included_articles.title: A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children
included_articles.abstract: Identiﬁcation of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in children is challenging due to the complexity and heterogeneity of ASD. Currently, most existing methods mainly rely on a single modality with limited information and often cannot achieve satisfactory performance. To address this issue, this paper investigates from internal neurophysiological and external behavior perspectives simultaneously and proposes a new multimodal diagnosis framework for identifying ASD in children with fusion of electroencephalogram (EEG) and eye-tracking (ET) data. Speciﬁcally, we designed a two-step multimodal feature learning and fusion model based on a typical deep learning algorithm, stacked denoising autoencoder (SDAE). In the ﬁrst step, two SDAE models are designed for feature learning for EEG and ET modality, respectively. Then, a third SDAE model in the second step is designed to perform multimodal fusion with learned EEG and ET features in a concatenated way. Our designed multimodal identiﬁcation model can automatically capture correlations and complementarity from behavior modality and neurophysiological modality in a latent feature space, and generate informative feature representationswith betterdiscriminabilityand generalizationfor enhanced identiﬁcation performance. We collected a multimodal dataset containing 40 ASD children and 50 typically developing (TD) children to evaluate our proposed method. Experimental results showed that our proposed method achieved superior performance compared with two unimodal methods and a simple feature-level fusion method, which has promising potential to provide an objective and accurate diagnosis to assist clinicians.

included_articles.title: AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
included_articles.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by social deficits that affects a considerable percentage of the global population. Early detection of ASD allows for early intervention and ensures a better prognosis; however, there is a lack of screening tools that can objectively measure social deficiency and calculate the probability of ASD. Joint attention is a social skill that develops from an early age, and poor joint attention skills are thought to be a characteristic feature of ASD. We have devised a protocol for the collection of video data for joint attention from toddlers and preschool-aged children. Ten-second video clips of instances where the participant is expected to initiate joint attention are used as input data for the convolutional neural network-long short-term memory-attention classification model. The model distinguished children with ASD and those demonstrating with typical developmental patterns with high accuracy and precision. We validated our model using an attention mechanism to ascertain that the classifications were made based on certain social gestures rather than on random chance. To that end, this work could be further developed into an automatic computational system for autism screening in the general population, as well as an assistive diagnostic tool for mental health specialists to objectively measure the severity of social deficits.

included_articles.abstract: Research Article Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Mengyi Liao ,1,2 Hengyao Duan ,1 and Guangshuai Wang 2 1Department of Education, Pingdingshan University, Pingdingshan 467000, China 2National Engineering Laboratory for Technology of Big Data Application in Education, Central China Normal University, Wuhan 430079, China Correspondence should be addressed to Mengyi Liao; liaomengyi83@163.com and Hengyao Duan; 3144@pdsu.edu.cn Received 16 February 2022; Revised 5 March 2022; Accepted 8 March 2022; Published 25 March 2022 Academic Editor: Bhagyaveni M.A Copyright © 2022 Mengyi Liao et al. +is is an open access article distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution License, which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited. Early detection of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly beneﬁcial to the health sustainability of children. Existing detection methods depend on the assessment of experts, which are subjective and costly. In this study, we proposed a machine learning approach that fuses physiological data (electroencephalography, EEG) and behavioral data (eye ﬁxation and facial expression) to detect children with ASD. Its implementation can improve detection eﬃciency and reduce costs. First, we used an innovative approach to extract features of eye ﬁxation, facial expression, and EEG data. +en, a hybrid fusion approach based on a weighted naive Bayes algorithm was presented for multimodal data fusion with a classiﬁcation accuracy of 87.50%. Results suggest that the machine learning classiﬁcation approach in this study is eﬀective for the early detection of ASD. Confusion matrices and graphs demonstrate that eye ﬁxation, facial expression, and EEG have diﬀerent discriminative powers for the detection of ASD and typically developing children, and EEG may be the most discriminative information. +e physiological and behavioral data have important complementary characteristics. +us, the machine learning approach proposed in this study, which combines the complementary information, can signiﬁcantly improve classiﬁcation accuracy.

included_articles.title: An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images
included_articles.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurological condition that affects how a person interacts and learns. The early and accurate diagnosis of ASD is vital to developing a comprehensive rehabilitation plan that improves the quality of life and the integration of the ASD person in the social, family, and work environment. However, the accurate diagnosis of ASD is usually affected since it is linked to the judgment of an expert, which produces biases related to the lack of objectivity. In consequence, several works have been dedicated to developing early detection techniques for ASD based on Machine Learning (ML) technologies and eye-tracking tools. The present work aims to introduce a new methodology for ASD classification, which uses Kernel Extreme Learning Machine (KELM), an objective dataset based on gaze tracking, feature extraction techniques, and data augmentation for training the model. In turn, to enhance the accuracy in ASD classification, the KELM model is optimized through the Giza Pyramids Construction (GPC) algorithm. The proposed approach includes pipeline data augmentation, dimensionality reduction, and a posterior normalization to classify ASD subjects accurately. Statistical tests and analyses were performed to validate the performance of the proposed methodology, resulting in an average accuracy of 98.8% in ASD classification. © 2022 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

The 98.8% figure cannot be compared with participant-level results, and the same underlying images yielded approximately 71% when the dataset's originators computed accuracy per child.

included_articles.title: Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals
included_articles.abstract: Background: Across behavioral studies, autistic individuals show greater variability than typically developing individuals. However, it remains unknown to what extent this variability arises from heterogeneity across individuals, or from unreliability within individuals. Here, we focus on eye tracking, which provides rich dependent measures that have been used extensively in studies of autism. Autistic individuals have an atypical gaze onto both static visual images and dynamic videos that could be leveraged for diagnostic purposes if the above open question could be addressed. Methods: We tested three competing hypotheses: (1) that gaze patterns of autistic individuals are less reliable or noisier than those of controls, (2) that atypical gaze patterns are individually reliable but heterogeneous across autistic individuals, or (3) that atypical gaze patterns are individually reliable and also homogeneous among autistic individuals. We collected desktop-based eye tracking data from two different full-length television sitcom episodes, at two independent sites (Caltech and Indiana University), in a total of over 150 adult participants (N = 48 autistic individuals with IQ in the normal range, 105 controls) and quantified gaze onto features of the videos using automated computer vision-based feature extraction. Results: We found support for the second of these hypotheses. Autistic people and controls showed equivalently reliable gaze onto specific features of videos, such as faces, so much so that individuals could be identified significantly above chance using a fingerprinting approach from video epochs as short as 2 min. However, classification of participants into diagnostic groups based on their eye tracking data failed to produce clear group classifications, due to heterogeneity in the autistic group. Limitations: Three limitations are the relatively small sample size, assessment across only two videos (from the same television series), and the absence of other dependent measures (e.g., neuroimaging or genetics) that might have revealed individual-level variability that was not evident with eye tracking. Future studies should expand to larger samples across longer longitudinal epochs, an aim that is now becoming feasible with Internet- and phone-based eye tracking. © The Author(s) 2022. included_articles.title: Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech
included_articles.abstract: Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder that results in altered behavior, social development, and communication patterns. In recent years, autism prevalence has tripled, with 1 in 44 children now affected. Given that traditional diagnosis is a lengthy, labor-intensive process that requires the work of trained physicians, significant attention has been given to developing systems that automatically detect autism. We work toward this goal by analyzing audio data, as prosody abnormalities are a signal of autism, with affected children displaying speech idiosyncrasies such as echolalia, monotonous intonation, atypical pitch, and irregular linguistic stress patterns. Objective: We aimed to test the ability for machine learning approaches to aid in detection of autism in self-recorded speech audio captured from children with ASD and neurotypical (NT) children in their home environments. Methods: We considered three methods to detect autism in child speech: (1) random forests trained on extracted audio features (including Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients); (2) convolutional neural networks trained on spectrograms; and (3) fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0—a state-of-the-art transformer-based speech recognition model. We trained our classifiers on our novel data set of cellphone-recorded child speech audio curated from the Guess What? mobile game, an app designed to crowdsource videos of children with ASD and NT children in a natural home environment. Results: The random forest classifier achieved 70% accuracy, the fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 model achieved 77% accuracy, and the convolutional neural network achieved 79% accuracy when classifying children’s audio as either ASD or NT. We used 5-fold cross-validation to evaluate model performance. Conclusions: Our models were able to predict autism status when trained on a varied selection of home audio clips with inconsistent recording qualities, which may be more representative of real-world conditions. The results demonstrate that machine learning methods offer promise in detecting autism automatically from speech without specialized equipment. (JMIR Pediatr Parent 2022;5(2):e35406) doi: 10.2196/35406

included_articles.title: Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection
included_articles.abstract: Variability in expressive and receptive language, difficulty with pragmatic language, and prosodic difficulties are all features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Quantifying language and voice characteristics is an important step for measuring outcomes for autistic people, yet clinical measurement is cumbersome and costly. Using natural language processing (NLP) methods and a harmonic model of speech, we analyzed language transcripts and audio recordings to automatically classify individuals as ASD or non-ASD. One-hundred fifty-eight participants (88 ASD, 70 non-ASD) ages 7 to 17 were evaluated with the autism diagnostic observation schedule (ADOS-2), module 3. The ADOS-2 was transcribed following modified SALT guidelines. Seven automated language measures (ALMs) and 10 automated voice measures (AVMs) for each participant were generated from the transcripts and audio of one ADOS-2 task. The measures were analyzed using support vector machine (SVM; a binary classifier) and receiver operating characteristic (ROC). The AVM model resulted in an ROC area under the curve (AUC) of 0.7800, the ALM model an AUC of 0.8748, and the combined model a significantly improved AUC of 0.9205. The ALM model better detected ASD participants who were younger and had lower language skills and shorter activity time. ASD participants detected by the AVM model had better language profiles than those detected by the language model. In combination, automated measurement of language and voice characteristics successfully differentiated children with and without autism. This methodology could help design robust outcome measures for future research. Lay Summary: People with autism often struggle with communication differences which traditional clinical measures and language tests cannot fully capture. Using language transcripts and audio recordings from 158 children ages 7 to 17, we showed that automated, objective language and voice measurements successfully predict the child’s diagnosis. This methodology could help design improved outcome measures for research. K E Y W O R D S autism, automated measures, communication, disfluency, natural language processing, pragmatic language, prosody, voice

included_articles.title: Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study
included_articles.abstract: Differences in speech prosody are a widely observed feature of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). However, it is unclear how prosodic differences in ASD manifest across different languages that demonstrate cross-linguistic variability in prosody. Using a supervised machine-learning analytic approach, we examined acoustic features relevant to rhythmic and intonational aspects of prosody derived from narrative samples elicited in English and Cantonese, two typologically and prosodically distinct languages. Our models revealed successful classification of ASD diagnosis using rhythm-relative features within and across both languages. Classification with intonation-relevant features was significant for English but not Cantonese. Results highlight differences in rhythm as a key prosodic feature impacted in ASD, and also demonstrate important variability in other prosodic properties that appear to be modulated by language-specific differences, such as intonation.

included_articles.title: Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings
included_articles.abstract: Background: Deficits in the ability to use language in social contexts, including storytelling skills, are observed across the autism spectrum. Development in machine-learning approaches may contribute to clinical psychology and psychiatry, given its potential to support decisions concerning the diagnosis and treatment of psychiatric conditions and disorders. Aims: To evaluate the usefulness of deep neural networks for detecting autism spectrum disorder (ASD) from textual utterances, specifically from narrations produced by individuals with ASD. Methods & Procedures: We examined two text encoders: Embeddings from Language Models (ELMo) and Universal Sentence Encoder (USE), and three classification algorithms: XGBoost, support vector machines, and dense neural network layer. We aimed to classify 25 participants with ASD and 25 participants with typical development (TD) based on their narrations produced during the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, Second Edition (ADOS-2) picture book task. The results of computational approaches were compared with the results of standardized testing and classifications made by two psychiatrists (raters). The raters were asked to read utterances produced by a participant (without an examiner’s statements and additional information) and assign a participant to one of the two groups: ASD or with typical development (TD). Outcomes & Results: The computer-based models had higher sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive values and negative predictive values than the raters, and lower than the two standardized instruments: ADOS-2 and Social Communication Questionnaire (SCQ). Conclusions & Implications: Our findings lay the groundwork for future studies involving deep neural network-based text representation models as tools for augmenting the ASD diagnosis or screening. included_articles.title: Development of a visual attention based decision support system for autism spectrum disorder screening
included_articles.abstract: Visual attention of young children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has been well documented in the literature for the past 20 years. In this study, we developed a Decision Support System (DSS) that uses machine learning (ML) techniques to identify young children with ASD from typically developing (TD) children. Study participants included 26 to 36 months old young children with ASD (n = 61) and TD children (n = 72). The results showed that the proposed DSS achieved up to 87.5% success rate in the early assessment of ASD in young children. Findings suggested that visual attention is a unique, promising biomarker for early assessment of ASD. Study results were discussed, and suggestions for future research were provided.

included_articles.abstract: ARTICLE OPEN Evaluation of an artiﬁcial intelligence-based medical device for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder Jonathan T. Megerian1,2, Sangeeta Dey3,4, Raun D. Melmed5, Daniel L. Coury6,7, Marc Lerner1,2, Christopher J. Nicholls8,9, Kristin Sohl 10, Rambod Rouhbakhsh11,12, Anandhi Narasimhan13, Jonathan Romain1,2, Sailaja Golla14, Saﬁullah Shareef15, Andrey Ostrovsky 16,17, Jennifer Shannon18, Colleen Kraft18, Stuart Liu-Mayo18, Halim Abbas 18, Diana E. Gal-Szabo18, Dennis P. Wall18,19 and Sharief Taraman 1,2,18,20✉ Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) can be reliably diagnosed at 18 months, yet signiﬁcant diagnostic delays persist in the United States. This double-blinded, multi-site, prospective, active comparator cohort study tested the accuracy of an artiﬁcial intelligence- based Software as a Medical Device designed to aid primary care healthcare providers (HCPs) in diagnosing ASD. The Device combines behavioral features from three distinct inputs (a caregiver questionnaire, analysis of two short home videos, and an HCP questionnaire) in a gradient boosted decision tree machine learning algorithm to produce either an ASD positive, ASD negative, or indeterminate output. This study compared Device outputs to diagnostic agreement by two or more independent specialists in a cohort of 18–72-month-olds with developmental delay concerns (425 study completers, 36% female, 29% ASD prevalence). Device output PPV for all study completers was 80.8% (95% conﬁdence intervals (CI), 70.3%–88.8%) and NPV was 98.3% (90.6%–100%). For the 31.8% of participants who received a determinate output (ASD positive or negative) Device sensitivity was 98.4% (91.6%–100%) and speciﬁcity was 78.9% (67.6%–87.7%). The Device’s indeterminate output acts as a risk control measure when inputs are insufﬁciently granular to make a determinate recommendation with conﬁdence. If this risk control measure were removed, the sensitivity for all study completers would fall to 51.6% (63/122) (95% CI 42.4%, 60.8%), and speciﬁcity would fall to 18.5% (56/303) (95% CI 14.3%, 23.3%). Among participants for whom the Device abstained from providing a result, specialists identiﬁed that 91% had one or more complex neurodevelopmental disorders. No signiﬁcant differences in Device performance were found across participants’ sex, race/ethnicity, income, or education level. For nearly a third of this primary care sample, the Device enabled timely diagnostic evaluation with a high degree of accuracy. The Device shows promise to signiﬁcantly increase the number of children able to be diagnosed with ASD in a primary care setting, potentially facilitating earlier intervention and more efﬁcient use of specialist resources. npj Digital Medicine (2022) 5:57 ; https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-022-00598-6

included_articles.title: Extraction and Classification of Acoustic Features from Italian Speaking Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.
included_articles.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD) are a group of complex developmental conditions whose effects and severity show high intraindividual variability. However, one of the main symptoms shared along the spectrum is social interaction impairments that can be explored through acoustic analysis of speech production. In this paper, we compare 14 Italian-speaking children with ASD and 14 typically developing peers. Accordingly, we extracted and selected the acoustic features related to prosody, quality of voice, loudness, and spectral distribution using the parameter set eGeMAPS provided by the openSMILE feature extraction toolkit. We implemented four supervised machine learning methods to evaluate the extraction performances. Our findings show that Decision Trees (DTs) and Support Vector Machines (SVMs) are the best-performing methods. The overall DT models reach a 100% recall on all the trials, meaning they correctly recognise autistic features. However, half of its models overfit, while SVMs are more consistent. One of the results of the work is the creation of a speech pipeline to extract Italian speech biomarkers typical of ASD by comparing our results with studies based on other languages. A better understanding of this topic can support clinicians in diagnosing the disorder.

The authors invoke this mechanism to discard their loudness results but retain the others, and diagnosis rests on an undescribed clinical judgement with no severity or cognitive data on either side.

included_articles.title: Eye Tracking-Based Diagnosis and Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques
included_articles.abstract: Eye tracking is a useful technique for detecting autism spectrum disorder (ASD). One of the most important aspects of good learning is the ability to have atypical visual attention. The eye-tracking technique provides useful information about children’s visual behaviour for early and accurate diagnosis. It works by scanning the paths of the eyes to extract a sequence of eye projection points on the image to analyse the behaviour of children with autism. In this study, three artiﬁcial-intelligence techniques were developed, namely, machine learning, deep learning, and a hybrid technique between them, for early diagnosis of autism. The ﬁrst technique, neural networks [feedforward neural networks (FFNNs) and artiﬁcial neural networks (ANNs)], is based on feature classiﬁcation extracted by a hybrid method between local binary pattern (LBP) and grey level cooccurrence matrix (GLCM) algorithms. This technique achieved a high accuracy of 99.8% for FFNNs and ANNs. The second technique used a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) model, such as GoogleNet and ResNet-18, on the basis of deep feature map extraction. The GoogleNet and ResNet-18 models achieved high performances of 93.6% and 97.6%, respectively. The third technique used the hybrid method between deep learning (GoogleNet and ResNet-18) and machine learning (SVM), called GoogleNet + SVM and ResNet-18 + SVM. This technique depends on two blocks. The ﬁrst block used CNN to extract deep feature maps, whilst the second block used SVM to classify the features extracted from the ﬁrst block. This technique proved its high diagnostic ability, achieving accuracies of 95.5% and 94.5% for GoogleNet + SVM and ResNet-18 + SVM, respectively.

included_articles.title: Identification of Social Engagement Indicators Associated With
included_articles.abstract: Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a widespread neurodevelopmental condition with a range of potential causes and symptoms. Standard diagnostic mechanisms for ASD, which involve lengthy parent questionnaires and clinical observation, often result in long waiting times for results. Recent advances in computer vision and mobile technology hold potential for speeding up the diagnostic process by enabling computational analysis of behavioral and social impairments from home videos. Such techniques can improve objectivity and contribute quantitatively to the diagnostic process. Objective: In this work, we evaluate whether home videos collected from a game-based mobile app can be used to provide diagnostic insights into ASD. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study attempting to identify potential social indicators of ASD from mobile phone videos without the use of eye-tracking hardware, manual annotations, and structured scenarios or clinical environments. Methods: Here, we used a mobile health app to collect over 11 hours of video footage depicting 95 children engaged in gameplay in a natural home environment. We used automated data set annotations to analyze two social indicators that have previously been shown to differ between children with ASD and their neurotypical (NT) peers: (1) gaze fixation patterns, which represent regions of an individual’s visual focus and (2) visual scanning methods, which refer to the ways in which individuals scan their surrounding environment. We compared the gaze fixation and visual scanning methods used by children during a 90-second gameplay video to identify statistically significant differences between the 2 cohorts; we then trained a long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network to determine if gaze indicators could be predictive of ASD. Results: Our results show that gaze fixation patterns differ between the 2 cohorts; specifically, we could identify 1 statistically significant region of fixation (P<.001). In addition, we also demonstrate that there are unique visual scanning patterns that exist for individuals with ASD when compared to NT children (P<.001). A deep learning model trained on coarse gaze fixation annotations demonstrates mild predictive power in identifying ASD. Conclusions: Ultimately, our study demonstrates that heterogeneous video data sets collected from mobile devices hold potential for quantifying visual patterns and providing insights into ASD. We show the importance of automated labeling techniques in generating large-scale data sets while simultaneously preserving the privacy of participants, and we demonstrate that specific social engagement indicators associated with ASD can be identified and characterized using such data. included_articles.title: Investigation of Eye-Tracking Scan Path as a Biomarker for Autism Screening Using Machine Learning Algorithms
included_articles.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder is a group of disorders marked by difﬁculties with social skills, repetitive activities, speech, and nonverbal communication. Deﬁcits in paying attention to, and processing, social stimuli are common for children with autism spectrum disorders. It is uncertain whether eye-tracking technologies can assist in establishing an early biomarker of autism based on the children’s atypical visual preference patterns. In this study, we used machine learning methods to test the applicability of eye-tracking data in children to aid in the early screening of autism. We looked into the effectiveness of various machine learning techniques to discover the best model for predicting autism using visualized eye-tracking scan path images. We adopted three traditional machine learning models and a deep neural network classiﬁer to run experimental trials. This study employed a publicly available dataset of 547 graphical eye-tracking scan paths from 328 typically developing and 219 autistic children. We used image augmentation to populate the dataset to prevent the model from overﬁtting. The deep neural network model outperformed typical machine learning approaches on the populated dataset, with 97% AUC, 93.28% sensitivity, 91.38% speciﬁcity, 94.46% NPV, and 90.06% PPV (ﬁvefold cross-validated). The ﬁndings strongly suggest that eye-tracking data help clinicians for a quick and reliable autism screening.

included_articles.title: Machine learning models using mobile game play accurately classify children with autism
included_articles.abstract: Digitally-delivered healthcare is well suited to address current inequities in the delivery of care due to barriers of access to healthcare facilities. As the COVID-19 pandemic phases out, we have a unique opportunity to capitalize on the current familiarity with telemedicine approaches and continue to advocate for main­ stream adoption of remote care delivery. In this paper, we specifically focus on the ability of GuessWhat? a smartphone-based charades-style gamified therapeutic intervention for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) to generate a signal that distinguishes children with ASD from neurotypical (NT) children. We demonstrate the feasibility of using “in-the-wild”, naturalistic gameplay data to distinguish between ASD and NT by children by training a random forest classifier to discern the two classes (AU-ROC = 0.745, recall = 0.769). This performance demonstrates the potential for GuessWhat? to facilitate screening for ASD in historically difficult-toreach communities. To further examine this potential, future work should expand the size of the training sample and interrogate differences in predictive ability by demographic.

included_articles.title: Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction
included_articles.abstract: With the rise of Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD) incidence rate, a new screening method that is capable of diagnosing ASD in a more accurate and convenient way is urgently needed. Unlike traditional scales, electroencephalogram (EEG), and eye movement based methods, the acoustic analysis based method has inherent advantages in data collection and rich algorithms that can be employed in speech processing. In this paper, three methods are compared for the construction of acoustic features based on time-frequency independent component analysis (TF-ICA): (1) extracting and combining the rows of the unmixing matrix of each frequency point to build the feature vector; (2) using the separation results of each frequency point as time-frequency feature; (3) extracting time-domain features from the outputs of TF-ICA. Finally, the features are compared by a deep learning classiﬁer on an ASD speech dataset. It is concluded from the experimental results that method 1 obtained the highest recognition rate of 98.51%.

A single 80:20 split over recordings rather than children, with roughly six utterances per child distributed across both sides; no cross-validation of the classifier, no repetition, no confidence intervals; Method 2's figure is the maximum over 256 frequency sequences; and the two-channel configuration underpinning the feature construction is never described.

included_articles.title: The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation
included_articles.abstract: This paper presents a speech-based system for autism severity estimation combined with automatic speaker diarization. Speaker diarization was performed by two different methods. The first used acoustic features, which included MelFrequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC) and pitch, and the second used x-vectors – embeddings extracted from Deep Neural Networks (DNN). The speaker diarization was trained using a Fully Connected Deep Neural Network (FCDNN) in both methods. We then trained a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to estimate the severity of autism based on 48 acoustic and prosodic features of speech. One hundred thirty-two young children were recorded in the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) examination room, using a distant microphone. Between the two diarization methods, the MFCC and Pitch achieved a better Diarization Error Rate (DER) of 26.91%. Using this diarization method, the severity estimation system achieved a correlation of 0.606 (Pearson) between the predicted and the actual autism severity scores (i.e., ADOS scores). Clinical Relevance—The presented system identifies children's speech segments and estimates their autism severity score. I. INTRODUCTION Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder diagnosed by social communication impairments, repetitive behaviors, and confined interests [1]. A common clinical tool for assessing ASD severity is the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) [2], a 45min assessment where a clinician interacts with the child using a variety of tasks/games and scores the child’s behavior using a standardized scale. Raw ADOS scores range between 0 and 30, with higher values indicating more severe ASD symptoms. The vast majority of ASD children exhibit speech and expressive language abnormalities, which range from a total lack of speech (i.e., non-verbal children) to those who develop normal vocabulary and syntax, but exhibit difficulties with the use of appropriate prosody and pragmatics [3]. Previous studies have demonstrated that verbal children with ASD speak in abnormal ways, including strange prosody [4], increased pitch variability and pitch range [5], slower speech rate, and prolonged word production. These studies used manual annotation and inspection of the audio recordings. To perform automatic analysis of ADOS recordings, there is a need for a speaker diarization algorithm that divides the recording into segments of child and of other speakers. *Research supported by Israel Ministry of Science and Technology (Grant no. 3-17422). Speaker diarization is affected by the quality of the audio recording, the number of recording microphones, the distance between microphones and speaking subjects. included_articles.title: The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children
included_articles.abstract: The present study contributes to the research problem of applying social robots in autism diagnosis. There is a common belief that existing diagnostic methods for autistic spectrum disorder are not effective. Advances in Human–Robot Interactions (HRI) provide potential new diagnostic methods based on interactive robots. We investigated deﬁcits in turn-taking in preschool children by observing their interactions with the NAO robot during two games: (Dance with me vs. Touch me). We compared children’s interaction proﬁles with the robot (ﬁve autistic vs. ﬁve typically developing young children). Then, to investigate turn-taking deﬁcits, we adopted a rating procedure to indicate differences between both groups of children based on an observational scale. A statistical analysis based on ratings of the children’s interactions with the NAO robot indicated that autistic children presented a deﬁcient level of turn-taking behaviors. Our study provides evidence for the potential of designing and implementing an interactive dyadic game between a child and a social robot that can be used to detect turn-taking deﬁcits based on objective measures. We also discuss our results in the context of existing studies and propose guidelines for a robotic-enabled autism diagnosis system.
included_articles.authors: Arent K; Brown DJ; Kruk-Lasocka J; Niemiec TL; Pasieczna AH; Standen PJ; Szczepanowski R

assessments.support: Five per group is the smallest sample in the review, but selection is otherwise sound: both groups recruited from the same kindergartens, exactly matched on sex at four boys and one girl, and drawn from a 12-month age band. No cognitive, language or comorbidity characterisation.

The elicitation is standardised to a degree no human examiner could match - identical robot behaviour delivered to every child across two scenarios designed to dissociate command-response from imitation - and the rating instrument is published with definitions. But every measurement passes through human judgement and rater blinding to diagnosis is nowhere addressed.

Multidisciplinary clinical diagnosis by a psychiatrist, a psychologist and a pedagogue, recorded in kindergarten files - genuine clinical ascertainment, well above the folder-membership and questionnaire-threshold labels elsewhere in this review, though the instruments and dates are not stated.

All ten children completed both games in a single session under an identical protocol; no attrition or excluded recordings are reported; six raters scored the same material with reliability quantified.

risk_of_bias.summary: Unclear risk of bias, in a study whose design quality is high and whose sample is very small. The paradigm is the strongest element: two five-minute dyadic games with a NAO robot, delivered identically to every child by machine rather than by a human examiner, deliberately constructed so that a child touching the robot means command-response in one scenario and imitation in the other, administered in the children's own kindergartens with both groups seen under the same protocol. Measurement is by six trained raters against an observational scale published in full in an appendix, with inter-rater reliability quantified at Kendall's W = 0.65 and subscale alpha at 0.77 - reliability reporting that most observational work in this corpus omits. Diagnoses were multidisciplinary clinical judgements by a psychiatrist, psychologist and pedagogue. Ethics approval, guardian consent and separate consent for filming are all documented. Against this, the sample is five children per group, so only large effects are detectable and no individual-level inference is possible; no confidence interval or effect size accompanies the group comparisons; rater blinding to diagnosis is nowhere addressed, which is the principal internal-validity risk given that all measurement is human judgement; no cognitive or language measure separates general developmental level from autism as an explanation for reduced turn-taking; and no test-retest data exist for a five-minute protocol proposed as a supplementary assessment tool. No computational model is fitted and no accuracy is reported or claimed.

included_articles.title: Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach
included_articles.abstract: This study segmented the time series of gaze behavior from nineteen children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and 20 children with typical development in a face-to-face conversation. A machine learning approach showed that behavior segments produced by these two groups of participants could be classified with the highest accuracy of 74.15%. These results were further used to classify children using a threshold classifier. A maximum classification accuracy of 87.18% was achieved, under the condition that a participant was considered as ‘ASD’ if over 46% of the child’s 7-s behavior segments were classified as ASD-like behaviors. The idea of combining the behavior segmentation technique and the threshold classifier could maximally preserve participants’ data, and promote the automatic screening of ASD.
included_articles.authors: Zhao Z; Wei J; Xing J; Zhang X; Qu X; Hu X; Lu J

assessments.support: Case-control sampling with autistic children drawn from a specialist mental health centre and typically developing children from the surrounding community - a design QUADAS-2 flags explicitly as high risk for diagnostic accuracy. Eligibility further narrows the autistic group to children aged 6-13 with non-verbal IQ >= 70, adequate conversational ability, no ADHD or schizophrenia and no current medication, excluding by construction the more severely affected and the comorbid, who are the children a screening tool would most need to handle. Enrolment was consecutive or convenience - not stated. Four of 43 (9.3%) were dropped for tracking failure with no comparison of their characteristics. The groups differ significantly in IQ (100.8 versus 116.1, p = .019), which is not adjusted for.

The index test is not prespecified: both the segment window length (10 candidates) and the ASD-like proportion threshold were selected to maximise accuracy on the same 39 children whose accuracy is then reported, and the feature subset was selected by forward selection outside the cross-validation loop. QUADAS-2 asks whether the threshold was prespecified; here it was explicitly not. Interpretation of the index test was automated and so blind to the reference standard in the ordinary sense, but the tuning procedure had access to the labels of every child.

Diagnosis followed DSM-IV criteria applied by a licensed psychiatrist of at least five years' experience, re-evaluated by a senior psychiatrist, with adjudication by two further senior psychiatrists on disagreement. Multi-clinician consensus is a reasonable standard and is more than several studies in this corpus provide, but no standardised instrument was used - the authors state they had limited access to ADOS and ADI-R - no inter-rater reliability is quantified, DSM-IV rather than DSM-5 was applied in work published in 2022, and TD status rests on community recruitment plus self/parent report with no autism screening instrument administered, so undetected autistic traits in the control group cannot be ruled out.

The interval between clinical diagnosis and eye-tracking is not reported. All 39 analysed participants received both the index test and the reference standard and all were included in the analysis, but the four excluded for technical failure are not characterised. The decisive problem is the unit of analysis: segments rather than children were randomly assigned to cross-validation folds, so the same participant contributes to both training and test data, and the participant-level result is computed from those same labels rather than from an independent set of children.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias overall, driven by validation design rather than by conduct of the experiment itself. The data collection is careful - naive participants, unconstrained head movement, verified calibration, an explicit data-loss rule, a published protocol - and the reference standard, while instrument-free, is a genuine multi-psychiatrist consensus. But the two headline accuracies are both optimistically biased: 74.15% comes from cross-validation that partitions segments rather than children, so individual gaze signatures leak between folds, and 87.18% is the maximum over a joint search across ten window lengths and an unspecified threshold grid conducted on the same 39 children, with the neighbouring configurations giving 0.77-0.85. Add an unnested feature-selection step, an uncontrolled 15-point IQ difference favouring the controls, a spectrum-narrow autistic sample and a community control group with no autism screening, and the reported figures should be read as an upper bound on a proof-of-concept rather than as an accuracy estimate. The authors' own framing - 'proof-of-concept research which showed the feasibility' - is the appropriate reading.

items.notes: Multi-psychiatrist DSM-IV consensus with escalation on disagreement - defensible and clearly described - but no standardised instrument, no reliability statistic, DSM-IV rather than DSM-5, and no autism screening of the control group.

Feature computation and classification are automated and label-free at the point of measurement. The live interviewer was presumably not blind to group, which is an unaddressed avenue for differential elicitation, but the measurement itself is not human-rated.

Segments, not participants, were randomly partitioned into the ten cross-validation folds. With one continuous recording per child and windows as short as 1 s, near-duplicate segments from the same child sit on both sides of every split. No participant-level or subject-independent evaluation is reported at any point.

Forward feature selection was run to choose the feature subset and the same subset was then reused in all ten folds - the paper states this directly. Selection therefore saw the test data. No scaling or normalisation procedure is described.

At the segment level a majority-class baseline is computed and plotted at every window length - an empirically derived chance floor that correctly acknowledges the group-linked class imbalance, and better practice than most studies here. At the participant level there is no baseline, no permutation test, no AUC value and no confidence interval for 87.18%, and that figure is the maximum of a two-dimensional search.

items.notes: 39 children for a per-child claim; the ROC in Fig. 5 is built from 39 points and a single child moves accuracy by 2.6 points. The thousands of segments give an appearance of statistical power that the 39 independent units do not support.

Computational reporting is thin: SVM kernel, regularisation, scaling, seeds, the threshold search grid and the per-length segment counts (shown only as a bar chart) are all absent.

No code, no data, no preregistration, no analysis plan. The dataset is a reuse of the authors' own prior study, which is disclosed clearly, but neither release is available for independent checking.

No ethics approval statement, no Declaration of Helsinki statement and no parental consent or child assent statement appears in the report, despite minors, a clinical population and deliberate non-disclosure of the device's purpose. Funding (eight grants) and conflicts of interest (none) are declared in full.

Three real limitations are stated and the work is self-labelled proof-of-concept; the confound between oculomotor behaviour and visual attention is conceded outright. But nothing is said about segment-level splitting, post hoc threshold selection, unnested feature selection or the IQ difference.

included_articles.title: A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features
included_articles.abstract: Early screening, which can lead to early diagnosis and intervention for children with autism (ASD), can signiﬁcantly improve their life quality. Consequently, the observational process of the ASD diagnosis and the lack of experts make the technology-based ASD screening methods more demanding. On the other hand, early ASD screening based on behavioral patterns is one of the most reliable methods that could be accomplished by analyzing children’s playing patterns. Thus, in this paper, we present an extension of our initial sensorized toy car functionalities by adding shaft encoders to detect attention to details and interest in rotating objects in children with ASD. Using the two modalities to detect different ASD symptoms improved our screening accuracy by more than 10%. Having such a sensorized toy car, which can be used at homes or clinics for screening ASD without high expertise, can improve the life of children with ASD and their families by providing an initial screening for further evaluation. This is essential for sustainable development, especially considering the increased rate of children with ASD around the world.
included_articles.authors: Mehralizadeh B; Baradaran B; Nikkhoo S; Soleiman P; Moradi H

assessments.support: Case-control sampling at a single autism centre: 28 already-identified autistic children against 18 typically developing children, at 61% prevalence. No inclusion or exclusion criteria are stated for either group, no recruitment route is given for the TD children, and no consecutive or random enrolment is described. Four children with cerebral palsy and fragile X syndrome were recruited and then omitted from all analyses without explanation, removing the only available differential-diagnosis contrast. Five autistic children who ignored the toy entirely appear to have been retained, and the resulting engagement difference feeds a selected model feature.

The index test was not prespecified. Two rounds of backward elimination selected 10 features from 54 on the full sample, three algorithms and three SVM kernels were compared, four feature configurations were evaluated, and the maximum of that grid is reported as the result. No threshold or operating point was fixed in advance. Interpretation is automated and label-free at inference, but the entire pipeline that produced the reported configuration had access to all 46 children's labels.

No reference standard is described. The paper names no diagnostic criteria, instrument, clinician, procedure or date for the autism diagnoses, and does not state how typically developing status was established or whether those children were screened for autism or developmental delay. The ASD label is presumably service-eligibility status at the recruiting centre. Without any specification of the target condition's ascertainment, the reported accuracy cannot be interpreted.

The interval between diagnosis and testing is unreported. Fifty children were tested and 46 modelled, with the four-child discrepancy unexplained in the analysis sections. All modelled children received the index test in a single 3-5 minute session of variable length, with a parent or therapist present or absent unrecorded. No sampling rate or packet-loss accounting is given despite UDP transport, so it is not possible to confirm that all children's signals were of comparable completeness.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias, with the dominant contributor being the complete absence of a described reference standard: nothing in the paper states how autism was diagnosed in the 28 children or how typical development was established in the 18, which leaves the quantity being predicted undefined. Beyond that, the study has the standard case-control geometry at 61% prevalence, an unprespecified index test selected as the best of a grid spanning three algorithms, three kernels, four feature sets and two rounds of backward elimination performed on the full sample, and no chance baseline against a 60.9% majority-class floor. Two design details push in opposite directions. In its favour, the unit of analysis is the child, so there is no within-participant leakage, and the ablation across four feature configurations is reported in full with four metrics each rather than a single headline. Against it, the not-playing ratio - one of three encoder features selected into the final model - encodes the fact that five autistic children refused to engage with the toy while every typically developing child engaged enthusiastically, so an unknown share of the discriminative signal is toy engagement rather than the interest-in-rotation mechanism the hardware was built to measure. The reported metrics also do not reconcile internally with the class ratio for several rows. Read as an engineering feasibility demonstration of a low-cost instrumented toy - which is how the authors ultimately position it, as a warning system prompting expert referral - the work is a reasonable contribution; read as a diagnostic accuracy estimate, 85.56% is not supportable.

extracted_data.intervention: Not reported

items.notes: Convenience sample of 28 autistic and 18 typically developing children at one Tehran autism centre, with no stated inclusion or exclusion criteria for either group and no recruitment route given for the controls. Age 3-6 only. Spectrum position is unmeasured, so representativeness cannot be assessed at all.

Typically developing children only in the modelled analysis. Four children with cerebral palsy and fragile X syndrome were recruited, played with the car, were described qualitatively as less enthusiastic, and were then excluded from every classification result without comment - discarding the study's own opportunity for a differential contrast.

Age is well matched (4.63 versus 4.61 years) and that is the only matched variable. Sex is not reported, IQ and developmental level are not measured, and the authors' own observation that TD children 'played with more energy and moved the car in a wider area' points at a general developmental-level difference that no measured covariate can rule out. items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Fifty children tested, 46 modelled, with the four-child gap corresponding to the other-disorder group but never stated as an exclusion. The five non-engaging autistic children are described but their handling is not specified. No signal-quality or packet-loss accounting under UDP transport, and no sampling rate given.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: None described. No criteria, instrument, clinician, process or date for any diagnosis, and no autism screening of the comparison group. This is the weakest reference-standard reporting encountered so far in this corpus.
Feature subset, algorithm and kernel were all chosen by search on the analysis sample; six configurations are tabulated and the maximum is the abstract's claim. No prespecified operating point.

The apparatus is identical for all children and well specified down to part numbers, with electronics concealed to avoid distraction, which eliminates the acquisition-chain confounds seen elsewhere in this corpus. But the session is unstandardised: 3-5 minutes of free play, with a parent or therapist present or absent unrecorded, no instruction protocol, and no stated sampling rate.
All measurement is sensor-derived and automated; no human rating enters the feature pipeline, so differential observer bias in measurement is not a concern.

The split unit is the child, with one aggregate vector per participant, so no within-child leakage is possible - a real strength relative to most of this corpus. But the cross-validation description is terse and partly self-contradictory ('the training set with 80% of samples and the test set with 20% of the remaining samples'), and the relationship between the single 80/20 split and the 5 folds is not made precise.

Two consecutive rounds of backward elimination reduced 54 features to 10, described in a dedicated section preceding the results with the surviving features named as a fixed outcome and no indication of refitting inside folds. At 46 samples and 54 candidate features this is the regime in which unnested selection produces the largest optimism.

No majority-class baseline (which alone gives 60.9%), no permutation test, no confidence intervals or fold-level spread, no AUC. Test folds contain about nine children, so one child moves fold accuracy by 11 points. Reported accuracies also fail to reconcile with the stated sensitivity, specificity and class ratio in at least three of six rows.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: 46 children for a 54-feature selection problem plus a three-algorithm, three-kernel, four-configuration model search. The authors identify the feature-to-sample ratio as a problem and respond with feature reduction, but the reduction is itself performed on the same small sample.

Hardware reporting is excellent - board, sensor part numbers, encoder type and placement, transport protocol, firmware ecosystem, an ROS interface package - and both feature tables are complete with the final selected subset named. Analysis reporting is absent: no software, no hyperparameters for any of three algorithms, no augmentation scheme, no seeds, no sampling rate, and no diagnostic criteria.

Four metrics across six configurations is a good ablation table, and the SVM/random forest error-profile discussion is a genuine strength. But there is no uncertainty quantification of any kind, no AUC, and the accuracy column does not reconcile with sensitivity, specificity and the 28:18 ratio for several rows. The text also mis-references Table 5 as Table 4.

Data available on request from the corresponding author; hardware and firmware stack described well enough to rebuild; an ROS package developed for integration. No code repository, no preregistration, no analysis plan.

Informed parental consent under the Declaration of Helsinki, anonymised participant IDs, and psychologist supervision are all reported and appropriate. But formal ethics review was not obtained: the IRB statement asserts that non-intrusive screening 'does not require ethics approval as long as the privacy of the participants is considered', substituting an engineering-school proposal acceptance and the autism centre's internal guidelines. For research on 3-6 year old children with developmental disabilities that is not adequate. Funding (none) and conflicts (none) are declared.

No limitations section. The only concessions are that the reimplemented baseline underperformed the original because data and setup differed, and that the system should currently serve as a referral warning rather than a diagnosis. Nothing is said about the missing reference standard, the unnested feature selection, the model search, the engagement confound or the dropped clinical group.

included_articles.title: A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities
included_articles.abstract: Frontiers in Psychology 01 frontiersin.org A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities Nicola Milano 1†, Roberta Simeoli 1,2*†, Angelo Rega 1,2 and Davide Marocco 1 1 Department of Humanistic Studies, University of Naples Federico II, Napoli, Italy, 2 Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center, Ottaviano, Italy
included_articles.authors: Milano N; Simeoli R; Rega A; Marocco D

assessments.support: Case-control design at 50% prevalence with autistic children drawn from a rehabilitation centre - which is also two authors' employer - and typically developing children from a mainstream primary school. Inclusion criteria are clearly stated and reasonably strict on both sides, and the rule excluding any child about whom a clinician or teacher was uncertain is a genuine safeguard against contaminated controls. But comorbidity was excluded by design, IQ ranges are asymmetric with six autistic children below the TD floor, sex is not reported at all, and the autistic group was receiving active psychomotor therapy - a motor intervention - while controls were not, confounding motor training history with diagnosis in a study whose outcome is motor kinematics.

The index test is not prespecified in its decisive parameters: the latent dimensionality was reduced from 10 to 2 after PCA on a latent space learned from the full dataset, and the class-conditional Gaussians used for classification at inference and proposed as clinical thresholds were fitted to all 1,500 observations. No threshold was fixed in advance. Interpretation is automated and blind to labels at inference, but the analysis restricting the dataset to correctly performed tasks conditions the retained data on cognitive success, and per-group error rates are not reported so the differential effect of that rule is unknown.

Among the strongest reference standards charted in this review. Autism required both DSM-5 clinical criteria and ADOS-2, applied by qualified clinicians, with comorbidity excluded. Typical development required absence of any confirmed neurodevelopmental disorder plus explicit exclusion of suspected autism signs, developmental abnormality and psychiatric or neurological history, reinforced by excluding any child about whom a clinician or teacher expressed uncertainty. Downgrading considerations that do not reach the threshold for a higher-risk judgement: ADOS-2 module and scores are never reported, the diagnosing clinicians are described only generically, no autism screening instrument was administered to the control group, and the diagnosis-to-testing interval is unstated.

All 60 enrolled children received both the index test and the reference standard, with no attrition reported. The problem is the analysis unit and the trial filter. Each child contributes 25 task observations to a 1,500-row dataset that is then split by 10-fold cross-validation with no statement that a child's rows were kept together, so the same participant appears in training and test folds. Separately, only correctly performed tasks entered the analysis, so the number of trajectories retained per child is unreported and plausibly differs by group and by IQ, and the diagnosis-to-testing interval is not given.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias overall, with an unusual profile: this study has one of the best reference standards in the corpus and one of the weakest validation designs. Autism was established by DSM-5 plus ADOS-2 with comorbidity excluded and controls screened conservatively, ethics approval and guardian consent are documented, the task is a standardised clinical instrument rather than an ad hoc game, acquisition is identical across groups, and the interpretability analysis is the most sophisticated encountered here. Against that, the reported 91.2% +/- 5.6% is computed by 10-fold cross-validation over 1,500 task observations generated by 60 children at 25 rows each, with nothing indicating that a child's rows were kept within a fold - so roughly 22-23 sibling observations from the same child, session and hand accompany each test row into training. Movement kinematics are close to an individual motor signature, so the figure substantially measures within-child consistency rather than between-child generalisation, and the paper's own remark that clustering is clearer when participants are averaged, together with the absence of any participant-level accuracy, points the same way. Accuracy is the only metric reported - no sensitivity, specificity, AUC or confusion matrix - the latent dimensionality and the class-conditional densities were both fitted on all the data, and the restriction to correctly performed trials conditions the dataset on cognitive success in a group pair whose IQ ranges differ. The finding that motor kinematics carry autism-relevant signal is plausible and consistent with the wider motor literature; the specific accuracy figure is not an estimate of performance on an unseen child.

items.notes: DSM-5 plus ADOS-2 by qualified clinicians for the autism group, with comorbidity excluded; controls excluded for suspected autism signs, developmental abnormality or psychiatric/neurological history, plus exclusion of any child about whom a clinician or teacher was uncertain. Among the strongest in this corpus, weakened only by the non-reporting of ADOS-2 scores and the absence of a screening instrument for controls.

Latent dimensionality chosen by PCA on a latent space fitted to all the data; class-conditional Gaussians used for inference and proposed as clinical thresholds fitted to all 1,500 observations; no prespecified operating point or threshold.

Acquisition does not differ by group, which removes the recording-chain confound that undermines several other studies charted here.

Feature extraction and modelling are fully automated from logged coordinates; no human rating enters the measurement pipeline. The examiner administering the task was presumably not blind to group, but the examiner does not score anything.

The dataset is explicitly 60 children x 25 tasks = 1,500 observations, and 10-fold cross-validation is applied to those observations with no statement that a child's rows were kept together. Each test row therefore has ~22-23 same-child siblings in training. Kinematic profiles are close to individual motor signatures, so the model can separate children rather than groups.

All 12 features are used, so no feature selection occurs, but the two decisions that shape the representation - reducing the latent space from 10 to 2 dimensions via PCA, and fitting the class-conditional bivariate Gaussians - were both made on the complete dataset rather than within training folds.

Accuracy is the only metric: no sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, AUC or confusion matrix, so the error profile is unknown. The +/- 5.6% is a fold standard deviation, not a confidence interval, and carries little meaning under observation-level folds. Chance is unambiguously 50% given the balanced design, but no baseline or permutation test is reported, and no participant-level accuracy is computed despite the participant-level latent plot being presented.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Sixty children for a deep generative model plus predictor. The 1,500-row dataset gives an appearance of adequate sample that the 60 independent units do not support, and the paper itself attributes its need for supervised training to 'the sample size and its characteristics'.

Task, hardware, capture rate, seating, all 12 feature definitions, the extraction package and the full three-term loss with its weighting are specified precisely. The network itself is not: no layer widths, optimiser, learning rate, batch size, epochs, seeds or code, despite two pages of textbook exposition on what neural networks are. The fold-assignment procedure is not described.

One number for the entire classification result, with no class-conditional metrics, no confusion matrix, no AUC and no confidence interval. The participant-level accuracy that the paper's own Figure 3 invites is never computed. Feature effects from the Monte Carlo analysis are presented graphically without effect sizes or uncertainty.
Raw data offered by the authors without undue reservation - a real if informal commitment. No code, no preregistration, no analysis plan, and no deposited dataset.

Approved by the Ethical Committee of Psychological Research of the Department of Humanities, University of Naples Federico II, with written informed consent from legal guardians. The conflict-of-interest statement discloses that two authors were employed by the rehabilitation centre that supplied the autistic participants - material and correctly declared. Funding is not reported.

A single stated limitation, and a conceptual one: that supervision was needed so the model still depends on traditional assessment for ground truth. Nothing about the observation-level cross-validation, the single-metric reporting, the in-sample fitting of the latent structure and class densities, the restriction to correct trials, the IQ asymmetry, the unreported sex distribution, or the psychomotor-therapy confound.

included_articles.title: A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation
included_articles.abstract: The incidence rate of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has been rising in the past decades, and has reached 1 ∼ 2%. Clinical ASD screening requires long testing time, complicated doctor training and high cost. Therefore, an objective and accurate automated method is urgently needed for large-scale early screening of autistic children. The lack of response to one’s own name is one of the early warning signals of ASD. Response to name is included in various ASD early screening and diagnostic assessments. In this paper, we propose an algorithm that combines automatic name detection with human pose tracking and head pose estimation in computer vision. The final prediction is determined by the combination of shoulder rotation angle, head pose information and duration. The experimental data comes from the process of clinical screening for ASD, which has less laboratory control, more realistic child response, and a flexible number of accompanying parents. Thirty subjects including 29 children with ASD and 1 typical developing (TD) child participated in the experiment. The experimental results show that the consistency between our proposed method and clinical diagnosis achieves 93.3%, which indicates our method can play an effective auxiliary role in the early screening of ASD.
included_articles.authors: Song C; Wang S; Chen M; Li H; Jia F; Zhao Y

assessments.support: A consecutive or convenience clinical series of 30 children at one tertiary hospital, 29 of them already autistic and 1 typically developing, selected by ADOS-2 module (TM, M1 or M2). No inclusion or exclusion criteria beyond module are stated, no recruitment period is given, and the demographic description is limited to a single overall mean age of 3.65 years with no sex, IQ, language or severity data. Because the sample contains essentially no non-autistic children, the study cannot address discrimination even in principle, yet is framed throughout as supporting early screening.

The index test is not prespecified and is not validated on data separate from that used to construct it. All five decision constants (90 degree and 20 degree shoulder thresholds, 10-frame and 8-frame durations, 3 s window) were set by hand and evaluated on the same 30 children, and the retrained YOLOv3 detector was fitted on more than 1,700 images of those same children. The judgement is automated and does not consult the clinician's score at inference, but no part of the pipeline was ever exercised on an unseen participant.

The comparator for the reported agreement is a single experienced clinician's 0-5 response-to-name score, assigned in real time by the same person conducting the assessment and calling the child's name, with no blinding, no second rater and no reliability statistic. The scoring rule itself is explicit and well specified, which is a strength, but the item requires a live judgement about whether a head turn included eye contact, made from behind the child, and no evidence is offered that a second clinician would score the same sessions the same way. The autism diagnoses underlying the sample rest on ADOS-2 administered at the same department, with no scores reported.

All 30 children received both the index test and the reference standard within the same session, which eliminates any interval concern. The problems are structural: the 109 test events are analysed as independent units although they cluster within 30 children and are strongly serially dependent, since a child who does not respond to the first call generally does not respond to the remaining four; no chance-agreement baseline is computed against a sample in which 17 of 30 children scored 5; and no accounting is given of detection, tracking or landmark failures, two of which are known to have occurred and are described only anecdotally in the discussion.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias, though the profile differs from most studies in this review because the study is not really a diagnostic accuracy study. It is an agreement study between an automated scorer and a clinician for one ADOS-2 item, conducted on a clinical series of 29 autistic children and 1 typically developing child. Within that scope it does several things well: the data come from live clinical assessments rather than a laboratory analogue, the clinical protocol is left unmodified, the decision rule is fully transparent and auditable frame by frame, the modality ablation is reported at two aggregation levels, the full 6 x 6 score confusion matrix is published, and the two residual errors are diagnosed concretely rather than glossed. But there is no validation of any kind - the five decision thresholds were hand-set and reported on the same data, and the person detector was retrained on 1,700 images of the very children it is evaluated on - and no chance-agreement floor is computed although 17 of the 30 children scored 5, which makes the 98.2% event-level agreement largely uninterpretable in the absence of a weighted kappa. The reference standard is one unblinded clinician with no second rater. And the framing is inconsistent with the evidence: the methods correctly state that this is 'an assessment of the response to name, not an assessment of autism risk', while the abstract reports 93.3% consistency with 'clinical diagnosis' and the conclusion proposes deployment for early autism screening in underserved regions. Read as a feasibility demonstration that ADOS-2 item scoring can be instrumented inside a working clinic, the work is a reasonable contribution; read as a validated screening aid, it is not supported.

items.notes: Thirty children from one tertiary hospital, selected only by ADOS-2 module, with a single overall mean age of 3.65 years and no age range, sex, IQ, language or severity data. Twenty-nine of thirty are autistic. Nothing can be established about which children the pipeline works for, and body proportions and postural control vary widely across the 12-month-to-5-year span the included modules cover.

One typically developing child among 30 participants. This is not a comparison group, and no between-group analysis is attempted or possible, yet the paper's framing is early autism screening throughout.

No covariates are measured, so none can be controlled. The specific uncontrolled factor that matters is postural and motor variation with age: the 90 degree shoulder threshold is applied uniformly to children who may differ by several years in development, and it is measured in 2-D image coordinates from a single uncalibrated fixed camera, so seating position and orientation relative to camera C1 confound the angle.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: No attrition is reported and all 30 children appear in the results. Perception failures are acknowledged only anecdotally - one child's mask prevented facial landmark detection - with no systematic accounting of detection, tracking or landmark failure rates across the 109 events.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: A single experienced clinician scores each child, unblinded and while simultaneously conducting the assessment, with no second rater and no inter-rater reliability statistic - on an item requiring a real-time judgement about eye contact made from behind the child. The scoring rule is explicit and well specified, which prevents a worse rating, but the standard is one person's uncorroborated judgement.

Five decision constants set by hand and reported on the same data; the trained detector fitted on images of the same 30 children. No development set, no held-out participants, no prespecified operating point.

The camera rig is fixed and identical across sessions (four cameras, common 1.44 m height, stated focal length, 25 fps, 1280 x 720) and the clinical protocol is followed as written, so acquisition is consistent. But no camera calibration is performed, the caller's side varies between sessions so the contributing rear camera varies, and the number of accompanying parents is deliberately unconstrained - all accepted as realism, at the cost of standardisation.

The automated judgement is fully deterministic and never sees the clinician's score, so the index test is blind to the reference standard by construction. The converse does not hold - but the clinician scored in real time during the session, before any automated output existed.

No split of any kind. Decision thresholds hand-set and evaluated on the same 30 children; YOLOv3 retrained on more than 1,700 images drawn from those same 30 subjects, so the detector has seen every child it is evaluated on. No estimate exists of performance on an unseen participant.

No feature selection occurs - all features are hand-specified and both angle definitions are fixed a priori, which removes selection bias as a mechanism. The threshold constants nonetheless play the same role as fitted parameters and were chosen with the evaluation data in view.

No chance-agreement baseline despite 17 of 30 children scoring 5 and each contributing five non-response events, so the 98.2% event-level figure sits above an unstated and high floor. No weighted kappa or ICC for what is an ordinal agreement problem, no confidence intervals, and the 109 events are treated as independent although they cluster within 30 children and are serially dependent.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Thirty children, of whom one is not autistic. One misclassified child moves participant-level accuracy by 3.3 points, so the headline improvement from 83.3% to 93.3% rests on three children.

Unusually complete for the pipeline: camera count, height, focal length, resolution and frame rate with each camera's role; the clinical protocol and its full 0-5 scoring tree; the angle computation written out as three equations; every threshold constant stated numerically with a rationale for the duration constant; and every third-party model named, including the size of the custom detection training set. A competent group could rebuild the system from the text.

Results are reported at both aggregation levels with the full 6 x 6 score confusion matrix published and the two errors diagnosed concretely - all creditable. But there are no confidence intervals, no chance-corrected agreement statistic, no per-component error rates, and the inverted positive/negative convention, though stated, invites misreading of the sensitivity and specificity figures.

Data declared confidential; no code, no retrained detector weights, no annotations, no preregistration. The reliance on published third-party models partially offsets this at the level of reconstructibility but not of verifiability.

Parental informed consent obtained before each session and faces mosaicked in published figures - appropriate handling for clinical video of preschool children with disabilities. But the ethics statement is a single clause, 'these experiments have passed an ethical review', with no committee, institution or approval number named. Funding and competing interests are declared.

No limitations section. The two error cases are analysed well and the methods contain a correct and creditable scope disclaimer that the study assesses response to name rather than autism risk - but that disclaimer is contradicted by the abstract's 'consistency ... with clinical diagnosis' and by the conclusion's proposal of deployment for early autism screening in remote areas. Nothing is said about the absence of validation, the chance-agreement floor, the single unblinded rater, or the demographic gaps.
