included_articles.title: Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games
included_articles.abstract: With the increasingly growing incidence of autism disorder, the early diagnosis of this disorder is of utmost importance. The appropriate diagnosis of this condition depends on the correct and accurate decision of the specialist. Thus, given the limited number of specialists in this area, the development of an efﬁcient classiﬁcation system is necessary. This study aims to analyze the eye-tracking data obtained from computer games to classify autistic and normal children. Twenty normal children from Namjoo public elementary school and 20 autistic children from the Daily Rehabilitation Clinic for Children with Special Disorders from the Tehran metropolis were selected for this study. Data were analyzed using a multilayer perceptron neural network with a backpropagation learning algorithm and a scaled conjugate gradient training algorithm. The classiﬁcation results were evaluated using the confusion matrix. The graphs from the game and the children’s gaze ﬁxation data were analyzed in this study to achieve a person-to-person evaluation and extract suitable features to classify autistic and typical children. The highest output precision and accuracy were obtained as 76.6% and 73.8%, respectively, for the case with all features considered.
included_articles.authors: Aminoleslami S; Maghooli K; Sammaknejad N; Haghipour S; Sadeghi-Firoozabadi V

assessments.support: Case-control sampling with autistic children from a specialist rehabilitation clinic and comparison children from a mainstream school, at 50% prevalence. Filtering is asymmetric: the autistic group faced five inclusion and two exclusion criteria that removed 5 of 25 approached children (20%) for refusing to sit or failing calibration, with no characterisation of those excluded, while no criteria at all are stated for the school-recruited comparison group and no autism screening was applied to it. The autistic sample is further restricted to 'high-performance' children who could sit at a computer and whose face perception a therapist judged adequate. Both groups are entirely male, which is stated in the table and never discussed.

The index test was not prespecified: four nested feature subsets were evaluated on the same data and the best reported as the result, and the network's iteration count and learning coefficient were selected by minimising MSE on an unstated partition. The network's own architecture is never reported. Decisively, the figures quoted in the abstract and conclusion are pooled across training, validation and test rather than held-out, so the reported operating characteristics are not those of the test partition.

Autism status rests on clinic admission following diagnosis by a paediatric psychiatrist and a paediatric clinical psychologist plus an undescribed 'comprehensive evaluation'. Two clinicians of different disciplines is a reasonable clinical basis, but no instrument, no DSM or ICD version, no date, no interval to testing and no reliability statistic is reported. The comparison group's status rests on school recruitment and the descriptor 'normal', with no screening instrument, no exclusion criteria and no statement that autism or other neurodevelopmental conditions were ruled out.

Five of 25 approached autistic children were excluded before any data were recorded, with no comparable attrition reported for the comparison group. The interval between diagnosis and testing is unreported. Most importantly, the analysis units are 240 observations rather than 40 children, randomly partitioned 168/36/36, so each child's six rows are scattered across training, validation and test - a structural flow problem that makes even the test partition non-independent of training.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias. The experimental conduct has genuine merits - identical eye-tracking equipment and laboratory for both groups, excellent age matching (8.40 versus 8.45 years), an engaging purpose-built task with an objectively correct answer on every trial, a named ethics committee with a verifiable approval identifier, and unusually honest tables that disaggregate every metric by training, validation and test partition. But the study's headline claim is not supported by its own numbers. The abstract and conclusion report precision 76.6% and accuracy 73.8%, which the tables identify as the pooled total across all three partitions; the held-out test figures for the same configuration are 66.7% and 58.3% against a 50% chance level on 36 observations, and the roughly 20-point train-to-test gap recurs in all four feature subsets without comment. Arithmetic on the reported percentages further establishes that the 240 modelled rows come from 40 children at six rows each, randomly split, so each test row has five siblings from the same child in training - and since the features are per-region fixation counts and durations, which are stable individual characteristics, even the 58.3% is optimistic for a genuinely unseen child. Add asymmetric group filtering that removed 20% of approached autistic children, an unscreened comparison group, an entirely male sample, no cognitive measure on a visual matching task, no diagnostic instrument, an unidentified eye tracker, other-race facial stimuli whose relevance the paper's own citations flag, and ROC curves reported without AUC values, and the appropriate reading is that this study demonstrates a workable game-based eye-tracking protocol while providing little evidence that gaze features from it classify children better than chance on held-out data.

extracted_data.study_design: Cross-sectional two-group diagnostic-classification study using a purpose-designed computer game as the elicitation task
extracted_data.sample_size: ASD/index: ; comparison: 20
extracted_data.intervention: Not reported

items.notes: Twenty autistic boys with 'high-performance autism' from one Tehran clinic, restricted further to those who could sit at a computer, tolerate calibration and whose face perception a therapist judged adequate; 5 of 25 approached (20%) excluded on those grounds. All male. No severity or cognitive measure, so representativeness is unassessable.

Mainstream schoolchildren described as 'normal' and 'healthy', with no screening instrument, no stated exclusion criteria and no evidence that autism or other conditions were ruled out. No clinical comparison group, which the authors themselves identify as needed for differential diagnosis.

Age is matched to within three weeks and sex is constant by design, which are real strengths. Everything else is uncontrolled: no IQ or cognitive measure on what is fundamentally a visual matching task, no language measure, and no accounting for the fact that the JAFFE stimuli are other-race faces for an Iranian sample - a factor the paper's own literature review shows it is aware of.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Twenty per cent of approached autistic children were excluded before recording, for reasons (refusal to sit, calibration failure) that plausibly correlate with sensory and attentional difficulty, with no characterisation of those children and no comparable filter applied to the comparison group. Out-of-range gaze samples were retained by enlarging the analysis space rather than quantified, and no tracking-ratio or data-loss statistic is reported.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Clinic admission following diagnosis by a paediatric psychiatrist and a paediatric clinical psychologist, with no instrument, criteria version, date or reliability reported, and a comparison group established only by school recruitment and the label 'normal', with no screening.

Four feature subsets compared on the same data with the best reported; network architecture unreported; iteration count and learning coefficient tuned by MSE on an unstated partition; and the quoted operating characteristics taken from the pooled total rather than the test partition.

One eye tracker, one laboratory, one stimulus set and one protocol for both groups, with calibration required before recording - so acquisition does not differ by group. But the eye tracker is never identified by make, model or sampling rate, the fixation-detection parameters are unstated, and no calibration accuracy criterion is given, which matters because every feature is a fixation count or duration.
Feature extraction and classification are automated from logged gaze data; no human rating enters the measurement pipeline.

Arithmetic on the reported percentages fixes the dataset at 240 rows split 168/36/36, i.e. six rows per child randomly scattered across partitions, so every test row has five siblings from the same child in training. Region-level fixation counts and durations are stable individual characteristics, making this a direct leakage channel.

No selection algorithm was used, but four predefined feature subsets were each evaluated on the same data and the best-performing one reported as the study's result, which is selection by another route.

The headline precision and accuracy are pooled across training, validation and test; held-out test accuracies are 52.8-58.3% against a 50% chance floor on 36 observations. No baseline, permutation test or confidence interval is reported, and ROC curves are plotted without AUC values. The consistent ~20-point train-to-test gap across all four configurations is never mentioned.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Forty children, 240 rows, 18 features, and a neural network of unreported size. The 36-observation test partition means a single observation moves test accuracy by 2.8 points, and three observations separate the reported test result from chance.

Task design, stimulus source, region segmentation, feature definitions, MATLAB version, training algorithm and activation functions are all given. Missing: the eye tracker's identity, sampling rate and accuracy; the fixation-detection parameters; the MLP's hidden layers and node counts; the learning rate and iteration count actually used; the split procedure and seed; and the fact, recoverable only by arithmetic, that the modelled units are observations rather than children.

The tables are commendably disaggregated by partition, which is the only reason the held-out figures are recoverable at all. But the abstract, results narrative and conclusion all quote the pooled total, roughly 15 points above the test value, without noting the distinction; no confidence intervals are given anywhere; and ROC curves are shown without AUC.
Data available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. No code, no preregistration, no analysis plan, no deposited dataset.

Ethics approval from a named committee with a verifiable identifier (IR.IAU.SRB.REC.1401.152), stated in its own subsection - better than most reports charted here. But parental consent appears only as an inclusion criterion for the autistic group, with no consent statement for the school-recruited comparison children and no mention of child assent. Funding and competing interests are declared.

Three limitations are stated, of which one - the need for clinically overlapping comparison conditions - is genuinely important. None of the decisive issues is acknowledged: the pooled-versus-held-out reporting, the observation-level split, the train-to-test gap, the subset comparison, the all-male sample, the other-race stimuli, or the differential attrition.

included_articles.title: Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior
included_articles.abstract: Advances in computational behavior analysis via artificial intelligence (AI) promise to improve mental healthcare services by providing clinicians with tools to assist diagnosis or measurement of treatment outcomes. This potential has spurred an increasing number of studies in which automated pipelines predict diagnoses of mental health conditions. However, a fundamental question remains unanswered: How do the predictions of the AI algorithms correspond and compare with the predictions of humans? This is a critical question if AI technology is to be used as an assistive tool, because the utility of an AI algorithm would be negligible if it provides little information beyond what clinicians can readily infer. In this paper, we compare the performance of 19 human raters (8 autism experts and 11 non-experts) and that of an AI algorithm in terms of predicting autism diagnosis from short (3-minute) videos of N = 42 participants in a naturalistic conversation. Results show that the AI algorithm achieves an average accuracy of 80.5%, which is comparable to that of clinicians with expertise in autism (83.1%) and clinical research staff without specialized expertise (78.3%). Critically, diagnoses that were inaccurately predicted by most humans (experts and non-experts, alike) were typically correctly predicted by AI. Our results highlight the potential of AI as an assistive tool that can augment clinician diagnostic decision-making.
included_articles.authors: Sariyanidi E; Zampella CJ; DeJardin E; Herrington JD; Schultz RT; Tunc B
included_articles.journal: Joint Proceedings of the ACM IUI 20

assessments.support: Case-control sampling at a specialist research centre, with 15 autistic adults and 27 neurotypical controls recruited specifically as controls and characterised to raters as 'clear cases of individuals without autism'. Selecting the well-separated ends of the distribution is appropriate for a human-benchmark study but is the classic QUADAS-2 high-risk configuration for accuracy estimation, and the authors identify it themselves as their key external-validity limit. Mitigating factors that do not lift the judgement: groups were matched on age, sex ratio, full-scale IQ and verbal IQ; enrolment and the two exclusions are fully reported; and the eligibility requirement of native English fluency is stated. All participants are adults able to sustain a 3-minute unstructured conversation with a stranger.

The index test is essentially prespecified. A linear SVM at default regularisation was applied to a fixed 6,272-feature representation with no feature selection, and exactly one hyperparameter - the cross-correlation window, over four candidate values - was optimised, inside a nested cross-validation loop. Classification is automated and blind to the reference standard. The representation itself was designed a priori on stated principles (identity removal, localised bases, exclusion of nose and cheek regions and of Facial Action Coding System units on dimensionality grounds), and those choices are argued in the text rather than justified by their effect on accuracy. Researcher degrees of freedom are unusually low for this literature.

Diagnostic status was confirmed prospectively as part of this study using the Clinical Best Estimate process informed by ADOS-2 Module 4 and DSM-5 criteria - the accepted research gold standard, integrating a standardised observational instrument with clinical judgement. Control status was established by deliberate recruitment as neurotypical rather than by mere absence of a diagnosis. The reference standard was determined independently of the index test, and the conversation confederates who generated the index-test material were blind to diagnostic status. The only deductions, insufficient to change the judgement, are that no ADOS-2 severity score is reported and that no inter-rater reliability figure is given for the Clinical Best Estimate consensus.

All 44 enrolled participants underwent both the reference standard and the CASS; 2 were excluded for absent consent to this specific analysis or unprocessable data, both reasons stated, leaving 42 all of whom appear in the analysis. Each participant contributes exactly one feature vector, so there is no clustering or serial dependence in the evaluation units, and the nested cross-validation partitions participants. The reference standard and the index-test recording occurred within the same study visit battery. The one unaddressed flow point is that the bored condition of the CASS was collected and not analysed, which is a scope decision rather than a selective-reporting problem since it is stated plainly.

risk_of_bias.summary: Unclear rather than high risk overall - the best-conducted study charted in this review to date, limited principally by its sampling frame rather than by its methods. Three domains are at low risk. The reference standard is Clinical Best Estimate informed by ADOS-2 Module 4 and DSM-5, applied prospectively, with controls deliberately recruited and confederates blinded. The index test has almost no researcher degrees of freedom: a linear SVM at default C over a fixed 6,272-feature representation with no feature selection and a single hyperparameter tuned inside a nested loop. Flow is clean, with one feature vector per participant, full accounting of the two exclusions, and participant-level partitioning in 10-fold cross-validation repeated 100 times with shuffling. The representation itself is designed to remove, rather than exploit, facial identity - the one study here that treats individual appearance as a confound to be subtracted. Patient selection is high risk in the standard way: 15 autistic adults against 27 deliberately clear-cut neurotypical controls, cognitively able, verbally fluent, recruited at a specialist centre, which the authors themselves name as the limitation that matters. Two reporting issues temper the result without impugning its conduct. Sensitivity is 0.55 - the model detects just over half the autistic adults - and appears once without discussion while the abstract and conclusion quote only the 80.5% accuracy; and the 64.3% majority-class floor is not computed, so the improvement is 16 points rather than the 30 an unwary reader would infer. The study's actual claim, that AI and human errors do not overlap, is descriptively supported but rests on five hard cases with no confidence interval or significance test.

items.notes: Fifteen autistic adults, verbally fluent native English speakers with IQ comparable to controls, recruited at a specialist research centre and able to hold an unstructured conversation with a stranger. This is the cognitively able end of the adult spectrum, and no severity score is reported to characterise it further.

Neurotypical controls recruited specifically as such and described to raters as clear cases. No clinical comparison group. The authors state the limitation explicitly and call for future work on neurodiverse samples, which is the correct diagnosis of the problem but does not remedy it here.

Groups matched on chronological age, sex ratio, WASI-II full-scale IQ and verbal IQ, with a stated test of each - the most complete matching in this corpus. Native English fluency required of all participants. Confederates blind to diagnostic status and unaware of the dependent variables, so elicitation was not differentially shaped. Facial identity is explicitly modelled and removed at the feature stage.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Two of 44 enrolled participants excluded, with both reasons stated (absent consent for this specific set of experiments; data unavailable for processing), and the resulting 42 fully analysed. The consent-based exclusion indicates granular per-experiment consent.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Clinical Best Estimate informed by ADOS-2 Module 4 and adhering to DSM-5, established prospectively as part of the study rather than inherited from records. Controls deliberately recruited as neurotypical. The only gaps are the absence of a reported ADOS-2 severity score and of a consensus reliability figure.

Linear SVM at default C = 1, no feature selection, one hyperparameter tuned in a nested loop over four values. The representation choices - identity removal, localised basis, exclusion of nose and cheek components and of FACS units - are argued a priori on stated principles rather than selected for performance.

Identical dual-camera device, resolution, frame rate and placement for every participant; a semi-structured paradigm with specified confederate training rules, timing constraints and a verbatim prompt; camera parameters supplied to the 3DMM fitting to decouple expression from pose. No group-dependent acquisition differences.

The pipeline is fully automated and label-free at inference. Confederates were blind to diagnostic status and unaware of the dependent variables. Human raters were necessarily unblinded to the task but were told only that cases were clear-cut, not which was which, and viewed videos in randomised order with a single viewing and no revisiting.

One feature vector per participant makes the split unit the person by construction. Nested cross-validation with 10 folds repeated 100 times with shuffled participant order addresses fold-assignment variance. The 3DMM identity-removal step additionally strips the individual-appearance information that drives leakage elsewhere in this corpus.

No feature selection is performed, so selection bias cannot arise despite 6,272 features. The single tuned hyperparameter is optimised in the inner loop. Regularisation is left at default rather than searched.

Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV are all reported - the most complete metric set here - and per-participant error analyses go beyond summary statistics. But no majority-class baseline (64.3%), permutation test, AUC or confidence interval is given, and the sensitivity of 0.55 is stated once and never discussed while the abstract quotes only accuracy.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Forty-two participants and 6,272 features. The linear model, fixed regularisation and absence of feature selection mitigate the dimensionality, and the nested participant-level scheme means the estimate is honest, but one participant is 2.4 accuracy points and the error-overlap finding rests on five hard cases with no uncertainty quantification.

The paradigm (including confederate training rules and verbatim prompt), hardware, 3DMM method and its rationale, basis construction, exact cross-correlation scheme with lag convention and overlap, feature count derivation, classifier and its fixed C, hyperparameter grid, and validation scheme are all fully specified - as is the entire human-rating protocol. Table 1 demographics were not recoverable from the retrieved text.

Five operating characteristics for the model and three levels of human aggregation, plus two per-participant analyses with a quantified correlation. But no confidence intervals, no AUC, no significance test on the human-versus-AI comparison or the error-overlap claim, and the abstract and conclusion foreground accuracy while omitting the 0.55 sensitivity.

No code, no data, no preregistration, and the modified localised expression basis - the study's most reusable artefact - is not released. The reliance on published components (3DI) partially offsets this for reconstruction but not for verification.

IRB approval from the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia is stated, and the exclusion of two participants for not consenting to this specific set of experiments evidences granular per-experiment consent - a strong governance signal for identifiable facial video. Four NIH grants are itemised. No competing-interests statement appears in the retrieved text.

Six substantive limitations are stated, including several that comparable papers omit entirely: the neurotypical-only comparison group with an explicit call for neurodiverse samples, the adult-only sample, the monadic rather than dyadic analysis, the partial interpretability with a specific statement of where it stops, the sample-size constraint given as the actual reason for the modelling choice, and the need for user research before clinical benefit can be claimed. The unaddressed items are the 0.55 sensitivity, the missing chance baseline, and the unmatched information available to human raters.

included_articles.title: Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas
included_articles.abstract: Objective: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) affects nearly 1 in 44 children younger than 8 years old in the United States, and the situation may be even worse in remote areas of the world. However, it is difﬁcult to utilize existing approaches to screen patients with ASD in remote areas due to the lack of professionals and high-tech instruments. Therefore, we develop a fast and accurate scalable method for screening children with ASD. Methods: A deep weakly supervised artiﬁcial intelligence model is proposed for ASD screening based on the dynamic viewing patterns (DVP) over viewing time and visual stimuli. In training, we utilized a long short-term memory (LSTM) network to learn the mapping between the autoencoder-based encoded dynamic patterns and the labels. In testing, we fed the encoded DVP of each undiagnosed child into the trained network and predicted the diagnosis category based on the score on all stimuli. Results: Based on the multi-center evaluation on 165 subjects (95 typically developing children and 70 children with ASD) aged 3-6 years from different areas of China, our method achieves an average recognition accuracy of 96.73% (sensitivity 96.85% and speciﬁcity 96.63%). Conclusion: The DVP is a discriminating attribute to identify the atypical performance of ASD. The DVP-based model is an effective platform for enhancing auxiliary ASD screening accuracy. Signiﬁcance: We validated the importance of dynamic information on between-group differences and classiﬁcation. assessments.support: Case-control sampling at 42% autism prevalence, with autistic children recruited through hospitals and rehabilitation services and comparison children through schools. No inclusion or exclusion criteria are stated beyond normal or corrected vision, no recruitment process is described, and sex is markedly imbalanced between groups (80.0% versus 63.2% male) without matching, adjustment or comment. Mitigating features that do not lift the judgement: recruitment spans multiple hospitals and schools across two provinces, giving real site diversity; ages are well matched; and the sample of 333 is among the largest in this review.

The index test is not fully prespecified. The Otsu decision threshold is fitted on subject average scores computed across training and test subjects together, so the operating point is chosen with sight of the test distribution; and network size, epoch count, mini-batch size, learning rate and the minLength lower bound are compared in a single results table on the evaluation data with no separate development set. The stimulus-discriminability ranking used to argue for a shortened 60-image protocol is likewise computed in-sample. Classification is otherwise automated and blind to labels at inference, and the semantic encoder is trained on an external corpus.

No reference standard is described in the main text for either group. The paper states that 140 autistic and 193 typically developing children were recruited, without naming any diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or procedure, and without reporting any screening of the comparison group. Table IV tabulates the diagnostic instruments used by comparator studies while leaving the study's own unstated. Clinical co-authorship at a children's healthcare department and a rehabilitation centre implies clinical diagnosis but does not substitute for a description.

The split is by subject, so each child's 82 stimulus patterns stay together and the evaluation units are properly independent at subject level; five random permutations are reported with the minimum given. The minLength preprocessing rule is analysed rather than applied blindly, with the authors showing that a stricter threshold would preferentially discard autistic children's data. Against this: the interval between diagnosis and testing is unreported, no attrition or data-exclusion accounting is given for the 333 children, the composition of the 165-subject test set relative to the five permutations is not fully clear, and no calibration procedure is described for the eye tracker.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias overall, driven by an undescribed reference standard and by case-control selection, in a study whose computational conduct is otherwise among the most careful in this review. The strengths are real and worth stating precisely: 333 children recruited across multiple hospitals and schools in two provinces, the largest and most site-diverse sample charted here; a subject-level split repeated over five permutations with the minimum reported; a semantic encoder trained on an external image corpus so that representation learning cannot leak; reimplemented baselines rather than cited comparators; ablations that separate semantic from low-level feature contributions; a quantitative analysis of how between-group separability depends on temporal and stimulus context, which converts architectural choices into measured consequences; a preprocessing parameter analysed specifically because it would otherwise discard autistic children's data preferentially; and honest subgroup reporting that surfaces two awkward findings - sensitivity falls in older children who have had rehabilitation training, and specificity falls in the youngest children who cannot sustain attention. Against this, the main text never states how autism was diagnosed in the 140 autistic children or how typical development was established in the 193 comparison children, so the target of a 96.73% accuracy is undefined; the groups differ by 17 percentage points in the proportion of boys, unmatched and unmentioned, in a study that separately reports higher error rates in boys; the Otsu decision threshold is fitted across training and test subjects together, which is not label leakage but is transductive and would be unavailable in the sequential-arrival deployment the paper envisages; and the network parameters, the minLength value and the stimulus-subset selection were all compared on the evaluation data. The finding that intervention reduces sensitivity is the most substantively important observation in the paper and cuts both ways - it is candid reporting, and it indicates that what the model measures is modifiable by training rather than a fixed marker.

extracted_data.sample_size: ASD/index: ; comparison: 193
extracted_data.intervention: Not reported

items.notes: One hundred and forty autistic children recruited through hospitals and rehabilitation services with no stated inclusion or exclusion criteria beyond normal or corrected vision, no diagnostic characterisation and no severity or cognitive measure. Representativeness cannot be assessed. The sample is nonetheless large and drawn from multiple sites in two provinces, which is more than most studies here offer.

School-recruited typically developing children with no reported screening for autism or developmental concerns. No clinical comparison group, so the study cannot address whether the viewing signature is autism-specific or a general marker of atypical development or of reduced task engagement.

Age is well matched (4.66 +/- 1.00 versus 4.77 +/- 0.92). Sex is not: 80.0% male in the autistic group against 63.2% in the comparison group, unmatched, unadjusted and unmentioned, in a paper that separately reports higher error rates in boys. No cognitive or developmental measure exists to separate an autism-specific viewing pattern from a general attentional or developmental one, and the authors' own account of grey-mask fixations in 3-4 year olds shows the two are confusable.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Device-level noise handling is specified numerically (merge points below 0.02, delete merged points under 0.1 s) and the minLength filter is analysed rather than assumed, with the authors demonstrating that a stricter setting would preferentially discard autistic children's data - a genuinely careful piece of work. But no attrition, exclusion or data-quality accounting is reported for the 333 children, and no calibration procedure or tracking-ratio statistic is given.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Not described. No instrument, criteria, clinician or process for either group in the main text, and no screening of the comparison group. Table IV lists comparator studies' instruments while leaving the study's own blank.

The Otsu threshold is fitted across training and test subjects together; network size, epochs, batch size, learning rate and minLength were compared on the evaluation data with no development set; and the 60-stimulus shortened protocol is selected in-sample from the same data on which accuracy is reported.

Identical eye tracker, sampling rate, screen, image geometry, viewing distance, display and mask timing and stimulus set for every child, in a consistent therapy-room arrangement with at most two accompanying adults. Acquisition does not differ by group. The absence of a described calibration procedure is the one gap.
The entire pipeline from fixation detection through scoring is automated and label-free at inference; no human rating enters the measurement chain.

Subject-level 50% split repeated over five random permutations with the minimum reported, so all 82 patterns from a child stay together - the correct design for a model that scores individual stimuli. The semantic autoencoder is trained on MS COCO rather than participant data, closing a second potential leakage path.

No feature selection occurs and the full vector enters the model. But the Otsu threshold is fitted transductively across training and test scores, and the stimulus-discriminability ranking that motivates a shortened protocol is computed on the evaluation data.

Accuracy at two aggregation levels, sensitivity, specificity, AUC, ablations, subgroup breakdowns by sex and age, and a five-permutation stability range - a fuller reporting set than almost anything else in this corpus. Missing: confidence intervals, a majority-class baseline (57.6%), and any prevalence-adjusted metric such as PPV, which is the number that matters for the proposed community-screening use.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Three hundred and thirty-three children, 165 in the test set, with 82 stimulus patterns each - by a wide margin the largest sample charted here, and the paper argues explicitly and with supporting visualisation that samples under 100 subjects cannot characterise model performance.

The computational pipeline is specified to reimplementation standard - stimulus protocol, device and its noise rule, superpixel step, autoencoder corpus and loss, full LSTM equations, feature concatenation, weak-supervision labelling, aggregation, thresholding, and a parameter sensitivity table including a reported negative result. The clinical protocol that produced the labels is entirely absent, as are the final architecture dimensions and any calibration procedure.

Two aggregation levels, sensitivity and specificity, AUC, ablations, five-permutation robustness with the minimum reported, and honest subgroup breakdowns that surface unflattering findings. But no confidence intervals, no chance baseline, and no prevalence-adjusted metric for a tool proposed for universal screening.
No code, no data, no stimulus set, no preregistration. Supplementary figures and tables are available through the publisher.

Approval by the Medical Ethics Committee of Northwestern Polytechnical University under protocol 202002032 with Declaration of Helsinki conformity - a named committee with a protocol number, better than most reports here. But no parental consent or child assent statement appears for a study of 333 children aged 3-6, and no competing-interests statement is given. Funding is itemised.

Failure modes are analysed concretely (natural scenes, small objects, edge-placed objects) and the age restriction is stated. The subgroup findings on rehabilitation training and on younger children's inattention are reported honestly and are the paper's most important caveats, though their implications for what the marker measures are not drawn out. Nothing is said about the undescribed reference standard, the sex imbalance, the transductive threshold, or the in-sample parameter and stimulus selection.

included_articles.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts
included_articles.abstract: Detecting individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) remains a challenge due to the resources and specialized professionals needed for accurate diagnosis, particularly for children where time is a critical factor. Early diagnosis of ASD is crucial for improving the quality of life for affected individuals, as it allows for timely intervention and support. In this study, we underscore the importance of artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) in developing innovative diagnostic methods, with the primary objective of creating AI models that assist in identifying users who may have ASD. Although several studies have utilized traditional machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques to detect various illnesses, few have focused on detecting ASD using text as input. We employ natural language processing (NLP) techniques combined with AI models, speciﬁcally decision trees, extreme gradient boosting (XGB), k-nearest neighbors algorithm (KNN) as ML models, and bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT) as DL models. The core idea involves extracting tweets from Twitter users through the platform’s API, classifying the texts as written by individuals who claim to have ASD (ASD users) or by those without ASD (non-ASD users). We generated a dataset of 404,627 tweets and used a subset of 90,000 tweets, comprising 45,000 from each classiﬁcation group, for training and testing the models. The results demonstrate a predictive model with an accuracy of over 84% when classifying texts potentially originated from ASD users. This research paves the way for using DL models to enhance the accuracy of detecting and diagnosing ASD in individuals effectively, emphasizing the critical role of AI in advancing early diagnostic methods for better patient outcomes.
included_articles.authors: Rubio-Martín S; García-Ordás MT; Bayón-Gutiérrez M; Prieto-Fernández N; Benítez-Andrades JA

assessments.support: Convenience sampling of 252 public Twitter accounts, 221 selected by keyword search of biographies for autism-related terms and 31 comparison accounts whose selection process is never described. No demographic information exists for either group, no matching was attempted or possible, and the comparison group was not screened for undisclosed autism. The self-selection is severe: the positive class consists entirely of people who both are autistic and choose to say so publicly on social media, a group likely to be verbally fluent, digitally engaged and often diagnosed in adulthood.

Hyperparameters for the three classical models were grid-searched with no validation set distinct from the reported test data, and the winning configuration is the best of four models compared on the same split. No text representation is described for the classical models, and no operating point or threshold was prespecified. Classification is automated and blind to labels at inference, but nothing in the pipeline was ever exercised on a writer it had not seen.

The label is unverified self-disclosure in a public social-media biography, with no diagnosis, instrument, criterion or verification of any kind, and the authors acknowledge that biographies may be false and that accounts may be written by someone other than the owner. The negative label is weaker still: the 31 comparison users are defined only by not stating that they are autistic, with no screening, and their selection is not described at all. The quantity predicted is the presence of an autism keyword in a profile, not the presence of autism.

The 90,000 modelled tweets are treated as independent units although they come from 252 authors, with the entire negative class of 45,000 tweets drawn from just 31 people. A single random 75/25 split over tweets places the large majority of each author's output in training alongside their own test tweets. No user-level result is reported, no cross-validation or repeated split is performed, and the 60% corpus reduction during cleaning is not broken down by user or group.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias in every domain, and the concerns are severe enough to place the reported 84.3% outside the range of interpretable evidence about autism. The decisive problem is that the split is over tweets rather than authors: 90,000 tweets from 252 users were divided at random, so every writer in the test set has the great majority of their own output in training, and because 31 people supply the entire 45,000-tweet negative class, roughly three-quarters of each comparison user's tweets are available to help classify the rest. A transformer that learned to recognise 31 individual writing styles would score very well and would have learned nothing about autism. Compounding this, the positive class was assembled by searching biographies for autism-related keywords including the community hashtag ActuallyAutistic, no autism vocabulary was removed from the tweets, and no topic analysis was performed - so the classifier may equally be detecting subject matter. The label is unverified self-disclosure with no clinical component; the comparison group of 31 is undescribed, unmatched and unscreened for undisclosed autism; no demographic data exist for anyone; and the paper is framed around detecting autism in children before age three while its data are adult social-media users. What the study does well is its manual filtering of candidate accounts, excluding organisations, self-described advocates and family members with stated rules and examples, and its publication of full confusion matrices, which reveal that the decision tree assigned nearly every tweet to the positive class - behaviour its 61.2% accuracy and 0.72 F1 conceal. Separately from bias, the study reports no ethics approval, no consent and no discussion of the ethics of building an autism classifier from identifiable individuals' public health disclosures.

extracted_data.study_design: Retrospective classification study on scraped social-media text; a cross-sectional comparison of language produced by self-identified autistic Twitter users against language produc…
extracted_data.sample_size: ASD/index: ; comparison: 31
extracted_data.intervention: Not reported

items.notes: Two hundred and twenty-one accounts found by keyword search of public biographies, with no demographic, cognitive or severity information for anyone. Self-disclosure of autism on social media selects a narrow and self-organised slice of the population - verbally fluent, digitally engaged, frequently diagnosed in adulthood - and nothing characterises which slice.

Thirty-one users whose selection is never described, unmatched on any attribute and unscreened for undisclosed autism, supplying the entire 45,000-tweet negative class at roughly 1,450 tweets each. The negative label means 'did not state it publicly', not 'is not autistic'.

No covariate is known so none can be controlled. The specific uncontrolled confound is topic: the positive class was assembled by searching for autism keywords, autism-related vocabulary was not removed from the tweets, and no topic analysis was run, so subject matter is fully confounded with the label. Author identity is a second uncontrolled factor, since the split does not separate writers.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Four cleaning steps are stated clearly and removed 60% of the raw corpus (1,014,723 to 404,627 tweets) - duplicates, retweets, incompletely extracted tweets and cross-platform auto-posts. The reduction is appropriately reported in aggregate but is not broken down by user or group, and how the 90,000-tweet balanced subsample was drawn from the 404,627 is not described.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Unverified self-disclosure in a public biography, with no diagnosis, instrument or verification, and an undescribed, unscreened negative class. The manual exclusion of organisations, advocates and family members is careful and well documented, but it improves the precision of a keyword search rather than establishing a diagnosis.

Best of four models compared on the same split, with grid-searched hyperparameters and no separate validation set. The text representation given to the three classical models is never stated, so the model-family comparison cannot be interpreted.

There is no elicitation protocol at all: the behavioural sample is whatever each user chose to post over five years, unconstrained in topic, audience, length, purpose or timing, spanning both the 140- and 280-character limits. Nothing about the measurement is standardised across users or classes.
Classification is automated and does not consult labels at inference; labels were assigned from profile text before any modelling.

A single random 75/25 split over tweets, not authors. Each of the 31 comparison users has roughly 1,090 of their own tweets in training and 360 in test; the model can succeed by recognising individual writing styles rather than any autism-related property. No performance estimate exists for an unseen writer.

No feature selection is described, but no text representation is described either, and the grid search over classical-model hyperparameters had no validation set separate from the reported test data. No autism-related vocabulary was masked, so the most obvious confound was left in the input.

One random split with no cross-validation, no repetition, no confidence interval and no chance baseline (50% at the tweet level). Full confusion matrices are reported, which is a real strength and exposes the decision tree's near-degenerate behaviour, but sensitivity and specificity are never computed and no user-level metric is given.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Ninety thousand tweets is ample for the models used, but the effective sample is 252 writers and, for the negative class, 31 - which is the number that governs generalisation. The apparent statistical power of a 22,500-tweet test set is illusory given that it contains no new authors.

Data collection is well described - six keywords, three manual exclusion rules with examples, four cleaning steps, date range, counts before and after - and model hyperparameters and the BERT checkpoint are given. But the selection of the 31 comparison users, the text representation for the classical models, BERT's fine-tuning regime and any random seed are all absent.

Full confusion matrices for all four models are published, which is better practice than accuracy alone and is what makes the decision tree's degenerate behaviour visible. But no confidence intervals, no chance baseline, no sensitivity or specificity computed from the counts, no AUC, and no user-level result.

No code, no data, no preregistration. The dataset consists of identifiable individuals' posts and could not be shared straightforwardly, which is a reason to have addressed data governance rather than to omit it.

No ethics approval, no ethics committee, no consent, and no discussion of the ethics of training an autism classifier on identifiable people's public health disclosures harvested without their knowledge. The only privacy measure is redacting username, location and date of birth from two example biographies 'in compliance with Twitter's policies' - a platform-terms consideration, not a research-ethics one. No competing-interests statement. Funding is acknowledged.

Two limitations stated, both about label truthfulness, and both valid. Nothing about the tweet-level split, the 31-user negative class, topic confounding, the absent demographics, the missing user-level metric, or the mismatch between a paper titled 'Early Detection' and a dataset of adult social-media users.

included_articles.title: Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder
included_articles.abstract: Atypical facial expression is one of the early symptoms of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) characterized by reduced regularity and lack of coordination of facial movements. Automatic quantiﬁcation of these behaviors can offer novel biomarkers for screening, diagnosis, and treatment monitoring of ASD. In this work, 40 toddlers with ASD and 396 typically developing toddlers were shown developmentally-appropriate and engaging movies presented on a smart tablet during a well-child pediatric visit. The movies consisted of social and non-social dynamic scenes designed to evoke certain behavioral and affective responses. The front-facing camera of the tablet was used to capture the toddlers’ face. Facial landmarks’ dynamics were then automatically computed using computer vision algorithms. Subsequently, the complexity of the landmarks’ dynamics was estimated for the eyebrows and mouth regions using multiscale entropy. Compared to typically developing toddlers, toddlers with ASD showed higher complexity (i.e., less predictability) in these landmarks’ dynamics. This complexity in facial dynamics contained novel information not captured by traditional facial affect analyses. These results suggest that computer vision analysis of facial landmark movements is a promising approach for detecting and quantifying early behavioral symptoms associated with ASD.
included_articles.authors: Babu PRK; Di Martino JM; Chang Z; Perochon S; Carpenter KLH; Compton S; Espinosa S; Dawson G; Sapiro G

assessments.support: Recruitment is from consecutive well-child visits at four paediatric primary care clinics rather than from a specialist autism service, with autism identified prospectively at 9.2% prevalence through routine M-CHAT-R/F screening and ADOS-T evaluation - a substantially stronger sampling frame than the case-control designs that dominate this corpus, and the reason this domain is not rated high. Exclusion criteria are stated in full and are practical rather than diagnostic. Against this: the groups differ substantially in age (24.21 versus 20.62 months), sex (77.5% versus 48.9% male) and racial and ethnic composition (47.5% versus 77.7% White; 32.5% versus 7.3% Hispanic/Latino), none of which is adjusted for; caregiver education is very high (82.8% college degree); and per-movie analysed samples vary with the 40% validity threshold in ways shown only graphically.

The index test is largely prespecified. The two anatomical regions were chosen a priori with stated literature rationales; the entropy parameters m = 2 and r = 0.15 sigma were taken from prior work with a supplementary sensitivity analysis; the 15 Hz filter cut-off, the 20-scale integration window and the 40% validity threshold are all justified from domain reasoning or cited sources rather than tuned; and no feature selection occurs. The primary analyses are hypothesis tests with confound adjustment rather than a fitted model. The one in-sample decision is the restriction of the secondary classification analysis to social movies, based on effect sizes observed in the same data.

A two-stage clinical pathway: universal caregiver-completed M-CHAT-R/F as part of routine care, followed by ADOS-Toddler evaluation by a child psychologist for any child screening positive or prompting caregiver or clinician concern. ADOS-T totals are reported (7.64 +/- 1.69). The comparison group is screened rather than assumed non-autistic, and the single discordant case - one typically developing child who screened positive, was evaluated and was not diagnosed - is reported explicitly. The residual limitation, insufficient to raise the rating, is that screen-negative children without expressed concern did not receive ADOS-T, so comparison-group status rests on a screening instrument.

All participants received the index test and the reference standard within the same clinical encounter, and each contributes a single feature vector per movie, so leave-one-out cross-validation partitions participants cleanly. Missing data are handled explicitly inside the entropy computation with a stated rule and worked example, the 40% validity threshold is justified from prior literature, missing-data percentage is shown not to differ between groups, and it is entered as an ANCOVA covariate - unusually careful handling. Against this: per-movie analysed sample sizes are reported only in figures, no flow diagram accounts for how many of the 436 were excluded from each movie, and no class-handling procedure is described for the decision-tree analysis despite the reported precision and recall being inconsistent with the 40:396 ratio.

risk_of_bias.summary: Unclear rather than high risk - alongside the human-benchmark facial study, one of the two best-conducted studies charted in this review, and the one whose sampling frame comes closest to the intended use. Recruitment is from consecutive well-child visits at four paediatric primary care clinics, with autism identified prospectively at 9.2% prevalence by universal M-CHAT-R/F screening followed by ADOS-Toddler evaluation, so this is a screening cohort rather than a case-control contrast, and the comparison group is screened rather than assumed. The index test is prespecified in every substantive respect - two hypothesis-driven regions, entropy parameters taken from prior literature with a sensitivity appendix, a physiologically justified filter cut-off, no feature selection - and the primary claims rest on non-parametric group comparisons with effect sizes, ANCOVA adjustment for two prespecified confounds, and an internal social/non-social control condition, rather than on a cross-validated accuracy figure. Missing data are handled with a stated rule inside the entropy computation, shown not to differ between groups, and additionally entered as a covariate. Governance is exemplary: two IRB protocols, written caregiver consent, itemised funding with a no-role statement, the most detailed competing-interests disclosure in the corpus, and a named conflict-free co-author who independently reviews the analyses. The residual concerns are real but bounded. Three demographic differences - 3.6 months of age, 29 points of sex ratio, 30 points of racial composition - are reported plainly and adjusted for nowhere, and the racial difference interacts with the paper's own acknowledged limitation that the landmark and affect detectors were trained mainly on adults, since detector accuracy varies with facial morphology. The secondary classification analysis was restricted to social movies on the basis of effect sizes from the same data, no class-handling step is described although the reported precision and recall cannot arise from a 40:396 ratio, and no majority-class baseline is given for a classifier operating at 9.2% prevalence. ADOS-T scores were obtained but never related to the biomarker, leaving the severity association untested.

extracted_data.sample_size: ASD/index: ; comparison: 396
extracted_data.intervention: Not reported

items.notes: Consecutive well-child attenders at four primary care clinics, with autism ascertained prospectively at 9.2% prevalence - much closer to a deployment population than the case-control norm here. Limits: caregiver education is very high (82.8% college degree), ADOS-T scores are tightly clustered (7.64 +/- 1.69) suggesting a narrow severity band, no cognitive measure exists, and the 40% valid-data threshold silently removes children who could not sustain attention.

Typically developing toddlers from the same clinics, all screened with M-CHAT-R/F - screened rather than assumed, which is better than almost anything else in this corpus. But screen-negative children did not receive ADOS-T, and the developmental-delay comparison that would test differential specificity sits in a supplementary appendix rather than in the main analysis.

Two candidate confounds are handled properly: percentage of missing data and landmark variation are both shown to correlate weakly with the outcome, tested for group difference, and entered as ANCOVA covariates individually and jointly, with the group difference preserved. But three demographic differences - age (3.6 months), sex (29 points) and race/ethnicity (30 points White, 25 points Hispanic/Latino) - are reported and none is adjusted, in a paper that demonstrably knows how to run ANCOVA.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: The most careful treatment in this corpus. Missing points are excluded at the embedding-vector level inside the entropy computation, with a worked example showing why concatenation would bias the estimate; a 40% validity threshold is applied per movie with a cited justification; missing-data percentage is shown not to differ between groups and is used as a covariate. The only gap is that per-movie analysed counts appear graphically rather than in a table.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Universal M-CHAT-R/F within routine care, ADOS-Toddler by a child psychologist for screen-positives and concern-flagged children, ADOS-T totals reported, and the single discordant case disclosed explicitly. Comparison group screened rather than assumed.

Regions chosen a priori with cited rationales; entropy parameters taken from prior literature with a sensitivity appendix; filter cut-off justified physiologically; integration window and validity threshold specified in advance; no feature selection. The only in-sample choice is restricting the secondary classification to social movies.

Identical iPad, camera, frame rate, movie set and 60 cm placement for every child, with a standardised room arrangement (caregiver holds child, others stand behind). Head motion is removed by affine normalisation to a canonical face rather than left as a confound, and camera-relative pose angles are estimated explicitly.

The entire measurement chain from face detection through entropy is automated and label-free. The affect estimator used as comparator was previously validated against human frame-by-frame coding on 136,450 frames with an intraclass correlation of 0.9.

Leave-one-out cross-validation over participants, with one feature vector per child per movie, so within-participant leakage is impossible. The primary claims rest on group comparisons rather than on a fitted predictive model, where cross-validation is not the operative safeguard.
No feature selection occurs - two prespecified features. Preprocessing parameters are fixed a priori from literature and shown insensitive in an appendix, so none is fitted to the outcome.

Effect sizes reported for every statistical comparison and interpreted as a gradient, ANCOVA confound adjustment, DeLong AUC comparisons, and an internal non-social control condition - stronger than anything else here. But the classification arm lacks confidence intervals, quotes no numeric AUC, gives no majority-class baseline (about 91% at 9.2% prevalence), and reports precision and recall arithmetically incompatible with the stated class ratio, implying an undisclosed balancing step.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: 436 participants overall is large for this corpus, but only 40 are autistic, and the analysed number per movie is smaller still after the 40% validity threshold. The authors state directly that the sample 'did not have sufficient power to determine the impact of demographic characteristics on the results', which is the correct acknowledgement given three unadjusted demographic imbalances.

The most complete in this review: recruitment pathway, all exclusion criteria, room and device arrangement, all six movies with durations and content, the full preprocessing chain with justified parameters, the entropy formulation with its missing-data rule and a worked numerical example, the across-subject normalisation, and every statistical test named to the Python function. Five supplementary appendices carry sensitivity and secondary analyses.

Effect sizes accompany every significance test and are interpreted, confound adjustments are reported, and three convergent analyses support the redundancy conclusion. But the classification arm has no confidence intervals, no numeric AUC, no chance baseline, and an unexplained class-handling step.
No code, no data, no stimulus set, no preregistration. The pipeline rests on the group's own previously published components, which aids conceptual reconstruction but not verification.

Duke University Health System IRB approval under two named protocol numbers; written informed consent from caregivers or legal guardians; inability to consent in English or Spanish disclosed as an exclusion criterion. Funding from eight sources itemised with an explicit no-role statement. The competing-interests disclosure is the most detailed in this corpus, covering technology licensed to Apple, patents, company directorships, advisory boards and consulting - and is accompanied by a structural mitigation, with data analysis independently and continuously reviewed by a named conflict-free co-author.

Three limitations stated, all real, including the important one that adult-trained detectors were applied to toddlers and that the sample lacked power to assess demographic effects. Not acknowledged: the unadjusted age, sex and race differences specifically; the in-sample selection of social movies for the classification analysis; the undisclosed class handling; and the fact that ADOS-T scores were obtained but never related to the biomarker.

included_articles.title: Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders
included_articles.abstract: EDITED BY Lauren Franz, Duke University, United States REVIEWED BY Barbara Le Driant, EA7273 Centre de Recherche en Psychologie Cognition, Psychisme et Organisations, Université de Picardie Jules Verne, France, Xiaoli Li, Beijing Normal University, China *CORRESPONDENCE Kota Iwauchi iwauchi.kota.ig9@is.naist.jp SPECIALTY SECTION This article was submitted to Digital Mental Health, a section of the journal Frontiers in Digital Health RECEIVED 25 May 2022 ACCEPTED 30 January 2023 PUBLISHED 16 February 2023 CITATION Iwauchi K, Tanaka H, Okazaki K, Matsuda Y, Uratani M, Morimoto T and Nakamura S (2023) Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders. The use, distribution or reproduction in other forums is permitted, provided the original author(s) and the copyright owner(s) are credited and that the original publication in this journal is cited, in accordance with accepted academic practice. No use, distribution or reproduction is permitted which does not comply with these terms. Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders Kota Iwauchi 1*, Hiroki Tanaka 1, Kosuke Okazaki 2, Yasuhiro Matsuda 2,3, Mitsuhiro Uratani 2, Tsubasa Morimoto 2 and Satoshi Nakamura 1 1Augmented Human Communication Laboratory, Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Ikoma, Nara, Japan, 2Department of Psychiatry, Nara Medical University School of Medicine, Kashihara, Nara, Japan, 3Osaka Psychiatric Medical Center, Osaka, Japan Experienced psychiatrists identify people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and schizophrenia (Sz) through interviews based on diagnostic criteria, their responses, and various neuropsychological tests. To improve the clinical diagnosis of neurodevelopmental disorders such as ASD and Sz, the discovery of disorder- speciﬁc biomarkers and behavioral indicators with sufﬁcient sensitivity is important. In recent years, studies have been conducted using machine learning to make more accurate predictions. Among various indicators, eye movement, which can be easily obtained, has attracted much attention and various studies have been conducted for ASD and Sz. Eye movement speciﬁcity during facial expression recognition has been studied extensively in the past, but modeling taking into account differences in speciﬁcity among facial expressions has not been conducted. In this paper, we propose a method to detect ASD or Sz from eye movement during the Facial Emotion Identiﬁcation Test (FEIT) while considering differences in eye movement due to the facial expressions presented. We also conﬁrm that weighting using the differences improves classiﬁcation accuracy. Our data set sample consisted of 15 adults with ASD and Sz, 16 controls, and 15 children with ASD and 17 controls. Random forest was used to weight each test and classify the participants as control, ASD, or Sz. The most successful approach used heat maps and convolutional neural networks (CNN) for eye retention. This method classiﬁed Sz in adults with 64.5% accuracy, ASD in adults with up to 71.0% accuracy, and ASD in children with 66.7% accuracy. Classifying of ASD result was signiﬁcantly different (p<.05) by the binomial test with chance rate. The results show a 10% and 16.7% improvement in accuracy, respectively, compared to a model that does not take facial expressions into account. In ASD, this indicates that modeling is effective, which weights the output of each image.
included_articles.authors: Iwauchi K; Tanaka H; Okazaki K; Matsuda Y; Uratani M; Morimoto T; Nakamura S

assessments.support: Clinical case-control sampling with two psychiatric groups and screened controls, at engineered 50% prevalence. Control groups were reduced from 26 to 16 (adults) and 17 to 15 (children) by ranking on SRS-2 score, so sampling is conditioned on a variable related to the construct being classified and the direction of that selection is ambiguous from the text. The adult groups differ by up to six years in mean age with markedly different variances, the children's groups differ by 40 percentage points in sex ratio, autistic children have more than twice the ADHD Rating Scale score of controls, and no IQ was obtained for anyone - the authors state the sample comprises only mild, high-functioning cases.

The index test is prespecified in its essentials. Three gaze features fixed a priori from cited prior work, no feature selection, model architectures fixed in advance and justified by dataset size, and the single tuned hyperparameter - the learning rate - optimised inside the inner loop of a nested cross-validation. Classification is automated and blind to labels at inference. The random-forest weighting layer is trained within folds and its importances averaged across them rather than fitted once on all data.

DSM-5 research criteria with condition-specific re-evaluation - ADOS-2 for autism with total scores reported, PANSS for schizophrenia - and controls actively screened by physicians and psychologists who excluded anyone with psychiatric history, drug abuse, epilepsy, learning delay or communication problems. All three groups have an explicit ascertainment procedure and the two clinical groups have quantified symptom measures. Minor gaps that do not raise the rating: no inter-rater reliability, no diagnosis-to-testing interval, and ADOS-2 reported as total raw rather than calibrated severity score.

All participants received both the index test and the reference standard, and cross-validation partitions by participant so each person's trials stay together. Trial exclusion rules are stated (scan-path length of zero excluded; at least 40% of gaze samples retained) and the resulting per-emotion trial counts are listed exactly, so attrition is visible. Against this: the statistical analysis treats those trials as independent units in Welch's t-tests despite clustering within participants at two or three trials per person per emotion, no mixed-effects adjustment is made, and eight participants whose gaze did not move were retained and misclassified by every model - correctly identified in the error analysis but not excluded or handled.

risk_of_bias.summary: Unclear rather than high risk, and one of the better-conducted studies in this review despite modest accuracies - or rather, the modest accuracies are a consequence of the conduct. The reference standard is among the strongest here: DSM-5 research criteria with ADOS-2 re-evaluation for autism and PANSS for schizophrenia, scores reported for both, and controls actively screened by clinicians rather than assumed. The validation is nested leave-one-participant-out with the learning rate tuned inside the inner loop, so participant-level disjointness and honest hyperparameter selection are both guaranteed; group sizes were equalised so chance is 50%; and every accuracy is tested against chance with a binomial test, with the failing schizophrenia result reported as marginal rather than rounded up. The error analysis is exemplary and yields a genuine finding, identifying eight participants misclassified by all four models whose gaze never left the centre despite normal recognition scores, and naming peripheral vision as a systematic failure mode of gaze-based assessment affecting 6.5% of adults and 17% of children. Reporting is complete enough to reimplement. The residual concerns are the sampling and the statistics. Controls were selected from a larger pool by SRS-2 ranking, conditioning the sample on a construct-related variable; the adult groups differ substantially in age and the children's groups in sex ratio; autistic children carry a large unadjusted ADHD burden in a gaze task; no IQ was measured, which the authors acknowledge; and the per-emotion statistical analysis that motivates the method treats clustered trials as independent, so those p-values are anticonservative. Confidence intervals are absent throughout, and with 30-31 participants per problem a single person moves accuracy by roughly three points, so the 10-point and 16.7-point gains attributed to weighting rest on about three and five participants respectively.

items.notes: Fifteen autistic adults and fifteen autistic children recruited through psychiatric services, all without intellectual difficulties but with no IQ measured. The authors state the sample comprises 'only a small number of mild (high-functioning) cases' and that it remains unclear whether findings extend across the spectrum - an accurate self-assessment.

The strongest comparison structure in this review after the human-benchmark study: neurotypical controls actively screened by physicians and psychologists, plus a psychiatric comparison group of 15 adults with schizophrenia assessed with PANSS. The schizophrenia group is not used to build a differential classifier, which is a missed opportunity, but its presence supports the parallel analysis that yields the paper's most valuable finding.

Group sizes were equalised, but by ranking controls on SRS-2 - a variable related to the classified construct. Adult groups differ by up to six years in mean age with very different variances; children's groups are 87% versus 47% male; autistic children score 17.6 against 6.88 on the ADHD Rating Scale, an unaddressed attentional confound in a gaze task. None of these is adjusted. Against this, FEIT recognition scores were equivalent across all groups, so differential task success is excluded as an explanation for the gaze differences.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Two explicit exclusion rules - scan-path length of zero, and a minimum 40% gaze-sample retention - with the resulting per-emotion trial counts listed exactly so attrition is visible. But the eight participants whose gaze never left the centre were retained and misclassified by every model; the error analysis identifies them precisely and diagnoses the cause, which is more than any other study here does, though no handling procedure follows.

items.notes: DSM-5 research criteria with ADOS-2 re-evaluation for autism (adult mean total 46.5 +/- 11.9) and PANSS for schizophrenia (67.1 +/- 13.0); controls screened by clinician interview with stated exclusions for psychiatric history, drug abuse, epilepsy, learning delay and communication problems. Every group has an explicit ascertainment procedure.

Three gaze features fixed a priori from cited literature, no feature selection, architectures fixed in advance with a stated small-data rationale, and the learning rate as the only tuned quantity, optimised inside the nested inner loop.

Identical eye tracker, 120 Hz sampling, 65 cm viewing distance, display resolution, stimulus set and trial timing for all participants, with a one-second fixation cross standardising the starting gaze position. The I-VT threshold is stated at 100 degrees per second and areas of interest are redrawn per image so that mouth-region measurement is not biased by expression-dependent mouth size.
The measurement chain from gaze sampling through event classification to modelling is automated and label-free. Verbal emotion responses were scored against an objective key.

Nested leave-one-participant-out cross-validation with all of a held-out person's 21 or 32 trials excluded from training, and the learning rate tuned in the inner loop. Trial-level leakage is structurally impossible, which matters because the per-trial classifier operates on stimulus images shown identically to everyone.
No feature selection occurs. The random-forest weighting layer is trained within folds and its importances averaged across them rather than fitted once on the full sample.

Group sizes equalised so chance is 50%, every accuracy tested against it with a binomial test, and the failing result (schizophrenia, p = 0.052) reported as marginal rather than rounded into significance - the clearest chance handling in this corpus. Missing: confidence intervals, AUC, and any adjustment for the fact that four model variants were compared per problem.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Thirty to thirty-one participants per classification problem, so one person is roughly three accuracy points and the 10-point and 16.7-point weighting gains correspond to about three and five participants. The authors identify small sample size as their first limitation. Per-fold training sets of 630-651 trials give an appearance of adequacy that 30 independent participants do not support.

Instrument battery, FEIT protocol and timing, eye tracker and sampling rate, viewing distance, I-VT threshold, area-of-interest definitions and per-image redrawing, both exclusion rules with resulting trial counts, scan-path pseudocode, both architectures with layer and kernel sizes, optimiser, loss, epoch cap, early-stopping patience, heat-map construction with Gaussian sigma and downscaling, and the nested cross-validation with its inner split - all specified. Statistical procedures named including the Benjamini-Hochberg correction.

Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for all four variants across all three problems, plus binomial tests against chance with the failing p-value shown. Per-emotion means and standard deviations tabulated for every feature. But no confidence intervals anywhere, no AUC, and no correction for comparing four model variants per problem.

Raw data offered by the authors without undue reservation; model architectures fully tabulated and the scan-path algorithm published as pseudocode. No code repository and no preregistration. The FEIT stimuli are under copyright and could not be reproduced even as figures.

Approved by ethics committees at both Nara Medical University and Nara Institute of Science and Technology; the procedure explained and informed consent obtained at the start of recording, with written consent from legal guardians recorded in the formal statement. Funding from a single CREST grant stated; competing interests declared as none.

Three limitations, all substantive: small sample, absence of IQ data with an explicit statement that the sample is mild and high-functioning, and - unusually - a documented failure mode found by inspecting the participants that every model misclassified, showing that some people complete the task using peripheral vision without moving their eyes, quantified at 6.5% of adults and 17% of children. Not acknowledged: the trial-as-unit statistical analysis, the SRS-2-based control selection, and the age and sex imbalances.
