included_articles.title: Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders
included_articles.abstract: Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) applications are platforms that provide means for nonspeech communication. One class of AAC apps are speechgenerating devices (SGDs). These AAC apps utilize icons/pictures that when tapped, spoken words will be produced. These apps are widely used to support communication and language learning for individuals with disabilities such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD). While the common mechanism for data collection in individuals with disabilities such as ASD is complex, requires speciﬁc technical mastery in acquisition site’s staff, and often cumbersome for participants, the daily use of AAC apps (in home settings and at will) provides opportunity to collect large scales of usage patterns that contains a wealth of information regarding individuals’ usage patterns that are essential components in developing usage model proﬁles. Despite such potential, the utility of these streams of data are rarely explored from a data science and data modeling perspective. This study provides a comprehensive view on various mechanisms and methodologies for modeling the usage patterns and their potential for identifying differences in AAC usage patterns between users with and without ASD. Data streams acquired from an AAC app called FreeSpeech is used in the study. FreeSpeech is an AAC app that is speciﬁcally designed for individuals with learning disabilities and ASD. Data modeling mechanism is initiated using a pseudo-semantic representation of touched words and other events via unique numeric values. Both supervised and unsupervised learning methods are considered in the study. Temporal, sequential, and spectral usage pattern modelings are considered among which modeling mechanisms based on sequential key-press representations outperformed others achieving 70% diagnosis classiﬁcation accuracy using support-vector-machine. This performance is improved to 82% accuracy using deep learning methods such as stacked autoencoders. I. INTRODUCTION Augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) systems are tools that support communication via methods other than traditional speech [7]. AAC systems are usually used by individuals with expressive communication disorders who suffer from impairments in speech, language, reading, and/or writing. The American Speech-Language-Hearing Association has divided users of AAC devices into two categories: those with congenital disabilities (Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), cerebral palsy, developmental disabilities, intellectual disability, developmental apraxia of speech, and genetic disorders) and those with acquired disabilities (cerebrovascular accidents, traumatic or acquired brain injuries, neurodegenerative diseases, disability following surgeries and temporary conditions such as intubation (for patients in critical care settings)). Current AAC devices offer support for 1) exchanging information, 2) developing social relationships, and 3) communicating needs [9]. Th
included_articles.authors: Atyabi A; Boccanfuso L; Snider; J. .. C.; Kim M; Barney E; Ahn YA; Li B; Dommer KJ; Shic F

assessments.support: Self-selected users of a free commercial app, with the labelled subset consisting of the 3.4% who voluntarily completed an optional survey. No inclusion or exclusion criteria beyond a minimum event count. The comparison group is a heterogeneous aggregate of eight loosely specified categories, half of them 'other' or 'none', dominated by acquired adult-onset conditions while the autism group is predominantly children - so age, aetiology and communication history all differ systematically between groups, and none is reported by group, matched or adjusted.

Window size was swept with the best reported; tuning effort differed between compared classifiers by the authors' own account; no development set separate from the evaluation data is described; and the decisive step - k-means pseudo-labelling of roughly 5,192 unlabelled users - was applied before the headline result was computed, so the classifier is largely fitted to and evaluated against machine-generated labels.

Unverified voluntary self- or proxy-report through an optional in-app survey completed by 214 of 6,033 users, with no clinical assessment, instrument, clinician or verification of any kind, and no record of who completed it. For the great majority of the modelled data there is no human-reported label at all, only a k-means cluster assignment. Participant totals are internally inconsistent across the text and two tables.

The unit of cross-validation is never stated. Each user contributes many windows in proportion to their app use, so window-level partitioning - the natural reading of the description - would place a user's own data on both sides of every fold, and no user-level result is reported. 761 users (12.6%) were excluded for insufficient events with no characterisation. Data span two and a half years but are analysed cross-sectionally with no modelling of change, learning or disease progression.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias in every domain, and the headline figure should not be read as a diagnostic accuracy estimate. Two problems are individually decisive. The reference standard is voluntary self- or proxy-report from 3.4% of users with no clinical component, and for the roughly 5,192 users who never disclosed anything the labels used in the headline analysis were generated by k-means clustering - so the 82% is substantially a measure of how well a stacked autoencoder reproduces a clustering solution rather than how well it predicts diagnosis. The same data before pseudo-labelling produced 47-61% across all three modelling views and six window sizes, at or barely above a 50% chance level, and the paper's own t-tests on simple usage measures found no group difference at all. Second, the unit of cross-validation is never stated; each user contributes many windows and no user-level result is reported, so a classifier recognising individual users from their customised key-press habits would produce exactly these numbers. Beneath both sits an unexamined confound that is close to structural: the comparison group is dominated by stroke, dementia, ALS and brain injury - acquired conditions of adult and later life - while autism is congenital and the app's heaviest users were children under ten, and age is neither reported by group nor adjusted. Accuracy is the only metric reported; there is no chance baseline, no confidence interval, no class-conditional figure. There is also no ethics approval, no consent for research use of telemetry gathered for debugging from disabled children and adults, and no discussion of either. What the study does establish, and establishes well, is that AAC telemetry exists at a scale conventional autism research cannot reach, that simple usage statistics do not separate diagnostic groups, and that the field has not previously looked.

But it is a convenience aggregate of eight categories - 49 'other' and 32 'none' out of 99 - dominated by acquired adult-onset conditions, so it differs from the autism group in age and aetiology as well as diagnosis.

None attempted. Age is collected but reported only as a marginal distribution, never by group, never adjusted - in a design where congenital childhood autism is contrasted against stroke, dementia, ALS and brain injury. The paper's own background section describes older AAC users struggling with non-intuitive interfaces, which is a description of the usage difference the classifier may be detecting. No sex, IQ, language or severity data exist.

items.notes: 761 of 6,033 users (12.6%) excluded for too few events, with no characterisation of who they were or how exclusion differed by group. The data were logged for debugging with 'little attention... given to the data structure', so quality is unknown. Participant totals do not reconcile across the text and two tables.

items.notes: Voluntary self- or proxy-report in an optional in-app survey, no clinical assessment or verification, no record of who answered, and for approximately 97% of the modelled data no human-reported label at all - only a k-means cluster assignment.

Window size swept with the best reported; uneven tuning across compared classifiers acknowledged by the authors; no separate development set; and pseudo-labelling applied before the headline evaluation.

There is no standardisation of any kind: the app is fully user-customisable, so different users operate different icon sets; no context, purpose or communication partner is recorded; and sessions vary without constraint. The authors correctly reject spatial modelling for exactly this reason, which shows they recognised the problem for one representation without extending it to the others.
Logging and modelling are fully automated; labels were self-reported before and independently of any analysis.

The unit of cross-validation is never stated. Users contribute many windows each, no user-level result is reported, and window-level partitioning would place a user's own data on both sides of every fold - with customised icon layouts making key-press sequences close to individual signatures.
No feature selection, but k-means pseudo-labelling of roughly 5,192 users was performed on the whole corpus before classification, so the label set itself is derived from the data being evaluated.

Accuracy is the only metric - no sensitivity, specificity, AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval anywhere. No chance baseline is computed, although bootstrap balancing implies 50%, against which the pre-pseudo-labelling results of 47-61% are at or near chance.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Eighty-one autistic and 99 non-autistic users with human-reported labels, expanded to thousands by pseudo-labelling and to a far larger but unstated number of windows. The apparent scale is a property of the telemetry, not of the labelled evidence.

The data source, encoding scheme, modelling views and window sweep are described clearly, but the elements that determine what the results mean are not: the unit of cross-validation, the k-means configuration and pseudo-label assignment, and the architectures and training regimes of the deep models that produce the headline figure.

Accuracy alone, with no uncertainty quantification of any kind. The one properly reported analysis is the negative t-test result, presented honestly. Three participant totals in the text and tables do not reconcile.
No code, no data, no preregistration. The dataset is telemetry from a discontinued commercial app held by a third-party foundation and is not described as available.

No ethics approval, no ethics committee, no consent for research use of telemetry gathered automatically for debugging, and no discussion of either - in a population including many children under ten and adults with dementia and brain injury. The only safeguard reported is encryption and de-identification. No competing-interests statement despite three commercial or industry-lab affiliations and a commercial data source.

No limitations section. Several real constraints are stated candidly in the methods - the debug-oriented data structure, the unusability of spatial modelling, the window-size trade-off, the uneven classifier tuning - but nothing addresses the reference standard, the age confound, the pseudo-labelling, the splitting unit or the ethics.

included_articles.title: Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder
included_articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE Joint attention, composed of complex behaviors, is an early-emerging social function that is deficient in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Currently, no methods are available for objectively quantifying joint attention. OBJECTIVE To train deep learning (DL) models to distinguish ASD from typical development (TD) and to differentiate ASD symptom severities using video data of joint attention behaviors. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS In this diagnostic study, joint attention tasks were administered to children with and without ASD, and video data were collected from multiple institutions from August 5, 2021, to July 18, 2022. Of 110 children, 95 (86.4%) completed study measures. Enrollment criteria were 24 to 72 months of age and ability to sit with no history of visual or auditory deficits. EXPOSURES Children were screened using the Childhood Autism Rating Scale. Forty-five children were diagnosed with ASD. Three types of joint attention were assessed using a specific protocol. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES Correctly distinguishing ASD from TD and different levels of ASD symptom severity using the DL model area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), accuracy, precision, and recall. RESULTS The analytical population consisted of 45 children with ASD (mean [SD] age, 48.0 [13.4] months; 24 [53.3%] boys) vs 50 with TD (mean [SD] age, 47.9 [12.5] months; 27 [54.0%] boys). The DL ASD vs TD models showed good predictive performance for initiation of joint attention (IJA) (AUROC, 99.6% [95% CI, 99.4%-99.7%]; accuracy, 97.6% [95% CI, 97.1%-98.1%]; precision, 95.5% [95% CI, 94.4%-96.5%]; and recall, 99.2% [95% CI, 98.7%-99.6%]), low-level response to joint attention (RJA) (AUROC, 99.8% [95% CI, 99.6%-99.9%]; accuracy, 98.8% [95% CI, 98.4%-99.2%]; precision, 98.9% [95% CI, 98.3%-99.4%]; and recall, 99.1% [95% CI, 98.6%-99.5%]), and highlevel RJA (AUROC, 99.5% [95% CI, 99.2%-99.8%]; accuracy, 98.4% [95% CI, 97.9%-98.9%]; precision, 98.8% [95% CI, 98.2%-99.4%]; and recall, 98.6% [95% CI, 97.9%-99.2%]). The DL-based ASD symptom severity models showed reasonable predictive performance for IJA (AUROC, 90.3% [95% CI, 88.8%-91.8%]; accuracy, 84.8% [95% CI, 82.3%-87.2%]; precision, 76.2% [95% CI, 72.9%- 79.6%]; and recall, 84.8% [95% CI, 82.3%-87.2%]), low-level RJA (AUROC, 84.4% [95% CI, 82.0%- 86.7%]; accuracy, 78.4% [95% CI, 75.0%-81.7%]; precision, 74.7% [95% CI, 70.4%-78.8%]; and recall, 78.4% [95% CI, 75.0%-81.7%]), and high-level RJA (AUROC, 84.2% [95% CI, 81.8%-86.6%]; accuracy, 81.0% [95% CI, 77.3%-84.4%]; precision, 68.6% [95% CI, 63.8%-73.6%]; and recall, 81.0% [95% CI, 77.3%-84.4%]). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE In this diagnostic study, DL models for identifying ASD and differentiating levels of ASD symptom severity were developed and the premises for DL-based (continued) Key Points Question Can joint attention be quantified for detecting autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and assessing ASD symptom severities? included_articles.authors: Ko C; Lim JH; Hong J; Hong SB; Park YR

assessments.support: Case-control sampling with autistic children drawn exclusively from a national referral centre for high-risk children and comparison children from day care centres, and the paper states explicitly that conservative criteria were applied on both sides 'to select individuals belonging to clinically distinct groups to ensure development of an accurate and precise ASD vs TD classification model'. Best-estimate IQ differs by 44-50 points at p < .001, the autism sample is 62% preverbal or single-word, and there is no clinical comparison group. Age (p = .99) and sex (p > .99) are matched essentially perfectly and enrolment is prospective and consecutive within an eleven-month window, which prevents a worse rating on process - but the spectrum is deliberately truncated at both ends.

The index test is prespecified: three task-specific models with input dimensions fixed by task duration, a fixed classification threshold of 0.5 rather than a tuned one, no feature selection, and no post-hoc model or feature search reported. Interpretation is fully automated and blind to the reference standard. The interpretability analysis provides evidence that the models respond to the intended behavioural constructs rather than to arbitrary correlates.

A staged pathway with universal K-CARS-2 screening, referral of screen-positive or concern-flagged children to a child psychiatrist, and K-ADOS-2 administration with calibrated severity scores reported for the autism group; comparison status requires a below-cutoff K-CARS-2 plus no parent-reported developmental or psychiatric history. Cognitive functioning was assessed in every participant with an age-appropriate standardised battery. The one qualification, insufficient to raise the rating for the detection analysis, is that the severity prediction target derives from the caregiver-completed K-CARS-2 rather than from the clinician-administered K-ADOS-2 the study already holds.

Prospective enrolment with dates given, 110 screened and 95 (86.4%) analysed with the flow diagram supplied in supplementary material, and reference standard and index test performed within the same study episode. Cross-validation is group-wise by individual, stated explicitly, so each child's up-to-fifteen clips remain within a single fold. Compliance across repeated trials was monitored and analysed rather than assumed. The unreported item is the class distribution across the three severity bands.

risk_of_bias.summary: Unclear rather than high risk: the conduct is among the best in this review and the sampling is among the most extreme. Three domains are at low risk. The reference standard is a staged pathway combining universal K-CARS-2 screening, child psychiatrist diagnosis and K-ADOS-2 with calibrated severity scores, supported by standardised cognitive assessment of every participant. The index test is prespecified with a fixed 0.5 threshold, no feature selection and no model search, and is supported by coordinated Grad-CAM, attention and clustering analyses showing that the models respond to the triadic gaze shifts and orienting behaviours the tasks were designed to elicit. Flow is clean, prospective, STARD-reported, with 86.4% completion and cross-validation grouped by individual so that a child's up-to-fifteen video clips never straddle folds - the safeguard most of this corpus omits. Every metric carries a confidence interval. Against this, patient selection is high risk by explicit design: the paper states that conservative criteria were used to produce 'clinically distinct groups', and the participant table shows a 44-50 point IQ gap at p < .001 with an autism sample that is 62% preverbal or single-word and no clinical comparison group. Detection AUROCs of 99.5-99.8% should therefore be read as demonstrating that the protocol and pipeline function, not as an estimate of performance in the population a referral tool would encounter, where the discrimination required is autism versus developmental delay rather than autism versus a typically developing four-year-old with IQ 105. The severity result requires a further caution: its three classes include non-autism, so it substantially re-solves the detection problem, and no within-autism severity result is reported. Specificity is never given despite STARD adherence, the severity class distribution is unreported so no chance baseline is computable, and the compliance analysis showing autistic children disengaging early from RJA tasks is treated as a limitation for severity modelling but not for detection.

items.notes: Conservative criteria applied deliberately to produce clinically distinct groups, stated by the authors. The autism sample has mean IQ 55-60 and is 62% preverbal or single-word - a population valuably absent from the rest of this corpus, but one selected from the severe end while comparison children are selected from above the screening cutoff, truncating the spectrum at both ends.

Typically developing day care attenders with below-cutoff K-CARS-2 and no parent-reported developmental or psychiatric history. Screened rather than assumed, which is better than most here, but there is no developmental-delay or language-disorder group - a decisive omission when the autism group's mean IQ is in the 50s, since nothing distinguishes an autism signal from a general developmental one.

Age (p = .99), sex (p > .99) and ethnicity are matched or homogeneous, and an age-stratified sensitivity analysis is performed - genuinely careful. But best-estimate and verbal IQ differ by 44-50 points at p < .001 in both age strata, roughly three standard deviations, and no adjustment is attempted despite the authors using mixed ANOVA elsewhere. Recruitment channel also differs completely by group, so site is confounded with diagnosis for an end-to-end model trained on raw frames.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: 110 screened, 95 (86.4%) analysed, with the enrolment flow given in a supplementary figure and the completion rate stated in the abstract. A purpose-built compliance score was computed for every repeated trial and analysed by two-way mixed ANOVA, so engagement is measured rather than assumed - a level of data-quality accounting that few studies here attempt.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Universal K-CARS-2 screening, child psychiatrist diagnosis and K-ADOS-2 with total, social affect and restricted-repetitive calibrated severity scores plus module distribution reported; comparison group screened below cutoff with no parent-reported history. Standardised cognitive assessment of every participant with age-appropriate instruments.

Three task-specific models with input dimensions fixed by task duration, a fixed 0.5 threshold rather than a tuned one, no feature selection and no reported model or hyperparameter search on the evaluation data.

A single consumer camera at fixed resolution and frame rate, front-facing viewpoint, quiet room, height-adjustable chair and table, identical three-task protocol with defined repetition counts, and a single 10-minute session for every child. The protocol was designed for replicability without specialised equipment, calibration or trained raters.
The pipeline is fully end-to-end and automated from raw frames; no human rating enters the index test at any point, which is precisely the dependence the authors set out to eliminate.

Ten-fold group-wise cross-validation with grouping by individual, stated explicitly, so all of a child's up-to-fifteen clips from a single continuous session remain in one fold. This is the correct construction and is unambiguous.

AUROC, accuracy, precision and recall each with 95% confidence intervals by a named method for all six models - the most complete uncertainty reporting in this review. included_articles.title: Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking
included_articles.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) refers to a collection of conditions characterized by challenges in areas such as social interactions, communication, and repetitive behavior. Children with autism spectrum disorders often experience difficulties in processing and responding to social cues, which can lead to deficits in social skills and nonverbal communication. Children with ASD have been observed to have problems in maintaining eye contact. The main aim of this study is to use the eye tracking scan path images as a biological indicator to identify children with autism. The dataset used in this study has 547 visualized scanpath images collected from 59 children. The aim of this study is to utilize these scanpath images and formulate an autism diagnosis technique with the help of machine learning algorithms. The proposed model extracts the trainable features from the images and it is fed to a logistic regression classifier and a multi-layer perceptron classifier (MLP). A comparative study between the performance of the proposed model and a custom convolutional neural network is also presented.

included_articles.title: SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism
included_articles.abstract: Language and communication impairments are considered one of the core features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Quantifying the language atypicalities in autism is a challenging task. Prior works have explored acoustic, and text-based features to assess children’s language and communicative behaviours and have shown their relevance in the diagnosis of autism. In this work, we explore the semantic and pragmatic language features in children with autism (CwA) to understand their significance in the diagnosis of autism. We use natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning (ML) techniques to automatically extract relevant features and detect the existence of speech behaviours such as echolalia, semantic coherence, repetitive language, etc. We further analyse their correlation with the clinical diagnosis of autism. We conducted validation experiments on the transcripts of 76 children (35 ASD and 41 TD) extracted from the CHILDES databank. Our analysis shows that the semantic and pragmatic language features are representative candidates for autism diagnosis and are found to complement the syntactic and lexical features in the classification of CwA with an accuracy of 94%. Further, these features being more coherent and relatable to the standard diagnostic tools improves the interpretability of the diagnostic predictions made using speech signals.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias, driven by the pooling design and the evaluation rather than by the feature engineering, which is the study's genuine contribution. Corpus identity therefore carries diagnostic information by construction, and since every feature in the study is a language measure and the top SHAP contributor is the number of distinct word roots - a canonical developmental index - a developmental or corpus-level explanation of the headline result cannot be excluded. No demographic, cognitive or severity data exist for any child, and no reference standard is described. On evaluation: SHAP-based feature elimination appears to precede the split, six classifiers were compared with the best reported, and all accuracies are multiples of 1/17, so the test set holds 17 items and the difference between the headline 94.1% and the next configuration is one child, with no confidence intervals offered. The ordering of the ablation - that semantic-pragmatic features alone match lexical features and that the three families combine additively - is more robust than any of the point accuracies and is the finding worth carrying forward.

included_articles.title: A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths
included_articles.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a developmental disorder that encompasses difficulties in communication (both verbal and non-verbal), social skills, and repetitive behaviors. The diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder typically involves specialized procedures and techniques, which can be time-consuming and expensive. The accuracy and efficiency of the diagnosis depend on the expertise of the specialists and the diagnostic methods employed. To address the growing need for early, rapid, cost-effective, and accurate diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder, there has been a search for advanced smart methods that can automatically classify the disorder. Machine learning offers sophisticated techniques for building automated classifiers that can be utilized by users and clinicians to enhance accuracy and efficiency in diagnosis. Eye-tracking scan paths have emerged as a tool increasingly used in autism spectrum disorder clinics. This methodology examines attentional processes by quantitatively measuring eye movements. Its precision, ease of use, and cost-effectiveness make it a promising platform for developing biomarkers for use in clinical trials for autism spectrum disorder. The detection of autism spectrum disorder can be achieved by observing the atypical visual attention patterns of children with the disorder compared to typically developing children. This study proposes a deep learning model, known as T-CNN-Autism Spectrum Disorder (T-CNN-ASD), that utilizes eye-tracking scans to classify participants into ASD and typical development (TD) groups. The proposed model consists of two hidden layers with 300 and 150 neurons, respectively, and underwent 10 rounds of cross-validation with a dropout rate of 20%. In the testing phase, the model achieved an accuracy of 95.59%, surpassing the accuracy of other machine learning algorithms such as random forest (RF), decision tree (DT), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and multi-layer perceptron (MLP). Furthermore, the proposed model demonstrated superior performance when compared to the findings reported in previous studies. The results demonstrate that the proposed model can accurately classify children with ASD from those with TD without human intervention.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias, with one problem that goes beyond bias to verifiability. The study is the fifth reuse of the 547-image scan-path dataset from 59 children charted in this review, and it repeats the recurring flaw of that literature: cross-validation over images rather than children, so each held-out image has roughly eight siblings from the same child in training. It compounds this with an unusually large hyperparameter search - separate sweeps over kernel size, stride, pooling, batch size, six optimisers and thirteen architectures, well over a hundred configurations, all scored on the same cross-validation with the maximum reported and no held-out confirmation - in a setting where optimiser choice alone moves accuracy by 35 points. It has no limitations section and acknowledges no constraint. But the decisive issue is arithmetic. Table 9 reports the proposed model at 95.59% accuracy with 77.60% sensitivity and 79.91% specificity; at 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic images those class-conditional values imply an accuracy of about 79.0%, and the multilayer perceptron row shows the same incompatibility (94.69% reported, about 73.6% implied). The paper reports two irreconcilable characterisations of its own classifier and reconciles neither, and separately mislabels the harmonic mean of sensitivity and specificity as F1. Against this, the study does several things better than the other reuses of this dataset: it reports the source participant statistics including CARS severity, it cites the originating study's ethical approvals, it declines to use augmentation on explicit and correct grounds, and it reports class-conditional metrics at all - which is precisely why its internal inconsistency is visible.

included_articles.title: A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning
included_articles.abstract: Early detection of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is crucial for timely intervention, yet diagnosis typically occurs after age three. This study aimed to develop a machine learning model to predict ASD diagnosis using infants’ electronic health records obtained through a national screening program and evaluate its accuracy. A retrospective cohort study analyzed health records of 780,610 children, including 1163 with ASD diagnoses. Data encompassed birth parameters, growth metrics, developmental milestones, and familial and post-natal variables from routine wellness visits within the first two years. Using a gradient boosting model with 3-fold cross-validation, 100 parameters predicted ASD diagnosis with an average area under the ROC curve of 0.86 (SD < 0.002). Feature importance was quantified using the Shapley Additive explanation tool. The model identified a highrisk group with a 4.3-fold higher ASD incidence (0.006) compared to the cohort (0.001). Key predictors included failing six milestones in language, social, and fine motor domains during the second year, male gender, parental developmental concerns, non-nursing, older maternal age, lower gestational age, and atypical growth percentiles. Machine learning algorithms capitalizing on preventative care electronic health records can facilitate ASD screening considering complex relations between familial and birth factors, post-natal growth, developmental parameters, and parent concern.
included_articles.authors: Ben-Sasson A; Guedalia J; Nativ L; Ilan K; Shaham M; Gabis LV

assessments.support: A whole national population cohort of 780,610 children born 2014-2019 with at least two years of computerised records, drawn from a universal Ministry of Health surveillance programme covering 75% of the country with the remainder under identical guidelines. There is no recruitment, no case-control sampling and no spectrum truncation: the comparison group is every other child in the cohort. Exclusion logic is stated and reasoned, including the deliberate retention of Fragile X, tuberous sclerosis and other autism-associated aetiologies on the grounds that autism has multiple causes. The one caveat, insufficient to raise the rating, is that the 25% of the population followed by health maintenance organisations are absent.

Feature reduction from 100 to 59 was made a priori on clinical-relevance grounds rather than by data-driven selection; the milestone binarisation rule is stated with its rationale and its cost; the Youden threshold is an objective, prespecified criterion rather than a tuned operating point; no hyperparameter search is reported; and four modelling methods are compared with full confusion counts rather than the best being selected and reported alone.

Routine clinical diagnosis recorded in health records, with no research instrument and no autism-specific screening tool in the surveillance protocol. Ascertainment is split between ICD-9 coding (56.6%) and verified free-text keyword search (43.4%), with provider recording practice varying. Decisively, the authors state that 'based on the national incidence of ASD, the true positive ASD group is at least 10 times higher in the examined population', so the great majority of autistic children in the cohort are labelled as comparison cases - substantial and acknowledged outcome misclassification, described by the authors as adding 'a lot of noise to the outcome label'.

The interval between predictor and outcome is imposed by design: predictors capped at 24 months, outcomes restricted to diagnoses recorded after 24 months, adopted explicitly to prevent leakage from diagnosis to predictors, with mean age at diagnosis 37.5 months. Cross-validation partitions children. Training and test AUC are both reported with overfitting acknowledged. Variable follow-up by birth cohort is addressed by a sensitivity model excluding 2019 births, and an external validity check using a variable deliberately excluded from the model confirms that flagged children were independently referred for developmental assessment at 3.29 times the rate.

risk_of_bias.summary: Unclear rather than low risk overall, and the single reason is outcome ascertainment - every other domain is at low risk, which is unique in this review. The design is a whole national population cohort of 780,610 children with no recruitment, no case-control sampling and a comparison group consisting of every other child, so the spectrum-truncation and selection problems that dominate this corpus do not arise. Temporal leakage is prevented by construction, with predictors capped at 24 months and outcomes restricted to diagnoses recorded after 24 months, adopted for exactly that purpose. Feature reduction was made a priori on clinical grounds, the operating point is an objective Youden threshold rather than a tuned cutoff, four modelling methods are compared with full confusion counts, training and test AUC are both reported with the overfitting stated plainly, SHAP importance is checked for stability across folds and corroborated by independent significance tests, a boys-only sensitivity model tests whether performance rests on sex, and a variable deliberately withheld from the model confirms that flagged children were independently referred for developmental assessment. Governance is complete. The reference standard, however, is routine clinical recording with no research instrument, split between ICD-9 codes and verified free-text search, and the authors themselves estimate that the true number of autistic children in the cohort is at least ten times the 1,163 labelled - so most autistic children sit in the comparison group. That misclassification biases sensitivity and specificity in directions the data cannot resolve, and it means the reported positive predictive value of 0.60%, which the paper leaves uncomputed, is an underestimate by an unknown factor. The appropriate reading is that the study establishes what routinely collected developmental surveillance data can support at population scale, with the caveat that its outcome label is substantially incomplete and its own authors say so.

included_articles.title: AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: “A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System”
included_articles.abstract: autism spectrum disorder (ASD) diagnosis often benefits from early identification. This paper proposes an enhanced deep learning model for analyzing facial features in children to aid in early ASD detection. The model integrates the YOLO architecture with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) employing transfer learning. Trained on a Kaggle dataset of 2,836 facial images (1,418 autistic and 1,418 nonautistic children), the model achieves high accuracy with MobileNet (95%), Xception (94%), and InceptionV3 (89%). This approach has the potential to improve existing detection methods for ASD and contribute to better human-computer interaction for individuals with special needs. Notably, the model demonstrates high specificity, effectively distinguishing autistic from non-autistic cases across various facial expressions in benchmark datasets.
included_articles.authors: ElMahalawy J; ElSwaify YA; Elliboudy D; Abbas OM; Moustafa N; Wael N

assessments.support: There is no participant selection. Images were scraped from the internet with autistic images taken from autism-focused websites and non-autistic images gathered randomly, so the two classes are drawn from different populations by different processes. The number of distinct children is unknown, no demographic information exists, and no inclusion or exclusion criterion of any kind is stated or possible.

Three architectures were compared with the best reported; augmentation appears to precede partitioning; two mutually inconsistent input sizes are given; and the reported confusion matrix corresponds to no stated partition size. No threshold or operating point is prespecified and no analysis establishes what the classifier responds to.

The label is the source from which an image was retrieved. No diagnosis, criterion, instrument, clinician or verification underlies either class, and both false-positive and false-negative labelling are unbounded - an autism-website photograph may depict a non-autistic person and a randomly collected photograph may depict an autistic child.

A single fixed partition of 2,836 images into 2,536/200/100, with no cross-validation, no repeated splits and no confidence intervals; a 100-image test set in which one image is a full percentage point; an ambiguous ordering of augmentation and splitting; an unknown and unrecoverable image-to-child mapping making participant-level integrity impossible to establish; 100% training accuracy; and a confusion matrix summing to 280 images that matches neither stated partition.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias in every domain, and the design cannot support the claim regardless of how the analysis is conducted. The autism label is the internet location from which an image was retrieved: photographs appearing on autism-focused websites are labelled autistic and photographs gathered randomly are labelled non-autistic, with no diagnosis, criterion or verification behind either class. Because the two classes were assembled from different sources, every photographic property that source determines - resolution, compression, lighting, background, pose, cropping convention, and the demographic composition of the populations represented - is systematically confounded with the label and fully available to the classifier. No interpretability analysis is performed that could distinguish a model responding to facial morphology from one responding to image provenance, so the reported 95% accuracy carries no evidential weight about children. Secondary problems compound this: a single fixed 100-image test set, augmentation of ambiguous ordering relative to splitting, an unknown image-to-child mapping making participant-level integrity unestablishable, 100% training accuracy, a confusion matrix matching no stated partition, vertical flipping applied to faces, and sensitivity and specificity written throughout with a units error. There is no limitations section and no acknowledged constraint. Separately from bias, the study reports no ethics approval, no consent and no consideration of either, while building on photographs of identifiable children that assert a health status about them, and proposing distribution as a consumer mobile application for families.

included_articles.title: An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks
included_articles.abstract: Background: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by heterogeneous behavioral and neurological patterns, complicating timely and accurate diagnosis. Behavioral datasets are commonly used to diagnose ASD. In clinical practice, it is difficult to identify ASD because of the complexity of the behavioral symptoms, overlap of neurological disorders, and individual heterogeneity. Correct and timely identification is dependent on the presence of skilled professionals to perform thorough neurological examinations. Nevertheless, with developments in deep learning techniques, the diagnostic process can be significantly improved by automatically identifying and automatically classifying patterns of ASD-related behaviors and neuroimaging features. Method: This study introduces a novel multimodal diagnostic paradigm that combines structured behavioral phenotypes and structural magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI) into an interpretable and personalized framework. A Generalized Additive Model with Interactions (GAMI-Net) is used to process behavioral data for transparent embedding of clinical phenotypes. Structural brain characteristics are extracted via a hybrid CNN–GNN model, which retains voxel-level patterns and region-based connectivity through the Harvard–Oxford atlas. The embeddings are then fused using an Autoencoder, compressing cross-modal data into a common latent space. A Hyper Network-based MLP classifier produces subject-specific weights to make the final classification. Results: On the held-out test set drawn from the ABIDE-I dataset, a 20% split with about 247 subjects, the constructed system achieved an accuracy of 99.40%, precision of 100%, recall of 98.84%, an F1-score of 99.42%, and an ROC-AUC of 99.99%. For another test of generalizability, five-fold stratified cross-validation on the entire dataset yielded a mean accuracy of 98.56%, an F1-score of 98.61%, precision of 98.13%, recall of 99.12%, and an ROC-AUC of 99.62%. Conclusions: These results suggest that interpretable and personalized multimodal fusion can be useful in aiding practitioners in performing effective and accurate ASD diagnosis. Nevertheless, as the test was performed on stratified cross-validation and a single held-out split, future research should seek to validate the framework on larger, multi-site datasets and different partitioning schemes to guarantee robustness over heterogeneous populations.
included_articles.authors: Malik W; Fahiem MA; Farhat T; Alghazo R; Mahmood A; Alhajlah M

assessments.support: ABIDE-I aggregates 17 sites with distinct recruitment practices, scanners and protocols; no age, sex or IQ distribution is reported for either group because these variables were converted into model features, and no quality-control exclusions are described. Within-site case-control recruitment is nonetheless a genuine advantage over internet-assembled corpora.

One of the two input streams consists of ADOS, ADI-R and SRS totals - the scored output of the assessments through which the labels were established - together with IQ and age. No cross-site harmonisation is applied to the imaging stream and SITE_ID is label-encoded into preprocessing.

Clinical diagnosis at the contributing sites supported by ADOS and ADI-R - the strongest reference standard of any study in this review. The problem is not its quality but that its scored output was supplied to the model as a predictor.

The subject is the analytic unit under both evaluation schemes, so no within-subject leakage arises - but neither scheme is site-stratified despite 17 sites, the split is described inconsistently as 70:30 and as 20% with a subject count matching neither, missingness on the instrument fields is label-informative and unaddressed, and the headline accuracy differs between sections of the same paper.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias, from a study whose architecture is among the most carefully constructed in the review and whose data foundation is circular. The design is thoughtful at every stage - GAMI-Net for interpretable additive modelling of clinical variables, a CNN-GNN pair capturing voxel structure and inter-region relationships, autoencoder fusion into a shared latent space rather than naive concatenation, and a hypernetwork generating subject-specific classifier weights - with ablation studies, four baseline comparators, SHAP analysis and t-SNE visualisation. The reference standard behind the labels is the strongest in the corpus. The problem is that the scored output of that reference standard is fed to the classifier as input: ADOS_TOTAL, ADOS_COMM, ADOS_GOTHAM_SEVERITY, ADI_R_SOCIAL_TOTAL_A, ADI_R_VERBAL_TOTAL_BV and SRS_RAW_TOTAL are all predictors, and the study's own explainability analysis ranks ADOS first among them. Because ADOS and ADI-R are largely absent for controls in ABIDE-I, missingness on these fields carries the label independently of magnitude. A ROC-AUC of 99.99% follows from this arrangement rather than from anything the architecture achieves, and no partitioning scheme could alter it. Secondary problems: no site-stratified or leave-one-site-out evaluation despite 17 sites and a documented site confound; age and IQ entered as predictors rather than adjusted for; no confidence intervals; and accuracy reported as 99.40% in the abstract and 96.4% in the contributions section, with the split described as both 70:30 and 20%.

items.notes: One thousand one hundred and twelve subjects is among the largest samples in the review and is ample for the architecture; the problem lies in what the features contain rather than in how many there are.

The abstract concedes that the partitioning scheme limits confidence and calls for validation under different schemes - the right instinct in kind. The target leakage, the site confound, the covariate-as-feature treatment and the internal inconsistencies are unaddressed.

included_articles.authors: Zhao Z; Zhang X; Zhang X; Qu X; Hu X; Lu J

assessments.support: Case-control sampling with autistic children from a psychiatric hospital and typically developing children from local communities. Eligibility required at least average non-verbal intelligence and conversational competence, excluding autistic children with intellectual disability. The sample is 85% male, drawn from a single city, and the two groups differ significantly in non-verbal IQ (102 versus 118, p = .015) and by 15 months in mean age (p = .066), neither adjusted for. Two of 23 comparison children were lost to technical problems before analysis without characterisation.

The features producing the headline result were constructed from the six coherence values identified as significantly different in a group comparison using all 41 participants, so feature construction was informed by every participant's diagnosis. Four classifiers were compared across two feature conditions over 63 candidate features with the maximum reported, and it is not stated whether forward feature selection was nested within the cross-validation loop. No threshold or operating point was prespecified.

Multi-clinician DSM-IV consensus - licensed psychiatrist with at least five years' experience, evaluation by a senior clinician, and escalation to two further senior clinicians on disagreement - which is a defensible clinical standard and better than a single unblinded judgement. But no standardised instrument was administered, no inter-rater reliability is quantified, DSM-IV rather than DSM-5 was applied, no severity measure was obtained, and community-recruited comparison children were not screened with any autism instrument.

All 41 analysed participants contributed a single feature vector and leave-one-out cross-validation partitions participants, so evaluation units are independent and no within-participant leakage is possible. Inclusion required videos longer than 45 s and all qualified, so no differential exclusion occurred at that stage. Against this, two comparison children were lost before analysis without description, the interval between diagnosis and recording is unreported, and the recordings are shared with the group's other publications on this cohort without the overlap being flagged.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias overall, concentrated in feature construction and sampling rather than in the measurement, which is the study's strength. Three elements are done well and should be credited. The splitting is participant-level leave-one-out with one feature vector per child, so within-participant leakage is impossible. The chance-level control is a genuine surrogate null - pairing each child's movement with an adult from a different video, so that coherence in the pseudo group represents two people who never interacted - which is the correct control for a synchrony measure and is constructed by almost no other study in this corpus. And the measurement chain is minimal, well justified and fully specified: a fixed camera in stable lighting, motion energy analysis whose validity follows from those conditions, and cross wavelet analysis resolving coordination across 23 time scales. Against this, the headline 92.68% rests on 57 features built by summing the six coherence values that a group comparison on all 41 participants had already identified as significant, and those features were then evaluated on the same 41 participants; the paper presents this as an innovation and attributes the gain to larger effect sizes, which is the artefact rather than an explanation. Four classifiers over 63 candidate features were compared with the maximum reported, and the entire improvement over the original-feature result consists of three additional autistic children, with no confidence interval offered. The groups differ by 16 IQ points and 15 months of age, neither adjusted, in a study of motor coordination. And the paper does not confront the fact that its own prior analysis of these identical recordings, using complexity matching, found no significant coordination difference at all - which is the most informative thing the dataset has to say.

items.notes: Twenty autistic children from a single psychiatric hospital, required to have at least average non-verbal intelligence and the conversational competence to sustain a structured interview, 85% male, with no severity measure - so the sample is a cognitively able, verbal, predominantly male slice. The authors name sex ratio and severity range as limitations.

Community-recruited typically developing children with self-reported absence of psychiatric, motor, vision or physical disorder, and no autism screening instrument applied. No clinical comparison group, so the coordination difference cannot be shown to be autism-specific rather than a marker of atypical development generally.

Sex is matched (p = .413), but non-verbal IQ differs by 16 points at p = .015 and mean age by 15 months at p = .066, neither adjusted in the statistical or the classification analysis. Both are plausible drivers of motor coordination, and the age difference runs in the direction that would independently predict less mature coordination in the autistic group. A further uncontrolled factor is the interviewer, who supplies half the coherence signal and was presumably not blind to group.

items.notes: Two of 23 comparison children were lost to technical problems before analysis, stated but not characterised. The 45 s minimum video length was applied and all 41 remaining participants met it, so no differential exclusion occurred at that stage - which is worth noting given that duration-based criteria elsewhere in this corpus have removed autistic participants preferentially.

items.notes: Multi-clinician DSM-IV consensus with escalation on disagreement is a reasonable clinical basis, but no standardised instrument, no reliability statistic, DSM-IV rather than DSM-5, no severity measure, and no screening of the comparison group.

The 57 derived features were constructed from coherences selected for statistical significance on the full sample; four classifiers were compared across two feature conditions with the maximum reported; and nesting of forward feature selection within the cross-validation is not stated.

Identical camera, sampling rate, side-view framing with both people equally placed, 80 cm seating distance, fixed camera position and stable lighting for every participant, with the same conversation protocol and appendix questions. The authors justify the validity of motion energy analysis directly from these acquisition conditions. A 45 s minimum duration criterion was applied uniformly.

Feature extraction and classification are automated and label-free once the regions of interest are drawn. But the regions of interest were drawn manually, and more importantly the interviewer - who contributes half the coherence signal - was a live participant presumably aware of each child's group, so differential elicitation cannot be excluded.
Leave-one-out cross-validation at participant level, described iteration by iteration, with one feature vector per child so within-participant leakage is structurally impossible.

The derived features underpinning the headline result were built from coherences chosen for significance on all 41 participants, so feature construction saw every held-out participant's diagnosis. Whether forward feature selection was nested inside the loop for the original-feature result is not stated.

The pseudo-pair surrogate null is an exemplary empirical chance level for the synchrony statistics - constructed by pairing children with adults who were never in the room - and is better than anything comparable in this corpus. But no chance baseline, permutation test or confidence interval accompanies any classification figure, and the entire improvement from 85.37% to 92.68% consists of three additional autistic children with specificity unchanged to the decimal.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Forty-one participants and 23 original plus 57 derived features. One participant is 2.4 accuracy points, and the authors name sample size as their first limitation.

Conversation protocol with appendix questions, seating distance, camera model and sampling rate, framing convention, region-of-interest procedure, minimum duration criterion, the principle and justification of motion energy analysis, all 23 time scales, the surrogate construction, four classifiers, the feature-selection cap, the leave-one-out scheme, the combinatorial derivation of the 57 features, and the exact composition of the three winning features are all specified. Software packages are not named.

Sensitivity and specificity are reported alongside accuracy - which is what makes visible that the whole improvement is a sensitivity gain of three children - and effect sizes and ROC curves are given. But no AUC values, no confusion matrices, and no confidence intervals on any classification figure.
No code, no data, no preregistration, and no software specification.

Declaration of Helsinki conformity, written informed consent approved by the local ethics committee and signed by caregivers, a separate declaration confirming Helsinki 2013 conformity and removal of identifying details, disclosure of the 200 CNY participant payment, and itemised funding from seven sources.

Three limitations compressed into one abstract sentence - sample size, sex ratio, severity range - with no dedicated section. Nothing about the significance-based feature construction, the classifier search, the IQ and age differences, or the discrepancy with the group's own null finding on these same recordings.

included_articles.title: Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning
included_articles.abstract: This study explores the challenge of differentiating autism spectrum (AS) from non-AS conditions in adolescents and adults, particularly considering the heterogeneity of AS and the limitations of diagnostic tools like the ADOS-2. In response, we advocate a multidimensional approach and highlight lexicogrammatical analysis as a key component to improve diagnostic accuracy. From a corpus of spoken language we developed, interviews and storyrecounting texts were extracted for 64 individuals diagnosed with AS and 71 non-AS individuals, all aged 14 and above. Utilizing machine learning techniques, we analyzed the lexicogrammatical choices in both interviews and story-recounting tasks. Our approach led to the formulation of two diagnostic models: the first based on annotated linguistic tags, and the second combining these tags with textual analysis. The combined model demonstrated high diagnostic effectiveness, achieving an accuracy of 80%, precision of 82%, sensitivity of 73%, and specificity of 87%. Notably, our analysis revealed that interview-based texts were more diagnostically effective than story-recounting texts. This underscores the altered social language use in individuals with AS, a crucial aspect in distinguishing AS from non-AS conditions. Our findings demonstrate that lexicogrammatical analysis is a promising addition to traditional AS diagnostic methods. This approach suggests the possibility of using natural language processing to detect distinctive linguistic patterns in AS, aiming to enhance diagnostic accuracy for differentiating AS from non-AS in adolescents and adults.
included_articles.authors: Kato S; Hanawa K; Saito M; Nakamura K

assessments.support: Case-control sampling with autistic participants recruited through a university neuropsychiatry clinic and three-quarters of the comparison group recruited as college students, so clinical status and educational setting co-vary with group. The comparison group's cognitive level was not measured at all - grade point average was substituted for IQ testing - while the autistic group's full-scale IQ is 81-91, so a substantial ability gap is likely and unquantified in a study of grammatical complexity. Mitigating features that do not lift the judgement: the autistic cohort deliberately retains co-occurring conditions on well-argued grounds, the age floor is chosen on a principled linguistic rationale, and 17 comparison participants came through the same clinical pathway.

Hyperparameters were adopted from standard values and explicitly not searched; no feature selection is performed; four model configurations are reported in full rather than the best being selected; and model comparisons are tested with McNemar rather than read from point differences. The automatic annotation model, the one fitted preprocessing component, is retrained within each cross-validation fold. Classification is automated and blind to labels at inference.

DSM-5 diagnosis by experienced neurodevelopmental specialists with ADOS-2 confirmation by a research-reliability-certified administrator, supported by SRS-2, Wechsler IQ testing, Vineland-II, AQ and PARS-TR. Uniquely in this review, the comparison group also received the ADOS-2 and was confirmed non-spectrum against quoted published cut-offs, with means reported for both comparison subgroups. Residual gaps insufficient to raise the rating: no blinding statement and no inter-rater reliability beyond the administrator's certification.

Every participant contributed transcripts from both tasks and all 135 appear in the analysis, with leave-one-out cross-validation partitioning participants. Against this, the language samples were produced during the ADOS-2 administrations that generated the diagnostic labels, so sample and label arise from the same encounter; no attrition or transcript-exclusion accounting is reported; and the seven-year recruitment window is not broken down, so it is unclear whether the two comparison subgroups were recruited contemporaneously with the autistic cohort.

risk_of_bias.summary: Unclear rather than high risk, and one of the best-conducted studies in the review. Three domains are strong. The reference standard is the only one in this corpus to apply a gold-standard instrument to both groups: DSM-5 diagnosis with ADOS-2 confirmation by a certified administrator for the autistic cohort, supported by SRS-2, Wechsler IQ, Vineland-II, AQ and PARS-TR, and ADOS-2 administration with quoted non-spectrum cut-offs for every comparison participant. The index test involves no hyperparameter search - explicitly declined - no feature selection, and full reporting of four configurations rather than selection of the best. And the validation nests the automatic annotation model inside each leave-one-out fold, recognising that a fitted preprocessing component leaks if trained once on the whole corpus; almost no other study here identifies that problem, let alone solves it. Reporting is correspondingly disciplined, with 95% confidence intervals on all sixteen accuracy figures, McNemar tests for model comparisons, and explicit refusal to read non-significance as equivalence. The binding limitation is sampling. The autistic group's measured full-scale IQ is 81-91 while the comparison group's cognitive level was not measured at all, grade point average being substituted, and three-quarters of that group are university students - so a probable and unquantified difference in cognitive and educational level separates the groups in a study whose outcome is the range and complexity of grammatical choice. A second structural feature deserves flagging without being a bias in the usual sense: the transcripts come from the ADOS-2 sessions that produced the labels, so the speech analysed was elicited by an examiner assessing the participant for autism at that moment.

Every comparison participant received the ADOS-2 and was confirmed non-spectrum against quoted cut-offs, which is stronger screening than any other study here provides. But three-quarters are college students selected for average grade point average, so the group is not a clinical comparison in the differential sense, and the 17 who came through the clinical pathway were selected precisely for having no psychiatric diagnosis.

Age differs significantly but by about a year; sex is not significantly different. Accuracy with 95% confidence intervals for all sixteen conditions, plus precision, sensitivity, specificity and AUC, and McNemar tests for pairwise model comparison with non-significance explicitly not read as equivalence. No majority-class baseline is stated, but the confidence intervals serve the same interpretive function against a 52.6% floor.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: One hundred and thirty-five participants is at the upper end for this corpus and the confidence intervals are correspondingly informative, but the authors name sample size as their principal limitation, describe the work as exploratory, and interpret their statistical comparisons with explicit reference to limited power.

Participant selection rationale, full diagnostic battery, ADOS-2 cut-offs applied to both groups, both elicitation tasks with their provenance, the annotation scheme with headings, functions and tag types, the transfer-comparison method, input construction for each model, all training hyperparameters with the statement that they were not searched, the fold-nested annotation procedure, and the full evaluation scheme are all specified. Software packages and seeds are not named.

Sixteen conditions with accuracy, 95% confidence intervals, precision, sensitivity, specificity and AUC, plus a McNemar comparison table with test statistics and p-values, and explicit power-aware interpretation of non-significant results. The most disciplined uncertainty reporting in the review after the population EHR study.

A data availability statement is provided and supplementary files carry the tag frequency comparisons, but the corpus itself is described in a prior publication rather than deposited, and no code is released.

Hirosaki University Committee on Medical Ethics approval with IRB numbers and their update history, information security guidelines followed, age-appropriate written consent including guardian consent for those under 20, and anonymisation with removal of identifiable utterances from transcripts - a privacy measure specific to spoken personal narrative. Funding itemised and competing interests declared as none.

A dedicated limitations section naming sample size repeatedly, describing the study as exploratory, identifying the weakest annotation category with concrete remedies, and interpreting non-significant statistical comparisons with reference to power. Not acknowledged: the unmeasured comparison-group IQ and the substitution of grade point average for cognitive testing, and the fact that the language samples come from the diagnostic sessions themselves.

included_articles.title: Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms
included_articles.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) presents as a neurodevelopmental condition impacting social interaction, communication, and behavior, underscoring the imperative of early detection and intervention to enhance outcomes. This paper introduces a novel approach to ASD detection utilizing facial features extracted from the Autistic Children Facial Dataset. Leveraging transfer learning models, including VGG16, ResNet, and Inception, high-level features are extracted from facial images. Additionally, fine-grained details are captured through the utilization of handcrafted image features such as Histogram of Oriented Gradients, Local Binary Patterns, Scale-Invariant Feature Transform, PHASH descriptors. Integration of these features yields three distinct feature vectors, combining image features with VGG16, ResNet, and Inception features. Subsequently, multiple machine learning classifiers, including Random Forest, KNN, Decision Tree, SVM, and Logistic Regression, are employed for ASD classification. Through rigorous experimentation and evaluation, the performance of these classifiers across three datasets is compared to identify the optimal approach for ASD detection. By evaluating multiple classifiers and feature combinations, this work offers insights into the most effective approaches for ASD detection.
included_articles.authors: Sarwani IS; Bhaskari DL; Bhamidipati S
included_articles.journal: International Journal of Advanced Computer S

assessments.support: No participant selection. 2,936 images downloaded from Kaggle with the two classes assembled from different internet sources, no demographic information of any kind, an unknown number of distinct children, and no inclusion or exclusion criterion stated or possible.

Eighteen classifier-feature combinations evaluated with the maximum reported, no hyperparameters stated for any classifier, and no prespecified operating point. No analysis establishes what the classifiers respond to, and five of the eight feature families are descriptors sensitive to image quality rather than to facial structure.

The label is a directory name. Features are extracted 'by traversing through the directory structure' with a label column added to denote 'autistic' or 'non_autistic'. No diagnosis, criterion, instrument or verification underlies either class.

No evaluation protocol is described at all - no split, no cross-validation, no holdout proportion - yet twenty accuracy figures are reported. The image-to-child mapping is unknown, so partition integrity could not be established even if a partition had been specified.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias in every domain, and the reported accuracies cannot be interpreted as estimates of anything. The study analyses 2,936 photographs from the same publicly scraped Kaggle collection already charted in this review, in which the autistic class was assembled from autism-focused online sources and the non-autistic class gathered separately - so image provenance is confounded with the label. That confound is sharper here than in the companion study, because five of the eight feature families are handcrafted descriptors (HOG, LBP, ORB, PHASH, SIFT) that respond to gradient structure, texture, keypoint density and global image fingerprint, all functions of resolution, sharpness, compression and lighting rather than of the child - and this feature set alone reaches 84.5%, a result reported without comment. Labels are directory names with no diagnostic verification. No demographic information exists. No interpretability analysis is performed that could distinguish a face classifier from a photograph classifier. And uniquely among included studies, no evaluation protocol is described at all: the words 'split' and 'validation' do not appear, no cross-validation is reported, and no train-test partition is stated for any of the twenty tabulated accuracies, while the feature-extraction pipeline is narrated in step-by-step detail down to CSV export. There is no limitations section, no ethics approval, no consent and no discussion of either, for a study built on photographs of identifiable children that assert a health status about them.

included_articles.title: Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed
included_articles.abstract: Received: 12 April 2024 Revised: 7 August 2024 Accepted: 20 August 2024 Available online: 31 December 2024 Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) affects brain development, impacting socialization, communication, and creativity in children. Signs typically appear within the first three years, with many children struggling with language acquisition, affecting their learning abilities. Various treatments help manage behaviors, benefiting both children and their parents. The mechanisms by which visual information about facial expressions translates into emotional categories are not well understood. This study proposes a system-level explanation through predictive processing theory. An innovative method combining Fast Mask Recurrent Convolutional Neural Network (FMRCNN) and hybrid Weighed Quantum Particle Swarm Optimization (WQPSO) aims to improve recognition of abnormal facial movements in individuals with ASD. FMRCNN captures temporal relationships and extracts features from input data, while the fast mask mechanism enhances network speed and efficiency by focusing on relevant input regions. The proposed method leverages predictive processing to improve accuracy and efficiency in facial expression recognition. It can identify six emotions: anger, fear, joy, sadness, surprise, and disgust. Results show significant potential in supporting ASD-related challenges, achieving 99.8% accuracy, 99.8% precision, 100% recall, and 94% specificity, surpassing existing systems in ASD facial expression recognition.
included_articles.authors: Devaraj VS; Periyathambi E

assessments.support: No autistic participants exist. Both corpora comprise adult volunteers producing instructed expressions under laboratory conditions, with no clinical characterisation, no demographic reporting in this paper, and a population differing from the stated target - autistic children - in both age and diagnosis.

Preprocessing is described in reasonable detail and evaluated across four brightness variants. But KDEF images are geometrically pre-standardised with eyes and lips at fixed coordinates, and only peak frames of CK+ sequences are used, so the input represents the most favourable possible case for facial expression recognition and none of the variation a deployment would face.
Posed emotion category labels assigned through instructed expression production - a sound ground truth for the task actually performed, though carrying no information about autism.

No validation scheme is described anywhere: no split proportion, no cross-validation arrangement, no held-out set size and no partitioning unit. CK+ contributes roughly 2.8 peak frames per individual and whether images of the same person span partitions is unstated.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias with respect to any autism-related question, and not assessable with respect to the emotion-recognition task it actually performs. The study contains no autistic participants, no autism labels and no autism classification target: its data are posed prototypical expressions from adult volunteers in the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces and Extended Cohn-Kanade corpora, with only peak frames used from the latter and the former geometrically standardised so that eyes and lips occupy fixed image coordinates. Reported performance is 99.8% accuracy, 99.8% precision, 100% recall and 94% specificity for six-way emotion classification, with significance tests against three baselines - but no validation scheme, split proportion, cross-validation arrangement or partitioning unit is stated anywhere in the paper, so the figures cannot be located relative to any evaluation design. The metric combination is unusual for a multi-class problem and is unaccompanied by confusion matrices or class-wise results; the number of emotion classes is given variously as six, seven and five; and the architecture narrative repeatedly describes the optimiser as encoding physiological signal characteristics although no physiological signal is collected. The paper's framing - title, keywords, abstract, introduction and conclusion - is entirely about autistic people and the failure of conventional systems to read their faces, which is a genuine problem that the experiments do not address.
