included_articles.title: Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification
included_articles.abstract: In recent years, research has been demonstrating that movement analysis, utilizing machine learning methods, can be a promising aid for clinicians in supporting autism diagnostic process. Within this field of research, we aim to explore new models and delve into the detailed observation of certain features that previous literature has identified as prominent in the classification process. Our study employs a game-based tablet application to collect motor data. We use artificial neural networks to analyze raw trajectories in a "drag and drop" task. We compare a two-features model (utilizing only raw coordinates) with a fourfeatures model (including velocities and accelerations). The aim is to assess the effectiveness of raw data analysis and determine the impact of acceleration on autism classification. Our results revealed that both models demonstrate promising accuracy in classifying motor trajectories. The four-features model consistently outperforms the two-features model, as evidenced by accuracy values (0.90 vs. 0.76). However, our findings support the potential of raw data analysis in objectively assessing motor behaviors related to autism. While the fourfeatures model excels, the two-features model still achieves reasonable accuracy. Addressing limitations related to sample size and noise is essential for future research. Our study emphasizes the importance of integrating intelligent solutions to enhance and assist autism traditional diagnostic process and intervention, paving the way for more effective tools in assessing motor skills.
included_articles.authors: Luongo M; Simeoli R; Marocco D; Milano N; Ponticorvo M

assessments.support: Twenty children in a case-control arrangement, with autistic participants from a rehabilitation centre that is also a co-author affiliation and where they were receiving psychomotor therapy, and comparison children from a mainstream school recruited 'without specific assessment of their pre-existing abilities'. Comorbidity was excluded from the autistic group, narrowing it relative to the clinical population. No sex, IQ, developmental or severity data for either group, and the autistic group's age standard deviation is nearly ten times the comparison group's.

The two feature sets are prespecified and compared directly rather than selected, no feature selection occurs, and the preprocessing is fixed a priori and fully specified. But no model architecture or training hyperparameters are reported, so the comparison between the two models cannot be checked for differences in capacity or training, and no operating point is prespecified.

Autism required clinical diagnosis confirmed with ADOS-2, administered by professionals explicitly stated to be independent of the research laboratory and study - a clear statement of independence that few papers here provide. Against this, no ADOS-2 score is reported so the severity range cannot be characterised, and comparison-group status rests on parent and teacher report of no neurodevelopmental disorder with no instrument administered and no assessment of abilities.

Seven hundred and thirty-eight trajectories from 20 children, roughly 37 each, partitioned by trajectory rather than by child, with the validation set quoted as 110 samples out of 738 and no statement that folds respected child boundaries. No participant-level result is reported anywhere. Data-inclusion rules are stated clearly (completed drags only, 20-69 points), but the number of trajectories contributed by each child is not reported and session duration varied between children.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias, driven by the validation unit and by sampling rather than by conduct, which is otherwise careful. The study does several things well that are rare in this corpus. Its task is designed to minimise social demand in a study of motor behaviour - no verbal instructions, a video tutorial and a vibration cue introduced explicitly to avoid stressful social situations - which removes a confound other motor studies here carry unexamined. Its rotation normalisation is worked out from the eight-target geometry and written out in full. Its diagnoses were made by clinicians explicitly independent of the research team. Its interpretability analysis manipulates acceleration in synthetic trajectories and measures the prediction response, giving causal rather than correlational evidence with a stated direction and strength. Its data are published openly on GitHub, uniquely among included studies here. And its limitations section names four real constraints with concrete remedies. The binding problem is that 738 trajectories come from 20 children at roughly 37 each and are partitioned by trajectory, so each validation trajectory has around 36 siblings from the same child in training - and after rotation normalisation those siblings differ only in the noise of execution. Movement kinematics at this granularity approach an individual motor signature, so the reported 0.90 cannot be read as performance on an unseen child, and with 20 participants a leave-one-child-out scheme would have been trivial. Beneath that sit two uncontrolled factors: neither group received any developmental or cognitive assessment, so a general developmental explanation for the motor difference cannot be excluded; and the autistic children were receiving psychomotor therapy at the recruiting centre while the comparison children were not, confounding motor training history with diagnosis in a study of motor kinematics.

The one deviation is table height adjusted by child age.
Coordinates are logged automatically by the game software and modelling is fully automated; no human rating enters the pipeline, and the examiner gave no instructions that could differ by group.

Four-fold cross-validation over 738 trajectories from 20 children, with the validation set quoted in samples and no indication that folds respected child boundaries. Each validation trajectory has roughly 36 siblings from the same child, session and hand in training, and after rotation normalisation those siblings differ only in execution noise. No feature selection occurs and the rotation normalisation is a deterministic geometric transform applied uniformly, so no fitted preprocessing component exists to leak.

Accuracy is reported as a fold-wise distribution rather than a point estimate, and ROC curves are given for both models - better than a bare number. But no sensitivity, specificity, precision, confusion matrix, AUC value, confidence interval or chance baseline appears anywhere.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Twenty children, the smallest sample among included studies, with the 738-trajectory count giving an appearance of data volume that 20 independent units do not support. The authors name sample size as their first limitation.

Exceptional on task, apparatus and preprocessing - exact recruitment dates, task geometry, tablet model and tilt, seating arrangement, sampling rate, all inclusion rules, the rotation normalisation in three numbered equations, the simulation range and the seven simplification rates. Silent on model architecture, training hyperparameters, seeds and whether folds were constructed by child.

Fold-wise accuracy distributions and ROC curves, plus correlations with p-values for the simulation analysis. But no class-conditional metrics, no AUC value, no confidence intervals and no participant-level figure.

The trajectory data are published in a public GitHub repository at a stated URL - the only open data release among included studies in this review, and one that makes the central claim independently checkable. No code or preregistration.

Approval by the Ethical Committee of Psychological Research of the Department of Humanities at the University of Naples Federico II, written parental informed consent, two named funders with an explicit no-role statement covering design, collection, analysis, publication decision and manuscript preparation, and a declaration of no competing interests.

Four limitations named with concrete remedies - sample size, single-device tracking, absence of longitudinal observation, and absence of complementary measures with a specific proposal to add ocular movement data. Not acknowledged: the trajectory-level partitioning, the absence of developmental assessment in either group, the differing age spread, or the psychomotor-therapy confound.

included_articles.title: Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain
included_articles.abstract: An Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) affected individual has several difﬁculties with social-emotional cues. The existing model is observed with emotional face processing in adolescents and ASD and Typical Development (TD) by utilizing various body parameters. Scanning facial expressions is the initial task, and recognizing the face’s sensitivity to different emotional expressions is the next complex task. To address this shortcoming, in this work, a new autism and visual Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) detection model for supporting healthcare applications by processing facial expressions and sensory data of heart rate and body temperature. Here, initially, the individual data regarding facial emotions and other body parameters like heart rate and body temperature are collected from various subjects. Then, the selection of optimal features is executed by a hybrid algorithm named Density Factor-based Artiﬁcial Bee Honey Badger Optimization (DF-ABHBO), where the most essential features are attained and fed to the detection phase. The optimal feature selection is made by resolving the ﬁtness function with constraints like correlation, data variance, and cosine similarity for inter and intra-class. Finally, the autism and visual SPD detection are performed through a Hybrid Weight Optimized Deep Neural Recurrent Network (HWODNRN), where the hyperparameter and weights of “Deep Neural Network (DNN) and Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)” are optimized with the developed DF-ABHBO technique. From the result analysis, the accuracy and F1-score rate of the offered DF-ABHBO-HWODNRN method have attained 96% and 93%. The ﬁndings obtained from the simulations of the designed system achieve better performance.
included_articles.authors: Dedgaonkar S; Sachdeo R

assessments.support: No sample size, no group sizes, no demographics, no recruitment route, no eligibility criteria and no setting are reported anywhere. Data are described only as 'collected manually' from 'various subjects'. Selection cannot be assessed because nothing about it is stated.

Feature selection optimises a fitness function using inter- and intra-class similarity, and therefore class labels, with no statement of nesting within training partitions. The selected feature subset - the explicit output of the paper's central method - is never disclosed. Five model variants and four conventional classifiers were compared with the proposed method reported as best, and no operating point is prespecified.

None described. The label is a binary 'Detected' or 'Not detected' for a merged autism-and-visual-SPD construct, with no instrument, criterion, clinician or procedure. The dataset section's reference to a 'new dataset named AQ10 ... developed based on autism screening' conflates a dataset with an existing screening questionnaire whose items appear nowhere in the reported variables.

Two mutually inconsistent validation descriptions are given - a variable learning-percentage split illustrated at 65/35, and 5-fold cross-validation - neither tied to the reported results. No unit of splitting is stated and none is recoverable, since the number of contributing individuals is never given. Metrics are reported to five decimal places with no denominator.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias in every domain, and the study is uninterpretable rather than merely biased. It reports no sample size, no demographics, no recruitment, no setting, no task, no equipment and no diagnostic procedure; its prediction target merges autism with visual sensory processing disorder into a single binary label with no stated basis; its validation is described in two inconsistent ways, neither tied to the reported figures and neither specifying a unit of splitting that could in any case be identified without a participant count; and its metrics are reported to five decimal places without a denominator. No ethics approval or consent is stated for what is described as manual collection of heart rate, body temperature and facial data from human subjects. Feature selection optimises a label-dependent fitness function with no statement of nesting, and the selected feature subset - the explicit output of the paper's central algorithmic contribution - is never disclosed. The one substantive observation the paper permits comes from its single worked data table: of five illustrated individuals, the three labelled 'Detected' have body temperatures of 100.4, 95.5 and 103 degrees Fahrenheit with heart rates of 102, 62 and 133, while the two labelled 'Not detected' have 98.5 and 99.5 with heart rates of 85 and 89. In the only data displayed, the label separates people with clinically abnormal vital signs from people without, which is a more plausible account of the reported 96.4% than any mechanism the paper proposes.

included_articles.title: Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder
included_articles.abstract: Autistic Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a challenging neurological development disorder, which involves poor social interaction, communication, and repetitive behaviours. If autism is identified early enough it can be treated with better outcomes but present diagnostic tests are dependent on subjective opinion, consume a lot of time, and are vague. This study is aimed at optimizing one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) to improve the precision and speed of early ASD diagnosis. Four ASD datasets representing different age groups — toddlers, children, adolescents, and adults were modelled using one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN). These datasets are accessible to the public on the UCI Machine Learning Repository and Kaggle, they consist of behavioural features relevant to ASD diagnosis. Each dataset underwent feature selection, categorical encoding, and missing value handling. Then, baseline 1D CNN with predefined hyperparameters was modelled on each of the datasets. Subsequently, the baseline models were optimized using the Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE). An interactive web-based ASD diagnostic tool was developed, where user inputs are processed through age-specific pre-trained optimized models to determine ASD probability. The optimized 1D CNN models significantly outperformed the baseline models across all age groups and achieved scores of 100% in accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, MCC, and AUC ROC. This implies that the optimized models can reliably identify people in various age groups who have and do not have ASD. The development of an interactive web-based diagnostic tool extends the practical utility of the models, making them accessible for clinical and at-home use.
included_articles.authors: Omotehinwa TO; Lawrence MO; Oyewola DO; Dada EG
included_articles.journal: Journal of Computational Mathematics and Data Science, 13, Article 100105

assessments.support: Self-selected users of autism screening applications, aggregated by third parties, with positive rates of 69% among toddlers and 61% among adolescents that reflect help-seeking rather than population prevalence. Age, gender and ethnicity are present as fields but no distribution is reported for any of them.

Ten binary responses to a screening questionnaire, answered by a parent, relative or health professional for the child bands, together with registration metadata. Nothing measured, observed or elicited; and the index test's inputs determine the reference standard arithmetically.

No clinical diagnosis exists for any respondent. The class variable is the summed A1-A10 item score thresholded at the instrument's published cut-off - a deterministic function of the model's own inputs, with the sum additionally present among the tabulated fields.

Each respondent contributes one row, so the split unit is the person; 80/20 partitions are tabulated with absolute sizes for all four datasets; class distributions are reported and the decision not to oversample is explained. Sound mechanics on a degenerate task.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias, from the most complete instance of target leakage in the review. The class variable in the UCI and Kaggle autism screening datasets is not a diagnosis but a screening outcome computed by summing the A1 to A10 item responses and applying the instrument's published cut-off; those ten items are the model's principal inputs, and the summed score itself is among the tabulated fields. The outcome is therefore a closed-form function of the predictors, and scores of exactly 100% on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation coefficient and AUC-ROC across all four age bands simultaneously are the arithmetic consequence rather than evidence about detection. No respondent in any of the four datasets is known to have received a clinical assessment. The paper attributes the perfect scores to its Tree-structured Parzen Estimator optimisation and does not consider the alternative. Against this, the analytic reporting is genuinely careful by the corpus's standards: class distributions are given for every dataset, the decision not to apply oversampling is explained rather than assumed, split proportions are tabulated with absolute partition sizes, the Matthews correlation coefficient is included, and the methodological critique of exhaustive grid search is well reasoned. The study also deploys - an interactive web-based tool routes user input through the pre-trained models and is described as accessible for clinical and at-home use, presenting the output of the Q-CHAT-10 and AQ-10 scoring rules to families as an AI diagnosis, with no predictive value computed at any realistic prevalence.

included_articles.authors: Ohmoto Y; Terada K; Shimizu H; Kawahara H; Iwanaga R; Kumazaki H

assessments.support: Approximately 99% of the five-year-old residents of one municipality, assessed during routine preschool medical examinations, with both groups drawn from the same population cohort and differing only in SRS-2 score. There is no recruitment, no case-control geometry and no spectrum truncation, and the single-age inclusion criterion removes the age confound that affects every other motor study in this review. Age and sex ratio do not differ between groups, and the SRS-2 cut-off is sex-specific. The one limitation, insufficient to raise the rating, is that the sample comes from a single small Japanese town.

Feature selection and hyperparameter optimisation were performed jointly, reducing sixteen candidate variables to three to five per model and fixing the SVM cost parameter, with no statement of whether this occurred inside the leave-one-out folds. Three variable sets were compared on the same participants. No threshold or operating point is prespecified. On 126 participants with 19 positives, unnested joint selection would be sufficient to produce the reported perfect scores.

The target is a maternal-report SRS-2 total dichotomised at a published population cut-off, with no clinical assessment, diagnostic instrument or second informant for any participant. The authors state that clinical evaluation should be integrated alongside the SRS-2 to improve reliability. A single-informant questionnaire threshold is a legitimate screening target but is not autism, and no reliability estimate accompanies it.

All 126 participants received both the SRS-2 and the balance assessment, each contributing one feature vector, with leave-one-out cross-validation partitioning participants. No attrition is reported and coverage of the target population is near-complete. The reference standard and index test were obtained in the same period and independently of one another. Unreported: signal-quality criteria for the pressure and pose streams, and any handling of pose-estimation failure.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias overall, driven entirely by the index test and the reference standard - the sampling and flow are among the best in this review. The study assessed approximately 99% of one municipality's five-year-olds during their routine preschool medical examinations, so both groups come from the same population cohort, there is no case-control contrast and no spectrum truncation, and confining the sample to a single age year removes the developmental confound that affects every other motor study charted here. Measurement is a standard clinical balance test instrumented with a pressure mat and a consumer webcam, synchronised at 20 Hz, and the discriminative features are correlations between joint angles and centre-of-pressure movement that neither sensor could produce alone. Leave-one-out cross-validation partitions participants, SHAP attribution is reported, and the model's predicted probability is correlated with the continuous SRS-2 score - a check on whether the prediction tracks the trait dimension rather than the imposed threshold that few studies here perform. The limitations passage names the optimism of the authors' own validation scheme. Against this, two problems bound what the result means. The target is a maternal-report SRS-2 total dichotomised at a cut-off, with no clinical assessment of any participant, so what is predicted is a questionnaire threshold rather than autism - which the authors state plainly. And accuracy, sensitivity and specificity are all reported as exactly 1.000 for two of three configurations, following a joint feature-selection and hyperparameter-optimisation step that reduced sixteen variables to three to five and whose nesting within the cross-validation loop is nowhere stated. On 126 children with 19 positives that step alone would suffice to produce perfect separation, and perfect separation is not a plausible property of postural measurement in five-year-olds.

items.notes: Approximately 99% of one municipality's five-year-old population, assessed in situ during routine examinations. Coverage is near-complete and self-selection is minimal; the sample represents the full trait distribution of that cohort rather than a recruited slice.

The comparison group is the remainder of the same population cohort below the SRS-2 cut-off - a within-population contrast rather than a recruited control group, which is the correct design for a screening question and is unique in this review alongside the population health-records study.

Age is controlled by design, every participant being five years old, which removes the confound that troubles every other motor study here; sex ratio does not differ and the SRS-2 cut-off is sex-specific. But no cognitive, developmental or motor-maturation measure was obtained, so at an age when postural control is still developing a general developmental explanation cannot be separated from an autistic-trait-specific one.

items.notes: No attrition is reported and all 126 participants appear in the analysis. But no signal-quality criterion is described for either the pressure or the pose stream, and no handling of OpenPose failure is reported - relevant because the study's discriminative features depend entirely on the estimated joint angles.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: A maternal-report SRS-2 total dichotomised at a published cut-off, with no clinical assessment, diagnostic instrument, second informant or reliability estimate for any participant. The authors acknowledge this and recommend integrating clinical evaluation.

Feature selection and hyperparameter optimisation performed jointly, reducing sixteen variables to three to five per model, with nesting relative to the cross-validation loop unstated; three variable sets compared on the same participants; no prespecified operating point.

One pressure sensor, one webcam model and resolution, a fixed 20 Hz synchronised acquisition, a documented physical configuration, and a standard clinical balance test administered identically to every child within a single routine examination programme. The task requires no verbal or social demand, so a motor measurement is obtained without social confound.
Feature extraction and classification are automated from sensor and pose data; the SRS-2 was completed by mothers independently of the balance testing and before it entered any analysis.

Leave-one-out cross-validation over participants, each contributing a single feature vector, so within-participant leakage is impossible. But the joint feature-selection and hyperparameter-optimisation step is described without reference to the folds, leaving the most consequential leakage question unresolved.

Three to five of sixteen variables plus a cost parameter selected per model by a procedure whose nesting within the cross-validation is nowhere stated. On 126 participants with 19 positives this alone would be sufficient to produce the reported perfect scores.

Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity all exactly 1.000 for two of three configurations, reported without a majority-class baseline against an 84.9% floor, without confidence intervals on a sensitivity estimated from 19 positives, and without comment on the implausibility of perfect separation in a behavioural measurement. Sensitivity and specificity are at least reported separately, which is essential at this prevalence.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Nineteen above-threshold participants for a model selecting three to five features from sixteen. The authors identify this directly, noting that with 'only around 20 above-threshold samples and highly imbalanced sample overall' they were constrained in their choice of validation scheme.

Population and sampling basis, inclusion criterion, instrument and cut-offs with their source, sensor and camera specifications, synchronised sampling rate, pose-estimation method with joints figured, all sixteen variables named and categorised, the three variable sets, the SVM kernel and cost parameter and the selected variables for each best model, the validation scheme and the statistical software with version. Supplementary materials give per-variable rationale and calculation. The nesting of feature selection is the one substantive omission.

Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity per variable set with the selected variables named; SHAP across all participants; and correlation of predicted probability with continuous SRS-2. But no confidence intervals, AUC, confusion matrix, chance baseline or positive predictive value - the last being directly computable and directly relevant given the population-based design.
Contributions stated to be included in the article and supplementary material, with further inquiries directed to the corresponding author. No code, no dataset deposit, no preregistration.

Nagasaki University Ethics Committee approval with number 22051204, Declaration of Helsinki conformity, and written informed consent from both the children and their guardians after a comprehensive explanation. Four funding sources itemised and competing interests declared as none.

Four limitations named, including the screening rather than diagnostic nature of the target with a recommendation to integrate clinical assessment, the small above-threshold sample, the single algorithm family, and the need for external validation - and, unusually, an explicit statement that the chosen validation scheme 'can produce optimistic performance estimates due to the small test set in each iteration' with a call for cautious interpretation. The nesting question is not addressed.

included_articles.title: Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network
included_articles.abstract: Artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have made signiﬁcant advances in the early detection and diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), overcoming the limits of previous screening methods. These AI-based technologies offer more objective, scalable, and efﬁcient methods for identifying risk behaviors associated with ASD. This article presents a novel approach for enhancing the detection and classiﬁcation of ASD by integrating squeeze-and-excitation, multiscale attention mechanisms, and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with automated hyperparameter optimization using the white shark optimization (WSO) algorithm. By leveraging attention mechanisms to focus on relevant facial features across multiple scales, this method enhances feature extraction, improves classiﬁcation accuracy, and provides a robust framework for analyzing complex facial imaging data. An extensive autism dataset, encompassing both facial and multimodal datasets, was utilized in this study, including subjects from the non-ASD control (NC) group and individuals diagnosed with ASD. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model signiﬁcantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a high accuracy of 95.36%, precision of 92.62%, and an F1-score of 95.5% for ASD detection and classiﬁcation. This proposed model is a promising tool for the accurate and early identiﬁcation of ASD, which is crucial for effective treatment and management. By providing deeper insights into distinctive facial patterns and morphological features associated with ASD, the model enables physicians to make more informed decisions and develop targeted treatment plans, ultimately improving patient outcomes. Subjects Bioinformatics, Algorithms and Analysis of Algorithms, Artiﬁcial Intelligence, Data Science
included_articles.authors: Ismail WN; Ali MAS

assessments.support: No participants were selected. Class membership in the Piosenka corpus is determined by whether an image was found on 'websites and Facebook pages that included autism-related content', and in the YTUIA corpus by whether a video was collected into a self-stimulatory-behaviour set or was an unrelated kindergarten video. The number of distinct individuals is unknown, the sex distribution is recorded as unspecified in the paper's own table, and age, ancestry, cognitive level and comorbidity are absent for both classes. The 1:1 class ratio is an artefact of dataset assembly.

Raw RGB face crops from uncontrolled consumer photographs and video frames, with no control over pose, expression, illumination, resolution, compression or crop convention - all of which may vary systematically with class given the differing harvest sources. Hyperparameters were selected by a metaheuristic search whose evaluation partition is not stated. No prespecified operating threshold.

No reference standard of any kind exists. No child in either corpus is known to have received a diagnostic assessment, no instrument or clinician judgement is cited, and the label records image provenance. The paper nonetheless describes the positive class as 'individuals diagnosed with ASD' and does not identify the absence as a limitation.

Split sizes are reported exactly for both corpora and the leakage-detection procedure is given in pseudocode with its thresholds and cluster sweep - materially better than the rest of this branch. But the reassignment of high-similarity test images into training is a data-dependent edit of the test set, the number of MTCNN detection failures is not reported, the number of runs behind the reported means is not stated, and the reported confidence intervals are narrower than the value of one test image.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias, driven entirely by the data rather than by the analysis - which is the opposite of the usual pattern in this branch and is what makes the study instructive. The labels in both corpora encode where material was found on the internet, not any assessment of the child depicted: the paper states that the autism images were 'taken from websites and Facebook pages that included autism-related content', while the video positives come from a self-stimulatory-behaviour collection and the negatives from unrelated kindergarten videos. No child is known to have been diagnosed, the sex distribution is marked as unspecified in the paper's own table, and no demographic variable is available for either class. Against that foundation the paper mounts the most careful analysis in the facial-photograph branch of this review. It is the only such study to test for leakage rather than assume its absence, and its test found a maximum training-test cosine similarity of 0.9714 in the video-derived corpus before any intervention - direct evidence that the frame-level splitting practised by the studies it builds on does leak. It re-split by perceptual cluster, reported the sweep and the thresholds, archived its code on Zenodo with a DOI, reported a full metric suite with McNemar and paired t-tests, ran a four-way ablation whose result contradicts its own architectural contribution, and evaluated across datasets in both directions. None of this reaches the label problem. A classifier that has learned to recognise images sourced from autism-related web content will perform identically on perfectly subject-disjoint splits, and will transfer between two corpora built on the same harvesting principle exactly as a genuine facial phenotype would - so the 89-90% cross-dataset result is not the independent confirmation it is presented as. The confidence intervals, uniformly plus or minus 0.4 percentage points on a 68-image test set, are narrower than a single test image. And no ethics or consent statement appears anywhere in a study whose training data are identifiable photographs of children scraped from personal websites, Facebook pages and YouTube.

items.notes: None exists. No diagnostic instrument, clinician judgement or medical record for any image; the label is image provenance. The paper nonetheless describes the positive class as diagnosed individuals.
Hyperparameters selected by a metaheuristic search over six ranges whose evaluation partition is unstated; no prespecified operating threshold; four model configurations compared on the same data.

Uncontrolled consumer photographs and video frames with unknown and class-correlated acquisition conditions. Preprocessing standardises geometry and pixel range but cannot standardise camera, lighting, pose, expression or compression.
Classification is fully automated from image data with no human rater involved at inference.

The best treatment of this issue in the facial-photograph branch: leakage was measured rather than assumed, found at 0.9714 maximum similarity, and addressed by perceptual-cluster splitting with a documented sweep and threshold. But perceptual similarity is a proxy for identity rather than a measurement of it, the reassignment step edits the test set using the model's own feature space, and none of it touches the provenance confound that determines what the labels mean.

The white shark search over learning rate, layer widths, batch size, depth and kernel size does not state which partition its fitness was computed on. Fitness is described as evaluated 'across folds' although no cross-validation scheme is defined elsewhere.

Confidence intervals of plus or minus 0.4 percentage points are reported on test sets as small as 68 images, where one image is worth 1.47 points and an exact binomial interval around 95% spans roughly 87% to 99%. No chance or trivial baseline; no positive predictive value at any realistic prevalence despite an assembled 1:1 ratio.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: A deep attention architecture with metaheuristic hyperparameter search trained on 951 images and evaluated on 68 in the video corpus. Image counts also overstate the effective sample, since the number of distinct children is unknown in both datasets.

Dataset URLs, preprocessing, exact split sizes, the leakage algorithm in pseudocode with thresholds and cluster sweep, the full training regime, hyperparameter bounds, hardware and software environment, and the metric definitions are all reported. The computational description is among the most complete in the corpus; what is missing is entirely on the human side.

A broad metric suite with curves and significance tests, and an internally consistent headline triple - but intervals narrower than a single test image, no chance baseline, no prevalence-adjusted predictive value, and no statement of how many runs underlie the reported means.
Both datasets public with URLs given; code on GitHub and archived on Zenodo with a DOI and a version tag. Among the strongest availability records in this review.

No ethics statement, no institutional approval and no consent statement anywhere in the paper, for a study trained on identifiable photographs and video frames of children scraped from personal websites, Facebook pages and YouTube. Funding, competing interests, author contributions and generative-AI use are all declared, so the omission is specific to human-subjects considerations.

Computational cost is named, the absence of clinical validation of the Grad-CAM heatmaps is stated in the authors' own voice with a concrete remedy, and the ablation admits that the paper's own multiscale contribution underperforms without the hyperparameter search. But the provenance confound, the absent reference standard, the missing demographics and the implausible intervals are all unmentioned, and the conclusion tells clinicians that the highlighted facial traits 'indicate the condition'.

included_articles.title: Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]
included_articles.abstract: This study aims to leverage a promising avenue for the precise and early detection of Autism. Autism is a multifaceted neurodevelopmental condition marked by challenges in social interaction, communication, and repetitive behaviors. Traditional diagnosis relies on time-consuming behavioral assessments, necessitating reliable and non-intrusive biomarkers for early and accurate detection. This paper analyzes eleven linear and non-linear features across time and frequency domains from an EEG dataset. Four neural network models, such as convolutional neural network (CNN), deep neural network (DNN), long short-term memory (LSTM), and a custom neural network are employed for classification. The CNN achieves the lowest accuracy at 89.02%, while the custom neural network reaches the highest accuracy at 94.02%, and the DNN and LSTM achieve 91.98% and 93.83% accuracy, respectively. Other metrics such as precision, recall, specificity, and F1-score, are also evaluated. This research underscores the efficacy of neural network in detecting Autism, advancing diagnostic tools.
included_articles.authors: Hasan et al.

assessments.support: Seventeen participants - 13 autistic and 4 typically developing boys - with a comparison group too small to characterise typical EEG variation, no age distribution by group across a 9-to-16 window in which EEG spectra change substantially, no cognitive, comorbidity or medication information, and an all-male sample.

The acquisition chain is fully specified - 16-channel g.tec montage with named electrode positions, ground and reference, 0.1-60 Hz bandpass with 60 Hz notch, 256 Hz sampling - and both groups were recorded on the same equipment under the same resting protocol, so no acquisition asymmetry arises. But no artefact rejection is described, the eleven features are not individually identified, and medication effects on EEG are unrecorded.

No diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician qualification or date is described for the autistic group, and no screening procedure for the four comparison children; the labels are inherited from the source corpus with none of its documentation transmitted.

No train-test split, cross-validation scheme or partitioning unit is stated anywhere. With 17 participants the reported 89-94% must derive from epoch-level evaluation, and with four controls a participant-disjoint arrangement is barely constructible; the number and distribution of segments are not reported.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias. The acquisition is the study's strength and is reported unusually well - a 16-channel g.tec montage with every electrode position, ground and reference named, 0.1-60 Hz bandpass filtering with a 60 Hz notch, 256 Hz sampling, and both groups recorded on the same equipment under the same resting protocol, so the acquisition asymmetry that undermines several branches of this review does not arise. Everything downstream is unreported or too small. The sample is 13 autistic and 4 typically developing boys, giving a participant-level majority-class baseline of 76.5% that is never stated; accuracies of 89.02% to 94.02% cannot be computed over 17 people, so they must derive from EEG epochs, and no train-test split, cross-validation scheme, partitioning unit or segment count appears anywhere in the paper. With four controls, a participant-disjoint evaluation would place at most one control in any held-out set, so the natural reading is that epochs from the same children span the partition - the failure this review has documented in four other modalities. No diagnostic ascertainment is described for either group, no age distribution is given across a range in which EEG spectra mature substantially, medication is unrecorded, and there is no limitations section. The ethics declaration states without qualification that neither a human-rights statement nor informed consent is required.

included_articles.title: Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play
included_articles.abstract: Background Play is an indispensable and meaningful activity in children’s daily life. Research has shown that autistic children often exhibit differences in play development. The core traits of autism, such as distinct patterns in social interaction and communication, focused interests, and repetitive behaviors, frequently manifest in their play. Therefore, play may serve as an insightful measure of these differences. Unlike previous studies focusing on play behaviors only, we explored other behaviors associated with autism during free play, and constructed a clinical prediction model for effectively screening autistic children. Methods Participants, including 123 autistic children and 123 neurotypical children aged 1–6 years, engaged in a 1.5-min free play with fixed toys, which was videotaped. A novel behavior-coding scheme was used to code these videos for 19 autistic behaviors, including play. The coding details of the 19 behaviors were then converted and expanded to 81 digital behavior indicators, including counts, duration, and proportion. Results The autistic children showed less functional play and imaginative play and reduced social communication and interactions, such as eye contact, facial expressions, and vocalizations, compared to the neurotypical children during free play. Furthermore, 5 behavioral indicators were selected for the prediction model through stepwise logistic regression, including 1 on socially oriented vocalizations and 4 on count and duration of functional play. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve revealed a good prediction performance with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.826, a sensitivity of 85.4%, and a specificity of 68.3%. Conclusion Our findings highlight differences in play performance and social communication and interactions during free play among autistic children. Based on these findings, we constructed a good clinical prediction model, which might be a potential digital tool used by clinicians to effectively screen autistic children.
included_articles.authors: Liu Q; Ma Z; Jin Y; He R; Su X; Chen J; Yin T; Cheng J; Guo Y; Li X; Liu J

assessments.support: A matched case-control design with autistic children drawn from a hospital and intervention service centres and comparison children from a kindergarten, so recruitment route differs by group. Children with any other psychiatric diagnosis, major physical or neurological disease or prior psychotropic medication were excluded, and 23 clinically diagnosed children scoring below CARS-2 30 were removed - truncating the spectrum at precisely the point where screening is most difficult. The authors state this themselves and connect it to performance inflation. Age and sex are matched and formally tested, which is better than most of this corpus, and the 1:1 ratio is a design artefact rather than a prevalence.

The task instruction is verbatim and tightly constrained, the toy set is fixed, and the coding manual is supplied in full, with three coders trained over a month and inter-coder consistency of 83.7-91.7% on 30 shared cases. But every one of the 81 indicators originates in a human judgement, coder blinding to group is not stated, and the recording contexts differ by recruitment route, so group membership may be inferable from a video independently of the behaviours scored. Five predictors were selected from 81 candidates and the operating cut-off chosen from the same ROC curve.

Best-estimate clinical diagnosis by senior child and adolescent psychiatrists under DSM-5, corroborated by CARS-2 with the instrument's published psychometrics cited. This is genuine clinical ascertainment by qualified clinicians and among the strongest reference standards in the review. The severity restriction it was combined with is captured under patient selection rather than here.

All 246 children completed the task and contributed one indicator vector each; the 23 exclusions are accounted for with their reason and occurred before the analysis. Diagnosis preceded the play task and was independent of it. The unit of analysis is the child throughout, so no within-participant leakage is possible. No recordings are reported lost or excluded for quality.

risk_of_bias.summary: Unclear rather than high risk of bias, which places this study among the small group in the review whose principal weakness is analytic optimism rather than a broken foundation. The clinical work is done properly: diagnosis by senior child and adolescent psychiatrists as a DSM-5 best-estimate judgement corroborated by CARS-2, comparison children matched on age and sex with the tests reported, comorbidity and medication excluded rather than ignored, a verbatim task instruction, a fixed toy set, three coders trained for a month against a published manual with inter-coder consistency of 83.7-91.7% verified on 30 shared cases, and the whole coding guide supplied as supplementary material. Reporting is correspondingly full - AUC with a confidence interval, sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, a calibration curve, a goodness-of-fit test, and odds ratios with intervals for every candidate indicator at both analysis stages. The performance claimed is modest and credible: AUC 0.826, sensitivity 85.4%, specificity 68.3%. Two problems bound it. The five predictors were selected from 81 candidates and the operating threshold read off the same ROC curve, all on the 246 children whose data then supply the reported performance, and although a bootstrap was run no optimism-corrected estimate appears - so the headline figures are apparent rather than validated. And the autistic group was restricted to CARS-2 at or above 30, removing 23 clinically diagnosed children from the milder end, which the authors identify explicitly with the correct inference that performance may therefore be overestimated. Both problems push in the same known direction and neither is concealed.

extracted_data.intervention: Not reported

items.notes: Twenty-three clinically diagnosed children scoring below CARS-2 30 were excluded, restricting the autistic group to at least moderate severity. The authors state that this may have produced selection bias toward more pronounced characteristics and that model performance may consequently be overestimated - the clearest self-identification of spectrum truncation in this review.

Kindergarten-recruited typically developing children, deliberately matched on age and sex with both tests reported - considerably better than the convenience controls typical of this corpus. But no non-autistic clinical comparison group exists, which the authors identify as the harder and more clinically relevant contrast, and the recruitment route differs systematically by group.

Age and sex matched and tested; comorbidity, neurological disease and psychotropic medication excluded by criterion. But no cognitive or language measure was obtained, although the strongest predictor is duration of socially directed speech, and age is matched at the mean without being adjusted for in a 1-to-6-year sample where four of five predictors are play-quantity measures and the group age variances differ (SD 9.9 against 13.5).

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: All 246 included children completed the task and contributed complete indicator vectors; the 23 exclusions are stated with their reason and occurred before analysis. No missing data or lost recordings are reported.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: DSM-5 best-estimate clinical diagnosis by senior child and adolescent psychiatrists, corroborated by CARS-2 with published psychometrics cited. Genuine clinical ascertainment, among the strongest in the review.

The task, toy set and coding scheme were fully prespecified and directional hypotheses stated in advance, including the confirmed prediction that repetitive behaviours would not differ. But the five model predictors were selected from 81 candidates post hoc and the operating cut-off chosen from the ROC curve.

Verbatim instruction reproduced in the paper including the examiner's constrained response rule, a fixed toy set with defined categories, a standard rapport-building preamble, and a 90-second duration applied identically to every child.

Diagnosis was established before and independently of the play task, but coder blinding to group is not stated - and with autistic children recruited from clinical services and controls from a kindergarten, group membership may be inferable from the recordings. This matters more here than in automated studies, since all 81 indicators pass through human judgement.

The unit of analysis is the child throughout with one vector each, so no within-participant leakage is possible. But there is no held-out set, no cross-validation and no external cohort - the model is fitted and evaluated on the same 246 children.

Five predictors selected from 81 candidates by group-difference testing, univariate regression and stepwise regression on the full sample, with performance reported on that same sample. A bootstrap was run but no optimism-corrected AUC is reported, and the stepwise criterion is unstated.

AUC with a confidence interval, sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, calibration curve and goodness-of-fit test - the fullest reporting in the behavioural branch. But the cut-off was chosen from the same ROC curve, and predictive values are quoted at the matched 50% prevalence with no recalculation for a screening base rate, which is the figure the paper's own screening proposal depends on.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: One hundred and twenty-three events for five final predictors is comfortable, but 81 candidates entered the selection process, which is where the optimism arises. The authors describe the sample as small for prediction-model development and call for more data.

Recruitment sources and window, full eligibility criteria, diagnostic procedure and threshold with the count excluded by it, matched demographics with tests, verbatim task instruction, toy categories, the coder training programme with experience range, duration and the inter-coder reliability check and its formula, all 19 behaviour definitions in a supplementary guide, and all 81 indicator definitions. Missing: coding and statistical software, stepwise criterion, bootstrap resample count.

AUC with interval, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, calibration curve, Hosmer-Lemeshow, density plots, and odds ratios with confidence intervals and p-values for every indicator at both stages. The gap is the absent optimism-corrected estimate rather than the presentation.

Anonymised data from the corresponding author on request, restricted by data protection and the consent text; the full coding guide is supplied as supplementary material, which is the more useful disclosure for replication. No code, no software named, no preregistration - though directional hypotheses were stated in the introduction.

Institutional ethics approval, Declaration of Helsinki conformity, and written informed consent from primary caregivers before the study. No funding received. Competing interests declared at the level of individual authors, with six of eleven declaring two patent applications arising from this research; four authors are affiliated with a commercial autism-services company, which is visible in the affiliations but not itself discussed.

Five limitations enumerated, including task brevity, sex imbalance, the CARS-2 severity restriction with its explicit consequence that performance may be overestimated, small sample for model development, and the absence of a non-autistic clinical comparison group. Selection optimism from choosing five predictors out of 81 is the notable omission.

included_articles.title: Predictive model using autism
included_articles.abstract: Predictive model using autism diagnostic observation schedule, second edition for differential diagnosis between schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder Dan Nakamura 1,2*, Yoichi Hanawa 1, Shizuka Seki 1, Misato Yamauchi 1, Yuriko Iwami 1, Yuta Nagatsuka 1, Hirohisa Suzuki 1,2, Keisuke Aoyagi 1, Wakaho Hayashi 1, Takeshi Otowa 3,4 and Akira Iwanami 1,2 1Department of Psychiatry, Showa University School of Medicine, Tokyo, Japan, 2Department of Psychiatry, Showa University Karasuyama Hospital, Tokyo, Japan, 3Department of Psychiatry, Teikyo University School of Medicine, Tokyo, Japan, 4Department of Psychiatry, Teikyo University Hospital, Tokyo, Japan
included_articles.authors: Nakamura D; Hanawa Y; Seki S; Yamauchi M; Iwami Y; Nagatsuka Y; Suzuki H; Aoyagi K; Hayashi W; Otowa T; Iwanami A

assessments.support: Both groups recruited consecutively from the same hospital's outpatient and inpatient services with matched age, sex and education - removing the recruitment asymmetry that affects nearly every other case-control study in this review. But eligibility required IQ above 85 in both groups and excluded comorbidity from both, plus severe positive symptoms from the schizophrenia group, so the sample is the diagnostically clean end of a problem defined by diagnostic ambiguity. The two groups were also recruited in non-overlapping windows about two years apart.

ADOS-2 Module 4 administered by research-certified psychiatrists following a published protocol with published coding criteria - the most standardised behavioural measurement in the review, and the published algorithms were applied at their published cut-offs without modification. But administrator blinding to the established diagnosis is not stated and is unlikely given the setting, every item code is a clinician judgement, and no within-study inter-rater reliability was computed at the item level on which the analysis depends. The six-item model was selected from 32 candidates on the full sample.

DSM-5 consensus diagnosis by several psychiatrists with extensive experience in both conditions, drawing on assessment interactions and full psychiatric and medical history, with the explicit statement that neither ADOS-2 nor ADI-R contributed to it. The deliberate independence of reference standard from index test is what makes the study's central finding interpretable.

All 90 participants received both the reference standard and the index test, with diagnosis preceding ADOS-2 administration in every case. No attrition or indeterminate results are reported. The unit of analysis is the participant throughout and the holdout split partitions participants, so no leakage is possible.

risk_of_bias.summary: Unclear risk of bias overall, with the reference standard and flow both low and the residual concerns concentrated in blinding and in the selection of the six-item model. The design answers the question this review has repeatedly found unaddressed: both groups are clinical, drawn from the same Tokyo hospital service, matched on age, sex and education, and diagnosed by consensus among expert psychiatrists under DSM-5 - with ADOS-2 and ADI-R deliberately excluded from that diagnostic process, so the index test is independent of the label it predicts. The central result is negative and does not depend on any model the authors fitted: applied as published by research-certified administrators, the ADOS-2 Module 4 original and revised algorithms misclassified 45.0% and 52.5% of adults with schizophrenia as autistic and achieved AUCs of 0.562 and 0.569, with no domain score carrying predictive value. The explanatory analysis then shows that ADOS-2 positivity in schizophrenia tracks PANSS negative-symptom severity and is predicted by that scale alone. The study's own six-item model reached an apparent AUC of 0.938 and 86.6% accuracy but fell to 65.3% under holdout validation, and the authors report the drop and attribute it to fitting six variables in a sample of ninety. What limits the study is that administrator blinding is not addressed while every input is a clinician judgement made after diagnosis was known; that item-level inter-rater reliability was never established although the instrument's published reliability concerns algorithm totals; and that excluding comorbidity from both groups and severe positive symptoms from the schizophrenia group removes precisely the ambiguous presentations in which differential diagnosis is difficult.

extracted_data.intervention: Not reported
extracted_data.comparator: 40 adults with DSM-5 schizophrenia (27 men, 13 women), mean age 33.53 years (SD 10.95), all with JART-estimated full-scale IQ above 85

items.notes: Consecutive clinical recruitment from one hospital's services for both groups, but restricted to full-scale IQ above 85 and to verbally fluent adults suitable for ADOS-2 Module 4, with comorbidity excluded from both groups and severe positive symptoms from the schizophrenia group. The diagnostically ambiguous and comorbid cases the model targets are exactly those excluded.

The comparison group is another clinical population recruited from the same service and matched on age, sex and education - the design this review has repeatedly identified as missing across the corpus, and the only instance of it among included studies.

Age, sex and education matched and tested; the schizophrenia group extensively characterised on symptom severity, medication and illness course. But intelligence was measured with different instruments in each group - a reading-based premorbid estimate against a directly administered full-scale IQ - and the authors state that the groups therefore cannot be compared on it, which matters because several discriminating items concern conversational structure and content.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: All 90 participants completed both the diagnostic process and the ADOS-2, with no attrition, indeterminate results or missing item codes reported.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Consensus DSM-5 diagnosis by several psychiatrists with extensive experience in both conditions, drawing on clinical interaction and full history, with ADOS-2 and ADI-R explicitly excluded from the process - deliberate independence from the index test, and the strongest reference-standard arrangement in the review for a study of this kind.

Both published algorithms were applied at their published cut-offs with no modification, which fully prespecifies the study's principal analysis. The six-item model, by contrast, was selected post hoc from 32 candidates on the full sample.

ADOS-2 Module 4 administered by research-certified psychiatrists following a published protocol of 15 prescribed activities over 40 to 60 minutes with published coding criteria for all 32 items - the most standardised behavioural measurement in the review.

Administrator blinding to the established diagnosis is nowhere stated, and both groups were recruited from the same service with diagnosis preceding assessment, so blinding is unlikely. Every index-test input is a clinician's ordinal judgement, and no within-study inter-rater reliability was computed at item level.
The unit is the participant throughout, each contributing one set of item codes, and the holdout split partitions participants. No form of within-participant leakage is possible.

Six items selected from 32 candidates on the full sample, with the apparent accuracy and AUC computed from that same sample and whether selection was repeated inside the training split unstated. The authors identify the resulting overfitting explicitly.

Both training and test accuracies reported (85.4% and 65.3%); AUC interpretive bands prespecified; DeLong's test for the paired ROC comparison; odds ratios with confidence intervals throughout; and the baseline is the instrument's own published algorithms on the same participants rather than a nominal chance line. The abstract nonetheless presents the apparent AUC of 0.938 without the held-out figure attached.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Six binary predictors selected from 32 candidates in a sample of 90. The authors state this directly: 'The model had six variables, which was a large number compared to the number of samples; hence, the AUC may have increased due to overfitting.' Sample size was justified against a comparable prior study rather than by power calculation.

Site, separate recruitment windows, full eligibility criteria for both groups, the diagnostic procedure with the explicit exclusion of ADOS-2 and ADI-R, the complete battery per group, the module with activity count and duration and both algorithms' cut-offs, the item dichotomisation rule with a worked psychometric justification, significance thresholds including a stricter alpha for correlations, and the statistical software with version. Missing: blinding, item-level reliability, and the holdout split proportions.

Sensitivity, specificity and explicit false-positive rates for both algorithms; AUCs against prespecified bands with DeLong's test; odds ratios with confidence intervals for every domain and item; non-zero proportions for all 32 items with tests; and both holdout accuracies. The one presentational fault is that the abstract carries the apparent AUC without the held-out figure.

Contributions stated to be in the article and supplementary material with further inquiries to the corresponding author. No code, no data deposit, no preregistration - though a sample size justification by reference to a prior comparable study is provided.

Medical Ethics Committee approval at Showa University School of Medicine, Declaration of Helsinki conformity, and written informed consent from the adult participants themselves rather than through proxies. No financial support of any kind and no competing interests declared.

Four limitations stated, including the incomparability of the two intelligence instruments and - the notable one - an explicit account of the holdout accuracy drop with overfitting named as the cause and external validation stated as the requirement. Blinding and item-level reliability are the omissions.

included_articles.title: The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech
included_articles.abstract: EDITED BY Ashad Kabir, Charles Sturt University, Australia REVIEWED BY Chiranjibi Sitaula, The University of Melbourne, Australia Delaram Sadeghi, Islamic Azad University of Mashhad, Iran *CORRESPONDENCE Najla D. This is an open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY). The use, distribution or reproduction in other forums is permitted, provided the original author(s) and the copyright owner(s) are credited and that the original publication in this journal is cited, in accordance with accepted academic practice. No use, distribution or reproduction is permitted which does not comply with these terms. The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech Najla D. Al Futaisi 1*, Björn W. Schuller 1,2, Fabien Ringeval 3 and Maja Pantic 4 1GLAM – Group on Language, Audio & Music, Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom, 2Chair of Embedded Intelligence for Health Care and Wellbeing, University of Augsburg, Augsburg, Germany, 3Grenoble INP, LIG, University Grenoble Alpes, Inria, CNRS, Grenoble, France, 4iBUG – Intelligent Behaviour Understanding Group, Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom Early detection is crucial for managing incurable disorders, particularly autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Unfortunately, a considerable number of individuals with ASD receive a late diagnosis or remain undiagnosed. Speech holds a critical role in ASD, as a signiﬁcant number of affected individuals experience speech impairments or remain non-verbal. To address this, we use speech analysis for automatic ASD recognition in children by classifying their speech as either autistic or typically developing. However, due to the lack of large labelled datasets, we leverage two smaller datasets to explore deep transfer learning methods. We investigate two ﬁne-tuning approaches: (1) Discriminative Fine-Tuning (D-FT), which is pre-trained on a related dataset before being tuned on a similar task, and (2) Wav2Vec 2.0 Fine-Tuning (W2V2- FT), which leverages self-supervised speech representations pre-trained on a larger, unrelated dataset. We perform two distinct classiﬁcation tasks: (a) a binary task to determine typicality, classifying speech as either that of a typically developing (TD) child or an atypically developing (AD) child; and (b) a four-class diagnosis task, which further classiﬁes atypical cases into ASD, dysphasia (DYS), or pervasive developmental disorder-not otherwise speciﬁed (NOS), alongside TD. This research aims to improve early recognition strategies, particularly for individuals with ASD. The ﬁndings suggest that transfer learning methods can be a valuable tool for autism recognition from speech. For the typicality classiﬁcation task (TD vs. AD), the D-FT model achieved the highest test UAR (94.8%), outperforming W2V2-FT (91.5%). In the diagnosis task (TD, ASD, DYS, NOS), D-FT also demonstrated superior performance (60.9% UAR) compared to W2V2-FT (54.3%). These results highlight the potential of transfer learning for speech-based ASD recognition and underscore the challenges of multi-class classiﬁcation with limited labeled data.
included_articles.authors: Al Futaisi ND; Schuller BW; Ringeval F; Pantic M

assessments.support: Two convenience corpora assembled for other purposes. One contains only autistic children with no control group; the other contains clinical and typical groups recorded in different physical settings. Participant counts are internally inconsistent - 64 typically developing children are claimed within a corpus stated to have 67 participants in total, leaving three for all three atypical classes - and per-class child counts are never given. No age distribution, cognitive level, language ability or socioeconomic information is reported for any group.

Raw audio from unspecified recording equipment under unspecified conditions, with no acoustic normalisation or channel compensation reported, in a corpus where the two binary classes were recorded in different physical environments. No task or elicitation is described for either corpus, so the prosodic signal cannot be separated from differences in what the children were doing.

Labels inherited from the source corpora with no diagnostic procedure, instrument, criteria or clinician qualification described for either. The CPSD categories are pre-DSM-5, PDD-NOS having been eliminated in 2013, so the four-class task reproduces a superseded nosology. The typically developing group is defined only by absence of prior difficulties.

Partition sizes are reported completely for all classes and all evaluation sets, splitting is speaker-disjoint with the rationale stated, a development partition is maintained separately from test, and minority-class upsampling is confined to training with evaluation distributions left intact - all better than the corpus norm. But the development-to-test inversion (78.0% against 94.8%) is unexplained, the number of speakers per class is unknown, and no uncertainty estimate accompanies any figure.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias, arising almost entirely from the data rather than from the analysis - a pattern this review has now seen twice, and one worth stating carefully because the analytic work here is above the corpus norm. The splitting is speaker-disjoint and the reason is articulated precisely, in language sharper than most papers manage: samples from each child belong to one fold only, to stop the model 'learning speaker or recording idiosyncrasies, and therefore deceptively excelling'. A development partition is kept separate from test, unweighted average recall is the primary metric, minority-class upsampling is confined to training while evaluation distributions are deliberately left intact, results are benchmarked against a stated baseline and against published work on the same corpus, and equalised-odds fairness testing is performed on held-out gender partitions. That fairness analysis produces the study's most important finding and undermines its own headline: D-FT sensitivity falls from 94.8% pooled to 43.6% for girls and 61.5% for boys. Against this, three data problems bound what any figure means. The corpus on which both tasks are trained and tested recorded its atypical children in clinics and its typically developing children in schools - a recording-environment confound perfectly aligned with the binary label, stated in the paper's own dataset description, never revisited, and unmitigated by any reported normalisation; speaker-disjoint splitting offers no protection against a confound that operates at the class level. The participant counts are mutually incompatible and the number of children per diagnostic class is never stated, so the protective value of speaker disjointness cannot be assessed. And no diagnostic procedure is described for either corpus, whose categories predate DSM-5.

extracted_data.study_design: Retrospective algorithm-development study on two existing child speech corpora, with binary and four-class classification tasks, transfer-learning comparison, equalised-odds fairne…
extracted_data.sample_size: ASD/index: ; comparison: 1,109 typically developing samples in CPSD. The paper states the control group 'consists of 64 Typically Developing children (TD), 52 of which are males and 12 females'.
extracted_data.intervention: Not reported
extracted_data.comparator: 1,109 typically developing samples in CPSD. The paper states the control group 'consists of 64 Typically Developing children (TD), 52 of which are males and 12 females'.

items.notes: Convenience corpora collected for other purposes, one with no control group at all. Ages 4-18 with no distribution reported, no cognitive or language measure, and participant counts that cannot be reconciled between sections.

The four-class task includes dysphasia and PDD-NOS as non-autistic clinical comparison groups - a design almost absent from this review and its principal merit. But the binary comparison group was recorded in schools while the clinical groups were recorded in clinics, so the contrast confounds diagnosis with recording setting.

No age data by group in a corpus spanning 6-18 years, across which voice changes fundamentally; no language measure although one class is a language disorder; no control or normalisation for recording environment, which differs systematically by class. Sex is the one confounder taken seriously, through fairness testing, and the models fail that test substantially.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Complete partition tables are given for every class and every evaluation set. But no per-class participant counts, no account of excluded or unusable recordings, and no sample-duration statistics.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Diagnoses inherited from source corpora with no procedure, instrument or criteria described, using pre-DSM-5 categories. The typically developing group is defined by absence of reported difficulties rather than by assessment.

Two architectures compared on identical folds with a separate development partition and a prespecified primary metric. Hyperparameters and the number of runs are not reported, and no uncertainty estimate accompanies any figure.

No recording equipment, sampling rate, acoustic condition or preprocessing chain reported for either corpus, and the two binary classes were recorded in different physical settings with no normalisation or channel compensation applied. No task or elicitation is described.
Classification is fully automated from audio; no human rater is involved at inference.

Speaker-disjoint splitting with the rationale stated explicitly, and a separate development partition - among the best-articulated splitting practice in the review. But the number of speakers per class is unknown, and speaker disjointness cannot address the class-level recording-setting confound.

Representations are learned; minority-class upsampling is applied to training only, with development and test distributions deliberately left unchanged 'to be representative of real-world' - a correct and explicitly reasoned choice that very few papers in this corpus make.

Unweighted average recall as primary metric, full metric suite across all partitions, confusion matrices, subgroup sensitivity and specificity, and benchmarking against a stated baseline and prior work on the same corpus - including a table showing the study's own four-class result below both. No confidence intervals or run-to-run variance.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Deep transformer models fine-tuned on 62 minutes of labelled audio, with the four-class test partition containing 26 samples per clinical class from an unstated and possibly very small number of children. The authors acknowledge that the test sets are small and 'not fully representative of the real-world'.

Complete partition tables, split proportions, splitting rule with rationale, both architectures with their pre-training corpora, the resampling policy, the metric, and the fairness procedure with formulae. Missing: code, hyperparameters, sample durations, recording conditions, per-class participant counts, age distributions, and any diagnostic procedure.

Every model reported on every partition with four metrics plus confusion matrices, and benchmarked against baseline and prior work - including where the study loses. But no confidence intervals, no variance across runs, and no significance testing, on margins as small as 0.7 points and test sets as small as 26 samples per class.
Neither corpus is openly available and no code is released. Contributions are stated to be in the article and supplementary material with inquiries to the corresponding author.

Approval attributed to the dataset administrations rather than a named research ethics committee, and consent stated as not required for participants or guardians - in a study of recorded child speech, and in a paper whose own introduction reflects at length on ethics committees as safeguards for exactly this kind of data. No funding and no competing interests declared.

Six limitations stated in detail, including the abandonment of the study's original younger-age aim, domain shift between corpora, class and gender imbalance with the fairness consequence spelled out, small test sets, and an explicit caution that the headline UAR must be interpreted against the corpus's specific characteristics. The clinic-versus-school recording confound is the significant omission.
