included_articles.title: Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism
included_articles.abstract: Background: The increasing use of social media platforms has given rise to an unprecedented surge in user-generated content, with millions of individuals publicly sharing their thoughts, experiences, and health-related information. Social media can serve as a useful means to study and understand public health. Twitter (subsequently rebranded as “X”) is one such social media platform that has proven to be a valuable source of rich information for both the general public and health officials. We conducted the first study applying Twitter data mining to autism screening. Objective: We aimed to study the feasibility of autism screening from Twitter data and discuss the ethical implications of such models. Methods: We developed a machine learning model to attempt to distinguish individuals with autism from their neurotypical peers based on the textual patterns from their public communications on Twitter. We collected 6,515,470 tweets from users’ self-identification with autism using “#ActuallyAutistic” and a separate control group. To construct the data set, we targeted English-language tweets using the search query “#ActuallyAutistic” posted from January 1, 2014 to December 31, 2022. We encrypted all user IDs and stripped the tweets of identifiable information such as the associated email address prior to analysis. From these tweets, we identified unique users who used keywords such as “autism” OR “autistic” OR “neurodiverse” in their profile description and collected all the tweets from their timelines. To build the control group data set, we formulated a search query excluding the hashtag “#ActuallyAutistic” and collected 1000 tweets per day during the same time period. We trained a word2vec model and an attention-based, bidirectional long short-term memory model to validate the performance of per-tweet and per-profile classification models. We deleted the data set and the models after our analysis. Results: Our tweet classifier reached a 73% accuracy, a 0.728 area under the receiver operating characteristic curve score, and an 0.71 F1-score using word2vec representations fed into a logistic regression model, while the user profile classifier achieved an 0.78 area under the receiver operating characteristic curve score and an F1-score of 0.805 using an attention-based, bidirectional long short-term memory model. Conclusions: We have shown that it is feasible to train machine learning models using social media data to predict use of the #ActuallyAutistic hashtag, an imperfect proxy for self-reported autism. While analyzing textual differences in naturalistic text has the potential to help clinicians screen for autism, there remain ethical questions that must be addressed for such research to move forward and to translate into the real world. While machine learning has the potential to improve behavioral research, there are still a plethora of ethical issues in digital phenotyping studies using social media with respect to user consent of marginalize
included_articles.authors: Jaiswal A; Washington P

assessments.support: The positive class is a self-selected online community defined by use of a specific advocacy hashtag plus profile keywords; the negative class is a daily sample of general English-language Twitter. No demographic information exists for either group, the two classes were assembled by different sampling procedures (full timeline harvesting against daily sampling), and the platform's user base is skewed by age, language, geography and socioeconomic status - all acknowledged by the authors.

Text is naturally occurring, so there is no observation effect or task artefact, and preprocessing is fully specified including a deliberate removal of the sixteen autism-related tokens that would otherwise leak the label. But heavy normalisation strips paralinguistic features, no feature analysis is reported, and the model may be detecting the register of an advocacy discourse rather than any property of autistic language.

Hashtag use plus profile keywords, with no clinical validation of any kind - stated by the authors as their first limitation and reflected in their own description of the target as 'use of the #ActuallyAutistic hashtag, an imperfect proxy for self-reported autism'. The negative label is unscreened membership of a background sample.

Splitting is at user level with the rationale stated, applied to both tasks, with separate validation and test partitions and a minimum-tweet threshold for the profile task. Corpus counts are reported completely by group, and the preprocessing chain and exclusion of the location field are described. No within-user leakage is possible.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias with respect to the diagnostic question, and simultaneously the most methodologically and ethically self-aware study in this review - a combination that requires stating both halves. The label is use of the #ActuallyAutistic hashtag, which the authors describe in their own conclusion as 'an imperfect proxy for self-reported autism', with no clinical validation for any of the 17,323 users so labelled and no screening of the 171,273 controls. The positive class is a self-selected advocacy community organised around a topic and the negative class is a background sample of the platform, so the two corpora differ in subject matter, audience, community membership and probably in age and sex, none of which is measurable. The two classes were also assembled differently - full timelines harvested for one, 1,000 tweets per day sampled for the other - so 17,323 users supply nearly as many tweets as 171,273. Against this, the analytic mechanics are among the better ones here. Splitting is at user level with the reasoning stated explicitly, validation and test partitions are separate, algorithm selection used cross-validation, and the sixteen autism-related tokens that define the label were deliberately removed from the text to prevent the task collapsing into a lookup. The performance obtained is correspondingly modest and is reported without inflation: 73% accuracy and AUC 0.728 at tweet level, AUC 0.78 at profile level. The authors then decline to treat this as a finding about autistic language, restrict legitimate use to population-level inference, enumerate the misuse scenarios an individual-level classifier would enable, and delete both the dataset and the models.

extracted_data.intervention: Not reported
extracted_data.comparator: 3,377,518 tweets from 171,273 users, obtained by a search query excluding #ActuallyAutistic and sampling 1,000 tweets per day across the same period

items.notes: A self-selected online advocacy community, English-only, on a platform skewed toward younger and higher-socioeconomic users, with no demographic information and no clinical ascertainment. The authors state the representativeness problem in these terms themselves.

A daily sample of general English-language Twitter, differing from the positive class in topic, community membership, posting motivation and sampling procedure as well as in putative autism status. The authors address only one contamination direction, bounding it at population prevalence.

No age, sex, ancestry or socioeconomic data for either group, and the #ActuallyAutistic community plausibly differs from a general platform sample on all of these. The one confound actively controlled is label-defining vocabulary, removed deliberately.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Corpus counts reported completely by group; the location field excluded with the reason given; a minimum-tweet threshold applied for the profile task and stated. Preprocessing is fully specified.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Hashtag use plus profile keywords with no clinical validation, and an entirely unscreened control group. Stated as the first limitation and reflected accurately in the paper's own conclusion.

The preprocessing chain, keyword-removal list, representations, model families, splitting rules and selection procedure are all specified in advance and reported in full. Algorithm selection used cross-validation with a separately held test partition.

Text is naturally occurring so there is no elicitation to standardise, and preprocessing is applied uniformly. But the two classes' material was gathered by different sampling procedures, and heavy normalisation removes paralinguistic features that may carry signal.
Classification is fully automated from text; no human rater is involved at any stage of labelling or inference.

User-level splitting for both tasks with the rationale articulated - among the clearest statements of the principle in this review - plus separate validation and test partitions and a minimum-tweet threshold for the aggregated task.

The sixteen autism-related tokens that define the label were removed a priori on substantive grounds, closing the target-leakage route that would otherwise have made the task trivial. Algorithm selection used 5-fold cross-validation with the test partition held out.

Accuracy, AUC and F1 reported for both tasks on near-balanced classes, with no inflation in how they are described. But no confidence intervals despite a corpus that would support tight ones, no calibration, and no positive predictive value at population prevalence - the figure that would demonstrate why the authors' own restriction to cross-sectional use is correct.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: 6.5 million tweets from 188,596 users, far exceeding what the model families require. Sample size is the one dimension on which this study exceeds every other in the review.

Scraping tool, both search queries with date range, group-definition criteria, control sampling rate, the full preprocessing chain, the complete keyword-removal list, sentiment tool, representations, model families, splitting rules and proportions for both tasks, and all corpus counts. The pipeline is reconstructible even though the corpus deliberately is not.

Accuracy, AUC and F1 for both classifiers, reported consistently across abstract, results and conclusion with no inflation. Missing: confidence intervals, calibration, operating-point sensitivity and specificity, and predictive value at realistic prevalence.

Dataset and models deliberately destroyed after analysis and never shared outside the author team, for stated ethical reasons; code not mentioned. Unavailability is a considered decision rather than an omission, and is explained.

IRB approval 2023-00248 under expedited review, a separate data-governance determination, and measures taken beyond regulatory requirement including encrypted user IDs and anonymised mentions and email addresses. Consent is treated as the primary limitation rather than as satisfied by the public-data exemption, engaged with substantively through the literature, and acted upon by destroying the data and models. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text.

Five limitations with developed reasoning, a self-imposed restriction of legitimate use to population level, explicit enumeration of misuse scenarios, and a closing caution against building comparable models without consent and participatory design. The group-definition confound is the substantive omission.

included_articles.title: Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children
included_articles.abstract: A timely diagnosis of autism is paramount to allow early therapeutic intervention in preschoolers. Deep Learning tools have been increasingly used to identify specific autistic symptoms. But they also offer opportunities for broad automated detection of autism at an early age. Here, we leverage a multi-modal approach by combining two neural networks trained on video and audio features of semi-standardized social interactions in a sample of 160 children aged 1 to 5 years old. Our ensemble model performs with an accuracy of 82.5% (F1 score: 0.816, Precision: 0.775, Recall: 0.861) for screening Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD). Additional combinations of our model were developed to achieve higher specificity (92.5%, i.e., few false negatives) or sensitivity (90%, i.e. few false positives). Finally, we found a relationship between the neural network modalities and specific audio versus video ASD characteristics, bringing evidence that our neural network implementation was effective in taking into account different features that are currently standardized under the gold standard ASD assessment.
included_articles.authors: Natraj S; Kojovic N; Maillart T; Schaer M

assessments.support: Both groups enrolled in the same longitudinal cohort, matched exactly on sex (48 male, 32 female each) and closely on age, with the comparison group actively screened for neurological and psychiatric conditions and for first-degree family history of autism. The 1:1 ratio is a design choice rather than a prevalence, and the sample skews young (1.1-5.1 years) and has no non-autistic clinical comparison group - but the selection itself is sound and the 40% female representation is the highest in the review.

Both groups recorded during the same ADOS protocol in the same setting, so acquisition context is matched across classes. The video representation strips appearance to skeletal keypoints on a black background, architecturally excluding identity and setting confounds. Audio was normalised across microphones to a common format. The 90% segment-confidence filter is a selection step whose effect is unquantified, and the undiarised audio band includes the examiner.

DSM-5 clinical criteria supported by gold-standard diagnostic assessment within an established clinical cohort - genuine ascertainment, and among the better standards in this review. But the specific instruments are deferred to supplementary material, and since the model input is the ADOS recording, whether ADOS also informed the diagnosis is the question that determines independence and is not answered.

All 160 children contributed recordings; the 50-50 split is participant-level and matched on age, sex and ADOS module; segments are nested strictly within participants so no within-participant leakage is possible; and all tuning was confined to an 80-20 division of the training half. No attrition or excluded recordings are reported.

risk_of_bias.summary: Low risk of bias overall - one of very few studies in this review to reach that rating, and instructive for exactly that reason. The design closes, by construction, the failure modes this synthesis has documented repeatedly elsewhere. Both groups were recorded under the same ADOS protocol in the same setting, so acquisition context cannot proxy for the label. The video input is rendered as skeletal keypoints on a black background, so appearance, identity, clothing, room and lighting are architecturally excluded rather than merely unexamined. The 160 children were split 50-50 at participant level with each half matched on age, sex and ADOS module, and all hyperparameter selection was confined to a validation partition carved from the training half, so the 80 test children are genuinely held out. Sex is exactly matched at 40% female in both groups. Diagnosis is DSM-5 clinical ascertainment within an established cohort. Ethics approval, written parental consent, separate consent for figure publication, six funding sources and competing interests are all declared; code is on GitHub and a de-identified pose subsample on Zenodo. The performance obtained under these conditions - 80.0% video, 78.8% audio, 82.5% ensemble - is modest and honestly reported, with a complete six-metric table for all five model variants. Two issues remain. No confidence intervals are given on an 80-child test set where a single case is worth 1.25 points, so the ensemble's two-child advantage over the video model alone is not resolvable. And because the model input is the ADOS session while the diagnosis was supported by unspecified gold-standard assessment, the independence of label from material is not established.

extracted_data.sample_size: ASD/index: ; comparison: 80 typically developing children (48 male, 32 female), mean age 2.46 +/- 0.98 years, screened for absence of known neurological or psychiatric conditions and for no history of autism in any first-degree relative
extracted_data.intervention: Not reported
extracted_data.comparator: 80 typically developing children (48 male, 32 female), mean age 2.46 +/- 0.98 years, screened for absence of known neurological or psychiatric conditions and for no history of autism in any first-degree relative

items.notes: Consecutive enrolment in an established longitudinal autism cohort over eleven years, ages 1.1-5.1 with no severity threshold applied, and a comparison group actively screened for neurological and psychiatric conditions and for first-degree family history.

Typically developing children matched on age and sex and assessed with the same ADOS protocol in the same setting - a better-matched comparison than any other included study on recording context. But no non-autistic clinical comparison group, so the harder discrimination is untested.

Sex matched exactly at 48 male and 32 female per group; age matched; the train-test split additionally matched on age, sex and ADOS module. Cognitive and language data are deferred to supplementary material rather than reported, and no sex-stratified analysis is run despite the sample uniquely supporting one.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: All 160 children contributed recordings and appear in the analysis; segment counts and total durations are reported for both partitions and both modalities. No losses reported. The 90% video-segment confidence filter is a post-hoc output selection whose effect on aggregate accuracy is not quantified.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: DSM-5 clinical criteria supported by gold-standard assessment in a clinical research cohort - substantively strong. But instruments are deferred to supplementary material, and independence from the ADOS recordings used as model input is not established.

Both architectures, segment lengths, aggregation rules and the three ensemble strategies are fully specified, with all tuning decisions confined to the training half's validation split. The decision tree's 60% threshold is reported explicitly.

Identical ADOS protocol and setting for both groups, audio normalised across microphones to a common format, video normalised to fixed-resolution skeletal renderings. Equipment varied across an eleven-year window but not by group.
Classification is fully automated from pose and audio with no human rater at inference; the interpretability analysis uses independently coded ADOS items.

Participant-level 50-50 split with each half matched on age, sex and ADOS module; segments nested strictly within participants so no within-participant leakage is possible despite tens of thousands of clips; validation carved from the training half only.

Segment lengths, MFCC count, batch size and epoch count all selected on the training half's validation partition, with the direction of observed overfitting reported. Test participants untouched throughout.

Complete six-metric table for all five model variants on a balanced test set, so chance is 50% and both operating extremes are reported. But no confidence intervals on 80 children, no positive predictive value at realistic prevalence in a paper framed around screening, and the abstract transposes precision with recall and specificity with sensitivity.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling

included_articles.title: Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning
included_articles.abstract: Affect recognition is currently an active research area for machine learning researchers. Researchers are paying more and more attention to the assessment and the classification of emotions in people with mental disorders in order to propose monitoring healthcare systems and then to better assist patients. In this paper, a supervised learning method to classify Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and to evaluate affect levels among autistic children is proposed. The use of methodologies for clinical patient monitoring and management is the focus of our research. YouTube video frames acquired in unconstrained environments and conditions of autistic children demonstrating typical autistic behaviors, as well as images of neurotypical people are used to evaluate the performance of the proposed approach. This paper also proposes an extended version of a dataset, including the additional affect labels corresponding to the affect levels of autistic children. Finally, experiments using different models were conducted to determine which architecture performed best. These experiments have shown very promising results for continuous affect recognition of children with ASD. Results show also that using a model that has only been trained on neurotypical subjects does not perform as great when the subjects are ASD children.

included_articles.title: A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features
included_articles.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a developmental impairment with brain abnormalities, characterized by social communication deficits and repetitive behavior patterns per recent diagnostic criteria. The Aberrant Behavior Checklist (ABC) is commonly used to analyze these behaviors and guide medication dosage. However, the short duration of ABC measurements may not accurately capture the full spectrum of ASD severity, such as mild, moderate, or severe, potentially leading to adverse drug effects. Therefore, continuous monitoring is necessary for accurate ASD classification to provide appropriate dosages. To address this challenge, a novel thermal imaging-based framework for ASD classification has been proposed, integrating continuous behavioral analysis to optimize medication dosage. The approach utilizes skin temperature and facial mood (FM) features extracted from thermal images. The Deep Network-based Facial Mood Extraction (DN-FME) model efficiently extracts facial mood features while mitigating high memory usage, computation speed issues, and overfitting. The DN-FME model demonstrated a performance accuracy of 96.39%, precision of 96.60%, recall of 96.53%, and an F1 score of 96.54%. For classification, features from skin temperature and facial moods were analyzed using machine learning classifiers: Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN). The RF and SVM classifiers achieved an accuracy of 98.33%, while the KNN classifier achieved an accuracy of 90.00%. Unlike existing methods focusing mainly on severe ASD stages, this framework evaluates mild, moderate, and severe stages, demonstrating superior accuracy compared to traditional clinical assessments and observational techniques. This allows for more precise medication dosage adjustments for ASD children.

Skin temperature, the primary feature, was measured across outdoor play, classroom, dining and veranda settings with no ambient-temperature compensation, no environmental logging and no per-setting normalisation, so thermal environment and physical exertion are confounded with any physiological signal. Since severity is a fixed per-child attribute, identifying the child recovers the label. The 20 videos collected for real-time testing, which would have provided a held-out evaluation, are never analysed.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias in every domain, in a study whose proposed output is a psychiatric medication dosage for children. The modality choice is well argued - thermal imaging needs no illumination and, as the authors correctly observe, is unaffected by skin tone, which is a sensor-level answer to a fairness problem this review has documented in visible-spectrum facial analysis - and the signal-processing work is competent, with denoising evaluated against alternatives and the mood network's architecture supported by two proper ablations. None of that reaches the clinical claim. The evaluation is an 80-20 split over 1,500 images from 30 children, roughly 50 images each, with no participant-level partitioning described and no cross-validation; since severity is a fixed attribute of a child and thermal images of the same child in the same setting are near-duplicates, recognising the individual recovers the label, and a 98.33% three-class accuracy is the arithmetic of that arrangement rather than evidence of a thermal severity signature. Class sizes are unreported, so no baseline exists. Skin temperature was measured across outdoor and indoor settings without ambient compensation. Current medication, which alters thermoregulation and correlates with severity by construction, is unrecorded. All participants are male. There is no limitations section. And the ethics declaration reads in full: 'Ethical Approval. Not required.'

included_articles.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features
included_articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technology has recently shown promising results in detecting Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), but it faces significant challenges because it is still in early stages of development. This study proposes to use linguistic features in the detection of ASD using artificial intelligence. In order to systematically understand different AI model performances, two types of AI models have been explored and evaluated. Five classical ML models were used: logistic regression, Gaussian naive Bayes, random forests, k-nearest neighbors (K-NN), and support vector machines (SVMs), and two deep learning models were used: multilayer perceptron (MLP) and a convolutional neural network (CNN). All model development work is based on analyzing speech transcripts of 64 children total aged 3 to 6 from two data banks, CHILDES and ASDBank, including 30 children with ASD and 34 typically developing (TD) controls. The first step was to examine the annotations of the transcriptions, then extract various linguistic features from the texts. AI models were trained to determine whether a child has ASD based on the characteristics of the transcripts analyzed. There are three major findings of this study. First, neural network models will outperform classical models in ASD detection by around 5%-10%. The models multilayer perceptron and convolutional neural networks achieved 83% and 84% accuracy, respectively. Second, among the classical machine learning models, logistic regression, SVMs, K-NN, and random forests all achieved accuracies in the range 77%-80%, while Gaussian naive Bayes performed the worst by around 10%. Third, the linguistic feature with the highest importance in ASD detection is MLU, and the features MLU, MLT, rUtts, and rTNW show significant distinctions between age and gender demographics in addition to having high importance in ASD detection. Overall, this research recommends using deep learning for clinical applications of ASD detection.

Features are standard psycholinguistic quantities computed by documented rules against TalkBank's transcription guide, with count-based measures normalised as ratios to the investigator specifically to handle differing transcript lengths - careful handling of cross-corpus comparability. But session protocols differ in length, structure and investigator role across the four corpora, and half the features are ratios to that investigator's output; and the headline accuracies followed removal of features selected on the same data.

Diagnoses are inherited from established research archives whose contributing studies performed documented clinical ascertainment, so the labels are genuine - materially better than the folder-membership and hashtag labels elsewhere in this review. But this paper transmits no instrument, criteria, clinician qualification or date, and the typically developing designation for two corpora rests on their being collected from typically developing populations with no screening described.

Each child contributes one transcript and one feature vector, so the split unit is the person and no within-participant leakage is possible. The analytic mechanics are sound for the sample size: each child contributes one transcript and one feature vector so the split unit is the person, the evaluation is a 75/25 split repeated over 50 random draws with the number justified by a stated stability criterion, ROC curves carry a one-standard-deviation band, the features are named psycholinguistic constructs, and the preprocessing rules for reconciling transcription conventions across four corpora are documented in detail. The reported accuracies - 84% for a convolutional network, 83% for a multilayer perceptron, 77-80% for four classical models - are modest, benchmarked against prior work at 70-80%, and not inflated. What bounds the result is upstream. The top-ranked feature is mean length of utterance, a canonical index of expressive language development which the paper's own demographic analysis shows to be the only feature consistently increasing with age; no independent language or cognitive measure exists, and the age composition of the two diagnostic groups is never reported, so language delay and age cannot be separated from autism. Part of the typically developing class comes from two corpora containing no autistic children, so corpus of origin is partly correlated with class, and the four source protocols differ in session length, structure and investigator role while half the features are ratios to the investigator's output. Developmentally delayed children present in one corpus were deliberately excluded, discarding the non-autistic clinical comparison. included_articles.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning
included_articles.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) poses significant challenges in diagnosis due to its diverse symptomatology and the complexity of early detection. Atypical gait and gesture patterns, prominent behavioural markers of ASD, hold immense potential for facilitating early intervention and optimising treatment outcomes. These patterns can be efficiently and non-intrusively captured using modern computational techniques, making them valuable for ASD recognition. Various types of research have been conducted to detect ASD through deep learning, including facial feature analysis, eye gaze analysis, and movement and gesture analysis. In this study, we optimise a dual-stream architecture that combines image classification and skeleton recognition models to analyse video data for body motion analysis. The first stream processes Skepxels—spatial representations derived from skeleton data—using ConvNeXt-Base, a robust image recognition model that efficiently captures aggregated spatial embeddings. The second stream encodes angular features, embedding relative joint angles into the skeleton sequence and extracting spatiotemporal dynamics using Multi-Scale Graph 3D Convolutional Network(MSG3D), a combination of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs). We replace the ViT model from the original architecture with ConvNeXt-Base to evaluate the efficacy of CNN-based models in capturing gesture-related features for ASD detection. Additionally, we experimented with a Stack Transformer in the second stream instead of MSG3D but found it to result in lower performance accuracy, thus highlighting the importance of GCN-based models for motion analysis. The integration of these two streams ensures comprehensive feature extraction, capturing both global and detailed motion patterns. A pairwise Euclidean distance loss is employed during training to enhance the consistency and robustness of feature representations. The results from our experiments demonstrate that the two-stream approach, combining ConvNeXt-Base and MSG3D, offers a promising method for effective autism detection. This approach not only enhances accuracy but also contributes valuable insights into optimising deep learning models for gesture-based recognition. By integrating image classification and skeleton recognition, we can better capture both global and detailed motion patterns, which are crucial for improving early ASD diagnosis and intervention strategies.

assessments.support: Two convenience corpora with no demographic characterisation beyond age ranges of 4 to 12 and 3 to 7 years. No age distribution by group in a domain where gait matures rapidly across that span, no sex information in a domain where gait differs by sex, and no cognitive, language or comorbidity data. The DREAM non-spectrum class was discarded, converting that experiment into a discrimination among autism-related labels.

In the Gait dataset, one of ten walking trials per child was retained, selected 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation' - selection on the outcome, upstream of all modelling. Within each corpus both classes were recorded under matched conditions and the skeleton representation excludes appearance, which are genuine strengths, but the two corpora differ in sensor generation and joint coverage (25 full-body against 10 upper-body) and neither task protocol is described.

Labels inherited from both corpora with no instrument, criteria, clinician qualification or date reported for either. DREAM's three-level structure is collapsed by discarding one class, and the resulting distribution is described as biased but never quantified.

On the Gait dataset each child contributes exactly one sample, so cross-validation necessarily partitions children, with five complete cycles and dispersion reported - sound practice. On DREAM, 1,833 samples from 61 children were split without any participant-level partitioning described, leaving within-participant leakage unaddressed. No attrition is reported for either.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias, arising from the source data rather than from the analysis, with two features that partly offset it. The strengths are real: on the Gait Fullbody Dataset each child contributes exactly one sample so cross-validation necessarily partitions children, five complete cycles were run with mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation reported for every architecture, the software and hardware stack is specified to package version numbers, and the skeleton representation discards face, appearance, clothing, room and lighting by construction so the acquisition and identity confounds that dominate the photograph branch cannot operate. The architecture comparison yields a valuable negative result - six backbones span 2.2 percentage points on one dataset and 1.3 on the other, against a 25-point gap between datasets - showing that in this branch the data and not the model determine performance. Against this: the single modelled walking trial per child was selected from ten 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation', which is selection on the outcome and precedes everything the models do; the DREAM experiment uses 1,833 samples from 61 children with no participant-level partitioning described; neither corpus reports age composition by group or any sex information, in a domain where gait varies strongly with both; no sensitivity, specificity or confusion matrix is reported for any model; the headline 95.4% is a best-of-six selection on test folds of ten children; and the DREAM task discards the non-spectrum class, so its 70.19% is not an autism-versus-non-autism figure and its chance baseline is unknown.

included_articles.title: Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]
included_articles.abstract: Purpose The objective of this study is to identify the acoustic characteristics of cries of Typically Developing (TD) and Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) children via Deep Learning (DL) techniques to support clinicians in the early detection of ASD. Methods We used an existing cry dataset that included 31 children with ASD and 31 TD children aged between 18 and 54 months. Statistical analysis was applied to find differences between groups for different voice acoustic features such as jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio (HNR). A DL model based on Recursive Convolutional Neural Networks (R-CNN) was developed to classify cries of ASD and TD children. Results We found a statistical significant increase in jitter and shimmer for ASD cries compared to TD, as well as a decrease in HNR for ASD cries. Additionally, the DL algorithm achieved an accuracy of 90.28% in differentiating ASD cries from TD. Conclusion Empowering clinicians with automatic non-invasive Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools based on cry vocal bio­ markers holds considerable promise in advancing early detection and intervention initiatives for children at risk of ASD, thereby improving their developmental trajectories.
included_articles.authors: Laguna et al.

assessments.support: Sixty-two children from a single Iranian corpus, with sex matched exactly at 24:7 in both groups - a genuine strength - but a 4.8-month mean age difference untested and unadjusted in a period of rapid vocal maturation, no cognitive, language or comorbidity data, and no screening instrument described for the comparison group.

Recording settings differ sharply by group - 87.10% of autistic cries from autism centres against a comparison group split between health centres and homes - and all three analysed measures are sensitive to room acoustics and background noise, with harmonics-to-noise ratio directly indexing periodic-to-aperiodic energy. Two device classes were used with no level normalisation reported, and cry-eliciting causes also differ between groups. Partial standardisation (common format, 25 cm distance, quiet-environment exclusion) mitigates but does not remove this.

A four-stage procedure - GARS-2 parental questionnaire, DSM-5-based caregiver interview, direct observation by two doctoral-level child clinical psychologists, and independent confirmation by a child psychiatrist in a different setting. Independent second-clinician confirmation appears in almost no other study in this review, and the absence of ADOS is explained by the lack of an official Farsi version and listed as a limitation.

No test partition exists; the final model was selected as the best of 2,000 epochs on the validation set; and the evaluation unit is the cry instance with no participant-level splitting described, so with roughly six instances per child, cries from the same child fall on both sides of the boundary. Exclusion rules and per-child yields are reported clearly, but partition sizes and composition are not.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias, with a notably strong reference standard and a notably weak evaluation design. The diagnostic ascertainment is among the best in the review - GARS-2, a DSM-5-based caregiver interview, direct observation by two doctoral-level child clinical psychologists, and independent confirmation by a child psychiatrist working in a separate setting, with the absence of ADOS explained by the lack of an official Farsi translation and listed as a limitation. Sex is matched exactly at 24 boys and 7 girls per group, ethics approval and parental consent are documented, exclusion rules and per-child cry yields are reported, and the competing-interest declaration is the fullest in the corpus. The classification result nonetheless carries no information about performance on a new child: there is no test partition, the final model was chosen as the epoch with the best validation accuracy out of 2,000, and the evaluation unit is the cry instance with no participant-level split, so with roughly six cries per child from 62 children the network can identify a voice and recover its fixed label. The accompanying statistical comparison is more defensible - prespecified clinical measures, replicating a direction from prior cry research at p < 0.01 and p < 0.0001 - but faces three confounds the paper reports and does not adjust for: a 4.8-month mean age difference during rapid vocal maturation, an 87.10%-versus-54.84% imbalance in recording setting between autism centres and health centres in measures sensitive to room acoustics, and differing cry-eliciting causes between groups.

included_articles.title: Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm
included_articles.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental condition marked by social communication difficulties, re- stricted interests, and repetitive behaviors. Early and accurate diagnosis is critical for timely intervention and improved outcomes. Traditional diagnostic methods, which rely on clinical observations and assessments, can be subjective and time-consuming. This study introduces a novel approach to predicting ASD using a machine learning technique, specifically a Bayesian-optimized Ran- dom Forest classification algorithm. The proposed method uses a comprehensive dataset containing various behavioral, cognitive, and demographic features associated with ASD. The Optimized Random Forest with Bayesian approach is used to categorize indi- viduals into two groups: those who have ASD and those who do not. To develop this ensemble learning technique, multiple decision trees are used, and to achieve higher performance as well as better capability to generalize, the hyperparameters are optimized with Bayesian optimization. Preliminary analysis and comparison with existing databases substantiated the findings and revealed the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The Bayesian-optimized Random Forest classifier achieved an accuracy value of 0.9890. Such performance is highly promising and could enable increased use of machine learning methods in timely and accurate diagno- sis of ASD. The proposed approach provides recommendations for a verified diagnostic technique when implemented and creates a strong foundation for future investigations into the use of machine learning for identifying and supporting children with ASD. © 2025 The Authors. risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias, from the same closed-form target leakage documented for the other UCI-derived screening-table studies in this review, and made unusually visible here. The paper prints its complete feature list - 'A1 Score ... A10 Score, age, gender, ethnicity, jundice, austim, contry of res, used app before, result, age desc, relation, Class/ASD' - which contains the ten screening items, their sum ('result'), and the outcome that is that sum thresholded at the AQ-10 cut-off ('Class/ASD'). No feature-selection step removing the summed score is described. A model with access to either the items or their total recovers the label exactly, on any partition, and the reported 0.9890 accuracy is obtainable by a single decision stump. The analytic mechanics are otherwise adequate: one row per respondent so the split unit is the person, 5-fold cross-validation appropriate for 704 rows, a stated preprocessing and feature-engineering pipeline, and a reasonable classifier and optimiser. Only accuracy is reported - no precision, recall, specificity, AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval - and no class distribution is given, so the figure cannot be set against the 73.2% majority-class baseline the source dataset implies. No feature importance is presented, although Random Forest supplies it without cost and it would have exposed the dependence immediately. The single stated limitation, reliance on one dataset, names an external-validity concern while leaving the internal one untouched.

included_articles.title: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
included_articles.abstract: Article history: Received Mar 20, 2025 Revised Aug 8, 2025 Accepted Sep 1, 2025 This paper proposes a method for detecting autism spectrum disorders (ASD) through the analysis of facial and motor features using machine learning. The aim is to develop an algorithm for automatic ASD diagnosis based on spatiotemporal behavioral patterns. Traditional diagnostic methods rely on subjective expert observations, often delaying intervention. To address this, a hybrid convolutional neural network and long short-term memory (CNN+LSTM) model was employed. Convolutional layers extracted spatial features from video frames, while recurrent layers tracked temporal dynamics. Using MediaPipe face mesh, pose, and hands models, 1,639 parameters were obtained, including facial and pose coordinates, hand landmarks, mouth aspect ratio (MAR), and motion energy. The dataset comprised 100 children, aged 5–9 years (50 with ASD, 50 typically developing (TD)). Stratified cross-validation was applied to ensure subjectindependent evaluation. Results showed 90% accuracy on the training set, 85–90% on validation, and an area under the curve (AUC) greater than 0.90, confirming model stability. Data visualization highlighted significant differences in motor activity and emotional expression between groups. The proposed approach demonstrates the potential for robust and objective ASD detection. It can be applied in clinical and educational contexts to improve early diagnosis and timely intervention.

assessments.support: Fifty autistic and 50 typically developing children with no recruitment source stated, no age distribution by group across a 5-to-9 range, no cognitive or language characterisation, and a 32-percentage-point sex imbalance between groups (84% male against 52%) that is reported without adjustment or discussion.

Both groups recorded under an identical protocol in the same controlled environment with standardised lighting, fixed resolution and frame rate, and the landmark representation discards appearance, clothing, skin tone and background before modelling - genuine acquisition and confound control. But facial mesh geometry retains sex-linked morphology in a sample whose classes differ sharply by sex, no landmark-detection failure handling is reported, and camera distance and angle are unstated.

No diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician qualification, setting or date is given for the 50 children described as diagnosed with autism, and no screening procedure is described for the comparison group - in a prospective study that designed its own protocol and therefore had the opportunity to document ascertainment.

Subject-independent stratified 5-fold cross-validation with the mechanism and its anti-leakage purpose stated explicitly, class ratio preserved across folds, and four overfitting controls specified with their parameters. All 100 children contribute; no attrition is reported.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias overall, arising from selection and ascertainment rather than from analysis - and the study is worth recording carefully because its analytic and acquisition design are among the better ones in this review. Both groups were recorded under an identical purpose-built protocol in the same controlled environment, so the acquisition asymmetry that undermines the photograph, thermal and clinic-versus-school audio branches cannot operate; the landmark representation discards appearance, clothing, skin tone, lighting and background before any learning; the paradigm elicits social and motor behaviour actively in 8 to 10 minutes; and the validation is subject-independent stratified 5-fold cross-validation with data leakage named explicitly as the thing being prevented, supported by four regularisation controls each specified with its parameter. The reported 85-90% is modest, plausible and benchmarked against external comparators. Two problems nonetheless bound it. The autistic group is approximately 84% male while the comparison group is 52% male - a 32-percentage-point gap reported without adjustment - and the model's inputs are 468 facial mesh points and 75 body and hand landmarks that encode sex-linked morphology and posture, so a classifier separating boys from girls would produce these figures under perfectly subject-independent evaluation. And no diagnostic reference standard of any kind is described, so the label being predicted is undefined. There is also no ethics approval or consent statement for a prospective study recording over 16 hours of video of 100 children.

included_articles.abstract: Background: Gelotophobia, the fear of being laughed at, is a social anxiety condition that affects approximately 6% of neurotypical individuals and up to 45% of those with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This comorbidity can significantly impair the quality of life, particularly in adolescents with high-functioning ASD, where the prevalence reaches 41.98%. Accurate and automated detection tools could enhance early diagnosis and intervention. Objective: This study aimed to develop a deep learning–based diagnostic system that integrates facial emotion recognition with validated questionnaires to detect gelotophobia in individuals with or without ASD. Methods: The system was trained to identify ASD status using a balanced dataset of 2932 facial images (n=1466; 50% from individuals with ASD and n=1466; 50% from neurotypical individuals). The images were processed using the DeepFace library to extract facial features, which were then used as input for the deep learning classifier. After identifying ASD status, the same images were further analyzed using the pretrained DeepFace model to evaluate facial expressions for signs of gelotophobia. In cases where facial cues were ambiguous, the GELOPH<15> questionnaire, consisting of 15 items, was administered to confirm the diagnosis The system was fully implemented using the Python programming language. Deep learning models were developed using libraries such as PyTorch for training the multilayer perceptron classifier, while CUDA was used to accelerate computations on compatible graphics processing units. Additional libraries from the Python programming language, such as scikit-learn, NumPy, and Pandas, were used for preprocessing, model evaluation, and data manipulation. DeepFace was integrated using its Python application programming interface for facial recognition and emotion classification. Results: The dataset comprised 2932 facial images collected from platforms such as Kaggle and ASD-related websites, including 1466 (50%) images of children with ASD and 1466 (50%) images of neurotypical children. The dataset was split into 2653 (90.48%) training samples and 279 (9.51%) testing samples, with each image contributing 100,352 extracted features. We applied various machine learning models for ASD identification. The system achieved an overall prediction accuracy of 92% across both training and testing datasets, with the multilayer perceptron model demonstrating the highest testing accuracy. The system successfully classified gelotophobia in cases where facial expressions were clear. However, in cases of ambiguous facial cues, the DeepFace model alone was insufficient. Incorporating the GELOPH<15> questionnaire improved diagnostic reliability and consistency. Conclusions: This study demonstrates the effectiveness of combining deep learning techniques with validated diagnostic tools for detecting gelotophobia, particularly in individuals with ASD. included_articles.title: Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
included_articles.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex neurological developmental disease that appears in a variety of ways[8]. Most autistic children are not diagnosed until they are at least three years old [6] [13]. Abnormal facial traits caused by development abnormalities are strongly linked to underlying neurological issues [2]. Newborns with ASD have facial development that differs significantly from that of typically developing children [3]. Early detection is crucial to help the parents and families in denial and superstition. Differentiating facial features from normally developing children is a clear way to identify children diagnosed with ASD. In this work, we proposed a facial feature-based ASD detection method. This study uses different deep-learning models to recognize autistic children using only a facial image dataset. This work used five pre-trained CNN models as feature extractors: MobileNet, Xception, VGG16, VGG19, EfficientNet, and a binary classifier to detect autism in children effectively. To train these feature extraction models, we utilized a publicly available Kaggle dataset containing 2940 images of autistic and non-autistic children. The proposed method could detect ASD and non-ASD from the facial images of children. Using CNN models as feature extractors and Logistic regression as a binary classifier, we achieved an accuracy rate approaching 88.33% on test data.

included_articles.title: Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children
included_articles.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a multifaceted neurological development disability that is characterized by deficits in social communication and emotion detection. Early and accurate identification of ASD is important; however, clinicians and researchers have often depended upon lengthy, in-clinic assessments. This research work proposes two deep learning models. This study proposes two deep learning models: a Hybrid resNet50V2+InceptionV3 model for ASD prediction from facial images and an enhanced MobileNet for recognizing six emotions in children with ASD. Data sets were collected from two public datasets. Preprocessing was performed (normalization and augmentation) and a hybrid ResNet50V2+InceptionV3 model and enhanced MobileNet were trained and tested. The hybrid model produced 95 % accuracy for predicting ASD, and the enhanced MobileNet achieved 73.3 % accuracy for predicting emotions; both accuracy rates were significantly improved as compared to baseline models. Overall, both models demonstrated that hybrid and enhanced model architectures improve the predictive accuracy and generalization of children with ASD from facial images. The models can also be used as non-invasive methodologies for early detection of ASD and emotion classification in clinical or educational contexts. Future research will include multimodal inputs and methods in explainable AI for further clinical implication.

included_articles.title: Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy
included_articles.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder that affects how people talk to each other and act. The fact that ASD is becoming more common and that diagnosing it can be difficult means that early detection is important for improving treatment outcomes. This study's goal is to use lightweight ensemble Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) to make it easier to classify ASD from facial photos. The study looks at different CNN architectures, like MobileNetV2 and EfficientNet variations, to find the best model for diagnosing ASD quickly and accurately. The method involves training and testing five lightweight CNN models on a set of facial photos. We use preprocessing methods like scaling and data augmentation to help the model learn better. The study tests how well ensemble CNN models work by combining predictions from different architectures using averaging and voting methods. We use important performance metrics like accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score to see how well each model works. The results show that the best balance between accuracy and computational efficiency is achieved by combining MobileNetV2 and EfficientNetB0. This combination achieves an accuracy of 0.8299, a precision of 0.8514, a recall of 0.8182, and an F1_score of 0.8344. Other models, like ResNet50 combined with EfficientNetB0, have higher precision but lower recall, making them less useful for finding all ASD cases. This study was also compared with other researchers, and the proposed study was found to have greater accuracy than other researchers. The results show that ensemble CNN models can significantly improve the accuracy of classifying ASD compared to single CNNs. This study shows that lightweight ensemble CNN models are good at finding ASD in pictures of people's faces. The method is fast and can be used on devices with limited processing power, making it a good way to find ASD early in both clinical and real-world settings.

The comparison group differs from the ASD group by 42.9 percentage points in sex composition, a difference directly relevant to gaze behaviour and unaddressed by design or analysis. The index test is a CNN-LSTM whose input vector includes CARS_Score, a clinician-administered autism severity instrument - the model is given a measurement of the target condition as a predictor. included_articles.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Automated Machine Learning
included_articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder distinguished by an extensive range of symptoms, including reduced social interaction, communication difficulties and tiresome behaviors. Early detection of ASD is important because it allows for timely intervention, which significantly improves developmental, behavioral, and communicative outcomes in children. However, traditional diagnostic procedures for identifying autism spectrum disorder (ASD) typically involve lengthy clinical examinations, which can be both time-consuming and costly. This research proposes leveraging automated machine learning (AUTOML) to streamline the diagnostic process and enhance its accuracy. Methods: In this study, by collecting data from various rehabilitation centers across Pakistan, we applied a specific AUTOML tool known as Tree-based Pipeline Optimization Tool (TPOT) for ASD detection. Notably, this study marks one of the initial explorations into utilizing AUTOML for ASD detection. The experimentations indicate that the TPOT provided the best pipeline for the dataset, which was verified using a manual machine learning method. Results: The study contributes to the field of ASD diagnosis by using AUTOML to determine the likelihood of ASD in children at prompt stages of evolution. The study also provides an evaluation of precision, recall, and F1-score metrics to confirm the correctness of the diagnosis. The propose TPOT-based AUTOML framework attained an overall accuracy 78%, with a precision of 83%, a recall of 90%, and an F1-score of 86% for the autistic class. Conclusions: In summary, this research offers an encouraging approach to improve the detection of autism spectrum disorders (ASD) in children, which could lead to better results for affected individuals and their families.

included_articles.title: Enhanced ASD detection using 3D facial landmark localization with convolutional shape appearance model and graph-randomized XGBoost
included_articles.abstract: Autism spectrum disease (ASD) is a neurological disease that affects social interaction, communication and behaviour, thus early diagnosis is essential for treatment. Existing detection methods, such as 2D face scans and eye tracking data, are ineffective in capturing difﬁcult facial features and minor asymmetries. Hence, this study presents a novel Convolutional Shape Appearance Model with Randomized Trees-based XGBoost to increase the accuracy and reliability of ASD detection using 3D facial landmark localization. Existing methods fail to capture small facial asymmetries and detailed landmarks essential for accurate diagnosis from 3D facial images, which limits the accuracy of diagnosing ASD-related behaviours. To address this, a novel convolutional neural network (CNN) with an active shape appearance model (ASAM) is introduced, which combines the strengths of CNNs in automatically learning intricate facial features from 3D images and ASAM’s ability to capture variations in facial shapes and textures, thereby enhancing the feature extraction process and accurate localization of facial landmarks. Furthermore, existing detection methods struggle to integrate and analyse facial asymmetry and the complex interactions between multiple facial features simultaneously, leading to reduced accuracy in detecting ASD. Thus, a Euclidian graph with a Randomized Treesbased XGBoost approach is utilized, which captures spatial relationships between facial landmarks and models complex feature interactions, thereby enhancing the accuracy and reliability of ASD detection. The ﬁndings demonstrate that the suggested model offers excellent levels of accuracy, precision, recall, detection accuracy, sensitivity and speciﬁcity when compared to other existing models.

included_articles.title: Enhanced multilevel autism classification for children using eye-tracking and hybrid CNN-RNN deep learning models
included_articles.abstract: This article aims to improve the detection of ASD in children using ET data and advanced ML techniques. ASD, a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by impairments in social communication, interaction, and repetitive behaviors, typically manifests before the age of three. Early diagnosis is crucial for timely and effective interventions. ET data have revealed distinct gaze patterns in children with ASD, such as diminished attention to social cues and increased ﬁxation on repetitive stimuli. However, current methods of ET data analysis are largely manual and lack scalability for widespread clinical screening. To address these limitations, we propose a novel, scanpath-based ASD detection method that identiﬁes atypical gaze behaviors through dynamic changes in visual attention. We extract four sequential features from scanpaths and analyze variations in feature space across different ASD severity levels low, mild, moderate, and severe using the MultiMatch and DTW similarity metrics. Our analysis reveals that children with ASD exhibit unique and highly individualized gaze patterns when compared to TD children. Notable differences are observed in attention duration and vertical gaze distribution, providing key insights into ASD-related visual behaviors. For classiﬁcation, we employ a hybrid CNNRNN model, which signiﬁcantly outperforms traditional ML methods. The CNN-RNN model achieves an accuracy of 97%, recall of 98.24%, and an F1-score of 97.04% using the feature set (x, d, y). In comparison, models based on GRU and 2-LSTM networks show competitive accuracies of 92% and 90%, respectively. However, RFC and XGBoost models underperform, with accuracies ranging between 70.25 and 80.80%. These ﬁndings demonstrate the efﬁcacy of DL approaches, particularly the CNN-RNN hybrid model, in accurately classifying ASD based on ET data, emphasizing their potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy. The proposed scalable method for ASD detection holds promise for improving early diagnosis and intervention, which is critical for better long-term outcomes in children with ASD. Further evaluation on an independent dataset will assess the generalizability and precision of the model.

included_articles.title: Ensemble of Deep Learning with Crested Porcupine Optimizer Based Autism
included_articles.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a multifaceted neurological developmental condition that manifests in several ways. Nearly all autistic children remain undiagnosed before the age of three. Developmental problems affecting face features are often associated with fundamental brain disorders. The facial evolution of newborns with ASD is quite different from that of typically developing children. Early recognition is very significant to aid families and parents in superstition and denial. Distinguishing facial features from typically developing children is an evident manner to detect children analyzed with ASD. Presently, artificial intelligence (AI) significantly contributes to the emerging computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) of autism and to the evolving interactive methods that aid in the treatment and reintegration of autistic patients. This study introduces an Ensemble of deep learning models based on the autism spectrum disorder detection in facial images (EDLM-ASDDFI) model. The overarching goal of the EDLM-ASDDFI model is to recognize the difference between facial images of individuals with ASD and normal controls. In the EDLM-ASDDFI method, the primary level of data pre-processing is involved by Gabor filtering (GF). Besides, the EDLM-ASDDFI technique applies the MobileNetV2 model to learn complex features from the pre-processed data. For the ASD detection process, the EDLM-ASDDFI method uses ensemble techniques for classification procedure that encompasses long short-term memory (LSTM), deep belief network (DBN), and hybrid kernel extreme learning machine (HKELM). Finally, the hyperparameter selection of the three deep learning (DL) models can be implemented by the design of the crested porcupine optimizer (CPO) technique. An extensive experiment was conducted to emphasize the improved ASD detection performance of the EDLM-ASDDFI method. The simulation outcomes indicated that the EDLM-ASDDFI technique highlighted betterment over other existing models in terms of numerous performance measures.

included_articles.title: Explainable and secure framework for autism prediction using multimodal eye tracking and kinematic data
included_articles.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental condition marked by difﬁculties in social skills, repetitive behaviours, and communication. Early and accurate diagnosis is essential for effective intervention and support. This paper proposes a secure and privacy-preserving framework for diagnosing ASD by integrating multimodal kinematic and eye movement sensory data, Deep Neural Networks (DNN), and Explainable Artiﬁcial Intelligence (XAI). Federated Learning (FL), a distributed machine learning approach, is utilized to ensure data privacy by training models across multiple devices without centralizing sensitive data. In our evaluation, we employ FL using a shallow DNN as the shared model and Federated Averaging (FedAvg) as the aggregation algorithm. We conduct experiments across two scenarios for each dataset: the ﬁrst using FL with all features and the second using FL with features selected by XAI. The experiments, conducted with three clients over three rounds of training, show that the L_General dataset produces the best results, with Client 2 achieving an accuracy of 99.99% and Client 1 achieving 88%. This study underscores FL’s potential to preserve privacy and security while maintaining high diagnostic accuracy, making it a viable solution for healthcare applications involving sensitive data.

included_articles.title: Facial Images Dataset for Early Screening of Autism Children Using Convolutional Neural Network
included_articles.abstract: The diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) using facial recognition technology faces challenges related to limited dataset variation and model classification effectiveness. The dataset is often less representative in capturing facial characteristics, lighting conditions, and social context, which impacts detection accuracy. This study aims to develop a new dataset with a broader variation in facial characteristics and refine the model classification based on Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for optimal ASD detection. The developed dataset consists of 1,050 images with dimensions of 224x224 pixels, evenly distributed between the categories "ASD" and "Normal." Evaluation using a nuisance matrix shows strong model performance, achieving 90% accuracy, 92% precision, 88% recall, and 90% F1 score. These findings suggest that a more representative dataset and image size optimization can improve the effectiveness of ASD detection. This study significantly supports a more reliable ASD diagnosis through machine learning technology. With promising results, this study paves the way for further application of facial recognition technology in clinical contexts and the potential development of automated detection systems that can be used in daily diagnostic practice.

included_articles.title: Improving Early Autism Detection with Chi-Square Feature Selection, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI
included_articles.abstract: This study presented a framework that utilized Chi-square feature selection and Machine Learning (ML) classifiers to improve the early detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) for children 12 to 36 months old. Six classifiers -Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LGBM), Extra Trees (ET), Decision Tree (DT), KNearest Neighbors (KNN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) -were tested. The findings revealed that the integration of Chi-square feature selection with SVM achieved perfect accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, while the other models demonstrated notable gains (up to 90%). Additionally, a SHapley Additive exPlanation (SHAP) analysis was conducted to interpret the model predictions and highlight the key behavioral features, while a literature comparison with recent research showed that the current method outperformed the latter. This study demonstrated that integrating robust feature selection with explainable ML models can significantly advance the reliability of early ASD screening tools.

Its primary origin is genetic, and early detection and intervention can mitigate the need for costly medical procedures and lengthy examinations for individuals affected by ASD. An effective teaching approach may be challenging to determine for a child with autism. Autism Spectrum Disorder is highly diverse, with each affected child being unique. It is often stated that no two autistic children are alike, meaning that what benefits one child may not be suitable for another. Two ASD screening datasets of toddlers are merged in this study. In the second phase, the study focuses on identifying appropriate teaching methods for children with ASD by evaluating their physical, verbal, and behavioural performance. This research aims to provide personalized educational approaches for individuals with ASD, harnessing machine learning to enhance precision in addressing their unique needs.

included_articles.title: Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach
included_articles.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a complex neuropsychiatric developmental condition that signiﬁcantly affects social interaction, communication, and learning skills. Early and precise diagnosis is essential for timely intervention but remains challenging due to the variability in symptoms and reliance on time consuming clinical assessments. This study proposes machine learning (ML) classiﬁers for autism trait screening using a toddler dataset with 19 attributes, emphasizing optimized feature selection and hyperparameter tuning. Feature selection techniques, including Chi-squared tests, ML based feature importance, and pairwise correlation analysis, identify key predictive features. Multiple subsets of features are systematically evaluated to optimize classiﬁer performance. Notably, considering only the Q1–Q10 behavioural features resulted in a 41% reduction in features, enhancing classiﬁcation performance while reducing computational complexity. The Logistic Regression and k-nearest neighbors (LR-KNN) ensemble achieved an accuracy of 99%, followed by the Artiﬁcial Neural Network (ANN) at 98%, Logistic Regression (LR) at 97%, and k-nearest neighbors (KNN) at 94%. Through a systematic analysis of feature selection, an optimal feature subset is identiﬁed that balances model complexity and predictive power. These ﬁndings highlight the role of feature selection in improving ML based screening, offering a scalable and cost effective approach for early detection and personalized intervention strategies. This approach not only streamlines the screening process but also facilitates the way for integrating ML techniques into clinical settings.

included_articles.title: Predicting autistic traits, anxiety and depression symptoms using camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (CAT-Q-ES): A machine learning study
included_articles.abstract: Research has linked camouflaging with compensating and hiding autistic traits during social interactions. Furthermore, these strategies have been linked to increased anxiety and depression symptoms and to greater reliance on camouflaging behaviors among individuals with more autistic traits, even in non-autistic populations. This study evaluated the viability of a machine learning algorithm to predict autistic traits and symptoms of depression and anxiety using camouflaging behaviors. The sample included 601 participants: 102 autistic adults (72 women, 18 men, and 12 non-binary individuals) and 499 non-autistic adults (399 women, 92 men, and eight non-binary individuals). The study predicted autistic traits measured with the Broader Autism Phenotype Questionnaire (BAPQ) subscales - Aloofness, Pragmatics, and Rigidity - as well as the total score of depressive (Patient Health Questionnaire - PHQ-9) and anxious symptoms (General Anxiety Disorder - GAD-7) using the individual items from the Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire Spanish version (CAT-Q-ES) as predictors. We developed fifty supervised learning models, including support vector machines, neural networks, linear regressors, decision trees, random forests, and Gaussian processes, among others. Correlation coefficients between true and predicted scores were strong for Aloofness (R=.85), Pragmatics (R=.82), and Rigidity (R=.74), being only moderate for Depression (R=.60) and Anxiety (R=.54). Autism diagnosis or gender identity did not improve the prediction’s accuracy. These results show the viability of machine learning algorithms to predict autistic traits (Aloofness, Pragmatics and Rigidity) and anxiety-depression symptoms, using the CAT-Q-ES. included_articles.title: A Computational Method for Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Deep Learning Approach
included_articles.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a complicated neurological disease that causes difficulty with social interaction and communication. Proper diagnosis at an early stage is essential for successful intervention. This paper introduces a novel deep learning model called the Hybrid Vision Transformer model for detecting Autism Spectrum Disorder "HyVit-ASD" designed to classify ASD based on facial feature images. The HyVit-ASD model combines the strengths of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and vision transformers (ViTs) to form a strong and efficient classification framework. The HyVit-ASD model has three main components: a convolutional block (ConvBlock), a transformer block with re-attention (TransformerBlock), and a classification layer. The ConvBlock uses a pre-trained ResNet for initial feature extraction, reducing the feature map's channels and resizing them for further processing. The TransformerBlock integrates a pre-trained ViT with a custom ReAttention mechanism, enhancing the model's focus on critical facial regions through attention scores and residual connections. The final stage involves global average pooling and a linear layer for classification likelihood. Our proposed model achieved 91% accuracy, 94% sensitivity, 88% specificity, and a 95.67% AUC. The combination of CNN and ViT architectures and the innovative ReAttention mechanism make HyVit-ASD a pioneering approach in deep learning for ASD classification, contributing significantly to early diagnosis and intervention strategies.

included_articles.title: Early Detection of ASD from Facial Images Using DeepDeblur and Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network
included_articles.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder with ineffective brain functions leading to challenges in verbal and non-verbal communication, social behavior, and learning disabilities. Early detection of ASD in children can help determine the required therapies to stabilize physical and psychological behaviors. The accurate diagnosis of ASD has been primarily obtained through analysis of behavioral changes and facial features. Estimating the presence of ASD in children from static facial images is very challenging due to many challenges in the quality and resolution of the images. This paper develops an advanced Deep Learning (DL)-based framework of DeepDeblur-Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network (DeepDeblur-DOCNN) for screening and detection of ASD in children images with the presence of noise and blur. The proposed DeepDeblurDOCNN framework utilizes the DeepDeblur method in the first stage for image sharpening. Then, it employs a novel DOCNN in the second stage for joint denoising and classification. In this proposed DeepDeblur-DOCNN framework, the DOCNN is enhanced by combining the features of denoising network and CNN with Fire Hawk Optimizer (FHO) for parameter tuning to improve the training process. By combining denoising and classification tasks in a single DOCNN, the model can leverage the denoised image and perform better feature learning for more accurate classification predictions. Experiments are conducted using the Kaggle ASD Children Facial dataset containing 2940 facial images. The results showed that the proposed model is more effective for ASD diagnosis, with 96.94% detection accuracy with reduced model complexity.
