included_articles.title: Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI
included_articles.abstract: Background: As the demand for early and accurate diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) increases, the integration of machine learning (ML) and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is emerging as a critical advancement that promises to revolutionize intervention strategies by improving both accuracy and transparency. Methods: This paper presents a method that combines XAI techniques with a rigorous data-preprocessing pipeline to improve the accuracy and interpretability of ML-based diagnostic tools. Our preprocessing pipeline included outlier removal, missing data handling, and selecting pertinent features based on clinical expert advice. Using R and the caret package (version 6.0.94), we developed and compared several ML algorithms, validated using 10-fold cross-validation and optimized by grid search hyperparameter tuning. XAI techniques were employed to improve model transparency, offering insights into how features contribute to predictions, thereby enhancing clinician trust. Results: Rigorous data-preprocessing improved the models’ generalizability and real-world applicability across diverse clinical datasets, ensuring a robust performance. Neural networks and extreme gradient boosting models achieved the best performance in terms of accuracy, precision, and recall. XAI techniques demonstrated that behavioral features significantly influenced model predictions, leading to greater interpretability. Conclusions: This study successfully developed highly precise and interpretable ML models for ASD diagnosis, connecting advanced ML methods with practical clinical application and supporting the adoption of AI-driven diagnostic tools by healthcare professionals. This study’s findings contribute to personalized intervention strategies and early diagnostic practices, ultimately improving outcomes and quality of life for individuals with ASD.

assessments.support: Both clinical groups recruited from early childhood intervention centres with a formal clinician-made DSM-5 diagnosis as an inclusion criterion, and groups closely matched on age (p=0.959) - substantially better than the corpus norm. But the clinical groups are approximately 92% male against 50% in the TD group (chi-squared 20.15, p<0.01) and differ significantly in receptive vocabulary and basic attention, and none of these is adjusted for in the models.

All predictors derive from the eye-tracking record; no clinical instrument score, diagnostic measure or demographic variable enters the feature set. Algorithms were selected for interpretability and the four feature sets are pre-defined by granularity rather than by label-driven selection.

Diagnoses were made by a licensed, experienced clinical team following DSM-5, independently of this study, and the authors explicitly note the provisionality of early-age diagnoses and the limitations of the instruments available to them.

Participant-level stratified 5-fold cross-validation with one row per child and no within-participant duplication. However, up to 158 variables are used for 93 children, no interval or fold variance is reported, and the headline figures are the best over four feature sets, several algorithms and four group comparisons with no correction.

risk_of_bias.summary: Moderate rather than high risk of bias - one of only two studies charted so far to avoid the high overall rating. The design is sound where most of this literature fails: real clinical diagnoses, age-matched groups, participant-level cross-validation, no instrument scores in the feature set, complete ethics reporting, and pre-specified interpretive thresholds. Residual risk sits in three places: an untreated sex imbalance and significant language-ability differences between the clinical and TD groups, a high variable-to-participant ratio with no interval reporting, and headline figures selected as the maximum across four feature sets, several algorithms and four comparisons. The study's own central finding - F1 0.63 for ASD versus DLD against 0.86 for ASD versus TD - is the least affected by all of these, because the two comparisons share every methodological feature.

included_articles.title: Utilizing deep learning models in an intelligent eye-tracking system for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis
included_articles.abstract: distinctive characteristics and categorize children with ASD and healthy controls based on individual images. Elbattah et al. (24) developed a machine learning (ML)-based approach to aid in the diagnosing process. This approach relies on acquiring knowledge of sequence-oriented patterns in action eye motions. The primary philosophy was to represent eye-tracking data as written documents that analyze a sequence of rapid eye movements (saccades) and periods of gaze fixation. Therefore, the study utilized the natural language processing (NLP) technique to transform the unorganized eye-tracking information. Li et al. (25) introduced an automated evaluation framework for detecting typical intonation patterns and predictable unique phrases that are important to ASD. Their focus was on the linguistic and communication difficulties experienced by young children with ASD. At first, the scientists utilized the Open SMILE toolkit to extract high-dimensional auditory characteristics at the sound level. They also employed a support vector machine (SVM) backend as the standard baseline. Furthermore, the researchers suggested many DNN arrangements and structures for representing a shared prosody label derived directly from the audio spectrogram after the constant Q transform. Identification and intervention for ASD have enduring effects on both ASD children as well as their families, necessitating informative, medical, social, and economic assistance to enhance their overall wellbeing. Professionals have problems in conducting ASD assessments due to the absence of recognized biophysiological diagnostic techniques (25, 26). Therefore, the diagnosis is often determined by a thorough evaluation of behavior, using reliable and valid standardized techniques such as the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) (27) and the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R) (28). These tools, widely approved in investigation and research domains, are considered the most reliable method for diagnosing ASD in medical situations (29, 30). However, using them involves the use of many materials, a significant amount of time, and is somewhat expensive (25, 26). Furthermore, the diagnostic technique necessitates the involvement of skilled and knowledgeable interviewers, who have the potential to influence the process. This is accompanied by the inclusion of intricate clinical procedures (25, 31). Collectively, these difficulties frequently contribute to a postponed identification, leading to a delay in the initiation of early intervention (26). Research indicates that early treatments for children with ASD before the age of five result in a much higher success rate of 67%, compared to a success rate of just 11% when interventions begin after the age of 5 (32). included_articles.title: A novel hybrid deep learning model using MEResNext for autism spectrum disorder detection
included_articles.abstract: A neurological disease, named autism spectrum disorder (ASD), is portrayed through divergence with social interaction, communication, and repetitive activities. As heredity is an important source, initial identification and treatment can diminish the need for wide examinations and expensive medical procedures for those with ASD. Prolonged effects and severity can be avoided at a timely determination of ASD. This study develops a hybrid deep-learning method for ASD detection. Pre-processing, feature selection and ASD detection are three steps involved. In the pre-processing phase, input data is passed in which noise and artefacts present in the data are removed using Yeo-Jhonson transformation. Next, by integrating Double exponential Smoothing (DES) in Elk Herd Optimizer (EHO), Double exponential Smoothing-Elk Herd Optimizer (DeSEHO), is proposed to select features. At last, the features that are selected are subjected to the ASD detection phase. In this stage, the Mo­ ments Embedding ResNeXt (MEResNeXt), which is the combination of Moments Embedding Network (MoNet) and ResNeXt, is used for ASD detection. The results of the research show that MEResNeXt performed better in terms of traditional models which show accuracy of 95.3 %, sensitivity of 96.5 %, and specificity of 94.8 %.

included_articles.title: An assessment of autistic and parkinsonian movement profiles to inform selective classification algorithms
included_articles.abstract: Background Movement differences in autism have attracted growing attention in recent years. Anecdotally, autistic movement has been likened to that of Parkinson’s Disease (PD). Given that PD assessments are primarily movementbased, it is important to ensure that autistic individuals are not scoring highly on PD diagnostic criteria due to autismrelated movement differences. Quantifying overlap in movement profiles and identifying distinguishing features is essential, particularly given increased PD diagnosis rates in the autistic population. Methods We conducted the first direct comparison study of autistic and parkinsonian movement. Autistic individuals (N = 31), individuals with PD (N = 32) and control participants (N = 31) completed a Shapes Tracing Task and a Reaction Time Task. Kinematic features were compared between groups and classification algorithms were run to distinguish between groups. Results Groups were distinguishable based on kinematic features. The autistic group differed from both PD and control groups in speed modulation and sub-movements, and from the PD group in reaction time. Classification algorithms for clinical (autism and PD) versus non-clinical groups, and for autism versus PD, were most accurate when combining kinematic and questionnaire data. There were no kinematic similarities between autism and PD that were also distinct from controls. Conclusions Whilst kinematic features did not appear similar between autism and PD, they were informative for group classification. This proof-of-concept study highlights that movement-based metrics may aid in identifying whether someone belongs to a clinical group, and which one – suggesting potential for refining diagnostic approaches for both autism and PD.

Gender and non-verbal reasoning matched; both clinical groups age-matched to controls; the unmatched ASD-PD age difference, and the significant depression and anxiety differences, are controlled statistically and residualised from the classification inputs.

However, the discriminatory feature sets were selected by group-difference significance computed over all participants, so configurations using them saw held-out labels during selection.

risk_of_bias.summary: Moderate risk of bias, and one of only three studies in the charted corpus below the high rating. Recruitment, diagnosis, matching, statistical modelling, ethics and reproducibility are all handled to a standard the rest of this literature does not approach, and the primary finding is a negative result supported by Bayes factors rather than by absence of significance. Residual risk sits in the classification component: test partitions of roughly 13 to 19 participants with no intervals reported, and discriminatory feature sets chosen using group-difference tests computed on the full sample. Both qualify the accuracy figures rather than the study's main conclusion, which does not depend on them.

included_articles.title: An explainable deep learning framework for screening level autism severity using behavioural data
included_articles.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental condition characterized by heterogeneous behavioural manifestations that vary across age groups and severity strata. While questionnaire-based screening instruments enable large-scale ASD identification, reliable severity stratification remains challenging due to the absence of explicit clinician-annotated severity labels and the reliance of many existing approaches on fragmented or multi-stage pipelines. To address this gap, this study proposes a unified BiLSTM–CGBO framework for screening-level ASD identification and ordinal severity stratification under a controlled behavioural labeling paradigm. The proposed architecture integrates a Bidirectional Long ShortTerm Memory (BiLSTM) network, employed as a high-capacity representation learner for modeling non-linear interactions among behavioural attributes, with a Chaotic Grey Ball Optimizer (CGBO) that adaptively modulates learning dynamics to enhance numerical stability and convergence. The framework is evaluated on harmonized ASD screening datasets from the Kaggle and UCI repositories, comprising 2154 participants across four developmental cohorts: toddlers, children, adolescents, and adults. Experimental results demonstrate consistently high classification accuracy and AUROC values across age groups, reflecting the model’s effectiveness in approximating a deterministic behavioural severity-scoring function rather than independent clinical diagnostic performance. Comparative analysis indicates that the proposed framework achieves stable improvements over classical machine learning and deep learning baselines, including SVM, CNN, and standard LSTM, under identical preprocessing and validation protocols. Model interpretability is examined using SHapley Additive Explanations (SHAP), which elucidate how behavioural attributes are utilized within the learned scoring structure without asserting causal or diagnostic attribution. Overall, the proposed BiLSTM–CGBO framework establishes a transparent, reproducible, and computationally efficient methodology for screening-level autism severity modeling, providing a robust foundation for future validation using independently clinician-annotated data and multimodal extensions. Article highlights • A single-stage AI model enables efficient autism severity screening across all agegroups. Page 2 of 31 Rathod et al. Discover Applied Sciences (2026) 8:363
included_articles.authors: Rathod VN; Goudar RH; Sangani S

assessments.support: Secondary use of four harmonised public screening datasets with no recruitment, eligibility, setting or dates described; per-cohort and per-class sample counts are not reported anywhere, and sex, ethnicity, country and respondent type were removed during feature pruning.

The predictor set contains the A1-A10 items and the composite Q_SCORE while the target is a four-level discretisation of a weighted sum of those same items. Domain weights were calibrated on the full dataset before cross-validation, and SHAP-based feature pruning - which requires a fitted model - was also applied to the whole dataset.

There is no clinician-annotated severity label, a fact the paper states as its motivating gap. The single external anchor is a kappa of 0.72 against expert assessments on a randomly sampled subset, with the number of records, the experts' qualifications and the instrument used all unreported.

Stratified 10-fold cross-validation at record level with early stopping and class weighting, plus quantified sensitivity analyses on imputation, thresholds and weights. But no class counts, no per-cohort sample sizes and no confidence intervals or across-fold variance for any accuracy.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias, for the same structural reason as the rest of the questionnaire branch: the severity target is a deterministic function of the predictors. What separates this study is that it identifies that fact itself, states it in five separate sections, and instructs the reader that its 97-99% accuracies are function approximation rather than diagnostic accuracy. Within that declared scope the methodology is comparatively strong - stratified cross-validation, a fully specified labelling function, three quantified sensitivity analyses, author-fitted baselines under identical protocols, an ablation, and SHAP applied with an explicit prohibition on causal reading. Residual problems: weight calibration and SHAP-based pruning both performed on the full dataset, no class counts or accuracy intervals, an unspecified expert-labelling procedure behind the only external anchor, and an ablation crediting SHAP with an accuracy gain it cannot produce.

included_articles.title: An explainable machine unlearning algorithm framework for early detection of autism spectrum disorder and brain disabilities in newborns
included_articles.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a rising disorder in the brain among newborns aged 0 to 36 months, emphasizing the urgent need for early and accurate detection to mitigate potential developmental risks. Deep learning and machine learning techniques have shown promise in diagnosing ASD, particularly in children aged 36 to 72 months. However, the effectiveness of these diagnostic models heavily depends on the quality and accuracy of the training data. Inaccurate or mismatched data can lead to unreliable diagnoses and inappropriate clinical interventions. In this paper, we propose a machine unlearning-integrated explainable AI (XAI) framework for the early detection of autism spectrum disorder and brain disabilities in newborns. Central to our framework is the Machine Unlearning-Integrated Explainable AI Partitioning Autism Detection and Brain Disorder (MUXAI-ASDBD) algorithm, a novel partitioning-based XAI approach built on Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). This algorithm provides layer-wise explainability during training and incorporates a machine unlearning mechanism at the summation layer, along with probability distribution analysis, to enhance diagnostic accuracy and computational efficiency. The MUXAI-ASDBD framework was evaluated using multiple benchmark datasets, including Ages and Stages Questionnaires (ASQ), CSBS, PEDS, the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (M-CHAT), and the Screening Tool for Autism in Toddlers and Children (STAT). We also integrated neuroimaging data from brain disorder MRI and EEG datasets. This work extends our previously published implementation, in which we detected autism but did not correct errors, as we do here. Simulation results showed that the MUXAI-ASDBD framework reduced error rates by 23%, reduced false positives, improved accuracy to 98%, and reduced processing time for autism detection using the given multimodal data.

included_articles.title: Deep learning based approach for Behavior classification in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder using naturalistic videos
included_articles.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder that is marked by a lack of communication skills in social situations and repetitive and stereotypical Behaviors. The most widespread form of diagnosing ASD among children is based on psychological screening test along with monitoring of the Behavioral pattern, especially repetitive Behaviors. Some of these Behaviors include hand-ﬂapping, head banging and spinning which are common among ASD children. In our research, we examine abnormal Behavioral patterns that may reﬂect ASD through the videos of children engaged in the everyday activities in the unstructured settings. A publicly available multiclass Self-Stimulatory Behavior Dataset (SSBD) is use in classify autistic Behavior. Before training the model, the dataset is thoroughly pre-processed (region-of-interest (ROI) detection and image cropping to eliminate irrelevant background objects). Moreover, information-augmenting methods are used to reduce overﬁtting and increase training efciency and generalization efectiveness. In order to obtain spatiotemporal details successfully, a number of deep learning models are tested, such as studied CNN-GRU model, 3D-CNN + LSTM, MobileNet, VGG16, and EfcientNet-B7. The ﬁndings of the experiment prove that the proposed CNN-GRU model is superior to all competing methods. The model with a k- fold cross-validation provides a steady accuracy of 0.9284 ± 0.0039–0.9294 ± 0.0038, which means that the model is robust and consistent across the folds. The efectiveness of the proposed approach is additionally justiﬁed by the comparisons with state-of-the-art methods. The results show that the systems based on the action recognition can help clinicians monitor the Behavioral trends and facilitate the quick, accurate, and efective screening of ASD. The proposed approach works efectively in predicting Behavior in real-life, uncontrolled videos and shows tremendous potential for real-world clinical implementation as a decision-support tool.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias, though with more methodological credit than most of this corpus. The comparative design is controlled - five architectures under identical hyperparameters, per-fold standard deviations for every model, paired t-tests with a corrected threshold, and a sensible error analysis - and the data are the most ecologically valid in the review, being spontaneous behaviour recorded in children's own homes. Two problems dominate. Folds are formed over clips from only 75 videos with no recording-level grouping, so the 0.9294 is not a generalisation estimate across children, and the unusually small fold variance is evidence of that rather than against it. And the task performed - four-way movement classification within a dataset containing only autistic children - cannot support the screening and diagnostic claims made in the title and abstract, a gap the paper's own decision-support hedge implicitly acknowledges. No ethics statement accompanies the reuse of identifiable children's home videos.

included_articles.abstract: Explainable Children Autism Detection using Gaze Features in Audio-Visual Speech Comprehension MIGUEL ZARAGOZÁ-PORTOLÉS, Universitat Politècnica de València, Spain DAVID GIMENO-GOMEZ, Universitat Politècnica de València, Spain VICENTA ÁVILA, University of Valencia, Spain DR. INMACULADA FAJARDO, University of Valencia, Spain DR. ANTONIO FERRER, University of Valencia, Spain NADINA GOMEZ-MERINO, University of Valencia, Spain NOEMI SKROBISZEWSKA, University of Valencia, Spain CARLOS-D. MARTÍNEZ-HINAREJOS, Universitat Politècnica de València, Spain Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition marked by impairments in social interac- tion and delayed language acquisition. Early and accurate identification is crucial for timely interventions that support cognitive and social development. Motivated by the subjectivity of traditional behavior-based assessments, computational methodologies offer more objective and cost-effective alternatives. Among these, eye-tracking stands out for capturing subtle attentional and perceptual patterns. This paper investigates the use of eye-tracking data for automatic ASD detection in children during audio-visual storytelling interactions, emphasizing traditional yet explainable machine learning methods. Although performance remains modest, our analyses reveal that fixation duration and revisit patterns to facial regions may serve as potential biomark- ers. Further analyses highlight the impact of stimulus modality, suggesting that the inclusion of visual speech cues provides valuable discriminative information. These findings have the potential to support and guide the work of psychologists in the assessment of ASD within speech comprehension contexts. included_articles.title: Explainable Ensemble Learning Framework for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Enhancing Trust, Interpretability and Reliability in AI-Driven Healthcare
included_articles.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing healthcare by helping with diagnosis. However, for doctors to trust AI tools, they need to be both accurate and easy to understand. In this study, we created a new machine learning system for the early detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) in children. Our main goal was to build a model that is not only good at predicting ASD but also clear in its reasoning. For this, we combined several different models, including Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Networks, into a single, more powerful framework. We used two different types of datasets: (i) a standard behavioral dataset and (ii) a more complex multimodal dataset with images, audio, and physiological information. The datasets were carefully preprocessed for missing values, redundant features, and dataset imbalance to ensure fair learning. The results outperformed the state-of-the-art with a Regularized Neural Network, achieving 97.6% accuracy on behavioral data. Whereas, on the multimodal data, the accuracy is 98.2%. Other models also did well with accuracies consistently above 96%. We also used SHAP and LIME on a behavioral dataset for models’ explainability.

included_articles.title: Finding the forest in the trees: Using machine learning and online cognitive and perceptual measures to predict adult autism diagnosis
included_articles.abstract: Traditional subjective measures are limited in the insight they provide into underlying behavioral differences associated with autism and, accordingly, their ability to predict diagnosis. Performance-based measures offer an attractive alternative, being designed to capture neuropsychological constructs more directly and objectively. However, due to the heterogeneity of autism, differences in any one speciﬁc neuropsychological domain are inconsistently detected. Meanwhile, protracted wait times for diagnostic interviews delay access to care, highlighting the importance of developing better methods for identifying individuals likely to be autistic and understanding the associated behavioral differences. We administered a battery of online tasks measuring multisensory perception, emotion recognition, and executive function to a large group of autistic and non-autistic adults. We then used machine learning to classify participants and reveal which factors from the resulting dataset were most predictive of diagnosis. Not only were these measures able to predict autism in a late-diagnosed population known to be particularly difﬁcult to identify, their combination with the most popular screening questionnaire enhanced its predictive accuracy (reaching 92% together). This indicates that performance-based measures may be a promising means of predicting autism, providing complementary information to existing screening questionnaires. Many variables in which signiﬁcant group differences were not detected had predictive value in combination, suggesting complex latent relationships associated with autism. Machine learning’s ability to harness these connections and pinpoint the most crucial features for prediction could allow optimization of a screening tool that offers a unique marriage of predictive accuracy and accessibility.

included_articles.title: Hybrid ensemble learning for Autism Spectrum Disorder screening using eye-tracking scanpath
included_articles.abstract: Early and accurate detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is essential for effective intervention and lifelong support. Recent advances in machine learning and eye-tracking technologies have enabled objective screening approaches based on gaze behavior, providing a non-invasive alternative to traditional diagnostic methods. This study introduces a hybrid ensemble learning framework that integrates bagging, boosting, and stacking strategies to leverage the complementary strengths of diverse classifiers, including decision trees, random forests, k-nearest neighbors, AdaBoost, and gradient boosting. The framework was evaluated on a benchmark eye-tracking dataset of 28 participants (14 ASD, 14 TD) using five-fold cross-validation. The proposed stacking model achieved a mean accuracy of 0.960 ± 0.080 and an F1-score of 0.952 ± 0.095 across the five folds, outperforming individual base learners and performing comparably to image-based deep learning models. By operating directly on raw scanpath data, the proposed model enhances interpretability and reduces preprocessing overhead by eliminating the need for image generation and transformation steps, making it suitable for practical and real-time screening environments. Future work will focus on validating the framework on larger and more diverse datasets and integrating it within an end-to-end ASD screening platform.

included_articles.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Facial Images and AI-Based Deep Learning Models
included_articles.abstract: The condition in which an individual's communication abilities and social interactions are affected during early development is called autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Such people feel more anxious, react to emotions in different ways and experience sounds, lights or touch differently. Early diagnosis and timely interventions can significantly improve behavioural and language development. Traditional methods for ASD detection, such as subjective questionnaires and behavioural observations, are often time-consuming, costly and reliant on specialized expertise, leading to a delay in intervention. To address these challenges, this work introduces a novel approach for the early identification and detection of ASD in children using facial images. The research focuses on utilizing YOLOv8n for facial features identification and ASD classification, harnessing its advanced object detection capabilities to enhance both accuracy and efficiency. This paper also presents a comparative analysis of YOLOv8n and YOLOv9c to conclude with the most effective solution. This study facilitates real-time ASD screening, providing healthcare professionals with timely and effective interventions in clinical environments.

included_articles.title: Multimodal fusion of deep transfer learning with wavelet neural network for autism spectrum disorder detection using facial images
included_articles.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex psychological disease described by persis­ tent problems in restricted behaviours, speech, social interaction, and non-verbal commu­ nication. Individuals with ASDs have trouble identifying and connecting with others. The ASD symptoms might arise in an extensive range of conditions. Many dissimilar kinds of functions exist for individuals with ASD. Emerging expert methods for recognising ASD that depend on the facial signs of children are one of the foremost contributions for perceiving ASD at an initial phase. At present, deep learning (DL) models have delivered excellent performance in a diversity of pattern recognition tasks. The utilization of mod­ els that depend on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) was projected by numerous researchers to be utilized in the study of ASD. In this paper, an innovative methodology called Deep Feature Fusion Integrated with Wavelet Neural Network for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification (DFFWNN-ASDI) utilizing facial images is proposed. The primary goal of the DFFWNN-ASDI technique is to serve as a promising diagnostic aid in clinical settings for the early and non-invasive detection of autism. Initially, the DFFWNN-ASDI technique performs pre-processing by utilising the Gaussian Gabor Filter (GGF) to en­ hance relevant facial features and suppress noise. Furthermore, a feature fusion strategy is implemented by incorporating deep features extracted from VGG16, DenseNet-121, and XceptionNet models, ensuring a rich and diverse representation of facial cues relevant to ASD. Moreover, the wavelet neural network (WNN) technique is employed for detecting ASD. Additionally, the chimp optimisation algorithm (COA) technique is implemented for optimal tuning of WNN parameters to enhance classification performance. Eventually, the Grad-CAM + + technique is applied to provide visual interpretation and abnormality detection. To establish the improved performance of the DFFWNN-ASDI approach, an ex­ tensive set of simulations was conducted under the autism image dataset. The comparison outcomes of the DFFWNN-ASDI model established a greater accuracy value of 98.42% compared to existing approaches across diverse metrics.

included_articles.title: SHAP-based explainable AI framework for autism severity classification using 3D motor biomarkers
included_articles.abstract: Introduction: Early Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) diagnosis is critical for intervention, yet current methods rely on subjective clinical observations. This study develops objective tools to classify ASD severity using 3D motor movement analysis, addressing motor abnormalities as core diagnostic features. Methods: A Random Forest (RF) model classiﬁed three severity levels using 463 motor features from 25 Kinect V2 joint points. Data from 109 children (50 typical, 50 moderate ASD, 9 severe ASD) were validated via 5-fold cross-validation and two held-out test sets (20% each). Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) analysis identiﬁed critical motor biomarkers. Results: The model achieved 84.6±10.9% accuracy (5-fold cross-validation) and 86.4% accuracy (internal and held-out test sets). For severe ASD, the model achieved 100% classiﬁcation accuracy on synthetic test data (4/4 cases; 95% CI: 39.8%-100.0%). However, this result represents a methodological proof-of- concept rather than clinical validation, as severe ASD features were synthetically generated from moderate ASD data and the model has not been validated on real Kinect-derived severe ASD motor data. SHAP analysis identiﬁed wrist movements, knee trajectories, and elbow-to-foot distances as key motor biomarkers for severity classiﬁcation. Discussion: This Kinect-based approach with RF and SHAP offers effective, interpretable ASD severity assessment for typical and moderate ASD classes, with promising methodological foundations for severe ASD pending validation on real data.

For the two real classes the 463 pre-calculated features are applied to roughly 87 training cases, a high-dimensional regime; no hyperparameters or seed are reported.
The three-level severity grouping is inherited from the original collection with no named instrument behind the moderate/severe distinction, and the severe stratum has no corresponding measurements.

The severe class contributes n=2 per test set and n=4 in total, and the author reports the resulting confidence interval.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias, and the study identifies why itself. included_articles.title: Screening autism spectrum
included_articles.abstract: Screening autism spectrum disorder in children using machine learning on speech transcripts Rida Assaf1, Zein Shehabeddine1 & Vikram Ramesh2 Early detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) in children is crucial for timely interventions that can improve developmental outcomes. Traditional diagnostic methods are often resource-intensive, time-consuming, and may raise ethical concerns regarding privacy, particularly for minors. In this study, we evaluate the feasibility of privacy-preserving machine learning models for ASD detection using children’s speech transcripts. By exclusively leveraging structured text-based inputs, our method inherently avoids the direct use of identifiable biometric data, such as raw audio or video, thus significantly reducing privacy risks. Although we have not implemented explicit cryptographic privacy measures (e.g., differential privacy, encryption), our approach minimizes privacy concerns inherently associated with sensitive biometric data. We conducted experiments on two datasets from the TalkBank repository, focusing on linguistic features such as Mean Length of Utterance (MLU) and Mean Length of Turn Ratio (MLT Ratio). Our results demonstrate strong predictive performance, with models achieving accuracy above 86% across both datasets. Notably, we found that a small, focused subset of features was sufficient to maintain this level of performance, reducing the need for extensive data collection, thereby enhancing privacy. These findings highlight the promise of computational linguistics in advancing non-invasive, ethical approaches to ASD detection, providing a foundation for future applications in clinical and educational contexts.

Fifty-two interpretable linguistic and demographic features with grid-searched hyperparameters reported and a shallow random forest appropriate to the sample size, and importance coefficients averaged across folds rather than taken from a single fit. But age is in the feature set and is confounded with group.

Diagnoses inherited from two peer-reviewed developmental-language studies with their own procedures, accessed through a curated academic repository whose contribution rules require consent and ethical approval.

Its three-class result including developmental delay (ROC-AUC 0.71) is the least confounded number it reports and the most useful.

included_articles.title: Towards screening of children students with autism spectrum disorder based on executive functions with serious game and machine learning approaches
included_articles.abstract: Educators face challenges in accommodating children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), particularly those without a deﬁnitive clinical diagnosis. Full-day schools provide a convenient setting to implement ASD screening techniques. Children diagnosed with ASD can receive customized interventions, allowing educators to customize teaching to individual needs and promote inclusive education. However, screening methods must seamlessly integrate into the educational environment, ensuring they are noninvasive and engaging. This study proposes a Serious Game (SG) tablet application that combines user requirements for inclusive design with Machine Learning (ML) techniques for screening analysis, oﬀering a playful tool for ASD screening. This tablet application includes three classical games designed to analyze executive functions (EF) in children. We recruited three inclusive education teachers to supervise 12 children aged between 3 and 6 years old, including 6 with ASD and 6 typically developing children. The teachers also facilitated the children’s use of our tablet application. Over three months, children completed 640 game matches, and preprocessing these matches resulted in a comprehensive dataset. We compared seven well-known and commonly used ML approaches: Random Forest (RF), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN), Logistic Regression (LR), Deep Learning (DL), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Naive Bayes (NB). According to our results, the RF model performed best with an accuracy of 96 %. Our study sheds light on the integration of playful approaches based on SG and ML techniques in educational environments, laying the groundwork for future research and practical applications to screen for suspected ASD among children in school settings.
included_articles.authors: Martins SRAL; Souza FAD; Teixeira LC; Leal BRA; Silva DMPF; Silva CMRD

assessments.support: Twelve children recruited by convenience through three education professionals, with sex composition unreported and children with co-occurring disorders or disabilities affecting application use excluded by design. The authors identify the small sample and convenience sampling as threats to external validity.

A purpose-built executive-function game battery with session-level telemetry, full grid search published for all seven models, and code and data deposited. No label-informed feature selection is described.
Clinical diagnosis is an inclusion criterion and its absence defines the control group, but the diagnosing procedure, instrument and assessor are not described.

Six hundred and forty game sessions from 12 children are partitioned by session, with no participant grouping described in either the 20/80 split or the 5-fold cross-validation, so roughly 53 sessions per child are distributed across training and test.

risk_of_bias.summary: High risk of bias for a single reason: the analysis unit is the game session, not the child. Six hundred and forty sessions from 12 children were split without participant grouping, so every test fold contains sessions from children whose other sessions trained the model, and the reported 96% is a within-participant estimate. Everything else about the study is well executed - three months of primary collection in the real deployment setting, age-matched groups, enumerated inclusion and exclusion criteria for both children and staff, guardian and professional consent, a theoretically grounded purpose-built task, seven algorithms under one published grid search, deposited code and data, and a six-item threats section that includes the ethics of school-based screening and the risk of stigmatisation. The one threat not identified is the one that governs the number, and the paper argues the opposite, treating high accuracy as evidence against overfitting.

screening_log.reason: Full text confirms 106 children (76 autistic, 30 typically developing) viewing biological-versus-geometric motion videos on a Tobii Pro TX300, 28 pixel-level image features reduced by genetic algorithm, neural networks learned per group to predict pixel fixation, and subject-level five-fold cross-validation reporting precision, sensitivity, specificity and AUC against SVM and feature-selection alternatives.

screening_log.title: Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis
screening_log.reason: Multivariate supervised machine learning applied to eye gaze features recorded in an immersive virtual environment to recognise autism - a computational model on behavioral data with an autism recognition target.

screening_log.title: Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms 55 children (35 autistic, 20 typically developing) experiencing a 24-minute multisensory CAVE virtual mall while wearing Tobii Pro Glasses 2, 144 gaze features across areas of interest and scenes, recursive feature selection with five algorithms across ten datasets, and accuracy, kappa, AUC, F1, sensitivity and specificity reported with standard deviations from repeated cross-validation.

screening_log.title: Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms
screening_log.reason: Machine-learning classifiers trained on head movement kinematics extracted by computer vision during conversation to identify autism - a computational model on behavioral (motor) data with an autism identification target.

screening_log.title: Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms 38 analysed children (18 autistic, 20 typically developing) answering ten yes-no questions while nodding or shaking their heads, head pose extracted by OpenFace 2.0 in pitch, yaw and roll, six kinematic features, five classifiers with exhaustive feature-combination search and leave-one-out cross-validation, reporting accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC.

screening_log.title: Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset
screening_log.reason: Machine-learning classifiers applied to eye-tracking scanpath images to predict autism - a computational model on behavioral data with an autism prediction target.

screening_log.title: Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms secondary analysis of a public scanpath image dataset from 59 children (30 autistic, 29 non-autistic), k-means clustering into four groups, nine classifiers applied to each cluster and to the pooled data with ten-fold cross-validation, and accuracy, AUC, F-measure, G-mean, sensitivity, specificity, fall-out and miss rate reported for every combination.

screening_log.title: Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder
screening_log.reason: A support vector machine trained on reaching-grasping kinematics to discriminate autistic from typically developing children - a computational model on behavioral (motor) data with an autism classification target.

screening_log.title: Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms 26 preschool children (13 autistic, 13 typically developing) performing a reaching-grasping task with optoelectronic motion capture, 17 kinematic features including principal-component motor synergy measures, SVM classification with leave-one-subject-out validation, and accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC reported alongside correlations with ADOS severity.

screening_log.title: Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a robot-mediated therapy and assessment system for autistic children with an automated methodology for attention assessment, reporting that the system represents the patient's attention state with 82.4% accuracy. Human participants, an instrumented behavioural measurement and an autism-related assessment target are present.

screening_log.title: Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary clinical study: 11 autistic boys with CARS2 scores of 30-36.5 recruited from Al Ain Hospital, interacting with a NAO robot carrying a chest-mounted mobile display across an adaptive 13-section scenario, with an automated attention score computed in real time and a long-term intervention arm in the 6 children who continued. Included as part of the verified corpus, and charted with the record made explicit that no autism prediction or classification is attempted - all participants are autistic and there is no comparison group - and that the reported 82.4% is agreement between the system's attention trend and the therapist's ratings, not a diagnostic performance estimate.

screening_log.title: Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning
screening_log.reason: Nine machine-learning algorithms applied to a purpose-built questionnaire to classify autistic from non-autistic children - a computational model with an autism prediction target.

screening_log.title: Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms 200 children (100 autistic, 100 non-autistic) in Lahore, a 21-item caregiver questionnaire covering developmental milestones, early sensory behaviours and perinatal and parental history, nine classifiers under three feature-selection schemes with an 80/20 split, and accuracy and confusion matrices reported. Included at the boundary of the behavioral-data criterion: only about six of the 21 items concern the child's behaviour, and those are retrospective caregiver recollections rather than directly measured behaviour - a distinction recorded here and carried into the per-group analysis.

screening_log.title: Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism
screening_log.reason: Machine-learning models trained on automatically extracted acoustic and prosodic voice measures to detect autism - a computational model on behavioral (speech) data with an autism detection target.

screening_log.title: Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms 118 youth (90 autistic, 28 typically developing) whose speech was extracted from four conversational ADOS-2 tasks, harmonic-model-derived pitch, jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio plus loudness, cepstral and spectral entropy measures, linear SVM classification with five-fold cross-validation and iterative class balancing, and AUC with 95% confidence intervals reported against an explicit chance classifier.

screening_log.title: Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images
screening_log.reason: Machine-learning classification of children as autistic or typically developing from eye-tracking scanpaths recorded during free viewing of images, using features derived from image content, fixation behaviour and centre bias.

screening_log.title: Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a supervised classifier (TreeBagger random forest) trained on 30 engineered features to discriminate autistic from typically developing children using the public Saliency4ASD eye-tracking dataset, with accuracy, recall, precision, F1, specificity, false positive rate and false negative rate reported on the challenge test set and benchmarked against seven competing submissions.

screening_log.title: Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data
screening_log.reason: Two deep-learning approaches - a synthetic-saccade generative baseline combined with real scanpaths, and a holistic image-plus-fixation-map network - trained to classify children as autistic or typically developing from free-viewing eye gaze data, with accuracy reported on validation and held-out test sets.

screening_log.title: Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms supervised binary classification of autism from eye-tracking scanpaths on the public Saliency4ASD dataset, with multilayer perceptron, branched MLP, ResNet18/50 and LSTM architectures, extensive ablation over inputs and representations, and accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC reported on both a validation split and a blind test set whose labels were withheld and scored by the challenge organisers.

screening_log.title: Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children
screening_log.reason: A deep neural network trained on 2D pose-estimation skeletons extracted from videotaped diagnostic assessments to classify young children as autistic or typically developing, reporting 80.9% accuracy with the prediction probability correlated to symptom severity.

screening_log.title: Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a VGG16-LSTM classifier trained on OpenPose skeletal representations of ADOS interaction videos from 136 children, with participant-wise train/test partitioning, segment-level predictions aggregated to subject level, an additional 101-child validation sample, and accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1 reported alongside correlations with ADOS calibrated severity scores, VABS-II adaptive functioning and best-estimate IQ.

screening_log.title: Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities
screening_log.reason: A supervised neural network trained on kinematic features of dragging movements captured by a tablet touchscreen, classifying 30 autistic and 30 typically developing children with a reported 93% accuracy.

screening_log.title: Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a feedforward neural network trained on 12 kinematic and touch features plus five task-identity variables extracted from touchscreen trajectories of 60 children performing a digital Leiter-3 battery, with accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and ROC reported and a stepwise feature-removal analysis of variable importance.

screening_log.title: A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children
screening_log.reason: A deep multimodal fusion framework combining resting-state EEG with task-state eye-tracking to classify 40 autistic and 50 typically developing children, reporting accuracy, sensitivity and specificity against unimodal and simple-concatenation baselines.

screening_log.title: A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms supervised classification of autism using eye-tracking features extracted from gaze during dynamic social video - a behavioural modality - fused with EEG features via stacked denoising autoencoders, evaluated by subject-independent stratified ten-fold cross-validation with accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, ROC/AUC and confusion matrices reported for four model variants. The eye-tracking modality alone is also evaluated and reported (86.67% accuracy), so the study contributes a behavioural-input result as well as a fused one.

screening_log.title: AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
screening_log.reason: A CNN-LSTM-attention model trained on 10-second video clips of children during an initiation-to-joint-attention protocol, classifying autistic from typically developing children with accuracy and precision reported.

screening_log.title: AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms supervised binary classification of autism from raw video of a structured joint-attention paradigm in 94 children, with subject-disjoint training, validation and two testing sets, accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and confusion matrices reported, and a soft attention mechanism used to verify that classification tracked the targeted social gesture.

screening_log.title: Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
screening_log.reason: A machine-learning approach fusing eye-fixation and facial-expression behavioural data with EEG to classify 40 autistic and 40 typically developing children, reporting 87.50% accuracy for the fused model.

screening_log.title: Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms supervised binary classification of autism using two behavioural modalities - gaze fixation distribution across K-means-derived areas of interest and CNN-based facial expression recognition during a social video - evaluated alone and fused with EEG under leave-one-out cross-validation, with per-modality accuracies and confusion matrices reported.

screening_log.title: An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images
screening_log.reason: A metaheuristic-optimised Kernel Extreme Learning Machine trained on gaze-path images to classify autism, reporting 98.8% average accuracy on a public eye-tracking dataset.

screening_log.title: An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms supervised binary classification of autism from eye-tracking-derived gaze-path images using a Kernel Extreme Learning Machine whose parameters are tuned by the Giza Pyramids Construction metaheuristic, with accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, Matthews correlation coefficient, F1 and ROC/AUC reported and compared against five alternative optimisers and three alternative classifiers.

screening_log.title: Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals
screening_log.reason: Eye-tracking gaze patterns from 153 adults analysed with automated computer-vision feature extraction, supervised classification into diagnostic groups, and unsupervised clustering, testing whether autism can be identified from gaze.

screening_log.title: Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a supervised Gaussian naive Bayes classifier trained to distinguish autistic from typically developing adults on four gaze features with 10,000 cross-validation iterations and a permutation-derived chance level, alongside a multivariate gaze-fingerprinting identification analysis and unsupervised Gaussian mixture clustering. Classification accuracy is reported (0.618 against a 0.607 chance level) together with per-participant correct- and misclassification frequencies, so this is a computational autism-classification study with a behavioural input, notwithstanding that its principal result is that classification fails.

screening_log.title: Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech
screening_log.reason: Three machine-learning models - random forest on acoustic features, CNN on spectrograms, and fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 - trained to classify children's speech as autistic or neurotypical from crowdsourced smartphone recordings, with accuracy reported for each.

screening_log.title: Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms supervised binary classification of autism from 850 child speech clips collected via a mobile game, with three model families compared under five-fold cross-validation and accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUROC, ROC curves and confusion matrices reported.

screening_log.title: Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection
screening_log.reason: Natural language processing measures and harmonic-model voice measures extracted from ADOS-2 transcripts and audio, used with support vector machines to classify 158 children as autistic or non-autistic, with ROC AUC reported for language-only, voice-only and combined models.

screening_log.title: Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms supervised binary classification of autism from seven automated language measures and ten automated voice measures derived from one ADOS-2 conversational task in 158 children, evaluated by leave-one-subject-out cross-validation with accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC with confidence intervals, DeLong tests between models, recursive feature elimination, and analyses of which participants each model detected or missed.

screening_log.title: Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers
screening_log.reason: Computer vision measurement of head movement rate, acceleration and multiscale-entropy complexity in 457 toddlers during tablet-delivered movies, with machine learning classification distinguishing autistic from neurotypical toddlers.

screening_log.title: Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms an SVM classifier with RBF kernel trained on computer-vision-derived head movement acceleration and complexity features to discriminate 41 autistic from 416 neurotypical toddlers, evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation with AUC and 95% confidence intervals reported for single-movie and combined-movie feature sets.

screening_log.title: Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study
screening_log.reason: Supervised machine learning classification of autism from rhythm- and intonation-relevant acoustic features derived from narrative speech samples in English and Cantonese, with AUC reported within and across languages.

screening_log.title: Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms linear SVM classification of ASD versus typical development using multivariate acoustic features extracted from a structured narrative task in two languages, with nested repeated 10-fold cross-validation, permutation-based significance testing, and AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and confusion matrices reported for six model configurations.

screening_log.title: Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings
screening_log.reason: Deep neural text encoders and three classification algorithms applied to picture-book narratives to classify 25 autistic and 25 typically developing participants, with sensitivity, specificity and predictive values reported.

screening_log.title: Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms supervised binary classification of autism from transcribed narrative utterances using ELMo and Universal Sentence Encoder embeddings with XGBoost, SVM and dense-layer classifiers, evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation, and benchmarked against two standardised instruments and two human raters on the same participants.

screening_log.title: Development of a visual attention based decision support system for autism spectrum disorder screening
screening_log.reason: A machine-learning decision support system using eye-tracking visual attention features to identify toddlers with autism from typically developing toddlers, reporting up to 87.5% accuracy.

screening_log.title: Development of a visual attention based decision support system for autism spectrum disorder screening
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms supervised classification of autism from area-of-interest gaze features recorded during a preferential-viewing paradigm, with four classifiers crossed with three feature-selection methods on two stimulus sets, evaluated by participant-based 10-fold cross-validation with accuracy, ROC area, F-measure, precision and recall reported for all 24 configurations.

screening_log.title: Different Eye Tracking Patterns in Autism Spectrum Disorder in Toddler and Preschool Children
screening_log.reason: Support vector machine classification of autism from eye-tracking fixation time percentages across ten areas of interest, reported separately for toddler and preschool cohorts.

screening_log.title: Different Eye Tracking Patterns in Autism Spectrum Disorder in Toddler and Preschool Children
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms SVM classification of autistic versus typically developing children from area-of-interest fixation time percentages in 95 toddlers and 78 preschoolers, evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation with accuracy, sensitivity and specificity reported and single-AOI classification accuracies tested against permutation-derived confidence intervals.

screening_log.title: Evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based medical device for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
screening_log.reason: A prospective multi-site trial of a gradient-boosted decision tree Software as a Medical Device combining caregiver questionnaire, home video analysis and clinician questionnaire inputs to produce an autism diagnostic recommendation, with PPV, NPV, sensitivity and specificity reported against blinded specialist consensus.

screening_log.title: Evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based medical device for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a machine-learning classifier operating on behavioural features derived from caregiver report, scored home video of the child's natural behaviour, and clinician observation, evaluated prospectively in 425 children aged 18-72 months against a blinded multi-specialist DSM-5 consensus reference standard, with predictive values, sensitivity, specificity, confusion matrix and covariate breakdowns reported.

screening_log.title: Extraction and Classification of Acoustic Features from Italian Speaking Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.
screening_log.reason: Acoustic features extracted with openSMILE eGeMAPS from Italian-speaking children's storytelling and classified with four supervised machine-learning methods to distinguish autistic from typically developing children.

screening_log.title: Extraction and Classification of Acoustic Features from Italian Speaking Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms supervised binary classification of autism from 16 statistically selected acoustic parameters in 14 autistic and 14 typically developing Italian children, using decision trees, K-nearest neighbours, random forests and support vector machines with accuracy, recall, precision, F1 and AUC reported on training and test splits.

screening_log.title: Eye Tracking-Based Diagnosis and Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques
screening_log.reason: Machine learning, deep learning and hybrid classifiers applied to eye-tracking scanpath images to distinguish autistic from typically developing children, with accuracies up to 99.8% reported.

screening_log.title: Eye Tracking-Based Diagnosis and Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms supervised binary classification of autism from gaze-path images using neural networks on hand-engineered texture features, transfer-learned convolutional networks, and CNN-plus-SVM hybrids, with accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, AUC and confusion matrices reported across six model configurations.

screening_log.title: Identification of Social Engagement Indicators Associated With
screening_log.reason: Computer-vision analysis of gaze fixation and visual scanning in home gameplay videos from a mobile app, with an LSTM trained to predict autism status from gaze patterns.

screening_log.title: Identification of Social Engagement Indicators Associated With
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms automated gaze annotation of 449 home videos from 95 children, permutation-tested group comparisons of fixation and transition patterns, and an LSTM classifier evaluated on a child-disjoint held-out test set with macro- and weighted-average precision and recall reported.

screening_log.title: Investigation of Eye-Tracking Scan Path as a Biomarker for Autism Screening Using Machine Learning Algorithms
screening_log.reason: Machine learning and deep neural network classifiers applied to eye-tracking scan path images to screen for autism, with AUC, sensitivity, specificity and predictive values reported.

screening_log.title: Investigation of Eye-Tracking Scan Path as a Biomarker for Autism Screening Using Machine Learning Algorithms
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms supervised binary classification of autism from 547 public gaze-path images using boosted decision trees, deep SVM, decision jungle and a convolutional neural network, evaluated by five-fold cross-validation on original and augmented datasets and additionally by leave-one-out cross-validation on a one-image-per-participant subset.

screening_log.title: Machine learning models using mobile game play accurately classify children with autism
screening_log.reason: Machine learning classifiers trained on mobile game play metadata to distinguish children with autism from neurotypical children, with AU-ROC and recall reported.

screening_log.title: Machine learning models using mobile game play accurately classify children with autism
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms supervised binary classification of autism from behavioural features derived from charades gameplay - per-emotion accuracy and response duration - in 49 children, evaluated by repeated nested cross-validation across four classifier families with AU-ROC, recall, accuracy and precision reported.

screening_log.title: Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction
screening_log.reason: Three acoustic feature-construction methods based on time-frequency independent component analysis compared with SVM and CNN classifiers on a speech dataset of autistic and comparison children, with recognition rates reported.

screening_log.title: Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms supervised binary classification of autism from children's speech recordings using unmixing-matrix, frequency-point and cepstral feature representations derived from time-frequency ICA, with accuracy, precision, recall and F1 reported for two classifiers across three feature methods.

screening_log.title: The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation
screening_log.reason: A speech-based system combining automatic speaker diarization with a convolutional network to estimate autism severity scores from ADOS recordings, with correlation against clinician-assigned scores reported.

screening_log.title: The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a computational model trained on 48 prosodic and acoustic features of children's speech to predict ADOS severity scores in 132 children, evaluated over 50 repeated participant-level train-test splits with Pearson correlation and normalised RMSE reported, alongside a comparison of two diarization approaches.

screening_log.title: The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe the use of a social robot in autism diagnosis, comparing turn-taking behaviour in five autistic and five typically developing preschool children across two robot-mediated games and reporting significantly reduced turn-taking in the autistic group. Human participants, an instrumented behavioural paradigm and an autism-related discrimination target are present.

screening_log.title: The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary observational study: ten children aged 5.5 to 6.5, five autistic and five typically developing, each playing two purpose-designed games ('Touch me' and 'Dance with me') with a NAO humanoid robot, with behaviour rated from video by six trained raters on a bespoke observational scale and compared by non-parametric tests. Included as part of the verified corpus, and charted with the record made explicit that no computational model is fitted and no individual receives a predicted class or score - the robot serves as a standardised elicitation device and all measurement is by human raters, so the study contributes as a paradigm-design and construct-validation contribution rather than as a classification result.

screening_log.title: Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a machine-learning classification of children with ASD versus typical development from oculomotor (gaze) time series recorded during a face-to-face conversation, reporting segment-level accuracy of 74.15% and child-level accuracy of 87.18% via a threshold classifier. Human participants, a behavioural modality (eye movement), a computational model (SVM) and an autism classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study: 19 children with ASD and 20 with TD (after exclusion of 4 for tracking failure), head-mounted Tobii Pro Glasses 2 at 50 Hz during a structured conversation, six entropy/range features of gaze allocation computed over non-overlapping segments of 1-10 s, SVM with forward feature selection and tenfold cross-validation classifying segments, then a threshold classifier aggregating segment labels to a per-child decision. Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and an ROC are reported. Eligible on all criteria. Charted with the caveat that the validation design pools segments across children (see rubric and appraisal).

screening_log.title: A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a sensorized toy car that captures children's play patterns through an accelerometer and newly added wheel shaft encoders, with machine learning used to screen for autism and a reported accuracy improvement of more than 10% from combining the two modalities. Human children, a behavioural modality (object play and manipulation), a computational classifier and an autism screening target are all present.

screening_log.title: A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study: 50 children aged 3-6 recruited at an autism centre in Tehran, of whom 46 (28 ASD, 18 TD) enter the classification; an instrumented toy car carrying an ADXL345 MEMS accelerometer and two Hall-effect shaft encoders on the wheels, streamed over Wi-Fi from an ESP8266; 44 acceleration features plus 10 new rotation/state features; backward-elimination feature selection; SVM, random forest and MLP compared under an 80/20 split with 5-fold cross-validation; accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and precision reported for six model/feature configurations. Eligible on all criteria.

screening_log.title: A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a variational autoencoder applied to motion features captured by a tablet-based psychometric scale in order to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities, reporting that the motion features of autistic children differ consistently from those of typically developing children. Human participants, a behavioural modality (touchscreen movement kinematics), a deep computational model and an autism identification target are all present.

screening_log.title: A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study: 60 children aged 5-10 (30 ASD diagnosed by DSM-5 plus ADOS-2, 30 TD), a tablet reimplementation of the Leiter-3 cognitive battery capturing finger trajectories at 40 Hz, 12 kinematic and touch features per trajectory averaged per task, a variational autoencoder with an attached softmax predictor trained jointly, 10-fold cross-validation reporting 91.2% +/- 5.6% accuracy, and a Monte Carlo feature-perturbation analysis of the latent space. Eligible on all criteria. Charted with the caveat that the unit of cross-validation is the task observation rather than the child (see rubric and appraisal).

screening_log.title: A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a computer-vision method combining human pose tracking, head pose estimation and automatic speech-based name detection to judge the response-to-name behaviour of autistic children, reporting 93.3% consistency with clinical diagnosis across 30 subjects and framing the work as an aid to early autism screening. A behavioural modality and a computational model are clearly present, but the sample is 29 autistic children and 1 typically developing child, and the target appears to be a behavioural response judgement rather than a diagnosis, so full-text assessment was needed to determine whether an autism prediction, screening, classification or severity-estimation target exists.

screening_log.title: A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation
screening_log.reason: Borderline, included on the severity-estimation limb of the eligibility criteria and flagged as a boundary case in the charting. The system's output is a judgement of whether a child responded to their name within 3 s of each call, aggregated into the 0-5 score that constitutes an ADOS-2 response-to-name item, with the clinician's score for that item as the reference. That is quantification of a symptom on a standardised diagnostic instrument, which falls inside 'severity-estimation target' as pre-specified for this review, and it is a genuine computational pipeline (iFlytek ASR for name-call timestamps, YOLOv3 person detection trained on the study's own images, HRNet pose estimation, OSNet re-identification for multi-object tracking, OpenFace head pose, then a rule-based decision on shoulder rotation angle, head yaw and frame counts). It is charted with three explicit caveats recorded throughout: the sample of 29 autistic children and 1 typically developing child cannot support any diagnostic discrimination claim; the abstract's phrase 'consistency between our proposed method and clinical diagnosis' refers to agreement with the clinician's response-to-name score, not with the autism diagnosis; and the authors themselves state that 'our experiment is an assessment of the response to name, not an assessment of autism risk'. Retaining it lets the review chart the distinct and under-represented category of automated administration and scoring of individual diagnostic-instrument items.

screening_log.title: Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe classification of autistic versus non-autistic children from eye-tracking data collected during a purpose-built computer game, using a multilayer perceptron trained by backpropagation, in 20 autistic and 20 comparison children, with precision 76.6% and accuracy 73.8% reported. Human participants, a behavioural modality (gaze during a face-recognition and expression-matching game), a computational classifier and an autism classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study: 20 autistic boys recruited from a rehabilitation clinic in Tehran and 20 boys from a public elementary school, a two-stage computer game built on the JAFFE facial-expression database, stationary eye tracking, an 18-feature matrix of fixation counts and fixation durations over defined screen regions, and a MATLAB multilayer perceptron with scaled conjugate gradient training evaluated by confusion matrix with precision, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and ROC curves across four feature subsets. Eligible on all criteria. Charted with the caveat, established by arithmetic on the reported percentages, that the modelled units are 240 game observations rather than 40 children and that the headline figures are totals across training, validation and test rather than held-out performance (see rubric and appraisal).

screening_log.title: Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a head-to-head comparison of 19 human raters (8 autism experts, 11 non-experts) against a computer-vision pipeline in predicting autism diagnosis from 3-minute silent videos of naturalistic conversation in 42 adults, reporting AI accuracy of 80.5% against 83.1% for experts and 78.3% for non-experts, with little overlap between AI and human errors. Human participants, a behavioural modality (facial and head movement during conversation), a computational model and an autism classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior
