screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study: 42 adults (15 autistic, 27 neurotypical) diagnosed by Clinical Best Estimate informed by ADOS-2 Module 4 and DSM-5, recorded during the interested condition of the Contextual Assessment of Social Skills with a blinded confederate; a 3D morphable model (3DI) with a purpose-modified 60-component localised expression basis quantifying facial movement and head rotation; 6,272 windowed cross-correlation features; a linear SVM evaluated by nested cross-validation with the correlation window as the only tuned hyperparameter, using 10-fold cross-validation repeated 100 times; and a parallel human-rating experiment on the same videos. Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV and accuracy are reported, together with a per-participant analysis of error overlap between AI and humans. Eligible on all criteria.

screening_log.title: Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a deep weakly supervised model that classifies children with autism from dynamic viewing patterns recorded by eye tracking, using a deep autoencoder for feature encoding and an LSTM for sequence scoring, evaluated on 165 children aged 3-6 from multiple centres in China with 96.73% accuracy, 96.85% sensitivity and 96.63% specificity. Human participants, a behavioural modality (gaze), a deep computational model and an autism screening target are all present.

screening_log.title: Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study: 333 children aged 3-6 (140 autistic, 193 typically developing) recruited from hospitals and schools in Shaanxi and Fujian provinces, a 6-minute passive viewing protocol of 82 images in four stimulus categories recorded on a SciEye 2.0 eye tracker at 140 Hz, superpixel-based deep autoencoder encoding pretrained on MS COCO, an LSTM trained under weak supervision with subject labels propagated to all stimuli, per-subject score aggregation with an Otsu threshold, and evaluation by accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC under a 50% subject-level split repeated in five random permutations, with ablation studies and a stimulus-discriminability analysis. Eligible on all criteria.

screening_log.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe classification of individuals as autistic or not from the text of their tweets, using decision trees, XGBoost, k-nearest neighbours and BERT over a dataset of 404,627 tweets subsampled to 90,000, with accuracy over 84%. Human participants (Twitter users), a behavioural modality (written language production), computational models and an autism identification target are all present.

screening_log.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study: 252 Twitter users (221 who state in their biography that they are autistic, 31 who do not), 1,014,723 tweets reduced to 404,627 after cleaning and subsampled to 45,000 per class, four models compared under a random 75/25 split with GridSearchCV hyperparameter tuning for the machine-learning models, and confusion matrices, F1 and accuracy reported. Eligible on all criteria as a study of computationally derived autism prediction from behavioural data, here language produced in a naturalistic setting. Charted with the caveat that the label is self-disclosure in a social-media biography rather than any clinical assessment, and that the split is over tweets rather than users (see rubric and appraisal).

screening_log.title: Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe automatic computer-vision quantification of facial landmark dynamics in 40 autistic and 396 typically developing toddlers watching movies on a tablet during a well-child paediatric visit, using multiscale entropy to estimate complexity and reporting higher complexity in the autistic group with information complementary to traditional facial affect analysis. Human participants, a behavioural modality (facial movement), computational analysis and an autism detection target are all present.

screening_log.title: Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study: 436 toddlers aged 17-36 months recruited at four paediatric primary care clinics, screened with M-CHAT-R/F and evaluated with ADOS-T where indicated; six social and non-social movies presented on an iPad with the front camera recording; face detection, identity-based tracking to isolate the child, 49-landmark extraction, affine normalisation to a canonical face with head-pose estimation, and low-pass filtering; a modified multiscale entropy analysis handling missing data and normalised for across-subject comparison; group comparisons with Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank and ANCOVA adjusting for missing-data percentage and landmark variation; and a decision-tree classifier with leave-one-out cross-validation reporting accuracy, precision, recall and ROC/AUC with DeLong comparisons, plus logistic-regression odds ratios. Eligible on all criteria.

screening_log.title: Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe machine-learning classification of adults with autism, adults with schizophrenia and children with autism against controls, using eye movement recorded during a facial emotion identification test, with random forest weighting of per-image outputs and convolutional neural networks on gaze heat maps. Human participants, a behavioural modality (gaze during facial expression recognition), computational models and an autism classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study: two datasets - 15 autistic adults, 15 adults with schizophrenia and 16 controls; 15 autistic children and 15 controls - all diagnosed under DSM-5 research criteria with ADOS-2 re-evaluation for autism and PANSS for schizophrenia; the Facial Emotion Identification Test administered while gaze was recorded on a Tobii Pro Fusion at 120 Hz; fixation, saccade and scan-path features plus gaze heat maps; a multilayer perceptron baseline and a CNN, each aggregated across 21 or 32 per-image decisions by hard voting or by random-forest weighting; and nested leave-one-participant-out cross-validation reporting accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and binomial tests against chance. Eligible on all criteria.

screening_log.title: Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe modelling of augmentative and alternative communication app usage patterns to identify differences between users with and without autism, using sequential, temporal and spectral representations of key presses with support vector machines and stacked autoencoders, reporting 70% and 82% diagnosis classification accuracy. Human participants, a behavioural modality (patterns of interaction with a speech-generating device), computational models and an autism classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study: usage logs from 6,033 users of the FreeSpeech iPad AAC application collected between January 2012 and May 2014, comprising over 2.5 million button presses, of which 5,372 users had valid usage patterns and 180 disclosed a diagnosis through a voluntary online survey (81 autistic, 99 non-autistic); key presses and app events encoded as pseudo-semantic numeric identifiers and modelled sequentially, temporally and spectrally over fixed windows; classification with SVMs, probabilistic neural networks, logistic regression, stacked autoencoders and deep belief networks; and k-means pseudo-labelling used to extend the labelled set. Eligible on all criteria, with substantial caveats about the self-reported reference standard and the pseudo-labelling step recorded in the charting.

screening_log.title: Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe development and validation of a joint attention-based deep learning system for detecting autism and assessing symptom severity from video of children performing a purpose-designed joint attention protocol, in 45 autistic and 50 typically developing children, reporting AUROCs of 99.5-99.8% for detection and 84.2-90.3% for severity. Human participants, a behavioural modality (joint attention behaviour on video), deep computational models and both autism classification and severity-estimation targets are all present.

screening_log.title: Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study reported to STARD standards: a prospective diagnostic study of 110 children aged 24-72 months across multiple South Korean sites, of whom 95 were analysed (45 autistic, 50 typically developing); K-CARS-2 screening for all, K-ADOS-2 and child psychiatrist diagnosis for the autism group, and cognitive assessment with Korean Bayley-II or K-WPPSI-IV; a purpose-built three-task joint attention protocol derived from the Early Social Communication Scales, video-recorded in a single 10-minute session; a CNN-LSTM-attention architecture evaluated by 10-fold group-wise (by individual) cross-validation with AUROC, accuracy, precision and recall reported with confidence intervals; and Grad-CAM, attention plots and hierarchical clustering for interpretation. Eligible on all criteria.

screening_log.title: Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe classification of autistic and typically developing children from 547 visualised eye-tracking scanpath images collected from 59 children, using InceptionV3 transfer-learned features fed to logistic regression and multilayer perceptron classifiers and compared against a custom convolutional neural network. Human participants, a behavioural modality (gaze scanpaths), computational models and an autism classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study on a reused public dataset: the 547 scanpath images from 59 children published by Carette/Cilia and colleagues, split 382/108/57 into training, validation and test sets; images converted from RGBA to RGB, resized to 100x100 greyscale for a custom five-level CNN or 299x299 with pixel normalisation for InceptionV3; features taken from the final convolutional layer before global average pooling and passed to logistic regression or a two-hidden-layer MLP; accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and ROC/AUC reported with confusion matrices. Eligible on all criteria, and charted as the fourth independent reuse of this dataset encountered in the review, which makes it valuable chiefly as a comparison point.

screening_log.title: SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe automatic extraction of semantic and pragmatic speech features - echolalia, semantic coherence, repetitive language - from conversational transcripts of 76 children (35 autistic, 41 typically developing) using natural language processing, with machine learning classification reaching 94% accuracy and SHAP analysis of feature contributions. Human participants, a behavioural modality (conversational language), computational models and an autism classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study on reused public corpora: transcripts of 76 children drawn from the Eigsti, Nadig and Flusberg datasets in the CHILDES databank; 77 linguistic features extracted with CLAN, L2SCA and BERT embeddings spanning morphosyntactic, lexical, syntactic-complexity and semantic-pragmatic categories; SHAP-based reduction to 63 features; comparison of six classifiers under a 90:10 split with grid search and 5-fold cross-validation for SVM hyperparameters; and reporting of accuracy, macro precision, recall and F1 against a majority-classifier baseline, with a feature-set ablation and SHAP interpretation. Eligible on all criteria.

screening_log.title: Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe classification of autistic against typically developing children from eye-gaze scan-path images enriched with temporal and pupil-velocity information, using convolutional and dense neural networks over four established eye-tracking paradigms, in 55 autistic and 32 typically developing children. Human participants, a behavioural modality (gaze), deep computational models and an autism classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study: 99 children enrolled and 86 with valid data (54 autistic per Table 1, 32 typically developing) viewing video batteries for Activity Monitoring, Dyadic Bid, Social Referencing and Theory of Mind tasks; gaze rendered as scan-path images at 1680 x 1050 then resized to 100 x 100 greyscale; DNN and CNN classifiers evaluated on 7:3 and 75:25 splits with rotation-based augmentation; and a series of stratification experiments covering diagnosis, age band within autism, sex within autism, the age-by-sex interaction, per-video-clip ablation, temporal windowing and velocity-based colour coding. Eligible on all criteria, and unusually informative for this review because its own auxiliary experiments quantify how strongly scan-path images encode age and sex.

screening_log.title: A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a convolutional deep neural network (T-CNN-ASD) classifying children as autistic or typically developing from eye-tracking scan-path images, reporting 95.59% accuracy under 10 rounds of cross-validation and comparison against random forest, decision tree, k-nearest neighbours and multilayer perceptron. Human participants, a behavioural modality (gaze scanpaths), a deep computational model and an autism classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study on a reused public dataset: the 547 scan-path images from 59 children (29 autistic, 30 typically developing) published by Carette and Cilia and colleagues, with participant statistics, stimulus protocol and eye tracker inherited from the source; images downscaled to 100 x 100, converted to greyscale and flattened; a custom network compared against four classical classifiers under 10-fold cross-validation; and an extensive hyperparameter grid over kernel size, stride, pooling, batch size, optimiser and layer/neuron configuration, with accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and a balanced-accuracy measure labelled F1 reported. Eligible on all criteria, and charted as the fifth independent reuse of this dataset in the review.

screening_log.title: A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a gradient boosting model predicting later autism diagnosis from electronic health records of 780,610 children, using birth parameters, growth metrics, developmental milestones and familial variables recorded during routine well-baby visits in the first two years, with AUC 0.86 and SHAP feature attribution. Human participants, a behavioural component (nurse-recorded developmental milestone attainment), a computational model and an autism prediction target are all present.

screening_log.title: A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study: a retrospective cohort of 780,610 Israeli children born 2014-2019 with at least two years of computerised well-baby records, of whom 1,163 received an autism diagnosis after age two; 100 candidate features reduced to 59 clinically relevant ones spanning 38 developmental milestones across gross motor, fine motor, language and personal-social domains plus birth, familial, growth and parent-concern variables; a gradient boosting model with 3-fold cross-validation compared against logistic regression, random forest and naive Bayes; and reporting of AUC, sensitivity, specificity, full confusion counts, a Youden-threshold risk stratification and SHAP feature importance. Eligible on all criteria. Charted with the note that the behavioural data are clinician-recorded milestone attainment rather than sensor-derived, which places it at the boundary of this review's modality scope but makes it uniquely informative about deployment at population scale.

screening_log.title: AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: “A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System”
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a deep learning system classifying children as autistic or non-autistic from facial images, trained on a Kaggle dataset of 2,836 images with MobileNet, Xception and InceptionV3 transfer learning, reporting 95% accuracy. Human participants (in the form of photographs), a computational model and an autism classification target are present. Whether static facial appearance constitutes behavioural data required full-text assessment.

screening_log.title: AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: “A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System”
screening_log.reason: Included at the boundary of the review's modality scope and charted as a negative exemplar. The study has two components: classification of autism from static facial photographs, which is facial morphology rather than behaviour; and a facial expression recognition module trained on AffectNet, which is behavioural. The paper frames the whole as identifying 'emotional and facial symptoms' and positions the combined system as an autism detection tool, so it meets the criterion of a computational model with an autism classification target applied to human facial data. It is retained because the review needs to characterise this branch of the literature - autism classification from scraped face photographs - and because its dataset construction, in which autistic images are scraped from autism-focused websites and non-autistic images gathered randomly from the internet, exemplifies a validity failure that recurs across that branch.

screening_log.title: An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a multimodal deep learning framework for autism diagnosis combining structured behavioural phenotypes with structural MRI, using GAMI-Net, a hybrid CNN-GNN, autoencoder fusion and a hypernetwork classifier on ABIDE-I, reporting 99.40% accuracy. Human participants, a computational model and an autism diagnostic target are present.

screening_log.title: An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study on ABIDE-I: 1,112 subjects (539 autistic, 573 control) from 17 international sites, combining T1-weighted structural MRI processed by a CNN-GNN over the Harvard-Oxford atlas with approximately 65-70 tabular phenotype fields processed by GAMI-Net, fused through an autoencoder into a 32-dimensional latent space and classified by a hypernetwork-generated multilayer perceptron. Included as part of the verified corpus. The record notes that neither modality is behavioural data in the instrumental sense that most of this review covers - the imaging is neuroanatomical and the tabular fields are diagnostic-instrument scores rather than observations of what a person does - so the study is charted as the corpus's principal representative of the neuroimaging-plus-phenotype branch, and its findings are interpreted accordingly.

screening_log.title: Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe quantification of interpersonal motor coordination in autistic and typically developing children filmed in conversation with an interviewer, using motion energy analysis and cross wavelet analysis, with machine learning classifiers reaching 85.37% accuracy on original coherence features and 92.68% with derived features. Human participants, a behavioural modality (whole-body movement synchrony during live social interaction), computational models and an autism classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study: 20 autistic and 21 typically developing children aged 6-13 filmed from a fixed side-view camera during a structured conversation with an interviewer at 80 cm; motion energy analysis extracting whole-body movement time series for both parties from manually drawn regions of interest; cross wavelet analysis producing coherence at 23 time scales; a pseudo-pair surrogate control constructed by pairing each child with an adult from a different video; four classifiers with forward feature selection evaluated by participant-level leave-one-out cross-validation; and reporting of accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and ROC curves. Eligible on all criteria. Charted with the note that this is a further analysis of the same participant cohort and recordings already charted in this review under a different modality (Zhao et al., oculomotor behaviour), which makes the two records directly comparable.

screening_log.title: Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe development of a diagnostic assessment model differentiating autistic from non-autistic adolescents and adults through machine-learning analysis of lexicogrammatical choices in interview and story-recounting transcripts from 64 autistic and 71 non-autistic individuals, reporting 80% accuracy, 82% precision, 73% sensitivity and 87% specificity. Human participants, a behavioural modality (spoken language production), computational models and an autism classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study: 64 autistic and 71 non-autistic Japanese participants aged 14 and above, diagnosed under DSM-5 by experienced clinicians with ADOS-2 as the primary instrument supported by SRS-2, WISC-IV or WAIS-III/IV, Vineland-II, AQ and PARS-TR; spoken language transcribed from ADOS-2 Module 3 and 4 interview and picture-book recounting tasks; a Systemic Functional Linguistics annotation scheme of lexicogrammatical tags applied manually and, in parallel, by an automatic Bi-LSTM sequence labeller; logistic regression and Bi-LSTM classifiers over tags, text and their combination; and evaluation by participant-level leave-one-out cross-validation with accuracy, 95% confidence intervals, precision, sensitivity, specificity, AUC and McNemar tests between models. Eligible on all criteria.

screening_log.title: Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe autism detection from facial features of the Autistic Children Facial Dataset, combining transfer-learned features from VGG16, ResNet and Inception with handcrafted descriptors (HOG, LBP, SIFT, PHASH) and five classical classifiers. The title's reference to 'emotion-based' detection suggested a behavioural component, but the abstract describes only static facial images, so full-text assessment was needed to determine whether any behavioural modality is present.

screening_log.title: Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms
screening_log.reason: Included at the boundary of the review's modality scope and charted, like the companion study on the same dataset, as a negative exemplar. The input is 2,936 static facial photographs from the same publicly scraped Kaggle collection already charted in this review, in which autistic images are drawn from autism-focused online sources and non-autistic images gathered separately - so the modality is facial appearance rather than behaviour, despite the title's framing as 'emotion-based'. No emotion or expression analysis of any kind is performed anywhere in the paper. It is retained because the review must characterise the size and reporting conventions of this branch of the literature, and because this study adds a specific and instructive feature to the picture: an exhaustive comparison of feature families and classifiers reported without any statement of how training and test data were separated.

screening_log.title: Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe facial expression recognition for autism spectrum disorder using a hybrid weighted quantum particle swarm optimisation and fast mask recurrent convolutional network, reporting 99.8% accuracy and framing the work as supporting autistic people whose facial cues are misread. Facial expression is within the review's behavioural modality scope and an autism-related application is claimed.

screening_log.title: Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study on facial expression recognition, evaluated on the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces corpus and the Extended Cohn-Kanade corpus, using a hybrid metaheuristic-plus-deep-learning architecture and reporting 99.8% accuracy for six-way emotion classification. Included as part of the verified corpus, and charted with the record made explicit that neither dataset contains autistic participants or autism labels, and that no autism classification, screening or severity-estimation target is modelled anywhere - so the study contributes to the review as an instance of autism-framed emotion-recognition work rather than as evidence about autism detection.

screening_log.title: Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe machine-learning classification of autistic and typically developing children from raw motion trajectories captured by a game-based tablet application during a drag-and-drop task, comparing a two-feature model on raw coordinates against a four-feature model adding velocity and acceleration, with accuracies of 0.76 and 0.90. Human participants, a behavioural modality (fine motor trajectory), computational models and an autism classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study: 20 children aged 3-6 (10 autistic, 10 typically developing) recruited in Naples, playing a purpose-built Unity drag-and-drop game on a tablet with finger coordinates logged at 20 Hz; 738 trajectories of 20-69 points retained after filtering; rotation normalisation of coordinates; two artificial neural networks compared, one on raw x-y coordinates and one adding velocity and acceleration; four-fold cross-validation with accuracy and ROC reported; and a simulation analysis generating trajectories with systematically varied acceleration to test that feature's causal role. Eligible on all criteria. Charted with the note that this is the same research group and the same rehabilitation centre as another study already charted in this review, though with a different sample and a different task.

screening_log.title: Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a deep learning model for detecting autism and visual sensory processing disorder from facial expressions together with heart rate and body temperature, using a hybrid optimisation algorithm for feature selection and network weight tuning, reporting 96% accuracy and 93% F1. A behavioural modality (facial emotion) and an autism detection target appear to be present, but the conflation of autism with sensory processing disorder as a single target and the absence of any participant description in the abstract required full-text assessment.

screening_log.title: Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain
screening_log.reason: Included on a narrow reading and charted with the record that the study is largely uninterpretable. A behavioural modality is present - seven facial emotion probabilities (angry, disgust, fear, happy, neutral, sad, surprise) plus derived positive and negative emotion scores - alongside two physiological variables, heart rate and body temperature, and the prediction target is a binary 'autism and visual SPD detection' label. That meets the letter of the eligibility criteria. However, the full text contains no participant count, no demographics, no recruitment description, no diagnostic procedure, no ethics statement and no consent statement; the data are described only as 'collected manually' from 'various subjects'; and the target conflates autism with visual sensory processing disorder into a single undifferentiated label. It is retained because the review should record the existence and characteristics of this segment of the literature, and because the one worked data table the paper provides is itself informative about what the reported 96.4% accuracy is likely to reflect.

screening_log.title: Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe Bayesian optimisation of one-dimensional convolutional networks for early autism diagnosis across four age-group datasets described as consisting of behavioural features, reporting 100% on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation coefficient and AUC, with an interactive web-based diagnostic tool developed for clinical and at-home use. A computational model, an autism diagnostic target and human data are all present.

screening_log.title: Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study on four public tabular datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository and Kaggle, covering toddlers (1,054 instances), children (292), adolescents (104) and adults (704), each modelled with baseline and Tree-structured Parzen Estimator-optimised one-dimensional convolutional networks under 80/20 splits, with a deployed web tool. Included as part of the verified corpus, and charted with the record made explicit that the modelled inputs are screening-questionnaire item responses - Q-CHAT-10 for toddlers and AQ-10 for the three older groups - and that in these datasets the class label is computed from those same items, which is the fact that determines what the reported results mean.

screening_log.title: Machine learning’s effectiveness
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe machine-learning evaluation of movement during a one-legged standing test to predict high autistic trait in 126 five-year-olds, using pressure-sensor and video data with a support vector machine over 16 explanatory variables, reporting accuracy, sensitivity and specificity of 1.000. Human participants, a behavioural modality (postural control during balance), a computational model and an autistic-trait prediction target are all present.

screening_log.title: Machine learning’s effectiveness
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study: 126 five-year-olds comprising approximately 99% of that age cohort in Sazacho, Nagasaki Prefecture, assessed during routine preschool medical examinations; a 48 cm pressure sensor recording centre-of-pressure distribution synchronised at 20 Hz with a webcam from which OpenPose estimated ten joint angles; 16 explanatory variables spanning centre-of-pressure sway, overall balance and correlations between joint angles and centre-of-pressure movement; a linear-kernel support vector machine evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation across three variable sets; and SHAP feature attribution plus correlation of predicted probability with SRS-2 total score. Eligible on all criteria, with the important qualification that the target is a Social Responsiveness Scale screening cut-off rather than a clinical diagnosis - so this is autistic-trait screening in a general population rather than case-control diagnosis, which is why it is charted separately from the diagnostic studies.

screening_log.title: Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a convolutional network with squeeze-and-excitation and multiscale attention, hyperparameter-optimised by a white shark optimisation algorithm, applied to facial imaging data to detect and classify autism, reporting 95.36% accuracy. Facial appearance and expression are within the review's behavioural modality scope, an autism target is present, and the work is a primary computational study.

screening_log.title: Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study on two image corpora: the Piosenka Kaggle facial-photograph dataset (2,866 images, 1,433 per class, ages 1-11) and the YTUIA dataset of face crops extracted with MTCNN from the Self-Stimulatory Behaviours Dataset YouTube videos (1,163 images after preprocessing). Models are SE-CNN and SE-MSF-CNN with white shark optimisation, evaluated within each dataset and, unusually for this branch, across datasets in both directions. Included, with the qualification recorded throughout this review for the Piosenka corpus: the paper states directly that the autism images were 'taken from websites and Facebook pages that included autism-related content', so class membership is confounded with image provenance. The study is nonetheless charted rather than excluded, because it is the only paper in the facial-photograph branch to conduct an explicit leakage investigation and to report cross-dataset transfer - both of which bear on the review's methodological synthesis.

screening_log.title: Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe four neural network models classifying autism from eleven linear and non-linear time- and frequency-domain features of EEG, reporting accuracies from 89.02% to 94.02%. Human participants, a computational model and an autism detection target are all present.

screening_log.title: Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study on resting-state scalp EEG obtained from the brain-computer interface group at King Abdulaziz University: 13 autistic boys aged 10 to 16 and 4 typically developing boys aged 9 to 16, recorded with a g.tec 16-channel cap at standard 10-20 positions, bandpass filtered 0.1-60 Hz with a 60 Hz notch and digitised at 256 Hz. Eleven linear and non-linear features were extracted and four neural architectures compared. Included as part of the verified corpus, and charted with the record made explicit that the modelled signal is a direct neurophysiological recording during rest rather than any observed behaviour - so the study represents the electrophysiological branch of this literature rather than the behavioural one.

screening_log.title: Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe 123 autistic and 123 neurotypical children aged 1-6 engaging in a 1.5-minute videotaped free play with fixed toys, coded for 19 autistic behaviours expanded into 81 digital behaviour indicators, with a stepwise logistic regression prediction model reaching AUC 0.826, sensitivity 85.4% and specificity 68.3%. Human participants, an observed behavioural modality, a computational prediction model and an autism target are all present.

screening_log.title: Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a prospective primary study conducted at Peking University Sixth Hospital and associated intervention centres between January and August 2022. Two hundred and forty-six children were assessed; autism was established by best-estimate clinical diagnosis from senior child and adolescent psychiatrists under DSM-5 criteria and corroborated by CARS-2, with exclusions for comorbid psychiatric diagnosis, major physical or neurological disease and prior psychotropic medication. A standardised 90-second free play task was videotaped, coded by three trained coders against a purpose-built manual with inter-coder consistency of 83.7-91.7%, converted into 81 count, duration and proportion indicators, and reduced by univariate screening and stepwise logistic regression to a five-predictor nomogram evaluated with ROC, Hosmer-Lemeshow, bootstrap and a calibration curve. Eligible on all criteria. The behavioural coding is performed by humans rather than by an algorithm, which the review records but does not treat as disqualifying: the modelling step is computational, the indicators are quantitative and designed by the authors to serve as a substrate for later automatic recognition, and the study occupies the same evidential position as the automated studies while being far better specified on the clinical side.

screening_log.title: Predictive model using autism
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a predictive model built from ADOS-2 Module 4 item scores to differentiate schizophrenia from autism in 40 and 50 adults respectively, reporting that the standard ADOS-2 algorithms failed to discriminate the groups while a six-item logistic model did. Human participants, an observational behavioural measurement, a computational prediction model and an autism-related classification target are all present, and the comparison group is another clinical population rather than typical development - the contrast this review has repeatedly noted as missing.

screening_log.title: Predictive model using autism
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a prospective clinical study at Showa University Karasuyama Hospital, Tokyo. Ninety adults with full-scale IQ above 85 were assessed - 40 with schizophrenia recruited April 2022 to December 2023 and 50 with autism recruited October 2018 to December 2020 - with diagnoses established by consensus among several expert psychiatrists under DSM-5 criteria. Critically for eligibility, the paper states that 'ASD diagnosis was a good clinical estimate, as neither the ADOS-2 nor the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R) was employed in the assessment process', so the index measurement is independent of the reference standard and none of the circularity that disqualified the questionnaire-item studies applies here. The modelled inputs are ADOS-2 Module 4 item codes - trained-clinician ratings of behaviour the participant produced during 15 standardised interactive activities designed to elicit social interaction, communication and repetitive behaviour - which is a record of observed behaviour under a controlled paradigm, the same category as the human-coded free-play indicators included elsewhere in this review and a different category from a respondent's questionnaire judgements. Included.

screening_log.title: The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe transfer-learning models classifying children's speech as typically or atypically developing and, in a four-class task, as typically developing, autistic, dysphasic or PDD-NOS, using discriminative fine-tuning and Wav2Vec 2.0, with fairness testing across gender. Human participants, a speech behavioural modality, computational models and an autism classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a secondary-analysis computational study on two child speech corpora: the De-Enigma corpus (55 autistic children aged 4-10 from Serbia and the United Kingdom, no control group, 115 minutes) used for pre-training, and the Child Pathological Speech Database (monolingual French-speaking children aged 6-18 recruited in Paris, containing autism, dysphasia and PDD-NOS groups alongside typically developing controls, 62 minutes) used for fine-tuning and evaluation. Two tasks are run - binary typicality and four-class diagnosis - with speaker-disjoint partitioning, equalised-odds fairness testing by gender, and comparison against published results on the same dataset. Eligible on all criteria, and of particular value to the review because the four-class task includes two non-autistic clinical comparison groups, which almost no included study attempts.

screening_log.title: Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a machine learning study distinguishing self-identified autistic Twitter users from a control group using 6,515,470 tweets, with per-tweet and per-profile classifiers reaching 73% accuracy and AUC 0.78 respectively. Human participants, a behavioural modality (naturally produced written language), computational models and an autism classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study on a purpose-built corpus: 3,137,952 tweets from 17,323 users who used #ActuallyAutistic and carried autism-related keywords in their profile descriptions, against 3,377,518 tweets from 171,273 control users, collected across 2014-2022 and analysed with TF-IDF and word2vec representations, classical classifiers and an attention-based bidirectional LSTM, with user-level splitting. Naturally produced written language is behaviour the person generated, which places the study within the review's modality scope alongside the speech and conversation studies. The label is self-identification through hashtag use rather than clinical diagnosis, which is a reference-standard limitation charted below rather than an eligibility failure - and one the authors state themselves, describing their target as 'use of the #ActuallyAutistic hashtag, an imperfect proxy for self-reported autism'.

screening_log.title: Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe two neural networks trained on video and audio features of semi-standardised social interactions in 160 children aged 1 to 5, combined into an ensemble reaching 82.5% accuracy for autism screening, with an analysis relating each modality to specific diagnostic-instrument characteristics. Human participants, two behavioural modalities, computational models and an autism target are all present.

screening_log.title: Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary study within the Geneva Autism Cohort: 80 autistic and 80 typically developing children aged 1.1 to 5.1 years, matched for age, sex and ADOS module, recorded during ADOS assessments between September 2012 and September 2023. A video network operating on OpenPose skeletal renderings over a black background and an audio network operating on the full audio band were trained independently and combined, with a 50-50 participant-level train-test split. Ethics approval, written parental consent, funding and competing interests are all declared, code is published on GitHub and a de-identified pose-estimation subsample on Zenodo. Eligible on every criterion.

screening_log.title: Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a supervised deep-learning method that both classifies autism and estimates continuous affect levels in autistic children from YouTube video frames, with an extended dataset carrying new arousal and valence labels. Human participants, a behavioural modality (facial appearance and expression), computational models and an autism classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study with two components: an autism-versus-non-autism image classifier trained on face crops from the Self-Stimulatory Behaviours Dataset (75 YouTube videos of children performing stimming behaviours, 73 retained), evaluated with subject-disjoint splits of 44/15/14 children and 5-fold cross-validation; and a continuous arousal and valence regressor, for which the authors created new annotations by having five trained raters continuously rate the SSBD frames. Facial appearance and expression are within the review's behavioural modality scope. Included, with the qualifications recorded below: the autism label rests on trusting parental YouTube uploads, and the composition and provenance of the non-autistic image class are never stated.

screening_log.title: A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a thermal-imaging framework extracting skin temperature and facial mood features from autistic children to classify autism severity continuously and adjust medication dosage, with a deep facial-mood model at 96.39% accuracy and Random Forest and SVM severity classifiers at 98.33%. Human participants, a sensed behavioural and physiological modality, computational models and an autism-related classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary study collecting original data: 1,500 thermal images from 30 male autistic children aged 5 to 15 at Don Guanella Special School in Chennai, captured with a FLIR USB thermal camera at emissivity 0.98 across four settings - outdoor play, classroom, dining area and veranda - plus 20 videos for real-time testing. Facial expression and skin-temperature dynamics are behavioural and physiological correlates of observable state, within the review's modality scope. Included, with the qualification that the classification target is a three-level severity grade rather than diagnosis, that no non-autistic comparison group exists, and that the source of the severity labels is nowhere stated.

screening_log.title: Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe deep transfer-learning models classifying autism from facial images of children using a 2,940-image Kaggle dataset, reporting 98% accuracy. Facial appearance is within the review's behavioural modality scope, an autism classification target is present, and the work is a primary computational study.

screening_log.title: Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a secondary-analysis computational study on the Kaggle autistic-children facial image corpus - 2,940 RGB images of children aged 2 to 14, 1,327 labelled autistic and 1,613 non-autistic - with three ImageNet-pretrained architectures compared under an 80/10/10 image-level split. This is the sixth study in the review built on this corpus family. Included, with the qualification recorded throughout: the paper states directly that the non-autistic images were 'randomly retrieved from web searches', so class membership is confounded with image provenance.

screening_log.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe classical and deep learning models detecting autism from linguistic features extracted from speech transcripts of 64 children aged 3 to 6, drawn from CHILDES and ASDBank, with accuracies of 77% to 84%. Human participants, a language-behaviour modality, computational models and an autism classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a secondary-analysis computational study on transcribed child speech from TalkBank: 30 autistic and 34 typically developing children aged 3 to 6, drawn from the Eigsti and Nadig corpora in ASDBank and supplemented from the Warren and Kuczaj corpora in CHILDES. Six linguistic features were computed in child-alone and child-to-investigator ratio forms using the Stanza NLP package, and seven models were compared over 50 random 75/25 train-test splits. Spontaneous speech produced during play is behaviour the child generated, within the review's modality scope.

screening_log.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a dual-stream deep learning architecture detecting autism from skeleton-based body movement in video, combining a Skepxel image stream with a graph-convolutional angular-feature stream. Human participants, a motor behavioural modality, computational models and an autism classification target are all present.

screening_log.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a computational study on two public skeleton corpora: the Gait Fullbody Dataset (100 children aged 4 to 12, 50 autistic and 50 typically developing, Kinect v2, 25 joints, one selected walking trial each) and the DREAM dataset (61 children aged 3 to 7, Kinect v1, 10 upper-body joints, 1,833 samples after excluding the non-spectrum class). Six image architectures were compared in the first stream and MSG3D against a Stack Transformer in the second, evaluated by 10-fold cross-validation repeated five and three times respectively. Whole-body movement captured by depth sensor is squarely within the review's modality scope.

screening_log.title: Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe acoustic analysis and deep learning classification of cries from 31 autistic and 31 typically developing children aged 18 to 54 months, reporting group differences in jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio and 90.28% classification accuracy. Human participants, a vocal behavioural modality, statistical and computational analysis, and an autism target are all present.

screening_log.title: Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a secondary analysis of the Khozaei et al. cry corpus collected in Iran: 62 children aged 18 to 54 months, 31 autistic and 31 typically developing, 24 boys and 7 girls in each group, with roughly six cry instances per child. Praat-derived perturbation measures were compared statistically between groups and a recurrent convolutional network was trained on cry spectrograms. Crying is vocal behaviour the child produces and is within the review's modality scope; the study also occupies a distinct position in the corpus as the only one analysing pre-linguistic vocalisation as such.

screening_log.title: Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm
screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a Bayesian-optimised Random Forest predicting autism from a dataset of behavioural, cognitive and demographic features, reporting 0.9890 accuracy. A computational model, an autism classification target and human data are all present.

screening_log.title: Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary computational study on the Kaggle version of the adult autism screening dataset - 704 rows and 21 features - modelled with a Bayesian-optimised Random Forest under 5-fold cross-validation. Included as part of the verified corpus, and charted with the record made explicit that the feature list the paper prints includes both 'result', which in this dataset is the sum of the A1-A10 item scores, and 'Class/ASD', which is that sum thresholded at the instrument's cut-off - so the outcome is a deterministic function of a predictor the paper enumerates among its own inputs.

Human participants, facial and motor behavioural modalities, a computational model and an autism target are all present.

screening_log.title: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a primary study with original data collection: 50 autistic and 50 typically developing children aged 5 to 9, recorded on webcam in a controlled environment during structured interaction tasks comprising simple games, gesture imitation exercises and short conversational prompts, 8 to 10 minutes per child yielding over 16 hours of full-HD video at 30 fps under standardised lighting. MediaPipe face mesh, pose and hands produced 1,639 numerical parameters per frame, modelled by a hybrid CNN+LSTM with stratified subject-independent 5-fold cross-validation. Eligible on all criteria.

screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe a deep learning system classifying autism status from 2,932 facial images and then assessing gelotophobia from facial expression, reporting 92% accuracy for autism identification. screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a computational study on a public facial-image corpus: 2,932 images, 1,466 labelled autistic and 1,466 neurotypical, described as 'collected from platforms such as Kaggle and ASD-related websites', with DeepFace producing 100,352 features per image and a multilayer perceptron classifying autism status under a 90.48/9.51 image-level split with 10-fold cross-validation on the training portion. screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe deep learning feature extraction from children's facial images for autism detection, using five pretrained CNNs as feature extractors with logistic regression as the classifier on a 2,940-image Kaggle dataset, reaching 88.33% test accuracy. Facial appearance is within the review's behavioural modality scope, an autism classification target is present, and the work is a primary computational study.

screening_log.title: Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a computational study on the Kaggle autistic-children facial image corpus (2,940 images), comparing five ImageNet-pretrained convolutional networks as frozen feature extractors - MobileNet, Xception, VGG16, VGG19 and EfficientNet - with logistic regression as the binary classifier, across three preprocessing configurations and with augmentation applied. This is the eighth study in the review built on this corpus family. Included, with the record made explicit that the corpus's autistic class is harvested from autism-associated online sources so that class membership is confounded with image provenance.

screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe two deep learning models - a hybrid ResNet50V2 plus InceptionV3 for autism prediction from facial images and an enhanced MobileNet for six-way emotion recognition in autistic children - reporting 95% and 73.3% accuracy on two public datasets. Facial appearance and expression are within the review's behavioural modality scope, an autism classification target is present, and the work is a primary computational study.

screening_log.title: Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a computational study on two Kaggle corpora: a facial-image dataset labelled autism versus non-autism, split 2,526 training, 280 testing and 80 validation - the standard partition of the Piosenka autistic-children collection charted seven times elsewhere in this review - and a separate emotion dataset of 703 training and 130 testing images. A hybrid ResNet50V2-InceptionV3 was fitted for the autism task and an enhanced MobileNet for six-way emotion recognition. Included, with the record noting that the autism corpus's positive class is harvested from autism-associated online sources, and that the reported metric set for the autism model is internally inconsistent.

screening_log.reason: Title and abstract describe lightweight ensemble convolutional networks classifying autism from facial photographs, comparing MobileNetV2 and EfficientNet variants and reporting an accuracy of 0.8299 for the best pairing. screening_log.title: Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy
screening_log.reason: Full text confirms a computational study on 2,936 facial images - 1,468 labelled autistic and 1,468 labelled normal - drawn from Kaggle together with data from an autism centre in Semarang, Indonesia, split 80:20 and modelled with five lightweight CNN ensembles combining MobileNetV2, ResNet50 and VGG16 with EfficientNet variants under averaging and voting. Included, with the record noting that the corpus mixes a public web-scraped collection with clinic-sourced images without reporting the proportion from each, and that no clinical ascertainment is described for either.

evidence_spans.text: Previous efforts to build ASD-detection AI models showed promising results. The low precision and recall scores of these models may be due to a lack of targeted behavioral biomarkers that can readily discriminate ASD from TD.

synthesis_text:
This review charted 170 computation-based autism prediction studies that use behavioural data, published between 2013 and 2026, and extracted for each one the same 23 review questions on participants, study conduct and reporting, behaviours, computational methods, and publishing trends. What follows synthesises those 170 charts. It is organised around the finding that emerged from them: that reported performance in this literature is governed almost entirely by how the evaluation was constructed and how the outcome was defined, and only marginally by the modality, the algorithm or the year.

**1. The performance distribution and what produces it.** Reported headline accuracies span roughly 50% to 100%, and the distribution is bimodal. One mode sits between 90% and 100%; the other between 55% and 85%. The separating variable is not the behavioural signal but the analysis unit. Where the unit of analysis is smaller than the person - an image, a video frame, a gaze sample, an EEG epoch, a cry instance, a thermal frame, a game session, an eye crop - and the data are partitioned at that unit rather than by participant, reported accuracy clusters in the upper mode. Where the unit is the person and folds separate people, it clusters in the lower one. The review found this pattern in every modality it examined. In eye tracking, Al-Adhaileh et al. (local_7432ffd7) partitioned 1,048,575 gaze samples from 59 children by sample and reported 99.78%; Alsharif et al. (local_44d3aef5) partitioned 547 scanpath images by image and reported 100% on 55 test images; Cheekaty and Muneeswari (local_bb4d1f7a) generated exactly 100 eye crops per child from 40 children and reported 97%. Against these, Zaragoza-Portoles et al. (local_5f57ba19) used participant-independent nested cross-validation on 45 children with a purpose-built social-attention paradigm and reported F1 0.641; Alagha et al. (local_d7b6fa00) aggregated scanpaths to the participant, listed leakage prevention among their contributions, and reported 0.96 with a fold standard deviation of 0.08 on 28 people. The same contrast appears in video (Jabbar et al., local_8d43288c: clip-level folds over 75 YouTube videos, 0.929 with fold standard deviations below 0.004), in facial photography (Zainal et al., local_945300a5: 15 photographs per child from 70 children split at image level, 90%), and in serious-game telemetry (Martins et al., local_b26db2f2: 640 sessions from 12 children split by session, 96%, where leave-one-child-out validation was available and unused).

**2. Circular and instrument-contaminated outcomes.** A second mechanism produces near-perfect figures independently of the split. In twelve charted studies the outcome variable is a deterministic function of the predictors. The clearest form is the checklist-threshold label: the Q-CHAT-10, AQ-10 and M-CHAT datasets encode a class as the thresholded sum of the ten items that are then supplied as features. Abu-Errub (local_ed30e24c) classified 292 of 292 test cases correctly and read this as confirming suitability for reliable clinical screening; Hajjej et al. (local_b9de0d7f) additionally manufactured a six-way teaching-method target with numpy by binning the same Q-CHAT total, predicted it at 0.9917 from the items the total is computed from, and offered the result to educators as a basis for decisions about individual children's education. Sankari (local_14df790d) mapped the mechanism without naming it, showing that every feature subset containing either the total or its summands performs well, and that with only age and sex as predictors sensitivity reaches 99.5% on a 69%-positive dataset. Rathod et al. (local_af9f4c12) is the only study in the corpus to identify the structure explicitly, writing that because the severity labels are deterministically derived from the same behavioural attributes used as model inputs, the prediction task constitutes a structured function-approximation setting and high classification performance should not be read as diagnostic accuracy. A related form is instrument inclusion: Jeon et al. (local_183eaef4) supplied CARS, the Social Responsiveness Scale, the AQ-10 total and the Q-CHAT-10 score as predictors of an autism-traits label and obtained accuracy, precision, recall and F1 of exactly 1.0000, then investigated the result by re-running the cross-validation at 2, 4 and 5 folds - the correct instinct aimed at the partition rather than at the feature list.

**3. Data provenance.** Sixteen of the 170 studies reuse the same web-scraped corpus of children's facial photographs, reporting accuracies from 81.0% to 99.8% on it. Across those sixteen, reported accuracy tracks model capacity and evaluation looseness rather than signal: frozen-extractor designs with linear classifiers occupy the low end, end-to-end fine-tuning under image-level splits the high end. Several of the papers state the provenance confound in their own methods sections - images randomly retrieved from web searches, or from websites and Facebook pages that included autism-related content - and none tests a source-held-out evaluation. Two members of this branch describe the corpus as something it is not: Attar and Paygude (local_986436f2) report age bands, six ethnicity categories, urban/rural residence and a four-way facial-morphology partition for a Kaggle image folder that carries no metadata, and describe 2D photographs as 3D scans with a 0.9 mm landmark localisation error; Alsharif et al. (local_44d3aef5) report 547 images as 547 children in their abstract. The branch's own terminal case, Vasundhara et al. (local_e54c304c), inadvertently supplies its most informative result: in an out-of-distribution probe, one of its two detectors classified a photograph of a dog as Autistic and a leaf as Nonautistic. No other study in the branch tests a non-face input.

**4. Differential diagnosis.** The review's most consequential quantitative findings come from the small number of studies that included a second clinical group. Antoli et al. (local_b6ac2b98) ran one pipeline against both a typically developing group and a developmental-language-disorder group: F1 0.86 for ASD versus TD, and 0.63 for ASD versus DLD at near-balanced class sizes, concluding that the approach is more effective as a screening tool than for differential diagnosis. Assaf et al. (local_1b457442) found the same shape in speech transcripts - ROC-AUC 0.87 to 0.93 against typical development, 0.71 once developmental delay was included. Hickman et al. (local_69b10fe4) compared autistic and parkinsonian movement directly and found no kinematic feature that was shared between the two conditions while also differing from controls, refuting the anecdotal resemblance that motivates part of this literature. And local_cd7545e2 supplies the field's reference point: the ADOS-2 itself reaches AUC 0.562 and 0.569 when asked to discriminate autism from schizophrenia, with false-positive rates of 45.0% and 52.5%. Read together, these establish that a substantial part of the ASD-versus-typical-development performance reported across the corpus is a clinical-versus-non-clinical distinction rather than an autism-specific one.

**5. Demographic confounding.** Van der Burg et al. (local_7b19a959) quantified this directly, and are the only study to do so: the same models reached 81.8% accuracy on their unbalanced sample and 74.0% once age and gender were matched, and they reported the matched figure as primary. Roughly eight accuracy points were attributable to demographics alone. That number bears on many studies in this corpus that report large unadjusted between-group imbalances - a 42.9-point sex gap in local_7432ffd7 (86.2% male ASD against 43.3% male TD), a 32-point gap in local_4ceee075, an approximately two-year age gap between groups in the Nadig corpus used by local_1b457442 with age entered as a predictor, and a 22-point sex gap alongside significant receptive-vocabulary differences in local_b6ac2b98. Van der Burg et al. also diagnose the questionnaire branch's two failure modes in print: that higher published accuracies were obtained either by predicting an AQ cut-off rather than an official diagnosis, or by using groups unbalanced on demographic features that were themselves included as predictors.

**6. Reference standards.** Across the corpus, outcome ascertainment ranges from documented clinician diagnosis to a folder name. At the strong end, local_b6ac2b98 required formal DSM-5 diagnoses from licensed clinical teams and stated that early-age diagnoses are provisional and may evolve; local_bb4d1f7a diagnosed with DSM-5 criteria and CARS scores and explained candidly that ADI-R and ADOS evaluations are not widely available in India; local_7b19a959 drew participants from a national autism register. At the weak end, sixteen facial-image studies inherit labels from image folders with no diagnostic procedure of any kind, and twelve questionnaire studies use a checklist threshold. A distinct third category is the constructed label: local_b9de0d7f generated a teaching-method target with numpy, local_af9f4c12 constructed four severity strata as cut points on a weighted item sum, and Firat (local_231757c7) synthesised an entire severity class by averaging another class's feature vectors and adding Gaussian noise - and said so in the abstract.

**7. Ethics and governance.** Reporting is bimodal and the split does not follow the modality. Complete reporting - named committee, reference number, guardian consent, and in two cases separate consent for publication of images - appears in local_bb4d1f7a (IRB-2024-0057, with publication-specific consent), local_b6ac2b98 (Cordoba REC 4393), local_4da2b941 (USC 26/2023), local_7b19a959 (VCWE-2020-041R1), local_69b10fe4 (ERN_18-1800B and ERN_16-0281AP5) and local_945300a5 (036/EA/FK/2025, with teacher accompaniment during data collection). At the other end sit explicit exemptions granted on the ground that data are public: local_13c1f46d states that the study did not involve direct experiments on humans because publicly available Kaggle datasets were used; local_183eaef4 waives consent on the ground that prior reuse of a dataset establishes a general consensus regarding its use for research; local_24fefc5f declares ethical approval Not Applicable without reasoning; local_e4c2a776 declares that the article contains no studies with human participants while analysing 2,940 photographs of children, alongside a data-availability statement asserting that no dataset was analysed. Two studies invert the pattern in an instructive way. Lakhan et al. (local_367db0b6) build an entire machine-unlearning framework on the correct observation that once a newborn's data enters a training set there is usually no mechanism to remove it when parents withdraw consent - and obtain no ethical review or consent for their own use of that data. Almadhor et al. (local_e771fb69) propose a federated privacy architecture invoking GDPR and HIPAA, with no ethics statement and nine test cases. Against these, Assaf et al. (local_1b457442) make privacy the design criterion and state plainly that a major drawback of facial-image approaches is the invasion of privacy, especially for minors - a critique that applies directly to sixteen studies in this same corpus.

**8. What the careful studies find.** Fifty-three studies were rated below high overall risk of bias (17 low, 36 some concerns). The five whose designs most directly support a generalisation claim - participant-level or participant-disjoint partitioning, clinician-ascertained outcomes, and an explicit baseline or control - converge on a narrow range. local_4da2b941 (601 adults, participant-disjoint two-layer cross-validation, deposited code) reached R = 0.85 at best and 0.54 at worst on dimensional targets, with only 36.3% of individual predictions within 5% of the true score. local_7b19a959 reached 74.0% on matched data from performance tasks, 83% from the AQ alone, and 92% combined. local_5f57ba19 reached F1 0.641 with a majority-class baseline built into the design. local_b6ac2b98 reached F1 0.86 against typical development and 0.63 against another neurodevelopmental condition. local_69b10fe4 reached mean test accuracy 0.73 for clinical versus non-clinical and 0.93 for ASD versus Parkinson's on test partitions of roughly 13 to 19 people. The envelope these define - roughly 0.6 to 0.9 depending on the comparison, with wide uncertainty at realistic sample sizes - is the field's actual current performance, and it is not the envelope the corpus as a whole reports.

**9. Behaviours and modalities.** Where the behavioural analysis is done well it produces falsifiable claims rather than leaderboard entries. local_bb4d1f7a's feature ablation concluded that continuous attention rather than transition phases carries severity information; local_b6ac2b98 found that broad social/non-social areas of interest outperform fine decomposition by facial region and emotion; local_5f57ba19 localised the audio-visual advantage to the pre-speech phase; local_69b10fe4 found the ellipse - the shape most used in the drawing-task literature - the least discriminative of four; local_7d7f1fcc found that its audio model's top ADOS items were non-vocal (showing, pointing, sensory exploration, hand mannerisms); local_1b457442 identified mean length of utterance and mean length of turn ratio, the child's conversational share, as the leading discriminators. Against these, a large fraction of the corpus - and nearly all of the facial-image branch - reports no interpretable behavioural finding at all, and several studies name interpretability as a contribution while reporting no attribution output.

**10. Publishing trends.** Output rises steadily across the window (1 study in 2013, 17 in 2019, 22 in each of 2021 and 2022, 27 in 2025, 14 in the partial 2026), and venue composition shifts with it. Clinical and specialist journals in the corpus (Translational Psychiatry, Research in Autism, Journal of Neurodevelopmental Disorders, Frontiers in Psychiatry, Frontiers in Neuroscience) contain most of the well-designed studies; general engineering and computing venues contain most of the near-perfect ones. Review cycles are correspondingly short in the second group - 32 days for a paper with no ethics statement and no limitations section (local_7432ffd7), 40 days for one reporting accuracy 1.0000 (local_183eaef4), 44 days for one reporting 100% on 55 images (local_44d3aef5) - and long in the first (180 days for local_69b10fe4, 133 for local_4da2b941, 127 for local_b6ac2b98). Framing follows the same division: the specialist venues produce abstracts that concede modest performance, benchmark against published clinical-viability thresholds, and label the work proof-of-concept; the computing venues produce claims of clinical deployment, real-time screening and diagnostic replacement, expressed as a position above quoted figures from other papers.
bias_assessment:
Overall risk of bias was rated high for 108 of the 170 included studies, moderate for 36, low for 17 and unclear for 9, using QUADAS-2 domains supplemented by four PROBAST-derived appraisal domains.

The distribution is not evenly spread across the four QUADAS-2 domains. Patient selection was rated high in the great majority of studies, driven by convenience or secondary use of public corpora with no recruitment, eligibility or demographic reporting; by comparison groups that were not recruited but produced by scoring; and by unadjusted between-group differences in age, sex and language ability. The index test domain was rated high wherever preprocessing steps that use outcome information preceded the split - class-conditional mean imputation (local_e771fb69), feature selection or SHAP-based pruning computed on the full dataset (local_7432ffd7, local_183eaef4, local_af9f4c12), pre-split synthetic oversampling (local_ed30e24c), and augmentation applied before partitioning (local_1d856900). Reference standard was the most consistently high-risk domain: in sixteen studies the outcome is a folder name on a web-scraped photograph, in twelve it is a checklist threshold on the predictors, and in three it is a variable the authors constructed. Flow and timing was rated high wherever the analysis unit was smaller than the participant, which was the single most frequent defect in the corpus.

Three cross-cutting patterns deserve separate statement. First, methodological care and estimand validity are independent: local_183eaef4 applied child-level cross-validation, grid search, Wilcoxon and Friedman model comparison and three explanation methods, and obtained accuracy 1.0000 because four autism instruments were in its feature set. Second, several studies read the symptoms of leakage as evidence against it - near-zero fold variance treated as robustness (local_8d43288c), test accuracy exceeding training accuracy treated as good generalisation (local_e4c2a776), high accuracy treated as reducing the likelihood of overfitting (local_b26db2f2). Third, internal arithmetic frequently fails: confusion matrices that do not match the stated evaluation size (local_986436f2), a headline accuracy computed over the whole dataset including the training portion (local_e04bcd32), mAP@0.5:0.95 within 0.03 points of mAP@0.5 (local_e54c304c), 25,000 positive cases drawn from a 10,000-sample dataset and described as class-balanced (local_367db0b6), and a stated total exceeding the accounted-for participants (local_8ff20c48).

Against this, a minority of studies were assessed as low or moderate risk on design grounds, and they share identifiable features: clinician-ascertained diagnoses obtained independently of the data, participant-level or participant-disjoint partitioning, hyperparameter selection nested inside the training portion, an explicit trivial baseline or label-randomisation control, confidence intervals or fold variance reported, and limitations sections that reason about mechanisms rather than listing generic caveats.
limitations:
This review has five limitations that bear on how its conclusions should be read.

First, the corpus was supplied rather than searched.
