The 170 records are a human-verified set assembled by the reviewer requesting this synthesis, not the output of a documented database strategy, so no recall claim can be made and the search-provenance fields of the PRISMA flow are necessarily incomplete. Identification counts, database queries and date filters were not available; one duplicate was detected and removed during corpus construction, giving 171 records identified and 170 after deduplication. All 170 were assessed on full text, and none was excluded on eligibility grounds, per the reviewer's instruction that the set was already human-verified.

Second, screening and charting were performed by a single assessor without independent duplicate extraction, so no inter-rater reliability can be reported. The charting instrument was applied uniformly - all 170 records carry the same 23 review questions, the same QUADAS-2 domains and the same four appraisal domains - but consistency is internal rather than externally verified.

Third, no meta-analysis was attempted and none would be defensible. The reported performance figures are not commensurable: they are computed over different analysis units (persons, images, frames, gaze samples, sessions), against outcomes of radically different provenance (clinician diagnosis, checklist threshold, folder label, author-constructed variable), under evaluation designs that differ in whether participants can appear on both sides of a split. Pooling them would produce a number whose principal determinant is the prevalence of leakage in the corpus.

Fourth, the review charts what studies report, and reporting quality is itself a variable under study. Where a paper does not state its class balance, its split proportions or the number of distinct participants behind its images, the charting records that absence but cannot recover the missing quantity. Several conclusions in this review - particularly about the number of distinct children behind reused image corpora - therefore rest on inference from arithmetic rather than on stated fact.

Fifth, the modality grouping used in the per-group analysis is an approximate assignment derived from each record's charted data-type field, not a categorisation applied by the original authors. Studies that combine modalities, or that describe their data in the terms of an adjacent literature, may be assigned to a group that does not fit them well; the group-level statements should be read as descriptions of tendencies within loosely defined families rather than as properties of exhaustive, mutually exclusive categories.

Diagnostic accuracy of behavioural compu.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of behavioural computational models for autism (reported)

Risk of bias.explanation: 108 of 170 studies at high overall risk of bias; the dominant defects are analysis units smaller than the participant, outcomes that are deterministic functions of the predictors, and reference standards consisting of folder labels or checklist thresholds.

Inconsistency.explanation: Reported accuracy is bimodal (roughly 55-90% and 90-100%) and the modes are separated by evaluation design rather than by modality, population or algorithm.

Indirectness.explanation: The comparison in the great majority of studies is autism versus typical development, not autism versus the clinical alternatives a screening decision must distinguish; the four studies including a second clinical group show performance falling by 20-25 points.

Imprecision.explanation: Confidence intervals are almost never reported; several headline figures rest on test sets of 9 to 55 units, and one perfect result carries a computed 95% interval of 39.8-100.0%.

Publication bias.explanation: Sixteen reuses of one public image corpus report 81.0-99.8% with no negative results; the corpus contains almost no studies reporting that a modality did not work.

Diagnostic accuracy of behavioural compu.summary: Very low certainty that reported accuracies estimate diagnostic performance. The subset of studies with participant-level partitioning, clinician-ascertained outcomes and clinically meaningful comparison groups supports a screening-aid level of performance (roughly 0.6-0.9 depending on the comparison) with low to moderate certainty.

Discrimination of autism from other clin.outcome: Discrimination of autism from other clinical conditions

Risk of bias.explanation: The four studies addressing this question were among the best designed in the corpus, with clinician-ascertained diagnoses and participant-level evaluation.

Inconsistency.explanation: All four converge: performance falls substantially when the comparison is another clinical group.

Indirectness.explanation: This is the directly relevant comparison for a screening or diagnostic claim.

Imprecision.explanation: Sample sizes are 45 to 552 participants and confidence intervals are seldom reported.

Publication bias.explanation: Only four studies address the question; too few to assess.

Discrimination of autism from other clin.summary: Moderate certainty that computational behavioural models discriminate autism from other neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions substantially less well than from typical development (F1 0.63 versus 0.86; ROC-AUC 0.71 versus 0.87-0.93), and that the gold-standard ADOS-2 also performs near chance against a comparison clinical population (AUC 0.562).

data_charting_rubrics.title: Very early detection of Autism Spectrum Disorders based on acoustic analysis of pre-verbal vocalizations of 18-month old toddlers
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Santos JF; Brosh N; Falk TH; Zwaigenbaum L; Bryson SE; Roberts W; Smith IM; Szatmari P; Brian JA
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder (high-risk siblings later diagnosed)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Speech and vocalisation
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Very early screening/detection: binary classification of ASD vs typically developing 18-month-old toddlers from pre-verbal vocalisations
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of a prospective longitudinal infant-sibling cohort; cross-sectional classification at the 18-month assessment
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single 18-month assessment analysed; ADOS sessions 24-52 minutes; participants followed from 6 months with reassessment every 3-12 months and final diagnosis at 36 months
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Clinician-administered ADOS Module 1 session (semi-structured); child vocalisations manually segmented and labelled
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Clinic/laboratory - videotaped ADOS assessment sessions within the Canadian Infant Sibling Study
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Final diagnosis at age three by a blinded experienced clinician using gold-standard tools: medical history, ADOS and ADI-R
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported; authors note toddlers with other non-ASD language development disorders were not included and that this remains to be investigated
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported (binary ASD vs TD only)
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - low-risk age-matched typically developing controls from families without ASD history
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes - low-risk controls followed and assessed in the same longitudinal protocol
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes - explicitly age-matched
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not stated as matched (similar ratios: 15/8 vs 13/7)
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Audio: pre-verbal vocalisations (speech, babble, cry, squeal, laugh, whine, yell) extracted from video recordings
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: ADOS Module 1 administration; vocalisations manually segmented and labelled, then automatically re-segmented by energy thresholding (4522 instances)
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Video recordings of ADOS sessions (audio extracted, 44 kHz downsampled to 16 kHz); VoiceSauce (UCLA SPAP Lab) and in-house MATLAB scripts for feature extraction; DTREG software for classifier training/evaluation
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: No - subset of the existing Canadian Infant Sibling Database
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - not stated; clinical cohort data
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Sensitive data (video and audio of identifiable toddlers) used; no anonymization, consent or data-protection procedure described in the paper beyond acknowledging participating families
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted acoustic-prosodic features with per-instance summary statistics (mean, standard deviation, range)
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: F0; formants F1-F4 and bandwidths B1-B4; harmonic magnitudes H1, H2, H4, A1, A2, A3 and corrected differences (H1*-H2*, H2*-H4*, H1*-A1*, H1*-A2*, H1*-A3*); subharmonic-to-harmonic ratio; RMS energy; cepstral peak prominence; harmonic-to-noise ratio in three bands; jitter; shimmer; voiced ratio
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: VoiceSauce; custom MATLAB scripts; spectral subtraction for noise reduction
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes - via the classifiers' inherent feature selection in DTREG
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Built-in feature importance from SVM and PNN training in DTREG
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: PNN: means of H1*-A3* and H4, standard deviation of H1, range of F0 and shimmer. SVM: means of energy, H4, H1*-A3*, jitter and A2
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not quantified directionally; authors infer a difference in vocal quality between TD and ASD groups
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Support vector machine (RBF kernel) and probabilistic neural network
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 10-fold cross-validation for performance; leave-one-out cross-validation and 4-fold grid search for hyperparameter selection; no independent external test set; cross-validation performed over vocalisation instances rather than explicitly subject-independent folds
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, AUC
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: PNN with feature combination FC3 (mean, SD, range): 97.7% accuracy, 95.6% sensitivity, 100.0% specificity, AUC 0.97. Best SVM (FC1): 79.1% accuracy, 82.6% sensitivity, 75.0% specificity, AUC 0.87
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Sufficient discriminability exists in pre-verbal vocalisations of 18-month-olds to separate toddlers later diagnosed with ASD from typically developing controls; PNN outperformed SVM across all feature combinations, and vocal-quality measures (notably H1*-A3*) plus F0 range were the most discriminative features. The authors present this as the youngest age range reported in the acoustic-prosodic autism literature at the time.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Vocal quality measures (H1*-A3*, H4, H1 variability), F0 range and shimmer
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Test whether results hold once toddlers with other non-ASD language development disorders are included; extend the analysis to audio collected at the 9- and 12-month routine assessments
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Small sample (n=43). Cross-validation appears to be performed at the vocalisation-instance level with thousands of instances from 43 children, creating a substantial risk of subject leakage between folds and inflating the 97.7% accuracy; the paper does not state subject-independent partitioning. No external validation. Class composition of the instance-level data differs from the participant-level split.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: ASD group (n=23, high-risk siblings later diagnosed) and typically developing low-risk controls (n=20); both explicitly reported with sizes in Table 1. No other-diagnosis group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'toddlers with ASD', 'ASD group', 'typically developing (TD) controls', 'control', 'high-risk siblings', 'low-risk'. Person-first/diagnosis-first language throughout; no identity-first ('autistic') usage.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=23, 15M/8F, age 18 +/- 0.42 months; controls n=20, 13M/7F, age 18 +/- 0.23 months. Controls explicitly described as age-matched; gender matching not claimed.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Blinded experienced clinician at age three using medical history, ADOS and ADI-R; ADOS Module 1 sessions also provided the recordings.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Standardized developmental and language tests are mentioned as part of the cohort protocol but no cognitive, linguistic or adaptive scores are reported for the analysed sample. Comorbidities not described; other non-ASD language disorders explicitly absent from the sample.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: very early detection (screening) as binary ASD vs TD classification at 18 months. Main finding: PNN reached 97.7% accuracy / 95.6% sensitivity / 100% specificity (AUC 0.97), outperforming SVM by up to 55.6% relative accuracy, indicating ASD markers are present in pre-verbal vocalisations.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Clinic setting (videotaped ADOS assessments). Existing data: a subset of the ongoing Canadian Infant Sibling Study database, analysed retrospectively.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: ADOS Module 1 semi-structured assessment (24-52 min), designed for preverbal children; vocalisations manually segmented/labelled into speech, babble, cry, squeal, laugh, other, then automatically re-segmented by energy thresholding.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Underlying cohort is longitudinal (from 6 months, reassessed every 3-12 months, diagnosis at 36 months) but the analysis is cross-sectional at the 18-month visit. Data are highly sensitive (video/audio of identifiable toddlers); the paper describes no anonymization, consent or data-protection procedure.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: video recording of ADOS sessions (audio at 44 kHz, downsampled to 16 kHz). Software: VoiceSauce (UCLA SPAP Laboratory), in-house MATLAB scripts, DTREG for classifier training and evaluation.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No dataset access statement; the Infant Sibling Database is a restricted clinical cohort. No code availability, no seeds, no hyperparameter table; feature set and classifier settings are described narratively only. Not reproducible as reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported/identifiable bias: very small sample (n=43); single national cohort; high-risk-sibling recruitment means the ASD group is not a general-population sample; male-skewed (28/43 male); English-speaking homes only; instance-level analysis with unequal vocalisation counts per group (2592 control vs 1930 ASD instances). Authors acknowledge only that non-ASD language-disorder toddlers were not included. Reviewer-identified: probable subject leakage in cross-validation and absence of any external validation.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Include toddlers with other non-ASD language development disorders to test specificity; extend the acoustic analysis to the 9- and 12-month assessments.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Speech/voice: pre-verbal vocalisations (babble, cry, squeal, laugh, whine, yell, single words) - acoustic and prosodic properties, not linguistic content.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality; no fusion. No combination with clinical scores or demographics.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning. Algorithms: support vector machine with RBF kernel, and probabilistic neural network (Parzen-window Bayes network).
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted acoustic-prosodic features computed per 25 ms frame and summarised per vocalisation instance as mean, standard deviation and range (three nested feature combinations FC1-FC3).
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, AUC. Headline: 97.7% / 95.6% / 100.0% / 0.97 (PNN, FC3).
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Feature importance from the classifiers' inherent selection (DTREG). Most informative: vocal-quality measures H1*-A3* (selected by both classifiers) and H4, H1 variability, F0 range, shimmer, energy, jitter, A2.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: 10-fold cross-validation plus leave-one-out and grid search for hyperparameters, described as guarding against overfitting. No external or independent test set, no held-out site, no class-imbalance handling, no statistical comparison between classifiers, no deployment or real-time claim beyond 'may be used to assist clinicians'. Subject-independence of folds is not stated.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: Autism, biomarker, prosody, SVM, PNN. Task vocabulary: 'very early detection', 'automated acoustic-prosodic analysis', 'markers of autism', 'assist clinicians with very early diagnosis'.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: ICASSP 2013 (IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing) - a technology/computational (signal-processing) venue, not an autism or clinical venue.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2013 - the earliest study in this corpus. The paper characterises the field as having focused on verbal children over age three and positions itself as pushing the age range down to 18 months; it does not otherwise analyse field-level trends.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Use of Machine Learning to Identify Children with Autism and Their Motor Abnormalities
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Crippa A; Salvatore C; Perego P; Forti S; Nobile M; Molteni M; Castiglioni I
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder (low-functioning, preschool)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Motor and kinematics
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Proof-of-concept computer-aided diagnosis: binary classification of low-functioning preschool children with ASD vs typically developing children from a simple upper-limb movement, and identification of a candidate motor signature
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study (proof-of-concept)
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session; 10 trials per participant (5 left hand, 5 right hand); testing session ~15 minutes, ~30 minutes analysis per subject; ASD group recruited over an 18-month period
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Structured motor task: reach, grasp a rubber ball and drop it into a hole, demonstrated by the experimenter without verbal cues
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Clinic/laboratory - IRCCS Eugenio Medea Scientific Institute, Child Psychopathology Unit
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: DSM-IV-TR criteria by a child neuropsychiatrist with autism expertise, independently confirmed by a child psychologist through direct observation and parent discussion; ADOS administered to 7 of 15 children only
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: All participants drug-naive with normal or corrected-to-normal vision; TD children had no history of social/communicative disorders, developmental abnormalities or CNS-related medical disorders. Other neurodevelopmental conditions not included
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: ADOS Social 11 +/- 2.2, Communication 7 +/- 1.5, SBRI 2 +/- 1.6 - but only for the 7 children who received ADOS; not used in modelling
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developing children recruited by local pediatricians and from kindergartens
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes - no history of social/communicative, developmental or CNS disorders
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No - matched on mental age, not chronological age; chronological age differed significantly (p<0.001)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Yes - balanced (3 vs 2 girls; chi-square p>0.05)
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Motor kinematics: 3D upper-limb movement trajectories from passive markers on wrist and hand
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Reach-to-grasp a 6-cm rubber ball from a support, then transport and drop it through a 7-cm hole in a see-through box; 10 trials (5 per side), order counterbalanced, practice trials given
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: SMART D optoelectronic system (BTS Bioengineering, Italy) with eight infrared motion-analysis cameras at 60 Hz (spatial accuracy <0.2 mm); 1-cm passive markers on wrists, hand dorsum, ball and box; MATLAB R2013b with the bioinformatics/biolearning toolbox; fifth-order Butterworth 8-Hz low-pass filter; self-written segmentation software
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - newly collected kinematic data, but not released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Informed written consent obtained from all legal guardians; research approved by the institute's ethics board in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Marker-based kinematic data are less identifiable than video; no explicit anonymization procedure described
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted kinematic summary features per sub-movement
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 17 features across two sub-movements: total movement duration, number of movement units, peak velocity, time of peak velocity, peak acceleration, time of peak acceleration, peak deceleration, time of peak deceleration (per sub-movement), plus delta wrist angle at ball drop
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: MATLAB (MathWorks) with self-written movement segmentation and parameter estimation code
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Fisher discriminant ratio (FDR) based feature ranking, with the full 17-feature ranking reported across all 30 leave-one-out rounds
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Seven features, all from sub-movement 2 (transport-to-goal): total duration, delta wrist angle, number of movement units, time of peak deceleration, peak acceleration, time of peak velocity, peak velocity
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Children with ASD showed slower and more fragmented transport movements (longer total duration, more movement units) and inappropriate hand inclination at ball drop; ANCOVA confirmed lower peak velocity and acceleration and later peak timings in the ASD group
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Support vector machine with a linear kernel (Salvatore et al. 2013 pipeline), preceded by FDR-based feature selection
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-out cross-validation over 30 subjects, repeated for feature subsets of size 1 to 17; no independent test set. Feature selection is described as part of the pipeline but is not clearly nested inside the LOO loop
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, specificity, sensitivity (with the maximum and the mean across feature-subset sizes reported)
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Maximum accuracy 96.7% (specificity 93.8%, sensitivity 100%) with seven selected features; overall mean across feature-subset sizes 84.9% accuracy (mean specificity 89.1%, mean sensitivity 82.2%)
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Kinematic analysis of a simple reach-grasp-drop task discriminated low-functioning preschool children with ASD from mental-age-matched TD peers with up to 96.7% accuracy using only seven features, all belonging to the goal-directed transport sub-movement. The authors interpret slower, more fragmented goal-oriented movement with atypical wrist inclination as a possible motor signature of autism reflecting disrupted movement-sequence planning.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Goal-directed transport sub-movement features: longer total duration, more movement units, delayed peak deceleration and velocity, lower peak acceleration and velocity, atypical delta wrist angle
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Replicate in a larger sample and validate on data the classifier was not trained on; include females with ASD, high-functioning children and adults to generalise across the spectrum; train with chronological-age-matched TD participants as well; collect ADOS on the full clinical sample to correlate kinematics with clinical severity; include other neurodevelopmental conditions (intellectual disability, developmental delay, developmental coordination disorder) to test specificity to ASD rather than neurodevelopmental disorder in general
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: One of the earliest and most-cited motor-kinematics ASD classification papers. Groups matched on mental age but differing significantly on chronological age and IQ - so the classifier may partly separate developmental level rather than autism, despite ANCOVA covariate control at the univariate level. Maximum-accuracy-over-feature-subsets reporting (96.7%) is an optimistically selected value; the mean of 84.9% is the more defensible number, and the authors themselves foreground the maximum in the abstract.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: ASD (n=15, low-functioning preschool) and typically developing controls (n=15). Both explicitly reported with demographics in Table 1. No other-diagnosis comparison group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with autism (ASD)', 'children with ASD', 'low-functioning autistic children', 'patients', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'healthy controls', 'clinical group'. Predominantly person-first with occasional 'autistic children' and clinical framing ('patients').
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=15, 3F/12M, chronological age 3;5 +/- 7.7 (2.8-4.6 yrs), IQ 75 +/- 13.4; TD n=15, 2F/13M, chronological age 2;6 +/- 5.2 (1.7-2.9 yrs), IQ 105 +/- 12.7. Matched on mental age (2;6 vs 2;7, n.s.) and gender-balanced, but NOT chronological-age matched (p<0.001) and IQ differed (p<0.001).
custom_fields.RQ1.4: DSM-IV-TR diagnosis by a child neuropsychiatrist specialised in autism, independently confirmed by a child psychologist via direct observation and parent discussion. ADOS was administered to only 7 of the 15 ASD children, so the gold-standard instrument does not cover the whole clinical sample.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Yes - IQ and mental age assessed with the Griffiths Mental Development Scales for all participants; ADOS Social/Communication and Stereotyped Behavior and Restricted Interests subscores reported for the 7 children who received ADOS. Comorbidities: participants were drug-naive with normal/corrected vision; other neurodevelopmental conditions were excluded from the design and flagged as future work.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: proof-of-concept binary classification (computer-aided diagnosis) of low-functioning preschool ASD from a simple upper-limb movement. Main findings: maximum accuracy 96.7% (specificity 93.8%, sensitivity 100%) with seven features; overall mean accuracy 84.9%; all discriminative features belong to the goal-directed transport sub-movement, suggesting a motor signature tied to movement-sequence planning.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Clinical/laboratory setting at an Italian research hospital. Newly collected data (ASD group recruited over 18 months; controls via pediatricians and kindergartens); no existing dataset used.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A structured reach-grasp-drop task: grasp a 6-cm ball from a support and drop it into a 7-cm hole in a transparent box, 10 trials per child (5 per hand, counterbalanced), demonstrated non-verbally by the experimenter with individually varying practice trials.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional - a single ~15-minute session per child. Data are marker-based 3D kinematics rather than video or audio, so less directly identifying; informed written consent from legal guardians and institutional ethics-board approval under the Declaration of Helsinki are reported, but no anonymization or data-protection procedure is described.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: SMART D optoelectronic system (BTS Bioengineering) with eight infrared cameras at 60 Hz, sub-0.2 mm accuracy; 1-cm passive markers on wrists, hand dorsum, ball and box. Software: MATLAB R2013b with the biolearning toolbox, fifth-order Butterworth 8-Hz low-pass filter, self-written segmentation and parameter-estimation code.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No data availability statement and no code release; the SVM pipeline is cited to prior work (Salvatore et al. 2013) and the feature set and validation scheme are described in enough detail to re-implement in principle, but no hyperparameters beyond 'linear kernel', no seeds and no released data. Not reproducible as reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors: very small sample; classifier highly specific to the training sample (preschool, low-functioning); need for females, high-functioning children and adults; no ADOS on the full sample; no other neurodevelopmental comparison groups; predictive value constrained by population base rate. Identifiable in review: strong male skew (25/30 male); chronological-age and IQ imbalance between groups confounded with diagnosis; single-site recruitment; maximum-over-feature-subsets accuracy reporting; feature selection not demonstrably nested within the LOO loop.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Replicate in a larger sample with a truly held-out dataset; extend to females, high-functioning children and adults; also train against chronological-age-matched controls; collect full ADOS to correlate kinematics with clinical severity; add other neurodevelopmental conditions to test ASD specificity; guide follow-up neuroimaging or genetic work on the identified phenotype.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Motor behavior: 3D upper-limb kinematics (velocity, acceleration, deceleration profiles, movement units, movement duration and wrist orientation) during a goal-directed reach-grasp-drop action.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality; no fusion across behavioral modalities. IQ and chronological age are used as ANCOVA covariates in the group comparison but are not combined with kinematics in the classifier.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning. Algorithm: linear-kernel support vector machine, with Fisher discriminant ratio feature ranking as the selection step.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted kinematic summary features - 17 scalar measures derived from segmented sub-movements (durations, movement units, peak velocity/acceleration/deceleration and their timings, wrist-angle change), not raw time series.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, specificity, sensitivity. Headline: 96.7% / 93.8% / 100% at seven features; mean across feature-subset sizes 84.9% / 89.1% / 82.2%. No AUC, F1 or confidence intervals.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Fisher discriminant ratio scores rank the features, and the full 17-feature ordering across the 30 LOO rounds is reported. Most informative: total duration, delta wrist angle and number of movement units of the transport sub-movement - interpreted as slower, more fragmented goal-directed movement with atypical hand inclination.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Leave-one-out cross-validation over 30 subjects, described as returning an almost unbiased error estimate. No external or independent test set (the authors explicitly name this as the main limitation), no held-out site, no class-imbalance handling (groups are balanced 15/15), no statistical test on classification performance, and no real-time or deployment claim - though practical feasibility is argued from the 15-minute session and 30-minute analysis time.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: Autism spectrum disorder; Kinematics; Classification; Machine learning; Support vector machines. Task vocabulary: 'computer-aided diagnosis', 'pattern classification', 'predict group membership', 'motor signature of autism', 'proof-of-concept'.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders - an autism-specific clinical journal, not a computational venue.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2015. The paper characterises prior pattern-classification work in ASD as dominated by neuroimaging (structural MRI, DTI) with only isolated behavioral examples (automated vocal analysis), and positions kinematics as a cheaper, less intrusive alternative - an explicit statement of the field's shift from neuroimaging toward behavioral signals.

data_charting_rubrics.title: ADHD and ASD Classification Based on Emotion Recognition Data
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Uluyagmur-Ozturk M; Arman AR; Yilmaz SS; Findik OTP; Genc HA; Carkaxhiu-Bulut G; Yazgan MY; Teker U; Cataltepe Z
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Facial emotion recognition task performance
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Differential screening/classification: predict participant diagnosis (ASD vs ADHD vs typically developing, and several binary regroupings) from emotion-recognition task responses
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study with multiple redefined binary class groupings
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single computerised session per participant; 40 emotional images presented; no session duration reported
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Human children and adolescents (mean ages 9-10.5 years)
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Computerised emotion-recognition task: participants viewed facial expression images and answered 'What is the emotion of this person?'; response correctness and latency logged
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Clinic - Marmara University Medical Faculty Hospital Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Outpatient Department
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: ASD diagnosed by DSM-IV-R criteria; ADHD diagnosed using the Turkish version of K-SADS-PL; both under the clinical supervision of the department head
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 18 ASD; 30 ADHD
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: ASD mean 10.5 years; ADHD mean 9.46 years (no SD reported)
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported; ASD participants described as high-functioning
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described beyond 'typically developing'; recruited from the same outpatient clinic referrals
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not claimed; group mean ages are broadly similar (10.5 / 9.46 / 9.22) but no matching procedure or statistical test is reported
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not reported - no gender data at all
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Stated as typically developing; no confirmation procedure described
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Behavioral task logs: response correctness (binary) and response latency (milliseconds) per stimulus image
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Emotion-recognition judgement on 40 facial-expression images from the Cohn-Kanade database, shown at a certain expression strength
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Custom application presenting Cohn-Kanade images and logging responses; the acknowledgements mention an eye tracker and sensors from ITU Kullab and tazi Machine Learning Solutions, but no eye-tracking or sensor data are used in the reported analysis
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - newly collected application-log data, but not released; the stimuli come from the existing public Cohn-Kanade database
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Marmara University Medical Faculty Ethical Advisory Board approval obtained (protocol 09.2014.0194) and parental consent forms signed. The collected data are task logs rather than identifiable media, so re-identification risk is low; no anonymization procedure described
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Per-stimulus behavioral response features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Response correct (RC, 0/1) and response time (RT, ms) for each of 40 images, plus their combination (RC&RT); image identity is the feature index
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Not stated (application log processing); ReliefF and symmetric uncertainty implemented for selection/correlation analysis
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Partly - selected feature counts are reported and symmetric-uncertainty values per class grouping are tabulated, but the identity of the most informative images is not given
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: ReliefF feature weighting (k=10, Manhattan distance) and symmetric uncertainty correlation analysis
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not identified specifically; the paper reports how many images were selected (e.g. 15 features for the best control-vs-others result) but not which emotions or images were most discriminative
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported for individual features; the related-work section notes children with ASD make significantly more errors, but this study reports no direction of effect of its own
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Decision tree, random forest, support vector machine, k-nearest neighbour, AdaBoost - all five run per class grouping and data type
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Not stated - no cross-validation scheme, train/test split, or repetition count is reported anywhere in the paper. Random oversampling to n=30 per group was applied to correct class imbalance, with no statement that it was performed inside a validation loop
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy only (best and mean across data types)
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Best ASD-vs-others: 91.11% accuracy (AdaBoost with ReliefF on response-time data). Control-vs-others: 80% (k-NN, 15 selected features; 68.89% without feature selection). ADHD-vs-ASD: ~90% on response-time data with AdaBoost, and 80% on combined RC&RT; best mean accuracy across data types 85.56% for the ADHD-ASD grouping
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Response correctness and latency in a facial emotion-recognition task carry enough signal to separate ASD, ADHD and typically developing children; ReliefF feature selection improved accuracy in general, and redefining the three-class problem into binary groupings raised accuracy further. The strongest result was distinguishing ASD from the combined ADHD-plus-control group (91.11%) using response times.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Response-time (latency) data outperformed response-correctness data for ASD discrimination; symmetric uncertainty was highest for the ADHD-vs-ASD contrast (0.336 RC, 0.449 RT)
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: None stated - the conclusion restates the results without proposing future work
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Notable as an early differential-diagnosis attempt (ASD vs ADHD vs TD) rather than the usual ASD-vs-TD binary. However, methodological reporting is weak: no validation scheme is stated at all, random oversampling to balance classes appears to be applied to the whole dataset before classification (a standard leakage route that inflates accuracy), no gender data, no age matching test, and the 'group redefinition' procedure selects the most favourable class grouping post hoc. Accuracies should be treated as unvalidated. Acknowledgements mention an eye tracker that plays no part in the reported analysis.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Three groups: ASD (n=18), ADHD (n=30) and typically developing controls (n=13). Group sizes are reported; this is one of the few corpus studies with a non-autistic clinical comparison group. No demographic breakdown beyond mean age.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'participants with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)', 'participants with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)', 'typically developing children', 'control group', 'people with ASD', 'participants with asd'. Consistently person-first/diagnosis-first; no identity-first usage.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=18 (mean age 10.5), ADHD n=30 (mean 9.46), control n=13 (mean 9.22). No standard deviations, no age ranges, and no gender distribution for any group. No matching procedure and no statistical test of group comparability is reported. Class imbalance was handled after the fact by random oversampling to 30 per group.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: ASD: DSM-IV-R diagnostic criteria. ADHD: Turkish version of K-SADS-PL. Both applied at the Marmara University Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Outpatient Department under the supervision of the department head. No ADOS or ADI-R.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive-functioning measures reported. ASD participants are described as high-functioning and older than the low-functioning samples in prior work, but no IQ figures are given. Comorbidities are not described, and it is not stated whether ASD-ADHD co-occurrence was excluded - a material omission given the three-group design.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: differential classification of diagnosis (screening rather than diagnosis) from emotion-recognition task behavior, including several binary regroupings of the three classes. Main findings: ASD-vs-others 91.11% (AdaBoost + ReliefF on response time); ADHD-vs-ASD ~90% on response time; control-vs-others 80%; feature selection and group redefinition both improved accuracy.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Clinic setting - a child and adolescent psychiatry outpatient department. Newly collected application-log data; stimuli drawn from the existing public Cohn-Kanade facial-expression database.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A computerised emotion-recognition task: 40 facial-expression images shown up to a certain expression strength, with the participant answering 'What is the emotion of this person?'. Response correctness and latency were logged. Participants were recruited from outpatient referrals and randomly assigned to sessions.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session; no session duration or number of sessions reported. Data are behavioral logs (correctness and millisecond latencies), not identifiable media, so sensitivity is low. Ethics approval (Marmara University Medical Faculty Ethical Advisory Board, protocol 09.2014.0194) and signed parental consent are reported; no anonymization or data-protection procedure is described.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: A custom application displaying Cohn-Kanade images and logging responses and latencies; the platform, display hardware and timing precision are not specified. The acknowledgements credit an eye tracker (ITU Computer Engineering Kullab) and sensors (tazi Machine Learning Solutions), but neither contributes data to the reported analysis.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No data availability statement, no code release, no hyperparameters (beyond ReliefF k=10), no seeds, and - critically - no statement of the validation scheme. The Cohn-Kanade stimulus set is public, but the collected participant data are not. Not reproducible as reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors: class imbalance across groups, attributed to 'technical problems' and corrected by random oversampling to 30 per group. Identifiable in review: very small control group (n=13); no gender data at all, so sex bias cannot be assessed in a literature where ASD samples are typically male-skewed; no age matching; single-site outpatient recruitment; no reported handling of ASD-ADHD comorbidity despite a three-way design; post-hoc selection of the best-performing class grouping and classifier; oversampling apparently applied before rather than within validation; and no validation scheme reported, so all accuracies are of unknown optimism.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: None proposed. The conclusion summarises results only and states no open questions or future directions.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Behavioral task performance in response to facial-expression stimuli: response correctness and response latency. This is recorded behavior in a perceptual task rather than a directly sensed modality such as gaze, speech or motion.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Two behavioral streams (correctness and latency) are combined by simple feature concatenation (RC&RT) and compared against each separately - an early-fusion feature-level combination. No integration with clinical scores, demographics or parent report.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning. Algorithms: decision tree, random forest, support vector machine, k-nearest neighbour and AdaBoost, each evaluated with and without ReliefF feature selection across eight class-grouping definitions.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Symbolic/event-based per-stimulus features: a 40-dimensional vector of binary correctness values and a 40-dimensional vector of millisecond latencies, indexed by image identity, plus their concatenation. No raw time series, embeddings or images are fed to the models.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy only - reported as best and mean across the three data types. No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC or confidence intervals, which is a serious gap for imbalanced clinical classes.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: ReliefF weighting (k=10, Manhattan distance) selects informative images, and symmetric uncertainty quantifies feature-class correlation per grouping (highest for ADHD-vs-ASD: 0.336 on correctness, 0.449 on latency). The number of selected images is reported but not which images or emotions they were, so no interpretable behavioral feature emerges.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Effectively unaddressed. No cross-validation scheme, train/test split or repetition count is reported; no external validation; no held-out site; no statistical comparison between classifiers; no deployment or real-time claim. Class imbalance is handled by random oversampling to 30 instances per group, apparently applied to the full dataset before classification, which would leak duplicated samples across any train/test boundary.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: ReliefF feature selection; human-computer interaction; classification; emotion recognition; Autism; ASD; ADHD; ASD diagnosis; ADHD diagnosis. Task vocabulary: 'classification of the participants', 'predict the diagnosis', 'differentiate participant groups'.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: 15th IEEE International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications (ICMLA) 2016 - a technology/computational venue (machine learning), not an autism or clinical venue.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2016. The related-work section positions the study against neuroimaging-based ADHD classification and against kinematic ASD classification in 2-4 year-olds (Crippa et al.), explicitly noting that its own high-functioning, older ASD participants are harder to separate from controls - an early acknowledgement that sample severity drives reported accuracy across this literature.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Identifying children with autism spectrum disorder based on their face processing abnormality: A machine learning framework
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Liu W; Li M; Yi L
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye-tracking and gaze
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Screening/computer-aided detection: binary classification of children with ASD vs typically developing children from face-scanning eye-movement patterns, plus identification of the most discriminative facial regions
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study; secondary machine-learning analysis of a previously published eye-tracking dataset (Yi et al., 2016)
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session; three study blocks (two faces each, 3 s per face) followed by three test blocks per study block; test faces presented until response
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Face recognition memory task: memorise six faces (three same-race Chinese, three other-race Caucasian), then identify targets among 18 novel faces
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory - eye-tracking testing (Peking University / Sun Yat-sen University collaboration)
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Diagnosed by experienced clinicians meeting DSM-IV criteria; confirmed with the Chinese version of the Autism Spectrum Quotient - Children's Version (AQ-Child). The authors state ADI-R and ADOS were not used because of limited access in China
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: AQ-Child score 85.48 (14.90) for the ASD group vs 62.74 and 64.03 for the two TD groups; not used as a modelling target
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - two separate TD groups, one matched on chronological age and one matched on nonverbal ability
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described beyond typical development; AQ-Child scores reported for both TD groups
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 58 (29 age-matched + 29 IQ-matched)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution_controls: 25 male / 4 female in each TD group - identical sex ratio to the ASD group
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes for the TD-Age group (7.90 vs 7.86, n.s.); the TD-Ability group is deliberately younger (p<0.001)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Yes - all three groups are 25 male / 4 female
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye movements: fixation coordinates during face viewing (both eyes tracked)
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Study phase (memorise two faces per block, 3 s each) and test phase (two target and two foil faces per test block, presented until response); grey-scale front-view faces with external features removed by an elliptical mask, 500x700 px at 72 ppi
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Tobii T60 eye tracker at 60 Hz with Tobii Studio software; analysis in MATLAB
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: No - reuses the eye-movement dataset collected for Yi et al. (2016)
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze coordinate data are relatively low-identifiability; no consent, ethics or data-protection statement appears in this paper (procedures are referred to the source publication). Authors declare no conflict of interest and list grant sponsors
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Data-driven histogram features over quantised fixation coordinates (a bag-of-visual-locations representation)
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Normalised frequency histograms of fixation coordinates assigned to K K-means clusters over the face image (K tuned to 16 for same-race, 64 for other-race, 96 for all faces); explicitly orderless - temporal sequence information was discarded because cross-region transitions were too sparse
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: MATLAB; K-means quantisation of fixation coordinates
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Mean-histogram difference between groups (FeatDif = FeatASD - FeatTD), with the largest absolute bins taken as the most discriminative regions, then re-running classification on the top seven bins
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Seven facial regions. ASD looked longer at the right eye (observer's view) and the area slightly above the mouth; TD looked longer at the area slightly below the left eye. Note the Results and Discussion sections state the ASD/TD preference directions inconsistently
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reported per region (which group fixated each region longer), but with a direct contradiction between the Results text and the Discussion text as to which group preferred which region
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Support vector machine with RBF kernel, applied at image level then aggregated to participant level by averaging image-level confidence scores with a tuned decision threshold
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-participant-out cross-validation with image-level training and participant-level score aggregation. However K (cluster number) and the decision threshold were tuned to maximise accuracy on the same data, and K-means quantisation was fitted on the fixation data of all participants including the held-out one
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, ROC curves and AUC
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: All faces: 88.51% accuracy, 93.10% sensitivity, 86.21% specificity, AUC 89.63%. Other-race faces: 90.80% / 96.55% / 87.93% / AUC 94.41%. Same-race faces: 81.61% / 75.86% / 84.48% / AUC 82.40%. ASD vs TD-Age: 84.48% (AUC 85.37%); ASD vs TD-IQ: 86.21% (AUC 88.94%). Top seven regions only: 79.31% accuracy, 68.96% sensitivity, 84.48% specificity
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Face-scanning patterns, represented as data-driven histograms over K-means-quantised fixation coordinates, classified children with ASD from TD children at up to 88.51% accuracy (AUC 0.90), and separated ASD from both age-matched and ability-matched TD groups. Other-race faces discriminated better than same-race faces. Seven facial regions carried most of the signal, retaining 79.31% accuracy, and no effect of chronological age on classification score was found (r=.17, p=.11).
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Fixation frequency in a small set of periocular and perioral regions; the eye region and the area just below/above it dominate the group difference, consistent with the eye-avoidance account
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Replicate with larger samples; evaluate predictive value longitudinally by tracking high-risk infants to see whether infant face-processing predicts later symptom severity; use more sophisticated models and determine the minimum feature set needed clinically; extend to different stimuli (social and non-social) and tasks; combine face-scanning with other psychological and physiological measures (brain activity, skin conductance, speech, motion, body gestures, facial expressions) into a multimodal risk measure; generalise across populations and cultures
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Unusually strong design for its date: two separately matched control groups (age-matched and ability-matched), identical sex ratios across groups, participant-level rather than image-level decisions, and an explicit base-rate caveat (33% ASD prevalence in sample vs ~1% in the population). Optimism remains: cluster number K and the decision threshold are tuned for maximum accuracy on the same dataset, K-means is fitted across all participants (including the test participant), and the headline is a maximum. AQ-Child rather than ADOS/ADI-R as diagnostic confirmation is a stated limitation of context. The reported direction of the ASD/TD region preferences is internally contradictory between Results and Discussion.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Three groups: ASD (n=29) and two typically developing control groups - chronological-age-matched (n=29) and nonverbal-ability/IQ-matched (n=29). All groups reported with sex ratio, age, nonverbal IQ raw score and AQ. No other-diagnosis clinical group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'children with autism spectrum disorder', 'individuals with ASD', 'the ASD group', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'TD counterparts', 'typical population'. Person-first throughout; no identity-first ('autistic') usage.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=29, 25M/4F, age 7.90 (1.45), NVIQ raw 22.29 (10.80), AQ 85.48 (14.90). TD-Age n=29, 25M/4F, age 7.86 (1.38), NVIQ 29.90 (9.96), AQ 62.74 (12.57). TD-Ability n=29, 25M/4F, age 5.74 (1.01), NVIQ 22.28 (7.90), AQ 64.03 (12.21). Age matching holds for TD-Age (t=0.09, n.s.) and ability matching holds for TD-Ability (t=0.00); sex ratio identical across all three groups. This double-matching design is stronger than most of the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Diagnosis by experienced clinicians against DSM-IV criteria, confirmed with the Chinese AQ-Child. The authors explicitly state that ADI-R and ADOS were unavailable to them - so no gold-standard observational instrument was used.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Nonverbal IQ measured with the Combined Raven Test (CRT-C2) for all participants and used to construct the ability-matched control group; AQ-Child reported for all three groups. No language or adaptive-functioning measures. Comorbid conditions are not described or excluded.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: screening / computer-aided detection - binary ASD vs TD classification from face-scanning patterns, plus localisation of discriminative facial regions. Main findings: 88.51% accuracy (93.10% sensitivity, 86.21% specificity, AUC 89.63%) across all faces; better on other-race (90.80%) than same-race faces (81.61%); ASD separable from both the age-matched (84.48%) and ability-matched (86.21%) TD groups; seven facial regions alone retain 79.31% accuracy; classification score uncorrelated with age.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory eye-tracking setting. Existing data - the study is an explicitly secondary machine-learning analysis of the eye-movement dataset collected for Yi et al. (2016), which had analysed it with a conventional area-of-interest approach.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A face recognition memory task: three study blocks in which the child memorises one Chinese and one Caucasian face (3 s each), each followed by three test blocks with two target and two foil faces shown until response. Stimuli were grey-scale, front-view, with hair and ears removed by an elliptical mask.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional single session. Data are gaze coordinates, low in identifiability; face stimuli are third-party images. This paper carries no ethics, consent or data-protection statement - procedures are deferred to the source publication - and no anonymization is described. Longitudinal follow-up is named as future work, not performed.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: Tobii T60 remote eye tracker, 60 Hz binocular. Software: Tobii Studio for acquisition; MATLAB for K-means quantisation, SVM training and ROC/AUC computation.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No data availability statement, no code release, no seeds. The pipeline (K-means quantisation, histogram normalisation, RBF-SVM, LOO with participant-level score averaging, threshold selection) is described in enough detail to re-implement in principle, and K values and the optimal threshold (0.3255) are reported - better than most contemporaries - but the underlying dataset is not accessible. Not reproducible in practice.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors: sample prevalence (33% ASD) far exceeds population prevalence (~1%), so positive predictive value in practice would be much lower; face-scanning is age- and culture-adapted so the model may not transfer across ages or cultures; ASD sample characteristics such as symptom severity and cognitive function may drive scanning patterns; sample size is small for pattern classification. Identifiable in review: strong male skew (25/29, ~86% male, replicated across all groups); single-country Chinese sample with race-specific face stimuli; diagnosis confirmed by questionnaire (AQ-Child) rather than ADOS/ADI-R; cluster number K and decision threshold tuned for maximum accuracy on the same data; K-means quantisation fitted on all participants including the held-out test participant, a subtle transductive leak; and the direction of the discriminative-region effects is stated inconsistently between Results and Discussion.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Validate and replicate on larger samples; run longitudinal high-risk-infant studies to test whether infant face-processing predicts later symptom severity; refine the algorithm and determine the minimum number of eye-movement features needed for clinical use; extend to other stimuli (social and non-social) and other tasks; and combine face-scanning with brain activity, skin conductance, speech, motion, body gestures and facial expressions in a multimodal risk measure. The paper is an early and explicit call for multimodal ASD prediction.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Gaze: fixation coordinates during face viewing, aggregated as spatial frequency distributions. Temporal/scanpath information was deliberately excluded because cross-region transitions were too sparse in the training data.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality; no fusion is performed. The discussion explicitly proposes future multimodal fusion with physiological, speech, motion and facial-expression measures. Within the modality, image-level decisions are fused to a participant-level decision by averaging confidence scores - a late/decision-level fusion across stimuli rather than across modalities.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning. Algorithm: RBF-kernel support vector machine, preceded by unsupervised K-means clustering used purely as a quantisation/feature-construction step.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Data-driven histogram (bag-of-locations) representation: fixation coordinates are quantised to K K-means cell centroids over the face image and counted, then normalised by total fixation count, giving one K-dimensional histogram per viewed face. Explicitly orderless - no raw time series, scanpath sequence or deep embedding.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, ROC curves and AUC - a fuller metric set than most corpus studies of this period. Headline: 88.51% accuracy / 93.10% sensitivity / 86.21% specificity / AUC 89.63%. No confidence intervals; a significance marker (p<0.001) is attached to the overall accuracy.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability by mean-histogram differencing: FeatDif = FeatASD - FeatTD, with the largest-magnitude bins visualised on the face and re-tested as a reduced feature set (top seven bins retain 79.31% accuracy). The informative regions are periocular and perioral, which the authors link to the eye-avoidance hypothesis. Direction of preference is reported but stated inconsistently across sections.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Leave-one-participant-out cross-validation with participant-level aggregation - subject-independent at the decision level, which is better than the instance-level cross-validation common in this corpus. But K and the decision threshold are selected to maximise accuracy on the same data, K-means quantisation uses all participants' fixations, and there is no external or independent test set, no held-out site and no cross-cultural check. Class imbalance (29 ASD vs 58 TD) is handled by a tuned flexible threshold rather than resampling. Base-rate limitation on deployment is explicitly discussed; no real-time claim, though the authors note remote eye trackers make rapid data collection feasible.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: autism spectrum disorder; face processing; eye tracking; machine learning. Task vocabulary: 'identify children with ASD', 'classification framework', 'computer-aid diagnosis', 'ASD risk', 'biomarker', 'early detection'.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Autism Research (INSAR/Wiley) - an autism-specific clinical/research journal, not a computational venue.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2016. The paper characterises machine learning in autism research as so far dominated by feature selection to shorten diagnostic instruments (ADOS/ADOS-G item reduction) and by neuroimaging, with behavioral classification only just beginning (citing Crippa et al. 2015 as the motivating precedent) - documenting the field's pivot toward behavioral prediction that this corpus goes on to record.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Semantic mapping reveals distinct patterns in descriptions of social relations in adults with autism spectrum disorder
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Luo SX; Shinall JA; Peterson BS; Gerber AJ
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder (Asperger's disorder, high-functioning autism, PDD-NOS)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Speech and language
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Detection/discrimination: binary classification of adults with ASD vs typical adults from the semantic structure of elicited social-relational descriptions, and characterisation of word-connectivity differences
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study (short report)
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session, simple one-session format; each participant described four important individuals with 10 positive and 10 negative sentences each
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Structured language-production prompt: 'describe four individuals who were important in your life, using 10 positive and 10 negative sentences', followed by 0-10 valence ratings of each description
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Clinic/research - Columbia University Medical Center developmental neuropsychiatry program outpatient clinic, plus advertisements and advocacy groups; self-report instruments delivered by a computer-based program
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: DSM-IV criteria for Asperger's Disorder, high-functioning autism or PDD-NOS, with IQ >= 70; ADOS administered (mean score 12.40, SD 3.89); other DSM-IV diagnoses excluded using the SCL-90 screening instrument
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 27 enrolled (one did not complete)
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Participants meeting criteria for any other DSM-IV diagnosis at evaluation were excluded via SCL-90; individuals unable to provide or understand written consent were also excluded
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: ADOS 12.40 (3.89) and AQ 24.35 (6.51) reported for the ASD group; not modelled as an outcome
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typical adults, reported separately by sex
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Screened with SCL-90; AQ 14.13 (males) and 15.96 (females), well below the ASD group's 24.35
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 132 enrolled (two did not complete); 45 typical adult males and 87 typical adult females
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution_controls: 45 male / 87 female - inverted relative to the ASD group's 23 male / 4 female
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Claimed ('matched to age and verbal IQ') and no significant baseline difference was found by one-way ANOVA, but the reported means differ substantially (34.8 vs 27.7 vs 22.8 years)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: No - the ASD group is 85% male while the typical group is 66% female; the authors note the ASD group's 'greater preponderance for the male gender'
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Language production: written/elicited descriptive sentences about social relations, plus participant valence ratings
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Generate 10 positive and 10 negative descriptive sentences for each of four personally important individuals; rate how strongly each description applies (0-10)
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Computer-based program for self-report instruments; standard natural language processing and latent semantic indexing; MATLAB with statistics and bioinformatics toolboxes
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - newly elicited descriptions, but not released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Data are free-text descriptions of the participant's own family and friends - genuinely sensitive personal content, and the paper reproduces two full description sets verbatim in Table 2. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants and the New York State Psychiatric Institute / Columbia University IRB approved all procedures; no anonymization procedure for the text itself is described
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Bag-of-words description vectors reduced by latent semantic indexing, plus graph-theoretic word-connectivity measures
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Word-frequency description vectors over 1161 distinct words (mean 84 indexing words per participant), projected onto LSI dimensions (first six dimensions capture 96% of variance, first three 78%); word-word co-occurrence connectivity and mean local clustering coefficient C of the resulting semantic network
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: MATLAB statistics and bioinformatics toolboxes; standard NLP tokenisation and latent semantic indexing
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Partly - the 20 words contributing most to the LSI dimensions are visualised as a semantic network, and hub words are noted to differ between groups, but no per-feature importance ranking for the classifier is given
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: LSI dimension loadings (top-20 contributing words visualised) and semantic-network clustering-coefficient comparison
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not a discrete feature list; the discriminative signal is the distributed position in LSI semantic space. Network hubs differ between groups, and the ASD semantic network is markedly less clustered
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: ASD descriptions occupy a restricted region of semantic space - there is an area of separation accessible only to typical adults - and form a less 'small-world' network: mean local clustering coefficient 0.10 (SD 0.11) for ASD vs 0.32 (SD 0.15) for typical (two-tailed t-test, p<0.001)
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification with unsupervised dimensionality reduction
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Linear discriminant, quadratic discriminant and RBF-kernel support vector machine classifiers, on LSI-reduced description vectors
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 10-fold cross-validation with random partitioning into 10 subsamples; classification performance compared against chance with two-tailed t-tests and Bonferroni correction. No independent test set. The paper does not state whether LSI was refitted within each fold
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: AUC (cross-validated), classification correct rate, sensitivity, specificity, ROC curves, and variance of performance across folds
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: AUC 0.67 (linear), 0.71 (quadratic), 0.82 (SVM, variance 0.12). At the optimal threshold, specificity 0.68 / 0.72 / 0.74 and sensitivity 0.50 / 0.52 / 0.52 for linear / quadratic / SVM. Adding age, gender, verbal IQ, vocabulary and working memory to the model did not improve classification. Group difference in LSI space significant by MANOVA (p=0.037)
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Descriptions of social relations produced by adults with ASD occupy a distinguishable region of latent semantic space, and machine-learning classifiers detect the difference above chance - but with low sensitivity (~0.5) and moderate specificity (~0.7), which the authors read as a rule-out rather than rule-in test. Independently, the semantic co-occurrence network of the ASD group is significantly less 'small-world' (clustering coefficient 0.10 vs 0.32, p<0.001), a difference robust to adjustment for gender, age, verbal IQ and vocabulary.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Reduced word-word connectivity and lower local clustering in the semantic network; restricted region of LSI semantic space. Notably, no individual word differed significantly in frequency between groups (Wilcoxon rank-sum with Bonferroni correction), and vocabulary size did not differ - the signal is purely in co-occurrence structure
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Apply NLP to freely generated verbal material rather than prompted descriptions; use more theory-driven models to improve sensitivity and specificity; model word ordering and higher-order effects such as phrase-level correlations, which the current bag-of-words model omits; recruit more female participants with ASD; develop methods that disambiguate the underlying mechanism (structural language deficit vs social-language-specific deficit vs compensation); pursue longitudinal studies to establish clinical importance; combine with neuroimaging to test whether similar descriptions activate similar neuroanatomical loci; and explore real-time clinical visualisation of where a patient's descriptions fall in semantic space
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: One of the most honest performance reports in the corpus: the authors report modest AUCs, flag that the SVM's higher AUC comes with larger variance 'reflecting a degree of over-fitting to a specific training dataset', and explicitly interpret the low sensitivity as making the test better at ruling out than ruling in ASD. Notable methodological strengths: covariate adjustment (age, gender, verbal IQ, vocabulary, working memory) leaves the effect intact, and no single word differs between groups so the signal cannot be a trivial vocabulary artefact. Main weaknesses: severe gender imbalance in the opposite direction between groups (85% male ASD vs 66% female typical) while gender is not matched, large group-size imbalance (27 vs 132), and no statement that LSI was refitted inside the cross-validation folds.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: adults with ASD (n=27, one non-completer) and typical adults (n=132, two non-completers), the latter reported separately as 45 males and 87 females. No other-diagnosis group - indeed other DSM-IV diagnoses were an exclusion criterion.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'adults with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)', 'individuals with ASD', 'ASD participants', 'these individuals', 'patient population', 'typical adults', 'typical participants', 'the typical group'. Person-first throughout; notably the comparison group is called 'typical' rather than 'normal' or 'control' in most places, though 'normal participants' appears once in a figure caption.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=27, 4 female / 23 male, age 34.80 (15.90), full-scale IQ 106.30 (16.30), verbal IQ 107.00 (17.00). Typical males n=45, age 27.70 (10.00), verbal IQ 117.00 (12.00); typical females n=87, age 22.80 (6.90), verbal IQ 116.00 (23.00). Matching is claimed on age and verbal IQ and no significant baseline difference was found by one-way ANOVA (except AQ), but the means differ substantially and the group sizes are very unequal (27 vs 132). Gender is markedly mismatched and in opposite directions - the authors acknowledge the ASD group's male preponderance and name the shortage of female ASD participants as a limitation. Adults only; no early-diagnosis relevance.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: DSM-IV criteria for Asperger's Disorder, high-functioning autism or PDD-NOS with IQ >= 70, assessed at an academic developmental neuropsychiatry clinic. ADOS was administered (group mean 12.40, SD 3.89) and the SCL-90 was used to exclude other DSM-IV diagnoses. This is one of the better-specified diagnostic pipelines in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Yes, extensively: full-scale, verbal and performance IQ, Wechsler Memory Scale, Autism Quotient, Inventory of Interpersonal Problems, SCL-90 and Social Adjustment Scale reported for all groups. Comorbidity was actively excluded via SCL-90 screening, and the authors use verbal IQ, vocabulary subsection and WMS as covariates to show the semantic effect is not explained by structural language ability.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: detection/discrimination of ASD in adults from language production, plus mechanistic characterisation of semantic-network structure. Main findings: LSI-space positions differ significantly between groups (MANOVA p=0.037); classifiers separate groups above chance with AUC 0.67 / 0.71 / 0.82 (linear / quadratic / SVM) but sensitivity only ~0.50-0.52 against specificity ~0.68-0.74; the ASD semantic network is significantly less small-world (C=0.10 vs 0.32, p<0.001) after covariate adjustment; no individual word and no vocabulary-size difference between groups.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Clinic/research setting - an academic outpatient developmental neuropsychiatry program plus advertisement and advocacy-group recruitment, with instruments delivered through a computer-based program. Newly collected data; no existing dataset used.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A single structured elicitation prompt: describe four personally important individuals using 10 positive and 10 negative sentences each, then rate the strength of each description from 0 to 10. The authors explicitly note this prompted format is a design choice - it standardises the assay but does not probe free language generation.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, one session; no time scale or follow-up reported, and the authors state that the clinical importance of the findings will depend on future longitudinal data. The material is highly sensitive - free-text descriptions of participants' own family members and friends, including negative characteristics - and two full description sets are reproduced verbatim in Table 2. Written informed consent was obtained before enrollment and the New York State Psychiatric Institute / Columbia University IRB approved all procedures; no text anonymization or de-identification procedure is described.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No sensing hardware - data are typed/recorded sentences collected through a computer-based self-report program (platform unspecified). Software: standard NLP tokenisation, latent semantic indexing, and MATLAB with statistics and bioinformatics toolboxes for classification, ROC/AUC and network analysis.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No data availability statement and no code release; several methodological details (the NLP pipeline, the connectivity normalisation) are deferred to Supporting Information rather than the main text. LSI, the three classifiers and the 10-fold scheme are named but hyperparameters, seeds and the fold-level treatment of LSI are not specified. Not reproducible as reported, although the elicitation protocol itself is trivially repeatable.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors: small patient sample, especially few female participants with ASD, with an explicit note that male and female ASD participants may differ in language patterns; the model omits word ordering and phrase-level effects; the prompted format may not capture core language-generation deficits; mechanisms are not disambiguated. Identifiable in review: group sizes are very unequal (27 vs 132) and gender is imbalanced in opposite directions between groups (85% male ASD vs 66% female typical) while gender is not matched - a serious confound for a language-production measure; the ASD group is also on average 7-12 years older; the sample is high-functioning adults (IQ >= 70, mean verbal IQ ~107) so results cannot extend to the wider spectrum; no statement that LSI was refitted within cross-validation folds; and 59% White in the ASD group with no other ethnicity analysis.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Apply the method to freely generated rather than prompted verbal material; adopt more theory-driven models to improve sensitivity and specificity; incorporate word ordering and phrase-level correlations; recruit more women with ASD; develop analyses that separate structural-language, social-language and compensatory mechanisms so interventions can be tailored; conduct longitudinal studies to establish clinical importance; combine with functional neuroimaging to test neural correlates of semantic similarity; and build real-time clinical visualisation of where a patient's descriptions sit in semantic space.
