custom_fields.RQ3.1: Language: lexical/semantic content of elicited descriptive sentences about social relations. No acoustic, prosodic, gaze or motor data - this is one of the few purely linguistic-content studies in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality. Positive and negative descriptions are analysed both combined and separately (the network difference loses significance when split, which the authors attribute to reduced power). Demographic and cognitive variables (age, gender, verbal IQ, vocabulary, WMS) are added to the classifier as covariates and do not improve performance - an integration attempt that is reported as null rather than omitted.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning with unsupervised dimensionality reduction. Algorithms: linear discriminant, quadratic discriminant and RBF-kernel SVM; latent semantic indexing (an SVD-based technique related to PCA) provides the representation. Graph-theoretic network analysis (local clustering coefficient) is used descriptively alongside the classifiers.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted symbolic representation: each description is a word-frequency vector over a 1161-word vocabulary, reduced to a low-dimensional LSI projection (six dimensions capture 96% of variance). Word ordering, phrases and higher-order correlations are explicitly omitted. Separately, a word-word co-occurrence graph is built and summarised by its mean local clustering coefficient.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: AUC (the primary metric), classification correct rate, sensitivity, specificity, ROC curves, and - unusually - the variance of performance across folds. Headline: AUC 0.82 for SVM (variance 0.12), 0.71 quadratic, 0.67 linear; sensitivity 0.50-0.52 and specificity 0.68-0.74 at the optimal threshold. Chance comparison by two-tailed t-test with Bonferroni correction.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: The 20 words contributing most to the LSI dimensions are visualised as two semantic networks (ASD vs typical), showing different hubs and markedly fewer connections in the ASD network. The interpretable finding is structural rather than lexical: mean local clustering coefficient 0.10 (SD 0.11) for ASD vs 0.32 (SD 0.15) for typical, p<0.001, robust to adjustment for gender, age, verbal IQ and vocabulary. Critically, no individual word frequency and no vocabulary-size difference reached significance, so the discriminative information lies entirely in word co-occurrence structure.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: 10-fold cross-validation with random partitioning; performance tested against chance with Bonferroni-corrected t-tests; classifier variance across folds reported and explicitly interpreted as evidence of SVM overfitting. Covariate robustness is tested (age, gender, verbal IQ, vocabulary, WMS added to the model - no improvement) and the network result is re-tested under a generalized linear model with covariates. No external or independent validation, no held-out site, no class-imbalance handling despite a 27:132 split, and no deployment claim beyond a proposal for future real-time clinical visualisation. Whether LSI was refitted inside each fold is not stated.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: machine learning; semantic web; autism spectrum disorder; latent semantic indexing; classification; small-world network. Task vocabulary: 'automatically detect and discriminate between these two groups', 'quantifying language production', 'computer-assisted strategy', 'screen out an ASD diagnosis'. The 'semantic web' and 'small-world network' vocabulary is distinctive within this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Autism Research (INSAR/Wiley), as a Short Report - an autism-specific clinical/research journal, not a computational venue.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2016. The paper positions data mining of language production for psychopathology as previously proposed but never demonstrated quantitatively across diagnostic groups, presenting itself as a first step - an early marker of the linguistic-content strand that grows later in this corpus (social media text, picture-book narratives, conversation transcripts).

data_charting_rubrics.title: Toward the Autism Motor Signature: Gesture patterns during smart tablet gameplay identify children with autism
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Anzulewicz A; Sobota K; Delafield-Butt JT
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Childhood Autism (ICD-10)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Motor and kinematics
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Screening / early identification: determine whether motor information from tablet gameplay differentiates children with autism from typically developing children, and characterise which movements drive the difference (the 'autism motor signature')
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study (proof-of-concept)
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session; each of two games comprised a 2-minute training phase followed immediately by a 5-minute test phase (14 minutes total per child)
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Two commercial 'serious' tablet games: 'Sharing' (structured - slice a food item and distribute pieces to four cartoon characters, with distractor objects) and 'Creativity' (unstructured free-play outlining and colouring)
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Specialist therapeutic centres (autism group) and standard kindergartens (control group) - an applied, non-laboratory setting chosen deliberately for ecological validity
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Poland (recruitment and development) with UK collaboration (University of Strathclyde)
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Clinical diagnosis of Childhood Autism per ICD-10 (2010 Edition) by medical practitioners within specialist clinics; supplemented by a clinician questionnaire on symptom severity and intellectual/social functioning. No ADOS or ADI-R
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 37 recruited; 35 engaged in gameplay, 2 discarded for not focusing or resigning
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Of the 37, 30 were 'uncomplicated', 1 high-functioning, 2 had Asperger's Syndrome and 4 were co-morbid with intellectual impairment (only 2 of those 4 completed). Children who could not follow simple instructions were excluded, as were children whose clinician or teacher was uncertain about diagnosis or health
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: A clinician questionnaire on severity of autistic symptoms and intellectual/social functioning was administered but its scores are not reported or modelled
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developing children recruited at standard kindergartens
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Teacher questionnaire on functioning; any child whose teacher was uncertain about diagnosis or health was excluded. No formal screening instrument
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 45 (all engaged in gameplay)
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes - explicitly age-matched (4y5m vs 4y7m, both SD 11 months)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Yes - explicitly gender-matched (12/37 vs 13/45 female, i.e. 32% vs 29%)
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Touch-screen gesture data (taps, multi-touch, swipes, releases) and inertial sensor data (tri-axial accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer) capturing contact forces and device displacement
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: 'Sharing' game (divide a food item into four and distribute to four cartoon characters, repeated trials, with non-task distractor objects) and 'Creativity' game (choose a shape, trace its dotted outline, then colour freely with no rules)
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: iPad mini (Apple) running iOS 7.0; two commercial games by Duckie Deck Game Studio wrapped in a bespoke app that sequenced games, locked the device and logged data; iOS Core Motion framework sampling inertial sensors at 10 Hz; standard iOS touch acquisition; data gzipped as JSON to cloud storage in Microsoft Azure Table Storage (NoSQL); bespoke feature-computation engine
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - newly collected tablet gameplay data, but not released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement; the work is tied to a commercial entity (Harimata Sp. z o.o.) with stated commercialisation ambitions
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Written informed parental consent obtained; protocols carried out in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the University of Strathclyde Ethics Committee. Data are touch and inertial traces (low identifiability), but they are transmitted to and stored in third-party commercial cloud services (Microsoft Azure) - a data-protection consideration the paper describes technically but does not address as a privacy matter
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted summary features over touch gestures and inertial signals
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 262 features extracted (108 touch, 164 inertial); 26 highly correlated features (r>0.9) collapsed, leaving 247 plus age and gender. Touch features cover gesture kinematics (velocity, acceleration), gesture form (area of a minimal adaptive polygon, height, duration) and tap counts; inertial features cover accelerometer and gyroscope statistics (RMS, max magnitude, zero-crossing counts, attitude means/SDs, inter-axis rotation correlations). Per-feature values were reduced to their mean per game session
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Bespoke feature-computation engine running in cloud services; iOS Core Motion for acquisition
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between the autism and control distributions for each feature, with the ten largest-distance features per game examined and boxplotted. The authors describe this as 'a best approximation' of the contributing features rather than a model-internal importance measure
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Sharing: all ten top features were inertial (AccelZeroCrossing_x, RotationCorrelation_1_2, AttitudeStdDev_y, AttitudeMean_y, RotationCorrelation_0_1, AttitudeRMS_x, AttitudeZeroCrossRate_x, RotationMean_z, RotationMeanMagnitude, RotationMin_z). Creativity: four inertial and six touch features, including mean gesture velocity, mean gesture area, gesture height statistics and minimum gesture duration
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Children with autism showed greater impact force (higher AccelerationRMS_y and AccelerationMagnitudeMax), a different distribution of angular forces (gyroscope features), faster mean gesture velocity, larger gesture area, more distal gesture placement with greater variation, and shorter minimum tap duration (faster taps)
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification (decision-tree ensembles)
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: ExtraTrees (5000 trees), Random Forest (5000 trees), Regularized Greedy Forest (500 trees, L2=sL2=1.0, square loss), and RGF2 (RGF with age and gender excluded). SVMs and gradient boosting machines were deliberately avoided as overfitting-prone on this sample size
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 10 repetitions of 10-fold cross-validation per game, with predictions aggregated across repetitions (740 observations) to generate ROC curves. Parameter searches were performed per algorithm. No independent external test set
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: AUC (primary, with standard deviation across repetitions), sensitivity and specificity at two explicit thresholds (0.50 and 0.55), ROC curves
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Best model RGF2: AUC 0.848 (SD 0.025) for Sharing, 0.926 (SD 0.013) for Creativity, 0.932 (SD 0.016) for the two-game average. Creativity at threshold 0.50 gave 83% sensitivity and 85% specificity; at 0.55, 80% sensitivity and 88% specificity. ExtraTrees and Random Forest reached average AUCs of 0.881 and 0.885
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Motor patterns extracted from ordinary iPad gameplay identified children with autism at up to AUC 0.93. The unstructured free-colouring game outperformed the structured sharing game, which the authors argue shows the signal is motor rather than attentional. The characterised signature is greater contact force with an altered force distribution, faster and larger gestures placed more distally, and shorter minimum tap durations - interpreted as disrupted prospective, feed-forward control of goal-directed movement.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Greater impact and gesture forces (accelerometer and gyroscope statistics), faster mean gesture velocity, larger and more distal gesture area, shorter minimum tap duration
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Test specificity against other developmental conditions - particularly developmental coordination disorder and ADHD, and more generally 'ASD versus ASD-like clinical presentation', which the authors name as the ultimate clinical question; recruit more widely and in larger numbers to establish population-level generalisability and determine whether the algorithms need retraining; extend the paradigm to younger, undiagnosed children at risk; couple the gameplay to other psychometric tests, to the face-forward camera for social/emotional measures, and to sensorised toys; move toward individual functional assessment rather than categorical diagnosis
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Among the strongest early behavioral-prediction studies in the corpus. Genuinely ecological setting, both age- and gender-matched groups, deliberate avoidance of overfitting-prone algorithms with an explicit critique of the prior SVM/LOO literature (naming Crippa et al.), repeated cross-validation with reported variance, and thresholds stated rather than tuned silently. Remaining concerns: IQ was not controlled and the authors concede this; recruitment from specialist therapeutic centres introduces a selection bias they explicitly acknowledge may have 'facilitated machine learning differential power'; 247 features against 82 children; feature importance is assessed by univariate KS distance rather than model-internal importance; and two authors are affiliated with the commercial developer (Harimata) with stated commercialisation intent, though this is disclosed by affiliation rather than as a competing-interests statement.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: children clinically diagnosed with Childhood Autism (n=37 recruited, 35 with usable data) and typically developing controls (n=45). Group composition is reported in unusual detail - 30 'uncomplicated' autism, 1 high-functioning, 2 Asperger's Syndrome, 4 with co-morbid intellectual impairment (2 completing). No non-autistic clinical comparison group, which the authors identify as the key gap.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with autism', 'children with ASD', 'individuals with autism', 'the Autism group', 'children developing typically', 'typically developing children', 'the Control group', 'neurotypical individuals'. Predominantly person-first; the phrase 'children developing typically' is used in preference to deficit framing, and 'neurotypical' appears once.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Autism n=37 (12 female / 25 male), mean age 4 years 5 months (SD 11 months), range 3-6 years. Control n=45 (13 female / 32 male), mean age 4 years 7 months (SD 11 months). Explicitly both age-matched and gender-matched - one of relatively few corpus studies to match on both. Female representation (32%) is unusually high for this literature. Very young sample, directly relevant to early identification, though all children were already diagnosed.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Clinical diagnosis of Childhood Autism per ICD-10 (2010 Edition) by medical practitioners in specialist clinics, with a clinician questionnaire on symptom severity and intellectual/social functioning; children with uncertain diagnosis were excluded. No ADOS, ADI-R or other standardised observational instrument was used - a notable weakness given the strength of the rest of the design.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: A questionnaire on level of intellectual and social functioning and on prior mobile-device experience was administered to clinicians (autism group) and teachers (control group), but no scores are reported. IQ was explicitly not controlled - the authors state they 'were unable to exclude intelligence as a potential confounder' and mitigate by noting most children were clinician-classified as average (n=29) or high functioning (n=4), with only 2 low-functioning children contributing final data. Comorbidity is reported at the individual level (intellectual impairment in 4).
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: early screening and characterisation - can motor information from tablet gameplay differentiate autism, and which movements do so. Main findings: best AUC 0.932 (RGF2, two-game average), 0.926 for the Creativity game alone, with 83% sensitivity at 85% specificity; the unstructured game outperformed the structured one; the signature is greater contact force with altered force distribution, faster/larger/more distal gestures, and shorter minimum tap duration, interpreted as disrupted prospective motor control.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Applied real-world settings - specialist therapeutic centres for the autism group and standard kindergartens for the controls, explicitly chosen over a university laboratory because laboratory motion-capture paradigms with reflective markers 'under the watchful gaze of curious scientists' are difficult for autistic children and may invalidate the data. Newly collected data; commercially available games were adapted with logging code.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Two tablet games, each with a 2-minute guided training phase and a 5-minute unassisted test phase. 'Sharing': tap a food item to slice it into four, then drag pieces onto four cartoon children's plates, with characters reacting positively or negatively, plus non-task distractor objects. 'Creativity': choose a toy or animal shape, swipe to fill in its dotted outline, then select a colour and paint freely with no rules. The experimenter demonstrated verbally and gesturally during training but did not intervene during testing; the clinician or teacher was present and intervened only for challenging behaviour, in which case data were omitted.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single ~14-minute session per child with no follow-up. Data are touch coordinates and inertial signals - low identifiability, no video or audio. Written informed parental consent, Declaration of Helsinki compliance and University of Strathclyde Ethics Committee approval are reported. However, the data pipeline transmits gameplay data over the web to Microsoft Azure cloud storage operated in connection with a commercial company; the paper documents this as architecture but never as a privacy, anonymization or data-protection question.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: iPad mini (Apple) running iOS 7.0, positioned on a 65 cm children's table within 10 cm of the edge so that sensor readings reflect touch forces rather than device movement; tri-axial accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer sampled via iOS Core Motion at 10 Hz; standard iOS touch-event acquisition. Software: two Duckie Deck commercial children's games wrapped in a bespoke app that sequenced and time-boxed the games and disabled the home button; gzip/JSON transfer to Microsoft Azure Table Storage; a bespoke cloud-side feature-computation engine.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No data availability statement and no code release - unsurprising given the commercial affiliation and stated commercialisation ambition. Reproducibility support is nonetheless comparatively good: the full 262-feature list is provided in a supplemental table, algorithm hyperparameters are given (RGF 500 trees, L2=sL2=1.0, square loss; ET and RF 5000 trees), the correlation-based feature reduction threshold (r>0.9) is stated, the cross-validation scheme is fully specified, and classification thresholds (0.50 and 0.55) are reported explicitly rather than optimised silently. The games are commercially available. Method-reproducible, data-irreproducible.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors, unusually thoroughly: IQ was not controlled and could confound; recruitment from particular specialist institutions gives only a subgroup of the spectrum and this 'inherent selection bias in our autism group may have facilitated machine learning differential power'; machine learning is sensitive to sample size so wider recruitment and larger numbers are needed; and the comparison is against children with no concern for ASD rather than against the clinically relevant ASD-versus-ASD-like contrast. Identifiable in review: 247 features against 82 children; feature importance assessed univariately by KS distance rather than from the models; the reported AUC is the best of four algorithm variants across two games plus their average; and two authors are affiliated with the commercial developer with explicit commercialisation ambitions, disclosed by affiliation but not as a competing-interests statement.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Test differentiation between ASD and other developmental psychopathologies (developmental coordination disorder, ADHD) - framed as 'the ultimate clinical question'; substantiate with a larger, more generalised population and test whether the algorithms transfer or need retraining; apply the paradigm to younger, not-yet-diagnosed children; couple gameplay with other psychometric tests, with the face-forward camera for social-intelligence and emotional-reaction measures, and with sensorised toys; and shift toward individual functional assessment rather than broad diagnostic categorisation.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Motor behavior in two forms: gesture kinematics and form from the touch screen (velocity, area, height, duration, tap counts) and contact/angular forces from inertial sensors (accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer). No gaze, speech or facial data.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Two behavioral data streams from the same device - touch and inertial - are combined by feature concatenation into a single 247-dimensional vector (early/feature-level fusion). Predictions from the two games are additionally averaged per child, a decision-level fusion across tasks that produced the best AUC (0.932) - higher than either game alone. Age and gender are included as features in ET, RF and RGF, and deliberately excluded in RGF2, which performed best, showing the result does not depend on demographic inputs.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning with decision-tree ensembles: ExtraTrees, Random Forest and Regularized Greedy Forest (plus an RGF variant without demographics). The authors explicitly rejected SVMs and gradient boosting machines as overfitting-prone given more features than observations and strong inter-feature correlations - a deliberate model-selection rationale that is rare in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted statistical features over sensor streams: touch data are segmented into atomic gestures and summarised by kinematic and form variables; inertial data are summarised across the session by statistical moments, zero-crossing counts and inter-axis correlations. All per-feature values are reduced to their session mean before modelling. No raw time series, images or learned embeddings.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: AUC as the primary metric, reported with standard deviation across repetitions - a rarity in this corpus - plus sensitivity and specificity quoted at two explicitly stated thresholds (0.50 and 0.55) and full ROC curves. Headline: AUC 0.932 average, 0.926 Creativity, 0.848 Sharing; 83% sensitivity / 85% specificity at threshold 0.50 on Creativity. No accuracy figure is emphasised, though the abstract translates the result as 'up to 93% accuracy', conflating AUC with accuracy.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between group distributions, with the ten highest-distance features per game reported, described and boxplotted. Most informative: inertial force features dominate (all ten in the Sharing game), joined by touch-based gesture velocity, area, height and minimum duration in the Creativity game. The interpretation is substantive rather than decorative - greater impact force, altered angular force distribution, faster and larger, more distally placed gestures and faster taps - and is tied to a mechanistic account of disrupted prospective/feed-forward motor control.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: 10 repetitions of 10-fold cross-validation with AUC standard deviations reported, aggregating 740 predictions for the ROC; algorithm choice explicitly motivated by overfitting risk; redundant features (r>0.9) collapsed; a demographics-free model variant (RGF2) run to check that age and gender were not driving the result. Bias and generalisability are addressed narratively (selection bias, IQ confound, institution-specific sample, need for retraining on the general population) rather than by mitigation. No external or independent test set, no held-out site and no real-time/deployment evaluation, though commercial deployment as a screening device is an explicit ambition.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No formal keyword list in the extracted text; the paper's own vocabulary is distinctive: 'autism motor signature', 'computational marker', 'bio-behavioural marker', 'serious games', 'smart tablet', 'prospective motor control', 'motor agency', 'early identification'. The framing of a 'computational bio-behavioural marker' as an alternative to purely biological biomarkers is a notable conceptual contribution.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Scientific Reports (Nature Portfolio) - a broad multidisciplinary science journal, neither autism-specific nor computational.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2016. The paper positions itself as the first to use smart-device serious games to study motor patterns in autism, and notes only one prior machine-learning study of autism-specific motor patterns (Crippa et al., optical motion capture, n=30) - which it critiques directly for SVM plus leave-one-out cross-validation being 'prone to over-fitting'. This is the corpus's clearest early example of methodological self-correction within the field, and it documents the shift from laboratory optical motion capture to consumer-device sensing.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Applying machine learning to identify autistic adults using imitation: An exploratory study
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Li B; Sharma A; Meng J; Purushwalkam S; Gowen E
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum condition (verbally able adults)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Motor and kinematics
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Exploratory identification and feature/condition discovery: determine whether kinematic data recorded during voluntary imitation can differentiate autistic and neurotypical adults, and identify which imitation conditions and which kinematic parameters are most discriminative
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study; secondary machine-learning analysis of a previously published imitation experiment
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session split into four blocks (two Target, two No-Target); 64 analysed trials per participant (8 per condition across 8 conditions) plus 32 additional trials included to prevent behaviour becoming repetitive
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Voluntary imitation: observe a video clip of a demonstrator's hand performing a two-movement sequence, then copy it. Conditions crossed target presence (Target vs No Target) with speed (fast vs normal) and trajectory (short vs elevated), giving eight conditions
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory - University of Manchester
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Not specified in this paper - participants are described as ASC adults recruited for the original study, with methods referred to the source publication. No diagnostic instrument, criteria or confirmation procedure is reported here
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 16 recruited; 2 excluded for data capture issues, leaving 14 analysed
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Not reported numerically - the groups are described as sex-matched but no counts are given
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported; no autism severity or trait measure is given for the ASC group
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described beyond 'healthy controls' / 'neurotypical'; no screening instrument reported
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes - matched by design and confirmed statistically (t(28) = 0.7, p = 0.49)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Stated as sex-matched, but no counts are reported
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Motor kinematics: 3D hand position trajectories during imitation
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Observe-then-imitate hand movement sequences presented as video clips; each trial began with a fixation cross, then a still hand image, then the video, with imitation cued by an exclamation mark. Movement onset/offset defined at 10% of peak velocity sustained for six consecutive samples (48 ms)
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Polhemus Liberty electromagnetic motion sensor attached to the index finger of the dominant hand, sampling X, Y, Z at 120 Hz; MATLAB with a 120 Hz Butterworth filter for processing; LIBSVM for SVM implementation; Weka for the comparison against standard attribute evaluators
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: No new collection - reuses data from Wild et al. - but the dataset is newly released with this paper as Supporting Information
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes - 'All relevant data are within the paper and its Supporting Information files'; the kinematic dataset is supplied as S1_File.xlsx and the paper states it is 'available in S1 File for other researchers'. This is one of very few corpus studies to actually release its data
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not applicable - openly deposited with the article under a CC-BY licence
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Low-sensitivity data - numeric kinematic parameters rather than video or audio. Participants received written information at least 48 hours in advance, had the opportunity to ask questions, and gave written consent; the study, consent procedure and use of data were approved by both the University of Manchester and NHS research ethics committees. This is among the most complete consent-and-ethics reporting in the corpus, and the released data are inherently de-identified
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted kinematic parameters, summarised per participant per condition as means and standard deviations across trials
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 20 kinematic parameters per trial: movement duration, peak velocity, time to peak velocity, percent peak acceleration, percent time before/after peak velocity, peak acceleration, time to peak acceleration, percent time to peak acceleration, percent peak acceleration location, peak deceleration, time to peak deceleration, percent time to peak deceleration, percent peak deceleration location, dimensionless jerk, horizontal maximum amplitude, vertical amplitude, time to peak vertical amplitude, percent time of peak vertical amplitude, percent location of peak vertical amplitude. Means and SDs across 8 trials give 40 features per condition
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: MATLAB (filtering, segmentation, parameter extraction); LIBSVM; Weka
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes - extensively; feature selection is the paper's central contribution
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Four approaches compared: SVM weight magnitudes, leave-one-parameter-out accuracy impact, PCA first-component loadings, and a combined method taking the top 8 SVM-weight features plus the intersection of top-3 PCA and top-10 leave-one-out features. Additionally benchmarked against nine standard Weka attribute evaluators (correlation ranking, information gain, OneR, ReliefF, symmetrical uncertainty, and four wrapper-based evaluators)
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Nine parameters, all standard deviations, from two conditions. No-Target Fast: peak velocity SD, time to peak velocity SD, peak acceleration, horizontal max amplitude SD, percent time of vertical amplitude SD. No-Target Elevated: time to peak acceleration SD, percent time to peak acceleration SD, vertical amplitude SD, percent location of peak vertical amplitude SD. Vertical amplitude SD in the NTE condition was the single most consistently important
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reported and interpreted: standard deviations were higher in the ASC group for all but one No-Target Fast feature, but lower (with one exception) for the No-Target Elevated features. The authors interpret increased variability under fast imitation as impaired sensorimotor planning, and decreased variability under elevated imitation as the autistic group retaining their usual movement style rather than attempting the unusual trajectory
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Naive Bayes, support vector machine (linear and RBF kernels, LIBSVM, grid-searched C and gamma), decision tree C4.5 and random forest. Naive Bayes was chosen deliberately as the starting point because SVM overfitting was anticipated with 40 features and 30 samples
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-out cross-validation with a second layer of cross-validation inside the training fold: at each iteration the remaining 29 samples are split into training and development, features and classifier parameters are selected on development performance only, the classifier is then retrained on all 29 and tested on the held-out sample. The authors state explicitly that 'we treat the test sample as unknown when selecting features and parameters. All selections are based on the performance on the Training data, not test data'. The Weka comparison in Table 6 uses ordinary 10-fold cross-validation instead
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, with per-classifier breakdowns and averages, plus standard deviations across the comparison methods
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Best result 86.7% accuracy (85.7% sensitivity, 87.5% specificity) with linear SVM on the nine combined-selection features. Naive Bayes 80.0%, RBF-SVM 83.3%, random forest 70.0%, decision tree 66.7%; average across the five models 77.3%. Condition screening by Naive Bayes gave NTE 64.5% and NTF 56.7% average accuracy, rising to 83.3% when the standard deviations of both conditions were combined. The combined feature-selection method (77.3%, SD 8.6%) outperformed the average of nine standard Weka attribute evaluators (70.5%), with the best standard evaluator (OneR) at 75.8%
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Kinematic variability during goal-less imitation discriminates autistic from neurotypical adults at up to 86.7% accuracy. The two No-Target conditions (fast and elevated) were far more discriminative than any Target condition, replicating the authors' earlier mean-based finding that imitation differences are specific to goal-less movement. All nine selected features were standard deviations rather than means, and their direction differed by condition - greater variability in fast imitation, lower variability in elevated imitation - which the authors read as the autistic group failing to construct a new sensorimotor plan for an unusual trajectory. Naive Bayes matched SVM performance despite a quarter of the features, and simple statistical histogram comparison failed entirely where machine learning succeeded.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Trial-to-trial variability (standard deviations) of velocity, acceleration timing and vertical amplitude during goal-less imitation - not mean kinematic values
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Expand the range of movements to more complex, full-body motor control functions; train on larger ASC and control groups to test generalisation across the heterogeneity of the condition; compare imitation in ASC against other groups with known motor deficits such as developmental coordination disorder and ADHD to establish whether motor profiles are shared or distinct; investigate whether motor subgroups exist within the autistic population and how these affect daily living and therapy; and design imitation studies using actions dissimilar to the observer's existing movement repertoire in order to maximise group differences
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The validation design is the strongest in the corpus for a small-sample study: a genuine nested leave-one-out with an inner training/development split, with the explicit statement that feature and parameter selection never sees the test sample. The paper also releases its dataset, reports full ethics and consent, benchmarks its feature selection against nine standard alternatives, reports sensitivity and specificity rather than accuracy alone, and reports a failed analysis (statistical histograms) rather than hiding it. Remaining weaknesses are mostly of reporting: no diagnostic instrument is named for the ASC group, sex counts are never given despite sex-matching being claimed, no autism severity or trait measure is reported, and n=30 means an 86.7% accuracy corresponds to 26 of 30 correct. The choice of the best classifier and feature-selection method across a large grid is also a residual source of optimism the nested design does not fully remove.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: autistic adults (16 recruited, 14 analysed after two exclusions for data capture failure) and neurotypical adult controls (n=16). Both group sizes and the exclusion are reported explicitly. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the discussion identifies developmental coordination disorder and ADHD as the comparisons needed next.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'autistic adults', 'autistic individuals', 'people with ASC', 'individuals with ASC', 'the ASC group', 'the autistic group', 'neurotypical controls', 'neurotypical group', 'non-autistic controls', with 'healthy controls' appearing once. Notably this paper uses identity-first language ('autistic adults', 'autistic individuals') and 'neurotypical' consistently, and uses 'autism spectrum condition' rather than 'disorder' - the most neurodiversity-aligned terminology of any study in the corpus so far, and a deliberate contrast with the person-first, 'healthy control' framing typical elsewhere.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASC n=14 analysed (16 recruited), mean age 32 +/- 7.69 years, mean WASI IQ 118.5 +/- 12.02. Controls n=16, mean age 29.31 +/- 8.38, mean IQ 119.8 +/- 11. Age and IQ did not differ significantly (age t(28) = 0.7, p = 0.49; IQ t(28) = -0.31, p = 0.76) - so unusually for this corpus the groups are matched on IQ as well as age, and the matching is statistically verified rather than merely asserted. Sex matching is claimed but no male/female counts are given for either group. Adults only, so no early-diagnosis relevance. Both groups are high-IQ (mean ~119), which bounds generalisability considerably.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not reported in this paper. The ASC participants come from a previously published experiment and no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or confirmation procedure is described - the reader is referred to the source publication. Given that diagnostic status is the classification target, this is the study's most significant reporting gap.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Full-scale IQ measured with the Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence and reported for both groups (118.5 vs 119.8) and used as a matching variable - one of the few corpus studies to match and verify on IQ. No language or adaptive-functioning measures, no autism trait or severity scores (no AQ, ADOS or equivalent), and no comorbidity information.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: exploratory feasibility plus discovery of the most discriminative test conditions and kinematic parameters - explicitly framed as addressing which conditions and features to use, not only whether classification works. Main findings: best accuracy 86.7% (sensitivity 85.7%, specificity 87.5%) with linear SVM on nine features; the two No-Target (goal-less) conditions were the discriminative ones; all nine selected features were standard deviations rather than means; the combined feature-selection method (77.3% average across models) outperformed nine standard Weka attribute evaluators (70.5% average); and conventional statistical histogram comparison failed to separate the groups at all.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory setting at the University of Manchester. Existing data - the study is an explicitly secondary machine-learning re-analysis of an imitation experiment previously analysed with mean-based statistics on only five kinematic parameters. Its contribution is analytic rather than new collection, though it does newly release the dataset.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A voluntary imitation task: participants observed a video clip of a demonstrator's hand performing a two-movement sequence and then copied it, cued by an exclamation mark after a fixation cross and a still hand image. Eight conditions crossed target presence (pointing to visible targets vs no apparent targets) with speed (48 vs 58 beats per minute) and trajectory (15 cm flat, 10 cm short, or 15 cm curved/elevated). Four blocks (two Target, two No-Target) with speed and trajectory randomised within block; 8 analysed trials per condition, plus 32 filler trials specifically included to stop participants' behaviour becoming repetitive and stereotyped.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session; no longitudinal component. The data are numeric hand-position kinematics, not identifiable media, so sensitivity is low - and the released dataset is inherently de-identified. Consent and ethics are reported more completely than anywhere else in the corpus so far: written information provided at least 48 hours in advance, an explicit opportunity to ask questions, written consent, and approval of the study, the consent procedure and the use of data by both the University of Manchester and NHS research ethics committees.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: Polhemus Liberty electromagnetic motion sensor attached to the index finger of the dominant hand, sampling 3D position at 120 Hz; video presentation of stimulus clips. Software: MATLAB for filtering (120 Hz Butterworth), movement segmentation (10% of peak velocity over six consecutive samples) and parameter extraction; LIBSVM for SVM training with grid search over C and gamma; Weka for the standard-attribute-evaluator comparison.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: The best reproducibility profile in the corpus so far. The dataset is released as Supporting Information (S1_File.xlsx) under CC-BY with an explicit data availability statement and an invitation to other researchers; the full 20-parameter definition table is published; the sampling rate, filter, segmentation threshold and trial structure are specified; the SVM library and grid-search procedure are named; and the entire pipeline is benchmarked in Weka, a public tool, against nine named standard evaluators. No code is released and random seeds are not reported, but the analysis is reconstructible from the released data.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors: small sample size is named as the study's limitation; ASC heterogeneity means generalisation to a wider population 'remains to be tested'; and comparison against other motor-deficit groups (developmental coordination disorder, ADHD) is needed to know whether the profile is autism-specific. Identifiable in review: no diagnostic instrument is reported for the ASC group at all; both groups have mean IQ near 119, so the sample represents only high-IQ verbally able adults; sex counts are never given despite sex-matching being claimed; 6% of ASC trials and 2% of control trials were excluded for recording or imitation errors, an asymmetry that is disclosed but not analysed; and the reported 86.7% is the best cell of a grid spanning three feature-selection methods, four-plus classifiers and eight conditions, so some selection optimism survives even the nested validation.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Expand to more complex, full-body motor functions; train on larger groups to improve generalisation across ASC heterogeneity; compare against developmental coordination disorder and ADHD to test whether motor profiles are shared or distinct; investigate motor subgroups within autism and their implications for daily living and therapy; and design future imitation experiments around actions dissimilar to the observer's existing repertoire, since that is what maximised group differences here - a concrete, actionable design recommendation rather than a generic call for more data.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Motor behavior: 3D hand kinematics during imitation - velocity, acceleration and deceleration profiles and their timings, jerk, horizontal and vertical amplitudes, and movement duration. Single-point finger tracking rather than full-body pose.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality; no fusion across behavioral modalities. Within the modality there is a form of condition-level fusion: features from the two best conditions (No-Target Fast and No-Target Elevated) are combined into a joint 40-feature vector, which raised Naive Bayes accuracy from 70.0% and 66.7% individually to 83.3% jointly - an explicit demonstration that combining task conditions helps. IQ and age are used as matching variables, not as model inputs.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning, with unsupervised PCA used only for feature selection. Algorithms: Naive Bayes, SVM with linear and RBF kernels, decision tree C4.5 and random forest. The choice of Naive Bayes first is explicitly motivated by anticipated SVM overfitting given 40 features and 30 samples, and the paper reports the informative finding that Naive Bayes performed comparably to SVM even on a quarter of the features, speculating that the independence assumption may genuinely hold for these kinematic parameters.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted kinematic summary features: 20 scalar parameters per trial, aggregated per participant per condition into means and standard deviations across 8 trials, giving 40 features per condition. Critically, the discriminative signal turned out to lie entirely in the standard deviations rather than the means - i.e. in trial-to-trial variability rather than in average movement form. No raw time series, images or learned embeddings.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, reported per classifier with averages and standard deviations across methods; the true positive and true negative definitions and class sizes (P=14, N=16) are stated explicitly. Headline: 86.7% accuracy, 85.7% sensitivity, 87.5% specificity (linear SVM, nine features). No AUC, F1 or confidence intervals.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is the paper's core contribution rather than an afterthought. Four selection methods are compared (SVM weights, leave-one-parameter-out, PCA first-component loadings, and their combination) and benchmarked against nine standard Weka attribute evaluators, with agreement between methods reported (features 16, 29 and 37 recur across several). The nine selected features are all standard deviations from the two goal-less conditions, and their directions are interpreted substantively: higher variability in No-Target Fast, lower variability in No-Target Elevated, read as the autistic group failing to build a new sensorimotor plan for an unusual trajectory and instead retaining their habitual movement style - an interpretation supported by citation to the authors' own follow-up work.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Robustness is handled better than anywhere else in the corpus at this sample size. A nested leave-one-out design places feature selection and hyperparameter tuning inside an inner training/development split, with the explicit statement that all selections are based on training-data performance and the test sample is treated as unknown. Feature-selection stability across iterations is examined and reported (SVM-weight features being more stable than leave-one-out features). The method is benchmarked against nine standard alternatives. What is absent: any external or independent dataset, any held-out site, any class-imbalance handling (14 vs 16 is near-balanced), and any deployment or real-time analysis. Generalisation across ASC heterogeneity is explicitly flagged as untested.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No formal keyword list in the extracted text. The paper's vocabulary: 'kinematic biomarkers', 'motor bio-signatures', 'diagnostic classification', 'voluntary imitation', 'goal-less imitation', 'data-driven', 'discriminative test conditions', 'exploratory study'. The consistent use of 'autism spectrum condition', 'autistic adults' and 'neurotypical' is itself a distinctive terminological signature.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: PLOS ONE - a broad open-access multidisciplinary journal, neither autism-specific nor computational.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2017. The paper surveys the emergence of machine learning in autism research across neural markers, cognitive scores, diagnostic-instrument item reduction and pregnancy risk factors, and notes that 'to date, there have been few studies that have applied machine learning to autistic motor data', naming Crippa et al. (2015) as the only prior motor example. It positions itself as the first to apply machine learning to imitation kinematics and, unusually, contrasts its own design against that predecessor on specific methodological grounds - less constrained task, exploration of which test conditions discriminate, and adults rather than children where group differences should be smaller.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Automatic Detection of ADHD and ASD from Expressive Behaviour in RGBD Data
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Jaiswal S; Valstar MF; Gillott A; Daley D
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2017 12th IEEE International Conference on Automatic Face & Gesture Recognit
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, and comorbid ADHD+ASD
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Facial expression and head motion (video)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Diagnostic aid: automatic end-to-end prediction of the presence/absence of ADHD and ASD in adults from video, framed as a time-saving objective supplement to expert questionnaire-and-observation diagnosis
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study with a newly collected dataset (KOMAA)
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session; approximately 12 minutes of video per participant, segmented into 12 story segments
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Computer-mediated psychological assessment: participants read and listened to 12 short stories from the 'Strange Stories' task, each followed by 2-3 spoken-response questions, delivered on screen with a pre-recorded voice to simulate an interviewer while keeping the setup automated
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Controlled laboratory/clinic recording setting, with recruitment via the Nottingham City Asperger Service and ADHD Clinic
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Participants had previously been clinically diagnosed with ADHD and/or ASD (route not specified beyond prior diagnosis). Controls were screened with the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS Part A, threshold 4) and the Autism Spectrum Quotient AQ-10 (threshold 6); only those scoring below both thresholds were admitted as controls
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 37 in the combined condition group (ASD only n=22 by the classification tables, ADHD only n=4, comorbid ADHD+ASD n=11)
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not reported numerically - median age per group is shown only as a bar chart (Fig. 3)
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Adults over 18; no upper bound or range reported
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Not reported numerically - gender distribution per group is shown only as a bar chart (Fig. 2/3)
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Comorbidity is the explicit study focus: a separate ADHD+ASD group is defined and a dedicated comorbid-vs-ASD-only classifier is trained. No other comorbidities described
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not modelled; ASRS and AQ-10 are used only as control-group screening gates, and their scores for the clinical groups are not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - adults with no ADHD/ASD symptoms who had never been diagnosed with either
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes, and unusually rigorously - dual screening on ASRS (ADHD) and AQ-10 (autistic traits) with explicit numeric thresholds
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 18 (from the classification table: 16 correct + 2 incorrect)
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not claimed; median ages are plotted per group but no matching procedure or statistical comparison is reported
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not claimed; gender distributions are plotted per group but not matched or tested
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes - dual-questionnaire screened
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: RGBD video: facial action units, Kinect animation units, 3D head pose, head-motion speed and cumulative head displacement, plus behavioral response times
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Reading and listening to 12 Strange Stories with 2-3 spoken questions each; the video was manually divided into 12 segments corresponding to the stories, which the authors note could be automated because story timing is researcher-controlled
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Microsoft Kinect 2.0 RGBD sensor (high-resolution colour and depth); Kinect v2 library/software for animation units and head pose; a modified deep CNN for facial action unit intensity estimation (the architecture of Jaiswal & Valstar without the BLSTM layer); computer screen with pre-recorded audio delivery
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - the KOMAA dataset (Kinect Data for Objective Measurement of ADHD and ASD), presented as a 'first of its kind' RGBD database and one of the paper's three stated contributions
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not stated - the dataset is announced as a contribution for evaluating computer-vision algorithms but no access route, licence or repository is given anywhere in the paper
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Highly sensitive data - identifiable facial video and voice recordings of clinically diagnosed adults. The paper contains no ethics-approval statement, no consent statement and no anonymization or data-protection procedure, despite announcing the dataset as a community resource. Only funders are acknowledged
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: High-level handcrafted descriptors aggregated as per-segment histograms, deliberately chosen over raw pixels to limit overfitting
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Six feature sets per video segment: (1) deep-learned facial action unit intensities for AU1, AU2, AU4, AU12, AU15, AU20 plus AU45 blink frequency and duration, as 10-bin histograms concatenated to a 62-dim vector; (2) ten Kinect animation units (lip stretcher, lip corner puller, lip corner depressor, eye closed, brow lowerer, left and right) as 10-bin histograms; (3) 3D head pose - pitch, yaw, roll deviations from the median pose as 18-bin histograms spanning -45 to +45 degrees, 54 dimensions; (4) head-motion speed from stable eye-corner and nose landmarks, smoothed over 20 frames, as a 10-bin histogram; (5) cumulative head displacement over the segment; (6) a 12-dimensional response-time vector. All concatenated across 12 segments and Z-score normalised
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Modified deep CNN AU detector (Jaiswal & Valstar architecture without BLSTM); Kinect v2 library for animation units and head pose; custom landmark-centroid tracking for head speed
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Greedy forward feature selection, with the top three discriminative features visualised per task and the top 30 features ranked by individual classification power in supplementary figures
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Controls vs Condition: head-motion speed during story segments 1 and 2, and Animation Unit 8 (lip-corner depressor) during segment 10. Comorbid vs ASD-only: AU1 (inner brow raiser, segment 1), AnU6 (lip-corner puller, segment 3) and head rotation about the Y axis (segment 8)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported - the discriminative features are named and plotted but the direction of the group difference is never stated in the text
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification with deep-learned intermediate representations
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Support vector machine with RBF kernel for the diagnostic classification, preceded by greedy forward feature selection; a deep convolutional neural network is used upstream as a pre-trained facial action unit detector rather than as the diagnostic classifier
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, with the score averaged over test subjects. The paper does not state that greedy forward feature selection was recomputed inside each fold, and the feature vector is very high dimensional relative to 55 subjects
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Classification accuracy only, reported alongside raw correct/incorrect counts per class
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Controls vs Condition (ADHD/ASD/both): 96.4% accuracy - controls 16/18 correct, condition 37/37 correct. Comorbid (ADHD+ASD) vs ASD-only: 93.9% accuracy - comorbid 9/11 correct, ASD-only 22/22 correct. The ADHD-only group (n=4) was too small to model
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Facial expression, head pose and head motion extracted automatically from 12 minutes of RGBD video during a Strange Stories task discriminated adults with ADHD and/or ASD from screened controls at 96.4% accuracy, and separated comorbid ADHD+ASD from ASD-only at 93.9%. The authors present this as the first work to learn models predicting ADHD/ASD diagnosis directly from high-level facial features rather than detecting predefined behavioural markers, and as the first to establish a relationship between facial expression and these conditions.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Head-motion speed and lip-corner depressor activity for the condition-versus-control contrast; inner-brow raiser, lip-corner puller and head yaw for the comorbid-versus-ASD contrast - all localised to specific Strange Stories segments
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: None stated - the conclusions summarise the contribution and assert potential for other neurodevelopmental disorders, but propose no specific future work, and no limitations section is present
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Genuinely novel contributions - direct end-to-end diagnostic prediction rather than marker detection, an adult population (rare in this corpus), an explicit comorbidity contrast, and dual-questionnaire screening of controls. But the reporting is thin in ways that matter: participant ages and gender distributions appear only as bar charts with no numbers, no matching or comparability testing is reported, accuracy is the only metric for a 18-vs-37 imbalanced problem where predicting 'condition' always would score 67%, greedy forward feature selection over a very high-dimensional vector (roughly 12 x 200+ dimensions) against 55 subjects is not stated to be nested within the leave-one-subject-out folds - the most likely source of the near-perfect condition-class recall - and there is no ethics or consent statement despite the collection and announcement of an identifiable facial-video database.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Four groups: controls (n=18), ASD only (n=22), ADHD only (n=4) and comorbid ADHD+ASD (n=11), totalling 55 adults. Group sizes must be inferred from the classification tables and a bar chart rather than a participant table. The ADHD-only group was explicitly too small (n=4) to train a classifier for, so the reported analyses collapse to controls-vs-condition and comorbid-vs-ASD-only. This is one of very few corpus studies with both a non-autistic clinical group and an explicit comorbid group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'subjects who have been diagnosed with ASD', 'individuals with ADHD', 'people with ASD', 'subjects with ADHD/ASD', 'the ASD group', 'the Condition group', 'healthy controls', 'healthy individuals', 'control group'. Person-first for the clinical groups, but the comparison group is repeatedly framed as 'healthy', which implicitly positions autism as ill-health rather than difference - a framing choice worth noting against the more neutral 'typically developing' used elsewhere in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Poorly reported. Total n=55 adults over 18. Group sizes are recoverable (18 control, 22 ASD only, 4 ADHD only, 11 comorbid) but only from the results tables. Median age per group and gender distribution per group are presented solely as bar charts (Figs. 2 and 3) with no numeric values, no standard deviations and no age range. No matching procedure, and no statistical test of age or gender comparability between groups, is reported. Adults only, so no early-diagnosis relevance.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Clinical groups: prior clinical diagnosis of ADHD and/or ASD, recruited through the Nottingham City Asperger Service and ADHD Clinic; the diagnostic instruments and criteria behind those prior diagnoses are not described. Controls: actively screened out using two validated instruments with stated thresholds - Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale Part A (threshold 4) and AQ-10 (threshold 6). The control screening is more rigorously specified than the case ascertainment, which is the reverse of the usual pattern in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive-functioning measures are reported for any group. ASRS and AQ-10 are used only as control-admission gates and their scores are never reported for the ASD, ADHD or comorbid groups. Comorbidity, by contrast, is handled seriously - ADHD+ASD co-occurrence is a defined group and the subject of the second classification task, motivated by the observation that treatment differs across the three clinical groups.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: a fully automatic end-to-end diagnostic aid predicting presence/absence of ADHD and ASD in adults directly from video, explicitly contrasted with prior work that only detected predefined behavioural markers. Main findings: 96.4% accuracy for controls vs condition (16/18 controls and 37/37 condition correct) and 93.9% for comorbid vs ASD-only (9/11 and 22/22 correct); head-motion speed and lip-corner depressor activity were most discriminative for the first task, inner-brow raiser, lip-corner puller and head yaw for the second.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A controlled recording setting with a screen and Kinect camera, with clinical recruitment via an NHS Asperger and ADHD service. Newly collected data - the study contributes the KOMAA dataset and no existing dataset is used.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A computer-mediated version of the Strange Stories task: 12 short stories displayed on screen and simultaneously read aloud by a pre-recorded voice, each followed by 2-3 questions answered aloud. The design deliberately simulates a human interviewer while removing the interviewer, so that the stimulus is identical across participants. Video was manually segmented into the 12 story periods for feature aggregation.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single ~12-minute recording per participant with no follow-up. The data are highly sensitive - identifiable RGB facial video plus depth and recorded voice responses from clinically diagnosed adults. Despite this, and despite announcing the resulting database as a contribution to the research community, the paper contains no ethics-approval statement, no participant consent statement, and no anonymization, access-control or data-protection provision. Only funding bodies are acknowledged.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: Microsoft Kinect 2.0 RGBD sensor capturing high-resolution colour and depth; a computer screen with speakers for stimulus delivery. Software: Kinect v2 library for animation units and 3D head pose; a modified deep CNN facial-action-unit detector (the Jaiswal & Valstar architecture with the BLSTM removed); custom landmark-centroid head-speed computation; SVM with RBF kernel and greedy forward feature selection.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Weak. The KOMAA dataset is announced as a contribution but no access conditions, licence, repository or contact route is stated - so a dataset presented as a community resource is in practice unavailable. No code release. Feature construction is described in good detail (histogram bin counts, AU list, angle ranges, smoothing window, normalisation) and would be re-implementable, but SVM hyperparameters, the feature-selection stopping criterion and the final feature-vector dimensionality are not given, and nothing states whether feature selection was nested in the cross-validation. Not reproducible as reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: No limitations section exists, so nothing is acknowledged by the authors beyond the ADHD-only group being too small to model. Identifiable in review: severe class imbalance (18 controls vs 37 condition) reported only as accuracy, where always predicting 'condition' would already score 67%; group sizes of 4 and 11 in two of the four cells; ages and genders never reported numerically and never matched or tested, so demographic confounding cannot be assessed at all; a very high-dimensional feature vector (six feature families x 12 segments) against 55 subjects with greedy forward selection not stated to be nested inside the leave-one-subject-out loop - the single most likely explanation for 37/37 and 22/22 perfect recall on the majority classes; single-site recruitment; and no ethnicity data.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: None proposed. The conclusion asserts high potential for facial expressions to predict ADHD, ASD 'and other neurodevelopmental disorders' but sets out no specific research programme, no validation plan and no open questions - unusual even by the standards of a short conference paper.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Facial expression (FACS action units and Kinect animation units), head pose in 3D, head-motion speed and cumulative head displacement, plus response latency to spoken questions. Voice is recorded for the answers but no acoustic or linguistic analysis of it is performed - only the time taken to respond is used.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Six behavioral feature families are combined by concatenation into a single normalised vector before classification - early/feature-level fusion - with temporal structure preserved by computing each family separately per story segment and concatenating across the 12 segments, which the authors describe as trading a twelvefold dimensionality increase for retained temporal information. No integration with clinical scores or demographics.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning. The diagnostic classifier is an RBF-kernel SVM with greedy forward feature selection. A deep CNN (a modified dynamic deep-learning AU architecture) is used upstream as a pre-trained facial action unit detector. The authors explicitly reject end-to-end deep learning on raw pixels because the small training set would cause severe overfitting - a deliberate and well-reasoned choice to use deep learning for representation but not for diagnosis.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Histogram-based aggregation of frame-level descriptors: AU intensities, animation-unit intensities, head-pose angles and head speeds are each binned into per-segment histograms; cumulative distance and response times enter as scalars; everything is length-normalised by frame count and Z-scored. This is a handcrafted statistical representation built on top of deep-learned per-frame features rather than a learned embedding of the video.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Classification accuracy only, supported by raw per-class correct/incorrect counts (which is at least transparent enough to recover the confusion matrix). No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC or confidence intervals - a significant gap given the 18-vs-37 and 11-vs-22 class imbalances, where the reported accuracies of 96.4% and 93.9% cannot be compared against the relevant majority-class baselines of 67% and 67% without recomputation.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Greedy forward feature selection identifies the discriminative features, with the top three per task visualised and the top 30 ranked by individual classification power. Informative features: head-motion speed (stories 1-2) and lip-corner depressor (story 10) for controls vs condition; inner-brow raiser (story 1), lip-corner puller (story 3) and head yaw (story 8) for comorbid vs ASD-only. Notably the features are segment-specific, implying that particular Strange Stories items carry the signal - an interpretable finding the paper does not pursue. The direction of each group difference is never stated.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, which is subject-independent at the outer level. Overfitting is explicitly reasoned about in two places - rejecting raw-pixel deep learning, and motivating feature selection because 'any classifier trained directly on the entire feature-set is most likely to overfit'. But there is no statement that feature selection was nested within folds, no external or independent validation, no held-out site, no class-imbalance handling or metric, no statistical testing, and no deployment or real-time evaluation despite the time-saving clinical framing. The comorbid classifier is trained on 33 subjects total.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No formal keyword list. The paper's vocabulary: 'automatic detection', 'expressive behaviour', 'RGBD data', 'behaviomedical conditions', 'diagnostic predictions', 'facial action units', 'animation units', 'Strange Stories'. The term 'behaviomedical' - conditions that alter expressive behaviour - is distinctive to this line of work and does not recur elsewhere in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: IEEE International Conference on Automatic Face and Gesture Recognition (FG) 2017 - a technology/computational venue (computer vision), not an autism or clinical venue.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2017. The paper characterises computer vision for ADHD and ASD as 'still in its infancy', with prior work confined to detecting predefined behavioural markers (AOSI markers, self-stimulatory behaviour, social games, engagement) whose 'effectiveness in predicting the actual ADHD and ASD diagnosis still remains to be seen'. It positions itself as one of the first to pose diagnosis directly as a machine-learning problem and, unusually for this corpus, targets adults rather than children.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Earlier identification of children with autism
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Pokorny FB; Schuller B; Marschik PB; Brueckner R; Nyström P; Cummins N; Bölte S; Einspieler C; Falck-Ytter T
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder (younger siblings at heightened familial risk, later diagnosed)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Speech and vocalisation
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Earlier identification / feasibility: characterise ASD-related acoustic specificities in pre-linguistic vocalisations at the feature level, and evaluate whether automated vocalisation-based identification of infants later diagnosed with ASD is feasible
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective analysis nested in a prospective longitudinal high-risk sibling cohort (EASE, Early Autism Sweden); cross-sectional classification at the 10-month recording
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single 12-minute parent-child interaction recording per infant (240 minutes total across 20 infants); outcome diagnosis established at 3 years of age
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Semi-standardised free-play parent-child interaction: parents instructed to play with their child on a mat with toys as they would at home, with study personnel leaving the room
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory - a closed recording room configured to approximate home play, within the Uppsala Child and Baby Lab / EASE cohort
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Sweden (data collection), with Austrian, German and UK analysis collaborators
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Diagnosed with ASD at 3 years of age using DSM-5 criteria; ASD group drawn from a Swedish population at heightened risk (younger siblings of children already diagnosed with ASD). TD group drawn from a low-risk population with a normal outcome at 3 years
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 10 (5 male, 5 female)
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: 10 months (all infants exactly 10 months at recording)
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: 10 months - a tightly fixed age band by design
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported; the outcome is binary diagnosis at 3 years. Speech-language developmental level was annotated via SAEVD-R (whether any vocalisation exceeded a single canonical syllable) - 4 ASD and 4 TD subjects did so
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developing infants from a Swedish low-risk population with normal outcome at 3 years
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes - low familial risk plus confirmed normal outcome at the 3-year assessment
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 10 (5 male, 5 female)
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes - all infants recorded at exactly 10 months
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Yes - exactly 5 male / 5 female in both groups, and the authors describe the sample as 'well gender- and family-language-balanced'
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Audio: pre-linguistic infant vocalisations (excluding vegetative sounds) extracted from audio-video parent-child interaction recordings
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Unstructured toy play between parent and infant; 684 vocalisations manually segmented on the basis of distinct vocal breathing groups, with vegetative sounds (smacking, breathing, hiccups) excluded, and vocalisation types annotated against the Stark Assessment of Early Vocal Development-Revised
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Panasonic HC-V700 cameras ceiling-mounted in the room corners for orientation-independent capture; audio extracted from one camera and converted to single-channel 44.1 kHz AAC; Noldus Observer XT for video coding and segmentation; openSMILE for feature extraction; Weka (SMO) for SVMs; TensorFlow for the BLSTM
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: No - retrospective analysis of recordings from the existing EASE longitudinal cohort
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement; clinical cohort recordings
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Highly sensitive - audio-video recordings of identifiable infants and parents in their own interaction. Ethical review board approval from the participating centres is stated in a footnote; no consent statement, anonymization procedure or data-protection provision is described. Notably the segmenting annotator was blinded to group membership, which is a methodological rather than privacy safeguard
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Standardised handcrafted acoustic feature set (statistical functionals over low-level descriptors)
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: The extended Geneva Minimalistic Acoustic Parameter Set (eGeMAPS): 88 acoustic parameters comprising statistical functionals over 25 frequency-, energy- and spectral low-level descriptors, explicitly selected in the literature for clinical speech analysis. Top discriminative features by effect size: mean spectral slope 0-500 Hz (unvoiced), normalised SD of MFCC4, mean unvoiced segment length, mean Hammarberg index (unvoiced), mean spectral slope 500-1500 Hz (unvoiced), mean f0, mean alpha ratio (unvoiced), voiced segments per second, f0 20-80 percentile range, normalised SD of MFCC1
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: openSMILE open-source toolkit (audEERING)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Univariate Mann-Whitney U tests per feature with effect size r (z divided by the square root of the sample count), reported for the top ten features; this is a statistical rather than model-internal importance measure
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: 54 of 88 eGeMAPS features differed significantly between groups; five reached moderate effect size (|r| > 0.3). The single strongest was the arithmetic mean of spectral slope 0-500 Hz over unvoiced segments (r = 0.3966)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Direction is encoded in the sign of r per feature (e.g. mean unvoiced segment length and spectral slope 500-1500 Hz are lower in the ASD group, spectral slope 0-500 Hz and MFCC4 variability higher), and probability density distributions for the strongest feature are plotted per group, but the substantive interpretation of these directions is not developed
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Linear-kernel support vector machine trained with sequential minimal optimisation (Weka) as the baseline, and a one-layer bidirectional LSTM neural network with eight cells (TensorFlow, Adam optimiser, 10 ms time steps, patience-based early stopping)
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Subject-independent 3-fold cross-validation with three partitions matched for gender and diagnosis and balanced for vocalisation counts; each fold uses one partition for training, one for development (SVM complexity parameter C, BLSTM architecture search and early stopping) and one for testing, with train and development merged before final testing. Subject-level decisions are derived from per-vocalisation votes
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Unweighted average recall (UAR) and weighted average recall (WAR) with standard deviations across folds, full confusion matrices at the vocalisation level, and subject-wise accuracy at both a fixed 0.5 threshold and an optimised threshold
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Vocalisation-level: SVM UAR 64.5% +/- 3.3% (WAR 69.0% +/- 2.6%); BLSTM UAR 62.9% +/- 2.0% (WAR 70.7% +/- 2.6%). Subject-level: both approaches 70% accuracy at a 0.5 majority-vote threshold and 75% with optimised thresholds - 8 of 10 ASD and 7 of 10 TD infants correctly assigned. Volubility did not differ between groups (Mann-Whitney p = 0.104)
