data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Pre-linguistic vocalisations of 10-month-olds later diagnosed with ASD differ measurably from those of typically developing infants: 54 of 88 standardised acoustic features showed significant group differences, five with moderate effect sizes, with spectral-slope and unvoiced-segment measures strongest. Automated identification is feasible but modest - 64.5% UAR per vocalisation and 75% subject-level accuracy. Volubility did not differ, contradicting the reduced-volubility account, and a deep BLSTM did not outperform a linear SVM at this sample size.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Spectral slope in unvoiced segments, MFCC variability, unvoiced segment length, Hammarberg index and f0 measures - largely voice-quality and spectral-balance parameters rather than pitch or duration alone
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: More fine-grained studies on substantially larger datasets; systematic evaluation of alternative acoustic feature sets; alternative feature pre-processing strategies such as bag-of-words processing; and different classification approaches including other deep learning architectures. The discussion also sketches an application scenario in which early preventative judgements are made from vocalisations recorded during routine paediatric examinations in the first year of life
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Methodologically the most disciplined of the early speech studies in this corpus. Subject-independent partitioning with a genuine three-way train/development/test split, hyperparameters tuned only on development data, unweighted average recall reported with standard deviations, full confusion matrices, blinded segmentation, and exact gender balance in both groups. The results are correspondingly modest and, unusually, the authors report a negative finding (no volubility difference) and a null comparison (BLSTM does not beat SVM at n=20). Real limitations remain: only 20 infants and the subject-level 75% rests on 15 of 20 correct, so the confidence interval is very wide; the reported subject-level accuracy uses thresholds optimised per fold rather than the fixed 0.5 threshold (which gives 70%); 54 of 88 features are declared significant without multiple-comparison correction; and the high-risk-sibling design means the ASD group is not a general-population sample.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 10: infants at heightened familial risk (younger siblings of children with ASD) later diagnosed with ASD at 3 years, and typically developing infants from a low-risk population with normal 3-year outcome. Both groups fully specified per subject in Table 1, including vocalisation counts and cross-validation partition assignment - subject-level transparency that is rare in this corpus. No other-diagnosis group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with autism spectrum disorder', 'individuals with ASD', 'individuals later diagnosed with ASD', 'infants later diagnosed with ASD', 'the ASD group', 'typically developing (TD) infants', 'TD controls', 'affected individuals'. Consistently person-first, and notably careful in using 'later diagnosed with ASD' for the infants, which correctly avoids attributing a diagnosis to a 10-month-old who did not yet have one.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=10 (5 male, 5 female); TD n=10 (5 male, 5 female). All infants exactly 10 months old at recording, so age is matched by design with no variance. Gender is exactly balanced within and across groups, and the authors additionally describe the sample as family-language-balanced. This is one of the very few corpus studies with perfect sex balance - though at n=20 total it is also among the smallest. Highly relevant to early diagnosis: 10 months is the youngest recording age in the corpus, with outcome ascertained 26 months later.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: ASD diagnosis at 3 years of age using DSM-5 criteria within the EASE longitudinal cohort; TD status confirmed by normal outcome at the same 3-year assessment. The specific instruments used at the 3-year assessment are not named in this paper. Group membership was withheld from the annotator during segmentation.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Speech-language developmental level was annotated using the Stark Assessment of Early Vocal Development-Revised (SAEVD-R), recording whether each infant produced vocalisation types more complex than single canonical syllables - 4 ASD and 4 TD infants did, so the groups were comparable on this measure. No cognitive, adaptive or IQ measures are reported, and comorbid conditions are not described. Pacifier use during recording is noted for three infants, and one misclassified TD infant is flagged as having used one - an unusually granular disclosure of a potential acoustic confound.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: earlier identification - characterise ASD-related acoustic specificities in pre-linguistic vocalisations and test the feasibility of automated identification. Main findings: 54 of 88 eGeMAPS features differed significantly between groups (five with |r| > 0.3, strongest being mean spectral slope 0-500 Hz over unvoiced segments at r = 0.3966); vocalisation-level UAR 64.5% (SVM) and 62.9% (BLSTM); subject-level accuracy 75% with optimised thresholds (70% at a fixed 0.5 threshold), correctly assigning 8/10 ASD and 7/10 TD infants. Volubility did not differ between groups (p = 0.104), a negative result reported plainly.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory setting - a closed recording room with ceiling-mounted cameras, deliberately arranged so parents would play as they would at home and with study personnel absent during recording. Existing data: retrospective analysis of recordings collected within the EASE (Early Autism Sweden) longitudinal high-risk sibling study.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A semi-standardised free-play parent-child interaction on a mat with toys, 12 minutes per infant, with parents instructed to play as at home. No task demands were placed on the infant. Vocalisations were then manually segmented by vocal breathing groups using Noldus Observer XT, with vegetative sounds excluded, and annotated for developmental complexity against SAEVD-R by an annotator blinded to group membership.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: The parent study is longitudinal - infants recorded at 10 months with diagnostic outcome at 3 years, a 26-month prospective interval - but the acoustic analysis itself is cross-sectional at the single 10-month recording. Data are highly sensitive: audio-video of identifiable infants and their parents in intimate play interaction. Ethical review board approval at the participating centres is stated in a single footnote; there is no consent statement, no anonymization or de-identification procedure, and no data-protection or access-control provision despite the media type.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: Panasonic HC-V700 camcorders ceiling-mounted in the room corners so infant behaviour could be captured continuously regardless of orientation; audio extracted from one camera as single-channel 44.1 kHz AAC. Software: Noldus Observer XT for video coding and segmentation; openSMILE (audEERING) for eGeMAPS extraction; Weka with sequential minimal optimisation for SVM training; TensorFlow with the Adam optimiser for the BLSTM.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No data availability statement and no code release, but reproducibility of the method is comparatively strong: the feature set is a published open standard (eGeMAPS) extracted with an open-source tool (openSMILE), both classifiers use widely available toolkits (Weka, TensorFlow), the SVM complexity grid is stated, the BLSTM architecture search outcome (one layer, eight cells), time step (10 ms), optimiser and early-stopping rule are given, the exact cross-validation partitions are published per subject in Table 1, and the optimised per-fold decision thresholds are listed. This is among the most re-implementable pipelines in the corpus; only the cohort recordings are unavailable.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors: the small number of subjects limits the impact of the results, and a genuine performance difference between SVM and deep learning 'might only become evident on a dataset with a considerably higher number of vocalisations'. They also note that a proportion of ASD infants' vocalisations carry no acoustic atypicality, and disclose pacifier use as a possible source of error for one misclassified control. Identifiable in review: n=20 makes the 75% subject-level figure equivalent to 15/20 correct with a very wide confidence interval; the headline 75% uses per-fold optimised thresholds rather than the fixed 0.5 threshold (70%); vocalisation counts are unbalanced between groups (259 ASD vs 425 TD) and per subject (9 to 98), so subject-level ratios rest on very different amounts of evidence; 54 of 88 features are declared significant with no multiple-comparison correction, so a substantial share are likely false positives; and the high-familial-risk sibling design means the ASD group is not representative of general-population screening.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Larger and more fine-grained studies; systematic comparison of alternative acoustic feature sets; alternative feature pre-processing such as bag-of-words representations; and other deep learning architectures. The authors also sketch the intended deployment scenario - early preventative judgements from vocalisations captured during routine paediatric examinations in the first year of life - which frames the eventual clinical target rather than a research step.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Speech/voice: pre-linguistic infant vocalisations (babbling and other non-vegetative vocal breathing groups) characterised by spectral, energy and frequency-related acoustic parameters. No linguistic content, since the infants are pre-verbal. Parental voice is present in the recordings but is not analysed.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality; no fusion. Video was recorded but used only for segmentation and annotation, not as a modelling input - a notable choice given that the same recordings could have supported gaze or motor analysis. Within the modality, per-vocalisation decisions are aggregated into a subject-level judgement by computing an ASD ratio and thresholding it, which is a late/decision-level fusion across utterances.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning. Algorithms: linear-kernel SVM (Weka SMO) as the baseline, chosen for robustness and insensitivity to feature overfitting, and a one-layer bidirectional LSTM neural network with eight cells as the deep-learning alternative. The comparison is reported as effectively a tie, which the authors attribute to sample size rather than to the architectures.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted standardised acoustic features: the 88-parameter eGeMAPS set of statistical functionals computed over 25 smoothed low-level descriptors per vocalisation. The BLSTM additionally consumes the descriptors on 10 ms time steps, so the deep model sees a frame-level time series while the SVM sees utterance-level functionals - a representation difference the paper does not foreground.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Unweighted average recall as the primary metric with weighted average recall alongside, both reported with standard deviations across folds; full vocalisation-level confusion matrices for both classifiers; and subject-level accuracy at two explicitly stated thresholds. Using UAR rather than accuracy is the methodologically correct choice for the unbalanced 259-vs-425 vocalisation split, and this is one of the few corpus studies to make it.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Univariate Mann-Whitney U tests with effect size r, with the top ten features tabulated and the strongest visualised as per-group probability density estimates. Most informative features are voice-quality and spectral-balance measures over unvoiced segments - spectral slope 0-500 Hz and 500-1500 Hz, Hammarberg index, alpha ratio - together with MFCC variability, unvoiced segment length, f0 mean and range, and voiced segments per second. No model-internal importance (no SVM weights or BLSTM attribution) is reported, and the acoustic-phonetic interpretation of the differences is left undeveloped.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The strongest validation design among the early speech studies here: subject-independent 3-fold cross-validation with partitions matched for gender and diagnosis and balanced for vocalisation count, and a genuine three-way train/development/test split in which the SVM complexity parameter, the BLSTM architecture and the early-stopping point are all selected on development data only. Confusion matrices and fold standard deviations are reported. Weaknesses: the headline subject-level accuracy uses thresholds optimised on the merged training and development partitions of each fold, which is defensible but should be read alongside the 70% fixed-threshold result; there is no external or independent validation and no held-out site; class imbalance is handled by reporting UAR rather than by resampling; and no real-time or deployment evaluation is performed, though a paediatric-examination scenario is proposed.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: autism spectrum disorder, early identification, infant vocalisation analysis, speech-language pathology. Task vocabulary: 'earlier identification', 'automatic vocalisation-based approach', 'early acoustic markers', 'pre-linguistic vocalisations', 'feasibility', 'en-route to'. The framing is markedly more cautious than most of the corpus - the claim is feasibility and markers, not diagnosis.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: INTERSPEECH 2017 (18th Annual Conference of the International Speech Communication Association) - a technology/computational venue (speech science and signal processing), not an autism or clinical venue, though the author list spans developmental neuroscience, child psychiatry and machine learning.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2017. The paper notes that early speech-language development in ASD has repeatedly been characterised as delayed and deviant but that only a few studies examine vocalisation specificities at the feature level, and that most of those assessed crying with single acoustic features such as fundamental frequency or duration. It positions itself as one of the first to explore ASD-related pre-linguistic vocalisation specificities across a wide standardised parameter set - documenting the shift from single hand-picked acoustic measures to standardised high-dimensional feature sets that characterises the speech strand of this corpus.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Speech-based Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Condition by Generative
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Deng J; Cummins N; Schmitt M; Qian K; Ringeval F; Schuller B
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism disorders, PDD-NOS, and specific language impairment
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Speech and vocalisation
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Automatic diagnosis: four-way classification of clinician-assigned diagnostic condition (autism disorders vs PDD-NOS vs specific language impairment vs typically developing) from children's spontaneous speech, with the methodological aim of testing whether GAN-learned representations overcome the small-data limitation of hand-crafted acoustic features
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional multi-class classification study; secondary analysis of an existing speech corpus, framed as a methods paper
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Almost 12 hours of audio in total across 102 children (7h38m TD, 1h35m autism disorders, 1h12m PDD-NOS, 1h56m SLI), segmented into 6380 utterances; per-child session duration not stated
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Human children (monolingual, with communicative verbal skills)
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Spontaneous speech recordings designed to induce three emotional valence categories (positive, neutral, negative)
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Clinic and school - patients recruited in two university departments of child and adolescent psychiatry in Paris; controls recruited from elementary schools
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: France (data collection), with German, French and UK analysis groups
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: Autism disorders (AD), pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified (PDD-NOS), specific language impairment (SLI)
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Clinical diagnosis according to DSM-IV criteria, made in two university child and adolescent psychiatry departments. Control status established by asking teachers to complete a questionnaire excluding children with learning disorders. No ADOS or ADI-R
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 34 (11 autism disorders, 10 PDD-NOS, 13 specific language impairment)
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not reported - the paper states patients were matched for age but gives no numeric age anywhere
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Not reported numerically - only that patients were matched for sex
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: All children had communicative verbal skills; TD children with learning disorders were excluded by teacher questionnaire. No other comorbidity information
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported; the target is categorical diagnosis only
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developing children from elementary schools
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes - teacher questionnaire used to exclude children with learning disorders
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Stated - patients matched for age, sex, academic grades and lexical abilities among themselves, and TD children matched to patients for age and sex at a 2:1 ratio. No numbers or statistical tests are given to verify this
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Stated as matched, but no numbers reported
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes for the TD group
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Audio: spontaneous child speech, analysed as paralinguistic/acoustic signal rather than linguistic content
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Spontaneous speech elicitation inducing positive, neutral and negative emotional valence; recordings segmented into 6380 utterances
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: openSMILE feature extraction toolkit; GAN implemented as feed-forward networks trained by stochastic gradient descent; SVM classifiers. Recording hardware is not described
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: No - uses the existing Child Pathological and Emotional Speech Database (CPESD)
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not stated - CPESD is a named existing corpus but no access route, licence or availability statement is given
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Sensitive data - speech recordings of clinically diagnosed children. This paper reports no ethics approval, no consent statement and no anonymization procedure, referring only to the source corpus publications. A competing-interests declaration is present (none declared)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Two standardised hand-crafted acoustic feature sets, plus unsupervised deep representations learned from them
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: eGeMAPS (88 parameters: first two statistical moments over spectral, cepstral, prosodic and voice-quality low-level descriptors) and ComParE (6373 brute-forced features over 65 low-level descriptors comprising 4 energy-related, 55 spectral including MFCC 1-14 and RASTA-filtered auditory spectrum bands, and 6 voicing-related including F0, probability of voicing, log HNR, jitter and shimmer). GAN representations are taken as the outputs of each of the four discriminator hidden layers
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: openSMILE, chosen explicitly 'for transparency and reproducibility'
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None - the paper reports which discriminator hidden layer yields the best representation but performs no feature-level attribution or interpretation
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None. The only layer-level finding is that the third hidden layer was best for eGeMAPS while the first (bottom) hidden layer was best for ComParE
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported - no acoustic difference between groups is characterised at all; this is purely a representation-learning benchmark
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Unsupervised representation learning feeding supervised classification
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Generative adversarial network (generator: 100-unit input, three 256-unit hidden layers, tanh output; discriminator: four 256-unit hidden layers with LeakyReLU, batch normalisation and sigmoid output, binary cross-entropy objective), with discriminator hidden-layer activations fed to a linear-kernel SVM. Baselines: linear SVM, RBF-kernel SVM and a four-hidden-layer multilayer perceptron
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Fixed child-independent partitioning into training (3692 utterances, ~60%), validation (1281, ~20%) and test (1407, ~20%) sets, with all utterances from any given child confined to a single partition. All model parameters optimised on the validation set; the test partition used solely for final evaluation on unseen children. One-sided z-tests used to compare systems
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Unweighted average recall (chosen explicitly for the imbalanced four-class task), reported on both validation and test partitions, with full four-by-four confusion matrices and significance markers
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Chance UAR is 25%. With eGeMAPS: linear SVM 39.91%, RBF-SVM 39.09%, MLP 40.97% test UAR; best GAN representation (third hidden layer) 44.06% test UAR, a 10.40% relative improvement over the linear SVM baseline, significant at p<0.05. With ComParE: linear SVM 42.83%, RBF-SVM 40.40%, MLP 37.61%; best GAN representation (first hidden layer) 46.93%, significant. Confusion matrices show the autism-disorders class is very poorly recovered - 24 of 149 AD utterances correct with eGeMAPS and 16 of 149 with ComParE, with most AD utterances misassigned to SLI or TD
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: GAN-learned representations of standard acoustic feature sets modestly but significantly outperform hand-crafted features fed directly to SVMs or an MLP on a four-way clinical speech classification task, reaching 46.93% UAR against a 25% chance level. The authors present this as the first use of GAN representation learning in computational paralinguistics. The confusion matrices, however, show performance is carried almost entirely by the large typically developing class, with the autism-disorders class recognised barely above the floor.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None identified - the study makes no claim about which acoustic properties distinguish the groups
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Test the GAN-based system on other health tasks such as depression detection; extend GAN representation learning to other behavioural signals including video descriptors and physiological signals such as electrocardiogram and electrodermal activity; and compare and combine GAN-based feature learning with other unsupervised representation-learning techniques such as bag-of-words
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Methodologically careful where it counts for its own claim - genuinely child-independent partitions, a real validation set for all parameter tuning, UAR rather than accuracy for imbalanced classes, published confusion matrices, significance testing, and an open feature-extraction toolkit chosen for reproducibility. But it is a representation-learning benchmark rather than a clinical study: absolute performance is low (46.93% UAR on four classes), the autism class specifically is barely recognised (16-24 of 149 utterances correct), no participant ages or sexes are reported at all, and evaluation is at the utterance rather than child level despite child-independent partitioning, so no per-child diagnostic accuracy can be derived. Its real value in this corpus is as a counterweight to the 90%+ accuracies reported elsewhere: on a harder multi-class task with a proper held-out test set and a language-impairment comparison group, speech-based autism recognition performs close to floor.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Four groups: autism disorders (n=11), PDD-NOS (n=10), specific language impairment (n=13) and typically developing (n=68), totalling 102 children. Group sizes are reported. This is one of the few corpus studies to include a non-autistic clinical comparison group - and notably one (SLI) chosen to probe exactly the specificity question that most ASD-versus-TD studies leave open. It is also one of the few to separate autism disorders from PDD-NOS as distinct classes.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASC', 'children with autism', 'children suffering from ASC', 'children with AD', 'patients', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'control group'. Person-first but with an explicitly medical framing - 'patients', 'suffering from', 'pathological' (in the corpus name), 'automatic diagnosis'. The paper uses 'Autism Spectrum Conditions' rather than 'Disorders', a comparatively neutral choice, alongside otherwise clinical vocabulary.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Sample sizes are given (11 AD, 10 PDD-NOS, 13 SLI, 68 TD) but no age, no age range, no standard deviation and no gender distribution is reported anywhere in the paper. Matching is asserted - patients matched among themselves for age, sex, academic grades and lexical abilities, and TD children matched to patients for age and sex at a 2:1 ratio - but with no numbers and no statistical verification. Absence of any age data makes the study impossible to place in the early-diagnosis timeline.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Clinical diagnosis under DSM-IV criteria in two university departments of child and adolescent psychiatry in Paris. Control status established by teacher questionnaire excluding learning disorders. No standardised autism instrument (no ADOS, ADI-R or questionnaire measure) is reported, and no inter-rater reliability is given for the clinical diagnoses that serve as ground truth for a four-way task.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Lexical abilities and academic grades are named as matching variables for the patient groups, but no scores are reported for any group and they are not used in modelling. All children are stated to have communicative verbal skills - an important inclusion constraint that excludes minimally verbal autistic children. Comorbidities are not described beyond the exclusion of learning disorders from the TD group.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: automatic diagnosis framed as a four-way classification, with the methodological objective of testing GAN representation learning against hand-crafted acoustic features under data scarcity. Main findings: best test UAR 46.93% with ComParE-derived GAN representations and 44.06% with eGeMAPS-derived ones, both significantly above the corresponding linear-SVM baselines (42.83% and 39.91%) at p<0.05, against a 25% chance level. The optimal discriminator layer differed by feature set (bottom layer for ComParE, third layer for eGeMAPS). The autism-disorders class was recognised at close to floor in both systems.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Mixed clinic and school setting - patients recruited in two Paris university child and adolescent psychiatry departments, controls from elementary schools. Existing dataset: the Child Pathological and Emotional Speech Database (CPESD), used entirely as secondary data; no new collection.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Spontaneous speech recordings designed to induce three emotional valence categories (positive, neutral, negative). The elicitation procedure itself is not described in this paper - no prompts, stimuli, interlocutor or session structure are given, only the valence categories and the resulting utterance counts. Recordings were segmented into 6380 utterances by an unspecified procedure.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; nearly 12 hours of audio in total but no per-child session duration, number of sessions or follow-up. The data are identifiable child speech recordings from a clinical population. This paper contains no ethics approval, no consent statement and no anonymization or data-protection provision, deferring entirely to the source corpus citations - a notable gap for a paper published at a digital health venue. A competing-interests declaration is present (none declared), which makes the absence of an ethics statement more conspicuous.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition hardware is described - microphone, recording format, sampling rate and environment are all absent. Software: openSMILE for eGeMAPS and ComParE extraction, selected explicitly 'for transparency and reproducibility'; GAN generator and discriminator as feed-forward networks trained with SGD (mini-batch 128, LeakyReLU, batch normalisation, tanh output, binary cross-entropy); linear-kernel SVM for classification. The deep-learning framework is not named.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Mixed. Strong on the modelling side: the feature sets are published open standards extracted with an open-source toolkit chosen for reproducibility, full network architectures are specified (layer counts, hidden units, activations, normalisation, objective, optimiser, batch size), the SVM complexity parameter is stated to be tuned on validation, and partition sizes are given. Weak on the data side: CPESD access conditions are never stated, the elicitation protocol and recording setup are absent, no code is released, no random seeds are reported, and the exact child-to-partition assignment is not published, so the child-independent split cannot be reproduced.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors: small corpus size in ASC research generally is the paper's motivating problem, and they cite prior work warning that high accuracies on small datasets 'may lead to potential confounds'. Identifiable in review: severe class imbalance (68 TD versus 11 AD children, 4547 versus 149 test-set utterances by the confusion matrices) with the reported UAR concealing near-floor autism recognition; no age or sex data reported at all, so demographic bias cannot be assessed; matching is asserted without numbers; single-country, monolingual, verbally able children only, which excludes minimally verbal autistic children entirely; evaluation is at utterance rather than child level; and the best-layer selection differs between feature sets in a way that suggests the layer choice is being read off test performance rather than validation - the eGeMAPS validation UARs are essentially flat across layers (39.33-40.92%) while the test UARs vary by more than a point.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Apply the GAN-based system to other health tasks such as depression detection; extend GAN representation learning to other behavioural signals including video descriptors and to physiological signals such as electrocardiogram and electrodermal activity; and compare and combine GAN-based feature learning with alternative unsupervised representation-learning approaches such as bag-of-words. All the proposed directions are methodological rather than clinical - no validation, replication or population-extension work is proposed.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Speech: spontaneous child vocal production analysed paralinguistically through prosodic, spectral, cepstral and voice-quality descriptors. The introduction explicitly argues that linguistic markers may be unreliable because language skills vary across spectrum subtypes, and that paralinguistic cues are better suited to automatic detection - so linguistic content is deliberately excluded.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality; no fusion. Two acoustic feature sets are compared rather than combined, and no combination with clinical, cognitive or demographic data is performed. The future-work section proposes extending the approach to video and physiological signals, but no multimodal work is done here.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Unsupervised deep representation learning combined with supervised classification. Algorithms: a generative adversarial network whose discriminator acts as a non-linear feature extractor, with hidden-layer activations fed to a linear-kernel SVM. Baselines: linear SVM, RBF-kernel SVM and a four-hidden-layer multilayer perceptron. Notably the GAN is used purely for representation learning, not for the data augmentation that the introduction motivates - the generator's synthetic samples are never used to enlarge the training set.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Two-stage representation: hand-crafted acoustic functionals (eGeMAPS 88-dimensional, or ComParE 6373-dimensional) computed per utterance, then transformed into deep embeddings by taking the activations of one of four GAN discriminator hidden layers (256 units each). The comparison across layers is itself a study of representation depth, and yields different optima for the compact and the brute-forced feature set.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Unweighted average recall only, chosen explicitly because the four-class task is imbalanced - the methodologically correct choice, and reported on both validation and test partitions. Full four-by-four confusion matrices are published for the best system under each feature set, which is unusually transparent and is what makes the near-floor autism-class performance visible. One-sided z-tests compare systems. No accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1 or AUC, and no per-child metric.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No feature importance, saliency, attention or attribution analysis is performed, and no acoustic property is identified as characteristic of any group. The only interpretability-adjacent result is which discriminator hidden layer produces the most useful representation, which speaks to network depth rather than to behaviour. This is one of the least interpretable studies in the corpus, and unusually the paper makes no interpretive claim it cannot support.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Generalisability is addressed by design: partitioning is 'completely child independent', with all utterances from a given child confined to one partition, and a dedicated validation partition is used for all parameter optimisation while the test partition is 'solely used for the purpose of performance evaluation on unseen children'. This is the correct structure and better than most of the corpus. Class imbalance is addressed at the metric level (UAR) but not by resampling or class weighting, and the confusion matrices show the imbalance is not in fact overcome. No external validation on a second corpus, no held-out site, no bias mitigation, no calibration, and no real-time or deployment analysis.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: Autism Spectrum Condition; automatic diagnosis; generative adversarial networks; representation learning. CCS concepts: Applied computing - Life and medical sciences, Health informatics; Computing methodologies - Neural networks. Task vocabulary: 'speech-based diagnosis', 'objective marker', 'computational paralinguistics', 'data scarcity', 'representation learning'.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: DH'17 - the 2017 ACM International Conference on Digital Health, London. A technology/health-informatics venue rather than an autism or clinical journal, though more health-oriented than the pure signal-processing venues elsewhere in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2017. The paper characterises the field as showing that 'high levels of accuracy can be achieved' for discriminating typically developing children from children with ASC, but immediately qualifies that these results come from 'rather small datasets, and may lead to potential confounds', naming corpus size as 'a major obstacle in the development of robust models which are sufficiently reliable for clinical practice'. It positions itself as the first application of GAN representation learning in computational paralinguistics. This is one of the corpus's most explicit internal critiques of its own literature's headline accuracies.

data_charting_rubrics.title: ANN and SVM Classifiers in Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorder Gait Based on Three-Dimensional Ground Reaction Forces
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Hasan CZC; Jailani R; Tahir NM
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder (mild category)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Motor and kinematics
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Automated recognition to assist diagnosis and clinical decision-making: binary classification of ASD versus normal gait patterns from 3D ground reaction forces, and identification of dominant GRF gait biomarkers
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study; an explicit methodological extension of the authors' earlier KNN-based study on the same cohort
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session; a single left-limb stance from one selected valid trial per subject was analysed
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Straight barefoot walking along a 6.5-metre walkway at self-determined speed, with one foot landing on each of two embedded force plates
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory - Human Motion Gait Analysis laboratory, Universiti Teknologi MARA Shah Alam
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Previously diagnosed with a mild category of ASD; no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or confirmation procedure is reported
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: All subjects had no history of lower extremity injuries and were able to walk independently; no other comorbidity information
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: All ASD participants were of the mild category, but no severity instrument or score is reported and severity is not modelled
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developing healthy children from the local community
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Described as healthy with no lower-extremity injury history; no screening instrument or autism-trait measure reported
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not claimed and not tested; group means differ by roughly 0.9 years (8.63 vs 9.52) with no statistical comparison reported
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed - no gender data at all
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Kinetic gait data: three-dimensional ground reaction forces (medial-lateral, anterior-posterior, vertical) during the stance phase of walking
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Self-paced barefoot straight-line walking; a trial counted as valid only when a clean foot strike landed on each force plate. Amplitudes normalised to percentage of body weight and time components to percentage of stance phase to permit between-subject comparison
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Two independent AMTI force plates embedded consecutively in a 6.5 m walkway, sampling at 1000 Hz; second-order low-pass Butterworth filter at 30 Hz cut-off; IBM SPSS Statistics v21 for stepwise discriminant analysis; MATLAB R2015a with the Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox and Neural Network Toolbox for classification
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes in the sense of newly collected gait data within a larger project, but the data are reused from the authors' earlier work and are not released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Low-sensitivity numeric force data rather than identifiable media. The study is stated to be part of a larger project approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Universiti Teknologi MARA; no participant consent statement or anonymization procedure is described, though parents are thanked in the acknowledgements
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted time-series parameterisation features - local peak and minimum force amplitudes and their relative times of occurrence
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 20 features across the three GRF components. Medial-lateral: maximum supination force, peak force during foot flat, maximum pronation force and their relative times (Fx1-Fx3, Tx1-Tx3). Anterior-posterior: maximum braking force, zero force at mid-stance, maximum propulsion force and their relative times (Fy1-Fy3, Ty1-Ty3), with Fy2 excluded because its value is zero by definition. Vertical: first vertical peak, minimum force between peaks, second vertical peak and their relative times (Fz1-Fz3, Tz1-Tz3), plus loading rate, push-off rate and peak ratio
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Time-series parameterisation applied to GRF waveforms; SPSS for the stepwise discriminant feature selection; MATLAB for classification
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Stepwise discriminant analysis (SWDA) using the Wilks' lambda criterion with F-to-enter of at least 0.05 and F-to-remove below 0.10, with the full p-value distribution for all 20 features published
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Three features with p < 0.05: relative time to maximum supination force (Tx1, p = 0.005), relative time to zero force during mid-stance (Ty2, p = 0.000) and second vertical peak force (Fz3, p = 0.000). The other 17 features were discarded
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported - the three significant features are named and located within the gait cycle (loading response, mid-stance, terminal stance) but the direction of the ASD-versus-TD difference is never stated. The authors relate altered second vertical peak force to gait instability and difficulty supporting body weight by analogy with cerebral palsy, without giving the direction of effect in their own data
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Three-layer feed-forward artificial neural network trained with scaled conjugate gradient backpropagation (hidden neurons varied 1 to 50), and support vector machines with linear, polynomial (degree 2-4) and RBF kernels, with C grid-searched over {0.001, 0.01, 1, 10, 100, 1000} and RBF gamma varied from 1.4 to 1.6 in 0.01 steps
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 10-fold cross-validation with the dataset randomly partitioned into ten equal folds, repeated for ten iterations, with accuracy, sensitivity and specificity averaged across folds from two-class confusion matrices. Critically, both the SWDA feature selection and the exhaustive grid search over model hyperparameters were performed on the full dataset before cross-validation, not nested inside the folds
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity per classifier
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: ANN with scaled conjugate gradient: 93.3% accuracy, 96.7% sensitivity, 90.0% specificity. SVM-RBF 85.0% / 93.3% / 76.7%; SVM-polynomial 83.3% / 86.7% / 80.0%; SVM-linear 78.3% / 76.7% / 80.0%. The authors report this outperforms their previous KNN attempt on the same data
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Three ground-reaction-force features - relative time to maximum supination, relative time to zero anterior-posterior force at mid-stance, and second vertical peak force - were statistically significant discriminators of ASD from typically developing gait, and a small feed-forward neural network using only these three features classified at 93.3% accuracy, outperforming all three SVM kernel variants. The authors interpret the findings as gait variation spanning loading response, mid-stance and terminal stance.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Timing of maximum supination force, timing of zero anterior-posterior force at mid-stance, and magnitude of the second (push-off) vertical peak force
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: More in-depth exploration of kinematic and kinetic gait parameters beyond ground reaction forces, and evaluation on a larger dataset to confirm the current observations
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A clean, well-instrumented gait study whose headline accuracy is nonetheless not a generalisation estimate: the SWDA feature selection that reduced 20 features to 3 was performed on the whole dataset using group labels, and the exhaustive grid search over SVM kernels, C, gamma and ANN hidden-layer size (1 to 50) was likewise conducted outside the cross-validation loop. Both leak label information into every fold, and the reported 93.3% is additionally the best of four classifier configurations. Reporting gaps compound this: no gender data at all, no age-matching test despite a ~0.9-year group difference, no diagnostic instrument for a sample described only as 'mild category of ASD', and a single stance phase from a single limb of a single trial per child as the entire behavioral sample. Feature-selection transparency is a genuine strength - the complete p-value table for all 20 features is published.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 30: children with ASD (all mild category) and typically developing children. Group sizes, mean age, height and body mass are reported for both. Recruitment is split within the ASD group - 14 from the National Autism Society of Malaysia centre and 16 from the local community via parents approached through social media - which is unusually specific. No other-diagnosis comparison group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'ASD subjects', 'ASD group', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'TD healthy children', 'normal children', 'normal gait patterns', 'ASD population'. Person-first for the participants but the comparison condition is repeatedly framed as 'normal' rather than 'typical' - 'ASD and normal gait', 'normal children' - which positions autistic gait as pathological by contrast; the paper also groups ASD gait with 'pathological gait' alongside cerebral palsy, stroke and Parkinson's disease.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=30, mean age 8.63 +/- 2.16 years, height 1.29 +/- 0.14 m, mass 31.21 +/- 14.20 kg. TD n=30, mean age 9.52 +/- 1.96 years, height 1.27 +/- 0.13 m, mass 28.03 +/- 10.57 kg. No gender distribution is reported for either group, and no age matching is claimed or statistically tested despite a ~0.9-year mean difference - material for a gait study in children, where maturation changes force profiles. Height and body mass are reported, which is appropriate since GRF amplitudes are normalised to body weight, but the large mass SD in the ASD group (14.20 kg) is not discussed.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not reported. Participants are described only as 'previously diagnosed with a mild category of ASD' with no instrument, diagnostic criteria, diagnosing clinician or confirmation procedure named. Control status is asserted rather than screened. Since diagnostic label is the classification target, this is the study's most serious reporting gap.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive-functioning measures are reported for either group, and no autism severity instrument underlies the 'mild category' description. The only functional criteria are physical - no history of lower-extremity injury and ability to walk independently. Comorbidities are not otherwise described.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: automated ASD gait recognition to assist diagnosis, clinical decision-making and treatment targeting, plus identification of dominant GRF biomarkers. Main findings: three of 20 GRF features were statistically significant discriminators (Tx1 p=0.005, Ty2 p<0.001, Fz3 p<0.001); a three-input ANN achieved 93.3% accuracy, 96.7% sensitivity and 90.0% specificity, outperforming SVM-RBF (85.0%), SVM-polynomial (83.3%) and SVM-linear (78.3%) as well as the authors' earlier KNN approach.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory setting - a dedicated human motion gait analysis laboratory with force plates embedded in an instrumented walkway. Data were newly collected within a larger institutional research project but are reused here from the authors' earlier published work, so this paper is a secondary analysis of an in-house dataset rather than a new collection.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Straight barefoot walking along a 6.5-metre walkway at self-determined speed, with the two force plates positioned so that one foot strikes each. Trials were accepted only on a clean foot strike on each plate. Only a single left-limb stance phase from one selected valid trial per participant was analysed - an extremely small behavioral sample per child, and the selection criterion for which valid trial to use is not stated.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single walking session with no follow-up and no repeated measurement. The data are numeric force-plate traces rather than identifiable media, so privacy risk is minimal. Ethics approval is reported at the level of the parent project (Research Ethics Committee of Universiti Teknologi MARA), but no participant or parental consent statement and no anonymization or data-protection procedure is described.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: two independent Advanced Mechanical Technology Inc. force plates embedded consecutively in a 6.5 m walkway, recording medial-lateral, anterior-posterior and vertical forces at 1000 Hz. Software: second-order low-pass Butterworth filter with 30 Hz cut-off; IBM SPSS Statistics v21 for stepwise discriminant analysis; MATLAB R2015a Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox and Neural Network Toolbox for SVM and ANN classification.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No data availability statement, no code release and no random seeds. Method reporting is otherwise good: the full 20-feature definition table, the complete SWDA p-value distribution for every feature, the SWDA entry and removal criteria, the sampling rate and filter settings, the SVM kernel types with their C and gamma grids, the polynomial degree range, and the ANN architecture and training function are all specified. The pipeline is re-implementable in principle but the analysis cannot be reproduced without the data.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors: only that evaluation on a larger dataset is needed to confirm the observations - there is no limitations section as such. Identifiable in review: feature selection by SWDA used group labels on the full dataset before cross-validation, and the exhaustive hyperparameter grid search (three SVM kernels, six C values, three polynomial degrees, 21 gamma values, 50 ANN hidden-layer sizes) was likewise performed outside the folds, so 93.3% is not an unbiased generalisation estimate; the reported figure is also the best of four classifier configurations; no gender data at all, so sex bias cannot be assessed in a literature with strong male skew; groups differ by ~0.9 years in mean age with no matching test, and gait matures with age; body mass SD is large and unequal; ASD recruitment is split across a specialist centre and social-media outreach with no comparison between subgroups; only one stance phase of one limb from one trial represents each child, so within-subject gait variability - itself a reported feature of autistic movement - is entirely discarded.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Two directions only: deeper exploration of kinematic and kinetic gait parameters beyond ground reaction forces, and evaluation on a larger dataset. No proposals for external validation, for comparison against other motor-affected conditions, or for addressing the demographic and methodological gaps.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Motor behavior: ground reaction forces during walking - the kinetic rather than kinematic aspect of gait, measuring the forces generated against the ground in three directions rather than limb trajectories or joint angles.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality, but with a form of within-modality fusion: features from all three orthogonal GRF components (medial-lateral, anterior-posterior, vertical) are pooled into one candidate set, and the three surviving features happen to come one from each component - so the discriminative signal is genuinely distributed across all three force directions. No combination with clinical, cognitive or demographic data.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning. Algorithms: a three-layer feed-forward artificial neural network trained by scaled conjugate gradient backpropagation, and support vector machines with linear, polynomial and RBF kernels. Stepwise discriminant analysis serves as a statistical feature-selection stage. The authors note that comparative studies often favour SVM, which makes their ANN result a departure from expectation.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted time-series parameterisation: each GRF waveform is reduced to its local peaks, minima and the relative times at which they occur, with amplitudes normalised to percentage body weight and times to percentage of stance phase. This yields 20 scalar features, reduced to three by feature selection. No raw waveforms, time series or learned representations are used.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, reported for all four classifier configurations. Headline: 93.3% accuracy, 96.7% sensitivity, 90.0% specificity for the ANN. No AUC, F1, precision, confidence intervals or fold-level variance, despite averaging over ten folds and ten iterations where a standard deviation would have been readily available.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Stepwise discriminant analysis with Wilks' lambda provides the interpretability, and the paper publishes the complete p-value distribution for all 20 candidate features - unusually transparent, since it lets a reader see exactly how sharp the separation between selected and discarded features is (three at p<=0.005, next best Fy1 at 0.084). The three retained features are interpreted anatomically as spanning loading response, mid-stance and terminal stance, and the altered second vertical peak is related to gait instability and body-weight support difficulties by analogy with cerebral palsy. The direction of each group difference is not reported.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Weak. 10-fold cross-validation repeated over ten iterations is used and is explicitly motivated by small sample size, but both the label-using SWDA feature selection and the exhaustive hyperparameter grid search were performed on the complete dataset before the folds were drawn, so information from every test fold informed both the feature set and the model configuration. There is no external or independent validation, no held-out site, no class-imbalance issue (30/30), no statistical comparison between classifiers, no bias mitigation, and no real-time or deployment analysis - though clinical diagnosis and treatment evaluation are named as intended applications.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: artificial neural network, autism spectrum disorder, gait classification, ground reaction force, support vector machine. Task vocabulary: 'automated recognition', 'gait disturbances', 'prominent biomarkers', 'pathological gait', 'clinical decision-making'. The framing situates autism alongside cerebral palsy, post-stroke and Parkinson's gait as a pathological gait recognition problem.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: TENCON 2018 - the IEEE Region 10 Conference. A general engineering/technology venue, neither autism-specific nor clinical, and broader than the specialist computer-vision and speech venues elsewhere in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2018. The paper notes that machine learning has been proven effective for automated gait recognition in cerebral palsy, post-stroke and Parkinson's disease, but that 'research in the area of automated recognition of ASD gait using machine learning techniques based on GRFs gait features is less prevalent' - positioning autism gait analysis as lagging behind other clinical gait populations, and its own contribution as an incremental extension of the authors' prior KNN study on the same data.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Analyzing Human-Robot Interaction Using Machine Vision for Autism screening
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Moghadas M; Moradi H
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2018 6th RSI International Conference on Robotics and Mechatronics (IcRoM)
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Robot-mediated interaction
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Automated screening: automate a previously manual robot-interaction screening protocol by extracting machine-vision features of a child's spatial behaviour toward a social robot and classifying ASD versus typically developing
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study; an explicit automation of the manually-coded protocol of Soleiman et al.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session of 190 seconds of interaction per child, in a fixed scenario beginning with a robot greeting followed by scripted communication actions
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Human children (toddlers to early school age)
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Free interaction with a remotely operated parrot-like social robot (RoboParrot) that speaks, blinks, sings, laughs and moves; parents present but instructed not to get involved
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Clinic - the Center for Treatment of Autistic Disorders (Tehran Autism)
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Diagnosed by a clinical team comprising a developmental-behavioural pediatrician and a child psychologist, with a child psychiatrist evaluating to validate the psychologist's initial assessment. No standardised instrument (no ADOS, ADI-R or rating scale) is named
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not reported - only a range is given
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported; two ASD participants are described post hoc as 'high-functional in autism range'
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not measured; functioning level is mentioned only anecdotally when explaining misclassifications
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developing children attending normal daycares or kindergartens
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Selected as showing no cognitive deficit and attending mainstream childcare; no screening instrument reported
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No - the control age range (2.11-7.6 years) extends far beyond the ASD range (2.1-4.1 years), with no matching, no means and no statistical comparison
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed - no gender data at all
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted rather than assessed
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Video-derived spatial behaviour: the child's tracked position relative to the robot over time, from an overhead camera
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A fixed 190-second robot interaction scenario; the child's position tracked by a Kernelized Correlation Filter after initial detection by motion detection or manual tagging; the floor area in front of the robot partitioned into a 4x4 grid
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: RoboParrot parrot-like social robot in a cage, remotely controlled by a tablet; two cameras - one beside the robot for facial expressions (recorded but not analysed here) and one overhead for global movement; Kernelized Correlation Filter tracking, selected over MIL, Boosting and TLD trackers
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Newly recorded interactions within an existing robot-screening programme; not released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Sensitive data - video recordings of identifiable young children, including a close-range facial camera. No ethics approval, consent statement or anonymization procedure is reported anywhere; only funders and the recruiting clinic are acknowledged. A figure showing a child interacting with the robot is reproduced in the paper
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted spatial-occupancy features and pairwise similarity measures
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Three feature constructions over a 4x4 spatial grid: a Presence Vector (16-bit binary indicator of whether the child ever occupied each cell), a Weighted Presence Vector (16-dimensional vector of the percentage of time spent in each cell), and the ratio of time spent in cell 4 - the cell directly in front of the robot - to time across the whole grid. Classification features are the cosine similarities between a child's WPV/PV and those of others
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Kernelized Correlation Filter tracker; custom grid-partitioning and cosine-similarity computation
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, in the sense that the two feature families are statistically compared
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: t-tests comparing within-ASD (AA) versus within-TD (NN) similarity distributions, ANOVA across AA/NN/NA groups, plus a permutation-style control in which participants were randomly regrouped into pseudo-ASD and pseudo-TD groups and the analysis repeated
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The Weighted Presence Vector cosine similarity (t-test p = 0.001, ANOVA p = 1.09e-05) and the ratio of presence in the cell directly in front of the robot (ANOVA p < 0.05). The qualitative binary Presence Vector was explicitly found not to discriminate (t-test p = 0.160)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Implied but not quantified: children with ASD spent proportionally less time in the cell directly in front of the robot, interpreted as less attraction to and interaction with it. Table 1 reportedly gives the per-group ratios but the values are not recoverable from the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification with a two-layer stacking arrangement
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Decision tree, k-nearest neighbours, Gaussian-kernel SVM, linear discriminant and logistic regression, each applied separately to the cosine-similarity feature and to the presence-ratio feature, with their outputs combined by a second-layer classifier - described by the authors as 'sort of sensor fusion'
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 8-fold cross-validation, stated as being used 'in order to prevent overfitting'. With 16 subjects this means two subjects per fold. No nesting of feature or model selection is described, and the best of five classifiers across three feature configurations is reported
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy only, plus narrative reporting of false positives and false negatives
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Final Gaussian SVM stacked classifier: 81.3% accuracy (13/16 correct), with 2 false positives and 1 false negative. First-layer classifiers each misclassified 2 TD and 2 ASD children. On individual features: cosine similarity gave 75% for KNN and SVM, 68.8% for discriminant and logistic regression and 50% for decision tree; presence ratio gave 75% for all five classifiers; the stacked combination gave 81.3% for SVM but only 68.8% for the other four classifiers
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: The proportion of interaction time a child spends directly in front of a social robot, and the similarity of their spatial occupancy pattern to other children's, distinguishes ASD from typically developing children well enough for a Gaussian SVM to reach 81.3% accuracy on 16 children. The qualitative binary presence pattern carried no signal; only the time-weighted version did. A permutation control confirmed the group difference was not an artefact of arbitrary grouping. The authors report that misclassifications were interpretable - two shy TD children who avoided the robot and two high-functioning autistic children who engaged with it.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Reduced proportion of time spent in the zone directly in front of the robot, and a distinctive within-group similarity of time-weighted spatial occupancy patterns
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Test the system on more children for better accuracy and confidence; study child-parent interaction during screening sessions; develop a more robust protocol to reduce image-processing cost and complexity; use the front-facing camera to exploit facial emotion and other features; and integrate this approach with other intelligent screening methods to raise overall accuracy
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The design contains one genuinely good methodological idea rarely seen in this corpus - a permutation control in which participants were randomly regrouped and the same statistical pipeline rerun, confirming the group difference did not arise by chance. The authors also reason explicitly about the asymmetric cost of false positives versus false negatives in screening, and explain their errors concretely rather than glossing them. Against this: n=16 makes 81.3% equal to 13 of 16 children; control ages (2.11-7.6 years) span nearly twice the ASD range (2.1-4.1) with no matching, so age is badly confounded with group in a task where locomotion and social approach change rapidly with development; no gender data; no diagnostic instrument; no ethics or consent statement despite video of young children including a facial camera; and the reported figure is the best cell of a five-classifier by three-feature grid with no nesting. The stacked second layer actually degraded four of the five classifiers relative to the single presence-ratio feature.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 8: children with ASD and typically developing children, total n=16. Group sizes are reported; no other-diagnosis group. The predecessor study being automated (Soleiman et al.) used 32 children, so this automation paper works on half that sample.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with autism', 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'Typically Developed (TD) children', 'TD children', 'normal ones', 'autistic ones', 'suspicious cases'. Mixed usage - person-first in the formal descriptions, but the comparison group is called 'normal' in the hypothesis statements and misclassified controls are described as 'suspicious cases'. The paper also uses 'high-functional in autism range' when explaining errors.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=8, age range 2.1-4.1 years. TD n=8, age range 2.11-7.6 years. No means, no standard deviations, and no gender distribution for either group. The groups are not age-matched and the mismatch is substantial - the control range extends to 7.6 years while no autistic child was older than 4.1 - which is a serious confound for a measure based on where a child physically positions themselves relative to a robot, since approach behaviour, mobility and social confidence all change markedly between age 2 and age 7. Very young sample, so relevant in principle to early screening.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Diagnosis by a clinical team - a developmental-behavioural pediatrician and a child psychologist - with a child psychiatrist validating the psychologist's initial evaluation. This multi-clinician process is described in more detail than most corpus studies, but no standardised instrument is named (no ADOS, ADI-R, GARS or SCQ), despite the introduction reviewing exactly such instruments. Control status was established by attendance at mainstream daycare and absence of observed cognitive deficit, with no screening instrument.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None reported. No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive measures for either group, and no autism severity instrument. Functioning level enters only as a post-hoc anecdote - two misclassified autistic children are described as 'high-functional in autism range' - which is used to explain errors rather than as measured data.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: automate an existing manually-coded robot-interaction screening protocol. Main findings: the time-weighted spatial occupancy pattern (WPV cosine similarity) separated the groups significantly (t-test p=0.001, ANOVA p=1.09e-05) while the binary presence pattern did not (p=0.160); the ratio of time spent directly in front of the robot was also significant (p<0.05); a Gaussian SVM stacking both feature families reached 81.3% accuracy with 2 false positives and 1 false negative; a random-regrouping control produced no significant differences, confirming the effect was not an artefact.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Clinic setting - the Center for Treatment of Autistic Disorders (Tehran Autism), with the robot placed in a cage and cameras positioned overhead and beside it. Newly recorded interaction data, but building directly on an existing robot-screening platform and protocol from the same research group.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A fixed 190-second scenario of interaction with RoboParrot, beginning with a greeting from the robot followed by several communication actions designed to motivate the child to engage further. The robot speaks, blinks, sings, laughs and moves slightly, and is teleoperated from a tablet. Parents accompanied their child but were instructed not to get involved. The child is free to move within the space in front of the robot; there is no task instruction to the child.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single 190-second session per child with no repeat or follow-up. The data are highly sensitive - continuous video of identifiable young children from two angles, including a close-range facial camera, plus a published photograph of a child interacting with the robot. There is no ethics approval statement, no parental consent statement, and no anonymization or data-protection provision anywhere in the paper. Only the funding council and recruiting clinic are acknowledged.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: RoboParrot, a parrot-like social robot with speech, blinking, singing, laughing and limited movement, teleoperated by tablet and placed inside a cage; two cameras, one beside the robot for facial expression and one overhead for global movement. Software: motion detection or manual tagging for initial child detection; Kernelized Correlation Filter tracking, chosen after comparison against MIL, Boosting and TLD trackers; custom grid partitioning, cosine similarity, and classifiers. No specific software packages or versions are named.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Poor. No data availability statement, no code, no software versions, no hyperparameters (the Gaussian SVM kernel width and the KNN k are never given), no random seeds, and no specification of how the 4x4 grid maps onto physical space. Table 1, which holds the per-group presence ratios, is not recoverable as values. The method is describable in principle - grid occupancy, cosine similarity, standard classifiers - but no quantitative result other than the accuracies and p-values can be extracted from the paper.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors: the limited number of cases is explicitly named as a limitation, with a stated plan to run on more children; and the method is acknowledged to fail on shy typically developing children, which the authors address by arguing it should be combined with other screening methods rather than used alone. Identifiable in review: control age range (2.11-7.6 years) roughly doubles the ASD range (2.1-4.1) with no matching, confounding age with group in a spatial-approach measure; no gender data despite a strongly sex-skewed condition; no diagnostic instrument; the best of five classifiers across three feature configurations is reported with no nesting of that selection inside the 8-fold cross-validation; the stacking layer degrades four of five classifiers, so the 81.3% may reflect a fortunate combination rather than a real gain; and post-hoc explanations of the four first-layer errors (shyness, high functioning) are unmeasured narrative rather than data.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Test on more children for higher accuracy and confidence; study child-parent interaction during screening sessions; develop a more robust protocol to cut image-processing cost and complexity; exploit the front camera for facial emotion and other features; and integrate with other intelligent screening approaches. The last of these follows directly from their own finding that the method misclassifies shy typically developing children, so it is a limitation-driven rather than generic proposal.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Spatial/locomotor behaviour: the child's physical position and dwell time relative to a social robot, derived from overhead video tracking. Facial video is captured but not analysed. This is proxemic and approach behaviour rather than gaze, speech or fine motor kinematics.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Two feature families derived from the same modality - similarity of time-weighted spatial occupancy patterns, and the presence ratio in the robot-facing cell - are each fed to separate first-layer classifiers whose outputs are combined by a second-layer classifier. The authors describe this explicitly as a form of sensor fusion, though both inputs come from one sensor; it is decision-level fusion across feature views. Notably the fusion helped only the SVM (75% and 75% to 81.3%) and hurt the other four classifiers (dropping to 68.8%). No integration with clinical scores, demographics or parent report.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning. Algorithms: decision tree, k-nearest neighbours, Gaussian-kernel SVM, linear discriminant analysis and logistic regression, each evaluated on both feature families and on the stacked combination. Gaussian SVM was selected as the final model. Statistical hypothesis testing (t-test, ANOVA) is used alongside classification to establish that the features carry group information.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Symbolic/spatial-occupancy representation: continuous tracked position is discretised onto a 4x4 grid and summarised either as a 16-bit binary occupancy vector or a 16-dimensional dwell-time proportion vector, then converted into pairwise cosine similarities between children. The classification features are therefore relational - how similar this child's spatial pattern is to others' - rather than absolute, which is an unusual representation choice in this corpus and one that makes the features dependent on the composition of the sample.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy only, reported for five classifiers across three feature configurations, supplemented by narrative false-positive and false-negative counts (2 and 1 for the final model). No sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, AUC or confidence intervals, though the raw counts allow them to be derived: with 8 per group, 2 FP and 1 FN gives sensitivity 87.5% and specificity 75%.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability comes from statistical comparison rather than model attribution. The Weighted Presence Vector similarity is shown to separate groups (p=0.001) while the binary Presence Vector does not (p=0.160), which is an informative negative result: the discriminative signal lies in how long a child stays near the robot, not in which regions they ever visit. The presence ratio in the robot-facing cell is directly interpretable as attraction to the robot. Importantly, the authors ran a permutation-style control - randomly regrouping the children and repeating the analysis, which produced no significant differences - a check almost no other study in this corpus performs.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Limited. 8-fold cross-validation is used and explicitly motivated by overfitting prevention, but with 16 children this leaves two per test fold, and neither the choice among five classifiers nor the two-layer stacking design is nested inside it. The random-regrouping control is a genuine robustness check on the statistical claim, though not on the classifier. There is no external or independent validation, no held-out site, no class-imbalance issue (8/8), and no real-time or deployment evaluation despite screening being the stated application. Generalisability is addressed only by the authors' plan to test more children, and the known failure mode (shy typically developing children) is handled by proposing combination with other methods rather than by any modelling change.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords as printed: 'autism screening; human robot interactions; image processing; classification' (the keyword line retains an unedited template fragment, 'Keywords-component; formatting'). Task vocabulary: 'autism screening', 'human-robot interaction', 'vision-based approach', 'Presence Vector', 'Weighted Presence Vector', 'suspicious cases'.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: The 6th RSI International Conference on Robotics and Mechatronics (IcRoM 2018), Tehran - a technology/robotics venue, not an autism or clinical venue.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2018. The paper situates itself against traditional questionnaire-and-expert screening (3DI, ASD-OC), noting clinical guidance that no questionnaire can be recommended as a diagnostic test and that a combination of direct behavioural observation and caregiver report is recommended instead - then frames robot-based screening as 'a new trend'. Its own contribution is explicitly the automation of a previously manual feature-extraction step in an existing robot protocol, illustrating the corpus-wide progression from manually coded behavioural observation to automated sensing of the same behaviour.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Applying Eye Tracking to Identify Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Wan G; Kong X; Sun B; Yu S; Tu Y; Park J; Lang C; Koh M; Wei Z; Feng Z; Lin Y; Kong J
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye-tracking and gaze
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Early screening: test whether a deliberately short (10 second) eye-tracking paradigm carries enough information to distinguish ASD from typically developing children, and identify which facial or body regions do the discriminating
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study, described by the authors as preliminary and proof of concept, with a replication aim (extending an infant finding to 4-6 year-olds) and an extension aim (machine-learning discrimination)
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session; a single 10-second muted video clip after five-point calibration and a fixation correction task
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Passive free viewing of a 10 s silent video of a young Asian female mouthing the English alphabet, preceded by eye-position correction using a dynamic pink rabbit stimulus
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Clinic - outpatient ward of the Child Mental Health and Rehabilitation Center, Shenzhen Maternity and Child Healthcare Hospital, with testing in a dark soundproof room; controls recruited from a kindergarten in the same city
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: China (Shenzhen), with US collaborators at Massachusetts General Hospital / Harvard Medical School
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: DSM-5 diagnosis by experienced physicians combined with a Childhood Autism Rating Scale score above 30 as an inclusion criterion. The authors state explicitly that ADI-R and ADOS were unavailable in their setting and list this as the study's first limitation. Gesell Developmental Scale (Chinese version) administered to the ASD group for correlational analysis
