data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported for the ASD group; controls were screened by a licensed physician to exclude any history of psychiatric or neurological disorder including ASD
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: CARS score 34.4 +/- 7.8 reported for the ASD group; GDS subscores reported (adaptation 62.8, large motion 73.7, fine motion 59.2, language 46.9, personal-social 53.5). Severity is used for correlation with fixation time but is not a modelling target
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developing children from a local kindergarten
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes - screened by a licensed physician to exclude any history of psychiatric or neurological disorder including ASD
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes - matched by design and confirmed non-significant (p = 0.17)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Claimed as gender-matched and non-significant by chi-square (p = 0.14), though the distributions differ substantially in practice (33/4 vs 27/10, i.e. 89% vs 73% male)
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes - physician-screened
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye movements: fixation time on ten predefined areas of interest, plus three within-face ratios
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Five-point calibration, eye-position correction on a dynamic pink rabbit, then passive viewing of the 10 s muted speaking-face clip. Fixation times computed for background, body, hair, outer-face, eyes, nose, mouth, person, face and outer-person; eyes-to-face, nose-to-face and mouth-to-face ratios derived to adjust for the generally lower total fixation time of the ASD group
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: SMI RED250 portable eye-tracking system at 250 Hz with 0.03 degree spatial resolution; 22-inch widescreen LCD monitor at 1024x768 with a fixed 65 cm eye-to-monitor distance in a dark soundproof room; BeGaze data analysis software; SPSS 22.0 for statistics
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - newly collected eye-tracking data, but not released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze coordinate and fixation-duration data are low in identifiability. Ethics approval from the Shenzhen Maternity and Child Healthcare Hospital research committee is reported with explicit reference to the 1964 Helsinki Declaration, informed consent was obtained from all parents, and a conflict-of-interest disclosure is provided for one author (equity in a startup and pending patents in an unrelated neuromodulation area). Ethics and consent reporting are complete; no anonymization procedure is separately described, and none is materially needed for this data type
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted area-of-interest fixation-time features and derived ratios
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Fixation times at ten AOIs - background; body (neck, shoulders, chest); hair; outer-face (face excluding mouth, nose, eyes); eyes; nose; mouth; person (hair, body, face); face (outer-face, eyes, nose, mouth); outer-person (hair and body) - plus eyes-to-face, nose-to-face and mouth-to-face ratios
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: BeGaze (SMI) for gaze data processing; SPSS 22.0 for statistical analysis and the discriminant/SVM analysis
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: SVM discriminative weights per AOI, with statistical significance assessed by 1000-iteration permutation tests against the null hypothesis that the weight values are arbitrary - a genuine statistical test of feature importance rather than a ranking
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Only two of the ten AOIs significantly discriminated: fixation time at the mouth (p = 0.008) and at the body (p = 0.03). Notably the eyes, despite showing a large univariate group difference, did not survive as a discriminative feature
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Clear and reported: fixation times were significantly lower in the ASD group at the eyes, mouth, nose, body, person, face and outer-person (all p < 0.005 after Bonferroni correction across ten AOIs). However none of the three within-face ratios differed (eyes-to-face p = 0.39, mouth-to-face p = 0.95, nose-to-face p = 0.87), indicating a global reduction in looking rather than a redistribution of attention within the face
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Support vector machine applied to AOI fixation times, framed as discriminant analysis
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Five-fold cross-validation, with classification accuracy tested against chance by permuting child labels 1000 times and locating the observed accuracy within the permuted distribution, and with AOI discriminative weights separately tested by 1000 permutations
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, with a permutation-based p-value for the accuracy
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: 85.1% accuracy, 86.5% sensitivity, 83.8% specificity, significantly above chance by permutation test (p < 0.001). Note an internal inconsistency: the Discussion also reports the same result as 'accuracy of 82.8%, sensitivity of 79.3%, and specificity of 86.2%' in one passage, contradicting the abstract, results and conclusion figures
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A 10-second muted video of a speaking face was sufficient to discriminate 4-6 year-old children with ASD from matched typically developing children at 85.1% accuracy. Children with ASD showed globally reduced fixation across seven of ten areas of interest, but crucially the within-face ratios did not differ, so the effect is reduced overall looking rather than a shift away from the eyes specifically. Only mouth and body fixation times carried significant discriminative weight. Fixation time correlated with the Gesell large-motion subscore in the ASD group.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Reduced fixation time at the moving mouth and at the body; more broadly a global reduction in fixation across eyes, mouth, nose, body, face, person and outer-person
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Studies with larger samples to validate the findings; extension to other populations, particularly young infants, to determine whether the effect is specific to this age group; direct comparison of this short paradigm against other established eye-tracking paradigms; and combination of this paradigm with other paradigms
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Unusually careful statistics for this corpus: Bonferroni correction across the ten AOI comparisons, permutation testing of both the classification accuracy and the individual feature weights, ratio measures explicitly introduced to control for the ASD group's globally lower fixation, and a candid five-point limitations list. The ratio result is the most scientifically interesting finding and is reported honestly even though it complicates the standard eye-avoidance narrative - the groups differ in how much they look, not in where within the face they look. Two problems temper this. First, the paper reports two different sets of performance figures for the same analysis (85.1/86.5/83.8 in the abstract, results and conclusion; 82.8/79.3/86.2 in the discussion), an unresolved internal inconsistency. Second, whether the SVM's five-fold cross-validation encloses the AOI selection is not stated, and gender is imbalanced in practice (89% vs 73% male) despite a non-significant chi-square on a small sample.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 37: children with ASD recruited from a hospital child mental health outpatient ward, and typically developing children recruited from a local kindergarten. Both groups fully characterised in a demographic table. No other-diagnosis comparison group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'ASD children', 'the ASD group', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'TD group', 'individuals with autism', 'patients' (once, when discussing evaluation bias). Predominantly person-first with 'ASD children' used interchangeably; the comparison group is consistently 'typically developing' rather than 'normal', which is the more neutral convention.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=37, 33 boys / 4 girls, age 4.6 +/- 0.7 years, CARS 34.4 +/- 7.8. TD n=37, 27 boys / 10 girls, age 4.8 +/- 0.4 years. Age matched by design with no significant difference (p = 0.17), and gender difference non-significant by chi-square (p = 0.14) - though the actual distributions are 89% versus 73% male, so the matching is statistically defensible rather than close. Narrow 4-6 year age band by inclusion criterion, directly relevant to early screening but, as the authors note, leaving open whether the finding generalises to younger children.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: DSM-5 diagnosis by experienced physicians plus a CARS score above 30 as an explicit inclusion criterion. The authors state directly that ADI-R and ADOS were unavailable in China and list the absence of confirmation with validated diagnostic instruments as their first limitation - an unusually forthright acknowledgement. Controls were screened by a licensed physician to exclude any psychiatric or neurological history including ASD, which is a stronger control-status procedure than most corpus studies.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: The Gesell Developmental Scale (Chinese version) was administered to the ASD group, with adaptation, large motion, fine motion, language and personal-social subscores all reported - one of the fuller functional characterisations in the corpus. However the authors themselves list the absence of IQ and adaptive behaviour measures as their second limitation, and no GDS or other functional data were collected for the control group. Comorbidities are not described for the ASD group.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: early screening, with the specific design question of whether a very short paradigm suffices, plus replication of an infant speaking-face finding in an older age group. Main findings: fixation times significantly lower in ASD at seven of ten AOIs after Bonferroni correction; no differences in any within-face ratio; only mouth (p=0.008) and body (p=0.03) fixation carried significant discriminative weight; SVM accuracy 85.1%, sensitivity 86.5%, specificity 83.8%, above chance by permutation (p<0.001); fixation time correlated with the GDS large-motion subscore (p<0.01 corrected).
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Clinic setting for testing (a dark, soundproof room with fixed viewing geometry) with clinical recruitment from a hospital outpatient ward and control recruitment from a kindergarten in the same city. Newly collected data; no existing dataset used.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Passive viewing, deliberately minimal: five-point calibration, then eye-position correction on a dynamic pink rabbit, then a single 10-second muted video of a young Asian female mouthing the English alphabet. The brevity is the explicit design contribution - the authors argue that with young children the paradigm must be short as well as informative, since keeping such subjects focused on a monitor for long periods is difficult. The stimulus is muted, so the speaking face provides visual mouth motion without audio.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single 10-second measurement per child with no follow-up. The data are fixation durations on predefined regions - among the least identifiable data types in the corpus. Ethics approval from the hospital research committee is reported with explicit reference to the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its amendments, informed consent was obtained from parents of all participants, and a conflict-of-interest disclosure is given for one author. Ethics and consent reporting is essentially complete.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: SMI RED250 portable eye tracker sampling at 250 Hz with 0.03 degree spatial resolution; 22-inch widescreen LCD at 1024x768; fixed 65 cm eye-to-monitor distance; dark soundproof room. Software: BeGaze for gaze data analysis; SPSS 22.0 for statistics, group comparisons and the SVM discriminant analysis.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No data availability statement and no code release. Method reporting is nonetheless strong: eye-tracker model, sampling rate, spatial resolution, screen resolution, viewing distance, calibration procedure, stimulus content and duration, the full AOI definitions and the ratio definitions are all specified, as are the cross-validation folds and the permutation counts. The analysis is re-implementable in principle on comparable data; the specific SVM kernel and regularisation settings are not given.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors in an explicit five-point limitations list: ADOS/ADI-R unavailable so diagnoses rest on DSM-5 and CARS alone; no IQ or adaptive-behaviour measure of functional level; relatively small sample requiring larger-sample validation; unknown whether findings are specific to the 4-6 age group; and no direct comparison against or combination with other eye-tracking paradigms. Identifiable in review: gender is imbalanced in practice (89% vs 73% male) despite a non-significant chi-square on n=74; the control group has no GDS or functional data so the correlational analysis cannot be contrasted across groups; single-site recruitment with an ethnically homogeneous sample viewing an Asian female face, leaving cross-cultural transfer untested; whether AOI selection was nested inside the five-fold cross-validation is unstated; and the paper reports two mutually inconsistent sets of accuracy figures for the same analysis.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Larger-sample validation; extension to other populations, particularly young infants, where early detection would matter most; determination of whether the effect is age-group specific; direct head-to-head comparison of this short paradigm against established longer paradigms; and combination of the short paradigm with other paradigms. The authors also state a general principle rather than a research step - that current ASD biomarkers including eye tracking are supplementary and not replacements for clinical assessment.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Gaze: fixation duration on predefined facial and body regions during passive viewing of a speaking face. Aggregate dwell time per region rather than scanpath, saccade dynamics or pupillometry.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality; no fusion. Within the modality, ten regional fixation times plus three derived ratios are supplied jointly to the SVM, which is feature-level combination across regions. Gaze data are separately correlated with Gesell developmental subscores using age and gender as covariates - an integration with clinical measures for interpretation rather than for prediction.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning with a single algorithm: support vector machine, described as discriminant analysis. No comparison against alternative classifiers, which is unusual for this corpus and arguably a strength - it removes the best-of-many selection optimism that inflates other studies here.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted region-aggregated features: total fixation time per area of interest over the 10-second clip, plus three normalising ratios. Extremely low-dimensional - ten AOIs and three ratios against 74 children - which is a far healthier feature-to-sample ratio than most studies in this corpus and materially reduces overfitting risk.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, with a permutation-derived p-value establishing that accuracy exceeds chance. Headline: 85.1% / 86.5% / 83.8% (p<0.001). No AUC, F1 or confidence intervals. A contradictory second set of figures (82.8% / 79.3% / 86.2%) appears in the Discussion for what is described as the same analysis, and is never reconciled.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is handled better than in most of the corpus. SVM discriminative weights per AOI are tested by 1000-iteration permutation against the null that weights are arbitrary, so feature importance carries a p-value rather than a rank. Only mouth (p=0.008) and body (p=0.03) survive. The most informative result is a negative one: although fixation was globally reduced in ASD across seven AOIs, none of the eyes-to-face, mouth-to-face or nose-to-face ratios differed, so the group difference is in total looking rather than in the within-face distribution of attention - a finding that complicates the common eye-avoidance interpretation and which the authors report rather than suppress.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Five-fold cross-validation, with two separate permutation procedures - one testing whether classification accuracy exceeds chance (1000 label permutations) and one testing whether each AOI's discriminative weight is non-arbitrary (1000 permutations). Multiple comparisons across the ten AOI group tests are Bonferroni-corrected, and the correlational analysis with GDS subscores is likewise corrected, with the authors explicitly flagging which correlations did not survive correction. What is absent: external or independent validation, held-out site, any statement of whether AOI selection is nested within the folds, class-imbalance handling (not needed at 37/37), and any deployment or real-time analysis - though the authors explicitly position eye tracking as supplementary to clinical assessment rather than a replacement.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: Autism; Eye tracking; Fixation time; Machine learning; Face. Task vocabulary: 'early detection', 'screening', 'biomarkers', 'areas-of-interest', 'discriminant analysis', 'proof of concept'. The paper's framing of biomarkers as 'supplementary' rather than diagnostic is a distinctive and unusually cautious note.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders - an autism-specific clinical journal, not a computational venue.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2018 (published online August 2018, in the 2019 volume). The paper documents the field's trajectory in some detail: eye tracking as 'one emerging objective tool increasingly being applied in ASD clinics and research', machine learning recently applied to behaviour, brain activity and eye tracking with 'encouraging results', and ASD biomarker research having 'grown exponentially' with integration into future risk assessment 'almost certain'. It also situates itself against three specific predecessors (Shic et al. on infants, Liu et al. on face-scanning machine learning, Fujioka et al. on adults), comparing accuracies directly - one of the more explicitly cumulative papers in the corpus.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Automatic Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Everyday
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Gong Y; Yatawatte H; Poellabauer C; Schneider S; Latham S
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder, plus an at-risk younger-sibling group
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Speech and language
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Practical fully-automatic home screening: build an ASD screening solution deployable on child-specific smart devices that analyses everyday vocalisations at home without professional supervision, explicitly aimed at regions with limited access to diagnostic services
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Longitudinal observational data collection (17 months) with cross-sectional classification analysis at the subject level
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: 17 months of continuous data collection from April 2016 to September 2017; 1858 interaction recordings totalling 19.8 hours and 7427 monitoring recordings totalling 890.4 hours of detected voice activity
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Two data sources: four gamified structured exercises (picture description, word reading, sentence reading, story reading, with reading material drawn from the Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation) that the child or parent activates, and a passive monitoring mode that continuously listens and records on voice-activity detection
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Home - devices were sent to each family and all data collection was performed entirely inside the children's homes without professional supervision, with the device placed in the child's bedroom
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Not reported - children are described as 'diagnosed with ASD' with no instrument, criteria, clinician or date given anywhere. At-risk children are defined as younger siblings of ASD children who have not been diagnosed
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 18 diagnosed with ASD (all 18 used in the classification experiment); plus 8 at-risk siblings excluded from the experiment because undiagnosed
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not reported as a group statistic; individual ages given per subject in Table 1
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: 3 months to 17 years at recruitment across the whole sample - an extraordinarily wide range
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Reported per subject in Table 1 but not aggregated per group
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported; several children are described narratively as possibly non-verbal but no severity measure exists
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described; TD status is asserted with no screening instrument
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd_controls: Not reported as a group statistic
data_charting_rubrics.age_range_controls: Individual ages range from 3 years to 16 years among the TD subjects listed
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No - no matching procedure, no group age statistics and no statistical comparison. Ages span 3 months to 17 years across the sample, and several ASD children are toddlers while several TD children are teenagers
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: No - not addressed
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted, not assessed
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Audio: children's everyday vocalisations, analysed both acoustically (voice quality, spectral and prosodic descriptors) and linguistically (ASR transcripts analysed for lexical and task-performance features)
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Picture description (9 social-scenario pictures), word reading (5 lists of 10-11 words), sentence reading (2 sentences), story reading (2 stories of ~100 words), all drawn from GFTA-2-1 articulation test material; plus passive monitoring of everyday communication activated and deactivated by parents
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Apple iPod Touch with an iRig Mic Cast external microphone running a custom iOS app; Sookasa HIPAA-compliant encryption over Dropbox for cloud upload; COVAREP toolkit for acoustic features; Google Cloud Speech-to-Text for transcription; LIWC for linguistic features; an SVM trained by stochastic gradient descent with hinge loss; correlation-based feature subset selection (CFS)
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - a novel 17-month naturalistic home audio corpus, but not released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Extremely sensitive - continuous passive audio recording inside children's bedrooms capturing the child and everyone around them, including parents, over 17 months and 890 hours. The paper reports two concrete protections: HIPAA-compliant encryption (Sookasa over Dropbox) for cloud storage, and parental control to activate and deactivate monitoring mode at any time, described explicitly as 'for privacy considerations'. However there is no ethics approval statement, no participant or parental consent statement, no IRB reference, and no discussion of the consent status of third parties incidentally recorded
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted acoustic functionals plus lexical and task-performance linguistic features, fused across sources
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Per audio clip, 74 COVAREP acoustic features per 10 ms summarised by mean, max and min into a 222-dimensional vector, averaged across clips per recording. Linguistic features: 93-dimensional LIWC vectors for picture description and monitoring; task-specific features for reading tests (total words, correct/irrelevant/repeated word ratios, word error rate, audio length, words per second); monitoring-specific vocabulary, mean conversation length and repetition ratios. Plus 6 usage-pattern features. Total 1330 dimensions after fusion, scaled to 0-1, with missing data padded with -1 to explicitly encode absence
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: COVAREP (acoustics), Google Cloud Speech-to-Text (ASR), LIWC (linguistics), custom self-adaptive SVM-based voice-activity segmentation using the 10% highest and 10% lowest energy frames per recording
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes - extensively
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Correlation-based feature subset selection (CFS), chosen specifically because features from the same data source are highly inter-correlated and individual-score selection would return redundant sets; plus per-source correlation coefficients with the diagnostic label, and ablation experiments training on each single data source in turn
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: CFS selected features from every one of the five data sources - monitoring (LIWC_Interrog, HMPDM 8/14/19/22), picture description (max F0, MCEP 5 and 19), sentence reading (MCEP 23), story reading (seven HMPDM and MCEP features), word reading (MCEP 10 and 20). Highest label correlations: Max_QQQ from monitoring (r=0.64) and Mean_HMPDM_13/14 from story reading (r=0.64). Only one linguistic feature was selected by CFS
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported - correlations with the label are given as magnitudes without sign or interpretation, and no acoustic property is characterised as higher or lower in the ASD group
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification with feature selection
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Binary SVM trained by stochastic gradient descent with a hinge loss objective, preceded by correlation-based feature subset selection
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-subject-out with an explicit three-way split - for each round one subject is held out for testing, 18 subjects are used for training and 8 as a development set, with epoch count and learning rate grid-searched on the development set. CFS feature selection is stated to be conducted 'in the model training'. Class imbalance (9 TD vs 18 ASD) is handled at the metric level by using unweighted average F1
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Unweighted average F1-score as the primary metric (chosen explicitly because the classes are unbalanced), with classification accuracy and a confusion matrix, plus per-single-source F1 scores for the ablation
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Fused model: unweighted average F1 0.87, accuracy 88.9% (24 of 27 subjects correct), with three misclassified subjects individually identified. Single-source F1 scores: story reading 0.77, word reading 0.76, monitoring 0.72, picture description 0.68, sentence reading 0.49, usage pattern 0.47 - all substantially below the fused 0.87
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Everyday vocalisations captured passively and through gamified tests on a consumer device at home, over 17 months, supported ASD screening at unweighted F1 0.87 without any professional supervision or manual processing. Multi-source fusion was decisively better than any single source (0.87 versus a best single-source 0.77), and CFS selected features from all five sources, confirming they are complementary rather than redundant. Acoustic features - particularly high-order Mel cepstrum and harmonic phase-distortion measures - were far more discriminative than linguistic ones, which the authors attribute to ASR errors on atypical child speech. Usage pattern was explicitly tested and found not discriminative, contradicting the authors' own prior expectation.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: High-order Mel cepstrum envelope (MCEP) and harmonic model phase distortion mean (HMPDM) coefficients across all sources, plus quasi-open quotient from monitoring - all voice-quality and spectral measures rather than prosodic or lexical ones
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Develop a speaker diarization algorithm suited to everyday monitoring so the target child's speech can be separated from parents' and others', named as important future work; incorporate age and gender to enable age- and gender-dependent fine-grained inference; and extend the application beyond screening to evaluating intervention effectiveness and tracking child development
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The most ecologically ambitious data collection in the corpus - 17 months of genuinely unsupervised home recording on consumer hardware, explicitly motivated by global inequity in access to diagnosis. The analysis is unusually self-critical: the authors deliberately exclude age and gender as features because recruitment may have made them confounded with the label, they test and report that usage pattern is not discriminative against their own prior hypothesis, they run single-source ablations that quantify the fusion benefit, and they explain their misclassifications by data volume. Against this, the sample is severely problematic for the claim: 27 analysed children spanning 3 months to 17 years with no age or gender matching and no group statistics, 18 ASD versus 9 TD, and no diagnostic instrument reported at all. With ages that disparate and unmatched, a classifier separating a 2-year-old from a 16-year-old on voice-quality features would achieve much of this performance on developmental grounds alone - the very confound the authors correctly identified for age-as-a-feature but did not address for age-as-a-sample-property. There is also no ethics or consent statement for 890 hours of in-home audio.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Three groups recruited: 18 children diagnosed with ASD, 9 typically developing children, and 8 at-risk children defined as undiagnosed younger siblings of ASD children. Only the 27 with definite TD or ASD status entered the classification experiment; the at-risk group was excluded because undiagnosed, which is handled transparently. Per-subject characteristics are tabulated individually.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'ASD children', 'children diagnosed with ASD', 'affected individuals', 'affected children', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'at-risk children', and notably 'the child's health condition' when referring to diagnostic status. Predominantly diagnosis-first ('ASD children') with a medicalised framing of autism as a health condition; the paper also uses 'neurodevelopmental disability' and 'disorder' interchangeably.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: This is the study's weakest reporting. Sample sizes are clear (18 ASD, 9 TD, 8 at-risk) and every subject's individual age, gender and diagnosis is listed in Table 1, but no group-level age mean, SD or gender distribution is computed anywhere, and no matching or comparability test is performed. Ages span 3 months to 17 years at recruitment. Inspecting Table 1, the ASD group includes children aged 2, 3 and 4 years while the TD group includes 16-year-olds, so the groups are grossly unmatched on age - a decisive confound for acoustic voice features, which change dramatically across childhood and adolescence.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not reported at all. Children are described as 'diagnosed with ASD' with no instrument, no criteria, no diagnosing professional and no date. TD status is asserted without any screening. At-risk status is defined purely by sibling relationship. Given that diagnostic label is the classification target and the paper proposes a screening tool, the complete absence of reference-standard information is the study's most serious gap.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None reported. No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive-functioning measures, no autism severity instrument, and no comorbidity information for any group. The reading materials are drawn from the Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, so a standardised articulation instrument supplies the stimuli, but it is not scored as an assessment. The authors note narratively that 'some non-verbal children may not able to finish the reading test' but no verbal-ability data exist.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: a practical, affordable, fully automatic home screening tool requiring no professional help, explicitly motivated by the scarcity of psychiatrists in South East Asia, the Western Pacific and Africa (0.21, 0.28 and 0.05 per 100,000). Main findings: unweighted F1 0.87 and accuracy 88.9% (24/27) from fused multi-source features; every single source performed worse alone (best 0.77); acoustic features dominated linguistic ones; and usage pattern was not discriminative.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Home setting, and uniquely so in this corpus - devices were mailed to families and all collection occurred inside children's homes with no professional supervision, deliberately to emulate real deployment of child-specific smart devices. Newly collected data; no existing dataset used.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Two complementary protocols. Structured: four gamified exercises activated by child or parent - picture description of social scenarios (9 pictures), word reading (5 lists of 10-11 words), sentence reading (2 sentences) and story reading (2 ~100-word stories), with materials drawn from the Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation and reproduced in full in the appendix. Unstructured: a monitoring mode that continuously listens and begins recording on voice-activity detection, capturing everyday communication. Crucially the paper documents real-world protocol failure honestly, reproducing a transcript in which a parent prompts and speaks over the child throughout a word-reading test, and designing error-robust features (irrelevant-word and repeated-word ratios) in response.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Longitudinal in collection (17 months, April 2016 to September 2017) but cross-sectional in analysis - all of a subject's recordings are averaged into one feature vector, so no temporal or developmental modelling is performed despite the long span. The data are among the most sensitive in the corpus: 890 hours of passive in-home audio from children's bedrooms, inevitably capturing parents and other household members. Two protections are described - HIPAA-compliant encryption (Sookasa over Dropbox) for cloud storage, and parent-controlled activation/deactivation of monitoring mode 'for privacy considerations'. But there is no ethics approval statement, no IRB reference, no parental or child consent statement, and no consideration of consent for third parties recorded incidentally.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: Apple iPod Touch with an iRig Mic Cast external microphone (chosen to ensure data quality), sent to each family. Software: a custom iOS app implementing the four gamified tests and the monitoring mode with voice-activity-triggered recording and automatic cloud upload; Sookasa for HIPAA-compliant encrypted Dropbox storage; COVAREP for acoustic feature extraction; Google Cloud Speech-to-Text for ASR; LIWC for linguistic analysis; a custom self-adaptive SVM voice-activity segmentation using per-recording energy percentiles to handle varying background noise.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No data availability statement and no code release. Method reporting is otherwise strong: all toolkits are named and are standard (COVAREP, LIWC, Google Cloud Speech-to-Text), feature dimensions are tabulated per source and per type totalling 1330, the missing-data encoding (-1 padding rather than interpolation) is stated, normalisation is described, the grid-search ranges for epochs and learning rate are given, and the complete reading and picture stimulus materials are reproduced in an appendix. The pipeline is re-implementable; the corpus is not accessible.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors, unusually thoroughly for a conference paper: large variance in data volume per subject (4 to 1968 recordings) driven by device-usage preference rather than condition; real-life data errors including interrupted tests and parents completing tests on the child's behalf, which would overestimate development level; varying background noise across subjects; absence of speaker diarization so child and parent speech cannot be separated; ASR error rates that increase precisely when child speech is atypical, undermining the linguistic features; and misclassification associated with low data volume for two of the three errors. They also deliberately excluded age and gender as features because 'in the subject recruitment process, it is possible that age and gender information have some implicit connection with the label'. Identifiable in review: that same recruitment confound is not addressed at the sample level - ages span 3 months to 17 years with toddlers over-represented in the ASD group and teenagers among the TD group, entirely unmatched, so acoustic maturation is confounded with diagnosis; 18 ASD versus 9 TD with only 27 analysed; no diagnostic instrument whatsoever; no ethics or consent statement; and the 17-month longitudinal structure is collapsed to a single averaged vector, discarding the developmental information the design was uniquely placed to capture.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Develop a speaker diarization algorithm suited to everyday monitoring conditions, named as important future work because the absence of diarization degrades both acoustic and linguistic analysis; incorporate age and gender to enable age- and gender-dependent fine-grained inference; and extend beyond screening to evaluating intervention effectiveness and tracking child development over time.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Speech and language jointly: acoustic/paralinguistic properties (voice quality, spectral envelope, harmonic phase distortion, F0) and linguistic content derived from ASR transcripts (LIWC categories, vocabulary size, repetition, reading accuracy, words per second). The explicit joint acoustic-linguistic framing is unusual in this corpus, where most speech studies are purely paralinguistic.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Fusion is the paper's central methodological claim and is done at two levels. Across modalities: acoustic and linguistic features are extracted separately and concatenated. Across sources: features from four structured tests plus passive monitoring plus usage pattern are all concatenated into one 1330-dimensional vector, with missing sources explicitly encoded as -1 so the model can handle non-participation rather than requiring imputation. The benefit is quantified by ablation - every single source scored 0.47-0.77 alone against 0.87 fused - and confirmed by CFS selecting at least one feature from each source, which the authors correctly note implies the sources are complementary rather than redundant given CFS's redundancy penalty. No integration with clinical scores or demographics, deliberately.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning. Algorithm: binary SVM optimised by stochastic gradient descent with a hinge loss objective, preceded by correlation-based feature subset selection. No deep learning, and no comparison against alternative classifiers - the paper's contribution is the data collection and fusion scheme rather than the model.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted features at two levels of abstraction: acoustic functionals (mean, max, min over 74 COVAREP descriptors sampled at 10 ms, giving 222 dimensions per recording, then averaged across recordings) and symbolic linguistic features from ASR transcripts (LIWC psycholinguistic categories, plus task-performance counts such as correct, irrelevant and repeated word ratios and word error rate). Notably the task-specific features are designed to be robust to the real-world failure mode observed - a parent prompting the child - by counting irrelevant and repeated words rather than only correct ones.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Unweighted average F1-score as the primary metric, selected explicitly because the classes are unbalanced (18 ASD vs 9 TD) - the methodologically correct choice and one only a minority of corpus studies make. Accuracy (88.9%) and a confusion matrix are also reported, along with per-single-source F1 scores enabling the fusion ablation. No sensitivity, specificity, AUC or confidence intervals.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is handled through three complementary analyses. CFS selection reports exactly which features were chosen from which source. Per-source correlation coefficients with the diagnostic label are tabulated with the top five features per source. Single-source ablation quantifies each source's standalone contribution. The findings are substantive: acoustic features dominate, specifically high-order Mel cepstrum envelope and harmonic model phase distortion mean coefficients plus quasi-open quotient - all voice-quality measures; only one linguistic feature (LIWC_Interrog) survives CFS, and linguistic features appear in the top-five correlations of only the picture description test, leading the authors to conclude that linguistic features are discriminative mainly when speech content is not fixed. Directions of effect are not reported, only correlation magnitudes.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Leave-one-subject-out with a genuine three-way split - one test subject, 18 training and 8 development subjects, with epochs and learning rate grid-searched on development only - which is subject-independent and separates model selection from performance estimation. Class imbalance is addressed at the metric level via unweighted F1. Robustness to real-world data corruption is a design goal rather than an afterthought: missing sources are explicitly encoded, error-correcting linguistic features are designed against the observed parent-prompting failure, and voice-activity segmentation adapts per recording to differing noise levels. Age and gender are deliberately excluded to prevent the model exploiting recruitment-correlated demographics. Absent: external or independent validation, any held-out site or device, calibration, and any deployment measurement despite the app being the contribution. Whether CFS is recomputed inside each leave-one-out fold is stated only as being 'conducted in the model training', which is suggestive but not explicit.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: Autism spectrum disorders, pervasive health, data mining, speech processing, natural language processing. Task vocabulary: 'ASD screening tool', 'ASD biomarkers', 'fully automatic', 'everyday vocalizations', 'continuous and transparent monitoring', 'first ASD screening solution'. The 'pervasive health' and 'transparent monitoring' framing situates this in ubiquitous computing rather than clinical assessment.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: ACM-BCB'18 - the 9th ACM International Conference on Bioinformatics, Computational Biology and Health Informatics, in the mHealth session. A technology/health-informatics venue, not an autism or clinical journal.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2018. The paper characterises prior speech-based autism work as demonstrating that vocalisations contain usable biomarkers across infants, young children and teenagers, but criticises it on two specific grounds: recordings are 'mostly based on audio data obtained in very controlled environments' and are 'often manually reviewed, segmented, and processed by speech experts', which limits both practicality and recording length. It positions the emergence of affordable child-specific smart devices (Amazon Echo Kids Edition at $79, Xiaomi Kids Smartwatch at $45) as the enabling shift - documenting the corpus-wide movement from laboratory instrumentation toward consumer hardware and naturalistic settings, and framing it explicitly as a global health-equity argument.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Detecting Autism Based on Eye-Tracking Data from Web Searching
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Yaneva V; Ha LA; Eraslan S; Yesilada Y; Mitkov R
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: Proceedings of the 15th International Web for All Conference
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder - high-functioning autism or Asperger's syndrome, adults
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye-tracking and gaze
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Accessible large-scale screening: test whether gaze data from ordinary web tasks can distinguish autistic from non-autistic adults, and characterise how task type, area-of-interest definition, page visual complexity and participant gender affect classification - explicitly aimed at a future serious game for screening rather than at diagnosis
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study; secondary machine-learning analysis of eye-tracking data originally collected to study web accessibility difficulties in autistic users
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session; up to 2 minutes per web page for browsing and 30 seconds per web page for searching, across six web pages, in randomised page order with counterbalanced task order
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Two web tasks on screenshots of six real web pages: Browsing (free viewing for up to 2 minutes per page, participants free to read or ignore any part) and Searching (30 seconds per page to locate answers to two verbally posed questions, read aloud)
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory - eye-tracking testing at the University of Wolverhampton, with autistic participants recruited via a West Midlands charity and controls by open advertisement
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Confirmed clinical diagnosis of autism as verified by the recruiting charity organisation; no instrument named. Exclusion criteria: any formally diagnosed intellectual disability, age under 18, and inability to use a computer. Control participants were screened with the Autism Quotient, with all scoring below 32 ('little or no autistic traits')
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 18 recruited (12 male, 6 female); 3 discarded for calibration difficulties and head-movement data loss, leaving 15 analysed (9 male, 6 female)
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Adults over 18; no upper bound reported
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: 9 male / 6 female in the analysed sample - 40% female, by far the highest female representation in the corpus
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Formally diagnosed intellectual disability was an explicit exclusion criterion; no other comorbidity information
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported for the autistic group; AQ was administered only to controls as a screening gate
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - non-autistic adults recruited by open advertisement
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes - all completed the Autism Quotient screening test, described as widely used by UK general practitioners before formal diagnostic referral, with none scoring above 32
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 18 recruited (10 male, 8 female); 2 discarded for data quality and 1 further removed at random to balance classes, leaving 15 analysed (8 male, 7 female)
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not formally matched or tested; group means are close (37 vs 33.7) with overlapping standard deviations
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not formally matched but closely balanced (9M/6F vs 8M/7F)
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes - AQ-screened
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye movements: fixation timing, duration, count and revisit patterns within areas of interest on web pages
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Six web page screenshots of varying visual complexity as rated by the ViCRAM tool (Apple and Babylon low, AVG and Yahoo medium, GoDaddy and BBC high), each viewed under both a browse and a search condition, with two search questions per page listed in full in the paper. Web-use frequency and prior familiarity with each site were surveyed to control for over-familiarity; all participants were daily web users and none was over-familiar with the stimuli
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Gazepoint GP3 video-based eye tracker at 60 Hz with 0.5-1 degree accuracy; 19-inch LCD monitor at approximately 65 cm controlled by an integrated distance sensor; nine-point calibration; VIPS (Vision-Based Page Segmentation) algorithm for page-specific AOI definition; R for logistic regression
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - the gaze dataset is newly released with this paper, though originally collected for a different study
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes - the eye-tracking data, R code, visual stimuli and task descriptions are all made freely available at a named GitHub repository, with an explicit 'Open Data' section and the stated purpose of replication. This is the most complete open-science provision of any study in the corpus
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze coordinates over web pages are low in identifiability. Full ethical approval was obtained from the University of Wolverhampton Faculty of Arts Ethics Committee prior to data collection, all participants signed a consent form after being familiarised with the purpose and procedure, and participants were debriefed afterwards. The authors additionally raise unprompted ethical concerns about the future of the approach, noting that profiling for conditions via web-searching behaviour 'will raise ethical considerations which should not be treated lightly'
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted gaze features per area of interest plus contextual non-gaze features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Gaze: time to first view (seconds from page onset to first fixation on an AOI), time viewed in seconds, time viewed as a percentage of total page time for the task, number of fixations, and number of revisits to a previously viewed AOI. Non-gaze: media ID (which web page), AOI ID, whether the AOI contained the correct answer to a search task, participant gender, and level of visual complexity
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Gazepoint software for gaze capture; VIPS-based page segmentation for page-specific AOIs; a 2x2 grid for generic AOIs; R for modelling
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Partly - the paper systematically ablates feature sets and design variables rather than ranking individual features
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Systematic comparison across feature sets (gaze only, gaze plus AOI ID, gaze plus media ID, gaze plus selected pages), across tasks (browse vs search), across AOI definitions (page-specific vs generic 2x2 grid), and across page and participant variables, with 95% confidence intervals throughout
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Gaze features alone performed best; adding AOI ID or media ID generally lowered accuracy. Page-specific AOIs were essential for the search task (0.75 vs 0.56 for generic AOIs) but made little difference for browsing (0.71 vs 0.70). The Apple and AVG pages were the most predictive for browsing. Correct-answer AOI had a slight positive effect on search classifiers; gender and visual complexity had no significant influence
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: The prior analyses of the same dataset (cited by the authors) found that autistic participants had longer scan paths, more transitions between page elements, shorter fixations, and more fixations on irrelevant elements. This study does not itself report directional effects for its features
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Logistic regression in R, selected after several classification algorithms were tested
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 100-fold cross-validation with participant-level partitioning: data from 10 randomly selected participants per group used for training and the remaining 5 per group used for testing, in each of 100 folds, so no data from a test participant is ever used for training. Behaviour-level predictions are aggregated to a participant-level decision by majority vote across that participant's behaviours. Accuracies are averaged across folds and reported with 95% confidence intervals
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Classification accuracy with 95% confidence intervals for every reported configuration, plus confusion matrices for the two best results
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Best overall: 0.75 accuracy for the Search task with page-specific AOIs and all gaze features. Browse task best: 0.71 (95% CI 0.69-0.73) using gaze features on the Apple and AVG pages combined; all pages with gaze features gave 0.66 (0.64-0.68). Generic 2x2 AOIs gave 0.70 for browse but only 0.56 for search. Individual browse pages ranged from 0.45 (BBC) to 0.63 (Apple). Confusion matrix for the best browse result shows balanced class performance (control 0.722, ASD 0.706)
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Gaze data from ordinary web browsing and searching distinguished autistic from non-autistic adults at up to 0.75 accuracy under strictly participant-independent validation. The search task elicited larger between-group differences than free browsing. How areas of interest are defined matters and interacts with task: generic grid AOIs were adequate for browsing but collapsed performance for searching, where meaningful page-element segmentation was necessary. Participant gender, page visual complexity and the location of the correct answer had little influence. The authors position the result explicitly against fMRI-based classifiers (71-86.7%) and argue that comparable screening could eventually be achieved without an eye tracker at all, via mouse and interaction logs.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Not characterised directionally in this paper; the underlying differences reported in the authors' prior analyses of the same data are longer scan paths, more inter-element transitions, shorter fixations and more fixations on irrelevant elements
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Design tasks that deliberately amplify between-group visual processing differences to improve accuracy, since the present data were not collected for classification; explore capturing the same differences without eye tracking, via operation logs, mouse clicks, accuracy and miss rate; develop a serious game for large-scale screening; extend the approach to other conditions exhibiting visual attention differences such as dementia, schizophrenia and ADHD; and address the ethical considerations that profiling for conditions from web behaviour would raise
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The most methodologically self-aware study in the corpus so far. It devotes a full background subsection to criticising the validation practice of prior autism classification work - naming an EEG study reporting 94% and a French speech study reporting 93.5% and showing that both partitioned data segments rather than participants, so 'different data segments from the same participant to be used for training and testing, allowing for higher accuracy owing to similarity between the data in the two sets' - and then adopts strict participant-level partitioning itself, explicitly to emulate diagnosing a new person. It reports 95% confidence intervals on every number, publishes confusion matrices, releases data, code, stimuli and task descriptions openly, reports a modest 0.75 without inflation, and compares itself unfavourably to fMRI accuracies rather than favourably to weaker studies. It also raises ethical concerns about its own future application unprompted. Real limitations remain: n=30 adults, no diagnostic instrument named (diagnosis 'verified by the charity organisation'), intellectual disability excluded so the sample is high-functioning only, the task is unusable with young children where screening matters most (acknowledged), and the reported best figure is selected across tasks, AOI schemes, feature sets and page subsets - though every alternative is also reported with intervals, which makes the selection visible rather than hidden.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: adults with a confirmed clinical diagnosis of high-functioning autism or Asperger's syndrome (18 recruited, 15 analysed) and non-autistic control adults (18 recruited, 15 analysed after 2 data-quality exclusions and 1 random removal to balance classes). All recruitment, exclusion and balancing decisions are reported explicitly, including the random removal. No other-diagnosis group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'people with autism', 'participants with autism', 'people on the autism spectrum', 'autistic individuals', 'autistic readers', 'the group with autism', 'neurotypical participants', 'control group of participants without autism', 'non-autistic control participants'. Notably mixed and deliberately so - the paper uses 'people with autism' and 'autistic' interchangeably, consistently pairs them with 'neurotypical' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy', and uses 'condition' rather than 'disorder' in its own prose. It also frames misdiagnosis in terms of harm to 'a person's self-perception', a person-centred framing absent elsewhere in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=15 analysed (9 male, 6 female), mean age 37 +/- 9.14 years, mean 16 +/- 3.33 years of formal education. Control n=15 analysed (8 male, 7 female), mean age 33.66 +/- 8.6 years, mean 18.35 +/- 2.47 years of formal education. No formal matching procedure or comparability test is reported, though age and gender are close in practice. At 40% and 47% female, this is by a wide margin the most gender-balanced sample in the corpus - most comparable studies are 80-90% male. Adults only, and the authors explicitly acknowledge that web tasks are unsuitable for the young children where early detection would matter most. Education differs by about 2.3 years in the controls' favour, which is not discussed.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: A confirmed clinical diagnosis of autism 'as verified by the charity organisation' through which participants were recruited - no instrument, criteria or clinician is named, and verification is delegated to a third-party organisation. By contrast, control status is established rigorously with the Autism Quotient, with an explicit threshold (none above 32) and a rationale (the AQ is used by UK general practitioners as pre-referral screening). As in several other corpus studies, the control ascertainment is better specified than the case ascertainment.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Years of formal education reported for both groups; web-use frequency assessed for all participants (all daily users); familiarity with each of the six stimulus websites surveyed to rule out over-familiarity confounds. No IQ, language or adaptive-functioning measures, and no autism severity score for the autistic group. Comorbidity handled only by excluding formally diagnosed intellectual disability, which bounds the sample to high-functioning adults.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: accessible, unobtrusive, scalable screening from everyday behavioural data, explicitly framed as a route to a future serious game rather than as a diagnostic substitute. Main findings: 0.75 accuracy for the Search task with page-specific AOIs; 0.71 (CI 0.69-0.73) for Browse on the two most predictive pages; task type matters (search beats browse); AOI definition matters and interacts with task (generic 2x2 grid gives 0.70 for browse but only 0.56 for search); gender, visual complexity and correct-answer location had no significant influence; adding AOI ID or media ID lowered accuracy relative to gaze features alone.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory setting with a controlled eye tracker and fixed viewing distance. Existing data - the eye-tracking corpus was originally collected to investigate web-searching difficulties experienced by autistic users, and the authors are explicit that 'the data used in this study was not collected with this objective in mind', treating this as a limitation on achievable accuracy.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Two contrasting tasks over the same six web page screenshots. Browsing: up to two minutes per page, free to read or ignore anything, moving on when ready. Searching: 30 seconds per page to answer two questions posed verbally by the researcher, with the answer read aloud - the full set of twelve questions is published in a table. Pages were presented in randomised order per participant and the two tasks were counterbalanced. Pages spanned three ViCRAM-rated visual complexity levels, giving a designed manipulation of stimulus complexity.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single session with no follow-up. Gaze data over public web pages carry low re-identification risk, which is part of why the data can be released openly. Full ethical approval was obtained from the University of Wolverhampton Faculty of Arts Ethics Committee before collection, all participants signed consent forms after being familiarised with the purpose and procedure, and participants were debriefed. Uniquely in this corpus, the authors also flag prospective ethical risk in the discussion, warning that future profiling of conditions from web-searching behaviour 'will raise ethical considerations which should not be treated lightly'.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: Gazepoint GP3 video-based eye tracker at 60 Hz with 0.5-1 degree of visual angle accuracy, a 19-inch LCD monitor, and an integrated sensor controlling viewing distance at approximately 65 cm; nine-point calibration. Software: Gazepoint software for capture; the extended VIPS (Vision-Based Page Segmentation) algorithm for page-specific AOI definition; the ViCRAM tool for rating page visual complexity; R for logistic regression and cross-validation.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: The best in the corpus. An explicit 'Open Data' section states that the eye-tracking data, code, and materials are available at a named GitHub repository, and the abstract states the gaze data, R code, visual stimuli and task descriptions are 'made freely available for replication purposes'. Full replicability is listed as one of the paper's three stated contributions. Beyond the release, the paper publishes the complete search question set, the AOI definition methods, the eye tracker specifications, viewing distance, calibration procedure, cross-validation scheme, and confidence intervals for every configuration, and directs readers to the repository for results of page combinations not shown in the paper.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors in a dedicated Limitations subsection: the 0.75 accuracy compares unfavourably with the 71-86.7% range reported for fMRI classifiers, which they attribute partly to the data not having been collected for classification; web-searching tasks are unsuitable for the very young children in whom early detection would be most valuable, so a different task would be needed to reach them; and the sample is not large, though they note it exceeds the 12-per-group benchmark study they compare against. Identifiable in review: no diagnostic instrument is named, with verification delegated to the recruiting charity; formally diagnosed intellectual disability is an exclusion criterion so results apply only to high-functioning adults; control education exceeds autistic education by 2.3 years, undiscussed; the headline is selected across two tasks, two AOI schemes, four feature sets and multiple page subsets - though every alternative is reported with confidence intervals, making the selection auditable; and the participant-level aggregation rule (majority vote over behaviours) is a design choice whose sensitivity is not explored.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Design tasks specifically intended to amplify visual-processing differences between groups, since the present stimuli were repurposed; explore capturing the same differences without an eye tracker at all, using operation logs, mouse clicks, task accuracy and miss rate, so that screening could run on ordinary hardware; develop a serious game for large-scale accessible screening; extend the gaze-classifier approach to other conditions with visual attention differences such as dementia, schizophrenia and ADHD; and confront the ethical implications of profiling for clinical conditions from web behaviour.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Gaze: fixation timing, duration, count and revisit behaviour within areas of interest during naturalistic web interaction. Distinctively, the stimuli are real web pages rather than faces or social scenes, so the measured construct is general attention allocation and search strategy rather than social attention.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality. Gaze features are combined at feature level with non-gaze contextual variables (page identity, AOI identity, correct-answer location, gender, visual complexity), and the paper reports that these additions generally reduced accuracy relative to gaze features alone - a negative fusion result reported plainly. Behaviour-level predictions are aggregated to a participant-level decision by majority vote, a late fusion across observations. The discussion proposes future fusion with non-gaze interaction data (mouse clicks, operation logs) as a route to eye-tracker-free deployment.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning. Algorithm: logistic regression in R, chosen after testing several classification algorithms. The deliberate choice of a simple linear model with a small feature set, rather than a high-capacity model on 30 participants, is consistent with the paper's general conservatism about overfitting.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted per-AOI gaze summary features - time to first view, total and percentage viewing time, fixation count and revisit count - computed under two alternative AOI definitions (VIPS-derived page elements versus a generic 2x2 grid), plus categorical contextual variables. No raw scanpaths, time series or learned embeddings. The AOI-definition comparison effectively treats the representation itself as an experimental variable, which is unusual and produces one of the paper's most useful findings.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Classification accuracy, reported with 95% confidence intervals for every single configuration in every table - the only study in the corpus to do this systematically - plus confusion matrices for the two best results showing balanced per-class performance (0.722 control, 0.706 ASD for the best browse model). No sensitivity, specificity, F1 or AUC as such, though the confusion matrices permit their derivation.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No per-feature importance ranking or saliency analysis. Interpretability instead comes from systematic ablation across design variables, which yields several substantive findings: gaze features alone outperform gaze plus contextual features; page-specific AOIs are necessary for search but not for browse, because search requires locating specific elements while browse treats all screen regions as equal; the Apple and AVG pages showed the largest between-group differences during browsing; and gender and visual complexity do not matter. The authors also connect back to prior analyses of the same data identifying longer scan paths, more transitions, shorter fixations and more fixations on irrelevant elements as the underlying behavioural differences.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The strongest validation reasoning in the corpus. The background section explicitly critiques two prior studies (an EEG study reporting 94% and a French speech study reporting 93.5%) for partitioning data segments rather than participants, noting that this allows segments from the same participant into both training and test sets and produces 'potentially overoptimistic results' that do 'not account for real-world scenarios where the algorithm will have the task of correctly classifying a new person'. The study then adopts 100-fold cross-validation with strict participant-level partitioning (10 training and 5 test participants per group per fold) precisely to emulate diagnosing a new person, and reports 95% confidence intervals throughout. Class balance is enforced by design, including the random removal of one control. What is absent: external validation on an independent cohort, any held-out site or apparatus, calibration analysis, and any measurement of the proposed eye-tracker-free variant.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: Autism, Eye Tracking, Web, Screening, Diagnostic Classification. CCS concepts: user characteristics, people with disabilities, user studies, web-based interaction, empirical studies in accessibility, accessibility design and evaluation methods. Task vocabulary: 'screening for risk of autism', 'marker of the condition', 'serious games for autism screening', 'accessible and unobtrusive screening method'. The accessibility-research framing is unique in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: W4A '18 - the 15th International Web for All Conference (Lyon), themed 'The Internet of Accessible Things'. A technology venue, but specifically a web accessibility venue rather than a machine-learning or clinical one, which shapes the paper's framing around scalability, cost and access rather than diagnostic accuracy.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2018. The paper surveys autism classification from fMRI (71-86.7% across several studies) and EEG (94%), and argues that eye tracking 'has not been used to investigate whether it is suitable to detect autism by considering atypical visual attention patterns', claiming to be the first study to test gaze data for autism screening. It also documents an important methodological trend critically rather than approvingly - noting that several high-accuracy results in the literature rest on partitioning by data segment rather than by participant - and situates eye tracking as moving from research equipment into consumer hardware (Samsung Galaxy S4, Tobii gaming trackers, Acer notebooks), anticipating the consumer-device turn this corpus records.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Video Gesture Analysis for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Zunino A; Morerio P; Cavallo A; Ansuini C; Podda J; Battaglia F; Veneselli E; Becchio C; Murino V
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder without accompanying intellectual impairment
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Motor and kinematics
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Automatic objective diagnostic support: classify whether a simple grasping gesture was performed by an autistic or typically developing child from video alone, and produce an attention map that indicates which spatial and temporal regions drove the decision
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study with a newly released video dataset
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session of approximately 30 minutes per participant; 12 consecutive grasps per condition across four conditions, giving 48 movements per child, with 2 practice trials before each block and a 2-minute pause between blocks
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Structured reach-to-grasp: grasp a water-filled bottle in order to perform one of four subsequent actions - place it in a box, pour water into a glass, pass it to a co-actor who places it, or pass it to a co-actor who pours
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory/clinic - a quiet room with a fixed table and chair setup; recruitment from the Child Neuropsychiatry Unit of the IRCCS Giannina Gaslini Hospital and from primary schools in Genoa
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: DSM-5 criteria, with ADOS-2 and ADI-R both administered by two experienced professionals - the most complete diagnostic ascertainment in the corpus so far. Exclusion screening covered pharmacological treatment, dyslexia, epilepsy and any other neurological or psychiatric condition
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 20 recruited (18 male); one subject discarded from experiments because all their non-corrupted videos came from a single condition, leaving 19 analysed
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Explicitly excluded: pharmacological treatment, dyslexia, epilepsy and any other neurological or psychiatric condition. ASD group was specifically without accompanying intellectual impairment
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Pharmacological treatment was an exclusion criterion
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: ADOS-2 and ADI-R were administered but no severity scores are reported, and severity is not modelled
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developing children from primary schools in Genoa
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Screened for the same exclusion criteria and assessed on the same IQ and executive-function measures; no autism-trait screening instrument reported
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 20 (16 male); one discarded for the same data reason, leaving 20 in the reported per-subject table with subject 3 removed from the ASD side
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes - matched and confirmed non-significant (t38 = -0.665, p = 0.510)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Yes - stated as matched (18/20 vs 16/20 male)
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Video: lateral-view footage of the reach-to-grasp gesture, deliberately Gaussian-smoothed to suppress appearance detail so that only kinematics remain informative
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: 48 grasps per child across four intention conditions, with standardised start posture (pronated forearm, semi-pronated hand, pincer grip on a tape-marked point), fixed object geometry (bottle base 5 cm, height 18 cm, weight 225 g at 44 cm from midline) and movement initiated at natural speed after an auditory tone; block order pseudo-randomised. Videos trimmed exactly at the instant the hand grasps the bottle, so only the pre-contact reaching phase is modelled
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Vicon VUE video camera at 1280x720, 100 frames per second, lateral viewpoint; height-adjustable chair and fixed-dimension table; pre-trained GoogLeNet CNN for frame features; LSTM with spatial attention; dense trajectories with HOG/HOF and VLAD encoding as a baseline
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - explicitly presented as the first video dataset of simple gestures performed by ASD and TD children, with 1837 video sequences after discarding corrupted acquisitions
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes - the dataset is published at a stated URL (pavis.iit.it autism-spectrum-disorder-detection-dataset), given as a footnote in the paper. One of very few corpus studies to release a behavioral dataset, and the only one so far to release video
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not applicable - publicly posted, though the access terms are not described in the paper
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Highly sensitive in principle - video of identifiable children - though the modelling pipeline applies Gaussian smoothing to remove appearance information, and the released clips are trimmed to the reaching phase from a lateral viewpoint. The research protocol was approved by the local ethics committee (ASL3 Genovese) in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration, and parents provided written informed consent after a detailed description of the study. No explicit anonymization or data-protection statement accompanies the public dataset release
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Learned deep representations - CNN convolutional features with a learned spatial attention weighting, consumed by a recurrent network
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Frame-level 7x7x1024 feature maps from the last convolutional layer of a pre-trained GoogLeNet, preserving spatial structure; a learned 7x7 attention map weights these into a single 1024-dimensional vector per frame; the LSTM maintains a 128-dimensional hidden representation, passed through a 16-dimensional fully connected layer and a binary softmax. No handcrafted kinematic parameters are used
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Pre-trained GoogLeNet (CNN); custom LSTM with soft spatial attention; dense trajectories implementation with default parameters for the baseline
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes - via the attention mechanism rather than feature ranking
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: A learned soft spatial attention map (7x7 per frame, generated by the LSTM from its hidden spatio-temporal state) superimposed on the video frames for visual inspection, explicitly designed to give clinicians interpretable feedback about which image regions and time points drove the decision
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The attention maps concentrate on regions around the hand and arm of the subject, which the authors read as the model extracting kinematic patterns from the grasping movement. No specific kinematic parameter is named, since none is computed
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not applicable and not reported - the model learns an opaque representation and no directional kinematic difference between groups is quantified
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised deep learning (recurrent neural network with attention over CNN features)
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: GoogLeNet CNN feature extractor plus LSTM with a learned soft spatial attention mechanism and binary softmax output. Baseline: dense trajectories with HOG and HOF descriptors encoded by VLAD
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-subject-out: 39 models trained, each excluding one subject, with per-subject accuracy computed by averaging frame-level probabilities across all that subject's videos and the final result averaged over subjects. The authors state explicitly that this procedure is more challenging than standard cross-validation, whose scores 'are always higher', and that they consider it the correct procedure for a system intended to generalise to real-world use
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Per-subject averaged accuracy, detection accuracy (fraction of subjects whose averaged probability exceeds a threshold), standard deviations across subjects, a confusion matrix with precision and recall per class, and a sensitivity analysis of detection accuracy as the confidence threshold varies from 0.5 to 0.95
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Full-data model: 0.82 detection accuracy (32 of 39 subjects correctly classified), mean per-subject accuracy 0.75 +/- 0.22. Per-intention models: 0.72 detection accuracy (28 of 39), mean accuracy 0.69 +/- 0.22, with individual conditions ranging from 0.59 (pass-to-pour) to 0.77 (pouring). Confusion matrix: ASD recall 78.95% (15/19), TD recall 85.00% (17/20), ASD precision 83.33%, TD precision 80.95%. TD subjects classified more accurately and with lower variance (0.77 +/- 0.21) than ASD subjects (0.72 +/- 0.22). Dense trajectories baseline performed at random chance
