data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A CNN-LSTM with spatial attention classified whether a simple bottle-grasping movement was performed by an autistic or typically developing child from video alone at 0.82 detection accuracy, using only the pre-contact reaching phase and with visual appearance deliberately suppressed. A state-of-the-art handcrafted action-recognition baseline (dense trajectories with HOG/HOF and VLAD) performed at chance on the same data, which the authors take as evidence that classical features cannot encode the relevant kinematic subtlety. Per-subject accuracy varied enormously (standard deviation 0.22, individual subjects ranging from 0.15 to 1.00), which the authors interpret as reflecting genuine heterogeneity within the autism spectrum. Attention maps concentrated on the hand and arm.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Not identified in interpretable terms; the attention maps localise to the hand and arm region during reaching, but no kinematic property is named
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Exploit the additional intention labels to test whether intention classification itself is altered in ASD, which could serve as an extra diagnostic cue; and refine the spatial attention model to inspect the kinematic discriminants in the gestures more finely
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Methodologically among the most honest deep-learning entries in the corpus. Leave-one-subject-out with 39 separately trained models is the correct protocol and the authors say explicitly that it yields lower scores than the cross-validation others report. They publish the full per-subject accuracy table - which reveals that several ASD subjects are classified at 0.15-0.31, i.e. confidently wrong - report a confusion matrix with precision and recall, run a confidence-threshold sensitivity analysis showing the model becomes untrustworthy above 0.9, and include a handcrafted baseline that fails at chance. They also pre-process to remove appearance cues so the model cannot exploit incidental visual differences between groups. Genuine limitations: n=39 makes 0.82 equal to 32 of 39 children; the reported headline uses a 0.5 threshold on averaged frame probabilities, a somewhat generous decision rule; the sample is IQ-matched high-functioning children only; and there is no limitations section, so the heterogeneity finding is presented as a substantive result rather than as a constraint on the claim.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 20: children with ASD without accompanying intellectual impairment (18 male), and typically developing children (16 male). One ASD subject (subject 3) was discarded because all their non-corrupted videos came from a single condition, so 39 subjects enter the experiments. No other-diagnosis comparison group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'autistic subjects', 'ASD subjects', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'healthy subjects', 'patient and healthy children', 'pathological and healthy subjects', 'autism disease', 'this pathology'. Markedly medicalised framing - autism is repeatedly called a 'disease' and a 'pathology', and the comparison group is 'healthy' - which is at the opposite end of the corpus's terminological range from the identity-first, 'neurotypical' usage of studies like Li et al. (2017).
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=20 (18 male, 2 female), age 9.8 +/- 1.5 years, WISC-IV Full Scale IQ 98.5 +/- 11.1. TD n=20 (16 male, 4 female), age 9.5 +/- 1.5 years, Full Scale IQ 102.8 +/- 9.4. Matching is verified statistically on both age (t38 = -0.665, p = 0.510) and IQ (t38 = 1.325, p = 0.193), and gender is matched by design. This is among the best-matched samples in the corpus - age, gender and IQ all matched with tests reported - though both groups are male-dominated (90% and 80%) and the ASD group is restricted to children without intellectual impairment.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: DSM-5 criteria, with both ADOS-2 and ADI-R administered by two experienced professionals. This is the most complete diagnostic ascertainment encountered in the corpus to date - the two instruments that the literature identifies as having the highest sensitivity and specificity, both applied, by two independent experienced assessors.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Full Scale IQ measured by WISC-IV for both groups and used as a matching variable; executive function assessed in both groups by the Tower of London test with no significant difference (TD 29.35 +/- 3.54, ASD 29.35 +/- 2.80, t38 = 0, p = 0.999); handedness assessed by the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (all but two children right-handed). Comorbidity is handled by explicit exclusion of pharmacological treatment, dyslexia, epilepsy and any other neurological or psychiatric condition. This is unusually thorough functional characterisation for a computer-vision paper.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: automatic objective diagnostic support from video alone, framed explicitly as a first step toward a computer-aided tool usable in clinical and more open settings. Main findings: 0.82 detection accuracy (32/39 subjects) with full-data training, 0.72 (28/39) when training per intention condition; mean per-subject accuracy 0.75 +/- 0.22; ASD recall 78.95%, TD recall 85.00%; a dense-trajectories handcrafted baseline performed at chance; attention maps localised to hand and arm; per-subject variability was large and is interpreted as evidence of spectrum heterogeneity.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory setting - a quiet room with fixed table and chair geometry and a standardised start posture - with clinical recruitment from a hospital child neuropsychiatry unit and control recruitment from primary schools. Newly collected data, released as the first public video dataset of ASD/TD gestures.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A highly standardised reach-to-grasp protocol: fixed start posture with pincer grip on a marked point, a water-filled bottle of specified dimensions at 44 cm from the child's midline, and four intention conditions (grasp-to-place, grasp-to-pour, pass-to-place, pass-to-pour) with target objects at specified distances. 12 consecutive grasps per condition (48 total), initiated at natural speed after an auditory tone, with 2 practice trials before each block, pseudo-randomised block order, and a 2-minute pause between blocks to avoid fatigue. Crucially, video is trimmed at the moment of contact, so only the pre-grasp reaching phase is analysed - testing the neuroscientific claim that intention is encoded in the earliest stages of a motor act.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single ~30-minute session per child with no follow-up. Video of identifiable children is inherently sensitive, though the analysis pipeline applies Gaussian smoothing to suppress appearance and the released clips show only a lateral view of a reaching arm. Ethics approval from the local committee (ASL3 Genovese) under the Helsinki Declaration is reported, and parents gave written informed consent after a detailed study description. No anonymization or data-protection statement accompanies the public dataset release, which is a gap given that the dataset is posted openly.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: Vicon VUE video camera at 1280x720 and 100 frames per second, lateral viewpoint; height-adjustable chair and a table of specified dimensions; a plastic bottle, box and glass of specified dimensions. Software: pre-trained GoogLeNet for CNN features; a custom LSTM with soft spatial attention; dense trajectories with HOG and HOF descriptors and VLAD encoding for the baseline. Deep-learning framework and training hyperparameters are not named.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Mixed but above corpus average. The dataset is publicly released at a stated URL - the only video dataset released in this corpus - and the experimental protocol is specified in exhaustive physical detail (table dimensions, object weights and positions, start posture, trial counts, block structure, camera settings, trimming rule). The model architecture is described concretely (GoogLeNet last conv layer, 7x7x1024 features, 7x7 attention map, 128-dim LSTM hidden state, 16-dim FC layer, 15-frame clips). What is missing: no code release, no training hyperparameters (learning rate, optimiser, epochs, regularisation), no random seeds, and no statement of how the model handles the 15-frame clip splitting at test time beyond averaging.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: There is no limitations section, so nothing is formally acknowledged, though the authors do report the difficulty candidly in the results - the large per-subject standard deviation is presented as evidence that 'finding a very general pattern in the video, that could be unique in distinguishing autistic subjects, is a challenging task', and TD subjects being classified better than ASD ones is read as 'evidence of the fact that autistic spectrum disorders comprise indeed a very wide spectrum of variability'. Identifiable in review: n=39 makes 0.82 equal to 32 of 39 children; the ASD group excludes intellectual impairment and is IQ-matched to controls, so results cannot extend to the broader spectrum; both groups are 80-90% male; the per-subject table shows several ASD children classified confidently wrong (subjects 7, 17 and 20 at 0.15, 0.16 and 0.31), which a single aggregate figure would conceal; the 0.5 threshold on averaged frame probabilities is a lenient decision rule and performance collapses below chance above a 0.9 threshold; and single-site recruitment with one fixed camera viewpoint leaves transfer entirely untested.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Exploit the intention labels already in the dataset to test whether intention classification itself is altered in ASD, which could provide an additional diagnostic cue; and refine the spatial attention model to more finely inspect the kinematic discriminants in the gestures. Both are concrete and grounded in the existing data rather than generic calls for larger samples.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Motor behavior captured as raw video: the kinematics of a reach-to-grasp movement, with visual appearance deliberately degraded by Gaussian smoothing so that only movement information remains available to the model. No markers, no motion capture, no handcrafted kinematic parameters - the paper positions this freedom from 'invasive sensory devices (e.g., MRI, microphones, eye tracker, Motion Capture landmarks)' as its central practical advantage.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality, no fusion. There is a form of temporal-spatial integration internal to the model - the LSTM's learned attention map weights spatial CNN features at each time step based on its accumulated hidden state, so spatial and temporal information are combined adaptively rather than by fixed pooling. Frame-level probabilities are averaged into a per-subject decision, a late fusion across frames and clips. No combination with clinical scores, IQ or demographics, despite those being available.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised deep learning: a pre-trained GoogLeNet CNN as frame feature extractor feeding a recurrent LSTM with a learned soft spatial attention mechanism and a binary softmax classifier. A handcrafted alternative (dense trajectories with HOG/HOF and VLAD encoding) is included specifically as a baseline and is reported to perform at chance - an informative negative comparison that most corpus studies omit.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Learned deep embeddings over raw video, with no handcrafted features at all: 7x7x1024 convolutional feature maps per frame from GoogLeNet, adaptively pooled by a learned 7x7 attention map into a 1024-dimensional vector, then consumed recursively by a 128-dimensional LSTM. Videos are split into 15-frame clips for training, with each clip treated independently and probabilities averaged across frames at test time. This is one of the few genuinely end-to-end representations in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Per-subject averaged accuracy with standard deviation, detection accuracy at a stated threshold, a full confusion matrix with per-class precision and recall (ASD 83.33% precision / 78.95% recall; TD 80.95% precision / 85.00% recall), and a threshold sensitivity curve from 0.5 to 0.95. No AUC or confidence intervals, but the reporting is more complete than accuracy-only studies and the full per-subject accuracy table is published, which allows a reader to see the distribution rather than only its mean.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: A learned soft spatial attention map, generated per frame by the LSTM from its hidden spatio-temporal state and visualised superimposed on the video, is the interpretability mechanism - and it is designed into the model rather than applied post hoc. The maps concentrate on the hand and arm during reaching, which the authors read as the network attending to gesture kinematics, and they propose the maps as feedback clinicians could use in interpreting a diagnosis. The interpretation stops at localisation: no kinematic property (velocity, jerk, trajectory shape) is extracted or named, so the explanation identifies where the model looks but not what it sees there.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Robustness is handled unusually seriously. Leave-one-subject-out with 39 independently trained models is used deliberately, with the authors stating that it is 'more challenging than the usual cross-validation whose classification scores are always higher' and that they consider it the correct procedure for a system meant to generalise. Appearance information is removed by Gaussian smoothing so the model cannot exploit incidental visual differences. A handcrafted state-of-the-art baseline is run and reported to fail at chance. A confidence-threshold sensitivity analysis shows detection accuracy degrading from 0.82 to 0.67 between thresholds 0.5 and 0.7 and dropping below chance above 0.9, with the authors stating plainly that the model 'is not more trustable after a threshold of 0.9'. What is absent: any external or independent dataset, any held-out site or camera viewpoint, any class-imbalance issue (19/20), and any real-time or deployment measurement despite clinical use being the stated aim.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No formal keyword list. The paper's vocabulary: 'autism disease diagnosis', 'video gesture analysis', 'attention map', 'computer-aided diagnostic algorithms', 'objective quantitative tool', 'motor signals of Autism', 'first screening test', 'pathological vs healthy subjects'. The recurrent 'disease'/'pathology' framing is distinctive and contrasts sharply with the neurodiversity-aligned vocabulary elsewhere in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: The 24th International Conference on Pattern Recognition (ICPR) 2018, Beijing - a technology/computational venue (pattern recognition and computer vision), not an autism or clinical venue, though the author list spans a computer vision institute, a cognition and motion neuroscience group, a university psychology department and a hospital child neuropsychiatry unit.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2018. The paper surveys machine learning applied to autism across quotient-based diagnostic tools, MRI, kinematic data, eye tracking and language acoustics, and argues that these modalities are 'quite invasive or require specialized personnel, often affecting the behavior of the subjects under study', and that most rely on 'handcrafted features and simplified linear models that often fail to handle the complexity of human behaviors in less controlled settings'. It positions itself as the first to cast autism diagnosis as a video-based computational problem and as part of the shift toward deep learning - a shift this corpus documents accelerating sharply from 2018 onward.

data_charting_rubrics.title: A Novel Eye Movement Data Transformation Technique that Preserves Temporal Information: A Demonstration in a Face Processing Task
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Król M; Król ME
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye-tracking and gaze
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Methodological: introduce a technique for statistically comparing two groups of scanpaths in terms of their temporal features, demonstrated on an autism versus typical development contrast. Autism classification is the demonstration case, not the primary aim
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control methods-demonstration study using data from two laboratory experiments with the same participants
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Two experiments comprising five task blocks of 12 trials each, giving 60 trials per subject; each trial presented a 500 ms fixation cross, a 2000 ms facial image, and a 2000 ms blank screen or question prompt
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Five face-perception tasks: guessing the expressed emotion; judging whether the brows or the lips were wider; free viewing with no requirement; estimating the person's age; and judging whether the person appeared 'nice'. Tasks were split across two experiments, presented in blocks with the free-view block first in Experiment 1 and the remaining block order randomised
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory - SWPS University of Social Sciences and Humanities, Wroclaw
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: All ASD participants had clinical diagnoses prior to enrolment based on ICD-10 criteria, and all diagnoses were additionally confirmed by the research team using ADOS-2. None of the typically developing subjects had a history of autism spectrum or other neurodevelopmental disorders
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 21 (including 2 females)
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Mean 16.27 years (range 11-29); no standard deviation reported
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: All subjects had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no neurological conditions; all had full-scale IQ at least in the average range (>85)
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: ADOS-2 was administered for diagnostic confirmation but no severity scores are reported or modelled
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developing individuals age- and IQ-matched
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes - no history of autism spectrum or other neurodevelopmental disorders, no neurological conditions, and full-scale IQ above 85
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 23 (5 females)
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes - described as age-matched, with near-identical means (16.27 vs 16.31), though the ASD range extends to 29 against a control maximum of 21
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not claimed; proportions differ (10% vs 22% female) on very small female counts
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes - screened by history and IQ
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye movements: binocular fixation sequences with timing and duration, encoded as scanpath strings over facial-landmark-derived areas of interest
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: 60 face images from the FACES database (balanced for sex and across young, middle-aged and older age groups), each shown once per subject with one randomly chosen emotional expression from six, to avoid familiarity effects and face-emotion interactions. Fixations detected with a 60 ms minimum duration and 50 degrees/s velocity threshold. Trials in which no AOI transitions occurred in either eye were excluded
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: SMI RED250 Mobile remote eye tracker at 250 Hz with 0.4 degree gaze accuracy; 15-inch Dell Precision M4800 workstation at 1280x720; chinrest at 65 cm; 5-point calibration and 4-point validation with periodic data-quality checks prompting repositioning; experimental software in C#; SMI event detector; Wolfram Mathematica 11.3 for landmark detection and LightGBM; MATLAB for t-SNE; R for the Cramer test
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Data were collected for this and a companion paper; the data and code are released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes - 'The data and code used to obtain the results described below are available as supplementary information'
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not applicable - supplied as supplementary material
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze coordinates over third-party stimulus faces carry low re-identification risk. Ethics reporting is complete: approval by the local Faculty Research Ethics Committee of the University of Social Sciences and Humanities in Wroclaw, written consent from adult subjects or from guardians of underage subjects, and additionally oral consent from the underage subjects themselves - a two-tier consent procedure rarely reported in this corpus
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Dimension-reduced scanpath representations derived from pairwise sequence similarity, plus a spatial-only control representation
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Each fixation is assigned to the nearest of 76 areas of interest (68 machine-detected facial landmarks plus 8 equidistant points on a rectangular frame enclosing the face, added specifically to capture stray fixations far from the face, noted as relatively frequent among ASD subjects). Scanpaths are encoded as character strings with each AOI character repeated once per 50 ms of fixation duration. ScanMatch pairwise similarity uses a substitution matrix encoding both spatial and semantic AOI relationships - positive scores inversely proportional to distance within an anatomical group (face outline, mouth, nose, eyes, eyebrows, frame), negative scores proportional to distance across groups, rescaled to [-1, +1] - with scores normalised by the longer sequence length to avoid length bias. The similarity matrix is then reduced by t-SNE to two dimensions per eye, giving four spatial-plus-temporal features per trial. A spatial-only control is produced by randomly permuting the scanpath characters before repeating the identical pipeline, yielding four features that encode AOI hit frequencies but not order
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Machine-learning facial landmark detector trained on 120,000 examples (Wolfram Mathematica 11.3 implementation); ScanMatch with the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm; t-SNE (van der Maaten's original MATLAB code); LightGBM via Mathematica
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No per-feature importance, but the study's entire design is an importance test - isolating the contribution of temporal ordering by comparing against a permuted-order control
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not applicable; the finding is that temporal ordering information contributes beyond spatial information
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported directionally. The paper explicitly declines to interpret which temporal patterns differ, framing the contribution as methodological. Average scanpath string length was 29.22 (SD 10.18) for ASD and 30.87 (SD 10.99) for TD subjects, corresponding to about 1.5 seconds
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification with unsupervised dimensionality reduction, used as a hypothesis test
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Gradient boosted decision trees via LightGBM (maximum 50 boosting rounds, maximum tree depth 6, automatically chosen leaf sizes, class priors set to 0.5). ScanMatch/Needleman-Wunsch for sequence alignment and t-SNE for embedding. A benchmark comparison used Levenshtein distance with Kruskal's non-metric multidimensional scaling in place of ScanMatch and t-SNE
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 5-by-2 repeated cross-validation with explicit subject-level partitioning - 'each time the dataset was split into two folds, we ensured that each subject's data entered only one of them, and that both subject groups were evenly split across the folds'. The paired classifier comparison is tested statistically, and both models are additionally verified against chance by permutation testing with 1000 random permutations. Group distribution differences are tested separately with the non-parametric Cramer test using 1000 Monte-Carlo permutation replicates
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Classification accuracy averaged across cross-validation iterations and folds, with a paired t-test comparing models, confusion matrices for both models, and permutation-derived p-values against chance
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Spatial-only model 53.9% accuracy; spatial-plus-temporal model 55.5%; the difference significant at t(5) = -2.94, p = 0.032. Both significantly above chance by permutation test (p < 0.001, k = 1000). Cramer test on t-SNE point distributions: left eye statistic 358.84 against critical value 61.59, p < 0.001; right eye statistic 205.25 against critical value 62.33, p < 0.001. Benchmark using Levenshtein distance with non-metric MDS: 51.8% spatial versus 51.9% spatial-plus-temporal, not significantly different (p = 0.387). Adding face emotion, gender, age or task type as predictors did not significantly improve either model
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: The paper introduces a general technique for statistically comparing groups of scanpaths on temporal features: compute a pairwise similarity matrix with ScanMatch, embed it with t-SNE, and compare the resulting low-dimensional distributions. Demonstrated on autism, the distributions of ASD and TD scanpath embeddings differed highly significantly, and a classifier given the temporal representation outperformed one given only spatial information (55.5% versus 53.9%, p = 0.032), establishing that the difference is not purely spatial. Crucially the absolute accuracies are very low - barely above the 50% chance level, though significantly so by permutation test - and the paper presents them as evidence for a methodological claim about temporal information rather than as a diagnostic capability.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Not identified; the study establishes that temporal ordering carries group-discriminative information without characterising what that ordering is
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: The technique is proposed for general use 'in other problems in which one needs to compare two sets of eye movement sequences in terms of their temporal features'; no autism-specific future work is proposed
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Methodologically this is one of the most careful studies in the corpus, and it is careful precisely because its aim is a methodological claim rather than a diagnostic one. Three design features stand out. First, subject-level partitioning is stated explicitly and enforced, with both groups evenly split across folds - the leakage control that most of this corpus omits. Second, the spatial-only control is constructed by randomly permuting the scanpath characters and re-running the entire identical pipeline, which is an elegant way to isolate the contribution of temporal ordering while holding everything else constant. Third, a benchmark using more standard techniques (Levenshtein distance with non-metric MDS) is run and reported as showing no significant temporal contribution, which both validates the choice of ScanMatch/t-SNE and demonstrates that the effect is not an artefact of the general approach. Diagnosis is confirmed with ADOS-2 on top of prior ICD-10 clinical diagnosis, groups are age- and IQ-matched, data and code are released, and consent is obtained at two levels for minors. The essential point for this review is that the reported accuracies are 53.9% and 55.5% - a 1.6 percentage point difference that is statistically significant but diagnostically negligible. Read alongside the corpus's many 90%+ claims from comparable gaze data and comparable sample sizes, this study is a valuable calibration: when the unit of analysis is a two-second trial, subjects are partitioned properly, and the comparison is against a matched control representation, the recoverable signal is very small.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: 21 individuals with ASD and 23 age- and IQ-matched typically developing controls, total 44. Group sizes, sexes and IQ means are all reported. No other-diagnosis comparison group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'subjects with ASD', 'individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)', 'the ASD population', 'ASD subjects', 'autistic vs. typically-developing individuals', 'typically developing (TD) controls'. Mixed person-first and identity-first, with 'typically developing' rather than 'normal' throughout. Autism is described as 'a developmental disorder affecting social and communicative functioning and related to repetitive, limited patterns of behavior and interests' - a conventional clinical framing without pathologising language.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=21 (2 female, 10%), mean age 16.27, range 11-29, mean full-scale IQ 109.4. TD n=23 (5 female, 22%), mean age 16.31, range 10-21, mean full-scale IQ 112.3. Groups are described as age- and IQ-matched and the means are indeed near-identical, though the ASD age range extends to 29 while no control exceeded 21, and no standard deviations or formal comparison tests are reported. All participants had full-scale IQ above 85, so the sample is restricted to average-or-above intellectual ability. Both groups are heavily male. Adolescents and adults, so no early-diagnosis relevance.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Among the strongest in the corpus: all ASD participants had prior clinical diagnoses under WHO ICD-10 criteria, and all diagnoses were additionally confirmed by the research team using ADOS-2, described accurately as 'a standardized, validated instrument for the assessment of autism spectrum conditions'. Control status was established by absence of any history of autism spectrum or other neurodevelopmental disorders. Independent re-confirmation with a gold-standard instrument, rather than reliance on prior diagnosis alone, is uncommon here.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Intelligence measured with the Wechsler Scales for all participants, with group means reported (109.4 and 112.3) and a minimum threshold of 85 applied as an inclusion criterion - so IQ is both measured and controlled by restriction and matching. Vision was normal or corrected-to-normal and neurological conditions excluded for all subjects. No language or adaptive measures, and ADOS-2 severity scores are not reported despite the instrument being administered.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: primarily methodological - to enable statistical comparison of two groups of scanpaths on temporal features, with autism as the demonstration domain. Main findings: t-SNE embeddings of ASD and TD scanpaths differed highly significantly for both eyes (Cramer test p < 0.001); adding the temporal representation to a spatial-only feature set raised classification accuracy from 53.9% to 55.5% (p = 0.032), establishing a genuine temporal difference beyond the known spatial one; both models were above chance by permutation test; and a benchmark using Levenshtein distance with non-metric MDS found no significant temporal contribution, indicating the effect depends on the specific ScanMatch/t-SNE combination.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory setting with a chinrest, fixed viewing distance and periodic data-quality monitoring. The data were collected by the authors across two experiments, with Experiment 1 data also used in a separate publication on information extraction - disclosed transparently on the grounds that 'recruiting ASD subjects and validating their diagnoses is extremely costly'.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Five face-perception tasks spanning emotion recognition, a non-social perceptual judgement (brow versus lip width), free viewing, age estimation and a social evaluation ('nice' or not), across 60 trials per subject. Stimuli were 60 FACES database photographs balanced by sex and across three age bands, each shown once per subject with one randomly chosen expression from six to avoid familiarity effects and face-emotion confounds. Notably the study deliberately used images of the entire head with varying facial-feature locations, criticising the field's usual practice of using cropped images with standardised feature positions as 'somewhat unrealistic' - and solved the resulting AOI problem with automatic landmark detection.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; two experiments in a laboratory session series with no follow-up. The data are gaze coordinates over third-party stimulus faces, so re-identification risk is minimal and the public release is correspondingly low-risk. Consent handling is exemplary: ethics approval from the named Faculty Research Ethics Committee, written consent from adult subjects or from guardians of underage subjects, and additionally oral consent obtained from the underage subjects themselves - a two-tier assent procedure that only one other study in this corpus matches.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: SMI RED250 Mobile remote eye tracker at 250 Hz with 0.4 degree accuracy; 15-inch Dell Precision M4800 at 1280x720; chinrest at 65 cm; 5-point calibration with 4-point validation and automated periodic quality checks prompting repositioning. Software: C# experimental program; SMI event detector (60 ms minimum fixation, 50 degrees/s velocity threshold); Wolfram Mathematica 11.3 for the facial landmark detector and LightGBM; MATLAB (van der Maaten's original code) for t-SNE; R for the Cramer test.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: The strongest reproducibility profile in the corpus alongside Yaneva et al. Data and code are both released as supplementary information. The method is documented exhaustively: eye tracker specifications, calibration and validation procedure, fixation detection thresholds, the 68+8 AOI construction and why the extra 8 frame points were added, the 50 ms character-repetition encoding, the substitution matrix construction with its distance and group logic and its [-1,+1] rescaling, the length normalisation rationale, the t-SNE implementation used, the LightGBM hyperparameters, the class priors, and the subject-level fold constraint. The authors also report that manipulating t-SNE settings and LightGBM defaults produced no qualitative change - an informal robustness check.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The paper has no dedicated limitations section, since it is framed as a methods demonstration. It does report transparently that Experiment 1 data were reused from a companion paper and why. Identifiable in review: the absolute accuracies of 53.9% and 55.5% are barely above chance and correspond to a 1.6 percentage point improvement, so while the temporal claim is statistically supported the practical discriminability is negligible - a fact the paper does not emphasise; the unit of analysis is a single two-second trial rather than a person, so no participant-level diagnostic estimate exists; the ASD age range extends to 29 against a control maximum of 21 despite matched means; both groups are heavily male on very small female counts; all participants have IQ above 85, so the sample excludes much of the spectrum; and trials with no AOI transitions in either eye were excluded, which may remove disproportionately many ASD trials given the noted tendency toward stray fixations.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: No autism-specific future work is proposed. The methodological conclusion is that the technique 'could be used in other problems in which one needs to compare two sets of eye movement sequences in terms of their temporal features', positioning the contribution as a general tool for eye-movement research rather than an autism screening development.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Gaze: binocular fixation sequences with duration and order, encoded relative to automatically detected facial landmarks. The distinguishing feature is that temporal ordering is preserved and made the object of analysis, whereas the corpus's other gaze studies aggregate into dwell times or fixation counts that discard sequence.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality, but with an unusual internal contrast: spatial-only and spatial-plus-temporal representations of the same data are constructed through identical pipelines and compared, which is a form of ablation rather than fusion. Left and right eye representations are kept separate and both included as features, motivated by a possible lateral offset with each eye directed slightly toward its own side of the face. Face emotion, gender, age and task type were tested as additional predictors and reported as not significantly improving either model.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning with unsupervised embedding: gradient boosted decision trees (LightGBM) over t-SNE embeddings of a ScanMatch similarity matrix. The Needleman-Wunsch sequence alignment underlying ScanMatch is a classical bioinformatics algorithm repurposed for gaze. A benchmark condition substitutes Levenshtein distance and Kruskal's non-metric multidimensional scaling for the ScanMatch/t-SNE pair.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A distinctive three-stage representation: fixation sequences are first converted to character strings where each AOI symbol is repeated proportionally to fixation duration (one character per 50 ms), so that duration is encoded in string length; pairwise ScanMatch alignment then produces a similarity matrix incorporating spatial proximity and anatomical group membership through a purpose-built substitution matrix; and t-SNE finally embeds each scanpath as a point in two dimensions. This converts an inherently pairwise, non-vector representation into per-item coordinates that can be tested statistically - which is exactly the barrier the paper sets out to solve.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Classification accuracy averaged over folds and iterations, with a paired t-test between the two models, confusion matrices for both, and permutation-based verification against chance. Group-level distributional differences are tested separately with the non-parametric Cramer test with reported statistics, critical values and p-values for each eye. The reporting is statistically thorough, though absolute accuracy is the only classification metric and no sensitivity, specificity or AUC is given.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No feature-level interpretation is offered, and this is a deliberate choice: the paper establishes that temporal ordering carries group-discriminative information without claiming to characterise what the ordering difference is. The illustrative hypothesis it uses to motivate the design - that TD subjects might look at the eyes before the mouth while ASD subjects do the reverse - is offered as a possibility to be tested, not a finding. The permuted-character control is the interpretive mechanism: because it destroys order while preserving AOI frequencies, any accuracy gain over it must come from sequence.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Among the best in the corpus. Subject-level partitioning is explicit and enforced, with both groups evenly split across folds and class priors set to 0.5. The 5-by-2 repeated cross-validation design is a recognised procedure for comparing classifiers. Both models are permutation-tested against chance (p < 0.001, k = 1000), which matters given accuracies near 50%. A benchmark using alternative standard techniques is run and reported as null, guarding against the conclusion being an artefact of the general pipeline. Sensitivity to algorithm settings is informally checked for both t-SNE and LightGBM. Absent: external validation on an independent sample, and any participant-level aggregation that would yield a diagnostic estimate.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: eye tracking; scanpath comparison; dimensionality reduction; machine learning; autism; face perception. Task vocabulary: 'scanpath', 'areas-of-interest', 'temporal scanpath features', 'substitution matrix', 'dimension-reduced scanpath representation'. Notably the vocabulary is that of eye-movement methodology rather than diagnosis - words like 'screening', 'detection' and 'biomarker' are absent.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Sensors (MDPI) - an instrumentation and sensing journal, neither autism-specific nor clinical, consistent with the paper's methodological framing.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2019. The paper's field characterisation is methodological rather than clinical: it observes that 'most related studies rely on spatial information about which different areas of visual stimuli were looked at, without considering the order in which this occurred', and that 'even state-of-the-art analyses of this type are typically based on spatial but not temporal eye movement information'. It also criticises the prevailing stimulus convention - that existing studies 'typically use facial images with cropped peripheral regions... and such that the locations of the key facial regions are the same across images', which 'facilitates the analysis but can be seen as somewhat unrealistic'. Both observations identify structural simplifications in the gaze literature that this corpus otherwise leaves unexamined.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Applying Machine Learning to Identify Autism With Restricted Kinematic Features
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Zhao Z; Zhang X; Li W; Hu X; Qu X; Cao X; Liu Y; Lu J
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: High-functioning autism
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Motor and kinematics
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Diagnostic identification with a novel construct: test whether restricted kinematic features - the motor expression of restricted and repetitive behaviour, one of the two cardinal DSM symptoms - can identify ASD, and thereby provide an objective assessment of RRB
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session; three trials of 60 seconds each per participant, separated by 2-5 minute breaks to avoid fatigue, with the first and last 3 seconds of each trial discarded
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: One-dimensional left-right oscillatory hand movement performed as complex as possible - explicitly requiring variant amplitude and frequency rather than periodic oscillation, adapted from Slowinski et al.
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Clinic/laboratory - children with ASD recruited from the Department of Child Psychiatry at Shenzhen Kangning Hospital, with testing using a desktop LeapMotion setup
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Confirmed diagnosis of high-functioning autism by a licensed psychiatrist using DSM-IV criteria; Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices administered to confirm average non-verbal intellectual ability; ADHD, intellectual disability and schizophrenia explicitly excluded
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Reported in Table 1 (not recoverable from the extracted text); inclusion range 6-13 years
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Reported in Table 1 but not recoverable from the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Explicitly excluded: ADHD, mental retardation and schizophrenia. Only high-functioning autism was included, to ensure compliance with the experimental protocol
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported; no autism severity instrument administered
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developing children reporting no physical or mental disorders
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: By self/caregiver report of no physical or mental disorders; no screening instrument
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd_controls: Reported in Table 1 (not recoverable from the extracted text)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution_controls: Reported in Table 1 but not recoverable from the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes - described as age-matched, with a demographic comparison presented in Table 1
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not explicitly claimed; demographic comparison is tabulated
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Motor kinematics: hand palm position time series and derived velocity and acceleration during oscillatory movement
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Three 60-second trials of one-dimensional oscillatory hand movement above a string strung between two sticks 60 cm apart, with the subdominant hand held behind the back; the experimenter demonstrated the distinction between simple periodic oscillation and complex unpredictable oscillation, and practice trials preceded recording. Trials were reinitiated if the hand left the recording zone or movement stopped
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: LeapMotion hand-tracking device with a Lenovo Legion R720 computer; two sticks and a string defining a 60 cm movement zone; a solid mat for comfortable positioning where needed; MATLAB R2017b for machine learning; SPSS 17.0 for statistics
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - newly collected
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - the paper states explicitly that 'The dataset is not made publicly available'
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Low-sensitivity numeric hand-position data. Written informed consent was signed by participants' caregivers, the study conformed to the Declaration of Helsinki and followed the ethical guidelines of Shenzhen University. No anonymization procedure is separately described, and none is materially needed for this data type
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted complexity/variability features derived from distributions of kinematic quantities
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 18 features: Shannon entropy and central 95% range computed over the distributions of movement amplitude, velocity and acceleration, each summarised across the three trials by minimum, median and maximum. Noise thresholds were applied before computation (amplitude 0-60 cm, velocity -3 to 3 m/s, acceleration -130 to 130 m/s2), and distributions were binned into 101 equally spaced bins
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: MATLAB - piecewise cubic Hermite interpolation of the position series, second-order low-pass Butterworth filter at 5 Hz, numerical differentiation for velocity and acceleration
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Two-stage selection: independent t-tests on all 18 features with a liberal p<0.1 threshold to identify discriminative features, followed by forward feature selection evaluating classification accuracy at each step
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Nine features passed the t-test screen (velocity entropy median/max/min, acceleration entropy median/min, amplitude entropy min, amplitude range median/max, velocity range min). The best model used four: maximal amplitude range, minimal velocity range, median velocity entropy and minimal velocity entropy - three of the four relating to velocity
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Partially reported: children with ASD had significantly greater maximal amplitude range than controls, which the authors interpret as performing oscillations with greater amplitude and link to reported macrographia and fine motor control deficits in autism. Directions for the velocity entropy and range features are not stated, so it is not reported whether the ASD group was more or less restricted on the measures that dominate the model
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Five classifiers compared: support vector machine, linear discriminant analysis, decision tree, random forest and k-nearest neighbour (k tested at 1, 3, 5, 7). KNN with k=1 performed best
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-out cross-validation across all five classifiers. Critically, both selection stages precede or wrap the cross-validation: the t-test screen from 18 to 9 features used the full labelled dataset, and forward feature selection chose the feature combination by maximising classification accuracy, so the reported accuracy is the maximum over a search that used the evaluation criterion itself
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC, reported for the best model of each of the five classifiers together with the number of features in each best model, plus a confusion matrix for the winning model and an accuracy-versus-feature-count curve
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Best model KNN (k=1) with four features: accuracy 88.37%, AUC 0.8815. The abstract reports specificity 91.3% and sensitivity 85%, while the discussion reverses these to sensitivity 91.3% and specificity 85% - an internal inconsistency. All classifiers except the decision tree exceeded 75% accuracy with no more than five features
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Restricted kinematic features - entropy and spread of the amplitude, velocity and acceleration distributions during a task explicitly demanding variable movement - classified high-functioning autistic children from typically developing children at 88.37% accuracy with AUC 0.88 using just four features. Three of the four best features derive from the velocity distribution, which the authors connect to prior findings that velocity profiles characterise subtle individual motor differences. The conceptual contribution is operationalising restricted and repetitive behaviour, a cardinal DSM symptom that is otherwise assessed only by informant report, as a measurable motor property.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Greater maximal amplitude range (larger oscillations), and velocity-distribution entropy and range measures, in a task requiring maximally variable movement
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Extend classification beyond ASD-versus-TD to discriminating ASD from other groups such as ADHD; apply machine learning to other aspects such as engagement evaluation; integrate genetic, neurological, psychological and kinematic features toward an objective automated diagnosis; and address how to quantify higher-level restricted and repetitive behaviour such as circumscribed interest, which motion-capture approaches to stereotyped movement cannot reach
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The conceptual contribution is genuine and, within this corpus, novel: rather than measuring social attention or general motor coordination, the task is designed so that the restrictedness itself becomes the dependent variable - participants are asked to be maximally variable, and the failure to be so is the signal. That is a well-reasoned operationalisation of a DSM criterion that is otherwise only informant-rated. The limitations section is also unusually honest, conceding that the sample is high-functioning only, that low-functioning children may not manage the task, and explicitly that 'this motor task would not work for children less than 2 years old, which suggests that this motor task would not function for the early screening of ASD' - a rare acknowledgement that the method cannot serve the early-detection goal the field usually claims. Against this, the validation is optimistic in a way the paper does not acknowledge: the t-test screen from 18 to 9 features used all labels, and forward feature selection then chose the combination that maximised classification accuracy, with the best of five classifiers and four k values reported - so 88.37% is a maximum over a substantial search rather than a generalisation estimate. The paper also reverses sensitivity and specificity between abstract and discussion, does not report the direction of the velocity features that carry most of the signal, and excludes ADHD, intellectual disability and schizophrenia, which makes the sample cleaner but the task easier than the clinical question requires.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: 20 children with high-functioning autism and 23 age-matched typically developing children. Group sizes are clear. No other-diagnosis comparison group - indeed ADHD, intellectual disability and schizophrenia were explicit exclusions - though the conclusion identifies ASD-versus-ADHD classification as the needed next step.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with high functioning autism', 'children with ASD', 'patients with ASD', 'ASD patients', 'the patient', 'individuals with typical development (TD)', 'TD children', 'non-ASD individuals'. Consistently medicalised - 'patient' is the default noun throughout, and the framing is diagnostic rather than descriptive.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=20, TD n=23, described as age-matched with an inclusion range of 6-13 years. Demographic details including ages and sexes are presented in Table 1, which is not recoverable from the extracted text, so exact means, standard deviations and sex ratios cannot be charted here. Non-verbal IQ was assessed with Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices as an inclusion criterion (average ability required) but the values are likewise in the unrecoverable table. Age matching is claimed and a demographic comparison is tabulated, which is better practice than most of the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Confirmed diagnosis of high-functioning autism by a licensed psychiatrist using DSM-IV criteria, with Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices confirming average non-verbal intellectual ability and explicit exclusion of ADHD, intellectual disability and schizophrenia. No ADOS or ADI-R. The exclusion of common comorbidities is unusually explicit and is a design strength for internal validity, though it narrows the population.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Non-verbal IQ assessed by Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices and used as an inclusion criterion (average ability), so cognitive level is controlled by restriction rather than by matching or covariate adjustment. No language or adaptive-functioning measures and no autism severity instrument. Comorbidity is handled by exclusion: ADHD, mental retardation and schizophrenia ruled out for the ASD group; controls reported no physical or mental disorders.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: test whether restricted kinematic features derived from restricted and repetitive behaviour can identify ASD, providing an objective assessment of a symptom domain normally rated by informants. Main findings: KNN (k=1) with four features achieved 88.37% accuracy and AUC 0.8815; nine of 18 features differed between groups at p<0.1; three of the four best features derive from the velocity distribution; and all classifiers except the decision tree exceeded 75% accuracy with five or fewer features.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Clinical recruitment (hospital child psychiatry department) with laboratory-style testing on a desktop LeapMotion apparatus. Newly collected data; no existing dataset used.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A deliberately inverted task design: participants perform one-dimensional oscillatory hand movement 'as complex as possible', with the experimenter demonstrating the contrast between simple periodic oscillation (mono amplitude and frequency) and complex unpredictable oscillation (variant amplitude and frequency), followed by practice trials until the requirement was understood. Three 60-second trials with the subdominant hand held behind the back, breaks of 2-5 minutes between trials, and trial reinitiation if the hand left the recording zone or movement stopped. The design is the paper's key idea - restrictedness is measured as failure to comply with an instruction to be variable.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; three 60-second trials in a single session with no follow-up. Data are numeric hand-position traces, not identifiable media. Written informed consent was signed by caregivers, the study conformed to the Declaration of Helsinki, and it followed the ethical guidelines of Shenzhen University. No anonymization procedure is described, and none is materially required for this data type.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: LeapMotion hand-tracking device connected to a Lenovo Legion R720-15IKBN computer, with a physical rig of two sticks and a string defining a 60 cm movement zone and a mat for comfortable hand positioning. Software: MATLAB R2017b for signal processing (piecewise cubic Hermite interpolation, second-order 5 Hz low-pass Butterworth filter, differentiation) and machine learning; SPSS 17.0 for statistical comparison.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: The dataset availability is stated explicitly and negatively - 'The dataset is not made publicly available' - which is at least transparent, and rarer in this corpus than silence. No code release. Method reporting is otherwise strong: apparatus, movement-zone geometry, trial structure and durations, interpolation and filter settings, noise thresholds for each kinematic quantity, the 101-bin histogram construction, the Shannon entropy and range equations, the two-stage feature-selection procedure with its p<0.1 threshold, the five classifiers with the k values tested, and the software versions. Re-implementable in principle; not reproducible without the data.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors in a dedicated Limitations section that is notably candid: only high-functioning children were recruited to ensure task compliance, and whether low-functioning patients could perform the task 'remains an open question'; and 'obviously, this motor task would not work for children less than 2 years old, which suggests that this motor task would not function for the early screening of ASD' - an explicit concession that the method cannot serve early screening, which almost no other corpus study makes. They further note that motion-capture approaches can quantify low-level stereotyped movement but not higher-level RRB such as circumscribed interest. Identifiable in review: the t-test screen from 18 to 9 features used the full labelled dataset before cross-validation, and forward feature selection then selected the combination maximising classification accuracy, so 88.37% is a maximum over a search using the evaluation criterion; the best of five classifiers and four k values is reported; sensitivity and specificity are reversed between abstract and discussion; the direction of the velocity features carrying most of the signal is not reported; exclusion of ADHD, intellectual disability and schizophrenia makes the discrimination easier than the clinical task; and demographic detail resides in a table that is not reproduced in the running text.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Extend classification from ASD-versus-TD to ASD-versus-other-conditions, specifically ADHD; apply machine learning to adjacent problems such as engagement evaluation; integrate genetic, neurological, psychological and kinematic features toward automated objective diagnosis, while acknowledging the open problem of selecting relevant features from a very large pool; and develop ways to quantify higher-level restricted and repetitive behaviour such as circumscribed interest, which accelerometer and Kinect approaches to stereotyped movement cannot capture.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Motor behavior: one-dimensional hand kinematics, specifically the statistical distributions of oscillation amplitude, velocity and acceleration rather than their means. The construct measured is behavioural variability/complexity rather than speed, accuracy or coordination - a different target from every other motor study in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality; no fusion. Within the modality, three kinematic quantities (amplitude, velocity, acceleration) are each summarised by two complexity measures (entropy and 95% range) and three cross-trial aggregates (min, median, max), giving an 18-feature grid, and the selected model combines amplitude-range and velocity-range/entropy features - so the fusion is across kinematic derivatives and trial aggregates. The discussion proposes future integration with genetic, neuroimaging and psychological data.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning with a broad classifier comparison: SVM, linear discriminant analysis, decision tree, random forest and k-nearest neighbour with k in {1,3,5,7}. KNN with k=1 - effectively a nearest-neighbour lookup, the highest-variance choice available - gave the best result, which on 43 participants with four selected features warrants caution the paper does not express.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted distributional features: Shannon entropy over a 101-bin normalised histogram and the central 95% range, computed for amplitude, velocity and acceleration and aggregated across three trials by minimum, median and maximum. This is a distribution-shape representation rather than the point-statistic representation (peak velocity, duration, jerk) used by other motor studies in the corpus, and is well matched to the construct of restrictedness.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for the best model of each of the five classifiers, plus a confusion matrix for the winning model and a plot of accuracy against number of features for all classifiers - which usefully exposes how performance varies with model size. Headline: 88.37% accuracy, AUC 0.8815. Sensitivity and specificity values (91.3% and 85%) are reported but with their labels swapped between the abstract and the discussion, leaving the assignment formally ambiguous. No confidence intervals or significance testing against chance.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Two-stage and reasonably transparent: independent t-tests identify nine discriminative features from 18, and forward feature selection then builds up the model incrementally, with the accuracy-versus-feature-count curve published for all five classifiers. The substantive interpretation is developed - three of four selected features derive from the velocity distribution, connected to prior work showing velocity distributions characterise subtle individual motor differences, and greater maximal amplitude range in ASD is linked to reported macrographia and fine motor control deficits. However the direction of the velocity entropy and range differences is never stated, so the central claim that autistic children are more restricted is not directly evidenced for the features that matter most.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Leave-one-out cross-validation is applied uniformly across all five classifiers, and the comparison across classifiers and feature counts is systematic. But the two selection stages are not nested: the t-test screen used the full labelled dataset, and forward feature selection optimised the same accuracy metric that is then reported, so the headline is a maximum over a search rather than an unbiased estimate - the same failure mode that Vabalas et al. (2019) in this corpus identify and correct. There is no external or independent validation, no permutation or significance testing, no class-imbalance handling (20 vs 23 is near-balanced), and no deployment analysis. Generalisability is addressed honestly in narrative terms - high-functioning only, unusable below age 2 - but not tested.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: Autism, entropy, kinematic feature, machine learning, restricted and repetitive behavior. Task vocabulary: 'restricted kinematic features', 'kinematic complexity', 'rapid diagnostic tool', 'automated and objective diagnosis', 'locked into a specific thought or behavior'. The entropy and complexity vocabulary is distinctive within the corpus's motor strand.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: IEEE Access - a broad open-access engineering and computing journal, neither autism-specific nor clinical.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2019. The paper characterises machine learning in autism as having concentrated on two things: shortening existing diagnostic instruments by removing redundant ADOS and ADI-R items (citing a claimed 100% accuracy from an 8-item ADOS subset, later above 95% on a larger sample), and classifying from neuroimaging, eye gaze and kinematic data - with only 'a handful' of kinematic studies, none of which targeted restricted and repetitive behaviour. Its closing argument that integrating genetic, neurological, psychological and kinematic features 'might pose a considerable challenge to the current diagnostic criteria of ASD' is one of the corpus's more ambitious claims about where the field is heading.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Automatic Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Acoustic and Text Features from Brief Natural Conversations
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Cho S; Liberman M; Ryant N; Cola M; Schultz RT; Parish-Morris J
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Speech and language
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Prescreening and triage: build an automatic ASD detection system from very brief, generic, natural conversations that could eventually be deployed in real-world settings such as doctors' offices and schools, explicitly motivated by long diagnostic waitlists
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study with a parallel human-rater benchmark
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session; approximately 5 minutes of unstructured conversation per child
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Unstructured 'get-to-know-you' conversation with a novel young adult confederate; no conversational prompts were provided to either speaker, who were simply instructed to get to know each other, covering generic topics such as pets, family, hobbies and sports
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Clinic/research - the Center for Autism Research, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Clinical Best Estimate process informed by ADOS-2 and adhering to DSM-5 criteria, used both to confirm ASD and to rule it out in the control group. Symptom characterisation additionally used ADOS-2 Calibrated Severity Scores and the Social Communication Questionnaire
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 35 (13 female)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: 13 female (the demographic table also prints '13 f., 12 m.', which sums to 25 rather than 35 - an internal inconsistency)
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported; all participants were native English speakers
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: ADOS-2 overall Calibrated Severity Score 6.57 vs 1.23 (t=13.78, p<0.001), social affect 6.83 vs 1.71, restricted and repetitive behaviour 6.54 vs 1.57, and SCQ lifetime 17.68 vs 2.69 (t=10.99, p<0.001) - full severity characterisation of both groups
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developing children in whom ASD was actively ruled out
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes, and rigorously - the same Clinical Best Estimate process with ADOS-2 was used to rule out ASD in controls, with ADOS-2 and SCQ scores reported
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 35 (11 female)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution_controls: 11 female (the table prints '11 f., 14 m.', again summing to 25)
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not formally matched but tested and non-significant (t=1.33, p=0.19)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Yes - matched on sex ratio by design and confirmed non-significant (chi-square=0.06, p=0.8)
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes - ASD actively ruled out by Clinical Best Estimate
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Audio and text: acoustic-phonetic features from the speech signal and lexical/discourse features from verbatim transcripts, extracted for both the child and the conversation partner
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A single 5-minute unstructured dyadic conversation, audio and video recorded, then transcribed verbatim with time alignment by a trained annotation team using a double-annotation plus senior-review protocol
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: A 'Biosensor' device placed between speakers with two opposed HD video cameras and four directional microphones; XTrans for transcription; sox for audio conversion; openSMILE with the ComParE13 configuration for acoustic features; base R, qdap and LIWC for text features; scikit-learn in Python for imputation, PCA and gradient boosting
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - newly collected conversational corpus, but not released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Highly sensitive - audio and video recordings of identifiable children in free conversation, plus verbatim transcripts of personal talk about family and hobbies. Ethics reporting is complete: the study was conducted with approval from and oversight by the Institutional Review Board of the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, parents provided written informed consent for their minor children, and children provided verbal assent. No anonymization or data-protection procedure for the recordings is separately described
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted acoustic functionals and handcrafted lexical/discourse features, computed separately for both interlocutors
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 352 acoustic features (44 openSMILE ComParE13 low-level descriptors including voicing probability, pitch, jitter local and DDP, shimmer, harmonic-to-noise ratio, RMS energy, MFCC 1-14 and zero crossing rate, plus their first-order deltas, x 2 speakers x 4 functionals: mean, median, standard deviation, interquartile range) and 272 text features (136 per speaker across six groups: pause/overlap metrics, segment/turn metrics, speaking rate and word complexity, LIWC categories, lexical entropy and diversity, and parts of speech, plus conversation-level formality and polarity). Total 624
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: openSMILE (ComParE13 configuration, 25 ms window, 10 ms step); LIWC; qdap; base R; a custom script by one author; scikit-learn
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Per-fold univariate Pearson correlation with diagnostic status (p<0.025) computed inside each cross-validation fold, with selection frequency across the 70 folds reported; supplemented by post-hoc linear regression on individual features
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: 17 participant features and 16 confederate features selected in more than half of folds. Participant: interquartile range and standard deviation of voicing probability, median HNR-delta, IQR of RMS-delta, median of 6th and 7th MFCC-delta, IQR of HNR, plus text features overlap percent, see-related words, perception-related words, relative words and death-related words. Confederate: all four functionals of jitter DDP, three functionals of jitter local, IQR of F0-delta, median HNR-delta and MFCC-delta measures - notably the confederate's voice quality features were among the most consistently selected of all
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reported for several features with statistics: median HNR-delta was higher in ASD children (t=3.25, p=0.002) and higher in confederates when talking to ASD children than to controls (t=2.72, p=0.008); standard deviation of participants' voicing probability (t=2.92, p=0.004) and IQR of F0-delta (t=3.09, p=0.003) were lower in ASD; and all functionals of confederate jitter were lower when talking to ASD children (median jitter t=2.7, p=0.009)
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification with dimensionality reduction
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Gradient Boosting Classifier (scikit-learn), preceded by per-fold univariate correlation filtering and Principal Component Analysis retaining the first 10 components
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-out cross-validation over 70 children, with feature selection performed inside each fold - the paper states that features were selected using univariate Pearson correlation 'within each cross-validation fold', selecting 24-39 features per fold, and that the top 10 principal components were retained 'within each CV fold'. This is correctly nested selection
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 reported per class and averaged, plus a ROC curve with AUC, and the same metric set computed for human raters for direct comparison
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Overall accuracy 75.71%, AUC 75.43%. Per class: TD accuracy 85.71% (30/35), ASD accuracy 65.71% (23/35); ASD precision 0.82, recall 0.66, F1 0.73; TD precision 0.71, recall 0.86, F1 0.78. Human raters on a matched 12-conversation subset: mean accuracy 83.33% (Student A 91.7%, Student B 75%), ASD accuracy 67%, TD accuracy 100%
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Five minutes of unstructured conversation with a naive partner supported ASD classification at 75.71% accuracy (AUC 0.754), approaching but not matching two briefly-trained undergraduate raters who reached 83.33% on a matched subset. Both the model and the humans were markedly better at identifying typically developing children than autistic ones, which the authors attribute to phenotypic heterogeneity - and notably both students misclassified the same autistic child. A central finding is that features of the conversation partner's speech, particularly jitter and harmonic-to-noise measures, were among the most consistently selected predictors, meaning the confederate's voice changed measurably depending on who they were talking to. Adding age, sex or IQ did not help and IQ actively hurt, which the authors correctly attribute to the groups already being matched on those variables.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Child: higher median HNR-delta, lower voicing-probability variability, lower IQR of F0-delta (reduced pitch dynamism). Confederate: higher median HNR-delta and lower jitter across all functionals when speaking to an autistic child
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Engineer features that directly measure semantic and pragmatic appropriateness of conversation at a turn-by-turn level, since human raters attended to topicality, relevance, appropriateness and conversational flow that the current feature set captured only indirectly; increase dataset size to improve performance and enable real-world application; and test whether longer conversations (10 minutes rather than 5) and designated topics improve performance
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Among the strongest studies in the corpus on nearly every dimension that matters. The reference standard is the best encountered - Clinical Best Estimate informed by ADOS-2 under DSM-5, applied to both confirm cases and rule out controls, with ADOS-2 Calibrated Severity Scores and SCQ reported for both groups. Groups are matched on full-scale, verbal and non-verbal IQ and on sex ratio with all comparisons tested and reported. Feature selection and PCA are explicitly nested inside the cross-validation folds, avoiding the leakage that affects most of this corpus. The human-rater benchmark is a genuinely valuable addition that almost no other study attempts, and it establishes that the task is hard for people too, giving the 75.71% a meaningful ceiling to be read against. The authors also state plainly that the approach 'is not yet valuable as a method for diagnosing ASD, which still needs to be diagnosed by expert clinicians'. Two real caveats: the demographic table's sex counts sum to 25 rather than 35 in both groups, an evident transcription error that leaves the exact sex distribution ambiguous; and the confederate-feature finding, while fascinating, means part of the classifier's signal is an interlocutor's reaction to the child rather than the child's own behaviour, which complicates any claim about autistic speech per se and would not transfer to a self-administered screening tool.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 35: children with ASD and typically developing children, plus 22 young adult confederates (19 female) who served as conversation partners and whose speech was also analysed. The confederates are effectively a third participant group whose data enter the model - an unusual design in this corpus. No other-diagnosis comparison group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'children on the autism spectrum', 'ASD children', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'TDC', and one appearance of 'ASD patients' in the discussion. Predominantly person-first with the notable use of 'children on the autism spectrum' in the introduction, and 'typically developing' rather than 'normal' throughout.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=35, mean age 11.42 +/- 2.51, full-scale IQ 105.51, verbal IQ 104.97, non-verbal IQ 104.63. TD n=35, mean age 10.57 +/- 2.82, full-scale IQ 107.14, verbal IQ 105.83, non-verbal IQ 105.97. Age difference non-significant (t=1.33, p=0.19); IQ differences non-significant on all three measures (p=0.6, 0.78, 0.68); sex ratio matched by design and non-significant (chi-square=0.06, p=0.8). This is among the best-matched samples in the corpus - matched and tested on full-scale, verbal and non-verbal IQ as well as sex. The one defect is that the printed sex counts ('13 f., 12 m.' and '11 f., 14 m.') sum to 25 rather than the stated 35 per group.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: The strongest reference standard in the corpus: diagnoses were confirmed for the ASD group and ruled out for the TD group using the Clinical Best Estimate process informed by ADOS-2 and adhering to DSM-5 criteria. Crucially the same rigorous process was applied to controls, not just cases - the inverse of the common corpus pattern where control screening is better specified than case ascertainment. Symptom severity was additionally characterised with ADOS-2 Calibrated Severity Scores and the Social Communication Questionnaire for both groups.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Full-scale, verbal and non-verbal IQ measured with the WASI-II for both groups and used as matching variables with all comparisons tested. ADOS-2 Calibrated Severity Scores (overall, social affect, restricted and repetitive behaviour) and SCQ lifetime scores reported for both groups with group comparisons. All participants were native English speakers. Comorbid conditions are not described.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: automatic ASD prescreening and triage from brief natural conversation, explicitly aimed at community settings such as doctors' offices and schools and motivated by diagnostic waitlists. Main findings: 75.71% accuracy, AUC 0.754; markedly better at identifying TD (85.71%) than ASD (65.71%) children; human raters reached 83.33% on a matched subset, so the model approaches but does not match human performance; confederate speech features were among the most consistently predictive; and adding age, sex or IQ did not improve and IQ worsened performance because the groups were already matched on them.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Clinic/research setting at a hospital autism centre. Newly collected data; the design deliberately departs from the field's reliance on ADOS-derived or highly structured speech samples in favour of naturalistic conversation with a non-expert partner.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A 5-minute unstructured 'get-to-know-you' conversation with a novel young adult confederate blind to diagnostic status and assigned by availability. No conversational prompts were given to either speaker. Recordings were made with a device placed between the speakers carrying two opposed HD cameras and four directional microphones.
