Transcription used a rigorous protocol: two junior annotators (one segmenting pause groups, one transcribing words) plus a senior annotator with at least six months' experience reviewing and correcting every file, with all annotators having completed at least 10 hours of Quick Transcription training modified for clinical ASD interviews and having achieved over 90% agreement with a gold-standard transcript before independent work.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single 5-minute conversation per child with no follow-up. The data are highly sensitive - audio and video of identifiable children in unscripted personal conversation, plus verbatim transcripts. Ethics reporting is complete and among the best in the corpus: IRB approval and oversight from the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, written parental informed consent, and verbal assent from the children themselves. No anonymization or retention procedure for the recordings is described.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: a 'Biosensor' recording device placed on a table between the two speakers, with two HD video cameras facing opposite directions to capture both participants simultaneously and four embedded directional microphones. Software: sox for format conversion; openSMILE with the ComParE13 configuration (25 ms window, 10 ms step) for acoustic low-level descriptors; XTrans for time-aligned orthographic transcription; base R, qdap and LIWC plus a custom author script for text features; scikit-learn (SimpleImputer, PCA, GradientBoostingClassifier) in Python.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No data availability statement and no code release, which is a real gap for a corpus this valuable. Method reporting is otherwise strong: the openSMILE configuration and window/step sizes, the full list of 44 low-level descriptors, the exact feature arithmetic (44 x 2 speakers x 4 functionals = 352), the six text-feature groups totalling 272, the voiceless-frame exclusion rule, the pitch normalisation formula with the 5th-percentile baseline, the correlation threshold (p<0.025), the number of components retained (10), the classifier, the libraries, and the annotation training and reliability criteria are all specified. The pipeline is re-implementable; the conversations are not accessible.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors: performance is limited by 5-minute samples and generic topics compared with ADOS evaluations designed to elicit ASD-like features; human raters outperformed the model, which the authors read as evidence that the feature set fails to capture topicality, relevance, appropriateness and conversational flow at a turn-by-turn level; ASD is harder to predict than TD because of phenotypic heterogeneity; and the approach 'is not yet valuable as a method for diagnosing ASD, which still needs to be diagnosed by expert clinicians'. Identifiable in review: the demographic table's sex counts sum to 25 rather than 35 in both groups; the confederate features that are among the most consistently selected mean part of the signal is an interlocutor's response to the child rather than the child's own behaviour, which limits transfer to any self-administered or partner-free screening context; all participants were native English speakers at a single site, with no ethnicity or socioeconomic data; confederates were 19 of 22 female, so partner-sex variation is minimal; and n=70 makes 75.71% equal to 53 of 70 children.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Engineer features that directly capture semantic and pragmatic appropriateness turn by turn, since that is what human raters used and the model lacked; enlarge the dataset to improve performance and enable real-world deployment; and test whether longer conversations (10 rather than 5 minutes) and designated topics improve performance. All three are grounded in specific observed shortfalls rather than generic.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Speech and language jointly: acoustic-phonetic properties (voicing probability, pitch, jitter, shimmer, HNR, energy, MFCCs, zero-crossing rate and their deltas) and lexical/discourse properties (pause and overlap metrics, turn metrics, speaking rate, word complexity, LIWC psycholinguistic categories, lexical entropy and diversity, parts of speech, formality, polarity). Distinctively, all of these are computed for both the child and the adult conversation partner.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Two-way fusion. Across modality: 352 acoustic and 272 text features are concatenated into a single 624-dimensional vector, then reduced by correlation filtering and PCA - so acoustic and lexical information are combined at feature level. Across speaker: features from the child and the confederate are both included, and the results show confederate features were selected in all 70 folds for several jitter and HNR measures, making interlocutor behaviour an explicit part of the model. Demographic and clinical variables were tested as additional inputs and reported as unhelpful (age and sex) or harmful (IQ), which the authors correctly attribute to prior matching - a negative fusion result reported rather than omitted.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning: a Gradient Boosting Classifier from scikit-learn. Principal Component Analysis is used unsupervised for dimensionality reduction. No comparison against alternative classifiers, which removes best-of-many selection optimism but also leaves the algorithm choice unjustified empirically.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted features at two levels: frame-level acoustic descriptors summarised per speaker per conversation by four statistical functionals, and text-derived lexical, syntactic and discourse counts. These are then projected onto 10 principal components for modelling, so the classifier operates on a learned low-dimensional linear subspace of handcrafted features rather than on the features directly.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 per class and averaged, plus a ROC curve with AUC - and, unusually, the identical metric set computed for human raters so the two can be read side by side. Headline: 75.71% accuracy, AUC 75.43%, with the per-class asymmetry (TD 85.71%, ASD 65.71%) reported prominently rather than buried in an average. No confidence intervals.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Well developed. Selection frequency across the 70 folds is reported per feature, distinguishing features chosen in all folds from those chosen occasionally, which is a more informative importance measure than a single ranking. Post-hoc linear regressions give directions and significance for key features. The substantive findings are specific: autistic children showed higher median HNR-delta, lower voicing-probability variability and reduced pitch dynamism (lower IQR of F0-delta); and confederates showed higher HNR-delta and lower jitter when talking to autistic children. The paper also collects qualitative human-rater justifications - flat intonation, long response latency, brief responses, frequent 'I don't know', topic changes, few follow-up questions - and uses them to diagnose what the automatic feature set is missing.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Feature selection is explicitly nested: univariate correlation filtering is performed 'within each cross-validation fold' (selecting 24-39 features per fold, 60 distinct features overall) and PCA is applied 'within each CV fold', with leave-one-out cross-validation over 70 children. This is the correct structure and avoids the selection leakage that affects most of the corpus. Robustness is further probed by testing whether demographic and IQ variables improve the model - they do not - which is a form of confound check. What is absent: external or independent validation, any held-out site, calibration analysis, and any real-world deployment test despite community prescreening being the stated goal. The human-rater comparison functions as an informal ceiling estimate rather than a validation.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: clinical speech, machine learning, Autism Spectrum Disorder. Task vocabulary: 'automatic detection system', 'prescreening and triage', 'brief, generic, and natural conversations', 'naive conversation partners (confederates)', 'real-world settings such as doctor's offices and schools'. The prescreening-and-triage framing, explicitly distinguished from diagnosis, is more careful than most of the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: INTERSPEECH 2019 (Graz) - a speech science and technology venue, not an autism or clinical journal, though the author list spans a linguistic data consortium, a hospital autism centre and university paediatrics and psychiatry departments.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2019. The paper characterises the speech-and-autism literature as drawing overwhelmingly on either highly structured elicitation (reading sentences or word lists) or semi-structured clinical interviews with an autism expert, chiefly ADOS evaluations, and argues these 'produce results that may not generalize to the everyday conversations that impact the lives of children on the autism spectrum'. It cites specific prior accuracies for calibration - roughly 74% from pitch features on 146 children, roughly 69% from speech rate and rhythm on 69 children - and identifies interlocutor speech features as an emerging and underused signal, noting prior findings that psychologists' speech predicted children's symptom severity better than the children's own features. This move from clinical-elicitation corpora toward naturalistic interaction is one of the clearest trend statements in the corpus.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Classifying Individuals with ASD Through Facial Emotion Recognition and Eye-Tracking
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Jiang M; Francis SM; Srishyla D; Conelea C; Zhao Q; Jacob S
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye-tracking and gaze
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Classification and mechanism: test whether eye movements combined with task performance in facial emotion recognition can identify individuals with ASD, and interpret the resulting feature importance to understand social and attentional differences
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study with a preceding statistical analysis of group differences
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session; the entire protocol (two practice trials and twelve test trials) lasted approximately 10 minutes, with individual videos of 19-33 seconds (mean 23.33 +/- 3.75 s)
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Human children, adolescents and young adults (ages 8-34)
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Dynamic Affect Recognition Evaluation (DARE): watch a face video transitioning slowly from neutral into one of six emotions (anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise), press the spacebar as soon as the emotion is recognised, then select the emotion from six labels
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Clinic and community - recruitment from University of Minnesota clinics, university websites, local and regional registries, local advertising, and the 2015 Minnesota State Fair; testing on two different display setups depending on collection location
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Diagnosed based on testing with standardized instruments, review of diagnostic history and prior evaluations, and DSM criteria confirmed by clinical research staff. The specific instruments are not named, but the multi-source ascertainment (standardised testing plus history review plus DSM confirmation) is described
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 23 recruited (20 male); data from 5 subjects with ASD excluded for failure to capture eye movements in at least six trials
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported for the ASD group; controls were required to have no psychiatric history, developmental delay or previous special education
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported; IQ score range 58-137 is given for the ASD group but no mean, SD or use in analysis
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developing controls with no psychiatric history, developmental delay or special education history
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes - by explicit exclusion of psychiatric history, developmental delay and prior special education
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 35 (25 male)
data_charting_rubrics.age_range_controls: 8-34 years - substantially wider than the ASD range of 8-17
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not matched by design; the group difference was tested and found non-significant (t-test p=0.241), though control ages extend to 34 while no autistic participant was older than 17
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not matched by design; the difference in sex frequency was tested and found non-significant (p=0.171), though proportions differ (87% vs 71% male)
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes - screened by exclusion criteria
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye movements (fixation location, timing, duration, frequency, saccade amplitude), behavioural task performance (response time and accuracy), and deep visual features of the fixated face regions
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Two practice trials with two response choices followed by twelve test trials with six choices; stimuli were Cohn-Kanade Action Unit-Coded facial expression sequences rendered as silent videos at 640x480, uniformly scaled to screen height, viewed at approximately 65 cm
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Tobii Pro TX300 (300 Hz) for all ASD subjects and six controls, Tobii X2-60 (60 Hz) for the remaining controls, with Tobii Studio 3.3.2; 19-inch (1680x1050) and 27-inch (1920x1080) displays depending on collection site; 9-point calibration with error below 0.5 degrees for all subjects; OpenFace deep network for face features; Viola-Jones face detector; scikit-learn for random forests
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - newly collected, but not released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze and behavioural data are low in identifiability; face stimuli come from a published database rather than participants. All subjects were recruited with the approval of the University of Minnesota Institutional Review Board. No participant consent statement or anonymization procedure is separately described, and no competing-interests declaration appears
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Three families combined: handcrafted task-performance features, handcrafted gaze features, and learned deep face-region embeddings
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Task (2-dim per trial): response time and relative response time. Gaze (6-dim per fixation): horizontal and vertical fixation location, fixation time, fixation frequency, fixation duration, saccade amplitude. Face (640-dim per fixation): activations from the fifth Inception block (inception-4a) of a pre-trained OpenFace network applied to the Viola-Jones-detected face region of the video frame at the fixation's time, scaled to 96x96
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: OpenFace (37-layer convolutional network, 8 Inception blocks, pre-trained on LFW and used without fine-tuning); Viola-Jones face detector; Tobii Studio; scikit-learn
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Random forest feature importance averaged across all cross-validation runs and normalised to the maximum; face-feature channels additionally visualised by averaging network activations across all video frames and overlaying them on an average face
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Coarse temporal features dominated: relative response time, fixation time, fixation frequency and response time ranked highest, while fine-grained fixation statistics (horizontal and vertical location, fixation duration, saccade amplitude) contributed less. Individual face-feature channels contributed weakly but their visualisations localised to distinct facial regions - forehead, eyes, cheeks, nose and ears
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reported in detail. The ASD group spent longer observing stimuli (14.37 vs 11.43 s, p<0.001; relative 0.61 vs 0.49, p<0.001), made more fixations (16.15 vs 14.41, p=0.002) at lower frequency (1.06 vs 1.28 Hz, p<0.001) with longer durations (0.31 vs 0.25 s, p<0.001) and larger saccade amplitudes (2.54 vs 2.30 degrees, p=0.016). Recognition accuracy did not differ (77.89% vs 77.14%, p=0.841). Pixel-wise fixation density comparison showed controls more attracted to eyes and mouth while ASD subjects fixated more on forehead, hair, ears, chin and other regions not associated with emotion recognition
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification (tree ensemble) over deep and handcrafted features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Random forest with bootstrap sampling and majority voting, trained with balanced class weights to offset the unequal group sizes; fixation-level scores averaged (soft voting) to produce trial-level and subject-level decisions. OpenFace is used upstream as a frozen feature extractor
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, repeated 60 times so each subject is tested once. Fixation-level predictions are aggregated by averaging to trial and subject level. Class imbalance handled by balanced class weights in training
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: AUC, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, reported separately for each feature family and their combination, at each of three units of analysis (fixation, trial, subject)
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Subject level with combined features: AUC 0.935, accuracy 86.2%, sensitivity 91.3%, specificity 82.9%. Subject level by family: task alone AUC 0.789 / accuracy 81.0% but sensitivity only 56.5%; gaze alone AUC 0.904 / 84.5%; face alone AUC 0.917 / 84.5%. Trial level combined: AUC 0.824, accuracy 75.6%. Fixation level combined: AUC 0.743, accuracy 72.5%. Note the paper's equations define sensitivity using TN and specificity using TP, which is inverted relative to convention
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Individuals with ASD recognised facial emotions just as accurately as controls but took significantly longer and moved their eyes differently - fewer, longer fixations with larger saccades, and more fixations on regions irrelevant to emotion (forehead, hair, ears, chin) rather than eyes and mouth. Combining task performance, gaze dynamics and deep features of the fixated face regions classified subjects at 86.2% accuracy and AUC 0.935, with each feature family contributing complementary information: task features alone had high specificity but very low sensitivity (56.5%), which rose to 91.3% once gaze and face features were added. Feature-importance analysis showed coarse temporal measures mattered most, and the accuracy-versus-response-time dissociation is the study's clearest substantive finding.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Longer and relatively longer response times; fewer fixations per second but of longer duration; larger saccade amplitudes; and fixation density displaced from eyes and mouth toward forehead, hair, ears and chin
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Extend to more subjects across a wider range of developmental ages; develop a multimodal approach combining demographic information, autonomic nervous system data, functional MRI and other methodologies; and apply the same eye-tracking and machine-learning paradigm to differentiate schizophrenia or ADHD, which also show altered gaze patterns
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: One of the better-designed gaze studies in the corpus. Strengths: statistical group comparison precedes and motivates the classification rather than being replaced by it; three feature families are ablated separately and at three units of analysis, so the complementarity claim is evidenced rather than asserted; leave-one-subject-out with balanced class weights; feature importance is computed from the model and the deep face-feature channels are visualised anatomically; and the accuracy-versus-response-time dissociation is a genuinely informative negative result. Concerns: two different eye trackers at different sampling rates (300 Hz and 60 Hz) were used, and crucially the assignment is confounded with group - all ASD subjects and only six controls used the TX300, while the remaining 29 controls used the X2-60. The authors assert that the rate difference 'did not factor into the analysis', but fixation frequency, duration and saccade amplitude are precisely the quantities most sensitive to sampling rate, and these are among the most important features in the model. That is a serious unaddressed confound. Additionally, five ASD subjects were excluded for eye-tracking failure while no controls were, which may itself be group-related; control ages extend to 34 against an ASD maximum of 17 despite a non-significant test; and IQ is reported only as a range (58-137) for the ASD group with no control values, so IQ is uncontrolled.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: 23 individuals with ASD (5 later excluded for eye-tracking failure) and 35 typically developing controls, total 58 recruited. Group sizes, sexes and ages are reported, and control status is defined by explicit exclusions. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the discussion proposes extending the paradigm to schizophrenia and ADHD.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder', 'individuals with ASD', 'subjects with ASD', 'people with ASD', 'the ASD group', 'typically developing (TD) controls', 'patients with schizophrenia or ADHD'. Consistently person-first, with 'typically developing' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy' for the comparison group - and notably the paper frames its findings as revealing 'social and attentional deficits', a deficit framing, while simultaneously reporting that emotion recognition accuracy was unimpaired.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=23 (20 male, 87%), age 12.74 +/- 2.45 years, range 8-17, IQ range 58-137. TD n=35 (25 male, 71%), age 14.11 +/- 5.09 years, range 8-34. Neither age nor sex was matched by design, but both differences were tested and found non-significant (p=0.241 and p=0.171). The control age range nonetheless extends to 34 while no autistic participant exceeded 17, so the groups differ substantially in composition even though means do not differ significantly - the control SD is more than double the ASD SD. IQ is given only as a range for the ASD group with no control values and no use as a covariate.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Diagnosis based on testing with standardized instruments, review of diagnostic history and prior evaluations, and DSM criteria confirmed by clinical research staff - a multi-source ascertainment described in more procedural detail than most corpus studies, though the specific instruments are not named. Control status established by requiring no psychiatric history, no developmental delay and no previous special education.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: IQ score range (58-137) reported for the ASD group only, with no mean, SD or control comparison, and not used as a covariate despite the authors' own introduction noting that eye-tracking results 'can be impacted by sample size, age, developmental level and IQ'. No language or adaptive measures. Comorbidities not described for the ASD group; controls screened by exclusion of psychiatric history, developmental delay and special education.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: classify ASD from combined task performance and eye movements during facial emotion recognition, and interpret the features to understand social and attentional differences. Main findings: recognition accuracy did not differ between groups (77.89% vs 77.14%, p=0.841) but response time and every eye-movement measure did; combined features gave subject-level AUC 0.935, accuracy 86.2%, sensitivity 91.3%, specificity 82.9%; task features alone had only 56.5% sensitivity, rising to 91.3% when gaze and face features were added.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Mixed clinic and community setting - recruitment spanned university clinics, websites, registries, local advertising and the 2015 Minnesota State Fair, with testing at more than one location using different displays and different eye trackers. Newly collected data; the face stimuli come from the existing Cohn-Kanade database.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: The Dynamic Affect Recognition Evaluation task: silent videos of a face transitioning slowly from neutral into one of six emotions, with the participant pressing the spacebar upon recognition and then selecting the emotion from six labels. Two practice trials (two choices) preceded twelve test trials (six choices), with practice videos not reused. Videos lasted 19-33 seconds. The design yields both a behavioural measure (how quickly recognition occurs, and whether it is correct) and a gaze measure over the same stimulus - which is what enables the accuracy-versus-latency dissociation.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single ~10-minute session with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates and button-press latencies over third-party stimulus faces, so participant-identifiable content is minimal. Institutional Review Board approval from the University of Minnesota is reported for all recruitment. No participant or parental consent statement, no anonymization procedure and no competing-interests declaration appear.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: two Tobii Pro eye trackers - the TX300 at 300 Hz for all ASD subjects and six controls, and the X2-60 at 60 Hz for the remaining controls - with Tobii Studio 3.3.2; two display configurations (19-inch 1680x1050 and 27-inch 1920x1080) depending on collection site; viewing distance approximately 65 cm (camera range 50-70 cm); 9-point calibration with error below 0.5 degrees for every subject. Software: OpenFace pre-trained on LFW for face features, Viola-Jones for face detection, scikit-learn for random forests.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No data availability statement and no code release. Method reporting is otherwise detailed: eye tracker models and sampling rates, calibration procedure and error tolerance, display specifications, viewing distance, stimulus source and resolution, trial counts, feature definitions and dimensionalities, the exact OpenFace layer used (inception-4a, 640 channels at 6x6), the Gaussian kernel for fixation density maps (sigma=15 pixels), balanced class weighting, and the cross-validation scheme. The pipeline is re-implementable in principle; the data are not accessible.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: No dedicated limitations section. The introduction acknowledges at field level that eye-tracking results 'can be impacted by sample size, age, developmental level and IQ, variation in stimuli, and task effort and objective', but the study does not then control for these. Identifiable in review: the two eye trackers are confounded with group - all ASD subjects used the 300 Hz TX300 while 29 of 35 controls used the 60 Hz X2-60 - and the most important model features (fixation frequency, fixation duration, fixation time, saccade amplitude) are exactly the measures a fivefold sampling-rate difference would bias, yet the authors dismiss this in one sentence; five ASD subjects were excluded for eye-tracking capture failure with no controls excluded, a group-dependent attrition that could itself reflect the behaviour being measured; control ages extend to 34 versus an ASD maximum of 17, with a control SD more than double the ASD SD; IQ is reported only as an ASD range and never controlled; two display sizes were used; and the reported equations define sensitivity in terms of TN and specificity in terms of TP, inverting the standard definitions.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Extend to more subjects across a wider span of developmental ages; build a multimodal classifier incorporating demographic information, autonomic nervous system measures, functional MRI and other methodologies; and apply the same paradigm to schizophrenia and ADHD, which also show altered gaze patterns in visual tasks - a differential-diagnosis direction that addresses the specificity question left open by ASD-versus-TD designs.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Three streams: gaze (fixation location, timing, duration, frequency, saccade amplitude), behavioural task performance (response latency and recognition accuracy), and the visual content of what was fixated (deep embeddings of the face region at each fixation). The third is unusual - most corpus gaze studies use predefined anatomical areas of interest, whereas here the stimulus content at the point of gaze is encoded by a deep network without any manual region annotation.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Feature-level fusion across the three families into a single per-fixation vector, and the contribution of each is ablated separately at fixation, trial and subject level - so the complementarity claim is directly evidenced. The clearest demonstration is that task features alone reach 81.0% subject-level accuracy but only 56.5% sensitivity, while adding gaze and face features raises sensitivity to 91.3% at similar accuracy. Predictions are additionally fused across observations by soft voting from fixations to trials to subjects, with accuracy rising monotonically (72.5% to 75.6% to 86.2%) as the aggregation unit widens.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning: random forest with bootstrap sampling, majority voting and balanced class weights. A pre-trained deep convolutional network (OpenFace, 37 layers in 8 Inception blocks) is used upstream as a frozen feature extractor without fine-tuning, on the stated grounds that the LFW training set is sufficiently general.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Hybrid representation: handcrafted scalar features for task performance and gaze dynamics, combined with a 640-dimensional learned embedding of the fixated face region taken from an intermediate convolutional layer. This is a distinctive design in the corpus - it replaces manually annotated areas of interest with a learned encoding of stimulus content at the point of gaze, which the authors explicitly present as avoiding reliance on annotated AOIs.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: AUC, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, reported for every feature family at every unit of analysis - a 3x4 results table that is among the most complete in the corpus and permits direct assessment of what each component contributes. Headline subject-level combined: AUC 0.935, accuracy 86.2%, sensitivity 91.3%, specificity 82.9%. No confidence intervals or confusion matrices. The printed formulas define sensitivity as TN/(TN+FP) and specificity as TP/(TP+FN), which reverses the conventional definitions and is presumably a transcription error, though it leaves the labelling of the reported values formally ambiguous.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Well developed and multi-layered. Random-forest importance values are averaged across all cross-validation runs and normalised, showing that coarse temporal measures (relative response time, fixation time, fixation frequency, response time) dominate while fine-grained spatial fixation statistics matter less. Face-feature channels are visualised by averaging network activations across frames and overlaying them on an average face, revealing that the informative channels correspond to distinct anatomical regions (forehead, eyes, cheeks, nose, ears). Separately, pixel-wise fixation density maps with t-tests localise where the groups differ - controls more on eyes and mouth, ASD subjects more on forehead, hair, ears and chin. This combination of model-derived importance, activation visualisation and independent statistical mapping is the most thorough interpretability treatment charted so far.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation repeated so each of the subjects is tested once, with balanced class weights addressing the 23-versus-35 imbalance, and results reported at three aggregation levels so the effect of the decision unit is visible rather than hidden. What is absent: external or independent validation, any held-out site despite multi-site collection, and any analysis of the apparatus confound. Most seriously, generalisability is undermined rather than tested by the design - the eye tracker is confounded with diagnostic group, and the model's most important features are sampling-rate-sensitive. No calibration analysis, no real-time or deployment claim beyond noting efficiency advantages over standardized diagnostic scales.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No formal keyword list in the extracted text. Vocabulary: 'atypical scanning patterns', 'atypical visual attention', 'social and attentional deficits', 'facial emotion recognition', 'Dynamic Affect Recognition Evaluation', 'comparable with the standardized diagnostic scales', 'efficiency and objectiveness'. The explicit benchmarking of classifier performance against standardised diagnostic scales is a distinctive framing.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: The 41st Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC) 2019 - a biomedical engineering venue, technology-focused but clinically adjacent.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2019. The paper surveys the eye-tracking-plus-machine-learning literature specifically, citing SVM classification of children from face-recognition scanpaths, deep-learning extraction of fixated-region features achieving 92% in adults, and gaze-plus-demographics classification across ASD risk levels. Its critical observation is that 'these studies only considered the eye-tracking data, mainly what was looked at, without jointly taking into account the task performance', which it attributes to behavioural tasks being 'general but not specific enough' - identifying the integration of task performance with gaze as the field's next step. It also cites a systematic review noting that eye-tracking results have varied across studies and are sensitive to sample size, age, developmental level, IQ and stimulus variation.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Detecting Developmental Delay and Autism Through Machine
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Tariq Q; Fleming SL; Schwartz JN; Dunlap K; Corbin C; Washington P; Kalantarian H; Khan NZ; Darmstadt GL; Wall DP
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder, speech and language conditions, and typical development
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Video-based behavioural rating
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Cross-cultural scaling of remote screening: test whether a video-based machine-learning pipeline validated on US children generalises to Bangladeshi children, extend it to other developmental delays beyond autism, and improve performance through adaptive aggregation of crowdsourced labels - explicitly aimed at low-resource settings where ADOS and ADI-R are unaffordable
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional development and validation study with a three-class design and stacked classification layers
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Brief parent-submitted videos averaging 3 minutes 11 seconds (SD 1 minute 57 seconds), recorded during clinical evaluation visits; each rater scored videos in under approximately 6 minutes based on the authors' prior work
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Human children aged 18 months to 4 years
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Unstructured short home videos required to capture the child's face and hands, involve social interaction or attempts at it, and involve interaction between the child and a toy or object; non-expert raters then answered 31 multiple-choice questions corresponding to behavioural features of autism
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Home video capture by parents on mobile phones, with recruitment and clinical evaluation at the Child Development Center of the Bangladesh Institute of Child Health, Dhaka Shishu Children's Hospital; video rating performed remotely in the United States
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Bangladesh (data collection) and United States (rating and analysis)
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: ASD; speech and language conditions (receptive language delay, expressive language delay, both, or receptive and expressive language disorder)
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (Bangla version) administered to all children, followed by additional clinical evaluation by a developmental psychologist and a child health physician to diagnose ASD, SLC or TD. ADOS was administered to 28 of the 50 children with ASD; it could not be completed for the remaining 22 because families were unable to commit the required time, which the authors describe as a common problem in low-resource areas
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 55 ASD videos (50 children in the demographic table) plus 50 with speech and language conditions
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: ASD cohort 2.51 (0.70) years; SLC cohort 2.73 (0.51) years
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: ASD 36/50 male (72%); SLC 31/50 male (46%); full cohort 90/150 male (60%)
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Stunted growth reported: 32% stunting in ASD, 50% in SLC, with stunting information missing for the entire TD cohort. Preterm birth 10% ASD, 12% SLC, 0% TD
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: MCHAT total score 13.5 (3.04) for ASD, 2 (0) for TD, 0.08 (0.57) for SLC. ADOS subscores for the 28 assessed ASD children: social affect 11.57 (5.30), restricted and repetitive behaviour 3.46 (3.29), composite 5.14 (2.08)
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes - MCHAT plus clinical evaluation by a developmental psychologist and child health physician
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 54 videos (50 children in the demographic table)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution_controls: 23/50 male (62% as printed, though the count implies 46%)
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not formally matched; cohort means are close (2.40 to 2.73 years) but no comparability test is reported
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not matched - ASD 72% male versus SLC 46% male, a substantial imbalance across the two clinical groups being discriminated in the second classification layer
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes - clinically evaluated
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Video-derived behavioural ratings: 31 multiple-choice human judgements of autism-relevant behaviours per video per rater
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Parents submitted brief videos of their child; videos were quality-checked by trained clinical researchers at Stanford for video, sound and image quality, length and content, and against three explicit content criteria. Nine non-Bengali-speaking US-based raters with no clinical training scored the videos after a one-hour training session, with quality checks comparing a subset of 10 video scores against gold-standard scores agreed by two experienced clinical research coordinators
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Parent mobile phones for video capture; a secure HIPAA-compliant online rating website; Python 3.6.7 with pandas 0.23.4, scikit-learn 0.20.0, hyperopt 0.1.1, shap 0.24.0 and matplotlib 3.0.1
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - 159 videos of Bangladeshi children with parent consent, described as a resource whose expansion the authors advocate
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Highly sensitive - home videos of identifiable young children transmitted internationally from Bangladesh to the United States and viewed by nine non-clinical raters. Governance is reported: ethical clearance from the Bangladesh Institute of Child Health / Dhaka Shishu Children's Hospital and the Stanford University Institutional Review Board, consent obtained in Bengali, videos 'securely sent' to Stanford, and rating conducted on a HIPAA-compliant platform. No anonymization is possible for face video, and no retention or deletion policy is described
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Human-rated categorical behavioural features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 31 multiple-choice questions corresponding to behavioural features of autism, derived from the authors' prior US work. The source classifiers were originally trained on item-level ADOS (approximately 30 features) or ADI-R (over 90 parent-report items) medical records of US children
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Human raters via a web platform; no automated feature extraction from the video signal
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Approximate Shapley values computed with the shap package for all 159 videos in the second classification layer, exploiting the local accuracy property so that each video's predicted class probability decomposes into per-feature contributions; ensemble-level Shapley values derived by applying the same rater weights. Separately, features selected most often during elastic-net hyperparameter tuning were compared between the US and Bangladeshi models
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Both US and Bangladeshi models relied on sensory seeking and stereotyped interests and actions. US-trained models weighted social participation and stereotyped speech more heavily, while Bangladeshi-trained models relied more on eye contact - which the authors attribute to raters sharing a language with the US children but not the Bangladeshi ones, making non-language physical cues more important
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Shapley values capture both magnitude and the direction in which each feature pushes the predicted class probability, though specific directions are not enumerated in the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification with ensemble aggregation across annotators
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Random forest classifiers, one per rater, predicting the three-class label from that rater's annotations; combined by a softmax-weighted ensemble in which each rater's weight reflects their model's accuracy relative to a majority-vote baseline. Two stacked layers: layer one distinguishes typical from atypical (ASD or SLC), layer two distinguishes ASD from SLC among those classified atypical. Logistic regression with elastic net regularisation used separately for the cross-cultural transfer comparison, with balanced class weights
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Three-fold cross-validation with random train/test splits, 114 training videos and 45 test videos per fold, with demographics reported for both training and test sets. The source-classifier validation tested US-trained models on the Bangladeshi data across different train-test splits. For the cross-cultural comparison, models were trained on Bangladeshi data and tested on US data and vice versa, with a 20% holdout and cross-validated hyperparameter tuning on the training portion
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: AUC and sensitivity with standard deviations for both classification layers; AUC with standard deviation for the source-classifier transfer test
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Layer one (atypical versus typical among developmentally delayed children): AUC 76% (SD 3%), sensitivity 76% (SD 4%). Layer two (ASD versus other developmental delay): AUC 85% (SD 5%), sensitivity 76% (SD 6%). Previously published US-trained classifiers applied directly to Bangladeshi videos achieved a maximum AUC of 0.75 (SD 0.06), against the 92% accuracy (95% CI 88-97%) those same classifiers achieved on US videos
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A video-based machine-learning screening pipeline developed and validated on US children transferred to Bangladeshi children with substantially reduced but non-trivial performance - AUC 0.75 directly, improved to 0.85 for ASD versus other developmental delay after retraining with a novel rater-adaptive ensemble. The most consequential finding for the field is the size of the cross-cultural drop: the same classifiers achieving 92% accuracy on US videos reached AUC 0.75 on Bangladeshi videos. Nine non-Bengali-speaking, clinically untrained US raters were nonetheless able to score the videos usefully, suggesting shared language may not be necessary. Shapley analysis showed US models leaned on social participation and stereotyped speech while Bangladeshi models leaned on eye contact, which the authors attribute to raters' inability to evaluate language-based behaviours across the language barrier.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Sensory seeking and stereotyped interests and actions in both cultural contexts; eye contact specifically prominent in the Bangladeshi models
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Expand to larger samples across Bangladesh and other low-resource settings; train models on annotations from raters who share the linguistic and sociocultural background of the children, which the authors hypothesise would raise performance to US levels; build a large annotated video corpus enabling convolutional and recurrent networks to learn features directly from raw video and audio; and use location-tagged videos to develop epidemiological estimates of developmental disorder prevalence to inform policy
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The single most valuable contribution of this paper to the present review is its cross-cultural transfer result. Classifiers reported at 92% accuracy on US home videos fell to AUC 0.75 when applied unchanged to Bangladeshi videos - a direct empirical measurement of the generalisation gap that almost every other study in this corpus leaves untested, and one the authors report openly rather than burying. Their diagnosis of why is also careful and plausible: the source classifiers were trained on clinical scoresheets rather than video features, on US children whose behavioural nuances differ culturally, and for a two-class ASD-versus-typical problem rather than the three-class problem the Bangladeshi data pose. The rater-adaptive weighting scheme is a genuine methodological contribution, and Shapley attribution at both individual-rater and ensemble level is more interpretability than most of the corpus offers. Real limitations: the second-layer comparison (ASD versus SLC) is confounded by sex, with the ASD cohort 72% male against 46% in the SLC cohort, and by family income, with 96% of ASD families earning over 30,000 taka against 80% of SLC and 26% of TD families - so the classifier separating ASD from SLC could be exploiting demographic differences rather than behaviour. Stunting data are missing for the entire TD cohort. ADOS was completed for only 28 of 50 ASD children. The demographic table's gender percentages are internally inconsistent with their counts. And the senior author is founder of a company developing digital health solutions for paediatric care, disclosed properly as a conflict of interest but relevant to how the screening claims are framed.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Three groups: 55 videos of children with ASD, 50 with speech and language conditions, and 54 typically developing, totalling 159 videos (150 with complete demographic data). The inclusion of a non-autistic clinical comparison group - and the explicit design of a second classification layer to separate ASD from other developmental delay - directly addresses the specificity question that most ASD-versus-typical studies in this corpus leave open. SLC diagnoses are further broken down: 74% had both receptive and expressive language delay, 12% receptive and expressive language disorder, 10% expressive delay alone, 4% receptive delay alone.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with autism', 'children with ASD', 'the ASD cohort', 'children with an SLC', 'children with neurotypical development (TD)', 'children in need of therapeutic interventions', 'children with developmental delays'. Person-first throughout, and notably 'neurotypical development' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy'. The framing is service-access oriented - autism as a condition requiring diagnosis for intervention access - rather than deficit-focused.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=50 (36 male, 72%), mean age 2.51 (0.70) years. SLC n=50 (31 male, 46%), mean age 2.73 (0.51). TD n=50 (23 male, printed as 62% though the count implies 46%), mean age 2.40 (0.59). Ages are close across groups but no matching or comparability testing is reported. Sex is substantially imbalanced between the two clinical groups (72% versus 46% male), which is a material confound for the ASD-versus-SLC layer. The demographic table also shows a marked socioeconomic gradient: 96% of ASD families earned over 30,000 taka versus 80% of SLC and only 26% of TD families, and 100% of ASD and TD families were urban versus 78% of SLC. Very young sample (18 months to 4 years), directly relevant to early detection.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: MCHAT (Bangla version) administered to all children, followed by clinical evaluation by a developmental psychologist and a child health physician to assign ASD, SLC or TD. ADOS was administered to only 28 of 50 ASD children, with the reason given explicitly - families could not commit the time required, 'a common problem for families in low-resource areas'. This partial gold-standard coverage is disclosed transparently and is itself an informative observation about diagnostic feasibility in the target setting. MCHAT scores are reported per group (13.5 ASD, 2 TD, 0.08 SLC), giving some quantitative separation.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: MCHAT total scores and ADOS subscores (social affect, restricted and repetitive behaviour, composite) reported for the assessed subset. Additional health and social indicators are reported that no other corpus study collects: preterm birth, stunted growth, family income band, urban/semiurban/rural residence, and religion. Stunting information is missing for the entire TD cohort, which prevents its use as a covariate. No IQ, language or adaptive-functioning scores.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: scale a validated US video-based screening pipeline to another culture and to developmental delays beyond autism, for deployment in settings lacking clinical resources. Main findings: US-trained classifiers transferred to Bangladeshi videos at maximum AUC 0.75 (SD 0.06) against 92% accuracy on US videos; retrained stacked classifiers with rater-adaptive weighting achieved AUC 76% (SD 3%) and sensitivity 76% (SD 4%) for atypical versus typical, and AUC 85% (SD 5%) and sensitivity 76% (SD 6%) for ASD versus other developmental delay; and feature importance differed by culture, with eye contact more prominent for Bangladeshi videos and social participation and stereotyped speech more prominent for US videos.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Home setting for data capture - parents recorded brief videos on mobile phones - combined with clinical setting for diagnosis and recruitment at a Dhaka children's hospital, and remote US-based rating. Newly collected data. The design deliberately exploits Bangladesh's 95% mobile phone subscription rate as the deployment substrate.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Parents submitted brief unstructured videos, quality-screened against three content criteria: capturing the child's face and hands, involving social interaction or attempts at it, and involving interaction between the child and a toy or object. All 159 submitted videos passed quality inspection. Nine clinically untrained, non-Bengali-speaking US raters then answered 31 multiple-choice questions per video after a one-hour training session, with quality control comparing a 10-video subset against gold-standard scores agreed by two experienced clinical research coordinators.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single short video per child with no follow-up. The data are among the most sensitive in the corpus - identifiable home video of very young children, transmitted internationally and viewed by nine non-clinical raters in another country. Governance is reported reasonably fully: dual ethical clearance from the Bangladesh Institute of Child Health / Dhaka Shishu Children's Hospital and the Stanford IRB, consent obtained in Bengali, secure transmission, and a HIPAA-compliant rating platform. What is absent is any retention, deletion or re-use policy, and any discussion of the ethics of routing identifiable child video to non-clinical raters abroad.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: parents' own mobile phones for video capture - deliberately, since the deployment argument rests on mobile ubiquity. Software: a secure HIPAA-compliant web rating platform; Python 3.6.7 with pandas 0.23.4, scikit-learn 0.20.0 for models, hyperopt 0.1.1 for hyperparameter tuning, shap 0.24.0 for Shapley values, and matplotlib 3.0.1. Version numbers are given throughout, which is better practice than corpus norm.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No data availability statement and no code release. Method reporting is otherwise strong: all software packages with exact versions, the rater-weighting softmax formulation, the Shapley local-accuracy property and its ensemble extension, the elastic-net loss with its two hyperparameters and the grid-search procedure, the balanced class weighting, the three-fold cross-validation split sizes, and demographic breakdowns for both training and test sets. Full mathematical detail is deferred to a multimedia appendix. The pipeline is re-implementable in principle; the videos, being identifiable child media, could not reasonably be released.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors in a dedicated limitations section that diagnoses the transfer gap in three specific ways: the source classifiers were trained on clinical scoresheets rather than features obtained from live video; those scoresheets came from formal clinical assessments of US children and 'do not capture a culturally diverse set of behavioral nuances'; and the classifiers were built to separate typical development from autism whereas this dataset contains other delays including SLCs. They also hypothesise that raters sharing the children's linguistic and sociocultural background would improve performance. Identifiable in review: sex is markedly imbalanced between the ASD and SLC cohorts (72% versus 46% male), directly confounding the second classification layer; family income differs sharply across groups (96% of ASD families above 30,000 taka versus 26% of TD families), as does residence; stunting data are missing entirely for the TD cohort; ADOS covered only 28 of 50 ASD children; the demographic table's gender percentages are inconsistent with their counts; and the senior author founded a company developing paediatric digital health solutions, disclosed as a conflict of interest.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Expand to larger samples across Bangladesh and other low-resource settings; recruit raters who share the children's linguistic and sociocultural background, hypothesised to close the performance gap with US results; accumulate a large annotated video corpus so that convolutional and recurrent networks can learn features directly from raw video and audio rather than from human annotations; and use location-tagged videos to generate epidemiological prevalence estimates that could inform policy and resource allocation - a public-health framing of future work that is unique in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Behavioural observation mediated by human rating rather than direct sensing: 31 categorical judgements of autism-relevant behaviours (eye contact, social participation, stereotyped speech, sensory seeking, stereotyped interests and actions, and others) made by watching short video. This is the only approach in the corpus where the 'features' are human perceptual judgements of behaviour rather than automatically extracted signals - which is deliberate, since it removes any need for specialised sensing hardware in the deployment setting.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Fusion occurs across annotators rather than across modalities, and this is the paper's methodological contribution. Each rater's annotations train a separate random forest, and predictions are combined by a softmax-weighted ensemble whose weights reflect each rater's model accuracy relative to a majority-vote baseline. The authors argue this lets the ensemble exploit each rater's strengths (one may rate eye contact well, another language ability) while discounting their weaknesses, and note it permits distributed annotation where each rater sees only a subset of videos without requiring imputation. A second form of composition is the stacked two-layer architecture, where layer one's atypical classifications feed layer two.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning. Random forests per rater with softmax ensemble weighting for the main classification; logistic regression with elastic net regularisation and balanced class weights for the cross-cultural transfer analysis. The choice of a two-layer stack is motivated conceptually - layer one optimised for sensitivity so no atypical case is missed, layer two optimised for both sensitivity and specificity to separate ASD from other delays - which links model design to intended clinical use more explicitly than most of the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Categorical human ratings as features: 31 multiple-choice responses per video per rater. No signal-level representation of the video is used at all. The authors note in future work that a sufficiently large annotated corpus would allow convolutional and recurrent networks to learn features directly from raw video and audio - explicitly positioning the current human-rating approach as a bootstrapping stage.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: AUC and sensitivity with standard deviations for both layers, and AUC with standard deviation for the source-classifier transfer test, plus ROC curves. Reporting sensitivity alongside AUC is appropriate for a screening framing, and reporting standard deviations across folds is better than corpus norm. However specificity is not reported for either layer, which matters given that layer one is explicitly optimised for sensitivity - so the false-positive burden of the first-stage triage is not quantifiable from the paper.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Among the most thorough in the corpus. Shapley values are computed for all 159 videos in the second layer using the shap package, exploiting local accuracy so each video's predicted probability decomposes exactly into per-feature contributions with both magnitude and direction, and the same rater weights are applied to derive ensemble-level Shapley values. This permits interpretation at the level of an individual child's individual annotation. Separately, features selected most often during elastic-net tuning are compared across the US and Bangladeshi models, yielding the substantive cross-cultural finding that eye contact dominates for Bangladeshi videos while social participation and stereotyped speech dominate for US videos - with a plausible mechanism offered, namely that raters could evaluate language-based behaviours only when they shared the language.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The paper is unusual in this corpus for treating generalisation as an empirical question rather than an assumption. It applies previously published classifiers unchanged to a new cultural population and reports the resulting performance drop (92% accuracy on US videos to AUC 0.75 on Bangladeshi videos), then trains models on each dataset and tests on the other to compare feature reliance. Class imbalance is handled with balanced class weights. Three-fold cross-validation with reported training and test demographics gives some assurance of split stability. What is missing: whether cross-validation folds were partitioned at child level is not explicitly stated (though with one video per child this is largely moot); specificity is not reported; and no prospective or external validation of the retrained Bangladeshi models is performed.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: autism; autism spectrum disorder; machine learning; developmental delays; clinical resources; Bangladesh; Biomedical Data Science. Task vocabulary: 'risk scores', 'reduce-to-practice testing', 'rater-adaptive weighting', 'triage', 'cross-cultural validity', 'health care disparity'. The health-equity and health-systems vocabulary ('clinical resources', 'population-level burden', 'policy change') is distinctive in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Medical Internet Research - a digital health and health informatics journal, clinically oriented rather than computational or autism-specific.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2019. The paper documents the field's cross-cultural blind spot directly: empirically validated tools like ADOS and ADI-R 'are not always used in different countries, particularly in developing countries, as these tools are expensive, require trained clinicians to administer, and may be limited by available translations and cultural adaptations', and it notes that global autism prevalence is 'largely unknown' with estimates of 0.15-0.8% in Bangladesh and around 3% in Dhaka, most cases in semiurban and rural areas going unnoticed. It situates itself in a programme of prior work on rapid mobile ASD detection from short home videos, and its central empirical contribution - measuring how far those US-validated classifiers transfer - is the kind of external validation this corpus otherwise almost entirely lacks.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Exploiting Visual Behaviour for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Arru G; Mazumdar P; Battisti F
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2019 IEEE International Conference on Multimedia & Expo Workshops (ICMEW)
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye-tracking and gaze
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Identification/screening: classify a subject as ASD or typically developing from their scanpath over a natural image, by combining image-content, fixation-behaviour and centre-bias features - developed as an entry to the Saliency4ASD Grand Challenge
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional classification study on a shared benchmark dataset with an organiser-provided train/test split; the authors performed no data collection
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Not reported - viewing durations per image are not stated, and the unit of analysis is a single scanpath over a single image
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Human children (per the source dataset), though the paper notes age information was not available to it
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Free viewing of natural 2D scene images while eye movements were recorded (by the dataset creators)
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Not reported - the data were obtained from a public challenge dataset and the original acquisition setting is not described
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Analysis conducted in Italy (Roma Tre University); the origin of the source data is not stated in this paper
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Not reported - class labels come with the challenge dataset and no diagnostic instrument, criteria or procedure is described
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: Not reported - the paper gives image and scanpath counts but never states the number of participants in either group
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not reported and explicitly unavailable - the authors state age 'is not available in the given dataset'
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developing subjects, per the dataset
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Unknown - age data were unavailable to the authors, who identify this as a substantive limitation
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Unknown - no gender data
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted by dataset label only
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye movements: scanpaths comprising fixation coordinates and durations over natural scene images, combined with computed properties of the images themselves
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Viewing of 2D natural scene images; the analysis pipeline additionally runs object detection and saliency estimation over each image to define content regions
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: No acquisition hardware (secondary data). Analysis: YOLO object detector; SDSP (saliency detection by combining simple priors); mean-shift clustering for region-of-interest extraction; MATLAB TreeBagger random forest with 128 trees
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: No - uses the Saliency4ASD Grand Challenge dataset from IEEE ICME 2019
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes in effect - the source dataset is a public benchmark released for a Grand Challenge, though this paper provides no citation details for access beyond naming it
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Low sensitivity - fixation coordinates over public stimulus images, with subject identifiers randomised by the dataset providers. No ethics or consent statement appears in this paper, which is defensible for secondary use of a released benchmark but is not stated as such
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted features across three families: image content, fixation/saccade behaviour, and centre bias
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 30 features. Content (Cnf1-Cnf11): fixation counts, durations and rates on detected objects versus non-object regions, image coverage from a thresholded fixation binary map, refixation count, and a saliency-weighted fixation measure combining SDSP saliency at fixated pixels with fixation duration. Fixation (Fxf1-Fxf15): total fixation count, fixations per duration, total, mean, longest and standard-deviation of fixation duration, index position of the longest fixation, saccadic amplitude statistics (mean, min, max, total, standard deviation), and mean-shift-derived region-of-interest count with mean and maximum ROI fixation durations. Centre bias (Cbf1-Cbf4): image-to-ROI centre distance, mean fixation distance from image centre, number of fixations within 100 pixels of centre, and time spent near centre
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: YOLO for object detection; SDSP for saliency; mean-shift clustering with a distance/scale threshold of 100 for ROI extraction; MATLAB TreeBagger
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None - no feature importance, ranking or ablation is reported, despite random forests providing importance measures natively
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None reported
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported for the authors' own data. The rationale for each feature family is grounded in cited prior findings - that ASD subjects show stronger centre bias regardless of object distribution and tend to look at areas without socially prominent objects - but no directional result is measured here
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification (tree ensemble)
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: MATLAB TreeBagger random forest with 128 trees, using bootstrap aggregation. No comparison against alternative classifiers
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Organiser-provided held-out test set: 300 images with labelled ASD and TD scanpaths for training, 100 images with unlabelled scanpaths for testing. Results are the mean of per-image scanpath classification results. Critically, the dataset provides no consistent subject identity across images - the authors state that 'the subject generating the fixation data 1 for image 1 may not be the one who generated the fixation data 1 for image 2' - so subject-level partitioning is impossible and the same individual's scanpaths may appear in both training and test sets
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, recall/sensitivity, specificity, F1, precision and AUC-ROC - the most complete metric set of any study so far in the corpus
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Accuracy 59.30%, recall 68.43%, specificity 50.56%, F1 61.64%, precision 56.96%, AUC-ROC 59.50%. Specificity at 50.56% is essentially chance, meaning the model barely distinguishes typically developing scanpaths from random assignment
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Combining image-content, fixation-behaviour and centre-bias features from a single scanpath yielded only 59.3% accuracy and an AUC of 0.595 on the held-out Saliency4ASD test set, with specificity at chance level. The authors report this candidly as 'promising for future improvements' and devote most of their discussion to explaining why performance is limited: fixation behaviour in ASD changes substantially with age, age data were unavailable in the dataset, and generalising a single feature model across all ages and image contents is unlikely to work.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None identified empirically in this study
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Incorporate object semantics (the type of object being fixated) rather than only object presence, motivated by evidence that ASD subjects look at the mouth rather than the eye region of faces; and study in depth the areas of fixation coverage missed by ASD subjects, on the reasoning that what fails to attract attention may be as informative as what does. The discussion additionally implies that age-adaptive feature modelling is necessary
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Valuable to this corpus mainly as an honest low-performance benchmark result. The metric reporting is the most complete of any study charted so far - accuracy, recall, specificity, precision, F1 and AUC together - and it is precisely this completeness that reveals the weakness a single accuracy figure would have hidden: specificity of 50.56% is chance, so the model is effectively labelling most scanpaths as ASD. The evaluation uses an organiser-held test set, which is stronger than internal cross-validation, but the dataset's lack of consistent subject identity across images makes subject-independent evaluation impossible by construction, and the unit of analysis is a scanpath rather than a person - so this is not a person-level diagnostic estimate at all. Participant characteristics are entirely absent: no counts, ages, genders or diagnostic procedure. The authors' discussion of age-dependence in ASD fixation behaviour is the paper's most substantive contribution, and it amounts to an argument that the benchmark's own framing - one model across all subjects and images - is inadequate.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups by dataset label - ASD and typically developing - but the paper reports no participant counts for either group, only image counts (300 training, 100 test). The unit of analysis throughout is the scanpath rather than the person, and subject identifiers are explicitly randomised and inconsistent across images, so participant-level group composition is not recoverable.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'persons affected by autism spectrum disorder', 'persons with ASD', 'ASD subjects', 'ASD patient', 'the patient', 'Typically Developing (TD) infants', 'TD persons', 'non-ASD subjects', 'typically developed toddlers'. Notably medicalised - 'patient' and 'affected by' recur - though the introduction does acknowledge the alternative term 'Autism Spectrum Condition' in its opening sentence before using 'disorder' throughout.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Not reported at any level. No sample sizes, no ages, no age ranges, no standard deviations, no gender distribution, and no matching information for either group. The authors state explicitly that age 'is not available in the given dataset' and treat this as a substantive limitation on their model, since they cite evidence that ASD fixation behaviour differs markedly between toddlers, young children and grown-up children. This is the least participant-characterised study in the corpus so far.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not reported. Class labels are inherited from the Saliency4ASD challenge dataset with no description of how the original diagnoses were established, what instruments were used, or how typically developing status was confirmed.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None reported. No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or severity measures, and no comorbidity information - consistent with the complete absence of participant metadata in the source dataset as used here.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: identify ASD from visual behaviour during image viewing, developed for the Saliency4ASD Grand Challenge. Main findings: accuracy 59.30%, recall 68.43%, specificity 50.56%, F1 61.64%, precision 56.96%, AUC-ROC 59.50% on the organiser's held-out test set. The authors describe this as promising with room for improvement, and attribute the limitation primarily to the absence of age information and to the age-dependence of ASD fixation behaviour.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Setting not reported - this is entirely secondary analysis of an existing benchmark dataset (Saliency4ASD, IEEE ICME 2019 Grand Challenge), with no data collection by the authors and no description of the original acquisition conditions.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Free viewing of 2D natural scene images, per the source dataset. No task instruction, viewing duration, stimulus presentation details or calibration procedure is described, since none of it was performed by these authors. The analysis pipeline adds its own processing tasks - YOLO object detection and SDSP saliency estimation over each stimulus image.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single scanpath per subject per image with no temporal or longitudinal component. The data are fixation coordinates over public stimulus images, with subject identifiers already randomised by the dataset providers, so re-identification risk is minimal. No ethics approval, consent or data-protection statement appears - understandable for secondary use of a released challenge dataset but not acknowledged as such anywhere in the paper.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition hardware, since no data were collected. Software: YOLO (You Only Look Once) for object detection, chosen to segment images into object and non-object regions; SDSP (saliency detection by combining simple priors) for saliency, chosen for low computational complexity; mean-shift clustering with a Gaussian kernel and a distance/scale threshold of 100 for region-of-interest extraction; MATLAB TreeBagger for the random forest.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Mixed. The source dataset is a public benchmark with an organiser-defined train/test split, which is the strongest form of comparability in this corpus - results are directly comparable against other challenge entrants. The feature set is fully enumerated in a table with definitions and the saliency feature is given as an explicit equation, the ROI clustering threshold (100) and centre-proximity radius (100 pixels) are stated, and the classifier and tree count (128) are named. But no code is released, no random seeds are given, no software versions are specified, and the object-detection and saliency models are named without configuration details.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors, and unusually thoughtfully for a four-page workshop paper: ASD fixation behaviour changes with age, with toddlers, young children and grown-up children differing markedly and adults with ASD showing no visible difference in fixation duration between objects and non-objects, so 'the ASD subject age is very important for detecting the condition' - yet age was unavailable in the dataset; and fixation behaviour also depends on image content, since young ASD children do not differ from TD children on scenes containing both faces and objects of circumscribed interest, so 'ASD condition cannot be generalized over age, fixation behaviour, and image content' whereas the model generalises all features over all subjects. Identifiable in review: specificity of 50.56% is chance level and the model is therefore near-useless for ruling out ASD, which the summary framing of '60% accuracy' obscures; no participant counts, ages or genders exist at all; subject identity is not consistent across images so subject-independent evaluation is impossible and the same person's scanpaths can appear in both training and test sets; the unit of analysis is a scanpath not a person, so this is not a person-level diagnostic result; and no feature importance is reported despite the model providing it natively.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Incorporate object semantics - the type of object fixated rather than merely whether a fixation fell on an object - motivated by evidence that ASD subjects look at the mouth rather than the eye region of faces; and study in depth which areas of fixation coverage ASD subjects miss, on the argument that what fails to attract attention may be as diagnostic as what attracts it. The discussion additionally implies, without stating it as a formal direction, that features must be adapted by participant age.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Gaze: fixation coordinates, durations and derived saccadic amplitudes during natural-scene viewing. Uniquely in this corpus, gaze features are combined with computed properties of the stimulus itself - detected object regions and a bottom-up saliency map - so the representation is jointly behavioural and stimulus-derived rather than purely behavioural.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single behavioural modality, but with genuine cross-source integration: three feature families (image content, fixation behaviour, centre bias) are concatenated for the classifier, and two of them require fusing gaze data with image-analysis outputs (YOLO object masks and SDSP saliency maps). This gaze-plus-stimulus-content fusion is a distinctive design in the corpus, though its contribution is never ablated so the value of each family is unknown. No integration with clinical, cognitive or demographic data - the latter being impossible given the dataset.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning. Algorithm: random forest via MATLAB TreeBagger with 128 trees and bootstrap aggregation, selected on the stated grounds that it performs well on all-numeric feature sets with a numeric class label. Mean-shift clustering is used unsupervised as a feature-construction step. No alternative classifiers are compared.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted numeric features - 30 scalar statistics per scanpath spanning content-relative fixation allocation, fixation and saccade dynamics, spatial coverage and refixation, saliency-weighted attention, and centre-proximity measures. No raw scanpath sequences, images or learned embeddings are fed to the classifier, though deep models (YOLO) and a saliency model are used upstream to define the regions the features are computed against.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: The fullest metric set in the corpus so far: accuracy (59.30%), recall/sensitivity (68.43%), specificity (50.56%), F1 (61.64%), precision (56.96%) and AUC-ROC (59.50%), all reported together for the held-out test set. Reporting specificity alongside recall is what makes the result interpretable - it shows recall is achieved largely by over-calling ASD, with specificity at chance.
