No confidence intervals or per-class confusion matrix.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No feature importance, saliency analysis or ablation is performed, and no behavioural feature is identified as informative - a notable gap given that random forests supply out-of-bag importance measures for free and the feature set is explicitly organised into three interpretable families. The paper's interpretive content is instead a literature-grounded argument about why the features should work and why age moderates them.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Evaluation on an organiser-held-out test set with labels withheld is methodologically stronger than the internal cross-validation used by most of the corpus, and it makes the result directly comparable against other challenge entrants. But the design has a structural limitation the authors flag without connecting to validity: subject identity is randomised and inconsistent across images, so partitioning by subject is impossible and the same individual's scanpaths may fall on both sides of the split. Combined with per-image rather than per-person analysis, the reported figures estimate scanpath-level discriminability, not person-level diagnostic accuracy. No external validation beyond the challenge test set, no bias analysis, no class-imbalance handling, and no deployment or real-time consideration.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: Autism spectrum disorder, Object detection, Fixations, Centre bias, Classification, Visual saliency. Task vocabulary: 'revealing the presence of autism spectrum disorder', 'ASD identification', 'early detection', 'visual behaviour', 'scanpath', 'centre bias', 'saliency'. The computer-vision vocabulary (saliency, object detection, ROI) dominates over clinical vocabulary.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: IEEE International Conference on Multimedia and Expo Workshops (ICMEW) 2019, as an entry to the Saliency4ASD Grand Challenge - a multimedia/computer-vision venue, not an autism or clinical venue.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2019. The related-work section surveys the eye-tracking-plus-machine-learning turn in some breadth, citing web-browsing gaze classification, saccade-based classification on six subjects, and a 700-image saliency study finding stronger centre bias and reduced saliency for faces in ASD. It also cites contrary evidence - that social orienting is 'not qualitatively impaired' in ASD and that the excess-mouth, diminished-eye gaze hypothesis has poor support - making it one of the few corpus papers to acknowledge that the underlying behavioural claims are contested. The existence of a dedicated Grand Challenge with a shared dataset is itself evidence of the field's move toward benchmark-based evaluation around 2019.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Hierarchical POMDP Framework for a Robot-Assisted ASD Diagnostic Protocol
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Petric F; Kovacic Z
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2019 14th ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction (HRI). IEEE
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder, preschool
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Robot-mediated interaction
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Autonomous robot-administered diagnostic support: develop a hierarchical POMDP framework enabling a humanoid robot to infer a child's unobservable state from behavioural observations during an ADOS-derived protocol, and to select which diagnostic task to administer next based on that inference
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Exploratory proof-of-concept study evaluating belief-state outcomes from robot-administered sessions, with no formal classification evaluation
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session per child; four tasks each performed exactly once, mirroring ADOS structure. No repeated sessions were held, deliberately, to avoid learned behaviours
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Human preschool children (target age band 2-6 years)
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Four tasks closely modelled on ADOS: response to name call (eye contact after being called), joint attention (transferring attention between two robots), play request (eliciting vocalisations and eye contact coordinated with hand and body gestures to assess simultaneous multi-channel communication), and functional imitation (imitating simple actions with a toy frog and a cup)
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory with a fully equipped examination and observation room, two-way mirror, high-definition camera and overhead microphone; a therapist present in the room and a second therapist plus robot operator observing from behind the mirror; parent or caregiver present for comfort
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Children were 'already diagnosed with ASD' prior to the study; no diagnostic instrument, criteria or clinician is specified. The paper notes all children in the ASD group were undergoing intervention
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not reported; described as preschool age with the research targeting ages 2-6
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Not reported - the paper states explicitly that 'Gender was not considered'
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: All children in the ASD group were undergoing intervention and 'are trained to perform similar tasks almost daily', which the authors identify as materially affecting their behaviour toward the robot
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not measured. The POMDP state space distinguishes low-functioning ASD, high-functioning ASD and typical development as inferred latent states, but no severity instrument was administered
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Groups were matched by mental age, though no values or statistical comparison are given
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: No - gender was explicitly not considered
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted only
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Observed social cues during robot interaction: eye contact, vocalisations/utterances, imitation and gestures, coded per task
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Each task begins with a robot action intended to provoke a child response. Eye contact is tracked in all four tasks, utterances in all four, imitation only in functional imitation, and gestures only in play request. Audio and video from all sessions were analysed offline to extract all robot actions and child social cues, and final belief states were recomputed offline from the observed action-observation pairs
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Two NAO humanoid robots (one facing the child, one on the floor to its left, activated only for the joint attention task); high-definition camera behind a two-way mirror; overhead microphone; robot onboard camera; SARSOP solver for the POMDP; controllers running on a remote computer
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Session recordings were collected but no dataset is described as released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Highly sensitive - video and audio recordings of identifiable preschool children, captured by both a concealed camera behind a two-way mirror and the robot's onboard camera. No ethics approval, no parental consent statement and no anonymization or data-protection provision appears anywhere in the paper; only funding and thanks to families are acknowledged. The one privacy-adjacent measure reported is that interaction transcripts shared with the expert assessors excluded child identification
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Discrete observed social cues feeding Bayesian belief updates, rather than engineered feature vectors
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Task-level partially observable state space comprises child condition (low-functioning ASD, high-functioning ASD, typically developing), engagement level (high/low, updated on child-robot eye contact) and verbal activity (high/low, updated on detected vocalisation), plus a fully observable task-progress state set. Protocol-level observations are generated by partitioning the task belief space: 16 partitions over the condition belief simplex, 3 over engagement and 3 over verbal activity, giving 144 possible observation triplets
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Semi-automatic - social cue detection algorithms exist but 'are not accurate enough for fully autonomous execution', so a human operator supplied the critical observations in real time and the remainder were obtained offline from video analysis
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None; observation probabilities were elicited from experienced ASD clinicians surveyed for estimates of how often certain events occur during diagnosis, rather than learned from data
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not applicable - the model encodes clinician-elicited priors rather than measuring group differences
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Probabilistic sequential decision-making under uncertainty (not supervised classification)
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Hierarchical partially observable Markov decision process with a task-level model and a protocol-level model, interfaced by partitioning the task belief space to generate protocol observations; solved with the SARSOP point-based solver. State transitions for the child-condition, engagement and verbal-activity states are identity matrices, since robot actions are assumed not to change them
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: No cross-validation, train/test split or held-out evaluation. Belief outcomes for 15 children were computed offline and compared against an independent expert assessment: transcripts of child behaviour, stripped of child identification, were given to autism experts who judged whether each behaviour resembled typical development or ASD. Validity is argued from the qualitative correspondence between belief distributions and these expert behavioural categories
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: None in the classification sense. Belief distributions over the three child-condition states are plotted per expert-assigned behavioural category; no accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, AUC or confusion matrix is reported
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Experts classified the 15 sessions as: 5 children showing ASD-characteristic behaviour, 3 showing typically developing behaviour, 4 ambiguous, and 3 sessions too short for meaningful assessment. The framework's belief distributions separated the ASD-behaviour group clearly, separated the typical-development group less decisively with overlap between high-functioning-ASD and typical beliefs, assigned the ambiguous group to high-functioning ASD, and for the too-short sessions produced near-uniform beliefs clustered in approximately 0.27-0.43, indicating the robot had gained little information
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A hierarchical POMDP allowed a semi-autonomous humanoid robot to maintain and update a belief over whether a child was typically developing, high-functioning autistic or low-functioning autistic across an ADOS-derived four-task protocol, and to select the next task based on inferred engagement. Across 15 preschool children the resulting beliefs corresponded reasonably to independent expert judgements of the observed behaviour - crucially, the authors validated against expert-assessed behaviour rather than against diagnosis, having observed that typically developing children sometimes behaved autistically and vice versa. The most informative result is arguably the null one: for the three sessions experts judged too short, the model's belief remained near uniform, correctly signalling that insufficient information had been gathered.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None identified empirically
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Conduct more clinical sessions to obtain data on child engagement and verbal activity during robot-administered tasks, enabling richer reward models, evaluation of the robot's task-selection ability, and comparison of belief-based classification against other classification methods that could not be trained without such data; continue developing social cue detection algorithms toward full autonomy; increase the number of tasks in the protocol; and investigate whether children's behaviour changes when diagnostic tasks are administered by a robot rather than a human examiner
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: This is methodologically unlike anything else in the corpus and should be read on its own terms: it is a sequential decision-making architecture, not a classifier, and it reports belief distributions rather than accuracy. Several judgements are unusually sound. The authors deliberately down-weighted the information each task contributes (scaling confidence to 0.8) after noticing that four tasks were producing near-certain beliefs, reasoning correctly that since ADOS uses five modules of at least ten tasks each, four tasks 'should not be enough to reach a diagnosis' - a rare instance of a researcher deliberately degrading their own apparent performance because the result was implausibly good. They also validated against expert-assessed behaviour rather than diagnosis, having observed that their ASD group, all in daily intervention, showed no anxiety toward the robot while typically developing children were shy and wary - an honest recognition that diagnosis and observed behaviour diverged in their sample. And they conclude by conceding that with four tasks the robot makes only three decisions, which 'does not necessarily warrant a use of POMDP'. Against this: 15 children with no ages, no genders (explicitly not considered), no diagnostic instrument and no ethics or consent statement despite covert-angle video of preschoolers; observation probabilities elicited from clinician surveys rather than learned; the robot was semi-autonomous with a human operator supplying critical observations in real time; four sessions were terminated by robot failures; and no quantitative performance metric of any kind is reported, so this study contributes no accuracy estimate to the review.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: 8 preschool children already diagnosed with ASD and 7 typically developing children, total 15. Group sizes are reported. No other-diagnosis group. Notably the analysis is ultimately regrouped by expert-assessed behaviour rather than by diagnosis, producing four categories (ASD-like behaviour n=5, typical behaviour n=3, ambiguous n=4, session too short n=3) that cut across the original diagnostic grouping.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'people with ASD', 'child with low-functioning ASD', 'child with high-functioning ASD', 'typically developing children'. Person-first throughout, with the paper framing its motivation in terms of 'successful inclusion of people with ASD into the society'. The POMDP state labels (sLA, sHA, sNA for low-functioning, high-functioning and typically developing) formalise a three-level functioning taxonomy as latent model states.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Only group sizes are reported: 8 ASD and 7 typically developing preschool children, matched by mental age. No chronological ages, no age ranges, no standard deviations, and gender is explicitly disregarded - 'Gender was not considered'. Mental-age matching is claimed but no values or comparison are given. The research targets ages 2-6, so the sample is directly relevant to early diagnosis, but nothing about its composition can be verified.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not reported. Children are described as 'already diagnosed with ASD' with no instrument, criteria, clinician or date, and typically developing status is asserted without screening. The protocol tasks are modelled on ADOS, but ADOS itself was not administered as a reference standard. Instead, the validation comparator is a post-hoc expert judgement of behaviour from de-identified transcripts - which is a reasonable choice given the authors' observation that behaviour and diagnosis diverged, but it means no gold-standard diagnostic anchor exists in the study.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None reported. No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive measures, no severity instrument, and no comorbidity information. Mental age is used for matching but its values are not given. The one clinically relevant characteristic reported is that all ASD-group children were undergoing intervention and trained on similar tasks almost daily - which the authors correctly identify as a confound affecting their behaviour toward the robot.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: enable a humanoid robot to reason about a child's unobservable state during an ADOS-derived diagnostic protocol and to select tasks adaptively, addressing the reported problem of inter-clinician disagreement arising from the need to simultaneously observe, code and interpret many behaviours. Main findings: belief distributions separated expert-assessed ASD behaviour clearly and typical behaviour less decisively; behaviour experts judged ambiguous was assigned to high-functioning ASD; and sessions too short for expert assessment produced near-uniform beliefs (approximately 0.27-0.43), correctly signalling insufficient information. No accuracy figure is reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory setting - a purpose-built examination and observation suite with a two-way mirror, fixed camera position and overhead microphone, with a therapist in the room and a second therapist plus robot operator behind the mirror. Newly collected session data; no existing dataset used.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Four ADOS-derived tasks, each performed exactly once as in ADOS: response to name call (positive if eye contact detected), joint attention (transferring attention to a second robot that activates its lights, verified by eye contact), play request (eliciting vocalisations and eye contact coordinated with hand and body gestures to test simultaneous multi-channel communication), and functional imitation with real objects - a toy frog and a cup - which the authors distinguish from the simple motoric imitation used in comparable work. In every task the robot first performs an action intended to provoke a child response. A therapist placed objects into the robot's hand and triggered demonstrations via head tactile sensors, specifically to eliminate failed grasps and guarantee the imitation always occurred.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single session per child, with repeated sessions deliberately avoided to prevent learned behaviours. The data are video and audio of identifiable preschool children, recorded both by the robot's onboard camera and by a high-definition camera concealed behind a two-way mirror - among the most privacy-sensitive arrangements in the corpus. There is no ethics approval statement, no parental consent statement and no anonymization or data-protection provision anywhere in the paper. The only privacy-adjacent measure is that transcripts shared with the expert assessors omitted child identification.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: two NAO humanoid robots, one facing the child with its back to the two-way mirror and one on the floor to its left with lights off except during the joint attention task; a high-definition camera behind the two-way mirror; an overhead microphone in the examination room; the robot's onboard camera. Software: hierarchical POMDP models solved with the SARSOP point-based solver, with protocol and task controllers and the operator interface running on a remote computer.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No data or code release. The model specification is however documented in unusual detail: the state factorisation, the belief-space partitioning scheme (16 partitions over the condition simplex, 3 each over engagement and verbal activity), the full 3x16 observation probability matrix for the condition states, the 2x3 matrices for engagement and verbal activity, the centroid-based procedure for deriving those probabilities, the confidence-scaling equation with its chosen value of 0.8, the reward-shaping rules, and the solver used. The model is therefore reimplementable; the sessions are not reproducible, and the clinician survey that supplied the underlying observation rates is not documented.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors, with notable candour: the sample size 'is not large'; because each task runs once the robot makes only three decisions, which 'does not necessarily warrant a use of POMDP'; social cue detection algorithms are 'not accurate enough for fully autonomous execution' so the robot is only semi-autonomous with an operator supplying critical observations; not all children completed all tasks, some because of robot failures and some through fear or refusal; in four cases robot failure ended the session because children would not continue; and crucially, typically developing children 'sometimes exhibit autistic behavior, and vice versa', which the authors attribute to the ASD group being in daily intervention and unafraid of the robot while typically developing children were shy and wary. Identifiable in review: no ages, genders or diagnostic instrument; no ethics or consent statement despite two-way-mirror video of preschoolers; observation probabilities elicited by clinician survey rather than estimated from data; no quantitative performance metric whatsoever; and the confidence-scaling parameter was tuned until 'more appropriate' belief values emerged, which is a judgement call rather than a fitted value.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Run more clinical sessions to obtain data on child engagement and verbal activity during robot-administered tasks, which would enable richer reward models, permit evaluation of the robot's task-selection policy, and allow belief-based classification to be compared against conventional classifiers that currently cannot be trained for lack of data; continue developing social cue detection toward full autonomy; increase the number of protocol tasks; and investigate whether children behave differently when diagnostic tasks are administered by a robot rather than a human examiner - a question that bears directly on whether robot-administered protocols measure the same construct as clinician-administered ones.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Social-interaction behaviour observed as discrete cues: eye contact, vocalisations, imitation and gestures, each tracked in specified tasks. These are categorical behavioural events rather than continuously sensed signals, and in this study they were largely human-coded (in real time by the operator for critical observations, offline from video for the rest) rather than automatically detected.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Multiple cue types are combined within each task's observation set and jointly update a shared belief over child condition, engagement and verbal activity - so eye contact, utterances, imitation and gestures fuse probabilistically into one latent state estimate. The hierarchical structure adds a second fusion level: each task's terminal belief is discretised into a partition index that becomes an observation for the protocol-level model, so information accumulates across tasks. This belief-space-partitioning interface is the paper's central technical contribution and is a genuinely different fusion mechanism from the feature concatenation used everywhere else in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Not machine learning in the supervised sense. The method is probabilistic sequential decision-making: a hierarchical POMDP with task-level and protocol-level models, solved by the SARSOP point-based value iteration solver. Model parameters are specified rather than learned - transition matrices for child states are identity (robot actions cannot change the child's condition, and no data existed on their effect on engagement or verbal activity), and observation probabilities were elicited from a clinician survey. The authors themselves note that comparison against trained classifiers is not yet possible for lack of data.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Behaviour is represented as discrete observation symbols drawn from a defined set per task, and the child is represented as a probability distribution (belief) over a factored latent state space of condition, engagement and verbal activity. Between hierarchy levels, a continuous belief simplex is discretised into 16 partitions whose centroids define observation probabilities. There are no feature vectors, embeddings or time series.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: None. No accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1 or AUC is reported, and no confusion matrix. The outputs are belief distributions over three latent states, plotted as frequency histograms per expert-assigned behavioural category. This means the study contributes no diagnostic accuracy estimate, and it should be excluded from any quantitative synthesis of performance - a point worth recording explicitly since its framing as a diagnostic protocol might otherwise invite inclusion.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: The model is inherently interpretable in structure - beliefs over named clinical states, observations tied to specific social cues, and reward rules stated in plain language (penalise name-call if the child is already engaged; penalise joint attention if the child is not engaged; reward play request if disengaged; reward imitation if engaged). But no analysis identifies which cues or tasks were most informative, and the observation probabilities encode clinician priors rather than empirical relationships, so nothing about autistic behaviour is learned from the data.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: There is no validation in the machine-learning sense - no cross-validation, no held-out data, no independent test set. Robustness is addressed through two design decisions instead. First, the authors noticed that four tasks were driving belief close to certainty and judged this implausible given ADOS uses five modules of at least ten tasks each, so they introduced a confidence-scaling transformation and set it to 0.8 to deliberately reduce the information each task contributes - actively degrading apparent performance on principled grounds. Second, they validated against expert-assessed behaviour rather than diagnostic label, because they had observed the two diverging in their sample. Neither is a generalisation estimate. There is no external validation, no bias analysis, no class-imbalance consideration, and the system is not autonomous, so deployment readiness is explicitly not established.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: POMDP; NAO; robot-assisted; autism; diagnostics. Task vocabulary: 'robot-assisted ASD diagnostic protocol', 'belief state', 'social cues', 'semi-autonomous', 'Wizard-of-Oz'. The decision-theoretic vocabulary (belief, policy, reward, observation probability) is unique in this corpus and reflects a robotics rather than pattern-recognition framing.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: The 14th ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) 2019 - a robotics and human-robot interaction venue, not an autism, clinical or machine-learning venue.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2019. The paper positions itself as 'one of the first applications of humanoid robots in the diagnostics procedure', distinguishing diagnostic from the much commoner therapeutic robot applications and noting that diagnostic use 'brings forth some additional requirements and challenges, especially in terms of data acquisition and reasoning'. It observes that the complexity of the diagnostic process 'imposes constraints on the robotic applications in form of the need for efficient processing and reasoning algorithms', which results in a 'low number of robotic applications in ASD diagnosis'. It also documents that most robot-autism research still uses 'some form of Wizard-of-Oz approach with various degrees of autonomy', and that observations are typically 'collected through analysis of video recordings, which is a common technique in this field' - an accurate characterisation of the robot strand of this corpus.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Intelligent Gaze-Based Screening System for Autism
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Dris AB; Alsalman A; Al-Wabil A; Aldosari M
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2019 2nd International Conference on Computer Applications & Information Security (ICCAIS)
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye-tracking and gaze
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Early screening: build an Arabic-language automated gaze-based screening system that integrates eye tracking with a machine-learning prediction model to categorise a child's visual attention as typical (non-ASD) or atypical (ASD), explicitly aimed at speeding up diagnosis and at addressing the absence of such systems for Arabic populations
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Proof-of-concept cross-sectional classification study; largely a system-design paper with a results section reporting classification metrics
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Not reported - no session length, number of stimuli, or per-stimulus viewing duration is given for the authors' own data collection
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Viewing of Arabic visual stimuli described as closely aligned with existing English-language stimuli from a cited prior study; the results section states videos were used as stimuli
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Clinic intended - the system is designed for use in autism centres or hospitals in Saudi Arabia, with a therapist-led pre-analysis phase collecting patient information and medical history before eye-tracker setup
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Saudi Arabia (with a Cleveland Clinic collaborator)
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Not reported - no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or confirmation procedure is described anywhere for the authors' own participants
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported for the authors' sample; the literature review notes that ADHD comorbidity with ASD reaches 59%
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - a typically developing (non-ASD) group is referred to in the results
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not reported or addressed
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not reported or addressed
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted only
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye movements: fixation durations within predefined regions of interest during stimulus viewing
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Stimulus viewing with gaze capture; the paper specifies a three-phase workflow (pre-analysis with patient history and eye-tracker setup, gaze data collection during stimulus presentation, and prediction-model building) but gives no stimulus inventory, presentation timings or ROI definitions
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Tobii X120 eye tracker for data collection. No analysis software, library or platform is named
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes in principle - the paper refers to 'our collected eye movement data set' - but nothing about it is characterised and it is not released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze fixation data are low in identifiability, and the workflow involves collecting patient information and medical history. No ethics approval, consent statement or anonymization procedure is reported anywhere, despite the system being designed for clinical deployment with children and the pre-analysis phase explicitly involving medical-history collection
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted region-of-interest fixation-duration features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Three metrics are tabulated: fixation duration for each region of interest, total fixation duration across all ROIs in the stimulus, and mean fixation duration within a ROI. The methods state that mean fixation duration within each ROI is incorporated as a temporal and spatial feature, with a single feature vector per participant representing the time distribution of their visual attention. The number of ROIs, their definitions and the resulting feature-vector dimensionality are never stated
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Not named
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None - the results state only that 'using ROIs as features for analysis prove clearly the levels of discrimination between ASD and non-ASD patients' without identifying any specific region
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Support vector machine, chosen on the stated grounds of its use in the cited literature and its capability as a binary classifier. No alternative classifiers are evaluated, and the kernel is not specified
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-out cross-validation, described in the methods as selecting one participant at a time as the test case with the model learned from the remaining participants - a participant-level scheme. No hyperparameter tuning procedure, no repetition, and no significance testing are described
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and area under the ROC curve
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Accuracy 88.6%, specificity 92.31%, sensitivity 86.63%, AUC 0.96
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: The paper reports an SVM over region-of-interest fixation-duration features achieving 88.6% accuracy, 92.31% specificity, 86.63% sensitivity and an AUC of 0.96 for distinguishing ASD from typically developing children, and presents this as proof of concept for remote eye tracking as an objective screening tool. The substantive contribution is framed as system design - an Arabic-language automated screening pipeline integrating eye tracking with a prediction model for use by therapists - together with the observation, developed at length in the literature review, that no prior work had integrated an automatic prediction model within a deployable screening tool.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None identified
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Replicate the model and findings with larger datasets to validate machine-learning performance, and apply other classification techniques and compare their results against SVM
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: This is the weakest-reported study charted so far and must be treated with corresponding caution. It reports four performance figures - 88.6% accuracy, 92.31% specificity, 86.63% sensitivity, AUC 0.96 - without stating how many participants were tested, their ages, their genders, how ASD was diagnosed, how many stimuli were shown, how long they were shown for, how regions of interest were defined, how many features resulted, what SVM kernel was used, or what software performed the analysis. Sections III and IV are written partly in the future tense ('will be trained', 'we will evaluate'), which suggests the paper describes a planned system with preliminary results appended rather than a completed study. The literature review is genuinely useful - it is careful, accurate, and notably includes a critique of a prior study's reliance on structured face-recognition tasks limiting generalisability to young children - and the paper's motivating observation about the absence of Arabic-language screening resources and the uncertain ASD prevalence estimates across Gulf states (1.4, 29 and 59 per 10,000 in Oman, UAE and Saudi Arabia) is a legitimate contribution. But the reported metrics cannot be independently interpreted, compared or reproduced, and in any quantitative synthesis they should be excluded or heavily discounted.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups are referred to - ASD and typically developing (non-ASD) children - but no participant counts are reported for either group anywhere in the paper. The sample is described only as 'our collected eye movement data set'. This is the only study charted so far that reports classification performance without stating any sample size.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'ASD children', 'individuals with ASD', 'ASD patients', 'non-ASD patients', 'patients', 'Autistic or non-Autistic', 'typically developing children', 'individuals with disabilities'. Strongly medicalised: autism is described as 'a mental disorder', 'among the most upsetting disorders of childhood' and 'a harming developmental disorder', and participants are consistently 'patients'. This is the most pathologising terminology encountered in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Nothing is reported. No sample sizes, no ages, no age range, no standard deviations, no gender distribution and no matching information for either group. The paper's motivation depends on early screening before age 2, but the age of the children actually tested is never stated, so it cannot be established whether the system was evaluated in the population it targets.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not reported. No diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or confirmation procedure is described for the ASD group, and typically developing status is asserted without any screening. Since diagnostic label is the classification target and the paper proposes a clinical screening tool, the complete absence of reference-standard information is disqualifying for any diagnostic-accuracy claim.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None reported. No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or severity measures for either group. The workflow specifies that a therapist collects patient information and medical history in the pre-analysis phase, so such data are presumably gathered, but none is reported or used.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: early screening via an Arabic automated gaze-based system integrating eye tracking with machine learning, to speed up diagnosis and reduce dependence on subjective clinical observation. Main findings as reported: accuracy 88.6%, specificity 92.31%, sensitivity 86.63%, AUC 0.96. The authors claim the AUC is the best among comparable models and argue this means it 'works well regardless of the class distribution', which is an overstatement of what AUC guarantees.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Intended clinical setting - autism centres or hospitals in Saudi Arabia, with a therapist-operated workflow. Newly collected data, though nothing about the collection setting, session structure or conditions is described.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Stated only at the highest level: Arabic visual stimuli 'that closely align with the existing English language visual stimuli' of a cited prior study, with data collection following recommendations from the same source. The results section states videos were used as stimuli. No stimulus inventory, count, duration, presentation order, calibration procedure or region-of-interest definition is given, so the elicitation protocol cannot be reconstructed or repeated.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; no session duration, number of sessions or follow-up is reported. Gaze fixation durations are low-sensitivity data, but the described workflow has a therapist collect patient information and medical history at the pre-analysis stage, which is identifiable clinical data. No ethics approval, no parental consent statement, and no anonymization or data-protection provision appears anywhere - a serious omission for a system designed for clinical deployment with children.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: Tobii X120 remote eye tracker. That is the only technical specification given - no monitor, viewing distance, sampling rate, calibration procedure, or analysis software, library or platform is named. The literature review names WEKA and MATLAB as tools used by other researchers, but the paper never states what it used itself.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Effectively nil. No data availability statement, no code, no software or versions, no SVM kernel or hyperparameters, no ROI definitions, no feature-vector dimensionality, no stimulus materials, no sample sizes, and no random seeds. Neither the experiment nor the analysis could be reproduced from the paper. The only reproducibility-supporting detail is the eye tracker model and a pointer to the prior study whose stimuli and data-collection recommendations were adapted.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors: only that the model should be replicated with larger datasets to validate performance, and that other classification techniques should be compared. No limitations section exists. Identifiable in review: no sample size is reported, so the precision of the four performance figures is unknowable; no ages, genders or diagnostic procedure, so demographic and ascertainment bias cannot be assessed; no stimulus, ROI or feature specification, so the measurement cannot be evaluated; methods sections are written partly in the future tense, suggesting the system was planned rather than fully executed at time of writing; the claim that a high AUC means the model 'works well regardless of the class distribution (i.e. when data are new/unknown)' conflates class-distribution invariance with generalisation to new data; and the study is framed around screening before age 2 while never reporting the age of any participant.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Replicate with larger datasets to validate the machine-learning performance, and apply and compare other classification techniques against SVM. Both are generic; no specific validation design, population extension or deployment study is proposed.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Gaze: fixation durations within predefined regions of interest during viewing of visual stimuli. Aggregate dwell time only - no scanpath, saccade, pupillometric or temporal-sequence information.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality, no fusion. Per-ROI mean fixation durations are concatenated into a single feature vector per participant, described as capturing the time distribution of visual attention across regions - a within-modality spatial aggregation rather than multimodal fusion. No integration with clinical scores, demographics or the medical-history data the workflow collects.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning. Algorithm: support vector machine only, selected because it is used in the cited literature and is a capable binary classifier. No paradigm comparison, no alternative algorithms, and no kernel specification.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted low-dimensional features: mean fixation duration per region of interest, assembled into one feature vector per participant. The paper describes this as incorporating both temporal and spatial information, since duration is temporal and ROI identity is spatial. No raw scanpaths, images or learned embeddings.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy (88.6%), specificity (92.31%), sensitivity (86.63%) and AUC (0.96) - a reasonably complete metric set on its face, and the authors explicitly motivate reporting all four. But with no sample size reported, none of the figures carries an interpretable precision, and the two-decimal specificity (92.31%, consistent with 12 of 13) hints at a very small test set. No confusion matrix, confidence intervals or significance testing.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No feature importance, ROI ranking or ablation is reported. The results assert that 'using ROIs as features for analysis prove clearly the levels of discrimination between ASD and non-ASD patients' but identify no specific region, direction or effect, so nothing interpretable about autistic visual attention emerges from the study itself.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Leave-one-out cross-validation at the participant level is described and is an appropriate choice, with the rationale cited. Beyond that, nothing: no external or independent validation, no held-out site, no repetition, no permutation or significance testing, no class-imbalance handling or reporting, no calibration, no bias analysis, and no deployment or real-time evaluation despite clinical deployment in Saudi autism centres being the explicit goal. Generalisability is addressed only by the future-work statement that larger datasets are needed.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder, Intelligent, Machine Learning, early diagnoses, speed up screening, early intervention. Task vocabulary: 'intelligent screening', 'gaze-based screening', 'early biomarkers', 'automated data-driven prediction model', 'computer-aid diagnostic tool', 'transformative step'. The 'intelligent system' framing and the emphasis on speeding up screening throughput are distinctive.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: The 2nd International Conference on Computer Applications and Information Security (ICCAIS) 2019 - a general computing and information-security venue, neither an autism, clinical, nor machine-learning-specialist venue.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2019. The literature review is the paper's strongest section and characterises the field carefully: screening has 'evolved recently from subjective clinical assessments to objective metrics acquired from sensing devices such as gaze-tracking, motion sensors, and speech analytics'; machine learning in autism has 'largely focused on how to select the most effective features from a large feature set on the clinical diagnostic tools to shorten the diagnosis time'; and, most pointedly, 'all presented studies adopted machine learning differently yet there is no automatic prediction model integrated within a screening tool to be used in clinics'. It also documents a geographic gap - a shortage of Arabic-language autism research and uncertain prevalence estimates of 1.4, 29 and 59 per 10,000 children in Oman, the UAE and Saudi Arabia - which is a dimension of coverage bias not raised elsewhere in this corpus.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Kinematic features of a simple and short movement task to predict autism diagnosis
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Vabalas A; Gowen E; Poliakoff E; Casson AJ
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2019 41st Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering i
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum condition, adults
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Motor and kinematics
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Prediction of autism diagnosis at the individual level from a deliberately simple and short motor task, with the explicit methodological aim of obtaining unbiased performance estimates using nested cross-validation rather than the K-fold cross-validation used by prior kinematic studies
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session; 10 seconds of continuous pointing per hand, performed with both dominant and non-dominant hands
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Simple repetitive pointing: move the index finger between two markers 30 cm apart as quickly and accurately as possible for 10 seconds
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory - University of Manchester
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Not reported - participants are described as autistic adults with no diagnostic instrument, criteria or confirmation procedure named
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 24 (9 female)
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described; no screening instrument reported
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 22 (7 female)
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not explicitly claimed or tested, but group means are very close (31.5 vs 30.8 years)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not claimed; proportions are similar (37.5% vs 31.8% female)
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Motor kinematics: 3D index-finger position during repetitive pointing, plus spatial accuracy of touch locations
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Repetitive pointing between two 8 mm red target stickers 30 cm apart on a table, for 10 seconds, with each hand. Accuracy quantified by the area bounded by the touch points at each target and by the average distance between touch points
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Polhemus Fastrak motion tracker with a single sensor on the distal phalange of the index finger, sampling X, Y, Z at 120 Hz; scikit-learn for SVM and grid search; scikit-rebate for ReliefF
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - newly collected, but not released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Low-sensitivity numeric motion-tracking data. Experimental procedures were approved by the University of Manchester research ethics committee with the reference number given (2017-2541-4204). No participant consent statement or anonymization procedure is separately described
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted kinematic and spatial-accuracy features, summarised as means and standard deviations
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 20 movement measures per pointing movement - duration, peak velocity and its timing (absolute and percentage), horizontal amplitude at peak acceleration, time before and after peak velocity, peak acceleration and its timing, peak deceleration and its timing, dimensionless jerk, horizontal and vertical amplitude, peak vertical amplitude timing and location - plus accuracy features based on the area bounded by touch points and the mean inter-point distance. Means and standard deviations pooled across hands give 60 features total
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Custom kinematic computation from Polhemus traces; scikit-learn and scikit-rebate for selection and classification
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Partly - feature-selection methods are compared as whole pipelines rather than individual features being ranked, but the most discriminative behavioural measures are reported with effect sizes
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Four feature-selection methods compared as complete pipelines: SVM recursive feature elimination, two-sample t-test filter (top 10), ReliefF (K=23, top 10) and minimum redundancy maximum relevance (top 10). Separately, group-level t-tests with Cohen's d identify the most different behavioural measures
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Group-level: movement duration (d=0.74), mean velocity (d=0.77), percentage time of peak vertical amplitude (d=0.82), time to peak velocity (d=0.69) and overall pointing area (d=0.81). At the pipeline level, simple t-test filtering gave the best classification (71%) and ReliefF the second best (70%), while the more sophisticated SVM-RFE (62%) and mRMR (60%) failed to reach significance
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Clearly reported: autistic participants pointed more slowly (duration 0.42 vs 0.37 s; mean velocity 776 vs 912 mm/s), reached peak vertical amplitude earlier and peak velocity later in the movement, but were substantially more accurate - overall touch area 30.87 mm2 versus 64.01 mm2 for non-autistic participants
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Support vector machine with RBF kernel, with C and gamma optimised by grid search inside the nested cross-validation, coupled with each of four feature-selection methods
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 10-fold nested cross-validation, repeated 100 times with random splits to obtain performance distributions. The authors state explicitly that the entire model development pipeline - data normalisation, feature selection and parameter tuning - is performed inside the training portion of each fold, so test data never enters model development. Significance assessed by permutation testing with 1000 label permutations
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and a permutation-derived p-value for every one of the four pipelines, plus accuracy distributions and confusion matrices for all four
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: t-test feature selection: 71% accuracy, 75% sensitivity, 66% specificity, p = 0.021. ReliefF: 70%, 72%, 68%, p = 0.027. SVM-RFE: 62%, 65%, 59%, p = 0.113 (not significant). mRMR: 60%, 64%, 55%, p = 0.148 (not significant). Behavioural group differences were significant with medium-to-large effect sizes (Cohen's d 0.69 to 0.82)
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A 10-second pointing task discriminated autistic from non-autistic adults at 71% accuracy under nested cross-validation with permutation-tested significance. Autistic participants moved more slowly but pointed substantially more accurately - roughly half the spatial scatter - which is a speed-accuracy trade-off rather than a deficit. The paper's central methodological point is that group-level differences with large effect sizes (d up to 0.82) do not translate into high individual-level classification accuracy, and that the 86.7-96.7% figures reported by prior kinematic studies reflect K-fold cross-validation, which produces overoptimistic estimates on small samples.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Slower movement (longer duration, lower mean velocity), later peak velocity, earlier peak vertical amplitude, and smaller pointing scatter area indicating greater spatial accuracy
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Apply the approach to kinematic data from more complex movement imitation tasks, with preliminary results described as promising; and validate the models on a newly collected independent dataset to establish robustness
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: One of the most important methodological contributions in the corpus despite being a four-page conference paper. It names the three prior kinematic ASC classification studies reporting 86.7-96.7%, identifies K-fold cross-validation as the reason those figures are overoptimistic on small samples, adopts nested cross-validation with the entire pipeline inside the training fold, repeats it 100 times, permutation-tests significance, and reports a candid 71% - then states the general lesson explicitly, that large group-level effect sizes do not necessarily translate to high classification performance. It also reports two of its four pipelines as non-significant rather than dropping them. Notably the same first author's 2020 Scientific Reports paper is also in this corpus, so the pair together document a research programme built around correcting this specific validation error. Remaining weaknesses are reporting gaps rather than analytic ones: no diagnostic instrument is named, no IQ values are given despite IQ matching being claimed, no age standard deviations, and no data or code release. The 71% on 46 participants also carries a wide confidence interval that is not reported, though the accuracy distributions are plotted.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: 24 autistic adults and 22 non-autistic (typically developing) adults, IQ-matched. Both group sizes and sex counts are reported. No other-diagnosis comparison group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'autistic individuals', 'autistic adults', 'ASC participants', 'non-autistic adults', 'non-autistic individuals', 'typically developing (TD) individuals', 'affected individuals'. Predominantly identity-first ('autistic individuals') paired with 'non-autistic' rather than 'healthy' or 'normal', and the paper uses 'Autism Spectrum Condition' rather than 'Disorder' throughout - among the more neurodiversity-aligned terminology in the corpus, consistent with the same Manchester group's other entries here.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASC n=24 (9 female, 37.5%), mean age 31.5 years. TD n=22 (7 female, 31.8%), mean age 30.8 years. Groups are stated to be IQ matched, but no IQ values, no age standard deviations, no age ranges and no statistical comparisons are reported. Female representation is comparatively high for this literature. Adults only, so no early-diagnosis relevance.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not reported. Participants are described simply as autistic adults with no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or verification procedure named, and control status is asserted without screening. Given that diagnosis is the prediction target, this is the study's principal reporting gap - though the same research group's companion 2020 paper documents its ascertainment more fully.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: IQ matching is claimed but no IQ values are reported for either group, and no language, adaptive-functioning or autism-trait measures are given. Comorbidities are not described. This is unusually sparse given that the paper is otherwise meticulous about its analysis.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: predict autism diagnosis at the individual level from a short simple motor task, with the stated methodological aim of producing unbiased performance estimates. Main findings: 71% accuracy (75% sensitivity, 66% specificity, p=0.021) with t-test feature selection and 70% with ReliefF, while SVM-RFE (62%) and mRMR (60%) did not reach significance; autistic participants moved more slowly but pointed about twice as accurately; and large group-level effect sizes did not translate into high classification accuracy.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory setting at a UK university. Newly collected data using motion tracking; no existing dataset used.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A deliberately minimal task: point between two 8 mm stickers 30 cm apart on a table with the index finger, as quickly and accurately as possible, for 10 seconds, repeated with the dominant and non-dominant hand. The brevity and simplicity are the point - the paper tests whether a task this short can carry diagnostic signal, in contrast to the longer imitation and gameplay protocols elsewhere in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single session of a few seconds of task data per hand, with no follow-up. Data are numeric 3D position traces, not identifiable media, so sensitivity is low. Ethics approval from the University of Manchester research ethics committee is reported with the specific reference number (2017-2541-4204); no consent statement or anonymization procedure is separately described.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: Polhemus Fastrak electromagnetic motion tracker with a single sensor on the distal phalange of the index finger, sampling X, Y and Z at 120 Hz; two 8 mm red target stickers on a table. Software: scikit-learn for SVM and grid search, scikit-rebate for ReliefF; outlier handling following the Van Selst and Jolicoeur non-recursive procedure.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No data or code release and no random seeds, but the analytic pipeline is described in enough detail to reimplement: the full 20-measure table, the accuracy-feature definitions, the outlier-removal procedure and its citation, z-score normalisation, the four feature-selection methods with their parameters (ReliefF K=23, top 10 features for the filter methods), the SVM kernel and grid-searched parameters, the named libraries, the nested cross-validation structure with 10 folds repeated 100 times, and the 1000-permutation significance test. Analytically this is one of the more reproducible descriptions in the corpus; empirically it is not reproducible without the data.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: No dedicated limitations section, but the paper's entire framing is a limitation critique aimed at its own field: prior kinematic studies achieving 86.7-96.7% 'used K-fold Cross-Validation, which was demonstrated to produce overoptimistic performance estimates, especially when a sample size is small' and did not assess whether performance differed significantly from random guessing. The conclusion adds that large parametric effect sizes 'do not necessarily translate to high ML classification performance'. Identifiable in review: no diagnostic instrument named; IQ matching claimed without values; no age standard deviations or ranges; adults only; n=46 so 71% is roughly 33 of 46 correct, with no confidence interval reported though accuracy distributions are plotted; the best of four pipelines is highlighted, though all four including the two non-significant ones are reported in full; and outlier replacement with group means (1.4% of data points) uses group information, a minor leakage route not discussed.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Extend the approach to kinematic data from more complex movement imitation tasks, with preliminary results described as promising - which is exactly what the same group's 2020 Scientific Reports paper in this corpus goes on to do; and validate the models on newly collected independent data to establish robustness, directly addressing the absence of external validation.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Motor behavior: 3D index-finger kinematics during repetitive pointing (velocity, acceleration, deceleration, jerk, amplitude and their timings) together with spatial endpoint accuracy derived from where the finger contacted the table.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality, but with two distinct feature families combined - movement kinematics and endpoint accuracy - which is what allows the speed-accuracy trade-off to emerge. Features from dominant and non-dominant hands are pooled into means and standard deviations, a form of within-modality aggregation. No integration with clinical, cognitive or demographic data.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning. Algorithm: SVM with RBF kernel, with C and gamma grid-searched. Four feature-selection strategies are compared as complete pipelines: SVM recursive feature elimination (embedded), two-sample t-test (filter), ReliefF (filter with neighbour interactions) and mRMR (filter with redundancy penalty). The finding that the two simplest filters outperformed the two more sophisticated methods is reported without embellishment.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted kinematic summary features: 20 scalar movement measures per pointing movement plus spatial accuracy measures, aggregated to 60 features as means and standard deviations pooled across hands, then z-score normalised. No raw time series, images or learned embeddings.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and a permutation p-value for each of the four pipelines, plus accuracy distributions across the 100 nested cross-validation repetitions and confusion matrices for all four models. Reporting non-significant results with their p-values (0.113 and 0.148) alongside significant ones is rare in this corpus. No AUC or confidence intervals, though the plotted distributions convey spread.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No per-feature importance ranking from the final models. Interpretability comes from the group-level behavioural analysis, which reports the five most discriminative measures with means, t-statistics, p-values and Cohen's d, and from averaged velocity and vertical-amplitude profiles plotted across movement progression for both groups. The substantive finding is a speed-accuracy trade-off: autistic participants were slower but roughly twice as spatially precise (30.87 vs 64.01 mm2 scatter area), which is a difference in movement strategy rather than an impairment - a framing that contrasts with most motor studies in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The strongest validation design among the motor studies here. Nested 10-fold cross-validation with normalisation, feature selection and hyperparameter tuning all performed inside each training fold, so test data never informs model development; the whole procedure repeated 100 times with random splits to yield performance distributions; and permutation testing with 1000 label shuffles to establish that accuracy differs from chance. The authors cite Varma and Simon on nested cross-validation giving 'almost unbiased' estimates and K-fold producing 'significantly overoptimistic results'. Absent: external or independent validation (explicitly named as future work), any held-out site, class-imbalance handling (24 vs 22 is near-balanced), and any deployment analysis. Outlier replacement with group means is performed before the folds, a small residual leakage path.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No formal keyword list in the extracted text. The paper's vocabulary: 'predict autism diagnosis', 'ASC biomarkers', 'automated algorithms assisting with ASC identification', 'nested Cross-Validation', 'overoptimistic performance estimates', 'statistically significantly different from random guessing'. The validation vocabulary is unusually prominent and is effectively the paper's contribution.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: The 41st Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC) 2019 - a biomedical engineering venue, technology-focused but clinically adjacent, not an autism-specific journal.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2019. The paper explicitly characterises the state of kinematic autism classification: three prior studies using tablet gameplay sensors, reach-and-throw tracking and movement imitation achieved 'high classification accuracy rates of 86.7% to 96.7%', but 'these studies used K-fold Cross-Validation, which was demonstrated to produce overoptimistic performance estimates, especially when a sample size is small' and did not test significance against chance. This is the corpus's most direct statement that its own literature's headline accuracies are methodologically inflated, and the paper's 71% is offered as the corrected estimate for a comparable task.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Learning to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder based on the Visual
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Carette R; Elbattah M; Cilia F; Dequen G; Guérin JL; Bosche J
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye-tracking and gaze
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Assistive diagnosis for early detection: transform eye-tracking scanpaths into visual representations so that ASD prediction becomes an image classification task, and demonstrate this with simple models on a limited dataset
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study, with the unit of analysis being the scanpath image rather than the participant
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session; average eye-tracking experiment duration approximately 5 minutes per participant across multiple video scenarios of varying length
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Passive viewing of videos designed to stimulate eye movement across the screen, including colourful balloons and cartoons with moving elements, plus a human presenter directing the child's attention to visible or invisible elements; additional stimuli from the SMI Experiment Center comprised static and dynamic naturalistic scenes with and without receptive language, joint attention stimuli, static faces or objects, and cartoons
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory - a quiet room at university premises with physical white barriers to reduce visual distraction; typically developing children recruited from schools in Hauts-de-France, ASD-diagnosed children examined in multidisciplinary ASD specialty clinics
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: ASD-diagnosed children were examined in multidisciplinary ASD specialty clinics, with autism intensity estimated by psychologists using the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS). For the typically developing group, parental reports of any possible concerns were carefully considered. No ADOS or ADI-R
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not reported per group; whole-sample mean 7.88 years, median 8.1 years, with distributions shown only as box plots
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: School-aged, approximately 8 years on average; exact range shown only in a box plot
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Not reported per group; whole sample 38 male (64%) / 21 female (36%)
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: CARS mean 32.97, median 34.50 across ASD participants, with the distribution shown as a box plot. Severity is used as a modelling target in the multi-label experiment, banded as Low (CARS<30), Mild (30<=CARS<36) and Severe (CARS>=36)
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developing children from French schools
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Parental reports of any possible concerns were carefully considered; no screening instrument administered
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not claimed or tested; only whole-sample age statistics are given, with no per-group breakdown or comparison
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not claimed or tested; only whole-sample gender distribution is given
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted, supported only by consideration of parental concerns
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye movements: gaze coordinates over time, rendered into images encoding both spatial path and movement dynamics
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Video viewing at approximately 60 cm from a 17-inch 1280x1024 monitor, seated alone or on a parent's lap, with five-point calibration followed by verification procedures. Participants were examined for quality of eye contact with the presenter and level of focus on other elements
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: SMI Red-m remote eye tracker at 250 Hz; 17-inch monitor at 1280x1024; SMI Experiment Center software for stimulus presentation; Python with Matplotlib for scanpath visualisation; scikit-learn for conventional classifiers; Keras for augmentation and neural networks; Azure ML Studio and ASP.NET/JavaScript for the demonstration web application
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - a new image dataset of 547 scanpath visualisations
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes - 'the dataset along with metadata files were recently published and made publicly available on the Figshare data repository', with the stated intention that it be useful for further applications and data mining
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze-derived images are low in identifiability. Both informed consent from parents and assent from the children were confirmed for all cases, and all procedures were conducted in accordance with the ethical standards of the institutional and/or national research committee and the 1964 Helsinki declaration. The released dataset comprises rendered scanpath images rather than raw video, which limits re-identification risk
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Learned representations over engineered image renderings - scanpaths encoded as colour-gradient images, then grayscaled and PCA-compressed
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Each scanpath image draws a line for every transition between consecutive gaze coordinates, with RGB components encoding movement dynamics: velocity as a black-to-red gradient, acceleration as green and jerk as blue, with values capped at one-quarter of the screen diagonal so that saccades appear yellow or white and fixations cyan. Images are vertically mirrored and limited to 200 drawn points, a threshold chosen empirically after testing 100-150 produced too few lines to discriminate the classes. Images are then scaled to 100x100, converted to grayscale by the standard luminance weighting, and reduced by PCA from 10,000 features to 50 components
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Python with Matplotlib for rendering; Keras for augmentation; scikit-learn for PCA and conventional classifiers
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None - no feature importance, saliency or ablation analysis, though qualitative inspection of example visualisations is offered
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None formally. Qualitatively the authors note that in the illustrated ASD example the participant 'had a tendency to look at the bottom of the screen, where the eye-tracking device was placed' - an observation that, if systematic, would be an apparatus-related artefact rather than a behavioural finding
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not quantified; only qualitative description of two example images
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification with dimensionality reduction, framed as image classification
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Conventional baselines - Naive Bayes, logistic regression, SVM and random forests (all approximately AUC 0.7). Neural networks - single hidden layer with 50, 200 or 500 neurons, and a two-layer 80-40 architecture, trained for 100 epochs with 20% dropout. The single-layer 200-neuron model performed best
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 10 rounds of cross-validation with AUC and its standard deviation reported. Crucially the unit is the image, not the participant: 547 images from 59 children, augmented with 2,735 synthetic samples generated by random transformations of the same visualisations, and no statement anywhere that partitioning was participant-independent. Multiple images and their augmented derivatives from the same child can therefore appear in both training and test folds
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: AUC with standard deviation across folds, ROC curves for all architectures, and a normalised confusion matrix for the multi-label severity model
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Binary classification: conventional models approximately AUC 0.70; all neural networks above 0.90, with the single-layer 200-neuron model best at approximately 0.92. Multi-label severity classification (non-ASD, low, mild, severe): approximately 83% for the single-layer model and 81% for the two-layer model, with the confusion matrix showing non-ASD discriminated well and ASD labels at least 20% lower, especially for severe ASD
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Rendering eye-tracking scanpaths as colour-coded images that encode velocity, acceleration and jerk allowed ASD prediction to be treated as an image classification problem, reaching AUC above 0.90 with a single-layer neural network - substantially better than conventional classifiers on the same data (AUC approximately 0.70). Model complexity beyond a single hidden layer gave no improvement. A finer multi-label model predicting CARS severity bands reached approximately 83% but with markedly worse performance on the ASD categories, particularly severe ASD. The scanpath image dataset was released publicly, and a demonstration web application was built to deliver the pipeline as a service.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Not identified quantitatively
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Not framed as a future-work section, but the limitations note that longer video scenarios could allow richer visual representation of gaze behaviour, and the conclusion suggests the scanpath-visualisation approach may transfer to comparable diagnostic problems and other psychological disorders
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The representational idea is genuinely creative - encoding a scanpath's spatial path and its first, second and third temporal derivatives into a single RGB image so that a generic image classifier can be applied - and the dataset release on Figshare is a real contribution that later corpus studies build on. But the reported AUC above 0.90 is not a participant-level generalisation estimate and should not be read as one. The unit of analysis is the image: 547 images from 59 children, then augmented fivefold to 2,735 additional synthetic samples derived from those same images, with 10-fold cross-validation and no statement anywhere that folds were participant-independent. Under image-level partitioning, images from the same child - and augmented copies of the very same image - will appear in both training and test sets, which is precisely the leakage mechanism that Yaneva et al. (2018) in this corpus identify as producing inflated accuracy. The augmentation makes this worse rather than better, since synthetic variants of a test image are near-duplicates. Additionally, no per-group demographics are reported at all, so age and sex confounding cannot be assessed; the ASD example is described as looking toward the bottom of the screen where the eye-tracking device sat, raising the possibility that some signal is apparatus-related; the multi-label severity target is derived from CARS, which is also the instrument establishing the diagnosis, making that experiment partly circular; and the study was funded by a commercial healthcare IT company whose relationship is acknowledged but not declared as a competing interest.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: 29 ASD-diagnosed children and 30 non-ASD children, total 59. Group sizes are reported. For the multi-label experiment the ASD group is further split by CARS severity into Low, Mild and Severe bands, making four classes. No non-autistic clinical comparison group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'individuals diagnosed with ASD', 'ASD-diagnosed children', 'ASD-diagnosed participants', 'children with ASD', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'Non-ASD'. Predominantly diagnosis-first labelling driven by the classification framing, with the notable phrasing that individuals with ASD 'typically suffer from deficits' and that symptoms 'place a considerable strain on their lives and their families' - a deficit-and-burden framing.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Reported only at whole-sample level: 59 children, 38 male (64%) and 21 female (36%), mean age 7.88 years and median 8.1 years, with age and CARS distributions shown as box plots. No per-group age means, standard deviations, ranges or sex breakdowns are given, and no matching procedure or comparability test is reported. This makes it impossible to assess whether the ASD and non-ASD groups differ in age or sex - a material gap since gaze behaviour changes markedly across childhood. The sample is school-aged (around 8 years), so despite the paper's early-detection framing it does not test the youngest ages.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: ASD-diagnosed children were examined in multidisciplinary ASD specialty clinics, with autism intensity rated by psychologists using CARS. Typically developing status rests on recruitment from mainstream schools plus careful consideration of parental reports of any possible concerns. No ADOS, ADI-R or structured screening instrument is used, and CARS serves both as the severity measure and, implicitly, as part of the diagnostic characterisation - which matters because CARS bands are later used as the multi-label prediction target.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive measures are reported for either group, and no comorbidity information. CARS is the only clinical instrument, reported as a sample-level mean and median with a box-plot distribution.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: assistive diagnosis supporting early detection, achieved by converting scanpaths into images so the problem becomes image classification.
