Main findings: neural networks exceeded AUC 0.90 (best approximately 0.92 with a single 200-neuron hidden layer) against approximately 0.70 for Naive Bayes, logistic regression, SVM and random forests on the same data; increasing model depth or width gave no further gain; and a four-class CARS-severity model reached approximately 83% overall but performed at least 20% worse on ASD categories than on non-ASD, particularly for severe ASD.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory setting - a quiet university room with white barriers to reduce visual distraction, children seated alone or on a parent's lap at approximately 60 cm. Newly collected data, with the resulting image dataset released publicly on Figshare and described in more detail in an earlier publication by the same group.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Passive video viewing lasting about 5 minutes on average, with scenarios deliberately varied in content and length to allow ocular activity to be analysed from different perspectives. Stimuli were designed to attract children (colourful balloons, cartoons) with elements whose position changes during the experiment, and some videos featured a human presenter speaking in French who attempts to direct the child's attention to visible or invisible elements. Additional SMI Experiment Center stimuli spanned static and dynamic naturalistic scenes with and without receptive language, joint attention stimuli, static faces or objects, and cartoons. A five-point calibration with subsequent verification procedures preceded recording.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single approximately 5-minute session per child with no follow-up. The data are gaze coordinates rendered into abstract images, so identifiability is low and the public release is correspondingly low-risk. Consent handling is reported carefully: both informed consent from parents and assent from the children themselves were confirmed for all cases, and procedures followed institutional and/or national research committee ethical standards and the 1964 Helsinki declaration with later amendments.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: SMI Red-m remote screen-based eye tracker at 250 Hz mounted below a 17-inch monitor at 1280x1024, with the child approximately 60 cm away; physical white barriers around the setup. Software: SMI Experiment Center for stimulus presentation; Python with Matplotlib for scanpath rendering; Keras for image augmentation and neural network training; scikit-learn for PCA and conventional classifiers; Azure ML Studio hosting the models as web services with an ASP.NET and JavaScript front end for the demonstration application.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Unusually strong on data, weaker on process. The 547-image dataset with metadata is publicly released on Figshare with the explicit intention that others reuse it, and a working demonstration application is deployed at a stated URL. The rendering procedure is described in reproducible detail - the colour-gradient encoding of velocity, acceleration and jerk, the one-quarter-diagonal cap, the vertical mirroring, the 200-point threshold and how it was chosen, the 100x100 rescaling, the grayscale luminance equation, and the PCA reduction to 50 components. What is missing: no code release, no random seeds, no statement of how cross-validation folds were partitioned, no augmentation transformation parameters beyond 'rotation, shearing', and no per-group demographics.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors in a brief limitations section: the relatively small number of participants, and the fairly short duration of the video scenarios, with longer scenarios possibly allowing a richer visual representation. Identifiable in review and more consequential: the unit of analysis is the image not the child, with 547 images from 59 children plus 2,735 augmented synthetic derivatives, and no statement that cross-validation was participant-independent - so images and their own augmented near-duplicates can span the training and test folds, which would inflate the reported AUC substantially; no per-group age or sex data at all; the qualitative observation that the ASD exemplar looked toward the bottom of the screen where the eye tracker was physically located raises the possibility of apparatus-driven signal; the multi-label experiment predicts CARS bands from data collected on children whose diagnosis was itself characterised by CARS, which is partly circular; and the work was funded by a commercial healthcare IT company, acknowledged but not declared as a competing interest.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: No dedicated future-work section. The limitations imply that longer video scenarios should be tested, and the conclusion suggests the scanpath-visualisation approach may generalise to comparable diagnostic problems and to other psychological disorders. No proposals for participant-level validation, larger or independent samples, or addressing the demographic reporting gaps.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Gaze: raw point-of-regard coordinates over time, from which velocity, acceleration and jerk are derived and encoded chromatically. Distinctively, the representation preserves the full spatiotemporal trajectory rather than aggregating into area-of-interest dwell times, which is the dominant approach elsewhere in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality, but with an internal fusion of four kinematic quantities into one image: spatial path as line geometry, velocity as the red channel, acceleration as green and jerk as blue. This packs position and its first three temporal derivatives into a single representation that a generic image classifier can consume - an elegant encoding, though the subsequent grayscale conversion collapses the three colour channels back into a single luminance value, discarding the channel separation the encoding created.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning, with the problem deliberately recast as image classification. Conventional baselines (Naive Bayes, logistic regression, SVM, random forests) are compared against feed-forward artificial neural networks of increasing capacity (single layer with 50, 200 or 500 neurons; two layers of 80 and 40), trained with 100 epochs and 20% dropout. PCA provides unsupervised dimensionality reduction. Notably no convolutional architecture is used despite the image framing, since PCA-compressed grayscale vectors are fed to fully connected layers.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A two-stage engineered-then-learned representation: scanpaths are first rendered into RGB images encoding position and its derivatives via colour gradients, then compressed by rescaling to 100x100, grayscale conversion, and PCA from 10,000 dimensions to 50 components. The classifier therefore operates on a 50-dimensional linear projection of a grayscale rendering rather than on the image directly, which is a significant loss of the spatial structure the rendering was designed to create.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: AUC with standard deviation across cross-validation folds, plotted as ROC curves for all four neural architectures, plus a normalised confusion matrix for the multi-label severity model. AUC is a reasonable primary metric, and reporting fold standard deviations is better than corpus norm. However no accuracy, sensitivity, specificity or precision is given for the binary task, and no confidence intervals, so the per-class error profile of the main result cannot be assessed.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None quantitatively. Two example visualisations are compared qualitatively, with the observation that both show high-density central regions and that the ASD exemplar tended to look toward the bottom of the screen. The confusion matrix for the multi-label model does carry an interpretable finding - that non-ASD is discriminated well while ASD categories, especially severe ASD, are at least 20% worse - which suggests the representation captures the presence of atypicality better than its gradation.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: This is the study's weakest dimension. Ten-fold cross-validation is reported with AUC standard deviations, and dropout and augmentation are used as regularisers, but the fundamental question of what constitutes a fold is never addressed: 547 images derive from 59 children and 2,735 further synthetic images derive from those 547, so unless partitioning is by participant - which is never stated - the test folds contain images from children whose other images, and augmented copies of whose images, were used in training. Augmentation performed before rather than within the fold split compounds this. There is no external validation, no held-out site, no participant-level reporting, no class-imbalance treatment (328 non-ASD vs 219 ASD images), and no permutation or significance testing. The deployed web application demonstrates practical delivery but not validity.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder, Machine Learning, Eye-tracking, Scanpath. Task vocabulary: 'assistive tools to support the diagnosis process', 'learn the eye-tracking patterns of ASD', 'visual representation', 'image classification task', 'second opinion that is considered to be less biased and reproducible'. The framing of machine learning as a less biased second opinion is a recurring justification in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: HEALTHINF 2019, part of the 12th International Joint Conference on Biomedical Engineering Systems and Technologies (BIOSTEC) - a health informatics and biomedical engineering venue, technology-focused rather than clinical, though the work is described as interdisciplinary collaboration between psychology and AI research units.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2019. The related-work section surveys the eye-tracking evidence base - shorter and less frequent saccades in high autistic traits, longer fixation on dynamic geometric images in ASD toddlers, declining eye fixation in infants aged 2 to 6 months who later developed ASD, and cohort evidence for eye tracking as an objective measure of autism risk and severity - and then the machine-learning turn, citing RNN classification of Fragile X from gaze during conversation (86-91%) and the authors' own earlier saccade-feature model on 17 children. It positions the visual-representation approach as novel: 'It is claimed that such approach has not been applied before in the context of ASD, to the best of our knowledge'. The accompanying dataset release and deployed web service also document the field's move toward shared benchmarks and demonstrable tooling around 2018-2019.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Machine Learning to Study Social Interaction Difficulties in ASD
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Georgescu AL; Koehler JC; Weiske J; Vogeley K; Koutsouleris N; Falter-Wagner C
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: Frontiers in Robotics and AI, 6, Article 132
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: High-functioning autism and Asperger syndrome, adults
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Motor and kinematics
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Proof-of-principle classification plus methodological guidance: establish whether full-body non-verbal behaviour captured during naturalistic dyadic interaction can classify autistic adults, and set out minimum methodological requirements for machine-learning applications in autism research
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Perspective article containing a cross-sectional proof-of-principle classification analysis of data from an existing social interaction study
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Five 5-minute social interaction tasks per dyad, of which four were analysed after one task was abandoned; 116 videos entered final analysis from an original 145
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Dyadic social interaction tasks: an ice-breaker task (abandoned), two debating tasks, a meal-planning task and a roleplay, conducted in pairs that were either two typically developed individuals, two autistic individuals, or one of each
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory - a room with standardised artificial lighting and fixed camera and chair geometry; autistic participants recruited from the Autism Outpatient Clinic at University Hospital Cologne, controls from university student and staff populations
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: ASD (ICD-10 F84.0 high-functioning autism or F84.5 Asperger syndrome)
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Two medical specialists independently confirmed the diagnosis in clinical interviews according to ICD-10 criteria, supplemented by extensive neuropsychological examination. Independent double confirmation is unusually strong ascertainment, though no standardised observational instrument (ADOS/ADI-R) is named
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Sample restricted to high-functioning autism and Asperger syndrome; no other comorbidity information
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developed individuals recruited online from university student and staff populations
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described; no screening instrument reported for the control group
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not reported or addressed in this paper
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not reported or addressed in this paper
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted only
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Video-derived motion energy: continuous time series of movement amount in head and body regions, converted into intrapersonal synchrony measures
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Four analysed 5-minute dyadic tasks (two debates, meal planning, roleplay) recorded in a standardised setup, with two manually drawn regions of interest per participant (head; rest of body including legs), grayscale change detected per region, time series smoothed and scaled, then cross-correlated in non-overlapping 60-second windows at time lags of plus or minus 5 seconds in 0.04 s steps
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Panasonic DV C Pro HD P2 high-definition video camera on a tripod 320 cm from chairs set 60 cm apart, under standardised artificial lighting; Motion Energy Analysis (frame differencing); rMEA package in R; NeuroMiner open-source machine-learning tool
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: No new collection for this paper - the data come from a separate interpersonal coordination study by the same group
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No, with an explicit and well-reasoned statement: 'The video datasets generated and analysed during the current study are not publicly available due this being identifiable patient data from a sample that did not consent to their data being shared in any form'
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: No - sharing is precluded by the consent obtained
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Highly sensitive - video recordings of identifiable adults in extended social interaction. Handling is exemplary: written informed consent obtained in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, local ethics committee approval from the Medical Faculty of the University of Cologne, monetary compensation of 50 Euros, participants debriefed, and data sharing explicitly refused on the grounds that participants did not consent to it. This is the only study in the corpus so far to decline data sharing on a stated consent basis rather than by silence
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Automatically computed synchrony features derived from frame-differencing motion energy
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Lagged cross-correlations between head and body movement time series - intrapersonal synchrony - computed in non-overlapping 60-second windows at lags of plus or minus 5 seconds with 0.04 s steps, yielding 1004 lagged cross-correlations per window, z-standardised and aggregated over the four conditions to give 4016 features per participant
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Motion Energy Analysis following the Ramseyer and Tschacher pipeline; rMEA (Kleinbub and Ramseyer) in R for smoothing, scaling and cross-correlation; NeuroMiner for the machine-learning pipeline
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None - no feature importance, weight inspection or ablation is reported, though a per-participant decision-score plot is provided
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported - no direction of synchrony difference between groups is given in this paper, which refers to a companion manuscript under revision for the substantive interaction findings
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification with unsupervised dimensionality reduction
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Support vector machine with linear kernel, implemented in NeuroMiner; PCA for preprocessing with the slack parameter C estimated over eight values from 0.015625 to 16
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Repeated nested k-fold cross-validation: outer cycle (CV2) of 10 folds with five permutations, inner cycle (CV1) repeated 5-by-5-fold, with participants shuffled before each fold definition. Parameter optimisation performed only in CV1 and model performance evaluated only in CV2. PCA was applied within each CV1 fold, retaining components cumulatively explaining 80% of variance, followed by feature-wise scaling to 0-1
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, AUC, and raw true/false positive and negative counts, plus a per-participant decision-score plot
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Accuracy 75.9%, sensitivity 96.6%, specificity 55.2%, AUC 0.71, with 28 true positives, 16 true negatives, 13 false positives and 1 false negative. The classifier correctly identified all but one autistic participant but misclassified 13 of 29 controls
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Intrapersonal motion synchrony - the temporal coordination between a person's own head and body movement - extracted automatically from video of naturalistic conversation classified autistic from typically developed adults at 75.9% accuracy under repeated nested cross-validation. Sensitivity was very high (96.6%, all but one autistic participant identified) but specificity poor (55.2%), so the model over-calls autism. The paper's larger purpose is methodological: it argues that most machine-learning studies in autism have used simple cross-validation, which risks selecting overly optimistic models, and that leave-one-out validation in particular produces unstable outcomes given autism's phenotypic heterogeneity - proposing repeated nested k-fold cross-validation as a minimum standard.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Not identified - the synchrony features are high-dimensional and no interpretable direction is reported
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Apply the resulting algorithm to a completely new and larger dataset and test its transdiagnostic specificity across different psychiatric conditions; combine multiple non-verbal communication parameters with clinical data such as questionnaires; extend to eye-gaze and facial expression; and move from semi-automated Motion Energy Analysis, which requires manually drawn regions of interest and so retains a subjective component, to fully automated computer-vision pose and gaze estimation - while noting that such tools' validity against standard motion capture has not yet been demonstrated and that they vary in robustness to tracking failure
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The classification result itself is modest and the sample characterisation in this paper is thin - no ages, no sexes, no matching information, all deferred to a companion manuscript under revision. What makes the paper valuable to this review is that it is simultaneously a primary study and a methodological critique of the field, and the critique is precise and correct. It identifies circularity in studies that train on clinician-derived features, notes that most autism machine-learning work uses simple cross-validation which risks 'choosing an overly optimistic model', and argues specifically that leave-one-out validation 'creates overly variable test sets, rendering model outcomes unstable' for a phenotype as heterogeneous as autism - a critique that applies directly to a large share of this corpus. It then implements the alternative it recommends: repeated nested cross-validation with PCA inside the inner fold, and reports the resulting 75.9% as 'a conservative estimate on the basis of a state-of-the-art ML approach'. The sensitivity/specificity asymmetry (96.6% vs 55.2%) is reported openly with raw counts, making clear the model achieves its accuracy by over-calling autism. The data-sharing refusal on explicit consent grounds is the most careful such statement in the corpus.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 29: high-functioning autistic adults (ICD-10 F84.0 or F84.5) and typically developed adults. Dyads were composed in three configurations - two typically developed, two autistic, or mixed - which is a design feature no other corpus study uses, since it means each participant's behaviour is measured while interacting with partners of both diagnostic statuses. No other-diagnosis group, though transdiagnostic specificity testing is named as required future work.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'autistic individuals', 'individuals with ASD', 'autistic adults', 'patients', 'typically developed (TD) individuals', 'TD adults'. Mixed identity-first and person-first, with 'typically developed' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy'. The paper also refers to autism as 'an umbrella term for neurodevelopmental conditions' and uses 'conditions' alongside 'disorder'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Only the group sizes are reported in this paper: 29 autistic and 29 typically developed adults. No ages, no age ranges, no standard deviations, no sex distribution, and no matching information or comparability testing - all deferred to a companion manuscript described as under revision. For a Perspective article this is understandable, but it means the classification result cannot be assessed for demographic confounding from this paper alone. Adults only, so no early-diagnosis relevance.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Diagnosis confirmed independently by two medical specialists in clinical interviews according to ICD-10 criteria, supplemented by extensive neuropsychological examination, with the sample restricted to F84.0 high-functioning autism and F84.5 Asperger syndrome. Independent double confirmation by two specialists is stronger than most corpus studies, though no standardised observational instrument is named. Control status is asserted with no screening instrument reported.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Extensive neuropsychological examination is stated to have supplemented the diagnostic interviews for the autistic group, but no scores are reported and none are used in analysis. No IQ, language or adaptive measures for either group, no autism severity instrument, and no comorbidity information.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: proof-of-principle demonstration that full-body non-verbal behaviour from naturalistic interaction can classify autistic adults, alongside a methodological argument for cross-validation standards. Main findings: 75.9% accuracy, 96.6% sensitivity, 55.2% specificity, AUC 0.71, with 28/29 autistic participants correctly identified but 13/29 controls misclassified. The authors present 75.9% as a deliberately conservative estimate produced by a rigorous validation procedure.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory setting with standardised lighting and fixed camera and seating geometry, but with naturalistic unscripted conversation content. The data come from an existing study on interpersonal coordination in dyadic interactions by the same group, so this is a secondary analysis for classification purposes.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Five 5-minute dyadic social interaction tasks - an ice-breaker, two debating tasks, a meal-planning task and a roleplay - with dyads composed as TD-TD, ASD-ASD or mixed. The ice-breaker task was abandoned entirely because one mixed dyad did not understand the instructions, reducing 145 videos to 116. Recording used a fixed high-definition camera 320 cm from chairs placed 60 cm apart under standardised artificial lighting. Two regions of interest per participant (head; body including legs) were drawn manually, and grayscale change within them produced two continuous movement time series per person.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; four analysed 5-minute interactions per dyad in a single session with no follow-up. The data are video of identifiable adults in extended conversation - among the most sensitive in the corpus. Handling is the most careful encountered: written informed consent under the Declaration of Helsinki, local ethics committee approval, 50 Euro compensation, debriefing, and an explicit data availability statement refusing sharing because the data are 'identifiable patient data from a sample that did not consent to their data being shared in any form'. That is a substantive privacy-protective decision rather than an unexplained absence.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: Panasonic DV C Pro HD P2 high-definition video camera on a tripod at a fixed 320 cm distance, chairs 60 cm apart, standardised artificial lighting. Software: Motion Energy Analysis following the Ramseyer and Tschacher pipeline; the rMEA R package for smoothing, scaling and lagged cross-correlation; NeuroMiner for PCA, SVM training and nested cross-validation. Notably no wearable sensors are used, which the authors flag as an advantage given hypersensitivity in autism.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Data sharing is refused on explicit consent grounds and no code is released, but the analysis is described in unusual procedural detail: the MEA pipeline and its source, the region-of-interest definitions, the cross-correlation window length (60 s), lag range (plus or minus 5 s) and step size (0.04 s), the non-overlapping window rule, the resulting feature counts (1004 lagged cross-correlations, 4016 features per participant), the PCA variance threshold (80%) and its placement inside the inner fold, the feature scaling range, the full nested cross-validation structure (10 folds x 5 permutations outer, 5-by-5 inner), and the eight C values searched. The named open-source tools (rMEA, NeuroMiner) further support re-implementation.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors: the sample size is 'rather limited', so the next step must be applying the algorithm to a completely new and larger dataset; transdiagnostic specificity across psychiatric conditions is untested; and Motion Energy Analysis retains 'a subjective component' because regions of interest are drawn manually, even though pixel-change detection is automatic. The paper also criticises the wider literature for circularity where classifiers are trained on clinician-derived features. Identifiable in review: no participant ages, sexes or matching information are reported in this paper at all; specificity of 55.2% means the model misclassifies nearly half of controls, so the headline accuracy rests on an unbalanced error profile; the dyadic design means each participant's synchrony was measured while interacting with partners of differing diagnostic status, a potential source of variance that is not analysed; one entire task was dropped because a single dyad misunderstood instructions; and the sample is high-functioning adults only.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Apply the trained algorithm to a completely new and larger dataset, and test transdiagnostic specificity across different psychiatric disturbances; combine multiple non-verbal communication parameters with clinical data such as questionnaires to improve prediction and detect cross-domain associations; extend to eye-gaze and facial expression; and move toward fully automated computer-vision pose and gaze estimation to remove the manual region-of-interest step - while cautioning that such tools' validity against standard motion capture is not yet demonstrated and that they vary in susceptibility to tracking failure and in the video types they support.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Motor behavior: whole-body non-verbal movement captured as frame-differencing motion energy in head and body regions, converted into intrapersonal synchrony - the temporal coordination between a person's own head and body movement. This is a distinctive construct in the corpus: not movement quantity, speed or trajectory, but the internal temporal coupling of one's own body segments during social interaction.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality in this analysis. The parent study measured interpersonal coordination between dyad members, but this classification uses intrapersonal synchrony only. Features from four separate interaction tasks are aggregated per participant, a form of fusion across contexts. The future-work section explicitly proposes multimodal fusion with eye-gaze, facial expression and clinical questionnaire data, and Box 1 lists 'combination of objective variables and standard diagnostic measures as input features' as a minimum requirement for reliable clinical application.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning: linear-kernel support vector machine, with PCA used unsupervised for dimensionality reduction. A single algorithm with no best-of-many comparison, consistent with the paper's methodological conservatism.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Automatically computed high-dimensional synchrony representation: 1004 lagged cross-correlations per window between head and body motion energy time series, z-standardised and aggregated across four interaction conditions into 4016 features per participant, then projected onto principal components explaining 80% of variance within each inner fold. No handcrafted kinematic parameters and no manual behavioural coding.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, AUC and raw true/false positive and negative counts, plus a decision-score plot showing each participant's position relative to the decision boundary. Reporting the raw counts (28/16/13/1) is what makes the error profile legible - the model's 75.9% accuracy comes with 96.6% sensitivity but only 55.2% specificity, meaning 13 of 29 controls were called autistic. No confidence intervals.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None from the model - no feature importance, SVM weight inspection or ablation is reported, which is a real gap given 4016 features reduced by PCA to an uninterpretable subspace. The only interpretive output is the per-participant decision-score plot, which shows the distribution of confidence and highlights that only one autistic participant fell on the wrong side of the boundary. Substantive behavioural interpretation is deferred to the companion manuscript.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The methodological centrepiece. The paper argues explicitly that most autism machine-learning studies rely on simple cross-validation, which 'increases the likelihood of choosing an overly optimistic model', and that leave-one-out validation - used by several studies it names - 'creates overly variable test sets, rendering model outcomes unstable' given autism's heterogeneity. It implements repeated nested k-fold cross-validation instead: 10 outer folds with five permutations, a 5-by-5 inner cycle, participants shuffled before each fold definition, parameter optimisation confined to the inner cycle and performance evaluation confined to the outer, with PCA fitted inside each inner fold. It then presents 75.9% as a conservative estimate obtained under this regime, and codifies the standards in a Box listing minimum requirements. What remains absent: external validation on an independent sample (named as the immediate next step), transdiagnostic specificity testing, and any deployment analysis.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: autism spectrum disorder, machine learning, nonverbal synchrony, support vector machine, motion energy analysis, classification, intrapersonal synchrony, nested cross-validation. Including 'nested cross-validation' as a keyword is itself notable and signals the paper's methodological intent. Task vocabulary: 'behavioral marker', 'automatized and objective classification', 'external validity', 'predictive psychiatry', 'transdiagnostic specificity'.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Frontiers in Robotics and AI, in the Human-Robot Interaction specialty section, published as a Perspective article - a technology venue, though the author list is dominated by psychiatry departments and the content is clinical-methodological rather than robotic.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2019. The paper provides one of the corpus's most explicit critical surveys of its own field. It notes that early machine-learning work in autism aimed at shortening ADOS and ADI-R administration by item reduction, 'yielding a classification accuracy of autism vs. typically-developing individuals of up to 99.9%', but warns that in such studies 'the features utilized for classification are still highly subjective and not independent of the respective clinician who bases the diagnostic decision on just those features (circularity)'. It catalogues the kinematic strand (96.7%, 92.5%, 93% from staged movement tasks) and observes that 'the movements under investigation were staged, thus, highly unnatural', arguing for a move to naturalistic interaction. And it identifies simple cross-validation and leave-one-out as sources of unstable and optimistic estimates. Together these amount to a diagnosis of three distinct methodological problems in the 2015-2019 literature that this corpus documents.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Phase 3 diagnostic evaluation of a smart
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Millar L; McConnachie A; Minnis H; Wilson P; Thompson L; Anzulewicz A; Sobota K; Rowe P; Gillberg C; Delafield-Butt J
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Prospective, multi-site, phase III diagnostic classification study designed according to the Standards for Reporting Diagnostic Accuracy Studies; protocol publication with results embargoed until data collection is complete
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Sub-second touch-screen and inertial sensor time series recorded during two five-minute gameplay sessions
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Target 760 children
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: This trial is the external validation. The algorithm was developed and published on a separate Polish pilot cohort and is applied here to prospectively collected, blinded data from two other countries by investigators separate from the developers.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 280 typically developing (180 Glasgow, 100 Gothenburg) and 200 with another neurodevelopmental disorder (140 Glasgow, 60 Gothenburg)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not detailed in the retrieved text beyond the ethics approvals
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Two cartoon games from the Duckie Deck series, engineered with bespoke code to collect sensor data, with children engaged for five minutes per game. The protocol sets out the paradigm's practical properties precisely, and they are the most favourable of any assessment in this review: 'this methodology required no professional training to deploy, no verbal instructions were required to engage the child, and only limited supervision was necessary. The result of the assessment was purely statistical; no subjective coding was required.' Ten minutes of play on a consumer tablet, deployable at home, in clinic or in a classroom, with no examiner training, no verbal demand on the child and no human rating in the measurement chain.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Apple iPad with its built-in capacitive touch screen, triaxial accelerometer and gyroscope; Play.Care data acquisition and analysis software from Harimata sp. z o.o.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not stated in the retrieved text
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not applicable; Play.Care is a commercial product
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: West of Scotland Research Ethics Service Committee 3 and the University of Strathclyde Ethics Committee
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Performed by the third-party Play.Care algorithm, described as an adaptation of a previously developed and published method; the feature set is not enumerated in the protocol
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Not addressed for the algorithm, which is a commercial product applied as a black box in this trial. The construct-level interpretability is nonetheless strong, since the target is motor pattern rather than an aggregate behavioural impression, and the protocol grounds this in a specific hypothesis about movement disruption as a core component of autism.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not applicable to the trial - the algorithm is locked before the prospective data are seen, which is the defining methodological feature of a phase III evaluation and is what distinguishes it from every other study in this corpus
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: The strongest design in the review, and the reasoning is set out explicitly. The protocol identifies two limitations of the pilot study and states how the trial addresses each: 'The pilot study was based on a sample of 82 children recruited from a small number of specialist day-care centres in Poland. Such limited subject recruitment is prone to selection bias and site-specific effects and precludes assessment of predictive value in population-based settings. Furthermore, the pilot study employed the same dataset to train and test the machine learning algorithm. It did so with 10 repetitions of a 10-fold cross-validation procedure that is not prone to overfitting. Nevertheless, it only trained and tested patterns on that particular dataset.' The remedy is a locked algorithm applied to 'new, blinded data obtained independently of the Play.Care software engineers and commercial concerns in an international, multisite diagnostic evaluation'. That is prospective external validation with the classifier frozen, the analysts separated from the developers, results embargoed until collection closes, two countries, three cohorts, and a prespecified primary outcome - a design no other study in this corpus approaches. The sample size justification is stated in the terms that matter for a screening instrument: if sensitivity or specificity is as high as 90% there will be 80% power to show it exceeds 83.0% and 90% power to show it exceeds 81.9%, while 'if the sensitivity (or specificity) is only 70%, there will be 91% power to show that it is below 80%. That is, if the Play.Care assessment is underperforming, which is the major concern of healthcare services, this study has a high probability of detecting it.' Powering a trial to detect underperformance, and saying so, is unique in this review.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The protocol's Strengths and Limitations box and its discussion of the pilot together give an accurate account: the pilot's 82 children came from a small number of specialist day-care centres in Poland, which is 'prone to selection bias and site-specific effects and precludes assessment of predictive value in population-based settings', and the pilot trained and tested on the same dataset even though it used repeated ten-fold cross-validation. Both are named as the reasons for the present trial.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: A planned sample of 760 children aged 30 months to 5 years 11 months across two countries, allocated in a published table: Glasgow 100 autistic, 140 other neurodevelopmental disorder and 180 typically developing; Gothenburg 180 autistic, 60 other neurodevelopmental disorder and 100 typically developing. The composition is the most important feature of the design for this review. Two hundred children with a diagnosed neurodevelopmental condition that is not autism - intellectual disability, non-verbal disability, communication disability, ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, Down's syndrome and cerebral palsy - are recruited specifically to test whether the instrument distinguishes autism from other developmental difference rather than only from typical development. Children with subclinical or secondary expressions of autism are excluded from that cohort to keep the contrast interpretable. No participant data are reported, since the protocol was published before data collection closed and the results are embargoed.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Clinical and health-economic, and unusually precise about the problem being solved. Autism is 'a childhood neurodevelopmental disorder', with UK prevalence and an aggregate annual healthcare and support cost of £28 billion cited. The diagnostic argument is specific rather than dismissive: 'Diagnosis currently relies on specialist medical expertise with diagnostic instrumentation dependent on subjectively rated scores during child observations, parent interviews and testing' - an accurate description that identifies subjectivity of scoring as the issue rather than impugning clinical judgement, and the protocol's stated ambition is to be 'an attractive and useful addition to the assessment and diagnostic toolbox', explicitly alongside ADOS-2 and ADI-R rather than in place of them. Early identification is framed in terms of what it enables for families - 'opportunity to adjust' and access to healthcare intervention and children's services - rather than in terms of treatment or cure. No autistic person or organisation is reported as involved in the design.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Not reportable, since no participants had been analysed. The design nonetheless specifies more clinical characterisation than almost any completed study in this corpus: parents of children in both clinical cohorts complete the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, the ESSENCE Questionnaire, and either the Adaptive Behavior Assessment System-3 or the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales-II, so behavioural difficulties, neurodevelopmental symptom breadth and adaptive functioning will all be available alongside the diagnostic label. The pilot study on which the trial builds used age- and gender-matched controls, and the age window is tightly bounded at 30 months to 5 years 11 months.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Clinical diagnosis of autism made independently of the study on DSM-5 criteria or the equivalent ICD-10 framework, against which the algorithm's blinded classification will be compared once data collection closes. Two features distinguish this from every other reference standard in the review. The comparison is prospective and blinded - the classifier is locked and applied to data 'obtained independently of the Play.Care software engineers and commercial concerns', with results embargoed until collection is complete - so the index test cannot be tuned to the labels. And the standard is supplemented rather than replaced by questionnaire data: SDQ, ESSENCE and an adaptive behaviour scale are collected for both clinical cohorts, so a positive or negative classification can be examined against symptom breadth and adaptive functioning rather than only against a binary label.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Planned and comprehensive. The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, the ESSENCE Questionnaire and the Adaptive Behavior Assessment System-3 or Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales-II are all administered to parents of children in the autistic and other-neurodevelopmental-disorder cohorts. That combination gives a behavioural-difficulty measure, a neurodevelopmental symptom-breadth measure and an adaptive-functioning measure alongside the diagnostic label, which is the apparatus needed to ask whether the instrument's output tracks severity or only category - the analysis this review has repeatedly found missing in completed studies whose data would have supported it.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The aim is to test, under phase III conditions, whether a tablet-based serious game can identify autism in preschoolers - specifically whether the 93% accuracy obtained in an 82-child Polish pilot survives prospective, blinded, multi-site evaluation against clinical diagnosis. The primary outcome is sensitivity and specificity for distinguishing autistic from typically developing children; the secondary outcome is accuracy in distinguishing autistic children from those with other neurodevelopmental disorders. No results are reported: the trial is registered as NCT03438994 with status 'Pre-results' and 'the results are blind until data collection is complete'. The protocol's substantive contribution to this review is therefore methodological, and it is considerable - it is the only study in the corpus that locks its algorithm before seeing the evaluation data, separates the analysts from the developers, prespecifies sensitivity and specificity as primary outcomes, powers the study to detect underperformance, recruits a non-autistic clinical comparison group, registers prospectively and publishes the protocol in advance.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Two sites, Glasgow and Gothenburg, with recruitment through NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde Specialist Children's Services, other specialist children's centres, nurseries and schools, and via two streams for the clinical cohorts - children receiving a positive diagnosis following an NHS clinic assessment, and children already diagnosed. Multi-site international recruitment is itself a design feature aimed at the pilot's acknowledged weakness, that a sample drawn from 'a small number of specialist day-care centres in Poland' is 'prone to selection bias and site-specific effects'. The assessment is intended for use 'in the home, clinic or classroom', so the deployment envelope is broad and the trial's setting is the referral pathway rather than a research laboratory. The residual limitation, not stated, is that recruitment through specialist services and existing diagnoses means predictive value at population prevalence will still not be directly estimable.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Two commercially available children's cartoon games from the Duckie Deck series, engineered with bespoke code to capture touch-screen and inertial sensor data, played for five minutes each. This is the most deployable paradigm in the review and the protocol states its properties exactly: the method 'required no professional training to deploy, no verbal instructions were required to engage the child, and only limited supervision was necessary. The result of the assessment was purely statistical; no subjective coding was required.' Four consequences follow that no other included paradigm achieves together. There is no examiner, so examiner variability is eliminated rather than merely controlled. There is no verbal demand, so the assessment reaches pre-verbal and minimally verbal children whom the language-based measures in this review cannot assess. There is no human rating anywhere in the chain, so inter-rater reliability is not a consideration. And the apparatus is a consumer tablet running a children's game, so ten minutes in a nursery or a living room produces the data. Against this, what the child is doing is playing a game rather than interacting socially, so the construct measured is motor control rather than reciprocity - which the protocol presents as a deliberate choice.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Prospective and cross-sectional at the level of the index test, with each child assessed once, and prospective in the trial sense that the algorithm is fixed before any evaluation data are collected. Ethics approval was obtained from the West of Scotland Research Ethics Service Committee 3 and the University of Strathclyde Ethics Committee. The competing-interest handling is the most thorough in this review and is worth recording in full: the academic authors sit on the trial steering and management committees and declare no financial interest in the product or in the funding company, while two coauthors are board members of Harimata sp. z o.o., which intends to commercialise the technology, and hold options vesting in it. The funding is a subcontract from that company under a Horizon 2020 SME Instrument grant. A commercially sponsored diagnostic evaluation in which the analysis is blinded to the developers, the academic investigators hold no equity, and the governance structure is stated, is exactly what this review has found missing elsewhere - most notably in the commercially funded cry-analysis study, whose disclosure is comparably complete but whose design provides none of these separations.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: An Apple iPad and two children's games. The sensing is entirely built in - capacitive touch screen for contact kinematics, triaxial accelerometer and gyroscope for device movement - so nothing is purchased, worn, calibrated or maintained beyond a consumer tablet. Set against the eye trackers, depth cameras, thermal cameras, EEG amplifiers, force plates and MRI scanners charted elsewhere in this review, this is the lowest equipment barrier of any instrumented approach here, and it is the reason the protocol can propose deployment 'in the home, clinic or classroom'.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: The most complete protocol reporting in the corpus. Specified: the design and its STARD basis; the trial registration number and its pre-results status; both sites with participant allocation broken down by cohort and site in a table; inclusion and exclusion criteria for all three groups in a second table, including the exclusion of subclinical or secondary autism expressions from the comparison-disorder group; the age window; both recruitment streams; the games, their source and their duration; the sensor modalities; the third-party algorithm with its provenance in a published pilot; the questionnaire battery for the clinical cohorts; primary and secondary outcomes; the sample size justification with explicit power figures; both ethics approvals; the funding source with grant number; an itemised competing-interest statement distinguishing academic from commercial authors; and author contributions naming who performed the sample size calculations and who conducted technical development. What cannot be reported is any result.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The protocol's account of its predecessor's limitations is the most methodologically literate passage in this corpus, and it names both failure modes that this review has documented repeatedly. On selection: the pilot's 82 children came from 'a small number of specialist day-care centres in Poland. Such limited subject recruitment is prone to selection bias and site-specific effects and precludes assessment of predictive value in population-based settings.' On evaluation: 'the pilot study employed the same dataset to train and test the machine learning algorithm. It did so with 10 repetitions of a 10-fold cross-validation procedure that is not prone to overfitting. Nevertheless, it only trained and tested patterns on that particular dataset.' That second sentence is important - it concedes that repeated cross-validation, which most studies in this review treat as sufficient, does not establish generalisation beyond the dataset it is computed on. Both concerns are then addressed structurally rather than rhetorically. Two design points remain unstated: recruitment through specialist services means population-prevalence predictive value will still not be directly estimable, and the algorithm remains a commercial black box, so a positive result would show that the instrument works without showing what it measures.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Completion of recruitment and comparison of the blinded classifications against medical diagnosis, with dissemination through peer-reviewed publication and conferences. For the review, the protocol's value is that it specifies in advance what a credible answer would look like, which makes any eventual result interpretable in a way that retrospective studies cannot be.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Motor pattern during gameplay, chosen deliberately in preference to social and emotional variables - the protocol lists as a strength that 'a computational analysis of motor pattern variables, rather than social and emotional variables, is employed', grounded in the hypothesis that 'an underlying movement disruption may be a core component of autism spectrum disorder and a new, accessible early biomarker'. The measurement is sub-second: touch-screen contact kinematics and triaxial inertial signals sampled while a child plays. Three properties make this construct choice significant for the synthesis. Motor control is measurable without any social demand, so it does not require the child to engage with a person, which is both an advantage in accessibility and a limitation in construct coverage. It is measurable without language, reaching the pre-verbal and minimally verbal children that the transcript- and conversation-based measures in this review cannot assess. And it is measurable without human rating, so the entire chain from behaviour to classification is instrumented - the protocol notes that in the pilot 'the result of the assessment was purely statistical; no subjective coding was required'. The motor hypothesis aligns with the one-legged-standing and skeleton-movement studies charted elsewhere here, which target postural and gait control on similar reasoning.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Two synchronous sensor streams from a single consumer device - touch-screen contact patterns and triaxial accelerometer plus gyroscope - capturing both what the child does to the screen and how the device moves while they do it. The fusion is inherent to the platform rather than engineered, which is part of the design's practical appeal: no synchronisation, no calibration and no additional hardware is required to obtain two complementary views of the same motor behaviour.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A commercial third-party classifier, Play.Care, described as an adaptation of the algorithm developed and published from the pilot study. Its internals are not restated in the protocol, and for the trial's purposes this is by design: the point of a phase III evaluation is that the instrument is locked and applied unchanged to new data, so the algorithm's specification belongs to the development phase rather than to the evaluation. The trade-off is that the trial can establish whether the instrument works without establishing what it measures - a limitation the protocol does not name.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Sub-second touch-screen and inertial time series from two five-minute gameplay sessions per child. The feature set derived from these is not enumerated, being internal to the commercial product.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Sensitivity and specificity as prespecified primary outcomes for the autism-versus-typical comparison, and accuracy for the autism-versus-other-neurodevelopmental-disorder comparison as a secondary outcome. Choosing sensitivity and specificity rather than accuracy as the primary measures is correct for a diagnostic instrument and is done by almost no other study in this corpus, most of which report accuracy alone on balanced designs. The sample size justification is expressed in the same terms and is worth quoting for the synthesis: if sensitivity or specificity is as high as 90%, the study has 80% power to show it exceeds 83.0% and 90% power to show it exceeds 81.9%; and 'if the sensitivity (or specificity) is only 70%, there will be 91% power to show that it is below 80%. That is, if the Play.Care assessment is underperforming, which is the major concern of healthcare services, this study has a high probability of detecting it.' Powering a study to detect its own instrument's failure, and stating that this is the point, is unique in this review.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Not addressed for the algorithm, which is applied as a commercial black box. The construct-level interpretability is nonetheless strong: the target is motor pattern rather than an aggregate behavioural impression, grounded in a specific and falsifiable hypothesis about movement disruption, so a positive result would be interpretable at the level of the construct even if not at the level of the model.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The methodological benchmark for this review, and the only design in the corpus that closes every failure mode the synthesis documents elsewhere. The algorithm is locked before the evaluation data exist, so no tuning to the labels is possible. The data are collected prospectively and 'independently of the Play.Care software engineers and commercial concerns', so the developers cannot influence the evaluation. Results are embargoed - 'the results are blind until data collection is complete' - so no interim selection can occur. Recruitment spans two countries and multiple streams, addressing the site-specific effects the protocol identifies in its own pilot. Sensitivity and specificity are prespecified as primary outcomes rather than accuracy. A non-autistic clinical comparison group of 200 children is recruited specifically to test differential diagnosis, prespecified as a secondary outcome. The trial is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov before results exist and the protocol is published in advance. And the sample size is justified with power calculations framed around detecting underperformance rather than demonstrating success. Most significantly for this review, the protocol states explicitly why the pilot's evaluation was insufficient despite using repeated cross-validation: it 'only trained and tested patterns on that particular dataset'. That sentence identifies the exact inferential gap that most studies in this corpus leave open - cross-validation within a dataset establishes internal consistency, not generalisation - and the trial exists to close it. The one residual limitation is that recruitment through specialist services and existing diagnoses means predictive value at population prevalence will not be directly estimable even on completion.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No formal keyword list appears in the retrieved text. Terms carried through the protocol: serious game, smart tablet, inertial sensors, movement disruption, motor pattern, biomarker, diagnostic classification, phase III, STARD, sensitivity, specificity, other neurodevelopmental disorder.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: BMJ Open 2019;9:e026226, Protocol section, open access under CC BY-NC; received 6 September 2018, revised 26 March 2019, accepted 1 May 2019, first published 16 July 2019. A general medical journal with a dedicated protocol section, and the venue's requirements are visible throughout: STARD-based design, trial registration with status, a Strengths and Limitations box, tabulated participant allocation and eligibility criteria, explicit power calculations, named ethics committees, an itemised competing-interest statement distinguishing academic from commercial authors, and author contributions specifying individual roles. Publishing a diagnostic protocol before results exist is the practice that makes selective reporting detectable, and this is the only instance of it in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published July 2019 by a collaboration between the University of Strathclyde, the University of Glasgow, the University of Aberdeen, the Gillberg Neuropsychiatry Centre at Gothenburg, and Harimata sp. z o.o., funded through a Horizon 2020 SME Instrument subcontract. For this review the article is the methodological benchmark against which the rest of the corpus can be read, and it earns that position on six counts. The algorithm is locked before the evaluation data exist and applied by investigators separate from its developers, with results embargoed until collection closes - so none of the tuning, selection or leakage mechanisms documented across the other 130-odd included studies can operate. Sensitivity and specificity are prespecified as primary outcomes rather than accuracy. A 200-child cohort with other neurodevelopmental disorders is recruited to test differential diagnosis as a prespecified secondary outcome, making this the only powered study in the corpus to address the question the free-play and robot studies name as the hardest and that the ADOS-versus-schizophrenia study shows the field's gold-standard instrument failing. The sample size is justified with power calculations framed around detecting underperformance, with the protocol stating that 'if the Play.Care assessment is underperforming, which is the major concern of healthcare services, this study has a high probability of detecting it'. The commercial interest is managed structurally, with academic investigators holding no equity, company board members with vesting options identified individually, and the analysis blinded to the developers. And the protocol is registered and published before any result exists. Beyond the design, one passage deserves to be carried into the synthesis verbatim, because it states the inferential problem that most of this corpus leaves unexamined: the pilot 'employed the same dataset to train and test the machine learning algorithm. It did so with 10 repetitions of a 10-fold cross-validation procedure that is not prone to overfitting. Nevertheless, it only trained and tested patterns on that particular dataset.' Repeated cross-validation establishes consistency within a dataset and not generalisation beyond it - and the entire trial exists because its authors took that distinction seriously about a 93% figure of their own. What the article cannot supply is a result: it is registered as NCT03438994 with status 'Pre-results', and no participant data are reported.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Predicting Autism Diagnosis using Image with Fixations and Synthetic Saccade Patterns
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Wu C; Liaqat S; Cheung SC; Chuah CN; Ozonoff S
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2019 IEEE International Conference on Multimedia & Expo
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye-tracking and gaze
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Screening for early identification: classify ASD from free-viewing scanpath data, motivated explicitly by the gap between symptom onset in the first years of life and a mean US diagnosis age above 4, with fewer than 25% diagnosed before age 3
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional classification study on a shared benchmark with an organiser-provided held-out test set; entry to the Saliency4ASD Grand Challenge
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Each child viewed each image at original full resolution for 3 seconds
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Free viewing of natural images
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Not reported - the data come from a challenge dataset and the original acquisition setting is not described
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Analysis conducted in the United States (UC Davis, University of Kentucky); origin of the source data not stated
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Not reported - class labels are inherited from the challenge dataset with no diagnostic instrument, criteria or procedure described
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 14 children with ASD viewed each image (the total number of distinct ASD participants is not stated)
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Mean 8 years; range 5-12 years for the ASD group
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developing children, 14 per image
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 14 children viewed each image; total distinct participants not stated
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not reported or addressed; only the ASD group's age range and mean are given, with no control equivalent
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed - no gender data for either group
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted by dataset label only
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye movements: scanpath fixation coordinates and durations during free viewing, combined with the stimulus images themselves
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Free viewing of 300 natural images for 3 seconds each; the analysis pipeline additionally generates synthetic reference scanpaths for every image using a computational saliency model
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Tobii T120 eye tracker with a 17-inch monitor (per the source dataset); STAR-FC multi-saccade generator for synthetic scanpaths; ResNet-18 backbones; PyTorch on a Titan XP GPU
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: No - uses the Saliency4ASD Grand Challenge dataset
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes in effect - a public challenge benchmark, cited but with no access details given in this paper
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Low sensitivity - fixation coordinates over public stimulus images. No ethics, consent or data-provenance statement appears in this paper, which is common for secondary use of a released benchmark but is not stated as such
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Two contrasting representations: handcrafted scanpath-comparison features against a synthetic typical baseline, and learned convolutional features over rendered fixation channels
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Synthetic saccade approach: ten aligned points from the real scanpath and ten from a STAR-FC synthetic scanpath (aligned by dynamic time warping, with the synthetic scanpath's first central fixation removed and all coordinates scaled to image dimensions), plus total viewing duration, number of fixations, mean and variance of fixation duration, and three trajectory distance measures between real and synthetic paths (dynamic time warping, Hausdorff, Frechet). The small model uses only the 7 high-level features; the full model uses a 47-dimensional vector adding 20 real and 20 synthetic coordinate values. Image-based approach: the stimulus image plus 33 channels, one per data point, each all-zero except for the duration value at the fixation location, then Gaussian-filtered or dilated to a 5-pixel radius to avoid extreme sparsity
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: STAR-FC generative saccade model; dynamic time warping alignment; ResNet-18 (pretrained, one branch frozen); PyTorch
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None - no feature importance or ablation beyond comparing the small (7-feature) and full (47-feature) synthetic saccade models
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None named, though the small 7-feature model outperformed the 47-feature model on both validation and test sets, indicating the aggregate statistics and distance measures carried more usable signal than the raw coordinate sequences
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported - no behavioral difference between groups is characterised
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised deep learning
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Two fully connected networks for the synthetic saccade approach: a small model with eight layers of seven neurons each (492 trainable parameters, batch normalisation at input, SELU activations, 200 epochs, binary cross-entropy with L2 regularisation, Adam, batch size 128), and a deeper 10-layer model expanding to 1024 neurons and back down (1,402,560 trainable parameters, batch normalisation and 0.3 dropout throughout, SELU, 300 epochs, Adam at learning rate 0.001, batch size 32). Image-based approach: two ResNet-18 branches - one frozen and pretrained for the image, one with a 33-channel first convolution for the fixation channels - each producing a 512-dimensional vector, concatenated to 1024 dimensions and classified, totalling approximately 11.3 million trainable parameters
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Two-stage. An internal split partitioned by image - 240 training images with 5542 scanpaths and 60 testing images with 1411 scanpaths - which is image-independent but not participant-independent. Then evaluation on the organiser's held-out test set of 100 images whose labels were withheld. Data augmentation (colour jitter, fixation location jitter up to 20 pixels, duration scaling by a random coefficient in [0.75, 1.25], random Gaussian sigma in [0.1, 2], horizontal flips) was applied to alleviate overfitting
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC, reported for all three model variants on both the internal validation split and the organiser's blind test set
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Internal validation: synthetic saccade (small) 65.41% accuracy, 0.66 sensitivity, 0.65 specificity, 0.69 AUC; synthetic saccade (full) 63%, 0.69, 0.66, 0.66; image-based 61.62%, 0.60, 0.64, 0.63. Organiser's blind test set: synthetic saccade (small) 54.15%, 0.741 sensitivity, 0.351 specificity, 0.546 AUC; synthetic saccade (full) 53.88%, 0.807, 0.282, 0.545; image-based 55.13%, 0.635, 0.471, 0.553. Every model lost 6-11 accuracy points and 0.09-0.14 AUC on the blind test set, with specificity collapsing from around 0.65 to 0.28-0.47
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Two deep-learning approaches to classifying ASD from free-viewing scanpaths - one comparing each real scanpath against a computationally generated 'typical' baseline, one rendering fixations as image channels for a two-branch CNN - reached 61-65% accuracy on an internal image-partitioned split but only 54-55% on the organiser's blind test set, with AUC falling to 0.545-0.553 and specificity collapsing to 0.28-0.47. The authors attribute the gap to imbalanced training and test distributions and insufficient training images. The smallest model, with 492 parameters and only seven aggregate features, performed best on internal validation and essentially matched the 11.3-million-parameter CNN on the blind test.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None identified
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Not stated - the paper has no future-work section, noting only that the performance gap between validation and test sets may reflect distributional imbalance and a shortage of training images
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The most valuable feature of this paper for the present review is that it reports both an internal-split result and a blind held-out result for the same three models, and the gap is large and consistent: 65.41% falls to 54.15%, 63% to 53.88%, 61.62% to 55.13%, with AUC dropping to barely above 0.5 and specificity collapsing from around 0.65 to as low as 0.28. This is a direct measurement of how much an internally-validated gaze classification result overstates blind performance, on the same data, with the same models - and it is the kind of comparison almost no other study in the corpus provides. The authors report it plainly and offer a reasonable diagnosis. The synthetic-baseline idea is also genuinely novel within this corpus: rather than learning what autistic gaze looks like, the model measures how far a scanpath deviates from a computationally simulated typical viewer, which sidesteps the need to characterise autistic gaze directly. Weaknesses are those of the benchmark and the format: no participant counts, ages for one group only, no genders, no diagnostic information, and an internal split partitioned by image rather than by participant, so the same child's scanpaths appear in both internal training and validation. The paper also cites, without endorsing, the 92% adult result it builds on and correctly notes it 'may not be directly applicable to gaze patterns from children'.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups by dataset label - ASD and typically developing - with 14 of each viewing every image. The total number of distinct participants is never stated, only the per-image viewer counts, so the actual sample size is unrecoverable from this paper. No other-diagnosis group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'people on the autism spectrum', 'ASD subjects', 'typically developed (TD) viewers', 'neurotypical individuals', 'children who develop typically'. Mixed but generally neutral, with 'neurotypical' and 'typically developed' used rather than 'normal' or 'healthy'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Sparse. 14 ASD and 14 TD children viewed each of 300 images, but the number of distinct children is not reported. Age is given only for the ASD group: 5 to 12 years, mean 8. No control age data, no gender data for either group, no matching procedure and no comparability testing. Given that gaze behaviour changes substantially between ages 5 and 12, and that no control ages are reported at all, demographic confounding cannot be assessed.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not reported. Class labels are inherited from the Saliency4ASD challenge dataset with no description of diagnostic instrument, criteria or procedure for either group.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None reported. No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or severity measures, and no comorbidity information - consistent with the absence of participant metadata in the challenge dataset as used here.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: an easy-to-use ASD screening tool for infants and toddlers, motivated by the gap between early symptom emergence and a mean US diagnosis age above 4 with fewer than 25% diagnosed before age 3. Main findings: internal validation accuracies of 61.62-65.41% with AUC 0.63-0.69, falling on the organiser's blind test set to 53.88-55.13% with AUC 0.545-0.553 and specificity as low as 0.282. The 492-parameter model performed best on validation and was matched by the 11.3-million-parameter CNN on the blind test.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Setting not reported - entirely secondary analysis of the Saliency4ASD benchmark. The source dataset used a Tobii T120 eye tracker with a 17-inch monitor, but no room, distance, calibration or session details are given.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Free viewing of 300 natural images, each shown at original full resolution for 3 seconds. The paper adds a computational task of its own: generating a synthetic 'typical viewer' scanpath for every image using STAR-FC, a multi-saccade generator that fixates centrally, applies a retinal transform with anisotropic blurring, combines peripheral low-level and central high-level conspicuity streams into a priority map with inhibition of return, and iterates.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; 3 seconds of viewing per image with no temporal or longitudinal component. The data are fixation coordinates over public stimulus images, so re-identification risk is minimal. No ethics approval, consent or data-provenance statement appears - understandable for secondary use of a released challenge dataset, but not acknowledged as such.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition hardware used by these authors; the source data came from a Tobii T120 eye tracker with a 17-inch monitor. Analysis: STAR-FC for synthetic scanpath generation; dynamic time warping for alignment; ResNet-18 pretrained backbones; PyTorch on a Titan XP GPU. Notably the hyperparameters are reported in full for all three models - layer counts, neuron counts, activations, dropout, optimiser, learning rate, batch size, epochs and trainable parameter counts - which is better than corpus norm.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Mixed but above average for a workshop paper. The source dataset is a public benchmark with an organiser-defined blind test set, so results are comparable against other entrants. All three model architectures are specified in reproducible detail including trainable parameter counts, and the augmentation regime is fully described (colour jitter, up to 20-pixel location jitter, duration scaling in [0.75, 1.25], random Gaussian sigma in [0.1, 2], horizontal flips, with affine transforms deliberately excluded to avoid pushing fixations out of frame). What is missing: no code release, no random seeds, no participant counts, no STAR-FC configuration details, and no statement of how the 240/60 image split was drawn.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors only briefly: 'The performance gap may be caused by the imbalanced distribution of training and test dataset and lacking of training images'. They also note, when citing the prior 92% adult result, that it 'may not be directly applicable to gaze patterns from children' - a caution about transfer that few corpus papers offer about their own antecedents. Identifiable in review: the internal split is partitioned by image, not by participant, so the same child's scanpaths appear in both internal training and validation, which is the most likely reason internal accuracy exceeds blind test accuracy by 6-11 points; the number of distinct participants is never stated; no control ages, no genders, no diagnostic information; specificity on the blind test collapses to 0.282-0.471, meaning the models achieve their apparent sensitivity largely by over-calling ASD; and the unit of analysis is the scanpath rather than the person, so no person-level estimate exists.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: None proposed. The paper closes by noting the validation-to-test performance gap and its possible causes without setting out future work, consistent with its four-page challenge-entry format.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Gaze: fixation coordinates and durations during free viewing of natural scenes. The distinguishing conceptual move is that gaze is not analysed in isolation but relative to a computationally simulated typical scanpath, so the measured quantity is deviation from a modelled norm rather than an absolute gaze property.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Two forms of fusion. In the synthetic saccade approach, real and synthetic scanpaths are aligned by dynamic time warping and concatenated along with aggregate duration statistics and three trajectory distance measures - fusing observed behaviour with a model-generated reference. In the image-based approach, a two-branch architecture separately encodes the stimulus image (frozen pretrained ResNet-18) and the fixation channels (ResNet-18 with a 33-channel input layer), concatenating their 512-dimensional outputs into a 1024-dimensional vector - fusing stimulus content with gaze behaviour. Both are stimulus-plus-behaviour fusions rather than multi-behavioural fusions.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised deep learning throughout. Fully connected networks of two capacities for the synthetic saccade approach, and a dual-branch convolutional architecture built on pretrained ResNet-18 for the image-based approach. STAR-FC, a computational saliency and saccade generation model, is used upstream as a reference generator rather than as a classifier. No conventional machine-learning comparators are included.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Two contrasting representations tested side by side. First, handcrafted: aligned coordinate pairs plus duration statistics plus three trajectory distances, in 7- and 47-dimensional variants. Second, learned: each fixation rendered as a sparse image channel carrying its duration at its location, Gaussian-smoothed to counter sparsity, with 33 channels stacked in temporal order - an unusual encoding that preserves both fixation order (by channel index) and duration (by value) while letting a convolutional network read spatial position directly rather than from coordinates.
