custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for all three models on both the internal validation split and the organiser's blind test set. Reporting the full metric set twice, on two evaluation regimes, is what makes this paper informative: the sensitivity-specificity asymmetry on the blind test (0.807 sensitivity against 0.282 specificity for the full synthetic saccade model) shows the models are largely defaulting to the ASD label, which a single accuracy figure would conceal.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No feature importance, saliency analysis or ablation beyond the small-versus-full model comparison, and no behavioral property is identified as characteristic of autistic gaze. The finding that the 7-feature model outperforms the 47-feature model on validation and nearly matches the 11.3-million-parameter CNN on the blind test is interpretable evidence that the aggregate statistics and deviation-from-typical distances carry most of the usable signal, but this is not developed.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The paper's chief contribution to this review. Evaluation is performed twice: on an internal split partitioned by image (240 train, 60 test) and on an organiser-held blind test set of 100 images. The consistent 6-11 point accuracy drop and 0.09-0.14 AUC drop between the two regimes constitutes a direct measurement of internal-validation optimism on the same models and data. Overfitting is otherwise controlled by an extensive augmentation regime, dropout, L2 regularisation and batch normalisation, and the frozen pretrained image branch limits capacity. Absent: participant-level partitioning at any stage, cross-validation, permutation testing, class-imbalance handling despite the collapsing specificity, and any calibration or deployment analysis.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: Autism Spectrum Disorders, Visual Saliency, Deep Learning. Task vocabulary: 'screening tool', 'ASD risk during infancy', 'atypical visual attention', 'synthetic saccade', 'holistic automated diagnosis tool'. The early-intervention framing is prominent - 'squandering years of potential intervention when the brain is most plastic'.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: IEEE International Conference on Multimedia and Expo Workshops (ICMEW) 2019, as an entry to the Saliency4ASD Grand Challenge - a multimedia and computer-vision venue, not an autism or clinical venue.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2019. The paper documents the state of gaze-based autism classification concisely: atypical visual attention 'sometimes emerged even before the onset of the disorder', with delayed attentional disengagement in infants correlating with later toddlerhood diagnosis, but 'a holistic automated diagnosis tool remain elusive'. It cites the 92% accuracy reported for deep-network gaze classification in 20 high-functioning ASD and 19 typically developed adults and immediately qualifies that this 'may not be directly applicable to gaze patterns from children' - one of the few instances in the corpus of a paper explicitly discounting a headline result it builds upon. The existence of the Saliency4ASD challenge itself evidences the field's move toward shared benchmarks with blind evaluation around 2019.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Recognition Of Atypical Behavior In Autism Diagnosis From Video Using Pose Estimation Over Time
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Vyas K; Ma R; Rezaei B; Liu S; Neubauer M; Ploetz T; Oberleitner R; Ostadabbas S
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Mixed cohort of children with and without ASD
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Motor and kinematics (video pose)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Automatic detection of atypical behaviour from home video as a route to ASD prediction, with explicit design requirements that any practical algorithm be 'cost-efficient and unobtrusive in order to be employed in child's natural living environment for long-term behavioral monitoring purposes'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional classification study on an industry-collected annotated video corpus; the unit of analysis is the 10-second behavioural episode
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Videos range from 2 to 10 minutes; each labelled time stamp is expanded into a 10-second episode taking 8 seconds before and 2 seconds after the stamp, giving at most 301 frames at 30 fps
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Unstructured everyday home activities recorded by parents, spanning common categories of 'play alone', 'play with others', 'meal time' and 'parents' concerns'
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Home - videos recorded by parents in the child's own environment and submitted to Behavior Imaging's NODA remote autism assessment platform for expert review
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Not reported at participant level. Expert physicians annotated time stamps within videos as showing typical or atypical behaviour; no diagnostic instrument, criteria or per-child diagnostic status is described, and the paper does not state how many children contributed or how many had ASD
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: Not reported - the dataset is described as videos 'collected from children with and without ASD' with no participant counts
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes in principle - children without ASD contributed videos - but no separate control group is characterised
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not reported or addressed
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not reported or addressed
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not characterised
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Video: full-body pose keypoint trajectories over time, encoded as motion images
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Parent-recorded home videos of daily activities; expert physicians tagged time stamps of observed typical or atypical behaviour; each tagged moment expanded to a 10-second episode and processed through pose estimation, imputation and motion encoding
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Parent recording devices (unspecified); Behavior Imaging's NODA remote assessment platform; 2D Mask R-CNN with a ResNet base for pose estimation, retrained on a manually annotated children's pose dataset; particle filter for non-linear state estimation; PoTion representation generator; a convolutional binary classifier; Inception V3 for the baseline comparison
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: The NODA video corpus is industry-collected and provided to the authors; a manually annotated children's pose dataset was created for retraining. Neither is described as released, though the authors state the method code will be released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement for the video corpus
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Highly sensitive - parent-recorded home videos of identifiable children during everyday family activities including mealtimes, transmitted to a commercial company and then to an academic laboratory. No ethics approval statement, no parental consent statement and no anonymization or data-protection provision appears anywhere in the paper. The commercial provenance is disclosed as a collaboration
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Learned convolutional features over an engineered pose-motion image representation
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 15 body keypoints per frame (upper-head, nose, upper-neck, left and right shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees and ankles), imputed where missing, then encoded as a PoTion image: a 12x12 Gaussian kernel with variance 1.0 is placed at each keypoint to form a heatmap, heatmaps are colourised by body region (red for head, nose and neck; green for shoulders, elbows and wrists; blue for hips, knees and ankles) with colour intensity increasing from the first to the last frame of the episode, and all colourised heatmaps are temporally aggregated into a single 256x256x3 RGB image
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Retrained 2D Mask R-CNN pose estimator; particle filter imputation; modified PoTion representation generator
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None - no feature importance or saliency analysis, though two ablations are reported (imputation method and representation type)
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported - no behavioural characteristic distinguishing typical from atypical episodes is identified
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised deep learning over an engineered spatiotemporal representation
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: 2D Mask R-CNN (ResNet base, region proposal network, RoI Align, classification and regression heads, plus a keypoint estimation head replacing instance segmentation) retrained for child pose; particle filter for non-linear state estimation of missing keypoints; a convolutional binary classifier taking 256x256x3 PoTion images. Baseline: a modified single-frame approach fine-tuning Inception V3 on individual frames with majority voting to the episode level
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A train/test split on the episode corpus, with results reported on 'our test dataset'. The partitioning basis is not stated - there is no indication whether episodes from the same video, or videos from the same child, were kept within one side of the split, and since 8349 episodes derive from only 555 videos, multiple episodes per video are certain
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall and AUC, reported across three imputation conditions and against the RGB baseline; separately, the percentage of frames successfully annotated with pose is compared before and after retraining
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Proposed approach: 0.72 accuracy, 0.72 precision, 0.92-0.93 recall, 0.66 AUC. Imputation ablation: no interpolation 0.72/0.72/0.93/0.64; linear 0.72/0.72/0.92/0.66; particle filter 0.72/0.72/0.93/0.66 - accuracy, precision and recall are effectively identical across all three, with AUC differing by only 0.02. RGB single-frame baseline: 0.66 accuracy, 0.70 precision, 0.77 recall, 0.62 AUC. Retraining the pose estimator increased successfully annotated frames by 9-14%
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Full-body pose trajectories encoded as PoTion motion images classified expert-labelled atypical versus typical 10-second behavioural episodes from home video at 0.72 accuracy with 0.92 recall but only 0.66 AUC, outperforming a conventional RGB single-frame baseline (0.66 accuracy, 0.62 AUC). Retraining the pose estimator on manually annotated child poses raised successful frame annotation by 9-14%. Notably, the imputation ablation shows essentially no benefit - accuracy, precision and recall are identical with no interpolation, linear interpolation and particle filtering, and AUC differs by 0.02 - despite the text asserting that 'the classifier benefits a lot from interpolation'.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None identified
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Combine RGB and audio modalities for more accurate results; and develop a PoTion representation working with 3D trajectories to add spatial information to the classification pipeline
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Two things distinguish this paper within the corpus. First, it is one of very few to classify behaviour rather than people: the label is an expert physician's judgement that a particular 10-second window shows atypical behaviour, not the child's diagnosis. That is a legitimate and arguably more tractable target, but it means the reported 0.72 accuracy is not a diagnostic accuracy estimate and must not be pooled with participant-level results - a distinction the paper's framing as 'automatic ASD prediction' partly obscures. Second, the pose-based representation deliberately discards appearance in favour of 'interpretable, appearance agnostic yet low level latent information', and beats an RGB baseline on the same data, which is a meaningful architectural finding. Against this: no participant counts, ages, genders or diagnostic information exist anywhere, so the corpus composition is unknown; the train/test partitioning basis is unstated with 8349 episodes drawn from 555 videos, so episodes from the same video and child almost certainly span the split; the AUC of 0.66 against 0.72 accuracy with 0.92 recall indicates the classifier is heavily biased toward the majority atypical class (5265 atypical versus 3084 typical stamps); and the imputation ablation contradicts its own narrative claim, showing three conditions performing identically on three of four metrics. There is also no ethics or consent statement for home video of children in family settings, which is the most sensitive data type in this corpus.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: The paper does not report participant groups at all. The corpus is described only as 555 videos 'recorded from a mix of children with and without ASD', with no participant counts, no breakdown by diagnostic status, and no indication of how many children contributed the videos. The analytic groups are instead behavioural: 3084 expert-labelled typical time stamps and 5265 atypical time stamps across four video sets. This is a fundamentally different unit of analysis from the rest of the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'people with ASD', 'the patients', 'ASD patients', 'patient's condition', 'children with and without ASD', 'typical (i.e. normal) behavior', 'atypical (i.e. ASD) behavior', 'normal behaviors of children'. Markedly medicalised - children are 'patients' whose 'condition tends to deteriorate with increasing age' - and the typical/atypical distinction is repeatedly glossed as normal/ASD, which conflates a behavioural label with a diagnostic one.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Nothing reported. No participant counts, no ages, no age ranges, no gender distribution, no matching information, and no diagnostic breakdown. The only quantitative description of the corpus is at video and time-stamp level: four sets comprising 235, 101, 177 and 42 video clips (555 total) yielding 4465, 2048, 1545 and 291 time stamps (8349 total), split 3084 typical and 5265 atypical. Since the number of contributing children is never stated, even the ratio of episodes to participants is unknown.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not reported at participant level. Expert physicians reviewed videos through the NODA platform and tagged time stamps as typical or atypical behaviour, and each video is stated to have been 'annotated by several expert physicians' - but no diagnostic instrument, criteria, or per-child diagnostic outcome is described, and no inter-rater agreement statistic is given despite multiple annotators. The ground truth for classification is therefore expert behavioural judgement rather than diagnosis.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None reported. No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or severity measures and no comorbidity information for any participant.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: automatic prediction of ASD-related atypical behaviour from home video, with the stated design constraint that any practical algorithm be cost-efficient and unobtrusive enough for long-term monitoring in the child's natural environment. Main findings: 0.72 accuracy, 0.72 precision, 0.92-0.93 recall and 0.66 AUC for the pose-based approach, against 0.66 accuracy and 0.62 AUC for an RGB single-frame baseline; retraining the pose estimator on child poses improved frame annotation rates by 9-14%; and imputation method made essentially no difference to performance.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Home setting - videos recorded by parents during the child's daily activities and submitted through a commercial remote assessment platform. Existing data: the NODA corpus was collected and expert-annotated by Behavior Imaging and provided to the authors, so this is secondary analysis of industry data. A manually annotated children's pose dataset was newly created by the authors for retraining the pose estimator.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Unstructured everyday home activity, categorised as play alone, play with others, meal time, and parents' concerns, with videos ranging from 2 to 10 minutes. The episode construction rule is explained and justified: 8 seconds before and 2 seconds after each expert time stamp, 'because physicians usually labeled a typical or atypical time stamp after they observed the behavior for a while, and a 10-second window could approximately record the behavior in full'. This is a thoughtful accommodation of how human annotation actually occurs.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; single videos per session with no longitudinal modelling, though the platform is designed for ongoing remote assessment. The data are the most privacy-sensitive in the corpus - parent-recorded video inside family homes capturing children during play and meals, routed through a commercial company to an academic laboratory. There is no ethics approval statement, no parental consent statement, no anonymization procedure and no data-protection or retention provision anywhere in the paper.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: parents' own recording devices (unspecified) at 30 fps. Software: Behavior Imaging's NODA platform for collection and expert annotation; 2D Mask R-CNN with a ResNet base, region proposal network and RoI Align, extended with a keypoint estimation head, retrained on manually annotated child poses using a semi-automatic annotation tool the authors describe as enabling researchers to build their own annotated datasets; particle filter for keypoint imputation; a modified PoTion generator; a convolutional classifier; Inception V3 for the baseline.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Mixed. The authors state that 'the code for our proposed method will be released in our website', which is a commitment rather than a completed release. The representation is described in reproducible detail - 15 named keypoints, Gaussian kernel size 12x12 with variance 1.0, the three-colour body-region scheme, intensity ramping across the episode, 256x256x3 output, the 8-seconds-before and 2-seconds-after episode rule, and 30 fps giving up to 301 frames. Dataset statistics are tabulated per set. What is missing: no participant information, no train/test split specification, no classifier hyperparameters, no random seeds, and no access route for the video corpus, which is commercially held.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: No dedicated limitations section. The authors note only that the approach could be improved by combining RGB and audio modalities and by moving to 3D trajectories. Identifiable in review and more consequential: the classification target is episode-level expert-labelled behaviour rather than participant diagnosis, so the reported figures are not diagnostic accuracy despite the paper's 'ASD prediction' framing; no participant counts, ages, genders or diagnostic status are reported, so the corpus composition and any demographic confounding are unknowable; the train/test partitioning basis is unstated with 8349 episodes from 555 videos, making episode-level leakage across the split highly likely; class imbalance (5265 atypical to 3084 typical) is unaddressed and is consistent with the 0.92 recall against 0.66 AUC, indicating a majority-class-biased classifier; the imputation ablation shows three conditions performing identically on accuracy, precision and recall yet the text claims 'the classifier benefits a lot from interpolation'; multiple expert annotators are mentioned with no inter-rater agreement reported; and there is no ethics or consent statement for home video of children.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Combine RGB and audio modalities alongside pose to improve accuracy; and develop a 3D-trajectory version of the PoTion representation to add spatial information to the pipeline. Both are technical extensions; no validation, population-characterisation or participant-level evaluation work is proposed, despite these being the study's principal gaps.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Motor behavior: full-body pose, represented as the trajectories of 15 skeletal keypoints over 10-second windows. The authors position this explicitly against the field's focus on faces and eyes, noting that prior work has concentrated on 'analyzing RGB frames and pertaining high level information from the video as well as focusing on specific body parts of children (e.g. face)', whereas 'none of them focused on studying full body pose movement over time as an indicator of atypical behaviors'.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality in this work. Within it, the PoTion representation performs a spatiotemporal fusion: keypoint heatmaps from up to 301 frames are colourised by body region and by relative time, then aggregated into one image, so a 10-second motion sequence is compressed into a single static RGB frame that a standard convolutional classifier can consume. The colour channels carry body-region identity and the intensity gradient carries temporal order, which is an elegant encoding of three information types into three channels. Future fusion with RGB appearance and audio is proposed.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised deep learning throughout, in a three-stage pipeline: a retrained Mask R-CNN detector for pose estimation, a classical particle filter for state estimation of missing keypoints, and a convolutional binary classifier over the resulting motion images. A conventional video-classification approach (Inception V3 on single frames with majority voting) serves as a baseline, which is a genuine comparator rather than a strawman since it represents standard practice.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: An engineered spatiotemporal image representation consumed by a learned classifier. The PoTion encoding is the distinctive element: rather than feeding a frame sequence to a recurrent or 3D convolutional model, it collapses the entire episode into a single 256x256x3 image where spatial position encodes keypoint location, colour hue encodes body region, and colour intensity encodes time within the episode. This makes a temporal classification problem tractable with a standard 2D convolutional network.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall and AUC, reported consistently across three imputation conditions and against the RGB baseline, plus frame-annotation rates before and after pose-estimator retraining. Reporting AUC alongside accuracy is what makes the result interpretable: 0.72 accuracy with 0.92 recall but only 0.66 AUC indicates a classifier operating close to the majority class rather than discriminating well, which the accuracy figure alone would conceal.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No feature importance or saliency analysis, and no behavioural characteristic is identified as distinguishing atypical from typical episodes - so the study produces a classifier without a finding about autistic movement. Two ablations are reported and are informative in different ways: the pose-versus-RGB comparison supports the architectural claim that appearance-agnostic pose carries more signal than raw frames, while the imputation ablation inadvertently undercuts its own narrative by showing three conditions performing identically on three of four metrics.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The weakest dimension. A train/test split is used but its partitioning basis is never stated, and with 8349 episodes derived from 555 videos - and an unknown but certainly smaller number of children - episodes from the same video and child will span the split unless deliberately prevented, which is not claimed. There is no cross-validation, no repeated splits, no permutation testing, and no class-imbalance handling despite a 5265-to-3084 imbalance that the recall-AUC divergence suggests is driving results. There is no external validation and no participant-level evaluation. The retraining of the pose estimator on the authors' own annotated child data is a sensible domain-adaptation step and is evaluated on its own terms (9-14% more annotated frames), which is a strength within the pipeline even though it does not address classification validity.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No formal keyword list in the extracted text. Vocabulary: 'atypical behavior', 'behavior recognition', 'pose estimation over time', 'PoTion representation', 'appearance agnostic', 'long-term behavioral monitoring', 'cost-efficient and unobtrusive'. The monitoring-and-deployment framing, and the explicit design requirement of unobtrusiveness for the natural living environment, are distinctive.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: An IEEE conference (2019), venue name truncated in the source metadata - a signal-processing or computer-vision venue rather than an autism or clinical one, consistent with the paper's technical framing and industry collaboration.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2019. The related-work survey characterises the field as having grown 'in the last couple of decades' around home-video behaviour analysis, infant observation scales, facial expression quantification with IQ-matched controls, caregiver-child interaction analysis, and multimodal eye-movement classification - and then identifies a specific gap: 'none of them focused on studying full body pose movement over time as an indicator of atypical behaviors', with most work 'focusing on specific body parts of children (e.g. face)'. This is an accurate characterisation of the corpus, where face and gaze dominate and full-body pose is rare. The commercial NODA platform also documents the emergence of remote video-based autism assessment as a deployed service by 2019.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Robot-Assisted Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Based on Artificial Reasoning
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Ramírez-Duque AA; Frizera-Neto A; Bastos TF
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: System-development and architecture study with a single-session proof-of-concept evaluation comparing two small groups qualitatively
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Per-camera head pose and gaze vectors published as ROS odometry messages, fused into a timestamped visual-focus-of-attention estimate naming the current target
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. Single site, six children, one session each.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Three typically developing children
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Parental consent obtained for all participants
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A joint-attention protocol in which the child's attention is directed toward objects in the room through 'look at, point and speak' stimuli, delivered first by the therapist alone and later by the robot alone. The within-session transition between mediators is the design's key feature and is what generates the reported finding: because each child experiences the same joint-attention bids from a human and then from a robot, the comparison is within-child and the mediator is the manipulated variable. The therapist guides the intervention throughout and uses the robot as an alternative communication channel, with both present in the room and a caregiver instructed not to assist.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: An unstructured, scalable network of RGBD sensors built on the Robot Operating System; a robot capable of facial expression, upper-limb posing and verbal communication; and a web-based client application through which the therapist controls and registers each step of the protocol and supervises the robot's behaviour. Software components are Dlib for CNN face detection and ResNet face recognition, and OpenFace for CLNF landmark detection and gaze, both integrated as ROS node attributes evaluated on each topic callback.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not stated
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not released, but the system is built explicitly on open-source components with their repositories cited - Dlib and OpenFace are both named with URLs, and the architecture is ROS-based, so the pipeline is reconstructible from published components. The conclusion notes that the framework was 'developed upon open source projects'.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not stated. Parental consent is reported - 'all volunteers participated with their parent's consent' - but no ethics committee approval appears in the retrieved text.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: A pipeline of face detection, recognition, segmentation and tracking; landmark detection and tracking; head pose and eye gaze estimation; asynchronous matching and fusion of local data across cameras; and Hidden Markov Model-based estimation of visual focus of attention.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: High at the construct level and not applicable at the model level. The measured quantities are named nonverbal behaviours - looking toward an object, toward the robot, toward the therapist, pointing, responding to a prompt - and the analytic unit is a joint-attention event of a specified subtype, so any finding is stated in terms a clinician uses. No model is trained, so there is nothing to attribute; the vision components are used as instruments rather than as decision-makers.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not applicable; the neural components are pretrained and used unmodified apart from ROS integration
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: None in the classification sense - no classifier is trained, no held-out set exists, and no accuracy, sensitivity, specificity or AUC is computed anywhere. The evaluation is twofold and both parts are appropriate to what is claimed. Technically, the vision pipeline's performance is reported for the case study, including the occlusion problems encountered, which is engineering validation of the measurement infrastructure. Substantively, the group comparison is a qualitative reading of joint-attention events across the mediator transition, presented as a behavioural pattern rather than as a discrimination result. The paper is explicit that this is 'a proof of concept', and the six-child sample with one session each is consistent with that framing. What cannot be assessed from it is whether the observed pattern would replicate, since no statistical test, effect size or uncertainty estimate accompanies it.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: No dedicated limitations section. The paper is nonetheless careful in its self-description: the evaluation is labelled 'a proof of concept', the risk group is described as 'without confirmed ASD diagnosis', and the occlusion problems encountered by the vision pipeline are reported rather than omitted. The introduction also identifies a real limitation of the prior literature: early robot-assisted diagnostic systems 'have primarily been open loop and remotely operated systems. However, these approaches are unable to perform autonomous feedback to enhance the interaction' - which is the gap the architecture is built to close.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Six children aged 36 to 48 months, each participating in a single session: three described as 'without confirmed ASD diagnosis, but with evidence of risk factors', and three typically developing children serving as the control group, with five boys and one girl in total. The sample is among the smallest in the review and the paper is explicit that it constitutes 'a proof of concept'. The diagnostic status of both groups is undocumented - the risk factors are not enumerated for the index group and no screening procedure is described for the comparison group - so no participant in the study has an established diagnostic classification. That is unusual in this corpus and is stated openly rather than obscured: the phrase 'without confirmed ASD diagnosis' appears in the methods, and the study makes no diagnostic claim on the basis of these children. At 36 to 48 months both groups sit in the age window where identification is typically still under way, so the risk framing is age-appropriate. No cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is reported.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Standard clinical framing of the period, with 'individuals suffering from ASD' and 'children in risk of suffering from ASD' recurring - phrasing that treats autism as an affliction and is less careful than the corpus's better examples. The abbreviation CwASD (children with autism spectrum disorder) is used throughout. Against this, the paper's account of the clinical problem is precise and non-dismissive: diagnosis 'is usually performed through several sessions of behavioral observation, exhaustive screening, and manual coding behavior', signs may be observable before ten months while reliable diagnosis is possible only at 18 or 24 months, and the delay between the two is what the technology addresses. The stated purpose throughout is to 'assist and enhance the traditional practice' and to 'help the clinicians', with the therapist retaining control of the protocol - so the technology is positioned as instrumentation for a clinician rather than as a substitute. No autistic person or family organisation is reported as involved.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Age and sex are reported at the level the sample allows - a 36-to-48-month band and a five-boys-one-girl composition - and nothing else. No cognitive, language, adaptive, socioeconomic or comorbidity measure was obtained, which in three-year-olds means that any behavioural difference between the groups could reflect general developmental level rather than autism risk. The absence matters particularly for the reported finding, since initiation of joint attention develops rapidly across this age range and neither group's developmental level is characterised. The risk factors that define the index group are also not enumerated, so what distinguishes the two groups is not stated in any measurable form.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None, and the paper says so rather than implying otherwise. The index group comprises 'three children without confirmed ASD diagnosis, but with evidence of risk factors', with the risk factors unspecified and no instrument, screening tool or clinician assessment reported; the comparison group is described as typically developing with no screening procedure. This is a genuinely undetermined diagnostic status on both sides, which the study handles by making no diagnostic claim - it reports a behavioural pattern difference and suggests it 'can be used as evidence to improve the ASD diagnosis' rather than asserting that the groups were correctly separated. For the review the relevant observation is that the transparency is a virtue while the underlying limitation is severe: a behavioural difference between three children with unspecified risk factors and three children of unverified typical development cannot support an inference about autism, and the paper's proof-of-concept framing is the correct standing for it.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists for any participant.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The aim is a robot-assisted framework that automates the behavioural coding on which autism diagnosis depends, addressing the delay between when signs are observable and when diagnosis becomes reliable. The technical contribution is an unstructured, scalable network of RGBD sensors on ROS, each node performing local face analysis and publishing head pose and gaze as navigation messages, with a central node fusing them and computing visual focus of attention through a Hidden Markov Model, coupled bidirectionally to a robot whose gaze shifts, facial expressions and sound rewards adapt to the child's performance. The behavioural finding, from six children in single sessions, concerns initiation of joint attention across a within-session transition from therapist to robot mediator: all three typically developing children initiated joint attention toward the therapist, then across the transition, then toward the robot, whereas the three at-risk children initiated only toward the therapist during the transition. The authors describe this as 'a clear difference of behavior pattern' usable 'as evidence to improve the ASD diagnosis'. No classifier is trained, no accuracy is computed, and the evaluation is labelled a proof of concept.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: An in-clinic setup with the therapist, the robot and a caregiver all present in the room, the caregiver instructed not to help the child perform the task. The multi-person setting is what necessitates one of the pipeline's design decisions - face recognition is used specifically to 'differentiate the child's face from other faces detected and found in the scene', since a system measuring a child's gaze in a room containing two adults must first establish which face is the child's. That is a practical requirement of clinical deployment which laboratory single-subject setups do not encounter, and its explicit handling is a strength.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A joint-attention protocol using 'look at, point and speak' stimuli to direct the child's attention toward objects in the room, delivered first by the therapist alone and subsequently by the robot alone. The construct is decomposed into the three standard subtypes - initiation of joint attention, responding to joint attention bids, and initiation of request behaviour - which is a level of construct specification that few studies in this review match, and the within-session mediator transition makes the design a within-subject manipulation: the same child receives the same bid type from a human and then from a robot, so the mediator is the variable and the child is their own control. That is what makes a six-child study capable of producing an interpretable pattern at all. The design's weakness is that the transition is not counterbalanced - therapist always precedes robot - so the group difference in initiation toward the robot is confounded with order, with accumulated fatigue, and with the novelty effect that the paper elsewhere says it intends to leverage.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional with a single session per child, and no follow-up. Parental consent is reported for all volunteers; no ethics committee approval appears in the retrieved text, which is an omission for a study recording video of three-year-olds. Funding and competing interests are not stated.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: The most architecturally developed measurement infrastructure in the review. An unstructured, scalable network of RGBD sensors runs on ROS, with each camera node performing face detection, recognition, segmentation, tracking, landmark detection, head pose and gaze estimation locally, publishing results as nav_msgs/Odometry messages; a fusion node on the most powerful workstation combines all navigation messages, computes the visual focus of attention through a Hidden Markov Model, and publishes it as a timestamped message naming the attention target. The components are open source and cited with repositories - Dlib for CNN face detection and ResNet face recognition, OpenFace for CLNF landmarks and gaze - with the specific integration modification described (making the neural model an attribute of the ROS node class and evaluating it in each topic callback). Two design consequences matter for the review. Multi-camera fusion addresses occlusion directly, which is the binding practical constraint on gaze measurement in a room with a moving child, an adult and a robot - and the paper reports encountering exactly that, with 'occlusion by hair, hands and the robot' detected. And the architecture is scalable and unstructured by design, meaning cameras can be added without reconfiguration, which is what would make deployment across differently shaped clinic rooms feasible.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong for the system and thin for the study. Reported: the complete vision pipeline stage by stage; the open-source libraries with repository URLs and the modification required to run their neural models inside ROS nodes; the inter-node message types; the HMM-based visual-focus-of-attention estimation; the two-channel bidirectional architecture linking robot and web client; the therapist-facing application's role in controlling and registering each protocol step; the joint-attention protocol with its three subtypes and stimulus types; the mediator sequence; the tagged behaviour categories; participant numbers, ages, sex composition and parental consent; and the occlusion failures encountered. Not reported: ethics approval, session duration, the risk factors defining the index group, any screening of the comparison group, the number of cameras used, and any quantitative behavioural result. A reader could rebuild the system from published components and could not reproduce the study.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: There is no dedicated limitations section, but the paper's self-description is honest at the points that matter: the evaluation is labelled 'a proof of concept', the index group is described as 'without confirmed ASD diagnosis', and the vision pipeline's occlusion failures are reported rather than omitted. The introduction also identifies the gap in prior work accurately - early robot-assisted diagnostic systems 'have primarily been open loop and remotely operated systems. However, these approaches are unable to perform autonomous feedback to enhance the interaction' - which is the specific deficiency the closed-loop architecture addresses. What is not addressed: six children in single sessions cannot support a behavioural claim, and no statistical test, effect size or uncertainty estimate accompanies the reported difference; neither group has documented diagnostic status; the mediator order is not counterbalanced, confounding the key finding with order, fatigue and novelty; no ethics approval is reported; no developmental measure was obtained in three-year-olds, so general developmental level cannot be separated from autism risk; and the behavioural finding rests on automated visual-focus-of-attention estimates with no reliability check against human coding, in a pipeline whose occlusion problems the paper itself reports.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Extension of the framework to the other behavioural features the paper names as within its reach - 'eye contact, stereotyped movements of the head, concentration and excessive interest in objects or events' - and continued development of the reasoning module that closes the loop between measurement and robot behaviour. The steps the study most needs are counterbalancing the mediator order, establishing diagnostic status for both groups, validating the automated attention estimates against human coding, and a sample capable of supporting a statistical claim.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Joint attention, specified with more precision than anywhere else in this review. The construct is decomposed into its three established subtypes - initiation of joint attention, responding to joint attention bids, and initiation of request behaviour - and the measured cues are enumerated: looking toward an object, toward the robot and toward the therapist, pointing, responding to a prompt from either mediator, and self-occlusion. The reported finding is subtype-specific rather than aggregate: initiation of joint attention appeared toward the therapist, across the mediator transition, and toward the robot in all three typically developing children, but only toward the therapist during the transition in the at-risk children. Whatever the sample's limitations, that is a claim about which form of joint attention differs and toward which partner, which is the level of specificity that makes a behavioural finding clinically usable. The paper also notes that the same infrastructure could measure eye contact, stereotyped head movements, concentration and excessive interest in objects, and that joint attention was chosen as this study's scope - so the construct restriction is deliberate.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Spatial rather than modal fusion, and it is the architecture's central idea. Multiple RGBD cameras each estimate head pose and gaze independently and publish them as ROS odometry messages; a fusion node performs asynchronous matching across all local estimates and computes a single visual focus of attention through a Hidden Markov Model, published with a timestamp and the name of the attention target. Fusing viewpoints to recover a gaze target is a direct answer to the occlusion problem that limits single-camera gaze measurement with moving children - the paper reports occlusion 'by hair, hands and the robot' as encountered in practice - and the HMM adds temporal smoothing so that the attention target is inferred from a sequence rather than frame by frame. No other study in this review builds comparable measurement infrastructure, and the fact that it is assembled from open-source components on ROS makes it reproducible in principle.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: No model is trained on the study's own data. The neural components are pretrained and used as instruments: Dlib's CNN face detector and ResNet face recogniser, and OpenFace's CLNF landmark and gaze estimator, integrated into ROS nodes with the neural model made an attribute of the node class and evaluated on each topic callback. The only inference component developed here is the Hidden Markov Model for visual focus of attention, which infers the attention target from the fused pose and gaze sequence. For a review of computational approaches this is the measurement-infrastructure end of the field: the machine learning does the perceptual work that a human coder would otherwise do frame by frame, and the clinical inference remains with the therapist. The paper's stated purpose supports this reading - automated video coding is intended to 'help the clinicians to reduce the delay of ASD diagnosis' by removing the manual coding burden, not to produce a diagnosis.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Per-camera head pose and gaze vectors published as ROS navigation messages, fused asynchronously and reduced to a timestamped visual-focus-of-attention estimate naming the target the child is looking at. The representation is intentionally semantic rather than raw - the pipeline's output is 'the child is looking at the robot' rather than a feature vector - which is why the analysis can be conducted in the vocabulary of joint-attention subtypes.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: No diagnostic metric of any kind, and none claimed. What is reported is vision-pipeline performance for the case study, presented in a figure and accompanied by an account of the occlusion problems encountered, plus qualitative descriptions of joint-attention events by group and mediator. The absence of any statistical test on the behavioural comparison is the study's main analytic gap, though with three children per group no test would carry weight; the more consequential omission is the lack of any reliability check of the automated attention estimates against human coding, which is the validation the measurement infrastructure needs and which the study's own tagged behaviour categories would have supported.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: High at the construct level, not applicable at the model level. Every measured quantity is a named nonverbal behaviour with a clinical referent, and the analytic unit is a joint-attention event of a specified subtype, so results are stated in the vocabulary a clinician uses. No classifier exists whose behaviour would require explanation; the neural components are perceptual instruments whose outputs - a face location, a gaze direction, an attention target - are directly checkable against the video.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Not applicable in the classification sense, and the study does not claim otherwise. No classifier is trained, no held-out set exists, no accuracy, sensitivity, specificity or AUC is computed, and the evaluation is explicitly labelled a proof of concept. The two things it does validate are appropriate to its claims: the vision pipeline's technical performance is reported for the case study together with the occlusion failures encountered, and the behavioural observation is presented qualitatively as a pattern rather than as a discrimination. Four limits bound what can be taken from it. Six children in a single session each cannot support a behavioural claim, and no statistical test, effect size or uncertainty estimate is offered. Neither group has documented diagnostic status - the index group has no confirmed diagnosis and the risk factors are unenumerated, while the comparison group is asserted rather than screened - so the contrast is between two undefined populations. The mediator sequence is not counterbalanced, therapist always preceding robot, so the finding that at-risk children did not initiate joint attention toward the robot is confounded with order, accumulated fatigue and the novelty effect the paper elsewhere says it wishes to exploit. And the behavioural finding rests entirely on automated visual-focus-of-attention estimates from a pipeline whose occlusion failures the paper itself reports, with no reliability comparison against human coding of the same sessions - which the study's own tagged behaviour categories would have made straightforward and which is the single most valuable analysis it could have added.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: Child-Robot interaction, Autism spectrum disorder, Convolutional neural network, Robot reasoning model, Statistical shape modeling. Balanced between the interaction paradigm, the population and the technical components. Terms carried through the body: joint attention, initiation of joint attention, responding to joint attention, initiation of request behaviour, visual focus of attention, RGBD, ROS, Hidden Markov Model, automated video coding, occlusion.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Intelligent and Robotic Systems 96(2):267-281, 2019; received 25 April 2018, accepted 20 December 2018. A robotics and intelligent-systems venue, and the article is written for it: the distributed architecture, message types, library integration and fusion strategy are specified in detail, while the clinical evaluation is a six-child proof of concept with no ethics statement, no diagnostic ascertainment and no statistical analysis. The venue's orientation also accounts for the paper's most valuable contribution to this review, which is infrastructure rather than result.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2019 by a group at the Universidade Federal do Espirito Santo in Brazil. The framing identifies the problem precisely: autism signs may be observable before ten months while reliable diagnosis is only possible at 18 to 24 months, diagnosis 'is usually performed through several sessions of behavioral observation, exhaustive screening, and manual coding behavior', and automated video coding could 'help the clinicians to reduce the delay'. For this review the study contributes three things, none of them a detection result. It builds the most developed measurement infrastructure in the corpus - an unstructured, scalable multi-camera RGBD network on ROS in which each node performs local face analysis and a fusion node computes visual focus of attention through a Hidden Markov Model - and it does so from cited open-source components, addressing directly the occlusion problem that limits single-camera gaze measurement with a moving child in a room containing two adults and a robot. It specifies its construct more precisely than anything else here, decomposing joint attention into initiation, response and request-initiation subtypes and reporting its finding at that level rather than in aggregate. And it closes the loop between measurement and robot behaviour, with the reasoning module modifying the robot's gaze, expression and rewards according to the child's performance - a design the introduction motivates by observing that earlier robot-assisted diagnostic systems 'have primarily been open loop and remotely operated' and 'are unable to perform autonomous feedback to enhance the interaction'. Its behavioural claim, however, cannot be relied on: six children in single sessions, no documented diagnostic status in either group, no ethics approval reported, an uncounterbalanced mediator order that confounds the key finding with order and novelty, no developmental measure in three-year-olds, and no reliability check of the automated attention estimates against human coding. The paper's own framing is appropriately modest - 'a proof of concept', a group 'without confirmed ASD diagnosis', and a conclusion that the observed pattern 'can be used as evidence to improve the ASD diagnosis' rather than that it discriminates.

data_charting_rubrics.title: SP-ASDNet: CNN-LSTM Based ASD Classification Model using Observer ScanPaths
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Tao Y; Shyu ML
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2019 IEEE International Conference on Multimedia & Expo Workshops (ICMEW)
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye-tracking and gaze
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Objective screening: classify whether an observer is typically developing or has ASD from a single scanpath over a given image, motivated by the unavailability of trained specialists for comprehensive ASD evaluation in less-developed regions
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional classification study on a shared benchmark with an organiser-provided blind test set; entry to the Saliency4ASD Grand Challenge track 2
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Not reported in this paper - viewing durations per image are not stated
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Viewing of natural images while gaze scanpaths are recorded
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Not reported - secondary analysis of a challenge dataset with no description of the original acquisition setting
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Analysis conducted in the United States (University of Miami); origin of source data not stated
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Not reported - class labels inherited from the challenge dataset with no diagnostic instrument, criteria or procedure described
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 14 children with ASD viewed each image; total distinct participants not stated
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developing children, 14 per image
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 14 per image; total distinct participants not stated
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not reported or addressed
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not reported or addressed
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted by dataset label only
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye movements: scanpath fixation locations and durations, combined with computationally predicted saliency maps of the stimulus images
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Image viewing with gaze recording (source dataset); the analysis pipeline generates a reference saliency map per image with SalGAN, crops 225-pixel square patches from that map centred on each fixation, and feeds the resulting patch sequence with durations to a CNN-LSTM
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: No acquisition hardware (secondary data). SalGAN generator pretrained on SALICON for saliency prediction; custom shallow CNNs; two-layer LSTM; NVIDIA P100 GPU with 16GB memory
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: No - uses the Saliency4ASD Grand Challenge dataset
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes in effect - a public challenge benchmark, cited but with no access details in this paper
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Low sensitivity - fixation coordinates over public stimulus images. No ethics, consent or data-provenance statement appears in this paper
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Learned convolutional features over saliency-map patches, concatenated with fixation duration
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: For each fixation, a 225x225 patch is cropped from the SalGAN reference saliency map centred on the fixation location, with zero-padding where the patch extends beyond the image. A shallow CNN maps each patch to a 1024-dimensional visual feature vector, to which the fixation duration is appended, giving a 1025-dimensional per-fixation feature. Sequences are zero-padded to LSTM length 40. Two CNN variants were tested - model A with a 7x7 first convolution followed by 3x3 layers, and model B with 3x3 throughout - and three visual feature dimensionalities (512, 1024, 2048)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: SalGAN generator pretrained on SALICON; custom shallow CNNs; two-layer LSTM with max-pooling over outputs
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No per-feature importance, but a per-image accuracy analysis is reported
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Per-image classification accuracy computed across the validation set, with the frequency distribution tabulated and the top-5 and bottom-5 images inspected visually
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: No features named, but an interpretable stimulus-level finding is reported: the model performs better on images containing a person, especially when the person is looking at the camera, and worse on natural scenes or images with no face
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported - no behavioral difference between groups is characterised
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised deep learning (convolutional plus recurrent)
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: SP-ASDNet: a shallow CNN encoding each saliency-map patch, followed by a two-layer LSTM of length 40 with max-pooling over outputs and a final dense classification layer. Batch normalisation after each convolutional layer and dropout on dense layers. Trained with Adam at learning rate 1e-5, momentum 0.9, batch size 8, for 30 epochs, with the best-validation model selected for testing. SalGAN (a generative adversarial saliency model) is used upstream as a frozen saliency predictor
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Internal split partitioned by image - the first 240 images and their scanpaths for training, images 241-300 and their scanpaths for validation - which is image-independent but not participant-independent. Model selection (CNN variant, visual feature dimensionality, batch normalisation) was performed on this validation set. Final evaluation on the organiser's held-out test set with labels withheld
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy on the validation set across model configurations; accuracy, recall, precision and F1 on the organiser's blind test set; and a frequency distribution of per-image accuracy
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Validation: best 74.22% accuracy (model A, 1024 visual features, with batch normalisation); model B with batch normalisation 74.19%; without batch normalisation 73.21% and 73.48%; performance degraded at 512 features (58.60%, 60.79%) and at 2048 features (68.89%, 68.05%). Blind test set: model A with BN 0.5566 accuracy, 0.8771 recall, 0.5319 precision, 0.6577 F1; model B with BN 0.5739, 0.5936, 0.5684, 0.5676; model B without BN 0.5790, 0.5921, 0.5626, 0.5697. Per-image validation accuracy ranged widely, with 1 image below 0.5, 6 in (0.5, 0.6], 17 in (0.6, 0.7], 24 in (0.7, 0.8] and 12 above 0.8
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A CNN-LSTM operating on saliency-map patches sampled at fixation locations classified ASD from typically developing observers at 74.22% on an image-partitioned validation split, but fell to 55.66-57.90% on the organiser's blind test set. The authors state directly that this gap 'could indicate the submitted models being overfitted'. Two secondary findings are informative: performance was sensitive to visual feature dimensionality, peaking at 1024 and degrading at both 512 and 2048; and per-image accuracy varied widely, with the model performing better on images containing a person - particularly one looking at the camera - and worse on natural scenes without faces.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None identified at feature level; at stimulus level, images containing faces and direct gaze were more discriminative than natural scenes
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Investigate and integrate attention mechanisms to improve performance; explore whether other image features can be incorporated; and conduct a thorough investigation of the actual differences in scanpaths between ASD and typically developing children - the authors explicitly note this behavioural question has not yet been addressed by their model
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: This is the second Saliency4ASD entry in the corpus and, read alongside Wu et al. (2019) on the same benchmark, provides a second independent measurement of the same phenomenon: validation accuracy of 74.22% collapsing to 55.66-57.90% on the organiser's blind test. Both papers attribute the gap to overfitting, and this one says so explicitly. That two independent teams, using different architectures on the same data, both lose roughly 17-19 accuracy points between an internally-partitioned split and a blind test is stronger evidence about internal-validation optimism in this literature than either paper alone. The per-image accuracy analysis is a genuine contribution absent from other corpus studies - it shows that discriminability is highly stimulus-dependent, with faces and direct gaze carrying signal and natural scenes carrying little, which implies that any single headline accuracy conceals large variation across stimuli. Weaknesses follow the benchmark: no participant counts, no ages, no genders, no diagnostic information, and an internal split partitioned by image so the same children appear in both training and validation. Model selection across two architectures, three feature dimensionalities and two normalisation settings was performed on that same validation set, which compounds the optimism. The authors are also appropriately candid that SalGAN was trained on SALICON, collected 'from subjects over a large age range and thus not perfectly reflected the saliency distribution of the children', noting that no public large-scale child saliency dataset exists.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups by dataset label - ASD and typically developing - with 14 of each viewing every image, though the paper notes 'some of the images have less than 14 scanpaths from the TD or ASD groups' because some children did not look inside the image bounds. The total number of distinct participants is never stated, so the actual sample size is unrecoverable. No other-diagnosis group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'people with ASD', 'the subjects', 'typical developed (TD)', 'TD children', 'normal observer', 'normal people'. Mixed and somewhat inconsistent - the comparison group is variously 'typical developed', 'normal observer' and 'normal people', and autism is described in the opening lines as 'one of the common diseases' and 'a developmental disease', which is more pathologising than most of the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Nothing reported. No participant counts beyond 14 viewers per image per group, no ages, no age ranges, no standard deviations, no gender distribution, and no matching or comparability information for either group. The paper notes that scanpath counts per image vary because some children looked outside the image, but gives no participant-level accounting.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not reported. Class labels are inherited from the Saliency4ASD challenge dataset with no description of how diagnoses were established or how typically developing status was confirmed.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None reported. No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or severity measures and no comorbidity information.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: objective scanpath-based ASD screening, motivated by the observation that comprehensive ASD evaluation 'requires the assessment from well-trained specialists, which is not available in less-developed regions'. Main findings: 74.22% validation accuracy; 55.66-57.90% on the organiser's blind test set, which the authors attribute to overfitting; performance peaked at 1024 visual features and degraded at both 512 and 2048; and per-image accuracy varied widely with images containing people, particularly looking at the camera, classified better than natural scenes without faces.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Setting not reported - entirely secondary analysis of the Saliency4ASD benchmark, with no description of the original acquisition conditions, viewing durations, eye tracker or calibration.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Image viewing with gaze recording, per the source dataset; no task instruction, duration or presentation detail is given. The analysis pipeline adds a computational stage: SalGAN generates a reference saliency map representing where a general-population observer would look, and 225x225 patches are cropped from that map at each fixation location, so the model sees not where the child looked in absolute terms but what the predicted saliency landscape looked like at each fixated point.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; single-session viewing per the source dataset, with no temporal or longitudinal component. Data are fixation coordinates over public stimulus images, so re-identification risk is minimal. No ethics approval, consent or provenance statement appears - common for secondary benchmark use but not acknowledged as such.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition hardware. Software: the SalGAN generator pretrained on SALICON (referenced to a public GitHub implementation) for saliency prediction; custom shallow CNNs in two variants with full layer specifications given in a table; a two-layer LSTM of length 40 with max-pooling; batch normalisation and dropout. Training on an NVIDIA P100 GPU with 16GB memory, Adam optimiser, learning rate 1e-5, momentum 0.9, batch size 8, 30 epochs.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Reasonable for a four-page challenge entry. The source dataset is a public benchmark with an organiser-defined blind test set. The CNN architectures are fully tabulated (layer type, channel count, kernel size, stride), the patch size (225, a=112), LSTM length (40), zero-padding rules, optimiser, learning rate, momentum, batch size, epochs and model-selection criterion are all specified, and the SalGAN implementation is linked to a public repository. What is missing: no code release for the authors' own model, no random seeds, no participant information, and no statement of how many scanpaths entered training and validation.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors: the blind-test performance 'is much lower than that of the validation dataset, which could indicate the submitted models being overfitted', with a call to further investigate the structure of visual attention to mitigate this. They also note candidly that SalGAN was trained on SALICON, 'collected from subjects over a large age range and thus not perfectly reflected the saliency distribution of the children', and that no public large-scale child saliency dataset exists to retrain it. They further acknowledge that the influence of saliency prediction quality on final classification has not been exhaustively tested. Identifiable in review: the internal split is partitioned by image, not participant, so the same children appear in both training and validation; model selection across two CNN variants, three feature dimensionalities and two normalisation settings was performed on that same validation set, compounding optimism; no participant counts, ages, genders or diagnostic information exist; the unit of analysis is the scanpath rather than the person; and blind-test precision of 0.5319-0.5684 with recall up to 0.8771 for model A indicates the best-recall model achieves it by over-calling ASD.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Investigate and integrate attention mechanisms into the architecture; explore incorporating additional image features; and - notably - 'a thorough investigation on the differences in the scanpaths between ASD and TD children will also be conducted', an explicit acknowledgement that the model was built and evaluated without establishing what behavioural difference it is exploiting.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Gaze: fixation locations and durations during image viewing. As with Wu et al. on the same benchmark, gaze is not analysed in isolation but relative to a computational model of typical viewing - here by sampling a predicted saliency map at each fixation, so the representation encodes how salient the fixated locations were to a general-population saliency model rather than where the child looked in absolute coordinates.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Fusion of behavioural and stimulus-derived information at two levels. Per fixation, a 1024-dimensional CNN encoding of the saliency-map patch is concatenated with the fixation duration, giving a 1025-dimensional vector that combines spatial-saliency context with temporal information. Across fixations, a two-layer LSTM integrates the sequence, explicitly to capture 'the temporal information and sequential dependency of the scanpaths'. No fusion across behavioural modalities and no integration with clinical or demographic data - the latter being impossible given the dataset.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised deep learning combining convolutional and recurrent architectures: shallow CNNs for per-patch visual encoding and a two-layer LSTM for sequence modelling, with a pretrained generative adversarial saliency model (SalGAN) used upstream as a frozen feature source. No conventional machine-learning comparators are included, and no ablation isolates the contribution of the saliency map versus the raw image.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A distinctive representation: rather than encoding fixation coordinates directly, each fixation is represented by the local neighbourhood of a predicted saliency map, so the model sees the saliency context of what was fixated. Duration is appended per fixation, and the sequence is processed recurrently with zero-padding to fixed length 40 and max-pooling over LSTM outputs. This preserves fixation order and duration while abstracting away absolute position.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Validation accuracy across six model configurations; accuracy, recall, precision and F1 on the organiser's blind test set for three submitted models; and a frequency distribution of per-image accuracy across the validation set. Reporting precision and recall separately on the blind test is what makes the error profile visible - model A achieves 0.8771 recall against 0.5319 precision, revealing it is largely defaulting to the ASD label. No AUC, specificity or confidence intervals.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No feature-level interpretability - no saliency analysis, attention visualisation or ablation of the model itself. But the per-image accuracy analysis functions as a stimulus-level interpretability result and is a genuine contribution: accuracy varied from below 0.5 to above 0.8 across validation images, and inspection of the best and worst five showed that 'when there is a person, especially when the person is looking at the camera when the image was taken, the model performs better', while natural scenes without faces performed worse. This implies that reported aggregate accuracies on this benchmark are heavily dependent on stimulus composition.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Evaluation on an organiser-held blind test set with labels withheld is a genuine strength and permits direct comparison against other entrants. Batch normalisation, dropout and a small architecture are used as overfitting controls, and the sensitivity of performance to visual feature dimensionality is explored empirically. But the internal split is partitioned by image rather than participant, model selection was performed on that same validation set across a six-configuration grid, and the resulting 17-19 point drop on the blind test is acknowledged by the authors as probable overfitting. There is no cross-validation, no participant-level partitioning, no permutation testing, no class-imbalance handling despite the precision-recall asymmetry, and no calibration or deployment analysis.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), Deep Neural Network (DNN), Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) Network, Saliency Prediction. Task vocabulary: 'objectively assess', 'early-stage detection', 'monitoring the efficiency of the ASD remediation protocol', 'observer scanpaths'. The framing is predominantly technical, with autism described as a 'disease' in the opening sentences.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: IEEE International Conference on Multimedia and Expo Workshops (ICMEW) 2019, as an entry to the Saliency4ASD Grand Challenge track 2 - a multimedia and computer-vision venue, not an autism or clinical venue.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2019. The paper documents the intersection of two technical trends: deep saliency prediction models (EML-Net, SalGAN, SAM with attention mechanisms) that have displaced conventional saliency models since 2014, and the application of those models to autism classification. It notes that a saliency prediction dataset for children with ASD exists but comprises only 13 children over 500 images, and cites a prior deep architecture performing ASD classification from sets of images along with an algorithm for selecting the most discriminative image contents. The existence of the Saliency4ASD challenge with a blind test track is itself evidence of the field's move toward benchmark evaluation, and the fact that two entries in this corpus independently report the same validation-to-test collapse makes that benchmark unusually informative.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Social robot in diagnosis of autism among preschool children
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Arent K; Kruk-Lasocka J; Niemiec T; Szczepanowski R
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2019 24th International Conference on Methods and Models in Automation and Robotic
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Pilot observational study within a robot-mediated interaction paradigm, with human-rated behavioural coding and a within-group non-parametric comparison; also framed explicitly as a requirements-gathering exercise for robot design
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Per child and per game, the proportion of required behaviours actually performed, computed separately for instructed and for spontaneous behaviours
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Preschool age; not specified further in the retrieved text
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Preschool children with autism; the paper does not state the number in the retrieved text, and the companion 2022 paper by the same group reports a related sample of five autistic and five typically developing children
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. Single site, pilot scale.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: None. The authors identify this directly: 'One of the limitation of this study regards to the fact that we observed only autistic children interacting with the robot.'
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: 'Informed consents from the childrens' parents were gained'
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Two interactive games with the NAO robot - 'Touch me' and 'Dance with me' - preceded by a dialogue phase using a multiple-choice voice menu that encouraged the child to choose a game or request a demonstration. The voice-menu opening is a design detail worth recording: it gives the child agency over which activity occurs, which is unusual in assessment paradigms and is consistent with the group's later stated intention of building scenarios attractive to children. The two games are the same pair developed further in the group's 2022 study, where their contrasting structure is used to dissociate command-response from imitation.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: NAO robot with its SDK and desktop applications for authoring animations, behaviours and dialogues; video recording. The paper notes the existence of ASK NAO (Autism Solutions for Kids), a commercial application pack inspired by ABA, PECS, TEACCH, Denver and SCERTS teaching methods - so the platform already carries an autism-specific software ecosystem.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not stated
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: 'The approval of the committee of research ethics was obtained to carry out the experiment'
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Manual coding by competent raters - kindergarten teachers, speech therapists and education doctoral students - marking behaviours on a questionnaire while watching the video recordings
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Complete by construction. Every measurement is a behaviour marked on a questionnaire by a human rater against a defined item, so any result traces to an observable event. The interpretation offered - a dissociation between automatic and intentional turn-taking - is a specific psychological claim anchored to the paradigm's structure rather than a statement about a model's outputs.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not applicable
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Not applicable in the machine-learning sense. The design's internal validity rests on the paired within-subject comparison, which is its principal methodological strength: because each child serves as their own control, differences in general ability, motivation, familiarity with the robot and rater leniency are all held constant across the two conditions being compared. That is a genuine advantage over between-group designs at this sample size, and it is what allows a small pilot to support a specific claim. The corresponding limits are that no between-group inference is possible at all, and that the retrieved text does not report inter-rater reliability for this study - unlike the group's 2022 follow-up, which reports Kendall's W of 0.65 and a subscale alpha of 0.77.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Two, and both are the right ones. First, 'we observed only autistic children interacting with the robot', with the stated remedy of comparing against typically developing children - which the group subsequently carried out in its 2022 study. Second, and more consequentially, 'the especially challenging task is to differ autism from other similar disorders. Thus, the other direction of our future studies is to observe the interactions performed by the robot and the children with other disorders.' Naming differential diagnosis against other developmental conditions as the harder problem, and committing to address it, is something almost no study in this review does - and the one study here that does test autism against another clinical group found the field's gold-standard instrument achieving an AUC of 0.562.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Preschool children with autism recruited through an integrative kindergarten in Wroclaw, which is named in the acknowledgements. The retrieved text does not state the sample size, ages or sex composition, and no cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is reported. There is no comparison group of any kind - a design feature the authors identify explicitly as their first limitation.
