The absence of controls means the study cannot support any between-group inference, and it is not presented as doing so: the finding is a within-subject dissociation, where each child's rate of instructed behaviour is compared against their own rate of spontaneous imitation, so every child serves as their own control and the sample size constrains precision rather than validity.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Clinical and engineering registers combined, with the paper's distinctive framing being that autism assessment is a joint design problem. The opening argument is that using human-robot interaction diagnostically 'implies the need of close cooperation between psychologists and engineers', covering both the robot's behaviour and its psychological effects on the one hand, and user requirements and evaluation criteria on the other - so the study treats the autistic child as a user whose requirements shape the technology, which is a different stance from the corpus norm of treating the child as a source of data. Terminology is standard for the period ('children with autism', 'autistic children', 'autistic population'), and the language of 'abnormal social interactions' and 'abnormal interaction patterns' is used in the abstract. The theoretical framing is theory of mind and mentalisation, which locates the construct in social cognition rather than in deficit enumeration. No autistic person is reported as involved, though the group's 2022 follow-up names children among the target users to be consulted.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Not reported. The retrieved text gives no sample size, age, sex, cognitive level, language ability, socioeconomic background or comorbidity information for the participating children. For a paired within-subject design the omissions are less damaging than they would be in a group comparison - the contrast being tested is internal to each child, so demographic differences cannot confound it - but they prevent any statement about which children the finding applies to, and they leave developmental level unmeasured in a study whose construct is spontaneous imitation of a robot.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not described in the retrieved text. Children were recruited through an integrative kindergarten and are stated to have autism, with no instrument, criteria, clinician or date given. The group's 2022 study on a related sample reports that diagnoses were delivered by a multidisciplinary team of a psychiatrist, a psychologist and a pedagogue and recorded in kindergarten files, which is likely the same route; if so the underlying ascertainment is genuine clinical judgement, well above the folder-membership and questionnaire-threshold labels charted elsewhere in this review. As reported here, however, the standard is undocumented. The absence matters less than usual because the study makes no diagnostic claim - it does not attempt to distinguish autistic from non-autistic children, and its within-subject finding does not depend on the label being correct for any classification purpose.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure was obtained.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated aim is twofold and unusual: to test whether play with a social robot reveals abnormal interaction patterns in autistic preschoolers, and simultaneously to collect user requirements and evaluation criteria for designing such a robot. The psychological finding is specific and well constructed: autistic children performed significantly more behaviours when the robot instructed them to than they performed spontaneously in imitation of the robot (Wilcoxon signed-rank W = 21, p = 0.028), from which the authors conclude that 'autistic children have more deficits among automatic turn-taking (spontaneous, without instruction) as compared to intentional turn-taking (after being instructed)'. That is a dissociation within the construct rather than a difference in its overall level, and it is exactly the kind of claim that a paired within-subject design can support and a between-group design at this scale could not. The engineering finding - a set of requirements and evaluation criteria for robot design derived from the experimental experience - is presented as a co-equal output, which no other study in this review does.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: An integrative kindergarten in Wroclaw, named in the acknowledgements. Assessing children in their own everyday setting, with a portable robot brought to them, is the deployment scenario the work envisages, so the pilot data were collected under the conditions in which the method would be used. Integrative kindergartens in Poland enrol autistic and typically developing children together, which is also the setting that would make the group's stated next step - comparison against typically developing peers - straightforward to arrange without changing anything else about the protocol.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Two interactive games with the NAO robot, 'Touch me' and 'Dance with me', preceded by a dialogue phase in which a multiple-choice voice menu encouraged the child to choose a game or request a demonstration. Three properties of this paradigm bear on the review. The elicitation is delivered by a machine, so the social partner's behaviour is identical for every child - a form of standardisation no human examiner can supply, and one that removes examiner variability from a construct (reciprocal interaction) where the examiner is half the dyad. The voice-menu opening gives the child a choice of activity, which is a design decision oriented to engagement rather than to experimental control and is consistent with the group's later commitment to scenarios attractive to children. And the two games differ in a way the group's 2022 paper makes explicit: one uses a stationary robot issuing instructions, the other a moving robot inviting imitation, so that the same physical behaviour has different meanings in each. Here that structure is used to define the two conditions of the within-subject contrast - instructed against spontaneous - which is the paradigm's payoff.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional pilot, single session per child, with no follow-up or test-retest. Ethics reporting is brief but complete on the essentials: approval of the committee of research ethics was obtained to carry out the experiment, and informed consent was obtained from the children's parents. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text; the participating kindergarten is acknowledged by name.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: A NAO humanoid robot from Aldebaran Robotics - 57 cm tall, 5.4 kg - with its SDK and desktop applications for authoring animations, behaviours and dialogues, plus video recording. The paper notes the availability of ASK NAO (Autism Solutions for Kids), a commercial application pack 'inspired by commonly practiced special education teaching methods (ABA, PECS, TEACCH, DENVER, SCERTS)', which is a useful observation for the review: the platform already carries an autism-specific software ecosystem built around established educational approaches, so robot-mediated assessment can be layered onto infrastructure that exists in practice rather than requiring a purpose-built device. The equipment cost remains high relative to the webcam-and-toys protocols charted elsewhere here, and what it buys is exact reproducibility of the social partner.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Adequate for a short conference paper and incomplete on participants. Reported: both games, the voice-menu dialogue opening, the robot platform with physical specifications and software environment, the professional backgrounds of the competent raters, the questionnaire-based coding procedure, the normalisation of behaviour counts to proportions of behaviours required in each game, the statistical test with statistic and p-value, ethics approval, parental consent, and the participating kindergarten by name. Not reported in the retrieved text: sample size, ages, sex, diagnostic ascertainment, the questionnaire items themselves, and inter-rater reliability - the last being a real gap given that the competent-raters technique is the study's measurement instrument, and one the group closed in its 2022 follow-up by reporting Kendall's W and subscale alpha.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Two limitations are stated and both are correctly identified. The first is the absence of a comparison group - 'we observed only autistic children interacting with the robot' - with the remedy given as comparison against typically developing children, which the group subsequently carried out. The second is more valuable and is rare in this corpus: 'the especially challenging task is to differ autism from other similar disorders. Thus, the other direction of our future studies is to observe the interactions performed by the robot and the children with other disorders.' Committing to a non-autistic clinical comparison is a commitment almost no study in this review makes, and the one included study that does test autism against another clinical population found the field's gold-standard observational instrument achieving an AUC of 0.562 - which is the evidence that this stated priority is the right one. What is not addressed: sample size and participant characteristics are unreported; no diagnostic ascertainment is described; inter-rater reliability is not quantified for this study; rater blinding to the hypothesis is not discussed; and no developmental measure separates general cognitive level from autism as an explanation for reduced spontaneous imitation.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Three directions, two of them named as limitations and one as an engineering output. Compare autistic children's robot interaction against that of typically developing children - subsequently done. Observe interactions with children who have other developmental disorders, to address the differential-diagnosis problem the paper identifies as the hardest. And apply the collected user requirements and evaluation criteria to robot design, which the paper treats as a research product in its own right.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Turn-taking, decomposed into two forms - and the decomposition is the study's substantive contribution to the review. Behaviour performed in response to an explicit robot instruction is treated as intentional turn-taking; behaviour performed spontaneously, imitating the robot without being told to, is treated as automatic turn-taking. Each is expressed as a proportion of the behaviours required of the child in that game, so the two are directly comparable within a child. The finding is that autistic children reliably do what they are asked and rarely do it unprompted, which the authors read as a specific deficit in automatic rather than intentional turn-taking. Two things make this valuable for the synthesis. It is a within-construct dissociation rather than a level difference, so it says something about the structure of the difficulty rather than only its presence - which almost no other included study attempts. And it identifies a measurement principle with wide application: a paradigm that separates prompted from unprompted performance can distinguish capacity from spontaneous deployment, a distinction that most behavioural measures in this corpus collapse.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: None. A single video stream coded by human raters, with the robot's own sensors unused for measurement. The paper's engineering framing points toward using them - it is explicitly gathering requirements for an 'interaction diagnosis system' - but no automated sensing is implemented here.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: None. No computational or machine-learning model is fitted. The analysis is a Wilcoxon signed-rank test on paired within-subject proportions, which is the correct choice for small-sample paired ordinal data and is used appropriately. For a review of computation-based approaches, the study sits immediately upstream of the modelling work: it establishes that a robot-delivered paradigm produces a measurable and theoretically interpretable behavioural dissociation, which is the finding that a subsequent automated system would need to reproduce.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Proportions of required behaviours performed, computed separately for instructed and spontaneous conditions in each game. Normalising by the number of behaviours the game required of the child is the right construction, since it removes differences in game length and in how many opportunities each scenario afforded, and it makes the two conditions commensurable within a child.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: One inferential statistic - Wilcoxon signed-rank W = 21, p = 0.028 - and no diagnostic accuracy metric of any kind, which is appropriate given that no classification is attempted. What is missing is an effect size and a confidence interval, which on a small paired sample would have conveyed the magnitude of the dissociation rather than only its statistical detectability, and inter-rater reliability for the coding on which the statistic rests.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Complete, because nothing is opaque: every value is a human rater's mark against a questionnaire item describing an observable behaviour. The interpretation offered is a psychological claim - a dissociation between automatic and intentional turn-taking - anchored to prior literature on automatic turn-taking deficits, rather than a statement about what a model responded to.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Not applicable in the machine-learning sense; no model is fitted and no individual receives a predicted class. The design's validity rests instead on the paired within-subject comparison, and this is its principal strength: because each child's instructed-behaviour rate is compared against their own spontaneous-behaviour rate, general ability, motivation, familiarity with the robot, session-specific factors and rater leniency are all held constant across the two conditions. That is a genuine methodological advantage at pilot scale, and it is why a study with no comparison group and an unreported sample size can nonetheless support a specific and interpretable claim. Three limits bound it. No between-group inference is possible, which the authors state as their first limitation. Inter-rater reliability is not reported here, although the competent-raters technique is the measurement instrument and the group quantified it in the 2022 follow-up at Kendall's W = 0.65. And no effect size or confidence interval accompanies the test statistic, so the magnitude of the dissociation is not characterised. Set against the modelling studies in this review, the design illustrates a point worth carrying into the synthesis: a within-subject contrast can extract an interpretable finding from a sample far too small for any classifier, and several of the between-group studies charted here with comparable sample sizes would have been better served by the same approach.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No formal keyword list appears in the retrieved text. Terms carried through the paper: human-robot interaction, social robot, NAO, turn-taking, automatic and intentional turn-taking, competent raters, theory of mind, mentalisation, user requirements, evaluation criteria.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: 2019 24th International Conference on Methods and Models in Automation and Robotics (MMAR), IEEE. A robotics and automation venue, and the paper is written for that audience - its second stated output is a set of user requirements and evaluation criteria for robot design, framed as an engineering deliverable rather than a clinical one. The venue explains both the paper's strengths, in its explicit treatment of the assessment problem as a joint psychology-engineering design task, and its omissions, since participant characteristics and diagnostic ascertainment would be expected in a clinical venue and are absent here.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Presented in 2019 at an automation and robotics conference by a Polish collaboration between the Department of Cybernetics and Robotics at Wroclaw University of Science and Technology and the Research Unit for Cognitive and Applied Psychology at the University of Lower Silesia - the same group whose 2022 follow-up is charted separately in this review. The framing is distinctive: rather than presenting a method, the paper presents a stage in an interdisciplinary development process, arguing that diagnostic human-robot interaction 'implies the need of close cooperation between psychologists and engineers' and delivering both a psychological result and a set of engineering requirements as co-equal outputs. For the synthesis the study contributes three things. Its finding is a within-construct dissociation rather than a group difference: autistic children performed significantly more behaviours when instructed than spontaneously in imitation (W = 21, p = 0.028), which the authors read as a deficit in automatic rather than intentional turn-taking. That is a claim about the structure of the difficulty, and the measurement principle behind it - separating prompted from unprompted performance to distinguish capacity from spontaneous deployment - has wide application in a corpus where most behavioural measures collapse the two. Its design demonstrates that a paired within-subject contrast can extract an interpretable result from a sample far too small for any classifier, which several similarly sized between-group studies charted here might usefully have adopted. And its stated future direction identifies the field's hardest problem correctly: 'the especially challenging task is to differ autism from other similar disorders', with a commitment to observe robot interactions with children who have other developmental conditions. Almost no study in this review makes that commitment, and the one included study that does test autism against another clinical group found the field's gold-standard observational instrument achieving an AUC of 0.562 - which is the evidence that this priority is the right one. What the study cannot supply is any detection result: no comparison group, no model, no classification, no accuracy, an unreported sample size and no diagnostic ascertainment described.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Application of the Still-Face Paradigm in Early Screening for High-Risk Autism Spectrum Disorder in Infants and Toddlers
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Qiu N; Tang C; Zhai M; Huang W; Weng J; Li C; Xiao X; Fu J; Zhang L; Xiao T; Fang H; Ke X
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Infants and toddlers at high risk of autism, prospectively confirmed
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Video and social interaction behaviour
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Establish whether social behaviours elicited by the still-face paradigm differ between high-risk and typically developing infants before 24 months, and whether machine-learning models built on those behaviours can screen for autism early enough to close the gap between the age at which diagnosis becomes possible (24 months) and the age at which it typically occurs (40 months or later)
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Prospective cohort with case-control classification: high-risk infants enrolled at 8-23 months, followed to 24 months for diagnostic confirmation, then classified against a concurrently recruited typically developing group
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One still-face session at enrolment (2 minutes face-to-face interaction followed by 1 minute of maternal still face), with diagnostic follow-up at 2 years of age
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Human infants and toddlers with their mothers
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Still-face paradigm (Tronick): the mother sits opposite the child and interacts normally for 2 minutes under fixed instructions (face-to-face, FF episode), then stops interacting and holds a neutral expression for 1 minute (still-face, SF episode). The classic third reunion episode was omitted. The SF episode is a deliberate social-challenge scenario in which the mother's social signals disappear entirely
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Designated observation room, outpatient clinic of the Child Mental Health Research Center, Nanjing Brain Hospital
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Two-stage and unusually rigorous for this age band. At enrolment, high-risk status required a positive M-CHAT plus a pediatric psychiatrist's judgement that the child met DSM-5 core criteria for ASD but was under 24 months. At 2 years, children were evaluated with the ADI-R and ADOS and clinically diagnosed by two pediatric psychiatrists against DSM-5; all children in the confirmed ASD group reached cut-off on both instruments. Genetic and metabolic syndromes (Rett, fragile X), other neurodevelopmental disorders including isolated language disorder and intellectual disability, craniocerebral trauma and neurological illness were exclusions
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 45 high-risk at enrolment, of whom 40 were confirmed ASD at 24 months and 5 no longer met criteria (the N-ASD group). Classification models were trained on the 40 confirmed cases
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Explicitly excluded: genetic and metabolic diseases (Rett syndrome, fragile X), neurodevelopmental disorders other than ASD (isolated language developmental disorder, intellectual disability), clear history of craniocerebral trauma, history of nervous system disease and serious physical illness
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Medication history was collected via a general information questionnaire but is not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Graded with CSBS-DP (social communication, language and symbolic behaviour factors plus total), CARS and ABC, and correlated against the behavioural indicators
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - typically developing infants and toddlers recruited in the Nanjing area over the same period
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: By exclusion criteria only: no neurodevelopmental or mental disorder, no craniocerebral trauma, no nervous system disease or serious physical illness. Gesell developmental quotients were measured for all participants
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No. The high-risk group was significantly older (19.71 vs 16.40 months, t = 3.80, p < 0.01). The authors name this first among their limitations, explaining that because autistic children generally have delayed development the groups could not be matched on age without unmatching developmental level
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Nominally - the TD inclusion criteria specify sex matching to the HR group, and the chi-square comparison was non-significant (p = 0.08), but the distributions differ visibly (11% female in HR versus 26% in TD)
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Video of mother-infant interaction, converted by human coders into duration and frequency counts of five defined social behaviours
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Two trained graduate students coded the videos in Observer XT 12, recording duration (seconds) and frequency (count) of five indicators across both episodes: protest behaviour, non-social smiling, eye contact, social smiling, and active social engagement. Roughly 20% of videos (18) were double-coded for reliability
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Video recording in a designated observation room; The Observer XT 12 behavioural observation and coding system; Python with scikit-learn (SVC, GaussianNB, RandomForestClassifier); Gesell Developmental Scale, M-CHAT, CSBS-DP, CARS, ABC, ADI-R and ADOS as clinical instruments
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes in principle - the authors state that all datasets generated are included in the article or Supplementary Material, though what is provided is aggregate tables rather than participant-level behavioural data
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Partially - a data availability statement exists ('All datasets generated for this study are included in the article/Supplementary Material'), which is more than most of the corpus offers, but no participant-level release is evident
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Sensitive - video of identifiable infants with their mothers. Governance is well reported: approval by the Medical Ethics Committee of Nanjing Brain Hospital (2017-KY089-01), written informed consent from legal guardians including specific consent for publication of potentially identifiable images or data, and prospective trial registration (Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR-OPC-17011995)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Human-coded behavioural event statistics - duration and frequency of defined social behaviours
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Ten indicators: duration and frequency of eye contact, active social engagement and social smiling during the FF episode, plus duration and frequency of eye contact and active social engagement during the SF episode. Only behaviours that differed significantly between groups were carried into the models. Protest behaviour and non-social smiling were dropped, having shown no group difference in either episode
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Human coding in Observer XT 12 by two trained graduate students; inter-coder reliability by intraclass correlation on ~20% of videos (ICC 0.76 protest, 0.82 non-social smiling, 0.81 eye contact, 0.83 social smiling, 0.79 active social engagement)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Not as model-derived importance. Feature relevance is established upstream by t-tests, and the substantive comparison reported is between episodes rather than between individual features
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Independent-samples t-tests for group differences; Pearson correlation of each behaviour against age, Gesell developmental quotients and symptom severity scores
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Eye contact and active social engagement, which differed significantly in both episodes; social smiling differed only in the FF episode. Within the SF episode, eye contact duration correlated with CSBS-DP symbolic behaviour and total scores, and eye contact frequency with the social communication factor, language factor and total scores
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: High-risk infants showed shorter durations and lower frequencies of eye contact, social smiling and active social engagement during the FF episode, and shorter and less frequent eye contact and active social engagement during the SF episode. The direction of the symptom correlations is that more flexible and appropriate eye contact and active social engagement accompanied less severe autism symptoms. Notably, negative-emotion behaviours (protest, non-social smiling) did not differ between groups in either episode, contrary to the authors' expectation from prior emotion-regulation literature
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised binary classification on tabular behavioural counts
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Support vector machine, Gaussian naive Bayes and random forest, all from scikit-learn, fitted separately for the FF and SF episodes
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-out cross-validation over the 83 training samples (40 confirmed ASD, 43 TD): 'each subject within these 83 samples was used for testing the model that was trained on the rest 82 samples', with predictions pooled to compute overall accuracy. A separate verification step applied the SVM to the 45 high-risk children - but 40 of those are the same confirmed-ASD children the model was trained on, so only the 5 N-ASD children constitute genuinely unseen data
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Overall classification accuracy per algorithm per episode, plus a confusion matrix for the SVM. No sensitivity, specificity, AUC, precision or F1 is reported as such, though the confusion matrix permits their derivation. Accuracy was also stratified by age band (8-11, 12-15, 16-19, 20-23 months) to test whether errors clustered by age
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: SVM was best in both episodes: 81.18% (FF) and 83.35% (SF). Random forest reached 80.72% and 83.13%; naive Bayes 80.54% and 82.35%. The SF episode outperformed the FF episode for all three algorithms. The SVM confusion matrix for the SF episode shows 34 of 40 ASD and 36 of 43 TD correctly classified (sensitivity 85.0%, specificity 83.7%); for the FF episode, 35 of 40 ASD and 33 of 43 TD (sensitivity 87.5%, specificity 76.7%). The verification step failed outright: 'even though the average classification accuracy of SVM was more than 80%, the 5 N-ASD was not classified correctly' - none of the five children who resolved off the spectrum was identified. No relationship was found between accuracy and age band
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A three-minute mother-infant still-face session, coded for five social behaviours, distinguished high-risk from typically developing infants aged 8-23 months, and SVM models on ten of those indicators reached 83.35% accuracy against diagnoses confirmed prospectively at 24 months. The still-face episode outperformed the free-interaction episode for every algorithm, which the authors interpret as the social-challenge scenario exposing communication impairment more sharply than ordinary interaction does. Behaviours during the SF episode also correlated with CSBS-DP symptom severity, while FF-episode behaviours did not. The model failed completely on the five high-risk children who did not go on to meet criteria, misclassifying all of them - the discrimination the paper most needs and does not achieve.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Reduced eye contact and reduced active social engagement, in both ordinary interaction and under maternal non-responsiveness; reduced social smiling in ordinary interaction only. Negative-emotion behaviours were not discriminative
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Expand the sample, particularly the N-ASD group, so the model can be verified on children who resolve off the spectrum; build more effective machine-learning models; identify N-ASD from ASD as an explicit goal; repeat under controlled physiological and psychological ages to address the age-matching failure; and pursue a home-based self-screening mode given the paradigm's convenience
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The prospective design is the paper's real contribution and is rare in this corpus: children were enrolled at 8-23 months on M-CHAT plus psychiatrist judgement, then followed to 24 months for ADI-R, ADOS and DSM-5 confirmation by two psychiatrists, so the labels the classifier learns are outcomes rather than concurrent impressions. The ethics reporting, trial registration and inter-coder reliability statistics are also better than corpus norm. Three problems constrain what the accuracy means. First, the verification step is largely circular - 40 of the 45 high-risk children used to 'verify' the SVM are the same confirmed-ASD children in its training set, and the only genuinely held-out cases are the 5 N-ASD children, all of whom were misclassified. The authors report this failure plainly rather than burying it, which is to their credit, but it means the clinically decisive question - distinguishing infants who will resolve from those who will not - is answered negatively. Second, the groups differ significantly in age (19.71 vs 16.40 months) and in four of five developmental quotients, and the outcome features are developmentally sensitive social behaviours; the age-band analysis addresses whether errors cluster by age but not whether the group age gap itself carries signal. Third, the ten features are human-coded, so this is machine learning on manual behavioural coding rather than automated behavioural sensing - the throughput bottleneck the paper's home-self-screening ambition would need to remove remains fully in place. The reported accuracies also differ slightly from the confusion matrices (83.35% versus 70/83 = 84.3% for the SF episode), suggesting the headline figures come from a slightly different pooling than the tabulated matrix.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups plus a prospectively emergent third. At enrolment: 45 high-risk infants and 43 typically developing infants, 88 in total, aged 8-23 months. At 24-month follow-up the high-risk group split into 40 confirmed ASD and 5 who no longer met criteria (N-ASD). Classification used the 40 confirmed ASD against the 43 TD. The N-ASD subgroup is the corpus's clearest instance of a genuine clinical comparison group - children who present as high-risk but do not go on to be diagnosed - and the study's inability to classify any of them is the most informative negative result in this record.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'infants and toddlers with high-risk autism spectrum disorder (HR)', 'children with ASD', 'infants and toddlers with ASD', 'typical development (TD)', 'infants and toddlers with TD'. Person-first throughout, with 'typical development' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy'. Disorder-framed language dominates ('a serious neurodevelopmental disorder', 'social communication barriers'), and the discussion invokes the extreme male brain theory and the intense world theory as explanatory frames.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: High-risk: n = 45, 40 male / 5 female (11% female), mean age 19.71 +/- 3.43 months. Typically developing: n = 43, 32 male / 11 female (26% female), mean age 16.40 +/- 4.70 months. The age difference is significant (t = 3.80, p < 0.01) and is the authors' first stated limitation, with the explicit rationale that matching on age would unmatch developmental level. Gesell developmental quotients differ significantly on adaptive (80.29 vs 92.98), fine motor (86.64 vs 93.70), language (60.84 vs 86.51) and personal-social (78.80 vs 92.28) domains; only gross motor is comparable (92.02 vs 92.77). Sex distributions were nominally matched by design with a non-significant chi-square (p = 0.08) but differ visibly. All participants are from the Nanjing area of China, with no ethnicity or socioeconomic reporting.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: The strongest ascertainment in the corpus's infant-screening strand, because it is prospective rather than concurrent. Entry to the high-risk group required a positive M-CHAT plus a pediatric psychiatrist's judgement that the child met DSM-5 core criteria while under 24 months. At 2 years every high-risk child was re-evaluated with both the ADI-R and the ADOS, and clinically diagnosed by two pediatric psychiatrists against DSM-5; all confirmed cases reached cut-off on both instruments. Exclusions removed Rett syndrome, fragile X, isolated language disorder, intellectual disability, craniocerebral trauma and neurological illness. Typically developing status rests on exclusion criteria plus Gesell assessment rather than a positive screen.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Comprehensive by corpus standards. Gesell Developmental Scale developmental quotients across five domains (adaptive, gross motor, fine motor, language, personal-social) for all participants; CSBS-DP with three factor scores and total, CARS, and ABC for symptom severity in the high-risk group. All were used analytically - correlated against behavioural indicators - not merely tabulated. The requirement that the mother be the primary caregiver is also a stated inclusion criterion for both groups, controlling a variable that matters for a mother-infant interaction paradigm.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: determine whether still-face paradigm social behaviours differ before 24 months and whether machine learning on them can screen for autism prospectively. Main findings: high-risk infants showed less eye contact, social smiling and active social engagement in free interaction, and less eye contact and active social engagement under the maternal still face; negative-emotion behaviours did not differ; SVM reached 83.35% for the still-face episode and 81.18% for free interaction, with the still-face episode superior for all three algorithms; still-face behaviours correlated with CSBS-DP symptom severity while free-interaction behaviours did not; and the model misclassified all five children who resolved off the spectrum.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Outpatient clinic of the Child Mental Health Research Center, Nanjing Brain Hospital Affiliated to Nanjing Medical University, with typically developing controls recruited from the Nanjing area over the same period (December 2017 onward). Prospectively registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry as ChiCTR-OPC-17011995.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A two-episode still-face paradigm: 2 minutes of normal mother-infant interaction under fixed instructions, then 1 minute in which the mother holds a neutral, unresponsive face. The classic reunion episode was omitted, following the common two-episode variant. The design logic is that the still-face episode manufactures a controlled social challenge - all of the mother's social signals vanish at once - and the paper's central empirical claim is that this challenge is more diagnostically informative than ordinary interaction, since the SF episode beat the FF episode for every classifier and only SF behaviours correlated with symptom severity.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Prospective longitudinal in the essential respect: behavioural measurement at 8-23 months, diagnostic outcome at 24 months. The behavioural measurement itself is a single cross-sectional session. Data are video of identifiable infants with their mothers - among the most sensitive material in the corpus. Governance is correspondingly well reported: named ethics approval (2017-KY089-01), written guardian consent, specific consent for publication of potentially identifiable images or data, and prospective trial registration.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Video recording in a designated observation room; The Observer XT 12 behavioural observation and coding system; Python with scikit-learn (SVC, GaussianNB, RandomForestClassifier). Clinical instrumentation: M-CHAT, Gesell Developmental Scale, CSBS-DP, CARS, ABC, ADI-R, ADOS. No custom hardware and no automated behavioural sensing.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Above corpus average. A data availability statement exists, trial registration is prospective, ethics approval is named with its reference number, inter-coder reliability is quantified per behaviour, the behavioural coding definitions are stated in full, the classifier library and functions are named, and the validation scheme is described precisely enough to reproduce. What is missing: hyperparameters (SVM kernel and C, forest size), any code release, participant-level data despite the availability statement, and reconciliation between the headline accuracies and the confusion matrix.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Two limitations are stated: the groups could not be age-matched because autistic children generally have delayed development, so matching on age would unmatch developmental level; and the sample was small. The N-ASD failure is discussed candidly - 'the 5 N-ASD was not classified correctly', attributed to class imbalance and to only ten indicators per sample, with identifying N-ASD from ASD named as a goal for future work. The contrary finding on negative emotion is also flagged as needing further validation. Identifiable in review but not acknowledged: the verification step is largely circular, since 40 of the 45 high-risk children used to verify the SVM were in its training set; the age gap coincides with significant differences in four of five developmental quotients, so group separation may partly reflect developmental level rather than autism; features were selected by group-difference t-tests computed on the full dataset before cross-validation, which leaks label information into the feature set; and the reported accuracies do not exactly match the tabulated confusion matrices.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Expand the sample, especially the N-ASD group, to verify the model on children who resolve off the spectrum; make identifying N-ASD from ASD an explicit objective; develop more effective machine-learning models; repeat the analysis under controlled physiological and psychological ages to address the age-matching problem; and develop the still-face paradigm into a convenient, objective and standardised self-screening mode usable at home.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Dyadic social-interaction behaviour: eye contact, social smiling, non-social smiling, protest behaviour and active social engagement, each measured as both duration and frequency. Uniquely in the corpus, behaviour is measured relationally - against a caregiver whose responsiveness is experimentally manipulated - rather than as a property of the child alone, and the manipulation is what generates the discriminative signal.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No multimodal fusion. All features come from a single modality (video-coded social behaviour). The study's structural comparison is instead across conditions of the same modality: the still-face episode versus the free-interaction episode, and the still-face episode won for every classifier (83.35 vs 81.18 for SVM, 83.13 vs 80.72 for random forest, 82.35 vs 80.54 for naive Bayes). This is a useful counterpoint to the corpus's fusion studies - here the gain comes from choosing a better elicitation condition rather than adding a sensor.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Three classical supervised classifiers compared on identical tabular features: support vector machine, Gaussian naive Bayes and random forest, all from scikit-learn. No deep learning, which is appropriate at n = 83 with 10 features. The three algorithms perform within about three percentage points of each other, which is itself informative: with this feature set the choice of classifier matters far less than the choice of elicitation episode.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Ten hand-defined behavioural statistics per child: duration and frequency of eye contact, active social engagement and social smiling in the FF episode, and duration and frequency of eye contact and active social engagement in the SF episode. All are produced by human coders in Observer XT 12, not by automated sensing - so the representation is interpretable and clinically legible, but the pipeline is not automatable and the home self-screening application the paper envisages would require replacing this stage entirely.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Overall accuracy per algorithm per episode, plus an SVM confusion matrix. Deriving from the matrix: SF episode sensitivity 85.0% and specificity 83.7%; FF episode sensitivity 87.5% and specificity 76.7%, so the still-face episode's advantage lies in specificity. No AUC, precision, recall or F1 is reported directly, although the paper does discuss 'low recall rate of N-ASD samples'. Accuracy is additionally stratified across four age bands to test whether misclassification clusters by age; no regularity was found.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is inherent rather than post hoc: the features are named clinical behaviours, so the model operates on quantities a clinician already reasons about. Interpretation is supported by two separate analyses rather than by a model-explanation method - t-tests establishing which behaviours differ and in which episode, and Pearson correlations linking still-face behaviours to CSBS-DP symptom severity. The substantive interpretation is that the still-face episode's social challenge exposes communication impairment more sharply than ordinary interaction, evidenced by the SF episode both classifying better and being the only episode whose behaviours correlate with symptom severity. No feature importances, coefficients or ablations are reported.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Leave-one-out cross-validation over 83 samples, then an attempted verification on the 45 high-risk children. The verification is where the design breaks down: 40 of those 45 are the confirmed-ASD children the model trained on, so only the 5 N-ASD cases are genuinely unseen - and all 5 were misclassified. There is a further subtler problem: the ten features were chosen because t-tests on the full dataset showed them to differ significantly between groups, so feature selection preceded and stood outside the cross-validation loop, leaking label information into every fold. No independent site, no held-out cohort, no calibration analysis, and no comparison against the M-CHAT baseline that all high-risk children had already passed.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: high-risk autism spectrum disorder; the Still-Face Paradigm; social behavior; machine learning; model for early screening. The vocabulary is developmental-psychology first and computational second - 'social behavior', 'emotion regulation', 'social expectations', 'infant-mother interaction' - with machine learning entering as a screening instrument rather than as the object of study.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Frontiers in Pediatrics (Child and Adolescent Psychiatry section) - a clinical pediatrics venue, not a computational one, which matches the paper's weighting toward the behavioural and diagnostic findings over the modelling.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2020. The framing is the diagnostic delay gap: autism can currently be diagnosed at 2 years but 'age at ASD diagnosis is still 40 months or even later', and Chinese prevalence estimates rose from 0.07% to 1.8%. The authors position video-based behavioural coding as the objective alternative to the retrospective parent interviews and rating scales that dominated earlier work, which they characterise as 'highly subjective and unfavorable for widespread promotion'. They also note that machine-learning screening had by then reached over 80% accuracy using EEG and brain imaging, and argue that combining social behavioural indicators with biological indicators is the necessary next step - positioning this paper as supplying the behavioural half of that combination.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Applying Machine Learning to Kinematic and Eye Movement Features of a Movement Imitation Task to Predict Autism Diagnosis
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Vabalas A; Gowen E; Poliakoff E; Casson AJ
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autistic adults
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Motor and kinematics (with gaze)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Predict autism diagnosis from movement imitation, with an explicit primary emphasis on the reliability of the machine-learning methodology - avoiding overfitting through nested validation, verifying generalisation on an independent sample, and achieving stable feature selection so that results are interpretable
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study with a pre-specified independent hold-out test sample
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session; imitation trials organised into a general instruction block and an attention instruction block, each covering three movement conditions (elevated, fast-direct, direct)
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Movement imitation: participants watched then imitated video sequences of simple hand movements pointing between locations, with movement style manipulated across conditions (elevated amplitude, fast-direct, direct) and under two instruction regimes - a general instruction block and an attention instruction block explicitly directing attention to movement style
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory - University of Manchester
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Not described in this paper; the experimental protocol and stimuli are referred to a prior publication by Gowen et al.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 22 total - 15 in the development sample and 7 in the independent test sample
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Development sample 33.1 years; independent test sample 28.16 years
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Development sample 3 female / 12 male; independent test sample 4 female / 3 male
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported in this paper
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described in this paper
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 22 total - 15 in the development sample and 7 in the independent test sample
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd_controls: Development sample 32.2 years; independent test sample 27.90 years
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution_controls: Development sample 3 female / 12 male; independent test sample 4 female / 3 male
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes - matched for age with non-significant differences within both the development sample (p = 0.73) and the test sample (p = 0.95); the two samples differ from each other at p = 0.06
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Yes within each sample (identical distributions in autistic and non-autistic groups), but markedly different between samples - 20% female in the development set versus 57% in the independent test set, which the authors flag explicitly
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Motor kinematics of hand movement and eye movement behaviour during imitation
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Watch a video of a hand movement sequence, then imitate it, with hand and eye movements recorded concurrently. Only movements between two specified pointing locations were included in analysis. Two instruction blocks were compared - general instruction and attention instruction
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Motion tracking and eye tracking apparatus (specific models referred to the source protocol publication); MATLAB or equivalent implementation of nested cross-validation, SVM-RBF, and four feature selection algorithms
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Data derive from an experimental protocol published previously by Gowen et al.; no dataset release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement in the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Low-sensitivity numeric motion and gaze data. Ethics details are not restated in this paper, being referred to the source protocol publication
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted kinematic and gaze features, summarised as means and standard deviations across conditions
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Kinematic: 20 parameters per movement (duration, peak velocity and its timing, horizontal amplitude before peak acceleration, time before and after peak velocity, peak acceleration and deceleration with their timings in seconds and percentages, dimensionless jerk, horizontal and vertical amplitude, peak vertical amplitude timing and location), computed as 20 means and 20 standard deviations for each of three movement conditions (elevated, fast-direct, direct) within each of two instruction blocks. Eye movement: 24 means and 24 standard deviations per instruction block. This yields a high-dimensional feature space against 30 development participants
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Motion and eye tracking pipelines from the source protocol; custom feature computation
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, with explicit emphasis on selection stability
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Four feature selection algorithms compared (t-test filter, SVM recursive feature elimination, ReliefF, mRMR), evaluated on both classification accuracy and Kuncheva's index of selection stability. Three improved variants were then developed: an ensemble combining rankings from all four selectors, t-test with bagging over 100 half-sample subsamples, and a novel 'Wrapped t-test' that iteratively adjusts t-statistics up or down according to whether the selected feature set exceeds 50% classification accuracy, running until Kuncheva's index equals 1 for 100 consecutive iterations
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Seven of the ten features selected by the wrapped t-test came from the elevated-amplitude condition, which was also the condition showing significant group differences by conventional parametric statistics
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Clearly reported and interpreted: after watching videos of elevated movements to imitate, autistic individuals performed movements using a lower vertical amplitude than non-autistic individuals, and consequently reached peak acceleration earlier in the movement. The most discriminative features came from the condition in which non-autistic individuals successfully imitated unusual movement kinematics while autistic individuals tended to fail
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification with stability-oriented feature selection
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: SVM with RBF kernel as the classifier throughout, paired with four baseline feature selection methods (t-test, SVM-RFE, ReliefF, mRMR) and three developed variants (ensemble, t-test with bagging, wrapped t-test)
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Two-stage. At model development, nested cross-validation with feature selection performed inside each of ten nested CV folds. Then, independently, the developed models were applied to a pre-specified hold-out sample of 7 autistic and 7 non-autistic participants who took no part in development. Statistical significance of classification results was assessed. The authors state the rationale explicitly: nested CV was chosen 'because it was shown to produce reliable results' and they had previously shown 'that nested CV produces reliable results regardless of sample size'
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Classification accuracy at both development and independent testing stages, reported per algorithm and per instruction block, with Kuncheva's index quantifying feature selection stability and p-values for statistical significance; accuracy distributions shown as box plots
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Final models: 73% accuracy from kinematic features, 70% from eye movement features, and 78% from combined features. Baseline t-test selection in the general instruction block gave 66% development accuracy with Kuncheva's index 0.66 and 68% on independent testing. Development and independent-testing accuracies were comparable throughout, which the authors present as evidence that nested cross-validation successfully controlled overfitting. The general instruction block outperformed the attention instruction block for all data types, with the difference moderate for kinematics and more marked for eye movement and combined data
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Kinematic and eye-movement features of a movement imitation task predicted autism diagnosis at 73%, 70% and 78% respectively for kinematic, gaze and combined data, with combined data providing complementary information. The central methodological result is that development-stage and independent-test accuracies were comparable, demonstrating that nested cross-validation was sufficient to control overfitting - and this held even though the two samples differed markedly in sex composition (20% versus 57% female). Substantively, the discriminative signal came from the elevated-amplitude condition: autistic adults imitated the unusual elevated movement style with lower vertical amplitude than non-autistic adults, reaching peak acceleration earlier. A novel wrapped t-test feature selection algorithm achieved perfect selection stability while also improving independent-test performance.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Reduced vertical amplitude and earlier peak acceleration when imitating movements performed with unusually elevated trajectories - a failure to adopt the model's atypical movement style rather than a general motor difference
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Not extracted in detail from the available text; the paper's framing implies extension to larger samples and to the adult diagnostic context it identifies as under-served
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: This is the corpus's strongest demonstration that nested validation delivers what it promises. The same first author's 2019 EMBC paper, also in this corpus, argued that prior kinematic studies reporting 86.7-96.7% had used K-fold cross-validation that inflates estimates on small samples; here the group goes further by developing models under nested cross-validation and then testing them on a genuinely independent hold-out sample of 14 participants who took no part in development. Development and testing accuracies were comparable, which is direct empirical evidence that the nested procedure generalised - and it held despite a large sex-composition difference between samples that the authors flag rather than conceal. The critique of the prior literature is stated precisely: those studies 'did not avoid pooling training and validation data while developing their ML models and did not take other steps to control for the fitting of random noise', did not test with independent data, and 'did not assess the statistical significance of the results'. The feature-selection work is also substantive: Kuncheva's index is used to quantify stability explicitly, four standard selectors are benchmarked, and a novel wrapped t-test achieves complete stability while improving independent-test accuracy - and the resulting stable ten-feature set is what makes the behavioural interpretation possible. Limitations are scale and reporting: 44 adults in total with a 14-participant test set, so 78% is roughly 11 of 14 correct; the diagnostic ascertainment is not described in this paper at all, being referred to the source protocol; and both samples are high-IQ (means 122-126) adults, bounding generalisability.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups totalling 44 adults, split across two independently constituted samples: a development sample of 15 autistic and 15 non-autistic adults, and a hold-out testing sample of 7 autistic and 7 non-autistic adults, each internally matched. Having a pre-specified independent test sample rather than only cross-validation folds is rare in this corpus. No other-diagnosis comparison group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'autistic adults', 'autistic individuals', 'non-autistic adults', 'non-autistic individuals', 'individuals living with autism'. Consistently identity-first and paired with 'non-autistic' rather than 'healthy', 'normal' or 'typically developing' - among the most neurodiversity-aligned terminology in the corpus, consistent with the same Manchester group's other entries here.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Development sample: 15 autistic (3 female, 12 male), mean age 33.1, mean IQ 122.0; 15 non-autistic (3 female, 12 male), mean age 32.2, mean IQ 124.8. Age p = 0.73, IQ p = 0.51. Independent test sample: 7 autistic (4 female, 3 male), mean age 28.16, mean IQ 122.14; 7 non-autistic (4 female, 3 male), mean age 27.90, mean IQ 126.29. Age p = 0.95, IQ p = 0.46. Groups are matched for age, gender, handedness and IQ within each sample, with all comparisons tested and reported - unusually thorough. The two samples differ in sex composition (20% female in development versus 57% in testing) and marginally in age (p = 0.06), which the authors flag explicitly and turn into a strength: generalisation held despite the demographic shift. Both samples are high-IQ (means 122-126) adults, which bounds the population addressed.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not described in this paper. The experimental protocol, stimuli and by implication the diagnostic ascertainment are referred to a prior publication by Gowen et al. This is the study's principal reporting gap - as with the same group's 2019 paper, the diagnostic basis for the class labels is not stated in the analysis paper itself.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: IQ is reported for all four subgroups and used as a matching variable with statistical verification, and handedness is also matched. No language, adaptive-functioning or autism-severity measures are reported, and no comorbidity information. IQ means of 122-126 indicate a sample well above population average.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: predict autism diagnosis from imitation kinematics and gaze, with methodological reliability as the explicit primary focus. Main findings: 73% accuracy from kinematics, 70% from eye movements, 78% from combined features; development and independent-test accuracies comparable, demonstrating that nested cross-validation controlled overfitting; the general instruction block outperformed the attention instruction block across all data types; t-test feature selection outperformed SVM-RFE, ReliefF and mRMR on both accuracy and stability; and seven of ten selected kinematic features came from the elevated-amplitude condition, where autistic adults imitated with lower vertical amplitude and earlier peak acceleration.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory setting at a UK university. The data come from an experimental protocol previously published by the same group, so this is a machine-learning analysis of an existing behavioural dataset rather than a new collection.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Movement imitation with style manipulation: participants watched a video of a hand movement sequence pointing between four locations and then imitated it, with only movements between two designated locations analysed. Three movement styles were used - elevated amplitude, fast-direct, and direct - crossed with two instruction blocks, a general instruction block and an attention instruction block that directed attention to movement style. The elevated condition is the theoretically critical one, since imitating an unusually elevated trajectory requires adopting a movement style outside one's habitual repertoire.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single session with no follow-up. Data are numeric kinematic and gaze traces, not identifiable media. Ethics and consent details are not restated in this paper, being referred to the source protocol publication - a reporting gap even if the underlying governance was presumably adequate.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: motion tracking and eye tracking apparatus, with specific models deferred to the source protocol publication; a screen for video stimulus presentation. Software: implementations of SVM-RBF, four feature selection algorithms, nested cross-validation, and the authors' novel bagging and wrapped t-test variants; Kuncheva's index for stability quantification.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No data or code release stated. Method reporting is strong on the analytic side - the full 20-parameter kinematic definition list, the feature structure across conditions and blocks, the four baseline selectors, the three developed variants with their operating rules (100 subsamples of size n/2 for bagging; t-statistic adjustment up or down at a 50% accuracy threshold with termination at Kuncheva's index of 1 across 100 consecutive iterations for the wrapped t-test), the nested cross-validation structure with feature selection inside each of ten folds, and the classifier. Weak on the experimental side, where apparatus, protocol details and diagnostic ascertainment are all deferred to a prior publication.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The paper's framing is itself a critique of prior work's limitations rather than only its own. On the field: prior kinematic ML studies 'had small sample sizes and achieved high classification accuracy', but 'models developed with small sample/high dimensional data are prone to fit noise and not necessarily an underlying pattern separating classes', and those studies 'did not avoid pooling training and validation data while developing their ML models and did not take other steps to control for the fitting of random noise', were 'not tested with independent data', and did not assess statistical significance. On their own work they acknowledge the difficulty of small-sample high-dimensional pattern recognition requiring careful handling of both validation and feature selection. Identifiable in review: 44 adults total with a 14-participant test set means 78% is roughly 11 of 14 correct; the diagnostic ascertainment is entirely absent from this paper; both samples are high-IQ adults; the reported headline is the best across several feature-selection variants; and the marked sex-composition difference between samples, while turned into a generalisation argument, also means the independent test provides limited evidence about performance in a comparably composed sample.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Not set out as a discrete future-work section in the extracted text. The introduction's framing implies the priority - the paper notes that adult diagnostic instruments 'have only been validated for use with children', that with adults 'clinicians rarely rely on standardised diagnostic methods making diagnosis less accurate, more subjective and lengthier', and that researching adult diagnostic criteria is listed among the top ten priorities by a UK autism research charity. The work positions itself as contributing quantitative tests to supplement current qualitative ones in that under-served context.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Two modalities: hand movement kinematics (velocity, acceleration, deceleration profiles with their timings, amplitudes, jerk) and eye movement behaviour during the same imitation task. Measuring gaze and movement concurrently during imitation is distinctive - it captures both what the participant looked at while observing the model and how they subsequently moved.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Explicit multimodal fusion with quantified benefit: kinematic features alone gave 73%, eye movement features alone 70%, and combined features 78%. The authors state that the modalities 'provided complementary information for predictions', and the 5-point gain over the better single modality is one of the clearest quantified fusion benefits in the corpus, obtained under independent testing rather than internal cross-validation. Features are combined at feature level before selection and classification.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning with SVM-RBF as the fixed classifier, so that the experimental variable is feature selection rather than model family. Four established selectors are benchmarked (t-test filter, SVM-RFE, ReliefF, mRMR) and three variants developed (ensemble, bagging, wrapped t-test). Holding the classifier constant while varying selection is a clean design that isolates the contribution the paper is actually studying.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted kinematic and gaze summary features, structured hierarchically: 20 kinematic parameters computed as means and standard deviations for each of three movement conditions within each of two instruction blocks, plus 24 gaze means and 24 gaze standard deviations per block. This produces a feature space far larger than the 30-participant development sample, which is precisely the small-sample high-dimensional regime the paper's methodology is designed to handle.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Classification accuracy at both development and independent-testing stages, reported side by side per algorithm and per instruction block - the side-by-side presentation is what makes the generalisation claim checkable. Kuncheva's index quantifies feature selection stability as a second reported outcome, treated as co-equal with accuracy. Statistical significance p-values accompany the accuracies, and accuracy distributions are shown as box plots. No sensitivity, specificity or AUC.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is pursued as an explicit design goal rather than a by-product: feature selection methods were chosen and developed 'aimed at selection stability to assure result interpretability', and the wrapped t-test runs until it converges on an identical feature set across 100 consecutive iterations. The resulting stable ten-feature set supports a specific behavioural interpretation - seven of ten features come from the elevated-amplitude condition, where autistic adults produced lower vertical amplitude and consequently earlier peak acceleration, indicating a failure to adopt the model's unusual movement style rather than a general motor difference. This is corroborated by conventional parametric tests showing significant group differences in the same condition.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The strongest validation design in the corpus. Nested cross-validation at development, with feature selection performed inside each of ten nested folds; then a genuinely independent hold-out sample of 14 participants who took no part in development; then direct comparison of development and testing accuracies to verify that nesting controlled overfitting. Statistical significance is assessed. Feature selection stability is quantified with Kuncheva's index. The generalisation claim is additionally stress-tested by the incidental fact that the two samples differ substantially in sex composition, so the independent result holds across a demographic shift. What remains absent: external validation on a different site or protocol, sensitivity and specificity, and any deployment analysis.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No formal keyword list in the extracted text. Vocabulary: 'reliable machine learning application', 'nested validation', 'selection stability', 'independent data sample', 'Kuncheva's index', 'quantitative tests to supplement current qualitative ones'. The methodological-reliability vocabulary dominates and is the paper's identity.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Scientific Reports (Nature Portfolio) - a broad multidisciplinary journal, neither autism-specific nor computational.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2020. The paper gives one of the corpus's sharpest field characterisations. On the clinical problem: UK average waiting time between initial concerns and clinical diagnosis exceeds three years, adult diagnostic instruments 'have only been validated for use with children', and adult diagnosis is 'less accurate, more subjective and lengthier'. On the methodological problem: 'only a handful of ML studies used kinematic data for autism prediction. All studies had small sample sizes and achieved high classification accuracy', but such models 'are prone to fit noise', and to the authors' knowledge those studies 'did not avoid pooling training and validation data', were not tested with independent data, and did not assess statistical significance. This paper is the corrective demonstration that follows from that diagnosis.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Research and Design of Autism Smart Diagnosis Information System Based on Chinese Children's Facial Expression Data and Deep Convolution Neural Network
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Zhao W
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: Proceedings of the 53rd Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Preschool children with autism
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Facial expression
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Design and deploy a deployable clinical information system that diagnoses autism from children's facial expression imitation using deep convolutional neural networks, in order to reduce diagnostic subjectivity, cut the one-to-two hours a physician spends per assessment, and extend early diagnosis to remote and underdeveloped areas via an app or web deployment
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Systems engineering and development paper with a small two-group validation test; no model is trained on autism labels, and the diagnostic rule is a threshold applied to expression-recognition output
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One test session per child; the system displays each of seven target expressions three times and collects the child's imitation each time
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Facial expression imitation on demand: the system displays one of seven expressions and prompts the child by picture and sound to imitate it, with elicitation aids such as cartoon smiling faces, children's songs and animations used for situational simulation. The camera captures the child's response, the CNN classifies it into one of seven expression categories, and the system compares the classified expression against the target
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Quiet classrooms without noise or external interference; the normal group at Amy Education School in Zhengzhou and the autistic group at Guangzhou Children's Care Center. The system was designed against the workflows of Hubei Maternal and Child Health Hospital, Wuhan Children's Hospital and Guangzhou Women and Children's Medical Center
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Reported only as 'The selected children with autism were diagnosed by a professional physician'. No instrument, criteria, date or clinician detail is given, though the paper elsewhere discusses ICD-10, DSM-IV, ABC, CARS and CABS as the instruments used in the collaborating hospitals
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported. Distinguishing severe, moderate and mild autism is named as future work
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - ten typically developing children described as 'normal'
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: By parent report only: 'After asking the parents of the children who participated in the experiment, the parents answered that the children who participated in the experiment had no history of autism'
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No, and the mismatch is systematic: the control group is 5-8 years old and the autistic group 3-6, so the groups barely overlap and the autistic children are younger throughout. Because expression production and imitation compliance both develop rapidly across this range, and because the recognition model was tuned on 5-8 year old faces, the age difference runs directly parallel to the outcome
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Yes - 5 boys and 5 girls in each group
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted by parent report; no screening instrument or developmental assessment was applied
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Still facial expression images captured by camera during imitation
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: The client captures the child's face, detects and compresses the face region, and transmits it to the server, which preprocesses the image, extracts features via CNN, classifies it into one of seven expression categories, compares that against the target expression, and returns a per-expression correct/incorrect result; the per-child recognition rate over seven expressions is then compared against a 60% threshold
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: High-definition cameras; client applications for computers and smartphones; application server and SQL Server database over a four-layer network topology; HDF5 files for expression feature storage; JSON over TCP for client-server transfer; VGG-19 and ResNet-18 convolutional neural networks; response time specified as under 5 seconds
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: A small supplementary set of 112 images - seven expressions from each of 16 healthy Chinese children aged 5-8 (8 boys, 8 girls) recruited via Amy Education School in Zhengzhou. Establishing a dedicated children's facial expression database is named as future work
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Sensitive - facial images of identifiable children including a clinically diagnosed autistic group, with collection photographs reproduced in the paper. Governance is limited to parental information before collection ('parents have been informed of the purpose of collecting facial expression data'); no ethics committee approval, no written consent procedure, and no anonymization or retention policy is described. Images are stored in a server-side SQL Server database
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Learned CNN features from raw facial images
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: End-to-end learned convolutional features; no handcrafted descriptors. The paper contrasts this with traditional oriented gradient histogram, Gabor filter, local directional pattern and enhanced local binary features, arguing these are 'artificial design, time-consuming and laborious' and effective only on small image sets
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: VGG-19 and ResNet-18, with extracted expression features persisted as HDF5 feature files that can be reread and updated when new samples arrive
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reported at the level of expression categories rather than features. In the autistic group the system's per-expression recognition rates were angry 50%, disgust 10%, fear 30%, happy 60%, sad 60%, surprise 20%, neutral 10%; in the control group angry 80%, disgust 70%, fear 80%, happy 100%, sad 80%, surprise 70%, neutral 90%. Happy and sad were best recognised in the autistic group, and neutral and disgust worst - though the neutral result inverts the control pattern, where neutral was among the best recognised
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Deep supervised classification of facial expression, with a hand-set threshold on classification agreement serving as the diagnostic rule
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: VGG-19 and ResNet-18, described as trained separately and then synthesised; no fusion mechanism, weighting or ensembling procedure is specified
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: None in the machine-learning sense. No training/validation/test split, no cross-validation, no held-out set, and no hyperparameters are reported for the expression models. The clinical evaluation is a single test of 20 children, and the 60% diagnostic threshold is read off the same 20 children's results rather than derived on separate data
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Per-expression and per-child recognition rate (proportion of the seven target expressions the system classified in agreement with the prompt), plus group means. No sensitivity, specificity, AUC, confusion matrix or statistical test of the group difference
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Mean expression recognition rate 81.4% in the typically developing group (per-child: 85.7, 85.7, 85.7, 57.1, 85.7, 100, 71.4, 100, 85.7, 57.1) and 34.3% in the autistic group (28.5, 28.5, 28.5, 42.9, 42.9, 57.1, 28.5, 42.9, 28.5, 14.3). Applying a 60% threshold separates the groups completely on this sample - all ten autistic children fall below 60% and eight of ten controls above - but two typically developing children also score 57.1% and would be flagged. Errors in the control group concentrated on disgust and surprise, attributed to their subtle and locally confined facial changes
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A client-server system was built in which children imitate seven prompted facial expressions, a CNN classifies each attempt, and agreement with the prompt is scored. Typically developing children's expressions were recognised at 81.4% and autistic children's at 34.3%, and the authors propose a 60% recognition rate as the threshold below which a child 'would have a tendency to suffer from autism', with lower rates indicating higher tendency. The system is presented as deployable by app or web page to bring early diagnosis to remote and underdeveloped areas.
