data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Reduced correspondence between prompted and produced facial expression, most pronounced for neutral, disgust and surprise
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Deploy and test in a large number of cooperating hospitals; collect substantially more facial expression data from both typically developing and autistic children and establish a dedicated children's facial expression database; extend the system to recognise children's physical movement so that autism can be assessed from multiple perspectives; and grade autism severity into severe, moderate and mild to support treatment planning
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Included on the criteria but among the weakest studies in the corpus, and the weakness is structural rather than incidental. No model is ever trained on autism labels: VGG-19 and ResNet-18 learn seven-way facial expression classification from FER2013 and CK+, supplemented by 112 images from 16 typically developing Chinese children, and the diagnostic decision is a hand-set threshold on how often the classifier's output matches the prompt. The consequence is that a measurement failure is being read as a clinical sign - a low recognition rate can mean the child did not imitate, imitated atypically, was too young to follow the prompt, or simply produced a face outside the distribution the network was trained on, and the design cannot distinguish these from autism. Three confounds make that ambiguity concrete. The groups differ in age (3-6 versus 5-8) with barely any overlap, in recruitment site (a Guangzhou care centre versus a Zhengzhou education school), and in relation to the training data, since the supplementary Chinese samples came from typically developing 5-8 year olds - the control group's own population. The 60% threshold is also fitted to the same 20 children it is then evaluated on, and even so misclassifies two controls at 57.1%. The headline 81.4% in the abstract is the expression recognition rate in typically developing children, not any diagnostic accuracy, and the paper's framing ('the diagnosis results are objective and accurate', 'the system can diagnose autism for children and adults in different countries and regions') is far beyond what 20 children support. The record is nonetheless valuable to the review: it is the clearest instance of the corpus's deployment-oriented strand, where system architecture, hospital workflow integration and cost-of-access arguments are developed in detail while validation is left minimal, and it documents an important failure mode - substituting a proxy task's performance for a diagnostic outcome.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of ten: 10 autistic children aged 3-6 from Guangzhou Children's Care Center and 10 typically developing children aged 5-8 from Amy Education School in Zhengzhou. A separate group of 16 typically developing Chinese children aged 5-8 (8 boys, 8 girls) supplied 112 training images. No other-diagnosis comparison group. At 20 evaluation participants this is among the smallest clinical evaluations in the corpus, and it is a system test rather than a model validation.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'autistic children', 'normal children', 'autistic patients', 'children with autism', 'healthy children volunteers'. The autistic/normal contrast is used throughout, and disease framing is explicit - autism is described as 'a representative disease of generalized developmental disorders' undergoing 'a transition from rare diseases to epidemics', with extensive discussion of the financial and psychological burden on families and society. This is the most pathologising vocabulary in the corpus, standing at the opposite end from the identity-first, non-autistic-comparison usage of the Manchester kinematics papers.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Autistic group: 10 children, 5 boys and 5 girls, aged 3-6, recruited through Guangzhou Children's Care Center. Control group: 10 children, 5 boys and 5 girls, aged 5-8, recruited through Amy Education School in Zhengzhou. Sex is balanced within and across groups, which is unusual for this corpus. Age is not: the ranges barely overlap and the autistic children are systematically younger, which matters because facial expression production, imitation compliance and attention to a screen prompt all change substantially between 3 and 8 years. Recruitment site is fully confounded with group. No means, standard deviations, IQ, developmental level, ethnicity or socioeconomic information is reported for either group.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: One sentence: 'The selected children with autism were diagnosed by a professional physician.' No instrument, criteria, date or diagnostician detail. The paper describes ICD-10, DSM-IV, ABC, CARS and CABS as the instruments the collaborating hospitals use, and analyses their facial-expression-related items in detail to motivate the design, but does not state which if any were applied to these ten children. Typically developing status rests entirely on parents answering that their child had no history of autism.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No IQ, developmental quotient, language, adaptive functioning, symptom severity or comorbidity measure is reported for either group. Severity grading is named only as future work.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: build a deployable hospital information system that diagnoses autism from facial expression imitation using deep CNNs, reducing subjectivity and physician time and extending early diagnosis to underserved regions. Main findings: mean expression recognition rate of 81.4% in typically developing children versus 34.3% in autistic children; a proposed 60% threshold below which a child is said to show a tendency toward autism; recognition errors in typically developing children concentrated on disgust and surprise; and in autistic children happy and sad were best recognised while neutral and disgust were worst.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Testing was conducted in quiet classrooms at two cooperating institutions - Amy Education School in Zhengzhou for the typically developing group and Guangzhou Children's Care Center for the autistic group. System requirements were developed through repeated consultation with physicians at Hubei Maternal and Child Health Hospital, Wuhan Children's Hospital and Guangzhou Women and Children's Medical Center, including direct observation of how they administer the diagnostic scales.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Prompted facial expression imitation. The system randomly displays one of seven expressions (angry, disgust, fear, happy, sad, surprise, neutral) and prompts the child by picture and sound to reproduce it, presenting the same expression three times, with elicitation aids such as cartoon smiling faces, children's songs and animations for situational simulation. The design is explicitly modelled on how physicians administer the diagnostic scales - 'The doctor observes the tester's reaction to determine whether the tester is autistic after requesting the tester to make the corresponding expression' - and the paper justifies the choice by itemising the expression-related items in the CABS, ABC and CARS scales.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single session per child with no follow-up. Data are facial images of identifiable children including a clinically diagnosed group, stored server-side in a SQL Server database and with collection photographs reproduced in the paper. Governance reporting is the weakest in the corpus: parents were informed of the purpose of data collection, but no ethics committee approval, no written consent procedure, no anonymization and no retention or access policy is described - which is a serious omission for a system whose stated deployment path is public download by app or web page.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: High-definition cameras; client applications for computers and smartphones; a four-layer architecture (application, communication, application server with firewall, database server); SQL Server; HDF5 feature files; JSON over TCP; VGG-19 and ResNet-18. Public training corpora: FER2013 (35,887 images at 48x48, seven expressions) and CK+ (593 sequences from 123 people at 640x480, 69% female, including African American, Asian and South American subjects). A specified non-functional requirement - end-to-end response under 5 seconds - is one of the few deployment constraints stated anywhere in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Poor. The system architecture, network topology, module decomposition, data formats and interface flow are described in detail, but nothing needed to reproduce the machine learning is given: no training procedure, no train/validation/test split, no hyperparameters, no epochs, no augmentation, no accuracy on the source expression datasets, and no description of how the VGG-19 and ResNet-18 outputs were 'synthesised'. No code and no data are released. The clinical evaluation reports per-child recognition rates in full, which is welcome, but no statistical test accompanies them.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The authors acknowledge that the algorithm 'is affected by the environment and light' and that accuracy suffers accordingly, noting that two typically developing children scored 57.1%; that errors concentrate on disgust and surprise because those expressions involve only minor local facial change and some participants produced them weakly; and that more real samples are needed. They do not acknowledge the design's central problems. No model is trained on autism labels, so a proxy task's failure rate is being treated as a diagnostic signal, and the design cannot separate non-imitation, atypical imitation, developmental immaturity and out-of-distribution faces from autism. The groups differ in age (3-6 versus 5-8) and are fully confounded with recruitment site. The supplementary training images came from typically developing 5-8 year olds, the control group's own population, which biases the classifier toward recognising control-group faces. The 60% threshold is fitted to the same 20 children it is evaluated on. And the abstract's 81.4% is the expression recognition rate in typically developing children, not a diagnostic accuracy, yet is presented as 'the accuracy of facial expression recognition of this system'.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Test the system in a large number of cooperating hospitals; collect far more facial expression data from both typically developing and autistic children and build a dedicated children's facial expression database, since existing databases are built mainly from adults and children have rounder faces, larger eyes and less prominent bones that make their features harder to recognise; extend the system to recognise physical movement so autism can be assessed from multiple perspectives; and add severity grading into severe, moderate and mild.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: A single modality - facial expression, captured as still images during prompted imitation of seven categories (angry, disgust, fear, happy, sad, surprise, neutral). The behaviour targeted is expression production on demand rather than spontaneous expression or expression recognition ability, although the paper's motivating literature concerns autistic people's difficulty recognising others' expressions, which is a different construct from the one measured.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No multimodal fusion. Adding recognition of children's physical movement to achieve 'diagnosis of autism from multiple perspectives' is named as future work. There is a nominal model-level combination - VGG-19 and ResNet-18 are said to be trained and then 'synthesised' - but no mechanism, weighting or comparative result is given for either model separately, so the combination cannot be evaluated.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Deep supervised learning: VGG-19 and ResNet-18 convolutional neural networks for seven-way facial expression classification. The paper argues explicitly for deep over traditional approaches, on the grounds that handcrafted features (oriented gradient histograms, Gabor filters, local directional patterns, enhanced local binary patterns) are 'artificial design, time-consuming and laborious' and work well only on small image sets, whereas end-to-end deep models combine feature extraction and classification. Critically, neither network is trained on an autism label - the diagnostic layer is a hand-set threshold on classification agreement, not a learned model.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Raw facial images processed end-to-end, with learned convolutional features persisted as HDF5 feature files for reuse and incremental retraining. Training data are FER2013 (35,887 low-resolution 48x48 images), CK+ (593 sequences from 123 people at 640x480), and 112 images from 16 Chinese children aged 5-8. The mismatch between the training distribution - largely adult, largely posed, mostly non-Chinese - and the target population of 3-6 year old autistic children is the input-representation problem the paper's supplementary collection was meant to address but at 112 images cannot.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Only recognition rate: the proportion of seven prompted expressions the classifier assigned to the prompted category, reported per expression, per child and per group. No sensitivity, specificity, AUC, precision, recall, F1, confusion matrix or statistical test. Because the threshold rule reduces to a binary decision on 20 children, sensitivity of 10/10 and specificity of 8/10 could be derived, but the paper does not do so and the threshold was chosen on these same data.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No interpretability method - no saliency maps, no attention visualisation, no feature attribution. What the system exposes instead is a per-expression probability histogram shown to the user, with the maximum-probability bar taken as the prediction, and a per-expression breakdown of which categories failed. This is interface transparency rather than model interpretability: it shows what the model decided, not why. The clinical interpretation offered - that autistic children have facial expression recognition obstacles, so their expressions are harder to classify - is asserted from the prior literature rather than derived from the model.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The weakest validation in the corpus. No train/validation/test split, no cross-validation, no held-out set, and no reported performance on the source expression datasets. The clinical evaluation is a single pass over 20 children whose groups differ in age and recruitment site, with the decision threshold fitted to those same 20 results. There is no independent sample, no external site, no repeat measurement, and no comparison against the diagnostic scales the system is meant to support - which is notable given the paper analyses those scales item by item to justify its design but never compares its output against them.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No formal keyword list. Vocabulary: 'autism smart diagnosis information system', 'deep convolution neural network', 'facial expression recognition', 'system architecture', 'network topology', 'social benefits and application value'. The register is information-systems and deployment-oriented rather than clinical or statistical - the paper's own framing is that it addresses 'the actual business needs of the hospital'.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Proceedings of the 53rd Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS) - an information-systems conference, not a clinical or machine-learning venue, which explains the weighting toward architecture, workflow and deployment over validation. Published under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 with a stable handle.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2020. The framing is epidemiological and economic rather than methodological: prevalence rising from 3-5 per 10,000 in the 1980s to 2.76% among US children aged 3-14 by 2016; an estimated 10 million people with autism in China including 2 million children, growing by nearly 200,000 annually, with no national statistical survey; 33% of parents reporting that caregiving seriously affected their careers with an average annual income loss of 30,957 yuan. Against that, the paper identifies the bottleneck as clinical throughput and subjectivity - one to two hours per diagnosis, results 'easily disturbed by external factors such as hospital level, physician's subjective level, patient's education level, age' - and positions an app-deliverable CNN system as the answer, with explicit emphasis on remote and underdeveloped areas. The paper is a clear marker of the corpus's deployment-first strand, in which access and cost arguments substitute for validation.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Automated identification of postural control for children with autism spectrum disorder using a machine learning approach
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Li Y; Mache MA; Todd TA
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Motor and kinematics (postural control)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Develop and validate automated identification of ASD postural control patterns, and thereby test the open question of whether postural sway characteristics can serve as diagnostic biomarkers for autism
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study with a preceding mixed-model ANOVA of group differences
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single session; 20-second quiet stance per trial, three acceptable trials per condition, two conditions (eyes open, eyes closed) in randomised order
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Quiet standing balance: stand barefoot on two feet and maintain a stationary stance for 20 seconds with arms relaxed at the sides, once with eyes open and once with eyes closed
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Biomechanics laboratory
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Prior diagnosis of ASD by a physician or licensed psychologist as an inclusion criterion; no instrument, criteria or confirmation procedure is described. Additional inclusion requirements were the ability to understand and communicate with examiners and the ability to perform the required tasks
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Explicit exclusions for all children: neurological disorders other than ASD, chronic medical disorders, visual impairments, and physical impairments that could affect balance
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported; no severity instrument administered
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - age-matched typically developing children recruited as healthy controls
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: By the same exclusion criteria (no neurological or chronic medical disorders, no visual or balance-affecting physical impairments); no autism-trait screening instrument reported
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes - explicitly age-matched, with means of 6.9 and 7.2 years and overlapping standard deviations
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not claimed; distributions differ (56% female in ASD versus 40% female in TD), though both groups are unusually female-rich for this literature
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Kinetic postural data: centre-of-pressure time series from a force plate during quiet standing
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Three acceptable 20-second trials per condition, with acceptability criteria stated explicitly: maintaining the instructed eye condition, no obvious voluntary movement such as looking around, swinging arms or leaning, and remaining quiet. Foot placement was deliberately not strictly controlled so participants could adopt a natural stance reflecting the strategy they would use in their own environment. Investigators and guardians kept as quiet as possible to minimise distraction
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Kistler force plate sampling at 60 Hz; fourth-order low-pass Butterworth filter with a 10 Hz cutoff determined by residual analysis; MATLAB R2020a Machine Learning Toolbox
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - newly collected, but not released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Low-sensitivity numeric force-plate data. Institutional Review Board approval was obtained for the study protocol, eligibility was screened by phone with legal guardians, and informed consent was obtained from legal guardians on arrival. No anonymization procedure is described, and none is materially required for this data type
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted centre-of-pressure summary features spanning sway magnitude and sway complexity
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 12 features in total - six COP variables measured under each of two visual conditions. The six are: linear displacement in the mediolateral direction, linear displacement in the anteroposterior direction (each computed as maximum minus minimum), total distance (total length of the COP sway path), sway area (95% confidence interval elliptical area), and sample entropy in the mediolateral and anteroposterior directions (sequence length 2, matching tolerance 0.15 times the standard deviation of the COP data). Features were selected because they capture both magnitude and complexity of sway and had shown group differences in prior research
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: MATLAB for filtering, COP variable computation and sample entropy; Chauvenet's criterion applied to check for outliers, with none detected
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No model-derived feature importance, but a full univariate group comparison is reported
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Mixed-model ANOVA with group as the between-subject factor and test condition as the within-subject factor, at p < 0.05
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: No ranked feature list from the models. The ANOVA showed that displacements, total distances and sway areas were all significantly greater in the ASD group regardless of condition, with no significant interaction; mediolateral sample entropy was greater under eyes-closed than eyes-open in both groups; and anteroposterior sample entropy showed no difference
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Clearly reported: children with ASD exhibited significantly greater COP sway than typically developing children - larger linear displacements, longer total sway path distances and larger sway areas - across both visual conditions. Both groups swayed more with eyes closed than eyes open. Notably, the sample entropy complexity measures did not distinguish the groups, despite the introduction citing two prior studies that found reduced COP complexity in ASD
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification with a broad algorithm comparison
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Six classifiers compared: discriminant analysis, k-nearest neighbour, naive Bayes, decision trees, support vector machine and random forest, with specific parameters given in an appendix. The authors motivate the breadth explicitly, noting that 'no one algorithm works best for every dataset' and that researchers usually implement several variants and explore the best
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Five-fold cross-validation with the dataset randomly split into five equal-sized subsets, four used for training and one for testing, iterated five times with performance metrics averaged. Since each participant contributes one feature vector (12 features aggregated across trials), the folds are inherently participant-level. No nested structure is described for the classifier parameter choices, and the best of six algorithms is reported as the headline
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision and F1 score, with the formulas given explicitly and 'positive' defined as ASD, plus confusion matrices for all classifiers in an appendix
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: All six classifiers exceeded 0.800 accuracy. Naive Bayes was best: accuracy 0.900, specificity 1.000, precision 1.000, F1 0.898, sensitivity 0.826. K-nearest neighbour was second: accuracy 0.860 with other metrics between 0.833 and 0.950
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Twelve centre-of-pressure features from 40 seconds of quiet standing classified children with ASD from age-matched typically developing children at up to 0.900 accuracy, with all six tested algorithms exceeding 0.800. The underlying group difference is in sway magnitude - children with ASD showed significantly greater displacement, path distance and sway area in both eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions - while the complexity measures (sample entropy) did not differentiate the groups, contrary to two prior studies cited in the introduction. Naive Bayes achieved perfect specificity and precision with sensitivity of 0.826, meaning it never falsely labelled a typically developing child as autistic but missed roughly one in six autistic children.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Greater centre-of-pressure sway magnitude: larger mediolateral and anteroposterior linear displacements, longer total sway path, and larger 95% confidence ellipse sway area, present under both visual conditions
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Increase the sample size and analyse more postural control data and features, which the authors expect would yield better classification performance
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A clean, well-executed biomechanics study with several strengths uncommon in this corpus: an a priori power analysis is reported and justified against prior published data; six algorithms are compared with a stated rationale for breadth; five metrics plus confusion matrices are reported with formulas and the positive class defined; outliers are formally checked with Chauvenet's criterion; trial acceptability criteria are stated explicitly; exclusion criteria address competing causes of balance impairment; and the ANOVA establishes the univariate group differences that the classification then exploits, so the classifier is not doing unexplained work. The sample is also unusually female-rich (14 of 25 in the ASD group), which is rare and valuable given the male skew across this literature. The principal limitations are scale and selection optimism. With 50 children and five-fold cross-validation, each test fold contains about 10 children, so an accuracy of 0.900 corresponds to roughly 45 of 50 correct, and specificity of exactly 1.000 with precision of exactly 1.000 reflects zero false positives out of 25 controls - a result that will not be stable at this sample size. The reported figure is also the best of six algorithms selected on the same cross-validation, with no nested structure or external validation. No diagnostic instrument is named, and the ASD group's inclusion criteria require the ability to understand instructions and perform the task, which restricts the sample to more able children. The negative entropy finding is reported plainly and is arguably the more informative result, since it contradicts the complexity account the introduction sets up.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 25: children with ASD and age-matched typically developing children, total 50. Both groups are characterised in a demographic table with sample size, sex breakdown, body mass, height and age. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though neurological disorders other than ASD were an explicit exclusion for both groups.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with autism spectrum disorder', 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'autistic postural control patterns', 'typically developing children', 'children with typical development', 'healthy controls'. Predominantly person-first with 'typically developing' used consistently for the comparison group, though 'healthy controls' appears once. The paper's framing is biomechanical rather than pathologising.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=25 (14 female, 11 male), age 6.9 (1.8) years, body mass 32.7 (11.5) kg, height 126 (13) cm. TD n=25 (10 female, 15 male), age 7.2 (2.0) years, body mass 30.3 (12.4) kg, height 128 (12) cm. Recruitment range 5-12 years. Groups are explicitly age-matched with near-identical means and overlapping standard deviations, and anthropometrics are reported and closely comparable - which matters for postural measures since body mass and height affect sway. Sex is not matched, with the ASD group 56% female against 40% in controls, but both proportions are far higher than the corpus norm, making this one of very few studies here where autistic girls are well represented. Sample size is justified by an a priori power analysis (power 0.80) against previously published postural sway data, indicating 10-13 per group would suffice for the group comparison, with the larger n=25 chosen because 'a larger sample size will improve the accuracy and success of machine learning classifiers'.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: A prior diagnosis of ASD by a physician or a licensed psychologist was an inclusion criterion, but no diagnostic instrument, criteria or confirmation procedure is described, and no autism-trait screening was applied to controls. Two further inclusion requirements - the ability to understand and communicate with examiners and the ability to perform the required tasks - restrict the ASD sample to children who could follow standing instructions, which bounds generalisability toward more able children.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or autism-severity measures are reported. Anthropometrics (height, body mass) are measured and reported for both groups, which is the relevant covariate set for postural biomechanics. Comorbidity is handled by explicit exclusion of neurological disorders other than ASD, chronic medical disorders, visual impairments and physical impairments affecting balance - a well-targeted exclusion list that removes the most plausible competing explanations for balance differences.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: develop and validate automated identification of ASD postural control patterns, framed around the open question of whether postural sway can serve as a diagnostic biomarker. Main findings: all six classifiers exceeded 0.800 accuracy; naive Bayes achieved 0.900 accuracy with 1.000 specificity, 1.000 precision, 0.898 F1 and 0.826 sensitivity; k-nearest neighbour was second at 0.860. The underlying group difference is greater sway magnitude in ASD across displacement, distance and area, with no group difference in sample entropy complexity.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory setting - a biomechanics laboratory with force-plate instrumentation. Newly collected data; no existing dataset used.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Quiet standing balance, barefoot on two feet with arms relaxed, for 20 seconds, under randomised eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions, with three acceptable trials per condition. The 20-second duration is justified explicitly against the practical difficulty of keeping autistic children still for longer, citing evidence that 15 seconds gives acceptable construct and concurrent validity in children. Foot placement was deliberately left unconstrained 'to enable participants to adopt a natural stance to more closely reflect any strategy they might use to maintain balance in their natural environment' - an ecological-validity choice made at the cost of some standardisation. Trial acceptability criteria are stated explicitly, and environmental distraction was minimised by keeping investigators and guardians quiet.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single laboratory session totalling roughly two minutes of recorded standing per child, with no follow-up. The data are numeric force-plate traces, not identifiable media, so privacy risk is minimal. Institutional Review Board approval of the study protocol is reported, eligibility was screened by telephone with legal guardians, and informed consent was obtained from legal guardians on arrival at the laboratory. No child assent statement is reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: a Kistler force plate sampling centre-of-pressure at 60 Hz; standard anthropometric measurement of height and body mass. Software: MATLAB R2020a with the Machine Learning Toolbox for classification and performance evaluation; a fourth-order low-pass Butterworth filter with a 10 Hz cutoff selected by residual analysis; sample entropy computed with sequence length 2 and matching tolerance 0.15 times the COP standard deviation.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No data or code release. Method reporting is otherwise strong: force plate manufacturer and sampling rate, filter order and cutoff with the selection method, all six COP variable definitions, sample entropy parameters, the outlier check and its criterion, trial acceptability criteria, the ANOVA design, the cross-validation scheme, the metric formulas with the positive class defined, the software version, and classifier parameters supplied in an appendix. Confusion matrices for all classifiers are also provided in an appendix. The analysis is re-implementable in principle on comparable force-plate data.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors only briefly, in the abstract and conclusions: 'By increasing the sample size and analyzing more data/features of postural control, a better classification performance would be expected'. There is no dedicated limitations section. Identifiable in review: n=50 with five-fold cross-validation means roughly 10 children per test fold, so 0.900 accuracy is about 45 of 50 correct and the exact 1.000 specificity and precision reflect zero false positives among 25 controls - values that will not be stable at this scale; the headline is the best of six algorithms evaluated on the same cross-validation with no nested selection or external validation; no diagnostic instrument is named; inclusion criteria requiring comprehension of instructions and task performance restrict the ASD sample to more able children; sex is not matched (56% versus 40% female); and the negative sample entropy result contradicts two prior studies cited in the introduction without the discrepancy being discussed in the extracted text.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Increase the sample size and analyse more postural control data and features, with the expectation of better classification performance. No proposals for external validation, comparison against other developmental conditions, or clinical deployment are made.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Motor behavior: kinetic postural control, specifically centre-of-pressure excursion during quiet standing, capturing both the magnitude of sway (displacement, path length, area) and its temporal regularity (sample entropy). This is the only study in the corpus to measure static postural control with a force plate, complementing the gait, reach and imitation studies in the motor strand.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality, but with a designed within-modality manipulation: the same six COP variables are measured under eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions and both sets are supplied jointly to the classifiers, giving 12 features. This effectively fuses two sensory conditions, allowing the models to exploit how each child's sway changes when visual input is removed. No integration with clinical, cognitive or demographic data, though anthropometrics were collected.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning with an unusually broad comparison: discriminant analysis, k-nearest neighbour, naive Bayes, decision trees, support vector machine and random forest, each briefly explained with a citation. The rationale is stated explicitly - because features, sample sizes and data structures differ, 'no one algorithm works best for every dataset', so researchers usually implement several and explore the best. The authors also note that basic supervised algorithms are chosen because they are 'computationally efficient and relevant to small sample sizes'.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted low-dimensional biomechanical features: 12 scalar summaries of centre-of-pressure behaviour per child, spanning two theoretically distinct constructs - sway magnitude and sway complexity. The 12-features-to-50-participants ratio is among the healthiest in the corpus and materially reduces overfitting risk relative to the high-dimensional representations used elsewhere.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision and F1, with all five formulas printed explicitly and 'positive' defined as ASD - a level of metric transparency few corpus studies match - plus confusion matrices for every classifier in an appendix. Headline: 0.900 accuracy, 1.000 specificity, 1.000 precision, 0.898 F1, 0.826 sensitivity for naive Bayes. No AUC and no confidence intervals, which matters given that specificity and precision of exactly 1.000 on 25 controls carry wide uncertainty.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No model-derived feature importance, but interpretability is supplied by a properly conducted univariate analysis that precedes and motivates the classification. The mixed-model ANOVA establishes that children with ASD sway significantly more in displacement, distance and area regardless of visual condition, with no group-by-condition interaction, and that both groups sway more with eyes closed. The negative result is equally informative and is reported plainly: sample entropy did not differentiate the groups, despite the introduction citing two prior studies reporting reduced COP complexity in ASD and interpreting it as 'a repetitive and restricted postural control pattern'. So the classification signal here is magnitude, not complexity.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Five-fold cross-validation with participant-level folds by construction, since each child contributes a single 12-feature vector - this avoids the window-level and image-level leakage that affects much of the corpus. Outliers were formally checked with Chauvenet's criterion because they 'could influence the classification accuracy', and none were found. Sample size was justified by a priori power analysis. What is absent: any nested structure separating algorithm selection from performance estimation, so reporting the best of six on the same folds carries selection optimism; no external or independent validation; no permutation testing against chance; no class-imbalance issue (25/25); no confidence intervals despite metrics of exactly 1.000; and no deployment or real-time analysis, though efficiency and minimal human intervention are cited as practical advantages.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: Developmental disorder, Postural stability, Force plate, Artificial intelligence, Standing, Balance. Task vocabulary: 'diagnostic biomarkers', 'automated identification', 'computer-aided machine learning', 'postural control patterns'. The vocabulary is biomechanical rather than clinical-diagnostic, and the biomarker claim is posed as an open question rather than asserted.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Biomechanics - a biomechanics and movement science journal, neither autism-specific nor computational, and the only representative of that field in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2020. The paper situates itself carefully in two literatures. On postural control it notes that reduced postural stability in ASD is 'well-established', with prior force-plate studies reporting greater sway displacement, areas, standard deviations, velocities and root mean square, and two studies reporting decreased COP complexity. On machine learning it observes that classifiers have already distinguished impaired postural stability in multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease and vestibular dysfunction, and have been applied in autism to eye gaze, cognitive function, pregnancy risk factors and hand movements - but concludes that 'to our knowledge, there has been no study that utilized machine learning approaches to study postural control features in children with ASD'. It thus documents the transfer of an established clinical-biomechanics method into the autism domain.

data_charting_rubrics.authors: Javed H; Park CH
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: Companion of the 2020 ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction (pp
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum disorder
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Robot-mediated interaction
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Risk detection and triage: identify children at risk for ASD from behavioral data captured during naturalistic child-robot interaction, explicitly framed as a way to streamline standard diagnostic procedures through rapid detection and clinical prioritisation rather than as a diagnostic tool
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study reported as a two-page Late-Breaking Report
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Total interaction time 3931 seconds for the TD group (mean 561.57 s per child) and 3442 seconds for the ASD group (mean 688.4 s per child); single session, no repeated sessions
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Human children aged 5-10 years, all male
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Robot-assisted sensory maze: two robots (a small humanoid and an iPod-based mobile robot) walk around a maze to find stations and interact with sensory stimuli at each, with the activity designed to include opportunities for robot-initiated conversation encouraging the child's active participation in a joint sensory experience
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory - robots set up on a table with children standing or seated around it, at The George Washington University
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Not reported - no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or confirmation procedure is described anywhere
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 5 (all boys)
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Within the overall 5-10 year study range
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 7 (all boys)
data_charting_rubrics.age_range_controls: Within the overall 5-10 year study range
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not claimed or tested; group means differ by roughly 0.8 years with substantially different standard deviations (2.30 vs 1.10)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Both groups are entirely male, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation ('the inclusion of a single gender')
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted only
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Video-derived behavioral data: upper-body pose tracking and facial keypoints during robot interaction
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Free interaction within the sensory maze scenario, with children unrestricted in movement and no obtrusive sensors worn; video recordings processed post hoc
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Two robots (small humanoid and iPod-based mobile robot); video recording; OpenPose for pose and facial keypoint extraction; Laban movement analysis for movement-intent features; a custom 1D CNN, plus random forest and k-nearest neighbour comparators
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - a video dataset from child-robot interactions, but not released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Sensitive - video recordings of identifiable children, with a published figure showing children interacting with the robots. Institutional Review Board approval is reported with the specific protocol number (GW IRB#111540). No parental consent statement, no anonymization procedure and no data-protection provision is described
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted movement-intent features combined with pose-derived facial keypoints
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 71 features per time window: 3 Laban movement analysis features (weight, space and time, derived to characterise the intent behind human movement) computed over a 1-second moving window to capture temporal structure, combined with 68 facial keypoints originating from the nose and eyes
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: OpenPose for upper-body tracking and facial keypoint detection; Laban movement analysis implementation following cited definitions
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported - no behavioral difference between groups is characterised
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised deep learning with conventional comparators
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: A 1D convolutional neural network with two 1D convolution layers to extract high-level features from the temporal data, followed by three dense layers (the first two widening the feature dimensions, the last generating output), with four dropout layers at a 20% rate. Comparators: random forest and k-nearest neighbour
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A single 80/20 split of the interaction data, with 80% used for training and 20% for validation. Critically the unit is the data point rather than the child - the discussion notes approximately 18,597 data points per subject from 1-second moving windows - and there is no statement that the split was made at child level, so windows from the same child almost certainly appear in both training and validation sets. No cross-validation, no repeated splits, no held-out test set distinct from the validation set
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision and recall for all three classifiers, plus a confusion matrix for the CNN. Training accuracy and training loss are also reported
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: CNN accuracy 0.8846, precision 0.8912, recall 0.8853 (training accuracy 0.883, training loss 0.232). Random forest accuracy 0.8852, precision 0.8876, recall 0.8856. KNN accuracy 0.8874, precision 0.8920, recall 0.8878. False negative rate 0.1787 from the CNN confusion matrix
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Facial keypoints and Laban-derived upper-body movement features extracted from video of unconstrained child-robot interaction supported classification of at-risk ASD versus typical development at approximately 0.88-0.89 accuracy across a CNN, random forest and k-nearest neighbour, with all three performing near-identically. The authors read the similar performance as indicating that simpler methods suffice at this data scale, and explicitly decline to claim diagnostic utility on the basis of a 0.1787 false negative rate, positioning the method instead as an accessible screening layer. The stated methodological appeal is that no obtrusive sensors were used and the child's movement was unrestricted, so the approach could extend to naturalistic settings such as play at home.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None identified
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Larger participant numbers and repeated interaction sessions to grow the dataset, at which point a CNN may become the better choice over simpler methods; incorporation of additional modalities including physiological, eye gaze and vocal data to represent ASD behaviours more comprehensively and improve reliability; and generalisation to other naturalistic interactions such as play at home where much larger datasets could be obtained
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A two-page Late-Breaking Report, and should be weighted accordingly. Its genuine merits are the naturalistic, sensor-free interaction design, the inclusion of two conventional comparators alongside the CNN, and two candid interpretive judgements: that the near-identical performance of CNN, random forest and KNN indicates 'simpler machine learning methods suffice for the given dataset', and that given a false negative rate of 0.1787 'this method cannot be claimed to be ready to be used singularly as a diagnostic tool for ASD'. Both are more restrained than corpus norm. The decisive problem is the evaluation unit: with 12 children producing approximately 18,597 data points each from 1-second windows, and a single 80/20 split with no statement of child-level partitioning, windows from the same child will appear on both sides of the split. The reported ~0.88 accuracy is therefore a within-child window-classification figure, not a person-level detection estimate, and 12 children cannot support the latter in any case. No diagnostic instrument is reported, both groups are entirely male (acknowledged), ages are unmatched, and no feature-level interpretation is offered. The finding that three structurally very different classifiers all land within 0.003 of each other is itself a signature of a task made easy by data leakage rather than of a robust signal.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: 5 boys with ASD and 7 typically developing boys, total 12 children. Group sizes, sexes and mean ages are reported. No other-diagnosis comparison group. This is the smallest participant sample in the corpus charted so far.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)', 'children at risk for ASD', 'at-risk children', 'typically developing (TD)'. Person-first, and notably the paper consistently frames its target as 'risk detection' rather than diagnosis, which is reflected in the terminology throughout.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: ASD n=5 (all male), mean age 8.2 +/- 1.10 years. TD n=7 (all male), mean age 7.43 +/- 2.30 years. Overall age range 5-10 years. No matching procedure or comparability test is reported; the group means differ by about 0.8 years and the control group's standard deviation is more than double the ASD group's. Both groups are exclusively male, which the authors explicitly list as a limitation - 'the inclusion of a single gender' - making this one of the few corpus studies to name sex homogeneity as a limitation rather than leave it unremarked. Total interaction time is reported per group (3931 s TD, 3442 s ASD), described as making the datasets comparable in size.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not reported. No diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or confirmation procedure is described for the ASD group, and typically developing status is asserted without screening. Given that diagnostic label is the classification target, this is the study's most fundamental reporting gap, though it is partly a consequence of the two-page format.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None reported. No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or severity measures for either group, and no comorbidity information.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: behavior-based risk detection to streamline standard diagnostic procedures through rapid detection and clinical prioritisation of at-risk children. Main findings: CNN 0.8846 accuracy, 0.8912 precision, 0.8853 recall; random forest 0.8852/0.8876/0.8856; KNN 0.8874/0.8920/0.8878 - all three within 0.003 of one another; false negative rate 0.1787. The authors conclude that simpler methods suffice at this scale and that the method is not ready for standalone diagnostic use.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory setting with robots on a table and children standing or seated around it. Newly collected data from a user study; no existing dataset used.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A sensory maze scenario in which two robots - a small humanoid and an iPod-based mobile robot - walk around a maze to find stations and interact with sensory stimuli at each. The activity was designed to include multiple opportunities for robot-initiated conversation, encouraging active participation from the child in a joint sensory experience. Children's movement was deliberately unrestricted and no obtrusive sensors were worn, which the authors identify as the design's key advantage for generalisation to naturalistic settings.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single session per child averaging roughly 9-11 minutes, with no repeated sessions or follow-up. The data are video recordings of identifiable children, and a figure showing children interacting with the robots is published. Institutional Review Board approval is reported with a specific protocol number (GW IRB#111540), but there is no parental consent statement, no child assent statement, and no anonymization, retention or data-protection provision.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: two robots (a small humanoid and an iPod-based mobile robot) in a sensory maze setup on a table; video recording equipment (unspecified). Software: OpenPose for upper-body tracking and facial keypoint extraction; Laban movement analysis for deriving weight, space and time movement-intent features; a custom 1D CNN with specified layer structure and dropout rate; random forest and k-nearest neighbour comparators. No frameworks, versions or hyperparameters beyond the dropout rate and layer counts are given.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Weak, as expected for a two-page report. No data or code release, no software versions, no CNN training hyperparameters (optimiser, learning rate, epochs, batch size), no random seeds, no KNN k value or random forest configuration, and no specification of how the 80/20 split was drawn. The feature construction is described at a level that would allow approximate reimplementation - OpenPose, 68 facial keypoints from nose and eyes, three Laban features over a 1-second moving window, 71 features total - and the CNN architecture is sketched, but nothing could be reproduced quantitatively.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors, and unusually directly for the format: the work 'is limited by the number of participants, the inclusion of a single gender and the exclusive use of behaviors available from video data', and given the 0.1787 false negative rate 'this method cannot be claimed to be ready to be used singularly as a diagnostic tool for ASD'. Identifiable in review and more consequential: the evaluation unit is the 1-second data window rather than the child, with approximately 18,597 data points per subject and a single 80/20 split whose partitioning level is unstated - so windows from the same child are almost certainly split across training and validation, making the reported accuracy a within-child figure rather than a person-level detection estimate; 12 children cannot support a person-level estimate regardless; no diagnostic instrument is reported; ages are unmatched with markedly unequal variances; validation and test sets are not distinguished; and no feature-level interpretation is offered so nothing is learned about what distinguishes the groups behaviourally.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Increase participant numbers and add repeated interaction sessions, which the authors expect will grow the dataset rapidly and may then favour the CNN over simpler classifiers; incorporate physiological, eye gaze and vocal data to represent ASD behaviours more comprehensively and improve network reliability; and extend the approach to other naturalistic interactions such as play at home, where much larger datasets could be obtained - a direction the authors argue is enabled specifically by the absence of obtrusive sensors and movement restriction.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Two behavioral streams from video: upper-body movement (characterised through Laban weight, space and time features intended to capture movement intent) and facial configuration (68 keypoints from the nose and eye regions). Notably the facial keypoints are geometric landmark positions rather than expression classifications, so the model sees face shape and pose rather than interpreted emotion.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Feature-level fusion of the two modalities: 3 Laban movement features are concatenated with 68 facial keypoints into a single 71-dimensional vector per 1-second window, so movement and facial information are combined before classification. There is no ablation isolating either modality's contribution, so their relative value is unknown. The discussion proposes future fusion with physiological, eye gaze and vocal data.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised learning with a deliberate depth comparison: a 1D convolutional neural network chosen for its suitability to ordered temporal data, benchmarked against random forest and k-nearest neighbour, which the authors describe as having 'simpler structures than a deep CNN with fewer hyperparameters that require fine-tuning'. Reporting a null result from this comparison - that all three perform equivalently - is a strength.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Handcrafted temporal features over a sliding window: Laban movement analysis converts pose trajectories into three interpretable movement-quality dimensions (weight, space, time) computed over 1-second windows, concatenated with raw facial keypoint coordinates. The representation is therefore partly interpretable in principle - Laban features have established meanings in movement analysis - though no interpretation is pursued.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision and recall for all three classifiers, plus a confusion matrix for the CNN from which the 0.1787 false negative rate is derived and discussed. Reporting the false negative rate explicitly, and using it to disclaim diagnostic readiness, is better practice than the corpus norm of quoting accuracy alone. Training accuracy and loss are also given. No AUC, F1, confidence intervals or per-class breakdown beyond the confusion matrix, and no significance testing.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No feature importance, saliency or ablation analysis is performed, and no behavioral characteristic is identified as distinguishing the groups - so despite using Laban movement analysis, whose weight, space and time dimensions carry established interpretive meaning, nothing is reported about how autistic and typically developing children's movement qualities differed. The study yields a classifier without a finding.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The weakest dimension. A single 80/20 split with no cross-validation, no repeated splits and no separation between validation and test sets, and - decisively - no statement that partitioning occurred at child level, when the discussion makes clear the unit is the 1-second data window with approximately 18,597 per subject. Dropout at 20% across four layers is the only overfitting control described. There is no external validation, no permutation testing, no class-imbalance handling despite 5 versus 7 children, and no calibration or deployment analysis. The authors do reason about deployment readiness qualitatively, correctly declining to claim diagnostic utility, but generalisation is addressed only through the aspiration to collect more data.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: Autism spectrum disorder, child-robot interaction, multi-modal behaviors, deep learning, machine learning, diagnosis. CCS concepts span robotics, machine learning and human-centered computing user studies. Task vocabulary: 'risk detection', 'at-risk ASD', 'streamline existing diagnostic procedures', 'clinical prioritization', 'accessible layer of screening'. The triage-oriented vocabulary is consistent and the paper avoids diagnostic overclaiming.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: HRI '20 Companion - the Late-Breaking Report track of the 2020 ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction. A robotics and human-computer interaction venue, and specifically a short-format preliminary-results track, which bounds what can be expected of the reporting.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2020. The brief related-work statement characterises prior machine-learning approaches to ASD diagnosis as based on standardised assessment data, brain imaging datasets, and kinematic analysis of upper-body movement during specialised tasks. The paper positions its own contribution against these as using 'only behavioral data captured through video recordings of a naturalistic interaction with social robots' with unrestricted movement and no obtrusive sensors - articulating the corpus-wide trend away from constrained laboratory tasks and toward naturalistic, sensor-free observation.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation as a Scalable Method for Distinguishing Children With Autism
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Tunçgenç B; Pacheco C; Rochowiak R; Nicholas R; Rengarajan S; Zou E; Messenger B; Vidal R; Mostofsky SH
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autism spectrum conditions
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Motor and kinematics (imitation)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Develop an objective, continuous, scalable measure of motor imitation ability - explicitly as a measurement instrument rather than only a classifier - and establish its construct validity against human observation coding, its test-retest reliability, its diagnostic discriminative ability, and its association with core autism symptom severity
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control instrument-development and validation study, with classification as one of four evaluation strands
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Brief one-minute imitation trials; 14 trials at varying speeds were collected, of which 4 at 100% speed are analysed here - the first two and their repetitions at the end - across two movement sequences; participants attended two-day visits
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Whole-body motor imitation: copying dance-like movements of a young woman shown on a large TV screen without music or sound, using sequences of 14-18 individual movement types chosen to be relatively unfamiliar, goal-less and requiring simultaneous multi-limb movement
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Research centre - the Center for Neurodevelopmental and Imaging Research at the Kennedy Krieger Institute, with recruitment through local schools and community events
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: DSM-5 criteria confirmed on site by research-reliable assessors using ADOS-2 (module 3 for all participants), the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised, and the parent-report Social Responsiveness Scale, Second Edition. Inclusion required a full-scale IQ of at least 80 or at least one index score of at least 80 on the WISC-V. The Movement Assessment Battery for Children, Second Edition was additionally administered to account for autism-associated differences in general motor ability
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Reported in Table 1 (not recoverable from extracted text); inclusion range 8-12 years
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Reported in Table 1 but not recoverable from extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Full inclusion and exclusion criteria are deferred to a supplement; IQ threshold of 80 applied as an inclusion criterion
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Not reported in the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: ADOS-2 and SRS-2 administered and used quantitatively - correlations between imitation ability and both instruments' social affect, restricted and repetitive behaviour, and total scores are reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Assessed with the same instrument battery; full criteria deferred to supplement
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd_controls: Reported in Table 1 (not recoverable from extracted text)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution_controls: Reported in Table 1 but not recoverable from extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Group comparison statistics are tabulated in Table 1, though the values are not recoverable from the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Tabulated but not recoverable from extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: 3D motion capture: x-y-z coordinates of 20 body joints during imitation, compared against a gold-standard model performance
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A brief training phase familiarised participants with the movement types and the expected range of motion, followed by imitation trials. Children's movements were recorded by two Kinect cameras at 30 frames per second, one in front and one behind, with no sensors or special clothing required. The gold standard against which children were compared was the motion data of the video model imitating herself
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Two Microsoft Kinect Xbox depth cameras at 30 fps; large TV display; iPi Motion Capture Software (IpiSoft) for joint extraction; custom DTW and metric-learning algorithm; SVM classifier
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Data collected as part of a wider study on imitation skills in autism; no dataset release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no data availability statement in the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Moderately sensitive - depth-camera motion recordings of identifiable children, though the analysed data are skeletal joint coordinates rather than video. Ethics approval was received from the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine Institutional Review Board prior to study commencement, written informed consent was obtained from all legal guardians, and verbal assent was obtained from all children. Participants received $100 compensation for their two-day visits
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Three interpretable derived features combining spatial and temporal imitation accuracy
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: After preprocessing (translating hips to origin, normalising the child's limb lengths to the model's skeleton, and aligning first-frame spatial orientation), three features are computed: a distance score derived from DTW-aligned Euclidean distance between child and model trajectories weighted by automatically estimated joint importance; the duration the child lagged behind the model; and the duration the child moved in advance of the model. Joint importance is estimated automatically from how much each joint is displaced in the gold-standard data for each movement type, so joints that stay static contribute less
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: iPi Motion Capture Software for 20-joint extraction from Kinect depth data; custom dynamic time warping and metric learning implementation
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, structurally - joint importance is estimated automatically and the three features are explicitly designed to be interpretable
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Automatic joint importance estimation from gold-standard displacement magnitude per movement type; metric learning determines the linear weights combining the three features, learned in a data-driven manner within cross-validation folds
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The three-feature structure (spatial distance, delay duration, advance duration) is the model, so all three are retained by design. The authors emphasise that including timing features matters given known deficits in coordinating action timing in autism
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Children with autism spectrum conditions showed poorer imitation than typically developing children (p < .005), and poorer imitation was associated with greater core autism symptom severity - correlations of -0.48 to -0.52 with SRS-2 social affect, restricted and repetitive behaviour, and total scores, and -0.17 to -0.34 with ADOS-2 subscales within the ASC group
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Metric learning for continuous scoring, plus supervised classification for diagnostic grouping
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Dynamic time warping for temporal alignment; metric learning to determine the linear combination weights for the three features, optimised to maximise correlation with human observation coding on training folds; support vector machine for diagnostic classification. Weight learning and classification both use three-fold cross-validation, replicated with ten folds in supplementary analyses
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Three-fold cross-validation with folds containing equal proportions of ASC and TD children. Critically, the metric-learning weights are learned on two folds and applied to the held-out third, so that 'children's CAMI scores are calculated completely independently from and without reference to their HOC scores'. SVM classification also uses three-fold cross-validation. The fold count is justified against bias-variance trade-off literature and the analyses are repeated with ten folds, replicating the findings. Test-retest reliability is established separately by comparing repeated trials
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Classification accuracy for CAMI versus HOC scores; Spearman correlations for construct validity against HOC and for test-retest reliability; correlations with ADOS-2 and SRS-2 for clinical validity; group comparison p-values
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: CAMI classification accuracy 87.2% versus HOC 74.4%. A single one-minute trial without HOC scores (trial 2b) classified at 84.6%. Construct validity correlations between CAMI and HOC r = .69-.87. Test-retest reliability r = .73-.86. Group difference in imitation p < .005. Imitation-symptom correlations: SRS-2 total r = -0.50 (p < .05) for CAMI versus -0.43 for HOC; ADOS-2 total within the ASC group r = -0.34 for CAMI versus -0.42 for HOC
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A one-minute Kinect-based imitation task scored by a DTW and metric-learning algorithm distinguished children with autism spectrum conditions from typically developing children at 87.2% accuracy, outperforming expert human observation coding on the same data (74.4%) while correlating strongly with it (r = .69-.87). Test-retest reliability across repeated trials was high (r = .73-.86), imitation was poorer in the autistic group (p < .005), and poorer imitation correlated with greater symptom severity on both parent-report and observational instruments. The authors position the method explicitly as measuring imitation ability specifically, in contrast to prior motor classifiers where 'it is unclear if the observed differences represent general motor abnormalities or specific imitation impairments'.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Greater spatial deviation from the model's movement trajectories and greater temporal asynchrony (both lag and advance) relative to the model
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Improve scalability - the current Kinect-based pipeline requires some manual processing owing to motion-tracking imperfections, and future work should explore alternative capture technologies. The authors also position CAMI as a candidate biomarker for defining biologically meaningful autism subtypes and for tracking performance during imitation-based interventions
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: One of the strongest studies in the corpus, and notable for treating classification as one validation strand among four rather than as the whole contribution. Its distinctive strengths: a gold-standard diagnostic battery (DSM-5 confirmed on site with ADOS-2, ADI-R and SRS-2 by research-reliable assessors); construct validity established against the existing expert standard; test-retest reliability quantified across repeated trials, which almost no other study here reports; convergent validity through correlations with two independent symptom measures; and a direct head-to-head comparison against human expert coding on the same children, which the algorithm wins. The metric-learning weights are learned inside cross-validation folds specifically so that CAMI scores are computed without reference to the HOC scores they are validated against - a deliberate leakage control. The authors also confront the small-sample objection quantitatively rather than dismissing it, deriving an expected classification error of 5.9% from Raudys's formula against a 2.8% infinite-sample floor, and noting their parameter-to-sample ratio is more favourable than two named prior autism motor studies. Remaining limitations: 48 children means 87.2% is roughly 42 correct, and with approximately 13 training samples per class per fold the estimate carries real variance; the reported figure is the better of two scoring methods on the same folds; the sample is restricted to IQ at or above 80 and ages 8-12; and the demographic table is not recoverable from the extracted text, so age and sex matching cannot be verified here. The scalability claim is also tempered by the authors' own admission that Kinect imperfections still require manual processing.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: 27 children with autism spectrum conditions and 21 typically developing children, total 48. Group sizes are clear and participant characteristics are tabulated with group comparison test statistics, though the values are not recoverable from the extracted text. No other-diagnosis comparison group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with autism spectrum conditions (ASCs)', 'children with ASCs', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'TD peers'. Consistently person-first, and the paper uses 'autism spectrum conditions' rather than 'disorder' throughout - one of a minority in this corpus to do so. The framing is developmental and functional rather than pathologising, discussing imitation's role in 'social bond formation and learning' rather than deficit alone, though 'imitation deficits' and 'impairments' are used.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: 27 ASC and 21 TD children aged 8-12 years. Participant characteristics including means, standard deviations, ranges and group comparison test statistics are presented in Table 1, but the values are not recoverable from the extracted text, so age and sex matching cannot be independently verified in this charting. IQ is controlled by inclusion criterion - full-scale IQ of at least 80 or at least one WISC-V index score of at least 80 - which restricts the sample to children of broadly average or above cognitive ability. General motor ability was additionally measured with the Movement Assessment Battery for Children-2 specifically 'to account for autism-associated differences in general motor abilities', which is an unusually thoughtful covariate choice for an imitation study since it separates imitation-specific from general motor difficulty.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: The most complete diagnostic ascertainment in the corpus alongside Cho et al. (2019): DSM-5 criteria confirmed on site by research-reliable assessors using ADOS-2 (module 3 for all participants, ensuring comparability), the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised, and the parent-report SRS-2. Using all three of the field's principal instruments, applied by research-reliable assessors, and standardising the ADOS module across participants, is a materially stronger reference standard than the 'prior clinical diagnosis' that most of this corpus relies on.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Extensive. Full-scale and index IQ measured with WISC-V and used as an inclusion criterion; general motor ability measured with the Movement Assessment Battery for Children-2 explicitly to separate imitation-specific from general motor differences; ADOS-2 and SRS-2 administered and used quantitatively in correlational analyses of symptom severity. Full inclusion and exclusion criteria are deferred to a supplement. This is among the fullest functional characterisations in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: develop an objective, continuous, scalable measure of motor imitation, validated on four fronts - construct validity, test-retest reliability, diagnostic discrimination, and clinical association. Main findings: CAMI classified diagnostic groups at 87.2% versus 74.4% for human observation coding; a single one-minute trial reached 84.6%; CAMI-HOC correlations r = .69-.87; test-retest r = .73-.86; poorer imitation in ASC (p < .005); and poorer imitation correlated with greater symptom severity on SRS-2 (r = -0.50 total) and ADOS-2.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Research centre setting at a neurodevelopmental research institute, with community and school recruitment. Data were collected as part of a wider study of imitation skills in autism, so this is a focused analysis within a larger programme rather than a standalone collection.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Whole-body imitation of dance-like movements performed by a young woman on a large TV screen, deliberately without music or sound. Sequences comprised 14-18 individual movement types selected to be 'relatively unfamiliar (e.g., moving arms up and down like a puppeteer)', to lack an end goal, and to require moving multiple limbs simultaneously - chosen on the basis of prior research showing that autistic imitation difficulties are most pronounced for meaningless, goal-less actions. A brief training phase preceded testing. Of 14 collected trials at varying speeds, only the 4 at 100% speed are analysed to avoid confounding by speed, comprising two sequences each presented twice, which is what enables the test-retest analysis.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; two-day visits with repeated trials within session, and no longitudinal follow-up - though repeated trials within session provide the test-retest estimate. Data are depth-camera recordings reduced to skeletal joint coordinates, so identifiability is moderate rather than high. Ethics governance is complete: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine IRB approval prior to commencement, written informed consent from all legal guardians, verbal assent from all children, and $100 compensation.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware: two Microsoft Kinect Xbox depth cameras at 30 frames per second positioned in front of and behind the child, requiring no sensors or special clothing - an explicit design advantage for this population; a large TV screen for stimulus display. Software: iPi Motion Capture Software for extracting 20 joint coordinates from depth recordings; a custom dynamic time warping and metric learning pipeline with equations supplied in a supplement; SVM for classification.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: No data or code release is stated in the extracted text, and substantial methodological detail - the CAMI equations, parameter learning formula, parameter values, full inclusion and exclusion criteria, study setup, and supplementary ten-fold replication - is deferred to a supplement. What is in the main text is precise: the five-step algorithm is described in sequence, joint importance estimation is explained, the three features are defined, the cross-validation scheme and its rationale are given, and the software and hardware are named. The approach would be reimplementable with the supplement.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Reported by the authors, and addressed unusually rigorously rather than merely acknowledged. On sample size, they concede that 27 ASC and 21 TD 'can be considered relatively small' given phenotypic heterogeneity, then argue quantitatively that the method does not suffer from a sample size problem: invoking the 1-in-10 rule for the three-variable metric learning (30 samples needed, approximately 90 used), and applying Raudys's formula for SVM expected error with p=3, delta=3.83 and n=13 per class to derive a 5.9% expected error against a 2.8% infinite-sample floor. They also note their parameter-to-sample ratio is more favourable than two named prior autism motor studies (40 parameters from 30 subjects, and 7 parameters from 30 subjects). On scalability they concede that Kinect imperfections 'require some manual processing that can be time-consuming'.
