This is the design's central choice and its main practical strength: the data are generated by a procedure clinics already perform, so deployment requires only recording rather than a new protocol, and the model's target and its input come from the same session. The cost is that the input is contaminated with clinician, parent and environmental sound, which is why manual speaker labelling was necessary; and that module assignment varies by child, so the speech elicited is not identical across participants.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional - a single ADOS session per child, averaging 41.6 +/- 12.4 minutes. Longitudinal follow-up is named as necessary future work precisely because the intended application (tracking severity change over time and after treatment) requires it. Data are full audio of clinical sessions including parent and clinician speech - among the most sensitive material in the corpus - yet no ethics approval, consent procedure or anonymization statement appears in the extracted text, while funding and acknowledgements are reported in detail.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: AKG CHM99 microphone at 1-2 m; TASCAM US-16x08 sound card; 44.1 kHz downsampled to 16 kHz; in-house GUI software for manual speaker interval labelling; PRAAT for pitch and formant analysis; custom code for energy, ZCR, spectral slope, jitter and conversational features; deep models with RMSProp and MSE loss. No commercial analysis system - the paper argues explicitly against LENA on the grounds that it is not open source, so 'it is not possible to further develop the LENA algorithms nor assess their utility in estimating ASD severity'.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Among the best in the corpus for method reporting. All 60 features are enumerated individually with their computation; the segmentation algorithm is given with its equations and every threshold (40 ms frames at 10 ms rate, baseline as modal energy within +/- 20 s, onset at 90% above baseline held 50 ms, offset at 10% above baseline held 50 ms, 110 ms and 3 s duration bounds, under 1.5% excluded); the PRAAT voicing threshold is stated as 0.45; all six model architectures are specified layer by layer with epochs, batch sizes and dropout; the hyperparameter search grid is given (batch size from {4,8,16} or {32,64}, learning rate from {1e-5, 5e-5, 1e-4, 5e-4}); and the balanced-split acceptance criteria are stated numerically. Missing: code and data release, ethics documentation, and the selected hyperparameter values are relegated to a table that did not survive extraction.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged: that speaker labelling was manual and that automatic diarization is needed for a fully automated system; that recordings are short clinic sessions rather than naturalistic home recordings; that the shorter-response-latency finding contradicts prior English-language work and needs replication; that feature utility may change with age and requires longitudinal testing; and, implicitly but importantly, that single-split results overstate robustness. Identifiable in review but not stated: RMSE 4.65 on a 0-30 scale is a large absolute error against which the phrase 'remarkably accurate prediction' sits uneasily; architecture and hyperparameters were selected by trying combinations, apparently outside the 50-split evaluation, so the reported means carry model-selection optimism; only 6 typically developing children means the low end of the severity range is thinly sampled, which inflates correlation through range restriction at one end and thin support at the other; and no ethics approval is reported for full clinical session audio.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Incorporate automatic speaker diarization to remove the manual annotation step and enable a fully automated system; extend from clinic recordings to long home recordings of the kind LENA collects; adopt a longitudinal design testing which speech features are informative at which developmental periods; and reassess the anomalous finding that more severely affected children responded faster rather than slower.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Child speech during clinical interaction, analysed along three distinct behavioural dimensions: prosody and voice quality (pitch, formants, spectral slope, jitter), acoustic energy dynamics (normalised energy and its derivatives, zero crossing rate), and conversational behaviour (vocalisation rate, segment durations, turn-taking latency and rate, total vocalisation count). The turn-taking features are what distinguish this from purely acoustic work - they measure the child's behaviour in relation to the clinician's, requiring the whole session and both speakers, and they turn out to be the features that track social affect specifically.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-sensor fusion - audio only. But there is a meaningful within-modality fusion result with a clear cost: the conversational features cannot be computed on short sub-groups of segments because they require the entire recording, so FC-DNN models 2 and 3 and the CNN use only the 48 acoustic and prosodic features. The best models therefore discard exactly the feature family that correlates most strongly with social affect symptoms, and still outperform the 60-feature vector model - which suggests the gain from many sub-samples outweighs the loss of conversational information, and implies an architecture that could use both would do better still.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Six models spanning linear regression, kernel regression and three deep architectures, all on identical data, which makes the comparison genuinely informative. The decisive variable turns out to be input structure rather than model family: the same 100 x 48 matrix input produces the two best models (FC-DNN 3 and CNN) while the same sub-sampled features presented as independent 48-vectors (FC-DNN 2) produce the worst model of all six. The authors draw the right conclusion - that architectures exploiting multiple simultaneous samples of a child's speech have a large advantage, and that the non-linear models' margin over linear regression and SVR shows 'the optimal ADOS prediction model is not likely to be linear'.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Sixty handcrafted features across seven families, fully enumerated, computed over automatically detected vocal segments within manually labelled speaker intervals. Three input arrangements are compared: one 60-feature vector per child; 100 independent 48-feature vectors per child, each from 10 sequential vocal segments; and those same 100 vectors stacked into a 100 x 48 matrix per child. The sub-sampling is a deliberate data-augmentation strategy for a 72-child dataset, raising training samples from 51 to 5100 in model 2 - and the finding that this hurt while stacking the same samples into a matrix helped is one of the more useful negative-plus-positive results in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: RMSE and Pearson correlation against clinician-assigned ADOS total, reported as mean +/- standard deviation over 50 splits and shown as histograms, plus scatter plots for one representative split. Reporting the across-split standard deviation and interpreting it is the distinguishing feature: it reveals that models with respectable means (SVR at R = 0.51, FC-DNN 2 at 0.31) were also wildly unstable (SD 0.17 and 0.25), while the two matrix-input models were stable at SD 0.09. Because the task is regression, no sensitivity, specificity or AUC applies; but no calibration analysis or error-versus-severity breakdown is given, so whether error concentrates at particular ADOS ranges is unknown, and with only 6 typically developing children the low end is thinly supported.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No post hoc model explanation, but strong interpretability at the feature level and, unusually, at the symptom-domain level. Every feature's Pearson correlation against ADOS total, SA, RRB and age is reported with significance marking, sequential forward selection names the 15 features that minimise linear-model RMSE, and the resulting interpretation is specific: acoustic and prosodic features (pitch, formants, jitter, energy, ZCR) track restricted and repetitive behaviour, while conversational features (vocalisation rate, turn-taking, vocalisation count) track social affect. The authors correctly note why this matters - symptom heterogeneity means a single global severity estimate is less clinically useful than measures tied to specific domains. The age analysis serves a second interpretive purpose, showing that the severity-predictive features are largely distinct from the age-predictive ones.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The strongest validation design among the corpus's speech studies. Splitting is at the participant level (51 train, 21 test), so the 100 sub-samples per child never cross the boundary - the leakage failure mode that undermines most segment-level work here is avoided by construction. The split is then repeated 50 times under explicit distribution-matching constraints (mean, SD and kurtosis of ADOS within +/-10% of the whole sample, skewness within +/-0.3), with rejection sampling until satisfied, and every model is run on all 50. Feature selection for the linear model is nested inside 5-fold cross-validation on training data only. What is missing: the architecture and hyperparameter search appears to sit outside the 50-split loop rather than nested within it, so the reported means retain some selection optimism; there is no external site, no independent cohort and no second language; and no test-retest or longitudinal reliability, which the intended use as a treatment outcome measure would require.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: audio signals, autism, autism diagnostic observation schedule, autism spectrum disorder, convolutional neural network, deep neural network, early detection, outcome measure, pitch, speech, symptom severity, treatment efficacy, zero crossing rate. The presence of 'outcome measure', 'symptom severity' and 'treatment efficacy' alongside the signal-processing terms is diagnostic of the paper's position - it is proposing a measurement instrument for monitoring, not a screening test.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: IEEE Access, in a special section on emerging deep learning theories and methods for biomedical engineering - an open-access engineering venue (CC BY 4.0), with clinical co-authors from Soroka University Medical Center and the National Autism Research Center of Israel giving the work genuine clinical grounding.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2020. The framing is unusual in this corpus for arguing about tooling as much as about clinical need. It identifies LENA as the dominant platform for automated speech analysis in autism and objects on methodological grounds - LENA 'is not an open-source software and it is, therefore, not possible to further develop the LENA algorithms nor assess their utility in estimating ASD severity' - making open, inspectable pipelines part of the paper's motivation. It also notes that only a few studies had attempted severity estimation rather than binary classification, citing one that explained about 40% of the variance in Social Affect scores from 33 English-speaking children, and positions itself as the first application of these features and deep learning to Hebrew, arguing that the results 'highlight the utility of speech analyses for estimating ASD severity at very young ages, regardless of the child's spoken language or their cultural environment'.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Detecting High-Functioning Autism in Adults Using Eye Tracking and Machine Learning
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Yaneva V; Ha LA; Eraslan S; Yesilada Y; Mitkov R
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering, 28(6), 1254-1261
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Independent adults with high-functioning autism
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking and gaze
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Test whether visual processing differences captured by eye tracking during ordinary web-page use can detect high-functioning autism in adults - a group the authors identify as especially hard to diagnose - and to establish whether the effect holds across two independent collections with different participants, stimuli and tasks. The proposed use is explicitly stated as screening for referral, not replacement of clinical diagnosis
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Two independent case-control classification studies with different participants, web pages and tasks, analysed jointly and compared
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session per participant per study; 6 web pages in Study 1 and 8 in Study 2, each viewed under two tasks presented in counterbalanced order. Time limits: 120 s per page for Browse 1 and for the Synthesis task, 30 s per page for Browse 2, and 30 s for two questions per page for Search
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Information processing on real web pages, structured by a hierarchy of information needs. Browse: explore the page freely with no specific goal (120 s per page in Study 1, capped at 30 s in Study 2). Search: locate a specific element to answer a question, e.g. 'Can you find a telephone number for technical support and read it?' (30 s for two questions per page). Synthesis: locate at least two elements and combine them to infer an implicit answer, e.g. 'How much more would you have to pay compared to the basic plan if you wanted to have ultra HD?' (120 s per page). Questions were posed and answered verbally; no scrolling, clicking or typing was involved
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: A quiet room with only the researcher and participant present; University of Wolverhampton, UK
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: United Kingdom - Wolverhampton and Birmingham, with collaborating authors at Middle East Technical University Northern Cyprus
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: High-functioning autism, Asperger's syndrome, or ASD
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Formal clinical diagnosis, documented rather than self-reported: participants were recruited through a UK autism charity and the University of Wolverhampton Enabling Centre, both of which required a copy of the formal diagnosis to access services, and all participants met ADOS diagnostic criteria. Diagnoses predating DSM-5 as 'High-Functioning Autism' or 'Asperger's syndrome' were accepted. Exclusions were formal diagnosis of any degree of intellectual disability, reading disorder, or vision conditions not correctable by glasses or lenses
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 28 unique autistic participants retained (15 analysed in Study 1, 19 in Study 2, with 6 taking part in both)
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Reported in Table I, which did not survive text extraction
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: All over 18; no range recoverable from the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Not recoverable from the extracted text, though gender was tested as a classification variable and 'generally lowered the results'
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Intellectual disability and reading disorder were exclusions; three control participants were excluded for reporting school referrals for dyslexia diagnosis
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not scored, but functional level is characterised concretely: all participants were highly independent adults with no caregiver; 20 autistic participants were employed or in higher education and 8 lived independently in council housing on disability benefits. Education is reported in detail - among the autistic group, 8 completed high school, 8 held bachelor's degrees and 3 master's degrees
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes, and actively screened rather than assumed: all control participants completed the 50-item Autism Quotient, and one was excluded for a high score. This is the practice most control groups in this corpus omit
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 32 unique control participants retained (15 analysed in Study 1, 19-20 in Study 2, with 3 taking part in both)
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd_controls: Reported in Table I, which did not survive text extraction
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution_controls: Not recoverable from the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Table I reports demographic characteristics but did not survive extraction, so matching cannot be verified from the available text. Education level is reported in detail and is visibly unbalanced - the control group holds more advanced degrees (10 bachelor's, 5 master's, 1 PhD, 3 high school) than the autistic group (8 bachelor's, 3 master's, 8 high school) - and this is not adjusted for
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not stated; gender was included as a candidate classification variable and consistently reduced accuracy, which is weak evidence that it carries no group signal here
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Screened with the AQ-50 and by exclusion of dyslexia referrals
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Gaze fixation data recorded during web-page viewing
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Fixations were mapped onto Areas of Interest defined three ways: page-specific AOIs derived by the extended Vision-Based Page Segmentation algorithm at its fifth hierarchical level (112 AOIs across Study 1 pages, averaging 18.6 per page; 213 across Study 2 pages, averaging 26.6 per page), a 2 x 2 generic grid, and a 4 x 4 generic grid. Each row of each dataset is the feature vector for one AOI on one page for one participant, giving 12 experimental cases (2 studies x 2 tasks x 3 AOI definitions)
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Gazepoint GP3 video-based eye tracker at 60 Hz with 0.5-1 degree accuracy, recording the right eye at roughly 65 cm with distance controlled by an integrated sensor and nine-point calibration; 19-inch and 17-inch LCD monitors for Studies 1 and 2; Gazepoint's position-variance fixation algorithm; the extended VIPS page segmentation algorithm; the ViCRAM tool for computing web-page visual complexity; R for classification
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes, and released. Making new data available is stated as an explicit objective of the paper
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes - 'Eye-tracking data, code, and materials are available in our external repository at https://tinyurl.com/detectingautism', including page screenshots, task questions, comparison results for other classifiers, confusion matrices, and full results for every data split and page configuration. This is the most complete open release in the corpus
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze coordinate data with demographic variables; ethical approval was sought and granted by the University of Wolverhampton Ethics Committee (Faculty of Science and Engineering) before data collection, all participants signed consent forms, and participants were debriefed afterwards. The authors also raise ethics prospectively, naming 'how to do this ethically' as one of three general questions that must be addressed before recording such behaviours outside laboratory conditions
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Gaze-based AOI-level statistics plus page and participant metadata
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Enumerated in Table II, which did not survive extraction. From the text, they comprise gaze features computed per AOI (fixation counts and durations and related measures) together with non-gaze variables tested for their effect: AOI identifier, Media identifier, whether the AOI contained the correct answer for Search tasks, page visual complexity, and participant gender
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Gazepoint fixation extraction; VIPS for page-specific AOI definition; ViCRAM for visual complexity scoring
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Not as model coefficients, but the paper systematically ablates feature groups and reports the effect of each: AOI ID and Media ID generally reduced accuracy (except Media ID with page-specific AOIs in Browse 1, where it produced the best result); the correct-answer indicator slightly helped individual Search pages but reduced the best Search classifier from 0.75 to 0.73; page visual complexity showed no consistent pattern; and gender consistently lowered accuracy
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Systematic ablation across 12 task-by-AOI configurations, plus per-page and per-page-combination analysis
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: No individual features are named. The structural findings are about representation rather than feature identity: AOI granularity matters more than AOI type for unconstrained browsing, while meaningful page-specific AOIs matter more for search, and the 2 x 2 grid was consistently worst
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported at the feature level - the paper reports classification signal rather than directional group differences. The one directional inference offered is that autistic participants spent longer browsing when time was unlimited, which the 30-second Study 2 condition was designed to control for; the discrimination signal survived that control, establishing that the groups differ in browsing strategy and not merely in browsing duration
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised binary classification with per-participant aggregation by majority vote
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Logistic regression with default R parameters, selected as the best of a set of standard classification algorithms whose comparison is deposited in the repository
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Participant-level splitting repeated 100 times. In Study 1, five participants per group were randomly held out for testing and ten per group used for training; in Study 2, six per group for testing and 13 per group for training - a 70:30 ratio in both. The model classifies each 'behaviour' (a feature vector for one AOI on one page for one participant), then assigns each test participant to whichever group received more of their behaviour-level predictions. Accuracy is averaged over the 100 splits and reported with 95% confidence intervals. Cross-study replication with different participants, stimuli and tasks functions as an additional generalisation check
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Mean classification accuracy over 100 random splits with 95% confidence intervals, reported for all 12 task-by-AOI configurations and for individual pages and page combinations. Confusion matrices are deposited in the repository rather than printed. No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1 or AUC appears in the paper itself
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Best accuracies by task: Search 0.75 (Apple + Babylon pages), Browse 1 with the 120 s limit 0.74 (Apple + AVG), Synthesis 0.73 (Amazon + Outlook), and Browse 2 with the 30 s limit 0.65 (Outlook). AOI effects: for Browse 1, page-specific and 4 x 4 grid AOIs both gave 0.71 against 0.66 for the 2 x 2 grid; for Browse 2, page-specific 0.65 against 0.60 and 0.61 for the two grids. Every headline figure is the maximum over a large configuration space - task, AOI definition, page subset, feature set and split ratio - all evaluated on the same 100 splits
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Gaze recorded while adults look at ordinary web pages discriminates high-functioning autism from control at around 74-75% accuracy, and the effect replicates across two collections with different participants, different web pages and different tasks - the paper's central claim being consistency rather than peak accuracy. Capping browsing time at 30 seconds showed that the signal is not merely that autistic participants browse longer: the groups differ in browsing strategy under equal time. Making the task harder did not help - the inferential Synthesis task performed no better than simple Search, which the authors suggest is because inferential processing is covert and so leaves no gaze trace. Area-of-interest definition materially affects accuracy, with a trade-off between capturing page structure and introducing noise, while page visual complexity and participant gender contribute nothing.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Different visual scanning of web page elements independent of task and of time spent - the authors infer that autistic adults may scan elements in a different order or be drawn more to images than to text, but note further analysis is needed to confirm this
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Develop a serious game that logs visual processing differences without requiring an eye tracker; collect behavioural data in natural environments rather than the laboratory; test whether accumulating more simple Search tasks beats designing more complex ones; and extend the approach to other conditions with atypical attention patterns such as dementia, schizophrenia and ADHD. Three prior questions are named: what makes a good discriminating task, how to record such behaviour outside the laboratory, and how to do so ethically
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: One of the two or three most methodologically self-aware papers in the corpus, and the most open. It criticises by name the exact failure mode that recurs throughout this literature - noting that EEG and speech studies reporting 94% and 93% are 'potentially overoptimistic as different data segments from the same participant are assigned to the training and testing sets', which 'does not correspond to real-world applications where the system has to categorize a user, portions of whose data are not included in the training set' - and then avoids it, splitting by participant across 100 random draws and aggregating AOI-level predictions into a per-participant vote. It also releases data, code, materials, screenshots, alternative-classifier comparisons and full results for every configuration, and reports 95% confidence intervals throughout. Its control group is screened with the AQ-50 rather than merely assumed typical, and its participants are documented as formally diagnosed by requirement of the recruiting services. Two problems temper this. The first is multiplicity: the paper explores 12 task-by-AOI configurations, multiple feature sets, several train/test ratios and every subset of pages, and reports the maximum - the headline 0.74 and 0.75 come from two-page subsets chosen for being 'the most discriminatory', with the selection made on the same 100 splits that produce the reported accuracy. The honest reading is therefore that a discrimination signal exists and replicates across two collections, which the paper does establish, while the specific numbers are optimistic. The second is education imbalance: the control group is visibly more educated than the autistic group, and neither education nor any other demographic is adjusted for in the models. The paper's negative results are as valuable as its positive ones: increased task difficulty did not increase separability, page visual complexity contributed nothing, and gender consistently hurt - each reported plainly and each useful to anyone designing gaze-based screening tasks.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups across two independent collections: 71 adults recruited, 68 retained (28 autistic, 32 control), with 15 per group analysed in Study 1 and 19 per group in Study 2, and 9 participants (6 autistic, 3 control) taking part in both. Exclusions are itemised: in Study 1, three autistic and two control participants for calibration and head-movement problems plus one randomly chosen control to rebalance classes; in Study 2, five controls - one for a high AQ score, three for reported school dyslexia referrals and two for calibration. Adults with high-functioning autism are a substantially under-represented population in this corpus, which is dominated by preschool and school-age children.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'adults with and without high-functioning autism', 'participants with autism', 'people on the spectrum', 'people with ASD', 'neurotypical people', 'control group'. Mixed person-first and 'people on the spectrum'; 'neurotypical' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy'. The framing is notable for treating heterogeneity as definitional - 'the term spectrum is used to signify the different types and levels of support that different individuals might need' - and for locating the diagnostic problem in the procedure rather than the person: current diagnosis is 'a highly subjective assessment process' restricted to 'behavioural, historical, and parent-report information' that 'leads to a lack of consistency and reliability'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Group sizes and exclusions are fully itemised, and functional and educational characteristics are reported in unusual detail: all participants were highly independent adults with no caregiver; 20 autistic participants were employed or in higher education and 8 lived independently on disability benefits; among the autistic group 8 had completed high school, 8 held bachelor's and 3 master's degrees, against 3, 10 and 5 plus one PhD in the control group. All but one participant used the web daily. Ages and sex distributions were tabulated in Table I but that table did not survive extraction. The visible education imbalance favouring controls is not adjusted for, and matters for tasks that are fundamentally reading and information-search tasks. Ethnicity and socioeconomic status are not reported; recruitment was from Wolverhampton and Birmingham.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Documented formal diagnosis rather than self-report: autistic participants were recruited through a UK autism charity and a university Enabling Centre, both of which require a copy of the formal diagnosis for service access, and all met ADOS diagnostic criteria. Pre-2013 diagnoses of High-Functioning Autism or Asperger's syndrome were accepted, appropriately for an adult cohort. The control group is the more distinctive part: all completed the 50-item Autism Quotient and one was excluded for a high score, so control status is positively screened rather than assumed - a step almost no other study in this corpus takes.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Intellectual disability and reading disorder were formal exclusions, and three control participants were excluded for school dyslexia referrals, so reading ability is controlled at the eligibility level for a task that depends on reading. Vision not correctable by glasses or lenses was also excluded. No IQ, AQ score (for the autistic group), symptom severity or adaptive functioning measure is reported; functional level is characterised by employment, housing and education instead, which is arguably more informative for an adult cohort though not comparable across studies.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: test whether gaze during ordinary web-page use detects high-functioning autism in adults, and whether the effect holds across independent participants, stimuli and tasks. Main findings: all four tasks produced a discrimination signal, with best accuracies of 0.75 (Search), 0.74 (Browse, 120 s), 0.73 (Synthesis) and 0.65 (Browse, 30 s); capping browse time showed the groups differ in browsing strategy and not only in time spent; increased task complexity did not increase separability; AOI content and granularity both affect accuracy, with the 2 x 2 grid consistently worst; and page visual complexity and participant gender contribute nothing.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A quiet room at the University of Wolverhampton with only researcher and participant present. Autistic participants recruited through a UK autism charity and the university's Enabling Centre; controls by snowball sampling in the Birmingham area. Ethical approval obtained from the University of Wolverhampton Ethics Committee before collection began.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Real web pages under three task types drawn from a published hierarchy of information needs - browse (no goal), search (locate one element), synthesis (locate two elements and infer a third). Study 1 used six pages spanning low, medium and high visual complexity; Study 2 selected eight from the Alexa top 100 after removing duplicates, non-English pages, search engines and pages requiring authentication, then scoring visual complexity with the ViCRAM tool and randomly selecting four low- and four high-complexity home pages. The rationale for web pages is ecological: they offer mixed textual and visual stimuli organised for a semantic purpose, permitting multiple search strategies, and browsing is 'a highly familiar and naturalistic task' whose data could in principle be captured without laboratory equipment. Time limits were manipulated deliberately across studies to separate strategy differences from duration differences.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; one session per participant per study, with nine participants contributing to both. Data are gaze coordinates plus demographic questionnaire responses. Governance is properly reported - prior ethics committee approval, signed consent forms, debriefing - and the authors go further than compliance by naming ethics as an open research question for any future move to naturalistic recording.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Gazepoint GP3 at 60 Hz with 0.5-1 degree accuracy, right eye, roughly 65 cm with sensor-controlled distance and nine-point calibration; 19-inch and 17-inch LCD monitors; Gazepoint's position-variance fixation algorithm; extended VIPS for page segmentation into hierarchical elements, using the fifth level (or deeper where a task could be completed by fixating a single element); ViCRAM for visual complexity; R for classification. The eye tracker is deliberately a low-cost consumer-grade device, consistent with the paper's argument that gaze hardware is already commodity technology.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: The best in the corpus. Data, code, materials, page screenshots, task questions, confusion matrices, comparisons against other classifiers, and full results for every data split and page configuration are all deposited at a public repository, and releasing data is stated as an explicit objective of the paper. Apparatus, calibration, viewing distance, fixation algorithm, AOI construction and split procedure are all specified in the text, and results carry 95% confidence intervals. The one gap in the paper itself is that Tables I and II - demographics and the feature list - are the two most reference-critical tables and neither survived text extraction here, though both are presumably in the deposited materials.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged: that web-searching tasks are unsuitable for very young children; that the sample is small, 'comparable with those of state-of-the-art fMRI studies for autism detection but smaller than the number needed for large validation studies'; that the design cannot explain why some pages discriminate better than others, nor why the harder Synthesis task did not outperform Search; that testing on independently collected data is not currently feasible because the data are task-specific and no comparable independent dataset exists; and, in a footnote, that the better accuracy under the longer browse limit might reflect the different pages and participants rather than the time limit itself. Identifiable in review but not acknowledged: the headline accuracies are maxima over a large configuration space - task, AOI definition, feature set, split ratio and every page subset - selected on the same 100 splits that produce the reported means, so the confidence intervals describe split variability but not selection uncertainty; and the control group's visibly higher educational attainment is left unadjusted in tasks that are fundamentally reading and search tasks.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Develop a serious game that captures visual processing differences without a dedicated eye tracker; move to behavioural data collected in natural environments; test whether aggregating more simple Search tasks beats designing more complex ones, since complexity did not help; and apply the approach to other conditions with atypical attention patterns - dementia, schizophrenia, ADHD. The authors frame three prerequisites: what makes a good discriminating task, how to record outside the laboratory, and how to do so ethically.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Visual attention during naturalistic information-seeking - fixation behaviour across web-page regions during free browsing, targeted search and inferential synthesis. This is a distinctive behavioural target for the corpus: not social attention to faces or eyes, but general visual-information-processing strategy on non-social stimuli. The paper argues this is a feature rather than a limitation, since 'atypical visual-attention patterns reflect higher-order differences in information processing', and it sidesteps the dependence on social stimuli that characterises most gaze work here.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No multimodal fusion. Gaze only, with non-gaze metadata (AOI identity, media identity, correct-answer indicator, page visual complexity, participant gender) tested as additional variables and found in almost every case to reduce accuracy. That systematic negative result is itself the paper's fusion finding: on this data, adding non-gaze information hurt.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Logistic regression, chosen after testing a set of standard classification algorithms in R with the comparison deposited publicly. A deliberately simple model, appropriate at 30-38 participants, and consistent with the paper's emphasis on characterising the signal and the data representation rather than on architecture. The experimental variables are the task, the AOI definition and the feature set, not the learner.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: AOI-level gaze feature vectors: one row per AOI per page per participant, under three AOI definitions - VIPS page-specific elements at the fifth hierarchical level, a 2 x 2 grid, and a 4 x 4 grid. The AOI comparison is the paper's most transferable methodological result. Page-specific AOIs suit Search tasks, where areas have differing task relevance; grid AOIs lose less for Browse tasks, where all elements are equally relevant; the coarse 2 x 2 grid is always worst; and the finer page-specific segmentation in Study 2 (26.6 AOIs per page against 18.6 in Study 1) may have added noise rather than information, since the 4 x 4 grid outperformed it for Synthesis. The authors conclude there is 'a trade-off between having sufficiently detailed AOIs and not introducing too much noise' and that the optimal number 'is best defined empirically'. Grid AOIs have the additional property that no fixation is lost.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Mean accuracy over 100 random participant-level splits with 95% confidence intervals, reported for every one of the 12 task-by-AOI configurations and for individual pages and page combinations. Confidence intervals are used substantively - the authors read them as showing 'the models are robust in their predictions'. Confusion matrices exist but are deposited rather than printed, and no sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1 or AUC appears in the paper. For a screening application where the cost of false negatives and false positives differ, this omission matters more than for a purely comparative study.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No model-explanation method, but extensive experimental interpretation through ablation and design manipulation. The two substantive interpretive results come from controlled comparisons rather than from the model: capping browse time at 30 seconds isolates strategy from duration and shows the groups differ in how they scan, not just how long; and the AOI comparison separates the contribution of page structure from that of spatial granularity. The tentative behavioural reading offered - that autistic adults may scan elements in a different order or be drawn more to images than to text - is explicitly flagged as requiring further analysis rather than asserted from the classifier.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Participant-level splitting throughout, repeated 100 times, with per-participant classification by majority vote over that participant's AOI-level predictions - and the choice is argued for explicitly against the segment-level splitting the authors identify in prior EEG and speech work. Cross-study replication with different participants, stimuli and tasks provides a form of generalisation evidence stronger than repeated splitting alone. Two gaps remain. There is no external validation on independently collected data, which the authors address directly: it 'is currently not feasible for our approach due to the task-specific nature of the data, and the unavailability of comparable data collected independently' - an honest statement of a real constraint, and part of why they released their own data. And configuration selection sits outside the validation loop: task, AOI definition, feature set, split ratio and page subset were all chosen by their performance on the same 100 splits.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: autism, eye tracking, web, screening, diagnostic classification, detection. 'Screening' rather than 'diagnosis' is the operative word and the paper is careful about it - the method 'is not intended to substitute clinical diagnostic procedures where these are available. Rather, its purpose is to be used to identify autistic traits at a wider level and to provide the means to refer for further assessment those people who might be at risk.' That framing is rare in this corpus and materially changes what the accuracy figures need to support.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering, 28(6), 1254-1261 - an engineering journal with a rehabilitation and assistive-technology orientation, consistent with the authors' backgrounds in language processing and web accessibility rather than clinical psychiatry.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2020. The framing is unusual in taking the measure of its own field before contributing to it. It positions resting-state fMRI as the state of the art for adult autism detection from behavioural data, quoting 79-86% under leave-one-out and 71-83% on unseen data, and notes the practical objection that fMRI is expensive, obtrusive and unsuitable for pregnant women or people with sensory issues, metal implants, claustrophobia or head trauma. It then singles out the EEG (94%) and speech (93%) results as 'potentially overoptimistic' for segment-level splitting, and observes of a comparable child eye-tracking study reporting 85.1% that there was 'no note on how the data was split'. Against that background it positions its own 74-75% as comparable to fMRI at far lower cost, and frames the adult high-functioning population as the underserved case: symptoms are less obvious, lifelong coping strategies mask presentation, and 'unlike for children, critical incidents with adults are not monitored by school staff or parents'.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder via an Eye-Tracking Based
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Xia C; Chen K; Li K; Li H
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2020 7th International Conference on Bioinformatics Research and Appli
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Preschool and early school-age children with autism
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking and gaze
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Move eye-tracking autism identification from static fixation statistics to the dynamic structure of the scanpath - the sequence of and relationships between fixations - by learning a representation of scanpath segments rather than analysing fixation location and duration in isolation, and to do so with a short protocol suitable for young children
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Case-control classification study with a purpose-built eye-tracking dataset and repeated random participant-level splits
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One free-viewing session per child: 82 images presented for 3 seconds each with a 1-second mask between images
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Free viewing with no instruction beyond observing the images. Stimuli comprised 82 images in four categories - facial images, social scenarios, animated characters and synthetic patterns - resized to 800 x 600 and presented centrally, with an interstimulus mask to reduce carry-over from the preceding image
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: A therapy room, with a maximum of two people present besides the child
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: China - Xi'an, Shaanxi; autistic children recruited via the Children Rehabilitation Center, Shaanxi Rehabilitation Hospital
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Confirmed clinical diagnoses according to the Classification and Diagnostic Criteria of Mental Disorders in China, Third Edition (CCMD-3). No ADOS, ADI-R or DSM criteria were applied, and no severity instrument, diagnostician or assessment date is reported
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 31 recruited; 30 used in the reported experiments (15 training, 15 testing)
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Not reported, though recruitment through a rehabilitation centre implies the autistic children were receiving intervention
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported. Extending the model to grade severity is named as future work
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: By attendance at regular schools in Xi'an with 'no diagnosis or previous history of ASD' - no screening instrument was applied
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 43 recruited; 40 used in the reported experiments (20 training, 20 testing)
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Approximately but not verifiably. Means differ by about half a year (4.67 versus 4.15) with markedly different spread (SD 1.59 versus 0.98) and different ranges - the autistic group extends down to 1.8 years and up to 8, the control group spans 2.5 to 7. No statistical test of the age difference is reported, and age is not controlled for in the model despite free-viewing behaviour changing substantially across this range
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Cannot be assessed - sex is not reported for either group
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted from mainstream school attendance and absence of an autism diagnosis; no developmental screening was performed
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Gaze fixation sequences (saccadic scanpaths) recorded during free viewing of static images
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Each scanpath was segmented into overlapping pieces of length k for k = 1 to 5 fixations. For each fixation, a 79 x 79 x 3 central patch and a 158 x 158 x 3 surrounding patch (resized to 79 x 79) were fed to a two-stream pretrained CNN, and 33 visual saliency features were computed. Piece features are the concatenation of the constituent fixations' features. An SVM regression model was trained per scale, scores averaged across scales and across all 82 images per child, and the child classified against a threshold obtained by the maximum between-class variance (Otsu) method
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: SciEye 2.0 eye tracker at 140 Hz; 1920 x 1080 monitor at 0.5 m viewing distance; a pretrained two-stream CNN from prior published work; the LIBSVM toolbox; saliency computation drawing on Itti et al.'s conspicuity maps and Oliva-Torralba saliency, plus face, person and car detectors
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - an eye-tracking dataset of 74 children across 82 stimuli was constructed for this study
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - no availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze coordinate data over image stimuli, so not directly identifying, but collected from young clinical and non-clinical children. No ethics committee approval, consent procedure or governance statement appears anywhere in the paper, which is a substantive omission given the population
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Learned deep features plus handcrafted multi-level visual saliency features, both computed at fixation locations
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Per fixation: two-stream CNN features from centre and surround patches, plus 33 saliency features in three tiers. Low-level (28 dimensions): pyramid subbands in four orientations and three scales (13), three-channel colour (3), probability of the pixel value in the corresponding colour (3), Itti conspicuity maps for intensity, colour and orientation (3), probability of each colour from 3D colour histograms filtered at five scales (5), and Oliva-Torralba saliency (1). Mid-level gist (2): distance to image centre and a trained horizon-line detector. High-level semantic (3): face, person and car detector response maps. Per piece: these features stacked across k fixations, for k = 1 to 5
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Pretrained CNN from prior work; custom saliency pipeline; LIBSVM
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes - a leave-one-family-out ablation removing each feature category in turn
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Ablation across four feature groups, with accuracy, sensitivity and specificity reported at piece, scanpath and subject level for each
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: CNN features contribute most (removing them drops subject accuracy from 93.15% to 84.57%), followed by high-level semantic features (87.42%), low-level features (89.14%) and mid-level gist features (90.86%). The authors read the high-level result as evidence for 'the importance of semantic high-level attributes in ASD recognition' - consistent with the literature's emphasis on reduced attention to faces and people
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported directionally. The model produces a continuous per-child autism score with higher scores indicating autism, but no analysis identifies which image regions, categories or fixation patterns drive the score in which direction, so the substantive behavioural finding remains implicit in the classifier
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Representation learning with kernel classification - deep features feeding an SVM, aggregated hierarchically from fixation to piece to scanpath to subject
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: A pretrained two-stream CNN for feature extraction (not trained on this data), five scale-specific SVM regression models via LIBSVM, and Otsu maximum between-class variance thresholding for the final binary decision
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Participant-level division into 15 autistic and 20 typically developing children for training and a disjoint 15 and 20 for testing, repeated over five random permutations with per-permutation results tabulated. Prediction proceeds bottom-up: pieces scored by the SVMs, averaged into scanpath scores, averaged across all 82 images into a subject score, and thresholded. The decision threshold is not fixed from training but recomputed by Otsu on the score distribution at hand, so the test set's own scores inform where the boundary falls
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy at three granularities (piece, scanpath, subject), plus sensitivity and specificity, reported for each of five permutations and for each ablation condition. Reporting accuracy at all three aggregation levels is a genuine contribution - it quantifies how much the hierarchical voting buys
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Across five permutations, subject-level accuracy was 94.29, 91.43, 94.29, 94.29 and 91.43 percent, averaging 93.15% with mean sensitivity 94.66% and specificity 92.00%. Accuracy rises monotonically with aggregation: 87.16% at piece level, 88.03% at scanpath level, 93.15% at subject level. Ablation: without CNN features 84.57%, without high-level features 87.42%, without low-level 89.14%, without mid-level 90.86%. The paper compares these against 89% (Liu et al.) and 92% (Jiang and Zhao) reported on different datasets, and against 84% for a quotient-based diagnostic tool
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Encoding the dynamic structure of saccadic scanpaths - overlapping segments of one to five consecutive fixations, each represented by pretrained CNN features plus multi-level saliency features - and scoring them with scale-specific SVMs classified children as autistic or typically developing with 93.15% mean subject-level accuracy over five random participant splits. Accuracy improves monotonically as evidence is aggregated from individual fixation pieces to whole scanpaths to whole subjects, which the authors present as evidence that no single scanpath is reliable and that integration across stimuli is necessary. CNN features contribute most and high-level semantic (face, person, car) features next, supporting the view that reduced attention to socially meaningful content carries the signal. Errors fall more often on typically developing children, which the authors attribute to distraction producing uninformative gaze.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Not identified explicitly. The ablation implies that semantic content at fixated locations - especially faces and people - carries substantial discriminative information, consistent with the reduced social-attention literature the paper reviews, but no direct measurement of social versus non-social looking is reported
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Replicate on larger samples and address positive/negative class balance; extend the model from binary identification to subdividing or scoring autism severity; improve the eye-tracking protocol to hold children's attention better and so raise the proportion of valid data; incorporate fixation duration, which the authors note most identification models ignore; replace the fixed-length piece encoding with recurrent networks that can process variable-length sequences directly; and apply the framework to other recognition tasks including other diseases, gender and age
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A technically careful paper with one methodological blind spot. The strengths are real: the train/test division is at the participant level and repeated over five permutations with all five reported rather than only the best; accuracy is reported at three aggregation granularities, which makes the contribution of hierarchical voting measurable rather than assumed; a proper ablation isolates each feature family's contribution; and the protocol is short by design, which matters for the population. The blind spot is the decision threshold. Class assignment uses the maximum between-class variance (Otsu) method applied to the score distribution being classified, including at test time, so the boundary between groups is derived from the test data rather than fixed from training - a transductive step that would be unavailable in the deployment scenario the paper envisages, where a single child is assessed in isolation with no comparison population to threshold against. This is not leakage of labels, but it does mean the reported accuracies assume a batch of children with a roughly known class mix. Three lesser issues: the abstract's headline 94.28% is the maximum over five permutations while the average is 93.15%, and on a 35-child test set a single subject is worth 2.86 percentage points, so the spread across permutations is one child; the comparisons against Liu (89%) and Jiang and Zhao (92%) are across different datasets, stimuli and populations and cannot support the claim of outperforming them; and no ethics approval or consent statement appears anywhere. Diagnostic ascertainment by CCMD-3 rather than ADOS or DSM-5 also limits comparability with the rest of the corpus, and sex is not reported for either group. The paper's most transferable observation is its own error analysis - that typically developing children are misclassified more often because distraction produces uninformative gaze - which correctly identifies data validity rather than model capacity as the binding constraint.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: 31 autistic children recruited through the Children Rehabilitation Center at Shaanxi Rehabilitation Hospital and 43 typically developing children attending mainstream schools in Xi'an. The reported experiments use 30 and 40 respectively (15 + 20 training, 15 + 20 testing), so one autistic and three typically developing children are recruited but unaccounted for in the analysis, with no explanation given. No other-diagnosis comparison group; the authors themselves flag class balance as an issue needing attention.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'infants with ASD', 'subjects'. Mixed person-first and 'ASD children'. The framing is medical and burden-oriented - autism is 'a severe lifelong neurodevelopmental disorder', children with it 'usually struggle in school, which affects their quality of life', and families 'may also bear enormous psychological pressure and burden'. The paper also uses 'the hazards of the disease' and refers to a 'golden period' for treatment at ages 2-6.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Autistic group: n = 31, aged 1.8-8 years, mean 4.67 +/- 1.59. Typically developing group: n = 43, aged 2.5-7 years, mean 4.15 +/- 0.98. Age is reported but not tested: the means differ by about half a year, the spreads differ substantially (SD 1.59 versus 0.98), and the ranges are asymmetric, with only the autistic group including children under 2.5 or over 7. Free-viewing behaviour changes rapidly across 2-8 years, and age is not entered into or controlled by the model. Sex is not reported at all for either group, nor is IQ, developmental level, socioeconomic status or ethnicity. All participants are from Xi'an.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Autistic children had 'confirmed clinical diagnoses of ASD according to the Classification and Diagnostic Criteria of Mental Disorders in China-Third Edition' (CCMD-3), with no instrument, diagnostician, date or severity measure reported. Using CCMD-3 rather than DSM-5 or ADOS/ADI-R is a legitimate national standard but limits comparability with the rest of this corpus, where ADOS confirmation is the norm. Typically developing status rests on mainstream school attendance and absence of a prior autism diagnosis, with no screening instrument applied - so the control group is unscreened.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No IQ, developmental quotient, language, adaptive functioning or symptom severity measure is reported for either group, and no comorbidity information. Grading severity is named only as future work.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: identify autism from the dynamic structure of saccadic scanpaths rather than from static fixation statistics, using learned representations. Main findings: 93.15% mean subject-level accuracy across five participant-level permutations (94.29% maximum), with sensitivity 94.66% and specificity 92.00%; accuracy increases monotonically with aggregation from pieces (87.16%) to scanpaths (88.03%) to subjects (93.15%); CNN features contribute most and high-level semantic features next in ablation; and errors concentrate on typically developing children, attributed to distraction producing uninformative gaze.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A therapy room with at most two people present besides the child. Autistic participants came from the Children Rehabilitation Center at Shaanxi Rehabilitation Hospital, Xi'an; typically developing participants from mainstream Xi'an schools. Funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the China Postdoctoral Science Foundation and the Natural Science Foundation of Shaanxi Province.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Free viewing of 82 static images across four categories - facial images, social scenarios, animated characters and synthetic patterns - each shown for 3 seconds with a 1-second mask between images to suppress carry-over, at 0.5 m from a 1920 x 1080 monitor with no instruction beyond observing. The design choice is deliberate and argued: eye-tracking protocols for this population 'usually consider the limited attention of children with ASD, with each set of experiments lasting less than 10 minutes', and the paper contrasts its short protocol against comparators requiring 10 minutes or 10-45 minutes. Note that 82 images at 4 seconds each implies roughly 5.5 minutes of presentation, against the 'approximately 2.5 minutes for recording eye movement' claimed in the comparison - an unexplained discrepancy.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single session per child with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates over image stimuli. No ethics committee approval, parental consent procedure, anonymization or data governance statement appears anywhere in the paper, despite participants being children as young as 1.8 years recruited through a clinical rehabilitation service.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: SciEye 2.0 eye tracker at 140 Hz; 1920 x 1080 monitor at 0.5 m; a pretrained two-stream CNN taken from prior published work rather than trained here; LIBSVM; a saliency pipeline incorporating Itti et al.'s conspicuity maps, Oliva-Torralba saliency, a trained horizon-line detector and face, person and car object detectors. Sampling rate, viewing distance, presentation timing and image dimensions are all specified; calibration procedure, data loss rate and fixation-detection algorithm are not.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Mixed. The model is described in enough detail to reimplement - patch sizes (79 x 79 centre, 158 x 158 surround resized to 79 x 79), the full 33-dimensional saliency breakdown with dimension counts per component, the multi-scale piece construction for k = 1 to 5 with the scoring equations, the aggregation formula, the thresholding method and the toolbox used. Stimulus timing, count, categories and apparatus are given. Missing: SVM kernel and hyperparameters, calibration and data-quality procedures, the identity of the CNN's pretraining data, any code or data release, any ethics documentation, and an account of the four recruited children who do not appear in the experiments.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged and unusually specific: the sample of 31 and 43 children is small and needs large-scale replication; class balance 'is also a problem that needs attention in the validation of our machine learning based model'; severity subdivision is not addressed; and data validity is limited because distracted typically developing children 'may generate meaningless eye movement', which the error analysis identifies as the reason specificity trails sensitivity. Not acknowledged: the Otsu threshold is computed on the score distribution being classified, including at test time, so the decision boundary uses test data and would not be available when assessing a single child; the abstract's 94.28% is the best of five permutations rather than the average; comparisons against Liu and Jiang and Zhao are across different datasets and cannot establish superiority; age differs between groups in mean, spread and range without any test or adjustment; sex is unreported; the control group is unscreened; and no ethics approval is stated.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Larger-scale replication with attention to class balance; extension from binary identification to severity scoring; protocol improvements to hold children's attention and increase the proportion of valid data; incorporation of fixation duration, which the authors observe 'most identification models have ignored'; replacement of fixed-length piece encoding with recurrent networks able to consume variable-length scanpaths directly; and transfer of the framework to other recognition tasks including other diseases, gender and age.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Visual attention during free viewing, targeted specifically at its dynamic structure - the sequence of and transitions between fixations rather than where or how long the eye rests. This is the paper's defining choice and its stated critique of the field: existing methods 'tend to analyze the indicators based on individual static fixation, such as the fixation location and fixation duration. However, the actual eye movement is a dynamic process. The relationship between fixations also contains important information in visual attention.' Ironically, in operationalising the dynamic view the model discards fixation duration entirely, which the authors recognise and list as future work.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-modal fusion - gaze only. There is within-modality feature fusion between learned CNN representations and handcrafted multi-level saliency features, and the ablation quantifies each family's contribution: removing CNN features costs 8.6 accuracy points, high-level semantic features 5.7, low-level 4.0 and mid-level 2.3. The paper closes by expressing the hope that the work 'can contribute to the development of multimodal approaches in the early detection and diagnosis of ASD', positioning gaze as one future component rather than a complete solution.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A hybrid: a pretrained two-stream CNN as a fixed feature extractor (not fine-tuned on this data), scale-specific SVM regression models via LIBSVM, and Otsu thresholding for the final decision. Using a frozen pretrained CNN is a sensible response to 74 participants, avoiding the overfitting that end-to-end deep training would invite, and the SVM stage operates on a much larger effective sample because each child contributes many scanpath pieces. The multi-scale design - one model per piece length from 1 to 5 fixations - is the architectural contribution, and is explicitly contrasted with the alternative of zero-padding variable-length scanpaths to a fixed size.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Scanpath pieces of one to five consecutive fixations, each fixation represented by two-stream CNN features over centre and surround image patches concatenated with 33 saliency features spanning low-level (orientation subbands, colour, Itti conspicuity, colour histograms, Oliva-Torralba saliency), mid-level gist (distance to centre, horizon line) and high-level semantic (face, person and car detector responses) tiers. Crucially, features describe what was looked at - the image content at each fixation - rather than the gaze coordinates themselves, so the representation encodes the semantics of visual attention rather than its geometry. Fixation duration is deliberately excluded and its omission acknowledged.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy at three aggregation levels (piece, scanpath, subject) plus sensitivity and specificity, tabulated per permutation and per ablation condition. Reporting accuracy at all three granularities is a real methodological contribution: it makes the value of hierarchical evidence integration measurable (87.16 to 88.03 to 93.15 percent) rather than assumed, and it is the kind of reporting that would expose segment-level inflation in studies that report only the finest granularity. Missing: AUC, confusion matrices, confidence intervals, and any statistical comparison between conditions - on a 35-child test set, where one subject is worth 2.86 points, the differences between permutations and between some ablation conditions amount to one or two children.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No saliency maps, attention visualisation or attribution over the model's decisions, and no directional characterisation of what distinguishes the groups. Interpretability is confined to the feature-family ablation, from which the authors infer 'the importance of semantic high-level attributes in ASD recognition' - a reasonable but indirect inference, since the high-level features are face, person and car detector responses and their removal costs 5.7 accuracy points. Because the model scores image content at fixated locations rather than gaze geometry, a per-category or per-region analysis would have been straightforward and would have connected the classifier to the reduced-social-attention literature the paper reviews at length; it is not performed.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Participant-level splitting into disjoint training and testing sets, repeated over five random permutations with every permutation's result tabulated rather than only the best - a sound design, and better than most of the corpus. Two qualifications. First, the classification threshold is obtained by the maximum between-class variance method applied to the score distribution being classified, so at test time the boundary is set using the test subjects' own scores; this is transductive rather than inductive, and would not transfer to assessing an individual child, which is the deployment scenario the paper's cost and portability arguments envisage. Second, no independent cohort, external site or held-out stimulus set is used, and the cross-paper comparisons against 89% and 92% are drawn from studies on entirely different datasets and populations, so they establish nothing about relative performance.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), Machine Learning, Eye-Tracking, Saccadic Scanpath, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Representation Learning. 'Saccadic scanpath' and 'representation learning' together capture the contribution - the object of study is how to represent a gaze trajectory, with autism as the classification task on which the representation is evaluated.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: ICBRA 2020, the 7th International Conference on Bioinformatics Research and Applications (ACM, Berlin) - a computing conference, published open access with support from King's College London and Northwestern Polytechnical University.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2020. The framing combines an access argument with a methodological one. On access: autism diagnosis 'usually relies on a multidisciplinary team of experts, which is relatively difficult to achieve, especially for economically underdeveloped areas', and eye trackers are 'affordable, portable, and easy to operate' so 'they can also be used in poor and remote areas'. On method: the paper's specific criticism of the existing eye-tracking literature is that models 'have usually utilized statistical analysis to discover the differences between the two classes' and so 'have high requirements for selecting the stimuli and indicators of eye movement for analysis', and that they analyse static fixations while 'the actual eye movement is a dynamic process'. Protocol duration is treated as a competitive dimension in its own right - the paper contrasts its short recording against comparators needing 10 or 10-45 minutes - reflecting a field increasingly aware that attention span, not accuracy alone, bounds what is deployable with young children.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Machine Learning and Virtual Reality on Body Movements' Behaviors to Classify Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Alcañiz Raya M; Marín-Morales J; Minissi ME; Teruel Garcia G; Abad L; Chicchi Giglioli IA
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Preschool and early school-age children with autism
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Motor and kinematics (body movement in virtual reality)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Test whether quantitative body movement measured during ecologically framed virtual reality imitation tasks can discriminate autistic from typically developing children, and determine which body regions and which sensory stimulus conditions carry the most discriminative information - replacing the qualitative clinical judgement of stereotyped and repetitive behaviour with an objective measurement
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification with a factorial comparison across five body regions and three cumulative sensory conditions
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session of 14 minutes total, comprising three stimulus conditions of 2 minutes 40 seconds each, with a 2-minute baseline recorded before each condition
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Imitation of avatar actions inside a projected virtual city street intersection, under three cumulative sensory conditions presented in fixed order. Visual (V): a boy avatar walks in from the left, stops, waves hello three times and exits, followed by a girl avatar entering centrally and exiting right with the same three waves, the sequence repeated three times; the child is asked to wave three times. Visual-auditory (VA): the same avatars dance to an animated disco song for 10 seconds, three times; the child imitates the dance. Visual-auditory-olfactory (VAO): the same avatars bite a buttered muffin accompanied by an artificial butter odour; the child imitates biting a muffin. The escalating sensory load is motivated explicitly by the autism sensory literature - hypersensitivity to visual and auditory stimuli, hyposensitivity to olfactory ones
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: A three-surface CAVE (Cave Assisted Virtual Environment) of 4 x 4 x 3 m at the Institute for Research and Innovation in Bioengineering, Polytechnic University of Valencia, with the child standing 1.5 m from the central surface and a caregiver present according to the child's needs
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Both groups presented an individual assessment report including ADOS-2 and ADI-R. ADOS-2 module 1 was used for all participants - the module designed for children with little or no phrase speech, which implies a low-verbal autistic sample and makes its use for the typically developing group at ages 4-7 anomalous. ADOS-2 and ADI-R are described in detail with their reliability coefficients, but no scores, cut-offs or severity indices are reported for the participants
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 24 stated in the participants section and abstract; the results tables imply 22 (true positive rates are multiples of 1/22 and accuracies multiples of 1/47), so two autistic children appear to have been dropped without explanation
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Within the study range of 4-7 years, though the standard deviation implies some participants below 4
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported, and the authors state explicitly that groups were not matched on motor comorbidities such as dyspraxia
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Not reported; the autistic sample was drawn from a cognitive development centre, implying ongoing intervention
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: ADOS-2 and ADI-R were administered and both yield severity indices, but no scores are reported and no severity-stratified analysis is performed
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes - typically developing participants also presented individual assessment reports including ADOS-2 and ADI-R, so control status is instrument-based rather than assumed. This is stronger than most of the corpus, though administering module 1 of ADOS-2 to typically developing 4-7 year olds is a puzzling choice
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Approximately - means differ by 0.27 years with unequal spread (SD 1.35 versus 0.91), and no statistical test of the difference is reported
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: No - 87.5% male in the autistic group against 64% in the control group, a substantial imbalance that is neither tested nor discussed, and one that matters directly for a study whose outcome is body movement magnitude
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Established by ADOS-2 and ADI-R assessment reports rather than assumed
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: RGB-D video of the child during the virtual experience, converted to 3D joint trajectories
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: OpenPose detected 25 body joints per frame with a per-joint confidence value; joints with confidence below 0.5 were discarded; 3D positions were reconstructed using the camera's depth channel; displacement was computed as the Euclidean distance between consecutive frames; and the movement level of a joint during a condition was summarised as the mean of all displacements. Joints were grouped into head (eyes and ears, joints 15-18), trunk (neck and mid-hip), arms (shoulders, elbows, wrists), legs (hips, knees, ankles) and feet (big toes, small toes, heels)
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Three-surface CAVE with three ceiling ultra-short-throw projectors delivering a 100-degree image from 55 cm and a Logitech Z906 500W 5.1 sound system; Olorama Technology wireless scent diffuser with 12 pre-charged channels triggered by UDP packet and a programmable fan controlling duration and intensity; Intel RealSense D435 depth camera with Intel RealSense SDK 2.0; OpenPose on an Nvidia GTX1060; MATLAB R2016a with the LIBSVM toolbox
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: A 49-child VR movement dataset was collected but no release is described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Video of identifiable children is captured but reduced to joint coordinates. Governance is properly reported: written information and written consent from family caregivers, approval by the Ethical Committee of the Polytechnic University of Valencia, and conformity with the institutional and national research committee standards and the 1964 Helsinki Declaration
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Aggregate kinematic magnitude features derived from pose estimation
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Mean inter-frame Euclidean displacement per joint, aggregated into five body-region groups plus a whole-body measure, computed separately for each of the three stimulus conditions plus the whole experiment - a 24-cell design of body-region by stimulus-condition datasets. Each dataset was reduced by principal component analysis retaining 95% of variance, then further reduced by SVM recursive feature elimination inside each training fold. Note that the paper describes this quantity as movement 'frequency' throughout, but mean inter-frame displacement measures movement magnitude, not rate; no frequency-domain or event-count analysis is performed
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: OpenPose for 2D joint detection with confidence scores, RealSense depth for 3D lifting, PCA and nonlinear SVM-RFE with correlation bias reduction for dimensionality reduction
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes - as the factorial comparison itself. Every combination of body region and stimulus condition is reported with accuracy, TPR, TNR, kappa and the number of PCA features retained
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Wilcoxon tests on per-joint movement level for group differences; nonlinear SVM-RFE with a correlation bias reduction strategy performed on each training fold with median feature ranks computed across folds; and the 24-model factorial accuracy comparison
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The head is the most consistently discriminative region, ranging from 80.85% accuracy in the visual condition to 89.36% in the visual-auditory-olfactory condition, and reaching 82.98% pooled across conditions with 100% sensitivity. Trunk and feet also reach 82.98% pooled. Arms and legs are weaker overall (74.47% and 72.34%) though arms peak at 87.23% in the visual condition. Every model retained three or fewer features after selection
