data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Clearly reported: 15 joints showed significant group differences and in 13 of them autistic children moved more than typically developing children - four leg joints, two head joints and one trunk joint in the visual condition, one leg and two head joints in visual-auditory, and four head joints in visual-auditory-olfactory. The exception runs the other way: one head joint showed lower movement in autistic children during two of the baseline periods, which the authors note is partially at odds with the literature
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification with unsupervised dimensionality reduction and wrapper feature selection
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: C-SVM with a Gaussian kernel, cost and gamma searched over seven logarithmically spaced values between 0.1 and 1000, preceded by PCA at 95% variance retention and nonlinear SVM-RFE with correlation bias reduction as a wrapper inside each training fold
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, with normalisation statistics (median and median absolute deviation) computed on the training folds only and applied to the held-out subject, and SVM-RFE performed on each fold's training set rather than on the whole dataset. The unit of held-out data is the child, so there is no participant-level leakage. What sits outside the loop is model selection: 24 body-region by stimulus-condition models were built and 'the model was optimized to achieve best Cohen's kappa', so both the hyperparameters and the reported configuration were chosen on the same leave-one-out estimate that is presented as the result
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, true positive rate, true negative rate, Cohen's kappa and the number of PCA features retained, tabulated for all 24 models - a full factorial report rather than a headline figure. Reporting TPR and TNR separately is what makes the confusion-matrix imbalance visible: the pooled head model reaches 82.98% with 100% sensitivity but only 68% specificity, while the pooled trunk model reaches the same accuracy with 63.64% sensitivity and 100% specificity
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Best overall 89.36% (kappa 0.79) for all joints in the visual condition, with 100% TPR and 80% TNR, from a single retained feature out of 14; equal 89.36% (kappa 0.78) for head joints in the visual-auditory-olfactory condition with 77.27% TPR and 100% TNR. Pooled across conditions, head, trunk and feet each reach 82.98% (kappas 0.67, 0.65, 0.66), arms 74.47% and legs 72.34%. Accuracy declines as sensory load increases when all joints are used (89.36% visual, 74.47% visual-auditory, 70.21% visual-auditory-olfactory) but rises for the head across the same progression (80.85, 82.98, 89.36). The all-joints all-conditions model performs worst at 70.21% with 45.45% sensitivity
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Autistic children moved more than typically developing children during virtual imitation tasks, with significant differences at 15 joints and higher movement in 13 of them, concentrated in the head and legs. Machine learning over joint displacement classified the groups at up to 89.36% accuracy. Two structural findings emerge from the factorial design: the head is the most consistently discriminative body region and becomes more so as sensory load increases, while pooling all joints and all conditions performs worst of all - more data made the classification worse, not better. The visual-only condition was the single most discriminative stimulus for whole-body movement. Every model needed three or fewer features after selection.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Greater overall body movement during imitation, concentrated in head joints (increasingly so under multisensory load) and in leg joints (under visual stimulation)
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Validate on larger samples that would permit a genuine test set; include comparison groups with other neurodevelopmental conditions involving movement impairment such as ADHD and intellectual disability, so that classifiers become specific to autism rather than to neurodevelopmental difference in general; match groups on IQ, cognitive ability and motor comorbidities such as dyspraxia; and counterbalance the stimulus order, stratified by functioning level
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The instrumentation and clinical framing are strong, and the limitations section is one of the most honest in the corpus - it names the absence of IQ, cognitive and motor-comorbidity matching as directly 'limiting the confidence that the experimental differences observed in the experiment were due to a diagnosis of ASD, and not to differences in other cognitive or non-cognitive factors', and identifies the absence of other-disorder comparison groups as a specificity problem. Both groups were assessed with ADOS-2 and ADI-R, ethics reporting is complete, and the validation loop is properly constructed with leave-one-subject-out folds, training-fold-only normalisation and RFE nested inside each fold. Three problems bound the result. First and most consequential is multiplicity: 24 models were built and hyperparameters were tuned to maximise Cohen's kappa on the same leave-one-out estimate that is reported, so 89.36% is the best of 24 optimised configurations on 47 children, where a single child is worth 2.13 percentage points. The paper's tabulation of all 24 makes this visible and assessable, which is to its credit, but the abstract's headline does not carry that caveat. Second, the between-group comparison uses the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, a paired test, for two independent groups; the appropriate test is Mann-Whitney U, and the reported significances should be treated as unverified. Third, the sex distributions differ markedly (87.5% versus 64% male) on an outcome - movement magnitude during imitation - where sex differences in this age range are plausible, and this is neither tested nor mentioned. Two smaller inconsistencies: the accuracy denominators imply 47 rather than 49 analysed children, with two autistic participants unaccounted for; and the quantity described throughout as movement 'frequency' is in fact mean inter-frame displacement, a magnitude. The most interesting substantive result is one the paper does not emphasise - that pooling all joints and all conditions gave the worst performance of any model, which suggests the discriminative signal is localised and that indiscriminate aggregation adds noise.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: 24 autistic children recruited through Red Cenit, a cognitive development centre in Valencia, and 25 typically developing children recruited by a management company through mailings to families. Both groups presented individual assessment reports including ADOS-2 and ADI-R, so the comparison group is instrument-assessed rather than merely unscreened. No other-diagnosis comparison group, and the authors identify this as a specificity limitation, proposing ADHD and intellectual disability comparisons for future work. Note that the results tables imply 22 rather than 24 autistic children were analysed.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'children with typical development (TD)', 'children with typical neurodevelopment', 'ASD individuals', 'ASD population'. Mixed person-first and 'ASD children'. The framing is clinical but not burden-oriented; notably the paper's critique is directed at the assessment instruments rather than at the children - ADOS 'relies on the examiner's expertise and subjectivity' and ADI-R diagnosis 'is based on caregivers' reports rather than on objective evaluation'. The sensory-difference framing is also treated as explanatory rather than deficit-laden, with hyper- and hypo-sensitivity used to motivate the stimulus design.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Autistic group: n = 24, 21 male and 3 female (87.5% male), mean age 5.13 +/- 1.35 years. Typically developing group: n = 25, 16 male and 9 female (64% male), mean age 4.86 +/- 0.91 years. Overall range 4-7 years. The age difference is small but untested and the spreads differ. The sex imbalance is substantial and unaddressed, which matters because the dependent variable is body movement magnitude. Critically, the authors state plainly that 'the experimental groups were not matched on measures related to the intelligence quotient performance, cognitive abilities, and motor comorbidities (e.g., dyspraxia)' and that this limits confidence that the observed differences are attributable to autism. No ethnicity or socioeconomic reporting; single site in Valencia.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Both groups presented individual assessment reports including ADOS-2 and ADI-R, and both instruments are described in detail with their test-retest reliabilities (ADOS-2: 0.87 social affect, 0.64 repetitive behaviour, 0.88 global; ADI-R: 0.93-0.97). Applying the same instruments to both groups is a genuine strength. Two qualifications: no ADOS-2 or ADI-R scores, cut-offs or severity indices are reported for any participant, so the diagnostic evidence cannot be inspected; and ADOS-2 module 1 was used for all assessments, which is the module for children with little or no phrase speech - implying a minimally verbal autistic sample and making its application to typically developing 4-7 year olds difficult to interpret.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None reported, and their absence is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation. ADOS-2 and ADI-R were administered and yield severity indices in social affect and restricted/repetitive behaviour domains, but no scores appear and no severity-stratified analysis is performed. No IQ, cognitive, language or adaptive measure, and no motor comorbidity screening despite the outcome being motor.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: determine whether body movement during multimodal VR imitation tasks discriminates autistic from typically developing children, which body regions carry the signal, and which sensory conditions best elicit it. Main findings: 15 joints differed significantly with autistic children moving more in 13 of them, concentrated in head and legs; best classification 89.36% (all joints, visual condition; and head joints, visual-auditory-olfactory condition); head is the most consistent region and improves with increasing sensory load; whole-body accuracy declines with increasing sensory load; the all-joints all-conditions model performs worst at 70.21%; and every model needed three or fewer features.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A three-surface CAVE of 4 x 4 x 3 m at the Institute for Research and Innovation in Bioengineering, Polytechnic University of Valencia. Autistic participants came from Red Cenit, a Valencia cognitive development centre; controls were recruited by a management company through family mailings. Funded by the Spanish Ministry of Economy, Industry and Competitiveness ('Immersive virtual environment for the evaluation and training of children with autism spectrum disorder: T Room'), the Generalitat Valenciana REBRAND project, and ERDF Valencian Community funds.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Avatar imitation in a projected virtual city street, under three cumulative sensory conditions - visual (waving), visual-auditory (dancing to a disco track), and visual-auditory-olfactory (biting a buttered muffin with a butter scent released by a wireless diffuser). The design is the most theoretically motivated stimulus escalation in the corpus: the sensory ladder follows the autism sensory literature directly, adding modalities to which autistic children are reported hypersensitive (visual, auditory) before one to which they are reported hyposensitive (olfactory), on the hypothesis that sensory load provokes repetitive behaviour. The imitation framing is also apt, since imitation deficits are independently documented. Order was fixed rather than counterbalanced, deliberately, to avoid sensory overload - a defensible clinical choice that the authors correctly flag as a methodological cost.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single 14-minute session with three 2-minute-40-second conditions each preceded by a 2-minute baseline, no follow-up. Data are depth video of identifiable children reduced to joint coordinates. Governance is properly reported: written information and written consent from family caregivers, approval by the Ethical Committee of the Polytechnic University of Valencia, and conformity with institutional and national committee standards and the 1964 Helsinki Declaration.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: CAVE with three ceiling ultra-short-throw projectors (100-degree image from 55 cm) and a Logitech Z906 5.1 sound system; Olorama Technology wireless scent diffuser with 12 UDP-triggered channels and programmable fan control of duration and intensity; Intel RealSense D435 depth camera with SDK 2.0; OpenPose for 25-joint pose estimation on an Nvidia GTX1060; MATLAB R2016a with LIBSVM. The scent delivery hardware is unique in this corpus and is what makes the olfactory condition possible.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Good on apparatus and pipeline, thin on results provenance. Reported: CAVE dimensions and projector specification, viewing distance, condition durations and baselines, camera model and SDK, OpenPose joint indices with their anatomical mapping, the 0.5 confidence cutoff, the displacement computation, PCA variance threshold, SVM kernel and search grid, the LOSO normalisation scheme, the nested RFE with correlation bias reduction, the optimisation criterion, and the software versions. Missing: any data or code release; ADOS-2 and ADI-R scores; frame rate of the depth camera; the proportion of joints discarded by the confidence threshold; an explanation for the two autistic children apparently absent from the analysis; and any account of how the 24 reported models relate to the number actually run.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged with unusual candour: the sample is small and precludes a genuine test set; autism's heterogeneity means larger training groups would be needed for generalisation; other neurodevelopmental comparison groups are absent, so the classifier may separate neurodevelopmental difference generally rather than autism specifically; the groups were not matched on IQ, cognitive ability or motor comorbidities, which the authors say directly limits attributing the differences to autism; and the stimulus order was not counterbalanced. Not acknowledged: the Wilcoxon signed-rank test is a paired test applied here to independent groups, where Mann-Whitney U is required, so the reported per-joint significances are unverified; 24 models were built and hyperparameters tuned to maximise kappa on the same leave-one-out estimate reported as the result, making 89.36% a best-of-many figure on 47 children where one child is worth 2.13 points; the sex distributions differ substantially on a motor outcome; the analysed sample appears to be 47 not 49; and the quantity called 'frequency' throughout is mean displacement, a magnitude.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Larger samples permitting a held-out test set and better coverage of autism's heterogeneity; comparison groups with other neurodevelopmental conditions involving movement impairment - ADHD and intellectual disability are named - specifically so that 'taking also into account different neurodevelopment conditions could improve the specificity of the classifiers for ASD rather than for neurodevelopment disorders in general'; matching on IQ, cognitive ability and motor comorbidity; and counterbalanced stimulus orders stratified by functioning level.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Whole-body movement during imitation, decomposed anatomically into head, trunk, arms, legs and feet, and measured as mean inter-frame joint displacement. The behavioural target is repetitive and stereotyped motor behaviour - the DSM criterion domain the paper argues is under-studied relative to social communication - operationalised as movement magnitude under graded sensory provocation rather than as counts of identified stereotypies. Uniquely in the corpus, the behaviour is elicited by a designed sensory manipulation rather than merely observed.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Multimodality here is in the stimulus rather than the sensing: a single depth camera captures movement, while visual, auditory and olfactory channels are added cumulatively to the environment. The results are informative and partly counterintuitive. For whole-body movement, discrimination is best under visual stimulation alone (89.36%) and degrades as modalities accumulate (74.47%, then 70.21%). For the head alone the pattern reverses, improving from 80.85% to 82.98% to 89.36% as sensory load rises. And pooling everything - all joints across all conditions - gives the worst result of any model at 70.21% with 45.45% sensitivity. The lesson transferable to the corpus's sensor-fusion studies is that indiscriminate aggregation across conditions and channels can destroy a localised signal.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A conventional and appropriately conservative pipeline for 47 participants: PCA at 95% variance retention, then C-SVM with a Gaussian kernel, with nonlinear SVM-RFE including correlation bias reduction as a wrapper inside each training fold. No deep learning is used for classification - OpenPose supplies the deep component as a fixed, externally trained pose estimator, which is the right division of labour at this sample size. Hyperparameters were searched over seven logarithmically spaced values of cost and gamma between 0.1 and 1000.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Mean inter-frame Euclidean displacement per joint, aggregated by body region and stimulus condition into a 24-cell factorial of datasets, each reduced by PCA then by RFE to three or fewer retained features. The representation is deliberately minimal - a single scalar per joint per condition - which is defensible at this sample size but discards everything about the temporal structure, rhythmicity or repetitiveness of the movement, despite repetitive behaviour being the construct the study is about. The paper's own terminology reflects the gap: it calls the measure 'frequency' throughout, but nothing in the pipeline computes a rate or a period.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, true positive rate, true negative rate, Cohen's kappa and retained feature count, tabulated for all 24 models. Reporting the full factorial rather than a selected best is good practice and is what allows an external reader to see both the multiplicity problem and the confusion-matrix imbalances - the pooled head model achieves 82.98% with 100% sensitivity but 68% specificity, while the pooled trunk model achieves identical accuracy with 63.64% sensitivity and 100% specificity, which the paper notes explicitly. Including Cohen's kappa is unusual in this corpus and appropriate given the near-balanced classes. Missing: confidence intervals, AUC, and any statistical comparison between models, which matters when adjacent accuracies differ by one or two children.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No model-explanation method, but the factorial design itself is the interpretive instrument, and it yields anatomically specific conclusions: the head is the most consistently discriminative region and becomes more so under multisensory load, while arms and legs contribute less. This is supported independently by the joint-level statistical analysis showing more movement in autistic children at 13 of 15 significant joints, concentrated in head and legs, which the authors connect to documented stereotypies of head tilting and leg flapping. The interpretation is therefore anchored in observable anatomy rather than in abstract features - though the underlying group comparison uses an inappropriate paired test.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The cross-validation architecture is correct: leave-one-subject-out folds, normalisation statistics computed on training folds only and applied to the held-out child, and SVM-RFE performed within each fold's training set with median ranks aggregated across folds. There is no participant-level leakage and no feature selection on the full dataset. What sits outside the loop is model selection - both the SVM hyperparameters ('the model was optimized to achieve best Cohen's kappa') and the choice of which of 24 configurations to headline were determined by the same leave-one-out estimate reported as the result. On 47 children this is a large source of optimism. The authors recognise the underlying constraint, noting that larger samples 'could allow validating the ML method, providing also the possibility to test the model' - an acknowledgement that no independent test was possible here.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorder; body movements; repetitive behaviors; virtual reality; machine learning. The inclusion of 'repetitive behaviors' locates the work in a specific DSM criterion domain rather than in autism generally, and the paper argues that this domain has been comparatively neglected - 'ASD studies primarily examine the weaknesses in social interaction abilities, and less on the stereotyped and repetitive motor behaviors'.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 9(5), 1260 - an open-access clinical journal, matching the paper's clinical framing and its detailed treatment of ADOS-2 and ADI-R.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2020. The framing is a critique of the gold standard on two grounds simultaneously - objectivity and ecological validity. On objectivity: 'since in ADOS examiner has to judge a child's performance giving scoring and rating, evaluation relies on the examiner's expertise and subjectivity; likewise, in ADI-R ASD diagnosis is based on caregivers' reports rather than on objective evaluation'. On ecology: the limitation is 'the absence of both objective assessment methods and the ecological validity of the setting'. Virtual reality is offered as addressing both at once - a controlled, repeatable environment that is nonetheless a simulated real-life scene, with sensory content that can be manipulated in ways a clinic room cannot. The paper positions itself as 'the first attempt to discriminate ASD children from children with typical neurodevelopment using body movements parameters of an imitation VR task and machine learning', and situates repetitive behaviour as an under-studied criterion domain relative to social communication.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Responsive Social Smile: A Machine-Learning Based Multimodal Behavior Assessment Framework towards Early Stage Autism Screening
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Pan Y; Cai K; Cheng M; Zou X; Li M
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: Proceedings of the 25th International Conference on Pattern Recognition (ICPR), 2240-2245
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Toddlers referred for autism assessment
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Facial expression and social interaction
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Automate one specific, hard-to-score element of clinical autism screening - the responsive social smile - which unlike response-to-name or joint attention has no clear behavioural benchmark and is assessed by ambiguous emotion description, so that clinicians can run the protocol while the system does the scoring
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control with dual evaluation: the system's per-stimulus scores are validated against clinician consensus labels, and the resulting score vectors are used to classify autism
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session per child, comprising up to six scripted stimuli, each repeated at most three times if the child did not respond
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: The Responsive Social Smile protocol - five types of social stimulus delivered by a clinician plus one by a parent, selected to span different humour mechanisms and modelled on ADOS design: greeting smile ('Hello!' plus the child's name), praise words ('You are so cute/cool!'), hide and seek, hints of tickling ('I am going to tickle you!'), actual tickling, and a parent-delivered greeting smile. Each stimulus is opened by a scripted keyword phrase that marks its start time
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: A standardised room layout at the Third Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University, with the child, a clinician and a parent seated so that a camera records the child's front face directly
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: China - Guangzhou, with the engineering groups at Duke Kunshan University and Sun Yat-sen University
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Diagnosed by professional clinicians at the collaborating hospital against DSM-IV criteria. No instrument scores, ADOS or ADI-R administration, or diagnostician details are reported. Note that DSM-IV rather than DSM-5 is used, which is unusual for a 2020 publication
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Group means not reported separately; the whole cohort averages 23.34 months
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Not reported per group; the whole cohort is 33 boys and 8 girls
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported, though the framework produces a six-dimensional behaviour score vector that is graded in principle
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - 21 children labelled non-autistic. These are children assessed at the same hospital rather than a community sample, so the comparison group is clinically referred, which makes the classification task harder and more realistic
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: By the same clinical diagnostic process that produced the autism labels
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Cannot be assessed - only whole-cohort age statistics are given, with an age-by-diagnosis scatter shown as a figure but no group means, SDs or test
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Cannot be assessed - only the whole-cohort 33:8 male:female split is reported. The authors note this approximates the 4:1 population sex ratio in autism, which is a reasonable observation about representativeness but says nothing about balance between groups
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not established - the comparison group is defined by absence of an autism diagnosis at a specialist clinic, not by typical development
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Synchronised audio and video of the clinical interaction
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A five-stage pipeline: (1) temporal stimulus localisation, where a Kaldi ASR system trained on AISHELL-2 detects the scripted keyword phrases and marks each stimulus onset; (2) face detection on the following time window using the OpenCV-DNN detector, chosen for robustness on the small face regions toddlers occupy; (3) facial expression recognition by a two-branch 2D/3D CNN over 7-frame clips resized to 224 x 224; (4) stimulus scoring, counting smile-classified clips within the window and thresholding; (5) autism classification from the resulting six-dimensional binary score vector
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: A single camera and microphone in a fixed low-cost room setup; Kaldi with an AISHELL-2-trained Mandarin model (1,000 hours of clean read speech); OpenCV-DNN face detector; a custom 2D-3D CNN built from ResNet-18 and 3D-ResNet-18 components; decision tree, SVM, naive Bayes and logistic regression classifiers
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Two. A clinical multimodal database of 41 diagnosed toddlers with per-stimulus behaviour scores and autism labels; and a video facial expression database of 15,000 seven-frame clips from a separate 54 children under six years old, manually labelled smile or non-smile, built specifically because existing expression databases are drawn from adults
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Highly sensitive - frontal video of identifiable toddlers with their parents in a clinical setting, plus audio. Governance reporting is minimal: participation with consent is acknowledged in the acknowledgements ('With their consent, this research can continue successfully') but no ethics committee approval, formal consent procedure or data governance statement appears in the paper
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: A six-dimensional vector of binary per-stimulus behaviour scores derived from learned facial expression features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: One binary score per stimulus (greeting smile from clinician, praise words, hide and seek, hints of tickling, tickling, greeting smile from parent), each indicating whether the child produced a clear responsive smile within the post-stimulus window. Missing stimuli - children who did not complete every step - were imputed with the mean of that child's other stimulus scores
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Kaldi for stimulus localisation; OpenCV-DNN for face detection; the custom 2D-3D CNN pretrained on Oulu-CASIA and fine-tuned on the 15,000-clip children's database for binary smile classification, with the decision threshold set empirically at 0.9 so that 'the child must give a clear enough response to count as smiling'
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No per-stimulus importance analysis, though the six-dimensional feature space is small enough that the decision tree is inherently inspectable; the learned tree is not shown
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None reported
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported at the stimulus level - which of the six social stimuli best separates the groups is never analysed, despite the six-dimensional representation making this directly available and despite the stimuli having been chosen to span different humour mechanisms
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: A cascade of pretrained deep perception modules feeding a shallow tabular classifier
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Kaldi ASR; OpenCV-DNN face detection; a two-branch expression network in which a shared 2D residual block (first three ResNet-18 layers, output 128 feature maps at 28 x 28) feeds both a 3D-CNN branch (fourth and fifth layers of pretrained 3D-ResNet-18) and a 2D-CNN branch (first five ResNet-18 layers plus average pooling), each yielding a 512-dimensional vector, concatenated to 1024 dimensions and passed to a fully connected classification layer; then logistic regression, naive Bayes, SVM and decision tree compared for the final autism classification
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-out cross-validation for both the stimulus scoring evaluation (196 stimulus samples) and the autism classification (41 children). The expression model was pretrained on Oulu-CASIA and fine-tuned on a children's database recorded from 54 children with explicitly no overlap with the 41 clinical participants - a clean separation between the perception module's training data and the evaluation cohort. The scoring evaluation is at the stimulus level, so the same child contributes multiple samples across folds; the autism classification is at the child level
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity with full confusion matrices for both stimulus scoring and autism classification, plus a comparison of all four classifiers under two conditions - using the system's predicted stimulus scores and using the clinicians' own scores - which isolates how much of the classification error comes from the perception stage
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Facial expression: 89.10% on Oulu-CASIA (against 81.46-91.67% for published comparators), then 92.60% for binary smile classification after fine-tuning on the children's database. Stimulus scoring against three-clinician majority-vote ground truth: 85.20% accuracy (confusion matrix 62 / 13 / 16 / 105 over 196 samples). Autism classification from predicted scores: decision tree 80.49% accuracy, 85.00% sensitivity, 77.27% specificity (17/3/5/16); SVM 70.73%, naive Bayes 68.29%, logistic regression 63.41%. Using clinicians' own stimulus scores instead: decision tree 82.93%, SVM 75.61%, naive Bayes 73.17%, logistic regression 70.73% - so replacing automated scoring with human scoring buys only about 2.4 accuracy points for the best classifier
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A scripted six-stimulus social smile protocol, automatically segmented by speech recognition and scored by a two-branch 2D/3D expression CNN, reproduced clinician consensus stimulus scores at 85.20% and supported autism classification at 80.49% accuracy in toddlers averaging 23 months. The most informative result is the ablation against human scores: feeding clinicians' own stimulus ratings into the same classifiers raised decision tree accuracy only from 80.49% to 82.93%, showing that the ceiling lies in the protocol's information content rather than in the perception pipeline. The failure analysis is equally pointed - most scoring errors were smiles the system detected correctly but which clinicians judged spontaneous rather than socially responsive, so the residual error is a problem of attributing cause to an expression, not of recognising it. The authors state plainly that a single protocol cannot screen autism comprehensively and position score fusion across multiple protocols as the next step.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Absence of a clear smile response to scripted social stimuli, aggregated across the six stimulus types; no individual stimulus is identified as more discriminative
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Fuse scores and features from multiple complementary automated assessment protocols - the authors name response to name and joint attention - since 'using the responsive social smile score alone cannot give a very comprehensive ASD classification'; and address the spontaneous-versus-responsive smile distinction that dominates the residual errors
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The engineering is thoughtfully staged and the evaluation design is better than the sample size would suggest. Three things stand out. First, the perception module's training data is genuinely disjoint from the clinical cohort - the 15,000-clip children's expression database comes from 54 children with explicitly no overlap with the 41 participants - which is exactly the discipline most video studies in this corpus omit. Second, the paper runs the ablation that matters: substituting clinician-assigned stimulus scores for the system's own raises the best classifier from 80.49% to 82.93%, which quantifies the perception stage's contribution to total error as small and locates the real limit in the protocol itself. Third, the failure analysis identifies a conceptually important boundary - most errors were correctly detected smiles that clinicians judged spontaneous rather than socially responsive - meaning the unsolved problem is causal attribution of an expression to a stimulus, not expression recognition. Against this, the participant reporting is thin in ways that matter: ages and sexes are given only for the pooled cohort, so age and sex matching between the 20 autistic and 21 non-autistic children cannot be checked at all, and with a 12-32 month range in a study whose outcome is social smiling to scripted prompts, age is a first-order confound. Diagnosis rests on DSM-IV with no instrument reported. No ethics approval statement appears despite frontal video of toddlers. And the headline 80.49% is the best of four classifiers on 41 children, where one child is worth 2.4 percentage points - the same margin the human-score ablation produces, which should temper how much weight either comparison bears. The paper's own framing is appropriately modest about this, describing the result as approaching 'the average level of domain experts in this Responsive Social Smile protocol' rather than as a screening test.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups, 41 toddlers: 20 diagnosed autistic and 21 non-autistic, all assessed at the same specialist hospital. The comparison group is therefore clinically referred rather than community-recruited, which makes the discrimination task harder and more clinically realistic than most of the corpus. A separate, non-overlapping group of 54 children under six supplied 15,000 labelled expression clips for training the perception module. No other-diagnosis comparison group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'autism children', 'non-ASD', 'autistic children'. Mixed person-first and 'ASD children'; the comparison group is 'non-ASD' rather than 'typically developing' or 'healthy', which is accurate given they were clinically assessed rather than screened as typical. Autism is described as 'a mental disorder that may significantly impact people's lives' and as causing 'deficits in social lives'. The paper's stated aim is to equip clinicians rather than replace them - 'clinicians would be equipped with leading technology and rich experience and universally serve autism children'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Reported only for the pooled cohort: 41 children aged 12-32 months, mean 23.34 months, 33 boys and 8 girls. No group-wise ages, standard deviations, sex splits or matching tests are given, and an age-by-diagnosis figure is shown but its values are not tabulated. This is a material gap: with a 12-32 month range, responsive social smiling to scripted verbal prompts changes substantially with age, so an age difference between groups would directly produce the observed effect. The authors note the 4:1 male:female ratio matches autism epidemiology, which speaks to representativeness but not to between-group balance. No IQ, developmental, socioeconomic or ethnicity data; single site in Guangzhou.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: 'Professional doctors diagnose all these 41 children' at the Third Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University, according to DSM-IV standards. No instrument (ADOS, ADI-R, CARS or otherwise), no cut-off, no diagnostician count and no assessment date are reported, and the use of DSM-IV rather than DSM-5 is not explained. Separately and more strongly, the per-stimulus ground truth is well established: three clinicians independently watched the protocol videos and labelled each trial, with majority voting used as the final score - so the intermediate outcome the system is optimised against has a genuine consensus reference standard even though the diagnostic label does not.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No IQ, developmental quotient, language, adaptive or symptom severity measure is reported, and no comorbidity information. The six behaviour scores function as a within-protocol profile but are not related to any external severity measure.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: automate scoring of the responsive social smile, one element of clinical screening that lacks clear behavioural benchmarks, and use the resulting scores for autism classification. Main findings: 85.20% agreement with three-clinician consensus stimulus scores; 80.49% autism classification accuracy with 85.00% sensitivity and 77.27% specificity from a decision tree; substituting clinicians' own stimulus scores raises this only to 82.93%, locating the performance ceiling in the protocol rather than the perception pipeline; 92.60% smile classification after fine-tuning on a purpose-built children's expression database; and most residual scoring errors are correctly detected smiles that clinicians judged spontaneous rather than socially responsive.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A standardised low-cost room setup deployed at the collaborating Third Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou, with a fixed seating layout for child, clinician and parent and a single camera positioned to record the child's frontal face. Funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the Key Research and Development Program of Jiangsu Province, the Six Talent Peaks project and a Guangzhou municipal livelihood science and technology plan.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A purpose-designed protocol modelled on ADOS and organised around distinct humour mechanisms: greeting smile with the child's name, praise words, hide and seek, hints of tickling, actual tickling, and a parent-delivered greeting smile. Each stimulus opens with a scripted keyword phrase, which is what makes automatic temporal segmentation possible - the ASR system detects the phrase and thereby locates the response window, so protocol design and pipeline design are co-dependent by construction. Stimuli are repeated up to three times if the child does not respond, and children who do not complete every step contribute missing scores that are mean-imputed.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single session per child with no follow-up. Data are frontal video and audio of identifiable toddlers with a parent and clinician present - among the most sensitive material in the corpus. Governance reporting is a single clause in the acknowledgements referring to participants' consent; no ethics committee approval, formal consent procedure, anonymisation or retention policy is stated, and no data availability statement is given.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: A single camera at 24 FPS and a microphone in a fixed layout, explicitly framed as low-cost. Software: Kaldi with an AISHELL-2-trained Mandarin ASR model; OpenCV-DNN face detector chosen for robustness on small toddler faces; a custom 2D-3D CNN built from ResNet-18 and pretrained 3D-ResNet-18 components; standard classifiers for the final decision. Standardising the physical setup is treated as a contribution in its own right.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Good on architecture, thin on protocol provenance. Reported: the full network architecture layer by layer for both branches with feature map dimensions, the 7-frame clip length and 224 x 224 input size, the 24 FPS and 20-second default window (about 480 frames per stimulus), the 0.9 smile decision threshold with its rationale, the ASR training corpus, the mean-imputation rule for missing stimuli, and the leave-one-out evaluation. Missing: decision tree hyperparameters, the smile-count threshold for stimulus scoring, group-wise demographics, ethics documentation, and any data or code release. A typographical error in the stimulus scoring description states that the score is marked 0 in both branches of the threshold test.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged: that a single protocol is insufficient - 'using the responsive social smile score alone cannot give a very comprehensive ASD classification' - and that fusing multiple protocols is needed; that autistic children are heterogeneous, making single-aspect screening hard; and, through the failure case study, that most residual errors are smiles that occurred but were not responses to the designed stimulus. Not acknowledged: that group-wise ages and sexes are never reported, so age and sex confounding cannot be excluded in a 12-32 month cohort; that the diagnostic reference standard is a bare DSM-IV clinical judgement with no instrument; that 80.49% is the best of four classifiers on 41 children where one child is worth 2.4 points - the same size as the gap the human-score ablation reveals; that stimulus scoring is evaluated at the trial level so the same child appears across folds; and that no ethics approval is reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Fuse scores and features from multiple complementary automated protocols - response to name and joint attention are named as the natural partners - to move from a single-aspect indicator to a composite screen, and address the distinction between spontaneous and socially responsive smiling that accounts for most remaining scoring error.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Responsive social smiling - whether a toddler produces a clear smile in response to a specific social overture, across five humour mechanisms plus a parent-delivered greeting. The behaviour is deliberately chosen because it is the hard case: unlike response to name or joint attention it 'is evaluated by emotion description that usually remains an ambiguous classification result', so it is the element of screening where automation has the most to offer and where a defensible ground truth is hardest to obtain. That the paper builds a three-clinician consensus for exactly this reason is a considered response to the problem.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Genuinely multimodal, but with the modalities serving different functions rather than being fused as parallel evidence: audio drives temporal segmentation (locating each stimulus onset from its scripted keyword) while video drives measurement (detecting the face and classifying the expression). This division is the framework's structural idea - speech tells the system when to look, vision tells it what it sees - and it is what allows an unsegmented clinical recording to be parsed automatically. Within the vision branch there is a second fusion, between a 3D-CNN capturing temporal dynamics and a 2D-CNN capturing spatial detail, concatenated to 1024 dimensions before classification. No accuracy comparison between the branches is reported, so the contribution of each is unquantified.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A cascade rather than a single model: pretrained ASR, pretrained face detection, a fine-tuned two-branch expression network, and a shallow classifier over six binary scores. The design is well matched to the data regime - deep components are trained on large external corpora (AISHELL-2, Oulu-CASIA, and the purpose-built 15,000-clip children's database) while the only model fitted to the 41-child cohort is a decision tree over six features. Four classifiers are compared, with the decision tree best by a wide margin (80.49% against 70.73% for SVM), which for a six-dimensional binary feature space is plausible.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A six-dimensional binary vector, one element per stimulus. This is a deliberately clinical representation - it mirrors exactly what a clinician records on a screening sheet, so the classifier's input is inspectable and the system's intermediate output is directly usable by a human even if the final classification is ignored. The cost is that all temporal, intensity and latency information about the smile is collapsed to a single bit per stimulus, and missing stimuli are mean-imputed within the child, which for a binary feature produces values the classifier was not otherwise trained on.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity with full confusion matrices at both stages, and - most valuably - a four-classifier comparison run twice, once on predicted stimulus scores and once on clinicians' scores. That paired table is the paper's best methodological contribution: it decomposes total error into the perception stage and the protocol stage, showing the perception stage contributes about 2.4 accuracy points. No AUC, no confidence intervals, no statistical test, and no per-stimulus analysis. The cross-study comparison table against eye-movement, hand-imitation, prosody and neuroimaging methods is drawn from different populations and age ranges and cannot support relative claims, though the paper presents it as context rather than as competition, noting its own cohort is the youngest at 1-3 years.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No attribution or saliency method, but the pipeline is interpretable by construction: every intermediate output is a clinically meaningful quantity - stimulus onset time, face crop, smile or non-smile, per-stimulus score - so a clinician can inspect where a decision came from without any explanation technique. The failure case study is the interpretive high point, examining all 29 misscored trials and finding that most involve genuine smiles that clinicians attributed to spontaneous emotion rather than to the social stimulus, with four examples shown. This identifies a specific conceptual limit: the system measures whether a smile occurred in a time window, not whether it was caused by the stimulus, and closing that gap requires modelling attention or gaze direction rather than better expression recognition.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Leave-one-out cross-validation at both stages, with the autism classification held out at the child level. The perception module's training data is cleanly disjoint from the evaluation cohort - the fine-tuning database comes from 54 children with explicitly no overlap with the 41 participants - which prevents the most serious form of leakage in video-based work. Two weaker points: the stimulus scoring evaluation is at the trial level across 196 samples from 41 children, so the same child appears in training and test folds for that stage; and the decision tree was chosen as best of four on the same leave-one-out estimate reported as the result. There is no independent cohort, no external site, and no held-out test set, which the sample size precludes.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No formal keyword list. Vocabulary: 'responsive social smile', 'multimodal behavior assessment framework', 'early stage autism screening', 'standardize', 'stimulus scoring', 'temporal stimulus localization'. The recurring word is standardisation - the paper's claim is as much about making a protocol repeatable and machine-readable as about classification accuracy.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Proceedings of the 25th International Conference on Pattern Recognition (ICPR), Milan, pages 2240-2245 - a computer vision and pattern recognition venue, with clinical co-authorship from the Third Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2020. The framing is about clinician workload and the limits of subjective scoring in a specific, unusually difficult case. The paper argues that the responsive social smile differs from other screening indicators because it lacks clear benchmarks and is 'evaluated by emotion description', that assessing 'children's emotions on small faces' while simultaneously running the experiment is error-prone, and that 'remembering every score for different social stimuli during the screening or perform the behavior scoring after the test is very subjective and labor-intensive'. Its comparison table is a useful snapshot of the 2020 field - eye movement at 88.51%, hand imitation at 86.70%, prosody at 76.00%, neuroimaging at 70.00% - and its accompanying observation is that 'cost and age requirements prevent some accurate ASD screening methods among children', with neuroimaging singled out as both expensive and impractical for young children who cannot stay still. Its own cohort at 12-32 months is the youngest in that table.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Selection of Eye-Tracking Stimuli for Prediction by Sparsely Grouped Input Variables for Neural Networks: towards Biomarker Refinement for Autism
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Li B; Barney E; Hudac C; Nuechterlein N; Ventola P; Shapiro L; Shic F
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: ETRA '20 Full Papers: ACM Symposium on Eye Tracking Research and Applications
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: School-age children with autism
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking and gaze
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Not to maximise autism classification but to solve a biomarker-design problem: given hundreds of candidate eye-tracking paradigms, each containing dozens of stimuli and each stimulus yielding many derived measures, find a parsimonious subset of stimuli that preserves discriminative power - because session length is the binding constraint on whether an eye-tracking biomarker is ever practical with young children. Selection must operate at the level of whole stimuli rather than individual variables, which makes it a grouped variable selection problem
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Methodological study on a clinical eye-tracking cohort, comparing three sparsity-inducing selection methods for classification and for four regression targets
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session per child covering 109 stimuli in counterbalanced orders; individual stimuli last 15 s (Biomotion, Dyadic Bids, Social Referencing, Theory of Mind), 20 s (Activity Monitoring) or 60 s (Dynamic Scenes)
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Passive viewing of six purpose-designed paradigms with no instruction beyond watching the screen - deliberately, because 'individuals with ASD are differentially impacted by the nature of verbal instruction' so passive viewing 'without explicit verbal direction have some of the greatest applicability across levels of function as well as age'. The paradigms are: Activity Monitoring (two actors in play-based activity, tapping social motivation and shared play); Biomotion (point-light human figure against rotating or phase-scrambled control dots, tapping primitive social preference); Dyadic Bids (three actors conversing, periodically turning to address the camera, testing sensitivity to social overtures); Dynamic Scenes (60-second edited clips from child-appropriate films with a coherent narrative); Social Referencing (an actor in escalating stressful activities such as inflating a balloon to bursting, testing automaticity of information-seeking from others); and Theory of Mind (a protagonist pursuing goals while an unseen antagonist interferes, gauging spontaneous interest in others' intentions)
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory eye-tracking sessions with embedded quality control and behavioural management, protocols aligned with a published multi-site standard
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: United States - Seattle Children's Research Institute and Yale University
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Clinician-assigned diagnostic labels, with ADOS severity score, SRS total score and Vineland-3 Adaptive Behavior Composite obtained by clinicians and trained psychometrists for 30 of the 32 autistic participants, and Stanford-Binet IQ obtained for all 64. The paper describes each instrument and its role: ADOS as a direct assessment 'held as a gold standard for clinical, genetic, and neurobiological research', SRS-2 as a caregiver questionnaire, Vineland-3 as a structured caregiver interview covering communication, daily living skills and socialisation
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 32 (30 with full ADOS, SRS and Vineland measurement)
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Reported for the whole cohort only: 76.32 +/- 16.3 months
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Not reported; the authors note results 'may reflect developmental properties of ASD specific to the school-age period'
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Not reported per group; whole cohort 43 male, 21 female
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not excluded - the non-autistic group deliberately includes children with language delay and other developmental concerns
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Continuous and multi-instrument: ADOS severity, SRS total, Vineland-3 ABC standard score and Stanford-Binet IQ, all used as regression targets
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Partly - the comparison group is not a typical-development control group but a mixed non-autistic group comprising typical development, language delay and other developmental concerns. This is a clinically realistic contrast that makes the classification substantially harder than autism versus typical development
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Diagnostic labels assigned clinically; IQ measured for all participants
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Stated as matched - 'There is no significant difference for age and sex between the ASD and non-ASD population' - though group-wise means, SDs and the test statistics are not given
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Stated as non-significantly different, with no group-wise figures reported
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not applicable - the comparison group is explicitly heterogeneous and includes developmental concerns
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Binocular gaze data during passive viewing of video stimuli
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Fixations identified by a Dynamic Programming on Distance Dispersion algorithm using partial fixations weighted by gaze points per region; expert frame-by-frame ROI annotation for each video stimulus with non-overlapping composite regions plus combined variables (head = eyes + mouth + hair + skin); oculomotor statistics computed per ROI and within event-specific time windows. Features include mean fixation time, number of fixations, saccade duration, time of first saccade, valid eye-tracking duration, percentage of gaze on screen, percentage of missing data and gaze data quality, with visual response latency added for Dyadic Bids and Theory of Mind, and latency to orient to biological motion for Biomotion. Missing values were imputed by unsupervised Expectation-Maximization
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: SR EyeLink 1000 Plus sampling binocularly at 500 Hz; Samsung SyncMaster 2233RZ 22-inch monitor at 60 Hz and 1680 x 1050; participants at 650 mm; Neurobehavioral Systems Presentation with multiple embedded 5-point calibrations and the ability to insert video breaks to manage non-compliance; processing pipeline in C++, MATLAB, R and SPSS; PyTorch for the neural networks, sklearn for lasso, pyglmnet for group lasso
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: A 64-child, 109-stimulus, 9,647-feature eye-tracking dataset, described as available upon request
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Partially - the machine learning code is open sourced at github.com/beibinli/SGIN; the eye-tracking data and processing pipeline are 'available upon request'
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze data over video stimuli with linked clinical scores. Governance is properly reported: Institutional Review Board approval from both Yale University and Seattle Children's Research Institute covering the eye-tracking experiments, data acquisition and data analysis protocols
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Handcrafted oculomotor and ROI-based gaze statistics, organised into groups by stimulus
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 9,647 features arranged into 109 groups, one per stimulus, with group sizes varying by paradigm - Activity Monitoring 50 features per stimulus, Biomotion 58 (SD 2.41), Dyadic Bids 177 (SD 3.89), Dynamic Scenes 41, Social Referencing 48, Theory of Mind 106 (SD 8.64). Most groups have fewer than 50 features and 34 groups have more than 100. The problem is explicitly p >> k > n, with 9,647 features and 109 groups against 64 participants
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Dynamic Programming on Distance Dispersion fixation identification; expert ROI annotation; custom oculomotor statistics with quality control on calibration accuracy, calibration stability and data collection rate (95% trimmed mean calibration error 0.751 visual degrees)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, at two levels: paradigm-level discard probabilities across 100 bootstrap runs for all three methods, and feature-level SHAP importance for the trained neural network
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Group sparsity patterns aggregated over 100 bootstrap runs; SHAP (Shapley Additive exPlanations) values averaged in absolute value across participants
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Paradigm level: Dyadic Bids is least often discarded and therefore most useful (24.96% discard probability under SGIN), followed by Theory of Mind (49.62%), Activity Monitoring (65.25%), Biomotion (66.72%), Dynamic Scenes (71.00%) and - surprisingly to the authors - Social Referencing most often discarded (72.00%). Feature level, the top 10 by SHAP span gaze duration toward activities (Activity Monitoring stimulus 9), gaze duration on biological movements and response latency to non-biological motion (Biomotion), the proportion of events meeting quality requirements (Dyadic Bids stimulus 58), start times of the 4th, 9th and 10th fixations or explored regions (Dyadic Bids), gaze duration toward eyes and number of fixations toward the eyes of the actor with direct gaze (Dyadic Bids), and latency to first orient to the body (Theory of Mind)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported directionally. The SHAP analysis identifies which features matter but not which way they move, though the authors interpret one class substantively: data-quality features rank highly because 'children with ASD can provide poorer quality data due to non-compliance and attention issues during presentation of socially-oriented scene content' - an unusually honest observation that a quality-control variable is functioning as a behavioural signal
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Sparsity-regularised linear and neural models for grouped variable selection
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Lasso (l1 on individual features, with a group counted sparse only if all its features are zeroed); group lasso (l2 norm per group, weighted by the square root of group size); and SGIN - Sparsely Grouped Input Variables for Neural Networks - which imposes group l1 regularisation on the parameters between each input group and all first-hidden-layer neurons, using the Frobenius norm of the corresponding parameter block, optimised by a Stochastic Blockwise Coordinated Gradient Descent algorithm. Network: 2 hidden layers of 3,000 and 500 neurons, ReLU, no bias in the first hidden layer, initial learning rate 0.1 halved each epoch over 5 epochs, batch size 64 for classification and 1 for regression. Compared against SVM (linear and RBF), decision tree, random forest, linear and logistic regression over 100 runs each
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 10-fold cross-validation with the same training/validation splits across all models for fair comparison, and feature normalisation fitted on the training set before each fold. Selection stability was assessed by 100 bootstrap runs per method with discard frequencies tabulated per paradigm. The authors state the limitation directly: 'We acknowledge that the validation performance might be over-optimistic and does not represent real-world performance for ASD/non-ASD classification'
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and AUC for classification, all plotted as functions of the number of sparsified groups rather than as single points - so the entire accuracy-versus-parsimony trade-off curve is the result. Pearson correlation for the four regression targets, again plotted against sparsity
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: With 99 of 109 stimuli removed (89.9% sparsity), SGIN retained 78.13% accuracy and 82.91% AUC; with only 11 stimuli retained it still achieved good accuracy and AUC. Lasso with 71 stimuli removed reached only 65.6% accuracy and 70.8% AUC, about 15% worse. Group lasso performed comparably to SGIN on average (79.71% accuracy, 79.72% AUC) but 'either removes no groups or many, and rarely anything in-between', struggling to go below 60 groups even after tuning. Non-sparse baselines - linear regression, logistic regression, linear SVM - reached around 84% accuracy but with no sparsification at all. Regression: SGIN predicted IQ at r = 0.54 (p < 0.0001), but neither SGIN nor lasso fitted above chance for ADOS severity, SRS or Vineland scores
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Eleven of 109 eye-tracking stimuli were sufficient to retain 78% accuracy and 0.83 AUC in separating autistic from non-autistic children, demonstrating substantial redundancy in a standard research battery and showing that a much shorter session could carry most of the discriminative signal. SGIN was the only method that achieved sparsification and high accuracy simultaneously: lasso sparsified but lost 15 accuracy points, group lasso matched accuracy but behaved almost bimodally in what it removed, and the best-performing conventional models sparsified nothing. Dyadic Bids - direct conversational overtures to the camera - was the paradigm most consistently retained, while Social Referencing was most often discarded. The central negative result is that the same features and methods failed entirely at predicting autism severity: neither SGIN nor lasso beat chance on ADOS, SRS or Vineland, while IQ was predicted at r = 0.54.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Duration and latency of gaze toward socially informative regions during direct conversational bids, latency to orient to biological motion, exploration timing statistics, and - notably - eye-tracking data quality itself, which the authors interpret as reflecting non-compliance and attention difficulties during socially oriented content
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Extend sparsity to bi-level, hierarchical, tree-structured and overlapping group structures so paradigms can be organised into subgroups; replace expert-defined event windows with data-driven isolation of informative time periods; expand samples to characterise autism's heterogeneity, since limited power in a small autistic sample constrains severity prediction; design stimuli specifically for severity prediction rather than group separation, and develop new modelling techniques for those outcomes; and test the robustness of the selected stimuli on larger unseen data
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: This is the corpus's most sophisticated treatment of the problem that actually blocks eye-tracking biomarkers in practice: not accuracy, but session length. Framing stimulus selection as grouped variable selection is exactly right - selection has to happen at the level of whole stimuli because that is the unit of acquisition cost - and the paper demonstrates that a 109-stimulus battery contains enough redundancy that 11 stimuli preserve most of the signal. Several features of the design are notably strong. The comparison group is not typically developing children but a mixed non-autistic group including language delay and other developmental concerns, making the discrimination clinically realistic and much harder than most of this corpus attempts. Results are reported as accuracy-versus-sparsity curves rather than as point estimates, so the whole trade-off is visible. Selection stability is assessed over 100 bootstrap runs, which exposes group lasso's near-bimodal behaviour that a single fit would have hidden. IRB approval from two institutions is documented, code is open sourced, and data is offered on request. Most importantly the authors state their own validation limitation without prompting: performance 'might be over-optimistic and does not represent real-world performance'. The paper's most valuable contribution to this review is a negative one, and it should carry substantial weight in the synthesis: the same features that separate diagnostic groups at 78-84% accuracy fail completely to predict ADOS severity, SRS or Vineland scores, while predicting IQ at r = 0.54. That dissociation implies group separation in eye tracking may be driven substantially by general cognitive and compliance factors rather than by autism-specific severity, a reading reinforced by data-quality variables appearing among the top ten SHAP features. Remaining weaknesses are conventional: group-wise demographics are asserted as matched but never tabulated; the sparsity level, hyperparameters and best-performing method are all chosen against the same 10-fold estimate; and 64 children with 9,647 features is a severe p >> n regime that the methods manage rather than resolve.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: One cohort of 64 children split 32 autistic and 32 non-autistic, with the non-autistic group deliberately heterogeneous - 'typical development, language delay, and other developmental concerns'. This is one of only a few studies in the corpus whose comparison group is a clinically referred mixed-diagnosis sample rather than typically developing children, which raises the difficulty of the task and makes the result far more relevant to real screening. Clinical instrumentation is deep for a subset: ADOS severity, SRS total and Vineland-3 ABC for 30 of the 32 autistic children, and Stanford-Binet IQ for all 64.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with autism', 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'non-ASD', 'children without ASD', 'typical development'. Consistently person-first, and the non-autistic group is named by what it is not rather than being called healthy or normal - accurate given its composition. The framing is biomarker-development rather than deficit-focused, referencing the FDA-NIH Biomarker Working Group and treating eye tracking as 'a powerful marker of cognition and human variability'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Reported for the whole cohort only: 64 children, mean age 76.32 +/- 16.3 months (about 6.4 years), 43 male and 21 female. Group-wise ages and sexes are not tabulated; the paper states there is 'no significant difference for age and sex between the ASD and non-ASD population' without giving means or test statistics. Stanford-Binet IQ was obtained for all participants, which is unusual and important, though group-wise IQ is likewise not reported - a notable gap given that IQ turned out to be the one clinical variable the eye-tracking features could predict. No ethnicity or socioeconomic reporting. The authors flag that findings 'may reflect developmental properties of ASD specific to the school-age period'.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Clinician-assigned diagnostic labels supported by an unusually complete instrument battery: ADOS severity scores administered as direct assessment by trained administrators, SRS-2 caregiver questionnaire, Vineland-3 structured caregiver interview, and Stanford-Binet IQ administered directly to every child. Each instrument is described with its purpose and administration mode. The one gap is that the diagnostic decision procedure itself - which instruments determined the ASD label, against which criteria - is not stated, and ADOS, SRS and Vineland were obtained for only 30 of the 32 autistic participants.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: The most complete clinical characterisation in the corpus for a subset of participants: ADOS severity (autism symptom severity), SRS total (reciprocal social behaviour), Vineland-3 ABC across communication, daily living skills and socialisation (adaptive functioning), and Stanford-Binet IQ for the full cohort. Critically, these are not merely tabulated but used as regression targets, which is what allows the paper's central negative finding - that eye-tracking features predict IQ but not autism severity or adaptive functioning.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: select a parsimonious subset of eye-tracking stimuli that preserves discriminative and predictive power, treating selection as a grouped variable problem. Main findings: 11 of 109 stimuli retained 78.13% accuracy and 82.91% AUC; SGIN was the only method achieving sparsity and accuracy together, with lasso 15 points worse at comparable sparsity and group lasso behaving near-bimodally; Dyadic Bids was the most-retained paradigm and Social Referencing the most-discarded; and the features predicted IQ (r = 0.54) but failed above chance for ADOS severity, SRS and Vineland.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory eye-tracking at Seattle Children's Research Institute and Yale University, with acquisition protocols aligned to a published multi-site standard and a delivery system providing embedded 5-point calibrations and the ability to insert video breaks for behavioural management. Funded by NIH awards K01 MH104739, R21 MH103550 and R03 MH092618, an NSF Expedition in Socially Assistive Robotics, and a Simons Foundation award.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Six passive-viewing paradigms totalling 109 stimuli, each designed by clinical psychologists 'to characterize features known to be atypical or impaired in individuals with ASD' and each targeting a distinct construct: social motivation and shared play (Activity Monitoring), primitive social preference (Biomotion), sensitivity to social overtures (Dyadic Bids), naturalistic scene viewing (Dynamic Scenes), automaticity of information-seeking from others (Social Referencing), and interest in and comprehension of others' intentions (Theory of Mind). Passive viewing with no instruction is a deliberate design decision justified by the observation that autistic individuals are differentially affected by verbal instruction, so implicit-attention paradigms generalise better across ability and age. Stimuli were presented in counterbalanced orders.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single session per child with no follow-up, though the motivating application - monitoring treatment response and predicting later outcomes - is inherently longitudinal and the paper acknowledges much work remains before eye tracking can serve it. Data are gaze recordings with linked clinical scores. Governance is fully reported: IRB approval from both Yale University and Seattle Children's Research Institute covering experiments, acquisition and analysis.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: SR EyeLink 1000 Plus at 500 Hz binocular; Samsung SyncMaster 2233RZ 22-inch at 60 Hz, 1680 x 1050; 650 mm viewing distance; Neurobehavioral Systems Presentation with embedded calibration and behavioural management; Dynamic Programming on Distance Dispersion fixation identification; expert frame-level ROI annotation; PyTorch, sklearn and pyglmnet in Python 3.6. Quality control is quantified - 95% trimmed mean calibration error of 0.751 visual degrees - which almost no other eye-tracking study in this corpus reports.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Among the best in the corpus. Reported: all six paradigms with their construct rationale, stimulus counts, durations and per-stimulus feature counts with standard deviations; the eye tracker, monitor, refresh rate, resolution, viewing distance, calibration scheme and measured calibration error; the fixation identification algorithm; the ROI annotation scheme including the non-overlap rule and composite variables; the imputation method; the network architecture, layer sizes, activation, bias handling, learning rate schedule, epochs and batch sizes; the optimisation algorithm; and the identity of every comparator method. Code is open sourced on GitHub and the data and processing pipeline are offered on request. Missing: group-wise demographics, the diagnostic decision procedure, and the specific 11 stimuli that constituted the best sparse subset.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged with unusual directness: 'We acknowledge that the validation performance might be over-optimistic and does not represent real-world performance for ASD/non-ASD classification'; only 64 participants with just 30 having full ADOS, Vineland and SRS measurement; limited power to characterise autism heterogeneity; results possibly specific to the school-age period; selected paradigms not guaranteed stable across runs because the p > n problem may have no unique optimum; and that much remains before eye tracking can be used practically for treatment optimisation or long-term outcome prediction. Identifiable in review but not stated: group-wise ages, sexes and IQs are asserted as balanced but never tabulated, which matters greatly given that IQ is the one variable the features do predict; the sparsity operating point, the hyperparameters and the identification of SGIN as best were all determined against the same 10-fold estimate; and the non-autistic group's heterogeneity, while a design strength, means the classifier's target is 'autism versus other developmental presentations', which is not the same construct as 'autism versus typical development' and complicates comparison with the rest of this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Extend group sparsity to bi-level, hierarchical, tree-structured and overlapping group definitions so that paradigms can be organised into nested subgroups; replace expert-annotated event windows with data-driven identification of the informative time periods within stimuli; expand the sample to characterise heterogeneity, since limited power constrains severity prediction; design stimuli specifically for predicting ADOS, SRS and Vineland rather than reusing paradigms built for group separation, and develop modelling techniques suited to those outcomes; and test the robustness of selected stimuli on larger unseen data.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Passive visual attention across six distinct social-cognitive constructs, decomposed into oculomotor mechanics (fixation counts and durations, saccade durations, first-saccade timing, exploration order), region-of-interest allocation (bodies, heads, eyes, mouths, activities, distractors), event-locked response latency, and data-quality measures (percentage of gaze on screen, missing data, proportion of events meeting quality requirements). Including quality metrics as candidate features rather than as exclusion criteria is a distinctive choice, and it pays off - one such feature appears third in the SHAP ranking, which the authors interpret as non-compliance during socially oriented content being itself informative.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-modal fusion; the study is gaze-only. What it does instead is the inverse of fusion and arguably more useful: it asks how much of a large multi-paradigm battery can be discarded. The result is that 89.9% of stimuli can be removed with modest accuracy loss, and the paradigm-level analysis shows the retained signal concentrates in Dyadic Bids and Theory of Mind, both of which include visual response latency features, while Biomotion also has latency features but lacks discrete ROI measures on heads, faces, eyes and bodies. The authors hypothesise that Dyadic Bids and Theory of Mind features subsume information available in the other paradigms - a redundancy argument that is the mirror image of the fusion arguments elsewhere in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Three sparsity-inducing methods compared on identical splits - lasso, group lasso and the paper's SGIN - against a panel of non-sparse baselines (linear and RBF SVM, decision tree, random forest, linear and logistic regression) run 100 times each. SGIN extends group l1 regularisation to a multi-layer non-linear network by penalising the Frobenius norm of the parameter block connecting each input group to all first-hidden-layer neurons, and introduces a Stochastic Blockwise Coordinated Gradient Descent optimiser that converges faster and finds more sparse groups than plain SGD. The comparison is informative precisely because the winner is not the most accurate model: non-sparse linear baselines reach about 84% accuracy against SGIN's 78-80%, but they remove nothing, so they cannot shorten the battery at all.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: 9,647 features organised into 109 groups, one per stimulus - the grouping is the methodological point, since acquisition cost is incurred per stimulus and not per derived variable, so selection must respect that structure. Group sizes are unequal by paradigm (41 to 177 features per stimulus) and group lasso's square-root-of-group-size weighting accounts for this. The regime is p >> k > n, with 9,647 features and 109 groups against 64 participants, which the paper states explicitly as the reason standard variable selection is inapplicable. Missing values imputed by unsupervised Expectation-Maximization.
