custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and AUC, all plotted as functions of the number of sparsified groups rather than reported as single points - so the deliverable is a trade-off curve between battery length and discriminative power, which is exactly the quantity a biomarker designer needs. Pearson correlation for the four regression targets, likewise plotted against sparsity, with random guessing anchored at r = 0. Selection stability is quantified as discard probability per paradigm over 100 bootstrap runs. No confidence intervals on the accuracy curves and no statistical test between methods.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Two complementary interpretability layers. At the paradigm level, bootstrap discard probabilities rank the six paradigms and reveal a surprise the authors flag themselves - Social Referencing, designed to probe automaticity of information-seeking from others, is the most discarded. At the feature level, SHAP values over the trained network yield a top-10 list spanning gaze duration to activities and to eyes, latency to biological and non-biological motion, exploration timing (start times of the 4th, 9th and 10th fixations or regions), and data quality. The interpretation offered for the quality feature is candid and important: autistic children 'can provide poorer quality data due to non-compliance and attention issues during presentation of socially-oriented scene content', so a variable normally treated as measurement noise is functioning as behavioural signal.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: 10-fold cross-validation with identical splits across all methods and training-set-fitted normalisation per fold, plus 100 bootstrap runs to assess selection stability. Two limitations, one acknowledged and one not. Acknowledged: the authors state directly that validation performance may be over-optimistic and does not represent real-world performance. Not stated: the operating point on the sparsity curve, the hyperparameters and the conclusion that SGIN is best were all determined against that same 10-fold estimate, and no held-out cohort, external site or independent battery was used. The paper's own framing is careful about this - it describes the work as setting 'the stage for concerted techniques designed around engines to iteratively refine and define next-generation biomarkers' rather than as delivering a validated biomarker.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: eye-tracking, feature selection, group selection, stimuli selection, paradigm selection, neural network, autism. Four of seven concern selection and only one names autism - the paper is a methods contribution to biomarker refinement, with autism as the application domain.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: ETRA '20, the ACM Symposium on Eye Tracking Research and Applications (Stuttgart), full papers track - the field's dedicated eye-tracking venue, published open access with support from the University of Washington, Yale and Seattle Children's.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2020. The framing is explicitly regulatory and infrastructural rather than clinical-need-driven: it situates itself among 'large-scale ongoing efforts in progress to develop next generation biomarker applications', cites the FDA-NIH Biomarker Working Group, and identifies validation studies aimed at markers of treatment response, predictors of later outcomes and subgrouping for intervention response. Its diagnosis of the field's practical bottleneck is precise and rarely stated elsewhere in this corpus: 'the longer the session associated with a biomarker, the more burdensome that biomarker becomes, and the less likely it will be to see practical implementation', with long batteries 'often stressful for young children and infants' and shorter sessions reducing burden, improving data quality and requiring less staff time. It also criticises current selection practice - 'straightforward winnowing of experimental batteries based on independent trial discriminability' - for ignoring interrelationships between trials that machine learning can capture, while warning that overfitting risk in the large-p small-n regime demands specialised techniques.

data_charting_rubrics.title: The identification of children with autism spectrum disorder by SVM approach on EEG and eye-tracking data
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Kang J; Han X; Song J; Niu Z; Li X
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: Computers in Biology and Medicine, 120, Article 103722
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Preschool children with autism
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking and gaze (with EEG as a second modality)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Test whether combining two objective measurement modalities - resting-state EEG spectral power and gaze allocation during face viewing - yields better autism identification than either alone, on the argument that EEG on its own is insufficient because autism's heterogeneity means spectral abnormalities are inconsistent across the spectrum, particularly in high-functioning presentations
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification with a modality-by-modality accuracy comparison
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session per child: approximately 6 minutes of eyes-open resting EEG, a break, then eye tracking comprising 12 face presentations (6 own-race and 6 other-race) of 10 seconds each
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Free viewing with no response required. A series of photographs of a young girl's face - own-race or other-race - presented in random order, each type appearing 6 times for 10 seconds, with a dynamic kitten and sound shown between trials to re-engage attention. The resting EEG preceded this with the child seated quietly, eyes open, minimising head movement, teeth gritting and blinking
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: A shielded room for EEG recording and a separate eye-tracking setup; autistic children recruited clinically and typically developing children from a local kindergarten
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: China - Beijing Normal University with Hebei University and Yanshan University
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Diagnosed by experienced Chinese psychiatrists using the Psychoeducational Profile Third Edition (PEP-3) together with DSM-5 criteria. No ADOS or ADI-R, no severity scores and no diagnostician count are reported
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported. PEP-3 yields developmental and behavioural scores but none are given, and no severity-stratified analysis is performed - a notable omission given the paper's own argument that heterogeneity between high- and low-functioning autism explains inconsistent EEG findings
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Recruited from a local kindergarten with no genetic history of autistic family members. No screening instrument was applied, so control status rests on absence of family history and mainstream attendance
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes - means of 4.29 and 4.26 years with near-identical spreads, and the authors state there were no statistical differences in age between groups. This is one of the better-matched pairs in the corpus
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Yes - 39:10 versus 36:12, stated as non-significantly different
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted from kindergarten attendance and absence of family history of autism; no developmental screening reported
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Resting-state scalp EEG and gaze fixation data during face viewing
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: EEG: re-referenced to averaged left and right mastoid signals, band-pass filtered 0.5-45 Hz, downsampled to 250 Hz, 50 Hz notch filter for line noise, ICA-based removal of ocular and muscular artefacts, visual inspection to reject contaminated segments, segmentation into non-overlapping 4-second epochs, then Welch power spectral density with eight 50%-overlapping Hamming-windowed segments per epoch and FFT. Relative power computed per band as that band's share of total spectrum power. Eye tracking: eight areas of interest defined on each face photograph (background, body, face, eyes, right eye, left eye, mouth, nose), with an engagement index computed as fixation time in the AOI divided by total fixation time and a 60 ms threshold applied to exclude unconscious gaze
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: 128-channel HydroCel Sensor Net (Electrical Geodesics) at 1000 Hz with 62 electrodes retained and re-referenced to linked ears; Tobii TX300 eye tracker at 300 Hz with five-point calibration required to pass with small error vectors, at approximately 60 cm viewing distance; MATLAB R2016a with EEGLAB
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: A 97-child dual-modality dataset, described as available from the corresponding author upon request
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - available on request
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: EEG traces and gaze coordinates over face photographs; low identifiability in themselves. Governance is properly reported: conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki, approved by the ethics committee of Beijing Normal University, with parental informed consent obtained before participation
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Spectral power features and AOI fixation-proportion features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: EEG: relative power in delta (1-4 Hz), theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz), beta (13-30 Hz) and gamma (30-45 Hz) bands, computed per electrode across 62 channels. Eye tracking: percentage of total fixation time in each of eight AOIs, separately for own-race and other-race faces, giving 16 gaze features. The combined pool was reduced by mRMR, with 32 features selected at the reported optimum
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: MATLAB pwelch for spectral density; custom AOI analysis in MATLAB; minimum-redundancy-maximum-relevance feature selection based on mutual information
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Not per feature. mRMR ranks features by maximal statistical dependency with minimum redundancy, but the identity of the 32 selected features is never reported - so which modality or which AOIs and bands drove the fused result cannot be determined
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: mRMR mutual-information ranking; independent t-tests on each band and each AOI as a separate descriptive analysis
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None named. The statistical analysis identifies theta (higher in autism), beta and gamma (both higher in autism) as significantly different EEG bands, and background, face, mouth and nose as significantly different AOIs for own-race faces, with background, nose and mouth for other-race faces
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reported clearly and in both modalities. EEG: autistic children showed significantly higher theta relative power (1.96 vs 2.27, t = 3.22, p = .002 - note the tabulated means run opposite to the stated direction), and higher beta (0.28 vs 0.22, t = 3.875, p < .001) and gamma (0.12 vs 0.08, t = 4.352, p < .001), with delta and alpha not different. Gaze: autistic children looked more at the background (19.40% vs 3.27% for own-race faces; 9.62% vs 1.53% for other-race) and less at the face (51.13% vs 63.56%), nose (16.94% vs 24.88%) and mouth (4.33% vs 8.35%). Eye-region differences were in the expected direction but did not reach significance
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised classification on tabular features with mutual-information feature selection
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Linear support vector machine, with mRMR for dimensionality reduction
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: None described. The paper contains no statement of any train/test split, cross-validation scheme, held-out set or repetition procedure anywhere in the methods or results. Feature selection by mRMR uses class labels and there is no indication it was nested within any resampling. The reported accuracy is explicitly the maximum over a sweep of one to forty-five selected features, plotted as a curve, so both the feature count and the operating point were chosen against the same data the accuracy is reported on
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy and AUC, reported per modality and per stimulus type. No sensitivity, specificity, confusion matrix, confidence interval or statistical comparison between conditions
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: EEG alone (five relative power bands) 68%. Eye tracking alone: 72.33% with AUC 0.827 for own-race faces, 66.67% with AUC 0.746 for other-race faces, and 75.89% with AUC 0.865 combining both face types. EEG plus eye tracking: maximum 85.44% with AUC 0.93 at 32 selected features. The modality ladder is therefore 68% to 75.89% to 85.44%, a gain of roughly 10 points from fusion over the better single modality
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Combining resting-state EEG spectral power with gaze allocation during face viewing raised autism classification accuracy to 85.44% (AUC 0.93), against 68% for EEG alone and 75.89% for gaze alone - a substantial and cleanly reported fusion benefit. The behavioural findings are consistent with the reduced social-attention literature: autistic children spent far more fixation time on the image background (19.4% versus 3.3% for own-race faces) and less on the face, nose and mouth, although eye-region differences did not reach significance. Own-race faces classified better than other-race faces, which the authors relate to the other-race effect. EEG showed elevated theta, beta and gamma relative power with no differences in delta or alpha. The authors' motivating argument - that EEG alone is inadequate because prior studies find no differences particularly in high-functioning autism - is supported by their own EEG-only result of 68%.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Increased fixation on non-face background regions and reduced fixation on face, nose and mouth; elevated theta, beta and gamma relative EEG power
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Recruit younger children, aged two years or under, since 'diagnosis of autism at earlier ages is a pressing clinical need' and the present cohort begins at three; and extract more features from both modalities, on the expectation that multi-modal multi-feature fusion will improve accuracy further
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The design has real strengths and one disabling omission. Strengths first: the groups are among the best matched in the corpus on both age (4.29 versus 4.26 years) and sex, with matching stated as tested; ethics reporting is complete with named committee approval, Helsinki conformity and parental consent; data are offered on request; and the modality comparison is reported cleanly enough that the fusion benefit can be read directly - 68% for EEG alone, 75.89% for gaze alone, 85.44% combined. The other-race manipulation is also a thoughtful addition that few studies attempt, and it produces an interpretable result consistent with the established other-race effect. The disabling omission is that no validation scheme is described at any point. There is no train/test split, no cross-validation, no held-out sample and no repetition procedure stated in the methods or results, and mRMR - which uses the class labels - is applied with no indication of nesting. On top of that, the headline 85.44% is explicitly the maximum of a curve swept across one to forty-five selected features, so the feature count was chosen on the same data the accuracy is reported for. With 97 children and 310-plus EEG features from 62 electrodes across five bands, this is precisely the regime in which unnested selection produces large upward bias, and the reported figures cannot be interpreted as out-of-sample performance. Two lesser issues: the identity of the 32 selected features is never given, so it is impossible to tell whether the fusion gain comes from genuine complementarity or from the EEG features simply dominating a larger pool; and the tabulated theta means (1.96 for autism versus 2.27 for controls) run opposite to the text's claim of higher theta in autism, one of several small internal inconsistencies in the results tables. Finally, EEG is a neurophysiological rather than behavioural measure, so for this review only the eye-tracking arm bears directly on the research questions - which makes the gaze-only figure of 75.89% the number that matters here, not the 85.44% headline.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups, 97 children: 49 with confirmed autism diagnoses and 48 typically developing children recruited from a local kindergarten. No other-diagnosis comparison group. At 97 participants this is one of the larger single-site cohorts in the corpus, and the authors note they 'recruited a relatively large sample size for the sake of classification'.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'autistic children', 'ASD children', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'normal children', 'patients with autism', 'healthy children'. Mixed and inconsistent - person-first in places, 'autistic children' elsewhere, and 'normal' and 'healthy' both used for the comparison group. Autism is framed as 'a very complex neurodevelopmental disorder' and once as 'this complex disease', with aetiology attributed to 'biological factors such as genetic defects, brain inflammation, and abnormal conditions during pregnancy'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Autistic group: n = 49, 39 male and 10 female, mean age 4.29 +/- 1.07 years. Typically developing: n = 48, 36 male and 12 female, mean age 4.26 +/- 1.00 years. The authors state there were no statistical differences in age or gender between groups, and the reported means and SDs bear that out - this is among the best-matched pairs in the corpus, on the two variables most likely to confound gaze during face viewing at this age. Both groups span 3-6 years. No IQ, developmental level, socioeconomic or ethnicity data; recruitment routes differ between groups (clinical for autism, a local kindergarten for controls), which is not addressed.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Diagnosis by 'experienced Chinese psychiatrists based on the psychoeducational profile (Third Edition)' and DSM-5 criteria. PEP-3 is a developmental and autism-characteristic assessment rather than a diagnostic instrument in the ADOS or ADI-R sense, so the ascertainment is weaker than the corpus norm for well-documented studies, though DSM-5 clinical judgement by experienced psychiatrists is a reasonable standard. Control status rests on kindergarten recruitment and the absence of 'genetic history of autistic family members', with no screening instrument applied.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None reported. PEP-3 yields developmental scores that could have supported severity or functioning analyses, but no scores appear and no stratification is performed. This is a substantive gap given the paper's own explanation for inconsistent EEG findings in the literature - that 'autism can be divided into low function and high function according to behavioral ability' and that heterogeneity is why 'using only EEG evaluation may be insufficient'. Having advanced that argument, the study is unable to test it in its own data.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: test whether fusing resting-state EEG spectral power with face-viewing gaze features improves autism identification over either modality alone. Main findings: EEG alone 68%, gaze alone 75.89% (AUC 0.865) combining own- and other-race faces, and fused 85.44% with AUC 0.93 at 32 selected features; autistic children fixated the background far more (19.4% versus 3.3%) and the face, nose and mouth less; own-race faces classified better than other-race faces; and EEG showed differences in theta, beta and gamma but not delta or alpha.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A shielded room for EEG recording and a separate eye-tracking station, with autistic children recruited clinically and typically developing children from a local kindergarten. Funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and the National Key Research and Development Program of China.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Two distinct paradigms in one session. Resting-state EEG for about 6 minutes with eyes open, with the child kept as still and quiet as possible. Then passive viewing of face photographs - a young girl of the child's own race or of another race, each type presented 6 times for 10 seconds in random order, with a dynamic kitten and sound between trials to re-engage attention and no response required. The own-race/other-race manipulation is uncommon in this literature and yields a directly interpretable comparison; the attention-recapturing interstimulus is a practical design detail for this age group that few papers describe.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single session per child with no follow-up. Data are EEG traces and gaze coordinates over face photographs, low in identifiability. Governance reporting is complete: conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki, approved by the ethics committee of Beijing Normal University, with parental informed consent obtained before participation, and a data availability statement offering the data on request.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: 128-channel HydroCel Sensor Net (Electrical Geodesics) at 1000 Hz, with 62 electrodes selected and re-referenced to linked ears; Tobii TX300 at 300 Hz with a five-point calibration required to pass with small error vectors before the experiment proceeded, at roughly 60 cm; MATLAB R2016a with EEGLAB for preprocessing and pwelch for spectral estimation.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Good on signal processing, absent on evaluation. Fully reported: electrode count and selection, sampling rates, referencing scheme, filter bands, downsampling, notch filtering, ICA artefact removal, visual rejection, epoch length, Welch parameters (eight segments, 50% overlap, Hamming window), the five frequency bands with their boundaries, the eight AOIs, the fixation-proportion index definition, the 60 ms fixation threshold, viewing distance, calibration procedure, stimulus counts and durations, and the interstimulus attention device. Entirely absent: any statement of how the classifier was trained and evaluated - no split, no folds, no repetition - together with SVM hyperparameters, the identity of the 32 selected features, and any code release.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged: that the cohort begins at age 3 and that 'diagnosis of autism at earlier ages is a pressing clinical need', with a stated plan to recruit children aged 2 or younger; and that more features should be extracted from both modalities. The paper also usefully concedes a limitation of its own EEG modality, noting that 'no differences in EEG were found in some previous studies, especially for high functioning autism' and concluding that 'using only EEG evaluation may be insufficient to identify children with this complex disease'. Not acknowledged, and decisive: no validation scheme of any kind is described, so the reported accuracies have no established out-of-sample interpretation; mRMR uses class labels with no indication of nesting within any resampling; the headline 85.44% is the maximum of a curve swept over one to forty-five features, so the operating point was selected on the reported data; the identity of the selected features is never given; recruitment routes differ systematically between groups; and no severity or functioning measure is reported despite heterogeneity being central to the paper's own argument.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Recruit younger children, aged two years or under, to address the clinical need for earlier diagnosis; and extract additional features from both EEG and eye tracking, since 'multi-modal, multi-feature fusion will likely improve classification accuracy further'.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Two behavioural-adjacent targets of different kinds. The behavioural measure proper is visual attention allocation during face viewing, decomposed across eight regions from whole-face down to individual eyes, and manipulated by face race. The EEG measure is neurophysiological rather than behavioural - resting-state cortical rhythm power - and the paper interprets it in behavioural terms, linking theta to working memory encoding and retrieval, beta to alertness and motor behaviour, and gamma to sensory processing, working memory, attention and arousal.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: The clearest and most cleanly reported fusion result in the corpus, precisely because both single-modality baselines are given: EEG alone 68%, gaze alone 75.89%, fused 85.44% with AUC rising from 0.865 to 0.93. That is close to a 10-point gain over the better single modality, and the authors' rationale for expecting it is specific rather than generic - EEG abnormalities are inconsistent across the autism spectrum, particularly in high-functioning presentations, whereas 'atypical face processing' has been found 'for all types of ASD', so the modalities should fail on different subgroups. There is a second, within-modality fusion as well: own-race faces alone gave 72.33% and other-race faces 66.67%, but combining both face types gave 75.89%, better than either. The caveat is that with no validation scheme and feature selection over a much larger EEG feature pool, the size of the fusion gain cannot be taken at face value, and the identity of the 32 selected features is not disclosed so complementarity cannot be verified.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A single linear SVM throughout, preceded by mRMR feature selection based on mutual information, chosen for jointly maximising relevance to the class label and minimising redundancy among features. No model comparison is performed - the experimental variable is the modality and the number of selected features, not the learner. This is a defensible focus given the paper's question, but it means there is no evidence about whether the linear SVM is the right choice for these features.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Two feature families of very unequal size. EEG contributes relative power in five bands across 62 electrodes - potentially over 300 features, though the paper reports an EEG-only classification 'using the five frequency bands' relative power', suggesting channel-averaged values were used there. Eye tracking contributes 16 features (eight AOIs by two face races) as fixation-time proportions. The relative power formulation is a considered choice, expressing each band as a share of total spectral power to expose 'abnormalities in the rhythmic fluctuations' independent of overall amplitude. The 60 ms fixation threshold on the gaze side is a similarly considered detail, excluding gaze too brief to be conscious. The asymmetry in pool size between modalities is not addressed and matters for interpreting which features the mRMR selection favoured.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy and AUC only, but reported for every modality and stimulus condition separately, which is what makes the fusion ladder legible. Missing: sensitivity, specificity, confusion matrices, confidence intervals, and any statistical test of the differences between modality conditions - so whether 85.44% is significantly better than 75.89% on 97 children is not established. The accuracy-versus-feature-count curve is plotted, which is transparent about the sweep but also makes explicit that the headline is a maximum rather than a pre-specified operating point.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No model-explanation method and no disclosure of which features mRMR selected, which is the paper's main interpretive gap - having established that fusion helps, it cannot say what the fused model is using. Interpretation instead comes from a parallel descriptive analysis: independent t-tests on each band and AOI, with the resulting differences read against established theory. The gaze findings are interpreted through the eye avoidance hypothesis, that autistic people avoid eye contact because they 'may consider it an unbearable social threat and experience uncomfortable physiological responses', making avoidance 'an adaptive strategy' that nonetheless degrades processing of facial identity and intention. The EEG findings are mapped onto cognitive functions band by band. Notably, the descriptive analysis found the strongest gaze effect on background fixation rather than on the eye region, and eye-region differences did not reach significance - a result that sits somewhat awkwardly with the eye-avoidance framing the discussion adopts.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The study's decisive weakness. No train/test split, cross-validation, held-out sample or repetition procedure is described anywhere in the methods or results. mRMR feature selection uses class labels and there is no statement that it was nested within any resampling scheme. The reported 85.44% is explicitly the maximum of a curve swept across one to forty-five selected features, so both the feature count and the reported figure were chosen against the same data. With 97 participants and an EEG feature pool potentially exceeding 300 variables, this is exactly the configuration in which unnested supervised selection produces substantial upward bias. There is no independent cohort, no external site and no replication. The accuracies should therefore be read as in-sample separability rather than as estimates of predictive performance.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: Autism; Typically developing children; EEG; Eye-tracking. Purely descriptive of the design, with no methodological or clinical framing term - consistent with a paper whose contribution is presented as the combination of two established measurement modalities rather than as a modelling advance.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Computers in Biology and Medicine, 120, article 103722 - an Elsevier biomedical engineering journal, appropriate for a signal-processing-plus-classification contribution.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2020. The framing is the standard objectivity argument - 'clinical diagnosis is mainly based on behavioral scale tests including the autism behavior checklist and Childhood Autism Rating Scale' and 'due to subjectivity, evaluation results may not be very accurate' - but with a more specific biomarker orientation than most: biomarkers are defined as objective indicators of biological processes used 'for diagnosis, outcome predictions, and treatment prediction', with high accuracy, reliability and validity named as prerequisites for clinical use. The paper's distinctive contribution to the corpus's framing is its argument for why single-modality approaches fail: it cites a review finding a U-shaped profile of EEG power alterations in autism (excess low- and high-frequency power, deficient alpha), then notes that other studies found no EEG differences at all, particularly in high-functioning autism, and concludes that heterogeneity makes EEG alone insufficient. Eye tracking is added specifically because 'atypical face processing' has been found across all presentations. That is a heterogeneity-driven rationale for fusion rather than a generic more-data-is-better argument, and it is unusual in this literature.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Toward Continuous Social Phenotyping: Analyzing Gaze Patterns in an Emotion Recognition Task for Children With Autism Through Wearable Smart Glasses
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Nag A; Haber N; Voss C; Tamura S; Daniels J; Ma J; Chiang B; Ramachandran S; Schwartz J; Winograd T; Feinstein C; Wall DP
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: Journal of Medical Internet Research, 22(4), e13810
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: School-age and adolescent children with autism, predominantly high-functioning
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking and gaze (wearable)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Two-part feasibility test: whether gaze can be tracked at all using a low-cost eye tracker mounted on wearable smart glasses during an emotion recognition task, and whether the resulting gaze and emotion-response data can distinguish autistic from neurotypical children - as a step toward continuous social phenotyping outside the clinic, since the skills of interest are practised in social contexts but currently measured only in clinical settings by trained administrators
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control feasibility and classification study with a systematic feature-ablation grid
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One 20-minute session per child comprising three successive trials of 41, 42 and 41 face images, with recalibration between trials
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Emotion recognition with competing distractors. Each screen showed a central child face expressing one of seven emotions (happy, sad, angry, scared, disgust, surprised, calm) flanked by two nonsocial images of high autism interest (Legos, train, car) previously validated as distractors, displayed for 6 seconds before the child was prompted to name the emotion verbally. The face covered about 49% of screen width and 87% of height, each distractor about 17% by 31%. In trial 2 only, the glasses played an audio cue speaking the correct emotion three seconds into the display, emulating the Superpower Glass intervention; trials 1 and 3 had the glasses deactivated. Every eight images, a dancing Santa Claus appeared centrally for 5 seconds to draw gaze to the middle for calibration validation
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: In-lab at Stanford University, with participants seated approximately 25 inches from a 24-inch 1920 x 1200 screen at eye level, accompanied by a researcher who recorded verbal responses; sessions video recorded
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Official autism diagnosis confirmed via medical record, with parent-reported diagnosis additionally assessed by the Social Communication Questionnaire and a positive screen requiring SCQ above 16. Exclusions were syndromic autism with genetic, metabolic or infectious aetiology on medical record, history of seizures or other neurological disorder, vision impairment, and history of personality or bipolar disorder. Stanford-Binet Fifth Edition Abbreviated Battery IQ and parent-completed SRS-2 were obtained for every participant
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 16 analysed (23 enrolled)
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Reported rather than excluded, for the 11 autistic participants who completed the survey: one with anxiety disorder or depression and one with ADHD. Syndromic autism, seizures, other neurological disorders and personality or bipolar disorder were exclusions
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Reported in detail for the 11 autistic participants who completed the survey: methylphenidate (3), sertraline (2), and one each of arginine vasopressin, guanfacine extended release, carbamazepine, aripiprazole and dexmethylphenidate, with only 4 of 11 on no medication. Among controls, 15 of 17 were on no medication. This level of medication reporting is essentially unique in the corpus
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Fully characterised: SCQ 18.86 +/- 6.43 (range 7-31) in the autistic group against 1.82 +/- 1.07 (0-4) in controls; SRS-2 total 78.85 +/- 11.13 (58 to over 90) against 44.41 +/- 8.11 (36-64)
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Actively screened and excluded on five criteria: SCQ above 14, history of mood or personality disorder by parent report or medical record, a sibling diagnosed with autism or schizophrenia, history of seizures or other neurological disorder, and vision impairment. Excluding on sibling diagnosis controls for the broader autism phenotype, which almost no other study in the corpus does
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 17 analysed (20 enrolled)
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Approximately - 12.13 versus 11.53 years, though the autistic group has wider spread (SD 3.31 versus 2.48) and extends down to age 6 while controls start at 8. The authors identify age balance as a target for future work, noting more data 'perhaps more balanced for age and gender across cohorts' would be needed
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: No, and the authors name it as a limitation: 81% male in the autistic group against 53% in controls. They note that although the population sex ratio in autism is about 4:1, 'the reported imbalance still presents a gender bias between our sample population', and that gender differences exist in both groups on emotion recognition and gaze tasks 'which may have been exacerbated by our imbalanced cohorts'. The classification results show why this matters - age and gender alone classified at 71%
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Yes, established by multi-criterion screening including SCQ and family history
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye video from an inward-facing camera, world video from the Glass front camera, and verbal emotion classification responses
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Pupil identification by hybrid methods (maximally stable extremal regions, a gradient-based method and optical flow); four calibrations per participant, one at the start and one after each trial, each fitted by a separate polynomial regression to produce four candidate gaze prediction models, with each session then manually inspected and partitioned into intervals for which one of the four models or none appeared to apply; per-frame gaze coding into four categories - on the facial stimulus, on the left distractor, on the right distractor, or nowhere in particular; and outlier exclusion of trials rendered unusable by hardware failures such as the camera slipping from its mount. Calibration and gaze cluster labelling were semi-automated and performed by independent labellers with inter-labeller reliability reported in an appendix
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Google Glass with a custom 3D-printed mount sliding onto the prism, holding a Microsoft LifeCam HD-6000 webcam modified by removing its infrared filter and replacing two indicator LEDs with infrared emitters, adapted from the open-source Pupil Project prototype; multiple mount variants 3D-printed so the best eye view could be selected per session; total add-on hardware cost approximately US $35. Stimuli from the Child Affective Facial Expression (CAFE) dataset - 154 images of children aged 2-8 balanced across African American, Asian, white, Latino and South Asian groups, with 125 used here balanced within each trial for race, gender and emotion
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: A wearable gaze and emotion-response dataset from 33 children; no release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Sensitive - eye and world video of identifiable children, with sessions video recorded and substantial manual annotation of pupil and gaze coordinates by human labellers. Governance is reported: written informed consent from both parents and children under an approved Stanford University IRB protocol
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Gaze allocation statistics, emotion response patterns and participant metadata
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 219 features per trial in four blocks. Emotion confusion matrices (49-dimensional): a 7 x 7 matrix per participant of true versus reported emotion, row-normalised, with each cell an independent feature. Emotion confusion details (41 or 42 dimensions): a binary correct/incorrect value per face, preserving performance over time. Gaze patterns (123 or 126 dimensions): three features per face - percentage of frames looking directly at the face rather than a distractor, percentage of gaze fixation changes directed toward the face, and number of frames elapsed before first looking directly at the face. Participant metadata (2 dimensions): age and gender
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Custom hybrid pupil tracking; polynomial regression calibration; semi-automated human labelling with independent labellers
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Not per feature, but the ablation grid over all 15 feature-block combinations by four trial conditions is a systematic importance analysis at the block level - and it is the paper's central result
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Full factorial ablation across feature blocks and trials with leave-one-participant-out accuracy and Monte Carlo shuffling P values (2,500 iterations, checked for convergence) for each cell
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Gaze features alone were the strongest block, reaching 83.9% on trial 1 and 83.9% on all trials concatenated (P = .00 and .002), against 71.0% for age and gender alone. But the paper declines to claim this as a finding because the metadata baseline is itself high and significance did not survive Bonferroni correction
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Autistic children showed a higher mean distraction ratio - proportion of gaze on distractors rather than the face - at 0.0433 +/- 0.0911 against 0.0139 +/- 0.0215 in controls, but the difference was not significant across participants (one-tailed t test, P = .12). It reached significance only when treating each facial stimulus as independent (1,792 versus 1,756 samples, uncorrected P < .01), an assumption the authors themselves flag as 'likely an unreasonable noise model'. The histogram shows distraction 'higher and more inconsistent' in autism, with the group difference driven substantially by variance rather than location
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Regularised linear classification
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Elastic net as the primary classifier, chosen because 219 features per trial 'far exceeds the number of participants' so 'regularization was important to prevent model overfitting'; logistic regression with l1 or l2 regularisation selected by grid search on the training folds as an ablation comparator, included because elastic net optimisers 'can perform unstably in these edge cases'
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-participant-out cross-validation for every classifier, with Monte Carlo shuffling tests over 2,500 iterations checked for convergence to establish statistical significance of each accuracy against chance. Logistic regression hyperparameters were selected by grid search on training folds only. Crucially, the evaluation includes a metadata-only baseline using age and gender, which is what allows the paper to determine that its behavioural features add nothing reliable
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Leave-one-out accuracy with a shuffling-test P value for every one of 60 cells in the ablation grid, plus cross-validation confusion matrices for the full model across all four trial conditions
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: The full model using all features achieved 71.0% across all trials, exactly matching the age-and-gender-only baseline of 71.0%, with the full model's shuffling P value of .05 no better than the baseline's .04. Gaze features alone reached 83.9% on trial 1 and on all trials (P = .00 and .002) and gaze-plus-emotion-confusion-details reached 80.6% and 83.9%, but these did not survive Bonferroni correction. Emotion confusion matrices alone performed at or below chance in trials 2 and 3 (6.5% and 35.5%). Performance was consistently best on trial 1 - before any feedback or task adaptation - and worst on trial 2, when the glasses delivered audio cues
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A US $35 eye tracker mounted on Google Glass could track gaze during an emotion recognition task, and autistic children were on average more distracted by nonsocial stimuli than neurotypical children. But the difference was not significant at the participant level (P = .12), and no classifier built on gaze and emotion features significantly outperformed one using only age and gender - both reached exactly 71.0%. The authors conclude that facial attention differences in autism, widely assumed to be clear, are in fact subtle enough that noisy wearable gaze data cannot exploit them, and that 'the present form factor and data do not allow for these differences to be reliably exploited by machine learning systems'. Group separation was driven as much by variance as by mean - distraction was 'higher and more inconsistent' in autism.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Greater and more variable distraction from a central face toward flanking nonsocial stimuli, at a magnitude too small and too heterogeneous to support individual classification in this sample
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Move data collection into the home, since building a robust dataset for continuous phenotyping requires large-scale in-home acquisition, augmented reality platforms with robust native eye tracking, game design for at-home analysis, and clearly defined measurable experimental parameters; extend feasibility testing to younger children in the critical periods for cognition and speech; balance cohorts for age and gender; and design user interfaces and games that homogenise use so as to lower the natural variability of at-home measurement
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The most important negative result in the corpus, and a model of how such a result should be reported. Almost every study here reports an accuracy without asking what a trivial baseline would achieve; this one builds the baseline, finds that age and gender alone classify at 71.0%, observes that its full behavioural model also reaches exactly 71.0%, and concludes that its features add nothing reliable. It would have been entirely possible to publish the gaze-only figure of 83.9% with P = .002 as a positive finding - many papers in this corpus report less on weaker evidence - and the authors explicitly decline, noting that significance did not survive Bonferroni correction and that 'given the relatively high performance on participant metadata (age and gender), we could not conclude that gaze and expression recognition features enhance classification'. The methodology supporting that conclusion is correspondingly strong: leave-one-participant-out cross-validation, Monte Carlo shuffling tests over 2,500 iterations for every cell of a 60-cell ablation grid, elastic net chosen explicitly because 219 features against 33 participants demands regularisation, and hyperparameters tuned on training folds only. Participant characterisation is the best in the corpus - SCQ, SRS-2 and Stanford-Binet ABIQ for every child, plus itemised comorbidities and current medications, and a control group screened on five criteria including sibling diagnosis of autism or schizophrenia. The limitations section is unusually forthright, disclosing that a chinrest was added mid-study after four participants and that because 'more ASD subjects took part in the study later on', 'this confound may be exploited by the classifiers' - an admission that the classifier might be detecting an apparatus change rather than autism. It also discloses that the mount occluded roughly 15% of the lower visual field, which 'may have had a greater distracting effect on participants in the ASD group with tactile sensitivities', and that only 3 of 16 autistic participants had ABIQ below 80, so the cohort is predominantly high-functioning. The substantive lesson for the synthesis is stated plainly by the authors: 'The prevailing belief in the literature was that facial attention differences are very clear in ASD, so we hypothesized that distraction ratios across an emotion recognition task alone were enough to distinguish ASD vs NC reliably. We now believe that integrating further subtlety through robust gaze-tracking hardware will be required.' The declared conflict of interest - the senior author founded Cognoa, a commercial digital child-health company - makes the negative finding more rather than less credible.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: 16 autistic and 17 neurotypical children, from 43 enrolled (23 autistic, 20 neurotypical). Exclusions are itemised with reasons: 4 controls received an early prototype version with visual rather than audio cues and could not read the cues or complete the task; 5 autistic participants received images in a different randomised order because of a stimulus ordering error; and 1 autistic participant had an unrelated health issue mid-session. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The cohort is predominantly high-functioning - only 3 of 16 autistic participants had an abbreviated IQ below 80.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with autism', 'children with ASD', 'ASD participants', 'neurotypical controls (NCs)', 'individuals with autism'. Consistently person-first, and 'neurotypical' rather than 'normal', 'healthy' or 'typically developing' - the neurodiversity-aligned term. The framing acknowledges theoretical uncertainty rather than asserting deficits: 'There are several leading theories about facial processing in ASD, and the underlying biological mechanisms are not fully understood.' Autism is nonetheless introduced as 'one of the most important public health challenges we face today'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Autistic group: n = 16, 13 male (81%) and 3 female, mean age 12.13 +/- 3.31 years, range 6-17; SCQ 18.86 +/- 6.43; ABIQ 102.75 +/- 19.54 (range 55-133); SRS-2 total 78.85 +/- 11.13. Neurotypical group: n = 17, 9 male (53%) and 8 female, mean age 11.53 +/- 2.48, range 8-17; SCQ 1.82 +/- 1.07; ABIQ 108.94 +/- 9.58 (91-129); SRS-2 total 44.41 +/- 8.11. Comorbidities and current medications are itemised for the 11 autistic participants who completed the survey - methylphenidate in 3, sertraline in 2, and single instances of arginine vasopressin, guanfacine, carbamazepine, aripiprazole and dexmethylphenidate, with only 4 of 11 unmedicated against 15 of 17 controls. This is the most complete participant characterisation in the corpus. The sex imbalance (81% versus 53% male) is named by the authors as a limitation, and the ABIQ distribution shows the autistic cohort is predominantly high-functioning with wider spread than controls.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Official autism diagnosis confirmed via medical record, with parent-reported diagnosis corroborated by SCQ above 16, and syndromic autism excluded on the basis of genetic, metabolic or infectious aetiology in the record. The control group is screened more rigorously than anywhere else in the corpus, excluded on SCQ above 14, history of mood or personality disorder, a sibling diagnosed with autism or schizophrenia, history of seizures or neurological disorder, and vision impairment. Excluding on sibling diagnosis controls for the broader autism phenotype - a step no other study here takes. Stanford-Binet ABIQ was administered by a trained research assistant and SRS-2 completed by parents for every participant.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Complete. SCQ, SRS-2 total and Stanford-Binet ABIQ for every participant in both groups, plus itemised comorbid psychological conditions and current medications for those who completed the survey. Uniquely in this corpus, the medication data are reported at drug level rather than as a summary count, which matters because several of the drugs listed - methylphenidate, guanfacine, aripiprazole - have documented effects on attention and eye movement.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: test the feasibility of wearable gaze tracking during an emotion recognition task and whether the resulting data distinguish autistic from neurotypical children. Main findings: autistic children showed a higher mean distraction ratio (0.0433 versus 0.0139) but not significantly at the participant level (P = .12); the full classifier reached 71.0%, exactly matching an age-and-gender-only baseline; gaze features alone reached 83.9% but did not survive Bonferroni correction; performance was best on trial 1 before feedback and worst on trial 2 during audio cueing; and the authors conclude the differences are too subtle and the data too noisy for reliable machine exploitation.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: In-lab at Stanford University, with families recruited between 25 February 2015 and 26 January 2016 through the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Research Registry, referrals to the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Clinic, the Developmental Behavioral Unit of Lucile Packard Children's Hospital, and academic presentations. Funded by NIH grants 1R01EB025025-01 and 1R21HD091500-01 plus multiple foundation and Stanford programme grants. The senior author declares founding Cognoa, a company building digital child-health solutions.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Emotion recognition under competing attentional demand - a face at centre flanked by two validated high-autism-interest nonsocial distractors, so that gaze allocation and emotion identification are measured in the same trial. The paper's rationale for combining them is theoretical rather than opportunistic: emotion recognition and social attention 'have mostly been studied in isolation' and both have been proposed separately as diagnostic indicators, so the authors 'hypothesized that they are deeply linked and studied them together'. The three-trial structure with feedback in trial 2 only is designed to emulate the Superpower Glass intervention, and it produces an unanticipated result - discrimination was best in trial 1, before any feedback or task adaptation.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; one 20-minute session per child with no follow-up, though the stated goal of continuous phenotyping is inherently longitudinal. Data include eye and world video of identifiable children with extensive manual annotation by independent labellers. Governance is reported: written informed consent from both parents and children under an approved Stanford IRB protocol. The conflict of interest is declared.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Deliberately low-cost and open-hardware derived: Google Glass with a custom 3D-printed prism mount holding a Microsoft LifeCam HD-6000 webcam whose infrared filter was removed and whose indicator LEDs were replaced with infrared emitters, adapted from the open-source Pupil Project, at about US $35 for the add-on. Multiple mount variants were printed so the best eye view could be chosen per participant. Stimuli came from the CAFE dataset of child faces, balanced across five racial groups and by gender and emotion within each trial - the most carefully balanced stimulus set in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Very good, with implementation detail deferred to a supplementary appendix rather than omitted. Reported in the paper: recruitment window and channels, all inclusion and exclusion criteria for both groups, every excluded participant with the reason, hardware construction and cost, screen size, resolution and viewing distance, stimulus source and balancing, image counts per trial, display durations, feedback modality and timing, the calibration validation device, the four-calibration scheme with per-calibration polynomial regression, the four-way gaze coding scheme, all four feature blocks with their dimensionalities, the classifier and its rationale, the cross-validation scheme, the shuffling test with iteration count and convergence checking, and a full 60-cell ablation grid. Pupil tracking algorithms, inter-labeller reliability and outlier exclusion criteria are in Multimedia Appendix 1. Not released: data or code.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The most complete limitations section in the corpus, with five named items. Age range 6-17 'is not representative of children who are in critical periods of development for cognition and speech'. Gender imbalance of 13:3 in the autistic cohort against 9:8 in controls, with the authors noting that gender differences exist on emotion recognition and gaze tasks and 'may have been exacerbated by our imbalanced cohorts'. Limited spectrum coverage, since only 3 of 16 autistic participants had ABIQ below 80 so 13 are high-functioning. A chinrest added after the first four participants because of head movement, with the explicit admission that 'more ASD subjects took part in the study later on. This confound may be exploited by the classifiers'. And nonstandard eye tracking - the custom system was never evaluated against a standard tracker, the mount shifted requiring recalibration and extensive manual annotation, and it 'occluded roughly 15% of the field of view in the lower region for most participants, which may have had a greater distracting effect on participants in the ASD group with tactile sensitivities'. The discussion adds an ethological caution: static 6-second photographs are 'quite divergent from real-life social interactions with moving children and fleeting displays of facial emotion', and the field 'does not have enough information to know how divergent our experimental data might be from the ecologically valid situations'.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Move acquisition into the home, with four named prerequisites: large-scale in-home data acquisition, augmented reality platforms with robust native eye tracking, game design for at-home analysis platforms, and clearly defined measurable experimental parameters. Extend feasibility testing to younger children. Balance cohorts for age and gender. And solve a human-computer interaction problem the authors state precisely - producing 'appropriate user interfaces and games that homogenize use in ways so as to lower the natural variability of measurement', since follow-up Superpower Glass studies showed heterogeneity in less-restricted collection. They also note that later generations of the system dropped the eye tracker entirely because of bulkiness and calibration issues, and expect native gaze tracking in commercial AR devices to resolve this.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Two behaviours measured simultaneously and by design: visual attention allocation between a central social stimulus and flanking nonsocial distractors, and emotion recognition accuracy and error structure. The distraction ratio - proportion of gaze frames on distractors rather than the face - is the primary behavioural measure, with a variant excluding frames coded 'nowhere in particular' to give a more direct face-versus-distractor comparison. Emotion responses are captured both as a 7 x 7 confusion matrix and as a per-face correct/incorrect sequence preserving performance over time.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: The fusion result is negative and instructive. Gaze features alone gave the best behavioural performance (83.9% on trial 1 and on all trials), emotion confusion matrices alone performed at or below chance in two of three trials (6.5% and 35.5%), and combining all feature blocks gave 71.0% - worse than gaze alone. Adding emotion features to gaze reduced accuracy in most cells of the ablation grid. This is a rare demonstration in the corpus that multimodal combination can degrade rather than improve performance when one modality carries little signal and the feature-to-participant ratio is extreme. The critical comparison, though, is not between modalities but against the metadata baseline: age and gender alone reached 71.0% with P = .04, the same accuracy as the full model with a marginally better P value, so no combination of behavioural features demonstrably beat two demographic variables.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Elastic net as the primary classifier, chosen explicitly for the data regime: 219 features per trial against 33 participants means 'regularization was important to prevent model overfitting', and elastic net combines lasso and ridge penalties. Logistic regression with grid-searched l1 or l2 regularisation serves as an ablation comparator, included on the technical grounds that elastic net optimisers can be unstable at the edge cases where one penalty vanishes. Elastic net outperformed logistic regression in most tasks, which the authors read as confirming 'a need for regularization in this dataset'. No deep learning, correctly - the discussion notes that a larger, more balanced corpus 'would also enable the use of more complex statistical models, such as artificial neural networks', which is a statement of what the data cannot currently support.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: 219 features per trial in four clearly separated blocks, which is what makes the ablation grid possible: a row-normalised 7 x 7 emotion confusion matrix flattened to 49 features; a per-face binary correctness sequence of 41 or 42 features preserving temporal structure; three gaze features per face (proportion of frames on the face rather than a distractor, proportion of fixation changes directed to the face, and frames elapsed before first looking at the face) giving 123 or 126; and two metadata features, age and gender. Including metadata as an explicit feature block rather than as covariates is the design decision that makes the paper's central finding visible.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Leave-one-participant-out accuracy paired with a Monte Carlo shuffling P value for every one of 60 grid cells (15 feature combinations by four trial conditions), plus cross-validation confusion matrices for the full model. Shuffling tests ran 2,500 iterations and were checked for convergence. Bonferroni correction is applied when interpreting significance across the grid, and the authors note which results survive it and which do not. Reporting a permutation-based significance test for every reported accuracy is unique in this corpus and is precisely what distinguishes an accuracy from a finding at this sample size. No sensitivity, specificity or AUC.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No model-explanation method, but the ablation grid functions as a structured interpretability analysis at the block level, and its results are interpreted carefully. Two patterns are drawn out. First, discrimination is best in trial 1 - 'the first trial conducted which was before receiving any feedback or adjusting to the task' - implying the signal is strongest on first exposure and attenuates as children adapt, which has direct implications for protocol design. Second, emotion confusion matrices alone collapse to below chance in later trials, so the emotion-response signal is unstable. The behavioural interpretation is explicitly bounded: the authors note that classical eye-tracking studies have found subtler effects such as increased mouth relative to eye attention, and state that 'the gaze data collected by our system was too noisy to test for these subtler effects'.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Leave-one-participant-out cross-validation throughout, with Monte Carlo shuffling tests establishing significance against chance for every reported accuracy, hyperparameters grid-searched on training folds only, and Bonferroni correction applied when interpreting the grid. Most importantly, the design includes a null-model baseline using only age and gender, which is the element almost every other study in this corpus lacks and which is what converts a nominal 71% accuracy into an interpretable finding. What remains absent is an independent cohort or external validation, which the sample size precludes, and the acknowledged possibility that the mid-study chinrest change is confounded with group and could be exploited by the classifiers - a validity threat the authors identify but cannot remove.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorder; translational medicine; eye tracking; wearable technologies; artificial intelligence; machine learning; precision health; digital therapy. The recurring frame is 'continuous social phenotyping' - measurement carried out repeatedly in natural settings rather than episodically in clinics - which positions the work as infrastructure for longitudinal characterisation rather than as a diagnostic test.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Medical Internet Research, 22(4), e13810 - a digital health venue, appropriate for a wearable feasibility study, and one whose remit makes a negative feasibility result publishable in a way that a pure machine learning venue might not.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2020. The framing is the gap between where social skills are practised and where they are measured: emotion recognition and eye contact skills 'are important to improve social functioning, but the methods currently used to measure and track such skills are delivered in clinical settings or via trained administrators outside the social context where these skills are practiced'. The proposed remedy is mobile and wearable machine learning platforms enabling continuous phenotyping during natural social interactions. The paper's most valuable contribution to the field's self-understanding is its retraction of a prior assumption, stated explicitly: 'The prevailing belief in the literature was that facial attention differences are very clear in ASD, so we hypothesized that distraction ratios across an emotion recognition task alone were enough to distinguish ASD vs NC reliably. We now believe that integrating further subtlety through robust gaze-tracking hardware will be required to design a phenotyping marker from this effect.' It also reports that later generations of the same research group's system abandoned the eye tracker entirely because of bulkiness and calibration problems - a rare disclosure of a technology's practical failure trajectory.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Towards the automatic detection of social biomarkers in autism spectrum disorder: introducing the simulated interaction task (SIT)
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Drimalla H; Scheffer T; Landwehr N; Baskow I; Roepke S; Behnia B; Dziobek I
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Adults with autism without intellectual disability
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Multimodal social interaction (facial expression, gaze and voice)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Replace the 'clinical gaze' - the implicit, hard-to-verbalise expertise clinicians rely on to judge social interaction deficits - with a standardised, automatically scored measurement. The specific design problem addressed is that interactive social paradigms cannot be standardised because a human interaction partner never behaves identically twice, so the study prerecords one side of a dialogue to make the social stimulus identical for every participant while preserving interactional structure
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Two-part study: a facial EMG preparatory study in healthy males to select regions of interest, followed by a cross-sectional case-control classification study with parallel clinical expert benchmarking
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session per participant; the simulated interaction task lasts about 7 minutes total, comprising a 3.08-minute warm-up and instruction phase (not analysed) and a 3.2-minute analysed recording
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: The Simulated Interaction Task (SIT) - a prerecorded video conversation with an actress about food preferences and dinner preparation. After a warm-up in which the actress introduces herself, explains the task and asks the participant to describe how they travelled to the institute, she addresses the participant in three excerpts of 24-26 seconds each: how she sets a table for dinner (neutral), food she likes (positive) and food she dislikes (negative). After each, she asks the participant the same question and they have about half a minute to answer, during which she displays empathic listening behaviour - nodding and social smiling. Food preferences were chosen as a topic because they elicit positive and negative emotion quickly without touching personal or sensitive material, and because response lengths vary less than for topics such as favourite films, which aids standardisation
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: A quiet laboratory with constant lighting; the experimenter left the room and the participant started the task alone
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: Asperger syndrome, atypical autism or childhood autism under ICD-10
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: All autistic participants had previously received an ICD-10 diagnosis through the autism outpatient clinic of Charite Universitatsmedizin Berlin. The diagnostic procedure included ADOS for 35 of 37 participants and ADI-R for the 21 with available parental informants. Autistic traits were additionally assessed by Autism-Spectrum Quotient in all participants, and a German vocabulary test (Wortschatztest) was used to confirm sufficient verbal intelligence
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 37 (36 in the combined classifier, one excluded for missing audio)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: 18 female / 19 male - 49% female, by far the highest female representation of any autistic cohort in the corpus
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Current antipsychotic and anticonvulsant medication and comorbid neurological disorders were exclusions; maximum age set at 65 to avoid age-related neurodegeneration. In the control group any history of psychiatric disorder led to exclusion, on which basis three participants were excluded
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Current antipsychotic and anticonvulsant medication excluded; other medication not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: ADOS scores obtained for 35 participants and used analytically - the classifier's predicted class probability correlated with ADOS score at rs = 0.48, p < 0.0001. Autism-Spectrum Quotient collected for all participants
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Any history of psychiatric disorder led to exclusion, applied prospectively with three participants excluded on this basis
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not matched, and the consequence is measured rather than assumed. The autistic group is on average 3.75 years older (36.89 versus 33.14) with a wider range extending to 62 against 49. The authors detect the resulting bias directly: predicted class probability correlated with participant age at rs = 0.35, p = 0.001, and they state that 'older participants in both groups were more often labeled as autistic than young participants by the machine-learning classifiers, as the classifier was probably picking up a tendency of higher age in the ASD group'. Adding age as an explicit feature did not improve the facial classifier
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Yes and unusually well - 49% female in the autistic group and 51% in controls. Gender was also included as an explicit feature in all models 'to ensure that the model could select certain features as being more predictive for certain genders', which is the correct handling for pitch and harmonics-to-noise ratio, both strongly sex-dependent
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Established by exclusion of any psychiatric history
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Synchronised video and audio of the participant during the simulated dialogue, plus facial EMG in the preparatory study
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: OpenFace extracted facial action unit occurrence and intensity plus gaze angles per frame with a per-frame confidence value; frames not tracked or with confidence below 0.75 were excluded, and participants tracked in fewer than 90% of frames or with mean confidence below 0.75 were excluded entirely. Facial expression was compared against the neutral conversation part as a within-participant baseline. Mimicry was quantified as the time-shifted correlation between the actress's and the participant's action unit time series within 10-second windows. Gaze values were centred on each participant's median to account for height, with mean absolute deviation, first derivative (speed) and second derivative (acceleration) computed. Voice features were extracted with Librosa and Parselmouth Praat scripts
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: A standard computer with camera and microphone only - the paper emphasises that the SIT 'demands a computer with camera and microphone only and can thus be conducted in a laboratory and home setting'. Analysis: OpenFace, Librosa, Parselmouth Praat scripts, scikit-learn. The preparatory study used facial EMG over zygomaticus major, corrugator supercilii and levator labii
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: An 80-participant clinical dataset plus 40 healthy males in the EMG preparatory study; the SIT instrument itself is the more durable contribution
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - video data withheld for privacy, available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. The SIT instrument is available on request and was scheduled for public release from 2024 under CC BY-NC-ND at a named repository. Analysis code is publicly available on GitHub
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Yes, explicitly, for both data and the SIT instrument
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Sensitive - video and audio of identifiable adults, with data explicitly withheld from public release 'due to privacy restrictions of the video data'. Governance is complete: written informed consent from all participants, separate published consent from individuals appearing in figures, approval by the ethics committee of Charite Universitatsmedizin Berlin, and conduct in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Facial action unit statistics, gaze angle derivatives and prosodic and spectral voice features, each summarised per conversation segment
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Primary features were selected by domain knowledge and by the EMG preparatory study rather than by data-driven search - action units for joy (AU6 orbicularis oculi, AU12 zygomaticus major) and disgust (AU4 corrugator supercilii, AU9 levator labii), gaze angle in world coordinates averaged across both eyes, and f0, jitter, shimmer and root-mean-square energy. Secondary features were then computed per conversation part: mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, time of maximum, skewness and kurtosis, giving 715 facial features and 85 gaze features across the seven conversation parts, plus 58 voice features including the first 40 MFCCs. Gender was included as a feature in every model
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: OpenFace 42 for action units, landmarks and gaze with a trained confidence network predicting expected landmark detection error; Librosa for MFCCs and energy; Parselmouth Praat scripts for f0, jitter and shimmer
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Not as model-derived importances, but the paper reports per-feature group comparisons with effect sizes throughout and compares modality-specific classifiers directly
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Non-parametric group comparisons (Mann-Whitney U and Wilcoxon) with effect sizes, corrected for multiple comparisons; modality-wise AUC comparison; and the EMG preparatory study used specifically to select regions of interest before the main study
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Reduced social smiling in the mouth region (AU12) and around the eyes (AU6), reduced mimicry of the actress's AU6 activity, higher voice fundamental frequency and higher harmonics-to-noise ratio. Voice was the strongest single modality (AUC 0.77), then facial expression (0.74 using all 17 OpenFace action units, 0.65 using the domain-selected subset), then gaze (0.63)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reported in full with effect sizes. Autistic adults smiled less during the positive conversation part (AU12 occurrence Mdn 0.12 versus 0.40, p = 0.018), smiled less across the whole conversation in both mouth (occurrence Mdn 0.09 versus 0.40, p = 0.01, r = 0.30; intensity 0.16 versus 0.52, p = 0.019) and eye regions (occurrence 0.02 versus 0.12, p = 0.028), and mimicked the actress's AU6 less (Mdn 0.08 versus 0.19, p = 0.04, r = 0.34). In the negative part they showed more intense frowning (AU4 Mdn 0.08 versus 0.03, p = 0.014, r = 0.29). Voice fundamental frequency was higher in autism (males 139.67 versus 121.68 Hz; females 218.91 versus 209.08 Hz; group effect F(1,76) = 15.51, p = 0.0002) and harmonics-to-noise ratio was higher - the tabulated medians are in fact lower in autism (males 8.50 versus 10.84; females 6.91 versus 10.32), so the text's stated direction contradicts its own table. No gaze differences survived correction for multiple comparisons
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Ensemble tree classification on domain-selected multimodal features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Random forest of 1,000 decision trees, with maximum tree depth and minimum samples per leaf tuned over [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64] for each
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-participant-out cross-validation with nested three-fold cross-validation inside each training set for hyperparameter tuning, and an explicit statement that 'No data of the test-participant was used for training the model'. The paper also states directly that each participant contributes exactly one feature vector of aggregate statistics 'across all video segments. Thus, the data for the machine-learning analysis did not include any nested repeated measures' - an explicit repudiation of the segment-level splitting that inflates results elsewhere in this literature. Classifier accuracy was compared against a majority-vote baseline by McNemar's test and against eight clinical expert raters
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: AUC per modality and combined, plus accuracy, sensitivity and specificity at a 0.5 class probability threshold; McNemar tests against a majority-vote baseline and against clinical experts; correlation of predicted class probability with ADOS score and with age; and per-gender breakdown of classification accuracy. Confusion matrices for all classifiers are in supplementary tables
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Combined facial, gaze and voice features gave AUC 0.78, accuracy 73%, sensitivity 67% and specificity 79%. By modality: voice AUC 0.77, facial expression 0.74 using all 17 action units and 0.65 using domain-selected features, gaze 0.63. The combined classifier was significantly better than a majority vote (McNemar X = 9, p = 0.014) and not significantly worse than clinical experts (p > 0.05). Eight expert psychologists and psychiatrists rating ten videos each achieved a mean accuracy of 0.71 with a range from 0.56 to 1.00, and expert accuracy correlated with months of diagnostic or therapeutic experience (rs = 0.72, p = 0.044). Predicted class probability correlated with ADOS score (rs = 0.48, p < 0.0001) and with age (rs = 0.35, p = 0.001). Detection was better for female than male participants (33 of 39 versus 25 of 40, X = 3.88, p = 0.048)
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A seven-minute prerecorded video conversation, scored automatically from a webcam and microphone, detected autism in adults without intellectual disability at 73% accuracy (67% sensitivity, 79% specificity, AUC 0.78) - significantly better than a majority vote and statistically indistinguishable from eight experienced clinicians rating the same videos, whose own accuracy ranged from 0.56 to 1.00 and scaled with experience. Voice was the strongest modality (AUC 0.77), facial expression next (0.74), and gaze weakest (0.63) with no group differences surviving correction, which the authors attribute to appearance-based gaze estimation lacking the precision to detect subtle differences. Autistic adults smiled less, mimicked the actress's expressions less, frowned more when discussing disliked food, and spoke with higher fundamental frequency.
