Critically, the classifier's output correlated with ADOS severity (rs = 0.48) but also with age (rs = 0.35), and the authors identify the latter as a genuine age bias inherited from unmatched groups.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Reduced social smiling in both mouth and eye regions, reduced spontaneous mimicry of a partner's positive expressions, increased frowning when discussing negative content, and higher voice fundamental frequency
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Compare SIT behaviour against a live face-to-face control condition with the same topic and dialogue script to validate the simulated procedure; develop tailored actress responses adaptive to the length of participants' answers; provide interaction partners matched to participants' gender, age or ethnic background, since similarity enhances mimicry; implement automated camera and microphone checks for home use and evaluate accuracy in home settings, since self-administration often reduces accuracy; use state-of-the-art eye trackers to establish whether gaze carries information within a simulated interaction; and test specificity and sensitivity in larger clinical samples with other psychiatric conditions
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: One of the two or three strongest studies in the corpus, and the only one to benchmark a classifier against practising clinicians on the same material. The design solves a real problem elegantly - interactive social paradigms cannot be standardised because a human partner never behaves identically twice, so one side of the conversation is prerecorded, and the actress's own non-verbal behaviour is then quantified with the same computer vision pipeline to verify that the stimulus is what it is claimed to be. The validation is properly constructed: leave-one-participant-out with nested three-fold hyperparameter tuning inside each training fold, one aggregate feature vector per participant with an explicit statement that there are no nested repeated measures, gender entered as a feature so that sex-dependent voice features can be used correctly, non-parametric tests throughout with multiple-comparison correction, and a McNemar test against a majority-vote baseline. Feature selection was constrained a priori by domain knowledge and by a separate EMG study rather than searched over the data, which the authors justify as necessary for 'transparent and explainable diagnostic decisions'. Two findings deserve particular weight in the synthesis. First, the classifier's predicted probability correlates with ADOS severity at rs = 0.48 - one of very few demonstrations anywhere in this corpus that a diagnostic classifier's output tracks clinical severity rather than merely separating groups. Second, and reported with unusual candour, the same probability correlates with age at rs = 0.35 because the autistic group was older, leading the authors to conclude that 'this age bias points to the strong need of careful testing for confounders and biases in training data for all kind of machine-learning diagnostic methods'. The expert benchmark is equally valuable and is the paper's most quietly devastating result: the eight clinicians ranged from 0.56 to 1.00 accuracy on the same videos, with performance scaling with experience, which quantifies the very variability the tool is meant to reduce. Remaining weaknesses are modest. The reported direction of the harmonics-to-noise ratio effect contradicts the paper's own table, which shows lower rather than higher HNR in autism. The autistic sample is high-functioning adults with existing diagnoses, so the camouflaging that the introduction identifies as delaying diagnosis is present in the very population being classified. And the age confound, though detected, is not corrected for in the reported accuracy.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups in the main study: 37 autistic adults without intellectual disability recruited via the autism outpatient clinic of Charite Universitatsmedizin Berlin, and 43 healthy controls, with one autistic participant excluded from the combined classifier for missing audio. A separate preparatory study used 40 healthy males with facial EMG to select regions of interest before the main analysis - a two-stage design in which feature selection is performed on an entirely different sample, which is stronger than any within-study selection procedure. No other-psychiatric-diagnosis comparison group, though the authors identify testing 'in larger clinical samples with different psychiatric conditions' as necessary since the social interaction deficits targeted are common to many disorders.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'individuals with ASD', 'adults with ASD', 'autism spectrum disorder', 'healthy controls (HC)', 'neurotypical (NT)', 'individuals without autism'. Consistently person-first, with both 'healthy controls' and 'neurotypical' used. The framing locates the problem in clinical practice rather than in patients: clinicians rely on 'the so-called clinical gaze, the implicit knowledge based on experience', which is 'difficult to verbalize, teach, quantify, standardize, and validate', and 'interrater-variability may account for inconsistencies regarding diagnostic accuracy'. Camouflaging is described neutrally as a strategy adults develop to compensate, and is identified as a reason for late diagnosis rather than as a deficit.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Autistic group: n = 37, 18 female (49%), mean age 36.89 years, range 22-62. Control group: n = 43, 22 female (51%), mean age 33.14 years, range 18-49. The sex balance is the most striking feature - essentially even in both groups, against the 4:1 male predominance typical of autism cohorts including most in this corpus - and it enables the paper's per-gender analysis showing better detection of women (33 of 39 versus 25 of 40, p = 0.048), which the authors interpret through the finding that women require more severe symptoms to receive a diagnosis. Age is not matched, with the autistic group 3.75 years older and extending 13 years further, and the classifier demonstrably picks this up (class probability correlated with age at rs = 0.35, p = 0.001). Verbal intelligence was confirmed sufficient by the Wortschatztest but no IQ values are reported. No ethnicity or socioeconomic data; single clinic recruitment.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Prior ICD-10 diagnoses of Asperger syndrome, atypical autism or childhood autism, made through a specialist autism outpatient clinic, with ADOS administered to 35 of 37 participants and ADI-R to the 21 for whom parental informants were available. Autism-Spectrum Quotient was collected for all participants in both groups and the Wortschatztest confirmed verbal intelligence. Control status was established prospectively by excluding any history of psychiatric disorder, with three participants excluded on that basis. Both groups were also screened for current antipsychotic and anticonvulsant medication and comorbid neurological disorders. This is among the more rigorous ascertainments in the corpus, and the ADOS scores are used analytically rather than merely reported.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: ADOS scores for 35 participants, Autism-Spectrum Quotient for all participants in both groups, and Wortschatztest verbal intelligence as an inclusion screen. The ADOS data are used substantively: the classifier's predicted class probability correlates with ADOS score at rs = 0.48, p < 0.0001, establishing that the model's output tracks symptom severity and not merely group membership. No full-scale IQ, adaptive functioning or comorbidity scores are reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: build and validate a standardised, automatically scored measure of social interaction behaviour capable of supporting autism diagnosis in adults. Main findings: combined AUC 0.78 with 73% accuracy, 67% sensitivity and 79% specificity; voice was the strongest modality (0.77), facial expression next (0.74), gaze weakest (0.63) with no differences surviving correction; autistic adults showed less social smiling and less mimicry and higher fundamental frequency; the classifier beat a majority vote and matched eight clinical experts whose own accuracy ranged from 0.56 to 1.00 and scaled with experience; and predicted probability correlated with both ADOS severity (rs = 0.48) and age (rs = 0.35), the latter identified as a confound.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A quiet laboratory with constant lighting at Humboldt-Universitat zu Berlin, with participants recruited through the autism outpatient clinic of Charite Universitatsmedizin Berlin. The experimenter left the room before the task began, so the participant was alone with the screen. Ethics approval from the Charite ethics committee, Helsinki conformity, written informed consent from all participants and separate consent for figure publication.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: The Simulated Interaction Task - the corpus's most carefully constructed elicitation paradigm. A prerecorded actress conducts a small-talk conversation about food preferences and dinner preparation, structured into neutral, positive and negative segments of 24-26 seconds each, alternating between her speaking and the participant answering while she displays empathic listening (nodding, social smiling). The design reasoning is stated in unusual detail: food preferences were chosen because they elicit positive and negative emotion quickly without personal or sensitive content, and because response lengths vary less than for topics such as favourite films, which aids standardisation. To generate natural behaviour, the actress actually conversed with the film director during shooting rather than reading to camera. Naturalness was supported by informing participants the actress's part was prerecorded, by instructing and rehearsing three-to-four-sentence answers, and by opening with a practice exchange. Crucially, the actress's own behaviour was then verified with the same OpenFace pipeline, confirming she expressed more disgust and less joy when discussing disliked food and smiled more when listening than speaking - so the stimulus is quantified rather than assumed.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; one session per participant with no follow-up, though the stated applications include monitoring disorder course and treatment outcome. Data are video and audio of identifiable adults. Governance is complete and includes an unusual element - explicit separate consent from individuals appearing in published figures - and the data availability statement withholds the dataset specifically 'due to privacy restrictions of the video data' while making it available on reasonable request. The discussion also engages the downstream consequences of deployment, noting that 'especially screenings and unsupervised feedback might result in more individuals seeking care and lead to higher costs for the health system' and that 'it is warranted to carefully define the area of use and evaluate benefits, costs, and risks' - one of very few papers in the corpus to consider system-level effects of its own tool.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Deliberately minimal: a standard computer with a camera and microphone, which the paper contrasts against comparators using 'high-cost apparatus, not suited for large-scale testing'. Analysis used OpenFace for action units, landmarks and gaze with a trained confidence network, Librosa for MFCCs and energy, Parselmouth Praat scripts for fundamental frequency, jitter and shimmer, and scikit-learn. The preparatory study used facial EMG over zygomaticus major, corrugator supercilii and levator labii to establish which action units to target.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Among the best in the corpus. Reported: all recruitment, inclusion and exclusion criteria; the full SIT structure with segment durations and the reasoning behind topic choice; the actress's verified non-verbal behaviour; frame- and participant-level tracking confidence thresholds (0.75 confidence, 90% of frames) with actual achieved tracking rates (99% of frames, mean confidence 0.99, no group difference at p = 0.97); feature construction at both primary and secondary levels with counts per modality; the classifier, ensemble size and full hyperparameter grids; the nested cross-validation scheme with an explicit statement about the absence of repeated measures; the expert rating protocol; and all statistical tests with effect sizes. Analysis code is public on GitHub, and the SIT instrument was scheduled for open release from 2024 under a Creative Commons licence at a named repository. Video data are withheld for privacy but available on request.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged with unusual thoroughness. On the age bias: 'older participants in both groups were more often labeled as autistic than young participants by the machine-learning classifiers, as the classifier was probably picking up a tendency of higher age in the ASD group. This age bias points to the strong need of careful testing for confounders and biases in training data for all kind of machine-learning diagnostic methods.' On gaze: the null result is attributed to appearance-based estimation being 'not sensitive enough to detect the subtle gaze dysfunctions present in ASD', with a caution that the null 'has to be interpreted with caution'. On the paradigm: the prerecorded actress cannot adapt to answer length, and future versions should provide tailored responses and partners matched on gender, age or ethnicity since similarity enhances mimicry. On the HNR finding: interpretation 'is not straightforward, given the lack of reference studies', with conflicting prior findings acknowledged and the possibility raised that groups differ in speaking-to-pause ratios. On multiplicity: the authors note that automated analysis 'allows the comparison of many different aspects of behavior' so 'the problem of multiple testing remains', which is why they favour the multivariate machine learning approach. Not acknowledged: the reported direction of the HNR effect contradicts the tabulated medians, which are lower rather than higher in autism; and the age confound, though identified, is not adjusted for in the headline accuracy.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Compare SIT behaviour against a live face-to-face condition with the same topic and script to validate the simulation; make the actress's responses adaptive to participants' answer lengths; provide interaction partners matched on gender, age or ethnic background since similarity enhances mimicry; add automated camera and microphone checks and evaluate accuracy in home settings, since self-administration often diminishes accuracy; use state-of-the-art eye tracking to establish whether gaze carries information in this paradigm; and test sensitivity and specificity in larger clinical samples spanning other psychiatric conditions, since social interaction deficits are common to psychosis, depression, bipolar disorder and substance use disorders.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Three behavioural channels measured simultaneously during a single interaction: facial expression (action unit occurrence and intensity, and critically mimicry - the time-shifted correlation between the actress's and participant's expression time series), gaze (angle, deviation from personal median, speed and acceleration), and voice (fundamental frequency, jitter, shimmer, energy, harmonics-to-noise ratio and MFCCs). Measuring mimicry rather than expression alone is the distinctive choice: it captures a dyadic property that requires both partners' behaviour, and it is only possible because the partner's behaviour is identical for every participant.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: A clean modality comparison with an informative asymmetry. Voice alone reached AUC 0.77, facial expression 0.74 with all 17 action units and 0.65 with the domain-selected subset, gaze 0.63, and all three combined 0.78 - so fusion added essentially nothing over voice alone, and the combined result is carried by the two strong modalities. The gaze failure is diagnosed rather than glossed: appearance-based estimation from a webcam is judged insufficiently precise for the subtle differences reported in the eye-tracking literature, and the authors explicitly recommend state-of-the-art eye trackers to test whether gaze carries information in this paradigm. The comparison between domain-selected facial features (0.65) and all available action units (0.74) is also instructive - constraining features for interpretability cost about 9 AUC points, a trade-off the authors accepted deliberately for 'transparent and explainable diagnostic decisions'.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A single random forest of 1,000 trees with maximum depth and minimum samples per leaf tuned over seven values each, applied identically to each modality and to the combination. Model choice is deliberately conservative given 80 participants, and an earlier conference paper by the same group compared alternative approaches. The more consequential modelling decision is what enters the model: features were restricted 'strictly to features based on domain-knowledge or on the EMG preparatory study' for the primary analyses, which is a principled constraint that sacrifices accuracy for interpretability and is quantified by the parallel all-action-unit result.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Primary features chosen a priori from theory and from an independent EMG study, then expanded into secondary summary statistics (mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, time of maximum, skewness, kurtosis) computed separately for each of the seven conversation parts - yielding 715 facial, 85 gaze and 58 voice features. Segment-wise computation preserves the paradigm's designed structure, so the representation encodes not just how much a participant smiled but when relative to the emotional content of the conversation. Each participant contributes exactly one feature vector, which the authors state explicitly rules out nested repeated measures. Gender is included as a feature throughout so that the model can weight sex-dependent voice features appropriately.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: AUC per modality and combined, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity at a stated threshold, McNemar tests against a majority-vote baseline and against expert raters, correlations of predicted class probability with ADOS severity and with age, per-gender classification breakdowns, and supplementary confusion matrices and ROC curves for every classifier. Two of these are almost unique in the corpus. Comparing against a majority-vote baseline establishes that the accuracy exceeds trivial prediction. Correlating predicted probability with ADOS establishes that the model's continuous output has clinical meaning beyond the binary decision - and correlating it with age reveals the confound.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is designed in rather than added afterwards. Features were restricted to those with prior theoretical or EMG-based justification specifically 'for transparent and explainable diagnostic decisions', so every input has a stated behavioural meaning. Each is then reported as a univariate group comparison with effect size, so the multivariate result can be read against the individual behaviours: less social smiling in mouth and eye regions, reduced mimicry of the actress's cheek-raise, more intense frowning during negative content, higher fundamental frequency. The cost of this constraint is measured - all 17 action units reached AUC 0.74 against 0.65 for the selected subset. The clinical validity of the model's output is separately established by its correlation with ADOS score, and its principal bias by its correlation with age.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Leave-one-participant-out cross-validation with nested three-fold cross-validation inside each training set for hyperparameter tuning, and an explicit assurance that no test-participant data entered training. The paper states directly that each participant contributes a single aggregate feature vector so that 'the data for the machine-learning analysis did not include any nested repeated measures' - an explicit repudiation of the segment-level splitting that inflates results throughout this literature. Beyond internal validation, the study adds two external reference points that most of the corpus lacks: a majority-vote baseline, beaten significantly, and eight practising clinicians rating the same videos, whose performance the classifier matched. What remains absent is an independent cohort or external site, and the age confound is detected but not corrected in the reported figures.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No formal keyword list. Vocabulary: 'social biomarkers', 'simulated interaction task', 'clinical gaze', 'camouflaging', 'social phenotypes', 'time-effective and cost-effective'. The framing term that does most work is 'clinical gaze' - the implicit expertise the tool is designed to externalise and standardise.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: npj Digital Medicine 3:25 - a Nature Portfolio digital health journal, open access, with authorship spanning psychology, computer science and psychiatry across Humboldt-Universitat, University of Potsdam, Hasso Plattner Institute and Charite.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2020. The framing is distinctive in locating the problem in the measurement instrument rather than in access or cost alone. For general cognition, standardised tests exist - the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, the Mini Mental State Examination - but 'quantifying social interaction deficits is still in its infancy', so clinicians rely on the clinical gaze, which 'practitioners need many years of training to acquire' and which is 'difficult to verbalize, teach, quantify, standardize, and validate'. The paper's own expert-rating data then substantiate this claim empirically: eight experienced clinicians rating the same videos ranged from 0.56 to 1.00 accuracy, with performance correlating with months of experience. The population argument is equally specific - adults with average or above-average intelligence are diagnosed late because they develop camouflaging strategies, and 'to the best of our knowledge, no existing approach focuses on adults with ASD and normal intelligence levels despite the high need for access to diagnosis'. The paper is also careful about its own claim, stating that the SIT 'is not meant to substitute traditional clinical assessment but rather to allow additional information about the client's social communication abilities at an early stage of the diagnostic process'.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence to Diagnose Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Tracking Saccades
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Dinesh A
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2020 IEEE MIT Undergraduate Research Technology Conference (URTC)
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Not characterised
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking and gaze (saccadic oculomotor control)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Shorten the time, resource use and uncertainty of autism diagnosis by replacing the multidisciplinary developmental evaluation with a single eye-tracking test, on the argument that sensorimotor abnormalities appear before social and cognitive deficits become identifiable and so could support earlier diagnosis
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Secondary analysis of an existing saccade dataset with classifier comparison; no new data collection
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Per the source protocol: one block of 30 gap trials and one block of overlap trials per participant
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: The gap/overlap paradigm for measuring saccadic eye movement latency. In gap trials the central fixation point is extinguished before the peripheral target appears, releasing attention early; in overlap trials the fixation point remains visible when the target appears, so attention must be disengaged before the saccade can be made. The difference between the two isolates attentional disengagement from motor execution. All participants completed one block of 30 gap trials and one block of overlap trials
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Not stated - the data are secondary and their origin is never identified
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Not stated. The author is affiliated with Stanford University; the data provenance is unreported
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Described only as participants 'confirmed to have ASD'. No instrument, criteria, clinician, setting or date is reported, and because the dataset is secondary and uncited, the diagnostic basis cannot be traced
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - described as 'healthy patients' and 'no autism present'
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Asserted but unverifiable - the groups are said to be 'closely related in terms of patients of similar ages and genders', with no ages, no statistics and no test reported for either variable
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Asserted in the same clause with no supporting data. This matters particularly because the introduction singles out girls as harder to diagnose because they are 'better at copying stereotypical social patterns', so sex composition is directly relevant to the paper's own framing
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted without a stated basis
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye-tracking measures from saccade trials, supplied as a tabular attribute set
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Not performed by the author. The paper describes the analytic quantities available in the dataset - saccade latency measured as the absolute difference between peripheral target onset and saccade initiation, saccade accuracy as absolute error, velocity and acceleration dynamics, and trial-to-trial variability of each - but reports no procedure by which these were computed and no statistics for any of the comparisons it describes
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Microsoft Azure Machine Learning Studio for all modelling, preprocessing, feature selection, splitting and evaluation. No eye tracker is identified because no data were collected
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: No
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not stated, and the dataset is never named or cited, so its origin cannot be established
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: No ethics approval, consent procedure, data governance statement or data provenance appears anywhere in the paper. Because the dataset is secondary and unidentified, it is not possible to establish under what approvals the original data were collected or whether their reuse here was authorised
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Tabular eye-tracking summary attributes
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Nineteen attributes in the source dataset, of which the paper names average pupil area, percent time fixated, percent time not fixated relative to time in zone, and percent time fixated relative to time tracked, plus unspecified further fixation breakdowns and gaze-point measures. Ethnicity, blood type and eye colour were dropped as 'unrelated to tracking eye movement', leaving 16 inputs, which mutual-information filtering reduced to 6. The presence of blood type and eye colour among the attributes of an eye-tracking dataset is unexplained and is one of several signs that the data source is not well understood by the author
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: None - features arrive pre-computed in the source dataset
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, in narrative form: the six retained features are said to include mean amplitude of primary saccades, absolute error of saccades and latency 'among three others', with the remaining three never named
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Filter-based feature selection in Azure ML Studio scored by mutual information, described as 'a nonparametric, model-free method for scoring a set of features'
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Mean amplitude of primary saccades, absolute saccade error, and saccade latency; the other three retained features are not identified
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Described narratively with no supporting statistics anywhere - no means, standard deviations, effect sizes, p-values or confidence intervals appear in the paper. The claims are that mean saccade latency did not differ noticeably between groups but trial-to-trial variability was greater in autism; that autistic participants showed larger absolute saccade error and greater trial-to-trial variability of that error, amplified at higher target step amplitudes; and that maximum saccade velocity was distinctly lower in autism with a somewhat longer time to reach it, while acceleration rates were similar. The pattern - preserved central tendency with elevated variability - is the paper's most substantive observation and is consistent with the wider oculomotor literature, but nothing here substantiates it quantitatively
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised binary classification on tabular features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Two-Class Boosted Decision Tree, selected after comparison against linear regression, logistic regression, multiclass neural networks, support vector algorithms and quantile regression models. Three of those comparators - linear regression, quantile regression and a multiclass network - are not binary classifiers, so the comparison set is not well matched to the task
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: k-fold cross-validation, with k never stated. Critically, the pipeline order is given explicitly in both the methods narrative and the reproduced Azure workflow diagram: data are loaded, columns selected, mutual-information feature selection applied to the full dataset, and only then is the data split for cross-validation. Supervised feature selection therefore precedes and sits outside the resampling loop, so every fold's training set was chosen using label information from that fold's held-out data. The paper describes cross-validation as a safeguard against overfitting while implementing the step that defeats it
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy only, quoted as 88% in the text and as an 'estimated accuracy score of 88-91%' in the abstract. An ROC curve is displayed but no AUC value is given, and no sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, confusion matrix or confidence interval appears
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: 88% accuracy for the Two-Class Boosted Decision Tree (abstract: 88-91%), with an unlabelled ROC curve. No performance figures are reported for any of the compared algorithms, so the claim that boosted trees were best cannot be checked
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A boosted decision tree trained on six mutual-information-selected saccade features classified autism at a reported 88% accuracy. The descriptive observations - that mean saccade latency was similar between groups while trial-to-trial variability was elevated in autism, that absolute saccade error was larger and more variable especially at larger target amplitudes, and that maximum saccade velocity was lower with a longer time to reach it - point to increased variability rather than shifted central tendency as the oculomotor signature. None of these claims is supported by any statistic in the paper, and the classification result rests on supervised feature selection performed outside the cross-validation loop on a secondary dataset whose origin, participants and diagnostic basis are never described.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Greater trial-to-trial variability in saccade latency and accuracy, larger absolute saccade error increasing with target amplitude, and lower peak saccade velocity with longer time to peak
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Retain more than six features, since restricting to the top six may have cost accuracy; move the model out of Azure ML Studio to an environment allowing direct control of node count, leaf count and tree depth for hyperparameter tuning; and increase the participant count beyond 108 to build a more diverse and robust classifier and improve performance on edge cases
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: An undergraduate conference paper whose weaknesses are structural rather than incidental, and it is included here on the criteria rather than on its merits. The single decisive flaw is stated openly by the paper itself: the workflow applies mutual-information feature selection to the entire dataset and only afterwards splits for cross-validation, so label information from every held-out fold informed which six of sixteen features the model uses. The text presents cross-validation as protection against overfitting in the same passage where it describes the step that undermines it, which suggests the problem is not recognised rather than accepted. Beyond that, essentially nothing about the study can be verified. The dataset is secondary and never named, cited or described in provenance terms, so its participants, their ages, sexes, recruitment, diagnostic instruments and collection ethics are all unknown; the assertion that groups were of 'similar ages and genders' is unaccompanied by any figure. No statistic of any kind appears in the paper - the group differences in saccade latency, accuracy and velocity are asserted in prose with no means, no variances, no tests and no effect sizes, and read as a paraphrase of the source dataset's original publication rather than as analysis conducted here. Only accuracy is reported, at 88% in the text and 88-91% in the abstract, with an ROC curve whose AUC is never given and no sensitivity or specificity, which for a proposed diagnostic test is the omission that matters most. The comparator algorithms include linear regression and quantile regression, which are not binary classifiers, and no performance figures are given for any of them. The presence of blood type and eye colour among the attributes of a saccade dataset, dropped without comment on why they were there, further suggests the data source was not well understood. The record retains value for the review in two narrow ways: it is a clear instance of the gap/overlap paradigm being used for autism classification, and its descriptive claim that the oculomotor signature lies in elevated trial-to-trial variability rather than in shifted means is a hypothesis worth carrying into the synthesis and testing against the better-instrumented studies in the corpus.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups totalling 108 participants: 65 with autism and 43 without. No other-diagnosis comparison group. Nothing further is reported about either group, and because the dataset is secondary and unidentified, no additional characteristics can be recovered. The class imbalance (60:40) is never addressed in the modelling, and with accuracy as the only reported metric a classifier predicting the majority class throughout would score 60%.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'patients with ASD', 'ASD participants', 'affected patients', 'healthy patients', 'children with ASD'. Consistently medicalised - participants are 'patients' throughout and autism is repeatedly framed by severity, opening with the claim that 'symptoms range from completely debilitating to manageable'. The one nuanced observation concerns sex: the paper notes that 'patients with less noticeable symptoms, often girls, who are found to be better at copying stereotypical social patterns, are much harder to accurately diagnose, and often grow into adulthood without ever being diagnosed', which correctly identifies camouflaging as a diagnostic problem - though the study then reports no sex data at all.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: None reported. The entire participant description is 'a total of 65 participants with ASD and 43 with no autism present; these were closely related in terms of patients of similar ages and genders'. No ages, no age ranges, no sex counts, no ethnicity, no socioeconomic information, no country, no recruitment route and no statistical test of the asserted matching. This is the least participant characterisation of any included study in the corpus. It matters directly here because saccade latency, peak velocity and accuracy all change substantially across childhood and adolescence, so an unreported age difference would reproduce every group difference the paper describes.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Participants are described as 'confirmed to have ASD' with no further detail - no instrument, no criteria, no diagnostician, no date. Non-autistic status is asserted as 'no autism present' with no screening described. Because the dataset is secondary and is never named or cited, the diagnostic basis cannot be traced to a source publication either. The paper's own introduction emphasises that diagnosis requires a multidisciplinary team conducting in-depth neurological, cognitive and language testing, which makes the absence of any account of how these 108 labels were obtained more conspicuous.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No IQ, developmental, language, adaptive or severity measure, and no comorbidity information. Given the paper's opening claim that autism symptoms 'range from completely debilitating to manageable', the absence of any severity characterisation means nothing can be said about where on that range the classified sample sits.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: build a machine-learning classifier on saccade features to shorten and simplify autism diagnosis. Main findings: a Two-Class Boosted Decision Tree reached 88% accuracy (88-91% per the abstract); mutual-information filtering selected six of sixteen attributes, including mean primary saccade amplitude, absolute saccade error and latency; and descriptively, autistic participants showed comparable mean saccade latency but greater trial-to-trial variability, larger and more variable absolute saccade error amplified at higher target amplitudes, and lower peak velocity with longer time to reach it.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Not stated. No collection site, period, recruitment route or ethics approval appears, because the data are secondary and their origin is never identified. All modelling was performed in Microsoft Azure Machine Learning Studio.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: The gap/overlap paradigm, which is a well-chosen task for this question even though the paper does not explain why: extinguishing the fixation point before target onset (gap) versus leaving it visible (overlap) separates attentional disengagement from saccade execution, and the paper correctly reports that overlap latencies were substantially longer than gap latencies, confirming the manipulation worked in the source data. Each participant completed one block of 30 gap trials and one block of overlap trials. The paradigm is described but not motivated, and the gap-minus-overlap difference that gives it its diagnostic interest is never analysed as such.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis. No ethics approval, consent procedure, anonymisation statement, data governance policy or data provenance is reported anywhere. Since the dataset is neither named nor cited, it cannot be established under what approvals the original collection took place or whether this reuse was authorised - a governance gap that is qualitatively different from simply failing to report approval for one's own collection.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Microsoft Azure Machine Learning Studio for the entire pipeline - data ingestion, column selection, missing-value cleaning, filter-based feature selection, train/validation splitting, model training and evaluation - with a screenshot of the workflow reproduced as a figure. No eye-tracking hardware is identified. The paper notes that the Studio limited its ability to tune the model, being unable to 'adjust the number of nodes, leaves, and depth', which is an unusual admission that the tooling constrained the science.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Poor. The workflow diagram and the named Azure modules make the pipeline order legible - which is how the feature-selection leakage becomes visible - but almost nothing else is reproducible. Not reported: the dataset's identity or citation, k for the k-fold cross-validation, any hyperparameters, the random seed, the identity of three of the six retained features, performance figures for any comparator algorithm, the AUC value behind the plotted ROC curve, and any statistic supporting any descriptive claim. No code and no data.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged: that only 108 individuals were used and more would produce a more diverse and robust classifier with better performance on edge cases; that restricting to six features may have cost accuracy; and that Azure ML Studio prevented direct hyperparameter tuning. Not acknowledged, and decisive: mutual-information feature selection was applied to the full dataset before splitting, so supervised selection sits outside the cross-validation loop; no participant characteristics are reported so no confound can be excluded; the dataset's provenance, diagnostic basis and collection ethics are entirely unstated; only accuracy is reported for a proposed diagnostic test, with no sensitivity or specificity and an unlabelled ROC curve; the 60:40 class imbalance means a majority-class predictor scores 60%; the abstract's 88-91% range is unexplained against the text's single figure of 88%; the comparator set includes regression methods that are not binary classifiers; and every descriptive group difference is asserted without a statistic.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Retain more than six input features, since filtering may have discarded useful signal; move the model out of Azure ML Studio to permit tuning of node count, leaf count and tree depth; and expand beyond 108 participants for a more diverse and robust classifier better able to handle edge cases.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Saccadic eye movement - specifically latency, accuracy (absolute error), amplitude, peak velocity, acceleration and the trial-to-trial variability of each, measured under gap and overlap conditions, together with fixation-proportion and pupil-area measures carried in the dataset. The rationale offered for targeting saccades rather than social gaze is worth noting and is not made elsewhere in this corpus in quite these terms: sensorimotor abnormalities are said to be detectable 'prior to the identification of social and cognitive deficits', so an oculomotor marker could in principle precede the social behaviours on which clinical diagnosis depends.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No multimodal fusion - a single modality throughout, and no within-modality condition comparison is exploited either. The gap and overlap blocks are described and their latency difference noted, but the paradigm's defining contrast is never used as a feature or analysed as a group-by-condition interaction, which is the main analytic opportunity the design offers and the paper leaves unused.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A Two-Class Boosted Decision Tree, selected after comparing linear regression, logistic regression, multiclass neural networks, support vector algorithms and quantile regression models within Azure ML Studio. The stated justification - that ensemble boosting suits small tabular data better than the bagging of random forests or the hierarchical structure of neural networks - is reasonable in outline, and choosing a shallow tabular model over deep learning at n = 108 is the right instinct. But no performance figure is given for any comparator, so the selection cannot be assessed, and including linear and quantile regression in a binary classification comparison indicates the model set was not well matched to the task.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Nineteen tabular attributes reduced to sixteen by dropping ethnicity, blood type and eye colour, then to six by mutual-information filtering. The features arrive pre-computed, so no representation design was performed here. Two observations about the feature set are worth recording: the presence of blood type and eye colour in a saccade dataset is unexplained and suggests the source was not well understood; and dropping ethnicity as 'unrelated to tracking eye movement' removes the one variable that would have permitted any check on demographic confounding, which given the total absence of participant characteristics is a consequential deletion.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy alone, at 88% in the text and 88-91% in the abstract, with a plotted ROC curve whose AUC is never stated. For a paper proposing to replace multidisciplinary diagnostic assessment with a single test, the absence of sensitivity and specificity is the critical omission - these are the quantities that determine whether such a test would be usable, and with 60% of the sample autistic, accuracy alone cannot distinguish a useful classifier from one biased toward the majority class. No confusion matrix, no confidence interval, no per-fold variability and no statistical comparison against any baseline.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: The mutual-information filter is presented partly as an interpretability device - it 'communicates the attributes in the dataset which have the most predictive power in the model to drive future experimentation' - and three of the six retained features are named: mean amplitude of primary saccades, absolute saccade error and latency. The other three are never identified, and no model-derived importances, tree structure or decision rules are shown despite the classifier being a decision tree ensemble, which is among the more inspectable model families. The behavioural interpretation offered is that variability rather than central tendency distinguishes the groups, but the paper twice states that the implications are unclear - 'it is uncertain what further implications it has on sensorimotor activity' and 'it is still uncertain what the connections are between these dynamics and saccade error or latency'.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: k-fold cross-validation with k unstated, and with supervised feature selection performed on the complete dataset before the split. The paper sets out the sequence unambiguously - pass in data, select columns, apply filter-based feature selection, then split - and reproduces the Azure workflow confirming it. Because mutual information is computed against the class labels, every fold's feature set was chosen using information from that fold's test data, which biases the reported accuracy upward by an amount that cannot be estimated from what is reported. The paper's own description of cross-validation as a method that has 'been shown to lower bias and overfitting' sits directly alongside the step that defeats it. There is no held-out test set, no independent cohort, no external validation and no repetition.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No formal keyword list. Vocabulary: 'saccades', 'sensorimotor activity', 'predictive machine learning model', 'novel method of diagnosis', 'shorten time, resources, and uncertainty'. The register is throughput-oriented - the claim is about reducing the professionals, resources and waiting time required for diagnosis rather than about mechanism or accuracy per se.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: 2020 IEEE MIT Undergraduate Research Technology Conference (URTC) - an undergraduate research venue, which is relevant context for the depth of methodological scrutiny the work received.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2020. The framing is access and throughput: CDC prevalence of 1 in 54, an estimate of 'two undiagnosed cases for every three accurately diagnosed', and a description of comprehensive developmental evaluation as requiring 'a multidisciplinary team consisting of a psychologist, neurologist, psychiatrist, speech therapist, and may include others' conducting in-depth neurological, cognitive and language testing, with no single medical test available. Two framing points are distinctive within this corpus. First, the sex argument - girls with subtler presentations who are 'better at copying stereotypical social patterns' go undiagnosed into adulthood - correctly identifies camouflaging as a diagnostic failure mode, although the study then reports no sex data. Second, the rationale for choosing saccades over social gaze is temporal rather than practical: sensorimotor abnormalities are said to be present 'prior to the identification of social and cognitive deficits', which would make an oculomotor marker earlier-detectable in principle than the social behaviours clinical diagnosis relies on. The paper also states that saccades in autism are an under-researched area, which is broadly consistent with this corpus, where gaze studies overwhelmingly examine where people look rather than how their eyes move.

data_charting_rubrics.title: An Experimental Trial: Multi-Robot Therapy for Categorization of Autism Level Using Hidden Markov Model
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Ali S; Mehmood F; Ayaz Y; Sajid M; Sadia H; Nawaz R
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Children with autism at minimal and mild severity levels
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Robot-mediated interaction
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Add a categorisation layer to an existing robot-mediated intervention system, so that the performance data already generated during therapy can be used to infer a child's autism severity level without requiring a therapist to perform the categorisation. The stated gap is that robot therapies improve social and communication skills but 'no such model exists that can label the autism category based on the behavioral patterns of children'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Prospective intervention study with severity categorisation; single group of autistic children split into a training set and a prediction test set, with agreement against clinician CARS categories as the outcome
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: 15 weeks total - 9 weeks and 9 sessions per child for the 8 training participants (72 experiments), and 6 weeks and approximately 6 sessions per child for the 4 test participants (25 experiments)
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Two modules of the existing Multi-Robot-mediated Intervention System. The joint attention module delivers three escalating cue levels in least-to-most order - visual only ('Rasta', a cyclic change of the robot's eye colour, and blinking), then visual plus speech ('hi', 'Hello'), then visual plus speech plus motion ('move forward', 'move backward', 'stand up', 'sit down') - with the child's gaze monitored at each stage. The imitation module is gated by joint attention: the child must fixate one of the two robots for at least 5 seconds to activate it, after which that robot performs 'move forward', 'move backward', 'raise hands' and 'hands down' for the child to imitate. The child chooses which of the two robots to activate by making eye contact
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Autism Resource Center, Islamabad, with two robots placed in an arc approximately 1 m from the child, the child seated for joint attention and standing for imitation, and a Kinect positioned behind the robots
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Participants were recruited from the Autism Resource Center and 'evaluated clinically based on Childhood Autism Rating Scale Schedule (CARS) by the autism experts'. CARS also supplies the reference severity categories against which the model is compared. No CARS scores, cut-offs or inter-rater information are reported, and no DSM or ADOS assessment is described
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 12 (8 training, 4 test)
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Not reported. All participants were receiving services at an autism resource centre, so concurrent intervention is implied but uncharacterised
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Two: 'minimal' and 'mild', assigned by CARS. These are the classification target. Note that the paper's own introduction describes the DSM three-level scheme (level 1 mild, level 2 substantial support, level 3 severe) and states that 'this research focuses on autism level 1 and level 2', but the categories actually used - minimal and mild - correspond to neither that scheme nor standard CARS bands, and the mapping between them is never given
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: No - the study contains no non-autistic comparison group. The task is severity categorisation within autism, not case-control discrimination
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not applicable
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not applicable - single group. No analysis relates age to joint attention or imitation performance despite a 4.2 to 7.5 year span, over which both behaviours change substantially
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not applicable, though the sample is 11 boys and 1 girl and the single girl is in the test set
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not applicable
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Gaze direction from the robots' cameras and skeletal joint positions from a depth sensor
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Joint attention was measured by NAO camera gaze tracking using the ALGazeDetection module of the NaoqiPeoplesPerception SDK, computing delay in making eye contact with the robot and the duration for which eye contact was maintained. Imitation was measured by real-time Kinect tracking of the child's joints, comparing the child's movement against the robot's action to determine whether the action was imitated. Each module yields a percentage success rate per session, which is then binned into three ordinal categories
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Two NAO humanoid robots, chosen for human-like appearance and programmability; the Naoqi SDK with ALGazeDetection; a Microsoft Kinect for skeletal tracking; the previously published Multi-Robot-mediated Intervention System architecture
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: 97 session records from 12 children; no release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Video and depth recordings of identifiable children in a clinical setting, with a photograph of a child interacting with the robots reproduced in the paper. Governance reporting is partial: the study 'was approved by the autism specialist and director board of ARC' and 'parents have also signed the consent form', but no institutional review board or ethics committee approval is named, and no anonymisation or data-handling policy is described
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Two ordinal categorical variables derived from continuous session performance
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Joint attention binned as low (up to 50% success), delayed (above 50% and below 80%) or immediate (80% to 100%); imitation binned as partial (up to 50%), moderate (above 50% and below 80%) or full (80% to 100%). The bin boundaries were 'deduced in discussion with the therapist', which grounds them clinically but also means they were set with knowledge of the data. Reducing two continuous percentages to two three-level ordinal variables discards most of the measured information - the entire model input is one of nine possible cells
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: ALGazeDetection for gaze; Kinect skeletal tracking for imitation matching
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Not applicable - only two features exist
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not applicable
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Across all 12 children, average joint attention success was 65.47% and average imitation success 76.19%. Per-child averages are tabulated: joint attention ranged from 43.43% to 85.46% and imitation from 59.9% to 92.19%. Most children fell in the 'delayed' joint attention band and the 'moderate' or 'full' imitation bands. No relationship between these values and CARS severity is reported directly - the model is fitted to that relationship but the underlying association is never described statistically
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Probabilistic graphical model - a two-state Hidden Markov Model with categorical emissions
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: A Hidden Markov Model in which the hidden states are the two autism levels (minimal, mild) and the observable states are the joint attention and imitation categories, with posterior probabilities computed as the product of the two conditional probabilities P(category | joint attention) and P(category | imitation) - a conditional independence assumption between the two observables that is stated implicitly in the equations but never justified. The transition probabilities given (0.472, 0.543, 0.457, 0.528) do not form valid rows of a stochastic matrix as presented
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A held-out split by participant: 8 children and 72 sessions for training, 4 children and 25 sessions for testing, with test participants selected 'randomly'. Predictions are made per session rather than per child, so the 25 test predictions come from only 4 individuals - roughly 6 correlated observations each. The Cohen's kappa is computed with n = 25, treating those sessions as independent, which overstates the effective sample size by a factor of about six
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy (19 of 25 correct, 76%) and Cohen's kappa against clinician CARS categorisation (kappa = 0.52, p = 0.009, described as moderate agreement). No sensitivity, specificity, confusion matrix by class, confidence interval or per-child breakdown
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: The model matched the clinician's CARS category in 19 of 25 test sessions, giving 76% accuracy and a statistically significant moderate kappa of 0.52 (p = 0.009). The six errors are individually tabulated and are symmetric - three sessions predicted mild where CARS said minimal and three the reverse. The test data comprise 12 sessions with an actual category of mild and 13 with minimal, which is close to balanced
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: An HMM taking binned joint attention and imitation success rates from robot-mediated therapy sessions reproduced clinician CARS severity categories in 76% of 25 test sessions, with moderate agreement (kappa 0.52, p = 0.009). The practical claim is that severity categorisation can be derived from data the intervention already produces, so that 'this technique focuses on the prediction of the level of autism using robotic therapy, and therefore does not need a therapist for intervention or categorization prediction'. The design also carries a genuine engineering idea - gating the imitation module on the child's own gaze, so that the child chooses which of two robots to activate, making the interaction contingent rather than scripted.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Not applicable in the case-control sense. Within autism, lower joint attention and imitation success rates are treated as indicating greater severity, though this association is embedded in the fitted probabilities rather than reported directly
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: None stated as a distinct section. The conclusion asserts that robots integrated with HMM are useful for categorising severity, without identifying next steps, remaining limitations or required replication
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The engineering premise is reasonable and the clinical setting is real - a genuine intervention programme at an autism resource centre, running for 15 weeks, with severity categories assigned independently by clinicians using CARS. Two design ideas are worth recording: gating the imitation module on the child's own sustained gaze, so the child selects which robot to activate and the interaction becomes contingent rather than scripted; and the least-to-most cue hierarchy in the joint attention module, which is drawn from established prompting practice rather than invented. The analysis, however, does not support the conclusion drawn from it. The most serious problem is an internal contradiction between two tables. Table 2 assigns each of the four test children a single autism type - S9 mild, S10, S11 and S12 all minimal - so at most about six of the 25 test sessions should carry an actual category of mild. Table 4 instead shows 12 mild and 13 minimal actual categories across the 25 rows, which cannot be reconciled with per-child assignment unless the clinician's CARS category changed within child across sessions, which is never described or explained. Until that is resolved the reported 76% and kappa 0.52 cannot be interpreted. Second, the unit of analysis is the session, not the child: 25 predictions come from 4 individuals, and the kappa is computed as though they were 25 independent observations, overstating the effective sample by roughly sixfold and making the p = 0.009 unreliable. Third, the model's input is extraordinarily coarse - two continuous percentages binned into three levels each, giving nine possible input states - and the bin boundaries were set in discussion with the therapist who also supplied the labels. Fourth, the severity terminology is inconsistent with the paper's own introduction, which describes the DSM three-level scheme and states the study addresses levels 1 and 2, while the categories actually used are 'minimal' and 'mild', a mapping never provided. Fifth, the transition probabilities as printed do not form valid distributions, and the posterior is computed as a product of two conditionals, assuming conditional independence between joint attention and imitation - an assumption undermined by the study's own design, in which the imitation module is activated by joint attention and therefore cannot be independent of it. The claim that the approach removes the need for a therapist is also not supported: CARS categories assigned by clinicians are what the model is trained and evaluated against, so a therapist is required to create every label it learns from.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: A single group of 12 autistic children from the Autism Resource Center in Islamabad, split into 8 for training and 4 for the prediction test. There is no non-autistic comparison group and none is intended - the task is severity categorisation within autism rather than case-control discrimination, which makes this one of the few studies in the corpus targeting a graded clinical outcome rather than a binary diagnosis. The analysis unit is the intervention session rather than the child, so 97 sessions arise from 12 individuals and 25 test predictions from 4.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'autistic child', 'the patient', 'subjects'. Mixed person-first and 'ASD children', with 'patient' used for the severe end of the spectrum. The framing is medical and severity-graded, opening with an etymology of 'autism' as 'referring to the children with extreme inability to relate with others' and describing the spectrum as running from borders that 'overlap normality on one end' to 'extreme intellectual impairment caused by brain malfunctions on the other'. Robot-mediated therapy is justified on the ground that 'ASD children are more inclined towards robots because of their predictive behavior'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Twelve children, 11 male and 1 female, aged 4.2 to 7.5 years with a mean of 6.5 and standard deviation 0.98, described as of Asian background. Per-child age, sex, autism type and mean joint attention and imitation performance are tabulated individually, which is good practice and is what makes the internal inconsistency between the tables detectable. No IQ, language, adaptive functioning, comorbidity or socioeconomic information. The sex ratio of 11:1 is more extreme than population estimates and the single girl is in the test set. Age is not related to performance anywhere in the analysis despite a 3.3-year span across which joint attention and imitation both develop substantially.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Participants were recruited from an autism resource centre and 'evaluated clinically based on Childhood Autism Rating Scale Schedule (CARS) by the autism experts'. CARS then serves double duty as both the eligibility assessment and the reference standard for severity. No CARS scores are reported for any child, no cut-offs are given for the minimal and mild bands, no inter-rater reliability is established, and no DSM-5 or ADOS assessment is described. Because the model is evaluated purely by agreement with these CARS categories, the absence of any information about their reliability is the central weakness in the reference standard - a moderate kappa against an unquantified rater tells one little.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: CARS severity category only, as minimal or mild. No CARS total scores, no IQ, no language or adaptive measures, and no comorbidity information. The two performance measures the model consumes - joint attention and imitation success rates - are themselves clinically meaningful and are tabulated per child, but they are the model's input rather than an independent characterisation.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: use performance data already generated during robot-mediated therapy to categorise autism severity level without requiring a therapist to do the categorisation. Main findings: an HMM over binned joint attention and imitation categories matched clinician CARS categories in 19 of 25 test sessions (76% accuracy) with moderate agreement (kappa 0.52, p = 0.009); average joint attention success across all children was 65.47% and imitation 76.19%; and most children fell in the delayed joint attention and moderate-to-full imitation bands.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: The Autism Resource Center, Islamabad, with the study approved by the centre's autism specialist and director board and parental consent obtained. Two robots were placed in an arc approximately 1 m from the child, who sat for the joint attention module and stood for imitation, with a Kinect behind the robots. The authors state that the participant setting is illustrated 'to make the intervention replicable'. No external funding was received.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Two modules of an existing multi-robot intervention, each targeting a core impairment. The joint attention module escalates cues in a least-to-most hierarchy - visual (cyclic eye colour change, blinking), then visual plus speech, then visual plus speech plus motion - which is drawn from established prompting practice and allows the level of support required to be read off the cue level at which the child responds. The imitation module is contingent rather than scripted: the child must fixate one of the two robots for five seconds to activate it, then imitates four movements. Using two robots is a deliberate design choice presented as 'representing a triad human communication scenario', on the reasoning that dyadic robot interaction does not exercise the same social configuration as everyday multi-party interaction.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Longitudinal in structure - 9 sessions per training child over 9 weeks and about 6 per test child over 6 weeks - but the longitudinal dimension is not analysed. Sessions are treated as independent observations rather than as repeated measures within child, and no change over time in joint attention or imitation is examined despite the data being an intervention series. Data are video and depth recordings of identifiable young children, with a photograph of a child with the robots published. Governance is reported at centre level (autism specialist and director board approval, signed parental consent) but no institutional review board is named and no data-handling policy appears.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Two NAO humanoid robots with the Naoqi SDK, using the ALGazeDetection module of NaoqiPeoplesPerception to determine whether the child is looking at the robot and to compute eye-contact delay and duration; a Microsoft Kinect for real-time skeletal joint tracking to score imitation against the robot's action. The measurement is therefore fully automated within the intervention itself, requiring no separate assessment session - which is the practical strength of the approach.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Mixed. Well reported: the two intervention modules with their specific cues and actions, the physical setup with distances, the sensors and SDK modules used, the binning thresholds for both observable variables, the session and week counts for training and testing, and a per-child table of age, sex, autism type and mean performance. Poorly reported or absent: CARS scores and band definitions, how the HMM parameters were estimated from the 72 training sessions, the basis for the transition probabilities quoted, per-child test results, any code or data, and any statement of institutional ethics approval. The printed transition probabilities do not sum to valid distributions, and the posterior formula assumes conditional independence between joint attention and imitation without stating or justifying that assumption.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Essentially none. The paper has no limitations section, and the only self-critical remark is a defence of the sample size on the ground that 'the presented work is based on previous research that also uses a similar number of subjects'. Identifiable in review and unaddressed: Table 2 assigns each test child a single autism type (one mild, three minimal) while Table 4 records 12 mild and 13 minimal actual categories across 25 test sessions, which cannot be reconciled without an unexplained within-child change in CARS category, and until resolved makes the reported accuracy and kappa uninterpretable; the kappa treats 25 sessions from 4 children as independent, inflating the effective sample about sixfold; the two observables are binned to three levels each using thresholds set with the therapist who also supplied the labels; the conditional independence assumption is contradicted by the design, since the imitation module is activated by joint attention; the severity labels 'minimal' and 'mild' are never mapped to the DSM levels the introduction describes; and the claim that no therapist is needed is undercut by the fact that every training label comes from a therapist's CARS assessment.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: None stated. The conclusion asserts the model's usefulness without identifying required replication, larger samples, per-child validation, or the reconciliation of its own tables.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Two behaviours, both DSM-relevant core impairments: joint attention, operationalised as the delay before establishing eye contact with a robot and the duration for which it is sustained under escalating cue support; and imitation, operationalised as the proportion of four gross motor actions correctly reproduced. Measuring both within a single interaction, and gating one on the other, is the design's distinctive feature - most robot studies in this corpus measure a single behaviour.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Two behavioural channels are combined, but through a probabilistic model rather than a learned fusion: the posterior for each severity category is computed as the product of P(category | joint attention) and P(category | imitation). No single-channel baseline is reported, so the contribution of combining them cannot be assessed, and no ablation is performed. More problematically, the product form assumes the two observables are conditionally independent given severity - an assumption the study's own architecture violates, since the imitation module only activates once the child has sustained gaze on a robot for five seconds, making imitation performance conditional on joint attention performance by construction. There are also two sensing modalities (robot camera gaze and Kinect depth), but these map one-to-one onto the two behaviours rather than being fused.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A two-state Hidden Markov Model with the severity level as the hidden state and the two binned behavioural categories as observables. The choice is defensible for an intrinsically sequential intervention series with a latent clinical state, and the model is inherently interpretable. But the temporal structure that motivates an HMM is not actually exploited - sessions are treated as independent observations rather than as a sequence within child, no state transitions over the course of therapy are examined, and the reported posterior computation is a static Bayes calculation over two conditionals rather than a sequential inference. In effect the model functions as a naive Bayes classifier over nine input cells, with the HMM framing adding formalism rather than capability.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Two continuous session-level percentages, each collapsed into three ordinal bands at 50% and 80% thresholds - so the entire model input for a session is one of nine discrete combinations. This is by far the coarsest representation in the corpus. The thresholds were 'deduced in discussion with the therapist and according to the child's performance', which gives them clinical meaning but also means they were chosen with sight of the data by the same source that supplied the labels. The per-child averages in Table 2 show how much is discarded: joint attention values from 43.43% to 85.46% and imitation from 59.9% to 92.19% collapse into a handful of cells.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy (19 of 25, 76%) and Cohen's kappa (0.52, p = 0.009) against clinician CARS categorisation. Reporting kappa rather than accuracy alone is appropriate for an agreement study and is better practice than most of the corpus. But the kappa's n = 25 counts sessions rather than children, so its significance is overstated; no confidence interval accompanies it; and no sensitivity, specificity or per-class breakdown is given, though the individually tabulated 25 test rows allow these to be derived - three false-mild and three false-minimal errors, symmetric across classes.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: The model is interpretable by construction: every input is a named clinical category, every hidden state is a severity level, and the posterior is an explicit product of two conditional probabilities that a clinician could in principle compute by hand. All 25 test cases are tabulated with their joint attention category, imitation category, actual category and predicted category, so every prediction and every error is individually inspectable - a level of transparency almost no other study in the corpus offers. What is missing is any account of the fitted probabilities, so the direction and strength of the learned relationships cannot be read, and no analysis of which of the nine input cells the model handles well or badly.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: A held-out split by participant, with 8 children and 72 sessions for training and 4 children and 25 sessions for testing, and test participants selected randomly. Splitting by child rather than by session is the correct choice and is stated clearly. Two failures follow it, though. Prediction and evaluation both operate at the session level, so the 25 test observations are roughly six repeated measures from each of four children, and the kappa treats them as independent - the effective sample is 4 children, not 25 sessions. And the test set's composition is unbalanced at the child level (one mild, three minimal by Table 2), which cannot generate the 12-mild, 13-minimal distribution of actual categories reported in Table 4, leaving the evaluation internally inconsistent. There is no cross-validation, no repetition over alternative splits, no independent cohort and no confidence interval.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorder (ASD), imitation, joint attention, Hidden Markov Model (HMM), robot-mediated therapies, Multi-robot-mediated Intervention System (MRIS). Two of the six name the specific clinical constructs targeted, which reflects the paper's grounding in established autism intervention targets rather than in generic behavioural sensing.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Educational Computing Research, 60(3), 722-741 - an educational technology journal rather than a clinical or engineering venue, which is consistent with the intervention framing and with the limited statistical scrutiny the analysis received.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021. The framing combines prevalence growth (CDC estimates moving from 1 in 59 to 1 in 54) with a claim that autism is 'the fastest-growing developmental disorder in the USA with a 6% to 15% increase in rate per year'. Distinctively for this corpus, it invokes COVID-19 as a driver: 'especially under the current COVID-19 situation, the current research trends are focusing online for technology-based therapies', which situates robot-mediated intervention within a pandemic-era shift toward remote and technology-delivered care. The rationale for robots is given as controllability, accuracy, low cost and adaptability, plus the claim that autistic children are drawn to robots because of their predictable behaviour. The specific gap claimed is that existing robot therapies improve skills but cannot label severity, and the authors note a prior HMM attempt that 'failed to produce hidden Markov models that are indicative of a person's level of autism'.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis Based on Trajectories of Eye Tracking Data
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Cardoso TV; Michelassi GC; Franco FO; Sumiya FM; Portolese J; Brentani H; Machado-Lima A; Nunes FLS
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2021 IEEE 34th International Symposium on Computer-Based Medical Systems (CBMS), 50-55
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Children and adolescents with autism
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking and gaze
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Bring the joint attention paradigm within reach of automated analysis by solving the technical problem that has kept it there - that verifying joint attention requires following a gaze trajectory relative to objects that move and change appearance through a video, which fixed regions of interest cannot represent. The proposed solution is the floating region of interest, a region identified by its semantic identity rather than its screen position
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study with an engineering contribution in feature construction
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session per participant viewing three video stimuli of approximately 10 seconds each, divided into nine analysed segments
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Passive viewing of three purpose-built joint attention videos. In video A only the therapist's eyes move; in video B the gaze moves toward an object of interest; in video C the hand points to the object of interest. Each video is divided at the points where the set of relevant regions changes - for example, a video splits into three segments of 54, 115 and 90 frames as the therapist's gaze first rests, then moves to the object, then returns
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory eye tracking with participants seated 50-70 cm from the monitor; participants recruited through the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Sao Paulo's School of Medicine
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Evaluated by specialists using DSM-5 criteria together with the Childhood Autism Rating Scale, with CARS scores from 33 to 45 and a mean of 34.5.
