CARS was also administered to the typically developing group, all of whom scored below the diagnostic threshold of 30 - so both groups were assessed with the same instrument, which is stronger than the corpus norm
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Mean 10 years; no standard deviation reported
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: CARS scores reported as a group range (33-45, mean 34.5) but not used analytically - no severity-stratified analysis and no relation between CARS score and classifier output
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes, by CARS administration with all scores below the 30-point diagnostic threshold - an actively screened comparison group rather than an assumed one
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd_controls: Mean 10 years; no standard deviation reported
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Matched on mean (both groups average 10 years) but not on range - the autistic group spans 5-18 and the typically developing group 3-15, so the extremes differ by three years at each end. No standard deviations or statistical test are reported, and age is not entered into the model
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Closely similar proportions - 68% male in the autistic group and 67% in the typically developing group - though no test is reported
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Confirmed by CARS below threshold
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Gaze fixation and visit data during video viewing
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Regions of interest were demarcated semi-automatically: a specialist draws a rectangle on the first frame defining a region, and an automated procedure propagates it across subsequent frames until the region set changes. Frames are then processed to obtain Cartesian coordinates and centres of each region, with multiple simultaneous regions distinguished by colour, and an algorithm links regions across frames by semantic identity so that a moving, resizing object such as a hand is treated as one region throughout. Gaze records - approximately ten per video frame given the 300 Hz sampling rate - are assigned to these floating regions and summarised into 15 features per region per segment
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Tobii Pro TX300 with a removable 23-inch monitor, sampling up to 300 Hz and tolerating head movement up to 50 cm/s; viewing distance 50-70 cm; Python with scikit-learn for modelling
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: An 86-participant joint attention eye-tracking dataset with purpose-built video stimuli; no release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze coordinate data over purpose-recorded video stimuli. No ethics committee approval, consent procedure or data governance statement appears anywhere in the paper, despite participants being children as young as 3 recruited through a university psychiatry department - a notable omission given the otherwise careful clinical characterisation
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Trajectory and timing features computed per region of interest per video segment
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Fifteen features per region: mean distance from gaze to region centre, its standard deviation and coefficient of variation; binary visit and fixation indicators; start time of first visit and of first fixation, both measured in eye-tracking record units and permitting negative values; order of the longest visit and of the longest fixation; duration of first visit and first fixation; longest visit and longest fixation; and percentage of visits and of fixations relative to segment duration. Each individual is represented by a 15 x R vector per segment, where R is the number of regions in that segment, giving nine feature vectors per person. Ten of the fifteen features are described as newly defined for this study on the basis of specialist observation
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Semi-automatic specialist demarcation with automated propagation; custom image processing to track region centres; Tobii-derived fixation and visit definitions, where a visit spans from the first fixation inside a region to the subsequent fixation outside it
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Not per feature, but reported at the level of video segment and region type through the ensemble selection process
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Exhaustive search over all 511 possible combinations of the nine segment-specific classifiers, with the winning combination read as identifying the informative segments
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Segments 1, 3 and 8 formed the best ensemble, corresponding to the three fundamental stages of joint attention - the therapist's gaze resting on the screen, moving to the object of interest, and returning. Regions encompassing the eyes proved more discriminative than regions covering the therapist's hand. Every individual segment classifier scored below 75%, which the authors read as showing that 'the complete action process is necessary'
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: No directional group comparisons are reported - the paper gives no means, distributions or statistical tests for any feature by group. All group information is embedded in the classifiers, which is a substantive reporting gap for a study whose novelty lies in its feature construction
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Ensemble of tree-based classifiers with segment-wise decomposition
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Nine random forest classifiers, one per video segment, combined by weighted vote against a threshold. Three combination strategies were compared: all nine with equal weights and threshold swept 1-9; all nine weighted by their individual accuracies with threshold swept 1.0-5.9 in 0.1 steps; and variable configuration, testing all 511 non-empty subsets of the nine classifiers with equal weights and threshold swept up to the subset size. Random forest hyperparameters (max features, min samples leaf, n estimators) were tuned by GridSearchCV, and five SMOTE variants (Borderline, KMeans, standard, SVM, Tomek) were compared alongside the unbalanced original
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 10-fold cross-validation used to estimate performance for every ensemble strategy, classifier combination and threshold. SMOTE class balancing was applied to the training samples only, which is stated explicitly and is the correct handling. The decisive weakness is that the same 10-fold estimate served as the selection criterion for an extremely large search space - three ensemble strategies, 511 classifier subsets, dozens of threshold values, five balancing methods and a grid over three random forest hyperparameters per segment - and the reported result is the maximum over that space with no outer validation loop
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, precision, specificity and F1, reported for the best configuration of each of the three ensemble strategies. Reporting specificity alongside sensitivity is what makes the result interpretable and reveals its main weakness
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Best configuration (variable ensemble using segments 1, 3 and 8 at threshold 2): accuracy 0.75, sensitivity 0.87, precision 0.78, specificity 0.53, F1 0.82. Homogeneous configuration with equal weights: accuracy 0.71, sensitivity 0.93, precision 0.72, specificity 0.30, F1 0.81. Homogeneous configuration with accuracy-based weights: accuracy 0.71, sensitivity 0.77, precision 0.79, specificity 0.60, F1 0.76. All three configurations trade specificity heavily for sensitivity, and the highest-sensitivity model correctly identifies only 30% of typically developing participants
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Gaze trajectory features computed against semantically tracked floating regions of interest classified autism at 75% accuracy with 87% sensitivity and an F1 of 0.82, but only 53% specificity. The most interpretable result is the segment analysis: the best ensemble used the three segments corresponding to the therapist's gaze resting, moving to the object, and returning, and no single segment reached 75% on its own, indicating that the discriminative information lies in the complete joint attention sequence rather than in any one moment. Regions containing the eyes outperformed regions containing the pointing hand. The floating region concept is the paper's substantive contribution: it allows a moving, resizing object to be treated as one semantic region across frames, which is what makes trajectory-based analysis of a dynamic joint attention scene possible at all.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Not reported directionally. The classifier finds discriminative information in gaze timing and proximity relative to the therapist's eyes across the full sequence of gaze shift and return, but no group means or directions are given
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Expand the dataset to address class imbalance rather than relying on synthetic samples; develop a computational technique to identify regions of interest automatically, since demarcation still requires a therapist; and explore other machine learning methods such as genetic algorithms for constructing a meta-classifier
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The engineering contribution is genuine and well motivated. Joint attention is arguably the most clinically meaningful paradigm in this corpus - it is an early differentiator and it is what clinicians actually assess - and the reason it is under-represented in computational work is precisely the problem this paper identifies: analysing it requires following gaze relative to objects that move and change appearance, which fixed regions cannot represent. The floating region of interest, defined by semantic identity rather than screen coordinates, is a clean solution, and the anticipation feature that allows negative first-visit times to capture gaze arriving before the region appears is a thoughtful operationalisation of the anticipatory component of joint attention. The clinical characterisation is also above corpus average: DSM-5 plus CARS for the autistic group with scores reported, and CARS administered to the comparison group as well so that typical development is verified rather than assumed. SMOTE is correctly applied to training folds only, and the authors state this explicitly. Two problems bound what the numbers mean. The first is multiplicity on a large scale: the reported 75% is the maximum over three ensemble strategies, 511 classifier subsets, swept thresholds, five balancing methods and a grid search over random forest hyperparameters for each of nine segments - all evaluated on the same 10-fold cross-validation that produces the reported figure, with no outer loop. The finding that segments 1, 3 and 8 are the informative ones is a selection result from that search, not an independent test, and its clean correspondence to the three stages of joint attention is a post hoc interpretation. The second is specificity: at 0.53 the model correctly identifies barely half the typically developing participants, and the equal-weight ensemble at 0.30 specificity is close to useless as a discriminator despite a 0.81 F1. The authors defend high sensitivity as appropriate for a rule-out test in early diagnosis, which is a legitimate framing, but a test with 53% specificity would refer roughly half of all typically developing children for further assessment, and this consequence is not discussed. Finally, no ethics approval or consent statement appears anywhere despite participants as young as three, and no group-level feature comparisons are reported, so the paper's own novel features are never characterised descriptively.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups totalling 86 participants: 56 autistic (38 male, 18 female, aged 5-18, mean 10) and 30 typically developing (20 male, 10 female, aged 3-15, mean 10). The class ratio is 65:35 in favour of autism, which the authors identify as a limitation and address with SMOTE on training folds. No other-diagnosis comparison group. At 86 participants this is among the larger single-site eye-tracking cohorts in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'individuals with ASD', 'children with ASD', 'Typical Development (TD)', 'patients'. Person-first in most places, with 'patients' used once for the whole sample. The framing is neutral and developmental rather than deficit-laden, describing autism as 'a neurodevelopmental disorder with clinical presentation and varied functional impact' and grounding joint attention in normal development - infants follow gaze within days of birth and develop referential understanding of gaze cues over the first two years.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Autistic group: 56 participants, 38 male and 18 female, aged 5-18 with mean 10. Typically developing: 30 participants, 20 male and 10 female, aged 3-15 with mean 10. Means match exactly and sex proportions are close (68% versus 67% male), but the age ranges differ at both ends, no standard deviations are given, and no statistical test of matching is reported. The age span is wide - 3 to 18 years - across which gaze-following and anticipation in joint attention change substantially, and age is neither modelled nor controlled. CARS scores are reported for both groups (33-45, mean 34.5 for autism; below 30 for typical development), which is more clinical detail than most of the corpus provides. No IQ, language, comorbidity, ethnicity or socioeconomic data.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Specialist evaluation using DSM-5 criteria together with CARS, with the autistic group's scores reported as a range and mean. Notably, CARS was administered to the typically developing group as well, confirming all scored below the 30-point diagnostic threshold - so both groups were assessed on the same instrument and control status is verified rather than assumed. The paper also footnotes the CARS threshold explicitly. What is missing is any account of who performed the assessments, when, or with what reliability, and no ADOS or ADI-R is described.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: CARS scores for both groups, reported as ranges and a group mean. The autistic range of 33-45 spans mild-to-moderate through severe on standard CARS bands, so the sample covers meaningful severity variation - but this is never exploited. No severity-stratified analysis is performed, no relationship between CARS score and classifier output is examined, and no IQ, language or adaptive measure appears. Given that the discriminative signal is in anticipatory gaze during joint attention, which plausibly varies with severity, relating classifier confidence to CARS would have been a straightforward and valuable analysis.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: build gaze trajectory features that can represent the joint attention paradigm computationally, using semantically tracked floating regions of interest, and classify autism from them. Main findings: 75% accuracy, 87% sensitivity, 53% specificity and 0.82 F1 from an ensemble using three of nine video segments; the informative segments correspond to the therapist's gaze resting, shifting to the object, and returning; no single segment exceeded 75% alone; and regions containing the eyes outperformed those containing the pointing hand.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory eye tracking with participants recruited through the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Sao Paulo's School of Medicine, in collaboration with the School of Arts, Sciences and Humanities and the bioinformatics postgraduate programme. Funded by CNPq, FAPESP/INCT-MACC, CAPES and PRONAS/PCD. No ethics approval statement appears.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Three purpose-built 10-second joint attention videos at 1920 x 1080, forming a graded series: in video A only the therapist's eyes move; in video B the gaze shifts toward an object of interest; in video C the hand points to the object. Each is segmented at the points where the set of relevant regions changes, giving nine analysed segments in total. The design is unusually well matched to the construct - joint attention involves coordinated mutual engagement with a third entity, so a stimulus that isolates gaze-only, gaze-to-object and gaze-plus-point conditions decomposes the paradigm into its components, and the segment-level ensemble then reveals which components carry information.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single viewing session per participant with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates over purpose-recorded video of a therapist. No ethics committee approval, parental consent procedure, anonymisation or data governance statement appears anywhere in the paper, despite participants aged from 3 years recruited through a university psychiatry department - the most conspicuous reporting gap in an otherwise clinically careful study.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Tobii Pro TX300 with a removable 23-inch monitor, up to 300 Hz sampling and head-movement tolerance to 50 cm/s, at 50-70 cm viewing distance; Python with scikit-learn including GridSearchCV and SMOTE implementations. The 300 Hz sampling against video frame rate yields approximately ten gaze records per frame, which is what makes fine-grained trajectory features and the anticipation measure feasible.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong on the feature and modelling pipeline, absent on governance and descriptive results. Fully reported: all 15 features with their definitions and which were newly devised; the floating region identification procedure including specialist demarcation of the first frame and automated propagation; segment boundaries with frame counts; the missing-value imputation rule with its constant; Min-Max normalisation; the SMOTE variants and random forest hyperparameter grids; all three ensemble strategies with their threshold ranges; and the 10-fold cross-validation. Absent: any ethics or consent statement; any group-level descriptive statistics for the features; the identity of the selected hyperparameters; data or code release; and any account of missing or excluded data.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged: the dataset is imbalanced and synthetic sampling is a stopgap pending more real data; region demarcation still requires a therapist and automatic identification would make the method faster; and accuracy could be improved with other methods such as genetic algorithms for meta-classifier construction. The low specificity is noted and defended rather than treated as a limitation - the authors argue that 'our major goal is to capture all possible individuals with the disorder' and that highly sensitive tests suit early rule-out. Not acknowledged: the reported 75% is the maximum over 511 classifier subsets, three ensemble strategies, swept thresholds, five balancing methods and per-segment hyperparameter grids, all selected on the same 10-fold estimate with no outer validation loop, so the figure is optimistically biased and the segment-1-3-8 finding is a selection outcome rather than an independent result; the practical consequence of 53% specificity - referring roughly half of typically developing children onward - is not discussed; ages span 3-18 with different ranges per group and no adjustment; CARS scores are collected but never related to model output; and no ethics approval is reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Enlarge the dataset so that class balance can be achieved with real rather than synthetic samples; automate region-of-interest identification to remove the therapist from the loop and speed the method; and explore alternative machine learning approaches including genetic algorithms for meta-classifier construction. The authors also note the approach generalises to any joint attention video provided a therapist marks the first and last frame of each region.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Anticipatory and referential gaze during joint attention - specifically whether and when the participant's gaze arrives at, dwells on and returns from the regions a therapist's gaze or gesture directs it toward. The construct targeted is more specific than the social-attention measures elsewhere in the corpus: not how much a child looks at faces, but whether the gaze tracks a referential sequence in time, including whether it arrives before the referent appears. The anticipation feature, which permits negative first-visit times computed against records from the preceding segment, is the direct operationalisation of that.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-modal fusion - gaze only. The combination that does occur is across time and across regions: nine segment-specific classifiers are ensembled, and the finding is that the whole is greater than any part, with every individual segment classifier below 75% while the best three-segment combination reaches it. This is a temporal rather than sensory fusion result, and it carries a clear message for the corpus's video-based studies - that a joint attention response is a sequence and that classifying any single moment of it underperforms classifying the sequence. The authors' own reading is that segments 1, 3 and 8 'present three fundamental stages of JA' and that 'the complete action process is necessary', though this identification comes from an exhaustive search rather than an a priori hypothesis.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Random forests, one per video segment, combined into an ensemble by weighted voting - a design that mirrors the temporal structure of the stimulus rather than flattening it. Three combination strategies are compared systematically, and the exhaustive variant testing all 511 subsets is thorough as an exploration but constitutes a very large selection space when evaluated on the same cross-validation used for reporting. No deep learning, which is appropriate at 86 participants, and no single-model baseline over concatenated features is reported, so the benefit of the segment-wise decomposition itself is not isolated.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Fifteen trajectory and timing features per region per segment, giving nine feature vectors of 15 x R dimensions per participant. Three aspects are distinctive. First, distance-to-centre features (mean, standard deviation, coefficient of variation) capture how tightly gaze is held on a region rather than merely whether it was there. Second, ordinal features (order of longest visit, order of longest fixation) encode sequence position within a segment. Third, the anticipation features permit negative values by searching gaze records from the preceding segment, so a participant whose gaze arrives before the referent appears is distinguished from one who arrives promptly. Missing values, arising when a region was never visited or fixated, are imputed as the segment's final time or order multiplied by an empirically chosen constant of 4 - a defensible encoding of 'never' as an extreme value, though the constant was tuned rather than derived.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity, precision, specificity and F1 for the best configuration of each ensemble strategy. Reporting all five is what makes the result honestly interpretable and exposes the sensitivity-specificity imbalance that accuracy alone would conceal - the equal-weight ensemble achieves an F1 of 0.81 while correctly classifying only 30% of typically developing participants. No AUC, no confidence intervals, no per-fold variability and no statistical comparison between strategies, so whether 0.75 differs meaningfully from 0.71 on 86 participants is not established.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No model-explanation method, but the ensemble structure delivers interpretability at the level that matters clinically. Because each classifier corresponds to a specific video segment, the winning combination identifies which moments of the joint attention sequence carry discriminative information - here the gaze at rest, the gaze shifting to the object, and the gaze returning. The authors also report that regions containing the eyes outperformed regions containing the therapist's hand, which speaks directly to the gaze-versus-gesture distinction in joint attention. Both findings are interpretable and clinically legible; both are outcomes of an exhaustive search rather than tests of prior hypotheses, and no group-level feature statistics are reported to corroborate them.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: 10-fold cross-validation with SMOTE correctly restricted to training samples - a detail explicitly stated and often got wrong elsewhere in this corpus. The problem is scale of selection: three ensemble strategies, all 511 classifier subsets, thresholds swept in fine increments, five SMOTE variants plus the unbalanced original, and a GridSearchCV over three hyperparameters for each of nine random forests, with the best result across all of that reported from the same 10-fold estimate. There is no outer cross-validation loop, no held-out set, no independent cohort and no repetition over alternative fold partitions. The consequence is that both the headline accuracy and the substantive claim about which segments matter are selection outcomes rather than validated findings.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: Autism Spectrum Disorder; Ensemble Method; Eye tracking; Image processing; Joint attention; Machine Learning; Random Forest; Trajectory; Typical Development. 'Trajectory', 'joint attention' and 'image processing' together capture the contribution - the paper is about representing a dynamic referential sequence computationally, with classification as the demonstration.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: 2021 IEEE 34th International Symposium on Computer-Based Medical Systems (CBMS), pages 50-55 - a medical informatics conference, with authorship spanning computing, bioinformatics and a university psychiatry department.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021. The framing identifies a specific methodological gap rather than a general access problem: joint attention is 'an important marker to differentiate children with ASD from 12 months onwards', its verification 'requires the therapist's experience, attention and time spent, considering that the specialist's observation not using any tools is the most common practice', and the obstacle to automating it is technical - 'the studies cited in the literature that use ET signals combined with computational methods do not process trajectory data or ignore that the paradigm involves the displacement of regions of interest'. The developmental grounding is unusually explicit for this corpus, linking gaze-following to inferences about intentions and motivations and framing anticipation as 'the action of providing a view of the immediate future based on the immediate past', which 'appears to be difficult in ASD'. That framing directly motivates the anticipation feature, giving the paper a rare coherence between construct, feature design and analysis.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Autistic spectrum traits detection and early screening: A machine learning based eye movement study
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Lin Y; Gu Y; Xu Y; Hou S; Ding R; Ni S
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: Journal of Child and Adolescent Psychiatric Nursing, 35
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Two quite different groups: non-clinical adults dichotomised by autistic-trait questionnaire score in the preliminary experiment, and young diagnosed autistic males in the test experiment
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking and gaze (in virtual reality)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Provide a rapid, deployable first-round autism screening method for settings where clinical resources are scarce, by recording gaze in an immersive VR scene rather than to a face on a monitor - on the argument that static or isolated social stimuli do not elicit the atypical social attention that real-world viewing does, since 'for static images or those which present social information in isolation, social attention is normal in autism'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Two-stage study: a preliminary classification experiment on non-clinical adults dichotomised by questionnaire score, followed by a test experiment applying the fitted models to a separate group of diagnosed autistic participants
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One VR exposure of 15-20 seconds per participant
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Human adults (preliminary) and children and young people (test)
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Free viewing of a single 3D virtual reality scene built in Unity3D - a couple in a garden with their dog - containing social stimuli (figures), an animal and landscape. No instruction or response was required; the participant simply wore the headset while gaze was recorded
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory at Tsinghua University's Shenzhen campus; test participants recruited through the Shenzhen Autism Society
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: In the preliminary experiment, none - the positive class is an Autism-spectrum Quotient score at or above the sample median. In the test experiment, existing ASD diagnoses of unstated origin
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Preliminary experiment: the 50-item Autism-spectrum Quotient, covering social skills, attention switching, attention to detail, communication and imagination, with the class boundary set at 21 - the sample mean and approximate median - so that 52 participants scoring 21 or above were labelled '1 (ASD)' and 55 scoring below were labelled '0'. The standard AQ clinical cut-off is 32, so this threshold does not identify autism and the '1' label denotes above-median trait scores in a general population. Test experiment: participants 'already diagnosed with ASD' recruited via the Shenzhen Autism Society, with no instrument, criteria or diagnostician reported, and no AQ administered
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 52 above-median-AQ adults in the preliminary experiment; 22 diagnosed autistic participants in the test experiment
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Preliminary above-median group 24.7 +/- 5.2 years; test group 12.68 +/- 7.61 years
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Not reported; the test group's standard deviation of 7.61 years around a mean of 12.68 implies a very wide spread, plausibly from early childhood into adulthood
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Preliminary above-median group 25 female / 30 male; test group all male
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: AQ total scores are reported for the preliminary sample (mean 21.0, SD 5.2) but not for the test group, and no severity measure was obtained for the diagnosed participants
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Only in the sense that the preliminary experiment's below-median group serves as the negative class. There is no non-autistic comparison group in the test experiment at all, so only recall can be computed there
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: No - the preliminary sample is a general adult sample with no screening, and the below-median group is defined solely by scoring under 21 on the AQ
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 55 below-median-AQ adults in the preliminary experiment; 0 in the test experiment
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Within the preliminary experiment, yes - 24.7 versus 25.0 years with near-identical spreads. Between the preliminary and test experiments, no, and the mismatch is severe: models trained on adults averaging 24.84 years were applied to a group averaging 12.68 years, and because age is an explicit model feature, every test participant falls at or beyond the edge of the training distribution on a variable the classifiers use
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Balanced within the preliminary experiment (49 women, 58 men overall). The test group is entirely male, and sex is also an explicit model feature, so the test participants are additionally unrepresentative on a second modelled variable
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not established for either group
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Gaze point coordinates in a virtual scene
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Gaze coordinates from the aGlass infrared module were projected into a unit square and scaled to image dimensions. The scene image was manually segmented into figure, animal and landscape regions, each filled with a distinct RGB value, and K-means clustering over pixel colour recovered three clusters corresponding to those regions. Each gaze point was assigned to a cluster by the same K-means model, producing point-cluster pairs from which nine proportion features were computed
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: HTC Vive headset with an embedded aGlass eye-tracking module using infrared gaze detection; Unity3D for scene construction and gaze-recording scripts; scikit-learn with GridSearchCV for modelling
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Gaze data from 107 adults and 22 diagnosed autistic participants; available from the corresponding author on reasonable request
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - available on reasonable request
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze coordinates within a synthetic scene plus AQ scores and demographics; low identifiability. Governance is reported for both experiments: approval by the Institutional Review Board of the Department of Psychology, Tsinghua University (No. THUDP20), with participant safety emphasised throughout
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Region-occupancy and transition proportions derived from gaze clustering, plus demographic variables
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Eleven in total. Three total-time proportions - the share of gaze points falling in the landscape, figure and animal regions. Three continuity proportions - the share of gaze points falling continuously within each region. Three transition proportions - the share of conversions between landscape and figure, landscape and animal, and figure and animal. Plus age and sex as demographic features. Including age and sex as predictors is the decision that most undermines the test experiment, since the test group differs from the training population on both
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: K-means over pixel RGB values to define regions; custom counting of gaze points, continuous runs and transitions
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, from the tree-based models
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Feature importance from tree-based models, plus visual comparison of per-feature density distributions between the two label groups
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The two continuity features for the figure and animal regions (continuousnum1 and continuousnum2) were the most important across all tree-based models, which the authors interpret as showing that 'the proportion of time to observe figure and animal region continuously can distinguish participants with low and high levels of autistic traits effectively'. Sustained rather than total looking is therefore the discriminative quantity - a substantive and transferable observation
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reported only as density-distribution comparisons in a figure, with no group means, tests or effect sizes. The narrative claim is that for several features - total figure time, total animal time, continuous animal time, and the landscape-animal and figure-animal transitions - the data from diagnosed autistic participants show 'a higher concentration' than the preliminary sample. Whole-sample feature means are tabulated (landscape occupies 76% of gaze points, figures 17%, the animal 7%) but never broken down by group
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Comparison of classical classifiers with an ensemble combiner
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Logistic regression and naive Bayes, both preceded by PCA to address multicollinearity and the naive independence assumption respectively; KNN with normalisation and tuning of k and weights; SVM with tuning of C, gamma and kernel and standardised features; decision tree tuned on max depth, min impurity decrease and min samples split; random forest tuned on n_estimators and max_features; gradient boosting tuned on five parameters; and an ensemble combining the seven by both probability averaging (predict 1 if mean probability is at least 0.5) and majority voting (predict 1 if at least four models agree)
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A single 70/30 train/test split of the 107 preliminary participants, with threefold cross-validation and GridSearchCV inside the training portion for hyperparameter tuning. The test experiment then applied the fitted models to 22 diagnosed autistic participants, which functions as an external check but only on the positive class - with no negative cases, only recall is computable, and specificity in the diagnosed population is entirely unknown. Data cleaning replaced values identified as abnormal with the mean of normal data, with neither the outlier criterion nor the stage at which this occurred relative to the split reported
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUC for all eight models in the preliminary experiment, and recall only in the test experiment
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Preliminary experiment: ensemble best at accuracy 0.73, precision 0.68, recall 0.81, F1 0.74 and AUC 0.90; random forest and gradient boosting both 0.70 accuracy, 0.81 recall, 0.72 F1 and AUC 0.68 and 0.66; decision tree 0.70 accuracy and AUC 0.68; SVM 0.61 accuracy; logistic regression 0.61 with recall of only 0.44; naive Bayes 0.58; KNN 0.55. Test experiment recall: ensemble 0.77, naive Bayes highest at 0.82, random forest 0.73, decision tree 0.64, SVM 0.59, gradient boosting 0.55, KNN 0.45, and logistic regression 0.00. Note that the ensemble's reported AUC of 0.90 exceeds every constituent model's AUC (range 0.57-0.68) by a margin that combination alone cannot plausibly produce
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Gaze recorded during 15-20 seconds of free viewing in a VR garden scene, reduced to nine region-occupancy and transition proportions plus age and sex, separated above-median from below-median autistic-trait scorers among 107 adults at 73% accuracy with an ensemble classifier, and recalled 77% of 22 separately recruited diagnosed autistic participants. The most informative features across all tree-based models were the proportions of continuous - rather than merely total - looking at the figure and animal regions. The paper's own most revealing result is the instability of individual models between experiments: gradient boosting fell from 0.81 recall to 0.55 while naive Bayes rose from 0.56 to 0.82, which the authors correctly read as evidence that 'the data patterns of the adults we recruited in the preliminary experiment are somehow different from those autistic adults'.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Reduced sustained looking at social figures and altered continuity of attention to the animal region; no direction or magnitude is quantified
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Improve eye-tracking stability and accuracy, since aGlass precision was insufficient and VR headsets met resistance from some autistic participants; enlarge both samples to reduce small-sample bias; consult a specialist psychologist when designing scenes, since not all scenes with social stimuli discriminate; and construct several scenes and select the best-performing one
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The design idea is sound and the paper states its own rationale well: static or isolated social stimuli may not elicit atypical social attention because 'for static images or those which present social information in isolation, social attention is normal in autism', so an immersive scene containing people, an animal and a landscape should engage the mechanism that face-on-a-screen paradigms miss. Ethics approval is reported for both experiments, data are offered on request, eight models are compared transparently with all metrics tabulated, and the finding that continuity of looking rather than total looking carries the discriminative information is a genuinely useful observation. Three problems nonetheless undermine the central claim. The first is conceptual and decisive: in the preliminary experiment the positive class is defined by a median split of AQ scores in a non-clinical adult sample, with the boundary set at 21 because the histogram happened to be symmetric there. The standard AQ clinical cut-off is 32; the paper's own sample mean is 21.0 with SD 5.2, so essentially the entire training sample sits within the normal range. Labelling the upper half of a general population distribution '1 (ASD)' means the models were trained to detect being slightly above average on a trait questionnaire, not to detect autism - and the paper's Table 2 compounds this by reporting the high-trait group's mean AQ as 16.6 and the low-trait group's as 25.7, which are transposed. The second problem is that age and sex are model features while the test group differs sharply from the training population on both: models fitted to adults averaging 24.84 years, roughly evenly split by sex, were applied to an all-male group averaging 12.68 years with a standard deviation of 7.61. Every test participant therefore lies at or beyond the edge of the training distribution on two modelled variables, and the observed recall cannot be attributed to gaze behaviour rather than to demographics. The third is that the test experiment contains no negative cases, so only recall is computable and specificity in the diagnosed population is unknown - a classifier biased toward predicting '1' would score well by construction. Two smaller signals reinforce the concern: the ensemble's AUC of 0.90 exceeds every constituent model's AUC of 0.57-0.68 by a margin that averaging or voting cannot produce, and outlier values were replaced by the mean of 'normal data' with no criterion given and no statement of whether this preceded the train/test split. The authors deserve credit for reporting the recall instability across experiments and drawing the correct inference from it - that the two populations differ - but that inference is precisely the reason the headline figures should not be read as autism screening performance.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two entirely separate samples serving different roles. The preliminary experiment used 107 non-clinical adults (49 women, 58 men, mean age 24.84 +/- 5.24) split by AQ score into 52 above-median and 55 below-median. The test experiment used 22 young autistic males (mean age 12.68 +/- 7.61) recruited through the Shenzhen Autism Society, with no comparison group. The two samples differ in age by roughly twelve years on average, in sex composition (mixed versus all-male) and in clinical status (trait-scored general population versus diagnosed), so the second is not a held-out sample from the first population but a different population entirely.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'autistic persons', 'people with autism', 'patients', 'participants with obvious and unobvious autistic traits', 'typically developing (TD)', 'healthy children'. Predominantly person-first but with heavy disease framing - autism is repeatedly called 'a very complex disease' and 'a mental disease', and the aims include 'reducing the incidence of ASD', which conflates screening with prevention of an incident condition. The taxonomy given in the background is also outdated, listing Rett syndrome and childhood disintegrative disorder as ASD subtypes, which DSM-5 removed. Against that, the paper is careful to distinguish trait detection from diagnosis in its framing, positioning the work as identifying high autistic traits 'before making a definite diagnosis'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Preliminary experiment: 107 adults, 49 women and 58 men, mean age 24.84 +/- 5.24 years, mean AQ 21.0 +/- 5.2. The two label groups are closely matched - 25 women and 30 men at 24.7 +/- 5.2 years versus 24 women and 28 men at 25.0 +/- 5.3 - which is good practice, although the reported group AQ means of 16.6 for the high-trait group and 25.7 for the low-trait group are transposed relative to their labels. Test experiment: 22 participants, all male, mean age 12.68 +/- 7.61 years, with no age range, AQ, IQ, severity, comorbidity or socioeconomic data. The demographic gulf between the two samples is the study's central design flaw and is never addressed.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: The weakest ascertainment logic in the corpus, and it is structural rather than a reporting omission. In the preliminary experiment there is no diagnostic assessment at all: the positive class is created by dichotomising AQ at 21, a value chosen because 'this histogram was almost symmetrical in terms of the mean results of the questionnaire (21), with 55 out of 107 results lower than 21 and 52 results no less than 21'. The threshold is therefore a median split chosen for balance, not a clinical cut-off - the established AQ screening threshold is 32 - and the paper nonetheless labels the upper half '1 (ASD)'. In the test experiment, participants were 'already diagnosed with ASD' with no instrument, criteria, diagnostician or date reported, and no AQ was administered so their trait scores are unknown and the two experiments' labels are not commensurable.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: AQ total scores for the preliminary sample only, with the five subscale domains described but never analysed. No severity, IQ, language, adaptive or comorbidity measure for the diagnosed test participants, and no AQ administered to them - so it is not possible to establish whether the diagnosed group would even have scored above the study's own trait threshold.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: build a rapid VR-based gaze screening method for high autistic traits, deployable where clinical resources are limited. Main findings: an ensemble of seven classifiers reached 0.73 accuracy, 0.81 recall and reported AUC 0.90 on the median-split adult sample and recalled 77% of 22 diagnosed autistic participants; continuity of looking at the figure and animal regions was the most important feature family across tree-based models; and individual model recall shifted markedly between the two experiments, which the authors read as evidence that the two populations differ.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory sessions at Tsinghua University's Shenzhen International Graduate School, with diagnosed participants recruited through the Shenzhen Autism Society. Funded by Shenzhen Humanities and Social Sciences Key Research Bases, the Guangdong Natural Science Foundation, the National Philosophy and Social Sciences Foundation of China and a Tsinghua SIGS foundation. IRB approval from the Department of Psychology, Tsinghua University (No. THUDP20) covering both experiments.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A single Unity3D virtual scene - a couple in a garden with their dog - containing three semantic regions: human figures as social stimuli, an animal, and landscape. Free viewing for 15-20 seconds with no instruction. The design rationale is explicit and worth recording: previous Chinese eye-tracking work used 'merely a face on the computer screen', whereas static or isolated social presentations may fail to reveal group differences because 'for static images or those which present social information in isolation, social attention is normal in autism'. The 15-20 second exposure is by some margin the shortest stimulus in the corpus, which suits deployment but yields few gaze points per participant.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; one brief exposure per participant with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates within a synthetic scene, plus questionnaire scores and demographics - low sensitivity. Governance is properly reported: IRB approval with a reference number for both experiments and explicit attention to participant safety, which matters here because the authors note that some autistic participants rejected the VR headset.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: HTC Vive with an embedded aGlass infrared eye-tracking module, gaze coordinates delivered in a normalised unit square through the Unity console; Unity3D for scene construction and recording scripts; scikit-learn with GridSearchCV. The authors report the hardware's limitations candidly, stating that 'the stability and accuracy of aGlass are not high enough' and that they observed rejection of VR among autistic participants - two practical findings that bear directly on whether this modality is deployable with the target population.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Mixed. Reported: the scene contents, exposure duration, headset and tracking module, the K-means region segmentation procedure, all eleven features with definitions, the seven base models with the specific hyperparameters tuned for each and the rationale for PCA before logistic regression and naive Bayes, both ensemble combination rules, the 70/30 split with threefold cross-validated GridSearchCV, and full metric tables for both experiments. Not reported: the outlier criterion and the stage at which mean imputation was applied relative to the split, the selected hyperparameter values, the number of gaze points per participant, any calibration or data-quality statistics, the diagnostic basis of the test participants, and any code. Data are available on request.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged: aGlass stability and accuracy are insufficient; VR was rejected by some autistic participants; small samples in both experiments make bias inevitable; not all scenes containing social stimuli discriminate, so scene design should involve a specialist psychologist and several scenes should be compared. Most valuably, the authors report and interpret the recall instability across experiments, concluding that 'the data patterns of the adults we recruited in the preliminary experiment are somehow different from those autistic adults'. Not acknowledged: that the preliminary positive class is a median split of a general-population trait distribution well below the AQ clinical cut-off, so the models were never trained on autism; that Table 2's group AQ means are transposed; that age and sex are model features while the test sample differs sharply from the training population on both; that the test experiment has no negative cases so specificity is unmeasured and recall alone cannot distinguish a good model from one biased toward positive prediction; that the ensemble's AUC of 0.90 is inconsistent with constituent AUCs of 0.57-0.68; and that outlier replacement by the mean is unspecified in both criterion and timing.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Improve the accuracy and stability of the eye-tracking hardware and address VR acceptability among autistic participants; enlarge both samples to reduce small-sample bias; involve a specialist psychologist in scene construction since social stimuli do not automatically discriminate; and design multiple scenes and select the most discriminative.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Distribution of visual attention across three semantic region types in an immersive scene - human figures, an animal and landscape - characterised in three ways: total occupancy, continuity of occupancy, and transitions between region pairs. Including both total and continuous occupancy is the design's most productive choice, since the continuity features turned out to be the most important and total occupancy was not, which distinguishes sustained engagement from repeated brief glances - a distinction most gaze studies in this corpus collapse.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-modal fusion. What is combined is models rather than modalities: seven classifiers ensembled by probability averaging and majority voting, with the stated rationale that 'the best model that matches the pattern of this group of data well does not mean that it can be generalized to fit another group of data', so combining reduces variance and improves generalisation. That reasoning is sound and is borne out empirically - the ensemble's recall held at 0.81 then 0.77 across the two experiments while individual models swung from 0.81 to 0.55 (gradient boosting) or 0.44 to 0.00 (logistic regression). This is the corpus's clearest demonstration that ensembling buys stability under population shift, even though the underlying task here is not what the paper claims.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Seven classical classifiers plus an ensemble, with each model's assumptions and their consequences discussed individually - PCA applied before logistic regression because of multicollinearity and before naive Bayes because of its independence assumption, normalisation before KNN because distance is scale-sensitive, standardisation before SVM for convergence. This model-by-model reasoning is more careful than most of the corpus. The ensemble is then justified on generalisation rather than accuracy grounds, which is the right argument and is the one the test experiment supports.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Nine gaze features plus age and sex. The gaze features are proportions rather than counts, which normalises for exposure length, and the three-way split into total, continuous and transition proportions gives a compact description of both where attention rests and how it moves. Whole-sample means show the landscape dominating at 76% of gaze points against 17% for figures and 7% for the animal. The inclusion of age and sex as predictors is the consequential decision: it improves fit within a homogeneous adult sample but makes the model's behaviour on a demographically different test population uninterpretable, since the classifiers may be responding to the demographic features rather than the gaze features.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUC for all eight models in the preliminary experiment - a complete and transparent table - but recall alone in the test experiment, because the test sample contains no negative cases. That asymmetry matters: recall of 0.77 on an all-positive sample is uninformative about discrimination, since any model with a positive prediction bias scores well. The reported ensemble AUC of 0.90 against constituent AUCs of 0.57-0.68 is also internally implausible, since averaging or voting over models with AUC at most 0.68 cannot ordinarily yield 0.90.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Feature importances from the tree-based models identify continuousnum1 and continuousnum2 - continuous looking at figures and at the animal - as the most significant features, supported by density-distribution plots showing these features differing most between groups while others such as continuous landscape looking overlap closely. The interpretation offered is behaviourally specific and plausible: what distinguishes the groups is how long attention is sustained on social and animate content, not how much total time is spent there. What is missing is any directional statement or statistical test - no group means, no effect sizes, no significance testing for any feature - so the reader cannot tell whether high-trait participants sustained more or less continuous looking at figures.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: A single 70/30 split of 107 participants with threefold cross-validated GridSearchCV inside the training portion, followed by application to a separate group of 22 diagnosed participants. The two-stage structure is the right instinct - fitting on one sample and testing on another population is more than most of the corpus attempts - but its execution defeats the purpose. The test sample contains only positive cases, so nothing about specificity or overall discrimination can be established. It differs from the training population by roughly twelve years of mean age and entirely in sex composition, both of which are model inputs. And the labels are not commensurable: the training positive class is above-median AQ in a non-clinical adult sample, while the test positives are clinically diagnosed individuals whose AQ scores were never measured. There is no repetition over alternative splits, no confidence intervals and no independent replication.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorders (ASD), early screening, eye movement, machine learning, virtual reality (VR). 'Early screening' rather than diagnosis is the operative framing, and the paper is generally careful to describe its target as high autistic traits rather than autism - though the labelling of the above-median group as 'ASD' in the methods works against that care.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Child and Adolescent Psychiatric Nursing, 35(1), 83-92 - a nursing journal, which is an unusual venue for a machine learning contribution and is consistent with the emphasis on deployability and screening infrastructure over methodological rigour.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021. The framing is unusually specific about health-system context in China. It describes the two-stage screening structure recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics, notes that 'approximately 50% of the time is carried out with staff assistance' even for parent-completed tools, and that assessment can 'continue for months if the symptoms are not sufficiently obvious'. On China specifically it observes that 'the study of mental diseases used to be marginalized due to the conservative culture and weak science consciousness', that 'a majority of child health care institutions in China have not incorporated early ASD screening into their daily work', and that parents and primary health care staff lack awareness of early behavioural characteristics. It also positions itself against two named Chinese eye-tracking studies reporting 88.51% and 85.1%, criticising both for using only a face on a computer screen, and grounds that criticism in a substantive claim from the literature - that social attention in autism appears normal when social information is presented statically or in isolation, which is the argument for immersive scenes.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Automatic classification of children with autism spectrum disorder by using a computerized visual‐orienting task
data_charting_rubrics.authors: He Q; Wang Q; Wu Y; Yi L; Wei K
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Preschool children with autism, split by cognitive functioning level
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking and gaze
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Move beyond binary autism-versus-typical classification to a three-way distinction that includes cognitive functioning level, on the argument that binary classification 'fails to take into account the heterogeneity in the ASD population' and that low-functioning autistic children 'may exhibit behaviors that are confounded with those of individuals with developmental delays'. A secondary goal is to test whether directional cues carrying less social information also discriminate, which bears on whether the visual-orienting deficit is social-specific or domain-general
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional three-group classification study with a graded social-content manipulation and explicit cross-group generalisation tests
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session per child of approximately 15 minutes, comprising 5 practice trials and 160 test trials
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A gamified visual-orienting task. Each trial shows a central directional cue surrounded by four object pictures at 250 pixels' distance. The child must follow the cued direction to the target and hold fixation there for 1000 ms to earn a smiling-face reward and verbal praise; failure to do so within 4000 ms ends the trial without feedback. Four cue types of increasing social content are used - an arrow, a pointing finger, a cartoon animal's gaze and a human gaze - with 40 pictures per cue type, 10 per direction, and 640 distinct object pictures drawn from familiar categories (furniture, instruments, sports equipment, stationery, fruit, containers). The instruction was 'Look at the person/little animal, what is she/it looking at? Will you look at that, too?'
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory testing with children seated approximately 60 cm from the display; autistic participants recruited from a preschool specialised for autistic children
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: All autistic children had prior diagnoses made by professional pediatricians at licensed hospitals under DSM-5 criteria, and all scored above threshold on the Chinese version of the Social Communication Questionnaire. The authors state explicitly that ADOS and ADI-R could not be administered 'since the Chinese translated versions of these two scales have not been officially released and validated' - an unusually candid account of why the field's gold standard was unavailable. Functioning subgroups were assigned by Combined Raven's Test (CRT-C2) for nonverbal and Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test-Revised (PPVT-R) for verbal mental intelligence, with children who failed to complete the CRT-C2 or scored below the PPVT norm average assigned to the low-functioning group
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 50 - 26 high-functioning and 24 low-functioning
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Not reported; means and standard deviations indicate a preschool sample
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: High-functioning 23 male / 3 female; low-functioning 19 male / 5 female
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Not reported; all autistic participants attended a specialised preschool, so concurrent intervention is implied
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Characterised in two dimensions: SCQ scores (high-functioning 12.23 +/- 6.92, low-functioning 17.32 +/- 5.23, typically developing 8.50 +/- 5.13) and cognitive measures (Raven raw 20.77, 11.00 and 22.17; PPVT raw 77.44, 22.88 and 80.38 respectively). Functioning level is not merely reported but is the basis of the three-class design
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Assessed on the same cognitive and SCQ instruments as the clinical groups, with the typically developing group scoring significantly lower on SCQ than both autistic groups. No separate screening instrument beyond SCQ is described
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes - all three groups matched at 5.24, 5.08 and 4.98 years with no significant differences on any pairwise comparison. Age matching is stated as a design feature ('age-matched children') rather than an incidental finding
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not formally tested; proportions differ (75% male in the typically developing group, 88% in high-functioning, 79% in low-functioning). The authors identify the imbalance as a limitation, noting that 'autistic girls exhibit more typical social attention than do autistic boys' and that too few girls participated to test whether the method performs equally across sexes
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Raw binocular gaze samples during visual-orienting trials
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Left and right eye positions were averaged; a fixation was defined as continuous gaze within a 50-pixel radius for at least 100 ms. Four areas of interest were defined - cue, target, the three confounds pooled, and all remaining screen area. Trials with recording failure from large head movements or instruction non-compliance were excluded, constituting 1.16%, 3.54% and 0.81% of trials for the high-functioning, low-functioning and typically developing groups respectively. Because targets and confounds appeared at random locations, gaze samples in those regions were expressed in local rather than global coordinates
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Tobii X120 eye tracker at 120 Hz; 25.5 x 34 cm display at 1024 x 768; five-point calibration accepted only when mean visual angle error was below 1 degree at all five points; Psychtoolbox on MATLAB; SPSS 20 for statistics
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: A 74-child three-group visual-orienting eye-tracking dataset; no release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze coordinate data over picture stimuli; low identifiability. Governance is properly reported: conducted in accordance with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Committee for Protecting Human and Animal Subjects at the School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences, Peking University, with written parental consent obtained before the experiment. Photographs used as human-gaze cues were 'personally approved for publication'
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Distributional statistics of raw gaze sample positions, used without selection
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Sixty-eight features comprising, for each of x and y coordinates in each of four areas of interest, the mean, median, standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis, interquartile range, minimum and maximum (8 statistics x 2 coordinates x 4 regions = 64), plus the number of gaze samples in each region (4). Gaze samples were stacked across all trials in a condition, justified by the absence of any learning effect. The design principle is stated explicitly: features were 'arbitrarily specified without a prior assumption on how our participants would behave' and all were used without selection
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Custom computation of distributional statistics over raw gaze samples; no toolbox-derived summary measures
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No - deliberately. Reporting feature importance would require the selection process the authors are at pains to avoid
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None by design. The informativeness of cue conditions is instead assessed by retraining on subsets of conditions and observing accuracy loss
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None individually. At the condition level, removing either the gaze cues or the non-gaze cues reduced three-class accuracy from 81.08% to 78.4% and 77.0% respectively, showing both carry information
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reported in detail with effect sizes across four behavioural measures. Success rate ranked TD 74.7% > HFA 29.1% > LFA 5.7% (group F(2,71) = 119.83, p < .001, eta-squared .771). Response latency ranked LFA 1277 ms > HFA 1117 ms > TD 986 ms, with LFA significantly slower than both. All groups spent longer on face cues than on finger or arrow cues and had lower success rates with them. Both autistic groups spent longer in the confound and uninformative regions than typically developing children. Within the high-functioning group only, target-region dwell time was shorter for the two gaze conditions than the two non-gaze conditions - a cue-type effect absent in the low-functioning group, whose poor performance 'did not depend on the amount of social information contained in the cue picture'. No learning effect was found between the first and last 10 trials in any group or condition
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Instance-based classification on distributional features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: k-nearest neighbours, chosen for simplicity, for suitability to low-dimensional overlapping data and for performance at small sample sizes, with k set at 2 for two-group and 5 for three-group classification. Critically, k was fixed by piloting on data from a previously published external study rather than tuned on the present data - so the one hyperparameter is set outside the evaluation entirely
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Subject-wise leave-one-out cross-validation, with every model trained on all participants but one and tested on the held-out child. The authors argue for this choice explicitly against the alternative, citing published work on the point: feature selection with small samples 'leads to record-wise cross-validation of model predictions, as opposed to subject-wise cross-validation. Record-wise cross-validation typically inflates the prediction accuracy'. They further note that 'feature selection with a small sample size is currently prevalent among medical studies with the machine learning techniques, and its overestimation of prediction accuracy should be cautioned'. Beyond the internal validation, two cross-group generalisation tests were run in which one group was withheld entirely from training and used as an unseen test population
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Overall accuracy, per-class sensitivity and specificity, full confusion matrices and per-class ROC AUC for the three-class problem; the same for the collapsed binary problem; and accuracy for the two cross-group generalisation tests
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Three-class: 81.08% accuracy, with sensitivity and specificity of 73.1% and 85.4% for high-functioning, 79.2% and 90.0% for low-functioning, and 91.7% and 96.0% for typically developing; AUC 0.775, 0.908 and 0.927 respectively. Errors concentrated on mislabelling the other two groups as high-functioning, which the authors relate to that group's intermediate behavioural position. Collapsing to binary autism versus typical development raised accuracy to 93.24% with AUC 0.938, autism sensitivity 96% and specificity 87.5%. Restricting to gaze cues alone gave 78.4% and to non-gaze cues alone 77.0%. The cross-group tests produced a striking asymmetry: a model trained on typically developing versus high-functioning children classified all 24 unseen low-functioning children as autistic (100%), whereas a model trained on typically developing versus low-functioning children classified only 53.85% of unseen high-functioning children correctly
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Raw gaze distributions from a 15-minute gamified visual-orienting task classified three groups - typically developing, high-functioning autistic and low-functioning autistic children - at 81.08% accuracy under subject-wise leave-one-out cross-validation with no feature selection, rising to 93.24% when the two autistic groups were collapsed. Visual-orienting deficits were present for non-social cues (arrows, pointing fingers) as well as gaze cues, and removing either cue family reduced accuracy, indicating the deficit is domain-general rather than specific to social information. Behavioural performance ranked strictly by group, with success rates of 74.7%, 29.1% and 5.7%. The most consequential result is the cross-group asymmetry: a model trained to separate typically developing from high-functioning children identified every unseen low-functioning child, while a model trained on the more separable typically developing versus low-functioning contrast identified barely half of unseen high-functioning children - direct evidence that classifiers trained on severely affected samples do not transfer to milder presentations.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Reduced success in orienting to and sustaining fixation on a cued target, longer latency to disengage from the cue, and more time spent on confounding and uninformative screen regions - present for both social and non-social directional cues, and graded by cognitive functioning level
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Test dynamic rather than still directional cues, since dynamic cues are more common in daily life; determine whether the algorithms can distinguish autism from attention deficits, given that the paradigm's attention-sustaining phase may itself drive the group differences; recruit approximately equal numbers of girls and boys to test whether the method performs equally across sexes, since autistic girls show more typical social attention; and exercise caution when comparing machine learning performance against current diagnostic methods because predictive power is constrained by population base rate
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: One of the strongest studies in the corpus, and the one most explicitly designed around the methodological failures it sees in the field. Three design decisions distinguish it. First, three-class rather than binary classification, motivated by the argument that binary designs ignore autism's heterogeneity and that low-functioning autistic children may resemble children with developmental delay - and the paper then demonstrates the cost, with accuracy falling from 93.24% to 81.08% when the clinical groups are separated. Second, no feature selection at all: 68 distributional statistics are computed from raw gaze samples and used wholesale, with the authors explaining that selection on small samples leads to record-wise cross-validation and inflated accuracy, and noting that this practice 'is currently prevalent among medical studies'. Third, and most valuable, two cross-group generalisation tests in which an entire group is withheld from training. The asymmetry these reveal is the paper's most transferable finding and should carry weight in the synthesis: a model trained on the harder contrast (typically developing versus high-functioning) identified 100% of unseen low-functioning children, while a model trained on the easier contrast (typically developing versus low-functioning) identified only 53.85% of unseen high-functioning children. That is direct empirical evidence that the many corpus studies recruiting predominantly severely affected samples would not transfer to the milder presentations where screening is actually needed. Supporting practice is also strong: subject-wise leave-one-out, the single hyperparameter fixed by piloting on an external dataset rather than the present data, calibration accepted only below 1 degree of visual angle, trial exclusion rates reported per group, absence of a learning effect verified before pooling trials, matched ages across all three groups with statistical confirmation, HFA and TD matched on both verbal and nonverbal intelligence, and full ethics reporting. Two caveats bound the interpretation. The low-functioning group achieved a success rate of 5.7%, meaning these children largely failed the task, so their separation may reflect general task non-engagement rather than a specific visual-orienting deficit - and the same limitation partly applies to their group assignment, which was based in part on failure to complete the Raven's test. And the sex imbalance is substantial and untested, which the authors name as a limitation with a specific rationale about autistic girls' social attention. Neither undermines the central methodological contribution.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Three groups totalling 74 children: 26 high-functioning autistic, 24 low-functioning autistic and 24 typically developing, all age-matched. Splitting the autistic sample by cognitive functioning rather than treating it as homogeneous is the design's defining feature and is argued for explicitly, on the grounds that binary classification 'fails to take into account the heterogeneity in the ASD population' and that low-functioning autistic children may show behaviours confounded with developmental delay and even with 'normal people with autistic traits, such as stereotyped behaviors, aggression, and noncompliance'. No separate developmental-delay or other-diagnosis group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'children with HFA', 'children with LFA', 'individuals with ASD', 'typically developing children'. Consistently person-first, including for the functioning subgroups. 'Low-functioning' and 'high-functioning' are used as technical designations tied to measured cognitive scores rather than as informal descriptors, and the paper defines them operationally. The framing is developmental and mechanism-oriented, discussing superior temporal sulcus activation and intention inference rather than burden or deficit.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Typically developing: 24 children, 18 male and 6 female, 5.24 +/- 0.81 years, Raven raw 22.17 +/- 9.03, PPVT raw 80.38 +/- 30.16, SCQ 8.50 +/- 5.13. High-functioning autistic: 26 children, 23 male and 3 female, 5.08 +/- 0.83 years, Raven 20.77 +/- 10.83, PPVT 77.44 +/- 22.39, SCQ 12.23 +/- 6.92. Low-functioning autistic: 24 children, 19 male and 5 female, 4.98 +/- 1.09 years, Raven 11.00 +/- 2.00, PPVT 22.88 +/- 12.30, SCQ 17.32 +/- 5.23. All three groups are age-matched with no significant pairwise differences, and the high-functioning and typically developing groups are additionally matched on both nonverbal intelligence (t(48) = -.49, p = .624) and verbal intelligence (t(46) = -.95, p = .356) - so the critical contrast is IQ-controlled, which almost no other study in this corpus achieves. Sex proportions differ (75%, 88%, 79% male) and are not tested; the authors name this as a limitation. No ethnicity or socioeconomic data; recruitment from a Beijing specialised preschool for the clinical groups.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Prior DSM-5 diagnoses made by professional pediatricians at licensed hospitals, corroborated by above-threshold scores on the Chinese SCQ for every autistic participant. The authors state plainly why the field standard was unavailable: 'We were unable to administer the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule or the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised to confirm the ASD diagnosis in our study since the Chinese translated versions of these two scales have not been officially released and validated.' This is a more informative disclosure than the silent omission found elsewhere in the corpus. Functioning subgroups were assigned by CRT-C2 and PPVT-R, with children failing to complete the Raven's test or scoring below the PPVT norm average classed as low-functioning - a criterion that partly conflates cognitive level with capacity to complete a structured test, which matters given that the outcome measure is also a structured task.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: The most complete cognitive characterisation in the corpus. Combined Raven's Test for nonverbal and PPVT-R for verbal mental intelligence, plus SCQ, administered to all three groups with means and standard deviations tabulated and all pairwise comparisons tested. These are not merely reported but used structurally - they define the functioning subgroups, they establish that the high-functioning and typically developing groups are matched on both intelligence measures, and they support the interpretation that visual-orienting performance tracks cognitive level. No adaptive functioning or comorbidity measures.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: classify three groups defined by diagnosis and cognitive functioning from raw gaze during a visual-orienting task, and test whether less-social directional cues also discriminate. Main findings: 81.08% three-class accuracy rising to 93.24% for binary autism versus typical development; success rates ranked 74.7%, 29.1% and 5.7% across typically developing, high-functioning and low-functioning groups; deficits appeared for arrow and finger cues as well as gaze cues, with removing either cue family costing accuracy; and cross-group tests showed a model trained on typically developing versus high-functioning children identified 100% of unseen low-functioning children while the reverse transfer achieved only 53.85%.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory testing at Peking University, with autistic participants recruited from a preschool specialised for autistic children in Beijing. Funded by multiple National Natural Science Foundation of China grants, an NSFC/DFG collaborative research centre, a Guangdong key project on autism diagnosis and treatment tools, and a Beijing municipal science and technology grant.
