No conflicts of interest declared.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A gamified visual-orienting task with a graded social-content manipulation - arrow, pointing finger, cartoon animal gaze, human gaze - crossed with four directions across 160 trials, using 160 distinct cue pictures and 640 distinct object pictures so that no stimulus repeats. The task requires not just an orienting saccade but sustained fixation on the target for 1000 ms to earn a reward, a design choice the authors justify from piloting: autistic children 'might occasionally choose one target, but then change their mind and fixate on another', so the long fixation window gives them the opportunity to revise. The 4000 ms trial limit was likewise set by piloting because 'some children with ASD would lose their attention during a trial'. The authors also flag that this attention-sustaining phase distinguishes their paradigm from conventional visual-orienting tasks and 'arguably contributes to the poor performance of children with ASD' - an unusually self-aware statement about what their own task measures.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single 15-minute session per child with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates over picture stimuli. Governance is fully reported: Helsinki conformity, named ethics committee approval at Peking University, written parental consent obtained before the experiment, and separate personal approval for publication of the photographs used as human-gaze cues. The experimenter was blind to functioning subgroup - 'the experimenter did not know a priori whether a child with ASD belonged to the LFA group or the HFA group' - which is a rare and worthwhile control.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Tobii X120 at 120 Hz; a 25.5 x 34 cm display at 1024 x 768 viewed from approximately 60 cm; five-point calibration accepted only when mean visual angle error fell below 1 degree at all five points; Psychtoolbox on MATLAB for stimulus presentation; SPSS 20 for statistics. The calibration acceptance criterion is stated quantitatively, which few eye-tracking studies in this corpus do.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Excellent. Reported: full stimulus inventory with picture counts, dimensions, resolution and spatial separation; the exact instruction wording; trial timing with the empirical rationale for both the 1000 ms fixation requirement and the 4000 ms limit; calibration procedure and acceptance threshold; fixation definition (50-pixel radius, 100 ms); all four areas of interest; per-group trial exclusion rates; the local-versus-global coordinate handling for randomly positioned regions; all 68 features enumerated by type and count; the classifier with its k values and the external source used to fix them; the cross-validation scheme; and complete confusion matrices with per-class sensitivity, specificity and AUC for both the three-class and binary problems. Missing only: data or code release, and the authors' own choice not to report feature importances, which follows from their no-selection stance.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged with four specific limitations: still rather than dynamic directional cues, whereas dynamic cues predominate in daily life; the attention-sustaining phase distinguishes this paradigm from conventional visual-orienting tasks and may itself drive the group differences, so future work should test whether the algorithms can separate autism from attention deficits; too few girls to test sex-specific performance, with the specific rationale that 'autistic girls exhibit more typical social attention than do autistic boys'; and that 'the predictive power of automatic classification techniques is constrained by the base rate of ASD in the population', so direct comparison against current diagnostic methods requires caution. The absence of ADOS and ADI-R is disclosed with its reason. Identifiable in review but not stated: the low-functioning group's 5.7% success rate means these children largely failed the task, so their classification may reflect general non-engagement rather than a visual-orienting deficit specifically; and the criterion for assigning children to that group included failure to complete the Raven's test, which partly conflates cognitive level with capacity to complete a structured assessment of the same general kind as the outcome task.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Test dynamic directional cues; establish whether the method distinguishes autism from attention deficits, given that the attention-sustaining phase may be doing much of the work; recruit balanced numbers of girls and boys to test sex-specific performance; and treat base-rate constraints seriously when comparing automated classification against clinical diagnosis.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Visual orienting - shifting and sustaining attention toward a target indicated by a directional cue - decomposed across four cue types spanning a social-content gradient from arrow through pointing finger and cartoon gaze to human gaze. Four behavioural quantities are measured: success rate, latency to disengage from the cue, and dwell time in the target, confound and uninformative regions. The social gradient is what makes the study theoretically informative rather than merely predictive: it permits the question of whether the deficit is social-specific, and the answer is that it is not.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-modal fusion - gaze only. The condition-level analysis serves the analogous purpose and yields a clear result: three-class accuracy falls from 81.08% to 78.4% using gaze cues alone and to 77.0% using non-gaze cues alone, so both cue families carry non-redundant information and the full set is better than either. This supports the paper's substantive claim that visual-orienting deficits in autism 'are not only tied to social cues but appear to be domain-general'. The behavioural analysis reinforces it: all three groups found face cues harder than arrow and finger cues, but the high-functioning group showed a cue-type effect on target dwell time that the low-functioning group did not, whose 'poor performance did not depend on the amount of social information contained in the cue picture'.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: k-nearest neighbours, deliberately simple, chosen for the low intrinsic dimensionality of gaze coordinates, for tolerance of overlapping class distributions and for small-sample performance. The single hyperparameter k was fixed by piloting on a different published dataset rather than tuned on the present data - so the entire model specification is set outside the evaluation, which removes the model-selection optimism that affects most of the corpus. No comparison against alternative classifiers is reported, which is a minor gap, but the choice is consistent with a paper whose stated aim is to avoid optimising anything on the evaluation data.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Sixty-eight distributional statistics computed from raw gaze samples - eight moments and order statistics for x and y in each of four regions, plus sample counts per region - used in full without selection. Two design details matter. Samples were stacked across all trials within a condition, justified by the verified absence of a learning effect between the first and last 10 trials in any group or condition. And because targets and confounds appeared at random positions, gaze samples in those regions were converted to local coordinates while cue and other regions retained global coordinates, so that the distributional statistics describe gaze relative to the object rather than relative to the screen. The stated principle - features 'arbitrarily specified without a prior assumption' and used without selection - is the direct methodological answer to the selection-inflation problem the paper identifies in the literature.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Complete: overall accuracy, per-class sensitivity and specificity, full confusion matrices and per-class ROC AUC for the three-class problem, the same for the collapsed binary problem, and accuracy for both cross-group generalisation tests. The confusion matrix is interpreted substantively rather than merely reported - errors concentrate on mislabelling the other groups as high-functioning, which the authors relate to that group's intermediate behavioural position and which explains its lowest specificity. Reporting the binary result alongside the three-class result quantifies exactly what collapsing heterogeneity buys: 93.24% versus 81.08%.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No model-explanation method, and none is possible given the no-selection design - but interpretability is provided instead by an extensive parallel behavioural analysis with mixed-design ANOVAs, effect sizes and Bonferroni-corrected post hoc tests across four measures and four cue conditions. This establishes what the classifier is likely responding to: a strict group ordering in success rate and latency, longer dwell in confound and uninformative regions for both autistic groups, and a cue-type interaction present in the high-functioning group but absent in the low-functioning group. Scan-path visualisations for representative participants from each group make the qualitative differences legible. The interpretation offered - that low-functioning children's scan paths 'appeared to be more random and less purposeful' - is honest about being descriptive.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Subject-wise leave-one-out cross-validation with no feature selection and a hyperparameter fixed from external data - about as clean an internal validation as this sample size permits, and argued for explicitly against record-wise alternatives with citation to the methodological literature on accuracy inflation. Beyond that, the two cross-group tests constitute a genuine generalisation experiment rarely attempted in this corpus: an entire group is withheld from training and used as an unseen population. The resulting asymmetry - 100% correct on unseen low-functioning children from a model trained on typically developing versus high-functioning, against 53.85% on unseen high-functioning children from a model trained on typically developing versus low-functioning - is interpreted correctly as showing that 'a model trained with more similar groups can perform well with test data from a disparate group, and a model trained with data from more different groups will underperform with test data from an intermediate group'. What remains absent is an independent cohort, an external site and any replication.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism diagnosis; autism screening; autism spectrum disorder; automatic classification; machine learning; visual orienting. 'Visual orienting' anchors the work in a specific and long-studied cognitive construct rather than in generic behavioural sensing, which is what allows the social-gradient manipulation to be theoretically interpretable.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: PsyCh Journal, 10(4), 550-565 - a psychology journal published by the Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences with Wiley. The venue explains the depth of the behavioural analysis relative to the modelling, and the two joint first authors span psychology and cognitive science.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021. The framing is a systematic critique of three methodological patterns in the existing literature, each with a named remedy. First, that behavioural features in prior work 'often relied on manually labeled features such as the retrospective coding of children's behaviors in videotapes' which 'were essentially based on subjective ratings, which reduced the appeal of using machine learning algorithms' - remedied by using raw gaze samples. Second, that most studies performed binary classification, which 'fails to take into account the heterogeneity in the ASD population' - remedied by three-class classification including functioning level. Third, that brain-imaging classification 'is generally limited to adults or older children (over 7 years)' so that 'the application of machine learning to young children or infants, who are arguably in more need of automatic classification, is challenging' - remedied by a 15-minute child-friendly eye-tracking task. To these it adds the selection-inflation critique, singling out a named study reporting 96.7% after selecting an optimal feature set from 15 participants per group and noting that such practice 'is currently prevalent among medical studies with the machine learning techniques, and its overestimation of prediction accuracy should be cautioned'. That is the most precise methodological self-awareness in the corpus.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Auxiliary Diagnostic Method for Early Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Movement Data Analysis
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Fang H; Fan L; Hwang JN
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2021 IEEE 7th International Conference on Cloud Computing and Intelligen
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: School-age children with autism
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking and gaze (biological motion)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Develop an auxiliary autism diagnostic method from structured rather than unstructured eye-movement data, on the argument that most artificial intelligence work in this area uses unstructured inputs such as brain images or gaze over natural scenes, 'which has complicated correlations among numerous parameters', so a small set of interpretable engineered features would be preferable for clinical support
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification with a hypothesis-driven feature design and a single random train/test split
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session per child viewing a six-minute animation, sampled every 0.02 seconds and divided into 5 stages of 7 sub-stages each, giving 35 data segments per child
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Passive viewing of a point-light biological motion animation built from human skeletal figures with body keypoints, showing three behaviours: figures walking forward from distant to near, walking upside-down, and clapping hands. Children were initially asked to gaze directly at one of the two small figures, after which 'apart from simple guidance, there will be no excessive linguistic or behavioral interference'
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Autistic children recruited from the Shanghai Putuo District Zhanyi Children Cultivation Service Center; setting for the comparison group not stated
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None reported. Participants are described only as '39 autistic Chinese school children' recruited from a named children's service centre, with no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or date given anywhere in the paper. This is the study's most serious reporting omission, since the labels the classifiers learn have no stated basis
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 39 recruited; 33 retained after exclusions
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - described as 'normal Chinese school children'
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 53 recruited; 50 retained after exclusions
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No, and the mismatch is substantial. The autistic group spans 4-10 years while the comparison group spans 2-15, so the comparison group includes children both younger and older than any autistic participant. No means, standard deviations or statistical tests are reported, and age is not modelled. Attention to biological motion and the capacity to sit through a six-minute animation both change markedly between 2 and 15 years
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: No - 74% male in the autistic group against 51% in the comparison group, untested and unaddressed
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted as 'normal' with no screening or assessment described
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye and head deviation angles sampled during animation viewing
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: For each 0.02-second sample the eye deviation angle, head deviation angle and a per-child default value were recorded, with positive values denoting leftward and negative rightward. Gaze region was inferred by comparing the eye deviation angle against the default value with a tolerance epsilon: values within epsilon of the default map to central regions, values beyond it map to lateral regions, and an eye deviation angle of exactly zero was taken to mean the child was gazing at 'area0, which cannot be tracked by the device'. Head-eye co-movement was scored whenever the eye and head deviation angles shared the same sign
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Tobii 4C eye tracker recording eye and head movements; 29WK500-P monitor; biological motion animation from previously published work by Fan et al.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Eye-movement data from 92 children; no release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Numeric gaze and head angle data; low identifiability in itself. No ethics committee approval, parental consent procedure or data governance statement appears anywhere in the paper, despite participants including children as young as two recruited through a children's service centre
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Hand-designed spatial-temporal rate features derived from three explicit behavioural hypotheses
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Forty-three features in three families. Gaze-region occupancy: the rate at which the child gazed at each of six screen areas (area0 through area5) in each of five stages, plus the mean rate across the whole animation - 36 features. Head-eye co-movement: the rate in each of five stages plus the mean - 6 features. Clap prediction: a single binary feature set to 1 if, after the first clap, the child gazed at either human figure at a rate above threshold before the second clap. Two hyperparameters govern the feature computation - the angular tolerance epsilon set to 2.25 and the prediction threshold tau set to 0.55, both 'empirically set', with the authors noting that 'different values could be set to gain a better performance'
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Custom rule-based computation from eye and head deviation angles; no toolbox-derived fixation or saccade detection
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, by Pearson correlation of each feature against the diagnostic label, displayed as a cluster heat map
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Pearson correlation coefficient between each of the 43 features and the binary label, computed on the full dataset
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The area0 features - the rate of gaze falling outside trackable screen regions - and the head-eye co-movement features are identified as accounting for 'a large proportion in classifying ASD and normal children'. Features 2-11 (head-eye co-movement and area0 across stages), plus features 15, 20, 30, 37, 38, 39 and 41, showed the strongest correlations with the label. The clap-prediction feature was found to be 'less significant in correlation'
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reported explicitly, and one prediction was refuted. Hypothesis 1 was supported - autistic children gazed more often at untrackable or off-screen areas, so 'ASD children tend to be more inattentive than normal children'. Hypothesis 2 was contradicted - head-eye co-movement rate correlated negatively with the autism label, so autistic children showed less rather than more head-eye co-movement, 'instead of positive correlation in the hypothesis 2'. Hypothesis 3 was supported in direction, with autistic children making fewer anticipatory gazes before the second clap, though the corresponding feature correlated weakly
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Comparison of classical classifiers on hand-engineered tabular features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: K-nearest neighbours with Euclidean distance over the 43-dimensional feature space (k not stated); Gaussian naive Bayes; and a support vector machine with a cubic polynomial kernel
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A single random split of the 83 valid samples into 43 training and 40 testing children, approximately 1:1, with no cross-validation, no repetition over alternative splits and no held-out validation set for tuning. The feature-computation hyperparameters epsilon and tau were set empirically with no stated procedure, and the Pearson correlation analysis used to validate the three feature hypotheses was computed over the entire dataset including the test half
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity with confusion matrices for each of the three classifiers. No AUC, precision, F1, confidence interval or statistical comparison between models
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: On the 40-child test set (25 typically developing, 15 autistic): cubic-kernel SVM 0.93 accuracy, 0.80 sensitivity, 1.00 specificity; Gaussian naive Bayes 0.90, 0.80, 0.96; KNN 0.80, 0.60, 0.92. Sensitivity of 0.80 corresponds to 12 of 15 autistic children detected, and specificity of 1.00 to 25 of 25 typically developing children correctly classified. All three models show markedly higher specificity than sensitivity, which the authors note as a general property - 'all three algorithms are excellent choices to ensure algorithm's performance in terms of specificity'
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Forty-three interpretable features derived from three explicit behavioural hypotheses about gaze during biological motion viewing classified autism at 93% accuracy with a cubic-kernel SVM on a 40-child test set, though with sensitivity of only 0.80 against perfect specificity. The correlation analysis produced a genuine and honestly reported refutation: head-eye co-movement, hypothesised to be elevated in autism because of stereotyped head-shaking, correlated negatively with the label, so autistic children moved head and eyes together less rather than more. The strongest single feature family was the rate of gaze falling in area0 - the region the tracker cannot resolve - which the authors interpret as inattention but which is equally a measure of tracking failure.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Higher rate of gaze falling outside trackable screen regions, lower rate of head-eye co-movement, and fewer anticipatory gazes to the human figures before a repeated clapping action
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Collect more samples, since 'given the limited datasets, comparisons cannot be simply drawn with other existing diagnostic methods'; and further justify whether the clap-prediction feature is genuinely an important diagnostic indicator, given its weak correlation
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A short conference paper with one genuine methodological virtue and several disabling gaps. The virtue is its hypothesis-driven feature design: three explicit behavioural predictions are stated in advance, features are constructed to test each, and the results are reported against them - including a refutation, with the authors stating plainly that head-eye co-movement went the opposite way to prediction and revising their interpretation accordingly. That is better scientific practice than the purely data-driven feature engineering found in much of this corpus, and it makes the resulting model interpretable in behavioural terms. The gaps are more consequential. No diagnostic instrument, criteria or clinician is reported anywhere, so the labels have no stated basis; participants are described simply as autistic children recruited from a service centre. No ethics approval or consent statement appears, for a sample including two-year-olds. The groups differ substantially and untestedly on both age - 4-10 years against 2-15, so the comparison group brackets the clinical group at both ends - and sex, at 74% against 51% male, on a task whose demands (sustaining attention to a six-minute abstract animation) vary strongly with age. Validation is a single random half-split with no cross-validation or repetition, so the 40-child test result has wide sampling uncertainty; the two feature-computation hyperparameters were set empirically with the explicit note that other values could improve performance; and the correlation analysis validating the feature hypotheses was computed over the whole dataset including the test half. Most substantively, the single strongest feature family is area0 - defined as the region where the eye deviation angle reads exactly zero because gaze 'cannot be tracked by the device'. Treating tracking failure as a behavioural measure of inattention is defensible as a hypothesis but conflates a genuine attentional signal with equipment dropout, head movement out of range and non-compliance, and in a study where the groups differ in age by up to a decade this is precisely the kind of variable that would separate groups for reasons unrelated to autism. The paper's own honest observation that all three classifiers achieve far higher specificity than sensitivity - 1.00 against 0.80 for the best model - is also worth carrying forward: the model rules typical development in confidently while missing one autistic child in five.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: 39 autistic children recruited from the Shanghai Putuo District Zhanyi Children Cultivation Service Center and 53 children described as normal, totalling 92. Nine samples were excluded for partial data loss or non-cooperation, leaving 83 - 33 autistic and 50 typically developing, so 6 autistic and 3 comparison children were removed, a differential exclusion rate of 15% versus 6% that is not commented on. No other-diagnosis comparison group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'autistic children', 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'normal children', 'normal people'. The comparison group is consistently 'normal' rather than 'typically developing'. The framing is strongly deficit-oriented, opening with 'the mental retardation of ASD, which increases with age' and describing the aim as reducing 'the intellectual deficiency of autistic children'. This is among the more pathologising registers in the corpus and the developmental claim it opens with - that intellectual impairment in autism increases with age - is not a standard finding.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Autistic group: 39 children, 29 boys and 10 girls, aged 4-10. Comparison group: 53 children, 27 boys and 26 girls, aged 2-15. No means, standard deviations, matching statement or statistical test is reported for either variable. Both differences are substantial: the comparison group is 51% male against 74%, and its age range brackets the clinical group at both ends, including children five years younger and five years older than any autistic participant. For a six-minute passive-viewing task with an abstract point-light stimulus, where the strongest feature is failure to maintain trackable gaze, an age spread from 2 to 15 years in one group only is a first-order confound. No IQ, language, severity, comorbidity or socioeconomic data.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None. The autistic group is identified only by recruitment from a named children's service centre, with no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician, date or severity information anywhere in the paper. The comparison group's status as 'normal' is asserted without any screening. This is the weakest ascertainment among the included studies in this corpus, and it is particularly striking given that the paper's own introduction criticises existing diagnosis for depending on 'doctors' level of experience, which makes the diagnostic results quite subjective and variable' - the labels its models learn from come from exactly that unexamined source.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No IQ, developmental, language, adaptive or severity measure, and no comorbidity information for either group.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: build an auxiliary autism diagnostic method from structured, interpretable eye-movement features rather than unstructured data. Main findings: cubic-kernel SVM achieved 0.93 accuracy, 0.80 sensitivity and 1.00 specificity; Gaussian naive Bayes 0.90/0.80/0.96 and KNN 0.80/0.60/0.92; gaze at untrackable regions and head-eye co-movement were the most label-correlated feature families; and the hypothesis that autistic children would show more head-eye co-movement was refuted, the correlation running in the opposite direction.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Autistic participants were recruited from the Shanghai Putuo District Zhanyi Children Cultivation Service Center; no setting is stated for the comparison group and no laboratory conditions, lighting or viewing distance are described. Acknowledged support from two university research teams at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Shanghai University of Engineering Science. The first author is affiliated with a Shanghai high school.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A six-minute point-light biological motion animation constructed from human skeletal figures with body keypoints, showing three behaviours in sequence: figures walking forward from distant to near, walking upside-down, and clapping hands. The stimulus choice is well motivated from the literature - typical viewers have 'a strong visual sensitivity to biological movement', autistic children show 'abnormal gaze towards scattered light points or rotating aperture', and have 'a lower tendency to immobilize biological moving objects'. Using abstract point-light figures rather than faces or naturalistic video isolates biological motion perception from face processing, which is a cleaner manipulation than most gaze studies in this corpus attempt. The upside-down walking condition in particular is the standard inversion control for biological motion, though the paper does not analyse it as such.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single six-minute session per child with no follow-up. Data are numeric eye and head deviation angles. No ethics committee approval, parental consent procedure, anonymisation or data governance statement appears anywhere, despite the sample including children as young as two recruited through a service centre for children with developmental needs.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Tobii 4C eye tracker, which records head as well as eye movement - the feature that makes the head-eye co-movement hypothesis testable and distinguishes this setup from the gaze-only trackers used elsewhere in the corpus; a 29WK500-P monitor; and the biological motion animation from prior published work. Sampling at 0.02-second intervals (50 Hz). No calibration procedure, viewing distance or data-quality criteria are described.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Mixed. Well specified: the three behavioural hypotheses, the six-region screen division, the rule mapping eye deviation angle to gaze region, the head-eye co-movement criterion, the clap-prediction rule, the complete 43-feature inventory with naming convention, the stage and sub-stage structure, the sampling period, both hyperparameter values, and the three classifiers with their mathematical definitions. Not specified: any diagnostic instrument; ethics approval; calibration procedure, viewing distance or data-quality thresholds; the value of k for KNN; how epsilon and tau were chosen; participant ages beyond ranges; and any data or code release. The complete absence of a diagnostic basis alongside a full derivation of the SVM kernel function is a striking imbalance of reporting effort.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged: the dataset is limited so 'comparisons cannot be simply drawn with other existing diagnostic methods, and more samples are needed for further analysis'; the clap-prediction feature 'needs to be further justified' given its weak correlation; and the hyperparameters were empirically set with the explicit note that 'different values could be set to gain a better performance'. The refutation of hypothesis 2 is reported clearly and the interpretation revised. Not acknowledged: no diagnostic instrument or criteria are reported for either group; no ethics approval; groups differ substantially in age (4-10 versus 2-15) and sex (74% versus 51% male) with no test or adjustment; validation is a single random split with no cross-validation or repetition, so the 40-child result carries wide sampling uncertainty; the correlation analysis validating the feature hypotheses used the full dataset including the test half; exclusion rates differ between groups (15% versus 6%); and the most predictive feature family, area0, is defined by the tracker's failure to resolve gaze, conflating attentional signal with equipment dropout.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Collect more samples to permit meaningful comparison against existing diagnostic methods, and establish whether the clap-prediction feature is genuinely diagnostic given its weak observed correlation.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Visual attention to point-light biological motion, decomposed three ways: where on the screen gaze falls across six regions and five animation stages, whether head and eye move together, and whether the child anticipates a repeated action. The head-eye co-movement measure is distinctive in this corpus - most eye-tracking studies discard head movement as a nuisance to be minimised, whereas here it is treated as a behavioural signal in its own right, hypothesised to index stereotyped head-shaking. That the hypothesis was refuted does not diminish the value of measuring it.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-modal fusion, but a within-session combination of eye and head channels from a single device, which is closer to fusion than most gaze studies here attempt. No ablation isolates the contribution of the head channel, though the correlation analysis identifies head-eye features among the most label-correlated, alongside the area0 gaze features. The temporal decomposition into five stages is a second axis of combination - features are computed per stage and pooled - but no analysis compares stages, so which phase of the animation carries the signal is not established despite the stage structure being built into the design.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Three classical classifiers compared on identical features: KNN with Euclidean distance, Gaussian naive Bayes and a cubic-kernel SVM. The choice is appropriate for 83 samples and 43 features, and the paper's stated rationale for the whole approach - preferring structured interpretable features over unstructured deep learning inputs - is coherent and is followed through. The cubic kernel is an unusual choice, more prone to overfitting than the standard RBF at this sample size, and no justification for the polynomial degree is given.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Forty-three features, every one traceable to one of three stated behavioural hypotheses, with a systematic naming convention (area-n-N for region n in stage N, plus per-region means). The representation is genuinely interpretable - each feature is a rate with a plain-language meaning - which serves the paper's clinical-support framing. Two design decisions bear scrutiny. Area0 is defined as an eye deviation angle of exactly zero, taken to mean gaze that 'cannot be tracked by the device', so a measurement artefact is promoted to a behavioural feature; this may capture real inattention but cannot distinguish it from tracker dropout, off-axis head position or non-compliance. And the region assignment depends on a single angular tolerance epsilon set to 2.25 by unspecified means, so the entire spatial feature family rests on one tuned constant.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity with confusion matrices for all three classifiers - adequate for a diagnostic framing and better than accuracy alone. The reported figures make the asymmetry visible: the best model detects 12 of 15 autistic children while correctly classifying 25 of 25 typically developing children, so it misses one autistic child in five. No AUC, precision, F1, confidence interval, per-split variability or statistical comparison between models, and with only 40 test children a single participant is worth 2.5 accuracy points, so the 0.93 versus 0.90 difference between the top two models is one child.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is the paper's organising principle rather than an afterthought. Every feature derives from a stated hypothesis, and the Pearson correlation heat map is used to test each hypothesis against the data and report the outcome - two supported, one refuted. The refutation is handled properly: head-eye co-movement correlated negatively with the label, so the conclusion states that autistic children 'show less head-eye co-movements than normal children (instead of positive correlation in the hypothesis 2)' while noting the feature remains diagnostically useful. The authors also draw a clinically directed conclusion, identifying which features 'doctors should pay attention to when diagnosing'. What is missing is any model-derived importance - the correlations are univariate and computed independently of the classifiers, so nothing establishes that the SVM actually uses the features the correlation analysis highlights.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The weakest element. A single random split of 83 children into 43 training and 40 testing, with no cross-validation, no repetition over alternative splits, no held-out tuning set and no independent cohort. The two feature hyperparameters were set empirically with no procedure stated and an explicit acknowledgement that other values could improve performance, and the correlation analysis used to justify the feature design was computed across the entire dataset including the test half - so the features whose relevance is demonstrated on all 83 children are the same features evaluated on 40 of them. With a 40-child test set, the reported accuracies carry sampling uncertainty of roughly plus or minus 8 percentage points that is never quantified.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: Auxiliary diagnosis, eye movement data, feature extraction, classification algorithms. 'Auxiliary diagnosis' is the operative framing - the tool is positioned as support for clinicians rather than as a replacement - and 'feature extraction' correctly identifies where the paper's effort went.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: 2021 IEEE 7th International Conference on Cloud Computing and Intelligent Systems (CCIS) - a computing conference. The first author is a high-school student, with university co-authors from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and the University of Washington, which is relevant context for the level of methodological review the work received.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021. The framing is the standard subjectivity argument - diagnosis 'mainly relies on experts' comprehensive clinical analysis of children, which is usually subjective and highly dependent on doctors' individual professional skills' - with an added emphasis on pre-verbal assessment, aiming to 'diagnose children without linguistic ability in an early stage'. Its distinctive contribution to the corpus's framing is a preference for structured over unstructured data: it observes that 'most of the studies focus on unstructured data, which has complicated correlations among numerous parameters' and argues that 'it is highly desired to develop an effective auxiliary diagnostic method for ASD with the utilization of structured data'. That is an argument for interpretability over raw predictive power, and it is one of the few places in this corpus where the trade-off is stated as a design principle rather than discovered after the fact. The biological motion rationale is also well grounded, citing the classic finding of strong visual sensitivity to biological movement in typical viewers against reports of abnormal gaze to point-light displays in autism.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Children ASD Evaluation Through Joint Analysis of EEG and Eye-Tracking Recordings With Graph Convolution Network
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Zhang S; Chen D; Tang Y; Zhang L
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Preschool children with autism
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking and gaze (with EEG as a second modality)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Improve on the simple feature-level and decision-level fusion strategies used in prior EEG-plus-gaze work, which the authors argue 'may not make full use of modality-cross information', by representing features as graph nodes and their covariances as edges so that a graph convolutional network can exploit relationships both within and across modalities. A secondary goal is to characterise which EEG features relate to which gaze behaviours
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification with a modality ablation and comparison against two published or standard alternatives
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Six minutes of resting EEG per child, followed by approximately seven eye-tracking tests in which each photograph type appeared six times for 10 seconds
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Two protocols in sequence. Resting-state EEG in a shielded room, then a battery of seven eye-tracking tests, each targeting a different construct: viewing unfamiliar own-race faces (two tests), viewing an unfamiliar other-race face, joint attention, gaze following (two 'ModJoint' tests) and social interaction. This is the widest set of distinct gaze paradigms in any single study in the corpus
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: A shielded room for EEG recording, with eye tracking conducted subsequently; the ethics approval indicates Beijing Normal University, with the analysis conducted at Wuhan University
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None reported. The paper describes participants only as '21 ASD and 21 TD children' aged 3-6, with no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician, setting or date given anywhere. The apparatus, age range, ethics committee and gaze paradigms match those of a separately published study from the same institutional source, suggesting this is a secondary analysis of an existing dataset, but no such provenance is stated
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Asserted but unverifiable - 'No statistical differences in age and gender are observed between ASD and TD groups', with no means, standard deviations, counts or test statistics given for either variable
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Asserted in the same clause with no supporting data
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted without a stated basis
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Resting-state scalp EEG and gaze fixation data across seven viewing paradigms
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: EEG: 128-channel recording re-referenced to linked ears, bandpass filtered 0.5-45 Hz, sampled at 256 Hz, ICA-based artefact removal in EEGLAB with visual inspection to reject heavily contaminated segments, reduction to 8 electrodes (F3, F4, T3, C3, C4, T4, O1, O2) 'in order to reduce computational overhead', and segmentation into non-overlapping 4-second epochs. Eye tracking: five-point calibration required to pass with small error vectors, cumulative fixation duration within each area of interest computed with a 60 ms threshold 'to rule out the invalid value caused by unconscious looking'
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: 128-channel HydroCel Sensor Net (Electrical Geodesics) at 256 Hz; eye tracking at 300 Hz; EEGLAB for ICA artefact removal
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: No new collection is described; the data appear to be an existing dataset reanalysed
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - the availability statement says only that 'the original contributions presented in the study are included in the article/supplementary material, further inquiries can be directed to the corresponding author'
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: EEG traces and gaze fixation summaries; low identifiability. Governance is reported: the study was conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the ethics committee of Beijing Normal University, with written informed consent provided
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Multi-domain EEG signal features and area-of-interest fixation features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Seven EEG features spanning three domains - a time-domain mean value; a short-time Fourier transform time-frequency feature; Pearson correlation coefficient as a synchronisation measure; and four complexity measures comprising approximate, sample, permutation and wavelet entropy. Seven eye-tracking features, one per test: exotic strange face, social interaction, joint attention, ModJoint1, ModJoint2, native strange face 1 and native strange face 2. Fourteen features in total form the nodes of the feature graph
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: EEGLAB for preprocessing; custom entropy and time-frequency computation; random forest for selecting the most significant eye-tracking features
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, through independent t-tests on every feature and through the covariance-derived adjacency matrix
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Independent t-tests of each feature against group, and covariance between every pair of features thresholded to build the graph adjacency matrix
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Among EEG features, the time-domain mean value (t = -22.20, p < .001), approximate entropy (t = -6.61, p < .001) and wavelet entropy (t = -3.83, p < .001) differed most between groups; permutation entropy did not differ at all (t = 0.20) and the Pearson synchronisation measure was non-significant. Among gaze features, native strange face 2 (t = -4.71, p < .001), native strange face 1 (t = -3.16, p < .005) and social interaction (t = -2.90, p < .01) differed most, while joint attention did not (t = -0.79) and ModJoint2 was non-significant
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reported only as t-statistics with signs and p-values, without group means, so magnitudes and directions cannot be interpreted substantively. The interpretive claims offered are that autistic and typically developing children differ most on own-race unfamiliar faces and on social interaction, which the authors relate to the social-communication criterion
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Graph neural network over a feature-relationship graph
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: A graph convolutional network in which each of the 14 features is a node and edges are placed where the covariance between two features exceeds a threshold, so that convolution propagates information along feature relationships within and across modalities. Random forest is used upstream to select the significant eye-tracking features. Comparators are a reimplementation of a published feature-engineering pipeline (band power plus AOI fixation percentages, mRMR selection, SVM) and a ResNet18 applied to concatenated features
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A single split with 'the ratio of training set against test samples is 8:2', with no cross-validation, no repetition and no held-out tuning set. The reported metrics imply the unit of splitting is not the child: with 42 participants an 80/20 split would yield about 8 test children, on which accuracies of 0.9500, 0.7368 and 0.7895 are arithmetically impossible; those values correspond instead to 19 of 20, 14 of 19 and 15 of 19 test samples. Since EEG was segmented into 4-second epochs yielding roughly 90 segments per child, the splitting appears to operate over derived samples rather than participants, which would place segments from the same child in both training and test sets
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for the proposed model and each comparator, plus t-statistics and p-values for every feature. No AUC, confusion matrices, confidence intervals or statistical comparison between models
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Proposed GCN 0.9500 on all four metrics. Single-modality baselines using the same features and pipeline: eye-tracking alone 0.7895 accuracy, 0.8000 precision, 0.9230 recall, 0.8571 F1; EEG alone 0.7368, 0.7500, 0.9231, 0.8276. External comparators: the reimplemented feature-engineering pipeline 0.8100 on all metrics, and ResNet18 on concatenated features 0.7000 accuracy, 0.8050 precision, 0.7150 recall, 0.6800 F1. Notably, eye tracking alone outperformed EEG alone
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Representing EEG and eye-tracking features as nodes in a graph whose edges are inter-feature covariances, then fusing them with a graph convolutional network, gave 95% accuracy against 79% for gaze alone and 74% for EEG alone, and beat both a conventional feature-concatenation-plus-SVM pipeline (81%) and a ResNet18 over concatenated features (70%). The authors interpret the ResNet result as showing that 'simply and rudely cascading EEG and eye-tracking recordings cannot make good use of multi-modality information'. Two substantive observations follow: gaze alone outperformed EEG alone, which the authors attribute to eye tracking recording outer behaviour that 'can portray the behavioral characteristics of children with ASD and TD more intuitively'; and the covariance graph reveals specific cross-modal relationships, with EEG synchronisation linked to face and joint-attention gaze features and entropy measures linked to face, joint attention and social interaction features, even though the two signals were recorded at different times.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Not characterised directionally. Group differences were largest for the EEG time-domain mean, approximate entropy and wavelet entropy, and for gaze during viewing of unfamiliar own-race faces and social interaction
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: None stated as a distinct section. The conclusion notes only that 'the solution holds potentials in the applications when concerning fusing much more data sources'
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The architectural idea is genuinely novel within this corpus and is well motivated: rather than concatenating features from two modalities or voting over separate classifiers, the paper builds a graph whose nodes are individual features and whose edges are covariances above a threshold, so that graph convolution propagates information along discovered feature relationships. The ablation supporting it is well constructed - the same features and pipeline are run on each modality alone and on both, and two external comparators are implemented, including a ResNet18 on concatenated features that performs worst of all, which is the clearest available evidence that the fusion mechanism rather than the model capacity is doing the work. The covariance analysis is also used interpretively rather than decoratively, identifying which EEG features relate to which gaze paradigms and noting the striking fact that these correlations appear even though EEG and eye tracking were recorded at different times. Three problems bound the claim. The most serious concerns the unit of analysis: with 42 children an 80/20 split gives roughly 8 test participants, on which the reported accuracies of 0.9500, 0.7368 and 0.7895 cannot arise, whereas they correspond exactly to 19 of 20, 14 of 19 and 15 of 19 samples. Combined with EEG being segmented into 4-second epochs at roughly 90 per child, this strongly indicates that splitting operates over derived samples rather than participants, so segments from the same child would appear in both training and test sets - the leakage mode that inflates accuracy throughout this literature. The paper never states the unit explicitly, which is itself a reporting failure for a result that turns on it. Second, no diagnostic instrument, criteria or clinician is reported for either group, and the participant description consists of two group sizes and an age range, with age and sex matching asserted but no figures given. Third, the t-tests and the covariance thresholds that define the graph structure were computed over the whole dataset, so the graph the model convolves over was built with knowledge of the test samples. Two smaller points deserve note: the reduction from 128 to 8 EEG electrodes is justified only by computational overhead, and the finding that gaze alone beats EEG alone is a useful and honestly reported result that runs against the paper's own neuroscience framing.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 21 children each, aged 3-6, totalling 42. No other-diagnosis comparison group. Nothing further is reported about either group - no ages beyond the shared range, no sexes, no clinical characterisation - and because no provenance for the dataset is given, nothing can be recovered from a source publication either.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'children with typically developing (TD)', 'ASD children', 'TD children', 'subjects'. Predominantly person-first with 'typically developing' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy'. The framing is neuroscience-oriented rather than deficit-focused, describing autism as 'an early-onset neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by the impairments in social communication and repetitive behaviors' and motivating the work by the claim that bio-signal analysis 'can provide more reliable evaluation of children ASD than traditional methods of behavior measurement relying on scales do'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Almost nothing. Two groups of 21 children aged between 3 and 6, with the single sentence 'No statistical differences in age and gender are observed between ASD and TD groups' offered in place of any figures - no means, standard deviations, sex counts or test statistics for either variable. For a study whose gaze features are cumulative fixation durations during face and social viewing, and whose EEG features include entropy measures that change substantially across early childhood, a three-year age band with no distributional information is a material gap. No IQ, language, severity, comorbidity, ethnicity or socioeconomic data.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None reported. There is no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician, assessment date or severity measure anywhere in the paper for the autistic group, and no screening described for the comparison group. The dataset's apparatus (128-channel HydroCel), age range (3-6), ethics committee (Beijing Normal University) and gaze paradigms (own-race and other-race face viewing) match a separately published study, which suggests secondary analysis of an existing cohort - but no such provenance, citation or diagnostic inheritance is stated, so the labels have no traceable basis within this paper.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No IQ, developmental, language, adaptive or severity measure, and no comorbidity information for either group.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: fuse EEG and eye-tracking features through a graph convolutional network over a covariance-derived feature graph, improving on simple feature- or decision-level fusion. Main findings: 95% accuracy for the fused model against 79% for gaze alone and 74% for EEG alone; 81% for a conventional mRMR-plus-SVM pipeline and 70% for ResNet18 on concatenated features; gaze alone outperformed EEG alone; and covariance analysis revealed cross-modal relationships between EEG synchronisation and entropy features and face, joint attention and social interaction gaze paradigms despite asynchronous recording.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: EEG recorded in a shielded room and eye tracking conducted subsequently; ethics approval indicates Beijing Normal University while the analysis was conducted at Wuhan University's School of Computer Science. No recruitment route, period or clinical setting is described.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: The broadest gaze battery in the corpus - seven distinct tests targeting own-race unfamiliar faces (twice), other-race unfamiliar faces, joint attention, gaze following (twice) and social interaction, each photograph type presented six times for 10 seconds. This design permits the informative negative finding that joint attention was the least discriminative gaze feature (t = -0.79, non-significant) while unfamiliar own-race face viewing was the most discriminative - the opposite of what much of this corpus assumes. Resting EEG precedes the gaze battery rather than being recorded concurrently, which is why the cross-modal covariances the paper reports are between asynchronously acquired signals.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single visit per child comprising sequential EEG and eye-tracking sessions, with no follow-up. Data are EEG traces and gaze fixation summaries. Governance is reported: conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki, approved by the ethics committee of Beijing Normal University, with written informed consent provided.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: 128-channel HydroCel Sensor Net (Electrical Geodesics) sampled at 256 Hz in a shielded room; eye tracking at 300 Hz with five-point calibration required to pass with small error vectors; EEGLAB for ICA-based artefact removal. Notably, only 8 of 128 electrodes (F3, F4, T3, C3, C4, T4, O1, O2) were retained, justified solely as being 'in order to reduce computational overhead' - a substantial discard of spatial information for a stated engineering rather than scientific reason.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Mixed. Well specified: EEG preprocessing chain with filter band, sampling rate, referencing, ICA artefact removal, electrode selection and 4-second non-overlapping epochs; the seven eye-tracking tests with their purposes and presentation schedule; the 60 ms fixation threshold; the fourteen features by name; both comparator architectures including ResNet18 channel configuration; and complete t-statistics for every feature. Not specified: any diagnostic instrument; participant ages, sexes or matching statistics; the unit of the 8:2 split; the covariance threshold used to build the adjacency matrix; GCN layer configuration, training hyperparameters or random seed; and the random forest configuration used for gaze feature selection. No code, and a data availability statement that points to the article itself.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Essentially none. The paper has no limitations section and offers no caveats on sample size, generalisability or validation design. Identifiable in review: the reported accuracies are arithmetically incompatible with a participant-level 80/20 split of 42 children and correspond instead to 19 of 20, 14 of 19 and 15 of 19 samples, which combined with 4-second EEG epoching implies segment-level splitting and hence leakage across the train/test boundary; no diagnostic instrument or criteria are reported for either group; age and sex matching is asserted with no figures; the t-tests and covariance thresholds defining the graph structure were computed on the full dataset including test samples; validation is a single unrepeated split with no confidence intervals; and the reduction from 128 to 8 electrodes is justified only computationally.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: None stated beyond the general remark that the approach 'holds potentials in the applications when concerning fusing much more data sources'.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Gaze allocation across seven distinct social-viewing paradigms - own-race and other-race unfamiliar faces, joint attention, gaze following and social interaction - each reduced to a cumulative fixation duration measure within areas of interest. The behavioural coverage is broader than any other single study in the corpus, and the per-paradigm t-tests make it possible to see which constructs actually discriminate: unfamiliar own-race faces and social interaction do, joint attention and one of the two gaze-following tests do not.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: The corpus's most architecturally ambitious fusion, and the ablation is properly constructed. Single-modality baselines using identical features and pipeline give 0.7368 for EEG and 0.7895 for gaze, against 0.9500 fused - a gain of over 15 points on the better single modality. Two comparators isolate the mechanism: a conventional pipeline concatenating features with mRMR selection and SVM reaches 0.8100, and a ResNet18 over concatenated features reaches only 0.7000 despite far greater capacity, which the authors read as showing that 'simply and rudely cascading EEG and eye-tracking recordings cannot make good use of multi-modality information'. The graph formulation itself is the contribution: features are nodes, thresholded covariances are edges, so convolution operates over discovered inter-feature structure rather than over a flat concatenation. The interpretive payoff is the cross-modal edge analysis, which identifies EEG synchronisation as related to exotic face, joint attention and gaze-following features, and entropy measures as related to face, joint attention and social interaction features - relationships that exist despite the two signals being recorded at different times. The caveat is that all of this rests on an accuracy figure whose validation unit is not stated and appears not to be the participant.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A graph convolutional network over a feature graph, with random forest for upstream gaze feature selection, compared against an SVM-based feature-engineering pipeline and a ResNet18. The GCN choice is well matched to the stated problem - modelling relationships between features across modalities where no explicit correlation exists between the raw signals - and using features rather than subjects as graph nodes is an unusual and defensible formulation. That the much deeper ResNet18 performs worst supports the argument that architecture matched to the fusion problem matters more than capacity at this sample size.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Fourteen features total - seven EEG spanning time domain, time-frequency, synchronisation and four complexity measures, and seven gaze features corresponding one-to-one with the seven viewing tests. This is an extremely compact representation, and the one-feature-per-paradigm structure on the gaze side means each node carries the summary of an entire experimental condition, which is what makes the covariance edges interpretable as relationships between constructs rather than between arbitrary statistics. The corresponding cost is that all spatial detail within each gaze paradigm - which areas of interest were fixated - is collapsed, and 120 of 128 EEG channels are discarded.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for the proposed model and all three comparators, plus t-statistics and p-values for every feature. Reporting all four metrics across a full ablation is good practice, and the single-modality baselines make the fusion gain directly readable. Missing: AUC, confusion matrices, confidence intervals and any statistical test between models - and with a test set of roughly 20 samples, the difference between 0.95 and 0.81 is about three samples. That all four metrics for the proposed method are exactly 0.9500 indicates a balanced test set of 20 with a single error.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is pursued at two levels and is the paper's strongest non-architectural contribution. Univariate t-tests establish which individual features differ between groups, with results interpreted against prior literature - reduced theta increase and stronger beta in autism for the comparator's band features, and greater differences in eye and body fixation. More distinctively, the adjacency matrix is analysed edge by edge to describe which features relate to which, both within EEG (mean value related to all but STFT; approximate entropy unrelated to sample entropy; STFT unrelated to entropy measures because 'entropy based features are calculated to measure the complexity of time series while STFT is a localized process in time and frequency domains') and across modalities. This turns the model's structure into a substantive claim about EEG-gaze relationships rather than leaving it as an implementation detail.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The weakest element and the one that governs how the headline should be read. A single 8:2 split with no cross-validation, no repetition and no held-out tuning set. The unit of splitting is never stated, and the reported figures indicate it is not the participant: 42 children split 80/20 gives roughly 8 test children, on which 0.9500, 0.7368 and 0.7895 are unattainable, whereas they correspond precisely to 19/20, 14/19 and 15/19 samples. With EEG divided into 4-second epochs yielding roughly 90 segments per child, sample-level splitting would place segments from the same child on both sides of the boundary. Additionally, the t-tests and the covariance thresholding that determines the graph's edge structure were computed across the entire dataset, so the graph topology the network convolves over was constructed using test-sample information. There is no independent cohort, no external site and no replication.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, EEG, eye-tracking, multi-modality fusion, graph convolution network. Three of five concern the fusion method rather than the clinical problem, which accurately reflects a paper whose contribution is architectural.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 15, article 651349, in the Cognitive Neuroscience section - a neuroscience venue, though the work is primarily a machine learning contribution and the authors are all from a computer science school.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021. The framing is a two-stage critique. First, that single-modality analysis is inherently limited because 'the bio-marker information carried by the bio-signal of a single-modality is likely insufficient or distorted' - an argument for fusion on information-theoretic rather than merely empirical grounds. Second, and more specific, that existing fusion work 'mainly rely on feature-level fusion or decision-level fusion' and that 'these simple kinds of fusion strategies may not make full use of modality-cross information, thus the performances are largely limited'. The paper then demonstrates this empirically by implementing both a feature-concatenation baseline and a deep network over concatenated features, and showing the latter performs worst. It also grounds the cross-modal premise in developmental neuroscience, citing work linking frontolimbic connectivity at 6 months to responding-to-joint-attention at 9 months, and studies finding eye-tracking and EEG measures correlated during social stimulation - so the fusion argument rests on a claimed functional relationship rather than on an assumption that more data helps.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Classification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Using Eye Tracking Data Based on Visual Attention Model
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Revers MC; Oliveira JS; Franco FO; Portolese J; Cardoso TV; Silva AF; Machado-Lima A; Nunes FLS; Brentani H
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2021 IEEE 34th International Symposium on Computer-Based Medical Systems (CBMS), 142-147
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Children and adolescents with autism across the severity range
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking and gaze (visual attention modelling)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Test whether autism severity can be classified from gaze, and specifically whether the interpretation of visual context degrades with severity - the hypothesis being that semantic, top-down attentional guidance is progressively impaired, so that a visual attention model fitted to each severity group will differ in which image attributes it relies on
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional severity classification within a single clinical population, with no non-autistic comparison group
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session per participant viewing nine videos in sequence with no break, 54 seconds total at 30 frames per second
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: The geometric-versus-social visual preference paradigm. Social scenes of children playing or doing yoga were shown on one side of the screen while randomly varying fractals were shown on the other, with attention competed between them. The authors note the paradigm's practical advantages explicitly: it is short, requires no audio, and 'can be used in nonverbal and at any age'
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Psychiatry Institute, University of Sao Paulo School of Medicine, with participants seated 50-70 cm from a 23-inch screen
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Assessment by a specialist in child and adolescent psychiatry, with inclusion requiring DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for autism and a CARS score above 30. The Repetitive Behavior Scale-Revised and Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales were administered where possible. Severity groups were defined by CARS, with above 36 classed as severe and 30-36 as non-severe
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 88 analysed from 91 recruited - 39 severe, 49 non-severe
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Severe group 8.7 +/- 3.9 years; non-severe group 8.8 +/- 3.2 years
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Severe group 12 male / 27 female (31% male); non-severe group 27 male / 22 female (55% male)
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported as a category, but clinical stability was an inclusion criterion - participants had to be on no medication or on unchanged medication for at least three months
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Stable condition required, defined as no medication or no medication change for at least three months
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: The classification target. CARS ranged 30-36 in the non-severe group (mean 33.1 +/- 2.0) and 36.5-46.5 in the severe group (mean 39.4 +/- 2.6). Vineland adaptive behaviour scores were significantly lower in the severe group (17.61% lower, p = 0.0006), providing independent corroboration of the CARS-based split, while Repetitive Behavior Scale scores did not differ (p = 0.104)
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: No - every participant is autistic with CARS above 30. This is a within-autism severity study, not a case-control design
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not applicable
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes - 8.8 versus 8.7 years with no significant difference (p = 0.900), and identical 3-16 ranges
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: No, and significantly so: 55% male in the non-severe group against 31% in the severe group (p = 0.02). The severe group is majority female, inverting the population sex ratio. The authors discuss this against literature on greater severity in autistic females but do not adjust for it in the model, so sex is a live confound for a classifier whose most important features are face and skin presence - domains where sex differences in social attention are documented
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not applicable
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Gaze fixation coordinates during dynamic video viewing
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Video frames were stripped of black background edges, resized to 350 x 200 pixels, and the ten frames either side of each video transition discarded. Frames differing by less than 33% of pixels from their neighbours were grouped, reducing 1,590 frames to 135 frame groups. Within each group, fixations from all participants of a severity class were summed into a class fixation map, smoothed with a Gaussian filter. Training pixels were sampled two ways - 350 fixated versus 350 non-fixated pixels, and the 350 most-fixated versus random non-fixated pixels - giving 700 training pixels per frame group per class
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Tobii Pro TX300 at 300 Hz with 1-3.3 ms processing latency; 23-inch screen at 50-70 cm; Tobii Pro Studio for recording; five-point calibration using animated figures at the four corners and centre; MATLAB 8.5 R2015a with mexopencv; RStudio 1.3.1093 for statistics
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: An 88-participant severity-stratified eye-tracking dataset; no release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze coordinate data over video stimuli. Governance is well reported: approval by the University of Sao Paulo School of Medicine research ethics board under a stated protocol number (17556019.8.0000.0068) in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Image attributes at three levels of abstraction, following the Feature-Integration Theory framework
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Twenty-seven features before selection. Pixel level (20): 13 steerable pyramid subbands at four scales and three orientations, colour contrast, intensity, orientation, and three RGB channel features. Object level (4): horizon line, movement, distance to the centre of the biological scene, and distance to the centre of the geometric scene. Semantic level (3): presence of skin, presence of face, presence of person. The three-level structure is the design's analytic point - pixel-level features index bottom-up attention driven by image statistics, semantic-level features index top-down attention driven by prior knowledge
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: MATLAB implementation of a Feature-Integration Theory-based visual attention model with mexopencv; ReliefF for feature selection with the criterion of retaining features weighted above the mean of all initial features
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, and it is the paper's substantive result rather than a supplementary analysis
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: ReliefF weighting performed independently for each severity group, with retention of features above the mean weight, so that the two groups' selected feature sets can be compared directly
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Fifteen features were selected for the non-severe group and twelve for the severe group. Critically, two of the three semantic features - presence of face and presence of skin - were selected only for the non-severe group. The severe group's model retained no face feature. Steerable pyramid features also differed, six selected for non-severe against five for severe, while RGB colour, horizon line and both distance-to-centre features were selected identically in both
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: The directional claim concerns which attributes guide attention rather than how much is looked at: the non-severe group's gaze is predicted in part by semantic content (faces, skin), while the severe group's is not, so attention in the severe group appears driven more by low-level image properties. The authors interpret this as evidence that 'the top-down mechanism seems to have a greater role in differentiating groups, than the bottom-up mechanism', consistent with the hypothesis that contextual interpretation degrades with severity
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Per-class generative attention model with similarity-based classification
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Two feedforward neural networks, one per severity group, each with a single hidden layer of ten neurons, sigmoid hidden activation and linear output, trained by backpropagation with Bayesian regularisation (MATLAB trainbr), learning rate 0.01, stopping at 1,000 epochs or error below 1e-7. Each network predicts whether a given pixel, represented by its feature vector, was fixated by that group. Predictions across pixels form a saliency map per frame group per class, binarised at 0.75. A participant's own fixation map is then compared against both class saliency maps frame group by frame group and assigned to whichever it more closely matches, with the participant labelled severe if 20 or more of 40 frame groups match the severe map
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Five-fold cross-validation with subject-level splitting, stated explicitly: 'in each fold, the classification phase was performed using data from 20% of the subjects and frames from the original stimulus video, whereas the VAM learning was performed using the remaining subjects and frames'. Folds were proportionally balanced. Two elements sit outside this loop: ReliefF feature selection is described as performed once per group with no statement of nesting within folds, and the 20-frame decision threshold was chosen by the Youden index applied to the ROC curve generated from the same evaluation
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Precision, sensitivity, specificity, error and accuracy, plus a ROC curve with mean and maximum area under the curve
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Mean AUC 0.85 with maximum 0.88. At the Youden-selected threshold of 20 frames, the reported averages are precision 70%, sensitivity 87%, specificity 60%, error 25% and accuracy 88%. These figures are mutually inconsistent - an error rate of 25% implies accuracy of 75%, and sensitivity of 87% with specificity of 60% on a 39/49 split implies accuracy of roughly 72%. The headline 88% appears to be the maximum AUC of 0.88 reported as accuracy; the internally consistent reading of the reported error rate is approximately 75% accuracy
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A visual attention model fitted separately to severe and non-severe autism groups distinguished them from gaze during a 54-second geometric-versus-social preference video, with mean AUC 0.85 and sensitivity 87% against specificity 60%. The substantive result is which features each group's model retained: presence of face and presence of skin were selected only for the non-severe group, so semantic content predicted where non-severe participants looked but not where severe participants looked. The authors read this as evidence that top-down, knowledge-driven attentional guidance degrades with severity while bottom-up image-driven guidance persists, and note that the CARS-based severity split was independently corroborated by significantly lower Vineland adaptive behaviour scores in the severe group.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Within autism, greater severity is associated with attention that is not predicted by semantic image content - faces and skin - while remaining predicted by low-level image statistics
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Test the methodology with different visual inputs to validate which features are genuinely relevant; extend beyond the 3-16 year range since autism is lifelong; address the small sample and the sex imbalance between groups; and analyse the impact of intelligence quotient as an additional model feature
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: This is one of only a handful of studies in the corpus targeting severity rather than diagnosis, and its analytic design makes the severity question mechanistic rather than merely predictive. Fitting a separate visual attention model to each severity group and comparing which image attributes each retains turns the classifier into an instrument for testing a specific hypothesis - that top-down semantic guidance of attention degrades with severity - and the result supports it cleanly: face and skin were retained only for the non-severe group.
