Because the feature hierarchy maps onto the bottom-up/top-down distinction from the attention literature, the finding has an interpretation independent of its predictive value, which is rare here. Other strengths: subject-level cross-validation stated explicitly, ethics approval with a protocol number, clinical stability required as an inclusion criterion, and independent corroboration of the CARS split by Vineland scores. Three problems bound the result. First and most serious, the reported metrics are internally inconsistent: error of 25% implies 75% accuracy, and sensitivity 87% with specificity 60% on a 39/49 split implies about 72%, yet 88% is reported as accuracy in both the abstract and conclusion. The value 0.88 is separately reported as the maximum ROC AUC, so the headline appears to be an AUC restated as accuracy. On the internally consistent reading the classifier achieves roughly 75% accuracy with specificity of only 60%. Second, the sex distributions differ significantly between groups (55% versus 31% male, p = 0.02) with the severe group majority female, and no adjustment is made - a live confound for a model whose distinguishing features are face and skin presence, given documented sex differences in social attention. The authors raise the issue but treat it as a substantive finding about female severity rather than as a threat to their classifier. Third, ReliefF feature selection is not stated to be nested within cross-validation folds, and the 20-frame decision threshold was fitted by the Youden index on the same ROC used for evaluation, so both the feature sets and the operating point were chosen with knowledge of the evaluation data. The absence of any non-autistic comparison group is a design choice rather than a flaw, but it means the finding speaks only to within-autism gradation.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: A single clinical population of 88 autistic children and adolescents, split by CARS into 39 severe and 49 non-severe, from 91 recruited. There is no typically developing comparison group and none is intended - the research question is whether severity can be graded within autism, which makes this one of very few studies in the corpus addressing gradation rather than detection. Exclusions were calibration problems, eye-tracking record rate below 80% and age over 17, applied to three participants.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'individuals with ASD', 'patients with ASD', 'ASD children', 'individuals with typical development'. Mixed person-first and 'patients', the latter reflecting recruitment from a psychiatry institute. The framing is clinical and severity-oriented, describing autism as classifiable by severity 'based on the degree of impairment in social communication, repetitive and restricted behavior patterns and also according to the need for support', and motivating the work by the claim that 'the categorization of individuals with ASD into levels contributes to the intervention, which directly impacts the prognosis'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Non-severe group: 49 participants, 27 male and 22 female, aged 3-16 with mean 8.8 +/- 3.2, CARS 30-36 with mean 33.1 +/- 2.0. Severe group: 39 participants, 12 male and 27 female, aged 3-16 with mean 8.7 +/- 3.9, CARS 36.5-46.5 with mean 39.4 +/- 2.6. Age is well matched (p = 0.900) with identical ranges. Sex is not: 55% male against 31%, p = 0.02, so the severe group is majority female against a population sex ratio of roughly 3:1 male. The authors engage with this substantively, citing literature both supporting and contesting greater severity in autistic females and noting that the ratio falls to 2:1 when restricted to low-functioning or intellectually disabled subgroups - but they do not adjust for sex in the model. Vineland scores were significantly lower in the severe group (p = 0.0006) while Repetitive Behavior Scale scores did not differ (p = 0.104). No IQ data, which the authors identify as a limitation.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Assessment by a specialist in child and adolescent psychiatry against DSM-5 criteria, with CARS above 30 required for inclusion, so every participant carries both a categorical diagnosis and a dimensional severity score. Clinical stability was additionally required - no medication or no change for at least three months - which controls a source of variability almost no other study in this corpus addresses. The severity split at CARS 36 follows a cited convention. What is missing is any account of who performed the CARS, with what training or reliability, and whether ADOS or ADI-R were available.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Strong for a severity study. CARS for all participants with group ranges and means; Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales and the Repetitive Behavior Scale-Revised administered 'when possible'. The Vineland result is used substantively - significantly lower adaptive functioning in the severe group corroborates the CARS-based split from an independent instrument, which is the correct way to validate a severity dichotomy. The absence of IQ is acknowledged as a limitation and proposed as a future model feature.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: test whether autism severity can be classified from gaze via a visual attention model, and whether semantic top-down attentional guidance degrades with severity. Main findings: mean ROC AUC 0.85 with sensitivity 87% and specificity 60%; presence of face and presence of skin were selected as predictive features only for the non-severe group; the non-severe model retained more features overall (15 versus 12); and the CARS severity split was corroborated by significantly lower Vineland scores in the severe group.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: The Psychiatry Institute of the University of Sao Paulo School of Medicine, with acknowledgement to the Autism Spectrum Disorder Program of the Clinics Hospital (PROTEA-HC). Funded by CAPES and the Brazilian National Program to Support Health Care for Persons with Disabilities. Ethics approval from the School of Medicine research ethics board under protocol 17556019.8.0000.0068.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: The geometric-versus-social preference paradigm - nine videos totalling 54 seconds at 30 fps and 1920 x 1080, with social scenes of children playing or doing yoga on one side of the screen competing against randomly varying fractals on the other. The paradigm is chosen for reasons of clinical reach rather than theoretical richness, and the reasons are stated: it 'has the advantage of being short and does not require audio, it can be used in nonverbal and at any age'. This matters for a severity study, since a paradigm requiring verbal instruction or sustained compliance would systematically exclude the severe end of the range being measured.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single 54-second viewing session per participant with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates over video stimuli. Governance is properly reported: research ethics board approval with a full protocol number and Helsinki conformity. Clinical stability over the preceding three months was required for inclusion.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Tobii Pro TX300 at 300 Hz with stated processing latency of 1-3.3 ms; 23-inch screen at 50-70 cm; Tobii Pro Studio; five-point calibration with animated figures at the corners and centre; MATLAB 8.5 R2015a with mexopencv for the attention model; RStudio for statistics. Data quality was enforced as an exclusion criterion - participants with an eye-tracking record rate below 80% were excluded, which is a stricter and more explicit quality gate than most of the corpus applies.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Good. Reported: full stimulus specification with duration, frame rate and resolution; viewing distance, screen size and calibration procedure; the exclusion criteria including the 80% record-rate threshold; all 27 candidate features itemised by level; the frame preprocessing chain including edge removal, resizing, transition-frame deletion and the 33%-difference grouping rule that reduced 1,590 frames to 135; both pixel-sampling strategies with counts; the complete neural network architecture, activation functions, training algorithm, learning rate and stopping criteria; the 0.75 binarisation threshold; the 20-frame decision rule and how it was chosen; the cross-validation scheme with its subject-level unit; and the statistical tests with normality checking. Missing: whether ReliefF was nested within folds, the identity of the selected features beyond their counts by category, any data or code release, and reconciliation of the inconsistent performance figures.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged: that the saliency-map approach needs testing with different visual inputs 'in order to validate the relevant features'; that the age range is restricted to 3-16 while autism is lifelong; that the sample is small; and that the sex imbalance between groups is a limitation. Analysing IQ as an additional feature is proposed. Not acknowledged: the reported accuracy of 88% is inconsistent with the reported error rate of 25% and with the reported sensitivity and specificity, and coincides exactly with the separately reported maximum ROC AUC; ReliefF feature selection is not stated to be nested within cross-validation folds, so the group-specific feature sets that constitute the paper's main finding may have been chosen using all the data; and the 20-frame decision threshold was fitted by Youden index on the same ROC used for evaluation.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Test the method with different visual inputs to validate which features are genuinely relevant rather than paradigm-specific; extend the age range beyond 3-16 given that autism is lifelong; enlarge the sample and address the sex imbalance; and incorporate intelligence quotient as an additional model feature.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Visual attention during competition between social and geometric content, analysed not as how much is looked at but as what predicts where gaze lands. The unit of analysis is the pixel: for each pixel, a 27-dimensional feature vector describing its image properties at pixel, object and semantic levels, with the model learning which properties predict fixation for each severity group. This reframes the behavioural question from a preference measure to an attentional-guidance measure, which is what allows the top-down versus bottom-up interpretation.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-modal fusion - gaze only. The combination that matters is across levels of image representation, and the design makes this an explicit test rather than an implicit one. The three feature levels map onto the two mechanisms the paper is interested in: pixel-level features index bottom-up attention driven by image statistics, semantic-level features index top-down attention driven by prior knowledge, and object-level features sit between. The finding that the two semantic features survive selection only in the non-severe group, while pixel-level features survive in both, is a direct within-modality dissociation supporting the hypothesis that severity impairs top-down more than bottom-up attentional guidance.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: An unusual architecture for this corpus: rather than training one discriminative classifier on participant-level features, the paper trains one small generative model per severity group - each a ten-neuron single-hidden-layer network with Bayesian regularisation, predicting whether a pixel was fixated by that group - and then classifies a new participant by which group's saliency map their own fixation map more closely resembles. This is a nearest-prototype scheme in saliency space. It has two consequences worth noting: the model is small enough to be well conditioned on the available data, and the comparison of the two fitted models is itself the scientific output, which is why the feature-selection difference is reported as the main finding rather than as an ablation.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Twenty-seven image features at three levels of abstraction, computed per pixel, reduced by ReliefF to 15 for the non-severe model and 12 for the severe model. The representation describes the stimulus rather than the participant, with the participant entering only through which pixels they fixated - an inversion of the usual arrangement in this corpus, where features describe gaze behaviour directly. Frame reduction from 1,590 to 135 groups by a 33% pixel-difference criterion is a sensible efficiency measure for 54 seconds of video, and discarding the ten frames either side of each video transition removes the change-detection artefacts that would otherwise dominate.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Precision, sensitivity, specificity, error and accuracy plus a ROC curve with mean and maximum AUC - a full set on paper, but the values do not reconcile. Error of 25% implies accuracy of 75%; sensitivity of 87% with specificity of 60% on a 39-severe, 49-non-severe split implies roughly 72%; and the headline 88% matches the separately reported maximum AUC of 0.88 exactly. The internally consistent reading is that the classifier achieves roughly 75% accuracy with 87% sensitivity and 60% specificity, and that mean AUC is 0.85. That specificity of 60% is the more informative figure for a severity-grading tool: two in five non-severe participants would be labelled severe.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is the paper's organising purpose rather than an add-on. By fitting a separate attention model per severity group and comparing their retained feature sets, the analysis yields a directly interpretable dissociation - presence of face and presence of skin predict fixation for non-severe participants but not for severe ones - which is then connected to the wider literature on reduced face and eye-region looking in autism and on face perception relating to social-impairment severity. The authors correctly note the partial redundancy between skin and face features as reinforcing rather than duplicating the finding, and identify the single differing non-semantic feature as a steerable pyramid component that indexes edges, texture and orientation and 'is not related to object recognition'. The conclusion drawn - that top-down mechanisms differentiate severity more than bottom-up ones - is well supported by the structure of the result, subject to the caveat that the feature selection may not have been nested within folds.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Five-fold cross-validation with splitting stated explicitly at the subject level, which is the correct unit and is clearly described. Folds were proportionally balanced. Two elements fall outside the loop. ReliefF feature selection is described once, per group, with no statement that it was repeated within folds - and since the group-specific feature sets are the paper's principal scientific claim, whether they were derived using all 88 participants or only training-fold participants materially affects their status. The 20-frame decision threshold was chosen by the Youden index applied to the ROC curve, which is the same curve used to characterise performance, so the operating point is fitted to the evaluation. There is no independent cohort, no external site and no held-out replication.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: Autism Spectrum Disorder, Severity Level, Supervised Machine Learning, Classifier, Eye Tracking. 'Severity Level' as a headline term marks this as one of the few corpus studies whose target is gradation rather than detection.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: 2021 IEEE 34th International Symposium on Computer-Based Medical Systems (CBMS), pages 142-147 - a medical informatics conference, with authorship spanning a university psychiatry department, a bioinformatics programme and a computing school. The same institution and venue as another corpus record on joint attention trajectories, from an overlapping author group.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021. The framing is that severity classification is under-explored relative to diagnosis - 'although we know little about its potential use in severity classification, in literature there are some important clues about the use of eye tracking in symptom severity' - and it assembles those clues carefully: a reported correlation of r = -0.52 between fixation on social stimuli and ADOS social scores; evidence that geometric preference predicts later symptom severity and joint-attention gaze shifting; and a finding that autistic children preferring the geometric side scored worse on ADOS, Mullen and Vineland alike. Its methodological argument is that region-of-interest analysis, which dominates the field, discards information: 'although using all the image information and visual attention models... could be more informative'. It builds directly on a 2015 three-level saliency study that found semantic features important in characterising autistic viewing and 'suggesting top-down impairments', and extends that from diagnosis to severity - which is a genuinely incremental and well-posed research question rather than a reapplication of an existing method to a new dataset.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Classification of Children With Autism and Typical Development Using Eye-Tracking Data From Face-to-Face Conversations: Machine Learning Model Development and Performance Evaluation
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Zhao Z; Tang H; Zhang X; Qu X; Hu X; Lu J
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: Journal of Medical Internet Research, 23(8), e29328
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: School-age children with autism of at least average nonverbal intelligence
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking and gaze (live social interaction)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Test whether gaze recorded during genuine face-to-face conversation - rather than while viewing images, videos or web pages - can classify autism, on the argument that gaze behaviour is highly context-sensitive and that 'findings obtained from image-viewing tasks could not be directly generalized to the scenario of natural social interaction'. A secondary aim was to test whether combining fixation features with conversation duration improves classification
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study using live dyadic interaction rather than screen-based stimuli
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One conversation per child, comprising four chronologically arranged sessions of variable duration
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A structured face-to-face conversation with a 33-year-old female interviewer blinded to group membership, seated 80 cm away, in four purposively designed sessions: general questions (name, school, best friend, an event from the previous week, summer plans) to establish familiarity; hobby sharing, on the reasoning that a self-selected topic may induce different gaze behaviour from generic ones; ten yes-no questions, designed to elicit head nodding or shaking; and question raising, in which the child is invited to ask the interviewer questions, examining initiative. The full question list is published
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory dyadic setup with two cameras - one capturing both parties in profile and one positioned beside the interviewer capturing the child's frontal view; autistic children recruited from the Child Psychiatry Department of Shenzhen Kangning Hospital and comparison children from local schools
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: A tiered clinical procedure reported in unusual detail: primary diagnosis by a licensed psychiatrist with at least five years of clinical experience following DSM-IV criteria, further evaluation by a senior psychiatrist, and consultation with at least two additional senior psychiatrists in the event of disagreement. The authors state plainly that ADOS and ADI-R were unavailable - 'owing to limited access to instruments such as the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule or the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised'. Inclusion additionally required at least average nonverbal intelligence, screened by the psychiatrist and measured with Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices, and absence of ADHD, schizophrenia or other clinical conditions
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 20 enrolled, 19 analysed
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: ADHD, schizophrenia and other clinical conditions were exclusion criteria
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not measured, and the authors acknowledge the consequence directly: 'the ASD severity level was not specifically measured in our study... The children with ASD included in this study could be viewed as representing individuals with minor severity'
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Healthy children with no mental or physical disorders and no autism or ADHD diagnosis in first-degree relatives, recruited from local schools. Excluding on first-degree relative diagnosis controls for the broader autism phenotype
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 23 enrolled, 20 analysed
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes - 99.6 versus 108.8 months, not significantly different (t37 = 1.09, p = .28)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Yes - 17:2 versus 17:3, not significantly different (chi-square = 0.17, p = .68), though only four girls participated in total, which the authors name as a limitation
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Established by absence of mental or physical disorder and absence of autism or ADHD in first-degree relatives
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Head-mounted eye-tracking data during live conversation, plus video from two cameras
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A snapshot image was drawn from the eye-tracking video to define four areas of interest - eyes, mouth, whole face and whole body. Tobii Pro Lab's real-world mapping algorithm projected gaze points from the moving scene video onto the snapshot, with correctness confirmed by a human observer and manual mapping performed wherever automatic assignment failed or was incorrect. Fixations were defined by a velocity-threshold filter at below 30 degrees per second for at least 60 ms. Percentage fixation time on each area of interest was computed per session as fixation duration divided by that session's total duration
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Tobii Pro Glasses 2 head-mounted eye tracker at 50 Hz with Tobii Pro Lab for dynamic-stimulus fixation analysis; Samsung HMX-F90 camera at 25 Hz capturing both parties and Logitech C270 at 30 Hz capturing the child's frontal view; Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices for nonverbal IQ
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Conversational eye-tracking data from 39 children, drawn from a larger project on behavioural markers of autism; no release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Video of identifiable children in dyadic interaction plus first-person scene video from head-mounted glasses - highly sensitive material. Governance is reported: the protocol followed the Declaration of Helsinki and the ethical guidelines of Shenzhen University, with written informed consent provided by caregivers. No committee approval number is given. Notably, participants were not informed of the eye tracker's function and a post-experiment interview confirmed none was aware their gaze was being recorded - a deception justified for behavioural naturalness but not discussed as an ethical matter
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Area-of-interest fixation percentages and conversation duration measures
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Twenty-one features. Sixteen visual fixation features: percentage of fixation time on each of four areas of interest (eyes, mouth, whole face, whole body) in each of four conversation sessions. Five session length features: the duration of each of the four sessions plus total duration across all four. Including conversation duration as a feature is the design's distinctive move - it captures an interactional outcome rather than a gaze property, and it turned out to be the single most informative feature
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Tobii Pro Lab with real-world mapping and human verification; velocity-threshold fixation filter
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, both through the forward selection ordering and through a full table of univariate group comparisons for all 16 area-of-interest features
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Forward feature selection, which adds features one at a time in order of the classification accuracy achieved, so the ordering is itself an importance ranking; plus Mann-Whitney U tests on every area-of-interest feature and on each session length
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The optimal three-feature model used total session length, mouth fixation in session 1, and whole body fixation in session 3. Total session length alone achieved 79.49% accuracy. Univariate comparisons found significant group differences for mouth, face and whole body fixation in sessions 1 and 2 and marginally in session 4, but never for the eyes area of interest in any of the four sessions
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reported in full with medians and effect statistics. Autistic children fixated less on the mouth (0.05 versus 0.19 in session 1, p < .001), face (0.21 versus 0.41, p = .001) and whole body (0.33 versus 0.55, p = .003), with the same pattern in session 2. Eye-region fixation did not differ in any session - a notable null given the prominence of eye-region avoidance in the wider literature. Autistic children took significantly longer to complete the same fixed number of questions, in sessions 1 (p < .01), 2 (p = .02) and 4 (p = .02) and overall (p < .01), but not in the yes-no session
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Classical supervised classification with wrapper feature selection
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Support vector machine, linear discriminant analysis, decision tree and random forest, each combined with forward feature selection that iteratively adds the feature yielding the highest classification accuracy at each step
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-out cross-validation with the test set containing a single participant, repeated until all participants were tested, described as implemented 'to minimize the potential overfitting problem'. The critical qualification is that forward feature selection operates by evaluating candidate features on classification accuracy, and the accuracy in question is the same leave-one-out estimate that is reported - so features were selected to maximise the reported metric. The paper additionally reports results for every feature-count from 1 to 21 across four classifiers and three feature sets, and quotes the maximum
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for every classifier and feature set, a confusion matrix for the best model, accuracy as a function of feature count for all four classifiers, and a full table showing the incremental effect of each added feature. A majority-class baseline is also computed and compared - 51.3% - which the authors use to confirm the result is not an artefact of class imbalance
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Combined features: SVM best at 92.31% accuracy with three features (specificity 100%, sensitivity 84.21%, AUC 0.92), then LDA 89.74% with four features (AUC 0.92), decision tree 84.62% with two features (AUC 0.86) and random forest 84.62% with sixteen features (AUC 0.86). Visual fixation features alone: maximum 84.62% by LDA with three features and by decision tree with two (both AUC 0.86). Session length features alone: maximum 84.62% by SVM with four features (AUC 0.87). Total session length as a single feature achieved 79.49%. The best model's confusion matrix shows all 20 typically developing children correctly classified and 3 of 19 autistic children missed
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Gaze recorded during a live structured conversation classified autistic from typically developing children at 92.31% accuracy, higher than fixation features alone or conversation duration alone (both 84.62%). The most striking finding is which feature carried most of the signal: total conversation length alone achieved 79.49%, meaning that how long a child took to answer a fixed set of questions was more informative than any gaze measure. Autistic children fixated less on the mouth, face and whole body of their conversational partner, but eye-region fixation did not differ in any of the four sessions. The three misclassified autistic children were shown by error analysis to fall within the typically developing distribution on all three selected features, which the authors present as evidence of heterogeneity rather than model failure.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Reduced fixation on the interviewer's mouth, face and body during conversation - but not specifically on the eyes - together with substantially longer time taken to complete a fixed set of conversational exchanges
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Validate with a larger autistic sample varying in severity and with a balanced sex ratio; include individuals with other clinical conditions such as developmental delay and ADHD, since the study only separated autism from typical development; recruit younger children given that mean age at diagnosis is around 60 months; develop contactless and calibration-free gaze recording, since head-mounted trackers may particularly affect autistic children's behaviour; extract richer gaze features including fixation counts, entropy, revisits and oculomotor measures; and combine modalities including eye tracking, kinematic, EEG and neuroimaging data
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The central contribution is the setting rather than the method, and it is well argued: essentially every other gaze study in this corpus records looking at a screen, whereas this one records looking at an actual conversational partner, on the correct reasoning that 'the presence of the social partner elicits a different pattern of both neural response and gaze behavior' and that image-viewing findings therefore may not transfer. The execution is careful in several respects that matter for a live-interaction study. The interviewer was blinded to group membership and required to behave consistently, and - unusually - this was checked empirically by quantifying her movement from the video recordings using image differencing and testing for a group difference. Participants were unaware the glasses recorded gaze, verified post hoc, so gaze was not self-conscious. Real-world gaze mapping was verified by a human observer with manual correction where automatic assignment failed. Diagnosis followed a tiered psychiatric procedure with escalation on disagreement, and the unavailability of ADOS and ADI-R is disclosed. A majority-class baseline is computed and compared, which almost no other study here does. The single most valuable substantive finding is that total conversation length alone classified at 79.49% - that is, the duration a child took to answer a fixed number of questions was more informative than any gaze feature, which reframes what the eye tracker is contributing and suggests that a far simpler measure captures much of the signal. Equally notable is the null result for the eye region, which did not differ between groups in any of the four sessions despite eye-region avoidance being the field's canonical finding. Two problems bound the accuracy claim. Forward feature selection chooses features by their classification accuracy, and that accuracy is the same leave-one-out estimate reported as the result, so the selection is not nested and the 92.31% is optimistically biased; the paper further reports every feature count from 1 to 21 across four classifiers and three feature sets and quotes the maximum, which compounds it. And IQ differs significantly between groups (100.8 versus 116.1, p = .02) with no adjustment, on a task requiring sustained conversational exchange, so verbal and cognitive ability is a live confound for the session-length feature that does most of the work. The authors' own scoping is appropriately modest, describing the work as 'proof-of-concept research' and noting that their autistic sample represents minor severity.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: 20 autistic children recruited from the Child Psychiatry Department of Shenzhen Kangning Hospital and 23 typically developing children from local schools, with four excluded for eye-tracking technical problems leaving 19 and 20. No other-diagnosis comparison group, and the authors identify this as a substantive limitation rather than a scope note: 'it remains unclear whether eye-tracking data could effectively detect ASD from other clinical phenotypes (eg, developmental delay and ADHD)'.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'children with typical development (TD)', 'healthy children'. Consistently person-first with 'typical development' as the comparison term, though 'healthy children' appears in the inclusion criteria. The framing locates the diagnostic problem in procedure rather than person: current diagnosis 'involves substantive subjective procedures that can be negatively impacted by various factors such as caregivers' reporting bias and clinicians' insufficient capability in differentiating ASD', and is 'highly labor- and time-demanding due to the shortage in clinical specialists'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Autistic group: 19 analysed, 17 male and 2 female, mean age 99.6 +/- 25.1 months, mean IQ 100.8 +/- 22.7. Typically developing group: 20 analysed, 17 male and 3 female, mean age 108.8 +/- 27.0 months, mean IQ 116.1 +/- 22.7. Age (p = .28) and sex ratio (p = .68) are well matched and formally tested. IQ is not - the groups differ by 15.3 points (p = .02) - and this is reported in the demographic table but not adjusted for anywhere in the modelling, which matters given that the single most informative feature is how long a child took to complete a conversation. Only four girls participated in total, which the authors name as a limitation with the specific rationale that autistic males and females differ in behavioural presentation, cognitive domains and emotions. No ethnicity or socioeconomic data.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: A tiered clinical procedure described in more detail than most of the corpus: DSM-IV diagnosis by a licensed psychiatrist with at least five years of experience, further evaluation by a senior psychiatrist, and escalation to at least two additional senior psychiatrists on disagreement. The unavailability of ADOS and ADI-R is disclosed explicitly as a resource constraint. Nonverbal IQ was screened by the psychiatrist and measured with Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices, and ADHD, schizophrenia and other conditions were exclusions. The comparison group was screened for absence of mental or physical disorder and for absence of autism or ADHD in first-degree relatives - the latter controlling for the broader autism phenotype, a step few studies here take.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Nonverbal IQ via Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices for both groups, with at least average intelligence required for inclusion in the autistic group. No autism severity measure of any kind, which the authors state candidly: severity 'was not specifically measured in our study' and the sample 'could be viewed as representing individuals with minor severity'. No language, adaptive functioning or comorbidity scores. The IQ data are reported but, unusually, the significant group difference they reveal is not carried into the analysis.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: determine whether gaze during live face-to-face conversation classifies autism, and whether combining fixation features with conversation duration improves on either alone. Main findings: 92.31% accuracy with SVM using three combined features against 84.62% for either feature family alone; total conversation length alone achieved 79.49%; autistic children fixated less on mouth, face and body but not differently on the eyes; and the three misclassified autistic children fell within the typically developing range on all selected features.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A laboratory dyadic setup at Shenzhen University with participants seated 80 cm from the interviewer, autistic children recruited from Shenzhen Kangning Hospital's Child Psychiatry Department and comparison children from local schools. Funded by seven Shenzhen and Guangdong municipal, medical-discipline and provincial research programmes. No conflicts declared.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A structured four-session conversation with a single blinded interviewer, each session designed to probe a different aspect of interaction: general questions for familiarisation, hobby sharing to test whether a self-selected topic changes gaze, yes-no questions to elicit head nodding or shaking, and question raising to examine initiative. The full question list is published, which makes the protocol reproducible in a way that most naturalistic-interaction studies are not. The design's key property is that the number of exchanges is fixed while the time taken is free, which is exactly what makes session length an interpretable behavioural measure rather than an artefact - and it is that measure which proved most discriminative.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; one conversation per child with no follow-up. Data are first-person scene video from head-mounted glasses plus two external camera feeds of identifiable children in dyadic interaction. Governance is partially reported - Helsinki principles, Shenzhen University ethical guidelines, and written caregiver consent - but no ethics committee approval number is given. Participants were deliberately not told the glasses recorded gaze, with a post-experiment interview confirming none had realised; this is methodologically well motivated for behavioural naturalness but the deception is not discussed as an ethical consideration.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Tobii Pro Glasses 2 head-mounted eye tracker at 50 Hz with Tobii Pro Lab for dynamic-stimulus analysis, plus two video cameras at 25 and 30 Hz. Two practical details are unusual and worth recording: an accuracy test was performed at the end of any conversation in which the participant had moved the glasses, and the authors report verifying that the device 'was reliably accurate even if the glasses were moved by participants during the conversation'. They nonetheless flag head-mounted tracking as a limitation, noting that autistic individuals 'are more sensitive to wearing devices' and recommending contactless, calibration-free alternatives.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong. Reported: full question list for all four sessions; interviewer age, sex, blinding and consistency requirement; seating distance; both camera models with sampling rates; eye tracker model and rate; the four areas of interest; the real-world mapping procedure with human verification and manual correction; the velocity-threshold fixation definition with its 30 deg/s and 60 ms parameters; the fixation-percentage computation; all 21 features; the forward selection procedure described step by step; the leave-one-out scheme; and a table giving accuracy, sensitivity and specificity at every feature count from 1 to 21. Missing: ethics approval number, data or code release, and classifier hyperparameters. The interviewer-consistency check by image differencing is itself reported with its test statistic.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged extensively and specifically: the sample excludes severe presentations and children below 6 or above 13, so the work is 'proof-of-concept research'; only four girls participated, and autistic males and females differ across behavioural, cognitive and emotional domains; severity was not measured; head-mounted eye tracking may itself affect autistic children's behaviour and contactless methods are needed; only fixation percentage was computed while counts, entropy, revisits and oculomotor measures were available; only autism versus typical development was tested, leaving discrimination from other clinical phenotypes unknown; and live interaction introduces uncontrollable subjective factors, with the honest observation that 'no human being can be expected to behave exactly the same way when interacting with different people'. Not acknowledged: forward feature selection maximises the same leave-one-out accuracy that is reported, so the headline is not an unbiased estimate, and the maximum is quoted across 21 feature counts, four classifiers and three feature sets; and IQ differs significantly between groups with no adjustment, despite the leading feature being conversation duration.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Validate on a larger autistic sample varying in severity with balanced sex ratio; include other clinical conditions such as developmental delay and ADHD; recruit younger children, citing a meta-analytic mean diagnosis age of 60.48 months overall and 43.18 months among children aged 10 or under; develop contactless calibration-free gaze recording, citing recent webcam-plus-computer-vision work whose accuracy was comparable to manual coding; generate richer gaze features including fixation counts, entropy, revisits and oculomotor performance; and combine eye tracking with kinematic, EEG and neuroimaging data.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Two behavioural channels from a single live interaction. Gaze allocation to a real conversational partner across four regions - eyes, mouth, whole face, whole body - and interaction duration, measured as the time taken to complete a fixed number of conversational exchanges. The second is not a gaze measure at all but an outcome of the interaction, and treating it as a feature alongside gaze is the design's most productive decision. The four-session structure adds a temporal dimension, since each feature is computed per session, allowing the analysis to show that group differences in mouth and face fixation are strong in the early sessions and attenuate later.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: A clean and well-quantified fusion result, with both single-modality baselines reported: fixation features alone reach 84.62%, session length features alone reach 84.62%, and combined they reach 92.31% - roughly an 8-point gain. What makes it more informative than most fusion claims in the corpus is that the two feature families are conceptually distinct rather than two views of the same signal: one measures where the child looked, the other how long the interaction took. The best three-feature model draws on both, taking total session length plus two fixation features. The finding that session length alone reaches 79.49% is the most consequential single number in the paper, since it implies most of the discriminative information is available without an eye tracker at all.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Four classical classifiers - SVM, linear discriminant analysis, decision tree and random forest - each wrapped in forward feature selection, with the paper giving a short rationale for each including the observation that decision trees offer 'strong interpretability, but it is prone to overfitting'. The model comparison is informative in one respect: random forest needed sixteen features to reach 84.62% while SVM reached 92.31% with three, which speaks to how concentrated the signal is. The wrapper design is also what creates the study's main methodological weakness, since the selection criterion is the reported metric.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Twenty-one features: sixteen fixation percentages (four areas of interest by four sessions) and five durations (four sessions plus total). The representation is compact, interpretable and clinically legible - every feature is a proportion of looking at a named body region during a named conversational activity, or a duration. Computing features per session rather than pooling across the conversation is what allows the temporal pattern to emerge, showing group differences concentrated in the earlier sessions. The authors note the representation's narrowness themselves, observing that fixation counts, entropy, revisits and oculomotor features were all available and unexploited.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Comprehensive. Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for every classifier under every feature set; a confusion matrix for the best model; an accuracy-versus-feature-count curve for all four classifiers; a table showing the incremental contribution of each successively added feature; and full Mann-Whitney comparisons for all 16 fixation features and all session lengths. Crucially, a majority-class baseline of 51.3% is computed and explicitly compared, which is the check almost every other study in the corpus omits. The one gap is that no confidence intervals accompany any figure, and with 39 participants a single misclassification is worth 2.6 accuracy points.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is served three ways. The forward selection ordering itself ranks features by contribution, showing that total session length alone reaches 79.49% and that only two fixation features are needed on top of it. The univariate table gives medians and effect statistics for every fixation feature, which is what reveals the eye-region null. And an error analysis examines the three misclassified autistic children individually, showing that on each of the three selected features they fell within the typically developing distribution - for instance, one had a total session length shorter than 75% of the typically developing group and mouth fixation higher than half of them. The authors read this as heterogeneity rather than model failure, which is the correct inference and is rarely drawn elsewhere in this corpus. The substantive interpretations offered - that the mouth matters because the task is conversational, and that longer conversations may reflect difficulty extracting social information - are plausible and appropriately hedged.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Leave-one-out cross-validation at the participant level, explicitly motivated as overfitting protection. The defect is that forward feature selection evaluates candidate features by their classification accuracy, and that accuracy is the leave-one-out estimate itself, so features were chosen to maximise the number subsequently reported. Compounding this, results are reported for every feature count from 1 to 21 across four classifiers and three feature sets - 252 cells - and the maximum is quoted as the headline. There is no outer validation loop, no held-out cohort and no repetition. The saving grace is that the paper prints the entire selection trajectory, so a reader can see that accuracy plateaus at 92.31% from three features through eleven and that the single-feature result is 79.49%, which makes the shape of the result assessable even though the peak is optimistic.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorder; eye tracking; face-to-face interaction; machine learning; visual fixation. 'Face-to-face interaction' is the distinguishing term and accurately identifies the contribution - the novelty is the recording context rather than the algorithm.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Medical Internet Research, 23(8), e29328 - a digital health venue, with authorship spanning a human factors and ergonomics institute, a district centre for disease control, and a hospital child psychiatry department.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021. The framing is a specific critique of ecological validity in the existing eye-tracking literature. The paper observes that prior data 'were primarily obtained by having participants watch images (ie, videos, pictures, web pages)' but that 'human gaze behavior is highly context-sensitive', that experimental setting and cognitive load influence visual attention, that face-to-face interaction is 'much more perceptually and cognitively difficult' than image watching, and that 'the presence of the social partner elicits a different pattern of both neural response and gaze behavior' - concluding that image-viewing findings 'could not be directly generalized to the scenario of natural social interaction'. It also situates itself on age, noting a meta-analytic mean diagnosis age of 60.48 months and arguing that future work should examine younger children than its own 6-13 range. And it is unusually explicit that the field has not yet addressed differential diagnosis: 'our study and most others only classified individuals with ASD and TD... More scientific endeavor is certainly required before a practical ML model that could detect ASD from different conditions is established.'

data_charting_rubrics.title: Combined Signal Processing Based Techniques and Feed Forward Neural Networks for Pathological Voice Detection and Classification
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Jayasree T; Shia S
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Children with autism, alongside a separate Down syndrome cohort
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Speech and vocalisation (acoustic voice quality)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Detect autism and Down syndrome from voice, and - the paper's distinctive aim - discriminate between the two conditions, on the observation that although prior work has analysed acoustic variability in autistic, Down syndrome and typically developing children separately, 'there has been no attempt to classify both'. A secondary aim is a systematic comparison of three acoustic feature families
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional three-way acoustic classification with sample-level analysis, comprising two detection tasks and one differential-classification task
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Multiple sustained phonations per child, yielding roughly 13 samples per participant
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Sustained phonation of the vowel /ah/. The authors position this deliberately against alternatives, noting that 'most of the existing voice based-autism detection techniques use either short speech utterances or utterances segmented from spontaneous speech to detect autism' and proposing sustained vowel phonation instead - a maximally controlled task that isolates voice source and vocal tract properties from linguistic and prosodic content
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: A noise-free location, with recording via Audio Editor 2016 software on a laptop
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None reported. The paper describes ADOS-R and ADI-R in its introduction as the instruments specially trained physicians and psychologists use, and criticises them as requiring 'standardized structures for capturing the behaviors and found to be very difficult', but gives no account of how the six autistic children in its own sample were diagnosed - no instrument, criteria, clinician, setting or date
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 6 autistic children (3 boys, 3 girls) providing 79 voice samples
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: 5 to 14 years, stated for all children collectively
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes - 7 control children (3 boys, 4 girls) providing 99 samples
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 7 children, 99 samples
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Cannot be assessed - a single 5-14 year range is given for all 19 children with no group-wise ages, means, standard deviations or test. This matters acutely for voice work, since fundamental frequency, jitter and shimmer change substantially across this age band and pubertal onset falls within it
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Approximately by count (3:3, 2:4, 3:4) but with no test, and with a total of only 19 children the balance carries little weight. Sex is a first-order determinant of the acoustic features used here
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted without a stated basis
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Audio recordings of sustained vowel phonation
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Pre-emphasis, framing and windowing with a 30 ms Hamming window, plus silence removal. Perturbation measures (jitter, shimmer) computed from the fundamental frequency; noise measures (harmonics-to-noise ratio, glottal-to-noise excitation ratio, signal-to-noise ratio) with mean, standard deviation, skewness and kurtosis computed across analysis windows; MFCCs from 30 ms windows at 15 ms shift, comprising 12 static coefficients plus log energy, the zeroth cepstral coefficient and delta and delta-delta features, summarised as means and standard deviations of 16 per-frame features; and 12 RASTA-PLP features from 11th-order all-pole modelling over 25 ms windows with 10 ms overlap, likewise summarised by mean and standard deviation
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Audio Editor 2016 on a laptop, recording PCM mono WAV at 16-bit resolution; MATLAB on an i5 processor for all feature extraction and modelling; LIBSVM for the SVM comparator. The stated sampling rate of '24,000 kHz' is evidently a typographical error for 24 kHz
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: A 255-sample voice corpus from 19 Indian children across three groups; no release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Voice recordings of identifiable children with clinical diagnoses. No ethics committee approval, parental consent procedure, anonymisation statement or data governance policy appears anywhere in the paper
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Three acoustic feature families spanning time-domain perturbation, noise energy and spectral-cepstral representations
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Perturbation: jitter (cycle-to-cycle frequency variation) and shimmer (cycle-to-cycle amplitude variation). Noise energy: harmonics-to-noise ratio, glottal-to-noise excitation ratio and signal-to-noise ratio, each summarised by mean, standard deviation, skewness and kurtosis. Spectral-cepstral: mel-frequency cepstral coefficients and RASTA-PLP. The paper motivates the progression through these families explicitly - perturbation measures are limited because fundamental frequency is hard to estimate in pathological voices, noise parameters are limited because 'the noise parameters depend on the voice recording environment', and spectral-cepstral features are proposed to overcome both
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Custom MATLAB implementations, with the authors noting that MFCC and RASTA-PLP 'can be calculated easily using the inbuilt routines present in the MATLAB'
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, as a systematic comparison of feature families across all three tasks rather than as within-model importance
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Exhaustive comparison of seven individual feature sets and four combined feature sets across three classification tasks, with accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, AUC and processing time reported for each
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: MFCC and RASTA-PLP for autism detection (both 100% accuracy, AUC 1); MFCC, RASTA-PLP and harmonics-to-noise ratio for Down syndrome detection (all 100%); MFCC and harmonics-to-noise ratio for autism-versus-Down-syndrome discrimination (both 100%). Perturbation and noise measures performed considerably worse throughout, with harmonics-to-noise ratio giving the weakest autism detection at 77.8%
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported. No group means, distributions, effect sizes or statistical tests are given for any acoustic feature, so nothing is established about how autistic voices differ acoustically - only that a classifier can separate them. The introduction summarises prior directional findings (higher mean fundamental frequency in Down syndrome, reduced pitch range, monotonic or sing-song autistic speech) but the study contributes no directional evidence of its own
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Shallow supervised neural network on engineered acoustic features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: A three-layer feed-forward neural network with one hidden layer, sigmoidal hidden activation and softmax output, trained by scaled conjugate gradient, learning rate 0.05, momentum 0.3, 2000 epochs to a mean squared error of 0.0001. The number of hidden neurons was set 'by means of trial rule' separately for each feature set and each task, ranging from 4 to 20. Compared against LIBSVM with an RBF kernel and a naive Bayes classifier
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 70% training, 15% cross-validation and 15% testing with six-fold cross-validation - but applied at the level of voice samples, not children. The corpus comprises 255 samples from only 19 children, so roughly 13 samples per child, and nothing indicates that samples from a given child were confined to a single partition. With repeated sustained phonations from the same speaker, speaker identity is far easier to learn than diagnostic category, and the reported perfect scores are consistent with the classifier recognising individuals rather than conditions. Compounding this, hidden neuron counts were selected by trial to maximise accuracy for each feature set and task, so every tabulated figure is a maximum over that search
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for every feature set on every task, plus processing time comparisons and hidden-neuron sensitivity curves. Reporting is extensive in coverage but contains no confidence intervals, no confusion matrices and no statistical comparison between conditions
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Autism detection: MFCC and RASTA-PLP both 100% accuracy with AUC 1; SNR 89.4%, jitter 88.88%, shimmer and GNE 83.33%, HNR 77.8%. Down syndrome detection: MFCC and RASTA-PLP both 100%, HNR 94.73%, SNR 92.4%, GNE 89.47%, jitter and shimmer 81.25%. Autism versus Down syndrome: MFCC and HNR both 100%, SNR 90.4%, RASTA-PLP 85.7%, jitter and shimmer 81.25%, GNE 73.68%. Comparators on MFCC for autism detection: SVM 78.5%, naive Bayes 91.2%, against the network's 100%. Combining feature families generally reduced performance - for autism detection, MFCC plus RASTA-PLP fell to 80.7% from 100% for either alone
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Feed-forward networks on spectral-cepstral features of sustained /ah/ phonation reportedly achieved 100% accuracy for autism detection, Down syndrome detection and autism-versus-Down-syndrome discrimination, with MFCC and RASTA-PLP consistently outperforming jitter, shimmer and noise-energy measures. Two findings are informative independent of the inflated absolute values. Combining feature families reduced rather than improved performance in almost every condition, which the authors report plainly. And the paper is one of very few in the corpus to attempt discrimination between two neurodevelopmental conditions rather than between one condition and typical development - the harder and more clinically relevant task.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Not characterised. The paper reports classification performance but no acoustic description of how autistic voices differ from those of controls or of children with Down syndrome
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: None stated as a distinct section beyond the general claim that the proposed method outperforms comparators
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Two aspects of this study are worth taking seriously and one problem invalidates its headline numbers. The valuable elements: it is one of very few papers in the corpus to attempt differential classification between two neurodevelopmental conditions rather than the much easier condition-versus-typical contrast, which is the discrimination clinical practice actually requires; and it conducts a systematic comparison of three acoustic feature families with a stated theoretical rationale for the progression between them - perturbation measures fail because fundamental frequency estimation is unreliable in disordered voices, noise measures fail because they depend on recording environment, and spectral-cepstral features are proposed to overcome both. Its finding that combining feature families degraded performance in almost every condition is also reported honestly and cuts against the fusion orthodoxy elsewhere in this corpus. The disabling problem is the unit of analysis. The corpus is 255 samples from just 19 children - about 13 sustained phonations each - and the 70/15/15 partition with six-fold cross-validation operates over samples with no indication that a child's samples were kept together. Repeated sustained vowel phonations from one speaker are close to a speaker-identification problem, and the features used (MFCC, RASTA-PLP, jitter, shimmer, HNR) are precisely those employed in speaker recognition. The reported 100% accuracies across three separate tasks are exactly what speaker-level leakage produces, and no other explanation is offered. Layered on top, the hidden neuron count was chosen by trial to maximise accuracy for each feature set and task, so every tabulated figure is already a maximum over a search. Beyond validation, the reporting gaps are severe: no diagnostic instrument for either clinical group, no group-wise ages in a 5-14 year sample where voice changes with maturation, no ethics or consent statement for recordings of identifiable children with clinical diagnoses, and no acoustic description of any group difference. The framing is also the most pathologising in the corpus - autism is presented as a 'voice disability' and a 'pathological voice' alongside a description of Down syndrome phenotype as including 'mental retardation' - language that is both outdated and conceptually confused, since autism is not a voice disorder.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Three groups, but 19 children in total: 6 autistic (3 boys, 3 girls), 6 with Down syndrome (2 boys, 4 girls) and 7 controls (3 boys, 4 girls), contributing 79, 77 and 99 sustained vowel samples respectively. The inclusion of a Down syndrome group is the design's most valuable feature - it is one of only a handful of studies in the corpus with an other-diagnosis comparison rather than only typical development, enabling the differential question the paper poses. But with six children per clinical group the analysis rests on a very small number of individuals however many samples each provides.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: The most pathologising language in the corpus, and conceptually as well as ethically problematic. Autism is repeatedly described as a 'pathological voice' and grouped under 'voice disability' alongside Down syndrome - a categorisation that misstates what autism is, since it is not a disorder of the voice. The Down syndrome phenotype is described as including 'mental retardation, general hypotonia... maxillary hypoplasia... with a relative macroglossia (unusually large tongue), short neck, and obesity'. Children are 'normal' versus 'affected'. Autistic speech is characterised as 'abnormal and is described as machine-like monotonic or sing-song'. Even allowing for a signal-processing venue's conventions, the register is markedly out of step with the rest of the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Almost none. Nineteen children aged 5-14, with sex counts by group but no ages, means, standard deviations or matching test for any group. The 5-14 range is the critical gap: fundamental frequency, jitter, shimmer and formant structure all change substantially across childhood and pubertal onset falls inside this window, so any group age difference would directly produce the acoustic differences the classifier exploits. Sex is likewise a primary determinant of these features and is balanced only by count across very small groups. No IQ, severity, comorbidity, language ability, socioeconomic or recruitment information.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None. The paper describes ADOS-R and ADI-R in its introduction and criticises them for requiring 'standardized structures for capturing the behaviors and found to be very difficult', but never states how the six autistic children in its own sample were identified - no instrument, criteria, clinician or setting. The same applies to the Down syndrome group, where the paper notes that 'Down Syndrome Screening tests are used for diagnosing Down Syndrome. Nevertheless, they cannot give appropriate results', without saying what was used here. Control status is asserted without any screening.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No IQ, developmental, language, adaptive or severity measure, and no comorbidity information for any of the three groups.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: detect autism and Down syndrome from sustained vowel phonation and discriminate between them, comparing three acoustic feature families. Main findings: MFCC and RASTA-PLP achieved 100% accuracy for autism detection and Down syndrome detection; MFCC and harmonics-to-noise ratio achieved 100% for autism-versus-Down-syndrome discrimination; perturbation and noise measures performed worse throughout; combining feature families reduced performance in almost every condition; and the feed-forward network outperformed SVM and naive Bayes comparators on the same features.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Recording in an unspecified 'noise free location' using consumer audio editing software on a laptop, at two engineering colleges in Tamil Nadu. No recruitment route, clinical setting or collection period is described, and no funding or ethics information appears.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Sustained phonation of the vowel /ah/, chosen explicitly against the alternative of connected or spontaneous speech. This is a defensible methodological position for voice-quality analysis - it holds linguistic content constant and isolates phonatory function - but it is a severe constraint for autism specifically, since the acoustic differences documented in autistic speech concern prosody, intonation contour and pragmatic use of voice, all of which are eliminated by a sustained vowel. The paper's own introduction describes autistic speech as 'machine-like monotonic or sing-song', properties that cannot manifest in an isolated sustained vowel, so the task may not be capable of capturing the phenomenon it is aimed at.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; multiple phonations per child in a single session with no follow-up. Data are voice recordings of identifiable children with clinical diagnoses. No ethics committee approval, parental consent procedure, anonymisation statement or data-handling policy appears anywhere in the paper - a complete absence rather than a partial omission, and one that matters given the population.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Audio Editor 2016 on a laptop recording PCM mono WAV at 16-bit resolution in a stated noise-free location; MATLAB on an i5 processor for all processing; LIBSVM for the SVM comparator. The recording chain is consumer-grade, which the paper does not treat as a limitation despite its own observation that 'the noise parameters depend on the voice recording environment. Hence the values of parameters also vary accordingly'. The stated sampling rate of '24,000 kHz' is a transcription error for 24 kHz.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Detailed on signal processing, absent on everything else. Fully specified: pre-emphasis, framing and windowing with 30 ms Hamming windows; the RASTA-PLP computation given as a seven-step procedure; MFCC parameters including window length, shift, coefficient count and dynamic features; RASTA-PLP order and window overlap; the network architecture, activation functions, training algorithm, learning rate, momentum, epoch count and target error; the hidden-neuron selection procedure; and the partition ratios. Absent: diagnostic instruments, group ages, ethics approval, recruitment, how samples were elicited or how many per child, whether the partition respected speaker boundaries, any group-level acoustic statistics, and any code or data.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: None. There is no limitations section and no caveat anywhere on sample size, validation design, generalisability or the absence of clinical characterisation. The nearest approach is the acknowledgement that hidden neuron counts have no exact formula and were fixed by trial. Identifiable in review: 255 samples derive from only 19 children with roughly 13 samples each, and the 70/15/15 partition operates over samples with no statement that speakers were kept together, which alone would explain the perfect accuracies; hidden neuron counts were tuned to maximise the reported accuracy for each feature set and task; no diagnostic instrument is reported for either clinical group; ages are given only as a collective 5-14 range in a domain where voice changes with maturation; no ethics or consent statement exists; and the sustained vowel task cannot express the prosodic properties the paper itself identifies as characterising autistic speech.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: None stated.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Voice quality during sustained phonation - specifically phonatory stability (jitter, shimmer), noise content of the glottal source (harmonics-to-noise, glottal-to-noise excitation and signal-to-noise ratios) and vocal tract spectral shape (MFCC, RASTA-PLP). This is the narrowest behavioural sample in the corpus: a single sustained vowel captures voice source and resonance properties but no prosody, no interaction, no linguistic content and no temporal structure of speech.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: The fusion result is clearly negative and is reported without spin, which makes it useful. Combining feature families reduced performance in nearly every condition: for autism detection MFCC plus RASTA-PLP fell to 80.7% from 100% for either alone, and HNR plus SNR fell to 53.2%; for Down syndrome detection MFCC plus RASTA-PLP fell to 78.3%. The single exception is HNR plus GNE reaching 100% for autism-versus-Down-syndrome discrimination. The authors state the conclusion plainly: 'the combined feature set provides less performance when compared to the individual features, for most of the cases'. Given the sample size this is more likely a dimensionality effect than a substantive finding, but it stands in useful contrast to the widespread assumption elsewhere in this corpus that combining features or modalities helps.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A single-hidden-layer feed-forward network trained by scaled conjugate gradient, chosen for its lack of user-dependent parameters and avoidance of line search, compared against RBF-kernel SVM and naive Bayes on identical features. The comparison is systematic and the network wins in every condition, though the margins - 100% against 78.5% for SVM and 91.2% for naive Bayes on the same MFCC features for autism detection - are large enough to be suspicious, since a shallow network and an RBF SVM on the same low-dimensional features would not normally diverge this far unless one is exploiting something the other is not.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Three feature families with an explicitly argued progression. Perturbation measures are introduced first and their limitation stated: 'a high degree of jitter consequences in a voice with roughness... Besides, it is very difficult to measure fundamental frequency, in the case of a pathological voice'. Noise energy measures follow, with their limitation likewise stated: they 'depend on the voice recording environment'. Spectral-cepstral features are then introduced to overcome both, with MFCC justified because it 'analyze the vocal tract independently of the vocal folds that can be injured due to voice pathologies' and RASTA-PLP because its bandpass filtering removes channel effects. This is a coherent and well-referenced design rationale, and the empirical ordering of results matches it. Each family is summarised to a fixed-length vector by statistical moments across frames.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for all seven individual and four combined feature sets across all three tasks - 33 conditions in total - plus processing time comparisons and hidden-neuron sensitivity curves. The coverage is unusually complete, and the processing time analysis is a practical dimension few studies report, showing MFCC and RASTA-PLP to be cheapest because jitter and shimmer require fundamental frequency estimation and GNE requires Hilbert envelope extraction and cross-correlation per glottal cycle. Missing: confidence intervals, confusion matrices, and any statistical test - and with perfect scores reported in six of 33 conditions, the metrics carry no information about where the model fails.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No model-explanation method and, more consequentially, no descriptive analysis of any group difference - no acoustic means, distributions, effect sizes or tests. The paper therefore establishes only that a classifier separates the groups, not what distinguishes them acoustically, which is a substantial gap for a study whose introduction reviews directional acoustic findings at length. The interpretation offered for why spectral-cepstral features win is at the level of feature family rather than individual parameter: they are Fourier-transform-based while jitter, shimmer, HNR and GNE are time-domain, and the result is said to be 'consistent with previous studies that, spectral and cepstral based features are best suited for discriminating voice with hoarseness from normal voice'.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The decisive weakness. Partitioning is 70/15/15 with six-fold cross-validation, but over 255 voice samples drawn from only 19 children - roughly 13 phonations each - with no statement that a child's samples were confined to one partition. Repeated sustained vowels from one speaker constitute a speaker-identification problem, and MFCC, RASTA-PLP, jitter, shimmer and HNR are the standard feature set for exactly that task, so a classifier can achieve near-perfect accuracy by recognising individuals and mapping them to their known group. Six of 33 reported conditions achieve exactly 100% accuracy with AUC 1, which is what speaker-level leakage produces and which is otherwise implausible for a clinical classification from a single vowel. Additionally, the hidden neuron count was chosen by trial to maximise accuracy separately for each feature set and task, so every figure is a maximum over that search. There is no independent cohort, no external validation and no held-out speaker test.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: Autism spectrum disorder; down syndrome; feed forward neural network; perturbation measures; noise parameters; cepstral features. Four of six name signal-processing constructs, accurately reflecting a paper whose contribution is a feature-family comparison with autism as one of two application labels.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Sound and Vibration, 55(2), 141-161 - an acoustics and signal-processing journal, not a clinical or machine-learning venue, published open access under CC BY 4.0. The venue explains both the depth of the signal-processing exposition and the absence of clinical reporting standards.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021. The framing is unusual and revealing: autism is introduced not as a neurodevelopmental condition but as one of two 'voice disabilities' within a paper about pathological voice detection, alongside Down syndrome, in a context where '1.2% of the world's total population is facing some type of voice disability'. Prevalence figures are given for both conditions in the United States and India (1 in 59 and 23 per 10,000 for autism; 1 in 700 and 1 in 1250 for Down syndrome). The critique of existing diagnosis is brief - ADOS-R and ADI-R 'require standardized structures for capturing the behaviors and found to be very difficult' - and the paper's real intellectual investment is in the acoustic literature, which it reviews carefully across five prior Down syndrome voice studies with their specific findings on fundamental frequency, jitter and shimmer. Its stated novelty is the differential task: prior work 'analyzed the variability of acoustic features in the voice produced by children with ADS, DS and normal children' but 'there has been no attempt to classify both'.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Computer-Aided Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Eye-Tracking Study Using Data Visualization and Deep Learning
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Cilia F; Carette R; Elbattah M; Dequen G; Guérin JL; Bosche J; Vandromme L; Le Driant B
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: School-aged children with autism
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking and gaze
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Recast autism screening from eye-tracking data as an image classification problem, by rendering gaze scanpaths as pictures in which spatial pattern and motion dynamics are both encoded - the latter through colour gradients keyed to velocity - so that a convolutional network can learn directly from the visual representation rather than from engineered fixation and saccade features
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study with an explicit comparison of image-level and participant-level validation, plus a correlational analysis against severity
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session per child of approximately 10 minutes, spanning multiple stimulus protocols
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Passive viewing of a heterogeneous battery drawn from several psychological protocols: three 58-second videos of joint attention initiation plus 18 corresponding 5-second photographs, in which a woman greets the child and then looks, verbalises and/or points toward a target present or absent from the child's visual field; twelve 4-second gaze-following videos in which an actor with a neutral face engages in direct gaze then shifts to one of three objects, with head-plus-eye shifts in six and eye-only shifts in six; static photographs of the same actors beside an object; and five minutes of cartoon scenes with emotional valence either contingent or non-contingent on the preceding scene. All conversation was in French, with a two-second central crosshair between stimuli
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: A quiet room at university premises with physical white barriers to reduce visual distraction, children seated alone or on a parent's lap approximately 60 cm from the screen
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Diagnosis was confirmed by health professionals in multidisciplinary autism specialty clinics using ADI-R and ADOS-G. The authors state candidly that 'we did not get permission to read the children's medical files', so ADI-R and ADOS-G scores were unavailable and were not analysed. Severity was independently estimated by psychologists using the French CARS, and communication level with the French Early Social Communication Scale (ECSP)
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Not reported; described as school-aged with a mean around 8 years
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: CARS administered to both groups by psychologists: 32.9 +/- 6.4 in the autistic group against exactly 15 with zero variance in the non-autistic group, the CARS floor. ECSP total score 141.1 +/- 50.3 versus 139.18 +/- 49.5, essentially identical between groups
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: For the non-autistic group 'parental reports of any possible concerns were carefully considered', and CARS was administered, returning the minimum possible score of 15 for every child
