data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Approximately - 7 years 7 months versus 8 years 0 months with near-identical spreads, though no statistical test of the difference is reported
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Closely - 19 male in each group out of 29 and 30 respectively, so 66% versus 63% male
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Established by parental report of concerns plus a floor CARS score
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Raw point-of-gaze coordinates over time, rendered as scanpath images
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Each participant's gaze coordinates were converted to images in three steps: a line drawn for every transition between consecutive gaze points; line colour varied on a greyscale spectrum according to the magnitude of gaze velocity computed from the change in point of gaze over time; and the image vertically mirrored because the coordinate origin sits at the screen bottom. The number of consecutive points drawn per image was capped at 200 - a value chosen after testing, since limits of 100-150 'turned out to poorly discriminate the 2 classes' while higher values risked cluttered visualisations - and velocity values were bounded at a quarter of the screen diagonal as physiologically implausible above that. Images were then background-cropped with OpenCV and scaled to 256 x 256
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: SMI RED250 screen-based remote eye tracker at 250 Hz; 17-inch monitor at 1280 x 1024; SMI Experiment Center for stimulus presentation; five-point calibration followed by verification procedures; Python with Matplotlib for visualisation, OpenCV for cropping, Keras for augmentation and modelling, a Tesla K80 GPU for training, and the Minerva R package for the maximal information coefficient analysis
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - a scanpath image dataset from 59 children, and the authors state that 'the data set was made freely available to be used by other studies investigating the potentials of eye tracking within the ASD context'
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes, per the authors' statement, though no repository link appears in the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not needed for the dataset; the demo application URL is available on request from the authors
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze coordinate data rendered as abstract scanpath images, low in identifiability, and released openly. Governance is reported and its basis explained: parents and guardians were informed of objectives, tasks and their right to withdraw at any time, written informed consent was obtained in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, all children gave their own agreement, and parents could remain in the experimental room. The authors state that 'this study did not require authorization from an ethics committee based on the recommendations for psychological research in France and in agreement with the national and institutional guidelines'
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Learned convolutional features over rendered scanpath images - no engineered gaze features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: None hand-specified. The representation is the image itself: spatial layout encodes where the gaze went, line colour encodes how fast it moved. The design intent is explicit - to 'compactly render eye movements into an image-based format while maintaining the dynamic characteristics of eye motion (eg, velocity) using color gradients' - so that a single visual object carries both the trajectory and its dynamics
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Convolutional layers of the CNN itself, with the authors noting that 'the features were extracted using the convolutional layers in the CNN model'
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No per-feature analysis, but the velocity encoding is validated indirectly through the maximal information coefficient analysis relating average velocity to CARS score
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Maximal information coefficient, chosen over Pearson correlation because inspection 'largely revealed the nonlinearity of the relationship between CARS scores and velocity', with the MIC value interpretable roughly as a coefficient of determination
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Gaze velocity, indirectly - MIC between CARS score and average velocity magnitude was 0.79, which the authors present as partly validating the classifier since velocity is what the colour gradient encodes
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported directionally for velocity, and the wider literature is presented as unsettled: one cited study found autistic children have faster eye movements with shorter saccadic latencies, favouring 'speed over accuracy'; another found high autistic traits associated with shorter and less frequent saccades; a third found greater saccade amplitude and higher frequency in autistic children. The authors note these divergences 'seem to depend largely on the equipment and data used', citing sampling rates of 60 Hz and 24 Hz in the conflicting studies against their own 250 Hz
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Deep convolutional classification on rendered visual representations
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: A convolutional neural network with four convolutional layers, four pooling layers and two fully connected layers, with dropout, implemented in Keras and trained over three epochs on a Tesla K80
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Three-fold cross-validation performed twice, under two different splitting units, and both results reported. In the first, folds are formed over the 547 scanpath images without regard to which child produced them. In the second, the 59 participants are randomly split into training and test sets first and images are then matched to those sets by participant ID, so no child contributes images to both. The paper reports the second explicitly as a check on the first: 'to further examine the model performance, the training and test sets were split based on the participants'. Data augmentation generated five synthetic samples per image, adding 2,735 samples
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: ROC curves with area under the curve and standard deviation across folds, plus accuracy, recall and precision, reported separately for the image-level and participant-level splits, and training and validation loss curves
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Image-level split: approximately 90% accuracy, 83% recall and 80% precision. Participant-level split: approximately 71% accuracy. The authors report the drop plainly - 'expectedly, the model performance declined' - and characterise 71% as 'still promising given the relatively small data set'. Separately, MIC between CARS score and average gaze velocity was 0.79
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Rendering eye-tracking scanpaths as images in which line colour encodes gaze velocity, then classifying them with a convolutional network, achieved about 90% accuracy when images were split without regard to participant and about 71% when the split respected participant boundaries. Reporting both is the paper's most valuable contribution: the 19-point gap is a direct, within-study measurement of how much accuracy segment-level splitting adds, on a design where the same participant contributes an average of 9.27 images. A maximal information coefficient of 0.79 between CARS severity and average gaze velocity supports the choice to encode velocity visually, and the authors note that the direction of velocity differences in autism remains unsettled across the literature, apparently varying with eye-tracker sampling rate.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Gaze velocity, which correlates strongly and non-linearly with CARS severity, though no direction is established
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: A larger cohort spanning different ages, analysing socio-cognitive and cognitive profiles alongside gaze; consideration of autism-specific data augmentation methods; longer video scenarios, since the short durations used may have limited the richness of gaze representation; and adaptation of more recent deep neural network methodologies. The authors also note the absence of a benchmark dataset in the autism literature as an obstacle to comparing machine learning approaches
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: This paper contains the single most useful methodological datum in the corpus: the same model, the same data and the same cross-validation procedure, run twice under different splitting units, giving approximately 90% accuracy when images are pooled and approximately 71% when participants are held out. With an average of 9.27 images per child, that 19-point gap is a direct within-study measurement of the inflation that segment-level splitting produces - the failure mode that recurs across this literature and that most affected studies never quantify because they only run the optimistic version. That the authors ran both, reported both, and described the decline as expected is the correct scientific behaviour and makes this record disproportionately valuable to the synthesis. Other strengths: the dataset was released openly, which almost no other eye-tracking study here does; ethics reporting is complete and its regulatory basis explained rather than merely asserted; diagnosis rests on ADI-R and ADOS-G administered in specialty clinics, with the inability to access the underlying scores disclosed as a limitation rather than concealed; the stimulus battery is described in unusual protocol-level detail; and the visualisation threshold of 200 points was selected empirically with the tested alternatives reported. The main residual concerns are interpretive rather than procedural. The MIC of 0.79 between CARS and velocity is computed per image rather than per child, so 547 observations derive from 59 individuals, and because every non-autistic child scores exactly 15 on CARS - the instrument floor, with zero variance - the correlation is substantially carrying the between-group difference rather than a within-autism severity gradient; it should not be read as evidence that velocity tracks severity across the spectrum. Training for only three epochs with three-fold cross-validation on 547 images plus 2,735 augmented samples is also thin, and the augmented copies of an image presumably share its participant, which would compound leakage in the image-level condition. Finally, the ECSP developmental-age scores of roughly 23-24 months in both groups reflect an instrument ceiling for eight-year-olds rather than a meaningful developmental measure, and the paper does not comment on this.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 59 children: 29 autistic and 30 non-autistic, closely matched at 19 males each. The authors explain the age composition candidly rather than presenting it as a design choice - they wanted younger participants for early detection, 'but in our region there were not enough diagnosed children younger than 6 years, and the time it takes to consult a doctor to make a diagnosis can be as long as 2 years'. That is an unusually direct statement of how diagnostic waiting times constrain the very research meant to shorten them. No other-diagnosis comparison group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'individuals diagnosed with ASD', 'children with ASD', 'ASD-diagnosed individuals', 'non-ASD', 'children with typical development'. Consistently person-first with 'non-ASD' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy' for the comparison group. The framing acknowledges family impact - deficits 'can unfortunately place a considerable strain on their lives and their families' - but is otherwise neutral, and the discussion notes that parents find eye-tracking results easier to understand than ADI cut-offs and that 'a lack of an objective measure can lead to delayed or diminished acceptance of the clinical diagnosis', which frames objectivity as serving families rather than only clinicians.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Autistic group: 29 children, 19 male, chronological age 7 years 7 months (SD 2 years 6 months), CARS 32.9 +/- 6.4, ECSP total 141.1 +/- 50.3. Non-autistic group: 30 children, 19 male, chronological age 8 years 0 months (SD 2 years 8 months), CARS exactly 15 with zero variance, ECSP total 139.18 +/- 49.5. Ages and sex ratios are closely comparable though no test is reported. Two features of the clinical data deserve note: the non-autistic group's CARS of 15 with zero standard deviation is the instrument's floor, so the measure carries no within-group variance; and ECSP developmental ages of approximately 23-24 months in both groups reflect a ceiling effect of an instrument designed for much younger children, not a meaningful developmental estimate for eight-year-olds. No IQ, ethnicity or socioeconomic data.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Diagnosis confirmed by health professionals in multidisciplinary autism specialty clinics using ADI-R and ADOS-G - the field's gold standard, and among the better ascertainments in the corpus. The important qualification is stated openly: 'we did not get permission to read the children's medical files', so the ADI-R and ADOS-G scores were unavailable and unanalysed, and the authors list this among their limitations, noting that access 'could have provided further interpretation of the results'. Independent severity and communication measures were obtained directly by the research team using French CARS and ECSP for both groups. Non-autistic status rests on careful consideration of parental concerns plus a floor CARS score.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: CARS for severity and ECSP for social communication, both in French versions, administered to both groups by psychologists. CARS is used analytically in the correlation analysis rather than merely tabulated. ECSP is reported but not used, and its near-identical group means at what appears to be a ceiling limit its informativeness. No IQ, adaptive functioning or comorbidity measures, and ADI-R and ADOS-G scores were inaccessible.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: represent eye-tracking scanpaths as velocity-coloured images so that autism screening becomes an image classification problem. Main findings: approximately 90% accuracy with image-level splitting and approximately 71% with participant-level splitting; a maximal information coefficient of 0.79 between CARS score and average gaze velocity; and a working demonstration application linking eye tracking, visualisation and prediction through a hosted model.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A quiet room at the University of Picardy Jules Verne with white barriers to reduce visual distraction, in an interdisciplinary collaboration between psychology and artificial intelligence research units. Children were recruited regionally, with autistic participants diagnosed at multidisciplinary specialty clinics. Supported by a university research quality bonus; no conflicts declared.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A composite battery assembled from several existing psychological protocols and described at unusual protocol-level detail: three 58-second joint attention initiation videos plus 18 matched 5-second photographs, opening with a hand-waving cartoon attention grabber before a woman greets the child and then looks, verbalises and points toward a target either present in or absent from the child's visual field; twelve 4-second gaze-following videos separating head-plus-eye shifts from eye-only shifts; static actor-plus-object photographs; and five minutes of cartoon scenes whose characters' emotional expressions are contingent or non-contingent on the preceding scene. Stimuli were counterbalanced and interleaved with a two-second central crosshair. The variety - dynamic versus static, human versus cartoon, human versus object - is deliberate, allowing 'analysis of the ocular activity of participants from different perspectives', and it is what produces multiple scanpath images per child.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single session of approximately 10 minutes per child with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates rendered as abstract scanpath images and released openly. Governance is fully reported and its regulatory basis explained: informed written consent from parents or guardians after explanation of objectives, tasks and the right to withdraw; assent from every child; parents permitted to remain in the room; Helsinki conformity; and an explicit statement that ethics committee authorisation was not required under French recommendations for psychological research. Explaining why approval was unnecessary, rather than simply omitting the matter, is better practice than the silence found in much of the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: SMI RED250 remote eye tracker at 250 Hz - among the highest sampling rates in the corpus, and material here because the authors attribute conflicting literature findings on saccade dynamics partly to trackers running at 60 Hz and 24 Hz; a 17-inch monitor at 1280 x 1024 viewed from about 60 cm; SMI Experiment Center; five-point calibration followed by verification procedures. Analysis in Python with Matplotlib, OpenCV and Keras on a Tesla K80, with the Minerva R package for the MIC computation, and Azure ML hosting the deployed demonstration model.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Good. Reported: the full stimulus battery with per-protocol durations, counts and content; recording geometry, calibration and verification; the three-step visualisation procedure including the mirroring correction and the velocity bound at a quarter of the screen diagonal; the empirical selection of the 200-point drawing threshold with the tested alternatives and their outcomes; image cropping and rescaling to 256 x 256; the augmentation factor and resulting sample count; the CNN layer composition; the three-fold cross-validation under both splitting regimes with the participant-level procedure described step by step; training epochs and hardware; and the MIC method with its rationale and software. Missing: CNN hyperparameters beyond layer counts, filter sizes, the repository link for the released dataset, and ADI-R and ADOS-G scores which were inaccessible.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged: the small participant count as the primary limitation; the inability to access ADI-R and ADOS-G scores, which 'limits the interpretation of our results'; the short duration of video scenarios, since 'perhaps longer scenarios might have allowed for a richer representation of the gaze behavior'; the restricted age group; the absence of a benchmark dataset in the autism literature making cross-study comparison difficult; and hardware and software costs as barriers to clinical adoption. The performance decline under participant-level splitting is reported as expected rather than hidden. Not acknowledged: the MIC of 0.79 is computed per image rather than per child, so 547 observations derive from 59 individuals; and because every non-autistic child scores the CARS floor of 15 with zero variance, that correlation largely reflects the between-group difference rather than a severity gradient within autism. Also unremarked: augmented copies of an image share its participant, which would compound leakage in the image-level condition, and three training epochs is very few.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: A larger cohort spanning different ages with analysis of socio-cognitive and cognitive profiles alongside gaze; autism-specific data augmentation methods; longer video scenarios for richer gaze representation; adaptation of more recent deep network methodologies; and, more broadly, transfer of the approach to other neurodevelopmental disorders. The authors also identify the field-level need for a benchmark dataset, which their own open release partly addresses.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Gaze trajectory and its dynamics across a heterogeneous battery spanning joint attention initiation, gaze following with head-plus-eye versus eye-only cues, static face-and-object viewing, and emotionally contingent versus non-contingent cartoon scenes. Rather than reducing these to fixation counts or dwell proportions, the study preserves the whole scanpath as a spatial object with velocity written into its colour - so the behavioural unit analysed is the shape of looking over time rather than any summary statistic of it.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-modal fusion. What is fused is spatial and temporal information within a single representation: the scanpath image simultaneously carries where gaze travelled and how fast, with velocity encoded as greyscale gradient along each line. This is a genuinely different answer to the multimodality problem from the feature-concatenation approaches elsewhere in the corpus - the two information types are combined at the representation level before any learning occurs, and the MIC analysis is offered as evidence that the velocity channel carries real signal, since velocity correlates with CARS at 0.79 and is exactly what the colour encodes.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A convolutional network with four convolutional layers, four pooling layers, two fully connected layers and dropout, trained for three epochs. The architectural choice follows directly from the representation decision: having converted gaze to images, the natural learner is a CNN, and the authors describe the whole approach as recasting diagnosis as 'a typical task of image classification'. No comparison against alternative classifiers or against engineered-feature baselines is reported, though the authors note this study builds on their own earlier work using fixation and saccade event features.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: The representation is the contribution. Scanpath images at 256 x 256 after cropping and rescaling, with three deliberate design decisions documented: a cap of 200 consecutive drawn points, selected empirically after finding that 100-150 'turned out to poorly discriminate the 2 classes' while higher values produced clutter; a velocity bound at a quarter of the screen diagonal on the grounds that faster movement 'would not be normal given the scenarios used'; and vertical mirroring to correct for the coordinate origin. Augmentation generated five synthetic variants per image. The heterogeneous stimulus battery is what yields an average of 9.27 images per child, which is simultaneously what makes the dataset large enough to train a CNN and what creates the leakage risk the paper then measures.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: ROC curves with AUC and cross-fold standard deviation, plus accuracy, recall and precision, reported twice - once for each splitting regime - together with training and validation loss curves. Reporting the same metrics under both regimes is what makes the comparison legible and is the paper's key methodological contribution. Missing: confusion matrices, confidence intervals on the accuracy figures, and per-class breakdown for the participant-level condition, where only accuracy is quoted.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No saliency or attribution analysis over the CNN, and the visual representation is not decomposed to show which regions of a scanpath image drive classification - a missed opportunity given that the images are directly human-interpretable and are reproduced in the paper for one participant from each group. Interpretability is instead pursued externally through the MIC analysis, which establishes that the velocity information encoded in colour correlates strongly with CARS severity and thereby argues that the model has something real to learn from. The authors connect this to the wider literature on saccade dynamics in autism, while noting honestly that the direction of the effect 'does not appear to be settled and seems to depend largely on the equipment and data used'.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The paper's most important element and the reason it matters to this review. Three-fold cross-validation is run twice on the same model and data under two splitting units. Pooling the 547 images regardless of origin gives approximately 90% accuracy. Splitting the 59 participants first and then assigning their images by ID - so that no child appears on both sides - gives approximately 71%. The authors describe the second explicitly as a further examination of model performance and note the decline as expected. With an average of 9.27 images per child, this constitutes a direct within-study quantification of segment-level inflation: roughly 19 accuracy points, on a design where images from one child are highly correlated. Residual issues: augmented samples presumably inherit their source image's participant, so the image-level figure may be further inflated; only accuracy is reported for the participant-level condition; three epochs is very few; and there is no independent cohort or external site.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorder; screening; eye tracking; data visualization; machine learning; deep learning; AI; ASS; artificial intelligence; ML; screening; adolescent; diagnosis. 'Data visualization' is the distinguishing term - the contribution is a representation strategy rather than an architecture or a clinical finding.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: JMIR Human Factors, 8(4), e27706 - a digital health and human factors venue, with all eight authors credited as contributing equally across psychology, computer science and anatomy research units at the University of Picardy Jules Verne.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021. The framing is conventional on diagnosis - hours of clinical examination, symptom variation, susceptibility to human bias - but two observations are distinctive. First, an unusually frank statement of how service capacity shapes research: the sample is school-aged rather than preschool because 'in our region there were not enough diagnosed children younger than 6 years, and the time it takes to consult a doctor to make a diagnosis can be as long as 2 years', so the very diagnostic delay the tool is meant to address prevented studying the age group where it would matter most. Second, an argument about acceptance rather than accuracy: 'parents seem to have high acceptance of eye tracking as part of the clinical evaluation because the visual results are easier to understand than is the ADI cutoff', and 'for some parents, a lack of an objective measure can lead to delayed or diminished acceptance of the clinical diagnosis'. That reframes the value of objective measurement as communicative as well as diagnostic, a consideration essentially absent elsewhere in this corpus. The paper also identifies the absence of a benchmark dataset as an obstacle to comparing methods, and responds by releasing its own.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Computer-aided autism diagnosis based on visual attention models using eye tracking
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Oliveira JS; Franco FO; Revers MC; Silva AF; Portolese J; Brentani H; Machado-Lima A; Nunes FLS
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Children and adolescents with autism, deliberately including those with comorbidities
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking and gaze (visual attention modelling)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Eliminate the region-of-interest bottleneck in eye-tracking diagnosis. The paper identifies two specific drawbacks of ROI-based methods - 'the need to demarcate each ROI on each frame of each video used in the experiments' and 'information waste regarding which visual features of sub parts of an image had a more fixed gaze' - and proposes learning a full visual attention model per group instead, so that any pixel of any frame can be scored without expert annotation. A further stated aim is stimulus independence, so that the video used to train the models need not be the video used for diagnosis
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification with a two-phase model-learning and diagnosis architecture, evaluated by subject-level cross-validation
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session per child viewing nine sequentially displayed videos of approximately 6 seconds each, 54 seconds in total
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: The biological-versus-geometric motion preference paradigm, with the screen split so that one half shows children interacting and the other shows fractal movement. Three biological-movement and three geometric-movement videos were combined into nine sequential clips at 1920 x 1080, with the side and order of biological versus geometric content varied throughout 'in order to avoid conditioning of the subjects'
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory eye tracking with participants seated 50-70 cm from the monitor; autistic participants recruited from the Psychiatry Institute of the University of Sao Paulo School of Medicine
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Clinical evaluation by a child psychiatrist against DSM-5 criteria, with severity measured by CARS. CARS was also applied to the typically developing group to confirm scores below 30. Functional cognitive evaluation by a trained neuropsychologist used the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, the Repetitive Behavior Scale and the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales where possible, and all clinical information for autistic individuals is published as supplementary material
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not reported; the whole sample spans 3 to 18 years
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Deliberately included, with an explicit rationale. The authors note that autism 'commonly co-occurs with other conditions', that anxiety appears in 30-50% and ADHD in 40% of cases, and that co-occurring emotional and behavioural problems 'contribute to different ASD trajectories' - concluding that 'individuals with comorbidities were not excluded from our study'. This is one of very few studies in the corpus to argue for inclusion rather than exclusion of comorbidity
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: CARS for all participants, with typically developing children confirmed below 30; WISC, Repetitive Behavior Scale and Vineland where obtainable. Per-participant clinical data are deposited as supplementary material, though not used analytically in the classification
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes, by CARS administration confirming scores below the diagnostic threshold of 30
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not addressed. A single 3-18 year range is given for the whole sample with no group-wise ages, means, standard deviations or test. The authors present the breadth as a strength - the dataset is described as 'heterogeneous in terms of age, gender and CARS' - which is a defensible argument for generalisability but leaves group age differences entirely unexamined across a fifteen-year span
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Similar proportions (64% versus 67% male) but not tested
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Confirmed by CARS below 30
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Gaze coordinates with timestamps during video viewing
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Frames were edge-trimmed, resized to 200 x 350 and stripped of the ten frames either side of each video transition. Consecutive frames were then aggregated wherever mean optical-flow motion between them fell below 0.33, a threshold set by visually identifying when consecutive frames were nearly identical. Group fixation maps were built by summing fixations across all subjects in a group and smoothing with a 5 x 5 Gaussian kernel. For each map, the 350 highest-valued coordinates supplied positive training pixels and 350 randomly chosen zero-fixation coordinates supplied negatives, giving 700 per map
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Tobii Pro TX300; five-point calibration repeated on failure, with exclusion after a second failure; participants seated 50-70 cm from the monitor with an expert or caregiver ensuring attention; MATLAB 2015a; Saliency Toolbox; XPaint for figures
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: A 106-participant eye-tracking dataset with accompanying clinical characterisation; the authors state an intention 'to continue our dataset formation in order to make it available for the scientific community' but do not release it here
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - per-participant clinical data are in supplementary material, but the eye-tracking data are not released
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze coordinates over video stimuli. Governance is fully reported: approval by the Ethics Committee of the University of Sao Paulo under protocol 57185516.9.0000.5390, informed consent from participants or legal guardians, Helsinki conformity, and separate informed consent for publication of identifying images from the people appearing in the stimulus videos
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Pixel-level image features spanning low-level saliency, semantic content and motion
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Twenty-eight candidate features: 13 steerable pyramids at four scales and three orientations; colour, intensity, orientation and skin presence from the Saliency Toolbox; three RGB channel features; horizon line detected by a mixture of linear regressions trained on a gist descriptor; presence of faces and presence of people; Euclidean distance to the screen centre and to the centre of the current half-screen scene; a motion magnitude from optical flow; and two binary indicators of whether the pixel lies in the biological or geometric half. A genetic algorithm reduced these to 15 per group
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Saliency Toolbox for Itti-model features; gist-based horizon detection; face and person detectors; optical flow for motion; genetic algorithm for feature selection, compared against ReliefF
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, as a direct comparison of which features each group's genetic algorithm retained
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Genetic algorithm selection performed independently for each group, with the retained feature sets tabulated side by side; ReliefF tested as an alternative and found inferior
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Two dissociations are reported. No RGB colour feature was selected for the autistic group while one was for the typically developing group. Conversely, distance to the frame centre was selected only for the autistic group, and presence of biological movement was selected only for the autistic group. Saliency Toolbox features were selected for both, which the authors read as evidence of their biological generality 'regardless of the presence of disorders such as ASD'
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported as group means or effect sizes - the analysis is entirely at the level of which features enter each model. The interpretations offered are that selection of the frame-centre feature only for the autistic group agrees with prior work finding 'the ASD group had a greater focus on the center of the image, even when there was nothing in the center', and that biological movement was not retained for the typically developing group because their attention is already captured by the face and person features, making the broader biological-movement region redundant
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Per-group generative attention model with similarity-vote classification
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Two neural networks, one per group, each with ten neurons in a single hidden layer, sigmoid hidden and linear output activations, binary cross-entropy loss, stochastic gradient descent at learning rate 0.01, stopping at 1000 cycles or error below 1e-7. Each predicts whether a given pixel will be fixated by a member of its group. Classification of a new individual proceeds by generating binary saliency maps from both models for each diagnosis frame, comparing each against that individual's own fixation map, and awarding a vote to whichever group's map matches more positions; the individual is labelled autistic if votes exceed a threshold. SVM was evaluated as an alternative learner
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Five-fold cross-validation performed over subjects, with the paper stating explicitly that 'no information of subjects used for testing is used in the learning phase, once the cross-validation was performed over the subjects'. In each fold, 20% of subjects supplied diagnosis data and the remaining 80% supplied model learning. Frames were also partitioned: 50 diagnosis frames were withheld from model learning, simulating the use of a different stimulus video. Two elements sit outside the loop - the genetic algorithm feature selection is reported once per group with no statement of nesting, and the 28-vote decision threshold was set by the Youden index on the ROC generated from the same cross-validation
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Precision, sensitivity/recall, specificity and AUC with standard deviation, plus ROC curves for all five folds and a comparison table of AUC across six classifier-and-feature-selection combinations, and a table of AUCs from three related published studies
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Average precision 90%, specificity 93%, sensitivity 69%, with AUC 0.822 (SD 0.015) for neural networks with genetic algorithm selection. Comparisons: neural network without selection 0.818 (0.053), with ReliefF 0.782 (0.026); SVM without selection 0.775 (0.027), with genetic algorithm 0.695 (0.023), with ReliefF 0.695 (0.042). Feature selection therefore helped the neural network only marginally in mean but substantially in stability, reducing the standard deviation from 0.053 to 0.015, while it markedly harmed the SVM
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Learning a separate visual attention model for each group - each a small network predicting whether any given pixel will be fixated, from 15 genetically selected image features - and classifying individuals by which group's predicted saliency their own fixation pattern more closely matches, achieved AUC 0.822 with 90% precision and 93% specificity but only 69% sensitivity. The approach removes the need for expert region-of-interest annotation entirely and is stimulus-independent in principle. The most interpretable results are the feature dissociations: distance to the frame centre and presence of biological movement were retained only for the autistic model, while colour features were retained only for the typically developing model. Feature selection improved the neural network's stability far more than its mean performance, and actively degraded the SVM.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Attention predicted by distance to the frame centre and by presence of biological movement, and not predicted by colour - a pattern the authors relate to the documented tendency of autistic viewers to fixate the image centre even when nothing is there
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Continue building the dataset with a view to public release, noting that 'obtaining eye tracking signals with the respective evaluation of experts is not a trivial task'; evaluate further machine learning techniques and extract additional features; and extend the approach beyond case-control comparison to discrimination between two disorders such as autism and ADHD
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The methodological argument is well posed and the engineering follows it through. The paper identifies a specific cost of the region-of-interest paradigm that dominates eye-tracking autism research - every ROI must be hand-drawn on every frame of every video, and the resulting aggregation discards which visual properties within a region actually drew the gaze - and replaces it with a per-pixel attention model that requires no annotation at all. The stimulus-independence claim follows naturally, since a model over image features can be applied to any video with comparable content, and the authors partially demonstrate this by withholding 50 frames from training and using them only for diagnosis. Several reporting practices are strong: full ethics approval with a protocol number, separate consent for publication of identifiable stimulus footage, per-participant clinical data deposited as supplementary material, subject-level cross-validation stated explicitly, and a six-way comparison of classifier and feature-selection combinations that shows genetic algorithm selection helping the network's variance while hurting the SVM - a nuance most papers would not report. The deliberate inclusion of participants with comorbidities, argued from prevalence data on anxiety and ADHD co-occurrence, is unusual and defensible for external validity. Four caveats bound the result. Sensitivity of 69% against specificity of 93% means roughly three in ten autistic children are missed, and on a 76:30 class ratio the high precision is partly a function of prevalence in the sample rather than of discriminative power. The genetic algorithm selection is reported once per group with no statement of nesting within folds, yet the resulting feature sets constitute the paper's main interpretive finding, so whether they were derived using all 106 participants materially affects their standing. The 28-vote decision threshold was fitted by Youden index on the same cross-validated ROC used to report performance. And the sample spans 3 to 18 years with no group-wise ages reported at all - the authors frame the breadth as heterogeneity supporting generalisability, which is reasonable, but it leaves open whether the groups differ in age on a task where developmental stage plausibly shapes preference for biological over geometric motion.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups totalling 106 children and adolescents: 76 autistic recruited from the Psychiatry Institute of the University of Sao Paulo School of Medicine and 30 typically developing. The class ratio of roughly 2.5:1 favouring autism is not addressed by any balancing procedure and matters for interpreting the reported 90% precision. Notably, participants with psychiatric and neurological comorbidities were deliberately retained rather than excluded, with the authors reasoning from co-occurrence prevalence that excluding them would misrepresent the population. No separate other-diagnosis group, though extending to autism-versus-ADHD discrimination is named as a future direction.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'individuals with ASD', 'ASD subjects', 'subjects with and without ASD', 'Typical Development (TD)', 'ASD patients'. Mixed person-first and abbreviated group labels, with 'patients' used when discussing comorbidity prevalence. The framing is neutral and mechanism-oriented, grounding the work in bottom-up and top-down attentional circuits and describing autism through 'alterations in early precursor of social behavior as biological motion, human face preference, and joint attention' rather than through deficit or burden.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Group sizes and sex splits are given - 76 autistic (49 male, 27 female) and 30 typically developing (20 male, 10 female) - with a single 3-18 year age range for the whole sample. No group-wise ages, means, standard deviations, matching statement or statistical test appears anywhere. The authors treat the breadth as a virtue, describing the dataset as 'heterogeneous in terms of age, gender and CARS' and citing this as a strength relative to comparison studies, which is a legitimate external-validity argument. But a fifteen-year age span with no group comparison is a gap on a paradigm where preference for biological over geometric motion is developmentally graded. Per-participant clinical data including WISC, Repetitive Behavior Scale and Vineland where obtainable are deposited in supplementary material, which is better practice than most of the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Clinical evaluation by a child psychiatrist against DSM-5 criteria with CARS-measured severity, plus neuropsychological assessment by a trained neuropsychologist using WISC, the Repetitive Behavior Scale and Vineland scales where possible. CARS was also administered to the comparison group and confirmed below the diagnostic threshold of 30, so typical development is verified rather than assumed. Per-participant clinical information is published as supplementary material. What is absent is ADOS or ADI-R, and no account is given of who performed the CARS or with what reliability.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Among the better-characterised samples in the corpus: CARS for all participants, plus WISC intelligence, Repetitive Behavior Scale and Vineland adaptive behaviour for autistic participants where obtainable, all deposited per participant. The limitation is that none of these measures is used analytically - there is no severity-stratified analysis, no relation between CARS or IQ and classifier output, and no examination of whether comorbidity status affects classification, despite comorbid participants having been deliberately retained.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: replace region-of-interest annotation with learned per-group visual attention models over video stimuli, and classify individuals by adherence to those models. Main findings: AUC 0.822 with 90% precision, 93% specificity and 69% sensitivity; genetic algorithm selection retained distance-to-centre and biological movement only for the autistic model and colour only for the typically developing model; selection improved the neural network's fold-to-fold stability far more than its mean AUC while degrading the SVM substantially.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory eye tracking with autistic participants recruited from the Psychiatry Institute of the University of Sao Paulo School of Medicine, in collaboration between computing, psychiatry and bioinformatics units. Ethics approval from the University of Sao Paulo under protocol 57185516.9.0000.5390.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: The biological-versus-geometric preference paradigm rendered as nine sequential 6-second clips totalling 54 seconds, with the screen split between children interacting and fractal movement, and with side and ordering varied to prevent conditioning. Two protocol details matter: calibration was repeated once on failure and the participant excluded after a second failure, and only subjects with more than 80% of total video time successfully captured were retained - a quantified data-quality gate. Where a child had to sit on an adult's lap, the adult wore a blindfold 'in order to avoid influencing the signals acquired', which is a control against caregiver gaze cueing that no other study in the corpus reports.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single 54-second viewing session per participant with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates over video stimuli. Governance is complete and detailed: named ethics committee approval with full protocol number, informed consent from participants or legal guardians, Helsinki conformity, and separately obtained consent for publication of identifying images from the individuals appearing in the stimulus videos - the last being a consideration almost never addressed elsewhere in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Tobii Pro TX300 with five-point calibration and a documented failure and exclusion policy; monitor viewed from 50-70 cm; MATLAB 2015a; Saliency Toolbox for Itti-model features; a gist-descriptor mixture of linear regressions for horizon detection; face and person detectors; optical flow for motion estimation.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Very good. Reported: stimulus construction with clip counts, durations, resolution and counterbalancing; positioning, calibration procedure and the two-failure exclusion rule; the 80% capture-rate inclusion threshold; the blindfold control for lap-seated children; frame preprocessing including edge removal, resizing to 200 x 350 and transition-frame deletion; the optical-flow aggregation threshold of 0.33 with its empirical derivation and an explicit note that it is video-specific and 'should be reviewed' for different stimuli; the 5 x 5 Gaussian smoothing kernel; the 350-positive and 350-random-negative pixel sampling; all 28 candidate features with their sources; the full network specification including loss, optimiser, learning rate and stopping criteria; the vote-based classification rule; and the subject-level cross-validation with the 50 held-out diagnosis frames. Missing: group-wise ages, whether genetic algorithm selection was nested within folds, and any code or eye-tracking data release.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged with unusual directness on one point. The authors anticipate the objection that using the same video for training and diagnosis constitutes contamination, state it themselves - 'although it could be interpreted as contamination and biasing of learning' - and describe their mitigation: only 700 sampled pixels per map enter learning, 50 frames are withheld entirely for diagnosis, and negatives are randomly drawn, which they argue 'approximates a scenario of usage of different videos'. They also note the optical-flow threshold is stimulus-specific, identify dataset construction as the field's binding constraint, and flag intent to release data. Not acknowledged: sensitivity of 69% is not discussed at all despite being the weakest metric and the one that matters for screening; the 2.5:1 class ratio inflates precision and is unaddressed; genetic algorithm selection is not stated to be nested within folds although the selected feature sets are the paper's main interpretive claim; the 28-vote threshold was fitted by Youden on the reported ROC; and no group-wise ages are given across a 3-18 year span.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Continue building the dataset toward public release, with the observation that assembling eye-tracking signals alongside expert clinical evaluation 'is not a trivial task'; evaluate further machine learning techniques and additional features; and extend from case-control comparison to discrimination between two disorders, specifically naming autism versus ADHD - the differential question the corpus almost never addresses.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Visual attention during competition between biological and geometric motion, analysed not as dwell proportions but as a mapping from image properties to fixation probability. The behavioural quantity modelled is which visual features attract a group's gaze, decomposed across low-level saliency (steerable pyramids, colour, intensity, orientation), semantic content (faces, people, skin, horizon), spatial position (distance to screen and scene centres) and motion (optical flow magnitude, biological versus geometric scene membership).
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-modal fusion. The combination is across feature families within a single modality, and the genetic algorithm's per-group selection is what makes it interpretable: the two models retain overlapping but non-identical feature sets, with distance-to-centre and biological-movement indicators appearing only in the autistic model and colour appearing only in the typically developing model. The authors' explanation for the biological-movement asymmetry is subtle and worth recording - the feature covers the whole region containing biological movement, and since typically developing attention 'is specifically more focused on the regions with people and faces' which are already captured by dedicated features, the broader region adds nothing for that group. That is a redundancy argument rather than an absence-of-effect argument, and it distinguishes a feature being uninformative from being subsumed.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Two small neural networks, one per group, each acting as a generative model of where that group looks, plus a similarity-vote decision rule - the same architecture as the severity study from the same laboratory but applied to diagnosis. SVM was tested as an alternative learner and performed worse (0.775 against 0.818 without selection). The comparison table across six classifier-and-selection combinations is genuinely informative: genetic algorithm selection raised the network's mean AUC only from 0.818 to 0.822 but cut its standard deviation from 0.053 to 0.015, while the same selection dropped the SVM from 0.775 to 0.695. Reporting a case where feature selection helps stability rather than accuracy, and helps one learner while harming another, is more nuanced than most of the corpus manages.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Twenty-eight pixel-level image features reduced to 15 per group by genetic algorithm, computed by averaging feature values across the frames aggregated into each group. The aggregation procedure is the paper's more distinctive representational contribution: because individual video frames contain too few fixations to support learning, consecutive frames are merged wherever mean optical-flow motion falls below 0.33, a threshold derived by visual inspection of when successive frames were nearly identical, and explicitly flagged as needing revision for any different stimulus. Training pixels are then sampled as the 350 most-fixated coordinates against 350 randomly chosen zero-fixation coordinates, giving a balanced 700 per map.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Precision, sensitivity, specificity and AUC with fold-wise standard deviation, ROC curves for all five folds, a six-row comparison of classifier and selection combinations, and a table of published AUCs from three comparable studies for external context. Reporting standard deviation across folds is what reveals the stability benefit of feature selection. The gap is that sensitivity of 69% is reported but never discussed, and no confusion matrix or confidence interval accompanies it - on a sample where 76 of 106 participants are autistic, missing 31% of them is the most consequential number in the paper.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is delivered by the per-group feature comparison rather than by any post hoc explanation method, and it works well because the features are semantically meaningful image properties. Three findings are drawn out and connected to prior literature: the frame-centre feature entering only the autistic model matches reports of centre fixation 'even when there was nothing in the center'; Saliency Toolbox features entering both models is read as evidence of biologically general attentional mechanisms; and biological movement entering only the autistic model is explained by redundancy with face and person features in the typically developing model. The absence of any group-level statistics on the features themselves limits how far these can be pushed, and the interpretive claims rest on which features a genetic algorithm happened to retain, which is a noisier basis than a direct comparison would be.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Five-fold cross-validation over subjects, stated explicitly and unambiguously - 'no information of subjects used for testing is used in the learning phase, once the cross-validation was performed over the subjects' - which is the correct unit and is rarely stated this plainly. A second partition operates over frames, with 50 held out from model learning for diagnosis only, deliberately simulating stimulus independence. The authors also pre-empt and address the same-video contamination objection. Two elements nonetheless sit outside the loop: the genetic algorithm feature selection is presented as a single result per group with no indication it was repeated per fold, and the 28-vote decision threshold was chosen by Youden index on the cross-validated ROC. There is no independent cohort or external site.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No formal keyword list. Vocabulary: 'visual attention model', 'region of interest', 'saliency map', 'fixation map', 'stimulus independence', 'computer-aided diagnosis'. The recurring conceptual pair is fixation map versus saliency map - what a person actually looked at against what a model predicts a group would look at - and classification is the comparison between them.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Scientific Reports, 11, 10131 - a broad open-access multidisciplinary journal, with authorship spanning a computing school, a university psychiatry department and a bioinformatics postgraduate programme.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021. The framing is a precise methodological critique rather than a general appeal to objectivity. Region-of-interest methods carry two costs: annotation burden, since every ROI must be marked on every frame of every video, and information loss, since aggregating within a region discards 'which visual features of sub parts of an image had a more fixed gaze'. The paper grounds its alternative in attention theory, distinguishing bottom-up circuits driven by image properties from top-down circuits using prior knowledge and social rules, and traces the computational lineage from the Koch model through Itti's implementation to the supervised saliency models of Borji and Judd. It positions its own advance as extending these from static images to video, citing the argument that video 'can contribute with more discoveries because the videos have temporal information'. It also situates itself quantitatively against prior work, tabulating AUCs of 0.71, 0.71 and 0.86 from three published studies against its own 0.82, and noting that its sample is larger and more heterogeneous in age, sex and severity than the comparators.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Alcañiz M; Chicchi‐Giglioli IA; Carrasco‐Ribelles LA; Marín‐Morales J; Minissi ME; Teruel‐García G; Sirera M; Abad L
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Preschool children with autism, minimally verbal
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking and gaze (immersive virtual reality)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Establish whether social attentional behaviour recorded in an ecologically rich immersive virtual environment can distinguish autistic from typically developing children, and which gaze parameters do the distinguishing - motivated by the argument that conventional assessment 'occurs in laboratories or clinical settings lacking ecological validity that could offer a deeper understanding of real-life abilities', and that behavioural biomarkers can capture 'unconscious processes' that explicit symptom observation cannot
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification with a general modelling approach and a parallel hypothesis-contrast approach testing eight predefined feature families
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session per child of 24 minutes 45 seconds, comprising 16 scenes ranging from 10 to 180 seconds each
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Free exploration of a multisensory virtual shopping mall projected in a CAVE, with visual, auditory and olfactory stimulation. Sixteen scenes were presented in counterbalanced order: a central hall where an avatar welcomes the child and asks their name; a train that appears four times and nearly runs over the avatar; a carousel with children riding and bubbles; an overflowing trash can at which the avatar shows disgust; an electronics shop with a clerk and a display in which the avatar plays peekaboo four times; a supermarket where the avatar offers a choice between an apple and a lollipop; a billboard; a game room where the avatar indicates three times verbally and by hand gesture that the child should look left, followed by a ball rotating right; and a cinema showing a scene from the film Inside Out. A forest scene with relaxing music was inserted at the start and between stores 'to avoid cognitive and sensory overload'
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: A 4 x 4 x 3 m three-wall CAVE at the Institute for Research and Innovation in Bioengineering, Polytechnic University of Valencia, with the child standing 1.5 m from the central wall except in the final seated scene
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: ADOS-2 and ADI-R, both described in detail with their test-retest reliabilities (ADOS-2: 0.87 social impairment, 0.64 repetitive behaviour, 0.88 global; ADI-R: 0.93-0.97). The paper states that 'both groups were individually evaluated with the same scales and procedure prior to the experiments'. ADOS-2 module 1 was used - the module for children aged 31 months and older 'who do not use coherent phrase language' - which places the autistic sample at the minimally verbal end. No scores are reported for any participant
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Within the study range of 4-7 years
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported. The only stated exclusions were wearing glasses or having any ocular alteration or pathology
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Not reported; autistic participants were recruited from a cognitive development centre, implying ongoing intervention
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: ADOS-2 and ADI-R were administered but no index or total scores are reported, and no severity-stratified analysis is performed. Module 1 administration is the only indication of functional level
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Stated to have received the same scales and procedure as the autistic group, though no scores are reported
data_charting_rubrics.age_range_controls: Within the study range of 4-7 years
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No. The autistic group is on average six months older (5.26 versus 4.75 years) with a narrower spread, and no statistical test of the difference is reported. The authors acknowledge the broader problem directly: 'experimental groups were not matched on sociodemographics, IQ, or cognitive ability, limiting the generalization of the model'
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Cannot be assessed - sex is not reported for either group anywhere in the paper, which is unusual for an autism study and prevents any assessment of representativeness or balance
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted, with the same assessment scales stated to have been applied but no scores given
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: First-person scene video with gaze overlay from head-mounted eye tracking in a projected virtual environment
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Recordings were processed by a custom program synchronising each participant's video, fixation patterns, frame-by-frame images of the virtual environment, and predefined area-of-interest definitions, producing a text file listing the frames in which each area of interest was seen. Frames in which no defined area was viewed were not reported. Scenes were grouped into seven categories - game room, cinema, electronics shop, supermarket, forest, central hall and carousel - and areas of interest were organised hierarchically into people (children and adults), their faces and bodies, items (dynamic and static) and background
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Three-wall CAVE of 4 x 4 x 3 m with three ultrashort-throw projectors, Logitech Z906 5.1 speakers and a wireless Olorama system regulating the presence and intensity of odours; Tobii Pro Glasses 2 with a front-facing scene camera, two cameras per eye using a 3D eye model, and an accelerometer and gyroscope allowing head and eye movement to be separated so that 'the impact of head movements on tracking data' is eliminated; R version 3.6.1 for analysis
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: A 55-child immersive VR eye-tracking dataset; no release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: First-person video of identifiable children in a monitored setting. Governance is reported: informed consent signed by relatives after explanation of objectives and procedure, explicit separate consent to video recording of the participating child, and approval from the Ethics Committee at the Polytechnic University of Valencia following Declaration of Helsinki guidelines
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Frame-count features describing what was looked at, computed globally and per scene
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 144 features in five families. General features: number of areas of interest seen, average number seen per scene with standard deviation. Background: frames in which nothing defined was viewed. Areas of interest: frames in which anything defined was viewed. Persons: frames in which any character was seen, decomposed by the main avatar versus other characters, and by faces versus bodies. Items: frames in which any item was seen, decomposed into dynamic and static. All except general features were computed both for the whole experience and per scene. Difference features were additionally constructed - faces minus bodies, children minus adults, avatar minus other characters, dynamic minus static items, and people minus items
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Custom synchronisation and area-of-interest mapping software; step backward sequential wrapper for feature selection
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, through both univariate significance testing and the hypothesis-contrast model comparison
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Shapiro-Wilk normality testing followed by t-test or Mann-Whitney per feature; plus eight predefined feature-family datasets modelled separately so their relative discriminative value can be compared directly
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Thirteen features differed significantly. Two concern overall area-of-interest counts. Three concern items in the game centre, where autistic children viewed more items and specifically more static items. In the hall, autistic children looked at adults and at non-avatar characters in significantly more frames. In the electronics shop, they looked more at other children - both faces and bodies - and at the main avatar. They looked at characters' faces in more frames in both the electronics shop and the game centre. At the model level, the people-versus-items family performed best (84% accuracy) and the adults'-faces-versus-bodies family worst (66%)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reported clearly and in a direction opposite to most of the literature: autistic children watched social elements - children's and adults' faces and bodies - in more frames than typically developing children, both overall and per scenario, and also looked more at static non-social items. The authors state plainly that 'this first result is partially in opposition with previous studies on social visual attention in ASD' and offer a specific explanation, that immersive VR provides high social content and that a meta-analysis found reduced social attention in autism chiefly when more than one person was present, so richer environments may activate rather than suppress visual exploration. A secondary directional finding is a preference for adults' faces over children's faces alongside greater attention to children's bodies than adults' bodies
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Comparison of classical supervised classifiers with wrapper feature selection
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Naive Bayes, XGBoost, k-nearest neighbours, random forest and support vector machine, each trained on each of ten datasets. Default hyperparameters were used throughout, deliberately - 'the models were built using the default hyperparameters so as not to increase the complexity of the problem by attempting to tune them'
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Five-fold cross-validation repeated four times, giving 20 iterations, with means and standard deviations reported for every metric. Feature selection used a step backward sequential wrapper capped at ten features 'in order to avoid overfitting', and the paper states that 'both the best feature subset and the best model were chosen using five-fold cross-validation (repeated four times)' - so selection and reporting share the same estimate. The authors are explicit that no independent sample exists: 'Data from all participants were used to validate the model; therefore, the reported results correspond to the cross-validation process'
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, Cohen's kappa, AUC, F1, sensitivity and specificity, each with a standard deviation across the 20 iterations, reported for the best model on each of the ten datasets
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: General approach: all 144 features with SVM and nine selected features gave 0.86 accuracy (SD 0.10), kappa 0.69, AUC 0.91, F1 0.87, sensitivity 0.91, specificity 0.82; restricting to the 13 statistically significant features and using kNN gave 0.77 accuracy, kappa 0.52, AUC 0.83, sensitivity 0.78, specificity 0.85 - notably with the lowest standard deviations of any model. Hypothesis-contrast approach: people versus items 0.84 (sensitivity 0.94, specificity 0.71); adults versus items 0.83 (sensitivity 0.82, specificity 0.85, the most balanced); children versus items 0.82; children versus adults 0.78; faces versus bodies 0.73; children's faces versus bodies 0.74; dynamic versus static items 0.69; adults' faces versus bodies 0.66 (kappa 0.25)
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Gaze recorded in a 24-minute multisensory virtual mall distinguished autistic from typically developing preschoolers at up to 86% accuracy with 91% sensitivity. The substantive finding runs against the prevailing literature: autistic children looked at social elements in more frames than typically developing children, both overall and within scenes, and also attended more to static non-social items. The authors attribute this reversal to the high social content of an immersive environment, citing meta-analytic evidence that reduced social attention in autism appears mainly when more than one person is present, and argue that a rich VR setting activates rather than suppresses visual exploration. Feature-family comparison showed that coarse contrasts between people and items discriminated well (84%) while fine-grained face-versus-body contrasts did not (66-74%), which the authors interpret as a limitation of macro-level area definitions.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Greater frame counts on social elements overall and per scene, greater attention to static non-social items, higher visual preference for adults over children, and preference for adults' faces over children's faces alongside greater attention to children's bodies
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Test on larger samples and on an independent dataset; treat sociodemographics, IQ and cognitive ability as possible moderators since groups were unmatched on them; refine areas of interest to include eyes and mouth and adopt a bottom-up or data-driven approach rather than predefined macro-areas; develop a portable system with integrated remote eye tracking, since eye-tracking glasses 'may not be accepted by all children, especially those who are particularly young' and both the glasses and the CAVE assembly are expensive; and include other neurodevelopmental conditions such as ADHD to improve discrimination and identify degrees of severity within each
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The scientific contribution here is a well-supported contradiction of an established finding, and the way the authors handle it is the record's chief value. Almost every gaze study in this corpus assumes and reports reduced social attention in autism; this one finds the opposite, with autistic children looking at faces and bodies in significantly more frames, and rather than burying the discrepancy it is stated plainly, situated against a meta-analysis showing reduced social attention chiefly at high social content, and explained by a specific mechanism - that a rich immersive environment with multiple agents may activate rather than suppress exploration, and that offline social cognition paradigms 'may not be generalizable across contexts'. The environment itself is the corpus's most elaborate: 24 minutes across 16 scripted scenes in a three-wall CAVE with synchronised auditory and olfactory channels, an avatar that greets the child by name, plays peekaboo, expresses disgust and issues joint-attention bids, and forest interludes inserted deliberately to prevent sensory overload. Reporting is strong in several respects: means and standard deviations across 20 cross-validation iterations for six metrics on all ten datasets, kappa alongside accuracy, ethics approval with explicit separate consent for video recording, ADOS-2 and ADI-R with module and reliability documented, and a deliberate decision not to tune hyperparameters so as to avoid an additional search dimension. The authors also state without prompting that all participants were used in validation and that no independent sample was tested. Three problems bound the accuracy claims. The feature subset and the model were both chosen using the same repeated cross-validation that produces the reported figures, across five algorithms and ten datasets - fifty model fits from which the best per dataset is reported - so the headline 86% is a maximum over a large search. Groups were not matched on sociodemographics, IQ or cognitive ability, which the authors acknowledge, and they differ by six months in mean age with no test reported. And sex is not reported for either group anywhere in the paper, an omission that is conspicuous in autism research and prevents any assessment of sample composition. A fourth consideration affects interpretation rather than validity: ADOS-2 module 1 targets children who do not use coherent phrase language, so the autistic sample sits at the minimally verbal end, and the reported reversal of the social-attention finding may be specific to that subgroup rather than to autism generally.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups totalling 55 children aged 4-7: 35 autistic recruited from the Red Cenit Neurocognitive Development Center in Valencia and 20 typically developing recruited by a management company through calls and mailings to families. The 35:20 imbalance is not addressed by any balancing procedure. Both groups are stated to have received the same evaluation scales and procedure before the experiment. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the authors name ADHD inclusion as a priority for future work specifically to 'identify with greater precision the degrees of severity in each disorder'.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'autistic children', 'children with ASD', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'autistic participants'. Predominantly identity-first ('autistic children') rather than person-first, which is unusual in this corpus and aligns with neurodiversity-community preference. The framing is measurement-oriented rather than deficit-oriented, centred on the argument that clinical assessment 'relies on children's observable behaviors and parents' interview responses, which clinicians rate according to their expertise and subjectivity', and that 'social desirability bias has been found to affect the veracity of parents' responses'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Autistic group: 35 children, mean age 5.26 +/- 0.51 years. Typically developing group: 20 children, mean age 4.75 +/- 0.77 years. Sex is not reported for either group anywhere in the paper - a striking omission in autism research. The six-month age difference is untested. Most importantly, the authors state directly that 'experimental groups were not matched on sociodemographics, IQ, or cognitive ability, limiting the generalization of the model', and recommend treating these as moderators in future work. The only stated exclusion criteria were wearing glasses or having an ocular alteration or pathology. ADOS-2 module 1 administration indicates the autistic sample is minimally verbal, which is important context for the study's central finding.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: ADOS-2 and ADI-R, both described in detail with their psychometric properties - ADOS-2 test-retest reliability of 0.87 for social impairment, 0.64 for repetitive behaviour and 0.88 for the global index; ADI-R ranging 0.93-0.97 - and the paper states that both groups were 'individually evaluated with the same scales and procedure prior to the experiments'. This is a strong ascertainment on paper. The gap is that no scores are reported for any participant or group, so neither the severity distribution nor the separation between groups can be inspected, and the assertion that typically developing children received the same instruments cannot be checked against data. ADOS-2 module 1 is specified, which locates the autistic sample among children who do not use coherent phrase language.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: ADOS-2 and ADI-R administered but with no scores reported and no severity-stratified analysis. No IQ, cognitive, adaptive or language measures, and the authors identify the absence of IQ and cognitive matching as a limitation requiring attention in future work. The only functional indicator available is the choice of ADOS-2 module 1.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: determine whether gaze in an immersive virtual environment distinguishes autistic from typically developing children and which parameters do so. Main findings: 86% accuracy with 91% sensitivity and AUC 0.91 using all features; autistic children looked at social elements in more frames than typically developing children, contrary to most prior work; they also attended more to static non-social items; people-versus-items contrasts discriminated best at 84% while adults'-faces-versus-bodies discriminated worst at 66%; and the model restricted to the 13 statistically significant features was less accurate but the most stable across iterations.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A three-wall CAVE of 4 x 4 x 3 m at the Institute for Research and Innovation in Bioengineering, Polytechnic University of Valencia, with autistic participants from the Red Cenit Neurocognitive Development Center and comparison children recruited by a management company. Funded by the Spanish Ministry of Economy, Industry and Competitiveness project 'Immersive Virtual Environment for the Evaluation and Training of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: T Room'.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: The most elaborate elicitation paradigm in the corpus: a 24-minute 45-second multisensory virtual mall with 16 scripted scenes and synchronised visual, auditory and olfactory channels. The scenes are designed to sample distinct social demands - an avatar greeting the child and asking their name, peekaboo through shop displays, a choice offered between an apple and a lollipop, explicit joint-attention bids where the avatar indicates three times verbally and by gesture that the child should look left, an emotional display of disgust at a trash can, and a startling event where a train nearly runs over the avatar. Two design decisions deserve note: forest scenes with relaxing music were inserted at the start and between stores specifically 'to avoid cognitive and sensory overload', and scene order was counterbalanced across participants. This is elicitation designed around the population's sensory needs rather than only around the constructs being measured.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single 24-minute session per child with no follow-up. Data are first-person video of identifiable children moving through a monitored environment. Governance is properly reported: informed consent from relatives after explanation of objectives and procedure, separate explicit consent to video recording of the child, ethics committee approval at the Polytechnic University of Valencia, and Helsinki conformity.
