A researcher remained present to monitor the child but 'attempted to intervene as little as possible (only in situations of device failure or cybersickness)' - the only mention of cybersickness in the corpus and a real consideration for immersive paradigms with children.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: A three-wall CAVE with three ultrashort-throw projectors, Logitech Z906 5.1 audio and a wireless Olorama olfactory system regulating odour presence and intensity; Tobii Pro Glasses 2 with a scene camera, two cameras per eye using a 3D eye model, and an accelerometer and gyroscope allowing head and eye movement to be separated so that head motion does not contaminate gaze data - a technical requirement for free movement that screen-based trackers cannot meet. Glasses were fitted and calibrated in an adjacent room, with researchers verifying both correct operation and that 'the subject did not reject them' before the child entered the CAVE. Analysis in R 3.6.1.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong on protocol, weaker on results provenance. Reported: every scene with its content and duration; CAVE dimensions, projector, audio and olfactory hardware; child positioning; the counterbalancing and the sensory-overload interludes; the calibration and acceptance procedure; the eye tracker's head-motion compensation; the hierarchical area-of-interest structure; all five feature families with construction rules including the difference features; the normality testing and choice between t-test and Mann-Whitney; the step backward wrapper with its ten-feature cap; the repeated cross-validation scheme; and six metrics with standard deviations for all ten datasets. Missing: participant sex, ADOS-2 and ADI-R scores, the identity of the selected features in the winning models (deferred to a supplementary table), any data or code release, and reconciliation of how many total model fits the reported maxima were selected from.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged with unusual completeness. The sample is small, the feature count high, and 'the models were not applied to an independent sample'; the authors state directly that 'data from all participants were used to validate the model; therefore, the reported results correspond to the cross-validation process', offering the 20 iterations and low standard deviations as partial mitigation. Groups were not matched on sociodemographics, IQ or cognitive ability. The macro-level area-of-interest approach 'presented some limitations in terms of recognition of specific eye gaze patterns related to specific areas, such as face areas (i.e., eyes and mouth)'. Eye-tracking glasses may not be accepted by young children and both they and the CAVE are expensive, limiting clinical deployment. Training took about 20 hours even parallelised. Not acknowledged: the feature subset and model were both chosen on the same repeated cross-validation that produces the reported metrics, across five algorithms and ten datasets, so the headline is a maximum over roughly fifty fits; participant sex is never reported; and the minimally verbal composition implied by ADOS-2 module 1 may bound the generality of the reversed social-attention finding.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Larger samples with testing on an independent dataset; treatment of sociodemographics, IQ and cognitive ability as moderators; refinement of areas of interest to include eyes and mouth, and adoption of a bottom-up data-driven definition rather than predefined macro-areas; development of a portable system with integrated remote eye tracking to replace glasses that young children may reject and a CAVE that is prohibitively expensive to assemble; and inclusion of other neurodevelopmental conditions such as ADHD to sharpen discrimination and characterise severity gradations.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Visual attention to social and non-social content during free exploration of a rich environment, decomposed hierarchically: people versus items versus background; within people, the main interacting avatar versus other characters, adults versus children, faces versus bodies; within items, dynamic versus static. Because features are computed both globally and per scene, the analysis can locate where in the 16-scene sequence group differences arise - and the significant differences cluster in the hall, the electronics shop and the game centre rather than being distributed evenly, which is information a whole-session summary would lose.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-modal fusion of sensor streams, but the stimulus is genuinely multisensory - visual, auditory and olfactory channels are synchronised, with odour presence and intensity under programmatic control. The analytic combination is across feature families, and the hypothesis-contrast approach makes it systematic: eight predefined families are modelled separately so their discriminative value can be compared. The resulting ordering is informative. Coarse social-versus-non-social contrasts perform best - people versus items at 84%, adults versus items at 83%, children versus items at 82% - while fine-grained within-social contrasts perform worst, with adults' faces versus bodies reaching only 66% and kappa 0.25. The authors draw the correct conclusion, that macro-area definitions capture the signal but cannot resolve face-internal patterns, and recommend adding eye and mouth areas.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Five classifiers - naive Bayes, XGBoost, kNN, random forest and SVM - trained on each of ten datasets, with the best per dataset reported. Default hyperparameters were used throughout, a decision the authors justify explicitly as avoiding an additional layer of search complexity. That is defensible and unusually candid, though it means the algorithm comparison reflects default behaviour rather than tuned potential, and different algorithms win on different datasets (SVM on two, kNN on two, naive Bayes on two, random forest and XGBoost on one each), which is what one would expect when nothing is tuned and sample sizes are small.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: 144 frame-count features spanning general, background, area-of-interest, person and item families, each computed globally and per scene, plus explicitly constructed difference features contrasting faces against bodies, children against adults, avatar against other characters, dynamic against static items, and people against items. Building the contrasts directly into the feature set rather than leaving them for the model to discover is a sensible choice at this sample size. The unit throughout is the number of frames in which something was seen, which measures how much of the session was spent looking at a category but discards fixation structure, dwell duration and sequence - a limitation the authors partly recognise in calling for finer area definitions.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Six metrics - accuracy, kappa, AUC, F1, sensitivity and specificity - each with a standard deviation across 20 cross-validation iterations, reported for the best model on every one of ten datasets. Including kappa alongside accuracy is appropriate given the 35:20 imbalance and is done consistently. The standard deviations are used substantively: the model on the 13 significant features is noted to have 'the lowest standard deviations, showing the highest consistency', which is a real finding distinct from mean accuracy. Missing: confusion matrices, confidence intervals, and any statistical comparison between the ten datasets, so whether 0.86 differs meaningfully from 0.84 on 55 children is not established - and the standard deviation of 0.10 on the best model spans that gap.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability comes from two complementary analyses rather than from any model-explanation method. Univariate testing with normality checking identifies 13 significantly differing features and localises them to specific scenes, and the eight hypothesis-contrast datasets rank feature families by discriminative value. Together these support a specific claim: coarse social-versus-non-social attention differentiates the groups while fine facial detail does not, at least at the area granularity used. The interpretation of the reversed direction is the most substantive interpretive work in the paper, connecting the finding to social-content level, to the static-versus-dynamic stimulus distinction, and to the argument that 'findings related to offline social cognition may not be generalizable across contexts'. The authors position their paradigm as 'an effective middle point' between contrived screen tasks and uncontrollable real settings.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Five-fold cross-validation repeated four times with means and standard deviations reported, which is better practice than single-split evaluation and gives some sense of variability. The limitation is stated by the authors themselves - no independent sample exists and all participants contributed to validation - and compounded by the fact that both the feature subset and the model were selected on that same repeated cross-validation, across five algorithms and ten datasets. The reported per-dataset maxima are therefore optimistically biased, and the general-approach figure of 0.86 is the best of roughly fifty fits. The ten-feature cap on selection is a sensible guard against overfitting given 144 candidates and 55 participants, and using default hyperparameters removes one further source of selection. There is no external site, no independent cohort and no held-out replication.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, behavioral biomarker, eye tracking, machine learning, multivariate supervised learning, virtual reality. 'Behavioral biomarker' is the organising concept - the paper's framing is that gaze can serve as an implicit, unconscious indicator complementing explicit symptom observation, situated alongside genetic, neural and physiological biomarker classes.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Autism Research, 15(1), 131-145 - the journal of the International Society for Autism Research, published open access under CC BY. Publishing in a specialist autism venue rather than an engineering one is consistent with the paper's substantive engagement with the social-attention literature and its willingness to contest an established finding.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021. The framing combines three arguments. On objectivity, that assessment 'relies on children's observable behaviors and parents' interview responses, which clinicians rate according to their expertise and subjectivity', with the specific addition that 'social desirability bias has been found to affect the veracity of parents' responses'. On ecological validity, that assessment 'occurs in laboratories or clinical settings lacking ecological validity that could offer a deeper understanding of real-life abilities'. And on timing, that 'many ASD dimensions are internal and do not manifest until 2-3 years of age', lengthening diagnosis. Its most valuable contribution to the corpus's framing is a careful review of the inconsistency in the social-attention literature: it catalogues studies finding reduced social attention, four finding increased social preference, and eight finding no difference, and identifies the moderators as static versus dynamic stimuli and level of social content - citing meta-analytic evidence that autistic children attended less to social stimuli specifically 'when the social content was higher (i.e., the number of people exceeded one)'. Its own contrary result is then argued within that framework rather than against it.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Zhao Z; Zhu Z; Zhang X; Tang H; Xing J; Hu X; Lu J; Qu X
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disord
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: School-age children with autism of at least average nonverbal intelligence
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Motor and kinematics (head movement)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Establish whether head movement dynamics carry information sufficient to identify autism, opening a behavioural channel the authors state has not previously been used for this purpose - 'to date, no study has been found to investigate whether head movement dynamics could be utilized to identify ASD' - despite extensive documentation of atypical head movement including rolling, shaking and banging
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification study using a single conversational session, drawn from a larger four-session protocol
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One yes-no question session per child within a longer conversation, comprising ten questions of variable duration
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Ten yes-no questions posed by an interviewer, with participants 'verbally required by the interviewer to use head nodding/shaking while doing so'. This instruction is the design's defining feature and also its principal interpretive constraint: it guarantees the behaviour will occur but converts it from spontaneous to intentional
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory dyadic setup with the child seated 80 cm from the interviewer's chair and two cameras, one capturing both parties from the side and one placed beside the interviewer capturing the child frontally; only the frontal camera feed was used for head movement analysis
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Confirmed diagnosis by a licensed psychiatrist with no less than five years of clinical experience strictly following DSM-IV criteria, with at least average nonverbal intelligence initially screened by the psychiatrist and confirmed by Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices at IQ of 70 or above, and absence of ADHD, schizophrenia and other pathological conditions
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 20 recruited, 18 analysed
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Reported in Table 1, which did not survive text extraction; the eligible range was 6-13 years
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Not recoverable from the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: ADHD, schizophrenia and other pathological conditions were exclusions
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not measured. The authors note the consequence for generalisation, calling for future work with 'larger samples of ASD individuals with different behavioral presentations'
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Recruited from nearby communities with no physical or mental disorders, and with no autism or ADHD reported in first-degree relatives - the latter controlling for the broader autism phenotype
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 23 recruited, 20 analysed
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd_controls: Reported in Table 1, which did not survive text extraction
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution_controls: Not recoverable from the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Compared in Table 1 and, more importantly, controlled analytically - age was entered as a random factor in the linear mixed-effects models used to test each feature, so the reported group differences in head movement are adjusted for age
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not recoverable from the extracted text. The companion study on the same cohort reports 17 male of 19 autistic and 17 of 20 typically developing children
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Established by absence of physical or mental disorder and absence of autism or ADHD in first-degree relatives
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Frontal video of the child during conversation, converted to head pose time series
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: OpenFace 2.0 head pose tracking produced angular displacement time series in pitch (nodding), yaw (shaking) and roll (lateral inclination). Series were smoothed by spline interpolation to exclude outliers and reduce noise. Rotation range was computed as the difference between the maximum positive and minimum negative angular displacement. Amount of rotation per minute was computed by differentiating displacement to obtain angular velocity, integrating the velocity time series to obtain total rotation, and normalising by trial duration in minutes - a normalisation adopted specifically 'to address the issue that participants spent different time to finish the conversation'. Separately, two female college students blind to both the experimental purpose and group membership independently coded whether each participant nodded or shook their head for each question
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Samsung HMX-F90 at 25 Hz for the side view and Logitech C270 at 30 Hz for the frontal view; OpenFace 2.0 for head pose tracking; MATLAB 2017b for feature computation and classification. The authors report OpenFace's published accuracy - mean absolute error of 2.4-3.1 degrees in pitch, 3.2-3.5 in yaw and 2.4-3.1 in roll - and justify its selection partly on its tolerance of face occlusion and poor lighting, which mattered because the camera was not directly frontal and self-occlusion occurred on far-left head rotations
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Head movement data from 38 children, drawn from a larger conversational dataset; no release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Frontal and side video of identifiable children in dyadic interaction. Governance is partially reported: the protocol followed the Declaration of Helsinki and caregivers signed written informed consent, with participants paid 200 CNY. No ethics committee approval number is given
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Kinematic amplitude and quantity measures of head rotation
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Six features - rotation range and amount of rotation per minute, each in pitch, yaw and roll. The pairing is deliberate: rotation range captures the extremity of movement while amount of rotation per minute captures its quantity, so the two dimensions of excessive movement are separated. Six features against 38 participants is among the most parsimonious feature-to-sample ratios in the corpus
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: OpenFace 2.0 head pose estimation; spline interpolation and numerical differentiation and integration in MATLAB
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, at two levels - statistical discrimination of each feature under mixed-effects modelling, and the exhaustive feature-combination search identifying which pairs classify best
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Linear mixed-effects models with each feature as dependent variable, group as fixed factor, and age, IQ, head nodding frequency, head shaking frequency and frequency of no nodding or shaking all entered as random factors, with likelihood ratio tests comparing models with and without the group term. All six features discriminated significantly and all were retained. Then a random feature combination approach tested every possible subset of the six features across all five classifiers
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The best model used two features. There is an internal inconsistency about which two: the abstract states 'RR_Pitch and ARPM_Yaw' while the results section states 'RR_Roll and ARPM_Yaw' twice. Either way, the discriminative pair combines a rotation-range measure with the yaw amount-of-rotation measure
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Clearly reported with an informative null alongside a positive finding. Autistic children showed significantly greater rotation range and greater amount of rotation per minute in all three directions - pitch, yaw and roll - after controlling for age, IQ and nodding and shaking frequencies. But the frequency of head nodding, head shaking and of using neither did not differ between groups (all p > 0.05, medians 8 versus 5.75 for nodding, 2 versus 3.25 for shaking), and only two participants used neither at all. The authors interpret this as autistic children nodding and shaking 'in a different fashion' rather than less often - the difference is in the kinematics of the gesture, not its occurrence
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Comparison of classical supervised classifiers with exhaustive feature-subset search
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Support vector machine, linear discriminant analysis, decision tree, random forest, and AdaBoost ensemble learning with decision-tree weak learners, each described with its rationale and known weaknesses - the decision tree noted to hold 'strong interpretability and computational efficiency, but it is prone to overfitting'
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-out cross-validation applied to all classifiers, described as implemented 'to prevent overfitting'. The random feature combination approach tested every possible subset of the six features, chosen over forward or backward selection because with only six features exhaustive search is tractable and 'typically yields equal or higher classification accuracy simply owing to the fact that all features and feature combinations could be tested'. The consequence is that 63 subsets across five classifiers - 315 model fits - were all evaluated on the same leave-one-out estimate, and the maximum was reported
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for the best model of each classifier, plus ROC curves for all five and an accuracy-versus-feature-count plot
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Decision tree best at 92.11% accuracy with two features, 88.9% sensitivity, 95% specificity and AUC 0.9167. All five classifiers exceeded 81% accuracy with no more than three features, and all produced AUC above 0.81. SVM reached its maximum with a single feature, decision tree with two, and LDA, random forest and ensemble with three
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Head movement kinematics extracted by computer vision from a conversational task classified autistic from typically developing children at 92.11% accuracy using just two features, with all five classifiers exceeding 81% using three features or fewer. The substantive finding is a dissociation between what the gesture is and how it is executed: autistic children nodded and shook their heads just as often as typically developing children, with no significant difference in nodding, shaking or non-use frequency, but did so with significantly greater rotation range and greater amount of rotation per minute in all three axes after adjusting for age, IQ and gesture frequency. The authors draw the methodological moral explicitly - human observers detect movement patterns well but 'not good at giving precise metric measures of movement', so head pose tracking finds motor differences that behavioural coding misses.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Greater rotation range and greater amount of rotation per minute in pitch, yaw and roll - excessive head movement in execution rather than reduced use of head gestures
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Larger samples spanning different behavioural presentations, given autism's heterogeneity; examination of unintentional rather than instructed head nodding and shaking, since prior findings of reduced gesture use may hold only in spontaneous contexts; and extension to younger children, since the 6-13 year range is well above the mean age at diagnosis of 60.48 months, with the authors arguing that head pose tracking is well suited to early screening because its 'constraint-free characteristics' allow data collection 'in natural settings without wearing sophisticated devices or following experimental instructions'
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The design has a clean logic and produces a result that is more interesting than its headline accuracy. By instructing every child to nod or shake while answering, the study guarantees the gesture occurs and can then ask a sharper question than whether autistic children gesture less - namely whether they gesture differently. The answer is a genuine dissociation: gesture frequency did not differ at all, while rotation range and amount of rotation per minute differed significantly in all three axes, and this held after entering age, IQ and the three gesture-frequency measures as random factors in mixed-effects models. That adjustment is unusually careful for this corpus and means the kinematic difference is not simply a by-product of doing more gesturing. The authors also draw the right general conclusion - that automated pose tracking measures the metric properties of movement that human coders cannot judge - and support it by having two blind coders independently rate gesture occurrence with good agreement, so the null on frequency is well established rather than merely unfound. The feature set is admirably parsimonious at six features for 38 participants. Three problems bound the accuracy figure. The exhaustive feature-combination search evaluated all 63 subsets across five classifiers on the same leave-one-out estimate that is reported, so 92.11% is the maximum over 315 fits with no outer loop; on 38 participants a single case is worth 2.6 accuracy points, and the gap between the best classifier and the others is roughly four cases. There is an unresolved internal inconsistency about which two features produced that result, with the abstract naming RR_Pitch and the results section naming RR_Roll. And most consequentially for validity, OpenFace failed to track 3.46% of frames for autistic children against 0.23% for typically developing children - a fifteenfold difference that the authors report but do not analyse. Since tracking failure arises from occlusion during large head rotations, this is plausibly downstream of the very excess movement being measured, but it also means data quality differs systematically by group in a way that could contribute to the features. The instructed-gesture design is also a two-edged choice, and the authors say so: it may explain why they found no frequency difference where prior work did, since 'the reduced use of head nodding/shaking in ASD individuals might only be observed in unintentional scenarios'.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups: 20 autistic children recruited from a local psychiatric hospital and 23 typically developing children from nearby communities, with five excluded for camera technical problems leaving 18 and 20. Participants are the same cohort as a companion study by the same group on conversational eye tracking, but the data come from a different conversational session - the yes-no question session rather than the full four-session conversation. No other-diagnosis comparison group. Participants were paid 200 CNY, which is disclosed.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'individuals with ASD', 'children with typical development (TD)', 'the affected children'. Mixed person-first and abbreviated forms. The framing locates the diagnostic problem in procedure and capacity rather than in children: diagnostic accuracy 'might be negatively affected by factors such as caregivers' report bias and clinicians' insufficient experiences of detecting ASD', and 'the shortage in specialists and the lengthy examinations make the diagnostic procedure a time-consuming process'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Eligibility required ages 6-13 in both groups, at least average nonverbal intelligence (IQ 70 or above by Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices) in the autistic group, and absence of physical or mental disorder plus no autism or ADHD in first-degree relatives for the comparison group. Group-wise ages, sexes and IQ appear in Table 1, which did not survive text extraction; the companion study on the same cohort reports mean ages of 99.6 and 108.8 months, sex ratios of 17:2 and 17:3, and a significant 15-point IQ difference favouring the comparison group. That IQ gap matters here too, and the study handles it better than most: age and IQ are both entered as random factors in the mixed-effects models used to establish which features discriminate, so the reported kinematic differences are adjusted for both. No ethnicity or socioeconomic data.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Confirmed diagnosis by a licensed psychiatrist with at least five years of clinical experience following DSM-IV criteria, with nonverbal IQ screened by the psychiatrist and confirmed by Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices, and ADHD and schizophrenia excluded. The companion study on the same cohort adds that diagnosis was further evaluated by a senior psychiatrist with escalation to two more on disagreement, and that ADOS and ADI-R were unavailable. Comparison children were screened for personal disorder and for first-degree relative diagnoses of autism or ADHD.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Nonverbal IQ via Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices, used both as an inclusion criterion and, importantly, as a covariate in the feature-discrimination models. No autism severity measure, which the authors acknowledge in calling for future samples with 'different behavioral presentations'. No language or adaptive functioning measures.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: determine whether head movement dynamics discriminate autistic from typically developing children, and which kinematic features do so. Main findings: 92.11% accuracy with a decision tree on two features, with all five classifiers above 81% using three features or fewer; head nodding, shaking and non-use frequencies did not differ between groups; but rotation range and amount of rotation per minute were significantly greater in autistic children in all three rotational axes after adjusting for age, IQ and gesture frequency.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A laboratory dyadic setup at Shenzhen University with the child seated 80 cm from a 33-year-old female interviewer blinded to group membership and required to behave and speak identically across participants; autistic children recruited from a local psychiatric hospital, comparison children from nearby communities. Funded by seven Shenzhen and Guangdong municipal, medical-discipline and provincial programmes.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Ten yes-no questions with an explicit verbal instruction to nod or shake the head while answering, drawn from the third of four chronologically arranged conversational sessions. The instruction is what makes the study possible - it ensures the target behaviour occurs in every participant, so kinematics can be compared on matched gestures rather than confounded with whether the gesture happened. The authors recognise the cost and state it: prior findings of reduced head gesture use in autism may hold only in spontaneous contexts, so 'our task may not a good one to reveal an ASD vs. TD difference in terms of head nodding/shaking frequency', and future work should examine unintentional gesture use.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single conversational session per child with no follow-up. Data are frontal and side video of identifiable children. Governance is partially reported - Helsinki conformity and written caregiver informed consent, with payment of 200 CNY disclosed - but no ethics committee approval or reference number is given.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Two consumer cameras, a Samsung HMX-F90 at 25 Hz and a Logitech C270 at 30 Hz, with only the frontal Logitech feed used for head pose; OpenFace 2.0; MATLAB 2017b. The equipment argument is worth noting: the whole pipeline runs from an ordinary webcam and open-source software, which underpins the authors' claim that head pose tracking suits early screening because it is 'constraint-free' and requires no worn devices or task compliance.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Good. Reported: seating distance, both cameras with sampling rates and their distinct purposes, the full ten-question list in an appendix, the instruction given to participants, interviewer blinding and consistency requirement, OpenFace version with published per-axis accuracy figures and the rationale for choosing it, per-group tracking failure rates, spline interpolation for smoothing, the exact definitions and computation of both features including the velocity-integration procedure and the per-minute normalisation with its rationale, the blind double-coding of gesture occurrence with Spearman reliabilities, the mixed-effects model specification with all fixed and random terms and the likelihood ratio testing approach, the exhaustive feature-combination rationale, all five classifiers, and leave-one-out cross-validation. Missing: ethics approval number, group-wise demographics in the extracted text, classifier hyperparameters, and any data or code release.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged: the small sample, attributed to 'the great difficulty of recruiting a large sample of ASD participants and having them complete the motor tasks', with leave-one-out cross-validation and the small number of retained features offered as mitigation against overfitting; autism's heterogeneity requiring larger and more varied samples; and the age range of 6-13 being 'much older than the mean age at diagnosis', so the study 'could only be viewed as an initial examination of social head behaviors in an older sample to establish proof of concept'. The instructed-gesture confound is also raised directly as an explanation for the frequency null. Not acknowledged: the exhaustive search evaluated 63 feature subsets across five classifiers on the same leave-one-out estimate that is reported, so the headline is a maximum over 315 fits; the abstract and results disagree on which two features produced it; and OpenFace tracking failure was fifteen times higher in the autistic group (3.46% versus 0.23%), which is reported but never examined as a possible source of the group difference.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Larger and more behaviourally varied samples given autism's heterogeneity; investigation of unintentional rather than instructed head nodding and shaking, to test whether reduced gesture use appears only in spontaneous contexts; and extension to younger children, with the argument that constraint-free computer vision is particularly suited to early screening since data can be collected in natural settings without worn devices or task instructions.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Head movement during conversational gesture, decomposed into three rotational axes - pitch for nodding, yaw for shaking, roll for lateral inclination - and characterised along two independent dimensions: extremity of rotation (range) and quantity of rotation per unit time. The behavioural target is therefore the manner of gesture execution rather than its occurrence, which is what allows the study to separate gesture use from gesture kinematics. Head gesture is also, unusually for this corpus, a communicative act rather than an incidental behaviour - nodding and shaking carry propositional content in a yes-no exchange.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No multimodal fusion; a single modality analysed across three axes. What the design does combine is two measurement approaches to the same behaviour - human coding of whether gestures occurred and automated kinematic measurement of how they were executed - and the divergence between them is the paper's most valuable result. Blind human coders found no group difference in gesture frequency; automated tracking found significant differences in every kinematic measure. The authors generalise this appropriately: the 'human perceptual system is good at detecting specific patterns of movement (e.g., head nodding, smiling), but it is not good at giving precise metric measures of movement', so pose tracking has 'an advantage over behavioral coding techniques - finding motor patterns that might be difficult to spot through human observations'. That is a specific, testable claim about what automation adds, and it is demonstrated within a single study.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Five classifiers compared on identical features, each with a short rationale and stated weaknesses, including the acknowledgement that decision trees are 'prone to overfitting' and that random forest 'could well address the overfitting problem of the DT algorithm' - which makes it notable that the decision tree nonetheless produced the highest accuracy, a pattern consistent with the exhaustive search finding a favourable split on a small sample. Reporting that all five classifiers exceeded 81% with three features or fewer is more informative than the single maximum, since it shows the signal is not classifier-specific.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Six features only - rotation range and amount of rotation per minute in each of pitch, yaw and roll. This is the most parsimonious representation in the corpus relative to sample size, and it is arrived at by design rather than by reduction: the two measures are chosen to separate the amplitude of movement from its quantity, and the per-minute normalisation explicitly corrects for participants taking different amounts of time. Spline interpolation is applied to smooth the raw series before computation. The small feature count is what makes exhaustive subset search feasible and also what limits overfitting risk.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for each classifier's best model, ROC curves for all five, and an accuracy-versus-feature-count plot. Reporting all five classifiers rather than only the winner allows the reader to see that the result is robust across model families. Missing: confusion matrices, confidence intervals and any statistical comparison between classifiers - on 38 participants one case is worth 2.6 accuracy points, so the spread from 81% to 92.11% is about four cases.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is strong because the features are physically meaningful angles and the mixed-effects analysis is conducted separately from the classification. Every feature is tested for group discrimination while controlling age, IQ and all three gesture-frequency measures as random factors, so the reported differences are adjusted rather than raw - a level of covariate control almost no other study in this corpus applies to its features. The resulting interpretation is concrete and clinically legible: autistic children move their heads through larger angles and accumulate more rotation per minute while making the same gestures with the same frequency. The blind human coding provides an independent check on the frequency null, with Spearman reliabilities of 0.787 for nodding and 0.895 for shaking.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Leave-one-out cross-validation at the participant level, correctly implemented and explicitly motivated as overfitting protection. The weakness is the search: the random feature combination approach deliberately tests every subset of the six features, and the authors justify it on the grounds that exhaustive search 'typically yields equal or higher classification accuracy simply owing to the fact that all features and feature combinations could be tested' - which is precisely the property that makes the resulting maximum optimistic. Sixty-three subsets across five classifiers gives 315 fits, all scored on the same leave-one-out estimate, with no outer loop and no held-out set. The mixed-effects feature screening also used all participants, though since all six features passed and all were retained, this contributed no additional selection. There is no independent cohort or external replication.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: Autism, Biomarkers, Diagnosis, Head movement, Machine learning. 'Head movement' is the novel term and the paper's claim to priority - the authors state theirs is 'the first to use head movement related features to detect ASD'.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, 52, 3038-3049 - a specialist autism journal rather than an engineering venue, which is consistent with the paper's substantive engagement with the motor-atypicality literature and its careful covariate handling.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021. The framing combines diagnostic delay with a specific argument for motor markers. On delay, it cites more than a year on average between initial screening and confirmed diagnosis in the United States, and a 35-country meta-analysis giving a mean diagnosis age of 60.48 months, falling to 43.18 months among children aged ten or under. On motor markers, it assembles evidence of atypical motor function in postural control, gait stability, arm movements and gross and fine motor control, and of delayed motor development in infancy that 'could subsequently contribute to the social impairments' - so motor features are argued to be developmentally upstream of the social criteria, not merely correlated with them. It then identifies head movement specifically as documented but unexploited, citing stereotyped head rolling, shaking and banging, greater head turning displacement and velocity when viewing social stimuli, and slower and less frequent head turning in response to name. Its closing claim is notably strong: 'the current diagnostic system of ASD, which are established on behavioral evaluation of social communication and restricted and repetitive behavior, would be greatly challenged' by combining features across neuroimaging, eye tracking, EEG and motion capture.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Akter T; Ali MH; Khan MI; Satu MS; Moni MA
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2021 2nd International Conference on Robotics, Electrical and Sign
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Children with autism, as characterised in the source dataset
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking and gaze
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Improve classification performance on an existing public scanpath image dataset by first partitioning it into more homogeneous subgroups. The stated problem is that 'these scanpath images were almost similar for normal and autistic children', so k-means clustering is applied to produce groups within which the two classes are, in the authors' phrase, 'more correlated' and therefore easier to separate
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Secondary computational analysis of a publicly released dataset; no new data collection, no new participants
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Not applicable - the source protocol collected approximately 10 minutes of viewing per child across multiple stimuli
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Not described in this paper. The source dataset derives from viewing photographs and videos related to social cognition, with scanpaths rendered as images encoding gaze trajectory and velocity
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Not applicable. The source data were collected in France; this analysis was performed in Google Colaboratory
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Analysis conducted in Bangladesh and Australia; source data from Hauts-de-France, France
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Inherited from the source dataset and reported at second hand: 'the severity of autism were classified by the psychologists using the Childhood Autism Rating Scale'. The source study additionally reports diagnosis confirmed by health professionals using ADI-R and ADOS-G, but that detail is not carried over here
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 30 children contributing 219 scanpath images
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Approximately 3 to 13 years, stated for the whole source sample
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Not reported per group; the source sample is 38 male (64%) and 21 female (36%) overall
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: CARS is mentioned as having been used in the source study but no scores are reported and no severity analysis is performed
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described in this paper
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 29 children contributing 328 scanpath images
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not addressed. No group-wise ages appear, only an approximate 3-13 year range for the whole sample
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed. Only a whole-sample sex split is given
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not described
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Pre-rendered scanpath images from a public repository
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Images were converted to greyscale, brightness increased, and resized to 128 x 128. K-means clustering was then applied to partition the image set into four clusters, with the standard iterative centroid-update procedure described mathematically. Nine classifiers were subsequently trained and evaluated within each cluster and on the pooled dataset
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: scikit-learn in Python running on Google Colaboratory; the source dataset from a public Figshare repository with the URL given
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: No - this is a reanalysis of a publicly released dataset
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes, and cited with its repository link - the analysis rests entirely on data another group released openly
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not needed; the source data are public
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Secondary analysis of pre-rendered abstract scanpath images with no personally identifying content. No ethics statement appears, which is defensible for public-data reuse though the reuse conditions are not discussed
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Raw greyscale pixel intensities of resized scanpath images
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: None engineered. The classifiers operate directly on 128 x 128 greyscale images after brightness adjustment, so the feature space is 16,384 raw pixel values per image with no dimensionality reduction described beyond the resizing itself
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: None beyond greyscale conversion, brightness adjustment and resizing
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported. No analysis of what distinguishes autistic from non-autistic scanpaths is attempted - the paper reports classification metrics only, and offers no account of what the clusters represent or what visual properties separate the classes
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Unsupervised partitioning followed by supervised classification on raw pixels
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: K-means clustering into four clusters, followed by decision tree, gradient boosting, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression, multilayer perceptron, naive Bayes, random forest, support vector machine and XGBoost applied within each cluster and to the pooled data
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Ten-fold cross-validation. The critical omission is that the unit is the scanpath image, not the child: the 547 images derive from 59 participants at an average of 9.27 images each, and nothing indicates that a child's images were confined to a single fold. The source study that released this dataset ran precisely this comparison and found accuracy falling from approximately 90% under image-level splitting to approximately 71% under participant-level splitting - a check this reanalysis does not repeat. Compounding this, k-means clustering was performed on the full image set before classification, so cluster membership was determined using all data including the images later used for testing
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, AUC, F-measure, G-mean, sensitivity, specificity, fall-out and miss rate, reported for all nine classifiers across four clusters and the pooled dataset - 45 rows of eight metrics
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Cluster 1 with multilayer perceptron: 88.89% accuracy, 79.2% AUC, 87.8% F-measure, 78.6% G-mean, 88.9% sensitivity, 69.4% specificity. Cluster 2 best 70.7% (logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost). Cluster 3 best 75.8% accuracy (random forest). Cluster 4 best 77.8% accuracy with 72.3% AUC (random forest). Pooled dataset best 74.2% accuracy with 71.5% AUC (random forest). Note that the abstract quotes 87% while the table gives 88.89%. Several cells are near-degenerate: in cluster 1, naive Bayes and SVM both show 73.3% accuracy with 73.3% sensitivity and 26.7% specificity - the signature of a classifier predicting almost exclusively one class - and SVM shows exactly 0.500 AUC in three of the five datasets
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Applying k-means clustering to a public scanpath image dataset before classification raised the best reported accuracy from 74.2% on the pooled data to 88.89% within one of four clusters. The authors interpret this as clustering having produced groups in which the classes are more separable. Read against the source study that released the dataset - which reported approximately 90% with image-level splitting and approximately 71% with participant-level splitting - the pooled result of 74.2% here is consistent with the source's optimistic figure, and the cluster-1 improvement is the best of thirty-six cluster-by-classifier combinations rather than a demonstrated gain.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None identified. The paper reports no behavioural or visual characterisation of what distinguishes the groups
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: None stated as a distinct section
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: This is a reanalysis of the openly released Cilia scanpath dataset, and it is instructive chiefly for what it does with that resource. The source study released its data explicitly to address the absence of a benchmark in this literature, and also reported - on the same images - that accuracy fell from approximately 90% when scanpath images were pooled to approximately 71% when participants were held out, with an average of 9.27 images per child. This reanalysis uses ten-fold cross-validation over the 547 images with no indication that a child's images were kept together, so it reproduces the optimistic configuration without the correction the source study supplied. Its pooled best of 74.2% sits close to the source's participant-pooled range, which is what one would expect. Two further problems compound this. The k-means clustering was performed on the whole image set before any classification, so cluster membership - which determines which images a model is trained and tested on - was established using data later used for testing, and the reported improvement is therefore not separable from that. And the headline 88.89% is the best of nine classifiers across four clusters plus the pooled set, forty-five cells in total, with no correction for multiplicity and no confidence intervals; the abstract quotes 87% while the table gives 88.89%, an unexplained discrepancy. The reported metrics also contain several near-degenerate results the paper does not flag: in cluster 1, naive Bayes and SVM both return 73.3% accuracy with 26.7% specificity, and SVM returns exactly 0.500 AUC in three of five datasets, which is the signature of a classifier predicting a single class throughout. Beyond validation, the paper contributes no behavioural interpretation - it does not say what the four clusters represent, what visual properties differ between classes, or why clustering should help - and it inherits its participant description at second hand without the diagnostic detail available in the source. Its one methodological idea, that partitioning a heterogeneous dataset into subgroups before classification may help, is worth taking seriously in principle, but it is not tested here in a way that distinguishes a real effect from selection across a large grid.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups inherited from the source dataset: 30 autistic and 29 non-autistic children, contributing 219 and 328 scanpath images respectively. The analysis operates on images rather than children throughout, and the 59 participants are never treated as the unit of anything. Following k-means partitioning, the effective analysis units become four image clusters of unstated composition - the paper does not report how many images, or how many children, fall in each cluster, nor the class balance within them, which makes the per-cluster metrics difficult to interpret.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'autistic children', 'ASD children', 'normal children', 'ASD patients', 'control instances'. The comparison group is 'normal' and autistic children are described as showing 'an unbearable social attitudes and unable to present regular physiological responses' - phrasing that is both pathologising and unclear. Autism is characterised in the abstract as 'reducing concentration on social activities and improving interest in non-social tasks', which restates a contested empirical claim as a definition.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Reported entirely at second hand and only for the whole sample: 59 participants, 38 male (64%) and 21 female (36%), aged approximately 3 to 13 years, recruited from schools in the Hauts-de-France region. No group-wise ages, sexes, means or standard deviations appear, and no matching is discussed. The source study reports mean ages of 7 years 7 months and 8 years 0 months by group, so the information exists but is not carried over.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Inherited and incompletely transmitted. The paper states only that 'the severity of autism were classified by the psychologists using the Childhood Autism Rating Scale' - describing a severity instrument rather than a diagnostic procedure. The source study reports diagnosis confirmed by health professionals using ADI-R and ADOS-G in multidisciplinary clinics, which is stronger ascertainment than this paper conveys. Non-autistic status is not described at all.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None used. CARS is mentioned as having been applied in the source study but no scores are reported, no severity stratification is performed, and no cognitive, language or adaptive measures appear. Since the source dataset's accompanying publication reports CARS and ECSP scores, the omission is a choice of this reanalysis rather than a constraint of the data.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: improve classification on an existing scanpath image dataset by clustering it first into more homogeneous subgroups. Main findings: best accuracy of 88.89% with a multilayer perceptron in cluster 1, against 74.2% for the best classifier on the pooled dataset; the other three clusters reached 70.7%, 75.8% and 77.8%; and the authors conclude that clustering produced groups in which classes were more separable.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No data collection. The source data were gathered from schools in Hauts-de-France; all analysis here was performed in Google Colaboratory using scikit-learn, by authors at institutions in Bangladesh and Australia.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Not described. The paper does not report what the children were looking at, how long the stimuli lasted, or how scanpaths were rendered into images - all of which are documented in the source publication and all of which bear on what the classifiers are learning. A reader of this paper alone cannot tell whether the images encode gaze position only or, as in the source, gaze velocity through colour gradient.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis of publicly released images. No ethics statement appears, which is largely defensible for reuse of open data, though the paper does not discuss the terms of that reuse. The Figshare repository is cited with its URL, and the originating study is credited.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: scikit-learn in Python on Google Colaboratory. No hardware, hyperparameters, random seeds or software versions are reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Poor for a computational paper. Reported: the source dataset with its repository link and originating citation, the preprocessing chain (greyscale, brightness increase, resize to 128 x 128), the number of clusters, the nine classifier names, ten-fold cross-validation, the eight evaluation metrics, and a complete 45-row results table. The k-means algorithm is set out in full mathematical detail, which is unnecessary for a standard method. Not reported: how many images or children fall in each cluster and their class balance; any hyperparameter for any classifier; the random seed; the rationale for choosing four clusters; whether images from a child were kept together; and any code. The mathematical exposition of k-means occupies more space than the entire account of how the classifiers were configured.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: None. There is no limitations section and no caveat on sample size, validation design, cluster interpretation or generalisability. Identifiable in review: ten-fold cross-validation operates over 547 images from 59 children with no statement that a child's images were confined to one fold, and the source study demonstrated on these same images that participant-level splitting reduces accuracy from approximately 90% to approximately 71%; k-means clustering was performed on the full image set before classification, so cluster membership was determined using test images; the headline is the best of 45 cluster-by-classifier cells with no multiplicity correction or confidence intervals; the abstract quotes 87% against the table's 88.89%; several reported cells are near-degenerate single-class predictors that are not flagged; and no clinical or behavioural interpretation of any result is offered.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: None stated.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Inherited from the source dataset: visual scanning behaviour rendered as a spatial trace. This paper adds no behavioural analysis of its own and does not characterise the target behaviour beyond the assertion in its introduction that autistic children show reduced attention to social content.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No multimodal fusion. The only combination performed is unsupervised partitioning followed by supervised classification, which is a pipeline rather than a fusion. The result - higher accuracy within one cluster than on the pooled data - is presented as evidence that clustering helps, but no cluster is characterised, no analysis explains what makes cluster 1 different, and the improvement is a maximum over 36 cluster-by-classifier combinations, so it cannot be distinguished from selection across the grid.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Nine classifiers spanning trees, ensembles, kernel methods, neural networks and probabilistic models, applied uniformly across all five datasets. Breadth is the only principle - no rationale is given for any individual choice, no hyperparameters are reported, and the winning algorithm differs by cluster (multilayer perceptron in cluster 1, random forest in clusters 3 and 4, three classifiers tied in cluster 2), which at these sample sizes is consistent with noise rather than with any property of the clusters.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Raw 128 x 128 greyscale pixels with brightness increased - 16,384 features per image, with no engineered representation, no dimensionality reduction and no convolutional structure. Applying classifiers such as naive Bayes, k-nearest neighbours and logistic regression directly to raw pixels of spatially structured images is a poor match of method to data, and is likely why the pooled results plateau around 74%: none of these models can exploit spatial locality. The source study used a convolutional network on the same images for exactly this reason.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Eight metrics for all nine classifiers on all five datasets, which is comprehensive in coverage and is the paper's strongest feature. Reporting specificity and fall-out alongside sensitivity is what makes the degenerate cells visible: in cluster 1, naive Bayes and SVM both show 73.3% accuracy with 26.7% specificity and exactly 0.500 AUC, and the best model itself pairs 88.9% sensitivity with only 69.4% specificity. Missing: confidence intervals, confusion matrices, cluster composition, and any statistical comparison - so whether 88.89% differs meaningfully from 77.8% is not established.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No feature importance, no saliency, no cluster characterisation and no behavioural interpretation. The paper does not state what the four clusters correspond to - whether they separate stimulus types, participants, image quality or something else - which leaves its central claim uninterpretable: the reader cannot tell whether clustering identified clinically meaningful subgroups or simply partitioned the images in a way that happened to make one subset easier. Given that images from the same child are visually similar, one plausible explanation is that clusters partly track individual participants, which would make the within-cluster accuracy gain a direct consequence of increased within-fold similarity.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The decisive weakness, and unusually well documented because the source study performed the missing check. Ten-fold cross-validation is applied over 547 scanpath images drawn from 59 children, with no statement that a child's images were confined to a single fold. The study that released these images ran both configurations and reported approximately 90% accuracy pooling images against approximately 71% holding out participants - so the inflation attributable to image-level splitting on this exact dataset is known and is roughly 19 points. This reanalysis does not repeat that check. Separately, k-means clustering used the entire image set, so the partition determining each model's training and test pool was fitted on data including the test images. There is no held-out set, no participant-level analysis, no confidence intervals and no independent cohort.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: ASD, Eye Tracking, K-Means Clustering, Classifier, Machine Learning. Three of five name generic methods, which reflects a paper whose contribution is a pipeline applied to someone else's data.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: 2021 2nd International Conference on Robotics, Electrical and Signal Processing Techniques (ICREST), pages 383-387 - a general engineering conference with no clinical or autism-specific remit.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021. The framing is brief and largely a literature enumeration, cataloguing prior eye-tracking autism work including the source dataset's own publications, web-page gaze studies, video-based screening paradigms, geometric-preference subtyping and autism risk indices. Its stated motivation is that 'there are needed a elaborated work that can explore significant factors of eye-signs for detecting autism', though the analysis performed does not in fact explore any factors. Its most interesting incidental observation is the honest one that motivates the clustering: 'these scanpath images were almost similar for normal and autistic children', which is a candid statement that the raw visual difference between groups is small - consistent with the source study's finding that participant-level accuracy sits near 71%.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Emanuele M; Nazzaro G; Marini M; Veronesi C; Boni S; Polletta G; D'Ausilio A; Fadiga L
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Preschool children with autism spectrum diagnoses
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Motor and kinematics (inter-joint coordination)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Identify a mechanistic substrate for the well-documented but poorly explained motor problems in autism, by testing whether motor synergies - the co-controlled blocks of redundant degrees of freedom through which the nervous system simplifies motor control - are impaired. The classification analysis is secondary to this, added to test translational feasibility. A distinctive further aim is to relate motor measures to symptom severity rather than merely to group label, on the observation that 'standardized assessments of autistic symptoms are often only used to assign group labels', which 'has prevented understanding the impact of motor differences in the heterogeneous expression of ASD symptoms'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control study combining group-level kinematic comparison, within-group severity correlation, and single-subject automatic classification
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Eight blocks of five trials each across two sessions of four blocks, giving 40 trials per child - ten per pen orientation
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A reaching-grasping task deliberately chosen for ecological validity and self-explanation. On the experimenter's vocal command, the child reaches for and grasps a felt-tip pen in order to complete a figure printed on a sheet of paper. The pen tip points in one of four orientations - upward right, upward left, downward right, downward left - varied 'to add more variability to the task and avoid the use of stereotyped actions'. The authors argue the paradigm's advantage explicitly: 'children of preschool age know perfectly well how to manipulate a felt-tip pen to draw on a sheet of paper, with no need for detailed task description'. Children were free to use any grip and either hand
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Laboratory motion capture with the child seated at a table; autistic children recruited from a local outpatient clinic for neurodevelopmental disorders, typically developing children from a local kindergarten
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: ICD-10 diagnoses spanning F84.9 pervasive developmental disorder unspecified (6 children), F84.0 autistic disorder (6) and F84.5 Asperger syndrome (1)
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Diagnosis by an experienced clinician according to ICD-10 and DSM-5 criteria. ADOS was then administered to all participants in both groups, both to corroborate the clinical diagnosis and to capture severity variation, with autistic children meeting the diagnostic cut-off and typically developing children scoring below it. Individual ADOS totals and modules are tabulated per participant
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Reported per participant rather than excluded: four children had F80.2 mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and one had G40.8 other epilepsy and recurrent seizures
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: ADOS total scores reported individually for every participant, ranging from 8 to 23 in the autistic group and 0 to 3 in the comparison group, with the module used also given per child. Severity is used analytically, correlated against every kinematic measure
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes - ADOS was administered to typically developing children as well, with all scoring below the diagnostic threshold and ten of thirteen scoring zero
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes, and formally tested - t(24) = 1.480, p = 0.152
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: No, and untested. The autistic group is 38% female and the comparison group 69% female, an inversion of the usual direction and a substantial imbalance in a 26-child sample; the paper reports sex per participant but never tests or discusses the difference
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Established by ADOS administration with all scores below the diagnostic threshold
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Three-dimensional marker trajectories from optoelectronic motion capture
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: The upper limb was modelled as a five-segment kinematic chain (clavicle, humerus, forearm, a segment joining the ulnar and radial markers, and hand) articulated through nine joint angles, with azimuth and elevation computed per segment and intersegmental angles derived by subtracting the proximal segment's angle. Pronosupination was computed as the elevation angle of the ulnar-radial segment after rotating both markers by the forearm azimuth. Movement onset was defined as tangential velocity of the ulnar marker rising for at least 100 ms, and offset as it rising again for at least 50 ms after falling below 20% of peak, with both criteria verified by visual inspection of individual trials. Principal component analysis was applied trial-wise to angular displacements after time-normalisation to 200 points and per-trial z-score normalisation to account for differing joint ranges of motion, and the variance accounted for by the first three components was extracted
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Qualisys optoelectronic motion capture with three infrared cameras at 200 Hz, low-pass filtered at 10 Hz with a third-order Butterworth filter; ten passive markers on the upper limbs and one on the sternum; MATLAB for kinematic computation; Python with scikit-learn for classification
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Kinematic recordings from 26 children; no release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Numeric marker trajectories with per-participant clinical data published in tabular form, including ICD-10 diagnosis codes and comorbidities but no identifiers. Governance is reported: written informed consent from parents or legal guardians, design according to the Declaration of Helsinki, and approval by the local ethical committee with a full reference number (EM185-2020_UniFe/170686_EM2)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Kinematic timing, amplitude, spatial and coordination measures
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Seventeen features per trial. Timing and dynamics: movement time, peak acceleration, peak velocity, peak deceleration, and relative time to each of these three normalised by movement time. Spatial endpoint: displacement along the x and y axes at movement offset, z-elevation at offset. Spatial mid-movement: proportion of total x and y displacement already covered at peak velocity, z-elevation at peak velocity. Path: total trajectory length. Coordination: variance accounted for by the first principal component, cumulatively by the first two, and cumulatively by the first three - the synergy measures. Including the synergy variables as classifier features alongside conventional kinematics is what allows the classification and the mechanistic analysis to speak to each other
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Custom MATLAB kinematic computation with cart2sph for joint angles; PCA for synergy extraction; scikit-learn for classification
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, computed per participant and reported in supplementary material
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Per-participant feature importance from the classifier, plus robustness analyses varying the number of test trials available and restricting features to those derivable from the ulnar marker alone
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Features indexing spatial displacement at peak velocity and at movement offset, together with the cumulative variance accounted for by the first three principal components, contributed significantly to classification - and the authors note this 'substantially confirmed the results obtained with univariate statistics', so the classifier and the group-level analysis converge on the same variables
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reported in full with test statistics and effect directions. Autistic children moved faster (mean movement time 743.7 ms against 839.5 ms, F(1,24) = 8.276, p = 0.008), showed a more symmetrical velocity profile with a larger relative time to peak velocity (0.503 against 0.463, p = 0.031), were more variable in trajectory length across trials (SD 45.96 against 34.22 mm, p = 0.0034), and showed lower cumulative variance accounted for by the first three principal components (97.53% against 98.20%, p = 0.009), indicating weaker coupling between joints. The two non-normal outcomes were confirmed by permutation tests with 5,000 permutations. Crucially, the synergy measure alone correlated with symptom severity, showing a significant negative Spearman correlation with ADOS total (rho = -0.650, p = 0.016), while movement time, relative time to peak velocity and trajectory-length variability did not (rho = 0.039, 0.257 and 0.138, all non-significant)
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Kernel-based supervised classification on trial-level kinematics with subject-level aggregation
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Support vector machine with a radial basis function kernel, with C and gamma optimised by grid search over C in {1, 10, 100} and gamma in {0.01, 0.001, 0.0001} at each iteration
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-subject-out, described unambiguously: the training set is formed by excluding all rows corresponding to one participant's trials, and that participant's data form the test set, repeated for every participant. Feature z-normalisation was fitted on the training set and applied to the test set using training-set means and standard deviations. The authors state the rationale explicitly - 'the data in the test dataset belonged to a participant that was never seen before by the classifier. Accordingly, the classifier accuracy was tested in a context that simulates as much as possible the diagnosis of a new patient in everyday life clinical settings'. Hyperparameters were grid-searched at each iteration. Two robustness analyses varied the number of test trials available and restricted features to those from the ulnar marker alone
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Trial-level classification accuracy averaged across participants and reported in bands, plus a subject-level ROC built from each participant's proportion of positive trial responses with area under the curve and sensitivity and specificity at the optimal operating point
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Average trial-level accuracy 0.739, with accuracy above 0.7 in 15 of 26 children, between 0.6 and 0.7 in 6, and below 0.6 in the remaining 5. At subject level the ROC gave an AUC of 0.947 with sensitivity 0.846 and specificity 0.923 at its optimal operating point. The abstract describes this as 'classification accuracy reached up to 0.947', which conflates AUC with accuracy; the trial-level accuracy is 0.739 and no subject-level accuracy is reported directly
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Autistic preschoolers showed faster, more ballistic reaching with a more symmetrical velocity profile, greater trial-to-trial spatial variability, and - the paper's central and novel result - weaker coupling between joint degrees of freedom, indicating impaired motor synergies. Only the synergy measure correlated with autism severity (rho = -0.650 against ADOS total), while the conventional kinematic measures did not, which is what elevates it from a group difference to a candidate mechanism. The authors argue that impaired synergies could produce the established but unexplained phenomena of fragmented action chains and abnormal trial-to-trial variability, and further that because synergies also provide a compact coding system for observed actions, their impairment could initiate 'bottom-up cascade effects, leading to pervasive impairments of social behaviour'. Classification reached AUC 0.947 at subject level under leave-one-subject-out validation, with sensitivity and specificity comparable to those reported for ADOS itself.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Reduced inter-joint coupling (lower variance accounted for by the first three principal components), faster and more ballistic movement with shorter deceleration, and greater trial-to-trial variability in trajectory length
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Evaluate intellectual disability, identified as 'an important source of inter-subject variability in ASD that seems to impact motor planning and coordination'; include additional diagnostic classes such as developmental coordination disorder and ADHD, since motor difficulties occur across neurodevelopmental disorders and a dimensional framing might reveal a common pathogenetic mechanism; and extend the synergy framework to speech and language coordination, which the authors argue shares key similarities with upper-limb action
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The strongest theoretically motivated study in the corpus. Rather than asking whether a classifier can separate groups, it asks what mechanism produces the separation, and answers with a specific and falsifiable proposal: that redundant motor degrees of freedom are less tightly co-controlled in autism, measurable as the variance a small number of principal components can account for across nine joint angles. The evidence for treating this as mechanism rather than epiphenomenon is the dissociation in the correlation analysis - the synergy measure correlates with ADOS severity at rho = -0.650 while movement time, velocity-profile symmetry and spatial variability all fail to, so the coordination index tracks the clinical dimension and the surface kinematics do not. The authors' framing of why this matters is unusually precise: standardised assessments in this literature 'are often only used to assign group labels', which 'has prevented understanding the impact of motor differences in the heterogeneous expression of ASD symptoms'. Methodologically the study is careful in several respects that most of the corpus is not. Leave-one-subject-out is implemented and justified explicitly as simulating diagnosis of a new patient; normalisation statistics are fitted on training folds only; hyperparameters are grid-searched within each iteration; non-normal outcomes are confirmed by permutation testing; ADOS is administered to both groups with per-participant scores, modules, ICD-10 codes, comorbidities and handedness all tabulated; ethics approval carries a full reference number; and two robustness analyses test performance under reduced trial counts and with only end-effector markers, motivated by the concrete observation that autistic children 'are indeed poorly compliant when required to wear something new or unusual' and may resist multiple markers. Three caveats. The headline figure is presented ambiguously - the abstract states 'classification accuracy reached up to 0.947' when 0.947 is the subject-level AUC, while the reported accuracy is 0.739 at trial level, and the sensitivity and specificity of 0.846 and 0.923 are taken at an operating point optimised on the same ROC. Sex is markedly imbalanced at 38% female in the autistic group against 69% in the comparison group, reported per participant but never tested or discussed, which matters in a 26-child sample. And the severity correlation rests on 13 points with a single high-ADOS participant visibly anchoring the relationship. The authors' own stated priorities - measuring intellectual disability and adding developmental coordination disorder and ADHD comparison groups - address precisely the right next questions.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 13 children each. The autistic group spans three ICD-10 diagnoses - six with F84.9 pervasive developmental disorder unspecified, six with F84.0 autistic disorder and one with F84.5 Asperger syndrome - and includes four children with comorbid mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and one with epilepsy, all reported per participant rather than excluded.
