No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the authors identify developmental coordination disorder and ADHD as necessary additions for establishing whether the motor finding is autism-specific or shared across neurodevelopmental conditions.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'neurotypical subjects', 'participants with ASD'. Consistently person-first with 'neurotypical' used for the general comparison. The framing is developmental and mechanistic rather than deficit-cataloguing - autism's heterogeneity is described at length, aetiology is acknowledged as 'far from being understood', and the theoretical argument runs from low-order sensorimotor processing upward to social cognition rather than treating social impairment as primary.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Autistic group: 13 children, 8 male and 5 female, aged 44-82 months, mean 66.23 +/- 11.56. Typically developing group: 13 children, 4 male and 9 female, aged 43-71 months, mean 60.08 +/- 9.54. Age matching is formally tested and confirmed (t(24) = 1.480, p = 0.152). Sex is not: 38% female against 69% female, an inversion of the usual direction, reported per participant but never tested or mentioned. Handedness was assessed behaviourally by asking children to draw and confirmed by caregivers or clinicians, with two left-handed children and two of unclear handedness, and left-hand trials from three autistic children were discarded because markers could not be placed on their left arms due to compliance problems. Per-participant ADOS totals, modules, ages, sexes, ICD-10 codes, comorbidities and handedness are all tabulated - the most complete individual-level characterisation in the corpus. No IQ or cognitive measures, which the authors name as a limitation.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Diagnosis by an experienced clinician under both ICD-10 and DSM-5, with specific ICD-10 subcodes reported per child. ADOS was then administered to every participant in both groups, with autistic children meeting the diagnostic cut-off and typically developing children scoring below it - ten of the thirteen scored zero, and the highest comparison score was 3. Applying the gold-standard instrument to both groups and publishing individual scores is stronger practice than almost anything else in the corpus. The authors also report ADOS's own published operating characteristics (sensitivity 0.94, specificity 0.80 across 12 studies) and use them as the benchmark against which to judge their classifier.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: ADOS total scores individually reported for all 26 participants with the module used, plus ICD-10 diagnostic subtype and comorbid diagnoses per child. Severity is used analytically rather than descriptively - correlated against all four kinematic outcomes - which is what produces the paper's key dissociation. The acknowledged gap is intellectual functioning: no IQ or developmental level was measured, and the authors state that future research 'will have to evaluate intellectual disability, which is an important source of inter-subject variability in ASD that seems to impact motor planning and coordination'.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: test whether motor synergies - the co-control of redundant degrees of freedom - are impaired in autism, and relate this to symptom severity. Main findings: autistic children moved faster with more symmetrical velocity profiles, showed greater trial-to-trial spatial variability, and showed significantly reduced variance accounted for by the first three principal components across nine joint angles; only the synergy measure correlated with ADOS severity (rho = -0.650, p = 0.016); and leave-one-subject-out SVM classification reached AUC 0.947 with 0.846 sensitivity and 0.923 specificity at the optimal operating point, on trial-level accuracy of 0.739.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Laboratory motion capture at the University of Ferrara and the Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia's Center for Translational Neurophysiology of Speech and Communication, with autistic children recruited from a local outpatient neurodevelopmental clinic and comparison children from a local kindergarten. Funded by two Italian Ministry of Health young-researcher grants and an EU H2020 project. No competing interests declared.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Reaching for and grasping a felt-tip pen to complete a printed figure - a task chosen because it is ecological and needs no explanation to a preschooler, with pen orientation varied across four positions specifically to prevent stereotyped movement. Forty trials per child across eight blocks in two sessions, with block order randomised and free choice of hand and grip. The design decisions are all in service of the mechanistic question: enough trials to estimate trial-to-trial variability and to fit trial-wise PCA, enough orientation variation to require genuine motor parameter selection rather than a rehearsed movement, and enough naturalness that task comprehension is not a confound.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; two sessions per child with no follow-up. Data are numeric marker trajectories, with per-participant clinical data published in tabular form but no identifiers. Governance is complete: written informed consent from parents or legal guardians, Helsinki-compliant design, and local ethical committee approval with a full reference number.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Qualisys optoelectronic motion capture with three infrared cameras at 200 Hz - the highest-fidelity motion measurement in the corpus - with ten passive markers on the upper limbs and one on the sternum, low-pass filtered at 10 Hz with a third-order Butterworth filter. Marker labelling was verified by offline visual inspection, and the movement onset and offset criteria were themselves validated by visual inspection of individual trials. The robustness analysis using only the ulnar marker is a direct response to the practical constraint that autistic children may not tolerate a full marker set.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Excellent. Reported: task geometry with all distances, stimulus dimensions, block structure and randomisation; camera count, sampling rate, filter type and cutoff; marker placement anatomy; the five-segment kinematic model with all nine joint angles and their derivation including the pronosupination computation; movement onset and offset criteria with their thresholds and durations; PCA preprocessing including time-normalisation to 200 points and per-trial z-scoring with its stated rationale; the justification for retaining three components; the full ANOVA model with both factors; permutation testing for non-normal outcomes with iteration count; all 17 classifier features defined individually in a table; the SVM kernel and full hyperparameter grid; the leave-one-subject-out procedure including how normalisation was applied across the split; and per-participant clinical data. Supplementary material covers pronosupination derivation, trial-count robustness, feature-restricted robustness and per-participant feature importance. Missing only: data or code release, and IQ measures.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged: the sample was 'relatively small and likely not able to capture the full heterogeneity of ASD'; intellectual disability was not measured despite being a known source of variability affecting motor planning and coordination; and only autism and typical development were contrasted, whereas motor difficulties occur across neurodevelopmental disorders so additional diagnostic classes would 'facilitate a dimensional acknowledgment of atypical development'. Practical constraints are also disclosed, including that left-arm markers could not be placed on three autistic children due to compliance problems. Not acknowledged: the abstract reports 0.947 as classification accuracy when it is the subject-level AUC, with trial-level accuracy being 0.739; the sensitivity and specificity are taken at an operating point optimised on the same ROC used to characterise performance; the sex imbalance of 38% versus 69% female is tabulated but never tested or discussed; and the severity correlation rests on 13 observations with a visibly influential high-ADOS point.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Measure intellectual disability as a source of inter-subject variability affecting motor planning and coordination; include developmental coordination disorder and ADHD comparison groups to test whether impaired synergies represent 'a common pathogenetic mechanism for these conditions' rather than an autism-specific marker; and extend the synergy framework to speech and language, on the argument that 'speech and language coordination share key similarity with upper limb action' and that language difficulties are common in autism.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Upper-limb reaching and grasping, analysed at two levels. Conventional kinematics capture the surface properties of movement - speed, velocity-profile shape, endpoint variability. The synergy analysis captures something different in kind: how tightly the nine joint angles covary, indexed by how much of their joint variance three principal components can absorb. That second level is the paper's contribution, and it targets a construct - co-control of redundant degrees of freedom - that no other study in this corpus measures.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No multimodal fusion. What the study combines is levels of description within a single modality, and it does so to informative effect: the 17 classifier features include both conventional kinematics and the three synergy measures, and the per-participant feature importance analysis finds that spatial displacement measures and the cumulative variance accounted for by three components both contribute. The authors note that this 'substantially confirmed the results obtained with univariate statistics', so the classifier's internal weighting agrees with the group-level analysis - a convergence that few studies in the corpus check and that here supports treating the classification as reflecting the same phenomenon as the hypothesis test rather than an unrelated pattern.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A single radial-basis-function SVM with hyperparameters grid-searched at each leave-one-subject-out iteration. No model comparison is reported, which is appropriate given that classification is explicitly secondary to the mechanistic question and the paper makes no claim about optimal architecture. The design decision that matters is aggregation: the classifier operates on trials, and subject-level inference is obtained by taking each participant's proportion of positive trial responses as an estimate of diagnosis probability, from which the ROC is built.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Seventeen trial-level features, each defined explicitly in a table, spanning movement timing, peak dynamics and their relative timing, spatial displacement at both peak velocity and movement offset, trajectory length, and the three cumulative variance-accounted-for measures. The representation is compact, physically interpretable and includes the theoretically motivated coordination variables alongside the descriptive ones. The PCA preprocessing is carefully specified - trial-wise application after time-normalisation to 200 points and per-trial z-scoring, the latter adopted specifically to account for the differing ranges of motion across joints, with the choice of three components justified by reference to prior work on three-dimensional movement.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Trial-level accuracy reported as a mean and in bands across participants, plus a subject-level ROC with AUC and the sensitivity and specificity at its optimal operating point. Reporting the distribution of per-child accuracy rather than only the mean is valuable - it shows five of 26 children classified below 0.6, which a summary figure would hide. The weakness is presentational: the abstract's 'classification accuracy reached up to 0.947' conflates AUC with accuracy, no subject-level accuracy is given directly, and the operating point yielding 0.846 sensitivity and 0.923 specificity is selected on the same curve. Comparison against ADOS's own published sensitivity and specificity is a useful external anchor that few studies provide.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is the paper's organising purpose. Every feature is a physical quantity with a motor-control meaning, the group differences are reported with effect directions and interpreted against specific literatures on feedforward versus feedback control, and the synergy result is developed into an explicit mechanistic account - that impaired co-control forces either learning motor commands for each degree of freedom separately, which is prohibitively slow, or mapping each behavioural goal to a whole set of muscle activations, which prevents generalisation, with either extreme producing the idiosyncratic and fragmented motor strategies observed clinically. The correlation analysis then provides the discriminating evidence, showing that only the synergy measure tracks severity. Per-participant feature importance is computed and reported, and the authors verify that it agrees with the univariate findings.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Leave-one-subject-out, correctly implemented and explicitly motivated as simulating 'the diagnosis of a new patient in everyday life clinical settings'. Normalisation is fitted on training folds and applied to test data using training statistics, and hyperparameters are grid-searched at each iteration rather than fixed globally. Two robustness analyses extend the validation usefully - varying the number of trials available in the test set, and restricting features to those derivable from the ulnar marker alone - both framed around deployment constraints rather than as statistical exercises. The residual issues are that the ROC operating point is chosen on the evaluation curve, and that no independent cohort or external site is tested, which the small sample precludes.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: Autism spectrum disorder, Motor synergies, Machine learning, Kinematics, Early diagnosis, Neurodevelopmental disorders. 'Motor synergies' is the novel term and the paper's claim - the authors state their result indicates 'for the first time, that motor synergies are impaired in ASD'.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Cognition, 213, article 104652, published open access in a special issue honouring the journal's founding editor - a cognitive science venue rather than a clinical or engineering one, which explains the depth of theoretical development relative to the modelling.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021. The framing is developmental and causal rather than diagnostic-efficiency driven. It argues that 'low-order impairments of sensory processing and motor coding during the early stages of life may impact the acquisition of more complex abilities, including socio-communicative skills and cognitive functions', and assembles evidence of pervasive sensorimotor impairment across posture, balance, gait, aiming movements, eye-hand coordination, force control and handwriting - proposing that these 'scattered disturbances presumably arise from a limited number of common dysfunctional mechanisms'. Its most distinctive contribution to the corpus's framing is a methodological criticism aimed at its own field: that standardised symptom assessments 'are often only used to assign group labels (i.e. ASD vs. neurotypical)', and that 'this approach has prevented understanding the impact of motor differences in the heterogeneous expression of ASD symptoms'. The paper then acts on that criticism by correlating every kinematic measure against ADOS totals within the autistic group, which is what yields its central dissociation.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Alnajjar F; Cappuccio M; Renawi A; Mubin O; Loo CK
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Single-arm clinical pilot and longitudinal intervention study, with concurrent validation of an automated attention-measurement system against therapist ratings
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A running attention score per session, accumulated at approximately 1 Hz across the 13-section scenario, together with per-session trend summaries used to adapt the next session
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 11 in the clinical setup, of whom 6 completed the long-term study
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. Single site, single therapist standard.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: None. There is no non-autistic comparison group of any kind, which is consistent with the study's purpose - it measures attention within an intervention rather than discriminating between groups.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Parents signed parental consent letters
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: An adaptive, semi-autonomous interaction scenario in 13 sections, delivered by a NAO robot with a mobile phone mounted on a custom chest holder displaying facial expressions from an Emotions Selector application. The system presents emotional cues and solicits appropriate emotional responses, and - the design's distinctive feature - the scenario adapts across sessions to each child's attention score history, so the intervention personalises itself from its own measurements. The chest-mount engineering is described carefully, with the authors noting that the added weight 'barely affects the center of mass of the robot body, hence the changes in the moment of inertia are negligible', preserving the robot's equilibrium and mobility so that built-in interactive behaviours still function.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Aldebaran/SoftBank NAO humanoid robot with a custom-designed chest mount holding a mobile phone; the phone camera configured as an IP camera via a mobile application; Haar cascade classifiers for face and ear detection. The algorithm runs continuously at approximately 1 Hz.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Approved by the Social Sciences Research Ethical Committee of UAE University and by Al Ain Hospital
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Rule-based. Face detected by Haar classifier increments the attention score by 5; face not detected decrements it by 1; a head turn matching the robot's directed gaze, detected via left or right ear detection, increments the joint-attention score by 15; and a sound-response increment is computed from speech-onset latency by a fixed linear formula.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Complete by construction, and unusually so. Every element of the attention score is a stated rule with a stated constant - plus 5 for a detected face, minus 1 for an undetected face, plus 15 for a joint-attention head turn, and a linear function of speech latency - so a clinician can read the score's derivation directly and an operator can adjust the weights for an individual child. There is no learned component whose behaviour would need explaining. Against the deep models charted elsewhere in this review, this is the opposite design point: nothing is fitted, so nothing is opaque, and the corresponding cost is that the constants are asserted rather than derived from data.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not applicable; the scoring constants are set by the operator rather than fitted
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Concurrent validation against an independent human standard, which is the appropriate design for the claim being made and is executed transparently. The system's session-level attention trend was compared against the treating therapist's 0-100 attention ratings across 34 sessions, with agreement on 28 and disagreement on 6, giving the reported 82.4%. This is an agreement rate between an automated measure and a clinician's judgement of the same construct - a concurrent-validity coefficient, not a diagnostic accuracy - and the paper's own conclusion describes it correctly as 'matching over 80% of therapist assessments'. Two limits follow. Agreement on a session-level trend is a coarse criterion, and no inter-rater reliability is available for the therapist ratings that serve as the standard, so the ceiling on achievable agreement is unknown. And with 34 sessions from 6 children, sessions from the same child are not independent and no adjustment for clustering is reported.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The introduction contains a well-judged analysis of the field's constraints that functions as a limitations discussion: most preprogrammed robot systems 'have fixed behavior (i.e., they are unable to autonomously perform adaptable closed-loop interactions), are not tailored to the individual needs of patients, and cannot keep track of their recovery progress', while semi-autonomous adaptive systems 'need high-performance hardware, such as GPUs chips, to process real-time data and update interactions' and 'are not yet reliable outside controlled research' settings. The discussion also reports the display-handling problem encountered in early sessions and how it was addressed. The causal claim about attention improvement is explicitly labelled a hypothesis.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Eleven autistic boys recruited from Al Ain Hospital in the United Arab Emirates, all with CARS2 scores between 30 and 36.5 - the mild-to-moderate band - under 16 years of age with a mean of 9.03 years (SD 2.56), and all required to have at least minimal verbal capability, being able to understand verbal communication and answer yes or no. Six of the eleven continued into the long-term study, with no explanation given for the other five. There is no comparison group of any kind, which is consistent with the design: the study measures attention within an intervention rather than discriminating between populations. Two features of the sample are worth recording for the review. Reporting a CARS2 range as an eligibility criterion is more severity characterisation than most included studies provide, and it bounds the population precisely - but because only the range is given rather than per-child scores, within-sample severity variation cannot be related to any outcome. And the eligibility requirements taken together - male, mild to moderate, verbally responsive - define a narrow population, so the system's behaviour with non-speaking or more severely affected children is untested despite the abstract describing the target group as having 'minimal verbal capabilities'.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Predominantly medical, with 'ASD patients' used throughout and 'recovery progress' appearing in the discussion of what current systems cannot track - a framing that treats autism as something one recovers from. Against this, the introduction opens with a genuinely thoughtful question about what social robots are for, asking whether robots might help people 'establish richer relationships with other humans, fulfilling their inherent empathic potential', and framing the issue as most pressing for 'individuals who are prevented by clinical factors from establishing typical social relations with others'. The clinical reasoning is also person-centred in a practical way: the authors note that assessment is usually done at enrolment and repeated occasionally, that more frequent assessment would let therapists adapt treatment and would help 'patients and their parents ... be better motivated to withstand long, repetitive therapy sessions', and that success depends on knowing which stimuli hold a particular child's attention. That is an argument for measurement in service of individualised therapy rather than for classification, and it is why the study has no diagnostic target. No autistic person is reported as involved in the design.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Age is reported as a mean with standard deviation and severity as a CARS2 eligibility range, both of which exceed the corpus norm. Sex is not a variable, since all eleven participants are male. What is absent is cognitive and language measurement: the verbal-response criterion is a functional floor rather than an assessed level, so the children's language ability is bounded below and not otherwise characterised, and no IQ, adaptive or developmental measure was obtained. Since the outcome is attention during a verbally mediated robot interaction, and the sound-response component of the score is a speech-latency measure, language ability is directly implicated in the measurement and is unmeasured. No socioeconomic, ancestry or comorbidity information is reported.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Clinical diagnosis established through the recruiting hospital, with severity quantified by CARS2 and reported as a 30-36.5 range for all participants. This is genuine clinical ascertainment, and specifying the severity band is a real strength - it makes the population interpretable in a way that a bare 'diagnosed with ASD' does not, and it bounds the claims to children with mild-to-moderate presentation. What is not reported is the instrument set beyond CARS2, the assessors, or the dates. Because the study makes no diagnostic claim, the reference standard's role here is to define the population rather than to serve as a target, and for that purpose it is adequate.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: CARS2 is used as an eligibility range rather than as a per-child variable, so no severity gradient is available for analysis - a missed opportunity, since relating attention trajectories to baseline severity across six children in a seven-week course would have been the natural individualisation question and the data existed to ask it. The study's own outcome measure, the automated attention score, functions as a repeated within-child measure and is used that way: its whole design rationale is that assessment could be 'repeated more frequently to trace the severity and development of symptoms'. That is a severity-tracking argument, and it is the clearest statement in this review of why continuous behavioural measurement might matter clinically for reasons other than diagnosis.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The aim is a robot-mediated therapy and assessment system that measures a child's attention automatically, adapts its own interaction scenario to that measurement, and thereby increases engagement over a course of sessions. Two results are reported. The automated attention score agreed with the treating therapist's assessment on 28 of 34 sessions, giving 82.4%, which the conclusion describes accurately as 'matching over 80% of therapist assessments'. And attention scores rose across a seven-week course in most of the six children who continued, from which the authors draw an explicitly hypothetical conclusion - 'our hypothesis is that a properly designed robot intervention system can increase the attention levels'. Neither claim concerns autism detection: all participants are autistic, there is no comparison group, and no classification is attempted. For this review the study contributes a different kind of evidence - a demonstration that an automated behavioural measure can track a clinician's judgement of the same construct well enough to be usable in a therapy loop, which is the closed-loop application that most of the corpus's detection-oriented work does not consider.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: An autism rehabilitation centre, with participants recruited from Al Ain Hospital - a clinical service setting, and the same setting in which the system would be deployed. That alignment between study setting and intended use setting is shared by only a few studies in this review. The clinical framing is specific: the authors note that assessment is typically performed at enrolment and repeated during long-term therapy, and that if it 'could be repeated more frequently to trace the severity and development of symptoms, then therapists could implement more efficacious diagnostic and therapeutic options' - so the setting defines the problem, which is the cost in expert time of repeated assessment.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A semi-autonomous adaptive scenario in 13 sections, delivered by a NAO robot with a mobile phone mounted on a purpose-built chest holder that displays facial expressions through an Emotions Selector application, presenting emotional cues and soliciting emotional responses. The paradigm's distinctive property is that it is closed-loop: the scenario adapts across sessions according to each child's attention score history, so the measurement feeds back into the intervention. No other study in this review implements that loop - the rest measure behaviour and stop. The engineering description is also careful in a way that matters practically: the chest mount was designed so that the added weight 'barely affects the center of mass of the robot body, hence the changes in the moment of inertia are negligible', preserving the robot's balance and its built-in interactive behaviours, which is the kind of detail that determines whether a modified platform actually works in a clinic. What is not reported is the session duration or the content of the 13 sections, so the paradigm cannot be reproduced from the paper.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Longitudinal in design - a seven-week course of sessions per child, with 34 sessions contributing to the agreement analysis - which distinguishes it from the almost uniformly cross-sectional remainder of this review. Repeated measurement within children is the study's methodological point rather than an incidental feature. Ethics reporting is complete: approval by the Social Sciences Research Ethical Committee of UAE University and by Al Ain Hospital, with signed parental consent letters. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text. Attrition is substantial and unexplained: 6 of 11 children completed the long-term study.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: An Aldebaran/SoftBank NAO robot with a custom-designed chest mount holding a mobile phone, the phone camera configured as an IP camera through a mobile application, and Haar cascade classifiers performing face and ear detection at approximately 1 Hz. The design point worth recording is that the sensing is the robot's own - the camera that measures the child is mounted on the thing the child is attending to - so the measurement apparatus and the social stimulus are the same object. That is more elegant than the arrangements charted elsewhere in this review, where a separate camera observes a child interacting with something else, and it means the face-detection geometry directly encodes orientation toward the robot. The cost is that the measure is only as good as the assumption behind it, and a low-frame-rate Haar cascade detecting a face is a coarse proxy for attending.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong on the system and incomplete on the study. Reported: eligibility criteria including the CARS2 band and the verbal-response requirement, mean age with standard deviation, recruitment site, both ethics approvals, the parental consent procedure, the robot and the custom chest-mount with its mass-distribution justification, the phone-as-IP-camera configuration, the detector types, all three scoring rules with their exact constants (+5, -1, +15 and a linear latency function), the 1 Hz update rate, the 13-section scenario structure, the adaptive personalisation mechanism, the number of sessions in the agreement analysis and the exact number of mismatches, and a practical failure mode with its fix. Not reported: session duration, the content of the 13 sections, why 5 of 11 children did not continue, the therapist rating procedure and its reliability, funding and competing interests. A reader could rebuild the scoring system and could not reproduce the study.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The introduction contains an unusually clear analysis of the field's constraints, which functions as a limitations discussion of the wider literature: most preprogrammed robot systems 'have fixed behavior (i.e., they are unable to autonomously perform adaptable closed-loop interactions), are not tailored to the individual needs of patients, and cannot keep track of their recovery progress', while adaptive systems 'need high-performance hardware, such as GPUs chips, to process real-time data' and 'are not yet reliable outside controlled research' settings. The discussion reports a practical failure - children handling the chest display in early sessions, depressing scores, addressed by fixing the display - and the causal claim about attention improvement is labelled a hypothesis. What is not addressed: there is no control condition, so the seven-week rise in attention scores cannot be separated from familiarisation with the robot, task practice, maturation or study attention, and the score's own components would be expected to rise as a child grows comfortable with the apparatus. Attrition of 5 of 11 children is unexplained, and if disengagement drove it then the trend is computed on the children who were already engaging. The 82.4% agreement is computed over sessions clustered within children with no adjustment, no chance-corrected statistic and no confidence interval, and no reliability estimate exists for the therapist ratings serving as the standard. Scoring constants are operator-set per child, so scores are not comparable across children. And equating a detected face with attending is a strong assumption for children who may attend without orienting.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: The authors propose sharing assessment data 'locally, within the same team or clinic, or globally as integrated clinical dataset sharable by professionals in different places through interoperable systems', and continued development of semi-autonomous adaptive robots that recognise behavioural cues and respond accordingly. The steps the study most needs are a control condition to separate intervention effect from familiarisation, an account of attrition, a chance-corrected agreement statistic with clustering adjustment, and reliability data for the therapist ratings.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Attention and engagement, decomposed into three operationally defined components with explicit rules. Face attention: orientation toward the robot's chest display, detected by Haar cascade, scoring +5 when the face is detected and -1 when it is not. Joint attention: a head turn matching the robot's directed gaze, detected through left or right ear detection, scoring +15 - the largest weight in the system, and appropriately so, since joint attention is the more specific construct. Sound response: latency from prompt to vocal response, converted by a fixed linear formula. The construct choice is well matched to the clinical purpose the paper sets out, which is not diagnosis but therapy targeting: the authors argue that 'one of the most important preconditions for the success of these interventions is the knowledge and availability of the kinds of stimuli that usually draw the attention of the child and increase his or her engagement over time'. Attention is what a therapist needs to know moment by moment to steer a session, and it is the quantity the system measures and feeds back. The weakness is the operationalisation of face detection as attention, which equates orienting with attending and will misclassify a child who listens without looking.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Three streams combined into one running score - face detection, ear-based head orientation, and speech-response latency - fused by weighted accumulation with operator-set constants rather than by a learned combiner. The weights encode a clinical judgement about relative importance (joint attention worth three times face attention, non-attention penalised lightly), which is transparent and adjustable but not empirically derived. No ablation examines what each stream contributes to the 82.4% agreement, which would have been informative about whether the joint-attention component - the most clinically specific and the hardest to detect from ear cascades - is carrying its weight.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: No model is trained. The system is rule-based throughout: off-the-shelf Haar cascade classifiers perform face and ear detection as measurement infrastructure, and the attention score is accumulated by hand-specified increments with operator-adjustable constants. There is no training set, test set, cross-validation or fitted parameter anywhere. For a review of computational approaches this is a useful boundary case, because it shows what can be achieved without learning: a transparent, adjustable, real-time measure that tracks a clinician's judgement on 82.4% of sessions and closes a therapy loop. The corresponding limitation is that the constants are asserted rather than derived, so the score's calibration rests on the operator's judgement rather than on evidence.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A scalar attention score accumulated at approximately 1 Hz across a session, with session-level trends used both for the agreement analysis and for adapting the next session's scenario. Every increment is traceable to a detection event and a stated constant.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: One agreement figure - 82.4%, from 6 mismatches in 34 sessions against the therapist's 0-100 attention ratings - plus session-by-session attention scores for the longitudinal arm. The metric is the right kind for the claim, since concurrent agreement with a clinician's judgement of the same construct is what a therapy-support measure needs to demonstrate, and the paper describes it correctly as matching therapist assessments rather than as diagnostic accuracy. Three gaps: no chance-corrected statistic such as Cohen's kappa, so the proportion of agreement attributable to the marginal distribution of therapist ratings is unknown; no adjustment for the clustering of 34 sessions within 6 children; and no reliability estimate for the therapist ratings themselves, so the achievable ceiling is unknown.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Complete and by design. Every component of the score is a stated rule with a stated constant, adjustable per child by the operator, so a therapist can read the derivation of any score directly and can tune the measure to a particular patient. Against the learned models charted throughout this review, this is the opposite design point: nothing is fitted, so nothing requires post-hoc explanation, and the trade-off is that calibration is asserted rather than derived. For a system intended to run inside a clinical session and inform a therapist's next move, that trade is defensible.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Not applicable in the classification sense - no model is trained, no individual is assigned a class, and no autism prediction is attempted. The relevant validation question is whether the automated attention measure tracks the construct it claims to measure, and the study answers it with concurrent validation against an independent human standard: agreement with the treating therapist's 0-100 attention ratings on 28 of 34 sessions, reported as 82.4%. That is the right design for the claim and it is described accurately, with the conclusion stating that the system matches 'over 80% of therapist assessments' rather than presenting the figure as diagnostic performance. Four qualifications bound it. The 34 sessions come from 6 children and are therefore clustered, with no adjustment reported, so the effective sample is closer to 6 than to 34. No chance-corrected agreement statistic is given, so how much of the 82.4% reflects the marginal distribution of the therapist's ratings is unknown. No reliability estimate exists for those ratings, so the ceiling on achievable agreement is unknown - and a measure agreeing 82.4% with a standard of unknown reliability could be tracking either the construct or that particular therapist. And the scoring constants are operator-adjustable per child, which is clinically sensible but means the score is not a fixed instrument and its agreement with a clinician may partly reflect tuning. The separate longitudinal claim - that attention rose across seven weeks - has no control condition at all, so it cannot be separated from familiarisation with a novel robot, practice on a repeated task, maturation, or the attention of being in a study; and with 5 of 11 children not completing and no reason given, the trend is computed on a self-selected subgroup. The authors label the causal claim a hypothesis, which is the correct standing for it.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: Autism, Robotics, Assessment, Attention, Therapy. Accurate and complete - naming the population, the technology, the purpose, the construct and the application. Unusually, the keyword set correctly signals that the study is about assessment within therapy rather than about diagnosis, which is not true of several titles in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: International Journal of Social Robotics 13:67-82, 2021; accepted 25 February 2020, published online 6 March 2020. A social robotics venue, and the article reads accordingly - the system engineering, the chest-mount mass distribution, the detector configuration and the scoring rules are all specified precisely, while the clinical evaluation carries no control condition, no chance-corrected agreement statistic and no account of attrition. The venue's orientation also explains the study's most valuable feature, the closed measurement-intervention loop, which is a robotics design idea rather than a clinical-trial one.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2021 by a group at United Arab Emirates University with Al Ain Hospital, and collaborators at RIKEN, the University of New South Wales, Western Sydney University and the University of Malaya. The framing separates it from most of this corpus: the problem identified is not detection but the cost of repeated assessment during therapy - assessment 'is typically performed at the time of enrollment and repeated during long-term therapy to measure progress', and if it 'could be repeated more frequently to trace the severity and development of symptoms, then therapists could implement more efficacious diagnostic and therapeutic options, and patients and their parents would be better motivated to withstand long, repetitive therapy sessions'. For this review the study contributes three things that the detection-oriented literature does not. It closes the loop: the automated attention measure feeds back into the interaction scenario, which adapts to each child's score history across sessions, so measurement serves intervention rather than terminating in a classification - no other study in the corpus implements this. It demonstrates what is achievable without any learned model: three transparent rules with operator-adjustable constants, running at 1 Hz on a phone camera mounted to the robot the child is attending to, agreeing with the treating therapist's judgement on 28 of 34 sessions. And it is longitudinal, tracking six children across a seven-week course, in a corpus that is otherwise almost entirely cross-sectional. Its evidential weight is nonetheless limited in ways that should be stated: there is no comparison group and no control condition, so the observed rise in attention cannot be separated from familiarisation, practice or maturation; 5 of 11 children did not complete and no reason is given; the 82.4% is an uncorrected agreement rate over sessions clustered within six children, against a therapist standard of unknown reliability; and the population is narrow - male, mild to moderate, verbally capable - despite the abstract describing the target as children with minimal verbal capabilities. The authors' own restraint is worth noting: the causal claim is presented as a hypothesis, and the system is positioned as a tool for therapists rather than as a diagnostic instrument.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Farooqi N; Bukhari F; Iqbal W
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2021 International Conference on Frontiers of Information Technology (FIT)
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Children with autism under 12 (stated elsewhere as under 10)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Questionnaire and caregiver report
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Create the first autism prediction dataset and model for Pakistan, a country the authors state does not track or report its autism cases, and to identify commonly co-occurring background factors so that 'appropriate lifestyle changes can be made accordingly'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification on a purpose-collected questionnaire dataset
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Single questionnaire completion per child
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: No behavioural task. A 21-item questionnaire administered in paper form at a private autism school and via Google Forms elsewhere, covering the child's sex, age and birth order; maternal pregnancy and delivery normality, prematurity, and oxygen supplementation in the first month; family history of cognitive disability; early behaviours (crib rocking, suspected deafness, insistence on particular music, reaction to bright lights, colours or unusual sounds); developmental milestones (age of independent walking, age of first words); parental education; and maternal vaccination, miscarriage history, smoking, antidepressant use and alcohol or drug use during or before pregnancy
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: The Child Psychiatry Department at Mayo Hospital, Lahore - described as the only government-run child psychiatry department in Pakistan, seeing on average two patients daily - and a private school for autistic children in Lahore
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None reported. Children are described as having autism spectrum disorder by virtue of attending a specialist school or the hospital's child psychiatry department, with no instrument, criteria, clinician or date given. The final questionnaire column is simply 'ASD diagnosed' answered yes or no
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Under 12 in the abstract, under 10 in the methods - the two statements are inconsistent
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Not reported numerically; a histogram is shown but no counts given
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported, though family history of cognitive disability is one of the questionnaire items
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Not reported for the children; maternal antidepressant use during pregnancy is a questionnaire item
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not described. No screening, assessment or recruitment source is given for the comparison group
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 100, collected 'to ensure that our model is trained without any class imbalance problem'
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not addressed. No ages are reported for either group and no matching is described or tested
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed. No sex counts are reported for either group
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted as 'healthy' with no basis stated
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Caregiver questionnaire responses
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Responses were encoded as binary values where items had two options, and one-hot encoded where items had more. Three feature-selection schemes were then applied: SelectKBest with k = 17, chosen because 'it gave the best results'; a variance threshold of 0.8, discarding any feature where 80% of values were identical; and SelectFromModel using importance weights
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Paper questionnaires and Google Forms for collection; Python with scikit-learn for modelling
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Yes - a 200-child questionnaire dataset described as the first of its kind for Pakistan; no release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Caregiver-reported clinical, developmental and family history including maternal substance use during pregnancy - sensitive material about identifiable families. No ethics committee approval, consent procedure, anonymisation policy or data governance statement appears anywhere in the paper
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Categorical and ordinal questionnaire responses
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Twenty-one items falling into three groups that differ fundamentally in kind. Child behaviour and development, six items: crib rocking as a baby, whether the child was ever thought to be nearly deaf, insistence on particular music, reaction to bright lights, colours or unusual sounds in the first year, age of independent walking, age of first words. Perinatal and birth history, five items: pregnancy normality, delivery normality, prematurity, oxygen in the first month, birth order. Parental and family background, eight items: family history of cognitive disability, paternal and maternal education, maternal vaccination during pregnancy, miscarriage history, parental smoking, maternal antidepressant use, parental alcohol or drug use. Plus sex and age. Only the first group constitutes behavioural data even in reported form
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Binary and one-hot encoding; scikit-learn SelectKBest, VarianceThreshold and SelectFromModel
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Only implicitly, through which features the three selection methods retained; the retained sets are never listed
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: SelectKBest score function, variance thresholding and model-based importance weights, with no results reported for any of them
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None named. The paper does not state which of the 21 items any selection method retained, so the substantive question of which factors predict the label is never answered despite being the stated aim
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reported only as a list of narrative observations in the conclusion, and reported for the autistic group alone with no comparison against the control group: that autism was 'quite often found in firstborns and males rather than females'; that around 50% of autistic children had a family member with a cognitive disability; that 'physically, it is observed that children with autism develop just like children without autism'; that most were considered deaf in early childhood and reacted to bright lights and loud sounds; that 'most of the mothers were vaccinated during pregnancies and had normal deliveries'; and that 'almost 50 percent of the parents smoked before giving birth to children with autism'. None of these is accompanied by a control-group rate, a base rate, a statistical test or an effect size, so none supports the comparative reading its phrasing invites
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Classical supervised classification on tabular questionnaire data
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Gaussian naive Bayes, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression, decision tree, random forest, support vector machine, AdaBoost, gradient boosting and XGBoost - each run under all three feature-selection schemes
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A single 80/20 train-test split, giving a test set of 40 children. No cross-validation, no repetition over alternative splits and no held-out tuning set. Feature selection was performed on the data with SelectKBest's k set to 17 explicitly because 'it gave the best results', so the selection parameter was tuned against the reported outcome. Twenty-seven algorithm-by-selection combinations were evaluated and the maximum reported
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy for all 27 combinations, plus a confusion matrix for each of the nine algorithms under SelectKBest and ROC curves. Sensitivity and specificity are said to have been calculated from the confusion matrices but their values are not tabulated
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Best accuracy 95% - achieved by random forest and SVM under SelectKBest, random forest and XGBoost under variance thresholding, and SVM and gradient boosting under SelectFromModel. The remaining cells range from 90% to 92.5%. Confusion matrices under SelectKBest show test sets of 40: random forest and SVM each gave 18 true positives, 2 false negatives, 0 false positives and 20 true negatives, corresponding to 90% sensitivity and 100% specificity
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A 21-item caregiver questionnaire administered to 100 autistic and 100 non-autistic children in Lahore supported classification at 95% accuracy across several algorithms, with the best confusion matrices showing 90% sensitivity and 100% specificity on a 40-child test set. The paper's stated broader aim - identifying 'common causes leading up to' autism - is not met: no feature importances are reported, no comparison against the control group accompanies any of the descriptive observations, and the listed observations about maternal vaccination and parental smoking are single-group frequencies presented without base rates or tests.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None established. The narrative observations are single-group frequencies with no control comparison, and the selected feature sets are never disclosed
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Expand the dataset; develop a mobile application for clinicians; maintain historical data and raise mental health awareness; and strengthen correlations between traits with more data. The authors also state that the model 'should be used with care and under supervision of some professional' and that 'this is a local dataset which should not be applied elsewhere in the world without consultation'
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: This record sits at the edge of the review's behavioral-data criterion and is retained with that qualification recorded. Only about six of its 21 items concern the child's behaviour - crib rocking, suspected deafness, music insistence, sensory reactivity, walking age and first-words age - and all are retrospective caregiver recollections rather than measured behaviour; the remainder are perinatal history, family history and parental background variables. That distinction matters for the synthesis, because it separates this study from the corpus's directly instrumented work in a way accuracy figures obscure. The paper's genuine contribution is infrastructural and is honestly framed: it documents that Pakistan does not track autism cases, that the country's only government-run child psychiatry department sees on average two patients a day, and that no data existed in any storable format, so the dataset had to be built from nothing. The closing caution that 'this is a local dataset which should not be applied elsewhere in the world without consultation' is more scoping discipline than most of the corpus offers. The methodological problems are nonetheless severe. Validation is a single 80/20 split producing a 40-child test set with no cross-validation or repetition, so a single case is worth 2.5 accuracy points and the spread from 90% to 95% is two children; SelectKBest's k was set to 17 explicitly because it gave the best results; and the maximum is reported across 27 algorithm-by-selection cells. No diagnostic instrument is reported for the autistic group and no screening at all for the comparison group, whose recruitment source is never stated. No ages, sexes or matching are reported for either group despite sex, age and birth order being model features - which means the classifier may be separating groups on demographics the study does not describe. No ethics approval or consent procedure appears, for data including maternal substance use and psychiatric medication during pregnancy. Most seriously for a paper intended to inform families, the conclusions list 'most of the mothers were vaccinated during pregnancies' and 'almost 50 percent of the parents smoked before giving birth to children with autism' among observations about autism, with no control-group rate, no base rate and no statistical test - phrasing that invites a causal reading the data cannot support and that is particularly hazardous in the case of vaccination. The stated aim of visualising 'common causes' is not achieved: the selected feature sets are never disclosed and no importance analysis is reported.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 100 children each: 100 autistic children recruited from the Child Psychiatry Department at Mayo Hospital Lahore and a private autism school, and 100 children described as healthy whose recruitment source is never stated. The comparison group was collected specifically 'to ensure that our model is trained without any class imbalance problem', so its purpose is stated as statistical rather than clinical. No other-diagnosis comparison group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with autism', 'autistic children', 'ASD individuals', 'healthy children'. The comparison group is 'healthy', and autism is introduced as 'a severe condition related to brain development that impairs communication and interaction with others'. The framing is disease-oriented, and the stated purpose of identifying 'common causes leading up to it so that appropriate lifestyle changes can be made accordingly' implies modifiable aetiology in a way the design cannot support.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Essentially none. No ages, means, standard deviations, sex counts or matching statistics are reported for either group. The age eligibility is stated inconsistently - under 12 in the abstract and under 10 in the methods. Sex, age and birth order are model features while remaining undescribed at group level, so the classifier's reliance on demographic separation cannot be assessed. Histograms of the distributions are presented as figures but no counts are given in text or table. No socioeconomic data beyond parental education, which is itself a model feature.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None. The autistic group is defined by recruitment from a child psychiatry department or a specialist school, with no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or date reported anywhere. The comparison group has no stated screening or source. The label is simply a questionnaire field, 'ASD diagnosed', answered yes or no. This is the weakest ascertainment among included records, and it is consequential because the entire study is a supervised classification of that label.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No severity, cognitive, language or adaptive measure. Family history of cognitive disability is collected as a predictor rather than as a characterisation.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: build the first autism prediction model for Pakistan from a purpose-collected questionnaire and identify commonly associated background factors. Main findings: 95% best accuracy across several algorithm-and-selection combinations, with 90% sensitivity and 100% specificity in the best confusion matrices on a 40-child test set; and a set of narrative single-group observations about birth order, sex, family history, sensory reactivity, maternal vaccination and parental smoking, none accompanied by control comparison or statistical test.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: The Child Psychiatry Department at Mayo Hospital Lahore, described as the only government-run child psychiatry department in Pakistan and seeing on average two patients daily, together with a private school for autistic children in Lahore. Questionnaires were administered on paper at the school and via Google Forms otherwise. No setting is described for the comparison group.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: No behavioural task and no observation of any kind. All data are caregiver responses to a 21-item questionnaire, most of it retrospective - the age at which a child first walked or spoke, whether they rocked in a crib as a baby, whether they were ever thought deaf, and maternal behaviours during a pregnancy that occurred years earlier. Recall accuracy for such items is known to be limited and to differ systematically between parents of diagnosed and undiagnosed children, since a diagnosis reframes recollection of early development. The paper does not address recall bias.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; a single questionnaire per family with no follow-up, though the items ask retrospectively about the perinatal period and early childhood. Data include maternal substance use, antidepressant use and miscarriage history - sensitive material about identifiable families collected partly through a commercial web form. No ethics committee approval, consent procedure, anonymisation policy or data-handling statement appears anywhere in the paper.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Paper questionnaires and Google Forms for collection; Python with scikit-learn for encoding, feature selection and classification. No hardware, versions, seeds or hyperparameters are reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Poor. Reported: the full 21-item questionnaire with each item's type and wording, the encoding scheme, the three feature-selection methods with their parameters, the nine algorithms with brief descriptions, the 80/20 split ratio, a complete 27-cell accuracy table, and confusion matrices for all nine algorithms under one selection scheme. Absent: any diagnostic instrument, ethics approval, group demographics, recruitment source for the comparison group, the identity of features retained by any selection method, all hyperparameters, the random seed, sensitivity and specificity values despite being said to have been computed, and any data or code. The questionnaire itself is the one element documented well enough to be reused.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged: the dataset should be enlarged for reliability; the model 'should be used with care and under supervision of some professional'; and 'this is a local dataset which should not be applied elsewhere in the world without consultation'. The last two are genuine scoping cautions that most of the corpus omits. Not acknowledged: no diagnostic instrument for either group; a single 80/20 split with a 40-child test set and no cross-validation; SelectKBest's k tuned to give the best results; the maximum reported across 27 cells; no group demographics despite sex, age and birth order being model features; no ethics approval; recall bias in retrospective caregiver report, which differs systematically between parents of diagnosed and undiagnosed children; and, most consequentially, the presentation of single-group frequencies about maternal vaccination and parental smoking as observations about autism without any control comparison or base rate.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Expand the dataset; build a mobile application for clinicians; maintain historical records and raise mental health awareness; and strengthen trait correlations with more data. The authors add two cautions that function as recommendations - that the model requires professional supervision in use, and that the dataset is local and should not be transferred to other populations without consultation.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: No behaviour is observed. Six of 21 items concern the child's behaviour as recalled by a caregiver - crib rocking, suspected deafness, insistence on particular music, reaction to bright lights, colours or unusual sounds, age of walking and age of first words - which together sample early sensory reactivity, repetitive movement and developmental milestone timing. The remaining fifteen items are perinatal, familial and parental variables that are not behavioural at all. This composition is the principal reason the record sits at the boundary of the review's scope and should be distinguished in the per-group analysis from directly instrumented behavioural studies.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No multimodal fusion. What the study does combine is heterogeneous variable types within one questionnaire - child behaviour, perinatal history, family history and parental lifestyle - but no analysis separates their contributions, no feature importances are reported, and the retained feature sets under each selection scheme are never disclosed. Since the design's stated purpose is to identify which factors matter, this omission removes the paper's principal claimed contribution: a reader cannot tell whether classification rests on the developmental items, on demographics such as sex and birth order, or on parental background variables.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Nine classifiers spanning probabilistic, instance-based, linear, tree, ensemble and kernel families, each described in a sentence with no rationale for inclusion and no hyperparameters. Breadth substitutes for justification. That six of the 27 cells reach 95% while the rest cluster between 90% and 92.5% - a spread of two test cases - indicates the comparison is not resolving real differences between algorithms.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Twenty-one questionnaire items binary- or one-hot-encoded, reduced by three alternative selection schemes. The representation is transparent and the questionnaire is fully documented, which makes it reproducible as an instrument even though the analysis is not. The critical gap is that the outcome of selection is never reported: SelectKBest retained 17 of the features, but which 17 is not stated, and the variance-threshold and model-based schemes likewise report no retained sets.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy for all 27 combinations, confusion matrices for nine algorithms under one scheme, and ROC curves. Providing the confusion matrices is what allows sensitivity and specificity to be derived - random forest and SVM both achieve 18 of 20 autistic children detected with all 20 comparison children correctly classified - even though the paper states these were calculated but does not tabulate them. Missing: confidence intervals, any statistical comparison, and any acknowledgement that a 40-child test set makes each case worth 2.5 accuracy points.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: The paper's stated aim includes helping 'visualize common causes leading up to' autism, and interpretability is therefore central to its purpose - but no interpretability analysis is performed. No feature importances, no selected feature lists, no coefficients, no decision rules. What is offered instead is a list of narrative observations in the conclusion, each a frequency within the autistic group presented without the corresponding control-group frequency. Two of these are actively hazardous as written: 'most of the mothers were vaccinated during pregnancies' and 'almost 50 percent of the parents smoked before giving birth to children with autism' both appear in a list introduced as observations about autism, in a paper whose abstract promises to identify causes so that lifestyle changes can be made. Without a comparison rate these statements are uninformative, and in the vaccination case the juxtaposition risks reinforcing a well-documented and thoroughly refuted misattribution.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The weakest element. A single 80/20 split of 200 children gives a 40-child test set, with no cross-validation, no repetition across splits and no separate tuning set. SelectKBest's k was chosen as 17 'as it gave the best results', which tunes a selection parameter against the reported evaluation. Twenty-seven algorithm-by-selection combinations were evaluated and the maximum quoted in the abstract. There is no independent cohort, no external validation and no confidence interval, so the reported 95% cannot be distinguished from the 90% cells by anything the paper provides.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: autism, autism spectrum disorder, machine learning, predictive analysis, ASD. Four of five are generic; 'predictive analysis' is the operative framing and signals an aetiological ambition the design does not support.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: 2021 International Conference on Frontiers of Information Technology (FIT), pages 305-309 - a general computing conference with no clinical remit.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021. The framing is about data absence rather than methodological gap, and on that point it is informative and specific. The authors note that 'no reliable epidemiological data on the prevalence of autism exists' for South Asia, that Pakistan does not track or report autism cases, that the country's only government-run child psychiatry department averages two patients a day, and that 'even in that department, no such reasonable measures have been taken to store data in any format', so data 'had to be collected from scratch'. That account of health-system data infrastructure is a genuine contribution to the corpus's picture of where this research happens and under what constraints, and it distinguishes the paper's problem from the throughput and objectivity arguments that dominate elsewhere. The scientific execution does not match the framing: the stated aim of identifying causes for lifestyle modification is beyond what a 200-child cross-sectional questionnaire without diagnostic ascertainment can address, and the conclusions drawn from it are single-group frequencies presented without comparison.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Asgari M; Chen L; Fombonne E
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: School-age children and adolescents with autism and fluent speech
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Speech and vocalisation (prosody)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Convert clinically recognised but unquantified prosodic abnormality into fine-grained automated measurement. The motivating observation is precise: only one ADOS-2 Module 3 item rates speech abnormalities at all, scoring intonation, volume, rhythm and rate together on a 0-2 scale where an abnormal score 'represents a composite of abnormal features crudely lumped together'; only one SRS item touches voice quality; and DSM-5 makes no reference to speech or voice quality in any of its seven diagnostic criteria
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification using speech extracted from a standardised diagnostic assessment, with an IQ-matched subsample replication
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One ADOS-2 administration per participant, with speech drawn from four conversational tasks within it
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Four purely conversational ADOS-2 Module 3 tasks, selected because they 'do not require objects, books or images': emotions conversation, social difficulties and annoyance conversation, friends and marriage conversation, and loneliness conversation. All occur in the second half of the administration and focus on the participant's understanding of emotions and social relationships, with preset open-ended interview questions and discretionary follow-up probes to maintain conversational flow
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Oregon Health and Science University, with participants recruited by community outreach and referrals from OHSU specialised clinics into a neuroimaging study; ADOS-2 sessions were videotaped and the recordings reused for this analysis
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Among the most thorough in the corpus. Diagnosis confirmed under DSM-5 by a research diagnostic team comprising an experienced child psychiatrist and a clinical psychologist, using best-estimate procedures after review of standardised diagnostic assessments including both videos and scored protocols. ADOS-2 Module 3 administered by research assistants or a senior clinical psychologist trained to research reliability. ADI-R administered to caregivers of the autistic group by trained interviewers and integrated into the best-estimate procedure. Autism was actively ruled out in the comparison group on the basis of ADOS-2 and SRS scores supplemented by expert clinical review
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 104 recruited, 90 analysed after 14 exclusions for poor recording quality
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: An unusually extensive exclusion list applied to all groups: seizure disorder, cerebral palsy, paediatric stroke, history of chemotherapy, sensorimotor handicaps, closed head injury, thyroid disorder, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, current major depressive episode, fetal alcohol syndrome, Tourette's disorder, severe vision impairment, Rett's syndrome, current psychoactive medication, and IQ below 70
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Participants currently taking psychoactive medications were excluded, which removes a plausible confound for voice measures that most speech studies leave uncontrolled
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Comprehensively characterised: ADOS-2 Social Affect (9.40 +/- 3.57 vs 1.04 +/- 1.86), Restricted and Repetitive Behavior (3.59 vs 0.52), total (12.99 vs 1.56) and Calibrated Severity Score (7.55 +/- 1.44 vs 1.22 +/- 1.04), plus SRS total t-score (77.35 +/- 10.93 vs 43.96 +/- 4.14), all significantly different. These are used analytically, correlated against the selected voice features
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes, and actively - autism was ruled out using ADOS-2 and SRS scores supplemented by expert clinical review, with comparison-group ADOS-2 totals averaging 1.56 and SRS t-scores 43.96
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes - 10.84 versus 10.96 years, p = 0.807, with race and ethnicity likewise non-significant
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: No, and substantially so: 80.6% male in the autistic group against 40.0% in the comparison group, p < 0.001. This is the study's most serious confound, since pitch is strongly sex-dependent and pitch is one of the two selected features. The authors acknowledge it, calling for replication in samples 'more balanced with respect to IQ and gender composition', but unlike the IQ confound they do not run a matched-subsample check
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Established by ADOS-2, SRS and expert clinical review
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Audio extracted from videotaped ADOS-2 administrations
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Speech segments belonging to each participant were located and grouped within each of four conversational activities. Analysis then proceeded through three cascaded levels. Short-term: speech sliced into 25 ms overlapping frames at 100 frames per second, silence removed by an energy-based detector, voiced and unvoiced frames separated by the harmonic model, and pitch, jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio extracted from voiced frames, with a first-order Markov smoothness constraint and Viterbi decoding applied to the pitch contour. Segment level: frame measures summarised separately across voiced and unvoiced regions by mean, median, variance, minimum and maximum, then augmented with duration and frequency statistics of voiced and unvoiced segments as proxies for speaking rate and fluency. Subject level: segment vectors summarised per activity by the same statistics, then the four activity vectors concatenated into one global feature vector
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Videotaped ADOS-2 recordings; a time-varying harmonic model of speech developed by the authors in prior work on Parkinson's disease and clinical depression; scikit-learn for classification, RobustScaler for feature scaling and RFECV for feature selection
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Speech data from 118 youth drawn from an existing neuroimaging cohort; no release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not stated in the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Audio extracted from videotaped clinical diagnostic assessments - highly sensitive material. Governance is reported: informed written consent or assent obtained from all participants and their parents, with review and approval by the Institutional Review Board of Oregon Health and Science University
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Harmonic-model-derived prosodic measures and standard spectral articulation measures
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Divided deliberately into two conceptual groups. Prosodic: pitch, jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio - all derived from the harmonic model - plus loudness computed as the root mean square of signal amplitude. Articulation: thirteen cepstral coefficients with their first and second time derivatives, plus spectral entropy of the log power spectrum, chosen as a proxy for voicing quality and 'speechiness'. Each is expanded through the three-level summarisation into distributional statistics separately for voiced and unvoiced regions and separately per conversational activity
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Time-varying harmonic model with maximum a posteriori parameter estimation, local smoothing during pitch candidate estimation to prevent octave errors, and Viterbi pitch contour decoding; energy-based silence detection; scikit-learn RFECV
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, through recursive feature elimination with cross-validation, and then followed up with clinical correlation analysis
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: RFECV ranking features by a scoring function and returning an optimal subset; the selected features were then correlated against clinical measures using partial Spearman coefficients adjusted for WISC IQ
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Pitch and loudness together formed the optimal prosodic subset. Both correlated significantly with autism severity as rated by independent informants - pitch against ADOS-2 CSS (-0.312) and SRS t-score (-0.264), loudness against ADOS-2 CSS (0.324) and SRS (0.323) - and with language profile, though loudness was unrelated to the SIDI pragmatic index (r = -0.170, p = 0.13)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reported with distributions and a two-dimensional visualisation. Pitch values were lower in autistic participants with comparable dispersion across groups, while loudness means exceeded those of comparison participants across all four ADOS-2 tasks and with much larger variability. The lower-pitch finding runs against a substantial part of the prosody literature, which more often reports elevated pitch and greater pitch variability in autism, and the paper does not comment on the discrepancy - a notable omission given that the comparison group is 60% female against the autistic group's 19%, and that female voices have higher fundamental frequency
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Regularised linear classification on harmonically derived speech features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Linear-kernel support vector machine with L1-norm regularisation, selected because it outperformed the non-linear alternative and because L1 assigns zero weights to uninformative coefficients; features scaled by RobustScaler because 'the range of derived features greatly differed from each other'. A chance classifier randomly assigning participants to classes was run as an explicit baseline
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Five-fold cross-validation with training, development and test sets rotated over the whole dataset, with the authors stating that 'the optimal parameters of SVM models were only learned from the training examples (four out of five sets), totally blinded from the test examples, and the fifth one only used for reporting the performance estimates'.
