Class imbalance was addressed by iterative undersampling: at each iteration 28 autistic participants were drawn at random to match the comparison group, five-fold cross-validation run on the matched sample, and scores accumulated, repeated until convergence at approximately 100 iterations. Ninety-five percent confidence intervals on AUC were computed. A separate IQ-matched subsample analysis paired 28 autistic with 28 comparison participants at equal mean IQ
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: AUC with 95% confidence intervals, sensitivity, specificity and accuracy, reported for each feature group, each conversational activity and each activity combination, all against a chance-classifier baseline
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Prosodic features 82.23% AUC (81.11-83.35), sensitivity 69.67%, specificity 76.83%, accuracy 73.30%. Articulation features alone 67.98% AUC. Combining prosodic and articulation features gave 78.52%, worse than prosody alone. Chance classifier 49.90% (48.17-51.63). By activity, friends and marriage conversation performed best at 83.04% AUC and 74.52% accuracy, then emotions conversation 81.63%, social difficulties 81.21% and loneliness 78.15%; combining activities did not improve on the single best. Critically, on 28 IQ-matched pairs at equal mean IQ of 113.4, friends and marriage conversation gave 77.6% accuracy and 88.27% AUC - higher than in the unmatched sample
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Prosodic voice measures derived from a time-varying harmonic model distinguished autistic from typically developing youth at 82% AUC against a chance baseline of 50%, using speech already captured during routine ADOS-2 administration. Prosody markedly outperformed articulation measures (68%), and combining the two was worse than prosody alone. Conversational context mattered: the friends and marriage conversation alone reached 83% AUC and combining tasks brought no gain, so a single well-chosen sampling context suffices. Recursive feature elimination reduced the prosodic set to pitch and loudness, both of which correlated with autism severity rated independently by a clinician (ADOS-2 CSS) and a parent (SRS) after adjusting for IQ. Most importantly, the result survived an IQ-matched subsample analysis at 88% AUC, addressing the group IQ difference directly.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Lower pitch with comparable dispersion, and higher loudness with substantially greater variability across all conversational contexts
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Replicate in larger samples better balanced for IQ and sex; compare voice-only against language-only analysis on the same participants and test whether combining them improves accuracy, building on the group's parallel natural-language work on ADOS-2 transcripts; develop these measures as outcome measures for treatment research, where the authors note 'a recognized dearth of outcome measures available', requiring longitudinal demonstration that they capture change; and extend voice analysis to preverbal toddlers at risk and to young children with minimal or no language
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The strongest speech study in the corpus on nearly every dimension. Its framing identifies a real and specific gap rather than a generic appeal to objectivity: prosodic abnormality is clinically recognised but measured by exactly one ADOS-2 item that lumps intonation, volume, rhythm and rate onto a 0-2 scale, one SRS item, and no DSM-5 criterion at all - so automated quantification is filling a documented void rather than duplicating existing instruments. The signal-processing contribution is substantive, using a time-varying harmonic model previously validated on Parkinson's disease and depression, with the specific technical justification that standard pitch detectors produce octave errors and lack the time-frequency resolution to capture the fine perturbations characteristic of disordered speech. Diagnostic ascertainment is exemplary - DSM-5 best-estimate by a psychiatrist and psychologist reviewing videos and scored protocols, ADOS-2 by research-reliable administrators, ADI-R, plus active rule-out in the comparison group - and the exclusion list controls seizure disorder, head injury, thyroid disorder, several psychiatric conditions and, critically for voice work, current psychoactive medication. Four analytic practices deserve particular note. A chance classifier is run as an explicit baseline and reported alongside every result, which almost no other study here does. Confidence intervals accompany every AUC. Class imbalance is handled by iterative undersampling repeated to convergence rather than by a single balanced draw. And the IQ confound is not merely acknowledged but tested: a 28-pair IQ-matched subsample reproduced and slightly exceeded the main result, which is the single most convincing robustness check in the corpus. The authors also state without prompting that results 'were not adjusted for multiple comparisons and should be viewed as preliminary'. Two problems remain. The sex imbalance is severe - 80.6% male against 40.0% female, p < 0.001 - and unlike IQ it receives no matched-subsample check, which matters acutely because pitch is one of the two selected features and is strongly sex-dependent; the finding that autistic participants had lower pitch than a comparison group that is 60% female is exactly what sex composition alone would produce, and the paper does not address this or note that lower pitch runs contrary to much of the prosody literature. Second, RFECV feature selection and the choice of the best conversational activity are both made across the reported cross-validation without an outer loop, so the 83% and the pitch-plus-loudness subset carry some selection optimism, though the IQ-matched replication mitigates this for the headline.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups from a single neuroimaging cohort: 104 autistic participants recruited of whom 90 were analysed, and 28 typically developing. All 14 exclusions for poor recording quality came from the autistic group, a differential attrition of 13.5% against 0% that is reported but not discussed - and one that plausibly removes the participants whose speech was hardest to capture, potentially the most severely affected. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The 90:28 imbalance is addressed analytically by repeated undersampling rather than left uncorrected.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'individuals with autism', 'youth with ASD', 'subjects with ASD', 'those with typical development', 'autistic'. Mixed person-first and identity-first, with 'typical development' throughout. The framing is measurement-focused and non-pathologising toward participants - the criticism is directed at instruments, describing the single ADOS-2 speech item as scoring 'a composite of abnormal features crudely lumped together'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Autistic group: 90 participants, 75 male (80.6%), mean age 10.84 +/- 2.20 (7.8-15.3), WISC-IV full-scale IQ 99.0 +/- 20.0. Comparison group: 28 participants, 12 male (40.0%), mean age 10.96 +/- 1.54 (7.0-15.0), IQ 113.4 +/- 12.3. Age, race and ethnicity show no significant difference. Two variables do: sex (p < 0.001) and IQ (p = 0.005). The IQ difference is addressed by a matched-pair replication; the sex difference is acknowledged but not tested. Given that pitch is sex-dependent and is one of the two features retained, and that the comparison group is 60% female against the autistic group's 19%, the sex imbalance is the more consequential of the two. Race is 86% white in both groups, and Hispanic ethnicity 14-18%, so the sample is demographically narrow but balanced.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Exemplary. DSM-5 diagnosis confirmed by a research diagnostic team comprising an experienced child psychiatrist and a clinical psychologist using best-estimate procedures after reviewing both videos and scored protocols of standardised assessments. ADOS-2 Module 3 administered by staff trained to research reliability level. ADI-R administered to caregivers of the autistic group by trained interviewers and integrated into the best-estimate procedure. Autism actively ruled out in comparison participants using ADOS-2 and SRS supplemented by expert clinical review. An extensive medical and psychiatric exclusion list applied to both groups, including current psychoactive medication - a control that matters directly for voice measures and that almost no other speech study in the corpus applies.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: The most complete clinical characterisation of any speech study in the corpus. ADOS-2 Social Affect, Restricted and Repetitive Behavior, total and Calibrated Severity Scores; SRS total t-scores; WISC-IV short-form full-scale IQ from Information, Block Design and Vocabulary subtests; and the Children's Communication Checklist-2 yielding both a General Communication Composite and a Social Interaction Difference Index designed so that more negative values indicate autism. All are reported with group means and p-values, and the ADOS-2 CSS, SRS, GCC and SIDI are used analytically as correlates of the selected voice features, with partial Spearman coefficients adjusted for IQ.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: quantify prosodic abnormality automatically and test whether voice alone predicts diagnosis better than chance, and whether ADOS-2 tasks differ in discriminative value. Main findings: prosodic features reached 82.23% AUC against a 49.90% chance baseline; articulation features alone reached only 67.98% and combining the two was worse than prosody alone; friends and marriage conversation was the single best sampling context at 83.04% with no gain from combining tasks; pitch and loudness formed the optimal subset and both correlated with independently rated severity after IQ adjustment; and an IQ-matched 28-pair subsample reproduced the result at 88.27% AUC.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Oregon Health and Science University, with participants recruited by community outreach and referral from OHSU specialised clinics into a neuroimaging study, and speech extracted from videotaped ADOS-2 administrations conducted as part of that study's screening. IRB approval from OHSU.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Four conversational ADOS-2 Module 3 tasks, chosen on an explicit criterion - they occur in the second half of the administration, 'do not require objects, books or images, and are purely conversational', so speech is elicited without competing manipulative demands. The design's central practical virtue is that no new protocol is required at all: the speech already exists in every videotaped ADOS-2, so the measure is retrofittable to routine assessment. The task-by-task comparison then produces a directly actionable finding - the friends and marriage conversation alone matches or exceeds all four combined, so a shorter sampling context suffices, and the authors note it 'could be selected in circumstances where reducing the false positive rate is required'.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; one ADOS-2 administration per participant with no follow-up, though the stated application as a treatment outcome measure would require longitudinal demonstration that the measures capture change, which the authors identify explicitly. Data are audio from videotaped clinical assessments. Governance is reported: informed written consent or assent from all participants and their parents, who also had to be fluent in English, and IRB review and approval at OHSU.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No dedicated recording equipment - the analysis reuses videotape from ADOS-2 administrations, which is what makes it deployable without protocol change. Analytically it rests on the authors' own time-varying harmonic model, developed to correct two specific failures of standard pitch detection algorithms: octave errors that estimate pitch at half or double its true value, and insufficient time-frequency resolution to capture the fine pitch and amplitude perturbation characteristic of disordered speech. The model is fitted by maximum a posteriori estimation to prevent overfitting from model complexity, and had been previously validated on Parkinson's disease and clinical depression.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Very good. Reported: the four ADOS-2 tasks with the criterion for their selection; the full three-level analysis cascade with frame length, frame rate, silence detection, voiced-unvoiced separation, the Markov smoothness constraint and Viterbi decoding; the summarisation statistics and the decision to summarise voiced and unvoiced regions separately; all feature families with their rationale; the classifier, kernel, regularisation and scaling; the cross-validation structure with explicit statement of how test folds were held blind; the undersampling procedure with its convergence criterion; the confidence interval computation; the RFECV method; the IQ-matched subsample construction; and the complete exclusion criteria list. Missing: SVM hyperparameter values, whether RFECV was nested within folds, data or code release, and the number of speech segments or total audio duration per participant.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Acknowledged directly: 'These results were not adjusted for multiple comparisons and should be viewed as preliminary. They require replication in larger samples, more balanced with respect to IQ and gender composition'. The study is described as a proof of concept and a pilot analysis. The IQ imbalance is not only acknowledged but addressed by a matched-pair replication. Not acknowledged: the sex imbalance receives no matched-subsample check despite being larger and more directly relevant, since pitch is sex-dependent and is one of the two retained features; the finding of lower pitch in autism runs contrary to a substantial part of the prosody literature and this discrepancy is never noted; all 14 exclusions for recording quality came from the autistic group; and RFECV and the choice of best conversational activity were both performed across the reported cross-validation without an outer loop.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Compare voice-only against language-only analysis on the same participants and test whether combining them helps, building on the group's parallel work applying natural language processing to ADOS-2 transcripts from this same sample; develop these measures as treatment outcome measures given 'a recognized dearth of outcome measures available for treatment research in autism', which requires longitudinal demonstration of sensitivity to change; and extend to preverbal toddlers at risk and to young children with minimal or no language, where the authors note identification of atypical voice patterns 'might enhance diagnostic procedures'.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Prosody during naturalistic conversation about emotions and social relationships, decomposed into pitch, cycle-to-cycle frequency perturbation (jitter), cycle-to-cycle amplitude perturbation (shimmer), harmonics-to-noise ratio and loudness, plus articulation indexed by cepstral coefficients and spectral entropy, and fluency indexed by voiced and unvoiced segment durations and counts. The behavioural target is the modulation of voice rather than its content, and the conversational rather than task-based elicitation means the speech is spontaneous.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: The fusion result is negative and cleanly reported: prosodic features alone gave 82.23% AUC, articulation alone 67.98%, and the two combined 78.52% - worse than prosody alone. The authors attribute this to articulation's poorer specificity dragging down the combination, and respond by using prosody alone for all subsequent analyses. A second combination test concerns sampling context rather than feature type: the best single conversational activity (83.04%) matched or exceeded every combination of two, three or four activities, so concatenating more speech did not help. Both results run against the assumption that more data or more feature families improve performance, and both are acted on rather than merely noted.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A single linear SVM with L1 regularisation, chosen after the non-linear variant underperformed and justified by L1's property of zeroing uninformative coefficients - appropriate for a high-dimensional feature space built by summarising frame measures across statistics, regions and activities. The more important modelling decision is the inclusion of an explicit chance classifier that randomly assigns participants, run through the same pipeline and reported in every results table at 49.90% AUC with its own confidence interval. That baseline is what converts the reported figures from numbers into evidence, and its presence distinguishes this study from most of the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A three-level cascade producing a fixed-dimension subject vector from variable-length speech: frame measures at 100 per second, summarised by five distributional statistics separately for voiced and unvoiced regions and augmented with duration statistics, then summarised again per conversational activity, then concatenated across four activities. The separation of voiced from unvoiced regions is a considered choice - 'features extracted from voiced regions tend to differ in nature compared to those from unvoiced regions' - and the per-activity structure is what enables the sampling-context comparison. Recursive elimination then reduces the prosodic set to two interpretable quantities, pitch and loudness.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: AUC with 95% confidence intervals, sensitivity, specificity and accuracy, reported for three feature configurations and seven activity configurations, every one alongside the chance baseline. Reporting confidence intervals on AUC allows the differences between conditions to be assessed - the prosody interval (81.11-83.35) does not overlap the articulation interval (66.62-69.35), so that comparison is supported, while the intervals for the four individual activities largely overlap, so the ranking among them is weaker than the point estimates suggest. Missing: confusion matrices and per-fold variability.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is pursued through three complementary routes. Recursive feature elimination reduces the prosodic set to pitch and loudness, both physically meaningful. Those two are then correlated against four clinical measures using partial Spearman coefficients adjusted for WISC IQ, establishing that both track severity as rated by a professional (ADOS-2 CSS) and independently by a parent (SRS) - the authors note this is 'a noticeable result since it was established with separate informants', which is the right emphasis, since agreement across informant types is stronger evidence than a single-source correlation. Finally, the distributions of both features are plotted by group across all four activities and jointly in a two-dimensional visualisation, showing lower pitch with comparable dispersion and higher loudness with much greater variability in autism. The one interpretive gap is that the direction of the pitch effect is not reconciled with the prosody literature.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Five-fold cross-validation with training, development and test sets rotated and an explicit statement that model parameters were learned only from training examples and were 'totally blinded from the test examples'. Class imbalance is handled by iterative undersampling to 28 per class, repeated until scores converged at around 100 iterations - a substantially more rigorous treatment than a single balanced draw, since it averages away the randomness of which majority-class participants are selected. Confidence intervals are computed on every AUC. The IQ-matched subsample analysis functions as an internal replication under a controlled confound and returns a higher AUC (88.27%) than the main analysis, which is strong evidence that IQ was not driving the result. What remains: RFECV and the best-activity selection were both performed across the same cross-validation used for reporting, with no outer loop; and no independent cohort or external site was tested.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: voice, speech analysis, autism spectrum disorder, harmonic model, prosody, machine learning. 'Harmonic model' is the technical core - the paper's distinctive contribution is a signal-processing method for extracting reliable pitch from quasi-periodic disordered speech, with autism as the application.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Frontiers in Psychology, 12, article 665096, in the Psychology for Clinical Settings section - a psychology venue, with authorship spanning a paediatrics institute on development and disability and departments of psychiatry and paediatrics, which explains the depth of clinical characterisation relative to the modelling.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021. The framing is the most precisely targeted in the corpus. Rather than arguing that clinical assessment is subjective in general, it identifies exactly where prosody falls through the diagnostic net: ADOS-2 Module 3 contains one item rating 'Speech abnormalities associated with autism (Intonation/Volume/Rhythm/Rate)' on a 0-2 scale where an abnormal score 'represents a composite of abnormal features crudely lumped together'; the SRS contains one item on unusual tone of voice; and 'there is no reference to speech or voice quality in any of the 7 diagnostic criteria laid out in' DSM-5. It also identifies a technical rather than clinical obstacle - that existing pitch detection algorithms produce octave errors on quasi-periodic disordered speech and lack the resolution to capture fine perturbation - and addresses it with a model previously validated on other clinical populations. Its account of why prior pitch findings conflict is likewise specific, attributing heterogeneity to variation in voice sampling context, from home recordings to structured caregiver interactions to professional evaluations 'with varying social and cognitive demands', and then testing that account directly by comparing four conversational contexts within one dataset.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Mazumdar P; Arru G; Battisti F
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Children with autism, from the Saliency4ASD benchmark
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking (free viewing of natural images)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Improve on the ICME 2019 Saliency4ASD Grand Challenge baselines by combining features that describe what is in the image with features that describe how it was looked at, rather than modelling scanpaths alone
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Secondary analysis of a public benchmark dataset with a fixed train/test image split, framed as a challenge submission with head-to-head comparison against other entries
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Not reported by this paper - viewing durations are properties of the original Saliency4ASD collection and are not restated
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Free viewing of 400 natural images spanning categories such as animals, buildings and natural scenes. No task instruction, response requirement or interaction is described - the paradigm is inherited wholesale from the benchmark, and the paper's contribution is entirely in feature engineering and classification rather than in data collection
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Not reported - the authors work from released scanpath files and never describe the acquisition setting, which belongs to the original Saliency4ASD collection
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Analysis performed in Italy (Roma Tre University and University of Padova); the participants' country is not stated and is a property of the source dataset
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Not reported anywhere in the paper. The label is taken as given from the dataset - no diagnostic instrument, clinician involvement, or diagnostic criterion is named, and the authors do not cite the source dataset's diagnostic procedure even in passing
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Not reported - a striking omission given that the paper's own Discussion argues at length that fixation behaviour differs between toddlers, children under ten and grown-up children, and concludes that 'age of a person is a very important factor and cannot be generalized for ASD detection'
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported - no ADOS, CARS, SRS or any severity measure
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye-tracking scanpaths (fixation coordinates and durations) paired with the image stimuli
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Thirty features were computed per subject-image pair and grouped into three families. Image content (11 features): YOLO trained on COCO detects objects, the top three highest-confidence bounding boxes are taken as object regions and the remainder as non-object regions, and fixation count, fixation duration, fixation rate and duration rate are computed separately for each region type; plus image coverage from a thresholded fixation heatmap, refixation count, and a saliency weight that combines SDSP saliency values at fixated pixels weighted by fixation duration. Fixations (15 features): total fixation count, total, mean, longest and standard deviation of fixation duration, the index of the longest fixation, fixations per unit duration, mean, minimum, maximum, total and standard deviation of saccadic amplitude, and three region-of-interest features obtained by mean-shift clustering of fixations with a distance threshold of 100. Centre bias (4 features): mean distance between image centre and ROI centres, mean distance of fixations from image centre, number of fixations within 100 pixels of the centre, and total fixation duration near the centre
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: YOLO object detector (9 convolutional plus 2 fully connected layers) trained on COCO; SDSP saliency algorithm, chosen over Itti-Koch, GBVS, BMS and neural approaches such as Salicon, SalGAN and SAM-ResNet explicitly for low computational complexity; mean-shift clustering; MATLAB TreeBagger
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: No - the Saliency4ASD benchmark from the IEEE ICME 2019 Grand Challenge is used unchanged
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes - Saliency4ASD is a public challenge dataset
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not discussed. No ethics statement, consent statement or IRB approval appears anywhere in the paper, which is defensible for secondary analysis of a released benchmark but is never addressed
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Hand-engineered features spanning stimulus content, oculomotor behaviour and spatial bias
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Thirty features in three named families - Cnf1-Cnf11 for image content, Fxf1-Fxf15 for fixation and saccade statistics, Cbf1-Cbf4 for centre bias - each individually defined and tabulated. The design is theory-driven: each family encodes a specific published claim about autistic viewing, namely reduced attention to objects and faces, shorter and fewer fixations with less image coverage, more refixation, and a strong bias toward the image centre independent of where objects are
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: YOLO/COCO for object regions, SDSP for saliency, mean-shift clustering for regions of interest, custom code for the fixation and centre-bias statistics
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No formal importance ranking. Instead the paper conducts a post-hoc diagnostic of which images the model handled best and worst, which serves a similar interpretive purpose
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Best-versus-worst image analysis rather than model-derived importance. For the five images with highest classification accuracy (88.5%) autistic children averaged 213 ms mean fixation duration against 574 ms for typically developing children, whereas for the five worst images (46.2%) the two groups averaged 318 ms and 313 ms respectively - so the feature the model relies on was simply absent as a group difference where the model failed. A follow-up dwell-time analysis binned fixation clusters at the 100 ms and 500 ms thresholds used in the reading literature to index information retention, finding 24% of autistic clusters under 100 ms against 15% for typically developing, and 21% over 500 ms against 35%
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Mean fixation duration (Fxf3) emerges from the error analysis as the feature carrying most of the discriminative load, with performance tracking almost exactly whether that group difference is present in a given image
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Shorter mean fixation durations and a greater proportion of very brief (<100 ms) fixation clusters in autistic children, with typically developing children showing more long (>500 ms) clusters - interpreted as autistic viewers processing less information per fixation
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Bagged decision-tree ensemble on hand-engineered features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: TreeBagger (bootstrap-aggregated random forest), selected after benchmarking 23 classifiers spanning three decision-tree depths, linear discriminant, logistic regression, two naive Bayes variants, six SVM kernels, five nearest-neighbour variants and five ensemble methods. Hyperparameters were tuned by minimising out-of-bag error over minimum leaf size, number of variables per split and number of trees, settling on minLS = 20, numPTS = 19, numTree = 128 at an OOB error of 0.3
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: The Saliency4ASD split of 300 training images and 100 test images, with the same 28 children appearing in both - so the split is by stimulus, not by participant. Hyperparameters were chosen by out-of-bag error on the training portion. The reported results are averaged across the individual scanpath classifications for each test image
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, recall, precision, F1, specificity, false positive rate and false negative rate, reported for the proposed model and all seven competing challenge submissions
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: On the challenge test set RM3ASD reached 0.59 accuracy, 0.68 recall, 0.57 precision, 0.61 F1, 0.50 specificity, 0.49 false positive rate and 0.32 false negative rate - tied for best accuracy with the TU entry (0.59) and ahead of SP-ASDNET (0.55-0.57) and the three UCK variants (0.53-0.55). Specificity of exactly 0.50 on a balanced two-class problem means the model performed at chance on typically developing children. The classifier-selection table in Section 4 reports much higher figures for the same model - TreeBagger 68.5%, medium Gaussian SVM 68.2%, RUSBoosted trees 67.9%, cubic SVM 67.7% - and the Discussion settles on 'at most 60% accuracy'
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Combining what an image contains with how it was looked at gives a modest but competitive classifier: 0.59 accuracy on the Saliency4ASD test set, tied for best among eight challenge entries and ahead of a CNN-LSTM scanpath model. The margin over the field is small and the absolute level is low - specificity was exactly chance - and the authors say so plainly, opening their Discussion with the concession that the model 'can reach at most 60% accuracy in detecting ASDs'. The more informative result is the error analysis: classification succeeded precisely on those images where autistic and typically developing children differed in mean fixation duration (213 versus 574 ms, 88.5% accuracy) and failed where they did not (318 versus 313 ms, 46.2%), which localises the whole effect in one feature and one stimulus-dependent group difference. The Discussion then argues that the feature set should have been conditioned on age, since fixation behaviour differs between toddlers, young children and older children, and the model uses no age information - a limitation the authors identify but cannot address, because the dataset supplies no ages.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Shorter mean fixation durations, more sub-100 ms fixation clusters and fewer clusters exceeding 500 ms in autistic children; the object-versus-non-object and centre-bias features are motivated from prior literature but no direction of effect is reported for them
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Condition feature selection on participant age, since the paper's own review indicates that discriminative viewing features differ for toddlers, children under ten and older children, and the model currently uses no age information; and study the image regions autistic viewers fail to cover, on the argument that what does not attract attention may be more informative than what does
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: An unusually honest paper about an unusually weak result, and valuable to this review for that reason. Where much of the eye-tracking literature reports 90%-plus accuracy from small samples and single splits, this reports 0.59 on a shared benchmark against seven other entries, none of which exceeded 0.59 either - a direct demonstration of what free-viewing scanpath classification actually achieves when the evaluation is standardised and competitive rather than self-administered. The error analysis is the strongest part of the paper: by showing that accuracy tracks whether the fixation-duration group difference exists in a given image, it establishes that the classifier is not learning a stable individual trait but exploiting a stimulus-dependent contrast, which explains both the low ceiling and why performance varies so widely across images. Three problems weigh against it. The unit of analysis is the subject-image pair, not the child: the split is by image with all 28 children in both partitions, and results are averaged over individual scanpath classifications, so the reported numbers are per-scanpath and not per-participant - the paper defines accuracy in terms of '#Subjects' while computing it over scanpaths, which is the same conflation that inflates results elsewhere in this corpus, though here it does not produce an inflated headline. Second, 23 classifiers and three hyperparameters were compared before selecting TreeBagger, and the resulting selection optimism is visible in the gap between the 68.5% in the selection table and the 0.59 on the test set. Third, participant reporting is essentially absent - no ages, no sex distribution, no diagnostic instrument, no severity, no ethics statement - and while much of that is inherited from the benchmark rather than chosen by the authors, they neither restate it from the source publication nor flag its absence, even while their own Discussion argues that age is decisive. That combination, a paper that identifies age as the critical uncontrolled variable while working from a dataset whose ages it never reports, is the clearest illustration in this corpus of what benchmark reuse costs in clinical interpretability.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups from the Saliency4ASD benchmark: 14 autistic children and 14 typically developing children, a balanced 28 in total. Both group sizes are reported, but nothing else about either group is. No other-diagnosis or subthreshold comparison group. The autistic and typically developing children are the same in the training and test partitions - the split is over the 400 images (300 train, 100 test), not over participants.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children affected by Autism Spectrum Disorder', 'ASD children', 'ASDs', 'ASD subjects', 'ASD patients', against 'Typically Developing (TD) kids', 'TDs', 'typically developed subjects'. Consistently person-with-condition or bare acronym, and the acronym is frequently pluralised into a noun for the people themselves ('ASDs', 'TDs'), which is the least person-centred usage in the corpus. 'Patients' appears for children who are not in any clinical encounter. The framing is deficit-based throughout, describing autism in terms of 'a deficit in social behaviour', children who 'avoid eye contact', and 'ASD syndrome'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Only group sizes are given: 14 and 14. Age, sex, IQ, language level and severity are all absent for both groups, and no matching of any kind is described or possible to verify. This is the least-characterised sample in the corpus. The gap matters more here than it would elsewhere because the paper's own Discussion devotes four bullet points to how fixation behaviour changes with age - contrasting toddlers around 21 months, children under ten and those over twenty - and concludes that 'selection of necessary features for modelling fixation behaviour of subjects should be varied based on the corresponding age', immediately followed by the admission that 'the presented model does not consider the age information'. The authors thus diagnose the omission precisely without being able to remedy it, because the benchmark they inherited does not carry the variable.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Nothing. No diagnostic instrument, clinical criterion, clinician role or diagnostic setting is mentioned at any point. The autism label is treated as an attribute of the dataset file, and even the source dataset's diagnostic procedure is not summarised or cited. Under the review's classification this is dataset-label-only ascertainment, in the weakest form encountered - some other benchmark-reuse papers here at least restate the original cohort's ADOS or CARS procedure.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No IQ, language, adaptive functioning, comorbidity or medication information for either group, and no exclusions described. Nor is there any severity measure, so the model's outputs cannot be related to any clinical gradient.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: build a classifier that combines image-content features with viewing-behaviour features, on the argument that competing entries modelled scanpaths without reference to what was being looked at. Main findings: 0.59 accuracy, 0.68 recall, 0.50 specificity on the challenge test set, tied for best of eight entries; performance concentrated on images where mean fixation duration separated the groups (88.5% on the best five images, 46.2% on the worst five); autistic children showed more brief fixation clusters under 100 ms (24% versus 15%) and fewer beyond 500 ms (21% versus 35%); and the authors conclude that age-conditioned feature selection is needed but unavailable.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Not reported. The eye-tracking sessions belong to the Saliency4ASD collection and the authors describe neither the room, the tracker, the viewing distance, nor the country. The only settings named are the two Italian universities where the analysis was performed. For a study whose entire signal is fixation duration, the absence of the acquisition sampling rate and calibration procedure is a substantive reproducibility gap rather than a formality.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Free viewing of 400 natural images from mixed categories, inherited from the benchmark. No instruction, response or trial structure is described. The paradigm is the most passive in the corpus - the child looks at pictures and nothing is asked of them - which is an advantage for feasibility in young or minimally verbal children and a disadvantage for interpretability, since there is no task performance against which viewing behaviour can be referenced. The best/worst image analysis shows how much the paradigm's yield depends on stimulus choice: three of the five best-performing images depict children, which the authors suggest 'might have moved the attention of the young participants', implying that stimulus curation rather than model capacity sets the ceiling.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis of a released benchmark; no follow-up. No ethics statement, consent statement or IRB approval appears anywhere - a defensible position for public challenge data, but the paper never states that position, nor does it point to where the original approvals were obtained. A competing-interests declaration is present, though it declares only a domain-based conflict.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition equipment is described - the eye tracker, its sampling rate, calibration and stimulus presentation are all properties of the source dataset and are not restated. Analysis tools are named specifically: YOLO with a stated architecture (9 convolutional plus 2 fully connected layers) trained on COCO for object detection; SDSP for saliency, with the selection rationale given as low computational complexity relative to Itti-Koch, GBVS, BMS, Salicon, SalGAN and SAM-ResNet; mean-shift clustering with an explicitly stated distance threshold of 100; and MATLAB's TreeBagger with tuned minLS, numPTS and numTree.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Mixed, and split cleanly along the boundary between what the authors did and what they inherited. Their own pipeline is reproducible in fine detail: all 30 features are individually named and defined in a table, the saliency-weight feature is given as an equation, the object-region rule (YOLO top-3 by confidence, remainder as non-object) is explicit, the clustering threshold is 100, the heatmap threshold is 0.1 with the source cited, the centre-proximity radius is 100 pixels, all 23 candidate classifiers are tabulated with their accuracies, and the selected hyperparameters and OOB error are stated. What is inherited is absent entirely: participant ages, sexes, diagnostic procedures, acquisition hardware, viewing durations. No code release is mentioned. The net effect is that the model could be re-implemented but the result could not be clinically interpreted.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Unusually forthright, and volunteered rather than buried. The Discussion opens by conceding the model 'can reach at most 60% accuracy in detecting ASDs' and then sets out four substantive reasons the task is hard - that fixation behaviour changes with age across toddlers, young children and adults; that at-risk toddlers can match typically developing toddlers on face fixation duration so the signal is age-dependent in kind rather than degree; that in scenes containing both faces and objects of circumscribed interest young autistic children do not differ from typically developing ones while older children show a non-object bias; and that consequently features should be selected per age band, which this model does not do. The Conclusion repeats that 'there is room for improvement'. What is not acknowledged: that classification is per scanpath rather than per child; that 23 classifiers were compared before one was selected; that specificity of exactly 0.50 means chance performance on the typically developing group; and the complete absence of participant characterisation and diagnostic provenance.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Two directions, both specific. Condition the feature set on participant age, given the age-dependence documented in the Discussion - though this requires demographic metadata the benchmark does not supply. And invert the analytic target by studying the regions of an image that autistic viewers fail to cover rather than those they fixate, on the reasoning that this 'might provide an insight on what does not attract the attention of a person with ASD'. The second is a genuinely different framing from the rest of the eye-tracking literature in this corpus, which almost uniformly models where gaze goes rather than where it does not.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Visual attention during free viewing, operationalised at three levels: what is looked at relative to image content (fixations on detected objects versus non-object regions, coverage, saliency-weighted fixation), how looking is temporally and spatially structured (fixation counts and durations, saccadic amplitudes, refixation, ROI clusters), and where looking is anchored spatially (distance of fixations and ROI centres from the image centre). Each family operationalises a specific published behavioural claim, so the feature set is a set of testable hypotheses rather than an undirected dump - which is what makes the error analysis interpretable when most of them turn out not to carry the result.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single-modality: eye tracking only. The paper nonetheless performs a fusion of a different kind - combining stimulus-derived features with observer-derived features - and this is its stated contribution. The comparison against competitors is argued in exactly these terms: the SP-ASDNET entries are said to fail because they 'do not consider the correlation between fixations and the corresponding image content', and the UCK entries because they discard the first fixation of each subject, which the authors argue is informative. The fusion is nonetheless only weakly supported by the results, since the best-performing competitor (TU, 0.59) matched RM3ASD exactly and also used a random forest over combined image and fixation features, while the error analysis attributes the model's success to a single fixation-duration feature that requires no image content at all.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A bagged decision-tree ensemble over 30 hand-engineered features - deliberately classical rather than deep, and justified by the comparison table showing that no classifier family separated meaningfully from any other. The spread across all 23 candidates is 59.3% (fine KNN) to 68.5% (TreeBagger), roughly nine points across decision trees, discriminant analysis, logistic regression, naive Bayes, six SVM kernels, five nearest-neighbour variants and five ensembles. That flatness is itself an informative negative result: when every model family lands within a few points of every other, the limiting factor is the feature representation and the data, not the learner - which supports the authors' focus on features and undercuts any claim that a deeper model would help.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: One fixed-length 30-dimensional vector per subject-image pair, computed by summarising the scanpath against the image. The representation choice determines the unit of analysis: because features are per subject-image, each child contributes one labelled instance per image, and the model classifies scanpaths rather than children. Nothing aggregates the multiple scanpaths belonging to the same child into a single participant-level prediction, and the reported metrics are means over per-image scanpath classifications.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Seven metrics - accuracy, recall, precision, F1, specificity, false positive rate and false negative rate - reported for the proposed model and all seven competing entries in a single table, which is the most complete comparative reporting in the corpus and allows failure modes to be read directly. It shows, for instance, that SP-ASDNET_1's apparently strong 0.87 recall comes with 0.25 specificity and a 0.75 false positive rate, meaning it classifies almost everything as autistic - a pathology that accuracy alone would have hidden. Applied to RM3ASD itself, the same table shows specificity of exactly 0.50 against recall of 0.68, so the model performs at chance on typically developing children and its accuracy advantage rests entirely on the autistic class. No confidence intervals, no significance testing, and no confusion matrices.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No model-derived interpretability method - no SHAP, no permutation importance, no tree-based importance despite using a random forest, where importance would have been available at no cost. In its place is a stimulus-level error analysis that turns out to be more informative: partitioning by classification accuracy shows that the five best images had autistic mean fixation duration of 213 ms against 574 ms for typically developing children, while the five worst had 318 versus 313 ms - so the model succeeds exactly where one feature separates the groups and fails where it does not. This localises the whole discriminative effect in mean fixation duration and simultaneously shows it is a property of particular stimuli rather than of the children. The dwell-time binning that follows (24% versus 15% of clusters under 100 ms; 21% versus 35% over 500 ms) links the finding to an existing reading-research framework in which sub-100 ms dwells indicate only partial information retention and dwells over 500 ms indicate further processing, giving the result a cognitive interpretation rather than leaving it as an unexplained numeric difference.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The benchmark's fixed 300/100 image split, with hyperparameters tuned by out-of-bag error on the training portion. Three weaknesses. The split partitions stimuli, not participants: all 28 children appear on both sides, so the model can learn subject-specific viewing idiosyncrasies from a child's training-image scanpaths and apply them to that same child's test-image scanpaths - the segment-level leakage pattern that recurs throughout this corpus, although here the low absolute performance suggests little was gained from it. Second, 23 classifiers plus a three-parameter grid were evaluated before one was chosen, and the resulting optimism is directly visible: the selection table reports 68.5% for TreeBagger while the test set returns 0.59, a nine-point gap that the paper presents without reconciling the two numbers. Third, no repeated splits, no cross-validation over participants, no confidence intervals and no significance test against the 0.59 competitor, so the claimed tie for first place rests on a single comparison of two point estimates on 100 images.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, object detection, fixations, classification, visual saliency. Three of the five are computer-vision terms and none is clinical, placing the paper firmly in the multimedia-signal-processing tradition rather than the clinical one - consistent with a venue, a challenge origin, and an evaluation framed as benchmark competition.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Signal Processing: Image Communication, volume 94, article 116184 (Elsevier), authored from Roma Tre University and the University of Padova. An image-processing journal with no clinical readership, and the paper is an extended write-up of an IEEE ICME 2019 Grand Challenge submission - a publication route that explains both its strengths (standardised data, common test set, direct comparison against seven other methods) and its weaknesses (no participant characterisation, no diagnostic provenance, no ethics statement, no clinical framing beyond the opening paragraphs).
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021 (submitted 2020, revised December 2020). Framed as early detection enabling early intervention, with the standard supporting claim that symptoms appear in the first two years and that early programmes let children enter kindergarten alongside typically developing peers - though the model is applied to school-age children of unstated age and could not address toddlers, whose viewing behaviour the paper's own Discussion says differs qualitatively. The more distinctive feature of the framing is what surrounds it: this is a challenge paper, so its comparative claim is against seven named competitor methods on a shared test set rather than against the literature at large, and its headline number is a modest 0.59 stated without inflation. The corpus contains few papers that report a result this weak, and its presence is a useful corrective - the same modality that yields 90%-plus in single-laboratory studies yields 0.53-0.59 across all eight entries when the data are fixed and shared.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Liaqat S; Wu C; Duggirala PR; Cheung SCS; Chuah CN; Ozonoff S; Young G
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Children with autism aged 5 to 12 from the Saliency4ASD benchmark
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking (free viewing of natural images)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Test whether a generative model of neurotypical scanning (STAR-FC) can serve as a per-image baseline against which an individual child's scanpath is compared, and whether a holistic image-plus-fixation network can outperform it - extending the authors' own ICME 2019 Grand Challenge submission with new architectures, representations and a full ablation study
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Secondary analysis of a public benchmark with a fixed train/validation split and a blind held-out test set scored by third parties, structured as a systematic ablation across architectures, input combinations and encoding schemes
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: 3 seconds of free viewing per image; 300 images in the training and validation pool and 100 in the test pool
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Free viewing of natural images at original full resolution, 3 seconds each, with no task instruction or response requirement
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Not reported for the data collection, which belongs to the Saliency4ASD source study; the analysis was performed at the University of Kentucky and the University of California, Davis
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Analysis in the United States; the participants' country is a property of the source dataset and is not stated
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Not reported. The label is inherited from the benchmark; no diagnostic instrument, criterion or clinician role is named, and the source collection is cited only for its recording conditions. This is notable because two senior authors are autism researchers whose group could have specified the diagnostic basis, and because the paper's own funding is an NIMH R01
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Mean 8 years; no standard deviation reported
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported - no ADOS, CARS, SRS or any severity or cognitive measure
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd_controls: Not reported - the 5-12 range and mean of 8 are stated only for the autistic children
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not reported; no age information is given for the comparison group at all, so matching cannot be assessed
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye-tracking scanpaths (ordered fixation coordinates with durations from 8 ms to 11483 ms) paired with the image stimuli
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Two parallel pipelines. Synthetic saccade approach: STAR-FC generates a temporally ordered synthetic scanpath for each image, taken as a proxy for neurotypical viewing; the child's real scanpath is zero-padded to a maximum of 33 fixations with coordinates normalised by image dimensions and durations divided by 5000, giving a 99-dimensional vector; 10 synthetic fixation points give a 20-dimensional vector; and seven statistical features are computed - total viewing duration, number of fixations, mean and variance of fixation duration, and Dynamic Time Warping, Hausdorff and Frechet distances between the real and synthetic scanpaths. These feed a branched MLP with three encoder channels (128-128-64, 128-128-64 and 64-64-32 neurons) concatenated into a 128-128-64 head. Image-based approach: each of the 33 fixations becomes its own image channel with the duration value placed at the fixation location, spread either by a Gaussian kernel or by replication to a 30-pixel radius, then passed through a ResNet branch whose first convolution accepts 33 channels; a second ImageNet-pretrained ResNet branch encodes the stimulus, and the two 512x7x7 feature maps are concatenated. An LSTM variant instead feeds each fixation triple plus a 49-dimensional image feature into a 5-layer recurrent network
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Tobii T120 eye tracker with a 17-inch monitor (source collection); STAR-FC saccade generator; ResNet18 and ResNet50 pretrained on ImageNet; 5-layer LSTM; PyTorch; Adam optimiser
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: No - the Saliency4ASD benchmark is used unchanged
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes, described as a publicly accessible collection; the test labels remain withheld by the challenge organisers
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not discussed. No ethics statement, consent statement or IRB approval appears, despite NIMH funding under award R01MH121344-01 being acknowledged
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Raw scanpath sequences, generative-model reference scanpaths, trajectory-distance statistics, and learned convolutional and recurrent representations
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Normalised fixation coordinates and durations (99 dimensions after zero-padding to 33 fixations); 10 STAR-FC synthetic fixation points with the first, always central, point discarded (20 dimensions); seven statistics comprising total viewing duration, fixation count, mean and variance of fixation duration and three trajectory distances (DTW, Hausdorff, Frechet) between real and synthetic paths; and, in the image-based branch, 33-channel fixation maps with Gaussian or replication spreading alongside ImageNet-pretrained ResNet image features
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: STAR-FC for synthetic scanpaths; DTW, Hausdorff and Frechet implementations for trajectory distance; ResNet18/ResNet50 for image and fixation-map encoding
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Not through a model-derived importance method, but through a systematic ablation that isolates the contribution of each input family, plus a post-hoc distributional analysis
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Twelve-way ablation across input combinations (scanpath, synthetic saccade, statistics and their combinations) and across architectures and encoding schemes, with each configuration evaluated on both validation and blind test sets; followed by a Kolmogorov-Smirnov comparison of total scanpath duration between groups
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The real scanpath alone. Removing it costs 2.61 percentage points on validation and 4.5 on test, while adding either the synthetic saccade or the statistical features to it yields no consistent gain and on the test set is actively harmful. Total scanpath duration emerges from the post-hoc analysis as the dominant single discriminator, matching the finding independently reported by the competing Startsev and Dorr entry
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Autistic children's scanpaths were substantially shorter in total duration than those of typically developing children, with the two histograms separating by a one-sided two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic of 0.278
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Deep learning - multilayer perceptrons, branched multi-encoder MLPs, convolutional networks and a recurrent network, compared head to head
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Baseline MLP (3 hidden layers, 128-128-64, ReLU, batch norm, dropout 0.2, 200 epochs, batch 24, Adam, learning rate 5e-4, weight decay 5e-5, L2-regularised binary cross-entropy); branched MLP with three encoder channels; CNN with a pretrained ResNet18 block replacing the first fully connected layer; ResNet18 and ResNet50 two-branch image models (30 epochs, batch 128, learning rate 2e-4); and a 5-layer LSTM (50 epochs). All hyperparameters, learning rates, weight decays, batch sizes and epoch counts are stated for every variant, and Table 4 and Table 9 tabulate exactly what changed relative to the original challenge submission
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: The benchmark's three-way split: 240 images with 5542 scanpaths for training, 60 images with 1411 scanpaths for validation, and 100 images with 2868 scanpaths as a blind test set whose diagnosis labels were withheld by the ICME 2019 organisers and whose performance numbers were computed by them. Validation results are averaged over two or three training runs with random initialisation and reported with standard deviations; test results are a single submitted run. The split partitions images, not children - all 28 participants appear in every partition
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for every configuration on both validation and test, with standard deviations across runs on validation; F1 added in the final cross-method comparison
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Best test result: ResNet50 image-based, 62.13% accuracy, sensitivity 0.71, specificity 0.537, AUC 0.667, F1 0.644 - the best of five methods compared, ahead of Scan-path & Saliency (59.84%, AUC 0.644), RM3ASD (59.30%) and SP-ASDNet (57.90%). Best synthetic-saccade result on test: BrMLP-SP at 61.39%, AUC 0.660, with the best specificity of any method (0.569). Best validation results were higher and pointed to different winners - LSTM at 67.23% and AUC 0.73, BrMLP-SP-F at 66.73% and AUC 0.72 - so the validation-optimal configuration was not the test-optimal one in either pipeline. Both pipelines improved substantially over the authors' own challenge submissions (synthetic saccade 53.88% to 61.39%; image-based 55.13% to 61.45% on test). Ablation showed the STAR-FC synthetic saccade contributed nothing: BrMLP-SP-STAR (60.27%) was worse than BrMLP-SP (61.39%) on test, and BrMLP-SP-STAR-F (58.94%) worse than BrMLP-SP-F (60.17%). Scanpath-only input matched scanpath-plus-image throughout (LSTM(s) 67.25% versus LSTM 67.23% on validation; ResNet18(s) 60.17% versus ResNet18 61.45% on test)
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: The paper's headline is a modest 62.13% accuracy and 0.667 AUC, best of five methods on a shared blind test set - but its substantive contribution is two negative results that the authors pursue rather than bury. First, the STAR-FC synthetic saccade, the paper's central methodological idea and the thing that distinguished the original challenge submission, contributes nothing: every configuration including it performs at or below the corresponding configuration without it, and the authors state plainly that removing it was one of the two changes responsible for their post-challenge improvement. Second, and more consequentially, scanpath-only input matches scanpath-plus-image input across every architecture tested - which should be impossible if the classifier were exploiting the well-documented interaction between social image content and autistic viewing, since a scanpath stripped of its stimulus carries no information about what was being looked at. The authors confront this directly, hypothesise that with only 14 children per group 'there might be a systematic bias in terms of the gaze patterns between these two groups', and support it by showing that total scanpath duration differs sharply between groups (KS statistic 0.278). The implication is that the models are substantially identifying individual children by their idiosyncratic viewing tempo rather than detecting autism from stimulus-dependent attention.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Markedly shorter total scanpath duration in autistic children, consistent with reduced visual exploration and independently identified as the top feature by a competing entry
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Map the learned features back to explainable scanpath entities, which the authors state they have not done; and, implicitly, collect data from more participants, since the small subject pool is offered as the explanation for the scanpath-only result
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The most methodologically self-aware paper in the eye-tracking portion of this corpus, and the one that comes closest to naming the corpus's central validity problem in its own words. Its strengths are substantial. The test set is genuinely blind - labels withheld by the ICME organisers, performance computed by them, not by the authors - which is the only truly external scoring arrangement in the corpus and removes any possibility of test-set tuning. Reporting is exhaustive: eleven tables covering every architecture, input combination and encoding scheme on both validation and test, with standard deviations across repeated runs, and two tables (4 and 9) that itemise exactly which hyperparameters changed from the original challenge submission and by how much. Negative results are foregrounded rather than suppressed - the paper's own named contribution, the STAR-FC synthetic saccade, is shown across four paired comparisons to be useless, and the authors say so. And the divergence between validation and test rankings is discussed rather than hidden, with the LSTM winning on validation (67.23%) and losing on test (60.40%) while ResNet50 does the reverse. The critical passage is the discussion of the scanpath-only result. Because a bare scanpath carries no stimulus information, its parity with scanpath-plus-image is logically incompatible with the social-saliency mechanism the entire approach is built on, and the authors recognise this: they call it 'surprising', note that 'all the studies discussed in Section 2 drew their conclusions conditioned on the same visual stimuli to the two groups of subjects', and then offer the correct explanation - with 14 children per group and every child appearing in every split, the network can learn each child's characteristic viewing tempo and recover the label from that. Their supporting evidence, the total-duration histograms, makes the point vividly. Two things they do not do. They do not act on the diagnosis by re-partitioning by participant, which would have converted the observation into a measurement of how much of the 62% is genuine; the benchmark's fixed splits make this impossible without abandoning the blind test, but the limitation should have been stated as bounding the result rather than only explaining it. And the KS test that supports the argument is computed over thousands of scanpaths as if independent, returning p = 4.09e-122 from 28 children - a p-value that, taken at face value, would be among the most extreme in the corpus, and which illustrates the very non-independence the surrounding paragraph is about. Participant reporting is minimal (ages for the autistic group only, no sex, no diagnostic instrument, no severity, no ethics statement) though better than the companion Mazumdar paper on the same data, and the acquisition conditions - Tobii T120, 17-inch monitor, 3 seconds per image at full resolution - are at least restated.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups from the Saliency4ASD benchmark: 14 autistic and 14 typically developing children, 28 in total. Every one of the 300 training and validation images was viewed by all 28 children, and the 100 test images likewise, so the three partitions are cuts through the same 28 people - 5542 training scanpaths, 1411 validation scanpaths and 2868 test scanpaths all originate from the same fourteen autistic and fourteen typically developing children. This is stated plainly by the authors and is the fact on which their own closing hypothesis turns. No other-diagnosis or subthreshold group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with autism spectrum disorder', 'ASD children', 'ASD subjects', 'individuals with ASD', 'ASD individuals', versus 'typically developed (TD) viewers', 'TD children', 'typically developing controls', and once 'IQ-matched normal peers' when describing prior work. Predominantly acronym-as-noun usage ('ASD and TD subjects') with occasional person-first phrasing. Autism is framed as 'defined by the deficits in social and communication development and the presence of stereotypical behaviors' - a deficit framing, though the paper is descriptively neutral about participants themselves and never uses 'patients'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Sample sizes are given (14 and 14) and, unlike the companion paper on the same dataset, ages are partially reported: 'the age of children with ASD lied in the range from 5 to 12 years old (8 years old on average)'. No standard deviation. Critically, no age information at all is given for the typically developing group, so age matching cannot be assessed even coarsely. Sex distribution, IQ, language level and severity are absent for both groups. The demographic reporting therefore covers one variable in one of two groups - better than nothing, but insufficient to know whether the two groups are comparable on the variable the authors' own literature review identifies as decisive for gaze behaviour.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not reported. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician role or setting is named; the label is an attribute of the released dataset. The paper cites the source collection for its recording parameters (Tobii T120, 17-inch monitor, 3-second presentations) but not for its ascertainment procedure. Under the review's classification this is dataset-label-only. The omission is more conspicuous here than in most benchmark-reuse papers because the author list includes established autism-research investigators and the work is funded by an NIMH R01, so the expertise to characterise or question the labels was present.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No IQ, adaptive functioning, language measure, comorbidity or medication information, and no exclusion criteria. Consequently nothing links model output to any clinical gradient, and the frequently cited possibility that IQ rather than diagnosis drives gaze differences cannot be examined.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: extend the authors' ICME 2019 challenge submission by testing whether a generative neurotypical scanning baseline (STAR-FC) improves classification and whether a holistic image-plus-fixation network beats it. Main findings: best test performance 62.13% accuracy and 0.667 AUC (ResNet50), best of five compared methods; substantial improvement over their own challenge entries (53.88% to 61.39% and 55.13% to 61.45%); the STAR-FC synthetic saccade contributes nothing across four paired comparisons; validation-optimal and test-optimal configurations differ in both pipelines; and, decisively, scanpath-only input matches scanpath-plus-image everywhere, which the authors attribute to systematic per-child gaze bias in a 28-participant pool and support with a large group difference in total scanpath duration.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Not reported for the data collection - the setting belongs to the Saliency4ASD source study. The acquisition conditions are partially restated: Tobii T120 eye tracker, 17-inch monitor, each image presented at original full resolution for 3 seconds. This is more than the companion paper on the same data provides but still omits room conditions, viewing distance, calibration procedure and sampling rate, all of which matter for a signal whose dominant discriminator turns out to be total fixation duration.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Free viewing of natural images for 3 seconds each, with no instruction, response or interaction. The paradigm is entirely inherited, and the paper's contribution lies in representation and architecture rather than task design. The 3-second window is worth noting against the finding that total scanpath duration is the dominant discriminator: within a fixed 3-second presentation, total scanpath duration is determined by how much of the window the tracker recorded valid fixations for, so the discriminating quantity is partly a function of tracking quality and compliance rather than of viewing strategy - a data-quality-as-signal pattern that recurs across this corpus and that the paper does not consider.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis; no follow-up. No ethics, consent or IRB statement anywhere, despite acknowledged NIMH funding (R01MH121344-01) and a full competing-interests declaration - so the omission is not a matter of the paper lacking front-matter sections. Data are public challenge material, which mitigates but does not remove the expectation of a statement about the source approvals.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Acquisition: Tobii T120 with a 17-inch monitor, restated from the source collection. Analysis: STAR-FC, described in enough detail to follow - central initial fixation, retinal transform giving anisotropic blurring, a conspicuity map fusing a low-level peripheral stream with a high-level deep-learned central stream, and a priority map incorporating inhibition of return - together with ImageNet-pretrained ResNet18 and ResNet50, a 5-layer LSTM, DTW, Hausdorff and Frechet distance implementations, and PyTorch. Every optimiser setting, learning rate, weight decay, batch size, dropout rate and epoch count is specified for each of the five architectures.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: The best-reported study in the eye-tracking group and among the best in the corpus for the parts under the authors' control. All preprocessing is specified: coordinate normalisation by image dimensions, duration normalisation by division by 5000, zero-padding to 33 fixations, the discarding of STAR-FC's always-central first point, Gaussian spreading with sigma = 20 versus 30-pixel replication, augmentation by up to 20-pixel fixation shifts and duration scaling in [0.8, 1.2], colour jitter and horizontal flip, and the explicit decision to exclude affine transforms because they could push fixations outside the image. Every architecture is given layer by layer with all training hyperparameters. Tables 4 and 9 go further than any other paper here by tabulating the exact delta between the published challenge submission and the improved version - preprocessing, layer count, inputs, learning rate, regularisation, epochs, dropout and batch size - which makes the source of the improvement auditable rather than asserted. What is missing: no code release, and none of the participant-level or diagnostic information, which is inherited.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Substantially acknowledged, and in the most important place. The authors state that scanpath-only performance rivalling scanpath-plus-image is 'a surprising result as the scan-path itself contains no direct information about the visual stimuli', note that it contradicts the premise of their own design and of every study in their related-work section, and offer the explanation that 'the dataset is too small in terms of the number of subjects - only 14 ASD and 14 TD children were included. As such, there might be a systematic bias in terms of the gaze patterns between these two groups'. They also concede they have not mapped learned features back to explainable entities. What is not acknowledged: that the same-28-children-in-every-split design makes this bias exploitable rather than merely present, so it bounds the validity of the 62.13% rather than only explaining an anomaly; that the validation-to-test ranking reversals (LSTM best on validation, worst of three on test) indicate the validation set is too similar to training to guide model selection, which they note descriptively without drawing the inference; that specificity is weak throughout, 0.537 for the best model and 0.44-0.57 across variants, so performance rests disproportionately on the autistic class; and that the supporting KS test treats thousands of scanpaths from 28 children as independent observations.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: One explicit direction: produce explainable features by mapping the learned representations back to interpretable scanpath properties, which the authors state is 'left for future studies'. One implicit: enlarge the participant pool, since small subject count is their own explanation for the anomalous scanpath-only result. Neither is elaborated, and notably the paper does not propose participant-wise partitioning, which is the direct remedy for the mechanism it identifies.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Visual attention during free viewing, represented at the level of the raw fixation sequence - coordinates, durations and their temporal order - rather than through hand-engineered behavioural constructs. Three encodings of the same behaviour are compared: a flat 99-dimensional vector, a 33-channel spatial fixation map preserving temporal order across channels, and a recurrent sequence. The comparison is informative in itself: the multi-channel encoding beat the single-channel version because it preserves ordering (66.06% versus 63.96% on validation), confirming that fixation sequence, not just fixation distribution, carries signal. The behavioural quantity that ultimately dominates, however, is the simplest - total scanpath duration.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single-modality eye tracking, but the paper performs and systematically ablates two distinct fusions, and both fail in ways that matter. The first fuses the child's real scanpath with a model-generated neurotypical reference scanpath, on the reasonable premise that deviation from a normative scanning pattern should be more diagnostic than the raw pattern; across four paired comparisons the synthetic saccade never helped, and the authors identify its removal as one of the two changes that produced their post-challenge improvement. The second fuses scanpath with stimulus image, on the premise that autistic viewing differs specifically in response to social content; scanpath-only matched or beat the fused model in three of four comparisons. Taken together the two negative fusion results carry more weight than the positive headline: the information the classifier uses is neither the deviation from normative scanning nor the interaction with image content, but something intrinsic to the scanpath itself - which the authors correctly suspect is subject identity.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Five architectures compared directly on the same data: baseline MLP, branched multi-encoder MLP, CNN over fixation maps, ResNet18/ResNet50 two-branch image models, and a 5-layer LSTM. The spread on the blind test set is 52.53% (CNN-SP-STAR) to 62.13% (ResNet50) - about ten points across shallow and deep, feedforward, convolutional and recurrent families - and the two best (62.13% and 61.39%) come from opposite ends of that range, a deep image model and a shallow MLP on raw coordinates. As in the companion paper on the same benchmark, the flatness across architecture families indicates that the limiting factor is the data rather than model capacity. The authors also note a specific failure mode with a plausible cause: the CNN over fixation maps performed worst, which they attribute to 'the mismatch between the fixation image maps and the CNN networked pretrained on natural images' - a sparse synthetic input passed through an ImageNet backbone.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: The most thorough exploration of input representation in the corpus. Scanpaths were encoded as (i) a zero-padded 99-dimensional flat vector of normalised coordinates and durations, (ii) a 33-channel image where each channel places one fixation's duration at its location, with two densification schemes (Gaussian sigma = 20 versus replication to a 30-pixel radius) and two channel schemes (one channel per fixation versus all collapsed into one), and (iii) a sequence fed to an LSTM alongside a 49-dimensional image feature taken from the ResNet 7x7 map before global pooling. The ablation over these choices is reported cleanly: separated channels beat collapsed channels because temporal order is preserved, and Gaussian spreading beat replication.
