Two representational decisions are also documented as corrections of earlier error - the original challenge entry had aligned real to synthetic scanpaths with dynamic time warping, which 'completely ignores the duration of each fixation point because no duration information is provided by the STAR-FC model' and thereby 'introduces distortion and omission to the real scan-path'; abandoning the warping and using raw 33-point scanpaths with durations was one of the two sources of the improvement.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for every one of roughly twenty configurations, on both validation and blind test, with standard deviations across two or three runs on validation - the most complete metric reporting in the corpus, and complete enough to read failure modes directly. Doing so is instructive: specificity is the consistent weakness, at 0.537 for the best test model and dropping as low as 0.35 for BrMLP-F and 0.44-0.48 for several others, against sensitivities of 0.71-0.78 - so most configurations lean toward calling children autistic, and accuracy alone would conceal this. The final comparison table adds F1 and flags, with an asterisk and a footnote, that two competitor AUCs were computed over binary labels as the mean of sensitivity and specificity because probability scores were unavailable - a precision about the comparability of borrowed numbers that is rare anywhere in this literature. No confidence intervals and no significance testing between methods, so the 62.13% versus 59.84% margin over the nearest competitor is a comparison of point estimates.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No formal interpretability method, and the authors say so: they 'have not conducted a full investigation to map these features back into explainable entities related to the scan-path data'. What they provide instead is more useful than a saliency map would have been. The ablation functions as an interpretability analysis by elimination, establishing which input families the model does and does not use - not the synthetic saccade, not the stimulus image, only the scanpath. That negative result then drives a direct distributional analysis: histograms of total scanpath duration by group, showing autistic scanpaths markedly shorter, with a one-sided two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic of 0.278. The finding converges with the competing Startsev and Dorr entry, which independently identified total fixation duration as its most discriminating feature - cross-method agreement on the same benchmark, which is stronger evidence about what the signal is than any single model's attribution would be. The accompanying p-value of 4.09e-122 should be disregarded: it is computed over several thousand scanpaths treated as independent when they come from 28 children, which is precisely the non-independence the surrounding paragraph is arguing exists.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The strongest external evaluation arrangement in the corpus paired with the weakest partitioning principle. On the strong side: the test labels were withheld by the ICME 2019 organisers and all test performance was computed by them, so no amount of iteration could tune to the test set - the only genuinely third-party-scored evaluation here - and validation results are averaged over repeated runs with standard deviations reported. On the weak side: the partition is over images (240 train / 60 validation / 100 test), not over children, so all 28 participants appear in all three sets, and a model that learns a child's characteristic viewing tempo from their training scanpaths can apply it to their test scanpaths. The authors identify this mechanism themselves as the explanation for scanpath-only parity, which makes it the corpus's only self-diagnosed instance of the leakage pattern - but they do not draw the consequence that it bounds the 62.13%. The benchmark's fixed splits preclude re-partitioning without forfeiting the blind test, which is a real constraint rather than an oversight; the appropriate response would have been to state the resulting ceiling explicitly. A further diagnostic sits unremarked in the tables: validation-optimal and test-optimal configurations differ in both pipelines (LSTM 67.23% on validation but 60.40% on test; BrMLP-SP-F best on validation, BrMLP-SP on test), which the authors attribute to training and validation being 'more similar to each other than to the test dataset' without noting that this makes the validation set unfit for model selection.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorders, eye gaze data, deep learning. Three terms, one clinical and two technical - the sparsest keyword set in the corpus, and consistent with a paper whose contribution is architectural and whose clinical content is inherited.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Signal Processing: Image Communication, volume 94, article 116198 (Elsevier) - the same issue as the Mazumdar RM3ASD paper, which it cites and benchmarks against. Authorship spans the University of Kentucky and UC Davis and combines signal-processing and networking engineers with two autism researchers from the MIND Institute tradition, and the work is supported by NIMH R01MH121344-01. The engineering-clinical composition is visible in the framing (the introduction cites mean US age at diagnosis over 4 years, fewer than 25% before age 3, and characterises the delay as 'squandering years of potential intervention when the brain is most plastic') but not in the participant reporting, which remains that of a benchmark paper.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021 (submitted May 2020, revised January 2021), extending a 2019 ICME Grand Challenge submission. The framing is the standard early-detection argument, sharpened by specific epidemiological figures on the diagnostic delay and by the claim that scanpath-only classifiers would be computationally light enough for mobile deployment. What distinguishes this paper's position in the literature is not its framing but its evaluative stance: it is one of the few here written in explicit competition with named alternatives on a shared blind test set, reporting its own prior submission's weaker numbers alongside the improved ones, and it treats the failure of its own central idea as a finding rather than an embarrassment. Its related-work section is also unusually careful about generalisation, noting that a 92%-accuracy adult study 'may not directly translate to ASD diagnosis among children' because children's and adults' gaze patterns differ - a caution that other papers in this corpus citing the same adult results do not observe.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Kojovic N; Natraj S; Mohanty SP; Maillart T; Schaer M
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Young children with autism, aged approximately 1 to 7 years
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Body pose and non-verbal social interaction (video-based motion)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Move beyond the single-behaviour digital phenotyping paradigm - gaze, head turn on name-calling, visual tracking - toward a holistic classifier that operates on the global pattern of non-verbal social interaction. The motivating argument is that autism 'comes with broad impairments that often transcend single behavioral acts' and manifests through 'global patterns of atypical postures and movements, fewer gestures used and often decoupled from visual contact, facial affect, speech', so a model that indexes one elicited behaviour at a time is measuring the wrong unit
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Case-control classification with a participant-wise training and testing partition, plus a second larger single-group validation sample, drawn from an ongoing longitudinal cohort study
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One videotaped ADOS assessment per child, averaging 42 minutes; total 47.8 hours in training, 48.7 in Testing Set 1 and 50.0 in Testing Set 2
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: The full ADOS assessment itself, filmed in its entirety. Only Modules Toddler, 1 and 2 were used, because these 'are conducted while moving around a room using a variety of attractive toys' and require fewer language abilities, whereas Modules 3 and 4 'happen mostly at a table and involve more discussion with lesser use of objects'. The choice was also pragmatic - ADOS is 'systematically administered in all children included in our study' - which is what makes the approach retrofittable to existing clinical archives
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: University of Geneva, Switzerland, within a larger longitudinal study of early development in autism. Assessments took place in several different rooms, were administered by different examiners and were filmed with different camera systems - heterogeneity the authors present as a robustness feature rather than a nuisance
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Clinical diagnosis under DSM-5 criteria, further corroborated using gold-standard diagnostic assessments (ADOS-G or ADOS-2). Typically developing children were screened for any known neurological or psychiatric illness and for autism in any first-degree relative - a stricter comparison-group criterion than most studies apply, since it excludes the broader autism phenotype in siblings and parents
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 68 in the training and Testing Set 1 pool (34 each), plus 101 in Testing Set 2
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: 2.80 +/- 0.92 years for the 68 in the main pool; 3.46 +/- 1.16 years for the 101 in Testing Set 2
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: 1.2 to 5.1 years in the main pool; 2 to 6.9 years in Testing Set 2
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Not stated in the main text; groups are described as matched for gender, with the distribution reported in supplementary Table S1
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not described for the autistic group; typically developing children were screened for any known neurological or psychiatric illness
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Fully characterised and used analytically: ADOS-2 Calibrated Severity Scores for total, social affect and repetitive and restricted behaviours, VABS-II Adaptive Behavior Composite with communication, socialisation, daily-living and motor subdomains, and a Best Estimate IQ combining the most representative cognitive measures for each child given that different instruments were used depending on age and ability to attend
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes - screened for any known neurological or psychiatric illness and for autism in any first-degree relative
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 68 (34 training, 34 in Testing Set 1); none in Testing Set 2
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution_controls: Not stated in the main text; reported as matched
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes - groups were matched for age (2.80 versus 2.55 years), and were also equally distributed across the training and testing partitions matched for diagnosis, age, gender and ADOS module
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Yes, stated as matched, with details in supplementary Table S1
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Confirmed by screening for neurological and psychiatric illness and for family history of autism
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Video of clinical diagnostic assessments, reduced to 2D skeletal keypoint sequences
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: OpenPose multi-person 2D pose estimation was applied frame by frame using the COCO model, yielding 18 keypoints per person (13 body, 5 facial). The video background was removed entirely and only skeletons on a black background retained, so the model sees no faces, rooms, toys, clothing or lighting. Feature vectors were computed from image output rather than raw keypoint coordinates to obtain invariance to rigid-body and affine transformations. Videos were downsampled from 696x554 to 320x240 and split into 5-second segments, a length selected because it gave lower validation loss than 10 or 15 seconds. Each segment's frames passed through ImageNet-pretrained VGG16, and the flattened high-dimensional features fed a 512-unit LSTM with 0.5 dropout, then ReLU dense layers with 0.5 dropout and a softmax over two classes. Segment predictions were averaged across the whole video to yield a continuous 'ASD probability', thresholded at 0.5 for classification
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Ordinary video recordings from multiple camera systems - explicitly 'a simple 2D camera input not requiring any external markers or sensors, thus allowing the retrospective analysis of videos'; OpenPose with the COCO model; VGG16 pretrained on ImageNet; Keras-style LSTM; rmsprop optimiser with categorical cross-entropy; University of Geneva Baobab HPC cluster with RTX 2080Ti, Titan X and Quadro P1000 GPUs; GraphPad Prism v.8 and SPSS v.25 for statistics
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: A corpus of 237 fully videotaped ADOS assessments from an ongoing Geneva longitudinal cohort; no public release is described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not stated in the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Yes, and by design rather than by policy. Reducing videos to skeletons on a black background was chosen for two stated reasons, one of which was 'to ensure de-identification of the persons involved' - so the representation that enables the analysis is also the one that removes identifiability. Ethics approval from the Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Medicine of Geneva University; informed written consent from a parent or legal guardian for all children; separate explicit consent obtained from the adults and the child's guardian for the identifying images reproduced in Figure 1
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Learned spatio-temporal representations of multi-person skeletal motion
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: No hand-engineered features. The input is the rendered skeleton image sequence itself, and all representation is learned - VGG16 supplying per-frame spatial encoding and the LSTM supplying temporal dependency across the 5-second window. What is deliberately excluded is as informative as what is included: no sound, no faces, no appearance, no scene, no manual annotation. The authors state that 'videos were not manually annotated; thus, we removed the human factor in the initial feature breakdown', which is the strongest claim to observer-independence in the corpus
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: OpenPose COCO 18-keypoint model; VGG16 pretrained on ImageNet
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Not at the level of network internals, which the authors concede. Interpretability is instead pursued externally, by relating the network's continuous output to 27 individual clinical symptom ratings
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Spearman rank correlations between ASD probability and ADOS calibrated severity scores, VABS-II composite and subdomains, and best-estimate IQ, all Bonferroni-corrected (p < 0.025 for two ADOS subdomains, p < 0.013 for four VABS subdomains, p < 0.002 for 27 ADOS items); followed by Partial Least Squares Correlation with 1000 permutations for significance and 1000 bootstrap resamples for salience stability, chosen because ADOS items are collinear and PLS-C carries 'no assumption of independence among tested variables'
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Of 27 ADOS items, 15 correlated significantly with ASD probability after Bonferroni correction, and they were predominantly non-verbal. The strongest were integration of gaze with other behaviours during social overtures (0.591), pointing (0.540), unusual eye contact (0.500), directed facial expressions (0.488), quality of social overtures (0.484), imagination (0.470), unusually repetitive interests and stereotyped behaviours (0.455), spontaneous initiation of joint attention (0.450), giving (0.438), gestures (0.435), unusual sensory behaviours (0.434), intonation (0.426), functional play (0.418), showing (0.396) and shared enjoyment (0.359). The PLS-C latent component was significant at p = 0.001 and loaded most on facial expressions, quality of social overtures and gestures; the lowest-loading items were the verbal ones - immediate echolalia and stereotyped language - which the authors attribute to the sample being largely pre-verbal
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Higher ASD probability accompanied greater symptom severity across social affect and repetitive behaviour domains, and lower adaptive functioning in communication, socialisation and daily-living autonomy - but notably not in the motor domain (-0.186, p = 0.066), a null the authors report without comment even though it bears directly on whether a pose-based model is capturing motor function
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Deep learning - convolutional feature extraction with recurrent temporal modelling over skeletal video
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: VGG16 (ImageNet-pretrained, 16 layers, 224x224 RGB input, feature maps reducing to 512 at 7x7) feeding a 512-unit LSTM with 0.5 dropout, then ReLU dense layers with 0.5 dropout and a two-class softmax. Trained with categorical cross-entropy and rmsprop at batch size 128 for 100 epochs on an 80-20 training-validation split of the 68 training videos, with the least-validation-loss checkpoint deployed. Segment length was itself selected by validation loss across 5, 10 and 15 seconds
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: The design's defining strength. The 136 children were split participant-wise into a Training set (34 autistic, 34 typically developing) and Testing Set 1 (34 and 34), matched on diagnosis, age, gender and ADOS module, so no child appears on both sides. Within the training set an 80-20 split supported hyperparameter tuning and early stopping. Crucially, although the network is trained and predicts on 5-second segments - roughly 505 per video, so about 34,000 training segments - the reported accuracy is computed after averaging every segment prediction within a video into a single per-child ASD probability. A second validation sample, Testing Set 2, comprised 101 further autistic children of somewhat older age. A sliding-window analysis from 20 seconds upward quantified how accuracy and prediction stability grow with the length of video used
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall (sensitivity), specificity and F1 on Testing Set 1; accuracy on Testing Set 2; accuracy as a function of video segment duration; and cumulative incidence of the segment length required for 100% within-child prediction consistency
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Testing Set 1 (68 children, balanced): accuracy 80.9%, precision 0.784, recall 0.854, specificity 0.765, F1 0.818. Testing Set 2 (101 autistic children): 80.2% accuracy, which since the sample is single-class is a sensitivity estimate. Roughly 70% accuracy was already reached using only 10 minutes of video, and for half the autistic sample a randomly drawn 10-minute segment gave 100% consistent class attribution. ASD probability correlated with ADOS total calibrated severity (0.451), social affect (0.509) and repetitive behaviours (0.409); negatively with VABS-II adaptive composite (-0.444), communication (-0.386), socialisation (-0.477) and daily-living autonomy (-0.397), but not motor functioning (-0.186, p = 0.066); and negatively with best-estimate IQ (-0.283, p = 0.012)
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A network seeing nothing but moving stick figures on a black background - no faces, no sound, no scene, no annotation - separated autistic from typically developing children at 80.9% accuracy with balanced sensitivity and specificity, on children held out at the participant level and predicted at the child level rather than the clip level. The result held at 80.2% in a second sample of 101 children, and was robust to the videos having been filmed in different rooms, by different examiners, with different cameras. Ten minutes of footage sufficed for about 70% accuracy and, for half the autistic sample, for perfectly stable classification. The network's continuous output behaved like a graded clinical measure rather than a binary flag, tracking ADOS severity in both symptom domains and inversely tracking adaptive functioning and IQ. Fifteen of 27 individual ADOS items correlated with it after Bonferroni correction, and a permutation-tested PLS-C confirmed that the items carrying the pattern were the non-verbal ones - gaze integration, gestures, directed facial expression, social overtures - with verbal items loading least.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Atypical global patterns of posture and movement during unconstrained social interaction, aligned with clinician ratings of gaze integration, pointing, eye contact, directed facial expression and gesture use
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Implement a spatio-temporal attention mechanism to identify which elements in space and time drive the network's decision, since the present analysis 'prevents us from drawing solid conclusions on what is represented in the NN'; and perform fine-grained annotation of the non-verbal behaviours that contributed most - incidence of communicative gestures, shared affective states, atypical social overtures - to establish what the network learned and to yield a more sensitive measure of how the disorder manifests. The authors also position the work toward finer-grained digital phenotyping capable of defining subtypes, arguing that gold-standard instruments 'still rely on somewhat coarse descriptions of symptoms' scored on 3- or 4-point scales while 'phenotypical differences between the behaviors brought on the same plane can be very pronounced'
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Methodologically the strongest classification study in this corpus, and the clearest demonstration of what the eye-tracking and image-classification papers here get wrong. Four design decisions carry it. The train/test partition is by child, matched on diagnosis, age, gender and ADOS module, so no participant's data appears on both sides - the failure mode that undermines Cilia, Akter, Liaqat, Mazumdar and several others. Predictions are made on 5-second segments but reported after aggregation to one probability per child, so the ~34,000 training segments never become ~34,000 apparent test cases; this is exactly the correction Cilia had to apply retrospectively (90% image-level falling to 71% participant-level), applied here by construction. The nuisance variation that other studies control away - different rooms, cameras, examiners - is left in, and the model's robustness to it is reported as a result. And the representation is stripped to skeletons on black, which simultaneously removes appearance confounds, removes identifiability, and makes it impossible for the model to exploit clinic decor, image quality or camera identity, all of which have been shown elsewhere in this literature to leak group membership. The clinical anchoring is likewise unusual: a continuous output correlated against three independent instruments with Bonferroni correction throughout, and a collinearity-aware PLS-C with 1000 permutations and 1000 bootstraps rather than 27 separate uncorrected tests. Three substantive caveats remain, none acknowledged. First and most important, OpenPose extracts keypoints for every person in the frame, and the ADOS videos contain the examiner and often a caregiver as well as the child; nothing in the design isolates the child's skeleton, so the classifier may be reading examiner behaviour - clinicians modulate prompting, positioning and press for joint attention according to how a child responds - rather than, or in addition to, the child's own movement. This is not a fatal objection to a screening tool operating on assessment video, but it changes what the 80.9% means and it is never raised. Second, the correlations offered as clinical validity are computed across a two-group sample in which ADOS severity is near-floor in one group and high in the other, so an r of 0.451 against total severity is substantially the group separation re-expressed; whether ASD probability grades severity within autistic children is not shown, and Testing Set 2 - 101 autistic children with the full range of severity - was the sample that could have shown it, but is used only for an accuracy figure. Third, ASD probability correlates inversely with IQ (-0.283) and with adaptive functioning (-0.444), raising the possibility that part of what the model detects is general developmental level; the one null in the whole correlation table is the motor subdomain (p = 0.066), which is where a pose-based model would most be expected to load, and neither the confound nor the anomaly is discussed. The paper also has no limitations section at all, which for a study of this quality is a conspicuous omission. Testing Set 2's status should be read carefully too: it contains no typically developing children, so its 80.2% is a sensitivity estimate on an older sample from the same cohort, not an external replication.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Three samples, all explicitly sized. Training set: 34 autistic and 34 typically developing children. Testing Set 1: a further 34 and 34, drawn from the same 136-child pool and 'equally distributed' with the training set, matched on diagnosis, age, gender and ADOS module. Testing Set 2: 101 videos from autistic children only, aged 2 to 6.9. The partition is by participant, so the 68 children in Testing Set 1 contributed no data to training - the defining structural strength of the study. Testing Set 2's single-class composition is a real limitation on what it can validate: with no typically developing children, its 80.2% figure is sensitivity alone and cannot detect a model that has drifted toward calling everyone autistic. No other-diagnosis or developmentally-delayed comparison group appears anywhere, so the model is never tested against the discrimination that matters clinically - autism versus other developmental concern - only against typical development.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with autism', 'children with ASD', 'individuals with autism', against 'typically developing (TD) children', 'their typically developing peers'. Consistently person-first, and the phrase 'their typically developing peers' in the abstract is a comparatively warm construction. 'Patients' never appears. Autism is described in DSM terms as 'impairments in social communication and interactions, and the presence of restricted, repetitive patterns of interests and behaviors', and the surrounding language is clinical rather than pathologising - 'atypical', 'aberrant' and 'unusual' applied to behaviours rather than to children. The Discussion is notably respectful in framing the purpose as supporting development during a plastic period rather than as detecting defect.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Autistic group in the main pool: 68 children, 2.80 +/- 0.92 years, range 1.2-5.1. Typically developing group: 68 children, 2.55 +/- 0.97 years, same range. Testing Set 2: 101 autistic children, 3.46 +/- 1.16 years, range 2-6.9. Groups are stated to be matched for diagnosis, age, gender and ADOS module, with the sex distribution given in supplementary Table S1 rather than the main text - the only demographic detail displaced to supplementary material. Matching on ADOS module is a subtler control than most studies apply: module assignment depends on expressive language level, so matching on it partially equates the groups on language, which for a non-verbal-behaviour classifier removes an obvious alternative explanation. The comparison group is nonetheless typically developing rather than developmentally delayed, so age and module matching cannot equate general developmental level - and best-estimate IQ, which is measured, is not reported as matched and correlates with the model output.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Clinical diagnosis under DSM-5, corroborated by gold-standard instruments (ADOS-G or ADOS-2) administered as part of an established longitudinal cohort study, with cohort recruitment procedures documented in three cited prior publications. Comparison children were screened not only for known neurological or psychiatric illness but also for autism in any first-degree relative - a criterion stricter than nearly any other study in this corpus, since it excludes children carrying familial liability who might show subthreshold features and thereby blur the contrast. Ethics approval from the Faculty of Medicine of Geneva University, written informed parental consent for all children, and separate explicit consent for the identifiable figure images.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Comprehensive and, unusually, used analytically rather than descriptively. ADOS calibrated severity scores for total, social affect and restricted/repetitive behaviour; VABS-II Adaptive Behavior Composite with communication, socialisation, daily-living and motor subdomains; and a Best Estimate IQ constructed to combine 'the most representative cognitive functioning measures for each child', since instruments varied with age and with each child's ability to attend demanding tasks - a pragmatic solution to a real problem in toddler cognitive assessment, and one that is documented rather than glossed. All three feed the validation analyses. Comorbidities are not described for the autistic group.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: test whether a network trained purely on non-verbal social interaction, represented as skeletal motion, can differentiate autistic from typically developing children - explicitly framed against prior digital phenotyping that focused on 'relatively isolated behaviors elicited by largely controlled prompts'. Main findings: 80.9% accuracy (precision 0.784, recall 0.854, specificity 0.765, F1 0.818) on 68 held-out children; 80.2% on a further 101 autistic children; ~70% from 10 minutes of video, with 100% within-child prediction consistency from a random 10-minute segment for half the autistic sample; robustness to different rooms, examiners and cameras; ASD probability correlated with ADOS severity (total 0.451, social affect 0.509, repetitive behaviours 0.409), inversely with adaptive functioning (-0.444) and IQ (-0.283); and 15 of 27 ADOS items significantly related after Bonferroni correction, predominantly non-verbal, confirmed by a permutation-tested PLS-C latent component (p = 0.001).
custom_fields.RQ2.2: University of Geneva, Switzerland, within an ongoing longitudinal study of early autism development. The assessments were not staged for this analysis - they are the cohort's routine clinical ADOS sessions, conducted 'in several different rooms', by 'different examiners', and 'filmed with different camera systems'. That heterogeneity is the study's most under-appreciated methodological asset: where other work in this corpus achieves high accuracy under a single fixed acquisition setup and therefore cannot distinguish diagnostic signal from site signature, here the acquisition varies within both classes, so camera, room and examiner cannot serve as proxies for group. The authors report classification robustness to this variability explicitly in supplementary analysis and treat it as evidence for generalisability rather than as noise to be apologised for.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: The ADOS assessment itself, filmed end to end and averaging 42 minutes - not a purpose-built task. Only Modules Toddler, 1 and 2 were used, on the stated grounds that these are conducted while moving around a room with attractive toys and demand less language, whereas Modules 3 and 4 are table-based and discussion-heavy. The paradigm's key property is that it requires no new protocol, instrumentation or examiner training: any clinic that already videotapes ADOS sessions holds the raw material. Against that, it inherits a structural feature the paper does not examine - the ADOS is an interactive assessment in which a trained examiner actively presses for social behaviours and adapts to the child's responses, so the recorded scene is a joint product of child and clinician, and the video contains the examiner and frequently a caregiver as well.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional analysis of data acquired within a longitudinal cohort; no longitudinal modelling is performed here, though the parent study follows children over time and the authors position the measure as suitable for tracking development. Ethics are reported in full: approval by the Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Medicine of Geneva University, methods stated to conform to that institution's guidelines and regulations, informed written consent obtained from a parent or legal guardian for every child, and separate explicit consent for publication of identifying images from both the adults and the guardian of the child appearing in Figure 1. The privacy engineering is stronger still: reducing video to skeletons on a black background was adopted partly 'to ensure de-identification of the persons involved', so the analytic representation is itself the anonymisation - among the few instances in this corpus where sensitive video data are handled by design rather than by assurance.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Deliberately minimal on the acquisition side. OpenPose 'uses a simple 2D camera input not requiring any external markers or sensors, thus allowing the retrospective analysis of videos' and is 'immune to variations in resolutions and setting' - so no motion capture suits, markers, depth sensors or calibrated rigs, and existing archives become usable. Analytically: OpenPose COCO model with 18 keypoints (13 body, 5 facial); VGG16 pretrained on ImageNet; a 512-unit LSTM; rmsprop with categorical cross-entropy; training on the Geneva Baobab HPC cluster across RTX 2080Ti, Titan X and Quadro P1000 GPUs; GraphPad Prism v.8 and SPSS v.25 for statistics, both with URLs. The contrast with the marker-based and depth-camera motor studies elsewhere in this corpus is the point - equivalent or better accuracy from ordinary video.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong on the pipeline, with one class of omission. Reported: OpenPose model variant and keypoint count; background removal; the decision to compute feature vectors from image output rather than raw coordinates, with the stated purpose of invariance to rigid-body and affine transformation; downsampling from 696x554 to 320x240; 5-second segmentation with the selection justified by validation loss against 10 and 15 seconds; full VGG16 layer geometry; LSTM size and both dropout rates; optimiser, loss, batch size, epochs and the 80-20 internal split; the least-validation-loss checkpointing rule; the 0.5 threshold on averaged ASD probability; the sliding-window procedure with its 20-second start and 20-second step; every Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold; and the PLS-C decomposition with its 1000 permutations and 1000 bootstrap resamples. Video-level statistics are tabulated (68/68/101 videos, 47.8/48.7/50.0 hours, ~505 segments per video). Missing: no code or model weights release, no data availability statement in the extracted text, no random seeds, and - the substantive gap - no statement of how many people appear per frame or whether any person-selection was applied to OpenPose's multi-person output, which is exactly the detail needed to know whose movement the classifier is reading.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The study's weakest aspect: there is no limitations section, and the Discussion is uniformly positive. Only one caveat is stated anywhere - that 'the current level of analysis prevents us from drawing solid conclusions on what is represented in the NN' - and it is offered in support of the future-work agenda rather than as a constraint on the claims. Four issues go unaddressed. OpenPose extracts keypoints for all persons present and the videos contain examiner and often caregiver alongside the child, so the model may be reading clinician behaviour, which is systematically different when a clinician is eliciting from a child who does not respond; nothing in the paper isolates the child. The clinical-validity correlations are computed across a mixed two-group sample where severity is near-floor in one group, so they largely re-express the group difference rather than demonstrating within-group grading. ASD probability correlates inversely with IQ and adaptive functioning, raising a developmental-level confound that is reported without comment. And the single null in the entire correlation table is the VABS-II motor subdomain (-0.186, p = 0.066) - the domain a pose-based classifier would most be expected to track - which passes without remark. Testing Set 2 is also presented as endorsing 'the model's stability' without noting that a single-class sample cannot detect loss of specificity.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Two concrete and well-motivated directions. Add a spatio-temporal attention mechanism 'to allow knowledge on the specific elements in space and time used to inform the diagnosis process in the network' - which, if it also resolved which person's skeleton drives the decision, would address the study's main unexamined confound. And perform fine-grained annotation along the non-verbal continuum for the behaviours that contributed most, specifically 'the precise annotation of the incidence of communicative gestures, shared affective states, atypical social overtures', to establish what the network learned and to build a measure more sensitive than a 3- or 4-point clinical scale. The broader agenda is finer-grained digital phenotyping able to process data 'at the spatio-temporal resolution that is off limits to human coding', to uncover manifestations not previously evidenced and to define subtypes for more precise clinical action.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Non-verbal social interaction taken as a global pattern rather than as an inventory of separable behaviours - the study's central conceptual commitment. The stated target is 'global patterns of atypical postures and movements, fewer gestures used and often decoupled from visual contact, facial affect, speech', with the emphasis on decoupling: the claim is that autistic non-verbal behaviour differs less in the presence or absence of individual acts than in how gesture, gaze, posture and affect are coordinated with one another and with the partner. That is a behavioural construct which single-behaviour paradigms cannot in principle capture, and it justifies both the whole-assessment input and the temporal modelling. The post-hoc symptom analysis supports the framing empirically: the items that tracked model output most strongly were integration of gaze with other behaviours (0.591), pointing (0.540) and unusual eye contact (0.500) - coordination items rather than frequency items.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single-modality by design, and the design is an argument. Sound is discarded, faces are discarded, appearance and scene are discarded, and what remains is 2D skeletal motion alone. The authors' case is that this isolates the non-verbal channel cleanly, and it is strengthened by the symptom analysis: of 27 ADOS items, the 15 that tracked model output were predominantly non-verbal, while the lowest-loading items on the PLS-C latent component were the verbal ones - immediate echolalia and stereotyped language - which the authors correctly attribute to a largely pre-verbal sample rather than to a modelling failure. Their handling of intonation, the one vocal item that loaded highly on a model that cannot hear, is the most careful piece of reasoning in the paper: rather than claiming the network recovered prosody, they explain that atypical intonation occurs in more severely affected, minimally verbal children who simultaneously score higher on atypical social overtures, atypical social response and undirected vocalisation, so the correlation runs through severity rather than through sound. Multi-person fusion is present but unexamined - skeletons of child, examiner and caregiver enter the same input without separation.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A CNN-LSTM action-recognition architecture - VGG16 for per-frame spatial encoding, a 512-unit LSTM for temporal dependency within 5-second windows - selected because it 'previously showed a good performance in video-based action classification'. The choice matches the construct: if what distinguishes the groups is the temporal coordination of non-verbal behaviours rather than their static configuration, a model without temporal structure could not capture it. The authors report that the final architecture 'was obtained upon testing various configurations', with the alternatives shown in supplementary Figure S2, and that 5-second segments beat 10- and 15-second segments on validation loss - so architecture and segment length were both selected on the internal validation split rather than on the held-out children, which is the correct separation.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: The most consequential representational decision in the corpus: rendered skeletons on a black background, with the background removed entirely. This forecloses whole classes of confound that demonstrably affect other studies here - clinic decor, lighting, camera model, image resolution, clothing, and the facial appearance that group-specific recording conditions can encode. It simultaneously delivers de-identification, which the authors name as a co-equal motivation. Two further choices support generalisation: features are computed from rendered image output rather than raw keypoint coordinates, explicitly 'to obtain feature vectors invariant to a rigid body and affine transformations', so a child positioned differently relative to the camera is not thereby a different input; and downsampling to 320x240 keeps the representation coarse. The residual limitation is that the rendering includes every person OpenPose detects, so the representation is of the interaction scene rather than of the child.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1 on the balanced held-out set - a complete set for a binary task, and one that shows the model is not trading sensitivity for specificity (0.854 against 0.765, the most balanced profile among the higher-accuracy studies in this corpus). Two additional evaluations go beyond the standard panel and are more informative than any of them. Accuracy as a function of input video length quantifies the deployment tradeoff directly, showing ~70% at 10 minutes rising to 81% at full length - a dose-response curve for evidence, which no other study here provides. And prediction consistency within an individual, reported as the cumulative incidence of the segment length needed for 100% stable class attribution across randomly drawn windows, measures whether a single child would receive the same answer twice - a reliability question distinct from accuracy and one that matters more for a screening tool than the point estimate does. Missing: no confidence intervals on any figure, no confusion matrix, and no significance test against a trivial baseline such as age.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No internal interpretability - no attention, no saliency, no layer analysis - and the authors state the limitation plainly: 'the current level of analysis prevents us from drawing solid conclusions on what is represented in the NN'. What replaces it is external validation against clinical ratings, executed with more statistical care than any comparable analysis in the corpus. Correlations against ADOS severity, VABS-II and best-estimate IQ are Bonferroni-corrected at explicitly stated thresholds (p < 0.025, p < 0.013, p < 0.002 for the 27-item analysis). Recognising that ADOS items are collinear and that 27 separate tests would be the wrong instrument regardless of correction, the authors then run a Partial Least Squares Correlation with 1000 permutations to test the latent component and 1000 bootstrap resamples to establish salience stability - a multivariate treatment that yields a single significant component (p = 0.001) rather than a list of individually surviving items. The resulting picture is coherent: non-verbal coordination items load highest, verbal items lowest. The inference is nonetheless indirect - it establishes that model output covaries with clinically rated non-verbal atypicality, not that the network computes it, and the correlations are inflated by being taken across two groups whose severity distributions barely overlap.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The corpus's reference implementation of correct validation for a segment-generating modality. Three properties matter. Participant-wise partition: the 136 children are split 68/68 into training and Testing Set 1, matched on diagnosis, age, gender and ADOS module, so no child's frames appear on both sides - and matching the partitions on covariates, not merely the groups, is a refinement almost nothing else here applies. Participant-level aggregation: the network trains and predicts on 5-second segments (~505 per video, ~34,000 in training), but every segment prediction within a video is averaged into one ASD probability per child before any metric is computed, so the reported 80.9% is over 68 children and not over 34,000 clips. This is precisely the correction that Cilia had to apply retrospectively, watching image-level accuracy of ~90% fall to ~71% at participant level, and applying it by construction is what makes this figure comparable to a clinical one. Hyperparameter selection is confined to an 80-20 split inside the training set, with the least-validation-loss checkpoint carried forward. Two limits persist. Testing Set 2, though larger, contains only autistic children and comes from the same cohort, so it estimates sensitivity in a slightly older sample rather than replicating externally - no independent site or cohort is tested. And the covariate matching does not extend to cognitive level: best-estimate IQ is measured, differs between a typically developing and an autistic group as a matter of course, and correlates with the model's output at -0.283, so some portion of the separation may reflect general developmental level rather than autism specifically. No leave-one-site-out or examiner-held-out analysis addresses the parallel possibility that examiner behaviour contributes.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No keyword list appears in the extracted text. The operative vocabulary is 'digital phenotyping', '2D pose estimation', 'deep neural network', 'non-verbal social interaction' and 'automated screening' - a framing that positions the work within clinical digital phenotyping rather than computer vision, notwithstanding that the machinery is entirely the latter.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Scientific Reports 11:15069 (2021), doi 10.1038/s41598-021-94378-z - a broad-scope journal reaching both clinical and computational readerships. The authorship is genuinely interdisciplinary and the division of labour shows in the paper: the Psychiatry Department at the University of Geneva supplies the cohort, the gold-standard clinical measures and the ADOS-item interpretation; AIcrowd supplies the deep learning; and the Geneva School of Economics and Management and Citizen Cyber Lab supply the scalability framing. Two authors are marked as contributing equally, one clinical and one computational. That composition explains why this study alone in the corpus combines competent deep learning with full clinical characterisation, correct partitioning and Bonferroni-corrected multivariate validation - most papers here have one side of that expertise or the other.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021 (received March, accepted July). The framing is the standard early-detection argument but stated with unusual precision and with quantities attached: autism is detectable at 14 months and with high certainty before two years, yet over 70% of affected children are not diagnosed before 51 months; children diagnosed before age two can gain up to 20 IQ points over the following year, while those diagnosed after four 'will not show any substantial cognitive gain even with adequate intervention'. That last figure converts the diagnostic delay from an inconvenience into a quantified loss and is the strongest version of the early-detection premise in this corpus. The critique of existing tools is equally specific - most screening tests are questionnaire-based, perform with low to moderate accuracy, and are 'prone to recall and subjectivity bias'. What most distinguishes the paper's positioning, though, is its critique of the prior computational literature rather than of clinical practice: it names the field's dominant paradigm - single-feature extraction from controlled prompts - as the limitation to be overcome, and argues that a construct defined by the decoupling of behaviours from one another cannot be measured by indexing those behaviours one at a time. The Discussion is also careful about scope in a way few papers here are, stating that diagnosis 'is unlikely to be set on the track of automated performance before long' and positioning the contribution as screening that catalyses referral.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Simeoli R; Milano N; Rega A; Marocco D
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: School-age children with autism, predominantly without intellectual disability
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Fine motor kinematics (touchscreen dragging trajectories)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Test whether the kinematics of an ordinary dragging movement, captured incidentally while a child performs a standard cognitive assessment, carry an autism-specific motor signature - so that assessment could yield a quantitative motor marker at no additional cost in time or child burden
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification, with autistic children recruited from a rehabilitation centre and comparison children from a primary school
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session per child; only the first five items of each of five Leiter-3 subtests were analysed
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A bespoke Unity/C# app reproducing the Leiter-3 nonverbal intelligence battery exactly - the same tasks in the same order under the original administration rules - across five cognitive domains: figure-ground (identify parts of figures within a complex stimulus, with invisible placeholders inside a target image), figure completion (recognise a whole object from randomly arranged parts), classification analogies (complete sequences of geometric shapes and matrices of increasing complexity), sequential order (place figures in logical order) and visual patterns (discriminate and match pictures). In every subtest but figure-ground the child drags moving cards from the bottom of the screen into placeholders at the top, with two to eight cards and placeholders per task and distractors present. Tasks ascend in complexity with progressively more distracting stimuli, requiring increasing attention and decision-making
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Naples, Italy - autistic children assessed at the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center, comparison children at a primary school
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Diagnosis under DSM-5 clinical criteria together with the ADOS-2, made by 'qualified doctors and professionals in the sector' who 'have no affiliation with our laboratory or our research' - an explicit statement of diagnostic independence from the research team that few studies in this corpus make. Comparison children were excluded for suspected signs of autism, developmental abnormalities, or current or past psychiatric or neurological disorder
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Not reported anywhere in the paper - neither counts nor proportions for either group
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: 'No existing comorbidities' was an inclusion criterion for the autistic group and 'No specific comorbidity was reported'. All participants had normal vision and no sensory or motor deficit - a notable exclusion given that the outcome is a motor measure. Any child whose clinician or teacher was uncertain about diagnosis or health was excluded
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Autistic participants were receiving ongoing psychomotor and speech therapy at the Neapolisanit Center; medication is not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: No ADOS severity scores, CARS or SRS are reported, despite the ADOS-2 having been administered for diagnosis - so severity was measured but not carried into the analysis. Cognitive level is reported only as an IQ range: 59-109 for the autistic group with six children between 59 and 70, and 74-110 for the comparison group. No means or standard deviations are given for either
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes, by exclusion criteria - suspected autism signs, developmental abnormalities and psychiatric or neurological history all excluded - though no standardised screening instrument is named
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Approximately - 7.0 versus 6.67 years - but no statistical test of the difference is reported and matching is not claimed as a design procedure
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Cannot be assessed; sex is not reported for either group
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Established by exclusion criteria applied through school and clinician report rather than by a standardised screening instrument
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Touchscreen coordinate time series
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: The app logged the position over time of every stimulus on screen and of the child's finger at 40 Hz, always tagged with which task was being performed. Coordinate streams were segmented into 'finite' trajectories, each running from the first tap to the lift of the finger at the end of a drag. Twelve features were computed per trajectory using the RStudio traj package and then averaged within task, giving one feature vector per child per task. To these were appended five one-hot task-identity variables encoding which of the five cognitive domains was being performed, 'in order to provide implicit information about the difficulty level of the task performed'. Only the first five items of each subtest were analysed, chosen because all participants performed them correctly - a deliberate step to limit cognitive interference - and the demonstration item FG1 was excluded because the examiner may have moved the cards
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Android 6.0 tablet, 9.6-inch screen, 1280x800 resolution, 60 Hz refresh; bespoke app in Unity and C#; touch sampling at 40 Hz; RStudio with the traj package for trajectory features; Leiter-3 materials supplied by Stoelting Co.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Touchscreen kinematics from 60 children; no repository is named
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No repository, but a data availability statement is present: raw data 'will be made available by the authors, without undue reservation'
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Yes - on request from the authors
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Coordinate data rather than video or audio, so intrinsically low-identifiability. Ethics approval from the Ethical Committee of Psychological Research of the Department of Humanities, University of Naples Federico II; written informed consent from legal guardians
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Kinematic and geometric trajectory descriptors plus task-identity indicators
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Twelve trajectory features: mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation of speed; mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation of acceleration; STH, a straightness index defined as the ratio of the straight-line distance between a trajectory's start and end points to its actual length, ranging 0 to 1 with 1 a straight line; DC, directional change over time, used as an index of nonlinearity; sdDC, the standard deviation of directional change, used as a measure of irregularity; and MeanLength, the average number of finite trajectories per task. Five additional one-hot variables encode the subtest. The design is economical - twelve interpretable quantities rather than hundreds - and each has a stated physical meaning
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: RStudio traj package (Leffondree et al. 2004; Sylvestre et al. 2006)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, by sequential removal
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: The 'Improved stepwise selection 1' procedure of Olden et al. (2004): starting from all 12 inputs, each is removed one at a time and the change in accuracy, sensitivity and specificity recorded; the variable with least impact is permanently removed and the process repeats until inputs are exhausted, yielding a full importance ordering. The five task-identity variables were always retained
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: In increasing order of importance, variables were removed as: sdAcc, STH, sdSpeed, sdDC, MaxSpeed, DC, MeanRow, MinSpeed, MeanSpeed, MinAcc, MaxAcc, MeanAcc. The last-removed - mean, maximum and minimum acceleration and mean speed - are therefore the most important, and the authors conclude that 'variables related to speed and acceleration of the finger seems more important than other measures, such as the straightness (STH) and the coherence (DC) of the entire trajectory'. Performance degraded gently until seven variables had been removed (78% accuracy) and then fell sharply to 52%
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Autistic children's trajectories were less straight (lower STH) with more changes of direction (higher DC), shorter on average (lower MeanLength, described as more fragmented), and simultaneously faster at their peaks and slower at their troughs - higher MeanSpeed and MaxSpeed but lower MinSpeed, higher MaxAcceleration but lower MinAcceleration - producing markedly larger standard deviations for both speed and acceleration. The authors read this as over- and under-compensation consistent with disrupted prospective guidance of goal-directed movement
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Shallow feedforward neural network on hand-engineered kinematic features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Feedforward multilayer perceptron with 17 input neurons, one hidden layer and 2 output neurons; tanh activation in the hidden layer, softmax output, Adam optimiser, sparse categorical cross-entropy loss, learning rate 0.01, Xavier weight initialisation, 500 training epochs. Hidden-layer width was chosen by grid search with cross-validation in a descending search from 10 neurons; accuracies were comparable from 10 down to 5 and degraded below 5, so 5 was selected on the stated principle that simpler networks overfit less. Features were standardised by mean-centring and division by standard deviation
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Ten-fold cross-validation with five repetitions over a dataset of 1,500 samples formed as 60 subjects x 25 tasks, described as 'randomized between subjects and tasks', with each fold taking 10% for testing and 90% for training 'regardless of the number of ASD or TD subjects in the test or training set'. Cross-validated accuracy was 88 +/- 3%. The headline 93% comes from a subsequent step: 'we used the best trained model across the 10-fold', that is the single best-performing fold model, on which sensitivity, specificity, the ROC curve and the entire feature-importance analysis were then computed
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and an ROC curve; accuracy across training epochs with mean and 90% bootstrapped confidence intervals across replications; and accuracy, sensitivity and specificity as functions of the number of retained features
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Ten-fold cross-validation with five repetitions: 88 +/- 3% accuracy. Best single fold model: 93% accuracy, sensitivity 0.87, specificity 0.98. Feature-removal curve: performance degrades slowly to 78% by the seventh removal, then falls steeply to 52% - chance - with a single feature. The 93%/0.87/0.98 figures are the ones reported in the abstract, the Discussion and the Conclusion; the 88 +/- 3% cross-validated figure appears once in the Results
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Kinematic features of ordinary dragging movements, logged at 40 Hz while children completed a digital Leiter-3 battery, supported classification of autism at 88 +/- 3% under ten-fold cross-validation and 93% for the best fold. The motor picture is coherent and clinically interpretable: autistic children's drags were shorter, less straight, more frequently redirected, and far more variable in speed and acceleration - fast at their peaks and slow at their troughs - which the authors interpret as repeated online correction consequent on impaired prospective motor control. Speed and acceleration measures carried more of the classification than the geometric straightness and directional-change indices, and performance was robust to removing up to six of twelve features. The practical claim is that the measure is free: it is extracted from a cognitive assessment the child is already taking, on consumer hardware, with no additional task, sensor or examiner time.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Shorter and more fragmented drag trajectories, lower straightness, more directional change, and much wider dispersion of speed and acceleration within a movement
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Replicate on a larger sample and test whether the algorithm remains predictive without retraining; control IQ explicitly rather than only limiting its influence by task selection; and, most importantly, include other neurodevelopmental conditions - the authors note that the motor signature 'may overlap with other disorders, such as attention deficit disorder, motor coordination disturbance, or general intellectual disabilities' and that sensory integration dysfunction, the mechanism they invoke, is also found in ADHD, so specificity to autism is untested. They also aim to extend the method to younger children
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A well-motivated and unusually economical study undermined by two validation choices, only one of which the authors appear to recognise. The strengths are real: diagnosis by DSM-5 plus ADOS-2 from clinicians explicitly unaffiliated with the research team; twelve interpretable features rather than an undirected feature dump; a principled feature-importance procedure with a published provenance; a coherent theoretical account linking the observed kinematics to prospective motor control; deployment on a consumer tablet with the measurement piggybacked on an assessment the child is taking anyway; and a genuinely thoughtful control for cognitive load, restricting analysis to the first five items of each subtest because all children completed those correctly, so trajectory differences cannot be attributed to some children failing the task. The limitations section is candid about sample size, the IQ confound and - most valuably - the possibility that the motor signature is shared with ADHD, developmental coordination disorder and intellectual disability rather than specific to autism. Against this, the validation has a structural flaw. The 1,500 samples are 60 children each contributing 25 task-level vectors, and the folds are drawn at random across subjects and tasks: the paper states the split proceeds 'regardless of the number of ASD or TD subjects in the test or training set', which means a given child's other 22 or 23 vectors sit in the training set while two or three are tested. Since the features are per-child averages of that child's habitual movement dynamics, the model can identify the individual and recover the label from that, and no participant-level split is reported anywhere. The second issue is the reporting choice: ten-fold cross-validation gave 88 +/- 3%, and 93% is the best of the ten fold models, selected after the fact and then used for the sensitivity, specificity, ROC and all feature-importance analyses. It is 93% that appears in the abstract, in the Discussion's summary and in the Conclusion, while 88 +/- 3% appears once. A third, smaller point: the Discussion's descriptive narrative dwells on straightness, directional change and trajectory length, but the study's own importance ranking places STH, sdDC and DC among the least useful variables and acceleration among the most - so the interpretation foregrounds features the model found least informative. Reporting gaps compound this: sex is not reported for either group, IQ is given only as a range with no means or standard deviations, ADOS-2 was administered but no severity scores are reported, and the recruitment asymmetry - autistic children from a rehabilitation centre where they receive ongoing psychomotor therapy, comparison children from a primary school - introduces a setting and familiarity difference that is never examined.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 30, both explicitly sized: 30 children with a DSM-5 and ADOS-2 diagnosis of autism recruited from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center, and 30 typically developing children recruited from a primary school. No other-diagnosis or developmentally-delayed comparison group, which the authors themselves identify as the key gap, noting that the motor signature 'may overlap with other disorders, such as attention deficit disorder, motor coordination disturbance, or general intellectual disabilities'. The two groups come from structurally different settings - a clinic where the autistic children receive ongoing psychomotor and speech therapy, versus a school - so group membership is confounded with familiarity with clinical testing, with the examiner's setting, and potentially with prior therapeutic work on exactly the fine-motor skills being measured. This is not discussed.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with autism', 'autistic children', 'ASD children', 'individuals with autism', 'ASD individuals', 'ASD participants', 'ASD group', against 'typically developing children', 'TD group', 'their typically developing peers', 'neurotypical group'. Person-first and identity-first are used interchangeably, sometimes in the same sentence. The clinical vocabulary is dated in one respect: intellectual disability is described as 'mild mental retardation' with a 2016 WHO citation, a term already superseded in DSM-5 and ICD-11 at the time of writing. Autism itself is framed in deficit terms throughout - 'communication impairment, a lack of social interaction' - though the theoretical framing is comparatively sympathetic, drawing on embodied cognition and on Sinha's account in which stereotyped behaviour is a rational response to an unpredictable world rather than a symptom to be suppressed.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Autistic group: 30 children, mean age 7 years (SD 1.4), IQ range 59-109 on the Leiter-3, with six children between 59 and 70. Comparison group: 30 children, mean age 6 years 8 months (SD 1), IQ range 74-110. Age is close but no test of the difference is reported and matching is not claimed as a procedure. Two reporting gaps are consequential. Sex is not reported for either group anywhere in the paper - no counts, no proportions, no statement that groups were balanced - which is a complete omission of a variable that affects both autism prevalence and fine motor development at these ages. And IQ is given only as a range, with no mean or standard deviation, so the extent of the cognitive difference between groups cannot be quantified even though the authors concede it is a confound: the autistic range extends 15 points lower at the bottom and the distributions within those ranges are unknown. The comparison group's lower bound of 74 is itself notable, sitting in the borderline range.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Among the better ascertainments in the corpus for a study of this size. Diagnosis required both DSM-5 clinical criteria and the ADOS-2, and was made by 'qualified doctors and professionals in the sector' who 'have no affiliation with our laboratory or our research' - an explicit assertion of independence between the diagnosing clinicians and the research team that almost no other study here makes, and which forecloses the possibility of diagnostic classification being influenced by knowledge of the study hypothesis. Comparison children were excluded for suspected autism signs, developmental abnormalities, or current or past psychiatric or neurological disorder, though the screening was by clinician or teacher judgement rather than a standardised instrument, and any child about whose diagnosis or health a clinician or teacher was uncertain was excluded outright. The one waste is that the ADOS-2 was administered but its severity scores are never reported or used.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Partial. IQ was assessed with the Leiter-3, a nonverbal intelligence test appropriate for this population and administered in its original form for the assessment, but reported only as a range per group. Comorbidity was handled by exclusion rather than measurement: 'no existing comorbidities' was an inclusion criterion, no specific comorbidity was reported, and all participants were required to have normal vision and no sensory or motor deficit - the last a genuinely relevant control for a study whose outcome is a fine-motor measure, and one that also narrows the sample away from the substantial proportion of autistic children who do have motor impairment. No adaptive functioning measure, no language level, and no ADOS severity scores despite the instrument being used for diagnosis. Medication is not reported, though ongoing psychomotor and speech therapy is.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: determine whether the kinematics of a simple dragging movement, recorded incidentally during a digital cognitive assessment, can classify autism, and describe the motor features that differentiate the groups. Main findings: 88 +/- 3% accuracy under ten-fold cross-validation with five repetitions, and 93% accuracy with sensitivity 0.87 and specificity 0.98 for the best fold model; classification degraded only gradually as features were removed, reaching 78% with five features and chance with one; speed and acceleration measures dominated the importance ranking over straightness and directional change; and autistic trajectories were shorter, less straight, more frequently redirected and far more variable in speed and acceleration.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Naples, Italy, across two different settings by group: autistic children at the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center, which provided 'the clinical ward for the experimentation' and where those children also receive ongoing psychomotor and speech therapy; comparison children at a primary school. The physical arrangement is specified precisely and identically for both - child seated at a table 65-70 cm high adjusted for age, experimenter opposite, tablet within 20 cm of the table edge - which controls posture and reach geometry, the most obvious physical determinants of drag kinematics. What is not controlled is the setting asymmetry itself. Recruiting cases from a therapy centre and comparisons from a school means group membership is entangled with familiarity with clinical assessment and with prior therapeutic exposure to fine-motor practice, either of which could shift drag dynamics independently of diagnosis.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A digital reimplementation of the Leiter-3 nonverbal intelligence battery, built in Unity and C#, playing 'exactly the same tasks of the Leiter-3, presented in the same order' under the original administration rules, with the examiner advancing subtests at the standard error threshold. Five subtests span figure-ground, figure completion, classification analogies, sequential order and visual patterns, with two to eight draggable cards and placeholders per item and distractors present, ascending in complexity. Three features of the design deserve note. The paradigm is entirely dual-purpose: the child takes a cognitive assessment they would take anyway and the motor data are a by-product, so there is no added task burden and the approach is retrofittable to any clinic already using the Leiter-3. The nonverbal character of the instrument makes it usable across language levels, which matters for autism specifically. And the cognitive-load control is carefully reasoned - only the first five items of each subtest were analysed 'since all participants correctly performed at least the first five items', so kinematic differences cannot be attributed to some children struggling with the cognitive demand, and the demonstration item FG1 was excluded because the examiner may have moved cards during it. The five one-hot task-identity variables then give the network explicit information about which cognitive context each movement came from.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, one session per child, no follow-up, though the authors state a future aim of applying the method to younger children. Ethics are reported: approval by the Ethical Committee of Psychological Research of the Department of Humanities, University of Naples Federico II, with written informed consent from legal guardians obtained before the study. The data are coordinate streams rather than video or audio, so re-identification risk is intrinsically low, and a data availability statement commits to sharing raw data 'without undue reservation'.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Deliberately commodity hardware: an Android 6.0 tablet with a 9.6-inch 1280x800 screen at 60 Hz refresh, dimensions given to the millimetre, with touch sampling at 40 Hz - so 40 coordinate pairs per second. No motion capture, markers, depth cameras or wearable sensors, which is the study's practical argument: the same measurement in the optical motion-tracking literature it cites requires a laboratory. Software is bespoke (Unity, C#), analysis uses RStudio with the traj package with its two source citations, and the Leiter-3 materials were supplied by Stoelting Co. The 40 Hz sampling rate is a meaningful constraint that goes unremarked: it bounds how finely acceleration - the feature family the importance analysis identifies as most discriminative - can be estimated from a differenced coordinate stream.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Good on instrumentation and modelling, thin on data structure. Reported: tablet model, screen size, resolution, refresh rate and sampling frequency; the seating geometry; the task battery with its five domains, item structure and administration rule; the definition of a finite trajectory; all twelve features with formal definitions including the STH ratio and the DC/sdDC interpretation; the traj package with citations; feature standardisation; the full network specification (17-5-2, tanh, softmax, Adam, learning rate 0.01, Xavier initialisation, sparse categorical cross-entropy, 500 epochs); the grid-search range for hidden units and the criterion for choosing five; the cross-validation scheme; and the feature-removal procedure with its source. Missing or ambiguous: the number of trajectories per child, the aggregation from 25 tasks to 1,500 samples is stated but the fold-assignment rule is described only as random 'regardless' of subject composition, so the reader must infer that subjects span folds; no code release; no random seeds; and no participant-level performance breakdown that would allow the segment-versus-subject question to be resolved from the reported numbers. A data availability statement is present.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Substantially candid on the scientific limitations and silent on the methodological one. Acknowledged, in a dedicated passage: the small sample, with replication needed 'to validate this method on a new not trained dataset' and an explicit question of whether the algorithm 'could remain predictive also for a greater sample or if it requires to be retrained'; the IQ confound, stated directly as 'we were not able to exclude intelligence as confounders', with the mitigation that most participants were high functioning and that analysing only universally-passed items limits cognitive interference; and - the most valuable admission in the paper - that the motor signature 'may overlap with other disorders, such as attention deficit disorder, motor coordination disturbance, or general intellectual disabilities', reinforced by the observation that sensory integration dysfunction, their explanatory mechanism, is also found in ADHD, so 'future extensions of this work should include other neurodevelopmental disabilities in order to verify the specificity of these motor signatures for ASD'. Not acknowledged: that the cross-validation folds split task-level samples rather than children, so the same child's data appears on both sides; that the headline 93% is the best of ten fold models while the cross-validated estimate is 88 +/- 3%; that hidden-layer width, feature ranking and the reported operating point were all selected on the same cross-validation used for reporting; and that cases and comparisons were recruited from systematically different settings.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Four directions, three of them named by the authors and one clearly implied. Replicate on a larger sample and determine whether the trained model transfers without retraining - a transfer question rather than a sample-size platitude. Control IQ explicitly as an independent variable rather than relying on task selection to suppress its influence. Include other neurodevelopmental conditions - ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, intellectual disability - to establish whether the signature is autism-specific rather than a general marker of atypical development; the authors give the mechanistic reason, that sensory integration dysfunction is not autism-specific. And extend the method to younger children, where earlier identification would matter most, which is where the motor-precursor literature they review predicts the signal should already be present.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: The kinematics of goal-directed dragging - how a finger travels from a card to a placeholder - decomposed into how fast (mean, max, min and SD of speed), how the speed changes (the same four for acceleration), how directly (STH straightness), how consistently in direction (DC and sdDC) and in how many separate pieces (MeanLength). The behaviour is not social and not autism-specific in its surface form; the claim is that autism manifests in the microstructure of any goal-directed movement because prospective motor control is impaired, which is why an arbitrary cognitive task can serve as the probe. The theoretical grounding is more developed than in most of this corpus, running from Kanner's original identification of disrupted movement patterns through Leary and Hill on motor-symptom links, the enactive mind account, Friston's predictive coding and Sinha's proposal that stereotypies are a response to an unpredictably 'magical' world - and the motor findings are read back into that frame as over- and under-compensation from interrupted feedforward control.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single-modality: touchscreen kinematics only.
