The paper nonetheless performs a within-modality combination that is worth noting - the network receives twelve kinematic features together with five one-hot task-identity variables, so movement is interpreted conditional on cognitive context rather than pooled across it, and the task variables 'were always provided to the ANN' and were never subject to the removal analysis. This is a defensible design given that different Leiter-3 subtests impose different spatial demands, but it has an unexamined consequence: because task identity is always available, the model can learn task-specific kinematic norms, and since the feature vectors are per-child per-task averages, the combination of task identity plus habitual movement dynamics is close to a subject fingerprint. No cross-modality fusion is attempted, and none is claimed.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A single small feedforward network - 17 inputs, one hidden layer of five tanh units, two softmax outputs - chosen for the stated reason that neural networks handle 'complex and nonlinear relationships between variables', which matches the paper's explicit epistemic position that no individual movement variable need differ between groups and that what is categorisable is 'the dynamic interaction of these features'. That position is argued rather than assumed, with a citation to Yarkoni and Westfall on prediction versus explanation, and it justifies choosing a predictive framework over group-difference testing. Model selection was equally restrained: a descending grid search from 10 hidden units found comparable accuracy down to 5 and degradation below, and 5 was chosen on the explicit principle that fewer hidden units reduce overfitting. Deliberate simplicity of this kind is rare in this corpus and is the right instinct for a 60-participant dataset; the difficulty is that it was verified against a cross-validation that does not hold participants out.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: One 17-dimensional vector per child per task: twelve kinematic features averaged over all finite trajectories in that task, plus five one-hot task indicators, yielding 60 x 25 = 1,500 rows. Two aspects of this construction determine what the results can mean. Averaging within task discards within-task variability and produces a stable per-child descriptor - which is exactly what makes each row informative about the individual as well as the group. And because every child contributes 25 such rows that share their individual movement characteristics, rows are strongly clustered within children; treating the 1,500 rows as exchangeable for the purpose of fold assignment is the analytic decision that undermines the headline figure. A representation of one vector per child would have given 60 rows and a much harder, but interpretable, problem.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and an ROC curve - an adequate panel, and the specificity/sensitivity asymmetry (0.98 versus 0.87) is reported rather than collapsed into accuracy. Two supplementary reporting choices are better than the corpus norm. Training-accuracy curves are shown with mean and 90% bootstrapped confidence intervals across all replications, so training stability is visible rather than asserted, and the authors state they 'checked that no overfitting is present in every fold'. And the feature-ablation curve reports accuracy, sensitivity and specificity jointly as a function of how many features are retained, which shows the graceful-then-sharp degradation pattern (78% at five features, 52% at one) and demonstrates that the result does not hinge on a single variable. What is missing bears directly on the headline: no confidence interval on the reported 93%, no confusion matrix, no per-fold table that would let a reader see the spread from which the best fold was drawn, and no comparison against a trivial baseline such as age or IQ - the latter especially relevant given that the authors concede IQ is an uncontrolled confound.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is pursued seriously and by an appropriate method. The stepwise-removal procedure of Olden et al. (2004) yields a complete importance ordering rather than a top-k list, and the accompanying curve shows how performance responds to progressive impoverishment of the input - more informative than a single importance ranking because it distinguishes redundant features from load-bearing ones. Boxplots of all twelve features by group then give the direction of every effect. The conclusions drawn are physically meaningful: speed and acceleration measures matter more than geometric straightness and directional coherence, and the movement picture that emerges - short, fragmented, non-straight trajectories with wide speed and acceleration excursions - is coherently linked to over- and under-compensation from disrupted prospective control, and cross-referenced to Anzulewicz's independent finding of greater impact force in autistic children's tablet interaction. There is one internal inconsistency: the Discussion's descriptive interpretation leads with STH, DC and MeanLength, but the study's own ranking removed STH second, sdDC fourth and DC sixth as the least impactful variables, while the acceleration measures the interpretation barely mentions were the last to be removed. The narrative therefore foregrounds the features the model found least useful. Both analyses were also run on the single best fold model rather than averaged across folds, so the ranking inherits that selection.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The study's decisive weakness, and the reason its numbers are not comparable to participant-level results elsewhere in this corpus. The dataset is 1,500 samples formed as 60 subjects x 25 tasks, explicitly 'randomized between subjects and tasks', and the folds are drawn so that 'for each fold, we take the 10% of the samples for testing and the remaining 90% for training, regardless of the number of ASD or TD subjects in the test or training set'. Every child therefore has roughly 22 or 23 of their 25 vectors in training whenever the remaining two or three are tested. Because each vector is an average of that child's habitual movement dynamics within a task, the network can identify the individual from their kinematic signature and recover the diagnosis from that identification rather than from any group-general motor property - the same mechanism Liaqat et al. diagnose explicitly in their own eye-tracking data and that Cilia quantified as a fall from ~90% to ~71% when the unit was corrected. No participant-held-out analysis is reported anywhere, so the magnitude of the inflation here is unknown. A second, independent issue concerns which number is reported: ten-fold cross-validation with five repetitions returned 88 +/- 3%, and the paper then states that 'for the successive analysis, we used the best trained model across the 10-fold', from which the 93% accuracy, 0.87 sensitivity, 0.98 specificity, ROC curve and complete feature-importance ordering are all derived. The best of ten is a maximum, not an estimate, and it is the figure carried into the abstract, the Discussion and the Conclusion while the cross-validated 88 +/- 3% appears once. Hidden-layer width was additionally selected on the same cross-validation. The compounded effect is that the reported operating characteristics come from a model chosen for performing best on data structurally related to what it was trained on.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, sensory-motor impairment, motion analysis, machine learning, classification, assessment technologies. The pairing of 'sensory-motor impairment' with 'assessment technologies' captures the paper's dual identity - a theoretical claim about embodied cognition and a practical claim about instrumenting existing clinical tools - and 'assessment technologies' rather than 'diagnosis' signals the intended scope correctly.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Frontiers in Psychology 12:635696 (2021), in the Health Psychology section, from the Department of Humanistic Studies at the University of Naples Federico II, the CNR Institute of Cognitive Sciences and Technologies, and the Neapolisanit rehabilitation centre. A psychology venue with a cognitive-science orientation rather than an engineering one, which is visible in the balance of the paper: the theoretical framing occupies more space than the model, the literature review traces motor abnormality in autism from Kanner forward, and the machine learning is deliberately modest. The clinical co-affiliation supplied the participants and the diagnostic pathway.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2021 (received November 2020, published May 2021). The framing is the standard critique of observational diagnosis - it 'requires a lot of time', relies on 'the interpretative skills of clinicians', and 'take a long time without being able to deliver an objective and shareable result' - but the paper adds a more specific diagnosis of the field's problem: 'one of the main gaps in the diagnosis of autism is related to the lack of a quantitative evaluation of the disorder; in fact, although the variability within the disorder is known, there is still no valid method to recognize and categorize these differences'. The target is therefore the absence of graded measurement rather than subjectivity as such. A second framing move is methodological and unusual for this corpus: the authors argue explicitly that classical group-difference statistics are the wrong instrument here, 'since several interactions of motion variables could, actually, affect the presumed typical autistic motor pattern, we cannot assume that there must necessarily be movement variables typical of autism', and cite Yarkoni and Westfall to justify a predictive rather than exploratory approach. That is a considered epistemic position rather than a default. The paper also positions itself in a specific lineage - Anzulewicz's iPad gameplay study with 262 features reaching 'up to 93% accuracy', Crippa's upper-limb kinematics at 96.7% - and its own 93% lands squarely on the number it cites, which the Discussion treats as convergent confirmation rather than as an occasion to ask whether the two studies share a validation design.

data_charting_rubrics.title: A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Han J; Jiang G; Ouyang G; Li X
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering, 30, 2003-2011
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Preschool children with autism, aged 3 to 6
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Multimodal - eye tracking (behavioural) fused with resting-state EEG (neurophysiological)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Test whether jointly modelling an internal neurophysiological signal and an external behavioural signal outperforms either alone, on the argument that autism 'is a complex and heterogeneous disease with abnormal manifestations from the cellular level to the behavioral level' so that no single modality can capture it - and specifically whether learned two-stage fusion beats naive feature concatenation
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification with a within-study ablation comparing two unimodal models, a feature-concatenation baseline and the proposed two-stage fusion model on identical data and folds
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session per child: at least five minutes of resting-state EEG, then a break, then two eye-tracking trials of about 30 seconds each
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Two distinct paradigms. EEG was recorded at rest with eyes open, the child seated comfortably in an armchair, usually accompanied by a caregiver, in a quiet room - so no task demand at all. Eye tracking used dynamic video stimuli drawn from the Chinese children's programme Tiger Qiao Hu depicting social interaction between a child and an adult, presented in two clips of about 30 seconds in random order, with a dynamic kitten and sound shown between trials to recapture attention. No response was required from the children at any point, which is what makes the protocol viable for 3-to-6-year-olds regardless of language or compliance
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Beijing, China. Typically developing children were recruited from a local kindergarten; the autistic children's recruitment site is not named beyond a reference to 'the school site' where reliable diagnostic information was limited. Ethics approval from the School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee of Beijing Normal University
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Stated as DSM-5 diagnostic confirmation, but immediately qualified: 'we had limited access to reliable information in the school site. Thus, the children were assessed by using the parent report on the Autism Behavior Checklist (ABC), Social Communication Questionnaire (SCQ), Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS), and Clancy Behavior Scale (CABS)'. The operative ascertainment for this study is therefore four parent-report screening questionnaires rather than a direct standardised observational assessment; no ADOS, ADI-R or clinician observation is reported. Comparison children were screened with ABC, SRS and SCQ completed by their teachers, and none reached the cut-off on any of the three
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Reported in Table I, not rendered in the extracted text; the stated age range is 3-6 years and group differences were tested with two-sample t-tests
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Reported in Table I, not rendered in the extracted text; no sex proportions appear in the running text
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Four parent-report instruments were administered to the autistic group - ABC, SCQ, SRS and CABS - with scores tabulated in Table I and group differences tested, so severity information exists but is used only for group description and is never related to model output
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes - ABC, SRS and SCQ completed by teachers, with no comparison child reaching the cut-off on any instrument
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd_controls: In Table I, not rendered in the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution_controls: In Table I, not rendered in the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Group differences in demographics were formally tested with two-independent-sample t-tests and reported with p values in Table I, though the values are not recoverable from the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not determinable from the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Screened on three standardised instruments by teachers, with no child reaching any cut-off
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: 128-channel resting-state EEG and eye-tracking gaze coordinates during dynamic social video
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: EEG: continuous eyes-open resting state recorded for at least five minutes at 1000 Hz from 128 Ag/AgCl passive electrodes (EGI), referenced online to Cz with impedances below 50 kOhm; preprocessed in EEGLAB with downsampling to 250 Hz, a 50 Hz notch, 0.5-45 Hz band-pass, segmentation into non-overlapping 4-second epochs, automated artifact detection covering eye movements, blinks, power supply, breathing, muscle, abrupt slopes and outliers, followed by visual inspection; channels exceeding 200 microvolts marked bad and interpolated, leaving 4.5 +/- 2.2 bad channels and 25.11 +/- 5.95 clean segments per child. Sixty-two electrodes were retained and grouped into ten regions. Eye tracking: Tobii TX300 at 300 Hz, screen 1024x768, viewing distance ~60 cm, five-point calibration required to pass with small error vectors before proceeding, Tobii fixation filter applied, gaps up to 100 ms filled by linear interpolation, binocular gaze averaged, and an inclusion threshold that all retained children had more than 70% screen-looking time
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Electrical Geodesics 128-channel Geodesic Sensor Net with Net Station; EEGLAB and MATLAB; Tobii TX300 eye tracker with the Tobii fixation filter; the DeepLearnToolbox MATLAB deep learning library, cited with its GitHub URL
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: A paired EEG and eye-tracking dataset from 90 preschool children; no release is described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not discussed beyond ethics. Approval from the School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee of Beijing Normal University, with informed consent obtained from all children with parental permission before enrollment
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Hand-engineered spectral, complexity and graph-theoretic EEG features, plus area-of-interest gaze statistics, then learned latent representations via denoising autoencoders
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: EEG, 125 features in three families. Relative power energy: mean relative power in delta (1-4 Hz), theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz), beta (13-30 Hz) and gamma (30-45 Hz) for each of ten brain regions, computed by FFT with a Hanning window on each 4-second epoch, giving 50 features - motivated by prior findings of reduced alpha and increased delta and theta power in autism. Multiscale entropy: sample entropy of coarse-grained series averaged over four scale ranges (1-5, 6-10, 11-15, 16-20) for each of ten regions, giving 40 features. Brain network: a 62-node graph with phase lag index as edge weight, from which seven global metrics - global efficiency, clustering coefficient, path length, normalised clustering coefficient, normalised path length, small-worldness and transitivity - are computed in each of five bands, giving 35 features. Eye tracking, 96 features: eight areas of interest (background, adult body, child body, adult eyes, child eyes, adult mouth, child mouth, joint attention) x six statistics (time to first fixation, fixations before, total fixation duration, fixation count, fixation duration, visit count) x two video clips. The AOI scheme is the analytically interesting part - separating adult from child, and eyes from mouth from body within each, plus an explicit joint-attention region, so the feature set encodes the specific social-attention distinctions the autism literature predicts
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: EEGLAB and MATLAB for EEG; the Tobii fixation filter for gaze; DeepLearnToolbox for the autoencoders
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No. No feature ranking, ablation over feature families, or attribution of any kind - the study's analytic attention is entirely on modality-level rather than feature-level contribution
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Modality-level ablation (EEG alone, eye tracking alone, naive concatenation, two-stage fusion) plus confusion-matrix decomposition and t-SNE visualisation of six feature spaces, but nothing that identifies which brain regions, frequency bands or areas of interest carry the signal
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None at feature level. At modality level, eye tracking outperformed EEG overall (86.67% versus 81.11%), and the confusion matrices show a genuine complementarity: EEG classified autistic children better (82.5% versus 77.7%) while eye tracking classified typically developing children markedly better (94% versus 80%), which is the concrete mechanism by which fusion helps
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported for any individual feature. The paper gives no group means, effect sizes or directional statements for any of the 221 features - the entire analysis is at the level of classifier output
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Deep unsupervised representation learning with supervised fine-tuning, applied hierarchically for late fusion
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Three stacked denoising autoencoders. EEG-SDAE with structure 125-64-50-2, ET-SDAE with 96-64-50-2, and Fusion-SDAE with 100-50-20-2 taking the concatenated 50-dimensional latent representations from the first two. Each SDAE is trained by greedy layer-wise unsupervised pre-training of denoising autoencoders with a zero-masking corruption at noise level 0.1 and sigmoid encoders and decoders minimising reconstruction mean square error, followed by removal of the decoders, addition of a softmax layer, and supervised backpropagation fine-tuning. Learning rates 0.1 for pre-training and 0.2 for fine-tuning, 100 and 200 iterations respectively, SGD optimisation. Three baselines share the same architecture family: EEG-SDAE alone, ET-SDAE alone, and CONCAT-SDAE trained on the raw concatenation of both feature sets
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Ten-fold cross-validation described explicitly as 'subject-independent', 'where each subject is regarded as a sample', with stratified sampling ensuring each fold preserves the autistic-to-typically-developing ratio; nine folds train, one tests, each fold tested once, and the average over the ten folds reported with standard deviations. Feature normalisation to [0,1] is fitted on the training set and the test set rescaled using the training minima and maxima - an explicit statement of correct normalisation discipline that most studies in this corpus omit. All four compared models are evaluated on the same dataset and folds
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity with standard deviations across folds; ROC curves with AUC for all four models; and full confusion matrices for all four models
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: MMSDAE (two-stage fusion): 95.56% accuracy, 92.5% sensitivity, 98% specificity, AUC 0.984, with the smallest standard deviation of any model. ET-SDAE: 86.67% accuracy. EEG-SDAE: 81.11%. CONCAT-SDAE (naive feature concatenation): intermediate, better than both unimodal models but worse than MMSDAE. Fusion improved overall accuracy by 14.45 points over EEG alone and 8.89 points over eye tracking alone. Confusion matrices: EEG classified autistic children at 82.5% and typically developing at 80%; eye tracking classified autistic at 77.7% and typically developing at 94%; fusion reached 92.5% and 98%, misclassifying three autistic children and one typically developing child
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Fusing resting-state EEG with gaze during social video classified preschool children at 95.56% accuracy under subject-independent cross-validation, against 86.67% for eye tracking alone and 81.11% for EEG alone. The gain is explained rather than merely asserted: confusion matrices show the two modalities fail in different directions - EEG identifies autistic children better while gaze identifies typically developing children much better (94% versus 80%) - so the modalities are genuinely complementary rather than redundant, and fusion inherits each one's strength. Learned two-stage fusion also beat naive feature concatenation, indicating that the benefit comes from combining high-level latent representations rather than from simply having more features. Eye tracking outperformed EEG despite EEG contributing more features and a far more elaborate acquisition, which is the result most relevant to a review of behavioural prediction: the behavioural modality was the stronger of the two.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Not reported at feature level - no group means, directions or effect sizes for any of the 125 EEG or 96 eye-tracking features
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Replace the three-model pipeline with more efficient architectures such as convolutional and attention networks; and, more substantively, develop fusion that tolerates a missing modality at training time, since the current design requires simultaneous EEG and eye-tracking data to deploy. Also to explore additional ASD-related features using advanced signal processing
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: One of the small number of studies in this corpus that gets the validation unit right and says so: cross-validation is described as subject-independent with each subject as a sample and stratified folds, and feature normalisation is explicitly fitted on training data and applied to test data. That combination places it well above the majority of the classification literature reviewed here, and its 95.56% is consequently a participant-level figure rather than a segment-level one. The ablation design is also a model of how to argue for fusion: four models on identical data and folds, with a confusion-matrix decomposition that identifies the specific asymmetry making fusion work - EEG better on the autistic class, gaze much better on the typical class - rather than asserting complementarity from an accuracy improvement alone. Including naive concatenation as a baseline, and showing the two-stage model beats it, is the right control for whether learned fusion adds anything beyond extra features. Against this, several things are missing or unexamined. Diagnostic ascertainment is the weakest element: DSM-5 confirmation is claimed but immediately qualified by an admission of 'limited access to reliable information in the school site', with the actual assessment resting on four parent-report questionnaires and no observational instrument - so the reference standard against which 95.56% is measured is parent report, and the model may be predicting questionnaire-derived group membership rather than clinically established autism. The eye-tracking inclusion rule that all children had more than 70% screen-looking time is a quality gate that plausibly excludes children differentially by group, and no exclusion count is reported. Relatedly, the EEG yield differs substantially between groups - 20.4 +/- 4.9 clean segments for autistic children against 27.2 +/- 5.3 for typically developing - a difference the paper reports and does not discuss, though it means EEG feature estimates are systematically noisier for the autistic group and raises the possibility that artifact burden itself is partly what distinguishes the groups. Hyperparameters (three network geometries, noise level, two learning rates, iteration counts) are stated but no selection procedure is described, so it cannot be determined whether they were tuned on the same folds used for reporting. There is no interpretability at all below the modality level: with 125 EEG and 96 gaze features, no group means, no directions of effect and no feature importance, the study yields no information about which brain measures or which areas of interest matter - a real loss given that the AOI scheme (adult versus child, eyes versus mouth versus body, joint attention) was designed to answer exactly that question. Finally the limitations section names only two issues, both engineering ones - the need for both modalities at deployment and the computational cost of three models - and does not raise sample size, single-site data, the diagnostic weakness or the absence of external validation.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups, both explicitly sized: 40 autistic children and 50 typically developing children, 90 in total, aged 3-6. Typically developing children came from a local kindergarten; the autistic children's site is identified only obliquely as 'the school site' where reliable diagnostic information was limited, which suggests a special-education setting but is never stated. No other-diagnosis or developmental-delay comparison group, so the model is tested only against typical development. The class imbalance (40:50) is handled correctly at the validation level by stratified fold construction, and both classes are large enough that the confusion-matrix decomposition is meaningful.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'individuals with ASD', 'ASD subjects', 'the ASD population', against 'typically developing (TD) children', 'TD subjects'. Acronym-as-modifier throughout with no person-first construction. The clinical framing is notably medicalised: autism is repeatedly called a 'disease' ('ASD is a complex and heterogeneous disease'), classification errors are framed as 'misdiagnosis rate', the ROC axes are relabelled 'diagnosis rate' and 'misdiagnosis rate', and the stated purpose is to 'assist clinicians to make a precise diagnosis decision'. Describing a neurodevelopmental condition as a disease and a false positive as a misdiagnosis positions the work as diagnostic rather than screening, which is a stronger claim than the parent-report reference standard can support.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Group sizes (40 and 50) and the 3-6 age range appear in the running text; ages, sex distribution and the four questionnaire scores are tabulated in Table I with p values from two-independent-sample t-tests, but the table did not render in the extracted text so the values cannot be recovered. That the comparison was made formally and reported with p values is to the study's credit and distinguishes it from the several studies here that report no demographic testing at all. What is not addressed is whether any demographic difference that did emerge was subsequently controlled for - no covariate adjustment or matched-subsample analysis appears anywhere. No IQ, developmental quotient, language level or adaptive functioning measure was collected for either group, which for a 3-6-year-old sample leaves the most obvious alternative explanation - general developmental level - entirely unaddressed.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: The study's weakest element, and unusually, the authors say so themselves. Diagnosis is stated to have been confirmed under DSM-5, but the very next sentence concedes 'we had limited access to reliable information in the school site' and explains that the children were therefore assessed using parent report on four instruments - the Autism Behavior Checklist, Social Communication Questionnaire, Social Responsiveness Scale and Clancy Behavior Scale. None is an observational or clinician-administered diagnostic instrument; all four are screening or symptom-report scales. No ADOS, ADI-R, CARS or direct clinical observation is reported. The consequence for interpretation is specific: the label the classifier is trained to predict is grounded in parent report, so a demonstration that a model recovers it at 95.56% shows agreement with parent-reported symptomatology, not with clinically established diagnosis. The comparison group is better handled - ABC, SRS and SCQ completed by teachers, with no child reaching any cut-off - so negative cases are screened on three instruments even though positive cases lack observational confirmation.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: No cognitive, language or adaptive measure of any kind for either group - a significant omission in 3-to-6-year-olds, where developmental level varies enormously and both resting EEG spectral power and social gaze allocation are strongly age- and ability-dependent. No comorbidity information and no exclusions described. Four symptom instruments (ABC, SCQ, SRS, CABS) were administered to the autistic group and three to the comparison group, and their scores are tabulated, so a severity gradient exists in the data; it is used only to characterise the sample and is never related to the model's continuous output, missing the opportunity to test whether the classifier's confidence tracks symptom level - the analysis that would have provided clinical anchoring.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: determine whether learned fusion of an internal neurophysiological modality and an external behavioural modality outperforms either alone, and whether hierarchical latent-space fusion beats naive feature concatenation. Main findings: MMSDAE reached 95.56% accuracy, 92.5% sensitivity, 98% specificity and AUC 0.984 under subject-independent stratified ten-fold cross-validation, improving on eye tracking alone (86.67%) by 8.89 points and EEG alone (81.11%) by 14.45; both fusion variants beat both unimodal models, and two-stage fusion beat naive concatenation; the modalities are complementary in a specific and demonstrated way, with EEG stronger on autistic children (82.5% versus 77.7%) and gaze much stronger on typically developing children (94% versus 80%); and the behavioural modality alone outperformed the neurophysiological one.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Beijing, China. Comparison children were recruited from a local kindergarten; the autistic children came from a school site whose identity is not given and where the authors report limited access to reliable diagnostic information. Both recordings took place under controlled conditions - EEG in a quiet room with the child in an armchair usually accompanied by a caregiver, eye tracking at a fixed ~60 cm viewing distance following a five-point calibration that had to pass with small error vectors before proceeding. Recruiting the two groups from different institutional settings is a structural feature the paper does not discuss, and it carries a specific risk for the eye-tracking modality here: the stimulus is Tiger Qiao Hu, a widely broadcast Chinese children's programme, so prior familiarity with the characters could differ systematically between children in a mainstream kindergarten and children in a special-education setting, and familiarity affects where a viewer looks.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Two paradigms with complementary demands, both requiring nothing of the child. EEG is eyes-open resting state for at least five minutes, so there is no task at all and no compliance requirement beyond sitting - the caregiver may be present. Eye tracking uses two ~30-second clips of a dynamic social interaction between a child and an adult, presented in random order, with an attention-grabbing animated kitten between trials, and 'no response was required from the children'. This is a well-judged design for the 3-6 age band: neither component depends on language, instruction-following or motor response, which is precisely what limits most computational paradigms in preschoolers. The eight areas of interest are the analytically substantive choice, distinguishing adult from child and, within each, eyes from mouth from body, plus a dedicated joint-attention region - a scheme built to test specific published claims about social attention. That the resulting 96 features are then fed undifferentiated into an autoencoder, with no analysis of which AOIs mattered, wastes the design's discriminative structure.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up. Ethics approval from the School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee of Beijing Normal University, with informed consent obtained from all children with parental permission before enrollment. Funding sources are itemised (NSFC grants 62003228 and 61761166003, a Beijing Municipal Education Commission project, and a National Key R&D programme grant). No data availability statement, no data sharing plan and no discussion of how the EEG and gaze recordings are stored or protected - though both modalities are lower-identifiability than the video and audio data used elsewhere in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Specified in detail on the acquisition side, which is a strength. EEG: Electrical Geodesics 128-channel Ag/AgCl passive electrode net, 1000 Hz sampling, at least five minutes, Cz online reference, impedances verified below 50 kOhm via Net Station, downsampling to 250 Hz, 50 Hz notch, 0.5-45 Hz band-pass, 4-second non-overlapping epochs, a cited automated artifact detector covering eye movements, blinks, line noise, breathing, muscle, abrupt slopes and outliers, supplementary visual inspection, a 200 microvolt bad-channel threshold with neighbour interpolation, and 62 of 128 electrodes retained across ten regions. Eye tracking: Tobii TX300 at 300 Hz, 1024x768 display, ~60 cm viewing distance, five-point calibration gated on small error vectors, Tobii fixation filter, linear interpolation of gaps up to 100 ms, binocular averaging, and a >70% screen-looking-time inclusion threshold. Modelling uses the publicly available DeepLearnToolbox, cited with its GitHub URL - so the learning machinery, at least, is reproducible off the shelf.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong on signal processing and network architecture, absent on selection procedure and data structure. Fully reported: every EEG acquisition and preprocessing parameter, every eye-tracking acquisition parameter, all three feature families with their band definitions, region groupings, MSE scale ranges and the seven graph metrics; the AOI scheme and the six per-AOI statistics with the arithmetic yielding 96 features; the normalisation formula together with the explicit statement that it is fitted on training data and applied to test; all three SDAE layer geometries; noise level, both learning rates, both iteration counts and the optimiser; the cross-validation scheme with its subject-independence and stratification; and the toolbox with its URL. Not reported: how the network geometries, noise level and learning rates were chosen, and whether that selection used the reporting folds; how many children were screened out by the >70% looking-time rule; whether any EEG recordings were excluded entirely; any group means or effect sizes for any feature; random seeds; and any data or code release beyond the third-party toolbox.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Only two limitations are stated, and both are engineering constraints rather than threats to validity: that deployment requires EEG and eye-tracking data to be available simultaneously, and that training three SDAE models costs more computation than one. Unaddressed: the diagnostic reference standard rests on parent-report questionnaires, which the authors themselves flag as a data-access compromise in the Methods but never carry into the interpretation of their results; the two groups were recruited from different institutional settings; no cognitive or developmental measure was collected in a 3-6-year-old sample, leaving developmental level uncontrolled; the >70% screen-looking-time gate may exclude children differentially by group with no count reported; the EEG segment yield differs markedly between groups (20.4 versus 27.2 clean segments), which the paper states in passing and never discusses despite its implication that artifact burden - and hence measurement noise - is itself group-dependent; hyperparameter selection is undescribed; there is no external validation cohort; and 90 children is a small sample for a model with three stacked networks. The Conclusion's claim that the framework 'can automatically learn and fuse useful information... without the need of much more diagnostic expert experience' is also stronger than a study whose labels came from parent questionnaires can support.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Two directions, both about model efficiency rather than about validity. Replace the three-model pipeline with convolutional or attention architectures to reduce computational cost; and, more interestingly, develop fusion that can operate 'even especially in the absence of one modality during the model training', which would address the practical barrier that the current design requires both an EEG net and an eye tracker for every child - a genuine obstacle to the scalability the paper claims. A third, briefer aim is to explore additional autism-related features via advanced signal processing. Absent from the agenda: external validation, direct diagnostic confirmation, developmental-level control, or any analysis of which features drive the result.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: The behavioural target is social visual attention: where a preschooler looks while watching a child and an adult interact, resolved to eight regions that separate the two people, separate eyes from mouth from body within each, and add an explicit joint-attention region. The six statistics per region capture both what was attended (fixation count, total and mean fixation duration, visit count) and the priority of attention (time to first fixation, number of fixations before first entering the region) - the latter pair encoding attentional precedence rather than mere allocation, which is the more theoretically pointed measure. The paired EEG modality is not behavioural at all, being eyes-open resting state with no task, so what the fusion combines is a behavioural response to social content with a task-free measure of intrinsic brain dynamics.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: The most carefully argued fusion analysis in the corpus, and one of very few where the mechanism of the fusion benefit is demonstrated rather than assumed. Four models are trained on identical data and folds: EEG alone, gaze alone, naive concatenation of raw features, and the proposed two-stage latent fusion. The ordering is informative at every step. Both fusion variants beat both unimodal models, so combining helps. Two-stage fusion beats naive concatenation, so the benefit comes from combining learned high-level representations rather than merely from having 221 features instead of 96 or 125 - the control that distinguishes a fusion architecture claim from a dimensionality claim. And the confusion matrices identify why: EEG classifies autistic children better (82.5% versus 77.7%) while gaze classifies typically developing children far better (94% versus 80%), so the modalities err in opposite directions and fusion recovers both strengths, reaching 92.5% and 98%. That asymmetry is a substantive finding in its own right and is the kind of evidence that most multimodal papers in this literature substitute an accuracy delta for. The t-SNE panels add a visual account, showing the fused representation separating classes where raw and concatenated features overlap. Two caveats: the paper does not test partial fusion (for instance gaze plus a single EEG family) so the minimum useful combination is unknown, and the behavioural modality alone at 86.67% already exceeds the EEG modality, which bears directly on cost-benefit given that eye tracking is far cheaper and faster to acquire than a 128-channel net in a preschooler.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Stacked denoising autoencoders used hierarchically - two for unimodal representation learning, a third for fusion - with greedy layer-wise unsupervised pre-training followed by supervised fine-tuning. The choice is well matched to the problem: 221 hand-engineered features from 90 children is a regime where supervised deep learning would overfit immediately, and unsupervised pre-training exploits the input data without consuming label information, while the denoising objective with zero-masking corruption prevents the identity mapping and encourages robustness. The paper justifies the choice by precedent in Alzheimer's diagnosis, ADHD classification and machinery fault diagnosis. The architecture is also deliberately shallow - two hidden layers per model, compressing 125 to 50 and 96 to 50 - which is appropriate for the sample size, though the t-SNE analysis reveals a cost the authors acknowledge: learned EEG features separate the classes less well than raw ones in the visualisation, which they attribute to dimension reduction discarding useful information.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A three-level representation. Level one is hand-engineered and theory-driven: EEG features chosen to test published claims about spectral power, signal complexity and network topology in autism, and gaze features chosen to test claims about social attention allocation. Level two compresses each modality to a 50-dimensional latent code via its own autoencoder. Level three concatenates the two 50-dimensional codes into a 100-dimensional vector and compresses again to 20 before classification. Two design points matter. Fusion occurs after each modality has been separately abstracted, so the fusion network operates on comparable representations rather than on raw features of wildly different scale and character - which is the paper's explanation for why it beats naive concatenation. And normalisation is fitted on training data only and applied to test data, a discipline stated explicitly and observed by very few studies in this corpus. The unit throughout is one vector per child, which is why the cross-validation can be genuinely subject-independent.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity with fold-wise standard deviations, ROC curves with AUC for all four models, and complete confusion matrices for all four - a full panel, and reported comparatively rather than only for the winning model. Reporting standard deviations across folds supports one of the paper's substantive claims, that MMSDAE 'presents the best stability and robustness with the smallest standard deviation among all compared methods', which is a claim about variance that accuracy alone cannot carry. The confusion matrices are the most useful element, since they convert an accuracy comparison into a diagnosis of where each model fails and thereby ground the complementarity argument. Missing: no confidence intervals on the reported means, no statistical test of the difference between models despite the word 'significantly' being used repeatedly of differences that are never tested, no per-fold table, and no comparison against a trivial baseline such as age - which for 3-to-6-year-olds is a real omission given that both resting EEG spectra and gaze behaviour change rapidly across that band.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: The weakest analytic dimension. There is no feature-level interpretability of any kind: no importance ranking, no per-family ablation, no group means, no effect sizes, no directional statements for any of the 221 features. This is a substantial loss because the feature set was designed to be interpretable - the ten brain regions, five frequency bands, four entropy scale ranges and seven graph metrics each correspond to a specific published hypothesis, and the eight areas of interest were constructed precisely to distinguish attention to eyes from mouth, to adult from child, and to joint-attention regions. A study that reported which of those differed would have contributed to the autism literature independently of its classifier; as written it contributes only a number. What interpretability exists is at modality level and is done well: the confusion-matrix decomposition establishing the EEG/gaze complementarity, and t-SNE projections of six feature spaces (raw EEG, raw gaze, raw concatenation, learned EEG, learned gaze, fused) showing progressive class separation. The t-SNE panels also surface an honest negative observation the authors do not hide - learned EEG features separate less well than expected, attributed to information loss in dimension reduction - though these projections are computed over the full dataset rather than per fold, so they illustrate rather than validate.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Done correctly, and stated in terms that leave no ambiguity: 'we perform a 10-fold subject-independent cross-validation to evaluate the performance of the proposed model, where each subject is regarded as a sample', with stratified sampling to preserve the class ratio in every fold, each fold tested exactly once, and the average across folds reported with standard deviations. Because every child contributes exactly one feature vector - EEG features are averaged across that child's clean segments, gaze features aggregated across their two trials - there is no possibility of the segment-level leakage that inflates results throughout this corpus, and the 95.56% is a genuine participant-level figure. Feature normalisation is also fitted on training data only. Two gaps remain. The three network geometries, the noise level, both learning rates and both iteration counts are stated as given, with no description of how they were arrived at, so selection optimism cannot be excluded and may be substantial across four compared architectures. And there is no external validation - no second site, no held-out cohort, no replication sample - so the estimate, though internally sound, rests entirely on 90 children from two institutions in one city. The correct comparison for this study's 95.56% is therefore not the segment-level 90%-plus figures elsewhere in the corpus but the small set of participant-level results, against which it stands as one of the highest and, on validation design, one of the better supported.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: autism spectrum disorders, multimodal fusion, electroencephalogram, eye-tracking, stacked denoising autoencoders, classification. Two modality terms, one architecture term, one fusion term - a keyword set entirely oriented to method, with 'multimodal fusion' rather than 'autism' functioning as the paper's actual subject.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering 30:2003-2011 (2022), a biomedical engineering venue. Authorship spans the School of Psychology at Capital Normal University, the School of Electrical Engineering at Yanshan University, and the State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Neuroscience and Learning at Beijing Normal University, with two first authors marked as contributing equally - one psychological, one engineering. Funded by three national and municipal Chinese grants. The psychology-engineering pairing explains the study's shape: rigorous signal acquisition and a validation design that respects subject independence, alongside an almost complete absence of clinical characterisation and of feature-level interpretation.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022 (submitted September 2021, published July 2022). The framing combines the standard prevalence appeal (1 in 54 per US CDC) with two more specific claims: that 'there is limited understanding of the neural patterns behind ASD and the severity of the disease', and that 'there is a lack of experienced experts for ASD diagnosis' - the second being a workforce argument that is more concretely relevant in the Chinese context the study is situated in than the objectivity arguments that dominate elsewhere in this corpus. The paper's distinctive positional claim is methodological: that 'most existing methods mainly rely on a single modality with limited information and often cannot achieve satisfactory performance', and that since autism has 'abnormal manifestations from the cellular level to the behavioral level' no single level of measurement can suffice. Its related-work section is unusual in citing single-modality accuracy figures from both literatures side by side - 92.34% and 96.44% for EEG, 88.51% and 85.1% for eye tracking - which sets up the fusion argument but also, unintentionally, shows that the highest reported unimodal figures already exceed this study's own unimodal results (81.11% and 86.67%), a discrepancy that goes unremarked and that most likely reflects differences in validation design rather than in signal quality.

data_charting_rubrics.title: AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Chanyoung K; Soyeon K; Yu Rang P; Soon-Beom H; Mindong S; Lim J; Bongkyung J
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Toddlers and preschoolers with autism, mostly with co-occurring intellectual disability
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Video of social behaviour - initiation of joint attention
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Build a screening tool around a single, clinically sanctioned social behaviour rather than an incidental motor or gaze correlate. The paper's stated positioning is explicit: it criticises the Cognoa-derived approach for feeding human ratings rather than video into the model, and criticises Zunino's grasping-kinematics work because 'the targeted gesture is not generally considered an indication of ASD behavior by most mental health specialists' - so the design goal is that both the input and the behaviour targeted should be clinically meaningful
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification with subject-disjoint training, validation and two separate testing sets, one of which is deliberately left unprocessed to test robustness
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session of approximately 10 minutes per child, yielding roughly 9 usable 10-second clips per participant
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A structured initiation-to-joint-attention protocol adapted from Mundy's Early Social Communication Scales with behaviour-extraction techniques from applied behaviour analysis. The child sits at a height-adjustable table with right elbow and wrist resting on it; a small toy (10 types, all 3x5x3 cm) is placed on the midline 70 cm from the child's edge - deliberately out of reach, because 'if the toy was placed too close to the child, they would simply pick up the toy and play with it without making any effort to interact with the examiner'. A trained examiner sits adjacent to the toy, positioned so the child must make an approximately 45-degree head turn or a substantial gaze shift to see their face. The examiner places the toy, waits 30 seconds and simply faces the child without any verbal instruction. When the child initiates joint attention - shifting gaze from toy to examiner and back, sometimes with a point - the examiner responds by turning to the toy. Each toy is used twice with a 30-second pause; toy order is pseudo-randomised. The examiner may substitute a toy if the child shows no interest after 30 seconds, and pauses the task if the child will not stay seated for at least 10 seconds
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Seoul, South Korea - children recruited from the Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Division of Seoul National University Hospital and from preschools; testing conducted individually in a quiet room, with a parent permitted to sit behind the child if needed
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Among the more thorough in the corpus for a conference paper. DSM-5 criteria applied; ADOS-2 administered to all children referred for suspected autism by two experienced professionals, with module-specific raw scores converted to calibrated severity scores (total, social affect, restricted and repetitive behaviours); the Korean CARS administered with a cut-off of 25.5 indicating high risk. Children with a calibrated severity score below 3 - the non-spectrum band - were excluded, and 6 of 50 initially recruited ASD-suspected children were removed on that basis, so the retained autistic group is diagnostically unambiguous (mean CSS 6.00, in the 'Autism' band)
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 44 retained from 50 recruited
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: An unusually targeted exclusion list, justified by the mechanism under study: because 'joint attention is believed to consist of complex neural processes including perception, attention, and motor coordination', all children were required to have normal or corrected-to-normal vision and normal hearing, and were screened out for pharmacological treatment, developmental coordination disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and any other neurological or psychiatric condition. Excluding ADHD and developmental coordination disorder specifically removes the two conditions most likely to impair the perceptual, attentional and motor components of the target behaviour
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Children receiving pharmacological treatment were excluded
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Well characterised: ADOS-2 total, social-affect and restricted/repetitive calibrated severity scores (6.00 +/- 1.56, 6.41 +/- 1.67 and 5.97 +/- 2.41 respectively), Korean CARS totals (30.9 +/- 5.94 versus 15.5 +/- 1.93), and a human-rated IJA score of 0 or 1 per trial summed to a maximum of 20 (4.59 +/- 5.75 versus 16.1 +/- 5.98). All are reported with group comparisons, though none is related to model output
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes - Korean CARS mean 15.5, far below the 25.5 high-risk cut-off, plus the same neurological, psychiatric, sensory and medication exclusions applied to both groups
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes, and formally tested - 47.9 versus 46.9 months, p = 0.697
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Yes, and formally tested - 54.0% versus 50.0% male, chi-squared p = 0.857
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Established by CARS score and by the same exclusion criteria applied to both groups
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: 2D RGB video of the child during the joint-attention protocol
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Video was recorded front-facing at 1920x1080 and 30 fps. Sequences were trimmed to begin the instant the toy was placed on the table and to end 10 seconds later, giving 300-frame clips. Corrupted acquisitions - frames with excessive blurring or with the child missing - were discarded, leaving 918 clips (484 typically developing, 434 autistic). For the training, validation and second testing sets, semantic segmentation isolated the human foreground so that background cues such as wallpaper colour and the child's clothing were suppressed, with the stated aim of ensuring 'that the algorithm considered only the kinematics of the gestures, such as gaze shift and head turns'. The first testing set was left unprocessed apart from resizing, to represent naturalistic data
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Sony DSC-RX100 IV digital camera at 1920x1080 and 30 fps; VGG-16 pretrained on ImageNet; a two-layer LSTM; a soft attention module; ten standardised toys selected per ADOS-2 and ESCS guidelines at a uniform 3x5x3 cm
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: 918 joint-attention video clips from 94 Korean children; no release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Video of identifiable young children is the raw material, and semantic segmentation of the foreground reduces but does not remove identifiability - unlike skeletonisation it retains the child's face. Governance is reported: approval by the Yonsei University IRB (no. 4-2021-0845), conduct in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and written informed consent from parents after a detailed description of the study. Two children appear in the published figures identified by participant codes
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Learned convolutional and recurrent representations of raw video, with no hand-engineered features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: None specified by hand. Features are taken from the last convolutional layer of ImageNet-pretrained VGG-16, chosen because 'owing to its convolutional nature, [it] preserves the spatial information', yielding a 512-dimensional vector at each of 7x7 spatial locations per frame. These enter a two-layer LSTM with 512-dimensional hidden state, and a soft attention module then weights the sequence positions. The design deliberately avoids hand-engineering gaze or head-pose estimates, which distinguishes it from the pose-estimation approaches elsewhere in this corpus
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: VGG-16 pretrained on ImageNet; semantic segmentation for foreground isolation
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, temporally - the attention weights are the interpretability instrument, and their inspection is the paper's most substantive analysis
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Soft attention weights (alpha) were extracted at each of the 300 LSTM time steps and plotted per clip. Every clip's plot was then checked against the corresponding video to determine whether a specific social gesture - such as a head turn to face the examiner - coincided with a rise in attention weight
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Temporal rather than featural. For typically developing children, attention weights invariably showed a distinct rise somewhere in the 300-frame sequence, peaking to at least twice baseline, though the onset and duration of that peak varied between children; for autistic children attention weights did not change significantly across the clip. Every attention peak in a typically developing child coincided with an observed initiation of joint attention, and across the entire dataset fewer than 1% of autistic children showed both an IJA behaviour and a corresponding attention peak
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Absence of the triadic gaze shift in the autistic group - the model's decision is grounded in the non-occurrence of a specific, clinically defined gesture rather than in a diffuse statistical difference
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Deep learning - convolutional feature extraction with recurrent temporal modelling and soft attention over raw video
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: VGG-16 (ImageNet-pretrained) supplying 512-dimensional features at 7x7 spatial locations per frame; a two-layer LSTM with 512-dimensional hidden state; a soft attention module producing a 512-dimensional attention-weighted encoding; then a 512-unit fully connected layer, ReLU, dropout at 0.5, and a final 512-to-2 fully connected layer for binary classification
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A subject-disjoint three-way partition rather than cross-validation. Twenty typically developing and 20 autistic children were split 8:2 into training (16+16) and validation (4+4). Two separate testing sets were then formed from the remaining participants: test set #1 with 20 typically developing and 16 autistic children, and test set #2 with 10 and 8. The three partitions account for all 94 children with no overlap. Test set #2 received the same semantic-segmentation preprocessing as training; test set #1 was left raw apart from resizing, so it functions as a domain-shift check. Clips were treated as independent during training, and the reported testing figures are computed over clips rather than over children
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy on training and validation; accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and full confusion matrices on both testing sets
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Training accuracy 98.9%, validation 97.0%. Test set #1 (raw video, 36 children, 416 clips): accuracy 0.916, precision 0.900, recall 0.945, F1 0.922, with 175 of 198 typically developing clips (88.4%) and 206 of 218 autistic clips (92.1%) correctly classified. Test set #2 (background-reduced, 18 children, 184 clips): accuracy 0.918, precision 0.880, recall 0.953, F1 0.915, with 88 of 99 (88.9%) and 81 of 85 (94.5%) correct. Performance on the unprocessed naturalistic set essentially matched the preprocessed set despite the model having been trained only on segmented video
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A CNN-LSTM-attention model reading 10-second video clips of a structured joint-attention probe separated autistic from typically developing children at 0.916 accuracy and 0.922 F1 on a subject-disjoint test set. The result held at 0.918 when the model was applied to raw, unsegmented video despite having been trained on background-removed clips, indicating that it is not relying on room or clothing cues. The most substantive contribution is the attention analysis: typically developing children showed a distinct attention peak at some point in each 300-frame sequence, autistic children showed flat attention profiles, and every peak in a typically developing child coincided with an observed triadic gaze shift - so the network's decision is anchored to the specific clinically defined behaviour the protocol was built to elicit, rather than to an unexamined correlate. Against this, the two groups differ by 45 IQ points (104 versus 58.8), which the authors acknowledge as the study's principal limitation.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Absence of the triadic gaze shift from object to social partner and back, indexed both by human rating (4.59 versus 16.1 of a possible 20) and by the model's flat attention profile
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Replicate with IQ-matched autistic and typically developing cohorts, which the authors state is required given the 45-point group difference; and extend the model from binary classification to prediction of social-function deficit severity, to serve as an objective adjunct to existing symptom-severity questionnaires and clinical scales
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A short conference paper that gets several things right which longer journal papers in this corpus get wrong. The partition is subject-disjoint across training, validation and two separate testing sets accounting for all 94 children - no participant appears twice - which removes the identity-leakage pathway that inflates Simeoli, Liaqat, Mazumdar and Akter. Age and sex are formally matched and tested (p = 0.697 and 0.857). Diagnostic ascertainment is strong for a four-page paper: DSM-5, ADOS-2 with calibrated severity scores, Korean CARS, and exclusion of six children whose severity scores fell in the non-spectrum band. The exclusion criteria are reasoned from the mechanism rather than applied by rote - ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, medication and sensory impairment are all removed precisely because joint attention depends on attention, motor coordination, vision and hearing. And the attention analysis is the best interpretability work in the corpus for a video model: rather than presenting a saliency heatmap and asserting plausibility, the authors inspected every clip against its attention plot and established a specific correspondence between attention peaks and observed triadic gaze, then quantified the converse (fewer than 1% of autistic children showed both). The domain-shift result is also genuinely informative - training on segmented video and testing on raw video at essentially identical accuracy is direct evidence against background-cue exploitation, and stronger evidence than the more common practice of simply asserting that a model attends to the child. Three problems bound the result. The IQ difference is enormous - 104 against 58.8, a mean in the intellectual disability range for the autistic group - so the model is separating children who differ in general cognitive level as much as in diagnosis, and joint attention is developmentally sensitive to cognitive level; the authors acknowledge this and call for IQ-matched replication, but their defence, that joint attention 'still proved to be an important trait to differentiate ASD from TD children' when IQ is considered, cites prior literature rather than testing it in their own data, and no matched-subsample analysis is attempted. Second, testing metrics are computed over clips (416 and 184) rather than over children (36 and 18), even though the paper describes averaging probabilities per subject for training and validation - so the confidence implied by the reported figures is not supported by 36 and 18 independent participants, and no per-child accuracy is given. Third, the target behaviour is already scored by a human rater in this very study, with near-complete separation (16.1 versus 4.59 of 20), so what the model demonstrates is automation of an existing measurement rather than detection of something clinicians cannot see; that is a legitimate and useful contribution, but the framing as discovering a 'behavioral biomarker' overstates it. The closing comparison - that the model outperforms prior work reporting 0.70-0.80 accuracy - is made without any statistical test and across studies with entirely different populations, tasks and IQ distributions.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups, both explicitly sized and accounted for: 50 typically developing children (27 male) and 44 autistic children (22 male), from an initial 50 ASD-suspected recruits of whom 6 were excluded for ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores below 3. Recruitment sources are named - the Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Division of Seoul National University Hospital for the clinical group and preschools for the comparison group. All 94 children are allocated across the three partitions without overlap: 40 to training and validation, 36 to test set #1, 18 to test set #2. No other-diagnosis comparison group, which matters here because ADHD and developmental coordination disorder were deliberately excluded rather than recruited as contrast groups - so the model is never asked to make the discrimination that would distinguish autism-specific joint-attention impairment from impairment secondary to attention or motor difficulty.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'ASD and TD children', 'individuals with ASD', against 'typically developing (TD) children', 'TD individuals'. Person-first in the fuller constructions, acronym-as-modifier elsewhere. Autism is framed conventionally as 'impairment in social interaction and communication, and restricted, repetitive patterns of interests and behaviors', and the socio-economic framing is burden-oriented, citing 'the socio-economic burden that stems from caring for ASD' in billions of dollars and, in the conclusion, a hope to 'reduce the burden on the parents'. The word 'patients' appears once for the children. The framing of joint attention itself is comparatively constructive, describing it as 'a high-level social skill and a valid indicator of social brain development' rather than as a deficit to be catalogued.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Fully reported and formally tested, which is uncommon in this corpus. Autistic group: 44 children, 22 male (50.0%), 46.9 +/- 13.0 months, median 49.0, range 24-68. Comparison group: 50 children, 27 male (54.0%), 47.9 +/- 12.5 months, median 48.5, range 25-72. Age p = 0.697 by t-test; sex p = 0.857 by chi-squared; both groups therefore genuinely matched on the two standard demographic variables and shown to be so. The decisive difference is cognitive: best-estimate IQ 104 +/- 17.4 in the comparison group against 58.8 +/- 18.6 in the autistic group, p < 0.001 - a 45-point gap placing the autistic group's mean firmly within the intellectual disability range. IQ was measured with the Korean WPPSI-IV or the Korean Bayley Scales depending on the child. The gap is acknowledged as the study's chief limitation but is not addressed analytically: no covariate adjustment, no IQ-matched subsample, no stratified analysis. Since joint attention emerges developmentally and is sensitive to cognitive level, and since the autistic group averages roughly a 45-point deficit, a substantial part of the classification could reflect developmental level rather than autism specifically.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Strong for a four-page conference paper. Diagnosis was made under DSM-5 criteria. The ADOS-2 was administered by two experienced professionals to all children referred for suspected autism, and because different modules were used according to age and language level, raw scores were converted to calibrated severity scores - total, social affect and restricted/repetitive - which is the correct procedure for comparing across modules and is done in only a minority of studies here. The paper states the CSS interpretation bands explicitly (1-3 non-spectrum, 4-5 ASD, 6-10 Autism) and applies them: 6 of the 50 initially recruited ASD-suspected children scored below 3 and were excluded, leaving a group with a mean CSS of 6.00, in the 'Autism' band. The Korean CARS was also administered with its 25.5 high-risk cut-off, and comparison children averaged 15.5 against 30.9 for the autistic group. The ascertainment therefore combines DSM-5 criteria, a module-calibrated observational instrument, a rating scale, and an explicit exclusion rule applied to borderline cases.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: IQ was measured for every child using an age-appropriate instrument - Korean WPPSI-IV for older children, Korean Bayley Scales-II for younger - and combined into a best-estimate figure, which is the right approach for a sample spanning 24 to 72 months. The result is the study's central confound rather than a control. Comorbidity was handled by exclusion and the exclusions are mechanistically reasoned: because joint attention depends on 'perception, attention, and motor coordination', children were required to have normal or corrected vision and normal hearing and were excluded for pharmacological treatment, developmental coordination disorder, ADHD, and any other neurological or psychiatric condition. This is a more thoughtfully constructed exclusion set than most in the corpus, since each element removes a plausible non-autism cause of failing the specific target behaviour. No adaptive functioning or language measure is reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: build a screening tool whose input is raw video and whose target behaviour is one that clinicians already regard as diagnostically meaningful, addressing two named shortcomings in prior work - that the Cognoa-derived system feeds human ratings rather than video into the model, and that Zunino's grasping-kinematics approach targets a gesture 'not generally considered an indication of ASD behavior by most mental health specialists'. Main findings: 0.916 accuracy, 0.900 precision, 0.945 recall and 0.922 F1 on a subject-disjoint raw-video test set of 36 children; 0.918 accuracy on a second, background-reduced test set of 18 children; and an attention analysis showing that typically developing children produce a distinct attention peak coinciding with an observed triadic gaze shift while autistic children produce flat attention profiles, with fewer than 1% of autistic children showing both.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Seoul, South Korea. The clinical group came from the Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Division of Seoul National University Hospital and the comparison group from preschools - a recruitment asymmetry of the kind that elsewhere in this corpus introduces setting confounds, but mitigated here because the paradigm itself is identical for both groups and highly constrained: same quiet room arrangement, same height-adjustable chair, same 70 cm toy placement, same 45-degree examiner offset, same ten toys, same 30-second waits. The paper also states that videos 'were acquired at different locations with various background noises' and treats the model's robustness across them as evidence for generalisability - which the train-on-segmented, test-on-raw result supports more directly than the assertion alone would.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: The most carefully constructed elicitation paradigm in the corpus, and the design reasoning is unusually visible. It adapts Mundy's Early Social Communication Scales, a validated manual for eliciting and scoring joint-attention behaviours, together with behaviour-extraction techniques from applied behaviour analysis. Three geometric decisions are justified explicitly. The toy sits 70 cm away on the midline, out of reach, because a nearer toy means the child 'would simply pick up the toy and play with it without making any effort to interact with the examiner' - so the design forces the social bid rather than merely permitting it. The examiner is offset such that seeing their face requires an approximately 45-degree head turn or a substantial gaze shift, which makes the target behaviour large enough to register in 2D video from a front-facing camera. And the examiner provides no verbal instruction and simply waits, so any initiation is spontaneous rather than prompted. The toys are standardised in size (3x5x3 cm) and drawn from ADOS-2 and ESCS guidelines, with pseudo-randomised order and a substitution rule if the child shows no interest. Ten seconds from toy placement defines the analysis window. The whole session takes about 10 minutes. The one unexamined element is that the examiner responds contingently - turning to the toy once the child initiates - so the examiner's behaviour is a function of the child's, and the paper does not state whether the examiner is in frame or whether the model could be reading their response rather than the child's initiation.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up. Ethics are reported in full for a conference paper: approval by the Yonsei University IRB under number 4-2021-0845, conduct in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and written informed consent from parents 'after receiving a detailed description of the study'. The data are identifiable video of young children, and although semantic segmentation removes background it retains faces; two children appear in published figures identified by participant codes. No data availability statement, no code release and no description of how the video corpus is stored or protected.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Acquisition is a single consumer camera - a Sony DSC-RX100 IV at 1920x1080 and 30 fps, front-facing - with no depth sensor, marker, wearable or eye tracker, which is the practical argument for the approach: the same behaviour is measured elsewhere with eye-tracking hardware or motion capture. Physical setup is specified to the centimetre (70 cm toy distance, 3x5x3 cm toys, 45-degree examiner offset, height-adjustable chair with the child's right elbow and wrist on the table). Modelling uses ImageNet-pretrained VGG-16 with the last convolutional layer retained for its spatial structure, a two-layer 512-dimensional LSTM, a soft attention module, and a classifier head of 512-unit FC, ReLU, dropout 0.5 and a 512-to-2 FC layer. Semantic segmentation isolates the foreground human, though the segmentation method itself is not named.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Good on protocol and architecture, thin on training procedure. Fully specified: the elicitation protocol with all distances, timings, toy specifications and examiner rules; camera model, resolution and frame rate; clip trimming rule (from toy placement, 10 seconds, 300 frames); the discard criterion for corrupted acquisitions; final clip counts by group (484 and 434 of 918); the exact composition of all four partitions by group and by clip count; the full network specification layer by layer; the attention formulation; and the difference in preprocessing between test sets. Not reported: optimiser, learning rate, batch size, epochs, loss function, any regularisation beyond the single dropout layer, the semantic segmentation method, random seeds, or any statement of how architecture or hyperparameters were selected. No code or data release. For a conference paper the protocol reporting is exemplary and the training reporting is incomplete.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: One limitation is stated and it is the right one: 'there is a statistically significant difference in IQ between the ASD and TD children. IQ is known to affect one's ability to perform behavioral tasks and joint attention', followed by the conclusion that 'a replication study using a sample of IQ-matched ASD and TD cohorts is therefore required'. The framing is honest, though the accompanying defence - that 'even when IQ is considered, joint attention still proved to be an important trait to differentiate ASD from TD children' - rests on a citation to prior literature rather than on any analysis of the present data, and no covariate adjustment or matched subsample is attempted despite IQ being measured for every child.
