Unaddressed: that test metrics are computed over clips rather than children, so effective sample sizes are 36 and 18 rather than 416 and 184; that the training set comprises only 32 children; that the target behaviour is separately scored by a human rater in this very study with near-complete group separation, so the model automates an existing measurement rather than revealing a new one; that ADHD and developmental coordination disorder were excluded rather than used as contrast groups, leaving specificity untested; that the examiner responds contingently to the child; and that the closing comparison against prior models reporting 0.70-0.80 accuracy is made without any statistical test and across incomparable populations.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Two directions, both well chosen. Replicate with IQ-matched cohorts - which follows directly from the acknowledged confound and is the single analysis that would establish whether the result is about autism or about developmental level. And extend from binary classification to continuous prediction of social-function deficit severity, to serve 'as an objective assessment tool that can be used in conjunction with currently available symptom severity measurement questionnaires and clinical scales'. The second is well supported by data already in hand, since ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores, CARS totals and human-rated IJA scores were all collected and none was related to model output; the severity-regression analysis is available in this dataset and simply was not run.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: A single, precisely defined social behaviour: initiation of joint attention, operationalised as the triadic gaze - 'a triadic gaze where the child shifts their gaze from the object at hand to the person they wish to interact with and back to the object, or from the person to the object and back to the person', sometimes accompanied by a point. This is the narrowest behavioural target in the corpus and the choice is deliberate and defended: joint attention is described as 'a high-level social skill and a valid indicator of social brain development', develops early in typical children, and is measured by a validated manual (ESCS). The contrast with the rest of this literature is instructive - where most studies extract many features from an unconstrained behaviour stream and let a model find what discriminates, this study constructs a paradigm to elicit one behaviour that clinicians already regard as diagnostic, then asks whether a model can see it. That inverts the usual relationship between the computational method and the clinical construct.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality - 2D RGB video only, with no audio, depth, gaze tracking or motion capture. No fusion is attempted or claimed. Within the modality the paper does run a preprocessing comparison that functions like an ablation: training, validation and test set #2 used semantically segmented video with the foreground human isolated so that 'most of the background noise (color of wallpaper, color of child's clothes, etc.) was reduced', while test set #1 was left raw. Accuracy was 0.918 on the segmented test set and 0.916 on the raw one, with autistic-class accuracy 94.5% versus 92.1%. Because the model was trained only on segmented video, its near-equivalent performance on raw video is a domain-shift result rather than a like-for-like comparison, and it constitutes direct evidence that the classifier is not depending on room or clothing cues - the confound that the skeletonisation approach elsewhere in this corpus removes by construction. The authors read the small drop as expected background distraction, which is a reasonable interpretation.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: CNN-LSTM with soft attention over raw video - a standard action-recognition architecture, applied without modification and without comparison to alternatives. Only one model is reported: no baseline, no ablation over architecture, no simpler comparator such as a frame-averaged CNN or a hand-engineered gaze-shift detector, and no chance or trivial baseline. The architectural choices are nonetheless well reasoned for the task. The last convolutional layer of VGG-16 is retained specifically because it 'preserves the spatial information' as a 7x7 grid of 512-dimensional vectors rather than a globally pooled summary, which matters when the discriminative event is a head turn at a particular image location. The LSTM supplies temporal structure, necessary because the target behaviour is a sequence - object, then person, then object - not a static configuration. And the attention module is included not for performance but for inspectability, which is how it is actually used.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Raw video reduced only by clip trimming and, for three of four partitions, foreground segmentation. There is no hand-engineered representation at all: no head pose, no gaze vector, no skeleton, no facial landmarks. This is a meaningful methodological position given that the target behaviour is a gaze shift, which the pose-estimation literature would extract explicitly. The tradeoff is visible in the results - the model works, but nothing about the representation is inspectable, and interpretability has to be recovered afterwards through the attention weights. The temporal unit is fixed at 10 seconds from toy placement, which encodes an assumption that a genuine initiation will occur within that window; the paradigm's 30-second wait before each trial makes that assumption defensible but it is not tested.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and full confusion matrices for both testing sets, plus training and validation accuracy - a complete panel for a conference paper, and reported for both test sets rather than only the better one. The confusion matrices make the error structure legible: on test set #1, 23 of 198 typically developing clips were called autistic against 12 of 218 autistic clips called typical, so the model errs toward false positives, and precision (0.900) sits below recall (0.945) accordingly. Two things are missing and one is consequential. There are no confidence intervals and no per-child accuracy, and since the metrics are computed over 416 and 184 clips originating from only 36 and 18 children, clips from the same child are not independent and the apparent precision of the estimates is overstated - the paper itself describes averaging probabilities per subject for training and validation but does not do so for testing. And there is no comparison against a trivial baseline; given a 45-point IQ gap, a baseline using developmental level alone would be the informative comparator.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: The strongest video-model interpretability analysis in the corpus, and the reason this short paper matters. Rather than presenting an attention heatmap and asserting that it looks sensible, the authors used the soft attention weights as a testable hypothesis about mechanism: they plotted the alpha values across all 300 frames for every clip and then checked each plot against the corresponding video to see whether a rise coincided with a specific social gesture. The finding is stated with appropriate precision - for typically developing children a distinct rise to at least twice baseline was 'invariably noted' somewhere in the sequence, though its onset and duration varied between children, while for autistic children attention weights 'did not change significantly throughout the duration of the video clip'. Crucially both directions are checked: every attention peak in a typically developing child coincided with an observed IJA behaviour, and across the whole dataset fewer than 1% of autistic children showed both an IJA behaviour and a corresponding peak. That establishes correspondence rather than mere plausibility, and it means the model's decision can be traced to the occurrence or non-occurrence of the clinically defined behaviour the protocol was designed to elicit - which is exactly the claim most deep-learning studies in this corpus make without evidence. The illustrative figure showing frames 80, 140, 180 and 240 for one child from each group makes the mechanism concrete. What is not done: attention is temporal only, with no spatial attribution showing which part of the frame is used, so it cannot be verified that the model is watching the child rather than the contingently responding examiner.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Correct in its most important respect and incomplete in a secondary one. The partition is subject-disjoint: 40 children in training and validation (16+16 and 4+4), 36 in test set #1, 18 in test set #2, accounting for all 94 participants with no child in more than one partition. This forecloses the identity-leakage route that inflates several other studies here, and it is the reason 0.916 can be compared to Kojovic's 80.9% and Han's 95.56% rather than to segment-level figures. Two independent test sets rather than one is a further strength, and making them differ in preprocessing turns the second into a domain-shift check rather than a redundant repetition. What is incomplete: the reported test metrics are clip-level, computed over 416 and 184 clips rather than over 36 and 18 children, so within-child correlation inflates the apparent precision even though it does not bias the point estimate; the paper describes per-subject probability averaging for training and validation but not for testing, and no per-child accuracy appears. There is also no cross-validation - a single fixed split with 32 training children - so the estimate carries no measure of split-to-split variability, and no external cohort or site. Finally, whatever architecture and hyperparameter selection occurred is undocumented, so it cannot be established that the validation set was used only once.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: AI-assisted diagnosis, autism spectrum disorder, behavioral biomarker, early detection model, joint attention. 'Behavioral biomarker' is the term doing the conceptual work - the paper's claim is that joint attention functions as a biomarker in the absence of any biological one, stated directly as 'there is no definitive biomarker for ASD'. 'AI-assisted diagnosis' rather than 'screening' in the keyword list sits slightly ahead of what the study demonstrates, though the body of the paper is more careful, describing the intended use as screening plus an assistive tool for specialists.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: IEEE 3rd International Conference on Human-Machine Systems (ICHMS) 2022, DOI 10.1109/ICHMS56717.2022.9980778 - an engineering conference, four pages. The author list is genuinely clinical-computational: the Department of Biomedical Systems Informatics at Yonsei University College of Medicine, the Division of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry at Seoul National University College of Medicine, the Department of Child Development and Family Studies at Seoul National University, and one industry author. That composition explains the paper's characteristic shape - protocol design and diagnostic characterisation at journal standard, training details at conference standard. Funded by the Korean government's IITP programme (2022-0-00234).
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022. The framing combines the usual prevalence and early-intervention arguments (1 in 59, billions in socio-economic burden, improved outcomes from early detection) with a workforce argument that is more specific and more relevant to the deployment claim: early detection 'does not appear to be feasible, especially in regions where there is a scarcity of mental health specialists'. What distinguishes this paper's positioning is its critique of the immediately preceding work rather than of clinical practice in general. It observes that the Cognoa system, which obtained FDA marketing authorisation, 'may be considered not fully automated as it uses as input for the machine learning model not the actual videos, but human ratings corresponding to the quality of behavior conveyed in each video' - a precise and correct distinction between automating inference and automating measurement that no other paper in this corpus draws. And it criticises Zunino's grasping-kinematics classifier on the ground that 'the targeted gesture is not generally considered an indication of ASD behavior by most mental health specialists', which is a criterion of clinical construct validity rather than of accuracy. Those two criticisms jointly define the paper's design: raw video in, and a behaviour clinicians already accept as diagnostic as the target. The conclusion's comparative claim - higher accuracy and F1 than prior models reporting 0.70-0.80 - is asserted without statistical test and across studies with different populations and IQ distributions, which sits oddly against the care of the critique that opens the paper.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Liao M; Duan H; Wang G
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Preschool children with autism, aged 3 to 6
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Multimodal - eye fixation and facial expression (behavioural) fused with EEG (physiological)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Determine the relative discriminative power of three modalities and whether hybrid fusion - feature fusion of the two behavioural streams, then weighted decision fusion with the physiological stream - improves on any single one. The framing includes a specific developmental argument for including EEG: 'atypical brain development in children with ASD appears earlier than atypical behavior, and the critical period of early intervention will be missed if the detection is based on behavioral data'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification with a per-modality ablation and a two-level fusion architecture, evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: A single 40-second video stimulus per child, with all three modalities recorded simultaneously
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Passive viewing of one 40-second video clip constructed to contain both social and non-social content in the same frame - social being 'comedians with happy facial expressions, funny actions, and laughter', non-social being backgrounds and two spinning wheels. The clip was chosen from a pool of ten by having three graduate students in special education rate each on valence and arousal, with the clip having the highest mean positive arousal selected. No response was required of the children
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: China - children recruited from special education schools and from regular kindergartens; recording conditions are described only as varying across days
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: China - Henan/Hubei (Pingdingshan University and Central China Normal University)
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: DSM-5 criteria only. No standardised observational instrument, no ADOS, ADI-R, CARS or any rating scale is reported, and no information is given about who applied the criteria or in what setting. Comparison children were 'screened to exclude any with psychiatric or neurological disorders, including ASD', with no instrument named for that screening either
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported for the autistic group; comparison children were screened for psychiatric and neurological disorders
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: None. No severity, cognitive, language or adaptive measure of any kind for either group
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Stated as screened to exclude psychiatric or neurological disorders including autism, but no screening instrument is named
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution_controls: 33 boys, 7 girls - identical to the autistic group
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes - 4.6 versus 4.8 years, with the paper stating no significant difference in age, though the test statistic is not given
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Yes, and exactly - both groups comprise 33 boys and 7 girls, an unusually precise match
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted by exclusion screening with no named instrument
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye-tracking fixation coordinates, video of the child's face, and 14-channel EEG
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Three simultaneous streams. Eye fixation: fixation coordinates were clustered by K-means into K areas of interest, with the loss function, assignment rule and centroid update given explicitly; the frequency of fixation points falling in each cluster became one feature, so K clusters yield K features. K was tested at 8, 12, 16 and 20 and 'the final value of K was determined from the experimental results'. Facial expression: the expression appearing in the stimulus was defined as the target expression, and the number of frames in every 40 in which the child displayed that target expression was counted as a feature - so the measure is expression imitation or contagion rather than expression per se. EEG: signals were low-pass filtered above 45 Hz and high-pass filtered below 0.2 Hz, segmented into effective epochs, with epochs containing eye blinks, eye movements or muscle movement removed, then FFT applied to obtain band powers in theta (4-6 Hz), alpha (6-13 Hz), low beta (13-20 Hz), high beta (20-30 Hz) and gamma (30-45 Hz) across six regions; independent-samples t-tests were then run across all 80 children and the 12 region-band combinations reaching significance were retained as the EEG feature set
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Tobii Eye Tracker; a video camera for facial expression; Emotiv EPOC+ 14-channel consumer EEG headset (AF3, F7, F3, FC5, T7, P7, O1, O2, P8, T8, FC6, F4, F8, AF4, with P3 and P4 as references); VGG16 for the facial expression base classifiers
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Simultaneous eye-tracking, facial video and EEG from 80 Chinese preschoolers; no repository
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Yes - 'available from the corresponding author on reasonable request'
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not discussed. Facial video of identifiable young children is collected. Ethics approval from the Institutional Review Board of Pingdingshan University (protocol 068, 20 October 2020), conducted per the Declaration of Helsinki, with informed consent from all subjects
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Cluster-frequency gaze features, imitation-count expression features, and region-band EEG power features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Gaze: K distribution frequencies, one per K-means cluster, where 'the higher the distribution frequency is, the higher the interest in information will be'. The design is unusual in that areas of interest are discovered from the data rather than drawn by hand around stimulus objects, which removes the experimenter's judgement about what counts as a region but also detaches the regions from any semantic content - a cluster is a place on the screen, not 'the comedian's face'. Facial expression: counts of target-expression frames per 40-frame window, produced by a CNN with soft labels. EEG: twelve features, being the region-band combinations that reached significance - theta at left frontal, right frontal, right temporal, parietal and occipital; alpha at parietal and occipital; low beta at left frontal, right frontal, parietal and occipital; gamma at left frontal
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: K-means clustering with the iterative algorithm specified; a CNN with soft labels and VGG16 base classifiers from the authors' prior work; FFT band-power analysis
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: At modality level only, via a per-modality ablation and confusion-matrix comparison. At feature level, the EEG t-test table reports every region-band comparison with F, t, p, mean difference and standard error, giving effect directions for that modality; no importance is reported for gaze or expression features
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Independent-samples t-tests across all 80 children for EEG band powers; three classifiers (random forest, SVM, K-nearest neighbour) applied to each modality separately with both best and average accuracy reported; confusion matrices and pairwise confusion graphs comparing per-class accuracy across modalities
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: EEG emerged as the most discriminative modality both at best (83.75%) and average (74.69%) accuracy. Within EEG, the theta band carried the strongest and most widespread differences, significant in five of six regions with the largest t (5.82 at left frontal). At the modality level the confusion analysis is more informative than the ranking: EEG classified autistic children best (90.0%) while facial expression classified typically developing children best (92.5%), and eye fixation was weakest overall but still better than EEG on the typical class (85.0% versus 77.5%)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Theta power was significantly higher in the autistic group across left frontal, right frontal, right temporal, parietal and occipital regions - the only direction reported anywhere in the paper. Alpha differed only at parietal and occipital, low beta at left and right frontal, parietal and occipital, gamma only at left frontal, and high beta nowhere. No directions are given for any gaze or facial-expression feature
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Classical classifiers with a two-level hybrid fusion architecture using an attribute-weighted naive Bayes combiner
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Random forest, support vector machine and K-nearest neighbour applied to each modality. Fusion proceeds in two levels: at level 1 the facial-expression and eye-fixation feature vectors are concatenated and classified together to give a behavioural subdecision, while EEG features are classified separately to give a physiological subdecision; at level 2 the two subdecisions are combined by a naive Bayes classifier with attribute weighting, where the weight for each subdecision is computed from the training-set counts so that 'the attributes that are highly correlated with the classification results will have a large weighting coefficient'. The weighting formula is given explicitly and is constructed so that a weight can never be zero
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-out cross-validation over the 80 children, so each child is held out once and the unit of analysis is the participant. However, the EEG feature set was selected by t-tests computed across all 80 children before cross-validation began, and the number of gaze clusters K was 'determined from the experimental results', so both feature selection and a preprocessing hyperparameter used the labels of every participant including the held-out one
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy per modality per classifier, with best and average across classifiers; accuracy for physiological, behavioural and hybrid fusion; and confusion matrices with per-class rates for all four configurations, plus pairwise confusion graphs
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Single modality best accuracies: EEG 83.75% (random forest), facial expression 77.50%, eye fixation 73.75%; averages across the three classifiers 74.69%, 71.56% and 67.50% respectively. SVM was the weakest classifier on every modality (65.00%, 61.25%, 65.00%). Fusion: physiological alone 83.75%, behavioural (gaze plus expression) 85.00%, hybrid fusion with weighted naive Bayes 87.50%. Per-class rates: EEG 90.0% on autistic and 77.5% on typically developing children; facial expression 72.5% and 92.5%; eye fixation 62.5% and 85.0%; hybrid fusion 85.0% and 90.0%. Eye fixation misclassified 37.5% of autistic children as typically developing, while EEG misclassified 22.5% of typically developing children as autistic
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Three modalities recorded simultaneously during a single 40-second social video were compared head to head and then fused. EEG was the strongest single modality (83.75% best, 74.69% average), facial expression next (77.50%, 71.56%) and eye fixation weakest (73.75%, 67.50%), and hybrid fusion reached 87.50%. The more substantive result is the confusion analysis, which shows the modalities failing in systematically different directions: EEG identified autistic children well (90.0%) but over-called autism in typical children (22.5% false positives), while both behavioural modalities were the reverse - facial expression reached 92.5% on typically developing children but only 72.5% on autistic ones, and eye fixation missed 37.5% of autistic children. Fusion recovers both sides, reaching 85.0% and 90.0%. Within EEG, theta power was elevated in the autistic group across five of six regions, the most widespread band effect. The behavioural modalities combined (85.00%) essentially matched EEG alone (83.75%), which is notable given the far lower cost of a camera and eye tracker than an EEG headset.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Elevated theta band power across frontal, right temporal, parietal and occipital regions in the autistic group; no directional findings are reported for gaze or facial expression
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Increase the sample size to improve accuracy and stability; and address the non-stationarity of the recordings, since 'the recording environments are changing' and 'across-day variability exists in recording conditions', by developing detection models that adapt over time
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The comparative design is the paper's real contribution and the analysis of it is better than the headline number suggests. Recording three modalities simultaneously from the same children during the same stimulus is the only way to compare their discriminative power without confounding modality with sample, task or setting, and the confusion-matrix decomposition then converts a set of accuracies into a statement about complementary failure directions - EEG over-calls autism, the behavioural modalities under-call it, and fusion recovers both. Reporting both best and average accuracy across three classifiers for every modality is also more honest than the corpus norm, since it exposes how much of any single figure is classifier-specific (the EEG spread runs from 65.00% for SVM to 83.75% for random forest, an 18-point range on identical features). Sex matching is exact and age matching is stated. Leave-one-out cross-validation operates at the participant level, so there is no within-subject leakage of the kind that inflates results elsewhere in this corpus. Two flaws nonetheless undercut the numbers. The EEG feature set was chosen by running t-tests across all 80 children and retaining the 12 region-band combinations that reached significance, and only then was leave-one-out cross-validation performed on those features - so every held-out child's label had already contributed to deciding which features to use. That is textbook selection bias, and it inflates the EEG modality specifically, which is precisely the modality the paper concludes is 'the most discriminative'. The gaze cluster count K was likewise 'determined from the experimental results'. Second, diagnostic ascertainment is DSM-5 criteria with no instrument, no assessor described and no severity, cognitive or language measure for either group - so in a 3-to-6-year-old sample recruited from special education schools versus regular kindergartens, developmental level is entirely uncontrolled and confounded with recruitment setting. Two further points bear on interpretation. The EEG is an Emotiv EPOC+, a 14-channel consumer headset worn by preschoolers, and the paper reports removing epochs containing blinks, eye movements and muscle activity without stating how much data survived in each group - the differential-artifact question that Han et al. at least reported. And the band definitions are non-standard (theta 4-6 Hz, alpha 6-13 Hz), which complicates comparison with the EEG literature the paper cites. The limitations section names only sample size and across-day recording variability, and does not raise the feature-selection procedure, the diagnostic weakness or the recruitment asymmetry.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 40, recruited from special education schools and from regular kindergartens respectively. Both are explicitly sized and their sex composition is identical (33 boys, 7 girls each). No other-diagnosis or developmental-delay comparison group. The recruitment asymmetry is the structural weakness: children attending special education schools and children attending regular kindergartens differ in developmental level, in daily environment, and in familiarity with being assessed, and none of these is measured. With no cognitive or language measure taken, group membership in this study is inseparable from educational placement, and a classifier that separates the two groups at 87.5% cannot be shown to be separating them on autism rather than on the correlates of placement.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'ASDs' used as a plural noun for people in the results discussion ('Eye fixation misclassified more ASDs as TDs'), against 'typically developing (TD) children', 'TD controls', 'TDs'. The acronym-as-noun usage is the least person-centred in the corpus alongside Mazumdar. The framing is burden-oriented - autism is 'a worldwide medical problem and a tremendous economic and mental burden to society' - but the paper also carries an unusually non-deterministic aetiological framing, citing 'an emerging view is that the atypical behavior of ASD children may be caused by early brain adaptation to an adverse environment, rather than a result of ongoing neural pathology', which motivates early intervention as prevention of maladaptive adaptation rather than as remediation of pathology.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Autistic group: 40 children, 33 boys and 7 girls, aged 3-6, mean 4.6 years with a standard deviation of 9 months. Comparison group: 40 children, 33 boys and 7 girls, aged 3-6, mean 4.8 years, SD 7 months. The paper states 'no significant difference in age or sex existed between the two groups' but reports no test statistic or p value for either. Sex is matched exactly, which is a stronger match than most studies here achieve. What is entirely absent is any measure of cognitive, language or adaptive functioning - a serious gap in a 3-to-6-year-old sample where developmental level varies widely, where EEG spectral power changes rapidly with age and maturation, and where the two groups were drawn from educational settings that themselves sort on developmental level. No IQ, no developmental quotient, no language measure, no severity score.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: The weakest ascertainment in the 2022 cohort. Autism is established by 'the criteria of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition' with nothing further: no ADOS, ADI-R, CARS, SRS or any other standardised instrument; no statement of who applied the criteria, with what training, or in what setting; and no indication whether diagnosis was made for this study or taken from school records. Comparison children were 'screened to exclude any with psychiatric or neurological disorders, including ASD', again with no instrument named and no cut-off stated. Under the review's classification this is clinical-diagnosis-only in its least documented form, and it means the reference standard cannot be independently evaluated.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None whatsoever. No IQ, developmental quotient, language level, adaptive functioning measure, severity score, comorbidity list or medication information for either group. This is the most complete absence of clinical characterisation among the studies in this corpus that nonetheless report high accuracy, and it compounds the recruitment asymmetry: with children drawn from special education schools versus regular kindergartens and no cognitive measure taken, there is no way to determine whether the classifier separates autism or separates developmental level.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: compare the discriminative power of eye fixation, facial expression and EEG collected simultaneously, and test whether hybrid fusion - behavioural feature fusion followed by weighted decision fusion with the physiological stream - outperforms any single modality. Main findings: EEG most discriminative (83.75% best, 74.69% average), facial expression next (77.50%, 71.56%), eye fixation weakest (73.75%, 67.50%); hybrid fusion 87.50% against 85.00% for behavioural data alone and 83.75% for physiological data alone; modalities fail in opposite directions, with EEG best on autistic children (90.0%) and facial expression best on typically developing children (92.5%); and theta power elevated in the autistic group across five of six brain regions.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: China, with the two groups drawn from different institutional settings - special education schools for the autistic children and regular kindergartens for the comparison children. Recording conditions are described only obliquely and only in the limitations, where the authors note that 'the recording environments are changing' and that 'across-day variability exists in recording conditions'. That acknowledgement is candid but incomplete: if recording conditions varied across days and the two groups were recruited from different institutions, sessions may have been clustered by group, in which case environmental variation is partially confounded with diagnosis. The paper does not report whether recordings were interleaved across groups.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A single 40-second video clip designed so that social and non-social content compete within the same display - social being comedians with happy expressions, funny actions and laughter, non-social being backgrounds and two spinning wheels. The selection procedure is documented and is the more careful part of the design: ten candidate clips were rated by three graduate students in special education on valence and arousal, mean positions on the arousal-valence plane were computed, and the clip with the highest mean positive arousal was chosen. That grounds the stimulus in an explicit affective criterion rather than in the experimenters' intuition, though three raters is a thin basis and the raters were adults rating their own emotions rather than children's. The paradigm's strength is that one stimulus simultaneously probes three constructs - where the child looks (social versus non-social competition), whether the child mirrors the displayed expression (imitation), and the concurrent EEG response - so the three modalities are genuinely commensurate. Its limitation is duration: 40 seconds is the shortest observation window in the corpus, and with a single clip there is no test-retest or within-child replication.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: approval by the Institutional Review Board of Pingdingshan University under protocol code 068 dated 20 October 2020, conduct in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and informed consent from all subjects involved. A data availability statement commits to sharing 'from the corresponding author on reasonable request'. Facial video of identifiable preschoolers is collected and no statement about its storage, retention or de-identification appears.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Three consumer-grade sensors, which is the practical argument of the paper: a Tobii eye tracker (model not specified), an unspecified video camera, and an Emotiv EPOC+ 14-channel wireless headset with all electrode positions named (AF3, F7, F3, FC5, T7, P7, O1, O2, P8, T8, FC6, F4, F8, AF4, referenced to P3 and P4). The EPOC+ is a consumer device with saline electrodes and no impedance control, applied here to children aged 3-6; the paper cites its noninvasiveness, low cost and high temporal resolution as advantages and does not discuss its known signal-quality limitations. Preprocessing is stated (0.2-45 Hz band, epoching, removal of epochs containing blinks, eye movement or muscle activity, FFT band power) but the number of surviving epochs per group is not reported - the differential-data-quality question that Han et al. at least quantified for their comparable design.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Uneven, with the mathematics fully specified and the empirical procedure underdocumented. Reported in detail: the K-means loss function, assignment rule, centroid update and convergence criterion; the attribute-weighting formula for naive Bayes with its zero-avoidance property; the two-level fusion architecture; all 14 EEG electrode positions; the filter cut-offs and the five band definitions; the complete t-test table with F, t, p, mean difference and standard error for all 30 region-band combinations; the stimulus selection procedure; and both best and average accuracy for every modality-classifier pair. Not reported: the Tobii model, the camera specification, the sampling rates of any device, the number of EEG epochs retained per child or per group, the final chosen value of K, the CNN architecture and training details beyond a reference to prior work, any hyperparameters for random forest, SVM or KNN, and the order in which feature selection and cross-validation were performed - which has to be inferred from the text's sequence and is the study's decisive ambiguity.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Two limitations are stated. The sample is 'relatively small' and should be extended. And the data 'have nonstationary characteristics, and the recording environments are changing', so that 'across-day variability exists in recording conditions', motivating future work on models that adapt over time - a limitation rarely raised in this corpus and a real one for consumer EEG. Not acknowledged: that the 12 EEG features were selected by t-tests computed across all 80 children before leave-one-out cross-validation, so the held-out child's label informed feature selection; that the gaze cluster count K was chosen from the experimental results; that the headline 87.50% is the best across three classifiers; that autism was established by DSM-5 criteria alone with no instrument, assessor or setting described; that no cognitive, language or severity measure was taken in a preschool sample; and that the two groups were recruited from special education schools and regular kindergartens respectively, so educational placement is confounded with diagnosis.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Two directions, both modest. Enlarge the sample to improve accuracy and stability. And address non-stationarity by 'adopting detection models over time' given the across-day variability in recording conditions - which points toward domain adaptation and is a sensible response to the consumer-EEG constraint the study operates under. Absent from the agenda: any proposal to strengthen diagnostic ascertainment, to measure developmental level, to recruit comparison children from comparable settings, or to validate on an external cohort.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Two behavioural constructs, each operationalised in a way that departs from convention. Social attention allocation is measured not by fixation on hand-drawn regions of interest but by the distribution of fixations across K-means clusters discovered from the data - so the analysis asks where gaze concentrates without the experimenter deciding in advance what counts as a region. This removes one source of investigator judgement and is defensible when a stimulus has no clean object boundaries, but it also severs the link between a feature and any interpretable content: a cluster is a screen location, so a group difference cannot be reported as 'less looking at the comedian's face'. That is why the paper reports no directional gaze findings at all. Facial expression is operationalised as imitation rather than as expression: the expression displayed in the stimulus is defined as the target, and the feature is the count of frames in each 40-frame window in which the child displays that same expression - so the measure is expression contagion or mirroring in response to a specific social display, motivated by prior work suggesting 'spontaneous expression imitation could be used as a behavioral marker'. This is a sharper construct than generic expression frequency and one of the few instances in this corpus of a behavioural feature defined relative to what the stimulus is doing at that moment.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: The corpus's most explicit study of fusion architecture, with three design choices argued rather than assumed. First, fusion is hybrid rather than purely early or late: the two behavioural streams are fused at feature level, because they are homogeneous enough that concatenation exploits their correlation, while the physiological stream is fused at decision level with the behavioural subdecision, because feature-level fusion across such different data types would not work - the paper states hybrid fusion 'utilizes the merits of feature fusion and decision fusion and overcomes their disadvantages'. Second, the decision combiner is not plain naive Bayes but an attribute-weighted variant, on the explicit reasoning that 'the naive Bayes algorithm assumes that each attribute has the same influence on the classification result; in fact, they are different', with weights derived from training-set co-occurrence counts and constructed so they cannot vanish. Third, and most valuably, the paper demonstrates why fusion works rather than merely that it does: confusion matrices and pairwise confusion graphs show EEG achieving 90.0% on autistic children but only 77.5% on typical ones while facial expression achieves 92.5% on typical children but only 72.5% on autistic ones, with eye fixation missing 37.5% of autistic children - so the modalities err in opposite directions and the fused model recovers 85.0% and 90.0%. This is the same mechanism-level demonstration Han et al. provide, arrived at independently and with three modalities rather than two, and the convergence between the two studies on the finding that neurophysiological and behavioural streams fail in opposite directions is worth carrying into the synthesis. The one deflating observation is that the two behavioural modalities together (85.00%) essentially match EEG alone (83.75%), and the full fusion adds only 2.5 points over the behavioural pair - so on a cost-benefit view the EEG headset buys very little over a camera and an eye tracker.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Deliberately conventional classifiers - random forest, SVM and K-nearest neighbour - with all three applied to every modality, and both best and average accuracy reported. Running the full grid rather than reporting one model is informative: the spread on EEG features runs from 65.00% (SVM) to 83.75% (random forest), an 18-point range on identical inputs, and SVM is the weakest learner on all three modalities. That variability is a caution about single-classifier results generally, and its reporting here is more transparent than the corpus norm. The modelling novelty sits in the combiner rather than the base learners: an attribute-weighted naive Bayes whose weights are computed from training-set counts, with the formula given and its zero-avoidance property noted. No deep model is used for classification, which is appropriate given 80 participants, though a CNN is used upstream for facial expression recognition.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: One feature vector per child per modality, so the unit is the participant throughout - which is what permits genuine leave-one-out cross-validation. The gaze representation is the most distinctive: rather than manually delineating areas of interest, K-means partitions the fixation space and cluster occupancy frequencies become the features, with K tested at 8, 12, 16 and 20. The approach adapts the region structure to where children actually looked, but it carries two costs the paper does not discuss - the clusters are fitted to the pooled data of both groups, and the choice of K was made on the basis of classification results. The expression representation is a time series of target-expression counts per 40-frame window, preserving some temporal structure. The EEG representation is 12 scalar band powers, reduced from 30 candidate region-band combinations by significance testing.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy only, plus confusion matrices - no sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, ROC or AUC is reported by name, though the confusion matrices supply per-class rates from which sensitivity and specificity can be read (85.0% and 90.0% for the fused model). No confidence intervals, no variance across leave-one-out iterations, and no statistical test of any comparison, despite the text repeatedly describing differences as significant ('significantly greater than that obtained using a single modality', 'can significantly improve the classification accuracy') where no test was performed. The reporting of both best and average accuracy per modality is a genuine strength that partly offsets this, since it makes classifier-dependence visible. The absence of any trivial baseline is a real gap given that the two groups differ in educational placement and no developmental measure was taken.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is strongest for EEG and absent for the behavioural modalities. The EEG t-test table is complete - all 30 region-band combinations with F, t, p, mean difference and standard error - and the directions and interpretations are given: theta power significantly higher in the autistic group in five of six regions with the largest effect at left frontal (t = 5.82), and interpretations offered for each band ('theta waves mainly reflect the emotional experience of individuals', 'the low-beta band is related to the capacity for concentration', gamma 'related to the abilities of learning, memory, and information processing'). Those band-to-function attributions are loose and would not survive scrutiny in the EEG literature, but the underlying statistics are fully reported and the theta finding is placed in the context of prior work. For gaze and facial expression there is nothing: no group means, no directions, no effect sizes, no indication of which clusters or which time windows differ. This asymmetry follows from the representations - clusters and frame counts have no semantic content to report - and it means the study, despite recording two behavioural modalities, contributes no behavioural finding beyond classification accuracy. The confusion-graph analysis is a genuine interpretability contribution at modality level, showing exactly which class each modality handles and which it fails.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Leave-one-out cross-validation over 80 children with the participant as the unit - structurally the right design, and it forecloses the within-subject leakage that inflates Simeoli, Liaqat, Mazumdar and Akter. But two selection steps precede it and contaminate it. The EEG feature set was determined by running independent-samples t-tests on band power across all 80 children and retaining the 12 region-band combinations reaching significance; only then was classification with leave-one-out cross-validation performed on those features. Every held-out child therefore contributed their label to the choice of features used to classify them - the classic selection-bias pattern, and one that inflates the EEG modality specifically, which is the modality the paper concludes is most discriminative and which anchors its central claim. Second, the number of gaze clusters was tested at four values and 'the final value of K was determined from the experimental results', so a preprocessing hyperparameter was also chosen on classification performance across the full sample. A third, milder issue is that the headline 87.50% is the best of three classifiers; the paper reports averages for single modalities but not for the fusion. There is no external validation, no independent cohort and no repeated-split estimate of variability. The correct reading is that the participant-level design is sound but that the reported figures - particularly for EEG and for the fusion that depends on it - are optimistic by an unmeasured margin.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No keyword list appears in the extracted text. The operative vocabulary is multimodal fusion, hybrid fusion, weighted naive Bayes, eye fixation, facial expression recognition, EEG, and early detection - a method-dominated register with 'early detection' as the only clinical term.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Healthcare Engineering, volume 2022, article 9340027, an open-access Hindawi title. Authorship is from the Department of Education at Pingdingshan University and the National Engineering Laboratory for Technology of Big Data Application in Education at Central China Normal University - an educational-technology rather than clinical or biomedical-engineering provenance, which explains the paper's shape: careful engineering of the fusion architecture and the stimulus selection, competent statistics on the EEG, and essentially no clinical characterisation of the participants. The review timeline is notably compressed (received 16 February 2022, revised 5 March, accepted 8 March, published 25 March - eleven days from submission to acceptance). Funded by Henan provincial science and social science programmes.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022. The framing is standard in its premises - 1 in 54 prevalence, 'a tremendous economic and mental burden to society', existing methods 'depend on the assessment of experts, which are subjective and costly' - but two elements are distinctive. The critique of current tools is concrete rather than generic, citing the M-CHAT as a case where a parent questionnaire 'is administered by specialists in rigorously controlled clinical settings, usually taking hours to complete', so the objection is to throughput rather than to validity. And the aetiological framing is unusually non-deterministic for this literature: the paper cites 'an emerging view is that the atypical behavior of ASD children may be caused by early brain adaptation to an adverse environment, rather than a result of ongoing neural pathology', which recasts early intervention as preventing maladaptive adaptation during a period of plasticity rather than as treating a fixed pathology. That framing then does argumentative work, supplying the paper's justification for including EEG at all - that 'atypical brain development in children with ASD appears earlier than atypical behavior, and the critical period of early intervention will be missed if the detection is based on behavioral data'. The claimed contributions are explicitly comparative: that prior work has applied each modality separately, that 'studies on data fusion are few', and that 'the discriminative powers of different data modalities are unclear' - a gap the study does address, and the modality-ranking result is its most transferable finding whatever the absolute accuracies are worth.

data_charting_rubrics.title: An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Gaspar A; Oliva D; Hinojosa S; Aranguren I; Zaldivar D
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Children, per the source dataset; no characteristics are given
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking, re-encoded as gaze-path images
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Demonstrate that the Giza Pyramids Construction metaheuristic is an effective optimiser for Kernel Extreme Learning Machine hyperparameters, using autism classification from gaze-path images as the test application. The contributions are framed in that order - the paper's stated aims are to 'test the GPC over a real application' and to 'improve the KELM accuracy in the classification of ASD by using GPC' - so autism is the benchmark and the optimiser is the subject
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Secondary analysis of a public image dataset, structured as an algorithm benchmarking study with 30 independent runs per method
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Not reported by this paper; the underlying recordings belong to the source dataset and their duration is referred to only obliquely as 'short'
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Human children (secondary data; the number of children is never stated)
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Viewing of videos 'containing stimulating scenarios for the movement of the eye in the entire screen', inherited wholly from the source dataset. No stimulus content, trial structure, instruction, duration or number of viewings is described
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Not reported - the recordings belong to the source dataset; the analysis was performed at Universidad de Guadalajara and Tecnologico de Monterrey
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Analysis in Mexico; the participants' country is a property of the source dataset and is never stated
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Not reported. The paper states only 'For more information about participants diagnosed with ASD and non-ASD, see [44]' and gives no diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician role or setting. Under the review's classification this is dataset-label-only ascertainment with no restatement of the source procedure
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: Not reported in terms of people - only that 219 of the 547 images belong to the autistic class
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes, as a non-ASD image class
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Not reported in terms of people - 328 of the 547 images belong to the non-ASD class
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Pre-rendered images in which gaze coordinates and their derivatives (velocity, acceleration, jerk) are encoded as RGB colour gradients
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: The pipeline is entirely image processing. Data augmentation: horizontal flip, translation along x and y at multiple magnitudes, and blur at multiple levels, applied individually and in combination, increasing the dataset by 1300% in both classes. Dimensionality reduction: images resized from 640x480 to 28x28 using Lanczos interpolation and converted to 8-bit grayscale via the ITU-R 601-2 luma transform - a step the paper explicitly identifies as its feature selection ('the entire DR process is also the feature selection used in the proposed method'). Normalisation: contrast stretching of pixel intensities to [0,1]. The resulting 784 pixel values per image, plus a class label, are flattened into a CSV with 785 columns and fed to the classifier
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: SMI RED screen-based eye tracker (source dataset only); Lanczos interpolation; Kernel Extreme Learning Machine with RBF kernel; six metaheuristic optimisers (GPC, PSO, ABC, ALO, BA, HHO); experiments run on an AMD Ryzen 7 2700X with 16 GB RAM and a GTX 1050 Ti
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: No - a public dataset of 547 gaze-path images (328 non-ASD, 219 ASD) is reused, with its figshare URL given
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes - the source dataset and metadata are downloadable from a figshare link reproduced in the paper
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not discussed. No ethics statement, consent statement or IRB approval appears anywhere, nor any pointer to the source dataset's approvals - defensible in principle for a public dataset but never addressed
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Raw downsampled grayscale pixel intensities
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 784 pixel values from a 28x28 grayscale rendering of the gaze-path plot. There is no domain feature engineering of any kind: no fixation counts, durations, saccade amplitudes, areas of interest or scanpath statistics. The velocity, acceleration and jerk information that the source dataset encodes as colour is in fact discarded at the grayscale conversion step, so the model sees only the spatial trace's luminance pattern at 28x28 resolution - a representation with no obvious connection to any behavioural construct
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Lanczos interpolation for resizing; ITU-R 601-2 luma transform for grayscale conversion; contrast stretching for normalisation
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No. No feature importance, attribution, saliency or interpretation of any kind, and none is possible in principle given that the features are individual pixels of a downsampled plot
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None. The paper reports no group difference, effect size or behavioural characteristic of any kind - only classification metrics. The single interpretive remark is that 'the amount of information in the images and the use of space in the x and y coordinates are essential factors when classifying ASD', which is an observation about image density rather than about gaze behaviour
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Kernel Extreme Learning Machine with metaheuristic hyperparameter search
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Kernel Extreme Learning Machine with an RBF kernel, whose regularisation parameter C and kernel width gamma are searched by the Giza Pyramids Construction metaheuristic - a population-based optimiser whose update rules derive from a metaphor of workers pushing stone blocks up a ramp, with gravity 9.8, ramp angle 10 degrees, friction bounds 1 to 10 and substitution probability 0.5. Five comparator optimisers (PSO, ABC, ALO, BA, HHO) were run at matched population size 10, dimension 2 and 10 iterations with their originally published internal parameters. Three comparator classifiers were also run: naive Bayes, logistic regression, and a multilayer perceptron with 100 neurons, ReLU activation, Adam optimiser and learning rate 0.001
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: No train/test split, cross-validation scheme or held-out set is described anywhere in the paper. The only replication described is that each method was 'run 30 times' and averages, medians and standard deviations reported across those runs. The optimiser's objective function is the KELM's own mean squared error, and Figure 4 plots accuracy rising across optimiser iterations, indicating that the hyperparameter search is scored on the same predictions that are subsequently reported. Data augmentation was applied to the whole dataset before any partitioning, and the authors state directly that they used it 'to enlarge the training and testing data'
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, Matthews correlation coefficient and F1, each reported as average, median and standard deviation over 30 runs; a confusion matrix; ROC curves with AUC; and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests comparing the proposed optimiser against each comparator
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: GPC-KELM: accuracy 0.9881, precision 0.9859, sensitivity 0.9843, specificity 0.9906, MCC 0.9752, F1 0.9851, with standard deviations below 0.0015 on every metric. Comparator optimisers all fell between 0.9736 and 0.9800 accuracy. Comparator classifiers were far lower: multilayer perceptron 0.8179, naive Bayes 0.7306, logistic regression 0.7243, with AUCs of 79.17, and 66.55 for logistic regression against 98.18 for GPC-KELM. The confusion matrix reports TP 847, TN 560, FP 8, FN 8 - 1,423 classified instances, roughly 20% of the 7,111 images produced by 1300% augmentation of the original 547. Wilcoxon tests returned p-values between 5.4e-12 and 1.1e-11 for every optimiser comparison. Optimal parameters were C = 26.644 and gamma = 23.603
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A Kernel Extreme Learning Machine whose two hyperparameters are tuned by the Giza Pyramids Construction metaheuristic classified gaze-path images at 98.8% accuracy, outperforming five alternative metaheuristics (97.4-98.0%) and three conventional classifiers (72.4-81.8%) on the same data, with Wilcoxon tests confirming the optimiser differences. The result is not interpretable as a finding about autism. The dataset is 547 gaze-path images from an unstated number of children with no reported demographics, diagnoses, ages or sexes; the images were augmented thirteenfold by flipping, translation and blurring before, by the authors' own statement, being used to 'enlarge the training and testing data'; the features are the 784 pixel values of a 28x28 grayscale downsample, which discards the velocity, acceleration and jerk information the source encoding carried in colour; and no train/test split or cross-validation is described anywhere. The comparator classifiers' much lower figures on identical data (81.8% for a multilayer perceptron) indicate how much of the 98.8% is attributable to the optimisation of two kernel parameters against the same data on which performance is reported.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None reported
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Enhance and 'democratize' eye-tracking technologies; and improve the classifier by incorporating multi-class information such as medical records or clinical evaluations. The authors also note that a larger dataset would improve performance and that longer video scenarios would yield images with more information
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: This is a metaheuristics paper that uses autism classification as a benchmark, and it should be read as such. The optimiser comparison is competently executed on its own terms - six algorithms at matched population size, dimension and iteration count, using each one's originally published internal parameters, repeated 30 times, with averages, medians and standard deviations reported for six metrics and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for every pairwise comparison. As evidence about autism, however, the study is uninformative and its headline figure is not comparable to any participant-level result in this corpus. The dataset is the same 547-image gaze-path collection that Cilia and colleagues produced, and the direct comparison is instructive: on those images Cilia reported roughly 90% at image level and approximately 71% once accuracy was computed per child, since each child contributed about nine images. This paper reports 98.8% and never mentions children at all - not their number, ages, sexes, diagnoses or severity - so the image-to-participant correction cannot even be applied. Three compounding problems produce the inflation. Data augmentation multiplied the dataset thirteenfold by flipping, translating and blurring, and the authors state explicitly that this was done 'to enlarge the training and testing data', so near-duplicate transforms of the same image appear on both sides of whatever split was used; the confusion matrix's 1,423 instances is about a fifth of the 7,111 augmented images, consistent with an 80/20 split over augmented copies. Independently, images from the same child span any split, since roughly nine images per child exist and no participant grouping is possible without participant identifiers. And no train/test protocol is described anywhere in the paper - the word 'split' does not appear, no cross-validation is specified, and the accuracy-versus-iteration curve shows the metaheuristic driving accuracy upward on what appears to be the reported data. The representation choice compounds the interpretive problem: converting to grayscale discards the colour channel in which the source dataset encoded velocity, acceleration and jerk, and downsampling to 28x28 leaves 784 pixel intensities that correspond to no behavioural quantity, so even a valid result would say nothing about gaze. Two things in the paper are nonetheless worth carrying forward. The comparator table is unusually informative as an internal check: a multilayer perceptron on identical augmented data reached 81.8% and logistic regression 72.4%, so the 17-to-26-point gap between the tuned KELM and standard classifiers on the same inputs is itself a signal that the tuning, rather than the data, is producing the headline. And the authors' own limitation statement - that augmentation was used to enlarge training and testing data - is a rare instance of a leakage mechanism being described in plain terms by the authors who used it.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Not answerable from this paper. Groups are described only as image classes - 328 non-ASD images and 219 ASD images, 547 in total - and the number of children contributing them is never stated. The paper's entire treatment of participants is one sentence directing the reader elsewhere: 'For more information about participants diagnosed with ASD and non-ASD, see [44]'. This is the only study in the corpus that reports no participant count at all, in either group. Because the source is the same gaze-path collection Cilia and colleagues assembled - 547 images with roughly nine images per child - the underlying sample is a few dozen children, but nothing in this paper permits that inference, and no participant identifier is available to group images by child.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'the ASD person', 'ASD patients', 'ASD subjects', 'challenged kids with severe disabilities', 'patients', against 'non-ASD' as the comparison label. The consistent use of 'patients' for children in a non-clinical dataset, and of 'the ASD person' as a category noun, is at the deficit end of the corpus's usage. The background section is the most pathologising in the review, describing autistic people as ranging from 'gifted children with exceptional learning and problem-solving capabilities to challenged kids with severe disabilities that require care-support throughout their whole life', framing behaviours as 'red flags', stating that 'there is no known cure for ASD', and arguing that early diagnosis helps 'children with medical prescriptions to prevent further deterioration of their condition' - a progressive-disease framing that misdescribes autism. The comparison class is named 'non-ASD' rather than typically developing, which is accurate to what is known about it but reflects that nothing is known about it.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Nothing. No ages, no sexes, no group sizes in people, no cognitive or language measures, no matching, and no statement that any of these are unavailable. The only quantities reported about the sample are image counts per class. This is the least characterised sample in the corpus, exceeding even Mazumdar, which at least reported that 14 autistic and 14 typically developing children contributed the data.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Nothing. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician role or setting, and no summary or citation of the source dataset's ascertainment procedure beyond a pointer to the source paper. The class labels are treated as properties of image files. This matters more than usual because the study reports 98.8% accuracy against a reference standard whose nature is entirely unspecified within the paper.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Nothing. No IQ, language, adaptive functioning, comorbidity, medication or severity data, and no exclusions described. Consequently there is no possibility of relating model output to any clinical gradient, and no way to assess whether developmental level rather than diagnosis distinguishes the classes.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: demonstrate the Giza Pyramids Construction metaheuristic as an optimiser for Kernel Extreme Learning Machine parameters, benchmarked on autism classification from gaze-path images. Main findings: GPC-KELM reached 0.9881 accuracy, 0.9859 precision, 0.9843 sensitivity, 0.9906 specificity, 0.9752 MCC and 0.9851 F1, with sub-0.0015 standard deviations across 30 runs; it beat PSO, ABC, ALO, BA and HHO variants (0.9736-0.9800) with Wilcoxon p-values below 1.1e-11; and it beat a multilayer perceptron (0.8179), naive Bayes (0.7306) and logistic regression (0.7243) on the same data, with AUC 98.18 against 79.17 and 66.55. Optimal parameters were C = 26.644 and gamma = 23.603, converging by the sixth of ten iterations.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Not reported. The recordings belong to the source dataset and the paper describes neither the room, the country, the recruitment route nor the acquisition protocol. The only setting information is the hardware on which the experiments were computed - an AMD Ryzen 7 2700X with 16 GB RAM, a GTX 1050 Ti and a 250 GB SSD - which is specified more precisely than anything about the children.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Described in a single clause: participants 'were shown different videos containing stimulating scenarios for the movement of the eye in the entire screen'. No stimulus content, category, duration, number, order or instruction is given, and no response was apparently required. The only substantive remark about the paradigm appears in the discussion, where the authors note that 'the short duration of the video scenarios' limits the information in each image and that 'more extended scenarios should be allowed to obtain images with more information in both classes' - which is an observation about image density rather than about behavioural sampling, and it inadvertently identifies the study's core interpretive problem: the quantity being classified is how much of the plot is filled in, not what the child looked at.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis of a public dataset; no follow-up. No ethics statement, consent statement or IRB approval appears anywhere, and no pointer is given to where the source dataset's approvals were obtained - an omission that is common for benchmark reuse in this corpus but is not acknowledged here either. A competing-interests declaration and a CRediT contribution statement are both present, so the absence of an ethics statement is not a matter of missing front matter.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition equipment beyond a single mention of the SMI RED screen-based eye tracker used for the source recordings, with no sampling rate, calibration procedure or viewing geometry. Analysis tools are specified in more detail: Lanczos interpolation for resizing (with the justification that it 'provides the best properties for preserving details'), the ITU-R 601-2 luma transform for grayscale conversion at 8-bit depth, contrast stretching with the normalisation equation given, the KELM formulation with its Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse solution and RBF kernel, and the full GPC update equations with their physical parameters. The asymmetry is characteristic: every step of the image pipeline is documented and nothing about the measurement is.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Reproducible as an algorithm, not as a study. Fully specified: the three augmentation operations and the resulting 1300% expansion; the resize target, interpolation kernel, colour transform and bit depth; the normalisation equation; the CSV structure of 785 columns; the KELM equations; the GPC pseudo-code with all four operations and their parameter values; the internal parameters of all five comparator optimisers in a table; the multilayer perceptron's architecture, activation, optimiser and learning rate; the search space for C and gamma; population size, dimension and iteration count; the number of independent runs; and the compute hardware. Entirely absent: any train/test split or cross-validation protocol, the sizes of any partition, the criterion by which the optimiser's fitness was evaluated relative to reported performance, any participant-level information, and any code release. The single most important methodological fact - how performance was estimated on data not used to fit or tune the model - is not stated at any point in the paper.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Three limitations are stated and none concerns validity. The dataset has a 'low number of participants'; the video scenarios were short, so images carry limited information and 'more extended scenarios should be allowed'; and 'the current version of this work is limited by the reduced number of samples of the eye-tracking dataset. We included a data augmentation step to generate synthetic samples to enlarge the training and testing data to overcome this issue'. That last sentence is the paper's most significant disclosure and is offered as a solution rather than as a problem: augmenting the testing data means near-duplicate transformations of the same source images populate both sides of the evaluation, which is exactly what a test set must exclude. Unaddressed: that no split or cross-validation protocol is described at all; that images from the same child cannot be separated because no participant identifiers exist; that the metaheuristic optimises hyperparameters against what appears to be the reported data; that grayscale conversion discards the velocity, acceleration and jerk information encoded in colour; that no participant characteristics or diagnostic procedures are known; and that the 17-to-26-point gap over conventional classifiers on identical data warrants explanation.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Two lines are proposed, neither addressing the study's weaknesses. First, 'the enhancement and democratization of eye-tracking technologies' - an infrastructure aim rather than a research one. Second, improving the classifier 'by incorporating multi-class information such as medical records or clinical evaluations', which would move the work toward the multimodal designs elsewhere in this corpus but would require exactly the clinical data this study does not have. Notably absent: any proposal to validate at participant level, to obtain participant metadata, to test on an independent cohort, or to separate augmentation from evaluation.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Nominally gaze during free viewing, but the behavioural construct is entirely lost in the representation. The source dataset encodes gaze coordinates together with their first, second and third derivatives - velocity, acceleration and jerk - as RGB colour gradients in a plot of the scanpath. This paper converts those images to grayscale, which discards the colour channel and hence the derivative information, then downsamples from 640x480 to 28x28, leaving 784 luminance values. What the classifier sees is a coarse silhouette of where the trace fell on the screen, with no fixation, saccade, duration or velocity quantity recoverable. The authors' own concluding observation that 'the amount of information in the images and the use of space in the x and y coordinates are essential factors' confirms this: the discriminative property is how much of the frame the trace covers, which is a plot-density statistic. No behavioural finding is reported and, given the representation, none could be.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality throughout, and no fusion is attempted. The paper's comparative apparatus is entirely internal to the optimisation problem: six metaheuristics searching the same two-dimensional hyperparameter space, and four classifier families on the same features. The most informative comparison for a reader of this review is the classifier table rather than the optimiser table. On identical augmented inputs, a multilayer perceptron reached 0.8179 accuracy with AUC 79.17, naive Bayes 0.7306 and logistic regression 0.7243 with AUC 66.55, against 0.9881 and AUC 98.18 for the tuned KELM. A 17-point accuracy gap and a 19-point AUC gap between a tuned kernel machine and a neural network on the same 784 pixel features is not what one expects if the features carry a robust class signal; it is what one expects if two kernel hyperparameters are being optimised against the evaluation data. The authors read the table as evidence of their method's superiority and do not consider this alternative reading.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A Kernel Extreme Learning Machine - a single-hidden-layer feedforward network with randomly assigned input weights and an analytically computed output layer, kernelised with an RBF - chosen for computational economy over deep models, with the paper explicitly excluding deep learning from comparison 'since they require many computational resources and time for training'. The KELM has exactly two tunable parameters, C and gamma, and the entire modelling contribution is how they are chosen. The Giza Pyramids Construction algorithm searches that two-dimensional space via a metaphor of workers pushing stone blocks up a ramp, with gravity, ramp angle, kinetic friction and a worker-substitution probability as parameters. It is worth stating plainly that a two-parameter search over a grid of powers of two from 2^-7 to 2^7 does not require a population-based metaheuristic - exhaustive enumeration of 225 combinations would be cheaper than 10 iterations of a 10-member population - so the algorithmic apparatus considerably exceeds the difficulty of the problem it is applied to. The convergence result reported (optimal values found by iteration six) reflects this.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: 784 grayscale pixel intensities from a 28x28 downsample of a 640x480 gaze-path plot, contrast-stretched to [0,1] and flattened into CSV rows. The paper describes this resizing as its dimensionality reduction and states explicitly that 'the entire DR process is also the feature selection used in the proposed method' - so there is no feature engineering, no domain representation and no learned encoding, only downsampling. Two consequences follow. The colour encoding of velocity, acceleration and jerk that the source dataset was constructed to carry is destroyed by the grayscale conversion, so the very information that made the images more than plots of position is discarded before modelling. And at 28x28 the trace is a coarse blob, meaning the retained signal is essentially spatial coverage and density. Augmentation by horizontal flipping is also questionable for this representation: mirroring a scanpath about the vertical axis produces an image that no eye could have generated on the original stimulus, so the synthetic examples are not merely redundant but physically impossible.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: The most complete metric panel in the corpus in form - accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, Matthews correlation coefficient and F1, each with average, median and standard deviation over 30 runs, plus a confusion matrix, ROC curves with AUC for four classifiers, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for every optimiser comparison. Including MCC is good practice for imbalanced classes and is rare here. The apparatus is nonetheless measuring the wrong thing. The 30 runs vary only the metaheuristic's random seed, not the data partition, so the sub-0.0015 standard deviations quantify optimiser stability rather than generalisation variance, and they should not be read as precision of the accuracy estimate. The Wilcoxon p-values of 5e-12 test whether one optimiser reliably beats another across seeds - a valid question about algorithms and an irrelevant one about autism.
