And the confusion matrix's 1,423 instances cannot be located in any described partition, since no split is specified; it corresponds to about 20% of the 7,111 augmented images, which is the only reading consistent with the paper's own statement that augmentation enlarged the testing data.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None, and none is possible. There is no feature importance, attribution, saliency map or ablation, and the representation - individual pixels of a 28x28 downsampled plot - admits no behavioural interpretation even if attribution were computed. The paper offers no group difference, no effect direction and no descriptive statistic about gaze. Its one interpretive sentence, that 'the amount of information in the images and the use of space in the x and y coordinates are essential factors when classifying ASD', is a statement about how much of the frame the trace fills. Placed against the rest of this corpus, that is a meaningful observation in an unintended way: it is consistent with the classifier keying on trace density, which is a property of how much usable gaze data the tracker captured, and hence potentially on data quality rather than on viewing behaviour - the pattern seen in Li 2020's SHAP quality feature, Fang 2021's untracked-gaze 'area0' and Zhao 2021's differential OpenFace failure rates.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The corpus's weakest evaluation design, and the weakness is threefold. First, no train/test split, cross-validation scheme, held-out set or partition of any kind is described anywhere in the paper; the only replication is 30 reruns of the optimiser. Second, augmentation preceded whatever evaluation occurred, and the authors state their purpose plainly: 'We included a data augmentation step to generate synthetic samples to enlarge the training and testing data.' Flips, translations and blurs of a source image are near-duplicates of it, so populating a test set with them guarantees that the model has effectively seen every test instance. Third, and independently of augmentation, the 547 source images come from a small number of children contributing roughly nine images each, and no participant identifiers exist in the released image set, so images from the same child necessarily span any partition. Layered on top, the metaheuristic optimises C and gamma against the KELM's mean squared error with the accuracy-versus-iteration curve in Figure 4 rising monotonically over ten iterations, which indicates the search is scored on the same predictions that are reported. The instructive comparison is with Cilia and colleagues, who built this dataset and reported that image-level accuracy near 90% fell to approximately 71% when computed per child. This paper reports 98.8% on the same images, cannot compute a per-child figure because it records no participants, and does not cite the correction. The gap between 71% and 98.8% is the measure of what these three compounding decisions add.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), Machine Learning, Kernel Extreme Learning Machine (KELM), Eye tracking, Metaheuristic algorithms. Three of five are optimisation or learning terms and the ordering of the paper's stated contributions confirms the priority: propose a tool, 'test the GPC over a real application', improve KELM accuracy. Autism is the application domain for a metaheuristics contribution.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Applied Soft Computing, volume 120, article 108654 (Elsevier) - a computational intelligence journal with no clinical readership. Authorship is from the Division of Technologies for Cyber-Human Integration at Universidad de Guadalajara and the School of Engineering and Sciences at Tecnologico de Monterrey, with no clinical or psychological co-authorship. The venue and authorship together account for the paper's profile completely: rigorous treatment of the optimisation problem, six-metric reporting with non-parametric testing, full algorithmic specification, and no participants, no ethics statement, no diagnostic information and no validation protocol. Its related-work section surveys classifiers and data sources broadly and accurately but engages with no methodological literature on evaluation.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022 (received October 2021, revised February 2022). The framing is the standard objectivity argument in a strong form: 'the accurate diagnosis of ASD is usually affected since it is linked to the judgment of an expert, which produces biases related to the lack of objectivity', with the gold standard characterised as requiring 'multiple sessions and a qualified professional', hence 'time and... high cost'. The proposed role is appropriately modest - 'automatic screening tools can accelerate the diagnosis by identifying which individual require a complete autism assessment' - and the discussion repeats that the method 'permits the experts to provide a preliminary overview that guides diagnosis to more complex stages and tests'. Two features of the background are worth noting against the corpus. The clinical description is the least accurate here, framing autism as a condition from which children 'deteriorate' without early medical prescription and cataloguing 'red flags' at 12, 14 and 18 months. And the paper's positioning of its own novelty - 'to the best of our knowledge, this is the first time KELM is used for ASD classification by using gaze tracking images' - is a claim about the pairing of an algorithm with a dataset rather than about any question concerning autism, which is a fair statement of what the study contributes.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Keles U; Kliemann D; Byrge L; Saarimäki H; Paul LK; Kennedy DP; Adolphs R
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Autistic adults with IQ in the normal range
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking during naturalistic video viewing
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Decompose the well-documented excess variability of autistic participants in behavioural studies into its two possible sources - unreliability within individuals versus heterogeneity between them - by testing three competing hypotheses: that autistic gaze is noisier and less reliable than control gaze; that it is individually reliable but heterogeneous across autistic people; or that it is individually reliable and also homogeneous among them. The framing identifies the omission directly: 'our prior study suffered a major limitation that is ubiquitous in autism studies: we do not know whether the atypical gaze patterns reflect a temporally stable group difference, or whether they reflect variability within individuals'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Two-site cross-sectional case-control study with repeated measurement across two stimuli in the same session, combining group-difference estimation, within-individual test-retest reliability, multivariate identification, supervised classification and unsupervised clustering on the same data
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Two full television episodes per participant on the same day separated by a break - approximately 22 and 21 minutes, combined into a 43-minute dataset for the sampling analyses
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Free viewing of two episodes of the television sitcom 'The Office' (NBC Universal, 2005). Episode A (Season 1 Episode 1, 22 minutes) was shown in three consecutive parts with no intervening task; Episode B (Episode 4, 21 minutes) was shown in a separate session with pauses for verbal social-comprehension questions, and gaze during those pauses was excluded. Naturalistic video was chosen deliberately over the 'much more impoverished and artificial stimuli typically employed in earlier studies (such as cropped photographs of grayscale faces)' for its high participant engagement and its reduction of data-quality confounds including sleepiness and motion artifacts
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Two independent sites - the California Institute of Technology and Indiana University - using otherwise identical eye trackers and video stimuli, with participants recruited through flyers at outpatient treatment programmes, community support groups, college campuses and other community locations
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Site-specific and documented in detail. At Caltech, three criteria were required: a prior diagnosis by a qualified clinician (MD or PhD); confirmation through a clinical interview with the participant, and parent where available, conducted by a named licensed clinical psychologist; and ADOS-2 Module 4 scores at or above the diagnostic cutoff on at least two components of the original algorithm and within one point on the third, or within one point of the total cutoff under the Hus and Lord algorithm (Social Affect plus Restricted Repetitive Behaviors >= 7). At Indiana University, participants had a prior community diagnosis of ASD, autism, Asperger's syndrome or PDD-NOS, and ADOS-2 Module 4 was administered by research-reliable administrators with scores within one point of the total cutoff under the same revised algorithm. Comorbid depression, anxiety and ADHD were deliberately not excluded, though participants scoring in the moderate-to-severe range (25+) on the Beck Depression Inventory II were excluded, as were those taking antipsychotic medication at the Indiana site
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 48 analysed, from 67 initially recruited
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Deliberately inclusive - depression, anxiety and ADHD were permitted rather than excluded, on the reasoning that they are common comorbidities; only moderate-to-severe depression by BDI-II and antipsychotic medication were excluded. The authors then list this inclusiveness among their own limitations, noting it 'leav[es] open questions about the extent to which these may have contributed to our findings'
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Participants taking antipsychotic medication were excluded at the Indiana University site
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: ADOS-2 Overall Calibrated Severity Score derived by the Hus and Lord algorithm, mean 7.04 +/- 1.98 with a full range of 3 to 10, and the Autism Spectrum Quotient in both groups (28.06 +/- 7.67 versus 15.70 +/- 6.41, t(151) = -10.314, p < 0.001). Severity was used analytically, being correlated against all four gaze features
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Autism Spectrum Quotient administered to both groups, with the comparison group averaging 15.70 against 28.06
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 105 analysed, from 116 initially recruited
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes and formally tested - 27.69 versus 27.09 years, t(151) = -0.501, p = 0.617
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Yes and formally tested - 79.2% versus 70.5% male, chi-squared = 0.864, p = 0.353
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Screened via the Autism Spectrum Quotient
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Gaze coordinates at 300 Hz during naturalistic video, with areas of interest derived automatically by computer vision
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Areas of interest were generated automatically frame by frame rather than hand-drawn. DensePose within Detectron2 detected 24 body parts per person, merged into head, hands and other body regions, with undetected regions treated as non-social content; RetinaFace within InsightFace detected face areas and five facial keypoints (two eyes, nose, two mouth corners), from which eye and mouth regions were constructed by a stated geometric rule involving nested bounding boxes split at the horizontal line through the nose. Across 61,724 frames, 96.2% depicted at least one person and 94.9% yielded face and face-part detections; reconstructed videos with overlaid segmentations were watched manually to verify the automatic estimates. Gaze was downsampled to the 24 Hz video frame rate, each average gaze point represented as a 1-degree-diameter disk, and assigned to whichever area of interest it maximally overlapped. Gaze-time percentages to each area were computed as a fraction of frames with successful on-screen gaze rather than of total frames, explicitly to prevent individual differences in tracking success from biasing the area-specific measures. In parallel, per-participant gaze heatmaps were built for each 1-second bin by convolving gaze points with a 0.5-degree isotropic Gaussian and correlated against group reference heatmaps constructed leave-one-participant-out
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Tobii TX300 eye tracker at 300 Hz with 0.4-degree spatial resolution, on a movable 23-inch 1920x1080 monitor at approximately 65 cm; nine-point calibration followed by nine-point validation, repeated if any point exceeded 1.5 degrees of error, and repeated before each of the three parts of Episode A; Detectron2 with DensePose; InsightFace with RetinaFace; scikit-learn for the Gaussian mixture model
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Eye tracking from 153 adults across two sites, collected within a larger study also including behavioural assessment and neuroimaging; no release statement in the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not stated in the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not stated in the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not discussed in the extracted text. The stimulus is copyrighted commercial television, and the authors note in the supplementary material that copyright restrictions prevented reproducing frames, substituting a royalty-free image for the figure
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Area-of-interest gaze-time proportions and heatmap-correlation similarity measures
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Eight features for the fingerprinting analysis: percentage of time spent looking at the screen, at faces, at non-social content, at non-head body parts, at hands, at eyes, at mouth, and the average correlation of the participant's gaze heatmap with the typically developing reference heatmap. Four of these - on-screen, face, eye and heatmap correlation - were used for classification and clustering, after removing non-social, non-head-body, hand and mouth features because of their high correlation with the retained ones; fingerprinting with the reduced set gave nearly identical accuracy to the full set
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: DensePose/Detectron2 for body-part segmentation; RetinaFace/InsightFace for face and keypoint detection
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Addressed at the level of feature families rather than by an importance ranking. The authors report 'a rather distributed effect over heatmaps and facial features, with no single feature driving the effect', and demonstrate that four features fingerprint as well as eight
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Comparison of fingerprinting accuracy under the full eight-feature and reduced four-feature sets; bootstrap-estimated Cohen's d with confidence intervals for every area of interest in both episodes; and a partial correlation analysis testing whether reliability in face-, eye- and heatmap-based measures could be explained by individual differences in on-screen gaze time alone
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: No single dominant feature. Group differences were largest for heatmap correlation with the typically developing reference (d = 0.820 in Episode A, 0.692 in Episode B), then faces (0.618, 0.604) and eyes; the effect was distributed across features rather than localised
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Autistic adults looked less at faces (77.4% versus 80.7% of on-screen gaze in Episode A; 70.8% versus 73.9% in Episode B) and less at eyes within faces (52.0% versus 60.2%; 47.0% versus 54.9%), and more at other body parts and non-social content. Their gaze heatmaps correlated less with the typically developing reference (r = 0.61 versus 0.67 in Episode A). Critically, the group reference heatmaps themselves were near-identical (r = 0.966 and 0.963 between the autistic and typically developing references), and autistic individuals were less correlated with the autistic reference heatmap than typically developing individuals were - so there is no shared autistic gaze pattern for the group to converge on
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Group-difference estimation with bootstrap effect sizes, multivariate nearest-neighbour identification, supervised probabilistic classification, and unsupervised variational Bayesian clustering
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Gaussian naive Bayes for supervised ASD-versus-TD classification; L2 nearest-neighbour matching over standardised eight- or four-dimensional gaze vectors for identity fingerprinting, with significance from a 10,000-iteration label-shuffling permutation test; and a variational Bayesian Gaussian mixture model (scikit-learn) for unsupervised clustering, initialised at five clusters with tests at 10 and 20 yielding the same result
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Deliberately constructed to avoid the failure modes of the surrounding literature. Classification used a held-out third of each group (16 autistic, 35 control) with a 10-minute epoch randomly sampled from the combined 43-minute dataset, repeated over 10,000 cross-validation iterations, and - decisively - the chance level was established empirically from a null distribution rather than assumed to be 50%, giving 0.607 at the 95th percentile. Reliability was assessed across two non-overlapping randomly sampled epochs from the combined data with 10,000 repetitions, and separately across the two distinct episodes. Effect sizes were bootstrap-estimated over 10,000 resamples with percentile confidence intervals. Reference heatmaps were always constructed leave-one-participant-out 'to eliminate bias'. Gaze-time percentages were normalised by frames with successful on-screen gaze to prevent tracking-success differences from biasing area-specific measures, and a partial correlation analysis confirmed that reliability survived partialling out on-screen gaze time. Prior familiarity with each episode was measured and verified not to affect any reported result. Analyses were repeated across epoch durations from 10 minutes down to 1 minute or less, and multiple comparisons were false-discovery-rate corrected throughout
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Cohen's d with bootstrap confidence intervals for group differences; Spearman's rho for within-individual reliability with bootstrap tests of between-group differences in reliability; fingerprinting identification accuracy against a permutation-derived chance level; classification accuracy against an empirical null; per-participant correct- and misclassification frequencies across cross-validation iterations; and cluster membership counts with stability across 33 sliding-window iterations
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Classification accuracy was 0.618 +/- 0.058 against an empirical chance level of 0.607 - a difference of about one percentage point, p = 0.039. Of 153 participants, 95 (15 of them autistic) were correctly classified in more than 75% of iterations, while 32 (22 of them autistic) were misclassified in more than 75% of iterations - so 22 of 48 autistic adults, 46%, were reliably assigned to the wrong group. Fingerprinting, by contrast, identified individuals at 35.4% for autistic and 29.5% for control participants across the two episodes against chance levels of 6.2% and 2.9%, and remained above chance for epochs as short as 2 minutes (20.4% and 18.9%). Within-individual reliability was high and statistically indistinguishable between groups (Spearman's rho > 0.635 for all measures at 10-minute epochs, all p < 0.001; between-group difference p > 0.333 at every epoch duration tested). Group differences were moderate and stable across both episodes (Cohen's d 0.60-0.82) and detectable from epochs as short as 2 minutes. No gaze feature correlated significantly with ADOS calibrated severity. Clustering returned two clusters of approximately 104 and 49 members containing approximately 25.5 and 22.5 autistic participants respectively - splitting the autistic group nearly in half rather than separating it from controls
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: The same dataset that yields moderate, replicable group differences in gaze to faces and eyes (Cohen's d 0.60-0.82, stable across two episodes and detectable in 2 minutes of video) yields classification performance at essentially chance: 0.618 accuracy against an empirically derived chance level of 0.607, with 46% of autistic adults reliably misclassified. The reason is established rather than speculated. Autistic gaze is not noisier - within-individual reliability across episodes was high and statistically identical to controls at every epoch duration tested, and individuals could be identified from their own gaze patterns at five to ten times chance from as little as 2 minutes of viewing. Nor is it homogeneously atypical - the autistic group's own reference heatmap was almost perfectly correlated with the control group's (r = 0.966), and autistic individuals matched the autistic reference less well than controls did, indicating there is no shared autistic gaze pattern. Unsupervised clustering split the autistic group nearly in half rather than separating it from controls. Autistic gaze is therefore individually reliable and heterogeneous between individuals, which is precisely the combination under which a group-level classifier cannot succeed however reliable the underlying measurement.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Less gaze to faces and to eyes within faces, more to other body parts and non-social content, and lower correlation with the typically developing reference heatmap - all moderate in size, replicated across both episodes, and none correlating with ADOS severity
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Expand to much larger samples and longer longitudinal epochs, which the authors argue is now feasible via internet-based (WebGazer) and smartphone-based eye tracking; collect longitudinal data incorporating dense state-dependent measures such as sleepiness and mood to distinguish measurement error from genuine state-dependent within-individual change; investigate autism subtypes now that reliability has been established as a prerequisite; design stimuli with specifically chosen visual features to maximise within-individual reliability and between-individual differences, which might in principle improve classification; and combine gaze with neuroimaging and genetics, noting that gaze differences would be expected to translate into BOLD differences and may constitute an endophenotype with substantial genetic effects
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The most important methodological paper in this corpus, and the one that supplies the explanatory framework the rest of the review needs. Three of its results bear directly on how every other classification study here should be read. First and most consequential, the gaze-fingerprinting analysis demonstrates that gaze to naturalistic video carries a strong individual signature: participants were identified out of 153 at 35% against a 3-6% chance level, and remained identifiable from as little as 2 minutes of viewing. That is a direct, quantified measurement of exactly the quantity that leaks when a participant's data appears on both sides of a train/test split - the mechanism Liaqat and colleagues hypothesised to explain their own scanpath-only anomaly, and the mechanism that inflates Cilia's image-level figure, Simeoli's task-level folds and Gaspar's augmented images. Second, the study shows that individual reliability and group classifiability are separable properties: gaze here is highly reliable within individuals, statistically as reliable in autistic as in control participants at every epoch duration, and yet classification runs at chance because the autistic group is heterogeneous. A classifier can therefore be measuring something real, stable and individually characteristic while carrying no diagnostic information whatsoever. Third, the empirical chance level - 0.607 rather than 0.500 in an imbalanced 48/105 sample - is established by permutation rather than assumed, and had it been assumed, 0.618 would have been reported as a modest success rather than as the null result it is. The design that produces these results is correspondingly careful: two independent sites, groups matched and formally tested on age, sex and full-scale IQ (111.4 versus 110.0, p = 0.525 - the only corpus study to equate IQ in a well-powered adult sample), ADOS-2 Module 4 with the Hus and Lord algorithm at both sites plus licensed-clinician confirmation at one, automated computer-vision area-of-interest definition verified by manual review, leave-one-out reference heatmap construction, normalisation of area-specific gaze by successful on-screen gaze to neutralise tracking-quality differences, a partial correlation check that reliability is not an artefact of on-screen time, a measured and tested familiarity covariate, FDR correction throughout, and 10,000-iteration bootstrap or permutation procedures behind every reported statistic. Two limitations qualify the generalisation and the authors name both. The sample is adults with IQ in the normal range, deliberately restricted 'reducing variation related to general inattention, difficulty following instructions, or difficulty understanding the video stimuli', so the findings need not extend to children or to those with intellectual disability - which is the population most of this corpus studies. And only two temporal blocks were collected, both on the same day, so the reliability demonstrated is over roughly an hour rather than over weeks or years. One issue the authors report but do not discuss is differential exclusion: 10 of 58 autistic participants (17%) were dropped for gaze data quality against 3 of 108 controls (3%), so the analysed autistic sample is the subset whose gaze could be tracked reliably - which if anything makes the failure of classification more striking, since the harder-to-track participants were removed.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups, with complete flow accounting. 183 individuals were initially recruited (67 autistic, 20 female, 22 at Caltech; 116 typically developing, 33 female, 34 at Caltech). 176 watched Episode A (62 autistic) and 167 watched Episode B (59 autistic); analyses were restricted to the 166 who watched both (58 autistic). Thirteen were then excluded for eye-tracking data quality - specifically, missing or off-screen gaze for more than half of one or both episodes - leaving 48 autistic and 105 typically developing participants. The exclusion was strongly differential: 10 of 58 autistic participants (17.2%) against 3 of 108 controls (2.8%), a figure reported precisely but not discussed. Its direction matters for interpretation: the analysed autistic sample is the subset whose gaze could be tracked reliably throughout 43 minutes of video, which if anything strengthens rather than weakens the paper's conclusion that classification fails, since the participants most likely to produce noisy data were removed. Participants were split across two independent sites, with 17 autistic and 33 control participants at Caltech and the remainder at Indiana University. No other-diagnosis comparison group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Identity-first throughout: 'autistic individuals', 'autistic adults', 'autistic people', 'autistic participants', used consistently in the title, abstract and body, against 'typically developing (TD) controls'. 'ASD group' appears as a technical label for the analytic group but 'patients' never does, and no individual is described as 'an ASD'. The framing is notably non-deficit even where deficits are reported: autism is characterised as 'a complex and heterogeneous disorder that has so far defied any simple diagnostic markers or cognitive mechanisms', gaze differences are described as 'atypical' rather than impaired, and heterogeneity is treated as a scientific finding to be explained rather than as noise to be controlled. This is the most careful terminology in the corpus and is consistent with the paper's substantive argument, which is that treating autistic people as an interchangeable group is what makes classification fail.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Fully reported with formal testing on every variable, in a table with test statistics and p values. Autistic group: 48 adults, 79.2% male, 27.69 +/- 5.37 years (18-41), full-scale IQ 111.38 +/- 14.98 (84-150), ADOS CSS-Overall 7.04 +/- 1.98 (3-10), AQ 28.06 +/- 7.67. Comparison group: 105 adults, 70.5% male, 27.09 +/- 7.29 years (19-55), full-scale IQ 110.01 +/- 10.20 (85-136), AQ 15.70 +/- 6.41. None of age (t(151) = -0.501, p = 0.617), sex (chi-squared = 0.864, p = 0.353) or IQ (t(140) = -0.637, p = 0.525) differed; only AQ did (t(151) = -10.314, p < 0.001), as it should. Eleven participants with missing IQ scores were explicitly excluded from that comparison and the exclusion is footnoted. This is the only study in the corpus to equate IQ between groups in a well-powered sample rather than acknowledging an IQ gap as a limitation, and the equating was achieved by restricting recruitment to adults with IQ in the normal range - a design choice the authors justify on the grounds of reducing 'variation related to general inattention, difficulty following instructions, or difficulty understanding the video stimuli', while acknowledging that it limits generalisation.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Thorough and site-specific. Caltech required three conditions jointly: a prior diagnosis by a qualified clinician holding an MD or PhD; confirmation via clinical interview with the participant, and a parent where available, conducted by a named licensed clinical psychologist among the authors; and ADOS-2 Module 4 scores meeting a precisely stated criterion - at or above cutoff on at least two components of the original algorithm and within one point on the third, or within one point of the total cutoff under the Hus and Lord revised algorithm with Social Affect plus Restricted Repetitive Behaviors >= 7. Indiana University required a prior community diagnosis of ASD, autism, Asperger's syndrome or PDD-NOS, plus ADOS-2 Module 4 administered by research-reliable administrators meeting the same revised-algorithm criterion. Naming the exact scoring algorithm and the tolerance around cutoffs, and stating that the two sites differed in whether independent clinical confirmation was additionally required, is more precise ascertainment reporting than any other study in this review provides. The comparison group was characterised with the AQ rather than by exclusion alone.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Comprehensive and used analytically rather than descriptively. Full-scale IQ was measured in both groups and reported with range and test statistic; the AQ was administered to both groups; and ADOS-2 Overall Calibrated Severity Scores derived by the Hus and Lord algorithm were obtained for the autistic group with a full range of 3 to 10, meaning the sample spans the severity spectrum rather than clustering at one end. Severity was then correlated against all four gaze features, with the finding that none reached significance - a negative result that matters, since it means the gaze measures that do differentiate groups on average do not index how autistic an individual is. Comorbidity handling is deliberate and unusual: depression, anxiety and ADHD were permitted rather than excluded on the grounds that they are common in autism, with only moderate-to-severe depression (BDI-II >= 25) and antipsychotic medication ruled out. The authors then list this inclusiveness among their own limitations, noting it leaves open how much comorbidity contributed to the findings - a rare instance of a design decision being defended and then flagged as a threat in the same paper.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: determine whether the excess behavioural variability of autistic participants reflects within-individual unreliability or between-individual heterogeneity, by testing three mutually exclusive hypotheses. Main findings, in the order they eliminate hypotheses: within-individual reliability was high and statistically indistinguishable between groups at every epoch duration (Spearman's rho > 0.635, between-group difference p > 0.333), and individuals were identifiable from their own gaze at 35% against a 3-6% chance level from as little as 2 minutes of video, ruling out hypothesis 1; the autistic and typically developing reference heatmaps were correlated at r = 0.966 and autistic individuals matched the autistic reference less well than controls did, and unsupervised clustering split the autistic group nearly in half rather than separating it from controls, ruling out hypothesis 3; supervised classification reached 0.618 against an empirical chance level of 0.607 with 22 of 48 autistic adults reliably misclassified, confirming hypothesis 2. Group differences themselves were moderate and robust: Cohen's d 0.60-0.82, replicated across two episodes and detectable from 2-minute epochs.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Two independent sites - Caltech and Indiana University - using 'otherwise identical eye trackers and video stimuli', with the two-site design adopted explicitly 'to optimize generalizability'. Recruitment was through flyers distributed at outpatient treatment programmes, community support groups and community locations including college campuses and YMCAs, so the sample is community-recruited rather than clinic-referred - which matters for representativeness, though the authors note the sample 'is not representative of ASD in general'. Site membership is carried through the analysis and displayed in every figure by marker shape, so site effects remain visible rather than being pooled away. This is the only multi-site study in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Free viewing of two episodes of a commercial television sitcom, chosen on an argued rationale rather than by convenience. The authors state that naturalistic video was selected over 'much more impoverished and artificial stimuli typically employed in earlier studies (such as cropped photographs of grayscale faces)' because movies deliver 'high participant engagement, and reducing confounds to data quality including sleepiness and motion artifacts', and because the same stimuli had proved effective in the group's prior neuroimaging work. Two distinct episodes were used specifically to test whether within-individual reliability holds across stimuli rather than merely across time, which is the stronger test. Three design controls attach to the stimulus. Prior familiarity with each episode was measured on a nine-point scale, participants split into familiar and unfamiliar, and every reported result verified not to differ between them. Gaze during the social-comprehension question pauses in Episode B was excluded. And the analysis showed that gaze to faces differed substantially between the two episodes (Cohen's d 1.15 in the autistic group, 1.70 in controls) while the between-group differences remained stable - establishing that the group effect is a property of the participants rather than of the particular video, which is precisely the confound that stimulus-specific studies elsewhere in this corpus cannot exclude.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional with two measurement blocks on the same day separated by a break, drawn from a larger study that also included extensive behavioural assessment and neuroimaging. The authors identify the temporal limitation themselves as their second main limitation: 'we collected only two [blocks], both close in time and for similar (but distinct) video episodes', and argue that longer-term longitudinal data with dense state measures such as sleepiness and mood would be needed to distinguish measurement error from genuine state-dependent within-individual change. No ethics or consent statement appears in the extracted text, though the study is embedded in an established multi-site research programme. Copyright constraints on the sitcom prevented reproducing stimulus frames, and a royalty-free substitute image was used for the segmentation figure.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Tobii TX300 at 300 Hz with 0.4-degree spatial resolution on a movable 23-inch 1920x1080 monitor at approximately 65 cm. Calibration discipline is the most rigorous in the corpus and is reported with its failure handling: a nine-point calibration followed by a nine-point validation quantifying error at all nine locations spanning the full screen, with results displayed immediately to the experimenter, who would adjust the screen or participant and repeat if any point exceeded 1.5 degrees of error - and the procedure repeated before each of the three parts of Episode A. The authors also report, against their own interest, that 'a computer error resulted in the loss of the validation data, so further quantitative assessment of validation accuracy is not possible', and that 12 participants were recorded at 120 Hz rather than 300 Hz 'because of a user error', noting that downsampling to the 24 Hz video frame rate compensated for the difference. Reporting both errors is a form of candour absent elsewhere in this corpus. Feature extraction used Detectron2 with DensePose and InsightFace with RetinaFace, and clustering used scikit-learn.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Among the most reproducibly reported studies in the corpus. Specified: recruitment channels; both sites' diagnostic criteria including the exact ADOS-2 algorithm, cutoff and tolerance; the complete flow from 183 recruited to 153 analysed with reasons and counts at each step; eye tracker model, sampling rate, resolution, monitor size, viewing distance, calibration and validation protocol with its error threshold and repetition rule; both recording errors; stimulus identity, duration and part structure; the familiarity questionnaire and its cut-point; the complete area-of-interest construction including the specific models used, the merging of 24 DensePose parts into three, and the geometric rule for deriving eye and mouth regions from five keypoints; detection rates across all 61,724 frames; the manual verification of automatic segmentation; the downsampling to video frame rate, the 1-degree gaze disk and the maximum-overlap assignment rule; the normalisation of area-specific gaze by successful on-screen frames with its stated rationale; heatmap construction with Gaussian width, bin duration and the leave-one-out reference rule; the bootstrap, permutation and sampling procedures with their 10,000 iteration counts; classifier, held-out sizes and cross-validation repetitions; the mixture-model initialisation and its robustness checks; and the FDR correction. What is missing from the extracted text is an ethics statement, a data availability statement and any mention of code release.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Three limitations are stated, each substantive and each with a proposed remedy - the most serious limitations section in the corpus. First, the sample is relatively small and 'not representative of ASD in general', and consists of adults with IQ in the normal range, so 'it remains unclear if our findings would generalize to children and individuals with lower IQ'; the inclusion of comorbid depression, anxiety and ADHD is folded into this as a further open question. Second, only two temporal blocks were collected, both on the same day, so within-individual precision is limited both by measurement error and potentially by state-dependent change, and longer-term longitudinal data across more diverse stimuli would be needed. Third, and most carefully argued, the interpretation rests on having measured only eye movements: 'It remains possible that other dependent measures - performance tasks or questionnaires based on interpreting the videos, or neuroimaging - would have revealed higher variability in ASD', including the specific alternative that autistic people might have unreliable cognition that they compensate for. The authors then argue against their own alternative rather than merely listing it, noting that 'eye movements are not under strong volitional control' and the stimuli are highly engaging, so 'a top-down compensatory mechanism thus seems implausible'. Two issues go unremarked: the differential exclusion rate for gaze data quality (17% of autistic participants versus 3% of controls), and the fact that the two sites used different diagnostic confirmation procedures.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: The agenda follows directly from the findings and is unusually specific. Scale up via internet-based (WebGazer) and smartphone-based eye tracking to obtain the sample sizes needed to identify subtypes, which the authors argue is now feasible and is made more so by their own finding that 2-minute epochs suffice. Collect longitudinal data with dense state-dependent measures - sleepiness, mood - to separate measurement error from genuine within-individual variation across weeks or years, and to assess intervention efficacy while revealing what an intervention changes ('gaze to faces but not to other features might change throughout training'). Design stimuli with specifically chosen visual features to maximise within-individual reliability and between-individual differences, which 'possibly... could also improve the classification analyses'. And integrate with neuroimaging and genetics, on the reasoning that systematic gaze differences 'would be expected to translate to differences also in evoked BOLD-fMRI activations' and 'may be an endophenotype reflecting substantial genetic effects'. The through-line is that establishing individual-level reliability was a prerequisite for all of these, which is the paper's framing of its own contribution.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Social visual attention during naturalistic viewing, resolved into a hierarchy of automatically detected regions: faces, eyes within faces, mouth, hands, non-head body parts, and non-social content, plus two global measures - total on-screen gaze time and the correlation of a participant's moment-by-moment gaze heatmap with a group reference. The heatmap measure is the conceptually distinctive one, since it captures moment-to-moment conformity with what other viewers looked at rather than aggregate time in a region, and it produced the largest group effects (d = 0.820 and 0.692). Its use also generates the paper's most consequential single analysis: constructing a reference heatmap from the autistic group and finding that it correlates at r = 0.966 with the control reference, while autistic individuals nonetheless match it less well than controls do. That result establishes directly that there is no shared autistic pattern of looking - the average autistic viewer looks where the average control viewer looks, and individual autistic viewers depart from that average in individually different directions.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality by design, and the paper is explicit that this is a limitation of its interpretation rather than a methodological choice to be defended: other measures 'would have revealed higher variability in ASD' is entertained as a live possibility. No fusion is attempted. The paper does perform an internal combination that is informative for the fusion literature elsewhere in this corpus: fingerprinting with all eight gaze features and with a reduced set of four gave nearly identical identification accuracy (32.6% versus 35.4% for the autistic group), because the removed features were highly correlated with the retained ones - non-social, non-head-body and hand gaze with face gaze, and mouth with eyes. That redundancy check, performed and reported rather than assumed, is the discipline missing from studies that report improvements from adding correlated features.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: The modelling is deliberately simple and the choice is argued: a Gaussian naive Bayes classifier on four features, because the study's question is whether diagnostic information exists in the gaze data at all, not how much a flexible model can extract from 153 participants. The complementary unsupervised analysis uses a variational Bayesian Gaussian mixture model, which learns the number of clusters from the data rather than being told it - an important property here, since forcing two clusters would have guaranteed a partition that could be compared against diagnosis, whereas learning the number allows the data to indicate no meaningful split. It returned predominantly two clusters (25 of 33 windows) and was robust to initialisation at 5, 10 or 20 components. Pairing a supervised classifier with an unsupervised clustering that asks the same question from the opposite direction, and finding that both fail to recover diagnosis, is stronger evidence than either alone.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Eight, then four, interpretable scalar features per participant per epoch - each a percentage of gaze time to an automatically detected region, or a correlation with a reference heatmap. Two representational decisions carry substantial methodological weight. Areas of interest were generated frame by frame by pretrained computer vision models rather than hand-drawn, removing experimenter judgement about what counts as a face or a hand and making the approach applicable to arbitrary naturalistic video; detection rates are reported (96.2% of 61,724 frames containing a person; 94.9% with face parts) and the automatic segmentations were manually verified by watching reconstructed overlay videos. And gaze-time percentages to each region were normalised by the number of frames with successful on-screen gaze rather than by total frames, explicitly so that individual differences in tracking success could not bias the region-specific measures - the direct remedy for the data-quality-as-signal pattern that recurs throughout this corpus, where tracking failure rates differ by group and can masquerade as behaviour. A partial correlation analysis then verified that the reliability findings were not explained by on-screen gaze time alone.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: The most statistically careful reporting in the corpus, and the one that determines the paper's central conclusion. Group differences are reported as Cohen's d with bootstrap confidence intervals from 10,000 resamples rather than as p values alone, with the authors stating they 'preferred Cohen's d to provide a practical estimate for the magnitude of an effect of interest... rather than just reporting the results of statistical tests'. Reliability is reported as Spearman's rho with a bootstrap test of the between-group difference in reliability - testing not whether each group is reliable but whether they differ in reliability, which is the actual hypothesis. Fingerprinting accuracy is tested against a permutation null with 10,000 label shuffles. Most importantly, classification accuracy is compared to an empirically derived chance level of 0.607 rather than to an assumed 0.500 - a distinction that entirely changes the reading of the 0.618 result, since against a nominal 50% baseline it would have appeared as a modest success. FDR correction is applied throughout. And per-participant classification frequencies across 10,000 iterations are reported, revealing that the aggregate accuracy conceals a bimodal structure: 95 participants classified correctly more than 75% of the time and 32 misclassified more than 75% of the time, 22 of those autistic. Reporting who is misclassified, rather than only how often, is what converts a null accuracy into a substantive finding about heterogeneity.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is pursued through study design rather than through model attribution, and is stronger for it. Four analyses jointly characterise what the gaze data contain. The effect-size profile across areas of interest, with bootstrap confidence intervals in both episodes, shows where the group differences lie and that they replicate. The reference-heatmap comparison establishes that the autistic and control group averages are nearly identical (r = 0.966) while individual autistic participants depart from both - which localises the phenomenon at the individual rather than group level. The fingerprinting analysis quantifies how much individually distinctive information the same features carry, and the four-versus-eight-feature comparison shows the information is distributed rather than concentrated. And the per-participant classification and clustering frequencies show which individuals the group-level model can and cannot place. The authors summarise the feature-level picture honestly as 'a rather distributed effect over heatmaps and facial features, with no single feature driving the effect', and note the caveat that their features were intercorrelated and their videos always contained people. The absence of a correlation between any gaze feature and ADOS severity is also reported, and is an important negative: the measures separate groups on average without indexing individual severity.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The reference standard for this corpus, and the source of its most transferable methodological lesson. The classification procedure holds out a third of each group, samples a 10-minute epoch at random from the combined 43-minute dataset, trains on the remainder and repeats 10,000 times - so the estimate is not a single split and every participant is held out repeatedly. Decisively, the chance level is derived empirically from a null distribution and comes to 0.607 rather than the 0.500 that an imbalanced 48/105 design might naively suggest; the observed 0.618 therefore exceeds chance by about one percentage point at p = 0.039, which the authors correctly describe as 'only slightly greater than would be expected by chance' and as confirming that heterogeneity 'precludes diagnostically robust classification'. Had the same number been compared against 50%, it would have been reported as a 12-point improvement. Beyond classification, the validation apparatus includes: leave-one-participant-out construction of every reference heatmap 'to eliminate bias'; normalisation of area-specific gaze by successful on-screen frames so that tracking quality cannot leak into the behavioural measures; a partial correlation control confirming reliability is not driven by on-screen time; measurement of stimulus familiarity and verification that it affects no result; replication of every analysis across two distinct stimuli and across epoch durations from 10 minutes down to seconds; bootstrap confidence intervals on all effect sizes; permutation testing for fingerprinting; FDR correction throughout; and two independent sites with site membership displayed rather than pooled. The single most important output for this review is the fingerprinting result itself: gaze identifies an individual out of 153 at five to ten times chance from 2 minutes of data. That is a direct measurement of the individual-identity signal that any train/test split failing to separate participants will allow a classifier to exploit, and it explains quantitatively why studies here that split by image, segment, task or augmented copy report accuracies far above what participant-level designs achieve.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: eye tracking, autism, heterogeneity, individual differences, videos. Three of five name the study's actual subject - heterogeneity and individual differences - rather than a method or a performance target, which is unique in this corpus and accurately signals a paper whose contribution is conceptual rather than algorithmic.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Molecular Autism 13:39 (2022), an autism-specific journal with a mechanistic and clinical readership, published open access. Authorship spans Caltech's Division of the Humanities and Social Sciences with computation and neural systems affiliations, the University of Iowa, Indiana University, Tampere University and a joint senior authorship shared between the two site leads. The group's prior work is cited as motivation and critiqued in the process - the paper explicitly identifies the limitation of its own earlier study as the gap it now addresses. Publishing a null classification result in an autism journal, framed as informative rather than as a failed experiment, is itself notable given that the corpus's positive-accuracy studies appear predominantly in engineering venues.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022. The framing is a deliberate inversion of the rest of this literature. Rather than arguing that clinical diagnosis is subjective and that automated classification would be objective, the paper starts from the premise that autism 'has so far defied any simple diagnostic markers or cognitive mechanisms' and asks what property of the data would have to hold for classification to be possible at all. It then names the field's characteristic omission precisely: 'Across ASD eye tracking studies, this is a major unanswered question: what portion of the variance in findings can be assigned to between-individual variability, and what portion can be assigned to within-individual variability?' - and observes that 'individual-level reliability is a prerequisite for successful classification and prediction'. That reframing converts a methodological question into a substantive one and produces a result the accuracy-maximising literature could not have produced: a demonstration that the measurement is reliable, the group difference is real and replicable, and the classifier nonetheless fails, because reliability and classifiability are different properties. The paper's positioning of eye tracking is correspondingly measured - it emphasises the modality's practical advantages, its applicability from infancy to adulthood, its resistance to volitional control and its emerging feasibility on phones and over the internet - while directing those advantages toward subtype discovery, longitudinal monitoring and intervention assessment rather than toward diagnosis.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Chi NA; Washington P; Kline A; Husic A; Hou C; He C; Dunlap K; Wall DP
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Children with a parent-reported autism diagnosis
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Speech and vocalisation (acoustic, non-linguistic)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Remove the equipment and setting barriers that the authors identify as blocking deployment of automated speech screening. The critique of prior work is specific and is the paper's organising argument: earlier studies achieving comparable or better accuracy used 'a specialized biosensor device with 4 directional microphones' or 'multiple wireless microphones, providing high purity recordings at a central recording location (a hospital)', and such research 'does not accelerate the process of autism detection because it requires the use of specialized equipment and centralized recording locations'. The additional argument is behavioural rather than logistical - 'interacting with unknown adults in foreign environments could be stressful and possibly affect the behavior of children with autism, thus leading to observations that are not generalizable to the real world'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification on a crowdsourced convenience sample, structured as a three-way model comparison under identical child-disjoint folds
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: 90-second gameplay sessions; each child contributed a mean of 1.32 videos and 14.7 clips, totalling 115.5 minutes of audio across the whole dataset
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Play within the Guess What? mobile game, designed for prosocial interaction at home between children aged 2 to 8 and their parents. Families choose either a charades game - acting out emotions, characters, sports, chores or objects - or a quiz game identifying colours, shapes, numbers and word spellings. The child follows the gameplay rules while the parent acts as mediator, holding the smartphone against their own forehead with the front camera facing the child. After each 90-second session parents can review the recording and choose whether to share it
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Participants' own homes, recorded by parents on their own smartphones; the research group is at Stanford University
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: United States (implied by recruitment through a US-distributed app; not stated explicitly)
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Parent report only, and the authors state the limitation plainly: 'while we require parents to disclose their child's clinical diagnosis by choosing from options not widely known to those who have not received a clinical evaluation, these labels are self-reported and thus unverified'. No standardised instrument, clinician contact or record verification of any kind. The mitigating argument - that the diagnostic options offered are unfamiliar to families who have not been through evaluation - is a plausible partial safeguard but is not itself validated
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 20 children (19 male, 1 female) contributing 425 clips
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Median 5 years; no mean or standard deviation reported
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Within the overall 3-12 range; group-specific ranges not reported
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported; no exclusion criteria of any kind are described
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: None. No severity, cognitive, language or adaptive measure for either group
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Parent report only; no screening instrument
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 38 children (15 male, 22 female, 1 unspecified) contributing 425 clips
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd_controls: Median 9.5 years; no mean or standard deviation reported
data_charting_rubrics.age_range_controls: Within the overall 3-12 range; group-specific ranges not reported
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No, and the gap is large - median 5 years in the autistic group against 9.5 in the comparison group, a 4.5-year difference. No statistical test is reported and, unlike the sex imbalance, the age difference is never mentioned as a limitation or discussed anywhere in the paper
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: No - 95% male against 39% male. This imbalance is acknowledged, quantified and benchmarked against the expected 4:1 to 3:1 population sex ratio, with the authors noting their split exceeds what that ratio would produce
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Parent report only
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Smartphone-recorded audio extracted from gameplay videos
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Audio was extracted from shared gameplay videos and manually spliced to isolate segments containing only the child's voice, because 'parents or children would often join in gameplay simultaneously, resulting in a variety of voices, sometimes overlapping with one another'. The resulting 850 clips - deliberately balanced at 425 per class - were partitioned into five folds under the constraint that all clips from a given child fall in the same fold. Three parallel pipelines then operated on the same folds: hand-engineered acoustic features for a random forest, Librosa-generated mel spectrograms for a CNN, and raw waveforms for a fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Participants' own smartphones (no model constraint); the Guess What? mobile game; Librosa for spectrogram synthesis; scikit-learn for the random forest; Keras for the CNN with Visualkeras for visualisation; the facebook/wav2vec2-base checkpoint
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: 850 child speech clips from 77 videos of 58 children, collected between 2018 and 2021 - described as a novel dataset; no release statement
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not directly addressed, but privacy receives a dedicated Discussion subsection - unusually for this corpus. The authors note that privacy 'is particularly important for studies involving commonly stigmatized disorders like autism', and argue that because their models are lightweight they 'could feasibly be deployed at home on mobile devices, allowing for private offline symptom detection as well as privacy-preserving federated learning approaches', addressing 'parents who wish for a diagnostic signal but hesitate to share videos with strangers'. Parental consent to share videos is described as part of the collection process; no IRB approval statement appears in the extracted text
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Standard speech-recognition acoustic descriptors; learned spectrogram representations; and self-supervised waveform representations
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: For the random forest: Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, chroma features, root mean square energy, spectral centroids, spectral bandwidths, spectral rolloff and zero-crossing rates - a conventional speech-recognition feature set rather than a prosody-specific one. Notably, despite the paper's motivating claim that autism involves 'echolalia, monotonous intonation, atypical pitch, and irregular linguistic stress patterns', no pitch, intonation, stress or rhythm feature appears anywhere in the feature set, and the two deep models learn their own representations without constraint. The gap between the stated prosodic rationale and the actual features is never addressed
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Librosa for spectrograms and acoustic features; wav2vec 2.0 for self-supervised representations
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No. No importance ranking, attribution or ablation over features, and no analysis of what distinguishes the classes acoustically
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None. No group means, effect sizes or acoustic characterisations are reported for any feature, so the paper contributes no descriptive finding about how autistic children's speech differed
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Three-way comparison: ensemble tree classifier on hand-engineered features, convolutional network on spectrograms, and fine-tuned self-supervised transformer on raw audio
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Random forest in scikit-learn with all hyperparameters stated (max_depth 20000, n_estimators 56, max_features 15, min_samples_split 10, min_samples_leaf 20, min_weight_fraction_leaf 0.1), described as manually chosen; logistic regression, Gaussian naive Bayes and AdaBoost were also tried and reported to perform worse. A 9-layer CNN with alternating convolution and max-pooling plus 3 dense layers and L2 penalty 0.01, trained 15 epochs to 8,724,594 parameters; a fine-tuned Inception v3 with ~33 million parameters was also tried and performed slightly worse, which the authors attribute to 'the irrelevance of ImageNet features to spectrograms'. Wav2vec 2.0 (facebook/wav2vec2-base), fine-tuned for 264 steps to 95 million parameters, justified by prior demonstration of its utility 'for suprasegmental tasks such as emotion prediction'
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Five-fold cross-validation with an explicitly child-disjoint constraint: 'we included the restriction that all clips spliced from a given child's video had to be included in the same fold to prevent models from learning from child-specific recording idiosyncrasies, including environmental background noise and audio quality'. Fold composition is tabulated (81-87 clips per class per fold). The best-performing model weights were saved per fold and metrics averaged across folds with standard deviations. Reported metrics are nonetheless computed over clips rather than over children
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUROC, each as mean and standard deviation across the five folds; per-fold and mean ROC curves for each model; and confusion matrices for all three models
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: CNN: 79.3% accuracy (SD 0.013), 80.4% precision, 79.3% recall, 79.0% F1, AUROC 0.822 (SD 0.010). Wav2vec 2.0: 76.9% accuracy (SD 0.005), 78.2% precision, 74.6% recall, 76.8% F1, AUROC 0.815 (SD 0.077). Random forest: 69.7% accuracy (SD 0.013), 68.7% precision, 74.4% recall, 69.4% F1, AUROC 0.740 (SD 0.09). Notably the random forest's recall standard deviation is 0.247 - larger than the differences between models. All three showed correlated fold-to-fold variation, performing well on fold 2 and poorly on fold 3, which the authors interpret as evidence that the folds are too small to be interchangeable. The CNN and wav2vec models produced relatively few false positives while the random forest produced many; all three had similar false negative rates
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Speech recorded on ordinary parental smartphones during 90-second home gameplay sessions supported autism classification at 79.3% accuracy and 0.822 AUROC using a small CNN over mel spectrograms, with a fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 close behind at 76.9% and a random forest on conventional acoustic features clearly worse at 69.7%. The result rests on only 115.5 minutes of audio from 58 children, and the cross-validation folds were constructed so that all of a child's clips stay together, explicitly to prevent the model from learning child-specific recording idiosyncrasies. Two transfer-learning observations are reported: an ImageNet-pretrained Inception v3 underperformed a purpose-built 8-million-parameter CNN, attributed to the irrelevance of natural-image features to spectrograms, while a self-supervised audio transformer transferred usefully. The authors also report that all three models rose and fell together across folds, which they read as an indication that the folds are too small. Against these results, the two groups differ by 4.5 years in median age (5 versus 9.5) and by 56 percentage points in proportion male, and diagnostic labels are unverified parent report.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None reported
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Collect more data from a wider selection of both groups, since 115.5 minutes already yielded reasonable accuracy; replace manual splicing of child speech - 'a time-intensive process that may not be scalable' - with automatic blind source separation, which the authors call 'an exceptionally challenging task' but 'possibly a necessary hurdle'; explore wearable collection via devices such as Google Glass, which the group has used to deliver social cues; add a crowdsourced human workforce for audio feature extraction; and combine audio with computer-vision quantification of hand stimming, upper-limb movement and eye contact toward an interpretable multimodal system
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The engineering contribution is genuine and the validation discipline is above the corpus norm, but the sample composition undermines the diagnostic claim in a way the paper never confronts. On the credit side, the fold construction is explicitly child-disjoint and the reason is stated in exactly the right terms - to prevent the model 'learning from child-specific recording idiosyncrasies, including environmental background noise and audio quality' - which is the leakage mechanism that Keles and colleagues quantify directly and that Cilia, Simeoli, Liaqat and Gaspar all fall into. Three model families are compared on identical folds with five metrics apiece, standard deviations across folds, per-fold ROC curves and confusion matrices, and negative results are reported without embarrassment: logistic regression, naive Bayes and AdaBoost underperformed, and a fine-tuned Inception v3 lost to a smaller purpose-built CNN. The observation that all three models rise and fall together across folds is a thoughtful diagnostic that the authors interpret correctly as fold-size limitation rather than model instability. The deployment argument is also more concrete than most: parental smartphones, no equipment constraint, 90-second sessions, and a privacy discussion proposing on-device inference and federated learning specifically because autism is stigmatised. Against this, the decisive problem is that the two groups differ by 4.5 years in median age - 5 against 9.5 - and this is not mentioned anywhere in the paper, not in the limitations, not in the discussion. Child speech changes profoundly across that interval in fundamental frequency, formant structure, articulatory precision, fluency and utterance length, and mel spectrograms encode all of it. A classifier separating median-5-year-olds from median-9.5-year-olds would be expected to reach roughly this accuracy on age alone, and nothing in the analysis excludes that explanation: no age-matched subsample, no age covariate, no age-only baseline. The sex imbalance compounds it - 95% male against 39% male - and although this one is acknowledged and quantified against the population ratio, sex likewise shapes child voice acoustics. Together the groups differ on the two variables that most determine how a child's voice sounds. Diagnostic labels are unverified parent report, which the authors do concede. And there is a mismatch between motivation and method that goes unremarked: the paper is framed throughout on prosodic abnormality - echolalia, monotonous intonation, atypical pitch, irregular stress - yet no pitch, intonation, stress or rhythm feature appears in the feature set, and no acoustic finding of any kind is reported, so the study contributes classification numbers without any characterisation of how the two groups' speech differed. A senior author declares founding Cognoa, a company developing digital autism diagnostics, which is disclosed appropriately.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups from a crowdsourced convenience sample: 20 children with a parent-reported autism diagnosis and 38 neurotypical children, 58 in total, contributing 77 videos over four years from 2018 to 2021. Clip counts were deliberately balanced at 425 per class, which means the 20 autistic children contributed roughly 21 clips each against roughly 11 each for the 38 comparison children - so the autistic class is built from fewer children sampled more densely, and each autistic child exerts about twice the influence on the class representation. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The recruitment mechanism is itself distinctive: families downloaded a mobile game, played it at home, and then chose whether to share the recording, so the sample is self-selected among app users willing to disclose a diagnosis and share video of their child.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'children with autism', 'affected children', 'individuals affected', against 'neurotypical (NT) children'. Person-first throughout, and the use of 'neurotypical' rather than 'typically developing' or 'normal' is the more neurodiversity-aligned choice, though it sits alongside conventional deficit framing of autism as 'delayed linguistic development, social interaction deficits, and behavioral impairments' and speech features described as 'peculiarities' and 'abnormalities'. The paper is unusual in explicitly naming stigma as a design consideration, noting that privacy 'is particularly important for studies involving commonly stigmatized disorders like autism' and motivating on-device inference for parents who 'hesitate to share videos with strangers'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Reported, and the reporting reveals the study's central problem. Autistic group: 20 children, 19 male (95%) and 1 female, median age 5 years. Comparison group: 38 children, 15 male (39%), 22 female (58%) and 1 unspecified, median age 9.5 years. Overall age range 3-12. Two large imbalances follow. The 4.5-year median age gap is the more serious and is never mentioned anywhere in the paper - not in the limitations, not in the discussion - despite being the single variable that most determines the acoustics of a child's voice across this range: fundamental frequency falls, formants shift with vocal-tract growth, articulation stabilises, disfluency declines and utterance length increases substantially between 5 and 9.5 years. The sex imbalance is the reverse - 95% versus 39% male - and this one is acknowledged, quantified and benchmarked, with the authors noting that even the naturally skewed 4:1 to 3:1 population ratio would predict only 75-80% male, so their split exceeds expectation, and concluding that the dataset 'may still not be completely representative of real-world conditions'. Combining the two, the autistic group is younger and almost entirely male while the comparison group is older and majority female, so the groups differ systematically on both determinants of child vocal acoustics before diagnosis is considered. No IQ, language level, developmental measure or matching procedure is reported.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Parent report alone, and the authors state the limitation directly: 'while we require parents to disclose their child's clinical diagnosis by choosing from options not widely known to those who have not received a clinical evaluation, these labels are self-reported and thus unverified'. No standardised instrument, no clinician involvement, no medical record check. The safeguard offered - that the diagnostic labels presented in the app are unfamiliar to families who have not been through an evaluation - is a reasonable heuristic against casual mislabelling but does nothing to establish which diagnosis a child actually received, when, by whom, or against what criteria. The comparison group's neurotypical status likewise rests on parental assertion with no screening instrument. This is the weakest reference standard in the corpus alongside the benchmark-reuse studies, and it is a consequence of the crowdsourcing design rather than an oversight: a fully remote app-based collection cannot verify diagnoses without a separate clinical pathway.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, language, adaptive or severity measure for either group, and no comorbidity or medication information. This matters more than usual for a speech study, since expressive language level directly determines what a child produces in a 90-second game and would be expected to differ between a median-5-year-old autistic group and a median-9.5-year-old comparison group on both developmental and diagnostic grounds. Nothing in the data allows that to be examined, and no exclusion criteria of any kind are described.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: test whether autism can be detected from self-recorded home speech captured on ordinary smartphones, removing the specialised equipment and centralised recording locations that the authors argue make prior work undeployable. Main findings: a purpose-built 8.7-million-parameter CNN over mel spectrograms reached 79.3% accuracy and 0.822 AUROC; a fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 reached 76.9% and 0.815; a random forest over conventional acoustic features reached 69.7% and 0.740; folds were constructed child-disjoint to block recording-idiosyncrasy leakage; all three models covaried across folds, suggesting the folds are too small; an ImageNet-pretrained Inception v3 underperformed the smaller purpose-built CNN; and the whole result rests on 115.5 minutes of audio from 58 children.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Participants' own homes, with no researcher present, no controlled acoustics and no equipment standardisation - the design's defining property and its explicit purpose. The authors' argument is twofold and both parts are worth noting. Logistically, prior speech studies used directional microphone arrays or multiple wireless microphones at a hospital, which 'pos[es] significant barriers to the widespread availability of automatic diagnosis tools', reinforced by the observation that 83.86% of American counties have no autism diagnostic resources at all and that the delay from first consultation to diagnosis averages over two years. Behaviourally, the authors argue that 'interacting with unknown adults in foreign environments could be stressful and possibly affect the behavior of children with autism, thus leading to observations that are not generalizable to the real world' - a validity argument for home recording rather than merely a convenience one. The consequence embraced rather than lamented is heterogeneous audio quality, which the paper treats as fidelity to deployment conditions.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Ninety-second sessions of the Guess What? mobile game, structured as either charades - acting out emotions, characters, sports, chores or objects - or a quiz on colours, shapes, numbers and word spellings. The child follows the gameplay while the parent mediates, holding the smartphone against their own forehead with the front-facing camera on the child. Three properties matter. The interaction partner is the child's own parent rather than a clinician or a stranger, which is what makes the elicited speech naturalistic. The session is extremely short, and the total corpus is only 115.5 minutes across 58 children, which the authors turn into a positive by noting that so little data still yielded workable accuracy. And the task structure is only semi-standardised: families choose between two game types and the resulting speech differs accordingly, so the linguistic and prosodic demands are not equated across children - a source of variation the paper does not examine, and one that could interact with age given that a median-5-year-old and a median-9.5-year-old will engage very differently with a spelling quiz.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, with data accumulated opportunistically over four years from 2018 to 2021 rather than in a defined recruitment window; no follow-up. Parental consent to share each recording is built into the app flow - families view the video after each session and choose whether to send it - which is a stronger form of ongoing consent than a single upfront authorisation, though no IRB approval statement appears in the extracted text. Privacy is treated substantively rather than as boilerplate, with a dedicated Discussion subsection arguing that the models' small size permits on-device inference and privacy-preserving federated learning, motivated explicitly by autism's stigmatisation and by parents who want a diagnostic signal but are unwilling to share video. A senior author declares founding Cognoa, a company developing digital paediatric health solutions.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Deliberately none beyond what families already own: participants' own smartphones, with no model, microphone or sampling-rate constraint, held against the parent's forehead during play. This is the study's contribution and its cost. The benefit is that the recordings carry the acoustic heterogeneity of real deployment - varying room acoustics, distances, device microphones, background noise - so a model that works here has already survived conditions that laboratory studies control away. The cost is that none of that variation is characterised: no distribution of device types, recording levels, signal-to-noise ratios or sampling rates is reported, so it cannot be determined whether any acoustic property covaries with group.
