Given that the two groups were recruited through the same app but differ in age and sex, a systematic difference in, say, microphone distance for younger children is plausible and unexamined. Analysis tools are named precisely: Librosa, scikit-learn, Keras with Visualkeras, and the facebook/wav2vec2-base checkpoint.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Good on modelling, thin on data. Reported: the app, the two game types, the 90-second session length, the recording arrangement, the manual splicing criterion (segments containing no voice but the child's), clip counts by class, the mean of 1.32 videos and 14.7 clips per child, the fold composition table, the child-disjoint fold constraint with its rationale, the complete random forest feature list and all six hyperparameters, the CNN's layer structure, regularisation penalty, epoch count and exact parameter count, the wav2vec checkpoint and fine-tuning step count, the alternative models tried and rejected, and the total 115.5 minutes of audio. Not reported: any acoustic property of the recordings, the group-specific age ranges or means, any splicing reliability check or inter-splicer agreement, clip durations, the criterion for how many clips were taken per child, any data or code release, and random seeds. The manual splicing step is the least reproducible element - it is a human judgement applied to every clip, performed by unspecified people to an unspecified standard, and the authors identify its non-scalability as a limitation without addressing its consistency.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Three limitations are stated, one of them thoroughly. The sex imbalance is quantified precisely (95% versus 39% male), benchmarked against the expected 4:1 to 3:1 population ratio, and the conclusion drawn that the dataset 'may still not be completely representative of real-world conditions' - among the more careful demographic self-assessments in the corpus. The unverified nature of parent-reported diagnoses is conceded directly. The small dataset and the non-scalability of manual splicing are both raised, with automatic blind source separation named as the necessary but difficult alternative. What is absent is the study's largest problem: the 4.5-year median age gap between groups appears once, in a single sentence of the demographics paragraph, and is never mentioned again - not in the limitations, not in the discussion, not as a caveat on the accuracy figures. No age-matched analysis, age covariate or age-only baseline is attempted. Also unaddressed: that the autistic class is built from 20 children sampled at roughly 21 clips each while the comparison class draws on 38 children at roughly 11 each; that metrics are clip-level rather than child-level despite the folds being child-disjoint; that no acoustic characterisation of any kind is reported; and that the prosodic rationale in the introduction is not reflected in any feature actually used.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Five directions, with the most substantive being technical. Collect more data across a wider selection of both groups, argued from the observation that 115.5 minutes already sufficed. Replace manual splicing with automatic blind source separation - the authors are realistic about this, calling it 'an exceptionally challenging task' while noting it is 'possibly a necessary hurdle to overcome to develop widely available and consistently effective autism machine learning diagnosis resources', which correctly identifies the bottleneck for any home-recording pipeline where parents and children speak simultaneously. Explore wearable collection through devices such as Google Glass, building on the group's prior work delivering social cues through wearables. Add crowdsourced human annotation of audio features. And combine audio with computer-vision quantification of hand stimming, upper-limb movement and eye contact toward an interpretable multimodal system. Notably absent: any proposal to verify diagnoses, to match on age, or to characterise what acoustically distinguishes the groups.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Nominally prosody. The introduction rests its case entirely on prosodic abnormality, citing 'echolalia, monotonous intonation, and atypical pitch and linguistic stress patterns' as 'among the most notable signs of autism', and this is the paper's justification for looking at speech at all. What is actually modelled is broader and less specific: the random forest uses a generic speech-recognition feature set - MFCCs, chroma, RMS energy, spectral centroid, bandwidth and rolloff, zero-crossing rate - containing no pitch, intonation contour, stress or rhythm measure whatsoever, while the CNN and wav2vec models learn unconstrained representations from spectrograms and waveforms. The behavioural target is therefore 'whatever in the acoustic signal separates these two groups of children', which given the sample composition includes vocal-tract size, fundamental frequency range and articulatory maturity - all direct functions of the age and sex on which the groups differ. Because no acoustic finding is reported, the paper cannot say whether anything prosodic was involved. The contrast with Asgari and colleagues elsewhere in this corpus is instructive: that study modelled pitch, jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio explicitly, reduced to two interpretable features, and correlated them with independently rated severity.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality - audio only - with no fusion attempted, though multimodal extension is proposed as future work. The paper does run a genuine three-way representation comparison on identical child-disjoint folds, which is more informative than most single-modality studies here and yields two transferable observations. First, learned representations beat hand-engineered ones by roughly ten points (79.3% and 76.9% against 69.7%), and the gap is largest in AUROC (0.822 and 0.815 against 0.740), suggesting that whatever separates the classes is not well captured by the conventional descriptor set. Second, the two transfer-learning results point in opposite directions and the authors interpret both correctly: an ImageNet-pretrained Inception v3 with 33 million parameters lost to a purpose-built 8.7-million-parameter CNN, attributed to 'the irrelevance of ImageNet features to spectrograms', while a self-supervised audio transformer transferred usefully, justified by prior evidence of wav2vec's utility 'for suprasegmental tasks such as emotion prediction'. Domain-matched pretraining helped; domain-mismatched pretraining hurt, even at four times the parameter count.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Three families compared on identical folds - an ensemble tree model on hand-engineered features, a convolutional network on spectrograms, and a fine-tuned self-supervised transformer on raw waveforms - which spans the realistic design space for a small audio classification problem. The comparison is conducted honestly: alternatives that lost are named rather than omitted (logistic regression, Gaussian naive Bayes, AdaBoost for the shallow family; Inception v3 for the deep one), and the winning CNN is the smallest deep model tried. Full hyperparameters are given for the random forest and described as 'manually chosen', with no tuning procedure stated - which leaves open whether the shallow model was tuned as carefully as the deep ones and hence whether the ten-point gap partly reflects unequal effort. The fold-to-fold correlation across all three models is the most thoughtful analytic observation in the paper: 'each model appears to perform well on fold 2 while performing relatively poorly on fold 3. This suggests that the data in each fold may be too limited', which correctly attributes the variance to the data partition rather than to model instability.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Three representations of the same 850 clips. Hand-engineered acoustic descriptors for the random forest; Librosa-generated mel spectrograms treated as images for the CNN; and raw waveforms for wav2vec 2.0. The unit throughout is the clip, not the child, and this is the study's one residual validation gap: the folds are child-disjoint, which correctly prevents a child's clips appearing on both sides, but the metrics are averaged over clips, so the reported figures aggregate 850 correlated observations from 58 people. A child who contributes 21 clips influences the accuracy twenty-one times over, and no per-child prediction or per-child accuracy is reported. Since clip counts differ systematically by group - roughly 21 per autistic child against 11 per comparison child - the clip-level metrics also weight the two classes' children unequally.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Five metrics per model, each as mean and standard deviation across five folds, plus per-fold and mean ROC curves and confusion matrices for all three - complete and comparative reporting. The standard deviations do real work here and are worth reading closely: the random forest's recall SD is 0.247, larger than the entire performance gap between models, indicating that its per-fold recall swings wildly, while its accuracy SD is only 0.013 - a pattern signalling that it trades sensitivity against specificity differently in each fold. Wav2vec's AUROC SD of 0.077 against the CNN's 0.010 similarly shows the CNN is the more stable model despite the authors' expectation that the 95-million-parameter transformer would be 'more robust'. The confusion matrices add a real finding: both deep models produce few false positives while the random forest produces many, with all three having similar false negative rates. What is missing is any comparison against a trivial baseline - given a 4.5-year median age difference between groups, an age-only classifier is the obvious comparator and would establish how much of the 79.3% is diagnostic at all.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No feature importance, attribution, saliency, spectral analysis or group comparison of any acoustic quantity is reported, and no interpretation is offered of what distinguishes the classes. This is a substantial gap given that the paper's entire motivation is a specific set of prosodic claims - echolalia, monotonous intonation, atypical pitch, irregular stress - none of which is tested, measured or discussed after the introduction. The random forest's feature set would have supported at least a permutation-importance analysis at no cost, and mel spectrograms admit standard saliency methods. The consequence is that the study yields three accuracy figures and no knowledge about autistic children's speech, so it cannot be evaluated for construct validity: there is no way to tell whether the models are keying on prosody, on vocal-tract size, on recording distance, or on utterance length. The authors do gesture at interpretability as a future goal, proposing that combining audio features with computer-vision measures 'could possibly result in interpretable models', which acknowledges the present absence.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Correct on the dimension that matters most in this corpus and incomplete on a secondary one. The fold constraint is stated explicitly and reasoned exactly right: 'all clips spliced from a given child's video had to be included in the same fold to prevent models from learning from child-specific recording idiosyncrasies, including environmental background noise and audio quality'. That names both the mechanism and its two concrete forms, and it is the discipline missing from Cilia's image-level folds, Simeoli's task-level folds, Liaqat's image-wise splits and Gaspar's augmented copies. Fold composition is tabulated so the balance can be checked, all three models are evaluated on the same folds, and metrics are averaged with standard deviations. Three gaps remain. Metrics are clip-level rather than child-level, so 850 correlated observations from 58 children are treated as the effective sample and no per-child accuracy is available. There is no held-out test set beyond cross-validation, and the random forest's hyperparameters were 'manually chosen' with no procedure described, so some selection optimism is unquantified. And most importantly, no analysis addresses whether the classifier is separating diagnosis or separating age and sex - there is no age-matched subsample, no covariate adjustment, and no age-only or sex-only baseline, despite both variables differing markedly between groups and both directly determining child vocal acoustics. The validation protocol is therefore sound against leakage and silent on confounding.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism, mHealth, machine learning, artificial intelligence, speech, audio, child, digital data, mobile app, diagnosis. The presence of 'mHealth' and 'mobile app' alongside 'diagnosis' locates the work in digital health delivery rather than in speech science, which matches the paper's actual contribution - a deployment architecture rather than an acoustic finding.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: JMIR Pediatrics and Parenting 5(2):e35406 (2022), an open-access digital-health journal for paediatric readers. Authorship spans Stanford's Division of Systems Medicine in Pediatrics, Bioengineering, Computer Science, Biomedical Data Science and Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, with the senior author's group having produced a substantial body of prior work on mobile autism screening, wearable social-cue delivery and crowdsourced annotation - much of it cited here. Funding is extensive, listing four NIH grants, an NSF award and numerous foundations. The senior author declares founding Cognoa, a company developing digital paediatric diagnostics, disclosed appropriately; the same company's FDA-authorised screening product is critiqued by name in the Ko et al. paper elsewhere in this corpus for feeding human ratings rather than raw video into its model - a critique that this study's raw-audio approach implicitly answers.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022. The framing combines the usual epidemiological appeal with two access statistics that are more concrete than the corpus norm: 83.86% of American counties have no autism diagnostic resources at all, and the delay from first consultation to diagnosis averages over two years, pushing typical diagnosis past age four with documented downstream consequences including higher psychotropic medication use, lower IQ and reduced language aptitude. The distinctive positioning, though, is a critique of the immediately preceding speech literature on deployability rather than on accuracy. The authors name two studies achieving comparable or better results - one using 'a specialized biosensor device with 4 directional microphones', another 'multiple wireless microphones, providing high purity recordings at a central recording location (a hospital)' - and argue that such work 'does not accelerate the process of autism detection' precisely because the conditions that produce clean data are the conditions that prevent scaling. They then add a validity argument alongside the logistical one: recording in unfamiliar settings with unfamiliar adults may itself alter the behaviour being measured. That pairing - that laboratory control buys signal quality at the cost of both reach and ecological validity - is the sharpest statement of the deployment-versus-fidelity tradeoff in this review, and it is the axis along which this study should be compared with Asgari and colleagues, who took the opposite position and gained interpretability, clinical characterisation and confound control in exchange for requiring a clinical ADOS session.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection
data_charting_rubrics.authors: MacFarlane H; Salem AC; Chen L; Asgari M; Fombonne E
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: School-age children and adolescents with autism and fluent speech
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Multimodal within speech - automated language measures fused with harmonic-model voice measures
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Not diagnosis. The stated aim is to establish the discriminant validity of automated communication measures against an already-established diagnosis, in order to build outcome measures for research: 'This work (past and current) is not currently intended to be employed for diagnostic or screening purposes. Rather, our methodology uses already-established diagnosis as an external criterion against which we can validate (in the sense of discriminant validity) these voice and language measures.' The underlying problem is that quantifying language and voice is 'costly, difficult to administer, and of limited accuracy', that caregiver reports are 'susceptible to the placebo effect' in treatment studies, and that the ADOS and SRS 'include only one item each on voice quality' despite prosodic difference being a cited characteristic of autism
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional classification with three specific aims - replicate two prior single-modality models within one sample using one methodology, quantify the gain from combining them, and characterise the clinical profiles of participants each model detects or misses
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One ADOS-2 Module 3 administration per participant, with analysis confined to a single conversational task averaging 6.5 to 7.9 minutes
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: The Friends, Relationships, and Marriage Conversation task of ADOS-2 Module 3, selected on three explicit grounds: it is administered in the second half of the assessment 'after the warm up period of the testing situation'; it 'consistently yields the most c-units of all ADOS tasks'; and it 'has a high standardization of conversational questions, leading to good comparability between participants', using pre-established open-ended interview questions designed to facilitate conversational flow. Both prior studies from this group had independently identified it as the most discriminative task
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Oregon Health & Science University, Portland, with participants recruited by community outreach and referral from OHSU specialty clinics into an fMRI study; the microphone was suspended in a cage on a table approximately three feet from where the child sat, positioned so as to capture the child's language even when they moved around the room
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Among the most rigorous in the corpus. All children in the autistic and ADHD groups were directly assessed by experienced child psychiatrists and clinical psychologists who confirmed diagnosis under DSM-IV-TR criteria; a research diagnostic team then reviewed the standardised diagnostic assessments - both videos and scored protocols - and applied best-estimate procedures. Autism was actively ruled out in both the typically developing and ADHD groups using the ADOS, clinical interview and parent-completed autism questionnaires. ADOS-2 Module 3 was administered to every participant by research assistants or a senior clinical psychologist trained to research reliability level. A strict screening list excluded seizure disorder, cerebral palsy, paediatric stroke, chemotherapy history, sensorimotor handicaps, closed head injury, thyroid disorder, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, current major depressive episode, fetal alcohol syndrome, Tourette's disorder, severe vision impairment, Rett syndrome, current psychoactive medication use, non-English speakers, and IQ below 70. Of 289 screened, 104 were excluded for not meeting strict diagnostic criteria
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: An extensive medical and psychiatric exclusion list applied to all groups, including current psychoactive medication - a control that matters directly for voice measures - and IQ below 70. ADHD was deliberately retained as part of the comparison group rather than excluded
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Participants currently using psychoactive medications were excluded
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: ADOS-2 Social Affect (9.31 +/- 3.53 versus 1.13 +/- 1.58) and Restricted and Repetitive Behavior (3.48 +/- 1.60 versus 0.46 +/- 0.64) scores, plus the parent-completed Children's Communication Checklist-2 yielding Structural (6.53 +/- 2.44 versus 10.21 +/- 1.97) and Pragmatic (4.92 +/- 1.86 versus 10.24 +/- 2.17) scale scores. All differ at p < 0.001 and all are used analytically as predictors of which participants each model detects
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Yes, but the comparison group is deliberately mixed
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Autism ruled out in both the typically developing and ADHD subgroups on the basis of the ADOS, clinical interview and parent-completed autism questionnaires
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 70, comprising typically developing children and children with ADHD combined into a single non-ASD group
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes and formally tested - 11.4 versus 11.5 years, Mann-Whitney p = 0.6044
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: No - 83.0% versus 57.1% male, Fisher's exact p = 0.00065. The imbalance is addressed directly by training the combined model separately in boys (AUC 0.8901) and girls (AUC 0.8067), neither differing significantly from the full-sample AUC (p = 0.4428 and p = 0.178)
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: The comparison group is intentionally not uniformly typical - it merges typically developing children with children carrying an ADHD diagnosis, justified on two grounds: preliminary analyses showed the two did not differ significantly on any language measure, and 'including a non-autistic clinical group alongside TD participants provided an opportunity to more adequately test for the specificity of the results with respect to the presence or absence of autism'
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Transcribed language and denoised audio from a single ADOS-2 conversational task
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Two parallel pipelines from the same recording. Language: all ADOS administrations were transcribed under modified SALT guidelines by trained research assistants blind to diagnostic status and intellectual ability, with speech segmented into communication units comprising a main clause plus subordinate or modifying clauses, or fragments constituting a whole utterance; disfluencies (mazes) were specially notated, unintelligible speech marked, transcriber disagreements resolved by discussion with a clinician to consensus, and transcribers subjected to biannual consistency checks. Voice: a three-module pipeline segmented the recording into frames by timestamp, retained only frames belonging to the child during the Friends task, applied a pretrained fully automated deep-neural-network denoiser, extracted ten harmonic features per frame, and averaged each feature across all frames for each participant
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Microphone suspended in a cage approximately three feet from the child; a pretrained deep-neural-network denoiser (Defossez et al. 2020) with no parameters to set; a harmonic model of speech with model-based jitter and shimmer estimation; linear-kernel SVM; mSVM-RFE for feature ranking; R for all statistics; analysis code released on GitHub
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Transcripts and audio from 158 children, drawn from a larger OHSU neuroimaging cohort and previously used by Salem et al. (2021) and in part by Asgari et al. (2021)
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No, but de-identified data are available on request and the analysis code is publicly released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Yes - 'De-identified data is available upon request from the authors', with analysis code at a stated GitHub URL
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Audio and transcripts from clinical diagnostic assessments. Governance is reported: IRB review and approval at OHSU, with informed written consent or assent obtained from all participants and their parents at the initial visit. De-identified data sharing is offered
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Automated language measures from transcripts and harmonic-model acoustic measures from audio
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Seven automated language measures: mean length of utterance in morphemes and number of distinct word roots (both computed only on complete, fluent, intelligible c-units), um proportion (um divided by um plus uh), content maze proportion (non-filler disfluencies divided by content mazes plus fillers), unintelligible proportion, c-units per minute, and repetition proportion (child words repeated in runs of two or more from the examiner's immediately preceding turn, divided by total child words). Ten automated voice measures: 13 cepstral coefficients with first and second time derivatives, log spectral entropy, F0, jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio, H1H2 as an indicator of breathiness, and RMS energy capturing loudness. Jitter and shimmer used a model-based rather than standard estimation because 'standard methods for calculating jitter and shimmer are sensitive to the pitch estimation'. The design is deliberately restrained - the authors describe 'a streamlined, purposeful inclusion of established voice and language measures' rather than a large undirected feature set, and each measure was previously validated in one of the group's two prior papers
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Modified SALT transcription protocol; harmonic model of speech with model-based jitter and shimmer estimation; DNN denoiser
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, and with an honest negative result
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Multiple support vector machine recursive feature elimination (mSVM-RFE) ranking features across 10-fold cross-validation to find the combination with lowest generalisation error; 10-fold rather than leave-one-out was used because the software could not be applied to leave-one-out
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The optimal subset comprised eight features, evenly split across modalities - content maze proportion, c-units per minute, mean length of utterance in morphemes and um proportion from language; RMS, F0, shimmer and log spectral entropy from voice. Critically, the optimal subset's AUC (0.9344) did not differ significantly from the full model's (0.9235, DeLong p = 0.1592), so feature selection produced no real gain and the authors report it as such rather than promoting the higher figure
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Descriptive statistics and between-group comparisons for all 17 measures are provided in supplementary Table S1 rather than in the main text. The directional finding that the paper foregrounds is not about features but about people: the language model detected autistic participants with poorer structural and pragmatic language and less language output, while the voice model detected those with better language profiles
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Linear support vector machines on interpretable hand-engineered features, compared in single-modality and combined configurations
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Linear-kernel SVM with the soft-margin constant selected per model (C = 10 for voice, C = 1 for language, C = 100 for combined), with all features normalised to [0,1]. Non-linear SVMs and formal hyperparameter tuning were also run and reported in supplementary Table S2, with the linear configuration reported in the main text for its performance. mSVM-RFE for feature ranking, and DeLong's test for comparing correlated ROC curves
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, adopted explicitly to 'limit over-fitting to the idiosyncratic characteristics of our participants' and justified by citation to Saeb et al. (2017) 'due to its approximation of the clinically relevant use-case of diagnosis in unseen participants'. Robustness was checked against 10-fold cross-validation, giving AUC 0.9235 versus 0.9205 with a non-significant difference (p = 0.9219). Model comparisons used DeLong's test for correlated ROC curves rather than informal comparison of point estimates, and 95% confidence intervals accompany every AUC. Sex-stratified models were fitted separately and compared against the full-sample AUC
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and ROC AUC with 95% confidence intervals for all three models; DeLong tests for all pairwise AUC comparisons; sex-stratified AUCs; and Mann-Whitney comparisons of age, IQ, four clinical scores and three task indices between correctly and incorrectly classified participants for each model
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Voice-only: accuracy 0.7215, sensitivity 0.7500, specificity 0.6857, AUC 0.7800 (95% CI 0.7076-0.8525). Language-only: accuracy 0.7975, sensitivity 0.7727, specificity 0.8286, AUC 0.8748 (0.8199-0.9297) - significantly better than voice (DeLong p = 0.036), the advantage lying entirely in specificity. Combined: accuracy 0.8671, sensitivity 0.8977, specificity 0.8286, AUC 0.9205 (0.8768-0.9641), significantly better than voice (p < 0.001) and than language (p = 0.033). The combined model's gain is entirely in sensitivity - specificity is unchanged at 0.8286 - so adding voice recovered autistic participants the language model missed without adding false positives. Only nine autistic participants (10.2%) were missed by the combined model. Sex-stratified AUCs were 0.8901 for boys and 0.8067 for girls, neither differing from the full sample. Feature selection to eight features gave 0.9344, not significantly better than the full model
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Language measures and voice measures extracted automatically from a single seven-minute ADOS-2 conversation classified autism at AUC 0.8748 and 0.7800 respectively, and their combination at 0.9205 - a statistically significant gain over both, established by DeLong tests on correlated ROC curves rather than by comparing point estimates. The mechanism of the gain is identified rather than assumed: the two modalities detect different children. Participants caught by the language model had significantly poorer structural and pragmatic language, less language output and were a year younger; participants caught by the voice model had consistently better language profiles, and no CCC-2 score or task index distinguished the voice model's hits from its misses, indicating that the acoustic measures 'assess paralinguistic features (e.g., prosody, loudness) that are truly independent of language level and output'. Combining them therefore lifted sensitivity from 0.77 to 0.90 while leaving specificity untouched at 0.83. The nine autistic participants still missed had the highest IQ and the most language output of any subgroup. Neither ADOS severity nor IQ was significantly associated with misclassification in any of the three models, and sex-stratified models performed equivalently - so the measures appear unconfounded by cognitive level, symptom severity and sex.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Reported in supplementary material rather than the main text; the paper's foregrounded finding concerns which participants each modality detects rather than which features differ
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Recruit adults and younger children, and include individuals with lower IQ and less verbal participants who cannot be assessed with Module 3; systematically test each component feature to identify which contribute; determine which voice features drive the voice model's false positives, with the specific hypothesis that 'loudness is a general non-specific feature of young children interviewed on sensitive topics... in an unfamiliar setting'; control microphone quality and placement tightly to reduce reliance on denoising; establish test-retest reliability and short-term stability, which the authors state they do not yet know; extend to naturalistic conversational sampling outside the clinic, 'aiming at minimizing interference by strangers and capturing naturally occurring conversations in the ecological niche of the participants'; and replace manual transcription with automatic speech recognition, re-evaluating model performance on ASR transcripts
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: One of the two or three strongest studies in this corpus, and the clearest demonstration of what a multimodal fusion claim looks like when it is properly evidenced. Four things distinguish it. The validation is leave-one-subject-out, adopted with an explicit citation to Saeb et al. on subject-wise versus record-wise cross-validation - the only paper here to name that literature - and cross-checked against 10-fold with a non-significant difference. Model comparisons use DeLong's test for correlated ROC curves with confidence intervals on every AUC, so the claim that combining beats either modality is a tested claim rather than a comparison of point estimates; almost every other fusion paper in this review asserts improvement from an accuracy delta alone. The complementarity mechanism is established empirically by profiling who each model catches: language features find children with poorer language and less output, voice features find children with better language profiles, and crucially no language measure distinguishes the voice model's hits from its misses - which is what licenses the interpretation that acoustic measures index something orthogonal to language level. That is a substantive clinical finding in its own right, and it converges with the clinical observation the authors cite that 'voice atypicalities often persist among older individuals who have achieved the most typical outcomes'. And the comparison group deliberately merges ADHD with typically developing children specifically 'to more adequately test for the specificity of the results', which is the design almost every other study in this corpus identifies as necessary and does not perform. Confound handling is equally disciplined: the groups differ on IQ (99.5 versus 112.1) and sex (83% versus 57% male), and rather than acknowledging these as limitations the authors test both directly - IQ and ADOS severity were never significantly associated with misclassification in any of the three models, and sex-stratified AUCs did not differ from the full sample. Scope discipline is exceptional: the paper states plainly that the work 'is not currently intended to be employed for diagnostic or screening purposes' and positions diagnosis as an external criterion for validating outcome measures, which is the correct framing for what the data support and one that no other high-performing study here adopts. Analysis code is released. The limitations are correspondingly candid and include several the authors were not obliged to raise - that ADOS administration focuses on eliciting autistic features so 'it is possible that our results are overestimated compared to what would be obtained with more naturalistic conversational samples'; that test-retest reliability is unknown; that transcription reliability statistics were not computed despite extensive training and biannual checks; and that examiners may have interacted with more able participants in ways that maximised their language output, citing Bone et al. Two residual issues. The denoising step is acknowledged as of unknown effect but its necessity is stated in striking terms - 'if denoising is not performed, the acoustic features mainly represent the noise instead of participants and the classifier cannot distinguish between groups' - which means the voice result depends entirely on a pretrained black-box denoiser applied identically to both groups, and while identical application is the right control, the interaction between denoising and group-specific vocal characteristics is unexamined. And the sample is restricted to fluent English speakers with IQ at or above 70 assessable with Module 3, which the authors flag; the measures cannot currently speak to minimally verbal children, who are a substantial part of the population the framing invokes.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two analytic groups from three clinical ones: 88 autistic participants and 70 non-autistic participants, the latter formed by merging children with ADHD and typically developing children. The merge is justified on two stated grounds and both are substantive - preliminary analyses showed no significant difference between the ADHD and typically developing subgroups on any automated language measure, and 'including a non-autistic clinical group alongside TD participants provided an opportunity to more adequately test for the specificity of the results with respect to the presence or absence of autism'. This is the corpus's clearest instance of a study building the specificity test into its comparison group rather than naming it as future work. Flow accounting is complete: 289 screened, 104 excluded for not meeting strict diagnostic criteria, 10 for failing to complete initial assessment, leaving 175 in the parent neuroimaging study (102 ASD, 45 ADHD, 28 TD); 6 autistic participants excluded for untranscribable ADOS sessions due to poor sound quality or non-compliance; and 11 more excluded for analysis - 6 with undefined um proportion because neither um nor uh occurred in the task, 4 without IQ results, and 1 with an acoustically corrupted file. Note that the exclusions fall disproportionately on the autistic group (14 of 17), and that the 6 excluded for producing no filled pauses at all are plausibly among the least verbally fluent.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'autistic people', 'autistic children', 'autistic individuals', 'people with and without autism', 'children with ASD', 'individuals with autism' - identity-first and person-first used interchangeably and comfortably, with identity-first predominating in general statements about the population. 'Patients' never appears. The framing is explicitly respectful and says so: 'this growing detection and awareness of autism requires thoughtful and respectful research to help facilitate communication between people with and without autism' - which frames the goal as bidirectional communication rather than as remediating a deficit. Communication is described as involving 'differences' and 'variability' at least as often as 'difficulties', and the lay summary opens with 'People with autism often struggle with communication differences which traditional clinical measures and language tests cannot fully capture' - locating the inadequacy in the measures rather than in the people. This is among the most careful terminology in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Fully reported with formal testing on every variable. Autistic group: 88 participants, 73 male (83.0%), 11.4 +/- 2.1 years, IQ 99.5 +/- 19.9. Non-autistic group: 70 participants, 40 male (57.1%), 11.5 +/- 1.7 years, IQ 112.1 +/- 12.9. Race and ethnicity are tabulated for both groups (predominantly white, 13 and 8 Hispanic). Age matches (Mann-Whitney p = 0.6044); sex does not (Fisher's exact p = 0.00065); IQ does not (p < 0.001). What distinguishes this study is that both mismatches are tested rather than merely conceded. For sex, the combined model was refitted separately in boys (n = 113, AUC 0.8901, 95% CI 0.8261-0.9541) and girls (n = 45, AUC 0.8067, 95% CI 0.6493-0.9640), neither differing significantly from the full-sample AUC (p = 0.4428 and p = 0.178). For IQ, the misclassification analysis found that IQ was never significantly associated with correct or incorrect classification in any of the three models. The authors nonetheless list loose matching among their limitations - 'Participants were not tightly matched between groups which could result in reduced fit for analysis' - rather than treating the confound tests as closing the question.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Among the strongest ascertainments in the corpus and comparable to its companion paper. Diagnosis was confirmed by experienced child psychiatrists and clinical psychologists who directly assessed every participant in the autistic and ADHD groups under DSM-IV-TR criteria, followed by a research diagnostic team reviewing 'results of the standardized diagnostic assessments (both videos and scored protocols)' and applying best-estimate procedures. ADOS-2 Module 3 was administered to all participants by research assistants or a senior clinical psychologist trained to research reliability level. Autism was actively ruled out in both comparison subgroups using the ADOS, clinical interview and parent-completed autism questionnaires - so negative cases are excluded on three independent sources rather than assumed. The screening list is extensive and clinically targeted, excluding seizure disorder, cerebral palsy, paediatric stroke, chemotherapy history, sensorimotor handicaps, closed head injury, thyroid disorder, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, current major depressive episode, fetal alcohol syndrome, Tourette's disorder, severe vision impairment, Rett syndrome, current psychoactive medication, non-English speakers and IQ below 70. That 104 of 289 screened participants were excluded 'for not meeting strict diagnostic criteria' indicates the criteria were applied stringently rather than nominally.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Complete and used analytically throughout. IQ was estimated from a three-subtest WISC-IV short form (Information, Block Design, Vocabulary) with the Sattler and Dumont formula, and the authors note honestly that separate verbal and non-verbal estimates cannot be derived from this short form. The Children's Communication Checklist-2 was completed by parents, with its structure described in detail - ten subscales, the first four averaged into a Structural Language scale and four more into a Pragmatic scale, with the last two measuring behaviours characteristic of autism. ADOS-2 Social Affect and Restricted and Repetitive Behavior scores were computed under the Gotham et al. algorithm. Three objective language-output indices were additionally computed from the task itself: total c-units, total words and activity time. All of these then serve as predictors in the misclassification analysis, which is the paper's most original contribution - they are not merely descriptive but are the variables through which the complementarity of the two modalities is established.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Three explicit aims, each addressed. First, replicate the voice model of Asgari et al. (2021) and the language model of Salem et al. (2021) and compare their discriminant validity using the same methodology in the same sample - achieved, with language (AUC 0.8748) significantly better than voice (0.7800, DeLong p = 0.036), the difference lying in specificity (0.83 versus 0.69). Second, quantify the gain from combining them - the combined model reached AUC 0.9205, significantly better than voice (p < 0.001) and language (p = 0.033), with accuracy 0.8671, sensitivity 0.8977 and specificity 0.8286; the entire gain is in sensitivity while specificity is unchanged. Third, characterise which participants each model detects - the language model caught children with poorer structural and pragmatic language, less output and one year younger; the voice model caught children with better language profiles and showed no association between language measures and classification success; only nine autistic participants (10.2%) escaped the combined model, and these had the highest IQ and most language output of any subgroup.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Oregon Health & Science University, with participants recruited through community outreach and referral from OHSU specialty clinics into an fMRI study - so the sample is a research cohort rather than a consecutive clinical series. Recording arrangements are described precisely and with their rationale: 'The microphone was suspended in a cage and placed on a table approximately 3 feet from where the child sat. This allowed the recording to accurately capture the child's language, even if, as is common in ADOS Module 3 administrations, the child sometimes moved around the room before being reminded to sit down.' That sentence does two things few papers here manage - it specifies the acquisition geometry and it explains the specific behaviour the geometry was designed to accommodate. The authors nonetheless flag microphone quality and placement as insufficiently controlled and recommend tightening it in future work to reduce reliance on denoising.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A single ADOS-2 Module 3 conversational task, chosen on three stated criteria that jointly amount to a principled sampling argument: it occurs in the second half of the assessment after the warm-up period, so the child is acclimatised; it 'consistently yields the most c-units of all ADOS tasks', so the sample is maximally dense; and it 'has a high standardization of conversational questions, leading to good comparability between participants', using pre-established open-ended interview questions. Two independent prior analyses from this group had converged on this task as the most discriminative. The paradigm's practical strength is that it requires no new protocol - the recording already exists in any videotaped ADOS - and its analytic strength is that all 158 participants completed the identical task, so between-participant differences are not confounded with differences in what was asked. The corresponding limitation is stated by the authors themselves: 'ADOS administration focuses on eliciting autistic features, thus it is possible that our results are overestimated compared to what would be obtained with more naturalistic conversational samples'.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; one assessment per participant, with the intended application being longitudinal outcome measurement rather than cross-sectional classification. The authors are explicit that the reliability evidence needed for that application does not yet exist: 'we do not yet know the reliability (test-retest) and short-term stability of the measures we generated from transcripts and audio recordings', though they state they are currently undertaking those studies. This is an important self-limitation, since an outcome measure without demonstrated test-retest stability cannot distinguish treatment effect from measurement noise. Ethics reporting is complete: IRB review and approval at OHSU, with informed written consent or assent obtained from all participants and their parents at the initial visit. A data availability statement offers de-identified data on request and gives a public GitHub URL for the analysis code.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Acquisition is minimal and reusable - a single suspended microphone three feet from the child during a routine ADOS administration - which is what makes the measures retrofittable to existing clinical archives. The analytic pipeline is where the equipment complexity sits: a harmonic model of speech with model-based jitter and shimmer estimation, adopted because 'standard methods for calculating jitter and shimmer are sensitive to the pitch estimation'; a pretrained fully automated deep-neural-network denoiser applied before feature extraction; and R for all statistical analysis with code released. The denoising step warrants attention because its necessity is stated unusually starkly: 'Recordings from both groups contain similar, ubiquitous noise not caused by participants. If denoising is not performed, the acoustic features mainly represent the noise instead of participants and the classifier cannot distinguish between groups.' Applying the denoiser identically to both groups is the correct control, and stating that raw acoustics were noise-dominated is candid, but it means the entire voice result is conditional on a black-box preprocessing step whose interaction with group-specific vocal characteristics is, as the authors concede, unknown.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Among the best in the corpus. Reported: the complete participant flow from 289 screened to 158 analysed with a reason and count at every step; the full exclusion criteria list; the diagnostic procedure at each stage; the ADOS module, administrator training level and task selection with rationale; microphone type, placement distance and its justification; the transcription protocol, unit definition, disfluency notation, blinding of transcribers to diagnosis and IQ, consensus resolution procedure and biannual consistency checks; the three-module audio pipeline; the precise definition of all seven language measures and all ten voice measures; the SVM kernel, the soft-margin constant for each of the three models, feature normalisation, and the fact that non-linear SVMs and formal tuning were also run and reported in supplementary material; the cross-validation scheme with its citation-backed justification and its 10-fold robustness check; the DeLong test for AUC comparison; the mSVM-RFE procedure with an explicit note that 10-fold was used because the software could not run under leave-one-out; and the statistical tests for every comparison. Analysis code is publicly released and de-identified data offered on request. What is missing, and acknowledged: transcription reliability statistics, despite the training and consistency checks; and the effect of the denoiser.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The most complete limitations section in the corpus, running to ten distinct items, several of which the authors were under no obligation to raise. Sample scope: ages 7-17 only; all participants had IQ in the normal range; all were fluent English speakers assessable with Module 3, so 'it is important for future studies to include individuals with lower IQ and less verbal participants'. Design: 'Participants were not tightly matched between groups which could result in reduced fit for analysis', notwithstanding the confound tests. Features: the set was deliberately limited to previously validated measures and should be expanded and tested component by component. Preprocessing: 'We do not know the full impact of denoising on voice features and results', with a recommendation to control microphone quality and placement to reduce the need for it. Setting: the samples come from ADOS administrations in a clinical research setting and cannot be generalised to other contexts, and because 'ADOS administration focuses on eliciting autistic features... it is possible that our results are overestimated compared to what would be obtained with more naturalistic conversational samples'. Reliability: test-retest and short-term stability are unknown. Transcription: manual transcription is costly and labour-intensive, and 'though the transcribers went through extensive training and regular consistency reviews, we do not have transcription reliability results'. In the discussion the authors additionally raise, unprompted, that examiners may have facilitated and maximised the language output of the more able participants, citing Bone et al., and that parents' CCC-2 scores 'could have been negatively biased in this subset due to their child's ASD diagnosis'.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Seven directions, each traceable to a stated limitation. Extend to adults and younger children, and to lower-IQ and minimally verbal participants who cannot complete Module 3. Test each component feature systematically to establish individual predictive power. Determine which voice features drive the voice model's false positives, with a specific and testable hypothesis - 'it could be that loudness is a general non-specific feature of young children interviewed on sensitive topics (as those covered by the Friends task) in an unfamiliar setting; if so, removal of these non-contributory features might improve the classification performance of voice-only models'. Control microphone quality and placement to reduce dependence on denoising. Establish test-retest reliability and short-term stability, which are prerequisites for the intended outcome-measure application. Sample naturalistic conversation outside the clinic, 'aiming at minimizing interference by strangers and capturing naturally occurring conversations in the ecological niche of the participants'. And replace manual transcription with automatic speech recognition, with the explicit caveat that 'future studies based on ASR transcription will need to re-evaluate performance of the models relying on ALMs' - recognising that ASR errors would propagate into disfluency and maze measures that depend on precise transcription.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Two distinct behavioural constructs measured from the same recording. Language targets expressive complexity and pragmatic function through mean length of utterance, lexical diversity, disfluency structure, rate of production, intelligibility and echoic repetition of the examiner's immediately preceding words - the last of these operationalising a specifically autism-relevant behaviour. The um-versus-uh proportion is the subtlest measure and reflects a well-established finding that the two filled pauses signal different planning difficulties. Voice targets paralinguistic production: pitch, cycle-to-cycle frequency and amplitude perturbation, harmonics-to-noise ratio as a hoarseness index, H1H2 as a breathiness index, spectral envelope and entropy, and RMS loudness. The paper's central empirical claim about these constructs is that they are separable in the participants they identify - the language measures track language ability, the voice measures do not, and the voice measures therefore capture 'paralinguistic features (e.g., prosody, loudness) that are truly independent of language level and output'.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: The best-evidenced fusion result in the corpus, on three counts. The improvement is statistically tested rather than asserted: DeLong's test for correlated ROC curves gives p < 0.001 against the voice model and p = 0.033 against the language model, with 95% confidence intervals on all three AUCs (0.7800, 0.8748, 0.9205). The improvement's structure is diagnosed: the combined model's specificity is identical to the language model's (0.8286) while sensitivity rises from 0.7727 to 0.8977, so the voice features recovered autistic participants the language model missed without importing the voice model's false-positive tendency - which is exactly the asymmetric gain one would predict if the modalities are complementary rather than redundant, and the authors note it explicitly. And the mechanism is established at participant level rather than inferred from the numbers: children detected by the language model had significantly lower CCC-2 structural and pragmatic scores and less output, while for the voice model 'the CCC-2 scores and the Friends task indices did not differentiate correctly or incorrectly classified participants', which is the direct evidence that the acoustic channel indexes something orthogonal to language level. The clinical implication the authors draw follows properly from that evidence: voice analysis is needed 'to detect communication differences among subjects with ASD who have achieved high language skills', concurring with the observation that voice atypicalities persist in individuals with otherwise typical outcomes. Compared with Han et al. and Liao et al., who also demonstrate complementary failure directions via confusion matrices, this study goes further by characterising the complementarity in terms of participant clinical profiles rather than class labels.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Linear-kernel SVMs throughout, chosen deliberately over more flexible alternatives and justified by prior use in speech-and-autism work. Non-linear SVMs and formal hyperparameter tuning were run and relegated to supplementary material with the linear configuration reported in the main text - which is the correct ordering when the goal is validating interpretable measures rather than maximising accuracy, though it does mean the reported soft-margin constants (C = 10, 1 and 100 for the three models) were selected on performance. The restraint is consistent with the study's stated purpose: 17 interpretable features, a linear classifier, and an emphasis on which participants are detected rather than on how high the number can be pushed. The mSVM-RFE analysis then delivers a genuinely useful negative result - the optimal eight-feature subset (0.9344) did not significantly outperform the full 17-feature model (0.9235, p = 0.1592), so feature selection bought nothing, and the authors report this rather than promoting the higher figure as their headline.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: One 17-dimensional vector per participant, produced by averaging frame-level acoustic measures across the task and computing transcript-level language measures over the same interval, then normalising all features to [0,1]. The unit is therefore the participant throughout, which is what makes leave-one-subject-out cross-validation meaningful. One representational property is worth noting because the authors use it defensively and correctly: almost every measure is length-normalised, being either an average over frames or c-units or a proportion computable on any sample length, the sole exception being number of distinct word roots. This lets them rebut the objection that the nine missed autistic participants escaped because their unusually long transcripts broke the measures - 'it is highly unlikely that the measures did not perform well for high language output, and more likely that high IQ and older children had fewer communication difficulties, making them harder to detect'. That is an argument about measurement invariance made from the construction of the features rather than from post hoc testing.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC with 95% confidence intervals for all three models, with DeLong tests for every pairwise AUC comparison - the appropriate test for correlated ROC curves derived from the same participants, and one that almost no other study in this corpus uses. The confidence intervals do real work: the voice model's interval (0.7076-0.8525) and the combined model's (0.8768-0.9641) do not overlap, so that comparison is visibly supported, whereas the language and combined intervals do overlap and the DeLong test is correspondingly marginal at p = 0.033. Reporting sensitivity and specificity separately is what makes the complementarity finding legible - the voice model's specificity of 0.6857 is the weakness that the language model repairs, and the combined model's unchanged specificity alongside raised sensitivity is the signature of the two modalities catching different people. The misclassification analysis adds a class of evidence absent elsewhere: Mann-Whitney comparisons of age, IQ, two CCC-2 scales, two ADOS domains and three task indices between detected and missed participants, for each of the three models separately, with the counterpart analysis for non-autistic participants in supplementary material. No chance or trivial baseline is reported, which is the one gap.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is built into the design rather than added afterwards, and it operates at three levels. The features are individually meaningful by construction - mean length of utterance, filled-pause ratio, disfluency proportion, F0, shimmer, loudness - so any model weight is directly interpretable, in contrast to the learned representations used by the deep-learning speech studies elsewhere in this corpus. mSVM-RFE ranks them and identifies an optimal eight, evenly split between modalities, though the selection is honestly reported as producing no significant gain. And the misclassification analysis functions as the deepest interpretive layer, answering not 'which features matter' but 'which children does this measure see', which is the question that determines clinical utility. Its findings are specific and consequential: the language model is biased toward younger children with poorer language and less output; the voice model is unbiased with respect to language level; the residual misses have the highest IQ and most language output; and neither ADOS severity nor IQ predicts misclassification in any model - from which the authors draw the appropriately hedged conclusion that 'if replicated, this result could confirm that our voice and language measurement methodology specifically taps aspects of communication skills that are not confounded by autism severity or developmental delay'.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, and uniquely in this corpus the choice is justified by citation to the methodological literature on exactly this issue - Saeb et al. (2017) on subject-wise versus record-wise validation - with the rationale that it approximates 'the clinically relevant use-case of diagnosis in unseen participants'. Because each participant contributes a single averaged feature vector, there is no possibility of the within-subject leakage that inflates results throughout this review. Robustness was checked against 10-fold cross-validation, giving 0.9235 against 0.9205 with p = 0.9219, confirming the estimate is not an artefact of the resampling scheme. Comparisons between models use DeLong's test rather than informal inspection. Sex-stratified models were fitted to test whether the sex imbalance drove the result. The confounding variables were tested rather than acknowledged. What remains: the soft-margin constants were chosen per model on performance and the linear configuration was selected for reporting over tuned non-linear alternatives, so some selection optimism is present though bounded by the small hyperparameter space; feature selection was performed under 10-fold rather than leave-one-out for software reasons; and there is no independent replication cohort - the sample is a single site and overlaps with the two prior papers whose findings are being replicated, so the 'replication' is of models rather than of data. The authors' own framing is appropriately cautious about all of this, describing the results as 'preliminary but very encouraging'.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism, automated measures, communication, disfluency, natural language processing, pragmatic language, prosody, voice. Six of eight are linguistic or communicative constructs rather than computational methods - 'disfluency', 'pragmatic language' and 'prosody' name specific behavioural phenomena - which accurately signals a paper whose subject is communication measurement with machine learning as instrument, rather than the reverse.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Autism Research 15(7):1288-1300 (2022), the journal of the International Society for Autism Research - a specialist autism venue with clinical and behavioural-science readership rather than an engineering one. Authorship spans OHSU's Department of Psychiatry, the Institute on Development and Disability and the Department of Pediatrics, with the senior author being a prominent autism epidemiologist and the two first authors marked as contributing equally, one from the language side and one from computation. Funding is from NIH and specifically the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders. The venue and authorship explain the paper's balance: full clinical characterisation, careful terminology, statistical inference appropriate to a clinical audience (DeLong tests, confidence intervals, non-parametric group comparisons), and modelling that is deliberately conservative.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022. The framing is unusual for this corpus in three respects. First, it declines the diagnostic frame outright: 'This work (past and current) is not currently intended to be employed for diagnostic or screening purposes. Rather, our methodology uses already-established diagnosis as an external criterion against which we can validate (in the sense of discriminant validity) these voice and language measures.' The target is outcome measures for trials and longitudinal studies, and the paper closes on that application. Second, the critique of existing instruments is specific rather than generic - conventional tests like the CELF-4 and PPVT 'evaluate structural aspects of language' and must be augmented by natural language sampling; parent-report instruments such as the CCC-2 have validity limits 'as illustrated in treatment studies that have shown caregiver reports to be susceptible to the placebo effect'; and, echoing the group's companion paper, the ADOS and SRS 'include only one item each on voice quality' despite prosodic difference being a cited characteristic of autism. Third, the epidemiological framing is calibrated rather than alarmist, citing a worldwide prevalence range of 0.043% to 2.68% and noting that 'reasons for the increasing prevalence rate are uncertain' - written by an author who has published extensively on exactly that question. The comparison against prior work is likewise careful, noting that Tanaka et al.'s sample of four autistic and two typically developing participants made its findings 'unreliable', and that the sampling contexts of the compared studies differed from this one so that 'examination of contextual effects should be vigorously pursued'.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Krishnappa Babu PR; Di Martino JM; Chang Z; Perochon S; Aiello R; Carpenter; K. L. .. H.; Compton S; Davis N; Franz L; Espinosa S; Flowers J; Dawson G; Sapiro G
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Toddlers subsequently diagnosed with autism during routine primary-care screening
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Head movement dynamics measured by computer vision from tablet-front-camera video
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Extend the group's prior finding that autistic toddlers move their heads more frequently while watching dynamic stimuli, in two ways: replicate it in a substantially larger sample with redesigned movies, and move beyond movement rate to acceleration and to complexity - the latter quantified by multiscale entropy to index 'the level of predictability and stability of head movements'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Prospective cross-sectional study embedded in routine primary-care well-child visits, with diagnostic outcome ascertained subsequently through a screen-and-refer pathway
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One app administration per child during a well-child checkup, comprising seven brief movies totalling roughly five minutes
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Passive viewing of seven brief developmentally appropriate movies presented on a tablet, split by design into four with high social content and three with low social content. Social: Blowing-Bubbles (~64 s, an actor blowing bubbles while smiling and frowning with limited verbal expression), Spinning-Top (~53 s), Rhymes (~30 s, an actress reciting nursery rhymes while smiling and gesturing) and Make-Me-Laugh (~56 s). Nonsocial: Floating-Bubbles (~35 s, bubbles moving randomly across the frame), Mechanical-Puppy (~25 s, a toy puppy barking and walking toward toy vegetables) and Dog-in-Grass-RRL (~40 s, a puppy appearing at random screen positions then following a fixed right-right-left pattern). No response was required of the child
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Four Duke pediatric primary care clinics, during routine well-child checkups. A quiet room with few distractions was identified at each clinic, though 'it was not otherwise controlled as in a laboratory setting'; the four rooms were similar in size, lighting and presence of distractions. The caregiver held the child on their lap with no instructions on how, sat quietly and was asked not to guide the child's behaviour, and siblings and the administering assistant stayed behind both caregiver and child
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: A prospective screen-and-refer pathway rather than a pre-selected clinical sample. All participants received the M-CHAT-R/F as part of routine clinical care. Toddlers scoring 3 or more initially, or 2 or more after follow-up questions, or for whom the pediatrician or parent raised developmental concerns, were referred for diagnostic evaluation by the study team psychologist. ADOS-2 Toddler Module was administered by research-reliable licensed psychologists who determined whether the child met DSM-5 criteria. The neurotypical group is defined by either a negative M-CHAT-R/F with no concerns raised, or a positive screen or raised concern followed by a psychologist's determination on the ADOS-2 and clinical judgment that the child had no developmental or autism-related concerns - so a substantial part of the comparison group was actively evaluated rather than assumed typical. Mean age at diagnosis was 23.9 months, with a mean of 0.7 months between diagnosis and app administration
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Exclusions were practical and applied at recruitment: known hearing or vision impairments; child too upset during the visit; caregiver uninterested or short of time; child unable to complete procedures, including refusing to stay on the caregiver's lap or app/device upload failure; and significant sensory or motor impairment precluding seeing the movies or sitting upright. A separate group of 12 children who screened positive and received a non-autism diagnosis such as language delay without autism was excluded from analysis on grounds of small sample size
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: ADOS-2 Toddler Module calibrated severity score 7.56 +/- 1.67 (range 2-10), and Mullen Scales of Early Learning giving an Early Learning Composite of 63.64 +/- 10.17 (range 49-87), Expressive Language T 28.08 +/- 7.41, Receptive Language T 23.14 +/- 4.93, Fine Motor T 34.11 +/- 10.76 and Visual Reception T 33.94 +/- 10.63. All were obtained for the autistic group only and the Mullen composite was used analytically as a correlate of head movement measures
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Partly by instrument - a negative M-CHAT-R/F with no caregiver or physician concern for most, and an ADOS-2 plus psychologist judgment of no developmental or autism-related concern for those who screened positive
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No - 20.59 versus 24.38 months, a significant difference by ANOVA. The imbalance is handled analytically: age was entered as a covariate in ANCOVA alongside the proportion of missing data, and 'these two covariates did not affect our between-group analyses'
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: No - 70.7% male in the autistic group against 50.2% in the neurotypical group, significant by chi-squared. The authors note the sample 'did not offer sufficient power to determine the influence of biological and demographic characteristics, such as sex'
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Established by negative M-CHAT-R/F without concerns, or by ADOS-2 and psychologist judgment for those who screened positive
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Video from a tablet front-facing camera, reduced to facial landmark and head-pose time series
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Faces were detected in each frame by a computer vision algorithm, with 'scarce human supervision' triggered by a face-tracking algorithm to ensure only the participant's face was tracked - an explicit safeguard against tracking the caregiver on whose lap the child sat. Forty-nine 2D facial landmarks were extracted and time-synchronised with the movies, and head pose angles (yaw, pitch, roll) computed relative to the tablet. Analysis was restricted to segments where the child was attending, defined by a yaw criterion of |theta| < ~20 degrees as a proxy for attention supported by central-bias theory for gaze estimation, and additionally confirmed by an automatic gaze estimation algorithm. Head movement rate was computed as the average Euclidean displacement of three central landmarks between consecutive frames, normalised by a one-second running average of inter-eye distance to remove the effect of varying child-to-camera distance, and smoothed over a 10-frame (1/3 s) moving window. Acceleration was the frame-to-frame difference of that rate averaged over 1/3 s. Complexity was multiscale entropy: the time series was coarse-grained to 30 scales and sample entropy computed at each with embedding dimension m = 2 and tolerance r = 0.15 times the population-wide standard deviation, chosen deliberately so that 'this choice defined a distance threshold r consistent across participants'; a global estimate integrated sample entropy across the first 10 scales. Participants with under 40% valid data for a given movie were excluded from that movie's analysis, on the stated ground that below this threshold the entropy estimate may not be reliable
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: An iOS-compatible app on a tablet mounted on a tripod approximately 60 cm in front of the child; the tablet's own front-facing camera; dlib-based face detection; a 49-landmark facial landmark extractor; an automatic gaze estimation algorithm from the group's prior work; Python with the pingouin statistical package
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Video and derived head-movement time series from 457 toddlers across four primary care clinics; no release statement
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Video of identifiable toddlers recorded in clinical settings. Governance is reported: caregivers provided written informed consent and the study protocols were approved by the Duke University Health System Institutional Review Board under two named protocol numbers (Pro00085434, Pro00085435). No de-identification procedure is described, though the analysis operates on extracted landmark coordinates rather than on imagery
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Kinematic and information-theoretic descriptors of a one-dimensional head movement time series
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Three per movie: mean head movement rate, mean absolute acceleration, and integrated multiscale entropy across the first ten scales. The feature set is deliberately minimal - three interpretable physical or information-theoretic quantities rather than a large engineered set - and each is motivated by a distinct hypothesis: rate replicates the prior finding, acceleration 'relates to the magnitude of the instantaneous forces involved in head movement', and entropy indexes 'the regularity of the one-dimensional time-series on multiple scales'. Total movement energy was also computed but reported as less discriminative than acceleration and not carried forward
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Facial landmark detection with 49 2D landmarks; head pose estimation; automatic gaze estimation; multiscale entropy following Costa et al. with sample entropy per Richman and Moorman
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Addressed through the classification ablation rather than by attribution: single features are compared against pairs, and single features across movies against all features across all movies
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: AUC comparison across feature configurations with Hanley-McNeil 95% confidence intervals, and formal model comparison using the true-difference criterion dt = d +/- 1.96 x sigma_d, with models judged not significantly different if the interval spans zero
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Mean acceleration was the strongest single feature, reaching AUC 0.85 when combined across the four social movies against 0.80 for integrated entropy across the same movies. Combining both features across all four movies into an eight-dimensional space performed worse (AUC 0.73) than either feature alone across movies - a negative result the authors report and explain as the expected consequence of increasing dimensionality on a moderate-sized dataset
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Autistic toddlers showed significantly higher head movement rate, higher acceleration and higher multiscale entropy than neurotypical toddlers, across both social and nonsocial movies. Effect sizes were medium to large for social movies (rate r = 0.39-0.73; entropy r = 0.40-0.68) and small to medium for nonsocial (rate r = 0.25-0.39), with the Mechanical-Puppy movie showing no significant group difference on any measure. Higher entropy is interpreted as movements being 'less predictable and less stable'. The within-group comparison is the more informative direction: neurotypical toddlers moved significantly more, with higher acceleration and higher complexity, during social than nonsocial movies (r = 0.47, 0.62 and 0.51), whereas 'the autistic group did not exhibit differences in Mean_rateHM, Mean_accelHM, and Integrated_entropyHM during the social versus nonsocial movies'
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Support vector machine with radial basis function kernel on three interpretable kinematic features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: SVM with RBF kernel, chosen because it 'is popular when used on relatively smaller datasets'; leave-one-out cross-validation, adopted with an explicit citation to Vabalas et al. (2019) to 'minimize the risk of overoptimistic classification'; Hanley-McNeil confidence intervals on AUC; and a variance-based true-difference test for comparing classifiers. Statistical inference elsewhere used Mann-Whitney U for between-group comparisons, Wilcoxon signed-rank for within-group, 2x2 mixed ANOVA for group-by-movie-type effects, and ANCOVA with age and missing-data proportion as covariates
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-out cross-validation over participants, with AUC and Hanley-McNeil 95% confidence intervals. Classifier configurations were compared using a formal true-difference criterion rather than by inspecting point estimates. The unit is the participant throughout, since all measures are per-child summaries over a movie. Group differences were separately protected by ANCOVA covarying age and the proportion of missing data, and by reporting effect sizes for every comparison. A per-movie data-quality gate excluded participants with under 40% valid data for that movie, with the resulting per-movie sample sizes reported explicitly in every figure
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: AUC with 95% confidence intervals for every feature configuration and every movie; effect size r for all group comparisons; F statistics and p values for the mixed ANOVAs; and per-scale p values for the entropy comparisons across all 30 multiscale resolutions
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Best classification: AUC 0.85 for mean acceleration combined across the four social movies, and 0.80 for integrated entropy combined across the same movies. Combining both features across all four movies gave 0.73 - worse than either alone. Individual movies were weaker: Rhymes was best, while Blowing-Bubbles gave 0.71 for acceleration, 0.68 for entropy and 0.73 for both; Spinning-Top 0.68, 0.67 and 0.71; Make-Me-Laugh 0.70, 0.69 and 0.72. Confidence intervals were wide throughout, for instance 0.53-0.75 for Blowing-Bubbles entropy, reflecting the 41-participant autistic group. Group differences by mixed ANOVA were highly significant for all three measures (rate F(1,427) = 42.48; acceleration F(1,427) = 38.65; entropy F(1,427) = 29.68; all p < .0001), with significant movie-type main effects and no significant interaction. Attention to the app was near-equivalent between groups at 95% and 93%
