data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: In an unselected primary-care sample of 457 toddlers of whom 41 were subsequently diagnosed with autism, computer vision applied to tablet front-camera video showed that autistic toddlers moved their heads more, with greater acceleration and greater multiscale-entropy complexity, while watching brief movies - replicating and extending the group's earlier rate-only finding with medium to large effect sizes. The most informative result is a within-group contrast rather than a between-group one: neurotypical toddlers modulated their head movement by content, moving substantially more during social than nonsocial movies (r = 0.47-0.62), while autistic toddlers showed no such difference and moved at consistently high levels throughout. That pattern contradicts the prior interpretation, from Martin and colleagues, that increased head movement in autism serves to modulate perception of social stimuli specifically. Classification using acceleration combined across the four social movies reached AUC 0.85, with entropy reaching 0.80; combining both feature types into eight dimensions reduced performance to 0.73. The differences were not attributable to attention, since measures were computed only during attending segments and attention rates were 95% and 93% across groups, nor to age or missing data, both entered as covariates.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Higher rate, higher acceleration and higher multiscale entropy of head movement, present during both social and nonsocial content, with the autistic group failing to show the content-dependent modulation seen in neurotypical toddlers
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Explore the developmental course of head movement differences and their nature and neurobiological basis; extend the computer vision to the trunk and shoulders, since examining videos revealed that 'the movement involves not just the head but also the upper body including trunk and shoulders, which were not captured by our computer vision algorithm'; and combine head movement with gaze, facial dynamics and response to name toward 'a multimodal computer vision-based digital phenotyping tool'
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The most deployment-realistic study in the corpus and among the strongest in design. Its decisive property is the sampling frame: 457 toddlers recruited consecutively during routine well-child visits at four primary care clinics, with autism diagnosed afterwards through a screen-and-refer pathway rather than participants being recruited because they were already diagnosed. The resulting 41:416 ratio approximates real screening prevalence, which means the AUC of 0.85 is estimated under something close to the base rate a deployed tool would face - unlike the balanced 50:50 designs that dominate this corpus, where a given AUC implies far better positive predictive value than it would in practice. The comparison group is also partly ascertained rather than assumed, since children who screened positive but were judged not to have developmental concerns after ADOS-2 remain in it. Validation is participant-level by construction, uses leave-one-out cross-validation with an explicit citation to Vabalas et al. on overoptimistic classification, reports Hanley-McNeil confidence intervals on every AUC, and compares classifier configurations by a formal variance-based criterion rather than by eye. Measurement engineering is equally careful: landmark displacement is normalised by inter-eye distance to remove camera-distance effects; the entropy tolerance uses a population-wide rather than per-participant standard deviation so the threshold is comparable across children; a data-quality gate of 40% valid data is applied per movie with the resulting sample sizes shown in every figure; face tracking is human-supervised to ensure the child rather than the caregiver is measured; and analysis is confined to attending segments with attention verified by two independent criteria. The scientific contribution is the within-group finding, which is stronger evidence than the between-group difference and is used correctly to adjudicate against a competing published interpretation. Three caveats. The groups differ significantly on age, sex, ethnicity and caregiver education, and while age and missing data are covaried, sex is not - the authors state the sample lacked power to examine it - and neither is caregiver education, which in a primary-care sample is a plausible proxy for factors affecting how a child is held and settled on a caregiver's lap. Cognitive ability differs and is acknowledged: 'it is not clear the degree to which differences in cognition contributed to our findings'. Most substantively, the authors report on inspection that the movement being measured extends to trunk and shoulders and is not confined to the head, which means the construct is closer to whole-body postural instability than to head movement per se - a possibility they raise themselves by connecting it to the postural-sway literature. There is also an internal inconsistency worth noting: the Results report positive correlations between Mullen Early Learning Composite and all three head movement measures during social movies (r = .36, .39, .34), meaning higher cognitive ability accompanied more movement, while the Discussion states the opposite, that 'autistic children with lower cognitive abilities showed higher levels of head movement rate, acceleration, and complexity'. The interpretation offered - that lower-ability children found the social movies harder to interpret - follows from the Discussion's version and not from the reported coefficients. Conflicts of interest are extensive and fully disclosed: five authors developed the app technology, which has been licensed with financial benefit to them and to Duke.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Three groups identified, two analysed. Of 457 toddlers recruited during well-child checkups at four pediatric primary care clinics, 41 were subsequently diagnosed with autism under DSM-5 and 416 were classified neurotypical. A third group of 12 who screened positive on the M-CHAT-R/F and received a non-autism diagnosis - language delay without autism is the example given - was excluded from analysis because of small sample size. That exclusion is the design's one substantive omission, since those 12 are precisely the children against whom a screening tool must discriminate, and their removal means the reported AUC reflects autism versus typical development rather than autism versus developmental concern. The neurotypical group is nonetheless better ascertained than most comparison groups in this corpus, being formed of two subsets - children with a negative M-CHAT-R/F and no caregiver or physician concern, and children who screened positive or raised concern but were then judged on the ADOS-2 and psychologist clinical judgment to have no developmental or autism-related concerns. The 41:416 ratio is the study's most consequential structural feature: it approximates the base rate a deployed screening tool would encounter, in contrast to the balanced designs that dominate this review.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'autistic toddlers', 'autistic children', 'autistic individuals', 'young autistic children', consistently identity-first including in the title, against 'neurotypical toddlers'. 'Patients' never appears and 'typically developing' is replaced throughout by 'neurotypical'. The framing of the phenomenon is descriptive rather than deficit-oriented - head movements are 'differences' in 'dynamics', autism is 'characterized by differences in social communication', and the interpretive discussion entertains the possibility that the movements 'might also serve a regulatory function' rather than treating them as symptoms to be catalogued. This is among the most careful terminology in the corpus and is consistent with the senior authorship's position in the autism research community.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Reported in full and tested, and the picture is one of multiple significant imbalances. Autistic group: 41 toddlers, 70.7% male, 24.38 +/- 4.73 months. Neurotypical group: 416 toddlers, 50.2% male, 20.59 +/- 3.18 months. Age differs significantly by ANOVA, sex by chi-squared. Two further significant differences appear in the demographic table and are less commonly reported elsewhere in this corpus: Hispanic ethnicity (29.3% versus 7.5%) and caregiver education, where 85.6% of neurotypical caregivers held a four-year college degree or more against 53.7% of autistic caregivers. Age and the proportion of missing data were entered as ANCOVA covariates and did not affect the between-group results; sex was not covaried, with the authors stating that the sample 'did not offer sufficient power to determine the influence of biological and demographic characteristics, such as sex'; ethnicity and caregiver education are reported but never revisited. The last is worth attention in this particular paradigm, since the measurement is of a toddler sitting on a caregiver's lap with 'no special instructions given regarding how to hold the child', so any systematic difference in how caregivers positioned or settled their children would enter the signal directly. Cognitive ability differs markedly - the autistic group's Mullen Early Learning Composite averages 63.64 - and no Mullen data were collected for the neurotypical group, so the difference cannot be quantified or adjusted.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: A genuine prospective screening pathway, which is rare in this corpus and is the study's principal methodological asset. Every participant received the M-CHAT-R/F as part of routine clinical care. Referral for diagnostic evaluation was triggered by a total score of 3 or more initially, 2 or more after follow-up questions, or developmental concerns raised by the pediatrician or parent. Referred children received the ADOS-2 Toddler Module from research-reliable licensed psychologists who determined DSM-5 status, supported by the Mullen Scales of Early Learning. Diagnosis therefore followed rather than preceded enrolment, and the mean interval between diagnosis and app administration was 0.7 months, so the behavioural measurement and the diagnostic determination are close in time. The comparison group's status is partly instrumented rather than assumed, since screen-positive children judged to have no concerns are retained in it. The one gap is that children with a negative M-CHAT-R/F and no raised concern were not directly assessed, so the neurotypical group will contain some proportion of children whose autism was not detected by screening - which biases toward underestimating the group difference rather than inflating it.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Comprehensive for the autistic group and absent for the comparison group. ADOS-2 Toddler Module calibrated severity scores average 7.56 +/- 1.67 across a range of 2-10, so the sample spans the severity spectrum. The Mullen Scales of Early Learning provide an Early Learning Composite of 63.64 +/- 10.17 alongside Expressive Language (T = 28.08), Receptive Language (T = 23.14), Fine Motor (T = 34.11) and Visual Reception (T = 33.94) T-scores - all substantially below average, indicating a group with considerable developmental delay, and the Fine Motor score is directly relevant since the outcome is a motor measure. The Mullen composite is used analytically, correlated against all three head movement measures. Because no Mullen data exist for the neurotypical group, the cognitive difference between groups cannot be estimated or adjusted, and the authors list this among their limitations: 'The autistic and neurotypical group differed in cognitive ability and, thus, it is not clear the degree to which differences in cognition contributed to our findings.' Comorbidity is not otherwise characterised, and the 12 children with non-autism diagnoses were removed.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: replicate a prior head-movement-rate finding in a larger sample with redesigned stimuli, and extend it to acceleration and multiscale-entropy complexity, testing whether differences are more pronounced for social content and whether the measures can be combined for classification. Main findings: autistic toddlers showed significantly higher rate (F(1,427) = 42.48), acceleration (F(1,427) = 38.65) and complexity (F(1,427) = 29.68), all p < .0001, with medium to large effect sizes for social movies and small to medium for nonsocial; a significant main effect of movie type with no group-by-type interaction; neurotypical toddlers modulated all three measures by content while autistic toddlers did not; classification reached AUC 0.85 for acceleration across the four social movies and 0.80 for entropy, with the eight-dimensional combination performing worse at 0.73; and neither age nor missing data affected the group comparisons.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Four Duke pediatric primary care clinics during routine well-child checkups - the only truly point-of-care setting in the corpus. The description of environmental control is unusually honest: a quiet room with few distractions was identified at each clinic, but 'although it was quiet and without a lot of distraction, it was not otherwise controlled as in a laboratory setting', with the four rooms noted as similar in size, lighting and presence of distractions. The social arrangement is specified in detail and matters for the measurement: the caregiver held the child on their lap with no instructions on how to do so, sat quietly, and was asked not to guide the child's behaviour or give instructions, while siblings and the administering assistant stayed behind both caregiver and child to reduce distraction. The tablet sat on a tripod approximately 60 cm in front of the child. That the caregiver's holding is uninstructed is a deliberate choice for ecological validity and an uncontrolled source of variance for a measure of postural movement.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Seven brief movies totalling about five minutes, split four social and three nonsocial by explicit design, each described with its duration and content. The social movies feature actors smiling, frowning, gesturing and using limited verbal expression; the nonsocial movies feature bubbles moving randomly, a mechanical toy puppy and a puppy appearing at screen positions in a fixed right-right-left pattern. The social/nonsocial split is the analytic instrument rather than a background feature: it enables the within-group contrast that produces the paper's most informative result, and it permits the group-by-content interaction test that adjudicates against Martin and colleagues' interpretation. The paradigm requires nothing of the child beyond sitting and watching, which is what makes it viable at 17 months in a clinic waiting room, and the near-equivalent attention rates of 95% and 93% across groups indicate that it holds toddlers' attention in both groups - an important equivalence, since differential attention would otherwise confound any movement measure. One movie, Mechanical-Puppy, showed no significant group difference on any of the three measures, and this is reported consistently rather than omitted.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional in analysis but embedded in a prospective screening pathway, with diagnosis ascertained after app administration at a mean interval of 0.7 months (range -0.1 to 5.9). No longitudinal follow-up of the measures themselves, and the authors identify the developmental course of head movement differences as a future direction. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: written informed consent from caregivers and approval by the Duke University Health System Institutional Review Board under two named protocol numbers. Conflicts of interest are declared at length and are substantial: five authors developed technology related to the app which has been licensed, with both they and Duke University benefiting financially; the senior clinical author sits on four scientific advisory boards, consults for three companies including Apple and receives book royalties; both senior authors have invention disclosures and patent applications registered with Duke's licensing office; and the senior engineering author is affiliated with Apple, with a note that the work was done before and independently of that affiliation. The disclosure is exemplary in its completeness, and the commercial interest in the app is relevant context for a paper reporting the app's discriminative performance.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Deliberately minimal and entirely commodity: an iOS tablet on a tripod, using its own front-facing camera, running a purpose-built app. No external camera, depth sensor, marker, wearable or motion capture. That is what permits administration in a primary-care room by a non-specialist assistant with a caregiver holding the child. The analytic chain is specified in detail - face detection with human-supervised tracking to ensure only the participant's face is followed, 49 2D facial landmarks, head pose angles relative to the tablet, an automatic gaze estimation algorithm, and Python with pingouin for all statistics. Two engineering decisions deserve note because they neutralise obvious confounds. Landmark displacement is normalised by a one-second running average of inter-eye distance, which removes the effect of the child moving closer to or further from the camera - a variance source that would otherwise dominate in a lap-held toddler. And the sample-entropy tolerance uses the population-wide standard deviation rather than each participant's own, chosen explicitly so that 'this choice defined a distance threshold r consistent across participants', which prevents children with more variable movement from being scored on a correspondingly wider tolerance and hence appearing artificially regular.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Among the most completely reported studies in the corpus. Specified: recruitment setting and inclusion and exclusion criteria; the full screen-and-refer diagnostic pathway with M-CHAT-R/F cut-points; instrument names and administrator qualifications; the demographic table with race, ethnicity, caregiver education and statistical tests; all seven movies with durations and content descriptions; the physical setup including tripod distance, caregiver instructions and positioning of other people; the landmark count and pose angles; the |yaw| < 20 degree attention criterion with its theoretical justification and the additional gaze-based confirmation; the inter-eye normalisation with its rationale; the 10-frame smoothing window; the complete multiscale entropy formulation with the coarse-graining equation, the sample entropy definition, m = 2, r = 0.15 sigma, the use of population-wide sigma with its rationale, integration across the first 10 scales, and the missing-data handling; the 40% data-quality threshold with its justification and the resulting per-movie sample sizes shown in every figure; every statistical test with its Python function; the classifier, kernel, cross-validation scheme and confidence-interval method; and the model-comparison criterion. Missing: no data or code release, no random seeds, and no reporting of how many of the 457 were excluded per movie in aggregate, though per-movie counts are given.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Three limitations are stated and each is substantive. The sample, though large overall, contained only 41 autistic children and therefore 'did not offer sufficient power to determine the influence of biological and demographic characteristics, such as sex'. Data from all participants were not used in every analysis because of the 40% attendance threshold. And 'the autistic and neurotypical group differed in cognitive ability and, thus, it is not clear the degree to which differences in cognition contributed to our findings' - a direct acknowledgement that the study's most likely alternative explanation is unresolved. A fourth limitation appears not in the limitations section but in the discussion, and is arguably the most important: inspection of videos from high-movement toddlers 'revealed that the movement involves not just the head but also the upper body including trunk and shoulders, which were not captured by our computer vision algorithm, as we focused solely on the face in this study'. That reframes the construct from head movement to whole-body postural instability, and the authors follow it with a serious engagement with the postural-sway literature. What goes unaddressed: the significant ethnicity and caregiver-education differences, never revisited after the demographic table; the exclusion of the 12 children with non-autism diagnoses, which removes the clinically decisive contrast; the wide confidence intervals on the per-movie AUCs; and the internal contradiction between the Results' positive Mullen correlations and the Discussion's statement that lower-ability children moved more.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Three directions, each following from a stated limitation. Explore the developmental course of head movement differences and 'elucidate their nature and neurobiological basis', with several concrete hypotheses already advanced - that the movements modulate sensory information generally rather than social perception specifically, that they reflect postural control difficulties that increase with sensory demand, or that like some repetitive behaviours they serve a regulatory function when stimuli are arousing. Extend the computer vision beyond the face to the trunk and shoulders, following directly from the observation that the movement is not confined to the head. And combine head movement 'with other behavioral biomarkers such as gaze, facial dynamics, and response to name' toward a multimodal digital phenotyping tool - which is the group's programmatic direction and is supported here by the demonstration that a single behavioural channel reaches AUC 0.85 in a prevalence-realistic sample.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Head movement dynamics during passive viewing, decomposed into three levels: how much the head moves (rate), how sharply that movement changes (acceleration, motivated as relating 'to the magnitude of the instantaneous forces involved in head movement'), and how predictable the movement time series is across temporal scales (multiscale entropy, indexing 'the level of predictability and stability'). The complexity measure is the study's conceptual contribution and is well chosen: rate and acceleration are magnitude measures that could be produced by any source of extra motion, whereas entropy captures the structure of the movement over time and licenses the specific claim that autistic toddlers' movements were 'less predictable and less stable'. The behaviour is explicitly sensorimotor rather than social, and the paper situates it in a substantial literature on motor differences in autism - stereotypies, fine and gross motor impairment, motor planning and coordination, asymmetry in home-video studies of infants later diagnosed, and difficulties in gait, balance, postural control, movement accuracy, manual dexterity and praxis. The authors' own inspection finding, that trunk and shoulders move too, suggests the underlying construct is postural rather than cephalic.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality, with the fusion result confined to combining features within it - and that result is a clean negative. Two features (acceleration, entropy) across four movies gives an eight-dimensional space and AUC 0.73, worse than either feature alone combined across the same four movies (0.85 and 0.80). The authors report this plainly and explain it correctly as the expected behaviour of a moderate-sized dataset as dimensionality grows. Two aspects make the negative result more useful than most. The two features are moderately correlated (r = 0.4-0.5), so combining them adds dimensionality without much independent information - which is the situation in which such degradation is predicted, and the authors report the correlation that makes it interpretable. And combining a single feature across movies did help substantially, lifting acceleration from around 0.68-0.71 on individual movies to 0.85 across four - so aggregation over stimuli was worth far more than aggregation over feature types. The paper's stated future direction is genuine multimodal fusion with gaze, facial dynamics and response to name, which is the group's programme; this study establishes what one channel contributes.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A single SVM with RBF kernel on two or three interpretable features, chosen because it 'is popular when used on relatively smaller datasets' and paired with leave-one-out cross-validation explicitly 'to minimize the risk of overoptimistic classification', citing Vabalas et al. (2019) - one of only two studies in this corpus to cite the methodological literature on validation bias directly. The modelling is deliberately subordinate to the statistical analysis: the paper's primary evidence is a set of mixed ANOVAs, Mann-Whitney and Wilcoxon tests with effect sizes and ANCOVA covariate control, and classification is used to answer a specific supplementary question - whether the measures 'can be integrated to distinguish autistic and neurotypical toddlers'. That ordering is appropriate for a study whose contribution is a behavioural finding rather than a screening product, and it is unusual in this corpus, where classification accuracy is typically the primary and often the only evidence. Classifier configurations are compared by a formal variance-based true-difference criterion, so the claim that combining across movies beats single movies is tested rather than asserted.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: One scalar per feature per movie per child, so the unit of analysis is the participant throughout and no segment-level inflation is possible. Three representational decisions do substantial confound-neutralising work. Displacement is normalised by a running average of inter-eye distance, removing the effect of a lap-held toddler moving toward or away from the camera, which would otherwise dominate the raw landmark displacement signal. The entropy tolerance uses the population-wide standard deviation rather than each child's own, so a child with more variable movement is not scored against a correspondingly wider tolerance and thereby made to appear more regular - a subtle and correct choice, with a prior paper cited for its detailed justification. And analysis is restricted to segments where the child is attending, established by two independent criteria: a head-yaw threshold justified by central-bias theory for gaze estimation, and an automatic gaze estimation algorithm confirming the child was looking at the screen. That restriction is what allows the authors to argue that the differences 'do not appear to reflect the degree of attention to the movies', and it is reinforced by the near-equal attention rates of 95% and 93%.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: The most complete statistical reporting in the corpus for a study of this kind. Every group comparison carries an effect size r alongside its p value; the mixed ANOVAs report F with degrees of freedom for group, movie type and their interaction; entropy comparisons are reported per scale across all 30 multiscale resolutions rather than only for the integrated summary; every AUC carries a Hanley-McNeil 95% confidence interval; and classifier configurations are compared by a stated variance-based criterion with the explicit rule that models are 'considered not significantly different' if the interval spans zero. The confidence intervals are essential to reading the result honestly and the paper does not hide what they show: for Blowing-Bubbles the entropy AUC interval runs 0.53 to 0.75, so that single-movie result barely excludes chance, and the intervals on the individual-movie AUCs are uniformly wide because only about 30 autistic children contribute to each. The headline 0.85 is correspondingly better supported than the per-movie figures. Also reported are the attention rates for both groups and the per-movie participant counts after the data-quality gate, both of which bear on whether the measurement was equally successful in the two groups.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is pursued through the design of the measures rather than through model attribution, and the analysis that carries most weight is the within-group contrast. Because the measures are three physically meaningful quantities, the finding can be stated directly in behavioural terms. The decisive analysis compares social against nonsocial movies within each group: neurotypical toddlers moved more, faster and less predictably during social content (r = 0.47, 0.62, 0.51), while autistic toddlers showed no content-dependent difference at all. That single contrast does three things a between-group difference cannot. It shows the effect is not simply 'autistic children move more' but that neurotypical children modulate movement by content and autistic children do not. It adjudicates directly against Martin and colleagues' published interpretation that increased head movement in autism serves to modulate perception of social stimuli, since on that account the difference should be confined to social content, and here it is not. And it rules out the reading that the measure indexes social engagement, since the group difference persists for nonsocial content. The paper then engages seriously with alternative mechanisms - general sensory modulation, postural control under multisensory demand, a regulatory function analogous to repetitive behaviour - rather than settling on one. The Mullen correlation analysis is the interpretively weakest element and contains an internal contradiction: the Results report positive correlations between Early Learning Composite and all three movement measures during social movies (r = .36, .39, .34), implying higher cognitive ability accompanied more movement, while the Discussion asserts that 'autistic children with lower cognitive abilities showed higher levels of head movement rate, acceleration, and complexity' and builds an interpretation on that reading.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Sound in every respect that this corpus commonly gets wrong, with the residual weakness being confounding rather than leakage. The unit is the participant, since all features are per-child summaries; leave-one-out cross-validation is used and justified by citation to Vabalas et al. on overoptimistic classification; AUCs carry Hanley-McNeil confidence intervals; and classifier configurations are compared by a formal criterion rather than by inspecting point estimates. Two further design properties strengthen the estimate beyond what the cross-validation alone provides. The class ratio of 41:416 approximates real screening prevalence, so the AUC is not estimated under an artificially balanced design - a distinction that matters enormously for translation, since the same AUC implies very different positive predictive value at 9% prevalence than at 50%. And diagnosis followed rather than preceded enrolment, so the sample is not conditioned on already being diagnosed, removing the referral filter that shapes almost every other study here. What remains unaddressed: age and missing data were covaried but sex was not, on stated power grounds; ethnicity and caregiver education differ significantly and are never revisited; cognitive ability differs and cannot be adjusted because Mullen data exist only for the autistic group; the 12 children with non-autism diagnoses were excluded, so the discrimination tested is against typical development rather than against developmental concern; and there is no independent replication cohort, though this study is itself a replication and extension of the group's earlier rate-only finding in a larger sample with redesigned stimuli.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: Autism; head movements; computer vision; complexity analysis. Four terms, two naming the behavioural construct and two the method - a compact and accurate description of a paper that measures one behaviour precisely rather than surveying many.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry 64(1):156-166 (2023, published online 2022), a clinical child mental health journal rather than an engineering venue. Authorship spans Duke's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Center for Autism and Brain Development, Global Health Institute, Office of Information Technology, and Department of Biomedical Engineering, Mathematics and Computer Sciences, with two co-senior authors - one clinical, one engineering. Funded by an NIH Autism Centers of Excellence award and two NIMH R01s, with additional support to the engineering authors from NSF, the Department of Defense and industry gifts. The genuinely joint clinical-engineering leadership is visible throughout: the statistical inference is what a clinical journal would require (effect sizes, mixed ANOVA, ANCOVA covariates, non-parametric tests), the measurement engineering is what a computer vision group would produce (landmark normalisation, population-wide entropy tolerance, dual attention criteria), and neither is subordinated to the other. The paper includes a 'Key points' box in the journal's clinical format.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022-2023. The framing is developmental and mechanistic rather than diagnostic, positioning head movement as 'one of the early sensorimotor signs associated with autism' and situating it within an established literature on motor differences - stereotypies, fine and gross motor impairment, motor planning and coordination, asymmetry in home videos of infants later diagnosed, and documented difficulties in gait, balance, postural control, movement accuracy, manual dexterity and praxis. What distinguishes the positioning is that the paper engages directly with a competing published interpretation and produces evidence against it: Martin and colleagues found head movement differences only during social stimuli and proposed that autistic children use head movements to modulate their perception of social scenes, whereas this study finds differences during both content types and states plainly that 'our data do not support the hypothesis that the head movements of the autistic toddlers were used to modulate the perception of social stimuli, per se'. It then offers alternatives without overclaiming, noting that 'the nature of these differences in head movement dynamics is not fully understood'. The translational claim is correspondingly modest - computer vision 'offers a scalable means of detecting subtle differences' that 'may be helpful in identifying early behaviors associated with autism' - and the stated endpoint is a multimodal digital phenotyping tool combining this channel with gaze, facial dynamics and response to name, not a standalone diagnostic. Given the disclosed commercial interest in the app, that restraint is notable.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Lau JCY; Patel S; Kang X; Nayar K; Martin GE; Choy J; Wong PCM; Losh M
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: English-speaking and Cantonese-speaking autistic individuals with IQ in the average range
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Speech prosody - rhythm and intonation from narrative speech
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Determine which prosodic differences in autism are robust across typologically distinct languages and which are shaped by language-specific properties. The motivating gap is stated precisely: 'most studies have concentrated on studying prosody in English-speaking groups. Language is fundamentally cultural, and how specific aspects of prosody are used can vary substantially across languages', so cross-linguistic study 'is therefore critical to address the variability of ASD symptomatology, and its underlying mechanisms'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-linguistic case-control classification with within-language and combined-language models, comparing two feature classes on the same participants
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One narration per participant of a 24-page wordless picture book, from which 20 utterances were selected for analysis
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Narration of the wordless picture book Frog, Where Are You? - a 24-page story about a boy and his dog searching for a missing pet frog. Pages were presented one at a time on a computer monitor while narration was audio recorded, with no examples provided. The book 'has been used extensively in studies of narrative discourse in ASD and other neurodevelopmental disabilities and in cross-linguistic work', which is the reason for its selection: because it is wordless, the same stimulus elicits comparable narrative content in any language without translation, making it one of the few paradigms that permits genuine cross-linguistic comparison of spontaneous connected speech
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Two sites - the United States, where participants were drawn from a larger family-genetic study of autism including probands, parents and controls, and Hong Kong, where recruitment used social media advertisements, direct approaches to schools and organisations serving autistic people, and employment programmes designed for adults previously diagnosed with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: ADOS-2 with research-reliable administration and scoring, using Overall, Social Affect and Restricted and Repetitive Behavior calibrated severity scores to index severity. No ADI-R, clinician best-estimate procedure or DSM criterion is described - the ADOS-2 alone establishes and confirms status. Exclusions applied to all participants were history of brain injury, major psychiatric disorder, known genetic syndrome, or neurodevelopmental disorder other than autism; comparison participants in both language groups were additionally screened for personal or family history of autism or related genetic disorders such as fragile X syndrome, which is a stricter criterion than most studies apply and reflects the family-genetic origins of the English cohort
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 55 recruited in English and 28 in Cantonese; 33 English and 24 Cantonese analysed
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: English 29 male : 4 female (87.9% male); Cantonese 19 male : 9 female (67.9% male)
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Excluded: brain injury, major psychiatric disorder, known genetic syndrome, and any neurodevelopmental disorder other than autism
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: ADOS-2 total calibrated severity scores of 7.02 +/- 1.85 (range 3-9.5) for the English autistic group and 6.00 +/- 2.33 (range 3-10) for the Cantonese, with Social Affect and Restricted and Repetitive Behavior severity scores also stated to have been derived. IQ was measured but with different instruments in each language group
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Screened for personal or family history of autism or related genetic disorders in both language groups
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 39 recruited in English and 24 in Cantonese; 33 English and 24 Cantonese analysed
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution_controls: English 15 male : 18 female (45.5% male); Cantonese 17 male : 7 female (70.8% male)
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Cantonese groups matched (17.83 versus 18.88); English groups differ (15.96 versus 19.31), flagged in the demographic table and described in the text as 'differences in gender and age observed between the English (but not Cantonese) groups', with a post-hoc analysis run to rule out age as a confound in the English intonation classification
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Cantonese groups matched (67.9% versus 70.8% male); English groups differ markedly - 87.9% male in the autistic group against 45.5% in the comparison group, a 42-point gap addressed by post-hoc analysis in supplementary material
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Established by exclusion of neurodevelopmental disorders and by screening for personal and family history of autism and related genetic conditions
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Audio recordings of narrative speech
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Recordings were transcribed and segmented into individual utterances defined by natural pauses, and 20 utterances per participant were selected for analysis. Two feature classes were then extracted using the MATLAB Audio Toolbox and scripts from prior published work. Rhythm: three representations of the temporal envelope - the envelope spectrum, intrinsic mode functions, and the temporal modulation spectrum - motivated by the observation that envelope rhythmicity, 'especially those of 2-8 Hz, is crucial in the neural processing of intelligible speech as it aligns with in brain areas in the spoken language processing pathway that oscillate at a similar rate', yielding 8,640 features across the 20 utterances per participant. Intonation: rather than the mean or variance of f0 used in prior work, entire time-normalised f0 contours were retained - 20 f0 values per utterance concatenated across 20 utterances, giving 400 features per participant. The analytic level is the utterance rather than the syllable, chosen because 'the utterance is associated with the intonational phrase, the most fundamental unit of prosody argued to be universal across all languages', which is what makes the two languages commensurable
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Audio recording during narration; MATLAB Audio Toolbox with scripts from prior published studies for envelope spectrum, intrinsic mode function and temporal modulation spectrum extraction; principal component analysis; linear-kernel SVM
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Narrative speech from 114 analysed participants across two languages; the English samples were previously used in a study of syllable-level measures not included here
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Partly - 'The minimal dataset and analytic scripts are available from the OSF database (https://osf.io/9ta65/)'
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Minimal dataset and analysis scripts publicly deposited
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not directly discussed, but a minimal dataset is deposited publicly rather than raw audio, which is the appropriate compromise for identifiable speech. Informed assent and consent were obtained from all participants and guardians as applicable, with approval by each institution's ethics committee and conformity to the Declaration of Helsinki stated
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Multivariate time- and frequency-domain acoustic representations of rhythm and intonation
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Rhythm (8,640 features): envelope spectrum, intrinsic mode functions and temporal modulation spectrum, all derived from the amplitude envelope of the speech signal and capturing temporal regularities that correlate with syllabic rhythm. Intonation (400 features): time-varying f0 values from time-normalised contours spanning each utterance. The design choice that distinguishes this study is the rejection of scalar summaries: the authors argue explicitly for 'moving beyond more reductionist approaches (e.g., averaging or picking extreme values) often used in traditional univariate acoustic analyses on pitch, stress, and speech rate, to capture the dynamicity of speech prosodic profiles', so an f0 contour is retained as a trajectory rather than collapsed to a mean and range
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: MATLAB Audio Toolbox with published scripts for envelope-based rhythm measures; time-normalisation of f0 contours
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Not at the level of individual features, which would be uninterpretable across 8,640 dimensions. Importance is addressed at the level of feature class - rhythm versus intonation - which is the study's actual research question
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Comparison of classification performance between the two feature classes, within each language separately and in the combined dataset, with permutation testing establishing whether each classification exceeds chance
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Rhythm-relevant features throughout. Rhythm classified successfully in English (median AUC 0.900), Cantonese (0.962) and the combined dataset (0.886), all at p < 0.001. Intonation classified successfully only in English (0.695, p = 0.007) and failed in Cantonese (0.620, p = 0.507) and in the combined dataset (0.559, p = 0.509)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not reported, and by design - the features are multivariate trajectories and spectra rather than scalar quantities, so no directional group difference is extractable. The paper's substantive claim is about which class of prosodic information carries diagnostic signal in which language, not about whether a given quantity is higher or lower. The introduction reviews the directional literature it departs from, noting that autistic speakers have been reported to show higher f0 and larger f0 range in English but lower f0 range in Thai and Japanese - a discrepancy that itself motivates the cross-linguistic design
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Linear support vector machine on principal components of high-dimensional acoustic features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Linear-kernel SVM applied to principal components. The kernel choice is argued rather than assumed: linear kernels are 'preferable to non-linear kernels because theoretically it is always possible to find a linear decision boundary that separates data, in spite of high data dimensionality and small sample size', with reference to precedent in neuroimaging and gene expression studies where features outnumber samples
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Repeated 10-fold cross-validation in which 'data reduction (into principal components) and hyperparameter tuning were performed in a nested fashion' - so dimensionality reduction and tuning occur inside each training fold rather than on the whole dataset. Statistical significance was established by a permutation approach with 5,001 iterations, and performance is reported as the median AUC across those iterations with the full distribution shown as boxplots. The stated purpose of the pipeline is explicit: 'Several procedures were performed in the classification pipeline to further avoid overfitting and optimistic bias due to limited sample size and the high-dimensionality of data'
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Median AUC across 5,001 iterations with permutation-derived p values, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for all six model configurations, boxplots of the AUC distributions, and aggregated confusion matrices
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Model 1, within language: English rhythm AUC 0.900 (accuracy 0.819, sensitivity 0.788, specificity 0.849), p < 0.001; Cantonese rhythm AUC 0.962 (accuracy 0.880, sensitivity 0.917, specificity 0.833), p < 0.001; English intonation AUC 0.695 (accuracy 0.683, sensitivity 0.758, specificity 0.606), p = 0.007; Cantonese intonation AUC 0.620 (accuracy 0.605), p = 0.507, not significant. Model 2, languages combined: rhythm AUC 0.886 (accuracy 0.835, sensitivity 0.790, specificity 0.877), p < 0.001; intonation AUC 0.559 (accuracy 0.566), p = 0.509, near chance
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Rhythm-relevant acoustic features classified autism at AUC 0.900 in English and 0.962 in Cantonese, and continued to classify at 0.886 when the two languages were pooled into a single model despite their typological distance - English being a stress-timed Indo-European non-tone language and Cantonese a syllable-timed Sino-Tibetan tone language. Intonation features behaved entirely differently: they classified significantly in English (0.695) but not in Cantonese (0.620, p = 0.507), and fell to near chance when languages were combined (0.559, p = 0.509). The dissociation is theoretically motivated rather than incidental. In tone languages pitch carries lexical meaning, so f0 is constrained by phonology in a way it is not in English, and the authors propose that 'the prolific usage of linguistic pitch in tone languages provides a compensatory effect ameliorating intonational differences in ASD'. The finding also reconciles a discrepancy in the prior literature, where higher f0 and wider f0 range have been reported repeatedly in English but lower f0 range in Thai and Japanese. The methodological contribution is the treatment of prosody as multivariate trajectory rather than scalar summary - retaining entire time-normalised f0 contours and envelope spectra rather than means and ranges.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Rhythm-relevant temporal envelope characteristics, robust across both languages; intonation contour characteristics in English only
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Confirm the findings in larger samples covering both sexes and wider age ranges; use more comprehensive assessments of language ability for group matching, 'since baseline language ability may covary with age and autism severity, influencing prosody and pitch in particular'; extend to languages from other typological classes - German and Dutch as rhythmically similar to English, Japanese as distant from both; examine the structural and functional neurophysiology of prosody production across language groups, noting existing findings of increased right inferior frontal gyrus and right caudate activation during prosody comprehension in autism; and investigate the ASPM gene as a potential genetic contributor to cross-linguistic differences in prosodic phenotype
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Methodologically among the more careful classification studies in the corpus, and conceptually the most ambitious. The validation pipeline is explicitly constructed against optimistic bias: dimensionality reduction and hyperparameter tuning are nested inside cross-validation folds rather than applied to the whole dataset, which is the correct handling of a problem with 8,640 features and 66 participants and is done by almost no other study here; significance is established by permutation with 5,001 iterations rather than assumed; and results are reported as median AUC with the full distribution displayed. The feature-class comparison is the right experimental design for the question, since it contrasts two hypotheses on identical participants and identical utterances rather than comparing across studies. The cross-linguistic design is what makes the study valuable to this review: it is the only paper in the corpus to test whether a behavioural marker generalises across languages, and it produces a clean dissociation - rhythm survives pooling across typologically distant languages while intonation does not even reach significance in Cantonese. That result has a direct implication the rest of the corpus should absorb: an English-derived prosodic classifier would be expected to transfer poorly to a tone language on its intonation features, so the near-universal practice of reporting accuracy from a single language and single cultural context leaves generalisation entirely untested. The paper also uses its own negative result constructively, explaining the Cantonese intonation failure through the phonological role of pitch in tone languages and using it to reconcile the conflicting f0 findings between English, Thai and Japanese studies. Four problems qualify the result. Attrition from the English sample is large and unexplained: 55 autistic and 39 comparison participants were recruited, but only 33 and 33 were analysed, so 40% of the autistic group and 15% of the comparison group were dropped with no reason stated and no comparison of retained against dropped participants. The English groups differ by 42 percentage points in proportion male and by more than three years in mean age; a post-hoc analysis is run and reported in supplementary material, but the imbalance falls on exactly the classification - English intonation - where f0 is most sex-dependent, and that is the one intonation result that reached significance. Diagnostic ascertainment rests on the ADOS-2 alone, without ADI-R or best-estimate clinical procedure, and part of the Cantonese sample was recruited through employment programmes for adults with prior Asperger or high-functioning autism diagnoses whose original ascertainment is unknown. And IQ was measured with different instruments in the two language groups - Wechsler scales in English, TONI-4 in Cantonese - so the two samples are not comparable on cognitive level even though both show a group difference favouring the comparison participants. The speculative discussion linking the Cantonese intonation null to ASPM allele frequencies in Han Chinese populations is loose and unsupported by any genetic data collected here; it is offered as a hypothesis but sits awkwardly against a paper that is otherwise disciplined. Data and analysis scripts are deposited on OSF, which is rare in this corpus and materially improves the study's verifiability.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Four groups across two languages, with recruitment and analysis counts that do not match. Recruited: 55 English-speaking autistic, 39 English-speaking comparison, 28 Cantonese-speaking autistic, 24 Cantonese-speaking comparison. Analysed: 33, 33, 24 and 24 respectively, stated in a parenthesis within the narrative-elicitation section - so 22 of 55 English autistic participants (40%) and 6 of 39 English comparison participants (15%) do not appear in the analysis, with no reason given, no flow diagram, and no comparison between retained and dropped participants. The demographic table reports 28 for the Cantonese autistic group where the analysis text says 24, a further inconsistency. The English participants come from a larger family-genetic study of autism that also enrolled parents and controls; the Cantonese participants were recruited via social media, schools and organisations serving autistic people, and employment programmes for adults previously diagnosed with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism. No other-diagnosis comparison group in either language.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)' and 'individuals with typical development (TD)' throughout, and uniquely in this corpus the choice is explained rather than defaulted: 'We acknowledge the variability in preferences related to person-first and identity-first terminology (i.e., individuals with ASD versus autistic individuals). We do not endorse one style over the other. For the purpose of this manuscript, to ensure that language is parallel when referencing both participant groups, we remain consistent with the following terminology.' The stated reason - parallelism across the two groups so that neither is described in a grammatically different form from the other - is a considered linguistic argument rather than a convention, and no other paper in the corpus addresses the question at all. Substantively, prosodic variation is framed as 'differences' rather than deficits throughout, including in the title, though the paper does report that such differences 'can contribute to an impression of oddness reported by listeners' when reviewing prior work.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Tabulated with within-language significance testing, and the picture differs sharply between the two language groups. Cantonese: autistic 19 male : 9 female, 17.83 +/- 9.24 years, IQ 108.54 +/- 10.92; comparison 17 male : 7 female, 18.88 +/- 8.70 years, IQ 115.08 +/- 10.13 - well matched on sex and age, with an IQ gap. English: autistic 29 male : 4 female, 15.96 +/- 7.38 years, IQ 104.13 +/- 14.34; comparison 15 male : 18 female, 19.31 +/- 5.35 years, IQ 111.03 +/- 13.79 - a 42-percentage-point sex imbalance in opposite directions, a three-year age gap, and an IQ gap. The authors identify this asymmetry themselves, referring to 'differences in gender and age observed between the English (but not Cantonese) groups', and run a post-hoc analysis in supplementary material to rule them out as confounds in the English f0 classification. That the confounds are concentrated in the English sample matters because the English intonation model is the only intonation classification that reached significance, and f0 is strongly sex-dependent: an autistic group that is 88% male compared against a group that is 55% female differs in mean pitch for reasons unrelated to diagnosis. Age ranges are wide in every group (6-35 years overall), spanning pre- and post-pubertal voice change. IQ was assessed with Wechsler scales in English and the TONI-4 in Cantonese, so cognitive level is not comparable across languages even though both language groups show a difference favouring comparison participants.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: ADOS-2 with research-reliable administration and scoring, using Overall, Social Affect and Restricted and Repetitive Behavior calibrated severity scores. This is a real observational instrument correctly administered, but it is the only diagnostic evidence described - there is no ADI-R, no DSM criterion application, no clinician best-estimate procedure and no statement of who made the final determination. For a subset of the Cantonese sample recruited through 'employment programmes particularly designed for adults previously diagnosed with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning Autism', the original diagnosis was made elsewhere under unknown procedures and the ADOS-2 serves as confirmation. The comparison groups are handled more stringently than in most studies here, screened for personal or family history of autism or related genetic disorders such as fragile X - a criterion that follows from the English cohort's family-genetic origins and that excludes the broader autism phenotype in relatives. General exclusions of brain injury, major psychiatric disorder, known genetic syndrome and other neurodevelopmental disorders were applied to all participants.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: IQ was measured in every participant, but with different instruments by language group: the WASI, WAIS-III/IV or WISC-IV for English participants and the TONI-4 for Cantonese participants. The TONI-4 is a nonverbal reasoning measure while the Wechsler scales yield full-scale IQ incorporating verbal subtests, so the two sets of scores are not interchangeable and cross-language comparison of cognitive level is not possible. Within each language group the comparison participants score higher (111.03 versus 104.13 in English; 115.08 versus 108.54 in Cantonese). ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores are reported for both autistic groups (7.02 English, 6.00 Cantonese) with full ranges spanning 3-9.5 and 3-10, so both samples cover the severity spectrum. No language ability measure was administered, and the authors identify this as a limitation that matters specifically for their outcome: 'future studies should employ more comprehensive assessments of language abilities for group matching, since baseline language ability may covary with age and autism severity, influencing prosody and pitch in particular'. No adaptive functioning or comorbidity data.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: identify prosodic differences in autism that span typologically distinct languages and those shaped by language-specific properties, by comparing rhythm-relevant and intonation-relevant acoustic feature classes within English, within Cantonese and across both combined. Main findings: rhythm classified successfully in English (median AUC 0.900), Cantonese (0.962) and combined (0.886), all p < 0.001; intonation classified significantly only in English (0.695, p = 0.007), failing in Cantonese (0.620, p = 0.507) and falling near chance when combined (0.559, p = 0.509). The dissociation is attributed to the phonological role of pitch in tone languages and is used to reconcile the conflicting f0 literature, where higher f0 and wider range are reported in English but lower f0 range in Thai and Japanese.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Two sites in different countries with different recruitment routes - a research setting in the United States, where participants came from an established family-genetic study of autism, and community recruitment in Hong Kong through social media, schools, autism organisations and employment programmes. The recording setting itself is described minimally: pages presented on a computer monitor with narration audio recorded, and no information about room, microphone, distance or recording equipment in either site. For a study whose primary features are the amplitude envelope and its spectral structure, the absence of any acoustic-recording specification is a genuine reproducibility gap, and it is compounded by the two-site design: if recording conditions differed systematically between the United States and Hong Kong, that difference would be absorbed into the envelope features. The combined-language model would be sensitive to this, though the fact that rhythm classification succeeds within each language separately - where recording conditions are presumably homogeneous - substantially mitigates the concern.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Narration of Frog, Where Are You?, a 24-page wordless picture book, presented one page at a time on a monitor with no examples given. The choice is the study's enabling methodological decision. Because the book contains no words, the identical stimulus can be administered in any language without translation, and it elicits connected spontaneous narrative rather than repetition, reading or single-word production - so the speech is naturalistic while the content is controlled across participants and across languages. The task has a long history in narrative discourse research in autism and in cross-linguistic work, which the authors cite. Twenty utterances per participant, segmented at natural pauses, were selected for analysis. The analytic level is deliberately the utterance rather than the syllable, on the grounds that 'the utterance is associated with the intonational phrase, the most fundamental unit of prosody argued to be universal across all languages' - the linguistic argument that makes English and Cantonese commensurable, since syllable-level units (final-syllable excursion in English, sentence-final particles in Cantonese) are language-specific and had been the focus of the group's prior work in each language separately.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, one narration per participant, no follow-up. Ethics reporting is adequate but generic: informed assent and consent from all participants and guardians as applicable, approval by each institution's ethics committee, and conformity with the Declaration of Helsinki, without naming the committees or protocol numbers. Data sharing is a genuine strength and rare in this corpus - 'The minimal dataset and analytic scripts are available from the OSF database' with a working URL, so the analysis is independently verifiable even though raw audio is not shared, which is the appropriate handling of identifiable speech. A competing interest is declared: one author owns a startup company supported by a Hong Kong government technology scheme, with a statement that the reported research is not associated with it.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Essentially nothing on the acquisition side - no microphone, recording device, sampling rate, room or distance is specified for either site, which for a study built on amplitude-envelope spectra is the most consequential reporting omission. Analysis tools are named: the MATLAB Audio Toolbox together with scripts from four prior published studies for the envelope spectrum, intrinsic mode function and temporal modulation spectrum extraction, with further technical detail relegated to supplementary material. The intonation pipeline extracts time-normalised f0 contours at 20 points per utterance. Principal component analysis and a linear-kernel SVM complete the chain. The reliance on published scripts rather than bespoke implementations, together with the OSF deposit of the analysis code, makes the computational half of the pipeline substantially more reproducible than the acquisition half.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Split sharply between the computational and the empirical. Fully specified or deposited: the two feature classes with their theoretical motivation, the counts (8,640 rhythm features, 400 intonation features), the utterance selection rule and count, the analytic level with its linguistic justification, the classifier and kernel with an argument for the choice, the nested structure of dimensionality reduction and hyperparameter tuning within cross-validation, the permutation testing with 5,001 iterations, and the analysis scripts on OSF. Not specified: any recording equipment or acoustic condition; the reason 22 English autistic and 6 English comparison participants were dropped between recruitment and analysis; how the 20 utterances per participant were selected from the full narrative; who performed transcription and segmentation, with what training or reliability; the number of principal components retained; and the SVM hyperparameter ranges searched. The supplementary file carries the post-hoc confound analysis, the technical feature-extraction detail and a supplementary demonstration that the rhythm features do contain systematic cross-linguistic differences - the last being an important internal check that the combined-language rhythm result is not simply detecting language.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Three limitations are stated, each substantive. The wide age range across groups and the small number of females are raised together, with the authors arguing that robust classification despite these may indicate 'aspects of prosodic profiles of ASD which are relatively age and gender invariant', supported by the post-hoc analysis, while conceding that 'future studies with larger samples are needed to confirm whether findings reported here extend to both males and females and different age ranges where prosodic abilities may vary'. The absence of language ability measures for group matching is identified with a precise mechanism - baseline language ability covaries with age and autism severity and influences pitch in particular. And the restriction to two languages is named, with specific proposals for extension. What goes unaddressed: the unexplained loss of 40% of the English autistic sample between recruitment and analysis; the discrepancy between the demographic table and the analysis counts for the Cantonese autistic group; the absence of any recording specification; the use of different IQ instruments across language groups, which makes the two samples non-comparable on cognitive level; and the fact that the sex imbalance falls precisely on the English intonation model, the one f0 classification that reached significance.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Five directions, four of them well grounded. Larger samples covering both sexes and wider age ranges. Comprehensive language-ability assessment for group matching, with the mechanism stated. Extension to further typological classes, with named candidates chosen for their position relative to the two languages studied - German and Dutch as rhythmically similar to English, Japanese as distant from both. Neurophysiological investigation of prosody production across language groups, building on existing findings of increased right inferior frontal gyrus and right caudate activation during prosody comprehension in autism, with the observation that such findings 'would be particularly compelling if replicated in individuals with ASD who are speakers of languages other than English'. The fifth is a proposal to examine the ASPM gene as a marker for prosodic differences, on the basis that most Han Chinese people carry a T allele favouring linguistic pitch processing which 'may implicate a role of genetic factors in contributing to cross-linguistic differences of ASD phenotypes'. This last is speculation built on a population-genetic association applied to a null classification result, with no genetic data collected in the study, and it is the one place where the paper's interpretive discipline lapses - it offers an ancestry-based genetic explanation for a language-based finding when the language explanation the authors themselves give (that lexical tone constrains f0) is sufficient.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Prosody decomposed into its two canonical components and operationalised as multivariate structure rather than summary statistics. Rhythm is captured through the amplitude envelope - its spectrum, its intrinsic mode functions and its temporal modulation spectrum - with a neurobiological rationale that envelope rhythmicity in the 2-8 Hz band 'is crucial in the neural processing of intelligible speech as it aligns with brain areas in the spoken language processing pathway that oscillate at a similar rate'. Intonation is captured as the full time-normalised f0 contour across each utterance, on the argument that the contour 'encompasses the dynamicity of speech intonation which varies across time within the most fundamental utterance-sized linguistic unit known as the intonational phrase'. The theoretical framing distinguishes affective prosody, which expresses emotion and intent and is broadly recognisable across cultures with possible evolutionary homologies in other mammals, from linguistic prosody, which encodes lexical and grammatical structure and varies drastically across languages - and this distinction predicts the study's result, since rhythm carries more affective and less linguistic load than pitch does in a tone language.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Not multimodal, but the study performs the corpus's most informative feature-class comparison, which serves an analogous function. Two feature classes representing the two components of prosody are tested on identical participants and identical utterances, within each language and combined, giving six models whose pattern is interpretable as a whole. The result is a dissociation rather than a fusion gain: rhythm classifies in both languages and survives pooling, intonation classifies in one language and collapses on pooling. Crucially the authors do not attempt to combine the two feature classes into a single model - which would have been the obvious accuracy-maximising move and would have obscured the dissociation. That restraint is what makes the study informative: the purpose is to determine which prosodic dimension is cross-linguistically robust, and combining them would have answered a different and less useful question. A supplementary analysis reported in the paper demonstrates that the rhythm features do contain systematic cross-linguistic differences, which is the necessary check that the successful combined-language model is separating diagnosis rather than exploiting language as a proxy - though with the two languages recruited at different sites through different routes, that check carries real weight and would ideally have appeared in the main text.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A single linear-kernel SVM applied consistently across all six configurations, with the kernel choice argued from the structure of the problem rather than selected empirically: linear kernels are 'preferable to non-linear kernels because theoretically it is always possible to find a linear decision boundary that separates data, in spite of high data dimensionality and small sample size', with precedent cited in neuroimaging and gene expression, where features routinely outnumber samples. Holding the model fixed across all six configurations is the right design for a study whose question is about features rather than about learners - any performance difference between rhythm and intonation, or between English and Cantonese, is attributable to the data rather than to differential model tuning. No alternative classifier is compared, which is appropriate given that no classification-performance claim is being made against competing methods.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: One feature vector per participant, formed by concatenating measures across the 20 selected utterances - so the unit of analysis is the participant and there is no possibility of the utterance-level leakage that would arise if each utterance were treated as an independent sample. Given 8,640 rhythm features against 66 English or 48 Cantonese participants, dimensionality reduction is unavoidable, and the handling is the correct one: principal component analysis is performed inside each cross-validation training fold rather than once on the full dataset, so the components are not informed by test-fold participants. The representational commitment that distinguishes the study is retaining trajectories rather than summaries - a full f0 contour instead of mean and range, an envelope spectrum instead of a speech rate. The cost is interpretability, since no directional statement about any acoustic quantity can be recovered from a principal component of an envelope spectrum, and the paper accordingly reports no group means or effect sizes for any feature. That is a defensible trade for a study whose question is about generalisation across languages rather than about characterising a difference.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Median AUC across 5,001 iterations with permutation-derived p values, reported alongside accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for every one of the six configurations, with the full AUC distributions displayed as boxplots and aggregated confusion matrices provided. Reporting the median across iterations with its distribution rather than a single point estimate is the correct summary for a repeated cross-validation, and it makes the stability of each result visible. The permutation testing is what carries the paper's central negative claims - without it, a Cantonese intonation AUC of 0.620 and a combined intonation AUC of 0.559 might have been reported as weak but positive results, whereas the permutation p values of 0.507 and 0.509 establish them as indistinguishable from chance. The sensitivity and specificity breakdown adds a further observation the authors draw out: the significant English intonation model has good sensitivity (0.758) but poor specificity (0.606), so it tends to call typically developing participants autistic, while the rhythm models are balanced across classes. No confidence intervals accompany the AUCs, and no formal test compares one model against another - the rhythm-versus-intonation contrast rests on one being significant and the other not, rather than on a test of their difference.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No feature-level interpretability, and none is possible given principal components of 8,640-dimensional envelope representations - the paper reports no group means, no effect sizes and no directional statements. What it provides instead is interpretability at the level of theoretical construct, which is the level its question operates at. The rhythm-versus-intonation contrast is itself the interpretive result, and the authors connect it to the existing descriptive literature ('the ML algorithms identified in this study appeared to capture patterns from acoustic features that were representative of these prosodic characteristics, paralleling such descriptive observations by clinicians and researchers') and to prior objective measures of speech rate, lexical stress and cross-syllabic durational variability. The Cantonese intonation failure is then given a mechanistic account grounded in phonology - pitch carries lexical meaning in tone languages, so f0 is under phonological constraint - and used to reconcile conflicting prior findings across English, Thai and Japanese. That is a stronger form of interpretation than a feature-importance ranking would have provided, because it generates a testable prediction: intonational differences in autism should be attenuated in tone-language speakers generally. The one interpretive overreach is the ASPM allele speculation, which substitutes a population-genetic explanation for a linguistic one that the paper has already established.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The strongest aspect of the study, and stated in the terms that matter: 'Several procedures were performed in the classification pipeline to further avoid overfitting and optimistic bias due to limited sample size and the high-dimensionality of data'. Three properties follow. Repeated 10-fold cross-validation is used rather than a single split. Dimensionality reduction into principal components and hyperparameter tuning are both performed 'in a nested fashion' inside the cross-validation, so neither the components nor the hyperparameters are informed by held-out data - the single most common source of optimistic bias in high-dimensional small-sample classification, and one that Liao and colleagues elsewhere in this corpus violate directly by selecting features on the full sample before cross-validating. Significance is established by permutation rather than assumed from a nominal chance level, with 5,001 iterations, and the resulting p values are what license the paper's negative claims. The unit is the participant throughout. What remains: no independent replication cohort, though the two-language design provides a form of internal generalisation test that is arguably stronger for the question at hand; no confidence intervals on the AUCs; no formal test comparing feature classes; and the unexplained 40% attrition from the English autistic sample, which is a selection concern that no amount of validation discipline can address. The combined-language model's validity also rests on the supplementary demonstration that language differences in the rhythm features do not account for the classification, a check that is performed but reported outside the main text.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No keyword list appears in the extracted text. The operative vocabulary is cross-linguistic, prosody, rhythm, intonation, tone language, machine learning classification, and autism phenotype - a register that places the work in linguistics and communication science with machine learning as instrument, which matches its actual contribution.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: PLOS ONE 17(6):e0269637 (2022), open access. Authorship spans the Roxelyn and Richard Pepper Department of Communication Sciences and Disorders at Northwestern University, the Department of Linguistics and Modern Languages and Brain and Mind Institute at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Chongqing University, and St. John's University - a genuinely bi-national collaboration, which is what the design requires and which is unique in this corpus. Funding comes from NIH grants in the United States and the Health and Medical Research Fund and two private foundations in Hong Kong. The communication-sciences provenance is visible throughout: the theoretical framing of prosody, the choice of a standard narrative elicitation task, the distinction between affective and linguistic prosody, and the interpretation of results in phonological terms all reflect a speech-language rather than an engineering orientation.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022. The framing is unusual for this corpus in being about scientific generalisation rather than about diagnostic deployment.
