The stated problem is not that clinicians are subjective or that diagnosis is slow, but that 'most studies have concentrated on studying prosody in English-speaking groups' while 'language is fundamentally cultural, and how specific aspects of prosody are used can vary substantially across languages' - so the field's evidence base may describe an English-specific phenotype without knowing it. The paper documents the concrete consequence: higher f0 and larger f0 range are reported repeatedly in English-speaking autistic groups, yet a Thai study found lower f0 range and a Japanese study likewise, and the existing cross-linguistic comparisons have all been between closely related languages (English and Danish, both Germanic; Cantonese and Mandarin, both Sinitic). The clinical implications drawn are correspondingly framed around intervention and cultural sensitivity rather than screening - that cross-linguistic differences 'may also help to optimize culturally sensitive diagnostic and intervention practices', and that if extensive pitch experience ameliorates intonational differences then pitch is 'a fruitful target for speech interventions in ASD for those who do not speak a tone language'. Diagnostic application is mentioned only in the conclusion and hedged: 'although further study with larger samples, and with additional language comparisons, is needed to support adaptation of the current models into clinical use'. The methodological argument against scalar summaries - that averaging or taking extreme values discards the dynamics that constitute prosody - is also a positional claim about how the field measures, and it is the study's most transferable methodological contribution.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Wawer A; Chojnicka I
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: International Journal of Language & Communication Disorders, 57(5), 948-962
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Fluently speaking autistic children, adolescents and young adults without intellectual disability
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Language content - narrative discourse (text, not acoustics)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Evaluate whether pre-trained deep neural text encoders can detect autism from narrative transcripts, and - the distinguishing feature of the design - situate that performance against two reference points on the same 50 participants: the standardised instruments ADOS-2 and SCQ, and two experienced psychiatrists reading the same transcripts. The stated framing is deliberately modest: 'due to the multidimensionality and complexity of the diagnosis problem, the role of such automatic analyses of narratives may only be complementary or supportive'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification with a within-study benchmarking design comparing computational models, human expert judgement on identical input, and standardised diagnostic instruments
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One narration per participant during a single ADOS-2 administration, averaging 4 minutes 24 seconds (range 2:28-7:22)
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Human children, adolescents and young adults
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: The ADOS-2 'Telling a Story from a Book' task, using the wordless picture book Tuesday by David Wiesner - a 15-page story in which frogs begin floating on lily pads one Tuesday evening and fly to a nearby town. The authors note that 'the pictures show unreal and humorous situations, and several mental and emotional states of the characters', which is the reason for its use: it demands inference about characters' internal states rather than simple description, and it is wordless so the narrative is entirely the participant's construction
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Poland - participants contacted through a university clinic, diagnostic or therapeutic centres, or schools, and assessed as part of a research evaluation
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: A prior clinical diagnosis of idiopathic autism determined by a multidisciplinary team including a psychiatrist under ICD-10 criteria was an inclusion requirement. For the study, ADOS-2 was administered by research-reliable clinicians supervised by an author who is an ADOS-2 trainer, and the SCQ was completed by parents. Importantly, 'prior to this study, participants were not evaluated using SCQ and ADOS-2 measures', so these instruments were administered fresh rather than being the basis of the original diagnosis - which is what makes their sensitivity and specificity in this sample meaningful as a comparator. The Polish ADOS-2 and SCQ are both stated to have good psychometric properties with published validation, and the SCQ's agreement with clinical diagnosis and with ADI-R is reported as Cohen's kappa 0.84 and 0.81
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Stated as matched to the comparison group for sex, but no counts are given
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Only idiopathic autism was included in the autistic group. Comparison participants were excluded for personal or family history of autism, history of developmental disorders, and neurological or psychiatric conditions or suspected genetic syndromes. Non-verbal IQ below 80 and any hearing, sight or mobility impairment excluded all participants
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: ADOS-2 overall scores of 13.60 +/- 5.23 for the autistic group against 2.48 +/- 3.22 for the comparison group, and SCQ overall scores of 22.19 +/- 6.01 against 3.60 +/- 5.78, both p < 0.001. Verbal and non-verbal IQ measured for all participants with Wechsler scales. Severity is used to characterise the sample and as a diagnostic comparator, not related to model output
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes and stringently - excluded for personal or family history of autism, developmental disorder history, and neurological or psychiatric conditions or suspected genetic syndromes, with ADOS-2 and SCQ additionally administered (mean 2.48 and 3.60)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution_controls: Matched to the autistic group; no counts given
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes and formally tested - 14.55 versus 14.38 years, p = 0.92
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Stated as matched, but without counts or a test statistic
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Established by a three-part exclusion covering personal and family autism history, developmental disorder history, and neurological, psychiatric or suspected genetic conditions
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Transcribed narrative text
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Narrations were video recorded and transcribed independently by two experienced transcribers blind to diagnosis, following the Codes for Human Analysis of Transcripts convention, with word-level reliability averaging 91%; one trained transcriber then compared the transcripts word for word and resolved discrepancies against the video recordings. Text was then encoded in three ways. Single: all of a participant's utterances concatenated with spaces into one text and encoded as one vector (1024 dimensions for ELMo, 512 for USE). Pages with zeros: a separate embedding computed for the utterances associated with each of the 15 book pages and concatenated, with zero vectors substituted for pages where the participant said nothing - which occurred in about 15% of cases - giving vectors of 15,360 or 7,680 dimensions. Pages with masking: the same page-level structure but using the neural masking mechanism to tell the model which slots to ignore, which is only compatible with the dense-layer classifier
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Video recording of ADOS-2 sessions; ELMoForManyLangs Polish ELMo, pre-trained on a 20-million-word sample from Wikipedia and Common Crawl; Google's Universal Sentence Encoder large variant version 3, transformer-based and supporting 16 languages including Polish; XGBoost; scikit-learn NuSVC with radial and linear kernels; TensorFlow 2 for the dense layer
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Narrative transcripts from 50 Polish participants; not publicly released
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Yes - available from the authors on request, with the stated reason for non-publication being that 'the data are not publicly available due to them containing information that could compromise the privacy of the research participants'
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Narrative transcripts from clinical assessments, withheld from public release on explicit privacy grounds. Ethics approval from the Faculty of Psychology, University of Warsaw Research Ethics Committee, with informed consent obtained separately from parents of participants under 16, parents of participants aged 16 and over, and the participants themselves - a three-tier consent structure more granular than most studies here describe
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Pre-trained contextual sentence embeddings, with no hand-engineered linguistic features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: None hand-engineered. Representations are 1024-dimensional ELMo vectors from a bidirectional LSTM language model with a character-level CNN front end, and 512-dimensional Universal Sentence Encoder vectors from a transformer that sums context-aware word representations across positions. The design choice being tested is not which features to use but at what granularity to represent the narrative - whole narration versus page by page - and how to handle pages where the participant said nothing
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: ELMoForManyLangs Polish model at default settings; Universal Sentence Encoder large v3
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No. The authors identify this as a limitation and propose a remedy: 'Neural network encoders followed by classifiers can take into account a wide variety of utterance characteristics but does not help to identify which particular aspects of language are crucial', with model explanation techniques such as LIME proposed to 'compute the contribution of each word in an utterance to the classifier's decision'
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None applied; the comparison across the three representation schemes serves as the only analysis of what carries the signal
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None at feature level. At representation level, page-level embeddings with zero vectors for silent pages outperformed both whole-narration embeddings and page-level embeddings with masking, and the two encoders reached identical top scores, which the authors read as indicating 'that the text encoding method might be of less importance' than the representation granularity
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None reported. The paper cites its authors' own prior work finding lower language abstraction and fewer positive-sentiment words in autistic narrations, but contributes no directional linguistic finding of its own
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Transfer learning from pre-trained language models with conventional classifiers on the resulting embeddings
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: ELMo and Universal Sentence Encoder as frozen text encoders, feeding XGBoost with default settings, scikit-learn NuSVC with radial and linear kernels, or a single dense layer with ReLU activation tuned over epochs (50, 80, 100), dropout (0.2, 0.3, 0.4) and units (128, 256, 512). Recurrent classifiers were also tried and reported in a footnote as 'far from satisfactory and substantially worse than those obtained using the Dense layer'
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-out cross-validation with the participant as the held-out unit - 'the number of folds equals the number of occurrences (utterances of one person, in our case) in the data set' - chosen because it 'maximizes the size of the training set (which is an advantage in the case of a relatively small amount of data)'. All six encoder-by-representation configurations are reported. Within each configuration, however, only the best-performing classifier is reported: 'For each input combination we only report the results of the best performing classifier'
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value, reported identically for six computational configurations, two human raters and two standardised instruments in a single table
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Best computational models: ELMo with page-level representation, zero vectors and SVM, and USE with page-level representation, zero vectors and XGBoost, both at sensitivity 0.72, specificity 0.68, PPV 0.69 and NPV 0.71. ELMo with a single whole-narration vector and SVM gave the highest sensitivity at 0.76 but specificity of only 0.60. USE with a single vector was weakest at 0.56 sensitivity. The two psychiatrists reading the same transcripts achieved sensitivity 0.56 and 0.60 with specificity 0.60 and 0.64 - close to chance. The two standardised instruments substantially outperformed everything else: ADOS-2 at sensitivity 1.00 and specificity 0.92, and SCQ at 0.92 and 0.96
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Pre-trained deep text encoders applied to picture-book narratives classified autism at sensitivity 0.72 and specificity 0.68 - modestly better than two experienced psychiatrists given the same transcripts (0.56-0.60 sensitivity, 0.60-0.64 specificity, near chance) and far worse than the standardised instruments administered to the same participants (ADOS-2 at 1.00 and 0.92; SCQ at 0.92 and 0.96). Representation granularity mattered more than encoder choice: page-level embeddings with zero vectors for pages the participant skipped beat whole-narration embeddings, and the two structurally different encoders reached identical top scores. The authors interpret the zero-vector result as informative in itself, since 'even missing out certain pages may provide clues to identify ASD participants'. The three-way benchmark is the paper's substantive contribution: it establishes both a floor - narrative text alone carries enough signal that a model beats an expert reading the same text - and a ceiling well below what a full observational assessment achieves, and the authors state the implication plainly, that automated narrative analysis 'may only be complementary or supportive'.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None reported by this study
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Replicate in larger samples permitting subgroup analysis by age, sex and IQ; include participants with non-spectrum disorders and other psychiatric conditions rather than only typically developing comparisons; test other narrative contexts, noting prior evidence that autistic participants perform worse on less structured tasks such as personal-experience narratives and conversation than on structured picture-book tasks; apply model explanation techniques such as LIME to identify which words drive classification and thereby 'discover new dimensions of language relevant to ASD'; combine text with speech and extra-linguistic features; and take advantage of improving automatic speech-to-text to remove the manual transcription bottleneck
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A small study whose value lies almost entirely in what it chose to measure alongside its model. Placing ADOS-2, SCQ, two human raters and six computational configurations in a single table with identical metrics on identical participants is the most useful comparative framing in the corpus, and it produces two findings that the accuracy-maximising literature cannot generate. The floor: two experienced psychiatrists reading the same transcripts performed near chance (0.56-0.60 sensitivity), so the models are extracting something from narrative text that trained clinicians cannot extract from the same text - a genuine, if modest, demonstration. The ceiling: the standardised instruments reached 1.00 and 0.92 sensitivity on the same 50 people, which places the models' 0.72 in a context that a paper reporting 0.72 alone could not provide. The authors then draw the correct conclusion rather than the flattering one, stating that automated narrative analysis 'may only be complementary or supportive' and that outperforming psychiatrists on isolated transcripts 'does not indicate that neural networks can replace clinical judgment' because 'an experienced clinician does not learn, in contrast to the ANNs, to diagnose patients based on their isolated statements'. That is the most disciplined interpretation of a positive result in this review. The design supporting it is sound in its essentials: groups matched on age (p = 0.92) and near-matched on verbal and non-verbal IQ with tests reported; comparison participants excluded for family as well as personal autism history; ADOS-2 administered by research-reliable clinicians under an ADOS-2 trainer's supervision and, crucially, administered fresh rather than being the basis of the original diagnosis, so it functions as an independent comparator; transcription performed independently by two blind transcribers with word-level reliability reported at 91% and discrepancies resolved against video - the only study in the corpus to report a transcription reliability figure; and leave-one-out cross-validation at the participant level. Four limitations bound the result. Only the best classifier per input combination is reported, and with three classifier families plus a 27-point hyperparameter grid for the dense layer, that selection is unquantified and applied on the same leave-one-out folds used for reporting. No AUC, confidence interval or permutation test accompanies any figure, so with 50 participants a sensitivity of 0.72 rests on 18 of 25 correct and carries a confidence interval spanning roughly 0.51 to 0.88. The instruments' near-perfect performance is partly an artefact the authors identify themselves: 'participants in our sample were carefully selected with clear signs of ASD among individuals in the ASD group and lack of developmental problems among individuals in the TD group', whereas the ADOS-2 validation sample included non-spectrum clinical cases - so the ceiling shown here is higher than the instruments achieve in practice, and the models' relative disadvantage is correspondingly overstated. And the sample is restricted to fluent speakers with non-verbal IQ of 80 or above, which the authors note may mean the results 'show the upper limit of diagnostic possibilities from the closed text data only'. Sex composition is claimed as matched but never reported.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 25, recruited through a university clinic, diagnostic or therapeutic centres and schools, and 'matched for age, sex and ethnicity, and nearly matched for intelligence quotients'. The autistic group required a prior clinical diagnosis of idiopathic autism from a multidisciplinary team including a psychiatrist under ICD-10 criteria; the comparison group was excluded for personal or family history of autism, history of developmental disorders, and neurological or psychiatric conditions or suspected genetic syndromes. No other-diagnosis comparison group, which the authors identify as a limitation and propose for future work: 'as we compared individuals with ASD and controls with TD, future studies should include individuals with non-spectrum disorders and other psychiatric conditions'. The design's distinguishing feature is that two further comparators operate on the same 50 participants - two standardised instruments and two human raters - so the study contains four independent classification approaches on one sample rather than one model evaluated in isolation.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'individuals with ASD', 'participants with ASD', 'people with ASD', 'individuals with typical development', 'participants with TD' - consistently person-first, with 'controls with TD' used for the comparison group. 'Patients' appears once in a general statement about clinical practice. The framing acknowledges heterogeneity explicitly at the outset - 'the clinical expression of the disorder is heterogeneous, and symptoms may vary widely from person to person. The cognitive abilities of people with ASD can range from gifted to severely challenged' - and describes autistic people as those who 'may communicate, interact, behave and learn differently from most other people', which is a difference rather than deficit construction. Narrative characteristics are nonetheless described in deficit terms throughout the literature review ('poor narrative skills', 'struggle with conveying the gist', 'deficits in pragmatic language'), reflecting the source literature.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Reported with tests for every variable. Autistic group: 25 participants, 14.55 +/- 5.46 years (7.1-24.6), non-verbal IQ 109.08 +/- 13.04 (80-140), verbal IQ 106.62 +/- 19.70 (72-131). Comparison group: 25 participants, 14.38 +/- 5.83 years (7.3-25.3), non-verbal IQ 114.64 +/- 12.50 (80-134), verbal IQ 113.12 +/- 14.33 (85-141). Age matches closely (p = 0.92) and both IQ measures are non-significant (p = 0.13 and p = 0.20), though the authors describe the match as 'nearly matched' and list imperfect IQ matching among their limitations - an appropriately cautious reading, since a five-to-six point gap in both verbal and non-verbal IQ at n = 25 per group is underpowered to detect. Verbal IQ matters particularly here because the outcome is narrative language. The one reporting gap is sex: the groups are stated to be matched on sex and ethnicity, but no counts, proportions or test are given for either, so the claim cannot be verified. The age range is wide (7 to 25 years), spanning most of narrative development, and the authors note they could not stratify by age, sex or IQ at this sample size.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Two-stage and well structured. Entry required a prior clinical diagnosis of idiopathic autism made by a multidisciplinary team including a psychiatrist under ICD-10 criteria - so ascertainment is clinical and independent of the research team. For the study itself, ADOS-2 was administered by research-reliable clinicians under the supervision of an author who is an ADOS-2 trainer, and parents completed the SCQ. The critical design detail is stated explicitly: 'Prior to this study, participants were not evaluated using SCQ and ADOS-2 measures.' That independence is what makes the instruments usable as comparators rather than as circular confirmations - though not entirely, since group membership was determined by the prior clinical diagnosis and the instruments are then evaluated against that same clinical determination. The Polish versions of both instruments have published psychometric validation, and the SCQ's reported agreement with clinical diagnosis (kappa 0.84) and with ADI-R (kappa 0.81) is cited. The comparison group's negative status is established by three separate exclusions plus fresh ADOS-2 and SCQ administration.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Both verbal and non-verbal IQ measured in every participant using age-appropriate Wechsler scales - the WISC-R for those aged 6.0-16.11 and the WAIS for those older - with means, standard deviations, ranges and t-tests reported for both. Reporting verbal and non-verbal IQ separately is appropriate and uncommon, and matters directly for a narrative-language outcome. Non-verbal IQ of 80 or above was an inclusion criterion, so the sample is confined to participants without intellectual disability, which the authors identify as limiting generalisation: 'our study included only fluently speaking participants with ASD with no intellectual disability and might not apply to everyone on the autism spectrum'. ADOS-2 overall and SCQ overall scores characterise severity in both groups. No adaptive functioning or language-specific standardised measure was administered, and no comorbidity information is reported beyond the idiopathic-autism inclusion requirement.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: evaluate deep neural text encoders for detecting autism from narrative transcripts and compare them against standardised instruments and human expert judgement on the same participants. Main findings: best computational configurations reached sensitivity 0.72 and specificity 0.68; two psychiatrists reading identical transcripts achieved 0.56-0.60 sensitivity and 0.60-0.64 specificity, close to chance; ADOS-2 achieved 1.00 sensitivity and 0.92 specificity and SCQ 0.92 and 0.96 on the same sample; page-level representation with zero vectors for skipped pages outperformed whole-narration representation; and ELMo and USE reached identical top scores despite different architectures, suggesting representation granularity matters more than encoder choice.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Poland, with participants contacted through a university clinic, diagnostic or therapeutic centres, or schools, and assessed as part of a research evaluation. The narratives themselves come from ADOS-2 administrations conducted by research-reliable clinicians, so the elicitation context is a standardised clinical assessment rather than a naturalistic setting. This has the same double edge noted in the OHSU studies: the standardisation makes narratives comparable across participants and the data are a by-product of an assessment already being conducted, but the assessment is specifically designed to elicit autism-related behaviour, so performance may not transfer to spontaneous narration. The authors raise the related point about narrative context, citing evidence that 'participants with ASD exhibit lower performance in less structured tasks (i.e., narratives of personal experiences, conversation) than more structured picture book tasks' - which implies, though the authors do not draw the inference explicitly, that a less structured elicitation might yield stronger rather than weaker classification.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: The ADOS-2 Telling a Story from a Book task using Tuesday by David Wiesner, a 15-page wordless picture book in which frogs float on lily pads and fly over a town at night. The choice is substantively motivated: the book presents 'unreal and humorous situations, and several mental and emotional states of the characters', so producing a coherent narrative requires inference about characters' internal states, causal linking of unusual events, and management of a fantastical premise - exactly the pragmatic demands the narrative literature identifies as difficult in autism. Being wordless, it supplies no linguistic scaffolding, so the entire narrative is the participant's construction. The resulting samples are short: on average 22 sentences, 323 tokens and 4 minutes 24 seconds, with participants producing utterances for a mean of 13.6 of 15 pages. That brevity is the practical constraint on the whole study - a few hundred words per person is a thin basis for a 15,360-dimensional representation - and the paper's honest performance figures should be read against it.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, one narration per participant, no follow-up. Ethics reporting is complete and unusually granular on consent, which was obtained separately from three parties as applicable: parents of participants under 16, parents of participants aged 16 and older, and the participants themselves - a structure that respects the assent of older adolescents and adults alongside parental consent. Approval came from the Faculty of Psychology, University of Warsaw Research Ethics Committee, with Declaration of Helsinki conformity stated. Data are withheld from public deposit on an explicit and appropriate privacy rationale - narrative transcripts of identifiable clinical assessments 'containing information that could compromise the privacy of the research participants' - with availability on request from the named authors. No competing interests, with Polish National Science Centre and University of Warsaw funding declared.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No specialised acquisition equipment - narratives were video recorded during ADOS-2 sessions already being conducted. The methodological weight sits on transcription, which is described more carefully than in any other study here: two experienced transcribers worked independently and blind to diagnosis, following the Codes for Human Analysis of Transcripts convention, achieving word-level reliability averaging 91%; one trained transcriber then compared the two transcripts word for word and resolved discrepancies by reference to the video. Reporting an actual reliability figure for transcription is unique in this corpus - MacFarlane and colleagues describe extensive transcriber training and consistency checks but state explicitly that they have no reliability results. Computational tools are named precisely: the Polish ELMo from ELMoForManyLangs pre-trained on 20 million words from Wikipedia and Common Crawl, at default settings; Universal Sentence Encoder large v3; XGBoost with default settings; scikit-learn NuSVC; and TensorFlow 2, with package URLs given in footnotes.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Good on the computational pipeline and the language sample, thinner on the participants. Reported: inclusion and exclusion criteria for both groups; the ADOS-2 task and the specific book; the transcription protocol with its convention, blinding, reliability figure and discrepancy resolution; descriptive statistics of the transcripts (sentences, tokens, duration, pages narrated); all three representation schemes with their vector dimensions and the 15% missing-page rate; every encoder with its version, pre-training corpus and settings; the classifier families with the dense layer's full hyperparameter grid; the leave-one-out scheme; and package URLs. A footnote even records that recurrent classifiers were tried and performed substantially worse. Not reported: sex composition despite matching being claimed; how the narrative was divided into page-level subsets, described only as done manually and acknowledged as 'sometimes ambiguous, especially when a participant skips one of the pages'; the number of trials or seeds; and any AUC, confidence interval or significance test. Data are available on request rather than deposited, for stated privacy reasons; no code release.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Six limitations are stated, all substantive. The sample is small with a wide age range and imperfect IQ matching, so 'we were not able to divide our sample into subgroups based on age, sex or IQ level'. The sample includes only fluently speaking participants without intellectual disability, so results 'might not apply to everyone on the autism spectrum' - followed by an unusually thoughtful observation that this may mean the figures 'show the upper limit of diagnostic possibilities from the closed text data only'. Only one narrative context was tested, with the authors noting prior evidence that less structured tasks are harder for autistic participants. No non-spectrum clinical comparison group was included. The approach requires high-quality transcription, which remains difficult to automate for spontaneous speech. And the models offer no interpretability. The authors additionally volunteer, when discussing why their instruments outperformed published validation figures, that 'participants in our sample were carefully selected with clear signs of ASD among individuals in the ASD group and lack of developmental problems among individuals in the TD group' - a candid acknowledgement that the sample is easier than a clinical population, which qualifies their own headline comparison. Not addressed: that only the best classifier per input combination is reported, over three families and a 27-point grid; the absence of any confidence interval on figures derived from 25 cases per class; and the unreported sex composition.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Six directions, each following from a stated limitation. Larger samples permitting stratification by age, sex and IQ. Inclusion of non-spectrum and other psychiatric groups. Other narrative contexts, with the specific prediction that less structured elicitation may behave differently. Model explanation techniques applied to word-level contributions, with the goal that 'giving meaning to collections of important words may lead to discovering new dimensions of language relevant to ASD' - which frames explainability as a route to linguistic discovery rather than only to trust. Combination of text with speech and extra-linguistic features, citing Asgari and colleagues and Fusaroli and colleagues. And automatic speech-to-text to eliminate the transcription bottleneck. The authors also express a clear preference between their own representations for translational purposes: 'the single vector approach, rather than the pages approach, seems to have the greatest possible clinical utility', because page segmentation is ambiguous and manual whereas the single vector 'enables full automation and objectification of the measurement' - choosing the marginally worse-performing option on deployability grounds, which is the right kind of reasoning and rare in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Narrative discourse as linguistic content, deliberately abstracted from acoustics. What is modelled is the semantic and syntactic structure of what the participant said, encoded by language models pre-trained on general Polish text - so the target is pragmatic and structural narrative ability rather than prosody or voice quality. The literature review specifies the constructs at stake: conveying the gist of a story, appropriate use of referential devices, coherence and causal connection, avoidance of irrelevant components, lexical diversity, and internal state language describing characters' perceptions, emotions and cognitive states. None of these is measured directly; the embeddings are expected to capture them implicitly, which is the study's bet and also the source of its interpretability gap. The complement to this design is Asgari and colleagues elsewhere in this corpus, who model the acoustics of the same kind of ADOS-derived speech while discarding the content, and MacFarlane and colleagues, who show that the two channels detect different participants.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality - text only, with no acoustic or extra-linguistic input, and combination with speech features named as future work. Within the modality the study performs a systematic representation comparison that functions as its main experimental variable: two encoders crossed with three representation schemes, reported as six configurations. The pattern is informative. Page-level representation with zero vectors beat whole-narration representation for both encoders, which the authors attribute to information loss in aggregation - 'the aggregation that occurs in the single vector approach for the whole narration causes some key information to be lost' - and to the possibility that particular pages matter more than others. The zero-vector scheme also beat masking, which is the more interesting of the two comparisons: masking tells the model to ignore pages the participant skipped, while zero vectors leave a marked absence, and the better performance of the latter supports the authors' reading that 'even missing out certain pages may provide clues to identify ASD participants'. Silence is treated as signal rather than as missing data. And the two encoders reaching identical top scores despite one being a bidirectional LSTM and the other a transformer suggests the architecture is not the limiting factor at this sample size.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Frozen pre-trained encoders feeding conventional classifiers, rather than end-to-end fine-tuning - the appropriate choice for 50 participants and roughly 300 words each, and justified on exactly those grounds: 'Thanks to the properties of embedding vectors, classification algorithms can successfully learn from relatively small labelled data sets.' Three classifier families were tried (XGBoost, SVM with two kernels, and a single dense layer with a 27-point hyperparameter grid), and a footnote records that recurrent classifiers were also tested and performed substantially worse. Reporting the failed recurrent experiments is good practice. The problem is the reporting rule for the successful ones: 'For each input combination we only report the results of the best performing classifier', so each of the six reported figures is the maximum over at least three classifier configurations and, for the masking rows, over a 27-point grid - all selected on the same leave-one-out folds used for reporting, with no held-out estimate of the selection cost.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: One feature vector per participant in every configuration, so the unit is the person and leave-one-out cross-validation is genuinely participant-level. The representation question is the study's actual experiment, and it is framed as a trade-off rather than an optimisation. The page-level scheme carries far more information - 15,360 dimensions for ELMo against 1024 for the single vector - and performs marginally better, but requires manually segmenting the narrative by book page, which the authors describe as 'sometimes ambiguous, especially when a participant skips one of the pages during storytelling' and which they were only able to resolve because they had video recordings; with audio alone it 'may require arbitrary decisions whether the utterance should be assigned to one page or the next'. They then recommend the single-vector approach for clinical use despite its slightly lower scores, because it is fully automatable. That is a deployability argument overriding a performance argument, made explicitly, and it is the kind of reasoning almost absent from the rest of this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value - clinically appropriate metrics reported identically for all ten rows of the comparison table. Reporting PPV and NPV alongside sensitivity and specificity is uncommon here and is meaningful in this design because the class balance is 25:25, so the predictive values are directly interpretable as performance at 50% prevalence. The table's real contribution is its scope: six model configurations, two human raters and two standardised instruments, all evaluated on the same 50 participants with the same four metrics, which allows the reader to locate the models between a human floor and an instrument ceiling rather than against an absent baseline. What is missing matters at this sample size. There is no AUC, no confidence interval and no significance test anywhere, so a sensitivity of 0.72 represents 18 of 25 correct and carries a binomial confidence interval running from roughly 0.51 to 0.88 - wide enough that the differences among the six configurations, and between the models and the raters, are not established. Nor is any chance or trivial baseline reported, though the balanced design makes 0.50 the natural reference and the human raters serve a similar function empirically.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None, and the authors treat this as the study's principal scientific shortcoming rather than a minor gap: 'Neural network encoders followed by classifiers can take into account a wide variety of utterance characteristics but does not help to identify which particular aspects of language are crucial.' They frame the remedy as a route to discovery rather than to trust, proposing LIME-style word-level attribution so that 'giving meaning to collections of important words may lead to discovering new dimensions of language relevant to ASD', and connecting it to their own prior work identifying sentiment and language abstraction as relevant dimensions - while noting 'it is very likely that this list is not exhaustive'. That framing is correct: for a study whose motivating literature is entirely about specific narrative constructs (coherence, causal connection, referential devices, internal state language), a classifier that cannot say which of these it is using contributes no linguistic knowledge. The one indirect interpretive finding is that skipped pages carry signal, inferred from zero-vector representation outperforming masking.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Leave-one-out cross-validation with the participant as the held-out unit, chosen deliberately for small-sample efficiency, and correctly described. Because each participant is represented by a single vector there is no possibility of utterance-level leakage. What is not controlled is selection: only the best classifier per input combination is reported, across three families and, for the masking configurations, a 27-point hyperparameter grid, all evaluated on the same folds that produce the reported numbers. With 50 participants and six reported configurations each maximised over several classifiers, the optimism is unquantified and could plausibly account for a substantial part of the 12-point gap between the best models (0.72) and the human raters (0.60). No permutation test, confidence interval or AUC is reported to bound this. Set against that, the study's benchmarking design provides a form of validation that internal resampling cannot: the human raters constitute an empirical performance floor obtained on identical input, and the standardised instruments an empirical ceiling obtained on identical participants, both of which anchor the model figures in a way no single-model study can achieve. The authors themselves qualify the ceiling, noting that their instruments exceeded their own published validation figures because the sample was selected for clear-cut cases while the validation sample included non-spectrum clinical participants.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorders (ASD), deep neural networks, deep learning, language processing, narrative. The inclusion of 'narrative' alongside three method terms signals the study's dual location in computational linguistics and communication disorders, and the journal's structured 'What this paper adds' box frames the contribution in clinical rather than technical terms.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: International Journal of Language and Communication Disorders 57(5):948-962 (2022), published on behalf of the Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists - a speech and language therapy journal, so the readership is clinical rather than computational. Authorship pairs the Institute of Computer Science of the Polish Academy of Sciences with the Faculty of Psychology at the University of Warsaw, with equal contribution declared, and the psychology author is an ADOS-2 trainer who supervised the assessments. That composition explains the study's shape: the clinical measurement is handled to research standards (research-reliable ADOS-2 administration, blind dual transcription with reliability, three-tier consent) while the computational work is competent but modest, and the interpretation is oriented toward what a speech and language therapist could use. The journal's format requires an explicit statement of clinical implications, which the authors use to state the supportive rather than replacement role of the method.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022 (submitted October 2020, accepted April 2022). The framing is unusual in this corpus for beginning from the strength of existing practice rather than its weakness: 'the validity and reliability of diagnosis of ASD improves considerably when diagnostic evaluation is carried out using standardized tools with good psychometric properties', and computational models are positioned as tools that 'may provide tools that, similarly to psychological testing, support clinicians in their decision-making'. The limiting statement follows immediately - 'due to the multidimensionality and complexity of the diagnosis problem, the role of such automatic analyses of narratives may only be complementary or supportive' - and the paper then proves its own point by measuring the gap between its models and the standardised instruments. The specific clinical gap it identifies is narrower and better argued than the usual appeals to cost or delay: hand-coding of narratives 'is time and labour intensive, and requires extensive training for coders to achieve reliability', which 'limit[s] sample sizes and may be difficult to implement across different research sites', while 'objective, valid and reliable measures of narration ability among individuals with ASD with no clear structural language deficits are limited' and 'standardized tests often miss evident-in-naturalistic-settings differences'. The target population is therefore explicitly the group for whom current instruments are least sensitive - 'participants with less severe autism spectrum-related symptoms, more advanced language, and no intellectual disability' - and the sample is constructed to match, with non-verbal IQ of 80 or above and fluent speech required.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Development of a visual attention based decision support system for autism spectrum disorder screening
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Ozdemir S; Akin-Bulbul I; Kok I; Ozdemir S
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Toddlers aged 26 to 36 months with a clinical autism diagnosis
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking - preferential viewing of paired social and non-social stimuli
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Build a deployable decision support system for early autism screening in toddlers under three years, and test which class of non-social competitor stimulus - familiar toys or spinning animations - better exposes atypical visual attention. The applied framing is explicit: the authors 'expect the output of this study to be an off-the-shelf and ready-to-use software package that will help professionals screen young children for early ASD risks'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification with a factorial comparison of two stimulus sets, three feature-selection methods and four classifiers, plus a single-feature baseline
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session containing both stimulus sets; each set comprised three 16-second paired videos, giving 48 seconds per set with a 2-second central fixation dot between videos
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A preferential-viewing paradigm in which social and non-social content compete side by side within a single display separated by a central vertical line. Six pairs were presented, split into two sets. In the first, social interaction videos - a male actor and a toddler in conversation and play, filmed in a naturalistic playroom with a colourful carpet, shelves and toys - were paired with videos of three toys with music and lights. In the second, the same class of social videos was paired with colourful spinning animations. Left-right position was counterbalanced across the experiment. No response was required. The non-social stimuli were chosen empirically rather than arbitrarily: the toys 'were selected because many young children with ASD highly preferred these toys during their free play activities at the university-based research center', and the animations because 'many young children with ASD's parents report that their children are highly interested in screen time'
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: A university-based research centre for children with special needs in Ankara, Turkey, using a purpose-built eye-tracking laboratory with controlled lighting; autistic participants recruited from a university research centre database, speech and language clinics and child psychiatrists at accredited hospitals across metropolitan and rural Ankara, and comparison children from the local community
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Clinical diagnosis by licensed child psychiatrists under DSM-5 criteria, established before study entry. The M-CHAT-R/F was additionally administered and its distribution reported (55 high risk, 6 medium risk among the autistic group; all 72 comparison children at no risk), with the authors noting they used it 'as it is the only available standardized screening instrument in the participants' native language' while acknowledging the literature on its low to moderate accuracy. No ADOS, ADI-R or other observational diagnostic instrument was administered. Exclusions were comorbid conditions such as seizure disorder or known genetic disorder, and hearing or visual impairment uncorrectable with glasses; comparison children were required to have no first- or second-degree relative with autism and no sibling with developmental, behavioural or emotional symptoms
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 61 recruited; the classification analyses appear to use a substantially smaller balanced subset
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Seizure disorder, known genetic disorder and uncorrectable hearing or visual impairment excluded
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: No autism severity instrument was administered. Developmental level was measured with the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Third Edition, giving cognitive scores of 77.79 for the autistic group against 98.0 for comparisons, and language scores of 67.70 against 101.27, both p < 0.001 - so the groups differ by roughly 20 and 34 standard score points respectively. The M-CHAT-R/F risk distribution is reported by group
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes and stringently - no autism history in any first- or second-degree relative, no sibling with developmental, behavioural or emotional symptoms, and all 72 classified as no risk on the M-CHAT-R/F
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 72 recruited
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes, and the authors state matching was performed on chronological age; 34.85 versus 32.90 months, p = 0.07
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: No - 37:24 versus 38:34, reported as p = 0.00. Acknowledged in the limitations: 'The study is also limited by a difference in the proportion of males and females between groups'
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Established by family-history exclusion and M-CHAT-R/F screening
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye-tracking gaze data over defined areas of interest
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Gaze was recorded at 250 Hz while toddlers viewed the six paired displays. Areas of interest were drawn in BeGaze for the social and non-social halves of each display, and thirteen gaze metrics were computed per area of interest, then averaged across the three videos within each stimulus set to give one value per feature per area of interest per participant. The two stimulus sets were treated as two separate datasets so that toys and animations could be compared as competitors. Three feature-selection methods - ReliefF, Information Gain and a Wrapper approach - were applied, and four classifiers (decision tree, naive Bayes, random forest, SVM) trained on each resulting feature set, giving 24 reported configurations
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: SMI RED250 remote eye tracker at 250 Hz mounted below a 17-inch LCD monitor at 1680x1050, viewing distance approximately 60 cm with screen height and distance adjusted per child; SMI Experiment Suite for presentation and Experiment Center 3.6 for data collection; BeGaze for drawing areas of interest; WEKA for feature selection and classification
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Eye-tracking data from 133 Turkish toddlers aged 26-36 months
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes - 'The study data for all machine learning experiments are available at https://aiot.cs.hacettepe.edu.tr/etjasd/'
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Publicly posted at a stated URL
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze coordinates and derived metrics rather than video, so intrinsically low identifiability, and the machine-learning dataset is publicly posted. No ethics approval statement, IRB number or consent statement appears anywhere in the extracted text - an omission for a study of toddlers with clinical diagnoses, though national research council funding is acknowledged
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Standard commercial eye-tracking area-of-interest metrics
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Thirteen metrics per area of interest: time to first appearance, appearance count, entry time, net dwell time, dwell time, glance duration, diversion duration, first fixation duration, glances count, revisits, fixation count, fixation time and average fixation duration. Definitions are given for several, including the less familiar ones - net dwell time as the sum of sample durations for all gaze samples hitting the area, and diversion duration as glance duration plus the duration of the saccade leaving the area. Because features are computed for both the social and non-social area of interest, each participant is described by 26 values per stimulus set
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: SMI BeGaze and Experiment Center 3.6
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, through three feature-selection algorithms whose selections are tabulated in full for both areas of interest and both stimulus sets, and through a single-feature baseline comparison
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: ReliefF (filter), Information Gain (described here as embedded) and a Wrapper approach, run in WEKA's attribute-selection mode under 10-fold cross-validation, with agreement across the three algorithms used as the criterion for calling a feature discriminative; supplemented by classification using net dwell time alone as a single-feature comparator
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: For the social area of interest, net dwell time, diversion duration and first fixation duration were selected by all three algorithms in both stimulus sets. Dwell time, glance duration and fixation time were selected by two. For the non-social areas, net dwell time and diversion duration were each selected by two algorithms. The authors highlight diversion duration as 'the most discriminative feature of our research and this feature was not used in the eye-tracking literature in general', contrasting it against their own prior systematic review finding that fixation count, fixation time, average fixation duration and dwell time dominate published work
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reported as group mean looking times, and the direction is informative. In the social-animation set, autistic toddlers looked at the animation for 6.061 s against 3.204 s for comparisons - nearly double - while looking at the people for 5.679 s against 10.370 s, roughly half. In the social-toys set the separation is much weaker: object looking was 6.607 s against 5.759 s and people looking 5.938 s against 8.587 s. The animation competitor therefore produces a far larger divergence on both halves of the display than the toy competitor, which is the direct behavioural basis for the study's stimulus-comparison finding
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Conventional classifiers on hand-computed gaze metrics, compared factorially
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Decision tree, naive Bayes, random forest and support vector machine, all in WEKA, with features min-max normalised to [0,1]. No hyperparameters are reported for any classifier. A decision tree is reproduced as a figure with its split thresholds shown, and the authors walk through how a clinician would traverse it - for instance comparing a child's social interaction fixation time against 5,879 ms at the root - as an argument for the interpretability of the tree despite its lower accuracy
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Ten-fold cross-validation with folds formed over participants, stated explicitly: 'the data is divided into ten subsets based on participants... Using participant-based subsets in 10-fold cross-validation ensured that all participants' data appeared either in the training or test set'. The authors also state that 'only training data is employed for the feature selection process'. Datasets were balanced between classes: 'We used balanced datasets in our study in terms of ASD and TD children distribution... in which all classes had the same number of training samples'
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: True positive rate, false positive rate, precision, recall, F-measure, ROC area and accuracy, reported per class and per configuration across six tables covering all 24 classifier-by-feature-selection-by-stimulus-set combinations, plus summary tables and figures
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Best result: 87.5% accuracy with ROC area 0.888 (random forest) and 0.875 (SVM), both using ReliefF-selected features on the social-animation dataset, with true positive rate 0.800 for the autistic class and 0.950 for comparisons. Best on the social-toys dataset: 85.0% (naive Bayes with Information Gain). Across all 24 configurations accuracy ranges from 67.5% to 87.5%. Averaged across feature-selection methods, the animation dataset outperformed the toys dataset (84.37% against 78.12% for the best method in each). Single-feature classification using net dwell time alone gave 70.67% and 79.17% for the toys and animation sets respectively, below the multi-feature results. Sensitivity for the autistic class is consistently the weaker side: even the best model detects 80% of autistic toddlers while correctly classifying 95% of comparisons
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A preferential-viewing paradigm pitting social interaction against non-social content classified toddlers aged 26-36 months at up to 87.5% accuracy with ROC area 0.888. The substantive finding is the stimulus comparison: spinning animations were a markedly more effective competitor than familiar toys, producing both larger raw looking-time divergences (autistic toddlers looked at animations for 6.06 s against 3.20 s for comparisons, and at people for 5.68 s against 10.37 s) and higher classification accuracy across most classifier and feature-selection combinations. A second contribution is featural: diversion duration and net dwell time were selected as discriminative by all three feature-selection algorithms, and the authors note that diversion duration is essentially unused in the eye-tracking autism literature, which their own prior systematic review found dominated by fixation count, fixation time, average fixation duration and dwell time. A single-feature baseline using net dwell time alone reached 70.67% and 79.17%, below the selected-feature results, establishing that the multivariate combination adds real information. The consistent asymmetry is that autistic toddlers are harder to detect than comparisons are to rule out, with 12.5% false negatives even in the best model.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Greater looking at animations and less at people, with diversion duration, net dwell time and first fixation duration on the social area of interest emerging as the most consistently selected discriminative metrics
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Collect more training data including children with developmental delays as a third group; test the system at the true population prevalence of roughly 1 in 54 rather than on balanced classes, to establish how it would perform in deployment; investigate the symptom profiles of false-negative children, since 'the relatively high number of false negatives may result from the clinical heterogeneity of children with ASD'; address the sex imbalance given the established gap in autism prevalence; and develop the system into an off-the-shelf software package for professionals
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The paradigm design is the strongest part of this study and its most transferable contribution. Pitting social against non-social content within a single display, and then systematically comparing two classes of non-social competitor chosen on empirical grounds - toys the centre's autistic children actually preferred in free play, and animations parents reported their children preferred - converts stimulus selection from an arbitrary choice into an experimental variable. The result is clear and clinically actionable: animations discriminate substantially better than toys, visible both in raw looking times and in classification accuracy across most configurations. The full factorial reporting of all 24 configurations rather than only the winner, the single-feature baseline showing that multivariate selection beats net dwell time alone, the identification of diversion duration as a discriminative metric essentially absent from the published literature, the public posting of the machine-learning dataset, and a genuinely critical literature review - which notes that in Pierce's geometric-preference study only 40% of autistic participants showed the preference and that repeated viewing may have affected attention, and which cites Frazier's meta-regression finding that poorly designed and poorly reported studies overestimate group differences - all indicate an author group thinking carefully about the field's weaknesses. Three problems nonetheless bear heavily on the reported numbers. First and most serious, the classification sample cannot be reconciled with the recruited sample. The paper describes 61 autistic and 72 comparison toddlers, but every reported accuracy across all six results tables is an exact multiple of 2.5 percentage points and every true positive rate a multiple of 0.05, which is arithmetically consistent with a balanced set of roughly 20 per class and inconsistent with 133 participants; the statement that 'all classes had the same number of training samples' acknowledges balancing without stating what was discarded or on what basis. No reconciliation, flow accounting or exclusion count appears anywhere, so it is not possible to determine how many children the 87.5% is computed over or how they were chosen. Second, the groups differ enormously on developmental level - Bayley cognitive scores of 77.79 against 98.0 and language scores of 67.70 against 101.27, both p < 0.001 - and this is neither adjusted for nor listed as a limitation. The authors' justification for not matching, that 'the study involved a passive viewing paradigm and did not require cognitive or language processing skills', does not hold: preferential attention to social interaction is developmentally graded, and a 34-point language gap in 26-to-36-month-olds is precisely the kind of difference that would produce reduced looking at a conversing adult and child. Third, the paper reports 87.5% as the maximum across 24 configurations while also conducting feature selection, and although it states that only training data informed feature selection, the Wrapper method is by construction driven by classification accuracy and the implementation is not described in enough detail to verify nesting. The class-balance discussion is candid in identifying the prevalence problem - explicitly noting the need to test at 1 in 54 - but then concludes that performing above 80% on balanced data 'indicates that the proposed DSS can also handle class imbalance', which does not follow. There is also no ethics approval or consent statement anywhere in the text.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups recruited: 61 toddlers with a clinical DSM-5 autism diagnosis and 72 typically developing toddlers, all aged 26-36 months, from a university-based research centre in Ankara. Recruitment was multi-source for the autistic group - a research centre database, speech and language clinics, and child psychiatrists at accredited hospitals, across both metropolitan and rural areas - and community-based for comparisons. No developmental-delay comparison group, which the authors identify as needed: future work should include 'children with developmental delays'. The critical unresolved issue is that the classification analyses do not appear to use all 133 recruited children. The paper states that 'we used balanced datasets in our study in terms of ASD and TD children distribution... in which all classes had the same number of training samples', and every reported accuracy across all six results tables falls on a 2.5-percentage-point grid while every per-class true positive rate falls on a 0.05 grid - a pattern arithmetically consistent with roughly 20 participants per class and inconsistent with 61 and 72. No exclusion count, flow accounting or subsampling rule is given anywhere, so the number of children behind the headline 87.5% and the basis on which they were selected are both unstated.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'young children with ASD', 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', against 'TD children' and 'typically developing children'. Consistently person-first, with 'young children' rather than 'subjects' or 'patients' throughout, which suits a toddler sample. The framing is deficit-oriented in describing attention - 'diminished attention to social stimuli', 'social orienting impairment', 'attentional bias toward non-social stimuli may compete with social cognition development' - but the paper is notably even-handed in one respect that most of this corpus is not: it repeatedly frames the phenomenon as involving 'both diminished and superior processing', treating heightened attention to animations and objects as a positive preference rather than only as a failure to attend socially. Autism is described as 'a spectrum rather than a distinct clinical disorder... which means that the symptoms can present in various combinations and range from mild to severe', invoked specifically to explain the study's false negatives.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Reported with tests, and the picture is one of a single successful match against two large failures. Age: 34.85 months for the autistic group against 32.90 for comparisons, p = 0.07 - matched, though marginally, and matching on age was the stated design intention. Sex: 37:24 against 38:34, reported as p = 0.00, acknowledged in the limitations. Development: Bayley-III cognitive scores of 77.79 against 98.0 and language scores of 67.70 against 101.27, both p < 0.001. The language gap of 33.6 standard score points is the largest developmental difference reported in any study in this corpus, and the cognitive gap of 20 points places the autistic group's mean more than one standard deviation below the comparison group's. Neither is adjusted for, stratified on, or listed as a limitation. The authors' stated reason for matching only on age is that 'the study involved a passive viewing paradigm and did not require cognitive or language processing skills', which conflates task demands with developmental sensitivity: no response was required, but where a 30-month-old looks when a conversing adult and child compete against a spinning animation is itself a developmental milestone, and a group averaging a 34-point language deficit would be expected to attend differently to a social interaction scene for reasons that are not specific to autism. Standard deviations are not reported for age or for either Bayley score.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Clinical diagnosis by licensed child psychiatrists under DSM-5 criteria, established before study entry and applied as an eligibility criterion, with subsequent exclusion of comorbid conditions including seizure disorder, known genetic disorder and uncorrectable sensory impairment. No observational diagnostic instrument - no ADOS, ADI-R or CARS - was administered, so ascertainment rests on clinical judgement whose procedures are not described beyond the practitioners' qualification. The M-CHAT-R/F was administered and its distribution reported by group (55 high risk and 6 medium risk among autistic participants; all 72 comparisons at no risk), which provides useful confirmation that the groups separate on a standardised screener but is not itself a diagnostic instrument, and the authors are clear-eyed about its limits, citing evidence of 'low to moderate accuracy' and explaining their use of it on the practical ground that it 'is the only available standardized screening instrument in the participants' native language'. The comparison group's negative status is established more stringently than the autistic group's positive status: no autism in any first- or second-degree relative, and no sibling with developmental, behavioural or emotional symptoms.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Developmental level was measured properly, with the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Third Edition - an age-appropriate instrument covering 1 to 42 months, cited with its psychometric properties - administered to both groups and reported separately for cognition and language. That both groups were assessed is a genuine strength relative to studies here that measure cognition in the autistic group only or not at all. The problem is that the resulting data are used descriptively and never analytically: the 20-point cognitive gap and 34-point language gap are tabulated and then absent from every subsequent analysis, with no covariate adjustment, no matched subsample, and no mention in the discussion or limitations. No autism severity instrument was administered, so the model's outputs cannot be related to a severity gradient and the false-negative analysis the authors themselves call for - assessing 'the symptom profiles of false-negative children' - is not possible with the data collected. No comorbidity or medication information beyond the exclusion criteria.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: develop and test a decision support system for early autism screening in toddlers, and determine whether toys or animations are the more effective non-social competitor in a preferential-viewing paradigm. Main findings: best accuracy 87.5% with ROC area 0.888 (random forest and SVM with ReliefF features on the animation dataset); animations outperformed toys across most configurations, with mean looking times showing autistic toddlers viewing animations for 6.06 s against 3.20 s for comparisons and people for 5.68 s against 10.37 s; diversion duration, net dwell time and first fixation duration on the social area of interest were selected as discriminative by all three feature-selection algorithms; multivariate feature sets beat net dwell time alone (78.12% and 84.37% against 70.67% and 79.17%); and 12.5% of autistic toddlers were false negatives even in the best model.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A purpose-built eye-tracking laboratory at a university research centre for children with special needs, with lighting described as optimised for tracking. The acquisition arrangement is described with the care a toddler paradigm requires: children sat approximately 60 cm from the screen either alone or on a parent's lap, screen distance and height adjusted individually, a researcher accompanying each parent-child pair throughout, a five-point calibration using a crying cartoon as the attention-catching target, and calibration repeated for each child until deviation in both x and y fell below one degree. Repeating calibration to a stated tolerance rather than accepting the first attempt is a discipline few studies here report. The setting is a controlled laboratory rather than a clinic or home, which the authors implicitly acknowledge as a limitation of the field when they call for 'less intrusive screening instruments that do not require tightly controlled environments' - a requirement their own paradigm does not yet meet.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A paired preferential-viewing paradigm with social and non-social content presented simultaneously on either side of a central dividing line, six pairs in total, each a 16-second video preceded by a 2-second central red fixation dot, with the 2-second segments excluded from analysis and left-right position counterbalanced. The design's distinctive feature is treating the non-social competitor as an experimental variable rather than a fixed choice. Two competitor classes were used, both selected on empirical rather than theoretical grounds - toys 'selected because many young children with ASD highly preferred these toys during their free play activities at the university-based research center', and spinning animations chosen because 'many young children with ASD's parents report that their children are highly interested in screen time compared to playtime and reading together'. The social videos were deliberately naturalistic, filmed in a playroom with a colourful carpet, shelves and toys, 'to observe how children view a natural environment' - which raises the competitive demand, since the social scene itself contains objects. The comparison then answers a design question the rest of the eye-tracking literature leaves implicit: which competitor best exposes the attentional bias. The answer, that animations beat toys, is directly usable by anyone constructing such a paradigm.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up. The most conspicuous reporting omission in the paper is ethical: no ethics committee approval, protocol number, consent or assent statement appears anywhere in the extracted text, despite the participants being toddlers with clinical diagnoses recruited through hospitals and clinics. Funding by the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Turkey is acknowledged and a conflict-of-interest declaration is present, so the absence is not a matter of missing front matter. Against this, data sharing is handled well: an open practices statement provides a URL at which 'the study data for all machine learning experiments are available', which is more than most studies here offer and which would in principle allow the sample-size discrepancy to be resolved externally.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Fully specified and appropriate to the age group. An SMI RED250 remote eye tracker at 250 Hz - remote rather than head-mounted, which is necessary for toddlers - mounted below a 17-inch LCD at 1680x1050 resolution, with stimuli presented via SMI Experiment Suite and data collected and stored in Experiment Center 3.6. Viewing distance approximately 60 cm with both distance and screen height individually adjusted, five-point calibration with a crying cartoon target repeated until x and y deviation fell below one degree, and a researcher present with each parent-child pair. Areas of interest were drawn in BeGaze, and all analysis performed in WEKA. Reporting the calibration tolerance and the repeat-until-criterion rule is important for a study whose features are all derived from gaze position, and it is done here where most studies in the corpus simply state that calibration was performed.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong on acquisition and stimulus design, weak on the analytic sample and the modelling. Reported in full: recruitment sources; inclusion and exclusion criteria for both groups; the complete stimulus structure with durations, pairing, counterbalancing and the rationale for each non-social class; tracker model, sampling rate, monitor, resolution, viewing distance, calibration procedure and tolerance; all thirteen features with definitions for the less familiar ones; the three feature-selection algorithms with their selections tabulated feature by feature and area by area for both datasets; all 24 classifier-by-selection-by-dataset results with seven metrics each; a worked decision tree with split thresholds; group mean looking times per area of interest per stimulus set; and a public data URL. Not reported: how many participants entered the classification analyses and how the balanced subset was formed; any hyperparameters for any of the four classifiers; standard deviations for age or Bayley scores; the number of participants excluded for tracking failure; ethics approval; and how feature selection was nested within cross-validation beyond the assertion that only training data were used.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Four limitations are stated. Class balance is treated most carefully and is the best-argued passage in the paper: the authors note that 'we need the true ratio of children with ASD to TD children, 1 in every 54 children, to test the usefulness of the DSS for predicting how DSS would perform on a sample representative of the population' - correctly identifying that a balanced design overstates deployment performance, which very few studies in this corpus acknowledge. They then undercut it with a non-sequitur: 'Despite missing this class imbalance, our results show over 80% accuracy and AUC ROC values (for SVM and RF) which indicates that the proposed DSS can also handle class imbalance.' Performance on balanced data carries no information about performance under 1-in-54 prevalence, where positive predictive value would collapse. The sex imbalance is acknowledged. The 12.5% false-negative rate is acknowledged and attributed to clinical heterogeneity, with a call to characterise those children's symptom profiles. Sample size is acknowledged. Not acknowledged: the 20-point cognitive and 34-point language gaps between groups; the discrepancy between recruited and analysed sample sizes; that 87.5% is the maximum across 24 configurations; the absence of an observational diagnostic instrument; the laboratory setting relative to the paper's own call for less intrusive screening; and the absence of any ethics statement.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Five directions, the first two substantive. Recruit a developmental-delay comparison group alongside autistic and typically developing children - the specificity test that the paradigm currently cannot support, and which matters particularly for a preferential-viewing task since developmental delay would be expected to affect social attention. Test at true population prevalence rather than balanced classes, to establish deployment performance. Characterise the symptom profiles of false-negative children, on the hypothesis that the 12.5% miss rate reflects clinical heterogeneity - though this requires severity data the study did not collect. Address the sex imbalance with reference to the established prevalence gap. And develop the system into 'an off-the-shelf and ready-to-use software package'. The last sits uneasily against the preceding four: a system that has not been tested at realistic prevalence, against developmental delay, or with characterised failure modes is not ready for packaging, and the paper does not sequence these.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Competitive social attention - specifically, how a toddler allocates looking when social interaction and an attractive non-social alternative are visible simultaneously. This is a stronger operationalisation than measuring attention to social content alone, because it makes the measurement relative rather than absolute and therefore less sensitive to overall engagement or tracking success. The theoretical framing is explicitly two-sided, distinguishing 'diminished' from 'superior' processing and noting that autistic attention 'is captivated by non-social stimuli such as objects, lights, and geometric shapes' - so the target behaviour is a preference rather than only a deficit. The thirteen area-of-interest metrics then decompose that preference into how long (dwell time, net dwell time, fixation time), how often (fixation count, glances count, revisits, appearance count), how quickly (time to first appearance, entry time), how sustained per visit (average fixation duration, first fixation duration, glance duration) and how the eye leaves (diversion duration).
