That last dimension is the one the authors highlight as novel, and it captures something the others do not - the temporal cost of disengaging from an area, which connects to the attention-disengagement literature in early autism that the introduction reviews.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality, and no cross-modal fusion is attempted. Two within-modality combinations are studied instead, and both are informative. The first is the stimulus comparison: two competitor classes tested as separate datasets so that toys and animations can be compared directly, with animations winning on both raw looking times and classification. The second is a feature-combination test structured as a genuine ablation - net dwell time alone, the single most consistently selected feature, was used to classify and reached 70.67% and 79.17% on the two datasets, against 78.12% and 84.37% for the multivariate selected sets, and the authors report having 'made similar observations for all other single features as well'. That comparison establishes that the multivariate combination contributes real information beyond the best individual metric, which is the check that distinguishes a feature-selection claim from a dimensionality claim and which most studies here omit. What is not tested is combining the two stimulus sets, so whether toys and animations elicit complementary information from different children remains open.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Four conventional classifiers spanning distinct inductive biases - a decision tree, naive Bayes, random forest and SVM - each run on each of three feature-selection outputs for each of two datasets, giving 24 configurations all of which are reported. Running the full grid and publishing all of it is good practice and exposes the spread: accuracy ranges from 67.5% to 87.5%, an 20-point range on the same participants, and no single classifier dominates across configurations (naive Bayes wins on the toys dataset, random forest and SVM on the animation dataset). The authors read this correctly as indicating that decision trees overfit small data while noting the tree's compensating virtue - it 'can be visualized' and traversed by a clinician, which they illustrate with a worked example walking through the split on social interaction fixation time at 5,879 ms. Choosing conventional classifiers over deep models is appropriate at this sample size. No hyperparameters are stated for any of the four, so the comparison cannot be assessed for equal tuning effort.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: One value per feature per area of interest per participant, averaged across the three videos within each stimulus set - so 26 values per participant per dataset, and the unit of analysis is the child. Features were min-max normalised to [0,1]. Averaging across the three videos within a set discards between-video variability, which is defensible for a screening measure but means the paradigm's internal consistency is never examined. Computing every metric for both the social and the non-social area of interest is the representational choice that makes the design work: it lets the classifier use the relationship between the two halves of the display rather than absolute looking at either, which is what a preferential paradigm is for. The two stimulus sets are kept as separate datasets throughout, so no participant contributes to a combined model.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Seven metrics per class per configuration - true positive rate, false positive rate, precision, recall, F-measure, ROC area and accuracy - across six full tables, plus two summary tables and two figures. This is among the most complete metric reporting in the corpus, and reporting per class rather than only overall is what makes the study's central asymmetry visible: across every configuration the true positive rate for the autistic class is lower than for comparisons, and in the best model it is 0.800 against 0.950, so the system misses one autistic toddler in five while correctly clearing nineteen comparisons in twenty. For a screening instrument that asymmetry is the wrong way round, and the authors flag the 12.5% false-negative rate explicitly. What is missing: no confidence intervals on any of the 24 accuracy figures, no significance test between configurations, and no chance or demographic baseline - the last being consequential given the 34-point language gap, since a classifier using Bayley language score alone would likely perform comparably and would establish how much of the 87.5% is attributable to gaze rather than to development.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is pursued at two levels and both are useful. At feature level, the selections of all three algorithms are tabulated feature by feature and area by area for both datasets, with agreement across algorithms used as the criterion for calling a feature discriminative - a more conservative approach than trusting any single ranking. The resulting claim is specific and checkable: net dwell time, diversion duration and first fixation duration on the social area were selected by all three algorithms in both stimulus sets. The authors then situate this against their own published systematic review of eye-tracking features in autism, noting that fixation count, fixation time, average fixation duration and dwell time dominate the literature while diversion duration is essentially absent - so the finding is that the field's default feature set may not contain its most discriminative member. At model level, the decision tree is reproduced with its thresholds and its traversal explained in clinical terms, presented as a transparency argument rather than a performance one. What is absent is any link between model output and clinical characteristics: no severity measure was collected, so the authors' own proposal to examine the symptom profiles of false negatives cannot be executed on these data.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Two claims are made and both are the right ones to make, but neither can be verified from what is reported. The cross-validation is stated to be participant-based - 'the data is divided into ten subsets based on participants... ensuring that all participants' data appeared either in the training or test set' - which forecloses within-participant leakage, though since each child contributes a single feature vector the safeguard is structural rather than earned. Feature selection is stated to use training data only. Against these, three issues remain. The analysed sample cannot be reconciled with the 133 recruited: the accuracy grid across all six results tables is consistent with roughly 20 per class and inconsistent with 61 and 72, and the balancing statement acknowledges that classes were equalised without saying how or how much was discarded. The Wrapper feature-selection method is by definition driven by classification accuracy, and while WEKA's attribute-selection mode can be run under cross-validation, the description does not establish that selection was refitted inside each classification fold rather than performed once and then used throughout - a distinction that determines whether the reported figures carry selection optimism. And the headline 87.5% is the maximum over 24 reported configurations, with no correction, no confidence interval and no held-out confirmation. The public data posting is the mitigating factor: it is the only route by which an external reader could resolve the sample question.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorders, eye tracking, visual attention, screening, machine learning, biomarker. The presence of both 'screening' and 'biomarker' signals the applied framing, and 'visual attention' rather than 'gaze' or 'fixation' indicates that the construct rather than the measurement is the intended subject.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: International Journal of Psychophysiology 173:69-81 (2022), a psychophysiology journal with a methods-oriented readership. Authorship pairs two special education departments (Hacettepe and Gazi Universities) with two computer engineering departments (Pamukkale and Hacettepe), and the pairing shows in the paper's shape: the paradigm design, stimulus rationale, calibration discipline and literature critique are of special-education quality while the machine learning is competent but conventional and under-specified. Funded by the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Turkey. The authors' own prior systematic review of eye-tracking features in autism is cited and used substantively to position the diversion-duration finding.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022. The framing is the standard early-screening argument but with more specific and better-sourced grounding than most in this corpus. The clinical problem is stated in concrete terms: 'many clinicians adopt a wait and see approach during the early years, delaying their diagnosis'; assessments are 'time-intensive processes that make many children are waitlisted for a long time'; and access depends on 'financial resources available to a child, the number of clinicians in a region, and governmental policy around access to resources'. The instrument critique is quantitative rather than rhetorical, citing the M-CHAT-R/F's reported positive predictive value of 54% for autism against 98% for developmental delay in a low-risk group, and noting that 'currently, no screening instrument can identify young children with ASD from non-ASD peers with high accuracy'. What most distinguishes the framing, though, is a genuinely critical reading of the machine-learning literature the paper is contributing to. The introduction surveys eight prior studies with their reported accuracies and then observes that 'the results of the reviewed studies indicated a large variance in prediction of ASD diagnosis', attributing it to 'the age of the participants, validation methods, and sample size but also... processing of noise, training dataset imbalances, feature selection, ranking, and data cases that overlap in features', and concluding that 'the variability of ASD classification performance require a careful reading of improvements in ML research related to ASD classification'. The discussion goes further, noting that many machine-learning studies in autism are 'limited by diverse methodological problems such as unreliable evaluation measures, small sample size, class imbalances in data, and invalid diagnostic procedures', citing Frazier's meta-regression that poorly designed and poorly reported studies overestimate group differences, and dissecting Pierce's geometric-preference finding to point out that only 40% of the autistic participants actually showed the preference and that the number of repeated trials was never reported. That level of critical engagement with the surrounding literature is unmatched in this corpus - which makes the study's own unreported sample reduction and unaddressed developmental confound the more striking.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Different Eye Tracking Patterns in Autism Spectrum Disorder in Toddler and Preschool Children
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Kong XJ; Wei Z; Sun B; Tu Y; Huang Y; Cheng M; Yu S; Wilson G; Park J; Feng Z; Vangel M; Kong J; Wan G
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Toddlers aged 1.5-3 years and preschoolers aged 3-5 years with autism
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking - fixation distribution across social and non-social areas of interest
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Establish whether gaze patterns differentiating autistic from typically developing children are the same at 1.5-3 years as at 3-5 years, on the reasoning that 'brain functional and structural alterations associated with ASD may differ across different age groups, which indicates that pathophysiology associated with ASD may vary across different ages'. The authors state that to their knowledge 'no study has been carried out to investigate/compare eye tracking patterns between toddlers (ages 1-3) and preschoolers (ages 3-5) with and without ASD'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control study with two independent age cohorts analysed both jointly, via diagnosis-by-age-group ANCOVA, and separately, via cohort-specific classification
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One session per child comprising five short paradigms totalling approximately 40 seconds of stimulus
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Five brief paradigms, each with two defined areas of interest. (i) A 10-second silent video of a woman mouthing the alphabet, with eyes and mouth as the two areas - the mouth chosen because it 'represents functional responses related to (early) stages of normative language development'. (ii) Two 5-second point-light displays of a person walking upright shown beside the same figure rotated 180 degrees, with left-right position switched between the two versions and results averaged. (iii) Two 5-second displays pairing a woman mouthing the alphabet against a white dot moving along a circular path, again position-switched and averaged. (iv) A clipart duck moving horizontally for 5 seconds followed by a clipart helicopter moving vertically for 5 seconds, with the movement pathways as areas of interest, testing 'the ability of keeping attention on a moving animal and object'. (v) A 5-second still image pairing an infant's face against an electric fan. No response was required
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Shenzhen Maternity and Child Healthcare Hospital, China - autistic participants from the hospital's Child Mental Health and Rehabilitation Center, comparison children from a local kindergarten or from routine annual check-ups in the hospital's child psychiatry outpatient ward; testing in a dark, soundproof room
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Diagnosis by experienced physicians under DSM-5 criteria, with a Childhood Autism Rating Scale score above 30 required for children aged 2 and over. The absence of an observational diagnostic instrument is stated plainly as a limitation with its reason: 'the ASD diagnoses were made by licensed pediatric psychiatrists based on the DSM-V and CARS (for those 2 years or older), but not confirmed by the ADOS/ADI-R due to limited access to these diagnostic tools in China'. Comparison children were screened by a study physician using three instruments - the Ages and Stages Questionnaires (Chinese Version), the Chinese children warning signs checklist, and the Developmental Screening Parent Questionnaire for Children Aged 0-6 - covering communication and language, physical ability, social skills, problem solving and intelligence, with onsite assessment and parent interview, and only children passing all screening and with no psychiatric or neurological history included
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 55 toddlers and 37 preschoolers
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: 1.5 to 5 years across both cohorts, with eight toddlers aged 1.6-1.8 years
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Toddlers 50 boys / 5 girls; preschoolers 33 boys / 4 girls
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported for the autistic group; comparison children were excluded for any history of psychiatric or neurological disorder. All participants required normal or corrected vision, and children who could not follow the calibration target did not continue
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: CARS scores of 32.3 +/- 1.5 in the toddler autistic group and 33.0 +/- 2.1 in the preschool group, obtained only for children aged 2 and over and only in the autistic group. Severity was used analytically: a multiple regression including age and gender as covariates found no significant association between fixation time percentage on any area of interest and CARS score, with p values ranging from 0.13 to 0.99
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Yes, and through three separate screening instruments administered by a study physician with onsite assessment and parent interview, though CARS was not administered to comparison children - a gap the authors identify themselves
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 40 toddlers and 41 preschoolers
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution_controls: Toddlers 33 boys / 7 girls; preschoolers 33 boys / 8 girls
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Yes in both cohorts and formally tested - toddlers 2.4 versus 2.2 years, p = 0.27; preschoolers 4.6 versus 4.8, p = 0.11 - and age was additionally entered as a covariate in every ANCOVA
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Yes in both cohorts by chi-squared test (p = 0.22 and p = 0.29), and gender was additionally entered as a covariate in every ANCOVA
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Established through three screening instruments plus exclusion of psychiatric and neurological history
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye-tracking fixation data over predefined areas of interest
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Gaze was recorded at 250 Hz while children viewed the five paradigms. Fixations were defined in BeGaze with a duration threshold above 100 ms and maximum displacement below one degree of visual angle, with the software applying filtering, interpolation and smoothing including for missing data. The single derived measure was fixation time percentage per area of interest, computed automatically as time allocated to the area divided by the duration of stimulus presentation. Position-switched versions of the biological motion and face-versus-dot paradigms were averaged. Quality control was applied twice: children unable to follow the five-point calibration target did not proceed, and Gaze Replay path playback was inspected before analysis 'to exclude the subjects whose fixation point deviates from the screen to reduce systematic errors'
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: SMI RED250 portable eye tracker at 250 Hz with 0.03 degree spatial resolution, 22-inch widescreen LCD at 1024x768, viewing distance 65 cm, in a dark and soundproof room; five-point calibration using a dynamic pink rabbit; BeGaze for fixation detection and area-of-interest analysis; R-studio 3.5.2 for statistics
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Eye-tracking data from 173 Chinese children across two age cohorts; a portion of the preschool video-clip data was used in a prior publication by the same group, which is disclosed
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Yes - 'The raw data supporting the conclusions of this article will be made available by the authors, without undue reservation'
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Gaze coordinates and derived percentages rather than video. Ethics approval from the Ethics Committee of Shenzhen Maternity and Child Healthcare Hospital, written informed consent from legal guardians, and separate written consent obtained for publication of potentially identifiable images or data
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: A single metric - fixation time percentage - computed across ten areas of interest
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Ten values per child: mouth and eye (from the mouthing-face video); walking upright and walking inverted (biological motion); dynamic character and dynamic moving dot (face versus geometry); duck and helicopter (moving objects); and baby face and electric fan (still image pair). The feature set is deliberately minimal - one metric, ten regions - which makes every value directly interpretable and makes the single-AOI classification analysis possible. The design pairs each social area against a matched non-social competitor of the same size within the same display, so five of the ten values are directly comparable against their partner
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: SMI BeGaze with fixation thresholds of duration above 100 ms and displacement below one degree
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, through per-AOI classification accuracy compared against a permutation-derived significance threshold, reported separately for each cohort
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Single-area-of-interest SVM classification for each of the ten areas, with red dashed lines in the results figures 'represent[ing] the 95% confidence interval obtained from non-parametric permutation testing' so that areas failing to exceed chance are visibly identified. Effect sizes (Cohen's d) are additionally reported for every group contrast in each cohort
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The rankings differ by age, which is the study's central claim. For toddlers, the moving mouth, walking upright, moving dot and baby face gave the highest single-area accuracies, while the moving duck, moving helicopter, electric fan and eyes did not exceed the permutation threshold. For preschoolers the picture largely inverts: the eyes, moving duck, infant face and electric fan were the four most discriminative, while the dynamic character and moving helicopter ranked lowest. Effect sizes follow the same pattern - the mouth separates toddlers at d = 0.81 but preschoolers at only d = 0.44, while the eye area separates preschoolers at d = 0.74 but toddlers at d = 0.12
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Autistic children showed reduced fixation time percentage in nine of the ten areas of interest, the exception being the moving helicopter. Crucially the reduction is not confined to social content: fixation on the dynamic moving dot was 20.1% against 39.4% in toddlers (d = 1.05, the largest effect in the study), on the electric fan 16.9% against 29.3% in preschoolers (d = 0.73), and on the inverted point-light figure 19.4% against 35.5% in toddlers (d = 0.81). The one interaction of substantive interest concerns the eye area: toddler autistic and comparison children did not differ (15.4% against 17.6%, p = 0.93) whereas preschool children did (15.1% against 29.2%, p = 0.006), because comparison children's eye-looking rose with age while the autistic groups' did not
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Support vector machine on ten interpretable gaze percentages, fitted separately per age cohort
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Support vector machine, chosen because 'it does not require any prior assumptions about the underlying relationship between variables'. No kernel, hyperparameters or implementation are specified. Statistical analysis used ANCOVA with diagnosis group, age group and their interaction as fixed effects and age and gender as covariates; Levene's test for equality of variance with weighted least squares substituted where the assumption failed; Tukey-corrected post-hoc contrasts; linear regression with multivariate-t multiple comparison adjustment for the two areas showing significant interactions; paired t-tests for within-group biological motion preference; and multiple regression of fixation percentage on CARS
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-out cross-validation over participants, described explicitly: 'dividing N participants into N-1 training samples and 1 test sample. The same procedure was repeated N times to make sure that each participant was used as a test sample once. We then predicted the group assignment for each subject with a separate classifier, determined using only the data from the other subjects, omitting the one predicted.' Toddler and preschool cohorts were modelled separately rather than pooled. Single-area classifications were tested against non-parametric permutation to establish which exceeded chance
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for the full ten-area model in each cohort; per-area accuracy, sensitivity and specificity against permutation thresholds; Cohen's d for every group contrast; F statistics and p values for all ANCOVA effects
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Toddler cohort: 80% accuracy, 80% sensitivity, 82% specificity. Preschool cohort: 71% accuracy, 81% sensitivity, 61% specificity - so performance was better in the younger cohort, and the preschool model's specificity is weak. ANCOVA showed a significant main effect of diagnosis on nine of ten areas (p < 0.001 for six of them), a main effect of age group on only one area (the dynamic moving dot, p = 0.003), and significant diagnosis-by-age interactions for the eye area (p = 0.048) and the helicopter (p = 0.05). Within-group biological motion analysis found that only preschool comparison children preferentially attended to upright over inverted walking (p = 0.01), with no preference in preschool autistic, toddler comparison or toddler autistic groups (p = 0.84, 0.59, 0.69). No fixation measure correlated with CARS
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Across five short paradigms, autistic children showed reduced fixation time percentage in nine of ten areas of interest, but the pattern of which areas discriminate changes with age. The clearest developmental finding is on the eyes: toddlers with and without autism did not differ (15.4% against 17.6%, p = 0.93), whereas preschoolers did (15.1% against 29.2%, p = 0.006), because typical eye-looking increased with age while autistic eye-looking did not - so the classic reduced-eye-contact marker is absent before three and emerges thereafter. The single-area classification rankings invert correspondingly, with the mouth, upright walking, moving dot and baby face discriminating toddlers while the eyes, duck, infant face and fan discriminate preschoolers. Full-model classification reached 80% accuracy in toddlers and 71% in preschoolers. Two negative results are reported without softening: no fixation measure correlated with CARS severity, and only preschool comparison children showed the expected preference for upright biological motion, with toddler comparison children failing to show it - which the authors flag as inconsistent with prior work rather than glossing over. The reduction in fixation is not confined to social content, appearing also for a moving dot, an electric fan and an inverted point-light figure.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Globally reduced fixation time percentage across social and non-social areas alike, with age-specific patterns - mouth and biological motion discriminating toddlers, eyes and object areas discriminating preschoolers
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Validate on independent datasets; include a broad spectrum of autistic and non-autistic participants rather than clear-cut cases, since the current design 'may have produced spectrum bias' and performance 'may be overestimated in medical practice'; add developmental assessment alongside chronological age; resolve the inconsistency with prior work on biological motion preference in toddlers; and use the age-specific paradigm rankings to design stimuli optimised for earlier detection, 'particularly for toddlers between 1.5 and 3 years old or even younger'
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The statistical and interpretive discipline here is among the best in the corpus, and the paper is notable chiefly for what it declines to claim. Three passages stand out. First, the authors deliberately do not report positive and negative predictive value and explain why with an actual calculation: 'using the above toddler values of 80% sensitivity and 82% specificity, and assuming 1% prevalence in the population, the PPV is approximately 4.2%. On the other hand, using these same values, NPV is greater than 99%.' No other study in this corpus performs that translation, and it is the single most useful number in the review for reading everyone else's accuracy figures - an 80%/82% classifier applied at real prevalence would be wrong about 24 of every 25 children it flagged. Second, spectrum bias is named as such and its direction stated: 'we compared typical cases of ASD with a group of TD with no clear ASD symptoms. Children with a history of psychiatric or neurological disorders were excluded from the TD sample, which may have produced spectrum bias. Thus, the ability of the eye tracking to discriminate between the ASD and non-ASD as shown in our study may be overestimated in medical practice.' Third, two negative findings are reported plainly - no fixation measure correlated with CARS severity, and toddler comparison children failed to show the preference for upright biological motion that prior work reports, an inconsistency the authors flag and attribute to a possible age-range difference rather than explaining away. The statistical handling is correspondingly careful: age and gender entered as covariates in every ANCOVA despite both being matched, Levene's test with weighted least squares substituted where variance assumptions failed, Tukey correction for post-hoc contrasts, multivariate-t adjustment for the interaction contrasts, effect sizes for every comparison, and permutation-derived thresholds so that single-area classifications failing to exceed chance are visibly marked. Leave-one-out cross-validation is participant-level and the two cohorts are modelled separately rather than pooled, which is what allows the developmental claim to be made. Two substantive problems remain. Diagnosis rests on DSM-5 plus CARS with no ADOS or ADI-R, acknowledged with its reason, and CARS was not administered to comparison children - so the reference standard is weaker than the analysis it supports. More importantly, the finding that fixation time percentage is reduced in nine of ten areas including a moving dot, an electric fan and an inverted point-light figure sits uneasily with a social-attention interpretation. Fixation percentages across paired areas do not sum to 100%, and the residual is time spent looking at neither area or off-screen; a group that looks less at every defined region is a group whose gaze is elsewhere or untracked, which points toward general attentional or compliance differences rather than selective social disinterest. The paper does not report the off-AOI residual by group, examine whether tracking loss differed between groups, or discuss this reading at all, even though it applied a quality-control step excluding children whose fixation deviated from the screen - a step that would itself remove the most affected children and whose exclusion counts are not reported. There is also an unreconciled discrepancy between the preschool cohort of 78 in the results table and the N = 74 stated for the preschool leave-one-out analysis.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two cohorts, each with two groups. Toddler cohort: 55 autistic children (aged 1.5-3, including eight aged 1.6-1.8) and 40 typically developing. Preschool cohort: 37 autistic children (aged 3-5) and 41 typically developing. Autistic participants came from the Child Mental Health and Rehabilitation Center of a maternity and child healthcare hospital; comparison children from a local kindergarten or from routine annual check-ups in the same hospital's outpatient ward. No developmental-delay or other-diagnosis comparison group, and the authors identify the consequence explicitly as spectrum bias. The two-cohort structure is the study's design contribution: rather than treating age as a covariate to be adjusted away, the cohorts are analysed both jointly through a diagnosis-by-age-group interaction and separately through cohort-specific classifiers, which is what permits the finding that different areas of interest discriminate at different ages. A discrepancy sits unreconciled between the 37 + 41 = 78 preschoolers reported in the results and the 'N = 74 for preschool' stated in the leave-one-out description, and exclusion counts from the two quality-control steps - calibration failure and off-screen fixation - are not reported for either cohort.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'ASD children' and 'toddler ASD' used interchangeably, against 'TD children' and 'typically developing individuals'. The acronym is frequently used adjectivally and occasionally as a bare group label ('toddler ASD, and TD is similar'). The framing is conventional and deficit-oriented - autism 'involves deficits in face processing', gaze is 'aberrant', and the literature on 'gaze abnormalities' is reviewed at length - but the paper is careful about the state of the evidence in a way that softens this: it notes that 'the precise nature of these deficits and the relationships between anomalous face processing and atypical socio-emotional function in ASD remain unclear', and cites a review finding that 'the excessive mouth and diminished eye gaze hypothesis of ASD is not generally supported'. That willingness to report that a widely repeated claim lacks support is uncommon in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Reported per cohort with tests, and both cohorts are matched on both variables. Toddlers: autistic 2.4 +/- 0.5 years and 50 boys to 5 girls, comparison 2.2 +/- 0.6 years and 33 boys to 7 girls, with p = 0.27 for age and p = 0.22 for gender. Preschoolers: autistic 4.6 +/- 0.5 years and 33 boys to 4 girls, comparison 4.8 +/- 0.3 years and 33 boys to 8 girls, with p = 0.11 and p = 0.29. Age and gender were then additionally entered as covariates in every ANCOVA despite already being matched, which is belt-and-braces and appropriate. What is absent is any measure of developmental or cognitive level in either group - no Mullen, Bayley, Griffiths or equivalent - and the authors address this directly rather than omitting it, arguing that 'predominant ASD studies used chronological age instead of developmental age' and that 'in practice, a child transition from Toddler to preschooler is typically based on the chronological age without developmental testing', while conceding that 'future studies may also need to consider adding a developmental test'. The argument is reasonable for defining the cohorts but does not address the confound: two groups matched on chronological age but differing in developmental level would differ in where they look for reasons unrelated to diagnosis, and nothing in the data can separate these.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: DSM-5 diagnosis by experienced physicians with a CARS score above 30 required for children aged 2 and over, described as 'in line with the ADOS standard'. The absence of an observational instrument is stated as the study's first limitation together with its cause - limited access to ADOS and ADI-R in China - which is a candid acknowledgement of a resource constraint rather than a methodological choice. The comparison group is screened more thoroughly than in most studies here: three instruments (the Ages and Stages Questionnaires Chinese Version, the Chinese children warning signs checklist, and the Developmental Screening Parent Questionnaire for Children Aged 0-6) covering communication and language, physical ability, social skills, problem solving and intelligence, administered by a study physician through onsite assessment and parent interview, with exclusion of any psychiatric or neurological history. The authors nonetheless flag the asymmetry: 'we did not assess the CARS in TD Children', so comparison participants were screened on general development but never on autism-specific symptomatology with the same instrument used to establish the cases.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: CARS scores were obtained for the autistic groups only and only for children aged 2 and over, at 32.3 +/- 1.5 in toddlers and 33.0 +/- 2.1 in preschoolers - both close to the cut-off of 30, so the samples sit at the milder end of the CARS range with narrow standard deviations, which limits the severity gradient available for correlation. The severity data are nonetheless used analytically, in a multiple regression of fixation time percentage on CARS with age and gender as covariates across all autistic children, returning no significant association on any area of interest (p values from 0.13 to 0.99). That null is reported without qualification and is important: it means the gaze measures separate the groups on average without tracking how autistic an individual child is, which converges with the same finding in the Keles adult study and bears on whether such measures could serve as severity or outcome measures rather than only as classifiers. No cognitive, language or adaptive measure was collected for either group, and no comorbidity or medication information.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: determine whether eye-tracking differences between autistic and typically developing children are the same in toddlers and preschoolers, and identify which paradigms discriminate at which age. Main findings: reduced fixation time percentage in nine of ten areas of interest with a main effect of diagnosis, but a main effect of age group on only one area; significant diagnosis-by-age interaction on the eye area, where toddlers did not differ (p = 0.93) but preschoolers did (p = 0.006); single-area classification rankings that largely invert between cohorts, with mouth, upright walking, moving dot and baby face discriminating toddlers and eyes, duck, infant face and fan discriminating preschoolers; full-model accuracy of 80% in toddlers and 71% in preschoolers; only preschool comparison children showing the expected preference for upright biological motion; and no association between any fixation measure and CARS severity.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A hospital-based child mental health and rehabilitation centre in Shenzhen, with testing conducted in 'a dark and soundproof room' at a fixed 65 cm viewing distance with the child's centre of vision aligned to the monitor centre. This is a tightly controlled laboratory environment rather than a point-of-care setting, which suits the measurement but limits the deployment claim - a dark soundproof room with a calibrated remote tracker is not a paediatric waiting area. The recruitment asymmetry is present but mitigated: autistic children came from the hospital's rehabilitation centre while comparison children came either from a local kindergarten or from routine check-ups at the same hospital's outpatient ward, so a proportion of the comparison group was recruited within the same institution.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Five short paradigms totalling roughly 40 seconds, each pairing a social element against a non-social competitor within a single display, and each with a stated theoretical rationale drawn from a specific prior literature. The design's strongest feature is its use of position-switched replicates: both the biological motion and the face-versus-dot paradigms were presented twice with left and right positions swapped and the fixation percentages averaged, which controls for any lateral gaze bias - a source of artefact that most paired-display studies in this corpus do not address. The paradigms also span a graded range of social content, from a full face with moving mouth, through point-light biological motion, to a still infant face, against competitors ranging from an abstract moving dot to an electric fan to clipart animals - which is what makes the age-specific ranking analysis informative, since it identifies which level of social content carries signal at which age. The brevity is a practical virtue for 18-month-olds and a limitation for reliability: a 5-second still-image trial yields one fixation percentage per child with no within-child replication from which stability could be estimated.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional with two age cohorts sampled independently rather than followed longitudinally - so the developmental claim rests on a cross-sectional age contrast, which the design cannot distinguish from cohort effects, though this is a standard and reasonable compromise. Ethics reporting is complete: approval by the Ethics Committee of Shenzhen Maternity and Child Healthcare Hospital, written informed consent from legal guardians, and separate written consent obtained specifically for publication of potentially identifiable images or data. Partial overlap with a prior publication by the same group is disclosed rather than concealed: 'A portion of preschool data using paradigm (video clip) data had been used in a previous study... However, this study used more comprehensive paradigms and the findings presented in this study have never been published before.' Raw data are offered on request.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: An SMI RED250 remote tracker at 250 Hz with 0.03 degree spatial resolution, viewing a 22-inch LCD at 1024x768 from 65 cm in a dark, soundproof room, with the child's centre of vision aligned to the screen centre. Calibration used five points with a dynamic pink rabbit as the target, and - importantly - 'those who failed to follow the dynamic pink rabbit fixation did not continue in the experiment', so calibration failure was an exclusion rather than a tolerated source of noise. A second quality step used Gaze Replay path playback before analysis 'to exclude the subjects whose fixation point deviates from the screen to reduce systematic errors'. Both steps are good practice for a toddler paradigm and both are likely to remove children differentially by group, since compliance with a calibration target and sustained on-screen looking are themselves plausibly reduced in autism - yet no exclusion counts are given for either step in either group, which is the most consequential reporting omission in the paper. Fixation detection thresholds are stated (duration above 100 ms, displacement below one degree) and analysis used BeGaze and R-studio 3.5.2.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong on statistics and stimuli, weak on flow and on the classifier. Fully reported: recruitment sources and screening instruments for both groups; the diagnostic basis with its acknowledged limitation; demographics per cohort with tests; every paradigm with duration, content, area-of-interest definition and rationale; the position-switching and averaging procedure; tracker model, sampling rate, spatial resolution, monitor, resolution, viewing distance, room conditions and calibration procedure with its exclusion rule; fixation detection thresholds; the complete statistical model including covariates, variance assumption testing, the weighted least squares substitution, post-hoc correction method and the multivariate-t adjustment for interaction contrasts; means and standard deviations for all ten areas in all four groups; F statistics and p values for all three ANCOVA effects on all ten areas; Cohen's d for every contrast; and the leave-one-out procedure. Not reported: exclusion counts at either quality-control step; the SVM kernel, hyperparameters or implementation; the reconciliation between 78 and 74 preschoolers; and any code. Raw data are offered on request.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Five limitations are stated and each is substantive, but two passages go considerably beyond the corpus norm. The prevalence discussion is the most valuable: rather than reporting predictive values, the authors explain why they will not, and then calculate the answer - 'using the above toddler values of 80% sensitivity and 82% specificity, and assuming 1% prevalence in the population, the PPV is approximately 4.2%. On the other hand, using these same values, NPV is greater than 99%.' They note that readers can perform the calculation themselves and that omitting predictive values 'is consistent with previous ASD studies on this topic', citing three. The spectrum bias passage is equally direct, naming the phenomenon, identifying its cause in the exclusion of psychiatric and neurological histories from the comparison group, and stating its direction: discriminative ability 'may be overestimated in medical practice'. The other three limitations are the absence of ADOS/ADI-R confirmation with its stated cause, the absence of CARS in comparison children, the small sample without independent validation, and the absence of developmental assessment with a reasoned defence of using chronological age. What is not addressed: that fixation reduction appears across non-social as well as social areas and may therefore index general attention rather than social attention; that the off-area residual is never reported by group; that the two quality-control exclusions may operate differentially by group and their counts are unreported; and the 78-versus-74 discrepancy.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Five directions, tightly tied to the stated limitations. Validate on independent datasets. Recruit 'a broad spectrum of the ASD and non-ASD participants' to address spectrum bias - the direct remedy for the acknowledged overestimation. Add developmental assessment alongside chronological age. Resolve the biological motion inconsistency, where their toddler comparison group failed to show a preference that prior work reports, with the authors noting that 'the age range for our study is between 1.5 and 3, while the previous study focused only on 2-year-olds, so we cannot exclude the possibility that the discrepancy is due to age range difference'. And exploit the age-specific paradigm rankings: 'elucidating the role of different paradigms in ASD classification across different stages may shed light on developing paradigms for earlier ASD detection, particularly for toddlers between 1.5 and 3 years old or even younger' - which is the concrete translational implication of the study's central finding.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Visual attention allocation, operationalised as the proportion of stimulus time spent fixating each of ten predefined regions. The construct is deliberately layered across paradigms, moving from face parts (eyes versus mouth), through configural biological motion (upright versus inverted point-light figures), to social-versus-geometric competition (mouthing face versus moving dot), to non-social object tracking (duck, helicopter), to static social-versus-object preference (infant face versus fan). That gradation is what makes the age-comparison informative, since it can localise which level of social content is discriminative at which age. The finding that reduction appears at nearly every level, including for an abstract moving dot and an electric fan, is the study's most consequential result for construct validity and is left uninterpreted: a child who fixates less on the fan as well as less on the baby face is not showing selective social disinterest, and the measure may be indexing how much of the stimulus period was spent fixating anything at all.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality with no cross-modal fusion, but two forms of within-modality combination are examined and both are informative. The first is combining the ten areas into a single classifier versus using each alone: the full ten-area model reached 80% and 71% while individual areas ranged from significant to indistinguishable from chance under permutation testing, and critically the set of areas exceeding chance differs between cohorts. The second is the within-paradigm pairing, where each social area sits opposite a size-matched non-social competitor in the same display, so the design supports comparing relative preference rather than absolute looking. The biological motion paradigm is analysed this way explicitly, with paired t-tests comparing upright against inverted within each of the four groups - and the result is a clean negative for three of them, with only preschool comparison children showing the expected preference. That the paper runs and reports this within-subject preference analysis, rather than only the between-group percentage comparison, is what allows it to engage substantively with the prior biological motion literature and to identify where it does not replicate.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A support vector machine on ten interpretable percentages, fitted separately for each age cohort. Modelling is subordinate to the statistical analysis throughout: the paper's primary evidence is a set of ANCOVAs with covariates, variance-assumption testing, post-hoc correction and effect sizes, and classification is used to answer the supplementary question of whether the measures combine usefully and which paradigms contribute at which age. That ordering suits a study whose contribution is a developmental finding rather than a screening product. Fitting the cohorts separately rather than pooling with an age covariate is the decision that makes the age-specific feature rankings possible and is the right one given that the entire hypothesis concerns differential patterns. The classifier itself is under-specified - no kernel, no hyperparameters, no implementation named - which matters less here than it would in a study whose headline was the accuracy, but which prevents replication of the classification component.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Ten scalar percentages per child, so the unit is unambiguously the participant and leave-one-out cross-validation is genuinely participant-level. Two representational choices deserve note. Averaging the position-switched replicates before analysis removes lateral bias but also discards the only within-child replication in the design, so no reliability estimate is available. And normalising by stimulus duration rather than by on-screen looking time is the choice that produces the study's interpretive ambiguity: because the denominator is total presentation time rather than valid tracked time, a child who looks away, blinks, or loses tracking accrues a lower percentage on every area simultaneously. That is consistent with the observed pattern of reduction across nine of ten areas including non-social ones, and it is precisely the normalisation that Keles and colleagues explicitly avoid by dividing by frames with successful on-screen gaze specifically 'to control for possible individual differences between participants in their total on-screen gaze time'. The contrast between the two studies on this single methodological point is instructive.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Comprehensive and appropriately chosen. Means and standard deviations for all ten areas across all four groups; F statistics with degrees of freedom and p values for diagnosis, age group and interaction effects on every area; Cohen's d for every group contrast within each cohort; accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for the full model in each cohort; and per-area classification performance plotted against permutation-derived 95% confidence intervals so that non-significant areas are visually identifiable. Reporting effect sizes alongside p values is what makes the developmental comparison legible - the mouth separates toddlers at d = 0.81 and preschoolers at d = 0.44, the eyes separate preschoolers at d = 0.74 and toddlers at d = 0.12 - and these are more informative than the significance pattern alone. Reporting sensitivity and specificity separately exposes the preschool model's weakness, where 81% sensitivity comes with 61% specificity, meaning nearly two in five typically developing preschoolers would be flagged. The deliberate omission of predictive values, with the reasoning and the calculated 4.2% PPV given in the limitations, is a more useful treatment than reporting them uncritically would have been.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is inherent in the design rather than added afterwards, since each feature is a named percentage on a named region and every group difference is reported with its direction and effect size. The per-area classification analysis then functions as a formal importance ranking, tested against permutation rather than asserted, and the finding that the rankings differ substantially between cohorts is the study's central claim. The eye-area result is the clearest example and is properly interpreted: comparison children's eye-looking rises from 17.6% at toddler age to 29.2% at preschool age while autistic children's stays flat at 15.4% and 15.1%, so the group difference emerges developmentally rather than being present from the outset. The authors offer a mechanistic account - that toddlers with typical development use visual mouth information for language acquisition, reducing eye attention, and that as language becomes more auditorily meaningful preschool attention shifts to the eyes - which is testable and which explains both the mouth and eye interactions coherently. Against this, the paper offers no interpretation at all of the finding that fixation is reduced on non-social areas, which is the observation most in tension with the social-attention framing it works within.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Participant-level leave-one-out cross-validation, described in enough detail to confirm that each held-out child's classifier was 'determined using only the data from the other subjects, omitting the one predicted'. Cohorts were modelled separately, so no information crosses between them. Single-area classifications were tested against non-parametric permutation, which is what establishes that several areas do not exceed chance rather than leaving weak accuracies to be read as weak positives. The statistical analyses are protected by covariate adjustment, variance-assumption testing with an appropriate substitution, Tukey correction and multivariate-t adjustment for the interaction contrasts. Three gaps remain. There is no independent validation cohort, acknowledged. The two quality-control exclusions - calibration failure and off-screen fixation - are described but their counts are not reported, and both plausibly operate differentially by group, so the analysed sample is a compliant subset of unknown size and composition. And the reference standard is DSM-5 plus CARS without observational confirmation, which bounds what any validation can establish. The most valuable validation-adjacent contribution, though, is not internal: by calculating that 80% sensitivity and 82% specificity yields a 4.2% positive predictive value at 1% prevalence, the paper supplies the translation step that converts a cross-validated accuracy into a statement about deployment, and it is the only study in the corpus to do so numerically.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism, eye tracking, percentage of fixation time, machine learning, toddler, preschool, support vector machine. Two of the seven name age bands, which accurately signals that the developmental comparison rather than the classification is the paper's subject.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Frontiers in Psychiatry 13:899521 (2022), in the Child and Adolescent Psychiatry section - a clinical psychiatry venue. Authorship spans the Athinoula A. Martinos Center for Biomedical Imaging and the Departments of Psychiatry and Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School with the Department of Child Psychiatry and Rehabilitation at Shenzhen Maternity and Child Healthcare Hospital, with two co-first authors and two corresponding authors spanning the two sites. The inclusion of a biostatistician from MGH's Department of Medicine is visible in the analysis, which is more statistically careful than any comparable study in the corpus. Funded by Chinese national and provincial sources. The international collaboration also explains the diagnostic constraint being stated so directly: a US-based team publishing on a Chinese cohort has every reason to flag the absence of ADOS and to name its cause.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022. The framing is the standard early-detection argument, but the paper's positioning is developmental rather than translational. Its motivating observation is that 'few studies have investigated the eye tracking differences across different chronological age groups' despite evidence that brain alterations in autism differ across ages, and its specific clinical rationale for the 3-year boundary is that 'a proportion of the children identified with possible autism before age 3 do not meet criteria for autism at later follow-up' while 'many children are not diagnosed with ASD until age 3 or older despite displaying symptoms much earlier'. The literature review is unusually careful about what is and is not established, reporting Frazier's meta-analysis of 122 studies as finding a reliable pattern of gaze abnormality that 'persists across ages and worsens during perception of human interactions' while also noting that 'adding perceptual complexity to stimuli or increasing cognitive load during attention-heavy tasks does not increase gaze abnormalities in autism', and citing a review concluding that 'the excessive mouth and diminished eye gaze hypothesis of ASD is not generally supported'. The comparative claims are likewise measured: rather than asserting superiority, the authors situate their 80% and 71% against a meta-analysis of MRI-based classification reporting sensitivity 0.83 and specificity 0.84 for structural and 0.69 and 0.66 for functional imaging, concluding only that 'our findings based on the eye tracking are comparable with results obtained from sophisticated brain imaging tools' - a comparison whose point is cost and accessibility rather than accuracy.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based medical device for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Jonathan T. Megerian
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Children aged 18-72 months for whom a caregiver or clinician had raised a developmental delay concern but who were not yet diagnosed
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Multimodal behavioural report and observation - caregiver questionnaire, expert-scored home video, and clinician questionnaire
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Enable primary care clinicians to diagnose autism directly rather than referring every concerning child to a specialist, addressing a specific bottleneck: 'only ~1% of patients with ASD are diagnosed by primary care HCPs in the US', while '~60% of children who fail screenings are neither referred to a specialist nor diagnosed in the primary care setting'. The trial was conducted to support FDA market authorisation, with PPV and NPV thresholds agreed with the regulator in advance
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Double-blinded, multi-site, prospective, active comparator cohort pivotal trial, prospectively registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04151290) before initiation
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One assessment episode per child: caregiver questionnaire (median 4 min 56 s), two home videos of 1.5-5 minutes each scored by an analyst (median 10 min 54 s), and a 30-minute clinician visit with a questionnaire (approximately 10 minutes)
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Human children aged 18 to 72 months with identified developmental delay concerns
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Three parallel inputs rather than a single elicitation. Input 1: an 18- or 21-item age-dependent caregiver questionnaire completed on a smartphone. Input 2: two caregiver-recorded home videos of the child 'interacting, playing, or talking in natural settings', a minimum of 1 minute 30 seconds and up to 5 minutes each, with the application instructing caregivers on recording quality such as showing the child's hands and face with sufficient lighting; these are scored on 33 or 28 items by trained analysts. Input 3: a 13- or 15-item questionnaire completed by the primary care clinician after a 30-minute in-person or telemedicine visit. The three inputs are blinded from one another and from the Device output. Across both age bands each child yields 64 questions in total. The behavioural constructs probed are enumerated in full and span integration of communication forms, joint attention, pretend play with toys and with others, aggression, expressive receptive and non-verbal language, quality of social responses, anxiety, range of facial expression, reciprocal communication, eye contact appropriateness, repetitive mannerisms, engagement, responsive and socially directed smiling, directed gaze, self-injury, group play, obsessive-compulsive features, sensory interests, hyperactivity, offering comfort, shared interests, imitation, unusual interests and interest in others
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Fourteen sites across six US states, recruiting children 'representing a population of patients that HCPs would see in their primary care practice'. The 15 participating clinicians were physicians who had completed residency in general pediatrics or family medicine, working across a variety of primary care settings, 47% male, with 1 to 38 years post-residency experience (mean 16), and were 'not recruited on the basis of any special interest or experience of ASD diagnosis, beyond what was delivered as part of their standard training'
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: The most rigorous reference standard in the corpus. Specialist assessments were conducted by board-certified child and adolescent psychiatrists, child neurologists, developmental-behavioural pediatricians or child psychologists with more than five years of experience diagnosing autism, using 'structured clinical observation, clinician interview and examination, medical/developmental review, and standardized assessment instruments' to reach a DSM-5 diagnosis, with the structured observation including conversation or free play, symbolic interactive play and sensory stimulation. Standardised medical history, physical examination findings and a video recording of the initial specialist assessment were then given to a blinded reviewing specialist who independently determined whether DSM-5 criteria were met; where the two disagreed a third specialist was consulted and the majority decision defined the reference standard. The rationale is stated: 'blinded consensus diagnosis introduced an additional level of rigor to the study design, reducing risks associated with confirmation bias, deindividuation, and homogenized group thinking'. Specialists also self-rated diagnostic certainty on a four-point scale, and the resulting agreement statistics are reported
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 122 of 425 completers (28.7%)
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: 2.96 +/- 1.06 years for completers with autism; 2.81 +/- 0.94 years for those receiving an autism-positive Device output
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: 18 to 72 months across the whole cohort
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Not reported separately for the autistic group; the full completer cohort was 36.2% female and 63.8% male, and performance is broken down by sex
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Comorbidity was the norm rather than an exclusion, and this is central to the design. Among completers, specialists diagnosed language disorder in 57.4%, global developmental delay in 31.1%, ADHD in 24.9%, phonological disorder in 16.0%, anxiety disorder in 8.2%, oppositional defiant disorder in 3.8%, stereotypic movement disorder in 3.1%, and smaller numbers with mood, separation anxiety, intellectual disability, learning, selective mutism, tic and other disorders. Overall 61.9% had one or more non-autism developmental or behavioural conditions and only 9.4% were both autism-negative and neurotypical. Non-English-speaking families were excluded
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: DSM-5 support-level severity scores were recorded by the diagnosing specialist for both social communication and restricted and repetitive behaviour domains in all autism-positive children, using the maximum where site and reviewing specialists differed. Of 121 with recorded scores, 5 were Level 1, 51 Level 2 and 65 Level 3 - so the sample skews toward greater support need. These are broken down by Device output, showing that of the 65 Level 3 children 44 received an autism-positive output and 21 were indeterminate, while of the 5 Level 1 children only 1 received a positive output and 4 were indeterminate. No IQ testing was conducted, with the stated reason that 'a large portion of participants were below the age threshold where non-verbal cognitive abilities can be reliably tested with traditional measures of intelligence'
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: No conventional control group. The comparison is against all other children referred with developmental concerns, of whom 263 had a non-autism developmental or behavioural condition and only 40 were neurotypical
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: The 40 neurotypical children were identified by the same blinded specialist consensus process as the autistic and other-condition groups
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 303 autism-negative completers, comprising 263 with at least one non-autism condition and 40 neurotypical
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd_controls: Not reported separately; the completer cohort averaged 3.33 +/- 1.15 years
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not applicable - this is a consecutive referral cohort rather than a matched case-control design, and age effects are analysed rather than eliminated. Children with autism averaged 2.96 years against 3.33 for the whole cohort, so the autism group is somewhat younger, and Device performance is reported separately for under-3 and 3-6 bands
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not applicable; the cohort is 36.2% female overall, and performance is broken down by sex
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Only 9.4% of the cohort - the design deliberately samples children with developmental concerns rather than a typical comparison group
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Structured questionnaire responses from caregivers and clinicians, and item-level scores derived by trained human analysts from caregiver-recorded home video
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: The three inputs are combined into a mathematical vector for machine-learning classification, producing an autism-positive, autism-negative or indeterminate output immediately on completion. The indeterminate output is a deliberate abstention mechanism: 'an indeterminate output is given when Device inputs are insufficiently granular for the algorithm to render a highly predictive output', described as 'a standard method of risk control in machine-learning algorithms'. The abstention thresholds were set by tuning: 'We worked in conjunction with the FDA to establish minimum thresholds for PPV and NPV... Once established, we used these values (PPV greater than 65% and NPV greater than 85%) as the boundaries to govern the model's range of acceptable outcomes during model hyperparameter tuning. We tuned on training/testing data to evaluate combinations of PPV and NPV at or above the FDA thresholds with variable abstention rates. We used cross-validation to maintain the PPV and NPV minimums and to arrive at the current Device abstention thresholds'
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: A caregiver-facing mobile application for iOS and Android; a video analyst portal; a healthcare provider web portal; a gradient boosted decision tree algorithm; HIPAA-compliant encryption and infrastructure. Video analysts required at least a master's degree in psychology, occupational therapy, physical therapy, speech-language pathology, special education or a related field with specific autism training, plus at least five years of professional or clinical experience with autistic children, standardised training, certification testing on unseen videos against minimum PPV, NPV and abstention-rate performance guarantees, and ongoing performance review
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Prospective trial data from 425 completers across 14 US sites
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No - 'Data are not publicly available because they contain sensitive patient information', though de-identified participant data and the protocol may be released to qualified researchers on request under a data-sharing agreement, and the full protocol is on ClinicalTrials.gov
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Yes, on reasonable request with a signed data-sharing agreement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Home video of young children is the raw material and is handled within a HIPAA-compliant encrypted infrastructure. Ethics approval from a centralised IRB (IntegReview, protocol Q170886, approved 19 July 2019, subsequently acquired by Advarra), with informed consent from all caregivers, and prospective trial registration
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Behavioural features from three independent report and observation channels, selected by prior machine-learning feature-ranking work
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Sixty-four items per child across the three inputs, with content 'stem[ming] from feature ranking experiments conducted previously to identify behavioral, executive functioning, and language and communication features that are maximally predictive of an ASD diagnosis'. The full list of probed constructs is published in the methods and spans social, communicative, play, repetitive and regulatory domains. Two age-band versions (18-47 and 48-71 months) differ slightly in item content 'in order to best capture the ASD phenotype among children based on developmental trajectories', with the classifier trained to perform equivalently across both
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Trained and certified human video analysts scoring 28 or 33 items per child from home video; caregiver and clinician questionnaires completed directly
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No feature-level importance is reported in this paper, which cites prior publications for the feature-selection work. Interpretability is instead pursued at the level of which children the Device can and cannot classify
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Analysis of the indeterminate group by specialist diagnosis and comorbidity; breakdown of Device output by DSM-5 severity level; breakdown of performance by age, sex, race and ethnicity, parental income and education; and comparison of specialist diagnostic certainty between cases the Device classified and cases it abstained on
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not reported at feature level. At case level, the informative finding is which children the Device declines to classify: 91.0% of the 290 indeterminate cases had at least one neurodevelopmental disorder, comprising 71.0% who were autism-negative with another condition, 20.0% who were autism-positive, and 9.0% with no developmental diagnosis. Severity mapped onto output, with 44 of 65 DSM-5 Level 3 children receiving a positive output against only 1 of 5 Level 1 children
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not applicable - the Device outputs a classification rather than a graded behavioural measure
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Gradient boosted decision tree with an abstention option, deployed as a regulated Software as a Medical Device
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: A gradient boosted decision tree trained initially on 'patient record data from thousands of children with diverse conditions, presentations, and comorbidities who were either diagnosed with ASD or confirmed not to have ASD based on standardized diagnostic tools', then 'iteratively improved, supplemented with ASD-expert input, and prospectively validated for 7 years prior to this study'. Abstention thresholds were tuned by cross-validation on training and testing data to hold PPV above 65% and NPV above 85% at the lowest achievable abstention rate
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A prospective pivotal trial rather than internal resampling: participants were enrolled consecutively from primary care referral, all Device inputs were collected blind to one another and to the output, and every completer then underwent an independent specialist evaluation whose result was determined by blinded consensus among two or three specialists. The Device was locked before the trial - its thresholds having been set on prior training and testing data - so this is an external validation of a fixed model rather than a fit-and-report exercise. The three inputs were mutually blinded and blinded to the output, and the specialists were blinded to the Device
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: PPV and NPV as pre-specified primary endpoints with Clopper-Pearson 95% confidence intervals, plus sensitivity, specificity, determinate-result rate, a full three-by-three confusion matrix against a three-level reference standard, performance stratified by age, sex, race and ethnicity, parental education and income, severity breakdowns by output, comorbidity frequencies by output, inter-specialist agreement rates, and specialist certainty ratings
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: The Device returned a determinate output for 31.8% (135/425) of participants. Within that subset: PPV 80.8% (95% CI 70.3-88.8), NPV 98.3% (90.6-100), sensitivity 98.4% (91.6-100), specificity 78.9% (67.6-87.7). The confusion matrix gives 63 true positives, 15 false positives, 1 false negative and 56 true negatives among determinate cases. Critically, the paper reports what happens if abstention is disallowed: across all 425 completers sensitivity would fall to 51.6% (63/122, 95% CI 42.4-60.8) and specificity to 18.5% (56/303, 95% CI 14.3-23.3). Of the 290 indeterminate cases, 91.0% had at least one neurodevelopmental disorder. None of the 15 false positives were neurotypical - all had a non-autism developmental-behavioural condition, and a third had one specialist who judged that they met autism criteria. Determinate rate was higher under age 3 (39% versus 26%, p = 0.006) while specificity was higher at 3 and over (88% versus 67%, p = 0.03). No differences were detected across sex, race and ethnicity, income or education by confidence-interval overlap, though PPV point estimates were 60% (12/20) for girls against 88% (51/58) for boys. Inter-specialist agreement: the first reviewer agreed with the diagnosing specialist 79% of the time, with 21% requiring a third
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: In a prospectively registered, double-blinded, 14-site trial of 425 children aged 18-72 months referred with developmental concerns, a Device combining caregiver report, expert-scored home video and primary care clinician observation achieved PPV 80.8% and NPV 98.3% against blinded specialist consensus - but only for the 31.8% of children on which it was willing to render a verdict. The paper's most consequential disclosure is what the abstention buys: forced to classify every child, sensitivity would fall to 51.6% and specificity to 18.5%. The abstention is not arbitrary, since 91% of the children the Device declined to classify had at least one neurodevelopmental disorder, and severity tracked output, with 44 of 65 children needing very substantial support classified positive against only 1 of 5 needing minimal support. Errors were clinically adjacent rather than random: all 15 false positives had a non-autism developmental-behavioural condition, none were neurotypical, and a third had one specialist who judged them autistic. There was a single false negative. The comparison population is the clinically realistic one - 61.9% of the cohort had a non-autism developmental or behavioural condition and only 9.4% were neurotypical - and the specialist reference standard itself was imperfect, with the first blinded reviewer disagreeing with the diagnosing specialist 21% of the time.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Not reported at feature level in this publication
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Reduce reliance on human video analysts to improve scalability of the video component in future algorithm generations; establish the training and education primary care clinicians need to use the Device confidently; conduct a registrational study monitoring stability of Device results against diagnosis over time, 'including establishing a diagnosis later in children who at the time of initial evaluation did not meet diagnostic criteria for ASD'; power future studies for covariate subgroups; confirm performance across intellectual levels; develop Mandarin and Spanish versions; and obtain cost and reimbursement data to determine whether the Device can be used equitably, including by families without smartphones or health insurance
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: This is the reference study for the entire review on every dimension of translational validity, and it should anchor the synthesis. Its design properties are unmatched here: prospective registration on ClinicalTrials.gov before initiation; 14 sites across six states; consecutive enrolment from primary care referral rather than from diagnosed cohorts; a model locked before the trial with thresholds set on prior data, making this an external validation rather than a fit-and-report exercise; mutual blinding of all three inputs and blinding of specialists to the Device; a reference standard consisting of DSM-5 diagnosis by a specialist with over five years of experience using structured observation, interview, medical review and standardised instruments, then independently confirmed by a blinded second specialist with a third adjudicating disagreements; predictive values as pre-specified primary endpoints with Clopper-Pearson intervals; a full flow diagram; and performance stratified by age, sex, race and ethnicity, income and education. Two features make it uniquely informative for this review. First, the comparison group is the one every other study here names as future work and does not recruit: 61.9% of participants had a non-autism developmental or behavioural condition and only 9.4% were neurotypical, so the Device is tested on the discrimination that actually matters in practice - autism versus other developmental concern - rather than autism versus typical development. Second, and more valuable still, the paper reports what its performance would be without its abstention mechanism: sensitivity 51.6% and specificity 18.5% across all completers, against 98.4% and 78.9% within the determinate third. That is the clearest demonstration available anywhere in this corpus of how much apparent accuracy depends on which cases a system is allowed to decline, and it is disclosed voluntarily. The associated caveat follows directly: the headline PPV of 80.8% applies to 31.8% of referred children, so two in three still require specialist evaluation, and the paper is explicit that 'the goal of the Device is not to enable diagnosis of all presentations of ASD'. Three further points bear on interpretation. The 'AI' is a fusion layer over human expert judgement rather than automated behaviour analysis - the video input is scored by analysts holding at least a master's degree and five years of autism experience, which Ko and colleagues elsewhere in this corpus criticise by name as meaning such a system 'may be considered not fully automated' - and the authors themselves identify decreasing this reliance as a scalability priority. The reference standard is itself uncertain, with blinded reviewers disagreeing 21% of the time and diagnosing specialists 'completely certain' only 67% of the time when diagnosing autism, which bounds what any device validated against it can achieve. And the sex finding deserves more caution than it receives: PPV was 60% (12 of 20) in girls against 88% (51 of 58) in boys, and while the confidence intervals overlap, concluding no difference from overlapping intervals in a study explicitly 'not powered for statistical inference on covariates' understates the uncertainty on a question - diagnostic disparity by sex - that the paper itself raises as a motivation. Commercial interest is substantial: seven authors are affiliated with Cognoa Inc., the corresponding author's address is a Cognoa email, and the code is proprietary and unavailable.
