custom_fields.RQ1.1: One consecutively enrolled cohort rather than contrasted groups, with the three-level reference standard producing the comparison structure. Of 711 enrolled, 425 completed both the Device inputs and the specialist evaluation; specialists classified 122 (28.7%) as autism-positive, 263 (61.9%) as autism-negative with at least one other developmental or behavioural condition, and 40 (9.4%) as autism-negative and neurotypical. That composition is the study's decisive structural advantage over every other study in this corpus: the comparison against which the Device is judged is overwhelmingly children with other developmental concerns rather than typically developing children, which is the discrimination a primary care tool actually has to make. Attrition is documented in a flow diagram and its causes disclosed - 126 dropped out before completing Device inputs and a further 160 after completing inputs but before the specialist evaluation, with the COVID-19 national emergency in March 2020 closing 9 of 14 sites, preventing an estimated 100 specialist visits, and the authors estimating the drop-out rate absent COVID at 26.2%. Completers and non-completers are shown to be demographically similar in a side-by-side table.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'patients with ASD', 'a child diagnosed with ASD', 'ASD positive' and 'ASD negative' as output labels. Person-first throughout, with the acronym used as an attribute rather than as a noun for people. The framing is diagnostic and health-systems oriented rather than pathologising: the problems named are wait times, referral bottlenecks, diagnostic disparity and specialist capacity, not deficits in children. The paper is notably careful about the population it serves, repeatedly framing autism as one possibility among many overlapping developmental presentations - 'ASD can co-occur with and/or share many overlapping features of other disorders diagnosed in childhood' - and treating the false positives as children who 'had a non-ASD developmental-behavioral pediatric condition that could potentially benefit from similar early interventions as ASD', which is a clinically constructive reading of an error rather than a defensive one.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Reported for the whole cohort in unusual demographic depth and used analytically rather than descriptively. Completers were 36.2% female, distributed across five age bands from 18 months to over 5 years, and characterised by race and ethnicity (53.9% non-Hispanic white only, 13.2% Black only, 11.5% Hispanic or Latino only, 13.4% multiple, 4.2% Asian only), parental education across six levels, and parental income across six brackets. Performance is then broken down across every one of these strata with Clopper-Pearson intervals, which no other study in this corpus attempts. The authors are appropriately careful about what this shows: the study 'was not powered for statistical inference on covariates' and differences were assessed 'by examining the overlap of corresponding 95% CIs'. Two age effects did reach significance - a higher determinate rate under 3 (39% versus 26%, p = 0.006) and higher specificity at 3 and over (88% versus 67%, p = 0.03). The sex comparison warrants more caution than the paper gives it: PPV was 60% (12/20) for girls against 88% (51/58) for boys, a 28-point gap resting on 20 determinate positive girls, and reading overlapping intervals as evidence of no difference in an underpowered analysis is the weakest inference in the paper - particularly since diagnostic disparity by sex is one of its stated motivations. The cohort had higher parental education and lower household income than the general US population, both acknowledged, with the income difference attributed plausibly to 'reduced parental participation in the workforce as a result of participants' developmental delays'.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: The strongest reference standard in the corpus, and the one against which others should be judged. Diagnosis was made by board-certified child and adolescent psychiatrists, child neurologists, developmental-behavioural pediatricians or child psychologists with more than five years of autism diagnostic experience, using structured clinical observation (comprising conversation or free play, symbolic interactive play and sensory stimulation), clinician interview and examination, medical and developmental review, and standardised assessment instruments, to reach a DSM-5 determination. That determination was then independently reviewed by a blinded second specialist working from standardised medical history, physical examination findings and video of the initial assessment, with a third specialist adjudicating disagreements and the majority decision defining the standard. The stated purpose is to reduce 'confirmation bias, deindividuation, and homogenized group thinking'. Crucially, the paper also quantifies the reference standard's own reliability rather than treating it as ground truth: the first reviewer agreed with the diagnosing specialist 79% of the time; of the 21% requiring a third opinion, the third sided with the diagnosing specialist 43% of the time and the first reviewer 57%; and diagnosing specialists reported being 'completely certain' only 67% of the time when diagnosing autism, 74% when ruling it out in favour of another condition, and 95% when the child was neurotypical. Reporting the imperfection of one's own gold standard is rare and consequential: it places a ceiling on what any device validated against it can be shown to achieve.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Extensive on comorbidity and severity, absent on cognition. Specialists recorded all comorbid conditions, tabulated across fifteen diagnostic categories with frequencies, and then cross-tabulated against Device output - showing for instance that children with phonological disorder were classified indeterminate 82.4% of the time while those with intellectual disability received a positive output 66.7% of the time. DSM-5 support-level severity was recorded separately for social communication and restricted repetitive behaviour domains in every autism-positive child, using the maximum where site and reviewing specialists differed, and broken down by output: of 121 with scores, 5 were Level 1, 51 Level 2 and 65 Level 3, with the Device classifying 44 of 65 Level 3 children positive against 1 of 5 Level 1 children. That gradient is the clearest evidence in the paper of what the abstention mechanism is doing - declining on milder and more ambiguous presentations. No IQ or developmental quotient was obtained, and the reason given is sound: 'a large portion of participants were below the age threshold where non-verbal cognitive abilities can be reliably tested with traditional measures of intelligence'. The authors nonetheless flag that 'appropriately powered follow-up studies are needed to confirm Device performance across a range of intellectual levels'.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: test whether an AI-based diagnostic aid can allow primary care clinicians to diagnose autism directly, reducing referral load and diagnostic delay. Main findings: for the 31.8% of children on which the Device rendered a verdict, PPV was 80.8% and NPV 98.3%, with sensitivity 98.4% and specificity 78.9%; if abstention were removed, sensitivity across all completers would fall to 51.6% and specificity to 18.5%; 91% of the children the Device declined to classify had at least one neurodevelopmental disorder; all 15 false positives had a non-autism developmental condition and none were neurotypical, with one specialist judging a third of them autistic; there was a single false negative; the mean age at which an autism-positive output was rendered was 2.81 years against a national average diagnosis age above 4; and no performance differences were detected across sex, race and ethnicity, income or education, though the study was not powered to test them.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Fourteen sites across six US states, recruiting children 'representing a population of patients that HCPs would see in their primary care practice' - so the sampling frame is the referral population the tool is intended for, not a research cohort. The participating clinicians are equally representative: 15 physicians trained in general pediatrics or family medicine, spanning 1 to 38 years of post-residency experience, and explicitly 'not recruited on the basis of any special interest or experience of ASD diagnosis, beyond what was delivered as part of their standard training'. That last detail matters more than it might appear: a diagnostic aid evaluated only with enthusiastic autism-interested clinicians would not establish that ordinary primary care physicians can use it. Thirteen point nine percent of clinician assessments were conducted by telemedicine rather than in person, with 'no evidence of performance degradation' when done remotely - an incidental finding produced by the COVID-19 disruption that speaks directly to rural and low-access deployment.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Three mutually blinded inputs, deliberately mirroring the components of a standard evaluation: 'use of multimodular Device inputs is consistent with current guidelines and recommendations for an evaluation of ASD that include having both caregiver and clinician input, as well as a structured observation of the child'. The video component is the element that distinguishes it from a questionnaire battery, and the rationale given is behavioural rather than technical - clinicians assess 'within a time-constrained clinical encounter where the child may not display behavior characteristic of that seen in the home environment or may become newly behaviorally reactive due to change in environment', so caregiver-recorded home video supplies observation of the child in their ordinary setting. The practical constraints are modest and reported: two videos of 1.5 to 5 minutes, with in-app guidance on framing and lighting; a caregiver questionnaire taking a median 4 minutes 56 seconds; and a clinician questionnaire taking about 10 minutes after a 30-minute visit. Age-banded questionnaire versions differ slightly to reflect developmental trajectories, with the classifier trained to perform equivalently across both.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Prospective and prospectively registered (NCT04151290) before initiation, conducted August 2019 to June 2020, with each child assessed once by the Device and once by specialists. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: centralised IRB review by IntegReview under protocol number Q170886, approved 19 July 2019, with the subsequent acquisition by Advarra noted, and informed consent from all caregivers. The COVID-19 disruption is disclosed in detail rather than smoothed over - the date of the national emergency, the number of sites closed (9 of 14), the reduced availability of those remaining, the estimate that 100 specialist visits could not be completed, the 97 that were completed afterwards, and the estimated drop-out rate absent the pandemic (26.2%). Data are withheld from public release on patient-sensitivity grounds but offered to qualified researchers under a data-sharing agreement, with the full protocol public on ClinicalTrials.gov. The code is proprietary and not available.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Consumer smartphones for caregivers plus web portals for clinicians and analysts - no specialised hardware. The substantive resource requirement is human: video analysts must hold at least a master's degree in psychology, occupational therapy, physical therapy, speech-language pathology, special education or a related field with specific autism training, and have at least five years of professional or clinical experience with autistic children. They receive standardised training, must pass certification on previously unseen videos meeting minimum PPV, NPV and abstention-rate guarantees, and undergo ongoing performance review during the study. This is the element that most complicates the scalability claim, and the authors identify it themselves as a research priority: 'improving the scalability of the video component of the Device by decreasing reliance on human video analysts in subsequent generations of the algorithm'. The Device also requires smartphone access, which the authors note 'not all low-income American families may have', and functions only in English, with Mandarin and Spanish versions in development.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Reporting is at regulatory-trial standard and exceeds every other study in the corpus. Fully specified: trial registration number and protocol availability; IRB name, protocol number and approval date; site count and states; recruitment population; clinician qualifications and experience distribution; participant flow with reasons at each stage and COVID-19 impact quantified; baseline demographics for both completers and all enrolled across age, sex, race and ethnicity, education and income; the complete list of behavioural constructs probed by the questionnaires; item counts per input per age band; video duration requirements and caregiver guidance; video analyst qualification, training and certification requirements; the reference standard procedure including the blinding and adjudication structure; specialist qualifications; the certainty rating scale; median completion times for two of three inputs with the third's estimation method disclosed; the confusion matrix against a three-level standard; performance across every demographic stratum with intervals; severity and comorbidity breakdowns by output; the statistical software, packages and interval method; and the abstention threshold-setting procedure including the FDA-agreed PPV and NPV floors. Not available: the algorithm itself, the feature weights, and the code, all proprietary; and the specific standardised instruments the specialists used are described generically rather than named.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Substantial and candid, with the central limitation stated as a headline result rather than buried. The abstention rate is not framed as a caveat but as a design feature whose cost is quantified: the Device declined to classify 68.2% of children, and the paper states plainly what would happen otherwise - sensitivity 51.6%, specificity 18.5%. The stated scope follows: 'the goal of the Device is not to enable diagnosis of all presentations of ASD, but to aid primary care HCPs to diagnose the subset of children the Device can confidently determine a recommendation for'. Other limitations acknowledged: not powered for covariate inference; no IQ testing, with the reason and the need for follow-up stated; English only, with non-English families excluded and translations in development; parental education higher and income lower than the general population; smartphone access required; cost and reimbursement data absent, with explicit concern about equitable access for low-income and uninsured families; reliance on human video analysts limiting scalability; and the expectation that abstention rates will vary with the population's composition, being lower in more neurotypical or higher-prevalence populations. What receives insufficient weight: the sex difference in PPV, dismissed on interval overlap in an admittedly underpowered analysis; and the fact that the reference standard's own 21% disagreement rate bounds the achievable ceiling, which is reported but not carried into the interpretation of the results.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Six directions, all operationally concrete. Reduce dependence on human video analysts in future algorithm generations - the scalability bottleneck. Determine what training primary care clinicians need to use the Device confidently in practice, which is a human-factors question the trial did not address since it used a study protocol rather than routine deployment. Run a registrational study monitoring the stability of Device results against diagnosis over time, 'including establishing a diagnosis later in children who at the time of initial evaluation did not meet diagnostic criteria for ASD' - the follow-up that would establish whether indeterminate and negative outputs remain correct as children develop, and the single most important missing evidence for a tool used at 18-72 months. Power future studies for demographic subgroups. Confirm performance across intellectual levels. And obtain cost and reimbursement data to establish whether deployment would be equitable, with explicit reference to Medicaid sustainability and to families without smartphones or insurance.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Behaviour is captured through three complementary observational vantage points rather than a single measurement channel, and the design rationale is explicitly clinical rather than technical. Caregiver report captures behaviour across settings and time; home video captures 'rich insight into the child's natural behavior outside of the clinic setting'; and the clinician questionnaire captures structured professional observation within a visit. The constructs probed are enumerated in full and are recognisably the constructs of a clinical autism evaluation - joint attention, integration of communication forms, reciprocal communication, quality of social responses and overtures, directed and responsive smiling, eye contact appropriateness, pretend and creative play alone and with others, imitation, shared interests, offering comfort, repetitive mannerisms, sensory interests, unusual interests - rather than proxy signals such as gaze coordinates or acoustic features. This is the one study in the corpus where the computational input is the same behavioural vocabulary a clinician would use, which is why its outputs can be interpreted directly and why its false positives can be characterised as children with other conditions that would benefit from similar intervention.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: The most consequential fusion result in the corpus, though the fusion itself is inherited from prior work: 'previously published analysis of earlier algorithm iterations demonstrated that combining inputs significantly improved the performance of the algorithm'. What this trial adds is not a demonstration that fusion helps but a demonstration of what fusion plus abstention achieves under prospective conditions on the clinically relevant population. Two properties of the fusion deserve note. The three inputs are mutually blinded, so no channel is contaminated by another - the caregiver does not know what the clinician said, the video analyst does not know either, and none sees the output. And the channels are deliberately heterogeneous in vantage point rather than in modality, combining retrospective caregiver knowledge, naturalistic home observation and structured clinical observation, which is a different fusion logic from the modality-combining designs elsewhere in this review and is justified by reference to diagnostic guidelines rather than to information theory. The trial does not report per-input performance, so the marginal contribution of each channel in this cohort cannot be assessed - a gap relative to the fusion ablations reported by MacFarlane, Han and Liao.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A gradient boosted decision tree, chosen for a regulated diagnostic aid over deep architectures, and locked before the trial. The model's provenance is described across seven years of prior development: initially trained 'using patient record data from thousands of children with diverse conditions, presentations, and comorbidities' with labels from standardised diagnostic tools, then 'iteratively improved, supplemented with ASD-expert input, and prospectively validated for 7 years prior to this study'. The abstention mechanism is the modelling contribution and is handled with unusual explicitness: thresholds were tuned by cross-validation on training and testing data to hold PPV above 65% and NPV above 85% - floors agreed with the FDA in advance - while minimising the abstention rate. The justification for abstaining rather than always deciding is stated in three parts: it 'provides a safeguard against known machine-learning failure modes, fosters clinician trust through model transparency, and helps flag cases where additional human expertise or data may be needed'. That framing - abstention as a transparency and triage mechanism rather than a performance trick - is the right one, and the paper earns it by quantifying the alternative.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Three input vectors combined into a single mathematical representation, with 64 questionnaire items per child spread across the channels. The representation is entirely in the vocabulary of clinical behavioural observation rather than in derived signal features, which is what allows the outputs to be audited clinically - the paper can report which comorbidities and which severity levels are associated with each output because the inputs are commensurable with the reference standard's own constructs. The age-banded versions are a considered detail: item content differs slightly between 18-47 and 48-71 months 'in order to best capture the ASD phenotype among children based on developmental trajectories', with the classifier trained to perform equivalently across both, and the trial then reports performance separately by age band and finds a genuine difference in determinate rate and specificity. That is representation design responding to a developmental fact, and it is validated rather than assumed.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Predictive values were the pre-specified primary endpoints, and the reason given is exactly right for a diagnostic aid: 'the selection of predictive values as primary endpoints reflects the utility of the Device in a broad spectrum of subjects, as these values measure how often in the study population the Device correctly identifies a patient with ASD and how frequently it correctly determines that a patient does not have ASD'. Because the cohort's 28.7% prevalence is that of the referral population the tool would actually serve, these predictive values are directly interpretable in deployment - which is precisely what the accuracy figures reported throughout the rest of this corpus are not. Clopper-Pearson exact intervals accompany every estimate. The confusion matrix is three-by-three against a three-level reference standard rather than two-by-two, so the composition of the errors is visible: all 15 false positives came from the other-condition column and none from the neurotypical column. Performance is stratified across five demographic dimensions with intervals throughout, severity and comorbidity are cross-tabulated against output, and reference-standard reliability and specialist certainty are reported alongside. The one substantive gap is the absence of per-input performance, which would show how much each channel contributes.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No feature-level interpretability, and the algorithm and code are proprietary - so at the level of mechanism the Device is opaque. What the paper offers instead is case-level interpretability, and it is more clinically useful than a feature ranking would be. The indeterminate group is characterised diagnostically: 91.0% had at least one neurodevelopmental disorder, 71.0% were autism-negative with another condition, 20.0% were autism-positive and 9.0% had no developmental diagnosis - so the abstentions concentrate on the genuinely ambiguous rather than falling randomly. Output is cross-tabulated against DSM-5 severity, showing a clear gradient from 44 of 65 Level 3 children classified positive to 1 of 5 Level 1 children. Output is cross-tabulated against every comorbidity, showing for example that phonological disorder yields abstention 82.4% of the time. And specialist certainty is compared between cases the Device classified and cases it declined - 71% versus 64% completely certain, p = 0.40 - testing whether the Device abstains where clinicians are also uncertain, and finding no significant difference. Taken together these establish what the Device is doing at the level a clinician needs, even though they say nothing about how.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The validation design is the study's principal contribution to this review and differs in kind from everything else charted here. Rather than resampling within a dataset, the model was locked with thresholds fixed on prior training and testing data, and then evaluated prospectively on consecutively enrolled children whose diagnoses were established afterwards by an independent blinded specialist consensus. All three Device inputs were blinded from one another and from the output; the specialists were blinded to the Device. The trial was registered before initiation, so the endpoints - PPV and NPV with FDA-agreed floors - were pre-specified rather than selected post hoc. Participant flow is fully documented with attrition causes including the COVID-19 disruption quantified. The two features that make this the corpus's benchmark are the population and the disclosure. The population is the referral cohort the tool is meant for, with 28.7% prevalence and only 9.4% neurotypical, so predictive values are directly deployable rather than requiring prevalence correction - the calculation Kong and colleagues perform hypothetically is here unnecessary because the design supplies it directly. The disclosure is the counterfactual: sensitivity 51.6% and specificity 18.5% without abstention, against 98.4% and 78.9% with it. No other paper in this corpus reports what its performance would be under a less favourable operating decision. What remains open is the temporal question the authors themselves identify - whether children given indeterminate or negative outputs at 18-72 months go on to receive autism diagnoses later - which the planned registrational study is designed to address and without which the NPV of 98.3% is a cross-sectional rather than a prognostic figure.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No keyword list appears in the extracted text. The operative vocabulary is Software as a Medical Device, diagnostic aid, active comparator, predictive value, indeterminate output, abstention, risk control and primary care - a regulatory and health-services register rather than a machine-learning one, which accurately reflects a paper whose contribution is a trial rather than an algorithm.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: npj Digital Medicine 5:57 (2022), a digital health journal published in partnership with Seoul National University Bundang Hospital. Authorship spans 20 affiliations including CHOC Children's, UC Irvine, Stanford, Nationwide Children's, Ohio State, University of Missouri, Arizona State, Children's National, and seven authors affiliated with Cognoa Inc., the device manufacturer, with the corresponding author reachable at a cognoa.com address and also holding a CHOC and UC Irvine appointment. The senior author list includes the Stanford investigator whose group also produced the crowdsourced speech study elsewhere in this corpus and who declares founding Cognoa there. The commercial relationship is transparent from the affiliations and the paper is framed as a regulatory submission, which explains both its methodological rigour - a pivotal trial must satisfy FDA review - and its limits, since the algorithm and code are proprietary and unavailable for independent scrutiny.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022. The framing is a health-systems argument rather than a technical or clinical-deficit one, and it is the most concretely evidenced in the corpus. The problem is specified with figures at each link in the chain: US prevalence 1.9%; mean age of diagnosis over 4 years despite reliable diagnosis being possible at 18 months; an estimated three-year delay between first caregiver concern and diagnosis, longer for children who are non-white, female, of lower socioeconomic status or rural; 27% of autistic children still undiagnosed at age 8; waits of up to 18 months between primary care screening and specialist diagnosis; only about 1% of autistic patients diagnosed by primary care clinicians; roughly 60% of children who fail a screen neither referred nor diagnosed; and 61% of 454 children with an eventual autism diagnosis having screened negative on a common screener in a cohort of over 20,000. The barriers to primary care diagnosis are then named specifically - low confidence with diagnostic tools, lack of specialist training, insufficient time to administer or to review results, and inadequate reimbursement - as is the observation that existing instruments risk overdiagnosis 'in populations with a lower prevalence of ASD, as is the case in primary care' and lose reliability when combination instruments are used stand-alone by time-pressured clinicians. The proposed role follows from this analysis and is correspondingly bounded: not to replace specialist assessment but to let primary care resolve the straightforward cases so that specialist capacity concentrates on the complex ones, with the authors observing that 'reducing tertiary referral loads by even a third could significantly shorten wait times for interventions to begin'.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Extraction and Classification of Acoustic Features from Italian Speaking Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Beccaria F; Gagliardi G; Kokkinakis D
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: Proceedings of the RaPID Workshop - Resources
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Italian-speaking children with autism aged 6 to 10
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Speech acoustics - prosody, voice quality, loudness and spectral distribution
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Determine whether acoustic markers of autism reported in English and other languages also hold in Italian, for which the authors state there are few studies. The stated aim is explicitly not classification: 'this work aims to test the feature extraction effectiveness and not automatically classify ASD from new speech data', with the classifiers serving to evaluate whether the selected features carry signal
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control acoustic comparison with a supervised classification step used as a validity check on feature selection, drawing on a previously collected autistic corpus and a newly collected comparison corpus
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One storytelling interview per child; recording durations are not reported
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Semi-spontaneous narrative elicited by asking the child to tell a story from six pictures depicting a birthday party, taken from the Shubi toy collection 'Storie da raccontare', described as 'easily interpretable by neurotypical children of different ages'. For the autistic group the interview 'started with activities generally done during the treatment session so the child would act in the most spontaneous way', conducted 'in the room where they usually play' with a setting 'designed so that the child would feel comfortable'
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: A homogeneous geographical area in Tuscany between Florence, Pistoia and Prato. Autistic children were recorded in June 2019 by a designated speech therapist in their usual therapy playroom, using a video camera on a three-legged support; comparison children were recorded subsequently by their own parents using the parents' phones, because COVID-19 made in-person collection impossible
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Diagnosis 'made by a neuropsychiatrist according to DSM-5 criteria'. No standardised observational or interview instrument is named, no severity measure was obtained, and no information is given about when the diagnosis was made or by what procedure. Children were recruited from the speech and language therapy service of AUSL Toscana Centro and the Onlus foundation Opera Santa Rita
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not reported; the stated range is 6 to 10 years
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: All autistic participants were receiving speech and language therapy, since they were recruited through a therapy service and recorded during a treatment session in their usual therapy room
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: None. No severity, cognitive, language or adaptive measure for either group
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: No screening instrument or exclusion criteria are described for the comparison group beyond their being described as having typical neurodevelopment
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd_controls: Not reported; stated as the same range as the autistic group
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Stated as matched - 'the children are 14 for each group with the same age (from 6 to 10 years)' - but no means, standard deviations or statistical test are reported, so only the range is known to be shared
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Yes and exactly, at 11 male and 3 female in each group. The sex ratio was chosen deliberately: 'Gender disparity is taken from the epidemiology of the disorder recorded by the DSM-5, i.e., four males every one female'
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Asserted rather than established; no screening instrument is named
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Audio extracted from video and phone recordings of narrative speech
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: The eGeMAPS parameter set was extracted with openSMILE version 2.1, yielding 88 parameters spanning frequency-related features (pitch on a semitone scale from 27.5 Hz, jitter, first three formant frequencies and bandwidths), energy and amplitude features (harmonics-to-noise ratio, loudness, shimmer) and spectral balance features (alpha ratio, formant relative energies, Hammarberg index, H1-H2 and H1-A3 harmonic differences, MFCCs 1-4, spectral flux, spectral slope in two bands). Mann-Whitney U-tests were then applied across the two groups and the 16 parameters showing significant differences retained. These were normalised and used to train four classifiers under three-fold stratified cross-validation on an 80/20 train-test split, giving 22 training and 6 test samples. Ten models were run per method and the best selected
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: For the autistic group, a video camera on a three-legged support in a therapy playroom; for the comparison group, parents' own mobile phones at home. openSMILE 2.1 with the eGeMAPS parameter set; Python with scikit-learn and Jupyter Notebook; code publicly released on GitHub
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: 28 narrative recordings from Italian children; the autistic recordings were reused from a prior thesis project on discourse and storytelling in autism, and the comparison recordings were newly collected for this study
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not stated. The analysis code is publicly released at https://github.com/federica-bcc/speech-autism
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not discussed. Written consent from caregivers is stated for the autistic group; no consent or ethics statement is given for the comparison group, and no ethics committee approval is reported for either
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: The eGeMAPS standard clinical paralinguistic parameter set
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Sixteen parameters survived Mann-Whitney selection, spanning four families. Frequency: standard deviation of pitch falling slope, and standard deviation of second formant frequency and bandwidth. Voice quality: mean and standard deviation of jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio. Loudness: mean, standard deviation of rising slope, and 20th percentile. Spectral: mean spectral flux overall and in voiced segments, and mean spectral slope in unvoiced segments over 0-500 Hz and 500-1500 Hz. The choice of eGeMAPS over the alternatives is argued rather than defaulted: ComParE was rejected because 'the size of the feature space (n = 6376) vastly outnumbers the sample size of our dataset' and would cause overfitting, and eGeMAPS was chosen over GeMAPS because it 'extracts features based on their relation to various psychological changes in voice production'
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: openSMILE 2.1 with the eGeMAPS parameter set
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, in the sense that all 16 selected features are reported with group means, standard deviations, outlier counts and p-values, and each is discussed individually against the prior literature
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Mann-Whitney U-test comparing each of the 88 extracted parameters between groups, with the significant subset retained
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The strongest separations were shimmer standard deviation (p = 0.0010), harmonics-to-noise ratio mean (p = 0.0012), shimmer mean and harmonics-to-noise ratio standard deviation (both p = 0.0016), spectral slope for unvoiced segments in 500-1500 Hz (p = 0.0026), second formant frequency standard deviation (p = 0.0030) and the 20th percentile of loudness (p = 0.0035)
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Autistic children showed higher mean jitter (0.036 versus 0.024) and shimmer (1.23 versus 1.04) but lower standard deviations of both, which the authors interpret as these features varying 'consistently less in children with autism but hav[ing] higher values on average'. Harmonics-to-noise ratio was substantially lower on average (5.04 versus 7.88) and more variable (SD 1.03 versus 0.64). Loudness was higher on all three functionals. Spectral flux was higher overall (0.72 versus 0.42) and in voiced segments (0.86 versus 0.51). Mean pitch was higher but not significantly so, which the authors read as 'chasing away the idea that the speech of people with ASD is robotic, monotonous and without melodic variation'
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Four conventional classifiers on a statistically preselected acoustic feature subset
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Decision trees, K-nearest neighbours, random forests and support vector machines, implemented in scikit-learn. No kernel, depth, neighbour count or other hyperparameters are reported for any of the four. Ten models were run per method and the best selected for the headline table, with the means and standard deviations across the ten also reported
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: An 80/20 train-test split producing 22 training and 6 test samples, with three-fold stratified cross-validation applied within the training set. Feature selection by Mann-Whitney U-test was performed across the whole dataset before splitting. Ten runs per method were performed and both the best model and the ten-run means are reported
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, recall, precision, F1 and AUC, reported separately for the training and test sets for the best model of each method, plus means and standard deviations across ten runs per method
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Best models on the six-sample test set: decision tree 83% accuracy, 100% recall, 96% precision, 80% F1, 88% AUC; SVM 83%, 100%, 67%, 80%, 88%; random forest 83%, 50%, 100%, 67%, 75%; KNN 67%, 100%, 50%, 67%, 75%. Means across ten runs are substantially lower and more informative: SVM 79.8% accuracy (SD 6.75) with AUC 84.9 (SD 5.44); random forest 70.1% (SD 10.33); decision tree 68.2% (SD 16.40) with AUC 76.3 (SD 12.92); KNN 58.5% (SD 12.02). The authors identify SVM as the most consistent and note that decision trees 'likely overfit more than RF and SVM', with 'half of the ten best models... good in the classification task' while the others 'decrease their performances drastically from the train to the test sets'
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Sixteen of 88 eGeMAPS acoustic parameters differed significantly between 14 Italian autistic and 14 typically developing children narrating a picture story, spanning voice quality (higher mean jitter and shimmer, lower harmonics-to-noise ratio), loudness (higher on all functionals), pitch dynamics (greater variability in falling slope) and spectral distribution (higher spectral flux, steeper unvoiced slopes). Classifiers trained on the selected subset reached 83% accuracy on a six-sample test set, with SVM the most consistent across repeated runs at a mean of 79.8%. The authors position the work as a feature-extraction validity study rather than a classification tool and are explicit that the feature-selection step makes the classification figures non-generalisable. The decisive interpretive problem is that the two groups were recorded on entirely different equipment in entirely different settings - autistic children on a tripod-mounted video camera in a therapy room, comparison children on their parents' phones at home - and every one of the reported acoustic families is directly sensitive to microphone type, distance and room acoustics. The authors discard the loudness results for precisely this reason but retain jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio and the spectral measures, which are no less affected.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Higher mean jitter and shimmer with lower variability, markedly lower harmonics-to-noise ratio, higher loudness, greater pitch falling-slope variability, higher spectral flux and steeper unvoiced spectral slopes
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Collect larger datasets and compare different feature subsets to establish 'a standard set of typical acoustic features for children with ASD'; rethink the recording process so that pitch and intensity can be analysed reliably, with the specific recommendation that 'it would be necessary that all the participants wear [a microphone] simultaneously from their mouths to ensure that all the variations are due to the actual speech production'; investigate the correlation of voice features with speaker age, sex and height; adopt common feature sets across studies so that results can be compared across languages, citing De La Fuente et al.; and determine whether the jitter and shimmer pattern observed here in children and reported elsewhere in adults persists across the lifespan
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A workshop paper whose scholarship substantially exceeds its data. The feature-family discussion is the most thorough in the corpus, treating each of the four groups separately, situating every finding against named prior studies including those that contradict it, and repeatedly declining to overclaim - the loudness literature is described as containing higher values, lower values and null results in roughly equal measure, the pitch literature as 'opposite findings', and the spectral findings as lacking comparators. The choice of eGeMAPS is argued from first principles about feature-space size relative to sample size, and the code is publicly released on GitHub, which almost nothing else in this corpus does. The authors also state their scope correctly, positioning the study as a test of feature-extraction validity rather than a classifier, and concede in advance that feature selection on the full dataset 'can lead to high performances of the classifier, which are not reproducible on new data', citing Luz and colleagues on exactly this effect in dementia speech. That is unusually honest. The problem is that these virtues are applied to data that cannot support acoustic conclusions. The autistic recordings were made in June 2019 by a speech therapist using a video camera on a tripod in a therapy playroom; the comparison recordings were made later by parents on their own phones at home, because COVID-19 prevented in-person collection. Every acoustic family reported - jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio, loudness, spectral flux, spectral slope - is directly determined by microphone type, mouth-to-microphone distance, room reverberation and the recording chain. The harmonics-to-noise result is the clearest case: it is by construction a signal-to-noise measure, it differs by nearly three units in the direction predicted by a distant tripod-mounted camera in a therapy room versus a close-held phone, and the paper itself notes that the original comparison recordings from the source project were unusable because 'the background noise was so high that it was impossible to identify the child's voice automatically'. The authors demonstrate that they understand the mechanism, because they invoke it to discard their own loudness findings - 'this difference in the results could be caused by the most reported problems: the recording environment and the microphone's position... For these reasons, we decided not to consider the results obtained as relevant' - and then recommend head-mounted microphones for future work. They do not apply the same reasoning to the voice-quality or spectral results, and their stated defence, that the impact 'will not have that significant impact because the storytelling task remained the same, and the quality of the recordings was high', addresses task comparability and absence of noise rather than the systematic acoustic differences between two recording chains. The classification component adds little independently: feature selection was performed on all 28 samples before splitting, the test set contains six children, and the headline 83% figures are the best of ten runs against ten-run means of 58.5% to 79.8%. Diagnosis rests on a neuropsychiatrist's DSM-5 judgement with no instrument, no severity data and no comparison-group screening, and no ethics approval is reported for either group.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 14, drawn from a homogeneous Tuscan area between Florence, Pistoia and Prato, and matched by construction on group size, age range and sex ratio. The autistic children came from the speech and language therapy service of AUSL Toscana Centro and the Opera Santa Rita foundation, and their recordings were reused from a prior thesis project on discourse and storytelling in autism. The comparison children were recruited separately for this study 'from the same geographical area' with 'the same demographic characteristics'. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The critical structural fact is that the two groups were not merely recruited separately but recorded separately, at different times, by different people, using different equipment, in different environments - a distinction that matters far more for acoustic analysis than for the behavioural comparisons elsewhere in this corpus, and one that the paper discloses fully while underweighting its consequences.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'people with autism', 'autistic people', 'the ASD group', with person-first and identity-first used interchangeably. The register is inconsistent in one respect that stands out: autism is repeatedly referred to as 'the disease' and 'the disorder' - 'to be able to use it during the diagnosis', 'distinguish the speech productions of the disease', 'a turning point in the early diagnosis of the disease' - and participants are twice called 'patients'. Against this, the paper is unusually attentive to correcting a stereotype, arguing from its own pitch data that 'the increasing pitch could suggest chasing away the idea that the speech of people with ASD is robotic, monotonous and without melodic variation, as reported in the past literature', and returning to the point again in the loudness discussion. The historical framing is careful too, quoting Kanner's original observation and noting that 'the researchers ignored this part of Kanner's study in the decades that followed'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Matched by design and reported only at that level. Both groups comprise 14 children aged 6 to 10 with 11 males and 3 females. No means, standard deviations or statistical tests are given for age, so the groups are known to share a range rather than shown to be equivalent - and across ages 6 to 10 children's vocal tracts, fundamental frequencies and narrative abilities change substantially, so a within-range imbalance would matter. The sex ratio was chosen deliberately to reflect the DSM-5 epidemiological figure of four males per female, which is a defensible design choice for representativeness though it means only three girls contribute to each group. No IQ, language, adaptive or severity measure was obtained for either group, so cognitive and linguistic level are entirely uncontrolled in a study whose outcome is narrative speech production. The authors identify a related gap themselves, noting that formant and fundamental frequency features are 'sensitive to the speaker's age, gender, and height' and recommending that future work investigate 'the correlation of voice features to the personal characteristics of the speakers'.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: One sentence: 'The diagnosis was made by a neuropsychiatrist according to DSM-5 criteria.' No standardised observational instrument such as ADOS, no interview such as ADI-R, no rating scale, no statement of when the diagnosis was made, whether it was made for this study or taken from clinical records, or what the diagnostic procedure comprised. Recruitment through a speech and language therapy service and a disability foundation indicates that all participants were receiving services, but nothing further is established. The comparison group's status is asserted rather than screened - no instrument, no exclusion criteria, and no statement about family history or developmental concerns. This is among the weakest ascertainments in the corpus and is not acknowledged as a limitation.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None whatsoever - no cognitive, language, adaptive, severity or comorbidity measure for either group. The absence is particularly consequential here because the outcome is narrative speech elicited from a picture sequence: expressive language level determines how much a child says, how fluently, and with what syntactic complexity, all of which shape the acoustic signal, and it would be expected to differ between a group recruited from speech and language therapy services and a community comparison group. Nothing in the data permits this to be examined, and the paper does not raise it.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: establish whether acoustic markers of autism reported for English and other languages also appear in Italian, using a standard clinical parameter set, with classification as a check on whether the selected features carry signal. Main findings: 16 of 88 eGeMAPS parameters differed significantly, spanning voice quality (jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio), loudness, pitch dynamics and spectral distribution; best classifiers reached 83% accuracy on a six-sample test set with SVM most consistent across ten runs at a mean of 79.8%; jitter and shimmer were higher on average but less variable in the autistic group, matching a pattern reported in Italian-language-independent adult work; and mean pitch was higher though not significantly, which the authors use to argue against the monotone-speech stereotype.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Two entirely different settings, and this is the study's defining problem. Autistic children were recorded in June 2019 by a designated speech therapist, in the room where they usually play, during a session that 'started with activities generally done during the treatment session so the child would act in the most spontaneous way', with 'a video camera placed on a tree-legged support'. Comparison children were recorded later by their own parents at home on the parents' phones, because 'due to the COVID-19 pandemic, it was impossible to collect the data in situ'. The clinical setting was designed carefully for the autistic children's comfort, which is good practice for eliciting natural speech and simultaneously guarantees a fixed, distant, uncontrolled microphone position in a room with unknown reverberation. A parent holding a phone produces a close-miked, low-noise, high-signal recording. Since the paper's entire yield is acoustic, the recording chain is not a nuisance variable but a direct competitor for every reported effect.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Semi-spontaneous narrative from a six-picture sequence depicting a birthday party, from a commercially available storytelling toy, chosen as 'easily interpretable by neurotypical children of different ages'. This is a reasonable elicitation - picture-sequence narration is the standard paradigm in the narrative literature, it produces connected spontaneous speech rather than repetition or reading, and holding the task constant across groups is what the authors correctly identify as the one thing they did preserve when the recording arrangements diverged. Two limitations follow from the design's reuse. The autistic recordings were collected for a different study, on discourse and storytelling, so the elicitation was optimised for qualitative narrative analysis rather than acoustic measurement - which is precisely why the original comparison recordings from that project were unusable. And recording durations, utterance counts and speech quantity are not reported for either group, so it is not known whether the two groups produced comparable amounts of speech, which bears on the stability of every averaged acoustic functional.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, one recording per child, with the two groups recorded at different times separated by the onset of the pandemic. Ethical reporting is incomplete: written consent from caregivers is stated for the autistic group, but no consent statement appears for the comparison group and no ethics committee approval is reported for either. Data are not shared. The analysis code, however, is publicly released on GitHub, which is rare in this corpus and materially improves verifiability of the computational steps even though the recordings themselves are unavailable.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: The acquisition equipment is the study's decisive variable and is reported with enough candour to be evaluated. Autistic group: a video camera on a three-legged support, at an unspecified distance, in a therapy playroom. Comparison group: parents' own phones, model unspecified, at home. No sampling rates, microphone specifications, distances or room characteristics are given for either. The analysis chain is by contrast well specified - openSMILE 2.1 with eGeMAPS, chosen over ComParE because 6,376 features 'vastly outnumbers the sample size', and over GeMAPS for its psychological grounding - with Python, scikit-learn and Jupyter, and public code. The authors' own recommendation for future work is the correct diagnosis of what went wrong: 'it would be necessary that all the participants wear [a microphone] simultaneously from their mouths to ensure that all the variations are due to the actual speech production'.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Uneven. Fully reported: the elicitation stimulus with its source; both recording arrangements including their divergence and its cause; the feature set with its version, the rationale for choosing it over two alternatives, and a complete table of all extracted feature families with definitions; the selection test; all 16 selected features with group means, standard deviations, outlier counts and exact p-values; the four classifiers; the split proportions and resulting sample sizes; the cross-validation scheme; the number of runs; both best-model and ten-run mean performance; and public code. Not reported: participant age means or tests; any cognitive, language or severity measure; the diagnostic procedure beyond one clause; recording durations, distances, sampling rates or device models; any classifier hyperparameters; comparison-group consent or ethics approval for either group; and any characterisation of speech quantity per child.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Partially, and in a revealing pattern. The recording divergence is disclosed in full and then defended: 'Even though we are aware that this might eschew our results, we consider that it will not have that significant impact because the storytelling task remained the same, and the quality of the recordings was high (i.e., there was no background noise).' The defence addresses task comparability and the absence of noise in the new recordings, neither of which is the issue - the issue is a systematic difference between two recording chains, which shifts every spectral and voice-quality measure regardless of how clean each chain is individually. The authors nonetheless demonstrate that they grasp the mechanism, because they apply it correctly to their own loudness findings: 'This difference in the results could be caused by the most reported problems: the recording environment and the microphone's position... For these reasons, we decided not to consider the results obtained as relevant for the present.' Having discarded loudness on exactly this reasoning, they retain jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio and the spectral measures, which depend on the same variables. The feature-selection bias is likewise acknowledged in advance with a citation to comparable work in dementia speech, and the scope is explicitly narrowed to feature-extraction validity rather than classification. Not acknowledged: the six-sample test set; that the headline figures are best-of-ten against much lower means; the absence of any diagnostic instrument, severity measure or comparison-group screening; the absence of cognitive and language measures; and the missing ethics approval.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Five directions, of which two are unusually well targeted. Redesign the recording process so that intensity and pitch can be analysed at all, with the concrete specification that all participants should wear a microphone at a fixed mouth distance - the authors note this must be balanced against 'the necessity of maintaining some environmental comforts for the patients in a clinical condition', which correctly identifies the tension between naturalistic elicitation and acoustic control. Adopt common feature sets across studies so results are comparable across languages, citing De La Fuente and colleagues - a standardisation argument that this review's cross-linguistic study (Lau and colleagues) makes in a different form. The remaining three are larger datasets with feature-subset comparison to build a standard acoustic set for autism; investigation of how voice features relate to speaker age, sex and height; and testing whether the jitter and shimmer pattern seen here in children and reported by Kissine and Geelhand in adults persists across the lifespan, which the authors suggest would be 'a turning point in the early diagnosis'.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Paralinguistic voice production during narrative, decomposed into four theoretically motivated families rather than treated as an undifferentiated feature vector. Frequency-related parameters index intonation and vocal-tract configuration; voice quality parameters (jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio) index the regularity of vocal fold vibration and are framed as measuring 'the difficulty in controlling the vocal fold vibrations, transforming the production into hoarseness, breathiness, and creaky voice'; loudness indexes intensity and, via its variability, 'the dynamic intonation of autistic speech production'; and spectral parameters index energy distribution. The theoretical grounding distinguishes pragmatic or linguistic prosody, carrying illocutionary force and sentence type, from affective prosody, carrying emotional state - the same distinction Lau and colleagues make - and locates the autism-relevant impairment in the affective channel, with consequences for both production and comprehension. The construct is coherent and the discussion of each family is genuinely scholarly; what it cannot survive is that all four families are equally functions of the recording apparatus.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality with no fusion. The paper's comparative work is instead across classifiers, and the reporting of it is better than the headline suggests. Four methods are run ten times each and both the best model and the ten-run mean with standard deviation are given, which makes the instability visible: the decision tree's best model reaches 83% accuracy and 100% recall on the test set but its ten-run mean is 68.2% with a standard deviation of 16.40, and the authors read this correctly as overfitting - 'half of the ten best models of all the ones trained for DT are good in the classification task, but the others tend to decrease their performances drastically from the train to the test sets'. SVM is identified as most consistent (mean 79.8%, SD 6.75) and preferred on that basis rather than on peak performance, with the reasoning that linear SVM 'is the best to use when dealing with small datasets'. Choosing a model for stability over peak accuracy, and reporting the distribution that justifies it, is the right instinct and is rare in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Four conventional classifiers - decision tree, K-nearest neighbours, random forest and SVM - run ten times each on 16 preselected features. The classification is explicitly instrumental rather than the contribution: 'the final aim of these implementations is to test whether these acoustic features are typical in the speech production of Italian-speaking children with ASD. Good results in the performances of the classifiers would confirm this assumption.' That framing is coherent but it does not escape the underlying problem, since features selected for significance on the same 28 samples will by construction classify those samples well regardless of what produced the difference. No hyperparameters are reported for any method, so the comparison across classifiers cannot be assessed for equal tuning effort, and no baseline of any kind is provided - not a chance level, not a demographic comparator, not the unselected 88-feature set, which would have been the most informative control given the authors' own citation of Luz and colleagues showing that performance 'drop[s] consistently if applied to the same dataset without performing the feature selection'.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: One feature vector per child, so the unit is the participant and there is no within-subject leakage. The representational contribution is the argued choice of eGeMAPS: ComParE was rejected on an explicit dimensionality argument relative to sample size, and eGeMAPS chosen over GeMAPS on grounds of psychological interpretability, with the whole parameter set tabulated and defined. Using a published standard parameter set rather than a bespoke feature collection is also what makes the study's cross-language comparison possible - the authors compare their selected features directly against those reported by Pokorny and colleagues using the same set and find agreement on unvoiced spectral slope in the 0-500 Hz range - and it is the basis of their recommendation that the field standardise on common feature sets. That is a genuine methodological contribution independent of this study's data.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, recall, precision, F1 and AUC, reported on both training and test sets for the best model of each method, plus means and standard deviations across ten runs. Reporting training alongside test performance is what allows overfitting to be diagnosed and the authors use it that way. Reporting the ten-run distribution rather than only the maximum is better practice still, and it substantially deflates the headline: SVM's mean accuracy is 79.8% against a best of 83%, the decision tree's mean is 68.2% against a best of 83%, and KNN's mean is 58.5%. What no metric can repair is the denominator. The test set contains six children, so 83% accuracy is five of six and 100% recall is three of three; a single reclassified child moves accuracy by 17 percentage points, and no confidence interval accompanies any figure. With 22 training and 6 test samples, and a further split into three cross-validation folds within the training set, the effective sample at every stage is too small for the metrics to discriminate between methods.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: The strongest part of the paper, and the reason it is worth charting despite its data problems. Every one of the 16 selected features is reported with group means, standard deviations, outlier counts and exact p-values, and then discussed individually against named prior work - with contradictory findings reported rather than suppressed. The pitch literature is described as containing 'opposite findings'; a proposed link between pitch excursions and 'motherese' speech is cited and then noted to have been 'disprove[n]' by later work; the loudness literature is enumerated as containing higher values, lower values, null results, and studies that avoided intensity entirely 'to avoid the risk of obtaining unclear results'; and the spectral findings are flagged as lacking comparators, with the authors stating plainly that 'we did not find any other relevant studies to confirm the importance of spectral features to detect ASD'. The jitter-shimmer-HNR discussion is the most substantive, correctly identifying the expected inverse relationship between jitter and harmonics-to-noise ratio, verifying it in their own data, and connecting it to the voice-pathology literature on breathiness and hoarseness. The interpretive irony is that this same literature supplies the reason to doubt the finding: harmonics-to-noise ratio is a signal-to-noise measure, and the two groups' signals were acquired through different chains.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The weakest dimension, and the authors say so more clearly than most. Feature selection by Mann-Whitney test was performed across all 28 samples before any split, so the 16 retained features are those that best separate the very children on whom the classifiers are then evaluated. The consequence is stated in advance and with a supporting citation: 'the feature selection operated on clinical recorded data can lead to high performances of the classifier, which are not reproducible on new data considering all the speech production. This aspect produces a bias in the results obtained by the classifier when used to create a tool able to distinguish the speech productions of the disease. For instance, while performing the same task on people with Alzheimer Dementia's speech, Luz et al. (2020) report that the performance evaluation metrics drop consistently if applied to the same dataset without performing the feature selection.' The scope is then narrowed accordingly - 'this work aims to test the feature extraction effectiveness and not automatically classify ASD from new speech data' - which is the right response to a known bias, though it does not remove it from the reported numbers. Three further limits compound it: an 80/20 split leaves six test samples; ten runs per method were performed with the best reported alongside the means; and there is no independent validation, no permutation test, no confidence interval and no baseline. The single most important validity threat, however, is not statistical at all: features selected for their ability to separate two groups recorded on different equipment will select for the equipment difference, and no amount of validation discipline within the dataset can detect that.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorders, acoustic analysis, machine learning, openSMILE, eGeMAPS. Naming both the toolkit and the parameter set is deliberate and consistent with the paper's argument that the field should standardise on shared feature sets so that findings become comparable across studies and languages.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Proceedings of the RaPID-4 workshop at LREC 2022 (Resources and Processing of linguistic, para-linguistic and extra-linguistic Data from people with various forms of cognitive or psychiatric impairment), published by ELRA under CC-BY-NC. Authorship spans the Department of Classical Philology and Italian Studies at the University of Bologna and the Department of Swedish, Multilingualism, Language and Technology at the University of Gothenburg, with the first author a student. This is a computational linguistics workshop rather than a clinical or engineering venue, which explains the paper's profile precisely: the linguistic and acoustic scholarship is of a high standard, the engagement with the prosody literature is extensive and critical, and the clinical characterisation, ethics reporting and validation design are correspondingly thin. The clinical data were collected by a third party for a prior thesis, acknowledged by name.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022. The framing is linguistic rather than translational: the motivating gap is that 'there are already many English contributions showing abnormalities of autistic speech at the prosodic level' but 'few studies on this promising field in Italian', so the question is whether findings established in one language transfer to another - the same question Lau and colleagues address between English and Cantonese, approached here for a language typologically closer to English but still untested. The historical framing is distinctive and well handled, quoting Crystal's characterisation of prosody research as 'the Cinderella of speech' that remains 'in the cellar, with few visitors', and tracing the neglect back to Kanner's original 1943 description, which described a child for whom 'it made no difference whether one spoke to him in a friendly or a harsh way' - an observation the authors note 'the researchers ignored... in the decades that followed'. The clinical ambition is stated modestly and consistently: the aim is a tool that 'may evolve, through further studies' and could 'support clinicians in diagnosing the disorder', with the classification component explicitly disclaimed as not intended for use on new speech data. That restraint distinguishes the paper from most in this corpus and makes its data problems more regrettable rather than less, since the scholarship would have supported a stronger study.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Eye Tracking-Based Diagnosis and Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Ahmed IA; Senan EM; Rassem TH; Ali MAH; Shatnawi HSA; Alwazer SM; Alshahrani M
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Children from the Carette et al. gaze-path image dataset
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking, re-encoded as scanpath images and treated as a texture classification problem
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Compare three families of artificial-intelligence technique - neural networks on hand-engineered texture descriptors, transfer-learned convolutional networks, and hybrid CNN-feature-plus-SVM pipelines - on a public autism gaze-path image dataset, with the applied aim that such systems 'could help experts and autism treatment centres in the early detection of autism in children'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Secondary analysis of a public image dataset, structured as a three-way comparison of modelling pipelines with a single fixed image-wise train/validation/test split
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Not reported; recording durations are properties of the source dataset and are not restated
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Not described. The paper reproduces no information about what the children viewed, for how long, or under what instruction - the eye-tracking paradigm belongs entirely to the source collection and is not restated at any point
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Not reported for the data collection; the analysis was performed at Najran University in Saudi Arabia with collaborators in India, the UK and Malaysia
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Analysis in Saudi Arabia; the participants' country is a property of the source dataset and is not stated
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Not reported. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician role or setting is named, and the source dataset's ascertainment procedure is not summarised. The labels are treated as attributes of the released image files
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 29 children (25 male, 4 female) contributing 219 images
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 30 children (13 male, 17 female) contributing 328 images
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not reported - no age information is given for either group
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: No. The autistic group is 86.2% male against 43.3% male in the comparison group, a 43-percentage-point difference that the paper restates from the source dataset without any comment, analysis or acknowledgement
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Pre-rendered scanpath images in which gaze position and its derivatives are visualised
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: The pipeline is entirely image processing. Enhancement: a 5x5 average filter smooths each image by replacing each central pixel with the mean of its 24 neighbours, a Laplacian filter detects edges, and the Laplacian result is subtracted from the averaged image. Segmentation: an active contour (snake) model isolates the eye-tracking path region as a region of interest, with the level-set formulation, energy function, stopping criterion and contour direction rules all given in equations. Morphological cleaning removes holes left by segmentation using union ('fits') and intersection ('hits') tests. Feature extraction: local binary pattern with a 4x4 configuration produces 203 features per image and grey-level co-occurrence matrix produces the remainder, concatenated into a 216-dimensional vector. In parallel, GoogleNet and ResNet-18 pretrained on ImageNet are fine-tuned for deep feature extraction, and their feature maps are alternatively passed to an SVM
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: No acquisition equipment described. Analysis used MATLAB-style average and Laplacian filtering, an active contour segmentation model, LBP and GLCM feature extractors, GoogleNet and ResNet-18 pretrained on ImageNet, feedforward and artificial neural networks with 216 input neurons and 10 hidden layers, and SVM; executed on a fifth-generation i5 processor with 8 GB RAM and a 4 GB GPU
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: No - the Carette et al. dataset of 547 gaze-path images from 59 children (29 autistic, 30 typically developing) is reused unchanged
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes - a figshare URL for the source dataset is given in the data availability statement
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not discussed. No ethics statement, consent statement or IRB approval appears, nor any pointer to the source dataset's approvals
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Hand-engineered image texture descriptors and learned convolutional feature maps
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Two hand-engineered families concatenated into a 216-dimensional vector: local binary patterns, computed at a 4x4 neighbourhood with each central pixel replaced by a code derived from its 15 neighbours, yielding 203 features; and grey-level co-occurrence matrix statistics supplying the remaining 13. Both are generic image texture descriptors developed for problems such as face recognition and material classification, and neither corresponds to any gaze, fixation, saccade or attention quantity. The alternative representations are deep feature maps from GoogleNet and ResNet-18, likewise generic
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Local binary pattern and grey-level co-occurrence matrix implementations; GoogleNet and ResNet-18 as feature extractors
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No. No feature importance, attribution or interpretation of any kind, and none is meaningful given that the features are texture codes over a rendered plot
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None. No group difference, effect size, gaze statistic or behavioural characteristic is reported anywhere - the paper contributes no finding about how autistic children's viewing differed
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Three parallel pipelines: shallow neural networks on texture features, fine-tuned CNNs, and CNN-feature-plus-SVM hybrids
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Feedforward and artificial neural networks with 216 input neurons, 10 hidden layers and 2 output neurons; GoogleNet fine-tuned with Adam, mini-batch 20, 4 epochs, learning rate 0.0003, validation frequency 3; ResNet-18 fine-tuned with Adam, mini-batch 15, 8 epochs, learning rate 0.0001, validation frequency 5; and SVM applied to the deep feature maps of each network
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A single fixed split of the 547 images: 80% for training and validation (subdivided 80:20, giving 350 training and 88 validation images) and 20% for testing (109 images). The split is by image, not by child - 59 children contributed 547 images, roughly 9.3 each, and no participant grouping is described or possible from the released data. Data augmentation by flipping, multi-angle rotation, displacement and shearing expanded the training and validation set sevenfold for the autistic class and tenfold for the comparison class (175 to 1,750 and 262 to 1,834) to balance the classes; the test set was left unaugmented at 44 and 66 images. The headline 99.8% is described as 'the overall accuracy', pooling training, validation and testing phases, against a test-phase accuracy of 98.7% for the same model
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for each of six configurations, with confusion matrices and separate training, validation and test performance for the neural network pipeline
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Neural networks on LBP-plus-GLCM features: FFNN and ANN both 99.8% overall accuracy, with the ANN reaching 100% on all measures in training and validation and 98.7% accuracy, 100% precision, 100% sensitivity, 98.2% specificity and 99.77% AUC in testing; FFNN precision 99.8%, sensitivity 99.5%, specificity 100%, AUC 99.85%. Deep models: ResNet-18 97.6% accuracy (precision 97.5%, sensitivity 97%, specificity 97%, AUC 97.56%) and GoogleNet 93.6% (precision 93%, sensitivity 94.5%, specificity 94.5%, AUC 99.48%). Hybrids: GoogleNet plus SVM 95.5% and ResNet-18 plus SVM 94.5%. Per-class accuracies are given for the deep models - GoogleNet 97.7% on the autistic class and 90.9% on the comparison class, ResNet-18 95.5% and 99%
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Six modelling pipelines were compared on 547 public gaze-path images, with shallow neural networks on concatenated local binary pattern and grey-level co-occurrence matrix texture features reaching 99.8%, transfer-learned ResNet-18 reaching 97.6%, GoogleNet 93.6%, and CNN-plus-SVM hybrids 95.5% and 94.5%. The result that hand-engineered texture descriptors outperform fine-tuned deep networks by two to six points is presented as the study's principal finding. Two features of the design determine how these numbers should be read.
