The split is by image rather than by child, so with roughly nine images per participant, images from the same children appear in training and test - the correction that the dataset's own originators applied, finding image-level accuracy near 90% falling to approximately 71% per child. And the headline 99.8% is described as an overall figure pooling training, validation and testing, against 98.7% for the same model on the test phase alone. The features themselves are generic image texture codes computed over a rendered scanpath plot after averaging, Laplacian filtering, active contour segmentation and morphological cleaning, so no gaze, fixation or attention quantity survives into the model and the paper reports no behavioural finding of any kind.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None reported
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Concatenate CNN-derived feature maps with the LBP and GLCM features into a single vector and classify with all three of ANN, FFNN and SVM - a purely architectural extension with no proposal to address participant grouping, demographic characterisation, diagnostic provenance or external validation
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A methods-comparison paper on a public dataset whose reported figures cannot be interpreted as diagnostic performance, and which is most useful to this review as a companion case to Gaspar and colleagues on the identical images. Three problems compound. First, the split is by image with no participant grouping: 59 children produced 547 images, roughly 9.3 each, and the 80/20 image-wise partition therefore places images from the same child on both sides. Cilia and colleagues, who created this dataset, quantified exactly this effect - image-level accuracy near 90% falling to approximately 71% when computed per child - and neither that correction nor the underlying issue is mentioned here. Second, the headline 99.8% is described as 'the overall accuracy' and is reconciled in the text with a training and validation accuracy of 100% and a test accuracy of 98.7% for the same model, so the abstract figure includes performance on data the model was fitted to. The correct number to compare against other studies is 98.7%, and that in turn is an image-level figure on 109 images from children the model has already partly seen. Third, and most consequential for interpretation, the features carry no behavioural content: after average filtering, Laplacian edge enhancement, active contour segmentation and morphological cleaning, the model receives local binary pattern and grey-level co-occurrence texture codes over a rendered plot. These are generic descriptors designed for texture and face recognition, and they retain nothing about fixations, saccades, dwell times or areas of interest - which is why the paper reports no group difference, no effect size and no gaze statistic anywhere in 27 pages. The finding that texture descriptors beat fine-tuned ResNet-18 and GoogleNet is consistent with the discriminative information being low-level plot morphology rather than viewing behaviour. Two things are done correctly and should be noted against the Gaspar comparison: augmentation is confined to the training and validation partitions with the test set left unaugmented, which is the right handling and which Gaspar violated by augmenting testing data as well; and the source dataset's sex composition is at least restated - 25 male and 4 female in the autistic group against 13 male and 17 female in the comparison group. That restatement reveals a 43-percentage-point sex imbalance running in opposite directions, which for a study classifying visual scanning patterns is a substantial uncontrolled confound, and it passes without a single sentence of comment. No age, diagnostic instrument, severity measure or ethics statement appears, no code is released, and no limitations section exists.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups inherited from the Carette et al. dataset: 29 autistic children contributing 219 images and 30 typically developing children contributing 328 images, 547 images from 59 children in total. This paper is more informative than Gaspar and colleagues on the same data, which reported only image counts, since it restates the participant counts and sex composition from the source publication. But the participant structure is then entirely disregarded in the analysis: the 80/20 partition operates on images, so children are not the unit at any stage and images from the same child necessarily span the training and test sets at roughly nine images per participant. No other-diagnosis or developmental-delay comparison group. The class imbalance of 219 to 328 is addressed by differential augmentation of the training and validation partitions - sevenfold for the autistic class, tenfold for the comparison class - rather than by any participant-level consideration.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'children with autism', 'people with autism', against 'TD' and 'typically developing children'. Person-first in the main, though 'patients with autism spectrum disorder' appears and autism is once described as 'autism disease' and elsewhere as something requiring 'effective treatments to improve responses in children with autism'. The framing is medical and treatment-oriented in a way that misdescribes the condition, referring to 'the heterogeneous response to treatment and the search for effective treatments' and to children 'who are less responsive to the currently available treatment methods'. The introduction also contains a confused clinical passage - 'Many symptoms of ASD appear, such as genetic, cognitive, neurological and cognitive factors' - listing aetiological factors as symptoms and repeating 'cognitive' twice, which is symptomatic of the paper's general disengagement from the clinical subject matter.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Sex composition is restated from the source publication and is the only demographic information given: the autistic group comprises 25 males and 4 females (86.2% male) and the comparison group 13 males and 17 females (43.3% male). That 43-percentage-point difference, running in opposite directions between groups, is reported in a single sentence and never mentioned again - not analysed, not covaried, not listed as a limitation, and not discussed anywhere in a 27-page paper. It matters because the classifier operates on rendered scanpath images, and any systematic difference in viewing behaviour, screen coverage or trace density associated with sex would be absorbed directly into the texture features. No ages, no age range, no IQ, no language level, no severity and no matching of any kind. Given that the same dataset elsewhere in this corpus is analysed by Gaspar and colleagues with no participant information at all, the restatement here is an improvement in reporting that is not accompanied by any improvement in analysis.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Nothing. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician role, setting or timing is reported, and the source dataset's ascertainment procedure is not summarised even in a sentence. The class labels are treated as file attributes throughout. Under this review's classification this is dataset-label-only ascertainment in its least documented form. The omission is compounded by the paper's framing, which repeatedly describes the systems as tools for 'diagnosis' and 'early diagnosis' and proposes that they 'could help experts and autism treatment centres in the early detection of autism in children' - claims about diagnostic utility made against a reference standard whose nature is entirely unknown to the reader.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, language, adaptive, severity, comorbidity or medication information for either group, and no exclusions described. Nothing therefore relates model output to any clinical dimension, and the possibility that the classifier separates developmental level rather than diagnosis cannot be examined.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: compare three artificial-intelligence approaches - shallow neural networks on hand-engineered texture features, transfer-learned CNNs, and CNN-plus-SVM hybrids - for classifying autism from gaze-path images. Main findings: FFNN and ANN on concatenated LBP and GLCM features reached 99.8% overall accuracy (98.7% at test phase); ResNet-18 reached 97.6% and GoogleNet 93.6%; the hybrids reached 95.5% and 94.5%; and the hand-engineered pipeline was concluded to be 'the best performance amongst the proposed systems'. No behavioural finding, group difference or gaze characteristic is reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Not reported. The paper describes neither the room, the country, the recruitment route, the eye tracker nor the acquisition protocol for the source recordings. The only settings named are the four institutions where the analysis was carried out and the hardware on which it ran - a fifth-generation i5 processor with 8 GB RAM and a 4 GB GPU, specified more precisely than anything about the children.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Entirely absent. Unlike Gaspar and colleagues on the same dataset, who at least state that participants 'were shown different videos containing stimulating scenarios for the movement of the eye in the entire screen', this paper reproduces nothing at all about what was viewed, for how long, or under what conditions. The reader is given no basis on which to judge what behaviour the scanpaths represent. Since the analysis proceeds by treating the resulting plot as a texture image, the absence is internally consistent with the method - the pipeline does not require knowing what generated the trace - but it means the study cannot connect its result to any behavioural construct, and the paper accordingly makes no attempt to.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis of a public dataset; no follow-up. No ethics statement, consent statement or IRB approval appears anywhere, and no pointer is given to where the source dataset's approvals were obtained. A data availability statement supplies the figshare URL for the source images with an access date, funding is acknowledged from the Najran University Scientific Research Deanship under a named grant, and a conflict-of-interest declaration is present - so the absence of an ethics statement is not a matter of missing front matter but of the section not being written.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition equipment is described at any point. The analysis chain is specified in unusual mathematical detail: the average filter with its 5x5 window and neighbour-averaging equation, the Laplacian operator, the subtraction combining them, the active contour formulation including the level-set function, the energy terms, the Heaviside and Dirac delta smoothing functions, the sign convention determining whether the contour shrinks or expands, and the stopping criterion comparing successive masks. Morphological operations are named, LBP is given with its neighbourhood size and feature count, and the CNN training options are tabulated with optimiser, mini-batch size, epochs, learning rate, validation frequency and execution environment for both networks. The asymmetry is total: every arithmetic step is documented and nothing about the measurement is.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Reproducible as an image-processing pipeline, not as a study. Fully specified: all filtering, segmentation and morphological steps with equations; LBP neighbourhood and feature count; the 216-dimensional concatenated vector; the network architectures with layer counts; both CNNs' complete training hyperparameters; the augmentation operations and the resulting counts before and after; the exact split into 350 training, 88 validation and 109 test images with per-class breakdowns; the evaluation formulae; and the compute hardware. Not reported: anything about the participants beyond counts and sex; the stimuli; the eye tracker; the diagnostic procedure; the final chosen contour parameters; whether the split was stratified or randomised and with what seed; and any code. The data availability statement points to the public source images.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: There is no limitations section, and no limitation is stated anywhere in the paper. Nothing is acknowledged about the image-wise split, the pooled headline accuracy, the absence of participant information, the sex imbalance restated in the methods, the lack of diagnostic provenance, the absence of any behavioural interpretation, or the single fixed split without repetition or confidence intervals. The conclusion instead asserts that all three systems 'achieved superior results' and 'promising results', and the future work proposes only to concatenate the feature families - an architectural extension that would address none of the above. This is the least self-critical paper in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: One direction: 'to extract features using CNN models and combine them with features extracted by LBP and GLCM algorithms into a single feature vector for each image and classify it using all three ANN, FFNN and SVM algorithms.' This proposes more feature concatenation on the same 547 images with the same split, and addresses none of the study's substantive weaknesses. No proposal is made to group by participant, obtain demographic or diagnostic metadata, validate externally, interpret the features behaviourally, or test on an independent dataset.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Nominally visual attention, but no behavioural construct survives the pipeline. The source dataset encodes gaze coordinates and their derivatives as a rendered plot; this study then applies average filtering, Laplacian edge enhancement, active contour segmentation of the trace region, morphological hole-filling, and finally local binary pattern and grey-level co-occurrence texture descriptors. What reaches the classifier is a 216-dimensional summary of the local texture statistics of a processed image of a line drawing. No fixation, saccade, dwell time, area of interest, coverage measure or any other quantity with a gaze interpretation is computed at any stage, and consequently the paper reports no group difference in viewing behaviour, no effect direction and no interpretation. The introduction's extensive discussion of social versus non-social orientation, social attention deficits and visual biomarkers has no connection to anything the method actually measures - a gap of several sections between the stated construct and the operationalisation.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality with no cross-modal fusion. Two within-pipeline combinations are performed. The first concatenates LBP and GLCM outputs into a single 216-dimensional vector, justified on the general ground that 'extracting the features from several methods and combining them are two of the most important recent methods that have an effect on accurate diagnosis' - an assertion rather than an argument, with no ablation showing what either family contributes alone. The second replaces each CNN's classification head with an SVM operating on its deep feature maps. That second comparison is the more informative because it is properly controlled: the same features are classified two ways, and the result is mixed - the SVM head improves GoogleNet from 93.6% to 95.5% but degrades ResNet-18 from 97.6% to 94.5%. The paper reports both directions without comment. Across all six configurations the pattern that hand-engineered texture beats learned representation is presented as the headline conclusion but never examined, though it is the observation most consistent with the discriminative signal residing in low-level plot morphology rather than in anything a pretrained visual network would find semantically salient.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Six configurations spanning three families, all reported, which is a reasonable comparative design in itself. The shallow networks use 216 input neurons and 10 hidden layers, an unusually deep configuration for a fully connected network on 216 features and 547 samples, with no justification, no hidden-layer widths and no regularisation described. The CNN training is more conventionally specified with full hyperparameters for both networks. The SVM is unspecified as to kernel or parameters. What is missing throughout is any baseline: no chance level, no permutation test, no simple comparator such as image mean intensity or trace pixel count, and no repetition across splits - so a 6.2-point spread between the best and worst configuration is reported without any means of judging whether it exceeds split-to-split variation on 109 test images.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: The representational chain is the study's core and its central problem. Four preprocessing stages precede feature extraction - average filtering, Laplacian enhancement, active contour segmentation, morphological cleaning - each documented with equations and each progressively removing information that might have carried gaze meaning. Segmentation isolates 'the eye-tracking path region', converting a trajectory into a binary or near-binary shape; morphological cleaning then modifies that shape further. LBP and GLCM are then computed over the result. Local binary patterns encode the relative intensity of a pixel against its neighbours and were developed for texture and face recognition; grey-level co-occurrence matrices summarise second-order intensity statistics. Neither has any relationship to where a child looked. The consequence is visible in the paper's own output: 27 pages containing six accuracy tables, multiple confusion matrices and ROC curves, and not one statement about what distinguishes autistic children's scanning from that of their peers.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for all six configurations, with confusion matrices and, for the neural network pipeline, separate training, validation and test figures. Reporting the three phases separately is genuinely useful and is what allows the headline to be diagnosed: the ANN achieved 100% on training and validation and 98.7% at test, and the abstract's 99.8% is described as 'the overall accuracy' - so it pools performance on data the model was fitted to with performance on held-out data. The correct held-out figure is 98.7%, on 109 images. Two internal inconsistencies also appear: GoogleNet is reported with 93.6% accuracy but 99.48% AUC while ResNet-18 has higher accuracy (97.6%) and lower AUC (97.56%), a pattern that would require explanation and receives none; and GoogleNet's per-class accuracies of 97.7% and 90.9% are difficult to reconcile with its stated 94.5% sensitivity and 94.5% specificity. No confidence intervals, no repeated splits, no significance tests and no baseline of any kind accompany any figure.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None, and none is possible. There is no feature importance, attribution, saliency or ablation, and the representation - texture codes over a segmented, morphologically cleaned rendering of a gaze trace - admits no behavioural interpretation even in principle. No group means, effect sizes, directions or descriptive statistics about viewing behaviour appear anywhere. The paper therefore contributes six accuracy figures and no knowledge about autism, gaze or visual attention, despite an introduction devoting several pages to social orientation, attention biomarkers and the clinical significance of atypical visual attention. That disconnection between the stated motivation and the delivered content is the study's defining characteristic.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Two distinct problems, one shared with several studies in this corpus and one specific to this paper. The shared problem is the unit of analysis: 547 images come from 59 children at roughly 9.3 images each, and the 80/20 partition is by image with no participant grouping described, so images from the same child appear in both training and test. Cilia and colleagues, who produced this dataset, measured the consequence directly, reporting image-level accuracy near 90% falling to approximately 71% when recomputed per child; that correction is neither cited nor applied here. The specific problem is that the headline figure pools phases: the abstract and conclusion report 99.8% while the results text states the same model achieved 100% in training and validation and 98.7% in testing, and describes 99.8% as 'the overall accuracy'. One element is handled correctly and deserves credit - augmentation by flipping, rotation, displacement and shearing was applied only to the training and validation partitions, expanding them from 175 and 262 to 1,750 and 1,834 images, while the test set remained unaugmented at 44 and 66. This is the correct discipline and is precisely what Gaspar and colleagues violated on the same dataset by augmenting the testing data as well. Against that, there is a single fixed split with no repetition, no cross-validation, no confidence intervals and no external validation, so the reported differences among six configurations rest on one partition of 109 test images.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, eye tracking, machine learning, neural networks, convolutional neural network, GLCM, local binary pattern. Five of seven are computational and two of those name specific texture descriptors, which accurately identifies the paper as a texture-classification study that happens to use autism-labelled images.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Electronics 11(4):530 (2022), an MDPI open-access engineering journal. Authorship spans the Applied College at Najran University in Saudi Arabia, Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar Marathwada University in India, Bournemouth University in the UK and the University of Malaya in Malaysia, with no clinical, psychological or autism-research affiliation among the seven authors. The review timeline is compressed - received 15 January 2022, accepted 6 February, published 10 February, twenty-six days from submission to publication - and the paper contains no limitations section, no ethics statement and several internal inconsistencies in its reported metrics. Funded by the Najran University Scientific Research Deanship.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022. The framing is the standard early-detection argument with the usual supporting claims: prevalence of one in 160 per WHO, diagnosis typically delayed to age 4 despite symptoms appearing earlier, and eye tracking recommended as 'fast, inexpensive, easy to analyse and applicable to all ages'. The related-work section is a list of prior studies with their reported accuracies and no critical assessment, and it includes an error that indicates limited engagement with the clinical literature - the ADOS is attributed to Lord et al. as 'a method... for assessing autism' consisting of 'unstructured observational tasks', when the instrument is explicitly semi-structured and standardised, and the CARS is described as being 'based on the doctor's assessment of children's behaviour through two scales, a social communication questionnaire and a social responsiveness scale', which conflates three distinct instruments. One passage is worth noting because it states a caveat the paper then ignores: 'evidence regarding positive eye-tracking outcomes as a strong predictor of long-term outcomes in children with ASD is lacking'. Having noted that the predictive validity of the modality is unestablished, the paper proceeds to report 99.8% accuracy and to propose the systems as aids for diagnosis and early detection without returning to the point.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Identification of Social Engagement Indicators Associated With
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Varma M; Washington P; Chrisman B; Kline A; Leblanc E; Paskov K; Stockham N; Jung JY; Sun MW; Wall DP
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Children with a parent-reported autism diagnosis, aged 2 to 15
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Gaze direction and visual scanning from smartphone video, without eye-tracking hardware
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Establish whether diagnostic gaze signals can be recovered from unstructured home video captured on an ordinary phone, removing three requirements that the authors identify as limiting prior work: manual frame-level annotation, eye-tracking hardware, and structured scenarios or clinical environments. The claim is stated as a first: 'to the best of our knowledge, this is the first study that attempts to obtain diagnostic insights into ASD from social gameplay videos without the use of eye-tracking hardware, manual frame-level annotations, and structured scenarios or environments'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional analysis of a crowdsourced home-video corpus, combining permutation-tested group comparisons with a child-disjoint supervised classification experiment
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: 90-second gameplay sessions, with each child contributing a mean of 4.7 videos (SD 7.3); 449 videos totalling 11.1 hours and 1,084,267 frames
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Charades within the GuessWhat mobile app. The parent places the smartphone on their own forehead with the front camera facing the child; the child acts out a prompt displayed on the device - emotions, sports, animals or chores - while the parent guesses, and the game ends at a 90-second limit. The parent may then review the recording and choose whether to share it. The authors argue the format supplies 'inherent structure, with factors such as the position of the phone camera, location of the child relative to the camera, and game-based social interactions between the parent and child remaining generally consistent between videos' while leaving the child 'unencumbered by bulky hardware such as eye trackers or head mounts'
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Participants' own homes, with recruitment via social media advertisements and research email lists; the research group is at Stanford University
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: United States (implied by recruitment; not stated explicitly)
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Parent report. Parents 'completed a survey to provide the age, sex, and diagnostic status of their children'. No instrument, clinician contact or record verification, and - unlike the companion speech study from the same group and app - the unverified nature of the labels is not acknowledged as a limitation anywhere in this paper
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 68 children (53 male, 15 female) contributing 380 videos
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not reported; the overall sample spans 2 to 15 years with the distribution shown only in a figure
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Within the overall 2-15 range; group-specific ranges not reported
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported; no exclusion criteria of any kind are described
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: None. No severity, cognitive, language or adaptive measure for either group
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Parent report only; no screening instrument
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 27 children (18 male, 9 female) contributing 69 videos
data_charting_rubrics.age_range_controls: Within the overall 2-15 range; not reported separately
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution_controls: 18 male (66.7%), 9 female, with one neurotypical male not providing his age
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not reported and not addressed. The sample spans 2 to 15 years - a thirteen-year range across which gaze behaviour, attention and gameplay engagement change profoundly - and no group means, medians or tests are given in the text, with the distribution relegated to a figure
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not tested. The autistic group is 77.9% male against 66.7% in the comparison group, an 11-point difference that is smaller than in most studies here but is not reported as a comparison or discussed
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Parent report only
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Smartphone front-camera video, reduced to per-frame gaze direction estimates
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A fully automated annotation pipeline, adopted explicitly to avoid exposing video to human annotators. Amazon Rekognition produced noisy labels for 30 facial landmarks and facial bounding boxes per frame, with frames containing zero or more than two faces discarded because 'other adults or siblings would often join in gameplay'. OpenFace then estimated gaze direction per frame as a coordinate pair with x from -1 (leftward) to 1 (rightward) and y from -1 (downward) to 1 (upward), expressed relative to the smartphone camera so that a direct gaze into the lens is (0,0). Frames where OpenFace confidence fell below 75%, because of occluded eyes or poor image quality, were removed. This reduced 1,084,267 frames to 619,620 annotated frames - 520,536 from autistic children and 99,084 from comparison children. The continuous gaze map was then discretised into a 4x4 grid of 16 areas of interest, and each frame assigned to one
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Participants' own smartphones running the GuessWhat app; Amazon Rekognition for facial landmark and bounding-box detection; OpenFace for gaze direction estimation; an LSTM implemented with the Adam optimiser
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: 449 gameplay videos from 95 children, 11.1 hours and over a million frames; no release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Privacy is a stated design driver rather than an afterthought. The entire annotation pipeline is automated specifically so that no human annotator sees participant video: 'we performed these tasks without sharing participant videos or private patient information with human annotators', and the discussion returns to this as a contribution, noting that prior manual-annotation approaches 'may compromise the privacy of participants by providing annotators with access to video footage'. Ethics approval from the Stanford Institutional Review Board under eProtocol 39562, with parental consent to share
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Discretised gaze direction sequences over a 16-cell grid
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Two derived representations from the same annotation. Fixation: the percentage of frames in a 90-second video falling in each of the 16 areas of interest, giving a 16-dimensional profile per video. Scanning: a graph in which each area of interest is a node and each gaze shift between areas is an undirected weighted edge, converted to a 16x16 adjacency matrix normalised by total transitions, with 61 unique non-zero cells. For classification, the frame-level area sequence is one-hot encoded into a w x 16 matrix using a sliding window of w frames with shift s. The critical property, acknowledged by the authors, is that the areas are directions relative to the phone camera rather than regions of the parent's face, so they carry no semantic content
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Amazon Rekognition and OpenFace, both off-the-shelf and applied without task-specific training
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, at the level of individual areas of interest and transition pairs, each tested separately with Bonferroni correction
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Two-sided permutation tests with 100,000 permutations at each of the 16 areas of interest, Bonferroni-corrected to a threshold of 0.0031; and the same procedure at each of the 61 unique non-zero cells of the transition matrix, Bonferroni-corrected to 0.0008. The authors note that 'because the AOIs are correlated, the Bonferroni correction is extremely stringent and will reduce the likelihood of Type 1 errors'
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: One of 16 areas of interest reached significance - location BC (p < .001) - and one of 61 transition pairs, the BB-to-BC transition (p < .001). Children of both groups fixated overwhelmingly on the four central locations nearest the camera; autistic children concentrated on BB and CB while comparison children concentrated on BB and BC. Transitions between BB and BC constituted 13% of all gaze shifts in comparison children against 9.4% in autistic children
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Reduced fixation and reduced transition frequency at a single off-centre location adjacent to the camera direction, with autistic children distributing their gaze differently among the four central cells. Because the grid is defined in camera-relative coordinates rather than on the parent's face, no anatomical or semantic interpretation of this location is available
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Recurrent sequence model on discretised gaze trajectories
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: A long short-term memory network with w cells, each accepting a one-hot 16-dimensional vector, with the final cell connected to a fully connected layer with a single output and sigmoid activation, thresholded at 0.5. Trained with Adam at learning rate 0.001, batch size 5, and a weighted binary cross-entropy loss to accommodate class imbalance. Window sizes from 50 to 500 frames (roughly 2 to 20 seconds) and shift values from 10 to 100 were explored on the validation set
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A three-way split by video with an explicit child-level constraint: 324 videos to training (275 autistic, 49 comparison), 71 to validation (62 and 9), and 54 to a held-out test set (43 and 11), 'ensuring that all videos corresponding to a single child were assigned to the same set'. Window and shift parameters were selected on the validation set and the three best configurations then evaluated once on the held-out test set. Group comparisons used permutation testing with Bonferroni correction throughout
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Macro-averaged and weighted-average precision and recall, chosen deliberately over accuracy because 'our data set exhibits class imbalance with cases outnumbering controls, these metrics provide the most accurate representation of model performance'. No accuracy, AUC or confidence intervals are reported
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Best configuration (window 100, shift 10) on the held-out test set: weighted-average precision 0.661, weighted-average recall 0.656, macro-averaged precision 0.595, macro-averaged recall 0.598. The two other configurations performed similarly or slightly worse (window 200: 0.635 / 0.662 / 0.577 / 0.561; window 500: 0.624 / 0.625 / 0.577 / 0.576). The authors describe this as 'mild predictive power' and note that 'macroaveraged statistics are lower than weighted-average statistics, suggesting that the accuracy of prediction differs between the 2 classes'. For the group comparisons, one of 16 fixation locations and one of 61 transition pairs survived Bonferroni correction
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Automated gaze estimation applied to 449 unstructured 90-second home gameplay videos from 95 children detected statistically robust but numerically small group differences: one of 16 gaze-direction regions and one of 61 transition pairs survived Bonferroni correction across 100,000-permutation tests, with comparison children making 13% of their gaze shifts between two adjacent central regions against 9.4% for autistic children. An LSTM trained on the discretised gaze sequences and evaluated on a child-disjoint held-out set reached macro-averaged recall of 0.598 and weighted-average recall of 0.656, which the authors characterise honestly as 'mild predictive power'. The methodological contribution is the pipeline rather than the performance: gaze was estimated from ordinary phone video with no eye tracker, no structured stimulus, no controlled lighting or camera distance, and - by design - no human ever viewing the footage, since annotation was performed entirely by off-the-shelf computer vision specifically to preserve participant privacy. The corresponding cost is that the resulting regions are directions relative to a phone held on a moving parent's forehead rather than locations on a face, which the authors state prevents any anatomical interpretation of the one significant region they found.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Reduced fixation on and reduced transitions to a single central gaze-direction region, with no anatomical interpretation available because the coordinate frame is camera-relative
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Expand the experimental population; analyse additional motion-based features such as limb movements and coordination; conduct qualitative human-centred investigations or pragmatic randomised controlled trials to evaluate clinical usability; and evaluate real-world diagnostic capability across diverse environmental settings. Dataset augmentation is proposed specifically to correct the class-imbalance effect on per-class accuracy
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: An unusually honest study that reports a weak result without inflating it, and whose value to this review lies in three methodological positions rather than in its numbers. First, the split is by child, stated explicitly - 'ensuring that all videos corresponding to a single child were assigned to the same set' - which is the discipline that separates this from Cilia, Simeoli, Gaspar and Ahmed, and it is applied even though the sliding-window feature construction generates thousands of overlapping training samples per video. Second, the statistics are conservative to a degree almost no other study here matches: two-sided permutation tests with 100,000 permutations at every one of 16 fixation regions and 61 transition cells, with Bonferroni correction applied and its stringency explicitly acknowledged, yielding exactly one significant finding in each family. Reporting one hit from 16 and one from 61, rather than presenting uncorrected p-values, is what makes the group-difference claim credible. Third, the metric choice is reasoned from the data structure - macro- and weighted-average precision and recall rather than accuracy, 'as our data set exhibits class imbalance with cases outnumbering controls' - and the authors then read the gap between the two as evidence that per-class performance differs. The result itself is close to the floor. The held-out test set contains 43 autistic and 11 comparison videos, so a classifier predicting the majority class throughout would achieve weighted-average recall of about 0.80; the reported 0.656 is well below that, and the macro-averaged recall of 0.598 is under ten points above chance. The authors say 'mild predictive power' and do not overstate it, but the paper does not make the majority-baseline comparison, which would have framed the finding more sharply. Three further issues are unaddressed. The sample spans ages 2 to 15 with no group means, medians or tests given in the text - a thirteen-year range over which gaze behaviour and gameplay engagement change radically - and age is never entered as a covariate or discussed. Diagnostic labels are unverified parent report, conceded as a limitation in the companion speech study from the same group and app but not mentioned here. And the areas of interest are, by the authors' own account, uninterpretable: 'due to camera motion and variation in the location of the smartphone relative to the parent's face, the gaze fixation maps are difficult to interpret qualitatively, and AOIs cannot be definitely matched to a parent's specific facial regions'. That concession is important and honest, but it means the single significant region cannot be connected to eye contact, mouth-looking or any other construct the introduction motivates the study with - so what the study establishes is that a difference exists in camera-relative gaze distribution, not what that difference is.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups from a crowdsourced app population: 68 children with parent-reported autism (53 male, 15 female) contributing 380 videos and 27 neurotypical children (18 male, 9 female) contributing 69 videos, 95 children and 449 videos in total, from approximately 1,000 individuals who downloaded the app. The imbalance is substantial and runs opposite to the direction usual in this corpus - cases outnumber controls by more than two to one at child level and by more than five to one at video level, which the authors identify as the reason for choosing macro- and weighted-average metrics over accuracy. After frame filtering the imbalance is similar (520,536 autistic frames against 99,084), so per-video frame retention was comparable between groups, which is a useful check that the automated quality filters did not operate differentially. No other-diagnosis comparison group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'the ASD cohort', against 'neurotypical (NT) children'. Person-first throughout, and 'neurotypical' rather than 'typically developing' or 'normal', which is the more neurodiversity-aligned term. Autism is described conventionally as 'characterized by social impairments, communication difficulties, and restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior', and the behavioural framing is deficit-oriented in places ('impaired social interactions', 'difficulty with maintaining eye contact'), though the analytic language is neutral and descriptive - differences in fixation distribution and transition frequency rather than abnormality. The privacy framing is notable for treating participants as people with interests to protect rather than as data sources.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Reported only in aggregate and incompletely. Sex is given as 53 male and 15 female in the autistic group against 18 male and 9 female in the comparison group - 77.9% versus 66.7% male - with no test and no discussion. Age is reported only as an overall range of 2 to 15 years, with the distribution shown in a figure and no group means, medians, standard deviations or tests in the text, and one comparison-group child not providing an age at all. That is the study's most consequential reporting gap: gaze allocation, sustained attention, and willingness to engage in a charades game with a parent all change enormously between a 2-year-old and a 15-year-old, and the analysis pools the entire range without stratifying, covarying or reporting whether the groups are comparable. No IQ, language, adaptive or severity measure for either group, and no exclusion criteria described.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Parent report alone. Parents who chose to share videos 'completed a survey to provide the age, sex, and diagnostic status of their children'. No instrument, no clinician involvement, no record verification, and no description of how diagnostic status was elicited. The companion study from the same group using the same app for speech analysis concedes this directly, noting that such labels 'are self-reported and thus unverified' and describing the mitigating design of offering diagnostic options unfamiliar to families who have not been evaluated. Neither the concession nor the mitigation appears here, and the limitations section does not mention the reference standard at all. Comparison-group status likewise rests on parental assertion with no screening.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, language, adaptive, severity or comorbidity measure for either group. Nothing therefore relates the gaze findings to any clinical dimension, and with an age span of 2 to 15 years and no developmental measure, neither age nor ability can be separated from diagnosis as an explanation for the observed differences.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: determine whether gaze fixation and visual scanning differences associated with autism can be detected from unstructured home video on consumer phones, without eye trackers, manual annotation or structured tasks. Main findings: one of 16 gaze regions (BC, p < .001) and one of 61 transition pairs (BB-BC, p < .001) differed significantly after Bonferroni correction across 100,000-permutation tests, with comparison children making 13% of transitions between these regions against 9.4% for autistic children; an LSTM on the discretised gaze sequences reached macro-averaged recall 0.598 and weighted-average recall 0.656 on a child-disjoint held-out set, described by the authors as mild predictive power; and the entire pipeline operated without any human viewing participant video.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Participants' own homes with no researcher present, no environmental control and no equipment standardisation - and the paper's positioning depends on this. The related-work section is unusually specific in critiquing prior computer-vision studies on precisely this point, noting that Hashemi and Chang 'controlled the room lighting and distance of the camera from the participant's face' and concluding that 'the ability of these techniques to translate to natural nonclinical environments and unstructured tasks remains to be explored'. The consequences are then reported rather than hidden: 'excessive camera movement and poor lighting conditions rendered some frames in our data set too blurry for use', and 'other adults or siblings would often join in gameplay, resulting in multiple faces in the frame'. Roughly 43% of frames were discarded by the automated quality filters. This is the most uncontrolled acquisition setting in the corpus and the paper treats that as its subject rather than as noise.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Ninety-second charades within a mobile game, with the child acting out prompts - emotions, sports, animals, chores - while the parent guesses, and the phone held on the parent's forehead with the front camera facing the child. The design achieves something specific: because the parent must watch the child to guess, the game creates a genuine dyadic social interaction in which the child's gaze toward the parent's face is functionally motivated, rather than a passive viewing task. The authors describe this as supplying 'inherent structure' in camera position, child location and interaction type while leaving the child free of hardware. The corresponding weakness is that the phone is mounted on a moving head, so the coordinate frame in which gaze is measured drifts continuously - which is why the resulting regions cannot be mapped to facial features. The prompts also vary between videos, so the elicited behaviour is not held constant across children.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, with videos accumulated opportunistically as families played and chose to share; no follow-up. Ethics approval from the Stanford IRB under a named eProtocol number, with parental consent to share each recording built into the app flow. Privacy is treated as a design constraint rather than a compliance step, and is one of the paper's three stated contributions: annotation was performed entirely computationally so that no human annotator ever viewed the footage, and the discussion explicitly contrasts this with prior manual-annotation work that 'may compromise the privacy of participants by providing annotators with access to video footage'. The senior author declares founding Cognoa and a co-author declares part-time consulting for the same company.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No specialised hardware at all - participants' own phones, with no model, camera specification, resolution or frame rate reported. The analytic chain uses two off-the-shelf systems applied without task-specific training: Amazon Rekognition for 30 facial landmarks and bounding boxes, and OpenFace for gaze direction. Both are used as noisy annotators with explicit quality gates - frames with zero or more than two faces removed, and frames with OpenFace gaze confidence below 75% removed - and the authors are appropriately cautious about what survives, stating that 'we expected the final annotations to be of high quality, but the presence of some noise and incorrect labels was to be expected'. Using general-purpose vision tools as automated annotators rather than training bespoke models is what makes the privacy-preserving claim credible and the pipeline reproducible, and it is a deliberate architectural choice rather than a convenience.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Good on pipeline, weak on participants. Fully reported: the app, game format, 90-second limit and recording arrangement; video and frame counts before and after filtering, broken down by group; both annotation tools with their outputs and the exact exclusion rules including the 75% confidence threshold; the gaze coordinate convention with its sign meanings; the 4x4 discretisation; the graph construction and normalisation for the transition analysis; the permutation test specification with 100,000 permutations and both Bonferroni thresholds; the sliding-window parameterisation with the ranges explored; the LSTM architecture, optimiser, learning rate, batch size and loss function; the three-way split with per-group video counts and the child-level constraint; and the metric choice with its rationale. Not reported: group-specific ages; any statistical comparison of demographics; the diagnostic elicitation; phone models or video specifications; the number of children excluded at any stage; and any data or code release.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Two limitations are stated and both are real. Class imbalance is identified as the reason macro-averaged and weighted-average statistics diverge, with dataset augmentation proposed as the remedy. More importantly, the interpretability of the areas of interest is conceded directly: 'due to camera motion and variation in the location of the smartphone relative to the parent's face, the gaze fixation maps are difficult to interpret qualitatively, and AOIs cannot be definitely matched to a parent's specific facial regions'. That is the central caveat on the whole study and the authors state it plainly rather than gesturing at eye contact or mouth-looking. What is not acknowledged: that diagnostic labels are unverified parent report, conceded by the same group in their companion speech paper but absent here; that the sample spans thirteen years of childhood with no age reporting, matching or covariate adjustment; that weighted-average recall of 0.656 falls below the roughly 0.80 a majority-class predictor would achieve on a test set of 43 autistic and 11 comparison videos; and that no confidence intervals, permutation tests or baselines accompany the classification results, in contrast to the rigour applied to the group comparisons.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Four directions, of which two are unusually practical. Expand the population and correct the class imbalance by augmentation. Analyse additional motion features such as limb movements and coordination, which the charades format would support naturally since the child is acting out prompts with their whole body. And - the most substantive - 'performing qualitative human-centered investigations or pragmatic randomized controlled trials to evaluate clinical usability' and 'evaluating the real-world diagnostic capabilities of our approach across diverse environmental settings'. Proposing a pragmatic randomised trial and human-centred usability work as the next step, rather than a larger dataset or a better architecture, is a translational rather than technical research agenda and is rare in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Two constructs drawn deliberately from clinical instruments: gaze fixation, 'which represent[s] regions of an individual's visual focus', and visual scanning, 'which refer[s] to the ways in which individuals scan their surrounding environment', both described as 'included in standard clinical diagnostic instruments'. The theoretical grounding is specific - fixation on the eyes signals communicative intent in dyadic interaction, and autistic individuals are reported to fixate instead on the mouth or other regions; scanning is grounded in Pelphrey's finding that neurotypical viewers transition between core facial features while autistic viewers scan non-feature areas such as the forehead and cheeks. Both constructs are then operationalised in a coordinate frame that cannot distinguish eyes from forehead from background, which the authors concede. The scanning analysis is nonetheless the more original contribution: modelling gaze shifts as a weighted graph and comparing adjacency matrices captures the sequential structure of looking rather than only its aggregate distribution, and it is what yields the interpretable finding that comparison children move between two adjacent central regions 13% of the time against 9.4% for autistic children.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality, and no fusion is attempted, though the companion speech study from the same group and app processes audio from the same recordings - so the two papers together represent an unexploited multimodal opportunity on a shared corpus, which neither notes. Within the modality, two representations of the same annotation are compared: a static fixation profile and a dynamic transition graph. Both yield exactly one significant finding after correction, and interestingly they converge on the same location - fixation differs at region BC and the significant transition is between BB and BC - which is a form of internal corroboration the paper does not draw attention to. Only the fixation representation is carried into the classifier; the transition matrices, which encode sequence and might plausibly carry more information, are used only descriptively.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: An LSTM chosen to exploit temporal structure, with the architecture kept minimal - w cells each taking a 16-dimensional one-hot vector, a single fully connected output and a sigmoid - and a weighted binary cross-entropy loss to handle the class imbalance. Only window size and shift are varied, explored across 50 to 500 frames and 10 to 100 respectively on the validation set, with the three best carried to the held-out test set. No alternative architecture, no baseline classifier and no chance comparator is reported, which is the main gap: given the imbalance, a majority-class predictor and a permutation null are both necessary to interpret a macro-averaged recall of 0.598, and neither is provided. The restraint in model complexity is appropriate for 95 children, but the absence of any comparator makes the modest result harder to situate than the group-difference analysis, where permutation testing does exactly that job.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: The representation is where the study's tradeoff is concentrated. Frame-level gaze is discretised from continuous (x, y) direction estimates into a 4x4 grid, then one-hot encoded and windowed. Discretisation is defensible given noisy estimates from uncalibrated phone video, and the sliding window with shift smaller than window generates overlapping samples, which multiplies the effective training set from 449 videos into many thousands of sequences - a legitimate augmentation given that the split is child-disjoint so the overlap cannot cross the partition. The decisive property, however, is the coordinate frame: gaze is expressed relative to the camera, which sits on the parent's forehead and moves with them. A region in this space is a direction, not a target, and the authors state that it cannot be matched to facial anatomy. The consequence is that the representation supports detecting that gaze distributions differ but not saying what they differ about - which is precisely the distinction between a signal and a behavioural finding, and the paper is clear about which it has.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Two very different standards are applied to the two halves of the paper, and the contrast is instructive. The group comparisons are analysed with exemplary conservatism: two-sided permutation tests with 100,000 rearrangements at every location, Bonferroni correction applied to both families, and the correction's stringency explicitly noted as reducing Type 1 error at the cost of power. Reporting one significant region from 16 and one transition from 61 under that regime is a credible finding precisely because 15 and 60 negatives are reported alongside. The classification results receive no equivalent treatment - four metrics for three configurations with no confidence intervals, no permutation null and no baseline. The metric choice is nonetheless well reasoned, with macro- and weighted-average precision and recall selected over accuracy because of the imbalance and the divergence between them correctly interpreted as class-dependent performance. What is missing is the comparison that would locate the result: with 43 autistic and 11 comparison videos in the test set, always predicting autism yields weighted-average recall around 0.80, above the reported 0.656.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is pursued through the design of the analysis rather than through model attribution, and the outcome is honest about its own limits. The two group-comparison analyses are fully interpretable in their own terms - which regions, which transitions, what percentages - and the graph representation adds a sequential dimension that a fixation profile alone would miss. The reported effect is concrete: 13% of comparison children's gaze shifts occur between two adjacent central regions against 9.4% for autistic children. What is missing, and is conceded, is the mapping from those regions to anything in the world. Because the phone moves with the parent's head, region BC is a direction relative to a moving camera, not the parent's eyes or mouth, so the finding cannot be connected to eye contact, mouth-looking, or the Pelphrey and Chawarska results the introduction builds on. The LSTM receives no attribution analysis at all. The net position is that the study establishes a difference exists without being able to characterise it, and says so.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The split is child-disjoint and stated as such, which is the single most important property and is applied correctly even under a feature construction that generates heavily overlapping windows: 324 videos to training, 71 to validation and 54 to a held-out test set, 'ensuring that all videos corresponding to a single child were assigned to the same set'. Hyperparameters were selected on validation and only the three best configurations evaluated on the test set, so the held-out estimate is not tuned. Group comparisons are protected by permutation testing with Bonferroni correction across both feature families. Three limits remain. There is no independent cohort. There is no baseline or null for the classification results, which matters acutely given a test set of 43 autistic and 11 comparison videos where the majority-class weighted-average recall of roughly 0.80 exceeds the reported 0.656 - a comparison the paper does not make. And the split is by video within child rather than being balanced on any covariate, so with an unreported age span of 2 to 15 years the training and test partitions could differ substantially in age composition without this being detectable. The overall picture is a study that validates its statistical claims rigorously and its predictive claim only loosely, while describing the latter as mild.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: mobile health, autism spectrum disorder, social phenotyping, computer vision, gaze, mobile diagnostics, pattern recognition, autism, diagnostic, pattern, engagement, gaming, app, insight, vision. The presence of 'social phenotyping' alongside 'mobile health' and 'gaming' locates the work in digital phenotyping delivered through consumer software rather than in vision research or clinical assessment.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Medical Internet Research 24(2):e31830 (2022), a digital health venue. Authorship spans Stanford's Departments of Computer Science, Bioengineering, Pediatrics and Biomedical Data Science, and Neuroscience, from the same group that produced the crowdsourced speech study on the same GuessWhat corpus. Funding is extensive, listing four NIH grants, an NSF award and numerous foundations. The senior author declares founding Cognoa and a co-author declares part-time consulting for the same company - relevant context given that the corpus's FDA pivotal trial paper evaluates a Cognoa device, and that the present study's honest reporting of a weak result sits in a portfolio that also contains a regulated commercial product.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022. The framing is the standard access and delay argument - 1 in 44 prevalence, lengthy parent questionnaires and clinical observation producing 'long waiting times for results', and a goal of 'mitigating the problems associated with limited diagnostic resources for neurodevelopmental disorders, especially in regions where access to care is limited'. What distinguishes the positioning is the structure of the related-work critique, which sorts prior video-based work into three categories and identifies a specific cost for each: manual annotation 'require[s] large numbers of trained annotators when implemented on a large scale, which is expensive and time-consuming' and 'may compromise the privacy of participants'; eye trackers 'require custom hardware that can often be expensive and inaccessible, especially for individuals living in resource-limited regions'; and structured-environment studies controlled 'room lighting and distance of the camera from the participant's face', leaving translation to natural settings untested. The study then removes all three constraints simultaneously and reports what remains, which is a small but statistically defensible difference and a weak classifier. Read that way the paper is a deliberate test of how much signal survives the removal of every experimental control - and the answer, reported without inflation, is not much.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Investigation of Eye-Tracking Scan Path as a Biomarker for Autism Screening Using Machine Learning Algorithms
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Kanhirakadavath MR; Chandran MSM
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Children from the Carette et al. gaze-path image dataset
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Eye tracking, re-encoded as scan path images
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Test whether eye-tracking scan path images can support autism screening, comparing three conventional classifiers against a convolutional network, and - unusually - determine whether apparent performance survives when the analysis is restricted to one image per child. The stated positioning is screening rather than diagnosis: 'Rather than being a diagnostic tool, the research model we proposed in this work is meant to be used for ASD screening using ET data'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Secondary analysis of a public image dataset, structured as a staged experiment across three data conditions - original images, rotation-augmented images, and a one-image-per-participant subset
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Not reported; the recordings belong to the source dataset
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Not described in the methods. The literature review, summarising the source publication, notes that participants 'watched a series of videos to stimulate eye movement across the screen', but no stimulus content, duration or instruction is restated for the analysis
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Not reported for the data collection; the analysis was performed at Vellore Institute of Technology in India and Ajman University in the United Arab Emirates
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Analysis in India and the UAE; the participants' country is a property of the source dataset
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Not reported for the analysis. The literature review notes that the source study's authors 'developed a four-level severity-based classifier model for ASD, with classes such as TD, low, medium, and severe based on Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) score', so CARS scores exist in the source dataset, but no diagnostic instrument, criterion or procedure is stated as applying to the participants analysed here
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 29 children contributing 219 images
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not reported. The literature review, describing a different Carette study, mentions children aged 8 to 10, but no ages are given for the participants whose images are analysed
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not used. CARS-based severity exists in the source dataset and is mentioned in the literature review, but is not applied in this analysis
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 30 children contributing 328 images
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Pre-rendered scan path images in which gaze coordinates and derivatives are encoded as colour gradients
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A five-stage pipeline. Images of 640x480x3 were converted to greyscale by equal weighting of the three colour channels, resized to 100x100 and flattened to 10,000-element vectors with a class label appended, giving a 547x10,001 array. Principal component analysis on this array yielded 500 components, used as features for the conventional classifiers. Separately, a convolutional network took the 100x100 greyscale images directly, with four convolutional layers of 16, 32, 64 and 128 filters at 3x3 with interleaved 2x2 max pooling, a flatten layer producing 4,608 features, two dense layers of 256 and 128 and a sigmoid output. Augmentation rotated every image by 45, 60, 90 and 180 degrees, producing 2,566 images (1,047 autistic, 1,519 comparison), on which PCA yielded 1,750 components. Finally a 'mini batch' dataset was formed containing a single image from each of the 59 participants and evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: No acquisition equipment described. Microsoft Azure Machine Learning Studio Classic for the conventional models, Google Colaboratory for the neural network, and a Dell XPS 15 laptop with an Intel i7-10750H; Adam optimiser, binary cross-entropy loss, 50 epochs, batch size 16, learning rate 0.001
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: No - the Carette et al. dataset of 547 images from 59 children is reused unchanged
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes - described throughout as publicly available
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not discussed. No ethics statement, consent statement or IRB approval appears, nor any pointer to the source dataset's approvals
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Principal components of flattened greyscale pixel arrays, and learned convolutional feature maps
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: For the conventional models, 500 principal components derived from 10,000 greyscale pixel values per image (1,750 components after augmentation). For the neural network, 4,608 features produced by the convolutional stack. Neither representation contains any gaze, fixation, saccade or attention quantity - and note that greyscale conversion by equal channel weighting destroys the colour encoding through which the source dataset represents velocity, acceleration and jerk, so the derivative information the images were built to carry is discarded before any modelling
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Principal component analysis; a four-layer convolutional stack
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No feature importance, attribution or interpretation of any kind
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None. No group difference, effect size or gaze statistic is reported
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Conventional classifiers on principal components, compared against a convolutional neural network
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Boosted decision tree, deep support vector machine and decision jungle in Azure Machine Learning Studio Classic; and a purpose-built convolutional network arrived at by iterative modification - 'we continued modifying configurations of the above model, such as various combinations of convolutional, pooling, and dense layers until we found an optimal model' - with hyperparameters tuned from defaults 'until the model produced the highest score'
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Five-fold cross-validation applied within a 70:30 split (382 training, 165 test) for the original and augmented datasets, and leave-one-out cross-validation for the 59-image participant-level subset. Both principal component analysis and rotation augmentation were applied to the complete dataset before any partitioning. Neither the original nor the augmented analysis groups images by child, and the 547 images derive from 59 children at roughly 9.3 images each
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: AUC, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value for every model in every data condition. The choice is argued explicitly against the field's convention: 'In contrast to the previously reported studies, we evaluate the model performance using the area under the ROC curve (AUC), specificity, sensitivity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative prediction value (NPV)'
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Three data conditions produce three very different pictures. On the original 547 images, conventional models performed near chance - deep SVM AUC 51.50%, decision jungle 60.40%, boosted decision tree 67.60% - while the neural network reached AUC 78.00% with sensitivity 78.57% and specificity 75.47%. On the rotation-augmented 2,566 images, conventional models improved modestly (boosted decision tree AUC 74.60%) while the neural network reached AUC 97.00% with sensitivity 93.28%, specificity 91.38%, PPV 94.46% and NPV 90.06% - the abstract's headline. On the participant-level subset of one image per child evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation, the same network achieved 72.88% overall accuracy, correctly identifying 17 of 29 autistic children (sensitivity 58.62%) and 26 of 30 comparison children (specificity 86.67%), with PPV 80.95% and NPV 64.00%
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: The same convolutional network applied to the same 547 public gaze-path images produced AUC 97.00% on a rotation-augmented set, AUC 78.00% on the unaugmented set, and 72.88% accuracy with 58.62% sensitivity when restricted to one image per child under leave-one-out cross-validation. The authors themselves attribute the augmented result to leakage - 'the discrepancy between the results using original and augmented datasets may be due to possible data contamination as similar replicates are entered into the training set, as seen in the testing dataset' - and construct the participant-level subset explicitly to address it. Their limitations section then generalises the point to the whole class of available data: existing open-access eye-tracking datasets 'combine multiple ETSP images from a small set of participants rather than a single trial from a large group, making them unsuitable for reliable ASD screening'. Conventional classifiers on principal components of the same images performed at or near chance throughout, with deep SVM reaching AUC 51.50% on the original data.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None reported
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Obtain an extensive dataset comprising single trials from a large group rather than multiple images from few participants; ensure during collection that the child is attending to the tracker and the environment is free of distraction; explore electrooculography as an alternative signal; and package the classifier into a mobile application for parents to screen toddlers aged 6 to 24 months
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The most analytically valuable paper in the corpus for quantifying validation-induced inflation, because it performs all three comparisons on the same images with the same network and reports all three. The sequence is: 97.00% AUC with rotation augmentation at image level, 78.00% AUC without augmentation at image level, and 72.88% accuracy with 58.62% sensitivity when restricted to one image per child. That last figure converges closely with the approximately 71% that Cilia and colleagues obtained when recomputing their own image-level result per participant, and it is reached here by an independent group using a different architecture - which makes the convergence a genuine replication of the corrected estimate rather than a coincidence. More remarkably, the authors diagnose the mechanism themselves and in the correct terms: 'the discrepancy between the results using original and augmented datasets may be due to possible data contamination as similar replicates are entered into the training set, as seen in the testing dataset', and they construct the participant-level subset specifically 'to mitigate the above issue'. Their limitations section then generalises it into a criticism of the available data infrastructure - open datasets 'combine multiple ETSP images from a small set of participants rather than a single trial from a large group, making them unsuitable for reliable ASD screening' - which is the sharpest statement of that problem anywhere in this review, and it appears in a paper whose own abstract leads with the contaminated figure. Two further strengths deserve note. Reporting AUC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV rather than accuracy is an explicit departure from the field's convention and is argued as such. And running conventional classifiers alongside the network provides an informative internal control: deep SVM on principal components of the same images reached AUC 51.50%, indistinguishable from chance, which locates whatever signal exists in the convolutional representation rather than in the pixel statistics. Against these, three problems remain. The abstract, keywords and conclusion all foreground the 97.00% figure that the discussion attributes to contamination, so the paper's headline contradicts its own analysis - a reader who stops at the abstract takes away exactly the number the authors have shown to be an artefact. Even the participant-level subset does not fully escape the underlying issue, since it uses a single arbitrarily chosen image per child and evaluates 59 samples by leave-one-out, so the 72.88% rests on 43 correct classifications with no confidence interval. And the augmentation itself compounds the problem beyond mere duplication: rotating a scan path by 45 or 60 degrees produces a gaze trajectory that no eye could have generated on a rectangular screen, so the synthetic training examples are physically impossible rather than merely redundant. Principal component analysis was also fitted on the complete dataset before splitting, which contaminates the conventional-model results independently of the augmentation. No participant demographics, diagnostic procedure, ethics statement or code release appears, and the greyscale conversion discards the colour channel through which the source dataset encodes velocity, acceleration and jerk.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups inherited from the Carette dataset: 29 autistic children contributing 219 images and 30 typically developing children contributing 328 images, 547 images from 59 children. The participant structure is not merely restated but actually used, which distinguishes this paper from the other two reuses of the same data in this corpus: a 'mini batch dataset that encapsulated only single trials from each of 59 participants' is constructed and evaluated separately. That analysis is the study's most valuable output. The main analyses nonetheless proceed at image level, so in the 70:30 split of 547 images and in the augmented analysis of 2,566 images, images from the same child appear in both training and test at roughly 9.3 images per participant. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The class imbalance of 219 to 328 is not corrected in the original analysis and is partly amplified by uniform augmentation, which preserves the ratio at 1,047 to 1,519.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'autistic children', 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', against 'typically developing (TD)' and 'TDs'. Person-first and identity-first are used interchangeably, and the comparison group is frequently reduced to the bare plural acronym 'TDs'. Autism is described as 'a chronic illness that lasts a lifetime' and elsewhere as a 'disease' and a 'condition' one may 'have', a framing that misdescribes a neurodevelopmental condition as a progressive illness. The introduction does include one observation that is clinically apt and rarely made in this corpus, noting that autism 'is diagnosed four times more frequently in boys than in girls; compared to boys, many girls with ASD show fewer visible signs' - though the study collects no sex data and cannot examine this.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Nothing. No ages, no sexes, no group sizes beyond the participant and image counts, no IQ, no language level and no matching of any kind for either group. The literature review mentions in passing that a different Carette study involved children aged 8 to 10, but no demographic information is given for the participants whose images are analysed here. This is a lesser omission than in the two companion reuses of the same data only in that participant counts are stated and, uniquely, used; on every other demographic variable the study is silent.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not reported for the analysis. The literature review does note that the source group 'developed a four-level severity-based classifier model for ASD, with classes such as TD, low, medium, and severe based on Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) score', which establishes that CARS scores accompany the source dataset - so this paper is aware that a severity instrument exists and does not use it. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician role or setting is stated as applying to the participants analysed, and the class labels are treated as image attributes. Under this review's classification this is dataset-label-only ascertainment, though better documented in its literature review than in its methods.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None used. CARS-based severity exists in the source data and is referenced in the literature review, but no cognitive, language, adaptive, severity or comorbidity measure enters the analysis, and no exclusions are described. Consequently nothing relates model output to any clinical dimension, and the paper's speculation that 'ML models could quantify heterogeneities in ASD symptoms, allowing for accurate ASD severity grading using ET data' is untested despite the severity data being available in the source.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: identify an accurate model for autism screening from scan path images and determine whether performance survives restriction to one image per child.
