Main findings: conventional classifiers performed at or near chance on the original images (deep SVM AUC 51.50%, decision jungle 60.40%, boosted decision tree 67.60%); the convolutional network reached AUC 78.00% on the same images; rotation augmentation raised the network to AUC 97.00%, which the authors attribute to data contamination; and the participant-level subset of 59 images evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation yielded 72.88% accuracy with sensitivity 58.62% and specificity 86.67%.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Not reported for the data collection. The literature review states, summarising the source publication, that recordings used 'an SMI RED series mobile eye tracker' while participants 'watched a series of videos to stimulate eye movement across the screen', but nothing about the room, country, recruitment or protocol is restated in the methods. The only settings named are the two analysing institutions and the compute environments - Microsoft Azure Machine Learning Studio Classic, Google Colaboratory, and a specified Dell laptop.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Not described. The methods section begins from the images and never states what the children viewed. The literature review's one-line summary of the source study is the only information available, and it is not carried into the analysis or used to interpret any result. The limitations section does return to the acquisition question with a substantive recommendation - 'the clinician must ensure that the child is staring at the eye tracker throughout the trials and that the recording environment is free from any distractions that may impact the child's attention' - which correctly identifies attention and environmental control as determinants of data quality, but this is offered as guidance for future collection rather than as a characterisation of the data analysed.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis of a public dataset; no follow-up. No ethics statement, consent statement or IRB approval appears anywhere, and no pointer is given to the source dataset's approvals - an omission that is common for benchmark reuse in this corpus but is not acknowledged. Funding is not declared in the extracted text. The dataset is described throughout as publicly available but no URL or accession is given in the extracted portion.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition equipment is described beyond a literature-review mention of the source study's SMI RED tracker. The analytic environment is specified in unusual detail for a computational paper: Microsoft Azure Machine Learning Studio Classic for the conventional models, Google Colaboratory for the neural network, and a Dell XPS 15 9500 with an Intel i7-10750H at 2.60 GHz with six cores. Model hyperparameters are stated - binary cross-entropy loss, 50 epochs, batch size 16, learning rate 0.001 with Adam - along with the full convolutional architecture layer by layer with filter counts, kernel sizes, pooling dimensions and output feature dimensions.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Reproducible as a pipeline, silent on the data. Fully reported: greyscale conversion with its channel weighting; resizing to 100x100 and flattening to 10,000 elements; the resulting array dimensions; the number of principal components retained in each condition; the complete convolutional architecture with all layer dimensions; the hyperparameters and the tuning procedure; the 70:30 split with exact image counts; the five-fold cross-validation; the augmentation rotations and the resulting class counts; the mini-batch construction and its leave-one-out protocol; the compute platforms and hardware; and full performance tables for every model in every condition. Not reported: participant demographics, diagnostic procedure, stimulus, acquisition protocol, the criterion by which one image per child was selected for the mini batch, random seeds, ethics approval, or any code.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Two limitations are stated and the first is the most substantive limitation statement in this part of the corpus. It identifies the structural problem with the available data infrastructure: 'A few open-access ET datasets are available; however, they combine multiple ETSP images from a small set of participants rather than a single trial from a large group, making them unsuitable for reliable ASD screening.' That is a correct and generalisable diagnosis, and it is reinforced in the discussion where the authors attribute their own augmented result to 'possible data contamination as similar replicates are entered into the training set, as seen in the testing dataset'. The second limitation concerns collection quality, recommending that clinicians ensure the child attends to the tracker in a distraction-free environment. What is not acknowledged: that the abstract, keywords and conclusion all lead with the 97.00% figure the discussion attributes to contamination; that images from the same child span the training and test partitions even without augmentation; that principal component analysis was fitted on the full dataset before splitting; that rotation by 45 and 60 degrees produces physically impossible gaze traces; that the participant-level result rests on 59 samples with no confidence interval; and that greyscale conversion discards the colour-encoded derivative information the source images carry.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Four directions. The first follows directly from the stated limitation and is the right one: obtain a dataset of single trials from a large group rather than multiple images from few participants. The second concerns collection quality - ensuring attention to the tracker and a distraction-free environment. The third proposes electrooculography as an alternative signal. The fourth is a deployment proposal that outruns the evidence considerably: 'a mobile app with an incorporated DNN-based ASD classifier and an extensive ET dataset of children aged 6 to 24 months may assist parents in independently screening their toddlers for ASD using a mobile device' - proposed for an age band entirely outside the analysed data, using a modality that requires an eye tracker, on the basis of a participant-level sensitivity of 58.62%.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Nominally atypical visual preference, with the introduction grounding this in the claim that autistic individuals 'pay less attention to faces and other social stimuli such as the human voice and hand gestures when compared to nonsocial stimuli' and that 'this unique pattern of eye movements appears in autistic children well before behavioral symptoms of ASD start showing'. Nothing of this construct survives into the analysis. The images are converted to greyscale - discarding the colour channel through which the source dataset encodes velocity, acceleration and jerk - resized to 100x100, and either flattened into pixel vectors for principal component analysis or passed through convolutional layers. No fixation, saccade, dwell time or area-of-interest quantity is computed at any stage, and no group difference in looking behaviour is reported anywhere. The construct discussed in the introduction and the quantity modelled in the methods are unconnected.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality with no fusion. The paper's comparative structure is instead across model families and, more importantly, across data conditions, and the second of these is the study's real contribution. Running the same convolutional network across three data conditions - original, rotation-augmented, and one image per participant - constitutes an ablation over validation design rather than over features, and it is the only such experiment in the corpus. The model-family comparison is also informative as an internal control: deep SVM on principal components of the same images reached AUC 51.50% on the original data, indistinguishable from chance, and decision jungle 60.40%, so the conventional pipeline extracts essentially nothing. That places whatever signal exists in the convolutional representation and simultaneously indicates that the pixel statistics captured by principal components carry no class information - a useful negative result that the authors note but do not pursue.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Four algorithms across two families. The three conventional models were run in a graphical cloud environment with 'minimal settings, making them lightweight and suited for low-power computers', which is a deployment argument rather than a methodological one. The convolutional network was arrived at by iterative search - 'we continued modifying configurations of the above model, such as various combinations of convolutional, pooling, and dense layers until we found an optimal model' - and its hyperparameters likewise tuned 'until the model produced the highest score', so both architecture and hyperparameters were selected on performance with no held-out confirmation of that selection. The authors do report an honest interim observation, that 'we found that all models were overfitting, which could be due to two factors: model complexity or the limited size of the dataset', and their response - augmenting the data - is a reasonable inference that turns out to have created a worse problem, which they then diagnose correctly.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Two representations of the same images, both stripped of behavioural content. For the conventional models: greyscale conversion by equal channel weighting, resizing to 100x100, flattening to a 10,000-element vector, then principal component analysis retaining 500 components (1,750 after augmentation). For the network: the same greyscale 100x100 image passed through four convolutional stages producing 4,608 features. The greyscale step is the most consequential and passes without comment: the source dataset's distinguishing property is that gaze velocity, acceleration and jerk are encoded as colour gradients, and averaging the three channels equally discards precisely that information, leaving a monochrome trace of position only. Both this study and Gaspar and colleagues make the same conversion on the same images, so the two independent reuses of this dataset both destroy the derivative encoding it was constructed to carry.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: The metric panel is a deliberate improvement on the field's convention and is argued as such: 'In contrast to the previously reported studies, we evaluate the model performance using the area under the ROC curve (AUC), specificity, sensitivity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative prediction value (NPV).' Reporting PPV and NPV alongside sensitivity and specificity is uncommon here and is what makes the participant-level result legible - sensitivity 58.62% against specificity 86.67% shows immediately that the model detects comparison children far better than autistic ones, which a single accuracy figure would conceal. All four models are reported in every data condition with all five metrics, so the deterioration of the conventional models and the improvement of the network under augmentation are both fully visible. Two gaps: no confidence intervals accompany any figure, which matters most for the 59-sample participant-level result; and Table 6 labels 72.88 as AUC while the discussion describes it as 'an overall accuracy of 72.88%', with the arithmetic (17 + 26 correct of 59) confirming it is accuracy, so the participant-level table header is mislabelled.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No feature-level interpretability of any kind, and none possible given that the features are principal components of pixel arrays or convolutional activations over a rendered plot. No group means, effect sizes, directions or descriptive statistics about gaze appear anywhere. What the paper offers instead is interpretability at the level of experimental design: by running the same model across three data conditions it makes visible what each condition contributes, which is a more useful form of insight for this review than a saliency map would be. The discussion also contains speculation not supported by anything done here - that 'by leveraging the capabilities of complex CNN-based algorithms, ML models could quantify heterogeneities in ASD symptoms, allowing for accurate ASD severity grading using ET data' - which is notable because the source dataset contains CARS-based severity labels that would have permitted a direct test.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: This is simultaneously the study's weakest and its most valuable dimension, because it fails and then measures its own failure. Three separate contaminations affect the headline analyses. Rotation augmentation was applied to all 547 images before partitioning, so rotated copies of the same source image appear in training and test. Principal component analysis was fitted on the complete 547x10,001 array (and later the 2,566x10,000 array) before splitting, so the components for the conventional models are informed by test images. And images from the same child span the partition regardless of augmentation, at roughly 9.3 per participant. The authors identify the first of these explicitly - 'possible data contamination as similar replicates are entered into the training set, as seen in the testing dataset' - and respond by constructing a one-image-per-participant subset evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation, which removes both the augmentation and the within-child duplication. The result is 72.88% accuracy with 58.62% sensitivity, against 97.00% AUC in the contaminated condition. That within-study drop of roughly 24 points, produced by the same architecture on the same source images, is the cleanest quantification of validation-induced inflation available in this review, and its close agreement with the approximately 71% Cilia and colleagues obtained by the same correction on the same data amounts to an independent replication of the corrected figure. The remaining weakness is that the participant-level analysis itself is thin - 59 samples, one arbitrarily selected image per child, leave-one-out, no confidence interval - so 72.88% is 43 correct classifications and carries a wide interval.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: ASD screening, autism spectrum disorder, machine learning, convolutional neural network (CNN), eye-tracking scan path images. The use of 'screening' rather than 'diagnosis' in the first keyword matches the paper's explicit positioning that the model 'is meant to be used for ASD screening' rather than as a diagnostic tool - a scope statement that several higher-profile studies in this corpus do not make.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Diagnostics 12(2):518 (2022), an MDPI open-access clinical diagnostics journal. Authorship is from the Schools of Electronics and Electrical Engineering at Vellore Institute of Technology in India and the Department of Biomedical Engineering at Ajman University in the UAE, with no clinical or autism-research affiliation. The review timeline is compressed - received 27 January 2022, accepted 12 February, published 17 February, twenty-one days from submission to publication - and no ethics statement appears. The literature review is nonetheless the most substantive of the three studies reusing this dataset, summarising six prior works with their samples, equipment, stimuli and reported figures, and correctly identifying which prior study reported what.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022. The framing is the standard screening argument with the usual claim that current procedures 'are highly subjective, leading to misdiagnoses or missed diagnoses' and that an objective biomarker 'would substantially impact current diagnosis practices'. Two features of the positioning are better than that suggests. The scope is explicitly bounded - a dedicated Clinical Implications subsection states that 'rather than being a diagnostic tool, the research model we proposed in this work is meant to be used for ASD screening using ET data' - which is the correct claim for what the evidence supports and is stated before any results are discussed. And the literature review engages with prior figures specifically rather than generically, comparing its own augmented AUC of 97.00% against 'the performance (AUC: 90%) reported in the research work on the same dataset with augmentation' - that is, against the source authors' own result on the same images. What the paper does not do is carry its own contamination diagnosis into that comparison: having established that the augmented condition is contaminated, it compares its contaminated 97% favourably against another group's similarly obtained 90%, when the informative comparison is between its own participant-level 72.88% and the source group's participant-level result of approximately 71%.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Machine learning models using mobile game play accurately classify children with autism
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Deveau N; Washington P; Leblanc E; Husic A; Dunlap K; Penev Y; Kline A; Mutlu OC; Wall DP
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Children aged 3 to 12 with a parent-reported formal autism diagnosis
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Gameplay behaviour - emotion enactment accuracy and response latency, captured as app event metadata
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Test whether a smartphone charades game already deployed as a therapeutic intervention generates enough behavioural signal, from event metadata alone, to screen for autism - with the equity argument that questionnaire-based screening 'require[s] literacy and perform[s] worse with non-white and lower education caregivers', so that 'naively deploying digitized versions of diagnostic questionnaires risks exacerbating current disparities in the early identification of ASD'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional classification on a remotely collected convenience sample, structured as a comparison of four classifier families with a feature-family ablation
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: 90-second gameplay sessions; data accumulated between April 2017 and February 2021
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: The GuessWhat charades game. The parent holds the smartphone against their forehead with a prompt displayed on the screen facing away from them; the child acts out the prompt, the parent guesses, and the parent labels the outcome by tilting the phone forward for a correct guess or backward for an incorrect one, advancing to the next prompt through a 90-second session. Prompts analysed here were drawn from the CAFE dataset - photographs of young children displaying angry, fearful, sad, happy, surprised, disgusted and neutral faces - so the child's task is to recognise a facial emotion and enact it recognisably. In-app coins, unlockable decks and achievement badges are described as reinforcing engagement over time
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: Participants' own homes, conducted entirely remotely; recruitment through the app's existing user base, the Hartwell Foundation's KidsFirst autism research database, ResearchMatch.org and Facebook advertisements
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Parent report with a described safeguard: 'To safeguard against the potential for self-reporting bias, we required the caregiver to confirm that their child's autism diagnosis came from a formal medical assessment. We asked the caregiver to choose a diagnostic label from a menu of choices including Autism Spectrum Disorder, Autistic Disorder, Pervasive Developmental Disorder-Not Otherwise Specified, Asperger Syndrome, ADHD/ADD, Anxiety, Speech and Language Delay. In addition, we required participants to report on the specific type(s) of therapy being administered to their child. This information requires a specialized understanding of the autism diagnosis and subsequent treatment prescriptions.' No instrument, clinician contact or record verification
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 28 children (19 male, 9 female)
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: The whole sample is reported as 7.10 +/- 5.82 years; no group-specific ages are given, and a standard deviation of 5.82 is arithmetically implausible for a sample restricted by inclusion criteria to ages 3 to 12
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported, though the diagnostic menu offered to parents included ADHD/ADD, anxiety and speech and language delay as alternative labels, and parents were required to report the therapies their child was receiving
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Parents were required to report 'the specific type(s) of therapy being administered to their child', though the resulting information is used only as a validity check on the diagnostic report and is not described or analysed
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: None. No severity, cognitive, language or adaptive measure for either group
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Parent report only; no screening instrument
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 21 children (10 male, 7 female, 4 not providing sex information)
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not reported and not addressed. No group-specific ages are given, so comparability cannot be assessed; the only age figure covers the whole sample and its standard deviation is implausible
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not tested. The autistic group is 67.9% male against 47.6% male among comparison children who reported sex, but four comparison children did not report it, and no comparison or discussion appears
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Parent report only
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: App event metadata only - no video, no audio, no images
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: The app records four event-level fields per trial: prompt start time, prompt end time, whether the prompt was labelled correct, and whether it was skipped. Analysis was restricted to the most frequently presented prompts, the 17 CAFE facial-emotion images, to minimise missing-data imputation. Two feature families were derived per child. Accuracy: for each of the 17 prompt types, the percentage of trials the parent labelled correct. Duration: for each of the 17 prompt types, the mean interval between prompt start and prompt end - 'the amount of time it took for a child to act out the prompt and for the parent to label it' - computed regardless of correctness. This gives 34 features
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Participants' own iOS or Android smartphones running the GuessWhat app; Python with scikit-learn; XGBoost
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Gameplay metadata from 49 children collected over nearly four years; no release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: The modality is intrinsically privacy-preserving and this is presented as a design advantage: because only event timestamps and outcome labels are used, no video or image of the child leaves the device, and the authors argue the approach can 'screen for ASD in a privacy-preserved manner', noting that 'privacy concerns are at the forefront of behavioral phenotyping efforts'. Stanford Institutional Review Board approval is stated without a protocol number
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Per-emotion task accuracy and per-emotion response latency
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Thirty-four features in two families of seventeen each, one per CAFE facial-emotion prompt. The construct targeted is emotion recognition, grounded in the observation that differences on such tasks 'stem[] from the ability to correctly identify an emotion and the reaction time required to do so'. The authors are explicit that the duration measure is not purely the child's: it spans the interval from prompt onset to the parent's tilt, so it includes the parent's recognition and labelling time as well as the child's enactment
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Direct computation from app event logs; no signal processing or computer vision involved
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Yes, and analysed at length across all 28 cross-validation iterations for all four classifier families, displayed as heatmaps and aggregated by emotion
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Model-derived feature importances extracted from the best model at each of the 28 nested cross-validation iterations, visualised as per-iteration heatmaps for each classifier family, compared statistically between the two feature families, and aggregated by emotion category
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Duration-based features were significantly more important than accuracy-based features (t = 5.15, p = 1e-5), a separation described as 'clear' and most pronounced in the tree-based models. Within duration features, those corresponding to disgust were consistently most important in the best-performing random forest, with surprise and sadness also consistently important across all classifier families except XGBoost
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: No group means or effect directions are reported for any feature. The authors do report one distributional observation that bears on interpretation: accuracy features 'were skewed heavily towards 1.0 (i.e., always correct)' for both groups, 'suggesting that these features may not discriminate well between the two conditions'
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Four conventional classifier families on 34 tabular behavioural features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: XGBoost, random forest, logistic regression and linear SVM, chosen on three stated criteria - no a priori assumption about linearity, the need for regularisation given a small sample, and interpretability 'to gain insight into the specific aspects of gameplay that predict ASD'. Hyperparameter grids are tabulated for all four, and the search space was deliberately restricted 'to include hyperparameters that would lead to more regularization and less overfitting' because of the sample size
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Repeated nested cross-validation with explicit leakage control. The outer loop splits the data into four partitions; the inner loop performs a four-fold grid search on three of them to select hyperparameters by AU-ROC; the selected model is then evaluated on the held-out fourth partition. The outer loop is repeated seven times, yielding 28 sets of performance metrics from which distributions were bootstrapped. Preprocessing was performed separately within each split, and the reason is stated: 'To avoid incorporating information from the distribution of the training data into the test set (i.e., data leakage), we carried out the following preprocessing steps separately for each test-train split of the data' - outlier removal at three standard deviations, k-nearest-neighbour imputation with k = 3, standardisation, and SMOTE upsampling of the minority class
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Mean AU-ROC, recall, accuracy and precision across the 28 cross-validation iterations, reported for all four classifiers under both the full 34-feature set and the 17-feature duration-only subset
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Full feature set: XGBoost best at AU-ROC 0.74 and recall 0.76, random forest 0.73 and 0.76, linear SVM 0.70 and 0.70 with the highest precision at 0.70, logistic regression 0.67 and 0.67. Duration-only subset: random forest best at AU-ROC 0.75, recall 0.77, accuracy 0.72 and precision 0.67; linear SVM 0.71 and 0.74; logistic regression 0.69 and 0.69; XGBoost fell to 0.70 and 0.72, the only model to worsen on the reduced set. Three of four classifiers improved or held when accuracy features were dropped
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Event metadata alone - prompt onset, prompt end, and a parent's correct-or-incorrect label - supported autism classification at AU-ROC 0.745 and recall 0.769 in 49 children, using no video, audio or imagery of any kind. The signal resides almost entirely in response latency rather than task accuracy: duration features were significantly more important than accuracy features (t = 5.15, p = 1e-5), and dropping the accuracy features improved or maintained performance in three of four classifier families. Accuracy features were uninformative because they were 'skewed heavily towards 1.0' in both groups, which the authors attribute either to lenient parental labelling or to a game too easy for most children. Within the duration features, prompts depicting disgust were consistently most important, with surprise and sadness following - a pattern the authors connect to evidence that these expressions require more cognitive development to discriminate. The critical caveat is stated by the authors themselves: the duration interval runs from prompt onset to the parent's tilt, so 'the duration-based measures in this study could capture the speed with which a parent marks a prompt as correct as opposed to the speed with which it takes the child to answer the prompt'.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Longer or otherwise distinctive response latencies, particularly for prompts depicting disgust, surprise and sadness; direction of effect is not reported
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Expand the sample to permit validation across demographic subgroups including gender, ethnicity, nationality, age and co-occurring diagnoses such as ADHD and dyslexia; reproduce the study in a clinical setting 'in which the person displaying the prompts to the child is neither a parent nor informed of the child's diagnosis', to remove both parental leniency and unblinding; extend the prompt set beyond CAFE images to video prompts; and elucidate how dimensions of the parent-child dyadic relationship shape the observed signal
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Methodologically the most disciplined of the three GuessWhat studies in this corpus, and one of the few papers anywhere in the review to name data leakage as such and design against it. Preprocessing - outlier removal, imputation, standardisation and SMOTE - is performed inside each train-test split with the reason stated explicitly, which is the correct handling and which several higher-profile studies here violate by fitting scalers, imputers or resamplers on the full dataset. The validation is repeated nested cross-validation with an inner grid search and an outer held-out fold, repeated seven times to give 28 estimates from which distributions were bootstrapped, and the hyperparameter search space was deliberately biased toward regularisation because of the sample size. Four classifier families are compared on identical folds with four metrics each under two feature conditions, and all sixteen results are reported. The feature-family ablation is genuinely informative rather than decorative: duration features are shown to dominate accuracy features by a large and tested margin, dropping the accuracy features improves three of four models, and the reason is diagnosed - accuracy scores cluster at ceiling in both groups, so they carry no information. Most importantly, the authors identify the study's central confound themselves and in precise terms: the duration measure spans prompt onset to the parent's tilt, so it may be measuring how fast the parent recognises and labels rather than how fast the child enacts, and their proposed remedy - reproduce with an examiner who is neither a parent nor informed of the diagnosis - would address both that confound and the unblinding of the labeller. That the single most important feature family may be an artefact of who is holding the phone is stated plainly rather than buried. Four limitations bound the result. AU-ROC of 0.745 in 49 children is modest and is reported as such, with the abstract describing it as demonstrating feasibility rather than accuracy. Diagnostic labels are parent report, mitigated by requiring confirmation of formal assessment and by asking parents to name therapies, but unverified. Demographic reporting is poor even by the standards of this corpus: no group-specific ages are given, the whole-sample figure of 7.10 +/- 5.82 years is arithmetically impossible given inclusion criteria of 3 to 12, four comparison children did not report sex, and no demographic comparison is made. And the unit of analysis is ambiguous - features are described as computed 'for a single session of gameplay' while the sample is described as 49 children, so whether a child contributing multiple sessions supplies multiple rows is not stated, and if it does the nested cross-validation would not be child-disjoint. Given how carefully leakage is handled elsewhere in the paper this is most likely one row per child, but it is not said.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups from a remotely recruited convenience sample: 28 children with a parent-reported formal autism diagnosis (19 male, 9 female) and 21 neurotypical children (10 male, 7 female, 4 not reporting sex), 49 in total, with data accumulated between April 2017 and February 2021. Recruitment ran through four channels - the app's existing user base, the Hartwell Foundation's KidsFirst autism research database, ResearchMatch.org and Facebook advertisements - which is a more diverse sampling frame than the single-channel recruitment typical here, though all routes select for families with smartphones, internet access and English literacy, and the last two select for research-engaged families. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the diagnostic menu presented to parents included ADHD/ADD, anxiety and speech and language delay, so children with those labels would presumably have been identifiable had they been recruited. The class imbalance is modest (28 to 21) and is handled by SMOTE upsampling applied within each cross-validation split rather than to the whole dataset.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'children with autism', 'individuals with ASD', against 'neurotypical (NT) children'. Person-first throughout, with 'neurotypical' preferred over 'typically developing'. The framing is oriented toward access and equity rather than deficit: the introduction is organised around rural and low-socioeconomic disparities in identification, the observation that 'up to 80 pct. of counties in the U.S. lack sufficient diagnostic resources', and the argument that questionnaire-based screening performs worse for non-white and lower-education caregivers. The game itself is described as 'a gamified therapeutic intervention' designed to be 'an engaging and fun way for parents and children to interact', so the data collection is framed as a by-product of something intended to benefit the family rather than as extraction. The paper also engages briefly with the ethics of framing, noting 'some disagreement about the patient as a consumer model' before arguing that user experience nonetheless matters for engagement.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: The weakest demographic reporting relative to the paper's methodological care elsewhere. Sex is given as 19 male and 9 female among autistic children and 10 male, 7 female and 4 unspecified among comparison children - so 67.9% versus 47.6% male among those reporting - with no comparison or discussion. Age is reported only as a whole-sample figure of 7.10 +/- 5.82 years, with no group-specific means, and that figure is arithmetically implausible: with inclusion restricted to ages 3 to 12, a standard deviation of 5.82 cannot arise, since the entire range spans nine years. Whether this is a transcription error or a computation over a different variable cannot be determined. No IQ, language, adaptive or severity measure for either group. The authors identify the consequence in their limitations - 'the sample size was too small to evaluate the predictive power of our models across various demographic dimensions, including gender, ethnicity, nationality, age and other diagnosis' - and commit to demographic fairness validation as recruitment expands, which is the right commitment but does not substitute for reporting what was collected.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Parent report, with a described mitigation that is more substantive than most. Caregivers were required to confirm that the diagnosis 'came from a formal medical assessment', to select a diagnostic label from a menu including several distinctions that a family without evaluation experience would be unlikely to navigate - Autism Spectrum Disorder, Autistic Disorder, PDD-NOS, Asperger Syndrome, ADHD/ADD, anxiety, speech and language delay - and to report the specific therapies their child was receiving, on the reasoning that 'this information requires a specialized understanding of the autism diagnosis and subsequent treatment prescriptions'. That is a coherent design: it uses the specificity of diagnostic and treatment vocabulary as an indirect check on whether a formal evaluation occurred. It remains parent report, with no instrument, clinician contact or record verification, and the therapy information collected as part of the check is never described or analysed. Comparison-group status rests on parental assertion with no screening at all.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None analysed. No cognitive, language, adaptive or severity measure was obtained for either group, and no comorbidity data are reported despite the diagnostic menu having captured alternative labels and despite therapy type having been collected. The absence matters for the specific construct at issue: response latency in an emotion-enactment task depends on receptive language, processing speed and motor planning, none of which is measured, and the sample spans ages 3 to 12 with no age reported by group. The authors list co-occurring diagnoses among the dimensions they cannot examine at this sample size.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: determine whether the GuessWhat game generates a signal separating autistic from neurotypical children using only objective gameplay metadata, as a step toward an easily deployed remote screening tool. Main findings: AU-ROC 0.745 with recall 0.769 for the best model (random forest on duration features); duration features significantly more important than accuracy features (t = 5.15, p = 1e-5); accuracy features uninformative because they cluster at ceiling in both groups; three of four classifiers improved or held when accuracy features were removed; and disgust, surprise and sadness prompts carried the most importance among duration features.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Participants' own homes with no researcher present, no equipment provision and no environmental control - 'this study was conducted remotely' - which is the design's entire point. The equity argument is developed at length and with specifics rather than as a gesture: prevalence is similar in rural (0.9%) and urban (1.0%) areas but rural communities face limited access to identification and intervention services; up to 80% of US counties lack sufficient diagnostic resources; and existing questionnaire-based screening 'require[s] literacy and perform[s] worse with non-white and lower education caregivers', so digitising those questionnaires 'risks exacerbating current disparities'. The proposed alternative - deriving signal from behaviour rather than from caregiver report - would in principle be insensitive to caregiver literacy, though the game itself still requires a smartphone, internet access and English.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A 90-second charades game in which the parent holds the phone against their forehead displaying a prompt they cannot see, the child acts it out, and the parent guesses and labels the outcome by tilting the phone. The prompts analysed are 17 CAFE facial-emotion photographs spanning anger, fear, sadness, happiness, surprise, disgust and neutrality, so the task requires the child to recognise an emotion and enact it recognisably to another person - a compound demand the authors characterise carefully as 'a complex interaction between child performance and parent interpretation', functioning as 'a proxy for emotion recognition' that 'likely captures components of theory of mind, metacognition and many other phenomena, as well'. The design's strength is that the parent's guessing behaviour makes the child's enactment functionally consequential rather than performed for a camera. Its corresponding weakness, which the authors state, is that the parent is inside the measurement loop: they set the end of every timed interval and they generate every accuracy label.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, with data accumulated opportunistically across nearly four years as families played and shared. Stanford Institutional Review Board approval is stated, though without a protocol number, and recruitment channels are named. The privacy position is a genuine design property rather than a claim: because the analysis uses only four event fields per trial - start time, end time, correct flag, skip flag - no imagery, audio or identifiable content is involved at all, which the authors present as enabling screening 'in a privacy-preserved manner' and contrast with computer-vision approaches where 'privacy concerns are at the forefront'. Among the three GuessWhat studies in this corpus, this is the only one whose modality raises no confidentiality question.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: None beyond a smartphone the family already owns - iOS or Android, with internet access, and no model, sensor or specification requirement, because the data are event timestamps rather than recordings. This is the most minimal data-collection footprint in the review and it is the paper's principal translational argument: a screening signal derived from four fields per trial imposes no bandwidth cost for video upload, no storage burden, no annotation pipeline and no privacy exposure. Analysis used Python with scikit-learn and XGBoost, with hyperparameter grids tabulated for all four classifier families.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong on modelling, weak on participants, with one substantive ambiguity. Fully reported: the game mechanics including the tilt-labelling convention; the four event fields recorded; the rationale for restricting to CAFE prompts; both feature definitions with their formulae; the complete preprocessing sequence with its ordering, the three-standard-deviation outlier rule, k = 3 for imputation, and SMOTE; the explicit statement that preprocessing occurs within each split; the nested cross-validation structure with outer and inner fold counts and the seven repetitions; the selection criterion of AU-ROC in the inner loop; hyperparameter grids for all four classifiers; the deliberate bias of the search space toward regularisation; and all sixteen performance figures across two feature conditions. Not reported: group-specific ages; any demographic comparison; the therapy information collected as a diagnostic check; whether a child contributing multiple sessions supplies multiple rows to the dataset; the IRB protocol number; and any data or code release. The unit-of-analysis ambiguity is the most consequential gap given the paper's otherwise careful leakage handling.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Two limitations are stated and both are substantive, and one further caveat appears in the discussion that is arguably more important than either. The stated limitations are that the sample is too small to evaluate performance across demographic dimensions - gender, ethnicity, nationality, age and co-occurring diagnoses - with a commitment to demographic fairness validation as recruitment expands; and that the study should be reproduced 'in a clinical setting in which the person displaying the prompts to the child is neither a parent nor informed of the child's diagnosis', which would remove both parental leniency in labelling and the unblinding of the person generating the labels. The discussion caveat is the one that bears on the headline: 'the duration-based measures in this study could capture the speed with which a parent marks a prompt as correct as opposed to the speed with which it takes the child to answer the prompt' - so the feature family carrying nearly all the signal may be measuring the parent. The authors also diagnose why the accuracy features failed, attributing the ceiling effect to 'parents incorrectly labeling or a game design that was too easy for the majority of children regardless of diagnosis'. Not acknowledged: the implausible age standard deviation; the absence of any group-specific demographics; and the unit-of-analysis ambiguity.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Four directions, two of which would directly test the study's own weaknesses. Reproducing the paradigm with an examiner who is neither the parent nor informed of the diagnosis would isolate the child's contribution to the duration measure from the parent's and would blind the labeller - addressing the confound and the unblinding in a single design change, and it is the right experiment. Expanding recruitment to permit demographic subgroup validation follows directly from the equity framing that motivates the study, since a tool proposed to reduce disparities must be shown not to perform differentially across the groups it is meant to serve. The remaining two are extending prompts beyond CAFE images to video, and investigating how the parent-child dyadic relationship shapes the signal - the latter framed as scientific rather than merely methodological.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Emotion recognition, targeted through a compound behaviour whose composite nature the authors are unusually careful about. The stated construct is grounded in prior work showing that autistic and neurotypical children differ both in 'the ability to correctly identify an emotion and the reaction time required to do so', and the two feature families map onto exactly those two components. But the measured behaviour is not the child's recognition alone: it is the child recognising the emotion, planning and executing an enactment, and the parent interpreting that enactment and responding. The paper states this rather than eliding it, describing the process as 'a complex interaction between child performance and parent interpretation' and noting that treating it as a proxy for emotion recognition risks 'an oversimplified understanding', since it 'likely captures components of theory of mind, metacognition and many other phenomena, as well'. That is the right level of caution for a construct that no single measurement isolates, and it is rarer in this corpus than it should be.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality with no fusion, but the feature-family comparison functions as a well-executed ablation and yields the study's clearest finding. Two families of seventeen features each - accuracy and duration - are compared in three ways: by model-derived importance across all 28 cross-validation iterations for all four classifiers, by a statistical test of the difference in mean importance (t = 5.15, p = 1e-5), and by retraining on the duration subset alone. All three converge: duration dominates, and removing accuracy improves or maintains performance in three of four classifiers, with XGBoost the only exception. The diagnosis of why is equally clean - accuracy scores cluster at ceiling in both groups, so the feature carries no variance to exploit - and the authors offer two candidate explanations, lenient parental labelling or a game too easy for most children, either of which would be actionable in redesign. This is what a feature ablation should look like, and it is more informative than the several fusion claims elsewhere in this corpus that rest on an accuracy delta alone.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Four classifier families selected on three reasoned criteria rather than by convention: no a priori assumption about linearity, so both linear and non-linear families are tested; the small sample, motivating families 'that offered considerable flexibility to prevent overfitting through regularization'; and interpretability, 'to gain insight into the specific aspects of gameplay that predict ASD'. The hyperparameter grids are tabulated in full and were deliberately restricted 'to include hyperparameters that would lead to more regularization and less overfitting' - so the search space itself was biased against complexity because of n = 49, which is a considered decision rather than a default. The spread across families is informative: tree-based methods reach AU-ROC 0.73-0.75 while linear methods reach 0.67-0.71, and linear SVM achieves the highest precision at 0.70 while tree methods achieve the highest recall, so the choice among them is a genuine operating-point decision. Model selection is stated as 'the simplest model resulting in the highest average of AU-ROC and Recall', a criterion declared before the comparison rather than fitted to it.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Thirty-four scalar features per child, derived directly from four event fields with no signal processing, feature learning or dimensionality reduction. The representation is maximally interpretable - each feature is 'percent correct on the disgust prompt' or 'mean response duration on the surprise prompt' - which is what makes the feature-importance analysis meaningful and what allows the finding to be stated in behavioural terms. Restricting to the 17 most commonly presented prompts 'in order to minimize missing-data imputation' is a sensible data-quality decision that is stated and justified. The one unresolved representational question is aggregation: features are described as computed 'for a single session of gameplay' while the sample is 49 children, and the paper does not state whether a child playing several sessions contributes several rows. If it does, the nested cross-validation would not be child-disjoint and the estimates would inherit the within-subject leakage that the paper is otherwise careful to avoid.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Mean AU-ROC, recall, accuracy and precision reported for all four classifiers under both feature conditions - sixteen complete result rows - with the values being means across 28 nested cross-validation iterations rather than single-split point estimates, and with distributions bootstrapped from those 28 sets. Reporting the full grid rather than only the winner exposes the tradeoff structure: linear SVM has the best precision on the full feature set while tree methods have the best recall, and XGBoost is the only model that degrades on the reduced set. The metric-selection reasoning is also made explicit, with the authors arguing for choosing 'the model that results in the highest average of AU-ROC and Recall' and undertaking to discuss the practical considerations of each metric. What is missing: no confidence intervals are printed despite distributions having been bootstrapped, and no chance or trivial baseline is reported - which matters at n = 49, where an AU-ROC of 0.745 estimated over 28 folds of roughly 12 held-out children each carries substantial uncertainty.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: The most thorough feature-importance analysis in the corpus relative to the size of the study. Importances are extracted from the best model at each of the 28 cross-validation iterations for each of the four classifier families and displayed as per-iteration heatmaps, so stability across folds is directly visible rather than asserted from a single fit. The two feature families are then compared statistically, yielding a large and significant separation (t = 5.15, p = 1e-5), and importances are aggregated by emotion category to give an interpretable ranking. The finding that disgust prompts carry the most importance, followed by surprise and sadness, is then connected to independent evidence that 'younger children are worse at discriminating facial expressions of disgust and surprise when images of these expressions are presented alongside specific other emotions', suggesting these emotions require more cognitive development to process - a mechanistic account that generates a testable prediction rather than a post hoc rationalisation. The authors immediately temper it, warning against 'an oversimplified understanding of these features'. The one weakness is that no direction of effect is reported: it is not stated whether autistic children took longer or shorter on disgust prompts, so the finding is that the feature discriminates without saying how.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Among the best-handled in the corpus on the dimensions the paper controls. Leakage is named explicitly and designed against: 'To avoid incorporating information from the distribution of the training data into the test set (i.e., data leakage), we carried out the following preprocessing steps separately for each test-train split of the data' - covering outlier removal, k-nearest-neighbour imputation, standardisation and SMOTE upsampling. Performing imputation and resampling inside the fold rather than on the full dataset is the correct handling and is violated by several studies here, including Liao and colleagues who select features on the whole sample and Kanhirakadavath and colleagues who fit principal components before splitting. The validation structure is genuine nested cross-validation - inner four-fold grid search selecting hyperparameters by AU-ROC, outer held-out fold estimating performance, repeated seven times for 28 estimates - so hyperparameter selection cannot contaminate the reported figures. Two residual issues. Feature selection was performed by inspecting importances across the 28 iterations and then retraining on the duration subset, so that selection used information from all folds; the effect is likely small since the selection is a binary family choice made on a large and statistically tested difference, but it is not nested. And the unit of analysis is not stated, so whether the folds are child-disjoint cannot be confirmed. Set against the corpus, the reported AU-ROC of 0.745 is modest precisely because these controls are in place, and the paper presents it as feasibility rather than accuracy.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No keyword list appears in the extracted text. The operative vocabulary is digital phenotyping, gamified therapeutic, remote screening, telehealth and health equity - a digital-health and access register rather than a machine-learning one, matching a paper whose contribution is a deployment argument supported by a modest classifier.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Intelligence-Based Medicine 6:100057 (2022), an Elsevier open-access journal. Authorship spans Stanford's Departments of Biomedical Data Science, Bioengineering, Pediatrics and Electrical Engineering, from the same group and the same GuessWhat platform as the crowdsourced speech study and the gaze study elsewhere in this corpus - three papers analysing three different data streams from one app. No competing-interest declaration appears in the extracted text, though the senior author declares founding Cognoa in both companion papers. The paper carries some marks of light editing, including a placeholder left in the methods ('need figure/graphic showing this') and a misspelling in the introduction.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022. The framing is a health-equity and access argument built around the COVID-19 transition to remote care, and it is more specific than the corpus norm at each step. Prevalence is similar in rural (0.9%) and urban (1.0%) areas, but rural communities face limited access to identification and intervention, and 'up to 80 pct. of counties in the U.S. lack sufficient diagnostic resources'. The critique of existing screening is where the paper is sharpest, and it is a critique this review should record: caregiver-report questionnaires 'require literacy and perform worse with non-white and lower education caregivers', so 'naively deploying digitized versions of diagnostic questionnaires risks exacerbating current disparities in the early identification of ASD'. That argument - that digitising an instrument inherits and can amplify its demographic bias - is made by no other paper here, and it motivates the study's choice to derive signal from a child's behaviour rather than a caregiver's report. The paper also engages with adoption as a design problem, noting that 'delays in the adoption of telehealth have been attributed to unengaged and resisting users' and that 'simply providing the current physician interaction through a smartphone may not be the best way of providing remote care', which is why the data collection is embedded in a game with progression mechanics rather than an assessment. Whether the resulting AU-ROC of 0.745 supports the deployment ambition is a separate question, and the abstract is appropriately hedged, claiming feasibility and 'potential' rather than accuracy.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Chen L; Zhang C; Gao X
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2022 IEEE 34th International Conference on Tools with Artificial
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Chinese children with autism attending special education services
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Speech acoustics - blind source separation of single-word utterances
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Compare three ways of deriving acoustic features from time-frequency independent component analysis, motivated by the argument that acoustic screening avoids the drawbacks of the alternatives: 'Methods based on eye movement, EEG, gastrointestinal flora analysis all require expensive equipment, and the detection process is complex' while 'the scale based method highly depends on the subjective experience of doctors'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional case-control classification comparing three feature-extraction pipelines on a purpose-collected speech corpus
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One-second speech samples at 48 kHz; each child contributed multiple samples, with roughly 4,000 autistic and 3,000 comparison recordings collected over about two years
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Elicited speech production. The corpus comprises words, phrases and sentences, with words accounting for 95% of the data, and children were asked to pronounce items - the authors note that 'the quality of children's word pronunciation was poor because some ASD children can't pronounce normally, or it's difficult for them to pronounce as required'. No task protocol, prompt list, elicitation procedure or examiner role is described
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: China, in cooperation with Anhui Medical University, the Anhui Autism Association and special education schools; a photograph of the collection setup is referenced but the recording arrangement is not described in text
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Not reported. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician role or setting is named anywhere in the paper. Recruitment is described only as being in cooperation with a medical university, an autism association and special education schools
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 'more than 80' children, contributing 511 of the analysed utterances
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 'more than 60' children, contributing 506 of the analysed utterances
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Not reported - no age information is given for either group
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not reported - no sex information is given for either group
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: One-second speech recordings at 48 kHz sampling
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Recordings were framed and windowed, transformed by short-time Fourier transform with a window length of 512 and frame offset of 256, giving 256 frequency sequences. Complex-valued independent component analysis was applied at each frequency point using negative entropy as the independence criterion, with a fixed-point update rule, followed by permutation sorting and amplitude compensation. Three feature representations were then derived. Method 1 extracts the row vectors of the unmixing matrix at each frequency point and concatenates them. Method 2 uses the sorted and amplitude-compensated separation outputs at each frequency point directly. Method 3 applies the inverse Fourier transform and window-gain elimination to recover separated time-domain speech, then extracts MFCC, LPCC and perceptual linear prediction features from it
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Recording equipment not described; a photograph of the collection setup is referenced. Analysis used short-time Fourier transform, a negative-entropy fixed-point ICA, SVM with a radial basis function kernel and cross-validated selection of C and gamma, and a convolutional neural network
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: A Chinese-language paediatric speech corpus of roughly 7,000 recordings from more than 140 children, described as addressing the absence of any public speech dataset for autistic children; no release is offered
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not discussed. No ethics statement, consent statement or institutional approval appears anywhere in the paper, despite the corpus having been purpose-collected from children through special education schools
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Blind-source-separation unmixing coefficients, separated frequency-domain sequences, and conventional cepstral features computed on separated speech
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Method 1: the complex row vectors of the 2x2 unmixing matrix at each of 256 frequency points, concatenated into a sequence. Method 2: the separated component sequences at each frequency point, with the 126th frequency sequence reported after being identified as the best-performing among the 256. Method 3: Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, linear prediction cepstral coefficients and perceptual linear prediction coefficients computed on the reconstructed separated signals
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Custom time-frequency ICA implementation; standard MFCC, LPCC and PLP extractors
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No feature importance, attribution or interpretation of any individual coefficient
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None; the comparison operates at the level of whole feature-construction methods
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Method 1, the unmixing-matrix representation, substantially outperformed both alternatives. Within Method 2 the 126th of 256 frequency sequences performed best but still only reached 59.71%. Within Method 3, perceptual linear prediction outperformed linear prediction cepstral coefficients, which outperformed MFCCs
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None reported. No group means, effect sizes or acoustic characterisations appear anywhere, and the representation admits none - an unmixing matrix coefficient has no interpretation as a property of a child's voice
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Blind source separation feature construction with conventional and convolutional classifiers
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Support vector machine with a radial basis function kernel, with C and gamma selected by cross-validation and the search surface illustrated; and a convolutional neural network, whose architecture, depth, training regime and hyperparameters are not reported. SVM is preferred on the argument that it 'still has good generalization ability under finite small samples', and the CNN's weaker performance is attributed to its needing 'a large number of labeled data for training, while the existing dataset is still small'
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A single 80:20 split of utterances - 408 autistic and 428 comparison recordings for training, the remainder for test - described as randomly selected. The split is over recordings rather than children, and the 511 and 506 analysed recordings derive from more than 80 and more than 60 children respectively, so several recordings per child are distributed across training and test. No cross-validation of the classifier, no repetition, no confidence intervals
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy (described as speech recognition rate), precision, recall and F1, reported for both classifiers under all three methods and, for Method 3, separately for each of the three cepstral feature families
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Method 1: SVM 98.51% accuracy, 97.36% precision, 98.15% recall, 97.25% F1; CNN 95.59%. Method 2: SVM 59.71%, CNN 55.19% - near chance, and this is the best of 256 frequency sequences. Method 3: with PLP features SVM 92.89% and CNN 90.43%; with LPCC SVM 91.47% and CNN 85.92%; with MFCC SVM 91.00% and CNN 89.34%
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: Three feature representations derived from the same time-frequency ICA pipeline gave sharply divergent results on the same 1,017 one-second utterances. Features taken from the unmixing matrix reached 98.51% accuracy with an SVM; conventional cepstral features computed on the ICA-separated signals reached 91-93%; and the separated frequency-domain sequences themselves reached only 59.71%, barely above chance and that only after selecting the best of 256 frequency sequences. The authors interpret the Method 1 advantage through their generative assumption that autistic speech is neurotypical speech convolved with filters representing 'dysfunctional' factors, so that 'the unmixing matrix can be regarded as the inverse matrix of these filter banks' and extracting it recovers 'the inherent distinguishing features representing the vocal system of both'. The internal inconsistency is that Method 2 uses the outputs of the very separation that Method 1's matrix performs, and those outputs discriminate near chance - so the separation is not producing acoustically distinct signals while the matrix that produced it appears nearly perfectly discriminative.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None reported
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Enrich the dataset, on the reasoning that the convolutional network underperformed because it needs more labelled data than currently exist
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A conference paper whose headline of 98.51% rests on a feature construction whose validity cannot be assessed from what is reported, and whose own results contain an unexplained internal contradiction. Three problems dominate. First, the split is by recording rather than by child: 511 autistic and 506 comparison utterances come from more than 80 and more than 60 children, so roughly six recordings per child are randomly distributed between a training set of 836 and a test set of 181, and utterances from the same child appear on both sides. With one-second single-word samples from the same speaker, that is close to speaker identification. Second, and more fundamentally, the two-channel structure that time-frequency ICA requires is never explained, and the equations as written suggest a construction that would invalidate the whole approach. Equation 2 states that the observation vector's components are 'the ASD children's speech signal and the normal children's speech signal, respectively', which would mean each ICA runs on a pair consisting of one autistic and one comparison utterance - so the unmixing matrix used as Method 1's feature would depend on which comparison sample the autistic sample was paired with, and the pairing requires knowing the labels. If instead the two channels are two microphones, no microphone arrangement is described anywhere and the photograph referenced in place of a methods description cannot supply it. Either reading is fatal to interpreting the 98.51%, and the paper does not disambiguate. Third, the paper's own Method 2 result argues against its Method 1 conclusion: the separated frequency-domain outputs classify at 59.71% even after the best of 256 sequences is selected, so whatever the separation is doing, the signals it produces barely discriminate - yet the matrix performing that separation is reported as almost perfectly discriminative. The Method 3 results, at 91-93% from ordinary MFCC, LPCC and PLP features, are the most interpretable in the paper and are in the range other speech studies here report under similar recording-level splits. Beyond these, the study reports nothing at all about its participants - no ages, no sexes, no diagnostic instrument, no severity, no exclusions - and contains no ethics or consent statement despite having purpose-collected roughly 7,000 recordings from children through special education schools. The generative framing deserves separate note: modelling autistic speech as neurotypical speech convolved with a filter bank of 'dysfunctional' factors treats the comparison group's speech as the undistorted reference signal, which is the most explicitly normative framing in this corpus and is embedded in the method rather than merely in the prose. One reported detail is genuinely useful and honest: less than a third of collected recordings were usable, 'because some ASD children can't pronounce normally, or it's difficult for them to pronounce as required', which documents a differential data-loss problem that speech studies here rarely quantify.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups described only in aggregate: 'more than 80 ASD children and more than 60 normal children', from whom about 4,000 and 3,000 recordings respectively were collected in cooperation with Anhui Medical University, the Anhui Autism Association and special education schools. After quality exclusion 'less than 1/3 of the data was usable', and 511 autistic and 506 comparison recordings were randomly selected for analysis. Participant counts are given imprecisely ('more than'), no exact numbers are stated, and the mapping between children and recordings is never specified - so the analysed sample is roughly six recordings per child but the actual distribution is unknown. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The critical structural fact is that all analysis, splitting and reporting operates on recordings, and children are never used as a unit at any stage.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'ASD children' throughout, against 'normal children' - the comparison group is called normal in the title framing, the abstract, every table and every figure caption, with 'typically developing' never used. That alone would place the paper at the normative end of this corpus, but the framing goes further and is embedded in the method rather than only in the wording. The generative model states that 'we consider the speech data of a ASD children as the convolution of pure normal children's speech data with all the filter banks representing the "dysfunctional" factors', so neurotypical speech is formally the undistorted source signal and autism is a distortion applied to it, alongside noise. The discussion repeats this, describing autistic speech as 'formed by the convolution of normal children's speech signals and all filter sets representing physiologically dysfunctional factors'. This is the only study in the corpus in which the deficit framing is a mathematical assumption of the model rather than a descriptive choice, and it determines the feature construction: Method 1's features exist only because the unmixing matrix is interpreted as the inverse of a hypothesised dysfunction filter.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Nothing whatsoever. No ages, no age ranges, no sexes, no IQ, no language level, no matching and no statistical comparison of any kind for either group. Even the participant counts are approximate. This is the least characterised sample in the corpus among studies that collected their own data rather than reusing a public benchmark - the benchmark-reuse papers at least have the excuse of inheriting an undocumented dataset, whereas this group recruited the children themselves over roughly two years and reports none of what they must have known. For a speech study the omission of age is especially consequential, since fundamental frequency, formant structure and articulatory precision change substantially across childhood and would separate any two groups differing in age composition.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Nothing. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician role, setting or timing is reported anywhere in the paper. The only relevant information is the recruitment route - cooperation with a medical university, an autism association and special education schools - which establishes that participants were engaged with autism services but not how their diagnoses were made or verified. The comparison group's status is likewise unestablished, with 'normal children' asserted and no screening described. The paper's introduction observes that 'ASD diagnosing can be difficult because there are no standard and quantified medical tests like blood tests to diagnose the disorder', which makes the absence of any account of how the reference labels were obtained more conspicuous rather than less.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, language, adaptive, severity, comorbidity or medication information for either group, and no exclusion criteria. One relevant observation is made in passing and is important: 'the quality of children's word pronunciation was poor because some ASD children can't pronounce normally, or it's difficult for them to pronounce as required, finally, less than 1/3 of the data was usable'. That establishes that expressive speech ability varied substantially within the autistic group and that data loss was driven by it, but no measure of that ability was collected and the retention rate is not reported separately by group.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: compare three acoustic feature constructions derived from time-frequency ICA for distinguishing autistic from comparison children's speech. Main findings: unmixing-matrix features reached 98.51% accuracy with SVM and 95.59% with CNN; separated frequency-point sequences reached only 59.71% and 55.19%, this being the best of 256 sequences; cepstral features on separated signals reached 91.00-92.89% with SVM, with PLP best and MFCC worst; and SVM outperformed CNN under every condition, which the authors attribute to the small dataset.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: China, with collection organised through Anhui Medical University, the Anhui Autism Association and special education schools. The recording environment is not described in text at all - a figure is referenced showing the collection setup, but no room, distance, microphone or channel configuration is stated. This gap is not merely a reporting deficiency here but a methodological one, because time-frequency ICA is a multichannel technique: it requires at least two observation channels to separate sources, and which two signals constitute those channels determines entirely what the unmixing matrix represents. Without the recording configuration the paper's central feature construction cannot be reconstructed or evaluated.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Elicited single-word production, with words constituting 95% of the corpus and phrases and sentences the remainder, each analysed sample trimmed to exactly one second at 48 kHz - a duration chosen because it 'not only ensured the integrity of the speech signal but also reduced the computational effort'. No prompt list, elicitation script, examiner instruction or session structure is described. Single-word production is the most constrained speech paradigm in the corpus, which has one methodological advantage - lexical content can in principle be held constant across children, removing a source of acoustic variation - and one significant cost, that prosodic, pragmatic and conversational features cannot be measured at all, so the study cannot address the prosodic constructs that motivate most speech work in autism. Whether lexical content was in fact matched between groups is not stated.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, with recordings accumulated over roughly two years and no follow-up. No ethics committee approval, consent statement or institutional review is mentioned anywhere, despite the study having purpose-collected approximately 7,000 speech recordings from more than 140 children recruited through special education schools and an autism association. Funding from two Anhui provincial science programmes is acknowledged. The dataset is presented as a contribution, with the authors noting that 'currently, there is no available public speech dataset for ASD children, which creates a big obstacle for related research', but no release, access route or sharing commitment is offered.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: The most consequential reporting gap in the paper. No microphone, recording device, sampling arrangement beyond the 48 kHz rate, room, distance or channel count is described; a photograph is referenced in place of a methods description. This matters because the entire analysis rests on a two-input two-output convolutive mixing model, and the paper's own equations describe the two observation channels ambiguously. Equation 1 sets up a general M-receiver model, which implies multiple microphones. Equation 2 then simplifies to two channels and states that 'x(n) are the ASD children's speech signal and the normal children's speech signal, respectively' - which describes not two microphones recording one speaker but one recording from each group. Under that reading each ICA would operate on a paired autistic and comparison utterance, and the resulting unmixing matrix would depend on the pairing, which requires the labels. The analytic chain is otherwise well specified: STFT with window 512 and offset 256 giving 256 frequency sequences, negative entropy as the independence criterion with the definition given, a fixed-point update rule, and permutation sorting with amplitude compensation before reconstruction.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Mathematically detailed and empirically opaque. Fully specified: the convolutive mixing model, the frequency-domain formulation, the negative-entropy independence criterion with its definition, the fixed-point update equation, the STFT window and offset, the resulting number of frequency sequences, the three feature constructions and the SVM kernel with its cross-validated parameter search. Not reported: recording equipment or channel configuration; participant ages, sexes, diagnoses or severity; the elicitation protocol or prompt set; whether lexical content was matched between groups; the CNN architecture, depth, training regime or any hyperparameter; how the 1,017 analysed recordings map to children; the retention rate by group; the criterion for selecting the 126th frequency sequence beyond it performing best; ethics approval; and any data or code release.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: There is no limitations section and only one limitation is acknowledged anywhere - that the dataset is small, offered as the explanation for the CNN underperforming the SVM and as the motivation for the sole future direction.
