Not acknowledged: that recordings from the same child are distributed across training and test; that the sample is entirely uncharacterised demographically and clinically; that no diagnostic procedure is reported; that the 59.71% figure for Method 2 is the maximum over 256 frequency sequences; that Method 2's near-chance result is difficult to reconcile with Method 1's near-perfect one; that the two-channel configuration underpinning the whole method is never described; that less than a third of collected recordings were usable and the loss was driven by the autistic children's pronunciation difficulty, so the analysed autistic sample is the more verbally able subset; and that no ethics approval is reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: One direction: 'One of our main tasks in future is to further enrich the dataset', motivated by the observation that the CNN needs more labelled data than are available. No proposal is made to group by child, characterise the participants, document the diagnostic procedure, describe the recording configuration, or validate on independent data.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Nominally the acoustic properties of autistic children's speech, but the construct is defined by a generative assumption rather than by any behavioural theory. The paper's model is that an autistic child's utterance equals a neurotypical utterance convolved with a filter bank representing 'all the dysfunctional factors', plus noise - so the target is whatever linear transfer function distinguishes the two groups' vocal production, treated as a property of 'the vocal system' rather than of prosody, articulation, phonation or pragmatics. Nothing in the analysis identifies which acoustic dimension is involved, and no group difference in any interpretable quantity is reported. The paper opens with a figure asserting 'noticeable distinctions' between an autistic and a comparison child's waveform, spectrum and spectrogram for the same content, but this is a single illustrative pair with no quantification. Compared with the other speech studies in this corpus - which measure pitch, jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio, rhythm or disfluency and report directions of effect - this study contributes no characterisation of speech at all.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Single modality with no fusion, but the three-method comparison is the paper's structure and its internal inconsistency is the most informative thing in it. Methods 1 and 2 are two views of the same computation: the ICA produces an unmixing matrix, which is applied to the observations to produce separated components. Method 1 uses the matrix, Method 2 uses its outputs. The reported results are 98.51% and 59.71%. If the separation were extracting genuinely different vocal sources for the two groups, the separated signals should carry that difference, yet they classify barely above chance even after the most favourable of 256 frequency sequences is selected. Method 3, which reconstructs time-domain speech from those same separated components and extracts standard cepstral features, then recovers 91-93% - which suggests the discriminative information is present in the reconstructed audio but not in the individual frequency-point sequences, and is consistent with ordinary speaker- and speech-level acoustic differences. Taken together the three results do not form a coherent picture, and the paper's explanation - that the unmixing matrix captures 'the essential distinctions between the two types of children's speech' - does not address why the separation those same matrices perform yields near-chance signals.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Two classifiers applied uniformly across all three feature methods, which makes the method comparison interpretable in that respect. The SVM is specified - radial basis function kernel with C and gamma selected by cross-validation, with the search surface plotted - and justified on small-sample grounds, that it 'still has good generalization ability under finite small samples'. The CNN is not specified at all: no layer count, filter sizes, depth, optimiser, learning rate, batch size or epoch count appears, only the general claim that convolution 'provides translation invariant convolution in time and space'. It underperforms the SVM under every one of the six conditions, by margins from 2.9 to 5.6 percentage points, which the authors attribute to insufficient training data. No baseline, chance level or permutation test is reported for any condition, which matters most for Method 2 where 59.71% needs to be judged against both chance and the 256-way selection that produced it.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Three representations of the same recordings, differing in where they intercept the ICA pipeline, and the choice among them is the paper's contribution. Method 1's representation is the unusual one and the one carrying the headline: the coefficients of the 2x2 unmixing matrix at each of 256 frequency points, concatenated. These are not properties of the child's voice in any direct sense - they are the parameters of a linear demixing operator estimated from the observation channels - and their interpretation depends entirely on what those channels are, which the paper does not establish. Method 2's representation is the separated component sequences, one per frequency point, of which the single best-performing was reported. Method 3's is conventional: MFCC, LPCC and PLP computed on reconstructed audio, and the authors note that separation 'eliminates the influence of certain noises and makes the speech data more pure', while sensibly cautioning that speech processing 'need not overly pursue the complete elimination of noise' since aggressive denoising distorts speech.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 reported for both classifiers under all six feature conditions - a complete and consistently applied panel, and the metric definitions are given. Reporting all three methods including the near-chance one is to the paper's credit, since Method 2's 59.71% could easily have been omitted. What is missing bears directly on how the numbers should be read. There is no confidence interval anywhere, on a test set of 181 recordings where a single reclassification moves accuracy by half a percentage point. There is no chance or trivial baseline, so Method 2's result is uninterpretable as stated - especially given that it is the maximum over 256 candidate frequency sequences, a selection that would elevate the apparent performance of pure noise. And there is no per-child aggregation, so the reported figures describe how well one-second recordings are classified rather than how well children are.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No feature importance, attribution, group comparison, effect size or acoustic characterisation appears anywhere, and Method 1's representation admits none in principle - an unmixing-matrix coefficient at frequency point k has no interpretation as a property of a child's voice. The one interpretive claim offered is theoretical rather than empirical: that because autistic speech is modelled as neurotypical speech convolved with dysfunction filters, 'the unmixing matrix can be regarded as the inverse matrix of these filter banks', so extracting it 'is equivalent to extracting the inherent distinguishing features representing the vocal system of both, reflecting the essential distinctions between the two types of children's speech'. This is an argument from the assumed generative model to the meaning of the features, not evidence that the features mean what is claimed, and it is not tested. Method 3, using standard cepstral features, would have supported conventional acoustic interpretation and none is attempted.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The weakest dimension, with three compounding problems. The split is by recording: 408 autistic and 428 comparison recordings train, the remainder test, described as randomly selected from 511 and 506 recordings originating in more than 80 and more than 60 children - so approximately six utterances per child are randomly assigned between the two sets and utterances from the same child appear on both sides. For one-second single-word samples from the same speaker in the same session, this approaches speaker identification rather than group classification, and it is the same failure that Kanhirakadavath and colleagues quantified on gaze images as a fall from 97% to 73% when the unit was corrected. There is no cross-validation of the classifier, no repetition and no confidence interval, so the reported figures come from one partition of 181 test recordings. And Method 2's headline of 59.71% is the best of 256 frequency sequences, chosen after inspecting all of them, with no correction and no report of the distribution across the other 255. Layered over all of this is the unresolved question of what the two ICA observation channels are: if the equations mean what they say, each unmixing matrix is estimated from a paired autistic and comparison utterance, so Method 1's features would be functions of a label-dependent pairing and the 98.51% would not measure classification at all. The paper provides no information with which to exclude that reading.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: Autism Spectrum Disorders, Independent Component Analysis, Deep Learning, Time-Frequency Feature. Three of four are signal-processing or machine-learning terms and none is clinical, which accurately identifies a paper whose contribution is a feature-construction comparison rather than a finding about speech.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Proceedings of the 2022 IEEE 34th International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI), DOI 10.1109/ICTAI56018.2022.00164. All three authors are from the School of Computer Science and Technology at Anhui University, with no clinical, psychological or speech-science affiliation, though the data collection is credited to cooperation with Anhui Medical University, the Anhui Autism Association and special education schools. Funded by two Anhui provincial science programmes. The venue is an artificial intelligence tools conference, and the paper's profile matches: the signal-processing derivation is developed at length with full equations while the participants, the diagnostic basis, the recording configuration and the ethics are absent.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022. The framing is a comparative argument for acoustic screening over the alternatives, and it is made concretely: methods based on eye movement, EEG and gut microbiome analysis 'all require expensive equipment, and the detection process is complex', while 'the scale based method highly depends on the subjective experience of doctors', so acoustic analysis 'provides a new path which is more simple and reliable for autism screening'. The related work is engaged specifically rather than generically, contrasting the study's use of speech against a prior study using infant cry - 'they focused on cry which is more random than the speech voice' - which is a reasonable methodological distinction. The paper also identifies a genuine infrastructure gap that this review can corroborate: 'currently, there is no available public speech dataset for ASD children, which creates a big obstacle for related research', a statement consistent with the fact that no speech study in this corpus shares its recordings, in contrast to the eye-tracking literature where a single public image dataset supports at least three of the charted studies. The paper's own corpus, roughly 7,000 recordings from over 140 children, would have been a substantial contribution to that gap had it been released.

data_charting_rubrics.title: The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Eni M; Gorodetski A; Dinstein I; Zigel Y
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2022 44th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine &
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_cohort: Hebrew-speaking young children, mostly not verbally fluent
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Speech acoustics and prosody, with automatic speaker diarization as an enabling component
data_charting_rubrics.primary_goal: Build an end-to-end system that can locate a child's speech within a full ADOS recording and estimate their symptom severity from it, removing the manual annotation step that prior acoustic work depended on. The stated gap is specific: prior speech studies 'reported high classification performance' but 'did not estimate the severity of autism symptoms in individual children'
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional regression study on consecutively recorded clinical assessments, with a within-study comparison of two diarization methods against manual annotation as baseline
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: One ADOS-2 session per child, mean duration 41.96 +/- 11.51 minutes, yielding approximately 11 hours of child vocalisation across the cohort
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Human children aged approximately 1 to 7 years
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: The ADOS-2 assessment itself - a 45-minute standardised examination in which a clinician engages the child in a variety of tasks and games and scores their behaviour. No purpose-built elicitation task was used; the speech analysed is whatever the child produced during routine diagnostic assessment, which is what makes the approach retrofittable to any clinic that records ADOS sessions
data_charting_rubrics.study_setting: The Azrieli National Centre for Autism and Neurodevelopment Research, Israel, in the ADOS examination room, with sessions administered by a clinician holding ADOS-2 research reliability
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: ADOS-2 administered by a trained clinician with ADOS-2 research reliability, with raw scores on the 0-30 scale used as the regression target. The comparison group's status is also clinically established - children were 'diagnosed with language or developmental delays or were defined as typically developing' - so the non-autistic group carries clinical diagnoses rather than being assumed typical. No additional instrument, and no statement of who made the categorical diagnosis or by what criteria beyond the ADOS
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: The cohort as a whole is described as aged 1 to 7 years; group-specific ranges are not reported
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported for the autistic group. The comparison group is deliberately clinical rather than screened-typical, comprising children with language or developmental delays alongside typically developing children
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: ADOS raw scores are the study's dependent variable rather than a descriptive covariate: 14.6 +/- 6.5 in the autistic group and 3.2 +/- 3.7 in the comparison group, on a 0-30 scale where higher values indicate more severe symptoms. This is the only study in the corpus to treat severity as the prediction target
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_controls_included: Partly - the 27-child comparison group mixes typically developing children with children carrying language or developmental delay diagnoses
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: The comparison group's ADOS scores are reported (3.2 +/- 3.7), so their low symptom level is instrument-verified, but the proportion who were typically developing rather than developmentally delayed is not stated
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: Approximately - 3.7 versus 3.1 years - but no statistical test is reported and matching is not claimed as a design procedure
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Closely - 80.0% versus 77.8% male, though no test is reported
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Only partly, by design: the comparison group includes children with language and developmental delays as well as typically developing children
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Single-channel audio recorded in the clinical assessment room
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Recordings were manually labelled into six categories - child, therapist, parent, movement, simultaneous speech, and silence by default - to provide diarization training targets and a segmentation baseline. Two diarization feature sets were compared: 13 MFCCs plus pitch with first derivatives (28 features), and 512-dimensional x-vectors computed with a 1.5-second window at 10 ms rate. Both fed the same fully connected deep network with two stacked softmax layers, followed by Viterbi decoding, and only child-detected segments were retained. Child segments were then split into individual vocalisations including those longer than 3 seconds, and for each recording a 100x48 feature matrix was built, each row being 48 prosodic and acoustic features - pitch, formants, zero-crossing rate, duration among them - computed over a random set of 10 sequential child vocalisations. A convolutional network then regressed the ADOS score from this matrix
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: A single AKG CHM99 microphone positioned 1-2 metres from the child, recording at 44.1 kHz and downsampled to 16 kHz; in-house labelling software; x-vector extraction using the Brno University of Technology system; the dscore tool with a 0.25-second collar for diarization error rate; RMSprop optimisation with random-search hyperparameter tuning under five-fold cross-validation
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Approximately 11 hours of child vocalisation from 132 Hebrew-speaking children recorded during ADOS-2 assessments; no release described
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not discussed. The data are audio recordings of clinical diagnostic assessments involving children, parents and clinicians. No ethics approval, consent statement or institutional review appears in the extracted text, though funding from the Israel Ministry of Science and Technology is acknowledged
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Prosodic and acoustic descriptors computed per vocalisation, plus diarization features
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Forty-eight prosodic and acoustic features per feature-matrix row, named only in part - pitch, formants, zero-crossing rate and duration are given as examples with the full set deferred to a prior publication. For diarization, 13 MFCCs plus pitch and their first derivatives, or 512-dimensional x-vector embeddings. The design choice of interest is the aggregation: each of 100 rows summarises a randomly drawn run of 10 sequential vocalisations, so the representation samples repeatedly from within a session rather than averaging across it, preserving variability that a single mean vector would discard
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Custom vocalisation segmentation from prior work by the same group; BUT x-vector system; standard prosodic and acoustic extractors
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: No feature-level importance or attribution. The comparison operates at the level of segmentation method rather than feature
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Comparison of severity-estimation performance under three segmentation conditions - manual labelling, MFCC-plus-pitch diarization, and x-vector diarization - with the same downstream architecture in each case
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not reported at feature level. At segmentation level, MFCC plus pitch produced the lowest diarization error rate (26.91%) and the best downstream severity estimate, while x-vectors gave higher child-segment accuracy (89.84%) but slightly worse severity estimation
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Not applicable - the model outputs a continuous severity estimate rather than a group contrast, and no directional acoustic finding is reported
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Deep regression on prosodic feature matrices, preceded by a deep classification model for speaker diarization
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: A fully connected deep network with two sequential softmax layers for six-class diarization, followed by Viterbi decoding; and a convolutional network with linear output for ADOS score regression, trained with RMSprop and hyperparameters selected by random search under five-fold cross-validation, with batch size, epoch count and learning rate reported separately for each segmentation condition
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Participant-level and repeated. Children were divided 80:20 into training and test sets, with splits constructed so that the distribution of ADOS scores - mean, standard deviation, kurtosis and skewness - was preserved in each partition relative to the whole dataset, and the procedure was executed 50 times. Reported figures are means and standard deviations across those 50 repetitions. Diarization was evaluated separately by leave-one-out
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: For diarization: diarization error rate decomposed into substitution, false accept and missed detection components, plus recall, precision and accuracy on child segments, with silence classification errors excluded on the stated ground that silence frames are removed downstream anyway. For severity estimation: normalised root mean square error and Pearson correlation between predicted and clinician-assigned ADOS scores, each reported as mean +/- standard deviation across the 50 splits
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Diarization: MFCC plus pitch achieved the lowest diarization error rate at 26.91%; x-vectors achieved recall 73.42%, precision 74.06% and accuracy 89.84% on child segments. Total detected child vocalisation duration was closely comparable across conditions (10.85 hours for manual labelling, 11.11 for MFCC plus pitch, 10.72 for x-vectors). Severity estimation: manual labelling baseline gave Pearson R 0.567 +/- 0.120 with NRMSE 0.261 +/- 0.036; MFCC plus pitch diarization gave R 0.606 +/- 0.099 with NRMSE 0.248 +/- 0.028; x-vectors gave R 0.581 +/- 0.115 with NRMSE 0.254 +/- 0.032
data_charting_rubrics.summary_key_findings: A convolutional network regressing ADOS raw scores from 48 prosodic and acoustic features of child speech, extracted from full-length clinical assessment recordings, achieved a correlation of 0.606 with clinician-assigned severity across 132 children and 50 repeated participant-level splits. The system's distinguishing property is that it estimates a continuous severity score rather than a binary group label, addressing a gap the authors identify precisely: prior speech studies 'reported high classification performance' but 'did not estimate the severity of autism symptoms in individual children'. The headline methodological result is counterintuitive and well-explained - automatic diarization slightly outperformed manual annotation as the segmentation input (R 0.606 against 0.567), which the authors attribute to manual labelling itself being imperfect for quiet child speech captured by a distant microphone in a reverberant room at an average signal-to-noise ratio of 12 dB. The two diarization approaches diverged: MFCC plus pitch gave the lower error rate and the better downstream estimate, while the more sophisticated x-vector embeddings gave higher child-segment accuracy but slightly worse severity prediction. The cohort is deliberately difficult - young children aged 1 to 7 who 'mostly do not speak fluently or use little or no phrase speech' - which the authors contrast against a prior study using 499 hours of speech from verbally fluent children.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Not reported; the study predicts a severity score rather than characterising acoustic differences
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Not stated as a separate section. Two limitations are named that imply directions: the audio quality achieved with a single distant microphone at 12 +/- 5 dB signal-to-noise ratio, contrasted against prior work using four microphones with beamforming; and the requirement for a minimum of 20 seconds of child speech comprising at least 50 vocalisations, which excludes the least verbal children
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Distinctive in this corpus for three reasons, and it should be cited in the synthesis for each. First, it is one of very few studies to predict a continuous severity score rather than a binary label, and it identifies the gap in the terms the review has repeatedly encountered - that classification studies 'did not estimate the severity of autism symptoms in individual children'. Keles and colleagues and Kong and colleagues both report, as negative findings, that gaze measures separating groups fail to correlate with severity; this study takes the correlation with severity as its primary endpoint. Second, the validation is participant-level and repeated in a form more careful than the corpus norm: children are split 80:20 with the ADOS score distribution matched between partitions on four moments - mean, standard deviation, kurtosis and skewness - and the whole procedure repeated 50 times with means and standard deviations reported. Matching the outcome distribution across splits is the right control for a regression on a bimodally distributed target and is not attempted elsewhere here. Third, the comparison group is clinically ascertained rather than screened-typical, comprising children with language or developmental delays alongside typically developing children, so the model is fitted across a genuine developmental-concern population. Two problems qualify the headline. The correlation of 0.606 is computed across the full 132-child sample, in which the autistic group averages ADOS 14.6 and the comparison group 3.2 - two well-separated clusters - so a substantial part of the explained variance reflects group membership rather than within-group severity grading. No within-autism correlation is reported, which is the quantity that would establish whether the system grades severity or merely detects the diagnostic contrast, and it is the same conflation that affects Kojovic and colleagues' clinical-validity analysis. And the requirement for at least 20 seconds and 50 vocalisations of child speech, acknowledged as a limitation, systematically excludes the minimally verbal children for whom an objective severity measure would be most valuable - the restriction is stated but its selection effect on the analysed sample is not quantified. Reporting is otherwise strong for a four-page conference paper: microphone model and distance, sampling rate, session duration, signal-to-noise ratio, diarization error decomposition, hyperparameters per condition, and total detected duration under each segmentation method, which allows the reader to verify that the three conditions recovered comparable amounts of speech. No ethics or consent statement appears.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: One cohort of 132 children recorded during routine ADOS-2 assessments, partitioned by diagnosis into 105 autistic and 27 non-autistic. The comparison group is the design feature worth noting: it comprises children 'diagnosed with language or developmental delays or were defined as typically developing', so it is a clinically referred population rather than a screened-typical one. That means the model is fitted across the range of children who actually present for autism assessment, and the regression target spans a continuum from ADOS 0 to 30 rather than two discrete classes. The proportion of the 27 who were developmentally delayed rather than typically developing is not reported, which limits how far the specificity claim can be pushed. No exclusion criteria are stated beyond the downstream requirement of at least 20 seconds and 50 vocalisations of child speech, and how many children that requirement removed is not reported.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'verbal children with ASD', against 'non-ASD' and 'typically developed (TD)'. Person-first and acronym-adjectival usage alternate. The clinical description is conventional and largely accurate, and one passage is notably careful about heterogeneity: autistic children 'exhibit speech and expressive language abnormalities, which range from a total lack of speech (i.e., non-verbal children) to those who develop normal vocabulary and syntax, but exhibit difficulties with the use of appropriate prosody and pragmatics'. Speech is described as 'abnormal' and 'strange prosody' is quoted from prior work, so the register is deficit-oriented, but the paper is precise about the range rather than treating autistic speech as a single phenotype - and that precision matters here, because the sample is drawn from the less verbal end of that range, which the authors state explicitly when comparing their corpus against prior work on 'verbally fluent children'.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Reported compactly and adequately for both groups: 105 autistic children aged 3.7 +/- 1.3 years, 80.0% male, ADOS 14.6 +/- 6.5; and 27 non-autistic children aged 3.1 +/- 1.5 years, 77.8% male, ADOS 3.2 +/- 3.7. The groups are close on sex (a 2.2-point difference) and reasonably close on age (0.6 years), though neither is formally tested and matching is not claimed. The overall age range of 1 to 7 years is given in the discussion. What is absent is any cognitive, language or adaptive measure, which is a real gap for a study whose predictor is speech and whose sample is described as 'mostly do not speak fluently or use little or no phrase speech' - expressive language level would be the obvious covariate, and it plausibly mediates both the acoustic features and the ADOS score. Ethnicity and socioeconomic information are not reported.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: The reference standard is the ADOS-2 itself, administered by a clinician with ADOS-2 research reliability, and it functions here as a continuous outcome rather than a categorical label - raw scores on the 0-30 scale are the regression target. That is a defensible use of the instrument and is more demanding than binary classification, since it requires the model to track a graded clinical judgement rather than a dichotomy. Two caveats. The categorical diagnoses used to describe the groups - autistic versus language delay, developmental delay or typical development - are stated without describing who assigned them or under what criteria, so the group composition rests on unspecified clinical judgement even though the regression target does not. And using a single instrument as both the sole clinical characterisation and the prediction target means the system is validated against one clinician's scoring on one occasion, with no second rater, no test-retest interval and no independent confirmation of the score's stability.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: ADOS raw scores are reported for both groups and are the dependent variable, so severity is characterised more centrally here than anywhere else in the corpus. Nothing else is measured: no IQ, developmental quotient, language level, adaptive functioning or comorbidity data for either group. The omission is consequential for interpretation because the sample is explicitly a young and largely non-fluent one, so expressive language ability varies widely and is not quantified. Since the predictors are acoustic properties of speech and the outcome is a clinical score that itself weights communication heavily, an unmeasured language-ability variable sits between the two and could account for a substantial part of the reported correlation without any autism-specific acoustic signal being involved.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: build an end-to-end system that locates child speech within a full ADOS recording and estimates autism severity from it, and determine whether automatic diarization can replace manual annotation. Main findings: MFCC-plus-pitch diarization achieved a 26.91% diarization error rate against x-vectors' 89.84% child-segment accuracy; severity estimation reached Pearson R 0.606 +/- 0.099 with NRMSE 0.248 with automatic diarization, against 0.567 +/- 0.120 and 0.261 with manual segmentation; and automatic diarization therefore matched or slightly exceeded manual annotation, which the authors attribute to imperfect manual labelling of quiet child speech in a reverberant room.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: The ADOS examination room at a national autism research centre, with recording conditions described honestly rather than idealised: a single microphone 1-2 metres from the child, in an environment with 'background noise, reverberation, and overlapping speech', and with both child and therapist free to move during the session. The resulting average signal-to-noise ratio of child speech is reported as 12 +/- 5 dB and named as a limitation. The authors position this deliberately against better-equipped prior work, noting that another group 'applied a diarization method for speech signals using four microphones, including a beamforming algorithm that improved their recordings' SNR' and that 'even though our proposed diarization methods achieved higher DER values, we used only one distant microphone recorded in a noisy environment'. Accepting worse acquisition in exchange for deployability in an ordinary clinic room is a defensible trade and is argued as such.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: No purpose-built task - the speech analysed is whatever the child produced during a standard 45-minute ADOS-2 administration. This is the design's principal translational strength: any clinic already recording ADOS sessions holds the raw material, no additional child burden is imposed, and the sampling context is by construction the one in which the reference score is generated. The corresponding limitation is the one the review has noted for other ADOS-derived studies: the assessment is designed to elicit autism-related behaviour, so acoustic differences observed within it may not generalise to spontaneous conversation. The paper does not raise this. A second, more specific constraint is imposed downstream: the severity model requires at least 20 seconds of child speech comprising at least 50 vocalisations, so children who spoke less than this could not be analysed - and in a cohort described as mostly not verbally fluent, that threshold plausibly excludes a meaningful proportion, though the number is not given.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, one recorded session per child, with no follow-up and no test-retest assessment of the severity estimate's stability. The absence of any ethics, consent or institutional review statement is the most conspicuous reporting gap: the study analyses audio recordings of clinical diagnostic assessments involving young children, their parents and clinicians, manually labelled by researchers, and no approval is mentioned in the extracted text. Funding from the Israel Ministry of Science and Technology is acknowledged with a grant number. No data availability statement and no code release.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Fully specified and deliberately minimal: a single AKG CHM99 microphone at 1-2 metres, 44.1 kHz downsampled to 16 kHz, in the ADOS room. Reporting the microphone model, its distance, the sampling and downsampling rates, the mean session duration and the achieved signal-to-noise ratio is more complete acquisition reporting than most speech studies in this corpus provide, and it matters here because the paper's central claim - that automatic diarization matches manual annotation - depends on the audio being genuinely difficult. Analysis tools are named specifically: the Brno University of Technology x-vector system with its window size and rate, the dscore tool with a 0.25-second collar, and RMSprop with random-search tuning under five-fold cross-validation, with the selected batch size, epoch count and learning rate tabulated separately for each of the three segmentation conditions.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Good within the constraints of a four-page conference paper, with one systematic deferral. Reported: microphone model, distance, sampling and downsampling rates, session duration, signal-to-noise ratio; the six manual labelling categories; both diarization feature sets with dimensionality and, for x-vectors, window size and rate; the shared network structure with its dual softmax and Viterbi post-processing; the vocalisation splitting including the treatment of segments over 3 seconds; the 100x48 matrix construction with its 10-vocalisation sampling rule; the optimiser and per-condition hyperparameters; the diarization error decomposition with its collar and the rationale for ignoring silence errors; the split construction with its four matched distributional moments and 50 repetitions; and the total detected duration under each segmentation condition. Deferred to a prior publication: the identity of the 48 features beyond four examples, the vocalisation separation method, and the CNN architecture details. Absent: ethics approval, data or code release, and the number of children excluded by the 20-second threshold.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Two limitations are stated, both technical and both substantive. The audio quality achieved with a single distant microphone in a reverberant room, quantified as 12 +/- 5 dB signal-to-noise ratio for child speech, is named and contextualised against prior work using four microphones with beamforming. And the requirement for a minimum of 20 seconds of child speech comprising at least 50 vocalisations is acknowledged as a constraint of the deep-learning approach. What is not acknowledged is the more consequential interpretive issue: the correlation of 0.606 is computed across a sample containing two well-separated clusters, with the autistic group averaging ADOS 14.6 and the comparison group 3.2, so a large part of the association reflects group membership rather than graded severity within either group. No within-autism correlation is reported, and without it the claim to estimate severity rather than to detect diagnosis is not established. Also unaddressed: the absence of any language or cognitive measure in a cohort defined by limited verbal fluency; the use of a single ADOS administration as both the only clinical characterisation and the prediction target; and the absence of an ethics statement.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: No dedicated future-work section, but both stated limitations imply directions and one is developed comparatively. Improving acquisition - the authors' contrast with a four-microphone beamforming setup indicates that better signal-to-noise ratio is the obvious lever, though it would trade against the deployability that a single-microphone setup buys. And relaxing the 20-second, 50-vocalisation minimum, which is framed as a constraint of the deep-learning architecture and which currently excludes the least verbal children. The paper also positions its result against two prior severity-estimation studies - one on Japanese-speaking adolescents using support vector regression and one on English-speaking children achieving a correlation of 0.634 in 33 children - and notes that it achieves 'a similar correlation value (0.606) while using a larger dataset of 132 children', which implicitly frames sample size as the axis along which the field should progress.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Prosodic and acoustic properties of spontaneous child speech during clinical assessment, grounded in a specific prior literature that the introduction summarises accurately: autistic children have been reported to show 'strange prosody', 'increased pitch variability and pitch range', 'slower speech rate, and prolonged word production', with the observation that 'these studies used manual annotation and inspection of the audio recordings' - which is precisely the dependency the present work is designed to remove. The 48 features are named only in part (pitch, formants, zero-crossing rate, duration), so the operationalisation cannot be fully evaluated from this paper. The construct that the model actually targets, though, is not an acoustic property but a clinical score: the system predicts ADOS raw scores, which aggregate social affect and restricted repetitive behaviour ratings across a 45-minute observation, most of which concerns behaviour the microphone cannot capture. That the model recovers 37% of the variance in such a score from speech acoustics alone is the substantive finding, and it is also the reason the result is hard to interpret mechanistically.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-modal fusion, but the study performs a well-designed three-way comparison of segmentation inputs feeding an identical downstream model - manual annotation, MFCC-plus-pitch diarization, and x-vector diarization - which isolates the contribution of the segmentation stage cleanly. The result is the paper's most interesting finding and runs against expectation in two ways. Automatic diarization matched or slightly beat manual annotation (R 0.606 and 0.581 against 0.567), which the authors explain rather than merely report: 'the manual segmentation is not perfectly accurate, especially for the child segments. The child speech is often quiet and is sometimes masked by noises, especially when using a distant microphone in a reverberant environment.' And the more sophisticated representation lost: 512-dimensional x-vectors achieved better child-segment accuracy (89.84%) than MFCC plus pitch, yet produced worse downstream severity estimation - so segment-classification accuracy and downstream utility diverge, and optimising the intermediate metric would have selected the worse system. That dissociation between an intermediate objective and the end-to-end outcome is a transferable lesson for any pipeline architecture.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Two networks in sequence, each matched to its task. Diarization uses a fully connected network with two stacked softmax layers, the second added on cited grounds that it improves final classification, followed by Viterbi decoding to impose temporal coherence on the frame-level outputs - a sensible structure for a sequence-labelling problem. Severity estimation uses a convolutional network with a linear output for regression, trained with RMSprop and hyperparameters selected by random search under five-fold cross-validation, with the selected values reported separately for each segmentation condition. Reporting per-condition hyperparameters is a small but meaningful detail: it shows the comparison between segmentation methods was made with each given its own tuned configuration rather than one set imposed across all three. Neither architecture is described in enough depth to reimplement, with details deferred to a prior publication.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: The representation choice is the study's most considered technical decision. Rather than reducing each recording to a single averaged feature vector - which is what most speech studies in this corpus do - the system builds a 100x48 matrix per child, where each row summarises 48 features over a randomly drawn run of 10 sequential vocalisations. This preserves within-session variability, which matters for a construct like prosodic atypicality that is expressed as inconsistency rather than as a shifted mean, and it supplies a two-dimensional input that a convolutional architecture can exploit. Because the matrix is the input and one prediction is produced per recording, the unit of analysis remains the child despite the internal resampling, so no leakage arises from the 100 correlated rows. The design also implicitly handles variable session length: a child with more vocalisations contributes more distinct draws, but every child yields the same fixed-size matrix.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Appropriate to a regression problem and reported with variability. Severity estimation uses Pearson correlation and normalised RMSE, each as a mean and standard deviation across 50 repeated splits - so the reader sees not only that R is 0.606 but that its standard deviation is 0.099, which places the manual baseline of 0.567 +/- 0.120 well within the automatic method's variation and correctly supports the paper's cautious claim of 'equivalent or slightly better' rather than a claim of superiority. Diarization is evaluated with the standard diarization error rate, decomposed into substitution, false-accept and missed-detection components with the collar specified, plus recall, precision and accuracy on child segments, and with a stated and reasonable justification for excluding silence errors. The most useful supplementary figure is the total detected vocalisation duration under each condition - 10.85, 11.11 and 10.72 hours - which demonstrates that the three segmentation methods recovered comparable amounts of speech and so that the downstream differences are not simply a matter of one method finding more data. No confidence intervals on the correlations beyond the across-split standard deviations, and no significance test between conditions.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No feature-level interpretability: the 48 features are not individually reported, no importance analysis is performed, and no acoustic characterisation of severity is offered, so the study contributes a prediction system rather than a finding about how autistic children's speech varies with symptom level. The interpretability that is present operates at the level of the pipeline. The three-way segmentation comparison establishes which stage contributes what, and the finding that automatic diarization outperforms manual annotation is given a mechanistic account grounded in the recording conditions. The dissociation between x-vectors' better segment accuracy and their worse severity estimate is reported without explanation, but it is reported, and it is the kind of intermediate-versus-final metric divergence that a paper optimising only for diarization performance would never have surfaced.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Among the better-designed validations in the corpus for a regression problem, with one important limitation that is interpretive rather than procedural. The split is by child and repeated 50 times, and - distinctively - each split is constructed so that the ADOS score distribution matches the full sample on four moments: 'we divided the children into training and testing datasets while balancing the distribution of ADOS scores (mean, standard deviation, kurtosis, and skewness) in each dataset'. Matching skewness and kurtosis as well as mean and variance is the right control for a bimodally distributed target, since an unlucky split could otherwise place most of the low-scoring comparison children on one side and inflate or deflate the correlation. Reporting means and standard deviations across the 50 repetitions rather than a single split follows properly. Hyperparameters were tuned by random search under five-fold cross-validation, though whether that tuning sat inside the 50 outer splits or was performed once beforehand is not stated - which leaves some selection optimism unquantified. The substantive limitation is what the correlation measures rather than how it was estimated: computed across a sample where the autistic group averages ADOS 14.6 and the comparison group 3.2, R = 0.606 conflates between-group separation with within-group severity grading, and no within-autism correlation is reported. That is the analysis that would distinguish a severity estimator from a diagnostic classifier expressed on a continuous scale, and it is the same conflation this review has flagged in Kojovic and colleagues.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No keyword list appears in the extracted text. The operative vocabulary is speaker diarization, severity estimation, diarization error rate, ADOS score and prosodic features - a speech-engineering register applied to a clinical regression target, which accurately describes a paper contributed to a biomedical engineering venue by a signal-processing group working with a clinical centre.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Proceedings of the 2022 44th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC), DOI 10.1109/EMBC48229.2022.9871523. All authors are at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, spanning biomedical engineering and the Azrieli National Centre for Autism and Neurodevelopment Research, so signal-processing and clinical autism expertise are co-located in a single institution - which shows in the study's access to research-reliable ADOS administration and in the realism of its recording setup. Funded by the Israel Ministry of Science and Technology with a grant number. The work builds explicitly on the same group's prior publications for the vocalisation segmentation method, the 48-feature set and the CNN architecture, so this paper reports an increment - the substitution of automatic diarization for manual labelling - rather than a standalone system.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2022. The framing is unusually precise about what the field has and has not done. Prior speech studies 'reported high classification performance' but 'did not estimate the severity of autism symptoms in individual children', and the two exceptions are named and characterised - one on Japanese-speaking adolescents using support vector regression, one on English-speaking children reaching a correlation of 0.634 in 33 participants. The paper also identifies the specific practical dependency it is removing: the earlier acoustic findings on prosody, pitch variability and speech rate all 'used manual annotation and inspection of the audio recordings', which is what makes them non-scalable. Its comparative positioning is likewise concrete rather than promotional: it acknowledges achieving worse diarization error than a four-microphone beamforming study, explains why, notes that a prior 499-hour corpus comprised verbally fluent children whereas this cohort 'mostly do not speak fluently or use little or no phrase speech', and describes its own correlation as 'similar' to the 0.634 of a smaller study rather than as an improvement. Adding a Hebrew-language cohort also extends the linguistic coverage of this corpus, which is otherwise dominated by English with single studies in Italian, Polish, Cantonese and Chinese.

data_charting_rubrics.title: The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Arent K; Brown DJ; Kruk-Lasocka J; Niemiec TL; Pasieczna AH; Standen PJ; Szczepanowski R
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Small controlled observational comparison study within a robot-mediated interaction paradigm, with human-rated behavioural coding and non-parametric group comparison
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Rater-assigned counts and 0-5 severity scores per child per game, aggregated into turn-taking indicators for each scenario
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. Single site, ten children, no replication.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 5 typically developing children (four boys, one girl)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Legal guardians were acquainted with the research aims and procedures and signed consent forms both for the children's participation and specifically for the filming of the study - separate consent for video recording is a level of specificity that few studies in this review report
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Two purpose-designed dyadic games of about five minutes each, preceded by a five-minute familiarisation session in which NAO introduces itself and performs two short rhythmic dances. 'Touch me' uses a stationary robot issuing voice commands; 'Dance with me' uses a moving robot inviting imitation. The paradigm is the study's principal output and its design logic is worth recording for the review: it is short, it is delivered identically to every child by a machine rather than by a person, it takes place in the child's own kindergarten, it requires no verbal response, and its two conditions are constructed to dissociate two routes to the same observable behaviour. Robot-delivered elicitation also removes the examiner-variability problem that affects human-administered protocols, and the authors note that the robot 'can provide predictable and reliable situations in which the complexity of interactions can be efficiently observed'.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: NAO humanoid robot operated remotely through its standard graphical interface, with video recording of each session. No sensing beyond the camera is used for measurement.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not stated; the observational scale itself is published in an appendix, which is the more useful disclosure for replication
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not applicable; no code was written for analysis
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Approved by the local committee for research ethics at the University of Lower Silesia
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Manual rating by six competent raters from the special education field, who watched the video recordings and scored behaviour on a purpose-built observational scale - counting movement activities and rating interest and additional movements on 0-5 severity scales for each of a defined set of positions specified in an appendix.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Complete by construction. Every measurement is a named behaviour scored against a definition published in an appendix, so any finding can be traced to an observable event and checked by another rater - which is what the reliability analysis does. The study's conclusion states the intended use in explicitly human terms: 'If a specialist has a sense of how a typical child plays with NAO, then they will be able to see possible deficits in the turn-taking of a child with autism by observing him/her.' That is an unusually honest description of what the work supports - a trained observer's calibrated judgement, aided by a standardised elicitation device - and it makes no claim that a machine performs the discrimination.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not applicable
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Not applicable in the machine-learning sense, and the corresponding measurement-validation work is done properly. Inter-rater reliability across the whole scale was assessed with Kendall's W and reported at 0.65 (p < 0.001), and the Additional movements subscale returned Cronbach's alpha of 0.77. Six independent raters scored the same material, the rating definitions are specified in an appendix, and the analysis uses non-parametric tests appropriate to five-per-group ordinal data. No model is trained, so no partitioning question arises; the relevant limitation is statistical power, since group comparisons on five children per arm can detect only large effects and provide no basis for individual-level prediction.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A dedicated 'Limitations and Further Directions of Study' section is provided, and its central statement is the most appropriately scoped translational claim in this review: NAO with the proposed software 'can be treated as a supplementary tool, thanks to which specialists can acquire additional diagnostic intuition to be used with standard tools'. The authors add that the games 'need to be improved and further developed', that this should be done 'by having close and extensive cooperation with the target users, including children, psychiatrists/psychologists and therapists', and that the goal is to identify a set of scenarios that would be attractive to children. Naming children among the target users whose cooperation is required is a form of participatory intent that appears nowhere else in this corpus.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Ten children aged 5.5 to 6.5 years (mean 6.08, SD 0.4), recruited through the kindergartens they attended in Poland: five diagnosed with autism and five typically developing, each group comprising four boys and one girl. The sample is the smallest in the review, and its composition is nonetheless carefully constructed - exact sex matching, a 12-month age band, and both groups drawn from the same kindergartens, so the recruitment asymmetry that affects nearly every case-control study charted here does not arise. Diagnoses were taken from kindergarten records and had been delivered by a multidisciplinary team of a psychiatrist, a psychologist and a pedagogue, which is genuine clinical ascertainment even though the instruments and criteria are not stated. No cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is reported. With five children per group, the study can support group-level inference about large effects and cannot support any statement about individual-level discrimination, which is consistent with what it claims.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Clinical and diagnostic in register, with an unusually clear-eyed account of why existing assessment is difficult. The introduction reviews the screening instruments - M-CHAT, ADEC, CARS-2, ASRS - and observes that because they rest on information from parents and caregivers 'their reliability is limited', with ADOS singled out as the exception 'enriched with interactive protocols'. It then names the differential-diagnosis problem directly: effectiveness 'is compromised by difficulties in differentiating autism from other developmental disorders (for instance, sensory integration disorder, dysphasia, minimal brain dysfunction, e.g., ADHD)', concluding that diagnosis 'often employs a range of clinical tools complemented with long-term observation of the autistic child, often leading to ambiguous diagnostic outcomes'. That is an accurate and specific account of the clinical problem, and the identification of differential diagnosis as the hard case matches the finding of the ADOS-versus-schizophrenia study charted elsewhere in this review. The paper also notes that most robotics work in autism concerns therapy rather than assessment, and positions itself in the smaller assessment literature. 'Autistic children' and 'children with autism' are used interchangeably; no neurodiversity framing appears, but the future-work section names children themselves among the target users whose cooperation is needed to improve the games, which is a participatory commitment absent from the rest of this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Age and sex are reported and controlled by design - a 12-month band and exact four-to-one sex matching in each group - which is proportionate handling for a ten-child study and better than several much larger studies in this review manage. What is absent is cognitive and language level, and the omission matters for the construct: turn-taking in a five-minute game depends on understanding the game, and without any developmental measure a general cognitive explanation for reduced turn-taking cannot be separated from an autism-specific one in six-year-olds. No socioeconomic, ancestry or comorbidity information is reported, and the sample is drawn from kindergartens in one Polish city.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Multidisciplinary clinical diagnosis by a team comprising a psychiatrist, a psychologist and a pedagogue, recorded in kindergarten files. This is real clinical ascertainment and places the study well above the folder-membership, hashtag and questionnaire-threshold labels charted elsewhere in this review - the diagnoses were made by qualified clinicians working together, which is closer to best practice than a single-instrument threshold. Two limitations attach. The instruments, criteria and dates behind those records are not stated, so the standard cannot be characterised further. And the diagnoses were obtained from records rather than confirmed for the study, which means they were known in advance to whoever recruited and, potentially, to the raters - and rater blinding is nowhere addressed, in a study where every measurement is a human judgement.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: No independent severity instrument was administered, but the study's own observational scale carries graded 0-5 severity ratings for interest in the robot and for additional movements at each defined position, so a within-study severity dimension exists. The authors use the group differences on these subscales to argue that the findings 'support the initial ASD diagnoses by showing that autistic symptoms are present in children diagnosed with ASD' - which is a convergent-validity argument for the measurement rather than a severity analysis, and is a reasonable use of the data. No relationship between turn-taking indicators and any severity score is examined.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The aim is to test whether a dyadic game with a social robot can elicit and reveal turn-taking deficits, as a step toward a robot-enabled diagnostic aid. Five autistic and five typically developing preschoolers each played 'Touch me' and 'Dance with me' with a NAO robot for about five minutes per game, and six raters from special education scored their behaviour from video on a purpose-built scale. Autistic children produced significantly fewer turn-taking behaviours in both scenarios, and group differences also appeared on interest in the robot and on additional movements. Inter-rater reliability was satisfactory (Kendall's W = 0.65, p < 0.001) with subscale alpha 0.77. The study's contribution is the paradigm and its validation rather than a detection result: no model is fitted, no child is assigned a predicted class, and no accuracy is computed or claimed. The authors state the intended use precisely - 'If a specialist has a sense of how a typical child plays with NAO, then they will be able to see possible deficits in the turn-taking of a child with autism by observing him/her' - which is a claim about calibrating human observation, not about automating it.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: The kindergartens the children attended, with a maximum of three children assessed per visit. Both groups were assessed in the same settings under the same protocol, which removes the clinic-versus-school recruitment asymmetry that this review has documented as a confound across the photograph, audio and thermal branches. Bringing a portable robot to a child's own nursery is also the deployment scenario the work envisages, so the data were collected under the conditions in which the method would be used - a property shared with only a few studies in this corpus, notably the population-based one-legged-standing study and the routine-examination work.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Two purpose-designed five-minute dyadic games preceded by a five-minute familiarisation session, and the paradigm is the study's principal output. Its design merits recording in detail. 'Touch me' uses a stationary robot issuing voice commands; 'Dance with me' uses a moving robot inviting imitation. The two are constructed to dissociate routes to the same observable behaviour, and the authors state the logic explicitly: in 'Dance with me' a child touching the robot 'cannot be classified as a response to the robot's voice command. If at all, this is a phase of some kind of imitation process', while 'the Touch me scenario precludes the emergence of spontaneous child reactions because the NAO robot in this case was not moving'. Designing two conditions so that a single behaviour can be attributed to command-response in one and imitation in the other is a level of construct care that almost nothing else in this review matches - most included studies collect a behavioural stream and ask what separates the groups, whereas this one asks what a given behaviour would mean and builds the paradigm to answer it. Four further properties make the paradigm well suited to the review's concerns: it is short, it requires no verbal response, it is delivered identically to every child by a machine rather than a person - removing examiner variability, which the authors note gives 'predictable and reliable situations' - and it is portable to a kindergarten.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session per child, with no follow-up or test-retest - the last being a real gap for a five-minute protocol proposed as a diagnostic aid, since the stability of a six-year-old's engagement with a novel robot across occasions is unknown and is exactly what a supplementary assessment tool would need. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: approval from the local research ethics committee at the University of Lower Silesia; legal guardians acquainted with the research aims and procedures; and signed consent forms covering both participation and, separately, the filming of the study. Separate consent for video recording is reported by very few studies in this review. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: A NAO humanoid robot operated remotely by an experimenter through its standard graphical interface, plus video recording. NAO's onboard sensing is not used for measurement at any point, so the robot is a standardised stimulus rather than an instrument - which is the study's defining methodological characteristic and the reason it contains no automated measurement. The equipment cost is nonetheless the highest of the elicitation devices in this review after MRI and thermal imaging: a NAO is a research-grade humanoid platform costing several thousand euros, against the webcam-and-toys protocols charted elsewhere. What it buys is exact reproducibility of the social partner's behaviour, which no human examiner can provide, and the authors identify this as the point.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong for an observational study. Reported: participant numbers, ages with mean and standard deviation, sex composition by group, the diagnostic source and the disciplinary composition of the diagnosing team, the kindergarten setting and the maximum of three children per visit, the two-session structure with familiarisation and both games and their durations, the robot and its remote operation, the number and professional background of the raters, both reliability statistics with their p-value, the statistical tests used, and - most usefully - the complete observational scale with its rating definitions published in an appendix. Publishing the instrument is what makes the paradigm reusable and is the single most valuable disclosure a study of this design can make. Not reported: rater blinding, the diagnostic instruments behind the kindergarten records, funding and competing interests.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: A dedicated limitations section is provided and its principal content is a scoping statement rather than a list of defects: NAO with the proposed software 'can be treated as a supplementary tool, thanks to which specialists can acquire additional diagnostic intuition to be used with standard tools'. The authors add that the games need further development through close cooperation with target users 'including children, psychiatrists/psychologists and therapists', and that the aim is a set of scenarios attractive to children. What is not addressed: the sample of five per group is not named as a constraint, though it permits only large effects to be detected and no individual-level inference at all; rater blinding to diagnosis is nowhere discussed, and is the study's main internal-validity risk since all measurement is human judgement and the diagnoses were on file; the instruments behind those diagnoses are unstated; no cognitive or language measure was obtained, so general developmental level cannot be separated from autism as an explanation for reduced turn-taking; and no test-retest data exist.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Improve and further develop the game scenarios in close cooperation with target users, explicitly including children alongside psychiatrists, psychologists and therapists; identify scenarios attractive to children; and extend toward a human-robot-interaction-enabled system that supports differentiation of autism symptoms beyond turn-taking. The inclusion of children themselves among the users to be consulted is the only participatory-design commitment in this corpus. The obvious additional steps, not proposed, are blinded rating, a larger sample, a developmental-level covariate, and test-retest assessment.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Turn-taking, treated as a specific and theoretically motivated construct rather than as a generic behavioural signal - and this is the study's main contribution to the review. Most included studies collect a rich behavioural stream and ask a model what separates the groups; this one names a single element of reciprocal social interaction, designs two contrasting scenarios to elicit it, defines the observable positions that constitute it in a published appendix, and tests whether the groups differ. Two secondary constructs are also measured on 0-5 severity scales: interest in the robot, and additional movements, the latter capturing motor behaviour that the authors treat as stereotypy-adjacent. The finding that autistic children produced significantly fewer turn-taking behaviours in both scenarios is consistent with the free-play study charted elsewhere in this review, which found the social-communication dimension separable in a brief structured sample while the restricted-repetitive dimension was not - here the additional-movements subscale did differ, which is worth noting since it suggests that a robot-mediated task may elicit motor behaviours that a 90-second free-play sample does not.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: None. A single video-recorded interaction stream, coded by human raters. The robot's own sensors - microphones, cameras, sonar, tactile sensors - are all present in the NAO platform and none is used for measurement, which is the study's clearest missed opportunity and the direction its own future-work section points toward. A robot that both elicits and records the interaction would supply exactly the standardised multimodal stream that several other studies in this review construct with far more improvised equipment.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: None. No computational or machine-learning model is fitted at any point, and no automated measurement is performed. The analysis is non-parametric group comparison - Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis and chi-squared - which is the appropriate choice for ordinal ratings from five children per group and is used correctly. For a review of computation-based approaches this study occupies the position immediately upstream of the modelling work: it establishes that a robot-delivered paradigm elicits a measurable group difference on a defined construct, which is the prerequisite for any subsequent automation, and it does not attempt the automation itself.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Rater-assigned counts of movement activities and 0-5 severity scores per defined position, aggregated into turn-taking indicators for each game. Every value is traceable to a named behaviour with a published definition, so the representation is fully auditable - the opposite end of the interpretability spectrum from the 100,352 DeepFace features or 1,639 landmark values used elsewhere in this review, and a reminder that the constructs those studies attempt to learn were originally defined by exactly this kind of manual specification.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: None of the diagnostic kind, and none claimed. The metrics reported are measurement-quality and inferential statistics: Kendall's W = 0.65 (p < 0.001) for inter-rater reliability across the whole scale, Cronbach's alpha = 0.77 for the Additional movements subscale, and Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis and chi-squared statistics with p-values for the group comparisons. Reporting inter-rater reliability at all is something most observational work in this corpus omits, and it is the appropriate primary metric for a study whose measurements are human judgements. What is absent is any confidence interval or effect size on the group comparisons, which on five per group would have been informative about how large the difference actually is rather than only whether it reached significance.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Complete, because nothing is opaque. Every measurement is a named behaviour scored against a definition published in an appendix, so any result can be traced to an observable event and independently re-scored - which is precisely what the six-rater reliability analysis does. The conclusion states the intended use in human terms: 'If a specialist has a sense of how a typical child plays with NAO, then they will be able to see possible deficits in the turn-taking of a child with autism by observing him/her.' That formulation is worth recording for the review because it describes an alternative to automation that most of this corpus does not consider - a standardised elicitation device that improves a clinician's calibration, rather than a model that replaces the clinician's judgement.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Not applicable in the machine-learning sense, since no model is fitted and no individual receives a predicted class - and the corresponding measurement-validation work is done properly. Six independent raters scored the same video material against definitions published in an appendix, inter-rater reliability was assessed with Kendall's W and reported at 0.65 (p < 0.001), and the Additional movements subscale returned an internal-consistency alpha of 0.77. Non-parametric tests appropriate to small ordinal samples were used throughout. The binding limitation is statistical power: with five children per group, only large effects are detectable, no confidence interval or effect size is reported, and nothing in the design supports individual-level inference - which is consistent with the study's own claims, since it asserts a group difference and a paradigm, not a classifier. Two internal-validity issues are unaddressed. Rater blinding to diagnosis is nowhere discussed, and since diagnoses were held in kindergarten records and every measurement is a human judgement, this is the study's main risk of bias. And no cognitive or language measure was obtained, so reduced turn-taking in a game requiring the child to understand the game cannot be separated from general developmental level. Set against the modelling studies in this review, however, the study has one structural advantage that no amount of downstream methodology can substitute for: its measurement instrument is published, its reliability is quantified, and its construct is named in advance.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorder; diagnostics; humanoid robot NAO; turn-taking. Compact and accurate, naming the population, the purpose, the apparatus and - unusually - the specific behavioural construct. Very few keyword sets in this corpus identify the construct being measured rather than the method being used.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Applied Sciences 12(17):8399, MDPI, open access under CC BY; received 10 June 2022, accepted 17 August, published 23 August 2022. An applied-sciences venue with a robotics editorial team. The paper's clinical apparatus - multidisciplinary diagnosis, ethics approval, separate filming consent, inter-rater reliability, a published observational scale - is more complete than that of many papers in clinical venues charted in this review, which suggests the standard came from the authors rather than from the venue: the author list spans robotics, cognitive and applied psychology, psychology, and rehabilitation medicine across four Polish and two British institutions, with all seven authors noted as contributing equally.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published August 2022 by a Polish-British collaboration spanning robotics, cognitive psychology, education and rehabilitation medicine. The framing is a well-informed critique of existing assessment: parent- and caregiver-report screening instruments have limited reliability, ADOS is the exception because it is 'enriched with interactive protocols', and diagnostic effectiveness is compromised by the difficulty of differentiating autism from sensory integration disorder, dysphasia and ADHD - so assessment often depends on long-term observation and 'often leading to ambiguous diagnostic outcomes'. For this review the study is valuable in four respects, none of which is a performance figure. It is the corpus's clearest example of construct-first design: rather than collecting a behavioural stream and asking what separates the groups, it names turn-taking as the target, builds two contrasting game scenarios to dissociate command-response from imitation, publishes the observational scale that defines the measurement, and quantifies its reliability across six raters. It brings the assessment to the child - both groups were seen in their own kindergartens under an identical protocol - so the recruitment and setting asymmetry that this synthesis has documented across the photograph, audio and thermal branches does not arise. Its translational claim is the best-calibrated in the corpus: the robot is 'a supplementary tool, thanks to which specialists can acquire additional diagnostic intuition to be used with standard tools', and the mechanism is described as a specialist learning what typical play with NAO looks like and thereby seeing deficits by observation - a proposal to calibrate human judgement rather than to replace it, which no other study here entertains. And its future-work section names children themselves among the target users whose cooperation is required to improve the games, the only participatory-design commitment in this review. What it cannot supply is evidence about detection: five children per group, no model, no individual-level prediction, no accuracy, no rater blinding, and no developmental-level covariate. Its role in the synthesis is therefore as the upstream complement to the modelling studies - a demonstration that a robot-delivered paradigm elicits a measurable group difference on a defined construct, which is the prerequisite that most of the automated work in this corpus assumes rather than establishes.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Zhao Z; Wei J; Xing J; Zhang X; Qu X; Hu X; Lu J
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional two-group diagnostic-classification study; secondary analysis of eye-tracking data collected for a previously published experiment (Zhao et al., 2021c), reusing the same participants and recordings with new features and a new modelling approach
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Hand-crafted summary statistics (entropy and range) over short fixed-length windows of the raw gaze coordinate time series; no image, no learned embedding, no areas of interest, and explicitly no temporal ordering within a segment
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not stated in this report
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Structured face-to-face conversation with an interviewer seated 80 cm away, comprising four sessions/topics: Generic question, Hobby sharing, Yes-no question, Question raising. Only the first session (Generic question, six questions intended to help the two people get familiar) was analysed, chosen because it was the longest and because gaze behaviour is sensitive to conversational topic so pooling sessions would blur the segment characteristics. Mean session length 191 s (ASD) versus 110 s (TD), a significant difference (Mann-Whitney U = 48, p < .01) attributed by the authors to social-processing difficulty.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Tobii Pro Glasses 2 head-mounted eye tracker, 50 Hz sampling, with a 1920 x 1080 scene camera; data exported through Tobii Pro Lab as pixel x/y coordinates
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not reported
