data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not stated in the retrieved text of this paper; the parent study (Zhao et al., 2021c) presumably carries it. Only a conflict-of-interest declaration and funding statement appear.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Six features per segment: Shannon entropy of gaze allocation on the x-axis (192 bins of 10 px), on the y-axis (108 bins of 10 px), and in the x-y plane (20,736 blocks of 10 x 10 px); plus the range (maximum distance between the two most remote gaze points) on the x-axis, the y-axis, and in the x-y plane. Segmentation is non-overlapping at lengths 1-10 s in 1 s steps; a k-second segment contains 50k consecutive gaze points.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Feature-level, and unusually explicit about mechanism. The single dominant feature is entropy of gaze allocation in the x-y plane, and the discussion reasons through what it means: TD children fixate preferentially on face and body and less on background, while ASD children distribute gaze more evenly between social and irrelevant information, producing more sparsely spread gaze points and hence higher entropy. Group-level feature statistics are tabulated for all six features at all ten window lengths with t-tests. The authors then concede that this makes the 'oculomotor' construct inseparable from visual attention in their data.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not reported for the SVM. The two decisions that were tuned - the segment length (10 candidate values) and the threshold percentage ('different percentage thresholds were tested ... and the optimal one that was associated with the highest classification accuracy was determined') - were both selected on the same 39 children on which the accuracy is reported.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Segment level: tenfold cross-validation with segments randomly partitioned into ten subsamples. The text states 'all behavior samples were randomly partitioned into 10 subsamples' - segments, not children, are the unit of partition, so segments from the same child appear in both training and test folds. Participant level: the threshold classifier is applied to the cross-validated segment labels of all 39 children, with both the window length and the threshold chosen to maximise accuracy on those same 39 children. There is no held-out participant set at either level.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Three, all genuine: (1) restricted phenotype - only children aged 6-13 with at least average non-verbal IQ and adequate conversational ability were included, so children with severe symptoms are absent, and the sample is overwhelmingly male, which matters given documented sex differences in presentation; the authors accordingly label the work 'proof-of-concept'. (2) Age - the benefits of early intervention and the reported mean diagnostic age of 43.18 months make classification in much younger children the clinically important target, which this study cannot address. (3) In the discussion rather than the limitations section, the authors state that existing eye-tracking ML studies including their own classify ASD against TD only, and that it 'remains unexplored whether ML is still an efficient tool in differentiating people with ASD from those with other clinical phenotypes (e.g., developmental delay and ADHD)'.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups. Enrolled: 20 ASD and 23 TD. Analysed: 19 ASD and 20 TD, after data from 1 ASD and 3 TD children were dropped for eye-tracking technical failure. Total analysed n = 39. No third or clinical comparison group. The unit of analysis for the model, however, is the gaze behaviour segment, not the child: at 9 s the two groups jointly contribute several thousand segments (exact counts shown only graphically in Fig. 2b), and because ASD sessions were 74% longer on average the ASD group supplies systematically more segments at every window length.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)' and 'children with typical development (TD)', used consistently. Person-first throughout ('children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'people with ASD'); the abbreviations ASD and TD are used as group labels in tables and figures. Deficit-oriented vocabulary is used freely in the interpretation - 'social deficits', 'attentional deficit', 'impairments', 'atypical oculomotor performance', 'ASD behaviors' - and the model's output classes are named 'ASD-like' and 'TD-like' behaviours. There is no engagement with neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement statement.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Age, sex and IQ reported per group with formal group comparisons: age 99.6 +/- 25.1 versus 108.8 +/- 27.0 months (t(37) = 1.09, p = .283); sex 17:2 versus 17:3 male:female (chi-square = .174, p = .676); IQ 100.8 +/- 22.7 versus 116.1 +/- 22.7 (t(37) = 2.45, p = .019). Age range 6-13 years by inclusion. Nothing else: no race or ethnicity, no socioeconomic status, no parental education, no language background, no medication status beyond the exclusion gate, no comorbidity counts. Both groups are drawn from Shenzhen, China, so the sample is culturally homogeneous - relevant because gaze-to-face norms are known to vary cross-culturally and the entire feature set is spatial gaze allocation during a face-to-face conversation. The significant IQ gap deserves emphasis: it is the one variable that separates the groups, and it is neither matched, regressed out, nor discussed as a confound.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Diagnosis was clinical and consensus-based rather than instrument-based, and the paper is candid about why: 'Due to a limited access to established ASD diagnostic instruments such as ADOS and ADI-R, the accuracy of the ASD diagnosis in the present study was assured through a variety of other rigorous procedures.' Those procedures were DSM-IV criteria applied by a licensed psychiatrist with at least five years' experience, re-evaluation by a senior psychiatrist, and adjudication by at least two further senior psychiatrists if they disagreed. Additional gates: non-verbal IQ >= 70 on Raven's APM, absence of schizophrenia or ADHD, no medication at the time of the experiment, and adequate conversational ability judged by a speech-language psychologist. TD children were community-recruited, Raven-screened to IQ > 70, self/parent-reported free of physical or mental disorder, and with no ASD/ADHD in first-degree relatives. Note the DSM edition: DSM-IV, not DSM-5, in a study published in 2022. Multi-psychiatrist consensus is a defensible reference standard and better than the single-clinician or registry labels used elsewhere in this corpus, but it is unblinded to everything the clinicians already knew about the child, is not quantified for reliability, and yields no severity gradation.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Cognitive ability: Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices in both groups, non-verbal only, used both as an eligibility gate (IQ >= 70) and as a reported demographic. Language: a qualitative judgement by a speech-language psychologist that the child could sustain average verbal communication - no standardised score. Severity: none. No ADOS calibrated severity score, CARS, SRS, ADI-R algorithm score or any other symptom-quantification instrument was obtained, which is a direct consequence of the stated lack of access to ADOS/ADI-R. The study therefore cannot relate its gaze-entropy features to symptom severity, cannot report where on the spectrum its 19 children sit, and cannot test whether misclassified children were the less severely affected ones. Combined with the exclusion of children with severe symptoms and of those with IQ below 70, the analysed autistic sample is a narrow, cognitively able, verbal slice of the population.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Two stated goals: first, to test whether gaze behaviour segments produced by autistic and TD children can be classified by machine learning; second, to test whether children themselves can be classified from the proportion of their segments the model labels ASD-like. The framing is explicitly novelty-driven - the authors assert that prior eye-tracking ML studies all extracted features from visual fixation patterns and that 'no study has been found to identify ASD with oculomotor behavior', drawing a conceptual distinction between where attention is directed (fixation) and how the eyes move in the sockets (oculomotor). Findings: segment classification peaked at 74.15% (9 s windows, single feature: entropy of gaze allocation in the x-y plane, sensitivity 75.45%, specificity 72.51%), above the majority-class baseline at every window length; child classification peaked at 87.18% (7 s windows, 46% threshold, sensitivity 89.47%, specificity 85.00%). Feature-level statistics show entropy differences significant at every window length from 1 to 10 s (all p <= .006 for the x-y plane), while range differences are significant only at the shortest windows and fall away beyond 4 s - so the discriminative signal is the irregularity of gaze allocation, not its spatial extent. Secondary observation of substantive interest: ASD children took 191 s to complete the same six-question session against 110 s for TD children (U = 48, p < .01).
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Single site in Shenzhen, China. Autistic children were recruited from a first-class mental health centre (Shenzhen Kangning Hospital / Shenzhen Mental Health Center, the affiliation of the child-psychiatry co-author); TD children came from nearby communities. The recording setting is a controlled but not screen-based one: a face-to-face structured conversation with an interviewer at a fixed 80 cm distance, with the child wearing eye-tracking glasses. This is a clinic-adjacent laboratory setting, not a naturalistic home or classroom setting and not a primary-care setting, so the recruitment path guarantees a spectrum-narrow, already-diagnosed autistic sample facing an unselected community control group - the classic case-control geometry whose accuracy does not transfer to a screening population.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: The paradigm is a structured dyadic conversation, notable in this corpus for being live and social rather than screen-based. Four topic sessions were arranged - Generic question, Hobby sharing, Yes-no question, Question raising - but only the first was analysed, for two stated reasons: gaze behaviour is topic-sensitive so pooling sessions would make segments heterogeneous and harder to classify, and the first session was the longest, yielding the most segments. The six questions of that session are published in an appendix. Two design features deserve credit. Head-mounted rather than remote tracking was chosen deliberately so that head movement is unconstrained and gaze in the scene-camera frame reflects eye-in-socket movement. And the participants were kept naive: they were not told the glasses recorded gaze, were not instructed to keep still, and post-experiment questioning confirmed none had guessed - a control against reactive gaze that most eye-tracking studies in this corpus do not report. The countervailing weakness is that the interviewer is a live human whose own behaviour is not standardised or measured, and who was presumably not blind to group; anything the interviewer did differently with the two groups is baked into the child's gaze.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional; no longitudinal component, no follow-up, no repeat testing, no test-retest reliability for the entropy features. Ethics reporting is the weakest element of the paper: the retrieved full text contains no institutional review board statement, no Declaration of Helsinki statement, and no description of parental consent or child assent, despite the study involving minors, a clinical population, and a deliberate withholding of the device's true purpose from participants. The parent study (Zhao et al., 2021c) may carry the approval, but a secondary analysis reusing identifiable behavioural recordings should restate it. What is declared is a conflict-of-interest statement (none) and a detailed funding list of eight grants.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Tobii Pro Glasses 2 head-mounted eye tracker sampling at 50 Hz, with an integrated 1920 x 1080 scene camera; gaze coordinates exported in pixels by Tobii Pro Lab. Cognitive assessment by Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices. Analysis tooling is not named - no MATLAB, Python, R, scikit-learn or LIBSVM is identified, and the SVM implementation, kernel and hyperparameters are unspecified. Calibration was one-point at the interlocutor's body position within Tobii's recommended 0.5-1.5 m working distance, verified qualitatively by checking that the live-view gaze marker overlapped named targets; no numeric accuracy or precision criterion was applied, and no per-participant tracking-ratio statistic is reported beyond the rule that segments with >30% loss were discarded.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Split. The experimental side is highly reproducible: the conversation protocol and its six questions are published, the 80 cm distance and 50 Hz sampling are given, the segmentation arithmetic is written out index by index, the binning is exact (10 px bins giving 192 x-bins, 108 y-bins and 20,736 x-y blocks), the Shannon entropy formula is stated, and the 30% data-loss rule is cited to its source. The computational side is not: no code, no data, no preregistration, no SVM kernel or regularisation parameter, no random seed, no scaling procedure, no statement of how many segments existed at each window length in numbers rather than a bar chart, and no specification of the grid of thresholds searched. A reader could re-run the experiment on new children but could not reproduce the reported numbers from the authors' data.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The authors state three limitations - restricted phenotype (IQ >= 70, verbal, no severe symptoms, 34 of 39 male), restricted and relatively late age band (6-13 years when the clinically decisive window is nearer 3-4), and, in the discussion, the absence of any non-TD clinical comparison. They self-describe the work as 'proof-of-concept'. The unstated limitations are the ones that bear on the headline numbers. (i) Segments, not children, were randomly partitioned into the ten cross-validation folds, so a child's own segments appear in both training and test sets; with only 39 children and thousands of segments, an SVM can learn individual gaze signatures rather than a group property, and the 74.15% is therefore an upper bound of unknown tightness. (ii) The participant-level 87.18% is the maximum over ten window lengths crossed with an unspecified grid of thresholds, all evaluated on the same 39 children - Table 4 shows the neighbouring windows giving 0.77-0.85, so the reported figure sits at the top of its own selection distribution and the honest summary of the method is closer to 'around 0.79 typical, 0.87 at the best of ten'. (iii) Forward feature selection was performed once on all the data and the resulting feature set reused in every fold, so selection is unnested. (iv) The ASD group's IQ was 15 points lower (p = .019) and is never controlled; gaze dispersion during a demanding conversational task is plausibly related to cognitive ability. (v) ASD children spent 74% longer in the session, which both drives the segment-level class imbalance and means the two groups' segments come from conversations of different length and, presumably, different affective character. (vi) No ethics or consent statement. To the authors' credit, the one comparison they do make carefully is the majority-class baseline at the segment level, which is exactly the empirical chance floor the imbalance demands.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Fuse oculomotor with visual fixation features, since the authors' own earlier work on the same children reached 84.62% from fixation alone and 92.31% with fixation plus conversational length; build a representative ASD oculomotor template on the model of Eraslan et al.'s scan-path trend analysis and classify by similarity to it; pursue the neural basis of gaze irregularity; push the age range down towards the 43-month mean diagnostic age, motivated by evidence of atypical oculomotor behaviour in infants later diagnosed; test against developmental delay and ADHD rather than TD alone; extend to children with more severe presentations and a balanced sex ratio; and separate inherent oculomotor function from visual-attention allocation in unconstrained settings. The last of these is the most interesting, because it is an admission that the paper's central conceptual claim - that it measures oculomotor behaviour rather than attention - is not established by its own data.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Gaze allocation during live social interaction, reduced to two constructs: regularity, measured as Shannon entropy of the spatial distribution of raw gaze points over 10 px bins (x-axis, y-axis and the 20,736-cell x-y grid), and spatial extent, measured as the maximum distance between the two most remote gaze points on each axis and in the plane. Crucially the representation is deliberately atemporal - gaze allocation 'captured how gaze behavior was mapped spatially without taking into account the temporal information', so no scan path, no fixation/saccade parsing, no dwell time and no areas of interest. The behavioural claim being tested is that autistic children spread gaze more diffusely and less predictably across the visual field during conversation. The results support this for entropy at every window length and for range only at short windows. Two further behaviours are measured but not modelled: conversational duration (191 s versus 110 s, p < .01), which the authors interpret as social-processing difficulty, and, implicitly, the willingness to wear glasses and converse for several minutes, which the sample was selected to guarantee.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No fusion in this study - a single modality, six features, and the best model uses exactly one of them. The paper is nonetheless one of the more informative in the corpus about fusion, because the authors have a directly comparable prior study on the identical 39 children: Zhao et al. (2021a) reached 84.62% with visual fixation features alone and 92.31% by adding a single non-eye-tracking feature, conversational length. Set beside the present 87.18% from oculomotor features alone, this gives an unusually clean within-sample comparison of three feature families on the same participants - and it also shows how much of the gain in the earlier fusion result came from conversational length, a variable that is essentially a direct measure of the group difference in task duration reported here (191 s versus 110 s). That is worth flagging as a caution about multimodal gains: a fused feature that is itself a near-proxy for group membership will raise accuracy without adding behavioural insight. The authors' recommendation is to fuse oculomotor with fixation features, and, in the longer term, eye tracking with EEG, neuroimaging and kinematics, arguing that segmentation is the enabling technique because it preserves participants who would otherwise be dropped for data loss in any one stream.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Classical machine learning in two stages. Stage one is a support vector machine classifying individual gaze behaviour segments as ASD-like or TD-like, chosen because 'SVM has been often used in ML studies in the field of ASD' - a popularity rather than a suitability argument, with no comparison against any other classifier. Stage two is a threshold classifier: count the proportion of a child's segments labelled ASD-like and call the child autistic if it exceeds a cut-off tuned to maximise accuracy (46% at the optimal 7 s window). No deep learning, no ensemble, no probabilistic model. The two-stage design - weak per-segment classifier plus aggregation to a strong per-participant decision - is the same multiple-instance shape used by Kojovic et al. in this corpus, and it is a sound idea; the difference is that Kojovic partitioned children before generating segments and this study did not, which is precisely what separates a legitimate aggregation gain from an inflated one.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Six hand-crafted scalar features per fixed-length window of the raw gaze coordinate stream: entropy_x, entropy_y, entropy_xy, range_x, range_y, range_xy. The window length is itself a modelled hyperparameter, swept from 1 to 10 s. The binning that defines the entropy is spatial and fixed to the scene camera resolution (10 px cells), which means the features are defined in the wearer's own head-centred frame rather than in a world or face-referenced frame - an appropriate choice given head-mounted tracking, but one that makes the features depend on the geometry of where the interviewer sat. No normalisation, standardisation or per-participant centring is described, so between-child differences in absolute gaze spread enter the model directly - the same property that makes segment-level pooling risky.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity at both the segment and participant level, plus an ROC curve for the participant-level threshold sweep (the AUC is not stated numerically). Sensitivity and specificity are defined explicitly and correctly at the segment level. Missing: AUC value, PPV/NPV, F1, confidence intervals of any kind, calibration, and any significance test on the classification results (the t-tests reported are on the features, not the models). The absence of confidence intervals matters at this sample size: with 39 children, the difference between 87.18% (34/39 correct) and the 77% seen at four of the ten window lengths is four children.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Good by the standards of this corpus, and honest about the limits of its own interpretation. Forward feature selection produces an explicit ranking, and Table 3 shows the striking result that a single feature - entropy of gaze allocation in the x-y plane - achieves the maximum 74.15% and that adding any of the other five slightly reduces accuracy. Table 2 gives group means, SDs and t-tests for all six features at all ten window lengths, letting a reader see that entropy separates the groups at every scale while range does not beyond 4 s. The discussion then supplies a mechanistic account rather than a post-hoc story: higher entropy in the ASD group follows from gaze being distributed more evenly between social and irrelevant regions instead of concentrating on face and body, referencing the authors' own fixation analysis of the same children. And they close by conceding the interpretive cost - 'the atypical oculomotor performance in the children with ASD was inseparable from visual attention in our study' - which is a rare admission that a paper's headline construct is confounded with the one it set out to distinguish itself from. The model is not interrogated at the individual level: no per-child probabilities, no error analysis, no examination of which five children were misclassified.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: This is the paper's weak point and the reason its two headline numbers should be read very differently from each other. Segment level: tenfold cross-validation with random partition of segments. The text is unambiguous that the unit is the segment ('all behavior samples were randomly partitioned into 10 subsamples'), and there is no statement anywhere that a child's segments were kept together. With 19 + 20 children each contributing tens to hundreds of windows from one continuous recording, adjacent segments from one child are near-duplicates in feature space, and the classifier can exploit stable individual gaze idiosyncrasies - the exact leakage that Keles et al. in this corpus quantified directly by identifying individuals from gaze at 35.4% against 6.2% chance. So 74.15% is not an estimate of performance on an unseen child. Participant level: the aggregation is applied to those already-leaky segment labels, and then two further quantities are optimised on the same 39 children - the window length (10 candidates, Table 4 shows accuracies 0.77 to 0.87) and the threshold (a sweep whose grid is not specified, optimal values 0.40 to 0.56). Reporting the maximum of that joint search as the study's accuracy is best-of-many reporting; the median of Table 4 is 0.78. Feature selection is likewise unnested, run once on all data with the chosen subset reused in every fold. What the study does do right is the segment-level chance floor: the majority-class baseline is computed and plotted at every window length precisely because the class imbalance is group-linked, and the SVM beats it throughout. That is more care about chance than most studies here take, which makes the absence of the corresponding participant-level baseline or permutation test more conspicuous. A corrected design would partition the 39 children into folds, generate segments within folds, run forward feature selection inside each training fold, and select the window length and threshold on training children only - and would very likely report a materially lower number, as Cilia et al. found when they moved from image-level to participant-level evaluation of the same data.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: Autism; Behavior segmentation; Entropy; Eye-tracking; Machine learning; Oculomotor. Two are methodological signatures rather than topic labels - 'Behavior segmentation' names the paper's own technique of cutting a continuous gaze recording into short windows, and 'Entropy' names its single discriminative feature - so the keyword set advertises a method rather than a clinical application. 'Oculomotor' is the conceptual claim the paper stakes out against the existing visual-fixation literature. Neither 'diagnosis' nor 'screening' appears, although the abstract closes by proposing to 'promote the automatic screening of ASD'. Terms carried through the body: threshold classifier, gaze allocation, Shannon entropy, support vector machine, forward feature selection, majority class prediction, face-to-face conversation.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders 53:934-946, an Original Paper - a clinically oriented specialist autism journal rather than an engineering or machine-learning venue. The venue choice shows in the reporting profile: participant characterisation, diagnostic procedure, task protocol and feature-level statistics with t-tests at every window length are all reported to clinical standards, while the computational specification (SVM kernel, regularisation, scaling, code) is thin and the cross-validation unit is left ambiguous. The paper was received in an earlier form, accepted 13 July 2022 and published online 1 August 2022 in the 2022 volume year with a 2023 issue assignment.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published online 2022, issued 2023, from Shenzhen University's Institute of Human Factors and Ergonomics with the Shenzhen Guangming District Center for Disease Control and Prevention and Shenzhen Kangning Hospital - an engineering-plus-public-health-plus-psychiatry collaboration, funded by eight Chinese grants including the National Natural Science Foundation, the Shenzhen Science and Technology Innovation Committee and a Guangdong Key Realm R&D Program. The framing is incremental and explicitly novelty-staking: the authors argue that all prior eye-tracking classification work has used visual fixation patterns and that 'no study has been found to identify ASD with oculomotor behavior', then draw a conceptual distinction between where attention is directed and how the eyes move in the sockets. The clinical motivation is the standard one for the period - diagnosis depends on clinician experience and caregiver report, is time-consuming and may be biased by subjective factors - and the proposed role is complementary, that eye tracking 'might be incorporated in clinical practice to complement existing diagnostic procedure'. The paper is unusual for 2022 in explicitly flagging that the whole eye-tracking classification literature, its own work included, has only ever tested against typical development.

data_charting_rubrics.title: A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Mehralizadeh B; Baradaran B; Nikkhoo S; Soleiman P; Moradi H
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional two-group diagnostic-classification study; an incremental engineering extension of the same group's earlier sensorized toy car (Moradi et al., reference [13]), whose accelerometer-only method is reimplemented from scratch on the new data as an internal baseline
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Hand-crafted statistical, spectral and state-occupancy features aggregated over the whole 3-5 minute play session; one feature vector per child. No time series modelling, no windowing, no learned representation.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Informed parental consent obtained in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, with parents informed of the study, goals, procedure and their rights; data stored under an anonymous participant ID with no name or personal identifiers. A child psychologist from the centre supervised the process.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Free play with a sensorized toy car for 3-5 minutes in a 3 x 4 m room. Unstructured: no instruction, no script, no prompts, no examiner-led task. The child may be alone or accompanied by a parent or therapist, and this is not standardised or recorded as a variable.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: ESP8266 NodeMCU IoT board streaming over Wi-Fi via UDP; ADXL345 MEMS triaxial accelerometer; two Hall-effect magnetic shaft encoders on the front and rear wheels; battery powered; Arduino-based firmware with an ROS package provided for integration. Sampling rate is not stated - only that UDP was chosen 'to ensure a maximum data collection rate'.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: 'The data presented in this study are available on request from the corresponding author'
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not released, but the hardware stack is unusually well specified (ESP8266 NodeMCU, ADXL345, Hall-effect encoders, Arduino firmware) and an ROS package is described as developed for interfacing, which is a reproducibility asset even without a repository link
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Explicitly declined rather than obtained. The Institutional Review Board Statement reads: the proposal was 'accepted by the school of ECE at the University of Tehran considering the privacy of participants and non-intrusiveness of the screening nature of the work'; 'this is a non-intrusive screening that does not require ethics approval as long as the privacy of the participants is considered'; and the work followed the autism centre's own guidelines. So there is departmental sign-off and site guidelines but no ethics-committee review of a study on 3-6 year old children with disabilities.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 44 acceleration features carried over from the earlier version: per-axis mean (3), variance (3), the five most common frequencies per axis (15), the amplitudes of those frequencies (15), signal energy per axis (3), pairwise inter-axis correlations (3), number of jolts (1) and playing-time duration (1). Ten new features: the ratios of not-playing, wheels-only, ground and air play to total playtime; the ratios of wheels-only, ground and air play to interactive playtime (states 2-4); total wheel turn rate; and counts of fast tilt movements about the X and Y axes, derived by short-time Fourier transform of the acceleration signal to recover roll and pitch during wheel play.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Feature-level and mechanistically motivated. The four play states are defined by an explicit and physically interpretable signature - encoder active with accelerometer static means wheel spinning, accelerometer active with encoder static means the car is being moved through the air, both active means floor play, neither means no play - and the selected features are named individually. The design rationale is observational: the authors state that after testing version 1 they noticed autistic children 'spent a great amount of time on rotating the wheels and watching them rotate' while TD children were interested but spent significantly less time on it. No per-child explanation, no error analysis, no examination of which children were misclassified.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Only the SVM kernel choice is described ('by performing several tests on three kinds of SVM, SVM with a linear kernel was selected for its considerably better performance on our data'). The procedure that selected it, and the data on which it was selected, are not stated.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 'The collection of 46 subjects' data was divided into two groups: the training set with 80% of samples and the test set with 20% of the remaining samples. The K-fold cross-validation method separated the test set in k = 5 different ways to generalize the result.' This reads as 5-fold cross-validation over the 46 children, with each fold's ~9 held-out children forming a test set, and the reported figures being fold averages. The unit is the child, so there is no within-child leakage - but the feature selection that produced the final 10-feature vector is described as operating on 'all the features' with no statement of nesting inside the folds.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Essentially none as a dedicated section. Two admissions appear in passing: the baseline accuracy is lower than the earlier paper's because 'the data are different and the setups for collecting data were different too' and because the prior method was reimplemented from scratch and 'may differ in the way that it was optimized before'; and the future-work paragraph concedes that at this stage the system 'can be used as a warning system to inform parents and caregivers to turn to experts for further evaluation', which is an appropriately modest positioning of a 46-child result.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Three groups recruited, two modelled. Recruited: 28 children with ASD, 18 typically developing children, and 4 children with other disorders (cerebral palsy and fragile X syndrome), total 50, all aged 3-6 years and tested at an autism centre in Tehran. Modelled: 46 subjects, which is exactly 28 + 18, so the four-child other-disorder group is excluded from every classification result without the exclusion being stated. A further subgroup is described but not removed: five of the 28 autistic children 'did not seem interested in playing with the sensorized toy car and neglected it completely', so roughly 18% of the autism group contributed a session of near-zero play. Whether their data were retained is not stated explicitly, but the 46-subject count implies they were, and one of the three selected encoder features is the not-playing ratio.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'Children with autism (ASD)', 'children with ASD' and the abbreviation ASD throughout; 'Typically Developed (TD) children' - an idiosyncratic expansion of the usual 'typically developing'. Person-first construction is used consistently ('children with ASD', 'people with ASD'). The clinical framing is medical-model and unhedged: autism is 'a neurodevelopmental disorder that causes problems in social communication and interaction', the targeted behaviours are named as 'symptoms' including 'the obsessive attention to detail' and 'repetitive behaviors', and the conclusion refers to the system as screening 'cognitive deficits'. There is no engagement with neurodiversity perspectives and no autistic-community involvement statement, although the framing of purpose - equitable access to screening in low- and middle-income and rural settings, tied to the UN Sustainable Development Goals - is unusual in this corpus and reflects a genuine health-equity motivation.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Extremely thin. Table 2 reports only group size, mean age and median age: ASD n = 28, mean 4.63, median 4.0; TD n = 18, mean 4.61, median 4.0; others n = 4, mean and median 5.5. Age is therefore well matched between the two modelled groups, which matters for a motor-play task in 3-6 year olds. Nothing else is reported: no sex distribution for any group, no IQ or developmental quotient, no language level, no socioeconomic status, no race or ethnicity, no comorbidities, no medication. The absence of sex counts is a deliberate, argued choice rather than an oversight - the authors state they did not balance sex because play complexity and toy engagement with car-like toys have been shown to be similar across sexes in autistic children - but declining to balance a variable is not a reason to decline to report it, and without the counts a reader cannot check whether the two groups happened to differ. Given that all children were recruited at a single autism centre in Tehran, the sample is also culturally and geographically homogeneous, which is worth noting for a device whose selling point is deployment in homes worldwide.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not reported at all - this is the study's most serious gap. The paper never states how any child's autism diagnosis was established: no DSM or ICD criteria, no ADOS, ADI-R, CARS, GARS or M-CHAT, no named clinician or team, no date of diagnosis, no inclusion or exclusion criteria for either group. The only clue is the recruitment site, an autism centre, so the ASD label is presumably the child's existing service-eligibility status. TD status is equally unspecified: the typically developing children are not described as having been screened for autism or developmental delay by any instrument, and their recruitment route is not given. The four children in the other-disorder group are labelled with CP and fragile X, again with no source. The result is that the study's target variable - the thing the 85.56% accuracy is accurate about - is undefined. This places it at the weakest end of reference-standard reporting in this corpus, below even the studies that use a single unblinded clinician's DSM judgement, because here there is no statement of any process at all.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, developmental, adaptive, language or motor assessment was administered to any participant, and no autism severity measure was obtained. This is a substantive omission for two reasons specific to this design. First, the task is a fine and gross motor task performed by 3-6 year olds, and the extracted features - jolt counts, acceleration energy, tilt rates, spatial extent of movement - are all motor-competence-sensitive; without a developmental or motor measure it is impossible to separate an autism-specific play signature from a general developmental-level difference, particularly since the authors themselves observe that 'the TD children played with more energy and they moved the car in a wider area compared to the other two groups'. Second, the discussion rests its case for multimodality on within-spectrum heterogeneity - 'children with ASD may be at different parts of the ASD spectrum' - which is precisely the variable the study does not measure, so the claim cannot be tested against the data and the model cannot be checked for whether it succeeds only on more severely affected children.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: to extend the group's existing accelerometer-only sensorized toy car by adding wheel shaft encoders, testing whether autistic children's documented interest in rotating objects can be captured as a second sensing modality and whether fusing it with movement features improves screening accuracy. The comparison is deliberately internal - the authors state they do not wish to compare their accuracy against other modalities in the literature, only against their own version 1. Findings: the reimplemented accelerometer-only baseline achieved 71.11% accuracy on the new data (lower than the 85% reported for version 1, attributed to different data, different collection setup and a from-scratch reimplementation); adding encoder features gave 78.61%; adding new roll/pitch acceleration features instead gave 75.83%; adding both gave 85.56% with sensitivity 81.67%, specificity 81.00% and precision 87.67% - the claimed improvement of more than 10 percentage points over baseline. Of the ten features surviving two rounds of backward elimination, three came from the encoders: the ratio of wheels-only play to total playtime, the not-playing ratio, and the total wheel turn rate. A secondary and arguably more informative finding is that random forest on the full feature set gave lower accuracy (80.83%) but the best sensitivity and specificity of any configuration (85.48%, 83.67%), which the authors flag as a reason a deployer might prefer it - a rare instance in this corpus of explicitly preferring a model on error-profile grounds rather than on headline accuracy.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Single site: an autism centre in Tehran, Iran. Children played in a 3 x 4 m room at the centre for 3-5 minutes, alone or accompanied by a parent or therapist, with a child psychologist from the centre supervising. This creates a gap between the study as conducted and the study as framed: the paper's central argument is for a home-based IoT device usable 'at homes, daycares, or clinics' in natural settings without expert involvement, and it repeatedly criticises fMRI, EEG and robot-based approaches for requiring specialised centres - yet all the reported data were collected at a specialised centre under psychologist supervision. The recruitment geometry is also the standard case-control one: an already-identified autistic group from a service setting against a typically developing comparison group, at 61% autism prevalence, which is roughly 60 times the population base rate the device is proposed to screen at.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Three to five minutes of unstructured free play with a toy car in a small room. This is one of the least constrained paradigms in the corpus and that is largely a virtue - there is no script, no examiner prompt, no screen, no wearable, and the electronics are hidden inside the car body specifically so the child is not distracted by them, so what is measured is spontaneous object play. The cost of that freedom is that nothing is standardised: session length varies by up to 67% between children, the presence of a parent or therapist in the room varies and is not recorded, whether anyone interacted with or encouraged the child is not stated, and the floor surface, lighting and available space beyond the room dimensions are not described. Because several features are ratios normalised by total or interactive playtime, some of this variability is absorbed, but the absolute features (jolt count, wheel turn rate, energy) are not obviously duration-invariant. The four-state decomposition is the paradigm's real contribution: by defining not-playing, wheels-only, floor and air play through the joint accelerometer/encoder signature, the authors turn an unstructured session into an interpretable behavioural budget.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up, no test-retest reliability for any feature - which matters for a device intended for repeated home use. Ethics reporting is unusual and problematic. Consent is handled well: parents were informed of the study, its goals, the procedure and their rights, informed consent was obtained in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, a child psychologist supervised, and data were stored under anonymous participant IDs without names or personal information. But formal ethics review was not obtained and the Institutional Review Board Statement argues that it was not needed: the proposal was accepted by the University of Tehran's School of ECE 'considering the privacy of participants and non-intrusiveness of the screening nature of the work', and the authors assert that 'this is a non-intrusive screening that does not require ethics approval as long as the privacy of the participants is considered', supplemented by the autism centre's own guidelines. A departmental engineering-school sign-off plus site guidelines is not equivalent to ethics-committee review of research on 3-6 year old children with developmental disabilities, and the non-intrusiveness of the measurement does not remove the need for review of recruitment, consent and data handling in a vulnerable population.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Well documented at the hardware level, undocumented at the software level. Hardware: an ESP8266 NodeMCU IoT board streaming sensor data over Wi-Fi by UDP; an ADXL345 MEMS triaxial accelerometer; two Hall-effect magnetic shaft encoders mounted on the front and rear wheels; battery power; all electronics concealed inside the car. Firmware is built on the Arduino ecosystem explicitly to simplify future development, and an ROS package was written so the car can be integrated into other screening systems - a genuine and unusual contribution to reusability. Software for analysis: nothing is named - no Python, MATLAB, scikit-learn or equivalent, no SVM implementation or regularisation parameter, no MLP architecture or augmentation method, no random forest settings. Two acquisition parameters that a replicator would need are also missing: the sampling rate of the accelerometer and encoders, and any accounting of packet loss, which is a real concern because UDP was chosen precisely for throughput over reliability and offers no delivery guarantee.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Mixed, with an unusual profile: this is one of the few studies in the corpus where the physical apparatus is more reproducible than the analysis. A reader could rebuild the car from the part numbers given and would have the ROS interface and Arduino firmware ecosystem described. Both feature tables are complete, listing all 44 baseline acceleration features with their symbols and all 10 new features with their definitions, and the final selected subset is named feature by feature. The four play states are defined operationally. Room size and session duration are given. Data are available on request. Against this: no code repository, no sampling rate, no model hyperparameters for any of the three algorithms, no random seed or fold assignment, no statement of whether feature selection was refit inside each fold, and no diagnostic criteria - so the labels themselves could not be reproduced. There is also an internal reference error, with the text pointing to 'Table 4' for the results that appear in Table 5.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The paper has no limitations section, and the omission is felt. What it does concede is narrow but honest: that the reimplemented baseline underperforms the original because the data and collection setup differed and the optimisation may not have matched; and, in the future-work paragraph, that at this stage the system should serve as a warning to prompt expert referral rather than as a diagnostic tool. The unacknowledged limitations are substantial. (i) No reference standard is described for any group, so the classification target is undefined. (ii) Six model/feature configurations are reported in Table 5 and the maximum is presented as the result, with no penalty for selection; the honest reading of an SVM chosen among three kernels, three algorithms and four feature sets on 46 children is that 85.56% is the top of a search distribution whose other members run 71-81%. (iii) Feature selection by two rounds of backward elimination over all 46 children's data, described before and separately from the evaluation, appears unnested, which on a 54-feature vector and 46 samples is exactly the regime where selection bias is largest. (iv) The engagement confound is stated in the text and then never revisited: five autistic children ignored the car entirely, all TD children were 'very interested', and the not-playing ratio is one of the three encoder features selected into the final model - so part of the classifier's discriminative power is a measure of whether the child engaged with the toy at all, which is a real behavioural difference but not the attention-to-rotating-objects mechanism the paper claims to have captured. (v) No developmental or motor measure exists to rule out general developmental level as the driver, despite the authors' own observation that TD children 'played with more energy and moved the car in a wider area'. (vi) The four CP/fragile X children were recruited and dropped. (vii) The reported metrics do not fully reconcile: at 28 ASD and 18 TD, row 6's sensitivity of 81.67% and specificity of 81.00% imply an accuracy near 81.4%, not 85.56%, and rows 1 and 4 show similar discrepancies, so either the class balance within folds differs from the overall sample or the columns are not all computed on the same basis.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Three concrete directions, the first two of which address real gaps. Test on a wider population and on a variety of cognitive deficits to determine whether the device can differentiate autism from other conditions rather than only from typical development - which is precisely what the four excluded CP and fragile X children could have begun to address. Investigate how the toy car's size, shape and colour affect children's engagement with it and therefore the extracted features - a design-sensitivity question rarely raised in this literature and directly relevant to whether a play-based screen generalises across devices. And position the device as one component of a larger multimodal screening system rather than standalone, on the argument that different autistic children present different symptoms so a single modality will always miss some.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Two behavioural constructs, both explicitly named as autism symptoms and both operationalised through the child's manipulation of a single object. First, interest in rotating objects and attention to parts rather than wholes, captured by the wheels-only play state: the encoder registers wheel rotation while the accelerometer shows the car body stationary, meaning the child is spinning the wheels and watching them rather than driving the car. The design was prompted by direct observation with version 1 that autistic children spent a great deal of time rotating the wheels and watching them while TD children did so much less. Second, movement and repetitive-play patterns, captured by the triaxial acceleration signature of the car being driven - its spectral content, energy, inter-axis correlation, jolt count and tilt dynamics. The four-state decomposition (not playing, wheels only, on the floor, in the air) is the behavioural core of the paper and yields an interpretable budget of how a child spends a play session. A third behaviour enters the model implicitly and without acknowledgement: engagement with the toy itself, via the not-playing ratio, which is dominated by the five autistic children who ignored the car completely against a TD group in which every child was 'very interested'.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Genuine two-stream fusion within a single physical device, and one of the cleaner ablation designs in the corpus. Streams: triaxial acceleration of the car body (movement pattern) and dual wheel shaft encoders (rotation). Fusion is early - after two rounds of backward elimination, first within each modality using inter-feature correlation and then across modalities, the selected features from both streams are concatenated into one vector for training. The ablation is fully reported and interpretable: 71.11% for acceleration alone, 78.61% for acceleration plus encoders, 75.83% for acceleration plus the new roll/pitch features, and 85.56% for all three sets, showing that each addition contributes and that the two contributions are partly complementary rather than redundant. The complementarity has a physical basis rather than a statistical one: the two sensors disambiguate states that either alone would confuse, since a stationary car with spinning wheels and a car carried through the air with static wheels are distinguishable only by looking at both signals together, and the new roll/pitch features are themselves derived by short-time Fourier transform of the accelerometer specifically to characterise what the body is doing during wheel play. The caution is that the ablation shares the sample and the feature-selection procedure with the final model, so the gains are measured under the same optimistic conditions as the headline accuracy; and that the largest single-feature contributor from the encoder side may be the not-playing ratio, which indexes engagement rather than rotation interest.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Classical machine learning throughout, with three algorithms compared: a linear-kernel SVM as the primary model, a random forest, and a multilayer perceptron trained with unspecified data augmentation. The SVM was retained because it outperformed the others on overall accuracy, and the linear kernel was chosen after testing three kernel types. No deep learning, no sequence model, no probabilistic or Bayesian approach; the whole session is collapsed to one fixed-length feature vector per child before any model sees it. The choice is defensible at n = 46 and the authors implicitly acknowledge the sample-size constraint by noting that 'the size of the training set is small compared to the size of the feature vector' as the motivation for aggressive feature reduction. The most interesting modelling observation in the paper is the discussion of the SVM/random forest trade-off: the random forest is 4.7 points worse on accuracy but better on both sensitivity and specificity, and the authors state plainly that a user may prefer it because it would miss fewer autistic children and mislabel fewer typically developing ones - an error-profile argument that most studies in this corpus never make.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A single 54-dimensional hand-crafted feature vector per child, reduced to 10 by feature selection. The 44 inherited acceleration features are per-axis means, variances, the five dominant frequencies and their amplitudes, signal energies, pairwise inter-axis correlations, a jolt count and the playing-time duration - i.e. a mix of time-domain statistics and coarse spectral descriptors computed over the whole session. The 10 new features are of two kinds: seven state-occupancy ratios derived from the joint encoder/accelerometer signature (fractions of total and of interactive playtime spent not playing, on wheels only, on the ground and in the air) plus the total wheel turn rate, and two tilt-count features (about X and about Y) obtained by short-time Fourier transform of the acceleration signal to recover the car's roll and pitch during wheel play. The representation is therefore entirely aggregate: no temporal ordering, no sequence, no windowing, and no per-episode analysis, so a child who spins the wheels once for ninety seconds and one who spins them thirty times for three seconds each are indistinguishable. The final selected set was seven acceleration features (Y-direction jolt, tilt about Y, X-direction energy, X-Y acceleration correlation, the fourth-highest X frequency, the fifth-highest Z frequency, and the relative amplitude of the highest Y frequency) and three encoder features (wheels-only play ratio, not-playing ratio, total wheel turn rate).
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and precision, reported for all six classifier/feature configurations in a single table, plus a confusion matrix for the best model. Reporting four metrics across a full ablation grid rather than one number for one model is better practice than much of this corpus. What is missing: AUC or ROC, F1, any confidence interval or standard deviation across the five folds, calibration, and any translation of the operating point to a screening context - no PPV or NPV at a plausible population prevalence, despite the paper's entire argument being about population-level screening access. At the study's own 60.9% prevalence a precision of 87.67% is unremarkable; at a 1-2% community prevalence, sensitivity 81.7% with specificity 81.0% would give a positive predictive value in the low single digits, which is the number that matters for a device proposed for home and daycare use. There is also an internal consistency problem: for several rows the reported accuracy cannot be recovered from the reported sensitivity and specificity given the 28:18 class ratio - row 6 implies about 81.4% rather than 85.56%, row 4 about 72.3% rather than 78.61%, and row 1 about 77.3% rather than 71.11% - so the columns appear not to be computed on a common basis.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Good, and grounded in physics rather than post-hoc attribution. Every feature is a named, humanly meaningful quantity, and the four play states are defined by an explicit and checkable sensor logic: encoder moving with accelerometer static means wheel spinning; accelerometer moving with encoder static means the car is airborne; both moving means floor play; neither means no play. The selected 10 features are listed individually so a reader can see exactly what the model uses, and the three encoder features that survived - wheels-only ratio, not-playing ratio, total wheel turn rate - map directly onto the behavioural hypothesis that motivated the hardware change. The mechanism itself came from observation of children playing with version 1, not from a literature-driven guess, which is a legitimate and transparent route to a feature. What is absent is any quantitative feature-level analysis: no group means or effect sizes for the wheels-only ratio or any other feature, no statistical test that autistic children actually spin the wheels more, no feature importances or coefficients, and no error analysis. So the paper can say which features the classifier used but cannot say by how much the groups differ on them, which is why the not-playing-ratio confound cannot be assessed from the reported results.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Better than most on the split unit, weaker on everything downstream. The unit of splitting is the child - one aggregate feature vector per participant - so the segment-level leakage that inflates results throughout this corpus is impossible here by construction, and the paper deserves credit for that even though it is a consequence of the aggregate representation rather than a deliberate safeguard. The reported scheme is an 80/20 division with 5-fold cross-validation rotating which 20% is held out, giving fold test sets of about 9 children and averaged metrics. The problems lie elsewhere. First, feature selection: two consecutive rounds of backward elimination were run over the feature set, described in a section that precedes the results and with the surviving 10 features named as a fixed outcome, with no indication that the procedure was repeated within each training fold. Selecting 10 of 54 features on all 46 children and then cross-validating the chosen subset is a well-characterised source of optimism, and it is most severe exactly in this regime of many features and few samples - the regime the authors themselves identify as the reason feature reduction was needed. Second, model selection: three algorithms, three SVM kernels and four feature configurations were evaluated on the same 46 children, and the maximum of that grid is the abstract's claim. Third, no chance baseline: the majority class alone gives 60.9%, and no permutation test or confidence interval is reported, so with roughly 9 children per test fold a single child's label moves fold accuracy by 11 percentage points and the difference between the 78.61% and 85.56% configurations is a handful of children. Fourth, prevalence: 61% autism in the modelled sample against a population rate near 1-2%, with no prevalence-adjusted metric. The corrective design is straightforward and worth stating for the synthesis - move both backward-elimination rounds and the kernel/algorithm choice inside the training folds, report the mean and spread across folds rather than the best cell of the grid, add a majority-class and a permutation baseline, and retain the CP and fragile X children as a differential-diagnosis check.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: autism spectrum disorder (ASD); sensorized toy; machine learning; IoT. The inclusion of 'IoT' rather than a clinical term signals where the paper locates itself - in connected-device engineering, not diagnostics - and 'sensorized toy' is the contribution rather than a topic. Neither 'screening', 'diagnosis' nor any behavioural term appears, despite screening being the stated purpose. Terms carried through the body: playing patterns, attention to details, interest in rotating objects, repetitive behaviors, shaft encoders, multi-modal features, early screening, sustainable development.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Sustainability 15(10), article 7790, MDPI, in a section handled by an academic editor from the image-processing field. This is an open-access multidisciplinary sustainability journal rather than a clinical, autism-specialist or biomedical-engineering venue, and the fit is achieved through an explicit framing device: the paper argues that low-cost widespread screening advances the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals by extending access to under-served and rural populations, and the argument recurs in the abstract, discussion and conclusion. That framing explains several features of the report - the emphasis on device cost and expert-independence, the comparison table of competing modalities by accessibility and cost, and the near-absence of clinical detail such as diagnostic criteria. Received 28 December 2022, revised 13 March 2023, accepted 25 April 2023, published 10 May 2023, CC BY.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2023 from the University of Tehran (Mechanical Engineering and ECE) with co-authors then at the University of Minnesota and UC Riverside, with no external funding. The framing is health-equity engineering rather than diagnostics: the opening premise is that many cases remain undiagnosed 'due to the limited access to experts, especially in low and middle-income societies', and the proposed answer is a device cheap enough to deploy in homes and daycares. Version 2 of an existing platform, so the framing is explicitly incremental - the contributions are stated as introducing a new modality and suggesting new features, and the authors state that they do not wish to compare their accuracy against other modalities in the literature but only against their own version 1. That restraint is unusual and appropriate. The paper is also of its moment in treating multimodality as an answer to within-spectrum heterogeneity - different autistic children show different symptoms, so a comprehensive screen needs several sensing channels - an argument that recurs across the 2022-2023 papers in this corpus.

data_charting_rubrics.title: A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Milano N; Simeoli R; Rega A; Marocco D
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional two-group diagnostic-classification study; a new modelling analysis of a dataset the same group collected and previously described descriptively (Simeoli et al., 2020, 2021), where the earlier descriptive analysis had been unable to distinguish the groups significantly
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Hand-crafted kinematic and touch descriptors aggregated to task level - 60 children x 25 tasks = 1,500 observations of 12 features, with a parallel 1,500 x 1 label vector carrying the child's diagnosis (0 = TD, 1 = ASD). No raw trajectory sequence, no image, no learned front end.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Written informed consent provided by participants' legal guardians / next of kin
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A Unity/C# Android tablet reimplementation of five subtests of the Leiter-3 Cognitive Battery, administered following the original test's instruction procedure. Each scene presents up to five draggable moving cards at the bottom and up to eight fixed placeholders at the top, with distracting stimuli and image detail increasing progressively across five difficulty levels. Each child performed 25 tasks, five per difficulty level. The examiner gave instructions using pointing and gesture guides without vocal aid, then left the child to perform unaided. A task counted as complete when every moving card had been placed in a placeholder, regardless of whether the answer was correct - but only trajectories from correctly performed tasks were analysed, 'to avoid the noise of the cognitive mistakes for the classification process'.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Android 6.0 tablet, 241.9 x 149.5 x 8.5 mm, 9.6 inch screen at 1280 x 800 and 60 Hz; custom software in Unity and C#; finger position logged at 40 Hz; features computed in RStudio with the traj package (Leffondree et al., 2004; Sylvestre et al., 2006)
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: 'The raw data supporting the conclusions of this article will be made available by the authors, without undue reservation'
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Reviewed and approved by the Ethical Committee of Psychological Research of the Department of Humanities, University of Naples Federico II
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: A trajectory is the set of coordinates from first tap to finger lift for one dragging movement. Twelve features per trajectory: mean, max, min and SD of speed; mean, max, min and SD of acceleration; STH (straightness, the ratio of start-to-end distance to path length, 0-1 with 1 a straight line, an index of linearity); DC (directional change over time, an index of nonlinearity); sdDC (SD of directional change, a measure of irregularity); and MeanLength (average number of finite trajectories per task). Trajectory-level values were averaged per task, giving one 12-dimensional vector per child per task.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: The strongest element of the paper and its actual contribution. Rather than reporting feature importances post hoc, the authors interrogate the learned latent space directly: they fit analytic bivariate Gaussians to each class's latent cloud, then perform Monte Carlo sampling of each input feature in turn while holding the other eleven fixed, tracking how the participant's latent projection moves and at what feature values the class assignment reverses. Figure 5 renders this as a per-feature density map over the latent space and Figure 6 as class-membership probability curves against raw feature values. The explicit clinical proposal is that these curves supply threshold values a clinician could use, singly or jointly, as quantitative indicators. Replacing the predictor network with the fitted densities at inference time is also motivated on interpretability and safety grounds - it is intended to stop a new participant landing in an unvisited region of latent space and being confidently misclassified, an outlier-detection framing the authors relate to Zhou and Paffenroth (2017).
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Only the latent dimensionality is described: a model with 10 latent variables was trained, PCA on the latent space showed the first two components explained 95% of its variance, and subsequent analyses were restricted to two latent variables. No layer sizes, neuron counts, learning rate, optimiser, batch size, epoch count or activation functions beyond tanh and softmax are reported, despite a full section of the Methods being devoted to explaining what an artificial neural network is.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 10-fold cross-validation over the 1,500 task observations, reporting mean accuracy 91.2% +/- 5.6% on the test folds. The unit of partition is the observation, not the child: each child contributes 25 rows to the dataset and there is no statement that a child's rows were kept within a single fold, so under a standard k-fold split roughly 22 to 23 of any test child's own task observations sit in the training data.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: One, and it is a conceptual rather than a methodological limitation: that a supervised classification step was needed at the outset, so 'we had to rely on the traditional assessment method to provide the ground truth to the model', whereas 'optimal VAE functioning could be entirely unsupervised'. The authors attribute this to sample size and sample characteristics and present unsupervised latent organisation as the goal of future work.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 30, total 60 children aged 5-10 years. ASD group: 30 children, mean age 7 years +/- 1.4, recruited from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center where they were receiving psychomotor and speech therapy, all diagnosed under both DSM-5 criteria and ADOS-2, with no existing comorbidities as an inclusion requirement. TD group: 30 children, mean age 6 years 8 months +/- 1, recruited from a primary school, with no confirmed neurodevelopmental disorder and excluded for suspected autism signs, developmental abnormalities, or any current or past psychiatric or neurological history. All 60 had normal vision and no sensory or motor deficits, and any child about whom a clinician or teacher was uncertain was excluded. No attrition or exclusions after enrolment are reported. The modelled dataset, however, is not 60 rows but 1,500: each child contributed 25 task observations (five tasks at each of five difficulty levels), and it is these observations, not the children, that are the unit of the reported cross-validation.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'Children with autism', 'autism spectrum disorder (ASD)', 'ASD group', 'typically developing (TD) group'. Person-first phrasing predominates but slips into group-as-noun usage in the results and discussion ('classify ASD and TD individuals', 'ASD trajectories', 'the ASD one'). The framing is firmly medical: autism is 'a by-birth neurodevelopmental disorder', characterised by 'communication and social impairment and restricted, repetitive, and stereotyped behaviours', and the target construct is 'motor abnormalities' throughout - abnormality rather than difference. One usage requires comment: the six autistic children with IQ 59-70 are described as having 'mild mental retardation', with the WHO (2016) cited as the source of the classification. That terminology is outdated in English-language practice, where intellectual disability is standard, and its appearance in a 2023 paper is worth noting even allowing for translation from Italian and for the cited WHO/ICD source. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement statement, though the stated purpose - to give clinicians objective quantitative indicators to supplement a process the authors criticise as subjective and examiner-dependent - is a clinician-support rather than a replacement agenda.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Partial. Reported: group sizes (30/30), mean and SD of age per group (7 +/- 1.4 versus 6 years 8 months +/- 1), age range 5-10, and IQ ranges per group from the Leiter-3 (ASD 59-109, TD 74-110), with the note that six autistic children scored between 59 and 70 and that no severe or profound impairment was present. Recruitment source is given for both groups. Not reported: sex distribution for either group - a striking omission in a 60-child study where sex ratio is both clinically salient and trivially available; race or ethnicity; socioeconomic status; parental education; language level; medication; and any positive comorbidity data, since comorbidity was an exclusion criterion. Two features of what is reported deserve emphasis. First, IQ is given only as a range, with no mean or SD, so the distributions cannot be compared - yet the ranges are visibly asymmetric and six autistic children sit below the TD group's floor of 74, which matters because the index task is a reimplementation of a cognitive test and the analysis is restricted to correctly performed trials. Second, the two groups differ systematically in more than diagnosis: the autistic children were recruited from a rehabilitation centre and were actively receiving psychomotor therapy, i.e. motor intervention, while the controls came from a mainstream school, so exposure to motor training is confounded with group membership in a study whose outcome is motor kinematics.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Among the better-specified in this corpus. Autism required satisfaction of two independent criteria - DSM-5 clinical criteria and the ADOS-2 - with diagnoses made by 'qualified doctors and professionals in the sector', and the absence of comorbidity was an explicit inclusion requirement. This is a dual-criterion standard including a gold-standard observational instrument, which places it above the single-clinician, registry-label or unspecified approaches seen elsewhere here. Typically developing status was established negatively rather than by instrument: no confirmed neurodevelopmental disorder, no suspected signs of autism, no developmental abnormality, no psychiatric or neurological history, plus an unusual and sensible catch-all whereby 'any child whose clinician or teacher was uncertain about the child's diagnosis or health was excluded'. That conservative rule reduces the risk of undetected autistic traits in the control group, though no screening instrument (SCQ, SRS, CAST) was administered to confirm it. Three details limit the standard's usefulness. The ADOS-2 module, algorithm scores and comparison scores are never reported, so the instrument is used as a gate and then discarded as data. Diagnosing clinicians are described only generically. And there is no statement of the interval between diagnosis and testing.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Cognitive ability was measured in every participant with the Leiter-3 International Performance Scale, a non-verbal instrument appropriate for this population, and reported as a per-group range (ASD 59-109, TD 74-110) with the six autistic children in the 59-70 band identified. No means, SDs or statistical comparison are given. Autism severity was not measured or reported at all: ADOS-2 was administered for diagnosis but no severity, comparison or algorithm score is carried into the paper, so the position of these 30 children on the spectrum is unknown, no analysis relates model output to symptom severity, and it cannot be checked whether the model succeeds preferentially on more affected children. No language, adaptive-functioning or motor-competence measure was obtained, the last being a notable gap in a study whose entire signal is motor. There is also a structural entanglement peculiar to this design: the Leiter-3 serves simultaneously as the cognitive measure and, in tablet form, as the experimental task, so the kinematic features are recorded while children perform the very test used to characterise their cognitive ability, and only trials they completed correctly are analysed. Cognitive ability is therefore not an independent covariate here - it conditions which trajectories exist in the dataset.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: to move beyond descriptive comparison of touchscreen motion features - which the group's own earlier work (Simeoli et al., 2020) had found insufficient to distinguish the groups significantly - by using a variational autoencoder to learn a low-dimensional latent distribution of movement, and then to interrogate that latent space to identify which kinematic features drive classification and at what values. The framing is explicitly dual: not merely a diagnostic classifier but 'a new quantitative method to assess ASD', with the theoretical grounding in embodied cognition and predictive coding and the claim that motor abnormality is an underrated defining feature of autism. Findings: task-level cross-validated accuracy 91.2% +/- 5.6%; a latent space in which the two groups occupy distinct, approximately Gaussian regions, with cleaner separation when participants are plotted as the mean of their 25 tasks than task by task; latent structure stable across initialisations up to rotation; and, from Monte Carlo perturbation of one feature at a time, the finding that sdSpeed, MaxAcceleration, MinAcceleration and sdAcceleration have the largest capacity to move a participant across the latent space and reverse their classification, while sdDC, MeanSpeed, MaxSpeed and MeanLength map preferentially into the TD region and are judged marginal. The fitted class densities give signed rules - higher MaxAcceleration and sdAcceleration, and lower MaxSpeed and MinAcceleration, increase the probability of ASD assignment - which the authors offer to clinicians as candidate threshold values.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Two sites in Campania, Italy, and the pairing is itself a confound. Autistic children came from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center, which is also the employer of two of the four authors, and were undergoing psychomotor and speech therapy there. Typically developing children came from a mainstream primary school. Testing conditions were standardised across both groups - the same tablet, a table 65-70 cm high with the tablet within 20 cm of the edge, the examiner seated opposite, the same instruction protocol - so the acquisition chain does not differ by group in the way it does in some other studies in this corpus. But the recruitment geometry is the classic case-control one at 50% prevalence, and it carries a specific extra risk here: the autistic group's ongoing psychomotor therapy is an intervention directed precisely at the motor system whose kinematics constitute the study's entire feature set. Whether that therapy makes autistic movement more or less like typical movement, it makes the two groups differ in motor training history as well as in diagnosis.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A tablet reimplementation, built in Unity and C#, of five subtests of the Leiter-3 Cognitive Battery, administered following the original test's instruction procedure with the examiner switching between subtests as the manual prescribes. Each scene shows up to five draggable cards at the bottom and up to eight placeholders at the top that capture cards dragged nearby, with distracting stimuli and image detail increasing across five difficulty levels; each child completed 25 tasks, five per level. Instructions were delivered by pointing and gesture without vocal aid, after which the child worked unaided. The design has real strengths: it is a standardised, clinically meaningful task rather than an ad hoc game, it varies difficulty systematically, and it captures fine motor behaviour as a by-product of a cognitive assessment the child would plausibly undergo anyway - which is the most translationally attractive property of the whole approach, since it means no additional testing burden. Two design decisions constrain interpretation. A task counted as complete when all cards had been placed regardless of correctness, but only correctly performed tasks were analysed 'to avoid the noise of the cognitive mistakes for the classification process'. This conditions the analysed sample on cognitive success and, if the groups differ in error rate - which is likely given the IQ ranges and six autistic children below the TD floor - removes trials differentially by group, changing what the retained trajectories represent. No error rates per group are reported, so the size of this effect cannot be assessed.
