And features are averaged to task level, so within-task temporal structure and trial-to-trial variability, both plausibly informative about motor control, are discarded before modelling.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up, no test-retest reliability for any kinematic feature - which matters for a proposal to use feature values as clinical thresholds, since a threshold is only useful if the measurement is stable within a child across occasions. Ethics reporting is complete and appropriate: the study was reviewed and approved by the Ethical Committee of Psychological Research of the Department of Humanities, University of Naples Federico II, and written informed consent was obtained from participants' legal guardians. The conflict-of-interest statement discloses that two authors were employed by Neapolisanit S.R.L., the rehabilitation centre from which the autistic participants were recruited - a material disclosure, correctly made. Funding is not reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Hardware and capture: an Android 6.0 tablet, 241.9 x 149.5 x 8.5 mm with a 9.6 inch 1280 x 800 screen at 60 Hz refresh, running custom software written in Unity and C# that logged finger position at 40 Hz. Cognitive assessment: Leiter-3 International Performance Scale. Feature extraction: RStudio with the traj package, citing Leffondree et al. (2004) and Sylvestre et al. (2006) - a specific, checkable toolchain. Modelling software is not named at all: no TensorFlow, PyTorch, Keras or equivalent, and no architecture details beyond 'a simple multilayer perceptron' predictor with a tanh intermediate layer and softmax output. The imbalance in the Methods is conspicuous - roughly two pages explain what a feed-forward neural network and backpropagation are, at textbook level, while the actual network used in the experiments has no stated layer sizes, learning rate, optimiser, batch size or epoch count.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Split, in the same pattern as several engineering-led studies in this corpus. Reproducible: the tablet specification, the 40 Hz sampling, the seating and table geometry, the five Leiter-3 subtests and 25-task structure, the definition of a trajectory (first tap to finger lift), all 12 features with their formulas or plain definitions in Table 1, the extraction package, and the three-term VAE loss written out in full with the equal weighting stated. Not reproducible: the network architecture and every training hyperparameter, the fold assignment procedure, random seeds, the Monte Carlo perturbation's sampling distribution parameters beyond 'N(mu_fi, sigma_fi)', and any code. Raw data are offered on request without undue reservation, which is a genuine commitment though weaker than deposition. The paper also reports no participant-level accuracy despite plotting participant-level latent means, so the single most useful number for a reader wanting to compare against other studies is absent.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The stated limitation is real but tangential: that supervision was required at the outset, so the ground truth still comes from traditional assessment, whereas an ideal VAE application would organise the latent space unsupervised. The unstated limitations are more consequential. The decisive one is the validation unit. The dataset is described unambiguously as 1,500 x 12 observations built from 60 children x 25 tasks, and 10-fold cross-validation is applied to those observations. Nothing indicates that a child's 25 rows were kept together, so in a standard k-fold split roughly 22-23 of each test observation's sibling rows - same child, same hand, same session, adjacent difficulty levels - are in the training set. A model with a 12-dimensional input and a 2-dimensional latent bottleneck can readily encode a child's individual motor signature, and the reported 91.2% is therefore substantially a measure of within-child consistency rather than of between-child generalisation. The tell is in the paper's own figures: Figure 3, which averages a participant's 25 tasks to a single point, shows cleaner separation than the task-level Figure 2, yet no accuracy is computed at that level, which is exactly the number a participant-disjoint evaluation would produce. Beyond validation: accuracy is the only metric reported, with no sensitivity, specificity, AUC or confusion matrix; the reduction from 10 to 2 latent dimensions was chosen by PCA on a latent space fitted to all the data; the analysis is restricted to correctly performed tasks, conditioning on cognitive success in a way that plausibly differs by group and is never quantified; IQ ranges are asymmetric with six autistic children below the TD floor and no means, SDs or test reported; sex is not reported at all; and the autistic group was in active psychomotor therapy while controls were not, confounding motor training with diagnosis in a study of motor kinematics.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Four directions. Enlarge the dataset in both size and feature relevance so that the latent space organises without supervision, which is the authors' stated ambition and would remove their reliance on clinical labels as ground truth. Generate as many candidate features as possible so a globally optimal feature set for autism identification can be determined, citing Zhao et al. (2021). Collect more clinical data so the latent space is more densely covered and new participants are less likely to fall into unvisited regions - a coverage argument that follows directly from their decision to classify by fitted density rather than by the predictor network. And combine these kinematic measures with traditional behavioural and cognitive scales into a multimodal risk indicator supporting clinicians rather than replacing them. Absent from the list, and more pressing than any of these, are participant-level validation, an independent cohort, a clinical comparison group, and test-retest reliability for the features proposed as clinical thresholds.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Fine motor control during goal-directed touchscreen dragging - specifically the kinematic profile of moving a finger from a card to a target placeholder, characterised along three dimensions. Speed: mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation. Acceleration: mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation. Path geometry: STH (straightness, the ratio of start-to-end distance to actual path length, an index of linearity), DC (directional change over time, an index of nonlinearity), sdDC (its standard deviation, a measure of irregularity), and MeanLength (the number of finite trajectories drawn per task). The behavioural hypothesis, grounded in embodied cognition and predictive coding, is that impaired active perception in autism produces abnormalities in planning and in serial and prospective coordination, which should surface as measurably different movement kinematics even in a simple drag. The group's earlier descriptive work had found autistic trajectories to show low linearity, high maximum speed and acceleration, and low minimum speed and acceleration, but without significant group separation; the present analysis partly reverses the speed direction, finding that lower MaxSpeed increases ASD probability while higher MaxAcceleration does. Note what is not modelled: no social behaviour, no gaze, no language, no gross motor activity - this is one of the most narrowly motoric behavioural targets in the corpus, and deliberately so.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: None - a single modality with 12 features from one sensor stream. The study is nonetheless relevant to the fusion question in two ways. First, the authors' explicit future direction is to combine these kinematic measures with 'the traditional behavioural and cognitive scale' into a multimodal risk measure - a clinician-facing rather than sensor-facing conception of fusion, in which the computational signal supplements standardised assessment rather than being fused with another sensor. Second, and more interestingly, the design already contains an implicit two-channel structure that goes unexploited: the tablet records both what the child does cognitively (which cards go where, and whether the answer is correct) and how the child moves while doing it. The paper deliberately discards the first channel, analysing only correctly performed tasks so that cognitive errors do not contaminate the motor signal. Since Leiter-3 performance is itself diagnostically informative and the two groups' IQ ranges differ, the discarded channel is not noise but a second modality that the design chose to suppress rather than fuse.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A variational autoencoder with an attached supervised predictor - the only VAE in this corpus and one of few genuinely generative models here. The encoder maps the 12 features to the parameters (mean and standard deviation) of a diagonal Gaussian latent distribution; a latent vector is sampled and passed both to a symmetric decoder that reconstructs the input and to a predictor MLP with a tanh intermediate layer and a softmax output over the two classes. The composite loss has three equally weighted terms: mean squared reconstruction error, the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the learned latent distribution and a zero-mean unit-variance diagonal Gaussian, and binary cross-entropy on the prediction. The architectural rationale is stated clearly and is the paper's conceptual contribution: the KL regularisation forces a well-behaved latent geometry, and the predictor loss forces the two classes into separable regions of it, because if the class-conditional latent distributions overlap too much the stochastic sampling makes the prediction loss stagnate. The result is a latent space in which classification and generative description coexist. At inference the predictor is then set aside in favour of two fitted bivariate Gaussians over the latent points, on the explicit grounds that density-based assignment is more conservative for inputs that land in unvisited regions - a deliberate outlier-aware design choice that is unusual and clinically sensible.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Twelve hand-crafted scalar features per task observation: four speed statistics (mean, max, min, SD), four acceleration statistics (mean, max, min, SD), and four path-geometry descriptors (STH straightness, DC directional change, sdDC directional-change variability, MeanLength). Features are computed per trajectory - one dragging movement from first tap to finger lift - using the R traj package, then averaged across the trajectories within a task, giving one 12-vector per child per task and 1,500 rows overall. The 40 Hz raw coordinate stream is therefore reduced twice before the network sees anything: once to per-trajectory summary statistics, once again by averaging across trajectories. No sequence model, no raw-signal input, no learned front end, and no representation of within-task variability across trajectories except through the SD features. The bottleneck is 10 latent dimensions at training, reduced to 2 for analysis after PCA showed the first two components carried 95% of the latent variance - so the effective representation of a child's movement on a task is a point in a plane.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy alone: 91.2% +/- 5.6% across 10 folds. This is the thinnest metric reporting of any study charted in this review that reports a headline number at all. There is no sensitivity, no specificity, no precision or recall, no F1, no AUC or ROC curve, no confusion matrix, and no per-class breakdown, so it is impossible to tell whether errors fall preferentially on autistic or typically developing observations - which is precisely the information a clinician evaluating a screening aid needs. The +/- 5.6% is a fold standard deviation, not a confidence interval, and with observation-level folds it does not carry the meaning it would under participant-level splitting. There is also no participant-level accuracy at all, despite Figure 3 plotting exactly the per-participant aggregation that would yield one, and despite the paper's own observation that the separation is clearer at that level. The balanced design (750 versus 750) at least makes 50% the unambiguous chance floor, so no prevalence adjustment is needed to read the number - but nor is any positive or negative predictive value offered for the screening use the discussion proposes.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: The best interpretability work in this corpus, and it is not an add-on but the paper's purpose. Three techniques are layered. First, the latent space is made analytically tractable by construction: the VAE's KL term drives it towards a diagonal Gaussian, so two-dimensional class-conditional Gaussians can be fitted to the ASD and TD point clouds and a genuine probability density function evaluated for any point rather than a black-box score. Second, feature influence is measured causally within the model rather than by correlation: for each participant, each of the 12 features is resampled 100 times from a Gaussian while the other 11 are held fixed, and the resulting displacement of that participant's latent projection is tracked, identifying not only which features move a subject but at which values the class assignment flips. Figure 5 aggregates this into per-feature density maps over the latent space and Figure 6 into class-probability curves against raw feature values. Third, the outputs are expressed in clinically usable form: signed, feature-specific rules (higher MaxAcceleration and sdAcceleration, lower MaxSpeed and MinAcceleration increase ASD probability) explicitly offered as candidate threshold values for joint use by clinicians. The design also embeds an interpretability-motivated safety property, replacing the predictor with density evaluation at inference so a participant in an unpopulated region is not confidently misassigned. The caveats are that no uncertainty is attached to any of these feature effects, no group-level statistics on the features themselves are reported (the earlier descriptive paper failed to find significant differences, which is the stated motivation for this analysis), and the whole latent geometry was learned on data containing the test observations, so the thresholds are in-sample.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The critical weakness, and it is unacknowledged. The dataset is stated plainly: 60 participants x 25 tasks = 1,500 observations of 12 features, with a parallel 1,500-element label vector repeating each child's diagnosis 25 times. Cross-validation is 10-fold over that observation set, giving 91.2% +/- 5.6%. There is no statement that a child's 25 rows were assigned to a single fold, and the description ('we used the k-fold cross-validation with k = 10 and returning the average accuracy', applied to 'the collected dataset') implies observation-level partitioning. Under that scheme every test observation has roughly 22-23 siblings from the same child, same session and same hand in the training data, differing only in Leiter-3 subtest and difficulty level. Movement kinematics are strongly individual - speed and acceleration profiles are close to a motor signature - so a 12-input, 2-latent model can separate children rather than groups and score highly, exactly the leakage Keles et al. quantified directly elsewhere in this corpus by identifying individuals from behaviour at many times chance. Two internal signals support this reading: the authors themselves note that the clustering is 'even more evident' when participants are plotted as the mean of their tasks than task by task, which is what one expects when within-child consistency is high; and they never compute the participant-level accuracy that this observation invites. Secondary issues compound it. The choice of two latent dimensions was made from PCA on a latent space learned from the entire dataset. The class-conditional Gaussians used for the interpretability analysis and proposed as clinical thresholds are fitted to all 1,500 points. Only accuracy is reported. And the balanced 50/50 design, while making chance interpretable, is 25-50 times the population prevalence at which the proposed screening support would operate. The corrective is straightforward and would be a genuinely valuable result: split the 60 children into folds, train on one set of children and test on unseen children, report participant-level sensitivity and specificity as well as accuracy, and refit the latent Gaussians within training folds only. Given 60 children and a well-specified reference standard including ADOS-2, that study is within reach of this dataset.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: machine learning, autism spectrum disorder, ASD, motor abnormalities, deep learning, early detection, diagnosis. Unusually, both 'early detection' and 'diagnosis' appear, which is a stronger clinical claim than the paper's own discussion supports - the text positions the method as supplying 'additional indicators of disorder or suspected diagnosis' and supporting clinicians rather than diagnosing. 'Motor abnormalities' is the theoretical stake, asserting that motor difference is a hallmark rather than an incidental correlate. Terms carried through the body: variational autoencoder, latent variable model, latent space, generative model, kinematics, touch-based functions, trajectory, straightness, directional change, embodied cognition, predictive coding, threshold values.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Frontiers in Psychology 14, article 1194760, Original Research, in a psychology rather than an engineering or clinical venue - which shows in the structure. Roughly two pages of the Methods are a textbook exposition of artificial neural networks and backpropagation aimed at a psychology readership, while the network actually used has no reported layer widths, learning rate, optimiser or epoch count; conversely the theoretical framing in embodied cognition and predictive coding is developed at length. Editorial and review handling is disclosed by name, as Frontiers requires. Received 27 March 2023, accepted 21 April 2023, published 18 May 2023 - a 25-day review turnaround - under CC BY.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2023 from the Department of Humanistic Studies, University of Naples Federico II, in collaboration with the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center, where two of the four authors were employed and from which the autistic participants were recruited - disclosed appropriately in the competing-interests statement. No funding is reported. The framing is a critique of existing assessment: the authors list four specific constraints of gold-standard tools - no explicit sensory-functioning assessment, dependence on examiner expertise and subjective evaluation, limited ecological validity, and the time demanded - and position quantitative motor measurement as the remedy. The paper is explicitly a second pass at the group's own earlier dataset, whose descriptive analysis had failed to separate the groups significantly, which makes it an unusually transparent instance of a common pattern in this corpus: conventional statistics find nothing, a deep model is applied to the same data, and separation appears. The stated ambition is to move eventually to unsupervised latent organisation so that the model no longer depends on clinical labels for ground truth - a 2023-era aspiration that the paper's own sample size prevents it from testing.

data_charting_rubrics.title: A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Song C; Wang S; Chen M; Li H; Jia F; Zhao Y
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional method-development and agreement study; a computer-vision pipeline is applied to video of routine clinical ADOS-2 assessments and its per-call response judgements are compared against an experienced clinician's scoring of the same sessions. No group comparison, no training/test split of participants, and no diagnostic classification.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Two scalar angle time series per 3 s window (25 fps, so up to 75 frames), reduced to threshold-crossing frame counts. No learned representation is fitted to the behaviour itself - the deep networks are all off-the-shelf perception components upstream of a hand-written rule.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Not stated as a range; participants were selected as those assessed with ADOS-2 modules TM, M1 or M2, which cover children from 12 months upward with little or no fluent language
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: 'Before each experiment, we obtained informed consent from the children's parents.' Participants' faces are mosaicked in the published figures for privacy, with the authors noting this may obscure the displayed facial joints.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: The ADOS-2 response-to-name press, embedded in a real clinical assessment. The child sits at a table engaged with toys; the clinician stands behind and to one side and calls the child's name in a natural tone. If the child turns and makes eye contact the item ends; otherwise the call is repeated up to three times at ~3 s intervals, after which the clinician reinforces by changing tone or asking a parent to call, up to two more times. Scoring: 0 for a response to the first call, 1 to the second, 2 to the third, 3 to the first reinforced call, 4 to the second, and 5 for no response after all five.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Four Hikvision RGB cameras with 2.8 mm focal length mounted at a uniform height of 1.44 m, recording 1280 x 720 at 25 fps; three are used - C1 at the child's left front for body pose, C3 and C4 at left and right rear for head pose, the rear pair being needed because the clinician may stand on either side. Software: iFlytek (HKUST Xunfei) real-time speech transcription for name-call timestamps; YOLOv3 for person detection; HRNet for 2-D human pose estimation; OSNet person re-identification for multiple-object tracking; OpenFace for facial landmarks and 3-D head Euler angles. Implementation in Python with PyTorch. Audio was converted to 16 kHz, 16-bit PCM for the ASR service.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: 'The data that has been used is confidential.'
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not reported. All the deep components are published third-party models (YOLOv3, HRNet, OSNet, OpenFace) plus a commercial ASR service, so the pipeline is reconstructible in outline, but the retrained YOLOv3 weights, the annotation of the 1,700-image detection dataset and the rule implementation are not released.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: 'These experiments have passed an ethical review' - no committee, institution or approval number is named.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Per frame within each 3 s window: (i) shoulder rotation angle theta_t, computed as the arccosine of the normalised dot product between the shoulder vector at frame t and at frame 0, converted from radians to degrees; (ii) head yaw angle from OpenFace's 3-D Euler decomposition, together with a binary indicator of whether a face was detected at all. Aggregation is by frame counting rather than by statistics.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Complete by construction. The decision is a transparent rule over two physically meaningful angles and a frame count, and the paper walks through worked examples with plotted time series (Fig. 6 for shoulder angle against the 90 degree threshold, Fig. 7 for head yaw), so any judgement can be audited frame by frame against video. The rationale for the cascade is also given in behavioural terms: shoulder rotation alone fails both ways, because some responsive children turn only the head while some unresponsive children rotate slightly while playing, so head pose is brought in exactly for the ambiguous band. This is the most fully interpretable system charted in this review, at the cost of having no learned decision component at all.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None reported for any component. The five decision constants - the 90 degree and 20 degree shoulder thresholds, the 10-frame and 8-frame duration thresholds, and the 3 s response window - are asserted rather than fitted. The only justification offered is for the duration threshold: human gaze fixation during concentration is not less than 0.2 s (citing reference [33]), doubled to 0.4 s to allow for error in children's shoulder rotation timing. The 3 s window follows the clinical protocol's inter-call interval.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: None in the machine-learning sense. There is no training/test split, no cross-validation, no held-out participants and no separate development set. The decision thresholds were set by hand and evaluated on the same 30 children and 109 test events on which they are reported. The one component that was trained - YOLOv3 - was trained on more than 1,700 images taken from the same 30 subjects, so the detector has seen every child it is later evaluated on.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: No limitations section. Two error sources are analysed concretely in the discussion - a mask preventing facial landmark detection combined with a slow response, and a head turn too fast to meet the frame-count threshold - and one important scope statement appears in the methods: 'although RTN deficiency is closely associated with ASD, our experiment is an assessment of the response to name, not an assessment of autism risk'. That disclaimer is correct and creditable, but it sits in tension with the abstract's framing of 93.3% 'consistency ... with clinical diagnosis' and with the conclusion's claim to 'assist in the screening of RTN in children with autism'.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Thirty children in total: 29 with autism and 1 typically developing, mean age 3.65 years. Selection was by ADOS-2 module - only children assessed with the TM, M1 or M2 modules were included, i.e. children from 12 months upward with little or no fluent oral expression, excluding the M3 and M4 modules used for verbally fluent older children and adults. There is no comparison group in any meaningful sense; the single typically developing participant cannot support a between-group contrast and the paper never attempts one. A second and more relevant unit of analysis exists: 109 individual name-call test events, since each child receives up to five calls (three in natural tone at about 3 s intervals, then up to two reinforced calls by clinician or parent). These 109 events are the denominator for the study's highest reported figure of 98.2%, but they are not independent - they cluster within 30 children and are strongly serially dependent, because a child who ignores the first call usually ignores the remaining four. Table 2 shows the consequence: 17 of the 30 children scored 5, meaning they did not respond to any of the five calls.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'Autistic children' and 'children with ASD' are both used, with 'autistic children' predominating in the title, abstract and conclusion - identity-first language, which is unusual in this corpus and may reflect translation from Chinese as much as a deliberate stance. Other usages are less careful: 'the number of autistic patients has been rising', 'more than 10 million people have been diagnosed with ASD', and 'children with autism have a low quality of life, require family care, and bring huge economic costs to society'. That last sentence, in the opening paragraph, frames autistic children primarily as a burden and is the starkest instance of deficit-and-cost framing encountered so far in this review. Clinically the vocabulary is standard medical-model: 'neurodevelopmental disorder', 'incidence rate', 'RTN deficiency', 'symptoms', 'no medicine can reliably relieve the symptoms of ASD'. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. Set against this, the study's practical stance towards children is respectful in a way several others here are not: it works within a real clinical assessment rather than imposing an experimental protocol, accepts a flexible number of accompanying parents, and mosaics participants' faces in published figures for privacy even at the cost of obscuring the detected landmarks.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: The thinnest demographic reporting of any included study charted so far. What is given: n = 30, of whom 29 autistic and 1 typically developing; a single overall mean age of 3.65 years; and the ADOS-2 modules from which participants were drawn (TM, M1, M2), which implies limited or absent fluent language across the sample. What is absent: sex distribution, age range or standard deviation, per-group age, IQ or developmental quotient, language level beyond the module implication, socioeconomic status, race or ethnicity, comorbidity, medication, and any ADOS-2 total, algorithm or comparison score. Because the sample is 29 autistic children and 1 control, the usual concern about group matching does not arise, but a different problem does: without age spread, sex, or developmental level it is impossible to judge for whom the vision pipeline works. Body proportions, head size, motor control and sitting posture all vary sharply across the 12-month to roughly 5-year span that modules TM through M2 encompass, and a shoulder-rotation threshold of 90 degrees measured in 2-D image coordinates is not obviously age-invariant. All data come from one hospital in Changchun, so the sample is also geographically and culturally homogeneous.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Two distinct reference standards operate in this study and the paper does not clearly separate them. For group membership, the 29 autistic children were assessed by professional clinicians using ADOS-2 at the Department of Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics of a university teaching hospital, with module assignment reported; but no ADOS-2 score, no DSM or ICD criteria, no diagnosing-clinician description and no diagnostic date are given, and the single typically developing child's status is not characterised at all. For the study's actual outcome, the reference is an experienced clinician's 0-5 response-to-name score, assigned during the same session under an explicitly stated rule set. This second standard is well defined operationally - the rule tree in Fig. 2 is unambiguous - and it is the appropriate comparator for what the system does. Its weaknesses are that a single clinician scored each child, that this clinician was necessarily unblinded (they were conducting the assessment and calling the child's name), that no second rater or reliability statistic exists, and that the score is therefore an individual judgement rather than a consensus. Since response to name is exactly the kind of item where a clinician standing behind a child must judge in real time whether a head turn counted as a response with eye contact, the absence of any inter-rater reliability is a real gap: the paper's headline number is agreement with one person's uncorroborated judgement.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: No cognitive, language, adaptive or global severity measure was administered or reported. The only quantitative symptom measure in the study is the response-to-name score itself, and it is genuinely informative: Table 2 shows that 17 of the 30 children failed to respond after all five calls, with the remainder distributed across the lower scores. That distribution is a symptom-severity profile for one ADOS-2 item, and it is reported honestly. But it is also the paper's undoing statistically, because a majority of children and a larger majority of the 109 calls fall into the single 'no response' category, and no chance-corrected agreement statistic is computed against that floor. Beyond this item, nothing: no ADOS-2 calibrated severity score despite ADOS-2 having been administered in full to every child, no developmental quotient, no language measure beyond the coarse module assignment, and no motor assessment - the last being relevant since the system's primary signal is torso rotation and children in this age and module range vary widely in postural control.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: to automate the judgement of response to name during real clinical ADOS-2 assessments, by combining automatic speech recognition (to timestamp the name calls) with human pose tracking (to measure shoulder rotation) and head pose estimation (to measure head yaw), and to show that adding body pose to the head-pose-only approach used in prior work improves agreement with clinicians. Three contributions are claimed: a four-camera multi-view capture rig; a 'Response to name Dataset' drawn from live ADOS-2 screening rather than a controlled laboratory protocol, with more natural child behaviour and an unrestricted number of accompanying parents; and the finding that combining shoulder rotation angle, head pose and response duration improves accuracy over pose alone. Findings: shoulder pose alone agreed with the clinician for 25 of 30 children (83.3%) and 104 of 109 calls (95.4%); adding head pose raised this to 28 of 30 (93.3%) and 107 of 109 (98.2%), with sensitivity 84.6% and specificity 100% under an inverted convention in which the 'positive' class is non-response. The two residual participant-level errors are diagnosed concretely: one child responded too slowly to accumulate the required 10 frames above the shoulder threshold and was also wearing a mask, which blocked the facial-landmark fallback; the other turned their head too fast for 8 frames of yaw to be detected. The score-level confusion matrix shows the modal outcome to be clinician 5 / predicted 5 in 17 children.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Single site: the Department of Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics, The First Hospital of Jilin University, Changchun, with engineering from Jilin University's School of Communication Engineering. The setting is the study's most distinctive feature and is used deliberately rather than incidentally. Recording took place during actual ADOS-2 screening sessions rather than in a purpose-built experiment, with four fixed cameras installed in the assessment room and the clinical protocol left untouched: the clinician stands where the protocol requires, calls in a natural tone, repeats and reinforces as the manual specifies, and an unspecified and varying number of parents may be present. The authors argue explicitly that this yields 'less laboratory control, more realistic child response, and a flexible number of accompanying parents', and they are right that this is the correct target distribution for a tool meant to sit inside a clinic. It also creates the engineering problem the pipeline is built to solve - the scene contains multiple adults, so person re-identification is needed simply to know which skeleton belongs to the child. The countervailing point is that the sample is a referred clinical series at a tertiary hospital with 29 of 30 children already autistic, which is the opposite of the community screening population the conclusion invokes when it proposes deployment 'in remote areas with underdeveloped medical care'.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: The ADOS-2 response-to-name press, executed as the manual prescribes and left unmodified. The child sits at a table absorbed in toys; the clinician stands behind and to one side and calls the child's name in a natural voice; if the child turns and makes eye contact the item ends, otherwise the call is repeated up to three times at roughly 3 s intervals; then up to two reinforced calls follow, delivered with a changed tone or by a parent. Scoring runs 0 (responds to the first call) through 5 (no response after all five). Two properties make this paradigm unusually well suited to automation. It has a precise onset - the moment the name is spoken - which the ASR component recovers automatically and which the authors correctly identify as removing a source of manual-annotation error; and it has a precise, short response window of 3 s fixed by the protocol itself. Two properties make it hard. The clinically defined response is 'turn and face the implementer with eye contact rather than glance to the side', which is a conjunction of orientation and gaze that no single sensor captures, and which the cascade approximates rather than measures - eye contact per se is never assessed, only head yaw and whether a face was detected by the rear camera. And the caller's position varies between left and right rear, which is why two rear cameras are required and why the head-pose channel depends on the child turning towards whichever camera happens to be behind the caller.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional single session with no follow-up and no test-retest assessment. Since the pipeline is proposed as a clinical scoring aid, the absence of any repeat measurement means nothing is known about whether the same child assessed twice would receive the same automated score. Ethics reporting is minimal but present in both required elements: 'these experiments have passed an ethical review', with no committee, institution or approval number named, and informed consent obtained from the children's parents before each session. A privacy measure is also implemented and disclosed - participants' faces are mosaicked in the published figures, with the authors noting that this may obscure the facial joints they wish to illustrate - and the data are declared confidential rather than released. For video recorded on preschool children with disabilities during clinical assessment, the consent and privacy handling is appropriate; the ethics statement is thinner than the norm and would not satisfy most journals' current reporting requirements.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Capture: four Hikvision RGB cameras with 2.8 mm lenses mounted at a common height of 1.44 m, recording 1280 x 720 at 25 fps, of which three are used - C1 at the child's left front for body pose and C3/C4 at left and right rear for head pose, the pair being necessary because the clinician may stand on either side. Audio is captured alongside and converted to 16 kHz 16-bit PCM for the speech service. Software stack, all named and all off-the-shelf except for retraining: iFlytek (HKUST Xunfei) real-time speech transcription, a deep fully-convolutional ASR that returns timestamped text and thereby locates each name call; YOLOv3 for person detection, deliberately retrained on more than 1,700 images from the study's own 30 subjects rather than using COCO weights, on accuracy grounds; HRNet for top-down 2-D pose estimation, chosen for its high-resolution feature maintenance and repeated multi-scale fusion; OSNet person re-identification to associate detections across frames and assign a stable ID, without which the child's skeleton could not be distinguished from the clinician's and the parents'; OpenFace for face detection, landmarks and 3-D head Euler angles. Implementation in Python and PyTorch. What is missing is any calibration: the cameras' geometry is fixed and stated but no intrinsic or extrinsic calibration is performed, and the shoulder rotation angle is computed directly in 2-D image coordinates, so a given physical torso rotation maps to different measured angles depending on where the child is seated and how they are oriented with respect to C1.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong on specification, absent on artefacts. Every decision constant is stated numerically - the 3 s response window, the 90 degree and 20 degree shoulder thresholds, the 10-frame (0.4 s) and 8-frame duration thresholds - and the angle computation is written out as three equations from the shoulder vector through the arccosine to the degree conversion. The camera rig, frame rate, resolution, focal length and mounting height are given, as are the roles of each camera, the clinical protocol and its full scoring rule, the exact third-party models used, and the size of the custom detection training set. A competent group could rebuild the system from the paper. What cannot be reproduced is any number in it: the data are declared confidential, the retrained YOLOv3 weights and the 1,700-image annotations are not released, no code is available, and the ASR component is a commercial service whose behaviour may change. There is also no preregistration and no independent evaluation of the perception components (detection, tracking, landmark) in isolation, so their error rates on this population are unknown and are folded silently into the end-to-end figure.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: There is no limitations section, though the discussion analyses the two residual errors carefully and the methods contain an important and creditable scope disclaimer - 'although RTN deficiency is closely associated with ASD, our experiment is an assessment of the response to name, not an assessment of autism risk'. The unaddressed limitations are substantial and several are structural. First, there is no validation of any kind: the five decision constants were chosen by hand and reported on the same 30 children, and the one trained component, YOLOv3, was retrained on 1,700 images of those same 30 children, so the detector has seen every participant it is evaluated on. Nothing in the paper estimates performance on an unseen child. Second, no chance baseline is computed, and the sample makes one essential: 17 of 30 children scored 5, so a rule that always predicted non-response would agree with the clinician on a majority of children and on a still larger majority of the 109 calls, since each non-responding child contributes five non-response events. For an ordinal agreement problem of this shape the natural statistic is a weighted kappa, and none is reported. Third, the 109 events are treated as independent for the headline 98.2% although they cluster within 30 children and are strongly serially dependent. Fourth, the reference standard is one unblinded clinician with no second rater and no reliability statistic, on an item that requires a real-time judgement about eye contact from behind the child. Fifth, the shoulder angle is a 2-D image-plane measurement from an uncalibrated fixed camera, so it confounds true rotation with seating position and posture. Sixth, the demographic reporting is too thin to establish for whom the method works. Finally, the framing is inconsistent: the abstract reports agreement with 'clinical diagnosis' and the conclusion invokes early autism screening in underserved regions, while the actual comparator is one clinician's score of one behavioural item in a sample that contains a single non-autistic child.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: No future-work section is provided. The conclusion's forward-looking claims are about deployment rather than research: that the method reduces the professional-knowledge requirement for assessment, provides efficient and objective computer-aided screening, and could support early autism screening in remote areas with underdeveloped medical care. Judged against the evidence, the research steps that would need to come first are clear and unstated: evaluation on children not used to train the detector; a balanced sample containing a meaningful number of non-autistic children so that the item score's discriminative value can be assessed; a second, blinded clinician rater with reported reliability so the reference standard is not one person's judgement; chance-corrected agreement statistics appropriate to an ordinal score; and threshold selection on a development set separate from the evaluation set. The wider point this study raises for the review, and does not itself pursue, is whether automating individual ADOS-2 items one at a time is a viable route to instrument automation - it is the only paper in this corpus attempting it, and the answer depends on error rates the paper cannot currently estimate.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: One behaviour, examined more closely than any other single behaviour in this corpus: response to one's own name. The clinical definition adopted is precise - the child should turn and face the caller with eye contact rather than glance to the side - and the paper's decomposition of it into measurable components is the substantive contribution. Torso orientation is captured as the angle between the left-right shoulder vector at each frame and the same vector at the first frame after the call, so the measurement is relative to the child's own starting posture rather than to an absolute frame. Head orientation is captured as the yaw Euler angle from facial landmarks, with the mere detection of a face by the rear camera also serving as evidence that the child turned towards the caller. Response latency is captured by the ordinal 0-5 score, which encodes how many calls and reinforcements were needed. The authors are explicit about why body pose is needed alongside head pose, and the reasoning is behavioural rather than technical: prior work used head pose and gaze only, but some responsive children turn only the head with little shoulder movement, while some unresponsive children rotate slightly while manipulating toys, so neither channel alone separates response from non-response. What is not measured, despite being in the clinical definition, is eye contact itself - gaze is approximated by head direction on the stated assumption that the two agree, an approximation that is reasonable in general but is exactly the point at which a glance to the side, which the protocol says does not count as a response, becomes indistinguishable from a genuine orienting response.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Three-stream fusion with a clearly reported ablation, and the fusion architecture is a hand-written cascade rather than a learned combination. Audio and video are fused at the segmentation stage: the ASR stream supplies timestamps for each name call, which cut the video into 3 s response windows, and the authors note that this removes the manual-annotation error that would otherwise attach to onset marking. Body pose and head pose are then fused at the decision stage in a three-branch rule: shoulder rotation above 90 degrees for more than 10 frames gives a positive response outright; shoulder rotation below 20 degrees on every frame gives a negative response outright; and only in the ambiguous 20-90 degree band does head yaw adjudicate, with more than 8 frames of detected yaw giving a positive response. The ablation is reported for the two visual streams and is the paper's central quantitative claim: pose alone gives 83.3% of participants and 95.4% of events, pose plus head pose gives 93.3% and 98.2%. In participant terms that is three additional children correctly scored out of 30, so the confidence interval on the improvement is wide even though the direction is plausible. Two features of this fusion design are worth carrying into the synthesis. It is complementary by explicit behavioural argument rather than by empirical search - each stream is introduced to cover a named failure mode of the other - which is a more defensible basis for multimodality than the accuracy-chasing seen in several other studies here. And the multi-view arrangement is itself a form of fusion driven by the clinical protocol: two rear cameras are required because the caller may stand on either side, so which camera contributes the head-pose evidence depends on the geometry of the assessment rather than on a fixed sensor assignment.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A hybrid that is unusual in this corpus: four deep neural networks are used as perception front ends, but no model is trained on the behaviour and the decision itself is a hand-written rule. The deep components are YOLOv3 for person detection (retrained on the study's own images rather than using COCO weights, on accuracy grounds), HRNet for top-down 2-D pose estimation (selected for its high-resolution feature maintenance and repeated multi-scale fusion), OSNet re-identification for multi-object tracking (necessary because the scene contains the child, the clinician and a variable number of parents, so the child's skeleton must be identified and followed), OpenFace for facial landmarks and 3-D head Euler angles, and a commercial deep fully-convolutional ASR for name-call timestamps. Above these sits a three-branch threshold cascade with five hand-set constants. The architectural choice is defensible for the task - the clinical scoring rule is itself a deterministic decision tree over observable orienting behaviour, so encoding it directly rather than learning it from 109 examples is the right call at this sample size, and it makes every judgement auditable. The cost is that nothing adapts: the thresholds cannot accommodate a child whose habitual posture or motor control differs, the paper's own two error cases are both threshold-boundary failures, and there is no probability or confidence attached to any judgement, so no case can be flagged as uncertain and referred back to the clinician - which is precisely what an assistive scoring tool ought to do.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Two scalar angle time series per 3 s response window, each sampled at 25 fps and therefore up to 75 frames long, reduced to threshold-crossing frame counts before the decision. The shoulder rotation series is computed frame by frame as theta_t = arccos(v_0 . v_t / |v_0||v_t|) converted to degrees, where v_t is the vector from the right to the left shoulder joint at frame t and v_0 is the same vector at the first frame after the name call - so the measurement is self-referenced to the child's posture at call onset rather than to any absolute frame, which is a sensible choice that removes dependence on how the child happened to be sitting. The head series is the OpenFace yaw Euler angle, accompanied by an implicit binary of whether a face was detected at all by the relevant rear camera. Both series are then summarised only by counting frames that satisfy a threshold, so the representation discards the shape of the movement entirely: peak angular velocity, smoothness, whether the turn was completed or aborted, and whether the child returned to the toys are all invisible. Nothing is learned from the raw joint coordinates, and no representation of the temporal profile of orienting survives into the decision.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy at two aggregation levels (30 participants and 109 test events), sensitivity, specificity, and a 6 x 6 confusion matrix of clinician against predicted 0-5 scores. The positive/negative convention is inverted from ordinary usage and stated explicitly - a true positive is a non-response correctly judged as a non-response - so sensitivity 84.6% refers to detecting failures to respond and specificity 100% to correctly recognising genuine responses. Reporting both aggregation levels and publishing the full score-level confusion matrix is better practice than most of this corpus. But the metric set is wrong for the problem in two ways. First, this is an ordinal agreement task between an automated scorer and a human scorer, for which the appropriate statistic is a weighted kappa or an intraclass correlation, and none is reported - so nothing corrects for the very high chance agreement created by 17 of 30 children scoring 5 and by every one of a non-responding child's five calls being a non-response event. The 98.2% event-level figure in particular is close to uninterpretable without that correction. Second, no confidence intervals are given, and with 30 children a single misclassification moves the participant-level accuracy by 3.3 points, so the reported improvement from 83.3% to 93.3% rests on three children. There is also no AUC, which is defensible since the system emits no score, and no evaluation of the perception components in isolation, so detection, tracking and landmark failures are folded silently into the end-to-end number.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Fully interpretable by construction, and this is the study's clearest methodological strength. Every judgement reduces to two physically meaningful quantities - degrees of shoulder rotation relative to the child's posture when their name was called, and degrees of head yaw - together with counts of how many of the 75 frames satisfied a stated threshold. Figures 6 and 7 plot both series for worked examples against their thresholds, so a clinician or auditor can replay any decision frame by frame against the video and see exactly why it came out as it did. The design rationale is also explained in behavioural terms rather than defended by performance: shoulder rotation alone fails in two named directions, missing responsive children who turn only the head and falsely flagging unresponsive children who shift slightly while playing with toys, and head pose is introduced specifically to adjudicate that band. Even the duration constant is argued from evidence rather than tuned, being derived from the observation that gaze fixation during concentration lasts at least 0.2 s and then doubled to 0.4 s to allow for timing error in children's rotation. Three interpretability limits remain. Nothing quantifies how close a judgement was to its threshold, so no case can be surfaced as borderline. The perception layer beneath the rule is entirely opaque and unevaluated on this population, so a wrong answer caused by a tracking identity switch would look identical to one caused by a genuine behavioural boundary case. And eye contact, which the clinical definition requires, is never measured - head direction stands in for gaze on an assumption stated but not tested.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: There is no validation strategy, and this is the study's decisive methodological gap. No training/test split, no cross-validation, no development set, no held-out participants: the five decision constants were set by hand and are reported on the same 30 children and 109 calls used to define them, and the single trained component, YOLOv3, was retrained on more than 1,700 images drawn from those same 30 subjects, so the person detector has seen every child it is subsequently evaluated on. Nothing in the paper estimates how the pipeline would behave on a child it has never encountered. Compounding this, no chance-agreement floor is computed although the data make one essential: with 17 of 30 children scoring 5 and each of those children contributing five non-response events, a trivial always-predict-non-response rule would already agree with the clinician on well over half the participants and on a substantially larger share of the 109 calls, so the 98.2% event-level figure is being reported against an unstated and high baseline. For an ordinal agreement problem the correct summary is a weighted kappa or ICC; accuracy without chance correction systematically overstates agreement in exactly this configuration. The 109 events are also treated as independent although they cluster within 30 children and are serially dependent by the protocol's own logic. Finally, the reference standard against which all of this is measured is a single unblinded clinician with no second rater, so even a perfectly validated system could only be shown to reproduce one person's uncorroborated judgements. The corrective study is well within reach of this group and would be worth more than the current numbers: fix the thresholds on a development subset, evaluate on children whose images never entered detector training, add a second blinded rater and report inter-rater reliability, and report weighted kappa alongside accuracy at both aggregation levels.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD); Response to name; Human pose tracking; Head pose estimation; Early screening. Three of the five are computer-vision technique names and one is the specific behaviour targeted, which accurately reflects a paper whose contribution is a perception pipeline for one clinical item. 'Early screening' is the only application term and it overstates the work, since the sample contains a single non-autistic child. Terms carried through the body: multimodal discrimination, shoulder rotation angle, automatic name calling detection, multiple object tracking, person re-identification, Euler angle, yaw, Response to name Dataset, computer-aided diagnosis, ADOS-2 modules.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Displays 76, article 102360, Elsevier - a display-technology and human-visual-interface journal, recommended for publication by a named handling editor. The venue is an unusual home for a clinical assessment study and explains the emphasis: camera geometry, multi-view capture, pose and landmark estimation and frame-level signal processing are described in detail, while the clinical apparatus around them - demographics, diagnostic scores, rater reliability, chance-corrected agreement - is thin or absent. Received 2 November 2022, revised 25 November 2022, accepted 18 December 2022, available online 5 January 2023.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2023 by Jilin University's School of Communication Engineering with the Department of Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics of The First Hospital of Jilin University, funded by the Science and Technology Development Plan of Jilin Province and the National Natural Science Foundation of China. The framing is capacity-driven and quantified: the opening cites autism prevalence rising to 1-2%, more than 10 million diagnosed people in China of whom about 3 million are children, and the striking statistic that 'globally, less than 5% of assessments use the ASD gold standard diagnostic tool, which is mainly due to the long test time, complex training of evaluators and high cost'. That last figure is the clearest statement in this corpus of why instrument automation, as opposed to diagnosis replacement, might matter. The paper positions its own contribution against three named prior response-to-name systems (Bidwell, Petric, Liu, Wang), arguing that all previous work relied on face, head pose and gaze while ignoring body pose - so the framing is incremental within a small, well-identified subliterature. Its most creditable move is the methods-section disclaimer that the work assesses response to name and not autism risk, which sits in unresolved tension with the abstract and conclusion.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Aminoleslami S; Maghooli K; Sammaknejad N; Haghipour S; Sadeghi-Firoozabadi V
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional two-group diagnostic-classification study using a purpose-designed computer game as the elicitation task
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Hand-crafted region-based counts and durations. No scan-path sequence, no transition matrix, no temporal ordering, no image features, no learned representation. Four nested feature subsets were evaluated: features around the figures, features on the figures, features on and around the figures, and all features.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Parental consent is listed as an inclusion criterion for the autistic group. No consent statement is given for the comparison group and no child assent is described.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A purpose-built two-stage computer game designed with expert guidance and modelled on picture-exchange approaches. Stage S1 targets face recognition: three photographs of Japanese women are shown in a row alongside one target figure and the child must identify which candidate matches the target. Stage S2 targets expression matching: the same women are shown displaying happy, sad and surprised expressions, with 'happy' as the target expression. Children were first shown a familiarisation set, and after conditions were judged suitable the full sequence was run. A total of 240 game images were presented.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: A stationary (remote) eye-tracking system at Shahid Beheshti University, shown in a figure but never identified by manufacturer, model, sampling rate or accuracy specification. Analysis in MATLAB R2020b.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: 'The datasets generated during the current study are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.'
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Research Ethics Committee of Islamic Azad University, Tehran Science and Research Branch, approval ID IR.IAU.SRB.REC.1401.152 - a named committee with a verifiable identifier, which is better than most reports in this corpus
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Fixations were detected and characterised in MATLAB by start time, duration, end time and spatial (X, Y) position. The stimulus space was segmented into regions - on FIG 1, 2 and 3; on the Reference FIG; around each of these; and two OUT regions - and fixations were clustered by location of node aggregation. Two quantities were computed per region: the number of fixation nodes and the fixation time, giving an 18-feature matrix. Eye movement is also described in graph-theoretic terms, with fixations as vertices and saccades as edges, and a per-child gaze graph is illustrated, but no graph-theoretic metric (degree, path length, centrality, transition entropy) is actually computed or used as a feature.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Modest but real. The 18 features are region-based fixation counts and durations, so each is directly interpretable as 'how often and how long the child looked here', and the region definitions are given diagrammatically. The comparison across four nested feature subsets is itself an interpretive device, showing that neither the figures alone nor their surroundings alone outperform the union. A worked single-child example (Fig. 7) walks through one trial, showing that the child concentrated fixations on the target and the correct candidate and identified it correctly. What is missing is any group-level analysis of the features themselves - no means, no effect sizes, no statistical comparison of where autistic and comparison children looked - so the study cannot say what visual behaviour distinguishes the groups, only that a network achieves a certain accuracy. The graph-theoretic framing introduced at length in the introduction is never operationalised.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Iteration count and learning coefficient were selected by minimising MSE, but on which partition is not stated. The number of hidden layers and the number of nodes per layer are described as problem-dependent and are never reported for the network actually used.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: '70 percent of data in the neural network were used for training and the remaining 30 percent for tests and validation' - the MATLAB Neural Network Toolbox default of 70/15/15. Critically, the split is over data rows rather than children, and the reported percentages identify the row count exactly: with N = 240, training accuracy 78.6% of 168 rows is 132, validation 66.7% of 36 is 24, test 58.3% of 36 is 21, and (132 + 24 + 21) / 240 = 73.75%, matching the reported 73.8% total to the decimal. The same arithmetic reproduces all four feature-subset tables. So each of the 40 children contributes six observations that are randomly scattered across training, validation and test.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Three, all in the final paragraph and all forward-looking rather than self-critical: that a system designed for children does not transfer to adults because the training parameters differ; that further work should enhance classification precision and accuracy from eye-tracking graph features; and that 'the classifier should include conditions overlapping with autism for differential diagnosis'. The third is a genuine and important acknowledgement. The conclusion also frames the modest accuracy as 'desirable given the status of children with high-performance autism disorder', i.e. as reflecting task difficulty in a high-functioning sample.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of 20, total 40 children, all male, aged roughly 4 to 12 years. The autistic group was drawn from the Daily Rehabilitation Clinic for Children with Special Disorders in Tehran, affiliated to the Family Institute of Shahid Beheshti University; the comparison group came from Namjoo public elementary school. Enrolment and attrition are reported for the autistic group only: 25 children with 'high-performance autism' were selected, of whom 5 (20%) were excluded under the study's stated exclusion criteria - refusing to sit on the chair, or failure to calibrate the eye tracker - and their data were never recorded. No exclusions, and indeed no exclusion criteria at all, are reported for the comparison group, so the two groups passed through different filters. The modelled dataset is not 40 rows but 240: arithmetic on the reported training, validation and test percentages fixes the row count exactly (168 + 36 + 36 = 240, with 132 + 24 + 21 = 177 correct and 177/240 = 73.75% matching the reported 73.8% total), so each child contributes six observations to a randomly partitioned dataset.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: The dominant contrast throughout is 'autistic and normal children', with 'normal' used in the title, abstract, results, discussion and conclusion, supplemented by 'healthy children' and 'typical children'. Framing autistic children against 'normal' peers is the least considered terminology encountered in this corpus and carries an implication - abnormality - that 'typically developing' does not. Autism itself is 'autism disorder' or 'the autism spectrum disorder', characterised by 'communication deficits', 'impairment in social interactions' and the statement that autistic children 'lack the ability to learn the socio-cognitive skills with normal development'. Severity is expressed as 'high-performance autism' and, in one passage discussing robot-assisted education, the text refers to 'students with mental retardation' - outdated in current English usage. Against this, the study's motivation is service-oriented rather than dismissive: it is framed around the shortage of specialists relative to a growing autistic population and the goal of supporting, not replacing, clinical judgement, and the introduction is unusually positive about autistic children's engagement with technology, citing evidence of 'inherent dependence on technology and positive behavior toward computer-based training'. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement statement.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Table 1 reports sex, group size, and mean and standard deviation of age: autistic 20 male, 8.40 +/- 2.45 years; comparison 20 male, 8.45 +/- 1.90 years, with an overall span of about 4 to 12 years. Age matching is excellent - the means differ by three weeks - though the autistic group is more dispersed. Beyond this, nothing: no IQ or developmental quotient despite the autistic group being labelled high-functioning, no language measure, no adaptive functioning, no comorbidity, no medication, no socioeconomic status, no race or ethnicity, and no autism severity. Two features of the reported demographics deserve emphasis. The sample is 100% male in both groups. This is stated in the table and never mentioned again - not as a design decision, not as a limitation, not in the conclusion - even though the introduction itself notes that autism prevalence is higher in boys, which is a reason to sample boys but not a reason to leave the restriction undiscussed. And the participants are Iranian children in Tehran while the facial stimuli are Japanese women from the JAFFE database, so every trial involves other-race face processing. The paper's own literature review cites work on differences between autistic and typically developing children in processing same-race versus other-race faces, and even reports that study's 70% accuracy as a comparator, yet never connects that literature to its own stimulus choice.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Weak and under-specified. Autistic status rests on admission to the recruiting clinic, where 'the children were admitted into this clinic based on the diagnosis made by a pediatric psychiatrist and a pediatric clinical psychologist and underwent a comprehensive evaluation', restated in the inclusion criteria simply as 'the diagnosis of autism spectrum disorders made by specialists'. Two clinicians of different disciplines is better than one, and the involvement of a psychiatrist and a clinical psychologist is a reasonable clinical standard, but no diagnostic instrument is named, no DSM or ICD version is cited, the 'comprehensive evaluation' is not described, no diagnosis date or interval to testing is given, and no reliability is quantified. The comparison group is weaker still: children were recruited from a mainstream public elementary school and are called 'normal' and 'healthy', with no screening instrument administered, no exclusion criteria listed and no statement that autism or developmental concerns were ruled out - so undetected autistic traits or other neurodevelopmental conditions in the comparison group cannot be excluded. The autistic group additionally passed two functional gates that shape who was studied: a therapist's judgement that the child had 'relative perception of people's faces', and the ability to sit at a computer and attend to images. Both are defensible for a face-processing task but both further narrow an already high-functioning sample.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: No cognitive, language, adaptive or severity instrument was administered to any participant in either group. The autistic sample is described only as having 'high-performance autism disorder', a label with no accompanying score, cut-off or source, and the conclusion leans on it interpretively - arguing that accuracy above 73% is 'desirable given the status of children with high-performance autism disorder', i.e. that the task is intrinsically harder in a less impaired sample. That is a reasonable argument but it cannot be evaluated, because no measure of functioning or severity exists to place the sample on any scale, nor to check whether the misclassified children were the less affected ones. Two informal proxies appear in the inclusion criteria - a therapist's judgement of the child's face perception, and the capacity to sit and attend at a computer - and both operate as gates rather than as measurements. The absence of IQ is particularly consequential here because the index task is a visual matching task drawn from the same family as nonverbal reasoning tests: any group difference in fixation distribution over candidate figures could as easily reflect differences in matching strategy or task comprehension as differences in social attention, and there is no covariate with which to separate them.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Goal: to classify autistic from non-autistic children by analysing eye-tracking data captured while they play a purpose-designed computer game, motivated explicitly by the shortage of diagnostic specialists relative to a growing autistic population and the wish for a system 'easily applicable by not-so-expert users'. The game was designed with expert guidance around two objectives drawn from picture-exchange practice: face recognition and facial-expression matching. Findings as reported: precision 76.6% and accuracy 73.8% with all 18 features, which the paper presents as the best of four nested feature subsets and describes as 'a suitable diagnostics system'. Findings as they should be read: those numbers are the TOTAL column of Table 5, pooling training, validation and test rows, and the held-out test values in the same table are precision 66.7%, accuracy 58.3%, sensitivity 57.1% and specificity 60.0% - between 6 and 10 points above a 50% chance level on 36 observations. Across all four feature subsets the pattern is identical and consistent: total accuracies of 65.0-73.8% concealing test accuracies of 52.8-58.3%, with training accuracies of 67.9-78.6%. The gap between training and test performance is present in every configuration and is never remarked on. Two subsets also show unstable held-out behaviour, with test sensitivity of 33.3% for 'around FIGs' and test specificity of 33.3% for 'on FIGs'.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Single-city, two-source recruitment in Tehran, with testing centralised at one laboratory. Autistic children came from the Daily Rehabilitation Clinic for Children with Special Disorders, a specialist service affiliated to the Family Institute of Shahid Beheshti University; comparison children came from Namjoo public elementary school. All eye tracking took place on one stationary system at the Faculty of Education and Psychology, Shahid Beheshti University, so unlike some studies in this corpus the acquisition chain is identical for both groups and no equipment confound arises. The recruitment geometry is nonetheless the standard clinic-versus-school case-control arrangement at 50% prevalence, and here it is compounded by asymmetric filtering: the autistic group faced five inclusion criteria and two exclusion criteria that removed 20% of those approached, while no criteria at all are stated for the school-recruited comparison group. The children who could not tolerate sitting at the computer or could not be calibrated - plausibly those with greater sensory or attentional difficulty - are precisely those absent from the analysed autistic sample.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A two-stage computer game built specifically for this study, informed by picture-exchange approaches in which cards depicting facial expressions convey concepts non-verbally. Stage S1 (face recognition): three photographs of Japanese women are displayed in a row beside a target figure, and the child must identify which candidate matches the target. Stage S2 (expression matching): the same women are shown with happy, sad and surprised expressions, with 'happy' as the target. All stimuli come from the JAFFE database. Children were familiarised with example images first, and conditions were checked as suitable before the full run of 240 game images. The design has clear merits - it is engaging rather than passive, it has an objectively correct answer on every trial so gaze can be interpreted against task demands, and it targets a behaviour (facial expression processing) with strong theoretical links to autism. Three features constrain what it can show. The stimuli are other-race for this sample, and the other-race face effect is a documented modulator of both face-processing performance and gaze distribution - the paper cites this literature but not in relation to its own design. Only static images are used, so no dynamic or interactive social content is present. And the analysis discards trial structure entirely: fixations are pooled into region counts and durations, so whether the child looked at the correct candidate, in what order, or how their strategy evolved across 240 trials is not represented, even though the single-child illustration in Fig. 7 shows exactly that kind of trial-level reasoning being informative.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up, no test-retest reliability. Ethics reporting is the strongest element of the paper's governance: approval was obtained from the Research Ethics Committee of Islamic Azad University, Tehran Science and Research Branch, with the approval identifier IR.IAU.SRB.REC.1401.152 stated in a dedicated Ethics subsection and repeated in the declarations - a named committee and a verifiable reference number, which most reports in this corpus do not provide. Consent is handled less completely: parental consent appears as an inclusion criterion for the autistic group only, with no consent statement for the school-recruited comparison children and no mention of child assent. Funding (none received) and competing interests (none) are declared.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Stimuli: the Japanese Female Facial Expression (JAFFE) database, presented at 1024 x 768. Capture: a stationary eye-tracking system at Shahid Beheshti University, depicted in a photograph but never identified - no manufacturer, model, sampling rate, spatial accuracy or precision figure appears anywhere in the paper, which is a significant omission because every feature is a fixation count or duration and fixation detection depends directly on sampling rate and on the detection algorithm's parameters, neither of which is stated. Analysis: MATLAB R2020b, using fixation detail output (start, duration, end, X, Y) and the Neural Network facilities for the MLP. Calibration was performed and used as a gate, with failure to calibrate an explicit exclusion criterion, but the protocol, point count and accuracy threshold are not described. Out-of-range samples were retained by enlarging the analysis space beyond the stimulus and labelling the surplus 'OUT', which is a pragmatic choice but implies non-trivial tracking error that is never quantified.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Split between a well-specified experiment and an under-specified model. Reproducible: the game's two stages and objectives, the JAFFE stimulus source, the 240-image protocol, the stimulus resolution and the region segmentation with its named zones, the 18-feature definition as fixation count and fixation time per region, the MATLAB version, the training algorithm (scaled conjugate gradient backpropagation) and the activation functions (tanh hidden, sigmoid output), and the ethics approval identifier. Not reproducible: the eye tracker itself, the fixation-detection parameters, the MLP's hidden-layer count and node counts, the learning rate and iteration count that were 'optimised' by MSE, the random split and seed, and the code. Data are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. The single most consequential reporting gap is not technical but presentational: because the abstract and conclusion quote the pooled total rather than the test column, a reader who does not open the tables will take away a figure roughly 15 points higher than the study's own held-out result.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The three stated limitations are real but peripheral - no transfer to adults, a desire for richer graph features, and the need for clinically overlapping comparison conditions, the last being a genuinely important acknowledgement that the study can only separate autistic children from unscreened schoolchildren. The unstated limitations dominate. First and most serious, the reported precision and accuracy are pooled across training, validation and test. The tables disaggregate honestly, so the information is present, but the abstract, results narrative and conclusion all quote the total. For the best configuration the held-out accuracy is 58.3% against a 50% chance level - on 36 observations, a difference of three. Second, the modelled rows are not children. Arithmetic on the reported percentages fixes the dataset at 240 rows split 168/36/36 in the MATLAB default proportions, so each of the 40 children contributes six rows that are randomly scattered across the three partitions, and every test row has five siblings from the same child in training. Given that the features are region-level fixation counts and durations, which are strongly stable within an individual, this is a direct route for identity information to leak. Third, four feature subsets were compared on the same data and the best reported as the study's result. Fourth, the stimuli are other-race faces for this sample, an effect the paper's own citations show it is aware of. Fifth, 20% of the approached autistic children were excluded for non-cooperation or calibration failure with no comparable filter on the comparison group and no description of those excluded.
