Sixth, the sample is entirely male and this is never discussed. Seventh, no IQ or cognitive measure exists to separate social-attention differences from task-comprehension differences on what is essentially a visual matching task. Eighth, ROC curves are displayed without any AUC value, so the one metric that would summarise discriminability across thresholds is shown graphically and not reported numerically.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Three directions are stated. Enrich the feature set derived from the eye-tracking graph in order to improve precision and accuracy - a reasonable ambition, and one the study has itself left unexploited, since the introduction develops a graph-theoretic framing of fixations as vertices and saccades as edges but no graph metric is ever computed. Extend the classifier to include conditions that overlap with autism so that differential diagnosis becomes possible - the most valuable of the three, and an acknowledgement that separating autistic children from unscreened schoolchildren does not establish clinical utility. And note that a system trained on children will not transfer to adults without retraining. Not mentioned, and more pressing: participant-level validation, reporting held-out rather than pooled performance, an independent cohort, culturally matched stimuli, inclusion of girls, and any cognitive covariate.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Visual attention during face recognition and facial-expression matching, operationalised entirely spatially. For each defined region of the display - on each of the three candidate figures, on the reference figure, around each of these, and in two regions outside them - two quantities are computed: the number of fixation nodes falling there and the total fixation time spent there. The behavioural hypothesis is the standard one for eye tracking in autism, that autistic and non-autistic children distribute gaze differently when required to compare faces and match expressions, with the paper's own framing that 'the recorded data on eye movements suggest a clear difference between the eye fixation patterns of normal subjects and subjects with autism spectrum disorders'. Two aspects of the operationalisation are worth noting for the synthesis. The regions are defined by task structure (which figure) rather than by facial anatomy - there are no eye, mouth or face-interior areas of interest - so the classic autism finding of reduced eye-region fixation cannot be tested by this feature set at all; what is measured is which stimulus the child compared and how long they dwelt on it, which is closer to a matching-strategy measure than to a social-attention measure. And the distinction between 'on' and 'around' a figure is the study's one attempt to capture a qualitative gaze property, on the implicit reasoning that fixating adjacent to rather than on a face is itself informative; the ablation shows neither subset alone outperforms their union.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No fusion. A single modality with 18 features from one sensor, and the four reported conditions are nested subsets of that same feature set rather than distinct modalities. One near-miss is worth recording: the discussion states that 'the children's verbal responses to the observed game were also recorded during the test' and that 'the results indicate the significant matching of the provided responses to the recorded eye-tracking patterns'. A second behavioural channel - whether the child correctly identified the target, and what they said - was therefore captured and would have been straightforward to fuse with gaze, all the more so because the task has an objectively correct answer on every one of 240 trials, so accuracy, latency and error patterns were available at no additional cost. None of it is quantified, analysed or entered into the model; the claimed correspondence between speech and gaze is asserted without a single supporting number. This is the same pattern seen in the tablet-based motor study charted elsewhere in this review, where the cognitive-performance channel was deliberately discarded to isolate the motor signal: a second modality present in the raw data and suppressed rather than fused.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A single shallow multilayer perceptron, trained by error backpropagation using the scaled conjugate gradient algorithm, with hyperbolic tangent activation in the hidden layer and sigmoid activation at the output, implemented in MATLAB R2020b. No alternative classifier was evaluated - no SVM, random forest, logistic regression or even a linear baseline - despite the introduction surveying several such methods, so there is no evidence that the neural network is better suited to 18 features and 240 rows than a simpler model would be. Nor is the network itself specified: the paper devotes a paragraph to explaining that the number of hidden layers and nodes is problem-dependent and then never states what was used, and the iteration count and learning coefficient are described as optimised by MSE without saying on which partition. For a dataset of 240 rows and 18 features, a shallow MLP is a defensible choice and overfitting is the expected risk; the reported train-to-test gaps of roughly 20 points in every configuration are consistent with that risk having materialised.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: An 18-dimensional vector of region-based fixation statistics per observation. The stimulus space, 1024 x 768, was augmented beyond its true extent to accommodate out-of-range gaze samples, then partitioned into named regions: on FIG 1, FIG 2 and FIG 3; on the Reference FIG; around each of these; and two OUT regions below the outer figures. Fixations were clustered by location of node aggregation and two quantities extracted per region - the number of fixation nodes and the fixation time. Four nested subsets of this matrix were evaluated separately: around the figures, on the figures, on and around the figures, and all features. The representation carries no temporal information: no scan-path order, no saccade amplitudes or directions, no transition probabilities between regions, no within-trial dynamics, and no trial-to-trial evolution across the 240 images. This is a notable gap given the introduction's extended development of a graph-theoretic view in which fixations are vertices and saccades are edges - Fig. 6 even displays such a graph for one autistic child - because every quantity that graph representation would naturally yield (degree distribution, edge weights, path structure, transition entropy) is left uncomputed, and the model receives only vertex-region tallies.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Precision, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, each reported separately for the training, validation and test partitions and for the pooled total, across all four feature subsets - sixty-four numbers in total. The disaggregation is a real reporting virtue and is what makes it possible to see what the study actually achieved: it is only because the tables separate the columns that a reader can recover the held-out test accuracy of 58.3% behind the abstract's 73.8%. Two summary tables then compare precision and accuracy across subsets, again by partition. ROC curves are plotted for all four configurations, but no AUC is reported for any, so the single number that would summarise discriminability independent of threshold is presented only as a picture. Also missing: confidence intervals of any kind, F1, calibration, and any participant-level metric. Given that the test partition contains 36 observations, a confidence interval would have been the most informative addition - at 58.3% on 36 observations the interval comfortably includes chance.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Limited but honest. The features are individually meaningful - counts and durations of looking at specified places - and the region diagram makes each one concrete. The four-subset comparison functions as a coarse importance analysis, showing that the full set outperforms either the figure regions or their surroundings alone, and the paper's interpretation of this is straightforward and reasonable: more regions provide more detail. A single-child worked example traces the fixation points and times for one trial and shows the child concentrating on the target and the matching candidate before answering correctly, which usefully demonstrates that the raw data are behaviourally interpretable. Against this, no group-level feature analysis is reported at all - no means, no distributions, no effect sizes, no statistical comparison of where the two groups looked - so the paper never states, and cannot state, what visual behaviour distinguishes autistic from comparison children in its own data. It reports only that a network reached a certain accuracy. For a study whose stated purpose is to support specialist decision-making, the absence of any description of the discriminative behaviour is a substantive gap: a clinician can act on 'autistic children fixated less on the reference face' but not on 'an unspecified MLP scored 73.8% pooled across partitions'.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The weakest element, and it fails on two counts that compound one another. First, the reported performance is not held-out. The abstract, results narrative and conclusion all quote 76.6% precision and 73.8% accuracy, which Table 5 identifies as the TOTAL column - the pooled figure across training, validation and test. The test column of the same table reads 66.7% precision and 58.3% accuracy, with sensitivity 57.1% and specificity 60.0%. The same pattern holds for every feature subset: total accuracies of 65.0-73.8% against test accuracies of 52.8-58.3%, with training accuracies of 67.9-78.6%. A roughly 20-point train-to-test gap in all four configurations is the signature of overfitting on a small dataset, and it is neither reported nor discussed. Second, the split is over observations rather than children. The paper says only that '70 percent of data ... were used for training and the remaining 30 percent for tests and validation', but the reported percentages determine the arithmetic exactly: with 240 rows split 168/36/36 in the MATLAB Neural Network Toolbox default proportions, 78.6% of 168 is 132, 66.7% of 36 is 24, 58.3% of 36 is 21, and (132 + 24 + 21)/240 = 73.75%, reproducing the reported total to the decimal, and the same reconstruction works for the other three subsets. Forty children therefore contribute six rows each, randomly scattered, so every test row has five siblings from the same child in the training set. Because the features are per-region fixation counts and durations - quantities that are highly stable within an individual and reflect that person's habitual looking style as much as their diagnosis - this is a direct channel for identity leakage, and it means even the 58.3% test figure is optimistic relative to a genuinely unseen child. Two further issues: four feature subsets were compared on the same data and the best reported, and no chance baseline, permutation test or confidence interval accompanies any figure, although the balanced design makes chance exactly 50% and the test partition is small enough that three observations separate the reported result from it. The corrective is available and would be worth doing: partition the 40 children, generate observations within partitions, tune the network on training children only, choose the feature subset on a development set, and report test-column figures with confidence intervals as the study's result.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: Artificial neural network; Autism spectrum disorder; Computer games; Eye-tracking. 'Computer games' rather than 'serious games' or 'gamified assessment' reflects the paper's framing of the task as a therapeutic-game artefact repurposed for measurement, and the introduction devotes several paragraphs to games as therapy before turning to classification. No application term - screening, diagnosis, classification - appears in the keywords, although the body text uses 'diagnosis system' freely. Terms carried through the body: therapeutic games, facial emotion recognition, expression matching, fixation duration, fixation count, graph theory, eye-tracking graph, multilayer perceptron, scaled conjugate gradient, confusion matrix.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Signal, Image and Video Processing 17:4357-4365, Springer - a signal-processing engineering journal, published as an Original Paper. The venue accounts for the reporting balance: the metric tables are exhaustive and correctly disaggregated by training, validation and test partition, and ROC curves are plotted for every configuration, while the clinical apparatus is minimal (no diagnostic instrument, no cognitive measure, no screening of the comparison group) and the eye tracker is never identified. Received 30 March 2023, revised 25 May 2023, accepted 10 June 2023, published online 4 July 2023.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2023 from the Islamic Azad University Science and Research Branch and Tabriz Branch, with the Institute for Cognitive and Brain Sciences and the Faculty of Education and Psychology of Shahid Beheshti University, Tehran; no funding received. The framing is workforce scarcity: 'since the proper diagnosis of this condition depends on the correct and accurate decision of the specialist, the availability of adequate specialists in this area seems necessary. Unfortunately, the number of these specialists is low with respect to the growing autistic population', leading to the goal of a system 'easily applicable by not-so-expert users'. That is a task-shifting rationale rather than an accuracy-improvement one, and it recurs across the Iranian and Chinese papers in this corpus. The introduction is unusually wide-ranging for a short engineering paper, surveying therapeutic games, socially assistive robots, brain-computer interfaces and fuzzy learning before arriving at its own design, and it conspicuously cites work on same-race versus other-race face processing in autism without applying that literature to its own choice of Japanese stimuli for Iranian children. The conclusion's call to include 'conditions overlapping with autism for differential diagnosis' is a 2023-typical acknowledgement that the case-control geometry is the field's binding constraint.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Sariyanidi E; Zampella CJ; DeJardin E; Herrington JD; Schultz RT; Tunc B
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: Joint Proceedings of the ACM IUI 20
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional diagnostic-classification study with an embedded human-benchmark comparison. The distinguishing design feature is that the same 3-minute silent videos were given to a computer-vision pipeline and to 19 human raters, allowing accuracy and, more importantly, per-participant error patterns to be compared directly.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A single 6,272-dimensional vector of pairwise temporal-coordination statistics per participant. No raw video, no learned embedding, no per-frame classification, and no sequence model - the representation is explicitly about how facial and head movements co-vary in time rather than about which expressions occur.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Adults; exact range not reported in the retrieved text
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Consent is implied and referenced - two participants were excluded precisely because of 'their lack of consent for this particular set of experiments', which indicates a granular, per-experiment consent regime and is a positive signal about data governance
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A slightly modified Contextual Assessment of Social Skills (CASS), a semi-structured assessment of conversational ability designed to mimic a first-time encounter. Participants held two 3-minute face-to-face conversations with two different confederates: an interested condition in which the confederate engaged verbally and non-verbally, and a bored condition in which the confederate signalled disengagement through one-word answers, limited follow-up, neutral affect and reduced eye contact and gesture. Only the interested condition is analysed. Confederates were trained to speak no more than 50% of the time, to wait 10 s before initiating and 5 s before re-initiating after a pause, and otherwise to converse naturally. The scripted prompt given to both parties is quoted verbatim in the paper.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: An in-house dual-camera device with two 1080p HD cameras at 30 fps pointing in opposite directions on a floor stand placed between participant and confederate, allowing simultaneous recording of both. WASI-II for cognitive assessment. Analysis used the 3DI 3D morphable model fitting method with camera parameters supplied as input.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not reported. The pipeline is built on published components (3DI, and a modification of an existing localised expression basis), so it is reconstructible in outline.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: 'All aspects of the study were approved by the Institutional Review Board The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP)'
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Frame-wise 3D morphable model fitting via 3DI, which models facial identity, pose and expression jointly so that identity bias is explained away rather than left in the signal. The default PCA expression basis was replaced by a purpose-constructed basis of 60 localised components so that each component maps to a nameable facial region; the 7 nose and cheek components were discarded, leaving 53 expression dimensions. Head rotation was reduced to yaw, pitch and roll, giving a 56 x T behaviour matrix per participant. Windowed cross-correlation was then applied to every ordered pair of the 56 time series, using windows of length Tw with 50% overlap and forward lag only on the second series (so the pair (i,j) is not equivalent to (j,i), preserving directionality), and each pair was summarised by the mean and standard deviation of its maximal cross-correlation across windows - yielding 56 x 56 x 2 = 6,272 features per participant.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Deliberate and multi-layered, and unusually honest about its own limits. The expression basis was purpose-rebuilt: the paper notes that the 3DI method's default PCA basis 'limits the interpretability as PCA components are not localized', and replaces it with 60 localised components each associated with a nameable facial region, accepting a modelling cost to gain semantic traceability. Feature importance is then analysed at two levels - the individual top-10 weighted features are named, and the four anatomical categories (eyes, brows, mouth, pose) are compared against their baseline representation in the 6,272-feature pool, which correctly avoids the trap of concluding that mouth features matter simply because there are many of them. The findings are related to prior literature on blinking, nodding, social orienting and backchannel feedback. The authors then state plainly what their design cannot support: they cannot distinguish upper lip from mouth corner because the localised regions are not that granular, and a fuller semantic account 'is beyond the scope of this study'. The discussion also makes interpretability a precondition rather than an ornament, arguing that a clinician cannot rationally weigh an AI second opinion without knowing which behaviours produced it.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Only one hyperparameter was tuned - the cross-correlation window Tw, over the values 1, 2, 4 and 6 seconds - and it was tuned inside a nested cross-validation loop. Tw = 2 s was selected in most folds. The SVM's C was fixed at its default rather than tuned, which further reduces the search space.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Nested cross-validation with the window length as the only optimised hyperparameter, reported as 10-fold cross-validation repeated 100 times with the participant order shuffled between repetitions. Because each participant contributes exactly one feature vector, the split unit is the participant by construction and no within-participant leakage is possible. Repetition with shuffling addresses fold-assignment variance, which very few studies in this corpus do.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Several, and they are the right ones. The sample is too small to train deep models, stated as the reason for choosing a linear SVM. The interpretability achieved is partial - the localised basis cannot resolve sub-regions of the mouth, and the analysis of why particular features matter is explicitly deferred. The comparison group is neurotypical, and the conclusion states that 'in a real life scenario, the problem of interest would be more difficult as a potential patient may not be NT but may not have ASD either', calling for future work on neurodiverse samples. The participants are adults, and the paper notes that research on younger participants is needed given the value of early diagnosis. The analysis is monadic - it discards the confederate's behaviour - and the authors name dyadic analysis as a future direction. And they note that whether clinicians' diagnoses actually improve with AI assistance requires user research not yet done.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Forty-four adults enrolled (17 autistic, 27 neurotypical), of whom two were excluded because they had not consented to this particular set of experiments or their data could not be processed, giving a final sample of 42: 15 autistic and 27 neurotypical, i.e. 35.7% autism prevalence. All were native and fluent English speakers. A second sample is central to the design and is reported with equal care: 19 human raters, comprising 8 expert clinicians (doctoral-level, with extensive autism training at the Center for Autism Research) and 11 non-experts (mostly BA-level psychology staff with some familiarity with autism but no specialised training), all of whom rated all 42 videos. A third group also participates without being analysed: 10 conversation confederates (3 male, 7 female, all native English speakers, undergraduate or BA-level research assistants), semi-randomly assigned by availability and clinical judgement, and blind to participant diagnostic status. The unit of analysis for the model is the participant - one 6,272-dimensional vector each - which is why no within-participant leakage is possible.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)' and 'adults with autism' predominate, paired with 'neurotypical (NT) individuals' rather than the more common 'typically developing' or, worse, 'normal'. 'Neurotypical' is a term originating in the autistic community and its use here, in a paper from a major autism research centre, is a meaningful marker: it frames the comparison group as one neurotype among others rather than as a standard of normality. The conclusion goes further, calling for future work 'in predicting ASD diagnosis from neurodiverse samples' - importing 'neurodiverse' as a technical descriptor of a clinically mixed population, which is both an accurate usage and an unusual one in this literature. Clinical description is measured throughout: autism is 'defined by observable behavioral cues - what a person does well or not well, too little or too much', its core traits are 'observable differences in social communication, social reciprocity, nonverbal communication, and relationships', and the word 'differences' rather than 'deficits' is used where most papers in this corpus use the latter. The framing of purpose is also non-replacement: the stated aim is to establish whether AI adds anything beyond clinician judgement, on the explicit premise that 'clinicians would have little interest in or benefit from incorporating AI algorithms if their decisions - and errors - highly overlap with their own'. There is no autistic-community involvement statement.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: The retrieved text states that the groups did not differ significantly on mean chronological age, full-scale IQ, verbal IQ or sex ratio, with the statistics themselves in a table not recoverable from the extracted text. That set of matched variables is nonetheless the most complete in this corpus for a study of this size, and two elements are worth emphasising because their absence undermines so many other studies charted here. IQ was measured with a standardised instrument (WASI-II) in both groups and matched on both full-scale and verbal estimates - so the classification cannot be attributed to a cognitive-ability gap, which is an uncontrolled confound in the majority of studies in this review. And sex ratio was matched rather than left uncontrolled or eliminated by sampling only boys. All participants were native and fluent English speakers by inclusion, which removes language proficiency as a confound in a conversational paradigm but also narrows generalisability. What is not reported in the retrieved text: race or ethnicity, socioeconomic status, comorbidity, medication, and - notably given that ADOS-2 was administered - any severity score. The sample is adults, cognitively able enough to complete an unstructured 3-minute conversation with a stranger, and it is a research-registry population at a specialist centre rather than a community sample.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: The strongest reference standard encountered in this review. Diagnostic status was 'confirmed as part of this study' - established prospectively rather than inherited from records - using the Clinical Best Estimate process, informed by ADOS-2 Module 4 and adhering to DSM-5 criteria. Clinical Best Estimate is the accepted research gold standard precisely because it integrates a standardised observational instrument, developmental history and clinical judgement rather than resting on any single source, and Module 4 is the correct ADOS-2 module for verbally fluent adolescents and adults. Neurotypical status was not merely the absence of a diagnosis: controls were 'recruited specifically as neurotypical controls', and raters were told they were 'clear cases of individuals without autism'. That framing is a genuine strength for a benchmark study - it means the human raters' 80.3% accuracy is not depressed by ambiguous controls - but it is simultaneously the study's central external-validity limit, since the two groups are drawn from the well-separated ends of a distribution that a real screening population fills continuously. The authors say so themselves in the conclusion. Two further points: the ADOS-2 was administered but no calibrated severity score is reported, so the autistic sample's position on the spectrum is unquantified; and the conversation confederates were blind to diagnostic status and unaware of the dependent variables, so the elicitation itself was not differentially shaped by knowledge of group membership - a control that few conversational studies in this corpus implement.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Cognitive ability was measured properly: WASI-II full-scale and verbal IQ estimates were obtained for the whole sample and compared between groups, with no significant difference. This is the correct handling and it removes the single most pervasive confound in this literature. Language ability is indexed by verbal IQ and by the requirement that all participants be native and fluent English speakers, which matters for a task whose entire stimulus is spontaneous conversation. Autism severity, however, is not reported. ADOS-2 Module 4 was administered as part of the diagnostic process, so calibrated severity scores were almost certainly available, yet none appears - so it is impossible to say where the 15 autistic adults sit on the spectrum, whether the 45% the model failed to detect were the less severely affected, or whether the four participants that humans misjudged but the model caught differed systematically in severity. That last question is the one the paper's own error-overlap analysis makes most interesting, and severity data would have gone a long way towards answering it. No adaptive-functioning, comorbidity or motor measure is reported either.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is not primarily to build a better classifier but to answer a prior question the field has left open: how do AI predictions correspond to human ones? The framing is explicit and is the paper's organising logic - 'the utility of an AI algorithm would be negligible if it provides little information beyond what clinicians can readily infer' - so the study is designed as a benchmark rather than a demonstration. Nineteen raters (8 doctoral-level autism experts, 11 non-experts) and a computer-vision pipeline were given the same 3-minute silent videos of 42 adults in casual conversation. Findings: AI accuracy 80.5%, expert clinicians 83.1%, non-experts 78.3%, all humans 80.3% - so the model performs at approximately expert level on this evidence. The operating characteristics show why accuracy alone is misleading: PPV 0.86, NPV 0.79, specificity 0.95 and sensitivity 0.55, meaning the classifier is highly conservative and detects only just over half the autistic adults. The paper's real result is the error analysis. Of five participants misclassified by a majority of human raters, four were correctly classified by the model, including the hardest case, which only 21% of raters got right. Per-participant accuracy of humans and AI correlated at just rho = 0.35, falling to 0.19 once the participants nearly all raters got right are removed, and the lower-left quadrant of the scatter - hard for both - is essentially empty. Feature weights point to head pose and its coordination with eye movement, and to mouth-related coordination, as the dominant signal, with both categories over-represented in the top-weighted features relative to their share of the feature pool.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Single site: the Center for Autism Research at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, with the University of Pennsylvania. This is a specialist research centre, and both arms of the study reflect that - the participants are a research-registry sample assessed by Clinical Best Estimate on site, and the 19 raters are the centre's own doctoral clinicians and BA-level staff. The rater sample is therefore an unusually strong human benchmark (these are people who assess autistic adults professionally) and simultaneously a narrow one (they share an institution, a training culture and, plausibly, prior exposure to similar video material). The recording setting is a laboratory room with a floor-standing dual-camera device between the two conversation partners, and the paradigm is a semi-structured assessment rather than a clinical encounter. The recruitment geometry is case-control at 35.7% prevalence with deliberately clear-cut controls, which the authors flag as the key generalisation limit. Against that, the paradigm itself is deliberately designed for scalability outside such settings: the conversation partner is a non-clinician, the interaction lasts three minutes, and the only equipment is a camera - which is the basis for the claim that this could serve as a screening procedure.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: The Contextual Assessment of Social Skills, slightly modified - a semi-structured assessment of conversational ability designed to mimic a real-life first-time encounter. Each participant held two 3-minute face-to-face conversations with two different confederates: an interested condition, in which the confederate engaged verbally and non-verbally, and a bored condition, in which the confederate signalled disengagement through one-word answers, few follow-up questions, neutral affect and reduced eye contact and gesture. Only the interested condition is analysed here. The confederate protocol is specified to an unusual degree: 10 confederates (3 male, 7 female, all native English speakers, undergraduate or BA-level research staff), blind to diagnostic status and unaware of the dependent variables, trained to speak no more than 50% of the time, to wait 10 s before initiating and 5 s before re-initiating after a pause, and otherwise to converse naturally; the prompt given to both parties is quoted verbatim. That combination - a live, unscripted, genuinely social task with a standardised and blinded partner - is close to the ideal for this literature, since it preserves naturalism without letting the partner's behaviour vary with what they believe about the participant. Two design choices constrain the result. Audio was discarded from both the AI and human conditions, so speech content, prosody and turn-taking timing - all diagnostically informative and all captured on the recording - are excluded by design in order to make the human-AI comparison fair. And only the participant's video enters the model, an approach the authors name explicitly as monadic and identify as a limitation: 'even if the context of the conversation is dyadic, our AI-based analysis is not dyadic since it discards the information from the confederate'. The bored condition, which would test whether the coordination signature survives a change in the partner's behaviour, was collected and left unanalysed.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session per participant, no follow-up and no test-retest assessment of the coordination features. Ethics governance is well handled: the study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, and consent was evidently granular rather than blanket, since two of the 44 enrolled participants were excluded specifically because of 'their lack of consent for this particular set of experiments' - a per-experiment consent regime that is a positive marker of data governance in a study involving identifiable facial video. Confederates were blinded to diagnostic status. The human raters were not blinded in the ordinary sense - they were told that every participant was either a confirmed autism case or a deliberately recruited clear control - which is appropriate for calibrating a benchmark but does mean their task was easier than a real screening decision. Funding from four NIH grants is fully itemised. No competing-interests statement appears in the retrieved text, which is a gap given that the work develops a potential clinical tool.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Recording used a purpose-built in-house device with two 1080p cameras at 30 fps mounted back to back on a floor stand between the participant and the confederate, so both parties are captured simultaneously from a fixed and identical geometry. Cognitive assessment used the WASI-II. Diagnosis used ADOS-2 Module 4. The analysis stack is the study's technical core and is described precisely: 3DI, a 3D morphable model fitting method chosen for two specific properties - it learns facial identity from multiple frames, so identity bias can be modelled and explained away rather than left to contaminate the expression signal, and it accepts camera parameters as input, which the authors state is critical for decoupling expression from head pose. The default PCA expression basis was replaced with a purpose-built basis of 60 localised components; 7 corresponding to nose and cheek were discarded, leaving 53 expression dimensions plus 3 rotation angles. Classification used a linear SVM at default C. The decision to reject Facial Action Coding System units is argued rather than assumed: the analysis needs continuous intensities for cross-correlation, automated AU detectors supply intensity for only a small number of AUs, and adding AUs would inflate a feature space that already grows quadratically in the number of time series.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Among the best-specified methods in this corpus, with the usual artefact gap. Reproducible from the text: the CASS protocol including confederate selection, training rules, timing constraints and the verbatim prompt; the camera hardware, resolution, frame rate and placement; the choice of 3DI with its stated rationale; the construction of the 60-component localised basis and the principled exclusion of nose and cheek components; the exact windowed cross-correlation scheme, including 50% window overlap, forward-lag-only convention and the explicit note that the pair (i,j) is therefore not equivalent to (j,i); the derivation of the 6,272 feature count; the SVM kernel and the fixed C = 1; the single tuned hyperparameter and its four candidate values; and the nested 10-fold cross-validation repeated 100 times with shuffling. The human-rating protocol is equally complete - head-and-neck crops, side-by-side layout, audio removed, randomised order, one viewing per video, no revisiting, completed in one to three sessions. Not available: code, data, the modified expression basis, preregistration, and the Table 1 demographics in the retrieved text. As a workshop paper (CEUR/ACM IUI joint proceedings) it is also shorter than a journal article, which accounts for some of the compression.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The stated limitations are unusually well chosen and include several that comparable papers omit: the sample is too small for deep learning, and this is given as the actual reason for the modelling choice rather than left implicit; the interpretability achieved is partial, and the authors specify exactly where it stops (they cannot resolve upper lip from mouth corner); the comparison group is neurotypical, and the conclusion states that a real patient 'may not be NT but may not have ASD either', calling for neurodiverse samples; the participants are adults when early diagnosis is where the clinical value lies; the analysis is monadic and discards the confederate; and whether clinicians actually benefit requires user research not yet performed. What is not addressed matters too. The sensitivity of 0.55 appears in a single sentence alongside three other operating characteristics and is never revisited, yet it is arguably the study's most consequential number: a tool that misses 45% of autistic adults cannot function as the screening technology the conclusion proposes, at least not in the direction the conclusion proposes it - though it could function well in the opposite direction, since NPV 0.79 and specificity 0.95 make a positive prediction informative. The abstract and conclusion report only accuracy. No majority-class baseline is computed, though at 15 versus 27 the floor is 64.3%, so the model's 80.5% represents a 16-point gain rather than the 30-point gain a reader assuming balance would infer. The human and AI conditions are not strictly matched - raters saw participant and confederate side by side while the model saw only the participant, so if anything the humans had more information, which strengthens rather than weakens the paper's conclusion but should be stated. Raters were also told that every case was clear-cut. No confidence intervals accompany any figure, and with 42 participants one case is 2.4 percentage points. And the bored condition was collected and never used.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Five directions, all following directly from what the study found. Examine which behaviours drive a predicted diagnosis, framed not as a nicety but as a precondition for clinical use - 'clinicians should understand how the AI algorithm makes a prediction before taking this prediction into account' - and requiring more granular expression models than the current localised basis provides. Extend to younger participants, since early diagnosis is where the developmental benefit lies. Move from monadic to dyadic analysis by incorporating the confederate's behaviour, which the recording setup already captures and the paradigm's interactive nature makes theoretically apt. Test on neurodiverse samples rather than autism-versus-neurotypical, the authors' own diagnosis of their key external-validity gap. And conduct user research to determine whether clinician decisions actually improve when AI assistance is available - the step that would convert a demonstrated non-overlap of errors into demonstrated clinical value. Absent from the list: raising sensitivity, external validation on an independent cohort, and analysis of the bored condition.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Facial movement and head movement during spontaneous conversation, and specifically their temporal coordination. The behavioural target is defined broadly and deliberately: the authors reject restricting analysis to the six basic emotions on the grounds that 'other kinds of facial movements (e.g., communicative expressions, speech-related mouth movements) are also important for diagnosing autism', and so quantify all observable facial motion via a morphable model rather than an emotion taxonomy. The coordination framing is grounded in the diagnostic instrument itself: the paper notes that ADOS criteria evaluate how an individual combines speech with gestures and eye contact with facial expression, and reasons by analogy that coordination within the facial channel - across regions, and between face and head - should be similarly informative. Empirically this is borne out. Head-pose-to-pose correlations carry the greatest average classifier weight, pose-eye correlations feature prominently in the top 10, and mouth-related correlations account for six of the top 10 including three mouth-mouth pairs; relative to their share of the 6,272-feature pool, pose features are about 2.5 times over-represented in the top 10 and mouth features about 1.6 times. The authors connect these to established findings on blinking and nodding as conversational signals and on head and eye movement as indices of social attention. Two behaviours present in the recording are excluded by design: speech, because audio was removed to keep the human comparison fair, and the confederate's behaviour, because the analysis is monadic.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-sensor fusion - a single camera stream - but the study is one of the most informative in this corpus about fusion of a different kind, because its entire feature construction is a within-modality coordination analysis. The 56 time series (53 localised facial expression components plus yaw, pitch and roll) are combined pairwise by windowed cross-correlation with directional lag, producing 6,272 features that encode not what the face did but how its parts moved together in time. The results locate the discriminative signal squarely in the cross-channel pairs: the highest-weighted features on average are pose-pose, and pose-eye combinations appear among the top individual features - so the signal is in how head movement coordinates with itself and with eye-region movement, not in either channel alone. This is a concrete demonstration that the useful information in multimodal behaviour can lie in the coordination structure rather than in the constituent signals, which is a stronger and more testable claim than the generic 'fusion improved accuracy' reported by most multimodal studies here. Two limits are stated by the authors. Feature count grows quadratically in the number of time series, which is why Facial Action Coding System units were not added and why nose and cheek components were dropped - a rare instance of a paper declining extra features on principled dimensionality grounds rather than adding everything available. And the analysis is monadic: the confederate's synchronised video was recorded by the same device and discarded, so interpersonal synchrony, which is the natural extension of a within-person coordination analysis and is theoretically central to conversation, remains untested and is named as future work.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A linear support vector machine at the default regularisation C = 1, over 6,272 engineered coordination features. The choice of a simple model is argued rather than defaulted: deep learning was rejected because 'the sample size is insufficient for reliably training deep learning models from scratch', and transfer learning was rejected because, to the authors' knowledge, no publicly available pre-trained model is directly applicable to the problem, so fine-tuning a classification head was also unavailable. Leaving C at its default further shrinks the search space, so the entire modelling procedure has exactly one tuned quantity - the cross-correlation window - and that is tuned inside a nested loop. The result is a pipeline with very few researcher degrees of freedom, which is the main reason its 80.5% is more credible than several higher figures elsewhere in this corpus. The intellectual weight of the paper sits in the representation rather than the classifier: the modelling contribution is the 3DMM-based identity-removed localised expression basis and the directional cross-correlation feature construction, with the SVM as a deliberately transparent read-out.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A single 6,272-dimensional vector per participant, built in three steps. First, frame-wise 3D morphable model fitting via 3DI, which jointly models identity, pose and expression so that the person's facial identity is estimated and removed rather than left to confound the expression signal - the authors cite identity bias explicitly, and this is one of very few studies in this corpus that treats individual identity as something to be subtracted rather than as an accidental source of accuracy. Second, replacement of the model's default PCA expression basis with 60 purpose-built localised components, of which 53 are retained (nose and cheek discarded), so that each dimension corresponds to a nameable facial region; concatenated with yaw, pitch and roll, this gives a 56 x T matrix per video. Third, windowed cross-correlation on every ordered pair of the 56 series, using 50% overlapping windows of length Tw and permitting only forward lag on the second series so that direction is preserved and the (i,j) pair differs from (j,i); each pair contributes the mean and standard deviation of its maximal cross-correlation across windows. The representation is therefore about temporal relationships rather than about static or averaged expression content, and it deliberately discards absolute expression magnitude, which is exactly the quantity most vulnerable to identity and recording differences. The dimensionality - 6,272 features for 42 participants - is extreme, mitigated by a linear model, fixed regularisation, no feature selection and participant-level nested cross-validation.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: The most complete metric set in this corpus for a study of this type. The AI model is characterised by accuracy (80.5%), sensitivity (0.55), specificity (0.95), positive predictive value (0.86) and negative predictive value (0.79) - reporting PPV and NPV alongside sensitivity and specificity is rare here and is the reporting that lets a reader see the model's actual clinical shape, namely a conservative rule whose positive calls are trustworthy and whose negative calls are not. Human performance is reported at three levels of aggregation: all raters (80.3%), experts (83.1%) and non-experts (78.3%). Beyond summary metrics, the study reports two per-participant analyses that carry more information than any accuracy figure: a table listing the five participants misclassified by a majority of human raters together with the AI's prediction for each, and a scatter plot of per-participant human accuracy against per-participant AI accuracy with the correlation quantified (rho = 0.35, and rho = 0.19 after excluding participants that 95%+ of raters classified correctly). Missing: AUC, confidence intervals, and any statistical test of the human-versus-AI difference or of the error-overlap claim - the rho values and the empty lower-left quadrant are reported descriptively, with no significance test or bootstrap, and with 42 participants and five hard cases the error-overlap finding rests on a small number of observations.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is treated as a design constraint rather than a post-hoc report, and the study is the clearest example in this corpus of a modelling choice being made to preserve semantic traceability. The authors note that the 3DI method's PCA expression basis 'limits the interpretability as PCA components are not localized - we cannot associate any PCA component with a specific facial region', and therefore rebuild the basis with 60 localised components before any modelling occurs. The linear SVM then makes weights directly readable. The importance analysis is done at two levels and, critically, against the right baseline: individual top-10 features are named, and the four anatomical categories are compared with their proportion of the full 6,272-feature pool, so the conclusion that mouth features matter is not an artefact of there being many mouth features (25.5% of the pool, 40% of the top 10) and the pose finding is stronger than it looks (5.3% of the pool, 13.3% of the top 10). Findings are then related to independent literature on blinking, nodding, social orienting and backchannel feedback rather than left as bare weights. The authors are equally explicit about the ceiling: they cannot distinguish upper lip from mouth corner, a fuller account would require 3D versions of localised bases, and 'further analysis to uncover why these features are important is beyond the scope of this study'. Finally, the discussion argues that interpretability is a precondition for the assistive use case the paper proposes - a clinician cannot rationally weigh a dissenting AI opinion without knowing which behaviours produced it - which correctly makes explanation a functional requirement rather than a courtesy.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The strongest validation design encountered so far in this review, with one important caveat about how the result should be read. Each participant contributes exactly one feature vector, so the unit of splitting is the person by construction and the segment-level leakage that inflates most studies in this corpus is structurally impossible. Validation is nested cross-validation with a single tuned hyperparameter, the correlation window Tw over four candidate values, optimised inside the inner loop; the SVM's regularisation is left at its default rather than tuned, further reducing researcher degrees of freedom; and no feature selection is performed at all, so selection bias cannot arise despite 6,272 features. The outer evaluation is 10-fold cross-validation repeated 100 times with participant order shuffled between repetitions, which addresses fold-assignment variance - a source of instability that very few studies here even acknowledge. The identity-modelling step deserves separate credit as leakage control of a different kind: because the 3DMM estimates and removes facial identity, the representation is explicitly stripped of the individual-appearance information that, elsewhere in this corpus, silently drives high accuracy. The caveat is the base rate and the operating point. At 15 autistic and 27 neurotypical participants, majority-class prediction yields 64.3%, so 80.5% is a 16-point improvement rather than the 30 points a reader assuming balance might infer, and no permutation test or confidence interval is offered. The class imbalance also shapes the classifier: at sensitivity 0.55 and specificity 0.95 the model has learned to be conservative, so its accuracy is carried disproportionately by correctly identifying neurotypical participants. None of this undermines the study's actual claim - which concerns the non-overlap of AI and human errors, evaluated per participant - but it does mean the headline accuracy should not be read as evidence of a strong autism detector.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Author keywords: autism; assistive healthcare technologies; digital phenotyping. The choice is revealing. 'Digital phenotyping' locates the work in a measurement tradition rather than a diagnostic one, and 'assistive healthcare technologies' states the intended role explicitly - neither 'diagnosis', 'screening', 'classification', 'machine learning' nor 'deep learning' appears, even though the paper performs classification with machine learning. Terms carried through the body text include computational behavior analysis, 3D morphable model, windowed cross-correlation, monadic versus dyadic analysis, Clinical Best Estimate, Contextual Assessment of Social Skills, and neurodiverse samples.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: CEUR Workshop Proceedings volume 3359, the ITAH (Intelligent Technologies for Assistive Healthcare) track of the Joint Proceedings of the ACM IUI 2023 Workshops, pages 48-57 - a workshop paper at a human-computer interaction venue rather than a clinical or machine-learning journal. The venue choice fits the contribution: the question of whether AI predictions add anything beyond human judgement is an interaction question, and the paper's framing around assistive rather than autonomous use is native to the IUI community. It also explains some of the reporting compression, since workshop papers are short. The article is deposited as an HHS Public Access author manuscript, reflecting the NIH funding, and is available under CC BY 4.0.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2023 (author manuscript available in PMC from November 2023), from the Center for Autism Research at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and the University of Pennsylvania, funded by four NIH grants (R01MH118327, R01MH122599, 5P50HD105354-02, R21HD102078). The framing is deliberately corrective rather than promotional. The opening premise is that psychiatry, unlike the rest of medicine, relies almost exclusively on observational and paper-and-pencil instruments, and that computational behaviour analysis could supply the missing instrumentation - with the explicit acknowledgement that clinical assessment reliability is currently limited, citing the DSM-5 field trial kappa of 0.69 for autism. The central rhetorical move is to identify a gap the field has left open: 'to our knowledge, no study has directly compared AI algorithms and human raters with respect to overall predictive capacity or specific decisions on individual cases'. That reframing - from 'can AI classify autism?' to 'does AI tell a clinician anything they did not already know?' - is the paper's real contribution and is the question most of this corpus does not ask. The positioning is consistently augmentative: AI as an assistive tool that could prompt a clinician to re-evaluate when the two disagree, with the caveat that this is only workable if the algorithm can say why.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Xia C; Zhang D; Li K; Li H; Chen J; Min W; Han J
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional two-group diagnostic-classification study with multi-centre recruitment, combined with a substantial descriptive analysis of gaze features and a methodological investigation of how temporal and stimulus-set parameters affect between-group separability
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A sequence of per-fixation feature vectors per stimulus, and 82 such sequences per child. The design choice that defines the paper is that no aggregation over fixations occurs before modelling - the ordered sequence enters the LSTM directly, in contrast to the histogram and stacked-fixation baselines the authors implement for comparison.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None on an independent cohort, though recruitment across two provinces and multiple hospitals and schools gives the sample more site diversity than most studies in this corpus. The autoencoder's pretraining on MS COCO is external but is a generic vision corpus, not a validation set.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not explicitly stated, although mothers were present during testing
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Passive free viewing. Eighty-two images from four categories chosen 'according to the behavioural characteristics of children with ASD' - facial images, social scenarios, animated characters and synthetic patterns - presented in two sessions of about three minutes each, six minutes in total. Each image was shown for 3 s separated by a 0.5 s grey mask. Children were positioned 0.5 m from the monitor and given 'no particular instructions except to observe the images'. Deliberately short and undemanding, on the stated grounds that the procedure must be child-friendly and hold attention.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: SciEye 2.0 eye tracker sampling at 140 Hz, using infrared corneal and retinal reflection; 1920 x 1080 monitor. Modelling used a deep autoencoder pretrained on 10,000 MS COCO images, SLIC superpixel segmentation, and an LSTM network trained by backpropagation through time.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not reported. Supplementary material is available through the publisher.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Medical Ethics Committee of Northwestern Polytechnical University, protocol 202002032, with all procedures conducted in accordance with the latest revision of the Declaration of Helsinki - a named committee with a protocol number
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Each stimulus was segmented into superpixels by SLIC, and for each fixation the bounding box of the containing superpixel was resized and passed through a deep autoencoder pretrained on MS COCO to yield a c-bit compressed semantic code. The authors note that using the full resized superpixel bounding box outperformed a fixed patch at the superpixel centre, 'implying the importance of utilizing the complete information of the superpixels'. Each fixation is then represented by the concatenation of its semantic code with four low-level descriptors: position, duration, saccade amplitude and saccade orientation. A viewing pattern of m+1 fixations becomes a length-m sequence of such feature vectors.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Substantial and multi-layered, though the model itself remains opaque. Three distinct interpretive strands run through the paper. First, an extensive descriptive analysis of hand-crafted low-level and semantic gaze features with between-group comparisons, including region-of-interest labelling and first-fixation timing, presented before any modelling and honestly concluding that these differences are 'not sufficiently significant to directly use these hand-crafted features for classification'. Second, a methodological analysis using time-delay embedding to quantify how between-group and within-group distances change with the amount of temporal information and the number of stimuli - which is the study's actual scientific argument and is unusual in this literature for treating separability as a quantity to be measured rather than assumed. Third, qualitative inspection of model scores identifying three factors that drive predictions: whether the pattern stays on the image or drifts to the grey mask, whether fixations on salient objects are missing, and whether the order and duration of fixations are reasonable, illustrated with worked successful and failed cases. What is absent is any attribution method applied to the trained LSTM itself - no saliency, no gate analysis, no per-fixation contribution - so the account of what the model uses is inferred from ablations and examples rather than measured.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Table II reports classification results under varying LSTM hidden units and fully connected size (reported to have slight effect), maximum epochs (accuracy increases with iterations), mini-batch size, learning rate, and the minLength lower bound (2 best). These comparisons are presented as ablation and sensitivity analyses rather than as a tuning protocol, and there is no statement that a separate development set was used, so the parameter values reported were compared on the same evaluation data.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Subject-level random split: 50% of subjects for training and the remainder for testing, repeated in five random permutations with all five exceeding 95.76% accuracy. Because the unit of splitting is the child, all 82 stimulus-based patterns from one child stay on the same side of the split, so within-child leakage is avoided by construction - an important design property given that the model scores individual stimuli. The autoencoder is trained on an external image corpus (MS COCO) rather than on participant data, so it introduces no leakage either. The one qualification is the final thresholding step: the paper states that subject average scores were computed 'for each subject in training and testing' and the Otsu threshold selected on that combined distribution, so the decision threshold is fitted transductively using the test subjects' scores. Otsu does not consult labels, but it does consult the test data.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The model is trained only on 3-6 year olds and is therefore currently suitable only for initial screening in that band. Failure cases are analysed concretely: natural scenes with slight between-group difference and few training samples; small objects whose semantic identity the encoder cannot resolve; and scenes with objects near the image edge, where typically developing children's fixations also fall on the grey mask during exploration, causing false positives. The subgroup analysis surfaces two further constraints as findings rather than caveats - reduced sensitivity in children who have had rehabilitation training, and reduced specificity in the youngest children. The discussion also acknowledges that hand-crafted features alone cannot classify adequately, and that individual stimulus-based patterns are 'not robust' so aggregation is necessary.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups, with a corpus considerably larger than most in this review. Total recruited: 333 children aged 3-6, comprising 140 with autism (112 boys, 28 girls; mean age 4.66 +/- 1.00 years) and 193 typically developing (122 boys, 71 girls; mean age 4.77 +/- 0.92 years), all with normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Recruitment was multi-centre, from several hospitals and schools across Shaanxi and Fujian provinces. The evaluation set is 165 subjects - 70 autistic and 95 typically developing - formed by a 50% subject-level random split, with robustness checked over five permutations. The paper explicitly frames sample size as a methodological argument rather than a logistical fact: Fig. 14(a) visualises how group separability degrades as more subjects are added, and the discussion states that 'when the number of subjects is less than 100, the test cannot accurately reflect the performance of the model' - a direct criticism of the small-sample studies that dominate this corpus, and one this study is entitled to make. A second unit of analysis exists and is handled correctly: each child contributes 82 stimulus-based viewing patterns, and these are scored individually before being aggregated to a subject-level decision, but the split is by child so the 82 patterns never straddle training and test.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'Children with ASD' and 'typically developing (TD) children' are the working terms, used consistently and person-first. But the surrounding framing is the most burden-oriented in this corpus. The introduction states that 'most patients diagnosed with ASD cannot independently live, study and work when they grow up, which places a heavy burden on their families and society', and autistic children are referred to throughout as 'patients' - including in the abstract, where the aim is 'to screen patients with ASD'. Early intervention is motivated by 'reducing the harm caused by the disorder'. Elsewhere the vocabulary is that of deviation from a norm: 'atypical performance', 'abnormalities in ASD', 'abnormal distribution values', and children whose viewing is 'passive in the information exploration process'. Set against this, the study's practical orientation is genuinely equity-driven and its design is respectful of children in a way several others here are not - six minutes of passive viewing, no instructions, no restraint, mother present, stimuli chosen partly to hold attention. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. One passage complicates the picture in an interesting way: the finding that 5-6 year olds who had undergone rehabilitation training scored lower and were more often missed is reported neutrally as a limitation of the model, without remarking that it implies the measured signal is modifiable by intervention - which is a substantive point about what the 'AI-marker' is actually marking.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Reported: group sizes, sex counts and mean and standard deviation of age for both groups, plus normal or corrected vision as the only participant criterion. Age is well matched (4.66 +/- 1.00 versus 4.77 +/- 0.92). Sex is not: the autistic group is 80.0% male (112 of 140) and the comparison group 63.2% male (122 of 193), a difference of nearly 17 percentage points that is neither tested, matched, adjusted nor mentioned. This omission is more consequential here than in most studies because the paper's own subgroup analysis reports that 'the groups of boys presented higher error rates than the groups of girls' - so sex is demonstrably related to model performance and is also unequally distributed between the classes. Not reported at all: IQ or developmental level, language ability, socioeconomic status, comorbidity, medication, and any autism severity measure. Recruitment sites are described qualitatively as areas 'where medical conditions are relatively poor', which is the closest the paper comes to a socioeconomic characterisation and is offered as a strength of external validity rather than as a demographic variable. The absence of any cognitive measure is a real limitation for a passive-viewing task in 3-6 year olds, since the capacity to sit still and attend to a screen for six minutes varies sharply with developmental level - and the paper's own analysis of why specificity is lowest in the youngest children turns on exactly that capacity.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not described. This is the study's most serious reporting gap and it sits oddly alongside the sophistication of everything else. The Data Acquisition section states only that 140 children with autism and 193 typically developing children were recruited and that all had normal or corrected vision; no diagnostic instrument, no DSM or ICD criteria, no clinician, no assessment procedure and no diagnostic date appears anywhere in the main text for either group. Two clinical co-authors are affiliated with the Children Healthcare Department of the Affiliated Hospital of Northwest University and the Children Rehabilitation Center of Shaanxi Rehabilitation Hospital, so clinical diagnosis is clearly implied, and the multi-centre recruitment from hospitals suggests service-identified children - but none of this is stated. The irony is sharpened by Table IV, in which the authors tabulate the diagnostic instruments used by comparator studies in the literature - Autism Behaviour Checklist, M-CHAT, ADOS, ADI-R - as a characteristic worth reporting, while leaving their own blank. Typically developing status rests on school recruitment with no screening instrument reported. Supplementary material was not retrieved and may contain more; on the main text alone, the quantity the model predicts with 96.73% accuracy is not defined.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, developmental, language, adaptive or severity measure was administered to any of the 333 children, and no autism severity score of any kind is reported. Three consequences follow that the paper does not address. First, the autistic sample cannot be positioned on the spectrum, so it is unknown whether the model's performance would hold in a less clearly affected group - a particular concern given that the discussion itself observes that adding subjects makes 'more unclear and atypical cases' appear. Second, the paradigm demands six minutes of sustained attention to a screen from 3-6 year olds, and the ability to comply is developmentally graded; without a cognitive measure it is impossible to separate an autism-specific viewing signature from a general attentional or developmental one, and the authors' own explanation of why specificity is lowest in 3-4 year olds - younger children 'find it difficult to focus on the screen the entire time, resulting in meaningless fixations that fall on the gray mask' - shows that this is not hypothetical. Third, the conclusion proposes that dynamic viewing patterns 'can also be employed to quantitatively assess subjects' ASD risk', but with no severity instrument in the study there is nothing against which such a continuous risk score could be calibrated or validated.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The goal is explicitly infrastructural rather than merely methodological: to build a screening method that works where the constraints are affordability, child-friendliness and the absence of professionals, which the authors identify as the three barriers to autism screening in remote areas. The technical contribution is the dynamic viewing pattern - gaze treated as an ordered trajectory over both viewing time and the stimulus set, rather than as a static distribution of fixations - together with a pipeline that encodes each fixation semantically via an autoencoder, scores each stimulus sequence with an LSTM, and aggregates 82 stimulus scores into a subject decision. Findings: subject-level accuracy 96.73% with sensitivity 96.85% and specificity 96.63% on 165 test children, stable above 95.76% across five random subject-level splits. The supporting analyses are more informative than the headline. Conventional hand-crafted features reproduce the expected group differences - autistic children make fewer fixations with longer saccades, look less at faces and other salient objects, take longer to notice them, and dwell more on background and on the grey mask - but the authors state plainly that these differences are 'not sufficiently significant to directly use these hand-crafted features for classification'. A time-delay embedding analysis then shows that between-group distance grows with the length of the pattern section used and with the number of stimuli included, and that for sections shorter than five fixations the within-autism variability exceeds the between-group difference - a quantitative argument that separability is manufactured by using more temporal and more stimulus context, not merely asserted. Ablation confirms both feature families contribute (semantic 94.85%, low-level 93.33%, combined 96.73%) and that sequence modelling beats fixation-histogram and stacked-fixation baselines.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Multi-centre, and deliberately so: children were recruited from multiple hospitals and schools in Shaanxi and Fujian provinces, chosen because 'medical conditions are relatively poor' there. This is one of only a few studies in this corpus with genuine site diversity, and the framing is consistent throughout - the paper's entire motivation is that screening in remote and low-income areas is understudied, and the design constraints follow from that premise rather than being retrofitted to it. Recording took place in a therapy room with the child 0.5 m from the monitor and at most two other people present, the mother and one researcher, which is a realistic community-clinic arrangement rather than a laboratory. The counterweight is the usual one: recruitment pairs hospital- or rehabilitation-identified autistic children against school-recruited comparison children at 42% prevalence, so the geometry remains case-control and the accuracy does not transfer to a community screening population. The authors do not compute what their operating point would mean at population prevalence, which for a proposed universal screening tool is the omission that matters most.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Passive free viewing of 82 static images, presented in two sessions of roughly three minutes each with each image shown for 3 s and a 0.5 s grey mask between images, with the only instruction being to observe. Four stimulus categories were chosen 'according to the behavioural characteristics of children with ASD': facial images, social scenarios, animated characters and synthetic patterns. Three properties make this among the better-designed paradigms in the corpus. It is short and undemanding by explicit design, because the authors treat children's limited sustained attention as a constraint on the method rather than as a nuisance. It varies stimulus type systematically, which permits the study's most practically useful analysis - a ranking of all 82 images by discriminative power, showing facial images strongest (499.59) and animated characters weakest (356.27), and demonstrating that dropping to the best 60 images costs no accuracy while dropping to a random 60 costs a great deal. That result is a concrete contribution to protocol design that most eye-tracking studies here are not positioned to make. And the grey mask, introduced as a simple inter-stimulus interval, turns out to carry signal, since fixations landing on it are one of the three factors the authors identify as driving model scores. That last point is also the paradigm's weakness: dwelling on a blank grey screen is at least as much a measure of disengagement from the task as of atypical social attention, and the paper's own observation that 3-4 year olds in the comparison group generate 'meaningless fixations that fall on the gray mask' concedes that the same behaviour arises from ordinary inattention.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up, and no test-retest reliability - which is a real gap for a tool proposed for repeated community screening. The nearest thing to a temporal analysis is Fig. 8, which tracks how the sample and the classification results evolved across the four quarters of 2021, showing 2-4 misclassified cases in an initial 40-child phase and stable results thereafter; this is a development log rather than a validation, but it is unusually transparent about how the model matured alongside the dataset. Ethics reporting is complete for approval and thin for consent: the study was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Northwestern Polytechnical University under protocol 202002032, with all procedures conducted in accordance with the latest revision of the Declaration of Helsinki - a named committee and a protocol number, better than most reports here - but no parental consent or child assent statement appears, despite the participants being 3-6 year olds. Funding from three National Natural Science Foundation of China grants is itemised. No competing-interests statement appears.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: A SciEye 2.0 eye tracker sampling at 140 Hz, using infrared illumination with corneal and retinal reflection, feeding a 1920 x 1080 monitor on which 1040 x 780 images were centred; the child sat 0.5 m away. The device's own preprocessing is specified numerically and is a genuine reporting strength: gaze points separated by less than 0.02 in normalised coordinates were merged, and merged points shorter than 0.1 s deleted, to suppress noise. No calibration procedure is described, which is the notable gap in an otherwise well-specified acquisition chain. On the analysis side: SLIC superpixel segmentation, a deep autoencoder trained layer-wise then fine-tuned globally with a cross-entropy reconstruction loss on 10,000 MS COCO images, and an LSTM with fully connected and regression heads trained by backpropagation through time, with the full gate equations reproduced. Otsu's maximum between-class variance method supplies the decision thresholds. Two baselines were reimplemented for comparison rather than merely cited - a fixation-count histogram with SVM, and stacked deep features of up to 10 fixations with SVM - which is more effort than most papers here expend on their comparators. Software frameworks and hardware for training are not named.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong on method, absent on artefacts, with an unusual amount of parameter transparency. Reproducible from the text: the complete stimulus protocol including image count, categories, display and mask durations, session structure and viewing distance; the eye tracker, its sampling rate and its exact noise-suppression rule; the superpixel step; the autoencoder's external training corpus, loss function and two-stage training strategy; the full LSTM equations; the feature concatenation; the weak-supervision label assignment; the aggregation and Otsu thresholding; and a sensitivity table spanning hidden units, fully connected size, epochs, mini-batch size, learning rate and the minLength lower bound. The finding that the resized superpixel bounding box outperforms a centred patch is reported as a negative result, which is rare and useful. Not available: code, data, the 82-image stimulus set, the specific final architecture dimensions, and - most importantly - the diagnostic procedure that generated the labels. Ten supplementary figures and three supplementary tables exist but were not retrieved. As an IEEE TBME paper the reporting standard is engineering-first, which shows in the asymmetry between an exhaustively specified pipeline and an unspecified clinical protocol.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The stated limitations are concrete and unusually specific about failure modes: the model is trained only on 3-6 year olds and applies only there; natural scenes with small between-group differences and few training examples are hard; small objects defeat the semantic encoder; and images with objects near the edge cause false positives because typically developing children's exploratory fixations also land on the grey mask. Two further constraints appear as subgroup findings rather than caveats and are more interesting than either: sensitivity is lowest in 5-6 year olds because some had undergone rehabilitation training teaching them to attend to social information, prompting the statement that 'the model is more suitable for the initial screening of children who have not undergone rehabilitation training'; and specificity is lowest in 3-4 year olds because they cannot sustain attention to the screen. Taken together these say that the measured signal is erased by intervention at one end of the age range and mimicked by ordinary inattention at the other, which bears directly on what the proposed 'AI-marker' represents - a point the paper reports but does not draw out. The unstated limitations are led by the absence of any described diagnostic reference standard, without which the target of a 96.73% accuracy is undefined. Others: sex is imbalanced between groups by 17 percentage points and never mentioned, despite the paper's own finding that error rates differ by sex; the Otsu decision threshold is fitted on training and test scores together, so the operating point is chosen with sight of the test distribution; architecture, learning parameters and the minLength value were compared on the evaluation data with no separate development set; the stimulus-discriminability ranking used to justify a shortened protocol is derived from the same data on which accuracy is reported; there is no majority-class baseline (57.6%) or confidence interval; and no prevalence-adjusted metric is offered despite the paper proposing population-scale screening.
