custom_fields.RQ2.9: Four directions, all substantive. Collect data from other age bands both to extend the model beyond 3-6 years and to characterise how dynamic viewing patterns change developmentally. Investigate diversity and individuality within the autistic group through subcategory classification and, notably, through explicit comparison of children who have and have not undergone rehabilitation training - which would convert the study's incidental finding about trained attention into a proper analysis. Predict stimulus discriminability directly with deep models, so that screening image sets can be designed rather than curated, building on the study's own demonstration that 60 well-chosen images match the full 82 while 60 random ones do not. And fuse gaze with fMRI, EEG, facial expression and observation-scale scores, described as an important and understudied challenge. What is missing from the list is the step that would matter most for the stated purpose: prospective evaluation in an unselected community population at realistic prevalence, with a described diagnostic reference standard.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Visual attention during passive free viewing, reconceived as a temporally ordered process rather than a spatial distribution. The paper's construct - the dynamic viewing pattern - encompasses where each fixation lands, in what order, for how long, and with what saccade amplitude and direction connecting it to the next, across all 82 stimuli. The descriptive analysis identifies the component behaviours: autistic children make fewer fixations with larger saccade amplitudes; they fixate faces less than typically developing children, with the largest between-group difference of any region appearing in facial areas; they fixate other salient objects less across food, animals, toys, gazed objects and touched objects; they are slower to notice most object types; and they spend more time on background regions and on the inter-stimulus grey mask. The mechanistic account offered is information-theoretic rather than social-motivational: typically developing children are described as fixating regions of continuous salient information under an information-maximisation principle, while autistic children are 'passive in the information exploration process'. The temporal analysis locates the difference at the extremes of each trial - autistic children's first fixation is often random or outside the image while typically developing children's lands near salient objects, the middle of the trial shows convergence, and the final stage diverges again as autistic children drift to non-salient background. One measured behaviour deserves separate flagging because the authors identify it as a top-three driver of model scores: whether the fixation pattern stays on the image or moves to the grey mask. This is as much a measure of task engagement as of visual preference, and the paper's own age analysis shows the same behaviour arising in typically developing 3-4 year olds from ordinary inattention.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-sensor fusion - a single eye tracker - but two feature families are combined within the modality and their contributions are separately quantified, which is more than most multimodal papers here achieve. The semantic stream encodes what the child is looking at, by locating each fixation in a SLIC superpixel and passing that region through an autoencoder pretrained on MS COCO to yield a compressed code; the low-level stream encodes the mechanics of looking - position, duration, saccade amplitude and saccade orientation. The ablation is clean and reported in the discussion: semantic features alone give 94.85% accuracy with 97.14% sensitivity and 93.16% specificity, low-level features alone 93.33% with 90.71% and 95.26%, and the combination 96.73% with 96.85% and 96.63%. The two are therefore complementary in a specific and interpretable way - semantic content drives sensitivity while movement mechanics drive specificity - and combining them raises both rather than trading one against the other. That is a more informative fusion result than the usual report of a single accuracy gain. A second, structural form of integration operates at the stimulus level: 82 per-stimulus scores are aggregated into one subject decision, and the paper shows both that individual stimulus scores are unreliable (Fig. 9(a) shows typically developing children scoring high on particular images) and that between-group separation grows with the number of stimuli pooled, so multi-scene aggregation is doing work analogous to multimodal fusion. On genuine cross-modality, the authors list fMRI, EEG, facial expression and observation-scale scores as future work and describe the problem of relating data across modalities as important and understudied.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A three-stage deep pipeline with an unsupervised front end, a weakly supervised middle and an unsupervised decision rule. Stage one is a deep autoencoder used purely as a nonlinear dimensionality reducer, trained layer-wise then fine-tuned globally with cross-entropy reconstruction loss on 10,000 MS COCO images - so the semantic encoder never sees participant data, which is a clean separation and removes one potential leakage path. Stage two is an LSTM over the per-fixation feature sequence for each stimulus, chosen for its capacity to model sequential dependence and to avoid the vanishing-gradient problems of plain recurrent networks, ending in a fully connected layer and a single-neuron regression head that scores the pattern. Stage three aggregates the 82 stimulus scores into a subject average and binarises it with Otsu's maximum between-class variance threshold. The weak supervision is explicit and correctly reasoned: the authors note that an autistic child's viewing will be atypical on only some stimuli but that labels for which specific stimuli are unavailable, so each child's diagnostic label is propagated to all 82 of their patterns and the aggregation step is relied upon to recover the subject-level decision from noisy per-stimulus targets. This is the appropriate formulation for the problem and is stated as such rather than adopted implicitly. Two baselines are reimplemented for comparison - a fixation-count histogram with SVM and stacked deep features of up to 10 fixations with SVM - and both underperform, which is the study's evidence that sequence structure, not merely deep features, carries the signal.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Per fixation: a c-bit semantic code obtained by locating the fixation's SLIC superpixel, resizing that superpixel's bounding box to d x d and passing it through the pretrained autoencoder, concatenated with four low-level descriptors - normalised position, duration, saccade amplitude and saccade orientation. A viewing pattern of m+1 fixations on one stimulus becomes a length-m sequence of these vectors, and each child yields 82 such sequences. The defining property is that no aggregation precedes the model: sequences enter the LSTM in their original order and length, in deliberate contrast to the histogram baseline (which discards order entirely) and the stacked-feature baseline (which fixes the fixation count at 10 by zero-padding or truncation). The authors' analysis of the minLength parameter is a good illustration of how carefully this was handled - raising the minimum sequence length from 2 to 4 fixations improves nothing and causes 'significant data loss in the ASD group', because autistic children produce fewer fixations, so filtering by pattern length would systematically discard the very participants the model must detect. Recognising that a preprocessing threshold interacts with the group difference it is meant to measure is a subtlety absent from most of this corpus. One reported negative result adds to the representation's credibility: using a fixed patch at each superpixel's centre performed worse than the resized full bounding box.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy at two levels of aggregation (A1 for stimulus-based patterns, A2 for subjects), sensitivity, specificity, ROC analysis and AUC, with results additionally broken down by sex and by age band and by ablation condition. Reporting sensitivity and specificity alongside accuracy is the minimum this literature should meet and is met here; adding subgroup breakdowns, and reporting them honestly when they are unflattering, goes beyond it. Robustness is addressed by repeating the subject-level split five times and reporting the minimum (95.76%) rather than only the mean. What is missing: confidence intervals; a majority-class baseline, which at 42.4% autism in the test set would be 57.6%; and any prevalence-adjusted metric such as positive predictive value, which is the number that matters for the community-screening application the paper proposes. At a population prevalence near 1-2%, sensitivity 96.85% with specificity 96.63% would yield a positive predictive value in the range of roughly 22-37% - far better than most operating points in this corpus, and a calculation the paper would have benefited from making explicit given how strongly it frames itself as a universal screening tool. The 82 stimulus-level scores are also not independent within a child, which affects the interpretation of A1 though not of A2.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: The paper does substantial interpretive work, but almost none of it is attribution on the trained model. Three strands. First, an extensive pre-modelling descriptive analysis with low-level and semantic gaze features, region-of-interest labelling, first-fixation timing and object-category breakdowns, which establishes the expected group differences and then concludes candidly that they are 'not sufficiently significant to directly use these hand-crafted features for classification' - an honest admission that the interpretable features do not do the work. Second, and most distinctive, a quantitative analysis of separability itself using time-delay embedding to compute Hausdorff and mean-minimal distances, showing how between-group distance and within-group variability change as a function of how much temporal context and how many stimuli are used. The finding that with pattern sections shorter than five fixations the within-autism variability exceeds the between-group difference is a genuinely useful result about the structure of the problem, and it turns the paper's architectural choices into consequences of measurement rather than assertions. Third, qualitative inspection of model scores, from which three drivers are named: whether the pattern stays on the image or drifts to the grey mask, whether fixations on salient objects are missing, and whether fixation order and duration are reasonable - each illustrated with worked successful and failed cases against the two baselines. The gap is that no attribution method is applied to the LSTM: there is no saliency analysis, no gate inspection, no per-fixation contribution, and no way to say for an individual child which of their 82 patterns or which fixations produced their score. For a system proposed as an aid to non-specialists in remote clinics, per-child explanation is exactly what would be needed, and the paper's own emphasis on an 'AI-marker' makes its absence more noticeable.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Among the stronger validation designs in this corpus at the level of splitting, with two specific weaknesses further down the pipeline. The split unit is the subject: 50% of the 333 children are held out, so all 82 stimulus-based patterns from a child stay together and within-child leakage is structurally impossible - which matters here more than usual, because the model scores individual stimuli and a naive pattern-level split would have placed 41 of each test child's own patterns in training. The procedure is repeated over five random permutations with the minimum reported (95.76%), addressing split-assignment variance. The semantic autoencoder is trained on MS COCO rather than on participant data, so the representation learning introduces no leakage. Two ablation baselines are implemented on the same data rather than cited from other papers. Against this: first, the decision threshold is fitted transductively. The paper states that subject average scores were computed 'for each subject in training and testing' and the Otsu maximum between-class variance threshold selected on that combined distribution, and the same is described for the stimulus-level threshold. Otsu does not use labels, so this is not label leakage, but the operating point is nonetheless chosen with sight of the test subjects' score distribution, and in a deployment where children arrive one at a time no such distribution exists - the threshold would have to be fixed in advance from training data alone, and no result is reported under that constraint. Second, several choices were compared on the evaluation data with no separate development set: LSTM hidden units and fully connected size, epoch count, mini-batch size, learning rate, and the minLength lower bound, all reported in a single results table with the best configuration carried forward. The stimulus-discriminability ranking used to argue that 60 images suffice was likewise computed on the same data, so the proposed shortened protocol is selected in-sample. Third, no majority-class floor (57.6%) or confidence interval is given. None of these undermine the subject-level split, which is the hard part and is done correctly; they mean the 96.73% is a mildly optimistic estimate under a transductively chosen threshold rather than a fully prospective one.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: Autism spectrum disorder, deep autoencoder, deep learning, dynamic viewing patterns, long short-term memory (LSTM) network. Four of the five are architectural or methodological, and the one novel construct - dynamic viewing patterns - is the paper's own coinage, which the abstract, title and body use consistently as a named attribute (abbreviated DVP throughout). Terms carried through the body: weakly supervised learning, between-group and intra-class difference, time-delay embedding, Hausdorff distance, superpixel, semantic hashing code, maximum between-class variance, AI-marker, scalable screening, medical cloud service centers. Neither 'diagnosis' nor 'classification' appears among the index terms despite both being performed, and 'screening' appears only in the title.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering 70(5):1622-1632, May 2023 - a high-profile biomedical engineering journal, submitted 17 June 2022, revised 15 October 2022, accepted 14 November 2022, published online 21 November 2022. The venue accounts for the paper's characteristic asymmetry: the signal-processing and machine-learning pipeline is specified to a standard that would permit reimplementation, complete with LSTM gate equations, a parameter sensitivity table, reimplemented baselines, ablations and a reported negative result, while the clinical apparatus that generated the labels is not described at all. Supplementary material comprising ten figures and three tables is hosted by the publisher. The paper adopts the journal's structured abstract format (Objective, Methods, Results, Conclusion, Significance), which is unusual in this corpus and enforces an explicit statement of clinical significance.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2023 by Northwestern Polytechnical University's School of Automation with the Institute of Artificial Intelligence at the Hefei Comprehensive National Science Center, in collaboration with the Children Healthcare Department of the Affiliated Hospital of Northwest University, the Children Rehabilitation Center of Shaanxi Rehabilitation Hospital, Beijing University of Chinese Medicine and Nanchang University - a broad engineering-clinical consortium, funded by three National Natural Science Foundation of China grants. The framing is health-equity infrastructure and is stated with more precision than most: the introduction identifies three specific barriers to screening in remote areas - affordability, child-friendliness and the availability of professionals - and every subsequent design choice is justified against one of them, including the explicit contrast with fMRI as an unaffordable alternative and the proposal that storage and analysis run on a cloud computing centre. The prevalence trajectory is cited precisely (1/68 in 2014, 1/59 in 2018, 1/44 in 2021 per US CDC), with the claim that developing-country prevalence is comparable. Two aspects of the positioning are notable for the synthesis. The paper explicitly criticises the small-sample norm in this literature, arguing from its own visualisation that 'when the number of subjects is less than 100, the test cannot accurately reflect the performance of the model' - a methodological argument that a 333-child multi-site study is entitled to make and that indicts much of the surrounding corpus. And the burden framing in the opening paragraph ('most patients diagnosed with ASD cannot independently live, study and work when they grow up, which places a heavy burden on their families and society') is the starkest deficit language encountered in this review, sitting uncomfortably beside an otherwise child-centred and access-oriented design.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Rubio-Martín S; García-Ordás MT; Bayón-Gutiérrez M; Prieto-Fernández N; Benítez-Andrades JA
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective classification study on scraped social-media text; a cross-sectional comparison of language produced by self-identified autistic Twitter users against language produced by a small comparison set of users
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: One tweet per instance, classified independently; there is no user-level aggregation, no thread or conversational context, and no temporal ordering
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Unknown. No age information is available for any user, and Twitter's terms require account holders to be at least 13, so the sample is adolescents and adults - despite the paper being motivated throughout by early detection in children.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: None. Users were not contacted and did not consent; the only privacy measure described is the removal of username, location and date of birth from the two example biographies reproduced as a figure, 'in compliance with Twitter's policies'.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. There is no task, protocol, prompt or elicitation of any kind; the data are whatever the users chose to post between January 2017 and January 2022.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Twitter developer API accessed by a Python script; Python 3.9 in two Jupyter notebooks; an Intel Core i7-9700K at 3.60 GHz with 32 GB RAM and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080. Libraries named: GridSearchCV for hyperparameter search; BERT-base-multilingual-cased as the deep model.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not reported. The dataset consists of tweets from identifiable public accounts and is not described as deposited or shareable.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: None stated. No institutional review board, ethics committee or research-ethics statement of any kind appears in the paper.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Not described. The paper states that natural language processing techniques were combined with the models but specifies no tokenisation, vectorisation, embedding or feature-engineering step for the three classical machine-learning models, so it is not stated what decision trees, XGBoost and k-nearest neighbours were actually operating on. BERT uses its own tokeniser and contextual embeddings by construction.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Absent. No feature importance, attention analysis, error analysis, example inspection or linguistic characterisation is offered for any model, so the paper cannot say what distinguishes the two classes of text. This is a particularly consequential gap here, because the most obvious explanation for the result - that people who identify as autistic in their biography also write about autism, disability, advocacy and related topics in their tweets - is never tested, and no autism-related vocabulary was removed from the tweets during preprocessing. The paper therefore cannot distinguish a linguistic-style signal from simple topic detection.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: GridSearchCV was used to select hyperparameters for the three classical models, with the selected values reported. The partition on which the search was conducted is not stated, and with only a single 75/25 random split described there is no separate validation set, so the search was most likely conducted using the same data on which results are reported. BERT was deliberately left untuned as a design choice.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 'The dataset was split randomly, 75% for training the models and 25% for testing them.' The unit of splitting is the tweet, not the user. Since each of the 252 users contributes hundreds or thousands of tweets, every user in the test set has the large majority of their own tweets in the training set - and with only 31 comparison users supplying 45,000 tweets, roughly 1,090 of each comparison user's tweets are available in training to help classify their remaining 360. No cross-validation, no repeated splits, no held-out users, and no confidence intervals.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Two, both concerning label validity: that users may provide false information in their biographies, and that tweets may be authored by someone other than the profile owner. These are real and correctly identified. Nothing else is acknowledged.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of Twitter accounts rather than of assessed people: 221 users whose public biography states that they are autistic and 31 users who do not, totalling 252. The imbalance is severe and consequential. Because the modelled dataset was balanced at the tweet level - 45,000 per class from a cleaned pool of 404,627 - each of the 31 comparison users contributes on average about 1,450 tweets while each of the 221 autistic users contributes about 200, a sevenfold difference in per-user concentration. The entire negative class is therefore the writing of 31 individuals. No user was recruited, contacted or aware of the study; the data are historical public posts from 1 January 2017 to 31 January 2022. Cleaning removed 60% of the raw corpus (1,014,723 to 404,627 tweets) by deleting duplicates, retweets, incompletely extracted tweets and cross-platform auto-posts, which is a substantial and appropriately reported reduction, though it is not broken down by user or by group.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: The terminology is the most internally contradictory in this corpus, and the contradiction is instructive. The search keywords include 'ActuallyAutistic' and 'Aspie' - terms coined and used by autistic people themselves, the first being an identity hashtag that exists precisely to distinguish autistic voices from those speaking about autism, and one that carries an explicit rejection of pathologising language. The paper harvests those self-identifications and then describes the people who wrote them as 'ASD patients', as 'individuals who suffer from ASD', and as 'people that suffer from ASD'; the comparison group is 'people that do not suffer from ASD'. Autism is 'a developmental disability' that 'affects the social and interactive skills of those who have it', which 'appears before the age of three and can last a lifetime'. The framing of value is entirely deficit-and-outcome: 'people who are not diagnosed in childhood have a poorer quality of life'. So the study takes its ground truth from a community that names itself in one register and reports its findings in the opposite one, without noticing. There is no neurodiversity framing, no autistic-community involvement, and no acknowledgement that the data subjects are a self-organised community with stated views about how they are described - or about being classified by algorithms trained on their own posts.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: None whatsoever. No age, sex, race or ethnicity, socioeconomic status, education, nationality, language background, comorbidity or medication is available for any of the 252 users in either group, and none is estimated or discussed. Three consequences follow. First, the sample is necessarily adolescents and adults, since Twitter requires account holders to be at least 13 - which sits at odds with a paper titled 'Early Detection' and motivated in its opening pages entirely by the value of diagnosing children before the age of three, a mismatch the text never addresses. Second, no matching of any kind was possible between the 221 autistic and 31 comparison users, and none was attempted, so any demographic difference between the groups - in age, sex, nationality, education, topic interests, or how much they tweet - is fully confounded with the label. Third, the only English-language requirement is stated for the tweets, but the chosen model is BERT-base-multilingual-cased, a multilingual checkpoint, which suggests the corpus may not be uniformly English. The one participant characteristic that is described in detail is not demographic but procedural: the manual exclusion of organisational accounts, self-described advocates and family members from the autistic group, which is careful work and is the paper's strongest methodological passage.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Self-disclosure in a public social-media biography, with no clinical component of any kind. Users were located by keyword search over biographies for 'Autism', 'ASD', 'Asperger', 'Aspie', 'Autistic' and 'ActuallyAutistic', and each candidate profile was then reviewed by hand and discarded if it belonged to an organisation or society, to someone describing themselves as an 'ASD advocate', or to a family member using phrasing such as 'father of an ASD kid' or 'mother of an ASD kid'. That filtering is thoughtful, is described in enough detail to repeat, and removes the most obvious sources of false positives - it is the best-executed part of the study. What it cannot do is establish that anyone is autistic. There is no diagnosis, no instrument, no criterion, no date and no verification, and the authors themselves note that biographies may contain false information and that tweets may be written by someone other than the account holder. The comparison label is weaker still and is not described at all: the paper never states how the 31 non-autistic users were found or chosen, whether they were sampled at random or selected for any property, or whether any effort was made to exclude autistic people who simply do not disclose - which, given that undiagnosed and undisclosed autism is common, means the negative class is defined by the absence of a public statement rather than by the absence of the condition. What the models therefore predict is whether a tweet came from an account whose biography contains an autism keyword.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, language, adaptive or severity measure exists, and none could exist given the data source. This matters more than in most studies here because language is the entire modality: a paper classifying people by their writing reports no lexical, syntactic, readability or pragmatic measure of that writing, and no characterisation of how the two corpora differ. Severity appears only in the introduction, where Asperger syndrome is described as 'the one that is labelled as severity 1' and is included among the search keywords, but no severity information is extracted, used or reported. The absence has a specific analytical cost: because self-disclosure of autism on social media is likely to be associated with particular parts of the spectrum - verbally fluent, self-aware, digitally engaged, often diagnosed later in life - the sample is drawn from a narrow and self-selected slice of the autistic population, and nothing in the study characterises which slice.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated objective is to build models 'capable of diagnosing ASD through the analysis of texts posted by users who disclose their condition in their biographies', motivated by the scarcity of specialists and the value of early diagnosis. Three contributions are claimed: a new Twitter dataset of 404,627 tweets from 252 users of whom 221 disclose autism; application of several machine-learning techniques to build predictive models; and comparison of classical machine learning against deep learning. Findings: BERT-base-multilingual-cased, used untuned, reached 84.3% accuracy and F1 0.84, outperforming XGBoost at 71.6% (F1 0.74), decision trees at 61.2% (F1 0.72) and k-nearest neighbours at 60.8% (F1 0.67), all three of which were hyperparameter-tuned by grid search. The authors present this as the paper's headline - that a default deep model beats optimised classical ones - and describe the result as 'quite astonishing'. The confusion matrices they report, to their credit, reveal more than the accuracies do: the decision tree produced 11,229 true positives against just 41 false negatives, meaning it labelled nearly every tweet autistic and achieved 99.6% sensitivity at 22.6% specificity - close to a degenerate classifier, which its 61.2% accuracy and 0.72 F1 conceal. BERT's counts correspond to sensitivity 82.1% and specificity 86.5%. No user-level result is reported for any model.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: There is no setting in the usual sense. No participants were recruited, contacted, assessed or informed; the study consists of harvesting five years of public posts from 252 identifiable Twitter accounts through the developer API and classifying them offline. The research group is at Universidad de Leon in Spain, and the compute is a single desktop workstation. Two features of this design deserve comment for the review. It is the only study in the corpus with no acquisition protocol at all, which means it is free of every acquisition confound that troubles the video and audio studies here - no equipment differences, no examiner effects, no laboratory artificiality - and simultaneously free of every control those protocols provide, since nothing about who wrote what, when, why, or to whom is known or standardised. And it is the only study here whose data subjects are neither aware of nor consenting to their participation, on a topic they disclosed publicly about themselves, which raises governance questions the paper does not engage with at all.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: None. This is the only included study with no elicitation paradigm: the behavioural sample is whatever 252 people chose to post on Twitter over five years, unconstrained in topic, audience, purpose, length or timing. The consequence that matters most is topic confounding, and it goes unaddressed throughout. The autistic group was assembled by searching biographies for autism-related keywords including 'ActuallyAutistic', a hashtag whose function is to mark autistic people's own commentary on autism; people who identify that way in their profile will frequently tweet about autism, disability, sensory experience, diagnosis, accommodation and advocacy. No preprocessing step removed autism-related vocabulary from the tweets, no topic model or lexical analysis was run, and no ablation tested whether the classifier still works with such terms masked. So the most parsimonious explanation of the 84.3% figure - that BERT is detecting subject matter rather than communication style - is neither tested nor mentioned. The paper's own framing invites this reading, since its introduction speaks of identifying 'linguistic patterns, emotional expressions, and communication styles', which is a style hypothesis, while its method offers nothing that could separate style from topic.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional in analysis though the data span five years, with no temporal modelling: tweets from 2017 and 2022 are pooled and classified independently, so nothing is learned about stability or change over time, and no test-retest or within-user consistency is examined. Ethics is the study's most serious deficiency and is entirely absent. There is no institutional review board approval, no ethics committee, no research-ethics statement, no consent, and no discussion of the ethics of the enterprise. The data are health-related disclosures made by identifiable individuals about themselves, harvested without their knowledge and used to train a classifier whose stated purpose is to identify people who may be autistic. The only privacy measure described is the redaction of username, location and date of birth from two example biographies reproduced as a figure, done 'in compliance with Twitter's policies' - a platform-terms consideration rather than a research-ethics one. The paper does not consider whether the autistic Twitter community, which is organised and vocal, would regard such a classifier as acceptable; whether a model that infers autism from public text could be used against the people it identifies; or whether public availability implies availability for this purpose. Given that several of the search keywords are terms this community coined for itself, the omission is conspicuous.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Data collection used a Python script against the Twitter developer API, exporting to CSV. Analysis ran in two Jupyter notebooks under Python 3.9 on a single workstation (Intel Core i7-9700K at 3.60 GHz, 32 GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080). The models are named with their selected hyperparameters - decision tree (max depth 9, min samples leaf 2, min samples split 4), XGBoost (colsample_bytree 0.8, gamma 5, max depth 5, min child weight 1, subsample 0.8), k-nearest neighbours with k = 1 - and the deep model is identified precisely as BERT-base-multilingual-cased, used without tuning by deliberate design. GridSearchCV is named as the search tool. What is conspicuously missing is the representation layer for the three classical models: the paper states that natural language processing techniques were combined with the models but never says how text became numbers - no tokenisation, no bag of words, no TF-IDF, no n-gram range, no embedding - so it is not possible to say what the decision tree, XGBoost and k-nearest neighbours were actually fitted to, which makes their comparison against BERT uninterpretable as a claim about model families.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Partial, and unusually asymmetric. The data-collection procedure is described well enough to repeat in principle: the six search keywords are listed, the three manual exclusion rules (organisations, advocates, family members) are stated with examples, the four cleaning steps are enumerated, the date range is given, and the tweet counts before and after cleaning are reported. Model configuration is also specified, with selected hyperparameters for all three classical models, the exact BERT checkpoint, the split ratio and the compute hardware. Against this: how the 31 comparison users were chosen is never stated, which alone prevents reconstruction of the dataset; the text representation for the classical models is undescribed; BERT's fine-tuning regime (epochs, learning rate, batch size, maximum sequence length) is not given; no random seed is reported for a study whose single result rests on one random split; and neither code nor data is available. The data could not straightforwardly be shared in any case, since they consist of identifiable individuals' posts, which is a reason to have addressed data governance rather than a reason to omit it.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The two stated limitations are correctly identified and concern label validity: users may give false information in their biographies, and tweets may be written by someone other than the account owner. Everything else is unaddressed, and several of the omissions are decisive. The split is random over 90,000 tweets, not over the 252 users, so every author in the test set has the great majority of their own tweets in training; for the comparison class this is extreme, since 31 people supply all 45,000 negative tweets, meaning roughly 1,090 of each comparison user's tweets are available to help classify their remaining 360. A model that learned to recognise 31 individual writing styles would score very well and would have learned nothing about autism. There is no control for topic, in a design where the positive class was assembled by searching for autism keywords and no autism vocabulary was removed from the text. The 31 comparison users are undescribed, unmatched and unscreened, so undisclosed autistic people may sit in the negative class and any group difference in age, nationality, profession or interests is confounded with the label. No demographic data exist. Hyperparameters were grid-searched with no separate validation set. No user-level metric is reported although per-user aggregation is the only form in which such a system could be used. And the framing gap is never acknowledged: a paper titled 'Early Detection', motivated by diagnosing children before age three, is trained entirely on adult social-media users.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Two directions, both narrow: tune BERT's hyperparameters, since it was deliberately left at defaults and might improve further; and train additional deep and classical models 'to ensure that no high-performing models are overlooked'. Both extend the leaderboard rather than test the finding. The steps that would matter are absent from the list: splitting by user rather than by tweet, masking autism-related vocabulary to separate topic from style, describing and expanding the comparison group, reporting user-level performance, and obtaining any form of clinical validation for the label. So is any consideration of research ethics or of engagement with the community whose posts constitute the dataset.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Written language produced spontaneously on social media - the only study in this corpus whose behavioural sample is entirely self-initiated public communication rather than behaviour elicited under a protocol. That is genuinely interesting as a modality: it is ecologically valid in a way no laboratory task can be, it is longitudinal by default (five years per user), it costs nothing to collect at scale, and it captures communication in its natural social context with real audiences and real stakes. But the study does nothing to characterise the behaviour it collects. No linguistic construct is named or measured - not lexical diversity, sentence length, pronoun use, sentiment, pragmatic markers, disfluency, figurative language or any of the features the autism-language literature has examined - and no analysis reports how the two corpora differ. The introduction gestures at 'linguistic patterns, emotional expressions, and communication styles' but nothing in the method operationalises any of these. The result is a study in which the behavioural target is left entirely to the classifier to define, with no account of what it found. Given that the positive class was assembled by searching for autism keywords and that no autism vocabulary was removed from the tweets, the behaviour actually being detected may be talking about autism rather than any property of autistic communication.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No fusion, and no possibility of it in this design - text alone, one tweet at a time. Two structural forms of integration that the data support were also not used. The first is user-level aggregation: 252 users each contribute hundreds or thousands of tweets, and pooling per-tweet predictions into a per-user decision would be the natural analogue of the multi-stimulus aggregation used to good effect by several eye-tracking studies in this corpus, and is the only form in which a screening application could work, since no one would be assessed on a single tweet. It is neither performed nor discussed, and no user-level metric appears. The second is metadata: the Twitter API returns posting time, reply and thread structure, follower and following counts, engagement figures and interaction partners, all of which are behavioural signals about social communication and all of which are discarded in favour of raw text. The paper's own framing - that social media offers insight into 'the social experiences and challenges faced by individuals with ASD' - points directly at interaction structure, which is precisely what is thrown away.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Four models compared: a decision tree, XGBoost, k-nearest neighbours with k = 1, and BERT-base-multilingual-cased. The comparison is framed as a deliberate test - the three classical models were hyperparameter-tuned by grid search while BERT was left entirely at defaults, 'to see if the DL model just with the basic model gives more accurate results than ML models that have been optimised' - and BERT won by 13 accuracy points over the best classical model. Setting up an asymmetric comparison and reporting it transparently is a reasonable framing, but the comparison is not interpretable as stated, because the text representation given to the classical models is never described. BERT builds its own contextual representation from subword tokens; the decision tree, XGBoost and k-nearest neighbours must have been given something, and what that was is unstated. If it was a sparse bag-of-words vector, then the finding is about representation rather than model family, and the paper cannot tell the two apart. Two of the classical results also look near-degenerate rather than merely weak: k = 1 nearest neighbours over a high-dimensional text representation is close to a memorisation baseline, and the decision tree assigned nearly everything to the positive class. Neither observation is drawn out.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: For BERT, subword tokens and contextual embeddings from the multilingual cased checkpoint, applied to one tweet at a time. For the three classical models, unspecified - the paper says natural language processing techniques were used but names no tokenisation, vectorisation or feature scheme, so the representation those models consumed is unknown. In every case the unit is a single tweet treated independently: no thread context, no reply structure, no temporal ordering, no user-level aggregation, and no metadata. The maximum sequence length is not stated, which matters because tweets in the 2017-2022 window span both the 140- and 280-character limits. Nothing was masked or normalised beyond the four corpus-cleaning steps, so hashtags, mentions, URLs, emoji and autism-related vocabulary all remain in the text the models see - the last of these being the reason the results cannot be read as evidence about communication style.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy and F1 for each model, together with full confusion matrices giving true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives - and the confusion matrices are the most valuable thing in the results, because they expose behaviour the summary metrics hide. The decision tree's counts (tp 11,229, fn 41, tn 2,540, fp 8,690) show a model that assigned almost every tweet to the autistic class: 99.6% sensitivity against 22.6% specificity, reported as 61.2% accuracy and F1 0.72, both of which make it look like a mediocre classifier rather than a near-degenerate one. BERT's counts give sensitivity 82.1% and specificity 86.5%, reasonably balanced. Publishing the raw counts for all four models is good practice and lets a reader recover what the headline numbers conceal. What is missing: sensitivity, specificity, precision and recall are never named or computed even though the counts are present; there is no AUC; there are no confidence intervals; there is no majority-class baseline, though the balanced tweet-level design makes it 50%; and there is no user-level metric, which is the only level at which the proposed application would operate. F1 is also computed with the autistic class as positive, which given the balanced tweet-level design is defensible but is never stated.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No feature importance for the tree-based models, despite decision trees and XGBoost both supporting it natively and both having been fitted; no attention or probing analysis for BERT; no error analysis; no inspection of misclassified examples; no lexical comparison between the two corpora; no topic modelling. The paper's entire interpretive content is the observation that BERT 'utilizes neural networks to recognize intricate patterns within the input data' and that this 'demonstrates the potential of deep learning models to extract relevant patterns'. The absence is not merely a missed opportunity but the reason the study's central claim cannot be assessed: the difference between a classifier that has learned something about autistic communication and one that has learned that certain accounts discuss autism, or that has memorised 31 people's writing styles, would be visible in even a cursory look at the most predictive tokens, and no such look is reported.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The weakest validation design in the corpus, and the failure is structural rather than marginal. A single random 75/25 split was applied to 90,000 tweets, with the tweet as the unit. Those tweets come from 252 users, so every user is represented on both sides of the split, and the imbalance makes this acute for the negative class: 31 comparison users supply all 45,000 non-autistic tweets, roughly 1,450 each, of which about 1,090 land in training and 360 in test. A model needs only to recognise those 31 writing styles - vocabulary, topics, habitual phrasings, recurring names, professional jargon, regional idiom - to classify the negative test set almost perfectly, and BERT is exactly the kind of model that will do so. The positive class is less concentrated at roughly 200 tweets per user but is leaky by the same mechanism. Nothing in the paper estimates performance on a writer the model has never seen, which is the only quantity relevant to the stated application. Compounding this: there is no cross-validation and no repeated split, so the single reported figure carries no stability estimate; hyperparameters were grid-searched with no validation set distinct from the test set; no chance baseline or confidence interval is given; and no user-level aggregation is performed, so the study never reports the metric its own use case requires. The corrective is simple and would be a genuinely informative experiment: hold out entire users, expand the comparison group well beyond 31 people, mask autism-related vocabulary, and report user-level sensitivity and specificity. On the current design, the 84.3% cannot be interpreted as evidence about autism at all.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: Machine Learning, Deep Learning, ASD, tweets, NLP. Four of the five are method or data-source labels and the fifth is the condition; no term describes a behaviour, a linguistic construct or a clinical application, which accurately reflects a paper with no behavioural hypothesis. Terms carried through the body: early detection, early diagnosis, social media texts, biographies, ActuallyAutistic, Aspie, hyperparameters search, BERT-base-multilingual-cased, GridSearchCV. The title's 'AI-Powered' is doing rhetorical rather than descriptive work.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: 2023 IEEE 36th International Symposium on Computer-Based Medical Systems (CBMS), pages 235-238 - a four-page conference paper at a computer-science venue oriented to medical systems. The format explains some of the compression, though not the absence of an ethics statement, which conference length limits do not excuse. The venue also explains the paper's evaluative frame: the result is presented as a model comparison with a winner, in the idiom of a benchmark leaderboard, rather than as a clinical or linguistic finding. Two DOIs appear in the retrieved text (10.1109/CBMS58004.2023.00051 and .00223), an artefact of the proceedings metadata.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2023 by the SALBIS and SECOMUCI research groups in the Department of Electric, Systems and Automatics Engineering at Universidad de Leon, Spain, partially supported by a university internal research programme. The framing is the familiar access-and-scarcity argument - diagnosis 'remains a challenge due to the resources and specialized professionals needed', existing methods rest on interviews and questionnaires that 'take too much time' - combined with a strongly stated case for early diagnosis occupying most of the introduction. The positioning within the field is explicitly as a gap-filler: the authors note that prior autism machine-learning work has used images and eye tracking, that 'few have focused on detecting ASD using text as input', and that there is 'a notable gap in research utilizing the information found in Twitter users' biographies'. That gap is real, and social-media language is a legitimate and under-explored modality. What makes the paper a cautionary case for this review is the distance between its framing and its evidence: a study motivated in its opening pages by identifying autistic children before the age of three, using adult self-disclosure on a platform with a minimum age of 13, claiming to 'pave the way' for diagnosis on the basis of a tweet-level classification whose validation design cannot distinguish autism from authorship. It is also the only study in the corpus that builds a health classifier from identifiable individuals' public disclosures with no ethics approval, no consent and no discussion of either.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Babu PRK; Di Martino JM; Chang Z; Perochon S; Carpenter KLH; Compton S; Espinosa S; Dawson G; Sapiro G
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional two-group study embedded in routine paediatric primary care; primarily a biomarker-characterisation study with statistical group comparison, extended by a secondary classification analysis and an explicit test of incremental value over the group's own prior affect-based measure
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Two scalar summary features per participant per movie - integrated entropy of eyebrow landmarks and of mouth landmarks - optionally joined by the positive-affect energy. The full MSE curve across 30 scales is used for the statistical comparison; only the integrated value enters the classifier.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None on an independent cohort. The affect estimator was previously validated against human coding on 136,450 frames with an intraclass correlation of 0.9, which is external validation of a component rather than of the study's finding.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Written informed consent from caregivers/legal guardians. Inability to give consent in English or Spanish was an explicit exclusion criterion, which is transparent about a real access limitation.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Passive viewing of six short developmentally appropriate movies (each under 90 s) presented on an iPad held 60 cm from the child, who sat on the caregiver's lap while all other family members and practitioners stood behind them to minimise distraction. Four movies are social - Blowing Bubbles (64 s), Spinning Top (53 s), Rhymes and Toys (49 s), Make Me Laugh (56 s) - featuring human actors making eye contact, smiling, gesturing, reciting rhymes and acting silly, including both successful and failed attempts to elicit affective response. Two are non-social - Mechanical Puppy (25 s) and Dog in Grass Right-Right-Left (40 s) - showing dynamic toys or animations, the latter using a spatially structured right-right-left appearance sequence. The social/non-social contrast is used as an internal control on the specificity of the finding.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Apple iPad with front-facing camera recording at 30 frames per second, running a purpose-built application; standard clinic environment. Analysis used published face detection, low-dimensional facial embedding for identity tracking, and a 49-point landmark detector, with statistics in Python via pingouin and scipy and modelling via scikit-learn.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not reported; the pipeline is built on the group's previously published components
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Duke University Health System Institutional Review Board, protocols Pro00085434 and Pro00085435 - named committee with two protocol numbers
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: 49 facial landmarks tracked per frame at 30 fps; the child's face isolated from caregiver, siblings and clinicians by facial embedding; affine normalisation to a canonical face; low-pass filtering at 15 Hz; averaging of landmark points within each region to give one-dimensional time series for eyebrows and for mouth. Multiscale entropy is then computed by coarse-graining each series over scales 1-30 and calculating sample entropy at each scale with embedding dimension m = 2 and tolerance r = 0.15 sigma, both values justified from prior literature and shown insensitive in a supplementary appendix. The summary feature, integrated entropy, is the cumulative sum of sample entropy across the first 20 scales. Separately, affect probabilities (neutral, positive, negative) are estimated with a pose-invariant method from the group's prior work, and their energy computed as a 10-frame moving average of the rate of change followed by cumulative sum.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Strong, and grounded in the measure rather than in post-hoc attribution. Because the feature is a single interpretable quantity - how predictable a facial region's movement is over time - the paper can reason directly about what it means, and does so explicitly: a highly periodic time series with large excursions yields low entropy, as does a nearly stable series with small excursions (the typically developing case), while an irregular non-periodic series yields high entropy (the autistic case). The authors are careful to distinguish complexity from mere variability, and demonstrate the distinction empirically by showing weak correlation between integrated entropy and landmark variation. The regions were chosen a priori with stated rationales, and the social/non-social contrast provides an internal test of whether the signal is social-content-specific. The interpretation offered is speculative but clearly labelled as such: that typically developing toddlers may respond more predictably because they share an understanding of the movies' social meaning, while autistic toddlers respond more idiosyncratically. The affect analysis functions as a discriminant-validity check rather than as an accuracy booster. What is not done is any individual-level explanation or error analysis.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Essentially none. The decision tree uses Gini impurity with no reported depth, leaf or pruning parameters; the entropy parameters m = 2 and r = 0.15 sigma are taken from prior literature and their insensitivity demonstrated in an appendix; the 20-scale integration window and the 15 Hz filter are justified from domain reasoning rather than tuned. The one selection made on the data is the restriction of the classification analysis to the four social movies, chosen because the statistical tests had shown larger effect sizes there.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-out cross-validation over participants for the decision-tree classifier, so the split unit is the child and no within-participant leakage is possible. The statistical analyses that constitute the paper's primary claims are conventional hypothesis tests with effect sizes rather than predictive models, and are supported by ANCOVA adjustment for two prespecified confounds. The restriction of the classification analysis to social movies was made after inspecting the group-difference effect sizes on the same data, so that selection is in-sample.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Three, stated concisely and all real: the landmark and affect detection algorithms were trained primarily on adults, though the group's prior work showed them reliable for toddlers; other complexity measures might discriminate better than multiscale entropy; and the sample, while relatively large, contains a limited number of autistic participants and lacked sufficient power to determine the impact of demographic characteristics on the results - which is an implicit acknowledgement of the unadjusted age, sex and race differences.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Four hundred and thirty-six toddlers aged 17-36 months, comprising 40 with autism and 396 typically developing, recruited at four paediatric primary care clinics during routine well-child visits. The recruitment route is the defining feature and separates this study from almost every other in the corpus: children were not enrolled as known cases and known controls, but as consecutive clinic attenders who received the M-CHAT-R/F as part of standard care and were referred for ADOS-Toddler evaluation only if they screened positive or if a caregiver or clinician raised a developmental concern. The resulting 9.2% autism prevalence is far closer to a real screening population than the near-balanced designs elsewhere here. Exclusion criteria are stated in full and are practical rather than diagnostic: known hearing or vision impairment, child too upset, caregiver not interested or without time or needing to care for siblings or unable to consent in English or Spanish, child did not complete the procedures, and missing clinical information. The analysed sample varies by movie because only participants with at least 40% valid landmark data for a given movie were included, and those per-movie counts are shown graphically rather than tabulated - the one place where the participant accounting is less transparent than the rest of the paper.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'Toddlers with ASD' and 'typically developing (TD) toddlers', used consistently and person-first throughout, with 'children with autism' also appearing. The register is notably measured for this literature. Autistic children are described as experiencing 'challenges in establishing social communication' and 'differences in use of facial expressions', and the paper speaks of 'atypical' and 'ambiguous' expressions rather than of deficits or abnormality - though 'atypical facial expression' is called an 'early symptom' and the language of biomarkers, symptoms and risk is used throughout. There is no burden framing, no cost-to-society argument, and no claim that autistic people cannot live independently, all of which appear in other papers charted here. Two interpretive passages are worth noting for their care. The explanation offered for the finding is framed as speculation and is symmetrical rather than deficit-laden: typically developing toddlers may respond more predictably because they share an understanding of the movies' social meaning, whereas autistic children's responses 'may be more idiosyncratic' - idiosyncrasy rather than impairment. And the authors note that neutral expressions 'might be interpreted by others as more ambiguous', locating the communicative difficulty in the interpretation as much as in the expression. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement statement.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: The most complete demographic reporting in this corpus, and the completeness is what makes the imbalances visible. Table 1 gives, per group: sex (autistic 77.5% male versus typically developing 48.9%), race (White/Caucasian 47.5% versus 77.7%; African American 15.0% versus 8.6%; other 37.5% versus 13.6%), Hispanic/Latino ethnicity (32.5% versus 7.3%), M-CHAT-R/F positivity (87.5% versus 0.25%), ADOS-T total (7.64 +/- 1.69 in the autistic group), and age in months (24.21 +/- 4.72 versus 20.62 +/- 3.21). Caregiver education is reported for the whole sample: 82.8% college degree, 15.5% more than high school, 1.8% no high school. Three of these differences matter and none is adjusted for. The age gap of 3.6 months is large at 17-36 months, a period of rapid change in facial expressivity, affect regulation and attention, and it runs in the direction that would be expected to produce more, not less, behavioural regulation in the older autistic group - so it does not obviously explain the finding, but it is a live confound in a study that goes to the trouble of ANCOVA-adjusting two other covariates. The sex difference reflects autism's true sex ratio rather than a sampling error, but sex differences in facial expressivity in toddlerhood are documented. The racial and ethnic difference is the one with a technical as well as a demographic dimension: the autistic group is 30 percentage points less White and over four times as likely to be Hispanic/Latino, and the paper's own stated limitation is that landmark and affect detectors were trained primarily on adults - detector accuracy is also known to vary by skin tone and facial morphology, so differential measurement error across groups cannot be excluded. The authors acknowledge the general problem, stating that the sample 'did not have sufficient power to determine the impact of demographic characteristics on the results'.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Among the strongest in this review, and structurally different from the case-control norm because the diagnostic pathway is the clinical one rather than a research recruitment. Every toddler received the M-CHAT-R/F, a validated caregiver screening instrument, as part of routine well-child care. Children screening positive, and children about whom a caregiver or clinician expressed developmental concern, were then evaluated by a child psychologist using the ADOS-Toddler module, the age-appropriate observational gold standard. Mean ADOS-T total in the autistic group was 7.64 +/- 1.69. Two features deserve particular credit. The comparison group is screened rather than assumed: 396 typically developing toddlers all completed M-CHAT-R/F, so undetected autism in the comparison group is reduced (though not eliminated, since M-CHAT-R/F sensitivity is imperfect and only screen-positive or concern-flagged children received ADOS-T). And the single discordant case is reported explicitly - one typically developing child screened positive, was evaluated with ADOS-T, and was not diagnosed - a level of transparency about the reference-standard pathway that no other study charted here provides. The limitation is the one intrinsic to a two-stage design: children who screened negative and prompted no concern did not receive ADOS-T, so the comparison group's status rests on a screening instrument rather than on the diagnostic one.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Partial, and better than most here on severity while silent on cognition. ADOS-Toddler total scores were obtained for the diagnosed children and are reported as a group mean of 7.64 +/- 1.69, giving a genuine quantitative severity index - the study is one of relatively few in this corpus where such a score exists at all. But it is used only descriptively. No analysis relates integrated entropy to ADOS-T score, so the question that would most strengthen the biomarker claim - whether facial-dynamics complexity tracks symptom severity within the autistic group, rather than merely separating groups - is not asked. The tight standard deviation (1.69) also indicates a fairly homogeneous severity range, which limits what such an analysis could have shown and constrains generalisation to more or less affected children. No cognitive, developmental or language measure was administered to either group, which matters for a paradigm requiring 17-36 month olds to attend to a screen for several minutes: developmental level governs sustained attention, and the paper's own 40% valid-data threshold removes children who looked away too much, so cognitive and attentional capacity silently shapes who is analysed. The authors partly address this by verifying that missing-data percentage does not differ significantly between groups and by entering it as an ANCOVA covariate, which is a good empirical substitute for a developmental measure but not a replacement for one.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Three questions, stated as hypotheses in advance. Whether the complexity of facial landmark dynamics differentiates autistic from typically developing toddlers; whether that complexity is higher specifically in the eyebrow region, on the basis of prior work on eyebrow raising in this cohort, and the mouth region, on the basis of atypical vocalisation literature; and whether the complexity measure adds information beyond the group's own previously published affect-based analysis or merely duplicates it. Findings: autistic toddlers showed significantly higher multiscale entropy in both regions, with a clear social/non-social gradient - during social movies p < .0001 with large to very large effect sizes (r = .51-.82), during non-social movies still significant but only medium (r = .32-.40). Integrated entropy over the first 20 scales gave p < .00001 with large or very large effects for all social movies. Eyebrows and mouth did not differ from each other (p > .05, r < 0.1), so the hypothesis of regional specificity was not supported in the sense of one region dominating. The autistic group also showed a significantly wider range of integrated entropy across the six movies (eyebrows p = .001, r = .33; mouth p = .0002, r = .39), meaning their facial responsiveness varied more between contents. On the third question, correlations between integrated entropy and positive-affect energy were moderate for two movies and negligible for four, and adding affect to the classifier did not improve on entropy alone - while affect alone performed worse - so the measures are largely independent and the complexity measure is the more informative of the two. Classification with a decision tree on social movies gave 76.6-78.3% accuracy with entropy alone; logistic regression gave odds ratios up to 1.8 for entropy against 0.8 for affect.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Four paediatric primary care clinics in the Duke Children's Primary Care network, with data captured during routine well-child visits. This is the study's most consequential design property and it addresses the corpus's most pervasive external-validity problem. Because recruitment is by clinic attendance rather than by diagnostic status, the sample is not a set of specialist-clinic cases contrasted with community controls but a screening cohort in which autism is identified prospectively at 9.2% prevalence. The measurement is embedded in the visit rather than added to it: the child sits on the caregiver's lap, an iPad is placed at 60 cm, and the movies play for a few minutes while the front camera records. Practical constraints of the setting are reported honestly as exclusion criteria - the child was too upset, the caregiver had no time or needed to mind siblings, consent could not be given in English or Spanish - which is a realistic account of what limits deployment in primary care and is more informative than a laboratory study's silence on the same issues. The one respect in which the setting is not fully representative is socioeconomic: 82.8% of caregivers held a college degree, which is far above the US population and reflects the catchment of an academic health system.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Six short movies, each under 90 seconds, presented on a tablet during the clinic visit, with the social/non-social split used as an internal control rather than as incidental variety. The four social movies feature human actors making eye contact, smiling, gesturing, reciting nursery rhymes and behaving comically - Blowing Bubbles (64 s), Spinning Top (53 s), Rhymes and Toys (49 s) and Make Me Laugh (56 s) - and two of them deliberately include both successful and failed attempts, which creates natural moments for affective response. The two non-social movies show dynamic toys or animations: Mechanical Puppy (25 s) and Dog in Grass Right-Right-Left (40 s), the latter using a structured spatial sequence. The design has three strengths worth carrying into the synthesis. It is short, passive and requires nothing of the child, so it can be administered opportunistically to 17-36 month olds in a clinic room. The social/non-social contrast provides a within-subject test of whether the measured signal is specific to social content, and the answer - large effects for social movies, medium effects for non-social - is more informative than a single accuracy figure, because it shows the complexity difference is amplified by social content but not created by it. And the environment is controlled in a low-tech way that suits the setting: caregiver holds the child, tablet at a fixed 60 cm, everyone else stands behind the pair to reduce distraction. The limitation is that passive viewing elicits a narrower behavioural range than interaction, and the authors identify live interpersonal interaction as the natural next step.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up, and no test-retest reliability of the entropy measure - which matters for a biomarker proposed for treatment monitoring, since sensitivity to change requires knowing the measurement's stability. Governance is exemplary by the standards of this corpus. The study was approved by the Duke University Health System Institutional Review Board under two protocol numbers (Pro00085434, Pro00085435), written informed consent was obtained from caregivers or legal guardians, and inability to consent in English or Spanish is disclosed as an exclusion criterion rather than passed over. Funding from eight sources including four NIH grants and four technology companies is itemised, with an explicit statement that 'the funders had no direct role in the study design, data analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript'. The competing-interests statement is the longest in this corpus and is unusually forthcoming: several authors developed technology licensed to Apple and have benefited financially, one is CEO of a company and holds a granted patent plus three applications alongside numerous advisory and consulting relationships, and another was affiliated with Apple at publication. Crucially, a structural mitigation is described rather than merely asserted: 'Data analysis for this project is constantly independently reviewed by Scott Compton, who has no conflict of interest related to this work', and Compton is a named co-author. Given the commercial stakes attached to a tablet-based autism screening app, an independent analysis reviewer is the right safeguard and is worth noting as a practice other groups could adopt.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: An ordinary consumer iPad with its front-facing camera at 30 frames per second, running a purpose-built application - no research-grade sensor, no eye tracker, no wearable, no additional hardware. That choice is the point: the entire measurement chain is a device already present in most homes and clinics, which is what makes the scalability claim credible rather than aspirational. Analysis components are all published and cited: a face detection algorithm, a low-dimensional facial embedding used to identify and track the child's face specifically among those of caregiver, siblings and clinical staff, a 49-point landmark detector, and the group's own pose-invariant affect estimator, itself previously validated against human frame-by-frame coding of 136,450 frames with an intraclass correlation of 0.9. Statistical work used Python with pingouin (Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon, ANCOVA), scipy (Spearman) and scikit-learn (logistic regression), each named at function level. The one component with a stated weakness is the perception layer: the landmark and affect algorithms were trained primarily on adults, which the authors list as a limitation while noting their prior validation in toddlers.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: The strongest methods reporting encountered in this review. Reproducible from the text: the full recruitment and screening pathway, all five exclusion criteria, the seating and device arrangement with the 60 cm distance, all six movies with durations and content, the 30 fps capture, the complete preprocessing chain including the affine canonical-face normalisation, the 15 Hz low-pass cut-off with its physiological justification (260 ms to produce an expression, 150-250 ms for a valid one), the removal of non-attending intervals, the entropy parameters m = 2 and r = 0.15 sigma with their literature sources and a supplementary sensitivity analysis, the exact rule for handling missing data inside the entropy computation with a worked numerical example, the 40% validity threshold and its consequence for per-movie sample size, the 20-scale integration window, the affect-energy definition with its 10-frame moving average, and every statistical test named down to the Python function. Two methodological contributions are presented as such rather than buried: the modification of multiscale entropy to handle partially missing time series without concatenation artefacts, and its normalisation to permit across-subject comparison - the latter accompanied by the pointed footnote that despite MSE's popularity in health research 'this problem has never been addressed before, and often authors report lower MSE for data that is clearly more complex and vice-versa'. Not available: code, data, the movies, and the decision-tree configuration. Five supplementary appendices hold further analyses, including the developmental-delay comparison and the head-motion work.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The three stated limitations are accurate and appropriately weighted: adult-trained landmark and affect detectors applied to toddlers, the possibility that other complexity measures would discriminate better, and insufficient power to determine how demographic characteristics affect the results. The last is an honest acknowledgement of a real problem, since the groups differ substantially on three demographic axes. The unstated limitations are fewer than in any other study charted here but include some that matter. The 3.6-month age gap between groups is never adjusted for, which is conspicuous in a paper that constructs ANCOVA models for two other covariates - the direction of the gap makes it an unlikely explanation of the finding, but it should have been modelled. The racial and ethnic composition differs sharply (47.5% versus 77.7% White; 32.5% versus 7.3% Hispanic/Latino), and this interacts with the acknowledged limitation about the detectors: landmark localisation accuracy varies with facial morphology and skin tone, so differential measurement error is a specific possibility, not a generic caveat. The decision to run the classification only on social movies was taken after seeing which movies produced larger effect sizes in the same data. No class handling is described for the decision tree, and the reported precision of about 70% with recall near 89% cannot arise from a 40:396 ratio without some balancing, so an undisclosed step exists in the classification pipeline. Per-movie analysed sample sizes appear only in figures. And ADOS-T totals were collected but never correlated with the entropy measure, leaving the biomarker's relationship to severity untested.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Four directions, each following from a specific gap. Study complexity and coordination of facial dynamics during live interpersonal interaction rather than passive viewing, motivated by evidence that autistic people have difficulty with affect coordination in social exchange - the natural extension of a measure built on temporal predictability. Apply the same complexity analysis to head motion as an index of postural control, exploiting data the pipeline already produces. Pursue the preliminary supplementary finding that integrated entropy may separate autism from developmental or language delay, which is the differential-diagnosis question most of this corpus avoids. And combine the facial-complexity biomarker with gaze indices, response to name, motor signatures and other measures before any automated decision tool is deployed - stated as a precondition rather than an aspiration. Absent from the list, and worth adding: test-retest reliability, prospective external validation, and the relationship between entropy and ADOS-T severity.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Spontaneous facial movement, characterised by its temporal predictability rather than its content - which is the study's conceptual contribution and distinguishes it from the affect-recognition tradition. Two regions were prespecified with stated rationales: the eyebrows, following the group's earlier finding about eyebrow raising in this cohort and the possibility that it indexes attentional engagement; and the mouth, on the basis of literature linking atypical vocalisation and mouth movement to autism. For each region the landmark points are averaged into a one-dimensional signal, head motion having first been removed by affine normalisation so that what remains is facial deformation rather than head movement. Multiscale entropy then quantifies how unpredictable that signal is across temporal scales. The authors are careful to explain what this does and does not capture, and the explanation is worth stating precisely because the distinction is often blurred elsewhere: a signal with large but highly periodic excursions gives low entropy, and so does a nearly stable signal with small excursions, while only irregular non-periodic movement gives high entropy. So the measure is not amplitude, not frequency and not variability, but predictability - and the paper backs this up empirically by showing that integrated entropy correlates only weakly (0.2-0.42) with landmark variation. The finding is that autistic toddlers' facial movement is less predictable in both regions, that the difference is amplified by social content, and that their responsiveness also varies more across different movies. The interpretation offered is that typically developing toddlers respond more predictably because they share an understanding of the movies' social meaning while autistic toddlers respond more idiosyncratically - explicitly labelled as speculation.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-sensor fusion, but the paper contains the corpus's cleanest test of whether two measures from the same modality carry redundant information, and the test is designed as discriminant validity rather than as an accuracy chase. The comparison measure is the group's own previously published affect analysis - the energy of the first derivative of neutral, positive and negative affect probability time series, computed as a 10-frame moving average of the rate of change followed by cumulative sum. Three lines of evidence are brought to bear. Correlation: Spearman r between integrated entropy and positive-affect energy is moderate for Blowing Bubbles (.49 eyebrows, .60 mouth) and Mechanical Puppy (.41, .49) but negligible for the other four movies (.01-.15), and the mouth correlates more strongly than the eyebrows, which the authors note is expected because smiling is a mouth event.
