Classification: decision trees using entropy alone reach 76.6-78.3% accuracy, using affect alone 61.6-75.0%, and using both 63.3-79.5% - so adding affect does not help and in two of four movies hurts, while AUCs compared by DeLong's method favour entropy alone in three of four movies. Logistic regression: entropy gives odds ratios up to 1.8 while affect gives 0.8, i.e. below unity. The conclusion that the two measures are largely independent and that entropy is the stronger is therefore supported by three convergent analyses rather than by a single accuracy comparison. The general lesson for the review is that a partially correlated second measure can be genuinely non-redundant, and that testing for redundancy explicitly - rather than reporting that fusion improved accuracy - is the more informative design.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Deliberately simple, and the simplicity is appropriate to the claim. The primary analyses are conventional non-parametric statistics: Mann-Whitney U for between-group comparison, Wilcoxon signed-rank for within-group, with effect size r reported for every significant test, and ANCOVA to adjust for two prespecified confounds. The modelling contribution is not a classifier but the entropy estimator itself - a modification of multiscale entropy that handles partially missing time series by admitting only fully observed embedding vectors into the coefficient counts, and that normalises per participant so complexity can be compared across people. The authors flag the second point sharply, noting in a footnote that despite MSE's popularity in health research the across-subject comparison problem 'has never been addressed before, and often authors report lower MSE for data that is clearly more complex and vice-versa'. The classification component is a secondary demonstration using a decision tree with Gini splitting and leave-one-out cross-validation, plus logistic regression for odds ratios. No deep learning appears anywhere. Given 40 autistic participants and two features, this is the right choice, and the paper does not pretend otherwise - the classifier is presented as evidence of feasibility rather than as the result.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Two scalar features per participant per movie: integrated entropy of the eyebrow region and of the mouth region, each being the cumulative sum of sample entropy across the first 20 coarse-grained scales of the landmark time series. The pipeline that produces them is where the work sits. Forty-nine landmarks are tracked at 30 fps; the child's face is isolated from those of caregiver, siblings and clinicians by facial embedding; eye-corner and nose landmarks drive an affine transform to a canonical face so that head motion is removed rather than confounded with expression; head-pose angles are estimated separately; signal above 15 Hz is filtered as noise on the physiologically motivated grounds that a facial expression takes at least 260 ms; non-attending intervals are excised; and the remaining landmark points within each region are averaged into a single time series. Sample entropy uses m = 2 and r = 0.15 sigma, both taken from prior literature with an appendix showing insensitivity to the choice. The missing-data rule is stated with a worked numerical example: only embedding vectors free of missing points contribute to the counts, because concatenating across gaps would inflate Cm without inflating Cm+1 and so bias the entropy. A minimum 40% valid-data requirement per movie applies. The representation deliberately discards expression identity, amplitude and timing, retaining only predictability - which is what makes it complementary to the affect measure rather than a variant of it.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Two metric sets for two purposes, both appropriate. For the primary group comparisons: exact p-values with effect size r reported for every test at every scale and every movie, ANCOVA-adjusted significance after controlling for missing-data percentage and landmark variation individually and jointly, Spearman correlations for the redundancy analysis, and within-group Wilcoxon tests for the eyebrow-versus-mouth comparison. Reporting effect sizes systematically alongside p-values, and interpreting them (medium for non-social, large to very large for social), is better statistical practice than anything else in this corpus and is what allows the social/non-social gradient to be read as a graded finding rather than a binary significant/not-significant one. For the secondary classification: accuracy, precision and recall for three feature sets across four movies under leave-one-out cross-validation, ROC curves with AUCs compared by DeLong's method, and logistic-regression odds ratios. Gaps: no confidence intervals on any classification metric; AUC values are shown graphically but not quoted numerically in the retrieved text; no majority-class baseline, which at 9.2% prevalence would be about 91% and therefore above the reported accuracies; and no positive or negative predictive value at the study's own prevalence, which for a primary-care screening tool is the number that would matter most. The precision-recall combination reported (about 70% and about 89%) is also arithmetically incompatible with a 40:396 class ratio, implying an undisclosed balancing step.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is structural rather than added afterwards, because the feature is a single quantity with a stated physical meaning. The paper explains precisely what integrated entropy measures and, importantly, what it does not: not amplitude, not variability, not frequency, but predictability, with the specific consequence that both a highly periodic large-excursion signal and a nearly stable small-excursion signal yield low entropy. That distinction is then tested rather than asserted, through the weak correlation (0.2-0.42) between integrated entropy and landmark variation, and through ANCOVA adjustment for variation as a covariate. Region selection was hypothesis-driven and prespecified with citations, so the analysis is confirmatory rather than exploratory in its choice of features. The social/non-social contrast functions as an interpretive control, showing that the effect is amplified by social content but present without it. The redundancy analysis against affect is itself an interpretability exercise - establishing that the measure is not simply detecting smiles. And the substantive interpretation offered is clearly labelled as speculation and is symmetrical rather than deficit-framed. What is missing is individual-level explanation: no error analysis, no examination of which children were misclassified, and no link between entropy and ADOS-T severity, which would have been the strongest available evidence that the measure tracks the construct it claims to index.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Sound at the level that matters most and loose at the margins. The classifier uses leave-one-out cross-validation over participants, so the split unit is the child and no within-participant leakage is possible - though this is easier to achieve here than elsewhere because each participant contributes a single feature vector per movie rather than many segments. More importantly, the paper's primary claims are not predictive at all: they are group comparisons with effect sizes, supported by ANCOVA adjustment for two prespecified confounds and by an internal control condition (non-social movies), which is a design where cross-validation is not the relevant safeguard and where the reported statistics carry their own uncertainty. Three looser points. The classification analysis was restricted to the four social movies because the group comparisons on the same data had shown larger effect sizes there, so that restriction is in-sample; the effect is modest, since the choice was made on a prespecified social/non-social distinction rather than by searching over movies individually, but it should be stated. No class handling is described for the decision tree, and reported precision near 70% with recall near 89% cannot be produced from 40 autistic against 396 typically developing participants - so an undisclosed balancing or subsampling step exists, and without knowing it the accuracy figures cannot be placed against the correct baseline. And no majority-class baseline is given, which at 9.2% prevalence would be about 91%, so the reported 76-79% accuracies would be below trivial on the unbalanced sample and are only meaningful under whatever balancing was applied. None of this affects the study's principal finding, which rests on non-parametric group comparisons with large effect sizes, confound adjustment and an internal control - a design that is more robust than a cross-validated accuracy figure and that this corpus contains too few of.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: Autism spectrum disorder, affective state, facial dynamics, complexity, sample entropy, multiscale entropy. Four of the six name the measurement rather than the application, and neither 'machine learning', 'deep learning', 'classification' nor 'diagnosis' appears - which accurately reflects a paper whose contribution is a biomarker and its statistical characterisation rather than a classifier. 'Complexity' and 'sample entropy' locate the work in the physiological time-series tradition rather than the affective-computing one, despite the venue. Terms carried through the body: integrated entropy, landmarks' dynamics, coarse-graining, canonical face model, pose-invariant affect, social versus non-social movies, biomarker, well-child visit.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: IEEE Transactions on Affective Computing 14(2):919-928, April-June 2023; manuscript received 30 April 2021, revised 4 September 2021, accepted 16 September 2021, published online 20 September 2021 - so the work predates its issue date by nearly two years. The venue is an affective-computing journal, and the paper is in part an argument against that field's dominant framing: rather than recognising emotions, it discards expression identity entirely and measures only the predictability of movement, then demonstrates that this carries information the affect pipeline misses. Five supplementary appendices are hosted with the article, containing the entropy-parameter sensitivity analysis, the across-subject normalisation discussion, the developmental-delay comparison, the head-motion analysis and the confound correlation values. The paper is unusually well supplied with methodological detail for its length, and the appendices carry material that would otherwise have been omitted.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2021/2023 by the Duke University Electrical and Computer Engineering department with the Duke Center for Autism and Brain Development and Duke Children's Primary Care - an engineering-psychiatry-primary care collaboration, funded by an NIH Autism Center of Excellence award, two further NIMH R01s, the Marcus and Simons Foundations, NSF, ONR and NGA, plus Apple, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services and Google. The framing is scalability of assessment: standardised observational assessment requires highly trained clinicians, manual facial coding from video is complex and time-intensive, and neither deploys at scale, so computer vision is proposed to make quantification universal. The positioning within the group's own programme is explicit and unusually candid - the paper states that it replicates the affect-related analysis of its own prior work on a larger dataset with redesigned stimuli, and then argues that the new complexity measure is 'an independent and more powerful measure' than the group's earlier one. Self-supersession of this kind is rare in this literature. The paper also carries an internal methodological critique of its own field, noting in a footnote that multiscale entropy is widely used in health research without addressing the across-subject comparability problem, with the result that 'often authors report lower MSE for data that is clearly more complex and vice-versa'. Commercially, this is one of the most conflicted studies in the corpus - several authors have licensed the underlying app technology to Apple and benefited financially - and it is also the only one to describe a structural mitigation, with data analysis independently reviewed throughout by a named conflict-free co-author.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Iwauchi K; Tanaka H; Okazaki K; Matsuda Y; Uratani M; Morimoto T; Nakamura S
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional multi-group classification study with two independent datasets (adults, children) and three diagnostic groups, combined with a per-emotion statistical analysis of gaze features. The distinguishing methodological proposal is to model the fact that group differences in gaze vary by which facial expression is presented, by weighting per-image classifier outputs rather than pooling them.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Two alternatives. The baseline model receives three scalar features per trial - number of fixations, number of saccades, scan-path length. The CNN receives a 34 x 34 greyscale gaze heat map together with the stimulus image. In both cases the unit of classification is a single trial, and the 21 or 32 per-trial binary decisions are then aggregated to a participant-level decision.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Adults: control 29.3 +/- 3.72, ASD 32.1 +/- 9.13, Sz 26.0 +/- 5.85 years. Children: control 10.0 +/- 1.55, ASD 10.9 +/- 1.39 years.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 61 analysed across two datasets: adults 46 (15 ASD, 15 Sz, 16 control, selected from 26 available controls); children 30 (15 ASD, 15 control, selected from 17 available controls)
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 16 control adults and 15 control children
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: The procedure was explained and informed consent obtained at the beginning of recording; the ethics statement records written informed consent provided by participants' legal guardian or next of kin
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: The Facial Emotion Identification Test (FEIT), a validated instrument using morphing to produce facial expressions of varying intensity, including weak expressions. Each trial began with a one-second fixation cross, then the face was displayed for 5 seconds, after which the participant verbally named the expression. Adults saw 21 images, three each of happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust and neutral, in random order; children saw 32 images, eight each of happiness, sadness, anger and surprise. FEIT score is the number of correct identifications. Because the task has an objectively correct answer, recognition accuracy and gaze behaviour are both available - and the recognition scores turn out to be essentially identical across groups.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Tobii Pro Fusion eye tracker sampling at 120 Hz; 1920 x 1080 display at approximately 65 cm; Tobii Pro Lab version 1.145 with the attention filter for fixation and saccade classification; Python for scan-path computation; PyTorch for the models.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: 'The raw data supporting the conclusions of this article will be made available by the authors, without undue reservation'
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not reported; the model architectures are fully tabulated and the scan-path algorithm is published as pseudocode
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Approved by ethics committees at both Nara Medical University and Nara Institute of Science and Technology
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Fixations and saccades were classified by Tobii Pro Lab's I-VT velocity-threshold algorithm at 100 degrees per second. Areas of interest were drawn on the eyes (extending up to the eyebrows), nose and mouth, and were redrawn per image because mouth size varies with expression - a small but important standardisation step. Scan-path length was computed in Python as the mean displacement between consecutive valid gaze samples, with a published pseudocode algorithm that handles invalid samples by segmenting rather than bridging them. For the CNN, gaze positions were rendered as a binary map, blurred with a Gaussian kernel (sigma = 10), centre-cropped and downscaled to 34 x 34 greyscale.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Good and integrated with the design rather than added afterwards. The random-forest aggregation layer produces a per-image importance, averaged across cross-validation folds, so the paper can say which facial expressions carried the classification - and it then checks those importances against the independent statistical analysis. For adult autism the highest-weighted images are two of the three neutral faces, and the statistical tests independently show all three gaze features differing on neutral trials, which the authors relate to documented difficulty with subtle expressions. For children, surprise and anger are weighted highest and anger is the one emotion showing a significant gaze difference. For schizophrenia the importances are uninterpretable, and the authors say so plainly - 'we do not think that feature importance has any particular significance' - explaining it by the observation that schizophrenia gaze differs from controls for every emotion, so no image is distinctive. Declining to interpret an importance ranking when the underlying statistics do not support it is a level of restraint absent from most of this corpus.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The learning rate was optimised by nested leave-one-participant-out cross-validation - i.e. inside the outer loop - which is the correct placement and is stated explicitly. Architecture sizes were fixed a priori and justified by dataset size. No other hyperparameter search is described.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Nested leave-one-participant-out cross-validation. In each outer fold one participant is held out entirely as test data and the rest are used for training, with the inner loop (8:2 training/validation split) used to optimise the learning rate. Test results across all participants are then pooled for accuracy, sensitivity and specificity. Because the split unit is the participant, all 21 or 32 trials from a held-out person are excluded from training, so the segment-level leakage that inflates most eye-tracking studies in this corpus cannot occur. Results are additionally tested against chance with a binomial test.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Three, all substantive and one genuinely novel. First, small sample size, with an explicit statement that more participants are needed to establish validity. Second, and unusual: a documented failure mode discovered by error analysis. Eight participants (two autistic adults, one adult with schizophrenia, one control adult, four autistic children, one control child) were misclassified by all four models, and inspection showed that their gaze did not move from the centre at all - yet their FEIT recognition scores were not low (18, 19, 15, 15 for the adults; 19, 25, 22, 17 for the children). The authors conclude that 'people with wide peripheral vision may be able to successfully complete the task without moving their eyes', and quantify the affected proportion as 6.5% of adults and 17% of children. Third, no IQ was measured: participants were recruited without intellectual difficulties but no actual values were obtained, and the authors note that the sample comprises 'only a small number of mild (high-functioning) cases'.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two independent datasets and three diagnostic groups. Adults: 15 with autism (9 male, 6 female), 15 with schizophrenia (7 male, 8 female) and 16 controls (8 male, 8 female), the latter selected from 26 available controls in order to equalise group sizes, with the selection made by ranking on SRS-2 score in descending order. Children: 15 with autism (13 male, 2 female) and 15 controls (7 male, 8 female), again reduced from 17 by SRS-2 ranking. The presence of a schizophrenia group is what distinguishes this sample from almost every other in the corpus: it supplies a psychiatric rather than merely a neurotypical contrast, and although no autism-versus-schizophrenia classifier is built, the parallel analyses against a common control group produce the study's most useful finding. Note also that the modelled unit is the trial rather than the participant - each adult contributes 21 trials and each child 32 - but the cross-validation splits by participant, so the two levels are handled correctly in the modelling even though the statistical analysis treats trials as independent.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'People with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)' and 'people with schizophrenia (Sz)' predominate, person-first, with 'the ASDs' and 'the Szs' appearing as shorthand in the participants section and 'disorder groups' used throughout as the collective term for the clinical samples. The register is clinical-psychiatric and uses 'abnormalities' freely - 'ASD and Sz have abnormalities in cognitive functions, particularly social cognitive functions', 'abnormalities in eye movement during facial expression recognition have also been reported' - and 'atypical gaze patterns' and 'social cognitive deficits' elsewhere. Autism is described as 'a neurodevelopmental disorder, meaning that it does not appear in adulthood but is an innate trait', which is an accurate developmental statement rather than a deficit claim. One passage is notably person-centred in a way the corpus rarely manages: the introduction explains that some people 'have spent their childhood without being diagnosed with ASD' and that in adulthood 'difficulties in real social life may become emerged', sometimes with secondary depressive states leading to a first psychiatric presentation - a description of late diagnosis framed around the person's experience rather than around missed screening opportunities. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement, but there is also no burden or cost rhetoric and no overstated claim.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Reported per group in two tables and more completely than most in this corpus, though with gaps. Adults: n and sex ratio, age, Kikuchi's Scale of Social Skills 18-item, SRS-2, FEIT score, ADOS-2 and PANSS as applicable. Children: n and sex ratio, age, SRS-2, FEIT score, ADHD-RS and CBCL. Three imbalances are visible and none is adjusted. The adult groups span six years of mean age (Sz 26.0 +/- 5.85, control 29.3 +/- 3.72, ASD 32.1 +/- 9.13) with very different variances, and age affects both gaze behaviour and face processing. The children's groups differ sharply in sex - 13:2 male:female in the autistic group against 7:8 in controls, so 87% versus 47% male - which is the largest sex imbalance in a matched-design study charted here. And autistic children scored more than twice as high on the ADHD Rating Scale as controls (17.6 +/- 10.2 versus 6.88 +/- 9.40), so attentional difficulty is confounded with diagnosis in a task whose outcome is where the eyes go. Not measured at all: IQ, which the authors identify as a limitation and which matters because they characterise the sample as high-functioning without being able to quantify it; and race or ethnicity, relevant here because Japanese participants viewed the FEIT's Western facial stimuli, an other-race configuration that goes unremarked. What is unusually well reported is the phenotypic battery: SRS-2 in both datasets, ADOS-2 totals for autistic adults, PANSS for schizophrenia, plus social-skills and behaviour-checklist measures, with a clear explanation of why SRS-2 was not administered to the schizophrenia group.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Among the strongest in this review, and the only one applying condition-specific re-evaluation to two different diagnoses. Diagnoses were determined according to DSM-5 research criteria and then re-evaluated with the appropriate instrument: ADOS-2 for the autistic participants, with the adult group's mean total raw score reported (46.5 +/- 11.9), and the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale for the schizophrenia group (67.1 +/- 13.0). Controls were not merely assumed neurotypical but were actively screened - 'physicians and psychologists interviewed them and excluded' anyone with learning delays or communication problems, and no control had a history of psychiatric disorder, drug abuse or epilepsy. So all three groups have an explicit ascertainment procedure, the two clinical groups have quantified symptom measures, and the control group has a stated exclusion protocol applied by clinicians. The residual gaps are minor by comparison: no inter-rater reliability is reported for the ADOS-2 or PANSS administrations, no interval between diagnosis and testing is given, and the ADOS-2 figures are total raw scores rather than calibrated severity scores, which limits comparability with other studies.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Rich on symptom severity and empty on cognition - an unusual combination in this corpus, where the reverse is more common. Severity and phenotype are measured with four or five instruments per dataset. Adults: SRS-2 total raw score (control 55.2 +/- 20.9, ASD 73.3 +/- 36.0 - note the very large SD in the autistic group, indicating wide variation in social-communication severity), ADOS-2 (46.5 +/- 11.9), PANSS for the schizophrenia group (67.1 +/- 13.0), and Kikuchi's Scale of Social Skills 18-item (control 64.7 +/- 11.0, ASD 45.3 +/- 9.46, Sz 59.1 +/- 9.14, so the autistic group scores lowest on self-reported social skill). Children: SRS-2 (control 19.2 +/- 11.5, ASD 74.7 +/- 26.9 - a very wide separation), ADHD-RS and CBCL. SRS-2 was deliberately not administered to the schizophrenia group because it has not been validated in that population, an omission explained rather than glossed. Against this, no IQ or developmental measure was obtained for anyone. The authors state the limitation squarely: participants were recruited without intellectual difficulties but 'we did not obtain any actual IQ values', so the study 'does not adequately take into account the influence of intellectual level', and the sample comprises 'only a small number of mild (high-functioning) cases'. Two consequences follow. Because the FEIT is a cognitive task with a correct answer, intellectual level plausibly affects both recognition accuracy and viewing strategy. And because SRS-2 was used to select which controls were retained, a severity-related variable enters the sampling as well as the description. Notably, no analysis relates any of these severity scores to model output, so the rich phenotyping is used descriptively rather than analytically.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated aim is to test whether modelling the specificity of gaze to particular facial expressions improves classification, on the premise - supported by prior basic research but not previously operationalised - that groups differ in gaze for some emotions and not others. The proposal is to classify each of the 21 or 32 FEIT images separately and then aggregate the per-image decisions with a random forest that learns which images matter, rather than by unweighted voting. Findings, all reported with binomial tests against chance and none oversold. For autistic adults versus controls the weighted CNN reached 0.710 accuracy (sensitivity 0.733, specificity 0.688), significantly above chance and 10 points above the unweighted CNN. For autistic children the weighted models reached 0.667 (weighted CNN sensitivity 0.600, specificity 0.733), significant and 16.7 points above the unweighted CNN, with the weighting raising sensitivity from 0.286 to 0.600. For schizophrenia the best models reached 0.645, only marginally above chance (p = 0.052), and weighting produced no improvement at all. The statistical analysis explains why the method behaves differently across conditions and is the more interesting result: in adults, reduced fixation at the eyes distinguished the schizophrenia group from controls for every one of the seven emotions, but the autistic group from controls for only two (anger and neutral), while scan-path length distinguished autism from controls for six of seven emotions. So the classic reduced-eye-looking signature was present uniformly in schizophrenia and only selectively in autism - which is exactly the condition under which per-image weighting helps for one and not the other. In children, almost no gaze feature reached significance at all, yet the weighted models still exceeded chance.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Single-country, clinic-linked laboratory testing in Nara and Osaka, Japan, with participants recruited through the psychiatry department of Nara Medical University School of Medicine and Osaka Psychiatric Medical Center and tested on equipment at the Nara Institute of Science and Technology. The setting is a controlled screen-based assessment at a fixed 65 cm viewing distance rather than a naturalistic or point-of-care one, and no deployment scenario is proposed. Recruitment geometry is the standard clinical case-control arrangement, with the important qualification that both clinical groups come from psychiatric services and both are contrasted against the same actively screened control group, which is what makes the parallel comparison meaningful. One setting-related feature is unaddressed: the FEIT is a Western instrument and the participants are Japanese, so every trial involves other-race face processing, in a task whose entire outcome is where on a face the participant looks. Cross-cultural differences in face-scanning are well documented and the paper does not mention them.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: The Facial Emotion Identification Test, a validated instrument that uses morphing to generate expressions at varying intensity, including deliberately weak ones - which is central to the paper's argument, since the finding it converges on concerns subtle rather than prototypical expressions. Each trial: a one-second central fixation cross, then a face for 5 seconds, then a verbal response naming the emotion. Adults saw 21 images (three each of happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust, neutral) and children 32 (eight each of happiness, sadness, anger, surprise), all in random order. Three properties make this among the better paradigms in the corpus. It has an objectively correct answer on every trial, so task performance and gaze behaviour are separately measurable - and the result is striking: FEIT scores were essentially identical across groups (adults 15.5, 14.5 and 14.3 out of 21 for controls, autism and schizophrenia; children 22.1 and 22.2 out of 32), meaning the groups recognised the emotions equally well while looking at the faces differently. Any gaze difference therefore cannot be attributed to differential task success. The stimulus set is systematically structured by emotion, which is what makes per-image weighting meaningful and interpretable rather than an arbitrary ensemble. And the one-second fixation cross standardises the starting gaze position across trials and participants, so scan-path measures begin from a common origin. The paradigm's limitations are the short trial (5 seconds, giving at most 600 gaze samples), the static stimuli, and the copyright restriction that prevents the images being reproduced or shared.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session per participant, no follow-up and no test-retest reliability for any gaze feature. The two datasets are age-stratified rather than longitudinal - adults and children are separate samples, not the same people at two ages - although the introduction motivates the design partly by an interest in 'the developmental trajectory in processing emotional stimuli in neurodevelopmental conditions', and the parallel analysis does permit a cautious comparison across age groups, which the discussion makes: anger is highly weighted in both the adult and child autism models, suggesting a possible common specificity. Ethics reporting is complete for approval and consent: the data collection was approved by ethics committees at both Nara Medical University and Nara Institute of Science and Technology, the procedure was explained at the start of recording and informed consent obtained, and the formal ethics statement records written informed consent from participants' legal guardian or next of kin. Funding from a single CREST grant is stated, and competing interests are declared as none.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: A Tobii Pro Fusion eye tracker sampling at 120 Hz, with participants seated approximately 65 cm from a 1920 x 1080 display. Fixation and saccade classification used Tobii Pro Lab version 1.145 with its attention filter and the I-VT velocity-threshold algorithm, with the threshold stated explicitly at 100 degrees per second - a level of specificity about event detection that most eye-tracking papers in this corpus omit entirely, and one that matters because fixation counts are meaningless without it. Areas of interest were drawn on the eyes (extending up to the eyebrows), nose and mouth, and were redrawn for each image because mouth size varies with expression, which prevents a systematic bias in mouth-region measurement across emotions. Scan-path length was computed in Python with an algorithm published as pseudocode that segments rather than bridges invalid samples. Modelling used PyTorch with fully tabulated architectures. Clinical instruments: ADOS-2, PANSS, SRS-2, Kikuchi's Scale of Social Skills 18-item, ADHD-RS and CBCL. No calibration procedure is described.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Among the best-specified studies in the review. Reproducible from the text: the full instrument battery per group, the FEIT protocol with image counts per emotion and exact trial timing, the eye tracker and sampling rate, the viewing distance, the I-VT algorithm with its velocity threshold, the area-of-interest definitions and the per-image redrawing rule, both trial-exclusion rules with the resulting per-emotion trial counts listed exactly, the scan-path computation as pseudocode, both model architectures in a table giving neuron counts and kernel sizes and channel counts, the optimiser, loss function, epoch cap and early-stopping patience, the heat-map construction including the Gaussian sigma and the 34 x 34 centre-cropped downscaling, the three-step strategy adopted specifically because the dataset is small, and the nested leave-one-participant-out scheme with its 8:2 inner split. Statistical procedures are equally explicit, including Welch's t-test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Not available: code, and the FEIT images, which are under copyright and could not even be reproduced as figures. Raw data are offered on request without undue reservation.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The three stated limitations are well chosen and one is a genuine contribution. Small sample size is acknowledged first. The IQ limitation is stated with unusual candour - participants were recruited without intellectual difficulties but no actual values were obtained, so the study 'does not adequately take into account the influence of intellectual level', and the sample is 'only a small number of mild (high-functioning) cases'. Most valuable is the error analysis, which is the kind of work almost no study in this corpus performs: the authors identified the eight participants misclassified by all four models, inspected their raw data, found that their gaze did not move from the centre at all, checked whether they had simply not engaged with the task, and found that their FEIT recognition scores were normal (18 and 19 of 21 for two autistic adults; 19, 25, 22 and 17 of 32 for four autistic children). The conclusion - that some people complete the task using peripheral vision without moving their eyes - identifies a failure mode intrinsic to gaze-based assessment, quantifies it at 6.5% of adults and 17% of children, and names it as a target for future work. Unstated limitations remain. The statistical analysis treats trials as independent when they cluster within participants at roughly two or three per person per emotion, so Welch's t-tests on 101-172 trials overstate the effective sample size. Control selection by SRS-2 ranking introduces a construct-related variable into the sampling, and the direction of the selection is ambiguous from the text. The adult groups differ by up to six years in mean age and the children's groups by 40 percentage points in sex ratio, neither adjusted. Autistic children scored more than twice as high on the ADHD Rating Scale as controls, an unaddressed comorbidity confound in a gaze task. And Japanese participants viewed Western faces without comment.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Three directions, each tied to a specific finding. Collect more data to establish validity, the standard response to a small sample. Develop a method that works for participants whose gaze barely moves - which follows directly from the error analysis and is a real methodological problem rather than a generic wish, since a gaze-based classifier that fails on 17% of children because they use peripheral vision has a systematic blind spot that more data alone will not close. And obtain actual IQ values and other individual characteristics so that the relationship between the model and the heterogeneity of the conditions can be examined - an acknowledgement that a high-functioning sample of 15 cannot speak for a spectrum. Not proposed, and worth noting: a direct autism-versus-schizophrenia classifier, which the dataset already supports and which would be the natural differential-diagnosis test; and validation on an independent cohort.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Visual attention during facial emotion recognition, measured in three ways and analysed separately for each emotion presented. Fixation counts within anatomically defined areas of interest - the eyes region extending up to the eyebrows, the nose and the mouth - index where attention is allocated on the face. Saccade counts index how often gaze shifts. Scan-path length, defined as the mean displacement between consecutive gaze samples, indexes how far and how restlessly the eyes travel. The paper's behavioural hypothesis is the one the field takes for granted, that autistic people look less at the eyes; its finding is that this holds much more clearly for schizophrenia than for autism in these data. In adults, fixation at the eyes separated the schizophrenia group from controls for all seven emotions with p values from .0001 to .01, but separated the autistic group from controls for only two of seven (anger and neutral). What did separate autistic adults from controls, across six of seven emotions, was scan-path length - they moved their gaze further per sample. Fixation at the mouth separated autism from controls for five of seven emotions but never separated schizophrenia from controls. So the two conditions produce distinguishable gaze signatures: schizophrenia is characterised by uniformly reduced eye-region fixation, autism by increased mouth fixation and longer scan paths that vary with the expression shown. In children, almost nothing reached significance - only eye fixation for anger. A secondary behaviour is measured and turns out to be null: emotion recognition accuracy, which was essentially identical across all groups in both datasets, so the gaze differences occur without any difference in task success.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-sensor fusion, but two forms of within-study integration are central to the design. The first is the CNN's dual input: the gaze heat map is presented alongside the stimulus image, so the network can 'explicitly learn the facial regions and expressions' rather than treating gaze positions as coordinates divorced from what was at those coordinates. Since the same 21 or 32 images are shown to every participant, the image channel functions as a conditioning signal identifying which trial the heat map came from. The second, and the paper's actual contribution, is the aggregation layer: each of the 21 or 32 trials is classified independently and the per-trial decisions are then combined either by unweighted hard voting or by a random forest that learns which stimuli to trust. That is a form of stimulus-level fusion, and unlike most fusion claims in this corpus it is tested against its own ablation across three separate problems with informative results - weighting adds 10 points for autistic adults and 16.7 for autistic children but nothing for schizophrenia. The differential outcome is explained mechanistically rather than left as a number: weighting helps precisely when group differences are selective across stimuli, and is useless when they are uniform. That is a more transferable finding about when multi-stimulus aggregation should be weighted than any of the accuracy comparisons in this review.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Deliberately small models with a classical aggregation layer, and the modesty is justified rather than incidental. The per-trial classifiers are a three-hidden-layer multilayer perceptron with five neurons per layer, taking three scalar gaze features, and a two-convolutional-layer CNN with 3 x 3 kernels and 8 and 16 channels plus one fully connected layer, taking a 34 x 34 greyscale heat map and the stimulus image. The authors describe a three-step strategy adopted explicitly because the dataset is small: downscale the images to 34 x 34 greyscale after centre-cropping, reduce the CNN to two layers plus one fully connected layer, and use leave-one-participant-out cross-validation to maximise training data. Above the per-trial classifier sits the paper's contribution, an aggregation over the 21 or 32 per-trial decisions by either hard voting or a random forest, the latter learning which stimuli should count. Training used Adam with cross-entropy loss, a 300-epoch cap and early stopping after 15 epochs without validation improvement, with the learning rate optimised inside the nested cross-validation. The authors also justify not using a support vector machine, on the grounds that the per-fold sample size of 630 or 651 trials is adequate relative to a cited prior study - an argument about sample adequacy rather than an unexamined preference for deep learning.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Two parallel representations, compared directly. The baseline uses three interpretable scalars per trial: number of fixations, number of saccades and scan-path length. The CNN uses a spatial representation: gaze sample positions are set to 1 in an otherwise zero image, blurred with a Gaussian kernel of sigma 10, centre-cropped and downscaled to 34 x 34 greyscale, then paired with the stimulus image so the model sees both where the person looked and what was there. Two observations about this representation. It discards temporal order entirely - a heat map is a spatial density, so the sequence in which regions were visited, which the paper's own scan-path measure partly captures, is unavailable to the CNN. And the aggressive downscaling to 34 x 34 from a 1920 x 1080 display means each pixel spans roughly 56 x 32 display pixels, so the representation can distinguish eyes from mouth but not, say, one eye from the other or the pupil from the eyelid; this is a reasonable trade for a dataset of this size but bounds what the model can learn. One reporting inconsistency: fixation counts of 200-300 in a five-second trial exceed the number of possible fixation events at 120 Hz, so these are gaze samples classified as fixation rather than discrete fixation events, and the label is used loosely throughout.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for four model variants across three classification problems - twelve complete metric triples, reported in a single table with the best in bold. Reporting all three metrics for every ablation condition rather than accuracy alone lets a reader see what the weighting actually does: for children it raises the baseline's sensitivity from 0.333 to 0.667 and the CNN's from 0.286 to 0.600, which is where the accuracy gain comes from, and the paper says so explicitly. The chance-level handling is the most straightforward in the corpus: group sizes were equalised so chance is approximately 50%, and each headline accuracy is tested against it with a binomial test, with all three p-values reported including the one that fails - schizophrenia at p = 0.052, described as marginally significant rather than rounded into significance. Feature importances from the random forest are averaged across cross-validation folds rather than fitted once. Missing: AUC or ROC, confidence intervals, and any precision or predictive-value figure. Given accuracies of 0.645 to 0.710 on samples of 30-31 participants, confidence intervals would be wide and their absence is the main reporting gap - a single participant moves accuracy by about 3 percentage points.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is built into the aggregation design and is then cross-checked against independent evidence, which is the part that distinguishes it. The random forest that weights the 21 or 32 per-image decisions yields an importance per stimulus, averaged over cross-validation folds, and a table maps each face number to its emotion so the importances can be read semantically. The authors then test each importance ranking against the separate statistical analysis. For autistic adults the two highest-weighted images are neutral faces, and the statistics independently show all three gaze features differing significantly on neutral trials - a convergence the authors relate to documented difficulty with subtle expressions, since neutral is the least prototypical stimulus in the set. For autistic children the highest weights fall on surprise and two anger images, and anger is the single emotion showing a significant gaze difference in that dataset. For schizophrenia the top-weighted images are disgust and anger, and here the authors decline to interpret: 'we do not think that feature importance has any particular significance', because the statistics show eye-region fixation differing for every emotion, so no image is distinctive and the ranking is noise. Refusing to build a story around an importance ranking that the underlying statistics do not support is a discipline absent elsewhere in this corpus, and it makes the two interpretations that are offered more credible. The error analysis adds a second layer of interpretability at the individual level, identifying the specific participants the models could not classify and diagnosing why.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: One of the two or three soundest validation designs in this review. The scheme is nested leave-one-participant-out cross-validation: in each outer fold a single participant is held out entirely, with all 21 or 32 of their trials excluded from training, and the inner loop with an 8:2 training/validation split is used to optimise the learning rate. Placing hyperparameter selection inside the outer loop is stated explicitly and is the correct construction; the great majority of studies in this corpus either tune on the test set or do not say. Because the split unit is the participant, the trial-level leakage that inflates results throughout this literature - where a person's own segments appear on both sides of the split - is structurally impossible here, and this matters more than usual because the per-trial classifier operates on individual FEIT images that would otherwise be trivially matched across folds. Class balance was engineered in advance by equalising group sizes, so chance is approximately 50% and is not an artefact of prevalence. And every reported accuracy is tested against that chance level with a binomial test, with the failing result reported as failing. The consequences are visible in the numbers: accuracies of 0.645 to 0.710 rather than the 90-plus figures common in this corpus, which is what a properly participant-disjoint, chance-tested evaluation of gaze features in 30 people looks like. Three residual weaknesses. No confidence intervals accompany any figure, and with 30-31 participants one person is roughly 3 accuracy points, so the 10-point gain from weighting in adults corresponds to about three people. The controls were selected from a larger pool by SRS-2 ranking, so sampling is conditioned on a construct-related variable. And the statistical analysis that motivates the whole approach - and that is used to validate the feature importances - treats trials as independent units when they cluster within participants, without any mixed-effects adjustment, so those p-values are anticonservative even after Benjamini-Hochberg correction.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia, convolutional neural networks, eye movement, facial emotion recognition. The inclusion of schizophrenia alongside autism is the distinguishing feature and signals the paper's differential-psychiatric framing rather than an autism-screening one; neither 'diagnosis', 'screening' nor 'classification' appears, and the application terms in the body are 'biomarkers' and 'behavioral indicators'. Terms carried through the text: Facial Emotion Identification Test, scan-path length, heat map, hard voting, random forest weighting, nested leave-one-participant-out cross-validation, areas of interest, I-VT, feature importance, peripheral vision.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Frontiers in Digital Health 5:952433, Digital Mental Health section, Original Research, CC BY. Received 25 May 2022, accepted 30 January 2023, published 16 February 2023 - an eight-month review, longer than the Frontiers norm, with two named reviewers and a handling editor from Duke University disclosed as the journal requires. The venue is a digital-health rather than an engineering or clinical-psychiatry journal, and the reporting reflects that mixed audience: clinical instruments and diagnostic procedure are described to psychiatric standards while model architectures, optimiser settings and cross-validation structure are tabulated to engineering standards, and both the statistical analysis and the machine learning are given roughly equal space. Supplementary materials hold the nose-fixation and saccade analyses.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2023 by the Augmented Human Communication Laboratory at Nara Institute of Science and Technology with the Department of Psychiatry at Nara Medical University School of Medicine and Osaka Psychiatric Medical Center, funded by a single JST CREST grant (JPMJCR19A5). The framing is diagnostic refinement within psychiatry rather than population screening: the opening premise is that experienced psychiatrists identify autism and schizophrenia through interviews, responses and neuropsychological tests, and that 'the discovery of disorder-specific biomarkers and behavioral indicators with sufficient sensitivity is important' to improve that process. Two aspects of the positioning are distinctive for this corpus. The paper's central concern is differentiation between two conditions rather than detection of one - 'since ASD and Sz are often difficult to differentiate, we propose to examine eye movement differences during facial expression recognition for the distinction' - which puts it among the very few studies here that treat the clinically realistic problem. And its contribution is framed as a modelling gap rather than a performance gap: prior basic research had established that gaze differences vary by presented emotion, but 'machine learning models that take this into account have not been examined', so the paper's claim is that a known behavioural fact should be built into the model architecture. The resulting accuracies are modest and are reported without inflation, with binomial tests against chance and a failing result left visible - a tone that stands out against the corpus's prevailing register.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Atyabi A; Boccanfuso L; Snider; J. .. C.; Kim M; Barney E; Ahn YA; Li B; Dommer KJ; Shic F
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of naturalistic app-usage telemetry, combining descriptive characterisation of a large uncontrolled user population with a diagnostic-classification analysis on the small labelled subset; partly a replication and extension of the same group's earlier report on the same dataset
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Fixed-length windows of consecutive key-press identifiers (sequential), of inter-press intervals (temporal), or per-session frequency vectors (spectral). Each user contributes many windows, in proportion to how much they used the app - so heavy users dominate the sample count. The authors note the trade-off explicitly: longer windows capture more cohesive patterns but yield fewer pseudo-samples and exclude short sessions, while shorter windows yield more samples but distort the patterns.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Full lifespan. Table II reports 36 users aged 0-5, 39 aged 6-10, 20 aged 11-18, 23 aged 19-30, 45 aged 31-50, 50 aged over 50, and 22 unspecified - totals that do not reconcile with the stated 180 or 214 survey respondents.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 6,033 app users; 5,372 with valid usage patterns after 761 were excluded for generating too few events; over 2.5 million individual button presses
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 99 users who disclosed a non-autism reason, comprising - per Table III - 32 with no diagnosis, 49 'other', 12 stroke, 4 ALS, 4 dementia, 4 brain injury and 3 ADHD
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: No consent process is described for the usage data, which were collected automatically as app telemetry for developer debugging. Survey completion was voluntary and 'refusal to answer the survey did not cause denial of service'. The only data-protection statement is that 'all the recorded data were encrypted and de-identified'. Many users were children under the age of 10.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. There is no task, protocol, prompt or elicitation: the data are whatever users chose to do with a communication app in daily life over two and a half years. This is the study's principal attraction and its principal limitation.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: FreeSpeech, an iPad-based speech-generating AAC application with a customisable, programmable interface supporting flexible arrangement of user-modifiable visual icons, sentence generation and mapping to synthesised or recorded voices; logs of key order, timing and event type transmitted automatically to a backend database on internet connection.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not reported. The acknowledgements thank the GiveSpeech Foundation 'for their provision of data'.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: None stated. No institutional review board, ethics committee or approval number appears anywhere in the paper.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: All events and unique keys were enumerated, yielding 69 unique keys and events across the corpus despite users being able to add their own vocabulary. These were partitioned into four categories - normal keys, complex keys, normal app events, complex app events - and assigned non-overlapping ranges of numeric identifiers so that category membership is recoverable from the identifier, described by the authors as a pseudo-semantic representation. The resulting numeric stream was then windowed into non-overlapping segments of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 or 100 consecutive key presses, each window becoming a pseudo-sample. Temporal modelling substitutes the inter-press interval in milliseconds for the key identifier; spectral modelling counts key or key-category frequencies per session and needs no window.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Weak on the models, moderately good on the data. There is no feature importance, attention analysis, error analysis or examination of what the stacked autoencoder learned, and no attempt to identify which key-press patterns distinguish the groups. The interpretive content is descriptive rather than model-based: usage by age band, average time in app by diagnosis, the top 14 phrases used across the corpus, and the number of unique words per diagnostic group. The pseudo-semantic identifier scheme is designed to preserve category information in the numeric encoding, which is a thoughtful representation choice, but nothing downstream exploits or interrogates it. The one reasoned negative result is the rejection of spatial modelling, on the grounds that user customisation makes screen positions incomparable between people.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Window size is swept over 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 100 and the best reported. The authors note that the deep belief network was tuned specifically for the 20-key-press window and speculate that 'more comprehensive tuning of the classifier to each window size sample specification (as it is done with the 20 key press samples) is likely to help this classifier' - an admission that tuning effort was applied unevenly across the compared models. No other hyperparameter procedure is described, and no separate development set is mentioned.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Two schemes are described. The earlier analysis used five repetitions of leave-one-out cross-validation nested with 100 bootstraps; the present extension uses ten repetitions of 20-fold cross-validation nested with ten bootstraps. In neither case is the unit of splitting stated. Given that each user generates many windows and that the modelling operates on windows, the natural reading is that windows rather than users are partitioned, in which case a user's own windows appear on both sides of every split. This is not clarified anywhere, and no user-level performance is reported. The far larger issue is that the headline result is obtained after k-means clustering has been used to assign pseudo-labels to approximately 5,192 unlabelled users, so most of the data on which 82% accuracy is computed carry machine-generated rather than reported labels.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: No limitations section. Several constraints are stated candidly in the methods rather than framed as limitations: that the data were collected for developer debugging and not configured for any analytic aim, so the data structure required significant reprocessing; that spatial modelling is unusable because the app is customisable; and that window size trades pattern fidelity against sample count. The conclusion notes that future work could examine the stability of predictions over time and the prediction of quantitative clinical traits such as adaptive skills and autism severity, which implicitly acknowledges that neither is available here.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: A very large uncontrolled user population with a very small labelled subset. FreeSpeech attracted 6,033 users between January 2012 and May 2014, of whom 5,372 generated enough events to be usable (761 excluded), collectively producing over 2.5 million button presses. Of these, 214 users voluntarily completed an online survey and 180 disclosed a diagnosis - 81 autistic and 99 non-autistic, which is 3.4% of the usable user base. The non-autistic group is itself clinically diverse: Table III lists 32 users reporting no diagnosis, 49 'other', 12 stroke, 4 ALS, 4 dementia, 4 brain injury and 3 ADHD alongside 88 with autism. Two internal inconsistencies should be recorded: Table III sums to 196 and Table II (age bands) to 235, against stated totals of 180 disclosing a diagnosis and 214 completing the survey, and Table III's 88 autistic users does not match the 81 stated in the text. The modelled unit is neither the user nor the session but the window - a fixed-length run of 10 to 100 consecutive key presses - so a heavy user contributes far more pseudo-samples than a light one, and the effective sample size for the classification experiments is never stated. Critically, the headline result is obtained after k-means clustering has assigned pseudo-labels to the roughly 5,192 users who never disclosed anything, so most of the data underlying the 82% figure carry machine-generated labels.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)' and 'individuals with disabilities' predominate, person-first and generally neutral, with the field's own vocabulary of augmentative and alternative communication used precisely throughout. The register is mostly that of assistive-technology research rather than pathology, and the paper is notably interested in what users do with the app rather than in what is wrong with them - the descriptive sections report which phrases people used, how many unique words they produced, and how long they engaged, framed as evidence of the app's usefulness across populations. Against this, deficit language appears in places: AAC systems 'are usually used by individuals with expressive communication disorders who suffer from impairments in speech, language, reading, and/or writing', autism is 'associated with deficits in social interaction', and 'individuals affected with autism' appears once. One passage is garbled in a way that matters: the text states that people with non-autistic communication challenges 'are typically interested in communicating with others, whereas individuals with ASD may be more motivated', which as written contradicts the contrast it is drawing and appears to have lost a negation - a claim about differential communicative motivation in autism that is contentious in the first place and is here left incoherent. There is no neurodiversity framing and no involvement of AAC users or autistic people in the research, which is a notable absence for a study built entirely on the communication attempts of disabled people.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Almost nothing usable, and the one variable that is reported creates the study's central problem. Age is given only as a distribution over six bands for survey respondents (0-5: 36, 6-10: 39, 11-18: 20, 19-30: 23, 31-50: 45, over 50: 50, unspecified: 22) with no breakdown by diagnosis, and the totals do not reconcile with the stated respondent counts. No sex, race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, IQ, language level or comorbidity data were collected at all. Geographic distribution is reported at country level: 66% of users in the United States, with Europe and Oceania represented. The decisive omission is age by diagnostic group, because the composition of the comparison group makes the confound near-certain rather than speculative. Autism is congenital and the app's heaviest and most frequent users were children aged 10 and under; the non-autistic comparison group is dominated by acquired conditions of adult and later life - stroke, dementia, ALS, brain injury - which the paper's own background section describes as the 'acquired disabilities' category of AAC users, explicitly contrasted with congenital ones. A classifier separating these groups from key-press sequences may therefore be separating a five-year-old learning to request food from a seventy-year-old adapting to post-stroke aphasia, and nothing in the analysis distinguishes that possibility from a genuine autism signature. The paper itself observes in its background that older AAC users approach these systems with greater communicative experience but less technological intuitiveness, producing struggle, frustration and abandonment - which is a description of precisely the age-related usage difference that the classifier could be detecting.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: The weakest reference standard in this review alongside the social-media study. Diagnosis is voluntary self- or proxy-report through an optional online survey embedded in a free commercial app: users 'were asked to disclose their reason for using the application', 214 of 6,033 chose to respond, and 180 named a diagnosis. There is no clinical assessment, no diagnostic instrument, no clinician involvement, no verification, no date of diagnosis, and no record of who completed the survey - the AAC user, a parent, a spouse or a speech-language therapist, each of which would be plausible for a device used by people with communication impairments spanning early childhood to advanced dementia. Because 'refusal to answer the survey did not cause denial of service', respondents are self-selected on unknown characteristics, and they represent 3.4% of usable users. The 'no diagnosis' category (32 users) is particularly ambiguous, since a person using a speech-generating device while reporting no diagnosis may be a therapist, a family member, a curious downloader or someone with an undisclosed condition. The comparison group's composition is simultaneously the study's most interesting feature and a further source of uncertainty: contrasting autism against other communication-impaired populations rather than against typical development is exactly the differential framing this literature usually avoids, but here the comparison group is a convenience aggregate of eight loosely specified categories, one of which is literally labelled 'other' and accounts for half of it.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, language, adaptive-function or autism-severity measure exists for any participant, and none could exist given the data source. This is a substantive gap for a study whose modality is language production: the dataset consists of hundreds of thousands of communicative acts, and the paper reports descriptively that autistic users produced a considerably higher number of unique words than most other diagnostic groups, but no linguistic or communicative competence measure is derived, validated or used. The conclusion identifies the gap without naming it as one, proposing future work on 'how usage patterns can be used to predict quantitative traits of clinical relevance (such as adaptive skills and the severity of the autism presentation)'. Two consequences follow. There is no way to characterise where on the spectrum the 81 autistic users sit, and since they are people who need a speech-generating device they are by construction from the minimally verbal end - a population systematically under-represented in the rest of this corpus, which is a genuine strength of the dataset that the absence of any severity measure prevents the study from exploiting. And the number of unique words used, which the paper reports as evidence of the app's usefulness, is equally readable as a proxy for expressive language level, unmeasured and uncontrolled, and plausibly one of the features the classifier exploits.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Two goals, and the paper is clearer about the first than the second. The first is to demonstrate that the dense telemetry generated by digital AAC systems is worth analysing at all, which the authors argue has been almost entirely neglected: 'with the exception of one prior report, no efforts have been made to use the dense streams of data collected by digital AACs to derive insights of clinical importance'. The second is the classification question, posed precisely and unusually well: 'can we distinguish individuals with ASD from individuals without ASD (but who have need for AAC systems), based solely on patterns of use?' - the parenthesis matters, because it commits the study to a differential rather than an autism-versus-typical contrast. Findings: conventional usage statistics separate nothing. Session length was 2.14 versus 2.10 minutes (p = 0.86), word selects per use 5.6 versus 4.31 (p = 0.166) and word-select frequency 2.99 versus 2.28 per minute (p = 0.147), none significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction, and the authors present this explicitly as motivation for more advanced modelling. The prior analysis of the same data reached 47-61% across sequential, temporal and spectral views - sequential SVM peaking at 58% at window size 40, temporal at 60%, spectral at 61% with LogitBoost - which is at or barely above chance. Accuracy rose to 70% with sequential modelling only after k-means pseudo-labelling enlarged the training set, and to 82% in the present study with stacked autoencoders at window size 40. Descriptively the study also reports that use spanned the whole lifespan with heaviest engagement among under-10s, that autistic users had the highest average number of app accesses, and that the commonest phrases concerned food, sleep, sport and greetings.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: There is no research setting: the data are telemetry from a free commercial iPad app used by people at home and in daily life across at least three continents over two and a half years, transmitted automatically to a backend server. This is the most naturalistic dataset in the corpus by a wide margin, and the authors are right that it represents a kind of scale that conventional autism research cannot reach - approximately 200 new users per month even at the end of the app's life, and around 1,800 in the busiest month. The corresponding losses are total. Nothing about the context of any interaction is known: whether the user was communicating with a person or exploring the interface, whether a therapist was present, whether the device was being used for its intended purpose, whether the account holder was the person using the screen. The logs were not designed for research and the authors say so plainly - collected 'for developers' debugging purposes and general system usage statistics', with 'little attention... given to the data structure and representation during the app development'. So the study inherits both the reach of consumer telemetry and its complete absence of experimental control, and it is candid about the latter in a way that makes the work easier to appraise.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: None, and its absence defines what the study can and cannot show. There is no task, protocol, prompt, stimulus or elicitation; the behavioural sample is whatever thousands of people chose to do with a communication app over two and a half years. This yields ecological validity that no laboratory paradigm can match - these are real communicative acts serving real needs, not responses to a screen in a clinic - but it also means the behaviour is confounded with everything that varies between users: how the app was configured, who set it up, what vocabulary was loaded, what the user was trying to say, how much support they had, and how long they had owned the device. One design consequence is handled well and is worth recording: the app was fully customisable, so different users operate on different icon arrangements, and the authors correctly reject spatial modelling on this basis - 'between participant or between group analyses are difficult due to the customizability of the app which allows different participants to all potentially create a different base (i.e. set of icons) upon which they operate'. That is a clear-sighted rejection of a representation that would have appeared informative while measuring only how each user had arranged their own screen. The windowing scheme is the substitute for a trial structure, and its trade-off is stated explicitly: longer windows capture more cohesive patterns but produce fewer pseudo-samples and discard short sessions, shorter windows produce more samples but distort the patterns.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Longitudinal in data span and cross-sectional in analysis: usage covers January 2012 to May 2014 with per-month user and event counts charted, but the classification treats windows as exchangeable and models nothing about change over time. This is a striking missed opportunity, since AAC usage is expected to develop as a user learns the system and, in the acquired-condition groups, may decline with disease progression - and the conclusion identifies 'the stability of predictions over time' as future work. Ethics is the study's most serious deficiency and is entirely absent. There is no institutional review board approval, no ethics committee, no research-ethics statement and no consent process for research use of the telemetry, which was gathered automatically for debugging from a commercial product. The only safeguard reported is that 'all the recorded data were encrypted and de-identified', and the only choice offered to users concerned the optional survey. The population includes 75 users aged 10 or under and a further 20 aged 11-18 among survey respondents alone, plus an unknown number among the roughly 5,192 unlabelled users, and every one of them is a person with a communication impairment whose attempts to speak are the data. Retrospective research use of consumer telemetry from disabled children, without consent or ethical review and without any discussion of either, is a governance gap that a four-page conference format does not excuse. No competing-interests statement appears despite three commercial or industry-lab affiliations among the authors and the app itself having been a commercial product.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: FreeSpeech, an iPad speech-generating AAC application commercially available on the Apple iTunes store from January 2012 to May 2014, with a customisable programmable interface supporting user-modifiable icon arrangement, sentence generation and mapping to synthesised or recorded voices. The app logged all key presses, their timings and other on-screen events and transmitted them automatically to a secure backend on internet connection. No research instrument, sensor or assessment tool was used at any point - the entire measurement apparatus is a consumer application's debug logging. Analysis software, frameworks, library versions and compute are not named anywhere, and neither are the architectures or training settings of the stacked autoencoders and deep belief networks that produce the headline result. The asymmetry is notable: the data-collection platform is described in useful detail while the modelling that generates the paper's claim is described only by algorithm name.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Partial and uneven. Reproducible in principle: the app's identity and deployment window, the user and event counts, the 12.6% exclusion rule for insufficient events, the survey response numbers, the four-category pseudo-semantic identifier scheme with its non-overlapping ID ranges and the count of 69 unique keys and events, the definitions of sequential, temporal and spectral modelling, the window sizes swept, the classifier inventory, and the repetition and bootstrap counts for both cross-validation schemes. Not reproducible: the unit of cross-validation, which is never stated and determines whether the results mean anything; the k-means configuration, how pseudo-labels were assigned and whether any were checked; the stacked autoencoder and deep belief network architectures and training regimes; the survey instrument; any hyperparameter, seed, code or data. The dataset is telemetry from a discontinued commercial app held by a third-party foundation and is not described as available. Internal consistency is also weak, with three different participant totals recoverable from the text and tables.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: There is no limitations section, and the paper's candour is concentrated in the methods rather than in self-appraisal. What is stated plainly and deserves credit: the data were collected for developer debugging with no analytic aim in mind, so the structure required substantial reprocessing; spatial modelling is unusable because the app is customisable; window size trades pattern fidelity against sample count; and the deep belief network was tuned only for one window size, so its poorer results elsewhere may reflect tuning effort rather than capability. What is not addressed is more consequential. The reference standard is unverified voluntary self-report from 3.4% of users with no clinical component. Age is confounded with diagnosis by the structure of the comparison group, which mixes congenital autism against predominantly acquired adult-onset conditions, and no age adjustment or even age-by-group reporting is performed. The headline 82% is computed after k-means assigned pseudo-labels to roughly 5,192 users, so the great majority of the evaluation data carry labels generated by an unsupervised algorithm rather than reported by any person - which makes the accuracy partly a measure of agreement with a clustering solution. The unit of cross-validation is never stated, and with each user contributing many windows, window-level splitting would put a user's own data on both sides of every fold. Accuracy is the only metric. No chance baseline appears. The three participant totals in the text and tables do not reconcile. And there is no ethics approval, no consent for research use, and no discussion of either.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Three directions, all in the conclusion and all reasonable. Examine the stability of predictions over time - the obvious next step for a dataset spanning two and a half years that is currently analysed cross-sectionally. Predict quantitative traits of clinical relevance such as adaptive skills and the severity of the autism presentation, which acknowledges that the present labels are binary and unverified. And develop 'next generation digital markers and fingerprints for understanding change, variation, and opportunities for growth' - a framing oriented towards monitoring and personalisation rather than diagnosis, which is the more defensible use of this kind of data. Not proposed, and more pressing: obtaining any clinically verified labels, adjusting for or matching on age, reporting user-level rather than window-level performance, evaluating without pseudo-labelling, and addressing the ethical basis for research use of the telemetry.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Interaction with a speech-generating communication device, treated as a behavioural signal in its own right rather than as a means to an end. Three representations of that behaviour are constructed and compared. Sequential modelling captures which keys are pressed in what order, encoded as a stream of numeric identifiers whose ranges preserve category membership - normal keys, complex keys, normal app events, complex app events - so that the encoding is 'pseudo-semantic' rather than arbitrary. Temporal modelling replaces the identifiers with inter-press intervals in milliseconds, capturing the rhythm of interaction independent of content. Spectral modelling counts how often each key or key category is pressed within a session, discarding order entirely. Spatial modelling is considered and rejected on the well-reasoned grounds that user customisation makes screen positions incomparable across people. What is measured, then, is the pattern of a person's attempts to communicate: how they sequence icons into utterances, how quickly they move between selections, and which parts of their vocabulary they use. Descriptively the paper reports that autistic users accessed the app most frequently and used a considerably higher number of unique words than most other groups, and that the commonest phrases across all users concerned food, sleep, sport and greetings. This is the only study in the corpus whose behavioural sample consists of real communicative acts serving real purposes - and also the only one where the behaviour is fully confounded with how the device happened to be configured, by whom, and for what.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No fusion.
