Other weaknesses compound the picture: a 57-image test set with no confidence intervals, so the three-way model comparison rests on differences of one or two images; no cross-validation or repeated splits; no chance baseline against an implied 59.6% floor; and one architectural choice (greyscale conversion) made with reference to observed accuracy on the same data.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, scan path, eye tracking, deep learning, transfer learning. Four of five name the method or modality and none names an application - neither screening, diagnosis nor classification appears, although the body text uses 'autism diagnosis technique' and 'second opinion'. Terms carried through the text: visualised scanpath images, biomarker, gaze disparities, fixation abnormality, hybrid classifier model, InceptionV3, feature extraction.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: 2023 2nd International Conference on Vision Towards Emerging Trends in Communication and Networking Technologies (ViTECoN), IEEE - a general communications and networking engineering conference, not a clinical, biomedical or machine-learning venue. That placement explains the paper's balance: substantial textbook exposition of convolutional networks and InceptionV3 architecture aimed at a non-specialist engineering audience, minimal clinical context, and no participant characterisation at all. It also explains the absence of ethics, funding and competing-interests statements, which such venues do not typically require. The paper is short and does not overreach; the reporting gaps are those of the format as much as of the authors.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2023 by the Department of Computer Science at Vellore Institute of Technology, India, with no reported funding. The framing is the standard workload-and-subjectivity argument: there is no definitive biological test for autism, diagnosis depends on a chain of specialist referrals and subjective instruments, and 'the process of diagnosis itself consumes a lot of time and energy of both the children and parents', so computer-aided methods offering a reliable 'second opinion' are attractive. The paper positions itself within an eye-tracking-for-diagnosis literature that it surveys across several conditions - Parkinson disease, dementia, dyslexia, schizophrenia - before turning to autism, which is a useful reminder that the same modality and often the same architectures are being applied across diagnoses, and that a scanpath classifier reported at 95% for dyslexia and 78.85% for schizophrenia in the cited work is not obviously measuring anything condition-specific. For this review the study's value is not its result but its position: it is the fourth independent reuse of the 547-image dataset encountered here, it applies a different modelling family from the others, and its comparatively modest 81% - obtained under the same image-level splitting that has yielded 97-99% elsewhere - is a useful data point on how much of those higher figures is attributable to method rather than to signal.

data_charting_rubrics.title: SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Narayan V; Shukla J
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: ICASSP 2023 - 2023 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processin
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Secondary computational analysis of pooled public child-language corpora; a feature-engineering and ablation study testing whether automatically extracted semantic and pragmatic language measures add discriminative power beyond morphosyntactic and lexical features. No new data collection and no clinical involvement.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A single fixed-length feature vector per child derived from an entire conversational session, with count-based features length-normalised. No sequence modelling, no utterance-level analysis, no acoustic information, and no temporal structure beyond the local coherence measures.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: 12 months to 8 years across corpora - Eigsti 3-6 years, Nadig 3-7 years, Flusberg 12-26 months
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. The three corpora are pooled rather than used as independent training and test sets, which is the obvious available design and would have been far more informative than a 17-item random split.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 41 typically developing (Eigsti 16, Nadig 25; Flusberg contributes none)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not applicable to this study; not discussed
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Three different paradigms pooled, which is the study's principal design weakness. The Eigsti corpus records 30-minute free play sessions; the Nadig corpus records approximately 10 minutes of parent-child free play; the Flusberg corpus records natural mother-child interaction in children aged 12-26 months. The conversation partner therefore varies (referred to variously as 'therapist', 'trainer' and 'parent' within the same paper), session length varies threefold, and transcription conventions differ by corpus and era. Duration-dependent features are normalised over conversation length, which addresses one component of this heterogeneity but not the others.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: CLAN (Computerized Language ANalysis) for transcription-based morphosyntactic measures; L2SCA for syntactic complexity; BERT embeddings for discourse coherence; TF-IDF for unexpected-word detection; an AutoML tool for model comparison; SHAP for feature attribution.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: The source corpora are public through the CHILDES databank and are cited to their originators.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not reported. CLAN, L2SCA, SHAP and the AutoML tool are named and publicly available.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: None stated. As a secondary analysis of a public research corpus this is defensible, though CHILDES transcripts of children's speech carry their own access conditions and no reference to the source studies' approvals appears.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Seventy-seven features in three groups. Automated stereotypical and repetitive speech characteristics (9 features): mean length of utterance in morphemes, number of distinct word roots, count of questions initiated by the child, proportion of immediately repeated phrases, child-child discourse coherence (cosine similarity between BERT embeddings of the child's consecutive sentences), child-partner discourse coherence (the same between partner and child sentences), echolalia (communication units with immediate repetition of the partner's bigrams), proportion of unintelligible units, and unexpected words identified via TF-IDF vectors. Lexical features (45): part-of-speech tag frequencies. Syntactic complexity (23): clause-per-sentence, mean sentence length and related measures from L2SCA. Count-based features are normalised over conversation length.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: A genuine strength and the paper's stated motivation, not an afterthought. Interpretability is built in at three levels. The feature set is designed to mirror ADOS criteria, so each measure has a clinical referent - echolalia, discourse coherence, initiative in asking questions, vocabulary extent - rather than being an arbitrary statistic. The ablation quantifies what each family contributes, showing that the semantic-pragmatic set alone matches part-of-speech features and that the three families are complementary. And SHAP analysis attributes the model's predictions to individual features, with the top contributors then checked against independent literature: number of distinct word roots as the dominant feature is linked to prior work on vocabulary in autism, and the prominence of unexpected words and of both discourse-coherence measures is related to evidence that autistic children lack global coherence in conversation. The authors argue explicitly that this is the point - the features 'improve the interpretability of diagnosis as these features are coherent and understandable to non-experts as well'. What is missing is any error analysis, any per-child examination, and any check on whether the top features differ systematically between the three source corpora.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Grid search with 5-fold cross-validation to select the SVM's regularisation parameter C and RBF width gamma. Model family selection was performed by comparing six classifiers with an AutoML tool and retaining the best-performing one, so the reported headline is the maximum of that comparison.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A single 90:10 train-test split, with 5-fold cross-validation used inside the training data only for SVM hyperparameter selection. Two problems attach. First, all reported accuracies are exact multiples of 1/17 - 64.7%, 70.59%, 76.5%, 82.3%, 88.2%, 94.1% - which fixes the test set at 17 items, roughly 22% of 76 rather than the stated 10%; the discrepancy is unexplained and may reflect a different sample unit. Second, SHAP-based elimination from 77 to 63 features is described as performed on 'the initial set of features extracted' with no statement that it was nested inside the split, so feature selection appears to have seen the evaluation data.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: None as a section. Two constraints are acknowledged in passing: that there is 'inconsistency in the dataset used in the literature for similar analysis', which motivates the majority-classifier comparator, and implicitly that severity and differential diagnosis are not addressed, both named as future work.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Seventy-six children assembled from three independent corpora in the CHILDES databank: Eigsti (16 autistic, 16 typically developing, aged 3-6, 30-minute free play), Nadig (13 autistic, 25 typically developing, aged 3-7, approximately 10 minutes of parent-child free play) and Flusberg (6 autistic, no comparison children, aged 12-26 months, natural mother-child interaction), giving 35 autistic and 41 typically developing overall. The composition matters more than the totals. Flusberg contributes autistic children only, so corpus membership is partially informative about diagnosis by construction, and it contributes them from an age band - infancy and early toddlerhood - that no comparison child occupies. The three corpora also differ in session length by a factor of three, in conversation partner, and in transcription era and convention. The paper notes that the Eigsti corpus contains a developmental delay group alongside autism and typical development, but that group is not used. No child-level information beyond corpus, group and corpus-level age range is reported anywhere.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'Children with autism (CwA)' is used throughout as the working abbreviation, alongside 'typically developing (TD)' and 'neurotypical', which is a more current pairing than the 'normal' contrast used elsewhere in this corpus. The clinical framing is nonetheless firmly deficit-based and in one respect dated: autism is characterised by 'repetitive and stereotypic behaviours and impaired social and communicative skills collectively called the triads of impairments', a formulation superseded by DSM-5's two-domain structure a decade before this paper. Language differences are described as 'language and communication impairments', 'language atypicalities' and 'aberrant receptive and expressive language development', and the targeted behaviours are 'stereotypic language behaviours'. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. Against this, the paper's motivating concern is a reasonable one about assessment rather than about people - that quantifying behavioural traits 'is cumbersome, and the efficacy of such methods primarily depends on the evaluators' expertise' - and its stated goal is interpretable measurement that a non-expert could follow, which is a service orientation rather than a replacement one.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Almost nothing at the individual level. Table 1 reports, per corpus, the number of autistic and typically developing participants and an age range: Eigsti 16/16 aged 3-6, Nadig 13/25 aged 3-7, Flusberg 6/0 aged 12-26 months. No sex, IQ, language level, socioeconomic status, race or ethnicity, comorbidity or severity is given for any child, and no group means or matching statistics of any kind are reported. Three consequences follow, all unaddressed. Because the pooled age range spans 12 months to 8 years while the comparison group is confined to 3-7 years, the two groups differ in age distribution by construction - and every feature in the study is a language measure, which in children is dominated by developmental stage. Mean length of utterance and number of distinct word roots, the latter identified by SHAP as the single largest contributor to the model's predictions, are canonical expressive-language milestones that change dramatically between 12 months and 8 years, so an age difference between groups is not a nuisance covariate here but a direct alternative explanation for the headline result. And without IQ or language-level data there is no way to separate an autism-specific pragmatic signature from a general language-delay one, which is precisely what the unused developmental delay group in the Eigsti corpus could have tested.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Absent as a described procedure. The paper's entire statement on this point is that it 'considered the binary classification problem of classifying a child as having ASD or not, as all three datasets had binary labelling of the clinical status' - so the labels are inherited from three separately assembled research corpora with no account of how autism was diagnosed in any of them, by whom, against which criteria or in which era. Given that the Flusberg corpus records children aged 12-26 months, its labels must derive from a very different ascertainment process from corpora recruiting 3-7 year olds, and pooling them without comment means the target variable is heterogeneous in an unexamined way. ADOS is invoked repeatedly, but as the source of the behavioural constructs the features are designed to mirror - echolalia, back-and-forth interchange, building on statements - rather than as an instrument administered to these children. That is a legitimate and rather elegant use of a diagnostic instrument as a specification for feature engineering, and it should not be confused with having a reference standard.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: No external cognitive, language or severity measure exists, and the absence is more consequential here than in most studies because language is simultaneously the modality, the feature set and the plausible confound. The study computes mean length of utterance in morphemes and number of distinct word roots - both standard expressive-language indices used clinically to characterise developmental level - and uses them as classifier inputs, with the second identified by SHAP as the dominant predictor. In a sample where the autistic group extends down to 12 months and the comparison group does not go below 3 years, that finding is compatible with the model having learned a developmental-language gradient rather than an autism-specific one. Nothing in the analysis distinguishes the two, because no independent measure of language level exists to adjust for. Severity is likewise absent and is named as future work. The gap also blocks the more interesting question the feature set was built to answer: whether pragmatic atypicality - echolalia, poor discourse coherence, failure to initiate questions - is present over and above general language level, which is the clinically meaningful version of the claim.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated objectives are threefold: to automatically extract semantic and pragmatic language features including echolalia, semantic coherence and repetitive language usage; to compare them systematically and identify the most significant; and to build an interpretable assessment system on that basis. The gap the paper identifies in the literature is specific and fair - prior work on semantic-pragmatic features for autism has examined individual measures such as echolalia or pronoun usage in isolation, and 'the cumulative effect of the features and how they complement the lexical, syntactic and other text-based features in the diagnosis of autism has not been analysed'. Findings: the best classifier, an RBF SVM on all 63 retained features, reached 94.1% accuracy with 94% macro F1 against a majority-classifier baseline of 56.4% accuracy and 32% macro F1. The feature-set ablation is the substantive result and is reported in full: morphosyntactic baseline 70.59%, syntactic complexity alone 70%, part-of-speech frequencies alone 82%, semantic-pragmatic features alone 82.3%, part-of-speech plus semantic-pragmatic 88.2%, and all three families 94.1%. So the semantic-pragmatic set matches the lexical set on its own and the three families are complementary rather than redundant, which is exactly the claim the study set out to test. SHAP attribution places the number of distinct word roots first, with unexpected words and both child-child and child-partner discourse coherence in the top ten, and the authors relate each to prior findings on vocabulary extent and on global coherence in autistic conversation.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting: this is a computational reanalysis conducted at IIIT Delhi on transcripts collected years earlier in North American research laboratories. The three source settings are described only briefly and differ substantially - 30-minute free play sessions in one corpus, roughly 10 minutes of parent-child play in another, and natural mother-child interaction with 12-26 month olds in the third. That heterogeneity is the study's central unexamined problem, because it is not random with respect to the label: one corpus supplies autistic children exclusively. Any systematic difference between the corpora - transcription conventions, how disfluency and unintelligibility were marked, who the partner was, how long the session ran, what era the recording belongs to - is therefore partially aligned with diagnosis. Length-dependent features are normalised over conversation length, which handles the most obvious component, but transcription and partner effects are not addressable by normalisation and are not discussed.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Three different paradigms pooled as though equivalent. Eigsti recorded 30-minute free play sessions; Nadig recorded approximately 10 minutes of parent-child free play; Flusberg recorded natural mother-child interaction in infants and toddlers. The conversation partner is not held constant and the paper's own terminology drifts - the echolalia feature is defined by repetition of bigrams 'originally spoken by the therapist', the discourse-coherence feature is described as similarity 'between BERT embeddings of consecutive sentences of therapist and child', SHAP results refer to 'trainer-child (t-c) discourse', and the corpus descriptions say the partner was a parent or the mother. Whoever the partner was, they are a live participant whose own language shapes every child-partner feature, and pragmatic behaviour in a child differs systematically with whether the interlocutor is a parent or a clinician. Since child-partner discourse coherence ranks among the top contributing features, this is not a peripheral concern. The countervailing strength is the paradigm's ecological character: these are unstructured natural conversations rather than elicited tasks, so the pragmatic behaviours the features target - taking initiative, building on statements, sustaining a topic - had a genuine opportunity to occur.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional by inheritance, with one session per child and no temporal analysis. The pooling of corpora spanning 12 months to 8 years creates something that looks like developmental range but is not a developmental design, since age is confounded with corpus and with label. No ethics statement appears, which is defensible for a secondary analysis of a public research corpus but is still an omission - the CHILDES databank operates under its own conditions of use and no reference to the source studies' approvals is made. Funding from an Indian government start-up research grant with partial industry-linked centre support is acknowledged; no competing-interests statement is provided.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: An entirely software-based pipeline, well specified for its scale. CLAN, the standard CHILDES analysis toolkit, supplied the morphosyntactic baseline features. L2SCA, an established second-language syntactic complexity analyser, supplied the 23 syntactic complexity measures. BERT embeddings with cosine similarity supplied the two discourse-coherence measures. TF-IDF vectors supplied the unexpected-word count. An AutoML tool was used to compare classifier families, and SHAP for attribution and for feature elimination. Using off-the-shelf, community-standard tools throughout is appropriate and makes the pipeline reconstructible in outline, though the specific BERT variant is not named and no code is released. Notably absent, given publication at ICASSP and repeated reference to 'speech signals' and 'speech features', is any acoustic analysis: the study operates entirely on transcripts, and the prosodic properties the introduction cites from prior work - increased pitch range and variability in autistic children - are not measured.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Better than most conference papers of this length. Reproducible: the three source corpora are public, named and cited with their participant counts and age ranges; every one of the 77 features is named with a definition in a two-column table, including the exact construction of the BERT-cosine coherence measures and the TF-IDF basis of unexpected words; the normalisation of count features over conversation length is stated; the tools are named; the reduction from 77 to 63 features and its SHAP basis is described; the classifier family, kernel and the grid-search-with-5-fold-CV procedure for C and gamma are given; and both the six-classifier comparison and the seven-configuration feature ablation are reported with four metrics each. Not available: code, the split or seed, the identity of the 63 retained features, the per-corpus composition of the training and test sets, the BERT variant, and the AutoML configuration. The stated 90:10 split is also inconsistent with the reported accuracies, all of which are exact multiples of 1/17.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: There is no limitations section, and the omissions matter more than in most studies of this type because several are specific to the pooling strategy. The three corpora differ in age band, session length, conversation partner and transcription convention, and - decisively - the Flusberg corpus contributes 6 autistic children and no comparison children, so corpus membership is partially predictive of diagnosis and corpus-specific artefacts are available to the classifier as diagnostic cues. The autistic group therefore extends to 12 months while the comparison group starts at 3 years, in a study whose features are language measures and whose top SHAP contributor is the number of distinct word roots - a canonical developmental index. Feature elimination by SHAP from 77 to 63 features is described before the train-test split with no statement of nesting, so the retained set saw the evaluation data. Six classifiers were compared and the best reported. All accuracies are multiples of 1/17, implying a 17-item test set rather than the 7 or 8 that a 90:10 split of 76 children would give, and no confidence interval accompanies a comparison in which one child moves accuracy by 5.9 points - so the 94.1% versus 88.2% difference between the best model and the next is one child. No demographic or cognitive data exist for any participant. And the Eigsti corpus's developmental delay group, which would have supported the differential comparison the conclusion identifies as needed, was present in the source material and not used. What the paper does do well on the evaluation side is report a majority-classifier baseline as a named comparator in both results tables, which is better practice than most of this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Two directions, both apt: identify autism severity from speech, and explore differential diagnosis using speech-based analysis. The second is the more important and is unusually actionable, because the Eigsti corpus the study already uses contains a developmental delay group alongside autism and typical development. Distinguishing autistic children from children with developmental delay on pragmatic features - rather than from typically developing children on measures dominated by general language level - is the clinically meaningful version of this study's claim, and the material for it was in hand. Not proposed, and needed: leave-one-corpus-out validation, which the three-corpus structure makes available and which would test whether the model generalises across settings rather than learning corpus identity; adjustment for age and language level; and nesting of feature selection.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Conversational language, targeted at the pragmatic and semantic level rather than the acoustic or syntactic one, and specified against a clinical instrument rather than by exploration. The design principle is stated plainly: features were extracted 'following the standard diagnostic tool for ASD - Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule', and the resulting measures map onto behaviours ADOS actually rates - echolalia, the ability to sustain back-and-forth interchange, asking questions, building upon statements, use of pronouns. Operationally this yields nine semantic-pragmatic measures: mean length of utterance in morphemes, number of distinct word roots, questions initiated by the child, immediate phrase repetition, coherence between the child's own consecutive utterances, coherence between the partner's and the child's utterances, echolalia as immediate repetition of the partner's bigrams, proportion of unintelligible units, and unexpected word use. Two design decisions are worth noting. Echolalia and child-partner coherence are inherently dyadic, defined by the relationship between what the partner said and what the child said next - so unlike almost every other behavioural measure in this corpus, these features encode interaction rather than individual output. And unintelligibility is retained as a feature rather than discarded as noise, which is behaviourally defensible since articulation and intelligibility are clinically relevant, though it also means transcription-quality differences across corpora enter the model.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-modal fusion, and the absence is conspicuous for a paper at a speech-signal-processing venue: the introduction cites acoustic findings on pitch range and variability in autistic children, the abstract refers to 'diagnostic predictions made using speech signals', and the title names speech features - yet the study operates entirely on transcripts and computes nothing acoustic. What it does instead is a careful within-modality fusion across three linguistic levels, and reports the ablation in full: syntactic complexity alone 70%, part-of-speech frequencies alone 82%, semantic-pragmatic features alone 82.3%, the last two combined 88.2%, and all three 94.1%. That progression is the study's real contribution and is more informative than a single accuracy figure, because it establishes that the semantic-pragmatic family carries as much signal alone as the lexical family and that the three are complementary rather than overlapping - the specific question the authors identified as unanswered in the prior literature. The caution is that the ablation shares its data, its unnested feature selection and its 17-item test set with the headline result, so the ordering is more reliable than the individual numbers.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Six classifier families compared by an AutoML tool - majority baseline, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting and support vector machine - with an RBF-kernel SVM retained on the basis of best accuracy and its C and gamma tuned by grid search with 5-fold cross-validation. The choice of simple, interpretable models is appropriate to 76 samples and 63 features and is consistent with the paper's stated priority of interpretability over raw performance. Two aspects of the comparison need stating. Selecting the best of six families on the same small evaluation set means the reported 94.1% is the maximum of a search, and the spread across families is wide (64.7% to 94.1%), so the choice is doing real work. And SHAP serves a dual role - as the feature-elimination criterion reducing 77 features to 63, and as the post-hoc attribution method interpreting the final model - which is efficient but means the interpretation is being read off a feature set that SHAP itself selected on the full data.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: One fixed-length vector per child summarising an entire conversational session, comprising 45 part-of-speech tag frequencies, 23 syntactic complexity measures and 9 semantic-pragmatic measures, reduced from 77 to 63 by SHAP-guided elimination that removed non-informative tags such as SYM and MD and an um-propagation artefact. Count-based features - echolalia, unintelligible units, unexpected words - are normalised over conversation length, which is a necessary and correctly applied step given that source sessions range from about 10 to 30 minutes. Two of the features are computed with contextual embeddings rather than surface statistics: child-child and child-partner discourse coherence are cosine similarities between BERT representations of consecutive sentences, which is a reasonable operationalisation of topic maintenance and is more sensitive than lexical overlap would be. The representation discards temporal structure beyond that local coherence, so trajectory across a session - whether a child warms up, disengages, or shifts topic progressively - is not represented.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, macro precision, macro recall and macro F1, reported for every one of six classifiers and every one of seven feature-set configurations, with a majority classifier as the first row of both tables. Macro averaging suits the near-balanced 35:41 split, and including the majority baseline as a named comparator - with improvements quantified against it - is better practice than most studies charted here, particularly given the authors' explicit rationale that inconsistency in the datasets used across the literature makes cross-study comparison unreliable. The gaps are nonetheless serious at this sample size. No confidence interval is reported anywhere, and since every accuracy is an exact multiple of 1/17 the test set contains 17 items, so one child is 5.9 percentage points and the difference between the headline 94.1% and the next-best 88.2% is a single child. No confusion matrix, no AUC, and no sensitivity or specificity named as such. The majority-classifier figure of 56.4% also does not correspond to the 53.9% implied by the overall class ratio, so it appears to be computed on a particular split, which is not stated.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: The study's strongest dimension, and interpretability is treated as the objective rather than as a diagnostic afterthought. Three layers support it. The feature set is specified against ADOS, so every measure has a clinical referent and the model's inputs are quantities a clinician would recognise - echolalia, discourse coherence, initiative in asking questions, vocabulary extent - rather than embeddings or spectral coefficients. The feature-family ablation quantifies what each level of linguistic description contributes, which is itself an interpretive result: semantic-pragmatic features alone reach 82.3%, matching part-of-speech features, and the families combine additively to 94.1%. And SHAP attribution identifies which individual features drive predictions, with the findings then checked against independent literature rather than asserted - the number of distinct word roots emerges as the largest contributor and is linked to prior work on vocabulary extent in autistic children, while the prominence of unexpected words and of both discourse-coherence measures is connected to evidence that autistic children show reduced global coherence in conversation. The authors' claim that these features are 'coherent and understandable to non-experts as well' is defensible. Two limits: no error analysis or per-child examination is performed, and no check is made on whether the top features differ systematically across the three source corpora - which, given that one corpus supplies only autistic children, is the analysis that would distinguish a linguistic finding from a corpus artefact.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The weakest dimension, and the problems compound. The reported scheme is a single 90:10 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation used inside the training data only for SVM hyperparameter selection - which is the correct placement for hyperparameter tuning and is stated clearly. But three issues sit above it. First, the arithmetic does not match the description: every reported accuracy is an exact multiple of 1/17 (64.7, 70.59, 76.5, 82.3, 88.2, 94.1 per cent), which fixes the test set at 17 items, roughly 22% of 76 rather than the stated 10%, and the discrepancy is unexplained. Whatever the intended design, a 17-item test set means one child is worth 5.9 percentage points, so the headline 94.1% is 16 of 17 correct and its margin over the next-best configuration is one child - a difference no confidence interval is offered for and none would support. Second, SHAP-based elimination from 77 to 63 features is described as performed on the initially extracted set with no indication of nesting inside the split, so the retained feature set was chosen with sight of the evaluation data; on 76 samples and 77 candidate features this is exactly the regime in which unnested selection produces substantial optimism. Third, six classifier families were compared and the best retained, with a 30-point spread between the worst and best, so the reported figure is the maximum of a search. Beneath all of this lies the pooling problem, which no amount of correct splitting would fix: because the Flusberg corpus contributes autistic children only and from a much younger age band, corpus identity partially predicts diagnosis, and a random split across pooled corpora cannot separate a linguistic signature from a corpus signature. The corrective design is available in the data and would be far more informative - leave-one-corpus-out validation, which would show directly whether features learned on Eigsti and Flusberg transfer to Nadig and vice versa, together with nesting the SHAP elimination and reporting the ablation ordering rather than point accuracies.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Index terms: speech analysis, autism spectrum disorder, human-computer interaction. All three are broad, and the third is a venue-fit choice rather than a description of the work. The acronym SPASHT is glossed in the abstract as meaning 'unambiguous', a deliberate reference to the paper's interpretability claim. Terms carried through the body: semantic and pragmatic features, echolalia, discourse coherence, repetitive language, stereotypic language behaviours, morphosyntactic features, syntactic complexity, CHILDES, CLAN, L2SCA, SHAP, majority classifier, interpretability.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: ICASSP 2023, the IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing - the principal venue for speech signal processing, and a slightly incongruous home for a study that performs no acoustic analysis at all. The paper operates entirely on transcripts, computing lexical, syntactic and semantic-pragmatic measures, while the abstract refers to 'diagnostic predictions made using speech signals' and the introduction reviews acoustic findings on pitch range and variability that the study does not build on. The four-page format accounts for the absence of a limitations section, an ethics statement and a competing-interests declaration, though not for the unexplained mismatch between the stated 90:10 split and the 17-item test set implied by the reported accuracies.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2023 by the Human-Machine Interaction Lab at IIIT Delhi, funded by an Indian government Science and Engineering Research Board start-up grant with partial support from a TCS Foundation centre and the Infosys Centre for Artificial Intelligence. The framing is the standard objectivity argument - autism diagnosis depends on behavioural assessment because 'the unavailability of genetic tests or biological markers' leaves no alternative, and 'quantifying these behavioural traits is cumbersome, and the efficacy of such methods primarily depends on the evaluators' expertise'. What distinguishes the paper's positioning is the specificity of the gap it claims: prior computational work on semantic-pragmatic language in autism has examined individual features such as echolalia or pronoun use in isolation and 'focused only on smaller feature sets', so 'the cumulative effect of the features and how they complement the lexical, syntactic and other text-based features in the diagnosis of autism has not been analysed'. That is a well-identified and genuinely open question, and the feature-family ablation is a direct answer to it. The paper's other distinctive commitment is to interpretability as a design constraint rather than a reporting nicety - features are specified against ADOS so that predictions can be explained in clinically recognisable terms - which puts it in the same small group as the joint-attention and facial-complexity studies charted here. For this review its main value is as the corpus's clearest demonstration that pragmatic language measures carry as much discriminative signal as lexical ones and combine with them additively; its main caution is that this was established on three pooled corpora, one of which contains autistic children exclusively.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Atyabi A; Shic F; Jiang J; Foster CE; Barney E; Kim M; Li B; Ventola P; Chen CH
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional classification study with an explicit stratification agenda: rather than only separating autism from typical development, the paper systematically tests whether scan-path images can also separate age bands and sexes within the autistic group, on the argument that these are the principal sources of heterogeneity obstructing biomarker discovery
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A 100 x 100 greyscale (or colour-coded) image per participant per video clip, so each participant contributes as many images as clips they viewed - roughly sixteen on average across 86 participants and 1,414 viewings. Augmented copies generated by rotation add further images.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: 0 to 18+ years, grouped into five bands. Autistic: 3 aged 0-1, 11 aged 2-4, 23 aged 5-9, 13 aged 10-17, 4 aged 18+. Typically developing: 5 aged 0-1, 6 aged 2-4, 16 aged 5-9, 5 aged 10-17, none 18+.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 99 enrolled; 86 with valid eye-gaze data
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None on an independent cohort. One partial external check is performed and is worth noting: the DNN is additionally run on the separate public scan-path dataset of 547 images from 59 children (219 autistic, 328 non-autistic) used by several other studies in this corpus, reaching 76.97% test accuracy with AUC 0.79 - broadly consistent with this paper's own 74.4% and with the participant-level figures reported by that dataset's originators.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not stated in the retrieved text
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Four video-based eye-tracking tasks selected on three stated criteria - strong construct performance, demonstrated between-group discrimination, and relation to autism symptoms in prior research on school-aged children - and noted to share similarities with the Autism Biomarkers Consortium for Clinical Trials battery. Individual video clips within each task were viewed very unevenly: Table 6 shows several clips viewed 90-92 times and many viewed once, with a total of 1,414 viewings across 43 named clips.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Not described in the retrieved text - no eye tracker make, model, sampling rate, display or viewing distance is given. Scan-paths were generated on a black background at 1680 x 1050 then resized to 100 x 100 greyscale.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not stated in the retrieved text
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: None hand-crafted; gaze coordinates are rendered directly as images. Three representations are compared. Spatial scan-paths draw the gaze trajectory on a black background with no temporal encoding. Spatio-temporal scan-paths restrict the drawing to non-overlapping 3-second windows (0-3, 3-6, 6-9, 9-12, 12-15 s) or to 1-second sub-windows, so time is encoded by which image a segment appears in. Velocity-infused spatio-temporal scan-paths additionally colour each segment according to the average velocity between consecutive gaze points, computed as Euclidean distance divided by time interval, with velocity mapped to colour through a stated threshold scheme.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Structural rather than model-based. No saliency, class activation or attention analysis is applied to any network, so nothing is reported about what visual property of a scan-path image drives a prediction. What the paper does instead is ablate systematically at the level of inputs and representations: removing individual video clips to rank their contribution, restricting scan-paths to successive temporal windows to locate when in a trial the signal lies, and adding velocity colour coding to test whether dynamics carry information beyond position. These ablations are genuinely informative - the finding that the first three seconds discriminate best and that discrimination decays over the trial is a substantive result about social attention - but they characterise the input, not the model.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Dropout (0.2 versus 0.5) and epoch count (50 versus 100) are swept and both settings reported, with the best bolded in each table. Architecture is shown only as a figure. No separate development set is described, so these comparisons were made on the reported test data.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Fixed random splits of images at 7:3 or 75:25, repeated three times in the temporal experiments with results averaged. The unit of splitting is the scan-path image, not the participant, and no participant-level or subject-disjoint evaluation is reported anywhere in the paper. With 86 participants contributing roughly sixteen images each, every test image has around eleven sibling images from the same child in training. Augmentation compounds this: augmented image counts are quoted as totals for the whole dataset rather than for the training partition alone, so rotated copies of a given scan-path may fall on both sides of the split.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: No limitations section. Two constraints are acknowledged in passing during the analyses: that the small number of female autistic participants restricts the sex-stratification analysis to the 5-9 year band and 'negatively impacts DNN's training', prompting the use of augmentation; and that class imbalance between autistic and typically developing images 'hinders the network training' and depresses AUC. Both are framed as problems to be solved by augmentation rather than as limits on inference.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Ninety-nine children were enrolled and 86 had valid eye-gaze data - 54 autistic and 32 typically developing according to Table 1 and the participant text, though the abstract states 55 autistic, an unresolved inconsistency. The 13 excluded participants are not characterised. Participants span the full paediatric age range and are grouped into five bands, with the autistic group distributed 3/11/23/13/4 across 0-1, 2-4, 5-9, 10-17 and 18+ years and the comparison group 5/6/16/5/0. Sex composition differs sharply: 44 male and 10 female among autistic participants (81.5% male) against 15 male and 17 female among comparison participants (46.9% male). The paper states plainly that 'each subject has a different number of recorded ET videos and the data is unbalanced with respect to diagnosis, age, and gender'. The modelled unit is not the child but the scan-path image, one per participant per video clip: 1,012 autistic and 380 typically developing images before augmentation, from 1,414 total clip viewings across 86 children - roughly sixteen images per child, unevenly distributed since Table 6 shows individual clips viewed anywhere from once to 92 times.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)' and 'Typically Developing (TD)' throughout, person-first and consistent, in the register of a computational health-informatics paper. Clinical description is deficit-framed but restrained: autism is 'a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with social communication deficits and repetitive behaviors', with 'deficit in social attention' and 'atypicality in social attention' as the operative constructs. One passage uses 'ASD patients' when summarising prior work. The framing of purpose is unusual for this corpus in being oriented towards heterogeneity rather than detection: the stated motivation is that 'the observed heterogeneity in autism' compounds the subjectivity of clinical assessment, and that 'ASD heterogeneity and proven difficulty to identify generalizable markers of ASD have led to the presumption of the presence of multiple etiologies rather than a single disorder'. That is a defensible scientific position and it drives the study's most interesting experiments. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. One factual error should be noted: the paper states that 'ASD prevalence is found to have a gender bias with one in four individuals with ASD diagnosis being male', which inverts the well-established ratio.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Age band and sex are reported per group in two tables and nothing else is. No IQ, language level, severity, comorbidity, medication, socioeconomic status, race or ethnicity appears anywhere, and no exact ages, means or statistical comparisons are given. The two variables that are reported are the two that matter most here, and both are badly imbalanced. Sex: 81.5% male in the autistic group against 46.9% in the comparison group, a difference of nearly 35 percentage points. Age: 31.5% of autistic participants are aged 10 or over against 15.6% of comparison participants, and all four participants aged 18 or over are autistic while all remaining comparison participants are under 18. Ordinarily these would be recorded as uncontrolled confounds of unknown magnitude. What makes this study distinctive is that it measures their magnitude itself: its own experiments show that scan-path images predict sex within the autistic group at 78.0% accuracy with AUC 0.850, and age band within the autistic group at 80.5% with AUC 0.868. Both figures exceed the 74.4% achieved for diagnosis. So the study demonstrates that its input representation carries demographic information at least as strongly as diagnostic information, in a sample where the demographics differ substantially between diagnostic groups - and the two results are presented in consecutive sections without the connection being drawn.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not described. The retrieved text contains no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician, procedure, date or setting for either group; participants are simply designated ASD or TD. This is a notable omission for a study from a group closely associated with the Autism Biomarkers Consortium for Clinical Trials, whose tasks the paper says its battery resembles, and it sits awkwardly with an introduction that criticises clinical assessment for being subjective and providing 'minimal information about the underlying mechanism of the disorder'. Whatever the actual ascertainment - and given the authorship it was very likely rigorous - the paper as published does not state it, so the target being predicted is undefined from the report alone.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, language, adaptive or severity measure is reported for any participant. The absence is more consequential here than in most studies because the paper's opening claim is explicitly about clinical gradation: 'in children with ASD, these patterns change with intellectual and social impairments, suggesting that patterns of social attention provide indices of clinically meaningful variation in ASD'. That is a claim about the relationship between looking patterns and intellectual and symptom severity, and the study collects no data with which to examine it. What it substitutes is demographic stratification - age and sex - which are sources of variation in autism but are not the clinically meaningful ones the abstract invokes. The result is a study framed around parsing heterogeneity that measures none of the clinical variables by which heterogeneity is defined, and which therefore cannot distinguish a scan-path difference that indexes symptom severity from one that indexes being a twelve-year-old rather than a three-year-old.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated objective is to test whether scan-path images - spatial representations of gaze - can stratify autism from typical development, and then whether they also capture the age and sex variation that makes autism biomarkers hard to generalise. The two contributions claimed are incorporating temporal information into scan-path images and infusing gaze velocity into them. Findings, in the paper's own summary order: spatial scan-paths separate autism from typical development at 74.4% test accuracy (AUC 0.68-0.72); scan-paths separate 2-4 year old from 10-17 year old autistic children at 80.5% (AUC 0.868); scan-paths separate male from female autistic children at 78.0% (AUC 0.850); and within the 5-9 year autistic subgroup they separate male from female at 98.8%. Temporal windowing shows the first three seconds of viewing discriminate best (76.3%) with a monotone decline to 70.2% by 12-15 seconds. Velocity-based colour coding raises the 3-6 second window from 71.74% to 80.25% (AUC 0.839), the paper's headline representational result. Per-clip ablation ranks the contribution of individual videos, with Theory of Mind and Dyadic Bid clips mattering most. The authors read the age and sex results as evidence that scan-paths capture heterogeneity; they can equally be read as evidence that the diagnostic result is confounded, since the two groups differ substantially on both variables.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Described only as a naturalistic study with a battery of eye-tracking video stimuli; no site, room, equipment or procedure is given in the retrieved text. The authorship spans seven United States institutions including the Yale Child Study Center and Seattle Children's Research Institute, and the paper notes that its paradigm 'share similarities with recent studies of autism biomarker Consortium for Clinical Trials (ABC-CT)', which locates the work within a serious clinical-research programme even though the report itself supplies no setting detail. The recruitment geometry cannot be assessed because recruitment is not described.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: The best-designed stimulus battery in this corpus, and described with a care that the rest of the methods does not match. Four tasks were chosen on three explicit criteria - strong construct performance, demonstrated between-group discrimination, and relation to autism symptoms in prior work with school-aged children. Activity Monitoring shows two actresses using child-directed speech and directing gaze to each other or to the activity between them, with clusters of colourful but irrelevant toys as deliberate distractors. Dyadic Bid is the most carefully constructed: an actor periodically addresses the camera while the two non-speaking actors either look silently at the viewer - included both as a control, to ensure the participant is not merely following a face that looks at them, and as a competing-face distractor - or look down with subtle hand movements, included as a foil controlling for the salience of the speaker's mouth movements. Social Referencing films escalating stressful episodes with distinct escalation, critical-event and resolution phases, such as a balloon inflated until it bursts. Theory of Mind implements a naturalistic false-belief scenario in which an antagonist repeatedly relocates objects unbeknown to a protagonist. Building explicit controls and foils into the stimuli rather than relying on post-hoc statistical adjustment is the kind of design reasoning that most studies here omit entirely. Against this, exposure to individual clips was extremely uneven - Table 6 shows clips viewed 92, 90, 62, 61 or 60 times alongside eighteen clips viewed exactly once - so the effective stimulus set is much smaller than the 43 clips listed, and participants did not all see the same material.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional with no follow-up and no test-retest assessment. The study is nonetheless the most thorough in this corpus on within-trial temporal structure: gaze is analysed in successive non-overlapping 3-second windows across the first 15 seconds, and separately in 1-second sub-windows, revealing that discrimination is highest in the first three seconds (76.3%) and declines steadily thereafter (71.7%, 69.3%, 71.0%, 70.2%). That is a substantive finding about when social attention differentiates, and it has a practical implication the paper does not draw out - that a shorter protocol may lose little. No ethics approval, consent statement, or competing-interests declaration appears in the retrieved text, which for a study of children including infants is a significant reporting omission whatever the underlying governance. Funding from an NIH K01 award and a Simons Foundation grant is stated.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Not reported. The paper describes no eye tracker, sampling rate, display, viewing distance, calibration procedure or recording software - a striking gap in a study whose entire input is eye-tracking data and which computes gaze velocity, a quantity whose meaning depends directly on sampling rate. What is specified is the downstream rendering: scan-paths are drawn on a black background at 1680 x 1050, resized to 100 x 100 and converted to greyscale, with velocity encoded as colour in the final experiments through a stated threshold mapping. Modelling used DNN and CNN architectures shown only as a figure.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Sharply uneven. The stimulus design, the per-clip view counts, the rendering resolution and downsampling, the temporal windowing scheme, the velocity formula and colour mapping, the dropout and epoch settings, the split ratios and the image counts for every one of fourteen experimental tables are all specified precisely - so the analysis pipeline is largely reconstructible. Almost everything about the data is not: no eye tracker or acquisition parameters, no diagnostic procedure, no demographics beyond age band and sex, no ethics or consent statement, no mapping from images to participants, no augmentation parameters, no seeds or split specifications, and no code or data. The mapping from images to participants is the single most consequential omission, because without it a reader cannot verify whether any evaluation in the paper is subject-disjoint - and nothing in the text suggests any of them is.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: There is no limitations section, and the two constraints acknowledged in passing - too few female autistic participants for sex analysis outside the 5-9 band, and class imbalance depressing AUC - are both treated as problems that augmentation solves rather than as bounds on inference. The unaddressed issues are severe and partly self-documented. The splitting unit is the scan-path image, and with roughly sixteen images per child each test image has about eleven siblings from the same participant in training; no subject-disjoint result appears anywhere in the paper. Augmentation compounds this: image counts after augmentation are quoted for the whole dataset rather than for the training partition, and the sex-by-age experiment shows test accuracy rising monotonically with augmentation level - 85.07% at 961/957 images, 85.81% at 1,276/1,259, and 98.84% at 3,121/2,905 - which is the characteristic signature of rotated duplicates falling on both sides of the split, since a genuine signal does not strengthen with synthetic replication. The 98.8% is nonetheless presented as evidence of 'substantial difference' between male and female autistic children. Training accuracy is 100% or within a fraction of it in essentially every table while test accuracy ranges from 67% to 81%, a twenty-to-thirty point gap noted once as 'a gap in performance' and never analysed. And the study's own results contain the material for its strongest self-critique: it shows that scan-path images encode age at 80.5% and sex at 78.0% within the autistic group, both higher than the 74.4% achieved for diagnosis, in a sample where the autistic group is 81.5% male against 46.9% and twice as likely to be aged 10 or over. Those two facts are reported four pages apart and never brought together. Beyond this: no reference standard, no IQ or severity measure despite an abstract that invokes intellectual impairment, no ethics or consent statement, no eye-tracker description, no sensitivity or specificity, no confidence intervals, and an unresolved discrepancy between 55 and 54 autistic participants.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: No future-work section. The conclusion restates the finding that velocity-infused spatio-temporal scan-paths capture patterns associated with age, sex and their interaction, framed as progress on the heterogeneity problem. The steps the study's own results most clearly call for are absent from the paper: subject-disjoint evaluation, augmentation applied only within training folds, and - most importantly - a diagnosis classifier stratified or matched on age and sex, since the paper has itself established that both are strongly encoded in the representation and both differ substantially between its diagnostic groups.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Social attention, decomposed into four constructs with distinct developmental and clinical significance rather than treated as a single quantity. Activity monitoring - attending to what others are doing together - is targeted with deliberate irrelevant distractors present. Dyadic bid sensitivity - responsiveness to another person's overture for engagement - is targeted with two built-in controls that distinguish genuine responsiveness from mere gaze-following and from mouth-movement salience. Social referencing - seeking clarifying information from others' faces in uncertain situations - is targeted with escalating stressful episodes containing a discrete critical event. Theory of mind - spontaneous processing of another's beliefs - is targeted with a naturalistic false-belief scenario. The measured behaviour is where and when the child looks within these scenes, rendered as a trajectory image. Two further behavioural findings emerge from the analysis rather than the design. Discrimination is strongest in the first three seconds of a clip and declines steadily thereafter, suggesting that the initial orienting response carries more diagnostic information than sustained viewing. And gaze velocity, added as colour, improves discrimination substantially over position alone in the same time window (71.74% to 80.25%), indicating that how fast the eyes move between points carries information the trajectory shape does not.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-sensor fusion, but the paper is one of the more informative in this corpus about fusing information types within a single modality, and it reports the ablation cleanly. Three representations are compared on the same data. Spatial scan-paths encode position only and give 74.4% for diagnosis. Spatio-temporal scan-paths encode position within bounded time windows, which allows the temporal locus of discrimination to be identified (76.3% in the first three seconds, declining to 70.2% by 12-15 seconds) but does not by itself improve peak performance. Velocity-infused spatio-temporal scan-paths encode position, time window and speed simultaneously by using velocity as the colour channel, and raise the 3-6 second window from 71.74% to 80.25% with AUC improving from 0.790 to 0.839 - a gain of 8.5 accuracy points from adding a derivative of the same underlying signal. That is a well-controlled demonstration that a rendered-image representation can be enriched with dynamics rather than discarding them, and it addresses head-on the central weakness of scan-path-image approaches, which is that drawing a trajectory throws away time. The caveat is that all three representations were evaluated under the same image-level splitting and the same whole-dataset augmentation, so the ordering is more trustworthy than the absolute values.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A dense neural network and a convolutional neural network, compared throughout at two dropout rates (0.2, 0.5) and two epoch counts (50, 100), with both reported and the better bolded in each table. No classical baseline, no majority classifier, and no architecture search beyond dropout and epochs; the networks are shown only as a schematic figure. The modelling is deliberately simple and the paper's intellectual investment sits in the input representation rather than the classifier, which is a reasonable division for a study whose claimed contributions are representational. The consistent pattern across every table is diagnostic of the setup rather than of the models: training accuracy reaches 100% or 99.9% almost everywhere while test accuracy sits between 67% and 81%, so both architectures memorise the training images completely at every setting tried, and dropout at either level does not prevent it.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A 100 x 100 image per participant per video clip, produced by drawing the gaze trajectory on a 1680 x 1050 black background and downsampling. The downsampling is aggressive - each output pixel spans roughly 17 x 11 input pixels - so fine spatial structure such as whether gaze fell on an eye or a cheek is not preserved, and what survives is the coarse geometry of the trajectory: its extent, its density, how many times it crosses itself. Three enrichments are then tested. Temporal restriction to 3-second or 1-second windows, which encodes time by segmentation rather than within the image. Velocity colour coding, which maps average speed between consecutive points - Euclidean distance over time interval - onto a colour scale with stated thresholds. And rotation-based augmentation, which generates additional images and is applied at three levels in one experiment. Two properties of this representation matter for interpretation. Because the image is a drawing, incidental graphical characteristics such as total ink and plotted extent are available to the network alongside behavioural ones, and no analysis distinguishes them. And because velocity depends on sampling rate, which is never stated, the velocity encoding cannot be reproduced or compared across studies.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Training accuracy, test accuracy and AUC for every configuration across fourteen tables - and the decision to report training accuracy is worth crediting, because it makes visible what most papers in this corpus conceal: the models reach 100% training accuracy in essentially every experiment while testing between 67% and 81%. A reader can therefore see the overfitting directly rather than having to infer it. AUC is also reported throughout, which is better than accuracy alone, and the paper reasons about the gap between accuracy and AUC, correctly attributing the low AUC to class imbalance in the training data. Against this, no sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1 or confusion matrix appears anywhere, so nothing is known about the error profile or about which class the models fail on. No confidence intervals are given; the temporal experiments are repeated three times and averaged, which gives some sense of stability, but the diagnosis and stratification headlines rest on single splits. And no chance baseline is stated, although after augmentation the classes are near-balanced.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No model interpretability whatsoever - no saliency, class activation, filter visualisation or error analysis is applied to either network, so the study cannot say what feature of a scan-path image produces a prediction. Its interpretive work is entirely at the input level and is systematic: individual video clips are removed one at a time and the models retrained, ranking each clip's contribution and showing that Theory of Mind and Dyadic Bid clips matter most while one Social Referencing clip matters least; scan-paths are restricted to successive temporal windows to locate when in a trial the discriminative information lies; and velocity encoding is added and removed to test whether dynamics contribute beyond position. These ablations yield findings a clinician could act on - that the first three seconds carry the most signal, that certain stimulus types are more informative than others - and are more useful than a saliency map would have been for stimulus design. But they say nothing about whether the network is responding to where the child looked or to how much of the canvas the drawing covers, which is the question a scan-path-image method most needs to answer.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The weakest element, and the paper contains the evidence for its own strongest critique. The splitting unit is the scan-path image at 7:3 or 75:25, and no participant-level or subject-disjoint evaluation is reported anywhere in twenty pages. With 86 participants generating 1,414 clip viewings, each child contributes roughly sixteen images, so a random image-level split places about eleven of a test child's own scan-paths in training - and scan-paths from one child viewing different clips share that child's habitual gaze extent, saccade amplitude and scanning style. Rotation-based augmentation makes this worse rather than better, because augmented counts are quoted for the whole dataset rather than for training partitions, implying that rotated copies of a single scan-path can appear on both sides of the split. The sex-by-age experiment then supplies near-direct evidence of this: test accuracy rises monotonically with augmentation level, from 85.07% at 961/957 images through 85.81% at 1,276/1,259 to 98.84% at 3,121/2,905. A real signal does not strengthen when synthetic copies are added; a duplicate-leakage artefact does exactly this. The 98.8% is nevertheless reported as the paper's most striking stratification result. Training accuracy of 100% in almost every table confirms complete memorisation at every setting. Layered on top of the leakage is a confound the paper documents without recognising: it establishes that scan-path images predict age band at 80.5% and sex at 78.0% within the autistic group - both above the 74.4% achieved for diagnosis - while its diagnostic groups differ by 35 percentage points in sex composition and by a factor of two in the proportion aged 10 or over. Taken together these mean the headline diagnosis figure cannot be attributed to autism-related looking patterns rather than to age and sex. The corrective design is straightforward and would be genuinely valuable given the quality of the stimulus battery: split by participant, augment only within training folds, and evaluate diagnosis within age-and-sex-matched strata using the paper's own demographic classifiers as a check.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: CCS concepts: supervised learning by classification, neural networks, health informatics. Additional keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder, eye tracking, eye-gaze scan-path, Convolution Neural Network. All are method or modality labels; no application term such as screening or diagnosis appears, consistent with a paper whose stated contribution is representational. The organising term throughout the body is 'stratification' rather than classification or detection - used both for separating autism from typical development and for separating subgroups within autism - which reflects the paper's heterogeneity framing. Other recurring terms: spatio-temporal scan-paths, velocity fusion, ASD heterogeneity, biomarker discovery, social attention.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data 17(2), Article 25, published 20 February 2023; received 15 July 2021, accepted 8 May 2022, online 3 June 2022 - a ten-month review at a data-mining journal. The venue explains the paper's shape: twenty pages with fourteen results tables systematically varying representation, temporal window, stimulus subset and augmentation level, alongside almost no clinical reporting - no diagnostic procedure, no demographics beyond age band and sex, no ethics statement, no sensitivity or specificity. Open access support is provided by six institutions. The article had accumulated 18 citations and 2,645 downloads at retrieval.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2023 by a seven-institution United States consortium including the Yale Child Study Center, Seattle Children's Research Institute and the University of Washington, funded by an NIH K01 award and a Simons Foundation grant, with a first author who also leads the AAC-telemetry study charted elsewhere in this review and a senior author (Shic) whose eye-tracking work recurs throughout this literature. The framing is heterogeneity rather than detection, and it is argued rather than asserted: clinical assessment is subjective and expert-dependent, autism heterogeneity has 'led to the presumption of the presence of multiple etiologies rather than a single disorder', and the quest for personalised medicine is obstructed by it - so a method that can parse subgroups is more valuable than one that only separates cases from controls. The literature review is the most thorough of any study in this corpus on the specific question of scan-path classification, surveying Carette's LSTM work (83% on 32 children), Li's oculomotor behaviour framework (80% on 49 children), Elbattah's autoencoder clustering, the Saliency4ASD grand challenge submissions of Tao and Shyu (74.22% validation falling to 55.66% on test, attributed to overfitting) and Wu (65.41% and 55.13%), and Pusiol's Fragile X work - and it criticises several of them on exactly the right grounds, noting where validation-to-test performance collapsed and where the stratification comparisons needed to support a heterogeneity claim were not reported. The paper's own most valuable contribution to this review is an unintended one: by demonstrating that scan-path images classify age at 80.5% and sex at 78.0% within a single diagnostic group, it quantifies how much demographic information this widely used representation carries, and therefore how much caution the many scan-path autism classifiers in this corpus require.

data_charting_rubrics.title: A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Alsaidi M; Obeid N; Al-Madi N; Hiary H; Aljarah I
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Secondary computational analysis of a public eye-tracking scan-path dataset; a hyperparameter-optimisation and model-comparison study aimed at maximising classification accuracy on a fixed image set. No new data collection and no clinical involvement.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A 100 x 100 greyscale scan-path image, flattened to a one-dimensional vector. A parallel set of experiments retains colour, giving slightly lower accuracy (94.69% versus 95.59%).
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Not reported as a range; mean 7.88 years, median 8.1 years across the whole sample
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 59 children yielding 547 scan-path images
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 30 children, 328 images
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not applicable to this study; not discussed
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Inherited: participants viewed a set of videos containing scenarios designed to elicit eye movement across the screen, seated alone or on a parent's lap about 60 cm from the display, in a quiet room with white barriers reducing distraction. Some videos included a live host verbally guiding the child's attention. The number of videos, their duration and how many scan-paths each child contributed are not stated in this paper.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Inherited: SMI Experiment Center Software with a Red-m remote eye tracker at 250 Hz; source images 640 x 480. Analysis used Python 3.6.8 with Keras/TensorFlow, OpenCV, scikit-learn and Matplotlib on an Intel Core i7 10th-generation machine with 16 GB RAM and an NVIDIA GeForce MX230.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: The source dataset is public and cited to its originators
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Inherited and reported at second hand: the source study's procedures 'were conducted following the ethical standards set by the institutional and/or national research committee, as well as in compliance with the 1964 Helsinki Declaration'. No approval is claimed or needed for the present secondary analysis, and none is stated.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: None hand-crafted. Images were scaled from 640 x 480 to 100 x 100, converted from colour to greyscale (100 x 100 x 3 to 100 x 100 x 1) and then flattened from three dimensions to one before entering the network - a step described and figured explicitly, and one that sits oddly with the model being called convolutional, since flattening destroys the spatial adjacency that convolution exploits.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Absent. No saliency, class activation, filter visualisation or error analysis is performed, and no statement is made about what property of a scan-path image drives a prediction. The discussion attributes the model's superiority to generic architectural virtues - that convolutional networks are 'successfully used for image denoising' and that convolution 'reduces the high dimensionality of images without losing its information' - rather than to anything observed in this data. The gap is compounded by the flattening step, which removes the spatial structure a convolutional explanation would rely on.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Exhaustive, and the study's principal activity. Separate tables sweep kernel size (3, 6, 9), stride (1, 2), pooling, batch size, optimiser (six) and layer/neuron configuration (thirteen), each crossed with the full set of architectures - well over a hundred configurations in total, every one evaluated by the same 10-round cross-validation and the maximum reported as the headline. The best result (two layers of 300 and 150 neurons, kernel size 3, stride 1, Adam, 20% dropout, 100 epochs) is the top cell of that grid.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: '10 rounds of cross-validation' applied to the 547 images. The unit is the image, not the child: 59 children produced 547 images, roughly nine each, and nothing in the paper indicates that a child's images were kept within a fold. No participant-level or subject-disjoint evaluation is reported. The same cross-validation was used to select among more than a hundred hyperparameter configurations, so the reported figure is the maximum of a large search evaluated on the same data.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: None. The paper has no limitations section and identifies no constraint on its findings. Its self-assessment is uniformly positive - the results 'demonstrate that the proposed model can accurately classify children with ASD from those with TD without human intervention', and the model 'demonstrated superior performance when compared to the findings reported in previous studies'.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Fifty-nine children producing 547 scan-path images - the fifth independent reuse of this dataset encountered in the review. Unlike the other reuses charted here, this paper reports the source participant statistics in a dedicated table: 29 autistic and 30 typically developing children, 38 male (64%) and 21 female (36%), mean age 7.88 years and median 8.1, with CARS mean 32.97 and median 34.50. The image split is 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic, so roughly nine images per child. None of the demographic or clinical variables is broken down by diagnostic group, so it cannot be determined whether the groups were matched on age or sex - the sex ratio of 64% male across the whole sample is compatible with anything from a balanced split to a heavily male autistic group and a balanced comparison group. The 547 images, not the 59 children, are the unit of cross-validation throughout.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'Children with ASD' and 'typically developing (TD) children' predominate, person-first, alongside 'individuals with ASD' and 'people with ASD'. Autism is 'a developmental disorder that encompasses difficulties in communication (both verbal and non-verbal), social skills, and repetitive behaviors' and 'a neurodevelopmental disorder that impacts the behavioral and cognitive abilities of children'. The register is medical-model but not pejorative, and the introduction is unusually attentive to autistic people's communicative experience for an engineering paper - it discusses difficulty grasping 'deeper implications in dialogues, resulting in literal understandings and struggles in recognizing indirect messages like sarcasm', and notes that 'clear and specific instructions are necessary for their understanding'. It also engages seriously with heterogeneity, comorbidity (ADHD, anxiety, mood disorders) and the interpersonal-coordination framing of diagnostic conversation. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. One framing choice should be flagged: early detection is motivated partly by 'reduced costs for both individuals and society as a whole', a cost-benefit argument that recurs across this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Better than the other reuses of this dataset, which typically report nothing, but still incomplete and entirely inherited. Table 1 gives, for the sample as a whole: 59 participants, 38 male and 21 female (64%/36%), 29 autistic and 30 typically developing, mean age 7.88 years and median 8.1, and CARS mean 32.97 and median 34.50. No variable is reported by group, so age matching, sex balance between groups and the severity distribution within the autistic group are all unavailable.
