The register is that of clinical linguistics rather than of deficit cataloguing, and the introduction engages seriously with autistic experience in ways rare here: it discusses masking behaviour, compensation strategies and learned camouflaging as phenomena that 'can conceal critical information about impairment, potentially leading to misdiagnosis', and notes that adult diagnosis is hampered because caregiver developmental reports are usually unavailable while 'patient self-insight is unreliable'. That framing treats diagnostic difficulty as a property of the encounter rather than of the person. Deficit vocabulary does appear - 'impairment', 'dysfunction', 'core deficits' - and there is no neurodiversity framing or autistic-community involvement, but the paper's characterisation of what it is measuring is more precise and less totalising than the corpus norm.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Reported asymmetrically, and the asymmetry is the study's principal weakness. For the autistic group: age 18 +/- 3.48, sex 24 male to 40 female, ADOS-2 Module 3 and 4 totals, SRS-2 total 85.53 +/- 9.00, WISC-IV full-scale IQ 81.22 +/- 14.42 and WAIS-III full-scale IQ 91.33 +/- 20.12, Vineland-II adaptive composite 64.83 +/- 22.53, AQ 36.64 +/- 8.04, and PARS-TR scores for preschool and for adolescent/adult items. This is the most complete clinical characterisation of an autistic sample anywhere in the review. For the comparison group: age 19 +/- 2.77, sex 39 male to 32 female, ADOS-2 totals - and then nothing except a college grade point average range of 2.4 to 2.8, with the authors stating plainly that 'IQ testing was not part of our methodology'. The consequence is a confound that cannot be assessed: the autistic group has measured full-scale IQ between 81 and 91, while the comparison group is three-quarters university students selected for average academic standing, so the groups almost certainly differ substantially in cognitive and educational level, in a study whose entire outcome is the range and complexity of grammatical choices a speaker makes. Two further features deserve note. Age differs significantly (p = 0.00) but by only about a year, so the significance reflects sample size rather than a meaningful gap. And the autistic sample is 62.5% female - the only female-majority autistic cohort in this review, and by a very wide margin - which is unremarked despite the paper's own extended discussion of camouflaging, a phenomenon reported disproportionately in autistic women and directly relevant to whether linguistic markers would be detectable in this sample.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: The most thorough reference standard in the review alongside the joint-attention study, and the only one that applies a gold-standard instrument to both groups. Autism diagnosis followed DSM-5 criteria applied by experienced clinicians specialising in neurodevelopmental disorders, with ADOS-2 as the primary confirming instrument administered by someone holding research reliability certified through Western Psychological Services, and supported by a full battery: SRS-2, age-appropriate Wechsler IQ testing, Vineland-II, AQ and PARS-TR caregiver interview. What distinguishes it further is the comparison group. Every non-autistic participant received the ADOS-2 and was confirmed non-spectrum against the published cut-offs, which are quoted (6 or below on Module 3; combined communication and social interaction of 7 or below on Module 4), with group means reported separately for the clinically assessed and the recruited subgroups. Almost every other study in this corpus establishes comparison status by absence of a diagnosis or by parent report; this one administers the same instrument to both sides. The inclusion of co-occurring conditions in the autistic cohort is also a deliberate and well-argued choice rather than an oversight. Two qualifications remain: the diagnosing clinicians were not blind to anything and no inter-rater reliability is reported beyond the administrator's certification, and the language samples analysed come from the same ADOS-2 sessions that generated the labels.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Extensive for the autistic group and absent for the comparison group. Available and reported: ADOS-2 Module 3 (6.93 +/- 1.38) and Module 4 (11.42 +/- 3.55) totals; SRS-2 total 85.53 +/- 9.00, indicating substantial social-communication difficulty; AQ 36.64 +/- 8.04, above the usual screening threshold; Vineland-II adaptive composite 64.83 +/- 22.53, well below the normative mean and with a very wide spread; PARS-TR 13.54 +/- 6.27 for preschool items and 24.30 +/- 11.49 for adolescent and adult items; and full-scale IQ from WISC-IV (81.22 +/- 14.42) or WAIS-III (91.33 +/- 20.12). Taken together these characterise a sample with average-to-borderline cognitive ability, marked adaptive-functioning impairment and clear social-communication difficulty - a genuinely informative clinical picture, and one that positions this cohort quite differently from the high-functioning verbal samples that dominate the rest of the review. Two things are not done with this material. None of it is related to model output, so the natural questions - whether linguistic distinctiveness scales with SRS-2 or AQ score, whether misclassified participants have lower ADOS-2 totals - are unasked despite the data being in hand. And no equivalent measure exists for the comparison group, so the severity information cannot be used to characterise the contrast, only one side of it.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The study begins from a specific and well-evidenced clinical problem rather than from a technical opportunity: ADOS-2, the gold standard, has documented limitations for adolescents and adults, because it does not clearly separate autism from ADHD or from the negative symptoms of schizophrenia and other psychiatric comorbidities, and because masking, compensation and camouflaging can conceal impairment. The proposed remedy is a comprehensive mapping of pragmatic impairment through lexicogrammatical analysis, which the authors note has not previously been attempted - prior linguistic work examined single grammatical areas such as modality, relative clauses or syntax, leaving 'the overall picture of the impairment... uncharted'. Findings: on interview transcripts the combined text-plus-tag Bi-LSTM reached 0.82 accuracy (95% CI 0.75-0.89) with AUC 0.90 under automatic annotation, and 0.80 (0.73-0.87) with sensitivity 0.73 and specificity 0.87 under manual annotation. The tag-only linear model reached 0.78 and the text-only model 0.80, and McNemar tests found no significant differences between them on the interview task. The substantive result is the task contrast: every model performed better on interviews than on picture-book recounting, where the linear model fell to 0.60-0.64 and the best model reached 0.78. The authors interpret this as evidence that the discriminative signal lies in socially interactive language use rather than in narrative production generally, which is exactly what a pragmatic-impairment account predicts and is a stronger form of evidence than a single accuracy figure.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Hirosaki University's Department of Neuropsychiatry, with natural language processing collaboration at Tohoku University. Language samples were drawn from ADOS-2 administrations conducted by a research-reliable administrator, so the recording setting is the standardised diagnostic assessment itself. Recruitment ran from September 2013 to October 2020, combining prospective enrolment with retrospective examination of diagnostic records under the same ethical framework. The recruitment geometry is the study's weak point relative to its reference standard: autistic participants come through a university neuropsychiatry clinic while three-quarters of the comparison group are college students recruited for the study, so clinical status, educational setting and probably cognitive level all co-vary with group. The 17 clinically assessed comparison participants partially mitigate this by coming through the same clinical pathway, but they are under a quarter of that group.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Two tasks, both taken from ADOS-2 Modules 3 and 4 as administered rather than constructed for the study: interview responses and picture-book story recounting. The choice has one clear advantage and one clear cost. The advantage is standardisation - the same certified administrator elicited both from every participant under a protocol designed to sample social communication, so the elicitation is as comparable across participants as anything in this review. The cost is that the speech analysed was produced during the diagnostic session itself, so the examiner's behaviour toward each participant is part of the context and is unobserved, and the language sample is not independent of the encounter that produced the label. The paper is explicit about what it does with the material: the entire spoken output is evaluated 'without setting specific requirements for text length, speaking duration, or word count', and the analysis addresses 'patterns of lexicogrammar selection from participants' responses' rather than the dynamics of interaction - so turn-taking, latency and interactional contingency are outside scope by design. The contrast between the two tasks is the most valuable feature of the paradigm and is exploited properly: interview is dialogic and socially demanding, picture-book recounting is monologic and scaffolded by the stimulus, and the consistent superiority of interview transcripts across all four models and both annotation methods is a within-study replication of the paper's theoretical claim.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional in analysis, though the corpus was assembled over seven years, with prospective recruitment and retrospective record examination running concurrently. No follow-up, no repeat sampling and no test-retest assessment of the linguistic measures - which matters for an instrument proposed as a diagnostic aid, since stability across occasions is unestablished. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: approval by the Hirosaki University Committee on Medical Ethics under IRB 2013-142, subsequently updated to 2018-168 with the previous number 2015-055 also given; the committee's information security guidelines followed; written consent from participants aged 20 and above and from both participants and guardians for those 19 and under; and anonymisation by alphanumeric identifier with identifiable utterances removed from transcripts. The last of these is a specific privacy measure appropriate to a corpus of personal spoken narratives and is not standard practice in this corpus. Funding from two JSPS KAKENHI grants is itemised and competing interests are declared as none.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No instrumentation - the data are transcribed ADOS-2 sessions. The apparatus is analytical and is specified adequately: logistic regression on normalised tag frequencies; Bi-LSTM models with 300-dimensional word and hidden vectors trained with Adam at learning rate 0.001, batch size 32, for 50 epochs; and a separate Bi-LSTM sequence labeller for automatic annotation. The most consequential methodological statement concerns what was not done: the hyperparameters 'were adopted from commonly used values and not explored, as preliminary experiments determined that the impact of the search for hyperparameters' was limited. Declining to search hyperparameters on a 135-participant dataset removes a source of optimism that most studies in this corpus exploit heavily, and doing so deliberately and saying so is exceptional. No software package or version is named, which is the one specification gap.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong on conceptual and procedural specification, weaker on artefacts. Reproducible from the text: the participant selection rationale with its critical-period justification, the full diagnostic battery, the ADOS-2 non-spectrum cut-offs applied to the comparison group with observed means, the two elicitation tasks and their ADOS-2 provenance, the Systemic Functional Linguistics annotation scheme with its lexicogrammatical headings, linguistic functions and tag types tabulated at category level, the transfer-comparison method by which the Japanese system network was built, the input construction for each of the four models, all training hyperparameters with the statement that they were not searched, the leave-one-out procedure with the annotation model retrained within each fold, and the evaluation metrics with confidence intervals and McNemar comparisons. Supplementary files carry the tag frequency comparisons. Not available: code, the corpus itself (described in a prior publication rather than deposited), the specific software stack, and any random seed. The annotation scheme's full tag inventory is summarised rather than exhaustively listed in the main text.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The limitations section is substantive and correctly prioritised. Sample size is named repeatedly as the principal constraint, with the conclusion that the study 'should be viewed as exploratory, aimed at providing initial insights rather than definitive conclusions' - a self-assessment few papers in this corpus offer and fewer still act on. The infeasibility of manual annotation in clinical settings is acknowledged as the reason the automatic annotator exists, and its weakest category (te-clauses, subdivided into eight classifications) is identified with two concrete remedies. Most notably, the McNemar results are interpreted with explicit reference to statistical power: 'the absence of statistically significant differences in our McNemar test results does not definitively indicate the absence of a performance difference between models, particularly in the context of small sample sizes'. Correctly refusing to read non-significance as equivalence is a discipline absent everywhere else in this review. What is not addressed matters nonetheless. IQ was measured in the autistic group at 81-91 and not measured at all in the comparison group, which was selected for average college grade point average - so an unquantified cognitive and educational gap separates the groups in a study of grammatical complexity, and the substitution of grade point average for IQ testing is presented as a selection criterion rather than acknowledged as a limitation. The language samples come from the ADOS-2 sessions that produced the labels, so the elicitation context is the diagnostic encounter itself. The comparison group is three-quarters university students against an autistic group whose educational status is unreported. And the 62.5% female composition of the autistic sample goes unremarked despite the paper's own emphasis on camouflaging.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Three directions, all concrete. Comprehensive verification with a substantially larger and more diverse participant pool, with the logistical difficulty of achieving this acknowledged rather than waved away. Improvement of the automatic annotation system, particularly for te-clauses, either by sharpening category definitions or by expanding training data - a specific and testable target derived from the study's own error analysis. And extension to other languages through transfer comparison, the same method used to build the Japanese system network, which the authors argue makes the annotation scheme 'applicable to any language'. That last is an unusually ambitious but well-grounded claim, since it rests on a documented linguistic methodology rather than on an assumption that features transfer. Not proposed, and needed: cognitive assessment of the comparison group, and analysis relating model output to the SRS-2, AQ, Vineland-II and ADOS-2 data already collected.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Lexicogrammatical choice - which options a speaker selects from the grammatical resources their language offers - as an operationalisation of pragmatic impairment. The theoretical grounding is Systemic Functional Linguistics, in which language is a system network of choices and meaning is made by selecting among them, and the clinical construct is defined with care as difficulty in 'adapting language formality based on the situation, interpreting non-literal language (such as idioms, metaphors, irony, and sarcasm), and understanding the nuances of language that affect interpersonal interactions... rather than with the basic structural or grammatical components'. The annotation scheme operationalises this across multiple lexicogrammatical systems, of which the paper details several: modality, where prior work by the first author found autistic individuals less likely to use probability expressions (must, will, may) and evidentiality expressions (seems, looks like, likely, is said, according to) and connected this to inferential reasoning; te-clauses with eight functional subtypes; negotiating particles, comprising twelve Japanese sentence-final and medial particles such as kana, ne, yo and yone that mark attitudinal stance toward a proposition and signal the speaker's claim on the information; and explanative mood. Two features distinguish this target from the rest of the corpus. It is language-specific in a principled way - the particles carrying much of the signal have no English equivalent and were identified through a system network built for Japanese - which is the opposite of the usual practice of applying an English-derived feature set across languages. And the empirical result localises the signal to socially interactive language: interview transcripts discriminated better than narrative recounting in every configuration tested, which is what a pragmatic account predicts and a purely structural account does not.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Two representations of the same speech are fused and their contributions separately established. The tag stream encodes the linguistic-theoretical description - which lexicogrammatical options were selected - while the text stream encodes the words themselves, and the combined model concatenates tag and word embeddings at each time step so the Bi-LSTM sees both simultaneously. The ablation is reported across four configurations, two tasks and two annotation methods, and its result is instructive precisely because it is modest: on interviews the tag-only linear model reached 0.78, the tag-only Bi-LSTM 0.80, the text-only Bi-LSTM 0.80 and the combined model 0.80-0.82, with McNemar tests finding no significant differences between them. So the theoretically motivated tag representation and the raw word sequence carry largely overlapping information, and combining them adds at most a point or two. The authors report this honestly rather than claiming a fusion benefit, and note that 'the text-DNN and text+tag-DNN models performed almost the same, with the text+tag-DNN model being marginally higher'. That is a more useful contribution to the review's treatment of multimodality than a claimed gain would have been: it shows that an expensive, theory-driven annotation layer can be approximately recovered from surface text by a sequence model, while remaining far more interpretable - which is why the authors retain it.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Four configurations spanning two model families, with the trade-off between them argued rather than resolved by accuracy. Logistic regression on normalised tag frequencies serves as the interpretable model, retained explicitly because 'in the medical context, interpretability is crucial because we are dealing with human lives' and because it 'allowed us to identify tags that impacted the outputs and quantify these effects'. Bi-LSTM models serve as the performance-oriented alternative, in three variants: tags only, text only, and tags plus text concatenated at each time step. A fifth model, a separate Bi-LSTM sequence labeller, performs automatic annotation and is retrained within each cross-validation fold. Two aspects of the modelling deserve particular credit. Hyperparameters were adopted from standard values and deliberately not searched, on the stated basis that preliminary work showed the search had little impact - which removes a large source of optimism on a 135-participant dataset. And the authors decline to declare a winner: after observing that the linear model was less precise, they write that 'it is not possible to make an unconditional judgment of which model is better', because interpretability and accuracy are not commensurable in a clinical setting. No other study in this corpus refuses to rank its models by accuracy.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Two representations, both derived from the same transcripts. Tags come from a Systemic Functional Linguistics annotation scheme built for Japanese through transfer comparison, comprising four system networks and eleven or more lexicogrammatical headings each with multiple tag types - modality, te-clauses with eight subtypes, twelve negotiating particles, explanative mood and others. For the linear model the input is a tag-frequency vector normalised by total word count, which discards order. For the Bi-LSTM variants the input is the ordered sequence of tag sets, with each word represented by the sum of the embedding vectors of its tags, giving 300-dimensional tag embeddings; the text model uses 300-dimensional word embeddings; and the combined model concatenates the two at each time step. Annotation was performed both manually and automatically, with both evaluated in parallel throughout, and the automatic annotator achieving a mean F of 0.88 against manual - so the study reports both the ceiling achievable with perfect annotation and the performance obtainable in a setting where manual annotation is impossible.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: The best-calibrated metric reporting in the review after the population EHR study. Accuracy is reported with a 95% confidence interval for every one of sixteen conditions - four models by two tasks by two annotation methods - alongside precision, sensitivity, specificity and AUC. Reporting confidence intervals is what makes the results interpretable at this sample size: the best interview model's interval of [0.75, 0.89] sits clearly above the 52.6% majority-class floor, while the weakest picture-book configuration at 0.60 [0.51, 0.69] does not. Model comparisons are then tested formally with McNemar rather than being asserted from point differences, and the results are tabulated with test statistics and p-values. Most importantly, non-significant comparisons are interpreted correctly: the authors state that non-significance 'does not definitively indicate the absence of a performance difference between models, particularly in the context of small sample sizes', citing the literature on statistical power. Across this corpus, model rankings resting on differences of one or two participants are routinely presented as findings; this is the only study that tests such comparisons and then declines to over-read them. Absent: confusion matrices, and any relation between predictions and the clinical severity variables collected.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is a design constraint, an argument and a reported finding rather than a post-hoc gloss. The features are categories from an explicit linguistic theory, so a model contribution attaches to a nameable grammatical choice - a modality expression, a particular sentence-final particle, a te-clause subtype - rather than to an embedding dimension, and the linear model is retained specifically so those contributions can be identified and quantified. The authors' refusal to declare the deep model superior on accuracy grounds, on the reasoning that interpretability matters differently when 'we are dealing with human lives', is the clearest statement of that principle in the corpus. Group differences in tag frequencies are tabulated in supplementary material. The annotation system's own errors are analysed rather than assumed away, with an overall F of 0.88 and the te-clause identified as the dominant error source together with an explanation of why - it subdivides into eight classifications whose boundaries are hard to define. What is missing is the individual level: no error analysis identifies which participants were misclassified, and no analysis relates model output to the SRS-2, AQ, Vineland-II or ADOS-2 scores the study holds, which would have tested whether the linguistic signal tracks clinical severity.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Among the two or three soundest validation designs in the review, and sound in ways that require deliberate effort rather than good fortune. The split unit is the participant, with leave-one-out cross-validation formally specified: each of the 135 samples serves once as the test case with the remaining 134 as training data. The step that distinguishes it is the handling of the annotation model. Automatic tag annotation is itself a fitted component, and fitting it once on the whole corpus would leak information from held-out participants into their own annotations; instead the procedure trains the annotator on the training partition of each fold and then uses that fold-specific annotator to label the held-out sample. Very few studies in this corpus recognise that a preprocessing model is a fitted component at all, and none other nests one this carefully. Hyperparameters were adopted from standard values and deliberately not searched, removing the model-selection optimism that inflates most results here. Confidence intervals accompany every accuracy, and model comparisons are tested with McNemar rather than read from point differences, with non-significance correctly not interpreted as equivalence. Two residual concerns are not validation failures but bound what the result means. The comparison group's cognitive and educational level is unmeasured while the autistic group's full-scale IQ is 81-91, so an unquantified ability gap may contribute to the separation. And the transcripts come from the ADOS-2 sessions that produced the labels, so the language sample and the diagnostic judgement arise from the same encounter - which does not leak the label into the features but does mean the model is trained on speech elicited by an examiner who was assessing the participant for autism at that moment.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No formal keyword list appears in the retrieved text. The organising terms are lexicogrammatical choices, pragmatic impairment, Systemic Functional Linguistics, system network, annotation scheme, corpus of spoken language, Bi-LSTM, leave-one-out cross validation, transfer comparison, differential diagnosis, masking and camouflaging. The vocabulary is drawn from clinical linguistics rather than from machine learning, and the title's framing - 'creating a diagnostic assessment model... by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices' - names a linguistic mechanism rather than an architecture, which is the reverse of the corpus norm.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: PLOS ONE 19(9), article e0311209, published 27 September 2024; received 19 March 2024, accepted 15 September 2024, open access under CC BY, with a named academic editor. Twenty-nine pages, of which a substantial proportion is devoted to the linguistic theory, the annotation scheme and the interpretation of what the tags mean - so the balance is unusual for this corpus, with the machine learning occupying perhaps a quarter of the paper and the linguistic framework the rest. The venue's reporting requirements produce the data availability, funding and competing-interests statements, and the length permits the annotation scheme to be documented at a level that a conference paper could not accommodate. Two supplementary files carry the tag frequency comparisons between groups.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2024 by the Department of Neuropsychiatry at Hirosaki University with Aomori Chuo Gakuin University and the Natural Language Processing Lab at Tohoku University, funded by two JSPS KAKENHI grants. The framing is diagnostic supplementation grounded in a specific, well-evidenced critique of the gold standard rather than in generic complaints about subjectivity: ADOS-2 does not clearly differentiate autism from ADHD or from the negative symptoms of schizophrenia and other psychiatric comorbidities; masking, compensation and camouflaging can conceal impairment; and adult diagnosis is further hampered because caregiver developmental reports are usually unavailable while self-insight is unreliable. That is a more precise diagnosis of what automated assessment is for than any other paper in this corpus offers, and it leads to a correspondingly bounded claim - language analysis as one input among several, not a replacement. Four features make the study particularly valuable to this review. It is the only one that applies a gold-standard instrument to both groups, so its comparison group is screened rather than assumed. It is the only one that nests a fitted preprocessing component inside its cross-validation. It is the only one that tests model comparisons statistically and then declines to over-read non-significant differences. And it is the only one that refuses to rank its models by accuracy, retaining an interpretable linear model on the explicit ground that interpretability is not commensurable with accuracy in clinical use. Set against these, its unmeasured comparison-group IQ is a real limitation, and its reliance on ADOS-2 transcripts means the speech analysed was produced inside the diagnostic encounter itself - a form of dependence between sample and label that no other language study here faces and that the paper does not discuss.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Sarwani IS; Bhaskari DL; Bhamidipati S
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: International Journal of Advanced Computer S
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Secondary computational analysis of a scraped public image dataset; a feature-family and classifier comparison, crossing three transfer-learning backbones and five handcrafted descriptor types against five classifiers. No participants, no data collection, no clinical involvement.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A concatenated feature vector of 3,315 dimensions per image, in three variants distinguished only by which backbone supplies the deep component
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 2,936 facial images; the number of distinct children is unknown and unrecoverable
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 1,468 images
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: None; not discussed
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None; pretrained VGG16, ResNet and Inception networks used as fixed feature extractors, with scikit-learn-style classical classifiers
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: The Kaggle dataset is cited by reference number
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: None stated and none discussed. The dataset consists of photographs of identifiable children obtained without consent, with the autistic class assembled from autism-focused sources so that the collection itself asserts a health status about identifiable minors.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Eight feature families with counts tabulated: 3,000 features each from VGG16, ResNet and Inception with fully connected layers excluded; 100 HOG features capturing gradient distributions; 50 LBP features representing texture; 50 ORB keypoint and descriptor features; 65 perceptual hash features encoding image fingerprints; and 50 SIFT features. These are combined into three feature vectors, each pairing the 315 handcrafted features with one backbone's 3,000.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None. No feature importance, saliency, activation visualisation or error analysis is performed for any of the eighteen model-feature combinations, so nothing is reported about which visual properties drive classification. This matters particularly here because the handcrafted feature set - gradient histograms, texture patterns, keypoint descriptors and perceptual hashes - consists precisely of quantities that respond to image resolution, sharpness, compression and lighting, so a source-provenance explanation for the results is not merely possible but the one the feature set is best suited to capture.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not described for any classifier
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Not described. The words 'split' and 'validation' do not appear anywhere in the paper, no cross-validation is reported, and no train-test partition, holdout proportion or resampling scheme is stated for any of the eighteen classifier-feature combinations whose accuracies are tabulated. The methods section describes feature extraction in step-by-step procedural detail - loading libraries, traversing directory structures, building DataFrames, adding label columns, saving to CSV - and then reports classification results without any statement of how the data were divided. This is the only included study in the review that reports classification performance without describing an evaluation protocol at all.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: None. There is no limitations section and no constraint on the findings is identified anywhere.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: There are no participants - 2,936 facial photographs from a Kaggle collection, evenly divided at 1,468 per class, described only as colour images of autistic and non-autistic children. The number of distinct children behind them is unknown and unrecoverable. This is the same publicly scraped 'Autistic Children Facial Dataset' already charted in this review in a companion study which used a 2,836-image version, and the two counts imply different snapshots of a dataset that has been revised. The companion study documents the provenance that this one does not mention: autistic images sourced from online platforms focused on autism, non-autistic images gathered separately from the internet.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'Autistic children' and 'non-autistic children', person-first in most constructions but with 'normally developing youngsters' appearing when summarising prior work. The clinical description in the introduction is drawn accurately from DSM criteria and is comparatively careful - reduced sharing of emotions and interests, deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, difficulty adapting behaviour to social contexts, difficulty making friends. The framing of purpose includes an unusual note: technological advancement is described as 'a blessing to the parents who are clueless about managing the condition', which positions the work as parent-facing. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement - a notable absence given that the dataset's autistic images were collected from autism-focused online spaces created by and for that community. The premise that 'autistic children show distinctive patterns' in facial and emotional expression is asserted without citation to any evidence about facial morphology.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: None whatsoever - no age, sex, race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, cognitive level, language, comorbidity or severity data for any image, and no statement that such information is unavailable. The paper does not report even the age range that the dataset's own description carries. As with the companion study, the omission is consequential because the two classes were assembled from different internet sources, and autism-focused online spaces will differ from general internet image collections in the demographics they represent as well as in photographic convention.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Absent. The labels are the names of two subdirectories in a downloaded folder, and the methods section describes exactly this: features are extracted 'by traversing through the directory structure', with 'a label column added to denote the class label (autistic or non_autistic)'. No diagnosis, instrument, criterion, clinician or verification underlies either class. The quantity the models predict is therefore which folder an image was filed in, and given that the folders were populated from different parts of the internet, the reported accuracies are best read as measures of how distinguishable the two source collections are as image sets.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None, and none is possible. No severity, cognitive, language or adaptive information exists for any image.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated aim is to improve autism detection accuracy from facial images by combining transfer-learned deep features with handcrafted image descriptors, and to identify the best classifier and feature combination. Findings: handcrafted features alone gave 78.0-84.5% across five classifiers, with random forest best; adding ResNet features raised the range to 84.4-90.2%, with SVM best; and adding Inception features gave 83.2-94.6%, with SVM best at 94.6%. The reported progression - handcrafted alone, then fused with each backbone - is a systematic ablation and is the paper's substantive content. What it cannot establish is what the improvement means, because no evaluation protocol is stated: the words 'split' and 'validation' appear nowhere, no cross-validation is described, and no train-test partition is specified for any of the eighteen reported accuracies. Whether these are held-out figures, training figures, or something else is not determinable from the paper.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting. Work was performed on a downloaded Kaggle dataset at two universities in Visakhapatnam, India, with no contact with any participant and no acquisition of any kind.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: None. There is no task, protocol or elicitation - the data are photographs. The framing gap is worth stating plainly: the title announces 'Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection' and the introduction argues that 'facial expressions and emotional expressions can help in early detection and diagnosis of ASD', but no expression is labelled, detected, elicited or analysed anywhere in the paper. The features extracted are generic image descriptors, and the classification target is the image's folder. The word 'emotion' does not recur in the method, results or conclusion. So the study measures no behaviour at all while describing itself as behavioural, which places it further outside this review's modality scope than the companion study on the same dataset, that one at least having attached a genuine facial-expression module trained on AffectNet.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional in the trivial sense. No ethics statement, consent, funding declaration or competing-interests statement appears anywhere. As with the companion study, the dataset consists of identifiable photographs of children obtained without their families' knowledge, with one class assembled specifically because those images appeared in autism contexts - so the collection asserts a health status about identifiable minors, and training and publishing on it propagates that assertion. None of this is acknowledged.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: None. Pretrained VGG16, ResNet and Inception networks used as fixed feature extractors with fully connected layers excluded, and five classical classifiers. No hardware, software package, version or hyperparameter is reported. The imaging characteristics of the source photographs - the properties that differ between the two source collections and that HOG, LBP, PHASH and SIFT are designed to capture - are neither reported nor examined.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Curiously uneven. The feature-extraction pipeline is described at unusual procedural length, narrating library imports, directory traversal, per-image processing, DataFrame construction, label-column addition, merging and CSV export, with exact feature counts tabulated for all eight families. The evaluation is described not at all. A reader is given enough to reconstruct how a 3,315-dimensional feature vector was built and nothing whatever about how the reported accuracies were computed. Also absent: the Kaggle dataset identifier and version, any classifier hyperparameters, any seed, and code.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: There is no limitations section and no constraint is acknowledged. The unaddressed problems are the same as for the companion study on this dataset, plus one that is specific to this paper. The dataset's two classes come from different internet sources, so image provenance is confounded with the label - and here the confound is sharper than usual, because five of the eight feature families are handcrafted descriptors that respond directly to gradient structure, texture, keypoint density and perceptual hashing, all of which are functions of resolution, sharpness, compression and lighting rather than of anything about the child. That the handcrafted features alone reach 84.5% is therefore not evidence that facial morphology is informative; it is equally consistent with the two collections being distinguishable as image sets. No diagnostic verification exists for either class. The number of distinct children is unknown. No demographic data are available. Eighteen classifier-feature combinations were evaluated and the maximum reported. And, uniquely among included studies, no evaluation protocol of any kind is described.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: None proposed. The conclusion restates the method and the comparison without identifying any next step.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: None is measured. The paper's framing is behavioural - emotion, facial expression, distinctive patterns shown by autistic children - and its method is not. HOG captures gradient orientation distributions, LBP captures local texture, ORB captures keypoints and their descriptors, PHASH computes a perceptual fingerprint of the whole image, SIFT detects scale-invariant local features, and the three backbones supply generic ImageNet activations. None of these is a measure of expression, movement or any behaviour, and no expression labels exist in the dataset. For the review this study marks the far end of a boundary the companion paper already approached: automated autism detection that has left behaviour behind entirely while retaining behavioural vocabulary.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Fusion within a single modality and across feature families, systematically ablated. Three feature vectors are constructed, each concatenating the same 315 handcrafted features with one backbone's 3,000 deep features, and results are reported for the handcrafted set alone and for each fused vector across five classifiers. The ablation shows a consistent gain from adding deep features - best accuracy rising from 84.5% with handcrafted features alone to 90.2% with ResNet and 94.6% with Inception - which is a clean comparison and is the paper's only methodological contribution. Its interpretability is destroyed by the absence of an evaluation protocol: without knowing how the accuracies were computed, the gain cannot be attributed to better representation rather than to greater capacity to fit the data.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Three ImageNet-pretrained backbones used as fixed feature extractors with fully connected layers excluded, and five classical classifiers - random forest, k-nearest neighbours, decision tree, SVM and logistic regression - applied to each of four feature conditions, giving twenty reported model-condition combinations of which eighteen are tabulated. The design is a systematic grid rather than a single proposed model, which is reasonable for a comparison study. No hyperparameters are reported for any classifier, and no rationale is given for the choice of backbones or descriptors beyond their being commonly used.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A 3,315-dimensional concatenation per image: 3,000 activations from one backbone plus 100 HOG, 50 LBP, 50 ORB, 65 PHASH and 50 SIFT features. The handcrafted component is worth characterising because it determines what a source-provenance confound would look like. HOG encodes gradient distributions, which depend on image sharpness; LBP encodes local texture, which depends on resolution and compression; PHASH is a whole-image fingerprint, which encodes global tone and layout; SIFT and ORB encode keypoint structure, which depends on contrast and focus. Every one of these is a property of the photograph rather than of the face, and all differ systematically between images collected from different sources. That this feature set alone achieves 84.5% is therefore the paper's most diagnostic result, and it is reported without comment.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Precision, recall, F1 and accuracy, reported as whole percentages for five classifiers across four feature conditions. The set is nominally adequate, but three problems undercut it. Precision, recall and F1 are reported as identical values to the percentage point in almost every row, which for a balanced binary problem is arithmetically possible but is presented without the confusion counts that would let a reader verify it. No AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval appears. And most fundamentally, no evaluation protocol is stated, so it is not determinable what population any of these numbers estimates - they may be held-out, resubstitution, or cross-validated figures, and the paper provides no basis for choosing between those readings.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No feature importance, saliency map, activation visualisation, error analysis or example inspection appears for any of the eighteen combinations. The absence is decisive rather than incidental in this design, because the study's own results contain the material for an interpretability check it does not perform: handcrafted descriptors sensitive to image quality reach 84.5% alone, and a single analysis of which descriptors carry that performance - or a single visualisation of what distinguishes the two classes - would establish whether the model responds to faces or to photographs.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: There is no validation strategy. This is not a case of an inadequate or leaky protocol but of no stated protocol at all: the words 'split' and 'validation' do not occur in the paper, no cross-validation is described, no holdout proportion is given, and no resampling scheme is mentioned, yet twenty accuracy figures are tabulated across four feature conditions and five classifiers. The methods section narrates the feature-extraction pipeline in step-by-step detail down to CSV export and then moves directly to results. Consequently none of the reported numbers can be interpreted as an estimate of performance on unseen data, and the comparison the paper is built around - handcrafted versus fused features, and among the three backbones - cannot be evaluated either, since a resubstitution comparison would favour the higher-dimensional representations regardless of their generalisation. Beneath this sits the same structural problem as in the companion study on this dataset: the two classes were assembled from different internet sources, so no split, however constructed, could separate a model that has learned about faces from one that has learned about photographs; and the number of distinct children is unknown, so images of one child may fall on both sides of any partition undetectably.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder; transfer learning; image features; VGG; ResNet; Inception. Five of six name architectures or feature types; no behavioural, clinical or application term appears. The title's 'Emotion-based' has no counterpart in the keywords, the method or the results, and is the paper's clearest instance of behavioural vocabulary applied to non-behavioural work.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications 15(5), 2024, pages 566 onwards - a general computer-science journal published by The Science and Information Organization, outside the clinical and biomedical literature. The venue accounts for the reporting profile: extensive procedural description of feature extraction, a large comparison grid, and no ethics, funding, competing-interests or limitations statement. It does not account for the absence of an evaluation protocol, which is a scientific rather than a formatting omission.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2024 by the Department of Computer Science and Systems Engineering at Andhra University with the Department of Applied Psychology at GITAM Deemed to be University, Visakhapatnam. The framing is early detection and parental support, with the observation that diagnosis 'depends predominantly on the aberrations in the functioning of the brain that may not surface in the very early stages' and that technology has been 'a blessing to the parents who are clueless about managing the condition'. The presence of a psychology co-author makes the absence of any diagnostic verification, demographic reporting or ethical consideration more striking rather than less. For this review the study's value is entirely as a second data point on the facial-photograph branch of the literature, and it strengthens three observations already recorded from the companion study on the same dataset. The branch is not small - two independent groups publishing in the same year on the same scraped collection, with a literature review here citing at least half a dozen further examples using facial images, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet and hybrid vision transformers at accuracies from 88% to 92.5%. Its reported accuracies are comparable to or higher than the best-conducted studies in this review, so accuracy in this literature does not order studies by evidential quality. And its methodological reporting can omit the evaluation protocol entirely without that omission preventing publication - which is the strongest available evidence that peer review in this branch is not filtering on the properties that determine whether a number means anything.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Devaraj VS; Periyathambi E
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective algorithm-development study on two public posed-expression corpora, comparing a proposed hybrid optimiser-network architecture against three baselines
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Grayscale cropped face images at two resolutions for the two processing stages
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Not reported. Both corpora consist of adult volunteers, so the population is decades older than the children the paper's motivation concerns.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 118 individuals contributing 327 sequences in CK+, of which only the peak frame of each sequence is used; the KDEF sample size is not stated in the paper
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: CK+ is described as testing the model 'on unseen data' after KDEF, which would constitute cross-corpus evaluation - the design this review values most highly. It is not reported as a separate result, so the strongest element of the design is also the least documented.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Not applicable - the task is multi-class emotion recognition rather than a group contrast
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Obtained by the original corpus creators
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Instructed posed expression production, as designed by the original corpus creators. The paper itself identifies why this matters, noting that 'research indicates a lack of studies utilizing static or dynamic facial stimuli displaying real, spontaneous emotions' and that 'staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones' - then evaluates exclusively on staged emotions.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None for acquisition. Preprocessing used grayscaling and resizing to 120x110 for a Gabor filter stage and 100x100 for the convolutional network, with normalisation, histogram equalisation, face detection and realignment, and landmark or local binary pattern feature extraction.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Both corpora are established public resources; no availability statement is given
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not stated. Both corpora were collected with participant consent by their original creators and are widely used in affective computing; secondary analysis conventionally proceeds without fresh approval.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Gabor filtering at 120x110 followed by convolutional feature learning at 100x100, with landmark and local binary pattern descriptors described in the preprocessing account
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None. No attribution, saliency or feature analysis is reported. The optimiser's quaternion formulation is given in mathematical detail but is a search-space device rather than an interpretability mechanism, and the accompanying claim that it encodes 'physiological signal characteristics' has no referent in this study's data.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The quantum particle swarm optimiser is itself the tuning mechanism; its own control parameters, population size and iteration count are not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Not described. No train-test split proportions, cross-validation scheme, participant-level partitioning or held-out arrangement is stated anywhere in the paper. CK+ is described as being used 'to test the WQPSO-FMRCNN model on unseen data', which implies training on KDEF and testing on CK+ - a genuine cross-corpus evaluation that would be a real strength if stated and quantified separately. But no cross-corpus result is reported as such, no partition sizes are given, and the headline figures are not attributed to a specific evaluation arrangement. Since CK+ contributes 327 sequences from 118 individuals and only the peak frame of each is used, roughly 2.8 images come from each person; whether images of the same individual span any partition is unstated.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: None. The paper has no limitations section, and the conclusion restates the aims in the language of achievement.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: There are no autistic participants. The Extended Cohn-Kanade corpus supplies 327 sequences from 118 adult volunteers, of which only the peak frame of each sequence is used, giving roughly 2.8 images per person; the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces corpus supplies posed adult expressions photographed under fixed conditions, with its sample size not stated in this paper. Both are general-population affective-computing resources with no autism component, no autism labels and no clinical ascertainment of any kind. The paper's results section mentions once, in passing, 'the Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression (ASD-FE) dataset and the Extended Cohn-Kanade (CK+) dataset adapted for ASD research', but no such dataset is described, cited, sized or characterised anywhere in the methods and no adaptation procedure is specified, while the experiments reported in the results and figures are conducted on brightness variants of KDEF and on CK+ peak frames. The sample is therefore adult, non-autistic, and posed - three respects in which it differs from the population the study's stated purpose concerns, which is autistic children experiencing spontaneous distress.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: The framing is entirely autism-focused and the content is not, which is the record's central observation. The introduction is written with some care about autistic experience: it notes that autistic people 'frequently struggle with self-regulation, emotional interpretation, and understanding and labeling others' emotions', and that 'these differences can lead to social withdrawal, especially when others react negatively to the atypical responses of individuals with ASD' - which locates part of the difficulty in other people's reactions rather than solely in the autistic person, a formulation better than most in this corpus. The conclusion likewise frames the goal as addressing 'the existing challenges faced by conventional facial expression recognition systems when applied to ASD populations, where nuanced facial cues may be misinterpreted or overlooked', which correctly identifies a technology failure rather than a personal deficit. Against this, autism is described as 'a neurological illness', and the phrase 'the minor changes and quirks typical of the facial movements' of autistic people is dismissive. No autistic person is reported as involved, and no autistic person's face appears in the data.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Not applicable to a study with no clinical groups, and unreported for the corpora used. No age distribution, sex composition or ancestry is given for either KDEF or CK+, although both are documented in their originating publications. The one demographic fact that matters here is implicit and unremarked: both corpora consist of adult volunteers, while the paper's motivating application concerns autistic children, so the modelled population differs from the target population by several decades of facial development as well as by diagnosis.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None is required by the task as executed, since no autism classification is attempted - the labels are posed emotion categories, which are a strong ground truth for emotion recognition and carry no information about autism. The consequence for this review is that the study cannot contribute evidence on any of the diagnostic questions. Its relevance is instead to the review's treatment of how autism framing attaches to work containing no autism data: a reader relying on the title, abstract, keywords and conclusion would record this as an autism study, and it is not one.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists, and none could, since no clinical population was studied.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated aim is to improve recognition of altered facial expressions in autistic people, on the argument that conventional systems misread the nuanced cues that autistic faces produce - a real and under-addressed problem, and the strongest idea in the paper. The executed work is six-way emotion classification on KDEF and CK+, reporting 99.8% accuracy, 99.8% precision, 100% recall and 94% specificity, with significance tests against CNN, linear SVM and k-nearest-neighbour baselines at p < 0.01. The gap between the two is the study's defining feature. The paper's own introduction supplies the reason the executed task cannot address the stated aim, observing that 'research indicates a lack of studies utilizing static or dynamic facial stimuli displaying real, spontaneous emotions' and that 'staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones' - after which the evaluation uses only staged emotions from instructed adult volunteers. A separate study charted in this review tests the transfer question directly and finds that affect models trained on neurotypical faces perform poorly on autistic children and improve substantially only after fine-tuning on autistic data, which is the evidence this study would have needed and did not seek.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting. Both corpora were collected under laboratory conditions by their original creators, with KDEF in particular geometrically standardised so that eyes and lips fall at fixed image coordinates across all images. That standardisation is the opposite of the conditions the paper's motivating application would face - an autistic child in spontaneous distress, filmed at whatever angle and distance the situation allows - and the mismatch is not discussed. The one robustness check reported, evaluation across four brightness variants of KDEF, addresses illumination but not pose, spontaneity, age or population.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Instructed posed expression production, as designed into both corpora. This is the canonical easy case for facial expression recognition: prototypical, maximally intense, produced deliberately, and captured at the peak frame - CK+ explicitly uses 'the peak frame of each sequence' because 'it includes the greatest information relating to emotions'. Selecting peak frames maximises separability and is standard practice for benchmarking, but it removes precisely the subtlety the paper claims to address. The paradigm gap is therefore twofold: posed rather than spontaneous, and peak rather than continuous.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element. No ethics statement appears, which is conventional for secondary use of two established consented affective-computing corpora. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition equipment. Preprocessing is described in reasonable detail - grayscale conversion, resizing to 120x110 for a Gabor filter stage and 100x100 for the convolutional network, intensity normalisation, histogram equalisation, face detection with realignment, and landmark or local binary pattern feature extraction. The two-resolution arrangement for the two processing stages is a specific and reproducible detail.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Partial. Reported: both corpora by name, CK+'s 327 sequences from 118 individuals, the peak-frame selection rule, the full preprocessing chain with both working resolutions, the quaternion algebra underpinning the optimiser given as explicit Hamilton relations, the three baseline comparators, and t-values and p-values for the comparisons. Not reported: KDEF's sample size, class distributions for either corpus, any train-test split or cross-validation scheme, the swarm optimiser's own population size and iteration count, the network's hyperparameters, how many runs contributed to the reported means, over what units the t-tests were computed, code, funding and competing interests. The mathematical apparatus is documented and the experimental protocol is not.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: There is no limitations section. The most consequential omission is the mismatch between the paper's framing and its content: every framing element - title, abstract, keywords, introduction, problem statement and conclusion - is written in terms of autistic people, while the data are posed expressions from non-autistic adults and no autism label, participant or classification target exists anywhere. The paper also identifies, in its own introduction, the reason its evaluation cannot support its aim - that staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones and that spontaneous stimuli are what the field lacks - without connecting that observation to its own design. Further unstated issues: no validation scheme, split proportion or partitioning unit is given anywhere; the reported metric combination (100% recall with 94% specificity in a six-class problem) is unusual and is presented without confusion matrices, class-wise results or a definition of multi-class specificity; the number of emotion classes is stated as six in the abstract, seven in the KDEF description and five in a CK+ figure caption; and the architecture narrative repeatedly describes the optimiser as encoding 'physiological signal characteristics' although no physiological signal is collected or used.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: None stated. The directions the study most needs are evident from its own framing: evaluate on autistic participants, evaluate on spontaneous rather than posed expression, and test whether a model optimised on posed adult faces transfers to autistic children's faces at all - the last being a question another study in this review answers negatively for a comparable pipeline.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Prototypical posed emotion in adult volunteers - anger, fear, joy, sadness, surprise and disgust - captured at peak intensity. The construct the paper claims to address is different and considerably harder: the atypical, low-intensity, idiosyncratic facial signalling that autistic people may produce and that conventional recognition systems misread. The paper states that problem clearly and does not test it. For this review the distinction matters because the two constructs have opposite difficulty profiles: posed peak-frame expression is the benchmark case on which affect recognition has long achieved very high accuracy, whereas spontaneous atypical expression in autistic children is where every reported system in this corpus degrades. A 99.8% figure on the first tells a reader nothing about the second.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: None. A single static image modality throughout. The recurring references to encoding 'physiological signal characteristics' and 'physiological signal properties' in quaternion space describe the optimiser's original application domain rather than anything in this study, where no physiological signal is acquired.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A hybrid of Weighted Quantum Particle Swarm Optimisation with a Fast Mask Recurrent Convolutional Neural Network. The optimiser's distinguishing feature is that it encodes the swarm in quaternion rather than Euclidean space, and the quaternion algebra is set out explicitly through Hamilton's relations, on the stated rationale that this concentrates the search on more productive regions. Comparison against CNN, linear SVM and k-nearest-neighbour baselines with significance tests is more than many papers in this branch offer. What is not reported is the optimiser's own configuration - population size, iteration count, inertia and weighting parameters - or the network's hyperparameters, so the mechanism credited with the improvement cannot be reproduced.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Grayscale cropped faces at 120x110 for Gabor filtering and 100x100 for convolutional processing, after normalisation, histogram equalisation, face detection and realignment. KDEF images are additionally pre-standardised by the corpus creators so that eyes and lips occupy fixed coordinates, which removes pose and scale variation entirely - a property that raises accuracy and reduces the relevance of the result to any uncontrolled setting.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy 99.8%, precision 99.8%, recall 100% and specificity 94%, with t-values and p-values against three baselines at p < 0.01. Three problems. The combination is unusual for a balanced multi-class problem - perfect recall alongside 94% specificity - and no confusion matrix, per-class breakdown or definition of multi-class specificity is supplied to make it interpretable. No confidence intervals accompany any figure, and the number of runs behind the reported means is not stated, so the significance tests cannot be assessed. And no chance baseline is given, though six-way classification would place it near 17% under balance.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No attribution, saliency, feature-importance or error analysis is reported for the classifier. The quaternion formulation is presented in mathematical detail but is a search-space construct, not an explanation of what the network responds to, and the associated claim that it captures physiological signal properties has no referent in the data.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Not assessable, because no validation scheme is described. The paper states no train-test split proportion, no cross-validation arrangement, no held-out set size and no partitioning unit anywhere. The one hint is that CK+ is used 'to test the WQPSO-FMRCNN model on unseen data' after KDEF, which would be cross-corpus evaluation - the design this review regards most highly, since it tests transfer across acquisition conditions and populations. It is not reported as a separate result, so what would have been the study's strongest methodological feature goes unquantified. Two further points bound the figures. CK+ contributes 327 peak frames from 118 individuals, roughly 2.8 images per person, and whether images of the same individual span any partition is unstated. And KDEF is geometrically standardised with eyes and lips at fixed coordinates, so a classifier operating on it faces none of the pose, scale or framing variation that any real deployment would present. A 99.8% accuracy on peak-frame posed expressions from geometrically aligned adult faces is close to the ceiling that this benchmark has long supported, and is not evidence about the harder problem the paper describes.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: hybrid WQPSO, FMRCNN, facial expression recognition, ASD, computational intelligence, healthcare. The inclusion of ASD in the keyword list, alongside an autism-framed title, ensures the paper is indexed and retrieved as autism research - which is how it entered this corpus - although it contains no autism data. That indexing effect is itself a finding for the review: searches for computational autism work will return studies of this kind, and their reported accuracies will enter informal impressions of the field's performance without ever having concerned autistic people.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Traitement du Signal 41(6), IIETA, open access under CC BY, doi 10.18280/ts.410628; received 12 April 2024, revised 7 August, accepted 20 August, available online 31 December 2024. A signal-processing venue. The review process accepted a paper whose title and abstract promise autism facial expression recognition while its experiments use two general-population posed-expression corpora; whose class count differs across three locations in the text; whose architecture narrative refers repeatedly to physiological signals that are never collected; and which states no validation scheme of any kind.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published December 2024 by a computer science and engineering group at R.M.D. Engineering College, Thiruvallur. For this review the study's value lies in what it illustrates rather than in what it measures, and two lessons carry into the synthesis. The first concerns the boundary between autism-framed and autism-evidenced work. Every framing element here - title, keywords, abstract, introduction, problem statement, conclusion - is written in terms of autistic people and the failure of conventional systems to read their faces, which is a real and under-addressed problem stated with some sympathy; and the entire experimental content is six-way emotion classification on posed expressions from non-autistic adult volunteers, evaluated at peak frames on a corpus whose images are geometrically standardised. A reader relying on title and abstract would record 99.8% as an autism result. The second concerns what such figures mean. The paper's own introduction notes that 'staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones' and that the field lacks work on spontaneous stimuli, which is precisely why 99.8% on peak-frame posed adult expressions is near the long-established ceiling for that benchmark and carries no implication for autistic children in spontaneous distress - the application the conclusion invokes. Another study charted in this review tests exactly that transfer and finds that affect models trained on neurotypical faces perform poorly on autistic children and improve materially only after fine-tuning on autistic data. Read together, the two studies make the point cleanly: the emotion-recognition benchmark is solved, the autism-relevant problem is not, and the two are frequently reported as though they were the same. Three further defects should be recorded: no validation scheme, split or partitioning unit is stated anywhere; the reported metrics (100% recall with 94% specificity across six classes) are presented without confusion matrices or class-wise results; and the number of emotion classes is given as six, seven and five in three different places.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Luongo M; Simeoli R; Marocco D; Milano N; Ponticorvo M
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional two-group classification study with a purpose-built serious game, combined with a simulation experiment in which trajectories are computationally modified to probe the causal contribution of acceleration to the model's predictions
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A sequence of 20-69 points per trajectory, each represented by two or four values, fed to a sequential neural network. Unlike the group's companion study on a different sample, which averaged trajectory features to a single vector per task, this study retains the full temporal sequence - so the model sees the shape of the movement over time rather than summary statistics.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. The discussion calls for 'further validations in real-world contexts and across larger populations' and for 'cross-validation with other diagnostic tools'.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Parents of all participants read and signed informed consent before the experiment, described as guaranteeing full understanding of their child's participation
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A purpose-built Unity 2D drag-and-drop game for tablets. The child drags an image from the screen centre at coordinate (0,0) to a target placed at one of eight positions spaced 45 degrees apart, while avoiding distractor images. A settings panel allows the experimenter to vary image category (geometric shapes, fruits or animals), the number of game scenes and the number of distractors, but identical settings were used for every participant in this study. Notably, no verbal instructions were given: 'the examiner did not provide specific instructions on how to play the game, but the child was encouraged to interact with the tablet independently, giving him the opportunity to understand the logic of the game', with a video tutorial triggered by the play button and a vibration cue on the image to be moved - both introduced explicitly 'to avoid stressful social situations and improve engagement and autonomy'. Each child completed a single session, with total duration varying between children.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: A 12.3-inch Dell Latitude tablet, raised and tilted at approximately 60 degrees to the table surface, running purpose-built software in Unity 2D and C#; finger coordinates logged at 20 Hz with asynchronous programming used for storage.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: 'The data underlying the results presented in the study are available from https://github.com/marialuongo/Trajectory-Autism' - an open repository, which is exceptional in this corpus and makes the trajectory dataset independently checkable
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not reported separately from the data
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Approved by the Ethical Committee of Psychological Research of the Department of Humanities, University of Naples Federico II
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Coordinates were rotation-normalised: the angle between consecutive points relative to the origin was computed with atan2, mapped into 0-360 degrees, and used to rotate each point, so that trajectories to targets at different angular positions become comparable. The mathematics is written out in full across three numbered equations. The two-feature model then receives only the rotated x and y coordinates; the four-feature model adds velocity and acceleration derived from them.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Strong for the study's specific question, and pursued by causal manipulation rather than attribution. Rather than asking a post-hoc method which features mattered, the authors generated synthetic trajectories with acceleration systematically varied across a stated range and measured how the models' predictions moved in response - establishing not only that acceleration matters but in which direction and with what strength for each model. The finding that the two-feature model, which has no access to acceleration, still correlates with it at r = 0.69 is an informative negative control on the ablation, showing that the difference between models is one of representational convenience rather than of information availability. The trajectory-simplification analysis at seven rates from 35% to 90% serves a similar robustness purpose. What is not done is any individual-level analysis, any error inspection, or any relation between predictions and the severity range the autistic group is said to span.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not described. Architecture details are not given in the retrieved text beyond the models being sequential neural networks distinguished by input dimensionality.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Four-fold cross-validation, chosen for the small dataset, with a validation set of 110 samples described as 15% of the 738-trajectory dataset. The unit is the trajectory, not the child: 738 trajectories come from 20 children, roughly 37 each, and nothing indicates that a child's trajectories were kept within a fold. Under a random trajectory-level split, each validation trajectory has approximately 36 siblings from the same child in training. No participant-level result is reported.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A dedicated limitations passage naming four constraints. Small sample size, stated first. Exclusive reliance on a tablet as the motion-tracking device, with the suggestion that a more extensive data-collection approach would allow more accurate analysis even from raw data alone. The absence of longitudinal observation, with the recommendation that the sample be expanded and followed over time. And the absence of complementary measures, with a specific proposal that manual and ocular movement data be coordinated to give information about hand-eye movement patterns. The authors also call for cross-validation against other diagnostic tools.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Twenty children aged 3-6, recruited between 13 February and 21 March 2023: 10 autistic (mean age 4 years, SD 0.94) from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center where they were receiving psychomotor and speech therapy, and 10 typically developing (mean 3 years 9 months, SD 0.1) from a pre-primary and primary educational institute in the province of Naples. Inclusion for the autistic group required a clinical diagnosis, age 3-6 and absence of comorbid conditions; the only criterion for the comparison group was parent and teacher report of no neurodevelopmental disorder, with the paper stating explicitly that they were recruited 'without specific assessment of their pre-existing abilities'. The modelled unit is not the child but the trajectory: 738 trajectories were retained after filtering, roughly 37 per child, and a further set of computationally generated trajectories brought the correlation analysis to 932 samples. Twenty children is the smallest sample of any included study in this review, and the discrepancy between 20 participants and 738 modelling units is the central interpretive issue.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'Children with autism', 'children with a diagnosis of autism' and 'individuals with ASD', person-first and consistent, alongside 'typically developing (TD) children'. Autism is 'a complex and heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder' with the standard two-domain description, and motor differences are called 'motor abnormalities' and 'motor disorders'.
