The framing is otherwise notably measured and contains one argument worth recording: the paper's opening critique is that autism diagnosis 'is based on subjective observations of behavior' focused on the two core domains, and that 'many other characteristics are overlooked in the diagnostic process, considered non-central to the disorder' - specifically motor characteristics, which 'have always been considered secondary symptoms and not closely related to the syndrome' despite evidence that they precede language and social difficulties. That is an argument for widening what is measured rather than for replacing clinicians, and it is grounded in embodied-cognition theory rather than in an appeal to objectivity alone. The paper also reports the literature on visuospatial ability in autism honestly as conflicting - some studies finding deficits, some no difference, some better performance - rather than selecting the supportive citations. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Thin, and thinner for the comparison group than for the autistic group. Reported: group sizes, age means and standard deviations, recruitment source, and for the autistic group the requirement of an ADOS-2-confirmed diagnosis and absence of comorbidity. Not reported: sex, IQ, developmental level, language ability, socioeconomic status, race or ethnicity, or any severity score. Two features of what is reported deserve attention. The autistic group's age standard deviation is 0.94 years against 0.1 for the comparison group - nearly a tenfold difference in spread - so although the means differ by only three months the autistic group spans a much wider developmental range, which matters for a fine-motor outcome in children aged 3 to 6 where motor control changes rapidly. And no cognitive or developmental assessment was performed on either group; the comparison children were recruited without any assessment of pre-existing abilities, and the autistic group's functioning is inferred rather than measured, from the fact that all 'were able to engage with a tablet, suggesting a moderate level of functioning'. Since the outcome is the smoothness and dynamics of a dragging movement, and both groups were selected without reference to developmental level, a general developmental explanation for the difference cannot be separated from an autism-specific one. A further asymmetry is that the autistic children were undergoing psychomotor therapy at the recruiting centre - direct motor intervention - while the comparison children were not.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Solid for the autistic group and absent for the comparison group. Autism required a clinical diagnosis confirmed with the ADOS-2, and the paper states something few in this review do: the diagnoses were made 'by healthcare professionals and industry experts who were independent of our research laboratory and study'. Explicit independence between the diagnosing clinicians and the research team removes one route by which knowledge of the study could influence the reference standard, and is worth crediting. Against this, no ADOS-2 score of any kind is reported, so the severity range the autistic group is said to span cannot be characterised; comorbidity was excluded by criterion, narrowing the sample relative to the clinical population; and typically developing status rests entirely on parent and teacher report of no neurodevelopmental disorder, with no screening instrument administered and no assessment of abilities - so undetected autistic traits or developmental difficulty in the comparison group cannot be ruled out.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None for either group. No IQ, developmental quotient, language, adaptive or severity measure was obtained, and the paper says so implicitly by describing the autistic group's functioning as inferred from their ability to use a tablet. The absence has two specific costs in this design. Because the outcome is fine motor kinematics in 3-6 year olds and neither group was assessed developmentally, the difference between groups cannot be attributed to autism rather than to general developmental level - and the autistic group's much wider age spread makes this more rather than less pressing. And because the autistic group is described as covering 'a range of symptom severity levels within the spectrum' without any score, the natural question of whether the model's confidence tracks severity cannot be asked, even though the study's simulation methodology is well suited to it.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Two objectives, both methodological rather than clinical. First, to test whether raw motion trajectories alone - unprocessed x and y coordinates - carry enough information to classify autistic from typically developing children, or whether derived kinematic features are needed; the comparison is motivated by the group's own prior work, which had found that maximum and minimum acceleration and standard deviations of speed and acceleration were the leading contributors in a feature-based model. Second, to test the specific role of acceleration by generating synthetic trajectories with systematically varied acceleration and observing how the models respond. Findings: the four-feature model reached 0.90 accuracy against 0.76 for the two-feature model, with a consistently higher fold-wise distribution and a better ROC curve, so derived features help substantially. But the simulation analysis complicates the simple reading: acceleration correlated with the two-feature model's predictions at r = 0.69 despite that model never receiving acceleration as an input, and with the four-feature model's at r = 0.82, both at p < 0.001 over 932 samples, with higher acceleration increasing the probability of an autism prediction in both. So the information is present in the raw coordinate sequence and the four-feature representation makes it easier to use rather than supplying something new - a conclusion the authors reach and state, writing that their findings 'support the potential of raw data analysis in objectively assessing motor behaviors related to autism' while the four-feature model 'excels'.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Two recruitment sites in the Naples area with a familiar asymmetry: autistic children from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center, which is also a co-author affiliation and where the children were receiving psychomotor and speech therapy, and comparison children from a mainstream pre-primary and primary school. The testing arrangement is described in unusual physical detail - table height 45-60 cm adjusted to the child's age, experimenter seated to the child's right at about 30 cm, a 12.3-inch tablet raised and tilted at approximately 60 degrees to give a full view of the game - and this level of specification is a genuine reproducibility asset. One element of it is also a small confound: adjusting table height by age introduces a systematic postural difference correlated with a variable whose spread differs sharply between groups. The wider recruitment geometry is the standard clinic-versus-school case-control arrangement, compounded here by the autistic group receiving active motor therapy at the recruiting site.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A purpose-built drag-and-drop game, and the design reasoning behind it is the paradigm's most valuable feature. The child drags an image from the screen centre to a target at one of eight positions spaced 45 degrees apart while avoiding distractors, with the settings panel allowing category, scene count and distractor number to be varied - all held constant here. Three design decisions address problems that recur throughout this review. No verbal instructions were given: the examiner deliberately withheld them so the child could work out the game's logic independently, and the two support mechanisms provided - a video tutorial triggered by the play button and a vibration cue on the image to be moved - were introduced explicitly 'to avoid stressful social situations and improve engagement and autonomy'. Designing the elicitation to minimise social demand, in a study measuring motor rather than social behaviour, removes a confound that several other studies here carry unexamined. The eight-target arrangement at fixed angular spacing then makes rotation normalisation possible, so trajectories to different targets become comparable - a design choice that pays off directly in the analysis. And recording is restricted to completed drags from image to target, with incomplete drags and stray touches excluded, so the measured behaviour is well defined. The costs are that session duration varied between children without being modelled, and that a single session per child leaves no within-child stability estimate.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session per child, with recruitment compressed into five weeks. No follow-up and no test-retest reliability for any kinematic measure - which the authors identify as a limitation and address directly, recommending that 'the sample should be expanded and observed longitudinally'. Governance is complete: approval by the Ethical Committee of Psychological Research of the Department of Humanities at the University of Naples Federico II, written informed consent from parents of all participants described as guaranteeing full understanding, funding from two named sources with an explicit statement that the funders had no role in design, data collection, analysis, publication decision or manuscript preparation, and a declaration of no competing interests. The data are deposited in a public GitHub repository, which is the only open data release among the included studies in this review.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: A 12.3-inch Dell Latitude tablet running purpose-built software written in Unity 2D and C#, logging finger x and y coordinates at 20 Hz with asynchronous programming used for storage so that recording did not degrade game performance. No sensor, marker, camera or wearable is involved. The 20 Hz sampling rate is modest - one sample every 50 ms - and bounds what can be said about rapid acceleration changes, though it is adequate for the trajectory-shape features the study models. No analysis software or framework is named, and the neural network architectures are not specified in the retrieved text, which is the one substantive gap in an otherwise well-documented apparatus.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Among the strongest in this review, and uniquely so on data. Reproducible from the text: exact recruitment dates, inclusion criteria for both groups, the game platform and task geometry with eight targets at 45-degree spacing, the settings panel contents and the statement that identical settings were used for all participants, the tablet model and its 60-degree tilt, the table-height range and experimenter position, the 20 Hz sampling rate, all three data-inclusion rules including the 20-69 point trajectory-length window, the rotation normalisation written out across three numbered equations with the atan2 construction and the angle-range mapping, both feature sets, the four-fold cross-validation with its 110-sample validation size, the acceleration-variation range for the simulation, and the seven trajectory-simplification rates. The trajectory data are published on GitHub at a stated URL - the only open data release among included studies here, and one that makes the central claim independently checkable. Not reported: the network architectures, training hyperparameters, seeds, and, critically, whether cross-validation folds were constructed by child or by trajectory.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The stated limitations are four and are well chosen: small sample size, exclusive reliance on a tablet as the tracking device, the absence of longitudinal observation, and the absence of complementary measures - with the specific and useful suggestion that manual and ocular movement data be coordinated to characterise hand-eye patterns. The authors also call for cross-validation against other diagnostic tools. What is not addressed is the relationship between 20 children and 738 modelling units. Cross-validation partitions trajectories, and with roughly 37 trajectories per child each validation trajectory has around 36 siblings from the same child in training; movement kinematics are close to an individual motor signature at this granularity, so a model can separate children rather than groups and report high accuracy. No participant-level result appears anywhere, and the paper does not state whether folds respected child boundaries. Three further omissions matter. Neither group received any developmental or cognitive assessment, and the comparison children were recruited explicitly without assessment of pre-existing abilities, so a general developmental explanation cannot be excluded in a fine-motor task with 3-6 year olds. The autistic group's age standard deviation is nearly ten times the comparison group's, so the groups differ in developmental spread. And the autistic children were receiving psychomotor therapy at the recruiting centre while the comparison children were not, confounding motor training with diagnosis in a study of motor kinematics - the same confound this review recorded in the group's companion study on a different sample, and unaddressed in both.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Four directions, all concrete and following from stated limitations. Expand the sample and observe it longitudinally, to establish predictive capacity over time. Move beyond a single tablet as the tracking device, on the reasoning that richer data collection would improve analysis even from raw coordinates. Coordinate complementary measures, specifically manual and ocular movement data together, to characterise hand-eye patterns - a well-targeted proposal given that the drag-and-drop task is inherently visuomotor and the study measures only the manual half. And cross-validate against other diagnostic tools. Not proposed, and needed: participant-level validation, developmental assessment of both groups, and relating model output to the severity range the autistic sample is said to span.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Fine motor control during goal-directed touchscreen dragging, represented as a full temporal sequence rather than as summary statistics. The behavioural claim is that motor differences in autism are prevalent, early-appearing - present 'even before the onset of language and social interaction difficulties' - and clinically neglected, with the paper stating that despite their relevance 'currently there are no adequate tools available to accurately assess motor function in children with autism'. The theoretical grounding is embodied cognition: how a person moves shapes how they learn from and explore the environment, so motor patterns are informative about cognition rather than peripheral to it. Empirically the study localises the signal to acceleration: synthetic trajectories with higher average acceleration are more likely to be classified as autistic, with correlations of 0.69 and 0.82 for the two models. That is a specific, directional and testable behavioural claim - faster or more abruptly accelerating dragging movements are associated with autism in this sample - and it is arrived at by manipulation rather than by correlation with observed data. Two things the representation does not capture: the visual half of the visuomotor task, since only finger position is recorded and gaze is not, which the authors identify as the priority extension; and any measure of task success beyond the requirement that a drag reach its target.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No cross-sensor fusion. The study's ablation is between two representations of the same signal - raw coordinates alone versus coordinates plus velocity and acceleration - and its result is more interesting than a simple fusion gain. The four-feature model outperforms the two-feature model substantially (0.90 versus 0.76), which would ordinarily be read as the derived features adding information. But the simulation analysis shows that acceleration correlates with the two-feature model's predictions at r = 0.69 even though that model never receives acceleration as an input, so the information is already present in the raw coordinate sequence and is being recovered from it. The 14-point accuracy difference therefore reflects how easily a network of this size and training regime can extract a derivative from a 20 Hz position sequence, not what information the sequence contains. That is a genuinely useful distinction for the review's treatment of feature engineering: it shows a case where explicit derived features improve performance without adding information, which is the opposite of the usual assumption and is established by manipulation rather than asserted. The authors' own conclusion follows this reading, noting that raw data analysis has potential while the four-feature model excels.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Two artificial neural networks trained on sequential data, differing only in input dimensionality - two features (rotated x and y coordinates) versus four (adding velocity and acceleration). No architecture details, layer counts, activation functions, optimiser or training hyperparameters are given in the retrieved text, which is the study's main reporting gap and is conspicuous against the exceptional specification of the task, the preprocessing and the simulation procedure. No alternative model families are compared and no baseline classifier is reported. The modelling is deliberately minimal because the study's question is representational rather than architectural: whether raw trajectories suffice. Given 20 children, keeping the model simple is the right choice, but the absence of any specification means the comparison between the two models cannot be checked for confounds such as differing capacity or training duration.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A rotation-normalised sequence of 20-69 points per trajectory. The rotation step is the representational contribution and is worked out carefully: because targets sit at eight positions 45 degrees apart, raw trajectories to different targets are not comparable, so the angle between consecutive points relative to the origin is computed with atan2, mapped from the atan2 range into 0-360 degrees, and applied as a rotation - with all three steps written out as numbered equations and the resulting endpoint coordinates given. This makes trajectories to any target directly comparable while preserving their shape, and it is the kind of preprocessing that reflects thought about the construct rather than convention. The two-feature model then receives only these rotated coordinates and the four-feature model adds velocity and acceleration. Crucially, unlike the group's companion study on a different sample - which averaged twelve kinematic features across a task to give one vector per child - this study preserves the full temporal sequence, so the model sees the unfolding of the movement rather than its summary. The 20-69 point length window standardises comparability at the cost of discarding both very brief and very extended drags.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Binary accuracy, reported as a distribution across cross-validation folds rather than as a single point, which conveys stability better than a bare figure; ROC curves for both models; and Pearson correlations with p-values for the acceleration analysis. Reporting the fold-wise distribution is good practice and is rare in this corpus. But the metric set is otherwise thin for a diagnostic claim: no sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1 or confusion matrix is given, so the error profile is unknown and it cannot be determined whether the models fail preferentially on autistic or comparison trajectories; no AUC value is quoted despite ROC curves being plotted; and no confidence interval accompanies either headline accuracy. No majority-class baseline is stated. Since the modelled unit is the trajectory rather than the child, no participant-level metric of any kind is available - which is the figure a clinical claim would require.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: The strongest element of the study, and methodologically distinctive. Rather than applying a post-hoc attribution method, the authors manipulate the input: synthetic trajectories are generated with average acceleration systematically varied between -5 and +5 cm/s squared, and the models' predictions are measured as a function of that variation, yielding correlations of r = 0.69 and r = 0.82 with a stated direction - higher acceleration increases the probability of an autism prediction. This is causal rather than correlational evidence about the model's decision function, it is quantified, and it is directional. A second robustness analysis simplifies trajectories at seven rates from 35% to 90% and re-tests, with generated trajectories under 20 points excluded. And the analysis produces an informative incidental finding: the two-feature model, which has no acceleration input, still correlates with acceleration at 0.69, showing that the raw sequence carries the information. What is absent is any individual-level interpretation - no error analysis, no examination of which children were misclassified, and no relation between predictions and the severity range the autistic group reportedly spans.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The decisive weakness, and it is structural rather than procedural. The dataset is 738 trajectories from 20 children, roughly 37 each, and evaluation uses four-fold cross-validation with a 110-sample validation set described as 15% of the trajectory dataset. The unit is explicitly the trajectory: the validation size is quoted in samples out of 738, and nothing in the paper indicates that a child's trajectories were kept within a fold. Under a random trajectory-level split, each validation trajectory is accompanied by approximately 36 siblings produced by the same child in the same session with the same hand, differing only in which of eight targets was approached - and after rotation normalisation even that difference is removed. Fine motor kinematics at this granularity function close to an individual motor signature, so a model can separate children rather than groups and report high accuracy; the reported 0.90 is therefore not an estimate of performance on a child the model has not seen, and no participant-level figure appears anywhere. With only 20 children, a participant-disjoint scheme would have been straightforward - leave-one-child-out would give exactly 20 folds - and would have produced the number a clinical claim requires. Three secondary points compound this. No chance baseline, confidence interval or class-conditional metric accompanies either accuracy. The simulation and simplification analyses, which are the study's strongest contribution, are conducted on the same trained models and the same underlying trajectories. And the two feature sets were compared without model architecture being specified, so the 14-point difference cannot be checked against differences in capacity. The corrective is simple and the open data release makes it possible for others to perform: partition the 20 children, retrain, and report participant-level accuracy alongside sensitivity and specificity.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: No formal keyword list appears in the retrieved text. The organising terms are raw motion data, motor trajectories, drag and drop, artificial neural networks, embodied cognition, sensorimotor activity, serious game, simulated trajectories, and early autism diagnosis. The framing vocabulary is drawn from developmental psychology and cognitive science rather than from machine learning, and 'raw' does substantial work in the title and throughout - the study's question is precisely whether unprocessed coordinates suffice.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: PLOS ONE 19(4), article e0302238, published 22 April 2024; received 9 January 2024, accepted 28 March 2024, open access under CC BY, with a named academic editor. The venue's requirements produce the data availability statement with its GitHub URL, the funder no-role statement and the competing-interests declaration - and the first of these is what makes this the only included study in the review with openly published data. Eighteen pages, with substantial space given to the theoretical framing, the task design and the preprocessing mathematics, and comparatively little to the model architecture, which is not specified.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2024 by the Natural and Artificial Cognition Lab in the Department of Humanistic Study at the University of Naples Federico II with the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Research and Rehabilitation Center, funded by a PNRR MUR project and a University of Naples internal line. Three of the five authors also appear on the variational-autoencoder study charted elsewhere in this review, and both studies recruit autistic participants from the same rehabilitation centre - though the samples, tasks and analyses differ, so this is a related programme rather than a reanalysis. The framing is a clinical-gap argument rather than an accuracy claim: motor differences are prevalent in autism and appear before language and social difficulties, yet they are treated as secondary symptoms and 'there are no adequate tools available to accurately assess motor function in children with autism' - so the contribution sought is an instrument for something currently unmeasured, not a replacement for something already measured. That is a more defensible position than most in this corpus and it is grounded in embodied-cognition theory rather than in appeals to objectivity. For the review the study's value is threefold. It is the only included study to publish its data openly, at a stated GitHub URL, which makes its central claim independently checkable and sets a standard the rest of the corpus does not meet. Its causal-manipulation interpretability method - generating synthetic trajectories with systematically varied acceleration and measuring how predictions respond - is a template other studies could adopt in place of post-hoc attribution. And its incidental finding that a model without acceleration as an input still correlates with acceleration at r = 0.69 is a useful counterweight to the assumption, common across this literature, that a feature-engineering gain means additional information rather than easier access to information already present. Set against these, its 738 trajectories come from 20 children and are partitioned by trajectory rather than by child, so the headline 0.90 is not an estimate of performance on an unseen child - and with only 20 participants, leave-one-child-out validation would have been trivial to perform.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Dedgaonkar S; Sachdeo R
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Algorithm-development study presented as a detection model; a metaheuristic optimisation contribution (a hybrid of artificial bee colony and honey badger algorithms) applied to feature selection and neural network weight tuning, evaluated on an undescribed dataset
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A tabular feature vector per individual; no temporal, sequential or image representation
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported anywhere in the paper. Table 2 displays five individuals as illustrative samples, but no total is given at any point.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: None stated
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None described. No stimulus, task, protocol or elicitation condition is reported, so it is unknown what the individuals were doing when their expressions, heart rate and temperature were recorded.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Not reported. No camera, expression-recognition system, heart rate monitor or thermometer is named.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not reported
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: None stated. Data described as collected manually from human subjects including physiological measurements, with no ethics committee, approval reference or governance statement of any kind.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Eleven variables per individual are shown in Table 2: seven emotion probabilities, positive and negative emotion aggregates, body temperature and heartbeat rate. The optimisation stage then selects an optimal subset by resolving a fitness function combining correlation, data variance, and inter- and intra-class cosine similarity.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None. No feature importance, attribution or error analysis is reported, and the selected feature subset is never named. Because the optimisation stage explicitly selects features, the identity of the selected subset would have been the single most informative output and it is not given.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The optimisation algorithm is itself the tuning mechanism, adjusting hidden neuron count, DNN and RNN weights and RNN epoch count. Its own parameters - acceleration coefficient, constant, iteration count - are not specified with values.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Ambiguous and inconsistently described. One passage reports varying the 'learning percentage' across five values with the complement used for testing, illustrated with 65% training and 35% testing. Another passage defines 5-fold cross-validation among the evaluation measures. Neither is tied to the reported headline figures, and no unit of splitting is stated - which is in any case unrecoverable, since the number of individuals contributing the data is never given.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: None. There is no limitations section and no constraint on the findings is identified.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Not reported. The paper states only that 'different data utilized for the analysis are collected manually, including physical and facial expression data' and that measurements 'are collected from various subjects'. No total sample size, no group sizes, no recruitment route, no eligibility criteria and no setting appear anywhere in the paper. Table 2 displays five individuals as illustrative samples, of whom three are labelled 'Detected' and two 'Not detected', but these are presented as examples of the data format rather than as the study population. A reader cannot determine whether the reported 96.44886% accuracy was computed on tens or thousands of individuals. This is the only included study in the review that reports no sample size at all.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'ASD-affected individuals' and 'autism-affected individuals' predominate, with 'ASD-affected children', 'affected children' and 'the individual affected with ASD' appearing throughout - a consistently affliction-framed register. Autism is described as affecting 'the neurological function and also the speech function of children' and as leading to 'uncontrolled aggressive behavior in the affected children', and the case for early detection is made in explicitly economic and burden terms: undetected autism 'may create more economic pressure, affect the family relationship, and also become a burden in social and medical care', and 'the occurrence of ASD has brought a large economic and mental burden to society that leads to severe public health problems'. Elsewhere autism is referred to as a 'defect' and as 'disease growth'. This is the most consistently deficit- and burden-oriented framing in the review, and it is paired with the conflation of autism and sensory processing disorder into a single detection target. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: None. No age, sex, race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, cognitive level, language ability, severity or comorbidity information appears for any individual, and no statement acknowledges the absence. The only individual-level variables reported anywhere are the eleven columns of Table 2 - seven emotion probabilities, two emotion aggregates, body temperature and heart rate - shown for five people.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None. The label is a binary 'Detected' or 'Not detected' for a combined 'autism and visual SPD' construct, with no diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician, assessment or source described. Two features of the labelling deserve specific note. First, the target conflates two distinct conditions - autism and visual sensory processing disorder - into a single undifferentiated binary, so even if the label were valid it would not identify which condition a positive prediction refers to, and the paper nowhere addresses how a model trained on a merged label could support either diagnosis. Second, the dataset section asserts that 'a new dataset named AQ10 is developed based on autism screening performed in individuals and holds 20 features', which conflates a dataset with the AQ-10, an existing published autism screening questionnaire, and in any case none of the AQ-10 items appears among the eleven variables the paper actually shows. The quantity being predicted is therefore undefined.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No severity, cognitive, language or adaptive measure exists, and the binary target does not distinguish autism from sensory processing disorder, let alone grade either.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated aim is a detection model for autism and visual sensory processing disorder that combines facial expression data with heart rate and body temperature, using a purpose-designed hybrid optimisation algorithm to select features and tune network parameters. Findings: the proposed method reached 96.44886% accuracy, 96.2963% sensitivity, 96.50485% specificity and 91% precision. Four metaheuristic comparators using the identical network architecture clustered within one percentage point (95.45-95.74%), and four conventional classifiers were substantially lower (81.5-86.6%). The tight clustering of the metaheuristic variants is the most interpretable result in the paper: it indicates that the choice among optimisation algorithms contributes about one accuracy point while the network architecture contributes about ten, which somewhat undercuts the paper's central claim that the novel optimiser is the contribution. Against this, the results cannot be evaluated because the dataset on which they were computed is never described, and the two accounts of the validation scheme - a variable learning-percentage split illustrated at 65/35, and 5-fold cross-validation defined among the evaluation measures - are not reconciled or tied to the reported figures.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Not reported. No site, clinic, laboratory, school or other setting is named, and the data collection is described only as manual. The authors are at engineering departments in Pune, India, with no clinical affiliation listed.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: None described. The paper does not state what the individuals were doing when their facial expressions, heart rate and body temperature were recorded - whether they were viewing stimuli, engaged in a task, at rest, or in any other condition. This matters directly for the variables measured: emotion probabilities, heart rate and body temperature are all state-dependent, so without knowing the eliciting condition their values are uninterpretable, and any systematic difference in condition between the two label groups would be indistinguishable from a group effect.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional as far as can be determined; no temporal structure is described. There is no ethics approval statement, no ethics committee, no consent statement and no governance description of any kind, for a study that reports manual collection of physiological measurements - heart rate and body temperature - and facial data from human subjects. This is the most complete governance absence among included studies that involve primary data collection. No funding or competing-interests statement appears either.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Not reported. No camera, facial expression recognition software, heart rate monitor, thermometer or any other instrument is named, and no computational environment or framework is specified. The optimisation algorithm and network are described mathematically but nothing is said about their implementation.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Sharply divided and instructively so. The computational contribution is documented in detail: the density-factor update equation, the threshold rule switching between artificial bee colony and honey badger updates at alpha = 0.5, the network composition, and all ten evaluation metrics written out as numbered equations with their standard definitions. A reader could reimplement the algorithm. Nothing about the data is available: no sample size, no participants, no collection procedure, no equipment, no task, no label provenance, no code and no dataset. The paper specifies exactly how a number was computed and not at all what it was computed on, which is the inverse of the profile this review has found in the clinically led studies.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: There is no limitations section and no constraint is acknowledged. The unaddressed problems begin with the impossibility of assessment: without a sample size, participant description, recruitment procedure, task, equipment or diagnostic standard, the study cannot be evaluated, replicated or interpreted, and its reported metrics - given to five decimal places - have no stated denominator. The target conflates autism with visual sensory processing disorder into one binary label. The validation scheme is described twice in mutually inconsistent terms and neither description is connected to the reported results. Feature selection optimises a fitness function involving inter- and intra-class similarity, which requires class labels, with no statement that this was confined to training data. No ethics approval or consent is reported for manual collection of physiological and facial data from human participants. And the paper's own worked example is the clearest evidence about what its labels track: of the five individuals in Table 2, the three labelled 'Detected' have body temperatures of 100.4, 95.5 and 103 with heart rates of 102, 62 and 133, while the two labelled 'Not detected' have 98.5 and 99.5 with heart rates of 85 and 89. Two of the three positives are febrile or hypothermic and two are tachycardic; both negatives are within normal range on both measures. In the only data the paper displays, the label separates people with abnormal vital signs from people without.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: None stated.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Nominally facial emotional expression, reduced to seven probability values per individual across angry, disgust, fear, happy, neutral, sad and surprise, plus derived positive and negative emotion aggregates. But no elicitation condition, stimulus, recording apparatus or expression-recognition method is described, so it is unknown what produced these probabilities or what the individuals were expressing about. Two physiological variables sit alongside them, and the paper's framing does not distinguish behaviour from physiology at any point - facial expressions and 'sensory data of heart rate and body temperature' are treated as interchangeable inputs to a detection model. The theoretical discussion also concerns recognition of emotions in others ('impaired identification of sad and fearful expressions', 'facial affect identification deficiency'), which is a perceptual capacity, while the measured variables are expression production; the paper does not note the distinction.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Three data sources are concatenated - emotion probabilities, heart rate and body temperature - with no ablation isolating their contributions, no rationale for combining state physiology with expression measures, and no reporting of which features the optimisation stage selected. Since the selected feature subset is the explicit output of the paper's central algorithmic contribution, its omission is the study's most conspicuous reporting gap: the method is designed to identify essential features and never says which they were. The one available clue is Table 2, where the physiological variables separate the two label groups cleanly and the emotion probabilities do not obviously do so.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A metaheuristic contribution presented as a detection model. DF-ABHBO hybridises artificial bee colony with the honey badger algorithm, motivated by the observation that the former suffers from local optima and slows under sequential processing while the latter offers dynamic and global search, and switching between them according to an adaptive density factor thresholded at 0.5. This tunes the hidden neuron count and weights of a deep neural network, and the weights and epoch count of a recurrent network, which together form HWODNRN. The comparison against PSO, WOA, ABC and HBO variants of the same architecture is the appropriate ablation for an optimisation contribution and shows differences under one percentage point, while the comparison against decision tree, ANN, RNN and ensemble learning shows ten-point differences - so the architecture rather than the optimiser accounts for most of the reported advantage, a reading the paper does not draw.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A tabular vector of eleven variables per individual, reduced by the optimisation-based selection stage to an unnamed subset. The fitness function combines correlation, data variance and inter- and intra-class cosine similarity, which is a reasonable multi-objective formulation for filter-style selection but depends on class labels and is therefore a candidate leakage route if applied outside training folds - a question the paper does not address. No temporal, sequential or image representation is used, so whatever dynamics the underlying facial or physiological recordings contained are absent from the model input.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Ten metrics defined by numbered equation - accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, false positive rate, false negative rate, negative predictive value, false discovery rate, F1-score and Matthews correlation coefficient - reported across two comparison tables to five decimal places. The precision of the reporting is inversely related to its informativeness: five decimal places imply a sample size in the hundreds of thousands, while the sample size is never stated. The metrics are also internally revealing in one respect: precision of 91% alongside sensitivity of 96.3% and specificity of 96.5% implies a positive class comprising roughly a quarter of the sample, information the paper does not supply directly. Three different headline figures appear - 96% accuracy with 93% F1 in the abstract, 96.44% accuracy with 91% precision in the conclusion, and 96.44886% with 91% in Table 3 - and the abstract's F1 value is not reproduced anywhere else. No confusion matrix, confidence interval or AUC appears.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No feature importance, attribution or error analysis is reported. The omission is particularly consequential here because the paper's central algorithmic claim is that its optimiser identifies 'the most essential features', and the identity of those features is never disclosed - so the one output that would connect the computational contribution to any clinical or behavioural interpretation is withheld. Given that the paper's only displayed data show the label tracking body temperature and heart rate rather than emotion probabilities, naming the selected features would have been directly informative about what the model detects.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Not assessable, and not assessable in a stronger sense than any other study in this review. The paper gives two accounts of its evaluation that are not reconciled: one describing a variable 'learning percentage' divided into five values with the complement used for testing, illustrated at 65% training and 35% testing; and another defining 5-fold cross-validation within the list of evaluation measures. Neither is linked to the reported figures, and neither states a unit of splitting - which is unrecoverable in any case, since the number of individuals contributing the data is never given, so it cannot be determined whether the rows being split are people or repeated measurements from people. Feature selection optimises a fitness function that uses inter- and intra-class similarity, and therefore class labels, with no statement that it was confined to training partitions. No chance baseline, class distribution, confusion matrix or confidence interval is reported. Underneath all of this lies the fact that the reported 96.44886% accuracy has no stated denominator: a reader cannot say whether it was computed on ten individuals or ten thousand, nor what proportion of them carried each label, nor what condition they were in when measured. The figure is not an estimate of anything that can be identified.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism and visual sensory processing disorder, density factor-based artificial bee honey badger optimization, hybrid weight optimized deep neural recurrent network, multi-objective function, optimal feature selection. Four of five name the paper's own coined methods; none names a behaviour, a clinical construct or an application. The keyword list accurately reflects the paper's centre of gravity, which is metaheuristic optimisation rather than autism.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Intelligent Decision Technologies 18(1):533-559, IOS Press, 2024; received 26 September 2022, accepted 28 October 2023 - a thirteen-month review at a decision-technologies journal outside the clinical and biomedical literature. Twenty-seven pages, of which the great majority document the optimisation algorithm, the network architecture and the metric definitions, with a single paragraph and one five-row table describing the data. The venue explains the balance and the absence of clinical reporting conventions; it does not explain the absence of a sample size, which no venue's norms would require to be omitted.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2024 by computer science and engineering departments at MIT-ADT University and the Vishwakarma Institute of Information Technology, Pune, with no funding statement and no clinical collaboration. The framing is the economic-burden argument in its strongest form in this review: undetected autism 'may create more economic pressure, affect the family relationship, and also become a burden in social and medical care', and the condition 'has brought a large economic and mental burden to society'. For the review the study is worth recording for three reasons, none of them to do with its result. It is the only included study that reports no sample size at all, which marks the outer limit of what this literature will publish. Its target conflates autism with visual sensory processing disorder into a single binary label, which no other included study does and which makes even a valid result uninterpretable clinically. And its one worked data table shows the three 'Detected' individuals carrying body temperatures of 100.4, 95.5 and 103 and heart rates of 102, 62 and 133 against 98.5 and 99.5 with heart rates of 85 and 89 for the two 'Not detected' - so in the only data the paper displays, the label separates abnormal from normal vital signs. Read alongside the facial-photograph studies charted here, it indicates that the segment of this literature driven by algorithmic novelty rather than by a clinical question can reach the high nineties on data it does not describe, with a target it does not define, and pass peer review at a journal with a thirteen-month review period.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Omotehinwa TO; Lawrence MO; Oyewola DO; Dada EG
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: Journal of Computational Mathematics and Data Science, 13, Article 100105
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective algorithm-development study on four public tabular screening datasets, comparing baseline against Bayesian-optimised architectures, with deployment of a public-facing diagnostic web tool
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A 17-dimensional tabular vector per respondent, comprising ten binary item scores plus registration metadata
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Four bands: 18-36 months, 4-11 years, 12-16 years, and 17 years and older
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 2,154 instances across four datasets - toddler 1,054, children 292, adolescent 104, adult 704
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. Four datasets are used but each is modelled separately with its own age-specific model, so no cross-dataset or cross-population transfer is tested.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Toddler 326, children 151, adolescent 41, adult 515
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. Respondents completed a screening questionnaire.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None. The screening data were collected through mobile and web screening applications by third parties.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: All four datasets are public on the UCI Machine Learning Repository and Kaggle
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not reported; a deployed web tool is described and figured
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not stated. The datasets are public aggregations of screening-app responses collected by third parties.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Feature selection, categorical encoding and missing-value imputation, with the 'Who_completed_the_test' field among those discussed
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None reported. No feature-importance, attribution or ablation analysis is presented, and dropping the item fields to test what the remaining metadata contribute is not attempted - which would have been the single most informative experiment available, since it would have separated any genuine signal in the registration metadata from the arithmetic recovery of the label from the items.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Tree-structured Parzen Estimator, argued as an adaptive alternative to the exhaustive grid search used in prior work on these datasets, which the authors correctly describe as 'computation-intensive and inefficient'
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: An 80/20 train-test split per dataset, with the resulting partition sizes tabulated for all four bands (843/211, 233/59, 83/21, 563/141). The unit is the respondent and each contributes one row, so no within-participant leakage arises, and the splits are reported completely - both of which are better practice than much of this corpus. None of it bears on the reported result, because the outcome variable in these datasets is computed from the input variables: the class is the summed A1-A10 score thresholded at the instrument's cut-off, and the summed score itself ('result') is among the tabulated fields. A model with access to the items, or to their sum, can recover the label exactly on any partition, and 100% on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation coefficient and AUC across all four datasets simultaneously is the arithmetic consequence rather than a measurement of detection.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The paper's critical discussion is directed outward rather than inward: it identifies limitations in prior work - small sample sizes, narrow diagnostic focus, reliance on predefined hyperparameters, and the inefficiency of exhaustive grid search - and positions its own contribution as remedying them. No limitation of the present study is stated, and no limitations section exists.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two thousand one hundred and fifty-four respondents across four public screening datasets, modelled separately by age band: toddlers aged 18-36 months (1,054 instances, 728 above and 326 below the screening cut-off), children aged 4-11 (292; 141 and 151), adolescents aged 12-16 (104; 63 and 41), and adults aged 17 and over (704; 189 and 515). The datasets originate from autism screening applications and are aggregated on the UCI Machine Learning Repository and Kaggle. Reporting the class distribution for every band, and discussing whether oversampling was warranted, is better practice than much of this corpus - and the counts also make plain what the 'positive' class is: respondents whose summed responses to ten screening items exceeded the instrument's published cut-off. No participant is known to have received any clinical assessment, no age or sex distribution is reported although both fields are present, and no ethnicity, socioeconomic or comorbidity distribution is given although jaundice at birth and family history of autism are among the tabulated fields.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Clinical and deficit-oriented, with one formulation that is factually wrong. Autism is described as 'a disorder specified by a genetic neurological condition linked to developmental delays in communication skills, recurring attitudes, difficulties switching between activities, and unexpected responses to senses', and the introduction states that 'if autism is identified early enough it can be treated with better outcomes' - a treatment framing that misdescribes what early intervention does. Against this, the paper's account of the access problem is well sourced and is the most concrete statement of it in the review: it cites over 125,000 individuals waiting for a mental health service examination in England in July 2022 against a recommended three-month wait, with the consequence that 'parents and caregivers [do] not have the necessary support and services early'. That is a real and quantified problem, and it is the reason work of this kind is published, funded and cited. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person or family organisation is reported as involved in designing a tool intended for at-home use by families.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Present as data fields and absent as reported characteristics. Age, gender, ethnicity, jaundice at birth, family history of autism, country of residence, prior app use and who completed the test are all columns in the datasets, and all but two of the twenty-one fields were retained for modelling - but no distribution, group comparison or descriptive statistic is reported for any of them. Age is handled structurally rather than statistically, by fitting a separate model per band, which is defensible since Q-CHAT-10 and AQ-10 are age-calibrated instruments. The one field whose treatment deserves comment is 'Who_completed_the_test', which the paper discusses: for the toddler and child datasets the items are answered by a parent, relative or health professional rather than by the person being screened, so the modelled data are one person's report about another, and the identity of that reporter is itself a predictor. That the respondent's relationship to the person is available as a feature underlines what the dataset contains - a record of someone's judgements, not of anyone's behaviour.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None, and its absence is structural rather than incidental. The class variable in the UCI and Kaggle autism screening datasets is not a clinical diagnosis: it is computed by summing the A1 to A10 item responses and applying the instrument's published cut-off, so it is a screening outcome derived arithmetically from the same fields supplied to the model. The paper describes the scoring rule itself - 'each question is scored as either 0 or 1 based on the individual's response. Only responses that indicate autistic traits are given a score of 1' - without drawing the consequence. Two facts follow. No respondent in any of the four datasets is known to have undergone diagnostic assessment, so nothing here is validated against autism as clinically established. And because the label is a deterministic function of the modelled inputs, the classification task has no uncertainty in it: 100% on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation coefficient and AUC across all four age bands simultaneously is the expected output of the arrangement, obtainable by a single summation and comparison, and no optimisation, architecture or validation scheme bears on it. This is the second study in the review resting on these datasets, and the pattern is identical in both.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None used as an outcome, although one is present. The 'result' field in these datasets is the summed A1-A10 score - a continuous screening total that could have supported a graded analysis - and it is retained as a model input rather than examined as a severity dimension. No cognitive, adaptive, language or clinical measure exists for any respondent.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated aim is to improve the precision and speed of early autism diagnosis by optimising one-dimensional convolutional networks with the Tree-structured Parzen Estimator across four age-specific datasets, and to deploy the result as an interactive diagnostic tool. The methodological argument is coherent and specific: prior work on these datasets relied on predefined hyperparameters or on exhaustive grid search, which the authors correctly characterise as 'computation-intensive and inefficient', and an adaptive Bayesian alternative is a sensible remedy. The result reported is 100% on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation coefficient and AUC-ROC in every age band, attributed to the optimisation. The alternative explanation is complete and requires nothing of the model: the class label in these datasets is the summed item score thresholded at the instrument's cut-off, the items are among the inputs, and the sum itself is among the tabulated fields, so the model is being asked to reproduce a deterministic function of its own predictors. On that reading the baseline models' shortfall reflects optimisation difficulty rather than any information limit, and the optimised models' perfection reflects the arithmetic. The paper's own literature review is consistent with this: it tabulates the subliterature at 97.15% to 100% on these datasets, and notes one comparator - using physical fitness tests, brain scans and severity assessments on recruited participants - reaching 77.99%, roughly twenty-two points lower.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting. The four datasets aggregate responses submitted through autism screening applications, collected by third parties and deposited publicly. The absence of a setting is consequential for the deployment claim rather than for the analysis: the proposed tool is intended for 'clinical and at-home use', so the population that would use it is the general public, while the datasets consist of people who had already sought out an autism screening app - a self-selected group with an above-population base rate, which is visible in the class distributions (69% positive among toddlers, 61% among adolescents).
custom_fields.RQ2.3: None. Respondents completed a ten-item screening questionnaire, answered by a parent, relative or health professional in the toddler and child bands and by the person themselves in the adult band. The distinction from the observational paradigms elsewhere in this review is total: nothing was elicited, observed or measured, and the record contains one person's answers to questions about another person's characteristics.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis of public repositories, with no longitudinal element. No ethics statement, consent statement, funding declaration or competing-interest declaration appears in the retrieved text. Secondary use of public tabular repositories conventionally requires no fresh approval; the absence of a competing-interest statement is more notable given that the study's output is a deployed public-facing diagnostic tool.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: None. The data were collected through mobile and web screening applications by third parties, and the analysis is tabular. The equipment argument is the whole basis of the deployment claim - a screening questionnaire needs nothing but a phone - and it is genuinely the lowest barrier of any approach in this review. What the low barrier delivers here is the ability to re-administer an existing instrument through a neural network.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong on the computational protocol and empty on provenance. Reported: all four datasets with their repositories and instance counts; class distributions for every band; the 80/20 split with absolute partition sizes for all four (843/211, 233/59, 83/21, 563/141); the feature counts before and after dropping two fields; the preprocessing chain of feature selection, categorical encoding and missing-value handling; the baseline and optimised architectures; the Tree-structured Parzen Estimator with an explicit justification for preferring it to grid search; and all six metrics for baseline and optimised models in all four bands. Not reported: search ranges for the optimisation, the partition on which its objective was evaluated, code, and any account of how the class variable in these datasets is derived - which is the one piece of provenance that determines what the results mean.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: No limitations section exists, and the paper's critical attention is directed entirely at prior work: small sample sizes, narrow diagnostic focus, dependence on predefined hyperparameters, and the inefficiency of grid search. What should have been stated: the class variable is computed from the modelled features by summation and thresholding, so the task contains no uncertainty and the perfect scores are arithmetic rather than empirical; no respondent in any dataset is known to have received a diagnostic assessment; no positive predictive value is computed at any realistic prevalence for a tool proposed for at-home use, where the base rate would be far below the 61-69% positive rates in the training data; no feature ablation isolates what the registration metadata contribute independently of the items, which would have been the single most informative experiment available; and the deployed tool presents the output of the Q-CHAT-10 and AQ-10 scoring rules to parents as an artificial-intelligence diagnosis without indicating that this is what it is.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: None separately stated. The most useful next step is available from the data already held: refit with the A1-A10 items and the 'result' field removed, which would establish whether the registration metadata - age, gender, ethnicity, jaundice, family history, country - carry any independent information about screening outcome. That experiment would convert the study from a demonstration of arithmetic into a substantive one, and the architecture and optimisation machinery already built would serve it without modification.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: None observed. The A1-A10 fields record whether a respondent endorsed each of ten statements about a person's social-communication characteristics - the person's own answers in the adult band, and a parent's, relative's or professional's answers about a child in the younger bands. These are judgements about behaviour, and the review's line is that a record of behaviour a person produced counts as behavioural data while a respondent's characterisation of that person does not. The remaining fields are administrative: age, gender, ethnicity, jaundice at birth, family history of autism, country of residence, prior app use and who completed the test. Nothing in the dataset is a measurement of anything anyone did. The contrast with the review's other administratively recorded data is instructive: nurse-recorded developmental milestone attainment counts as behaviour because it records whether a child performed an action, whereas a ten-item checklist total records what an informant concluded.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: None. A single tabular modality throughout.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: One-dimensional convolutional networks fitted separately per age band, with a baseline configuration and a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator-optimised version. The methodological argument for the optimiser is the paper's best contribution and is correctly reasoned: prior work on these datasets used predefined hyperparameters or exhaustive grid search, and an adaptive Bayesian method that concentrates sampling in promising regions is both cheaper and more likely to find good configurations. Fitting a separate model per age band is also appropriate, since Q-CHAT-10 and AQ-10 are distinct age-calibrated instruments. The difficulty is that neither choice can be evaluated on this task: when the label is a deterministic function of the features, an optimiser that reaches 100% and a baseline that does not are distinguishable only in how efficiently they discover a summation rule, which is not what the comparison is presented as measuring.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A 17-dimensional tabular vector per respondent, retained from 19 or 21 available fields after dropping two judged irrelevant. Ten of the seventeen are the binary screening item responses. The critical structural fact is that the outcome is computed from those ten by summation and thresholding, and that the sum is itself present among the fields in these datasets - so the representation contains the answer twice over, once implicitly across the items and once explicitly in the total.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Six metrics reported for baseline and optimised models across all four datasets - accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation coefficient and AUC-ROC. Including the Matthews correlation coefficient is good practice for imbalanced tabular data and is rare in this corpus, and class distributions are reported for every band so that majority-class baselines are computable at 69%, 52%, 61% and 73%. None of those baselines is stated or compared against, and no confidence intervals are given. The decisive reporting failure is not in the metric set but in its interpretation: six independent-looking metrics all reaching exactly 100% simultaneously, in four separate datasets, is a signature of a degenerate task rather than a converging body of evidence, and the paper reads it as the latter.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No feature-importance, attribution or ablation analysis is reported. The omission is the single most consequential methodological gap in the study, because the one experiment that would have distinguished a real finding from an arithmetic one - refitting without the A1-A10 items and the summed result - requires nothing that the study has not already built.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The mechanics are sound and irrelevant. Each respondent contributes one row, so the split unit is the person and within-participant leakage cannot occur; the 80/20 partition sizes are tabulated for all four datasets; class distributions are reported and the decision not to oversample is explained rather than assumed, which avoids the synthetic-minority inflation affecting several comparators in the paper's own literature review. All of this is better practice than much of this corpus. It has no bearing on the reported result, because the target in these datasets is computed from the predictors: the class is the summed A1-A10 score thresholded at the instrument's published cut-off, the ten items are model inputs, and the sum itself appears among the tabulated fields. A model with access to either can recover the label exactly, on any partition, under any validation scheme, with any architecture. Scores of 100% on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation coefficient and AUC-ROC across four independent datasets simultaneously are the arithmetic consequence of that arrangement, and the paper's attribution of them to Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation misidentifies the cause. This is target leakage in its most complete form - more complete than the neuroimaging study charted alongside it, where the features summarised a clinical judgement, since here the label is a closed-form function of the inputs. The paper's own comparison table is the strongest available evidence that this is systematic rather than idiosyncratic: it places the subliterature on these datasets at 97.15% to 100%, and records one comparator using genuinely independent measurements - physical fitness tests, brain scans and severity assessments on recruited participants - at 77.99%.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: machine learning, one-dimension convolution neural networks, 1D CNN, tree-structured parzen estimator, autistic spectrum disorder. Four of five name the method or its components, with the population named once and no term identifying the data source, the modality or the fact that the inputs are questionnaire responses.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Computational Mathematics and Data Science 13:100105, Elsevier, 2024. A computational mathematics venue, and the reviewing focus followed accordingly: the optimisation methodology, the architecture comparison, the class-distribution reporting and the metric set are all handled to a reasonable standard, while a paper reporting 100% on six metrics across four datasets - and deploying a public diagnostic tool on that basis - was accepted without the derivation of the class variable being examined.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2024 by mathematics and computer science departments at four Nigerian universities. The framing is an access argument stated with more precision than anywhere else in this review: over 125,000 individuals were reported waiting for a mental health service examination in England in July 2022 against a recommended three-month wait, so 'parents and caregivers [do] not have the necessary support and services early'. That problem is real, quantified and correctly identified, and it is why work of this kind is written, published and cited. For the review the study contributes three things, all cautionary. It is the corpus's most complete instance of target leakage: the class variable in the UCI and Kaggle autism screening datasets is the summed A1-A10 item score thresholded at the instrument's published cut-off, the items are the model's inputs, and the sum is itself among the tabulated fields - so the outcome is a closed-form function of the predictors and 100% on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation coefficient and AUC across four independent datasets is the expected arithmetic, obtainable by a summation and a comparison. Second, the paper's own literature review documents that this is systematic rather than isolated, tabulating the subliterature on these datasets at 97.15% to 100% while recording one comparator that used independent measurements - fitness tests, brain scans and severity assessments on recruited participants - at 77.99%, roughly twenty-two points below. Third, and most consequentially, the study does not stop at reporting: it deploys. An interactive web-based diagnostic tool was built, illustrated in the paper, and described as routing user input through age-specific pre-trained models to give 'immediate diagnostic feedback', 'accessible for clinical and at-home use'. A parent using it answers the Q-CHAT-10 or AQ-10 items and receives back, presented as an artificial-intelligence diagnosis, the output of those instruments' own scoring rule - with no positive predictive value computed at any realistic prevalence, and with the training data drawn from screening-app users whose positive rates run to 69%. What should be said in the study's favour is that its analytic reporting is careful where the corpus norm is not: class distributions are given for every band, the decision not to oversample is explained, split sizes are tabulated in full, the Matthews correlation coefficient is included, and the methodological critique of grid-search hyperparameter tuning is well reasoned. The gap between that care and the unexamined provenance of the label is the review's clearest illustration of how rigorous analysis above a corrupted target produces a confidently wrong deployment.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Machine learning’s effectiveness
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Ohmoto Y; Terada K; Shimizu H; Kawahara H; Iwanaga R; Kumazaki H
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional population-based screening study embedded in routine preschool medical examinations, with a classification analysis distinguishing children above and below an SRS-2 screening cut-off
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A 16-dimensional summary vector per child, derived from the time-series pressure and pose data. Temporal structure is compressed into summary statistics (path length, speed, entropy, correlation) rather than modelled directly.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: All participants were 5 years old - an inclusion criterion, giving an unusually tight age band
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. The authors identify it as needed: 'validation using external datasets from different regions or institutions would help confirm whether the findings hold across different populations'.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 107 in the low autistic trait group (55 male, 52 female)
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Written informed consent from participants' legal guardians, and the participants section states that 'all subjects and their guardians provided written informed consent' after a comprehensive explanation - so assent as well as consent
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: The one-legged standing test, a standard clinical balance assessment, administered with the child standing on the pressure sensor facing the experimenter. Multiple trials were conducted, since one variable is the duration of the longest stand across trials. The task is brief, familiar, requires no instruction beyond the standing request and no social or verbal demand, and was already part of the routine medical examination - so the measurement adds essentially nothing to the burden on the child.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: A 48 cm square LL pressure sensor (NEWCOM Inc.) for plantar pressure distribution; a Logitech c615n webcam at 640 x 480 and 30 fps placed in front of the child; synchronised acquisition at 20 Hz; OpenPose for estimating ten joint positions from the video. Statistical analysis in SPSS version 27.0.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: 'The original contributions presented in the study are included in the article/Supplementary Material. Further inquiries can be directed to the corresponding author.'
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Approved by the Ethics Committee of Nagasaki University, Japan, approval number 22051204, with procedures conducted in accordance with institutional and national standards and the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its amendments
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Sixteen variables in three categories. Centre-of-pressure sway: total path length, mean speed, entropy and convex-hull area. Total balance ability: duration of the longest trial. Body-pressure relationship: the difference between centre-of-mass and centre-of-pressure, and ten correlation variables between centre-of-pressure movement and the angle of each of neck, shoulder, left and right elbow, left and right trunk, left and right hip, and left and right knee. Joint angles were estimated by OpenPose from the video.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Well handled and integrated with the study's substantive claim. Every feature is a named biomechanical quantity - path length, sway entropy, convex-hull area, or the correlation between a specific joint's angle and centre-of-pressure movement - so a contribution attaches to an identifiable aspect of postural control. SHAP values are computed for each variable set and displayed across all participants, and the selected variables for each model are reported by name. The convergent finding that shoulder, hip and trunk correlations dominate supports a specific mechanistic reading: what differs is not sway magnitude but how upper-body and waist movement is coordinated with the shifting base of support. The correlation between SRS-2 total and predicted probability is the strongest interpretive element - it shows the model's output varies continuously with trait level rather than merely reproducing the dichotomy, which is the check that distinguishes a genuine gradient from a threshold artefact, and it is performed for all three variable sets.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The paper states that the procedure 'simultaneously selected the 16 explanatory variables and optimized the hyperparameter to screen High autistic trait group and, thereby, improve the performance and generalization of all SVM classification models'. Between three and five variables were selected from the sixteen for each of the three models, and the cost parameter is reported alongside each. Whether this joint selection and optimisation was nested within the leave-one-out loop is not stated.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Leave-one-out cross-validation over the 126 participants, with each child contributing a single 16-dimensional feature vector, so the split unit is the person and no within-participant leakage is possible. The unresolved question is whether the joint feature-selection and hyperparameter-optimisation step was performed inside each fold or once on the full sample; the text describes it in a single sentence preceding the description of the cross-validation, and does not say. Given that three to five variables plus a cost parameter were chosen from sixteen candidates on 126 participants of whom 19 are positive, unnested selection would be sufficient to produce the perfect scores reported.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: An unusually candid limitations passage. The target is an SRS-2 screening cut-off rather than a diagnosis, and the authors state that the method should be 'part of a comprehensive assessment process that includes clinical evaluation and other standardized measures', and that 'integrating more robust diagnostic tools for ASD, such as clinical assessments or standardized behavioral tests, alongside the SRS-2, would improve the reliability of the screening process'. The above-threshold sample is small - 'with only around 20 above-threshold samples and highly imbalanced sample overall, we were forced to use LOOCV to avoid polarization of prediction toward the Low autistic trait group'. And, most notably, they state the specific risk their own choice creates: 'LOOCV can also produce optimistic performance estimates due to the small test set in each iteration. In addition, it can be unstable when the dataset contains noise or outliers, as individual data points can disproportionately influence the results. These limitations emphasize the need for cautious interpretation of our results.' They also note that only an SVM was tried and that external validation is needed.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: One hundred and twenty-six five-year-olds - 64 boys and 62 girls - constituting approximately 99% of the five-year-old residents of Sazacho, Nagasaki Prefecture, assessed during their routine preschool medical examinations. This is a whole-population age cohort rather than a recruited sample, and it is the second study in this review with genuinely population-based sampling, alongside the Israeli well-baby records study.
