Group assignment used the Social Responsiveness Scale, Second Edition completed by mothers, dichotomised at published sex-specific Japanese cut-offs of 53.5 for boys and 52.5 for girls: 19 children (9 boys, 10 girls) fell above and 107 (55 boys, 52 girls) below, giving a 15.1% above-threshold rate. The groups differ sharply on the defining variable (SRS-2 69.79 +/- 23.66 against 31.24 +/- 11.48, t = -6.956, p < 0.001) and not on age (all five) or sex ratio (p = 0.81). The unit of analysis is the child, with one 16-dimensional feature vector each.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: 'Children with autism spectrum disorder' and 'children with high autistic trait' are used precisely and the distinction is maintained throughout - the outcome is consistently named 'High autistic trait group' rather than autism, in the title, abstract, methods, results and conclusion. That precision is unusual in this corpus and matters, because the study measures a screening-questionnaire threshold rather than a diagnosis and says so. Clinical description is standard medical-model - 'deficits in social communication and social interactions and repetitive, restricted behaviors', 'motor impairments', 'balance impairments', 'deficiency in balance ability' - and the introduction opens with a cost framing, citing an estimated lifetime social cost of approximately $3.6 million per individual. Against this, the discussion of why balance matters is developmental and person-centred rather than diagnostic: poor balance 'increases the risk of falls among affected children which diminishes their motivation to participate in physical activities', and balance impairments 'can hinder the development of communication and motor skills, limit the children's integration into mainstream society, and adversely affect their social adaptation abilities'. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Sparse but well controlled by design rather than by adjustment. Reported: group sizes, sex ratio with a chi-square test (p = 0.81), age with a t-test (non-significant, and in any case every participant was five years old by inclusion criterion), and SRS-2 total scores per group with a t-test. Not measured: IQ, developmental level, language, adaptive functioning, socioeconomic status, comorbidity or medication. Two features of the design substitute effectively for adjustment on the variables that matter most in a postural study. Restricting the sample to a single age year removes the age confound that troubles most motor studies in this review - postural control changes rapidly between three and six, and every other motor study charted here spans several years. And the sex-specific SRS-2 cut-off means that sex is handled within the outcome definition rather than left as a group difference, which combined with the balanced observed ratio makes sex an unlikely driver. What remains unaddressed is developmental level: no cognitive or motor-development measure was obtained, so at an age when balance is still maturing a general developmental explanation cannot be distinguished from an autistic-trait-specific one. The sample is also drawn entirely from one small Japanese municipality, so the SRS-2 cut-offs, though taken from published Japanese population distributions, are applied to a single local cohort.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: There is none in the diagnostic sense, and the study is explicit about this. Group membership rests entirely on maternal completion of the SRS-2 and application of published sex-specific screening cut-offs; no child received a clinical assessment, ADOS, ADI-R or diagnostic evaluation of any kind. The authors state the consequence directly, recommending that the method form 'part of a comprehensive assessment process that includes clinical evaluation and other standardized measures' and that 'integrating more robust diagnostic tools for ASD, such as clinical assessments or standardized behavioral tests, alongside the SRS-2, would improve the reliability of the screening process'. This places the study in a different category from the diagnostic studies charted elsewhere in this review: what is predicted is whether a mother's questionnaire responses about her child exceed a threshold, which is a legitimate screening target but not autism. Three specific consequences follow. Single-informant report carries known biases and no second informant or reliability statistic is available. A dichotomy imposed on a continuous scale creates borderline cases whose classification is arbitrary, which matters for a model reporting perfect separation. And the 19 above-threshold children are a screening-positive group of whom, at a population SRS-2 cut-off, a substantial proportion would not receive an autism diagnosis on assessment.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: The SRS-2 total score is the study's only clinical measure, and it serves three roles - defining the groups, characterising them (69.79 +/- 23.66 against 31.24 +/- 11.48), and, most valuably, functioning as a continuous validity check. The authors correlate SRS-2 total with the model's predicted probability of high-trait membership for each of the three variable sets and report a positive relationship in every case. This is the analysis most studies in this corpus fail to perform even when the data are available: it tests whether the model's output tracks the underlying trait dimension or merely reproduces the imposed dichotomy, and a positive continuous relationship is evidence for the former. The authors also identify the natural extension, stating that they 'intend to consider developing a continuous SRS score prediction model as a next step' - which would convert a screening classifier into a trait-estimation instrument. No cognitive, language, adaptive or motor-development measure was obtained for any child.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The aim is to test whether machine-learning analysis of movement during the one-legged standing test can identify five-year-olds with high autistic traits, motivated by a specific timing gap: autism can be detected at 14 months and diagnosed reliably by two years, yet over 70% of affected children are not diagnosed until after 51 months, so screening before elementary school entry is needed. Balance is chosen because prior behavioural work reports that autistic children show smaller centre-of-pressure shift, more repetitive centre-of-pressure patterns and less complex postural control in both static and dynamic states, and because the one-legged standing test is already a standard clinical assessment - so the measurement can be added to a routine examination at essentially no cost. Findings: accuracy, sensitivity and specificity all reached 1.000 for the study's proposed variable set (correlations between centre-of-pressure and shoulder, right trunk and right knee angles) and for the combined set, while the conventional variable set based on prior literature performed less well on accuracy and sensitivity though it also achieved specificity of 1.000. SHAP attribution identified shoulder, hip and trunk as the dominant contributors. And SRS-2 total correlated positively with predicted probability across all three variable sets. The substantive claim is therefore not that balance differs in magnitude but that the coordination between upper body and the shifting base of support differs - the conventional sway measures are the weaker predictors and the novel correlation measures are what produce the separation.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A local preschool in Sazacho, Nagasaki Prefecture, during the pupils' routine medical examinations, capturing approximately 99% of the town's five-year-olds. Three features of this setting distinguish it from the recruitment geometry of almost every other study in this review. There is no case-control contrast: both groups come from the same population and differ only in where their SRS-2 score falls, so the spectrum-truncation problem that inflates diagnostic studies does not arise. The measurement is embedded in an examination the children were attending anyway, so it imposes no additional burden and the participation rate is near-total, eliminating the self-selection that affects recruited samples. And the setting is exactly the deployment setting the paper proposes - preschool screening before elementary education - so the data were collected under the conditions in which the method would be used. The corresponding limitation is geographic narrowness: a single small municipality, which the authors identify when calling for validation on datasets from different regions or institutions.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: The one-legged standing test, administered on a pressure sensor with the child facing the experimenter and multiple trials conducted. Four properties make it well suited to the purpose. It is a standard clinical balance assessment with an established literature, so the construct is not invented for the study. It is brief and requires no verbal instruction beyond the request to stand on one leg, no stimulus, no screen and no social interaction - so a motor measurement is obtained without the social demand that confounds several other motor studies in this review. It was already part of the routine medical examination, which is what made near-complete population coverage feasible. And the authors identify a specific analytic target within it that most balance studies overlook: the transition from two-legged to one-legged standing, which they treat as 'a feed-forward process that is necessary to achieve the one-legged standing outcome' and therefore as informative about anticipatory postural control rather than only about steady-state sway. Limitations of the paradigm are that a single brief task samples a narrow slice of balance ability - the authors call for 'a broader range of balance cues' - and that no test-retest data exist, so the stability of the measures within a child is unknown.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up and no test-retest reliability. The absence of repeat measurement is a real gap for a proposed screening instrument, since a threshold decision on a single brief balance trial requires knowing how stable that trial is within a child. Ethics reporting is complete: approval by the Ethics Committee of Nagasaki University under number 22051204, procedures conducted in accordance with institutional and national standards and the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its amendments, and written informed consent obtained from both the children and their guardians after a comprehensive explanation - the participants section specifies 'all subjects and their guardians provided written informed consent', so assent as well as parental consent. Funding from two JSPS Grants-in-Aid, JST MIRAI and JST CREST is itemised, and competing interests are declared as none.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Deliberately modest and fully specified. A 48 cm square LL pressure sensor from NEWCOM Inc. captured plantar pressure distribution; a Logitech c615n webcam at 640 x 480 and 30 fps, placed in front of the child, captured full-body images; the two streams were acquired synchronously at 20 Hz, and the physical configuration of participant, experimenter, camera and sensor is documented in a figure. Joint angles at ten body points were estimated from the video using OpenPose. Statistical analysis used SPSS 27.0. The equipment choice matters for the translational claim: a consumer webcam plus a single pressure mat, with open-source pose estimation, is deployable in a preschool examination room, which is the setting the paper targets. What is not reported is any calibration, signal-quality criterion or handling of pose-estimation failure - relevant because OpenPose accuracy on 640 x 480 video of a five-year-old at unspecified distance is not guaranteed and the study's proposed features depend entirely on the joint angles it produces.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Well reported. Available from the text: the population, its 99% coverage and the single-age inclusion criterion; the SRS-2 with its sex-specific cut-offs and their published source; the pressure sensor make and size; the webcam model, resolution and frame rate; the 20 Hz synchronised acquisition; OpenPose with its ten joints figured; all sixteen variables named and grouped into three categories; the composition of the three variable sets; the SVM kernel and the cost parameter for each best model; the named variables selected by each model; the leave-one-out scheme; and the statistical software with version. Supplementary materials carry the rationale and calculation method for each explanatory variable and further detail on model construction and evaluation. Not available: code, the dataset, and - the one gap that affects interpretation - whether the joint feature-selection and hyperparameter-optimisation procedure was performed inside or outside the cross-validation loop.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The limitations passage is among the most self-critical in this review and names four constraints, one of them unprompted by convention. The target is a screening cut-off rather than a diagnosis, and the authors recommend that clinical assessment be integrated alongside the SRS-2. The above-threshold sample is small at around 20, and the class imbalance is acknowledged as the reason for choosing leave-one-out cross-validation 'to avoid polarization of prediction toward the Low autistic trait group'. Only an SVM was tried. And external validation on other regions and institutions is needed. Most notably, the authors state the specific hazard their own validation choice creates: 'LOOCV can also produce optimistic performance estimates due to the small test set in each iteration. In addition, it can be unstable when the dataset contains noise or outliers, as individual data points can disproportionately influence the results. These limitations emphasize the need for cautious interpretation of our results.' Naming the optimism of one's own evaluation scheme is rare here. What is not addressed is the more consequential question. The paper states that the procedure 'simultaneously selected the 16 explanatory variables and optimized the hyperparameter', with three to five variables plus a cost parameter chosen per model from sixteen candidates on 126 participants of whom 19 are positive - and it does not say whether that selection occurred inside each leave-one-out fold. If it did not, unnested selection on this configuration would by itself be sufficient to produce accuracy, sensitivity and specificity of exactly 1.000, and the perfect scores would carry no information. Also unaddressed: no majority-class baseline against an 84.9% floor, no positive predictive value despite a genuinely population-based design that could support one, no developmental measure to separate autistic-trait effects from general motor maturation in five-year-olds, and single-informant SRS-2 with no reliability estimate.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Six directions, all specific. Develop a continuous SRS score prediction model rather than a dichotomous classifier - the most valuable of them, since it would convert a threshold decision into a trait estimate and is already supported by the observed correlation between SRS-2 and predicted probability. Integrate clinical assessments or standardised behavioural tests alongside the SRS-2 to strengthen the reference standard. Obtain a larger and more balanced sample above the threshold. Compare the SVM against random forests or deep learning. Validate on external datasets from different regions or institutions. And incorporate a broader range of balance cues. Not proposed, and needed: reporting whether feature selection was nested, and computing positive predictive value at the observed population prevalence.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Postural control during single-leg stance, decomposed into three families with a clear theoretical rationale. The conventional family follows prior work: centre-of-pressure path length, mean speed, entropy and convex-hull area, together with the duration of the longest stand, capturing how much and how variably the base of support moves. The proposed family is the study's contribution and captures something different - the correlation between centre-of-pressure movement and the angle of each of ten joints (neck, shoulder, both elbows, both trunk sides, both hips, both knees), plus the difference between centre-of-mass and centre-of-pressure. These measure not how much the child sways but how the body's segments move in relation to the sway, which is a coordination rather than a magnitude construct. The empirical result supports the distinction: the conventional sway variables alone performed less well, while the proposed correlation variables achieved perfect separation, and SHAP attribution identified shoulder, hip and trunk as the dominant contributors. The authors' reading - that upper-body and waist coordination with the base of support is what differentiates children with high autistic traits - is a specific, mechanistically interpretable claim about anticipatory and compensatory postural control rather than about balance ability in general. The paper also flags the transition from two-legged to one-legged stance as a feed-forward process worth examining separately, which is a construct-level insight most balance studies do not articulate.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Genuine two-sensor fusion, and the fusion is constitutive rather than additive. A pressure sensor supplies centre of pressure and a webcam supplies joint angles via pose estimation, synchronised at 20 Hz - and the study's proposed variables are precisely the correlations between the two streams, so neither sensor alone could produce them. The ablation is reported across three configurations and is informative: conventional variables derived from the pressure sensor alone gave the weakest accuracy and sensitivity, the proposed cross-sensor correlation variables reached perfect scores on their own, and the combined set also reached perfect scores. That ordering says that the information distinguishing the groups lies in the relationship between body movement and base-of-support movement rather than in either measured separately, which is a more specific and more mechanistically meaningful fusion result than the accuracy gains reported by most multimodal studies in this corpus. The caveat is that all three configurations share the same feature-selection procedure and the same evaluation, so the ordering is more trustworthy than the absolute values - and with two of the three reaching exactly 1.000, the comparison has no headroom to discriminate further.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A linear-kernel support vector machine, with the cost parameter reported (0.01 for the two best models) and between three and five variables selected from sixteen per configuration. The choice of a linear SVM on interpretable biomechanical features is well matched to 126 participants with 19 positives, and the reported model equations - high autistic trait group as a function of named variables - make each fitted model fully transparent. Only one algorithm family was tried, which the authors identify as a limitation and propose remedying by comparison against random forests or deep learning. The more consequential modelling detail is that feature selection and hyperparameter optimisation were performed jointly in a single procedure described in one sentence, with the stated purpose of improving 'performance and generalization of all SVM classification models' - so the search is doing substantial work, reducing sixteen candidates to three to five while also fixing the regularisation, and its relationship to the cross-validation loop is not specified.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A 16-dimensional summary vector per child. Time-series pressure and pose data are compressed into scalar descriptors: path length, mean speed, entropy and convex-hull area for centre-of-pressure; longest-trial duration for overall balance; and ten joint-wise correlations plus the centre-of-mass to centre-of-pressure difference for the body-pressure relationship. This is aggregation rather than sequence modelling, so the temporal unfolding of a stance is not represented except insofar as entropy and correlation capture it. The correlation features are nonetheless well chosen for the construct: a correlation between a joint angle and centre-of-pressure position is inherently relational and cannot be computed from either stream alone, and it summarises coordination in a single interpretable number. Every variable is named, categorised and explained, with the rationale and calculation method for each given in supplementary material.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for each of three variable sets, reported alongside the named variables and cost parameter of each best model; SHAP values displayed for all participants; and correlations between SRS-2 total and predicted probability. Reporting sensitivity and specificity separately is essential at 15.1% prevalence and is done. But three gaps matter. No majority-class baseline is stated, so the reported 1.000 is not placed against the 84.9% floor that a trivial all-negative classifier would achieve - although sensitivity of 1.000 does establish that all 19 positives were caught, which a trivial classifier could not do. No AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval appears; on 19 positives, an exact binomial interval around a sensitivity of 1.000 would extend below 0.82, which is the figure a reader needs. And no positive predictive value is computed, despite the population-based design making it directly meaningful - at the observed 15.1% prevalence and perfect specificity it would be 1.000, but any realistic degradation in specificity would move it sharply, and that sensitivity analysis is exactly what a screening proposal requires.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Strong, and directed at the study's substantive question rather than at post-hoc justification. Every one of the sixteen variables is a named biomechanical quantity with its rationale and calculation given in supplementary material, so an attribution is interpretable without further translation. SHAP values are computed for each of the three variable sets and displayed across all participants, and the variables selected by each model are named in the results table - so a reader can see not only which features mattered but which entered each fitted model. The convergent finding across SHAP and model selection, that shoulder, hip and trunk correlations dominate, supports a specific claim about where in the body the difference lies. Most valuable is the continuous check: predicted probability is correlated with SRS-2 total score for each variable set, testing whether the model tracks the underlying trait dimension or merely reproduces the imposed threshold, with a positive relationship reported in every case. That analysis is the one this review has repeatedly noted as absent elsewhere, and it is performed here on the study's own severity variable. What is missing is per-participant error analysis - though with perfect classification there are no errors to analyse, which is itself a reason for scepticism about the perfect scores.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Correct on the split unit and ambiguous on the step that matters. The evaluation is leave-one-out cross-validation over 126 participants, each contributing one 16-dimensional vector, so the unit is the person and within-participant leakage is impossible. The class imbalance is acknowledged and drives the choice of scheme, with the authors stating that with around 20 above-threshold samples they 'were forced to use LOOCV to avoid polarization of prediction toward the Low autistic trait group'. They then state the risk this creates in their own words - that leave-one-out 'can also produce optimistic performance estimates due to the small test set in each iteration' and 'can be unstable when the dataset contains noise or outliers' - and conclude that their results need cautious interpretation. That is the right instinct, but it does not reach the decisive issue. The methods state that the procedure 'simultaneously selected the 16 explanatory variables and optimized the hyperparameter', and three to five variables plus a cost parameter were retained per model from sixteen candidates on 126 participants of whom 19 are positive. Whether that joint selection was repeated inside each of the 126 folds is not stated anywhere in the main text. If it was not - and the sentence's placement before the description of cross-validation suggests it may not have been - then the selection saw every participant's label, and on this configuration that alone is sufficient to produce accuracy, sensitivity and specificity of exactly 1.000. Perfect scores on all three metrics for a behavioural measurement in five-year-olds are not a plausible property of the phenomenon, and unnested selection is the most parsimonious explanation. Three further points: no majority-class baseline is given against an 84.9% floor; no confidence interval accompanies a sensitivity estimated on 19 positives; and the three variable sets were compared on the same 126 participants. The corrective is straightforward and would leave the study's substantive contribution intact - nest the selection, report the resulting accuracy with an interval, and add the positive predictive value that the population-based design uniquely permits.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autistic trait, machine learning, balance, one-legged standing, screening. The set is precise and honest - 'autistic trait' rather than autism, and 'screening' rather than diagnosis, both of which accurately describe what the study does. Terms carried through the body: centre of pressure, convex hull, sway entropy, centre of mass, joint angle correlation, feed-forward process, anticipatory postural control, SHAP, leave-one-out cross-validation, Social Responsiveness Scale.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Frontiers in Psychiatry 15:1464285, Original Research, open access under CC BY; received 13 July 2024, accepted 30 September 2024, published 17 October 2024. Editorial and review handling is disclosed by name as Frontiers requires, and the reviewers include a researcher whose own work on movement analysis in autism is cited in this review's corpus - an indication that the paper was assessed within the relevant specialist community. The venue's structure produces the ethics, funding, competing-interests and data-availability statements, and supplementary materials carry the per-variable rationale and calculation methods that would not fit the main text.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2024 by informatics and engineering groups at Shizuoka and Gifu Universities with neuropsychiatry and medical sciences at Nagasaki University, funded by two JSPS Grants-in-Aid together with JST MIRAI and JST CREST. The framing is a timing gap stated with unusual precision: autism can be detected at 14 months and diagnosed with high accuracy by two years, yet more than 70% of affected children are not diagnosed until after 51 months, so identifying autistic traits before elementary school entry is the target. The chosen route is to instrument an assessment that already happens - the one-legged standing test within a routine preschool medical examination - which is why near-complete population coverage was achievable. For this review the study is valuable on four counts. It is one of only two with genuinely population-based sampling, and the only one whose comparison group is simply the rest of the same age cohort, so the spectrum-truncation problem that inflates the diagnostic studies does not arise at all. Its measurement is embedded in an existing examination with a consumer webcam and a single pressure mat, so the deployment claim is credible rather than aspirational. Its cross-sensor fusion is constitutive rather than additive, with the discriminative features being correlations between body movement and base-of-support movement that neither sensor could produce alone - and the ablation shows those features outperforming the conventional sway measures drawn from prior literature. And it correlates its model's output with the continuous SRS-2 score, testing whether the prediction tracks the trait dimension rather than only the imposed threshold. Against all this stands a single unresolved question: whether the joint feature-selection and hyperparameter-optimisation procedure was nested within the leave-one-out loop. On 126 children with 19 positives, selecting three to five of sixteen variables plus a cost parameter would by itself explain accuracy, sensitivity and specificity of exactly 1.000, and the paper does not say. The authors' own warning that their validation scheme 'can produce optimistic performance estimates' should be read as applying with more force than they intend.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Ismail WN; Ali MAS
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective algorithm-development study on two secondary public image corpora, with within-dataset evaluation, an ablation study, statistical comparison of model variants and bidirectional cross-dataset evaluation
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: RGB face crops. No landmark coordinates, no morphometric measurements, no temporal information - so the craniofacial and expression-dynamics literature invoked as motivation is not operationalised in the representation.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Stated as 1-11 for dataset 1; not stated for dataset 2 beyond 'the relevant age range'
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 2,866 images in dataset 1 and 1,163 images in dataset 2, from an unknown and unreported number of individuals. The paper's own table labels the 2,866 as 'Total individuals', conflating images with people.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Bidirectional cross-dataset evaluation between the two corpora - training on one and testing on the other - reaching 89-90% accuracy in both directions. This is genuine external evaluation in the technical sense and is rarer in this branch than in the corpus as a whole. Its interpretation is the difficult part, and the paper does not attempt it. Both corpora share the same construction principle: autism-labelled material was harvested from autism-related online content and control material from general online content. A confound that is common to both datasets will transfer between them exactly as a real facial phenotype would, so successful transfer between two corpora built the same way is not the independent confirmation it appears to be. Transfer to a clinically ascertained cohort with documented diagnoses would be, and is not attempted.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 1,433 images labelled non-ASD control in dataset 1; controls in dataset 2 are frames from 'YouTube videos featuring kindergarten activities within the relevant age range'
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. No task was administered - the children in the images were not participating in any study and in most cases were photographed or filmed for unrelated reasons.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU on Google Colab, Python 3.8, Jupyter notebooks, 12 GB RAM and 16 GB GPU memory. MTCNN for face detection in dataset 2; pretrained ResNet-50 for the leakage analysis. No data-acquisition equipment exists, since the images were harvested from the internet.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Both datasets are public and their URLs are given - the Piosenka Kaggle collection and the SSBD page hosted at rolandgoecke.net. Supplemental information is provided through the journal.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Yes, and fully: code on GitHub at walaanagyis/Autism-Detection with a Zenodo archive at doi 10.5281/zenodo.16410536, version 1.0.0. This is among the better code-availability records in the review.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: None stated. The paper contains no ethics statement, no institutional review board approval and no consent statement anywhere - a search of the full text returns no occurrence of 'ethic' or 'consent'. For secondary analysis of public datasets this is common practice, but the datasets here consist of identifiable photographs and video frames of named or nameable children, scraped from personal websites, Facebook pages and YouTube, whose parents did not consent to their use as autism training data and in many cases posted the material to seek support or raise awareness. The paper does not raise the question.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Learned end to end by the convolutional network. Squeeze-and-excitation blocks reweight channels; a multiscale fusion module concatenates feature maps across scales; white shark optimisation tunes hyperparameters.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Grad-CAM heatmaps are overlaid on face crops for each attention module, and the authors state that this 'ensures transparency and reliability in decision-making'. They then supply, unprompted, the caveat that most papers in this branch omit: 'clinical users or experts did not validate our heatmaps, limiting our ability to assess their potential clinical utility', with a recommendation to collaborate with psychiatrists or autism specialists to evaluate whether the highlighted regions carry diagnostic meaning. That acknowledgement is the correct one. What the heatmaps cannot address is the question the corpus construction raises: a heatmap showing that the model attends to the face does not distinguish a facial phenotype from image-quality, crop-convention or demographic differences that also live in the face region, so saliency is uninformative about the provenance confound.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: White shark optimisation over learning rate (0.0001-0.1), neurons in two layers (10-200 each), batch size (32/64/128), number of convolutional layers (3 or 5) and kernel size (3/5/7). The configuration is reported as 10 search agents, dimension 3 and two iterations - a total of roughly 20 fitness evaluations, which is a very shallow search, and the stated dimension of 3 is inconsistent with the six parameter ranges listed. Fitness is defined over accuracy, F1 and loss 'across folds', though no cross-validation scheme is described elsewhere. Whether the fitness was evaluated on the validation or the test partition is not stated.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: The most developed part of the paper, and the reason it is charted rather than dismissed. For dataset 2 the authors recognised that frame-level splitting of video-derived images risks subject-level and temporal leakage, extracted ResNet-50 features for all 1,163 images, and measured the maximum cosine similarity between training and test images - obtaining 0.9714, which they correctly read as indicating 'a substantial likelihood of leakage'. They then applied K-Means clustering over the deep features, swept the cluster count from 30 to 150, split clusters rather than images into 80/10/10 partitions, and reassigned any test image whose similarity to a training image exceeded 0.90 back into training. The adopted 100-cluster configuration gives 951 training, 144 validation and 68 test images with a final maximum similarity of 0.8989 and 28 images reassigned. For dataset 1 the same check was applied, the maximum similarity was 0.90, and the original 2,526/80/280 split was retained. Two problems limit what this achieves. Perceptual similarity is a proxy for identity, not a measure of it: two frames of the same child in different lighting can fall below 0.90 while two different children in identical conditions can exceed it, so the procedure does not establish subject disjointness and the paper's claim of 'confirming the absence of subject- or frame-level leakage' overstates what a cosine threshold can confirm. And the reassignment step is a data-dependent edit of the test set - the images most similar to training data are moved out of it - which makes the reported test performance conditional on a curation step defined by the model's own feature space.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Two limitations are named. The first is computational: the deep architecture with multiscale attention plus the bio-inspired optimisation raises deployment cost, introducing 'added complexity and resource-consumption iterative processes, which can compromise scalability and efficiency, particularly in real-time applications'. The second is the one that matters more and is stated well: 'clinical users or experts did not validate our heatmaps, limiting our ability to assess their potential clinical utility', with a specific remedy proposed. The ablation section also states honestly that multiscale fusion alone did not improve on squeeze-and-excitation alone.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: There are no participants. The units are images: 2,866 in the Piosenka Kaggle collection, split 1,433 autism-labelled and 1,433 control, described as ages 1-11; and 1,163 face crops extracted with MTCNN from the YTUIA/SSBD video corpus, split after re-clustering into 951 training, 144 validation and 68 test. The number of distinct children behind either figure is unknown and unreported - the paper's own table labels the 2,866 images as 'Total individuals', which is the conflation this review has repeatedly recorded in the image-classification branch. The provenance of each class is stated plainly and is the decisive fact: the autism images were 'taken from websites and Facebook pages that included autism-related content', while the YTUIA positives derive from 100 videos assembled to depict self-stimulatory behaviour, of which 50 came from YouTube and 50 from therapists and professional organisations, with controls being 'YouTube videos featuring kindergarten activities within the relevant age range'. In both corpora, therefore, the class label records where material was found rather than any assessment of the child depicted.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Consistently medical and deficit-framed, with the diagnostic label used as an attribute of appearance. Autism is 'a complex neurodevelopmental disorder that affects both cognitive and social development' posing 'a significant concern in modern healthcare'. The facial framing is the distinctive feature: the introduction assembles a physiognomic case - 'craniofacial anomalies make neuro-developmental disorders like ASD more likely to happen', autism severity 'has been associated with a wider intercanthal distance and a lower height of the facial midline', and 'facial asymmetry and facial masculinity are good signs that someone has significant ASD symptoms'. The conclusion instructs clinicians that they 'must recognize these facial traits or regions, as they indicate the condition'. Person-first phrasing appears alongside 'individuals diagnosed with ASD' and 'the non-ASD control group'. There is no neurodiversity framing, no autistic-community involvement, and no acknowledgement that a facial-appearance classifier trained on photographs of children scraped from support and awareness pages carries a different set of ethical questions from a behavioural measurement.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Almost entirely absent, and the paper marks the absence in its own table. Age is given as a range of 1-11 for dataset 1 and not at all for dataset 2; the sex distribution is recorded as 'Females/Males: -' with the note 'Gender distribution unspecified'; and no information exists on ancestry, socioeconomic status, cognitive level, language, comorbidity or medication for either class. No between-class comparison of any characteristic is possible, and none is attempted. Two consequences follow directly. Because autism is diagnosed roughly four times more often in boys, and because facial classifiers are known to key strongly on sex-linked morphology, an unmeasured sex imbalance between classes is a live and untestable alternative explanation for the entire result. And because the two classes were harvested from different regions of the internet - autism advocacy and support content on one side, general and kindergarten content on the other - they are likely to differ in the geography, ancestry and photographic circumstances of the children depicted, none of which can be checked. The reported cross-dataset transfer does not resolve this, since both corpora were constructed on the same principle.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: There is none. No child in either corpus is known to the authors to have received a diagnostic assessment. In the Piosenka dataset the positive label means an image was found on a website or Facebook page with autism-related content; in the YTUIA dataset it means a video was collected into a corpus of self-stimulatory behaviour, half from YouTube and half from therapists and professional organisations. Neither carries a clinician judgement, a diagnostic instrument, a medical record or any documented ascertainment. The paper cites no reference standard, does not identify the absence as a limitation, and describes the positive class throughout as 'individuals diagnosed with ASD' - a description the data cannot support. The YTUIA positives at least depict a behaviour that is associated with autism, which places them a step above pure provenance labelling; but the modelling target is the face crop rather than the behaviour, so even that association does not transfer to what the model is trained on. This is the same reference-standard failure recorded for the other Piosenka-based papers in this review, and it bounds every figure the paper reports.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, severity, adaptive or language measure exists for any image in either corpus, and none could, given how the data were assembled. The introduction cites literature relating intercanthal distance and facial midline height to autism severity, which would make a severity analysis the natural test of whether the model has learned anything morphological - but no severity data exist to run it against, and the point is not raised.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated aim is to improve facial-image-based autism detection by combining squeeze-and-excitation channel attention, multiscale feature fusion and convolutional networks with automated hyperparameter search using the white shark optimisation algorithm, motivated by four claimed gaps in prior work: limited modelling of long-range dependencies by CNNs, insufficient local inductive bias when images are treated as token sequences, weak interpretability, and inadequate splitting strategies. The headline finding is 95.36% accuracy, 92.62% precision and 95.5% F1 - a triple that is arithmetically consistent with a recall of 98.6% and a specificity of 92.2% at the reported 1:1 ratio, which is worth noting because internal inconsistency is common in this branch. Three secondary findings carry more weight than the headline. The ablation shows that the paper's own multiscale fusion contribution reduces accuracy relative to squeeze-and-excitation alone when the hyperparameter search is removed (0.85 against 0.89), and the authors state this plainly rather than burying it. The leakage investigation on the video-derived corpus found a maximum training-test cosine similarity of 0.9714 before intervention, which is direct evidence that naive frame-level splitting of that dataset - the standard practice in the papers it is drawn from - leaks. And bidirectional cross-dataset evaluation reached 89-90%, which the paper presents as robustness and which is better read as evidence that whatever the model has learned is common to two corpora built by the same web-scraping principle.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting exists. Both corpora are secondary web collections assembled by third parties, and the computational work was done on Google Colab. This matters more here than in most secondary-data studies in this review, because the setting is precisely what generates the labels: the Piosenka positive class is defined by having been found on autism-related websites and Facebook pages, and the YTUIA classes are defined by being drawn from a self-stimulatory-behaviour video corpus versus unrelated kindergarten videos. In a study where the data collection setting differs systematically between classes and no other ascertainment exists, the setting is the confound rather than a background detail.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: None. No task, paradigm or elicitation procedure exists in either corpus. The children in the Piosenka images were photographed for reasons unrelated to any study, and the YTUIA videos were recorded by families and organisations for their own purposes. This has a specific analytic consequence the paper does not draw: the introduction motivates the work through evidence about facial expression dynamics - that autistic infants 'exhibit more complex facial expressions than their typically developing classmates, particularly in the eyebrows and lips' - but nothing in an uncontrolled still photograph or an isolated video frame holds expression, pose, gaze, emotional context or elicitation constant, so a difference in expression between classes cannot be distinguished from a difference in the circumstances under which the two classes of image were taken.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional and retrospective, with no longitudinal element and no repeat measurement. The ethics reporting is the notable gap: the paper contains no ethics statement, no institutional review board approval and no consent statement of any kind - a full-text search returns no occurrence of 'ethic' or 'consent'. Analysis of public datasets frequently proceeds without fresh approval, and PeerJ's declaration structure elicited funding, competing-interests, author-contribution and data-availability statements from these authors, so the omission is specific to human-subjects considerations. The data are identifiable photographs and video frames of children, harvested from personal websites, Facebook pages and YouTube, whose families posted them to seek support or raise awareness and did not consent to their use as training data for an autism classifier. The paper's conclusion envisages clinical deployment of a model built on that material without touching the question. Funding from King Faisal University grant KFU250488 is declared with a no-role statement, competing interests are declared as none, and the authors disclose that generative AI was used to correct the English.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition equipment exists. Computation used an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU on Google Colab under Python 3.8 with 12 GB RAM and 16 GB GPU memory, batch sizes between 32 and 128. MTCNN performed face detection on the video frames, followed by alignment, cropping and resizing; pixel values were normalised to [0, 1]. A pretrained ResNet-50 supplied the feature space for the leakage analysis. Because the images come from unknown consumer cameras and phones under unknown conditions, every acquisition variable that a purpose-built study would control - focal length, sensor, resolution, illumination, distance, compression - varies freely and, critically, may vary systematically with class, since the two classes were harvested from different kinds of online source.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Better than most of this branch on the computational side and empty on the human side. Fully reported: both dataset URLs, the preprocessing pipeline, the final split sizes for both corpora, the leakage-detection procedure in pseudocode with its cosine thresholds, cluster sweep from 30 to 150 and reassignment rule, the training regime including early stopping with patience 5, checkpointing on best validation loss and learning-rate reduction by a factor of 0.1 on a plateau of 3, the hyperparameter search bounds, the white shark configuration, the hardware and software environment, and the full metric suite with McNemar and paired t-tests. Code is on GitHub and archived on Zenodo with a DOI, which places this paper in the minority of the corpus that permits computational replication. Not reported: the number of distinct individuals behind either image count, any demographic composition, which data partition the hyperparameter fitness was evaluated on, the number of runs behind the reported means, and how the confidence intervals were computed. The stated search dimension of 3 is also inconsistent with the six hyperparameter ranges tabulated.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Two limitations are stated and both are real. The computational cost of a deep multiscale attention architecture combined with metaheuristic search is acknowledged as a barrier to real-time deployment. And the interpretability claim is qualified honestly: 'clinical users or experts did not validate our heatmaps, limiting our ability to assess their potential clinical utility', with a concrete remedy proposed. The ablation discussion adds a third, unprompted admission - that multiscale fusion alone did not improve on squeeze-and-excitation alone. What is not stated is more consequential. The provenance confound is never raised, although the paper supplies the evidence for it in its own description of where the images came from. No diagnostic reference standard exists for either corpus and this is not identified as a limitation. Demographics are absent and marked as absent, yet the possibility that age, sex or ancestry imbalance drives the result is not discussed. The 1:1 class ratio bears no relation to prevalence and no positive predictive value is computed. The confidence intervals - uniformly the mean plus or minus 0.4 points, on a test set of 68 images where one image is worth 1.47 points - cannot be describing the uncertainty in the accuracy estimate; an exact binomial interval around 95% on 68 images runs from roughly 87% to 99%. The cross-dataset result is offered as robustness without noting that both corpora were built the same way. And the ethics of the underlying images is untouched.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Two directions are named: clinical validation of the Grad-CAM heatmaps by psychiatrists or autism specialists, which is the right next step for the interpretability claim; and reduction of the computational cost for real-time use. Not proposed, and needed before any of the reported figures could support the paper's clinical claims: evaluation on a cohort with documented diagnoses, reporting of the demographic composition of each class, a test of whether the model's output survives matching on age and sex, and an assessment of whether the classifier's decisions track image provenance rather than facial phenotype.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Nominally facial morphology and expression; operationally, whatever separates two sets of internet images. The motivating literature is specific - intercanthal distance, facial midline height, facial asymmetry, facial masculinity, and increased complexity of eyebrow and lip movement in autistic infants - but none of it is operationalised. The representation is a raw RGB face crop, so no morphometric measurement is extracted, no landmark geometry is computed, and no temporal information is retained, which rules out expression dynamics entirely. What the network can key on is unconstrained: craniofacial shape, but equally facial expression at the captured instant, head pose, apparent age, ancestry, image resolution, compression artefacts, illumination, background and crop convention. The paper's leakage analysis inadvertently demonstrates how much non-diagnostic structure the images carry - a maximum training-test cosine similarity of 0.9714 in a pretrained ResNet-50 feature space, on a corpus that supposedly contains different children.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: None in the sense this review uses the term. The paper's 'multiscale fusion' combines feature maps at different spatial resolutions within a single network operating on a single image modality, and the abstract's reference to 'both facial and multimodal datasets' is not borne out by the methods - both corpora are collections of still images. The multiscale ablation is nonetheless informative and is reported honestly: without the hyperparameter search, adding multiscale fusion lowered accuracy from 0.89 to 0.85, and the authors state that 'adding multi-scale fusion may not have yielded better results'. Only in combination with white shark optimisation does the fuller architecture win, which means the architectural contribution and the search contribution are not separable in the reported comparison.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Deep convolutional networks with channel attention and multiscale feature fusion, in four configurations - SE-CNN and SE-MSF-CNN, each with and without white shark optimisation. White shark optimisation is a swarm metaheuristic that adjusts learning rate, layer widths, batch size, depth and kernel size against a fitness combining accuracy, F1 and loss. The reported configuration is ten agents over two iterations, roughly twenty fitness evaluations, which is a very shallow search for a six-dimensional space - and the tabulated dimension of 3 does not match the six ranges given. The evaluation partition for the fitness function is not stated, which matters: if fitness was computed on the test partition, the reported test performance is a selection maximum rather than a held-out estimate. Comparison across configurations is supported by McNemar's test and paired t-tests with p below 0.01, more statistical care than is usual in this branch, applied to a comparison whose foundation - the labels - is the unexamined part.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: RGB face crops, normalised to [0, 1], obtained by third-party cropping in dataset 1 and by MTCNN detection with alignment, cropping and resizing in dataset 2. No landmark coordinates, no morphometric derivations, no temporal sequence. The representation therefore cannot express any of the specific craniofacial or expression-dynamic constructs the introduction invokes, and it retains every source-dependent property of the image - resolution, compression, illumination, pose, background - that is free to vary with class given how the two classes were harvested.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: The broadest metric set in this branch: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Cohen's kappa, specificity, AUC and AUC-PR, with confusion matrices, ROC and precision-recall curves, means and standard deviations across runs, 95% intervals, McNemar's test and paired t-tests. The apparatus is well beyond what most facial-image papers in this review report, and the headline triple is internally coherent - 95.36% accuracy with 92.62% precision and 95.5% F1 implies recall 98.6% and specificity 92.2% at a 1:1 ratio, which reproduces the stated accuracy exactly. Two failures nonetheless undercut the reporting. The intervals are not compatible with the data: every one is the mean plus or minus 0.4 percentage points, accompanied by a standard deviation of 0.03, on test sets as small as 68 images where a single misclassification moves accuracy by 1.47 points; an exact binomial interval around 95% on 68 images spans roughly 87% to 99%. And no positive predictive value is computed for any realistic prevalence, despite a 1:1 class ratio that exists only because the datasets were assembled that way - at a population rate near 1-2%, a specificity of 92% would place the great majority of positive calls on non-autistic children.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Grad-CAM heatmaps are computed over the attention-generated feature maps and presented as ensuring 'transparency and reliability in decision-making'. The authors then add the qualification that distinguishes this paper from others in the branch: the heatmaps were never shown to clinicians, so their diagnostic meaning is unassessed, and collaboration with psychiatrists or autism specialists is recommended to establish whether the highlighted regions are informative. That is the correct caveat and it is stated in the authors' own voice. Its limits should be clear, though. Saliency identifies where in the image the model looked, not what property it responded to, and every candidate explanation for the result - craniofacial shape, expression, apparent age, ancestry, image resolution, crop convention - is located in the same face region. A heatmap centred on the eyes and mouth is therefore equally consistent with a facial phenotype and with the model having learned to recognise the photographic style of images that appear on autism support pages. The conclusion nevertheless instructs clinicians that they 'must recognize these facial traits or regions, as they indicate the condition', which asserts precisely what the heatmaps cannot establish.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The most developed validation section in the facial-image branch of this review, and worth recording carefully because it is the one place where a paper in that branch takes leakage seriously. The authors recognised that the video-derived corpus risks subject-level and temporal leakage under frame-level splitting, and rather than asserting the problem away they measured it: ResNet-50 features for all 1,163 images, maximum training-test cosine similarity of 0.9714, correctly interpreted as 'a substantial likelihood of leakage'. They then applied K-Means over the deep features, swept cluster counts from 30 to 150, split clusters rather than images 80/10/10, and reassigned test images exceeding 0.90 similarity to a training image back into the training set, adopting the 100-cluster configuration for its balance of test-set size (68 images), final similarity (0.8989) and reassignment count (28). The same check on the Piosenka corpus returned 0.90, and the original split was kept. Compared with the four other Piosenka-based papers charted here, all of which split images without comment, this is a substantial advance. Three qualifications bound it. Perceptual similarity is a proxy for identity and not a measurement of it - two images of one child under different lighting can fall below any threshold while two different children in matched conditions can exceed it - so the paper's claim to have confirmed 'the absence of subject- or frame-level leakage' asserts more than a cosine threshold can support. The reassignment step edits the test set using the model's own feature space, moving out precisely the images most similar to training data, which makes the reported performance conditional on a data-dependent curation rule. And the leakage machinery addresses only within-corpus duplication; it does nothing about the confound that determines what the labels mean, since a model that has learned to recognise images sourced from autism-related web content will do so equally well on perfectly disjoint subjects. The cross-dataset evaluation deserves the same reading. Training on one corpus and testing on the other reached 89-90% in both directions, which the paper offers as robustness. But both corpora were built by the same principle - autism-labelled material harvested from autism-associated online sources, controls from general online sources - so a confound common to both transfers exactly as a genuine phenotype would. Transfer between two datasets that share a construction bias is not independent confirmation; transfer to a clinically ascertained cohort would be, and is not attempted. The remaining gaps are the unstated evaluation partition for the hyperparameter fitness, the absence of any chance or prevalence baseline, and confidence intervals incompatible with the test set sizes.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: artificial intelligence (misspelled as 'artificial intellgent' in the published keyword list), multi-scale view convolutional neural network (SE-MSF-CNN), autism spectrum disorder, white shark optimisation. The set is entirely method-facing - three of four terms name the architecture or the optimiser - with no term describing the population, the data source, the behaviour or the clinical question. That distribution is characteristic of the branch and is one reason these papers are hard to locate from a clinical search. Terms recurring in the body: squeeze-and-excitation, multiscale attention, Grad-CAM, explainable artificial intelligence, transfer learning, craniofacial anomalies, facial masculinity, cosine similarity, K-Means, leakage.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: PeerJ Computer Science 11:e3134, submitted 8 April 2025, accepted 29 July 2025, published 2 October 2025, open access under CC-BY 4.0, academic editor Davide Chicco, with subject areas listed as bioinformatics, algorithms, artificial intelligence and data science. The venue is a computer science journal, which shapes what the review process attended to: the paper's statistical comparison of model variants, its ablation design, its code archiving on Zenodo and its leakage analysis are all above the norm for this branch, while the absence of any ethics statement, any diagnostic reference standard and any demographic description passed without comment. PeerJ's declaration structure elicited funding, competing-interests, author-contribution and data-availability statements from these authors but has no field that would have prompted a human-subjects declaration. The bibliographic record also carries an inconsistency worth noting for the corpus: the supplied metadata dates the article to 2024 while the article itself is a 2025 publication.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2025 by information systems and computer science groups at Al Yamamah University Riyadh, Minia University and King Faisal University, funded by King Faisal University grant KFU250488. The framing is the standard early-detection appeal - screening is subjective, expertise is scarce, and a facial-image classifier would be objective, scalable and non-invasive - built on a physiognomic literature the introduction reviews approvingly and the conclusion endorses, telling clinicians that facial traits 'indicate the condition'. For this review the paper occupies an unusual position, and its value lies in the tension between its two halves. Methodologically it is the best-executed study in the facial-photograph branch: it is the only one to test for leakage rather than assume its absence, and it found a maximum training-test similarity of 0.9714 in the video-derived corpus, which is direct evidence that the naive frame-level splitting practised by the papers it draws on does leak; it is one of the few in the whole corpus to archive its code with a DOI; it reports a full metric suite with significance testing; its ablation honestly records that its own architectural contribution underperforms without the accompanying hyperparameter search; and it evaluates across datasets in both directions. Substantively, none of that reaches the problem, because the labels in both corpora encode where an image was found rather than any assessment of the child in it - a fact the paper states in its own methods and never revisits. The cross-dataset result sharpens rather than resolves this: two corpora built by the same principle, autism-labelled material from autism-associated online sources against controls from general online sources, will share their confounds, so 89-90% transfer between them is what a provenance-driven model would produce as readily as a phenotype-driven one. The lesson the review should carry from this paper is that methodological rigour applied downstream of a corrupted label does not repair it, and can make an uninterpretable result look better validated than the less careful papers alongside it. Two further points belong in the discussion: no ethics or consent statement appears anywhere in a paper whose training data are identifiable photographs of children scraped from personal websites, Facebook pages and YouTube; and the reported confidence intervals of plus or minus 0.4 percentage points on a 68-image test set are narrower than a single test image, which is a reporting failure that the journal's statistical framing did not catch.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Hasan et al.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective algorithm-development study on an existing resting-state EEG corpus, comparing four neural architectures
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: An eleven-dimensional feature vector per analysed EEG segment. The number of segments, their duration and their distribution across participants are not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. Single corpus, single site.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 4 typically developing boys aged 9 to 16
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Stated as not required
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None - resting state with eyes in an unspecified condition. The absence of a task is a deliberate design choice by the originating group, intended to minimise artefact, and it has a specific consequence for interpretation: without an elicitation there is no behavioural or cognitive event to which any spectral difference can be anchored, so a group difference in resting EEG is a difference in ambient neural state rather than in any response.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: g.tec EEG cap with 16 Ag/AgCl electrodes, g.tec GAMMAbox and g.tec USBamp, driven by the BCI2000 system. Electrodes at FP1, FP2, F7, F3, Fz, F4, F8, T3, C4, Cz, C3, T5, Pz, O1, Oz and O2 under the international 10-20 system, with AFz as ground and the right earlobe as reference. Bandpass filtered 0.1-60 Hz, notch filtered at 60 Hz, digitised at 256 Hz. This is a complete and reproducible acquisition description - montage, ground, reference, filter settings and sampling rate all specified - and is better acquisition reporting than most studies in this review provide for their own modalities.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: The corpus is available from the King Abdulaziz University brain-computer interface group with permission, and the paper gives the access URL and acknowledges the data provider by name.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: The declarations state: 'For this type of study, statement of human rights is not required' and 'For this type of study, informed consent is not required.' The recordings are of identifiable children obtained from another institution's research group, so the declaration concerns secondary use rather than the original collection, but the two are not distinguished and no reference to the original approvals is given.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Eleven linear and non-linear features spanning time and frequency domains. The paper's own comparison table indicates that the feature family follows Peketi and Dhok, and the related-work section enumerates the descriptors typical of this subliterature - power spectrum, wavelet transform, fast Fourier transform, fractal dimension, correlation dimension, Lyapunov exponent, entropy, detrended fluctuation analysis and synchronisation likelihood.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None. No feature-importance, attribution or spectral-localisation analysis is reported, so which of the eleven features or which electrode positions drive the classification is unknown - a notable gap given that the features are individually interpretable quantities (spectral power, entropy, fractal dimension) with an established electrophysiological literature, and that identifying which of them separates the groups would have been the study's most transferable output.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not described
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Not described. The paper states no train-test split, no cross-validation scheme, no held-out arrangement and no participant-level partitioning - the words describing any partitioning rule are absent from the text. This matters more here than usual because of the sample structure: accuracies of 89% to 94% cannot have been computed over 17 participants, so they must be computed over EEG epochs or windows, and with four control children any participant-disjoint evaluation would place at most one control in a held-out set. The natural reading is that epochs from the same children appear in both training and evaluation, which is the failure mode this review has documented for scanpath images, video frames, thermal images and cry instances, arising here in an electrophysiological modality. Nothing in the paper contradicts that reading and nothing in it confirms an alternative.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: None. The paper has no limitations section, and the conclusion states that the research 'underscores the efficacy of neural network in detecting Autism, advancing diagnostic tools'.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Seventeen boys: 13 autistic aged 10 to 16 and 4 typically developing aged 9 to 16, drawn from the global autism EEG corpus held by the brain-computer interface group at King Abdulaziz University and used with permission. The comparison group of four is the smallest in the review and is too small to characterise typical variation in any EEG measure, let alone to support a claim about detection. The sample is entirely male, which removes sex as a confound and means nothing reported can be assumed to apply to autistic girls. No age distribution by group is given beyond the two ranges, and none of the descriptors this review usually records - cognitive level, language ability, comorbidity, medication, socioeconomic background - is available. The 13:4 ratio also sets the participant-level majority-class baseline at 76.5%, against which the reported 89-94% should be read and never is.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Conventional clinical framing, brief and largely accurate. Autism is 'a complex neurodevelopmental condition characterized by a spectrum of challenges, including difficulties in communication, response, attention, social behavior, and repetitive activities', with the addition that autistic people 'exhibit atypical neural activity patterns'. The diagnostic argument is the branch standard: current practice 'predominantly depends on subjective and time-consuming behavioral assessments', so an objective non-intrusive biomarker is needed. Person-first phrasing is used throughout and no pathologising excess appears. No neurodiversity framing is present and no autistic person is reported as involved. The framing is worth recording for the synthesis because it is identical to that of the behavioural studies charted elsewhere in this review - the same dissatisfaction with behavioural assessment motivates both branches, while the electrophysiological branch requires equipment and expertise that the behavioural work is generally chosen to avoid.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Almost entirely absent. Sex is fully controlled by the sample being all-male; age is given only as two overlapping ranges (10-16 and 9-16) with no distribution or group comparison; and no cognitive, language, comorbidity, medication or socioeconomic information exists. Two specific risks follow. EEG spectral characteristics change substantially across the 9-to-16 window - the alpha peak rises in frequency, slow-wave power declines, and the maturational trajectory is well documented - so an age difference between a 13-child and a 4-child group would be sufficient to separate them on spectral features, and nothing reported allows the check. And medication is unrecorded, although antiepileptics and antipsychotics both alter EEG spectra and are more common in an autistic than in a comparison sample.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None described. The 13 autistic participants are stated to be 'diagnosed with ASD' with no instrument, criteria, clinician qualification, setting or date, and no screening procedure is reported for the 4 comparison children. The labels derive from the originating corpus and this paper transmits none of its documentation. The consequence is the same as for several studies in this review: the quantity the models predict is a label of unknown provenance, and no reported figure can be located relative to any clinical standard.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists for any participant, so no gradient analysis is possible and the models' outputs can be related only to group membership.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The aim is to compare a broader range of neural architectures on EEG-derived features than prior work has done, on the argument that existing studies have explored a limited set of models and feature combinations. Four architectures were fitted to eleven linear and non-linear time- and frequency-domain features: a custom neural network reached 94.02% accuracy, an LSTM 93.83%, a deep neural network 91.98% and a convolutional network 89.02%, with precision, recall, specificity and F1 reported for each. The comparison is even-handed and includes the lowest performer rather than only the winner. What the study cannot establish is what those figures mean. With 17 participants the accuracies must have been computed over EEG epochs rather than people, no validation scheme of any kind is described, and with four control children a participant-disjoint evaluation would leave at most one control in any held-out set. The paper's own comparison table is the most useful thing in it for this review, and its pattern is discussed below.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No primary collection. Recordings were made by the originating group under controlled laboratory conditions with participants at rest, described as ensuring artefact-free and reliable data. Both groups were recorded on the same equipment under the same protocol, so the acquisition asymmetry that undermines several branches of this review - clinic against school, autism websites against general internet - does not arise here. That is a genuine structural advantage of purpose-built physiological corpora over the assembled behavioural ones.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: None, by design. The EEG was recorded 'during participants' relaxed states to ensure artifact-free data', so no task was administered, no stimulus presented and no behaviour elicited. This is the defining difference between the electrophysiological branch and the behavioural studies charted elsewhere in this review, and it cuts both ways. Resting-state acquisition is maximally undemanding - it requires no cooperation with instructions, no verbal ability and no social engagement, which is why it reaches participants that task-based paradigms cannot - and it also means there is no behavioural or cognitive event to which any observed difference can be anchored. A group difference in resting spectral power is a difference in ambient neural state, interpretable only against a physiological literature, whereas a group difference in gaze during a social scene or in utterance length during play is interpretable directly.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element. The ethics declarations read in full: 'For this type of study, statement of human rights is not required' and 'For this type of study, informed consent is not required.' The data are EEG recordings of identifiable children obtained from another institution's research group with permission, so the declaration concerns secondary use rather than the original collection - but the paper does not distinguish the two, gives no reference to the originating approvals, and states the exemption in absolute terms. The data provider is acknowledged by name with the corpus URL, and competing interests are declared as none.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: The most completely specified acquisition chain in the review. A g.tec EEG cap with 16 Ag/AgCl electrodes, a g.tec GAMMAbox and g.tec USBamp, driven by BCI2000; electrodes at FP1, FP2, F7, F3, Fz, F4, F8, T3, C4, Cz, C3, T5, Pz, O1, Oz and O2 under the international 10-20 system; AFz as ground and the right earlobe as reference; bandpass 0.1-60 Hz with a 60 Hz notch; digitised at 256 Hz. Montage, ground, reference, filter settings and sampling rate are all given, which is more acquisition detail than most behavioural studies in this review report for their own instruments and is exactly what would be needed to replicate the recording. The corresponding practical point is that this apparatus - a research EEG amplifier, a gel cap, a trained operator and a cooperative child who will sit still - is at the opposite end of the deployment spectrum from the webcam-and-toys protocols charted elsewhere, and the review's synthesis should note that the electrophysiological branch shares the behavioural branch's motivation while requiring the equipment that motivation exists to avoid.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Sharply divided. Fully reported: the data source with its URL and a named acknowledgement of the provider, both group sizes and age ranges, the complete electrode montage with ground and reference positions, the filter settings and sampling rate, the recording condition, the count of features and their domain families, all four network architectures with layer sizes and activation functions given as explicit equations, and five performance metrics for each model. Entirely absent: any train-test split, cross-validation scheme or partitioning unit; the number of EEG segments analysed and how they distribute across the 17 participants; the identity of the eleven features; hyperparameters; and any account of how autism was ascertained. A reader could replicate the recording and the architectures and could not evaluate or reproduce the result.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: There is no limitations section. What should have been stated, in order of consequence: no validation scheme of any kind is described, so the reported 89-94% cannot be placed relative to any evaluation design, and with 17 participants those figures must derive from epoch-level evaluation where a participant-disjoint arrangement is barely constructible from four controls. The participant-level majority-class baseline is 76.5% and is never stated. The comparison group of four children is too small to characterise typical EEG variation. No age distribution by group is given across a 9-to-16 window in which EEG spectra change substantially, and medication - which alters EEG directly and differs between such groups - is unrecorded. No diagnostic ascertainment is described. No feature-importance analysis identifies which of the eleven descriptors separates the groups, which would have been the study's most transferable finding. And the paper's own comparison table displays a pattern it does not comment on, discussed below.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: None stated. The steps this study most needs are participant-disjoint evaluation with the scheme reported, a stated majority-class baseline, feature-importance analysis over the eleven descriptors, and a comparison group larger than four.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: None. No behaviour is observed, elicited or measured at any point: the recordings capture spontaneous cortical electrical activity while participants rest. The construct is neurophysiological - spectral power, signal complexity, fractal and entropy characteristics of the resting EEG - and the paper's motivating premise is that 'individuals with ASD exhibit atypical neural activity patterns'.
