For the review this places the study in a parallel evidence stream: it addresses the same clinical problem as the behavioural work and answers it with a different kind of measurement, one that is more direct physiologically and further from anything a clinician, parent or teacher observes. The related-work section shows the branch's feature vocabulary clearly - recurrence quantification analysis, power spectrum, wavelet transform, fast Fourier transform, fractal dimension, correlation dimension, Lyapunov exponent, entropy, detrended fluctuation analysis and synchronisation likelihood - none of which corresponds to an observable behaviour.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: None. A single electrophysiological modality throughout, with no behavioural, imaging or clinical data fused. The eleven features span time and frequency domains, which is within-modality diversity rather than fusion.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Four architectures compared on a common feature set: a convolutional network, a three-layer dense network (128 ReLU, 64 ReLU, single sigmoid, with the layer equations written out explicitly), an LSTM, and a custom design. Presenting four architectures with their formulations, and reporting the weakest alongside the strongest, is more even-handed than much of this corpus. The comparison's informativeness is limited by the spread being small - 89.02% to 94.02%, five points across four quite different architectures - which on a 17-participant sample is well within the range that resampling variation alone would produce, and by no hyperparameter or training detail being reported. The pattern nonetheless matches the one found in the skeleton-movement study charted elsewhere in this review, where six architectures spanned two percentage points on one dataset: in this literature the data determine the result and the architecture rarely does.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: An eleven-dimensional vector of linear and non-linear time- and frequency-domain descriptors per EEG segment. The features are individually interpretable and have an established electrophysiological literature, which makes the absence of any feature-importance analysis a real loss - identifying which descriptors and which electrode positions separate the groups would have produced a transferable finding independent of the classification accuracy. The number and duration of segments and their distribution across participants are not reported, which is the missing information needed to judge the sample structure.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1 for all four architectures. Reporting specificity is appropriate at a 13:4 class ratio and more than several studies in this review provide. Three gaps: no confidence intervals on figures derived from 17 participants; no confusion matrices or class-wise breakdowns; and no chance or majority-class baseline, although the participant-level ratio places a trivial all-autistic classifier at 76.5%, so the reported 89-94% represents a much smaller increment over the trivial solution than the raw numbers suggest.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No feature-importance, attribution, spectral-band or electrode-localisation analysis is reported. In a study whose features are interpretable physiological quantities and whose electrodes have known anatomical correspondences, this is the clearest missed opportunity: a ranking of the eleven descriptors, or a topographic map of discriminative channels, would have been comparable across the branch's literature and would have survived any subsequent revision of the accuracy figure.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The study reports no validation scheme at all, and the sample structure makes the omission decisive. With 13 autistic and 4 typically developing participants, accuracies of 89.02% to 94.02% cannot have been computed over people - 17 cases cannot produce those percentages - so they must be computed over EEG epochs or windows, and the paper never states how many segments were extracted, how long they were, how they distribute across participants, or how they were partitioned. With four control children, any participant-disjoint evaluation would place at most one control in a held-out set, which would make the reported specificity uninterpretable; the natural reading is therefore that segments from the same children appear on both sides of the boundary, and that the networks are separating individuals rather than groups. This is the same failure the review has documented for scanpath images, video frames, thermal images and cry instances, arising here in a fifth modality, and it is compounded by the absence of a stated majority-class baseline: at 13 against 4, a classifier that predicts autism for everything scores 76.5% at participant level, so the headline numbers represent a far smaller gain than they appear to. The paper's own comparison table is the most useful evidence in the study and it points the same way. It lists participant counts of 16/46, 10/5, 34/11, 10/10, 15/0 and 13/4 alongside accuracies of 92.9%, 93%, 72.77%-90.57%, 81%, 91.12% and 89.02%-94.02% - and one outlier at 212/199 participants reporting 56% to 64%. The single study in the table with a sample an order of magnitude larger than the rest reports by far the lowest accuracy, and the authors reproduce this pattern without comment. That inverse relationship between sample size and reported performance is the same one this review has traced through the behavioural branches, and its appearance in a table assembled by the authors themselves makes it the study's most transferable contribution.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: Autism, detection, EEG, machine learning, neural network. Compact and accurate, naming the population, the task, the modality and the method. The keyword set would place the study in searches for computational autism detection alongside the behavioural work, which is how it entered this corpus, and the review should note that the two branches are not distinguished at the indexing level.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Advances in Technology Innovation 9(4):287-300, 2024, doi 10.46604/aiti.2024.13951; received 1 July 2024, revised 31 July, accepted 2 August 2024 - a 32-day cycle. A technology-innovation venue, and the reviewing pattern is consistent with that: the acquisition chain, the feature families and the four architectures with their layer equations are all documented, while the complete absence of any validation scheme, of any majority-class baseline, of a limitations section and of any account of diagnostic ascertainment passed without comment, as did an ethics declaration stating in absolute terms that no human-rights statement or informed consent is required.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2024 by the School of Computer Engineering and Mathematical Sciences at the Defence Institute of Advanced Technology, Pune, with a collaborator at Manipal University Jaipur, using data provided by the brain-computer interface group at King Abdulaziz University. The framing is identical to that of the behavioural studies charted throughout this review - diagnosis 'predominantly depends on subjective and time-consuming behavioral assessments', so a 'reliable and non-intrusive biomarker' is needed - which is itself worth recording, because the two branches share a motivation while differing entirely in what they measure and in what they require. For the synthesis the study contributes three things. It is the review's representative of the electrophysiological branch, and it makes clear both that branch's advantage - a purpose-built corpus with both groups recorded on identical equipment under an identical protocol, removing the acquisition confound that undermines the scraped-image and clinic-versus-school studies - and its cost, since a research EEG amplifier, a gel cap, a trained operator and a child who will sit still is precisely the apparatus that the webcam-and-toys approaches exist to avoid. Second, it reproduces the methodological pattern the review has traced across five behavioural modalities: 17 participants, accuracies necessarily computed over epochs, no stated partitioning rule, and a majority-class baseline of 76.5% that goes unmentioned. Third, and most usefully, its own comparison table supplies independent evidence for the review's central quantitative observation. The table lists six prior studies with participant counts from 15 to 80 reporting accuracies of 81% to 93%, and one study with 411 participants reporting 56% to 64% - so within a table the authors assembled themselves, the single study with a sample an order of magnitude larger than the rest reports by far the lowest performance. The inverse relationship between sample size and reported accuracy that this review documents in the scanpath, facial-image and speech branches is therefore visible in the electrophysiological branch too, and visible in a summary constructed without any intention of demonstrating it.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Liu Q; Ma Z; Jin Y; He R; Su X; Chen J; Yin T; Cheng J; Guo Y; Li X; Liu J
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Prospective case-control diagnostic prediction-model development study, with internal bootstrap validation and calibration assessment, reported in nomogram form
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: An 81-dimensional vector of counts, durations and proportions per child, reduced to five predictors in the final model. Every element is a directly interpretable quantity - how many times a behaviour occurred, for how long, or what fraction of a related total it represented - so the representation is transparent from end to end.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. Internal bootstrap and calibration only, on the development sample. The authors call for more data, for evaluation of the coding scheme's reliability and validity, and for assessment across age groups, language levels and diverse presentations.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 123 typically developing children (103 male, 20 female), median CARS 15.0
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Written informed consent obtained from primary caregivers before the study began
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A 90-second free play episode with a fixed toy set. The child was first seated with warm-up toys while an instructor spent 5-10 minutes building rapport; the warm-up toys were then removed and the play materials presented. The written instruction is reproduced in full in the paper: set up materials and allow the child to explore and play independently for 90 seconds; do not initiate any conversation or interaction; give appropriate and neutral responses if the child initiates spontaneously - the example given is that if the child hands the examiner a toy, the examiner should smile and say thank you but should not start a new conversation. The design is deliberately minimal and its economics are stated: 1.5 minutes of child time and 10-15 minutes of coder time. The authors also identify what the brevity costs, noting that certain social interaction, communication and repetitive behaviours were not fully captured and that lengthening the session and creating opportunities for the child to initiate interaction would help - a prediction they made in advance, having hypothesised that repetitive behaviour frequency would not differ between groups because the session is too short for it to emerge.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Video recording in a playroom; no instrumentation beyond the camera. No software package for coding is named, and no statistical software is identified.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not public. Anonymised data are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request, with the restriction attributed to data protection and to the study-specific consent text. The full behaviour coding guide is provided as supplementary Table S1, which is the more useful disclosure for replication.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not reported. No statistical software is named.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Approved by the ethics committee of the corresponding institute (anonymised for blind review in this version), conducted in accordance with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Manual coding by trained human coders against a purpose-written manual, capturing onset and offset on a video timeline so that duration and overlap could be computed, plus behaviour form and function. The 19 coded behaviours were then converted arithmetically into 81 indicators of count, duration and proportion, with functional and imaginative play alone accounting for 18 of them.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Complete and intrinsic, and one of the strongest cases in the review. Each predictor is a directly observable quantity with an odds ratio and confidence interval, the model is a five-term logistic regression displayed as a clinician-readable nomogram, calibration between predicted and observed probabilities is plotted, and density plots for the retained indicators show the distributions behind the coefficients. Nothing requires post-hoc attribution because nothing is opaque. The substantive reading is coherent too: what the model detects is reduced quantity and variety of functional object play together with reduced socially directed speech, which is a recognisable and clinically meaningful pattern rather than an uninterpretable signal. Two interpretive checks are absent. Predicted probability is not related to CARS-2 score, so whether the model tracks a severity gradient or only the group boundary is untested. And no adjustment for age is reported in the final model, which matters because four of five predictors quantify how much a child plays with objects, in a sample spanning 1 to 6 years where that quantity changes rapidly with development.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: None in the machine learning sense. The analogous step is variable selection: 81 indicators were narrowed by group-difference tests and clinical judgement, then by univariate logistic regression, then by stepwise selection. The number of candidates entering the univariate stage is not stated precisely, and the stepwise criterion is not specified.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Internal only, and this is the study's principal methodological limitation, standing in contrast to how well everything upstream of it is done. The five predictors were selected from 81 indicators using the same 246 children on whom the model's AUC, sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values are then reported; the ROC cut-off of 0.399 was likewise chosen from that same curve. The bootstrap and calibration curve address model stability and probability calibration rather than out-of-sample discrimination, and no held-out set, cross-validation or external cohort is used. The consequence is that AUC 0.826 is an apparent rather than a validated figure, and the selection of five predictors from 81 candidates on 123 events is more than enough to inflate it. The authors do not raise selection optimism, though they raise the related severity-restriction optimism explicitly.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Five, enumerated and unusually well chosen. First, the 90-second task is efficient but does not fully capture social interaction, communication or repetitive behaviours, and lengthening it and providing opportunities for the child to initiate interaction would help. Second, the sample is predominantly male, which limits generalisability across gender-specific presentations, and stratified analyses are needed. Third - the most important admission - children with CARS-2 below 30 were excluded, 'which may have resulted in selection bias by including only those with more pronounced characteristics of autism. Consequently, the performance of the clinical prediction model may be overestimated.' Fourth, the sample is small for prediction-model development and the reliability and validity of both the coding scheme and the model need further evaluation across age groups, language levels and diverse presentations. Fifth, only autistic and typically developing groups were included: 'in the real clinical setting, it is more challenging to distinguish ASD children from non-ASD children, such as those with IDD, than distinguish ASD children from TD children', so non-autistic clinical comparison groups must be studied before the tool's discrimination can be judged.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two hundred and forty-six children aged 1 to 6, recruited in Beijing between January and August 2022 in a matched 1:1 design: 123 autistic (105 male, 18 female, mean age 54.0 months, SD 9.9) and 123 typically developing (103 male, 20 female, mean age 51.1 months, SD 13.5). The autistic children came from a hospital and from autism intervention service centres; the comparison children from a local kindergarten. Groups were matched and formally tested on age (t(224.10) = 1.90, p = 0.0591) and sex (chi-square = 0.031, p = 0.860), and separated on severity as expected (median CARS-2 37.0 against 15.0, Z = -13.90, p < 0.001). Two sample-definition decisions shape what the study can show. Children with current or previous psychiatric diagnoses other than autism, major physical or neurological disease, or any prior psychotropic medication were excluded, which produces an uncomplicated autism group at the cost of representativeness. And 23 children who met clinical criteria but scored below 30 on CARS-2 were removed, so the autistic group is restricted to the more clearly affected end of the spectrum - a restriction the authors identify themselves and connect explicitly to performance inflation. The unit of analysis is the child throughout, with one 81-dimensional indicator vector each.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Notably careful, and the most consistent use of identity-first language in this corpus. The title and abstract say 'autistic children' and 'neurotypical children'; the body alternates between 'autistic children' and 'children with ASD' without the deficit-laden hedging common elsewhere. Differences are described as differences rather than as deficits - autism is 'a neurodevelopmental condition with distinct patterns in social interaction, communication, and repetitive behavior', autistic children 'often show differences in play development', and the core traits are 'distinct patterns in social interaction and communication, focused interests, and repetitive behaviors'. The opening frames play in terms of what it gives children rather than what it diagnoses: play 'can provide satisfaction and joy, promote quality of life, engender social inclusion, and foster better social outcomes and friendships later in life'. The literature review is also candid about disagreement, noting that 'some studies report no significant differences in symbolic and functional play' and treating the inconsistency as a reason for further work rather than something to be argued past. Two elements pull the other way: the coded behaviour set uses 'unusual' and 'abnormal' as category labels ('unusual sensory seeking behaviors', 'unusual and repetitive hand/body/limb movements', 'abnormal eye contact'), and no autistic person or community organisation is reported as involved in designing the coding scheme, choosing which behaviours count as targets, or interpreting the findings.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Age and sex are reported per group with formal matching tests, severity is reported with a group comparison, and comorbidity and medication are controlled by explicit exclusion criteria - a considerably fuller demographic account than most of this corpus. What is absent is cognitive and language level, and that absence is consequential rather than incidental. The strongest single predictor in the final model is the duration of socially oriented vocalisations and verbalisations, and the candidate pool contained counts and proportions of vocalisations using words; without an expressive language measure, a group difference in language level cannot be separated from a group difference in the social orientation of speech. The age matching also deserves a closer reading than the p-value alone gives it. The means differ by 2.9 months at p = 0.0591, but the standard deviations differ substantially (9.9 against 13.5), so the distributions are not the same shape - and in a sample spanning 1 to 6 years, functional and imaginative play increase steeply with age. Four of the five retained predictors are quantities of object play, and the model does not adjust for age, so part of what the nomogram encodes may be developmental level rather than autism. Socioeconomic status, ancestry and parental education are not reported, and the sample is drawn entirely from Beijing.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Among the stronger reference standards in this review. Diagnosis was made by senior child and adolescent psychiatrists as a best-estimate clinical judgement against DSM-5 criteria, corroborated by CARS-2 with the instrument's psychometric properties cited from the literature (internal consistency 0.93, meta-analytic alpha 0.90, sensitivity 88%, specificity 86%). The corroboration is real clinical assessment rather than a questionnaire threshold standing in for one, and it is applied by clinicians qualified to make it. Two qualifications matter. First, the CARS-2 floor of 30 was applied as an exclusion: 23 children with a clinical diagnosis but a score below 30 were removed from the study. This converts the reference standard from 'clinically diagnosed autism' into 'clinically diagnosed autism of at least moderate severity', truncating exactly the part of the spectrum on which a screening tool would be hardest and most useful. The authors state the consequence directly - selection bias toward more pronounced characteristics, with the model's performance therefore possibly overestimated - which is the correct inference and one that few papers here draw about their own inclusion rules. Second, whether the video coders knew each child's group is not stated, and because the autistic children were recruited from hospitals and intervention centres while controls came from a kindergarten, group membership may have been inferable from the recordings independently of any behaviour coded.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: CARS-2 total is the only clinical measure and it does three jobs: it corroborates diagnosis, it gates inclusion at a score of 30, and it characterises the groups (median 37.0, IQR 33.5-41.5 against 15.0, IQR 15.0-15.5; Z = -13.90, p < 0.001). What it is not used for is the analysis that the data would support and that this review has repeatedly found missing: relating CARS-2 to the model's predicted probability. That correlation would test whether the nomogram tracks a continuous severity dimension or only the group boundary, and it is a stronger validity check than any of the internal statistics reported. No cognitive, adaptive or language measure was obtained for either group, and no developmental level was recorded - which, in a study whose predictors are quantities of object play across ages 1 to 6, leaves developmental maturity as an unmeasured competitor to the autism explanation.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The aim was to measure functional and imaginative play together with other core autistic traits during a brief free play task, characterise the group differences, and build from them a clinical prediction model capable of screening children aged 1 to 6 - explicitly extending prior work that had examined play behaviours alone. Directional hypotheses were stated in advance, including the prediction that repetitive behaviour frequency would not differ between groups because the session would be too short for it to emerge. The findings: autistic children showed less functional and less imaginative play, and reduced eye contact, facial expression and vocalisation. Restricted and repetitive behaviours did not separate the groups, exactly as predicted - the reported odds ratios for stereotyped language use, repetitive hand and body movements and unusual sensory seeking are numerically enormous with confidence intervals spanning zero to infinity and p-values near 1, the signature of behaviours almost never observed in a 90-second window. Stepwise regression retained five predictors, all in the protective direction: duration of socially oriented vocalisations (OR 0.940), total counts of functional play (OR 0.639), and play time with miniature or representational toys (OR 0.985), cause-and-effect toys (OR 0.973) and construction toys (OR 0.958). The nomogram reached AUC 0.826 (95% CI 0.776-0.877) with sensitivity 85.4% and specificity 68.3% at a cut-off of 0.399. The confirmed negative prediction about repetitive behaviour is worth as much as the positive findings: it demonstrates that the task samples the social-communication and play dimensions of the phenotype and not the restricted-repetitive dimension, which bounds what any model built on it can claim to detect.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A playroom, with the child seated at a table and an instructor beside them, preceded by 5-10 minutes of rapport building with warm-up toys that were then removed. The recruitment settings differ by group: autistic children from a hospital and autism intervention service centres in Beijing, comparison children from a local kindergarten. That asymmetry is the default arrangement across this literature and it carries two consequences the paper does not discuss. Children recruited through intervention services have by definition been identified and are receiving support, so they differ from a screening population in ways beyond diagnosis. And because the recording context is not identical across groups, an unblinded coder could plausibly infer group membership from the video independently of the behaviours being scored - a risk that matters here more than in automated studies, since every indicator originates in a human judgement.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A 90-second free play episode with a fixed toy set spanning miniature or representational toys, cause-and-effect toys and construction toys, preceded by 5-10 minutes of rapport building. The instruction is reproduced verbatim in the paper and is tightly specified: allow the child to explore and play independently for 90 seconds; do not initiate any conversation or interaction; respond appropriately and neutrally if the child initiates - if the child hands the examiner a toy, smile and say thank you but start no new conversation. This is a well-designed paradigm for its purpose. It is genuinely brief, it places almost no demand on the child, it requires no screen or instrumentation, and the examiner's role is constrained precisely enough to be reproducible. The authors state its cost in the same terms as its benefit: 1.5 minutes of child time and 10-15 minutes of coder time, against a session too short to elicit repetitive behaviours or to give the child an opportunity to initiate social interaction. Both halves of that trade-off are confirmed in the results - the play and communication indicators separate the groups while the restricted-repetitive indicators are degenerate - and the authors' proposed fix, lengthening the session and building in opportunities for initiation, follows directly.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional with a single session, no follow-up and no test-retest. The absence of repeat measurement matters for a proposed screening instrument built on a 90-second sample of a young child's behaviour, since day-to-day variation in a toddler's play is substantial and unquantified here. Ethics reporting is complete: approval by the institute's ethics committee (anonymised in this version for blind review), conformity with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki, and written informed consent from primary caregivers before the study began. The competing-interest declaration is more informative than most and deserves recording: six of the eleven authors declare two patent applications arising from this research (202310300588.1 and 202310315701.3) while five declare none, and four authors are affiliated with ALSOLIFE, a Beijing autism-services company, alongside the Peking University Sixth Hospital group. The paper states it received no funding of any kind. The patents are declared without their claims being described, which is the relevant detail when the paper proposes the coding scheme and model as a deployable clinical tool.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Minimal and deliberately so: a video camera in a playroom and a fixed set of physical toys. No sensor, screen, wearable or eye tracker is involved. That is the design's practical argument - the equipment barrier to using this protocol in a clinic or kindergarten anywhere is a camera and a box of toys, which is lower than for any other included study except the population health-records analysis. The cost is transferred to the analysis: 10-15 minutes of trained-coder time per 90-second video, which is where the scalability constraint now sits, and which is why the authors describe the coding scheme as 'a feeding database with low granularity for automatic behavior recognition through machine learning in the future'. Neither the coding software nor the statistical software is named.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong on the human protocol and thin on the computational one. Fully reported: recruitment sources and window, inclusion and exclusion criteria, the diagnostic procedure and CARS-2 threshold with the count excluded by it, group demographics with matching statistics, the verbatim task instruction including the examiner's response rule, the rapport-building preamble, the toy categories with definitions, the coder training programme - three coders with 3 months to 11 years of relevant experience, one month of training under the manual's authors with weekly review meetings, and an inter-coder consistency check in which all three independently coded the same 30 children, reaching 83.7-91.7% with the reliability formula given - the definitions of all 19 behaviours in a supplementary coding guide, all 81 indicators with definitions, and the complete univariate and multivariate regression output with odds ratios, confidence intervals and p-values. This is enough for another group to run the protocol. Not reported: the coding software, the statistical software, the stepwise selection criterion, the number of bootstrap resamples, and the optimism-corrected AUC that the bootstrap should have produced. Data are available from the corresponding author on request only, with the restriction attributed to data protection and the consent text.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Five limitations are enumerated and they are well chosen - three of them identify problems that most papers in this corpus leave to the reader. The 90-second task does not fully capture social interaction, communication or repetitive behaviours, and should be lengthened with opportunities for child-initiated interaction. The sample is predominantly male, limiting generalisability across gender-specific presentations. Children scoring below 30 on CARS-2 were excluded, 'which may have resulted in selection bias by including only those with more pronounced characteristics of autism. Consequently, the performance of the clinical prediction model may be overestimated' - a statement of spectrum truncation and its effect on performance that is more direct than anything else in this review. The sample is small for prediction-model development and both the coding scheme and the model need further reliability and validity evaluation across age groups, language levels and presentations. And only autistic and typically developing groups were compared, whereas 'in the real clinical setting, it is more challenging to distinguish ASD children from non-ASD children, such as those with IDD, than distinguish ASD children from TD children'. What is missing is the optimism arising from the analysis itself: five predictors were selected from 81 candidates using the same 246 children whose data yield the reported AUC, sensitivity and specificity, and the operating cut-off was chosen from the same ROC curve, so the headline figures are apparent performance and no optimism-corrected estimate is reported although a bootstrap was run. Also unaddressed: predictive values are quoted at the matched 50% prevalence with no recalculation for a screening base rate; no language or cognitive measure exists although the strongest predictor is socially directed speech; age is matched at the mean but not adjusted for, in a 1-to-6-year sample where four of five predictors are play-quantity measures; the recruitment asymmetry between clinical services and a kindergarten is not discussed; and coder blinding to group is not stated.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Six directions, each tied to a named limitation. Lengthen the free play session and create opportunities for child-initiated interaction, so that social communication and repetitive behaviours can actually be observed. Recruit a sex-balanced sample and analyse behavioural features by gender. Include children with subtler or atypical presentations rather than restricting to CARS-2 at or above 30, to make the model applicable where screening is hardest. Collect more data and formally evaluate the reliability and validity of both the coding scheme and the model, including across age groups and language levels. Add non-autistic clinical comparison groups, particularly intellectual developmental disorder, since that is the discrimination that real clinical practice requires. And use the coding scheme as a training substrate for automatic behaviour recognition - the paper is explicit that the count, duration and proportion indexes were designed to suit 'future application scenarios of machine learning automation'. Not proposed, and needed: an optimism-corrected or externally validated performance estimate, and predictive values recomputed at a realistic screening prevalence.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: The broadest behavioural coverage of any single task in this review. Nineteen behaviours were coded and expanded into 81 quantitative indicators of count, duration and proportion, spanning functional play, imaginative or symbolic play, eye contact, facial expression, vocalisations and verbalisations with a socially oriented subclass and a word-use subclass, stereotyped use of language, unusual and repetitive hand, body and limb movements, unusual restricted and stereotyped behaviours, and unusual sensory seeking. Play was further resolved by object category - miniature or representational toys, cause-and-effect toys, construction toys - so that play duration could be attributed to the kind of play the toy affords, and functional and imaginative play alone generated 18 of the 81 indicators. Behaviour form and function were coded alongside occurrence, and the timeline representation records overlap so that simultaneous behaviours can be identified. Two results from this breadth matter for the review. Only two behavioural families entered the final model - socially oriented speech and functional play with objects - so the informative signal is narrower than the coding scheme. And the restricted-repetitive indicators are statistically degenerate, with odds ratios in the millions and confidence intervals from zero to infinity, because these behaviours essentially did not occur in 90 seconds. That is a clean demonstration, made against a pre-registered prediction, that a brief structured play sample accesses the social-communication and play dimensions of the phenotype while leaving the restricted-repetitive dimension unobserved - a boundary that applies to every short-observation study in this corpus and is rarely made visible.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No sensor fusion - a single camera supplies everything. But the final model combines information across behavioural channels rather than within one: duration of socially oriented vocalisations from the communication channel together with four measures of functional play from the object-manipulation channel, one of them a count and three of them durations resolved by toy type. That cross-channel structure is meaningful. It says that neither the social nor the play dimension alone accounted for the group difference in the stepwise selection, and it aligns with the clinical description of autism better than a single-channel model would. The play predictors also carry an internal ordering worth noting: total counts of functional play has by far the strongest odds ratio (0.639), while the three toy-specific durations sit close to 1 per unit of time (0.985, 0.973, 0.958), so the discriminative work is done mainly by how often a child engages in functional play at all rather than by how long any particular episode lasts.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Univariate logistic regression for candidate screening followed by stepwise logistic regression for model construction, with the result presented as a nomogram. No machine learning algorithm is used and none is needed - with 246 children, 123 events and 81 candidate predictors, a regularised or stepwise regression is the statistically appropriate choice, and the transparency it buys is substantial: five interpretable coefficients with odds ratios and confidence intervals, displayed in a form a clinician can read off a chart. The model is accompanied by a Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test (chi-square 15.329, p = 0.053), a bootstrap procedure and a calibration curve. This is prediction-model methodology as the clinical literature practises it, and it is markedly better matched to the data than the deep architectures applied to smaller samples elsewhere in this corpus. The methodological gap is not the algorithm but the evaluation: stepwise selection from 81 candidates, on the sample that then supplies the performance estimate, without an optimism-corrected figure.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: An 81-dimensional vector per child of counts, durations and proportions, derived arithmetically from human coding of a 90-second video with onset and offset times on a timeline. Every element is directly interpretable and directly auditable - a coder's judgement about a named behaviour, aggregated by a stated rule. The final representation is five numbers: one speech duration and four play quantities. The proportion indicators are a thoughtful design element, since normalising socially oriented vocalisations by total vocalisations, or word-use vocalisations by total vocalisations, separates the social direction of speech from the amount of speech - and indeed the proportional versions had the strongest univariate odds ratios in the vocalisation family (0.367 and 0.345). It is notable that stepwise selection nonetheless retained the raw duration measure rather than a proportion, which leaves the model's strongest predictor confounded with how much the child spoke at all, and thus with expressive language level, which was never measured.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: The fullest metric reporting in the review's behavioural branch. AUC 0.826 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.776-0.877; sensitivity 85.4%; specificity 68.3%; positive predictive value 72.9%; negative predictive value 82.4%, all at a stated cut-off of 0.399; Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness of fit; a calibration curve relating predicted to observed probabilities; density plots for the retained indicators; and odds ratios with confidence intervals and p-values at both the univariate and multivariate stages for every indicator. Reporting discrimination, calibration, predictive values and per-predictor uncertainty together is what a prediction-model study should do and what almost no other paper in this corpus does. Three qualifications. The predictive values are computed at the 1:1 prevalence the matched design created; at a realistic screening base rate, a specificity of 68.3% would place the great majority of positive calls on non-autistic children, and this recalculation is exactly what the paper's screening proposal requires and does not perform. The reported AUC is apparent rather than optimism-corrected, despite a bootstrap having been run for that purpose. And the operating cut-off of 0.399 was chosen from the same ROC curve on which the sensitivity and specificity are then quoted, so that pair is a best-of-curve selection rather than a prespecified operating point.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Intrinsic and complete, with no post-hoc machinery needed. The model is five logistic coefficients over directly observable quantities, each reported with an odds ratio and confidence interval, and displayed as a nomogram that a clinician can use by hand. Calibration between predicted and observed probability is plotted rather than asserted, density plots show the underlying distributions, and the full univariate-to-multivariate progression is tabulated so that a reader can see which candidates were considered and which survived. The substantive interpretation is coherent and clinically recognisable: reduced frequency of functional object play, reduced play time across all three toy categories, and less socially directed speech. This is one of the few models in the review whose output could be discussed with a family in ordinary language. Two interpretive gaps remain, both concerning what the coefficients might be measuring other than autism. Predicted probability is never related to CARS-2, so whether the model tracks severity or only group membership is untested on data already collected. And no age term appears in the model, although four of five predictors are quantities of object play in a sample spanning 1 to 6 years, where those quantities rise steeply with development and where the two groups' age distributions differ in spread even after matching on the mean.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The weakest link in an otherwise carefully executed study, and instructive precisely because everything upstream is done well. Eighty-one indicators were reduced by group-difference testing and clinical judgement, then by univariate logistic regression, then by stepwise logistic regression, and the resulting five-predictor model's AUC, sensitivity, specificity and predictive values were computed on the same 246 children that drove every one of those selection steps. The operating threshold of 0.399 was likewise read off that same ROC curve. Selecting five predictors from 81 candidates on 123 events produces substantial optimism, and the standard remedy - bootstrap resampling that repeats the entire selection procedure within each resample to yield an optimism-corrected estimate - was partially performed but not reported that way: the bootstrap is described as validating the model, and the calibration curve and Hosmer-Lemeshow test address probability calibration and fit rather than out-of-sample discrimination, so no corrected AUC appears anywhere. There is no held-out set, no cross-validation and no external cohort. What makes this worth stating carefully is that the study's other validity properties are unusually sound - the split unit is the child throughout with no possibility of within-participant leakage, the diagnosis is a real clinical best-estimate judgement rather than a questionnaire threshold, the groups are matched and tested on age and sex, the comparison prediction about repetitive behaviour was made in advance and confirmed, and the authors themselves identify spectrum truncation as a source of performance inflation. The likely direction of error is therefore known and the likely magnitude is modest by this corpus's standards: an AUC of 0.826 with sensitivity 85.4% and specificity 68.3% is a plausible figure for this task, and the paper's own honesty about the CARS-2 floor points the same way. Two further items belong here. Coder blinding to group is not stated, and with autistic children recruited from hospitals and intervention centres and controls from a kindergarten, the recordings themselves may reveal group membership - which matters more in a human-coded study than in an automated one, because every one of the 81 indicators passes through a coder's judgement. And the predictive values that a screening claim depends on are quoted at the 50% prevalence of a matched design, with no recomputation for the base rate of any population in which the tool would be used.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: free play, autism, digital behavioral feature, prediction model, screening. The set is well chosen and unusually balanced - one term for the paradigm, one for the population, one for the data representation, one for the method and one for the intended use - which makes the paper findable from either a clinical or a computational search, unlike the method-only keyword sets typical of the engineering venues in this corpus. The phrase 'digital behavioral feature' is worth flagging as a term of art: the features are digital in the sense of being quantified and machine-readable, but they are produced by human coders, not by any automated recognition system.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: BMC Psychiatry 24:799, 2024, open access under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; received 10 May 2024, accepted 30 September 2024, doi 10.1186/s12888-024-06129-9. A clinical psychiatry venue, and the difference from the engineering venues that dominate this corpus is visible throughout: the paper reports matching statistics and their tests, cites the psychometrics of its diagnostic instrument, describes coder training and inter-rater reliability, reports odds ratios with confidence intervals, tests calibration and goodness of fit, enumerates five limitations including its own selection bias, and supplies the full coding manual as supplementary material. It is comparably weak where clinical journals are typically weak: the statistical software is not named, the code is not available, the stepwise criterion is unstated and no optimism-corrected estimate is reported. The version under review is the blinded submission, with the recruiting hospital and ethics committee anonymised in the text.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2024 by the Peking University Sixth Hospital group - NHC Key Laboratory of Mental Health and the National Clinical Research Center for Mental Disorders - together with authors from ALSOLIFE, a Beijing autism-services company, with no external funding and two patent applications declared by six of the eleven authors. The framing is developmental and clinical rather than technological: play is introduced as a meaningful activity in its own right that supports quality of life, social inclusion and later friendships, and the argument for using it as a measure is that the core traits of autism naturally manifest there. The intended contribution is a time- and cost-efficient screening aid that could 'remove the geographic barriers' to early identification. For this review the study is valuable on four counts. It has the most complete clinical characterisation of any behavioural study charted here - real DSM-5 best-estimate diagnosis by psychiatrists, CARS-2 corroboration with cited psychometrics, deliberate matching on age and sex with tests reported, and comorbidity and medication handled by explicit exclusion. It demonstrates what a brief observation can and cannot access: the social-communication and play dimensions separated the groups while the restricted-repetitive indicators were statistically degenerate in 90 seconds, confirming a hypothesis the authors stated in advance and bounding what every short-observation study in this corpus can claim. It reports honest and modest performance - AUC 0.826, sensitivity 85.4%, specificity 68.3% - with calibration, predictive values and per-predictor confidence intervals, in a literature where accuracy alone above 95% is the norm. And its limitations section contains the clearest statement of spectrum truncation and its effect anywhere in this review: children below CARS-2 30 were excluded, 'consequently, the performance of the clinical prediction model may be overestimated'. Two cautions travel with it. The five predictors were selected from 81 candidates and the operating threshold from the same ROC curve, all on the development sample, so the reported figures are apparent rather than validated, and the bootstrap that was run is not reported as an optimism correction. And the screening claim rests on predictive values computed at the matched 50% prevalence; at any realistic base rate a specificity of 68.3% would make most positive calls false, which is the calculation that determines whether this tool is deployable in the settings its authors envisage.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Predictive model using autism
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Nakamura D; Hanawa Y; Seki S; Yamauchi M; Iwami Y; Nagatsuka Y; Suzuki H; Aoyagi K; Hayashi W; Otowa T; Iwanami A
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional clinical comparison and diagnostic prediction-model development study, contrasting two clinical groups rather than a clinical group against typical development, with internal holdout validation
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Two representations were compared. The instrument's own algorithm domain scores - communication and reciprocal social interaction for the original algorithm, social affect and restricted repetitive behaviour for the revised algorithm - and a binary vector of per-item non-zero indicators from which the six-item model was built.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Adults over 18; no upper limit was applied
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None, and the authors identify it as the required next step: 'additional validation of the model using external data is required'.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 40 adults with DSM-5 schizophrenia (27 men, 13 women), mean age 33.53 years (SD 10.95), all with JART-estimated full-scale IQ above 85
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Written informed consent obtained from all participants - and, as adults with capacity, from the participants themselves rather than proxies, which distinguishes this study from most in the review
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: ADOS-2 Module 4: 15 standardised interactive activities over 40 to 60 minutes, administered by research-certified psychiatrists, designed to create social presses that elicit social interaction, communication and repetitive behaviour. Module 4 is the version intended for verbally fluent adolescents and adults. This is the most heavily standardised behavioural paradigm in the review - the instrument's reliability rests, as the paper puts it, on 'its well-structured (semi-structured) form of administration, direct observation of individuals, and strict training requirements for administration and scoring'. The trade-off relative to the automated paradigms charted elsewhere is that it requires an hour of certified clinician time per participant.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None beyond the instrument itself. Statistical analysis in SPSS version 29.0.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: 'The original contributions presented in the study are included in the article/supplementary material. Further inquiries can be directed to the corresponding author.'
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not reported; SPSS version 29.0 is named
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Showa University School of Medicine, conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and with local legislation and institutional requirements
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: ADOS-2 item codes were dichotomised into zero versus non-zero (scores of 1, 2, 3, or 8 for item B3). The rationale is stated and is a genuine psychometric argument rather than a convenience: for several items higher scores do not indicate greater autism severity but different phenotypic presentations, and the paper gives item B11, quality of social response, as its example - a rating of 1 describes limited, awkward or inconsistent reactions while a rating of 2 describes odd, stereotyped or contextually inappropriate reactions, and 'there was no clear difference between scores 1 and 2 regarding the severity of ASD symptoms'. Dichotomising to presence-or-absence of atypicality avoids treating an unordered distinction as ordinal.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Complete and clinically substantive. Every predictor is a named ADOS-2 item with a published behavioural definition, reported with an odds ratio and confidence interval and a direction. The item-level analysis is presented as a table of non-zero-score proportions for all 32 items with chi-square tests, so a reader can see the whole behavioural profile of each group rather than only the retained six - and the profile is coherent. The autism group scored non-zero more often on asking for information (90.0% against 50.0%), emphatic or emotional gestures (74.0% against 40.0%), unusual eye contact (72.0% against 22.5%), language production linked to nonverbal communication (90.0% against 55.0%) and quality of social overtures (88.0% against 47.5%). The schizophrenia group scored non-zero more often on reporting of events (60.0% against 24.0%), conversation (57.5% against 32.0%), communication of own affect (80.0% against 54.0%) and comments on others' emotions or empathy (75.0% against 34.0%). That pattern supports the paper's clinical reading - that both conditions produce social-communication atypicality but of distinguishable kinds - and it is far more useful to a clinician than a discrimination statistic.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not applicable. The analogous step is item selection: per-item logistic regressions on the full sample were used to find 'the combination of assessment items with the highest diagnostic predictive accuracy', which was then designated the Predictive Model.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Holdout validation of the six-item model, and the reporting of it is the study's most valuable methodological act. The dataset was randomly divided into training and test samples, and the paper reports both figures: 85.4% correct in training against 65.3% in test. The authors then state the inference plainly - 'The model had six variables, which was a large number compared to the number of samples; hence, the AUC may have increased due to overfitting. Therefore, additional validation of the model using external data is required.' Almost every paper in this corpus that performs a held-out check reports only the favourable number; this one reports the drop and attributes it to its own design. The apparent AUC of 0.938 and apparent accuracy of 86.6% should therefore be read against the 65.3% held-out figure, and the honest reading of this study is that a six-item model selected from 32 candidate items on 90 participants does not yet generalise. The holdout is a single random split rather than repeated cross-validation, and the split proportions and the number of repetitions are not stated.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Four, stated plainly. The sample is small and findings should be interpreted carefully. No upper age limit was applied, which may have caused an age imbalance, though the authors judge the impact limited given similar ranges, means and standard deviations. Intelligence could not be compared between groups because different instruments were used - JART for schizophrenia and WAIS-III for autism. And, most importantly, 'the holdout validation result of the Predictive Model showed a decrease in diagnostic accuracy. The model had six variables, which was a large number compared to the number of samples; hence, the AUC may have increased due to overfitting. Therefore, additional validation of the model using external data is required.'

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Ninety adults recruited from the outpatient and inpatient services of Showa University Karasuyama Hospital in central Tokyo: 40 with schizophrenia (27 men, 13 women, mean age 33.53 years, SD 10.95) recruited between April 2022 and December 2023, and 50 with autism (35 men, 15 women, mean age 33.80 years, SD 8.39) recruited between October 2018 and December 2020. Both groups required a full-scale IQ above 85 and both were diagnosed under DSM-5 by consensus among several psychiatrists with extensive experience in both conditions. Three features distinguish this sample from almost every other in the review. Both groups are clinical, drawn from the same service, so there is no clinic-versus-community recruitment asymmetry and no typically developing comparison group at all. Both are adults with fluent speech and average or above-average measured ability, which is the population in which differential diagnosis is genuinely difficult and in which most of this corpus's paediatric work has nothing to say. And roughly a third of each group is female (30% and 33%), against the heavy male preponderance typical of autism research samples - a consequence of studying adults presenting to psychiatric services rather than children referred to developmental research. Groups did not differ on age, sex or years of education. The unit of analysis is the participant, with one set of ADOS-2 item codes each.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Consistently medical and diagnostic, which fits the venue and the question. Autism is 'a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and restricted or repetitive behavioral patterns of interest'; participants are 'patients with schizophrenia' and 'participants with ASD'. The framing throughout is nosological rather than functional - the question is which category a person belongs to and how to tell, not what support they need - and the language of the instrument itself supplies terms like 'unusual eye contact' and 'speech abnormalities associated with autism'. What lifts the paper above simple deficit framing is its treatment of overlap. The introduction traces the shared history seriously, from Bleuler's use of 'autistic' as a basic symptom of schizophrenia through modern evidence of co-occurrence, familial clustering and shared genetic risk, and it describes the distinguishing features in clinical detail - the content and duration of delusions, the presence or absence of self-disturbance, the developmental timing of onset - rather than asserting a clean boundary. The discussion then treats the overlap as substantive rather than as measurement error, proposing that negative symptoms in schizophrenia and social-communication features in autism may share underlying deficits in social cognition. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person is reported as involved in the work, but the paper does not pathologise its participants beyond the diagnostic task it sets itself.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Better characterised on the clinical side than any other included study and weaker on one specific comparison. Reported and compared: age, sex, years of education, and Autism Spectrum Quotient totals for both groups. The schizophrenia group additionally has PANSS positive, negative, general psychopathology and total scores, DIEPSS drug-induced extrapyramidal symptom severity, chlorpromazine-equivalent antipsychotic dosage, age at onset and duration of illness - and all of these are used analytically, in correlations with ADOS-2 scores and in comparisons between cut-off-positive and cut-off-negative subgroups. That depth is what allows the study's most important finding, that ADOS-2 positivity in schizophrenia tracks negative-symptom severity. The gap is intelligence. Both groups were screened at a full-scale IQ above 85, but with different instruments - WAIS-III administered directly to the autism group, the Japanese Adult Reading Test estimating premorbid ability in the schizophrenia group - and the authors state that they were therefore 'unable to accurately compare intelligence between patients with schizophrenia and ASD'. This is not a minor asymmetry: JART is a reading-based estimate of premorbid rather than current function, and schizophrenia commonly involves cognitive decline from premorbid levels, so the two groups may be matched on a threshold while differing substantially in current cognitive ability. Since ADOS-2 Module 4 requires fluent speech and several discriminating items concern the structure and content of conversation, an uncontrolled difference in current verbal ability is a live alternative explanation for part of the item-level pattern. Ancestry and socioeconomic status beyond education are not reported.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: The strongest reference standard in the review for the specific question at hand, and its strength lies in what was deliberately left out of it. Diagnoses in both groups were made under DSM-5 by consensus among several psychiatrists with extensive experience in both conditions, drawing on interactions during diagnostic assessment and on prior psychiatric and medical histories. The paper then states the crucial fact: 'ASD diagnosis was a good clinical estimate, as neither the ADOS-2 nor the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R) was employed in the assessment process.' Because ADOS-2 items are the index test, any contribution of ADOS-2 to the diagnosis would have made the analysis circular - the model would be predicting a label partly derived from its own inputs, which is the failure this review has documented in the questionnaire-item studies where the class label is an arithmetic function of the modelled features. Here the separation is explicit and deliberate, and it is what makes the headline negative finding meaningful: when the ADOS-2 algorithm labels 45% to 52% of schizophrenia patients as autistic, that is a genuine disagreement with an independent clinical judgement rather than an artefact of shared information. Two qualifications. Best-estimate consensus diagnosis is the accepted standard in adult psychiatry but has no external criterion, so disagreement between algorithm and clinicians is evidence about the algorithm only if the clinicians are taken as correct. And whether the ADOS-2 administrators were blind to the established diagnosis is not stated, which matters more here than in an automated study because every item code is a clinician's judgement.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: The most thorough severity characterisation in the review, and it is used to answer a question rather than to describe the sample. The Autism Spectrum Quotient was administered to both groups as a self-report measure of autistic traits. The schizophrenia group additionally received PANSS across all four scales, DIEPSS, antipsychotic dosage in chlorpromazine equivalents, age at onset and duration of illness. These measures then carry the study's explanatory finding. All ADOS-2 domains and totals from both algorithms correlated positively with the PANSS negative scale in the schizophrenia group, with strong correlations for the original algorithm's social domain and the revised algorithm's total. Schizophrenia participants meeting the autism cut-offs had substantially higher negative-scale scores than those who did not - 27.61 against 18.36 on the original algorithm (p < 0.001) and 26.29 against 18.37 on the revised - while the positive and general psychopathology scales did not differ. And logistic regression entering all variables that differed between cut-off-positive and cut-off-negative subgroups found that cut-off positivity was predicted by the PANSS negative scale score alone. The conclusion is specific and important: what the ADOS-2 detects in adults with schizophrenia is negative-symptom severity, not autism. This is the kind of construct-validity analysis that this review has repeatedly found missing from studies whose severity data would have supported it, performed here on the group where it matters most.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The aim was to identify similarities and differences in the symptoms of schizophrenia and autism, establish a more objective method of differential diagnosis, and characterise autistic features in schizophrenia - motivated by a clinical problem the introduction sets out at length: the two conditions co-occur, cluster in families, share genetic risk and produce overlapping presentations, while the features that distinguish them (the content and duration of delusions, self-disturbance, developmental timing) are precisely the ones that become unavailable when verbal expression is poor, when symptoms are concealed, or when a high-functioning autistic adult's characteristics did not surface until adolescence. The findings answer that question in three parts. The ADOS-2's own algorithms failed: 45.0% and 52.5% of the schizophrenia group screened positive on the original and revised algorithms, AUCs were 0.562 and 0.569, and no domain score of either algorithm carried significant predictive value. An item-level model built on six items - A7 reporting of events, A10 emphatic or emotional gestures, B1 unusual eye contact, B6 comments on others' emotions or empathy, B8 responsibility, B9 quality of social overtures - reached apparent accuracy 86.6% and AUC 0.938, significantly outperforming both algorithms by DeLong's test, but dropped to 65.3% under holdout validation. And the autistic-looking features in schizophrenia proved to be negative symptoms: ADOS-2 scores correlated with the PANSS negative scale, cut-off-positive patients had higher negative-symptom scores than cut-off-negative patients, and cut-off positivity was predicted by the negative scale alone. The negative finding is the durable one. The positive finding is a promising direction whose own validation shows it is not yet ready.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Outpatient and inpatient services of a single university psychiatric hospital in central Tokyo, with both groups drawn from the same institution. This removes the recruitment asymmetry that affects nearly every case-control study in this review, where the autistic group comes from clinical services and the comparison group from schools, kindergartens or community advertising - an asymmetry that introduces differences in ascertainment, motivation and setting alongside the diagnostic difference of interest. Here both groups are patients of the same service, assessed in the same place by the same certified administrators. The setting is also the deployment setting: a differential-diagnosis aid for autism versus schizophrenia would be used in exactly this kind of adult psychiatric service. The corresponding limitation is a single site in one country with one clinical culture, and the two groups were recruited in non-overlapping windows about two years apart, which the paper does not discuss.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: ADOS-2 Module 4 - 15 standardised interactive activities over 40 to 60 minutes, administered by research-certified psychiatrists, with behaviour rated on 32 items against published criteria. Module 4 is the version for verbally fluent adolescents and adults. This is the most rigorously standardised behavioural paradigm anywhere in this review: the activities are prescribed, the coding criteria are published and detailed, administrators require formal certification, and the instrument's psychometrics are established in the literature (the paper cites sensitivity 89.6 and specificity 82.2 for the algorithms in their validation populations, figures that refer to autism against non-autism rather than against schizophrenia). Two properties of the paradigm are directly relevant to the review's synthesis. It is designed around social presses - the examiner actively creates situations that require reciprocity, so it samples behaviour under demand rather than passively - which is why it elicits far more of the phenotype in an hour than the 90-second free-play or 3-minute video paradigms charted elsewhere. And its cost is the mirror image of the automated approaches: an hour of certified clinician time per participant, which is exactly the bottleneck those approaches exist to relieve. This study is therefore useful as a reference point for what a full-cost, fully standardised behavioural assessment achieves - and the answer, for the autism-versus-schizophrenia question, is an AUC of about 0.56.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional with a single assessment session per participant and no follow-up, though the schizophrenia group's clinical characterisation includes age at onset and duration of illness, giving a longitudinal dimension to the covariates if not to the design. No test-retest data. Ethics reporting is complete: approval by the Medical Ethics Committee of Showa University School of Medicine, conduct in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and with local legislation and institutional requirements, and written informed consent from the participants themselves - who, being adults with measured IQ above 85, consented on their own behalf rather than through proxies, which is true of very few studies in this review. The authors declare no financial support of any kind and no competing interests, and acknowledge a named colleague for teaching them ADOS-2 administration and an editing service for language.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: None. The instrument, a trained administrator and a scoring sheet are the entire apparatus; analysis used SPSS 29.0. The absence of equipment is worth stating explicitly in a review otherwise populated by eye trackers, pressure sensors, motion capture, webcams and wearables, because it inverts the usual cost structure. Nothing needs to be bought, calibrated or maintained, and nothing can fail to acquire - but the assessment consumes 40 to 60 minutes of a psychiatrist who holds research certification in the instrument, plus scoring time. Every automated approach in this corpus is, in effect, an attempt to move cost from that clinician to a device. This study measures what the clinician-borne version delivers on a question the automated work has not attempted.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong on the clinical protocol, silent on computation. Reported: the site, the separate recruitment windows, full inclusion and exclusion criteria for each group, the diagnostic procedure with the explicit statement that ADOS-2 and ADI-R were excluded from it, the complete battery administered to each group, the ADOS-2 module with its activity count, duration, item count and both algorithms' cut-offs, the item dichotomisation rule with the psychometric argument for it and a worked example, the non-zero proportions for all 32 items with chi-square tests, the complete regression output including odds ratios and confidence intervals for every domain and every retained item, the prespecified AUC interpretive bands, DeLong's test for the paired ROC comparison, both training and test accuracies from holdout validation, the significance thresholds including a stricter alpha of 0.01 for correlations, the sample size justification by reference to a prior comparable study, and the statistical software with version. Not reported: administrator blinding, within-study inter-rater reliability at item level, the holdout split proportion and whether the split was repeated, and code. Data are available from the corresponding author on request.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Four limitations are stated and the fourth is the most consequential and the most creditable. The sample is small and the findings require careful interpretation. No upper age limit was applied, which may have caused an age imbalance, though the authors judge the impact limited given the similar ranges, means and standard deviations. Intelligence could not be compared because JART was used in one group and WAIS-III in the other. And: 'the holdout validation result of the Predictive Model showed a decrease in diagnostic accuracy. The model had six variables, which was a large number compared to the number of samples; hence, the AUC may have increased due to overfitting. Therefore, additional validation of the model using external data is required.' Reporting a held-out accuracy of 65.3% against a training accuracy of 85.4%, and naming overfitting as the explanation, places this paper in a very small minority within this corpus - most studies that perform such a check report only the favourable figure, and several report perfect scores without any check at all. What is not stated: whether ADOS-2 administrators were blind to diagnosis, which matters because every input is a clinician judgement; that item-level inter-rater reliability was never established within this study although the analysis operates at that granularity while the instrument's published reliability is at algorithm level; that the two groups were recruited two years apart in non-overlapping windows; that the abstract and results still present AUC 0.938 as the model's discriminative ability with the 65.3% figure confined to the body; that excluding comorbidity from both groups and severe positive symptoms from the schizophrenia group removes precisely the ambiguous cases the model is for; and that no positive predictive value is computed for any realistic clinical case mix.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: External validation of the six-item model on independent data is stated as the explicit requirement and follows directly from the holdout result. The discussion also opens a mechanistic direction: since the ADOS-2's apparent autism signal in schizophrenia tracks negative symptoms, and since negative symptoms and autistic social-communication features may both reflect deficits in social cognition supported by overlapping brain regions, the two may be partly the same construct measured under different diagnostic labels. Not proposed, and needed if the model is to progress: blinded administration, item-level inter-rater reliability, a sample that includes the diagnostically ambiguous and comorbid cases the model is intended for, comparable cognitive measurement across groups, and predictive values computed for realistic clinical mixes.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: The full 32-item behavioural repertoire of ADOS-2 Module 4, spanning communication (spoken language level, speech abnormalities, echolalia, stereotyped word use, offering and asking for information, reporting of events, conversation, descriptive gestures, emphatic gestures) and reciprocal social interaction (unusual eye contact, facial expressions directed to the examiner, language production linked with nonverbal communication, shared enjoyment, communication of own affect, comments on others' emotions or empathy, insight into social situations and relationships, responsibility, quality and amount of social overtures, quality of social response), plus imagination and restricted repetitive behaviour items. The item-level table is the study's richest contribution to this review's behavioural synthesis, because it shows that both conditions produce social-communication atypicality but of distinguishable kinds. The autism group scored non-zero more often on asking for information (90.0% against 50.0%), emphatic or emotional gestures (74.0% against 40.0%), unusual eye contact (72.0% against 22.5%), language production linked to nonverbal communication (90.0% against 55.0%) and quality of social overtures (88.0% against 47.5%). The schizophrenia group scored non-zero more often on reporting of events (60.0% against 24.0%), conversation (57.5% against 32.0%), communication of own affect (80.0% against 54.0%) and comments on others' emotions or empathy (75.0% against 34.0%). Roughly speaking, the autistic profile concentrates in the mechanics of nonverbal social exchange - gaze, gesture, the coordination of speech with nonverbal behaviour, the initiation of overtures - while the schizophrenia profile concentrates in the content and organisation of discourse and in affective and empathic commentary. The finding that matters for every behavioural study in this review is that a measure sensitive to social-communication atypicality in general will flag both groups, and that separating them requires attending to which atypicalities are present rather than how many.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: None in the sensor sense - a single observational instrument supplies everything. But the retained six-item model is cross-channel in the same way that the free-play model charted elsewhere is: it combines a discourse-content item (reporting of events), a gesture item (emphatic or emotional gestures), a gaze item (unusual eye contact) and three social-reciprocity items (comments on others' emotions or empathy, responsibility, quality of social overtures). No single channel would have sufficed, and the directions differ by channel - gaze, gesture and overture atypicality point toward autism while discourse and empathic-commentary atypicality point toward schizophrenia. That opposition of signs within one model is what allows a six-item combination to reach an apparent AUC of 0.938 where the algorithm totals, which simply add atypicality across channels, reach 0.56. It is a clean demonstration that summing behavioural abnormality destroys the information needed for differential diagnosis, and it should temper the widespread practice in this corpus of building composite atypicality scores.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Logistic regression throughout, at three levels: domain scores from each published algorithm as predictors of clinical diagnosis; per-item regressions on dichotomised non-zero indicators to identify predictive items; and a combined six-item model. A further logistic regression within the schizophrenia group predicted ADOS-2 cut-off positivity from the clinical variables that differed between cut-off-positive and cut-off-negative subgroups, returning the PANSS negative scale alone. ROC curves were compared by DeLong's test. With 90 participants and a differential-diagnosis question, regression is the correct tool and no machine learning is attempted or needed - the value of the analysis lies in what the coefficients say, not in maximising a discrimination statistic. The one modelling weakness is the size of the search: six items were chosen from 32 candidates on 90 participants by seeking 'the combination of assessment items with the highest diagnostic predictive accuracy', which is an unregularised selection over a large space, and the holdout result confirms the cost.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Two representations, compared directly. The instrument's own algorithm domain scores - communication and reciprocal social interaction under the original algorithm, social affect and restricted repetitive behaviour under the revised - which aggregate item ratings into totals against published cut-offs. And a binary per-item vector recording whether each of the 32 items received a non-zero score. The dichotomisation is the more interesting choice and is justified on psychometric rather than convenience grounds: for several items a higher rating denotes a different presentation rather than a more severe one, and the paper works through item B11, quality of social response, where a rating of 1 describes limited, awkward or inconsistent reactions and a rating of 2 describes odd, stereotyped or contextually inappropriate ones - 'there was no clear difference between scores 1 and 2 regarding the severity of ASD symptoms, and the differences were considered to be limited to phenotypic differences in symptoms'. Treating such a scale as ordinal and summing it is exactly what the algorithms do, and the collapse to presence-or-absence of atypicality is part of why the item-level analysis recovers information the totals lose.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Well chosen for the question and honestly reported.
