data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Minimal and largely unreported - maximum iterations for the multilayer perceptron and the convolutional architecture are stated, but no search procedure is described for any model. Given 64 children, restraint in tuning is appropriate, but it is not presented as a deliberate choice.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Better reasoned than the sample size would lead one to expect, and explained rather than asserted. Each child contributes one transcript and one feature vector, so the unit of analysis is the person and no within-participant leakage is possible - which distinguishes this study from the image and frame-level branches of the review. The evaluation is a 75/25 train-test split repeated over 50 random splits with results averaged, and the paper justifies both the choice and the number: 'Due to small data size, K-fold cross validation is not used, but the models are trained and evaluated on 50 random train-test splits. This number is chosen to achieve sufficient consistency with the results (evaluation metric values have stabilized and do not vary more than 1% as the number of splits is increased) while maintaining a relatively quick runtime.' Reporting a stability criterion for the number of repetitions is a level of methodological care that very few papers in this corpus show. Three limits remain. With 64 children, a 25% test partition holds 16, so each averaged estimate rests on very small folds and no confidence interval is reported. The reported accuracies of 83% and 84% are described elsewhere in the paper as obtained 'after the removal of certain features', and that removal was informed by results on the same data, so the headline is a post-selection figure. And repeated random splitting addresses variance rather than the confounds - age composition, language level, corpus of origin - that determine what the model is separating.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Two are named. The amount of data is limited, and 'having a greater variety of datasets from children of different backgrounds would also further improve model performance'. And residual noise remained after feature computation, 'though slight noise is inevitable since speech is transcribed in different ways across datasets', with the proposed remedy being preprocessing algorithms to raise the signal-to-noise ratio. The second acknowledges cross-corpus heterogeneity at the transcription level, which is the right issue partially identified.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Sixty-four children aged 3 to 6 - 30 autistic and 34 typically developing - assembled from four archived TalkBank corpora. The autistic children come from ASDBank's Eigsti and Nadig collections; the typically developing children come partly from those same collections and partly from CHILDES's Warren and Kuczaj corpora, added deliberately 'to try to balance demographic (gender and age) representations'. The paper is honest about the residual imbalance, stating that 'most participants are male, and there are more children aged 3-4 than aged 5-6', and it explains the sex imbalance correctly as a consequence of autism being 'almost 4 times as common in boys than in girls'. Numerical age and sex compositions by diagnostic group are not reported, which matters because the paper's own analysis finds that mean length of utterance - the top-ranked predictor - is the only feature that consistently increases with age. Developmentally delayed children present in the Eigsti corpus were deliberately excluded to keep the task binary, which removes the non-autistic clinical comparison group the source data could have supported. The unit of analysis is the child, one transcript and one feature vector each.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Standard clinical-deficit framing, brief and without the physiognomic or pathologising excesses found elsewhere in this corpus. Autistic children 'commonly have difficulty communicating and interacting with others, show repetitive and restricted behaviors, and have delayed cognitive and movement skills'; the phrase 'there is no permanent cure for ASD' appears, and children are once referred to as 'patients with ASD'. Person-first language predominates. The framing of the access problem is accurate and non-alarmist: diagnosis is difficult because 'there is no medical test', a professional diagnosis from age 2 is considered reliable, and 'some patients with ASD are not diagnosed until after their childhood, and many do not receive a diagnosis at all'. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person is reported as involved. The paper's most careful language is about sex: rather than treating the male preponderance in its sample as a nuisance, it names the four-to-one diagnostic ratio as the cause and then analyses features separately for boys and girls - one of very few studies in this review to treat sex as a substantive variable rather than a sampling artefact.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Partially reported and, unusually, analytically used. The paper states the age range (3 to 6), acknowledges that boys predominate and that the 3-4 band is larger than the 5-6 band, and explains the sex imbalance by reference to the diagnostic ratio. It does not give numerical age or sex breakdowns by diagnostic group, and no cognitive, language, socioeconomic or ancestry information is available. What distinguishes it from the rest of this corpus is what it does with the demographics it has: rather than reporting them and moving on, it computes every feature separately for autistic and typically developing children, for the two age bands and for boys and girls, and reports the interactions. The results are substantive - mean length of utterance rises with age; boys aged 3-4 exceed girls of the same age on the key features while girls aged 5-6 exceed boys; and mean length of turn is lower in autistic boys than typically developing boys but higher in autistic girls than typically developing girls. That last sex-by-diagnosis interaction, if real, would mean a single classifier trained mostly on boys could systematically misread girls - which is exactly the failure mode a speech study charted elsewhere in this review demonstrated empirically, with sensitivity falling from 94.8% pooled to 43.6% for girls. The gap here is that the paper stops at feature-level description and never evaluates model performance by subgroup, so the implication of its own finding goes untested.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Inherited from the source corpora and not transmitted. Children are designated autistic or typically developing by the original Eigsti and Nadig investigators, but this paper reports no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician qualification or assessment date. The labels are nonetheless in a different class from those in the web-scraped branches of this review: ASDBank and CHILDES are established research archives whose contributing studies performed documented clinical ascertainment, so the underlying labels are real diagnoses rather than folder membership or hashtag use. The specific weaknesses are that the paper does not tell the reader what those diagnoses rested on, and that the typically developing designation for the Warren and Kuczaj children means only that those corpora were collected from typically developing populations, without any screening described in this paper.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists independently of the modelled features - and this absence is the study's central interpretive problem rather than a routine gap. Mean length of utterance is the single most important predictor in both feature-importance analyses, and MLU is one of the oldest and best-established indices of expressive language development in child language research. Autistic children in this age range frequently have language delay, so a model whose leading feature is MLU may be detecting delayed expressive language rather than autism. Distinguishing the two requires an independent measure of language ability, which the archived transcripts do not supply here and which the paper does not seek. The point is sharpened by the paper's own demographic analysis: it reports that MLU is 'the only feature that consistently significantly increased with age', so the top predictor is simultaneously a developmental index and a diagnostic one, in a sample whose age composition by diagnostic group is not reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated aim is to compare classical machine learning against deep learning for autism detection from linguistic features, using more than one data source and paying attention to how features differ across age and sex - three gaps the paper identifies in prior work, the second of which ('all previous studies based their research on a single data source') is a fair criticism of much of this literature. Findings: the convolutional network reached 84% accuracy and the multilayer perceptron 83%, against 77-80% for logistic regression, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbours and random forests, and roughly ten points lower for Gaussian naive Bayes; mean length of utterance was the top-ranked feature for both models that supply importances, confirming one prior study and contradicting another on total number of words; and the demographic analysis found MLU rising with age, a reversal of the sex gap between the 3-4 and 5-6 bands, and a sex-by-diagnosis interaction on mean length of turn. The performance figures are modest, honestly reported, and benchmarked against three prior studies at 70-80%, which places them in a credible range for this task and in sharp contrast to the 95-100% figures elsewhere in this review. What the study cannot establish is what the models detect: its leading feature is a developmental language index, no independent language measure exists, and the age composition of the two groups is unreported.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting; four archived corpora with different recording protocols. The heterogeneity is presented as a strength - two data banks used 'to better represent the population and make the detection model systems more reliable' - and it is a defensible position against the single-corpus practice the paper criticises. It also creates a partial provenance confound that goes unexamined. The autistic children come only from Eigsti and Nadig; the typically developing children come from those two plus Warren and Kuczaj, which contain no autistic children at all. For that supplemented fraction, corpus of origin is perfectly correlated with class, and the corpora differ in ways that bear directly on the features: session lengths of 30 minutes, 10 minutes, unspecified and 30 minutes respectively; a structured cleanup period in one and not the others; and different investigator roles, which matters because half the features are ratios of the child's output to the investigator's. The paper addresses the transcription-convention side of cross-corpus variation in detail and does not address the protocol side.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Play-based spontaneous speech, but not one paradigm - four. Eigsti recorded 30-minute play sessions, Nadig 10-minute free play followed by a cleanup period, Warren toy play of unspecified duration and Kuczaj 30-minute spontaneous speech samples. Spontaneous play speech is a good elicitation context for the constructs of interest: it produces enough utterances to estimate MLU stably, it imposes minimal demand, and it captures conversational turn-taking with an adult, which the ratio features exploit. The heterogeneity is handled only partly. The paper normalises the three count-based features as ratios to the investigator specifically 'to normalize for different transcript lengths', which is the right instinct and addresses the most obvious threat. It does not address that a 10-minute free-play session with a cleanup period and a 30-minute spontaneous speech sample differ in more than length - in topic structure, in how much the adult initiates, and in what kinds of utterance are elicited - or that one corpus's session duration is simply unknown.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis of archived transcripts, one session per child, with no follow-up. The ethics position is stated briefly and is defensible: 'The data used in this research is from a publicly available database. The information was gathered with informed consent. This research will not involve any personal information.' Unlike the web-scraping and institutional-imaging studies charted elsewhere in this review, the underlying material was collected for research purposes with consent obtained at source and archived under a governance framework designed for reuse, so a secondary analysis of it raises materially different questions from harvesting children's photographs from support pages or thermally imaging pupils at a special school. Funding and competing interests are not stated.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No instrumentation. Stanford's Stanza NLP package parsed sentences and tokens; scikit-learn supplied five classical models and the multilayer perceptron; Keras supplied the convolutional network. The computational cost is trivial and the input is text that already exists in a public archive, so this is among the least resource-intensive designs in the review - which is also its limitation, since it inherits whatever the original recordings and transcriptions captured and can add nothing.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Good for a short conference paper, and notably strong on the preprocessing that determines whether cross-corpus features are comparable. Reported: all four source corpora by name with recording protocols where known, the deliberate exclusion of developmentally delayed children, group sizes, the age range, all six features with both their child-alone and ratio definitions and the reason ratios were used, the NLP package, the token-cleaning rules in detail - symbols removed, bracketed and parenthesised tokens removed as unspoken, 'xxx' and '@<letters>' special-form markers stripped because they are used inconsistently across datasets, '&=' tokens removed as non-speech sounds - the seven models with their library provenance, the convolutional architecture layer by layer, the 75/25 split, the 50 repeated splits with the stability criterion that justified that number, and all five metrics with ROC variability bands. Not reported: age and sex composition by diagnostic group, the source corpora's diagnostic procedures, which features were removed before the headline accuracies, and code.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Two limitations are stated: limited data, with a call for greater variety of participant backgrounds; and residual noise after feature computation, acknowledged as partly inevitable 'since speech is transcribed in different ways across datasets'. The second identifies cross-corpus heterogeneity at the transcription level, which is the right issue seen from one side. What is not addressed: mean length of utterance, the top predictor, is a developmental language index that the paper's own analysis shows increasing with age, and with no independent language measure and no reported age composition by group, language delay and age cannot be separated from autism; part of the typically developing class comes from corpora containing no autistic children and using different protocols, so corpus of origin is partly correlated with class; session lengths differ threefold where stated and are unknown for one corpus, and the investigator's role differs across protocols although half the features are ratios to the investigator; developmentally delayed children were deliberately excluded, removing the clinical comparison that would have made the result far more informative; the headline accuracies were obtained 'after the removal of certain features' selected on the same data; no confidence intervals accompany estimates from test folds of sixteen children; and no model performance is reported by age band or sex despite the feature analysis being stratified and despite that analysis finding a sex-by-diagnosis interaction.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Larger and more varied datasets; better preprocessing to reduce transcription noise; and, implied by the mean-word-length finding, lexical complexity measured in phonemes or morphemes rather than characters. Not proposed, and needed: an independent language measure to separate delay from autism; reporting of age and sex composition by diagnostic group; model evaluation stratified by sex, given the interaction the paper itself reports; and reinstatement of the developmentally delayed children as a third class, since the source corpus contains them and the resulting three-way discrimination is what clinical practice requires.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Structural and quantitative properties of spontaneous speech, operationalised as six standard psycholinguistic descriptors: mean length of utterance, mean length of turn, mean word length, number of utterances, total number of words and number of different words. Two design decisions distinguish this from a generic bag-of-features approach. Each feature was computed both for the child alone and as a ratio to the investigator's value in the same session, and the two versions were compared empirically to see which carried more information - a construct-level question about whether autistic children's speech differs absolutely or relative to their conversational partner's. And the count-based features were used only in ratio form to normalise for transcript length. The results locate the discriminative information in utterance and turn length and in the child's output relative to the adult's, with typically developing children higher on cMLU, rMLU, rMLT, rUtts and rTNW - a coherent picture of shorter utterances, shorter turns and proportionally less talk. Mean word length carried no signal, and the paper draws the right conclusion, that characters are a poor proxy for lexical complexity and that phonemes or morphemes would be the correct unit. The construct that this cannot separate from autism is expressive language level, of which MLU is a canonical index.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: None across modalities - text only, with no acoustic, prosodic or visual information. The ratio features constitute a form of dyadic fusion in that they combine the child's output with the investigator's within a session, which is conceptually similar to the interaction-level modelling in the pose-based studies charted elsewhere in this review and is more than most transcript-based work attempts. Its vulnerability is that the investigator's behaviour is not standardised across the four source corpora, so the denominator of every ratio feature varies by protocol.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A systematic seven-model comparison spanning logistic regression, Gaussian naive Bayes, random forests, k-nearest neighbours, support vector machines, a multilayer perceptron and a small convolutional network. Comparing classical against neural models on the same features is the paper's stated purpose and is executed evenly - same features, same splits, same metrics. The scale is appropriate for 64 children and twelve features, and the classical models are the ones such data can support. The conclusion drawn from the comparison, however, exceeds it: a 5-to-10-point advantage for neural models on 64 children, with test folds of sixteen and no confidence intervals, is not a stable basis for the recommendation to use deep learning clinically, and the one-to-two-point margin between the multilayer perceptron and the convolutional network is certainly not.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A vector of at most twelve interpretable linguistic values per child, reduced after a first round comparing the child-alone and ratio forms of each feature. This is the most parsimonious representation in the review and is well matched to the sample: every dimension is a quantity with a published psycholinguistic literature, computed by documented rules from a public archive, so the representation is auditable end to end. Its limitation is that transcript-level aggregation discards everything about how the speech unfolded - no sequence, no timing, no prosody - so constructs such as turn-taking latency or intonation, which the wider literature associates with autistic speech, are outside its reach.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUC for all seven models, with ROC curves that plot the individual splits, the mean curve and a one-standard-deviation band. That variability band is worth singling out: on 64 children with 50 repeated splits it conveys the instability of the estimate more honestly than a point figure, and it is a form of uncertainty reporting that almost no other study in this review provides. Precision and recall are also interpreted correctly in clinical terms, with recall of 80-81% read as a low false-negative rate 'important for ensuring that children with ASD are diagnosed correctly' and precision of 84-86% as protecting children without autism from being misdiagnosed. Missing: confidence intervals, confusion matrices, calibration, and any positive predictive value at a realistic prevalence - the last mattering because the reported precision holds only at the near-balanced sample ratio.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Among the better-handled in the review, because the features are interpretable by construction and the interpretation is pursued rather than asserted. Feature-importance plots are given for logistic regression and random forests; mean length of utterance emerges as the top predictor in both; and the finding is compared explicitly against prior literature, confirming one study's MLU result and contradicting another's conclusion that total number of words does not differ. The stratified analysis goes beyond importance to describe how each feature behaves across diagnosis, age band and sex, producing the specific and testable claims recorded above. And the negative result on mean word length is interpreted correctly rather than ignored - characters are the wrong unit for lexical complexity, and phonemes or morphemes would be better. What interpretability cannot settle here is the identity of the underlying construct: MLU is a developmental language index and no independent measure of language ability exists in the data, so the models' leading signal is compatible with autism-specific pragmatic difference and with generic expressive language delay, and the paper does not raise the distinction.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Sound on the mechanics for a study of this size, and unresolved on the confounds. Each child contributes one transcript and one feature vector, so the split unit is the person and no within-participant leakage is possible - which places this study among the minority in the review not exposed to the failure that dominates the image, frame and thermal branches. The evaluation is a 75/25 split repeated over 50 random draws with results averaged, and the choice is both explained and empirically justified: cross-validation was rejected because of small sample size, and 50 repetitions were selected because metrics stabilised, varying by no more than 1% as further splits were added. Stating a stability criterion for the number of repetitions is a level of care that very few papers in this corpus show, and the ROC plots with a one-standard-deviation band around the mean curve carry that honesty into the presentation. Three qualifications bound what this buys. Test folds contain sixteen children, so each averaged estimate rests on very small samples and no confidence interval is given; the headline 83-84% is stated elsewhere in the paper to have been obtained 'after the removal of certain features', a selection made on the same data, so it is a post-selection figure; and repeated random splitting addresses sampling variance and not the three confounds that determine what is being separated. Those are, in order of importance: that the top-ranked feature is a developmental language index with no independent language measure available and no age composition reported by group; that part of the typically developing class comes from corpora containing no autistic children, so corpus of origin is partly correlated with class; and that the four source protocols differ in session length, structure and investigator role, while half the features are ratios to that investigator's output. None of these would be revealed by any splitting scheme, and none is addressed.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder, Natural Language Processing, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Linguistics. Balanced across population, modality and method, and 'Linguistics' in particular signals that the features are psycholinguistic constructs rather than learned embeddings. Terms carried through the body: mean length of utterance, mean length of turn, total number of words, number of different words, TalkBank, CHILDES, ASDBank, Stanza, feature importance, train-test split.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: 2024 IEEE 3rd International Conference on Computing and Machine Intelligence (ICMI), doi 10.1109/ICMI60790.2024.10585946. A short computing-conference paper, single-authored by a student at The Harker School in San Jose - a secondary school - which is worth recording factually because it contextualises both the scale and the character of the work. The paper is careful where a beginner might not be: it splits by participant, justifies its repeated-split design with a stated stability criterion, documents its token-cleaning rules against TalkBank's transcription guide, plots ROC variability bands, compares its feature findings explicitly against three named prior studies including where it contradicts them, and reports modest accuracies without inflation. It is weaker on the clinical reasoning that a conference in computing and machine intelligence would not have prompted: no independent language measure, no age composition by group, a non-autistic clinical comparison deliberately discarded, and a recommendation about clinical model choice resting on a one-to-two-point margin. Set beside several journal papers in this review that report 98-100% from image-level splits on web-scraped corpora, its 84% from a participant-level split on a consented research archive is the more informative result.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Presented at an IEEE computing conference in 2024 by a single secondary-school author in California. The framing is the standard early-detection argument, stated accurately: 1 in 36 children affected, no medical test, professional diagnosis reliable from age 2, and many children diagnosed late or never. For this review the study is valuable on four counts that have little to do with its accuracy figure. It is one of a small number of included studies whose split unit is the participant and whose evaluation design is both explained and empirically justified - 50 repeated 75/25 splits chosen because metrics stabilised within 1% - and it reports estimate variability through ROC standard-deviation bands rather than a bare point figure. Its features are named psycholinguistic constructs with an established literature, so its results are directly comparable with prior findings, and it makes those comparisons explicitly, confirming one study's mean-length-of-utterance result and contradicting another's on total word count. Its accuracy of 83-84%, benchmarked against three prior studies at 70-80%, sits in a credible range for a genuinely hard task and provides a useful calibration point against the 95-100% figures produced elsewhere in this review by leaked or confounded designs. And its sex-stratified feature analysis reports a diagnosis-by-sex interaction - mean length of turn lower in autistic boys than typically developing boys but higher in autistic girls than typically developing girls - which, if real, means a classifier trained predominantly on boys would misread girls, exactly the failure another study in this review demonstrated empirically with sensitivity falling from 94.8% pooled to 43.6% for girls. Three cautions travel with it. The top-ranked predictor is mean length of utterance, a canonical index of expressive language development that the paper's own analysis shows rising with age, and with no independent language measure and no age composition reported by group, language delay and age cannot be separated from autism as explanations. Part of the typically developing class was drawn from corpora containing no autistic children and using different recording protocols, so corpus of origin is partly correlated with class, and the four protocols differ in session length, structure and investigator role while half the features are ratios to the investigator's output. And the developmentally delayed children present in one source corpus were deliberately excluded to keep the task binary, discarding the non-autistic clinical comparison that would have made the study far more informative and that the review has found almost nowhere else.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Shin J; Miah ASM; Kakizaki M; Hassan N; Tomioka Y
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective algorithm-development and architecture-comparison study on two public skeleton datasets, with repeated cross-validation and an ablation across six image backbones and two sequence models
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Three-dimensional joint coordinates - 25 joints from Kinect v2 in the Gait dataset, 10 upper-body joints from Kinect v1 in DREAM - re-expressed either as Skepxel images or as angle-augmented graph sequences. The skeleton representation is worth noting as a confound control of the same kind used by the Geneva pose study charted elsewhere in this review: it discards appearance, face, clothing, room and lighting entirely, so a classifier operating on it cannot exploit the identity and setting confounds that dominate the image-based branch.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: 4 to 12 years (Gait Fullbody); 3 to 7 years (DREAM, with ages recorded in months)
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 100 children in the Gait Fullbody Dataset and 61 in DREAM
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None across datasets in the evaluative sense - the two corpora are used in parallel rather than one held out from the other, and their sensor and joint differences would in any case prevent direct transfer. Evaluating on two independent corpora is nonetheless more than most of this branch attempts, and the 25-point difference between them is itself the study's most useful finding about generalisability.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 50 typically developing children in Gait Fullbody. In DREAM the non-spectrum class was excluded from the analysis, following the prior study the architecture is derived from.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Obtained by the original data collectors; not addressed here
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Walking trials in the Gait Fullbody Dataset - ten per child, of which one was retained - and robot-assisted therapy sessions in DREAM. Neither paradigm is described in detail here, and the DREAM sessions involve interaction with a robot, so what the child was doing when each sample was recorded is not characterised.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Microsoft Kinect v2 (25 joints) for the Gait Fullbody Dataset and Kinect v1 (20 joints, of which 10 upper-body joints are recorded) for DREAM, with the difference in joint coverage documented explicitly. Analysis used Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.5.1, Torchvision, NumPy, scikit-learn, SciPy, Seaborn, Pandas and OpenCV, on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 with 48 GB RAM under Ubuntu, with SGD at learning rate 0.001 and batch size 12. The software stack is reported with version numbers throughout, which is unusually complete.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Both datasets are public and identified: the Gait Fullbody Dataset by Dryad DOI 10.5061/dryad.s7h44j150 with an access date, and DREAM by citation.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not released by these authors, though the paper states that the GitHub code from the prior study was used and identifies a specific configuration requirement - that the cluster_distance_loss option must be set to True to enable Skepxels - which is a genuinely useful reproducibility detail.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: None stated. Both datasets are public secondary sources collected by other groups under their own governance, so no fresh approval would ordinarily be sought, and the paper contains no institutional review statement. It does engage with a related question in its introduction, noting that prior eye-tracking work 'raised concerns about ensuring anonymity' and that gaze data pose 'the issue of privacy protection' - and it positions skeleton data as an answer, since joint coordinates carry no facial or appearance information. That is a real privacy advantage of the modality and is stated as a motivation rather than merely a side effect.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Stream one: skeleton sequences encoded as Skepxels and passed to an image backbone. Stream two: relative joint angles embedded into the skeleton sequence, then MSG3D for spatiotemporal extraction. Both are learned representations over engineered inputs.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None attempted. No attribution, joint-importance analysis or kinematic characterisation is reported, so which aspects of movement drive the classification is unknown. This is a missed opportunity that the modality makes unusually accessible: skeleton data are inherently interpretable, joint-level or phase-level importance would map directly onto describable gait features such as stride variability, arm swing asymmetry or postural sway, and the clinical literature the paper cites is framed in exactly those terms. The Geneva pose study charted elsewhere in this review demonstrates what such an analysis can yield.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: SGD at learning rate 0.001, batch size 12, 30 epochs initially and extended to 100 after inspecting preliminary learning curves. The extension is explained by reference to observed convergence behaviour rather than asserted.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Two different arrangements with very different properties, and the paper reports both in full. On the Gait Fullbody Dataset, each of the 100 children contributes exactly one sample - one selected walking trial - so 10-fold cross-validation splits 90 training against 10 test children, and the unit is unavoidably the participant. Each configuration was run through a complete cross-validation cycle five times, giving 50 training runs, with mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation reported across runs. That is sound, and the reporting of dispersion across repetitions is better than most of this corpus. On DREAM the arrangement is materially weaker: 1,833 samples from 61 children were split 1,650 against 183 per fold with no participant-level partitioning described, so roughly 30 samples per child are distributed across folds and within-participant leakage is unaddressed. The interesting result is that the leak-prone dataset produced the lower accuracy - 70.19% on DREAM against 95.4% on Gait Fullbody - which indicates that the difference between the two figures is driven by something other than leakage, most plausibly by the far richer 25-joint full-body gait representation against 10 upper-body joints. Two further issues bound the Gait figure despite its clean split unit. Each child's single sample was chosen from ten trials on the basis of the diagnosis and a clinician's recommendation, so the data were selected on the outcome before any model saw them. And the paper reports the maximum across runs alongside the mean, with the abstract quoting the best-performing architecture's 95.4% rather than the reference model's 94.8%, on a test fold of ten children where one child is worth ten percentage points.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The conclusion names three: generalisability requires further optimisation, 'particularly for datasets with biased label distributions'; the computational complexity of dual-stream models 'poses challenges for real-time clinical applications'; and future work should pursue lightweight architectures, improved augmentation and pre-training. Naming its own computational cost as a barrier to the clinical use it proposes is a candid admission. There is no separate limitations section.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two public corpora used in parallel. The Gait Fullbody Dataset, created by Al-Jubouri and colleagues, contains 100 children aged 4 to 12 - 50 autistic and 50 typically developing - recorded with a Kinect v2 capturing 25 joint coordinates, with each child performing ten walking trials of which one was retained, giving 100 samples. A separate subset of nine children with severe symptoms is available and is not analysed here. The DREAM dataset contains 61 children aged 3 to 7, recorded with Kinect v1 during robot-assisted therapy, yielding 3,121 samples of which 1,833 were used after the non-spectrum class was excluded; only 10 upper-body joints are recorded, since Kinect v1 detects 20 joints and DREAM omits the lower body. No age distribution, sex, cognitive level, language ability or clinical characterisation is available for either corpus. Two structural facts shape everything downstream. In the Gait dataset each child contributes exactly one sample, so cross-validation necessarily partitions children - a property that arises from the data rather than from a design decision, but that gives this study the participant-level split unit most of the video branch lacks. And that single retained sample was chosen from ten trials 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation', so the modelled data were selected with knowledge of the outcome.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Predominantly medical, with 'patients with ASD' used repeatedly and autism described as a set of 'complex developmental disabilities' with symptoms such as 'a lack of eye contact and an obsession with certain behaviours'. Two passages show more thought than the register suggests. The introduction gives an accurate and unusually careful account of rising prevalence, noting that the doubling of diagnoses between 2015 and 2024 occurred despite the stricter DSM-5 criteria expected to reduce it, and attributing the net increase to awareness and earlier diagnosis - concluding that 'many patients with ASD have not yet surfaced'. That is the correct reading of the epidemiological trend and stands against the alarm framing used elsewhere in this corpus. And the account of the access barrier is concrete rather than rhetorical: 'the high barrier to visiting a hospital, along with the fact that many children are not yet able to speak. Deciding to visit a hospital often requires recognising signs within the household', with the proposed role for the technology being to give families 'a clearer motivation to visit a hospital' rather than to substitute for assessment. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person is reported as involved.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Absent for both corpora beyond the stated age ranges of 4 to 12 and 3 to 7 years. No age distribution by diagnostic group, no sex, no cognitive or language measure, no ancestry and no comorbidity. Two of these are specifically damaging for a gait study. Walking kinematics mature substantially across 4 to 12 years - stride length, cadence, arm swing, double-support time and postural stability all change - so if the autistic and typically developing groups differ in age composition, a gait classifier and an age classifier would be behaviourally indistinguishable, and nothing reported allows the check. And gait differs by sex from middle childhood, with no sex information available in either corpus. The DREAM corpus additionally spans 3 to 7 years with ages recorded in months, so finer age information exists in the source data and is not used. The paper does not report demographic composition for either dataset or acknowledge these as confounds.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Inherited and undescribed for both corpora - no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician qualification or assessment date appears anywhere. The Gait Fullbody Dataset carries binary autistic and typically developing labels from its creators; DREAM carries a three-level label - non-spectrum, ASD and AUT - of which the non-spectrum class was discarded, following the prior study whose architecture this work extends. Discarding the non-spectrum group has a consequence the paper does not draw: the DREAM experiment is then a discrimination between two autism-related categories rather than between autism and non-autism, so its 70.19% is not comparable to the Gait dataset's autism-versus-typical task and the two figures cannot be read as measurements of the same thing. The reference-standard issue that most affects validity, however, is procedural rather than definitional. The methods state that in the Gait dataset each child performed ten walking trials and 'the most optimal trial was selected based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation'. Selecting which of a child's trials enters the dataset on the basis of that child's diagnosis is selection on the outcome: it means the 100 modelled samples are not a random sample of each child's walking but the trial a clinician judged most suitable given what the child was known to have. Whatever separation the models achieve is conditioned on that choice, and no splitting scheme downstream can undo it.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None used. The Gait Fullbody Dataset includes a subset of nine children with severe symptoms, and the paper's methodology section states that the architecture is proposed 'for ASD detection and severity assessment' - but no severity analysis is performed, no result for the severe subset is reported, and severity appears nowhere in the results. DREAM's three-level labelling likewise encodes a gradient that is collapsed by discarding one class. No cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists for either corpus.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The aim is to optimise a dual-stream skeleton architecture for autism detection, replacing the vision transformer of a prior design with a convolutional backbone to test whether CNN-based models capture gesture features effectively, and comparing MSG3D against a Stack Transformer in the temporal stream. The headline results are 95.4% on the Gait Fullbody Dataset and 70.19% on DREAM. The more informative findings are in the ablation tables. Across six image backbones the Gait results span 93.2% to 95.4% and the DREAM results 68.92% to 70.19% - so architecture choice moves accuracy by around two points on one dataset and one point on the other, while the gap between the two datasets is 25 points. That is a clean demonstration that in this branch the data determine performance and the model barely matters, which is a useful corrective to a literature organised around architectural novelty. The paper also reports that substituting a Stack Transformer for MSG3D lowered accuracy, and it reports its own reference implementation (ViT-B at 94.8%) alongside the alternatives rather than only the winner. What the study does not establish is what the 25-point gap means: the two corpora differ in sensor generation, joint coverage (25 full-body against 10 upper-body), task (walking against robot-assisted therapy), label structure (autism versus typical against two autism-related classes) and splitting unit (child against sample), and no analysis separates these.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting. The Gait Fullbody Dataset records walking trials captured by Kinect v2, and DREAM was collected during robot-assisted therapy sessions with Kinect v1. The paper documents the sensor difference carefully - Kinect v2 detects 25 joints, Kinect v1 detects 20, and DREAM omits the lower body leaving 10 - which is exactly the kind of acquisition detail that determines cross-corpus comparability and that most secondary-analysis studies in this review omit. It does not, however, examine the settings themselves: what the children were doing during DREAM sessions, how a robot's presence shapes movement, or whether the walking protocol was standardised in distance, speed or footwear. Within each corpus, both classes were recorded under the same conditions, so the acquisition confound that affects the photograph and clinic-versus-school audio studies charted elsewhere in this review does not arise here - a genuine structural advantage of using purpose-built research corpora.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Walking trials in one corpus and robot-assisted therapy sessions in the other, neither described in detail. The gait paradigm is well chosen for the review's purposes: walking requires no verbal ability, imposes no social demand, is producible by very young children, and yields a motor signal that can be measured objectively - which the paper argues explicitly, noting that diagnosis 'often requires speech-based tests' but 'at the early detection stage, many young children may not yet be able to speak'. That argument identifies a real gap in the assessment landscape, since the language-based measures charted elsewhere in this review are inapplicable to precisely the youngest and least verbal children for whom early detection matters most. Two things weaken the execution. Only one of ten walking trials per child is retained, and that trial was chosen with knowledge of the diagnosis, so within-child variability - which is itself a candidate marker in motor studies - is discarded by a non-blind procedure. And in DREAM the recorded movements arise from therapy interaction with only upper-body joints available, so the gait construct that motivates the paper is not measurable in the second dataset at all.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element. No ethics statement appears, which is conventional for analysis of two public corpora collected under their originators' governance. The paper does address a related concern substantively, and its argument deserves recording: it notes that prior eye-tracking work 'raised concerns about ensuring anonymity' and identifies 'the issue of privacy protection associated with gaze data', then positions skeleton representation as the answer. Joint coordinates carry no face, appearance, clothing, room or lighting information, so a skeleton corpus is inherently less identifying than the video or photograph corpora that dominate this branch. That is a real privacy property of the modality, argued as a motivation rather than noted as a side effect, and it aligns with the same reasoning that led the Geneva group charted elsewhere in this review to render pose as skeleton-on-black and to release a de-identified pose subsample when raw video could not be shared. Funding from the University of Aizu Competitive Research Fund is declared, competing interests are declared as none, and both datasets are identified with public locations.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Microsoft Kinect v2 for the Gait Fullbody Dataset, giving 25 three-dimensional joint coordinates, and Kinect v1 for DREAM, giving 20 joints of which 10 upper-body positions are recorded. The paper explains the difference and its consequence for comparability, with a figure contrasting the two joint layouts. Kinect-class depth sensing is consumer hardware, which matters for the deployment argument: skeleton capture requires no markers, no wearables, no calibration by the family and no clinical instrumentation, and produces data that cannot identify the child by appearance. Analysis used Python 3.10 with nine named packages at stated versions on an RTX 3090 with 48 GB RAM, trained with SGD at learning rate 0.001 and batch size 12 - a fuller software and hardware specification than almost any other study in this review provides.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Among the more reproducible computational records in the corpus. Reported: both datasets with public access locations, one with a Dryad DOI and access date; sensor models, joint counts and the difference between the two Kinect generations with a figure; sample counts for both corpora; the exclusion of the non-spectrum class; the complete software stack with version numbers for nine packages; the hardware; optimiser, learning rate and batch size; the epoch schedule with the reason for its extension; the cross-validation scheme with fold sizes and repetition counts stated separately for each dataset, including why DREAM was run three times rather than five; mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation for every architecture on both datasets; and the specific configuration flag needed to enable Skepxels in the inherited codebase. Not reported: whether DREAM splitting respected participants, any demographic composition, per-class counts for DREAM, sensitivity and specificity, and the authors' own code.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The conclusion names three limitations: generalisability requires further optimisation, 'particularly for datasets with biased label distributions'; 'the computational complexity of dual-stream models also poses challenges for real-time clinical applications'; and future work should pursue lightweight architectures, improved augmentation and pre-training. Naming one's own computational cost as an obstacle to the clinical use one proposes is candid, and identifying label imbalance as the source of the DREAM shortfall is a reasonable diagnosis even if not the only one. There is no separate limitations section, and several substantial issues go unaddressed. The Gait dataset's single retained trial per child was selected 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation' - the methods quote it and nothing follows. No participant-level partitioning is described for DREAM, where 1,833 samples come from 61 children. No demographic information exists for either corpus, in a domain where gait varies strongly with age and sex. No sensitivity, specificity, AUC or confusion matrix is reported for any proposed model, so a screening claim rests on accuracy alone. The 95.4% is a best-of-six architecture selection on test folds of ten children, where one child is worth ten percentage points and the six backbones span 2.2 points. And the paper reports, without comment, that the Gait dataset's own creators moved from approximately 60% accuracy without augmentation to 92% with seven augmentation techniques - a 32-point gain from augmentation alone, which is as clear a statement of augmentation-driven inflation as this review has found, quoted as background rather than treated as a warning.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Lightweight architectures to make dual-stream inference tractable in real time; improved augmentation and pre-training; and multimodal extension combining audio and visual data with skeleton. Not proposed, and needed: participant-level partitioning for DREAM; sensitivity and specificity alongside accuracy; demographic reporting and age-stratified analysis; use of all ten walking trials per child rather than one clinician-selected trial, which would both remove the outcome-informed selection and make within-child movement variability available as a feature; and joint-level attribution, which skeleton data make straightforward and which would connect model behaviour to describable gait characteristics.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Whole-body movement kinematics, and the construct argument is one of the better ones in this review. Gait and gesture are presented as 'prominent behavioural markers' that can be 'efficiently and non-intrusively captured', and the case for preferring them to language-based assessment is made explicitly: diagnosis 'often requires speech-based tests', yet at the early detection stage 'many young children may not yet be able to speak'. That identifies a genuine coverage gap - the transcript-based and conversational measures charted elsewhere in this review are inapplicable to non-speaking and pre-verbal children, who are precisely the population early detection targets. The operationalisation is only partly matched to the argument. In the Gait dataset the construct is walking, measured across 25 full-body joints, which is the right instrument for the claim. In DREAM only 10 upper-body joints are available and the movements arise from therapy interaction, so gait is not measurable and the second experiment addresses a different construct under the same label. And no interpretability analysis connects the models to any nameable movement characteristic, so what aspect of gait the 95.4% reflects - stride variability, arm swing, postural sway, turning - is unknown, despite skeleton data making such an analysis unusually accessible.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Two representational streams over one sensor, aligned by a pairwise Euclidean distance loss during training and then tested separately. Stream one encodes skeleton sequences as Skepxels for an image backbone; stream two embeds relative joint angles and applies MSG3D, combining graph convolution over the skeletal topology with temporal convolution over time. The design rationale is stated clearly - the loss 'minimises the distance between the Skepxel embedding, which captures spatiotemporal features, and the GCN embedding, which models structural joint relationships', promoting co-learning of complementary representations - and the ablation supports the graph component, with a Stack Transformer substitution lowering accuracy. This is representational rather than sensor fusion, but it is a coherent idea coherently tested. What is missing is a decomposition of how much each stream contributes to the final figure, which would be the natural complement to the architecture ablation that is reported.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A dual-stream architecture derived from a prior design, with two deliberate substitutions tested: ConvNeXt-Base replacing the original ViT-B in the image stream to assess whether CNN backbones capture gesture features effectively, and a Stack Transformer trialled against MSG3D in the sequence stream. Six image backbones were compared in total - ViT-B, ConvNeXt-Base, Swin-V2-B, ShuffleNetV2-X2, ResNet-152 and MaxViT-T - spanning transformer, convolutional and hybrid families. The comparison is even-handed and the reference implementation is reported alongside the alternatives rather than only the winner. Its most valuable outcome is a negative one: across six architectures the accuracy spread is 2.2 points on one dataset and 1.3 on the other, against a 25-point gap between the datasets, so architectural choice is nearly irrelevant to performance here. For a literature in which most papers are organised around a new architecture, that is a finding worth propagating.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Three-dimensional joint coordinate sequences, re-expressed two ways - as Skepxel images and as angle-augmented graph sequences. The skeleton representation functions as a designed confound control of the same kind used by the Geneva pose study charted elsewhere in this review: face, expression, clothing, body habitus, room, lighting and background are all absent by construction, so a classifier operating on it cannot exploit the appearance and setting confounds that dominate the photograph branch. It also carries the privacy property the paper argues for, since joint coordinates do not identify a child by appearance. The limitation is coverage: 25 full-body joints in one corpus against 10 upper-body joints in the other, so the two experiments do not measure the same thing, and the paper's own figure contrasting the joint layouts makes this visible without drawing the inference for the 25-point performance gap.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy only, but reported with dispersion - average, maximum, minimum and standard deviation across repeated cross-validation cycles for every architecture on both datasets, plus per-epoch accuracy and loss curves. The dispersion reporting is a real strength and is what makes the architecture comparison interpretable: standard deviations of 0.71 to 1.82 on the Gait dataset against a 2.2-point spread between backbones show immediately that the architectural differences are barely larger than run-to-run noise, and the paper is able to note that ShuffleNet was more stable than MaxViT at the same mean accuracy. What is absent is everything a screening claim requires. No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC or confusion matrix is reported for any proposed model, so the balance between missed cases and false alarms is unknown, and no positive predictive value at any realistic prevalence is computed. Accuracy on a 50:50 corpus tells a clinician very little, and on DREAM - where the class distribution is described as biased but never quantified - it tells them nothing at all.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None attempted, and the omission is more notable here than in most of this review because the modality invites it. Skeleton data are inherently interpretable: joints have names, angles have physical meaning, and time is explicit, so a joint-level or phase-level attribution would map directly onto describable gait characteristics - stride variability, arm swing amplitude and asymmetry, trunk sway, turning smoothness - which are the terms in which the clinical motor literature the paper cites is written. The Geneva pose study charted elsewhere in this review shows what such an analysis yields when its model confidences are regressed on clinical item scores. Here nothing connects the 95.4% to any nameable property of how the children walked, so the study establishes that a classifier can separate the groups and contributes nothing to understanding what it separates them on. Given that no demographic data exist either, the possibility that the models respond to age- or sex-related gait maturation rather than to autism cannot be examined from any direction.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Two arrangements with materially different properties, reported clearly enough that both can be assessed. On the Gait Fullbody Dataset the split unit is necessarily the child, because each of the 100 children contributes exactly one sample, so 10-fold cross-validation partitions 90 children against 10; each configuration was run through five complete cycles giving 50 training runs, with mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation reported. That is sound practice and the dispersion reporting is better than most of this corpus. On DREAM, 1,833 samples from 61 children were split 1,650 against 183 per fold with no participant-level partitioning described - roughly 30 samples per child distributed across folds - so within-participant leakage is unaddressed. The instructive result is the direction of the difference: the leak-prone dataset produced the lower figure, 70.19% against 95.4%, which means the gap between them cannot be explained by leakage and must lie in sensor coverage, task, label structure or class balance. That inversion is worth carrying into the synthesis, because it is a counterexample to the assumption that leakage always explains the highest numbers in a branch. Three issues nonetheless bound the Gait figure despite its clean split unit. The single sample per child was chosen from ten trials 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation', so the modelled data were selected with knowledge of the outcome - a threat that operates entirely upstream of cross-validation and that no splitting scheme addresses. The 95.4% is the best of six architectures whose spread is 2.2 points against run-to-run standard deviations reaching 1.82, on test folds of ten children where a single child moves accuracy by ten percentage points, so the difference between the reported winner and the reference implementation's 94.8% is not resolvable. And the DREAM experiment discards the non-spectrum class, making it a two-way discrimination among autism-related labels rather than an autism-versus-non-autism task, with the resulting class balance never quantified so that no chance baseline exists for its 70.19%. Finally, the paper transmits without comment the single clearest piece of evidence in this review for augmentation-driven inflation: the Gait dataset's own creators reported approximately 60% accuracy without augmentation and 92% after applying seven augmentation techniques including noise addition, scaling and flipping. A 32-point gain from augmenting a 100-sample dataset is a statement about the augmentation, not about gait, and it is quoted here as motivating background.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism diagnosis; Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs); Convolutional Neural Network (CNN); Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs); effective feature extraction; MSG3D; skeleton points. Almost entirely architectural - six of seven terms name a method or component, with 'autism diagnosis' the only clinical term and no reference to gait, movement, children or screening. Terms carried through the body: Skepxels, dual-stream, pairwise Euclidean distance loss, Kinect, joint angles, gait, gesture, early detection.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Electronics 14(11):2231, MDPI, open access under CC BY; received 26 April 2025, revised 21 May, accepted 26 May, published 30 May 2025 - a 34-day review cycle. An electronics and computing venue, and the profile matches: the software stack is versioned to nine packages, the hardware is specified, the cross-validation scheme is stated separately for each dataset with fold sizes and repetition counts, and every architecture is reported with mean, max, min and standard deviation. What a clinical venue would have required is absent: no sensitivity or specificity, no demographic composition, no examination of the outcome-informed trial selection quoted in the methods, and no discussion of what the 25-point gap between the two datasets implies about the construct being measured.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published May 2025 by the School of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Aizu, Japan, funded by the university's Competitive Research Fund. The framing is screening-oriented and modest in its target: because 'deciding to visit a hospital often requires recognising signs within the household', a video-based assessment could give families 'a clearer motivation to visit a hospital' - an aim scoped as prompting help-seeking rather than replacing assessment, which is among the better-calibrated translational positions in this review. For the synthesis the study contributes four things. Its modality argument fills a real gap: diagnosis 'often requires speech-based tests' yet 'many young children may not yet be able to speak', so a movement-based measure reaches the youngest and least verbal children whom the language-based studies charted elsewhere here cannot assess. Its skeleton representation is a designed confound control, discarding face, appearance, clothing, room and lighting entirely, and the paper argues the accompanying privacy advantage explicitly against the anonymity concerns raised for eye-tracking and video data - the same reasoning that led the Geneva group to render pose as skeleton-on-black. Its architecture comparison produces a valuable negative result: across six image backbones the accuracy spread is 2.2 points on one dataset and 1.3 on the other, against a 25-point gap between the two datasets, so in this branch the data determine performance and the architecture barely matters - a corrective to a literature organised around architectural novelty. And the direction of that 25-point gap is instructive, since the corpus with unaddressed within-participant leakage produced the lower figure, which is a counterexample to the assumption that leakage always explains the highest numbers. Three cautions travel with it. The Gait dataset's single modelled trial per child was chosen from ten 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation' - selection on the outcome, quoted in the methods and never examined. No sensitivity, specificity or confusion matrix is reported for any model, and no demographic data exist for either corpus in a domain where gait varies strongly with age and sex. And the paper transmits, as motivating background, the clearest evidence of augmentation-driven inflation in this review: the Gait dataset's own creators went from approximately 60% accuracy without augmentation to 92% with seven augmentation techniques applied to 100 samples.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Laguna et al.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Secondary analysis of an existing cry corpus, combining group-level statistical comparison of acoustic perturbation measures with a deep learning classification experiment
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: 128x128 grayscale spectrogram images per cry instance. The unit of analysis is the cry instance rather than the child, which Table 1 confirms by defining sensitivity as 'true positives, number of ASD instances' and specificity as 'true negatives, number of TD instances'.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. Single corpus, single country, no held-out cohort.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 31 typically developing children (24 boys, 7 girls), mean age 30.8 months
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: 'Comprehensive informed consent was acquired from the parents or legal guardians of the participants' before enrolment, with the paper specifying that this ensured they were informed about objectives, procedures, and possible advantages and risks
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None - cries were recorded opportunistically when they occurred. The reasons for crying were recorded and differ between groups: complaining or discomfort accounted for 74.20% of autistic and 67.75% of typically developing cries, with sleepiness, hunger and anxiety making up 25.80% and 32.25% respectively. Reporting the eliciting cause at all is good practice and rare, but the difference between groups means that cry aetiology is a further variable covarying with class, and it is not adjusted for.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Sony UX560 and UX512F voice recorders for 74.2% of recordings and smartphones with a custom recording application for 25.80%, all in WAV format at 16-bit and 44.1 kHz to ensure consistency across devices. Parents and trained voice collectors were instructed to record in quiet environments at approximately 25 cm from the child's mouth. Analysis used Praat for acoustic feature extraction.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: The source corpus is described as publicly available and is cited to Khozaei et al. 2020; supplementary material accompanies the article.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Approval from the ethics committee at Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences and Health Services, Tehran, obtained for the original collection
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Two parallel routes. For the statistical analysis, Praat computed pitch-based features including jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio per cry pattern. For the classification, cry audio was converted to spectrograms rendered as 128x128 single-channel images.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Good at the feature level and absent at the model level. The three perturbation measures are standard clinical voice-quality metrics with a physiological interpretation - jitter and shimmer index cycle-to-cycle instability in laryngeal vibration, and harmonics-to-noise ratio indexes the proportion of periodic to aperiodic energy - so the statistical findings translate directly into a claim about vocal motor control that a clinician could evaluate. Nothing connects the network's decisions to those or any other acoustic properties: no attribution over the spectrogram, no comparison between what the network responds to and what the significant features capture, and no analysis of whether the classifier's errors relate to age, recording setting or cry cause. Since the paper's two analyses could have been linked - by asking whether the network's confidence tracks jitter, shimmer or HNR - the omission leaves the deep learning result disconnected from the interpretable one.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The architecture and optimisation settings are reported in detail, but the model-selection rule is the study's decisive methodological problem: 'The training process spanned 2000 epochs, with the model exhibiting superior validation accuracy being designated as the final trained classifier.' The reported 90.28% is therefore the maximum validation accuracy observed across 2,000 epochs, selected on the same partition it is reported from.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: The weakest element, and it fails in three compounding ways. First, no test partition exists: the reported accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision and F-score are all validation-set figures, and the paper contains no held-out evaluation of any kind. Second, the final model was selected as the epoch with the best validation accuracy out of 2,000, so the reported figure is a maximum over 2,000 draws on the partition it is measured on - an optimistic selection whose expected inflation on a small validation set is large. Third, the evaluation unit is the cry instance rather than the child, and no participant-level partitioning is described anywhere; with roughly six instances per child from 62 children, instances from the same child almost certainly appear in both training and validation, so the network can recognise an individual voice and recover its fixed label. Any one of these would inflate the estimate; together they mean that 90.28% carries essentially no information about performance on a new child. No cross-validation is reported. The accompanying statistical analysis is not affected by these problems and stands on its own - jitter and shimmer higher and harmonics-to-noise ratio lower in the autistic group, at p < 0.01 and p < 0.0001 - though it too is computed at the cry-instance level rather than with a per-child summary, so the effective sample for those tests is unclear.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Four, stated in a dedicated section. Generalisability is limited by sample size, demographic variation and the 18-to-54-month age range, with a call for larger and more diverse populations across age groups and cultural backgrounds. Cry characteristics may change as children grow, making age-specific models necessary - which comes close to identifying the age confound without naming it as one. The diagnosis rested on GARS-2, a DSM-5-based caregiver interview and psychiatrist confirmation rather than ADOS, because no official Farsi version exists. And expanding the dataset and refining diagnostic methods will be needed for broader application. The authors also note that clinical implementation 'would require clinician training and addressing ethical considerations'.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Sixty-two children aged 18 to 54 months drawn from the publicly available Khozaei cry corpus collected in Iran: 31 autistic and 31 typically developing, with 24 boys and 7 girls in each group, mean ages 35.6 and 30.8 months. The exact sex matching at 24:7 is a genuine design strength and gives the sample 22.6% girls, higher than most autism research samples in this review. Two features of the sample are less favourable and both are reported without being examined. The mean ages differ by 4.8 months - about 16% of the younger group's mean, in a period of rapid vocal-tract and laryngeal maturation - with no test or adjustment reported, which matters because jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio all vary with vocal development. And the recording settings differ sharply by group: 87.10% of the autistic children's cries were recorded at autism centres and 12.90% at home, while 54.84% of the typically developing children's were recorded at health centres and 45.16% at home. Roughly six cry instances were retained per child (6.10 +/- 5.05 for the autistic group, 5.39 +/- 3.66 for the comparison group), giving an instance-level dataset of around 355 cries from 62 children. No cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is available.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Clinical and developmental, without pathologising excess. Autism is 'a neurodevelopmental condition', described through 'a wide range of cognitive, social, and communicative challenges' and framed in terms of impact on the child, the family and society across education, healthcare and employment - a systemic rather than individual framing. Person-first phrasing is used consistently ('children with ASD', 'individuals diagnosed with ASD'), and the early-detection argument is made in terms of neuroplasticity and long-term prognosis rather than urgency or alarm. One formulation deserves note for its restraint: the paper states that 'any behavioral cues that raise concerns should be diligently combined with clinical assessments to enable the early identification of atypical development', positioning the technology as an input to clinical judgement rather than a substitute for it. The phrase 'children at risk of ASD' recurs and carries the usual risk framing. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person or family organisation is reported as involved in the work, which is worth noting for a study whose proposed product is an at-home screening tool for caregivers.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Better than most secondary analyses in this review on sex and worse on age. Sex is matched exactly - 24 boys and 7 girls in both groups - so it is fully controlled, and at 22.6% girls the sample is less male-skewed than most autism research. Mean ages are reported per group at 35.6 and 30.8 months, but no statistical comparison is made and no adjustment is applied, despite a 4.8-month difference spanning a developmental window in which laryngeal control, vocal-tract length and respiratory coordination all change substantially. The three features that reached significance - jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio - are exactly the measures known to vary with vocal maturation, so an age difference of this magnitude is a competing explanation for the group findings and no analysis distinguishes them. The authors come close to the point in their limitations, noting that 'cry characteristics may evolve as children grow, potentially influencing model accuracy, making it essential to explore age-specific models', but treat it as a generalisability issue rather than as a confound within their own comparison. No cognitive, language, adaptive, socioeconomic or comorbidity data are available, and the sample is entirely Iranian and Farsi-speaking, which the authors identify as limiting cultural generalisability.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Among the stronger ascertainment procedures in this review and described with unusual completeness for a secondary analysis. The process ran in four stages: the Gilliam Autism Rating Scale, Second Edition completed by parents; a caregiver interview conducted against DSM-5 criteria; direct evaluation and observation of the child by two child clinical psychologists holding doctorates; and separate confirmation of the diagnosis by at least one child psychiatrist in a different setting. Independent confirmation by a second clinician working in a different setting is a real safeguard against single-assessor error and appears in almost no other study charted here. The authors also state plainly why ADOS was not administered - 'the official version of Autism Diagnostic Observational Schedule (ADOS) is not available for Farsi' - and repeat it in their limitations rather than leaving the omission unexplained. Two qualifications remain. The GARS-2 is a parental questionnaire, and its position at the front of the process means the pathway begins with parental report; and the typically developing group's status is not described as having been screened by any instrument.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: GARS-2 was administered to every autistic child as the first step of the diagnostic process, so a quantified severity measure exists in the source data - and no score is reported, no group summary is given, and no analysis relates severity to any acoustic feature or to the model's output. That is the analysis this review has repeatedly found missing where the data would support it, and here the data plainly do: correlating jitter, shimmer or harmonics-to-noise ratio with GARS-2 total would test whether the acoustic differences track autistic trait severity or only group membership, and would distinguish a graded biological signal from a categorical artefact. No cognitive, language or adaptive measure is available for either group.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Two aims: to identify acoustic differences between autistic and typically developing children's cries, and to test whether deep learning can classify them. The statistical result is coherent and physiologically interpretable - significantly higher jitter (p < 0.01) and shimmer (p < 0.01) and significantly lower harmonics-to-noise ratio (p < 0.0001) in the autistic group, which together describe greater cycle-to-cycle instability in both pitch and amplitude and a noisier, less periodic voice signal, consistent with less stable laryngeal and respiratory control. The direction replicates prior cry work the authors cite. The classification result was 90.28% accuracy with AUC 90.83%, sensitivity and specificity both 88.64%, precision 95.12% and F-score 91.75%. The two halves of the study are of very different evidential weight. The acoustic comparison is a straightforward group contrast on prespecified clinical measures and stands or falls on the confounds - age, recording setting, cry cause - none of which is adjusted. The classification figure additionally rests on a validation-set maximum selected across 2,000 epochs with no held-out test partition and no participant-level splitting, so it carries essentially no information about performance on a new child, and the paper does not connect the network's behaviour to the interpretable acoustic features it identified.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: The recording settings are reported group by group and their distribution is the study's most consequential unexamined feature. For the autistic children, 87.10% of recordings came from autism centres and 12.90% from homes; for the typically developing children, 54.84% came from health centres and 45.16% from homes. The paper describes this variety as deliberate - 'a variety of devices and recording locations ... were used to avoid bias and increase generalizability' - but variety across a study is not the same as balance across groups, and here almost nine in ten autistic recordings come from one type of setting while the comparison recordings are split between two others. Jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio are all sensitive to reverberation, background noise and microphone distance, and harmonics-to-noise ratio in particular is a direct measure of the ratio of periodic to aperiodic energy, so ambient noise depresses it mechanically. The strongest statistical finding in the paper (HNR, p < 0.0001) is therefore in the direction that a noisier recording environment would produce.
