Partial standardisation was applied - a common WAV format at 16-bit and 44.1 kHz, a 25 cm microphone distance instruction, exclusion of recordings not made in quiet conditions - which mitigates but cannot remove the imbalance, and no per-setting stratified analysis is reported although the data to run one plainly exist.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: None, by the nature of the behaviour - cries were captured opportunistically when they occurred. That is appropriate and unavoidable, and the paper handles the resulting variability better than most: it excluded pain-associated cries, retained 'only pure crying sounds' with segments containing other vocalisations or non-empty-mouth cries eliminated, and recorded the eliciting cause for each cry. Reporting the cause distribution is genuinely good practice and appears nowhere else in this review. It also reveals a further imbalance: complaint or discomfort accounted for 74.20% of autistic and 67.75% of typically developing cries, with sleepiness, hunger and anxiety making up the remainder at 25.80% and 32.25%. Cry acoustics vary with what prompted the cry, so aetiology is a third variable covarying with class alongside age and setting, and it is not adjusted for.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element, though the paper argues that the modality would support one - cry 'allows for longitudinal assessment, enabling researchers to track developmental changes over time', which is a real advantage of a signal that can be captured repeatedly at home at no cost. Ethics reporting is complete for the original collection: approval by the ethics committee of Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences and Health Services in Tehran, with 'comprehensive informed consent ... acquired from the parents or legal guardians' before enrolment, specified as covering objectives, procedures and possible advantages and risks. The competing-interest declaration is the fullest in this review and is itemised by individual: two authors are employed by Zoundream AG, a commercial infant-cry-analysis company, one of them being a co-founder holding stock; a third received compensation as a member of its scientific advisory board; the fourth declares none; and the company funded the research alongside four public and quasi-public funders. Naming employment, founder status, equity and advisory compensation separately is exactly what a commercially sponsored diagnostic-technology study should do, and it allows a reader to weigh the translational claims accordingly.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Sony UX560 and UX512F voice recorders for 74.2% of recordings and smartphones running a custom recording application for the remaining 25.80%, all captured in WAV at 16-bit and 44.1 kHz specifically 'to ensure consistency across devices', with parents and trained voice collectors instructed to record in quiet environments at approximately 25 cm from the child's mouth. Praat performed acoustic analysis. The equipment story is the strongest part of the translational argument: a smartphone recording of a cry costs nothing, requires no clinic visit, no specialist operator, no cooperation from the child and no language ability, and can be repeated indefinitely at home - which is why the authors propose 'continuous remote monitoring'. Two device classes with different microphones nonetheless introduce acoustic variation that no level normalisation or channel compensation is reported to address, and the device mix by group is not stated.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Strong on the human and acoustic protocol, incomplete on the modelling. Reported: the source corpus with citation and public availability, group sizes with exactly matched sex composition, mean ages, the four-stage diagnostic procedure with instruments and clinician qualifications and the stated reason ADOS was unavailable, recorder models and their proportions, the audio format and sampling rate with the rationale, the 25 cm distance instruction, the recording-setting distribution by group, the cry-cause distribution by group, the exclusion rules for pain cries and impure segments, per-child cry yields with standard deviations, the acoustic software and the definitions of the perturbation measures, and the network architecture with layer counts, kernel size, channel count, dropout, augmentation methods, optimiser, cyclic learning-rate bounds, batch size and epoch count. Not reported: any test partition, the split proportions, whether splitting respected participants, the number of cry instances per partition, and code. A reader could reproduce the acoustic analysis and could not evaluate the classification result.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Four limitations are stated in a dedicated section and they are reasonable as far as they go: generalisability limited by sample size, demographic variation and the 18-to-54-month age range; cry characteristics changing with growth, making age-specific models necessary; the absence of ADOS because no official Farsi version exists; and the need for larger datasets and refined diagnostic methods. The second of these comes close to identifying the age confound but treats it as a generalisability question rather than as a threat to the group comparison in hand. What is not addressed is more consequential. The classification result has no held-out test partition, the final model was selected as the best of 2,000 epochs on the validation set, and the evaluation unit is the cry instance with no participant-level splitting described - so with roughly six instances per child, the network can identify a voice and recover its fixed label, and 90.28% is a selection maximum on data it has partly seen. The recording-setting imbalance is reported in the methods and presented as a strength when 87.10% of autistic recordings came from autism centres against a comparison group split between health centres and homes, and the three significant acoustic measures are all sensitive to room acoustics and background noise. The 4.8-month age difference is not tested or adjusted. Cry causes differ between groups and are not adjusted. Two device classes are used with no normalisation reported. GARS-2 scores exist and are not used for any severity analysis. And the statistical tests appear to be computed over cry instances rather than per-child summaries, so their effective sample size is unclear.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: The authors propose larger and more culturally diverse samples, age-specific models to accommodate developmental change in cry acoustics, refined diagnostic methodology, and real-world testing and integration - adding that implementation 'would require clinician training and addressing ethical considerations', which is an appropriate acknowledgement from a commercially sponsored group. Not proposed, and prerequisite to interpreting the classification result: a held-out test partition, participant-level splitting, and a model-selection rule that does not maximise over the evaluation set. Also needed and readily available: a stratified analysis by recording setting, an age-adjusted group comparison, and a correlation between the acoustic features and the GARS-2 scores already collected.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Cry acoustics, and specifically voice quality rather than cry structure. Three perturbation measures were analysed - jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio - selected because of their established clinical use in voice assessment. The construct choice is the study's strongest conceptual contribution and is unique in this review: cry is available before any language develops, is produced by every child regardless of cognitive or verbal level, requires no cooperation, no task compliance and no social engagement, and directly reflects neuromuscular control of the larynx and respiratory system. The paper's formulation is apt - 'infant cries provide a unique window into the neurological and physiological state of the infant' - and it identifies prior work reporting atypical cry acoustics in autistic toddlers under 18 months, which is younger than any other behavioural measure charted here can reach. The findings are physiologically legible: higher jitter and shimmer mean greater cycle-to-cycle instability in the frequency and amplitude of vocal fold vibration, and lower harmonics-to-noise ratio means a greater proportion of aperiodic energy, so the composite picture is of less stable phonatory control. Two constructs are conspicuously not addressed: the temporal and prosodic structure of the cry, which prior work also implicates, and the communicative function of crying, which is discarded when only 'pure crying sounds' are retained.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: None. A single acoustic modality, with two analysis routes over the same signal - Praat-derived perturbation measures for the statistical comparison and spectrogram images for the network. The two routes are never joined: the paper does not test whether the network's confidence relates to jitter, shimmer or harmonics-to-noise ratio, which would have connected its interpretable finding to its opaque one and is the single most useful additional analysis the existing data would support.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A recurrent convolutional network trained from scratch, combining three convolutional layers (kernel size 3, 32 output channels) for spatial feature extraction from spectrograms with LSTM layers for temporal structure - a standard and well-motivated architecture for audio, and the paper justifies the hybrid by reference to its success in video and speech recognition. Regularisation is taken seriously: dropout at 0.2 in each LSTM layer, and frequency masking and time masking augmentation applied specifically to the training split, which is the correct restriction. Optimisation used Adam with a cyclic learning rate between 1e-6 and 1e-5 and batch size 16. All of this is competently specified. The problem is not the model but the selection rule: training ran for 2,000 epochs and 'the model exhibiting superior validation accuracy being designated as the final trained classifier', so the reported figure is the maximum of 2,000 validation-accuracy draws, reported from the partition on which the maximum was taken.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Two representations. For the statistical analysis, Praat-derived scalar features per cry pattern - jitter as the mean absolute difference between consecutive pitch periods, shimmer as the amplitude analogue, and harmonics-to-noise ratio - each with a clinical interpretation and an established literature. For the classification, 128x128 single-channel spectrogram images per cry instance. The spectrogram representation retains time-frequency structure that the scalar perturbation measures discard, which is the right complement in principle; but because each cry instance is treated as an independent observation and roughly six come from each child, the representation also carries whatever is idiosyncratic to an individual voice, which is what an instance-level split allows the model to exploit.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: A fuller metric set than most of this branch: accuracy 90.28%, AUC 90.83%, sensitivity 88.64%, specificity 88.64%, precision 95.12% and F-score 91.75%, with sensitivity and specificity reported separately and defined explicitly in the table as counts of autistic and typically developing instances. The statistical analysis reports means with standard errors and codes significance at three thresholds. Two problems limit what any of it means. Every classification figure is a validation-set value with no held-out test, taken at the best of 2,000 epochs, so all six metrics inherit the same selection optimism. And the instance-level definition of sensitivity and specificity means these are not per-child operating characteristics: a screening tool's sensitivity is the proportion of autistic children it flags, not the proportion of their individual cries, and with six cries per child the two quantities can differ substantially. No confidence intervals accompany any figure, on an effective sample of 62 children.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Split between a well-interpreted feature analysis and an uninterpreted model. The three perturbation measures are clinical voice-quality metrics with direct physiological meaning, so the statistical result translates into a specific and evaluable claim about phonatory stability, and the paper articulates it correctly. The network is treated as a black box: no attribution over the spectrogram, no examination of which frequency bands or temporal regions drive its decisions, no error analysis by age, setting or cry cause, and - most importantly - no test of whether its confidence relates to the jitter, shimmer or harmonics-to-noise ratio the same study found significant. That last analysis is available from the data already collected and would have determined whether the network learned the acoustic phenomenon the paper identified or something else entirely, such as the recording environment. Its absence means the study's two halves neither corroborate nor constrain each other.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Three compounding failures make the reported 90.28% uninterpretable, and none is discussed. First, there is no test partition: accuracy, AUC, sensitivity, specificity, precision and F-score are all validation-set figures, and no held-out evaluation of any kind appears in the paper. Second, the final model was chosen as the epoch with the best validation accuracy out of 2,000 - so the reported number is a maximum over 2,000 draws taken on the very partition it is reported from, an optimistic selection whose inflation on a small validation set is substantial. Third, the evaluation unit is the cry instance rather than the child, as Table 1's own definitions confirm, and no participant-level partitioning is described anywhere; with roughly six instances per child from 62 children, cries from the same child will fall on both sides of the boundary, so the network can recognise an individual voice and recover that child's fixed label. This is the same failure documented in this review for scanpath images, video frames, EEG epochs and thermal images, appearing here in a fifth modality. Set against this, the statistical analysis is a separate and more defensible piece of work - a prespecified comparison of three clinically established measures, replicating a direction reported in prior cry research, with significance at p < 0.01 and p < 0.0001. But it faces its own confounds, all reported in the paper and none adjusted: the groups differ by 4.8 months in mean age during a period of rapid vocal maturation, using measures that change with that maturation; 87.10% of autistic recordings came from autism centres against a comparison group split between health centres and homes, and all three measures are sensitive to room acoustics and background noise, with harmonics-to-noise ratio - the strongest finding - being a direct measure of periodic-to-aperiodic energy that ambient noise depresses mechanically; the eliciting causes of the cries differ between groups; two device classes were used; and the tests appear to be computed over cry instances rather than per-child means, leaving their effective sample size unclear. The corrective analyses are all available from data the paper already reports - stratify by recording setting, adjust for age, aggregate per child, and correlate the acoustic features with the GARS-2 scores already collected.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: cry analysis, early childhood, autism spectrum disorder, deep learning. Compact and well balanced across modality, population, condition and method. Terms carried through the body: vocal biomarker, jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio, fundamental frequency, spectrogram, R-CNN, Praat, GARS-2, at-home screening, continuous remote monitoring.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, Brief Report, accepted 18 March 2025, open access under CC BY-NC-ND, doi 10.1007/s10803-025-06811-1. A clinical autism journal, and the venue's influence is visible in what is reported well: the four-stage diagnostic procedure with clinician qualifications, the explanation of why ADOS was unavailable in Farsi, the ethics and consent statements, the exclusion rules, the per-group recording-setting and cry-cause distributions, and above all a competing-interest declaration that itemises employment, founder status, equity holding and advisory compensation by individual. The brief-report format constrains length, but the omissions that matter are not length-related - a test partition, a participant-level split and a model-selection rule that does not maximise over the evaluation set are design decisions rather than reporting ones, and the same journal's structure that elicited an exemplary conflict declaration did not elicit any account of how the 90.28% was obtained.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2025 by a group spanning Zoundream AG in Basel, the Barcelona Center for Maternal-Fetal and Neonatal Medicine, and the University of Bologna, funded by Zoundream AG together with Swiss and Spanish innovation agencies, with two authors employed by the company, one of them a co-founder holding stock, and a third compensated as a scientific advisory board member. For this review the study occupies a position no other paper does. Cry is the earliest behaviour any included study measures: it is present before language, requires no cooperation, no task compliance, no social engagement and no cognitive floor, and it can be captured on a phone at home and repeated indefinitely at no cost. That combination reaches a population - pre-verbal infants, and children whose developmental level precludes the tasks used everywhere else in this corpus - that nothing else charted here can assess, and the physiological rationale is coherent, since jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio index the stability of laryngeal control rather than any social or communicative construct. The diagnostic ascertainment behind the corpus is also among the better ones in the review, with four stages culminating in independent confirmation by a child psychiatrist in a separate setting, and the authors explain rather than conceal the absence of ADOS. And the competing-interest declaration is the most complete in the corpus. Against all of this, the evidential yield is limited by three things the paper reports and does not examine. The classification figure has no held-out test, was taken as the best of 2,000 epochs on the validation set, and is computed over cry instances with no participant-level split from 62 children contributing roughly six cries each - so it says nothing about performance on a new child. The recording settings are strongly imbalanced, with 87.10% of autistic cries captured at autism centres against a comparison group split between health centres and homes, and all three significant acoustic measures are sensitive to the acoustic environment, with the strongest finding being the one ambient noise would most directly produce. And the groups differ by 4.8 months in mean age, untested and unadjusted, in a window of rapid vocal maturation using measures that change with it. The study's most useful contribution to the synthesis is therefore its construct rather than its numbers: it demonstrates what a pre-linguistic, task-free, physiologically interpretable behavioural signal would look like, and simultaneously how easily such a signal is confounded by where the recording was made.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Babu T; Nair RR; Mahapatra S
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective algorithm-development study on a single public tabular screening dataset, with hyperparameter optimisation and cross-validated evaluation
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A tabular vector per respondent drawn from 21 fields, with the retained subset not enumerated
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Adults; age is a field in the dataset but no distribution is reported
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 704 rows
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None, and the authors identify its absence: 'A limitation of this work is its heavy reliance on a single public Kaggle dataset, which may limit the model's generalizability.'
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Not reported; 515 in the source dataset
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. Respondents completed a ten-item screening questionnaire.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None. Data were collected through a screening application by third parties.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: The dataset is public on Kaggle
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not stated; secondary analysis of a public tabular repository
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: A feature-engineering stage described as selecting and transforming relevant fields, guided by exploratory data analysis
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None reported. No feature importance is presented, despite Random Forest supplying it without additional cost - and despite it being the analysis that would have revealed immediately whether the model was splitting on the summed screening score.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Bayesian optimisation over the Random Forest hyperparameters, presented as the study's principal contribution
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Five-fold cross-validation, with each respondent contributing one row so that the split unit is the person and within-participant leakage cannot arise. The scheme is appropriate for 704 rows and is more than several comparators in this branch report. It has no bearing on the reported result, because the outcome variable is computed from the input variables: 'Class/ASD' is the summed A1-A10 score thresholded at the AQ-10 cut-off, and 'result' - that same sum - appears in the feature list the paper prints, with no feature-selection step removing it described. A model with access to either can recover the label exactly on any partition, and 0.9890 accuracy is what that arrangement produces.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: One, and it is correctly identified as far as it goes: 'A limitation of this work is its heavy reliance on a single public Kaggle dataset, which may limit the model's generalizability. Future studies should address this by incorporating diverse datasets to enhance the model's applicability across different populations.' Advanced techniques including deep learning and transfer learning are also proposed as future directions.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Seven hundred and four respondents to the AQ-10 adult autism screening instrument, drawn from a public Kaggle aggregation of screening-app submissions. The paper reports the row count and the field names and nothing else: no class distribution, no age or sex composition, no ethnicity breakdown, although age, gender and ethnicity are all among the 21 fields it prints. In the source dataset the positive class comprises 189 of 704, giving a majority-class baseline of 73.2% that the paper never states. No respondent is known to have received any clinical assessment. The population is self-selected users of an autism screening application, which is neither a clinical sample nor a population sample.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Brief and conventional. Autism is 'a complex neurological disorder that involves repetitive behaviors, limited interest, and has interpersonal interaction problems', with traditional diagnosis characterised as 'subjective and time-consuming'. Person-first phrasing predominates. The closing statement refers to 'identifying and supporting children with ASD', although the dataset is an adult screening corpus - a slippage between the population studied and the population invoked. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person is reported as involved.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Present as fields and absent as reported characteristics. Age, gender, ethnicity, jaundice at birth, family history of autism, country of residence, prior app use and who completed the test are all among the 21 columns the paper enumerates, and all are candidates for the model; none is described, summarised or analysed. The consequence is that nothing can be said about who the 704 respondents were, and no confounding can be assessed - though the question is largely moot given that the outcome is computable from the inputs.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None. The 'Class/ASD' variable in this dataset is not a clinical diagnosis but a screening outcome, computed by summing the A1-A10 item responses and applying the AQ-10 cut-off. No respondent underwent diagnostic assessment, and no instrument, clinician or record is cited. The distinctive feature of this particular study is that the derivation is visible in its own methods: the paper prints the complete field list - 'A1 Score, A2 Score, A3 Score, A4 Score, A5 Score, A6 Score, A7 Score, A8 Score, A9 Score, A10 Score, age, gender, ethnicity, jundice, austim, contry of res, used app before, result, age desc, relation, Class/ASD' - which contains both the ten items, their sum ('result'), and the thresholded outcome ('Class/ASD'). The model is therefore asked to predict a variable that is a deterministic function of another variable it is given.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None used as an outcome. The 'result' field is the summed AQ-10 score - a continuous screening total that could have supported a graded analysis - and it appears among the predictors rather than as a severity dimension. No cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated aim is to improve autism prediction with a Bayesian-optimised Random Forest, motivated by the subjectivity and slowness of conventional assessment. The reported result is 0.9890 accuracy, described as highly promising and as providing 'recommendations for a verified diagnostic technique when implemented'. The alternative explanation is complete: the class variable is the summed AQ-10 item score thresholded at the instrument's cut-off, the ten items are inputs, and the sum itself is printed among the study's own feature list with no removal step described - so the model is recovering a threshold rule from its own predictor, a task a single decision stump would solve. The paper attributes the accuracy to Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation of the ensemble.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting. The data are screening-app submissions aggregated on Kaggle by a third party, from respondents who sought out an autism screening tool - a self-selected population whose positive rate reflects help-seeking rather than prevalence.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: None. Respondents answered ten AQ-10 statements about themselves. Nothing was observed, elicited or measured.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis of a public tabular repository, with no longitudinal element. No ethics, consent, funding or competing-interest statement appears in the retrieved text; secondary use of a public tabular dataset conventionally requires no fresh approval.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: None. Data collection was by a screening application operated by third parties, and the analysis is tabular.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Partial. Reported: the dataset source, its 704 rows and 21 fields with every field name printed verbatim, the preprocessing stage of cleaning and missing-value handling, a feature-engineering stage guided by exploratory data analysis, the 5-fold cross-validation scheme, the Random Forest classifier and the Bayesian optimisation method. Not reported: which features survived the engineering stage - the single fact needed to determine whether 'result' entered the model - together with the class distribution, hyperparameter search ranges, any metric beyond accuracy, and code. Printing the full field list is nonetheless a useful piece of transparency, since it is what makes the leakage identifiable.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: One limitation is stated and is correct as far as it goes: 'A limitation of this work is its heavy reliance on a single public Kaggle dataset, which may limit the model's generalizability. Future studies should address this by incorporating diverse datasets to enhance the model's applicability across different populations.' That identifies an external-validity problem while leaving the internal one untouched - the issue is not that one dataset was used but that within it the label is computable from the features. Also unstated: no class distribution or majority-class baseline despite the source dataset's 73.2% negative rate; only accuracy reported, with no precision, recall, specificity, AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval; no feature importance despite Random Forest supplying it without cost, which would have exposed the dependence on 'result' immediately; and no clinical ascertainment for any respondent.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Incorporate diverse datasets to improve generalisability across populations, and explore deep learning and transfer learning. The more informative step, available from the data in hand, would be to refit with 'result' and the A1-A10 items removed and report what the registration metadata alone achieve - which would separate any genuine association from the arithmetic recovery of the label.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: None observed. The A1-A10 fields are a respondent's answers to ten statements about their own social-communication characteristics, and the remaining fields are registration metadata. These are self-characterisations rather than records of behaviour produced, which is the distinction this review applies when admitting app telemetry, written language or nurse-recorded milestone attainment as behavioural data.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: None. A single tabular modality.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A Random Forest with hyperparameters tuned by Bayesian optimisation, evaluated by 5-fold cross-validation. Ensemble trees are a sensible default for a small mixed-type tabular dataset, cross-validation is appropriate at 704 rows, and Bayesian optimisation is a reasonable alternative to grid search. The methodology is proportionate to the data; the difficulty is entirely in what the data contain.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A tabular vector per respondent drawn from 21 fields, with the retained subset unspecified after a feature-engineering stage. The decisive representational fact is that both the ten AQ-10 items and their summed total appear in the enumerated field list, and no removal of the total is described.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy alone, at 0.9890. No precision, recall, specificity, F1, AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval is reported, and no class distribution is given, so the figure cannot be compared against the 73.2% majority-class baseline that the source dataset implies. For a screening application, sensitivity and specificity are the quantities that matter and neither is provided.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No feature importance is reported, which is both the study's clearest missed opportunity and the analysis that Random Forest makes available at no cost. A single importance plot would have shown the model splitting on the summed screening score and would have identified the problem before publication.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Sound mechanics on a task with no uncertainty in it. Each respondent contributes one row so the split unit is the person, and 5-fold cross-validation is appropriate for 704 rows - both better than several comparators in this branch. Neither bears on the result. The outcome variable 'Class/ASD' is the summed A1-A10 score thresholded at the AQ-10 cut-off; the ten items are inputs; and 'result', the sum itself, is printed among the paper's own enumerated feature list with no feature-selection step removing it described. A model with access to either the items or the sum recovers the label exactly, on any partition, under any resampling scheme, with any classifier - and 0.9890 accuracy is a figure a single decision stump on the 'result' column would reach or exceed. This is the third study in the review resting on the UCI-derived autism screening tables, and the pattern is identical across all three: careful analytic practice above a label that is a closed-form function of the features. The paper's own stated limitation, that reliance on a single dataset may limit generalisability, correctly names an external-validity concern while leaving the internal one entirely unaddressed - which is the characteristic failure of this subliterature, since diversifying the datasets would change nothing if each new dataset carries the same arithmetic relationship between its items and its label.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD); Machine Learning; Bayesian Optimization; Random Forest; Early Diagnosis; Predictive Modeling. Method-facing with the population named once; no term identifies the data source or the fact that the inputs are questionnaire responses.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Procedia Computer Science 258:1576-1585, Elsevier, 2025, open access under CC BY-NC-ND, doi 10.1016/j.procs.2025.04.389, peer-reviewed under the scientific committee of the International Conference on Machine Learning and Data Engineering. A conference-proceedings venue with a short review cycle, and the reviewing engaged with the modelling rather than the data: a paper whose own methods section prints a feature list containing both the summed screening score and the thresholded outcome derived from it was accepted reporting 0.9890 accuracy without that relationship being examined.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 2025 by computer science and electrical engineering departments at Alliance University, Bengaluru, with a collaborator at Nitte Institute of Professional Education, Mangalore. The framing is the standard access argument - conventional diagnosis is subjective and time-consuming, so machine learning should make it faster and more accurate. For this review the study's value is corroborative rather than novel: it is the third built on the UCI-derived autism screening tables, and it makes the leakage visible in a way the others do not, because it prints its complete feature list including both 'result' - the summed A1-A10 score - and 'Class/ASD', the outcome that is that sum thresholded at the AQ-10 cut-off. The relationship between the two is a matter of arithmetic, and the reported 0.9890 accuracy is its consequence rather than a measurement of detection. Two features of the study make the case more useful than the bare finding. Its analytic practice is otherwise unremarkable but adequate - 5-fold cross-validation, one row per respondent, a stated preprocessing and feature-engineering pipeline, a reasonable classifier and a reasonable optimiser - which is the same pattern the review has now recorded across five modalities: rigour applied above a corrupted target produces a confidently wrong result. And its single stated limitation is diagnostic of how the subliterature understands itself: 'heavy reliance on a single public Kaggle dataset, which may limit the model's generalizability', with the remedy proposed as incorporating diverse datasets. That names an external-validity problem while leaving the internal one untouched, and would not help, because every dataset in this family carries the same closed-form relationship between its items and its label. The one analysis that would have settled the matter - a Random Forest feature-importance plot, available at no cost - is not reported.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Amirbay A; Baigabylov N; Mukhanova A; Mukhambetova K; Zaitov E; Burganova R; Khusanova K; Akhmedova F
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Prospective case-control classification study with purpose-designed multimodal video acquisition and subject-independent cross-validated evaluation
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A 1,639-dimensional per-frame vector sequence per child. Reducing video to landmark coordinates before modelling has the same confound-control property this review has noted for the pose-based studies: appearance, clothing, skin tone, room and lighting are discarded, so those cannot drive the classification. Facial mesh geometry does retain morphology, however, which is where the sex imbalance between groups becomes consequential.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. Single site, single cohort, single protocol.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 50 typically developing children, 52% male and 48% female
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed anywhere in the paper
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A purpose-designed structured interaction protocol lasting 8 to 10 minutes per child, comprising simple games, gesture imitation exercises and short conversational prompts, explicitly designed 'to elicit both social and motor behaviors'. This is a well-judged paradigm for the review's purposes: it is brief enough to be practical, it actively elicits the behaviours of interest rather than waiting for them, it spans social and motor domains in one session, and it was administered identically to both groups. The gesture-imitation component in particular is a targeted elicitation of a construct - motor imitation - with an established clinical literature. What is not reported is the content of the tasks in enough detail to reproduce them, or whether the examiner's behaviour was scripted.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: A webcam recording at 1920x1080 and 30 frames per second under standardised lighting. MediaPipe face mesh, pose and hands models for landmark extraction. The equipment requirement is a single consumer webcam and open-source software, which makes the deployment claim credible and places the study alongside the free-play and one-legged-standing work as an approach a clinic or school could actually adopt.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: 'The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author ... upon reasonable request. Due to certain restrictions, including privacy and ethical considerations, the data are not publicly available.' The restriction is appropriate for identifiable video of children, though landmark coordinates - which is what was actually modelled - are far less identifying than the source video and could have been released.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: None stated. The paper contains no institutional review board or ethics committee reference, and no consent or assent statement of any kind - a full-text search returns no occurrence of 'consent'. The only mention of ethics is in the data availability statement, which cites 'privacy and ethical considerations' as a reason for withholding data. This is a prospective study that recruited 100 children, including 50 autistic children, and recorded over 16 hours of video of them, so the absence is not attributable to secondary-data status as it is for several other studies in this review.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Per frame: 99 pose landmark coordinate values, 63 hand coordinate values per hand, facial landmark coordinates, the mouth aspect ratio and per-region motion energy, with a timestamp, totalling 1,639 numerical values.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Partial and descriptive. Heat map analysis and movement-energy graphs are used to show group differences in motor activity and facial expression, and because motion energy is computed per region - face, pose, each hand - these visualisations can in principle localise where the difference lies. Two features that were engineered specifically for interpretability, the mouth aspect ratio and per-region motion energy, are physically meaningful quantities. But no attribution over the model itself is reported: which of the 1,639 inputs or which of the three landmark streams drives the classification is unknown, no ablation separates face from pose from hands, and the visualisations are presented as group-level descriptive evidence rather than as explanations of model behaviour. Given the sex imbalance, a per-stream ablation would have been especially informative, since a face-mesh-driven result and a motion-energy-driven result carry very different confound risks.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Regularisation is specified in detail - early stopping with patience of 10 epochs monitoring validation loss, dropout at 0.5, L2 weight regularisation at 0.001, and batch shuffling each epoch 'to minimize temporal correlations in the data'. No hyperparameter search procedure is described, and the architecture sizes are stated rather than justified.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: The most explicitly reasoned anti-leakage design in this review's video branch, and the paper states its purpose directly: 'To provide strong model validation and prevent data leakage, a stratified 5-fold cross-validation strategy was utilized, preserving the ratio of ASD and TD participants in each fold. The dataset was divided on a subject-independent basis such that data from the same participant was not included in both training and validation datasets.' Subject-independence is named, stratification preserves class ratio across folds, and four separate overfitting controls are specified with their parameters. The concluding claim - that this 'provided a reliable estimate of the model's generalization ability while minimizing the risk of inflated accuracy due to overfitting' - is warranted as far as the leakage question goes, and the study is one of the few in this branch to close that route deliberately in a corpus of frame-level data. Three qualifications remain. All reported figures are cross-validation results with no independent held-out test set, so architecture and configuration choices were made on the same folds that supply the estimates. The reported range - '85-90% on validation' with '90% accuracy on the training set' - is a range rather than a point estimate with fold-level detail. And subject-independence protects against recognising an individual across the split; it does not protect against the sex imbalance, since a model that separates boys from girls will do so equally well on unseen children.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: No limitations section exists. Future work is identified in the introduction - 'extension of the parameter set, utilization of deeper architectures, growth of dataset size, and optimization towards real-time high-accuracy performance' - which concedes by implication that the parameter set, the architecture and the sample are all currently limited, but none of these is allowed to qualify a conclusion.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: One hundred children aged 5 to 9, recruited in Kazakhstan: 50 described as diagnosed with autism and 50 typically developing peers, recorded under a single purpose-designed protocol yielding over 16 hours of video. The sample is balanced 50:50 by group and the acquisition context is common to both, which removes the recruitment and recording asymmetry that affects most of this review's video and image work. Two demographic facts bound what follows. The sex composition differs sharply between groups - the autistic group is approximately 84% male and 16% female, while the comparison group is 52% male and 48% female - a 32-percentage-point gap reported in the results without comment, adjustment or stratified analysis. And no age distribution by group is given, only the shared 5-to-9 range, across which facial proportions, motor coordination and gestural repertoire all change substantially. No cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is available for either group, and no recruitment source is stated.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Conventional medical framing, more dated in places than most of this corpus. Autism is 'a neurodevelopmental disorder' but also 'this disorder' and, in the opening sentence, is placed within 'identification and investigation of diseases'. The characterisation is deficit-based - 'social deficits, difficulties in communication, and atypical patterns of behavior', with key characteristics given as 'avoidance of eye contact, lack of or excessive expression of emotions, and repetitive stereotypical movements'. 'Children with ASD' and 'neurotypical children' are the standard usages, and 'neurotypical' rather than 'normal' is a small point in the paper's favour. The access argument is stated in health-systems terms that are accurate for the setting - 'a shortage of qualified specialists and a high burden on healthcare systems' - and the proposed role is 'earlier identification and timely referral to specialists', which frames the technology as a routing mechanism rather than a replacement for assessment. No neurodiversity framing appears, and no autistic person or family organisation is reported as involved, which is worth noting for a study that recorded 16 hours of video of children without any documented consent process.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Sex is reported per group and is badly imbalanced; everything else is absent. The autistic group is approximately 84% male and the comparison group 52% male, so the two classes differ by around 32 percentage points on a variable that directly shapes every input the model receives. The feature vector comprises 468 facial mesh points, 33 pose points and 42 hand landmark points, together with a mouth aspect ratio derived from lip geometry - facial morphology, body proportion and posture are all sex-linked from middle childhood, and a network given these coordinates could achieve substantial separation by distinguishing boys from girls without representing anything about autism. This is the same failure mode that a speech study charted elsewhere in this review exposed empirically, where sensitivity collapsed from 94.8% pooled to 43.6% for girls; here the imbalance is in the sample rather than in the evaluation, so it inflates rather than conceals. No sex-stratified analysis, adjustment or discussion appears. No age distribution by group is reported despite a 5-to-9 range in which facial and motor development changes markedly; no cognitive, language, socioeconomic or ancestry information exists; and comorbidity is not recorded. The landmark representation does control for one class of confound well - appearance, clothing, skin tone, lighting and room are all discarded before modelling - which makes the uncontrolled demographic variables the more conspicuous.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None described. The 50 children are stated to be 'diagnosed with ASD' and nothing further is given - no instrument, no criteria, no clinician, no setting, no date - and no screening procedure is reported for the 50 comparison children. For a prospective study that designed its own acquisition protocol, recruited 100 families and recorded over 16 hours of video, this is a striking omission, and it contrasts sharply with the care taken over the technical description: the paper specifies the MediaPipe landmark counts, the composition of the 1,639-value feature vector, the dropout rate, the L2 coefficient and the early-stopping patience, while saying nothing at all about how autism was established in the children whose data those numbers describe. The consequence is that the label the model predicts is undefined, and the study's reported 85-90% cannot be located relative to any clinical standard.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure is reported for either group, so no gradient analysis is possible and the model's output cannot be related to anything other than group membership. The protocol includes conversational prompts, so verbal ability was engaged in producing the data without being measured.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The aim is an automated method for detecting autism from facial and motor features extracted from video, motivated by the subjectivity of expert observation, the weakness of early behavioural signs, and a shortage of specialists. The pipeline extracts 1,639 numerical parameters per frame using MediaPipe face mesh, pose and hands, adds a mouth aspect ratio and per-region motion energy, and models the sequence with a hybrid CNN+LSTM. Reported results: 90% accuracy on training data, 85-90% on validation, recall 0.95 and AUC above 0.9042, with the hybrid significantly outperforming single-architecture baselines at p < 0.05 by paired t-tests across folds. Heat map and movement-energy analyses showed group differences in motor activity and facial expression. The performance is modest and in a credible range for this task, and it is benchmarked against external comparators rather than presented in isolation. What the study cannot establish is what the separation reflects: the autistic group is 84% male against 52% in the comparison group, and the inputs are facial and body geometry, so sex is a live alternative explanation that no reported analysis excludes.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A controlled recording environment with standardised lighting, using a single webcam, with both groups recorded under the same protocol. That last point matters and is one of the study's real strengths: across the photograph, video-frame, thermal and clinic-versus-school audio branches, this review has repeatedly found the two classes recorded under systematically different conditions, so that acquisition context proxies for the label. Here the setting, lighting, camera, resolution, frame rate and task sequence are common to both groups, and the landmark representation additionally discards appearance and background before modelling. Whatever the study is detecting, it is not the difference between two recording environments. What is not stated is where the recordings took place, how children were recruited to each group, or whether the examiner differed between groups.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A purpose-designed structured interaction protocol of 8 to 10 minutes per child, comprising simple games, gesture imitation exercises and short conversational prompts, explicitly intended 'to elicit both social and motor behaviors'. This is among the better-judged paradigms in the review. It is short enough to be practical in a clinic or school, it actively elicits the target behaviours rather than waiting for them to occur, and it spans the social and motor domains within one session - which matters because a study charted elsewhere here demonstrated empirically that a 90-second free-play sample cannot reach the restricted and repetitive dimension at all. The gesture-imitation component is a targeted elicitation of motor imitation, a construct with an established clinical literature in autism, and its inclusion means the protocol probes something specific rather than sampling behaviour generically. Against this, the tasks are described only in outline: no script, no item list, no ordering, no statement of whether the examiner's prompts were standardised, and no report of how children who declined a task were handled. The protocol is therefore reproducible in spirit and not in detail.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session per child, with no follow-up or test-retest. The ethics position is the study's most serious reporting failure. There is no institutional review board reference, no ethics committee, no consent statement and no assent statement anywhere in the paper - a full-text search returns no occurrence of the word 'consent'. The only appearance of ethics is in the data availability statement, which cites 'privacy and ethical considerations' as grounds for withholding the data, so the authors evidently regard the material as ethically sensitive while documenting no approval for having collected it. This is a prospective study that recruited 100 children including 50 autistic children and recorded more than 16 hours of video of them, so unlike several other studies in this review the omission cannot be attributed to secondary-data status. Competing interests are declared as none; funding is not stated in the retrieved text.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: A single webcam recording at 1920x1080 and 30 frames per second under standardised lighting, with MediaPipe face mesh, pose and hands performing landmark extraction. The equipment requirement is the lowest of any instrumented study in this review apart from the free-play video work: one consumer camera and open-source software, with no eye tracker, depth sensor, force plate, wearable or thermal camera. That makes the proposed application in 'clinical and educational contexts' credible as an equipment matter, and it means the 1,639-parameter feature vector is obtainable anywhere a laptop and a room are available. What is missing is the acquisition detail that determines whether landmark coordinates are comparable across sessions: camera distance and angle, the child's seated or standing position, and any per-session calibration. No landmark-detection failure rate is reported, which matters because MediaPipe hand tracking fails intermittently when hands leave frame or overlap, and class-correlated missingness would be indistinguishable from a class-correlated behavioural difference.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Sharply divided. The technical protocol is documented well: task types, session duration, total video volume, resolution, frame rate, lighting standardisation, the three MediaPipe models with their landmark counts (468 face, 33 pose, 21 per hand), the composition of the 1,639-value vector with per-component counts, the definitions of the mouth aspect ratio and of motion energy as mean Euclidean landmark displacement between consecutive frames, the complete validation strategy with fold count, stratification rule, subject-independence, early-stopping patience of 10, dropout of 0.5, L2 coefficient of 0.001 and batch shuffling, the network architecture layer by layer with unit counts and activations, the loss function and optimiser, and the metric set with paired t-tests across folds. The human protocol is not documented at all: no recruitment source, no diagnostic procedure, no age distribution by group, no ethics approval and no consent process. A reader could rebuild the pipeline and could not evaluate, replicate or ethically justify the study that produced the data.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: There is no limitations section. The introduction's future-work sentence - calling for 'extension of the parameter set, utilization of deeper architectures, growth of dataset size, and optimization towards real-time high-accuracy performance' - concedes by implication that the parameter set, architecture and sample are limited, but nothing qualifies a conclusion. What should have been stated, in order of importance: the autistic group is 84% male against 52% in the comparison group, and the model's inputs are facial mesh and body landmark geometry, so a substantial part of the separation could be sex discrimination, and no stratified or adjusted analysis is reported. No diagnostic reference standard is described for a prospectively recruited sample, so the predicted label is undefined. There is no ethics approval or consent statement for a study recording 16 hours of video of 100 children. No age distribution by group is given across a 5-to-9 range in which facial and motor development changes substantially. All reported figures are cross-validation results with no independent held-out test, so architecture selection and performance estimation share data. No specificity or confusion matrix is reported, and with recall at 0.95 and accuracy at 85-90%, specificity must be materially lower than recall - a fact the reported metrics conceal. The stated 95% confidence intervals of plus or minus 1.5% are narrower than 100 children in 5-fold cross-validation would ordinarily support and their derivation is not given. And no ablation separates the face, pose and hand streams, so the study cannot say which behaviour carries the signal.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Four directions are named: a larger parameter set, deeper architectures, a larger dataset, and optimisation for real-time performance. All are engineering extensions. Not proposed, and prerequisite to interpreting the present result: a sex-stratified or sex-adjusted analysis, which is the single most informative check the existing data would support; an ablation across the three landmark streams, which would show whether the signal lies in facial geometry, posture or hand movement and therefore how exposed it is to the sex confound; documentation of how autism was ascertained in the 50 children; an independent held-out evaluation; and ethics and consent documentation.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: The broadest simultaneous behavioural coverage from a single camera in this review: facial configuration and expression through a 468-point face mesh, whole-body posture through 33 pose points, and manual gesture through 21 points per hand, all captured at 30 frames per second and reduced to a 1,639-value vector per frame. Two derived measures add interpretable structure. The mouth aspect ratio - the ratio of vertical to horizontal lip distance - is a compact index of mouth opening that relates to both expression and vocalisation. Motion energy, defined as the mean Euclidean displacement of landmark coordinates between consecutive frames and computed separately for the face, the pose and each hand, is a clean measure of how much each body region moves per unit time, and its per-region computation means motor activity can be localised rather than aggregated. The stated behavioural targets - reduced eye contact, atypical emotional expression, and repetitive stereotypical movement - map reasonably onto these streams, though gaze itself is not measured directly and stereotypy is not identified as such, only as elevated hand motion energy. The visualisations reported (heat maps and movement-energy graphs) show group differences in motor activity and facial expression, but no ablation determines which stream the classifier uses, which leaves the construct claim unresolved.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Three landmark streams from one camera, concatenated at the feature level and modelled jointly - within-camera multimodal fusion rather than multi-sensor fusion. The breadth is a genuine advantage: face, posture and hands are rarely combined in one model in this literature, and doing so at 30 frames per second with temporal modelling gives the network access to how expression, posture and gesture co-vary. The paper argues this explicitly, proposing a model that 'simultaneously analyzes facial expressions, head movements, hand gestures, and posture over time, combining spatial and temporal learning'. What is missing is any decomposition: no ablation reports performance with each stream removed, so the relative contribution of face, pose and hands is unknown. That omission is more costly here than usual, because the three streams carry very different confound exposure - facial mesh geometry is strongly sex-linked, hand motion energy much less so - and the study's 32-point sex imbalance between groups makes the distinction decisive for interpreting the result.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A hybrid CNN+LSTM: convolutional layers for spatial feature extraction from the per-frame landmark vector, then an LSTM(64, return sequences) and an LSTM(32) for temporal dependency, then dense(16, ReLU) and dense(1, sigmoid), trained with binary cross-entropy and Adam. The architecture is standard, appropriately sized for 100 participants, and compared against configurations using either component alone, with the hybrid winning at p < 0.05 by paired t-tests across folds. Regularisation is unusually well specified - early stopping at patience 10 on validation loss, dropout 0.5, L2 at 0.001 and per-epoch batch shuffling - and each control is given with its parameter rather than merely named. The gap is that no hyperparameter search is described and the layer sizes are stated without justification, so it is unclear whether the configuration was tuned on the same folds that supply the reported figures.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A per-frame vector of 1,639 values comprising a timestamp, 99 pose landmark coordinates, 63 coordinates for each hand, facial mesh coordinates, the mouth aspect ratio and per-region motion energy, formed into sequences for temporal modelling. Reducing video to landmark coordinates before any learning is a deliberate confound control of the same kind used by the pose-based studies elsewhere in this review: skin tone, clothing, background, lighting and room are all discarded, so none can drive the classification, and this is a substantive advantage over the whole-image approaches in the photograph branch. The residual exposure is facial mesh geometry, which retains craniofacial morphology and therefore retains the sex- and age-linked variation that the sample does not control.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, AUC, precision and recall, with paired t-tests across the 5-fold results at p < 0.05 and 95% confidence intervals for accuracy, precision, recall and F1 stated to lie within plus or minus 1.5%. Reporting intervals and fold-level significance testing at all places the study above most of this corpus. Three problems limit the reporting. Specificity is not given, and with recall at 0.95 and accuracy at 85-90% on a balanced sample, specificity must be substantially below recall - roughly 75-85% by arithmetic - so the metric that a screening application most needs is the one omitted, and the model's error profile is asymmetric in a direction the reported figures obscure. No confusion matrix appears. And the stated interval of plus or minus 1.5% is narrower than 100 children in 5-fold cross-validation would normally support, with 20 children per validation fold meaning a single child moves fold accuracy by 5 percentage points; the derivation of the interval is not stated, so whether it describes across-fold variation or something else cannot be determined.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Descriptive rather than model-directed. Heat map analysis and movement-energy graphs are presented to show that motor activity and facial expression differ between groups, and because motion energy is computed per region these could localise the difference - but they characterise the data rather than the classifier, and no attribution, ablation or feature-importance analysis is reported for the model itself. Two of the engineered features, the mouth aspect ratio and per-region motion energy, were designed to be interpretable and are physically meaningful, which makes the absence of any analysis relating them to model output the more conspicuous. The specific analysis that this study needed and did not perform is a stream-wise ablation: a result driven by hand motion energy and a result driven by facial mesh geometry would have very different standing given that the two groups differ by 32 percentage points in sex composition, and nothing reported distinguishes them.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Strong where this review's video branch is usually weakest, and unexamined where this particular sample is weakest. The splitting is subject-independent stratified 5-fold cross-validation, and the paper states both the mechanism and the purpose: 'To provide strong model validation and prevent data leakage ... The dataset was divided on a subject-independent basis such that data from the same participant was not included in both training and validation datasets.' In a corpus of frame-level data from 100 children, where naive splitting would place frames of the same child on both sides and produce a near-perfect figure, this is exactly the right control, and it is named as such - the clearest anti-leakage statement in this review's video branch. Stratification preserves class ratio across folds; four overfitting controls are specified with their parameters; and the resulting figure of 85-90% is modest and plausible, benchmarked against external comparators rather than presented in isolation. The remaining issues are of two kinds. Procedurally, all reported figures are cross-validation results with no independent held-out test, so architecture selection and performance estimation share the same folds; the reported accuracy is a range rather than a mean with fold-level detail; specificity is not reported although recall of 0.95 against 85-90% accuracy implies it is materially lower; and the stated plus-or-minus 1.5% intervals are narrower than 20-child validation folds would ordinarily support, with no derivation given. Substantively, and more importantly, subject-independence protects against recognising an individual across the split but offers no protection against a group-level confound, and this sample has a severe one: the autistic group is approximately 84% male and the comparison group 52%, while the model's inputs are 468 facial mesh points and 75 body and hand landmarks, all encoding sex-linked morphology and posture. A classifier that separates boys from girls would perform equally well on unseen children and would be entirely consistent with the reported figures. The study is therefore a clear illustration of a distinction the synthesis should draw: leakage control and confound control are different problems, and closing the first - which this paper does deliberately and well - leaves the second untouched.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Keywords: autism spectrum disorders, early diagnosis, facial analysis, long short-term memory, mouth aspect ratio, spatiotemporal patterns. Balanced across population, method and construct, with 'mouth aspect ratio' unusually specific for a keyword list and signalling that engineered interpretable features were part of the design. Terms carried through the body: MediaPipe, face mesh, pose, hands, motion energy, motor imitation, gesture, subject-independent, stratified cross-validation.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics 14(5):3985-4000, October 2025, open access under CC BY-SA; received 20 March, revised 8 August, accepted 1 September 2025. An electrical engineering and informatics venue, and the profile of what was and was not scrutinised follows: the acquisition protocol, the feature construction, the validation strategy, the regularisation parameters and the architecture are all specified in detail, while the absence of any diagnostic ascertainment procedure and of any ethics or consent statement for a prospective study recording 100 children passed review without comment. The journal's structure elicited conflict-of-interest and data-availability declarations - the latter citing 'privacy and ethical considerations' - but has no field that would have prompted a human-subjects statement.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published October 2025 by information systems and sociology groups at L.N. Gumilyov Eurasian National University in Astana, with collaborators at Esil University and the National University of Uzbekistan. The framing is health-systems oriented and accurate for the region - a shortage of qualified specialists and a high burden on healthcare systems - with the technology positioned as a route to 'earlier identification and timely referral to specialists' rather than as a substitute for diagnosis, which is among the better-calibrated translational positions in this review. For the synthesis the study contributes three things. Its acquisition design is one of the strongest here: both groups were recorded under an identical purpose-built protocol in the same controlled environment, so the acquisition confound that undermines the photograph, video-frame, thermal and clinic-versus-school audio studies charted elsewhere cannot operate; the protocol actively elicits both social and motor behaviour in 8 to 10 minutes; and the landmark representation discards appearance, clothing, skin tone, lighting and background before any learning, removing a further class of confound by construction. Its validation is the most explicitly reasoned anti-leakage design in the video branch, naming subject-independence and data leakage directly and specifying four overfitting controls with their parameters - and the resulting 85-90% is modest and credible, benchmarked against external comparators. And it is a clean illustration of a distinction worth stating in the synthesis: leakage control and confound control are separate problems. The autistic group is approximately 84% male against 52% in the comparison group, a 32-percentage-point gap, and the model's inputs are 468 facial mesh points and 75 body and hand landmarks that encode sex-linked morphology and posture; a classifier separating boys from girls would produce exactly these figures under perfectly subject-independent cross-validation. No stratified or adjusted analysis addresses this, and no stream-wise ablation shows whether the signal lies in facial geometry or in hand motion, which would bear directly on the exposure. Two further gaps: no diagnostic reference standard of any kind is described for a prospectively recruited sample, so the predicted label is undefined; and no ethics approval or consent statement appears anywhere, in a study that recorded over 16 hours of video of 100 children including 50 autistic children.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Eldawansy M; El Bakry H; M Shohieb S
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective algorithm-development study on a public facial-image corpus, with a second proposed diagnostic component for which no data were collected
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A 100,352-dimensional feature vector per image, fed to a multilayer perceptron. The dimensionality exceeds the number of images by a factor of about 34, which is an extreme ratio and is not commented on.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 2,932 images from an unreported number of individuals
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None, and the authors identify its absence as a limitation.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 1,466 images of neurotypical children
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not obtained and not required by the stated design, since no participant was contacted; the underlying images were collected from the internet by third parties without the depicted children's families having consented to this use, which the paper does not discuss
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. The children were photographed for reasons unrelated to any study, in unknown contexts.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None for acquisition. Analysis used an Intel Core i7-11800H with 16 GB RAM under Windows 10, Python 3.9.7, scikit-learn 0.24.2, TensorFlow 2.9.2, DeepFace 0.0.93, with PyTorch for the multilayer perceptron and CUDA for acceleration - a fully versioned software stack, which is good practice.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: 'The datasets generated or analyzed during this study are available in the Kaggle repository.'
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not reported; the full software stack is versioned
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Approved by the Faculty of Computers and Information Research Ethics Committee, approval code 2024 01 004, with procedures stated to conform to the Declaration of Helsinki and to ethical standards for data privacy and the responsible use of AI in health research. The statement further explains that the facial images came from 'a publicly available, anonymized dataset on Kaggle, ensuring no personally identifiable information was used' and that 'no direct contact with human participants occurred'. Obtaining and reporting a numbered ethics approval for a secondary image analysis is more than most studies in this branch do. The characterisation of a corpus of children's photographs as anonymised and free of personally identifiable information is nonetheless questionable, since a photograph of a face is among the most directly identifying data types there is, and the same paper uses a face-recognition library to process them.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: DeepFace, a pretrained face-recognition and emotion-classification library, applied to each image to produce 100,352 features. DeepFace's face-recognition embeddings are trained for identity verification on adult face corpora, and its emotion classifier is trained on neurotypical expression datasets - so both components were developed on populations and tasks other than the one they are applied to here. A study charted elsewhere in this review demonstrated empirically that affect models trained on neurotypical faces transfer poorly to autistic children and require fine-tuning on autistic data; DeepFace is used here without fine-tuning.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None. No attribution, saliency, feature analysis or error analysis is reported for either component. With 100,352 undifferentiated DeepFace features feeding a multilayer perceptron, nothing in the paper indicates what property of an image drives an autism prediction, which matters particularly here because DeepFace's principal embedding is an identity-verification representation - designed to encode who a face belongs to - so the features are optimised for exactly the individual-level information that an image-level split allows a model to exploit.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not described. Several machine learning models were compared and the multilayer perceptron reported as best on testing accuracy, so model selection used the reported evaluation.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A 90.48/9.51 split into 2,653 training and 279 testing images, with 10-fold cross-validation applied to the training portion. Two problems. The split is at image level with no participant-level partitioning described and the number of distinct children never stated, so in a web-assembled corpus where one child may appear in several images, images of the same child can fall on both sides - the standard failure of this branch, documented in this review for six other studies on the same corpus family. And the reported figure is given as '92% across both training and testing datasets', which conflates the two and leaves it unclear what the 279-image test partition alone yielded; a test set of 279 images would in any case give a 95% interval of roughly plus or minus 3 points even before the leakage question. The 10-fold cross-validation is applied within the training data rather than as the primary evaluation, which is the correct arrangement, and the authors correctly note in their limitations that 'while 10-fold cross-validation mitigates overfitting, the lack of an external validation cohort limits confidence in generalizability'.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Five, in a dedicated section, and they are candid. The dataset of publicly available 2D facial images 'may not fully represent the diversity of facial expressions in children with ASD or gelotophobia, as demographic variables, such as age, gender, and cultural background, were not explicitly controlled'. Ten-fold cross-validation mitigates overfitting but 'the lack of an external validation cohort limits confidence in generalizability'. Subtle emotional states such as fear and disgust remain hard to distinguish because they involve minimal facial muscle movement. The approach relies solely on static images while 'real-world interactions are dynamic and multimodal (including voice, gesture, and context)'. And the advanced architectures and multimodal inputs proposed as future directions 'were not implemented in this study'. Naming uncontrolled demographics and the absence of external validation directly is more than most papers in this branch offer.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: There are no participants. The units are 2,932 facial images, balanced at 1,466 per class, described in the results as 'collected from platforms such as Kaggle and ASD-related websites'. The number of distinct children behind those images is never stated, and no age, sex, ancestry, cognitive, language or clinical information is available for either class - an absence the authors acknowledge directly, noting that 'demographic variables, such as age, gender, and cultural background, were not explicitly controlled'. This is the seventh study in this review built on the Kaggle facial-image corpus family, and the description of the autistic class as sourced partly from autism-related websites places it squarely in the same category as the others: the label records where an image was found rather than any assessment of the child in it. For the paper's second target, gelotophobia, there are not even images with labels - no person was assessed for gelotophobia by any means, so that half of the study has no sample at all.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Standard clinical framing with an unusually sympathetic account of the second condition. Autism is 'a neurodevelopmental disorder' characterised by 'difficulties in social interactions, communication impairments, repetitive behaviors, and restricted interests', with the spectrum concept explained accurately as reflecting variation in severity and ability. The description of gelotophobia is the paper's best writing and is genuinely person-centred: individuals 'may perceive all laughter as negatively directed at them, interpreting it as a form of mockery or threat, which often leads to social withdrawal and isolation', and the account traces how the belief becomes internalised into 'heightened sensitivity to rejection, feelings of shame, and an increased tendency toward social avoidance'. Framing a condition through the person's experience of it, rather than through observable deficit, is rare in this corpus. The paper also refers to autistic people as 'populations considered socially vulnerable', which is an acknowledgement of social position rather than individual pathology. Against this, the study's method sits awkwardly with its own framing: a condition defined by an internal appraisal of others' intentions is to be detected from a photograph of a face. No autistic person or organisation is reported as involved.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Entirely absent, and acknowledged as such. No age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic, cognitive or comorbidity information exists for either image class, and the authors state plainly that age, gender and cultural background 'were not explicitly controlled'. Two consequences follow that the acknowledgement does not address. Facial classifiers key strongly on apparent age and on sex-linked morphology, and autism is diagnosed roughly four times more often in boys, so an unmeasured sex imbalance between a class harvested from autism-related sources and a class harvested elsewhere is a live and untestable alternative explanation for the reported 92%. And DeepFace, the feature extractor, is a face-recognition library whose embeddings are optimised to encode individual identity - which makes demographic attributes among the properties most strongly represented in the 100,352 features fed to the classifier. Comorbidity is a further specific gap here, since the paper's own second target is a comorbid condition whose prevalence in autism it puts at up to 45%, yet no comorbidity is recorded for any image.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None for autism and none for gelotophobia, with the second absence being the more remarkable.
