custom_fields.RQ5.3: Received 4 October 2024, revised 13 March 2025, accepted 24 August 2025 - the longest review cycle among the recently charted studies, and by far the least effective. Framing is diagnostic-replacement with an explicit efficiency argument: enabling more accurate and automated ASD screening, reducing reliance on subjective assessments, and facilitating timely interventions. Positioning is entirely comparative against numbers quoted from a single prior paper, with the contribution expressed as a higher AUC (0.98 against 0.74, 0.66 and 0.64) rather than as an estimate of anything.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Enhanced multilevel autism classification for children using eye-tracking and hybrid CNN-RNN deep learning models
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Cheekaty S; Muneeswari G
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed as scalable screening to replace largely manual eye-tracking analysis. No clinician-facing evaluation, threshold or deployment study.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Prospective single-site primary data collection followed by supervised four-class classification of autism severity, with a 70:15:15 image-level split. A secondary comparison experiment reuses the public Saliency4ASD dataset.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Within-study: GRU, 2-LSTM, RFC, XGBoost across four feature sets. Across-study: Saliency4ASD/ICME 2019 entries (Tao and Shyu 74.22%, Wu et al. 65.41% and 61.62%, Startsev and Dorr AUC 75 and 76.9), against which the proposed method is listed at 95.93% and 97.95%.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Children with an existing ASD diagnosis were recruited from a single special school. Eligibility required a CARS score of 30 or above and an age between 8 and 12 years.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Two parallel representations: variable-length scanpath sequences of the selected features, padded and masked; and 4,000 cropped eye images at 416x416 labelled with subject ID, frame number, severity range and left/right eye.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: India - participants recruited at Dakshinya Autistic School, Guntur, Andhra Pradesh; analysis at VIT-AP University, Amaravati. Ethics approval from Government Medical College, Guntur.
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: CARS, used both as the eligibility screen (score 30 or above) and as the source of the four severity classes. The class boundaries in Table 3 are Low CARS <=20, Mild 20<CARS<=40, Medium 40<CARS<=60, High CARS>60. Two of these are impossible. CARS is a 15-item scale scored 1 to 4 per item, so it ranges from 15 to 60 and no child can score above 60; the High class as defined is empty. And since eligibility required CARS >=30, no child can fall in the Low class (<=20) or in the lower half of the Mild class. The four groups of exactly ten participants each therefore cannot have been produced by the stated rule.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Diagnoses were made by experienced physicians using DSM-5 criteria together with CARS scores, with the paper explaining candidly that ADI-R and ADOS evaluations are not widely available in India. This is an honest account of a real constraint and is better documented than most of the corpus.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: All 40 participants have an ASD diagnosis, allocated 10 each to low, mild, medium and high severity classes.
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: The Gesell Developmental Scale (GDS) is stated to have been used to examine associations between eye-tracking data and behavioural/clinical outcomes, but no GDS score, distribution or analysis is reported anywhere in the paper.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: 8 to 12 years by eligibility criterion. No mean, SD or distribution is reported, and no per-severity-class age breakdown.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Not reported at all - no counts, no proportions, no acknowledgement that sex was not recorded.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 40 children. There is an earlier and irreconcilable statement in the introduction that in the initial training we enrolled a group of 8-10 children aged x years - the literal placeholder x survives into the published paper.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: Partial and self-described as incomplete. The Saliency4ASD experiment uses independent public data, but the task there is ASD versus TD binary classification while the model's own task is four-class severity, so it is not a validation of the trained model. The abstract states that further evaluation on an independent dataset will assess the generalizability and precision of the model.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: None. There is no typically developing group in the study, although the abstract states that children with ASD exhibit unique and highly individualized gaze patterns when compared to TD children. The only TD data in the paper come from the separate public Saliency4ASD set (14 ASD, 14 TD children) used in a side comparison.
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No. Single session per child.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Written informed consent from all parents before participation, plus separate written consent for publication of participant details and accompanying images. This two-tier consent is among the strongest ethics reporting in the corpus, comparable to local_7d7f1fcc.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: 25% for the four-class severity task by construction (1,000 images per class), never stated. The Saliency4ASD comparison is a two-class task with a 50% baseline, so the two sets of numbers are not on the same scale.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye tracking - gaze recordings at 250 Hz, converted into scanpath sequences and additionally into cropped left/right eye images extracted from video frames.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Passive viewing of a ten-second silent movie in which a young Asian woman articulates the English letters, preceded by five-point calibration. The workflow text elsewhere refers to a 2-minute eye-tracking video, which does not match the ten-second stimulus.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: SMI RED250 portable eye tracker at 250 Hz; display 1024x768 with stated spatial resolution 0.05. Analysis in MATLAB on Windows 10, Intel Core i5, 4 GB RAM.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Low to moderate. The acquisition protocol (device, sampling rate, calibration, stimulus, resolution) and the eligibility criteria are described well enough to repeat the data collection, and the feature sets and their ablation are clearly specified. But no code, no seed, no software versions, no convolutional architecture, no fold count for the asserted cross-validation, no route to the announced 4,000-image dataset, and severity class definitions that cannot have produced the reported groups.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not stated. The paper announces a novel dataset of 4,000 annotated 416x416 eye images that researchers and developers can leverage, but gives no access route, licence or deposit.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Yes, fully specified: Government Medical College, Guntur Ethics Committee, decision reference IRB-2024-0057.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Noise removal, calibration drift correction, fixation/saccade detection by dispersion- and velocity-threshold methods with saccades excluded from analysis, mapping of gaze coordinates to AOIs on the stimulus, normalisation, and image augmentation by rotation and shearing. Sequence padding to maximum scanpath length with a masking mechanism.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Four sequential scanpath features - horizontal position x, vertical position y, fixation duration d and velocity v - evaluated in four combinations: (y,x), (x,d,y), (x,y,v) and (x,y,d,v). Scanpath similarity computed with dynamic time warping and MultiMatch. Maximal information coefficient used to score feature relevance; PCA and recursive feature elimination also mentioned.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: MATLAB for the classification pipeline; Python for frame segmentation. No versions, no seed, no repository.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: None. No confidence intervals, no significance tests, no fold variance. Maximal information coefficient scores are reported for features but without inference.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Substantive by this corpus's standards, and the paper's real contribution. MIC scores rank individual scanpath features and similarity measures; the feature-set ablation is used to argue that velocity carries the least information about severity while continuous attention (fixation duration and vertical gaze position) carries the most; MultiMatch and DTW are contrasted, with DTW shown to be more sensitive to vertical gaze distribution. The conclusion drawn - that it is the continuous attention process, as opposed to the transition phases, that reflects atypical visual behaviour - is an actual empirical claim about behaviour rather than a leaderboard entry.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not systematically described. Learning rate 0.0001 and batch size 64 are stated; for the Saliency4ASD comparison, learning rate and epoch count were adjusted to account for varying data sizes with no criterion given.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Per-class accuracy is shown across training, validation and test sets, and the confusion matrix is discussed by class (low and medium separate better than mild and high). No demographic subgroup analysis, since no demographics beyond age band were collected.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Deep learning sequence models: hybrid CNN-RNN, GRU, two-layer LSTM, BiLSTM; classical comparators random forest and XGBoost.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: LSTM layers of 128 hidden units, final layer into a fully connected softmax; batch size 64, cross-entropy loss, learning rate 0.0001. The description says softmax regression for class probability prediction in binary classification although the task has four classes. Convolutional layer specifications are not given.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A 70:15:15 train/validation/test division of the 4,000 eye images. The split is at the image level: each of the 40 participants contributes exactly 100 images (50 frames x 2 eyes), so all three subsets necessarily contain images from every participant - and indeed both eyes from the same video frame can land on opposite sides of the split. Cross-validation is asserted repeatedly (cross-validation ensuring robustness) but no fold count, fold results or variance is ever reported. Augmentation is described before the split.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, false discovery rate, false omission rate and AUC are all defined by formula. Only accuracy, recall and F1 are actually tabulated for the within-study comparison; specificity, FDR and FOR are never reported as numbers. A four-class confusion matrix is shown as a figure.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: CNN-RNN with feature set (x,d,y): accuracy 97.00%, recall 98.24%, F1 97.04%. Other feature sets: (x,y,d,v) 95.23%, (y,x) 94.00%, (x,y,v) 90.00%. Comparators at the best feature set: GRU 92%, 2-LSTM 92%, XGBoost 80.25%, RFC 80.80%. On the Saliency4ASD comparison the proposed method is reported at 95.93% accuracy / 95.82% AUC (full dataset) and 97.95% / 97.84% (eye dataset).
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Visual attention dynamics during viewing of a speaking face: fixation location and duration, saccades, vertical gaze distribution, and scanpath shape.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Weight DTW by fixation duration to refine scanpath alignment; improve eye-tracking reliability and accessibility; evaluate on an independent dataset.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Brief: small-scale datasets typical of ASD research, the need to retain valid scanpaths across paradigms leading to inconsistent sample sizes across subjects, and eye-tracking technology challenges around calibration precision and data integrity arising from subject cooperation and equipment limits. The image-level split, the absent TD group, the impossible CARS bands and the incommensurable external comparison are not mentioned.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Forty children, all with an existing ASD diagnosis, recruited from Dakshinya Autistic School in Guntur, India, and divided into four severity classes of exactly ten each: low, mild, medium and high. There is no typically developing comparison group, which matters because the abstract nonetheless reports that children with ASD exhibit unique and highly individualized gaze patterns when compared to TD children - a comparison the design cannot support. The only TD data in the paper belong to the separate public Saliency4ASD set (14 ASD, 14 TD) used in a side experiment. Two internal inconsistencies affect the count: the introduction states that in the initial training we enrolled a group of 8-10 children aged x years, with the placeholder x left in the published text, and the analysis unit is not the child but the cropped eye image - 50 frames x 2 eyes x 40 children = 4,000 images, which is what the 70:15:15 split partitions.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, ASD children, autism applicants, participants, TD children, neurotypical. The paper is one of the few in the corpus to define neurotypical explicitly and to note that it refers to individuals whose neurological development conforms to societal norms and expectations - a formulation that recognises the norm as social rather than natural. Elsewhere the register slips (autism applicants as a table heading; the severity ladder low/mild/medium/high applied to children rather than to symptoms). The introduction is unusual in this corpus for framing the research motivation partly around reducing stigma, promoting inclusion, and improving educational and employment outcomes rather than solely around detection.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Thin. Age is given only as the 8-12 eligibility band, with no mean, SD or per-class distribution. Sex is not reported at all - not even a total male/female count - despite forty children being individually recruited and consented. Nothing on socioeconomic status, language, verbal ability or schooling level, and no per-severity-class characteristics of any kind. The Gesell Developmental Scale is said to have been used to relate eye-tracking data to behavioural and clinical outcomes, but no GDS number appears anywhere in the article.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Well handled and honestly reported. Diagnoses were made by experienced physicians applying DSM-5 criteria together with CARS scores, and the paper states plainly why gold-standard instruments were not used: ADI-R and ADOS evaluations are not widely available in India. That candour about a real infrastructural constraint compares favourably with the many studies in this corpus that simply assert diagnosis or inherit labels from a download. What undermines it is the severity banding rather than the diagnosis: eligibility required CARS >=30, yet Table 3 assigns ten children to a Low class defined as CARS <=20 and ten more to a Mild class spanning 20 to 40, and a High class defined as CARS >60 when the scale's maximum is 60. The four equal groups cannot have been generated by the stated rule, and the actual CARS distribution is never shown.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: CARS is the only reported measure, and it is the label rather than a covariate. The Gesell Developmental Scale is named but never reported. No IQ, adaptive-behaviour, language or comorbidity data.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is to replace largely manual, unscalable eye-tracking analysis with an automated scanpath-based method that classifies autism severity into four levels, and to characterise how gaze features vary across those levels using DTW and MultiMatch similarity. Headline findings: CNN-RNN with features (x, d, y) reaches accuracy 97.00%, recall 98.24%, F1 97.04%, against GRU 92%, 2-LSTM 92%, XGBoost 80.25% and RFC 80.80%. The more interesting finding is the feature ablation: velocity contributes least, and the authors conclude that it is the continuous attention process, as opposed to the transition phases, that reflects atypical visual behaviour - with differences concentrated in attention duration and vertical gaze distribution.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A single special school (Dakshinya Autistic School, Guntur) supplying participants, with ethics oversight from Government Medical College, Guntur, and analysis at VIT-AP University. Recording used a five-point calibration then passive viewing. Setting is described adequately for the acquisition but the recording room, examiner and session conditions are not characterised, and there is no discussion of whether recording conditions varied across severity groups.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Passive viewing of a ten-second silent movie in which a young Asian woman articulates the English letters, chosen on the reasoning - well argued from the prior literature reviewed - that a speaking face is a more discriminating stimulus than a static one, since gaze duration on inner facial features is reduced specifically while the face is speaking. The stimulus choice is one of the better-motivated in the corpus. Against that, the workflow section describes classifying autism severity from a 2-min ET video, which contradicts the ten-second stimulus and is never reconciled.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up. Ethics is a genuine strength: approval from the Government Medical College Guntur Ethics Committee with a stated decision reference (IRB-2024-0057), written parental informed consent before participation, and separate written consent for publication of participants' details and any accompanying images. That second, publication-specific consent places this study at the responsible end of the review's ethics gradient, alongside local_7d7f1fcc and well away from studies that report no ethics statement at all.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: SMI RED250 portable eye tracker at 250 Hz, 1024x768 display, stated spatial resolution 0.05, five-point calibration, with calibration drift correction applied in preprocessing. Fixation/saccade segmentation by dispersion-threshold and velocity-threshold algorithms. Classification implemented in MATLAB on Windows 10 with an Intel Core i5 and 4 GB RAM; frame segmentation in Python. The hardware is implausibly modest for the described deep models and no training time is given.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Mixed. The acquisition protocol is reported in enough detail to be repeated - device, sampling rate, calibration procedure, stimulus, display parameters, eligibility criteria - and the four feature sets and their ablation are fully specified, so the study's most interesting result could be re-tested. Everything downstream is opaque: no code, no seed, no MATLAB version, no convolutional architecture, no epoch count, no fold count for the cross-validation that is repeatedly asserted but never reported, and no access route for the 4,000-image dataset the paper announces as a contribution for researchers and developers to leverage. A further reproducibility concern is the literature review, which contains a run of citations on building energy consumption, distributed generation, solar-equipped neighbourhoods and electric vehicles - and the abbreviation list correspondingly defines DB as Design builder, DG as Distributed generation and ICME as Integrated Computational Materials Engineering. These belong to a different paper and indicate that portions of the manuscript were assembled rather than written for this study.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Three limitations are stated: small-scale datasets typical of ASD research; the practice of retaining valid scanpaths across paradigms, which produces inconsistent sample sizes across subjects; and eye-tracking reliability problems from calibration precision, subject cooperation and equipment limits. All three are real and specific. Unmentioned: that the 70:15:15 split is at the eye-image level so every participant appears in all three subsets; that there is no TD group despite the abstract's TD comparison; that the CARS bands defining the four classes are arithmetically impossible and inconsistent with the eligibility threshold; that the external comparison is against a different task on a different dataset; that specificity, FDR and FOR are defined but never reported; and that the asserted cross-validation is never quantified.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Weight DTW by fixation duration to improve scanpath alignment; address calibration precision and data-integrity problems in eye-tracking to improve reliability and accessibility for screening; and evaluate on an independent dataset to assess generalizability and precision. The last is stated in the abstract itself, which is an unusually forthright acknowledgement that the reported figures are not yet generalisation estimates.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Visual attention during viewing of a speaking face, decomposed into fixation position (x, y), fixation duration and inter-fixation velocity, and into scanpath shape compared by DTW and MultiMatch. The behavioural claims that emerge are specific and testable: attention duration and vertical gaze distribution differ most across severity levels, velocity least, and children with ASD show highly individualised rather than merely reduced gaze patterns.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No multimodal fusion - eye tracking alone. There is a within-modality fusion of two representations of the same recording (scanpath sequences for the RNN path, cropped eye images for the CNN path), which is what the hybrid designation refers to. The Gesell Developmental Scale was collected and could have supported a genuine behavioural-clinical fusion, but no GDS result is reported.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised sequence classification. Primary model is a hybrid CNN-RNN combining convolutional feature extraction with GRU and LSTM recurrence; comparators are GRU, a two-layer LSTM, BiLSTM, random forest and XGBoost. LSTM layers use 128 hidden units into a fully connected softmax; batch size 64, cross-entropy loss, learning rate 0.0001. The classification section describes the output as softmax regression for class probability prediction in binary classification although the task is four-class throughout.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Two representations. (i) Variable-length scanpath sequences over four features - x, y, fixation duration d, velocity v - padded to maximum length with a masking mechanism, evaluated in four combinations. (ii) 4,000 cropped eye images at 416x416, fifty frames per child times left and right eye, each labelled with subject ID, frame number, severity band and eye side. The image-level representation is what the 70:15:15 split partitions, and it is where the validity problem originates: with a fixed 100 images per child, the split cannot separate participants even in principle.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, false discovery rate, false omission rate and AUC are all defined by equation, which reads as thorough; only accuracy, recall and F1 are then reported for the within-study experiments, and specificity, FDR and FOR appear as numbers nowhere. A four-class confusion matrix is shown and discussed sensibly - low and medium separate better than mild and high. The Saliency4ASD table reports accuracy and AUC together (95.93/95.82 and 97.95/97.84). The 25% four-class chance level is never stated, and no metric carries an interval.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: The strongest interpretability work among the eye-tracking studies charted so far, and the reason this paper is worth more than its headline number. Maximal information coefficient scores rank individual scanpath features and the similarity measures; a systematic four-way feature-set ablation shows accuracy moving from 90.00% ((x,y,v)) to 97.00% ((x,d,y)) to 95.23% ((x,y,d,v)); and from that pattern the authors argue that velocity is uninformative for severity while fixation duration and vertical gaze position carry the signal. They further contrast the two similarity metrics, finding MultiMatch less sensitive to subtle temporal or spatial change and DTW more sensitive to vertical gaze distribution. These are claims about gaze behaviour that could be falsified by another laboratory, which is rare in this corpus. Their evidential weight is nonetheless limited by the same leakage that inflates the accuracies: an ablation computed under an image-level split ranks features by how well they support participant recognition as much as by how well they support severity discrimination.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The design is a 70:15:15 partition of 4,000 eye images derived from 40 children at exactly 100 images per child (50 frames, left and right eye). Because the per-child image count is constant and the split is at the image level, every participant is present in the training, validation and test subsets simultaneously; more finely still, the left and right eye of the same video frame - two crops of one instant of one recording - can land on opposite sides. This is frame-level leakage of the same kind documented in the video, EEG-epoch, thermal, cry and facial-image branches, and it is sufficient to explain a 97% four-class result from 40 children. Three further weaknesses compound it. Augmentation by rotation and shearing is described as a dataset-preparation step applied before partitioning. Cross-validation is asserted four separate times as ensuring robustness, but no fold count, no per-fold result and no variance is ever reported, so it cannot be assessed and may not have been run on the final model. And the external comparison in Table 7 places this study's four-class severity accuracies (95.93%, 97.95%) beside Saliency4ASD entries (74.22%, 65.41%, 61.62%) that solve a different, binary ASD-versus-TD task on different data - the numbers are not commensurable, and the higher figure is not evidence of a better method. To the authors' credit, the abstract itself concedes that further evaluation on an independent dataset will assess the generalizability and precision of the model, which is the correct reading of their own result.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Autism spectrum disorder; CNN-RNN hybrid network; Early diagnosis; Eye-tracking data; Machine learning; Scanpath analysis. Method- and modality-centred, with scanpath analysis correctly signalling the paper's actual analytic contribution; nothing about severity, participants or validation.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Neural Computing and Applications 37(33):27631-27654, in a special issue drawn from the 2023 India International Congress on Computational Intelligence. Special-issue routing is relevant to the review's venue analysis: the impossible CARS bands, the absent TD group behind a TD claim in the abstract, the surviving x placeholder in the participant count, and a literature review containing building-energy and distributed-generation citations all passed review in 53 days.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Received 12 August 2024, accepted 4 October 2024, published online 4 December 2024, issued 2025. Framing is assistive-to-transformative: the work is said to show how ML and eye tracking can transform the diagnosis and treatment of autism and to set a new standard in the field, with the method described as capturing spatial and temporal dynamics with unprecedented accuracy. Set against that rhetoric, the paper is also one of the few in the corpus whose abstract states outright that generalisability has not yet been assessed, and whose introduction motivates the work partly by stigma reduction, inclusion and long-term quality of life rather than solely by detection throughput.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Ensemble of Deep Learning with Crested Porcupine Optimizer Based Autism
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Balasubramani J; Rajendran S; Zakariah M; Alnuaim A
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed as computer-aided diagnosis that can aid families and parents in superstition and denial and support treatment and reintegration of autistic patients. No clinician, threshold or deployment evaluation.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of a public Kaggle facial-image dataset; supervised binary image classification with a metaheuristic hyperparameter search and a reported 5-fold cross-validation.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Literature-quoted figures for MobileNet (90.24%), VGG-16 with logistic regression (89.55%), random forest (91.00%), decision tree (90.11%) and gradient boosting (92.64%), multi-kernel SVM (91.98%) and KNN (89.90%). None was re-run by the authors on the same data or split.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None. The Autism Image Data set was downloaded from Kaggle (cihan063/autism-image-data, accessed 22 November 2024) - the same web-scraped autism face corpus reused repeatedly across this review.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Gabor-filtered RGB face crops at unspecified resolution, encoded as MobileNetV2 feature vectors.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: India and Saudi Arabia - Saveetha School of Engineering, Saveetha Institute of Medical and Technical Sciences, Chennai; and the College of Applied Studies and Community Service, King Saud University, Riyadh. No data collection setting.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None. Class labels are Kaggle folder names on photographs of unknown provenance. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or date exists for any image, and the paper does not discuss this.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: Not stated. Inferable as approximately 1,400 from the confusion-matrix arithmetic.
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not reported and not obtainable from image files.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Not reported. The abstract nonetheless asserts that the facial evolution of newborns with ASD is quite different from that of typically developing children, a claim about neonates that the data cannot address.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Stated as 2,926 facial samples in two classes. The confusion-matrix counts do not agree with this: at 1,000 epochs the model is said to have recognised 1,338 normal and 1,362 autism samples correctly, which against the reported per-class accuracies of 95.57% and 97.29% implies roughly 1,400 images per class, or about 2,800 in total.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. The comparison discussion refers to evaluating on a distinct benchmark dataset as a way to establish generalisation, but no second dataset is used.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Not stated; approximately 1,400 by the same inference. The paper simultaneously asserts that the dataset suggests a possible class imbalance requiring consideration and applies inverse-frequency class weights, although the source dataset is balanced by construction.
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: 50% by construction, never stated.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Two-dimensional facial photographs.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. Still images, no stimulus, task or session.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None for acquisition. Compute environment not described - no hardware, no runtime other than an unlabelled training time column in the Gabor ablation table.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Very low. The source dataset and access date are given, and the augmentation and normalisation settings are specified in unusual detail - but there is no code, no software, no hardware, no seed, no image resolution (the placeholder X, Y pixels survives in the text), no ensemble combination rule, no CPO configuration, no split specification, and no reconciliation between the stated 2,926 images and the roughly 2,800 implied by the confusion matrices.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Source Kaggle URL is given with an access date. No derived splits, features or trained models are shared.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Explicitly waived. The statement reads that the study did not involve direct experiments on humans or the use of human tissue samples, and that publicly available datasets from Kaggle were used instead. No consideration is given to the fact that the dataset consists of identifiable photographs of children carrying an unverified disability label.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Gabor filtering to emphasise facial texture and orientation; MTCNN face detection; median filtering for noise reduction; Z-score colour normalisation across channels; bicubic-interpolated resizing to unspecified dimensions - the text reads image resizing dimensions (X, Y pixels), leaving the placeholder unfilled; inverse-frequency class weighting; augmentation by random rotation between -15 and 15 degrees, horizontal flips, random cropping up to 10% and brightness scaling between 0.8 and 1.2.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: MobileNetV2 as a feature extractor over the Gabor-filtered images.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Not named. No library, version, seed or repository. Deep belief network and HKELM components are presented as Python-like pseudocode rather than as an implementation.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: None. No intervals, no tests, and no fold variance despite cross-validation being claimed.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None of the fitted model. The paper offers component-level ablation reasoning (Gabor filtering aids texture discrimination; removing MobileNetV2 would reduce performance; the ensemble beats individual classifiers) but only the Gabor ablation is actually run. No saliency, attribution or feature analysis.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Crested Porcupine Optimizer over the three models' hyperparameters, with no stated search space, budget or objective, and no statement of which data partition the optimiser's fitness was computed on. Separately, results are reported across five epoch settings and the best (1,000 epochs, 96.43%) is carried into the abstract and the comparison table.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None. No demographic variable exists in the data.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Ensemble of three heterogeneous learners over shared CNN features: long short-term memory, deep belief network (stacked restricted Boltzmann machines) and hybrid-kernel extreme learning machine, with hyperparameters selected by the Crested Porcupine Optimizer, a recent metaheuristic.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Structural descriptions and energy/kernel equations are given for the RBM and HKELM components, and the ensemble is sketched as pseudocode. Concrete settings - layer widths, learning rates, ensemble combination rule, CPO population and iteration counts, and the hyperparameter search space - are not reported. The use of an LSTM over static single-image features is never justified, as there is no sequence in the input.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Two incompatible accounts. The results section reports confusion matrices at 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 and 2500 epochs whose correct-classification counts (for example 1,338 plus 1,362 at 1,000 epochs) span essentially the whole dataset, indicating evaluation over all available images rather than a held-out portion; no train-test split is described anywhere in the experimental section. Separately, the comparison discussion states that 5-fold cross-validation was applied with 80% training and 20% testing per fold and that accuracy and F1 were consistently high with minimal variance - but no per-fold value, mean or standard deviation is reported.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, F-score and G-measure, per class and averaged, at five epoch counts; ROC curves; a Gabor filtering ablation with training time and a computational-cost index. Specificity, AUC as a number, calibration, predictive values and confidence intervals are all absent.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Average accuracy 96.43%, precision 96.44%, recall 96.43%, F-score 96.43%, G-measure 96.43% at 1,000 epochs. Per class at that setting: Normal accuracy 95.57%, precision 97.24%; Autism accuracy 97.29%, precision 95.65%. The Gabor ablation reports 96.43% with filtering against 92.80% without.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None. The target is static facial appearance - texture, contour and shape features under the premise that developmental problems affecting face features are often associated with fundamental brain disorders.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: None stated.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: None. The article has no limitations section and the word limitation does not appear.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: No participants. The unit is the image: a stated 2,926 facial samples in two classes, Normal and Autism, downloaded from Kaggle. The number of distinct children is unknown and never raised. The stated total does not survive contact with the results: the confusion matrix at 1,000 epochs reports 1,338 correctly recognised normal and 1,362 correctly recognised autism images, which against the per-class accuracies of 95.57% and 97.29% implies about 1,400 images in each class and about 2,800 overall. Those counts also span essentially the whole dataset, which means the reported confusion matrices are not computed on a held-out subset at all.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic children, autistic patients, individuals with ASD, normal controls, Normal class, typically developing children. The pathologising register is unusually strong even for this branch: autism is described as a set of intricate neuro-developmental brain diseases, the comparison class is labelled Normal throughout, and the stated benefit of early recognition is to aid families and parents in superstition and denial. Elsewhere autistic people are said to require treatment and reintegration. There is no autistic or community perspective anywhere in the article.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: None whatsoever. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography, socioeconomic status or recruitment source - the dataset carries none and the paper requests none. This is notable in comparison with local_986436f2, which reused a sibling of the same corpus and supplied an elaborate demographic table that the data cannot support; here the same absence is simply left unremarked. The abstract's claim about the facial evolution of newborns with ASD is particularly untethered, since nothing in the data identifies any subject's age, let alone a neonate.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None. Labels are Kaggle folder names on photographs of unknown origin. No clinical assessment, instrument, criterion, assessor, date or provenance record exists for a single image, and the paper does not acknowledge the issue at any point - including in its ethics statement, which cites the dataset's public availability as the reason no ethical review was required.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure, and none obtainable from photographs.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is to distinguish facial images of individuals with ASD from normal controls with an ensemble pipeline: Gabor filtering, MobileNetV2 feature extraction, an ensemble of LSTM, deep belief network and hybrid-kernel extreme learning machine, and Crested Porcupine Optimizer hyperparameter selection. Headline findings: average accuracy 96.43%, precision 96.44%, recall 96.43%, F-score 96.43% and G-measure 96.43% at 1,000 epochs, against literature-quoted comparators between 89.55% and 92.64%. The Gabor ablation - the paper's one genuinely executed experiment - gives 96.43% with filtering against 92.80% without, at less than half the training time.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No setting. Images were downloaded from Kaggle on 22 November 2024; the compute environment is not described at all, and the only timing information is an unlabelled training-time column (10.5 versus 26.0) in the Gabor ablation table.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: No task or paradigm. Static photographs with no stimulus, interaction or session. The construct is facial morphology and texture, justified by the premise that developmental problems affecting face features are often associated with fundamental brain disorders.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional. Ethics is handled by explicit exemption: the study did not involve direct experiments on humans or the use of human tissue samples, and publicly available Kaggle datasets were used instead. That reasoning treats identifiable photographs of children - carrying a disability label that no clinician assigned - as outside the scope of human-subjects consideration entirely. It is the clearest statement in the corpus of the assumption that makes this branch of the literature possible, and it is stated as a formal declaration rather than in passing.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: None for acquisition. Processing components named: Gabor filter bank, MTCNN face detection, median filter, Z-score colour normalisation, bicubic interpolation, MobileNetV2, LSTM, DBN built from restricted Boltzmann machines, hybrid-kernel ELM, Crested Porcupine Optimizer. No software, versions, seed, hardware or runtime environment is given, and the target image resolution is left as the literal placeholder (X, Y pixels).
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Very low. Some preprocessing choices are specified with real precision - rotation range -15 to 15 degrees, horizontal flips, random crops to 10%, brightness 0.8 to 1.2, inverse-frequency class weights, Z-score channel normalisation - and the source dataset is properly cited with an access date. Everything needed to actually rebuild the system is missing: no code, no libraries, no seed, no image size, no layer configuration, no ensemble combination rule, no CPO search space or budget, no split specification, and a stated sample size that the reported confusion matrices contradict.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: None. The article contains no limitations section, no threats-to-validity discussion, and no caveat of any kind. Nothing is said about the dataset's web provenance, the absence of diagnostic labels, the evaluation counts that span the whole dataset, the epoch-wise selection of the reported figure, or the fact that all comparator numbers are quoted rather than measured.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: None. There is no future-work section. The paper closes on the claim of superiority over existing methods.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: None. No behaviour is observed, elicited or measured. The target is static facial appearance - edges, contours and textures at multiple Gabor orientations and scales, described as capturing intricate details of face characteristics including the eyes, nose and mouth.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No fusion of modalities - a single image source. What the paper calls an ensemble is three classifiers (LSTM, DBN, HKELM) over one shared MobileNetV2 feature vector from one photograph. The LSTM's inclusion is unexplained: there is no temporal or sequential structure in a single still image for a recurrent model to exploit, and the paper never addresses this.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A four-stage pipeline: Gabor filtering, MobileNetV2 feature extraction, a heterogeneous ensemble of LSTM, deep belief network and hybrid-kernel extreme learning machine, and metaheuristic hyperparameter selection by the Crested Porcupine Optimizer. This is the corpus's most elaborate architecture stack applied to its simplest and least trustworthy data. Only one component's contribution is actually tested (Gabor filtering); the others are argued for in the conditional - removing MobileNetV2 may result in diminished performance, evaluating individual classifiers against the ensemble might reveal improvements - without those experiments being run.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Gabor-filtered RGB face crops at an unstated resolution, passed through MTCNN detection, median denoising and Z-score channel normalisation, then encoded as MobileNetV2 features. Augmentation adds rotation, horizontal flip, cropping and brightness variation, described as a preprocessing stage rather than as a training-time operation. Class weighting is applied on the stated grounds of imbalance, although the source Kaggle corpus is balanced by construction and the paper's own confusion matrices imply near-equal class sizes.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall, F-score and G-measure, per class and averaged, at 500 through 2,500 epochs; ROC curves described qualitatively; a Gabor ablation with training time and a computational-cost index whose units are not given. No specificity, no numeric AUC, no calibration, no predictive values at a stated prevalence, and no confidence interval anywhere. The reported average of 96.43% is not one measurement but the best of five epoch settings, carried into both the abstract and the comparison table against baselines evaluated under unknown conditions in other papers.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None of the trained model. The Gabor ablation shows that texture filtering helps (96.43% versus 92.80%) but says nothing about what the classifier attends to. No saliency, no attribution, no per-class error analysis beyond the raw confusion counts. In a study whose premise is that specific facial characteristics carry diagnostic information, no facial characteristic is ever identified.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The validation account is internally contradictory, and this is the study's central defect. The experimental section reports confusion matrices at five epoch settings whose correct-classification counts - 1,338 normal plus 1,362 autism at 1,000 epochs, and comparable figures at the other settings - account for essentially the entire stated dataset. No train-test division is described anywhere in that section. If those matrices are computed over all available images, then every reported metric is a resubstitution figure on the training data. Separately and much later, the comparison discussion asserts that 5-fold cross-validation was applied with 80% training and 20% testing per fold, and that the model consistently attained elevated accuracy and F1 scores across all folds, exhibiting minimal variance - yet not one per-fold number, mean or standard deviation is given, so the claim cannot be checked and does not reconcile with the confusion-matrix counts. On top of that: the reported headline is the best of five epoch settings with no selection criterion or held-out basis; the Crested Porcupine Optimizer searched hyperparameters against an unstated objective on an unstated partition; augmentation is described before any split; and the split, whatever it is, is at the image rather than the child level on a corpus known to repeat faces. The comparison in Table 3 sets this study's figure against seven baselines taken from other publications on unstated data and protocols, which is a comparison of numbers rather than of methods.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Autism spectrum disorder; ensemble learning; crested porcupine optimizer; facial images; computer-aided diagnosis. Four of five terms name the machinery; none names participants, validation or setting.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Computers, Materials & Continua 83(2) (Tech Science Press) - a broad-scope open-access computing journal covering materials, computing and engineering. This is the review's clearest venue-mismatch case: a diagnostic claim about children, resting on unlabelled web photographs and an explicit ethics exemption, published in a journal with no clinical review capacity, with no limitations section and no future work, in 81 days.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2025, published 16 April, 81 days from submission to acceptance. Framing is unqualified computer-aided diagnosis, with an unusual and revealing justification: early recognition is said to be significant to aid families and parents in superstition and denial, and AI is credited with aiding the treatment and reintegration of autistic patients. The contribution is expressed purely as a higher number than seven quoted baselines. There is no limitations section, no future work, and no acknowledgement that any part of the claim is provisional - the paper's closing position is that the method is superior, full stop.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Explainable and secure framework for autism prediction using multimodal eye tracking and kinematic data
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Almadhor A; Alasiry A; Alsubai S; Al Hejaili A; Kovac U; Abbas S
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed as a privacy-preserving diagnostic framework viable for healthcare applications involving sensitive data, with GDPR and HIPAA invoked in the abbreviation list. No clinical evaluation, threshold or deployment.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of a single small public dataset, reorganised into a simulated federated-learning experiment with three clients and three communication rounds; two local DNNs plus a global model, run with all features and with SHAP-selected features.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Internal only: all-features versus SHAP-selected features, across four feature subsets and three clients, for two local models and the global model. No external baseline is re-run.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None. An open-source movement dataset from Mendeley Data was downloaded. Its recruitment, setting, dates and inclusion criteria are not described, and the dataset is not cited by DOI or name in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Tabular feature vectors per instructional segment - 120 kinematic or 48 behavioural/eye features, MinMax scaled (or not, depending on which sentence is read).
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Saudi Arabia (Jouf University, King Khalid University, Prince Sattam bin Abdulaziz University, University of Tabuk), Slovakia (Comenius University Bratislava) and Pakistan (COMSATS University Islamabad). No data collection by the authors.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None described. Labels are the binary field of the downloaded dataset (1 autistic, 0 non-autistic). No instrument, criterion, assessor or date is given, and the source dataset's own diagnostic procedure is not summarised.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 22 individuals diagnosed with ASD
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Not reported. The introduction refers to both children and adults; the paper never states which the 44 examples are.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 44 examples. This is the entire empirical basis of the study.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 22 non-autistic individuals
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: 50% by construction (22 versus 22), never stated. On nine test cases the standard error of an accuracy estimate is about 17 percentage points, which is never acknowledged.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Two behavioural modalities from one archived dataset: kinematic/motion features (120 per instructional segment) and observational behavioural / eye-movement features (48 per instructional segment).
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Not described. The features are said to be recorded per instructional segment, but no task, stimulus, instruction set, session structure or duration is reported anywhere.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Not reported - no eye tracker, motion capture system or sensor is named, since the data were downloaded and the source acquisition is not summarised.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Very low. The dataset is neither cited nor linked; the preprocessing description contradicts itself on whether normalisation was applied; the client partition of the 44 examples is unstated; no split ratio, seed, layer configuration, learning rate, batch size or epoch count is given; code is available only on demand; and the reported headline accuracy differs between the abstract, the contributions list and the results section.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Contradictory. The methods describe an open-source dataset available via Mendeley Data, while the data-availability statement says the data supporting the findings are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. No accession, DOI or URL is given for the Mendeley record.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Stated as available from the authors on demand; not deposited.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Absent. The declarations contain funding, data and code availability, and a conflict-of-interest statement, but no ethics approval and no consent statement; the string ethic does not occur in the article. This is notable in a paper whose central claim concerns the ethical handling of sensitive health data.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Missing values and anomalies replaced by the class mean - that is, imputation using the outcome label, performed over the whole dataset. The text then states in one place that each feature is preserved in its original, continuous form without normalization and in another that MinMax scaling and normalisation were applied. Pearson correlation analysis was run to detect multicollinearity; it is referred to as Pearson Correlation Analysis (PCA).
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: None beyond selection. Four subsets of the archived features are used: K_General (generalised kinematic), K_Attention (attention-specific kinematic), L_General (generalised eye movement) and L_Attention (attention-specific eye movement, fixation and saccade). A second scenario replaces the full feature set with features ranked by SHAP values from an XGBoost model.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Not named beyond algorithm components: a shallow DNN with dense layers, ReLU and dropout; FedAvg aggregation; XGBoost with SHAP for feature selection; MinMaxScaler. No library, version, seed or hardware.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: None. No confidence intervals, no significance tests, no repeated runs.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: SHAP summary plots from an XGBoost surrogate rank feature importance, and the ranked features are then used to define the reduced-feature scenario. This is the paper's main methodological content, but no feature is ever named in the text, so the reader learns that explanation was performed without learning what it explained. The comparison of all-features against SHAP-selected features is genuinely informative in one respect: it shows the two scenarios disagreeing wildly and inconsistently across clients.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not described. Feature selection by SHAP was performed with an XGBoost model on the data before the federated experiments.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None. No demographic variables exist in the reported data.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Supervised deep learning in a simulated federated setting. Local Model 1 is a shallow DNN with dense layers and dropout for binary classification; Local Model 2 has five hidden layers with ReLU and dropout and is described as multi-class although the task is binary; outputs are aggregated by FedAvg into a global model.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Three clients, three communication rounds, two local models per client. Layer widths, dropout rates, learning rate, optimiser, batch size, epochs per round and the client data partition are all unspecified. The pseudocode gives only the round/client/model loop structure.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Not described as such. There is a train/test division mentioned in passing but no ratio, no seed, no cross-validation and no statement of how the 44 examples were distributed across the three clients. The test-set size is recoverable only from the confusion matrices, which contain nine cases (6 true negatives, 2 true positives, 1 false negative, 0 false positives for Model 1; 6 true negatives and 3 true positives for Model 2). Every accuracy in Tables 2-5 is a multiple of 1/9 (0.11, 0.22, 0.33, 0.44, 0.55, 0.66, 0.77, 0.88), confirming that each reported figure rests on nine test cases.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 per client, per feature subset, per local model and for the global model, in both scenarios; confusion matrices and training/validation accuracy and loss curves for the best configuration.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: The abstract reports the L_General dataset producing the best results, with Client 2 reaching accuracy 99.99% and Client 1 reaching 88%. The contributions list instead attributes 99.99% to Client 2 and 0.88 to Client 3. The results section reports Local Model 2, Client 2, L_General, all features achieving accuracy 1.00 and F1 1.00. Since the test set contains nine cases, 1.00 means nine of nine correct, and the 99.99% figure is that same result restated.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Movement kinematics during instructional segments, and eye-movement behaviour including fixation and saccade characteristics under general and attention-specific conditions.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: One paragraph, proposing integration of Physical Neural Networks based on stacked intelligent metasurfaces to process multimodal sensory data at the hardware level, reducing computational overhead and enhancing privacy. This is a hardware-research direction unconnected to any weakness of the present study.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: None concerning this study. The word limitations appears once, describing the strengths and limitations of methods reviewed in the related-work section. There is no limitations paragraph, and no acknowledgement of the sample size, the nine-case test sets, the class-mean imputation or the contradictory preprocessing description.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Forty-four examples in total - 22 individuals diagnosed with ASD and 22 non-autistic individuals - taken from an open-source movement dataset on Mendeley Data that is neither named nor cited. Nothing else is known about them: not their age band (the introduction discusses both children and adults without saying which these are), not their sex, not their recruitment, not the country, not the year. The 44 examples were divided among three simulated federated clients by an unstated rule, and each client's evaluation rests on nine test cases - a figure that appears nowhere in the text and is recoverable only from the confusion matrices (6 true negatives, 2 true positives, 1 false negative, 0 false positives) and from the fact that every accuracy in Tables 2 through 5 is a multiple of one ninth.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, individuals with ASD, autistic individuals, non-autistic individuals, ASD patients. The register is comparatively neutral for this corpus: the comparison group is called non-autistic rather than normal, autistic individuals is used alongside person-first phrasing, and the introduction notes that the spectrum makes each individual's experience unique. There is no autistic-community engagement and no discussion of how the people in the dataset were labelled or whether they knew their data would be reused.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: None. Not a single demographic characteristic is reported for the 44 people - no age, sex, ethnicity, geography, language or clinical background. This is a striking omission in a paper whose entire argument concerns the responsible, privacy-preserving handling of sensitive personal health data: the study invokes GDPR and HIPAA in its abbreviation table while reporting nothing at all about the individuals whose data it processes, and without asking whether they consented to this reuse.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not described. Labels come as a binary field in the downloaded dataset (1 autistic, 0 non-autistic). No diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor, setting or date is reported for either group, and the source dataset's own procedures are not summarised. The comparison group's non-autistic status is likewise asserted with no screening evidence.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No IQ, adaptive behaviour, language, severity or comorbidity measure of any kind.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is a secure, privacy-preserving ASD diagnostic framework combining multimodal kinematic and eye-movement data, deep neural networks, federated learning with FedAvg, and SHAP-based explanation, evaluated in two scenarios (all features versus SHAP-selected features) across three clients and three rounds. The reported headline is that L_General gives the best results with an accuracy of 99.99% and F1 of 99.99%, described as flawless classification performance. The substantive finding, once the tables are read, is different and more interesting: performance is wildly unstable. Across the four feature subsets and three clients, accuracies in the all-features scenario range from 0.01 to 0.88, and SHAP-based feature selection helps some client-subset combinations and badly hurts others (Client 2 on K_General rises from 0.22 to 0.66 while Client 2 on K_Attention falls from 0.55 to 0.33). The paper reports this variability but attributes it to data heterogeneity rather than to the estimator's variance at n=9.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: None described. No acquisition setting, no laboratory, no clinic, no country of origin for the data. The federated clients are simulated - the paper says they represent independent clients such as hospitals or personal devices, but all three run on the authors' own partition of one 44-row file, so no distributed data actually exists.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Not reported. Features are said to be extracted per instructional segment, and the eye-movement subsets are labelled General and Attention, but no task, stimulus, instruction, session length or protocol is described anywhere in the article. A reader cannot say what the participants were doing when the kinematic and gaze data were recorded.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis. Ethics reporting is absent - no approval, no consent, no exemption statement, and the word ethic does not appear in the article. This absence is the paper's most consequential internal contradiction: the entire contribution is framed as a privacy-and-security advance for sensitive health data, invoking GDPR and HIPAA, yet the study reuses identifiable behavioural recordings of 44 people without stating any ethical basis for doing so. Federated learning here protects data from a hypothetical future adversary while the actual governance question - whether these 44 people agreed to this - is never raised.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition instrumentation is named, because the data were downloaded and the source acquisition is not summarised. Computational components: a shallow DNN with dense layers, ReLU and dropout (Local Model 1), a five-hidden-layer DNN described as multi-class although the task is binary (Local Model 2), FedAvg aggregation, XGBoost with SHAP for feature ranking, MinMaxScaler. No library, version, seed, hardware or runtime.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Very low, and internally contradictory on a basic point. The preprocessing section states that each feature is preserved in its original, continuous form without normalization and then, one paragraph later, that the MinMax scaler was employed for scaling and the dataset normalised; the pseudocode also calls MinMaxScaler. The dataset is described as openly available on Mendeley but is given no name, DOI or URL, and the formal data-availability statement instead says the data are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. Code is available on demand only. No split ratio, no seed, no client partition rule, no layer widths, no learning rate, no epochs. The paper also refers to Pearson correlation analysis by the abbreviation PCA, which elsewhere denotes principal component analysis.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: None. There is no limitations section. Nothing is said about 44 examples being the entire dataset, about nine-case test sets, about accuracies quantised to multiples of one ninth, about class-mean imputation using the outcome label, about the contradictory normalisation account, about the absent ethics statement, or about the three federated clients being partitions of a single small file rather than independent institutions.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: A single paragraph proposing Physical Neural Networks based on stacked intelligent metasurfaces to process multimodal sensory data at the hardware level, reducing computational overhead and enhancing privacy through localised data handling. Computational overhead is not a difficulty encountered anywhere in a study that fits shallow networks to 44 rows, and the proposal addresses none of the study's actual weaknesses.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Movement kinematics and eye-movement behaviour, split into general and attention-specific variants: 120 kinematic features and 48 observational-behavioural features per instructional segment, with the attention-specific eye subset described as covering fixation and saccade characteristics. Because no task is described and no feature is ever named, the behavioural content of the study is opaque - the reader cannot identify a single behaviour that distinguishes the groups.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: This is one of the few charted studies with genuine cross-modal structure, and its fusion design is worth recording precisely. Two local models operate on separate files, one specialising in kinematic features and one in eye-movement features; their outputs are merged and passed to a global model with its own dense layers and dropout. That is late fusion at the model level, in contrast to the feature-concatenation fusion used elsewhere in the corpus. The design is sound in outline. What it cannot support is inference: with 44 examples divided among three clients and evaluated on nine cases, no comparison between the unimodal and fused configurations is distinguishable from noise, and the paper never makes that comparison explicitly in any case.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Supervised deep learning in a simulated federated architecture: two local DNNs per client (a shallow dense network for binary classification, and a five-hidden-layer network described as multi-class), three clients, three communication rounds, FedAvg aggregation into a global model. XGBoost with SHAP serves as a separate feature-ranking model. No classical baseline is fitted for comparison.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Tabular vectors of 120 kinematic or 48 behavioural/eye features per instructional segment, organised into four named subsets (K_General, K_Attention, L_General, L_Attention). Preprocessing includes one step that deserves separate note: missing values and anomalies were replaced with the mean value of each respective class - imputation conditioned on the outcome label, computed over the whole dataset before any split. Where a feature has missing values at different rates in the two groups, that step writes the label into the feature matrix directly, and it is a sufficient mechanism to produce a nine-of-nine result on its own.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1, reported per client, per feature subset, per local model and for the global model in both scenarios. No specificity, no AUC, no calibration, no predictive values and no confidence interval anywhere. The metric grid is dense and the reported values are internally revealing: they take only the values 0.11, 0.22, 0.33, 0.44, 0.55, 0.66, 0.77, 0.88 and 1.00, which are the achievable accuracies on nine test cases. The headline of 99.99% is that same 9/9 restated, and the paper describes it as flawless classification performance. One tabulated value, Client 3 on L_Attention at 0.01, is not a multiple of one ninth and is presumably a typographic corruption of 0.11.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: SHAP over an XGBoost surrogate produces a summary plot ranking feature importance, and the ranked features define the second experimental scenario. The intent is right and the framework is one of the review's few genuine attempts at explanation before rather than after modelling. Two things undercut it. First, no feature is ever named in the text, so the explanation is reported as an activity rather than a result and nothing can be learned about which movements or gaze behaviours matter. Second, SHAP values estimated from 44 rows are not stable quantities, and the all-features versus selected-features comparison bears this out - selection helps some client-subset combinations and severely harms others with no interpretable pattern, which the paper attributes to data heterogeneity rather than to sampling variance.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: This is the review's clearest case of a metric grid resting on almost nothing. The entire empirical base is 44 examples. Those are divided among three simulated federated clients by a rule that is never stated, and each client's reported accuracy is computed on nine test cases - a number that appears nowhere in the text and must be reconstructed from the confusion matrices (6+2+1+0 = 9; 6+3 = 9) and from the quantisation of every tabulated accuracy to multiples of one ninth. On nine cases the standard error of an accuracy estimate is roughly 17 percentage points, so the difference between the paper's best result (1.00, reported as 99.99%) and its worst (0.11) is barely more than sampling noise, and the four-subset by three-client by two-scenario by two-model grid amounts to dozens of comparisons among estimates that cannot be distinguished from each other. Three further problems compound it. Class-conditional mean imputation was applied across the full dataset, writing outcome information into the predictor matrix. SHAP-based feature selection was likewise performed on the whole dataset before the federated runs. And no split ratio, seed, cross-validation or repetition is reported, so none of the figures carries a variance estimate. Finally, the headline itself is unstable across the paper: the abstract credits 99.99% to Client 2 and 88% to Client 1, the contributions list credits 88% to Client 3, and the results section reports the best configuration as accuracy 1.00 - three descriptions of the same experiment. The framing of nine correct classifications out of nine as flawless classification performance and as high diagnostic accuracy suitable for healthcare applications is not supportable at any sample size this study has.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Multimodal data; Kinematic features; Eye movement; Federated learning; Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI); Security and privacy; Autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Seven terms, five of them naming machinery or infrastructure properties; the condition appears last and the participants not at all.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Complex & Intelligent Systems 11:173 (Springer) - a computational-intelligence journal. Relevant to the review's venue analysis in a specific way: this is a privacy-and-governance paper by construction, invoking GDPR and HIPAA, published without an ethics statement of any kind, and its headline accuracy of 99.99% on nine test cases passed review over 126 days.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2025, published online 19 February, 126 days from submission to acceptance. Framing is infrastructural rather than clinical - the contribution is offered as a viable solution for healthcare applications involving sensitive data that preserves privacy and security while maintaining high diagnostic accuracy. The claim of high diagnostic accuracy rests on nine test cases; the claim of privacy preservation rests on a federated architecture simulated over a single downloaded file; and the paper's own governance obligations - stating an ethical basis for reusing 44 people's behavioural recordings - go unmet. It is the corpus's clearest example of privacy engineering standing in for research ethics.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Facial Images Dataset for Early Screening of Autism Children Using Convolutional Neural Network
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Zainal Z; Melinda M; Away Y; Mawarpury M
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: 2025 10th International Conference on Computer and Communi
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed as paving the way for facial recognition technology in clinical contexts and automated detection systems usable in daily diagnostic practice. No clinician, threshold or prospective evaluation.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Prospective two-site primary data collection (posed facial photography) followed by supervised binary image classification with a single 70/20/10 image-level split.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: None re-run. Prior figures are quoted from the literature: VGG-19 and ShuffleNet at 88%, MobileNet at 87% test accuracy, ResNet-50 at 90% and 89.2% on thermal images, ResNet-18 at 81.4%, VGG16 at 87% test accuracy on a Pakistani autism-centre dataset, ResNet50 transfer learning at 92%.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: School-based. Children were called individually and photographed in a dedicated 2x2 m studio area within a 7x7 m room. Autistic participants were photographed before undergoing physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy; typically developing participants were recruited in the same manner.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: 224x224 RGB face crops at 1:1 aspect ratio.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Indonesia - Banda Aceh. Autistic participants recruited at a Special Elementary School, typically developing participants at a State Elementary School; analysis at Universitas Syiah Kuala.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None described. Group membership follows school placement - autistic children from a Special Elementary School, comparison children from a State Elementary School. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or record is reported, and the typically developing children were not screened.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 35 children with autism, 525 images
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not measured. Intellectual disability was an exclusion criterion for the autistic group but no cognitive measure is reported for anyone.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Contradictory. The narrative states 3 to 14 years; Table I states 5 to 15 years; the later methods text states 5 to 15. No mean, SD or per-group distribution.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Handled by exclusion rather than measurement. Children with colds, diarrhoea, lung infections, epilepsy or flu were excluded from both groups, and autistic participants with intellectual disability, cerebral palsy or Down syndrome were also excluded.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 70 children, yielding 1,050 photographs (15 per child).
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 35 typically developing children, 525 images
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No. Single session per child.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Parental written consent obtained; teacher accompaniment during sessions. No statement about consent for publication of the children's images, although sample face photographs are reproduced in Figures 3 and 6.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: 50% by construction (51 versus 51 test images), never stated.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Two-dimensional colour facial photographs.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Posed expression photography. The child sits one metre from the camera, facing a projection screen or prototype smart device; the room is surrounded by black curtains, sessions run from 09:00 to 12:00, and an acclimation period precedes capture. A 17-inch LCD screen and speakers are listed as present for video viewing, but no video content or viewing task is described.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Canon EOS M-100 digital camera with 256 GB storage on a tripod; ISO 800, aperture f/5.6, exposure 1/25 s; images captured at 6000x4000 and cropped to 1:1. Room lighting stated as 30 W in the narrative and 22 W in Table I. Temperature 25-27 degrees C; humidity 40-45% in the narrative and 50-60% in Table I; acclimation 10-15 minutes in the narrative and 3 minutes in Table I.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Split. The data acquisition protocol is among the most completely specified in the entire corpus - room dimensions, temperature, humidity, lighting wattage, acclimation time, session hours, camera model, ISO, aperture, exposure, capture resolution, subject distance, curtain arrangement, expression set and photograph counts - and the augmentation configuration is printed verbatim. The modelling is the opposite: no architecture, no optimiser, no learning rate, no batch size, no epoch count, no seed, no code, no dataset deposit. Several acquisition parameters also conflict between the narrative and Table I (age 3-14 versus 5-15, humidity 40-45% versus 50-60%, lighting 30 W versus 22 W, acclimation 10-15 minutes versus 3 minutes).
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not stated. The dataset is presented as the study's contribution but no deposit, licence or access route is given.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not available. Only the augmentation configuration is printed.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Yes, with a code number: 036/EA/FK/2025 (Faculty of Medicine). Parents signed a consent form (rendered as a concern form in the text) before data collection, and children were accompanied by their teachers during collection.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Resize to 224x224; noise removal and contrast enhancement (methods unspecified); rescale to [0,1]; augmentation by rotation up to 20 degrees, width and height shifts up to 0.2, shear 0.2, zoom 0.2 and horizontal flip. The paper states candidly that the study does not record the total number of augmentations applied in the code.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: End-to-end CNN; no hand-crafted features.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Keras/TensorFlow implied by the ImageDataGenerator augmentation code in Table II. No framework version, no seed, no hardware.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: None. No confidence interval on any figure; on 102 test images the 95% interval around 0.90 spans roughly 0.83 to 0.95.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None. No saliency, attribution, per-expression breakdown or error analysis beyond the confusion-matrix counts. The three collected expressions would have supported a natural interpretability analysis and are explicitly set aside.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not described. Training and validation accuracy are said to reach nearly 100% within the first few epochs with loss stabilising near zero, described as optimal and stable performance without signs of overfitting - although the held-out test accuracy is 90%.
