data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None - not by expression, age or sex, none of which is available in analysable form.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Convolutional neural network with a sigmoid output. The architecture is never specified - no layer count, filter sizes, pooling scheme, dense layer widths, optimiser, learning rate, batch size or epoch count appears anywhere, despite the introduction promising the design of custom layers as a contribution.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Only that CNNs use convolutional, pooling and fully connected layers, and that the final activation is sigmoid. The paper notes that because sigmoid is used, the output probabilities are independent and do not sum to one - a remark that makes no sense for a two-class single-output model.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A single 70/20/10 split at the image level: 369 training, 105 validation and 51 test images per class. Because every child contributes exactly 15 photographs and there are only 70 children, an image-level split cannot separate participants - the same child's flat, smiling and sad photographs, taken minutes apart in identical lighting at a fixed one-metre distance, are distributed across training, validation and test. Augmentation is applied to the training generator, which is correct; no cross-validation, no repetition, no seed.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and a confusion matrix; sensitivity and specificity are defined by formula but specificity is never reported as a number.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Accuracy 0.90, precision 0.92, recall 0.88, F1 0.90 on 102 test images. The confusion matrix gives 47 and 45 correct with 4 false positives and 6 false negatives, which reconciles exactly with the reported metrics (92/102 = 0.902; 47/51 = 0.922; 47/53 = 0.887).
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Posed facial expression. Each child was instructed to produce three expressions - flat/neutral, smiling and sad - with five photographs of each. The paper states explicitly that the analysis focuses solely on the final Normal versus Autism classification without independently assessing the individual expressions, so the expression manipulation is collected but never used as a variable.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: One sentence: explore augmentation technologies to generate larger and more diverse datasets, plus unspecified additional techniques.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: None. There is no limitations section and no caveat, apart from the incidental admission that the number of augmentations applied was not recorded.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Seventy children in two recruited groups: 35 with autism from a Special Elementary School in Banda Aceh and 35 typically developing children from a State Elementary School in the same city. Each contributed 15 photographs (three expressions x five shots), giving 1,050 images split evenly 525/525. The analysis unit throughout is the image, not the child: the 70/20/10 division yields 369/105/51 images per class, and the reported metrics rest on 102 test images drawn from the same 70 children who supplied the training images. This is genuine primary data collection with a real, separately recruited comparison group - which distinguishes it sharply from the twelve Kaggle-corpus reuses charted in this review - but the group difference is confounded with school of origin, since every autistic child comes from one institution and every comparison child from another.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with autism, autistic children, autistic condition, typically developing children, normal children, Normal class. The Normal/Autism class labelling runs throughout including in the figures and conclusion. One artefact of manuscript reuse is worth recording: the description of the testing workflow states that the output classifies the child as either a stunted child (label 1) or a normal child (label 0) - terminology from childhood stunting research that has no place in an autism study and that survived into the published text.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Thin, and internally inconsistent where present. Age is given as 3 to 14 years in the acquisition narrative and 5 to 15 years in Table I and again in the results; no mean, SD or per-group distribution is provided. Sex is not reported at all. No socioeconomic, ethnic, linguistic or verbal-ability information. The exclusion criteria are unusually explicit for this corpus - children with colds, diarrhoea, lung infections, epilepsy or flu were excluded from both groups, and autistic participants with intellectual disability, cerebral palsy or Down syndrome were excluded - which controls the sample tightly but also removes the co-occurring conditions most likely to be present in a real screening population and narrows the autistic group to those without intellectual disability.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None. Group membership is determined by school: the autism group is the set of children attending a Special Elementary School, the comparison group the set attending a State Elementary School. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor, date or record is reported for a single child, and the typically developing children were not screened with any instrument. The study's exclusion of intellectual disability, cerebral palsy and Down syndrome implies some clinical information was available, but its source is never described. School placement is a proxy for diagnosis that also carries administrative, geographic and socioeconomic structure into the label.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No IQ, developmental, adaptive or language measure, and no autism severity instrument. Intellectual disability appears only as an exclusion criterion.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is to address the limited variation and representativeness of existing autism facial-image datasets by building a new dataset with broader variation in facial characteristics, lighting and social context, and to refine a CNN classifier on it. Headline findings: accuracy 0.90, precision 0.92, recall 0.88, F1 0.90 on 102 test images, with 47 and 45 correct classifications against 4 false positives and 6 false negatives. The conclusion attributes the result principally to the choice of a 1:1 aspect ratio and 224x224 image size, which is a claim about preprocessing conventions rather than about autism.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Reported in more detail than any other study in this corpus. A 7x7 m room with a 2x2 m capture area, black curtains over the windows, air conditioning at 25-27 degrees C, controlled humidity, fixed room lighting, sessions restricted to 09:00-12:00 to limit lighting and temperature variation, a fixed one-metre subject-to-camera distance, a tripod-mounted camera, and a stated acclimation period before capture. The two groups were photographed at different institutions, however - a special school and a state school - and the paper does not report whether the studio setup was physically identical at both sites or whether the same operator ran both. Given how completely the acquisition is otherwise specified, this is the one variable that matters most and is left open.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Posed expression photography: each child produced flat, smiling and sad expressions on instruction, five photographs each. The paper states outright that the process focuses solely on the final classification between Normal and Autism without independently assessing the individual expressions. That is a striking design decision - the expression manipulation is the only behavioural content in the study, it was deliberately elicited, and it is then discarded as a variable. A per-expression analysis would have distinguished a model reading facial morphology from one reading expression production, which is precisely the question the design was built to answer.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session. Ethics reporting is solid: an ethics code number is given (036/EA/FK/2025, Faculty of Medicine), parents signed a consent form before collection, and children were accompanied by their teachers throughout - a safeguarding measure that no other study in this corpus mentions. What is missing is consent for publication of images, since sample photographs of identifiable children appear in Figures 3 and 6, and any statement about the dataset's future distribution, even though building a shareable dataset is presented as the study's primary contribution.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Canon EOS M-100 on a tripod, 256 GB storage, ISO 800, f/5.6, 1/25 s, 6000x4000 capture cropped to 1:1 and resized to 224x224. Room instrumentation includes a 17-inch LCD screen and speakers, listed for video viewing although no video task is described. Analysis software is not named; only the Keras ImageDataGenerator augmentation block is printed. Several environmental parameters conflict between the narrative and Table I: lighting 30 W versus 22 W, humidity 40-45% versus 50-60%, acclimation 10-15 minutes versus 3 minutes.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: The most sharply divided reproducibility profile in the corpus. The data side is exemplary: room dimensions, temperature, humidity, lighting, session hours, camera body, ISO, aperture, exposure, capture and output resolution, subject distance, curtain arrangement, expression protocol, per-child photograph counts and the verbatim augmentation configuration are all published, so another laboratory could recreate the acquisition closely. The model side is empty: no architecture, no layer specification, no optimiser, no learning rate, no batch size, no epoch count, no seed, no code, and no deposit for the dataset that the paper exists to introduce. The internal contradictions between narrative and Table I further undercut the acquisition detail, and the survival of stunted child in the workflow description indicates text carried over from an unrelated manuscript.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: None stated. There is no limitations section. The image-level split across 15 photographs per child, the school-based group assignment standing in for diagnosis, the confounding of group with institution, the absence of any per-expression analysis, and the 102-image test set all pass without comment. The one candid admission is incidental: the study does not record the total number of augmentations applied in the code.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: A single sentence proposing augmentation technologies to generate larger and more diverse datasets, plus unspecified additional techniques. Given that the study's own contribution is a dataset built to address representativeness, proposing synthetic augmentation as the route to further diversity moves away from the recruitment-based solution the paper has just demonstrated.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Posed facial expression - flat, smiling and sad - and, implicitly, static facial appearance. Because expressions are pooled before classification, the study cannot say whether the model distinguishes groups by how the children produce expressions or by how their faces look, and the paper does not raise the distinction.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No multimodal fusion - a single photographic modality. The introduction reviews thermal-imaging work at length (ResNet-50 on facial skin temperature across emotional states) and a thermal branch would have been a natural pairing with this acquisition setup, given that the protocol already controls room temperature and includes a body-temperature acclimation period. Only RGB photographs are collected.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A convolutional neural network with a sigmoid output, trained end to end. The architecture is never described. The introduction promises the design of custom layers to optimise detection of ASD-specific visual characteristics, and no custom layer, or indeed any layer, is ever specified. Prior architectures (VGG-19, ShuffleNet, MobileNet, ResNet-18/34/50, AlexNet, VGG16) are discussed only as literature figures.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: 224x224 RGB face crops at 1:1 aspect ratio, rescaled to [0,1], with training-time augmentation by rotation to 20 degrees, width and height shifts to 0.2, shear 0.2, zoom 0.2 and horizontal flip. Noise removal and contrast enhancement are mentioned without method. The conclusion treats the 1:1 ratio and 224x224 size as the study's principal finding, which places a preprocessing convention where an empirical result should be.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and a confusion matrix, with sensitivity and specificity defined by formula but specificity never reported numerically. The reported figures reconcile exactly with the confusion-matrix cells - 92 of 102 correct gives 0.902; 47 of 51 predicted-positive gives 0.922; 47 of 53 actual-positive gives 0.887 - which is a level of internal consistency several other studies in this corpus fail to achieve. What is absent is any interval: with 102 test images the 95% confidence interval around 0.90 runs from roughly 0.83 to 0.95, so the comparison against the quoted literature figures of 87%, 88%, 89.2%, 90% and 92% is not discriminating. The abstract also describes the evaluation as using a nuisance matrix.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No saliency, attribution or ablation, and no per-expression error breakdown despite expression being a designed factor. In a study whose premise is that specific facial characteristics reflect social and emotional traits relevant to autism, no facial characteristic is identified anywhere.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: A single 70/20/10 division at the image level - 369, 105 and 51 images per class - applied to 1,050 photographs from 70 children at exactly 15 photographs each. Participant separation is therefore impossible: five near-identical shots of the same child pulling the same expression, taken minutes apart under fixed lighting at a fixed one-metre distance with the same camera settings, are distributed across training, validation and test. This is the same frame-level leakage documented across the video, EEG-epoch, thermal, cry and facial-image branches of this review, and it is the study's decisive methodological failure - the more so because the acquisition protocol is so tightly controlled that the only systematic variation left between images of different children is the children themselves. Three further points. The split is unrepeated and unseeded, with no cross-validation and no interval on any figure. Training and validation accuracy are reported as reaching nearly 100% within the first few epochs with loss near zero, described as optimal and stable performance without signs of overfitting, while held-out accuracy is 90% - a gap the paper reads as success rather than as evidence about the split. And group membership is perfectly confounded with institution, since all autistic children were photographed at a special school and all comparison children at a state school, so any residual site difference in setup, operator or child preparation is available to the classifier. What would have rescued the design is available and unused: with 70 children, a participant-level split holding out, say, 7 autistic and 7 typically developing children entirely would have cost nothing and produced an interpretable, if less impressive, number.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: ASD; Normal; CNN; Confusion Matrix; Dataset. Five terms, two of which name an evaluation artefact and a data structure rather than a subject; Normal appears as a keyword in its own right.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: 2025 10th International Conference on Computer and Communication Engineering (ICCCE), IEEE, pages 351-355. A short engineering conference paper. The venue explains but does not excuse the asymmetry between a fully specified acquisition protocol and a completely unspecified model, and the survival of unrelated stunting terminology in the workflow description.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2025 IEEE conference proceedings. Framing is optimistic but hedged more than most: the study is said to pave the way for further application of facial recognition technology in clinical contexts and the potential development of automated detection systems that can be used in daily diagnostic practice. The novelty claim is placed on the dataset rather than on the accuracy - the paper's stated purpose is to remedy the poor representativeness of existing autism face datasets, and it does so by actually recruiting and photographing 70 children under a controlled protocol rather than by downloading images. That is a real contribution to a branch of this literature that has otherwise recycled the same web-scraped corpus twelve times over.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Improving Early Autism Detection with Chi-Square Feature Selection, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Abu-Errub A
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Described as confirming suitability for reliable clinical screening applications and as a practical tool for early screening; no clinician evaluation or prospective test.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of a single public tabular dataset; six classifiers compared with and without chi-square feature selection, tuned by Bayesian optimisation, evaluated on a 70/10/20 stratified split with SHAP explanation of the best model.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Internal: six classifiers, each with all features and with chi-square-selected features. External: literature-quoted figures only - LR 97.15%, SVM 97.82%, RF 93.69% - none re-run on this dataset.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None. The ASD Toddler dataset (Thabtah) was obtained from Kaggle. Its own recruitment, setting, dates and respondent characteristics are not summarised.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A short tabular row per toddler: ten binary Q-CHAT-10 items plus demographic and history variables, min-max scaled.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Jordan - Department of Computer Science, Faculty of Information Technology, Jadara University, Irbid. Single author. No data collection.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None. The outcome variable is Class/ASD_Traits, the Q-CHAT-10 screening outcome, not a clinical diagnosis. The paper nonetheless states that 735 cases were diagnosed with ASD. No instrument beyond Q-CHAT-10, no clinician, no criterion and no assessor exists for any case.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 735 cases labelled ASD (69.7%)
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not available in the dataset and not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: 12 to 36 months, per the dataset's scope. No mean, SD or distribution is reported.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Sex is present as a variable and appears in the SHAP analysis as a low-importance feature, but no counts or proportions are reported.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported. Jaundice at birth and family history of ASD are present as binary covariates.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 1,054 cases originally; expanded to 1,456 instances after SVM-SMOTE oversampling. The 402 additional instances are synthetic.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None, and identified as a limitation.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 319 cases labelled non-ASD (30.3%)
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: After SMOTE balancing the test set is 148 versus 144, so chance is 50.7%. In the original data the prevalence is 69.7% ASD, so a majority-class classifier would score 69.7% - neither baseline is stated.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Questionnaire - ten binary Q-CHAT-10 behavioural items plus seven demographic and history variables (sex, ethnicity, jaundice, family member with ASD, region, who completed the test, age).
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. A ten-item caregiver checklist; no observation, stimulus or session.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None. Tabular data only.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Moderate, and the best in the questionnaire branch. The dataset is public and cited, the preprocessing pipeline is described step by step in order, the split proportions and test-set composition are given, and Table I reports every tuned hyperparameter for all six classifiers to four significant figures. Missing: code, seed, library versions, the number of features retained by chi-square selection, the identity of the selected features, and any statement of whether feature selection was performed inside or outside the split.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Source dataset cited as available on Kaggle; no derived splits, synthetic instances or code shared.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not stated. The word ethical appears once, in the XAI discussion, listing ethical compliance among the reasons interpretability matters in healthcare. There is no ethics or consent statement for the study itself.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Removal of noisy or irrelevant records; label encoding of Sex, Jaundice, Ethnicity, Region, Family_mem_with_ASD and Class/ASD_Traits; MinMax scaling to [0,1]; SVM-SMOTE oversampling of the minority class to produce 1,456 instances. The class label itself is listed among the variables that were label-encoded, which is unremarkable in itself but underlines that Class/ASD_Traits is treated as one categorical column among others.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Chi-square ranking of each attribute against the class label, used to select a reduced feature subset. The number of features retained is never stated.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Not named. Components identifiable from the text: scikit-learn estimators (LGBM, ExtraTrees, DecisionTree, KNN, SVM, MLP), MinMaxScaler, SVM-SMOTE (imbalanced-learn), chi-square selection, Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation, SHAP. No versions, no seed, no hardware.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: None. No confidence intervals, no repeated splits, no variance across cross-validation folds.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: SHAP beeswarm and bar plots for the SVM with chi-square selection, reported as showing that joint attention (does your child follow where you are looking), use of simple gestures and empathy-related behaviours dominate, while sex and jaundice contribute minimally. The analysis is properly executed and clearly presented; its interpretive value is limited by the fact that the highlighted features are Q-CHAT-10 items and the label is the Q-CHAT-10 outcome, so their dominance is arithmetic rather than clinical.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Bayesian optimisation with cross-validation restricted to the training data; the validation split used for model selection. Correctly done and clearly described.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None. Ethnicity and region are present as variables but no performance is stratified by them.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Classical machine learning: LightGBM, Extra Trees, Decision Tree, K-Nearest Neighbours, Support Vector Machine (RBF) and Multi-Layer Perceptron.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Fully reported in Table I, which is a genuine strength. LGBM: gbdt, max_depth 10, 100 estimators, min_child_samples 100, num_leaves 127, subsample 0.7. ET: max_depth 16, min_samples_split 2, 184 estimators. DT: gini, max_depth 10, min_samples_leaf 1, min_samples_split 6, best splitter. KNN: Manhattan, k=4, distance weighting. SVM: RBF, C=635.234, gamma scale. MLP: ReLU, alpha 0.0002816, adaptive learning rate, 4 hidden layers of 148 neurons, Adam.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A stratified 70/10/20 split of the SMOTE-expanded 1,456 instances, giving a 292-case test set (148 ASD, 144 non-ASD), with Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation cross-validated inside the training portion and the test set held out for final reporting. The design is described with unusual care - the author explicitly anticipates the overfitting objection and lists four mitigations. The decisive flaw is nonetheless in the ordering: SVM-SMOTE was applied to the whole dataset before partitioning, so synthetic instances interpolated from cases that ended up in the test set were placed in the training set and vice versa.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and log loss for all twelve model-feature-set configurations, plus a confusion matrix and SHAP beeswarm and bar plots for the best model. The inclusion of log loss is notable - it is the only calibration-sensitive measure reported by any study charted in this review to date.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: SVM achieved accuracy, precision, recall and F1 of 1.000 both with all features and with chi-square-selected features, with log loss falling from 0.011 to 0.008; on the 292-case test set all 148 ASD and all 144 non-ASD instances were classified correctly, giving zero false positives and zero false negatives, described as 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity. MLP reached 0.997, ET 0.990, LGBM 0.980, KNN 0.973 and DT 0.969 after selection.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Parent-reported early social-communication behaviours: joint attention and gaze following, use of simple gestures, empathy-related behaviours (comforting a distressed person), response to name, eye contact, pretend play, early speech and repetitive staring.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: External validation on larger and more heterogeneous cohorts; integration of additional modalities (genetic, neuroimaging).
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Yes, a short but substantive paragraph: results rest on a single publicly available dataset that may not capture the full diversity of ASD presentations across populations and cultural contexts; real-world deployment would require external validation on larger and more heterogeneous cohorts; and additional modalities such as genetic or neuroimaging data might further improve accuracy. The circular label, the pre-split SMOTE and the 100% result itself are not questioned.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: No groups were recruited. The unit is the questionnaire record: 1,054 cases from the public ASD Toddler dataset (Thabtah, via Kaggle), of which 735 are labelled ASD and 319 non-ASD - a 69.7% positive rate. SVM-SMOTE then expanded the set to 1,456 instances, meaning 402 of the rows subsequently modelled and evaluated are synthetic interpolations rather than children. The 292-case test set (148 ASD, 144 non-ASD) therefore contains an unstated number of synthetic records, and the number of real children behind the reported 100% is never given.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, non-ASD, toddlers, children, ASD presentations. Register is clinical and restrained; the comparison class is called non-ASD rather than normal, and the limitations paragraph shows unusual awareness that ASD presentations vary across populations and cultural contexts. One phrase runs against this: the introduction describes ASD as a complex neuro-developmental abnormality. No autistic or community perspective is cited.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Almost none reported, though several demographic variables are present in the data and used as predictors. Age is given only as the dataset's 12-36 month scope. Sex, ethnicity and region exist as columns - sex and jaundice are named in the SHAP analysis as low-importance features - but no counts, proportions or distributions are printed for any of them, and no subgroup breakdown is performed. Ethnicity and region are label-encoded into ordinal integers, a transformation that imposes an arbitrary ordering on nominal categories and is not discussed.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None. The outcome is Class/ASD_Traits, the Q-CHAT-10 screening result, and no clinical diagnosis exists for any case. The paper describes this as 735 cases diagnosed with ASD, which overstates what the dataset contains: the ASD label here records that a caregiver's ten checklist answers summed above a cut-off, not that a clinician assessed the child. No assessor, criterion, instrument beyond Q-CHAT-10 or date is reported.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, developmental, adaptive, language or severity measure is available in the dataset or reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is to improve early ASD detection for toddlers aged 12-36 months by combining chi-square feature selection with six machine learning classifiers, SVM-SMOTE balancing, Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation and SHAP explanation, claimed as the first study to combine all four. Headline findings: chi-square selection improved every classifier (DT 0.938 to 0.969, KNN 0.959 to 0.973, LGBM 0.976 to 0.980, ET 0.986 to 0.990, MLP 0.993 to 0.997), and SVM reached 1.000 on accuracy, precision, recall and F1 both before and after selection, with all 292 test cases classified correctly - zero false positives and zero false negatives, reported as 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity and as confirming suitability for reliable clinical screening applications.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting. A single-author secondary analysis of a downloaded file; no computing environment or runtime is described.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: No task or paradigm. The instrument is the ten-item Q-CHAT-10 caregiver checklist, completed retrospectively about a toddler; the paper does not reproduce the items but names three of them via the SHAP results.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis. There is no ethics or consent statement for this study. The single occurrence of the word ethical is in the XAI section, which argues that interpretability is needed in healthcare for clinical adoption, risk reduction, ethical compliance, informed consent and patient engagement - the paper names informed consent as a value that explainable AI supports, while providing no consent or governance statement for its own reuse of 1,054 toddlers' screening records.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: None for acquisition. Analytical components: label encoding, MinMaxScaler, SVM-SMOTE, chi-square selection, six scikit-learn-family classifiers, Bayesian optimisation and SHAP. No library, version, seed, hardware or runtime is reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: The strongest reporting in this review's questionnaire branch, with one structural gap. The dataset is public and cited; the preprocessing sequence is given step by step in order; the split proportions and the exact test-set composition (292 cases: 148 ASD, 144 non-ASD) are stated; and Table I lists every tuned hyperparameter for all six classifiers to four significant figures, including C = 635.2340 and alpha = 0.0002816. Against that: no code, no seed, no versions, and - most consequentially - the number of features chi-square retained is never given, the selected features are never listed, and whether selection was fitted inside or outside the split is never stated. The paper's headline claim concerns the effect of feature selection, and the reader cannot determine how many or which features that selection produced.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: A real limitations paragraph, and better than most: the results rest on a single public dataset which may not capture the full diversity of ASD presentations across populations and cultural contexts, real-world deployment would require external validation on larger and more heterogeneous cohorts, and additional modalities such as genetic or neuroimaging data could be integrated. What it does not question is the result itself. A model that classifies 292 consecutive cases without a single error is treated as an achievement to be explained by good feature selection rather than as a signal that the target is recoverable from the inputs by construction. Also unmentioned: that SMOTE preceded the split, that the label is the Q-CHAT-10 outcome rather than a diagnosis, and that a fifth of the evaluated instances are synthetic.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: External validation on larger and more heterogeneous cohorts, and integration of genetic or neuroimaging modalities. The first directly addresses the stated limitation; the second proposes adding expensive modalities to a pipeline whose reported ceiling is already 100%, which is the characteristic move of this literature - scaling up inputs rather than questioning the estimand.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Parent-reported early social-communication behaviours drawn from Q-CHAT-10. The SHAP analysis names three specifically: joint attention (does your child follow where you are looking), use of simple gestures, and empathy-related behaviours. These are clinically sensible early markers, and the paper notes correctly that they correspond to established clinical markers - but their prominence in the model is a property of how the label was constructed, not independent evidence about them.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No fusion - a single questionnaire modality plus static demographic covariates. Multimodal extension with genetic and neuroimaging data is proposed as future work only.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Six classical supervised learners - LightGBM, Extra Trees, Decision Tree, KNN, RBF-kernel SVM and a four-layer MLP - each evaluated with the full feature set and with a chi-square-selected subset, all tuned by Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation with cross-validation inside the training data. No deep learning on raw signals; no ensemble of the six.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A tabular row per toddler: ten binary Q-CHAT-10 items plus sex, ethnicity, jaundice, family history, region, respondent and age, label-encoded and min-max scaled. Two features of this representation matter. First, the ten items are the constituents of the Q-CHAT-10 score whose threshold defines the label, so the predictor set arithmetically determines the outcome - the same structure as local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 (which reach 100% on six metrics) and the inverse of local_8ff20c48 (which deleted five of the ten items and consequently fell to 0.83). Second, ethnicity and region are nominal categories converted to ordered integers by label encoding, imposing an artificial ordering that the paper does not remark on.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and log loss for all twelve configurations, plus a confusion matrix and SHAP plots for the best model. The log loss column deserves credit: it is the only calibration-sensitive measure reported by any study charted in this review, and it does real work here - Decision Tree posts 0.938 accuracy with a log loss of 2.223, exposing badly miscalibrated probabilities that accuracy alone would hide. Against that, no confidence interval accompanies any figure, and neither baseline is stated (50.7% on the balanced test set, 69.7% majority-class on the original data). The F1 score is also described as the geometric mean of precision and recall, when it is the harmonic mean.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: SHAP beeswarm and bar plots for the SVM with chi-square selection, showing joint attention, simple gestures and empathy-related behaviours as the dominant predictors and sex and jaundice as negligible. This is properly executed explainability, presented as evidence of clinical trustworthiness on the grounds that the model's important features align with established clinical markers. The alignment is real but uninformative: the label is a threshold on the sum of exactly those items, so any model that recovers the label must weight them heavily, and any model that recovered the label from sex or jaundice instead would be the anomaly. SHAP here confirms that the pipeline learned the arithmetic it was given, and the paper reads that confirmation as external validation of the behavioural markers.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The validation section is, in most respects, the most carefully constructed in this review's questionnaire branch. A stratified 70/10/20 split is used, the roles of the three partitions are stated explicitly (fitting, hyperparameter tuning and model selection, final reporting), Bayesian optimisation is cross-validated inside the training data only, the test set is described as never used during training or tuning, and the author pre-empts the overfitting objection directly, listing four mitigations. Two problems defeat all of that care. The first is ordering: SVM-SMOTE was applied to the whole 1,054-case dataset before partitioning, expanding it to 1,456 instances, and only then was the balanced dataset randomly partitioned. Synthetic minority instances are interpolations between real minority cases, so synthetic rows in the training set are constructed from real rows that ended up in the test set, and synthetic rows in the test set are constructed from real training rows. The hold-out is therefore not independent, and this alone can produce near-perfect minority-class recall. The second is the estimand: the label Class/ASD_Traits is the Q-CHAT-10 outcome, a deterministic threshold on the sum of ten items that are supplied as features. No split scheme can make the reconstruction of that threshold into a diagnostic accuracy. Together these explain a result that the paper instead attributes to methodological quality - 292 of 292 test cases correct, zero false positives and zero false negatives, reported as 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity and as confirming suitability for reliable clinical screening. The external comparison in Table III compounds this by ranking the 100% against literature figures of 97.15%, 97.82% and 93.69% from other datasets and protocols, presenting the gap as a methodological advance.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD); chi-square feature selection; machine learning; explainable AI. Four terms, three naming technique. Neither the instrument (Q-CHAT-10) nor the population (toddlers) appears, despite both being central.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Engineering, Technology & Applied Science Research 15(5):27954-27959 - an open-access general engineering journal. A 100% diagnostic accuracy claim, a hold-out contaminated by pre-split synthetic oversampling, and a label that is a threshold on its own predictors passed review there in 48 days including a revision round.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2025, accepted 14 August, 48 days from submission. Framing is screening-tool improvement rather than diagnostic replacement, and is comparatively measured: integrating robust feature selection with explainable ML models can significantly advance the reliability of early ASD screening tools. The overreach is concentrated in one sentence - that 100% sensitivity and specificity confirm the model's suitability for reliable clinical screening applications - and in a comparison table that ranks the perfect score above three published figures from unrelated datasets. The paper's genuine contributions are its hyperparameter transparency, its inclusion of log loss, and a limitations paragraph that correctly identifies single-dataset dependence.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Novel Framework for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification and Tailored Education With Effective Data Mining and Ensemble Learning Techniques
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Hajjej F; Ayouni S; Alohali MA; Maddeh M
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Phase II is framed as directly actionable: the results are said to be valuable for educators and professionals working with children with ASD, helping them make informed decisions about teaching methods that can have a significant impact on the children's learning and development.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of two merged public tabular screening datasets; two phases of supervised classification (ASD traits, then teaching method), with SMOTE balancing, three feature-selection techniques, seven classifiers plus a voting ensemble, an 80:20 split and 10-fold cross-validation.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Internal: seven classifiers against the RF-XG ensemble, across four feature conditions. External: literature-quoted accuracies of 98.77%, 97.82%, 99.25% and 99.85%, none re-run.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None by the authors. Dataset 1: the ASD Toddler dataset from Kaggle (fabdelja/autism-screening-for-toddlers), 1,054 instances and 17 columns. Dataset 2: ASD screening data for toddlers aged 12-36 months in Saudi Arabia, gathered through an online questionnaire. Neither source's recruitment procedure, sampling frame or response rate is described.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A tabular row per toddler: ten binary Q-CHAT-10 items plus demographic and history variables.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Saudi Arabia - Princess Nourah bint Abdulrahman University and King Saud University, Riyadh. One of the two source datasets is described as collected from toddlers across regions of Saudi Arabia via an online questionnaire; the other is the Kaggle/Thabtah toddler set.
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: The Q-CHAT-10 total is used as a severity index in Phase II, with children binned into low, low-to-moderate, moderate, moderate-to-high and high severity bands. No validated severity instrument (CARS, ADOS calibrated severity score) is involved, and Q-CHAT-10 is not a severity measure.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None. The class label is the Q-CHAT-10 outcome, defined explicitly in the paper: a 1 is scored for each item answered Always, Usually or Sometimes, and a total above 3 points indicates the presence of potential ASD traits. No clinical diagnosis, instrument beyond the checklist, assessor or criterion exists for any record.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: 12 to 36 months for the Saudi dataset; the Kaggle toddler set covers the same band. No mean, SD or distribution.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Gender is present as a variable and is named in the Phase II rationale, but no counts or proportions are reported.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported. Jaundice and family history are present as covariates.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not clearly stated for the merged set. Dataset 1 contributes 1,054 instances; the size of the Saudi dataset and the size of the merged and SMOTE-balanced set are never reported, so the number of rows underlying every reported metric is unknown.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. Merging two datasets is presented as improving diversity, but the two are pooled rather than used as train and held-out cohorts, which would have made this the corpus's rare genuine external validation at no extra cost.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Never stated. After SMOTE the binary task is balanced, so chance is 50%; the Phase II task has seven classes (0 plus six teaching methods) whose distribution is not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Questionnaire - ten binary Q-CHAT-10 items plus demographic and history fields, from two merged online screening datasets.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. Online caregiver questionnaire.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None. Tabular data.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Low. One dataset is cited by URL and the label rule is stated explicitly, which is more than most; but the second dataset has no accession, the merged set is not deposited, no row counts are given at any stage, no hyperparameters are reported for any of eight models, no seed or versions are given, the number and identity of selected features are never stated, the order of SMOTE relative to the split is unspecified, and the headline 99.99% appears in no results table.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Dataset 1 is cited by Kaggle URL. The Saudi dataset is referenced but no accession is given, and the merged dataset presented as a contribution is not deposited.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Absent. There is no ethics statement, no consent statement and no data-governance statement; the string ethic does not appear in the article.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Merging of two regional datasets, SMOTE oversampling to balance classes, and feature selection. The order of SMOTE relative to the train-test split is not stated, and neither the pre- nor post-SMOTE row counts are reported.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Three feature-selection techniques compared: Bi-Directional Elimination, Boruta, and an ML-based feature selection (MFS). The number and identity of features retained by each are not reported, only a feature-ranking figure.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Python with scikit-learn; numpy is named as the tool used to create the Phase II teaching-method column. No versions, no seed, no hardware.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: None. Per-fold values are tabulated but no standard deviation or interval is computed, and the printed average (0.986) does not match the mean of the ten printed fold accuracies (0.9876).
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: A feature-ranking figure from the ML-based selection method. No SHAP, no per-class analysis, no examination of what distinguishes the teaching-method classes.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not described.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None, although the merged dataset spans two regions and the stated motivation for merging was regional diversity - a regional breakdown was directly available and is not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Classical machine learning: random forest, decision tree, logistic regression, KNN, SVM, gradient boosting machine, XGBoost, plus a proposed RF-XG voting ensemble.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: No hyperparameters are reported for any of the eight models. The ensemble is described only as combining RF and XGBoost through a voting mechanism.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: An 80:20 train-test split with feature selection applied and models then re-assessed on the 20% test data, followed by 10-fold cross-validation. The order of operations is stated ambiguously - models were trained using selected significant features through feature selection techniques, then assessed on the test data - with no statement of whether selection was fitted inside the training partition, and no statement of whether SMOTE preceded or followed the split.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for each model in each feature condition (Tables 3-6), per-fold cross-validation results (Table 7), Phase II classification results (Table 8), and a state-of-the-art comparison (Table 9). No AUC, no specificity, no calibration, no confidence intervals.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Phase I: with original features RF-XG reaches 0.94; with Bi-Directional Elimination 0.92; with Boruta 0.98; with ML-based feature selection 0.99. Ten-fold cross-validation gives an average accuracy of 0.986. The state-of-the-art comparison table, however, lists the proposed approach at 99.99%, a figure that appears in no results table and exceeds every value the study reports. Phase II: RF-XG predicts the teaching-method label with accuracy 0.9917.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Parent-reported early social-communication behaviours captured by Q-CHAT-10. Phase II additionally invokes physical, verbal and behavioural performance, though no such measurements exist in the data.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: None stated.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: None. The article has no limitations section; the only occurrence of limitations refers to challenges in prior work reviewed.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: No participants were recruited. Two public toddler screening datasets are merged: the Kaggle ASD Toddler set (1,054 instances, 17 columns) and an online questionnaire dataset covering toddlers aged 12-36 months across regions of Saudi Arabia. The size of the second dataset is never given, the size of the merged set is never given, and the size after SMOTE oversampling is never given - so the number of rows behind every table in the paper is unknown, and it cannot be determined how many are real records and how many synthetic. Class counts are likewise absent. The stated motivation for merging - improving diversity by combining two regions - is the paper's best idea and is never exploited: the two cohorts are pooled rather than used as development and held-out sets.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic children, children with ASD, individuals affected by ASD, high-level and low-level autistic children, autism students. The abstract opens with a genuinely thoughtful observation - that ASD is highly diverse, each affected child is unique, no two autistic children are alike, and what benefits one child may not suit another - and the whole paper is then organised around assigning children to one of six teaching methods on the basis of a checklist total. The severity vocabulary (high-level, moderate-to-high, low-level autistic children) applies the label to the child rather than to support needs, and the framing describes ASD as having a primary origin that is genetic and as significantly affecting cognitive abilities and object recognition.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: None reported. Gender is present as a variable and is named as a factor in the Phase II rationale; ethnicity, region and jaundice exist as columns; no counts, proportions or distributions are printed for any of them. The absence of a regional breakdown is the notable one, since regional diversity is the stated reason for merging the two datasets and the merged column would have made a two-cohort comparison immediate.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None, and the paper states the label rule plainly enough that this is not in doubt: a 1 is scored for each Q-CHAT-10 item answered Always, Usually or Sometimes, and a total above 3 indicates the presence of potential ASD traits. That threshold is the outcome variable. No clinician, diagnostic instrument, criterion or assessment date exists for any record in either dataset, and the online questionnaire origin of the Saudi data means the respondents were not verified either.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: No validated cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure. The Q-CHAT-10 total is repurposed as a severity index in Phase II, binning children into five severity levels. Q-CHAT-10 is a binary screening instrument with a single cut-off; it was neither designed nor validated to grade severity, and using its total as a severity scale is an unsupported extension that Phase II then rests on entirely.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Two goals. Phase I: identify ASD from merged toddler screening data using seven classifiers plus a proposed RF-XG voting ensemble, under three feature-selection schemes. Phase II: recommend an appropriate teaching method for each child from their physical, verbal and behavioural performance. Headline findings: RF-XG reaches 0.94 on original features, 0.92 with Bi-Directional Elimination, 0.98 with Boruta and 0.99 with ML-based feature selection; 10-fold cross-validation averages 0.986; and Phase II predicts the teaching-method label at 0.9917. The comparison table separately claims 99.99%, a number that appears in none of the results tables and exceeds every figure the study actually reports.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting. Two downloaded or pre-existing questionnaire datasets, analysed in Python. No computing environment, runtime or data-handling arrangement is described.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: No task or paradigm - an online caregiver questionnaire. Phase II claims to assess children's physical, verbal and behavioural performance, and this claim is unsupported at the most basic level: the dataset contains ten checklist items and a handful of demographic fields, and no physical, verbal or behavioural performance measure of any kind.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis. There is no ethics statement, no consent statement and no data-governance statement anywhere in the article. That absence is more consequential here than in most of this corpus, because the output is not a screening probability but a specific educational placement recommendation for individual children, offered to educators as a basis for decisions affecting their learning and development.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No instrumentation. Python with scikit-learn for modelling; numpy is named specifically as the library used to create the Phase II teaching-method column. No versions, seed, hardware or runtime.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Low. The one Kaggle dataset is linked and the Q-CHAT-10 label rule is stated explicitly, which is better than most of the branch. Everything else is missing: the second dataset has no accession, the merged dataset that is claimed as a contribution is not deposited, no row counts are reported at any stage (pre-merge, post-merge, post-SMOTE, per class, per split), no hyperparameters are given for any of eight models, no seed or library versions appear, the number and identity of features retained by each of the three selection methods are never stated, and the order of SMOTE relative to the split is unspecified. The manuscript is also visibly an unedited accepted version - the header retains Date of publication xxxx 00, 0000 and the placeholder DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2017.DOI, and the running footer reads VOLUME 4, 2016 throughout.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: None. There is no limitations section and no caveat anywhere. Unmentioned: that the label is a threshold on the summed predictors; that the Phase II target was manufactured by the authors from that same total; that the reported 99.99% appears in no table; that the printed cross-validation average does not equal the mean of the printed folds; that row counts are absent throughout; and that no ethics approval was sought for a study producing educational placement recommendations.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: None stated. There is no future-work section.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Parent-reported early social-communication behaviours from Q-CHAT-10 - response to name, eye contact, gestures, pointing, pretend play, gaze following, comforting, early speech, staring. No behaviour is observed, and the physical and verbal performance invoked in the Phase II framing does not exist in the data.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No modality fusion. The only fusion is the merging of two questionnaire datasets from different regions, which is dataset pooling rather than multimodal integration - and, as noted, the regional structure created by that merge is then discarded rather than used for cross-cohort validation.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Seven classical classifiers - random forest, decision tree, logistic regression, KNN, SVM, gradient boosting, XGBoost - plus an RF-XG voting ensemble presented as the novel contribution. Three feature-selection techniques (Bi-Directional Elimination, Boruta, ML-based selection) are compared. No hyperparameter is reported for any model.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Tabular rows of ten binary Q-CHAT-10 items plus demographic and history fields, SMOTE-augmented and feature-selected. The ten items are the constituents of the Q-CHAT-10 total whose threshold defines the Phase I label and whose bands define the Phase II label, so in both phases the predictor set arithmetically determines the outcome.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 across four feature conditions, seven classifiers and an ensemble; per-fold cross-validation values; Phase II results; and a state-of-the-art comparison. No AUC, no specificity, no calibration, no confidence interval, and no chance level for either the binary Phase I task or the seven-class Phase II task. Two internal inconsistencies matter. The 10-fold table prints an average accuracy of 0.986 while the ten listed fold accuracies average 0.9876, and it contains a fold reporting recall 0.999 against accuracy 0.988 and another reporting accuracy 0.999 - values out of line with their neighbours. More seriously, the comparison table credits the proposed approach with 99.99% accuracy, positioning it above four quoted literature figures (98.77%, 97.82%, 99.25%, 99.85%), when the study's own best tabulated result is 0.99 and its cross-validated average is 0.986. The headline claim of surpassing the state of the art rests on a number the paper never produced.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: A single feature-ranking figure from the ML-based selection method. No attribution analysis, no examination of which features drive the teaching-method assignment, and no interrogation of why three different feature-selection methods produce accuracies spanning 0.92 to 0.99 on the same data.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: Phase I follows the familiar pattern: an 80:20 split plus 10-fold cross-validation over data whose label is a threshold on the summed predictors, with SMOTE applied at an unstated point relative to the split and feature selection of unstated nesting. Row counts are absent at every stage, so no reported figure can be located to a sample. That much places the study alongside local_ed30e24c, local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 in the circular-label group. Phase II is a different and more serious matter, and it is the reason this record exists. The teaching-method target did not come from any school, therapist, assessment or record: the paper states that a new column named Teaching Method was added to the dataset using the numpy library, containing integers 1 to 6 for six specialised teaching methods plus 0 for no special education needed, and that these were assigned on the basis of severity as analysed from the Q-CHAT-10 score, which is the count of the A1-A10 values. The models are then trained to predict that manufactured column from the other columns - including A1 to A10 themselves. The reported 0.9917 accuracy therefore measures how well a classifier reproduces an arithmetic rule that the authors wrote, applied to the very features they wrote it from. It is not an estimate of anything about children, education or autism; a lookup table would score 1.00. Compounding this, the mapping from severity band to intervention (Pivotal Response Training for high-level, technology-aided instruction for moderate-to-high, PECS for moderate, task analysis for low-to-moderate, Intensive Behavioral Intervention for low) is asserted with no evidence base, no clinical input and no citation, and it inverts the usual intensity gradient by assigning the most intensive intervention to the least affected group. The results are then offered to educators and professionals as a basis for informed decisions about teaching methods that can have a significant impact on the children's learning and development. The merged two-region design offered a genuine external-validation opportunity - train on one cohort, test on the other - and it is not taken.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD); Autism Students Learning; SMOTE; Multi-model Learning; Feature Engineering. Three of five terms name technique; the educational claim that occupies half the paper appears only as Autism Students Learning.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: IEEE Access - a high-volume open-access multidisciplinary engineering journal. The published PDF is the unedited accepted version, retaining template placeholders in the header (Date of publication xxxx 00, 0000; DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2017.DOI) and a VOLUME 4, 2016 footer throughout. No reviewer questioned a fabricated educational-placement target, a 99.99% figure absent from the results, or the absence of any ethics statement in a paper recommending educational interventions for individual children.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2025 (accepted version, citation DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2024.3349988). Framing moves beyond diagnosis into intervention allocation: the aim is personalised educational approaches for individuals with ASD, harnessing machine learning to enhance precision in addressing their unique needs, with results said to help educators make informed decisions. The paper opens by insisting that no two autistic children are alike and closes by assigning them to six intervention categories on the basis of a ten-item checklist total that the authors themselves binned. It is the corpus's clearest example of a pipeline whose output is an action taken on a child rather than a probability, built on a target the authors wrote with numpy.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Sankari M S
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed as a scalable and cost-effective approach for early detection and personalized intervention strategies that facilitates the way for integrating ML techniques into clinical settings. No clinician evaluation or prospective test.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of a single public tabular screening dataset; four classifiers evaluated across a default feature set and four selected subsets, with hyperparameter tuning and k-fold cross-validation.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Internal: four classifiers across five feature configurations. External: literature-quoted accuracies in Table 8, none re-run.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None. The Toddler autism dataset (1,054 records) was taken from an open repository (described variously as UCI and an online open repository). The paper states that the data were collected via an ASD test screening application with no direct human interaction, with responses submitted by parents and other stakeholders.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Standardised tabular vectors of questionnaire items and demographic fields, in five different feature configurations.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: India - Department of Electronics and Communication, PSG College of Technology, Coimbatore. Single author. No data collection.
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: None. The Qchat-10-Score total is present as a variable and is used as a predictor in two of the four subsets.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None. The outcome is the Class/ASD traits field of the questionnaire dataset, which encodes the Q-CHAT-10 screening result. No clinician, diagnostic instrument, criterion or assessor exists for any record, and the responses were submitted through an app with no verification of respondent or child.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 728 records labelled autism (69.1%)
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Average age reported as 25 to 28 months, with the paper noting that autism cases increase between 25 and 30 months and become more noticeable by 35-36 months - an observation about label prevalence by age band rather than about development.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Reported only as a male predominance of 69.7% in the autism group. No figure is given for the control group and no overall count.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported. Jaundice and family history of ASD are covariates.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 1,054 records, 19 attributes.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 326 records labelled control (30.9%)
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not stated. With 728 of 1,054 positive, a majority-class classifier achieves 69.1% accuracy and 100% sensitivity.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Questionnaire - ten Q-CHAT behavioural items (A1-A10, five-point response scale collapsed to binary), the Qchat-10-Score total, and demographic fields (age in months, sex, ethnicity across eleven groups, jaundice, family member with ASD, who completed the test).
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. App-administered caregiver checklist.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None. Tabular data.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Moderate. The preprocessing pipeline is published as a numbered algorithm with the exact encodings and column operations; the source dataset is public; the four feature subsets are described by their contents; the statistical tests and their p-values are tabulated; and the metric set includes confusion matrices for every model. Missing: split proportions, the value of k in cross-validation, per-fold results, final hyperparameter values, the ANN architecture, the ensemble combination rule, a random seed, code, and any statement of whether selection and tuning were nested inside the training partition.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Source repository cited; no derived splits or code shared.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not obtained, and the statement made in its place is worth quoting: the dataset was collected via an ASD test screening application, with no direct human interaction, with responses submitted by parents and other stakeholders, ensuring ethical approval for research purposes. Absence of direct contact is treated as itself constituting ethical approval.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Documented as a numbered algorithm: load 1,054 rows and 19 columns, drop Case_no, handle missing values, one-hot encode ethnicity and who-completed-the-test, label-encode jaundice, sex, family history and the class label, standardise with StandardScaler, then separate X (all columns except Class/ASD traits) from Y. No resampling is applied - the 69/31 imbalance is left in place, which is unusual and preferable to the SMOTE approaches elsewhere in this branch.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Three selection methods producing four subsets: Chi-squared univariate selection (SelectKBest, p<0.05) and tree-based feature importance from RF and Extra Trees give Subsets 1 and 2; pairwise correlation analysis with Pearson, Spearman and variance inflation factor gives Subsets 3 and 4. A fifth condition uses Q1-Q10 alone. Feature reductions of 17%, 29%, 41%, 58% and 76% are tracked.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Not named; scikit-learn estimators are implied (SelectKBest, RF, Extra Trees, LR, KNN, ANN). No versions, no seed, no hardware.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Kruskal-Wallis tests of each Q-CHAT item against the class variable, all significant with extremely small p-values (for example Q9 p = 4.0e-106, Q6 p = 2.1e-101, Q10 p = 2.9e-20). Chi-squared univariate selection at p<0.05. No confidence intervals on any performance figure and no fold variance.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Substantial by this branch's standards: chi-squared and impurity-based feature rankings, Pearson and Spearman correlation analysis, variance inflation factors for multicollinearity, Kruskal-Wallis association tests, a mapping of each Q-CHAT item to DSM-5 behavioural domains, and an iterative feature-addition curve tracking sensitivity and specificity as Q1 through Q10 are added one at a time. Q9, Q6 and Q5 emerge as the strongest items and Q8 and Q10 as the weakest across all three ranking methods - a consistent result, though one determined by the label's construction.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Random search followed by manual fixing for LR; error-rate inspection for KNN's k; unspecified tuning for the ANN. The paper states that the manually tuned model is then trained and evaluated on the dataset to ensure generalization, which describes tuning and evaluation on the same data.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None by performance. Descriptively, the paper notes eleven ethnic groups with no significant ethnic differences in ASD diagnosis rates, White Europeans most represented followed by Asians.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Logistic regression, k-nearest neighbours, a feed-forward artificial neural network, and a proposed LR-KNN ensemble.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Partially reported. SelectKBest K is tuned; tree-based selectors have n_estimators, random_state, min_samples_split and min_samples_leaf tuned; LR is tuned by random search then manually fixed to the best values; KNN's k is chosen by inspecting the error rate across k; the ANN is described only as input, hidden and output layers with non-linear activation. Concrete final values are not tabulated, and the ensemble's combination rule is not specified.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: The dataset was divided into training, testing and validation sets (proportions not stated) and k-fold cross-validation is described generically with no value of k, no per-fold results and no variance. The confusion matrices imply a test set of 317 records, about 30% of 1,054. Whether feature selection and hyperparameter tuning were nested inside the training partition is never stated, and the selection methods rank features against the class label.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, F1, sensitivity, specificity, Matthews correlation coefficient and a confusion matrix for every model in the final configuration, plus per-subset accuracy, sensitivity and specificity in a bar chart, and an iterative feature-addition analysis of sensitivity and specificity. The inclusion of MCC is a genuine strength and is explicitly motivated: the author states that incorrect diagnoses can have significant implications for families and that MCC is included to ensure robust predictions under imbalance.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Parent-reported early social-communication behaviours: response to name, eye contact, pointing to express needs, and the remaining Q-CHAT items, each mapped in Table 1 to a behavioural description and related to DSM-5 domains.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: None in the extracted text; the article's conclusion section is not present in the extracted PDF text, which ends mid-discussion after Table 7.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: No limitations section. One candid remark appears in the discussion - that on reviewing performance across multiple feature subsets, the results obtained were not entirely satisfactory - and one methodological observation, that Subset 2 included both the Qchat-10-Score and Q1-Q10 features, which could sometimes mislead the model results. The latter is the closest anyone in this branch comes to naming the circularity, and it is not pursued.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: No participants. 1,054 records from the public toddler Q-CHAT dataset, 728 labelled autism and 326 control - a 69.1% positive rate that the paper reports and, unusually for this branch, leaves in place rather than resampling. The records were submitted through an ASD screening application by parents and other stakeholders, so neither respondent nor child was verified. The confusion matrices imply a test partition of 317 records, though no split proportion is stated; the row totals also differ across models within the same table (105/212 for LR, KNN and LR-KNN but 110/207 for the ANN), which they should not if all four were evaluated on the same partition.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autism traits, ASD traits, toddlers, individuals with ASD, controls, non-ASD individuals. The register is careful and the title is the most honest in this branch of the corpus: predicting autism traits, not diagnosing autism. ASD is described as a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition, controls rather than normals are used for the comparison class, and the stated motivation includes that incorrect diagnoses can have significant implications for families. One slip: the opening sentence calls ASD a complex neuropsychiatric developmental condition.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Better than most of the branch, though still descriptive only. Age averages 25 to 28 months with a note that labelled cases rise between 25 and 30 months and become more noticeable by 35-36 months. Sex is given only as 69.7% male within the autism group, with no control-group figure. Ethnicity is reported across eleven groups with White Europeans most represented followed by Asians, and the paper states there were no significant ethnic differences in diagnosis rates - the one ethnicity analysis in this branch. Jaundice, family history and respondent type are present. No performance is broken down by any of these, so the demographic detail informs the sample description but not the evaluation.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None. The outcome is the Class/ASD traits field, the Q-CHAT-10 screening result, applied to app-submitted responses with no clinical assessment, no clinician, no instrument beyond the checklist and no verification of who completed it. The paper's title and abstract are accurate about this - it predicts autism traits, not autism - and that accuracy distinguishes it from several neighbours in the corpus that describe the same label as a diagnosis.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity instrument. The Qchat-10-Score total appears as a predictor in two feature subsets rather than as a participant characteristic.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is to identify a minimal feature subset for ASD trait screening in toddlers through systematic feature selection and hyperparameter tuning, and to map Q1-Q10 and the Q-CHAT total onto DSM-5 behavioural domains. Headline findings: using Q1-Q10 alone (a 41% feature reduction) gives the best performance across all classifiers, with the LR-KNN ensemble at accuracy 0.99, precision 1.00, specificity 1.00 and MCC 0.98, followed by ANN 0.98, LR 0.97 and KNN 0.94. Q9, Q6 and Q5 rank consistently highest across chi-squared, tree-importance and correlation methods; Q8 and Q10 lowest.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No setting. A single-author secondary analysis of a downloaded file; no computing environment or runtime is described.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: No task or paradigm. The instrument is the ten-item Quantitative Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, administered through a screening app on a five-point frequency scale from never to always, collapsed to binary. Table 1 maps each question to its behavioural construct - response to name, eye contact, finger pointing and so on - which is more transparency about the instrument than most of the branch offers.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis. The ethics statement is the notable feature: the dataset was collected via an ASD test screening application, with no direct human interaction, with responses submitted by parents and other stakeholders, ensuring ethical approval for research purposes. Absence of contact between researcher and participant is presented as itself supplying ethical approval. No committee, protocol number, consent statement or data-governance arrangement appears, and no consideration is given to whether app users agreed to research reuse of their children's screening responses.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No instrumentation. Analytical components: StandardScaler, one-hot and label encoding, SelectKBest with chi-squared, RF and Extra Trees importance, Pearson and Spearman correlation, variance inflation factor, Kruskal-Wallis tests, logistic regression, KNN, a feed-forward ANN and an LR-KNN ensemble. No library names, versions, seed or hardware.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Moderate, and the strongest in this branch alongside local_ed30e24c. The preprocessing is published as a numbered algorithm specifying every encoding and column operation; the dataset is public; the composition of each of the four feature subsets is listed; the statistical tests and their exact p-values are tabulated; and confusion matrices are printed for all four final models. Missing: split proportions, the value of k in the cross-validation, any per-fold result, final hyperparameter values, the ANN architecture, the ensemble's combination rule, a seed, and code. The extracted PDF also ends mid-discussion after Table 7, so no conclusion or funding statement is available.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: No limitations section, but two candid remarks stand out. The author writes that on reviewing performance across multiple feature subsets, the results obtained were not entirely satisfactory - an unusual admission in a literature where every result is a success. And, discussing Subset 2, that it included both the Qchat-10-Score and Q1-Q10 features, which could sometimes mislead the model results. That second sentence is the closest any of the six Q-CHAT-based studies charted in this review comes to naming the circularity at the centre of the branch: the total and its own summands are both in the feature set, and the label is a threshold on the total. Having noticed it, the paper treats it as a redundancy nuisance and moves on.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Not available - the extracted text ends mid-discussion and contains no conclusion or future-work section.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Parent-reported early social-communication behaviours from the Q-CHAT: response to name, ease of eye contact, pointing to express desires, and the remaining seven items, each mapped to a DSM-5 behavioural domain. The item-level analysis produces a consistent ordering - Q9, Q6 and Q5 most informative, Q8 and Q10 least - which is the paper's substantive behavioural claim.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No fusion - a single questionnaire modality with demographic covariates. The systematic subset comparison is a study of feature configurations within one modality, not multimodal integration.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Four supervised learners: logistic regression, k-nearest neighbours, a feed-forward artificial neural network, and a soft LR-KNN ensemble presented as the contribution. No tree-based or boosted classifier is used for prediction, though RF and Extra Trees are used for feature ranking.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Standardised tabular vectors in five configurations: the default 19-attribute set; Subset 1 (chi-squared, ordered by Q1-Q10 with Q9, Q5, Q6 top); Subset 2 (tree importance, retaining both Qchat-10-Score and Q1-Q10); Subset 3 (correlation-based: Qchat-10-Score, sex, jaundice, age, family history, ethnicity, respondent); Subset 4 (minimal: Qchat-10-Score, age, sex, jaundice); and Q1-Q10 alone. The configurations are the study's real object, and their comparison is where its diagnostic value lies - Subsets 3 and 4 keep the Q-CHAT total and drop the items; Q1-Q10 keeps the items and drops the total; Subset 2 keeps both.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, F1, sensitivity, specificity, MCC and a confusion matrix for every model, plus per-subset comparisons and an iterative feature-addition curve. The metric set is the most complete in this branch: MCC is included deliberately because of the class imbalance, and its motivation - that incorrect diagnoses have significant implications for families - is stated. It also does real work, separating LR (accuracy 0.97, MCC 0.92) from ANN (0.98, 0.98). Two problems. No confidence interval accompanies any figure. And the confusion matrices are mutually inconsistent: LR, KNN and LR-KNN each have class totals of 105 and 212, while the ANN's are 110 and 207, so the four models were not all evaluated on the same 317-record partition.
