custom_fields.RQ4.4: The most thorough feature analysis in this branch: chi-squared scores, RF and Extra Trees impurity importance, Pearson and Spearman correlations, variance inflation factors, Kruskal-Wallis association tests with exact p-values, a DSM-5 domain mapping for each item, and an iterative curve tracking sensitivity and specificity as Q1 through Q10 are added one at a time. Three items (Q9, Q6, Q5) rank highest under all three methods. The analysis is careful and internally consistent; what limits it is that the label is a threshold on the sum of the very items being ranked, so the Kruskal-Wallis p-values of order 1e-100 and the convergence across three ranking methods are arithmetic consequences rather than empirical discoveries about which behaviours matter.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The validation design is under-reported - no split proportions, no value of k, no per-fold results, no statement of whether feature selection and tuning were nested inside the training partition, and a passage stating that the manually tuned model is then trained and evaluated on the dataset to ensure generalization, which describes tuning and evaluating on the same data. The confusion matrices imply a 317-record test partition but disagree on its class composition across models (105/212 for three of them, 110/207 for the ANN). Underneath that, the estimand is the branch's usual one: Class/ASD traits is the Q-CHAT-10 outcome and Q1-Q10 are its summands, so predicting the former from the latter is arithmetic recovery. What makes this study analytically valuable to the review is that its own feature-subset experiment maps the circularity almost completely without naming it. Subsets 3 and 4 retain the Qchat-10-Score and discard the items; Q1-Q10 retains the items and discards the total; Subset 2 retains both, and the author observes that this could sometimes mislead the model results. Every configuration containing either the total or its summands performs well, and the reported conclusion - that Q1-Q10 alone gives optimal performance with 41% fewer features - is a statement about which encoding of the label's own arithmetic is most compact. The single most revealing number in the paper is in the iterative analysis: with only the two least significant features, age and sex, sensitivity was 99.5%. With 69.1% of records positive, that is what a near-all-positive classifier produces, and the surrounding text treats it as a baseline from which adding Q1 (sensitivity 97.6%) and Q2-Q4 (92.8%, 91.3%) represents degradation. Read correctly it demonstrates that sensitivity alone is uninformative on this dataset and that the majority-class baseline is 69.1% accuracy - neither point is made, and no chance level appears anywhere in the article.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: machine learning; feature selection; hyperparameter tuning; logistic regression; k-nearest neighbors; artificial neural network. Six terms, all naming technique - autism, ASD, Q-CHAT, toddlers and screening appear in none of them, which is unusual and leaves the keyword list disconnected from the paper's subject.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Engineering Research Express 7(2):025269 (IOP Publishing) - an open-access general engineering journal. A 132-day review including one revision round did not surface the mutually inconsistent confusion matrices, the missing split proportions and cross-validation k, the unstated chance level, or an ethics statement that treats absence of direct human interaction as constituting ethical approval.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2025, published 28 May, 132 days from submission to acceptance. Framing is screening-support rather than diagnostic replacement and is among the most measured in the corpus - the title claims to predict autism traits, the abstract offers a scalable and cost-effective approach for early detection and personalized intervention strategies, and the discussion admits that results across subsets were not entirely satisfactory. The overreach is confined to the closing claim of facilitating the way for integrating ML techniques into clinical settings. Its distinguishing contribution is analytical rather than predictive: by systematically varying which parts of the Q-CHAT arithmetic enter the feature set, it produces the branch's most complete map of why these accuracies are what they are.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Predicting autistic traits, anxiety and depression symptoms using camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (CAT-Q-ES): A machine learning study
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Conde-Pumpido Zubizarreta S; Tubío-Fungueiriño M; Pozo-Rodríguez M; Carracedo A; Cernadas E; Fernández-Delgado M; Fernández-Prieto M
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed with unusual restraint: the models are proposed as screeners to accelerate referral for deeper and personalised attention but never to replace clinical evaluation, to be applied by clinicians following a personalised-medicine approach that considers autonomy and the patient's daily-life context.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional primary survey study nested within a broader instrument-validation project, followed by supervised regression. Fifty regression algorithms compared under two-layer 4-fold cross-validation with participant-disjoint partitions.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Fifty algorithms against one another, plus three input configurations (CAT-Q-ES alone; plus gender; plus autism diagnosis; plus both). No external benchmark.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: A REDCap survey disseminated through autism associations, institutions, federations, clinical units, autism-related research networks and social media. All participants were Spanish nationals or residents. Self-diagnosed respondents (n=12) and those not reporting gender (n=13) were excluded prospectively.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A 25-element vector of Likert item responses, optionally augmented with gender and/or autism diagnosis in three additional configurations.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Spain - Universidade de Santiago de Compostela (CiMUS and CiTIUS), FIDIS, IDIS, CIBERER/Instituto de Salud Carlos III, and Fundacion Publica Galega de Medicina Xenomica. Online survey administered through REDCap.
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: Dimensional rather than categorical: BAPQ Aloofness, Pragmatic Language and Rigid Personality subscales are the outcome variables, with internal consistencies computed in this sample (omega .94, .87, .92; full scale .96).
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Self-reported but constrained. Participants were asked about their clinically based diagnosis of autism and about which professional made it; those reporting self-diagnosis were excluded; participants were instructed to report only clinician-confirmed diagnoses and not diagnoses based on personal feelings of distress. The authors name the residual uncertainty as a limitation and recommend clinician-confirmed diagnosis in future work.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 102 autistic adults with a formal diagnosis from specialised clinicians (72 women, 18 men, 12 non-binary), mean age 36.0 (SD 10.6), mean age at diagnosis 32.0 (SD 12.3)
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not measured. Level of education is reported in full for both groups (from no studies through PhD), with 61.8% of autistic and 64.9% of non-autistic participants holding a degree and 3.9% versus 13.4% a PhD.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Adults; means and SDs reported by group with a significant 2.7-year difference (t(599)=2.24, p=.025, d=0.24, 95% CI .03-.46). The autistic group's mean age at diagnosis of 32.0 years is itself reported, which is unusual and directly relevant to the camouflaging hypothesis.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Self-reported gender rather than sex assigned at birth, with an explicit rationale that gender better reflects participants' identities. Autistic group 70.6% women, 17.6% men, 11.8% non-binary; non-autistic 80.0% women, 18.4% men, 1.6% non-binary. Group differences tested: fewer women in the autistic group (Z=-2.10, p=.036) and more non-binary participants (Z=5.21, p<.001).
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Reported in detail for both groups in Table 1: high abilities 32.4% vs 5.6%, ADHD 22.5% vs 4.4%, developmental coordination disorder, specific learning disorder, epilepsy, bipolar disorder, eating disorder 13.7% vs 5.4%, anxiety 49.0% vs 18.8%, depression 30.4% vs 11.8%, sleep disorder 18.6% vs 4.4%.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 601 adults
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None, and the authors state directly that these algorithms should be extensively cross-validated using data from health records before any implementation in mental health care.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 499 non-autistic adults (399 women, 92 men, 8 non-binary), mean age 33.3 (SD 11.0)
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No. Single administration.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Informed consent obtained; the survey's primary section provided study information and a consent statement before participation.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not applicable in the classification sense; these are regression targets. The comparison the paper does not make is against a trivial baseline such as predicting the sample mean, which would set a reference for the reported MAE and RMSE.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Self-report questionnaire - the 25 CAT-Q-ES items on a 1-7 Likert scale as predictors; BAPQ subscales, PHQ-9 and GAD-7 totals as outcomes.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. Online self-report battery completed in a single sitting via REDCap.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture) hosted at Fundacion Publica Galega de Medicina Xenomica, with audit trails and validated data-capture interfaces.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: High - the best in the charted corpus. Code and a sample dataset are on OSF; the fifty models, their packages and their hyperparameter grids are listed in a supplementary appendix; the cross-validation procedure is described step by step including partition roles and rotation; every instrument's internal consistency is computed in-sample; imputation is quantified (0.30% missing) and justified; exclusions are enumerated with reasons and counts. Only the full dataset is withheld.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: A small sample of the data accompanies the code on OSF; the full dataset is not deposited.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Yes - code and a small sample dataset are publicly available on OSF (https://osf.io/t5v62). This is the only study charted in this review to release working code.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Yes, fully specified: conducted in line with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Santiago de Compostela, code USC 26/2023, with participant anonymity preserved throughout data collection.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Minimal and fully described: person-level mean imputation for 15 participants with one or two missing PHQ-9 items (0.30% missing data), with the rationale that PHQ-9 is unidimensional. No resampling, no scaling described as necessary, no feature engineering.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: None. The 25 raw CAT-Q-ES items are the predictors. Subscale scores were tested as an alternative input and reported not to improve accuracy; that negative result is stated rather than omitted.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Fifty regression models implemented across Python, R, Matlab and Octave, with the package used by each model and its hyperparameter tuning details listed in Appendix 1 of the supplementary material.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Group comparisons by Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis with reported statistics and p-values; t-test and Wald tests for demographic differences with effect sizes and confidence intervals; McDonald's omega internal consistencies computed in this sample for every instrument. Performance metrics themselves are reported without confidence intervals or across-trial variance.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Limited at the model level - no feature importance or attribution for the fifty regressors. The three input-configuration comparisons function as a coarse ablation and support a substantive claim: gender and diagnosis add nothing beyond the camouflaging items.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Nested inside the cross-validation, selected on the validation partition by MAE, never on the test partition.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Gender is analysed as a variable of interest rather than a nuisance: non-binary participants scored significantly higher than women and men on CAT-Q-ES total, compensation, masking, assimilation and the BAPQ subscales, and higher than men on depression and anxiety; no differences were found between women and men. Predictive accuracy was explicitly tested for improvement when gender was added, and did not improve.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Fifty regression algorithms spanning support vector regression, neural networks, linear and regularised linear regressors, decision trees, random forests, boosting ensembles, k-nearest neighbours and Gaussian processes.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Per-model packages and hyperparameter grids are given in the supplementary appendix. Best performers: stochastic gradient descent for Aloofness (Python), support vector regression for Pragmatics (Matlab), Ridge regression for Rigidity (Matlab), k-nearest neighbours for Depression (Python), and a boosted regression-tree ensemble for Anxiety (R).
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Two-layer K-fold cross-validation with K=4, described in operational detail: the 601 participants were divided into four disjoint partitions stratified to span the full score range, each participant appearing in exactly one partition; in each of four trials two partitions trained, one validated and one tested, with the roles rotating; hyperparameters were selected by validation MAE, the model was then refitted on training plus validation, and test MAE was computed on the untouched partition; the four test MAEs were averaged. This is correct nested cross-validation at the participant level and is the most rigorous validation design in the charted corpus.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Pearson correlation between true and predicted scores, mean absolute error, mean absolute percentage error of the score range, root mean square error, per-model and per-outcome, averaged over the four trials; plus predicted-versus-true scatter plots with a diagonal reference line and a tolerance analysis (36.3% of predictions within 5% of the true value, over 60% within 10%). Correlation strength is interpreted against a pre-specified external criterion (Colton 1974: <.25 null, .25-.5 weak, .5-.75 moderate, >.75 strong).
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Best-regressor correlations: Aloofness R=.85 (MAE 5.55, MAPE 9.2%, RMSE 7.22), Pragmatics R=.82 (5.36, 8.9%, 6.90), Rigidity R=.75 (6.94, 11.6%, 8.92), Depression R=.58 (4.55, 16.9%, 5.71), Anxiety R=.54 (4.00, 19.1%, 4.91). Adding gender and/or autism diagnosis changed R by at most .03 and MAE by at most 0.10, from which the authors conclude that this information is already implicit in the CAT-Q-ES items.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Camouflaging - compensation (copying others' behaviour, preparing social scripts), masking (controlling facial and body expression to fit in), and assimilation (effortful engagement, pretending to be normal in social situations).
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Clinician-confirmed diagnoses and observational measures of camouflaging; dimensional continuous scales for anxiety and depression rather than criterion-based screeners; extensive cross-validation against health-record data before any clinical implementation.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A substantial and self-critical limitations section: over-representation of women, attributed to the source validation project and to online-study bias toward respondents with topic interest, higher cognitive ability and moderate-to-high socioeconomic status; inability to verify self-reported diagnoses, with the mitigation described and clinician confirmation recommended for future work; weaker performance for anxiety and depression, explained through the structure of the instruments (PHQ-9 and GAD-7 items map to distinct diagnostic criteria and so scatter more than the BAPQ's interrelated within-domain items); and measurement of generalised anxiety only, omitting social anxiety, which is the form most closely linked to masking.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two groups of adults recruited into one online survey: 102 autistic adults with a clinician-made diagnosis (72 women, 18 men, 12 non-binary) and 499 non-autistic adults (399 women, 92 men, 8 non-binary), 601 in total. The analysis unit is the person throughout, and the four cross-validation partitions are participant-disjoint by construction - each participant appears in exactly one partition. Exclusions are enumerated with reasons: 12 self-diagnosed respondents and 13 who did not report a gender they identified with. This is the only charted study in which the number of people, the number of analysis units and the number of rows in every reported metric are the same figure.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Autistic adults, autistic individuals, neurodivergent, non-autistic, camouflaging, masking, neurotypical behavior. The framing is identity-first and community-aligned throughout: camouflaging is described as an adaptive social coping strategy rather than a symptom, the paper states explicitly that adapting one's behaviour in social contexts - whether to avoid discrimination or to achieve personal goals - is not inherently pathological and does not necessarily indicate autism, and it warns that mental health professionals should be aware of unintentional reinforcement of stigma and the pathologization of (mal)adaptive social strategies like social camouflaging. Non-binary participants are analysed as a group in their own right rather than dropped, and the paper states its reason for using self-reported gender rather than sex assigned at birth: it better reflects participants' identities. This is the only study in the charted corpus whose language would be recognised as respectful by the population it studies.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: The most complete demographic and clinical reporting in the corpus. Age by group with means, SDs and a tested 2.7-year difference with effect size and confidence interval; mean age at autism diagnosis (32.0 years, SD 12.3); self-reported gender in three categories with between-group tests; full education distribution from no studies to PhD for both groups; and a complete self-reported comorbidity table covering high abilities, ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, specific learning disorder, epilepsy, bipolar disorder, eating disorder, anxiety, depression and sleep disorder, with percentages for both groups. Nationality/residence is stated (Spain). The women-heavy composition (78% overall) is not merely reported but explained and named as the study's most notable limitation, with a mechanism offered - the parent project validates an instrument designed for highly masked autistic adults, especially women, and online studies skew toward respondents with topic interest, higher cognitive ability and moderate-to-high socioeconomic status.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Self-reported but with real safeguards, and honestly characterised. Participants were asked about a clinically based diagnosis and about which professional made it; the 12 who reported self-diagnosis were excluded; and respondents were instructed to report only clinician-confirmed diagnoses and not diagnoses based on personal feelings of distress. The authors then name the residual uncertainty as a limitation and recommend clinician-based confirmation in future work. No diagnostic instrument was administered by the research team. Importantly, diagnosis is not the prediction target here - it is a covariate tested for incremental value - so the study's central claims do not rest on label accuracy in the way the rest of this corpus does.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Dimensional and psychometrically characterised. BAPQ Aloofness, Pragmatic Language and Rigid Personality are the autistic-trait outcomes; PHQ-9 and GAD-7 total scores the affective outcomes; CAT-Q-ES compensation, masking and assimilation subscales the predictors. McDonald's omega is computed in this sample for every instrument (CAT-Q-ES .96, GAD-7 .92, PHQ-9 .91, Aloofness .94, Pragmatics .87, Rigidity .92), and the known psychometric weakness of the Spanish BAPQ Pragmatic Language subscale is flagged in advance.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is to evaluate whether machine learning on self-reported camouflaging behaviours can predict dimensional autistic traits and anxiety/depression symptoms, and whether knowing a person's gender or autism diagnosis improves that prediction. Headline findings: correlations between true and predicted scores of R=.85 for Aloofness, .82 for Pragmatics and .75 for Rigidity (strong by the pre-specified Colton criterion), against .58 for Depression and .54 for Anxiety (moderate); and adding gender and/or diagnosis changes R by at most .03, from which the authors conclude that this information is already implicit in the camouflaging items. The stated implication is a possible screening aid for people whose autistic traits are masked or subthreshold and whose diagnosis is unclear or not yet established, regardless of gender identity.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: An online REDCap survey hosted at Fundacion Publica Galega de Medicina Xenomica, disseminated through autism associations, institutions, federations, clinical units, research networks and social media, within a broader project validating the CAT-Q for the Spanish population. Recruitment channel is stated and its selection consequences are analysed in the limitations rather than left implicit.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: No task or paradigm - a self-report battery completed in one sitting: the 25-item CAT-Q-ES (Likert 1-7) as predictors, and the 36-item BAPQ, the PHQ-9 and the GAD-7 as outcomes. This is the design's central methodological feature and its principal limitation, discussed under RQ4.5.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single administration. Ethics reporting is complete: Declaration of Helsinki, approval by the Ethics Committee of the University of Santiago de Compostela with the code USC 26/2023, informed consent presented in the survey's first section before participation, and participant anonymity preserved throughout collection. Beyond procedural ethics, the discussion contains a substantive ethical analysis absent from every other study charted here - it warns against reinforcing stigma and pathologising adaptive social strategies, insists that algorithmic models should never replace clinical evaluation, and requires that clinicians apply them within a personalised-medicine approach respecting patient autonomy and daily-life context.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: REDCap for capture, with validated data entry, audit trails for tracking data manipulation and export, and automated export procedures. Modelling used fifty regressors implemented in Python, R, Matlab and Octave, with the package and hyperparameter tuning grid for each listed in a supplementary appendix.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: The highest in the charted corpus. Code and a small sample dataset are publicly deposited on OSF - the only working code released by any study in this review. The fifty models, their implementation languages, packages and hyperparameter grids are enumerated in supplementary material. The cross-validation procedure is specified operationally, including partition disjointness, stratification across the score range, the rotation of training/validation/test roles across four trials, and the refit-on-train-plus-validation step. Missing data are quantified (0.30%) and the imputation justified. Exclusions are counted and reasoned. Internal consistencies are computed in-sample for every instrument. The only gap is the full dataset, withheld for confidentiality with a sample released in its place.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: A genuine limitations section, self-critical and mechanistic rather than formulaic. Four limitations are stated with reasoning: the over-representation of women, traced to the parent validation project and to online-recruitment bias toward respondents with topic interest, higher cognitive ability and moderate-to-high socioeconomic status; the inability to verify self-reported diagnoses, with the mitigation described and its residual risk acknowledged; the weaker anxiety and depression models, explained through instrument structure (PHQ-9 and GAD-7 items each map to a distinct diagnostic criterion and so scatter, whereas BAPQ items are interrelated within domain); and the restriction to generalised anxiety, omitting social anxiety, which is the form most closely tied to masking. The one limitation not stated is the shared-method dependence between predictors and outcomes.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Include clinician-confirmed diagnoses and observational measures of camouflaging alongside self-report; replace criterion-based screeners with dimensional continuous scales for anxiety and depression to reduce scatter; and, before any clinical implementation, cross-validate extensively against health-record data. Each future direction addresses a specific stated limitation, which is rare in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Camouflaging behaviour, decomposed into compensation (copying others' behaviours, preparing scripts for social situations), masking (controlling and adjusting facial and bodily expression to fit in) and assimilation (effortful engagement and pretending to be normal in social situations). The outcomes are dimensional autistic traits - aloof personality, pragmatic language, rigid personality - and depressive and anxious symptoms. The behaviour of interest is therefore an active social strategy rather than a deficit, and the study is the only one in the corpus to treat an autistic behaviour as adaptive rather than symptomatic.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No modality fusion - a single self-report modality throughout. The nearest analogue is the input-configuration comparison, which tests whether adding gender and/or autism diagnosis to the CAT-Q-ES items improves prediction and finds that it does not. The authors themselves identify observational measurement of camouflaging as the modality this study lacks and recommend adding it.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Fifty supervised regression algorithms compared under a common protocol - support vector regression, neural networks, linear and regularised linear regressors, decision trees, random forests, boosting ensembles, k-nearest neighbours and Gaussian processes among others. Different algorithms won for different outcomes (SGD for Aloofness, SVR for Pragmatics, Ridge for Rigidity, KNN for Depression, boosted trees for Anxiety), and the winners are simple regularised or instance-based methods rather than deep networks. This is regression to continuous scores rather than the binary classification that dominates the corpus, which removes the threshold and prevalence problems that make most of the charted accuracy figures uninterpretable.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: The 25 raw CAT-Q-ES Likert items, in four configurations: items alone, items plus gender, items plus autism diagnosis, and items plus both. Subscale scores were tested as an alternative input and did not improve accuracy - a negative result the paper reports rather than suppresses.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Pearson R between true and predicted scores, MAE, MAPE relative to the score range, and RMSE, per outcome and averaged across the four trials, with predicted-versus-true scatter plots against a perfect-agreement diagonal. Correlation magnitudes are interpreted against a pre-specified external criterion (Colton 1974), so strong and moderate are defined before the results rather than after. The tolerance analysis is the most practically informative reporting in the corpus: the best Aloofness model places 36.3% of predictions within 5% of the true score and just over 60% within 10%, which states plainly what the R=.85 does and does not deliver at the individual level. The paper also notes correctly that the lower MAE for Depression and Anxiety reflects their narrower score ranges rather than better prediction, and reads the MAPE accordingly. Two gaps: no confidence intervals or across-trial variance accompany the metrics, and no trivial baseline (for instance, predicting the sample mean) is reported against which the MAE and RMSE could be judged. A minor inconsistency: the abstract gives Rigidity R=.74 and Depression R=.60, while Table 3 gives .75 and .58 for the CAT-Q-ES-only configuration.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No model-level attribution for the fifty regressors - no coefficients, feature importances or SHAP values are reported, so which camouflaging items carry the signal is not established. The interpretive work is done instead by the input-configuration comparison, which supports a clean negative claim: gender and autism diagnosis add at most .03 to R and 0.10 to MAE, so neither provides information not already implicit in the camouflaging items. That result is the basis for the paper's central applied argument - that the tool could work regardless of gender identity and where a diagnosis is unclear or absent.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The validation design is the most rigorous in the charted corpus and is reported operationally rather than by name. Two-layer 4-fold cross-validation: 601 participants divided into four partitions that are disjoint at the participant level and stratified so that each spans the full score range; in each of four trials, two partitions train, one validates and one tests, with roles rotating so that every partition serves as test exactly once; for models with tunable hyperparameters, candidates are fitted on the training partitions, selected by MAE on the validation partition, then refitted on training plus validation before a single prediction on the untouched test partition; the four test MAEs are averaged. Hyperparameter selection therefore never sees the test data, the analysis unit is the person, and no participant contributes to both sides of any split - the three failures that account for most of the inflated figures elsewhere in this review are all absent here. Two real limitations remain. The first is the one the paper does not name: predictors and outcomes are self-report questionnaires completed by the same person in the same sitting, so the correlations are inflated by common-method variance, and there is direct construct overlap between camouflaging items (which describe effortful management of social interaction) and the BAPQ Aloofness and Pragmatic Language subscales (which measure social and pragmatic difficulty). The R=.85 for Aloofness should be read as agreement between two overlapping self-descriptions of social experience, not as prediction of an independently ascertained trait - which is precisely why the anxiety and depression models, whose outcomes are less conceptually adjacent to camouflaging, drop to .54 and .58. The authors explain that gap through instrument structure; construct proximity is at least as plausible. The second is that no external cohort is tested, which the paper itself insists on before any clinical use. Set against the corpus, this study is the reference point: a properly nested, participant-level, model-selection-clean design applied to a genuinely dimensional target yields R=.85 at best and .54 at worst, with only 36% of individual predictions landing within 5% of the truth - the realistic ceiling against which the 99% and 100% figures elsewhere in this review should be read.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: ASD; Autism; CAT-Q-ES; Camouflaging; Supervised machine learning; Mental health; Gender. Seven terms covering condition, instrument, construct, method, outcome domain and a demographic dimension analysed substantively - the most informative keyword set in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Research in Autism 128:202712 (Elsevier) - a specialist autism research journal rather than an engineering or general-science venue, and the difference is visible throughout: dimensional outcomes, in-sample psychometrics, effect sizes with confidence intervals for group comparisons, a self-critical limitations section, an ethics analysis of algorithmic screening in mental health, and deposited code. It is the only paper in the corpus published in a venue whose reviewers are subject-matter specialists in autism, and it is also the only one to release code, report internal consistencies, or discuss stigma.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2025, accepted 15 September, 133 days with a substantive revision round. Framing is deliberately bounded: the results show the viability of machine learning to predict traits and symptoms and suggest potential for developing a tool that may improve screening in individuals whose diagnosis is unclear or not yet established. The discussion then constrains that further - algorithms should be extensively cross-validated against health records before implementation, should be used as screeners to accelerate referral rather than replace clinical evaluation, and should be applied within a personalised-medicine approach respecting autonomy. Where the rest of this corpus claims diagnosis and delivers checklist arithmetic, this study claims correlation between self-reports and delivers exactly that, with the error bars in view.

data_charting_rubrics.title: A Computational Method for Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Deep Learning Approach
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Ibadi H; Lakizadeh A
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems, 18(3), 312-321
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed as contributing significantly to early diagnosis and intervention strategies and as a powerful tool to enhance ASD diagnosis and improve outcomes for individuals with ASD and their families. No clinician, threshold or prospective evaluation.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of a public facial-image dataset; supervised binary image classification with a single image-level train/validation/test split.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Two kinds. Table 1 reports validation-set accuracy for XGB (73), CNN (72), DenseNet121 (78), ResNet50 (80), VGG16 (71) and VGG19 (76) against the proposed model at 86.5 - these appear to be fitted by the authors. Table 5 and Table 7 report figures for MobileNetV2, MobileNetV3-Large, an integrated classifier, MobileNet-V1/V2 and Xception taken from prior publications, and a further list (MobileNet 87%, Xception 90%, MobileNet 88%, VGG16 68%, VGG16 88%) quoted from five other papers.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None. A dataset of 2,926 images was described as curated from public repositories covering diverse demographics; the citation and the comparison table identify it as the Kaggle autism facial-image corpus used by five of the cited prior studies.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: 224x224 RGB face images; internally re-encoded as a three-channel 224x224 tensor synthesised from ResNet features before entering the transformer.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Iran - Department of Information Technology and Computer Engineering, University of Qom. No data collection.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None. Labels are the autism/non-autism folder assignment of a public image corpus. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or provenance record exists for any image, and the paper does not raise the issue.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: Not stated. The confusion matrix and metrics imply a balanced 200-image test set.
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not reported and not obtainable from images.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Not reported. The dataset is described as paediatric but no age information exists.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 2,926 images at 224x224 pixels. The number of distinct children is unknown and never discussed.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. The conclusion states that further validation on larger, diverse datasets is needed.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Not stated.
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: 50% on a balanced 200-image test set, never stated.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Two-dimensional facial photographs at 224x224.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. Still images, no stimulus, task or session.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None for acquisition. Training used CUDA acceleration; no GPU model or runtime is given.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Low. The optimiser, learning rate, weight decay, loss and split sizes are stated, and the architecture is described in prose with three equations - more than several neighbours provide. But there is no code, no seed, no epoch or batch count, no ResNet or ViT variant specification, no ReAttention or ABAL parameterisation, no augmentation list, no dataset accession beyond a reference number, and no statement of how the 200/200 split was drawn.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: The source is cited as a public repository via reference [29]; no derived split, feature set or model is shared.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Absent. There is no ethics statement, no consent statement and no exemption claim; the string ethic does not appear in the article, and no consideration is given to the provenance of the children's photographs.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Described only as preprocessing and data augmentation techniques applied to enhance quality and prevent overfitting, plus a proposed Attention-Based Augmentation Layer (ABAL) said to apply non-destructive transformations. No specific transformation, parameter or ordering relative to the split is stated.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: A ConvBlock using a pre-trained ResNet whose 512-dimensional output is projected by a 1x1 convolution to three channels and resized to 224x224, then fed to a pre-trained ViT-base.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: PyTorch with torchvision (pre-trained ResNet) and a Hugging Face-style ViTModel. No versions, no seed, no repository.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: None. No confidence intervals; on 200 test images the 95% interval around 91% spans roughly 86% to 95%, which covers most of the comparison table.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Asserted rather than demonstrated. The ReAttention mechanism is described as amplifying diagnostically relevant regions such as eye gaze and mouth movements and as focusing on periocular regions, aligning with clinical studies linking ASD to reduced eye contact. No attention map, saliency visualisation or quantitative attribution is presented to support that claim, and no ablation isolates the ReAttention module's contribution.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not described beyond the fixed optimiser settings. Validation accuracy (86.5) is lower than test accuracy (91), which is reported without comment.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None. The dataset is described as covering diverse demographics but carries no demographic labels.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Hybrid deep learning: pre-trained ResNet convolutional block, pre-trained ViT-base transformer block with a custom residual ReAttention mechanism, global average pooling and a linear classification layer.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: AdamW optimiser, learning rate 1e-5, weight decay 1e-2, cross-entropy loss, CUDA. Epoch count, batch size, seed, ResNet depth, ViT variant details, ReAttention dimensions and the ABAL transformation set are all unspecified.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A single image-level split: 2,526 training, 200 validation and 200 test images. There is no cross-validation, no repetition, no seed, and no statement of how the split was drawn. The dataset is the widely reused web-scraped autism face corpus, which contains repeated images of the same faces - the paper itself notes that one cited study cleaned duplicates from the dataset using the MD5 hash algorithm, and does not do so here.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, AUC, F-measure, G-mean, sensitivity, specificity, fall-out and miss rate, for validation and test, with formulae given and a confusion-matrix figure.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Test set: accuracy 91%, sensitivity 94%, specificity 88%, AUC 95.67%, F-measure 90.99%, G-mean 90.95%, fall-out 0.12, miss rate 0.06. Validation: accuracy 86.5%, AUC 93.65%, F-measure 86.47%, G-mean 86.38%.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None observed. The paper's rationale invokes asymmetric facial movements, eye gaze and mouth movements as ASD biomarkers that the ReAttention mechanism is said to amplify, but the input is a single still photograph in which no movement exists.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Hybrid vision transformers and adaptive learning are offered as a promising direction for future research in ASD classification and medical imaging; validation on larger, more diverse datasets is named as needed.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: None as a section. The introduction is built entirely from a catalogue of other studies' limitations - roughly twenty prior approaches are each summarised with a named weakness (computational cost, pose sensitivity, annotation burden, domain shift, sensor quality, cost of eye tracking, privacy concerns of web tools, cultural variability of handwriting) - and this critical apparatus is not turned on the authors' own design. The conclusion contains a single hedge: while further validation on larger, diverse datasets is needed.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: No participants. 2,926 images at 224x224, described as curated from public repositories covering diverse demographics and labelled autism or non-autism; the comparison tables identify the source as the same Kaggle facial corpus used by all five of the studies it benchmarks against. The split is 2,526 training, 200 validation and 200 test images. Class counts are never stated for any partition, though the metric arithmetic implies a balanced 200-image test set. The number of distinct children is unknown - and the paper is aware that this matters, because it notes that one cited study cleaned duplicates from the dataset using the MD5 hash algorithm, an acknowledgement that the corpus contains repeated images. No deduplication is performed here.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic and non-autistic children, autistic individuals, ASD children, individuals with ASD and their families. The register is clinical and reasonably neutral - non-autistic rather than normal is used for the comparison class - though the opening sentence describes ASD as a complicated neurological disease and the introduction lists cognitive impairments among its defining characteristics. No autistic or community perspective appears.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: None. The dataset is asserted to cover diverse demographics and the model is claimed to address demographic variability, but no age, sex, ethnicity, geography or recruitment information exists for any image and none is reported. The diversity claim is therefore unverifiable, and the paper's stated advance over prior work on limited generalizability across diverse demographics rests on it.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None. Labels are the folder assignment of a public image corpus. No clinical diagnosis, instrument, criterion, assessor or date exists for a single image, and unlike several of its neighbours the paper does not even describe the labelling process in passing. The comparison table's premise - that the models being compared share a common foundation because they use the same dataset - makes this the shared and unexamined weakness of the whole benchmark line.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure; none obtainable from photographs.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is to overcome the limitations of prior facial-image ASD classifiers - computational cost, pose sensitivity, poor generalisation across demographics - with HyVit-ASD, a hybrid combining a pre-trained ResNet convolutional block, a pre-trained ViT with a custom residual ReAttention mechanism, and an Attention-Based Augmentation Layer. Headline findings: test accuracy 91%, sensitivity 94%, specificity 88%, AUC 95.67%, F-measure 90.99%, G-mean 90.95%, fall-out 0.12, miss rate 0.06, against six models the authors fitted (71-80% validation accuracy) and five literature figures on the same corpus (68-90%).
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting. Images were obtained from a public repository; training used CUDA acceleration with no hardware, runtime or environment described.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: No task or paradigm. Static photographs. The rationale nonetheless refers repeatedly to movement - the ReAttention mechanism is justified as capturing fine-grained local features critical for ASD biomarkers such as asymmetric facial movements, and as amplifying regions including eye gaze and mouth movements. None of these is present in a still image, so the architecture's stated motivation describes a modality the study does not use.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional. Ethics reporting is absent entirely - no approval, no consent, no exemption claim, and no mention of where photographs of identifiable children came from or under what terms they may be reused. The paper does note, in summarising prior work, that web-based screening tools raise privacy concerns, so the category is available to it and simply not applied to its own data.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition instrumentation. Modelling used PyTorch with a torchvision pre-trained ResNet and a ViT-base transformer, AdamW at learning rate 1e-5 with weight decay 1e-2, cross-entropy loss and CUDA. No versions, seed, epoch count, batch size or hardware.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Low. The architecture is described in prose with three equations, and the optimiser, learning rate, weight decay, loss function and split sizes are given - a better start than several neighbours. What is missing prevents replication: no code, no seed, no epoch or batch count, no ResNet depth or ViT variant, no parameterisation for either of the two components claimed as novel (ReAttention and the Attention-Based Augmentation Layer), no list of augmentation transformations, no dataset accession beyond a reference number, no class counts for any partition, and no statement of how the 200-image validation and test sets were drawn from 2,926.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: None of its own. This paper has the corpus's most extensive limitations apparatus pointed entirely outward: the introduction runs through roughly twenty prior approaches and attaches a specific weakness to each - high computational cost and limited generalizability across diverse demographics, sensitivity to non-frontal poses, dependence on iterative expert annotation, computational intensity of heterogeneous data fusion, susceptibility to noise in handcrafted features, laborious EEG preprocessing, expensive eye-tracking hardware, domain shift in EfficientNet on medical images, scarce labelled data, need for high-quality motion sensors, shallow architectures, accuracy sacrificed for deployability, privacy concerns and connectivity dependence in web tools, cultural variability in handwriting, cost and immobilisation requirements of fMRI, and overfitting risk in metaheuristic optimisation. It even observes that cross-validation may not reflect real-world variability, risking overfitting. None of this critical vocabulary is turned on its own single unrepeated image-level split of an unlabelled web corpus. The only self-directed hedge is a clause in the conclusion.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Hybrid vision transformers and adaptive learning as a direction for future research in ASD classification and medical imaging, and validation on larger, more diverse datasets. The second addresses the study's real gap; the first proposes more of what was just done.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: None. The classification target is static facial appearance. The paper's own account of what the model attends to - periocular regions, eye gaze, mouth movements, asymmetric facial movements - describes dynamic behaviours that a single photograph cannot contain, so the stated biomarker rationale and the actual input are mismatched.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No fusion of modalities. The hybrid designation refers to combining two vision backbones (ResNet and ViT) over the same image. The introduction reviews multimodal neuroimaging and EEG-plus-eye-tracking work and dismisses both on cost and complexity grounds.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A three-stage architecture: a ConvBlock in which a pre-trained ResNet produces a 512-dimensional feature vector that is projected by a 1x1 convolution to three channels and interpolated back to 224x224; a TransformerBlock applying a pre-trained ViT-base with a residual ReAttention mechanism; and global average pooling into a linear classifier. The intermediate step is unusual and unexplained - ResNet features are collapsed to a three-channel image-shaped tensor purely so that a pre-trained ViT's input interface can consume them, which discards most of the convolutional representation before the transformer sees it. No ablation tests whether the ConvBlock, the ReAttention module or the ABAL contributes anything.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: 224x224 RGB face crops from the public corpus, with unspecified preprocessing and augmentation plus a proposed Attention-Based Augmentation Layer applying unnamed non-destructive transformations. Neither the augmentation set nor its placement relative to the split is stated.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, AUC, F-measure, G-mean, sensitivity, specificity, fall-out and miss rate, with formulae given, reported for both validation and test, plus a confusion-matrix figure. This is a fuller and better-chosen metric set than most of the facial-image branch offers - specificity and fall-out are reported as numbers rather than merely claimed, and the figures are internally consistent (sensitivity 94% with miss rate 0.06; specificity 88% with fall-out 0.12; their mean 91% matching the reported accuracy on a balanced test set). Two problems. No confidence interval accompanies any figure, and on 200 test images the 95% interval around 91% runs from roughly 86% to 95% - a range that contains almost every entry in the comparison tables, so the claimed ordering among methods is not established. And validation accuracy (86.5%) is lower than test accuracy (91%) by 4.5 points on 200 images each, which is reported without comment.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Claimed, not shown. The ReAttention mechanism is described as adaptively amplifying diagnostically relevant regions such as eye gaze and mouth movements and as focusing on periocular regions, aligning with clinical studies linking ASD to reduced eye contact. No attention map, saliency overlay, feature attribution or region-level analysis appears anywhere in the paper to support this, and no ablation isolates the module. The claim that the model attends to the periocular region - which would be the study's most interesting finding if demonstrated - is asserted as a design intention and presented as though it were a result.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: A single image-level split of 2,926 images into 2,526 training, 200 validation and 200 test, with no cross-validation, no repetition, no seed and no description of how the split was drawn. Three problems follow. First, the corpus is the widely reused web-scraped autism face collection, which contains duplicate and near-duplicate images of the same individuals; the paper demonstrates awareness of exactly this, noting that a cited study cleaned duplicates from the dataset using the MD5 hash algorithm, and then does not deduplicate, so images of the same child can sit on both sides of the split. Second, the test set is 200 images, giving a 95% confidence interval around 91% of roughly 86-95% - wide enough to contain the great majority of the comparison entries the paper ranks itself above, including MobileNet-V1 at 90.67 and Xception at 92.01, so the reported ordering is not supported. Third, validation accuracy is 4.5 points below test accuracy on partitions of equal size, an inversion that normally indicates split variance rather than generalisation and is reported without remark. Underneath all three sits the problem the whole benchmark line shares and this paper states approvingly: the models being compared have a solid common foundation because they use the same dataset - a dataset with no diagnostic labels, no provenance and no demographic information. A common foundation of that kind makes the numbers comparable to each other and to nothing else.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Autism spectrum disorder; Vision transformers; Facial image analysis; ReAttention; Early diagnosis; CNN. Four of six terms name architecture; participants, validation and setting are absent.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems 18(3):312-319 - an open-access computing journal. Review appears to have been rapid (received 17 January 2025, revised 4 February 2025) and did not surface the absent ethics statement, the unreported class counts, the 200-image test set behind a four-way ranking claim, or the mismatch between a movement-based biomarker rationale and a still-image input.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2025. Framing is diagnostic and confident: the model is a pioneering approach contributing significantly to early diagnosis and intervention strategies, and a powerful tool to enhance ASD diagnosis and improve outcomes for individuals with ASD and their families, hedged only by a clause acknowledging that further validation on larger, diverse datasets is needed. The contribution is expressed as a position in a leaderboard over one public image corpus, and the paper is explicit that this shared corpus is what makes the comparison solid - which is the clearest statement in the review of how this branch understands evidence.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Early Detection of ASD from Facial Images Using DeepDeblur and Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Vijayan N; Vanitha DV
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems, 18(4), 1-11
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed as computer-aided diagnosis and as assisting the reintegration and treatment of autistic patients. No clinician, threshold or prospective evaluation.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of a public facial-image dataset; a two-stage deblurring-plus-classification pipeline with metaheuristic parameter tuning, evaluated on a stated image-level split.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Deblurring: Deepblur, Wiener filtering and blind deconvolution. Classification: literature-quoted figures for MobileNet (94.6% on 3,014 images), CNN-Xception (96.63% on 2,636), MobileNetV2 (92.0% on 2,940), VGG19 (94.8% on 2,940) and a hybrid attention model (96.5% on 2,926). None re-run by the authors.

data_charting_rubrics.country_region: India - Avinashilingam Institute for Home Science & Higher Education for Women, Coimbatore, and Adi Shankara Institute of Engineering and Technology, Kerala. No data collection.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None. Labels are the folder assignment of a Kaggle image corpus. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or provenance record exists for any image, and the paper does not mention the issue.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 1,470 autistic images
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not reported and not obtainable from images.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 2,940 facial images. The number of distinct children is unknown and never discussed.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 1,470 non-autistic images
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: 50% by construction (1,470 versus 1,470), never stated.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Two-dimensional facial photographs.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. Still images, no stimulus, task or session.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None for acquisition. Analysis in MATLAB R2021a; no hardware or runtime described.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Very low. The dataset source and class counts are given, the split sizes are stated, and MATLAB R2021a is named - but the reported result does not correspond to the stated split, no architecture is specified, no learning rate, batch size or epoch count appears, the Fire Hawk Optimizer's search space and budget are unstated, the image resolution is unstated, and there is no code or seed. The deblurring evaluation reports PSNR, MSE and SSIM, which require a sharp ground-truth reference that does not exist for downloaded web photographs; how those references were obtained is never explained.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Kaggle source cited by reference number; no derived splits, deblurred images or trained models shared.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Absent. There is no ethics statement, no consent statement and no exemption claim; the string ethic does not appear in the article.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Image resizing described as adjusting the facial image for ratio and resolution with the loss of pixels, followed by DeepDeblur sharpening (a convolution/deconvolution network learning a blurred-to-sharp mapping) and then joint denoising within the classifier.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: End-to-end within the Denoising Optimized CNN (DOCNN), in which one layer set performs denoising and the next performs classification, with a Fire Hawk Optimizer tuning parameters.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: MATLAB R2021a. No toolbox versions, seed or repository.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: None. No confidence intervals, no repeated runs, no variance.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None. No saliency, attribution or ablation isolating DeepDeblur, the denoising branch or the Fire Hawk Optimizer, although the pipeline has three separable components each claimed as a contribution.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Fire Hawk Optimizer over unstated parameters with an unstated objective and unstated budget; the data partition on which the optimiser's fitness was evaluated is not identified.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None. No demographic variable exists in the data.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Two-stage deep learning: DeepDeblur (CNN-based deblurring) followed by DOCNN, a joint denoising-and-classification CNN whose parameters are tuned by the Fire Hawk Optimizer, a swarm metaheuristic.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: A notation table of 25 symbols and a set of loss terms are given (L2 loss, total variation loss, facial semantic loss, total loss). Layer counts, filter sizes, learning rate, batch size, epoch count, FHO population and iteration budget, and the tuned parameter set are all unspecified.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Stated as an image-level split of 2,940 into 2,540 training (1,270 per class) and 400 test images (200 per class). The reported result does not come from that test set: the results section states that out of 2,940 images used for evaluation the model correctly classified 1,430 autism and 1,420 non-autism images, 2,850 correct against 90 wrong. 2,850/2,940 = 96.94%, exactly the headline accuracy, so the reported figure is a resubstitution estimate computed over the entire dataset including the 2,540 training images. No cross-validation, no repetition, no seed.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Classification: accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure, a confusion matrix and an ROC curve. Deblurring: percentage blur removed, PSNR, MSE and SSIM.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Accuracy 96.94%, precision 97.28%, recall 96.62%, F-measure 96.95%. Deblurring: 91.22% blur removed, PSNR 32.75 dB, MSE 0.115, SSIM 0.96, against Deepblur (87.67%, 30.43 dB, 0.176, 0.77), Wiener filtering and blind deconvolution.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None. Static facial appearance; the paper frames facial features as a diagnostic route alongside behavioural change analysis.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: None. There is no future-work section.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: None. There is no limitations section. The word limitations appears once, describing challenges of facial-feature analysis in general terms in the introduction.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: No participants. 2,940 images from the Kaggle ASD Children Facial dataset, balanced at 1,470 autistic and 1,470 non-autistic - the fourteenth charted reuse of this corpus in the review. The number of distinct children is unknown and never raised, and the corpus is known to contain repeated images of the same faces. The paper states a split of 2,540 training images (1,270 per class) and 400 test images (200 per class), but the confusion matrix it then reports covers all 2,940 images, so the population behind the headline figure is the whole dataset rather than the held-out 400.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic and non-autistic faces, autistic patients, children. The register is medical and dated: ASD is introduced as a neurodevelopmental disorder with ineffective brain functions and as a conventional developmental neuro-disorder, and deep learning is credited with developing interactive systems to assist in the reintegration and treatment of autistic patients. No autistic or community perspective appears.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography, socioeconomic status or recruitment source for any image, and no acknowledgement that this information is absent. One of the studies the paper summarises in its own literature review notes that model reliability depends on dataset quality and race factors, so the concern is present in the article's field of view and is not applied to its own data.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None. Labels are Kaggle folder names on photographs of unknown provenance. No clinical diagnosis, instrument, criterion, assessor or date exists for a single image. The paper opens by observing correctly that there is no medical screening or test like a blood test or scan for ASD and that diagnosis requires developmental history and behavioural assessment - and then treats folder labels on downloaded photographs as sufficient ground truth for a diagnostic classifier.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure; none obtainable from photographs.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is to make facial-image ASD screening robust to poor image quality by adding a deblurring stage and a joint denoising-classification network with metaheuristic parameter tuning. Headline findings: accuracy 96.94%, precision 97.28%, recall 96.62%, F-measure 96.95%, against five literature figures between 92.0% and 96.63%; and, for the deblurring stage, 91.22% blur removed with PSNR 32.75 dB and SSIM 0.96 against Deepblur, Wiener filtering and blind deconvolution.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting. Images downloaded from Kaggle; experiments run in MATLAB R2021a with no hardware, runtime or environment described.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: No task or paradigm. Static photographs with no stimulus, interaction or session. The construct measured is facial appearance, framed as a diagnostic route parallel to behavioural analysis.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional. There is no ethics statement, no consent statement and no exemption claim, and no consideration of where photographs of identifiable children came from or under what terms they may be reused, deblurred, denoised and redistributed in figures - the paper reproduces sample faces at five processing stages in Figure 3.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition instrumentation. Implementation in MATLAB R2021a. No toolbox versions, hardware, runtime, seed or code. The proposed pipeline's components - DeepDeblur, DOCNN and the Fire Hawk Optimizer - are described by loss functions and a notation table rather than by any reproducible configuration.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Very low, with one distinctive problem. The dataset source, class balance, split sizes and MATLAB version are stated, and a 25-symbol notation table with loss definitions (L2, total variation, facial semantic, total) is provided - superficially detailed. But no architecture, learning rate, batch size, epoch count, image resolution, optimiser budget or search space is given; there is no code or seed; the reported result does not correspond to the stated split; and the deblurring evaluation reports PSNR, MSE and SSIM, all of which are computed against a sharp ground-truth reference image. No such reference exists for a photograph downloaded from the web. Either the blur was synthetically added to already-degraded web images so that a reference existed - in which case the deblurring result describes recovery from artificial corruption and says nothing about real image quality - or the metrics were computed against something unstated. The paper does not say which.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: None. There is no limitations section, no threats-to-validity discussion and no caveat. The single occurrence of limitations is a generic sentence in the introduction about facial-feature analysis being affected by image quality and expression variation - which is the problem the paper sets out to solve, not a limitation of its solution. Nothing is said about the dataset's provenance, the absent diagnostic labels, the mismatch between the stated split and the reported evaluation, or the absence of any ablation.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: None. There is no future-work section; the paper ends on the claim of higher accuracy with reduced model complexity.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: None. No behaviour is observed, elicited or measured. The target is static facial appearance recovered from deblurring and denoising.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No fusion of modalities - a single image source. The pipeline stacks three processing stages (deblurring, denoising, classification) over one photograph, which is depth rather than multimodality.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A two-stage pipeline: DeepDeblur, a convolution/deconvolution network learning a blurred-to-sharp mapping, followed by DOCNN, a CNN in which one layer set denoises and the next classifies, with a Fire Hawk Optimizer tuning parameters. Three separable components are each claimed as a contribution and none is ablated, so the reader cannot tell whether the deblurring stage, the denoising branch or the metaheuristic contributes anything to the classification result.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Resized, deblurred and denoised RGB face images at unstated resolution. Resizing is described as adjusting the facial image for ratio and resolution with the loss of pixels - an unusual admission that information is discarded before the pipeline whose purpose is to recover information begins.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure, a confusion matrix and an ROC curve for classification; percentage blur removed, PSNR, MSE and SSIM for deblurring. Specificity is not reported, no AUC value is given numerically, no calibration or predictive values appear, and no confidence interval accompanies any figure. The reported accuracy of 96.94% reconciles exactly with the confusion-matrix counts - 2,850 correct out of 2,940 - which is the problem rather than a reassurance, because 2,940 is the entire dataset and not the 400-image test set the methods section defines.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No saliency, attribution or feature analysis, and no ablation of the three pipeline stages. In a paper whose thesis is that image quality restoration improves ASD detection, no experiment isolates the contribution of restoration to the classification outcome - the deblurring metrics and the classification metrics are reported side by side but never linked.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: This study's decisive problem is that the reported result does not come from its stated evaluation design. The methods define an image-level split of 2,940 images into 2,540 for training and 400 for testing, balanced within each. The results section then states that out of 2,940 images used for evaluation the model correctly classified 1,430 autism images and 1,420 non-autism images, 2,850 correct with 90 misclassified - and 2,850/2,940 is precisely 96.94%, the headline accuracy carried into the abstract and the comparison table. The reported performance is therefore a resubstitution figure computed over the whole dataset, with 86% of the evaluated images having been used to fit the model. The 400-image test set is defined and never used to produce a number. Three further issues compound this. The corpus is the web-scraped autism face collection that repeats individuals, so even a correctly executed image-level split would not separate children. The Fire Hawk Optimizer tuned unspecified parameters against an unspecified objective on an unspecified partition. And the comparison table ranks 96.94% against five literature figures spanning 92.0% to 96.63% obtained on different image counts (2,636 to 3,014) under unstated protocols, with the paper asserting that the comparisons are done under the same conditions used in the existing methods to ensure fair comparison - a claim that cannot hold when this study's own figure is a training-set score.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Autism spectrum disorder; Face recognition; DeepDeblur; Denoising optimized convolutional neural network; Fire hawk optimizer. Four of five terms name pipeline components; face recognition rather than screening or classification is used for the task.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems 18(4) - an open-access computing journal, the same venue as local_6e7174c0. Review did not surface the mismatch between the stated 400-image test set and the 2,940-image evaluation, the absent ethics statement, or the reporting of reference-dependent image-quality metrics for photographs that have no sharp reference.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2025 (received 26 October 2024, revised 1 March 2025). Framing is diagnostic and efficiency-oriented: the model is offered for screening and detection of ASD in children, as computer-aided diagnosis, and as achieving higher accuracy with reduced model complexity and less execution time. There is no limitations section and no future work; the contribution is stated entirely as a position above five quoted figures on the same public image corpus, and the paper's own account of why ASD diagnosis is difficult - that there is no blood test or scan and that developmental history and behaviour must be assessed - is not reconciled with what it then does.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Jeon I; Kim M; So D; Kim EY; Nam Y; Kim S; Shim S; Kim J; Moon J
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed as supporting the adoption of AI-driven diagnostic tools by healthcare professionals, with practical R-based guidelines offered for non-experts. Paediatric and psychiatric clinicians are co-authors and are credited with guiding feature selection, but no clinician-facing evaluation or prospective test is conducted.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of a single public tabular dataset, with an expert-guided preprocessing pipeline, eight classifiers compared under 10-fold cross-validation with grid-search tuning, non-parametric model-comparison tests, and post-hoc explanation by PFI, LIME and SHAP.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Internal, across the eight algorithms, with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests comparing the neural network against each other model on fold-wise metrics and a Friedman test across all models. No external benchmark is re-run.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None. The ASD Children Traits dataset was downloaded from Kaggle (uppulurimadhuri/dataset, accessed 1 June 2024). The originating collection procedure, setting, country and dates are not described.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A 19-field tabular row per child, with categorical variables integer-coded.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Republic of Korea - Soonchunhyang University (Departments of Medical Science, ICT Convergence, AI and Big Data) with clinical co-authors from the Departments of Paediatrics and Psychiatry at Soonchunhyang University Cheonan Hospital. No data collection.
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: Present as predictors rather than as descriptors: the Social Responsiveness Scale (0-10), CARS (recoded 1-4 as nothing/little/medium/severe), the AQ10 total score (1-10) and the Qchat_10_Score (0-10). None is reported as a participant characteristic - no mean, range or distribution by class.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None. The dependent variable is ASD_traits, a binary field indicating whether ASD traits are present. No clinician assessment, diagnostic instrument administration, criterion or assessor is described for any case; the paper nonetheless describes the task throughout as ASD diagnosis and the cases as patients.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: Not reported for either the raw or the preprocessed dataset.
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Global Developmental Delay / Intellectual Disability is present as a binary variable, but no cognitive measure and no distribution are reported.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: 1 to 18 years (Age_Years), fully populated. No mean, SD or distribution, and no per-class breakdown.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Sex is present as a variable (M/F, recoded 1=boy, 2=girl) but no counts or proportions are reported.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Recorded as binary variables and used as model inputs: speech delay/language disorder, learning disorder, genetic disorders, depression, global developmental delay/intellectual disability, social/behavioural issues, anxiety disorder. No prevalence figures are reported for any of them.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 1,985 cases with 28 variables before preprocessing; 634 cases with 19 variables after. Two thirds of the dataset (68%) was removed during preprocessing.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. The abstract nonetheless states that rigorous data-preprocessing improved the models' generalizability and real-world applicability across diverse clinical datasets, although only one dataset was used.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Not reported. The introduction notes that ASD assessment datasets typically over-represent ASD cases, but the study's own class balance is never given.
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Waived, with an explicit justification: the dataset is widely accepted and publicly available, has been used in numerous research studies establishing a general consensus regarding its use for research purposes, and all patient information has been de-identified.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not stated, and not derivable - the class balance of the 634-case analysis set is never reported. The introduction observes that ASD datasets typically over-represent ASD cases, which makes the omission more consequential.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Tabular questionnaire and clinical-record fields: ten AQ-10 behavioural items, four instrument scores (SRS, CARS, AQ10, Q-CHAT-10), seven comorbidity flags, and demographics (age, sex, ethnicity across 11 categories, family history, rater).
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. Tabular records with no observation, stimulus or session.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None. Tabular data.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Moderate to high on the artefacts, low on the decisive step. Strengths: the source dataset is cited with URL and access date; the preprocessed 634-case analysis dataset is deposited as supplementary Table S1; per-fold metrics for all eight models are given in Appendix A; the software environment is named with a version for caret; every model family is specified with equations; and the k-NN k-sweep is fully reported. Weakness: the preprocessing that removed 68% of the records and 9 of the 28 variables is described only as expert-guided outlier and inconsistency removal, with no criterion, no per-step counts, no class composition of the removed records and no seed - so the single step that most affects the result cannot be reproduced.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: The source Kaggle dataset is cited with a URL and access date, and - unusually - the preprocessed 634-case dataset is supplied as supplementary Table S1 (ASD_Preprocessed_Dataset.xlsx). Per-fold performance metrics are also given in Appendix A.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not available. R and caret are advocated at length as accessible to non-experts, and practical guidelines are offered, but no script is deposited.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Formally waived: ethical review and approval were waived due to the use of publicly available data without any identifiable information.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Outlier removal, missing-data handling and feature selection based on clinical expert advice, described as identifying inconsistencies and removing erroneous data to increase dataset reliability. The result is a reduction from 1,985 samples and 28 variables to 634 samples and 19 variables. Neither the outlier criterion, the number of records removed at each step, the class composition of removed records, nor whether removal was blind to the outcome is reported.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: None beyond expert-guided variable selection. The 19 retained variables include the ten AQ-10 items, the AQ10 total, the Q-CHAT-10 score, SRS, CARS, seven comorbidity flags and demographics.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: R with the caret package version 6.0.94, plus the iml package for SHAP and permutation feature importance and the lime package for LIME; glmnet and class packages named for logistic regression and k-NN. Package versions beyond caret are not given, and no seed is reported.
