data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Extensive and appropriate in form: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests of the neural network against each competitor on fold-wise metrics, and Friedman tests across all eight models for each metric, with chi-squared statistics and p-values reported. No confidence intervals accompany the point estimates.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Three methods applied to the best models: permutation feature importance, LIME and SHAP. The reported finding is that the A1-A10 behavioural items dominate predictions while demographic variables such as age and ethnicity contribute little, and that SHAP gives the most consistent and reliable explanations. LIME output is reported with probability and explanation-fit values.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Grid search within caret; the resampling scheme used for tuning relative to the outer 10 folds is not specified, so it is unclear whether tuning was nested.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None. Ethnicity is coded across 11 categories and sex is present, but no performance is stratified by either; both appear only as low-importance features in the XAI output.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Eight classical learners compared: random forest, SVM, gradient boosting machine, XGBoost, C5.0, a neural network, k-nearest neighbours and logistic regression.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Grid-search hyperparameter tuning within caret; equations are given for each model family. Concrete tuned values are not tabulated except for k-NN, where accuracy is reported across k=1 to 7 and k=7 selected. A neural network architecture figure is provided.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 10-fold cross-validation with grid-search tuning, with per-fold metrics reported in an appendix; then, prompted by the exceptionally high results, repeat experiments at 2-fold, 4-fold and 5-fold. The analysis unit is the child and folds partition children, so there is no within-participant leakage. What is not addressed is whether feature selection and the 68% record removal preceded the cross-validation - both are described as pipeline steps performed before modelling, so both were applied to the full dataset with the outcome in view.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, F1, precision, recall and area under the precision-recall curve, per model and per fold, at four different fold counts; Wilcoxon signed-rank p-values for pairwise comparison and Friedman chi-squared statistics across models; a k-value sweep for k-NN.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Under 10-fold cross-validation the neural network achieved accuracy 1.0000, F1 1.0000, precision 1.0000 and recall 1.0000, with prAUC 0.9601; GBM and XGBoost both reached accuracy 0.9984 with precision 1.0000; logistic regression 0.9858, SVM 0.9874, C5.0 0.9701, random forest 0.9463 and k-NN 0.8883. The neural network again reached perfect scores at 4-fold and 5-fold, but fell to 0.8691 at 2-fold.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Parent- or professional-reported autistic traits captured by the AQ-10 items, described in the XAI discussion as communication patterns, repetitive actions and frequency of eye contact.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Transition from R to Python to access more advanced machine-learning libraries and foster collaboration in the childcare research community.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: No dedicated limitations section, but the discussion is unusually self-critical in one respect: the authors state that they were concerned about the potential for overfitting because of the exceptionally high performance metrics, and ran additional 2-fold, 4-fold and 5-fold cross-validation experiments specifically to test it. They note that the neural network's perfect scores in certain folds indicate a potential risk of overfitting to specific data characteristics, and that identical metrics for the neural network and k-NN in some tables may indicate redundancy or overfitting in the model implementation or data processing. They nonetheless conclude that the models show some degree of generalizability.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: No participants were recruited. The ASD Children Traits dataset was downloaded from Kaggle: 1,985 cases with 28 variables, covering children aged 1-18. Preprocessing then reduced this to 634 cases and 19 variables - 68% of the records and a third of the variables removed as outliers, inconsistencies or erroneous data identified by clinical experts. Neither the raw nor the preprocessed dataset's class balance is reported anywhere, so the number of ASD and non-ASD cases behind every result in the paper is unknown. This matters more than usual because the introduction states explicitly that ASD assessment datasets tend to over-represent ASD cases and that this can bias models toward the majority class - a problem the authors identify and then never quantify in their own data.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, individuals with ASD, patients, ASD traits, non-ASD. The register is clinical and generally neutral, with person-first phrasing throughout and an explicit concern for quality of life for individuals with ASD. The consistent use of patient for records in a downloaded Kaggle file - patient case identifiers, patient consent, patient information - is worth noting: it treats spreadsheet rows as clinical subjects while the study has no clinical relationship with any of them.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Variables are present but distributions are not. Age spans 1-18 years with no mean or SD; sex is coded M/F with no counts; ethnicity is coded across 11 categories (Asian, Black, Hispanic, Latino, Middle Eastern, Mixed, Native Indian, Others, Pacifica, South Asian, White European) with no counts; family history and rater type (family member, healthcare professional, other) are recorded. Seven comorbidity flags are retained as model inputs - speech/language delay, learning disorder, genetic disorders, depression, global developmental delay/intellectual disability, social/behavioural issues, anxiety disorder - and not one prevalence figure is given for any of them. The dataset is described as comprehensively capturing socioeconomic status, but no socioeconomic variable appears in either variable table.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None. The dependent variable is ASD_traits, a binary yes/no field in a Kaggle spreadsheet. No clinical assessment, diagnostic instrument administration, criterion, assessor or date exists for any case, and the originating collection procedure is not described at all. The paper nonetheless frames the task as ASD diagnosis throughout, titles itself Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics, and opens by criticising clinician-administered instruments for introducing variability and potential bias - a criticism made in favour of a label whose provenance is entirely unknown.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Four instrument scores are present - Social Responsiveness Scale, CARS, AQ10 total and Q-CHAT-10 - and all four are used as model inputs rather than reported as participant characteristics. Not one mean, range or class-wise distribution appears for any of them. This is the study's central analytic problem, examined under RQ4.2 and RQ4.5.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is to combine explainable AI with a rigorous, clinically guided preprocessing pipeline to make ML-based ASD diagnosis both accurate and interpretable, and to provide practical R-based guidelines for non-expert clinicians. Headline findings: under 10-fold cross-validation the neural network reached accuracy, precision, recall and F1 of exactly 1.0000, with GBM and XGBoost at 0.9984 and logistic regression at 0.9858; Wilcoxon and Friedman tests confirmed significant differences between models; and PFI, LIME and SHAP all identified the A1-A10 behavioural items as dominant with demographic variables contributing little.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting. A downloaded Kaggle file analysed in R. The authorship is notable for this corpus - it includes practising paediatric and psychiatric clinicians from a university hospital, and their input is credited with guiding the feature-selection step.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: No task or paradigm. Tabular records combining AQ-10 item responses, four instrument scores, comorbidity flags and demographics, with a rater field recording whether a family member, healthcare professional or other person completed the assessment. The rater field is retained as a predictor rather than analysed as a source of measurement heterogeneity.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis. Ethics is formally addressed and formally waived: ethical review and approval were waived due to the use of publicly available data without any identifiable information, and patient consent was waived because the dataset is widely accepted and publicly available, has been used in numerous research studies establishing a general consensus regarding its use for research purposes, and has been de-identified. The reasoning is at least stated, which distinguishes it from the many charted studies with no ethics statement at all; but the specific argument - that prior reuse establishes a consensus legitimising further reuse - is a citation-count justification for a governance question, and it is offered for a dataset whose own collection consent is never established.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No instrumentation. R with caret 6.0.94, iml for SHAP and permutation importance, lime for LIME, glmnet and class for two of the models. The paper devotes an entire subsection to arguing that R is accessible to non-expert clinicians and offers practical guidelines for its use - a genuine attempt at translation - and then does not release the script that would make those guidelines operational.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Split. The artefact-level reporting is among the best in the charted corpus: the source dataset has a URL and access date, the preprocessed 634-case analysis dataset is deposited as a supplementary spreadsheet, fold-by-fold metrics for all eight models appear in an appendix, caret's version is given, each model family is defined by equation, and the k-NN k-sweep is reported in full. The decisive step is nevertheless irreproducible. Preprocessing removed 1,351 of 1,985 records and 9 of 28 variables on the basis of clinical experts identifying inconsistencies and erroneous data, with no criterion stated, no counts per step, no class composition for the removed records and no indication of whether the removal was made blind to the outcome. Since that step is credited in the abstract with improving generalizability and real-world applicability, and since it is the largest single transformation in the pipeline, the study cannot be reproduced in the respect that matters most.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: There is no limitations section, but the discussion contains the most genuine act of self-scrutiny in the charted corpus. The authors write that because of the exceptionally high-performance metrics observed in our initial model evaluations, we were concerned about the potential for overfitting, and they respond by re-running the entire comparison at 2-fold, 4-fold and 5-fold. They report that the neural network's perfect scores in certain folds indicate a potential risk of overfitting to specific data characteristics, and that identical metrics for the neural network and k-NN in some tables may indicate redundancy or overfitting in the model implementation or data processing. That instinct is correct and is exercised properly. What it does not reach is the cause: no fold count can diagnose a problem that lies in the feature set rather than the partition, and the one experiment that would have settled it - refitting without the SRS, CARS, AQ10 and Q-CHAT-10 scores - is never run. Unmentioned elsewhere: the unreported class balance, the unspecified 68% record removal, the absence of any external dataset behind a claim of applicability across diverse clinical datasets, and the unknown provenance of the label.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: A single direction: migrate from R to Python for access to more advanced machine-learning libraries and better collaboration with the childcare research community. This is a tooling preference rather than a scientific direction, and it addresses none of the study's own identified concerns - not the overfitting the authors flag, not external validation, and not the missing clinical ground truth.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Autistic traits as captured by the ten AQ-10 items, characterised in the XAI discussion as communication patterns, repetitive actions and frequency of eye contact. All behaviour is second-hand and questionnaire-mediated, reported by a family member, healthcare professional or unspecified other.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No modality fusion - a single tabular source. There is, however, a fusion of instrument types within the feature vector that is the study's defining characteristic: AQ-10 item responses, an AQ-10 total, a Q-CHAT-10 total, an SRS score and a CARS severity rating all sit in the same 19-variable input alongside the ASD_traits label they are designed to determine.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Eight classical classifiers compared under a common protocol - random forest, SVM, gradient boosting machine, XGBoost, C5.0, a neural network, k-nearest neighbours and logistic regression - with grid-search tuning in caret and formal statistical comparison by Wilcoxon signed-rank and Friedman tests. No deep learning on raw signals; the comparison is fair in form and the statistical apparatus is more rigorous than anything else in the charted corpus.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A 19-field tabular row containing, together: the ten AQ-10 behavioural items, the AQ10 total score, the Q-CHAT-10 score, the Social Responsiveness Scale score, the CARS severity rating, seven comorbidity flags and demographics - with ASD_traits as the target. This is the review's most concentrated instance of target leakage by instrument inclusion. CARS is a clinician-administered autism severity scale; SRS measures social impairment severity; AQ10 and Q-CHAT-10 are autism screening totals whose thresholds define exactly the kind of traits-present label being predicted; and the ten AQ-10 items are the summands of the AQ10 total. Four separate measurements of the target condition, plus the item-level constituents of one of them, are supplied to the model as predictors of that condition. A perfect neural-network score under this arrangement is the expected outcome, not an anomaly - and it explains why even logistic regression, a linear model on 19 variables, reaches 0.9858.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, F1, precision, recall and area under the precision-recall curve, per model and per fold, at four fold counts, with per-fold tables in an appendix. The choice of prAUC is thoughtful and explicitly justified by the expected class imbalance. Two absences matter. Specificity is never reported for any model, so the false-positive behaviour of a system proposed for paediatric screening is invisible; and the class balance is never given, so neither the prAUC baseline nor the majority-class accuracy can be computed. The reported neural-network figures are accuracy 1.0000, F1 1.0000, precision 1.0000 and recall 1.0000 - a model that misclassifies no child in any of ten folds - with prAUC 0.9601, a combination that is itself internally odd, since a classifier with perfect precision and recall should have a precision-recall curve area of 1.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Three methods, applied properly and to the best models only: permutation feature importance, LIME with reported probability and explanation-fit values, and SHAP, with the authors concluding that SHAP gives the most consistent and reliable explanations for both global and local behaviour. The substantive finding is that the A1-A10 behavioural items dominate while demographic variables such as age and ethnicity contribute little, which the paper reads as evidence that behaviour rather than demography drives ASD prediction and as grounds for clinician trust. The reading is understandable and wrong in an instructive way: the model weights the AQ-10 items heavily because the label is an autism-traits determination made from those items, so the explanation confirms the pipeline's internal arithmetic rather than validating a clinical insight. The XAI apparatus here is the most carefully executed in the charted corpus and is applied to a model whose behaviour it cannot make meaningful.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: On the axes that defeat most of this literature, the design is sound. The analysis unit is the child, the folds partition children, there is no within-participant leakage, hyperparameters are grid-searched, per-fold results are published, model differences are tested with Wilcoxon signed-rank and Friedman statistics rather than eyeballed, and the k-NN sweep is reported. The authors then did what almost no one in this corpus does: they distrusted their own result. Concerned about the potential for overfitting given exceptionally high metrics, they re-ran the full comparison at 2, 4 and 5 folds, observed that the neural network scored perfectly at 4 and 5 folds but fell to 0.8691 at 2, and noted that this indicates a potential risk of overfitting to specific data characteristics. That is the right instinct pointed at the wrong object. Varying the fold count tests partition sensitivity; it cannot detect leakage that lives in the feature set. Here the feature set contains four separate instrument measurements of the target condition - CARS, SRS, AQ10 and Q-CHAT-10 - plus the item-level constituents of the AQ-10 total, all predicting a binary ASD_traits label. Under those conditions accuracy 1.0000 is not overfitting; it is the model reading the answer off the input, and no resampling scheme will change it. Two further issues compound this. The preprocessing removed 68% of the records and a third of the variables through expert identification of inconsistencies and erroneous data, performed on the whole dataset before cross-validation and with no stated criterion, no per-class counts and no indication of outcome blinding - a step credited in the abstract with improving generalizability. And the class balance is never reported, so neither a majority-class baseline nor a prAUC reference exists, and the perfect scores cannot be positioned against anything. The abstract's claim that rigorous preprocessing improved real-world applicability across diverse clinical datasets is made from a single dataset with no external cohort.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: autism spectrum disorder; clinical diagnosis; data preprocessing; healthcare analytics; machine learning; patient outcomes; personalized intervention; explainable artificial intelligence. Eight terms spanning condition, method, application and aspiration; validation and participants are absent, and clinical diagnosis names something the study does not have.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Diagnostics 14(22):2504 (MDPI) - an open-access clinical diagnostics journal, with paediatric and psychiatric clinicians among the authors. The clinical involvement is real and shaped the feature selection; it did not surface that four instrument measurements of the target condition were sitting in the predictor set, which is precisely the observation clinical expertise is best placed to make. The paper cleared review in 40 days.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 8 November 2024 (indexed here under 2025), 40 days from submission. Framing is translational and confident: the integration of ML and XAI promises to revolutionize intervention strategies, the study successfully developed highly precise and interpretable ML models for ASD diagnosis, and the findings support the adoption of AI-driven diagnostic tools by healthcare professionals and contribute to personalized intervention strategies. The paper positions itself in a comparison table against ten prior studies, with the distinguishing contribution in every row being the absence of XAI in the others - so novelty is claimed on the explanation layer while the estimand goes unexamined. Its most interesting feature is that a team including practising clinicians, applying correct cross-validation, formal statistical testing and three explanation methods, arrived at accuracy 1.0000 and treated it as a result to be defended by resampling rather than as a signal to inspect the feature list.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Using explainable machine learning and eye-tracking for diagnosing autism spectrum and developmental language disorders in social attention tasks
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Antolí A; Rodriguez-Lozano FJ; Juan Cañas J; Vacas J; Cuadrado F; Sánchez-Raya A; Pérez-Dueñas C; Gámez-Granados JC
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed cautiously: the approach is described as a preliminary step toward computer-aided diagnosis, and the conclusion states outright that it is more effective as a screening tool than for differential diagnosis.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional primary study with three clinically defined groups, followed by supervised classification across every pairwise and pooled group combination, using four nested feature sets and stratified 5-fold cross-validation.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Internal across algorithms, across the four feature sets, and across every group combination: ASD vs TD, DLD vs TD, ASD vs DLD, and pooled ASD+DLD vs TD. No external benchmark.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Both clinical groups were recruited from early childhood intervention centres in the province of Cordoba. Inclusion required attendance at such a centre and a formal diagnosis of ASD or DLD made by a licensed, experienced team of clinicians following DSM-5 and international diagnostic manual guidelines.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: One tabular row per child, with 24, 60, 72 or 158 eye-tracking variables depending on the dataset.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Spain - University of Cordoba (Departments of Psychology and of Electronic and Computer Engineering), Maimonides Biomedical Research Institute of Cordoba, and the Mind, Brain and Behavioral Research Center, University of Granada.
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: None reported. No ADOS calibrated severity, CARS or equivalent; the study characterises groups by attention and receptive vocabulary rather than by autism severity.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Formal diagnosis of ASD or DLD by a licensed, experienced clinical team following DSM-5 and international diagnostic manual guidelines, made independently of this study as a condition of enrolment at an early intervention centre. The authors note as a limitation that their diagnostic tools could have been supplemented with further assessments but were the only ones available at the time, and that diagnoses made at early ages are provisional and may evolve.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 24 children with ASD (mean age 53.50 months, SD 10.35)
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Two measures reported with group comparisons: a basic attention score (TD 87.09, ASD 73.50, DLD 73.08; F=13.23, p<0.01) and PPVT-III receptive vocabulary standard score (TD 108.75, ASD 98.65, DLD 86.57; F=19.56, p<0.01). Both differ significantly across groups and both are reported as sample characteristics rather than fed to the models.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: 32 to 74 months. Groups are statistically indistinguishable on age (F(2,90)=0.041, p=0.959), which is reported explicitly.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: TD 22 boys / 22 girls; ASD 22 boys / 2 girls; DLD 23 boys / 2 girls (chi-squared 20.15, p<0.01). The imbalance is reported, tested and discussed - the authors note it is in line with the higher reported prevalence of both conditions in males - but it is not adjusted for in the models, so sex remains available to the classifiers as a route to separating the clinical groups from TD.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported beyond the group definitions themselves.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 93 children aged 32 to 74 months (mean 53.51, SD 10.6)
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. Named implicitly through the stated limitation on scope and sample size and the call to replicate.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Two comparison groups: 25 children with developmental language disorder (mean age 54.0, SD 12.14) and 44 typically developing children (mean age 53.23, SD 10.04). The presence of a second clinical group rather than only a typically developing control is the study's defining design feature.
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No, and the limitation section notes that early diagnoses are provisional and may evolve over time, so findings should be interpreted with caution.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Written informed consent from participants' legal guardians, obtained after families were informed of the study's purpose and assessment procedures.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not stated numerically. Group sizes are unequal (24, 25, 44), so the majority-class baselines differ by comparison - approximately 0.65 for ASD vs TD, 0.64 for DLD vs TD, 0.51 for ASD vs DLD and 0.47 for pooled clinical vs TD - which is relevant to reading the 0.63 for ASD versus DLD in particular.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye tracking - gaze during a paired social/non-social visual preference task.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: The eye-tracking paired preferences paradigm, in which social and non-social images are presented side by side. Faces displayed three emotions (happiness, anger, neutral) paired against objects, following established designs from the eye-gaze literature. Nine-point calibration with an animated target preceded testing.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Tobii X2-30 remote screen-based eye tracker at 30 Hz, mounted below a 15-inch laptop screen, with Tobii Studio for stimulus presentation. The reported spatial accuracy of 36 degrees is a typographic error for 0.36 degrees; as printed it would exceed the entire screen.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Moderate. The acquisition protocol is well specified - device, sampling rate, screen, calibration procedure, paradigm, stimulus composition - and the four feature sets are defined by variable count and content, the cross-validation scheme is stated, the F1 interpretive bands are pre-specified, and raw data are offered on request. Missing: the software or workbench used for modelling, hyperparameter settings, any tuning procedure, a random seed, per-fold results, and the full variable lists for the four datasets.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Raw data will be made available by the authors on request, without undue reservation.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Yes, fully specified: Research Ethics Committee of Cordoba, date 02/08/2019, reference number 4393, conducted in accordance with local legislation and institutional requirements and following the Declaration of Helsinki.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Eye-tracking output was transformed into per-participant variable sets. Four nested datasets were constructed: full variables (158), basic variables (24), prior variables (60) and secondary variables (72), differing in how finely stimuli and areas of interest were decomposed.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Standard eye-tracking metrics (fixation duration, fixation count, visit duration, latency to first fixation) computed over areas of interest at four levels of granularity - from a global social/non-social division down to individual facial features and emotional expressions.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Tobii Studio for acquisition. The classification toolkit is not named, although the algorithm set (naive Bayes, logistic model trees) points to a Java-based workbench.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Group characteristics tested with ANOVA (age, basic attention, PPVT-III) and chi-squared (sex), with F statistics and p-values reported. No confidence intervals or across-fold variance accompany the classification results.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Central to the design rather than added afterwards. Algorithms were chosen for interpretability, and the analysis identifies which eye-tracking variables discriminate: broad social versus non-social areas of interest carry the signal, finer decompositions add nothing, and mean duration of visits to objects distinguishes groups. The authors interpret this in attentional terms as difficulty disengaging attention from objects, linking to Landry and Bryson's disengagement account, rather than treating the model as an oracle.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not described; no statement of whether any tuning was nested inside the folds.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: The four group comparisons are themselves the analysis. No further stratification by sex, age or ability, although the marked sex imbalance and the significant PPVT-III differences would have supported it.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Classical interpretable classifiers, chosen for explainability rather than capacity. Naive Bayes and logistic model trees emerged as the most effective.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Not tabulated. No hyperparameter settings, tuning procedure or seed is reported for any algorithm.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Stratified 5-fold cross-validation with the participant as the unit - each fold trains on four fifths of the children and predicts the held-out fifth, and no child contributes data to more than one row. This is participant-level validation, correct in structure. Two design features nonetheless bear on interpretation: the full variable set contains 158 variables for 93 children, so p exceeds n by a wide margin in three of the four datasets; and the reported figures are the best result over four feature sets crossed with several algorithms and four group comparisons, with no correction for that selection and no external cohort.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: F1-score, with precision and recall defined by equation and an explicitly stated interpretive band (0.0-0.5 poor, 0.5-0.7 moderate, 0.8-0.9 good, 0.9-1.0 excellent) fixed in advance of the results.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: F1 0.912 for DLD versus TD; 0.88 for pooled ASD+DLD versus TD; 0.86 for ASD versus TD; and 0.63 for ASD versus DLD. The most informative variables were those grouping stimuli broadly into social and non-social categories; adding finer-grained variables about specific facial features or emotions did not improve classification. Mean duration of visits to objects emerged as a candidate disorder-specific marker.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Social attention: preferential looking to faces versus objects, with fixation duration, fixation count, visit duration and latency to first fixation as the underlying metrics, and areas of interest ranging from whole-stimulus categories down to specific facial regions (eyes, mouth) and emotional expressions.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Add further explainable algorithms (gradient boosting trees, explainable boosting machines) and extend to multimodal data combining eye tracking with behavioural, cognitive or neurophysiological measures.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A short but substantive paragraph: limited scope of the experiment and sample size; diagnostic tools that could have been supplemented with further assessments, with the honest note that these were the only tools available at the time; a call to replicate with current behavioural assessments; and the observation that diagnoses at early ages are provisional and may evolve, so the findings should be interpreted with caution.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Ninety-three children aged 32-74 months in three clinically defined groups: 24 with ASD, 25 with developmental language disorder, and 44 typically developing. Both clinical groups were recruited from early childhood intervention centres in Cordoba province and required a formal diagnosis made by a licensed, experienced clinical team. The analysis unit is the child throughout, and each child contributes exactly one row to each of four feature sets. The inclusion of a second clinical group is what distinguishes this study from almost the entire charted corpus: it makes the ASD-versus-DLD comparison possible, and that comparison is where the study's most informative result lies.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, developmental language disorder, neurodevelopmental disorders, typical development, children with ASD, clinical groups. The register is clinical and precise, using DSM-5 language (persistent deficits in social interaction and communication, repetitive and restrictive patterns) without editorialising. Groups are named by diagnosis rather than by normality - the comparison group is typically developing, never normal. There is no autistic-community engagement, but nothing in the language pathologises beyond the diagnostic criteria themselves.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Among the most complete in the corpus, and reported with statistical tests. Age: TD 53.23 (SD 10.04), ASD 53.50 (10.35), DLD 54.0 (12.14) months, F(2,90)=0.041, p=0.959 - the groups are closely matched on age, which is uncommon here and is demonstrated rather than asserted. Sex: TD 22 boys/22 girls, ASD 22/2, DLD 23/2, chi-squared 20.15, p<0.01 - a large and explicitly tested imbalance which the authors attribute to the higher prevalence of both conditions in males. Basic attention: 87.09 / 73.50 / 73.08, F=13.23, p<0.01. PPVT-III receptive vocabulary standard score: 108.75 / 98.65 / 86.57, F=19.56, p<0.01. Nothing on ethnicity, socioeconomic status or language background. The sex and vocabulary differences matter for the classification results and are not carried into the modelling as covariates.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Clinically ascertained and honestly qualified. Diagnosis of ASD or DLD was made by a licensed, experienced team of clinicians following DSM-5 and international diagnostic manual guidelines, independently of this study and as a precondition of enrolment at an early intervention centre. Typically developing children are defined by the absence of such enrolment. The authors then add two caveats that few in this corpus offer: that their diagnostic tools could have been supplemented with further assessments but were the only ones available at the time, and that diagnoses at early ages are provisional and may evolve over time, so the findings should be interpreted with caution.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: No autism severity instrument is reported. Instead the study characterises its groups on two dimensions relevant to the task: a basic attention score and PPVT-III receptive vocabulary, both with significant group differences. The absence of a severity measure is a real gap for interpreting the ASD group's heterogeneity, but the inclusion of a standardised language measure is directly to the point, since DLD is the comparison condition.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated aim is to apply explainable machine learning to eye-tracking data from a social attention task in children with ASD, DLD and typical development, to assess classification accuracy across all group combinations and to identify which variables best differentiate the groups. Headline findings: F1 0.912 for DLD versus TD, 0.88 for pooled ASD+DLD versus TD, 0.86 for ASD versus TD, and 0.63 for ASD versus DLD; broad social versus non-social areas of interest carried the signal while finer decompositions by facial region and emotion did not improve accuracy; naive Bayes and logistic model trees performed best; and mean duration of visits to objects emerged as a candidate disorder-specific marker.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Early childhood intervention centres in the province of Cordoba supplied both clinical groups; testing used a screen-based eye tracker below a 15-inch laptop, with nine-point calibration. The clinical recruitment route is stated, though the room, examiner and whether TD children were tested under identical conditions are not described.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: The eye-tracking paired preferences paradigm: social and non-social images presented side by side, with faces displaying happiness, anger and neutral expressions paired against objects, following established designs (Sasson and Touchstone; Vacas et al.). This is a purpose-built social-attention task drawn from the developmental literature rather than a repurposed video or free-viewing sequence, and the choice is justified by reference to the metrics - fixation duration, fixation count, latency to first fixation - shown to be sensitive to gaze differences across neurodevelopmental conditions.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional, single session. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: approval by the Research Ethics Committee of Cordoba dated 02/08/2019 with reference number 4393, conducted per the Declaration of Helsinki and local legislation, with families informed of the study's purpose and procedures and written informed consent obtained from legal guardians. The discussion adds an ethically relevant scientific caveat - that early diagnoses are provisional - which bears directly on how the labels should be read.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Tobii X2-30 remote eye tracker at 30 Hz on a 15-inch laptop screen with Tobii Studio and nine-point calibration using an animated target. The stated spatial accuracy of 36 degrees is a typographic error for 0.36 degrees - as printed the figure would exceed the visual angle of the entire display. The modelling software is not named, and no hyperparameters, tuning procedure or seed is reported for any algorithm, which is the main reporting gap in an otherwise well-specified study.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Moderate to good on acquisition, thin on modelling. Reproducible: the eye tracker, sampling rate, screen size, calibration procedure, paradigm, stimulus composition and emotion set; the four feature sets by variable count and content; the stratified 5-fold scheme; the F1 interpretive bands, fixed before the results; and an offer of raw data on request. Not reproducible: the modelling workbench, the algorithm settings, whether any tuning occurred and whether it was nested, the seed, per-fold results, and the full variable lists for the 158-, 72-, 60- and 24-variable datasets.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: A short but genuinely self-critical paragraph naming four things: the limited scope of the experiment, the sample size, the diagnostic tools (which could have been supplemented but were the only ones available at the time), and the provisional nature of early-age diagnoses, with an explicit instruction that findings should be interpreted with caution and a call for replication with current behavioural assessments. Not mentioned: that the full variable set has 158 variables for 93 children; that the reported figures are the maximum over four feature sets, several algorithms and four comparisons with no correction; that the sex imbalance between clinical and TD groups (approximately 92% male versus 50%) offers an alternative route to the ASD-vs-TD and DLD-vs-TD separations; and that the significant PPVT-III differences are similarly available.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Add further explainable algorithms such as gradient boosting trees and explainable boosting machines, and integrate multimodal data combining eye tracking with behavioural, cognitive or neurophysiological measures to improve robustness and clinical applicability. Both are proportionate to the study's own findings.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Social attention during simultaneous presentation of social and non-social stimuli: preferential looking to faces versus objects, indexed by fixation duration, fixation count, visit duration and latency to first fixation, across areas of interest from whole-stimulus categories down to eyes and mouth and across three emotional expressions. The substantive behavioural finding is about objects rather than faces - mean duration of visits to objects discriminates, which the authors interpret as difficulty disengaging attention from objects rather than as reduced interest in faces.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No multimodal fusion - eye tracking alone. What the study does instead is a granularity comparison within one modality: four nested feature sets ranging from 24 broad variables to 158 fine-grained ones. The result is a clean negative finding that broad social/non-social area-of-interest variables carry the discriminative information while adding specific facial features and emotion categories does not improve accuracy. Multimodal extension with behavioural, cognitive or neurophysiological measures is named as the next step.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Interpretable classical classifiers selected for explainability rather than capacity, with naive Bayes and logistic model trees performing best. No deep learning. The algorithm choice follows from the stated aim - to identify which eye-tracking variables discriminate, in a form clinicians can inspect - rather than from a search for maximum accuracy, and this is one of the few studies in the corpus where the modelling choice is subordinated to the scientific question.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Four nested tabular feature sets per child: full (158 variables), secondary (72), prior (60) and basic (24), differing in how finely stimuli and areas of interest are decomposed. All variables derive from the eye-tracking record; no clinical instrument score, demographic variable or diagnostic measure enters the feature set - a point worth stating explicitly, because it is exactly what separates this study from the corpus's leakage cases. With 93 children and up to 158 variables, three of the four datasets have more variables than participants.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: F1-score only, with precision and recall given by equation. The interpretive bands are stated in advance (0.0-0.5 poor, 0.5-0.7 moderate, 0.8-0.9 good, 0.9-1.0 excellent) and the results are then reported against them, so the descriptions excellent, good and moderate are pre-committed rather than chosen after the fact - a small but genuine discipline. Missing: accuracy, sensitivity and specificity separately, AUC, calibration, confidence intervals, across-fold variance, and any statement of the majority-class baseline. The last matters most for the ASD-versus-DLD comparison, where the classes are nearly balanced (24 versus 25) and F1 0.63 sits only modestly above chance, and for ASD-versus-TD, where the baseline is around 0.65 and the reported 0.86 represents a real but smaller gain than the number suggests in isolation.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Interpretability is the study's purpose rather than an appendix to it. The four-way feature-set comparison yields a negative result that is reported plainly - fine-grained variables about specific facial areas and emotions do not improve on broad social versus non-social groupings - and the surviving discriminative variable, mean duration of visits to objects, is interpreted theoretically as difficulty disengaging attention from objects, connected to an existing attentional account (Landry and Bryson). This is a claim about behaviour that another laboratory could test, generated by a model whose structure a clinician can inspect, which is the intended use of explainable methods and is rare in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The validation is participant-level and structurally correct: stratified 5-fold cross-validation over 93 children, one row per child, no within-participant duplication, and no clinical instrument score anywhere in the feature set. Three caveats qualify the numbers rather than invalidate them. First, dimensionality - the full dataset carries 158 variables for 93 children, and even the smallest carries 24, so the models operate in a regime where cross-validated estimates over five folds are noisy; no interval or fold variance is reported. Second, selection - the headline figures are the best over four feature sets crossed with several algorithms and four group comparisons, with no correction and no held-out cohort, so they are optimistic by an unquantified margin. Third, confounding - the clinical groups are approximately 92% male against 50% in the TD group (chi-squared 20.15, p<0.01) and differ significantly in receptive vocabulary and basic attention, all of which are plausible correlates of gaze behaviour in a paired-preference task; none is adjusted for, so part of the 0.86 and 0.912 against TD may reflect sex and language ability rather than diagnosis. The result that survives all of this is the one the authors themselves foreground: ASD versus DLD reaches only F1 0.63, at nearly balanced class sizes, and they conclude that the approach is more effective as a screening tool than for differential diagnosis. That conclusion is the correct reading of their own data and is the most valuable single sentence in this part of the corpus, because the two comparisons are internally controlled - same task, same equipment, same pipeline, same analyst - so the gap between 0.86 against typical development and 0.63 against another neurodevelopmental condition isolates how much of the apparent signal is autism-specific rather than clinical-population-general.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: explainable machine learning; autism spectrum disorder; developmental language disorder; eye-tracking; differential diagnosis; computer-aided diagnosis. Six terms naming method, both conditions, modality and - uniquely in this corpus - differential diagnosis, which is what the study actually attempts.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Frontiers in Neuroscience 19:1558621 - an open-access neuroscience journal, with a 127-day review. The venue's disciplinary fit shows in the reporting: matched group characteristics with ANOVA and chi-squared tests, a standardised language measure, a pre-specified interpretive scale for F1, an ethics reference number, and a limitations paragraph that includes the provisionality of early diagnoses.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2025, published 24 June, 127 days from submission to acceptance. Framing is deliberately restrained and, unusually, becomes more restrained as the paper proceeds: the abstract reports the ASD-versus-DLD F1 of 0.63 alongside the higher figures rather than burying it, and the conclusion states that the approach is more effective as a screening tool than for differential diagnosis. The clinical claim is limited to a preliminary step toward computer-aided diagnosis. Its contribution to the review is not a performance number but a controlled contrast: by running the same pipeline against a typically developing group and against a second clinical group, it converts the corpus's ubiquitous ASD-versus-TD figure into an interpretable quantity.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Utilizing deep learning models in an intelligent eye-tracking system for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Alsharif N; Al-Adhaileh MH; Al-Yaari M; Farhah N; Khan ZI
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed as usable by physicians and healthcare professionals to enhance the accuracy rate of ASD diagnosis. No clinician, threshold or prospective evaluation.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of a public eye-tracking scanpath image dataset; four deep learning classifiers compared on a single image-level train/validation/test split.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Internal across the four architectures. External: figures quoted from three prior studies on the same dataset - Akter et al. 2021 (87% accuracy, AUC 79%), Cilia et al. 2021 (CNN, 90%) and Elbattah et al. 2021 (variational autoencoder, 79%) - none re-run.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None. The dataset was obtained from a public repository of eye-tracking scanpath images (the Cilia/Carette collection, whose originators are cited in the comparison table).
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: 640x480 scanpath images normalised to [0,1].
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Saudi Arabia - King Salman Center for Disability Research, Albaha University, King Faisal University, Saudi Electronic University and Prince Sultan University. No data collection.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None described. Labels are inherited from the public image collection; no diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or date is reported, and the originating study's diagnostic procedure is not summarised.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 219 images labelled ASD
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 547 scanpath images at 640x480. The abstract describes these as 328 characteristically emerging children and 219 children with autism, converting an image count into a child count; the methods section states correctly that there were 328 images for the people without ASD and 219 images for the persons diagnosed with ASD. The number of distinct children behind the 547 images is never given and, in the source collection, is far smaller.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 328 images labelled non-ASD
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not stated. The test set is 33 non-ASD against 22 ASD, so the majority-class baseline is 60%.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye tracking rendered as images - scanpath visualisations of fixations and saccades, treated as pictures rather than as time series.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Not described. The viewing task, stimuli, session length and recording conditions of the original collection are not summarised, so what the children were looking at is unknown from this paper.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None for acquisition. The compute environment is tabulated (Table 5) but no hardware model or runtime is quoted in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Low to moderate. The per-model parameter tables are unusually complete for this corpus - base architecture, pooling, dense widths, dropout, output activation, loss, optimiser, learning rate, batch sizes and epoch count are all given - and the preprocessing order is stated correctly. But the dataset has no accession or URL, the split proportions are never stated (the test size of 55 must be recovered from a support column), there is no seed or code, the number of distinct children is unknown, and the hybrid model's construction is described only by a figure.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Described as a freely accessible public repository; no accession, URL or DOI is given, and no derived splits or models are shared.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Absent. There is no ethics statement, consent statement or exemption claim; the string ethic does not appear in the article.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Resize to 640x480, image enhancement, conversion to numerical arrays, pixel normalisation to [0,1], splitting into training, validation and test sets, then augmentation (rotation, shifting, flipping) via ImageDataGenerator applied during training. The ordering is stated explicitly and correctly - the split precedes augmentation, and augmentation is confined to training.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Transfer learning from ImageNet-pretrained backbones with the fully connected layers removed.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Keras/TensorFlow implied by the ImageDataGenerator augmentation module and the pre-trained ImageNet backbones. No versions, no seed, no repository.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: None. No confidence intervals; on 55 test images the 95% interval around 92% spans roughly 82% to 98%, and around 78% roughly 65% to 88%.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None. No saliency, attribution or analysis of which scanpath features drive the classification, and no ablation isolating the hybrid model's components.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not described as a search. Fixed settings are reported per model; training ran for 100 epochs with validation accuracy described as rising from 50% to 100%.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None. No demographic variable exists in the data.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Four deep learning classifiers: MobileNet, VGG19, DenseNet169, and a hybrid combining VGG19 and MobileNet.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Reported per model in parameter tables: ImageNet-pretrained base with the top removed, pooling, dense layers with ReLU, dropout 0.5, a two-unit softmax output, sparse categorical cross-entropy, RMSprop at learning rate 0.0001 for MobileNet and Adam at 0.0001 for DenseNet169, training batch size 16, validation batch size 32, 100 epochs, augmentation applied during training.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: A single image-level split into training, validation and test sets. The test partition contains 55 images (33 non-ASD, 22 ASD), recoverable from the support column of the per-class results tables. The split is at the image level on a dataset in which each child contributes multiple scanpath images, so images from the same child appear on both sides. No cross-validation, no repetition, no seed.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Per-class precision, recall, F1 and support, overall accuracy, macro averages, ROC curves, and training/validation accuracy and loss curves. Specificity is defined by equation but not tabulated.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: MobileNet accuracy 100% with perfect precision, recall and F1 for both classes and ROC 100%; VGG19 92%; DenseNet169 78% (non-ASD precision 74%, recall 97%; ASD precision 92%, recall 50%); the hybrid model is reported but its headline figure is not captured in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Visual scanning behaviour during viewing, encoded as the geometric trace of gaze across the stimulus.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: None. There is no future-work section.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: None. There is no limitations section and the word limitation does not appear in the article.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: No participants. 547 scanpath images from a public eye-tracking repository, 328 labelled non-ASD and 219 ASD. The abstract converts this image count into a participant count, describing the dataset as scan pathways obtained from 328 characteristically emerging children and 219 children with autism - which would make this one of the larger primary eye-tracking cohorts in the field. The methods section states the correct version, that these are image counts. The source collection is the Cilia/Carette scanpath set, whose originators are cited in the comparison table and in which a few dozen children contributed multiple scanpath images each; the number of distinct children behind the 547 images is never given here. Every reported metric rests on a test partition of 55 images, recoverable only from the support column of the per-class results tables.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, persons diagnosed with ASD, people without ASD, children with autism, characteristically emerging children, ASD children. The phrase characteristically emerging children appears to be a rewording of typically developing and, together with formulations like monotonous and stereotyped behaviors and the commonness of ASD, suggests heavy paraphrasing throughout. The register is otherwise clinical without being pejorative, and there is no autistic-community perspective.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography or recruitment source for any image, and no acknowledgement that this information is absent - despite the introduction discussing sex ratios in ASD prevalence and noting that girls with ASD often have fewer observable symptoms, a point directly relevant to a dataset whose sex composition is unknown.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None. Labels are inherited from a public image collection with no diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or date reported, and the originating study's diagnostic procedure is not summarised. The paper's opening argument is that conventional ASD assessment relies on subjective criteria and lacks objectivity - a criticism advanced in favour of a label whose ascertainment it never examines.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is to automate ASD categorisation from eye-tracking data using deep learning, in response to the cost, delay and subjectivity of conventional assessment. Headline findings: MobileNet reached 100% accuracy with perfect precision, recall and F1 for both classes and ROC 100%; VGG19 92%; DenseNet169 78%; the proposed model is ranked above three prior studies on the same dataset (87%, 90%, 79%). The paper attributes its advantage explicitly to preprocessing - our model achieved high accuracy because we have used a different preprocessing approach from improving dataset.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting. Images downloaded from an unnamed public repository; the compute environment is tabulated but not quoted in the extracted text. Critically, the acquisition setting of the original data - the viewing task, the stimuli, the eye tracker, the session structure - is nowhere summarised, so a reader cannot say what behaviour the scanpaths record.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Not reported. The paradigm behind the scanpaths is never described. This matters more than usual for a scanpath dataset, because the geometry of a scanpath image is jointly determined by the child and by the stimulus, and without knowing the stimulus set one cannot tell whether the classifier is reading gaze behaviour or stimulus identity.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional. There is no ethics statement, consent statement or exemption claim anywhere in the article, and no consideration of the provenance or consent basis of the underlying eye-tracking recordings of children.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition instrumentation described. Modelling used ImageNet-pretrained MobileNet, VGG19 and DenseNet169 backbones with custom heads, Keras ImageDataGenerator for augmentation, RMSprop or Adam at learning rate 0.0001, batch sizes 16 (training) and 32 (validation), and 100 epochs. Parameter tables per model are provided and are more complete than most in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Mixed. Strengths: per-model parameter tables covering base architecture, pooling, dense widths, dropout, output layer, loss, optimiser, learning rate, batch sizes and epochs; and an explicit, correctly ordered preprocessing sequence in which the split precedes augmentation and augmentation is confined to training. Weaknesses: the dataset is described only as a freely accessible public repository with no accession, URL or DOI; the split proportions are never stated and the test size must be inferred from a support column; there is no seed, no code, and no statement of how many children the images come from; and the hybrid model is specified only by a figure.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: None. There is no limitations section and the word limitation does not occur in the article. Nothing is said about the image-level split on a dataset with repeated images per child, about the 55-image test set, about the absence of any description of the underlying task, or about the fact that three architectures trained on the same data under the same protocol span 78% to 100%.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: None. There is no future-work section; the paper closes on the claim that healthcare professionals can use these classifiers to enhance the accuracy rate of ASD diagnosis.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Visual scanning behaviour, encoded as a rendered scanpath image showing the geometric trace of fixations and saccades. Because the images are treated as pictures rather than as sequences, no fixation duration, saccade amplitude, area-of-interest dwell or temporal ordering is extracted or reported - the behavioural content of the data is entirely implicit in the picture.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No fusion of modalities - one image source. The hybrid model combines two ImageNet backbones over the same image, which is architectural ensembling rather than multimodality.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Four transfer-learning classifiers: MobileNet, VGG19, DenseNet169 and a VGG19+MobileNet hybrid, each with ImageNet weights, the top layers removed, a pooling layer, dense layers with ReLU and dropout, and a two-unit softmax output.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: 640x480 scanpath images, enhanced, converted to arrays and normalised to [0,1], with rotation, shifting and flipping augmentation applied during training only. Augmentation of a scanpath image is worth a separate note: flipping and rotating a gaze trace changes its spatial relationship to the stimulus that produced it, so the augmented examples correspond to no possible viewing behaviour - a transformation that is standard for photographs and semantically incoherent for scanpaths.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Per-class precision, recall, F1 and support, overall accuracy, macro averages, ROC curves and training/validation curves. Specificity is defined by equation and never tabulated. No confidence interval accompanies any figure, and none is possible to infer without the split proportions, which are not stated. The support column is the only place the test-set size appears: 33 non-ASD and 22 ASD, 55 images in total. On 55 images the 95% interval around VGG19's 92% runs from roughly 82% to 98% and around DenseNet169's 78% from roughly 65% to 88%, so the reported ordering of the four architectures - and the ranking against the three prior studies at 87%, 90% and 79% - is not statistically distinguishable.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. No saliency, attribution or scanpath-feature analysis, and no ablation of the hybrid. In a study whose premise is that gaze patterns carry diagnostic information, no gaze pattern is identified, and the paper does not report what distinguishes the ASD scanpath images from the others.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The preprocessing order is handled correctly - the dataset is split before augmentation, and augmentation is applied during training via ImageDataGenerator - which is better than several neighbours in this corpus. Everything else about the evaluation undercuts the result. The split is at the image level on a scanpath collection in which each child contributes multiple images, so images generated from the same child's viewing session sit on both sides of the partition; this is the same within-participant leakage documented across the video, EEG-epoch, thermal, cry and facial-image branches, and it is sufficient to explain a perfect score. The test partition holds 55 images, a figure the paper never states and that must be recovered from a support column, so every reported metric carries roughly plus or minus 11 to 13 percentage points of sampling noise; MobileNet's 100% means 55 of 55 correct. There is no cross-validation, no repetition and no seed, and the spread across four architectures trained identically on the same data - 100%, 92%, 78% and the hybrid - is itself evidence of how unstable a 55-image estimate is, though the paper reads it as a genuine ranking of methods. The comparison against three prior studies on the same dataset (87%, 90%, 79%) is attributed to a different preprocessing approach, when the more parsimonious explanation is that the earlier figures came from evaluations that were less permissive. Finally, the paper never describes the viewing task behind the scanpaths, so it cannot exclude that the classifier is recognising which stimulus produced a trace rather than who produced it.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: autism spectrum disorder; eye tracking; deep learning; VGG19; MobileNet; DenseNet169; hybrid model. Four of seven terms name specific architectures; validation, participants and task are absent.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Frontiers in Medicine 11:1436646 - an open-access clinical journal, accepted in 44 days. A 100% diagnostic accuracy claim, an abstract that reports image counts as child counts, an absent ethics statement, an unstated test-set size and no limitations section all passed clinical review.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Published 19 July 2024 (indexed here under 2025), 44 days from submission. Framing is unqualified diagnostic assistance: the classifiers are said to demonstrate the potential of eye-tracking data to aid physicians in efficiently and accurately screening for autism, and users and healthcare professionals can utilize these classifiers to enhance the accuracy rate of ASD diagnosis. The contribution is stated as a leaderboard position - 100% against 87%, 90% and 79% on the same public dataset - and attributed to preprocessing. There is no limitations section, no future work and no hedge of any kind.

data_charting_rubrics.title: A novel hybrid deep learning model using MEResNext for autism spectrum disorder detection
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Rai S
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed as reducing the need for wide examinations and expensive medical procedures and enabling timely determination of ASD. No clinician, threshold or prospective evaluation.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of a single public tabular screening dataset; a three-stage pipeline (transformation, metaheuristic feature selection, hybrid deep classifier) evaluated across training-percentage and iteration sweeps.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Traditional models, unnamed in the extracted text, against which the proposed method is said to perform better. A long related-work table catalogues the advantages and disadvantages of prior studies but none is re-run.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None. The Autism screening data for toddler dataset was downloaded; no accession, URL or DOI is given beyond a dataset citation.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A tabular vector of Q-CHAT-10 items and individual characteristics after Yeo-Johnson transformation and metaheuristic selection.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: India - Department of Electronics Engineering, Vivekananda Institute of Professional Studies-Technical Campus, New Delhi. Single author. No data collection.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None. The label rule is stated plainly: if the Q-CHAT-10 score is higher than 3 the class value is YES implying ASD traits potential, otherwise NO. No clinical diagnosis, instrument administration, assessor or criterion exists for any record.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Not reported. The dataset is the toddler screening set, so 12-36 months by convention, but the paper does not state it.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Not reported. The number of records in the analysed dataset appears nowhere in the article.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Declared Not Applicable.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not stated and not derivable, since neither the sample size nor the class balance is reported. In the standard toddler Q-CHAT-10 dataset roughly 69% of records are positive, making the majority-class baseline approximately 69%.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Questionnaire - ten Q-CHAT-10 behavioural items plus additional individual characteristics.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. A caregiver checklist.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None. Tabular data; implementation in Python.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Very low, and lower than the page count suggests. The article contains roughly forty numbered equations specifying the MoNet sub-matrix square-root layer and its backward propagation in full detail, and reports none of the information needed to repeat the experiment: no sample size, no class balance, no split or cross-validation scheme, no test-set size, no metaheuristic search space or budget, no number or identity of selected features, no learning rate, epoch count or batch size in the running text, no seed, no library, no code and no dataset accession.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Only a dataset citation; no accession, URL or DOI.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Declared Not Applicable, with no reasoning offered.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Yeo-Johnson transformation, presented as removing noise and artefacts and justified at length against Box-Cox and log transformation on the grounds that it handles negative values. Applied to a feature set consisting largely of binary questionnaire items, for which the notion of noise and artefacts is not defined.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: DeSEHO - Double Exponential Smoothing integrated into the Elk Herd Optimizer - a metaheuristic feature selector. Neither the search space, the fitness function, the population size, the iteration budget, the number of features retained nor the identity of the selected features is reported.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Python. No library, version, seed or repository.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: None. No confidence intervals, no repeated runs, no variance.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None. The metaheuristic selects features and none is named; no importance, attribution or ablation is reported.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The DeSEHO metaheuristic performs feature selection against an unstated fitness function; model hyperparameters are tabulated without a search procedure. Results are reported across iteration and training-percentage sweeps with the maximum carried into the abstract.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: MEResNeXt - a hybrid of the Moments Embedding Network (MoNet) and ResNeXt, both convolutional image architectures, applied to tabular questionnaire data.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Table 2 is said to list MoNet and ResNeXt hyperparameters. The mathematical exposition is extensive - roughly forty numbered equations covering the sub-matrix square-root layer, homogeneous mapping, forward and backward propagation and the aggregated residual transformation - but no learning rate, batch size, epoch count, layer width or cardinality value is quoted in the running text, and no seed is given.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: No split, cross-validation or held-out set is described. Performance is presented as curves against training percentage (70%, 80%) and against iteration count (20 to 80), with the reported headline taken from the best point on those curves. There is no statement of what data the metrics are computed on, no test-set size, no repetition and no seed.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and F1, each plotted against training percentage and iteration count. The definitions given are partly incorrect: accuracy is defined as dividing the total number of instances by the number of correctly classified instances - the reciprocal of accuracy - and specificity is described in words as dividing the total number of false positives and true negatives by the sum of both, which evaluates to 1, although the accompanying equation is correct.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Accuracy 95.3%, sensitivity 96.5%, specificity 94.8%. Intermediate values on the curves include accuracy 0.927 at 70% training data and iteration 20.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Parent-reported early social-communication behaviours captured by Q-CHAT-10; no individual item is named or discussed.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Enhance preprocessing techniques, improve feature-selection efficiency, and ensure the model's adaptability across diverse datasets.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Two sentences, both about the model rather than the study: reliance on the Yeo-Johnson transformation for noise removal may not be sufficient for all types of data, and the complexity of the model may lead to overfitting, especially with smaller datasets. Nothing is said about the circular label, the absent sample size, the absent validation protocol or the absent ethics basis.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: No participants, and no sample size of any kind. The article never states how many records the analysed dataset contains, how many are ASD-positive, or how many are negative - a gap that persists through a results section built entirely on performance curves. The data source is identified only as Autism screening data for toddler, the public Q-CHAT-10 collection. Since no split, test set or fold structure is described either, there is no point in the paper at which a reader can say how many observations any reported number rests on.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic individuals, individuals with ASD, patient, ASD patients. The register is medical and dated - autism is introduced as a neurological disease, individuals are described as needing the right treatment as soon as possible to recover their condition and diminish the disorder's effects. One passage is more sympathetic, noting that individuals with ASD have uniqueness and a few have incomparable ability in academics, music skills and visual. No autistic or community perspective appears.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography, socioeconomic status or recruitment information, and no acknowledgement that any of it is missing.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None, and the paper states the substitute rule explicitly: if the Q-CHAT-10 score is higher than 3 then the class value is allocated as YES which implies ASD traits potential; if not, NO is allocated. The outcome is therefore a threshold on the sum of the ten checklist items that also constitute the feature set - the seventh instance of this structure in the review, after local_8253c2ec, local_a0d73248, local_8ff20c48, local_ed30e24c, local_b9de0d7f and local_14df790d. No clinician, instrument administration or diagnostic criterion enters at any point.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is a hybrid deep-learning method for ASD detection in three stages: Yeo-Johnson transformation to remove noise and artefacts, DeSEHO (Double Exponential Smoothing integrated into the Elk Herd Optimizer) for feature selection, and MEResNeXt (Moments Embedding Network combined with ResNeXt) for classification. Headline findings: accuracy 95.3%, sensitivity 96.5%, specificity 94.8%, described as performing better than traditional models.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting. A downloaded dataset analysed in Python; no hardware, runtime or environment is described.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: No task or paradigm - a caregiver checklist. The article does not reproduce or discuss a single Q-CHAT-10 item, so no behaviour is named anywhere in it.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis. Ethical approval and informed consent are both declared Not Applicable, without reasoning - the paper does not invoke the public-data exemption that comparable studies at least state, and offers nothing in its place. A related reporting anomaly: the article has a single author, Saloni Rai, whose CRediT contribution is listed only as Data curation, yet the author statements read All authors have made substantial contributions to conception and design and the acknowledgements thank the co-authors of this manuscript for their valuable and constructive suggestions.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition instrumentation. Implementation in Python with no library, version, seed or hardware. Method components: Yeo-Johnson transformation, the Elk Herd Optimizer with double exponential smoothing, the Moments Embedding Network and ResNeXt.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Very low, in an unusually instructive way. The article devotes several pages and roughly forty numbered equations to the internals of the MoNet sub-matrix square-root layer, including its forward and backward propagation and the symmetrisation of matrix derivatives - a level of mathematical specification exceeding anything else in the charted corpus. It reports none of what would be needed to repeat the study: no sample size, no class balance, no split or cross-validation scheme, no test-set size, no metaheuristic search space or budget, no count or identity of selected features, no learning rate, batch size or epoch count in the running text, no seed, no code, and no dataset accession. The detail is concentrated entirely on the parts that are reproduced from prior architecture papers and absent from the parts that are specific to this experiment.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Two sentences, both concerning the model rather than the study: the reliance on the Yeo-Johnson transformation for noise removal may not be sufficient for all types of data, and the complexity of the model may lead to overfitting, especially with smaller datasets. Notably, the article contains an extensive limitations apparatus pointed at other people's work - Table 1 tabulates the advantages and disadvantages of each prior study, and the related-work section names constraints for several of them - while none of that scrutiny reaches the circular label, the unreported sample size, the absent validation protocol or the Not Applicable ethics declaration.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Enhance preprocessing techniques, improve the efficiency of feature selection, and ensure the model's adaptability across diverse datasets. The last is the only one that addresses a genuine gap, and it is stated without reference to any external dataset.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Parent-reported early social-communication behaviour, entirely unspecified - the article names the Q-CHAT-10 instrument and describes its scoring rule but never states or discusses a single item, so no behaviour is identified anywhere in the paper.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No fusion - a single questionnaire modality. The hybrid designation refers to combining two convolutional architectures over the same tabular input.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: MEResNeXt, combining the Moments Embedding Network with ResNeXt. Both are convolutional architectures designed for images: MoNet's contribution is a bilinear second-order moment embedding with a sub-matrix square-root layer developed for fine-grained visual recognition, and ResNeXt's is the aggregated residual transformation with cardinality developed for ImageNet classification. Applying them to a short tabular vector of binary questionnaire responses is never justified, and neither the spatial structure that motivates convolution nor the fine-grained texture statistics that motivate moment embedding exists in the data.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A tabular vector of Q-CHAT-10 items and individual characteristics, Yeo-Johnson transformed and then reduced by the DeSEHO metaheuristic. Two observations.
