First, Yeo-Johnson is a variance-stabilising power transformation for continuous skewed variables; applying it to binary checklist responses to remove noise and artefacts, and justifying that choice at length against Box-Cox on the ground that it accommodates negative values, is a category error about the data. Second, the ten items are the summands of the score whose threshold defines the label, so whatever subset DeSEHO retains, the target remains an arithmetic function of the feature pool.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and F1, plotted against iteration count and training percentage. Two of the four definitions given in the text are wrong: accuracy is described as dividing the total number of instances by the number of correctly classified instances, which is the reciprocal of accuracy and would exceed 1; and specificity is described in words as dividing the total number of false positives and true negatives by the sum of both, which is identically 1. The accompanying equations for sensitivity and specificity are correct, so these are errors of exposition rather than of computation, but they appear in a section whose stated purpose is to define the evaluation measures. No confidence interval, no chance level and no class balance accompany any figure.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: None. The metaheuristic selects a feature subset and neither its size nor its membership is reported; no importance ranking, attribution or ablation appears; and no component of the three-stage pipeline is isolated. In a paper whose contribution is a specific combination of transformation, optimiser and architecture, no experiment shows that any of the three contributes anything.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: There is no validation design to assess. The article describes no train-test split, no cross-validation, no held-out set and no test-set size; it never states how many records the dataset contains or what its class balance is; and its results are presented as curves of accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and F1 against iteration count (20 to 80) and training percentage (70%, 80%), with the abstract's 95.3% / 96.5% / 94.8% taken from the best region of those curves. Reading performance off the maximum of a sweep is model selection on the reported quantity, and here there is not even a stated partition on which the sweep is evaluated. Underneath that sits the estimand: the label is a threshold on the sum of the ten Q-CHAT-10 items supplied as features, so the task is reconstruction of a checklist rule regardless of how the data are partitioned. The contrast with the rest of this branch is instructive. local_ed30e24c reached a flawless 292 of 292 with all items retained and pre-split SMOTE; local_14df790d reached 0.99 and mapped the mechanism through its feature-subset comparison; local_8ff20c48 fell to 0.83 after deleting five items. This study reports 95.3% after an unreported metaheuristic selection of an unreported number of features - a figure whose position in that range is determined by how much of the label's arithmetic the optimiser happened to retain, which the paper does not report and therefore cannot interpret.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Autism spectrum disorder; Disease detection; Hybrid deep learning; Optimization algorithm. Four terms, three naming machinery in the most generic possible way; neither the instrument, the population, the modality nor the validation appears.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Computational Biology and Chemistry 120:108619 (Elsevier), 2026 issue. A computational-biology venue, and the mismatch shows: a paper with no sample size, no validation protocol, no reported class balance, two incorrect metric definitions, image architectures applied to binary questionnaire responses, and author statements referring to co-authors of a single-authored manuscript.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2026 issue. Framing is early-detection and cost-saving: initial identification and treatment can diminish the need for wide examinations and expensive medical procedures, and prolonged effects and severity can be avoided at a timely determination of ASD. The contribution is expressed as architectural novelty - a named hybrid (MEResNeXt) built from two named components, fed by a named metaheuristic (DeSEHO) built from two further named components - with the accuracy figure as its warrant. It is the corpus's clearest example of method-naming as the unit of contribution: four new acronyms are introduced, forty equations specify borrowed architecture internals, and the number of children behind the result is never mentioned.

data_charting_rubrics.title: An assessment of autistic and parkinsonian movement profiles to inform selective classification algorithms
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Hickman LJ; Fraser DS; Galea JM; Happé F; Cook JL
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed cautiously and specifically. The motivating clinical concern is stated at the outset: because PD assessments are primarily movement-based, autistic individuals may score highly on PD diagnostic criteria for reasons unrelated to PD, which matters given increased PD diagnosis rates in autistic people. The proposal is that kinematic measures be used alongside clinical assessments, not in place of them, and the authors note that the tablet-based protocol could be deployed in community settings without laboratory equipment.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Cross-sectional three-group comparison with primary kinematic data collection over two testing days, followed by linear mixed-model analysis of group differences and supervised classification for clinical-versus-non-clinical and ASD-versus-PD contrasts.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Systematic: three algorithms crossed with predictor configurations spanning all kinematic features, discriminatory kinematic features, three questionnaire sets and their combinations, for two classification problems. Results are presented as a colour-coded heat map ordered by mean test accuracy, with cells above and below chance distinguished.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Three groups recruited through Parkinson's UK, Autistica, the University of Birmingham Psychology Autism Research Database, the University of Birmingham Older Adults Database and social media. Participants in the clinical groups had to provide evidence of a formal clinical diagnosis (for example a clinician's letter) or come from databases where such evidence had already been verified. Those reporting co-occurring movement or developmental disorders were excluded. The PD group was recruited first as an opportunity sample; autistic adults were then recruited to match it, and controls to match both.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: One row per participant, with 37 kinematic variables and/or questionnaire scores from three instrument sets (ASD, PD, ASD & PD), combined in a grid of predictor configurations.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: United Kingdom - MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit (Cambridge), University of Birmingham, and King's College London. Tasks were completed by participants at home on a supplied tablet.
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: Trait and symptom severity measured with validated instruments and reported with group comparisons: UPDRS Part II for parkinsonian traits (ASD 3.7, PD 11.91, CTRL 0.94), RAADS (32.97 / 10.7 / 6.32) and AQ (37.61 / 19.19 / 16.03) for autistic traits, PHQ for depression and GAD for anxiety. All show the expected group ordering with post-hoc tests reported.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Formal clinical diagnosis, evidenced by documentation (for example a clinician's letter) or verified in an existing research database, with mutual exclusion between the two clinical groups and exclusion of co-occurring movement or developmental disorders in all groups. The authors note explicitly that absence of a diagnosis does not exclude undiagnosed cases, and that the PD and control participants come from a generation in which ASD diagnoses were not prevalent.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 31 autistic adults (14 male, 16 female, 1 other; mean age 55.52, SD 8.01; mean 4.23 years since diagnosis)
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Non-verbal reasoning measured with the Matrix Reasoning Item Bank (MaRs-IB) and matched across groups (0.57 / 0.55 / 0.58, F(2,89)=0.43).
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Middle-aged to older adults. Both clinical groups were age-matched to controls (both p>0.05) but ASD and PD were not matched to each other (t(60.57)=-3.88, p<0.001), so age was entered as a control variable in the mixed models and residualised out before the classification inputs were computed.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Matched across groups (chi-squared(4)=3.25, non-significant): ASD 14M/16F/1 other, PD 19M/13F, CTRL 15M/16F. The autistic sample is close to balanced by sex, which is unusual for this corpus.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Depression and anxiety measured, found significantly elevated in the clinical groups, and controlled for statistically in the mixed models. Eight ASD and six PD participants were taking psychoactive medication at testing.
data_charting_rubrics.medications_therapies: Reported and controlled by protocol: participants with PD completed the tasks before their first dose of dopaminergic medication each morning, so testing occurred in a practically defined off-medication state. Psychoactive medication use is reported for both clinical groups.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 94 adults
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. The study is described as proof-of-concept.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Two comparison groups: 32 adults with Parkinson's disease (19 male, 13 female; mean age 63.16, SD 7.60; 3.69 years since diagnosis) and 31 controls (15 male, 16 female; mean age 59.00, SD 9.96). The second clinical group is the study's defining feature - the comparison is against another movement-affecting condition rather than only against non-clinical controls.
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No, and the authors identify this as a limitation - without a longitudinal design it cannot be known whether any autistic participant will later develop PD.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Fully informed consent from all participants, who received remuneration of GBP 10 per hour.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Explicitly used as the reference throughout - the classification heat map is colour-coded by whether each cell exceeds chance, and two models are reported as performing at chance (0.50).
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Kinematics - stylus trajectories on a touchscreen during shape tracing, plus reaction times - combined in some models with self-report questionnaire scores.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A Shapes Tracing Task using four shapes spanning the angular-frequency spectrum (clover, petals, ellipse, rounded square) and a Reaction Time Task, both completed with a stylus on a supplied touchscreen tablet across two testing days no more than three days apart. Programmed in PsychoPy and delivered through Pavlovia; the MaRs-IB was administered on Gorilla.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Samsung Galaxy Tab A7 (10.4-inch touchscreen, 2000x1200) with stylus; PsychoPy/PsychoJS via Pavlovia; Gorilla for the reasoning task. The authors acknowledge that the resistive forces of the stylus on the tablet and limits in sampling rate and spatial resolution may have reduced observable group differences relative to motion-tracking setups.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: High. Data and analysis scripts are deposited on OSF; software packages are named with versions (R Studio 2022.07.2, MATLAB 2022a, JASP 0.17.2.1, PsychoJS 2021.1.4); the device, screen resolution and stylus are specified; the outlier criterion and the exact percentage removed per feature are reported; the transformations applied to each variable are listed; the mixed-model formulae are given; the feature-selection rule is stated precisely; and the classification grid is presented in full as a heat map. Only the composition of the individual 80/20 draws and the nesting of JASP's tuning are unspecified.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes, at the same OSF repository.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Yes - data and analysis scripts are deposited at https://osf.io/5g7ft.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Yes, with two reference numbers: local Research Ethics Committee approvals ERN_18-1800B and ERN_16-0281AP5, conducted per the Declaration of Helsinki.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Outlier removal at 2 SD from the mean with the exact percentage removed reported per feature (3.7% speed, 3.4% acceleration, 2.1% jerk, 0.1% minimum speed, 0.1% maximum speed, 3.7% sub-movements, 3.1% speed modulation, 5.5% SPARC, 3.7% error measure); log transforms for speed, acceleration and jerk, reciprocal transform for minimum speed to meet normality assumptions; z-scoring before the mixed models. For the classification inputs, residuals were taken after controlling for age, depression and anxiety, then averaged across trials and days.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Nine kinematic features computed per shape plus one reaction time value, giving 37 input variables in the all-kinematic-features set. A second, reduced set of discriminatory kinematic features was defined by supervised filter selection: features (or feature-shape combinations) showing significant group differences in the mixed models were retained.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: R Studio 2022.07.2 for group matching, MATLAB 2022a (fitlme) for linear mixed models, JASP 0.17.2.1 for Bayesian analyses and classification.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Extensive and appropriate: ANOVAs and chi-squared for group matching, linear mixed models with group, shape and their interaction as fixed effects and random effects for trial, day and participant, post-hoc tests with beta estimates and confidence intervals, and Bayesian ANOVAs on residuals to quantify evidence for the null where no group difference was found, with BF01 interpretive bands stated in advance.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Central. The study reports which kinematic features differ and in which direction: autistic participants differed from both PD and controls in speed modulation and sub-movements, and from PD in reaction time. It also reports which task conditions were informative - the ellipse was the least useful shape for distinguishing groups - and recommends that future studies span the angular-frequency spectrum rather than using only ellipses or spirals as most of the prior literature does. Increased jerk in autism is discussed as possibly epiphenomenal on speed differences given how the two are mathematically linked.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Neighbour count and tree number optimised per analysis via JASP; no statement of whether this was nested inside the split.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: The two classification contrasts are the analysis. Age effects on kinematic features are modelled directly and reported, and age, depression and anxiety are residualised out of the classification inputs.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: K-nearest neighbours, random forest and support vector machine with a linear kernel, chosen because these three have been used together in comparably sized parkinsonian-movement studies. Neighbour counts and tree numbers were optimised through JASP's default functionality.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: KNN k and RF tree count optimised per analysis by JASP; SVM linear kernel. Full analysis scripts are deposited.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: An 80/20 participant-level split, with the model trained on 80% of participants and test accuracy computed on the remaining 20%; accuracy is reported per algorithm and as the mean across the three algorithms. The unit is the participant throughout. Two features limit the estimates: the test partitions are small (roughly 13 participants for the ASD-versus-PD contrast and 19 for clinical-versus-non-clinical), and the discriminatory feature sets were selected using group-difference tests computed over all participants, so those particular configurations are optimistically biased.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Test accuracy per algorithm and averaged across algorithms, displayed as a heat map with chance-level colour coding. For the group-difference analyses: F statistics, p-values, beta estimates with 95% confidence intervals, and Bayes factors (BF01) quantifying evidence for the null with interpretive thresholds stated in advance.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Clinical (ASD+PD) versus non-clinical: best mean test accuracy 0.73, from discriminatory kinematic features combined with both questionnaire sets. ASD versus PD: best mean test accuracy 0.93, again from kinematics plus both questionnaires, with discriminatory kinematic features alone reaching 0.80 under SVM. All models were above chance except two, which performed at chance (0.50). The principal negative finding is that no kinematic feature was similar between ASD and PD while also differing from controls - there is no kinematic-similarity basis for the anecdotal likeness between autistic and parkinsonian movement.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Fine motor control during constrained drawing: movement speed, acceleration, jerk, minimum and maximum speed, number of sub-movements, speed modulation (adaptation of speed to trajectory curvature), smoothness (SPARC) and tracing error, plus simple reaction time.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Use a range of shapes spanning the angular-frequency spectrum rather than only ellipses or spirals; investigate the utility of kinematic features for early screening in conjunction with clinical assessments; and distinguish movement decline arising from clinical conditions from normal ageing.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A substantial and specific limitations section: diagnosis-based group definition cannot exclude undiagnosed cases and no longitudinal follow-up establishes whether autistic participants later develop PD; the PD and control participants come from a generation in which ASD diagnoses were not prevalent, so undiagnosed autistic individuals may sit in those groups; stylus resistance and the tablet's sampling rate and spatial resolution may have suppressed group differences relative to motion-tracking; kinematic features are highly context-dependent and the results may be specific to this task; and the autistic sample comprised older adults, a group in which kinematic features have not previously been assessed, so discrepancies with findings from younger samples may reflect age rather than contradiction.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Ninety-four adults in three groups: 31 autistic adults, 32 adults with Parkinson's disease and 31 controls. Both clinical groups required documentary evidence of a formal clinical diagnosis or came from research databases where such evidence had been verified, with mutual exclusion between the two conditions and exclusion of co-occurring movement or developmental disorders. Recruitment order is reported and is itself methodologically informative - the PD group was recruited first as an opportunity sample, autistic adults were then recruited to match it, and controls to match both. The analysis unit is the participant throughout, and the 80/20 classification split partitions people. What limits the classification estimates is size rather than structure: the ASD-versus-PD test partition contains roughly 13 people and the clinical-versus-non-clinical partition roughly 19.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: Autistic individuals, autistic adults, autistic movement, individuals with PD, control participants, non-autistic individuals. Identity-first language is used consistently and without hedging, movement differences are described as differences rather than deficits or abnormalities, and the framing throughout treats autistic movement as a characteristic to be measured rather than a pathology to be detected. The paper also cites the proposal that movement differences be added as specifiers to autism diagnoses - condition-relevant but non-selective - which is a precise and non-inflationary way of positioning the finding.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: The most complete adult-sample reporting in the corpus, with formal matching tests. Gender is matched across groups (chi-squared(4)=3.25, ns) and the autistic sample is close to sex-balanced at 14M/16F/1 other - a composition no other autism study in this review achieves. Age: ASD 55.52 (8.01), PD 63.16 (7.60), CTRL 59.00 (9.96); both clinical groups matched to controls but ASD and PD not matched to each other (p<0.001), which the authors handle by entering age as a control variable and residualising it from the classification inputs. Non-verbal reasoning (MaRs-IB) is matched. Depression and anxiety differ significantly and are controlled for. Years since diagnosis, psychoactive medication use, and UPDRS, RAADS and AQ trait scores are all reported by group with post-hoc comparisons.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Clinically ascertained with documentation, and honestly bounded. Participants had to supply evidence of a formal clinical diagnosis such as a clinician's letter, or be drawn from databases where that evidence had been verified. The limitations section then names the two residual problems precisely: absence of a diagnosis does not exclude undiagnosed cases, and the PD and control participants belong to a generation in which autism diagnoses were not prevalent, so undiagnosed autistic people may sit in the comparison groups. That second observation is a genuine insight about ascertainment in older cohorts that appears nowhere else in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Comprehensive and instrument-based: UPDRS Part II for parkinsonian traits, RAADS and AQ for autistic traits, PHQ for depression, GAD for anxiety, MaRs-IB for non-verbal reasoning, and years since diagnosis. All are reported by group with ANOVA and post-hoc comparisons, and the ordering is as expected (autistic traits ASD>PD>CTRL; parkinsonian traits PD>ASD>CTRL). Crucially the trait instruments are used both as sample descriptors and, in some model configurations, as declared predictors alongside kinematics - so their role is explicit rather than hidden.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: Two aims, one confirmatory and one applied. First, to test directly whether autistic and parkinsonian movement resemble each other - a comparison previously possible only by juxtaposing separate studies with different designs and demographics. Second, to assess whether kinematic features can classify clinical versus non-clinical status and, within the clinical groups, ASD versus PD. Findings: autistic participants differed from both PD and controls in speed modulation and sub-movements, and from PD in reaction time; classification reached a best mean test accuracy of 0.73 for clinical versus non-clinical and 0.93 for ASD versus PD, in both cases from kinematics combined with questionnaires; and, most importantly, no kinematic feature was found to be similar between ASD and PD while also differing from controls. The anecdotal likeness between autistic and parkinsonian movement is not supported.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Home-based testing on a supplied tablet over two days no more than three days apart, following an online screening form, questionnaire battery and reasoning task. The PD group completed the tasks before their first dopaminergic dose each morning. Home administration is presented as an advantage for scalability - the protocol could be run in community settings without laboratory kinematic equipment - and its cost is acknowledged in the limitations, where stylus resistance and the tablet's sampling and spatial resolution are named as possible suppressors of group differences.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A Shapes Tracing Task with four shapes chosen to span the angular-frequency spectrum (clover, petals, ellipse, rounded square) plus a Reaction Time Task, both stylus-based. The shape design is deliberate and yields a methodological result the review should record: the ellipse was the least useful shape for distinguishing groups, and the authors point out that most drawing tasks in the literature index only elliptical or spiral movements, recommending that future studies span the full angular-frequency range. That is a concrete, actionable finding about task design derived from data.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional with two testing days; no longitudinal follow-up, which the authors identify as limiting their ability to know whether autistic participants later develop PD. Ethics reporting is complete: two Research Ethics Committee approval numbers (ERN_18-1800B and ERN_16-0281AP5), Declaration of Helsinki compliance, fully informed consent, and payment of GBP 10 per hour - remuneration being reported at all is uncommon in this corpus and is relevant to the ethics of research participation.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Samsung Galaxy Tab A7 with a 10.4-inch 2000x1200 touchscreen and stylus; tasks programmed in PsychoPy and delivered via Pavlovia (PsychoJS 2021.1.4); MaRs-IB on Gorilla. Analysis in R Studio 2022.07.2 (matching), MATLAB 2022a with fitlme (mixed models) and JASP 0.17.2.1 (Bayesian analyses and classification). Every package is named with a version.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: The highest in the charted corpus alongside local_4da2b941. Data and analysis scripts are deposited on OSF; all software is named with versions; the device and its screen specification are given; the outlier rule is stated with the exact percentage removed for each of the nine features; the normalising transformations are listed per variable; the mixed-model formulae are written out including random-effect structure; the feature-selection rule is specified precisely, including how group-by-shape interactions were handled; and the full classification grid is published as a heat map rather than reduced to a headline. The only gaps are the composition of the individual 80/20 draws and whether JASP's parameter optimisation was nested inside the split.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: A genuinely analytical limitations section with five distinct items, each carrying a mechanism: diagnosis-based grouping cannot exclude undiagnosed cases; the PD and control groups come from a generation in which autism diagnoses were not prevalent, so undiagnosed autistic people may be present in them; stylus resistance and tablet sampling and spatial resolution may have suppressed group differences relative to motion tracking; kinematic features are context-dependent and the results may be task-specific; and the autistic sample was older than those in the existing kinematic literature, so apparent contradictions with prior findings may be age effects. Two further issues go unstated: the classification test partitions contain roughly 13 to 19 participants, and the discriminatory feature sets were selected using group-difference tests computed on all participants.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Employ a range of shapes across the angular-frequency spectrum rather than only ellipses or spirals; investigate kinematic features for early screening in conjunction with clinical assessments; and separate clinically driven movement decline from normal ageing, a need the study itself establishes by demonstrating age effects on several kinematic features.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Fine motor kinematics during constrained tracing: speed, acceleration, jerk, minimum and maximum speed, number of sub-movements, speed modulation (how sharply speed adapts to trajectory curvature), smoothness via SPARC, and tracing error, plus simple reaction time. The discriminating features are specific and directional - autistic participants showed greater speed modulation and more sub-movements than both other groups, and differed from PD in reaction time - and the paper is careful about mechanism, noting that reported increases in jerk in autism may be epiphenomenal on speed differences because the two quantities are mathematically linked.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Genuine and declared multimodal fusion, and the study's most useful applied finding. Kinematic features and self-report questionnaire scores are combined in an explicit grid of predictor configurations - kinematics alone, questionnaires alone (ASD, PD, or both) and their combinations - and the combination outperforms either alone for both classification problems (0.73 clinical versus non-clinical; 0.93 ASD versus PD). Because the questionnaire sets are named and separated, the contribution of each modality is visible rather than buried, and the finding that both trait questionnaires together beat either individually is directly interpretable.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Three standard classifiers - KNN, random forest and linear-kernel SVM - selected on the explicit ground that these three have been used together in comparably sized studies of parkinsonian movement. No deep learning and no novel architecture; results are reported for all three separately and as a mean, so no single algorithm's best run stands in for the finding.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: One row per participant. Thirty-seven kinematic input variables (nine features across four shapes plus one reaction time value), computed as residuals after controlling for age, depression and anxiety and averaged across trials and days; plus three questionnaire sets. A reduced discriminatory kinematic feature set was defined by retaining features, or feature-shape combinations, that showed significant group differences in the mixed models. That selection rule is stated precisely - including that a group-by-shape interaction yielding a difference on only one shape contributes only that shape's value - which is both good reporting and the point at which the design leaks, since the significance tests were computed over all participants including those later held out.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Test accuracy per algorithm and averaged across the three, with the full grid published as a heat map colour-coded against chance and ordered by mean accuracy - so the reader sees every configuration, including the two that performed at chance, rather than only the maximum. For the group-difference analyses the reporting is fuller still: F statistics, p-values, beta estimates with 95% confidence intervals, and Bayes factors quantifying evidence for the null with interpretive bands stated in advance. What is absent is any interval on the classification accuracies, which matters because the test partitions hold roughly 13 to 19 participants; the 95% interval around the 0.93 headline spans approximately 0.66 to 1.00, and around 0.73 approximately 0.49 to 0.90.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Substantive and directional. The study identifies which features discriminate (speed modulation, sub-movements, reaction time), in which direction, and between which pairs of groups; which task conditions are informative (the ellipse least so); and where an apparent effect may be an artefact of another (jerk as a possible epiphenomenon of speed). It also uses Bayesian analysis to distinguish absence of evidence from evidence of absence, reporting that low Bayes factors mean there is not strong evidence to conclude that movements were the same between groups where differences were not found - a distinction almost never drawn in this literature.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The validation design is participant-level and honestly reported, with three qualifications that the review should record rather than treat as disqualifying. The structure is correct: an 80/20 split of participants, with test accuracy computed on held-out people and reported for each of three algorithms and as their mean, and with the entire configuration grid published so that the reported maximum sits visibly among its alternatives, including two models at chance. The qualifications are, first, size - 63 participants in the ASD-versus-PD contrast and 94 in clinical-versus-non-clinical give test partitions of roughly 13 and 19 people, so a 0.93 mean accuracy corresponds to about 12 of 13 correct and carries a confidence interval running from roughly 0.66 to 1.00; no interval is reported. Second, selection - the discriminatory kinematic feature sets were defined by group-difference significance from mixed models fitted on all participants, so configurations using those sets saw the held-out participants' labels during feature selection and are optimistically biased; the all-kinematic-features configurations are unaffected, and the paper's own observation that variability was seen in whether discriminatory or all features yielded stronger accuracy is consistent with the selection buying less than it might. Third, no external cohort, which the authors acknowledge by describing the work as proof-of-concept. Set against the corpus, what makes this study valuable is not its accuracy figure but its structure: the negative result is the primary finding, it is supported by Bayesian evidence for the null rather than by absence of significance, and the classification is offered as a secondary demonstration rather than as a diagnostic claim.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Autism; Parkinson's disease; Movement; Classification. Four terms, both conditions named, the behavioural domain named, and the analytic task named - with no architecture, no algorithm and no accuracy language.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Neurodevelopmental Disorders 18:8, a specialist neurodevelopmental journal, with a 180-day review - the longest among the charted 2026 studies. The disciplinary fit is visible throughout: formal group matching with equivalence tests, mixed models with appropriate random-effect structure, Bayesian evidence for the null, pre-specified interpretive thresholds, deposited data and scripts, complete ethics reporting including participant remuneration, and a limitations section that reasons about cohort effects in ascertainment.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2026, accepted 15 December 2025 after 180 days. The framing is unusual for this corpus in that its primary contribution is negative and clinically protective rather than a performance claim. The motivating concern is that PD assessments are primarily movement-based, so autistic people may score highly on PD diagnostic criteria because of autism-related movement differences - a differential-diagnosis risk that matters given rising PD diagnosis rates in autistic populations. The study then finds no kinematic similarity between autism and PD that is also distinct from controls, which addresses that concern directly. The classification work is labelled proof-of-concept, kinematics are proposed for use in conjunction with clinical assessments rather than instead of them, and the applied suggestion - that a tablet-and-stylus protocol could support community-scale assessment without laboratory equipment - is proportionate to what was demonstrated.

data_charting_rubrics.title: An explainable deep learning framework for screening level autism severity using behavioural data
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Rathod VN; Goudar RH; Sangani S
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Proposed for integration with electronic health record systems and e-learning platforms for real-time monitoring, but with the qualification that clinical deployment should incorporate human oversight and longitudinal validation to ensure ethical and context-aware use.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of four harmonised public tabular screening datasets; a single-stage BiLSTM with a chaotic optimiser performs joint binary screening and four-level ordinal severity classification, evaluated by stratified 10-fold cross-validation with an ablation study and SHAP analysis.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Internal baselines fitted by the authors under identical preprocessing and validation protocols: SVM (RBF) 0.911, random forest 0.928, logistic regression 0.902, three-layer MLP 0.944, unidirectional LSTM 0.932. Plus a literature comparison table spanning eight prior studies (0.869 to 0.978).
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None. Public ASD screening datasets were downloaded from Kaggle and the UCI Machine Learning Repository and harmonised.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A 15-attribute tabular row per participant, processed by a bidirectional recurrent network on the stated reasoning that the ordering of A1-A10 items is not arbitrary and that each question progressively evaluates social reciprocity.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: India - Visvesvaraya Technological University, Belagavi, and Manipal Institute of Technology Bengaluru, Manipal Academy of Higher Education. No data collection.
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: Constructed rather than measured. A continuous behavioural index B is computed as a weighted combination of the A1-A10 screening items under domain weights, normalised to [0,1] and discretised into four ordinal strata: No ASD below 0.30, Level 1 (Mild) 0.30-0.55, Level 2 (Moderate) 0.55-0.75, Level 3 (Severe) at or above 0.75, with thresholds chosen to align with DSM-5 functional-support descriptors and percentile interpretations from the Q-CHAT and ADOS-2 literature. Domain weights were calibrated by the chaotic optimiser to maximise Cohen's kappa against independent expert assessments on a randomly sampled subset, reaching kappa 0.72 (95% CI 0.69-0.76).
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None, and the paper says so directly. It states in the abstract that reliable severity stratification remains challenging due to the absence of explicit clinician-annotated severity labels, and constructs its own labels instead. The binary ASD field in the source datasets is the standard questionnaire screening outcome; no clinician assessment exists for any record.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: Not reported as a count. The derived severity label produces four strata whose class distribution is described as closely mirroring population-level screening statistics reported in prior paediatric ASD studies, but no counts are given.
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: A Cognitive Assessment variable appears in the correlation analysis but is not described as an instrument or reported as a distribution.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Four developmental cohorts - toddlers, children, adolescents and adults - with age retained as a normalised continuous feature. No mean, SD or per-cohort sample size is given in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 2,154 participants across four developmental cohorts (toddlers, children, adolescents, adults), after harmonisation of the source datasets.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None, and identified repeatedly as the necessary next step: external validation against independently clinician-annotated severity datasets is stated as a required direction for future work.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Declared not applicable on the same basis - no human participants were directly involved and no personal or sensitive information was collected.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not stated. The four-class severity distribution is described qualitatively as mirroring population screening statistics but no class counts are given, so neither a majority-class baseline nor a per-class prevalence can be computed.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Questionnaire - the ten A1-A10 screening items plus a composite Q_SCORE, age and derived behavioural domain variables, harmonised to 15 unified attributes across four source datasets.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. Caregiver or self-report screening checklists.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None. Tabular data.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Moderate. The labelling function is specified with its weights, normalisation and four threshold boundaries; imputation, harmonisation, normalisation and feature-pruning steps are described in order; sensitivity analyses on imputation, thresholds and weights are quantified; the cross-validation scheme is stated; and the ablation table isolates each component. Missing: code, seed, software and versions, network layer configuration, learning rate, batch size and epoch count, per-cohort and per-class sample counts, and the harmonised dataset itself, which is promised post-publication.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Source repositories named (Kaggle, UCI). The harmonised dataset is stated to be available on reasonable request and to be made public post-publication.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not deposited. Materials are available on reasonable request to the corresponding author.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Declared not applicable on the ground that the study did not involve direct experimentation with human participants or animals and used publicly available, fully anonymised, open-access de-identified datasets from Kaggle and UCI.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Harmonisation of four source datasets into 15 unified attributes with semantically and statistically comparable variables retained; mode imputation for missing values, with a sensitivity analysis against median and k-nearest-neighbour imputation showing under 1.0% deviation in macro-F1 and accuracy; min-max normalisation of continuous variables; label encoding of categorical fields; stratified sampling by age group during merging to preserve cohort proportions.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Correlation filtering plus SHAP-based feature importance used to prune variables, with Ethnicity, Country of Residence, Who Completed Test and Used App Before excluded as low-variance or irrelevant. Pearson correlation (p<0.05) was used to verify that retained features were significantly associated with the class labels.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Not named in the extracted text beyond the algorithm components (BiLSTM, chaotic optimiser, SHAP). No versions or seed.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Cohen's kappa with a 95% confidence interval for label-expert agreement; Pearson correlations with p-values; sensitivity analyses on imputation method, severity thresholds and domain weights with the resulting metric deviations quantified. No confidence intervals accompany the classification accuracies and no across-fold variance is reported for them.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: SHAP applied to analyse feature utilisation, with the scope explicitly bounded - the paper describes this as methodologically bounded explainability that examines how behavioural attributes are utilised within the learned scoring structure without asserting causal or diagnostic attribution. The correlation analysis separately relates Q_SCORE to social communication difficulties (r 0.64-0.67) and repetitive behaviour (r 0.45-0.63), and notes that age correlates weakly (r -0.21 to 0.12).
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The chaotic optimiser modulates learning dynamics during training; the domain weights of the labelling function were separately optimised by the same optimiser against expert-labelled agreement.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Performance is reported separately for all four developmental cohorts and per severity class via AUROC curves. No stratification by sex or ethnicity - both were removed during feature pruning.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: A bidirectional LSTM as representation learner combined with a chaotic optimiser for learning-rate modulation. The optimiser's expansion is inconsistent between the abstract (Chaotic Grey Ball Optimizer) and the methods (Chaotic Gradient-Based Optimizer), both abbreviated CGBO.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Categorical cross-entropy with softmax over four severity classes; stratified 10-fold cross-validation with early stopping and class weighting for imbalance. Layer widths, learning rate, batch size and epoch count are not quoted in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Stratified 10-fold cross-validation at the participant level with early stopping and class weighting. Threshold and weight sensitivity were assessed by perturbing severity thresholds by 5% and domain weights by 10% across the ten folds, with macro-F1 and kappa varying by no more than 0.6% and 0.03. The decisive feature, which the paper states plainly, is that the severity labels are deterministically derived from the same behavioural attributes used as model inputs, so the prediction task is function approximation rather than diagnosis. Two ordering issues remain: the domain weights were calibrated on the data before cross-validation, and SHAP-based feature pruning necessarily requires a fitted model and was likewise performed on the full dataset.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUROC per cohort and for the ablation variants; Cohen's kappa with a confidence interval for label-expert agreement; macro-F1 and kappa stability under threshold and weight perturbation; per-class AUROC curves for the four severity levels across age groups; a correlation heatmap with Pearson coefficients across all 2,154 records.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Accuracy 99.10% (toddlers), 97.10% (children), 98.50% (adolescents) and 98.10% (adults), with AUROC exceeding 0.99, described as a 3-6% absolute improvement over the strongest baselines. Ablation: unidirectional LSTM 0.932, BiLSTM without the chaotic optimiser 0.956, BiLSTM with Adam 0.968, BiLSTM with the chaotic optimiser 0.985, and BiLSTM plus optimiser plus SHAP 0.987.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Screening-item behaviours grouped into social communication difficulties, repetitive behaviour and a cognitive assessment domain, as evaluated through the A1-A10 items.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: External validation against independently clinician-annotated severity data; multimodal fusion; federated learning validation; prospective clinical trials to enhance sensitivity and ensure fairness across populations.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Substantial and, unusually, integrated into the methods rather than confined to a closing paragraph. The paper states that the severity labels are deterministically derived from the model's own inputs, that high performance should therefore be read as function approximation rather than diagnostic accuracy, that the labelling kappa supports internal consistency while not implying external diagnostic validity, and that current datasets are behaviourally constrained and exclude multimodal cues such as prosody or eye gaze. It repeats the scope restriction at least four times in different sections.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: No participants were recruited. Four public screening datasets from Kaggle and UCI were harmonised into 2,154 records spanning toddlers, children, adolescents and adults, with stratified sampling by age group during merging to preserve cohort proportions. The analysis unit is the record and the cross-validation folds are stratified over records. What is missing is arithmetic: the per-cohort sample sizes, the class counts for the binary screening outcome and the counts for each of the four constructed severity strata are all absent, so the denominator behind every reported accuracy is unknown. The class distribution is characterised only qualitatively, as closely mirroring population-level screening statistics reported in prior paediatric ASD studies.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, participants, developmental cohorts, severity strata. The register is technical and notably free of pathologising language for this corpus; severity is described in terms of DSM-5 functional-support levels rather than as degrees of impairment, and the paper avoids the diagnostic vocabulary its results cannot support. No autistic or community perspective appears.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Almost none, and by deliberate removal. Age is retained as a continuous normalised feature and cohort membership is preserved through stratified merging, but ethnicity, country of residence, who completed the test and whether the app had been used before were all excluded during feature pruning as low-variance, irrelevant or metadata noise, on the stated ground of eliminating demographic skew. Sex is not reported anywhere. The consequence is that no subgroup analysis by sex, ethnicity or respondent type is possible, and the fairness across populations named in the future-work section cannot be assessed in the present study - the variables required for it were removed.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None, and the paper is explicit rather than silent about this. The abstract states that reliable severity stratification remains challenging due to the absence of explicit clinician-annotated severity labels; the methods then construct severity labels from the A1-A10 items themselves; and the scope paragraph states that because the severity labels are deterministically derived from the same behavioural attributes used as model inputs, the subsequent prediction task constitutes a structured function-approximation setting. The one external anchor is the weight calibration, in which domain weights were optimised to maximise agreement with independent expert assessments on a randomly sampled subset, achieving Cohen's kappa 0.72 (95% CI 0.69-0.76) - and the paper immediately qualifies this as supporting the internal consistency of the labeling heuristic while not implying external diagnostic validity. Neither the number of expert-labelled records, the identity or qualification of the experts, nor the instrument they used is reported.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Constructed, not measured. The four ordinal strata are cut points on a weighted sum of A1-A10 normalised to [0,1]: No ASD below 0.30, Mild 0.30-0.55, Moderate 0.55-0.75, Severe at or above 0.75, with the boundaries said to align with DSM-5 functional-support descriptors and percentile interpretations from the Q-CHAT and ADOS-2 literature. No validated severity instrument was administered to anyone. The paper's own framing of this as a controlled behavioural labeling paradigm rather than as severity assessment is accurate and is what distinguishes it from local_b9de0d7f, which generated a six-way teaching-method label from a Q-CHAT total using numpy and then offered the resulting accuracy to educators as a basis for decisions.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is a single-stage framework performing joint screening-level ASD identification and four-level ordinal severity stratification, under an explicitly controlled labelling paradigm, with a bidirectional LSTM as representation learner and a chaotic optimiser for training stability. Headline findings: accuracy 99.10% for toddlers, 97.10% children, 98.50% adolescents and 98.10% adults with AUROC above 0.99, a 3-6 point gain over the authors' own baselines (SVM 0.911, logistic regression 0.902, random forest 0.928, MLP 0.944, unidirectional LSTM 0.932). The framing of these results is the study's distinguishing feature: they are presented as evidence of the model's effectiveness in approximating a deterministic behavioural severity-scoring function rather than independent clinical diagnostic performance.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting. Public datasets harmonised and analysed computationally; no environment, hardware or runtime is described.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: No task or paradigm - screening checklists completed by caregivers or self-report. The paper offers a substantive argument for its architecture choice that deserves recording: although the A1-A10 items are collected in a static format, their ordering is said to be non-arbitrary, with each question progressively evaluating social reciprocity, which is why a bidirectional sequence model is applied. The argument is stated but not tested - no experiment permutes item order to see whether the claimed sequential structure carries any signal.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis. Ethical approval and consent to participate are both declared not applicable, with the reasoning stated in full: no direct experimentation with human participants, and all analyses conducted on publicly available, fully anonymised, open-access de-identified datasets from Kaggle and UCI. The declaration is at least reasoned rather than blank. What it does not address is whether the original respondents consented to research reuse - the same gap present across this branch.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No instrumentation. Analytical components: BiLSTM, a chaotic optimiser (expanded inconsistently as Chaotic Grey Ball Optimizer in the abstract and Chaotic Gradient-Based Optimizer in the methods), SHAP, and standard preprocessing. No software, version, seed or hardware is named in the extracted text.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Moderate, and unusually strong on the parts that matter most for this branch. The labelling function is specified completely - the weighted index, its normalisation, the four threshold boundaries and the calibration objective - so another group could reconstruct the target variable, which is not true of any comparable study in this review. Three separate sensitivity analyses are reported with quantified deviations: imputation method (mode versus median versus kNN, under 1.0% deviation in macro-F1 and accuracy), severity thresholds perturbed by 5% and domain weights by 10% (macro-F1 within 0.6%, kappa within 0.03). The ablation table isolates each architectural component. Against this: no code, seed, software, versions, layer configuration, learning rate, batch size or epoch count; no per-cohort or per-class sample counts; and the harmonised dataset promised only post-publication.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: This is the study's defining characteristic and the reason it matters to the review. The scope restriction is not confined to a closing limitations paragraph but is stated in the abstract, the contributions list, the labelling section, the training section and the results discussion. Its clearest formulation is in section 3.3: because the severity labels are deterministically derived from the same behavioural attributes used as model inputs, the subsequent prediction task constitutes a structured function-approximation setting; accordingly, high classification performance should be interpreted as evidence of the proposed model's ability to learn stable and interpretable behavioural scoring functions, rather than as proof of clinical diagnostic accuracy. It further states that the labelling kappa supports internal consistency while not implying external diagnostic validity, that SHAP results carry no causal or diagnostic attribution, that performance gains are methodological improvements rather than evidence of clinical diagnostic superiority, and that the datasets are behaviourally constrained. What remains unstated: that the domain weights were calibrated on the full dataset before cross-validation, that SHAP-based feature pruning requires a fitted model and was likewise performed on the full data, that no class counts are reported, and that the ablation credits SHAP with a 0.002 accuracy gain when SHAP is a post-hoc explanation method that cannot alter a model's predictions.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: External validation against independently clinician-annotated severity datasets - named as necessary rather than desirable - plus multimodal fusion (prosody, eye-gaze dynamics), federated learning validation, and prospective clinical trials to enhance sensitivity and ensure fairness across populations. The first directly addresses the study's own stated boundary; the fairness objective is undercut by the removal of ethnicity and country of residence during preprocessing.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Screening-item behaviours from the A1-A10 instruments, organised into three domains - social communication difficulties, repetitive behaviour and a cognitive assessment component - which supply the weighted terms of the constructed severity index. The correlation analysis relates the composite Q_SCORE to social communication difficulties (r 0.64-0.67) and repetitive behaviour (r 0.45-0.63) and reports moderate inter-item correlations (r 0.10-0.46), read as each item adding unique variance.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No fusion - a single questionnaire modality. What the study does perform is dataset harmonisation across four age cohorts into a common 15-attribute schema with stratified merging, which is cross-cohort integration rather than multimodal fusion. Multimodal extension with prosody and gaze is named as future work, and the absence of such cues is acknowledged as a constraint of the current data.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A bidirectional LSTM as a high-capacity representation learner over static questionnaire attributes, trained with a chaotic optimiser that applies controlled chaotic perturbations to diversify gradient updates, described as an alternative to deterministic optimisers such as Adam or RMSProp. Baselines fitted by the authors under identical preprocessing and validation: SVM, random forest, logistic regression, MLP and unidirectional LSTM. The ablation reports a clean monotone progression from 0.932 to 0.987.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: A 15-attribute harmonised row per participant after pruning, with continuous variables min-max normalised and categorical fields label-encoded. The predictor set contains the A1-A10 items and the composite Q_SCORE; the target is a four-level discretisation of a weighted sum of those same A1-A10 items. The label is therefore an arithmetic function of the inputs by construction, and the paper says so.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUROC per cohort and per ablation variant; per-class AUROC curves across the four severity levels and four age groups; Cohen's kappa with a confidence interval for label-expert agreement; and quantified stability under three separate perturbation analyses. The metric set is broad and the sensitivity reporting is a genuine strength. Two gaps. No confidence interval or across-fold variance accompanies any classification accuracy, despite ten folds having been run and despite intervals being reported for the kappa. And no class counts are given for either the binary or the four-level target, so no baseline exists against which a 99.10% can be positioned - which matters particularly for a four-class ordinal problem whose stratum boundaries the authors chose.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: SHAP is applied with its scope explicitly bounded, and the bounding is the point: the contributions list describes it as methodologically bounded explainability, applied to analyse feature utilisation and model consistency without asserting independent clinical causality. That is the correct use of the method under a constructed label, and it is unique in this corpus - the six other Q-CHAT-labelled studies charted here all read their SHAP or feature-importance output as clinical corroboration. Two problems remain. SHAP was also used upstream, as a feature-pruning criterion, which requires a fitted model and was performed on the full dataset before cross-validation. And the ablation table lists BiLSTM + CGBO + SHAP at accuracy 0.987 against BiLSTM + CGBO at 0.985, attributing a 0.002 gain to the addition of SHAP - which is not possible, since a post-hoc explanation method computes attributions for an already-trained model and cannot change its predictions.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The evaluation is stratified 10-fold cross-validation at the record level with early stopping and class weighting, supported by three quantified sensitivity analyses - imputation method, severity thresholds perturbed by 5%, domain weights perturbed by 10% - showing macro-F1 stable within 0.6% and kappa within 0.03. That is more robustness checking than any other study in this branch performs. But the estimand is settled before any of it, and the paper states the conclusion itself: the severity labels are deterministically derived from the same behavioural attributes used as model inputs, so the task is function approximation and the accuracy figures are not diagnostic accuracy. Read that way, the results are internally coherent and even informative - a BiLSTM recovers a four-way threshold on a weighted sum of ten items with 97-99% accuracy, and simpler models recover it with 90-94%, which quantifies how much architectural capacity the reconstruction of a piecewise-linear scoring rule requires. Three residual issues qualify even that reading. The domain weights were calibrated on the full dataset by optimising kappa against expert labels before cross-validation, so the labelling function itself was fitted to the data the model is then evaluated on. SHAP-based feature pruning was likewise applied to the whole dataset and necessarily requires a fitted model. And the expert calibration - the only external anchor in the study - reports kappa 0.72 without stating how many records were expert-labelled, by whom, or with what instrument, so the one bridge between the constructed label and clinical severity is itself unspecified. Compared against the branch, the difference is not in the estimand but in the interpretation: local_ed30e24c reported 292 of 292 correct as confirming suitability for reliable clinical screening; local_b9de0d7f offered a numpy-generated teaching-method label at 0.9917 to educators; this study reports 99.10% and states in four separate places that it does not mean what it appears to mean.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Not captured in the extracted text.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Discover Applied Sciences 8(4):363 (Springer) - an open-access multidisciplinary applied-sciences journal. The venue is not clinical, yet the paper is the most careful in the branch about the boundary between computational and clinical claims, which suggests the discipline of the authors rather than of the reviewers is doing the work here.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2026. The framing is the study's principal contribution to this review. Where the rest of the questionnaire branch presents reconstruction of a checklist threshold as diagnostic accuracy, this paper presents the same task as what it is - approximation of a deterministic behavioural scoring function - and repeats that restriction in the abstract, the contributions, the methods, the results and the conclusion. It describes its own labelling as a heuristic with internal consistency but no external diagnostic validity, bounds its SHAP interpretation against causal claims, calls external validation against clinician-annotated data necessary rather than desirable, and requires human oversight for any deployment. The overreach that remains is modest and confined to the discussion, which speaks of diagnostic precision and of stratifying ASD into four functional levels, and to the clinical-integration proposal for electronic health records and e-learning platforms. It is the only study in the branch whose stated conclusions a reader could act on safely.

data_charting_rubrics.title: An explainable machine unlearning algorithm framework for early detection of autism spectrum disorder and brain disabilities in newborns
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Lakhan A; Mohammed MA; Hamouda H; Thaljaoui A; Baslem A; Al-Andoli MN
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Asserted strongly - the contributions list claims that leveraging past experience in implementing our system in clinical settings, the framework can effectively validate itself in real-world clinical implementations, ensuring it can indeed be implemented in hospital settings.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Simulation-based evaluation of a proposed algorithmic framework across several named behavioural screening datasets and imaging modalities. The experiments are described throughout as simulation results, and the article states it extends the authors' own previous implementation.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: CNN, GNN, ACNN, SVM, LSTM and FCNN-LSTM, reported in tables whose rows mix dataset description with algorithm scores.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None. Datasets are named as ASQ, CSBS, PEDS, M-CHAT and STAT, plus MRI and EEG collections, and are said to be publicly available at a GitHub repository maintained by the first author.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: 224x224 image inputs for the CNN backbones; the questionnaire modality's representation is not specified. Illustrative feature vectors are printed as literal example values.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Pakistan, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Tunisia and Malaysia - Dawood University of Engineering and Technology, University of Anbar, Al-Farabi University, Majmaah University, Jendouba University and Multimedia University. No data collection is described.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None described. No diagnostic instrument administration, criterion, assessor or date is reported for any record in any of the named datasets.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: Stated as 25,000 positive cases in one passage; no other count is given.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Also inconsistent. The title and abstract concern newborns aged 0 to 36 months; the MRI inclusion criteria restrict to children aged 12-36 months; the CSBS description says the dataset was aged 3-6 years; and another passage refers to extending previous work on children aged 12-36 months.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Subjects with confounding neurological conditions are said to have been excluded from the MRI set; no other comorbidity information appears.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Irreconcilable. The methods state that the study used MRI datasets of newborns comprising 10,000 samples, and then that the final dataset included 25,000 positive cases and 1200 negative cases, with class balance maintained. Twenty-five thousand positives cannot be drawn from 10,000 samples, and a 25,000-to-1,200 ratio is not class balance. Elsewhere the CSBS description reports 500 subjects. No consistent total exists anywhere in the article.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. The paper instead asserts that the framework can effectively validate itself in real-world clinical implementations.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Stated as 1,200 negative cases in the same passage.
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No, although the motivation section argues for handling longitudinal developmental data.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not obtained; declared unnecessary on the same basis.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not stated. With the reported 25,000 positives against 1,200 negatives the majority-class baseline would be 95.4%, which would place the headline 98% barely above it - but the counts are internally inconsistent, so no baseline can actually be computed.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Nominally multimodal - MRI, video, audio, text and EEG are named as modality symbols, and ASQ, CSBS, PEDS, M-CHAT and STAT as questionnaire sources. The worked example in the parameter table lists only MRI, video and text.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None described. Questionnaire responses and archived imaging.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: A testbed with 32 GB RAM and 2 TB storage is named for latency and runtime measurement. No acquisition equipment is described for any modality.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Nominally high, actually very low. A public repository is cited for code and data, configurations are said to be frozen, and CNN hyperparameters are tabulated. But the article's own account of its data is self-contradictory at every scale - 10,000 samples yielding 25,000 positives, 25,000 against 1,200 described as balanced, partition counts of six and four in different sections, age ranges of 0-36 months, 12-36 months and 3-6 years - so it is not possible to determine what would be reproduced. Table 4, presented as the standard dataset, is a results table in which the same subject ID range appears five times with different family relationships and different algorithm names.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: The same GitHub repository is cited as hosting the ASQ, CSBS, PEDS, M-CHAT and STAT datasets.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: A GitHub repository is cited for both code and datasets, and the paper claims the pipeline can be replicated end-to-end with frozen configuration files.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not obtained, and the reasoning is stated: because the work involved no hospital deployments, no site-specific approvals, patient consent or institutional governance processes were required. The same passage states that the datasets were fully identified and processed with strict subject-level partitioning - fully identified being the opposite of de-identified, presumably a typographic error for de-identified in a sentence about privacy safeguards.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Each modality is partitioned into non-overlapping segments for parallel training. The number of partitions is given as six in the methodology narrative and as four in the parameter table.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Per-partition CNN feature extraction (ResNet-50 or InceptionV3), aggregation into a modality-specific representation, and fusion across modalities into a single feature vector.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Not named beyond model families (ResNet-50, InceptionV3) and a stated code repository.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests are named; no test statistic, p-value or interval is reported anywhere in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Layer-wise explainability is the framework's central claim, with modality-specific outputs described as gradient spectrogram features for audio and spatiotemporal attention maps for video. No attribution figure or quantitative interpretability result is presented in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Multi-objective weights tuned by grid search on the validation set; configurations stated to be frozen in the repository.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: A partitioning-based CNN framework (MUXAI-ASDBD) with layer-wise explainability and a machine-unlearning mechanism at the summation layer, plus probability distribution analysis. Baselines are named as CNN, GNN, ACNN, SVM, LSTM and a proposed FCNN-LSTM.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: ResNet-50 (50 layers) or InceptionV3 (48 layers), input 224x224, Adam optimiser, learning rate 0.003 described as increasing, batch size 64, 150 epochs, binary cross-entropy. Threshold parameters, unlearning time (3.2 s) and retraining time (5.6 s) per partition are tabulated.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Described as a 70/15/15 train/validation/test partition with strict subject-level separation to avoid leakage across folds and stratified sampling to preserve class distribution, with thresholds set by the Youden index on validation data. That description is methodologically sound in wording. It cannot be reconciled with the rest of the article: the sample sizes it applies to are internally contradictory, the same section reports 25,000 positives from a 10,000-sample dataset, and the experiments are described elsewhere as simulations.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive value, ROC AUC and calibration scores are named as the evaluation set, said to be reported with 95 to 98% confidence intervals - a phrasing that conflates the confidence level with an interval. Paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests are named for significance. The figures actually presented are bar charts of error rate, false-positive counts and precision binned into low, medium and high categories before and after unlearning.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Maximum diagnostic accuracy of 98%, a 23% reduction in overall error rate, reduced false positives and reduced processing time. No confusion matrix, no per-dataset accuracy table and no numeric confidence interval accompanies these figures in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Developmental screening items - the CSBS description mentions communication via eye movements (straight, upward, leftward, downward) and repetitive hand and finger movements, with binary yes/no responses and 30-second monitoring windows.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Not separately detailed in the extracted text beyond the deployment concerns above.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Two sentences in the conclusion: the framework depends on the availability and quality of multimodal datasets, which may vary across clinical settings, and repeated unlearning operations can incur overhead in large-scale applications. Both concern deployment rather than the evidence.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: No participants and no coherent sample. The methods state within four consecutive sentences that the study utilised MRI datasets of newborns comprising 10,000 samples and that the final dataset included 25,000 positive cases and 1200 negative cases, with class balance maintained. Both claims cannot hold: 25,000 positives cannot come from 10,000 samples, and a ratio of nearly 21 to 1 is not balance. Elsewhere the CSBS description reports 500 subjects, and Table 4, labelled Standard dataset, lists the same identifier range 01-1000 five times over with different family relationships (son, daughter, niece) and a different algorithm name in each row, so it is a results table presented as a data description. No consistent count of children exists anywhere in the article.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, newborns, newborn babies, infants, children, brain disabilities, brain disorder. Autism is grouped throughout with brain disabilities and brain disorders as a single detection target, and the abstract describes ASD as a rising disorder in the brain among newborns. No autistic or community perspective appears. A distinct register intrudes in the results, where false positives are explained as occurring when the system flags safe/normal data as malicious or abnormal, and precision is explained in terms of how likely a nominated event is to be true when the model declares it malicious, fraudulent, or different from the expected behaviour - vocabulary from cybersecurity or fraud detection that has been carried into a paper about newborns.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: None. No sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic or geographic information for any dataset. Age is reported three incompatible ways: newborns aged 0 to 36 months in the title and abstract, children aged 12-36 months in the MRI inclusion criteria, and aged 3-6 years in the CSBS description. Since the paper's central claim is that existing tools are restricted to toddlers above 18 months and that it addresses the gap in newborns, the age of the analysed population is the single most consequential fact in the study and it is stated three different ways.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None. No diagnostic instrument administration, criterion, assessor or record is described for any dataset. The named sources - ASQ, CSBS, PEDS, M-CHAT and STAT - are developmental screening instruments, not diagnoses, and the paper does not describe how any label was assigned. One results passage categorises outcomes as yes (Y), random (R) - indicating a 50% probability of yes and a 50% probability of no - and not detected (N), which introduces a coin-flip category into what is presented as a diagnostic output.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is a machine-unlearning-integrated explainable AI framework for early ASD and brain-disability detection in newborns, motivated by a genuinely important argument: once a newborn's data is used in training, most models provide no mechanism to remove it if parents withdraw consent, which raises ethical and legal problems under GDPR and HIPAA. Headline findings: a 23% reduction in error rates, reduced false positives, accuracy improved to 98%, and reduced processing time. The results are described as simulation results.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting. Datasets are said to have been processed in different computing laboratories; a testbed with 32 GB RAM and 2 TB storage is named for timing measurements. The paper states that the work involved no hospital deployments while also claiming, in its contributions list, past experience implementing the system in clinical settings and that the framework can effectively validate itself in real-world clinical implementations.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: No task or paradigm. Developmental screening instruments and archived imaging. The most concrete behavioural description concerns CSBS items on communication via eye movements (straight, upward, leftward, downward) and repetitive hand and finger movements, recorded as binary responses over 30-second monitoring windows.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional. Ethics and consent are declared unnecessary on the stated ground that the work involved no hospital deployments, and the same passage claims that the datasets were fully identified and processed with strict subject-level partitioning, with fully authorised controlled access, audit logging and standard encryption. Fully identified is the opposite of de-identified and appears in a sentence listing privacy safeguards, so it is presumably an error - but it is the operative word in the article's only statement about the identifiability of newborn data. The irony is structural rather than incidental: the paper's entire motivation is that models must be able to forget a newborn's data when parents withdraw consent, and it obtains no consent and no ethical review for its own use of that data.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition instrumentation. Model components: ResNet-50 (50 layers) or InceptionV3 (48 layers) at 224x224 input, Adam at learning rate 0.003 (described as increasing), batch size 64, 150 epochs, binary cross-entropy; unlearning and retraining times of 3.2 s and 5.6 s per partition; an inter-modality correlation threshold of 0.65. A testbed with 32 GB RAM and 2 TB storage is named.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: The article makes strong reproducibility claims - a public GitHub repository for both code and data, frozen configuration files, and an explicit statement that the entire pipeline can be replicated end-to-end - and simultaneously makes reproduction impossible by contradicting itself about what was run. The partition count is six in the methodology and four in the parameter table; the sample is 10,000 MRI scans and also 25,000 positives plus 1,200 negatives; the age band is 0-36 months, 12-36 months and 3-6 years in three places; the modality set is MRI, video, audio, text and EEG in one section and MRI, video and text in another. Feature vectors are printed as illustrative example values rather than as results.
