A sentence from the revision process also survives in the published text, reporting that figures are revised with corrected captions, algorithm numbering is standardized, and placeholder references are replaced with accurate citations.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Two sentences, both about deployment: the framework depends on the availability and quality of multimodal datasets, which may vary across clinical settings, and repeated unlearning operations can incur overhead at scale. Neither addresses the evidence. Unmentioned: the contradictory sample sizes, the three different age ranges, the absence of any diagnostic label description, the absence of any numeric result table for the headline accuracy, the majority-class baseline implied by the reported class ratio, and the fact that the experiments are described as simulations.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Not separately developed beyond the deployment limitations. The paper closes on the claim that the framework improved interpretability and diagnostic reliability.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Developmental screening behaviours as captured by ASQ, CSBS, PEDS, M-CHAT and STAT items - communication through eye movements and repetitive hand and finger movements are the only behaviours described concretely - together with imaging and physiological modalities named but not characterised.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Multimodal fusion is the framework's structural claim: each modality is partitioned, processed by per-partition CNNs, aggregated into a modality representation, and fused into a single feature vector for a softmax classifier. The claim cannot be evaluated. The modality set differs between sections (MRI, video, audio, text and EEG versus MRI, video and text); no dataset is characterised well enough to know what any modality contains; the fused feature vectors are printed as illustrative example numbers; and no ablation isolates any modality's contribution except a reference to an MRI-only ablation whose results are not shown in the extracted text.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: MUXAI-ASDBD, described as a partitioning-based explainable CNN framework with layer-wise explainability and a machine-unlearning mechanism at the summation layer, using ResNet-50 or InceptionV3 as per-partition feature extractors. Baselines named are CNN, GNN, ACNN, SVM, LSTM and a proposed FCNN-LSTM - a list that does not match the framework the paper is proposing, since the title framework is a partitioned CNN and the proposed baseline is a fully connected LSTM.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: 224x224 images for the CNN backbones; the representation of questionnaire data is never specified, which matters because five of the seven named datasets are questionnaires and a 224x224 convolutional backbone cannot consume a checklist without a stated encoding. Aggregated feature vectors appear in the text as literal illustrative values such as [0.5, 0.6, ..., 0.8] and [0.45, 0.55, ..., 0.75].
custom_fields.RQ4.3: The named metric set is clinically appropriate and unusually complete for this corpus - sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, ROC AUC and calibration, with thresholds set by the Youden index and significance assessed by paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. None of it is reported. No sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, AUC or calibration value appears in the extracted text, no test statistic or p-value is given, and the phrase all reported with 95 to 98% confidence intervals conflates a confidence level with an interval width. What is actually presented is bar charts of error rate, false-positive count and precision binned into low, medium and high before and after unlearning, plus a headline accuracy of 98% and a 23% error reduction with no denominator. If the stated class ratio of 25,000 positives to 1,200 negatives held, the majority-class baseline would be 95.4% and the headline would be 2.6 points above it.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Layer-wise explainability is the framework's named contribution and no explainability result is presented. Modality-specific outputs are described in a single sentence as gradient spectrogram features for audio and spatiotemporal attention maps for video, each demonstrating interpretability in a clinically meaningful context, with no figure, attribution or quantitative measure to support the claim in the extracted text.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The validation section contains, in isolation, the most methodologically literate paragraph of any weak study in this review: a 70/15/15 partition with strict subject-level separation to avoid leakage across folds, stratified sampling to preserve class distribution, Youden-index thresholding on validation data, clinically meaningful metrics including PPV and NPV and calibration, paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, ablation of the MRI-only modality, runtime measurement with means and standard deviations, and a subject-level deletion threat model under which the unlearned model should remain statistically indistinguishable from one retrained without the deleted data, audited by removing specified subjects and validating forgetting against deletion audit sets. Every element of that is the right thing to do. None of it can be assessed, because the article does not report a single number from any of it and because the data description it would apply to is self-contradicting - 10,000 MRI samples yielding 25,000 positive cases, a 25,000-to-1,200 split called class balance, six partitions in one section and four in another, three mutually exclusive age ranges. The experiments are moreover described throughout as simulation results, and the only quantitative outputs shown are before-and-after bar charts binned into low, medium and high. The gap between the methodological vocabulary and the reported evidence is the finding here: this is the corpus's clearest instance of validation language functioning as a genre convention rather than as a description of work performed.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Autism spectrum disorder; Newborn babies; Machine un-learning; Convolutional neural network; Explainable artificial intelligence. Five terms; the population claim (newborn babies) is the one the article's own data description contradicts three times.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Alexandria Engineering Journal 145 (2026) 164-181 (Elsevier) - a general engineering journal. Review did not surface a sample description in which 25,000 positive cases are drawn from 10,000 samples and a 21-to-1 ratio is called balanced, three incompatible age ranges for the study population, partition counts differing between sections, a named metric set none of whose values are reported, cybersecurity vocabulary about malicious and fraudulent events in a paper about infants, or a surviving response-to-reviewers sentence in the body text.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2026. The framing rests on a genuinely important and under-addressed problem: that once a newborn's data enters a training set there is usually no mechanism to remove it when parents withdraw consent, and that this is a live obligation under GDPR and HIPAA. That argument is correct and is made nowhere else in this corpus. What follows it does not support any of the claims made from it - accuracy improved to 98%, error rates reduced by 23%, false positives reduced, and a framework said to be able to validate itself in real-world clinical implementations and to be implementable in hospital settings. The study reports no confusion matrix, no metric values from its own named metric set, no consistent sample size and no ethics approval, in a paper whose organising principle is the ethical handling of newborns' data.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Deep learning based approach for Behavior classification in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder using naturalistic videos
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Jabbar U; Waseem Iqbal M; Nechifor A; Abaker M; Khairalseed MA; Antohi VM; Fortea C; Stefanescu CA
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed with an explicit limit that the review should record: the system is described as intended to be used as a clinical decision support system and not an independent diagnostic system. The abstract nonetheless states that the approach facilitates quick, accurate and effective screening of ASD and shows tremendous potential for real-world clinical implementation.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of a public naturalistic video dataset; four-class behaviour classification with k-fold cross-validation, five architectures compared under identical hyperparameters, and paired significance testing.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: VGG16, MobileNet, EfficientNet-B7 and 3D-CNN+LSTM, all fitted by the authors on the same data under identical settings, with paired t-tests reported against the proposed model. Plus a related-work table of eleven prior studies with their datasets, methods, accuracies and named limitations.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None. The Self-Stimulatory Behaviour Dataset (SSBD) was used, which the paper describes accurately: parents and caretakers posted their videos on publicly accessible websites, and the dataset developers supplied URLs of 75 YouTube videos with start and finish annotations for the behaviours of interest.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Cropped frame sequences from annotated behaviour segments.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Pakistan, Romania, Saudi Arabia and Sudan - Superior University Lahore, Dunarea de Jos University of Galati, Transilvania University of Brasov, King Khalid University and University of Gadarif. No data collection.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None. The SSBD videos were uploaded by parents and caretakers to public websites; no clinical diagnosis, instrument, assessor or record exists for any child, and the annotations concern the timing of behaviours rather than diagnostic status.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: Not applicable in the usual sense - the dataset consists of videos of autistic children only, so all four classes come from the same population.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 75 videos of approximately 90 seconds each, segmented into frames. The number of distinct children is never stated. The k-fold confusion matrix reports 303 samples, so the analysis unit is a video segment or frame clip rather than a child.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. The independent test set is a held-out portion of the same 75-video dataset.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: There is no non-autistic comparison group. The fourth class, normal Behavior, is non-stereotyped movement drawn from the same autistic children's videos.
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not addressed.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: 25% for a four-class task if classes are balanced, never stated; the per-class sample counts are not reported so the actual baseline cannot be computed.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Video - naturalistic home recordings, decomposed into frames.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None imposed. Naturalistic home video of children engaged in everyday activities, with behaviour segments delimited by the dataset's original annotations.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None controlled - consumer recordings of unknown provenance uploaded to YouTube. Python OpenCV was used for frame extraction.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Low to moderate. Genuine strengths: the source dataset is public and correctly attributed, the preprocessing chain (frame extraction, ROI detection, cropping, augmentation) is described in order, five architectures were trained under deliberately identical hyperparameters, per-fold standard deviations are published for every model, and paired significance tests with a corrected threshold are reported. Missing: the value of k, the number of extracted frames or clips, the number of distinct children, per-class sample counts, the split unit, the learning rate, batch size and epoch count, a random seed, and any code or data statement.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: No data-availability statement appears in the extracted text. SSBD itself is a public URL list, and the paper notes that it is the only freely available dataset of this kind.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Absent. There is no ethics statement, consent statement or exemption claim; the string ethic does not appear in the article. No consideration is given to the provenance of the videos - which the paper itself describes as home recordings of identifiable autistic children uploaded by parents and caretakers to YouTube - or to whether their reuse for model training was contemplated by those who posted them.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Frame extraction with OpenCV; region-of-interest detection and image cropping to remove irrelevant background objects; augmentation to reduce overfitting. Segments were divided according to behavioural movement type using the dataset's annotations.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: CNN convolutional layers for per-frame spatial features, passed to a GRU for temporal modelling across frames.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Python with OpenCV for frame extraction; a deep learning framework is implied but not named with a version.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Paired t-tests between the proposed model and each baseline with t statistics, p-values and a stated significance threshold of 0.0125 - an explicit multiple-comparison correction that is rare in this corpus. Per-fold standard deviations are reported for every architecture.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None of the model. The confusion-matrix discussion is substantive, however: misclassifications concentrate between spinning and the repetitive classes, which the authors attribute to overlap in motion dynamics, and normal behaviour is moderately confused with the repetitive classes in the independent test set.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not described as a search. The same hyperparameter settings were deliberately used across all five models for comparability.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Per-class performance is reported and discussed. No demographic stratification is possible.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: A custom CNN-GRU hybrid, compared against VGG16, MobileNet, EfficientNet-B7 and a 3D-CNN+LSTM under identical hyperparameter settings.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Convolutional layers into flatten and fully connected layers with softmax output; GRU chosen over LSTM for simpler gating and fewer parameters, with the stated rationale that this improves training stability under repeated k-fold retraining. All five models were trained with the same hyperparameter settings to enable fair comparison - an explicit and welcome design choice. Specific layer widths, learning rate, batch size and epoch counts are not quoted in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: k-fold cross-validation, with per-fold means and standard deviations reported for all five architectures, plus a separate overall test evaluation with its own confusion matrix. The value of k is not stated. The decisive issue is the unit: the 75 source videos are segmented into frame clips and the k-fold confusion matrix covers 303 samples, so segments from the same video - and therefore the same child, setting, lighting and camera - are distributed across folds. No video-level or child-level grouping is described.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Validation accuracy and loss per architecture; precision, recall and F1 per architecture; per-fold mean and standard deviation for accuracy, precision, recall and two further columns; per-class F1; two confusion matrices (k-fold and independent test); learning curves; and paired t-tests with p-values against each baseline at a Bonferroni-style threshold of 0.0125.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: CNN-GRU k-fold accuracy 0.9294 +/- 0.0038 with per-fold standard deviations under 0.004 across all metrics; validation accuracy 0.96 with validation loss 0.16; precision 0.96, recall 0.95-0.96, F1 0.96. Baselines: MobileNet 0.9193, 3D-CNN+LSTM 0.8912, EfficientNet-B7 0.8808, VGG16 lowest. Per class, arm flapping and head banging reach F1 0.98 while normal behaviour and spinning reach 0.93 and 0.94. Paired t-tests: CNN-GRU versus MobileNet t=3.68 p=0.0028; versus VGG16 t=3.52 p=0.0051; versus 3D-CNN+LSTM t=10.82; versus EfficientNet-B7 t=16.67.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Four behaviour classes: arm flapping, head banging, spinning and normal behaviour. These are self-stimulatory motor behaviours recorded in unstructured everyday settings, which is a genuine strength - the behaviours are observed rather than reported and are recorded outside a laboratory.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Announced but not detailed in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: The paper announces that Section 4 discusses the paper's weaknesses and possible future study approaches, and the only self-directed observations in the extracted text concern the dataset - that SSBD is the only freely available dataset of its kind, that it is somewhat helpful but does not fully meet the study's conditions, and that no previous dataset fully meets the requirement. A detailed limitations table is applied to eleven prior studies instead.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: No participants and no groups. The data are 75 YouTube videos of approximately 90 seconds each from the Self-Stimulatory Behaviour Dataset, uploaded by parents and caretakers, segmented into frame clips by behaviour type using the dataset's original annotations. The number of distinct children is never stated - a consequential omission, since 75 videos may represent fewer than 75 children and the k-fold confusion matrix reports 303 samples, so the analysis unit is the clip. Crucially there is no non-autistic comparison group: all four classes, including normal Behavior, are drawn from videos of autistic children, so the study is a behaviour-recognition problem within one population rather than a diagnostic contrast between populations.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic children, ASD children, ASD youngsters, abnormal Behavioral patterns, stereotypical Behaviors, normal Behavior. The stereotyped/normal opposition is applied to movements rather than to children, which is the more defensible usage, but the framing describes self-stimulatory behaviours as abnormal throughout and the fourth class as normal. No autistic or community perspective appears, and there is no discussion of self-stimulatory behaviour as regulatory rather than pathological.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography or setting information for any child. The videos are consumer home recordings of unknown provenance, and the paper does not report even the age range of the children whose behaviour it classifies.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None, and not required by the task as executed - but required by the task as described. The videos are annotated for when a behaviour occurs, not for whether the child has a diagnosis; no clinical assessment, instrument or assessor exists for anyone in the dataset. The paper's title nonetheless places the work in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder and its abstract states that the approach facilitates quick, accurate and effective screening of ASD. Those claims do not follow from a four-way discrimination among arm flapping, head banging, spinning and other movement in videos of children who are all autistic.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is to classify four behaviour categories - arm flapping, spinning, head banging and normal behaviour - from naturalistic, unstructured video, using a CNN-GRU architecture, in order to help clinicians monitor behavioural trends. Headline findings: CNN-GRU reaches k-fold accuracy 0.9294 +/- 0.0038 and validation accuracy 0.96, outperforming MobileNet (0.9193), 3D-CNN+LSTM (0.8912), EfficientNet-B7 (0.8808) and VGG16, with paired t-tests significant against all four at a corrected threshold of 0.0125. Per class, the two clearly distinct repetitive behaviours (arm flapping, head banging) reach F1 0.98 while spinning and normal behaviour reach 0.94 and 0.93.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting - the defining property of the data is precisely that there is none. The videos are unstructured home recordings made by families in everyday environments, which is the source of both the design's principal strength (ecological validity, behaviours observed rather than reported) and its principal uncontrolled variance (camera, framing, lighting, distance and activity all vary by video and are perfectly confounded with the child).
custom_fields.RQ2.3: No imposed task. Naturalistic recordings of children engaged in everyday activities, with behaviour episodes delimited by the SSBD annotations of start and finish times. This is the most ecologically valid data source in the charted corpus - no laboratory, no stimulus, no instruction, and behaviours that occurred spontaneously in the child's own environment.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis. There is no ethics statement, consent statement or exemption claim anywhere in the article. The omission is more pointed than in the questionnaire studies because the paper itself describes the data's provenance: parents and caretakers posted their videos on websites that are accessible to the public, and the dataset consists of URLs to 75 YouTube videos of identifiable autistic children. Whether a parent posting a home video to YouTube thereby consents to its use as machine learning training data is exactly the question the study needed to address and does not raise.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No controlled acquisition equipment - the recordings are consumer video of unknown origin. Python OpenCV was used for frame extraction. Region-of-interest detection and cropping were applied to remove background objects, which is the appropriate response to uncontrolled framing. No deep learning framework, version, seed or hardware is named.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Mixed, with real strengths on the comparative design. Reproducible: the source dataset is public and correctly attributed to its originators, the preprocessing chain is described in order, all five architectures were deliberately trained under identical hyperparameters to make the comparison fair, per-fold standard deviations are reported for every model and metric, and paired t-tests with a corrected significance threshold of 0.0125 are tabulated. Not reproducible: the value of k, the number of frames or clips extracted, the number of distinct children, per-class sample counts, the unit at which folds were formed, the learning rate, batch size and epoch count, any seed, and any code or data-availability statement.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The paper announces that it will discuss its weaknesses, and the only self-directed remarks concern the data - that SSBD is the sole freely available dataset of its kind, that it is somewhat helpful but does not fully meet the study's conditions, and that no existing dataset does. Against that, a full column of Table 1 assigns a specific limitation to each of eleven prior studies (did not describe the pre-processing and model development steps; need to improve results; implemented a basic CNN model that performs binary classification and was tested on a small dataset). Unmentioned for this study: that folds are formed over clips from 75 videos with no video-level or child-level grouping; that the number of distinct children is unknown; that there is no non-autistic comparison group behind a screening claim; that no ethics statement accompanies the reuse of identifiable children's home videos; and that per-class counts and the chance level are unreported.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Announced in the paper's structure but not developed in the extracted text.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Self-stimulatory motor behaviour observed in natural settings: arm flapping, head banging and spinning, against a fourth class of non-stereotyped movement. This is the corpus's clearest instance of behaviour being observed directly rather than inferred from a photograph, a checklist or a questionnaire - the behaviours are the ones clinicians actually watch for, recorded where they actually occur. The confusion-matrix analysis adds a substantive behavioural observation: errors concentrate between spinning and the two repetitive classes, attributed to overlap in motion dynamics, and normal behaviour is moderately confused with the repetitive classes in the held-out test.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No fusion - video only. The CNN-GRU combination is spatial-plus-temporal modelling within one modality, and the architectural rationale is stated properly: convolutional layers extract spatial features from single frames while autism-related behaviour is a temporal phenomenon requiring sequence modelling across frames. That is a correct justification for a recurrent component, unlike the several studies in this corpus that apply LSTMs to single static inputs.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A custom CNN-GRU hybrid, with GRU selected over LSTM on the stated grounds of simpler gating, fewer parameters, greater training stability and less overfitting under repeated k-fold retraining. Four comparators - VGG16, MobileNet, EfficientNet-B7 and 3D-CNN+LSTM - were fitted by the authors on the same data under identical hyperparameters, which makes this one of the few architecture comparisons in the corpus that is actually controlled.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Cropped frame sequences from annotated behaviour segments, after region-of-interest detection to remove irrelevant background and augmentation to reduce overfitting. The ROI step is well motivated for uncontrolled home video, where background and framing differ systematically between recordings.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Validation accuracy and loss, precision, recall and F1 per architecture; per-fold means with standard deviations for every model and metric; per-class F1; two confusion matrices; learning curves; and paired t-tests with a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of 0.0125. The statistical reporting is among the better examples in this corpus - the standard deviations are given rather than implied, and the multiple-comparison correction is stated explicitly. What is missing bears directly on interpretation: per-class sample counts are not reported, so the 25% chance level for a four-class problem cannot be checked against the actual class balance; the value of k is never given; and the very small per-fold standard deviations (under 0.004 across five architectures) are read as evidence that the model is robust and consistent across the folds when, over clips drawn from only 75 videos, near-identical fold results are equally consistent with folds that are near-identical resamples of the same recordings.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No model interpretability, but a genuine and clinically sensible error analysis. Spinning is confused with the repetitive classes because of overlapping motion dynamics, and normal behaviour is confused with the repetitive classes in the independent test set - both of which are the errors one would predict from the physics of the behaviours, and both of which point at the harder discrimination (is this movement stereotyped or not?) rather than the easier one (is this flapping or banging?).
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The evaluation is better constructed than most in this corpus and still cannot support the claim the title makes. On the credit side: k-fold cross-validation with per-fold standard deviations reported for all five architectures, an independent test evaluation with its own confusion matrix, identical hyperparameters across models to make the comparison fair, and paired t-tests against every baseline at a corrected threshold. On the debit side, three things. First, the unit: 75 source videos are segmented into clips and the k-fold matrix covers 303 samples, with no video-level or child-level grouping described, so clips from the same recording - same child, same room, same camera, same clothing - fall on both sides of every fold. In naturalistic video this is the strongest available shortcut, because recording identity is far easier to learn than movement type. Second, the reported stability is read backwards: standard deviations below 0.004 across five different architectures are presented as robustness, whereas over clips from 75 videos they indicate that the folds contain much the same material. Third, and separately from any of this, the task is not the task claimed. Four-way discrimination among arm flapping, head banging, spinning and other movement, in videos of children who are all autistic, cannot yield screening for ASD, because no non-autistic person appears anywhere in the data - a screening claim requires a comparison the design does not contain. The paper's own hedge, that the system is intended as a clinical decision support system and not an independent diagnostic system, is the correct reading and sits uneasily beside a title placing the work in diagnoses of ASD and an abstract promising effective screening.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Autism Spectrum Disorder; Behavior analysis; CNN-GRU; deep learning; naturalistic video. Five terms, and naturalistic video is the one that matters - it names the study's genuine distinguishing property in a corpus dominated by downloaded photographs and checklists.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience 20:1626315, with a 174-day review including a substantial revision. The review did not surface the absent ethics statement for reuse of identifiable children's home videos, the unreported number of distinct children, the absence of a non-autistic comparison behind a screening claim, or the reading of near-zero fold variance as robustness.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2026, published 18 March, 174 days from submission with one revision round. The framing is internally split. The objectives section states that the system should be used as a clinical decision support system and not an independent diagnostic system - an accurate and unusually explicit limit. The title, abstract and conclusion pull the other way, placing the work in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder, claiming it facilitates the quick, accurate, and effective screening of ASD, and asserting tremendous potential for real-world clinical implementation. What the study actually demonstrates is that a CNN-GRU distinguishes four movement categories in home video at about 93% under a clip-level split, which is a behaviour-recognition result and a useful one; the screening language is added on top of it.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Explainable Children Autism Detection using Gaze Features in Audio-Visual Speech Comprehension
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Zaragozá-Portolés M; Gimeno-Gomez D; Ávila V; Fajardo DI; Ferrer DA; Gomez-Merino N; Skrobiszewska N; Martínez-Hinarejos CD
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 10(3), Article ETRA012 (ETRA)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Bounded with unusual precision. The paper states that its roughly 64% F1/AUC positions the work as a research exploration rather than a deployable diagnostic tool, given that benchmarks for clinical viability often exceed 80-90%, and proposes value only in preliminary screening contexts where sensitivity to early biomarkers is prioritised over perfect accuracy, as a complement to human judgement involving both educators and clinicians.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Secondary analysis of a purpose-collected eye-tracking corpus (BeGaze); supervised binary classification with six classical algorithms across a factorial design of two stimulus modalities and three temporal speech phases, under nested participant-independent cross-validation with bootstrap confidence intervals.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Six algorithms against one another across twelve experimental conditions (two modalities x three phases, plus global comparisons), and - importantly - against an explicit majority-class baseline computed within each cross-validation fold as a lower bound.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Not described in this paper, which analyses an existing corpus; diagnostic classification was conducted externally by qualified specialists (neuropaediatricians or clinical psychologists) prior to inclusion.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: A tabular vector of 18 AOI-based temporal gaze features per experimental instance (participant x story x modality x phase).
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Spain - Universitat Politecnica de Valencia (Pattern Recognition and Human Language Technology research centre) and University of Valencia (Reading Research Unit, Department of Developmental and Educational Psychology). The corpus is Spanish, collected in a Castilian/Valencian bilingual environment.
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: SCQ scores reported by group. No ADOS or calibrated severity metric.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Yes, and independent of the study: diagnostic classification was conducted externally by qualified specialists - neuropaediatricians or clinical psychologists - prior to inclusion in the corpus. The Social Communication Questionnaire was additionally administered as a symptomatology measure and its group difference reported (12.6 versus 4.7).
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 19 children with a specialist-confirmed ASD diagnosis; mean age 75.9 months (SD 19.4); SCQ 12.6 (5.3); KBIT-2 108.78 (16.77); PPVT-III 50.0 (28.5)
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Two standardised instruments administered by the research team in Spanish-adapted form: KBIT-2 for nonverbal intelligence, comparable across groups (104.3 versus 108.78), and PPVT-III for receptive vocabulary, substantially lower in the ASD group (50.0 versus 67.3). The paper reports both and notes the pattern explicitly.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Focused on the preschool-to-primary transition, ages 5-8 years, with group means of 78.1 and 75.9 months. The ASD group's age standard deviation is more than twice that of the comparison group (19.4 versus 8.8 months).
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 45 children (BeGaze corpus)
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. Named implicitly in the limitations through the small sample and the call for larger cross-linguistic cohorts.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 26 typically developing children; mean age 78.1 months (SD 8.8); SCQ 4.7 (5.6); KBIT-2 104.3 (12.7); PPVT-III 67.3 (22.6)
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Informed consent obtained from the legal guardians of all participants.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Explicitly operationalised as a per-fold majority-class baseline included in the design to test whether gaze features add value beyond class distribution - one of only two studies in the charted corpus to build a trivial baseline into the evaluation rather than leaving it implicit.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye tracking during audio-visual storytelling, with areas of interest defined on the narrator's face.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A storytelling comprehension task. Children watched pre-recorded clips of a professional storyteller narrating short children's stories with the face clearly visible, then answered comprehension questions. Six stories (N01-N06) were used, three presented audio-only and three audio-visually, counterbalanced across participants, with each story instance segmented into three temporal phases relative to speech onset (pre-speech, speech, post-speech).
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Screen-based eye tracking (device not named in the extracted text) with predefined AOIs over eyes, nose and mouth. Modelling on a standard desktop (Intel i7, 16 GB RAM, no GPU), which the authors note keeps the pipeline deployable without specialised hardware.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: High. The corpus is cited to its originating publications with its ethics approval; the participant table gives group sizes, ages, SCQ, KBIT-2 and PPVT-III with standard deviations; the 18 features are enumerated by AOI; the experimental grid (two modalities x three phases x six stories) is fully described including counterbalancing; the grid-search space is published per algorithm; the nested cross-validation scheme, participant independence, class balancing and bootstrap interval estimation are all specified; the software stack is named; and per-story results are tabulated. The main gaps are the eye-tracking device, a code or data statement, and the number of instances per condition.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Not stated in the extracted text; the BeGaze corpus is cited to its originating publications.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not stated in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Yes - the experimental protocol and data collection for the BeGaze corpus were approved by the Ethics Committee of the Universitat de Valencia and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Computation of temporal AOI-based features per experimental instance, with each story instance treated as a separate sample and segmented into three speech phases. The authors note explicitly that they did not stratify by story content.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Eighteen interpretable features - for each of the eyes, mouth and nose AOIs: fixation count, average fixation duration, dwell-time percentage, fixation-time percentage, revisits and normalised dwell coverage.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Scikit-learn, XGBoost and PyTorch.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on all performance estimates; paired t-tests comparing audio-only against audio-visual within each speech phase with full statistics tabulated; explicit statements of where differences did and did not reach significance, and repeated notes that the small number of observations limits what the comparisons can establish.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Two independent methods - model feature importance and SHAP - both computed on each fold's test set and then averaged, which is the methodologically correct placement. The convergent finding is that fixation times on the mouth and revisits across areas of interest are the most informative features, with eye revisits and mouth fixation count ranking highest. The authors connect this to existing cognitive literature on social attention in ASD rather than presenting it as a discovery.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Grid search inside the inner cross-validation loop only, with the search space published per algorithm.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Extensive by condition rather than by demographics: results are decomposed by stimulus modality, by speech phase, and by individual story, with the story analysis run specifically to test whether narrative content drove performance (it did not).
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Six classical, interpretable algorithms including SVM (linear kernel only, chosen deliberately to preserve interpretability), logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost and a shallow multi-layer perceptron.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Grid searches specified per algorithm - SVM C in {0.1, 1, 10, 100} with gamma in {scale, auto} and linear kernel throughout; MLP hidden layer sizes in {(12,), (24,), (36,), (48,), (24,12)}, activation in {relu, tanh}, learning rate schedule in {constant, adaptive}, solver in {adam, sgd}, alpha in {0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05}. Hyperparameters were selected in the inner cross-validation loop, then the model retrained on the full training data and evaluated on the held-out outer test fold.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Five-fold nested cross-validation with a participant-independent split and class balance preserved in each fold, with bootstrap-based 95% confidence intervals. Hyperparameter selection occurs in the inner loop and never touches the outer test fold. A majority-class baseline is computed per fold specifically to test whether the gaze features carry information beyond class distribution. This is the most complete validation design in the charted corpus alongside local_4da2b941.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Macro F1 and AUC prioritised explicitly because of small and imbalanced data, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals; per-condition results across modality and phase; per-story F1 with standard deviations; paired t-tests comparing modalities within each phase; feature importance and SHAP attributions computed on each fold's test set and averaged.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Best performance 64.1% F1 and 64.5% AUC, from logistic regression in the audio-visual speech-phase condition. Across conditions the speech phase was most stable at around 55% F1. Audio-visual stimuli significantly outperformed audio-only in the pre-speech phase; no significant modality difference emerged during or after speech. Per story, audio-only averaged 57.7 (SD 9.8) and audio-visual 64.1 (SD 9.1) with large within-story variability. All models exceeded the majority-class lower bound.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Social attention to a speaking face: fixation counts, average fixation durations, dwell time, fixation time percentages, normalised dwell coverage and revisits, computed separately for eyes, mouth and nose areas of interest.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Frameworks that capture the sequential structure of AOI-based fixations to exploit the dynamic nature of visual attention; larger cross-linguistic cohorts to assess bilingual exposure effects; and cost-benefit analysis of false positives to set meaningful performance thresholds for low-stakes screening.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: A dedicated limitations section plus two further discussion sections addressing constraints. Stated: the relatively small sample for specific modality/phase pairings limits generalisation and increases susceptibility to overfitting; the context-specific storytelling task may not transfer to other real-world situations; and predefined AOIs and fixed time intervals limit the granularity of the analysis. A separate section addresses cultural and linguistic constraints, noting that participants were recorded in a Castilian/Valencian bilingual environment, which may support cross-linguistic relevance while also introducing confounds relative to monolingual audio-visual speech processing.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Forty-five Spanish children from the BeGaze corpus: 19 with an ASD diagnosis made externally by neuropaediatricians or clinical psychologists before inclusion, and 26 typically developing children, focused on the 5-8 year preschool-to-primary transition. Each child contributed multiple samples - one per story, under two modality conditions and segmented into three temporal phases - and the cross-validation folds are explicitly participant-independent, so the multiplication of samples per child does not leak across the split. This is the correct handling of a repeated-measures design and it is rare in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, typically developing children, TYP. The register is measured and clinical without pathologising; gaze differences are framed as attentional and perceptual patterns and as potential biomarkers rather than as deficits, and the comparison group is typically developing throughout. One inherited phrase from the literature review describes eye tracking as quantifying social attention deficits. There is no autistic or community perspective, but nothing in the language overstates.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Well reported for the variables collected. Group sizes, mean ages with standard deviations, SCQ, KBIT-2 nonverbal intelligence and PPVT-III receptive vocabulary are all tabulated by group, and the pattern is described accurately: nonverbal intelligence comparable across groups (104.3 versus 108.78) while the ASD group shows higher SCQ (12.6 versus 4.7) and markedly lower receptive vocabulary (50.0 versus 67.3). Sex is not reported. Two features deserve note for interpretation. The ASD group's age variability is more than double the comparison group's (SD 19.4 versus 8.8 months), and the receptive-vocabulary gap is large and not adjusted for in the models - in a task whose stimulus is a narrated story, receptive vocabulary is a plausible driver of where a child looks. The paper does address linguistic background separately, devoting a discussion section to the Castilian/Valencian bilingual environment of the recordings.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Independent and clinician-made: diagnostic classification was conducted externally by qualified specialists (neuropaediatricians or clinical psychologists) prior to inclusion in the corpus, with the SCQ administered separately as a symptomatology measure. The label therefore predates and is unrelated to the gaze data - the property that separates this study from the checklist-threshold and folder-label branches of this review.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: SCQ for autism symptomatology, KBIT-2 for nonverbal intelligence and PPVT-III for receptive vocabulary, all administered by the research team using Spanish-adapted standardised instruments and reported by group with standard deviations. No ADOS or calibrated severity score.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is to investigate eye-tracking-based ASD detection during audio-visual storytelling using traditional but explainable machine learning, and to identify which gaze features and which phases of speech carry discriminative information. Headline findings: best performance 64.1% F1 and 64.5% AUC (logistic regression, audio-visual speech phase); around 55% F1 in the speech phase across both modalities; a statistically significant advantage for audio-visual over audio-only stimuli in the pre-speech phase but not during or after speech; and convergent feature-importance and SHAP evidence that mouth fixation time and revisits across facial areas of interest are the most informative features. The abstract states in its second-to-last sentence that performance remains modest.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: The BeGaze corpus was collected in a Spanish research setting with children viewing pre-recorded storytelling clips on screen with AOIs defined over the narrator's face. The bilingual Castilian/Valencian environment of the recorded participants is treated as a methodological factor in its own right rather than left unmentioned.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A well-designed and unusually informative paradigm. Children watched a professional storyteller narrating short children's stories with the face clearly visible, then answered comprehension questions. Six stories were used, three audio-only and three audio-visual, counterbalanced across participants, and each instance was segmented into pre-speech, speech and post-speech phases. This yields a factorial design in which modality and temporal phase can be varied independently, and it is the only study in the charted corpus that manipulates the stimulus systematically rather than presenting a single fixed stimulus set. The paper also notes what it did not control - that the data were not stratified by story content - and then tests that concern directly in a per-story analysis.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional. Ethics reporting is complete for the corpus: approval by the Ethics Committee of the Universitat de Valencia, conduct in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and informed consent from the legal guardians of all participants. Funding is fully itemised across six grants.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Screen-based eye tracking with predefined AOIs over eyes, nose and mouth; the device model is not named, which is the study's one notable acquisition-reporting gap. Analysis used Scikit-learn, XGBoost and PyTorch on an Intel i7 desktop with 16 GB RAM and no GPU, a configuration the authors highlight deliberately as evidence that the pipeline is deployable without specialised hardware.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: High. The corpus is cited to its source with its ethics approval; participant characteristics are tabulated with standard deviations on four measures; the 18 features are enumerated by area of interest; the factorial design is described in full including story counterbalancing; the grid-search space is published for every algorithm; the nested cross-validation, participant independence, per-fold class balancing and bootstrap interval procedure are all specified; the software stack is named; and per-story and per-condition results are tabulated with variability. Missing: the eye-tracking device, a code or data availability statement, and the number of instances contributing to each modality/phase cell.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: A dedicated limitations section naming three constraints - small sample for specific modality/phase pairings limiting generalisation and increasing overfitting risk; the context-specific storytelling task potentially not transferring to other situations; and predefined AOIs and fixed time intervals limiting analytic granularity - plus a separate section on cultural and linguistic constraints addressing the Castilian/Valencian bilingual environment, and a further section (7.3) that positions the work explicitly against clinical viability benchmarks. The self-assessment is distributed through the discussion rather than confined to a closing paragraph, and it is accurate. The one limitation not raised is the substantial receptive-vocabulary difference between groups, which is measured, reported, and then not adjusted for in a task built on comprehending narrated stories.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Sequential models that exploit the temporal structure of AOI fixations rather than aggregating them into summary features; larger cross-linguistic cohorts to assess bilingual exposure; and cost-benefit analysis of false positives to define what performance threshold would count as meaningful in low-stakes screening. The last of these is a form of future work no other study in this review proposes - defining the target rather than raising the number.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Social attention to a speaking face, decomposed by facial region and by time relative to speech onset: fixation count, average fixation duration, dwell-time and fixation-time percentages, normalised dwell coverage and revisits, for the eyes, mouth and nose separately. The substantive behavioural findings are specific and testable - eye revisits and mouth fixation count rank highest in importance, mouth fixation time and cross-AOI revisits emerge as candidate biomarkers under both attribution methods, and the audio-visual advantage is concentrated in the pre-speech phase, which the authors read as anticipatory attention to the mouth before speech begins.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Modality is manipulated experimentally rather than fused computationally, which is a different and arguably more informative use of the term. By presenting the same storytelling task audio-only and audio-visually and comparing gaze features across the two, the study isolates what the visual speech channel contributes to group discrimination - and finds that it contributes most before speech onset. That is a designed contrast producing an interpretable answer, in contrast to the corpus's several studies that concatenate modalities and report only the combined figure.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Six classical interpretable classifiers - SVM (linear kernel only, chosen deliberately to preserve interpretability), logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost and a shallow MLP among them - selected explicitly because the study prioritises explainability over capacity. SVM was most consistent across conditions; logistic regression gave the single best result. No deep sequence model is used, and the authors give the reason: the corpus is small and the features are lightweight.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Eighteen AOI-based temporal gaze features per experimental instance, where an instance is one participant viewing one story under one modality in one speech phase. No clinical instrument score, demographic variable or diagnostic measure enters the feature set - the SCQ, KBIT-2 and PPVT-III are reported as sample characteristics and kept out of the model.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Macro F1 and AUC, chosen explicitly because the data are small and imbalanced, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on every estimate; per-condition, per-phase and per-story breakdowns with standard deviations; paired t-tests between modalities within each phase with full statistics; and - critically - a per-fold majority-class baseline built into the design as a lower bound to test whether the gaze features add anything beyond class distribution. That last element is present in only one other charted study. The reported numbers are correspondingly modest and are described as such: about 55% F1 in the speech phase, 64.1% F1 and 64.5% AUC at best, with the paper noting where differences fail to reach significance and attributing that to the limited number of observations.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Two attribution methods - model feature importance and SHAP - applied convergently, and computed on each cross-validation fold's test set before averaging, which is the correct placement and is stated explicitly. The result is a ranked feature list dominated by eye revisits, mouth fixation count and mouth fixation-time percentage, interpreted against existing cognitive literature on social attention rather than presented as a novel discovery. The authors also note honestly where interpretation fails: for features beyond the leading ones no clear pattern emerged, which they attribute to the modest performance of the classifiers rather than explaining away.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: This is the most rigorously validated study in the charted corpus, and its result is the corpus's most useful single number. The design is five-fold nested cross-validation with participant-independent splits, class balance preserved within folds, hyperparameter selection confined to the inner loop, retraining on the full training portion before a single outer-fold evaluation, bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on every estimate, and a per-fold majority-class baseline included specifically to test whether the features beat class distribution. Each child contributes multiple samples across stories, modalities and phases, and the participant-independent split is what prevents that from becoming the leakage that inflates most of this literature. The outcome is 64.1% F1 and 64.5% AUC at best and around 55% in most conditions - and the authors state plainly that this positions the work as a research exploration rather than a deployable diagnostic tool, given that benchmarks for clinical viability often exceed 80-90%. Two qualifications remain. The sample is 45 children, and the paper repeatedly notes that the limited number of observations prevents modality differences from reaching significance. And the ASD group's receptive vocabulary is markedly lower (PPVT-III 50.0 versus 67.3), which is measured and reported but not adjusted for in a task requiring comprehension of narrated stories - so part of the gaze difference may be a comprehension difference. Neither qualification changes the study's value to this review, which is calibrative: run with correct participant-level nesting, an explicit trivial baseline, confidence intervals and a purpose-designed social-attention paradigm, eye-tracking classification of autism in children reaches the low sixties.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Autism spectrum disorder; Early identification in children; Eye-tracking; Audio-visual speech comprehension; Explainable Artificial Intelligence. Five terms covering condition, application, modality, task and method, with the task - audio-visual speech comprehension - named specifically rather than generically.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 10(3), Article ETRA012, the ETRA eye-tracking venue. The disciplinary fit shows in the reporting: participant-independent nested cross-validation, bootstrap intervals, a majority-class lower bound, paired significance testing between conditions, fold-level attribution computation, and an explicit comparison of the achieved performance against published clinical-viability thresholds.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2026 (May). The framing is the most disciplined in the review. The abstract concedes in its own body that performance remains modest; the results section opens by observing that the modest overall performances underscore the inherent challenges of detecting ASD from gaze-based features in data-scarce naturalistic settings; and section 7.3 states that roughly 64% F1/AUC positions the work as a research exploration rather than a deployable diagnostic tool, given benchmarks for clinical viability often exceed 80-90%. Value is claimed only for preliminary screening as a complement to human judgement, and the proposed future work includes defining, by cost-benefit analysis, what performance threshold would count as meaningful for low-stakes screening. Set beside the studies in this corpus reporting 99% and 100% from checklist thresholds and web-scraped photographs, its contribution is not a method but a demonstration of what the honest number looks like.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Explainable Ensemble Learning Framework for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Enhancing Trust, Interpretability and Reliability in AI-Driven Healthcare
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Alshammeri M; Tariq N; Jhanji NZ; Humayun M; Khan MA
data_charting_rubrics.journal_conference: Computer Modeling in Engineering & Sciences 146(1):41 (Tech Science Press)
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed around trust and interpretability for clinical adoption; no clinician evaluation, threshold or prospective test.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective analysis of two datasets under a common pipeline: a public behavioural screening dataset (binary ASD traits) and a smaller multimodal dataset (four severity classes), with base learners, voting and stacking ensembles, regularised neural networks, an ablation study and post-hoc explanation.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Eight model configurations reported side by side on Dataset 1, plus an ablation adding one pipeline component at a time, plus a state-of-the-art comparison table with named limitations for each prior study.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None for Dataset 1, which is taken from public ASD screening databases and is stated to be the same dataset reported in a cited prior study. For Dataset 2 no recruitment, site, country or citation is given - only that it consists of 100 original clinical samples.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Dataset 1: a reduced tabular vector after correlation filtering and F-test selection. Dataset 2: a concatenated 4,220-dimensional multimodal vector.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Malaysia, Taiwan and the UK - Jouf University, King Salman Center for Disability Research, National University of Computer and Emerging Sciences, Taylor's University, Asia University, University of Roehampton and Prince Mohammad bin Fahd University.
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: Dataset 1 contains the Autism Spectrum Quotient, Social Responsiveness Scale, Q-CHAT score and Childhood Autism Rating Scale as features. Dataset 2's four categories (Mild, Moderate, Severe, Very Severe) are the classification target with no measurement instrument stated.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None described for either dataset. Dataset 1's target is the presence of ASD traits as a binary field; Dataset 2's four severity classes are asserted with no instrument named, though clinical experts are said to have verified annotation consistency at Cohen's kappa 0.92.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: Dataset 1: 729 ASD-positive instances (36.72%). Dataset 2 has no non-ASD class - all 400 samples are distributed across four severity categories.
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not measured. Dataset 1 includes global developmental delay and learning disorder as binary indicators.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Dataset 1 includes age as a demographic feature; no range or distribution is reported. Dataset 2: not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Sex is listed among Dataset 1's demographic features; no counts are reported for either dataset.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Dataset 1 includes speech delay/language disorder, learning disorder, genetic disorders, depression, global developmental delay, social/behavioural issues and anxiety disorder as binary features; no prevalences are reported.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: Dataset 1: 1,985 instances with 28 attributes, 283 of which have missing values. Dataset 2: 100 original clinical samples augmented fourfold to 400.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. The two datasets are presented as a robustness check on one another, but they involve different tasks (binary traits versus four-class severity) and are not used as train/test cohorts.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Dataset 1: 1,256 ASD-negative instances (63.28%), which sets the majority-class baseline at 63.28%. Dataset 2: none.
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Written caregiver consent claimed for Dataset 2 with no further detail; not addressed for Dataset 1.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Reported for Dataset 1 and directly computable - 63.28% of instances are ASD-negative, so the majority-class baseline is 63.28%, which the paper does not state. For Dataset 2 the four severity classes are evenly distributed, so chance is 25%.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Dataset 1: tabular behavioural, demographic and clinical-assessment fields. Dataset 2: four modalities - facial images, 10-30 second voice recordings, vision-based body-keypoint motion, and wearable physiological signals (heart rate variability, galvanic skin response, temperature).
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None described for either dataset - no stimulus, task or session protocol is reported.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Dataset 2 names vision-based pose estimation and wearable sensors; no device models. No compute environment is described.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Split. Dataset 1's pipeline is among the best documented in this branch: the full preprocessing and modelling sequence is published as a numbered algorithm with the correlation threshold, the SMOTE trigger condition, the split ratio and the F-test formula given, and the dataset's class balance, feature counts and missing-value count are tabulated. Dataset 2 is the opposite - no source, no citation, no country, no institution, no ethics committee, no access route, and a description built entirely from asserted quality figures. Neither dataset comes with code, seeds, base-learner hyperparameters or a stated fold count.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Dataset 1 is described as coming from public ASD screening databases with details in a cited prior study. Dataset 2 has no accession, citation or access route.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Claimed for Dataset 2 - all participant data anonymised before processing, written consent obtained from caregivers, and Institutional Review Board approval granted for data collection and analysis - but no committee, protocol number, institution or country is named. No ethics statement covers Dataset 1.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Published as a numbered algorithm: label encoding, z-score normalisation, removal of features correlated above 0.90 (retaining whichever correlates more with the target), stratified 60:20:20 splitting, conditional SMOTE applied to the training set only when the minority-to-majority ratio falls below 0.8, and ANOVA F-test feature selection. The ordering is correct and the paper states explicitly that SMOTE is applied only on the training set, preventing data leakage - an ordering that several comparable studies in this review get wrong.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Dataset 1: correlation filtering and ANOVA F-test selection. Dataset 2: 4,220 features - 4,040 image features from three pretrained CNNs plus 200 texture, colour and shape descriptors; 80 acoustic features; 50 motion features; 50 physiological features.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Not named. Components identifiable: ResNet50, VGG16, MobileNetV2 for image features, MFCC and voice-quality extraction, SMOTE, SelectKBest ANOVA F-test, random forest, XGBoost, gradient boosting, SVM, logistic regression, soft-voting and stacking ensembles, regularised and deep MLPs, SHAP and LIME.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: None. No confidence intervals, significance tests or cross-validation variance accompany any reported figure.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: SHAP and LIME applied to Dataset 1 only, as stated in the abstract. No attribution analysis is reported for the multimodal dataset, where modality-level attribution would have been the informative result.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: k-fold cross-validation is said to optimise each classifier; the search space and fold count are not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Random forest, XGBoost, gradient boosting, SVM and logistic regression as base learners; soft voting and stacking with a logistic-regression meta-learner; a regularised MLP with L2, batch normalisation and dropout; and a deeper variant with early stopping and adaptive learning-rate scheduling.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Regularisation components are named for the neural networks; base-learner hyperparameters and the k of the cross-validation are not quoted in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Dataset 1: stratified 60:20:20 train/validation/test split with k-fold cross-validation for model optimisation, SMOTE confined to training, and a held-out test set for final metrics. Dataset 2: stratified 80/10/10 split with 5-fold stratified cross-validation - applied, critically, to the augmented set of 400 rather than to the 100 original samples, so augmented copies of the same clinical sample fall on both sides of the split, and the test partition contains 40 samples against 4,220 features.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC per model on Dataset 1; accuracy and F1 for each ablation configuration on both datasets. No confidence intervals, no cross-validation variance, and precision, recall and F1 are omitted for the two neural network rows.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Dataset 1: regularised neural network 97.60% accuracy (ROC-AUC 0.998); voting classifier 96.90%; SVM, logistic regression and stacking 96.10%; random forest and gradient boosting 94.50%; XGBoost 93.70%. Logistic regression reports recall 100.00% with precision 87.20% and ROC-AUC 1.000. Dataset 2 multimodal: 98.2%. Ablation on Dataset 1: 89.40% baseline, 92.80% with feature selection, 94.60% with SMOTE, 96.30% with ensemble fusion, 97.60% with neural-network regularisation.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Dataset 1: screening-questionnaire behaviours and comorbidity flags. Dataset 2: facial appearance, voice quality, movement kinematics including velocity, acceleration, jerk, coordination and repetitive behavioural patterns, and autonomic arousal.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Not captured in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: None as a section in the extracted text. A comparison table assigns a specific limitation to each of the prior studies reviewed.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two datasets with very different standing. Dataset 1 is 1,985 instances with 28 attributes from public ASD screening databases - the same 1,985-record ASD Children Traits collection analysed by local_183eaef4 - and here, unlike there, its class balance is reported: 729 ASD-positive (36.72%) against 1,256 negative (63.28%), with 283 instances carrying missing values. Dataset 2 consists of 100 original clinical samples augmented fourfold to 400, distributed evenly across four severity categories with no non-ASD class at all, and with no source, citation, country or institution given for the original 100. The number of distinct children behind either dataset is never stated.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, ASD traits. The register is clinical and unremarkable; the framing is service-oriented, opening on the need for clinicians to trust AI tools and closing on healthcare trustworthiness. One sentence in the introduction overreaches in a way worth recording - that machine learning algorithms assess the likelihood of a child being diagnosed with autism from behavioural information, making them a suitable replacement for routine and expensive screening tests. No autistic or community perspective appears.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Thin for Dataset 1 and absent for Dataset 2. Dataset 1 lists age, sex, ethnicity, jaundice and family history among its features and reports none of their distributions; seven comorbidity indicators are similarly listed as features with no prevalences. Dataset 2 reports no demographic information of any kind for its 100 clinical samples, despite claiming IRB approval and caregiver consent for their collection.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None for either dataset. Dataset 1's target is a binary ASD-traits field with no diagnostic procedure described, and the dataset's own feature list includes the Autism Spectrum Quotient, Social Responsiveness Scale, Q-CHAT score and Childhood Autism Rating Scale - four instruments used to determine autism status, supplied as predictors of it. This is the same instrument-inclusion leakage documented in local_183eaef4, which used the same 1,985-record dataset and reached accuracy 1.0000. Dataset 2's four severity categories are asserted with no instrument named; clinical experts are said to have verified annotation consistency at Cohen's kappa 0.92, but what they were rating and against what standard is not stated.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: Dataset 1 carries AQ, SRS, Q-CHAT and CARS as features rather than as reported participant characteristics - no mean, range or class-wise distribution appears for any of them. Dataset 2's severity categories are the prediction target with no underlying measure described.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is an ensemble framework that is both accurate and interpretable enough for clinicians to trust, evaluated on a behavioural dataset and a multimodal one. Headline findings: 97.6% accuracy on behavioural data from a regularised neural network (ROC-AUC 0.998) and 98.2% on multimodal data, with all other models above 93%; and an ablation showing accuracy rising from 89.40% (no feature selection, no resampling) through feature selection, SMOTE and ensemble fusion to 97.60% with neural-network regularisation.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No setting is described for either dataset. Dataset 1 is a public download; Dataset 2's 100 original clinical samples have no stated collection site, country, institution or period, which is difficult to reconcile with the claim that an Institutional Review Board granted approval for their collection.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: No task or paradigm for either dataset. Dataset 2's modality descriptions imply that facial images, 10-30 second voice recordings, body-keypoint motion and wearable physiological signals were captured simultaneously with synchronisation errors below 100 ms, which requires a structured session protocol - none is described.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional. Ethics is claimed only for Dataset 2, in a short paragraph stating that all participant data were anonymised, written consent was obtained from caregivers, and IRB approval was granted for data collection and analysis, with secure storage, encryption and restricted access. No committee, protocol number, institution or country accompanies any of this, and no ethics statement covers Dataset 1 at all. Given that Dataset 2 is otherwise entirely unsourced, the ethics paragraph is the only evidence offered that its 100 clinical samples exist as described.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: For Dataset 2, vision-based pose estimation and wearable sensors are named without models; ResNet50, VGG16 and MobileNetV2 supply image features at 224x224 with ImageNet normalisation; audio features include MFCC, spectral, temporal, rhythmic and voice-quality measures such as jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio. No software, version, seed or compute environment is given anywhere.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Sharply divided between the two datasets. Dataset 1's pipeline is one of the better-documented in this branch: the whole sequence is published as a numbered algorithm specifying label encoding, z-score normalisation, the 0.90 correlation-filtering threshold and its retention rule, the 60:20:20 stratified split, the exact SMOTE trigger condition (minority-to-majority ratio below 0.8) with the interpolation formula, the ANOVA F-score expression, and the SHAP and LIME definitions - and the dataset's instance count, feature count, missing-value count and class balance are all tabulated. Dataset 2 is unreproducible in principle: no source, citation, country, institution, ethics committee, participant description or access route exists for the 100 original samples, and its characteristics are conveyed entirely through asserted quality figures (complete data availability, synchronisation below 100 ms, inter-rater kappa 0.92). Neither dataset is accompanied by code, seeds, base-learner hyperparameters or a stated fold count.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: No limitations section appears in the extracted text. A comparison table instead assigns a named limitation to each of roughly fifteen prior studies (few participants, results may not apply widely; tested only in lab settings, not in daily life situations; works best only on similar data, not tested in real-world settings). None of that scrutiny is turned inward. Unmentioned: that four autism instruments sit in Dataset 1's feature set alongside the autism label; that Dataset 2's split partitions augmented copies rather than original samples; that Dataset 2's test partition holds 40 samples against 4,220 features; that Dataset 2 contains no non-ASD class, so its 98.2% is four-class severity rather than detection; that the 63.28% majority-class baseline on Dataset 1 is never stated; and that Dataset 2 has no provenance.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Not captured in the extracted text.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Dataset 1: screening-questionnaire responses and comorbidity flags, none of them examined individually. Dataset 2: the most behaviourally specific description in the paper - velocity, acceleration, jerk, movement range, coordination and repetitive behavioural patterns from body keypoints, alongside voice quality and autonomic arousal - describing exactly the kind of multimodal behavioural measurement this literature needs, for a dataset whose existence the paper does not evidence.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Dataset 2 is presented as genuine four-modality fusion - image, audio, motion and physiological features concatenated into a 4,220-dimensional vector - and the ablation attributes the final gain from 97.80% to 98.2% to multimodal integration. Three things make that uninterpretable. There are 4,220 features for 400 samples, of which only 100 are original. The 400 include augmented copies split across training and test, so the multimodal gain is measured on partly duplicated data. And no modality-level attribution is reported: SHAP and LIME are applied to Dataset 1 only, so the paper cannot say what any modality contributed. A 0.4-point accuracy gain on a 40-sample test set is a single case reclassified.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Five base learners (random forest, XGBoost, gradient boosting, SVM, logistic regression), soft-voting and stacking ensembles with a logistic-regression meta-learner, and two neural networks - a regularised MLP with L2, batch normalisation and dropout, and a deeper variant with early stopping and adaptive learning-rate scheduling. Predictions are combined by ensemble weighting proportional to validation performance.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Dataset 1: a reduced tabular vector after correlation filtering above 0.90 and ANOVA F-test selection, drawn from 28 attributes that include the AQ, SRS, Q-CHAT and CARS scores alongside the ASD-traits target. Dataset 2: a 4,220-dimensional concatenation dominated by 4,040 image features, against 400 samples - a ratio of more than ten features per sample, and more than forty per original clinical sample.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC for eight configurations on Dataset 1, plus accuracy and F1 for six ablation configurations on both datasets. Three problems. Precision, recall and F1 are omitted for both neural-network rows, so the two models carrying the headline figures are reported on accuracy and AUC alone. No confidence interval or cross-validation variance accompanies any value. And the reported logistic-regression row - recall 100.00%, precision 87.20%, ROC-AUC 1.000 - is the signature of a model that separates the classes perfectly on the test partition, which on a dataset containing four autism instruments as features is expected rather than notable, and which the paper reads as displaying more false-positive tendencies. The 63.28% majority-class baseline is computable from the paper's own table and is never stated.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: SHAP and LIME are applied, and applied only to Dataset 1 - a choice the abstract states plainly. The consequence is that the paper's interpretability contribution covers the dataset where the answer is predetermined by the presence of AQ, SRS, Q-CHAT and CARS among the features, and omits the dataset where attribution would have been genuinely informative, namely which of four fused modalities carries the signal. No SHAP or LIME output is described in the extracted text.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The two datasets require separate verdicts. On Dataset 1 the pipeline ordering is right and is unusually well documented: a stratified 60:20:20 split precedes SMOTE, SMOTE is applied only to the training portion and only when the class ratio falls below 0.8, and the paper states this explicitly as preventing data leakage - the ordering that local_ed30e24c got wrong and that most of this branch does not discuss.
