What the ordering cannot repair is the feature set, which contains the Autism Spectrum Quotient, the Social Responsiveness Scale, the Q-CHAT score and the Childhood Autism Rating Scale as predictors of a binary ASD-traits label. The same dataset produced accuracy 1.0000 for local_183eaef4; here it produces 97.60%, and the difference is attributable to preprocessing choices rather than to anything about autism. Dataset 2 is worse in kind. Its 100 original clinical samples were augmented fourfold to 400, and the stratified 80/10/10 split and 5-fold cross-validation were applied to the augmented set - so rotated, pitch-shifted, coordinate-scaled and noise-added copies of the same clinical sample sit on both sides of the split. The test partition therefore holds 40 samples, of which perhaps ten correspond to distinct originals, evaluated against a 4,220-dimensional feature vector. The reported 98.2% is roughly 39 of 40 correct on data the model has seen transformed versions of. It is also not a detection result: Dataset 2 contains four severity classes and no non-ASD class, so the abstract's presentation of 98.2% accuracy alongside the behavioural detection figure conflates a four-way severity task with binary ASD identification. Neither dataset carries a confidence interval, and the 63.28% majority-class baseline available in the paper's own Table 2 is never used.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Twelve keywords including ethical AI and healthcare trustworthiness. The list is longer than any other in the corpus and names trust, interpretability, ethics and reliability - all values the paper's Dataset 2 handling does not exemplify.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Computer Modeling in Engineering & Sciences 146(1):41 (Tech Science Press), 55 days from submission to acceptance. A modelling and engineering venue; review did not surface an entirely unsourced clinical dataset carrying an IRB claim with no committee or institution, a split performed over augmented copies, a four-class severity result reported alongside a binary detection result, or four autism instruments sitting in the predictor set.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2026, published 29 January. The framing is trust-centred - the stated goal is a model that is not only good at predicting ASD but also clear in its reasoning, with the title promising to enhance trust, interpretability and reliability in AI-driven healthcare. Against that, the paper reports a 98.2% figure from a dataset it does not source, whose split partitions augmented duplicates, and whose task is not the one the abstract implies; it applies its interpretability methods only to the dataset where they are least informative; and it reproduces the branch's characteristic overreach in describing machine learning as a suitable replacement for routine and expensive screening tests. Its genuine methodological contribution - explicitly confining SMOTE to the training partition and publishing the whole pipeline as an algorithm - is real and is the part of the paper most worth borrowing.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Finding the forest in the trees: Using machine learning and online cognitive and perceptual measures to predict adult autism diagnosis
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Van der Burg E; Jertberg RM; Geurts HM; Chakrabarti B; Begeer S
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed as a screening aid to triage individuals for expedited assessment given protracted diagnostic wait times, explicitly complementary to existing questionnaires rather than replacing clinical assessment, and with feature ranking proposed as a means of shortening the battery.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Secondary analysis pooling three prior online experiments with overlapping participants; supervised binary classification of autism diagnosis from performance-based measures, run separately on the full sample and on a fully age- and gender-matched subsample, with a label-randomisation negative control.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Three predictor configurations compared on the matched sample - objective task measures alone (74% maximum accuracy), the AQ alone (83%), and the two combined (92%) - plus a label-randomisation control model whose performance falls to chance.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Autistic participants through the Netherlands Autism Register (NAR); non-autistic participants through Prolific Academic - chosen with a stated justification that it produces particularly high quality data relative to popular alternatives - and additionally through the NAR. All participants were fluent in Dutch and naive to the purpose of the research.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: One row per participant with 54 performance variables, optionally augmented with the AQ and demographics.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Netherlands - Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and University of Amsterdam, with a UK collaboration (University of Reading). All testing conducted online in Dutch via the Neurotask platform.
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: AQ-28 total reported by group (83.4 versus 60.1 in the full sample; 81.6 versus 59.7 matched, both p<0.001) and used both as a comparator predictor and as a fusion partner. Age at diagnosis is also reported.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Self-reported formal diagnosis by a registered clinician for autistic participants, with non-autistic participants reporting no autism diagnosis. Autistic participants were drawn from the Netherlands Autism Register, a national research register. The population is explicitly characterised as late-diagnosed (mean age at diagnosis 35.6 years) and is described as particularly difficult to identify.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 286 autistic adults in the full sample (mean age 44.2, SD 13.6; 71.0% women; AQ 83.4, SD 10.7; mean age at diagnosis 35.6, SD 15.1); 125 in the matched subsample.
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: ICAR-16 abbreviated intelligence measure administered to all participants and matched across groups (0.54 versus 0.53 in the full sample; 0.54 versus 0.55 matched), with the instrument's strong correlation with full-scale IQ and its age and sex invariance cited.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Adults, with a large and reported group difference in the full sample (44.2 versus 32.2 years, p<0.001). The matched subsample is exactly age-matched at 37.6 (12.7) in both groups.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Full sample 71.0% women in the autistic group against 48.9% in the comparison group (p<0.001); matched subsample exactly 74.4% women in both. The autistic sample is majority-female, which is unusual and follows from a late-diagnosed register population.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 552 adults in the final dataset, from 959 recruited (538 autistic, 421 non-autistic). 407 were excluded for missing data from at least one experiment, arising from per-study exclusion criteria, technical issues or attrition - a substantial and clearly reported attrition.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None. The work is framed as an initial effort toward optimising a screening battery.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 266 non-autistic adults (mean age 32.2, SD 12.0; 48.9% women; AQ 60.1, SD 11.6); 125 in the matched subsample.
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Informed consent obtained from all participants prior to the experiments.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Established empirically rather than assumed: a random forest trained on randomised labels performs close to chance on both training and test data, which is reported alongside the substantive results as a control.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Online performance-based behavioural tasks in three domains - multisensory perception, emotion recognition and executive function - yielding 54 variables, plus the AQ-28 questionnaire and demographic fields.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A battery of online experiments administered through Neurotask, reused from three prior published studies with overlapping participants. Each contributing experiment carried its own exclusion criteria, which drive the reported attrition.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Participants' own devices; tasks programmed and delivered online via Neurotask (www.neurotask.com).
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: High. The analysis script is on OSF; the recruitment sources, exclusion count and reasons, and the matching procedure are all reported; demographic, ICAR and AQ characteristics are tabulated with standard deviations and significance tests for both samples; the tuning procedure, the tuned hyperparameters and the overfitting criterion are described; the decision not to resample is stated with its reasoning; and a label-randomisation control is reported. The primary data are restricted by register privacy rules with a documented request procedure - a limitation that is properly explained rather than left implicit.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Partial and clearly explained: NAR data are not publicly available due to privacy restrictions, and researchers may request access by submitting a research proposal and signing a Data Sharing Agreement with the NAR team, with a link to the procedure.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Yes - the machine learning Python script is publicly available on OSF.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Yes, with a reference number: approved by the ethical committee of the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam (VCWE-2020-041R1), in accordance with the Netherlands Code of Conduct for Research Integrity and the revised Declaration of Helsinki.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Listwise exclusion of participants missing data from any contributing experiment (407 excluded). No resampling: the authors state that they decided not to oversample the minority class with SMOTE or to undersample the majority class, and instead address imbalance and demographic confounding through the matched subsample.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: None beyond the 54 task-derived dependent variables from the three experimental batteries, plus AQ total and demographic variables in the configurations where they are included.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Python with scikit-learn (RandomForest, GridSearchCV). The analysis script is deposited on OSF.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: Mann-Whitney U tests for group differences on demographics and AQ with significance marked; Bonferroni correction applied to the variable-level group comparisons, described as highly conservative.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Feature importance rankings from the random forest, compared across predictor configurations and used substantively. The central interpretive finding is that several variables showing no significant group difference under Bonferroni-corrected testing nonetheless carried predictive value in combination, which the authors read as evidence of complex latent relationships. Reaction-time variables ranked consistently high. The authors also note that the feature-importance profile was very similar with and without the AQ, arguing that the two data types contribute in different ways.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: GridSearchCV with 3-fold cross-validation, followed by systematic single-parameter sensitivity visualisation against F1.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: The matched versus unmatched comparison is itself the key analysis, and the paper also notes that the most sensitive measures may differ by participant age, so its ranking may not generalise to all autistic populations.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Random forest, chosen with an explicit rationale - ability to detect sparse signals in high-dimensional data, provision of feature importance rankings, and, notably, that random forests capture any patterns that exist in the data and are therefore difference focused rather than deficit focused.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Hyperparameters (n_estimators, max_features, bootstrap, max_depth and others) tuned by GridSearchCV with 3-fold cross-validation, then each parameter systematically varied to visualise its effect on F1. Overfitting was controlled by adjusting parameters to minimise the gap between training and test performance, with the paper stating that a large disparity indicates overfitting.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Train/test split with 3-fold cross-validated grid search for hyperparameter selection, overfitting monitored by the train-test performance gap, and two analyses run in parallel: the full unbalanced sample and a subsample matched 100% on age and gender at 125 per group. The paper states explicitly that performance in the unmatched sample is inflated by the inclusion of age and gender as features given the group disparity in those factors, and that the matched sample therefore provides a better estimate of performance despite its smaller size - and reports the matched figures as its primary result.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and F1 for both the full and matched samples, for each predictor configuration, alongside the label-randomised control. Feature importance rankings are reported and compared across configurations.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Full sample: accuracy 81.8%, sensitivity 77.1%, specificity 84.1%, F1 77.9%. Age- and gender-matched sample (the primary result): accuracy 74.0%, sensitivity 69.2%, specificity 79.2%, F1 73.5%. On the matched sample, the AQ alone reached 83% and the combination of objective measures with the AQ reached 92%. The label-randomised model performed at chance.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Neuropsychological performance: multisensory temporal and perceptual integration, emotion recognition accuracy and reaction time across emotional categories and stimulus types, and executive function. Reaction-time variables emerge as consistently high in predictive value.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Refine the battery using feature ranking to remove uninformative measures and shorten administration; design manipulations that accentuate reaction-time differences in the most sensitive domains; and extend to populations differing in age.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Distributed through the discussion. Named: that performance in the unmatched sample is inflated by demographic features and that the matched estimate should be preferred; that the most sensitive measures may vary with participant age so the feature ranking may not generalise; that the work represents initial efforts with limitations on the conclusions that can be drawn; and, in comparing against prior work, that higher published accuracies were obtained either by predicting an AQ cut-off rather than an actual diagnosis or by using groups unbalanced on demographic features included as predictors, which risks sampling biases inflating performance.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Two recruited groups of adults: 286 autistic and 266 non-autistic in the final dataset, from 959 initially recruited, with 407 excluded for missing data from at least one contributing experiment (per-study exclusion criteria, technical issues, attrition). Autistic participants came from the Netherlands Autism Register and non-autistic participants principally from Prolific Academic. A second, fully age- and gender-matched subsample of 125 per group was drawn by random selection from the unbalanced sample, and it is this matched analysis the paper reports as its primary result. The analysis unit is the person throughout. The attrition is large and is stated plainly with its causes.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: The most carefully handled in the entire corpus, and explicitly so. The paper inserts a parenthetical statement in its opening paragraph that it alternates between person-first and identity-first language to address the varying preferences of the international autism community, citing a published recommendation. Its terminology is consistently difference-based rather than deficit-based - behavioural differences, differences from the norms seen in the non-autistic population - and it justifies its choice of algorithm partly in those terms, noting that random forests capture any patterns that exist in the data and are therefore difference focused rather than deficit focused. It is the only study in the review to make a language decision explicitly, to cite community preference as the reason, and to connect that framing to a methodological choice.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Complete and analytically load-bearing. Age, gender, ICAR-16 abbreviated IQ, AQ total and age at diagnosis are tabulated for both samples with means, standard deviations and Mann-Whitney tests. The full sample carries large group differences in age (44.2 versus 32.2 years) and gender (71.0% versus 48.9% women), both significant at p<0.001; the matched subsample is exact on both. Cognitive ability is matched in both samples (ICAR 0.54 versus 0.53). The autistic sample is 71% women and late-diagnosed at a mean of 35.6 years - a demographic profile that is the opposite of almost every other autism study in this corpus, and one the paper identifies as particularly difficult to identify. Nothing on ethnicity or socioeconomic status.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Self-reported formal diagnosis by a registered clinician, with participants drawn from a national research register (NAR) rather than a convenience sample, and non-autistic participants reporting no autism diagnosis. Diagnosis therefore predates and is independent of the task data. The population is explicitly characterised as late-diagnosed, which the paper treats as a strength for the research question - it is precisely the group that existing screening instruments miss - rather than glossing over it.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: AQ-28 total, ICAR-16 abbreviated intelligence, and age at diagnosis, all reported by group with standard deviations and significance tests. The AQ is additionally used as a comparator predictor and a fusion partner, so its role in the modelling is explicit rather than hidden inside a feature vector - the distinction that separates this study from the corpus's instrument-inclusion leakage cases.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is to test whether online performance-based measures can predict adult autism diagnosis, whether they add to the most widely used screening questionnaire, and which behavioural variables carry the predictive signal. Headline findings on the age- and gender-matched sample: objective task measures alone reach 74% accuracy (sensitivity 69.2%, specificity 79.2%, F1 73.5%); the AQ alone reaches 83%; the two combined reach 92%. On the unmatched full sample the objective measures reach 81.8%, which the paper states is inflated by including age and gender as features. A label-randomised control performs at chance. Several variables with no significant group difference under Bonferroni correction nevertheless contributed predictive value in combination.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: Entirely online, in Dutch, via the Neurotask platform, on participants' own devices - which the paper presents as the point rather than a compromise, arguing that online performance-based measures offer a marriage of more objective data types with the accessibility of surveys, against neuroimaging approaches that are costly, time-consuming and require laboratory attendance. The battery is described as briefer than a typical movie.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: A battery of online tasks spanning three neuropsychological domains - multisensory perception, emotion recognition and executive function - reused from three prior published experiments with overlapping participants, yielding 54 dependent variables. The design rationale is stated clearly: because autism is heterogeneous, differences in any one neuropsychological domain are inconsistently detected, so the study looks across domains rather than within one.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional. Ethics reporting is complete: ethical committee approval from the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam with reference VCWE-2020-041R1, compliance with the Netherlands Code of Conduct for Research Integrity and the revised Declaration of Helsinki, and informed consent from all participants prior to the experiments. Data governance is also handled properly - the register data are restricted for privacy reasons, and the procedure for requesting access through a research proposal and Data Sharing Agreement is documented.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Participants' own devices, with tasks programmed and delivered online through Neurotask. Analysis in Python with scikit-learn's RandomForest and GridSearchCV, with the script deposited on OSF.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: High, and complete on the axes that matter. The analysis script is publicly deposited; the recruitment sources are named with a justification for the platform chosen; the 407 exclusions are counted with their reasons; the matching procedure is described; demographic, cognitive and AQ characteristics are tabulated with standard deviations and significance tests for both samples; the tuned hyperparameters are enumerated; the tuning procedure and the overfitting criterion are stated; the decision not to resample is stated with its reasoning; and a label-randomisation control is reported. The primary data are restricted by register privacy rules, with the request procedure documented - the correct handling for a national register rather than a gap.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Distributed through the discussion rather than isolated, and unusually incisive. The paper states that the unmatched sample's higher accuracy is inflated by including age and gender as features and that the matched estimate should be preferred; that the feature ranking may not generalise across participant ages; and that the work represents initial efforts with limits on what can be concluded. Its most valuable limitation, though, is directed outward and applies to a large part of this review's corpus: it notes that studies reporting higher accuracy did so either by using the AQ-10 items to predict whether participants fell above or below an AQ cut-off score rather than whether they received an official diagnosis, or by using groups that were not balanced on demographic features included as predictors - and that this risks sampling biases inflating performance, which the authors accounted for through their matched analysis. That is a precise, published statement of the two mechanisms this review has documented across the questionnaire branch.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Use feature ranking to remove uninformative measures and shorten the battery; design manipulations that accentuate reaction-time differences in the most sensitive domains, since certain emotional categories and stimulus types are harder to categorise and leave more room for RT differences; and test whether the sensitive measures differ across age groups.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Neuropsychological performance across three domains rather than a single behavioural marker: multisensory perceptual integration, emotion recognition (with accuracy and reaction time varying by emotional category and stimulus type), and executive function. The substantive behavioural findings are specific - reaction-time variables consistently ranked high in predictive value, and executive function emerged as informative in this adult sample - and the paper is careful that the ranking is sample-dependent.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: Genuine, declared and quantified multimodal fusion, and the study's central result. Objective task measures and the AQ questionnaire are evaluated separately and together on the same matched sample: 74% for tasks alone, 83% for the AQ alone, 92% combined. Because each configuration is reported, the increment attributable to fusion is visible (9 points over the questionnaire alone), and because the feature-importance profile is very similar with and without the AQ, the authors can argue that the two data types contribute information in different ways rather than merely duplicating each other. This is the only study in the charted corpus to report all three configurations and thereby make the fusion claim checkable.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Random forest, selected with reasons given: capacity to detect sparse signals in high-dimensional data, provision of feature-importance rankings usable for battery optimisation, and the property of being difference-focused rather than deficit-focused. No deep learning and no architecture competition - the modelling is subordinated to the scientific question.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: One row per participant containing 54 task-derived dependent variables, with AQ total and demographic variables added in specified configurations. No dimensionality reduction or feature selection is applied, and no clinical instrument is smuggled in - the AQ's presence is the explicit object of one of the three comparisons.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and F1 for both samples and each configuration, plus a label-randomised control model. The specificity/sensitivity split is reported rather than collapsed into accuracy (matched sample: sensitivity 69.2%, specificity 79.2%), which shows that the model misses roughly a third of autistic adults at the reported operating point - visible precisely because the paper reports it. Missing: confidence intervals, cross-validation variance on the final estimates, and calibration. The chance level is established empirically by the randomisation control rather than asserted.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Feature importance is used as a scientific instrument rather than as decoration. The headline interpretive result is that several variables showing no significant group difference even under highly conservative Bonferroni correction nonetheless carried predictive value in combination - a finding that only a multivariate model can produce and that the authors read as evidence of complex latent relationships associated with autism rather than as a discovery of new markers. Reaction-time variables ranked consistently high; executive function was informative in this adult sample; and the near-identical importance profile with and without the AQ supports the claim that objective and subjective measures contribute differently. The authors also state the limit: the ranking may not generalise across ages.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: This is one of the two most rigorously evaluated studies in the charted corpus, and its distinctive contribution is the demographic-confounding analysis. The design uses a train/test split with 3-fold cross-validated grid search for hyperparameters and monitors overfitting by the train-test performance gap; adds a label-randomisation control that falls to chance, empirically establishing the baseline rather than assuming it; and declines to resample, stating that neither SMOTE nor undersampling was used. Its decisive move is to run the entire analysis twice - once on the full unbalanced sample and once on a subsample matched 100% on age and gender at 125 per group - and then to report the matched result as primary, stating that performance in the unmatched sample is inflated by the inclusion of age and gender as features given the disparity between groups in those factors. The difference is large: 81.8% unmatched against 74.0% matched, so roughly eight accuracy points in this study were attributable to demographic confounding alone. That number is directly relevant to the rest of this review, in which sex imbalances of 32 points (local_4ceee075) and 43 points (local_7432ffd7) between groups are reported and left unadjusted, and it is the only quantification of that effect anywhere in the corpus. Residual limitations: no confidence intervals or fold variance accompany the final estimates; the matched subsample is 250 people; diagnosis is self-reported rather than verified, albeit through a national register; and 407 of 959 recruited participants were excluded for missing data, which may not be at random. None of these undermines the study's central results, and the authors identify the most important of them themselves.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Not captured in the extracted text.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Translational Psychiatry 16:129 (Nature Portfolio) - a clinical and translational psychiatry journal, and the only such venue in the charted corpus. The disciplinary fit is evident throughout: matched-subsample analysis, Bonferroni-corrected group comparisons, a label-randomisation control, sensitivity and specificity reported separately, deposited analysis code, documented data-access procedures, an explicit language statement citing community preference, and a discussion that diagnoses the methodological failures of the prior literature it is compared against.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2026. The framing is screening-support and is bounded at every point: the measures may be a promising means of predicting autism, providing complementary information to existing screening questionnaires; the value proposition is triage for expedited assessment given protracted diagnostic wait times, not replacement of clinical assessment; and the reported gain is stated as 9 percentage points over the most popular adult screening questionnaire, with the authors noting that this matters in the context of an estimated 1% population prevalence. The paper is also unusual in reporting a result that undercuts its own headline - that the same models reach 81.8% on the unmatched sample and 74.0% once age and gender are matched - and in choosing the lower figure as its primary estimate.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Hybrid ensemble learning for Autism Spectrum Disorder screening using eye-tracking scanpath
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Alagha N; Elkhodiry AA; Copiaco A; Himeur Y; Mansoor W; Ritz C; Eapen V; Albanna A; Beheshti A
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed as supporting scalable, computationally efficient screening tools suitable for real-time clinical deployment, with the reduction of preprocessing overhead (no scanpath-to-image conversion) presented as the practical advantage.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of a public eye-tracking scanpath dataset; handcrafted feature extraction followed by a hybrid ensemble (bagging, boosting, stacking) with five-fold cross-validation, permutation-based feature relevance and non-parametric significance testing between classifiers.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: The five base learners against the stacking ensemble, all under the same five-fold cross-validation, with a Friedman test across folds; plus a comparative discussion against image-based deep learning approaches on the same dataset.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None. A public benchmark eye-tracking dataset released in anonymised form on Zenodo was used; no new data were collected.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: One aggregated feature vector per participant, formed from the mean and standard deviation of each scanpath descriptor across that participant's trials.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Australia - University of Dubai, American University in Baghdad, University of Wollongong, University of New South Wales, Al Amal Psychiatric Hospital (Emirates Health Services) and Macquarie University. The author list includes clinicians from a psychiatric hospital and a clinical medicine school.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Not described. Labels are inherited from the public dataset; no diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or date is reported, and the originating collection's ascertainment is not summarised.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 14 with ASD
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 28 participants
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None, and identified as the necessary next step.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 14 typically developing
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not applicable to this analysis; the originating collection's consent arrangements are not summarised.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: 50% by construction (14 versus 14), never stated.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Eye tracking - raw scanpath sequences of fixations, used directly rather than converted into scanpath images.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Not described. The viewing task and stimuli behind the scanpaths are not summarised, so what the participants were looking at is unknown from this paper.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None for acquisition. No compute environment is described.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Moderate. The source dataset is cited with a DOI; the nine handcrafted features are enumerated with their definitions; the fixed-length truncation/padding parameter (20 fixations), the subject-level aggregation rule and the standardisation are specified; every base learner's fold-wise mean and standard deviation is tabulated; and the permutation-importance procedure and its intended scope are described. Missing: code, seed, software and versions, base-learner and meta-learner hyperparameters beyond k=3, the number of scanpaths per participant, the viewing task behind the scanpaths, and the exact placement of the within-subject resampling relative to the fold split.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: The source dataset is cited with a Zenodo DOI.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not stated. Supplementary material is referenced.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Declared not required, with reasoning: the study used a publicly available eye-tracking dataset released in anonymised form, no new data were collected, the dataset creators anonymised the data prior to public release, and no identifiable personal information is included.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Each scanpath was converted to a fixed-length representation by truncating or zero-padding to the first 20 fixations. Scanpath-level features were then aggregated to the participant level by taking the mean and standard deviation of each feature across all of that participant's scanpaths, producing one feature vector per person. Features were z-score standardised. During model training, additional subject-level samples were generated by resampling scanpaths within each subject and recomputing the aggregated representation, described as increasing sample diversity while preserving subject-specific behavioural patterns.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Handcrafted scanpath descriptors computed per trial: number of fixations, mean fixation duration, total path length, mean saccade amplitude, dispersion (summed standard deviations of x and y coordinates), fixation duration entropy, first fixation duration, maximum fixation duration and total fixation duration.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Not named; scikit-learn-family estimators are implied (decision tree, random forest, KNN, AdaBoost, gradient boosting, stacking).
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: A non-parametric Friedman test on fold-wise F1 scores to assess whether performance differences between classifiers were significant. Standard deviations across folds are reported for every metric and every model. No confidence intervals on the point estimates.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Permutation-based feature relevance, with the scope stated explicitly - the analysis was performed independently of model selection procedures and served solely as an interpretability tool rather than as a feature selection mechanism. A full feature-importance ranking is presented.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not described beyond the stated k for KNN and the diversity-aware base-learner selection.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None; no demographic variable exists in the reported data.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: A hybrid ensemble integrating bagging, boosting and stacking, with decision tree, random forest, k-nearest neighbours (k=3), AdaBoost and gradient boosting as base learners and a stacking meta-learner. Base learners were chosen by a stated diversity-aware selection strategy intended to promote complementary decision boundaries.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: k=3 for KNN is stated; other base-learner hyperparameters and the meta-learner specification are not quoted in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Five-fold cross-validation with an explicitly stated subject-wise aggregation and evaluation protocol adopted, in the authors' words, to prevent data leakage and provide a more realistic estimate of model generalization in clinical settings. Because the analysis unit is the participant and there are 28 participants, each test fold contains approximately five or six people. The one ambiguity is the within-subject resampling step: additional subject-level samples were generated by resampling scanpaths within each subject during model training, and if those resampled vectors were created before rather than within the fold split, multiple aggregated representations of the same participant could cross folds.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 with mean and standard deviation across the five folds for every base learner and for the ensemble; a Friedman test on fold-wise F1 scores; and a permutation-based feature relevance ranking.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Stacking ensemble accuracy 0.9600 (SD 0.0800), precision 0.9750 (0.0500), recall 0.9500 (0.1000), F1 0.9524 (0.0952). Base learners: AdaBoost 0.9267 accuracy / 0.9181 F1; KNN (k=3) 0.8867 / 0.8781; random forest 0.8533 / 0.8374; decision tree 0.8200 / 0.7657; gradient boosting 0.7800 / 0.7181.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Visual scanning behaviour: fixation counts and durations, saccade amplitudes, spatial dispersion of gaze, irregularity of gaze allocation, and cumulative viewing time.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Validation on larger and more diverse datasets, and integration into an end-to-end ASD screening platform.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Stated directly and in the right place: although the proposed framework achieved high accuracy, it was evaluated on a single small-scale dataset (28 participants), which limits the statistical generalizability of the findings, and therefore the reported results should be interpreted as a proof-of-concept demonstration, pending validation on larger and more diverse populations.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Twenty-eight participants, 14 with ASD and 14 typically developing, from a public benchmark eye-tracking dataset released on Zenodo. This is the smallest participant base of any charted study apart from local_e771fb69, and it is the only quantity the paper reports about the people involved - no age, sex, cognitive ability, recruitment source, country or diagnostic procedure appears. Crucially, the analysis unit is the participant: scanpath-level features are aggregated to one vector per person by taking the mean and standard deviation across that person's trials, and the evaluation is described as subject-wise specifically to prevent data leakage. With 28 people and five folds, each test fold holds roughly five or six participants.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, TD, individuals with ASD. The register is clinical and unremarkable; the opening characterisation uses deficits in social communication and the presence of restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, standard DSM phrasing. No autistic or community perspective appears, and no demographic or personal description of the participants is offered at any point.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography, cognitive ability or recruitment information for any of the 28 participants, and no acknowledgement that this information is absent. The paper's own discussion notes that generalisation across demographics and hardware platforms remains a pressing issue in this literature - a concern it identifies and then cannot address, because it reports no demographic variable at all.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Not described. Labels are inherited from the public dataset with no diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or date reported, and the originating collection's ascertainment procedure is not summarised. This is the study's largest unforced omission, since two of its authors are clinicians - one at a psychiatric hospital and one at a clinical medicine school - and a paragraph characterising the source cohort would have been straightforward.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is a hybrid ensemble integrating bagging, boosting and stacking that operates directly on raw scanpath features rather than on scanpath images, so as to reduce preprocessing overhead and improve interpretability for real-time screening. Headline findings: the stacking ensemble reached accuracy 0.9600 (SD 0.0800), precision 0.9750, recall 0.9500 and F1 0.9524, above every base learner (AdaBoost 0.9267, KNN 0.8867, random forest 0.8533, decision tree 0.8200, gradient boosting 0.7800), and comparable to image-based deep learning models on the same dataset at a fraction of the preprocessing cost.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No study setting. A public dataset analysed computationally, with no compute environment, runtime or hardware described - which sits awkwardly with a contribution framed around computational efficiency and real-time deployment, since no timing measurement supports it.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Not reported. The viewing task, stimuli, eye tracker and session structure of the originating collection are nowhere summarised, so a reader cannot say what the participants were looking at when the scanpaths were recorded. For a scanpath analysis this matters, because scanpath geometry is jointly determined by the viewer and the stimulus, and without knowing the stimulus set one cannot exclude stimulus identity as a source of the signal.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis. Ethics is declared not required, with reasoning given: the dataset is publicly available, was released in anonymised form by its creators, contains no identifiable personal information, and no new data were collected. The declaration is at least argued rather than blank, and the paper additionally discloses that one author is an editorial board member of the journal and was excluded from the editorial decision - a disclosure no other charted study makes.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition instrumentation is described. Modelling components: decision tree, random forest, KNN (k=3), AdaBoost, gradient boosting and a stacking meta-learner. No software, version, seed or hardware.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Moderate. Reproducible: the source dataset has a DOI; the nine handcrafted scanpath descriptors are enumerated with definitions; the 20-fixation truncation/padding rule, the mean-and-standard-deviation aggregation to participant level, and z-score standardisation are all specified; fold-wise means and standard deviations are tabulated for every model; and the permutation-importance procedure is described with its intended scope. Not reproducible: no code or seed, no software or versions, no hyperparameters beyond k=3, no count of scanpaths per participant, no description of the source task, and no statement of where in the pipeline the within-subject resampling occurs relative to the fold split.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Stated plainly and correctly, in the discussion rather than in a boilerplate paragraph: although the framework achieved high accuracy, it was evaluated on a single small-scale dataset of 28 participants, which limits the statistical generalizability of the findings, so the reported results should be interpreted as a proof-of-concept demonstration pending validation on larger and more diverse populations. That is the right reading of a 28-person study and it is offered without hedging. What is not raised: that the fold-wise standard deviations (0.08 on accuracy, 0.095 on F1) are large precisely because each fold holds five or six people; that no demographic, task or diagnostic information about the source cohort is reported; and that the within-subject resampling step is not located relative to the split.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Validation on larger and more diverse datasets, and integration into an end-to-end screening platform. Both follow directly from the stated limitation.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Visual scanning behaviour reduced to nine interpretable descriptors: number of fixations, mean and maximum and first fixation duration, total fixation duration, total path length, mean saccade amplitude, spatial dispersion of fixations, and fixation-duration entropy as a measure of irregularity in gaze allocation. Operating on these rather than on rendered scanpath images is the paper's central methodological claim, and it is a defensible one - the features are inspectable and the permutation analysis can name which of them matter.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No modality fusion - eye tracking alone. What is fused is classifiers rather than data: bagging, boosting and stacking are combined within one architecture, with base learners selected by a stated diversity criterion to promote complementary decision boundaries.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A three-strategy ensemble - bagging, boosting and stacking - over five base learners (decision tree, random forest, KNN k=3, AdaBoost, gradient boosting) with a stacking meta-learner. The base-learner set is chosen by an explicit diversity-aware strategy rather than assembled arbitrarily, and every constituent's performance is reported separately so the ensemble's increment is visible: the best base learner reaches 0.9267 accuracy and the stack 0.9600, a gain of about 3.3 points.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: One vector per participant, formed by aggregating nine scanpath descriptors across that person's trials via mean and standard deviation, after each scanpath was truncated or zero-padded to 20 fixations and before z-score standardisation. The 20-fixation cap is a substantive modelling decision - it discards everything after the twentieth fixation in longer scanpaths and pads shorter ones - and its effect is not tested.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 with fold-wise means and standard deviations for all six models, plus a Friedman test on fold-wise F1 and a permutation-importance ranking. Reporting the standard deviations is a real strength and is also where the study's honest signal lies: an accuracy standard deviation of 0.0800 and an F1 standard deviation of 0.0952 on a five-fold split of 28 people means individual folds ranged widely, which is what five- or six-person test sets produce. On such folds, 0.9600 accuracy corresponds to roughly 27 of 28 participants classified correctly across the full cross-validation, and a single reclassification moves the figure by about 3.6 points. No confidence interval accompanies any estimate and the 50% chance level is never stated.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Permutation-based feature relevance, with an unusually precise statement of scope: the analysis was performed independently of model selection procedures and served solely as an interpretability tool rather than as a feature selection mechanism. That distinction matters and is drawn correctly - permutation importance computed for interpretation cannot leak into the model, whereas the same computation used to select features would. A full ranking is presented, though the extracted text does not name which descriptors dominated.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The design gets the structural question right and is limited by size rather than by construction. Subject-wise aggregation and evaluation are adopted explicitly to prevent data leakage and to provide a more realistic estimate of generalisation in clinical settings, and this is listed as one of the paper's four stated contributions - a rare instance in the eye-tracking branch of participant-level splitting being treated as a design requirement rather than overlooked. Set against the branch, that choice is what separates this study's 0.96 on 28 people from local_44d3aef5's 1.00 on 55 scanpath images and local_bb4d1f7a's 0.97 on 100 eye crops per child. Three qualifications remain. First, size: 28 participants across five folds gives test sets of five or six, and the reported standard deviations (0.08 accuracy, 0.095 F1) reflect that directly - the estimate is not wrong, it is imprecise, and the paper says as much in calling the work a proof of concept. Second, the within-subject resampling: additional subject-level samples were generated by resampling scanpaths within each subject and recomputing the aggregated representation, described as occurring during model training; if that augmentation was performed before the fold split rather than inside it, several aggregated vectors derived from the same participant's scanpaths would cross the partition and the subject-wise protocol would be undermined by the very step intended to increase sample diversity. The paper's wording suggests the correct placement but does not state it unambiguously. Third, the source cohort is uncharacterised - no task, no equipment, no diagnostic procedure, no demographics - so what the classifier separates cannot be independently assessed.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Autism Spectrum Disorder; Bagging; Boosting; Stacking; Ensemble learning; Eye-tracking. Four of six terms name ensemble strategies; participants, task and validation are absent.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Array 30 (2026) 100753 (Elsevier) - an open-access computer science journal. The author list spans engineering and clinical institutions including a psychiatric hospital, which makes the absence of any description of the source cohort's diagnosis or demographics more notable rather than less. The paper discloses an editorial conflict of interest for one author, which is good practice and uncommon in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2026. The framing is proportionate and, on the point that matters, correct: the reported results should be interpreted as a proof-of-concept demonstration, pending validation on larger and more diverse populations. The claims that go beyond that are about engineering rather than clinical accuracy - reduced preprocessing overhead by eliminating scanpath-to-image conversion, suitability for real-time screening environments, and a more direct and deployable solution bridging the gap between research prototypes and practical clinical tools - and even those are asserted without any timing measurement. Its contribution to the review is as the eye-tracking branch's demonstration that participant-level evaluation is achievable in this modality and that when it is applied, the resulting figure comes with a standard deviation of eight accuracy points on 28 people.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Facial Images and AI-Based Deep Learning Models
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Vasundhara; D. .. N.; Lakshmi Prasanna P; Moorthy C; Venkata Sailaja N
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed as facilitating real-time ASD screening and providing healthcare professionals with timely and effective interventions in clinical environments, with deployment as mobile or web applications proposed to improve accessibility in remote areas.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of a public annotated facial-image dataset; two object-detection architectures trained and compared, with an informal out-of-distribution probe on non-human images.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: YOLOv8n against YOLOv9c on the same data, plus a literature table of prior facial-image studies with reported accuracies from 79.56% to 98.8%.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None. A publicly available dataset was obtained from the Roboflow platform.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: 640x640 RGB images with bounding-box annotations.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: India - VNR Vignana Jyothi Institute of Engineering and Technology and Vasavi College of Engineering, Hyderabad. No data collection.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None. Labels are the autistic/non-autistic annotations attached to a Roboflow dataset; no diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or provenance record exists for any image, and the originating collection is not described.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: Not stated. Images are labelled autistic or non-autistic; no class counts are given.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 14,352 annotated facial images of children, each with bounding-box annotations. The number of distinct children is never stated, and the relationship of this count to the roughly 3,000-image public autism face corpus that the paper's own literature table cites repeatedly is not explained.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Not stated.
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Not obtained by the authors; consent by the original curators is presumed from platform sharing policy rather than verified.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not stated, and not computable since class counts are not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Two-dimensional facial photographs with bounding-box annotations.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. Still images, no stimulus, task or session.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None for acquisition; no compute environment described.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Low. The framework (Ultralytics), image size (640x640), epoch count (50) and the Roboflow-based preprocessing and augmentation pipeline are named, and the source platform is identified. Missing: the dataset URL, accession or version; class counts; split ratios and partition sizes; the number of distinct children; learning rate, batch size, optimiser and seed; and any code. The reported mAP@0.5:0.95 values are inconsistent with the mAP@0.5 values in a way that cannot be reconciled.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: The dataset is described as publicly available on Roboflow; no URL, accession or version is given.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not obtained, with reasoning given: the dataset is publicly available and comprises only de-identified facial images with no personally identifiable information; according to Roboflow dataset sharing policies, it is understood that before making this dataset public, the curators obtained adequate consent and ethical clearance; and there was no personal or clinical collection for this research. The paper also states directly that, given the child's facial data aspect, there is ethical sensitivity.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Performed through Roboflow's built-in export pipeline: automatic resizing to 640x640, conversion to RGB, normalisation, and augmentation by horizontal flipping and further transformations intended to reduce sensitivity to illumination, facial expression and head pose.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: End-to-end within the YOLO backbone (CSPDarknet), described as extracting facial symmetry, eye spacing, philtrum width and face shape at successive feature-map scales.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Ultralytics YOLO framework; Roboflow for dataset export, preprocessing and augmentation.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: None. Consistency across repeated runs is asserted without any variance figure.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: No formal attribution. The paper does report an informal out-of-distribution probe whose result is more informative than anything in its metric table: presented with non-human inputs, YOLOv8n correctly rejected a dog and a leaf, while YOLOv9c classified the dog as Autistic and the leaf as Nonautistic.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not described.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None. No demographic variable exists in the data.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Object detectors rather than classifiers: YOLOv8n and YOLOv9c, trained with the Ultralytics framework to localise a face and assign it an autistic or non-autistic class label.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: 50 epochs at 640x640 image size. No learning rate, batch size, optimiser, seed or split ratio is reported.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: The dataset is said to be divided into three groups for testing, validation and training, with the stated rationale that such splitting reduces the bias and overfitting possibility. No split ratio, no counts per partition, no cross-validation and no seed is reported, and the split is at the image level on a corpus of unknown per-child composition. Training and evaluation are said to have been carried out multiple times with highly consistent results, but no variance figure is given.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Precision, recall, F1, mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95 for both models; normalised confusion matrices with an additional Background class; precision-recall and F1-confidence curves; and a qualitative comparison on out-of-distribution test images.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: YOLOv8n: precision 91.95%, recall 92.77%, F1 92.36%, mAP@0.5 94.76%, mAP@0.5:0.95 94.73%. YOLOv9c: precision 91.29%, recall 90.29%, F1 90.79%, mAP@0.5 93.32%, mAP@0.5:0.95 93.21%. The near-identity of mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95 in both models (a gap of 0.03 and 0.11 points respectively) is not possible for a genuine detection metric, since mAP@0.5:0.95 averages precision over progressively stricter localisation thresholds and is always materially lower than mAP@0.5.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None. The targets are static facial morphology features named as facial symmetry, eye spacing, philtrum width and face shape.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: None stated.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: None for this study. A full column of the literature table assigns a specific limitation to each of roughly ten prior studies (limited dataset diversity; overfitting risk with limited data; poor generalization; lack of clinical validation; no multimodal analysis), and none is applied to the present work.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: No participants. 14,352 annotated facial images of children obtained from the Roboflow platform, labelled autistic or non-autistic and carrying bounding-box annotations. No class counts, no split sizes and no count of distinct children appear anywhere. The scale is worth noting against the branch: the paper's own literature table cites the Kaggle autism face corpus repeatedly, and that corpus contains roughly 3,000 images, so a 14,352-image Roboflow set is most plausibly an augmented export of the same underlying photographs - which the paper's description of Roboflow's built-in augmentation at export time supports but never states.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with autism, autistic, non-autistic. The introduction is unusually careful in one respect - it notes that while certain individuals with ASD may also experience cognitive impairment, the majority possess average to above-average intelligence, and that symptoms vary so that some face mild difficulties while others require full-time care. Elsewhere the register is standard for this branch. No autistic or community perspective appears.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography or recruitment information for any image, and no acknowledgement of the absence - although the paper's own literature table repeatedly lists limited dataset diversity and poor generalization as limitations of prior studies using the same kind of data.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None. Labels are annotations attached to a Roboflow dataset. No clinical diagnosis, instrument, criterion, assessor or date exists for a single image, and the originating collection is not described. The paper's introduction gives an accurate account of how ASD is actually diagnosed - paediatricians or psychologists using developmental history, behavioural observation and instruments including CARS for severity - and then treats platform annotations on downloaded photographs as an adequate substitute.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure; none obtainable from photographs.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is real-time ASD screening from facial images using object detection, with YOLOv8n compared against YOLOv9c to identify the more effective solution. Headline findings: YOLOv8n reached precision 91.95%, recall 92.77%, F1 92.36% and mAP@0.5 94.76%, against YOLOv9c at 91.29%, 90.29%, 90.79% and 93.32%; YOLOv8n showed higher true-positive rates for both classes with fewer misclassifications into the Background class; and, in an out-of-distribution probe, YOLOv8n rejected non-human inputs while YOLOv9c classified a dog as Autistic and a leaf as Nonautistic.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No setting. Images exported from Roboflow and models trained with the Ultralytics framework; no hardware, runtime or environment is described, which is a notable gap in a paper whose central claim is real-time deployability.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: No task or paradigm. Static photographs. The construct is facial morphology, with the backbone described as extracting facial symmetry, eye spacing, philtrum width and face shape - a list of dysmorphology features that would require calibrated measurement rather than a detection head trained on uncalibrated web images.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional. Ethics is not obtained but is genuinely reasoned about, which distinguishes this study from most of its branch: the authors note that the data comprise only de-identified facial images with no personally identifiable information, state that according to Roboflow dataset sharing policies it is understood that the curators obtained adequate consent and ethical clearance before publication, confirm that no personal or clinical collection took place, and - unusually - write explicitly that given the child's facial data aspect, there is ethical sensitivity. That last sentence is the only acknowledgement anywhere in the fifteen-study facial-image branch that photographing and labelling children's faces raises a question at all. Its weakness is the inference immediately preceding it: consent is presumed from a hosting platform's sharing policy rather than verified.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition instrumentation. Roboflow supplied preprocessing (640x640 resize, RGB conversion, normalisation) and augmentation (horizontal flipping and transformations for illumination, expression and pose variation) at export; training used the Ultralytics YOLO framework for 50 epochs. No learning rate, batch size, optimiser, seed or hardware.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Low. Named: the source platform, the export-time preprocessing and augmentation, the image size, the epoch count and the training framework. Missing: the dataset URL, accession or version; class counts and split proportions; the number of distinct children; optimiser, learning rate, batch size and seed; and any code. The reported metrics also contain an internal inconsistency that cannot be reconciled - mAP@0.5:0.95 sits within 0.11 points of mAP@0.5 for both models, which no genuine detection evaluation produces.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: None for this study. The literature table (Table 2) is unusually thorough in the opposite direction, assigning each of roughly ten prior works a named weakness - limited dataset diversity and challenges generalizing to real-world conditions; overfitting risk with limited data; overfitting in small datasets and poor generalization; low model interpretability and high training time; small and limited dataset, lack of clinical validation, no multimodal analysis. Every one of those applies to the present study and none is claimed by it. Unmentioned: the absent class counts and split ratios, the unstated number of distinct children, the impossible mAP relationship, and the fact that a model trained to detect autism from a face assigned a class label to a dog.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: None stated.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: None. No behaviour is observed or measured; the target is static facial appearance, described in terms of symmetry, eye spacing, philtrum width and face shape.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No fusion - a single image modality. The paper's own literature table lists no multimodal analysis as a limitation of a cited prior study and does not apply it to itself.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: YOLOv8n and YOLOv9c, single-stage object detectors, applied to a whole-image binary classification problem. The architectural choice is consequential and unexamined: an object detector localises instances within a scene and scores them against a Background class, so the confusion matrices contain Autistic, Non-Autistic and Background categories, and the reported mAP is a localisation-plus-classification measure rather than a diagnostic accuracy. Nothing in the task requires detection - each image contains one face - so the apparatus adds a spatial estimation problem and a third class to a two-class question.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: 640x640 RGB images with bounding boxes, preprocessed and augmented by Roboflow's export pipeline. Because augmentation is applied at export rather than at training time, augmented variants of an image may be distributed across the train, validation and test partitions - the paper gives no information that would exclude this, and gives no split ratio either.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Precision, recall, F1, mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95 for both models, with normalised confusion matrices, precision-recall curves and F1-confidence curves. The reporting looks complete and contains an impossibility. For YOLOv8n, mAP@0.5 is 94.76% and mAP@0.5:0.95 is 94.73%; for YOLOv9c, 93.32% and 93.21%. mAP@0.5:0.95 averages average precision across ten IoU thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95, so it is bounded above by mAP@0.5 and in practice falls well below it - gaps of twenty to forty points are typical for face-scale objects. A gap of 0.03 points implies that localisation quality is perfect at every threshold up to 0.95, which no detector trained for 50 epochs on uncalibrated web photographs achieves. The two numbers are therefore not both genuine mAP values. No class counts, no split sizes, no chance level and no variance across the repeated runs the paper claims to have performed are reported.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: No formal attribution, but the paper contains an out-of-distribution probe that is the single most informative result in it and is presented only as a robustness comparison between architectures. Given a picture of a dog and a picture of a leaf, YOLOv9c classified the dog as Autistic and the leaf as Nonautistic, while YOLOv8n rejected both. The authors read this as evidence of YOLOv8n's superior filtering. The more important reading is what it reveals about the task: a model trained to detect autism from a photograph will assign an autism label to whatever is placed in front of it unless something else stops it, and the difference between the two architectures here is a difference in background rejection rather than in anything about autism. No other study in this fifteen-strong branch tests its model on a non-face input, and this one does so almost incidentally.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The evaluation is thinly described and internally inconsistent. The dataset is said to be divided into three groups for testing, validation and training, with the reasoning that such splitting reduces the bias and overfitting possibility - and no ratio, no partition size, no seed and no cross-validation follows. The split is at the image level on a corpus whose per-child composition is unknown, and whose 14,352 images most plausibly derive by augmentation from a much smaller set of underlying photographs, since Roboflow's augmentation was applied at export rather than during training; if so, transformed variants of the same photograph sit on both sides of the partition. Training and evaluation are said to have been carried out multiple times with highly consistent results, and no variance figure supports that claim. Most concretely, the two mAP figures cannot both be genuine: mAP@0.5:0.95 within 0.11 points of mAP@0.5 is arithmetically achievable only under near-perfect localisation at IoU 0.95, which is not attainable here. And the informal robustness probe demonstrates directly that the system's decision surface extends to objects that are not faces, which no reported metric captures.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD); Facial Image Analysis; YOLO; Real-time screening; AI-based Diagnostics. Five terms, two of them deployment claims (real-time screening, AI-based diagnostics) that the paper does not measure - no inference latency or throughput figure appears anywhere despite real-time being the central selling point.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Journal of Pioneering Medical Sciences 15(1):137-145, a medical sciences journal, 90 days from submission to acceptance. Clinical review did not surface the absent class counts and split ratios, the mAP inconsistency, or the reported finding that one of the two models labels a dog as autistic.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2026, published 5 February. Framing is real-time clinical screening: the study is said to facilitate real-time ASD screening, providing healthcare professionals with timely and effective interventions in clinical environments, with mobile and web deployment proposed to reach remote areas. There is no limitations section and no future work, and the contribution is expressed as a position above one quoted prior YOLO result. Its distinguishing features within the branch are two: an ethics paragraph that at least names the sensitivity of children's facial data before proceeding, and an out-of-distribution test that inadvertently shows the model assigning an autism label to a photograph of a dog.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Multimodal fusion of deep transfer learning with wavelet neural network for autism spectrum disorder detection using facial images
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Shaik J; Shekhar R; Shelke CJ
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed as a promising diagnostic aid in clinical settings for the early and non-invasive detection of autism. No clinician, threshold or prospective evaluation.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of a public facial-image dataset; a multi-stage pipeline (Gabor filtering, three-backbone deep feature fusion, wavelet neural network classifier, metaheuristic parameter tuning) with results reported for a 70% training phase and a 30% testing phase.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Literature-quoted figures for CONCAT-SDAE, ViT-B, EfficientNet-B4, VGG-19, GBM, random forest and KNN, none re-run by the authors.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None. The autism image dataset was obtained by citation; the paper does not name the source repository, though the composition (2,940 images, 1,470 per class) identifies it as the widely reused public autism facial corpus.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: Gabor-filtered facial images encoded as a fused multi-backbone feature vector.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: None. Labels are the two class folders of a public image corpus; no diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or provenance record exists for any image.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 1,470 autistic
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 2,940 images
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None, and named as the next step: future work will assess the architecture on demographically different and stable datasets to evaluate fairness and generalisability.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 1,470 non-autistic
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Declared not applicable.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: 50% by construction (1,470 versus 1,470), never stated.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Two-dimensional facial photographs.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: None. Still images.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None for acquisition. Compute: Python 3.6.5 on a PC with an i5-8600K, 16 GB RAM, GeForce GTX 1050 Ti 4 GB, 250 GB SSD and 1 TB HDD.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Low. Reported: the compute configuration in full, the activation, learning rate, dropout, epoch count and batch size, the class composition of the dataset, and the pipeline stages in order. Missing: the dataset's identity or URL (it is cited only by reference number, and the formal statement denies any dataset was analysed), the split procedure and seed, the wavelet basis, the chimp-optimiser configuration, and any code. The stated 50 epochs and the 25-epoch learning curves do not agree.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Contradictory. The formal statement reads that data sharing does not apply to this article as no datasets were generated or analysed during the current study - in an article whose results section reports simulations on a 2,940-image dataset.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Declared unnecessary on a factually incorrect basis: the statement reads that this article does not contain any studies with human participants performed by any of the authors, in a paper analysing 2,940 photographs of children. Consent to participate and consent to publish are both marked not applicable.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Gaussian Gabor filtering to enhance relevant facial features and suppress noise.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Concatenated deep features from three pretrained backbones - VGG16, DenseNet-121 and XceptionNet - described as ensuring a rich and diverse representation.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Python 3.6.5. No library or version beyond that.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: None. No confidence intervals, significance tests or repeated-run variance.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Grad-CAM++ applied to highlight the most significant facial regions, described as improving the transparency of the model and as providing abnormality detection. Visual interpretation results are shown as a figure; no quantitative attribution or region-level analysis accompanies them, and no named facial region is reported as consistently salient.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: The chimp optimisation algorithm is used to tune wavelet-network parameters, with no stated objective, search space, population or iteration budget, and no statement of which data partition the optimiser's fitness was evaluated on.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None, and the paper says why - the dataset carries no demographic labels, so the influence of demographic factors on classification and feature learning cannot be examined.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: A wavelet neural network classifier over the fused features, with the chimp optimisation algorithm tuning its parameters, and Grad-CAM++ applied for visual interpretation.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: ReLU activation, learning rate 0.01, dropout 0.5, 50 epochs, batch size 5. The training and validation curves are described over 25 epochs, which does not match the stated 50. No seed, no wavelet basis specification, and no chimp-optimiser search space or budget.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Results are reported separately for a 70% training phase and a 30% testing phase, with confusion matrices, precision-recall and ROC analyses for each. No cross-validation, no repetition, no seed, and no statement of how the partition was drawn. The split is at the image level on a corpus known to repeat individuals. Notably, the reported testing-phase accuracy (98.42%) exceeds the training-phase accuracy (97.75%), and the paper reads the same inversion in its learning curves as evidence of good generalisation without overfitting.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure and AUC, per class and averaged, for both the training and testing phases; confusion matrices; precision-recall and ROC curves; and training/validation accuracy and loss curves.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Testing phase (30%): average accuracy 98.42%, precision 98.40%, recall 98.42%, F-measure 98.41%, AUC 98.42%; per class, autistic accuracy 98.02%. Training phase (70%): average accuracy 97.75%, precision 97.80%, recall 97.75%, F-measure 97.76%, AUC 97.75%; per class, autistic 96.56% and non-autistic 98.94%. Quoted comparators range from 92.10% to 97.76% on precision.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: None. Static facial appearance, described as facial cues relevant to ASD and as expression patterns and facial morphology.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Evaluate the architecture on demographically diverse and stable datasets to assess fairness and generalisability.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: One, and it is a real one: because the dataset carries no demographic information, and because expression patterns and facial morphology differ across demographic factors, their influence on ASD classification and facial-feature learning cannot be clearly examined. This is the most direct acknowledgement of the demographic-provenance problem anywhere in the sixteen-study facial-image branch. Not stated: the absence of diagnostic labels, the image-level split on a corpus that repeats individuals, the test-above-train inversion, the epoch discrepancy, or the contradictory data-availability and ethics declarations.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: No participants. 2,940 images in two balanced classes of 1,470 - the sixteenth charted reuse of the public autism facial-image corpus, identifiable from that exact composition although the paper names only a reference number rather than a repository. The number of distinct children is unknown and never discussed. Results are reported for a 70% training partition and a 30% testing partition with no counts, no seed and no statement of how the split was drawn.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, individuals with ASD, children with ASD. The register is medical and dated - ASD is introduced as a complex psychological disease and later as a critical neurodevelopmental condition with excessive medical expenses - and the symptom list includes repetitive and aggressive behaviours, hyperactivity, and cognitive impairment. Grad-CAM++ is described as providing abnormality detection, which frames the highlighted facial regions as abnormalities rather than as model attention. No autistic or community perspective appears.
