custom_fields.RQ1.3: None reported, and the paper is one of the few in this branch to say so and to explain why it matters: expression patterns and facial morphology differ across demographic factors, and because the dataset carries no such information, their influence on ASD classification and on facial-feature learning cannot be clearly examined. That is an accurate statement of the branch's central data problem, made by a study that then proceeds anyway.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: None. Labels are the folder assignments of a public image corpus, with no clinical diagnosis, instrument, criterion, assessor or date for any image, and no description of how the collection was assembled. The introduction gives a conventional account of ASD as requiring thorough clinical testing and then treats folder labels as sufficient ground truth for a system offered as a diagnostic aid in clinical settings.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure; none obtainable from photographs.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is a computationally efficient, privacy-preserving and optimised framework for ASD detection from facial images, combining Gaussian Gabor filtering, fused deep features from VGG16, DenseNet-121 and XceptionNet, a wavelet neural network classifier tuned by the chimp optimisation algorithm, and Grad-CAM++ for visual interpretation. Headline findings: average accuracy 98.42% with precision 98.40%, recall 98.42%, F-measure 98.41% and AUC 98.42% in the 30% testing phase, against quoted comparators from 92.10% to 97.76%.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No setting. A downloaded dataset analysed in Python 3.6.5 on a desktop with an i5-8600K, 16 GB RAM and a GeForce GTX 1050 Ti - a configuration reported in unusual detail for a study whose stated contribution includes computational efficiency, though no runtime or inference-time measurement accompanies it.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: No task or paradigm. Static photographs with no stimulus, interaction or session; the construct is facial morphology and expression.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional. The ethics declaration is factually wrong rather than merely permissive: this article does not contain any studies with human participants performed by any of the authors, stated for an analysis of 2,940 photographs of children, with consent to participate and consent to publish both marked not applicable. It is paired with a data-availability statement asserting that no datasets were generated or analysed during the current study, in an article whose results section reports a full metric grid computed on a 2,940-image dataset. Together the two declarations describe a paper that did not use any data, which is the opposite of what the article reports. The framing also claims the framework is privacy-preserving, with no privacy mechanism of any kind described.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: No acquisition instrumentation. Compute fully specified (Python 3.6.5, i5-8600K, 16 GB RAM, GTX 1050 Ti 4 GB, 250 GB SSD, 1 TB HDD). Training settings: ReLU, learning rate 0.01, dropout 0.5, 50 epochs, batch size 5 - though the accuracy and loss curves are described over 25 epochs, which does not match.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Low. The compute environment, the four principal training hyperparameters, the class composition and the pipeline order are all given, which is more than several neighbours provide. Against that: the dataset is identified only by a reference number while the formal data statement denies that any dataset was analysed; no split procedure, partition counts or seed appear; the wavelet basis and network topology are unspecified; the chimp optimiser has no stated objective, search space or budget; no code is released; and the epoch count in the text contradicts the epoch axis of the learning curves.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: One stated limitation, and it is the right one: the dataset lacks demographic information, expression patterns and facial morphology vary across demographic factors, and their influence on classification and feature learning therefore cannot be examined - with future work directed at demographically different datasets to assess fairness and generalisability. Within the facial-image branch this is the clearest statement of the problem that undermines all sixteen of its members. What is not stated: that the labels have no diagnostic basis, that the split is at the image level on a corpus that repeats individuals, that the testing-phase accuracy exceeds the training-phase accuracy, that the epoch counts disagree, and that the ethics and data-availability declarations contradict the article's own contents.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Assessment on demographically different and stable datasets to evaluate fairness and generalisability - proportionate to the stated limitation and the only future direction offered.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: None. No behaviour is observed or measured. The targets are static facial features enhanced by Gabor filtering, with the paper referring to facial cues relevant to ASD and to expression patterns and facial morphology without identifying any specific feature.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No modality fusion - a single image source. The paper's fusion is across three ImageNet backbones (VGG16, DenseNet-121, XceptionNet) applied to the same photograph, which is representational concatenation rather than multimodality, and no ablation isolates any backbone's contribution.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: A four-stage pipeline: Gaussian Gabor filtering, concatenated features from three pretrained CNNs, a wavelet neural network classifier, and chimp-optimisation parameter tuning, with Grad-CAM++ appended for visualisation. Each stage is named as a contribution and none is ablated, so the reader cannot tell whether the Gabor stage, the three-way fusion, the wavelet classifier or the metaheuristic contributes anything to the reported figure.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Gabor-filtered facial images encoded as a concatenation of three backbone feature vectors. Neither the input resolution, the fused vector dimensionality, nor the wavelet basis is stated.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure and AUC, per class and averaged, for both phases, with confusion matrices, precision-recall and ROC curves. The reporting is dense and contains one telling relationship: the 30% testing-phase average accuracy (98.42%) is higher than the 70% training-phase average accuracy (97.75%), and the per-class figures move in the same direction. A model that performs better on held-out data than on the data it was fitted to is normally a signal that the partition is not independent - shared or near-duplicate images across the split being the usual cause on this corpus - or that the reported training figure is not a resubstitution score. The paper reads the same inversion in its learning curves as good generalisation without overfitting. No confidence interval, no chance level and no variance across runs accompanies any value.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Grad-CAM++ is applied and a visual interpretation figure is shown, described as highlighting the most significant facial regions and improving model transparency. The description also calls this abnormality detection, which reframes model attention as pathology. No quantitative attribution is reported, no facial region is named as consistently salient across images, and no test establishes whether the highlighted regions correspond to anything anatomically meaningful rather than to image-provenance artefacts - the question the branch most needs answered and the one a saliency method is least able to settle on unlabelled web photographs.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The evaluation rests on a single image-level partition of 2,940 photographs into 70% training and 30% testing, with no cross-validation, no repetition, no seed and no statement of how the split was drawn. The corpus repeats individuals, so an image-level split does not separate children, and the number of distinct children is unknown - the same defect documented across the other fifteen members of this branch. Two further features are specific to this paper. First, the accuracy inversion: the testing phase reports 98.42% against the training phase's 97.75%, and the learning curves show validation accuracy exceeding training accuracy, which the authors interpret as evidence of good generalisation. The more usual explanation on this corpus is that the partitions are not independent. Second, the chimp optimisation algorithm tuned the classifier's parameters against an unstated objective on an unstated partition, so the reported test figure may be the outcome of a search evaluated on the data it is then reported against. On top of this, the comparison against seven quoted literature figures (92.10% to 97.76%) is drawn from other papers under unknown protocols, and no component of the four-stage pipeline is ablated.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Autism Spectrum Disorder; Facial Images; Wavelet Neural Network; Deep Learning; Chimp Optimisation Algorithm. Three of five terms name pipeline machinery; validation, participants and setting are absent.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Multimedia Tools and Applications 85:300 (Springer), 218 days with a revision round. A multimedia and computing venue. Review did not surface an ethics declaration stating that no human participants were involved in a study of 2,940 children's photographs, a data-availability statement denying that any dataset was analysed, a test accuracy above training accuracy read as good generalisation, or the mismatch between the stated 50 epochs and the 25-epoch learning curves.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2026. Framing is diagnostic-aid: the technique is offered as a promising diagnostic aid in clinical settings for the early and non-invasive detection of autism, and the stated research gap is a computationally efficient, privacy-preserving and accurately optimised framework - with no privacy mechanism described and no runtime measured. The contribution is expressed as a position above seven quoted figures. Its one substantive merit within the branch is its limitation paragraph, which states plainly that the dataset's lack of demographic information prevents any assessment of how facial morphology and expression vary across populations, and commits future work to demographically diverse data - the clearest statement of the branch's central problem made by any of its sixteen members, sitting alongside declarations asserting that the study used no data and involved no human participants.

data_charting_rubrics.title: SHAP-based explainable AI framework for autism severity classification using 3D motor biomarkers
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Fırat Y
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Bounded to proof-of-concept: the approach is described as demonstrating methodological feasibility as a potential future adjunct to autism screening and assessment, with low-cost Kinect sensors potentially implementable in clinical settings pending validation on larger independent datasets from multiple institutions.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of a public 3D motion-capture dataset; three-class severity classification with a random forest, evaluated by 5-fold cross-validation plus internal and held-out test sets, with SHAP feature attribution.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: A literature table of prior motor-based ASD studies (IMU, VR, Kinect, motion tracking, gait) with sample sizes and accuracies from 70% to 95.4%, against which the present study is listed at 86.4% on 109 children.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None. The public dataset Three-dimensional dataset combining gait and full-body movement of children with autism spectrum disorders was obtained from Zenodo and Dryad, with both repository URLs given and the original collection cited.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: One 463-dimensional feature vector per child.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Türkiye - Department of Computer Engineering, Mudanya University, Bursa. Single author. No data collection.
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: The three-level grouping is the outcome. No named severity instrument (CARS, ADOS calibrated severity) appears.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Inherited from the original collection, whose severity grouping (typical, moderate ASD, severe ASD) is used as the classification target. The instrument behind the moderate/severe distinction is not named in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 50 moderate ASD with real Kinect recordings, plus 9 severe ASD for whom only 2D video (Samsung Note 9) exists and no Kinect data were collected.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Not reported in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Not reported in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 109 children
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None, and the absence is stated explicitly rather than implied - both test sets are described as reserved subsets from the same data distribution rather than independent external validation.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 50 typically developing children with real Kinect recordings.
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No, and longitudinal study of how motor biomarkers track severity change is proposed as future work.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Written informed consent for participation was provided by the participants' legal guardians or next of kin in the original collection.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not stated numerically. With 50 typical, 50 moderate and 9 severe, the majority-class baseline for the three-class task is approximately 45.9%.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: 3D skeletal motion capture - X, Y and Z coordinates from 25 Kinect V2 joint points (head, neck, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hands, spine, hips, knees, ankles, feet) - for the typical and moderate groups; 2D video only for the severe group.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Gait and full-body movement recorded in a controlled laboratory environment by the original collectors; severe-ASD recordings were made in clinical settings on video because Kinect could not be set up for those children.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Microsoft Kinect V2 for the typical and moderate groups; a Samsung Note 9 phone camera for the nine severe-ASD video recordings.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: High for a secondary analysis. Both repository locations for the dataset are given with the note that they hold identical data with full documentation; the six preprocessing stages are enumerated in order with the exact dataframe dimensions; the class encoding is stated; the decision to use only original rather than augmented recordings is stated and justified; the synthetic-generation procedure is described precisely enough to reproduce (averaging moderate vectors plus Gaussian noise); and confidence intervals and fold standard deviations are reported. Missing: model hyperparameters, software and versions, a seed, and code.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Fully specified: the dataset is open-access with both a Zenodo record and a Dryad DOI given, and the paper notes that both repositories provide the same data with full documentation and metadata.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not stated in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Documented at both levels: ethics approval was obtained by the original data collectors from their institutional review board prior to data collection, and this secondary analysis used publicly available de-identified data from the Zenodo/Dryad repositories, conducted in accordance with local legislation and institutional requirements.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Six documented stages: extraction of raw data from 109 children; use of 463 pre-calculated video-level statistical features per child with timestamps omitted to give a single 463-dimensional vector; assembly into a 109 x 466 dataframe with class labels (typical 0, moderate 1, severe 2); stratified division into training, internal test and held-out test sets; z-score normalisation; and, for the severe class only, synthetic feature generation. Augmented versions of the typical and moderate data (seven geometric transformations - rotation, mirroring, scaling) were available in the source repository and deliberately not used; only original recordings were analysed.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: None by the author; the 463 features were pre-calculated by the dataset creators.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Not named in the extracted text beyond the algorithm components (random forest, SHAP).
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: A 95% confidence interval is computed and reported for the severe-class result (39.8%-100.0%), and the fold-wise standard deviation is reported for the cross-validated accuracy. No significance testing between models.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: SHAP applied per class with feature-importance, summary and waterfall plots. The reported biomarkers are anatomically specific - wrist movements, knee trajectories, elbow-to-foot distances - and the author connects them to motor impairments reported in the existing ASD literature. A systematic axis pattern across severity levels is also reported.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Not described in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: Per-class SHAP analyses. No demographic stratification; the author names age, gender and cultural background as dimensions on which generalisation should be tested in future work.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Random forest, selected for performance, flexibility and compatibility with SHAP-based clinical interpretation.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Not quoted in the extracted text beyond the algorithm choice.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: 5-fold cross-validation plus two held-out test sets of 20% each, with the second reserved solely for final validation, and the limits of this design stated explicitly: both test sets were drawn from the same original dataset using the same sensor, protocol and feature extraction pipeline, representing reserved subsets from the same data distribution rather than independent external validation. The analysis unit is the child. The decisive complication is the severe class: because no Kinect data exist for the nine severe-ASD children, its feature vectors were generated synthetically by averaging moderate ASD vectors and adding Gaussian noise, so the severe class is not a sample of children at all.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy with standard deviation across folds (84.6 +/- 10.9%), held-out accuracy (86.4%), per-class results, a 95% confidence interval for the severe-class result, and SHAP feature importance, summary and waterfall plots per class.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: 84.6 +/- 10.9% accuracy under 5-fold cross-validation and 86.4% on the internal and held-out test sets. For the severe ASD class, 100% classification accuracy on synthetic test data (4/4 cases, 95% CI 39.8%-100.0%). SHAP identified wrist movements, knee trajectories and elbow-to-foot distances as the leading motor biomarkers, with a reported gradient in axis composition across severity (Y-axis features 30% to 10% to 0%, X-axis features 70% to 90% to 100%).
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Motor function: inter-joint Euclidean distances, range-of-motion metrics, gait parameters (speed, step length, cycle time) and temporal characteristics, framed around balance, gait, postural control and stereotyped movement.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Collect real severe-ASD Kinect data with a stated minimum target of 20 to 50 children; test generalisation on larger and more diverse datasets across age groups, genders and cultural backgrounds; and conduct longitudinal studies of how motor biomarkers reflect changes in severity over time for evaluating intervention effectiveness.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Extensive, specific and placed centrally rather than in a closing sentence. Named: that the most critical limitation is the use of synthetic data for the severe ASD group combined with a sample of n=2 per test set and n=4 in total, which fundamentally affects the interpretation of all severe ASD results; that the original dataset contained only 2D video for severe cases because Kinect V2 could not be set up in controlled laboratory settings for those children; that synthetic features were generated by averaging moderate ASD vectors and adding Gaussian noise and therefore do not represent real Kinect-derived measurements; that consequently the model has not been validated on real severe ASD Kinect data and the reported 100% reflects the ability to distinguish real moderate ASD data from an artificially constructed distribution rather than true clinical severity levels; that the extremely wide confidence interval indicates high statistical uncertainty and a single misclassification would reduce recall to 75%; that the overall sample of 109 is small; and that the two test sets are not independent external validation.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: One hundred and nine children from a public Kinect V2 dataset: 50 typically developing, 50 moderate ASD and 9 severe ASD. The composition is uneven in a way that determines everything else about the study - the nine severe-ASD children have no Kinect recordings at all, only 2D phone video, because the original collectors could not set up Kinect V2 in controlled laboratory settings for children with severe autism. The severe class in the analysis therefore contains no real motor measurements from any child; its feature vectors were synthesised by averaging moderate ASD vectors and adding Gaussian noise. The analysis unit is the child, one 463-dimensional vector each, and the paper reports this structure openly rather than presenting three comparable groups.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, typical development, moderate ASD, severe ASD. The register is clinical and neutral; motor differences are described as impairments in line with the cited literature, and severity terms are applied to groups rather than to children as labels. One artefact intrudes: the keyword list ends with violence level classification, evidently carried over from an unrelated manuscript.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Not reported in the extracted text - no age, sex, ethnicity or socioeconomic information for any of the 109 children. The author names this as a gap prospectively rather than leaving it implicit, listing age groups, genders and cultural backgrounds among the dimensions on which generalisation must be tested in future work.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Inherited from the original collection and not independently established. The three-level grouping (typical, moderate, severe) is used as the classification target and the instrument behind the moderate/severe distinction is not named in the extracted text. What the paper does establish clearly is the provenance chain: ethics approval was obtained by the original collectors from their institutional review board before collection, guardian consent was given, and this study is a secondary analysis of de-identified public data.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: The severity grouping is the outcome rather than a covariate, and no validated severity instrument is named. Given that the study's subject is severity classification, the absence of a stated instrument behind the labels is its largest unaddressed gap - the synthetic-data problem is discussed at length, the label-provenance problem is not.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is objective classification of three ASD severity levels from 3D motor features, identification of the contributing motor biomarkers through SHAP, and evaluation across multiple validation strategies. Headline findings: 84.6 +/- 10.9% accuracy under 5-fold cross-validation and 86.4% on the held-out sets; 100% on the severe class (4 of 4) with a 95% confidence interval of 39.8% to 100.0%; and wrist movements, knee trajectories and elbow-to-foot distances as the leading biomarkers. The abstract itself states that the severe-class result is a methodological proof-of-concept rather than clinical validation because the severe features were synthetically generated.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: The original recordings were made in a controlled laboratory environment for the typical and moderate groups and in clinical settings for the severe group. The reason for that difference is reported and is substantive: Kinect V2 could not be deployed in controlled conditions for children with severe autism, so only phone video was obtained. That is a real, generalisable observation about who this class of technology can and cannot measure, and it is stated plainly rather than worked around silently.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Gait and full-body movement recorded with 25 Kinect V2 joint points at X, Y and Z coordinates, from which the dataset creators pre-calculated 463 features: inter-joint Euclidean distances, range-of-motion metrics, gait parameters (speed, step length, cycle time) and temporal characteristics. The severe-ASD group was recorded on a Samsung Note 9 in clinical settings, and the paper explains why extracting the same 463 features from that video was technically impossible - missing 3D coordinates, depth information and time-series data.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional secondary analysis. Ethics is documented at both levels - institutional review board approval obtained by the original collectors before data collection, guardian written informed consent, and a secondary analysis of publicly available de-identified data in accordance with local legislation and institutional requirements. Both repository locations are given. This is complete provenance reporting for a secondary analysis and is among the best in the corpus.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: Microsoft Kinect V2 capturing 25 joints in three dimensions in real time for the typical and moderate groups; a Samsung Note 9 phone camera for the nine severe-ASD children. The analysis software, versions and seed are not reported.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: High for a secondary analysis. Both repository URLs are given with the note that they contain the same data with full documentation and metadata; the six preprocessing stages are enumerated with exact dataframe dimensions (109 x 466) and class encodings; the decision to use only original rather than the repository's seven geometric augmentations is stated explicitly; the synthetic-generation rule is described precisely enough to reproduce; and both a fold standard deviation and a 95% confidence interval are reported. Missing: model hyperparameters, software and versions, seed and code.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: The most thorough and self-critical limitations discussion in the charted corpus, and the only one in which the paper's own headline result is dismantled by its author. The severe-class analysis is described as the most critical limitation of the study; the reason no real data exist is explained; the synthetic-generation method is named; and the consequence is stated in full - that the reported 100% reflects the model's ability to distinguish between real moderate ASD motor data and an artificially constructed distribution, not between true clinical severity levels. The author further notes that the extremely wide confidence interval indicates high statistical uncertainty and that a single misclassification would reduce recall to 75%, sets a minimum target of 20 to 50 real severe-ASD cases for future work, and states that the two test sets are reserved subsets from the same data distribution rather than independent external validation. The one limitation not raised is the provenance of the severity labels themselves.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Collect real Kinect-derived severe-ASD data with a stated minimum sample of 20 to 50; test generalisation across age groups, genders and cultural backgrounds on larger datasets from multiple institutions; and run longitudinal studies of how motor biomarkers track severity change, framed as a way to evaluate intervention effectiveness. Each addresses a specific stated limitation.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Motor function measured directly in three dimensions: inter-joint distances, range of motion, gait speed, step length and cycle time, and temporal characteristics, over 25 skeletal joints. The behavioural claims arising from SHAP are anatomically specific - wrist movements, knee trajectories and elbow-to-foot distances - and are related to motor impairments reported in the prior ASD literature rather than presented as novel discoveries. A structural pattern is also reported: Y-axis features decline (30% to 10% to 0%) and X-axis features increase (70% to 90% to 100%) with increasing severity, though the severe end of that gradient is synthetic.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No modality fusion - 3D skeletal motion alone. The study's most interesting observation is instead about modality availability: the severe-ASD group could not be captured with the same sensor as the other two, so the modality itself is unavailable for the group whose severity the study most wants to classify. That is a genuine finding about the deployability of depth-sensor assessment and it applies well beyond this paper.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Random forest, chosen for performance, flexibility and compatibility with SHAP-based interpretation. No architecture competition, no metaheuristic and no deep learning - the modelling is subordinated to the interpretability aim.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: One 463-dimensional feature vector per child, pre-calculated by the dataset creators, z-score normalised, with timestamps omitted. Two aspects deserve note. The dimensionality is high relative to the sample - 463 features for 109 children, of whom roughly 87 are available for training - so the model operates in a regime where a random forest's variable selection is doing most of the work. And the repository's seven geometric augmentations (rotation, mirroring, scaling) were available and deliberately not used, a restraint that several studies in this corpus do not exercise.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Accuracy with a fold-wise standard deviation (84.6 +/- 10.9%), held-out accuracy (86.4%), per-class results and, for the severe class, an exact binomial confidence interval (39.8%-100.0%) on a 4-of-4 result. Computing and reporting that interval is the single most useful reporting decision in this part of the corpus: it converts an apparently perfect result into a statement that the true accuracy could be anywhere above 40%, and the author draws exactly that inference. The fold standard deviation of 10.9 points is likewise reported rather than smoothed. What is missing: the three-class majority baseline (approximately 45.9%) is never stated, and no per-class sensitivity or specificity is given for the two real classes.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: SHAP applied per class with importance, summary and waterfall plots, yielding anatomically interpretable biomarkers (wrist, knee, elbow-to-foot) that the author relates to established motor findings in autism. The interpretation is properly bounded for the two real classes - the author states that for typical and moderate ASD the approach relies on biomarkers that are anatomically interpretable and reflect systematic motor patterns consistent with the literature - and implicitly withheld for the severe class, whose SHAP profile describes a distribution the author constructed. The reported axis gradient across severity is the clearest illustration: its severe endpoint (X-axis features 100%) is a property of the synthesis procedure rather than of any child.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The evaluation is competently constructed at the child level - 5-fold cross-validation with a fold standard deviation reported, plus two 20% held-out sets one of which is reserved solely for final validation, and an explicit statement that neither constitutes independent external validation because both are reserved subsets from the same data distribution with the same sensor, protocol and feature pipeline. Against most of this corpus that is exemplary. The decisive issue is the severe class, and the paper states it before any reader could raise it: because no Kinect recordings exist for the nine severe-ASD children, the severe class's feature vectors were created by averaging moderate ASD vectors and adding Gaussian noise. A classifier separating that construction from real moderate data is separating a smoothed, noise-perturbed version of one distribution from the distribution itself, which is a task with a known answer and no clinical content - and the author says so, writing that the 100% result reflects the ability to distinguish real moderate ASD motor data from an artificially constructed distribution, not true clinical severity levels. The 4-of-4 result carries a 95% confidence interval from 39.8% to 100.0%, which the author computes, reports and interprets. Two further qualifications apply to the real two-class portion: 463 features for 109 children is a high-dimensional regime with roughly 87 training cases, and the three-class majority baseline of about 45.9% is never stated against which 84.6% should be read. The study is nonetheless the corpus's clearest demonstration that a near-perfect number can be reported and simultaneously explained away by the person reporting it.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: autism spectrum disorder; motor biomarkers; random forest; SHAP analysis; violence level classification. The last term belongs to a different paper and survives in the published keyword list.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Frontiers in Psychiatry 17:1751654, 107 days with a revision round. A psychiatry venue, and the fit shows in the reporting - confidence intervals on a small-sample result, an explicit statement that held-out sets are not external validation, full provenance for a secondary analysis, and a limitations discussion that identifies the study's own most striking result as uninterpretable. The revision round appears to have strengthened rather than softened these statements, since the synthetic-data caveat appears in the abstract itself.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: 2026, published 23 March. The framing is the most restrained in the charted corpus relative to the numbers reported. The abstract states 100% accuracy for the severe class and, in the same sentence, that this represents a methodological proof-of-concept rather than clinical validation because the features were synthetically generated; the discussion adds that a single misclassification would reduce recall to 75%; the conclusion describes the work as proof-of-concept demonstrating methodological feasibility pending validation on independent datasets; and future work is specified with a minimum sample target. Its contribution to this review is therefore not its accuracy but its demonstration that an author can report a perfect score and simultaneously explain, in the abstract, why it means nothing - the exact move that the corpus's fifteen facial-image studies and seven checklist studies do not make.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Screening autism spectrum
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Assaf R; Shehabeddine Z; Ramesh V
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed as a foundation for future applications in clinical and educational contexts, with conversational agents or robotic assistants proposed as a scalable non-invasive screening route. No clinician evaluation or prospective test.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Retrospective secondary analysis of two public child-language corpora; supervised classification (binary ASD versus TD in each corpus and merged, plus three-class ASD/TD/DD in one) with grid-searched hyperparameters and 5-fold stratified cross-validation.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Three algorithms across four dataset configurations - Nadig binary, Eigsti binary, merged, and Eigsti three-class - with six metrics each.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: None. Two corpora were retrieved through TalkBank APIs: the Eigsti et al. dataset and the Nadig and Bang datasets, both within the CHILDES database and ASDBank English corpus. Selection criteria are stated - appropriate age groups for both cohorts, satisfactory sample size relative to alternatives, and availability of both ASD and TD children within the corpus.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: One tabular row per child with 52 linguistic and demographic features.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Lebanon and the United States - American University of Beirut and University of California, Los Angeles. No data collection.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Inherited from the two originating research studies, both of which are peer-reviewed developmental-language investigations with their own diagnostic procedures; the instruments used are not summarised in this paper. TalkBank's contribution requirements - informed consent from participants or guardians and ethical approval before data sharing - are cited as the governance basis.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 16 with ASD in Eigsti (12 male, 4 female; mean ages 56 and 55 months) and 12 in Nadig (10 male, 2 female; mean ages 61 and 53 months).
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not reported. The Eigsti developmental-delay group functions as a partial control for general developmental level.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: Eigsti children were aged 3-6 years; Nadig ASD children 36-74 months against TD children 12-57 months. The per-group mean ages tabulated by the authors show large gaps: in Nadig, TD means of 29 and 34 months against ASD means of 61 and 53 months.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Reported by group and by corpus in a full table - Eigsti TD 13M/3F, DD 14M/2F, ASD 12M/4F; Nadig TD 15M/11F, ASD 10M/2F. The ASD groups are more male-weighted than the TD group in Nadig (83% versus 58%).
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Not reported beyond the developmental-delay group definition.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 86 children across two corpora - 48 in Eigsti and 38 in Nadig.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None; the two corpora are analysed separately and merged rather than used as train and test cohorts - a missed opportunity given that they are independently collected.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: Eigsti: 16 typically developing (13 male, 3 female; mean ages 40 and 45 months) and 16 with developmental delay (14 male, 2 female; mean ages 57 and 54 months) - a genuine second clinical comparison group. Nadig: 26 typically developing (15 male, 11 female; mean ages 29 and 34 months).
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No, although the Nadig source data were collected at three time points over a year, that structure is not exploited.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Obtained at source under TalkBank's contribution requirements; not separately obtained for this reuse.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: Not stated numerically. Nadig is 26 TD against 12 ASD, so the majority-class baseline is 68.4%; Eigsti binary is balanced at 16 versus 16 (50%); the three-class Eigsti task is balanced at 16 per class (33%).
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Text - transcribed natural speech from parent-child interactions and free play, with no audio or video used.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: Naturalistic language sampling from the source studies - 30-minute free-play sessions in Eigsti, and parent-child interactions sampled at three time points over a year in Nadig.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: None. Transcripts retrieved through TalkBank APIs.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: Moderate to high. Both corpora are public and linked; the source studies are cited; participant counts, sex composition, per-group mean ages, total words and utterance statistics are tabulated; the feature count is stated; the tuned hyperparameters are reported for all three models; the SMOTE validation procedure and its KS statistics are given; and the overfitting check is quantified. Missing: code, seed, software and versions, the full 52-feature list, and the placement of SMOTE relative to the cross-validation folds.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Both corpora are publicly accessible via TalkBank and linked in the data-availability section.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Not stated in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: Not obtained for this secondary analysis, with the governance basis stated: TalkBank ensures compliance with ethical standards for data collection and explicitly requires researchers who contribute data to obtain informed consent from participants or their guardians and obtain necessary ethical approvals before data sharing.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Extraction of participant details, word tokens, utterances and transcript information via TalkBank APIs; cleansing; derivation of linguistic features including stem words and parts of speech, giving 52 features. SMOTE was applied to the Nadig dataset only, because of its 26-to-12 class imbalance, and the authors validated it by comparing feature distributions before and after with Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, reporting KS statistics below 0.15 with p-values around 0.99.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Fifty-two features covering participant details, utterance-level statistics, stem words and parts of speech, from which the analysis foregrounds Mean Length of Utterance, Mean Length of Turn Ratio, age and total words.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Not named beyond the algorithms (logistic regression, random forest, TabNet); TabNet implies PyTorch.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: P-values reported for every model, described as indicating the reliability and statistical significance of the observed results; Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests validating the SMOTE-generated distributions; and a train-validation gap check for overfitting.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: Logistic-regression coefficients accumulated across the five cross-validation folds and averaged, yielding a ranked feature list, followed by a reduced-model check in which the top four non-part-of-speech features alone reproduce nearly the same 86% accuracy. The named features are Mean Length of Utterance (lower MLU associated with higher ASD likelihood), Mean Length of Turn Ratio (lower ratio associated with ASD, indicating the child contributes less to conversational exchanges), age, and total words.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Grid search combined with 5-fold stratified cross-validation, with the selected values reported for all three models.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: The three-class Eigsti analysis is itself the key comparison, separating ASD from developmental delay as well as from typical development. Per-sex and per-group demographic characteristics are tabulated but performance is not stratified by them.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Logistic regression, random forest and TabNet (a tabular attention network), with logistic regression used for the interpretability analysis because of its strong performance.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Grid search with 5-fold stratified cross-validation gave 750 iterations for logistic regression; 200 trees at maximum depth 2 for random forest; and batch size 8 for TabNet. The very shallow random forest (depth 2) is an appropriate choice for 38-48 cases and is reported.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Five-fold stratified cross-validation on each configuration, with hyperparameters grid-searched under the same scheme. The analysis unit is the child. Overfitting was checked by comparing training and validation accuracy, with the authors reporting a gap of no more than 4% and citing the small corpus sizes (48 and 38) as the reason for the check. SMOTE was applied to the Nadig dataset with distributional equivalence verified by KS tests, though the placement of the oversampling relative to the cross-validation folds is not stated.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Six metrics - accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and p-values - for every model and configuration, with the rationale for each stated (precision and recall for medical evaluation, F1 to consolidate them, ROC-AUC for skewed data).
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Logistic regression reached ROC-AUC 0.93 on Nadig and 0.87 on Eigsti binary; TabNet reached approximately 0.96 on the merged dataset; and random forest reached only 0.71 on the three-class Eigsti task distinguishing ASD, TD and developmental delay. Accuracy above 86% is reported across both binary datasets, and a model using only the top four non-part-of-speech features achieved nearly the same 86%.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Expressive language and conversational participation: utterance length, turn length relative to the adult interlocutor, total words produced, stem words and parts of speech.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Broader age ranges, more diverse environments and dialects, transfer learning from larger speech corpora; features that better separate developmental delay from autism; conversational agents or robotic assistants for scalable screening; and multimodal extension combining linguistic features with limited prosodic cues to balance information against the privacy advantage of text.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: Several, stated specifically: the size and diversity of the datasets, particularly the limited 3-6 year age range; the absence of prosodic information (pitch, rhythm, intonation) that text cannot capture but that is indicative of atypical speech in autism; and the notably lower performance on the three-class Eigsti task, which the authors read as showing the need for features that capture nuances specific to developmental delay in order to reduce the risk of misdiagnosis. Overfitting risk from the small samples is also raised and addressed by a train-validation gap check.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Eighty-six children across two independently collected public corpora. Eigsti et al.: 48 children aged 3-6 in three balanced groups of 16 - typically developing, developmental delay and ASD - each recorded in a 30-minute free-play session, with ethnic composition reported (39 White, 3 LatinX, 6 African-American). Nadig and Bang: 38 children, 26 typically developing and 12 with ASD, sampled at three time points over a year in parent-child interactions. The analysis unit is the child throughout, and the two corpora are analysed separately, merged, and - for Eigsti - as a three-class problem. The presence of a developmental-delay group is the design's most valuable feature and is the reason this study can say something the rest of the speech branch cannot.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, typically developing, delayed development. The register is neutral and the paper's framing is unusually ethics-forward: it argues that a major drawback of facial-image approaches is the invasion of privacy, especially for minors, and the need to collect their images over prolonged periods of their childhood, and that MRI-based approaches rely on invasive data collection raising ethical and privacy concerns. One phrase slips - facial features recorded at the onset of the disease - but the overall orientation treats the children's data as something requiring protection rather than as a resource.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: The most complete demographic reporting in the speech branch. Sex, participant counts, mean ages, total words and mean and median utterance lengths are tabulated by group and by sex for both corpora, and Eigsti's ethnic composition is given. That reporting is what makes the study's central confound visible: in the Nadig corpus the typically developing children have mean ages of 29 and 34 months while the ASD children have mean ages of 61 and 53 months, a gap of roughly two years, and the ASD group is 83% male against 58% in the TD group. The authors note the age difference explicitly, attributing it to the significant language delays typically observed in children with ASD - but they then include age in the feature set.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Inherited from two peer-reviewed developmental-language studies, whose own diagnostic procedures are cited but not summarised. Governance is handled by reference to TalkBank's contribution requirements, which oblige contributing researchers to obtain informed consent from participants or guardians and the necessary ethical approvals before sharing. That is a reasonable basis for secondary analysis of a curated academic repository and is stated rather than assumed - a different situation from the web-scraped and platform-hosted collections elsewhere in this review.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: No severity or cognitive instrument is reported. The Eigsti developmental-delay group provides a partial control for general developmental level in the three-class analysis, which is the closest the study comes to separating autism-specific from delay-general language differences.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is to test whether privacy-preserving machine learning on speech transcripts can screen for ASD, on the argument that structured text avoids identifiable biometric data such as raw audio or video. Headline findings: ROC-AUC 0.93 on Nadig and 0.87 on Eigsti binary with logistic regression, approximately 0.96 on the merged data with TabNet, accuracy above 86% on both binary datasets, and a four-feature model reproducing nearly the same 86%. The result the authors themselves flag as important is the three-class Eigsti task, where the best ROC-AUC falls to 0.71.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: No setting of the authors' own. The source recordings were 30-minute free-play sessions (Eigsti) and parent-child interactions at three time points over a year (Nadig), both naturalistic language-sampling protocols from developmental research rather than screening paradigms.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Naturalistic language sampling rather than a designed classification task, which is a strength - the speech is spontaneous interaction, not an elicited response to a stimulus. The features derived from it are conversational as well as lexical: Mean Length of Turn Ratio measures the child's turn length relative to the adult's, capturing conversational participation rather than isolated production.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional analysis of longitudinally collected data. Ethics rests on TalkBank's stated requirement that contributors obtain informed consent and ethical approval before sharing, which the paper cites explicitly. The privacy argument is the paper's organising claim and it is stated with appropriate qualification: the authors acknowledge that they have not implemented explicit cryptographic privacy measures such as differential privacy or encryption, and claim only that text-based inputs inherently avoid identifiable biometric data. That qualification, placed in the abstract, is more careful than the unqualified privacy-preserving claims made elsewhere in this corpus.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: None for acquisition; transcripts retrieved through TalkBank APIs. Modelling used logistic regression, random forest and TabNet with grid-searched hyperparameters; no software, version or seed is named.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: Moderate to high. Both corpora are public and linked with their source studies cited; participant counts, sex, mean ages, total words and utterance statistics are tabulated by group; the feature count is given; the selected hyperparameters are reported for all three models; the SMOTE validation is quantified with KS statistics and p-values; and the overfitting check is reported as a numerical train-validation gap. Missing: code, seed, software versions, the complete 52-feature list, and the placement of SMOTE relative to the folds.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: Substantive and mostly well aimed. Stated: the small size and limited diversity of the corpora, particularly the narrow 3-6 year age range; the absence of prosodic information - pitch, rhythm, intonation - which text cannot represent and which is indicative of atypical speech in autism, an honest acknowledgement that the privacy advantage carries an information cost; the risk of overfitting given 48 and 38 participants, addressed by a quantified train-validation comparison; and the markedly lower performance on the three-class task, read as showing that features specific to developmental delay are needed to reduce misdiagnosis risk. Not stated: that the ASD and TD groups in the Nadig corpus differ in mean age by roughly two years and that age is one of the four features the paper identifies as carrying the signal.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Broader age ranges, more diverse environments and dialects, transfer learning from larger speech corpora, features capturing developmental-delay-specific nuances, conversational agents or robotic assistants for scalable screening, and a multimodal extension adding limited prosodic cues while preserving the privacy advantage of text. The last is a considered trade-off rather than a generic call for more modalities.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Expressive language and conversational participation in spontaneous interaction. The two leading features are behaviourally specific and directionally interpretable: Mean Length of Utterance, where lower values indicate shorter and simpler utterances and are associated with higher ASD likelihood, and Mean Length of Turn Ratio, the child's turn length relative to the adult's, where lower values indicate that the child contributes less to conversational exchange. Both correspond to well-established clinical observations, and the paper relates them accordingly rather than presenting them as discoveries.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No modality fusion - text alone, deliberately. The paper's argument is that excluding audio and video is the point, since transcripts avoid identifiable biometric data, and it acknowledges the cost: prosodic features indicative of atypical speech cannot be captured in text. Its future-work proposal to add limited prosodic cues while preserving text-level privacy is an explicit privacy-information trade-off, which no other study in this corpus formulates.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Three classifiers - logistic regression, random forest at maximum depth 2, and TabNet - with logistic regression selected for the interpretability analysis on the basis of its performance. The depth-2 random forest is an appropriate constraint for 38-48 cases and is reported rather than left implicit.
custom_fields.RQ4.2: Fifty-two tabular features per child spanning participant details, utterance statistics, stem words and parts of speech. The inclusion of age among the predictors is the study's principal unaddressed problem: the two groups in the Nadig corpus differ in mean age by roughly two years by the authors' own table, and age is reported as one of the four features that carry the result.
custom_fields.RQ4.3: Six metrics per model per configuration - accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and p-values - with the rationale for each stated. The reporting is complete and the paper draws the right comparison from it: ROC-AUC 0.93 for ASD versus TD in Nadig, 0.87 in Eigsti, roughly 0.96 merged, and 0.71 for the three-class task including developmental delay. Missing: confidence intervals, fold variance, and the majority-class baselines - which matter particularly for Nadig, where 26 TD against 12 ASD gives a 68.4% baseline against a reported accuracy above 86%.
custom_fields.RQ4.4: Well executed. Logistic-regression coefficients were accumulated across all five cross-validation folds and averaged rather than taken from a single fit, and the resulting ranking was then tested by refitting on the top four non-part-of-speech features alone, which reproduced nearly the same 86% accuracy. That reduced-model check is a genuine validation of the importance ranking rather than an assertion, and it supports the paper's privacy argument directly - fewer features means less data collection. The named features are clinically interpretable, and their directions are stated. The one problem is that age is among them, and age is confounded with group.
custom_fields.RQ4.5: The design is sound in structure and limited by two things the paper handles unevenly. Structurally: 5-fold stratified cross-validation at the child level, grid-searched hyperparameters under the same scheme, an explicit overfitting check reporting a train-validation gap of no more than 4% with the small sample sizes named as the reason for checking, SMOTE confined to the one imbalanced corpus and validated by Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests showing near-identical distributions, and six metrics reported for every configuration. That is careful work. Two problems remain. The first is confounding, and it is visible in the paper's own table: in the Nadig corpus the typically developing children average 29 and 34 months while the ASD children average 61 and 53 months - roughly a two-year gap - and the ASD group is 83% male against 58%. Age is then included as a feature and identified as one of the four that carry the signal. A classifier separating a four-year-old from a two-and-a-half-year-old on utterance length and vocabulary is doing developmental rather than diagnostic work, and the Nadig ROC-AUC of 0.93 cannot be separated from that. The Eigsti corpus is better matched (TD 40-45 months, ASD 55-56) and yields a lower 0.87. The second is the placement of SMOTE relative to the folds, which is not stated - though the distributional validation is more than most studies provide. Against these, the study's most valuable number is the one it foregrounds itself: 0.71 for the three-class task including developmental delay, against 0.87-0.93 for ASD versus typical development. The gap is internally controlled - same features, same corpus, same pipeline - and it quantifies how much of the binary performance is autism-specific rather than a general clinical-versus-typical distinction.
custom_fields.RQ5.1: Computational linguistics; Machine learning; Artificial intelligence; Feature importance; Autism spectrum disorder (ASD); Privacy. Privacy as a keyword reflects the paper's organising argument rather than being decorative.
custom_fields.RQ5.2: Scientific Reports 15(1):34134 (Nature Portfolio). A multidisciplinary venue. The reporting reflects it: demographic tables by group and sex, six metrics with stated rationales, a quantified overfitting check, KS validation of the oversampling, and a limitations section that names the information cost of the privacy choice.
custom_fields.RQ5.3: Framing is screening-support and privacy-forward, and both claims are qualified in the abstract itself - the models are described as a foundation for future applications in clinical and educational contexts, and the privacy claim is explicitly limited to the absence of biometric data rather than to any cryptographic guarantee, with the authors stating that they have not implemented differential privacy or encryption. The paper's contribution to this review is twofold. It is the only study in the corpus to make privacy the design criterion and to argue explicitly that facial-image approaches invade the privacy of minors - a critique that applies directly to the sixteen facial-image studies charted here, several of which reuse web-scraped photographs of identifiable children with no ethics statement. And its three-class result (ROC-AUC 0.71 including developmental delay, against 0.87-0.93 against typical development) joins local_b6ac2b98 and local_69b10fe4 as the review's differential-diagnosis calibration points.

data_charting_rubrics.title: Towards screening of children students with autism spectrum disorder based on executive functions with serious game and machine learning approaches
data_charting_rubrics.authors: Martins SRAL; Souza FAD; Teixeira LC; Leal BRA; Silva DMPF; Silva CMRD
data_charting_rubrics.primary_focus: Framed as a school-based screening aid rather than a diagnostic tool, with the paper stating that screening should be understood as an initial support for identifying warning signs and guiding the search for specialised clinical evaluation, not as a definitive diagnosis.
data_charting_rubrics.study_design: Prospective primary data collection in an inclusive-education setting followed by supervised binary classification of game-session telemetry, with grid-searched hyperparameters and 5-fold cross-validation across seven algorithms.
data_charting_rubrics.duration_frequency: Seven algorithms under identical grid search and cross-validation, with learning curves plotted for each.
data_charting_rubrics.subject_model: Convenience sampling of three inclusive-education professionals assigned to the day and time of the experiment, with stated inclusion criteria (authorised by their supervisor; trained in the data-collection tool) and an exclusion criterion (unavailable to apply and report activities). Children were recruited through those professionals with guardian authorisation as the first requirement.
data_charting_rubrics.task_type: One row per game session - 640 rows from 12 children.
data_charting_rubrics.country_region: Brazil - Universidade de Pernambuco, Recife and Arcoverde. Data collected in a specialised educational service (AEE/SEA) setting within full-day schools.
data_charting_rubrics.disorder_diagnosis: None reported. The exclusion criteria distinguish children with ASD alone from those with ASD combined with other disorders, so profile is controlled by design rather than measured.
data_charting_rubrics.diagnosis_assessment: Clinical diagnosis is an inclusion criterion for the ASD group and its absence for the control group; the diagnosing procedure and instrument are not described. Guardians additionally completed a behavioural anamnesis questionnaire.
data_charting_rubrics.n_disordered: 6 children with a clinical ASD diagnosis, three in the 3-4 year band and three in the 5-6 year band.
data_charting_rubrics.age_mean_sd: Not measured. Children with intellectual or physical disabilities that would impair use of the application were excluded, and the exclusion criteria are enumerated and justified.
data_charting_rubrics.age_range: 3 to 6 years, with children organised into age groups (G3, G4, G5) to make the samples more homogeneous and the clinical and control groups matched across those bands.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_distribution: Not reported in the extracted text.
data_charting_rubrics.comorbidities_included_excluded: Handled by exclusion. Three participant profiles are defined - ASD alone, ASD with co-occurring disorders, and children whose disabilities would impair use of the application - with the scope restricted to signs of ASD exclusively and other disorders explicitly outside the study.
data_charting_rubrics.severity_levels: 12 children aged 3-6 years, contributing 640 game sessions over three months.
data_charting_rubrics.healthy_status_confirmed: None; identified implicitly through the sample-size and convenience-sampling threats.
data_charting_rubrics.n_controls: 6 children without an ASD diagnosis, matched on the same age distribution, serving as the control group.
data_charting_rubrics.age_matched: No, though data were collected over three months; longitudinal protocols with repeated collections at different time points are recommended as future work to assess response stability.
data_charting_rubrics.gender_matched: Guardian written informed consent for every child, plus separate written consent from the education professional administering the tool.
data_charting_rubrics.neurodevelopmentally_typical: 50% by construction (6 children versus 6, with sessions approximately balanced), never stated.
data_charting_rubrics.data_types: Game telemetry - session-level performance data from three classical games on a tablet, capturing session duration, game identity and task-performance fields.
data_charting_rubrics.tasks_performed: A purpose-built serious-game tablet application containing three classical games designed to elicit executive-function behaviours, administered by a trained specialised-education professional in the child's own school setting, with guardians not present during play.
data_charting_rubrics.equipment_tools: Tablet running the study's own serious-game application.
data_charting_rubrics.new_dataset_contributed: High on artefacts, and the highest in the primary-data group. Code and dataset are publicly deposited with replication explicitly named as the purpose; the full hyperparameter search space and selected values are tabulated for all seven models; the data fields are listed with types and examples; inclusion and exclusion criteria for both children and professionals are enumerated; the consent procedure is described for both; and the games and their executive-function rationale are documented. Missing: an ethics committee reference, sex composition, a seed, software versions, and any statement of how sessions were assigned to partitions.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_openly_available: Yes, at the same repository.
data_charting_rubrics.dataset_available_request: Yes - code and dataset are publicly deposited at a GitHub repository, with the paper stating explicitly that this allows replication of the results.
data_charting_rubrics.sensitive_data_anonymized: An ethics committee approval is not quoted in the extracted text, but consent procedures are documented: guardians signed an Informed Consent Form as the first requirement for each child's participation, and the specialised-education professional signed a Free and Informed Consent Form after training on the data-collection tool.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_types: Game sessions were preprocessed into a tabular dataset with session-level fields (duration in seconds, game identity, and task-performance variables). The dataset was organised into three sets: 20% held out for validation, with the remaining 80% divided 70/30 into training and testing.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_features: Session-level performance and timing variables derived from game telemetry; the field list is tabulated with data types and example values.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_extraction_tools: Not named beyond the algorithms (random forest, MLP, deep MLP, KNN, logistic regression, SVM, naive Bayes); scikit-learn is implied by the hyperparameter names.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_importance_reported: None. No confidence intervals, significance tests or fold variance; learning curves are inspected qualitatively.
data_charting_rubrics.importance_method: None of the fitted models - no feature importance, attribution or ablation is reported despite random forest being the best performer and providing importances for free.
data_charting_rubrics.top_features_identified: Exhaustive grid search with 5-fold cross-validation, with the full search space and selected values published for all seven models.
data_charting_rubrics.feature_change_direction: None by performance. Children were organised into age bands for balance rather than for analysis.
data_charting_rubrics.model_category: Seven classical and neural approaches compared under a common protocol: random forest, multilayer perceptron, deep MLP, KNN, logistic regression, SVM and naive Bayes.
data_charting_rubrics.specific_algorithms: Fully tabulated. Random forest: 50 trees, max depth 10, min_samples_split 2, min_samples_leaf 1, bootstrap False. MLP: one hidden layer of 100, ReLU, Adam, alpha 0.0001, constant learning rate. Deep MLP: (128, 64, 32), tanh. Search grids are given alongside the selected values for every model.
data_charting_rubrics.validation_methodology: Grid search with 5-fold cross-validation for hyperparameter selection, followed by a training/testing/validation round also using 5-fold cross-validation, with learning curves generated per model. The unit throughout is the game session, not the child: 640 sessions from 12 children are partitioned without any participant grouping, so sessions played by the same child appear in training and test simultaneously. With roughly 53 sessions per child, this is the dominant determinant of the reported accuracy.
data_charting_rubrics.performance_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for each of the seven models, plus learning curves showing training and cross-validation accuracy against training-set size.
data_charting_rubrics.key_performance_results: Random forest 96% accuracy; MLP, deep MLP and SVM 94%; KNN 90%; logistic regression 82%; naive Bayes lower still.
data_charting_rubrics.features_associated_disorder: Executive functions: planning, cognitive flexibility, inhibitory control, working memory and performance monitoring, grounded in the Pennington and Ozonoff and Hill accounts of executive dysfunction in autism.
data_charting_rubrics.future_directions_recommended: Longitudinal protocols with additional collections at different time points; larger and more diverse samples; and professional training accompanying any deployment.
data_charting_rubrics.reviewer_notes: An extensive threats-to-validity section. Named: the small sample size as a major constraint on generalisation given the variability of characteristics among individuals with ASD; convenience sampling as a source of selection bias that restricts the variety of profiles and compromises external validity; the restriction of scope to signs of ASD exclusively, with each exclusion criterion enumerated and justified; the risk of overfitting associated with the reduced sample size; the absence of longitudinal data, with repeated collections recommended to assess response stability; and - distinctively - the ethical implications of early screening in educational settings, including the risk of stigmatisation, the responsible use of the generated information, and the need for training of education professionals to reduce misinterpretation. Not stated: that the 640 sessions come from 12 children and are partitioned without participant grouping.

custom_fields.RQ1.1: Twelve children aged 3-6 years - six with a clinical ASD diagnosis and six without, matched across the same age bands - who together completed 640 game sessions over three months in their own school setting. The recruitment structure is documented in unusual detail: three inclusive-education professionals were recruited with stated inclusion and exclusion criteria, trained on the tool, and supervised the children's use of it, with guardians absent during play. The gap between the number of children and the number of analysis rows is the study's decisive feature: 640 sessions from 12 children is roughly 53 per child, and the dataset is partitioned by session rather than by child.
custom_fields.RQ1.2: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, typically developing children, atypical and typical children, neurotypicals. The register is educational rather than clinical and the orientation is inclusive - the stated purpose is to let educators tailor teaching to individual needs and promote inclusive education, and the discussion warns against stigmatisation. One phrase dates the framing (ASD as a neuropsychiatric disorder), and the keyword list begins with Phishing, an artefact from an unrelated manuscript.
custom_fields.RQ1.3: Age is reported and controlled by design - children were organised into groups G3, G4 and G5 by age, and the ASD and control groups were matched across those bands specifically to make the samples more homogeneous. Sex is not reported. Nothing on socioeconomic status or ethnicity, though the school-based recruitment in a Brazilian public inclusive-education setting is described. Guardians completed a behavioural anamnesis questionnaire whose contents are not reported.
custom_fields.RQ1.4: Clinical diagnosis is an inclusion criterion - children with a diagnosis form the ASD group and children without form the control group - but the diagnosing procedure, instrument and assessor are not described. The framing is honest about why this matters in context: the study's motivating problem is that a significant number of children with ASD in Brazilian early and primary education remain without an appropriate clinical diagnosis, which leaves educators without information to tailor teaching. The tool is proposed for exactly those undiagnosed children, and is trained on children whose diagnostic status is already known.
custom_fields.RQ1.5: None. Comorbidity and severity are handled by exclusion rather than measurement: three participant profiles are defined - ASD alone, ASD with co-occurring disorders, and children whose disabilities would impair application use - and the scope is restricted to signs of ASD exclusively, with each exclusion criterion enumerated and justified. That is transparent design, and it also means the sample excludes the children for whom screening decisions are hardest.
custom_fields.RQ2.1: The stated goal is a serious-game tablet application combining inclusive-design requirements with machine learning, to give educators a playful, non-invasive ASD screening aid usable inside the school day. Headline findings: random forest reached 96% accuracy, MLP, deep MLP and SVM 94%, KNN 90%, logistic regression 82% and naive Bayes lower, with learning curves showing training accuracy above validation accuracy and no abrupt decline.
custom_fields.RQ2.2: A specialised educational service setting within Brazilian full-day schools, with the games administered by a trained education professional during the child's normal activities and guardians not present. This is the only study in the charted corpus whose data were collected in the setting where the resulting tool would actually be used, and the choice is argued: full-day schools provide a convenient setting, the professional's existing daily relationship with the children was leveraged, and the application was incorporated into planned educational demands.
custom_fields.RQ2.3: Three classical games on a tablet, purpose-designed around executive functions - planning, cognitive flexibility, inhibitory control, working memory and performance monitoring - with the theoretical grounding cited to Pennington and Ozonoff and to Hill. The paradigm is genuinely constructed for the question rather than repurposed, and the games' accessibility and usability requirements were derived from a prior review stage documented in the methodology flowchart.
custom_fields.RQ2.4: Cross-sectional analysis of three months of collection. Consent is documented at both levels - guardians signed an Informed Consent Form as the precondition for each child's participation, and the administering professional signed a Free and Informed Consent Form after training - though no ethics committee reference appears in the extracted text. The paper also contains an ethical discussion that no other study in this corpus offers: it states that the ethical implications of early screening in educational settings must be considered, including the risk of stigmatisation and the responsible use of the generated information; that screening should be understood as an initial support for identifying warning signs and guiding the search for specialised clinical evaluation, not as a definitive diagnosis; and that use of the tool should be accompanied by appropriate training for education professionals to reduce misinterpretations and promote an inclusive and respectful approach to differences. For a tool intended to be operated by teachers on undiagnosed children, that is the right set of concerns and it is stated without prompting.
custom_fields.RQ2.5: A tablet running the study's own serious-game application. Modelling used seven standard algorithms with grid-searched hyperparameters; no software, version, seed or compute environment is named.
custom_fields.RQ2.6: High on artefacts. Code and dataset are publicly deposited on GitHub with replication named as the explicit purpose - the second study in the charted corpus to release working code. The full hyperparameter grid and selected values are tabulated for all seven models; the collected data fields are listed with types and example values; inclusion and exclusion criteria are enumerated for both children and professionals; the consent procedure is described at both levels; and the game design and its executive-function rationale are documented through a methodology flowchart. Missing: an ethics committee reference, sex composition, a random seed, software versions, and - most consequentially - any statement of how the 640 sessions were assigned to the training, testing and validation partitions.
custom_fields.RQ2.7: One of the fullest threats-to-validity sections in the corpus, with six distinct items: small sample size as a major constraint on generalisation given the variability among individuals with ASD; convenience sampling as a source of selection bias restricting profile diversity and compromising external validity; the restriction of scope to ASD signs alone, with each exclusion criterion enumerated and justified; overfitting risk from the reduced sample; the absence of longitudinal data, with repeated collections recommended; and the ethical implications of school-based screening including stigmatisation risk. The one thing not identified is the thing that governs the result: that 640 sessions come from 12 children and are partitioned by session. The paper instead argues in the opposite direction, stating that the high accuracy observed in the models and the robust metrics reinforce the low likelihood of overfitting - which reads a symptom as reassurance.
custom_fields.RQ2.9: Longitudinal protocols with additional collections at different time points to assess response stability and tool robustness; larger and more diverse samples to address the convenience-sampling limitation; and training for education professionals as a condition of deployment. Each addresses a stated threat.
custom_fields.RQ3.1: Executive function as elicited by three purpose-built games - planning, cognitive flexibility, inhibitory control, working memory and performance monitoring - captured through session-level telemetry including duration and task-performance fields. This is behaviour observed during a designed task rather than reported on a checklist or inferred from an appearance, and the construct is theoretically motivated rather than chosen for convenience. What the paper does not do is say which behaviours distinguished the groups: no feature importance is reported, so the executive-function framing that justifies the whole design is never connected to a result.
custom_fields.RQ3.2: No modality fusion - game telemetry alone. The behavioural anamnesis questionnaire completed by guardians is collected and not used as a predictor, which keeps the model's inputs clean of parent-report information but also leaves an available modality unexploited.
custom_fields.RQ4.1: Seven algorithms under a single protocol - random forest, MLP, deep MLP, KNN, logistic regression, SVM and naive Bayes - with the full grid search published. The comparison is genuinely controlled and the spread it produces (96% down to 82% and lower) is informative in itself.
