narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The corpus's methodological benchmark: gold-standard Clinical Best Estimate ascertainment applied symmetrically to cases and controls, IQ- and sex-matched groups with every comparison tested, feature selection and PCA correctly nested inside cross-validation folds, complete per-class metrics, and - uniquely - a human-rater comparison establishing that the task is hard for people too. Its finding that a naive conversation partner's own voice quality shifts measurably depending on whether they are talking to an autistic child is the corpus's clearest evidence that the measurable signal in social interaction is dyadic rather than located in one person.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups of 35: children with ASD and typically developing children, plus 22 young adult confederates (19 female) who served as conversation partners and whose speech was also analysed. The confederates are effectively a third participant group whose data enter the model - an unusual design in this corpus. No other-diagnosis comparison group. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'children on the autism spectrum', 'ASD children', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'TDC', and one appearance of 'ASD patients' in the discussion. Predominantly person-first with the notable use of 'children on the autism spectrum' in the introduction, and 'typically developing' rather than 'normal' throughout. [RQ1.3] ASD n=35, mean age 11.42 +/- 2.51, full-scale IQ 105.51, verbal IQ 104.97, non-verbal IQ 104.63. TD n=35, mean age 10.57 +/- 2.82, full-scale IQ 107.14, verbal IQ 105.83, non-verbal IQ 105.97. Age difference non-significant (t=1.33, p=0.19); IQ differences non-significant on all three measures (p=0.6, 0.78, 0.68); sex ratio matched by design and non-significant (chi-square=0.06, p=0.8). This is among the best-matched samples in the corpus - matched and tested on full-scale, verbal and non-verbal IQ as well as sex. The one defect is that the printed sex counts ('13 f., 12 m.' and '11 f., 14 m.') sum to 25 rather than the stated 35 per group. [RQ1.4] The strongest reference standard in the corpus: diagnoses were confirmed for the ASD group and ruled out for the TD group using the Clinical Best Estimate process informed by ADOS-2 and adhering to DSM-5 criteria. Crucially the same rigorous process was applied to controls, not just cases - the inverse of the common corpus pattern where control screening is better specified than case ascertainment. Symptom severity was additionally characterised with ADOS-2 Calibrated Severity Scores and the Social Communication Questionnaire for both groups. [RQ1.5] Full-scale, verbal and non-verbal IQ measured with the WASI-II for both groups and used as matching variables with all comparisons tested. ADOS-2 Calibrated Severity Scores (overall, social affect, restricted and repetitive behaviour) and SCQ lifetime scores reported for both groups with group comparisons. All participants were native English speakers. Comorbid conditions are not described. [RQ2.1] Goal: automatic ASD prescreening and triage from brief natural conversation, explicitly aimed at community settings such as doctors' offices and schools and motivated by diagnostic waitlists. Main findings: 75.71% accuracy, AUC 0.754; markedly better at identifying TD (85.71%) than ASD (65.71%) children; human raters reached 83.33% on a matched subset, so the model approaches but does not match human performance; confederate speech features were among the most consistently predictive; and adding age, sex or IQ did not improve and IQ worsened performance because the groups were already matched on them. [RQ2.2] Clinic/research setting at a hospital autism centre. Newly collected data; the design deliberately departs from the field's reliance on ADOS-derived or highly structured speech samples in favour of naturalistic conversation with a non-expert partner. [RQ2.3] A 5-minute unstructured 'get-to-know-you' conversation with a novel young adult confederate blind to diagnostic status and assigned by availability. No conversational prompts were given to either speaker. Recordings were made with a device placed between the speakers carrying two opposed HD cameras and four directional microphones. Transcription used a rigorous protocol: two junior annotators (one segmenting pause groups, one transcribing words) plus a senior annotator with at least six months' experience reviewing and correcting every file, with all annotators having completed at least 10 hours of Quick Transcription training modified for clinical ASD interviews and having achieved over 90% agreement with a gold-standard transcript before independent work. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single 5-minute conversation per child with no follow-up. The data are highly sensitive - audio and video of identifiable children in unscripted personal conversation, plus verbatim transcripts. Ethics reporting is complete and among the best in the corpus: IRB approval and oversight from the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, written parental informed consent, and verbal assent from the children themselves. No anonymization or retention procedure for the recordings is described. [RQ2.5] Hardware: a 'Biosensor' recording device placed on a table between the two speakers, with two HD video cameras facing opposite directions to capture both participants simultaneously and four embedded directional microphones. Software: sox for format conversion; openSMILE with the ComParE13 configuration (25 ms window, 10 ms step) for acoustic low-level descriptors; XTrans for time-aligned orthographic transcription; base R, qdap and LIWC plus a custom author script for text features; scikit-learn (SimpleImputer, PCA, GradientBoostingClassifier) in Python. [RQ2.6] No data availability statement and no code release, which is a real gap for a corpus this valuable. Method reporting is otherwise strong: the openSMILE configuration and window/step sizes, the full list of 44 low-level descriptors, the exact feature arithmetic (44 x 2 speakers x 4 functionals = 352), the six text-feature groups totalling 272, the voiceless-frame exclusion rule, the pitch normalisation formula with the 5th-percentile baseline, the correlation threshold (p<0.025), the number of components retained (10), the classifier, the libraries, and the annotation training and reliability criteria are all specified. The pipeline is re-implementable; the conversations are not accessible. [RQ2.7] Reported by the authors: performance is limited by 5-minute samples and generic topics compared with ADOS evaluations designed to elicit ASD-like features; human raters outperformed the model, which the authors read as evidence that the feature set fails to capture topicality, relevance, appropriateness and conversational flow at a turn-by-turn level; ASD is harder to predict than TD because of phenotypic heterogeneity; and the approach 'is not yet valuable as a method for diagnosing ASD, which still needs to be diagnosed by expert clinicians'. Identifiable in review: the demographic table's sex counts sum to 25 rather than 35 in both groups; the confederate features that are among the most consistently selected mean part of the signal is an interlocutor's response to the child rather than the child's own behaviour, which limits transfer to any self-administered or partner-free screening context; all participants were native English speakers at a single site, with no ethnicity or socioeconomic data; confederates were 19 of 22 female, so partner-sex variation is minimal; and n=70 makes 75.71% equal to 53 of 70 children. [RQ2.9] Engineer features that directly capture semantic and pragmatic appropriateness turn by turn, since that is what human raters used and the model lacked; enlarge the dataset to improve performance and enable real-world deployment; and test whether longer conversations (10 rather than 5 minutes) and designated topics improve performance. All three are grounded in specific observed shortfalls rather than generic. [RQ3.1] Speech and language jointly: acoustic-phonetic properties (voicing probability, pitch, jitter, shimmer, HNR, energy, MFCCs, zero-crossing rate and their deltas) and lexical/discourse properties (pause and overlap metrics, turn metrics, speaking rate, word complexity, LIWC psycholinguistic categories, lexical entropy and diversity, parts of speech, formality, polarity). Distinctively, all of these are computed for both the child and the adult conversation partner. [RQ3.2] Two-way fusion. Across modality: 352 acoustic and 272 text features are concatenated into a single 624-dimensional vector, then reduced by correlation filtering and PCA - so acoustic and lexical information are combined at feature level. Across speaker: features from the child and the confederate are both included, and the results show confederate features were selected in all 70 folds for several jitter and HNR measures, making interlocutor behaviour an explicit part of the model. Demographic and clinical variables were tested as additional inputs and reported as unhelpful (age and sex) or harmful (IQ), which the authors correctly attribute to prior matching - a negative fusion result reported rather than omitted. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning: a Gradient Boosting Classifier from scikit-learn. Principal Component Analysis is used unsupervised for dimensionality reduction. No comparison against alternative classifiers, which removes best-of-many selection optimism but also leaves the algorithm choice unjustified empirically. [RQ4.2] Handcrafted features at two levels: frame-level acoustic descriptors summarised per speaker per conversation by four statistical functionals, and text-derived lexical, syntactic and discourse counts. These are then projected onto 10 principal components for modelling, so the classifier operates on a learned low-dimensional linear subspace of handcrafted features rather than on the features directly. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 per class and averaged, plus a ROC curve with AUC - and, unusually, the identical metric set computed for human raters so the two can be read side by side. Headline: 75.71% accuracy, AUC 75.43%, with the per-class asymmetry (TD 85.71%, ASD 65.71%) reported prominently rather than buried in an average. No confidence intervals. [RQ4.4] Well developed. Selection frequency across the 70 folds is reported per feature, distinguishing features chosen in all folds from those chosen occasionally, which is a more informative importance measure than a single ranking. Post-hoc linear regressions give directions and significance for key features. The substantive findings are specific: autistic children showed higher median HNR-delta, lower voicing-probability variability and reduced pitch dynamism (lower IQR of F0-delta); and confederates showed higher HNR-delta and lower jitter when talking to autistic children. The paper also collects qualitative human-rater justifications - flat intonation, long response latency, brief responses, frequent 'I don't know', topic changes, few follow-up questions - and uses them to diagnose what the automatic feature set is missing. [RQ4.5] Feature selection is explicitly nested: univariate correlation filtering is performed 'within each cross-validation fold' (selecting 24-39 features per fold, 60 distinct features overall) and PCA is applied 'within each CV fold', with leave-one-out cross-validation over 70 children. This is the correct structure and avoids the selection leakage that affects most of the corpus. Robustness is further probed by testing whether demographic and IQ variables improve the model - they do not - which is a form of confound check. What is absent: external or independent validation, any held-out site, calibration analysis, and any real-world deployment test despite community prescreening being the stated goal. The human-rater comparison functions as an informal ceiling estimate rather than a validation. [RQ5.1] Index terms: clinical speech, machine learning, Autism Spectrum Disorder. Task vocabulary: 'automatic detection system', 'prescreening and triage', 'brief, generic, and natural conversations', 'naive conversation partners (confederates)', 'real-world settings such as doctor's offices and schools'. The prescreening-and-triage framing, explicitly distinguished from diagnosis, is more careful than most of the corpus. [RQ5.2] INTERSPEECH 2019 (Graz) - a speech science and technology venue, not an autism or clinical journal, though the author list spans a linguistic data consortium, a hospital autism centre and university paediatrics and psychiatry departments. [RQ5.3] 2019. The paper characterises the speech-and-autism literature as drawing overwhelmingly on either highly structured elicitation (reading sentences or word lists) or semi-structured clinical interviews with an autism expert, chiefly ADOS evaluations, and argues these 'produce results that may not generalize to the everyday conversations that impact the lives of children on the autism spectrum'. It cites specific prior accuracies for calibration - roughly 74% from pitch features on 146 children, roughly 69% from speech rate and rhythm on 69 children - and identifies interlocutor speech features as an emerging and underused signal, noting prior findings that psychologists' speech predicted children's symptom severity better than the children's own features. This move from clinical-elicitation corpora toward naturalistic interaction is one of the clearest trend statements in the corpus.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control; 23 individuals with ASD (20 male, mean age 12.74, IQ range 58-137; 5 excluded for eye-tracking failure) vs 35 typically developing controls (25 male, mean age 14.11, range 8-34) recruited across US clinics, registries, advertising and a state fair; newly collected eye-tracking and behavioural data, not released.
narrative_rows.methods: Dynamic Affect Recognition Evaluation task with twelve silent Cohn-Kanade face videos transitioning neutral-to-emotion, spacebar response on recognition then six-choice emotion identification; Tobii TX300 (300 Hz) and X2-60 (60 Hz) eye tracking with 9-point calibration; features combining task performance (2-dim), gaze dynamics (6-dim) and 640-dim OpenFace embeddings of the fixated face region; random forest with balanced class weights under leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, with soft voting from fixations to trials to subjects.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Emotion recognition accuracy did not differ (77.89% vs 77.14%, p=0.841), but the ASD group responded slower (14.37 vs 11.43 s, p<0.001), with fewer fixations per second (1.06 vs 1.28 Hz), longer fixations (0.31 vs 0.25 s) and larger saccades (2.54 vs 2.30 degrees), and with fixation density displaced from eyes and mouth toward forehead, hair, ears and chin. Subject-level combined classification: AUC 0.935, accuracy 86.2%, sensitivity 91.3%, specificity 82.9%; task features alone gave only 56.5% sensitivity.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No limitations section. The eye tracker is confounded with group (all ASD at 300 Hz, 29 of 35 controls at 60 Hz) and the model's most important features are sampling-rate-sensitive; five ASD subjects but no controls were excluded for capture failure; control ages extend to 34 against an ASD maximum of 17; IQ reported only as an ASD range and never controlled; two display sizes; no external validation despite multi-site collection; and the printed sensitivity and specificity formulas are inverted.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The corpus's clearest demonstration that autistic differences in an emotion task can lie entirely in process rather than outcome - equal recognition accuracy with significantly slower, differently distributed looking - and the study whose ablation design most directly evidences that task performance and gaze carry complementary diagnostic information. It is also the corpus's most instructive example of an apparatus confound: a study strong on analysis and interpretation whose headline result is undermined by recording the two groups on different equipment.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups: 23 individuals with ASD (5 later excluded for eye-tracking failure) and 35 typically developing controls, total 58 recruited. Group sizes, sexes and ages are reported, and control status is defined by explicit exclusions. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the discussion proposes extending the paradigm to schizophrenia and ADHD. [RQ1.2] 'individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder', 'individuals with ASD', 'subjects with ASD', 'people with ASD', 'the ASD group', 'typically developing (TD) controls', 'patients with schizophrenia or ADHD'. Consistently person-first, with 'typically developing' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy' for the comparison group - and notably the paper frames its findings as revealing 'social and attentional deficits', a deficit framing, while simultaneously reporting that emotion recognition accuracy was unimpaired. [RQ1.3] ASD n=23 (20 male, 87%), age 12.74 +/- 2.45 years, range 8-17, IQ range 58-137. TD n=35 (25 male, 71%), age 14.11 +/- 5.09 years, range 8-34. Neither age nor sex was matched by design, but both differences were tested and found non-significant (p=0.241 and p=0.171). The control age range nonetheless extends to 34 while no autistic participant exceeded 17, so the groups differ substantially in composition even though means do not differ significantly - the control SD is more than double the ASD SD. IQ is given only as a range for the ASD group with no control values and no use as a covariate. [RQ1.4] Diagnosis based on testing with standardized instruments, review of diagnostic history and prior evaluations, and DSM criteria confirmed by clinical research staff - a multi-source ascertainment described in more procedural detail than most corpus studies, though the specific instruments are not named. Control status established by requiring no psychiatric history, no developmental delay and no previous special education. [RQ1.5] IQ score range (58-137) reported for the ASD group only, with no mean, SD or control comparison, and not used as a covariate despite the authors' own introduction noting that eye-tracking results 'can be impacted by sample size, age, developmental level and IQ'. No language or adaptive measures. Comorbidities not described for the ASD group; controls screened by exclusion of psychiatric history, developmental delay and special education. [RQ2.1] Goal: classify ASD from combined task performance and eye movements during facial emotion recognition, and interpret the features to understand social and attentional differences. Main findings: recognition accuracy did not differ between groups (77.89% vs 77.14%, p=0.841) but response time and every eye-movement measure did; combined features gave subject-level AUC 0.935, accuracy 86.2%, sensitivity 91.3%, specificity 82.9%; task features alone had only 56.5% sensitivity, rising to 91.3% when gaze and face features were added. [RQ2.2] Mixed clinic and community setting - recruitment spanned university clinics, websites, registries, local advertising and the 2015 Minnesota State Fair, with testing at more than one location using different displays and different eye trackers. Newly collected data; the face stimuli come from the existing Cohn-Kanade database. [RQ2.3] The Dynamic Affect Recognition Evaluation task: silent videos of a face transitioning slowly from neutral into one of six emotions, with the participant pressing the spacebar upon recognition and then selecting the emotion from six labels. Two practice trials (two choices) preceded twelve test trials (six choices), with practice videos not reused. Videos lasted 19-33 seconds. The design yields both a behavioural measure (how quickly recognition occurs, and whether it is correct) and a gaze measure over the same stimulus - which is what enables the accuracy-versus-latency dissociation. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single ~10-minute session with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates and button-press latencies over third-party stimulus faces, so participant-identifiable content is minimal. Institutional Review Board approval from the University of Minnesota is reported for all recruitment. No participant or parental consent statement, no anonymization procedure and no competing-interests declaration appear. [RQ2.5] Hardware: two Tobii Pro eye trackers - the TX300 at 300 Hz for all ASD subjects and six controls, and the X2-60 at 60 Hz for the remaining controls - with Tobii Studio 3.3.2; two display configurations (19-inch 1680x1050 and 27-inch 1920x1080) depending on collection site; viewing distance approximately 65 cm (camera range 50-70 cm); 9-point calibration with error below 0.5 degrees for every subject. Software: OpenFace pre-trained on LFW for face features, Viola-Jones for face detection, scikit-learn for random forests. [RQ2.6] No data availability statement and no code release. Method reporting is otherwise detailed: eye tracker models and sampling rates, calibration procedure and error tolerance, display specifications, viewing distance, stimulus source and resolution, trial counts, feature definitions and dimensionalities, the exact OpenFace layer used (inception-4a, 640 channels at 6x6), the Gaussian kernel for fixation density maps (sigma=15 pixels), balanced class weighting, and the cross-validation scheme. The pipeline is re-implementable in principle; the data are not accessible. [RQ2.7] No dedicated limitations section. The introduction acknowledges at field level that eye-tracking results 'can be impacted by sample size, age, developmental level and IQ, variation in stimuli, and task effort and objective', but the study does not then control for these. Identifiable in review: the two eye trackers are confounded with group - all ASD subjects used the 300 Hz TX300 while 29 of 35 controls used the 60 Hz X2-60 - and the most important model features (fixation frequency, fixation duration, fixation time, saccade amplitude) are exactly the measures a fivefold sampling-rate difference would bias, yet the authors dismiss this in one sentence; five ASD subjects were excluded for eye-tracking capture failure with no controls excluded, a group-dependent attrition that could itself reflect the behaviour being measured; control ages extend to 34 versus an ASD maximum of 17, with a control SD more than double the ASD SD; IQ is reported only as an ASD range and never controlled; two display sizes were used; and the reported equations define sensitivity in terms of TN and specificity in terms of TP, inverting the standard definitions. [RQ2.9] Extend to more subjects across a wider span of developmental ages; build a multimodal classifier incorporating demographic information, autonomic nervous system measures, functional MRI and other methodologies; and apply the same paradigm to schizophrenia and ADHD, which also show altered gaze patterns in visual tasks - a differential-diagnosis direction that addresses the specificity question left open by ASD-versus-TD designs. [RQ3.1] Three streams: gaze (fixation location, timing, duration, frequency, saccade amplitude), behavioural task performance (response latency and recognition accuracy), and the visual content of what was fixated (deep embeddings of the face region at each fixation). The third is unusual - most corpus gaze studies use predefined anatomical areas of interest, whereas here the stimulus content at the point of gaze is encoded by a deep network without any manual region annotation. [RQ3.2] Feature-level fusion across the three families into a single per-fixation vector, and the contribution of each is ablated separately at fixation, trial and subject level - so the complementarity claim is directly evidenced. The clearest demonstration is that task features alone reach 81.0% subject-level accuracy but only 56.5% sensitivity, while adding gaze and face features raises sensitivity to 91.3% at similar accuracy. Predictions are additionally fused across observations by soft voting from fixations to trials to subjects, with accuracy rising monotonically (72.5% to 75.6% to 86.2%) as the aggregation unit widens. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning: random forest with bootstrap sampling, majority voting and balanced class weights. A pre-trained deep convolutional network (OpenFace, 37 layers in 8 Inception blocks) is used upstream as a frozen feature extractor without fine-tuning, on the stated grounds that the LFW training set is sufficiently general. [RQ4.2] Hybrid representation: handcrafted scalar features for task performance and gaze dynamics, combined with a 640-dimensional learned embedding of the fixated face region taken from an intermediate convolutional layer. This is a distinctive design in the corpus - it replaces manually annotated areas of interest with a learned encoding of stimulus content at the point of gaze, which the authors explicitly present as avoiding reliance on annotated AOIs. [RQ4.3] AUC, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, reported for every feature family at every unit of analysis - a 3x4 results table that is among the most complete in the corpus and permits direct assessment of what each component contributes. Headline subject-level combined: AUC 0.935, accuracy 86.2%, sensitivity 91.3%, specificity 82.9%. No confidence intervals or confusion matrices. The printed formulas define sensitivity as TN/(TN+FP) and specificity as TP/(TP+FN), which reverses the conventional definitions and is presumably a transcription error, though it leaves the labelling of the reported values formally ambiguous. [RQ4.4] Well developed and multi-layered. Random-forest importance values are averaged across all cross-validation runs and normalised, showing that coarse temporal measures (relative response time, fixation time, fixation frequency, response time) dominate while fine-grained spatial fixation statistics matter less. Face-feature channels are visualised by averaging network activations across frames and overlaying them on an average face, revealing that the informative channels correspond to distinct anatomical regions (forehead, eyes, cheeks, nose, ears). Separately, pixel-wise fixation density maps with t-tests localise where the groups differ - controls more on eyes and mouth, ASD subjects more on forehead, hair, ears and chin. This combination of model-derived importance, activation visualisation and independent statistical mapping is the most thorough interpretability treatment charted so far. [RQ4.5] Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation repeated so each of the subjects is tested once, with balanced class weights addressing the 23-versus-35 imbalance, and results reported at three aggregation levels so the effect of the decision unit is visible rather than hidden. What is absent: external or independent validation, any held-out site despite multi-site collection, and any analysis of the apparatus confound. Most seriously, generalisability is undermined rather than tested by the design - the eye tracker is confounded with diagnostic group, and the model's most important features are sampling-rate-sensitive. No calibration analysis, no real-time or deployment claim beyond noting efficiency advantages over standardized diagnostic scales. [RQ5.1] No formal keyword list in the extracted text. Vocabulary: 'atypical scanning patterns', 'atypical visual attention', 'social and attentional deficits', 'facial emotion recognition', 'Dynamic Affect Recognition Evaluation', 'comparable with the standardized diagnostic scales', 'efficiency and objectiveness'. The explicit benchmarking of classifier performance against standardised diagnostic scales is a distinctive framing. [RQ5.2] The 41st Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC) 2019 - a biomedical engineering venue, technology-focused but clinically adjacent. [RQ5.3] 2019. The paper surveys the eye-tracking-plus-machine-learning literature specifically, citing SVM classification of children from face-recognition scanpaths, deep-learning extraction of fixated-region features achieving 92% in adults, and gaze-plus-demographics classification across ASD risk levels. Its critical observation is that 'these studies only considered the eye-tracking data, mainly what was looked at, without jointly taking into account the task performance', which it attributes to behavioural tasks being 'general but not specific enough' - identifying the integration of task performance with gaze as the field's next step. It also cites a systematic review noting that eye-tracking results have varied across studies and are sensitive to sample size, age, developmental level, IQ and stimulus variation.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional development and validation with three diagnostic classes; 159 parent-submitted mobile-phone videos of Bangladeshi children aged 18 months to 4 years (55 ASD, 50 speech and language conditions, 54 typically developing), diagnosed by MCHAT plus developmental psychologist and physician evaluation with ADOS on 28 of 50 ASD children; not released.
narrative_rows.methods: Nine clinically untrained, non-Bengali-speaking US raters scored 31 behavioural questions per video after one hour of training with gold-standard quality checks; per-rater random forests combined by softmax weighting on each rater's accuracy relative to majority vote; stacked two-layer classification (typical versus atypical, then ASD versus SLC) under three-fold cross-validation; Shapley value attribution at rater and ensemble level; elastic-net logistic regression trained on each country's data and tested on the other for cross-cultural comparison.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Previously published US-validated classifiers applied unchanged reached maximum AUC 0.75 (SD 0.06) on Bangladeshi videos, against 92% accuracy (95% CI 88-97%) on US videos. Retrained stacked models achieved AUC 76% (SD 3%) with sensitivity 76% (SD 4%) for atypical versus typical, and AUC 85% (SD 5%) with sensitivity 76% (SD 6%) for ASD versus other delay. Eye contact dominated Bangladeshi models; social participation and stereotyped speech dominated US models.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The ASD and SLC cohorts differ by 26 percentage points in sex and sharply in family income, confounding the layer-two comparison; all ASD and TD families were urban and predominantly higher-income, so the rural low-resource target population is barely represented; specificity is not reported for either layer despite layer one being sensitivity-optimised; ADOS covered only 28 of 50 ASD children; stunting data missing entirely for the TD cohort; demographic table percentages inconsistent with counts; senior author has a disclosed commercial interest in paediatric digital health.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The corpus's only direct measurement of cross-cultural generalisation: classifiers reported at 92% accuracy on US home videos fell to AUC 0.75 applied unchanged to Bangladeshi videos, with the drop reported openly and diagnosed specifically. It is also one of very few studies here with a non-autistic clinical comparison group built into the classification architecture, one of the few to compute Shapley attributions at individual-annotation level, and the only one to frame its contribution in health-systems terms - triage capacity, prevalence estimation and policy - rather than diagnostic accuracy alone.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Three groups: 55 videos of children with ASD, 50 with speech and language conditions, and 54 typically developing, totalling 159 videos (150 with complete demographic data). The inclusion of a non-autistic clinical comparison group - and the explicit design of a second classification layer to separate ASD from other developmental delay - directly addresses the specificity question that most ASD-versus-typical studies in this corpus leave open. SLC diagnoses are further broken down: 74% had both receptive and expressive language delay, 12% receptive and expressive language disorder, 10% expressive delay alone, 4% receptive delay alone. [RQ1.2] 'children with autism', 'children with ASD', 'the ASD cohort', 'children with an SLC', 'children with neurotypical development (TD)', 'children in need of therapeutic interventions', 'children with developmental delays'. Person-first throughout, and notably 'neurotypical development' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy'. The framing is service-access oriented - autism as a condition requiring diagnosis for intervention access - rather than deficit-focused. [RQ1.3] ASD n=50 (36 male, 72%), mean age 2.51 (0.70) years. SLC n=50 (31 male, 46%), mean age 2.73 (0.51). TD n=50 (23 male, printed as 62% though the count implies 46%), mean age 2.40 (0.59). Ages are close across groups but no matching or comparability testing is reported. Sex is substantially imbalanced between the two clinical groups (72% versus 46% male), which is a material confound for the ASD-versus-SLC layer. The demographic table also shows a marked socioeconomic gradient: 96% of ASD families earned over 30,000 taka versus 80% of SLC and only 26% of TD families, and 100% of ASD and TD families were urban versus 78% of SLC. Very young sample (18 months to 4 years), directly relevant to early detection. [RQ1.4] MCHAT (Bangla version) administered to all children, followed by clinical evaluation by a developmental psychologist and a child health physician to assign ASD, SLC or TD. ADOS was administered to only 28 of 50 ASD children, with the reason given explicitly - families could not commit the time required, 'a common problem for families in low-resource areas'. This partial gold-standard coverage is disclosed transparently and is itself an informative observation about diagnostic feasibility in the target setting. MCHAT scores are reported per group (13.5 ASD, 2 TD, 0.08 SLC), giving some quantitative separation. [RQ1.5] MCHAT total scores and ADOS subscores (social affect, restricted and repetitive behaviour, composite) reported for the assessed subset. Additional health and social indicators are reported that no other corpus study collects: preterm birth, stunted growth, family income band, urban/semiurban/rural residence, and religion. Stunting information is missing for the entire TD cohort, which prevents its use as a covariate. No IQ, language or adaptive-functioning scores. [RQ2.1] Goal: scale a validated US video-based screening pipeline to another culture and to developmental delays beyond autism, for deployment in settings lacking clinical resources. Main findings: US-trained classifiers transferred to Bangladeshi videos at maximum AUC 0.75 (SD 0.06) against 92% accuracy on US videos; retrained stacked classifiers with rater-adaptive weighting achieved AUC 76% (SD 3%) and sensitivity 76% (SD 4%) for atypical versus typical, and AUC 85% (SD 5%) and sensitivity 76% (SD 6%) for ASD versus other developmental delay; and feature importance differed by culture, with eye contact more prominent for Bangladeshi videos and social participation and stereotyped speech more prominent for US videos. [RQ2.2] Home setting for data capture - parents recorded brief videos on mobile phones - combined with clinical setting for diagnosis and recruitment at a Dhaka children's hospital, and remote US-based rating. Newly collected data. The design deliberately exploits Bangladesh's 95% mobile phone subscription rate as the deployment substrate. [RQ2.3] Parents submitted brief unstructured videos, quality-screened against three content criteria: capturing the child's face and hands, involving social interaction or attempts at it, and involving interaction between the child and a toy or object. All 159 submitted videos passed quality inspection. Nine clinically untrained, non-Bengali-speaking US raters then answered 31 multiple-choice questions per video after a one-hour training session, with quality control comparing a 10-video subset against gold-standard scores agreed by two experienced clinical research coordinators. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single short video per child with no follow-up. The data are among the most sensitive in the corpus - identifiable home video of very young children, transmitted internationally and viewed by nine non-clinical raters in another country. Governance is reported reasonably fully: dual ethical clearance from the Bangladesh Institute of Child Health / Dhaka Shishu Children's Hospital and the Stanford IRB, consent obtained in Bengali, secure transmission, and a HIPAA-compliant rating platform. What is absent is any retention, deletion or re-use policy, and any discussion of the ethics of routing identifiable child video to non-clinical raters abroad. [RQ2.5] Hardware: parents' own mobile phones for video capture - deliberately, since the deployment argument rests on mobile ubiquity. Software: a secure HIPAA-compliant web rating platform; Python 3.6.7 with pandas 0.23.4, scikit-learn 0.20.0 for models, hyperopt 0.1.1 for hyperparameter tuning, shap 0.24.0 for Shapley values, and matplotlib 3.0.1. Version numbers are given throughout, which is better practice than corpus norm. [RQ2.6] No data availability statement and no code release. Method reporting is otherwise strong: all software packages with exact versions, the rater-weighting softmax formulation, the Shapley local-accuracy property and its ensemble extension, the elastic-net loss with its two hyperparameters and the grid-search procedure, the balanced class weighting, the three-fold cross-validation split sizes, and demographic breakdowns for both training and test sets. Full mathematical detail is deferred to a multimedia appendix. The pipeline is re-implementable in principle; the videos, being identifiable child media, could not reasonably be released. [RQ2.7] Reported by the authors in a dedicated limitations section that diagnoses the transfer gap in three specific ways: the source classifiers were trained on clinical scoresheets rather than features obtained from live video; those scoresheets came from formal clinical assessments of US children and 'do not capture a culturally diverse set of behavioral nuances'; and the classifiers were built to separate typical development from autism whereas this dataset contains other delays including SLCs. They also hypothesise that raters sharing the children's linguistic and sociocultural background would improve performance. Identifiable in review: sex is markedly imbalanced between the ASD and SLC cohorts (72% versus 46% male), directly confounding the second classification layer; family income differs sharply across groups (96% of ASD families above 30,000 taka versus 26% of TD families), as does residence; stunting data are missing entirely for the TD cohort; ADOS covered only 28 of 50 ASD children; the demographic table's gender percentages are inconsistent with their counts; and the senior author founded a company developing paediatric digital health solutions, disclosed as a conflict of interest. [RQ2.9] Expand to larger samples across Bangladesh and other low-resource settings; recruit raters who share the children's linguistic and sociocultural background, hypothesised to close the performance gap with US results; accumulate a large annotated video corpus so that convolutional and recurrent networks can learn features directly from raw video and audio rather than from human annotations; and use location-tagged videos to generate epidemiological prevalence estimates that could inform policy and resource allocation - a public-health framing of future work that is unique in this corpus. [RQ3.1] Behavioural observation mediated by human rating rather than direct sensing: 31 categorical judgements of autism-relevant behaviours (eye contact, social participation, stereotyped speech, sensory seeking, stereotyped interests and actions, and others) made by watching short video. This is the only approach in the corpus where the 'features' are human perceptual judgements of behaviour rather than automatically extracted signals - which is deliberate, since it removes any need for specialised sensing hardware in the deployment setting. [RQ3.2] Fusion occurs across annotators rather than across modalities, and this is the paper's methodological contribution. Each rater's annotations train a separate random forest, and predictions are combined by a softmax-weighted ensemble whose weights reflect each rater's model accuracy relative to a majority-vote baseline. The authors argue this lets the ensemble exploit each rater's strengths (one may rate eye contact well, another language ability) while discounting their weaknesses, and note it permits distributed annotation where each rater sees only a subset of videos without requiring imputation. A second form of composition is the stacked two-layer architecture, where layer one's atypical classifications feed layer two. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning. Random forests per rater with softmax ensemble weighting for the main classification; logistic regression with elastic net regularisation and balanced class weights for the cross-cultural transfer analysis. The choice of a two-layer stack is motivated conceptually - layer one optimised for sensitivity so no atypical case is missed, layer two optimised for both sensitivity and specificity to separate ASD from other delays - which links model design to intended clinical use more explicitly than most of the corpus. [RQ4.2] Categorical human ratings as features: 31 multiple-choice responses per video per rater. No signal-level representation of the video is used at all. The authors note in future work that a sufficiently large annotated corpus would allow convolutional and recurrent networks to learn features directly from raw video and audio - explicitly positioning the current human-rating approach as a bootstrapping stage. [RQ4.3] AUC and sensitivity with standard deviations for both layers, and AUC with standard deviation for the source-classifier transfer test, plus ROC curves. Reporting sensitivity alongside AUC is appropriate for a screening framing, and reporting standard deviations across folds is better than corpus norm. However specificity is not reported for either layer, which matters given that layer one is explicitly optimised for sensitivity - so the false-positive burden of the first-stage triage is not quantifiable from the paper. [RQ4.4] Among the most thorough in the corpus. Shapley values are computed for all 159 videos in the second layer using the shap package, exploiting local accuracy so each video's predicted probability decomposes exactly into per-feature contributions with both magnitude and direction, and the same rater weights are applied to derive ensemble-level Shapley values. This permits interpretation at the level of an individual child's individual annotation. Separately, features selected most often during elastic-net tuning are compared across the US and Bangladeshi models, yielding the substantive cross-cultural finding that eye contact dominates for Bangladeshi videos while social participation and stereotyped speech dominate for US videos - with a plausible mechanism offered, namely that raters could evaluate language-based behaviours only when they shared the language. [RQ4.5] The paper is unusual in this corpus for treating generalisation as an empirical question rather than an assumption. It applies previously published classifiers unchanged to a new cultural population and reports the resulting performance drop (92% accuracy on US videos to AUC 0.75 on Bangladeshi videos), then trains models on each dataset and tests on the other to compare feature reliance. Class imbalance is handled with balanced class weights. Three-fold cross-validation with reported training and test demographics gives some assurance of split stability. What is missing: whether cross-validation folds were partitioned at child level is not explicitly stated (though with one video per child this is largely moot); specificity is not reported; and no prospective or external validation of the retrained Bangladeshi models is performed. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: autism; autism spectrum disorder; machine learning; developmental delays; clinical resources; Bangladesh; Biomedical Data Science. Task vocabulary: 'risk scores', 'reduce-to-practice testing', 'rater-adaptive weighting', 'triage', 'cross-cultural validity', 'health care disparity'. The health-equity and health-systems vocabulary ('clinical resources', 'population-level burden', 'policy change') is distinctive in this corpus. [RQ5.2] Journal of Medical Internet Research - a digital health and health informatics journal, clinically oriented rather than computational or autism-specific. [RQ5.3] 2019. The paper documents the field's cross-cultural blind spot directly: empirically validated tools like ADOS and ADI-R 'are not always used in different countries, particularly in developing countries, as these tools are expensive, require trained clinicians to administer, and may be limited by available translations and cultural adaptations', and it notes that global autism prevalence is 'largely unknown' with estimates of 0.15-0.8% in Bangladesh and around 3% in Dhaka, most cases in semiurban and rural areas going unnoticed. It situates itself in a programme of prior work on rapid mobile ASD detection from short home videos, and its central empirical contribution - measuring how far those US-validated classifiers transfer - is the kind of external validation this corpus otherwise almost entirely lacks.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional classification on a public benchmark; the Saliency4ASD IEEE ICME 2019 Grand Challenge dataset of natural images with ASD and TD scanpaths (300 training images, 100 held-out test images); no participant counts, ages or genders reported and subject identity inconsistent across images.
narrative_rows.methods: 30 handcrafted features across three families - image content (fixations on YOLO-detected objects versus non-objects, coverage, refixation, SDSP saliency-weighted attention), fixation behaviour (fixation and saccade statistics, mean-shift-derived ROI counts and durations) and centre bias (distance from and dwell time near image centre) - fed to a MATLAB TreeBagger random forest with 128 trees, evaluated on the organiser's held-out test set.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Accuracy 59.30%, recall 68.43%, specificity 50.56%, F1 61.64%, precision 56.96%, AUC-ROC 59.50%. Specificity is at chance, so recall is obtained largely by over-calling ASD.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No participant counts, ages, genders or diagnostic ascertainment; age unavailable in the dataset despite ASD fixation behaviour being strongly age-dependent, which the authors identify as the principal cause of limited performance; subject identity inconsistent across images so subject-independent evaluation is impossible and analysis is per-scanpath rather than per-person; no feature importance or ablation; single model, no comparison.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The corpus's most useful low-performance data point: an entry to a shared benchmark with an organiser-held-out test set, reporting the fullest metric set of any study charted and thereby exposing that a 59% accuracy conceals chance-level specificity. Its discussion is also the corpus's clearest statement that ASD gaze signatures are moderated by age and image content, so a single model generalised across all subjects and stimuli is unlikely to work - an argument that indicts the benchmark framing itself, not just this entry.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups by dataset label - ASD and typically developing - but the paper reports no participant counts for either group, only image counts (300 training, 100 test). The unit of analysis throughout is the scanpath rather than the person, and subject identifiers are explicitly randomised and inconsistent across images, so participant-level group composition is not recoverable. [RQ1.2] 'persons affected by autism spectrum disorder', 'persons with ASD', 'ASD subjects', 'ASD patient', 'the patient', 'Typically Developing (TD) infants', 'TD persons', 'non-ASD subjects', 'typically developed toddlers'. Notably medicalised - 'patient' and 'affected by' recur - though the introduction does acknowledge the alternative term 'Autism Spectrum Condition' in its opening sentence before using 'disorder' throughout. [RQ1.3] Not reported at any level. No sample sizes, no ages, no age ranges, no standard deviations, no gender distribution, and no matching information for either group. The authors state explicitly that age 'is not available in the given dataset' and treat this as a substantive limitation on their model, since they cite evidence that ASD fixation behaviour differs markedly between toddlers, young children and grown-up children. This is the least participant-characterised study in the corpus so far. [RQ1.4] Not reported. Class labels are inherited from the Saliency4ASD challenge dataset with no description of how the original diagnoses were established, what instruments were used, or how typically developing status was confirmed. [RQ1.5] None reported. No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or severity measures, and no comorbidity information - consistent with the complete absence of participant metadata in the source dataset as used here. [RQ2.1] Goal: identify ASD from visual behaviour during image viewing, developed for the Saliency4ASD Grand Challenge. Main findings: accuracy 59.30%, recall 68.43%, specificity 50.56%, F1 61.64%, precision 56.96%, AUC-ROC 59.50% on the organiser's held-out test set. The authors describe this as promising with room for improvement, and attribute the limitation primarily to the absence of age information and to the age-dependence of ASD fixation behaviour. [RQ2.2] Setting not reported - this is entirely secondary analysis of an existing benchmark dataset (Saliency4ASD, IEEE ICME 2019 Grand Challenge), with no data collection by the authors and no description of the original acquisition conditions. [RQ2.3] Free viewing of 2D natural scene images, per the source dataset. No task instruction, viewing duration, stimulus presentation details or calibration procedure is described, since none of it was performed by these authors. The analysis pipeline adds its own processing tasks - YOLO object detection and SDSP saliency estimation over each stimulus image. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single scanpath per subject per image with no temporal or longitudinal component. The data are fixation coordinates over public stimulus images, with subject identifiers already randomised by the dataset providers, so re-identification risk is minimal. No ethics approval, consent or data-protection statement appears - understandable for secondary use of a released challenge dataset but not acknowledged as such anywhere in the paper. [RQ2.5] No acquisition hardware, since no data were collected. Software: YOLO (You Only Look Once) for object detection, chosen to segment images into object and non-object regions; SDSP (saliency detection by combining simple priors) for saliency, chosen for low computational complexity; mean-shift clustering with a Gaussian kernel and a distance/scale threshold of 100 for region-of-interest extraction; MATLAB TreeBagger for the random forest. [RQ2.6] Mixed. The source dataset is a public benchmark with an organiser-defined train/test split, which is the strongest form of comparability in this corpus - results are directly comparable against other challenge entrants. The feature set is fully enumerated in a table with definitions and the saliency feature is given as an explicit equation, the ROI clustering threshold (100) and centre-proximity radius (100 pixels) are stated, and the classifier and tree count (128) are named. But no code is released, no random seeds are given, no software versions are specified, and the object-detection and saliency models are named without configuration details. [RQ2.7] Reported by the authors, and unusually thoughtfully for a four-page workshop paper: ASD fixation behaviour changes with age, with toddlers, young children and grown-up children differing markedly and adults with ASD showing no visible difference in fixation duration between objects and non-objects, so 'the ASD subject age is very important for detecting the condition' - yet age was unavailable in the dataset; and fixation behaviour also depends on image content, since young ASD children do not differ from TD children on scenes containing both faces and objects of circumscribed interest, so 'ASD condition cannot be generalized over age, fixation behaviour, and image content' whereas the model generalises all features over all subjects. Identifiable in review: specificity of 50.56% is chance level and the model is therefore near-useless for ruling out ASD, which the summary framing of '60% accuracy' obscures; no participant counts, ages or genders exist at all; subject identity is not consistent across images so subject-independent evaluation is impossible and the same person's scanpaths can appear in both training and test sets; the unit of analysis is a scanpath not a person, so this is not a person-level diagnostic result; and no feature importance is reported despite the model providing it natively. [RQ2.9] Incorporate object semantics - the type of object fixated rather than merely whether a fixation fell on an object - motivated by evidence that ASD subjects look at the mouth rather than the eye region of faces; and study in depth which areas of fixation coverage ASD subjects miss, on the argument that what fails to attract attention may be as diagnostic as what attracts it. The discussion additionally implies, without stating it as a formal direction, that features must be adapted by participant age. [RQ3.1] Gaze: fixation coordinates, durations and derived saccadic amplitudes during natural-scene viewing. Uniquely in this corpus, gaze features are combined with computed properties of the stimulus itself - detected object regions and a bottom-up saliency map - so the representation is jointly behavioural and stimulus-derived rather than purely behavioural. [RQ3.2] Single behavioural modality, but with genuine cross-source integration: three feature families (image content, fixation behaviour, centre bias) are concatenated for the classifier, and two of them require fusing gaze data with image-analysis outputs (YOLO object masks and SDSP saliency maps). This gaze-plus-stimulus-content fusion is a distinctive design in the corpus, though its contribution is never ablated so the value of each family is unknown. No integration with clinical, cognitive or demographic data - the latter being impossible given the dataset. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning. Algorithm: random forest via MATLAB TreeBagger with 128 trees and bootstrap aggregation, selected on the stated grounds that it performs well on all-numeric feature sets with a numeric class label. Mean-shift clustering is used unsupervised as a feature-construction step. No alternative classifiers are compared. [RQ4.2] Handcrafted numeric features - 30 scalar statistics per scanpath spanning content-relative fixation allocation, fixation and saccade dynamics, spatial coverage and refixation, saliency-weighted attention, and centre-proximity measures. No raw scanpath sequences, images or learned embeddings are fed to the classifier, though deep models (YOLO) and a saliency model are used upstream to define the regions the features are computed against. [RQ4.3] The fullest metric set in the corpus so far: accuracy (59.30%), recall/sensitivity (68.43%), specificity (50.56%), F1 (61.64%), precision (56.96%) and AUC-ROC (59.50%), all reported together for the held-out test set. Reporting specificity alongside recall is what makes the result interpretable - it shows recall is achieved largely by over-calling ASD, with specificity at chance. No confidence intervals or per-class confusion matrix. [RQ4.4] None. No feature importance, saliency analysis or ablation is performed, and no behavioural feature is identified as informative - a notable gap given that random forests supply out-of-bag importance measures for free and the feature set is explicitly organised into three interpretable families. The paper's interpretive content is instead a literature-grounded argument about why the features should work and why age moderates them. [RQ4.5] Evaluation on an organiser-held-out test set with labels withheld is methodologically stronger than the internal cross-validation used by most of the corpus, and it makes the result directly comparable against other challenge entrants. But the design has a structural limitation the authors flag without connecting to validity: subject identity is randomised and inconsistent across images, so partitioning by subject is impossible and the same individual's scanpaths may fall on both sides of the split. Combined with per-image rather than per-person analysis, the reported figures estimate scanpath-level discriminability, not person-level diagnostic accuracy. No external validation beyond the challenge test set, no bias analysis, no class-imbalance handling, and no deployment or real-time consideration. [RQ5.1] Index terms: Autism spectrum disorder, Object detection, Fixations, Centre bias, Classification, Visual saliency. Task vocabulary: 'revealing the presence of autism spectrum disorder', 'ASD identification', 'early detection', 'visual behaviour', 'scanpath', 'centre bias', 'saliency'. The computer-vision vocabulary (saliency, object detection, ROI) dominates over clinical vocabulary. [RQ5.2] IEEE International Conference on Multimedia and Expo Workshops (ICMEW) 2019, as an entry to the Saliency4ASD Grand Challenge - a multimedia/computer-vision venue, not an autism or clinical venue. [RQ5.3] 2019. The related-work section surveys the eye-tracking-plus-machine-learning turn in some breadth, citing web-browsing gaze classification, saccade-based classification on six subjects, and a 700-image saliency study finding stronger centre bias and reduced saliency for faces in ASD. It also cites contrary evidence - that social orienting is 'not qualitatively impaired' in ASD and that the excess-mouth, diminished-eye gaze hypothesis has poor support - making it one of the few corpus papers to acknowledge that the underlying behavioural claims are contested. The existence of a dedicated Grand Challenge with a shared dataset is itself evidence of the field's move toward benchmark-based evaluation around 2019.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Exploratory proof-of-concept robotics study; 8 preschool children already diagnosed with ASD and 7 typically developing children in Croatia, matched by mental age, with no ages, genders or diagnostic instrument reported; single-session robot-administered protocol with video and audio recordings, not released.
narrative_rows.methods: Four ADOS-derived tasks (response to name call, joint attention, play request, functional imitation) administered by NAO humanoid robots; a hierarchical POMDP maintained belief over child condition (low-functioning ASD, high-functioning ASD, typical), engagement and verbal activity, with task-level beliefs discretised into 16/3/3 partitions to generate protocol-level observations; observation probabilities elicited from a clinician survey; confidence scaling of 0.8 applied to reduce per-task information; solved with SARSOP; robot semi-autonomous with an operator supplying critical observations.
narrative_rows.outcomes: No accuracy metric reported. Expert assessment of de-identified transcripts categorised sessions as ASD-like behaviour (n=5), typical behaviour (n=3), ambiguous (n=4) and too short (n=3). Belief distributions separated ASD-like behaviour clearly, typical behaviour less decisively with high-functioning-ASD overlap, assigned ambiguous behaviour to high-functioning ASD, and for too-short sessions remained near-uniform at approximately 0.27-0.43.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No quantitative performance metric of any kind; 15 children with no ages, genders or diagnostic instrument; ASD group all in daily intervention and habituated to similar tasks, producing behaviour that diverged from diagnosis; observation probabilities elicited by clinician survey rather than learned; confidence-scaling parameter tuned by judgement; robot only semi-autonomous with human-supplied observations; four sessions ended in robot failure; no ethics or consent statement despite two-way-mirror video of preschoolers.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The corpus's only sequential decision-making architecture rather than a classifier, and its clearest example of a research team deliberately reducing their own apparent performance on principled grounds - introducing confidence scaling because four tasks producing near-certain diagnostic belief was implausible against ADOS's five modules of ten-plus tasks. It also documents an important confound for the whole robot-mediated strand: an intervention-experienced ASD group showed no anxiety toward the robot while typically developing children were shy and wary, so diagnosis and observed behaviour diverged, and the authors restructured their analysis around behaviour in response.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups: 8 preschool children already diagnosed with ASD and 7 typically developing children, total 15. Group sizes are reported. No other-diagnosis group. Notably the analysis is ultimately regrouped by expert-assessed behaviour rather than by diagnosis, producing four categories (ASD-like behaviour n=5, typical behaviour n=3, ambiguous n=4, session too short n=3) that cut across the original diagnostic grouping. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'people with ASD', 'child with low-functioning ASD', 'child with high-functioning ASD', 'typically developing children'. Person-first throughout, with the paper framing its motivation in terms of 'successful inclusion of people with ASD into the society'. The POMDP state labels (sLA, sHA, sNA for low-functioning, high-functioning and typically developing) formalise a three-level functioning taxonomy as latent model states. [RQ1.3] Only group sizes are reported: 8 ASD and 7 typically developing preschool children, matched by mental age. No chronological ages, no age ranges, no standard deviations, and gender is explicitly disregarded - 'Gender was not considered'. Mental-age matching is claimed but no values or comparison are given. The research targets ages 2-6, so the sample is directly relevant to early diagnosis, but nothing about its composition can be verified. [RQ1.4] Not reported. Children are described as 'already diagnosed with ASD' with no instrument, criteria, clinician or date, and typically developing status is asserted without screening. The protocol tasks are modelled on ADOS, but ADOS itself was not administered as a reference standard. Instead, the validation comparator is a post-hoc expert judgement of behaviour from de-identified transcripts - which is a reasonable choice given the authors' observation that behaviour and diagnosis diverged, but it means no gold-standard diagnostic anchor exists in the study. [RQ1.5] None reported. No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive measures, no severity instrument, and no comorbidity information. Mental age is used for matching but its values are not given. The one clinically relevant characteristic reported is that all ASD-group children were undergoing intervention and trained on similar tasks almost daily - which the authors correctly identify as a confound affecting their behaviour toward the robot. [RQ2.1] Goal: enable a humanoid robot to reason about a child's unobservable state during an ADOS-derived diagnostic protocol and to select tasks adaptively, addressing the reported problem of inter-clinician disagreement arising from the need to simultaneously observe, code and interpret many behaviours. Main findings: belief distributions separated expert-assessed ASD behaviour clearly and typical behaviour less decisively; behaviour experts judged ambiguous was assigned to high-functioning ASD; and sessions too short for expert assessment produced near-uniform beliefs (approximately 0.27-0.43), correctly signalling insufficient information. No accuracy figure is reported. [RQ2.2] Laboratory setting - a purpose-built examination and observation suite with a two-way mirror, fixed camera position and overhead microphone, with a therapist in the room and a second therapist plus robot operator behind the mirror. Newly collected session data; no existing dataset used. [RQ2.3] Four ADOS-derived tasks, each performed exactly once as in ADOS: response to name call (positive if eye contact detected), joint attention (transferring attention to a second robot that activates its lights, verified by eye contact), play request (eliciting vocalisations and eye contact coordinated with hand and body gestures to test simultaneous multi-channel communication), and functional imitation with real objects - a toy frog and a cup - which the authors distinguish from the simple motoric imitation used in comparable work. In every task the robot first performs an action intended to provoke a child response. A therapist placed objects into the robot's hand and triggered demonstrations via head tactile sensors, specifically to eliminate failed grasps and guarantee the imitation always occurred. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single session per child, with repeated sessions deliberately avoided to prevent learned behaviours. The data are video and audio of identifiable preschool children, recorded both by the robot's onboard camera and by a high-definition camera concealed behind a two-way mirror - among the most privacy-sensitive arrangements in the corpus. There is no ethics approval statement, no parental consent statement and no anonymization or data-protection provision anywhere in the paper. The only privacy-adjacent measure is that transcripts shared with the expert assessors omitted child identification. [RQ2.5] Hardware: two NAO humanoid robots, one facing the child with its back to the two-way mirror and one on the floor to its left with lights off except during the joint attention task; a high-definition camera behind the two-way mirror; an overhead microphone in the examination room; the robot's onboard camera. Software: hierarchical POMDP models solved with the SARSOP point-based solver, with protocol and task controllers and the operator interface running on a remote computer. [RQ2.6] No data or code release. The model specification is however documented in unusual detail: the state factorisation, the belief-space partitioning scheme (16 partitions over the condition simplex, 3 each over engagement and verbal activity), the full 3x16 observation probability matrix for the condition states, the 2x3 matrices for engagement and verbal activity, the centroid-based procedure for deriving those probabilities, the confidence-scaling equation with its chosen value of 0.8, the reward-shaping rules, and the solver used. The model is therefore reimplementable; the sessions are not reproducible, and the clinician survey that supplied the underlying observation rates is not documented. [RQ2.7] Reported by the authors, with notable candour: the sample size 'is not large'; because each task runs once the robot makes only three decisions, which 'does not necessarily warrant a use of POMDP'; social cue detection algorithms are 'not accurate enough for fully autonomous execution' so the robot is only semi-autonomous with an operator supplying critical observations; not all children completed all tasks, some because of robot failures and some through fear or refusal; in four cases robot failure ended the session because children would not continue; and crucially, typically developing children 'sometimes exhibit autistic behavior, and vice versa', which the authors attribute to the ASD group being in daily intervention and unafraid of the robot while typically developing children were shy and wary. Identifiable in review: no ages, genders or diagnostic instrument; no ethics or consent statement despite two-way-mirror video of preschoolers; observation probabilities elicited by clinician survey rather than estimated from data; no quantitative performance metric whatsoever; and the confidence-scaling parameter was tuned until 'more appropriate' belief values emerged, which is a judgement call rather than a fitted value. [RQ2.9] Run more clinical sessions to obtain data on child engagement and verbal activity during robot-administered tasks, which would enable richer reward models, permit evaluation of the robot's task-selection policy, and allow belief-based classification to be compared against conventional classifiers that currently cannot be trained for lack of data; continue developing social cue detection toward full autonomy; increase the number of protocol tasks; and investigate whether children behave differently when diagnostic tasks are administered by a robot rather than a human examiner - a question that bears directly on whether robot-administered protocols measure the same construct as clinician-administered ones. [RQ3.1] Social-interaction behaviour observed as discrete cues: eye contact, vocalisations, imitation and gestures, each tracked in specified tasks. These are categorical behavioural events rather than continuously sensed signals, and in this study they were largely human-coded (in real time by the operator for critical observations, offline from video for the rest) rather than automatically detected. [RQ3.2] Multiple cue types are combined within each task's observation set and jointly update a shared belief over child condition, engagement and verbal activity - so eye contact, utterances, imitation and gestures fuse probabilistically into one latent state estimate. The hierarchical structure adds a second fusion level: each task's terminal belief is discretised into a partition index that becomes an observation for the protocol-level model, so information accumulates across tasks. This belief-space-partitioning interface is the paper's central technical contribution and is a genuinely different fusion mechanism from the feature concatenation used everywhere else in the corpus. [RQ4.1] Not machine learning in the supervised sense. The method is probabilistic sequential decision-making: a hierarchical POMDP with task-level and protocol-level models, solved by the SARSOP point-based value iteration solver. Model parameters are specified rather than learned - transition matrices for child states are identity (robot actions cannot change the child's condition, and no data existed on their effect on engagement or verbal activity), and observation probabilities were elicited from a clinician survey. The authors themselves note that comparison against trained classifiers is not yet possible for lack of data. [RQ4.2] Behaviour is represented as discrete observation symbols drawn from a defined set per task, and the child is represented as a probability distribution (belief) over a factored latent state space of condition, engagement and verbal activity. Between hierarchy levels, a continuous belief simplex is discretised into 16 partitions whose centroids define observation probabilities. There are no feature vectors, embeddings or time series. [RQ4.3] None. No accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1 or AUC is reported, and no confusion matrix. The outputs are belief distributions over three latent states, plotted as frequency histograms per expert-assigned behavioural category. This means the study contributes no diagnostic accuracy estimate, and it should be excluded from any quantitative synthesis of performance - a point worth recording explicitly since its framing as a diagnostic protocol might otherwise invite inclusion. [RQ4.4] The model is inherently interpretable in structure - beliefs over named clinical states, observations tied to specific social cues, and reward rules stated in plain language (penalise name-call if the child is already engaged; penalise joint attention if the child is not engaged; reward play request if disengaged; reward imitation if engaged). But no analysis identifies which cues or tasks were most informative, and the observation probabilities encode clinician priors rather than empirical relationships, so nothing about autistic behaviour is learned from the data. [RQ4.5] There is no validation in the machine-learning sense - no cross-validation, no held-out data, no independent test set. Robustness is addressed through two design decisions instead. First, the authors noticed that four tasks were driving belief close to certainty and judged this implausible given ADOS uses five modules of at least ten tasks each, so they introduced a confidence-scaling transformation and set it to 0.8 to deliberately reduce the information each task contributes - actively degrading apparent performance on principled grounds. Second, they validated against expert-assessed behaviour rather than diagnostic label, because they had observed the two diverging in their sample. Neither is a generalisation estimate. There is no external validation, no bias analysis, no class-imbalance consideration, and the system is not autonomous, so deployment readiness is explicitly not established. [RQ5.1] Index terms: POMDP; NAO; robot-assisted; autism; diagnostics. Task vocabulary: 'robot-assisted ASD diagnostic protocol', 'belief state', 'social cues', 'semi-autonomous', 'Wizard-of-Oz'. The decision-theoretic vocabulary (belief, policy, reward, observation probability) is unique in this corpus and reflects a robotics rather than pattern-recognition framing. [RQ5.2] The 14th ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) 2019 - a robotics and human-robot interaction venue, not an autism, clinical or machine-learning venue. [RQ5.3] 2019. The paper positions itself as 'one of the first applications of humanoid robots in the diagnostics procedure', distinguishing diagnostic from the much commoner therapeutic robot applications and noting that diagnostic use 'brings forth some additional requirements and challenges, especially in terms of data acquisition and reasoning'. It observes that the complexity of the diagnostic process 'imposes constraints on the robotic applications in form of the need for efficient processing and reasoning algorithms', which results in a 'low number of robotic applications in ASD diagnosis'. It also documents that most robot-autism research still uses 'some form of Wizard-of-Oz approach with various degrees of autonomy', and that observations are typically 'collected through analysis of video recordings, which is a common technique in this field' - an accurate characterisation of the robot strand of this corpus.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Proof-of-concept classification study and system-design paper; ASD and typically developing children in Saudi Arabia, with no sample sizes, ages, genders or diagnostic procedure reported; newly collected Tobii X120 gaze data, not characterised and not released.
narrative_rows.methods: Three-phase workflow (therapist pre-analysis with patient history and eye-tracker setup, gaze capture during Arabic visual stimuli adapted from a cited English-language protocol, and prediction-model building); mean fixation duration per region of interest assembled into one feature vector per participant; SVM with participant-level leave-one-out cross-validation. Kernel, hyperparameters, ROI definitions, feature dimensionality, stimulus counts and analysis software are all unreported.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Accuracy 88.6%, specificity 92.31%, sensitivity 86.63%, AUC 0.96, reported without sample size, confidence intervals, confusion matrix or significance testing.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No sample size, ages, genders or diagnostic ascertainment reported; no stimulus, ROI or feature specification; no model configuration or software; methods partly written in the future tense; no ethics or consent statement despite a clinical child-facing workflow collecting medical history; no limitations section; and an overstated interpretation of AUC as evidence of generalisation to new data.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Charted primarily as a reporting-quality data point and for its literature review, which correctly identifies that prior work had not embedded an automatic prediction model inside a deployable clinical screening tool, and which raises a geographic coverage gap - the scarcity of Arabic-language autism screening research and the wide divergence of Gulf prevalence estimates - that no other study in this corpus addresses. Its performance figures are not interpretable as effect estimates and should be excluded from any quantitative synthesis.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups are referred to - ASD and typically developing (non-ASD) children - but no participant counts are reported for either group anywhere in the paper. The sample is described only as 'our collected eye movement data set'. This is the only study charted so far that reports classification performance without stating any sample size. [RQ1.2] 'ASD children', 'individuals with ASD', 'ASD patients', 'non-ASD patients', 'patients', 'Autistic or non-Autistic', 'typically developing children', 'individuals with disabilities'. Strongly medicalised: autism is described as 'a mental disorder', 'among the most upsetting disorders of childhood' and 'a harming developmental disorder', and participants are consistently 'patients'. This is the most pathologising terminology encountered in the corpus. [RQ1.3] Nothing is reported. No sample sizes, no ages, no age range, no standard deviations, no gender distribution and no matching information for either group. The paper's motivation depends on early screening before age 2, but the age of the children actually tested is never stated, so it cannot be established whether the system was evaluated in the population it targets. [RQ1.4] Not reported. No diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or confirmation procedure is described for the ASD group, and typically developing status is asserted without any screening. Since diagnostic label is the classification target and the paper proposes a clinical screening tool, the complete absence of reference-standard information is disqualifying for any diagnostic-accuracy claim. [RQ1.5] None reported. No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or severity measures for either group. The workflow specifies that a therapist collects patient information and medical history in the pre-analysis phase, so such data are presumably gathered, but none is reported or used. [RQ2.1] Goal: early screening via an Arabic automated gaze-based system integrating eye tracking with machine learning, to speed up diagnosis and reduce dependence on subjective clinical observation. Main findings as reported: accuracy 88.6%, specificity 92.31%, sensitivity 86.63%, AUC 0.96. The authors claim the AUC is the best among comparable models and argue this means it 'works well regardless of the class distribution', which is an overstatement of what AUC guarantees. [RQ2.2] Intended clinical setting - autism centres or hospitals in Saudi Arabia, with a therapist-operated workflow. Newly collected data, though nothing about the collection setting, session structure or conditions is described.
