Here that structure is used to define the two conditions of the within-subject contrast - instructed against spontaneous - which is the paradigm's payoff. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional pilot, single session per child, with no follow-up or test-retest. Ethics reporting is brief but complete on the essentials: approval of the committee of research ethics was obtained to carry out the experiment, and informed consent was obtained from the children's parents. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text; the participating kindergarten is acknowledged by name. [RQ2.5] A NAO humanoid robot from Aldebaran Robotics - 57 cm tall, 5.4 kg - with its SDK and desktop applications for authoring animations, behaviours and dialogues, plus video recording. The paper notes the availability of ASK NAO (Autism Solutions for Kids), a commercial application pack 'inspired by commonly practiced special education teaching methods (ABA, PECS, TEACCH, DENVER, SCERTS)', which is a useful observation for the review: the platform already carries an autism-specific software ecosystem built around established educational approaches, so robot-mediated assessment can be layered onto infrastructure that exists in practice rather than requiring a purpose-built device. The equipment cost remains high relative to the webcam-and-toys protocols charted elsewhere here, and what it buys is exact reproducibility of the social partner. [RQ2.6] Adequate for a short conference paper and incomplete on participants. Reported: both games, the voice-menu dialogue opening, the robot platform with physical specifications and software environment, the professional backgrounds of the competent raters, the questionnaire-based coding procedure, the normalisation of behaviour counts to proportions of behaviours required in each game, the statistical test with statistic and p-value, ethics approval, parental consent, and the participating kindergarten by name. Not reported in the retrieved text: sample size, ages, sex, diagnostic ascertainment, the questionnaire items themselves, and inter-rater reliability - the last being a real gap given that the competent-raters technique is the study's measurement instrument, and one the group closed in its 2022 follow-up by reporting Kendall's W and subscale alpha. [RQ2.7] Two limitations are stated and both are correctly identified. The first is the absence of a comparison group - 'we observed only autistic children interacting with the robot' - with the remedy given as comparison against typically developing children, which the group subsequently carried out. The second is more valuable and is rare in this corpus: 'the especially challenging task is to differ autism from other similar disorders. Thus, the other direction of our future studies is to observe the interactions performed by the robot and the children with other disorders.' Committing to a non-autistic clinical comparison is a commitment almost no study in this review makes, and the one included study that does test autism against another clinical population found the field's gold-standard observational instrument achieving an AUC of 0.562 - which is the evidence that this stated priority is the right one. What is not addressed: sample size and participant characteristics are unreported; no diagnostic ascertainment is described; inter-rater reliability is not quantified for this study; rater blinding to the hypothesis is not discussed; and no developmental measure separates general cognitive level from autism as an explanation for reduced spontaneous imitation. [RQ2.9] Three directions, two of them named as limitations and one as an engineering output. Compare autistic children's robot interaction against that of typically developing children - subsequently done. Observe interactions with children who have other developmental disorders, to address the differential-diagnosis problem the paper identifies as the hardest. And apply the collected user requirements and evaluation criteria to robot design, which the paper treats as a research product in its own right. [RQ3.1] Turn-taking, decomposed into two forms - and the decomposition is the study's substantive contribution to the review. Behaviour performed in response to an explicit robot instruction is treated as intentional turn-taking; behaviour performed spontaneously, imitating the robot without being told to, is treated as automatic turn-taking. Each is expressed as a proportion of the behaviours required of the child in that game, so the two are directly comparable within a child. The finding is that autistic children reliably do what they are asked and rarely do it unprompted, which the authors read as a specific deficit in automatic rather than intentional turn-taking. Two things make this valuable for the synthesis. It is a within-construct dissociation rather than a level difference, so it says something about the structure of the difficulty rather than only its presence - which almost no other included study attempts. And it identifies a measurement principle with wide application: a paradigm that separates prompted from unprompted performance can distinguish capacity from spontaneous deployment, a distinction that most behavioural measures in this corpus collapse. [RQ3.2] None. A single video stream coded by human raters, with the robot's own sensors unused for measurement. The paper's engineering framing points toward using them - it is explicitly gathering requirements for an 'interaction diagnosis system' - but no automated sensing is implemented here. [RQ4.1] None. No computational or machine-learning model is fitted. The analysis is a Wilcoxon signed-rank test on paired within-subject proportions, which is the correct choice for small-sample paired ordinal data and is used appropriately. For a review of computation-based approaches, the study sits immediately upstream of the modelling work: it establishes that a robot-delivered paradigm produces a measurable and theoretically interpretable behavioural dissociation, which is the finding that a subsequent automated system would need to reproduce. [RQ4.2] Proportions of required behaviours performed, computed separately for instructed and spontaneous conditions in each game. Normalising by the number of behaviours the game required of the child is the right construction, since it removes differences in game length and in how many opportunities each scenario afforded, and it makes the two conditions commensurable within a child. [RQ4.3] One inferential statistic - Wilcoxon signed-rank W = 21, p = 0.028 - and no diagnostic accuracy metric of any kind, which is appropriate given that no classification is attempted. What is missing is an effect size and a confidence interval, which on a small paired sample would have conveyed the magnitude of the dissociation rather than only its statistical detectability, and inter-rater reliability for the coding on which the statistic rests. [RQ4.4] Complete, because nothing is opaque: every value is a human rater's mark against a questionnaire item describing an observable behaviour. The interpretation offered is a psychological claim - a dissociation between automatic and intentional turn-taking - anchored to prior literature on automatic turn-taking deficits, rather than a statement about what a model responded to. [RQ4.5] Not applicable in the machine-learning sense; no model is fitted and no individual receives a predicted class. The design's validity rests instead on the paired within-subject comparison, and this is its principal strength: because each child's instructed-behaviour rate is compared against their own spontaneous-behaviour rate, general ability, motivation, familiarity with the robot, session-specific factors and rater leniency are all held constant across the two conditions. That is a genuine methodological advantage at pilot scale, and it is why a study with no comparison group and an unreported sample size can nonetheless support a specific and interpretable claim. Three limits bound it. No between-group inference is possible, which the authors state as their first limitation. Inter-rater reliability is not reported here, although the competent-raters technique is the measurement instrument and the group quantified it in the 2022 follow-up at Kendall's W = 0.65. And no effect size or confidence interval accompanies the test statistic, so the magnitude of the dissociation is not characterised. Set against the modelling studies in this review, the design illustrates a point worth carrying into the synthesis: a within-subject contrast can extract an interpretable finding from a sample far too small for any classifier, and several of the between-group studies charted here with comparable sample sizes would have been better served by the same approach. [RQ5.1] No formal keyword list appears in the retrieved text. Terms carried through the paper: human-robot interaction, social robot, NAO, turn-taking, automatic and intentional turn-taking, competent raters, theory of mind, mentalisation, user requirements, evaluation criteria. [RQ5.2] 2019 24th International Conference on Methods and Models in Automation and Robotics (MMAR), IEEE. A robotics and automation venue, and the paper is written for that audience - its second stated output is a set of user requirements and evaluation criteria for robot design, framed as an engineering deliverable rather than a clinical one. The venue explains both the paper's strengths, in its explicit treatment of the assessment problem as a joint psychology-engineering design task, and its omissions, since participant characteristics and diagnostic ascertainment would be expected in a clinical venue and are absent here. [RQ5.3] Presented in 2019 at an automation and robotics conference by a Polish collaboration between the Department of Cybernetics and Robotics at Wroclaw University of Science and Technology and the Research Unit for Cognitive and Applied Psychology at the University of Lower Silesia - the same group whose 2022 follow-up is charted separately in this review. The framing is distinctive: rather than presenting a method, the paper presents a stage in an interdisciplinary development process, arguing that diagnostic human-robot interaction 'implies the need of close cooperation between psychologists and engineers' and delivering both a psychological result and a set of engineering requirements as co-equal outputs. For the synthesis the study contributes three things. Its finding is a within-construct dissociation rather than a group difference: autistic children performed significantly more behaviours when instructed than spontaneously in imitation (W = 21, p = 0.028), which the authors read as a deficit in automatic rather than intentional turn-taking. That is a claim about the structure of the difficulty, and the measurement principle behind it - separating prompted from unprompted performance to distinguish capacity from spontaneous deployment - has wide application in a corpus where most behavioural measures collapse the two. Its design demonstrates that a paired within-subject contrast can extract an interpretable result from a sample far too small for any classifier, which several similarly sized between-group studies charted here might usefully have adopted. And its stated future direction identifies the field's hardest problem correctly: 'the especially challenging task is to differ autism from other similar disorders', with a commitment to observe robot interactions with children who have other developmental conditions. Almost no study in this review makes that commitment, and the one included study that does test autism against another clinical group found the field's gold-standard observational instrument achieving an AUC of 0.562 - which is the evidence that this priority is the right one. What the study cannot supply is any detection result: no comparison group, no model, no classification, no accuracy, an unreported sample size and no diagnostic ascertainment described.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Prospective cohort with case-control classification; 45 high-risk infants (mean 19.71 months, 40 male) recruited at a Nanjing child mental health clinic and followed to 24 months, where 40 were confirmed ASD by ADI-R, ADOS and DSM-5 and 5 were not, versus 43 typically developing infants (mean 16.40 months, 32 male); video of a two-episode still-face session, human-coded, no participant-level release.
narrative_rows.methods: Two-minute mother-infant free interaction followed by one minute of maternal still face, video-coded in Observer XT 12 by two trained graduate students (ICC 0.76-0.83) for duration and frequency of protest behaviour, non-social smiling, eye contact, social smiling and active social engagement; ten indicators showing significant group differences were fed to scikit-learn SVM, Gaussian naive Bayes and random forest classifiers, evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation over 83 samples and then applied to the 45 high-risk children.
narrative_rows.outcomes: SVM best in both episodes at 81.18% (free interaction) and 83.35% (still face); random forest 80.72% and 83.13%; naive Bayes 80.54% and 82.35%. The still-face episode beat free interaction for every algorithm, with the gain concentrated in specificity (83.7% versus 76.7%). Still-face behaviours correlated with CSBS-DP symptom severity while free-interaction behaviours did not. All five children who resolved off the spectrum were misclassified.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Feature selection by full-dataset t-tests outside the cross-validation loop; the verification cohort contains 40 of the model's own training cases so only 5 children were genuinely unseen; groups unmatched on age (p < 0.01) and on four of five developmental quotients, running parallel to the behavioural outcomes modelled; 11% female in the high-risk group; features human-coded rather than automatically sensed, leaving the throughput bottleneck the home-screening ambition would need to remove; reported accuracies do not reconcile exactly with the confusion matrices; no hyperparameters or code.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The corpus's clearest example of prospective outcome labelling in infancy - behaviour measured at 8-23 months, diagnosis confirmed at 24 by ADI-R and ADOS - which is a materially different evidential basis from the concurrent-label studies that dominate elsewhere. It is equally valuable as a negative result: the five children who presented as high-risk and then resolved were all misclassified, showing that high accuracy against typically developing controls says nothing about the discrimination that early screening actually requires. Its episode comparison also offers a counterpoint to the corpus's multimodal fusion studies, obtaining its gain by manipulating the elicitation condition rather than by adding a sensor.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups plus a prospectively emergent third. At enrolment: 45 high-risk infants and 43 typically developing infants, 88 in total, aged 8-23 months. At 24-month follow-up the high-risk group split into 40 confirmed ASD and 5 who no longer met criteria (N-ASD). Classification used the 40 confirmed ASD against the 43 TD. The N-ASD subgroup is the corpus's clearest instance of a genuine clinical comparison group - children who present as high-risk but do not go on to be diagnosed - and the study's inability to classify any of them is the most informative negative result in this record. [RQ1.2] 'infants and toddlers with high-risk autism spectrum disorder (HR)', 'children with ASD', 'infants and toddlers with ASD', 'typical development (TD)', 'infants and toddlers with TD'. Person-first throughout, with 'typical development' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy'. Disorder-framed language dominates ('a serious neurodevelopmental disorder', 'social communication barriers'), and the discussion invokes the extreme male brain theory and the intense world theory as explanatory frames. [RQ1.3] High-risk: n = 45, 40 male / 5 female (11% female), mean age 19.71 +/- 3.43 months. Typically developing: n = 43, 32 male / 11 female (26% female), mean age 16.40 +/- 4.70 months. The age difference is significant (t = 3.80, p < 0.01) and is the authors' first stated limitation, with the explicit rationale that matching on age would unmatch developmental level. Gesell developmental quotients differ significantly on adaptive (80.29 vs 92.98), fine motor (86.64 vs 93.70), language (60.84 vs 86.51) and personal-social (78.80 vs 92.28) domains; only gross motor is comparable (92.02 vs 92.77). Sex distributions were nominally matched by design with a non-significant chi-square (p = 0.08) but differ visibly. All participants are from the Nanjing area of China, with no ethnicity or socioeconomic reporting. [RQ1.4] The strongest ascertainment in the corpus's infant-screening strand, because it is prospective rather than concurrent. Entry to the high-risk group required a positive M-CHAT plus a pediatric psychiatrist's judgement that the child met DSM-5 core criteria while under 24 months. At 2 years every high-risk child was re-evaluated with both the ADI-R and the ADOS, and clinically diagnosed by two pediatric psychiatrists against DSM-5; all confirmed cases reached cut-off on both instruments. Exclusions removed Rett syndrome, fragile X, isolated language disorder, intellectual disability, craniocerebral trauma and neurological illness. Typically developing status rests on exclusion criteria plus Gesell assessment rather than a positive screen. [RQ1.5] Comprehensive by corpus standards. Gesell Developmental Scale developmental quotients across five domains (adaptive, gross motor, fine motor, language, personal-social) for all participants; CSBS-DP with three factor scores and total, CARS, and ABC for symptom severity in the high-risk group. All were used analytically - correlated against behavioural indicators - not merely tabulated. The requirement that the mother be the primary caregiver is also a stated inclusion criterion for both groups, controlling a variable that matters for a mother-infant interaction paradigm. [RQ2.1] Goal: determine whether still-face paradigm social behaviours differ before 24 months and whether machine learning on them can screen for autism prospectively. Main findings: high-risk infants showed less eye contact, social smiling and active social engagement in free interaction, and less eye contact and active social engagement under the maternal still face; negative-emotion behaviours did not differ; SVM reached 83.35% for the still-face episode and 81.18% for free interaction, with the still-face episode superior for all three algorithms; still-face behaviours correlated with CSBS-DP symptom severity while free-interaction behaviours did not; and the model misclassified all five children who resolved off the spectrum. [RQ2.2] Outpatient clinic of the Child Mental Health Research Center, Nanjing Brain Hospital Affiliated to Nanjing Medical University, with typically developing controls recruited from the Nanjing area over the same period (December 2017 onward). Prospectively registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry as ChiCTR-OPC-17011995. [RQ2.3] A two-episode still-face paradigm: 2 minutes of normal mother-infant interaction under fixed instructions, then 1 minute in which the mother holds a neutral, unresponsive face. The classic reunion episode was omitted, following the common two-episode variant. The design logic is that the still-face episode manufactures a controlled social challenge - all of the mother's social signals vanish at once - and the paper's central empirical claim is that this challenge is more diagnostically informative than ordinary interaction, since the SF episode beat the FF episode for every classifier and only SF behaviours correlated with symptom severity. [RQ2.4] Prospective longitudinal in the essential respect: behavioural measurement at 8-23 months, diagnostic outcome at 24 months. The behavioural measurement itself is a single cross-sectional session. Data are video of identifiable infants with their mothers - among the most sensitive material in the corpus. Governance is correspondingly well reported: named ethics approval (2017-KY089-01), written guardian consent, specific consent for publication of potentially identifiable images or data, and prospective trial registration. [RQ2.5] Video recording in a designated observation room; The Observer XT 12 behavioural observation and coding system; Python with scikit-learn (SVC, GaussianNB, RandomForestClassifier). Clinical instrumentation: M-CHAT, Gesell Developmental Scale, CSBS-DP, CARS, ABC, ADI-R, ADOS. No custom hardware and no automated behavioural sensing. [RQ2.6] Above corpus average. A data availability statement exists, trial registration is prospective, ethics approval is named with its reference number, inter-coder reliability is quantified per behaviour, the behavioural coding definitions are stated in full, the classifier library and functions are named, and the validation scheme is described precisely enough to reproduce. What is missing: hyperparameters (SVM kernel and C, forest size), any code release, participant-level data despite the availability statement, and reconciliation between the headline accuracies and the confusion matrix. [RQ2.7] Two limitations are stated: the groups could not be age-matched because autistic children generally have delayed development, so matching on age would unmatch developmental level; and the sample was small. The N-ASD failure is discussed candidly - 'the 5 N-ASD was not classified correctly', attributed to class imbalance and to only ten indicators per sample, with identifying N-ASD from ASD named as a goal for future work. The contrary finding on negative emotion is also flagged as needing further validation. Identifiable in review but not acknowledged: the verification step is largely circular, since 40 of the 45 high-risk children used to verify the SVM were in its training set; the age gap coincides with significant differences in four of five developmental quotients, so group separation may partly reflect developmental level rather than autism; features were selected by group-difference t-tests computed on the full dataset before cross-validation, which leaks label information into the feature set; and the reported accuracies do not exactly match the tabulated confusion matrices. [RQ2.9] Expand the sample, especially the N-ASD group, to verify the model on children who resolve off the spectrum; make identifying N-ASD from ASD an explicit objective; develop more effective machine-learning models; repeat the analysis under controlled physiological and psychological ages to address the age-matching problem; and develop the still-face paradigm into a convenient, objective and standardised self-screening mode usable at home. [RQ3.1] Dyadic social-interaction behaviour: eye contact, social smiling, non-social smiling, protest behaviour and active social engagement, each measured as both duration and frequency. Uniquely in the corpus, behaviour is measured relationally - against a caregiver whose responsiveness is experimentally manipulated - rather than as a property of the child alone, and the manipulation is what generates the discriminative signal. [RQ3.2] No multimodal fusion. All features come from a single modality (video-coded social behaviour). The study's structural comparison is instead across conditions of the same modality: the still-face episode versus the free-interaction episode, and the still-face episode won for every classifier (83.35 vs 81.18 for SVM, 83.13 vs 80.72 for random forest, 82.35 vs 80.54 for naive Bayes). This is a useful counterpoint to the corpus's fusion studies - here the gain comes from choosing a better elicitation condition rather than adding a sensor. [RQ4.1] Three classical supervised classifiers compared on identical tabular features: support vector machine, Gaussian naive Bayes and random forest, all from scikit-learn. No deep learning, which is appropriate at n = 83 with 10 features. The three algorithms perform within about three percentage points of each other, which is itself informative: with this feature set the choice of classifier matters far less than the choice of elicitation episode. [RQ4.2] Ten hand-defined behavioural statistics per child: duration and frequency of eye contact, active social engagement and social smiling in the FF episode, and duration and frequency of eye contact and active social engagement in the SF episode. All are produced by human coders in Observer XT 12, not by automated sensing - so the representation is interpretable and clinically legible, but the pipeline is not automatable and the home self-screening application the paper envisages would require replacing this stage entirely. [RQ4.3] Overall accuracy per algorithm per episode, plus an SVM confusion matrix. Deriving from the matrix: SF episode sensitivity 85.0% and specificity 83.7%; FF episode sensitivity 87.5% and specificity 76.7%, so the still-face episode's advantage lies in specificity. No AUC, precision, recall or F1 is reported directly, although the paper does discuss 'low recall rate of N-ASD samples'. Accuracy is additionally stratified across four age bands to test whether misclassification clusters by age; no regularity was found. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is inherent rather than post hoc: the features are named clinical behaviours, so the model operates on quantities a clinician already reasons about. Interpretation is supported by two separate analyses rather than by a model-explanation method - t-tests establishing which behaviours differ and in which episode, and Pearson correlations linking still-face behaviours to CSBS-DP symptom severity. The substantive interpretation is that the still-face episode's social challenge exposes communication impairment more sharply than ordinary interaction, evidenced by the SF episode both classifying better and being the only episode whose behaviours correlate with symptom severity. No feature importances, coefficients or ablations are reported. [RQ4.5] Leave-one-out cross-validation over 83 samples, then an attempted verification on the 45 high-risk children. The verification is where the design breaks down: 40 of those 45 are the confirmed-ASD children the model trained on, so only the 5 N-ASD cases are genuinely unseen - and all 5 were misclassified. There is a further subtler problem: the ten features were chosen because t-tests on the full dataset showed them to differ significantly between groups, so feature selection preceded and stood outside the cross-validation loop, leaking label information into every fold. No independent site, no held-out cohort, no calibration analysis, and no comparison against the M-CHAT baseline that all high-risk children had already passed. [RQ5.1] Keywords: high-risk autism spectrum disorder; the Still-Face Paradigm; social behavior; machine learning; model for early screening. The vocabulary is developmental-psychology first and computational second - 'social behavior', 'emotion regulation', 'social expectations', 'infant-mother interaction' - with machine learning entering as a screening instrument rather than as the object of study. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Pediatrics (Child and Adolescent Psychiatry section) - a clinical pediatrics venue, not a computational one, which matches the paper's weighting toward the behavioural and diagnostic findings over the modelling. [RQ5.3] 2020. The framing is the diagnostic delay gap: autism can currently be diagnosed at 2 years but 'age at ASD diagnosis is still 40 months or even later', and Chinese prevalence estimates rose from 0.07% to 1.8%. The authors position video-based behavioural coding as the objective alternative to the retrospective parent interviews and rating scales that dominated earlier work, which they characterise as 'highly subjective and unfavorable for widespread promotion'. They also note that machine-learning screening had by then reached over 80% accuracy using EEG and brain imaging, and argue that combining social behavioural indicators with biological indicators is the necessary next step - positioning this paper as supplying the behavioural half of that combination.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control with a pre-specified independent hold-out sample; 22 autistic and 22 non-autistic UK adults split into a development set (15 vs 15, mean age ~33, mean IQ ~123) and an independent test set (7 vs 7, mean age ~28, mean IQ ~124), matched within samples for age, gender, handedness and IQ; motion and eye tracking from a movement imitation task, not released.
narrative_rows.methods: Participants watched and imitated hand movement sequences under three style conditions (elevated, fast-direct, direct) and two instruction blocks; 20 kinematic parameters as means and SDs per condition plus 24 gaze means and SDs per block; SVM-RBF classifier held constant while four feature selectors (t-test, SVM-RFE, ReliefF, mRMR) and three developed variants (ensemble, bagging, wrapped t-test) were compared on accuracy and Kuncheva's index; nested cross-validation with selection inside each of ten folds at development, then application to the independent hold-out sample.
narrative_rows.outcomes: 73% accuracy from kinematic features, 70% from eye movement features, 78% from combined features. Development and independent-test accuracies were comparable throughout, demonstrating that nested cross-validation controlled overfitting despite a 20% versus 57% female difference between samples. The general instruction block outperformed the attention block for all data types. Seven of ten selected kinematic features came from the elevated-amplitude condition, where autistic adults imitated with lower vertical amplitude and earlier peak acceleration.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No diagnostic instrument, criteria or ethics statement appears anywhere in this paper, all deferred to a prior protocol publication; 44 adults total with a 14-participant test set, so 78% is roughly 11 of 14 correct; both samples are high-IQ (means 122-126) adults; several hundred features against 30 development participants; the headline is the best across several feature-selection variants; no external validation on a different site or protocol; sensitivity and specificity not reported.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The corpus's definitive demonstration that nested validation generalises. Where the same first author's 2019 paper argued that prior kinematic studies' 86.7-96.7% figures reflected K-fold cross-validation on small samples, this study develops models under nested cross-validation and then tests them on a genuinely independent hold-out sample, showing development and test accuracies to be comparable - and the result holds across a substantial sex-composition shift between samples. It also provides the corpus's cleanest quantified multimodal fusion benefit (73% and 70% singly, 78% combined) obtained under independent testing rather than internal cross-validation, and treats feature-selection stability as a reported outcome in its own right.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups totalling 44 adults, split across two independently constituted samples: a development sample of 15 autistic and 15 non-autistic adults, and a hold-out testing sample of 7 autistic and 7 non-autistic adults, each internally matched. Having a pre-specified independent test sample rather than only cross-validation folds is rare in this corpus. No other-diagnosis comparison group. [RQ1.2] 'autistic adults', 'autistic individuals', 'non-autistic adults', 'non-autistic individuals', 'individuals living with autism'. Consistently identity-first and paired with 'non-autistic' rather than 'healthy', 'normal' or 'typically developing' - among the most neurodiversity-aligned terminology in the corpus, consistent with the same Manchester group's other entries here. [RQ1.3] Development sample: 15 autistic (3 female, 12 male), mean age 33.1, mean IQ 122.0; 15 non-autistic (3 female, 12 male), mean age 32.2, mean IQ 124.8. Age p = 0.73, IQ p = 0.51. Independent test sample: 7 autistic (4 female, 3 male), mean age 28.16, mean IQ 122.14; 7 non-autistic (4 female, 3 male), mean age 27.90, mean IQ 126.29. Age p = 0.95, IQ p = 0.46. Groups are matched for age, gender, handedness and IQ within each sample, with all comparisons tested and reported - unusually thorough. The two samples differ in sex composition (20% female in development versus 57% in testing) and marginally in age (p = 0.06), which the authors flag explicitly and turn into a strength: generalisation held despite the demographic shift. Both samples are high-IQ (means 122-126) adults, which bounds the population addressed. [RQ1.4] Not described in this paper. The experimental protocol, stimuli and by implication the diagnostic ascertainment are referred to a prior publication by Gowen et al. This is the study's principal reporting gap - as with the same group's 2019 paper, the diagnostic basis for the class labels is not stated in the analysis paper itself. [RQ1.5] IQ is reported for all four subgroups and used as a matching variable with statistical verification, and handedness is also matched. No language, adaptive-functioning or autism-severity measures are reported, and no comorbidity information. IQ means of 122-126 indicate a sample well above population average. [RQ2.1] Goal: predict autism diagnosis from imitation kinematics and gaze, with methodological reliability as the explicit primary focus. Main findings: 73% accuracy from kinematics, 70% from eye movements, 78% from combined features; development and independent-test accuracies comparable, demonstrating that nested cross-validation controlled overfitting; the general instruction block outperformed the attention instruction block across all data types; t-test feature selection outperformed SVM-RFE, ReliefF and mRMR on both accuracy and stability; and seven of ten selected kinematic features came from the elevated-amplitude condition, where autistic adults imitated with lower vertical amplitude and earlier peak acceleration. [RQ2.2] Laboratory setting at a UK university. The data come from an experimental protocol previously published by the same group, so this is a machine-learning analysis of an existing behavioural dataset rather than a new collection. [RQ2.3] Movement imitation with style manipulation: participants watched a video of a hand movement sequence pointing between four locations and then imitated it, with only movements between two designated locations analysed. Three movement styles were used - elevated amplitude, fast-direct, and direct - crossed with two instruction blocks, a general instruction block and an attention instruction block that directed attention to movement style. The elevated condition is the theoretically critical one, since imitating an unusually elevated trajectory requires adopting a movement style outside one's habitual repertoire. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single session with no follow-up. Data are numeric kinematic and gaze traces, not identifiable media. Ethics and consent details are not restated in this paper, being referred to the source protocol publication - a reporting gap even if the underlying governance was presumably adequate. [RQ2.5] Hardware: motion tracking and eye tracking apparatus, with specific models deferred to the source protocol publication; a screen for video stimulus presentation. Software: implementations of SVM-RBF, four feature selection algorithms, nested cross-validation, and the authors' novel bagging and wrapped t-test variants; Kuncheva's index for stability quantification. [RQ2.6] No data or code release stated. Method reporting is strong on the analytic side - the full 20-parameter kinematic definition list, the feature structure across conditions and blocks, the four baseline selectors, the three developed variants with their operating rules (100 subsamples of size n/2 for bagging; t-statistic adjustment up or down at a 50% accuracy threshold with termination at Kuncheva's index of 1 across 100 consecutive iterations for the wrapped t-test), the nested cross-validation structure with feature selection inside each of ten folds, and the classifier. Weak on the experimental side, where apparatus, protocol details and diagnostic ascertainment are all deferred to a prior publication. [RQ2.7] The paper's framing is itself a critique of prior work's limitations rather than only its own. On the field: prior kinematic ML studies 'had small sample sizes and achieved high classification accuracy', but 'models developed with small sample/high dimensional data are prone to fit noise and not necessarily an underlying pattern separating classes', and those studies 'did not avoid pooling training and validation data while developing their ML models and did not take other steps to control for the fitting of random noise', were 'not tested with independent data', and did not assess statistical significance. On their own work they acknowledge the difficulty of small-sample high-dimensional pattern recognition requiring careful handling of both validation and feature selection. Identifiable in review: 44 adults total with a 14-participant test set means 78% is roughly 11 of 14 correct; the diagnostic ascertainment is entirely absent from this paper; both samples are high-IQ adults; the reported headline is the best across several feature-selection variants; and the marked sex-composition difference between samples, while turned into a generalisation argument, also means the independent test provides limited evidence about performance in a comparably composed sample. [RQ2.9] Not set out as a discrete future-work section in the extracted text. The introduction's framing implies the priority - the paper notes that adult diagnostic instruments 'have only been validated for use with children', that with adults 'clinicians rarely rely on standardised diagnostic methods making diagnosis less accurate, more subjective and lengthier', and that researching adult diagnostic criteria is listed among the top ten priorities by a UK autism research charity. The work positions itself as contributing quantitative tests to supplement current qualitative ones in that under-served context. [RQ3.1] Two modalities: hand movement kinematics (velocity, acceleration, deceleration profiles with their timings, amplitudes, jerk) and eye movement behaviour during the same imitation task. Measuring gaze and movement concurrently during imitation is distinctive - it captures both what the participant looked at while observing the model and how they subsequently moved. [RQ3.2] Explicit multimodal fusion with quantified benefit: kinematic features alone gave 73%, eye movement features alone 70%, and combined features 78%. The authors state that the modalities 'provided complementary information for predictions', and the 5-point gain over the better single modality is one of the clearest quantified fusion benefits in the corpus, obtained under independent testing rather than internal cross-validation. Features are combined at feature level before selection and classification. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning with SVM-RBF as the fixed classifier, so that the experimental variable is feature selection rather than model family. Four established selectors are benchmarked (t-test filter, SVM-RFE, ReliefF, mRMR) and three variants developed (ensemble, bagging, wrapped t-test). Holding the classifier constant while varying selection is a clean design that isolates the contribution the paper is actually studying. [RQ4.2] Handcrafted kinematic and gaze summary features, structured hierarchically: 20 kinematic parameters computed as means and standard deviations for each of three movement conditions within each of two instruction blocks, plus 24 gaze means and 24 gaze standard deviations per block. This produces a feature space far larger than the 30-participant development sample, which is precisely the small-sample high-dimensional regime the paper's methodology is designed to handle. [RQ4.3] Classification accuracy at both development and independent-testing stages, reported side by side per algorithm and per instruction block - the side-by-side presentation is what makes the generalisation claim checkable. Kuncheva's index quantifies feature selection stability as a second reported outcome, treated as co-equal with accuracy. Statistical significance p-values accompany the accuracies, and accuracy distributions are shown as box plots. No sensitivity, specificity or AUC. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is pursued as an explicit design goal rather than a by-product: feature selection methods were chosen and developed 'aimed at selection stability to assure result interpretability', and the wrapped t-test runs until it converges on an identical feature set across 100 consecutive iterations. The resulting stable ten-feature set supports a specific behavioural interpretation - seven of ten features come from the elevated-amplitude condition, where autistic adults produced lower vertical amplitude and consequently earlier peak acceleration, indicating a failure to adopt the model's unusual movement style rather than a general motor difference. This is corroborated by conventional parametric tests showing significant group differences in the same condition. [RQ4.5] The strongest validation design in the corpus. Nested cross-validation at development, with feature selection performed inside each of ten nested folds; then a genuinely independent hold-out sample of 14 participants who took no part in development; then direct comparison of development and testing accuracies to verify that nesting controlled overfitting. Statistical significance is assessed. Feature selection stability is quantified with Kuncheva's index. The generalisation claim is additionally stress-tested by the incidental fact that the two samples differ substantially in sex composition, so the independent result holds across a demographic shift. What remains absent: external validation on a different site or protocol, sensitivity and specificity, and any deployment analysis. [RQ5.1] No formal keyword list in the extracted text. Vocabulary: 'reliable machine learning application', 'nested validation', 'selection stability', 'independent data sample', 'Kuncheva's index', 'quantitative tests to supplement current qualitative ones'. The methodological-reliability vocabulary dominates and is the paper's identity. [RQ5.2] Scientific Reports (Nature Portfolio) - a broad multidisciplinary journal, neither autism-specific nor computational. [RQ5.3] 2020. The paper gives one of the corpus's sharpest field characterisations. On the clinical problem: UK average waiting time between initial concerns and clinical diagnosis exceeds three years, adult diagnostic instruments 'have only been validated for use with children', and adult diagnosis is 'less accurate, more subjective and lengthier'. On the methodological problem: 'only a handful of ML studies used kinematic data for autism prediction. All studies had small sample sizes and achieved high classification accuracy', but such models 'are prone to fit noise', and to the authors' knowledge those studies 'did not avoid pooling training and validation data', were not tested with independent data, and did not assess statistical significance. This paper is the corrective demonstration that follows from that diagnosis.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Systems development paper with a 20-child validation test; 10 autistic children aged 3-6 from Guangzhou Children's Care Center and 10 typically developing children aged 5-8 from a Zhengzhou education school; expression models trained on FER2013 and CK+ plus 112 images from 16 typically developing Chinese children, none released.
narrative_rows.methods: A client-server system prompts a child by picture and sound to imitate one of seven facial expressions three times, with cartoon and song aids; the client detects and transmits the face, and the server preprocesses, classifies via VGG-19 and ResNet-18, and compares the predicted expression against the prompt. Per-child recognition rate over seven expressions is compared against a 60% threshold to indicate a tendency toward autism.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Mean recognition rate 81.4% in typically developing children and 34.3% in autistic children; the 60% threshold separates all ten autistic children from eight of ten controls, with two controls at 57.1%. Errors in controls concentrated on disgust and surprise; in the autistic group happy and sad were best recognised, neutral and disgust worst. No sensitivity, specificity or statistical test reported.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No model is trained on autism labels - diagnosis is a threshold on a proxy task, so measurement failure cannot be distinguished from clinical signal; the threshold is fitted to the same twenty children it is evaluated on; groups differ in age (3-6 versus 5-8) and are fully confounded with recruitment site; supplementary training images came from the control group's own population; diagnosis reported only as by 'a professional physician' and control status by parent report; no ethics approval, written consent or anonymization reported for children's facial images; no training details, split, cross-validation, code or data; conclusions of worldwide applicability rest on twenty children.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The corpus's clearest case of the deployment-first strand: detailed system architecture, hospital workflow analysis, an explicit sub-5-second response requirement, and access arguments about remote and underdeveloped areas, paired with essentially no validation. It also documents a failure mode the review should name explicitly - substituting a proxy task's performance for a diagnostic outcome, so that a classifier's inability to recognise a child's face is read as evidence about the child. Its scale-item analysis (mapping CABS, ABC and CARS items to facial expression) is a genuinely useful piece of clinical-requirements work that the rest of the corpus rarely attempts.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups of ten: 10 autistic children aged 3-6 from Guangzhou Children's Care Center and 10 typically developing children aged 5-8 from Amy Education School in Zhengzhou. A separate group of 16 typically developing Chinese children aged 5-8 (8 boys, 8 girls) supplied 112 training images. No other-diagnosis comparison group. At 20 evaluation participants this is among the smallest clinical evaluations in the corpus, and it is a system test rather than a model validation. [RQ1.2] 'autistic children', 'normal children', 'autistic patients', 'children with autism', 'healthy children volunteers'. The autistic/normal contrast is used throughout, and disease framing is explicit - autism is described as 'a representative disease of generalized developmental disorders' undergoing 'a transition from rare diseases to epidemics', with extensive discussion of the financial and psychological burden on families and society. This is the most pathologising vocabulary in the corpus, standing at the opposite end from the identity-first, non-autistic-comparison usage of the Manchester kinematics papers. [RQ1.3] Autistic group: 10 children, 5 boys and 5 girls, aged 3-6, recruited through Guangzhou Children's Care Center. Control group: 10 children, 5 boys and 5 girls, aged 5-8, recruited through Amy Education School in Zhengzhou. Sex is balanced within and across groups, which is unusual for this corpus. Age is not: the ranges barely overlap and the autistic children are systematically younger, which matters because facial expression production, imitation compliance and attention to a screen prompt all change substantially between 3 and 8 years. Recruitment site is fully confounded with group. No means, standard deviations, IQ, developmental level, ethnicity or socioeconomic information is reported for either group. [RQ1.4] One sentence: 'The selected children with autism were diagnosed by a professional physician.' No instrument, criteria, date or diagnostician detail. The paper describes ICD-10, DSM-IV, ABC, CARS and CABS as the instruments the collaborating hospitals use, and analyses their facial-expression-related items in detail to motivate the design, but does not state which if any were applied to these ten children. Typically developing status rests entirely on parents answering that their child had no history of autism. [RQ1.5] None. No IQ, developmental quotient, language, adaptive functioning, symptom severity or comorbidity measure is reported for either group. Severity grading is named only as future work. [RQ2.1] Goal: build a deployable hospital information system that diagnoses autism from facial expression imitation using deep CNNs, reducing subjectivity and physician time and extending early diagnosis to underserved regions. Main findings: mean expression recognition rate of 81.4% in typically developing children versus 34.3% in autistic children; a proposed 60% threshold below which a child is said to show a tendency toward autism; recognition errors in typically developing children concentrated on disgust and surprise; and in autistic children happy and sad were best recognised while neutral and disgust were worst. [RQ2.2] Testing was conducted in quiet classrooms at two cooperating institutions - Amy Education School in Zhengzhou for the typically developing group and Guangzhou Children's Care Center for the autistic group. System requirements were developed through repeated consultation with physicians at Hubei Maternal and Child Health Hospital, Wuhan Children's Hospital and Guangzhou Women and Children's Medical Center, including direct observation of how they administer the diagnostic scales. [RQ2.3] Prompted facial expression imitation. The system randomly displays one of seven expressions (angry, disgust, fear, happy, sad, surprise, neutral) and prompts the child by picture and sound to reproduce it, presenting the same expression three times, with elicitation aids such as cartoon smiling faces, children's songs and animations for situational simulation. The design is explicitly modelled on how physicians administer the diagnostic scales - 'The doctor observes the tester's reaction to determine whether the tester is autistic after requesting the tester to make the corresponding expression' - and the paper justifies the choice by itemising the expression-related items in the CABS, ABC and CARS scales. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single session per child with no follow-up. Data are facial images of identifiable children including a clinically diagnosed group, stored server-side in a SQL Server database and with collection photographs reproduced in the paper. Governance reporting is the weakest in the corpus: parents were informed of the purpose of data collection, but no ethics committee approval, no written consent procedure, no anonymization and no retention or access policy is described - which is a serious omission for a system whose stated deployment path is public download by app or web page. [RQ2.5] High-definition cameras; client applications for computers and smartphones; a four-layer architecture (application, communication, application server with firewall, database server); SQL Server; HDF5 feature files; JSON over TCP; VGG-19 and ResNet-18. Public training corpora: FER2013 (35,887 images at 48x48, seven expressions) and CK+ (593 sequences from 123 people at 640x480, 69% female, including African American, Asian and South American subjects). A specified non-functional requirement - end-to-end response under 5 seconds - is one of the few deployment constraints stated anywhere in this corpus. [RQ2.6] Poor. The system architecture, network topology, module decomposition, data formats and interface flow are described in detail, but nothing needed to reproduce the machine learning is given: no training procedure, no train/validation/test split, no hyperparameters, no epochs, no augmentation, no accuracy on the source expression datasets, and no description of how the VGG-19 and ResNet-18 outputs were 'synthesised'. No code and no data are released. The clinical evaluation reports per-child recognition rates in full, which is welcome, but no statistical test accompanies them. [RQ2.7] The authors acknowledge that the algorithm 'is affected by the environment and light' and that accuracy suffers accordingly, noting that two typically developing children scored 57.1%; that errors concentrate on disgust and surprise because those expressions involve only minor local facial change and some participants produced them weakly; and that more real samples are needed. They do not acknowledge the design's central problems. No model is trained on autism labels, so a proxy task's failure rate is being treated as a diagnostic signal, and the design cannot separate non-imitation, atypical imitation, developmental immaturity and out-of-distribution faces from autism. The groups differ in age (3-6 versus 5-8) and are fully confounded with recruitment site. The supplementary training images came from typically developing 5-8 year olds, the control group's own population, which biases the classifier toward recognising control-group faces. The 60% threshold is fitted to the same 20 children it is evaluated on. And the abstract's 81.4% is the expression recognition rate in typically developing children, not a diagnostic accuracy, yet is presented as 'the accuracy of facial expression recognition of this system'. [RQ2.9] Test the system in a large number of cooperating hospitals; collect far more facial expression data from both typically developing and autistic children and build a dedicated children's facial expression database, since existing databases are built mainly from adults and children have rounder faces, larger eyes and less prominent bones that make their features harder to recognise; extend the system to recognise physical movement so autism can be assessed from multiple perspectives; and add severity grading into severe, moderate and mild. [RQ3.1] A single modality - facial expression, captured as still images during prompted imitation of seven categories (angry, disgust, fear, happy, sad, surprise, neutral). The behaviour targeted is expression production on demand rather than spontaneous expression or expression recognition ability, although the paper's motivating literature concerns autistic people's difficulty recognising others' expressions, which is a different construct from the one measured. [RQ3.2] No multimodal fusion. Adding recognition of children's physical movement to achieve 'diagnosis of autism from multiple perspectives' is named as future work. There is a nominal model-level combination - VGG-19 and ResNet-18 are said to be trained and then 'synthesised' - but no mechanism, weighting or comparative result is given for either model separately, so the combination cannot be evaluated. [RQ4.1] Deep supervised learning: VGG-19 and ResNet-18 convolutional neural networks for seven-way facial expression classification. The paper argues explicitly for deep over traditional approaches, on the grounds that handcrafted features (oriented gradient histograms, Gabor filters, local directional patterns, enhanced local binary patterns) are 'artificial design, time-consuming and laborious' and work well only on small image sets, whereas end-to-end deep models combine feature extraction and classification. Critically, neither network is trained on an autism label - the diagnostic layer is a hand-set threshold on classification agreement, not a learned model. [RQ4.2] Raw facial images processed end-to-end, with learned convolutional features persisted as HDF5 feature files for reuse and incremental retraining. Training data are FER2013 (35,887 low-resolution 48x48 images), CK+ (593 sequences from 123 people at 640x480), and 112 images from 16 Chinese children aged 5-8. The mismatch between the training distribution - largely adult, largely posed, mostly non-Chinese - and the target population of 3-6 year old autistic children is the input-representation problem the paper's supplementary collection was meant to address but at 112 images cannot. [RQ4.3] Only recognition rate: the proportion of seven prompted expressions the classifier assigned to the prompted category, reported per expression, per child and per group. No sensitivity, specificity, AUC, precision, recall, F1, confusion matrix or statistical test. Because the threshold rule reduces to a binary decision on 20 children, sensitivity of 10/10 and specificity of 8/10 could be derived, but the paper does not do so and the threshold was chosen on these same data. [RQ4.4] No interpretability method - no saliency maps, no attention visualisation, no feature attribution. What the system exposes instead is a per-expression probability histogram shown to the user, with the maximum-probability bar taken as the prediction, and a per-expression breakdown of which categories failed. This is interface transparency rather than model interpretability: it shows what the model decided, not why. The clinical interpretation offered - that autistic children have facial expression recognition obstacles, so their expressions are harder to classify - is asserted from the prior literature rather than derived from the model. [RQ4.5] The weakest validation in the corpus. No train/validation/test split, no cross-validation, no held-out set, and no reported performance on the source expression datasets. The clinical evaluation is a single pass over 20 children whose groups differ in age and recruitment site, with the decision threshold fitted to those same 20 results. There is no independent sample, no external site, no repeat measurement, and no comparison against the diagnostic scales the system is meant to support - which is notable given the paper analyses those scales item by item to justify its design but never compares its output against them. [RQ5.1] No formal keyword list. Vocabulary: 'autism smart diagnosis information system', 'deep convolution neural network', 'facial expression recognition', 'system architecture', 'network topology', 'social benefits and application value'. The register is information-systems and deployment-oriented rather than clinical or statistical - the paper's own framing is that it addresses 'the actual business needs of the hospital'. [RQ5.2] Proceedings of the 53rd Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS) - an information-systems conference, not a clinical or machine-learning venue, which explains the weighting toward architecture, workflow and deployment over validation. Published under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 with a stable handle. [RQ5.3] 2020. The framing is epidemiological and economic rather than methodological: prevalence rising from 3-5 per 10,000 in the 1980s to 2.76% among US children aged 3-14 by 2016; an estimated 10 million people with autism in China including 2 million children, growing by nearly 200,000 annually, with no national statistical survey; 33% of parents reporting that caregiving seriously affected their careers with an average annual income loss of 30,957 yuan. Against that, the paper identifies the bottleneck as clinical throughput and subjectivity - one to two hours per diagnosis, results 'easily disturbed by external factors such as hospital level, physician's subjective level, patient's education level, age' - and positions an app-deliverable CNN system as the answer, with explicit emphasis on remote and underdeveloped areas. The paper is a clear marker of the corpus's deployment-first strand, in which access and cost arguments substitute for validation.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control; 25 children with ASD (14 female, mean age 6.9) and 25 age-matched typically developing children (10 female, mean age 7.2), aged 5-12, in a US biomechanics laboratory; force-plate centre-of-pressure data from three 20-second quiet-stance trials per visual condition, not released.
narrative_rows.methods: Barefoot quiet standing for 20 seconds with eyes open and eyes closed in randomised order, three acceptable trials each, on a Kistler force plate at 60 Hz filtered at 10 Hz; six COP variables computed per condition (mediolateral and anteroposterior displacement, total path distance, 95% ellipse sway area, and mediolateral and anteroposterior sample entropy) giving 12 features; mixed-model ANOVA for group differences; six classifiers (discriminant analysis, k-nearest neighbour, naive Bayes, decision trees, SVM, random forest) under five-fold cross-validation in MATLAB.
narrative_rows.outcomes: All six classifiers exceeded 0.800 accuracy. Naive Bayes best at 0.900 accuracy, 1.000 specificity, 1.000 precision, 0.898 F1, 0.826 sensitivity; k-nearest neighbour second at 0.860. ANOVA showed significantly greater displacement, path distance and sway area in ASD under both conditions with no interaction, and no group difference in sample entropy.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: n=50 means 0.900 accuracy is about 45 of 50 children and the exact 1.000 specificity reflects zero false positives among 25 controls, with no confidence intervals; the headline is the best of six algorithms on the same cross-validation folds without nested selection; no diagnostic instrument named and controls unscreened; ASD inclusion required ability to understand instructions and perform the task, restricting the sample to more able children; sex unmatched; no external validation; no limitations section.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The corpus's only static postural-control study and one of its cleanest small-sample designs - participant-level folds by construction, twelve features against fifty children, five metrics with formulas and confusion matrices, formal outlier checking and an a priori power analysis. It is also one of very few studies here where autistic girls are well represented (14 of 25). Its most informative result is negative: sample entropy complexity did not distinguish the groups despite prior reports, so the discriminative signal is sway magnitude alone.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups of 25: children with ASD and age-matched typically developing children, total 50. Both groups are characterised in a demographic table with sample size, sex breakdown, body mass, height and age. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though neurological disorders other than ASD were an explicit exclusion for both groups. [RQ1.2] 'children with autism spectrum disorder', 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'autistic postural control patterns', 'typically developing children', 'children with typical development', 'healthy controls'. Predominantly person-first with 'typically developing' used consistently for the comparison group, though 'healthy controls' appears once. The paper's framing is biomechanical rather than pathologising. [RQ1.3] ASD n=25 (14 female, 11 male), age 6.9 (1.8) years, body mass 32.7 (11.5) kg, height 126 (13) cm. TD n=25 (10 female, 15 male), age 7.2 (2.0) years, body mass 30.3 (12.4) kg, height 128 (12) cm. Recruitment range 5-12 years. Groups are explicitly age-matched with near-identical means and overlapping standard deviations, and anthropometrics are reported and closely comparable - which matters for postural measures since body mass and height affect sway. Sex is not matched, with the ASD group 56% female against 40% in controls, but both proportions are far higher than the corpus norm, making this one of very few studies here where autistic girls are well represented. Sample size is justified by an a priori power analysis (power 0.80) against previously published postural sway data, indicating 10-13 per group would suffice for the group comparison, with the larger n=25 chosen because 'a larger sample size will improve the accuracy and success of machine learning classifiers'. [RQ1.4] A prior diagnosis of ASD by a physician or a licensed psychologist was an inclusion criterion, but no diagnostic instrument, criteria or confirmation procedure is described, and no autism-trait screening was applied to controls. Two further inclusion requirements - the ability to understand and communicate with examiners and the ability to perform the required tasks - restrict the ASD sample to children who could follow standing instructions, which bounds generalisability toward more able children. [RQ1.5] No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or autism-severity measures are reported. Anthropometrics (height, body mass) are measured and reported for both groups, which is the relevant covariate set for postural biomechanics. Comorbidity is handled by explicit exclusion of neurological disorders other than ASD, chronic medical disorders, visual impairments and physical impairments affecting balance - a well-targeted exclusion list that removes the most plausible competing explanations for balance differences. [RQ2.1] Goal: develop and validate automated identification of ASD postural control patterns, framed around the open question of whether postural sway can serve as a diagnostic biomarker. Main findings: all six classifiers exceeded 0.800 accuracy; naive Bayes achieved 0.900 accuracy with 1.000 specificity, 1.000 precision, 0.898 F1 and 0.826 sensitivity; k-nearest neighbour was second at 0.860. The underlying group difference is greater sway magnitude in ASD across displacement, distance and area, with no group difference in sample entropy complexity. [RQ2.2] Laboratory setting - a biomechanics laboratory with force-plate instrumentation. Newly collected data; no existing dataset used. [RQ2.3] Quiet standing balance, barefoot on two feet with arms relaxed, for 20 seconds, under randomised eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions, with three acceptable trials per condition. The 20-second duration is justified explicitly against the practical difficulty of keeping autistic children still for longer, citing evidence that 15 seconds gives acceptable construct and concurrent validity in children. Foot placement was deliberately left unconstrained 'to enable participants to adopt a natural stance to more closely reflect any strategy they might use to maintain balance in their natural environment' - an ecological-validity choice made at the cost of some standardisation. Trial acceptability criteria are stated explicitly, and environmental distraction was minimised by keeping investigators and guardians quiet. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single laboratory session totalling roughly two minutes of recorded standing per child, with no follow-up. The data are numeric force-plate traces, not identifiable media, so privacy risk is minimal. Institutional Review Board approval of the study protocol is reported, eligibility was screened by telephone with legal guardians, and informed consent was obtained from legal guardians on arrival at the laboratory. No child assent statement is reported. [RQ2.5] Hardware: a Kistler force plate sampling centre-of-pressure at 60 Hz; standard anthropometric measurement of height and body mass. Software: MATLAB R2020a with the Machine Learning Toolbox for classification and performance evaluation; a fourth-order low-pass Butterworth filter with a 10 Hz cutoff selected by residual analysis; sample entropy computed with sequence length 2 and matching tolerance 0.15 times the COP standard deviation. [RQ2.6] No data or code release. Method reporting is otherwise strong: force plate manufacturer and sampling rate, filter order and cutoff with the selection method, all six COP variable definitions, sample entropy parameters, the outlier check and its criterion, trial acceptability criteria, the ANOVA design, the cross-validation scheme, the metric formulas with the positive class defined, the software version, and classifier parameters supplied in an appendix. Confusion matrices for all classifiers are also provided in an appendix. The analysis is re-implementable in principle on comparable force-plate data. [RQ2.7] Reported by the authors only briefly, in the abstract and conclusions: 'By increasing the sample size and analyzing more data/features of postural control, a better classification performance would be expected'. There is no dedicated limitations section. Identifiable in review: n=50 with five-fold cross-validation means roughly 10 children per test fold, so 0.900 accuracy is about 45 of 50 correct and the exact 1.000 specificity and precision reflect zero false positives among 25 controls - values that will not be stable at this scale; the headline is the best of six algorithms evaluated on the same cross-validation with no nested selection or external validation; no diagnostic instrument is named; inclusion criteria requiring comprehension of instructions and task performance restrict the ASD sample to more able children; sex is not matched (56% versus 40% female); and the negative sample entropy result contradicts two prior studies cited in the introduction without the discrepancy being discussed in the extracted text. [RQ2.9] Increase the sample size and analyse more postural control data and features, with the expectation of better classification performance. No proposals for external validation, comparison against other developmental conditions, or clinical deployment are made. [RQ3.1] Motor behavior: kinetic postural control, specifically centre-of-pressure excursion during quiet standing, capturing both the magnitude of sway (displacement, path length, area) and its temporal regularity (sample entropy). This is the only study in the corpus to measure static postural control with a force plate, complementing the gait, reach and imitation studies in the motor strand. [RQ3.2] Single modality, but with a designed within-modality manipulation: the same six COP variables are measured under eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions and both sets are supplied jointly to the classifiers, giving 12 features. This effectively fuses two sensory conditions, allowing the models to exploit how each child's sway changes when visual input is removed. No integration with clinical, cognitive or demographic data, though anthropometrics were collected. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning with an unusually broad comparison: discriminant analysis, k-nearest neighbour, naive Bayes, decision trees, support vector machine and random forest, each briefly explained with a citation. The rationale is stated explicitly - because features, sample sizes and data structures differ, 'no one algorithm works best for every dataset', so researchers usually implement several and explore the best. The authors also note that basic supervised algorithms are chosen because they are 'computationally efficient and relevant to small sample sizes'. [RQ4.2] Handcrafted low-dimensional biomechanical features: 12 scalar summaries of centre-of-pressure behaviour per child, spanning two theoretically distinct constructs - sway magnitude and sway complexity. The 12-features-to-50-participants ratio is among the healthiest in the corpus and materially reduces overfitting risk relative to the high-dimensional representations used elsewhere. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision and F1, with all five formulas printed explicitly and 'positive' defined as ASD - a level of metric transparency few corpus studies match - plus confusion matrices for every classifier in an appendix. Headline: 0.900 accuracy, 1.000 specificity, 1.000 precision, 0.898 F1, 0.826 sensitivity for naive Bayes. No AUC and no confidence intervals, which matters given that specificity and precision of exactly 1.000 on 25 controls carry wide uncertainty. [RQ4.4] No model-derived feature importance, but interpretability is supplied by a properly conducted univariate analysis that precedes and motivates the classification. The mixed-model ANOVA establishes that children with ASD sway significantly more in displacement, distance and area regardless of visual condition, with no group-by-condition interaction, and that both groups sway more with eyes closed. The negative result is equally informative and is reported plainly: sample entropy did not differentiate the groups, despite the introduction citing two prior studies reporting reduced COP complexity in ASD and interpreting it as 'a repetitive and restricted postural control pattern'. So the classification signal here is magnitude, not complexity. [RQ4.5] Five-fold cross-validation with participant-level folds by construction, since each child contributes a single 12-feature vector - this avoids the window-level and image-level leakage that affects much of the corpus. Outliers were formally checked with Chauvenet's criterion because they 'could influence the classification accuracy', and none were found. Sample size was justified by a priori power analysis. What is absent: any nested structure separating algorithm selection from performance estimation, so reporting the best of six on the same folds carries selection optimism; no external or independent validation; no permutation testing against chance; no class-imbalance issue (25/25); no confidence intervals despite metrics of exactly 1.000; and no deployment or real-time analysis, though efficiency and minimal human intervention are cited as practical advantages. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: Developmental disorder, Postural stability, Force plate, Artificial intelligence, Standing, Balance. Task vocabulary: 'diagnostic biomarkers', 'automated identification', 'computer-aided machine learning', 'postural control patterns'. The vocabulary is biomechanical rather than clinical-diagnostic, and the biomarker claim is posed as an open question rather than asserted. [RQ5.2] Journal of Biomechanics - a biomechanics and movement science journal, neither autism-specific nor computational, and the only representative of that field in this corpus. [RQ5.3] 2020. The paper situates itself carefully in two literatures. On postural control it notes that reduced postural stability in ASD is 'well-established', with prior force-plate studies reporting greater sway displacement, areas, standard deviations, velocities and root mean square, and two studies reporting decreased COP complexity. On machine learning it observes that classifiers have already distinguished impaired postural stability in multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease and vestibular dysfunction, and have been applied in autism to eye gaze, cognitive function, pregnancy risk factors and hand movements - but concludes that 'to our knowledge, there has been no study that utilized machine learning approaches to study postural control features in children with ASD'. It thus documents the transfer of an established clinical-biomechanics method into the autism domain.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control Late-Breaking Report; 5 boys with ASD (mean age 8.2) and 7 typically developing boys (mean age 7.43), aged 5-10, at a US university; approximately 7373 seconds of child-robot interaction video, not released.
narrative_rows.methods: Sensory-maze scenario with a small humanoid and an iPod-based mobile robot designed to elicit conversation and joint sensory experience; OpenPose extraction of upper-body pose and 68 facial keypoints; three Laban movement analysis features (weight, space, time) over 1-second moving windows combined into 71 features; a 1D CNN with two convolution layers, three dense layers and four 20% dropout layers, compared against random forest and k-nearest neighbour; single 80/20 split.
narrative_rows.outcomes: CNN 0.8846 accuracy / 0.8912 precision / 0.8853 recall; random forest 0.8852/0.8876/0.8856; KNN 0.8874/0.8920/0.8878 - all within 0.003. False negative rate 0.1787. The authors conclude simpler methods suffice at this scale and that the method is not ready for standalone diagnostic use.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: 12 children, all male, with no diagnostic instrument reported and no age matching; the evaluation unit is the 1-second window with ~18,597 per child under a single 80/20 split with no stated child-level partitioning, so the reported accuracy is a within-child figure rather than a person-level estimate; validation and test sets not distinguished; no feature interpretation so no behavioral finding; no data, code or hyperparameters.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Charted mainly as an example of naturalistic sensor-free robot-mediated observation with commendably restrained conclusions - the authors report a null model-comparison result and explicitly decline diagnostic claims on the basis of their false negative rate. It is also the corpus's clearest illustration of window-level rather than person-level evaluation: three structurally very different classifiers landing within 0.003 of one another on 12 children is a signature of the evaluation design rather than of a discovered signal.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups: 5 boys with ASD and 7 typically developing boys, total 12 children. Group sizes, sexes and mean ages are reported. No other-diagnosis comparison group. This is the smallest participant sample in the corpus charted so far. [RQ1.2] 'children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)', 'children at risk for ASD', 'at-risk children', 'typically developing (TD)'. Person-first, and notably the paper consistently frames its target as 'risk detection' rather than diagnosis, which is reflected in the terminology throughout. [RQ1.3] ASD n=5 (all male), mean age 8.2 +/- 1.10 years. TD n=7 (all male), mean age 7.43 +/- 2.30 years. Overall age range 5-10 years. No matching procedure or comparability test is reported; the group means differ by about 0.8 years and the control group's standard deviation is more than double the ASD group's. Both groups are exclusively male, which the authors explicitly list as a limitation - 'the inclusion of a single gender' - making this one of the few corpus studies to name sex homogeneity as a limitation rather than leave it unremarked. Total interaction time is reported per group (3931 s TD, 3442 s ASD), described as making the datasets comparable in size. [RQ1.4] Not reported. No diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or confirmation procedure is described for the ASD group, and typically developing status is asserted without screening. Given that diagnostic label is the classification target, this is the study's most fundamental reporting gap, though it is partly a consequence of the two-page format. [RQ1.5] None reported. No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or severity measures for either group, and no comorbidity information. [RQ2.1] Goal: behavior-based risk detection to streamline standard diagnostic procedures through rapid detection and clinical prioritisation of at-risk children. Main findings: CNN 0.8846 accuracy, 0.8912 precision, 0.8853 recall; random forest 0.8852/0.8876/0.8856; KNN 0.8874/0.8920/0.8878 - all three within 0.003 of one another; false negative rate 0.1787. The authors conclude that simpler methods suffice at this scale and that the method is not ready for standalone diagnostic use. [RQ2.2] Laboratory setting with robots on a table and children standing or seated around it. Newly collected data from a user study; no existing dataset used. [RQ2.3] A sensory maze scenario in which two robots - a small humanoid and an iPod-based mobile robot - walk around a maze to find stations and interact with sensory stimuli at each.
