[RQ3.2] No multimodal fusion - a single modality throughout, and no within-modality condition comparison is exploited either. The gap and overlap blocks are described and their latency difference noted, but the paradigm's defining contrast is never used as a feature or analysed as a group-by-condition interaction, which is the main analytic opportunity the design offers and the paper leaves unused. [RQ4.1] A Two-Class Boosted Decision Tree, selected after comparing linear regression, logistic regression, multiclass neural networks, support vector algorithms and quantile regression models within Azure ML Studio. The stated justification - that ensemble boosting suits small tabular data better than the bagging of random forests or the hierarchical structure of neural networks - is reasonable in outline, and choosing a shallow tabular model over deep learning at n = 108 is the right instinct. But no performance figure is given for any comparator, so the selection cannot be assessed, and including linear and quantile regression in a binary classification comparison indicates the model set was not well matched to the task. [RQ4.2] Nineteen tabular attributes reduced to sixteen by dropping ethnicity, blood type and eye colour, then to six by mutual-information filtering. The features arrive pre-computed, so no representation design was performed here. Two observations about the feature set are worth recording: the presence of blood type and eye colour in a saccade dataset is unexplained and suggests the source was not well understood; and dropping ethnicity as 'unrelated to tracking eye movement' removes the one variable that would have permitted any check on demographic confounding, which given the total absence of participant characteristics is a consequential deletion. [RQ4.3] Accuracy alone, at 88% in the text and 88-91% in the abstract, with a plotted ROC curve whose AUC is never stated. For a paper proposing to replace multidisciplinary diagnostic assessment with a single test, the absence of sensitivity and specificity is the critical omission - these are the quantities that determine whether such a test would be usable, and with 60% of the sample autistic, accuracy alone cannot distinguish a useful classifier from one biased toward the majority class. No confusion matrix, no confidence interval, no per-fold variability and no statistical comparison against any baseline. [RQ4.4] The mutual-information filter is presented partly as an interpretability device - it 'communicates the attributes in the dataset which have the most predictive power in the model to drive future experimentation' - and three of the six retained features are named: mean amplitude of primary saccades, absolute saccade error and latency. The other three are never identified, and no model-derived importances, tree structure or decision rules are shown despite the classifier being a decision tree ensemble, which is among the more inspectable model families. The behavioural interpretation offered is that variability rather than central tendency distinguishes the groups, but the paper twice states that the implications are unclear - 'it is uncertain what further implications it has on sensorimotor activity' and 'it is still uncertain what the connections are between these dynamics and saccade error or latency'. [RQ4.5] k-fold cross-validation with k unstated, and with supervised feature selection performed on the complete dataset before the split. The paper sets out the sequence unambiguously - pass in data, select columns, apply filter-based feature selection, then split - and reproduces the Azure workflow confirming it. Because mutual information is computed against the class labels, every fold's feature set was chosen using information from that fold's test data, which biases the reported accuracy upward by an amount that cannot be estimated from what is reported. The paper's own description of cross-validation as a method that has 'been shown to lower bias and overfitting' sits directly alongside the step that defeats it. There is no held-out test set, no independent cohort, no external validation and no repetition. [RQ5.1] No formal keyword list. Vocabulary: 'saccades', 'sensorimotor activity', 'predictive machine learning model', 'novel method of diagnosis', 'shorten time, resources, and uncertainty'. The register is throughput-oriented - the claim is about reducing the professionals, resources and waiting time required for diagnosis rather than about mechanism or accuracy per se. [RQ5.2] 2020 IEEE MIT Undergraduate Research Technology Conference (URTC) - an undergraduate research venue, which is relevant context for the depth of methodological scrutiny the work received. [RQ5.3] 2020. The framing is access and throughput: CDC prevalence of 1 in 54, an estimate of 'two undiagnosed cases for every three accurately diagnosed', and a description of comprehensive developmental evaluation as requiring 'a multidisciplinary team consisting of a psychologist, neurologist, psychiatrist, speech therapist, and may include others' conducting in-depth neurological, cognitive and language testing, with no single medical test available. Two framing points are distinctive within this corpus. First, the sex argument - girls with subtler presentations who are 'better at copying stereotypical social patterns' go undiagnosed into adulthood - correctly identifies camouflaging as a diagnostic failure mode, although the study then reports no sex data. Second, the rationale for choosing saccades over social gaze is temporal rather than practical: sensorimotor abnormalities are said to be present 'prior to the identification of social and cognitive deficits', which would make an oculomotor marker earlier-detectable in principle than the social behaviours clinical diagnosis relies on. The paper also states that saccades in autism are an under-researched area, which is broadly consistent with this corpus, where gaze studies overwhelmingly examine where people look rather than how their eyes move.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Prospective intervention study with severity categorisation and no comparison group; 12 autistic children (11 male, 4.2-7.5 years, mean 6.5) at an Islamabad autism resource centre, split 8 for training (72 sessions over 9 weeks) and 4 for testing (25 sessions over 6 weeks); CARS severity categories assigned by centre clinicians; data not released.
narrative_rows.methods: Two modules of an existing Multi-Robot-mediated Intervention System with two NAO robots: joint attention with least-to-most escalating visual, speech and motion cues, gaze scored by the robots' cameras via ALGazeDetection; and imitation, activated only after five seconds of sustained gaze on a chosen robot, with four gross motor actions scored by Kinect skeletal tracking. Session success percentages were binned into three ordinal levels each at 50% and 80% thresholds and fed to a two-state Hidden Markov Model whose hidden states are the minimal and mild severity levels, with posteriors computed as the product of two conditional probabilities.
narrative_rows.outcomes: The model matched clinician CARS categories in 19 of 25 test sessions (76% accuracy) with Cohen's kappa 0.52 (p = 0.009), described as moderate agreement. Errors were symmetric - three false-mild and three false-minimal. Average joint attention success across all children was 65.47% and imitation 76.19%, with per-child values from 43.43% to 85.46% and 59.9% to 92.19% respectively.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Table 2 assigns each of the four test children a single severity type (one mild, three minimal) while Table 4 reports 12 mild and 13 minimal actual categories across the 25 test sessions, an irreconcilable contradiction that leaves the headline accuracy and kappa uninterpretable; the kappa treats 25 sessions from 4 children as independent, overstating the effective sample about sixfold; two continuous measures are collapsed into nine possible input cells using thresholds set with the label-providing therapist; the posterior assumes conditional independence between joint attention and imitation although imitation is gated by joint attention in the design; printed transition probabilities do not form valid distributions and no fitting procedure is described; severity terminology does not match the DSM scheme the introduction sets out; no limitations section, no institutional ethics approval named, and no data or code.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: One of few studies in the corpus to target graded severity rather than binary diagnosis, and the only one to derive that estimate from data an intervention already generates rather than from a separate assessment - which is the practically interesting idea here. Two design elements are worth carrying into the synthesis: gating the imitation module on the child's own sustained gaze, so the interaction is contingent and the child selects which robot responds; and the least-to-most cue hierarchy, which lets the level of support required be read directly off the cue level at which the child engages. The analysis supporting the severity claim is not usable: an internal contradiction between the participant and results tables, session-level statistics treated as independent across only four children, and an independence assumption the study's own architecture violates. It also illustrates a claim the review should treat sceptically wherever it appears - that an automated categoriser removes the need for a clinician, when the clinician's judgement is the only source of the labels it learns from.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] A single group of 12 autistic children from the Autism Resource Center in Islamabad, split into 8 for training and 4 for the prediction test. There is no non-autistic comparison group and none is intended - the task is severity categorisation within autism rather than case-control discrimination, which makes this one of the few studies in the corpus targeting a graded clinical outcome rather than a binary diagnosis. The analysis unit is the intervention session rather than the child, so 97 sessions arise from 12 individuals and 25 test predictions from 4. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'autistic child', 'the patient', 'subjects'. Mixed person-first and 'ASD children', with 'patient' used for the severe end of the spectrum. The framing is medical and severity-graded, opening with an etymology of 'autism' as 'referring to the children with extreme inability to relate with others' and describing the spectrum as running from borders that 'overlap normality on one end' to 'extreme intellectual impairment caused by brain malfunctions on the other'. Robot-mediated therapy is justified on the ground that 'ASD children are more inclined towards robots because of their predictive behavior'. [RQ1.3] Twelve children, 11 male and 1 female, aged 4.2 to 7.5 years with a mean of 6.5 and standard deviation 0.98, described as of Asian background. Per-child age, sex, autism type and mean joint attention and imitation performance are tabulated individually, which is good practice and is what makes the internal inconsistency between the tables detectable. No IQ, language, adaptive functioning, comorbidity or socioeconomic information. The sex ratio of 11:1 is more extreme than population estimates and the single girl is in the test set. Age is not related to performance anywhere in the analysis despite a 3.3-year span across which joint attention and imitation both develop substantially. [RQ1.4] Participants were recruited from an autism resource centre and 'evaluated clinically based on Childhood Autism Rating Scale Schedule (CARS) by the autism experts'. CARS then serves double duty as both the eligibility assessment and the reference standard for severity. No CARS scores are reported for any child, no cut-offs are given for the minimal and mild bands, no inter-rater reliability is established, and no DSM-5 or ADOS assessment is described. Because the model is evaluated purely by agreement with these CARS categories, the absence of any information about their reliability is the central weakness in the reference standard - a moderate kappa against an unquantified rater tells one little. [RQ1.5] CARS severity category only, as minimal or mild. No CARS total scores, no IQ, no language or adaptive measures, and no comorbidity information. The two performance measures the model consumes - joint attention and imitation success rates - are themselves clinically meaningful and are tabulated per child, but they are the model's input rather than an independent characterisation. [RQ2.1] Goal: use performance data already generated during robot-mediated therapy to categorise autism severity level without requiring a therapist to do the categorisation. Main findings: an HMM over binned joint attention and imitation categories matched clinician CARS categories in 19 of 25 test sessions (76% accuracy) with moderate agreement (kappa 0.52, p = 0.009); average joint attention success across all children was 65.47% and imitation 76.19%; and most children fell in the delayed joint attention and moderate-to-full imitation bands. [RQ2.2] The Autism Resource Center, Islamabad, with the study approved by the centre's autism specialist and director board and parental consent obtained. Two robots were placed in an arc approximately 1 m from the child, who sat for the joint attention module and stood for imitation, with a Kinect behind the robots. The authors state that the participant setting is illustrated 'to make the intervention replicable'. No external funding was received. [RQ2.3] Two modules of an existing multi-robot intervention, each targeting a core impairment. The joint attention module escalates cues in a least-to-most hierarchy - visual (cyclic eye colour change, blinking), then visual plus speech, then visual plus speech plus motion - which is drawn from established prompting practice and allows the level of support required to be read off the cue level at which the child responds. The imitation module is contingent rather than scripted: the child must fixate one of the two robots for five seconds to activate it, then imitates four movements. Using two robots is a deliberate design choice presented as 'representing a triad human communication scenario', on the reasoning that dyadic robot interaction does not exercise the same social configuration as everyday multi-party interaction. [RQ2.4] Longitudinal in structure - 9 sessions per training child over 9 weeks and about 6 per test child over 6 weeks - but the longitudinal dimension is not analysed. Sessions are treated as independent observations rather than as repeated measures within child, and no change over time in joint attention or imitation is examined despite the data being an intervention series. Data are video and depth recordings of identifiable young children, with a photograph of a child with the robots published. Governance is reported at centre level (autism specialist and director board approval, signed parental consent) but no institutional review board is named and no data-handling policy appears. [RQ2.5] Two NAO humanoid robots with the Naoqi SDK, using the ALGazeDetection module of NaoqiPeoplesPerception to determine whether the child is looking at the robot and to compute eye-contact delay and duration; a Microsoft Kinect for real-time skeletal joint tracking to score imitation against the robot's action. The measurement is therefore fully automated within the intervention itself, requiring no separate assessment session - which is the practical strength of the approach. [RQ2.6] Mixed. Well reported: the two intervention modules with their specific cues and actions, the physical setup with distances, the sensors and SDK modules used, the binning thresholds for both observable variables, the session and week counts for training and testing, and a per-child table of age, sex, autism type and mean performance. Poorly reported or absent: CARS scores and band definitions, how the HMM parameters were estimated from the 72 training sessions, the basis for the transition probabilities quoted, per-child test results, any code or data, and any statement of institutional ethics approval. The printed transition probabilities do not sum to valid distributions, and the posterior formula assumes conditional independence between joint attention and imitation without stating or justifying that assumption. [RQ2.7] Essentially none. The paper has no limitations section, and the only self-critical remark is a defence of the sample size on the ground that 'the presented work is based on previous research that also uses a similar number of subjects'. Identifiable in review and unaddressed: Table 2 assigns each test child a single autism type (one mild, three minimal) while Table 4 records 12 mild and 13 minimal actual categories across 25 test sessions, which cannot be reconciled without an unexplained within-child change in CARS category, and until resolved makes the reported accuracy and kappa uninterpretable; the kappa treats 25 sessions from 4 children as independent, inflating the effective sample about sixfold; the two observables are binned to three levels each using thresholds set with the therapist who also supplied the labels; the conditional independence assumption is contradicted by the design, since the imitation module is activated by joint attention; the severity labels 'minimal' and 'mild' are never mapped to the DSM levels the introduction describes; and the claim that no therapist is needed is undercut by the fact that every training label comes from a therapist's CARS assessment. [RQ2.9] None stated. The conclusion asserts the model's usefulness without identifying required replication, larger samples, per-child validation, or the reconciliation of its own tables. [RQ3.1] Two behaviours, both DSM-relevant core impairments: joint attention, operationalised as the delay before establishing eye contact with a robot and the duration for which it is sustained under escalating cue support; and imitation, operationalised as the proportion of four gross motor actions correctly reproduced. Measuring both within a single interaction, and gating one on the other, is the design's distinctive feature - most robot studies in this corpus measure a single behaviour. [RQ3.2] Two behavioural channels are combined, but through a probabilistic model rather than a learned fusion: the posterior for each severity category is computed as the product of P(category | joint attention) and P(category | imitation). No single-channel baseline is reported, so the contribution of combining them cannot be assessed, and no ablation is performed. More problematically, the product form assumes the two observables are conditionally independent given severity - an assumption the study's own architecture violates, since the imitation module only activates once the child has sustained gaze on a robot for five seconds, making imitation performance conditional on joint attention performance by construction. There are also two sensing modalities (robot camera gaze and Kinect depth), but these map one-to-one onto the two behaviours rather than being fused. [RQ4.1] A two-state Hidden Markov Model with the severity level as the hidden state and the two binned behavioural categories as observables. The choice is defensible for an intrinsically sequential intervention series with a latent clinical state, and the model is inherently interpretable. But the temporal structure that motivates an HMM is not actually exploited - sessions are treated as independent observations rather than as a sequence within child, no state transitions over the course of therapy are examined, and the reported posterior computation is a static Bayes calculation over two conditionals rather than a sequential inference. In effect the model functions as a naive Bayes classifier over nine input cells, with the HMM framing adding formalism rather than capability. [RQ4.2] Two continuous session-level percentages, each collapsed into three ordinal bands at 50% and 80% thresholds - so the entire model input for a session is one of nine discrete combinations. This is by far the coarsest representation in the corpus. The thresholds were 'deduced in discussion with the therapist and according to the child's performance', which gives them clinical meaning but also means they were chosen with sight of the data by the same source that supplied the labels. The per-child averages in Table 2 show how much is discarded: joint attention values from 43.43% to 85.46% and imitation from 59.9% to 92.19% collapse into a handful of cells. [RQ4.3] Accuracy (19 of 25, 76%) and Cohen's kappa (0.52, p = 0.009) against clinician CARS categorisation. Reporting kappa rather than accuracy alone is appropriate for an agreement study and is better practice than most of the corpus. But the kappa's n = 25 counts sessions rather than children, so its significance is overstated; no confidence interval accompanies it; and no sensitivity, specificity or per-class breakdown is given, though the individually tabulated 25 test rows allow these to be derived - three false-mild and three false-minimal errors, symmetric across classes. [RQ4.4] The model is interpretable by construction: every input is a named clinical category, every hidden state is a severity level, and the posterior is an explicit product of two conditional probabilities that a clinician could in principle compute by hand. All 25 test cases are tabulated with their joint attention category, imitation category, actual category and predicted category, so every prediction and every error is individually inspectable - a level of transparency almost no other study in the corpus offers. What is missing is any account of the fitted probabilities, so the direction and strength of the learned relationships cannot be read, and no analysis of which of the nine input cells the model handles well or badly. [RQ4.5] A held-out split by participant, with 8 children and 72 sessions for training and 4 children and 25 sessions for testing, and test participants selected randomly. Splitting by child rather than by session is the correct choice and is stated clearly. Two failures follow it, though. Prediction and evaluation both operate at the session level, so the 25 test observations are roughly six repeated measures from each of four children, and the kappa treats them as independent - the effective sample is 4 children, not 25 sessions. And the test set's composition is unbalanced at the child level (one mild, three minimal by Table 2), which cannot generate the 12-mild, 13-minimal distribution of actual categories reported in Table 4, leaving the evaluation internally inconsistent. There is no cross-validation, no repetition over alternative splits, no independent cohort and no confidence interval. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder (ASD), imitation, joint attention, Hidden Markov Model (HMM), robot-mediated therapies, Multi-robot-mediated Intervention System (MRIS). Two of the six name the specific clinical constructs targeted, which reflects the paper's grounding in established autism intervention targets rather than in generic behavioural sensing. [RQ5.2] Journal of Educational Computing Research, 60(3), 722-741 - an educational technology journal rather than a clinical or engineering venue, which is consistent with the intervention framing and with the limited statistical scrutiny the analysis received. [RQ5.3] 2021. The framing combines prevalence growth (CDC estimates moving from 1 in 59 to 1 in 54) with a claim that autism is 'the fastest-growing developmental disorder in the USA with a 6% to 15% increase in rate per year'. Distinctively for this corpus, it invokes COVID-19 as a driver: 'especially under the current COVID-19 situation, the current research trends are focusing online for technology-based therapies', which situates robot-mediated intervention within a pandemic-era shift toward remote and technology-delivered care. The rationale for robots is given as controllability, accuracy, low cost and adaptability, plus the claim that autistic children are drawn to robots because of their predictable behaviour. The specific gap claimed is that existing robot therapies improve skills but cannot label severity, and the authors note a prior HMM attempt that 'failed to produce hidden Markov models that are indicative of a person's level of autism'.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control classification; 86 Brazilian participants - 56 autistic (38 male, 5-18 years, mean 10, CARS 33-45) and 30 typically developing (20 male, 3-15 years, mean 10, CARS below 30) - assessed by DSM-5 and CARS at a university psychiatry department; gaze recorded on a Tobii Pro TX300 during three purpose-built joint attention videos; data not released.
narrative_rows.methods: Three 10-second videos isolating gaze-only, gaze-to-object and gaze-plus-point joint attention conditions were divided into nine segments; specialists demarcated regions of interest on the first frame of each segment and an automated procedure propagated and semantically linked them across frames as floating regions; 15 trajectory and timing features per region per segment - including distance-to-centre statistics, visit and fixation timing and duration, ordinal position, and anticipation features permitting negative first-visit times - fed nine segment-specific random forests, combined by weighted voting under three ensemble strategies with SMOTE applied to training folds only and evaluated by 10-fold cross-validation.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Best configuration (segments 1, 3 and 8, threshold 2): accuracy 0.75, sensitivity 0.87, precision 0.78, specificity 0.53, F1 0.82. Equal-weight nine-classifier ensemble: 0.71 accuracy, 0.93 sensitivity, 0.30 specificity, 0.81 F1. Accuracy-weighted ensemble: 0.71 accuracy, 0.77 sensitivity, 0.60 specificity, 0.76 F1. No individual segment classifier reached 75%, and regions containing the eyes outperformed regions containing the therapist's hand.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The reported result is the maximum over 511 classifier subsets, three ensemble strategies, finely swept thresholds, five SMOTE variants and per-segment hyperparameter grids, all scored on the same 10-fold cross-validation with no outer loop, so both the accuracy and the segment-selection finding are optimistically biased selection outcomes; specificity of 0.53 means roughly half of typically developing participants are misclassified, a consequence defended but not analysed; no ethics approval or consent statement appears despite participants aged from 3; ages span 3-18 with differing ranges by group and no adjustment; CARS scores are collected but never related to classifier output; and no group-level descriptive statistics are reported for any of the paper's own novel features.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The corpus's most serious attempt to make joint attention computationally tractable, and the floating region of interest - a region identified by semantic continuity rather than screen position, so that a moving and resizing hand or object remains one region across frames - is a transferable methodological contribution that addresses the specific reason joint attention has been under-represented in automated work. Its anticipation feature, allowing negative first-visit times computed against the preceding segment, is the corpus's only direct operationalisation of anticipatory gaze. The temporal ensemble result is also worth carrying forward: no single moment of the joint attention sequence classified above 75% while a three-segment combination did, indicating that the informative unit is the referential sequence rather than any instant within it. Against that, it is a clear illustration of selection bias at scale, with hundreds of configurations optimised on the reporting cross-validation, and of the specificity problem that accuracy and F1 conceal - the highest-F1 model here correctly identifies fewer than a third of typically developing participants.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups totalling 86 participants: 56 autistic (38 male, 18 female, aged 5-18, mean 10) and 30 typically developing (20 male, 10 female, aged 3-15, mean 10). The class ratio is 65:35 in favour of autism, which the authors identify as a limitation and address with SMOTE on training folds. No other-diagnosis comparison group. At 86 participants this is among the larger single-site eye-tracking cohorts in the corpus. [RQ1.2] 'individuals with ASD', 'children with ASD', 'Typical Development (TD)', 'patients'. Person-first in most places, with 'patients' used once for the whole sample. The framing is neutral and developmental rather than deficit-laden, describing autism as 'a neurodevelopmental disorder with clinical presentation and varied functional impact' and grounding joint attention in normal development - infants follow gaze within days of birth and develop referential understanding of gaze cues over the first two years. [RQ1.3] Autistic group: 56 participants, 38 male and 18 female, aged 5-18 with mean 10. Typically developing: 30 participants, 20 male and 10 female, aged 3-15 with mean 10. Means match exactly and sex proportions are close (68% versus 67% male), but the age ranges differ at both ends, no standard deviations are given, and no statistical test of matching is reported. The age span is wide - 3 to 18 years - across which gaze-following and anticipation in joint attention change substantially, and age is neither modelled nor controlled. CARS scores are reported for both groups (33-45, mean 34.5 for autism; below 30 for typical development), which is more clinical detail than most of the corpus provides. No IQ, language, comorbidity, ethnicity or socioeconomic data. [RQ1.4] Specialist evaluation using DSM-5 criteria together with CARS, with the autistic group's scores reported as a range and mean. Notably, CARS was administered to the typically developing group as well, confirming all scored below the 30-point diagnostic threshold - so both groups were assessed on the same instrument and control status is verified rather than assumed. The paper also footnotes the CARS threshold explicitly. What is missing is any account of who performed the assessments, when, or with what reliability, and no ADOS or ADI-R is described. [RQ1.5] CARS scores for both groups, reported as ranges and a group mean. The autistic range of 33-45 spans mild-to-moderate through severe on standard CARS bands, so the sample covers meaningful severity variation - but this is never exploited. No severity-stratified analysis is performed, no relationship between CARS score and classifier output is examined, and no IQ, language or adaptive measure appears. Given that the discriminative signal is in anticipatory gaze during joint attention, which plausibly varies with severity, relating classifier confidence to CARS would have been a straightforward and valuable analysis. [RQ2.1] Goal: build gaze trajectory features that can represent the joint attention paradigm computationally, using semantically tracked floating regions of interest, and classify autism from them. Main findings: 75% accuracy, 87% sensitivity, 53% specificity and 0.82 F1 from an ensemble using three of nine video segments; the informative segments correspond to the therapist's gaze resting, shifting to the object, and returning; no single segment exceeded 75% alone; and regions containing the eyes outperformed those containing the pointing hand. [RQ2.2] Laboratory eye tracking with participants recruited through the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Sao Paulo's School of Medicine, in collaboration with the School of Arts, Sciences and Humanities and the bioinformatics postgraduate programme. Funded by CNPq, FAPESP/INCT-MACC, CAPES and PRONAS/PCD. No ethics approval statement appears. [RQ2.3] Three purpose-built 10-second joint attention videos at 1920 x 1080, forming a graded series: in video A only the therapist's eyes move; in video B the gaze shifts toward an object of interest; in video C the hand points to the object. Each is segmented at the points where the set of relevant regions changes, giving nine analysed segments in total. The design is unusually well matched to the construct - joint attention involves coordinated mutual engagement with a third entity, so a stimulus that isolates gaze-only, gaze-to-object and gaze-plus-point conditions decomposes the paradigm into its components, and the segment-level ensemble then reveals which components carry information. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single viewing session per participant with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates over purpose-recorded video of a therapist. No ethics committee approval, parental consent procedure, anonymisation or data governance statement appears anywhere in the paper, despite participants aged from 3 years recruited through a university psychiatry department - the most conspicuous reporting gap in an otherwise clinically careful study. [RQ2.5] Tobii Pro TX300 with a removable 23-inch monitor, up to 300 Hz sampling and head-movement tolerance to 50 cm/s, at 50-70 cm viewing distance; Python with scikit-learn including GridSearchCV and SMOTE implementations. The 300 Hz sampling against video frame rate yields approximately ten gaze records per frame, which is what makes fine-grained trajectory features and the anticipation measure feasible. [RQ2.6] Strong on the feature and modelling pipeline, absent on governance and descriptive results. Fully reported: all 15 features with their definitions and which were newly devised; the floating region identification procedure including specialist demarcation of the first frame and automated propagation; segment boundaries with frame counts; the missing-value imputation rule with its constant; Min-Max normalisation; the SMOTE variants and random forest hyperparameter grids; all three ensemble strategies with their threshold ranges; and the 10-fold cross-validation. Absent: any ethics or consent statement; any group-level descriptive statistics for the features; the identity of the selected hyperparameters; data or code release; and any account of missing or excluded data. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged: the dataset is imbalanced and synthetic sampling is a stopgap pending more real data; region demarcation still requires a therapist and automatic identification would make the method faster; and accuracy could be improved with other methods such as genetic algorithms for meta-classifier construction. The low specificity is noted and defended rather than treated as a limitation - the authors argue that 'our major goal is to capture all possible individuals with the disorder' and that highly sensitive tests suit early rule-out. Not acknowledged: the reported 75% is the maximum over 511 classifier subsets, three ensemble strategies, swept thresholds, five balancing methods and per-segment hyperparameter grids, all selected on the same 10-fold estimate with no outer validation loop, so the figure is optimistically biased and the segment-1-3-8 finding is a selection outcome rather than an independent result; the practical consequence of 53% specificity - referring roughly half of typically developing children onward - is not discussed; ages span 3-18 with different ranges per group and no adjustment; CARS scores are collected but never related to model output; and no ethics approval is reported. [RQ2.9] Enlarge the dataset so that class balance can be achieved with real rather than synthetic samples; automate region-of-interest identification to remove the therapist from the loop and speed the method; and explore alternative machine learning approaches including genetic algorithms for meta-classifier construction. The authors also note the approach generalises to any joint attention video provided a therapist marks the first and last frame of each region. [RQ3.1] Anticipatory and referential gaze during joint attention - specifically whether and when the participant's gaze arrives at, dwells on and returns from the regions a therapist's gaze or gesture directs it toward. The construct targeted is more specific than the social-attention measures elsewhere in the corpus: not how much a child looks at faces, but whether the gaze tracks a referential sequence in time, including whether it arrives before the referent appears. The anticipation feature, which permits negative first-visit times computed against records from the preceding segment, is the direct operationalisation of that. [RQ3.2] No cross-modal fusion - gaze only. The combination that does occur is across time and across regions: nine segment-specific classifiers are ensembled, and the finding is that the whole is greater than any part, with every individual segment classifier below 75% while the best three-segment combination reaches it. This is a temporal rather than sensory fusion result, and it carries a clear message for the corpus's video-based studies - that a joint attention response is a sequence and that classifying any single moment of it underperforms classifying the sequence. The authors' own reading is that segments 1, 3 and 8 'present three fundamental stages of JA' and that 'the complete action process is necessary', though this identification comes from an exhaustive search rather than an a priori hypothesis. [RQ4.1] Random forests, one per video segment, combined into an ensemble by weighted voting - a design that mirrors the temporal structure of the stimulus rather than flattening it. Three combination strategies are compared systematically, and the exhaustive variant testing all 511 subsets is thorough as an exploration but constitutes a very large selection space when evaluated on the same cross-validation used for reporting. No deep learning, which is appropriate at 86 participants, and no single-model baseline over concatenated features is reported, so the benefit of the segment-wise decomposition itself is not isolated. [RQ4.2] Fifteen trajectory and timing features per region per segment, giving nine feature vectors of 15 x R dimensions per participant. Three aspects are distinctive. First, distance-to-centre features (mean, standard deviation, coefficient of variation) capture how tightly gaze is held on a region rather than merely whether it was there. Second, ordinal features (order of longest visit, order of longest fixation) encode sequence position within a segment. Third, the anticipation features permit negative values by searching gaze records from the preceding segment, so a participant whose gaze arrives before the referent appears is distinguished from one who arrives promptly. Missing values, arising when a region was never visited or fixated, are imputed as the segment's final time or order multiplied by an empirically chosen constant of 4 - a defensible encoding of 'never' as an extreme value, though the constant was tuned rather than derived. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity, precision, specificity and F1 for the best configuration of each ensemble strategy. Reporting all five is what makes the result honestly interpretable and exposes the sensitivity-specificity imbalance that accuracy alone would conceal - the equal-weight ensemble achieves an F1 of 0.81 while correctly classifying only 30% of typically developing participants. No AUC, no confidence intervals, no per-fold variability and no statistical comparison between strategies, so whether 0.75 differs meaningfully from 0.71 on 86 participants is not established. [RQ4.4] No model-explanation method, but the ensemble structure delivers interpretability at the level that matters clinically. Because each classifier corresponds to a specific video segment, the winning combination identifies which moments of the joint attention sequence carry discriminative information - here the gaze at rest, the gaze shifting to the object, and the gaze returning. The authors also report that regions containing the eyes outperformed regions containing the therapist's hand, which speaks directly to the gaze-versus-gesture distinction in joint attention. Both findings are interpretable and clinically legible; both are outcomes of an exhaustive search rather than tests of prior hypotheses, and no group-level feature statistics are reported to corroborate them. [RQ4.5] 10-fold cross-validation with SMOTE correctly restricted to training samples - a detail explicitly stated and often got wrong elsewhere in this corpus. The problem is scale of selection: three ensemble strategies, all 511 classifier subsets, thresholds swept in fine increments, five SMOTE variants plus the unbalanced original, and a GridSearchCV over three hyperparameters for each of nine random forests, with the best result across all of that reported from the same 10-fold estimate. There is no outer cross-validation loop, no held-out set, no independent cohort and no repetition over alternative fold partitions. The consequence is that both the headline accuracy and the substantive claim about which segments matter are selection outcomes rather than validated findings. [RQ5.1] Index terms: Autism Spectrum Disorder; Ensemble Method; Eye tracking; Image processing; Joint attention; Machine Learning; Random Forest; Trajectory; Typical Development. 'Trajectory', 'joint attention' and 'image processing' together capture the contribution - the paper is about representing a dynamic referential sequence computationally, with classification as the demonstration. [RQ5.2] 2021 IEEE 34th International Symposium on Computer-Based Medical Systems (CBMS), pages 50-55 - a medical informatics conference, with authorship spanning computing, bioinformatics and a university psychiatry department. [RQ5.3] 2021. The framing identifies a specific methodological gap rather than a general access problem: joint attention is 'an important marker to differentiate children with ASD from 12 months onwards', its verification 'requires the therapist's experience, attention and time spent, considering that the specialist's observation not using any tools is the most common practice', and the obstacle to automating it is technical - 'the studies cited in the literature that use ET signals combined with computational methods do not process trajectory data or ignore that the paradigm involves the displacement of regions of interest'. The developmental grounding is unusually explicit for this corpus, linking gaze-following to inferences about intentions and motivations and framing anticipation as 'the action of providing a view of the immediate future based on the immediate past', which 'appears to be difficult in ASD'. That framing directly motivates the anticipation feature, giving the paper a rare coherence between construct, feature design and analysis.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Two-stage study; preliminary experiment on 107 non-clinical Chinese adults (49 women, mean age 24.84 +/- 5.24, mean AQ 21.0) dichotomised at the sample median into 52 above and 55 below, then a test experiment on 22 separately recruited diagnosed autistic males (mean age 12.68 +/- 7.61) with no comparison group; VR gaze data available on request.
narrative_rows.methods: Free viewing of a 15-20 second Unity3D garden scene containing human figures, a dog and landscape, with gaze recorded by an aGlass infrared module in an HTC Vive; the scene was segmented by colour and K-means into three regions and gaze points assigned to clusters, yielding three total-occupancy, three continuous-occupancy and three transition proportions plus age and sex; seven classifiers (logistic regression and naive Bayes after PCA, KNN, SVM, decision tree, random forest, gradient boosting) plus an averaging-and-voting ensemble were fitted on a 70/30 split with threefold cross-validated GridSearchCV, then applied to the diagnosed sample.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Preliminary: ensemble accuracy 0.73, precision 0.68, recall 0.81, F1 0.74, AUC 0.90; best individual models random forest and gradient boosting at 0.70 accuracy and AUC 0.68 and 0.66. Test experiment recall: ensemble 0.77, naive Bayes 0.82, random forest 0.73, gradient boosting 0.55, KNN 0.45, logistic regression 0.00. Continuous looking at the figure and animal regions were the most important features across tree-based models.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The preliminary positive class is a median split of AQ at 21 in a non-clinical sample against a clinical cut-off of 32, so the models were trained to detect above-average trait scores rather than autism, and Table 2's group AQ means are transposed; age and sex are model features while the test sample differs from the training population by roughly twelve years of mean age and is entirely male; the test sample contains no negative cases so specificity is unmeasured and recall alone cannot distinguish discrimination from positive-prediction bias; the ensemble's AUC of 0.90 is inconsistent with constituent AUCs of 0.57-0.68; outlier replacement by the mean is unspecified in criterion and timing; 15-20 seconds of viewing yields few gaze points; and aGlass accuracy is described by the authors as insufficient.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Useful to the review on three counts despite its central flaw. It supplies the corpus's clearest statement of why immersive stimuli might matter - that social attention in autism can appear normal when social information is presented statically or in isolation - and tests it, finding continuity of looking rather than total looking to be the discriminative quantity. It provides the corpus's best demonstration that ensembling buys stability under population shift, with individual model recall swinging from 0.81 to 0.55 and from 0.44 to 0.00 while the ensemble held at 0.81 then 0.77. And it reports two practical deployment findings that other VR studies here do not: that consumer VR eye-tracking accuracy was inadequate, and that some autistic participants rejected the headset. Its principal value as a methodological case, however, is negative: it is the corpus's clearest instance of a trait questionnaire median split in a non-clinical sample being labelled and reported as autism classification, and of an apparent external validation that is neither demographically comparable nor capable of measuring discrimination.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two entirely separate samples serving different roles. The preliminary experiment used 107 non-clinical adults (49 women, 58 men, mean age 24.84 +/- 5.24) split by AQ score into 52 above-median and 55 below-median. The test experiment used 22 young autistic males (mean age 12.68 +/- 7.61) recruited through the Shenzhen Autism Society, with no comparison group. The two samples differ in age by roughly twelve years on average, in sex composition (mixed versus all-male) and in clinical status (trait-scored general population versus diagnosed), so the second is not a held-out sample from the first population but a different population entirely. [RQ1.2] 'autistic persons', 'people with autism', 'patients', 'participants with obvious and unobvious autistic traits', 'typically developing (TD)', 'healthy children'. Predominantly person-first but with heavy disease framing - autism is repeatedly called 'a very complex disease' and 'a mental disease', and the aims include 'reducing the incidence of ASD', which conflates screening with prevention of an incident condition. The taxonomy given in the background is also outdated, listing Rett syndrome and childhood disintegrative disorder as ASD subtypes, which DSM-5 removed. Against that, the paper is careful to distinguish trait detection from diagnosis in its framing, positioning the work as identifying high autistic traits 'before making a definite diagnosis'. [RQ1.3] Preliminary experiment: 107 adults, 49 women and 58 men, mean age 24.84 +/- 5.24 years, mean AQ 21.0 +/- 5.2. The two label groups are closely matched - 25 women and 30 men at 24.7 +/- 5.2 years versus 24 women and 28 men at 25.0 +/- 5.3 - which is good practice, although the reported group AQ means of 16.6 for the high-trait group and 25.7 for the low-trait group are transposed relative to their labels. Test experiment: 22 participants, all male, mean age 12.68 +/- 7.61 years, with no age range, AQ, IQ, severity, comorbidity or socioeconomic data. The demographic gulf between the two samples is the study's central design flaw and is never addressed. [RQ1.4] The weakest ascertainment logic in the corpus, and it is structural rather than a reporting omission. In the preliminary experiment there is no diagnostic assessment at all: the positive class is created by dichotomising AQ at 21, a value chosen because 'this histogram was almost symmetrical in terms of the mean results of the questionnaire (21), with 55 out of 107 results lower than 21 and 52 results no less than 21'. The threshold is therefore a median split chosen for balance, not a clinical cut-off - the established AQ screening threshold is 32 - and the paper nonetheless labels the upper half '1 (ASD)'. In the test experiment, participants were 'already diagnosed with ASD' with no instrument, criteria, diagnostician or date reported, and no AQ was administered so their trait scores are unknown and the two experiments' labels are not commensurable. [RQ1.5] AQ total scores for the preliminary sample only, with the five subscale domains described but never analysed. No severity, IQ, language, adaptive or comorbidity measure for the diagnosed test participants, and no AQ administered to them - so it is not possible to establish whether the diagnosed group would even have scored above the study's own trait threshold. [RQ2.1] Goal: build a rapid VR-based gaze screening method for high autistic traits, deployable where clinical resources are limited. Main findings: an ensemble of seven classifiers reached 0.73 accuracy, 0.81 recall and reported AUC 0.90 on the median-split adult sample and recalled 77% of 22 diagnosed autistic participants; continuity of looking at the figure and animal regions was the most important feature family across tree-based models; and individual model recall shifted markedly between the two experiments, which the authors read as evidence that the two populations differ. [RQ2.2] Laboratory sessions at Tsinghua University's Shenzhen International Graduate School, with diagnosed participants recruited through the Shenzhen Autism Society. Funded by Shenzhen Humanities and Social Sciences Key Research Bases, the Guangdong Natural Science Foundation, the National Philosophy and Social Sciences Foundation of China and a Tsinghua SIGS foundation. IRB approval from the Department of Psychology, Tsinghua University (No. THUDP20) covering both experiments. [RQ2.3] A single Unity3D virtual scene - a couple in a garden with their dog - containing three semantic regions: human figures as social stimuli, an animal, and landscape. Free viewing for 15-20 seconds with no instruction. The design rationale is explicit and worth recording: previous Chinese eye-tracking work used 'merely a face on the computer screen', whereas static or isolated social presentations may fail to reveal group differences because 'for static images or those which present social information in isolation, social attention is normal in autism'. The 15-20 second exposure is by some margin the shortest stimulus in the corpus, which suits deployment but yields few gaze points per participant. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; one brief exposure per participant with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates within a synthetic scene, plus questionnaire scores and demographics - low sensitivity. Governance is properly reported: IRB approval with a reference number for both experiments and explicit attention to participant safety, which matters here because the authors note that some autistic participants rejected the VR headset. [RQ2.5] HTC Vive with an embedded aGlass infrared eye-tracking module, gaze coordinates delivered in a normalised unit square through the Unity console; Unity3D for scene construction and recording scripts; scikit-learn with GridSearchCV. The authors report the hardware's limitations candidly, stating that 'the stability and accuracy of aGlass are not high enough' and that they observed rejection of VR among autistic participants - two practical findings that bear directly on whether this modality is deployable with the target population. [RQ2.6] Mixed. Reported: the scene contents, exposure duration, headset and tracking module, the K-means region segmentation procedure, all eleven features with definitions, the seven base models with the specific hyperparameters tuned for each and the rationale for PCA before logistic regression and naive Bayes, both ensemble combination rules, the 70/30 split with threefold cross-validated GridSearchCV, and full metric tables for both experiments. Not reported: the outlier criterion and the stage at which mean imputation was applied relative to the split, the selected hyperparameter values, the number of gaze points per participant, any calibration or data-quality statistics, the diagnostic basis of the test participants, and any code. Data are available on request. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged: aGlass stability and accuracy are insufficient; VR was rejected by some autistic participants; small samples in both experiments make bias inevitable; not all scenes containing social stimuli discriminate, so scene design should involve a specialist psychologist and several scenes should be compared. Most valuably, the authors report and interpret the recall instability across experiments, concluding that 'the data patterns of the adults we recruited in the preliminary experiment are somehow different from those autistic adults'. Not acknowledged: that the preliminary positive class is a median split of a general-population trait distribution well below the AQ clinical cut-off, so the models were never trained on autism; that Table 2's group AQ means are transposed; that age and sex are model features while the test sample differs sharply from the training population on both; that the test experiment has no negative cases so specificity is unmeasured and recall alone cannot distinguish a good model from one biased toward positive prediction; that the ensemble's AUC of 0.90 is inconsistent with constituent AUCs of 0.57-0.68; and that outlier replacement by the mean is unspecified in both criterion and timing. [RQ2.9] Improve the accuracy and stability of the eye-tracking hardware and address VR acceptability among autistic participants; enlarge both samples to reduce small-sample bias; involve a specialist psychologist in scene construction since social stimuli do not automatically discriminate; and design multiple scenes and select the most discriminative. [RQ3.1] Distribution of visual attention across three semantic region types in an immersive scene - human figures, an animal and landscape - characterised in three ways: total occupancy, continuity of occupancy, and transitions between region pairs. Including both total and continuous occupancy is the design's most productive choice, since the continuity features turned out to be the most important and total occupancy was not, which distinguishes sustained engagement from repeated brief glances - a distinction most gaze studies in this corpus collapse. [RQ3.2] No cross-modal fusion. What is combined is models rather than modalities: seven classifiers ensembled by probability averaging and majority voting, with the stated rationale that 'the best model that matches the pattern of this group of data well does not mean that it can be generalized to fit another group of data', so combining reduces variance and improves generalisation. That reasoning is sound and is borne out empirically - the ensemble's recall held at 0.81 then 0.77 across the two experiments while individual models swung from 0.81 to 0.55 (gradient boosting) or 0.44 to 0.00 (logistic regression). This is the corpus's clearest demonstration that ensembling buys stability under population shift, even though the underlying task here is not what the paper claims. [RQ4.1] Seven classical classifiers plus an ensemble, with each model's assumptions and their consequences discussed individually - PCA applied before logistic regression because of multicollinearity and before naive Bayes because of its independence assumption, normalisation before KNN because distance is scale-sensitive, standardisation before SVM for convergence. This model-by-model reasoning is more careful than most of the corpus. The ensemble is then justified on generalisation rather than accuracy grounds, which is the right argument and is the one the test experiment supports. [RQ4.2] Nine gaze features plus age and sex. The gaze features are proportions rather than counts, which normalises for exposure length, and the three-way split into total, continuous and transition proportions gives a compact description of both where attention rests and how it moves. Whole-sample means show the landscape dominating at 76% of gaze points against 17% for figures and 7% for the animal. The inclusion of age and sex as predictors is the consequential decision: it improves fit within a homogeneous adult sample but makes the model's behaviour on a demographically different test population uninterpretable, since the classifiers may be responding to the demographic features rather than the gaze features. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUC for all eight models in the preliminary experiment - a complete and transparent table - but recall alone in the test experiment, because the test sample contains no negative cases. That asymmetry matters: recall of 0.77 on an all-positive sample is uninformative about discrimination, since any model with a positive prediction bias scores well. The reported ensemble AUC of 0.90 against constituent AUCs of 0.57-0.68 is also internally implausible, since averaging or voting over models with AUC at most 0.68 cannot ordinarily yield 0.90. [RQ4.4] Feature importances from the tree-based models identify continuousnum1 and continuousnum2 - continuous looking at figures and at the animal - as the most significant features, supported by density-distribution plots showing these features differing most between groups while others such as continuous landscape looking overlap closely. The interpretation offered is behaviourally specific and plausible: what distinguishes the groups is how long attention is sustained on social and animate content, not how much total time is spent there. What is missing is any directional statement or statistical test - no group means, no effect sizes, no significance testing for any feature - so the reader cannot tell whether high-trait participants sustained more or less continuous looking at figures. [RQ4.5] A single 70/30 split of 107 participants with threefold cross-validated GridSearchCV inside the training portion, followed by application to a separate group of 22 diagnosed participants. The two-stage structure is the right instinct - fitting on one sample and testing on another population is more than most of the corpus attempts - but its execution defeats the purpose. The test sample contains only positive cases, so nothing about specificity or overall discrimination can be established. It differs from the training population by roughly twelve years of mean age and entirely in sex composition, both of which are model inputs. And the labels are not commensurable: the training positive class is above-median AQ in a non-clinical adult sample, while the test positives are clinically diagnosed individuals whose AQ scores were never measured. There is no repetition over alternative splits, no confidence intervals and no independent replication. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorders (ASD), early screening, eye movement, machine learning, virtual reality (VR). 'Early screening' rather than diagnosis is the operative framing, and the paper is generally careful to describe its target as high autistic traits rather than autism - though the labelling of the above-median group as 'ASD' in the methods works against that care. [RQ5.2] Journal of Child and Adolescent Psychiatric Nursing, 35(1), 83-92 - a nursing journal, which is an unusual venue for a machine learning contribution and is consistent with the emphasis on deployability and screening infrastructure over methodological rigour. [RQ5.3] 2021. The framing is unusually specific about health-system context in China. It describes the two-stage screening structure recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics, notes that 'approximately 50% of the time is carried out with staff assistance' even for parent-completed tools, and that assessment can 'continue for months if the symptoms are not sufficiently obvious'. On China specifically it observes that 'the study of mental diseases used to be marginalized due to the conservative culture and weak science consciousness', that 'a majority of child health care institutions in China have not incorporated early ASD screening into their daily work', and that parents and primary health care staff lack awareness of early behavioural characteristics. It also positions itself against two named Chinese eye-tracking studies reporting 88.51% and 85.1%, criticising both for using only a face on a computer screen, and grounds that criticism in a substantive claim from the literature - that social attention in autism appears normal when social information is presented statically or in isolation, which is the argument for immersive scenes.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional three-group classification; 74 Beijing preschoolers - 26 high-functioning autistic (5.08 years), 24 low-functioning autistic (4.98 years) and 24 typically developing (5.24 years), all age-matched, with the high-functioning and typically developing groups additionally matched on Raven's and PPVT scores; DSM-5 hospital diagnoses plus Chinese SCQ above threshold; 160 visual-orienting trials on a Tobii X120; data not released.
narrative_rows.methods: A gamified task presented a central directional cue - arrow, pointing finger, cartoon gaze or human gaze - surrounded by four objects, requiring the child to orient to the cued target and hold fixation for 1000 ms within a 4000 ms window to earn a reward; 68 distributional statistics of raw gaze samples across four areas of interest were computed without any selection and classified by k-nearest neighbours with k fixed from an external pilot dataset, evaluated by subject-wise leave-one-out cross-validation, with two additional tests withholding an entire group from training.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Three-class accuracy 81.08% (sensitivity/specificity 73.1/85.4 for high-functioning, 79.2/90.0 for low-functioning, 91.7/96.0 for typically developing; AUC 0.775, 0.908, 0.927); binary autism versus typical development 93.24% with AUC 0.938. Gaze cues alone gave 78.4% and non-gaze cues alone 77.0%. Success rates ranked 74.7%, 29.1% and 5.7%; response latencies 986, 1117 and 1277 ms. Cross-group transfer: 100% of unseen low-functioning children correctly identified by a model trained on typically developing versus high-functioning, against 53.85% of unseen high-functioning children from the reverse.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The low-functioning group achieved only 5.7% task success, so their classification may reflect general task non-engagement rather than a specific visual-orienting deficit, and their group assignment was based partly on failure to complete the Raven's test - a similar structured task; the attention-sustaining phase distinguishes the paradigm from conventional visual-orienting tasks and the authors note it may itself drive group differences; sex is 75-88% male across groups and untested; static rather than dynamic cues; no confidence intervals on any accuracy or AUC; no independent cohort or external site; and no data or code release.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The corpus's benchmark for methodological self-awareness. It names three specific failure patterns in the literature - subjective manual behavioural coding, binary classification that ignores heterogeneity, and feature selection on small samples producing record-wise validation and inflated accuracy - and adopts a concrete remedy for each, using raw gaze distributions, three-class classification by functioning level, and no feature selection whatever with a hyperparameter fixed from external data. Two results should carry weight in the synthesis. The first is the quantified cost of collapsing heterogeneity: 93.24% binary against 81.08% three-class on identical data. The second, and more important, is the cross-group transfer asymmetry - a model trained on typically developing versus high-functioning children identified every unseen low-functioning child, while the reverse transfer reached only 53.85% - which is direct evidence that the many studies in this corpus recruiting predominantly severely affected samples would not generalise to the milder presentations where screening is most needed. Its finding that non-social cues (arrows, fingers) discriminate nearly as well as gaze cues also bears on the corpus's widespread assumption that social attention is the relevant signal.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Three groups totalling 74 children: 26 high-functioning autistic, 24 low-functioning autistic and 24 typically developing, all age-matched. Splitting the autistic sample by cognitive functioning rather than treating it as homogeneous is the design's defining feature and is argued for explicitly, on the grounds that binary classification 'fails to take into account the heterogeneity in the ASD population' and that low-functioning autistic children may show behaviours confounded with developmental delay and even with 'normal people with autistic traits, such as stereotyped behaviors, aggression, and noncompliance'. No separate developmental-delay or other-diagnosis group. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'children with HFA', 'children with LFA', 'individuals with ASD', 'typically developing children'. Consistently person-first, including for the functioning subgroups. 'Low-functioning' and 'high-functioning' are used as technical designations tied to measured cognitive scores rather than as informal descriptors, and the paper defines them operationally. The framing is developmental and mechanism-oriented, discussing superior temporal sulcus activation and intention inference rather than burden or deficit. [RQ1.3] Typically developing: 24 children, 18 male and 6 female, 5.24 +/- 0.81 years, Raven raw 22.17 +/- 9.03, PPVT raw 80.38 +/- 30.16, SCQ 8.50 +/- 5.13. High-functioning autistic: 26 children, 23 male and 3 female, 5.08 +/- 0.83 years, Raven 20.77 +/- 10.83, PPVT 77.44 +/- 22.39, SCQ 12.23 +/- 6.92. Low-functioning autistic: 24 children, 19 male and 5 female, 4.98 +/- 1.09 years, Raven 11.00 +/- 2.00, PPVT 22.88 +/- 12.30, SCQ 17.32 +/- 5.23. All three groups are age-matched with no significant pairwise differences, and the high-functioning and typically developing groups are additionally matched on both nonverbal intelligence (t(48) = -.49, p = .624) and verbal intelligence (t(46) = -.95, p = .356) - so the critical contrast is IQ-controlled, which almost no other study in this corpus achieves. Sex proportions differ (75%, 88%, 79% male) and are not tested; the authors name this as a limitation. No ethnicity or socioeconomic data; recruitment from a Beijing specialised preschool for the clinical groups. [RQ1.4] Prior DSM-5 diagnoses made by professional pediatricians at licensed hospitals, corroborated by above-threshold scores on the Chinese SCQ for every autistic participant. The authors state plainly why the field standard was unavailable: 'We were unable to administer the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule or the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised to confirm the ASD diagnosis in our study since the Chinese translated versions of these two scales have not been officially released and validated.' This is a more informative disclosure than the silent omission found elsewhere in the corpus. Functioning subgroups were assigned by CRT-C2 and PPVT-R, with children failing to complete the Raven's test or scoring below the PPVT norm average classed as low-functioning - a criterion that partly conflates cognitive level with capacity to complete a structured test, which matters given that the outcome measure is also a structured task. [RQ1.5] The most complete cognitive characterisation in the corpus. Combined Raven's Test for nonverbal and PPVT-R for verbal mental intelligence, plus SCQ, administered to all three groups with means and standard deviations tabulated and all pairwise comparisons tested. These are not merely reported but used structurally - they define the functioning subgroups, they establish that the high-functioning and typically developing groups are matched on both intelligence measures, and they support the interpretation that visual-orienting performance tracks cognitive level. No adaptive functioning or comorbidity measures. [RQ2.1] Goal: classify three groups defined by diagnosis and cognitive functioning from raw gaze during a visual-orienting task, and test whether less-social directional cues also discriminate. Main findings: 81.08% three-class accuracy rising to 93.24% for binary autism versus typical development; success rates ranked 74.7%, 29.1% and 5.7% across typically developing, high-functioning and low-functioning groups; deficits appeared for arrow and finger cues as well as gaze cues, with removing either cue family costing accuracy; and cross-group tests showed a model trained on typically developing versus high-functioning children identified 100% of unseen low-functioning children while the reverse transfer achieved only 53.85%. [RQ2.2] Laboratory testing at Peking University, with autistic participants recruited from a preschool specialised for autistic children in Beijing. Funded by multiple National Natural Science Foundation of China grants, an NSFC/DFG collaborative research centre, a Guangdong key project on autism diagnosis and treatment tools, and a Beijing municipal science and technology grant. No conflicts of interest declared. [RQ2.3] A gamified visual-orienting task with a graded social-content manipulation - arrow, pointing finger, cartoon animal gaze, human gaze - crossed with four directions across 160 trials, using 160 distinct cue pictures and 640 distinct object pictures so that no stimulus repeats. The task requires not just an orienting saccade but sustained fixation on the target for 1000 ms to earn a reward, a design choice the authors justify from piloting: autistic children 'might occasionally choose one target, but then change their mind and fixate on another', so the long fixation window gives them the opportunity to revise. The 4000 ms trial limit was likewise set by piloting because 'some children with ASD would lose their attention during a trial'. The authors also flag that this attention-sustaining phase distinguishes their paradigm from conventional visual-orienting tasks and 'arguably contributes to the poor performance of children with ASD' - an unusually self-aware statement about what their own task measures. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single 15-minute session per child with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates over picture stimuli. Governance is fully reported: Helsinki conformity, named ethics committee approval at Peking University, written parental consent obtained before the experiment, and separate personal approval for publication of the photographs used as human-gaze cues. The experimenter was blind to functioning subgroup - 'the experimenter did not know a priori whether a child with ASD belonged to the LFA group or the HFA group' - which is a rare and worthwhile control. [RQ2.5] Tobii X120 at 120 Hz; a 25.5 x 34 cm display at 1024 x 768 viewed from approximately 60 cm; five-point calibration accepted only when mean visual angle error fell below 1 degree at all five points; Psychtoolbox on MATLAB for stimulus presentation; SPSS 20 for statistics. The calibration acceptance criterion is stated quantitatively, which few eye-tracking studies in this corpus do. [RQ2.6] Excellent. Reported: full stimulus inventory with picture counts, dimensions, resolution and spatial separation; the exact instruction wording; trial timing with the empirical rationale for both the 1000 ms fixation requirement and the 4000 ms limit; calibration procedure and acceptance threshold; fixation definition (50-pixel radius, 100 ms); all four areas of interest; per-group trial exclusion rates; the local-versus-global coordinate handling for randomly positioned regions; all 68 features enumerated by type and count; the classifier with its k values and the external source used to fix them; the cross-validation scheme; and complete confusion matrices with per-class sensitivity, specificity and AUC for both the three-class and binary problems. Missing only: data or code release, and the authors' own choice not to report feature importances, which follows from their no-selection stance. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged with four specific limitations: still rather than dynamic directional cues, whereas dynamic cues predominate in daily life; the attention-sustaining phase distinguishes this paradigm from conventional visual-orienting tasks and may itself drive the group differences, so future work should test whether the algorithms can separate autism from attention deficits; too few girls to test sex-specific performance, with the specific rationale that 'autistic girls exhibit more typical social attention than do autistic boys'; and that 'the predictive power of automatic classification techniques is constrained by the base rate of ASD in the population', so direct comparison against current diagnostic methods requires caution. The absence of ADOS and ADI-R is disclosed with its reason. Identifiable in review but not stated: the low-functioning group's 5.7% success rate means these children largely failed the task, so their classification may reflect general non-engagement rather than a visual-orienting deficit specifically; and the criterion for assigning children to that group included failure to complete the Raven's test, which partly conflates cognitive level with capacity to complete a structured assessment of the same general kind as the outcome task. [RQ2.9] Test dynamic directional cues; establish whether the method distinguishes autism from attention deficits, given that the attention-sustaining phase may be doing much of the work; recruit balanced numbers of girls and boys to test sex-specific performance; and treat base-rate constraints seriously when comparing automated classification against clinical diagnosis. [RQ3.1] Visual orienting - shifting and sustaining attention toward a target indicated by a directional cue - decomposed across four cue types spanning a social-content gradient from arrow through pointing finger and cartoon gaze to human gaze. Four behavioural quantities are measured: success rate, latency to disengage from the cue, and dwell time in the target, confound and uninformative regions. The social gradient is what makes the study theoretically informative rather than merely predictive: it permits the question of whether the deficit is social-specific, and the answer is that it is not. [RQ3.2] No cross-modal fusion - gaze only. The condition-level analysis serves the analogous purpose and yields a clear result: three-class accuracy falls from 81.08% to 78.4% using gaze cues alone and to 77.0% using non-gaze cues alone, so both cue families carry non-redundant information and the full set is better than either. This supports the paper's substantive claim that visual-orienting deficits in autism 'are not only tied to social cues but appear to be domain-general'. The behavioural analysis reinforces it: all three groups found face cues harder than arrow and finger cues, but the high-functioning group showed a cue-type effect on target dwell time that the low-functioning group did not, whose 'poor performance did not depend on the amount of social information contained in the cue picture'. [RQ4.1] k-nearest neighbours, deliberately simple, chosen for the low intrinsic dimensionality of gaze coordinates, for tolerance of overlapping class distributions and for small-sample performance. The single hyperparameter k was fixed by piloting on a different published dataset rather than tuned on the present data - so the entire model specification is set outside the evaluation, which removes the model-selection optimism that affects most of the corpus. No comparison against alternative classifiers is reported, which is a minor gap, but the choice is consistent with a paper whose stated aim is to avoid optimising anything on the evaluation data. [RQ4.2] Sixty-eight distributional statistics computed from raw gaze samples - eight moments and order statistics for x and y in each of four regions, plus sample counts per region - used in full without selection. Two design details matter. Samples were stacked across all trials within a condition, justified by the verified absence of a learning effect between the first and last 10 trials in any group or condition. And because targets and confounds appeared at random positions, gaze samples in those regions were converted to local coordinates while cue and other regions retained global coordinates, so that the distributional statistics describe gaze relative to the object rather than relative to the screen. The stated principle - features 'arbitrarily specified without a prior assumption' and used without selection - is the direct methodological answer to the selection-inflation problem the paper identifies in the literature. [RQ4.3] Complete: overall accuracy, per-class sensitivity and specificity, full confusion matrices and per-class ROC AUC for the three-class problem, the same for the collapsed binary problem, and accuracy for both cross-group generalisation tests. The confusion matrix is interpreted substantively rather than merely reported - errors concentrate on mislabelling the other groups as high-functioning, which the authors relate to that group's intermediate behavioural position and which explains its lowest specificity. Reporting the binary result alongside the three-class result quantifies exactly what collapsing heterogeneity buys: 93.24% versus 81.08%. [RQ4.4] No model-explanation method, and none is possible given the no-selection design - but interpretability is provided instead by an extensive parallel behavioural analysis with mixed-design ANOVAs, effect sizes and Bonferroni-corrected post hoc tests across four measures and four cue conditions. This establishes what the classifier is likely responding to: a strict group ordering in success rate and latency, longer dwell in confound and uninformative regions for both autistic groups, and a cue-type interaction present in the high-functioning group but absent in the low-functioning group. Scan-path visualisations for representative participants from each group make the qualitative differences legible. The interpretation offered - that low-functioning children's scan paths 'appeared to be more random and less purposeful' - is honest about being descriptive.
