[RQ4.5] Subject-wise leave-one-out cross-validation with no feature selection and a hyperparameter fixed from external data - about as clean an internal validation as this sample size permits, and argued for explicitly against record-wise alternatives with citation to the methodological literature on accuracy inflation. Beyond that, the two cross-group tests constitute a genuine generalisation experiment rarely attempted in this corpus: an entire group is withheld from training and used as an unseen population. The resulting asymmetry - 100% correct on unseen low-functioning children from a model trained on typically developing versus high-functioning, against 53.85% on unseen high-functioning children from a model trained on typically developing versus low-functioning - is interpreted correctly as showing that 'a model trained with more similar groups can perform well with test data from a disparate group, and a model trained with data from more different groups will underperform with test data from an intermediate group'. What remains absent is an independent cohort, an external site and any replication. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism diagnosis; autism screening; autism spectrum disorder; automatic classification; machine learning; visual orienting. 'Visual orienting' anchors the work in a specific and long-studied cognitive construct rather than in generic behavioural sensing, which is what allows the social-gradient manipulation to be theoretically interpretable. [RQ5.2] PsyCh Journal, 10(4), 550-565 - a psychology journal published by the Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences with Wiley. The venue explains the depth of the behavioural analysis relative to the modelling, and the two joint first authors span psychology and cognitive science. [RQ5.3] 2021. The framing is a systematic critique of three methodological patterns in the existing literature, each with a named remedy. First, that behavioural features in prior work 'often relied on manually labeled features such as the retrospective coding of children's behaviors in videotapes' which 'were essentially based on subjective ratings, which reduced the appeal of using machine learning algorithms' - remedied by using raw gaze samples. Second, that most studies performed binary classification, which 'fails to take into account the heterogeneity in the ASD population' - remedied by three-class classification including functioning level. Third, that brain-imaging classification 'is generally limited to adults or older children (over 7 years)' so that 'the application of machine learning to young children or infants, who are arguably in more need of automatic classification, is challenging' - remedied by a 15-minute child-friendly eye-tracking task. To these it adds the selection-inflation critique, singling out a named study reporting 96.7% after selecting an optimal feature set from 15 participants per group and noting that such practice 'is currently prevalent among medical studies with the machine learning techniques, and its overestimation of prediction accuracy should be cautioned'. That is the most precise methodological self-awareness in the corpus.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control classification; 92 Chinese children - 39 autistic (29 boys, 4-10 years) from a Shanghai children's service centre and 53 described as normal (27 boys, 2-15 years) - with 9 excluded for data loss or non-cooperation leaving 33 and 50; no diagnostic instrument reported; Tobii 4C eye and head tracking during a six-minute point-light biological motion animation; data not released.
narrative_rows.methods: Eye and head deviation angles sampled every 0.02 s across five animation stages of seven sub-stages each; the screen divided into six regions with gaze assigned by comparing eye deviation angle against a per-child default within an angular tolerance of 2.25; 43 features computed from three stated hypotheses - gaze-region occupancy rates per stage and overall, head-eye co-movement rates, and a binary clap-anticipation indicator thresholded at 0.55; KNN, Gaussian naive Bayes and cubic-kernel SVM trained on a single random split of 43 training and 40 testing children.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Cubic-kernel SVM 0.93 accuracy, 0.80 sensitivity, 1.00 specificity; Gaussian naive Bayes 0.90/0.80/0.96; KNN 0.80/0.60/0.92. Pearson correlations identified gaze at untrackable regions and head-eye co-movement as the most label-correlated features. Hypothesis 1 (greater inattention) was supported, hypothesis 3 (less clap anticipation) supported in direction but weakly correlated, and hypothesis 2 (more head-eye co-movement) refuted - the correlation ran negative.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No diagnostic instrument, criteria or clinician reported for either group, so the labels have no stated basis; no ethics approval or consent statement despite participants as young as two; groups differ untestedly in age (4-10 versus 2-15) and sex (74% versus 51% male) on an age-sensitive task; validation is a single unrepeated random split on 40 test children with no cross-validation and no confidence intervals; the two feature hyperparameters were set empirically with the authors noting other values could improve performance; the correlation analysis justifying the feature design used the full dataset including the test half; exclusion rates differ between groups; and the most predictive feature family, area0, is defined by the tracker's failure to resolve gaze.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Contributes two things to the review despite high risk of bias. First, it is the corpus's clearest example of hypothesis-driven feature engineering with honest reporting of a refuted prediction: three behavioural hypotheses are stated in advance, features are built to test each, and the authors report that head-eye co-movement went the opposite way to predicted and revise their interpretation accordingly. Second, it independently reproduces a pattern already visible elsewhere in the corpus - that the single strongest 'behavioural' feature is a measure of tracking failure. Here area0, gaze the device cannot resolve, is among the most label-correlated features and is interpreted as inattention; the same conflation of data quality with clinical signal appears in the Seattle Children's eye-tracking work, where a data-quality variable ranked third by SHAP importance. That convergence is worth carrying into the synthesis as a recurring measurement problem rather than an isolated quirk. Its use of head movement as a behavioural channel rather than a nuisance variable is also unusual and, despite the refuted hypothesis, methodologically suggestive.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups: 39 autistic children recruited from the Shanghai Putuo District Zhanyi Children Cultivation Service Center and 53 children described as normal, totalling 92. Nine samples were excluded for partial data loss or non-cooperation, leaving 83 - 33 autistic and 50 typically developing, so 6 autistic and 3 comparison children were removed, a differential exclusion rate of 15% versus 6% that is not commented on. No other-diagnosis comparison group. [RQ1.2] 'autistic children', 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'normal children', 'normal people'. The comparison group is consistently 'normal' rather than 'typically developing'. The framing is strongly deficit-oriented, opening with 'the mental retardation of ASD, which increases with age' and describing the aim as reducing 'the intellectual deficiency of autistic children'. This is among the more pathologising registers in the corpus and the developmental claim it opens with - that intellectual impairment in autism increases with age - is not a standard finding. [RQ1.3] Autistic group: 39 children, 29 boys and 10 girls, aged 4-10. Comparison group: 53 children, 27 boys and 26 girls, aged 2-15. No means, standard deviations, matching statement or statistical test is reported for either variable. Both differences are substantial: the comparison group is 51% male against 74%, and its age range brackets the clinical group at both ends, including children five years younger and five years older than any autistic participant. For a six-minute passive-viewing task with an abstract point-light stimulus, where the strongest feature is failure to maintain trackable gaze, an age spread from 2 to 15 years in one group only is a first-order confound. No IQ, language, severity, comorbidity or socioeconomic data. [RQ1.4] None. The autistic group is identified only by recruitment from a named children's service centre, with no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician, date or severity information anywhere in the paper. The comparison group's status as 'normal' is asserted without any screening. This is the weakest ascertainment among the included studies in this corpus, and it is particularly striking given that the paper's own introduction criticises existing diagnosis for depending on 'doctors' level of experience, which makes the diagnostic results quite subjective and variable' - the labels its models learn from come from exactly that unexamined source. [RQ1.5] None. No IQ, developmental, language, adaptive or severity measure, and no comorbidity information for either group. [RQ2.1] Goal: build an auxiliary autism diagnostic method from structured, interpretable eye-movement features rather than unstructured data. Main findings: cubic-kernel SVM achieved 0.93 accuracy, 0.80 sensitivity and 1.00 specificity; Gaussian naive Bayes 0.90/0.80/0.96 and KNN 0.80/0.60/0.92; gaze at untrackable regions and head-eye co-movement were the most label-correlated feature families; and the hypothesis that autistic children would show more head-eye co-movement was refuted, the correlation running in the opposite direction. [RQ2.2] Autistic participants were recruited from the Shanghai Putuo District Zhanyi Children Cultivation Service Center; no setting is stated for the comparison group and no laboratory conditions, lighting or viewing distance are described. Acknowledged support from two university research teams at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Shanghai University of Engineering Science. The first author is affiliated with a Shanghai high school. [RQ2.3] A six-minute point-light biological motion animation constructed from human skeletal figures with body keypoints, showing three behaviours in sequence: figures walking forward from distant to near, walking upside-down, and clapping hands. The stimulus choice is well motivated from the literature - typical viewers have 'a strong visual sensitivity to biological movement', autistic children show 'abnormal gaze towards scattered light points or rotating aperture', and have 'a lower tendency to immobilize biological moving objects'. Using abstract point-light figures rather than faces or naturalistic video isolates biological motion perception from face processing, which is a cleaner manipulation than most gaze studies in this corpus attempt. The upside-down walking condition in particular is the standard inversion control for biological motion, though the paper does not analyse it as such. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single six-minute session per child with no follow-up. Data are numeric eye and head deviation angles. No ethics committee approval, parental consent procedure, anonymisation or data governance statement appears anywhere, despite the sample including children as young as two recruited through a service centre for children with developmental needs. [RQ2.5] Tobii 4C eye tracker, which records head as well as eye movement - the feature that makes the head-eye co-movement hypothesis testable and distinguishes this setup from the gaze-only trackers used elsewhere in the corpus; a 29WK500-P monitor; and the biological motion animation from prior published work. Sampling at 0.02-second intervals (50 Hz). No calibration procedure, viewing distance or data-quality criteria are described. [RQ2.6] Mixed. Well specified: the three behavioural hypotheses, the six-region screen division, the rule mapping eye deviation angle to gaze region, the head-eye co-movement criterion, the clap-prediction rule, the complete 43-feature inventory with naming convention, the stage and sub-stage structure, the sampling period, both hyperparameter values, and the three classifiers with their mathematical definitions. Not specified: any diagnostic instrument; ethics approval; calibration procedure, viewing distance or data-quality thresholds; the value of k for KNN; how epsilon and tau were chosen; participant ages beyond ranges; and any data or code release. The complete absence of a diagnostic basis alongside a full derivation of the SVM kernel function is a striking imbalance of reporting effort. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged: the dataset is limited so 'comparisons cannot be simply drawn with other existing diagnostic methods, and more samples are needed for further analysis'; the clap-prediction feature 'needs to be further justified' given its weak correlation; and the hyperparameters were empirically set with the explicit note that 'different values could be set to gain a better performance'. The refutation of hypothesis 2 is reported clearly and the interpretation revised. Not acknowledged: no diagnostic instrument or criteria are reported for either group; no ethics approval; groups differ substantially in age (4-10 versus 2-15) and sex (74% versus 51% male) with no test or adjustment; validation is a single random split with no cross-validation or repetition, so the 40-child result carries wide sampling uncertainty; the correlation analysis validating the feature hypotheses used the full dataset including the test half; exclusion rates differ between groups (15% versus 6%); and the most predictive feature family, area0, is defined by the tracker's failure to resolve gaze, conflating attentional signal with equipment dropout. [RQ2.9] Collect more samples to permit meaningful comparison against existing diagnostic methods, and establish whether the clap-prediction feature is genuinely diagnostic given its weak observed correlation. [RQ3.1] Visual attention to point-light biological motion, decomposed three ways: where on the screen gaze falls across six regions and five animation stages, whether head and eye move together, and whether the child anticipates a repeated action. The head-eye co-movement measure is distinctive in this corpus - most eye-tracking studies discard head movement as a nuisance to be minimised, whereas here it is treated as a behavioural signal in its own right, hypothesised to index stereotyped head-shaking. That the hypothesis was refuted does not diminish the value of measuring it. [RQ3.2] No cross-modal fusion, but a within-session combination of eye and head channels from a single device, which is closer to fusion than most gaze studies here attempt. No ablation isolates the contribution of the head channel, though the correlation analysis identifies head-eye features among the most label-correlated, alongside the area0 gaze features. The temporal decomposition into five stages is a second axis of combination - features are computed per stage and pooled - but no analysis compares stages, so which phase of the animation carries the signal is not established despite the stage structure being built into the design. [RQ4.1] Three classical classifiers compared on identical features: KNN with Euclidean distance, Gaussian naive Bayes and a cubic-kernel SVM. The choice is appropriate for 83 samples and 43 features, and the paper's stated rationale for the whole approach - preferring structured interpretable features over unstructured deep learning inputs - is coherent and is followed through. The cubic kernel is an unusual choice, more prone to overfitting than the standard RBF at this sample size, and no justification for the polynomial degree is given. [RQ4.2] Forty-three features, every one traceable to one of three stated behavioural hypotheses, with a systematic naming convention (area-n-N for region n in stage N, plus per-region means). The representation is genuinely interpretable - each feature is a rate with a plain-language meaning - which serves the paper's clinical-support framing. Two design decisions bear scrutiny. Area0 is defined as an eye deviation angle of exactly zero, taken to mean gaze that 'cannot be tracked by the device', so a measurement artefact is promoted to a behavioural feature; this may capture real inattention but cannot distinguish it from tracker dropout, off-axis head position or non-compliance. And the region assignment depends on a single angular tolerance epsilon set to 2.25 by unspecified means, so the entire spatial feature family rests on one tuned constant. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity with confusion matrices for all three classifiers - adequate for a diagnostic framing and better than accuracy alone. The reported figures make the asymmetry visible: the best model detects 12 of 15 autistic children while correctly classifying 25 of 25 typically developing children, so it misses one autistic child in five. No AUC, precision, F1, confidence interval, per-split variability or statistical comparison between models, and with only 40 test children a single participant is worth 2.5 accuracy points, so the 0.93 versus 0.90 difference between the top two models is one child. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is the paper's organising principle rather than an afterthought. Every feature derives from a stated hypothesis, and the Pearson correlation heat map is used to test each hypothesis against the data and report the outcome - two supported, one refuted. The refutation is handled properly: head-eye co-movement correlated negatively with the label, so the conclusion states that autistic children 'show less head-eye co-movements than normal children (instead of positive correlation in the hypothesis 2)' while noting the feature remains diagnostically useful. The authors also draw a clinically directed conclusion, identifying which features 'doctors should pay attention to when diagnosing'. What is missing is any model-derived importance - the correlations are univariate and computed independently of the classifiers, so nothing establishes that the SVM actually uses the features the correlation analysis highlights. [RQ4.5] The weakest element. A single random split of 83 children into 43 training and 40 testing, with no cross-validation, no repetition over alternative splits, no held-out tuning set and no independent cohort. The two feature hyperparameters were set empirically with no procedure stated and an explicit acknowledgement that other values could improve performance, and the correlation analysis used to justify the feature design was computed across the entire dataset including the test half - so the features whose relevance is demonstrated on all 83 children are the same features evaluated on 40 of them. With a 40-child test set, the reported accuracies carry sampling uncertainty of roughly plus or minus 8 percentage points that is never quantified. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Auxiliary diagnosis, eye movement data, feature extraction, classification algorithms. 'Auxiliary diagnosis' is the operative framing - the tool is positioned as support for clinicians rather than as a replacement - and 'feature extraction' correctly identifies where the paper's effort went. [RQ5.2] 2021 IEEE 7th International Conference on Cloud Computing and Intelligent Systems (CCIS) - a computing conference. The first author is a high-school student, with university co-authors from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and the University of Washington, which is relevant context for the level of methodological review the work received. [RQ5.3] 2021. The framing is the standard subjectivity argument - diagnosis 'mainly relies on experts' comprehensive clinical analysis of children, which is usually subjective and highly dependent on doctors' individual professional skills' - with an added emphasis on pre-verbal assessment, aiming to 'diagnose children without linguistic ability in an early stage'. Its distinctive contribution to the corpus's framing is a preference for structured over unstructured data: it observes that 'most of the studies focus on unstructured data, which has complicated correlations among numerous parameters' and argues that 'it is highly desired to develop an effective auxiliary diagnostic method for ASD with the utilization of structured data'. That is an argument for interpretability over raw predictive power, and it is one of the few places in this corpus where the trade-off is stated as a design principle rather than discovered after the fact. The biological motion rationale is also well grounded, citing the classic finding of strong visual sensitivity to biological movement in typical viewers against reports of abnormal gaze to point-light displays in autism.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control classification with modality ablation; 42 Chinese children aged 3-6 (21 autistic, 21 typically developing) with no diagnostic instrument, ages, sexes or clinical characterisation reported; six minutes of 128-channel resting EEG plus seven eye-tracking paradigms; data not released.
narrative_rows.methods: EEG filtered 0.5-45 Hz, ICA-cleaned, reduced to 8 electrodes and epoched into 4-second segments, yielding seven features across time, time-frequency, synchronisation and four entropy domains; seven gaze features derived from cumulative area-of-interest fixation durations, one per viewing test, selected by random forest; all 14 features formed nodes of a graph whose edges were thresholded inter-feature covariances, convolved by a graph convolutional network and evaluated on a single 8:2 split against single-modality baselines, an mRMR-plus-SVM pipeline and a ResNet18 over concatenated features.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Fused GCN 0.9500 on accuracy, precision, recall and F1; gaze alone 0.7895 accuracy and EEG alone 0.7368; the conventional concatenation pipeline 0.8100 and ResNet18 0.7000. Feature-wise t-tests found the largest EEG differences for the time-domain mean, approximate entropy and wavelet entropy, and the largest gaze differences for unfamiliar own-race faces and social interaction, with joint attention non-significant. Cross-modal covariance edges linked EEG synchronisation and entropy features to face, joint attention and social interaction gaze paradigms despite asynchronous recording.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The unit of the 8:2 split is never stated and the reported accuracies are arithmetically incompatible with participant-level splitting of 42 children, corresponding instead to roughly 20 samples, which with 4-second EEG epoching implies segment-level division and leakage; no diagnostic instrument, criteria or clinician for either group and no dataset provenance; participant description limited to two group sizes and an age range with matching asserted but unquantified; t-tests and the covariance thresholds defining the graph structure computed over the full dataset; a single unrepeated split with no confidence intervals; 120 of 128 EEG channels discarded for computational convenience; and no limitations section.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Contributes the corpus's most architecturally considered fusion design - a graph whose nodes are features and whose edges are inter-feature covariances, so that convolution exploits relationships within and across modalities rather than treating concatenated features as a flat vector - together with the ablation needed to assess it, including a ResNet18 on concatenated features that performs worst of all and thereby separates fusion mechanism from model capacity. Its covariance edge analysis is a rare attempt to make a fusion model's internal structure interpretable as substantive claims about EEG-gaze relationships. Two findings should carry into the synthesis independently of the contested accuracy figure: gaze alone outperformed EEG alone in the same pipeline, and across seven distinct gaze paradigms it was unfamiliar own-race face viewing and social interaction that discriminated, while joint attention did not - which cuts against the prominence joint attention receives elsewhere in this corpus. The record is also a clear instance of a paper whose validation unit is unstated and whose reported metrics reveal it not to be the participant.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups of 21 children each, aged 3-6, totalling 42. No other-diagnosis comparison group. Nothing further is reported about either group - no ages beyond the shared range, no sexes, no clinical characterisation - and because no provenance for the dataset is given, nothing can be recovered from a source publication either. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'children with typically developing (TD)', 'ASD children', 'TD children', 'subjects'. Predominantly person-first with 'typically developing' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy'. The framing is neuroscience-oriented rather than deficit-focused, describing autism as 'an early-onset neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by the impairments in social communication and repetitive behaviors' and motivating the work by the claim that bio-signal analysis 'can provide more reliable evaluation of children ASD than traditional methods of behavior measurement relying on scales do'. [RQ1.3] Almost nothing. Two groups of 21 children aged between 3 and 6, with the single sentence 'No statistical differences in age and gender are observed between ASD and TD groups' offered in place of any figures - no means, standard deviations, sex counts or test statistics for either variable. For a study whose gaze features are cumulative fixation durations during face and social viewing, and whose EEG features include entropy measures that change substantially across early childhood, a three-year age band with no distributional information is a material gap. No IQ, language, severity, comorbidity, ethnicity or socioeconomic data. [RQ1.4] None reported. There is no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician, assessment date or severity measure anywhere in the paper for the autistic group, and no screening described for the comparison group. The dataset's apparatus (128-channel HydroCel), age range (3-6), ethics committee (Beijing Normal University) and gaze paradigms (own-race and other-race face viewing) match a separately published study, which suggests secondary analysis of an existing cohort - but no such provenance, citation or diagnostic inheritance is stated, so the labels have no traceable basis within this paper. [RQ1.5] None. No IQ, developmental, language, adaptive or severity measure, and no comorbidity information for either group. [RQ2.1] Goal: fuse EEG and eye-tracking features through a graph convolutional network over a covariance-derived feature graph, improving on simple feature- or decision-level fusion. Main findings: 95% accuracy for the fused model against 79% for gaze alone and 74% for EEG alone; 81% for a conventional mRMR-plus-SVM pipeline and 70% for ResNet18 on concatenated features; gaze alone outperformed EEG alone; and covariance analysis revealed cross-modal relationships between EEG synchronisation and entropy features and face, joint attention and social interaction gaze paradigms despite asynchronous recording. [RQ2.2] EEG recorded in a shielded room and eye tracking conducted subsequently; ethics approval indicates Beijing Normal University while the analysis was conducted at Wuhan University's School of Computer Science. No recruitment route, period or clinical setting is described. [RQ2.3] The broadest gaze battery in the corpus - seven distinct tests targeting own-race unfamiliar faces (twice), other-race unfamiliar faces, joint attention, gaze following (twice) and social interaction, each photograph type presented six times for 10 seconds. This design permits the informative negative finding that joint attention was the least discriminative gaze feature (t = -0.79, non-significant) while unfamiliar own-race face viewing was the most discriminative - the opposite of what much of this corpus assumes. Resting EEG precedes the gaze battery rather than being recorded concurrently, which is why the cross-modal covariances the paper reports are between asynchronously acquired signals. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single visit per child comprising sequential EEG and eye-tracking sessions, with no follow-up. Data are EEG traces and gaze fixation summaries. Governance is reported: conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki, approved by the ethics committee of Beijing Normal University, with written informed consent provided. [RQ2.5] 128-channel HydroCel Sensor Net (Electrical Geodesics) sampled at 256 Hz in a shielded room; eye tracking at 300 Hz with five-point calibration required to pass with small error vectors; EEGLAB for ICA-based artefact removal. Notably, only 8 of 128 electrodes (F3, F4, T3, C3, C4, T4, O1, O2) were retained, justified solely as being 'in order to reduce computational overhead' - a substantial discard of spatial information for a stated engineering rather than scientific reason. [RQ2.6] Mixed. Well specified: EEG preprocessing chain with filter band, sampling rate, referencing, ICA artefact removal, electrode selection and 4-second non-overlapping epochs; the seven eye-tracking tests with their purposes and presentation schedule; the 60 ms fixation threshold; the fourteen features by name; both comparator architectures including ResNet18 channel configuration; and complete t-statistics for every feature. Not specified: any diagnostic instrument; participant ages, sexes or matching statistics; the unit of the 8:2 split; the covariance threshold used to build the adjacency matrix; GCN layer configuration, training hyperparameters or random seed; and the random forest configuration used for gaze feature selection. No code, and a data availability statement that points to the article itself. [RQ2.7] Essentially none. The paper has no limitations section and offers no caveats on sample size, generalisability or validation design. Identifiable in review: the reported accuracies are arithmetically incompatible with a participant-level 80/20 split of 42 children and correspond instead to 19 of 20, 14 of 19 and 15 of 19 samples, which combined with 4-second EEG epoching implies segment-level splitting and hence leakage across the train/test boundary; no diagnostic instrument or criteria are reported for either group; age and sex matching is asserted with no figures; the t-tests and covariance thresholds defining the graph structure were computed on the full dataset including test samples; validation is a single unrepeated split with no confidence intervals; and the reduction from 128 to 8 electrodes is justified only computationally. [RQ2.9] None stated beyond the general remark that the approach 'holds potentials in the applications when concerning fusing much more data sources'. [RQ3.1] Gaze allocation across seven distinct social-viewing paradigms - own-race and other-race unfamiliar faces, joint attention, gaze following and social interaction - each reduced to a cumulative fixation duration measure within areas of interest. The behavioural coverage is broader than any other single study in the corpus, and the per-paradigm t-tests make it possible to see which constructs actually discriminate: unfamiliar own-race faces and social interaction do, joint attention and one of the two gaze-following tests do not. [RQ3.2] The corpus's most architecturally ambitious fusion, and the ablation is properly constructed. Single-modality baselines using identical features and pipeline give 0.7368 for EEG and 0.7895 for gaze, against 0.9500 fused - a gain of over 15 points on the better single modality. Two comparators isolate the mechanism: a conventional pipeline concatenating features with mRMR selection and SVM reaches 0.8100, and a ResNet18 over concatenated features reaches only 0.7000 despite far greater capacity, which the authors read as showing that 'simply and rudely cascading EEG and eye-tracking recordings cannot make good use of multi-modality information'. The graph formulation itself is the contribution: features are nodes, thresholded covariances are edges, so convolution operates over discovered inter-feature structure rather than over a flat concatenation. The interpretive payoff is the cross-modal edge analysis, which identifies EEG synchronisation as related to exotic face, joint attention and gaze-following features, and entropy measures as related to face, joint attention and social interaction features - relationships that exist despite the two signals being recorded at different times. The caveat is that all of this rests on an accuracy figure whose validation unit is not stated and appears not to be the participant. [RQ4.1] A graph convolutional network over a feature graph, with random forest for upstream gaze feature selection, compared against an SVM-based feature-engineering pipeline and a ResNet18. The GCN choice is well matched to the stated problem - modelling relationships between features across modalities where no explicit correlation exists between the raw signals - and using features rather than subjects as graph nodes is an unusual and defensible formulation. That the much deeper ResNet18 performs worst supports the argument that architecture matched to the fusion problem matters more than capacity at this sample size. [RQ4.2] Fourteen features total - seven EEG spanning time domain, time-frequency, synchronisation and four complexity measures, and seven gaze features corresponding one-to-one with the seven viewing tests. This is an extremely compact representation, and the one-feature-per-paradigm structure on the gaze side means each node carries the summary of an entire experimental condition, which is what makes the covariance edges interpretable as relationships between constructs rather than between arbitrary statistics. The corresponding cost is that all spatial detail within each gaze paradigm - which areas of interest were fixated - is collapsed, and 120 of 128 EEG channels are discarded. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for the proposed model and all three comparators, plus t-statistics and p-values for every feature. Reporting all four metrics across a full ablation is good practice, and the single-modality baselines make the fusion gain directly readable. Missing: AUC, confusion matrices, confidence intervals and any statistical test between models - and with a test set of roughly 20 samples, the difference between 0.95 and 0.81 is about three samples. That all four metrics for the proposed method are exactly 0.9500 indicates a balanced test set of 20 with a single error. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is pursued at two levels and is the paper's strongest non-architectural contribution. Univariate t-tests establish which individual features differ between groups, with results interpreted against prior literature - reduced theta increase and stronger beta in autism for the comparator's band features, and greater differences in eye and body fixation. More distinctively, the adjacency matrix is analysed edge by edge to describe which features relate to which, both within EEG (mean value related to all but STFT; approximate entropy unrelated to sample entropy; STFT unrelated to entropy measures because 'entropy based features are calculated to measure the complexity of time series while STFT is a localized process in time and frequency domains') and across modalities. This turns the model's structure into a substantive claim about EEG-gaze relationships rather than leaving it as an implementation detail. [RQ4.5] The weakest element and the one that governs how the headline should be read. A single 8:2 split with no cross-validation, no repetition and no held-out tuning set. The unit of splitting is never stated, and the reported figures indicate it is not the participant: 42 children split 80/20 gives roughly 8 test children, on which 0.9500, 0.7368 and 0.7895 are unattainable, whereas they correspond precisely to 19/20, 14/19 and 15/19 samples. With EEG divided into 4-second epochs yielding roughly 90 segments per child, sample-level splitting would place segments from the same child on both sides of the boundary. Additionally, the t-tests and the covariance thresholding that determines the graph's edge structure were computed across the entire dataset, so the graph topology the network convolves over was constructed using test-sample information. There is no independent cohort, no external site and no replication. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, EEG, eye-tracking, multi-modality fusion, graph convolution network. Three of five concern the fusion method rather than the clinical problem, which accurately reflects a paper whose contribution is architectural. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 15, article 651349, in the Cognitive Neuroscience section - a neuroscience venue, though the work is primarily a machine learning contribution and the authors are all from a computer science school. [RQ5.3] 2021. The framing is a two-stage critique. First, that single-modality analysis is inherently limited because 'the bio-marker information carried by the bio-signal of a single-modality is likely insufficient or distorted' - an argument for fusion on information-theoretic rather than merely empirical grounds. Second, and more specific, that existing fusion work 'mainly rely on feature-level fusion or decision-level fusion' and that 'these simple kinds of fusion strategies may not make full use of modality-cross information, thus the performances are largely limited'. The paper then demonstrates this empirically by implementing both a feature-concatenation baseline and a deep network over concatenated features, and showing the latter performs worst. It also grounds the cross-modal premise in developmental neuroscience, citing work linking frontolimbic connectivity at 6 months to responding-to-joint-attention at 9 months, and studies finding eye-tracking and EEG measures correlated during social stimulation - so the fusion argument rests on a claimed functional relationship rather than on an assumption that more data helps.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional within-autism severity classification with no non-autistic comparison group; 88 of 91 recruited Brazilian children and adolescents aged 3-16, split by CARS into 39 severe (mean 39.4) and 49 non-severe (mean 33.1), all DSM-5 diagnosed by a child psychiatry specialist and clinically stable for at least three months; gaze recorded on a Tobii Pro TX300 during a 54-second geometric-versus-social preference video; data not released.
narrative_rows.methods: Video frames were edge-trimmed, resized and grouped by similarity from 1,590 to 135 groups; class fixation maps were built by pooling fixations within each severity group; 27 image features spanning pixel, object and semantic levels were computed per pixel and reduced by ReliefF independently for each group; a ten-neuron single-hidden-layer network with Bayesian regularisation was trained per group to predict pixel fixation, generating class saliency maps binarised at 0.75; participants were classified by which class saliency map their own fixation map matched across frame groups, with a 20-of-40 threshold set by Youden index, under five-fold subject-level cross-validation.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Mean ROC AUC 0.85, maximum 0.88. At the selected threshold: precision 70%, sensitivity 87%, specificity 60%, error 25%, with a reported accuracy of 88% that is inconsistent with those figures and matches the maximum AUC. Feature selection retained 15 features for the non-severe model and 12 for the severe model, with presence of face and presence of skin selected only for the non-severe group. Vineland scores were 17.61% lower in the severe group (p = 0.0006).
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Reported performance figures are mutually inconsistent - error of 25% implies 75% accuracy while 88% is reported, matching the separately reported maximum AUC; specificity of 60% means two in five non-severe participants are misclassified; sex differs significantly between severity groups (55% versus 31% male, p = 0.02) with the severe group majority female and no adjustment, on a model whose discriminating features are face and skin presence; ReliefF feature selection is not stated to be nested within cross-validation folds although the group-specific feature sets are the main finding; the 20-frame decision threshold was fitted on the evaluation ROC; no IQ data; age restricted to 3-16; no data or code release.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: One of the few corpus studies targeting severity gradation rather than diagnosis, and the only one to make the classifier itself the instrument of a mechanistic hypothesis. By fitting a separate visual attention model to each severity group and comparing which image attributes each retains, it produces a dissociation with meaning independent of predictive accuracy: presence of face and presence of skin predict where non-severe participants look but not where severe participants look, while low-level pixel features predict both - evidence that top-down semantic guidance of attention degrades with severity while bottom-up guidance persists. Its paradigm choice is also instructive for severity work, being deliberately short, audio-free and usable with nonverbal participants, so it does not systematically exclude the severe end of the range being measured. Two cautions carry forward: its headline accuracy is internally inconsistent and appears to be an AUC restated, and its severe group is majority female against a population ratio favouring males, an imbalance the authors interpret substantively but do not control for.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] A single clinical population of 88 autistic children and adolescents, split by CARS into 39 severe and 49 non-severe, from 91 recruited. There is no typically developing comparison group and none is intended - the research question is whether severity can be graded within autism, which makes this one of very few studies in the corpus addressing gradation rather than detection. Exclusions were calibration problems, eye-tracking record rate below 80% and age over 17, applied to three participants. [RQ1.2] 'individuals with ASD', 'patients with ASD', 'ASD children', 'individuals with typical development'. Mixed person-first and 'patients', the latter reflecting recruitment from a psychiatry institute. The framing is clinical and severity-oriented, describing autism as classifiable by severity 'based on the degree of impairment in social communication, repetitive and restricted behavior patterns and also according to the need for support', and motivating the work by the claim that 'the categorization of individuals with ASD into levels contributes to the intervention, which directly impacts the prognosis'. [RQ1.3] Non-severe group: 49 participants, 27 male and 22 female, aged 3-16 with mean 8.8 +/- 3.2, CARS 30-36 with mean 33.1 +/- 2.0. Severe group: 39 participants, 12 male and 27 female, aged 3-16 with mean 8.7 +/- 3.9, CARS 36.5-46.5 with mean 39.4 +/- 2.6. Age is well matched (p = 0.900) with identical ranges. Sex is not: 55% male against 31%, p = 0.02, so the severe group is majority female against a population sex ratio of roughly 3:1 male. The authors engage with this substantively, citing literature both supporting and contesting greater severity in autistic females and noting that the ratio falls to 2:1 when restricted to low-functioning or intellectually disabled subgroups - but they do not adjust for sex in the model. Vineland scores were significantly lower in the severe group (p = 0.0006) while Repetitive Behavior Scale scores did not differ (p = 0.104). No IQ data, which the authors identify as a limitation. [RQ1.4] Assessment by a specialist in child and adolescent psychiatry against DSM-5 criteria, with CARS above 30 required for inclusion, so every participant carries both a categorical diagnosis and a dimensional severity score. Clinical stability was additionally required - no medication or no change for at least three months - which controls a source of variability almost no other study in this corpus addresses. The severity split at CARS 36 follows a cited convention. What is missing is any account of who performed the CARS, with what training or reliability, and whether ADOS or ADI-R were available. [RQ1.5] Strong for a severity study. CARS for all participants with group ranges and means; Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales and the Repetitive Behavior Scale-Revised administered 'when possible'. The Vineland result is used substantively - significantly lower adaptive functioning in the severe group corroborates the CARS-based split from an independent instrument, which is the correct way to validate a severity dichotomy. The absence of IQ is acknowledged as a limitation and proposed as a future model feature. [RQ2.1] Goal: test whether autism severity can be classified from gaze via a visual attention model, and whether semantic top-down attentional guidance degrades with severity. Main findings: mean ROC AUC 0.85 with sensitivity 87% and specificity 60%; presence of face and presence of skin were selected as predictive features only for the non-severe group; the non-severe model retained more features overall (15 versus 12); and the CARS severity split was corroborated by significantly lower Vineland scores in the severe group. [RQ2.2] The Psychiatry Institute of the University of Sao Paulo School of Medicine, with acknowledgement to the Autism Spectrum Disorder Program of the Clinics Hospital (PROTEA-HC). Funded by CAPES and the Brazilian National Program to Support Health Care for Persons with Disabilities. Ethics approval from the School of Medicine research ethics board under protocol 17556019.8.0000.0068. [RQ2.3] The geometric-versus-social preference paradigm - nine videos totalling 54 seconds at 30 fps and 1920 x 1080, with social scenes of children playing or doing yoga on one side of the screen competing against randomly varying fractals on the other. The paradigm is chosen for reasons of clinical reach rather than theoretical richness, and the reasons are stated: it 'has the advantage of being short and does not require audio, it can be used in nonverbal and at any age'. This matters for a severity study, since a paradigm requiring verbal instruction or sustained compliance would systematically exclude the severe end of the range being measured. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single 54-second viewing session per participant with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates over video stimuli. Governance is properly reported: research ethics board approval with a full protocol number and Helsinki conformity. Clinical stability over the preceding three months was required for inclusion. [RQ2.5] Tobii Pro TX300 at 300 Hz with stated processing latency of 1-3.3 ms; 23-inch screen at 50-70 cm; Tobii Pro Studio; five-point calibration with animated figures at the corners and centre; MATLAB 8.5 R2015a with mexopencv for the attention model; RStudio for statistics. Data quality was enforced as an exclusion criterion - participants with an eye-tracking record rate below 80% were excluded, which is a stricter and more explicit quality gate than most of the corpus applies. [RQ2.6] Good. Reported: full stimulus specification with duration, frame rate and resolution; viewing distance, screen size and calibration procedure; the exclusion criteria including the 80% record-rate threshold; all 27 candidate features itemised by level; the frame preprocessing chain including edge removal, resizing, transition-frame deletion and the 33%-difference grouping rule that reduced 1,590 frames to 135; both pixel-sampling strategies with counts; the complete neural network architecture, activation functions, training algorithm, learning rate and stopping criteria; the 0.75 binarisation threshold; the 20-frame decision rule and how it was chosen; the cross-validation scheme with its subject-level unit; and the statistical tests with normality checking. Missing: whether ReliefF was nested within folds, the identity of the selected features beyond their counts by category, any data or code release, and reconciliation of the inconsistent performance figures. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged: that the saliency-map approach needs testing with different visual inputs 'in order to validate the relevant features'; that the age range is restricted to 3-16 while autism is lifelong; that the sample is small; and that the sex imbalance between groups is a limitation. Analysing IQ as an additional feature is proposed. Not acknowledged: the reported accuracy of 88% is inconsistent with the reported error rate of 25% and with the reported sensitivity and specificity, and coincides exactly with the separately reported maximum ROC AUC; ReliefF feature selection is not stated to be nested within cross-validation folds, so the group-specific feature sets that constitute the paper's main finding may have been chosen using all the data; and the 20-frame decision threshold was fitted by Youden index on the same ROC used for evaluation. [RQ2.9] Test the method with different visual inputs to validate which features are genuinely relevant rather than paradigm-specific; extend the age range beyond 3-16 given that autism is lifelong; enlarge the sample and address the sex imbalance; and incorporate intelligence quotient as an additional model feature. [RQ3.1] Visual attention during competition between social and geometric content, analysed not as how much is looked at but as what predicts where gaze lands. The unit of analysis is the pixel: for each pixel, a 27-dimensional feature vector describing its image properties at pixel, object and semantic levels, with the model learning which properties predict fixation for each severity group. This reframes the behavioural question from a preference measure to an attentional-guidance measure, which is what allows the top-down versus bottom-up interpretation. [RQ3.2] No cross-modal fusion - gaze only. The combination that matters is across levels of image representation, and the design makes this an explicit test rather than an implicit one. The three feature levels map onto the two mechanisms the paper is interested in: pixel-level features index bottom-up attention driven by image statistics, semantic-level features index top-down attention driven by prior knowledge, and object-level features sit between. The finding that the two semantic features survive selection only in the non-severe group, while pixel-level features survive in both, is a direct within-modality dissociation supporting the hypothesis that severity impairs top-down more than bottom-up attentional guidance. [RQ4.1] An unusual architecture for this corpus: rather than training one discriminative classifier on participant-level features, the paper trains one small generative model per severity group - each a ten-neuron single-hidden-layer network with Bayesian regularisation, predicting whether a pixel was fixated by that group - and then classifies a new participant by which group's saliency map their own fixation map more closely resembles. This is a nearest-prototype scheme in saliency space. It has two consequences worth noting: the model is small enough to be well conditioned on the available data, and the comparison of the two fitted models is itself the scientific output, which is why the feature-selection difference is reported as the main finding rather than as an ablation. [RQ4.2] Twenty-seven image features at three levels of abstraction, computed per pixel, reduced by ReliefF to 15 for the non-severe model and 12 for the severe model. The representation describes the stimulus rather than the participant, with the participant entering only through which pixels they fixated - an inversion of the usual arrangement in this corpus, where features describe gaze behaviour directly. Frame reduction from 1,590 to 135 groups by a 33% pixel-difference criterion is a sensible efficiency measure for 54 seconds of video, and discarding the ten frames either side of each video transition removes the change-detection artefacts that would otherwise dominate. [RQ4.3] Precision, sensitivity, specificity, error and accuracy plus a ROC curve with mean and maximum AUC - a full set on paper, but the values do not reconcile. Error of 25% implies accuracy of 75%; sensitivity of 87% with specificity of 60% on a 39-severe, 49-non-severe split implies roughly 72%; and the headline 88% matches the separately reported maximum AUC of 0.88 exactly. The internally consistent reading is that the classifier achieves roughly 75% accuracy with 87% sensitivity and 60% specificity, and that mean AUC is 0.85. That specificity of 60% is the more informative figure for a severity-grading tool: two in five non-severe participants would be labelled severe. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is the paper's organising purpose rather than an add-on. By fitting a separate attention model per severity group and comparing their retained feature sets, the analysis yields a directly interpretable dissociation - presence of face and presence of skin predict fixation for non-severe participants but not for severe ones - which is then connected to the wider literature on reduced face and eye-region looking in autism and on face perception relating to social-impairment severity. The authors correctly note the partial redundancy between skin and face features as reinforcing rather than duplicating the finding, and identify the single differing non-semantic feature as a steerable pyramid component that indexes edges, texture and orientation and 'is not related to object recognition'. The conclusion drawn - that top-down mechanisms differentiate severity more than bottom-up ones - is well supported by the structure of the result, subject to the caveat that the feature selection may not have been nested within folds. [RQ4.5] Five-fold cross-validation with splitting stated explicitly at the subject level, which is the correct unit and is clearly described. Folds were proportionally balanced. Two elements fall outside the loop. ReliefF feature selection is described once, per group, with no statement that it was repeated within folds - and since the group-specific feature sets are the paper's principal scientific claim, whether they were derived using all 88 participants or only training-fold participants materially affects their status. The 20-frame decision threshold was chosen by the Youden index applied to the ROC curve, which is the same curve used to characterise performance, so the operating point is fitted to the evaluation. There is no independent cohort, no external site and no held-out replication. [RQ5.1] Index terms: Autism Spectrum Disorder, Severity Level, Supervised Machine Learning, Classifier, Eye Tracking. 'Severity Level' as a headline term marks this as one of the few corpus studies whose target is gradation rather than detection. [RQ5.2] 2021 IEEE 34th International Symposium on Computer-Based Medical Systems (CBMS), pages 142-147 - a medical informatics conference, with authorship spanning a university psychiatry department, a bioinformatics programme and a computing school. The same institution and venue as another corpus record on joint attention trajectories, from an overlapping author group. [RQ5.3] 2021. The framing is that severity classification is under-explored relative to diagnosis - 'although we know little about its potential use in severity classification, in literature there are some important clues about the use of eye tracking in symptom severity' - and it assembles those clues carefully: a reported correlation of r = -0.52 between fixation on social stimuli and ADOS social scores; evidence that geometric preference predicts later symptom severity and joint-attention gaze shifting; and a finding that autistic children preferring the geometric side scored worse on ADOS, Mullen and Vineland alike. Its methodological argument is that region-of-interest analysis, which dominates the field, discards information: 'although using all the image information and visual attention models... could be more informative'. It builds directly on a 2015 three-level saliency study that found semantic features important in characterising autistic viewing and 'suggesting top-down impairments', and extends that from diagnosis to severity - which is a genuinely incremental and well-posed research question rather than a reapplication of an existing method to a new dataset.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control classification using live dyadic interaction; 43 Chinese children enrolled and 39 analysed - 19 autistic (99.6 months, 17 male, IQ 100.8) recruited from a Shenzhen hospital child psychiatry department and 20 typically developing (108.8 months, 17 male, IQ 116.1) from local schools; diagnosis by tiered DSM-IV psychiatric assessment without ADOS or ADI-R; head-mounted eye-tracking data not released.
narrative_rows.methods: Children wore Tobii Pro Glasses 2 during a structured four-session conversation with a blinded female interviewer at 80 cm, covering general questions, hobby sharing, ten yes-no questions and question raising; gaze was mapped to four areas of interest (eyes, mouth, face, whole body) by Tobii Pro Lab real-world mapping with human verification and manual correction, using a 30 deg/s, 60 ms fixation filter; 16 fixation-percentage features and 5 session-duration features were fed to SVM, LDA, decision tree and random forest classifiers under forward feature selection with leave-one-out cross-validation.
narrative_rows.outcomes: SVM reached 92.31% accuracy with three features - total session length, mouth fixation in session 1 and whole body fixation in session 3 - at 100% specificity and 84.21% sensitivity (AUC 0.92). Fixation features alone and session length features alone each reached 84.62%. Total session length alone gave 79.49%. Autistic children fixated less on mouth, face and body in the early sessions but showed no difference in eye-region fixation in any session, and took significantly longer to complete the same fixed set of questions.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Forward feature selection maximises the same leave-one-out accuracy that is reported, with the maximum quoted across 21 feature counts, four classifiers and three feature sets and no outer loop, so 92.31% is optimistically biased; IQ differs by 15.3 points between groups (p = .02) with no adjustment, on a task whose leading feature is conversation duration; severity was not measured and severe presentations were excluded, with the sample described as representing minor severity; only four girls participated; no other-diagnosis comparison group; head-mounted tracking may itself alter autistic children's behaviour; only fixation percentage was computed from a much richer available feature space; no ethics approval number and no data or code release.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The corpus's only study to record gaze during an actual conversation rather than a screen-based task, and its argument for doing so - that gaze is context-sensitive, that face-to-face interaction is perceptually and cognitively harder than image viewing, and that a present social partner elicits different neural and gaze responses - is the clearest statement in the corpus of an ecological-validity problem affecting most of the rest of it. Two results deserve particular weight in the synthesis. First, total conversation length alone classified at 79.49%, so the time a child took to complete a fixed set of exchanges was more informative than any gaze feature - a finding that both reframes what the eye tracker contributes and suggests a far simpler and cheaper measure captures much of the signal. Second, eye-region fixation did not differ between groups in any of the four conversational sessions, a direct null against the field's canonical finding, obtained in precisely the setting where eye contact should matter most. The study also models good practice on several fronts other studies neglect: a computed majority-class baseline, an empirical check that the blinded interviewer behaved consistently across groups, participants unaware their gaze was recorded, and an individual-level error analysis showing the three missed autistic children fell within the typical range on every selected feature.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups: 20 autistic children recruited from the Child Psychiatry Department of Shenzhen Kangning Hospital and 23 typically developing children from local schools, with four excluded for eye-tracking technical problems leaving 19 and 20. No other-diagnosis comparison group, and the authors identify this as a substantive limitation rather than a scope note: 'it remains unclear whether eye-tracking data could effectively detect ASD from other clinical phenotypes (eg, developmental delay and ADHD)'. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'children with typical development (TD)', 'healthy children'. Consistently person-first with 'typical development' as the comparison term, though 'healthy children' appears in the inclusion criteria. The framing locates the diagnostic problem in procedure rather than person: current diagnosis 'involves substantive subjective procedures that can be negatively impacted by various factors such as caregivers' reporting bias and clinicians' insufficient capability in differentiating ASD', and is 'highly labor- and time-demanding due to the shortage in clinical specialists'. [RQ1.3] Autistic group: 19 analysed, 17 male and 2 female, mean age 99.6 +/- 25.1 months, mean IQ 100.8 +/- 22.7. Typically developing group: 20 analysed, 17 male and 3 female, mean age 108.8 +/- 27.0 months, mean IQ 116.1 +/- 22.7. Age (p = .28) and sex ratio (p = .68) are well matched and formally tested. IQ is not - the groups differ by 15.3 points (p = .02) - and this is reported in the demographic table but not adjusted for anywhere in the modelling, which matters given that the single most informative feature is how long a child took to complete a conversation. Only four girls participated in total, which the authors name as a limitation with the specific rationale that autistic males and females differ in behavioural presentation, cognitive domains and emotions. No ethnicity or socioeconomic data. [RQ1.4] A tiered clinical procedure described in more detail than most of the corpus: DSM-IV diagnosis by a licensed psychiatrist with at least five years of experience, further evaluation by a senior psychiatrist, and escalation to at least two additional senior psychiatrists on disagreement. The unavailability of ADOS and ADI-R is disclosed explicitly as a resource constraint. Nonverbal IQ was screened by the psychiatrist and measured with Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices, and ADHD, schizophrenia and other conditions were exclusions. The comparison group was screened for absence of mental or physical disorder and for absence of autism or ADHD in first-degree relatives - the latter controlling for the broader autism phenotype, a step few studies here take. [RQ1.5] Nonverbal IQ via Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices for both groups, with at least average intelligence required for inclusion in the autistic group. No autism severity measure of any kind, which the authors state candidly: severity 'was not specifically measured in our study' and the sample 'could be viewed as representing individuals with minor severity'. No language, adaptive functioning or comorbidity scores. The IQ data are reported but, unusually, the significant group difference they reveal is not carried into the analysis. [RQ2.1] Goal: determine whether gaze during live face-to-face conversation classifies autism, and whether combining fixation features with conversation duration improves on either alone. Main findings: 92.31% accuracy with SVM using three combined features against 84.62% for either feature family alone; total conversation length alone achieved 79.49%; autistic children fixated less on mouth, face and body but not differently on the eyes; and the three misclassified autistic children fell within the typically developing range on all selected features. [RQ2.2] A laboratory dyadic setup at Shenzhen University with participants seated 80 cm from the interviewer, autistic children recruited from Shenzhen Kangning Hospital's Child Psychiatry Department and comparison children from local schools. Funded by seven Shenzhen and Guangdong municipal, medical-discipline and provincial research programmes. No conflicts declared. [RQ2.3] A structured four-session conversation with a single blinded interviewer, each session designed to probe a different aspect of interaction: general questions for familiarisation, hobby sharing to test whether a self-selected topic changes gaze, yes-no questions to elicit head nodding or shaking, and question raising to examine initiative. The full question list is published, which makes the protocol reproducible in a way that most naturalistic-interaction studies are not. The design's key property is that the number of exchanges is fixed while the time taken is free, which is exactly what makes session length an interpretable behavioural measure rather than an artefact - and it is that measure which proved most discriminative. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; one conversation per child with no follow-up. Data are first-person scene video from head-mounted glasses plus two external camera feeds of identifiable children in dyadic interaction. Governance is partially reported - Helsinki principles, Shenzhen University ethical guidelines, and written caregiver consent - but no ethics committee approval number is given. Participants were deliberately not told the glasses recorded gaze, with a post-experiment interview confirming none had realised; this is methodologically well motivated for behavioural naturalness but the deception is not discussed as an ethical consideration. [RQ2.5] Tobii Pro Glasses 2 head-mounted eye tracker at 50 Hz with Tobii Pro Lab for dynamic-stimulus analysis, plus two video cameras at 25 and 30 Hz. Two practical details are unusual and worth recording: an accuracy test was performed at the end of any conversation in which the participant had moved the glasses, and the authors report verifying that the device 'was reliably accurate even if the glasses were moved by participants during the conversation'. They nonetheless flag head-mounted tracking as a limitation, noting that autistic individuals 'are more sensitive to wearing devices' and recommending contactless, calibration-free alternatives. [RQ2.6] Strong. Reported: full question list for all four sessions; interviewer age, sex, blinding and consistency requirement; seating distance; both camera models with sampling rates; eye tracker model and rate; the four areas of interest; the real-world mapping procedure with human verification and manual correction; the velocity-threshold fixation definition with its 30 deg/s and 60 ms parameters; the fixation-percentage computation; all 21 features; the forward selection procedure described step by step; the leave-one-out scheme; and a table giving accuracy, sensitivity and specificity at every feature count from 1 to 21. Missing: ethics approval number, data or code release, and classifier hyperparameters. The interviewer-consistency check by image differencing is itself reported with its test statistic. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged extensively and specifically: the sample excludes severe presentations and children below 6 or above 13, so the work is 'proof-of-concept research'; only four girls participated, and autistic males and females differ across behavioural, cognitive and emotional domains; severity was not measured; head-mounted eye tracking may itself affect autistic children's behaviour and contactless methods are needed; only fixation percentage was computed while counts, entropy, revisits and oculomotor measures were available; only autism versus typical development was tested, leaving discrimination from other clinical phenotypes unknown; and live interaction introduces uncontrollable subjective factors, with the honest observation that 'no human being can be expected to behave exactly the same way when interacting with different people'. Not acknowledged: forward feature selection maximises the same leave-one-out accuracy that is reported, so the headline is not an unbiased estimate, and the maximum is quoted across 21 feature counts, four classifiers and three feature sets; and IQ differs significantly between groups with no adjustment, despite the leading feature being conversation duration. [RQ2.9] Validate on a larger autistic sample varying in severity with balanced sex ratio; include other clinical conditions such as developmental delay and ADHD; recruit younger children, citing a meta-analytic mean diagnosis age of 60.48 months overall and 43.18 months among children aged 10 or under; develop contactless calibration-free gaze recording, citing recent webcam-plus-computer-vision work whose accuracy was comparable to manual coding; generate richer gaze features including fixation counts, entropy, revisits and oculomotor performance; and combine eye tracking with kinematic, EEG and neuroimaging data. [RQ3.1] Two behavioural channels from a single live interaction. Gaze allocation to a real conversational partner across four regions - eyes, mouth, whole face, whole body - and interaction duration, measured as the time taken to complete a fixed number of conversational exchanges. The second is not a gaze measure at all but an outcome of the interaction, and treating it as a feature alongside gaze is the design's most productive decision. The four-session structure adds a temporal dimension, since each feature is computed per session, allowing the analysis to show that group differences in mouth and face fixation are strong in the early sessions and attenuate later. [RQ3.2] A clean and well-quantified fusion result, with both single-modality baselines reported: fixation features alone reach 84.62%, session length features alone reach 84.62%, and combined they reach 92.31% - roughly an 8-point gain. What makes it more informative than most fusion claims in the corpus is that the two feature families are conceptually distinct rather than two views of the same signal: one measures where the child looked, the other how long the interaction took. The best three-feature model draws on both, taking total session length plus two fixation features. The finding that session length alone reaches 79.49% is the most consequential single number in the paper, since it implies most of the discriminative information is available without an eye tracker at all. [RQ4.1] Four classical classifiers - SVM, linear discriminant analysis, decision tree and random forest - each wrapped in forward feature selection, with the paper giving a short rationale for each including the observation that decision trees offer 'strong interpretability, but it is prone to overfitting'. The model comparison is informative in one respect: random forest needed sixteen features to reach 84.62% while SVM reached 92.31% with three, which speaks to how concentrated the signal is. The wrapper design is also what creates the study's main methodological weakness, since the selection criterion is the reported metric. [RQ4.2] Twenty-one features: sixteen fixation percentages (four areas of interest by four sessions) and five durations (four sessions plus total). The representation is compact, interpretable and clinically legible - every feature is a proportion of looking at a named body region during a named conversational activity, or a duration. Computing features per session rather than pooling across the conversation is what allows the temporal pattern to emerge, showing group differences concentrated in the earlier sessions. The authors note the representation's narrowness themselves, observing that fixation counts, entropy, revisits and oculomotor features were all available and unexploited. [RQ4.3] Comprehensive. Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for every classifier under every feature set; a confusion matrix for the best model; an accuracy-versus-feature-count curve for all four classifiers; a table showing the incremental contribution of each successively added feature; and full Mann-Whitney comparisons for all 16 fixation features and all session lengths. Crucially, a majority-class baseline of 51.3% is computed and explicitly compared, which is the check almost every other study in the corpus omits. The one gap is that no confidence intervals accompany any figure, and with 39 participants a single misclassification is worth 2.6 accuracy points. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is served three ways. The forward selection ordering itself ranks features by contribution, showing that total session length alone reaches 79.49% and that only two fixation features are needed on top of it. The univariate table gives medians and effect statistics for every fixation feature, which is what reveals the eye-region null. And an error analysis examines the three misclassified autistic children individually, showing that on each of the three selected features they fell within the typically developing distribution - for instance, one had a total session length shorter than 75% of the typically developing group and mouth fixation higher than half of them. The authors read this as heterogeneity rather than model failure, which is the correct inference and is rarely drawn elsewhere in this corpus. The substantive interpretations offered - that the mouth matters because the task is conversational, and that longer conversations may reflect difficulty extracting social information - are plausible and appropriately hedged. [RQ4.5] Leave-one-out cross-validation at the participant level, explicitly motivated as overfitting protection. The defect is that forward feature selection evaluates candidate features by their classification accuracy, and that accuracy is the leave-one-out estimate itself, so features were chosen to maximise the number subsequently reported. Compounding this, results are reported for every feature count from 1 to 21 across four classifiers and three feature sets - 252 cells - and the maximum is quoted as the headline. There is no outer validation loop, no held-out cohort and no repetition. The saving grace is that the paper prints the entire selection trajectory, so a reader can see that accuracy plateaus at 92.31% from three features through eleven and that the single-feature result is 79.49%, which makes the shape of the result assessable even though the peak is optimistic. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder; eye tracking; face-to-face interaction; machine learning; visual fixation. 'Face-to-face interaction' is the distinguishing term and accurately identifies the contribution - the novelty is the recording context rather than the algorithm. [RQ5.2] Journal of Medical Internet Research, 23(8), e29328 - a digital health venue, with authorship spanning a human factors and ergonomics institute, a district centre for disease control, and a hospital child psychiatry department. [RQ5.3] 2021. The framing is a specific critique of ecological validity in the existing eye-tracking literature. The paper observes that prior data 'were primarily obtained by having participants watch images (ie, videos, pictures, web pages)' but that 'human gaze behavior is highly context-sensitive', that experimental setting and cognitive load influence visual attention, that face-to-face interaction is 'much more perceptually and cognitively difficult' than image watching, and that 'the presence of the social partner elicits a different pattern of both neural response and gaze behavior' - concluding that image-viewing findings 'could not be directly generalized to the scenario of natural social interaction'. It also situates itself on age, noting a meta-analytic mean diagnosis age of 60.48 months and arguing that future work should examine younger children than its own 6-13 range. And it is unusually explicit that the field has not yet addressed differential diagnosis: 'our study and most others only classified individuals with ASD and TD... More scientific endeavor is certainly required before a practical ML model that could detect ASD from different conditions is established.'

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional three-way acoustic classification; 255 sustained /ah/ phonations from 19 Indian children aged 5-14 - 6 autistic (79 samples), 6 with Down syndrome (77) and 7 controls (99) - with no diagnostic instrument, group ages or ethics statement reported; data not released.
narrative_rows.methods: Recordings made with consumer audio software in a noise-free location, preprocessed by pre-emphasis, silence removal, framing and 30 ms Hamming windowing; three acoustic feature families extracted - perturbation (jitter, shimmer), noise energy (HNR, GNE, SNR with four moments each) and spectral-cepstral (MFCC with dynamic features, RASTA-PLP from 11th-order all-pole modelling), each summarised by frame-wise means and standard deviations; classified by a single-hidden-layer feed-forward network trained by scaled conjugate gradient with hidden neuron count set by trial, partitioned 70/15/15 with six-fold cross-validation over samples, and compared against RBF-kernel SVM and naive Bayes.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Autism detection: MFCC and RASTA-PLP each 100% accuracy with AUC 1; SNR 89.4%, jitter 88.88%, HNR lowest at 77.8%. Down syndrome detection: MFCC and RASTA-PLP 100%, HNR 94.73%. Autism versus Down syndrome: MFCC and HNR 100%, RASTA-PLP 85.7%, GNE lowest at 73.68%. Comparators on MFCC for autism detection reached 78.5% (SVM) and 91.2% (naive Bayes). Combining feature families reduced accuracy in nearly every condition, with MFCC plus RASTA-PLP falling to 80.7% for autism detection.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: 255 samples derive from only 19 children with roughly 13 phonations each, and the 70/15/15 partition is never stated to respect speaker boundaries, so speaker-level leakage is the most parsimonious explanation for perfect accuracy in six of 33 conditions using features standard in speaker recognition; hidden neuron counts were tuned by trial to maximise the reported accuracy for each feature set and task; no diagnostic instrument for either clinical group and no screening for controls; ages reported only as a collective 5-14 range where voice changes with maturation; no ethics or consent statement for recordings of clinically diagnosed children; no group-level acoustic statistics of any kind; no limitations section; and a sustained vowel cannot express the prosodic features the paper itself identifies as characterising autistic speech.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Retains value for the review on two counts despite uninterpretable performance figures. It is one of very few studies in the corpus to attempt discrimination between two neurodevelopmental conditions rather than the far easier condition-versus-typical contrast, and that differential question is the one clinical practice actually poses.
