And its feature-family comparison is theoretically motivated rather than exploratory, with stated reasons why perturbation measures fail in disordered voices (unreliable fundamental frequency estimation) and why noise measures fail across settings (dependence on recording environment) - reasoning that transfers to other acoustic work in the corpus. Its negative fusion result, that combining feature families degraded performance in nearly every condition, is reported without spin and stands against the prevailing assumption elsewhere. Methodologically it is the corpus's clearest case of sample-level partitioning over a tiny speaker pool, and the clearest illustration that the acoustic features common in this literature are the same ones used for speaker identification - a confound that any voice-based autism study must design against.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Three groups, but 19 children in total: 6 autistic (3 boys, 3 girls), 6 with Down syndrome (2 boys, 4 girls) and 7 controls (3 boys, 4 girls), contributing 79, 77 and 99 sustained vowel samples respectively. The inclusion of a Down syndrome group is the design's most valuable feature - it is one of only a handful of studies in the corpus with an other-diagnosis comparison rather than only typical development, enabling the differential question the paper poses. But with six children per clinical group the analysis rests on a very small number of individuals however many samples each provides. [RQ1.2] The most pathologising language in the corpus, and conceptually as well as ethically problematic. Autism is repeatedly described as a 'pathological voice' and grouped under 'voice disability' alongside Down syndrome - a categorisation that misstates what autism is, since it is not a disorder of the voice. The Down syndrome phenotype is described as including 'mental retardation, general hypotonia... maxillary hypoplasia... with a relative macroglossia (unusually large tongue), short neck, and obesity'. Children are 'normal' versus 'affected'. Autistic speech is characterised as 'abnormal and is described as machine-like monotonic or sing-song'. Even allowing for a signal-processing venue's conventions, the register is markedly out of step with the rest of the corpus. [RQ1.3] Almost none. Nineteen children aged 5-14, with sex counts by group but no ages, means, standard deviations or matching test for any group. The 5-14 range is the critical gap: fundamental frequency, jitter, shimmer and formant structure all change substantially across childhood and pubertal onset falls inside this window, so any group age difference would directly produce the acoustic differences the classifier exploits. Sex is likewise a primary determinant of these features and is balanced only by count across very small groups. No IQ, severity, comorbidity, language ability, socioeconomic or recruitment information. [RQ1.4] None. The paper describes ADOS-R and ADI-R in its introduction and criticises them for requiring 'standardized structures for capturing the behaviors and found to be very difficult', but never states how the six autistic children in its own sample were identified - no instrument, criteria, clinician or setting. The same applies to the Down syndrome group, where the paper notes that 'Down Syndrome Screening tests are used for diagnosing Down Syndrome. Nevertheless, they cannot give appropriate results', without saying what was used here. Control status is asserted without any screening. [RQ1.5] None. No IQ, developmental, language, adaptive or severity measure, and no comorbidity information for any of the three groups. [RQ2.1] Goal: detect autism and Down syndrome from sustained vowel phonation and discriminate between them, comparing three acoustic feature families. Main findings: MFCC and RASTA-PLP achieved 100% accuracy for autism detection and Down syndrome detection; MFCC and harmonics-to-noise ratio achieved 100% for autism-versus-Down-syndrome discrimination; perturbation and noise measures performed worse throughout; combining feature families reduced performance in almost every condition; and the feed-forward network outperformed SVM and naive Bayes comparators on the same features. [RQ2.2] Recording in an unspecified 'noise free location' using consumer audio editing software on a laptop, at two engineering colleges in Tamil Nadu. No recruitment route, clinical setting or collection period is described, and no funding or ethics information appears. [RQ2.3] Sustained phonation of the vowel /ah/, chosen explicitly against the alternative of connected or spontaneous speech. This is a defensible methodological position for voice-quality analysis - it holds linguistic content constant and isolates phonatory function - but it is a severe constraint for autism specifically, since the acoustic differences documented in autistic speech concern prosody, intonation contour and pragmatic use of voice, all of which are eliminated by a sustained vowel. The paper's own introduction describes autistic speech as 'machine-like monotonic or sing-song', properties that cannot manifest in an isolated sustained vowel, so the task may not be capable of capturing the phenomenon it is aimed at. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; multiple phonations per child in a single session with no follow-up. Data are voice recordings of identifiable children with clinical diagnoses. No ethics committee approval, parental consent procedure, anonymisation statement or data-handling policy appears anywhere in the paper - a complete absence rather than a partial omission, and one that matters given the population. [RQ2.5] Audio Editor 2016 on a laptop recording PCM mono WAV at 16-bit resolution in a stated noise-free location; MATLAB on an i5 processor for all processing; LIBSVM for the SVM comparator. The recording chain is consumer-grade, which the paper does not treat as a limitation despite its own observation that 'the noise parameters depend on the voice recording environment. Hence the values of parameters also vary accordingly'. The stated sampling rate of '24,000 kHz' is a transcription error for 24 kHz. [RQ2.6] Detailed on signal processing, absent on everything else. Fully specified: pre-emphasis, framing and windowing with 30 ms Hamming windows; the RASTA-PLP computation given as a seven-step procedure; MFCC parameters including window length, shift, coefficient count and dynamic features; RASTA-PLP order and window overlap; the network architecture, activation functions, training algorithm, learning rate, momentum, epoch count and target error; the hidden-neuron selection procedure; and the partition ratios. Absent: diagnostic instruments, group ages, ethics approval, recruitment, how samples were elicited or how many per child, whether the partition respected speaker boundaries, any group-level acoustic statistics, and any code or data. [RQ2.7] None. There is no limitations section and no caveat anywhere on sample size, validation design, generalisability or the absence of clinical characterisation. The nearest approach is the acknowledgement that hidden neuron counts have no exact formula and were fixed by trial. Identifiable in review: 255 samples derive from only 19 children with roughly 13 samples each, and the 70/15/15 partition operates over samples with no statement that speakers were kept together, which alone would explain the perfect accuracies; hidden neuron counts were tuned to maximise the reported accuracy for each feature set and task; no diagnostic instrument is reported for either clinical group; ages are given only as a collective 5-14 range in a domain where voice changes with maturation; no ethics or consent statement exists; and the sustained vowel task cannot express the prosodic properties the paper itself identifies as characterising autistic speech. [RQ2.9] None stated. [RQ3.1] Voice quality during sustained phonation - specifically phonatory stability (jitter, shimmer), noise content of the glottal source (harmonics-to-noise, glottal-to-noise excitation and signal-to-noise ratios) and vocal tract spectral shape (MFCC, RASTA-PLP). This is the narrowest behavioural sample in the corpus: a single sustained vowel captures voice source and resonance properties but no prosody, no interaction, no linguistic content and no temporal structure of speech. [RQ3.2] The fusion result is clearly negative and is reported without spin, which makes it useful. Combining feature families reduced performance in nearly every condition: for autism detection MFCC plus RASTA-PLP fell to 80.7% from 100% for either alone, and HNR plus SNR fell to 53.2%; for Down syndrome detection MFCC plus RASTA-PLP fell to 78.3%. The single exception is HNR plus GNE reaching 100% for autism-versus-Down-syndrome discrimination. The authors state the conclusion plainly: 'the combined feature set provides less performance when compared to the individual features, for most of the cases'. Given the sample size this is more likely a dimensionality effect than a substantive finding, but it stands in useful contrast to the widespread assumption elsewhere in this corpus that combining features or modalities helps. [RQ4.1] A single-hidden-layer feed-forward network trained by scaled conjugate gradient, chosen for its lack of user-dependent parameters and avoidance of line search, compared against RBF-kernel SVM and naive Bayes on identical features. The comparison is systematic and the network wins in every condition, though the margins - 100% against 78.5% for SVM and 91.2% for naive Bayes on the same MFCC features for autism detection - are large enough to be suspicious, since a shallow network and an RBF SVM on the same low-dimensional features would not normally diverge this far unless one is exploiting something the other is not. [RQ4.2] Three feature families with an explicitly argued progression. Perturbation measures are introduced first and their limitation stated: 'a high degree of jitter consequences in a voice with roughness... Besides, it is very difficult to measure fundamental frequency, in the case of a pathological voice'. Noise energy measures follow, with their limitation likewise stated: they 'depend on the voice recording environment'. Spectral-cepstral features are then introduced to overcome both, with MFCC justified because it 'analyze the vocal tract independently of the vocal folds that can be injured due to voice pathologies' and RASTA-PLP because its bandpass filtering removes channel effects. This is a coherent and well-referenced design rationale, and the empirical ordering of results matches it. Each family is summarised to a fixed-length vector by statistical moments across frames. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for all seven individual and four combined feature sets across all three tasks - 33 conditions in total - plus processing time comparisons and hidden-neuron sensitivity curves. The coverage is unusually complete, and the processing time analysis is a practical dimension few studies report, showing MFCC and RASTA-PLP to be cheapest because jitter and shimmer require fundamental frequency estimation and GNE requires Hilbert envelope extraction and cross-correlation per glottal cycle. Missing: confidence intervals, confusion matrices, and any statistical test - and with perfect scores reported in six of 33 conditions, the metrics carry no information about where the model fails. [RQ4.4] No model-explanation method and, more consequentially, no descriptive analysis of any group difference - no acoustic means, distributions, effect sizes or tests. The paper therefore establishes only that a classifier separates the groups, not what distinguishes them acoustically, which is a substantial gap for a study whose introduction reviews directional acoustic findings at length. The interpretation offered for why spectral-cepstral features win is at the level of feature family rather than individual parameter: they are Fourier-transform-based while jitter, shimmer, HNR and GNE are time-domain, and the result is said to be 'consistent with previous studies that, spectral and cepstral based features are best suited for discriminating voice with hoarseness from normal voice'. [RQ4.5] The decisive weakness. Partitioning is 70/15/15 with six-fold cross-validation, but over 255 voice samples drawn from only 19 children - roughly 13 phonations each - with no statement that a child's samples were confined to one partition. Repeated sustained vowels from one speaker constitute a speaker-identification problem, and MFCC, RASTA-PLP, jitter, shimmer and HNR are the standard feature set for exactly that task, so a classifier can achieve near-perfect accuracy by recognising individuals and mapping them to their known group. Six of 33 reported conditions achieve exactly 100% accuracy with AUC 1, which is what speaker-level leakage produces and which is otherwise implausible for a clinical classification from a single vowel. Additionally, the hidden neuron count was chosen by trial to maximise accuracy separately for each feature set and task, so every figure is a maximum over that search. There is no independent cohort, no external validation and no held-out speaker test. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Autism spectrum disorder; down syndrome; feed forward neural network; perturbation measures; noise parameters; cepstral features. Four of six name signal-processing constructs, accurately reflecting a paper whose contribution is a feature-family comparison with autism as one of two application labels. [RQ5.2] Sound and Vibration, 55(2), 141-161 - an acoustics and signal-processing journal, not a clinical or machine-learning venue, published open access under CC BY 4.0. The venue explains both the depth of the signal-processing exposition and the absence of clinical reporting standards. [RQ5.3] 2021. The framing is unusual and revealing: autism is introduced not as a neurodevelopmental condition but as one of two 'voice disabilities' within a paper about pathological voice detection, alongside Down syndrome, in a context where '1.2% of the world's total population is facing some type of voice disability'. Prevalence figures are given for both conditions in the United States and India (1 in 59 and 23 per 10,000 for autism; 1 in 700 and 1 in 1250 for Down syndrome). The critique of existing diagnosis is brief - ADOS-R and ADI-R 'require standardized structures for capturing the behaviors and found to be very difficult' - and the paper's real intellectual investment is in the acoustic literature, which it reviews carefully across five prior Down syndrome voice studies with their specific findings on fundamental frequency, jitter and shimmer. Its stated novelty is the differential task: prior work 'analyzed the variability of acoustic features in the voice produced by children with ADS, DS and normal children' but 'there has been no attempt to classify both'.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control classification with dual validation regimes; 59 French school-aged children - 29 autistic (7y7m, 19 male, CARS 32.9) diagnosed by ADI-R and ADOS-G in specialty clinics and 30 non-autistic (8y0m, 19 male, CARS 15) - viewing a battery of joint attention, gaze-following, face-object and emotional cartoon stimuli; 547 scanpath images averaging 9.27 per child, released openly.
narrative_rows.methods: SMI RED250 at 250 Hz recorded gaze during roughly 10 minutes of stimuli; scanpaths were rendered as images with a line per gaze transition, greyscale colour keyed to velocity, vertical mirroring, a 200-point drawing cap chosen empirically and a velocity bound at a quarter of the screen diagonal; images were cropped, rescaled to 256 x 256 and augmented fivefold, then classified by a CNN with four convolutional, four pooling and two fully connected layers under three-fold cross-validation run twice - once pooling images and once holding out participants.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Image-level split approximately 90% accuracy, 83% recall, 80% precision. Participant-level split approximately 71% accuracy, reported by the authors as an expected decline. Maximal information coefficient between CARS score and average gaze velocity 0.79, computed per image.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: 59 participants, named by the authors as the primary limitation; ADI-R and ADOS-G scores inaccessible so diagnostic detail could not be analysed; the MIC severity correlation is computed per image across 547 observations from 59 children and its comparison group sits at the CARS floor with zero variance, so it substantially reflects the between-group difference rather than a within-autism gradient; augmented samples are not stated to be confined to their source image's partition; only three training epochs; only accuracy reported for the participant-level condition; short stimulus scenarios; and school-age composition forced by regional diagnostic delays.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Supplies the corpus's single most useful methodological measurement: the same model, data and cross-validation run under two splitting units, yielding approximately 90% accuracy when scanpath images are pooled and approximately 71% when participants are held out. With 9.27 images per child, that 19-point gap directly quantifies the segment-level inflation that recurs throughout this literature and that most affected studies never measure, since they run only the optimistic version. It should anchor the synthesis's treatment of validation design. The paper is also notable for releasing its dataset openly - addressing the benchmark gap it identifies - for explaining rather than omitting the basis on which ethics committee approval was not required, and for two framing observations found nowhere else in the corpus: that regional diagnostic waiting times of up to two years prevented recruiting the preschool sample the research aimed at, and that parents may accept a clinical diagnosis more readily when an objective visual measure accompanies it.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups of 59 children: 29 autistic and 30 non-autistic, closely matched at 19 males each. The authors explain the age composition candidly rather than presenting it as a design choice - they wanted younger participants for early detection, 'but in our region there were not enough diagnosed children younger than 6 years, and the time it takes to consult a doctor to make a diagnosis can be as long as 2 years'. That is an unusually direct statement of how diagnostic waiting times constrain the very research meant to shorten them. No other-diagnosis comparison group. [RQ1.2] 'individuals diagnosed with ASD', 'children with ASD', 'ASD-diagnosed individuals', 'non-ASD', 'children with typical development'. Consistently person-first with 'non-ASD' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy' for the comparison group. The framing acknowledges family impact - deficits 'can unfortunately place a considerable strain on their lives and their families' - but is otherwise neutral, and the discussion notes that parents find eye-tracking results easier to understand than ADI cut-offs and that 'a lack of an objective measure can lead to delayed or diminished acceptance of the clinical diagnosis', which frames objectivity as serving families rather than only clinicians. [RQ1.3] Autistic group: 29 children, 19 male, chronological age 7 years 7 months (SD 2 years 6 months), CARS 32.9 +/- 6.4, ECSP total 141.1 +/- 50.3. Non-autistic group: 30 children, 19 male, chronological age 8 years 0 months (SD 2 years 8 months), CARS exactly 15 with zero variance, ECSP total 139.18 +/- 49.5. Ages and sex ratios are closely comparable though no test is reported. Two features of the clinical data deserve note: the non-autistic group's CARS of 15 with zero standard deviation is the instrument's floor, so the measure carries no within-group variance; and ECSP developmental ages of approximately 23-24 months in both groups reflect a ceiling effect of an instrument designed for much younger children, not a meaningful developmental estimate for eight-year-olds. No IQ, ethnicity or socioeconomic data. [RQ1.4] Diagnosis confirmed by health professionals in multidisciplinary autism specialty clinics using ADI-R and ADOS-G - the field's gold standard, and among the better ascertainments in the corpus. The important qualification is stated openly: 'we did not get permission to read the children's medical files', so the ADI-R and ADOS-G scores were unavailable and unanalysed, and the authors list this among their limitations, noting that access 'could have provided further interpretation of the results'. Independent severity and communication measures were obtained directly by the research team using French CARS and ECSP for both groups. Non-autistic status rests on careful consideration of parental concerns plus a floor CARS score. [RQ1.5] CARS for severity and ECSP for social communication, both in French versions, administered to both groups by psychologists. CARS is used analytically in the correlation analysis rather than merely tabulated. ECSP is reported but not used, and its near-identical group means at what appears to be a ceiling limit its informativeness. No IQ, adaptive functioning or comorbidity measures, and ADI-R and ADOS-G scores were inaccessible. [RQ2.1] Goal: represent eye-tracking scanpaths as velocity-coloured images so that autism screening becomes an image classification problem. Main findings: approximately 90% accuracy with image-level splitting and approximately 71% with participant-level splitting; a maximal information coefficient of 0.79 between CARS score and average gaze velocity; and a working demonstration application linking eye tracking, visualisation and prediction through a hosted model. [RQ2.2] A quiet room at the University of Picardy Jules Verne with white barriers to reduce visual distraction, in an interdisciplinary collaboration between psychology and artificial intelligence research units. Children were recruited regionally, with autistic participants diagnosed at multidisciplinary specialty clinics. Supported by a university research quality bonus; no conflicts declared. [RQ2.3] A composite battery assembled from several existing psychological protocols and described at unusual protocol-level detail: three 58-second joint attention initiation videos plus 18 matched 5-second photographs, opening with a hand-waving cartoon attention grabber before a woman greets the child and then looks, verbalises and points toward a target either present in or absent from the child's visual field; twelve 4-second gaze-following videos separating head-plus-eye shifts from eye-only shifts; static actor-plus-object photographs; and five minutes of cartoon scenes whose characters' emotional expressions are contingent or non-contingent on the preceding scene. Stimuli were counterbalanced and interleaved with a two-second central crosshair. The variety - dynamic versus static, human versus cartoon, human versus object - is deliberate, allowing 'analysis of the ocular activity of participants from different perspectives', and it is what produces multiple scanpath images per child. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single session of approximately 10 minutes per child with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates rendered as abstract scanpath images and released openly. Governance is fully reported and its regulatory basis explained: informed written consent from parents or guardians after explanation of objectives, tasks and the right to withdraw; assent from every child; parents permitted to remain in the room; Helsinki conformity; and an explicit statement that ethics committee authorisation was not required under French recommendations for psychological research. Explaining why approval was unnecessary, rather than simply omitting the matter, is better practice than the silence found in much of the corpus. [RQ2.5] SMI RED250 remote eye tracker at 250 Hz - among the highest sampling rates in the corpus, and material here because the authors attribute conflicting literature findings on saccade dynamics partly to trackers running at 60 Hz and 24 Hz; a 17-inch monitor at 1280 x 1024 viewed from about 60 cm; SMI Experiment Center; five-point calibration followed by verification procedures. Analysis in Python with Matplotlib, OpenCV and Keras on a Tesla K80, with the Minerva R package for the MIC computation, and Azure ML hosting the deployed demonstration model. [RQ2.6] Good. Reported: the full stimulus battery with per-protocol durations, counts and content; recording geometry, calibration and verification; the three-step visualisation procedure including the mirroring correction and the velocity bound at a quarter of the screen diagonal; the empirical selection of the 200-point drawing threshold with the tested alternatives and their outcomes; image cropping and rescaling to 256 x 256; the augmentation factor and resulting sample count; the CNN layer composition; the three-fold cross-validation under both splitting regimes with the participant-level procedure described step by step; training epochs and hardware; and the MIC method with its rationale and software. Missing: CNN hyperparameters beyond layer counts, filter sizes, the repository link for the released dataset, and ADI-R and ADOS-G scores which were inaccessible. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged: the small participant count as the primary limitation; the inability to access ADI-R and ADOS-G scores, which 'limits the interpretation of our results'; the short duration of video scenarios, since 'perhaps longer scenarios might have allowed for a richer representation of the gaze behavior'; the restricted age group; the absence of a benchmark dataset in the autism literature making cross-study comparison difficult; and hardware and software costs as barriers to clinical adoption. The performance decline under participant-level splitting is reported as expected rather than hidden. Not acknowledged: the MIC of 0.79 is computed per image rather than per child, so 547 observations derive from 59 individuals; and because every non-autistic child scores the CARS floor of 15 with zero variance, that correlation largely reflects the between-group difference rather than a severity gradient within autism. Also unremarked: augmented copies of an image share its participant, which would compound leakage in the image-level condition, and three training epochs is very few. [RQ2.9] A larger cohort spanning different ages with analysis of socio-cognitive and cognitive profiles alongside gaze; autism-specific data augmentation methods; longer video scenarios for richer gaze representation; adaptation of more recent deep network methodologies; and, more broadly, transfer of the approach to other neurodevelopmental disorders. The authors also identify the field-level need for a benchmark dataset, which their own open release partly addresses. [RQ3.1] Gaze trajectory and its dynamics across a heterogeneous battery spanning joint attention initiation, gaze following with head-plus-eye versus eye-only cues, static face-and-object viewing, and emotionally contingent versus non-contingent cartoon scenes. Rather than reducing these to fixation counts or dwell proportions, the study preserves the whole scanpath as a spatial object with velocity written into its colour - so the behavioural unit analysed is the shape of looking over time rather than any summary statistic of it. [RQ3.2] No cross-modal fusion. What is fused is spatial and temporal information within a single representation: the scanpath image simultaneously carries where gaze travelled and how fast, with velocity encoded as greyscale gradient along each line. This is a genuinely different answer to the multimodality problem from the feature-concatenation approaches elsewhere in the corpus - the two information types are combined at the representation level before any learning occurs, and the MIC analysis is offered as evidence that the velocity channel carries real signal, since velocity correlates with CARS at 0.79 and is exactly what the colour encodes. [RQ4.1] A convolutional network with four convolutional layers, four pooling layers, two fully connected layers and dropout, trained for three epochs. The architectural choice follows directly from the representation decision: having converted gaze to images, the natural learner is a CNN, and the authors describe the whole approach as recasting diagnosis as 'a typical task of image classification'. No comparison against alternative classifiers or against engineered-feature baselines is reported, though the authors note this study builds on their own earlier work using fixation and saccade event features. [RQ4.2] The representation is the contribution. Scanpath images at 256 x 256 after cropping and rescaling, with three deliberate design decisions documented: a cap of 200 consecutive drawn points, selected empirically after finding that 100-150 'turned out to poorly discriminate the 2 classes' while higher values produced clutter; a velocity bound at a quarter of the screen diagonal on the grounds that faster movement 'would not be normal given the scenarios used'; and vertical mirroring to correct for the coordinate origin. Augmentation generated five synthetic variants per image. The heterogeneous stimulus battery is what yields an average of 9.27 images per child, which is simultaneously what makes the dataset large enough to train a CNN and what creates the leakage risk the paper then measures. [RQ4.3] ROC curves with AUC and cross-fold standard deviation, plus accuracy, recall and precision, reported twice - once for each splitting regime - together with training and validation loss curves. Reporting the same metrics under both regimes is what makes the comparison legible and is the paper's key methodological contribution. Missing: confusion matrices, confidence intervals on the accuracy figures, and per-class breakdown for the participant-level condition, where only accuracy is quoted. [RQ4.4] No saliency or attribution analysis over the CNN, and the visual representation is not decomposed to show which regions of a scanpath image drive classification - a missed opportunity given that the images are directly human-interpretable and are reproduced in the paper for one participant from each group. Interpretability is instead pursued externally through the MIC analysis, which establishes that the velocity information encoded in colour correlates strongly with CARS severity and thereby argues that the model has something real to learn from. The authors connect this to the wider literature on saccade dynamics in autism, while noting honestly that the direction of the effect 'does not appear to be settled and seems to depend largely on the equipment and data used'. [RQ4.5] The paper's most important element and the reason it matters to this review. Three-fold cross-validation is run twice on the same model and data under two splitting units. Pooling the 547 images regardless of origin gives approximately 90% accuracy. Splitting the 59 participants first and then assigning their images by ID - so that no child appears on both sides - gives approximately 71%. The authors describe the second explicitly as a further examination of model performance and note the decline as expected. With an average of 9.27 images per child, this constitutes a direct within-study quantification of segment-level inflation: roughly 19 accuracy points, on a design where images from one child are highly correlated. Residual issues: augmented samples presumably inherit their source image's participant, so the image-level figure may be further inflated; only accuracy is reported for the participant-level condition; three epochs is very few; and there is no independent cohort or external site. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder; screening; eye tracking; data visualization; machine learning; deep learning; AI; ASS; artificial intelligence; ML; screening; adolescent; diagnosis. 'Data visualization' is the distinguishing term - the contribution is a representation strategy rather than an architecture or a clinical finding. [RQ5.2] JMIR Human Factors, 8(4), e27706 - a digital health and human factors venue, with all eight authors credited as contributing equally across psychology, computer science and anatomy research units at the University of Picardy Jules Verne. [RQ5.3] 2021. The framing is conventional on diagnosis - hours of clinical examination, symptom variation, susceptibility to human bias - but two observations are distinctive. First, an unusually frank statement of how service capacity shapes research: the sample is school-aged rather than preschool because 'in our region there were not enough diagnosed children younger than 6 years, and the time it takes to consult a doctor to make a diagnosis can be as long as 2 years', so the very diagnostic delay the tool is meant to address prevented studying the age group where it would matter most. Second, an argument about acceptance rather than accuracy: 'parents seem to have high acceptance of eye tracking as part of the clinical evaluation because the visual results are easier to understand than is the ADI cutoff', and 'for some parents, a lack of an objective measure can lead to delayed or diminished acceptance of the clinical diagnosis'. That reframes the value of objective measurement as communicative as well as diagnostic, a consideration essentially absent elsewhere in this corpus. The paper also identifies the absence of a benchmark dataset as an obstacle to comparing methods, and responds by releasing its own.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control classification via per-group attention modelling; 106 Brazilian children and adolescents aged 3-18 - 76 autistic (49 male) recruited from a university psychiatry institute and 30 typically developing (20 male), all CARS-assessed with the comparison group confirmed below 30, comorbid participants deliberately retained; gaze recorded on a Tobii Pro TX300 during 54 seconds of biological-versus-geometric motion video; clinical data deposited, eye-tracking data not released.
narrative_rows.methods: Frames were edge-trimmed, resized to 200 x 350, stripped of transition frames and aggregated wherever mean optical-flow motion fell below 0.33; group fixation maps were built by summing fixations across each group and Gaussian-smoothing; 350 most-fixated and 350 random unfixated coordinates per map supplied balanced training pixels described by 28 image features spanning steerable pyramids, Saliency Toolbox measures, RGB, horizon, faces, people, distance to screen and scene centres, optical-flow motion and biological/geometric scene membership, reduced to 15 per group by genetic algorithm; a ten-neuron network per group predicted pixel fixation, and individuals were classified by which group's binary saliency map their own fixation map matched more often across 50 held-out diagnosis frames, under five-fold subject-level cross-validation.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Average precision 90%, specificity 93%, sensitivity 69%, AUC 0.822 (SD 0.015). Alternatives: network without selection 0.818 (0.053), with ReliefF 0.782; SVM without selection 0.775, with genetic algorithm 0.695. Genetic algorithm selection retained distance-to-frame-centre and presence of biological movement only for the autistic model and an RGB colour feature only for the typically developing model, while Saliency Toolbox features were retained for both.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Sensitivity of 69% means roughly three in ten autistic participants are missed and is never discussed; the 76:30 class ratio inflates the reported precision and is unaddressed; genetic algorithm feature selection is not stated to be nested within cross-validation folds although the selected feature sets constitute the main interpretive finding; the 28-vote decision threshold was fitted by Youden index on the reported ROC; no group-wise ages are given across a 3-18 year span on a developmentally graded paradigm; and the eye-tracking data are not released.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The corpus's clearest articulation of why region-of-interest analysis constrains eye-tracking autism research - annotation burden on every frame of every video, plus loss of information about which visual properties within a region drew the gaze - and a worked alternative that removes annotation entirely by modelling fixation probability per pixel from image features. Its per-group feature comparison converts the classifier into an interpretable statement about attentional guidance, yielding a specific dissociation: centre distance and biological-movement membership predict autistic gaze while colour does not, with the reverse for typically developing gaze. Two practices deserve wider adoption: the blindfolding of adults holding lap-seated children to prevent caregiver gaze cueing, which no other corpus study reports, and separately obtained consent for publishing identifiable footage of the people appearing in stimulus videos. Its comparison table also supplies a rare nuance for the synthesis - feature selection improved the neural network's fold-to-fold stability (SD 0.053 to 0.015) far more than its mean AUC, while degrading the SVM by eight points, so the value of selection is learner-dependent and shows up in variance rather than in central tendency.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups totalling 106 children and adolescents: 76 autistic recruited from the Psychiatry Institute of the University of Sao Paulo School of Medicine and 30 typically developing. The class ratio of roughly 2.5:1 favouring autism is not addressed by any balancing procedure and matters for interpreting the reported 90% precision. Notably, participants with psychiatric and neurological comorbidities were deliberately retained rather than excluded, with the authors reasoning from co-occurrence prevalence that excluding them would misrepresent the population. No separate other-diagnosis group, though extending to autism-versus-ADHD discrimination is named as a future direction. [RQ1.2] 'individuals with ASD', 'ASD subjects', 'subjects with and without ASD', 'Typical Development (TD)', 'ASD patients'. Mixed person-first and abbreviated group labels, with 'patients' used when discussing comorbidity prevalence. The framing is neutral and mechanism-oriented, grounding the work in bottom-up and top-down attentional circuits and describing autism through 'alterations in early precursor of social behavior as biological motion, human face preference, and joint attention' rather than through deficit or burden. [RQ1.3] Group sizes and sex splits are given - 76 autistic (49 male, 27 female) and 30 typically developing (20 male, 10 female) - with a single 3-18 year age range for the whole sample. No group-wise ages, means, standard deviations, matching statement or statistical test appears anywhere. The authors treat the breadth as a virtue, describing the dataset as 'heterogeneous in terms of age, gender and CARS' and citing this as a strength relative to comparison studies, which is a legitimate external-validity argument. But a fifteen-year age span with no group comparison is a gap on a paradigm where preference for biological over geometric motion is developmentally graded. Per-participant clinical data including WISC, Repetitive Behavior Scale and Vineland where obtainable are deposited in supplementary material, which is better practice than most of the corpus. [RQ1.4] Clinical evaluation by a child psychiatrist against DSM-5 criteria with CARS-measured severity, plus neuropsychological assessment by a trained neuropsychologist using WISC, the Repetitive Behavior Scale and Vineland scales where possible. CARS was also administered to the comparison group and confirmed below the diagnostic threshold of 30, so typical development is verified rather than assumed. Per-participant clinical information is published as supplementary material. What is absent is ADOS or ADI-R, and no account is given of who performed the CARS or with what reliability. [RQ1.5] Among the better-characterised samples in the corpus: CARS for all participants, plus WISC intelligence, Repetitive Behavior Scale and Vineland adaptive behaviour for autistic participants where obtainable, all deposited per participant. The limitation is that none of these measures is used analytically - there is no severity-stratified analysis, no relation between CARS or IQ and classifier output, and no examination of whether comorbidity status affects classification, despite comorbid participants having been deliberately retained. [RQ2.1] Goal: replace region-of-interest annotation with learned per-group visual attention models over video stimuli, and classify individuals by adherence to those models. Main findings: AUC 0.822 with 90% precision, 93% specificity and 69% sensitivity; genetic algorithm selection retained distance-to-centre and biological movement only for the autistic model and colour only for the typically developing model; selection improved the neural network's fold-to-fold stability far more than its mean AUC while degrading the SVM substantially. [RQ2.2] Laboratory eye tracking with autistic participants recruited from the Psychiatry Institute of the University of Sao Paulo School of Medicine, in collaboration between computing, psychiatry and bioinformatics units. Ethics approval from the University of Sao Paulo under protocol 57185516.9.0000.5390. [RQ2.3] The biological-versus-geometric preference paradigm rendered as nine sequential 6-second clips totalling 54 seconds, with the screen split between children interacting and fractal movement, and with side and ordering varied to prevent conditioning. Two protocol details matter: calibration was repeated once on failure and the participant excluded after a second failure, and only subjects with more than 80% of total video time successfully captured were retained - a quantified data-quality gate. Where a child had to sit on an adult's lap, the adult wore a blindfold 'in order to avoid influencing the signals acquired', which is a control against caregiver gaze cueing that no other study in the corpus reports. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single 54-second viewing session per participant with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates over video stimuli. Governance is complete and detailed: named ethics committee approval with full protocol number, informed consent from participants or legal guardians, Helsinki conformity, and separately obtained consent for publication of identifying images from the individuals appearing in the stimulus videos - the last being a consideration almost never addressed elsewhere in this corpus. [RQ2.5] Tobii Pro TX300 with five-point calibration and a documented failure and exclusion policy; monitor viewed from 50-70 cm; MATLAB 2015a; Saliency Toolbox for Itti-model features; a gist-descriptor mixture of linear regressions for horizon detection; face and person detectors; optical flow for motion estimation. [RQ2.6] Very good. Reported: stimulus construction with clip counts, durations, resolution and counterbalancing; positioning, calibration procedure and the two-failure exclusion rule; the 80% capture-rate inclusion threshold; the blindfold control for lap-seated children; frame preprocessing including edge removal, resizing to 200 x 350 and transition-frame deletion; the optical-flow aggregation threshold of 0.33 with its empirical derivation and an explicit note that it is video-specific and 'should be reviewed' for different stimuli; the 5 x 5 Gaussian smoothing kernel; the 350-positive and 350-random-negative pixel sampling; all 28 candidate features with their sources; the full network specification including loss, optimiser, learning rate and stopping criteria; the vote-based classification rule; and the subject-level cross-validation with the 50 held-out diagnosis frames. Missing: group-wise ages, whether genetic algorithm selection was nested within folds, and any code or eye-tracking data release. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged with unusual directness on one point. The authors anticipate the objection that using the same video for training and diagnosis constitutes contamination, state it themselves - 'although it could be interpreted as contamination and biasing of learning' - and describe their mitigation: only 700 sampled pixels per map enter learning, 50 frames are withheld entirely for diagnosis, and negatives are randomly drawn, which they argue 'approximates a scenario of usage of different videos'. They also note the optical-flow threshold is stimulus-specific, identify dataset construction as the field's binding constraint, and flag intent to release data. Not acknowledged: sensitivity of 69% is not discussed at all despite being the weakest metric and the one that matters for screening; the 2.5:1 class ratio inflates precision and is unaddressed; genetic algorithm selection is not stated to be nested within folds although the selected feature sets are the paper's main interpretive claim; the 28-vote threshold was fitted by Youden on the reported ROC; and no group-wise ages are given across a 3-18 year span. [RQ2.9] Continue building the dataset toward public release, with the observation that assembling eye-tracking signals alongside expert clinical evaluation 'is not a trivial task'; evaluate further machine learning techniques and additional features; and extend from case-control comparison to discrimination between two disorders, specifically naming autism versus ADHD - the differential question the corpus almost never addresses. [RQ3.1] Visual attention during competition between biological and geometric motion, analysed not as dwell proportions but as a mapping from image properties to fixation probability. The behavioural quantity modelled is which visual features attract a group's gaze, decomposed across low-level saliency (steerable pyramids, colour, intensity, orientation), semantic content (faces, people, skin, horizon), spatial position (distance to screen and scene centres) and motion (optical flow magnitude, biological versus geometric scene membership). [RQ3.2] No cross-modal fusion. The combination is across feature families within a single modality, and the genetic algorithm's per-group selection is what makes it interpretable: the two models retain overlapping but non-identical feature sets, with distance-to-centre and biological-movement indicators appearing only in the autistic model and colour appearing only in the typically developing model. The authors' explanation for the biological-movement asymmetry is subtle and worth recording - the feature covers the whole region containing biological movement, and since typically developing attention 'is specifically more focused on the regions with people and faces' which are already captured by dedicated features, the broader region adds nothing for that group. That is a redundancy argument rather than an absence-of-effect argument, and it distinguishes a feature being uninformative from being subsumed. [RQ4.1] Two small neural networks, one per group, each acting as a generative model of where that group looks, plus a similarity-vote decision rule - the same architecture as the severity study from the same laboratory but applied to diagnosis. SVM was tested as an alternative learner and performed worse (0.775 against 0.818 without selection). The comparison table across six classifier-and-selection combinations is genuinely informative: genetic algorithm selection raised the network's mean AUC only from 0.818 to 0.822 but cut its standard deviation from 0.053 to 0.015, while the same selection dropped the SVM from 0.775 to 0.695. Reporting a case where feature selection helps stability rather than accuracy, and helps one learner while harming another, is more nuanced than most of the corpus manages. [RQ4.2] Twenty-eight pixel-level image features reduced to 15 per group by genetic algorithm, computed by averaging feature values across the frames aggregated into each group. The aggregation procedure is the paper's more distinctive representational contribution: because individual video frames contain too few fixations to support learning, consecutive frames are merged wherever mean optical-flow motion falls below 0.33, a threshold derived by visual inspection of when successive frames were nearly identical, and explicitly flagged as needing revision for any different stimulus. Training pixels are then sampled as the 350 most-fixated coordinates against 350 randomly chosen zero-fixation coordinates, giving a balanced 700 per map. [RQ4.3] Precision, sensitivity, specificity and AUC with fold-wise standard deviation, ROC curves for all five folds, a six-row comparison of classifier and selection combinations, and a table of published AUCs from three comparable studies for external context. Reporting standard deviation across folds is what reveals the stability benefit of feature selection. The gap is that sensitivity of 69% is reported but never discussed, and no confusion matrix or confidence interval accompanies it - on a sample where 76 of 106 participants are autistic, missing 31% of them is the most consequential number in the paper. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is delivered by the per-group feature comparison rather than by any post hoc explanation method, and it works well because the features are semantically meaningful image properties. Three findings are drawn out and connected to prior literature: the frame-centre feature entering only the autistic model matches reports of centre fixation 'even when there was nothing in the center'; Saliency Toolbox features entering both models is read as evidence of biologically general attentional mechanisms; and biological movement entering only the autistic model is explained by redundancy with face and person features in the typically developing model. The absence of any group-level statistics on the features themselves limits how far these can be pushed, and the interpretive claims rest on which features a genetic algorithm happened to retain, which is a noisier basis than a direct comparison would be. [RQ4.5] Five-fold cross-validation over subjects, stated explicitly and unambiguously - 'no information of subjects used for testing is used in the learning phase, once the cross-validation was performed over the subjects' - which is the correct unit and is rarely stated this plainly. A second partition operates over frames, with 50 held out from model learning for diagnosis only, deliberately simulating stimulus independence. The authors also pre-empt and address the same-video contamination objection. Two elements nonetheless sit outside the loop: the genetic algorithm feature selection is presented as a single result per group with no indication it was repeated per fold, and the 28-vote decision threshold was chosen by Youden index on the cross-validated ROC. There is no independent cohort or external site. [RQ5.1] No formal keyword list. Vocabulary: 'visual attention model', 'region of interest', 'saliency map', 'fixation map', 'stimulus independence', 'computer-aided diagnosis'. The recurring conceptual pair is fixation map versus saliency map - what a person actually looked at against what a model predicts a group would look at - and classification is the comparison between them. [RQ5.2] Scientific Reports, 11, 10131 - a broad open-access multidisciplinary journal, with authorship spanning a computing school, a university psychiatry department and a bioinformatics postgraduate programme. [RQ5.3] 2021. The framing is a precise methodological critique rather than a general appeal to objectivity. Region-of-interest methods carry two costs: annotation burden, since every ROI must be marked on every frame of every video, and information loss, since aggregating within a region discards 'which visual features of sub parts of an image had a more fixed gaze'. The paper grounds its alternative in attention theory, distinguishing bottom-up circuits driven by image properties from top-down circuits using prior knowledge and social rules, and traces the computational lineage from the Koch model through Itti's implementation to the supervised saliency models of Borji and Judd. It positions its own advance as extending these from static images to video, citing the argument that video 'can contribute with more discoveries because the videos have temporal information'. It also situates itself quantitatively against prior work, tabulating AUCs of 0.71, 0.71 and 0.86 from three published studies against its own 0.82, and noting that its sample is larger and more heterogeneous in age, sex and severity than the comparators.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control classification with parallel general and hypothesis-contrast modelling; 55 Spanish children aged 4-7 - 35 autistic (5.26 +/- 0.51 years) from a Valencia neurocognitive development centre and 20 typically developing (4.75 +/- 0.77 years) recruited by mailing, both assessed with ADOS-2 module 1 and ADI-R but with no scores or sex reported; gaze from Tobii Pro Glasses 2 during a 24-minute multisensory CAVE experience; data not released.
narrative_rows.methods: A three-wall CAVE with synchronised projection, 5.1 audio and programmable odour delivery presented a 16-scene virtual mall with an interacting avatar, counterbalanced in order and interleaved with calming forest scenes; head-mounted eye tracking with gyroscopic head-motion compensation was mapped frame-by-frame onto hierarchical areas of interest covering people (adults, children, avatar, faces, bodies), items (dynamic, static) and background, yielding 144 frame-count features globally and per scene plus explicit difference features; ten datasets were modelled by naive Bayes, XGBoost, kNN, random forest and SVM at default hyperparameters, with step backward wrapper selection capped at ten features and five-fold cross-validation repeated four times.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Best model 0.86 accuracy (SD 0.10), kappa 0.69, AUC 0.91, sensitivity 0.91, specificity 0.82 using all features with SVM; the 13-significant-feature model reached 0.77 with the lowest variability. Hypothesis-contrast families ranked people-versus-items 0.84, adults-versus-items 0.83, children-versus-items 0.82, children-versus-adults 0.78, children's faces-versus-bodies 0.74, faces-versus-bodies 0.73, dynamic-versus-static items 0.69 and adults' faces-versus-bodies 0.66. Thirteen features differed significantly, all in the direction of autistic children viewing social elements and static items in more frames.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Feature subset and model both selected on the same repeated cross-validation across five algorithms and ten datasets, so reported maxima are optimistically biased and no independent sample was tested - both stated by the authors; groups unmatched on age, sociodemographics, IQ and cognitive ability, also acknowledged; sex not reported for either group; no ADOS-2 or ADI-R scores reported; ADOS-2 module 1 indicates a minimally verbal autistic sample that may bound generality; macro-level areas of interest cannot resolve eye and mouth patterns; and both the eye-tracking glasses and the CAVE are described as too costly for clinical deployment.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The corpus's clearest well-argued contradiction of a canonical finding: autistic children here looked at social elements in significantly more frames than typically developing children, the opposite of what most gaze studies report, and the authors neither bury it nor overclaim it. They situate it against meta-analytic evidence that reduced social attention appears mainly when social content exceeds one person, propose that a rich immersive environment activates rather than suppresses exploration, and note that offline social cognition paradigms may not generalise across contexts. That argument, and the accompanying catalogue of studies finding reduced, increased and null social-attention effects, should inform how the synthesis treats the many corpus studies that assume reduced social looking as a given. The paradigm is also the corpus's most elaborate - 24 minutes across 16 scripted scenes with synchronised olfactory delivery, joint-attention bids and emotional displays, plus calming interludes designed around sensory overload - and its feature-family ranking supplies a transferable methodological result: coarse social-versus-non-social contrasts discriminate well while fine face-internal contrasts do not, at macro-area granularity. Its honest reporting of deployment barriers, that glasses may be rejected by young children and that CAVE assembly is prohibitively expensive, is equally useful for assessing translational claims elsewhere in the corpus.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups totalling 55 children aged 4-7: 35 autistic recruited from the Red Cenit Neurocognitive Development Center in Valencia and 20 typically developing recruited by a management company through calls and mailings to families. The 35:20 imbalance is not addressed by any balancing procedure. Both groups are stated to have received the same evaluation scales and procedure before the experiment. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the authors name ADHD inclusion as a priority for future work specifically to 'identify with greater precision the degrees of severity in each disorder'. [RQ1.2] 'autistic children', 'children with ASD', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'autistic participants'. Predominantly identity-first ('autistic children') rather than person-first, which is unusual in this corpus and aligns with neurodiversity-community preference. The framing is measurement-oriented rather than deficit-oriented, centred on the argument that clinical assessment 'relies on children's observable behaviors and parents' interview responses, which clinicians rate according to their expertise and subjectivity', and that 'social desirability bias has been found to affect the veracity of parents' responses'. [RQ1.3] Autistic group: 35 children, mean age 5.26 +/- 0.51 years. Typically developing group: 20 children, mean age 4.75 +/- 0.77 years. Sex is not reported for either group anywhere in the paper - a striking omission in autism research. The six-month age difference is untested. Most importantly, the authors state directly that 'experimental groups were not matched on sociodemographics, IQ, or cognitive ability, limiting the generalization of the model', and recommend treating these as moderators in future work. The only stated exclusion criteria were wearing glasses or having an ocular alteration or pathology. ADOS-2 module 1 administration indicates the autistic sample is minimally verbal, which is important context for the study's central finding. [RQ1.4] ADOS-2 and ADI-R, both described in detail with their psychometric properties - ADOS-2 test-retest reliability of 0.87 for social impairment, 0.64 for repetitive behaviour and 0.88 for the global index; ADI-R ranging 0.93-0.97 - and the paper states that both groups were 'individually evaluated with the same scales and procedure prior to the experiments'. This is a strong ascertainment on paper. The gap is that no scores are reported for any participant or group, so neither the severity distribution nor the separation between groups can be inspected, and the assertion that typically developing children received the same instruments cannot be checked against data. ADOS-2 module 1 is specified, which locates the autistic sample among children who do not use coherent phrase language. [RQ1.5] ADOS-2 and ADI-R administered but with no scores reported and no severity-stratified analysis. No IQ, cognitive, adaptive or language measures, and the authors identify the absence of IQ and cognitive matching as a limitation requiring attention in future work. The only functional indicator available is the choice of ADOS-2 module 1. [RQ2.1] Goal: determine whether gaze in an immersive virtual environment distinguishes autistic from typically developing children and which parameters do so. Main findings: 86% accuracy with 91% sensitivity and AUC 0.91 using all features; autistic children looked at social elements in more frames than typically developing children, contrary to most prior work; they also attended more to static non-social items; people-versus-items contrasts discriminated best at 84% while adults'-faces-versus-bodies discriminated worst at 66%; and the model restricted to the 13 statistically significant features was less accurate but the most stable across iterations. [RQ2.2] A three-wall CAVE of 4 x 4 x 3 m at the Institute for Research and Innovation in Bioengineering, Polytechnic University of Valencia, with autistic participants from the Red Cenit Neurocognitive Development Center and comparison children recruited by a management company. Funded by the Spanish Ministry of Economy, Industry and Competitiveness project 'Immersive Virtual Environment for the Evaluation and Training of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: T Room'. [RQ2.3] The most elaborate elicitation paradigm in the corpus: a 24-minute 45-second multisensory virtual mall with 16 scripted scenes and synchronised visual, auditory and olfactory channels. The scenes are designed to sample distinct social demands - an avatar greeting the child and asking their name, peekaboo through shop displays, a choice offered between an apple and a lollipop, explicit joint-attention bids where the avatar indicates three times verbally and by gesture that the child should look left, an emotional display of disgust at a trash can, and a startling event where a train nearly runs over the avatar. Two design decisions deserve note: forest scenes with relaxing music were inserted at the start and between stores specifically 'to avoid cognitive and sensory overload', and scene order was counterbalanced across participants. This is elicitation designed around the population's sensory needs rather than only around the constructs being measured. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single 24-minute session per child with no follow-up. Data are first-person video of identifiable children moving through a monitored environment. Governance is properly reported: informed consent from relatives after explanation of objectives and procedure, separate explicit consent to video recording of the child, ethics committee approval at the Polytechnic University of Valencia, and Helsinki conformity. A researcher remained present to monitor the child but 'attempted to intervene as little as possible (only in situations of device failure or cybersickness)' - the only mention of cybersickness in the corpus and a real consideration for immersive paradigms with children. [RQ2.5] A three-wall CAVE with three ultrashort-throw projectors, Logitech Z906 5.1 audio and a wireless Olorama olfactory system regulating odour presence and intensity; Tobii Pro Glasses 2 with a scene camera, two cameras per eye using a 3D eye model, and an accelerometer and gyroscope allowing head and eye movement to be separated so that head motion does not contaminate gaze data - a technical requirement for free movement that screen-based trackers cannot meet. Glasses were fitted and calibrated in an adjacent room, with researchers verifying both correct operation and that 'the subject did not reject them' before the child entered the CAVE. Analysis in R 3.6.1. [RQ2.6] Strong on protocol, weaker on results provenance. Reported: every scene with its content and duration; CAVE dimensions, projector, audio and olfactory hardware; child positioning; the counterbalancing and the sensory-overload interludes; the calibration and acceptance procedure; the eye tracker's head-motion compensation; the hierarchical area-of-interest structure; all five feature families with construction rules including the difference features; the normality testing and choice between t-test and Mann-Whitney; the step backward wrapper with its ten-feature cap; the repeated cross-validation scheme; and six metrics with standard deviations for all ten datasets. Missing: participant sex, ADOS-2 and ADI-R scores, the identity of the selected features in the winning models (deferred to a supplementary table), any data or code release, and reconciliation of how many total model fits the reported maxima were selected from. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged with unusual completeness. The sample is small, the feature count high, and 'the models were not applied to an independent sample'; the authors state directly that 'data from all participants were used to validate the model; therefore, the reported results correspond to the cross-validation process', offering the 20 iterations and low standard deviations as partial mitigation. Groups were not matched on sociodemographics, IQ or cognitive ability. The macro-level area-of-interest approach 'presented some limitations in terms of recognition of specific eye gaze patterns related to specific areas, such as face areas (i.e., eyes and mouth)'. Eye-tracking glasses may not be accepted by young children and both they and the CAVE are expensive, limiting clinical deployment. Training took about 20 hours even parallelised. Not acknowledged: the feature subset and model were both chosen on the same repeated cross-validation that produces the reported metrics, across five algorithms and ten datasets, so the headline is a maximum over roughly fifty fits; participant sex is never reported; and the minimally verbal composition implied by ADOS-2 module 1 may bound the generality of the reversed social-attention finding. [RQ2.9] Larger samples with testing on an independent dataset; treatment of sociodemographics, IQ and cognitive ability as moderators; refinement of areas of interest to include eyes and mouth, and adoption of a bottom-up data-driven definition rather than predefined macro-areas; development of a portable system with integrated remote eye tracking to replace glasses that young children may reject and a CAVE that is prohibitively expensive to assemble; and inclusion of other neurodevelopmental conditions such as ADHD to sharpen discrimination and characterise severity gradations. [RQ3.1] Visual attention to social and non-social content during free exploration of a rich environment, decomposed hierarchically: people versus items versus background; within people, the main interacting avatar versus other characters, adults versus children, faces versus bodies; within items, dynamic versus static. Because features are computed both globally and per scene, the analysis can locate where in the 16-scene sequence group differences arise - and the significant differences cluster in the hall, the electronics shop and the game centre rather than being distributed evenly, which is information a whole-session summary would lose. [RQ3.2] No cross-modal fusion of sensor streams, but the stimulus is genuinely multisensory - visual, auditory and olfactory channels are synchronised, with odour presence and intensity under programmatic control. The analytic combination is across feature families, and the hypothesis-contrast approach makes it systematic: eight predefined families are modelled separately so their discriminative value can be compared. The resulting ordering is informative. Coarse social-versus-non-social contrasts perform best - people versus items at 84%, adults versus items at 83%, children versus items at 82% - while fine-grained within-social contrasts perform worst, with adults' faces versus bodies reaching only 66% and kappa 0.25. The authors draw the correct conclusion, that macro-area definitions capture the signal but cannot resolve face-internal patterns, and recommend adding eye and mouth areas. [RQ4.1] Five classifiers - naive Bayes, XGBoost, kNN, random forest and SVM - trained on each of ten datasets, with the best per dataset reported. Default hyperparameters were used throughout, a decision the authors justify explicitly as avoiding an additional layer of search complexity. That is defensible and unusually candid, though it means the algorithm comparison reflects default behaviour rather than tuned potential, and different algorithms win on different datasets (SVM on two, kNN on two, naive Bayes on two, random forest and XGBoost on one each), which is what one would expect when nothing is tuned and sample sizes are small. [RQ4.2] 144 frame-count features spanning general, background, area-of-interest, person and item families, each computed globally and per scene, plus explicitly constructed difference features contrasting faces against bodies, children against adults, avatar against other characters, dynamic against static items, and people against items. Building the contrasts directly into the feature set rather than leaving them for the model to discover is a sensible choice at this sample size. The unit throughout is the number of frames in which something was seen, which measures how much of the session was spent looking at a category but discards fixation structure, dwell duration and sequence - a limitation the authors partly recognise in calling for finer area definitions. [RQ4.3] Six metrics - accuracy, kappa, AUC, F1, sensitivity and specificity - each with a standard deviation across 20 cross-validation iterations, reported for the best model on every one of ten datasets. Including kappa alongside accuracy is appropriate given the 35:20 imbalance and is done consistently. The standard deviations are used substantively: the model on the 13 significant features is noted to have 'the lowest standard deviations, showing the highest consistency', which is a real finding distinct from mean accuracy. Missing: confusion matrices, confidence intervals, and any statistical comparison between the ten datasets, so whether 0.86 differs meaningfully from 0.84 on 55 children is not established - and the standard deviation of 0.10 on the best model spans that gap. [RQ4.4] Interpretability comes from two complementary analyses rather than from any model-explanation method. Univariate testing with normality checking identifies 13 significantly differing features and localises them to specific scenes, and the eight hypothesis-contrast datasets rank feature families by discriminative value. Together these support a specific claim: coarse social-versus-non-social attention differentiates the groups while fine facial detail does not, at least at the area granularity used. The interpretation of the reversed direction is the most substantive interpretive work in the paper, connecting the finding to social-content level, to the static-versus-dynamic stimulus distinction, and to the argument that 'findings related to offline social cognition may not be generalizable across contexts'. The authors position their paradigm as 'an effective middle point' between contrived screen tasks and uncontrollable real settings. [RQ4.5] Five-fold cross-validation repeated four times with means and standard deviations reported, which is better practice than single-split evaluation and gives some sense of variability. The limitation is stated by the authors themselves - no independent sample exists and all participants contributed to validation - and compounded by the fact that both the feature subset and the model were selected on that same repeated cross-validation, across five algorithms and ten datasets. The reported per-dataset maxima are therefore optimistically biased, and the general-approach figure of 0.86 is the best of roughly fifty fits. The ten-feature cap on selection is a sensible guard against overfitting given 144 candidates and 55 participants, and using default hyperparameters removes one further source of selection. There is no external site, no independent cohort and no held-out replication. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, behavioral biomarker, eye tracking, machine learning, multivariate supervised learning, virtual reality. 'Behavioral biomarker' is the organising concept - the paper's framing is that gaze can serve as an implicit, unconscious indicator complementing explicit symptom observation, situated alongside genetic, neural and physiological biomarker classes. [RQ5.2] Autism Research, 15(1), 131-145 - the journal of the International Society for Autism Research, published open access under CC BY. Publishing in a specialist autism venue rather than an engineering one is consistent with the paper's substantive engagement with the social-attention literature and its willingness to contest an established finding. [RQ5.3] 2021. The framing combines three arguments. On objectivity, that assessment 'relies on children's observable behaviors and parents' interview responses, which clinicians rate according to their expertise and subjectivity', with the specific addition that 'social desirability bias has been found to affect the veracity of parents' responses'. On ecological validity, that assessment 'occurs in laboratories or clinical settings lacking ecological validity that could offer a deeper understanding of real-life abilities'. And on timing, that 'many ASD dimensions are internal and do not manifest until 2-3 years of age', lengthening diagnosis. Its most valuable contribution to the corpus's framing is a careful review of the inconsistency in the social-attention literature: it catalogues studies finding reduced social attention, four finding increased social preference, and eight finding no difference, and identifies the moderators as static versus dynamic stimuli and level of social content - citing meta-analytic evidence that autistic children attended less to social stimuli specifically 'when the social content was higher (i.e., the number of people exceeded one)'. Its own contrary result is then argued within that framework rather than against it.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control classification from a single conversational session; 43 Chinese children recruited and 38 analysed - 18 autistic aged 6-13 with DSM-IV diagnosis by an experienced psychiatrist and Raven's IQ of 70 or above, and 20 typically developing from nearby communities screened for personal and first-degree relative diagnoses; frontal video converted to head pose time series, not released.
narrative_rows.methods: Children answered ten yes-no questions while explicitly instructed to nod or shake their heads, seated 80 cm from a blinded interviewer; OpenFace 2.0 extracted pitch, yaw and roll angular displacement from a webcam feed, spline-smoothed, from which rotation range and amount of rotation per minute were computed in each axis; two blind coders independently rated gesture occurrence; linear mixed-effects models tested each feature with group as fixed factor and age, IQ and three gesture-frequency measures as random factors; all 63 feature subsets were then fed to SVM, LDA, decision tree, random forest and AdaBoost under leave-one-out cross-validation.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Decision tree best at 92.11% accuracy with two features, 88.9% sensitivity, 95% specificity, AUC 0.9167; all five classifiers exceeded 81% accuracy and 0.81 AUC using three features or fewer. Head nodding, shaking and non-use frequencies did not differ between groups (all p > 0.05). Rotation range and amount of rotation per minute were significantly greater in autistic children in all three axes after adjusting for age, IQ and gesture frequency.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: All 63 feature subsets were evaluated across five classifiers on the same leave-one-out estimate that is reported, so 92.11% is a maximum over 315 fits with no outer loop; the abstract and results disagree on which two features produced it; OpenFace tracking failed on 3.46% of autistic frames against 0.23% of typically developing frames, reported but not analysed despite being a plausible partial source of the kinematic difference; 38 participants with one case worth 2.6 accuracy points; the instructed-gesture design means the frequency null may not generalise to spontaneous contexts, as the authors note; ages 6-13 are well above the mean diagnosis age; severity unmeasured; and no ethics approval number, data or code.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Opens head movement as a behavioural channel for autism identification and does so with a design that isolates the right question. By instructing every child to nod or shake, it separates whether a gesture occurs from how it is executed, and finds a clean dissociation: blind human coders detected no difference in gesture frequency, while automated pose tracking found significantly greater rotation range and rotation per minute in all three axes after adjusting for age, IQ and gesture frequency. That within-study divergence substantiates a claim the corpus often asserts but rarely demonstrates - that automated measurement captures metric properties of movement human observation cannot judge. Its covariate handling, entering age, IQ and gesture frequency as random factors when establishing feature discrimination, is among the most careful in the corpus. Two cautions carry forward: the exhaustive subset search across five classifiers makes the headline a best-of-315 figure, and the fifteenfold group difference in tracking failure is a measurement-quality confound of exactly the kind seen elsewhere in this corpus, where data-quality variables turn out to carry group signal.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups: 20 autistic children recruited from a local psychiatric hospital and 23 typically developing children from nearby communities, with five excluded for camera technical problems leaving 18 and 20. Participants are the same cohort as a companion study by the same group on conversational eye tracking, but the data come from a different conversational session - the yes-no question session rather than the full four-session conversation. No other-diagnosis comparison group. Participants were paid 200 CNY, which is disclosed. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'individuals with ASD', 'children with typical development (TD)', 'the affected children'. Mixed person-first and abbreviated forms. The framing locates the diagnostic problem in procedure and capacity rather than in children: diagnostic accuracy 'might be negatively affected by factors such as caregivers' report bias and clinicians' insufficient experiences of detecting ASD', and 'the shortage in specialists and the lengthy examinations make the diagnostic procedure a time-consuming process'. [RQ1.3] Eligibility required ages 6-13 in both groups, at least average nonverbal intelligence (IQ 70 or above by Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices) in the autistic group, and absence of physical or mental disorder plus no autism or ADHD in first-degree relatives for the comparison group. Group-wise ages, sexes and IQ appear in Table 1, which did not survive text extraction; the companion study on the same cohort reports mean ages of 99.6 and 108.8 months, sex ratios of 17:2 and 17:3, and a significant 15-point IQ difference favouring the comparison group. That IQ gap matters here too, and the study handles it better than most: age and IQ are both entered as random factors in the mixed-effects models used to establish which features discriminate, so the reported kinematic differences are adjusted for both. No ethnicity or socioeconomic data.
