Testing Set 2's single-class composition is a real limitation on what it can validate: with no typically developing children, its 80.2% figure is sensitivity alone and cannot detect a model that has drifted toward calling everyone autistic. No other-diagnosis or developmentally-delayed comparison group appears anywhere, so the model is never tested against the discrimination that matters clinically - autism versus other developmental concern - only against typical development. [RQ1.2] 'children with autism', 'children with ASD', 'individuals with autism', against 'typically developing (TD) children', 'their typically developing peers'. Consistently person-first, and the phrase 'their typically developing peers' in the abstract is a comparatively warm construction. 'Patients' never appears. Autism is described in DSM terms as 'impairments in social communication and interactions, and the presence of restricted, repetitive patterns of interests and behaviors', and the surrounding language is clinical rather than pathologising - 'atypical', 'aberrant' and 'unusual' applied to behaviours rather than to children. The Discussion is notably respectful in framing the purpose as supporting development during a plastic period rather than as detecting defect. [RQ1.3] Autistic group in the main pool: 68 children, 2.80 +/- 0.92 years, range 1.2-5.1. Typically developing group: 68 children, 2.55 +/- 0.97 years, same range. Testing Set 2: 101 autistic children, 3.46 +/- 1.16 years, range 2-6.9. Groups are stated to be matched for diagnosis, age, gender and ADOS module, with the sex distribution given in supplementary Table S1 rather than the main text - the only demographic detail displaced to supplementary material. Matching on ADOS module is a subtler control than most studies apply: module assignment depends on expressive language level, so matching on it partially equates the groups on language, which for a non-verbal-behaviour classifier removes an obvious alternative explanation. The comparison group is nonetheless typically developing rather than developmentally delayed, so age and module matching cannot equate general developmental level - and best-estimate IQ, which is measured, is not reported as matched and correlates with the model output. [RQ1.4] Clinical diagnosis under DSM-5, corroborated by gold-standard instruments (ADOS-G or ADOS-2) administered as part of an established longitudinal cohort study, with cohort recruitment procedures documented in three cited prior publications. Comparison children were screened not only for known neurological or psychiatric illness but also for autism in any first-degree relative - a criterion stricter than nearly any other study in this corpus, since it excludes children carrying familial liability who might show subthreshold features and thereby blur the contrast. Ethics approval from the Faculty of Medicine of Geneva University, written informed parental consent for all children, and separate explicit consent for the identifiable figure images. [RQ1.5] Comprehensive and, unusually, used analytically rather than descriptively. ADOS calibrated severity scores for total, social affect and restricted/repetitive behaviour; VABS-II Adaptive Behavior Composite with communication, socialisation, daily-living and motor subdomains; and a Best Estimate IQ constructed to combine 'the most representative cognitive functioning measures for each child', since instruments varied with age and with each child's ability to attend demanding tasks - a pragmatic solution to a real problem in toddler cognitive assessment, and one that is documented rather than glossed. All three feed the validation analyses. Comorbidities are not described for the autistic group. [RQ2.1] Goal: test whether a network trained purely on non-verbal social interaction, represented as skeletal motion, can differentiate autistic from typically developing children - explicitly framed against prior digital phenotyping that focused on 'relatively isolated behaviors elicited by largely controlled prompts'. Main findings: 80.9% accuracy (precision 0.784, recall 0.854, specificity 0.765, F1 0.818) on 68 held-out children; 80.2% on a further 101 autistic children; ~70% from 10 minutes of video, with 100% within-child prediction consistency from a random 10-minute segment for half the autistic sample; robustness to different rooms, examiners and cameras; ASD probability correlated with ADOS severity (total 0.451, social affect 0.509, repetitive behaviours 0.409), inversely with adaptive functioning (-0.444) and IQ (-0.283); and 15 of 27 ADOS items significantly related after Bonferroni correction, predominantly non-verbal, confirmed by a permutation-tested PLS-C latent component (p = 0.001). [RQ2.2] University of Geneva, Switzerland, within an ongoing longitudinal study of early autism development. The assessments were not staged for this analysis - they are the cohort's routine clinical ADOS sessions, conducted 'in several different rooms', by 'different examiners', and 'filmed with different camera systems'. That heterogeneity is the study's most under-appreciated methodological asset: where other work in this corpus achieves high accuracy under a single fixed acquisition setup and therefore cannot distinguish diagnostic signal from site signature, here the acquisition varies within both classes, so camera, room and examiner cannot serve as proxies for group. The authors report classification robustness to this variability explicitly in supplementary analysis and treat it as evidence for generalisability rather than as noise to be apologised for. [RQ2.3] The ADOS assessment itself, filmed end to end and averaging 42 minutes - not a purpose-built task. Only Modules Toddler, 1 and 2 were used, on the stated grounds that these are conducted while moving around a room with attractive toys and demand less language, whereas Modules 3 and 4 are table-based and discussion-heavy. The paradigm's key property is that it requires no new protocol, instrumentation or examiner training: any clinic that already videotapes ADOS sessions holds the raw material. Against that, it inherits a structural feature the paper does not examine - the ADOS is an interactive assessment in which a trained examiner actively presses for social behaviours and adapts to the child's responses, so the recorded scene is a joint product of child and clinician, and the video contains the examiner and frequently a caregiver as well. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional analysis of data acquired within a longitudinal cohort; no longitudinal modelling is performed here, though the parent study follows children over time and the authors position the measure as suitable for tracking development. Ethics are reported in full: approval by the Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Medicine of Geneva University, methods stated to conform to that institution's guidelines and regulations, informed written consent obtained from a parent or legal guardian for every child, and separate explicit consent for publication of identifying images from both the adults and the guardian of the child appearing in Figure 1. The privacy engineering is stronger still: reducing video to skeletons on a black background was adopted partly 'to ensure de-identification of the persons involved', so the analytic representation is itself the anonymisation - among the few instances in this corpus where sensitive video data are handled by design rather than by assurance. [RQ2.5] Deliberately minimal on the acquisition side. OpenPose 'uses a simple 2D camera input not requiring any external markers or sensors, thus allowing the retrospective analysis of videos' and is 'immune to variations in resolutions and setting' - so no motion capture suits, markers, depth sensors or calibrated rigs, and existing archives become usable. Analytically: OpenPose COCO model with 18 keypoints (13 body, 5 facial); VGG16 pretrained on ImageNet; a 512-unit LSTM; rmsprop with categorical cross-entropy; training on the Geneva Baobab HPC cluster across RTX 2080Ti, Titan X and Quadro P1000 GPUs; GraphPad Prism v.8 and SPSS v.25 for statistics, both with URLs. The contrast with the marker-based and depth-camera motor studies elsewhere in this corpus is the point - equivalent or better accuracy from ordinary video. [RQ2.6] Strong on the pipeline, with one class of omission. Reported: OpenPose model variant and keypoint count; background removal; the decision to compute feature vectors from image output rather than raw coordinates, with the stated purpose of invariance to rigid-body and affine transformation; downsampling from 696x554 to 320x240; 5-second segmentation with the selection justified by validation loss against 10 and 15 seconds; full VGG16 layer geometry; LSTM size and both dropout rates; optimiser, loss, batch size, epochs and the 80-20 internal split; the least-validation-loss checkpointing rule; the 0.5 threshold on averaged ASD probability; the sliding-window procedure with its 20-second start and 20-second step; every Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold; and the PLS-C decomposition with its 1000 permutations and 1000 bootstrap resamples. Video-level statistics are tabulated (68/68/101 videos, 47.8/48.7/50.0 hours, ~505 segments per video). Missing: no code or model weights release, no data availability statement in the extracted text, no random seeds, and - the substantive gap - no statement of how many people appear per frame or whether any person-selection was applied to OpenPose's multi-person output, which is exactly the detail needed to know whose movement the classifier is reading. [RQ2.7] The study's weakest aspect: there is no limitations section, and the Discussion is uniformly positive. Only one caveat is stated anywhere - that 'the current level of analysis prevents us from drawing solid conclusions on what is represented in the NN' - and it is offered in support of the future-work agenda rather than as a constraint on the claims. Four issues go unaddressed. OpenPose extracts keypoints for all persons present and the videos contain examiner and often caregiver alongside the child, so the model may be reading clinician behaviour, which is systematically different when a clinician is eliciting from a child who does not respond; nothing in the paper isolates the child. The clinical-validity correlations are computed across a mixed two-group sample where severity is near-floor in one group, so they largely re-express the group difference rather than demonstrating within-group grading. ASD probability correlates inversely with IQ and adaptive functioning, raising a developmental-level confound that is reported without comment. And the single null in the entire correlation table is the VABS-II motor subdomain (-0.186, p = 0.066) - the domain a pose-based classifier would most be expected to track - which passes without remark. Testing Set 2 is also presented as endorsing 'the model's stability' without noting that a single-class sample cannot detect loss of specificity. [RQ2.9] Two concrete and well-motivated directions. Add a spatio-temporal attention mechanism 'to allow knowledge on the specific elements in space and time used to inform the diagnosis process in the network' - which, if it also resolved which person's skeleton drives the decision, would address the study's main unexamined confound. And perform fine-grained annotation along the non-verbal continuum for the behaviours that contributed most, specifically 'the precise annotation of the incidence of communicative gestures, shared affective states, atypical social overtures', to establish what the network learned and to build a measure more sensitive than a 3- or 4-point clinical scale. The broader agenda is finer-grained digital phenotyping able to process data 'at the spatio-temporal resolution that is off limits to human coding', to uncover manifestations not previously evidenced and to define subtypes for more precise clinical action. [RQ3.1] Non-verbal social interaction taken as a global pattern rather than as an inventory of separable behaviours - the study's central conceptual commitment. The stated target is 'global patterns of atypical postures and movements, fewer gestures used and often decoupled from visual contact, facial affect, speech', with the emphasis on decoupling: the claim is that autistic non-verbal behaviour differs less in the presence or absence of individual acts than in how gesture, gaze, posture and affect are coordinated with one another and with the partner. That is a behavioural construct which single-behaviour paradigms cannot in principle capture, and it justifies both the whole-assessment input and the temporal modelling. The post-hoc symptom analysis supports the framing empirically: the items that tracked model output most strongly were integration of gaze with other behaviours (0.591), pointing (0.540) and unusual eye contact (0.500) - coordination items rather than frequency items. [RQ3.2] Single-modality by design, and the design is an argument. Sound is discarded, faces are discarded, appearance and scene are discarded, and what remains is 2D skeletal motion alone. The authors' case is that this isolates the non-verbal channel cleanly, and it is strengthened by the symptom analysis: of 27 ADOS items, the 15 that tracked model output were predominantly non-verbal, while the lowest-loading items on the PLS-C latent component were the verbal ones - immediate echolalia and stereotyped language - which the authors correctly attribute to a largely pre-verbal sample rather than to a modelling failure. Their handling of intonation, the one vocal item that loaded highly on a model that cannot hear, is the most careful piece of reasoning in the paper: rather than claiming the network recovered prosody, they explain that atypical intonation occurs in more severely affected, minimally verbal children who simultaneously score higher on atypical social overtures, atypical social response and undirected vocalisation, so the correlation runs through severity rather than through sound. Multi-person fusion is present but unexamined - skeletons of child, examiner and caregiver enter the same input without separation. [RQ4.1] A CNN-LSTM action-recognition architecture - VGG16 for per-frame spatial encoding, a 512-unit LSTM for temporal dependency within 5-second windows - selected because it 'previously showed a good performance in video-based action classification'. The choice matches the construct: if what distinguishes the groups is the temporal coordination of non-verbal behaviours rather than their static configuration, a model without temporal structure could not capture it. The authors report that the final architecture 'was obtained upon testing various configurations', with the alternatives shown in supplementary Figure S2, and that 5-second segments beat 10- and 15-second segments on validation loss - so architecture and segment length were both selected on the internal validation split rather than on the held-out children, which is the correct separation. [RQ4.2] The most consequential representational decision in the corpus: rendered skeletons on a black background, with the background removed entirely. This forecloses whole classes of confound that demonstrably affect other studies here - clinic decor, lighting, camera model, image resolution, clothing, and the facial appearance that group-specific recording conditions can encode. It simultaneously delivers de-identification, which the authors name as a co-equal motivation. Two further choices support generalisation: features are computed from rendered image output rather than raw keypoint coordinates, explicitly 'to obtain feature vectors invariant to a rigid body and affine transformations', so a child positioned differently relative to the camera is not thereby a different input; and downsampling to 320x240 keeps the representation coarse. The residual limitation is that the rendering includes every person OpenPose detects, so the representation is of the interaction scene rather than of the child. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1 on the balanced held-out set - a complete set for a binary task, and one that shows the model is not trading sensitivity for specificity (0.854 against 0.765, the most balanced profile among the higher-accuracy studies in this corpus). Two additional evaluations go beyond the standard panel and are more informative than any of them. Accuracy as a function of input video length quantifies the deployment tradeoff directly, showing ~70% at 10 minutes rising to 81% at full length - a dose-response curve for evidence, which no other study here provides. And prediction consistency within an individual, reported as the cumulative incidence of the segment length needed for 100% stable class attribution across randomly drawn windows, measures whether a single child would receive the same answer twice - a reliability question distinct from accuracy and one that matters more for a screening tool than the point estimate does. Missing: no confidence intervals on any figure, no confusion matrix, and no significance test against a trivial baseline such as age. [RQ4.4] No internal interpretability - no attention, no saliency, no layer analysis - and the authors state the limitation plainly: 'the current level of analysis prevents us from drawing solid conclusions on what is represented in the NN'. What replaces it is external validation against clinical ratings, executed with more statistical care than any comparable analysis in the corpus. Correlations against ADOS severity, VABS-II and best-estimate IQ are Bonferroni-corrected at explicitly stated thresholds (p < 0.025, p < 0.013, p < 0.002 for the 27-item analysis). Recognising that ADOS items are collinear and that 27 separate tests would be the wrong instrument regardless of correction, the authors then run a Partial Least Squares Correlation with 1000 permutations to test the latent component and 1000 bootstrap resamples to establish salience stability - a multivariate treatment that yields a single significant component (p = 0.001) rather than a list of individually surviving items. The resulting picture is coherent: non-verbal coordination items load highest, verbal items lowest. The inference is nonetheless indirect - it establishes that model output covaries with clinically rated non-verbal atypicality, not that the network computes it, and the correlations are inflated by being taken across two groups whose severity distributions barely overlap. [RQ4.5] The corpus's reference implementation of correct validation for a segment-generating modality. Three properties matter. Participant-wise partition: the 136 children are split 68/68 into training and Testing Set 1, matched on diagnosis, age, gender and ADOS module, so no child's frames appear on both sides - and matching the partitions on covariates, not merely the groups, is a refinement almost nothing else here applies. Participant-level aggregation: the network trains and predicts on 5-second segments (~505 per video, ~34,000 in training), but every segment prediction within a video is averaged into one ASD probability per child before any metric is computed, so the reported 80.9% is over 68 children and not over 34,000 clips. This is precisely the correction that Cilia had to apply retrospectively, watching image-level accuracy of ~90% fall to ~71% at participant level, and applying it by construction is what makes this figure comparable to a clinical one. Hyperparameter selection is confined to an 80-20 split inside the training set, with the least-validation-loss checkpoint carried forward. Two limits persist. Testing Set 2, though larger, contains only autistic children and comes from the same cohort, so it estimates sensitivity in a slightly older sample rather than replicating externally - no independent site or cohort is tested. And the covariate matching does not extend to cognitive level: best-estimate IQ is measured, differs between a typically developing and an autistic group as a matter of course, and correlates with the model's output at -0.283, so some portion of the separation may reflect general developmental level rather than autism specifically. No leave-one-site-out or examiner-held-out analysis addresses the parallel possibility that examiner behaviour contributes. [RQ5.1] No keyword list appears in the extracted text. The operative vocabulary is 'digital phenotyping', '2D pose estimation', 'deep neural network', 'non-verbal social interaction' and 'automated screening' - a framing that positions the work within clinical digital phenotyping rather than computer vision, notwithstanding that the machinery is entirely the latter. [RQ5.2] Scientific Reports 11:15069 (2021), doi 10.1038/s41598-021-94378-z - a broad-scope journal reaching both clinical and computational readerships. The authorship is genuinely interdisciplinary and the division of labour shows in the paper: the Psychiatry Department at the University of Geneva supplies the cohort, the gold-standard clinical measures and the ADOS-item interpretation; AIcrowd supplies the deep learning; and the Geneva School of Economics and Management and Citizen Cyber Lab supply the scalability framing. Two authors are marked as contributing equally, one clinical and one computational. That composition explains why this study alone in the corpus combines competent deep learning with full clinical characterisation, correct partitioning and Bonferroni-corrected multivariate validation - most papers here have one side of that expertise or the other. [RQ5.3] 2021 (received March, accepted July). The framing is the standard early-detection argument but stated with unusual precision and with quantities attached: autism is detectable at 14 months and with high certainty before two years, yet over 70% of affected children are not diagnosed before 51 months; children diagnosed before age two can gain up to 20 IQ points over the following year, while those diagnosed after four 'will not show any substantial cognitive gain even with adequate intervention'. That last figure converts the diagnostic delay from an inconvenience into a quantified loss and is the strongest version of the early-detection premise in this corpus. The critique of existing tools is equally specific - most screening tests are questionnaire-based, perform with low to moderate accuracy, and are 'prone to recall and subjectivity bias'. What most distinguishes the paper's positioning, though, is its critique of the prior computational literature rather than of clinical practice: it names the field's dominant paradigm - single-feature extraction from controlled prompts - as the limitation to be overcome, and argues that a construct defined by the decoupling of behaviours from one another cannot be measured by indexing those behaviours one at a time. The Discussion is also careful about scope in a way few papers here are, stating that diagnosis 'is unlikely to be set on the track of automated performance before long' and positioning the contribution as screening that catalyses referral.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control study in Naples, Italy: 30 autistic children (mean age 7.0, SD 1.4; Leiter-3 IQ range 59-109, six between 59 and 70) recruited from the Neapolisanit rehabilitation centre and 30 typically developing children (mean age 6 years 8 months, SD 1; IQ range 74-110) from a primary school. Diagnosis by DSM-5 plus ADOS-2 from clinicians unaffiliated with the research team; comorbidities, sensory and motor deficits excluded. Sex is not reported for either group. Data are touchscreen coordinates, available from the authors on request.
narrative_rows.methods: A bespoke Unity/C# app reproduced the Leiter-3 nonverbal battery across five subtests, logging finger position at 40 Hz. Coordinate streams were segmented into finite drag trajectories and reduced by the RStudio traj package to twelve features - mean, max, min and SD of speed and of acceleration, straightness (STH), directional change (DC), its SD, and mean trajectory count - averaged within task and concatenated with five one-hot subtest indicators, giving 1,500 samples from 60 children x 25 tasks. Only the first five items of each subtest were analysed because all participants completed those correctly. A 17-5-2 feedforward network (tanh, softmax, Adam, lr 0.01, Xavier init, 500 epochs) was evaluated by ten-fold cross-validation with five repetitions, with folds drawn at random across subjects and tasks. Variable importance was obtained by the sequential-removal procedure of Olden et al.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Ten-fold cross-validation with five repetitions gave 88 +/- 3% accuracy. The best single fold model gave 93% accuracy, sensitivity 0.87 and specificity 0.98, and supplied the ROC curve and the feature-importance ranking. Performance degraded gradually to 78% with five features retained and fell to 52% with one. Acceleration and mean speed were the most important variables, straightness and directional-change measures the least. Autistic trajectories were shorter and more fragmented, less straight, more frequently redirected, and much wider in speed and acceleration range - higher maxima and lower minima, hence larger standard deviations.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Cross-validation folds split 1,500 task-level samples at random across 60 children 'regardless of the number of ASD or TD subjects in the test or training set', so each child's remaining 22-23 averaged vectors train the model that tests the rest, allowing per-child movement signatures to substitute for group-general signal; no participant-held-out analysis is reported. The headline 93% and all its accompanying operating characteristics come from the best of ten fold models against a cross-validated 88 +/- 3%. Hidden-layer width, operating point and feature ranking were all selected on the same cross-validation. Sex is unreported for both groups, IQ appears only as a range so the acknowledged cognitive confound cannot be quantified, ADOS-2 severity scores were obtained but never used, and cases and comparisons were recruited from a therapy centre and a school respectively. The Discussion's descriptive interpretation foregrounds the features the study's own ranking found least informative.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Valuable to the synthesis on three counts, the last of them cautionary. First, it demonstrates that consumer hardware suffices for the measurement that the motor-kinematics literature has generally required laboratory motion capture to obtain, and that the measurement can be free - piggybacked on a nonverbal cognitive assessment the child is taking anyway, requiring no extra task, sensor or examiner time. Second, its limitations section contains the corpus's clearest statement of the diagnostic-specificity problem: the authors observe that their motor signature may equally mark ADHD, developmental coordination disorder or intellectual disability, and that the sensory-integration mechanism they invoke is not autism-specific, so a case-versus-typical contrast cannot establish what a screening tool needs to establish. Almost no other study here confronts that. Third, it is a clean instance of the corpus's dominant validity failure occurring in a study that is otherwise careful - the same analytic decision that Cilia quantified (image-level ~90% falling to participant-level ~71%) and that Liaqat et al. diagnosed in their own data is made here without comment, alongside a second decision to report the maximum across folds rather than the cross-validated mean. The gap between the two figures the paper itself reports, 93% and 88 +/- 3%, is the smaller part of the problem; the unmeasured gap is what a participant-held-out split would have given.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups of 30, both explicitly sized: 30 children with a DSM-5 and ADOS-2 diagnosis of autism recruited from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center, and 30 typically developing children recruited from a primary school. No other-diagnosis or developmentally-delayed comparison group, which the authors themselves identify as the key gap, noting that the motor signature 'may overlap with other disorders, such as attention deficit disorder, motor coordination disturbance, or general intellectual disabilities'. The two groups come from structurally different settings - a clinic where the autistic children receive ongoing psychomotor and speech therapy, versus a school - so group membership is confounded with familiarity with clinical testing, with the examiner's setting, and potentially with prior therapeutic work on exactly the fine-motor skills being measured. This is not discussed. [RQ1.2] 'children with autism', 'autistic children', 'ASD children', 'individuals with autism', 'ASD individuals', 'ASD participants', 'ASD group', against 'typically developing children', 'TD group', 'their typically developing peers', 'neurotypical group'. Person-first and identity-first are used interchangeably, sometimes in the same sentence. The clinical vocabulary is dated in one respect: intellectual disability is described as 'mild mental retardation' with a 2016 WHO citation, a term already superseded in DSM-5 and ICD-11 at the time of writing. Autism itself is framed in deficit terms throughout - 'communication impairment, a lack of social interaction' - though the theoretical framing is comparatively sympathetic, drawing on embodied cognition and on Sinha's account in which stereotyped behaviour is a rational response to an unpredictable world rather than a symptom to be suppressed. [RQ1.3] Autistic group: 30 children, mean age 7 years (SD 1.4), IQ range 59-109 on the Leiter-3, with six children between 59 and 70. Comparison group: 30 children, mean age 6 years 8 months (SD 1), IQ range 74-110. Age is close but no test of the difference is reported and matching is not claimed as a procedure. Two reporting gaps are consequential. Sex is not reported for either group anywhere in the paper - no counts, no proportions, no statement that groups were balanced - which is a complete omission of a variable that affects both autism prevalence and fine motor development at these ages. And IQ is given only as a range, with no mean or standard deviation, so the extent of the cognitive difference between groups cannot be quantified even though the authors concede it is a confound: the autistic range extends 15 points lower at the bottom and the distributions within those ranges are unknown. The comparison group's lower bound of 74 is itself notable, sitting in the borderline range. [RQ1.4] Among the better ascertainments in the corpus for a study of this size. Diagnosis required both DSM-5 clinical criteria and the ADOS-2, and was made by 'qualified doctors and professionals in the sector' who 'have no affiliation with our laboratory or our research' - an explicit assertion of independence between the diagnosing clinicians and the research team that almost no other study here makes, and which forecloses the possibility of diagnostic classification being influenced by knowledge of the study hypothesis. Comparison children were excluded for suspected autism signs, developmental abnormalities, or current or past psychiatric or neurological disorder, though the screening was by clinician or teacher judgement rather than a standardised instrument, and any child about whose diagnosis or health a clinician or teacher was uncertain was excluded outright. The one waste is that the ADOS-2 was administered but its severity scores are never reported or used. [RQ1.5] Partial. IQ was assessed with the Leiter-3, a nonverbal intelligence test appropriate for this population and administered in its original form for the assessment, but reported only as a range per group. Comorbidity was handled by exclusion rather than measurement: 'no existing comorbidities' was an inclusion criterion, no specific comorbidity was reported, and all participants were required to have normal vision and no sensory or motor deficit - the last a genuinely relevant control for a study whose outcome is a fine-motor measure, and one that also narrows the sample away from the substantial proportion of autistic children who do have motor impairment. No adaptive functioning measure, no language level, and no ADOS severity scores despite the instrument being used for diagnosis. Medication is not reported, though ongoing psychomotor and speech therapy is. [RQ2.1] Goal: determine whether the kinematics of a simple dragging movement, recorded incidentally during a digital cognitive assessment, can classify autism, and describe the motor features that differentiate the groups. Main findings: 88 +/- 3% accuracy under ten-fold cross-validation with five repetitions, and 93% accuracy with sensitivity 0.87 and specificity 0.98 for the best fold model; classification degraded only gradually as features were removed, reaching 78% with five features and chance with one; speed and acceleration measures dominated the importance ranking over straightness and directional change; and autistic trajectories were shorter, less straight, more frequently redirected and far more variable in speed and acceleration. [RQ2.2] Naples, Italy, across two different settings by group: autistic children at the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center, which provided 'the clinical ward for the experimentation' and where those children also receive ongoing psychomotor and speech therapy; comparison children at a primary school. The physical arrangement is specified precisely and identically for both - child seated at a table 65-70 cm high adjusted for age, experimenter opposite, tablet within 20 cm of the table edge - which controls posture and reach geometry, the most obvious physical determinants of drag kinematics. What is not controlled is the setting asymmetry itself. Recruiting cases from a therapy centre and comparisons from a school means group membership is entangled with familiarity with clinical assessment and with prior therapeutic exposure to fine-motor practice, either of which could shift drag dynamics independently of diagnosis. [RQ2.3] A digital reimplementation of the Leiter-3 nonverbal intelligence battery, built in Unity and C#, playing 'exactly the same tasks of the Leiter-3, presented in the same order' under the original administration rules, with the examiner advancing subtests at the standard error threshold. Five subtests span figure-ground, figure completion, classification analogies, sequential order and visual patterns, with two to eight draggable cards and placeholders per item and distractors present, ascending in complexity. Three features of the design deserve note. The paradigm is entirely dual-purpose: the child takes a cognitive assessment they would take anyway and the motor data are a by-product, so there is no added task burden and the approach is retrofittable to any clinic already using the Leiter-3. The nonverbal character of the instrument makes it usable across language levels, which matters for autism specifically. And the cognitive-load control is carefully reasoned - only the first five items of each subtest were analysed 'since all participants correctly performed at least the first five items', so kinematic differences cannot be attributed to some children struggling with the cognitive demand, and the demonstration item FG1 was excluded because the examiner may have moved cards during it. The five one-hot task-identity variables then give the network explicit information about which cognitive context each movement came from. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, one session per child, no follow-up, though the authors state a future aim of applying the method to younger children. Ethics are reported: approval by the Ethical Committee of Psychological Research of the Department of Humanities, University of Naples Federico II, with written informed consent from legal guardians obtained before the study. The data are coordinate streams rather than video or audio, so re-identification risk is intrinsically low, and a data availability statement commits to sharing raw data 'without undue reservation'. [RQ2.5] Deliberately commodity hardware: an Android 6.0 tablet with a 9.6-inch 1280x800 screen at 60 Hz refresh, dimensions given to the millimetre, with touch sampling at 40 Hz - so 40 coordinate pairs per second. No motion capture, markers, depth cameras or wearable sensors, which is the study's practical argument: the same measurement in the optical motion-tracking literature it cites requires a laboratory. Software is bespoke (Unity, C#), analysis uses RStudio with the traj package with its two source citations, and the Leiter-3 materials were supplied by Stoelting Co. The 40 Hz sampling rate is a meaningful constraint that goes unremarked: it bounds how finely acceleration - the feature family the importance analysis identifies as most discriminative - can be estimated from a differenced coordinate stream. [RQ2.6] Good on instrumentation and modelling, thin on data structure. Reported: tablet model, screen size, resolution, refresh rate and sampling frequency; the seating geometry; the task battery with its five domains, item structure and administration rule; the definition of a finite trajectory; all twelve features with formal definitions including the STH ratio and the DC/sdDC interpretation; the traj package with citations; feature standardisation; the full network specification (17-5-2, tanh, softmax, Adam, learning rate 0.01, Xavier initialisation, sparse categorical cross-entropy, 500 epochs); the grid-search range for hidden units and the criterion for choosing five; the cross-validation scheme; and the feature-removal procedure with its source. Missing or ambiguous: the number of trajectories per child, the aggregation from 25 tasks to 1,500 samples is stated but the fold-assignment rule is described only as random 'regardless' of subject composition, so the reader must infer that subjects span folds; no code release; no random seeds; and no participant-level performance breakdown that would allow the segment-versus-subject question to be resolved from the reported numbers. A data availability statement is present. [RQ2.7] Substantially candid on the scientific limitations and silent on the methodological one. Acknowledged, in a dedicated passage: the small sample, with replication needed 'to validate this method on a new not trained dataset' and an explicit question of whether the algorithm 'could remain predictive also for a greater sample or if it requires to be retrained'; the IQ confound, stated directly as 'we were not able to exclude intelligence as confounders', with the mitigation that most participants were high functioning and that analysing only universally-passed items limits cognitive interference; and - the most valuable admission in the paper - that the motor signature 'may overlap with other disorders, such as attention deficit disorder, motor coordination disturbance, or general intellectual disabilities', reinforced by the observation that sensory integration dysfunction, their explanatory mechanism, is also found in ADHD, so 'future extensions of this work should include other neurodevelopmental disabilities in order to verify the specificity of these motor signatures for ASD'. Not acknowledged: that the cross-validation folds split task-level samples rather than children, so the same child's data appears on both sides; that the headline 93% is the best of ten fold models while the cross-validated estimate is 88 +/- 3%; that hidden-layer width, feature ranking and the reported operating point were all selected on the same cross-validation used for reporting; and that cases and comparisons were recruited from systematically different settings. [RQ2.9] Four directions, three of them named by the authors and one clearly implied. Replicate on a larger sample and determine whether the trained model transfers without retraining - a transfer question rather than a sample-size platitude. Control IQ explicitly as an independent variable rather than relying on task selection to suppress its influence. Include other neurodevelopmental conditions - ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, intellectual disability - to establish whether the signature is autism-specific rather than a general marker of atypical development; the authors give the mechanistic reason, that sensory integration dysfunction is not autism-specific. And extend the method to younger children, where earlier identification would matter most, which is where the motor-precursor literature they review predicts the signal should already be present. [RQ3.1] The kinematics of goal-directed dragging - how a finger travels from a card to a placeholder - decomposed into how fast (mean, max, min and SD of speed), how the speed changes (the same four for acceleration), how directly (STH straightness), how consistently in direction (DC and sdDC) and in how many separate pieces (MeanLength). The behaviour is not social and not autism-specific in its surface form; the claim is that autism manifests in the microstructure of any goal-directed movement because prospective motor control is impaired, which is why an arbitrary cognitive task can serve as the probe. The theoretical grounding is more developed than in most of this corpus, running from Kanner's original identification of disrupted movement patterns through Leary and Hill on motor-symptom links, the enactive mind account, Friston's predictive coding and Sinha's proposal that stereotypies are a response to an unpredictably 'magical' world - and the motor findings are read back into that frame as over- and under-compensation from interrupted feedforward control. [RQ3.2] Single-modality: touchscreen kinematics only. The paper nonetheless performs a within-modality combination that is worth noting - the network receives twelve kinematic features together with five one-hot task-identity variables, so movement is interpreted conditional on cognitive context rather than pooled across it, and the task variables 'were always provided to the ANN' and were never subject to the removal analysis. This is a defensible design given that different Leiter-3 subtests impose different spatial demands, but it has an unexamined consequence: because task identity is always available, the model can learn task-specific kinematic norms, and since the feature vectors are per-child per-task averages, the combination of task identity plus habitual movement dynamics is close to a subject fingerprint. No cross-modality fusion is attempted, and none is claimed. [RQ4.1] A single small feedforward network - 17 inputs, one hidden layer of five tanh units, two softmax outputs - chosen for the stated reason that neural networks handle 'complex and nonlinear relationships between variables', which matches the paper's explicit epistemic position that no individual movement variable need differ between groups and that what is categorisable is 'the dynamic interaction of these features'. That position is argued rather than assumed, with a citation to Yarkoni and Westfall on prediction versus explanation, and it justifies choosing a predictive framework over group-difference testing. Model selection was equally restrained: a descending grid search from 10 hidden units found comparable accuracy down to 5 and degradation below, and 5 was chosen on the explicit principle that fewer hidden units reduce overfitting. Deliberate simplicity of this kind is rare in this corpus and is the right instinct for a 60-participant dataset; the difficulty is that it was verified against a cross-validation that does not hold participants out. [RQ4.2] One 17-dimensional vector per child per task: twelve kinematic features averaged over all finite trajectories in that task, plus five one-hot task indicators, yielding 60 x 25 = 1,500 rows. Two aspects of this construction determine what the results can mean. Averaging within task discards within-task variability and produces a stable per-child descriptor - which is exactly what makes each row informative about the individual as well as the group. And because every child contributes 25 such rows that share their individual movement characteristics, rows are strongly clustered within children; treating the 1,500 rows as exchangeable for the purpose of fold assignment is the analytic decision that undermines the headline figure. A representation of one vector per child would have given 60 rows and a much harder, but interpretable, problem. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and an ROC curve - an adequate panel, and the specificity/sensitivity asymmetry (0.98 versus 0.87) is reported rather than collapsed into accuracy. Two supplementary reporting choices are better than the corpus norm. Training-accuracy curves are shown with mean and 90% bootstrapped confidence intervals across all replications, so training stability is visible rather than asserted, and the authors state they 'checked that no overfitting is present in every fold'. And the feature-ablation curve reports accuracy, sensitivity and specificity jointly as a function of how many features are retained, which shows the graceful-then-sharp degradation pattern (78% at five features, 52% at one) and demonstrates that the result does not hinge on a single variable. What is missing bears directly on the headline: no confidence interval on the reported 93%, no confusion matrix, no per-fold table that would let a reader see the spread from which the best fold was drawn, and no comparison against a trivial baseline such as age or IQ - the latter especially relevant given that the authors concede IQ is an uncontrolled confound. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is pursued seriously and by an appropriate method. The stepwise-removal procedure of Olden et al. (2004) yields a complete importance ordering rather than a top-k list, and the accompanying curve shows how performance responds to progressive impoverishment of the input - more informative than a single importance ranking because it distinguishes redundant features from load-bearing ones. Boxplots of all twelve features by group then give the direction of every effect. The conclusions drawn are physically meaningful: speed and acceleration measures matter more than geometric straightness and directional coherence, and the movement picture that emerges - short, fragmented, non-straight trajectories with wide speed and acceleration excursions - is coherently linked to over- and under-compensation from disrupted prospective control, and cross-referenced to Anzulewicz's independent finding of greater impact force in autistic children's tablet interaction. There is one internal inconsistency: the Discussion's descriptive interpretation leads with STH, DC and MeanLength, but the study's own ranking removed STH second, sdDC fourth and DC sixth as the least impactful variables, while the acceleration measures the interpretation barely mentions were the last to be removed. The narrative therefore foregrounds the features the model found least useful. Both analyses were also run on the single best fold model rather than averaged across folds, so the ranking inherits that selection. [RQ4.5] The study's decisive weakness, and the reason its numbers are not comparable to participant-level results elsewhere in this corpus. The dataset is 1,500 samples formed as 60 subjects x 25 tasks, explicitly 'randomized between subjects and tasks', and the folds are drawn so that 'for each fold, we take the 10% of the samples for testing and the remaining 90% for training, regardless of the number of ASD or TD subjects in the test or training set'. Every child therefore has roughly 22 or 23 of their 25 vectors in training whenever the remaining two or three are tested. Because each vector is an average of that child's habitual movement dynamics within a task, the network can identify the individual from their kinematic signature and recover the diagnosis from that identification rather than from any group-general motor property - the same mechanism Liaqat et al. diagnose explicitly in their own eye-tracking data and that Cilia quantified as a fall from ~90% to ~71% when the unit was corrected. No participant-held-out analysis is reported anywhere, so the magnitude of the inflation here is unknown. A second, independent issue concerns which number is reported: ten-fold cross-validation with five repetitions returned 88 +/- 3%, and the paper then states that 'for the successive analysis, we used the best trained model across the 10-fold', from which the 93% accuracy, 0.87 sensitivity, 0.98 specificity, ROC curve and complete feature-importance ordering are all derived. The best of ten is a maximum, not an estimate, and it is the figure carried into the abstract, the Discussion and the Conclusion while the cross-validated 88 +/- 3% appears once. Hidden-layer width was additionally selected on the same cross-validation. The compounded effect is that the reported operating characteristics come from a model chosen for performing best on data structurally related to what it was trained on. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, sensory-motor impairment, motion analysis, machine learning, classification, assessment technologies. The pairing of 'sensory-motor impairment' with 'assessment technologies' captures the paper's dual identity - a theoretical claim about embodied cognition and a practical claim about instrumenting existing clinical tools - and 'assessment technologies' rather than 'diagnosis' signals the intended scope correctly. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Psychology 12:635696 (2021), in the Health Psychology section, from the Department of Humanistic Studies at the University of Naples Federico II, the CNR Institute of Cognitive Sciences and Technologies, and the Neapolisanit rehabilitation centre. A psychology venue with a cognitive-science orientation rather than an engineering one, which is visible in the balance of the paper: the theoretical framing occupies more space than the model, the literature review traces motor abnormality in autism from Kanner forward, and the machine learning is deliberately modest. The clinical co-affiliation supplied the participants and the diagnostic pathway. [RQ5.3] 2021 (received November 2020, published May 2021). The framing is the standard critique of observational diagnosis - it 'requires a lot of time', relies on 'the interpretative skills of clinicians', and 'take a long time without being able to deliver an objective and shareable result' - but the paper adds a more specific diagnosis of the field's problem: 'one of the main gaps in the diagnosis of autism is related to the lack of a quantitative evaluation of the disorder; in fact, although the variability within the disorder is known, there is still no valid method to recognize and categorize these differences'. The target is therefore the absence of graded measurement rather than subjectivity as such. A second framing move is methodological and unusual for this corpus: the authors argue explicitly that classical group-difference statistics are the wrong instrument here, 'since several interactions of motion variables could, actually, affect the presumed typical autistic motor pattern, we cannot assume that there must necessarily be movement variables typical of autism', and cite Yarkoni and Westfall to justify a predictive rather than exploratory approach. That is a considered epistemic position rather than a default. The paper also positions itself in a specific lineage - Anzulewicz's iPad gameplay study with 262 features reaching 'up to 93% accuracy', Crippa's upper-limb kinematics at 96.7% - and its own 93% lands squarely on the number it cites, which the Discussion treats as convergent confirmation rather than as an occasion to ask whether the two studies share a validation design.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control study in Beijing: 40 autistic and 50 typically developing children aged 3-6, the latter from a local kindergarten and the former from an unnamed school site. Autism was assessed by parent report on ABC, SCQ, SRS and CABS after the authors report 'limited access to reliable information' for direct diagnostic confirmation; comparison children were screened by teachers on ABC, SRS and SCQ with none reaching cut-off. Paired resting-state EEG and eye-tracking data were collected in one session; no cognitive or developmental measure was obtained; the dataset is not released.
narrative_rows.methods: EEG: 128-channel EGI at 1000 Hz for at least five minutes eyes-open resting state, downsampled to 250 Hz, 50 Hz notch, 0.5-45 Hz band-pass, 4-second epochs with automated plus visual artifact rejection, 62 electrodes grouped into ten regions, yielding 125 features (50 relative band power, 40 multiscale entropy, 35 phase-lag-index graph metrics). Eye tracking: Tobii TX300 at 300 Hz during two ~30-second clips of adult-child social interaction, eight areas of interest x six statistics x two clips = 96 features, with a >70% screen-looking-time inclusion threshold. Three stacked denoising autoencoders (125-64-50-2, 96-64-50-2, and 100-50-20-2 for fusion) with zero-masking noise 0.1, greedy layer-wise pre-training and supervised fine-tuning. Evaluated by subject-independent stratified ten-fold cross-validation with training-only feature normalisation, against EEG-only, gaze-only and naive-concatenation baselines.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Two-stage fusion: 95.56% accuracy, 92.5% sensitivity, 98% specificity, AUC 0.984, with the smallest fold-wise standard deviation. Eye tracking alone 86.67%; EEG alone 81.11%; naive concatenation intermediate. Confusion matrices show complementary failure modes - EEG classified autistic children at 82.5% versus gaze at 77.7%, while gaze classified typically developing children at 94% versus EEG at 80% - with fusion reaching 92.5% and 98%, misclassifying three autistic and one typically developing child. t-SNE projections show progressive class separation from raw through learned to fused representations.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The reference standard is four parent-report questionnaires, which the authors themselves attribute to limited site access, so the model predicts parent-reported symptomatology rather than clinically confirmed diagnosis. Groups were recruited from different institutions, and the eye-tracking stimulus is a widely broadcast Chinese children's programme whose familiarity may differ between settings. No cognitive or developmental measure was collected in a 3-6-year-old sample. Usable EEG differed markedly by group (20.4 versus 27.2 clean segments), reported without discussion, and the >70% looking-time gate is applied with no exclusion count. Hyperparameters for four architectures are stated without any selection procedure. No feature-level results of any kind - no group means, directions or importance - despite an interpretable feature design. No external validation, no statistical testing of the differences repeatedly called significant, and a limitations section naming only computational cost and the need for both modalities.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Important to the synthesis for two reasons that pull in different directions. Methodologically it belongs with Kojovic and Asgari in the small group that got validation right: subject-independent stratified cross-validation with one vector per child and normalisation fitted on training data only, all stated explicitly, which makes its 95.56% a participant-level figure and therefore not comparable to the segment-level 90%-plus results reported by Cilia, Akter, Simeoli and others. Substantively it provides the corpus's cleanest evidence on multimodal fusion, because the fusion benefit is decomposed rather than asserted: four models on identical folds establish that fusion beats both unimodal models and that learned latent fusion beats naive concatenation, while the confusion matrices identify the mechanism as complementary failure directions - EEG better on the autistic class, gaze substantially better on the typical class. Most fusion claims in this literature rest on an accuracy delta alone; this one does not. Two findings should carry forward independently. The behavioural modality alone (86.67%) outperformed the neurophysiological one (81.11%) despite EEG requiring a 128-channel net, five minutes of cooperative sitting and a far more elaborate pipeline, which bears directly on the cost-effectiveness case for behavioural screening. And the group difference in usable EEG segments - 20.4 against 27.2 - is another instance of the data-quality-as-signal pattern recurring across this corpus, where the measurement's own failure rate differs systematically by group and is left unexamined.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups, both explicitly sized: 40 autistic children and 50 typically developing children, 90 in total, aged 3-6. Typically developing children came from a local kindergarten; the autistic children's site is identified only obliquely as 'the school site' where reliable diagnostic information was limited, which suggests a special-education setting but is never stated. No other-diagnosis or developmental-delay comparison group, so the model is tested only against typical development. The class imbalance (40:50) is handled correctly at the validation level by stratified fold construction, and both classes are large enough that the confusion-matrix decomposition is meaningful. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'individuals with ASD', 'ASD subjects', 'the ASD population', against 'typically developing (TD) children', 'TD subjects'. Acronym-as-modifier throughout with no person-first construction. The clinical framing is notably medicalised: autism is repeatedly called a 'disease' ('ASD is a complex and heterogeneous disease'), classification errors are framed as 'misdiagnosis rate', the ROC axes are relabelled 'diagnosis rate' and 'misdiagnosis rate', and the stated purpose is to 'assist clinicians to make a precise diagnosis decision'. Describing a neurodevelopmental condition as a disease and a false positive as a misdiagnosis positions the work as diagnostic rather than screening, which is a stronger claim than the parent-report reference standard can support. [RQ1.3] Group sizes (40 and 50) and the 3-6 age range appear in the running text; ages, sex distribution and the four questionnaire scores are tabulated in Table I with p values from two-independent-sample t-tests, but the table did not render in the extracted text so the values cannot be recovered. That the comparison was made formally and reported with p values is to the study's credit and distinguishes it from the several studies here that report no demographic testing at all. What is not addressed is whether any demographic difference that did emerge was subsequently controlled for - no covariate adjustment or matched-subsample analysis appears anywhere. No IQ, developmental quotient, language level or adaptive functioning measure was collected for either group, which for a 3-6-year-old sample leaves the most obvious alternative explanation - general developmental level - entirely unaddressed. [RQ1.4] The study's weakest element, and unusually, the authors say so themselves. Diagnosis is stated to have been confirmed under DSM-5, but the very next sentence concedes 'we had limited access to reliable information in the school site' and explains that the children were therefore assessed using parent report on four instruments - the Autism Behavior Checklist, Social Communication Questionnaire, Social Responsiveness Scale and Clancy Behavior Scale. None is an observational or clinician-administered diagnostic instrument; all four are screening or symptom-report scales. No ADOS, ADI-R, CARS or direct clinical observation is reported. The consequence for interpretation is specific: the label the classifier is trained to predict is grounded in parent report, so a demonstration that a model recovers it at 95.56% shows agreement with parent-reported symptomatology, not with clinically established diagnosis. The comparison group is better handled - ABC, SRS and SCQ completed by teachers, with no child reaching any cut-off - so negative cases are screened on three instruments even though positive cases lack observational confirmation. [RQ1.5] No cognitive, language or adaptive measure of any kind for either group - a significant omission in 3-to-6-year-olds, where developmental level varies enormously and both resting EEG spectral power and social gaze allocation are strongly age- and ability-dependent. No comorbidity information and no exclusions described. Four symptom instruments (ABC, SCQ, SRS, CABS) were administered to the autistic group and three to the comparison group, and their scores are tabulated, so a severity gradient exists in the data; it is used only to characterise the sample and is never related to the model's continuous output, missing the opportunity to test whether the classifier's confidence tracks symptom level - the analysis that would have provided clinical anchoring. [RQ2.1] Goal: determine whether learned fusion of an internal neurophysiological modality and an external behavioural modality outperforms either alone, and whether hierarchical latent-space fusion beats naive feature concatenation. Main findings: MMSDAE reached 95.56% accuracy, 92.5% sensitivity, 98% specificity and AUC 0.984 under subject-independent stratified ten-fold cross-validation, improving on eye tracking alone (86.67%) by 8.89 points and EEG alone (81.11%) by 14.45; both fusion variants beat both unimodal models, and two-stage fusion beat naive concatenation; the modalities are complementary in a specific and demonstrated way, with EEG stronger on autistic children (82.5% versus 77.7%) and gaze much stronger on typically developing children (94% versus 80%); and the behavioural modality alone outperformed the neurophysiological one. [RQ2.2] Beijing, China. Comparison children were recruited from a local kindergarten; the autistic children came from a school site whose identity is not given and where the authors report limited access to reliable diagnostic information. Both recordings took place under controlled conditions - EEG in a quiet room with the child in an armchair usually accompanied by a caregiver, eye tracking at a fixed ~60 cm viewing distance following a five-point calibration that had to pass with small error vectors before proceeding. Recruiting the two groups from different institutional settings is a structural feature the paper does not discuss, and it carries a specific risk for the eye-tracking modality here: the stimulus is Tiger Qiao Hu, a widely broadcast Chinese children's programme, so prior familiarity with the characters could differ systematically between children in a mainstream kindergarten and children in a special-education setting, and familiarity affects where a viewer looks. [RQ2.3] Two paradigms with complementary demands, both requiring nothing of the child. EEG is eyes-open resting state for at least five minutes, so there is no task at all and no compliance requirement beyond sitting - the caregiver may be present. Eye tracking uses two ~30-second clips of a dynamic social interaction between a child and an adult, presented in random order, with an attention-grabbing animated kitten between trials, and 'no response was required from the children'. This is a well-judged design for the 3-6 age band: neither component depends on language, instruction-following or motor response, which is precisely what limits most computational paradigms in preschoolers. The eight areas of interest are the analytically substantive choice, distinguishing adult from child and, within each, eyes from mouth from body, plus a dedicated joint-attention region - a scheme built to test specific published claims about social attention. That the resulting 96 features are then fed undifferentiated into an autoencoder, with no analysis of which AOIs mattered, wastes the design's discriminative structure. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up. Ethics approval from the School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee of Beijing Normal University, with informed consent obtained from all children with parental permission before enrollment. Funding sources are itemised (NSFC grants 62003228 and 61761166003, a Beijing Municipal Education Commission project, and a National Key R&D programme grant). No data availability statement, no data sharing plan and no discussion of how the EEG and gaze recordings are stored or protected - though both modalities are lower-identifiability than the video and audio data used elsewhere in this corpus. [RQ2.5] Specified in detail on the acquisition side, which is a strength. EEG: Electrical Geodesics 128-channel Ag/AgCl passive electrode net, 1000 Hz sampling, at least five minutes, Cz online reference, impedances verified below 50 kOhm via Net Station, downsampling to 250 Hz, 50 Hz notch, 0.5-45 Hz band-pass, 4-second non-overlapping epochs, a cited automated artifact detector covering eye movements, blinks, line noise, breathing, muscle, abrupt slopes and outliers, supplementary visual inspection, a 200 microvolt bad-channel threshold with neighbour interpolation, and 62 of 128 electrodes retained across ten regions. Eye tracking: Tobii TX300 at 300 Hz, 1024x768 display, ~60 cm viewing distance, five-point calibration gated on small error vectors, Tobii fixation filter, linear interpolation of gaps up to 100 ms, binocular averaging, and a >70% screen-looking-time inclusion threshold. Modelling uses the publicly available DeepLearnToolbox, cited with its GitHub URL - so the learning machinery, at least, is reproducible off the shelf. [RQ2.6] Strong on signal processing and network architecture, absent on selection procedure and data structure. Fully reported: every EEG acquisition and preprocessing parameter, every eye-tracking acquisition parameter, all three feature families with their band definitions, region groupings, MSE scale ranges and the seven graph metrics; the AOI scheme and the six per-AOI statistics with the arithmetic yielding 96 features; the normalisation formula together with the explicit statement that it is fitted on training data and applied to test; all three SDAE layer geometries; noise level, both learning rates, both iteration counts and the optimiser; the cross-validation scheme with its subject-independence and stratification; and the toolbox with its URL. Not reported: how the network geometries, noise level and learning rates were chosen, and whether that selection used the reporting folds; how many children were screened out by the >70% looking-time rule; whether any EEG recordings were excluded entirely; any group means or effect sizes for any feature; random seeds; and any data or code release beyond the third-party toolbox. [RQ2.7] Only two limitations are stated, and both are engineering constraints rather than threats to validity: that deployment requires EEG and eye-tracking data to be available simultaneously, and that training three SDAE models costs more computation than one. Unaddressed: the diagnostic reference standard rests on parent-report questionnaires, which the authors themselves flag as a data-access compromise in the Methods but never carry into the interpretation of their results; the two groups were recruited from different institutional settings; no cognitive or developmental measure was collected in a 3-6-year-old sample, leaving developmental level uncontrolled; the >70% screen-looking-time gate may exclude children differentially by group with no count reported; the EEG segment yield differs markedly between groups (20.4 versus 27.2 clean segments), which the paper states in passing and never discusses despite its implication that artifact burden - and hence measurement noise - is itself group-dependent; hyperparameter selection is undescribed; there is no external validation cohort; and 90 children is a small sample for a model with three stacked networks. The Conclusion's claim that the framework 'can automatically learn and fuse useful information... without the need of much more diagnostic expert experience' is also stronger than a study whose labels came from parent questionnaires can support. [RQ2.9] Two directions, both about model efficiency rather than about validity. Replace the three-model pipeline with convolutional or attention architectures to reduce computational cost; and, more interestingly, develop fusion that can operate 'even especially in the absence of one modality during the model training', which would address the practical barrier that the current design requires both an EEG net and an eye tracker for every child - a genuine obstacle to the scalability the paper claims. A third, briefer aim is to explore additional autism-related features via advanced signal processing. Absent from the agenda: external validation, direct diagnostic confirmation, developmental-level control, or any analysis of which features drive the result. [RQ3.1] The behavioural target is social visual attention: where a preschooler looks while watching a child and an adult interact, resolved to eight regions that separate the two people, separate eyes from mouth from body within each, and add an explicit joint-attention region. The six statistics per region capture both what was attended (fixation count, total and mean fixation duration, visit count) and the priority of attention (time to first fixation, number of fixations before first entering the region) - the latter pair encoding attentional precedence rather than mere allocation, which is the more theoretically pointed measure. The paired EEG modality is not behavioural at all, being eyes-open resting state with no task, so what the fusion combines is a behavioural response to social content with a task-free measure of intrinsic brain dynamics. [RQ3.2] The most carefully argued fusion analysis in the corpus, and one of very few where the mechanism of the fusion benefit is demonstrated rather than assumed. Four models are trained on identical data and folds: EEG alone, gaze alone, naive concatenation of raw features, and the proposed two-stage latent fusion. The ordering is informative at every step. Both fusion variants beat both unimodal models, so combining helps. Two-stage fusion beats naive concatenation, so the benefit comes from combining learned high-level representations rather than merely from having 221 features instead of 96 or 125 - the control that distinguishes a fusion architecture claim from a dimensionality claim. And the confusion matrices identify why: EEG classifies autistic children better (82.5% versus 77.7%) while gaze classifies typically developing children far better (94% versus 80%), so the modalities err in opposite directions and fusion recovers both strengths, reaching 92.5% and 98%. That asymmetry is a substantive finding in its own right and is the kind of evidence that most multimodal papers in this literature substitute an accuracy delta for. The t-SNE panels add a visual account, showing the fused representation separating classes where raw and concatenated features overlap. Two caveats: the paper does not test partial fusion (for instance gaze plus a single EEG family) so the minimum useful combination is unknown, and the behavioural modality alone at 86.67% already exceeds the EEG modality, which bears directly on cost-benefit given that eye tracking is far cheaper and faster to acquire than a 128-channel net in a preschooler. [RQ4.1] Stacked denoising autoencoders used hierarchically - two for unimodal representation learning, a third for fusion - with greedy layer-wise unsupervised pre-training followed by supervised fine-tuning. The choice is well matched to the problem: 221 hand-engineered features from 90 children is a regime where supervised deep learning would overfit immediately, and unsupervised pre-training exploits the input data without consuming label information, while the denoising objective with zero-masking corruption prevents the identity mapping and encourages robustness. The paper justifies the choice by precedent in Alzheimer's diagnosis, ADHD classification and machinery fault diagnosis. The architecture is also deliberately shallow - two hidden layers per model, compressing 125 to 50 and 96 to 50 - which is appropriate for the sample size, though the t-SNE analysis reveals a cost the authors acknowledge: learned EEG features separate the classes less well than raw ones in the visualisation, which they attribute to dimension reduction discarding useful information. [RQ4.2] A three-level representation. Level one is hand-engineered and theory-driven: EEG features chosen to test published claims about spectral power, signal complexity and network topology in autism, and gaze features chosen to test claims about social attention allocation. Level two compresses each modality to a 50-dimensional latent code via its own autoencoder. Level three concatenates the two 50-dimensional codes into a 100-dimensional vector and compresses again to 20 before classification. Two design points matter. Fusion occurs after each modality has been separately abstracted, so the fusion network operates on comparable representations rather than on raw features of wildly different scale and character - which is the paper's explanation for why it beats naive concatenation. And normalisation is fitted on training data only and applied to test data, a discipline stated explicitly and observed by very few studies in this corpus. The unit throughout is one vector per child, which is why the cross-validation can be genuinely subject-independent. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity with fold-wise standard deviations, ROC curves with AUC for all four models, and complete confusion matrices for all four - a full panel, and reported comparatively rather than only for the winning model. Reporting standard deviations across folds supports one of the paper's substantive claims, that MMSDAE 'presents the best stability and robustness with the smallest standard deviation among all compared methods', which is a claim about variance that accuracy alone cannot carry. The confusion matrices are the most useful element, since they convert an accuracy comparison into a diagnosis of where each model fails and thereby ground the complementarity argument. Missing: no confidence intervals on the reported means, no statistical test of the difference between models despite the word 'significantly' being used repeatedly of differences that are never tested, no per-fold table, and no comparison against a trivial baseline such as age - which for 3-to-6-year-olds is a real omission given that both resting EEG spectra and gaze behaviour change rapidly across that band. [RQ4.4] The weakest analytic dimension. There is no feature-level interpretability of any kind: no importance ranking, no per-family ablation, no group means, no effect sizes, no directional statements for any of the 221 features. This is a substantial loss because the feature set was designed to be interpretable - the ten brain regions, five frequency bands, four entropy scale ranges and seven graph metrics each correspond to a specific published hypothesis, and the eight areas of interest were constructed precisely to distinguish attention to eyes from mouth, to adult from child, and to joint-attention regions. A study that reported which of those differed would have contributed to the autism literature independently of its classifier; as written it contributes only a number. What interpretability exists is at modality level and is done well: the confusion-matrix decomposition establishing the EEG/gaze complementarity, and t-SNE projections of six feature spaces (raw EEG, raw gaze, raw concatenation, learned EEG, learned gaze, fused) showing progressive class separation. The t-SNE panels also surface an honest negative observation the authors do not hide - learned EEG features separate less well than expected, attributed to information loss in dimension reduction - though these projections are computed over the full dataset rather than per fold, so they illustrate rather than validate. [RQ4.5] Done correctly, and stated in terms that leave no ambiguity: 'we perform a 10-fold subject-independent cross-validation to evaluate the performance of the proposed model, where each subject is regarded as a sample', with stratified sampling to preserve the class ratio in every fold, each fold tested exactly once, and the average across folds reported with standard deviations. Because every child contributes exactly one feature vector - EEG features are averaged across that child's clean segments, gaze features aggregated across their two trials - there is no possibility of the segment-level leakage that inflates results throughout this corpus, and the 95.56% is a genuine participant-level figure. Feature normalisation is also fitted on training data only. Two gaps remain. The three network geometries, the noise level, both learning rates and both iteration counts are stated as given, with no description of how they were arrived at, so selection optimism cannot be excluded and may be substantial across four compared architectures. And there is no external validation - no second site, no held-out cohort, no replication sample - so the estimate, though internally sound, rests entirely on 90 children from two institutions in one city. The correct comparison for this study's 95.56% is therefore not the segment-level 90%-plus figures elsewhere in the corpus but the small set of participant-level results, against which it stands as one of the highest and, on validation design, one of the better supported. [RQ5.1] Index terms: autism spectrum disorders, multimodal fusion, electroencephalogram, eye-tracking, stacked denoising autoencoders, classification. Two modality terms, one architecture term, one fusion term - a keyword set entirely oriented to method, with 'multimodal fusion' rather than 'autism' functioning as the paper's actual subject. [RQ5.2] IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering 30:2003-2011 (2022), a biomedical engineering venue. Authorship spans the School of Psychology at Capital Normal University, the School of Electrical Engineering at Yanshan University, and the State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Neuroscience and Learning at Beijing Normal University, with two first authors marked as contributing equally - one psychological, one engineering. Funded by three national and municipal Chinese grants. The psychology-engineering pairing explains the study's shape: rigorous signal acquisition and a validation design that respects subject independence, alongside an almost complete absence of clinical characterisation and of feature-level interpretation. [RQ5.3] 2022 (submitted September 2021, published July 2022). The framing combines the standard prevalence appeal (1 in 54 per US CDC) with two more specific claims: that 'there is limited understanding of the neural patterns behind ASD and the severity of the disease', and that 'there is a lack of experienced experts for ASD diagnosis' - the second being a workforce argument that is more concretely relevant in the Chinese context the study is situated in than the objectivity arguments that dominate elsewhere in this corpus.
