The paper's distinctive positional claim is methodological: that 'most existing methods mainly rely on a single modality with limited information and often cannot achieve satisfactory performance', and that since autism has 'abnormal manifestations from the cellular level to the behavioral level' no single level of measurement can suffice. Its related-work section is unusual in citing single-modality accuracy figures from both literatures side by side - 92.34% and 96.44% for EEG, 88.51% and 85.1% for eye tracking - which sets up the fusion argument but also, unintentionally, shows that the highest reported unimodal figures already exceed this study's own unimodal results (81.11% and 86.67%), a discrepancy that goes unremarked and that most likely reflects differences in validation design rather than in signal quality.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control study in Seoul: 44 autistic children (22 male, 46.9 +/- 13.0 months, best-estimate IQ 58.8 +/- 18.6, ADOS-2 CSS 6.00, CARS 30.9) from Seoul National University Hospital's child psychiatry division, and 50 typically developing children (27 male, 47.9 +/- 12.5 months, IQ 104 +/- 17.4, CARS 15.5) from preschools; age and sex matched and tested (p = 0.697, p = 0.857), IQ differing by 45 points (p < 0.001). Six ASD-suspected recruits with CSS below 3 were excluded. ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, medication use, sensory impairment and other neurological or psychiatric conditions excluded. 918 ten-second video clips (484 TD, 434 ASD); not released.
narrative_rows.methods: A joint-attention protocol adapted from Mundy's ESCS: the child seated at a table with a 3x5x3 cm toy placed on the midline 70 cm away and out of reach, a trained examiner seated so that seeing their face requires a ~45-degree head turn, no verbal instruction, 30-second waits, ten toys in pseudo-randomised order, ~10 minutes per child. Front-facing Sony DSC-RX100 IV at 1920x1080 and 30 fps; clips trimmed from toy placement to 10 seconds (300 frames). ImageNet-pretrained VGG-16 supplied 512-dimensional features at 7x7 spatial locations per frame, feeding a two-layer 512-dimensional LSTM, a soft attention module, then FC-ReLU-dropout(0.5)-FC for binary classification. Partitions were subject-disjoint: 32 children training, 8 validation, 36 in test set #1 (raw video), 18 in test set #2 (background-reduced).
narrative_rows.outcomes: Training 98.9%, validation 97.0%. Test set #1 (raw, 36 children, 416 clips): accuracy 0.916, precision 0.900, recall 0.945, F1 0.922 - 175/198 TD and 206/218 ASD clips correct. Test set #2 (segmented, 18 children, 184 clips): accuracy 0.918, precision 0.880, recall 0.953, F1 0.915 - 88/99 and 81/85 correct. Attention analysis: typically developing children invariably showed an attention peak of at least twice baseline somewhere in the 300-frame sequence, coinciding in every case with an observed triadic gaze shift; autistic children showed flat attention profiles, and fewer than 1% showed both an IJA behaviour and a corresponding peak.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Best-estimate IQ differs by 45 points with the autistic group's mean in the intellectual disability range, on a behaviour that is developmentally sensitive to cognitive level; the authors acknowledge this but defend it by citation rather than by analysing their own data, and no covariate adjustment or IQ-matched subsample is attempted. Test metrics are computed over clips rather than children, so effective sample sizes are 36 and 18 rather than 416 and 184, and no per-child accuracy is given. Training used only 32 children on a single fixed split with no cross-validation and no confidence intervals. ADHD and developmental coordination disorder were excluded rather than recruited as contrast groups, so specificity is untested. Optimiser, learning rate, epochs, loss function and any selection procedure are unreported. The examiner responds contingently to the child and attention is temporal only, so it cannot be verified that the model watches the child rather than the examiner. The claim of superiority over prior models reporting 0.70-0.80 accuracy is untested and across incomparable populations.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Contributes three things to the synthesis. First, it is the corpus's clearest example of designing the paradigm around a clinically sanctioned construct rather than mining an unconstrained behaviour stream: the protocol is adapted from a validated manual, every geometric parameter is justified by what it forces the child to do, and the target is a behaviour clinicians already treat as diagnostic - a position the paper articulates as a criticism of prior work whose 'targeted gesture is not generally considered an indication of ASD behavior by most mental health specialists'. Second, its attention analysis is the best verification in the corpus that a deep video model attends to what it is supposed to: rather than presenting a plausible heatmap, the authors checked every attention plot against its video and established correspondence in both directions, with peaks coinciding with observed triadic gaze in typically developing children and fewer than 1% of autistic children showing both. Third, training on background-segmented video and testing on raw video at equivalent accuracy is direct evidence against the scene-cue exploitation that other video studies here can only exclude by assertion or by skeletonisation. The countervailing lesson is equally useful: this is the corpus's most extreme instance of an unaddressed IQ confound, with a 45-point group gap on a developmentally sensitive behaviour, and it illustrates that correct partitioning and verified attention do not by themselves establish what a classifier is detecting. It also raises a question the synthesis should carry: the target behaviour was scored by a human rater in this same study with near-complete separation (16.1 versus 4.59 of 20), so the demonstrated contribution is automation of an existing measurement rather than access to something clinicians cannot see - a legitimate goal, but a different one from discovering a behavioural biomarker.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups, both explicitly sized and accounted for: 50 typically developing children (27 male) and 44 autistic children (22 male), from an initial 50 ASD-suspected recruits of whom 6 were excluded for ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores below 3. Recruitment sources are named - the Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Division of Seoul National University Hospital for the clinical group and preschools for the comparison group. All 94 children are allocated across the three partitions without overlap: 40 to training and validation, 36 to test set #1, 18 to test set #2. No other-diagnosis comparison group, which matters here because ADHD and developmental coordination disorder were deliberately excluded rather than recruited as contrast groups - so the model is never asked to make the discrimination that would distinguish autism-specific joint-attention impairment from impairment secondary to attention or motor difficulty. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'ASD and TD children', 'individuals with ASD', against 'typically developing (TD) children', 'TD individuals'. Person-first in the fuller constructions, acronym-as-modifier elsewhere. Autism is framed conventionally as 'impairment in social interaction and communication, and restricted, repetitive patterns of interests and behaviors', and the socio-economic framing is burden-oriented, citing 'the socio-economic burden that stems from caring for ASD' in billions of dollars and, in the conclusion, a hope to 'reduce the burden on the parents'. The word 'patients' appears once for the children. The framing of joint attention itself is comparatively constructive, describing it as 'a high-level social skill and a valid indicator of social brain development' rather than as a deficit to be catalogued. [RQ1.3] Fully reported and formally tested, which is uncommon in this corpus. Autistic group: 44 children, 22 male (50.0%), 46.9 +/- 13.0 months, median 49.0, range 24-68. Comparison group: 50 children, 27 male (54.0%), 47.9 +/- 12.5 months, median 48.5, range 25-72. Age p = 0.697 by t-test; sex p = 0.857 by chi-squared; both groups therefore genuinely matched on the two standard demographic variables and shown to be so. The decisive difference is cognitive: best-estimate IQ 104 +/- 17.4 in the comparison group against 58.8 +/- 18.6 in the autistic group, p < 0.001 - a 45-point gap placing the autistic group's mean firmly within the intellectual disability range. IQ was measured with the Korean WPPSI-IV or the Korean Bayley Scales depending on the child. The gap is acknowledged as the study's chief limitation but is not addressed analytically: no covariate adjustment, no IQ-matched subsample, no stratified analysis. Since joint attention emerges developmentally and is sensitive to cognitive level, and since the autistic group averages roughly a 45-point deficit, a substantial part of the classification could reflect developmental level rather than autism specifically. [RQ1.4] Strong for a four-page conference paper. Diagnosis was made under DSM-5 criteria. The ADOS-2 was administered by two experienced professionals to all children referred for suspected autism, and because different modules were used according to age and language level, raw scores were converted to calibrated severity scores - total, social affect and restricted/repetitive - which is the correct procedure for comparing across modules and is done in only a minority of studies here. The paper states the CSS interpretation bands explicitly (1-3 non-spectrum, 4-5 ASD, 6-10 Autism) and applies them: 6 of the 50 initially recruited ASD-suspected children scored below 3 and were excluded, leaving a group with a mean CSS of 6.00, in the 'Autism' band. The Korean CARS was also administered with its 25.5 high-risk cut-off, and comparison children averaged 15.5 against 30.9 for the autistic group. The ascertainment therefore combines DSM-5 criteria, a module-calibrated observational instrument, a rating scale, and an explicit exclusion rule applied to borderline cases. [RQ1.5] IQ was measured for every child using an age-appropriate instrument - Korean WPPSI-IV for older children, Korean Bayley Scales-II for younger - and combined into a best-estimate figure, which is the right approach for a sample spanning 24 to 72 months. The result is the study's central confound rather than a control. Comorbidity was handled by exclusion and the exclusions are mechanistically reasoned: because joint attention depends on 'perception, attention, and motor coordination', children were required to have normal or corrected vision and normal hearing and were excluded for pharmacological treatment, developmental coordination disorder, ADHD, and any other neurological or psychiatric condition. This is a more thoughtfully constructed exclusion set than most in the corpus, since each element removes a plausible non-autism cause of failing the specific target behaviour. No adaptive functioning or language measure is reported. [RQ2.1] Goal: build a screening tool whose input is raw video and whose target behaviour is one that clinicians already regard as diagnostically meaningful, addressing two named shortcomings in prior work - that the Cognoa-derived system feeds human ratings rather than video into the model, and that Zunino's grasping-kinematics approach targets a gesture 'not generally considered an indication of ASD behavior by most mental health specialists'. Main findings: 0.916 accuracy, 0.900 precision, 0.945 recall and 0.922 F1 on a subject-disjoint raw-video test set of 36 children; 0.918 accuracy on a second, background-reduced test set of 18 children; and an attention analysis showing that typically developing children produce a distinct attention peak coinciding with an observed triadic gaze shift while autistic children produce flat attention profiles, with fewer than 1% of autistic children showing both. [RQ2.2] Seoul, South Korea. The clinical group came from the Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Division of Seoul National University Hospital and the comparison group from preschools - a recruitment asymmetry of the kind that elsewhere in this corpus introduces setting confounds, but mitigated here because the paradigm itself is identical for both groups and highly constrained: same quiet room arrangement, same height-adjustable chair, same 70 cm toy placement, same 45-degree examiner offset, same ten toys, same 30-second waits. The paper also states that videos 'were acquired at different locations with various background noises' and treats the model's robustness across them as evidence for generalisability - which the train-on-segmented, test-on-raw result supports more directly than the assertion alone would. [RQ2.3] The most carefully constructed elicitation paradigm in the corpus, and the design reasoning is unusually visible. It adapts Mundy's Early Social Communication Scales, a validated manual for eliciting and scoring joint-attention behaviours, together with behaviour-extraction techniques from applied behaviour analysis. Three geometric decisions are justified explicitly. The toy sits 70 cm away on the midline, out of reach, because a nearer toy means the child 'would simply pick up the toy and play with it without making any effort to interact with the examiner' - so the design forces the social bid rather than merely permitting it. The examiner is offset such that seeing their face requires an approximately 45-degree head turn or a substantial gaze shift, which makes the target behaviour large enough to register in 2D video from a front-facing camera. And the examiner provides no verbal instruction and simply waits, so any initiation is spontaneous rather than prompted. The toys are standardised in size (3x5x3 cm) and drawn from ADOS-2 and ESCS guidelines, with pseudo-randomised order and a substitution rule if the child shows no interest. Ten seconds from toy placement defines the analysis window. The whole session takes about 10 minutes. The one unexamined element is that the examiner responds contingently - turning to the toy once the child initiates - so the examiner's behaviour is a function of the child's, and the paper does not state whether the examiner is in frame or whether the model could be reading their response rather than the child's initiation. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up. Ethics are reported in full for a conference paper: approval by the Yonsei University IRB under number 4-2021-0845, conduct in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and written informed consent from parents 'after receiving a detailed description of the study'. The data are identifiable video of young children, and although semantic segmentation removes background it retains faces; two children appear in published figures identified by participant codes. No data availability statement, no code release and no description of how the video corpus is stored or protected. [RQ2.5] Acquisition is a single consumer camera - a Sony DSC-RX100 IV at 1920x1080 and 30 fps, front-facing - with no depth sensor, marker, wearable or eye tracker, which is the practical argument for the approach: the same behaviour is measured elsewhere with eye-tracking hardware or motion capture. Physical setup is specified to the centimetre (70 cm toy distance, 3x5x3 cm toys, 45-degree examiner offset, height-adjustable chair with the child's right elbow and wrist on the table). Modelling uses ImageNet-pretrained VGG-16 with the last convolutional layer retained for its spatial structure, a two-layer 512-dimensional LSTM, a soft attention module, and a classifier head of 512-unit FC, ReLU, dropout 0.5 and a 512-to-2 FC layer. Semantic segmentation isolates the foreground human, though the segmentation method itself is not named. [RQ2.6] Good on protocol and architecture, thin on training procedure. Fully specified: the elicitation protocol with all distances, timings, toy specifications and examiner rules; camera model, resolution and frame rate; clip trimming rule (from toy placement, 10 seconds, 300 frames); the discard criterion for corrupted acquisitions; final clip counts by group (484 and 434 of 918); the exact composition of all four partitions by group and by clip count; the full network specification layer by layer; the attention formulation; and the difference in preprocessing between test sets. Not reported: optimiser, learning rate, batch size, epochs, loss function, any regularisation beyond the single dropout layer, the semantic segmentation method, random seeds, or any statement of how architecture or hyperparameters were selected. No code or data release. For a conference paper the protocol reporting is exemplary and the training reporting is incomplete. [RQ2.7] One limitation is stated and it is the right one: 'there is a statistically significant difference in IQ between the ASD and TD children. IQ is known to affect one's ability to perform behavioral tasks and joint attention', followed by the conclusion that 'a replication study using a sample of IQ-matched ASD and TD cohorts is therefore required'. The framing is honest, though the accompanying defence - that 'even when IQ is considered, joint attention still proved to be an important trait to differentiate ASD from TD children' - rests on a citation to prior literature rather than on any analysis of the present data, and no covariate adjustment or matched subsample is attempted despite IQ being measured for every child. Unaddressed: that test metrics are computed over clips rather than children, so effective sample sizes are 36 and 18 rather than 416 and 184; that the training set comprises only 32 children; that the target behaviour is separately scored by a human rater in this very study with near-complete group separation, so the model automates an existing measurement rather than revealing a new one; that ADHD and developmental coordination disorder were excluded rather than used as contrast groups, leaving specificity untested; that the examiner responds contingently to the child; and that the closing comparison against prior models reporting 0.70-0.80 accuracy is made without any statistical test and across incomparable populations. [RQ2.9] Two directions, both well chosen. Replicate with IQ-matched cohorts - which follows directly from the acknowledged confound and is the single analysis that would establish whether the result is about autism or about developmental level. And extend from binary classification to continuous prediction of social-function deficit severity, to serve 'as an objective assessment tool that can be used in conjunction with currently available symptom severity measurement questionnaires and clinical scales'. The second is well supported by data already in hand, since ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores, CARS totals and human-rated IJA scores were all collected and none was related to model output; the severity-regression analysis is available in this dataset and simply was not run. [RQ3.1] A single, precisely defined social behaviour: initiation of joint attention, operationalised as the triadic gaze - 'a triadic gaze where the child shifts their gaze from the object at hand to the person they wish to interact with and back to the object, or from the person to the object and back to the person', sometimes accompanied by a point. This is the narrowest behavioural target in the corpus and the choice is deliberate and defended: joint attention is described as 'a high-level social skill and a valid indicator of social brain development', develops early in typical children, and is measured by a validated manual (ESCS). The contrast with the rest of this literature is instructive - where most studies extract many features from an unconstrained behaviour stream and let a model find what discriminates, this study constructs a paradigm to elicit one behaviour that clinicians already regard as diagnostic, then asks whether a model can see it. That inverts the usual relationship between the computational method and the clinical construct. [RQ3.2] Single modality - 2D RGB video only, with no audio, depth, gaze tracking or motion capture. No fusion is attempted or claimed. Within the modality the paper does run a preprocessing comparison that functions like an ablation: training, validation and test set #2 used semantically segmented video with the foreground human isolated so that 'most of the background noise (color of wallpaper, color of child's clothes, etc.) was reduced', while test set #1 was left raw. Accuracy was 0.918 on the segmented test set and 0.916 on the raw one, with autistic-class accuracy 94.5% versus 92.1%. Because the model was trained only on segmented video, its near-equivalent performance on raw video is a domain-shift result rather than a like-for-like comparison, and it constitutes direct evidence that the classifier is not depending on room or clothing cues - the confound that the skeletonisation approach elsewhere in this corpus removes by construction. The authors read the small drop as expected background distraction, which is a reasonable interpretation. [RQ4.1] CNN-LSTM with soft attention over raw video - a standard action-recognition architecture, applied without modification and without comparison to alternatives. Only one model is reported: no baseline, no ablation over architecture, no simpler comparator such as a frame-averaged CNN or a hand-engineered gaze-shift detector, and no chance or trivial baseline. The architectural choices are nonetheless well reasoned for the task. The last convolutional layer of VGG-16 is retained specifically because it 'preserves the spatial information' as a 7x7 grid of 512-dimensional vectors rather than a globally pooled summary, which matters when the discriminative event is a head turn at a particular image location. The LSTM supplies temporal structure, necessary because the target behaviour is a sequence - object, then person, then object - not a static configuration. And the attention module is included not for performance but for inspectability, which is how it is actually used. [RQ4.2] Raw video reduced only by clip trimming and, for three of four partitions, foreground segmentation. There is no hand-engineered representation at all: no head pose, no gaze vector, no skeleton, no facial landmarks. This is a meaningful methodological position given that the target behaviour is a gaze shift, which the pose-estimation literature would extract explicitly. The tradeoff is visible in the results - the model works, but nothing about the representation is inspectable, and interpretability has to be recovered afterwards through the attention weights. The temporal unit is fixed at 10 seconds from toy placement, which encodes an assumption that a genuine initiation will occur within that window; the paradigm's 30-second wait before each trial makes that assumption defensible but it is not tested. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and full confusion matrices for both testing sets, plus training and validation accuracy - a complete panel for a conference paper, and reported for both test sets rather than only the better one. The confusion matrices make the error structure legible: on test set #1, 23 of 198 typically developing clips were called autistic against 12 of 218 autistic clips called typical, so the model errs toward false positives, and precision (0.900) sits below recall (0.945) accordingly. Two things are missing and one is consequential. There are no confidence intervals and no per-child accuracy, and since the metrics are computed over 416 and 184 clips originating from only 36 and 18 children, clips from the same child are not independent and the apparent precision of the estimates is overstated - the paper itself describes averaging probabilities per subject for training and validation but does not do so for testing. And there is no comparison against a trivial baseline; given a 45-point IQ gap, a baseline using developmental level alone would be the informative comparator. [RQ4.4] The strongest video-model interpretability analysis in the corpus, and the reason this short paper matters. Rather than presenting an attention heatmap and asserting that it looks sensible, the authors used the soft attention weights as a testable hypothesis about mechanism: they plotted the alpha values across all 300 frames for every clip and then checked each plot against the corresponding video to see whether a rise coincided with a specific social gesture. The finding is stated with appropriate precision - for typically developing children a distinct rise to at least twice baseline was 'invariably noted' somewhere in the sequence, though its onset and duration varied between children, while for autistic children attention weights 'did not change significantly throughout the duration of the video clip'. Crucially both directions are checked: every attention peak in a typically developing child coincided with an observed IJA behaviour, and across the whole dataset fewer than 1% of autistic children showed both an IJA behaviour and a corresponding peak. That establishes correspondence rather than mere plausibility, and it means the model's decision can be traced to the occurrence or non-occurrence of the clinically defined behaviour the protocol was designed to elicit - which is exactly the claim most deep-learning studies in this corpus make without evidence. The illustrative figure showing frames 80, 140, 180 and 240 for one child from each group makes the mechanism concrete. What is not done: attention is temporal only, with no spatial attribution showing which part of the frame is used, so it cannot be verified that the model is watching the child rather than the contingently responding examiner. [RQ4.5] Correct in its most important respect and incomplete in a secondary one. The partition is subject-disjoint: 40 children in training and validation (16+16 and 4+4), 36 in test set #1, 18 in test set #2, accounting for all 94 participants with no child in more than one partition. This forecloses the identity-leakage route that inflates several other studies here, and it is the reason 0.916 can be compared to Kojovic's 80.9% and Han's 95.56% rather than to segment-level figures. Two independent test sets rather than one is a further strength, and making them differ in preprocessing turns the second into a domain-shift check rather than a redundant repetition. What is incomplete: the reported test metrics are clip-level, computed over 416 and 184 clips rather than over 36 and 18 children, so within-child correlation inflates the apparent precision even though it does not bias the point estimate; the paper describes per-subject probability averaging for training and validation but not for testing, and no per-child accuracy appears. There is also no cross-validation - a single fixed split with 32 training children - so the estimate carries no measure of split-to-split variability, and no external cohort or site. Finally, whatever architecture and hyperparameter selection occurred is undocumented, so it cannot be established that the validation set was used only once. [RQ5.1] Keywords: AI-assisted diagnosis, autism spectrum disorder, behavioral biomarker, early detection model, joint attention. 'Behavioral biomarker' is the term doing the conceptual work - the paper's claim is that joint attention functions as a biomarker in the absence of any biological one, stated directly as 'there is no definitive biomarker for ASD'. 'AI-assisted diagnosis' rather than 'screening' in the keyword list sits slightly ahead of what the study demonstrates, though the body of the paper is more careful, describing the intended use as screening plus an assistive tool for specialists. [RQ5.2] IEEE 3rd International Conference on Human-Machine Systems (ICHMS) 2022, DOI 10.1109/ICHMS56717.2022.9980778 - an engineering conference, four pages. The author list is genuinely clinical-computational: the Department of Biomedical Systems Informatics at Yonsei University College of Medicine, the Division of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry at Seoul National University College of Medicine, the Department of Child Development and Family Studies at Seoul National University, and one industry author. That composition explains the paper's characteristic shape - protocol design and diagnostic characterisation at journal standard, training details at conference standard. Funded by the Korean government's IITP programme (2022-0-00234). [RQ5.3] 2022. The framing combines the usual prevalence and early-intervention arguments (1 in 59, billions in socio-economic burden, improved outcomes from early detection) with a workforce argument that is more specific and more relevant to the deployment claim: early detection 'does not appear to be feasible, especially in regions where there is a scarcity of mental health specialists'. What distinguishes this paper's positioning is its critique of the immediately preceding work rather than of clinical practice in general. It observes that the Cognoa system, which obtained FDA marketing authorisation, 'may be considered not fully automated as it uses as input for the machine learning model not the actual videos, but human ratings corresponding to the quality of behavior conveyed in each video' - a precise and correct distinction between automating inference and automating measurement that no other paper in this corpus draws. And it criticises Zunino's grasping-kinematics classifier on the ground that 'the targeted gesture is not generally considered an indication of ASD behavior by most mental health specialists', which is a criterion of clinical construct validity rather than of accuracy. Those two criticisms jointly define the paper's design: raw video in, and a behaviour clinicians already accept as diagnostic as the target. The conclusion's comparative claim - higher accuracy and F1 than prior models reporting 0.70-0.80 - is asserted without statistical test and across studies with different populations and IQ distributions, which sits oddly against the care of the critique that opens the paper.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control study in China: 40 autistic children (33 boys, 7 girls, mean 4.6 years) from special education schools and 40 typically developing children (33 boys, 7 girls, mean 4.8 years) from regular kindergartens, aged 3-6, matched on sex exactly and stated to be matched on age. Autism established by DSM-5 criteria alone with no instrument or assessor reported; no cognitive, language, adaptive or severity measure for either group. Eye-tracking, facial video and 14-channel Emotiv EPOC+ EEG were recorded simultaneously during one 40-second video clip; data available from the corresponding author on request.
narrative_rows.methods: The stimulus was selected from ten candidates by valence-arousal ratings from three graduate students, and combined social content (comedians laughing) with non-social content (spinning wheels). Gaze features were the frequencies of fixations falling in each of K K-means clusters, with K tested at 8, 12, 16 and 20. Facial expression features were counts, per 40-frame window, of frames in which the child displayed the expression shown in the stimulus, detected by a CNN with soft labels. EEG features were band powers (theta 4-6, alpha 6-13, low beta 13-20, high beta 20-30, gamma 30-45 Hz) across six regions, reduced to the 12 region-band combinations reaching significance in t-tests across all 80 children. Random forest, SVM and KNN were applied to each modality; behavioural features were fused at feature level and combined with the EEG subdecision by an attribute-weighted naive Bayes classifier. Evaluation was leave-one-out cross-validation over the 80 children.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Best single-modality accuracies: EEG 83.75%, facial expression 77.50%, eye fixation 73.75%; averages across the three classifiers 74.69%, 71.56% and 67.50%. Behavioural fusion 85.00%, physiological alone 83.75%, hybrid fusion 87.50%. Per-class rates showed opposite failure directions: EEG 90.0% on autistic and 77.5% on typically developing children; facial expression 72.5% and 92.5%; eye fixation 62.5% and 85.0%; hybrid fusion 85.0% and 90.0%. Theta power was significantly higher in the autistic group in five of six regions, with the largest effect at left frontal (t = 5.82).
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The 12 EEG features were selected by t-tests computed across all 80 children before leave-one-out cross-validation, so each held-out child's label informed the choice of features used to classify them - selection bias that inflates the very modality the paper concludes is most discriminative; the gaze cluster count K was likewise chosen from classification results, and the headline 87.50% is the best of three classifiers. Autism was established by DSM-5 criteria alone with no instrument, assessor or setting documented, and no cognitive, language or severity measure was taken. Groups were recruited from special education schools versus regular kindergartens, confounding placement and developmental level with diagnosis. EEG came from a consumer headset with epoch survival unreported by group and non-standard band definitions. Only accuracy is reported, differences described as significant were never tested, and there is no external validation. The limitations section names only sample size and across-day recording variability.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The most useful thing this study contributes is a controlled modality comparison: three streams recorded from the same children during the same 40-second stimulus, so their relative discriminative power is compared without confounding modality with sample, task or setting - a design no other paper in this corpus achieves with three modalities. Its confusion-graph analysis then independently reproduces the finding Han et al. reach with two modalities, that neurophysiological and behavioural streams fail in opposite directions, EEG over-calling autism and behavioural measures under-calling it. That convergence across two Chinese cohorts, different stimuli, different EEG hardware and different fusion architectures is one of the more robust cross-study observations available in this review. Two secondary points are worth carrying. The two behavioural modalities together (85.00%) essentially matched EEG alone (83.75%) and the full three-modality fusion added only 2.5 points, which bears on the cost case for adding EEG to camera-and-eye-tracker screening. And reporting both best and average accuracy per modality exposes an 18-point spread across classifiers on identical EEG features - a caution applicable to every single-classifier accuracy figure in this corpus. Against all of this, the study is also a clear instance of a validity failure distinct from the segment-level leakage that dominates elsewhere: the cross-validation is correctly participant-level, but feature selection sits outside it, so the design is right and the number is still optimistic.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups of 40, recruited from special education schools and from regular kindergartens respectively. Both are explicitly sized and their sex composition is identical (33 boys, 7 girls each). No other-diagnosis or developmental-delay comparison group. The recruitment asymmetry is the structural weakness: children attending special education schools and children attending regular kindergartens differ in developmental level, in daily environment, and in familiarity with being assessed, and none of these is measured. With no cognitive or language measure taken, group membership in this study is inseparable from educational placement, and a classifier that separates the two groups at 87.5% cannot be shown to be separating them on autism rather than on the correlates of placement. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'ASDs' used as a plural noun for people in the results discussion ('Eye fixation misclassified more ASDs as TDs'), against 'typically developing (TD) children', 'TD controls', 'TDs'. The acronym-as-noun usage is the least person-centred in the corpus alongside Mazumdar. The framing is burden-oriented - autism is 'a worldwide medical problem and a tremendous economic and mental burden to society' - but the paper also carries an unusually non-deterministic aetiological framing, citing 'an emerging view is that the atypical behavior of ASD children may be caused by early brain adaptation to an adverse environment, rather than a result of ongoing neural pathology', which motivates early intervention as prevention of maladaptive adaptation rather than as remediation of pathology. [RQ1.3] Autistic group: 40 children, 33 boys and 7 girls, aged 3-6, mean 4.6 years with a standard deviation of 9 months. Comparison group: 40 children, 33 boys and 7 girls, aged 3-6, mean 4.8 years, SD 7 months. The paper states 'no significant difference in age or sex existed between the two groups' but reports no test statistic or p value for either. Sex is matched exactly, which is a stronger match than most studies here achieve. What is entirely absent is any measure of cognitive, language or adaptive functioning - a serious gap in a 3-to-6-year-old sample where developmental level varies widely, where EEG spectral power changes rapidly with age and maturation, and where the two groups were drawn from educational settings that themselves sort on developmental level. No IQ, no developmental quotient, no language measure, no severity score. [RQ1.4] The weakest ascertainment in the 2022 cohort. Autism is established by 'the criteria of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition' with nothing further: no ADOS, ADI-R, CARS, SRS or any other standardised instrument; no statement of who applied the criteria, with what training, or in what setting; and no indication whether diagnosis was made for this study or taken from school records. Comparison children were 'screened to exclude any with psychiatric or neurological disorders, including ASD', again with no instrument named and no cut-off stated. Under the review's classification this is clinical-diagnosis-only in its least documented form, and it means the reference standard cannot be independently evaluated. [RQ1.5] None whatsoever. No IQ, developmental quotient, language level, adaptive functioning measure, severity score, comorbidity list or medication information for either group. This is the most complete absence of clinical characterisation among the studies in this corpus that nonetheless report high accuracy, and it compounds the recruitment asymmetry: with children drawn from special education schools versus regular kindergartens and no cognitive measure taken, there is no way to determine whether the classifier separates autism or separates developmental level. [RQ2.1] Goal: compare the discriminative power of eye fixation, facial expression and EEG collected simultaneously, and test whether hybrid fusion - behavioural feature fusion followed by weighted decision fusion with the physiological stream - outperforms any single modality. Main findings: EEG most discriminative (83.75% best, 74.69% average), facial expression next (77.50%, 71.56%), eye fixation weakest (73.75%, 67.50%); hybrid fusion 87.50% against 85.00% for behavioural data alone and 83.75% for physiological data alone; modalities fail in opposite directions, with EEG best on autistic children (90.0%) and facial expression best on typically developing children (92.5%); and theta power elevated in the autistic group across five of six brain regions. [RQ2.2] China, with the two groups drawn from different institutional settings - special education schools for the autistic children and regular kindergartens for the comparison children. Recording conditions are described only obliquely and only in the limitations, where the authors note that 'the recording environments are changing' and that 'across-day variability exists in recording conditions'. That acknowledgement is candid but incomplete: if recording conditions varied across days and the two groups were recruited from different institutions, sessions may have been clustered by group, in which case environmental variation is partially confounded with diagnosis. The paper does not report whether recordings were interleaved across groups. [RQ2.3] A single 40-second video clip designed so that social and non-social content compete within the same display - social being comedians with happy expressions, funny actions and laughter, non-social being backgrounds and two spinning wheels. The selection procedure is documented and is the more careful part of the design: ten candidate clips were rated by three graduate students in special education on valence and arousal, mean positions on the arousal-valence plane were computed, and the clip with the highest mean positive arousal was chosen. That grounds the stimulus in an explicit affective criterion rather than in the experimenters' intuition, though three raters is a thin basis and the raters were adults rating their own emotions rather than children's. The paradigm's strength is that one stimulus simultaneously probes three constructs - where the child looks (social versus non-social competition), whether the child mirrors the displayed expression (imitation), and the concurrent EEG response - so the three modalities are genuinely commensurate. Its limitation is duration: 40 seconds is the shortest observation window in the corpus, and with a single clip there is no test-retest or within-child replication. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: approval by the Institutional Review Board of Pingdingshan University under protocol code 068 dated 20 October 2020, conduct in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and informed consent from all subjects involved. A data availability statement commits to sharing 'from the corresponding author on reasonable request'. Facial video of identifiable preschoolers is collected and no statement about its storage, retention or de-identification appears. [RQ2.5] Three consumer-grade sensors, which is the practical argument of the paper: a Tobii eye tracker (model not specified), an unspecified video camera, and an Emotiv EPOC+ 14-channel wireless headset with all electrode positions named (AF3, F7, F3, FC5, T7, P7, O1, O2, P8, T8, FC6, F4, F8, AF4, referenced to P3 and P4). The EPOC+ is a consumer device with saline electrodes and no impedance control, applied here to children aged 3-6; the paper cites its noninvasiveness, low cost and high temporal resolution as advantages and does not discuss its known signal-quality limitations. Preprocessing is stated (0.2-45 Hz band, epoching, removal of epochs containing blinks, eye movement or muscle activity, FFT band power) but the number of surviving epochs per group is not reported - the differential-data-quality question that Han et al. at least quantified for their comparable design. [RQ2.6] Uneven, with the mathematics fully specified and the empirical procedure underdocumented. Reported in detail: the K-means loss function, assignment rule, centroid update and convergence criterion; the attribute-weighting formula for naive Bayes with its zero-avoidance property; the two-level fusion architecture; all 14 EEG electrode positions; the filter cut-offs and the five band definitions; the complete t-test table with F, t, p, mean difference and standard error for all 30 region-band combinations; the stimulus selection procedure; and both best and average accuracy for every modality-classifier pair. Not reported: the Tobii model, the camera specification, the sampling rates of any device, the number of EEG epochs retained per child or per group, the final chosen value of K, the CNN architecture and training details beyond a reference to prior work, any hyperparameters for random forest, SVM or KNN, and the order in which feature selection and cross-validation were performed - which has to be inferred from the text's sequence and is the study's decisive ambiguity. [RQ2.7] Two limitations are stated. The sample is 'relatively small' and should be extended. And the data 'have nonstationary characteristics, and the recording environments are changing', so that 'across-day variability exists in recording conditions', motivating future work on models that adapt over time - a limitation rarely raised in this corpus and a real one for consumer EEG. Not acknowledged: that the 12 EEG features were selected by t-tests computed across all 80 children before leave-one-out cross-validation, so the held-out child's label informed feature selection; that the gaze cluster count K was chosen from the experimental results; that the headline 87.50% is the best across three classifiers; that autism was established by DSM-5 criteria alone with no instrument, assessor or setting described; that no cognitive, language or severity measure was taken in a preschool sample; and that the two groups were recruited from special education schools and regular kindergartens respectively, so educational placement is confounded with diagnosis. [RQ2.9] Two directions, both modest. Enlarge the sample to improve accuracy and stability. And address non-stationarity by 'adopting detection models over time' given the across-day variability in recording conditions - which points toward domain adaptation and is a sensible response to the consumer-EEG constraint the study operates under. Absent from the agenda: any proposal to strengthen diagnostic ascertainment, to measure developmental level, to recruit comparison children from comparable settings, or to validate on an external cohort. [RQ3.1] Two behavioural constructs, each operationalised in a way that departs from convention. Social attention allocation is measured not by fixation on hand-drawn regions of interest but by the distribution of fixations across K-means clusters discovered from the data - so the analysis asks where gaze concentrates without the experimenter deciding in advance what counts as a region. This removes one source of investigator judgement and is defensible when a stimulus has no clean object boundaries, but it also severs the link between a feature and any interpretable content: a cluster is a screen location, so a group difference cannot be reported as 'less looking at the comedian's face'. That is why the paper reports no directional gaze findings at all. Facial expression is operationalised as imitation rather than as expression: the expression displayed in the stimulus is defined as the target, and the feature is the count of frames in each 40-frame window in which the child displays that same expression - so the measure is expression contagion or mirroring in response to a specific social display, motivated by prior work suggesting 'spontaneous expression imitation could be used as a behavioral marker'. This is a sharper construct than generic expression frequency and one of the few instances in this corpus of a behavioural feature defined relative to what the stimulus is doing at that moment. [RQ3.2] The corpus's most explicit study of fusion architecture, with three design choices argued rather than assumed. First, fusion is hybrid rather than purely early or late: the two behavioural streams are fused at feature level, because they are homogeneous enough that concatenation exploits their correlation, while the physiological stream is fused at decision level with the behavioural subdecision, because feature-level fusion across such different data types would not work - the paper states hybrid fusion 'utilizes the merits of feature fusion and decision fusion and overcomes their disadvantages'. Second, the decision combiner is not plain naive Bayes but an attribute-weighted variant, on the explicit reasoning that 'the naive Bayes algorithm assumes that each attribute has the same influence on the classification result; in fact, they are different', with weights derived from training-set co-occurrence counts and constructed so they cannot vanish. Third, and most valuably, the paper demonstrates why fusion works rather than merely that it does: confusion matrices and pairwise confusion graphs show EEG achieving 90.0% on autistic children but only 77.5% on typical ones while facial expression achieves 92.5% on typical children but only 72.5% on autistic ones, with eye fixation missing 37.5% of autistic children - so the modalities err in opposite directions and the fused model recovers 85.0% and 90.0%. This is the same mechanism-level demonstration Han et al. provide, arrived at independently and with three modalities rather than two, and the convergence between the two studies on the finding that neurophysiological and behavioural streams fail in opposite directions is worth carrying into the synthesis. The one deflating observation is that the two behavioural modalities together (85.00%) essentially match EEG alone (83.75%), and the full fusion adds only 2.5 points over the behavioural pair - so on a cost-benefit view the EEG headset buys very little over a camera and an eye tracker. [RQ4.1] Deliberately conventional classifiers - random forest, SVM and K-nearest neighbour - with all three applied to every modality, and both best and average accuracy reported. Running the full grid rather than reporting one model is informative: the spread on EEG features runs from 65.00% (SVM) to 83.75% (random forest), an 18-point range on identical inputs, and SVM is the weakest learner on all three modalities. That variability is a caution about single-classifier results generally, and its reporting here is more transparent than the corpus norm. The modelling novelty sits in the combiner rather than the base learners: an attribute-weighted naive Bayes whose weights are computed from training-set counts, with the formula given and its zero-avoidance property noted. No deep model is used for classification, which is appropriate given 80 participants, though a CNN is used upstream for facial expression recognition. [RQ4.2] One feature vector per child per modality, so the unit is the participant throughout - which is what permits genuine leave-one-out cross-validation. The gaze representation is the most distinctive: rather than manually delineating areas of interest, K-means partitions the fixation space and cluster occupancy frequencies become the features, with K tested at 8, 12, 16 and 20. The approach adapts the region structure to where children actually looked, but it carries two costs the paper does not discuss - the clusters are fitted to the pooled data of both groups, and the choice of K was made on the basis of classification results. The expression representation is a time series of target-expression counts per 40-frame window, preserving some temporal structure. The EEG representation is 12 scalar band powers, reduced from 30 candidate region-band combinations by significance testing. [RQ4.3] Accuracy only, plus confusion matrices - no sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, ROC or AUC is reported by name, though the confusion matrices supply per-class rates from which sensitivity and specificity can be read (85.0% and 90.0% for the fused model). No confidence intervals, no variance across leave-one-out iterations, and no statistical test of any comparison, despite the text repeatedly describing differences as significant ('significantly greater than that obtained using a single modality', 'can significantly improve the classification accuracy') where no test was performed. The reporting of both best and average accuracy per modality is a genuine strength that partly offsets this, since it makes classifier-dependence visible. The absence of any trivial baseline is a real gap given that the two groups differ in educational placement and no developmental measure was taken. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is strongest for EEG and absent for the behavioural modalities. The EEG t-test table is complete - all 30 region-band combinations with F, t, p, mean difference and standard error - and the directions and interpretations are given: theta power significantly higher in the autistic group in five of six regions with the largest effect at left frontal (t = 5.82), and interpretations offered for each band ('theta waves mainly reflect the emotional experience of individuals', 'the low-beta band is related to the capacity for concentration', gamma 'related to the abilities of learning, memory, and information processing'). Those band-to-function attributions are loose and would not survive scrutiny in the EEG literature, but the underlying statistics are fully reported and the theta finding is placed in the context of prior work. For gaze and facial expression there is nothing: no group means, no directions, no effect sizes, no indication of which clusters or which time windows differ. This asymmetry follows from the representations - clusters and frame counts have no semantic content to report - and it means the study, despite recording two behavioural modalities, contributes no behavioural finding beyond classification accuracy. The confusion-graph analysis is a genuine interpretability contribution at modality level, showing exactly which class each modality handles and which it fails. [RQ4.5] Leave-one-out cross-validation over 80 children with the participant as the unit - structurally the right design, and it forecloses the within-subject leakage that inflates Simeoli, Liaqat, Mazumdar and Akter. But two selection steps precede it and contaminate it. The EEG feature set was determined by running independent-samples t-tests on band power across all 80 children and retaining the 12 region-band combinations reaching significance; only then was classification with leave-one-out cross-validation performed on those features. Every held-out child therefore contributed their label to the choice of features used to classify them - the classic selection-bias pattern, and one that inflates the EEG modality specifically, which is the modality the paper concludes is most discriminative and which anchors its central claim. Second, the number of gaze clusters was tested at four values and 'the final value of K was determined from the experimental results', so a preprocessing hyperparameter was also chosen on classification performance across the full sample. A third, milder issue is that the headline 87.50% is the best of three classifiers; the paper reports averages for single modalities but not for the fusion. There is no external validation, no independent cohort and no repeated-split estimate of variability. The correct reading is that the participant-level design is sound but that the reported figures - particularly for EEG and for the fusion that depends on it - are optimistic by an unmeasured margin. [RQ5.1] No keyword list appears in the extracted text. The operative vocabulary is multimodal fusion, hybrid fusion, weighted naive Bayes, eye fixation, facial expression recognition, EEG, and early detection - a method-dominated register with 'early detection' as the only clinical term. [RQ5.2] Journal of Healthcare Engineering, volume 2022, article 9340027, an open-access Hindawi title. Authorship is from the Department of Education at Pingdingshan University and the National Engineering Laboratory for Technology of Big Data Application in Education at Central China Normal University - an educational-technology rather than clinical or biomedical-engineering provenance, which explains the paper's shape: careful engineering of the fusion architecture and the stimulus selection, competent statistics on the EEG, and essentially no clinical characterisation of the participants. The review timeline is notably compressed (received 16 February 2022, revised 5 March, accepted 8 March, published 25 March - eleven days from submission to acceptance). Funded by Henan provincial science and social science programmes. [RQ5.3] 2022. The framing is standard in its premises - 1 in 54 prevalence, 'a tremendous economic and mental burden to society', existing methods 'depend on the assessment of experts, which are subjective and costly' - but two elements are distinctive. The critique of current tools is concrete rather than generic, citing the M-CHAT as a case where a parent questionnaire 'is administered by specialists in rigorously controlled clinical settings, usually taking hours to complete', so the objection is to throughput rather than to validity. And the aetiological framing is unusually non-deterministic for this literature: the paper cites 'an emerging view is that the atypical behavior of ASD children may be caused by early brain adaptation to an adverse environment, rather than a result of ongoing neural pathology', which recasts early intervention as preventing maladaptive adaptation during a period of plasticity rather than as treating a fixed pathology. That framing then does argumentative work, supplying the paper's justification for including EEG at all - that 'atypical brain development in children with ASD appears earlier than atypical behavior, and the critical period of early intervention will be missed if the detection is based on behavioral data'. The claimed contributions are explicitly comparative: that prior work has applied each modality separately, that 'studies on data fusion are few', and that 'the discriminative powers of different data modalities are unclear' - a gap the study does address, and the modality-ranking result is its most transferable finding whatever the absolute accuracies are worth.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Secondary analysis of a public collection of 547 gaze-path images (328 non-ASD, 219 ASD) recorded with an SMI RED eye tracker, in which gaze coordinates and their velocity, acceleration and jerk are encoded as RGB gradients. The number of children contributing the images, their ages, sexes, diagnoses and severity are not reported anywhere in the paper, which directs readers to the source publication. No ethics statement.
narrative_rows.methods: Images were augmented by horizontal flipping, translation and blurring applied individually and in combination, expanding the dataset by 1300%; resized from 640x480 to 28x28 by Lanczos interpolation; converted to 8-bit grayscale by the ITU-R 601-2 luma transform; contrast-stretched to [0,1]; and flattened into 785-column CSV rows of 784 pixel values plus a label. A Kernel Extreme Learning Machine with RBF kernel was fitted, its two parameters C and gamma searched over powers of two from 2^-7 to 2^7 by the Giza Pyramids Construction metaheuristic minimising the model's mean squared error, with population 10 and 10 iterations. Five comparator optimisers (PSO, ABC, ALO, BA, HHO) and three comparator classifiers (multilayer perceptron, naive Bayes, logistic regression) were run on the same data. No train/test split or cross-validation is described; each method was run 30 times.
narrative_rows.outcomes: GPC-KELM: accuracy 0.9881, precision 0.9859, sensitivity 0.9843, specificity 0.9906, MCC 0.9752, F1 0.9851, all with standard deviations below 0.0015 across 30 runs; AUC 98.18; confusion matrix TP 847, TN 560, FP 8, FN 8. Comparator optimisers 0.9736-0.9800; Wilcoxon p-values 5.4e-12 to 1.1e-11. Comparator classifiers far lower on identical data: multilayer perceptron 0.8179 (AUC 79.17), naive Bayes 0.7306, logistic regression 0.7243 (AUC 66.55). Optimal parameters C = 26.644, gamma = 23.603, converging by iteration six.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No train/test split, cross-validation or held-out set is described anywhere. Augmentation expanded the data thirteenfold before evaluation and, by the authors' explicit statement, was used 'to enlarge the training and testing data', so near-duplicate transforms of the same source image populate both sides. Images from the same child cannot be separated because no participant identifiers exist and no participants are described. Two kernel hyperparameters were optimised against the model's own error with accuracy rising monotonically across optimiser iterations. Grayscale conversion discards the velocity, acceleration and jerk information the source encoding carried in colour, and 28x28 downsampling leaves only coarse spatial coverage, so no behavioural quantity survives. Horizontal flipping generates physically impossible scanpaths. No participant characteristics, no diagnostic procedure, no ethics statement, no behavioural findings, and no comparison against the source dataset's own participant-level result.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The corpus's most instructive negative case, because it can be compared directly against a participant-level analysis of the identical images. Cilia and colleagues, who created this 547-image gaze-path dataset, reported approximately 90% at image level and roughly 71% once accuracy was computed per child, since each child contributed about nine images. This paper reports 98.8% on the same images, adds a thirteenfold augmentation that the authors state was applied to the testing as well as the training data, describes no split or cross-validation at all, and never mentions children - so the participant-level correction cannot even be attempted. The 27-point gap between 71% and 98.8% is a direct measurement of what these compounding decisions add. Two further observations transfer. The comparator table functions as an internal diagnostic: a multilayer perceptron on identical inputs reached 81.8% and logistic regression 72.4%, so a 17-to-26-point advantage for a two-parameter tuned kernel machine is more consistent with tuning against the evaluation data than with a robust class signal in 784 downsampled pixels. And the representation itself illustrates a distinct failure mode - converting to grayscale destroys the derivative information the source dataset existed to encode, leaving a plot-density statistic, which is consistent with the authors' own closing remark that 'the amount of information in the images and the use of space in the x and y coordinates are essential factors' and points toward tracker data quality rather than viewing behaviour as the operative variable.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Not answerable from this paper. Groups are described only as image classes - 328 non-ASD images and 219 ASD images, 547 in total - and the number of children contributing them is never stated. The paper's entire treatment of participants is one sentence directing the reader elsewhere: 'For more information about participants diagnosed with ASD and non-ASD, see [44]'. This is the only study in the corpus that reports no participant count at all, in either group. Because the source is the same gaze-path collection Cilia and colleagues assembled - 547 images with roughly nine images per child - the underlying sample is a few dozen children, but nothing in this paper permits that inference, and no participant identifier is available to group images by child. [RQ1.2] 'the ASD person', 'ASD patients', 'ASD subjects', 'challenged kids with severe disabilities', 'patients', against 'non-ASD' as the comparison label. The consistent use of 'patients' for children in a non-clinical dataset, and of 'the ASD person' as a category noun, is at the deficit end of the corpus's usage. The background section is the most pathologising in the review, describing autistic people as ranging from 'gifted children with exceptional learning and problem-solving capabilities to challenged kids with severe disabilities that require care-support throughout their whole life', framing behaviours as 'red flags', stating that 'there is no known cure for ASD', and arguing that early diagnosis helps 'children with medical prescriptions to prevent further deterioration of their condition' - a progressive-disease framing that misdescribes autism. The comparison class is named 'non-ASD' rather than typically developing, which is accurate to what is known about it but reflects that nothing is known about it. [RQ1.3] Nothing. No ages, no sexes, no group sizes in people, no cognitive or language measures, no matching, and no statement that any of these are unavailable. The only quantities reported about the sample are image counts per class. This is the least characterised sample in the corpus, exceeding even Mazumdar, which at least reported that 14 autistic and 14 typically developing children contributed the data. [RQ1.4] Nothing. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician role or setting, and no summary or citation of the source dataset's ascertainment procedure beyond a pointer to the source paper. The class labels are treated as properties of image files. This matters more than usual because the study reports 98.8% accuracy against a reference standard whose nature is entirely unspecified within the paper. [RQ1.5] Nothing. No IQ, language, adaptive functioning, comorbidity, medication or severity data, and no exclusions described. Consequently there is no possibility of relating model output to any clinical gradient, and no way to assess whether developmental level rather than diagnosis distinguishes the classes. [RQ2.1] Goal: demonstrate the Giza Pyramids Construction metaheuristic as an optimiser for Kernel Extreme Learning Machine parameters, benchmarked on autism classification from gaze-path images. Main findings: GPC-KELM reached 0.9881 accuracy, 0.9859 precision, 0.9843 sensitivity, 0.9906 specificity, 0.9752 MCC and 0.9851 F1, with sub-0.0015 standard deviations across 30 runs; it beat PSO, ABC, ALO, BA and HHO variants (0.9736-0.9800) with Wilcoxon p-values below 1.1e-11; and it beat a multilayer perceptron (0.8179), naive Bayes (0.7306) and logistic regression (0.7243) on the same data, with AUC 98.18 against 79.17 and 66.55. Optimal parameters were C = 26.644 and gamma = 23.603, converging by the sixth of ten iterations. [RQ2.2] Not reported. The recordings belong to the source dataset and the paper describes neither the room, the country, the recruitment route nor the acquisition protocol. The only setting information is the hardware on which the experiments were computed - an AMD Ryzen 7 2700X with 16 GB RAM, a GTX 1050 Ti and a 250 GB SSD - which is specified more precisely than anything about the children. [RQ2.3] Described in a single clause: participants 'were shown different videos containing stimulating scenarios for the movement of the eye in the entire screen'. No stimulus content, category, duration, number, order or instruction is given, and no response was apparently required. The only substantive remark about the paradigm appears in the discussion, where the authors note that 'the short duration of the video scenarios' limits the information in each image and that 'more extended scenarios should be allowed to obtain images with more information in both classes' - which is an observation about image density rather than about behavioural sampling, and it inadvertently identifies the study's core interpretive problem: the quantity being classified is how much of the plot is filled in, not what the child looked at. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis of a public dataset; no follow-up. No ethics statement, consent statement or IRB approval appears anywhere, and no pointer is given to where the source dataset's approvals were obtained - an omission that is common for benchmark reuse in this corpus but is not acknowledged here either. A competing-interests declaration and a CRediT contribution statement are both present, so the absence of an ethics statement is not a matter of missing front matter. [RQ2.5] No acquisition equipment beyond a single mention of the SMI RED screen-based eye tracker used for the source recordings, with no sampling rate, calibration procedure or viewing geometry. Analysis tools are specified in more detail: Lanczos interpolation for resizing (with the justification that it 'provides the best properties for preserving details'), the ITU-R 601-2 luma transform for grayscale conversion at 8-bit depth, contrast stretching with the normalisation equation given, the KELM formulation with its Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse solution and RBF kernel, and the full GPC update equations with their physical parameters. The asymmetry is characteristic: every step of the image pipeline is documented and nothing about the measurement is. [RQ2.6] Reproducible as an algorithm, not as a study. Fully specified: the three augmentation operations and the resulting 1300% expansion; the resize target, interpolation kernel, colour transform and bit depth; the normalisation equation; the CSV structure of 785 columns; the KELM equations; the GPC pseudo-code with all four operations and their parameter values; the internal parameters of all five comparator optimisers in a table; the multilayer perceptron's architecture, activation, optimiser and learning rate; the search space for C and gamma; population size, dimension and iteration count; the number of independent runs; and the compute hardware. Entirely absent: any train/test split or cross-validation protocol, the sizes of any partition, the criterion by which the optimiser's fitness was evaluated relative to reported performance, any participant-level information, and any code release. The single most important methodological fact - how performance was estimated on data not used to fit or tune the model - is not stated at any point in the paper. [RQ2.7] Three limitations are stated and none concerns validity. The dataset has a 'low number of participants'; the video scenarios were short, so images carry limited information and 'more extended scenarios should be allowed'; and 'the current version of this work is limited by the reduced number of samples of the eye-tracking dataset. We included a data augmentation step to generate synthetic samples to enlarge the training and testing data to overcome this issue'. That last sentence is the paper's most significant disclosure and is offered as a solution rather than as a problem: augmenting the testing data means near-duplicate transformations of the same source images populate both sides of the evaluation, which is exactly what a test set must exclude. Unaddressed: that no split or cross-validation protocol is described at all; that images from the same child cannot be separated because no participant identifiers exist; that the metaheuristic optimises hyperparameters against what appears to be the reported data; that grayscale conversion discards the velocity, acceleration and jerk information encoded in colour; that no participant characteristics or diagnostic procedures are known; and that the 17-to-26-point gap over conventional classifiers on identical data warrants explanation. [RQ2.9] Two lines are proposed, neither addressing the study's weaknesses. First, 'the enhancement and democratization of eye-tracking technologies' - an infrastructure aim rather than a research one. Second, improving the classifier 'by incorporating multi-class information such as medical records or clinical evaluations', which would move the work toward the multimodal designs elsewhere in this corpus but would require exactly the clinical data this study does not have. Notably absent: any proposal to validate at participant level, to obtain participant metadata, to test on an independent cohort, or to separate augmentation from evaluation. [RQ3.1] Nominally gaze during free viewing, but the behavioural construct is entirely lost in the representation. The source dataset encodes gaze coordinates together with their first, second and third derivatives - velocity, acceleration and jerk - as RGB colour gradients in a plot of the scanpath. This paper converts those images to grayscale, which discards the colour channel and hence the derivative information, then downsamples from 640x480 to 28x28, leaving 784 luminance values. What the classifier sees is a coarse silhouette of where the trace fell on the screen, with no fixation, saccade, duration or velocity quantity recoverable. The authors' own concluding observation that 'the amount of information in the images and the use of space in the x and y coordinates are essential factors' confirms this: the discriminative property is how much of the frame the trace covers, which is a plot-density statistic. No behavioural finding is reported and, given the representation, none could be. [RQ3.2] Single modality throughout, and no fusion is attempted. The paper's comparative apparatus is entirely internal to the optimisation problem: six metaheuristics searching the same two-dimensional hyperparameter space, and four classifier families on the same features. The most informative comparison for a reader of this review is the classifier table rather than the optimiser table. On identical augmented inputs, a multilayer perceptron reached 0.8179 accuracy with AUC 79.17, naive Bayes 0.7306 and logistic regression 0.7243 with AUC 66.55, against 0.9881 and AUC 98.18 for the tuned KELM. A 17-point accuracy gap and a 19-point AUC gap between a tuned kernel machine and a neural network on the same 784 pixel features is not what one expects if the features carry a robust class signal; it is what one expects if two kernel hyperparameters are being optimised against the evaluation data. The authors read the table as evidence of their method's superiority and do not consider this alternative reading. [RQ4.1] A Kernel Extreme Learning Machine - a single-hidden-layer feedforward network with randomly assigned input weights and an analytically computed output layer, kernelised with an RBF - chosen for computational economy over deep models, with the paper explicitly excluding deep learning from comparison 'since they require many computational resources and time for training'. The KELM has exactly two tunable parameters, C and gamma, and the entire modelling contribution is how they are chosen. The Giza Pyramids Construction algorithm searches that two-dimensional space via a metaphor of workers pushing stone blocks up a ramp, with gravity, ramp angle, kinetic friction and a worker-substitution probability as parameters. It is worth stating plainly that a two-parameter search over a grid of powers of two from 2^-7 to 2^7 does not require a population-based metaheuristic - exhaustive enumeration of 225 combinations would be cheaper than 10 iterations of a 10-member population - so the algorithmic apparatus considerably exceeds the difficulty of the problem it is applied to. The convergence result reported (optimal values found by iteration six) reflects this. [RQ4.2] 784 grayscale pixel intensities from a 28x28 downsample of a 640x480 gaze-path plot, contrast-stretched to [0,1] and flattened into CSV rows. The paper describes this resizing as its dimensionality reduction and states explicitly that 'the entire DR process is also the feature selection used in the proposed method' - so there is no feature engineering, no domain representation and no learned encoding, only downsampling. Two consequences follow. The colour encoding of velocity, acceleration and jerk that the source dataset was constructed to carry is destroyed by the grayscale conversion, so the very information that made the images more than plots of position is discarded before modelling. And at 28x28 the trace is a coarse blob, meaning the retained signal is essentially spatial coverage and density. Augmentation by horizontal flipping is also questionable for this representation: mirroring a scanpath about the vertical axis produces an image that no eye could have generated on the original stimulus, so the synthetic examples are not merely redundant but physically impossible. [RQ4.3] The most complete metric panel in the corpus in form - accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, Matthews correlation coefficient and F1, each with average, median and standard deviation over 30 runs, plus a confusion matrix, ROC curves with AUC for four classifiers, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for every optimiser comparison. Including MCC is good practice for imbalanced classes and is rare here. The apparatus is nonetheless measuring the wrong thing. The 30 runs vary only the metaheuristic's random seed, not the data partition, so the sub-0.0015 standard deviations quantify optimiser stability rather than generalisation variance, and they should not be read as precision of the accuracy estimate. The Wilcoxon p-values of 5e-12 test whether one optimiser reliably beats another across seeds - a valid question about algorithms and an irrelevant one about autism. And the confusion matrix's 1,423 instances cannot be located in any described partition, since no split is specified; it corresponds to about 20% of the 7,111 augmented images, which is the only reading consistent with the paper's own statement that augmentation enlarged the testing data. [RQ4.4] None, and none is possible. There is no feature importance, attribution, saliency map or ablation, and the representation - individual pixels of a 28x28 downsampled plot - admits no behavioural interpretation even if attribution were computed. The paper offers no group difference, no effect direction and no descriptive statistic about gaze. Its one interpretive sentence, that 'the amount of information in the images and the use of space in the x and y coordinates are essential factors when classifying ASD', is a statement about how much of the frame the trace fills. Placed against the rest of this corpus, that is a meaningful observation in an unintended way: it is consistent with the classifier keying on trace density, which is a property of how much usable gaze data the tracker captured, and hence potentially on data quality rather than on viewing behaviour - the pattern seen in Li 2020's SHAP quality feature, Fang 2021's untracked-gaze 'area0' and Zhao 2021's differential OpenFace failure rates. [RQ4.5] The corpus's weakest evaluation design, and the weakness is threefold. First, no train/test split, cross-validation scheme, held-out set or partition of any kind is described anywhere in the paper; the only replication is 30 reruns of the optimiser. Second, augmentation preceded whatever evaluation occurred, and the authors state their purpose plainly: 'We included a data augmentation step to generate synthetic samples to enlarge the training and testing data.' Flips, translations and blurs of a source image are near-duplicates of it, so populating a test set with them guarantees that the model has effectively seen every test instance. Third, and independently of augmentation, the 547 source images come from a small number of children contributing roughly nine images each, and no participant identifiers exist in the released image set, so images from the same child necessarily span any partition. Layered on top, the metaheuristic optimises C and gamma against the KELM's mean squared error with the accuracy-versus-iteration curve in Figure 4 rising monotonically over ten iterations, which indicates the search is scored on the same predictions that are reported. The instructive comparison is with Cilia and colleagues, who built this dataset and reported that image-level accuracy near 90% fell to approximately 71% when computed per child. This paper reports 98.8% on the same images, cannot compute a per-child figure because it records no participants, and does not cite the correction.
