The gap between 71% and 98.8% is the measure of what these three compounding decisions add. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), Machine Learning, Kernel Extreme Learning Machine (KELM), Eye tracking, Metaheuristic algorithms. Three of five are optimisation or learning terms and the ordering of the paper's stated contributions confirms the priority: propose a tool, 'test the GPC over a real application', improve KELM accuracy. Autism is the application domain for a metaheuristics contribution. [RQ5.2] Applied Soft Computing, volume 120, article 108654 (Elsevier) - a computational intelligence journal with no clinical readership. Authorship is from the Division of Technologies for Cyber-Human Integration at Universidad de Guadalajara and the School of Engineering and Sciences at Tecnologico de Monterrey, with no clinical or psychological co-authorship. The venue and authorship together account for the paper's profile completely: rigorous treatment of the optimisation problem, six-metric reporting with non-parametric testing, full algorithmic specification, and no participants, no ethics statement, no diagnostic information and no validation protocol. Its related-work section surveys classifiers and data sources broadly and accurately but engages with no methodological literature on evaluation. [RQ5.3] 2022 (received October 2021, revised February 2022). The framing is the standard objectivity argument in a strong form: 'the accurate diagnosis of ASD is usually affected since it is linked to the judgment of an expert, which produces biases related to the lack of objectivity', with the gold standard characterised as requiring 'multiple sessions and a qualified professional', hence 'time and... high cost'. The proposed role is appropriately modest - 'automatic screening tools can accelerate the diagnosis by identifying which individual require a complete autism assessment' - and the discussion repeats that the method 'permits the experts to provide a preliminary overview that guides diagnosis to more complex stages and tests'. Two features of the background are worth noting against the corpus. The clinical description is the least accurate here, framing autism as a condition from which children 'deteriorate' without early medical prescription and cataloguing 'red flags' at 12, 14 and 18 months. And the paper's positioning of its own novelty - 'to the best of our knowledge, this is the first time KELM is used for ASD classification by using gaze tracking images' - is a claim about the pairing of an algorithm with a dataset rather than about any question concerning autism, which is a fair statement of what the study contributes.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Two-site cross-sectional study at Caltech and Indiana University: 48 autistic adults (79.2% male, 27.69 +/- 5.37 years, full-scale IQ 111.38, ADOS CSS-Overall 7.04, range 3-10) and 105 typically developing adults (70.5% male, 27.09 +/- 7.29 years, IQ 110.01), matched and formally tested on age, sex and IQ (all p > 0.35), from 183 recruited. Diagnosis by prior clinician diagnosis plus ADOS-2 Module 4 under the Hus and Lord algorithm at both sites, with additional licensed-psychologist confirmation at Caltech; comorbid depression, anxiety and ADHD permitted. Thirteen participants were excluded for gaze data quality (10 autistic, 3 control). Gaze recorded during two episodes of 'The Office' totalling 43 minutes.
narrative_rows.methods: Tobii TX300 at 300 Hz with nine-point calibration and validation repeated whenever any point exceeded 1.5 degrees of error. Areas of interest were generated automatically per frame using DensePose/Detectron2 for body parts and RetinaFace/InsightFace for faces and five keypoints, from which eye and mouth regions were derived geometrically; 96.2% of 61,724 frames contained a person and segmentations were manually verified. Gaze was downsampled to 24 Hz, represented as a 1-degree disk, assigned by maximum overlap, and expressed as a proportion of frames with successful on-screen gaze. Per-participant 1-second gaze heatmaps were correlated against leave-one-out group reference heatmaps. Analyses comprised bootstrap-estimated Cohen's d for group differences, Spearman reliability across non-overlapping epochs with bootstrap tests of between-group difference, L2 nearest-neighbour gaze fingerprinting with permutation testing, Gaussian naive Bayes classification with a held-out third over 10,000 iterations against an empirical null, and variational Bayesian Gaussian mixture clustering.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Group differences were moderate and replicated: less gaze to faces (77.4% versus 80.7% in Episode A) and eyes (52.0% versus 60.2%), Cohen's d 0.60-0.82, detectable from 2-minute epochs. Within-individual reliability was high and statistically identical between groups (Spearman's rho > 0.635; between-group difference p > 0.333 at every epoch duration). Fingerprinting identified individuals at 35.4% (autistic) and 29.5% (control) against chance levels of 6.2% and 2.9%, remaining above chance at 2-minute epochs. Classification reached 0.618 +/- 0.058 against an empirical chance level of 0.607 (p = 0.039), with 22 of 48 autistic adults misclassified in over 75% of iterations. The autistic and control reference heatmaps correlated at r = 0.966, and autistic individuals matched the autistic reference less well than controls did. Clustering returned two clusters containing approximately 25.5 and 22.5 autistic participants - splitting the autistic group rather than separating it. No gaze feature correlated with ADOS severity.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The sample is adults with IQ in the normal range, deliberately restricted, so findings need not generalise to children or to those with intellectual disability - the populations most of this corpus studies. Only two temporal blocks were collected, both on the same day, so demonstrated reliability spans about an hour rather than weeks or years. Only eye movements were measured, leaving open whether other measures would show greater within-individual variability in autism, though the authors argue against this on the grounds that eye movements are not under strong volitional control. Comorbid depression, anxiety and ADHD were permitted and may have contributed. Unremarked: 17% of autistic participants versus 3% of controls were excluded for gaze data quality, and the two sites used different diagnostic confirmation procedures. No ethics, data availability or code statement appears in the extracted text.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This is the paper that supplies the interpretive framework for the entire review, and it does so through three results that no other study here provides. The gaze-fingerprinting analysis quantifies the individual-identity signal in gaze directly: participants were identified out of 153 at five to ten times chance from as little as 2 minutes of viewing. That is a measurement of precisely the quantity that leaks whenever a participant's data appears on both sides of a train/test split - the mechanism Liaqat and colleagues hypothesised to explain their own scanpath-only anomaly, that Cilia quantified as a fall from roughly 90% to approximately 71% when accuracy was recomputed per child, and that operates unexamined in Simeoli's task-level folds and Gaspar's augmented images. The classification result then separates two properties that the rest of this literature conflates: gaze here is highly reliable within individuals, as reliable in autistic as in control participants, and yet diagnostic classification runs at chance because the autistic group is heterogeneous. A classifier can therefore measure something entirely real, stable and individually characteristic while carrying no diagnostic information at all. And the empirically derived chance level - 0.607 rather than an assumed 0.500 in a 48/105 design - shows how much interpretation depends on getting the baseline right: the identical number would have read as a 12-point success against a nominal baseline. Against these, the study also establishes what a well-designed eye-tracking comparison actually yields in matched adults: moderate, replicable group differences of Cohen's d 0.60-0.82 that do not correlate with severity and do not support individual-level assignment. That figure is the appropriate benchmark for the effect sizes underlying the corpus's high-accuracy small-sample results, and its distance from them is the review's central quantitative finding.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups, with complete flow accounting. 183 individuals were initially recruited (67 autistic, 20 female, 22 at Caltech; 116 typically developing, 33 female, 34 at Caltech). 176 watched Episode A (62 autistic) and 167 watched Episode B (59 autistic); analyses were restricted to the 166 who watched both (58 autistic). Thirteen were then excluded for eye-tracking data quality - specifically, missing or off-screen gaze for more than half of one or both episodes - leaving 48 autistic and 105 typically developing participants. The exclusion was strongly differential: 10 of 58 autistic participants (17.2%) against 3 of 108 controls (2.8%), a figure reported precisely but not discussed. Its direction matters for interpretation: the analysed autistic sample is the subset whose gaze could be tracked reliably throughout 43 minutes of video, which if anything strengthens rather than weakens the paper's conclusion that classification fails, since the participants most likely to produce noisy data were removed. Participants were split across two independent sites, with 17 autistic and 33 control participants at Caltech and the remainder at Indiana University. No other-diagnosis comparison group. [RQ1.2] Identity-first throughout: 'autistic individuals', 'autistic adults', 'autistic people', 'autistic participants', used consistently in the title, abstract and body, against 'typically developing (TD) controls'. 'ASD group' appears as a technical label for the analytic group but 'patients' never does, and no individual is described as 'an ASD'. The framing is notably non-deficit even where deficits are reported: autism is characterised as 'a complex and heterogeneous disorder that has so far defied any simple diagnostic markers or cognitive mechanisms', gaze differences are described as 'atypical' rather than impaired, and heterogeneity is treated as a scientific finding to be explained rather than as noise to be controlled. This is the most careful terminology in the corpus and is consistent with the paper's substantive argument, which is that treating autistic people as an interchangeable group is what makes classification fail. [RQ1.3] Fully reported with formal testing on every variable, in a table with test statistics and p values. Autistic group: 48 adults, 79.2% male, 27.69 +/- 5.37 years (18-41), full-scale IQ 111.38 +/- 14.98 (84-150), ADOS CSS-Overall 7.04 +/- 1.98 (3-10), AQ 28.06 +/- 7.67. Comparison group: 105 adults, 70.5% male, 27.09 +/- 7.29 years (19-55), full-scale IQ 110.01 +/- 10.20 (85-136), AQ 15.70 +/- 6.41. None of age (t(151) = -0.501, p = 0.617), sex (chi-squared = 0.864, p = 0.353) or IQ (t(140) = -0.637, p = 0.525) differed; only AQ did (t(151) = -10.314, p < 0.001), as it should. Eleven participants with missing IQ scores were explicitly excluded from that comparison and the exclusion is footnoted. This is the only study in the corpus to equate IQ between groups in a well-powered sample rather than acknowledging an IQ gap as a limitation, and the equating was achieved by restricting recruitment to adults with IQ in the normal range - a design choice the authors justify on the grounds of reducing 'variation related to general inattention, difficulty following instructions, or difficulty understanding the video stimuli', while acknowledging that it limits generalisation. [RQ1.4] Thorough and site-specific. Caltech required three conditions jointly: a prior diagnosis by a qualified clinician holding an MD or PhD; confirmation via clinical interview with the participant, and a parent where available, conducted by a named licensed clinical psychologist among the authors; and ADOS-2 Module 4 scores meeting a precisely stated criterion - at or above cutoff on at least two components of the original algorithm and within one point on the third, or within one point of the total cutoff under the Hus and Lord revised algorithm with Social Affect plus Restricted Repetitive Behaviors >= 7. Indiana University required a prior community diagnosis of ASD, autism, Asperger's syndrome or PDD-NOS, plus ADOS-2 Module 4 administered by research-reliable administrators meeting the same revised-algorithm criterion. Naming the exact scoring algorithm and the tolerance around cutoffs, and stating that the two sites differed in whether independent clinical confirmation was additionally required, is more precise ascertainment reporting than any other study in this review provides. The comparison group was characterised with the AQ rather than by exclusion alone. [RQ1.5] Comprehensive and used analytically rather than descriptively. Full-scale IQ was measured in both groups and reported with range and test statistic; the AQ was administered to both groups; and ADOS-2 Overall Calibrated Severity Scores derived by the Hus and Lord algorithm were obtained for the autistic group with a full range of 3 to 10, meaning the sample spans the severity spectrum rather than clustering at one end. Severity was then correlated against all four gaze features, with the finding that none reached significance - a negative result that matters, since it means the gaze measures that do differentiate groups on average do not index how autistic an individual is. Comorbidity handling is deliberate and unusual: depression, anxiety and ADHD were permitted rather than excluded on the grounds that they are common in autism, with only moderate-to-severe depression (BDI-II >= 25) and antipsychotic medication ruled out. The authors then list this inclusiveness among their own limitations, noting it leaves open how much comorbidity contributed to the findings - a rare instance of a design decision being defended and then flagged as a threat in the same paper. [RQ2.1] Goal: determine whether the excess behavioural variability of autistic participants reflects within-individual unreliability or between-individual heterogeneity, by testing three mutually exclusive hypotheses. Main findings, in the order they eliminate hypotheses: within-individual reliability was high and statistically indistinguishable between groups at every epoch duration (Spearman's rho > 0.635, between-group difference p > 0.333), and individuals were identifiable from their own gaze at 35% against a 3-6% chance level from as little as 2 minutes of video, ruling out hypothesis 1; the autistic and typically developing reference heatmaps were correlated at r = 0.966 and autistic individuals matched the autistic reference less well than controls did, and unsupervised clustering split the autistic group nearly in half rather than separating it from controls, ruling out hypothesis 3; supervised classification reached 0.618 against an empirical chance level of 0.607 with 22 of 48 autistic adults reliably misclassified, confirming hypothesis 2. Group differences themselves were moderate and robust: Cohen's d 0.60-0.82, replicated across two episodes and detectable from 2-minute epochs. [RQ2.2] Two independent sites - Caltech and Indiana University - using 'otherwise identical eye trackers and video stimuli', with the two-site design adopted explicitly 'to optimize generalizability'. Recruitment was through flyers distributed at outpatient treatment programmes, community support groups and community locations including college campuses and YMCAs, so the sample is community-recruited rather than clinic-referred - which matters for representativeness, though the authors note the sample 'is not representative of ASD in general'. Site membership is carried through the analysis and displayed in every figure by marker shape, so site effects remain visible rather than being pooled away. This is the only multi-site study in the corpus. [RQ2.3] Free viewing of two episodes of a commercial television sitcom, chosen on an argued rationale rather than by convenience. The authors state that naturalistic video was selected over 'much more impoverished and artificial stimuli typically employed in earlier studies (such as cropped photographs of grayscale faces)' because movies deliver 'high participant engagement, and reducing confounds to data quality including sleepiness and motion artifacts', and because the same stimuli had proved effective in the group's prior neuroimaging work. Two distinct episodes were used specifically to test whether within-individual reliability holds across stimuli rather than merely across time, which is the stronger test. Three design controls attach to the stimulus. Prior familiarity with each episode was measured on a nine-point scale, participants split into familiar and unfamiliar, and every reported result verified not to differ between them. Gaze during the social-comprehension question pauses in Episode B was excluded. And the analysis showed that gaze to faces differed substantially between the two episodes (Cohen's d 1.15 in the autistic group, 1.70 in controls) while the between-group differences remained stable - establishing that the group effect is a property of the participants rather than of the particular video, which is precisely the confound that stimulus-specific studies elsewhere in this corpus cannot exclude. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional with two measurement blocks on the same day separated by a break, drawn from a larger study that also included extensive behavioural assessment and neuroimaging. The authors identify the temporal limitation themselves as their second main limitation: 'we collected only two [blocks], both close in time and for similar (but distinct) video episodes', and argue that longer-term longitudinal data with dense state measures such as sleepiness and mood would be needed to distinguish measurement error from genuine state-dependent within-individual change. No ethics or consent statement appears in the extracted text, though the study is embedded in an established multi-site research programme. Copyright constraints on the sitcom prevented reproducing stimulus frames, and a royalty-free substitute image was used for the segmentation figure. [RQ2.5] Tobii TX300 at 300 Hz with 0.4-degree spatial resolution on a movable 23-inch 1920x1080 monitor at approximately 65 cm. Calibration discipline is the most rigorous in the corpus and is reported with its failure handling: a nine-point calibration followed by a nine-point validation quantifying error at all nine locations spanning the full screen, with results displayed immediately to the experimenter, who would adjust the screen or participant and repeat if any point exceeded 1.5 degrees of error - and the procedure repeated before each of the three parts of Episode A. The authors also report, against their own interest, that 'a computer error resulted in the loss of the validation data, so further quantitative assessment of validation accuracy is not possible', and that 12 participants were recorded at 120 Hz rather than 300 Hz 'because of a user error', noting that downsampling to the 24 Hz video frame rate compensated for the difference. Reporting both errors is a form of candour absent elsewhere in this corpus. Feature extraction used Detectron2 with DensePose and InsightFace with RetinaFace, and clustering used scikit-learn. [RQ2.6] Among the most reproducibly reported studies in the corpus. Specified: recruitment channels; both sites' diagnostic criteria including the exact ADOS-2 algorithm, cutoff and tolerance; the complete flow from 183 recruited to 153 analysed with reasons and counts at each step; eye tracker model, sampling rate, resolution, monitor size, viewing distance, calibration and validation protocol with its error threshold and repetition rule; both recording errors; stimulus identity, duration and part structure; the familiarity questionnaire and its cut-point; the complete area-of-interest construction including the specific models used, the merging of 24 DensePose parts into three, and the geometric rule for deriving eye and mouth regions from five keypoints; detection rates across all 61,724 frames; the manual verification of automatic segmentation; the downsampling to video frame rate, the 1-degree gaze disk and the maximum-overlap assignment rule; the normalisation of area-specific gaze by successful on-screen frames with its stated rationale; heatmap construction with Gaussian width, bin duration and the leave-one-out reference rule; the bootstrap, permutation and sampling procedures with their 10,000 iteration counts; classifier, held-out sizes and cross-validation repetitions; the mixture-model initialisation and its robustness checks; and the FDR correction. What is missing from the extracted text is an ethics statement, a data availability statement and any mention of code release. [RQ2.7] Three limitations are stated, each substantive and each with a proposed remedy - the most serious limitations section in the corpus. First, the sample is relatively small and 'not representative of ASD in general', and consists of adults with IQ in the normal range, so 'it remains unclear if our findings would generalize to children and individuals with lower IQ'; the inclusion of comorbid depression, anxiety and ADHD is folded into this as a further open question. Second, only two temporal blocks were collected, both on the same day, so within-individual precision is limited both by measurement error and potentially by state-dependent change, and longer-term longitudinal data across more diverse stimuli would be needed. Third, and most carefully argued, the interpretation rests on having measured only eye movements: 'It remains possible that other dependent measures - performance tasks or questionnaires based on interpreting the videos, or neuroimaging - would have revealed higher variability in ASD', including the specific alternative that autistic people might have unreliable cognition that they compensate for. The authors then argue against their own alternative rather than merely listing it, noting that 'eye movements are not under strong volitional control' and the stimuli are highly engaging, so 'a top-down compensatory mechanism thus seems implausible'. Two issues go unremarked: the differential exclusion rate for gaze data quality (17% of autistic participants versus 3% of controls), and the fact that the two sites used different diagnostic confirmation procedures. [RQ2.9] The agenda follows directly from the findings and is unusually specific. Scale up via internet-based (WebGazer) and smartphone-based eye tracking to obtain the sample sizes needed to identify subtypes, which the authors argue is now feasible and is made more so by their own finding that 2-minute epochs suffice. Collect longitudinal data with dense state-dependent measures - sleepiness, mood - to separate measurement error from genuine within-individual variation across weeks or years, and to assess intervention efficacy while revealing what an intervention changes ('gaze to faces but not to other features might change throughout training'). Design stimuli with specifically chosen visual features to maximise within-individual reliability and between-individual differences, which 'possibly... could also improve the classification analyses'. And integrate with neuroimaging and genetics, on the reasoning that systematic gaze differences 'would be expected to translate to differences also in evoked BOLD-fMRI activations' and 'may be an endophenotype reflecting substantial genetic effects'. The through-line is that establishing individual-level reliability was a prerequisite for all of these, which is the paper's framing of its own contribution. [RQ3.1] Social visual attention during naturalistic viewing, resolved into a hierarchy of automatically detected regions: faces, eyes within faces, mouth, hands, non-head body parts, and non-social content, plus two global measures - total on-screen gaze time and the correlation of a participant's moment-by-moment gaze heatmap with a group reference. The heatmap measure is the conceptually distinctive one, since it captures moment-to-moment conformity with what other viewers looked at rather than aggregate time in a region, and it produced the largest group effects (d = 0.820 and 0.692). Its use also generates the paper's most consequential single analysis: constructing a reference heatmap from the autistic group and finding that it correlates at r = 0.966 with the control reference, while autistic individuals nonetheless match it less well than controls do. That result establishes directly that there is no shared autistic pattern of looking - the average autistic viewer looks where the average control viewer looks, and individual autistic viewers depart from that average in individually different directions. [RQ3.2] Single modality by design, and the paper is explicit that this is a limitation of its interpretation rather than a methodological choice to be defended: other measures 'would have revealed higher variability in ASD' is entertained as a live possibility. No fusion is attempted. The paper does perform an internal combination that is informative for the fusion literature elsewhere in this corpus: fingerprinting with all eight gaze features and with a reduced set of four gave nearly identical identification accuracy (32.6% versus 35.4% for the autistic group), because the removed features were highly correlated with the retained ones - non-social, non-head-body and hand gaze with face gaze, and mouth with eyes. That redundancy check, performed and reported rather than assumed, is the discipline missing from studies that report improvements from adding correlated features. [RQ4.1] The modelling is deliberately simple and the choice is argued: a Gaussian naive Bayes classifier on four features, because the study's question is whether diagnostic information exists in the gaze data at all, not how much a flexible model can extract from 153 participants. The complementary unsupervised analysis uses a variational Bayesian Gaussian mixture model, which learns the number of clusters from the data rather than being told it - an important property here, since forcing two clusters would have guaranteed a partition that could be compared against diagnosis, whereas learning the number allows the data to indicate no meaningful split. It returned predominantly two clusters (25 of 33 windows) and was robust to initialisation at 5, 10 or 20 components. Pairing a supervised classifier with an unsupervised clustering that asks the same question from the opposite direction, and finding that both fail to recover diagnosis, is stronger evidence than either alone. [RQ4.2] Eight, then four, interpretable scalar features per participant per epoch - each a percentage of gaze time to an automatically detected region, or a correlation with a reference heatmap. Two representational decisions carry substantial methodological weight. Areas of interest were generated frame by frame by pretrained computer vision models rather than hand-drawn, removing experimenter judgement about what counts as a face or a hand and making the approach applicable to arbitrary naturalistic video; detection rates are reported (96.2% of 61,724 frames containing a person; 94.9% with face parts) and the automatic segmentations were manually verified by watching reconstructed overlay videos. And gaze-time percentages to each region were normalised by the number of frames with successful on-screen gaze rather than by total frames, explicitly so that individual differences in tracking success could not bias the region-specific measures - the direct remedy for the data-quality-as-signal pattern that recurs throughout this corpus, where tracking failure rates differ by group and can masquerade as behaviour. A partial correlation analysis then verified that the reliability findings were not explained by on-screen gaze time alone. [RQ4.3] The most statistically careful reporting in the corpus, and the one that determines the paper's central conclusion. Group differences are reported as Cohen's d with bootstrap confidence intervals from 10,000 resamples rather than as p values alone, with the authors stating they 'preferred Cohen's d to provide a practical estimate for the magnitude of an effect of interest... rather than just reporting the results of statistical tests'. Reliability is reported as Spearman's rho with a bootstrap test of the between-group difference in reliability - testing not whether each group is reliable but whether they differ in reliability, which is the actual hypothesis. Fingerprinting accuracy is tested against a permutation null with 10,000 label shuffles. Most importantly, classification accuracy is compared to an empirically derived chance level of 0.607 rather than to an assumed 0.500 - a distinction that entirely changes the reading of the 0.618 result, since against a nominal 50% baseline it would have appeared as a modest success. FDR correction is applied throughout. And per-participant classification frequencies across 10,000 iterations are reported, revealing that the aggregate accuracy conceals a bimodal structure: 95 participants classified correctly more than 75% of the time and 32 misclassified more than 75% of the time, 22 of those autistic. Reporting who is misclassified, rather than only how often, is what converts a null accuracy into a substantive finding about heterogeneity. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is pursued through study design rather than through model attribution, and is stronger for it. Four analyses jointly characterise what the gaze data contain. The effect-size profile across areas of interest, with bootstrap confidence intervals in both episodes, shows where the group differences lie and that they replicate. The reference-heatmap comparison establishes that the autistic and control group averages are nearly identical (r = 0.966) while individual autistic participants depart from both - which localises the phenomenon at the individual rather than group level. The fingerprinting analysis quantifies how much individually distinctive information the same features carry, and the four-versus-eight-feature comparison shows the information is distributed rather than concentrated. And the per-participant classification and clustering frequencies show which individuals the group-level model can and cannot place. The authors summarise the feature-level picture honestly as 'a rather distributed effect over heatmaps and facial features, with no single feature driving the effect', and note the caveat that their features were intercorrelated and their videos always contained people. The absence of a correlation between any gaze feature and ADOS severity is also reported, and is an important negative: the measures separate groups on average without indexing individual severity. [RQ4.5] The reference standard for this corpus, and the source of its most transferable methodological lesson. The classification procedure holds out a third of each group, samples a 10-minute epoch at random from the combined 43-minute dataset, trains on the remainder and repeats 10,000 times - so the estimate is not a single split and every participant is held out repeatedly. Decisively, the chance level is derived empirically from a null distribution and comes to 0.607 rather than the 0.500 that an imbalanced 48/105 design might naively suggest; the observed 0.618 therefore exceeds chance by about one percentage point at p = 0.039, which the authors correctly describe as 'only slightly greater than would be expected by chance' and as confirming that heterogeneity 'precludes diagnostically robust classification'. Had the same number been compared against 50%, it would have been reported as a 12-point improvement. Beyond classification, the validation apparatus includes: leave-one-participant-out construction of every reference heatmap 'to eliminate bias'; normalisation of area-specific gaze by successful on-screen frames so that tracking quality cannot leak into the behavioural measures; a partial correlation control confirming reliability is not driven by on-screen time; measurement of stimulus familiarity and verification that it affects no result; replication of every analysis across two distinct stimuli and across epoch durations from 10 minutes down to seconds; bootstrap confidence intervals on all effect sizes; permutation testing for fingerprinting; FDR correction throughout; and two independent sites with site membership displayed rather than pooled. The single most important output for this review is the fingerprinting result itself: gaze identifies an individual out of 153 at five to ten times chance from 2 minutes of data. That is a direct measurement of the individual-identity signal that any train/test split failing to separate participants will allow a classifier to exploit, and it explains quantitatively why studies here that split by image, segment, task or augmented copy report accuracies far above what participant-level designs achieve. [RQ5.1] Keywords: eye tracking, autism, heterogeneity, individual differences, videos. Three of five name the study's actual subject - heterogeneity and individual differences - rather than a method or a performance target, which is unique in this corpus and accurately signals a paper whose contribution is conceptual rather than algorithmic. [RQ5.2] Molecular Autism 13:39 (2022), an autism-specific journal with a mechanistic and clinical readership, published open access. Authorship spans Caltech's Division of the Humanities and Social Sciences with computation and neural systems affiliations, the University of Iowa, Indiana University, Tampere University and a joint senior authorship shared between the two site leads. The group's prior work is cited as motivation and critiqued in the process - the paper explicitly identifies the limitation of its own earlier study as the gap it now addresses. Publishing a null classification result in an autism journal, framed as informative rather than as a failed experiment, is itself notable given that the corpus's positive-accuracy studies appear predominantly in engineering venues. [RQ5.3] 2022. The framing is a deliberate inversion of the rest of this literature. Rather than arguing that clinical diagnosis is subjective and that automated classification would be objective, the paper starts from the premise that autism 'has so far defied any simple diagnostic markers or cognitive mechanisms' and asks what property of the data would have to hold for classification to be possible at all. It then names the field's characteristic omission precisely: 'Across ASD eye tracking studies, this is a major unanswered question: what portion of the variance in findings can be assigned to between-individual variability, and what portion can be assigned to within-individual variability?' - and observes that 'individual-level reliability is a prerequisite for successful classification and prediction'. That reframing converts a methodological question into a substantive one and produces a result the accuracy-maximising literature could not have produced: a demonstration that the measurement is reliable, the group difference is real and replicable, and the classifier nonetheless fails, because reliability and classifiability are different properties. The paper's positioning of eye tracking is correspondingly measured - it emphasises the modality's practical advantages, its applicability from infancy to adulthood, its resistance to volitional control and its emerging feasibility on phones and over the internet - while directing those advantages toward subtype discovery, longitudinal monitoring and intervention assessment rather than toward diagnosis.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional classification on a crowdsourced convenience sample: 850 speech clips (425 per class) manually spliced from 77 home smartphone videos of 58 children collected via the Guess What? mobile game between 2018 and 2021 - 20 children with parent-reported autism (19 male, median age 5) and 38 neurotypical children (15 male, 22 female, 1 unspecified, median age 9.5), aged 3-12 overall. Total audio 115.5 minutes. Diagnoses unverified parent report; no cognitive, language or severity measures; dataset not released.
narrative_rows.methods: Parents recorded 90-second charades or quiz gameplay sessions on their own smartphones held against the forehead, then chose whether to share. Child-only speech segments were manually spliced out to exclude parental voices. Three pipelines ran on identical five-fold partitions constrained so that all of a child's clips fell in one fold: a scikit-learn random forest over MFCCs, chroma, RMS energy, spectral centroid, bandwidth and rolloff and zero-crossing rate; an 8,724,594-parameter 9-layer CNN over Librosa mel spectrograms trained 15 epochs with L2 penalty 0.01; and facebook/wav2vec2-base fine-tuned for 264 steps to 95 million parameters. Logistic regression, Gaussian naive Bayes, AdaBoost and a fine-tuned Inception v3 were also tried and underperformed.
narrative_rows.outcomes: CNN 79.3% accuracy (SD 0.013), 80.4% precision, 79.3% recall, 79.0% F1, AUROC 0.822 (SD 0.010). Wav2vec 2.0 76.9% accuracy, 78.2% precision, 74.6% recall, 76.8% F1, AUROC 0.815 (SD 0.077). Random forest 69.7% accuracy, 68.7% precision, 74.4% recall (SD 0.247), 69.4% F1, AUROC 0.740. All three models performed well on fold 2 and poorly on fold 3, which the authors read as evidence that folds are too small. Both deep models produced few false positives while the random forest produced many; false negative rates were similar. No acoustic feature importance or group difference of any kind is reported.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The two groups differ by 4.5 years in median age (5 versus 9.5) and by 56 percentage points in proportion male (95% versus 39%) - the two variables that most determine child vocal acoustics - with no matching, covariate adjustment, age-matched subsample or age-only baseline; the sex imbalance is acknowledged and quantified but the larger age gap is never mentioned after the demographics paragraph. Diagnostic labels are unverified parent report, as the authors concede, and comparison-group status rests on parental assertion with no screening instrument. Metrics are clip-level over 850 correlated clips from 58 children, with no per-child accuracy. The autistic class draws roughly 21 clips per child against 11 for the comparison class. No acoustic conditions are characterised, no splicing reliability check is described, no feature importance or group comparison is reported, and the prosodic rationale motivating the study is not reflected in any feature used. No IRB statement, data or code release.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Two contributions bear on the synthesis. First, this is one of the few studies in the corpus to construct cross-validation folds participant-disjoint and to state the reason in exactly the right terms - 'to prevent models from learning from child-specific recording idiosyncrasies, including environmental background noise and audio quality' - which names both the mechanism that Keles and colleagues quantify through gaze fingerprinting and the concrete forms it takes in audio. That its accuracy lands at 79.3% rather than in the nineties, on genuinely uncontrolled home recordings, is consistent with the pattern across the corpus that correct partitioning and realistic acquisition conditions together produce figures in the seventies to low eighties. Second, it defines one end of the deployment-versus-fidelity axis that this review should draw explicitly: parental smartphones, 90-second sessions, no clinician, no equipment, 115.5 minutes of total audio - against Asgari and colleagues at the other end, using speech already captured during a research-reliable ADOS session, with full clinical characterisation, an IQ-matched confound check, an explicit chance baseline and interpretable pitch and loudness features correlated with independently rated severity. The two studies reach comparable discriminative performance by opposite routes, and the comparison shows what each route costs: the crowdsourced design gains reach and ecological validity while giving up diagnostic verification, demographic matching and any acoustic interpretation whatsoever. The unaddressed 4.5-year age gap is the concrete instance of that cost, and it is the reason this study's 79.3% cannot be read as a diagnostic figure without an age-matched replication.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups from a crowdsourced convenience sample: 20 children with a parent-reported autism diagnosis and 38 neurotypical children, 58 in total, contributing 77 videos over four years from 2018 to 2021. Clip counts were deliberately balanced at 425 per class, which means the 20 autistic children contributed roughly 21 clips each against roughly 11 each for the 38 comparison children - so the autistic class is built from fewer children sampled more densely, and each autistic child exerts about twice the influence on the class representation. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The recruitment mechanism is itself distinctive: families downloaded a mobile game, played it at home, and then chose whether to share the recording, so the sample is self-selected among app users willing to disclose a diagnosis and share video of their child. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'children with autism', 'affected children', 'individuals affected', against 'neurotypical (NT) children'. Person-first throughout, and the use of 'neurotypical' rather than 'typically developing' or 'normal' is the more neurodiversity-aligned choice, though it sits alongside conventional deficit framing of autism as 'delayed linguistic development, social interaction deficits, and behavioral impairments' and speech features described as 'peculiarities' and 'abnormalities'. The paper is unusual in explicitly naming stigma as a design consideration, noting that privacy 'is particularly important for studies involving commonly stigmatized disorders like autism' and motivating on-device inference for parents who 'hesitate to share videos with strangers'. [RQ1.3] Reported, and the reporting reveals the study's central problem. Autistic group: 20 children, 19 male (95%) and 1 female, median age 5 years. Comparison group: 38 children, 15 male (39%), 22 female (58%) and 1 unspecified, median age 9.5 years. Overall age range 3-12. Two large imbalances follow. The 4.5-year median age gap is the more serious and is never mentioned anywhere in the paper - not in the limitations, not in the discussion - despite being the single variable that most determines the acoustics of a child's voice across this range: fundamental frequency falls, formants shift with vocal-tract growth, articulation stabilises, disfluency declines and utterance length increases substantially between 5 and 9.5 years. The sex imbalance is the reverse - 95% versus 39% male - and this one is acknowledged, quantified and benchmarked, with the authors noting that even the naturally skewed 4:1 to 3:1 population ratio would predict only 75-80% male, so their split exceeds expectation, and concluding that the dataset 'may still not be completely representative of real-world conditions'. Combining the two, the autistic group is younger and almost entirely male while the comparison group is older and majority female, so the groups differ systematically on both determinants of child vocal acoustics before diagnosis is considered. No IQ, language level, developmental measure or matching procedure is reported. [RQ1.4] Parent report alone, and the authors state the limitation directly: 'while we require parents to disclose their child's clinical diagnosis by choosing from options not widely known to those who have not received a clinical evaluation, these labels are self-reported and thus unverified'. No standardised instrument, no clinician involvement, no medical record check. The safeguard offered - that the diagnostic labels presented in the app are unfamiliar to families who have not been through an evaluation - is a reasonable heuristic against casual mislabelling but does nothing to establish which diagnosis a child actually received, when, by whom, or against what criteria. The comparison group's neurotypical status likewise rests on parental assertion with no screening instrument. This is the weakest reference standard in the corpus alongside the benchmark-reuse studies, and it is a consequence of the crowdsourcing design rather than an oversight: a fully remote app-based collection cannot verify diagnoses without a separate clinical pathway. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, language, adaptive or severity measure for either group, and no comorbidity or medication information. This matters more than usual for a speech study, since expressive language level directly determines what a child produces in a 90-second game and would be expected to differ between a median-5-year-old autistic group and a median-9.5-year-old comparison group on both developmental and diagnostic grounds. Nothing in the data allows that to be examined, and no exclusion criteria of any kind are described. [RQ2.1] Goal: test whether autism can be detected from self-recorded home speech captured on ordinary smartphones, removing the specialised equipment and centralised recording locations that the authors argue make prior work undeployable. Main findings: a purpose-built 8.7-million-parameter CNN over mel spectrograms reached 79.3% accuracy and 0.822 AUROC; a fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 reached 76.9% and 0.815; a random forest over conventional acoustic features reached 69.7% and 0.740; folds were constructed child-disjoint to block recording-idiosyncrasy leakage; all three models covaried across folds, suggesting the folds are too small; an ImageNet-pretrained Inception v3 underperformed the smaller purpose-built CNN; and the whole result rests on 115.5 minutes of audio from 58 children. [RQ2.2] Participants' own homes, with no researcher present, no controlled acoustics and no equipment standardisation - the design's defining property and its explicit purpose. The authors' argument is twofold and both parts are worth noting. Logistically, prior speech studies used directional microphone arrays or multiple wireless microphones at a hospital, which 'pos[es] significant barriers to the widespread availability of automatic diagnosis tools', reinforced by the observation that 83.86% of American counties have no autism diagnostic resources at all and that the delay from first consultation to diagnosis averages over two years. Behaviourally, the authors argue that 'interacting with unknown adults in foreign environments could be stressful and possibly affect the behavior of children with autism, thus leading to observations that are not generalizable to the real world' - a validity argument for home recording rather than merely a convenience one. The consequence embraced rather than lamented is heterogeneous audio quality, which the paper treats as fidelity to deployment conditions. [RQ2.3] Ninety-second sessions of the Guess What? mobile game, structured as either charades - acting out emotions, characters, sports, chores or objects - or a quiz on colours, shapes, numbers and word spellings. The child follows the gameplay while the parent mediates, holding the smartphone against their own forehead with the front-facing camera on the child. Three properties matter. The interaction partner is the child's own parent rather than a clinician or a stranger, which is what makes the elicited speech naturalistic. The session is extremely short, and the total corpus is only 115.5 minutes across 58 children, which the authors turn into a positive by noting that so little data still yielded workable accuracy. And the task structure is only semi-standardised: families choose between two game types and the resulting speech differs accordingly, so the linguistic and prosodic demands are not equated across children - a source of variation the paper does not examine, and one that could interact with age given that a median-5-year-old and a median-9.5-year-old will engage very differently with a spelling quiz. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, with data accumulated opportunistically over four years from 2018 to 2021 rather than in a defined recruitment window; no follow-up. Parental consent to share each recording is built into the app flow - families view the video after each session and choose whether to send it - which is a stronger form of ongoing consent than a single upfront authorisation, though no IRB approval statement appears in the extracted text. Privacy is treated substantively rather than as boilerplate, with a dedicated Discussion subsection arguing that the models' small size permits on-device inference and privacy-preserving federated learning, motivated explicitly by autism's stigmatisation and by parents who want a diagnostic signal but are unwilling to share video. A senior author declares founding Cognoa, a company developing digital paediatric health solutions. [RQ2.5] Deliberately none beyond what families already own: participants' own smartphones, with no model, microphone or sampling-rate constraint, held against the parent's forehead during play. This is the study's contribution and its cost. The benefit is that the recordings carry the acoustic heterogeneity of real deployment - varying room acoustics, distances, device microphones, background noise - so a model that works here has already survived conditions that laboratory studies control away. The cost is that none of that variation is characterised: no distribution of device types, recording levels, signal-to-noise ratios or sampling rates is reported, so it cannot be determined whether any acoustic property covaries with group. Given that the two groups were recruited through the same app but differ in age and sex, a systematic difference in, say, microphone distance for younger children is plausible and unexamined. Analysis tools are named precisely: Librosa, scikit-learn, Keras with Visualkeras, and the facebook/wav2vec2-base checkpoint. [RQ2.6] Good on modelling, thin on data. Reported: the app, the two game types, the 90-second session length, the recording arrangement, the manual splicing criterion (segments containing no voice but the child's), clip counts by class, the mean of 1.32 videos and 14.7 clips per child, the fold composition table, the child-disjoint fold constraint with its rationale, the complete random forest feature list and all six hyperparameters, the CNN's layer structure, regularisation penalty, epoch count and exact parameter count, the wav2vec checkpoint and fine-tuning step count, the alternative models tried and rejected, and the total 115.5 minutes of audio. Not reported: any acoustic property of the recordings, the group-specific age ranges or means, any splicing reliability check or inter-splicer agreement, clip durations, the criterion for how many clips were taken per child, any data or code release, and random seeds. The manual splicing step is the least reproducible element - it is a human judgement applied to every clip, performed by unspecified people to an unspecified standard, and the authors identify its non-scalability as a limitation without addressing its consistency. [RQ2.7] Three limitations are stated, one of them thoroughly. The sex imbalance is quantified precisely (95% versus 39% male), benchmarked against the expected 4:1 to 3:1 population ratio, and the conclusion drawn that the dataset 'may still not be completely representative of real-world conditions' - among the more careful demographic self-assessments in the corpus. The unverified nature of parent-reported diagnoses is conceded directly. The small dataset and the non-scalability of manual splicing are both raised, with automatic blind source separation named as the necessary but difficult alternative. What is absent is the study's largest problem: the 4.5-year median age gap between groups appears once, in a single sentence of the demographics paragraph, and is never mentioned again - not in the limitations, not in the discussion, not as a caveat on the accuracy figures. No age-matched analysis, age covariate or age-only baseline is attempted. Also unaddressed: that the autistic class is built from 20 children sampled at roughly 21 clips each while the comparison class draws on 38 children at roughly 11 each; that metrics are clip-level rather than child-level despite the folds being child-disjoint; that no acoustic characterisation of any kind is reported; and that the prosodic rationale in the introduction is not reflected in any feature actually used. [RQ2.9] Five directions, with the most substantive being technical. Collect more data across a wider selection of both groups, argued from the observation that 115.5 minutes already sufficed. Replace manual splicing with automatic blind source separation - the authors are realistic about this, calling it 'an exceptionally challenging task' while noting it is 'possibly a necessary hurdle to overcome to develop widely available and consistently effective autism machine learning diagnosis resources', which correctly identifies the bottleneck for any home-recording pipeline where parents and children speak simultaneously. Explore wearable collection through devices such as Google Glass, building on the group's prior work delivering social cues through wearables. Add crowdsourced human annotation of audio features. And combine audio with computer-vision quantification of hand stimming, upper-limb movement and eye contact toward an interpretable multimodal system. Notably absent: any proposal to verify diagnoses, to match on age, or to characterise what acoustically distinguishes the groups. [RQ3.1] Nominally prosody. The introduction rests its case entirely on prosodic abnormality, citing 'echolalia, monotonous intonation, and atypical pitch and linguistic stress patterns' as 'among the most notable signs of autism', and this is the paper's justification for looking at speech at all. What is actually modelled is broader and less specific: the random forest uses a generic speech-recognition feature set - MFCCs, chroma, RMS energy, spectral centroid, bandwidth and rolloff, zero-crossing rate - containing no pitch, intonation contour, stress or rhythm measure whatsoever, while the CNN and wav2vec models learn unconstrained representations from spectrograms and waveforms. The behavioural target is therefore 'whatever in the acoustic signal separates these two groups of children', which given the sample composition includes vocal-tract size, fundamental frequency range and articulatory maturity - all direct functions of the age and sex on which the groups differ. Because no acoustic finding is reported, the paper cannot say whether anything prosodic was involved. The contrast with Asgari and colleagues elsewhere in this corpus is instructive: that study modelled pitch, jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio explicitly, reduced to two interpretable features, and correlated them with independently rated severity. [RQ3.2] Single modality - audio only - with no fusion attempted, though multimodal extension is proposed as future work. The paper does run a genuine three-way representation comparison on identical child-disjoint folds, which is more informative than most single-modality studies here and yields two transferable observations. First, learned representations beat hand-engineered ones by roughly ten points (79.3% and 76.9% against 69.7%), and the gap is largest in AUROC (0.822 and 0.815 against 0.740), suggesting that whatever separates the classes is not well captured by the conventional descriptor set. Second, the two transfer-learning results point in opposite directions and the authors interpret both correctly: an ImageNet-pretrained Inception v3 with 33 million parameters lost to a purpose-built 8.7-million-parameter CNN, attributed to 'the irrelevance of ImageNet features to spectrograms', while a self-supervised audio transformer transferred usefully, justified by prior evidence of wav2vec's utility 'for suprasegmental tasks such as emotion prediction'. Domain-matched pretraining helped; domain-mismatched pretraining hurt, even at four times the parameter count. [RQ4.1] Three families compared on identical folds - an ensemble tree model on hand-engineered features, a convolutional network on spectrograms, and a fine-tuned self-supervised transformer on raw waveforms - which spans the realistic design space for a small audio classification problem. The comparison is conducted honestly: alternatives that lost are named rather than omitted (logistic regression, Gaussian naive Bayes, AdaBoost for the shallow family; Inception v3 for the deep one), and the winning CNN is the smallest deep model tried. Full hyperparameters are given for the random forest and described as 'manually chosen', with no tuning procedure stated - which leaves open whether the shallow model was tuned as carefully as the deep ones and hence whether the ten-point gap partly reflects unequal effort. The fold-to-fold correlation across all three models is the most thoughtful analytic observation in the paper: 'each model appears to perform well on fold 2 while performing relatively poorly on fold 3. This suggests that the data in each fold may be too limited', which correctly attributes the variance to the data partition rather than to model instability. [RQ4.2] Three representations of the same 850 clips. Hand-engineered acoustic descriptors for the random forest; Librosa-generated mel spectrograms treated as images for the CNN; and raw waveforms for wav2vec 2.0. The unit throughout is the clip, not the child, and this is the study's one residual validation gap: the folds are child-disjoint, which correctly prevents a child's clips appearing on both sides, but the metrics are averaged over clips, so the reported figures aggregate 850 correlated observations from 58 people. A child who contributes 21 clips influences the accuracy twenty-one times over, and no per-child prediction or per-child accuracy is reported. Since clip counts differ systematically by group - roughly 21 per autistic child against 11 per comparison child - the clip-level metrics also weight the two classes' children unequally. [RQ4.3] Five metrics per model, each as mean and standard deviation across five folds, plus per-fold and mean ROC curves and confusion matrices for all three - complete and comparative reporting. The standard deviations do real work here and are worth reading closely: the random forest's recall SD is 0.247, larger than the entire performance gap between models, indicating that its per-fold recall swings wildly, while its accuracy SD is only 0.013 - a pattern signalling that it trades sensitivity against specificity differently in each fold. Wav2vec's AUROC SD of 0.077 against the CNN's 0.010 similarly shows the CNN is the more stable model despite the authors' expectation that the 95-million-parameter transformer would be 'more robust'. The confusion matrices add a real finding: both deep models produce few false positives while the random forest produces many, with all three having similar false negative rates. What is missing is any comparison against a trivial baseline - given a 4.5-year median age difference between groups, an age-only classifier is the obvious comparator and would establish how much of the 79.3% is diagnostic at all. [RQ4.4] None. No feature importance, attribution, saliency, spectral analysis or group comparison of any acoustic quantity is reported, and no interpretation is offered of what distinguishes the classes. This is a substantial gap given that the paper's entire motivation is a specific set of prosodic claims - echolalia, monotonous intonation, atypical pitch, irregular stress - none of which is tested, measured or discussed after the introduction. The random forest's feature set would have supported at least a permutation-importance analysis at no cost, and mel spectrograms admit standard saliency methods. The consequence is that the study yields three accuracy figures and no knowledge about autistic children's speech, so it cannot be evaluated for construct validity: there is no way to tell whether the models are keying on prosody, on vocal-tract size, on recording distance, or on utterance length. The authors do gesture at interpretability as a future goal, proposing that combining audio features with computer-vision measures 'could possibly result in interpretable models', which acknowledges the present absence. [RQ4.5] Correct on the dimension that matters most in this corpus and incomplete on a secondary one. The fold constraint is stated explicitly and reasoned exactly right: 'all clips spliced from a given child's video had to be included in the same fold to prevent models from learning from child-specific recording idiosyncrasies, including environmental background noise and audio quality'. That names both the mechanism and its two concrete forms, and it is the discipline missing from Cilia's image-level folds, Simeoli's task-level folds, Liaqat's image-wise splits and Gaspar's augmented copies. Fold composition is tabulated so the balance can be checked, all three models are evaluated on the same folds, and metrics are averaged with standard deviations. Three gaps remain. Metrics are clip-level rather than child-level, so 850 correlated observations from 58 children are treated as the effective sample and no per-child accuracy is available. There is no held-out test set beyond cross-validation, and the random forest's hyperparameters were 'manually chosen' with no procedure described, so some selection optimism is unquantified. And most importantly, no analysis addresses whether the classifier is separating diagnosis or separating age and sex - there is no age-matched subsample, no covariate adjustment, and no age-only or sex-only baseline, despite both variables differing markedly between groups and both directly determining child vocal acoustics. The validation protocol is therefore sound against leakage and silent on confounding. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism, mHealth, machine learning, artificial intelligence, speech, audio, child, digital data, mobile app, diagnosis. The presence of 'mHealth' and 'mobile app' alongside 'diagnosis' locates the work in digital health delivery rather than in speech science, which matches the paper's actual contribution - a deployment architecture rather than an acoustic finding. [RQ5.2] JMIR Pediatrics and Parenting 5(2):e35406 (2022), an open-access digital-health journal for paediatric readers. Authorship spans Stanford's Division of Systems Medicine in Pediatrics, Bioengineering, Computer Science, Biomedical Data Science and Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, with the senior author's group having produced a substantial body of prior work on mobile autism screening, wearable social-cue delivery and crowdsourced annotation - much of it cited here. Funding is extensive, listing four NIH grants, an NSF award and numerous foundations. The senior author declares founding Cognoa, a company developing digital paediatric diagnostics, disclosed appropriately; the same company's FDA-authorised screening product is critiqued by name in the Ko et al. paper elsewhere in this corpus for feeding human ratings rather than raw video into its model - a critique that this study's raw-audio approach implicitly answers. [RQ5.3] 2022. The framing combines the usual epidemiological appeal with two access statistics that are more concrete than the corpus norm: 83.86% of American counties have no autism diagnostic resources at all, and the delay from first consultation to diagnosis averages over two years, pushing typical diagnosis past age four with documented downstream consequences including higher psychotropic medication use, lower IQ and reduced language aptitude. The distinctive positioning, though, is a critique of the immediately preceding speech literature on deployability rather than on accuracy. The authors name two studies achieving comparable or better results - one using 'a specialized biosensor device with 4 directional microphones', another 'multiple wireless microphones, providing high purity recordings at a central recording location (a hospital)' - and argue that such work 'does not accelerate the process of autism detection' precisely because the conditions that produce clean data are the conditions that prevent scaling. They then add a validity argument alongside the logistical one: recording in unfamiliar settings with unfamiliar adults may itself alter the behaviour being measured. That pairing - that laboratory control buys signal quality at the cost of both reach and ecological validity - is the sharpest statement of the deployment-versus-fidelity tradeoff in this review, and it is the axis along which this study should be compared with Asgari and colleagues, who took the opposite position and gained interpretability, clinical characterisation and confound control in exchange for requiring a clinical ADOS session.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional classification at Oregon Health & Science University: 158 children aged 7-17 from 289 screened - 88 autistic (83.0% male, 11.4 +/- 2.1 years, IQ 99.5 +/- 19.9, ADOS SA 9.31, RRB 3.48) and 70 non-autistic (57.1% male, 11.5 +/- 1.7 years, IQ 112.1 +/- 12.9) formed by deliberately merging children with ADHD and typically developing children to test specificity. Diagnosis by DSM-IV-TR from experienced child psychiatrists and clinical psychologists with best-estimate confirmation from a research diagnostic team reviewing videos and scored protocols; autism actively ruled out in both comparison subgroups. Extensive medical, psychiatric and medication exclusions plus IQ below 70. Data are transcripts and audio from one ADOS-2 Module 3 conversational task; de-identified data available on request and analysis code released.
narrative_rows.methods: Seven automated language measures (mean length of utterance in morphemes, number of distinct word roots, um proportion, content maze proportion, unintelligible proportion, c-units per minute, repetition proportion) were computed from modified-SALT transcripts produced by research assistants blind to diagnosis and IQ, with consensus resolution and biannual consistency checks. Ten automated voice measures (cepstrum with first and second derivatives, log spectral entropy, F0, jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio, H1H2, RMS) were computed from child-only frames after DNN denoising and averaged per participant. Three linear-kernel SVMs - voice, language and combined - were evaluated by leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, justified by citation to Saeb et al. on subject-wise validation and cross-checked against 10-fold. Model comparisons used DeLong's test for correlated ROC curves; mSVM-RFE ranked features; sex-stratified models tested the sex imbalance.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Voice-only AUC 0.7800 (95% CI 0.7076-0.8525), accuracy 0.7215, sensitivity 0.7500, specificity 0.6857. Language-only AUC 0.8748 (0.8199-0.9297), accuracy 0.7975, sensitivity 0.7727, specificity 0.8286 - significantly better than voice (p = 0.036), the advantage entirely in specificity. Combined AUC 0.9205 (0.8768-0.9641), accuracy 0.8671, sensitivity 0.8977, specificity 0.8286 - significantly better than voice (p < 0.001) and language (p = 0.033), with the gain entirely in sensitivity. Ten-fold cross-validation gave 0.9235 (p = 0.9219 versus leave-one-out). Sex-stratified AUCs were 0.8901 (boys) and 0.8067 (girls), neither differing from the full sample. Feature selection to eight features gave 0.9344, not significantly better. The language model detected participants with significantly poorer CCC-2 structural and pragmatic scores, less language output and one year younger; the voice model showed no such association. Nine autistic participants (10.2%) were missed by the combined model, and these had the highest IQ and most language output of any subgroup. Neither ADOS severity nor IQ predicted misclassification in any model.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Restricted to fluent English speakers aged 7-17 with IQ at or above 70 assessable with ADOS-2 Module 3, so the measures cannot currently speak to minimally verbal children or those with intellectual disability. Groups were not tightly matched, differing significantly on sex and IQ, though both were tested for effect. Fourteen of seventeen analysis exclusions fell on the autistic group, including six who produced neither um nor uh. The voice result is conditional on a pretrained black-box denoiser whose full impact the authors state is unknown, and without which 'the acoustic features mainly represent the noise instead of participants'. Samples come from ADOS administrations, which the authors note focus on eliciting autistic features so that 'it is possible that our results are overestimated compared to what would be obtained with more naturalistic conversational samples'. Test-retest reliability - a prerequisite for the intended outcome-measure application - is not yet established. Transcription reliability statistics were not computed. Single site, no independent replication cohort, and no chance or demographic-only baseline.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The corpus's benchmark for multimodal fusion and, alongside Keles and Kojovic, for validation practice generally. Three contributions carry into the synthesis. Its fusion claim is the only one here supported by DeLong tests on correlated ROC curves with confidence intervals rather than by comparing raw accuracies, and the improvement's structure is diagnosed rather than asserted: specificity is unchanged at 0.8286 while sensitivity rises from 0.7727 to 0.8977, which is the signature of complementary rather than redundant channels. Its mechanism for that complementarity is established at participant level and is a clinical finding in its own right - language measures detect autistic children with poorer language and less output, voice measures detect those with better language profiles, and no language measure predicts which children the voice model catches, so acoustic measures index something genuinely orthogonal to language level. That result directly supports the claim, echoed in the companion Asgari paper, that prosodic measurement is most needed precisely for the individuals conventional language assessment misses. And it is one of only two studies in the corpus to build the specificity test into its design by including a non-autistic clinical comparison group, addressing the concern that Simeoli and others identify as future work. Two further practices should be named in the synthesis as transferable: leave-one-subject-out cross-validation adopted with explicit citation to the subject-wise validation literature, which is the direct methodological answer to the leakage found in Cilia, Simeoli, Liaqat and Gaspar; and the misclassification profiling that asks not how accurate a model is but which patients it sees, which converts a performance number into information a clinician could act on. Its scope discipline - stating plainly that the work is not intended for diagnosis and that diagnosis serves only as an external criterion for validating outcome measures - is the framing most other high-performing studies in this review should have adopted.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two analytic groups from three clinical ones: 88 autistic participants and 70 non-autistic participants, the latter formed by merging children with ADHD and typically developing children. The merge is justified on two stated grounds and both are substantive - preliminary analyses showed no significant difference between the ADHD and typically developing subgroups on any automated language measure, and 'including a non-autistic clinical group alongside TD participants provided an opportunity to more adequately test for the specificity of the results with respect to the presence or absence of autism'. This is the corpus's clearest instance of a study building the specificity test into its comparison group rather than naming it as future work. Flow accounting is complete: 289 screened, 104 excluded for not meeting strict diagnostic criteria, 10 for failing to complete initial assessment, leaving 175 in the parent neuroimaging study (102 ASD, 45 ADHD, 28 TD); 6 autistic participants excluded for untranscribable ADOS sessions due to poor sound quality or non-compliance; and 11 more excluded for analysis - 6 with undefined um proportion because neither um nor uh occurred in the task, 4 without IQ results, and 1 with an acoustically corrupted file. Note that the exclusions fall disproportionately on the autistic group (14 of 17), and that the 6 excluded for producing no filled pauses at all are plausibly among the least verbally fluent. [RQ1.2] 'autistic people', 'autistic children', 'autistic individuals', 'people with and without autism', 'children with ASD', 'individuals with autism' - identity-first and person-first used interchangeably and comfortably, with identity-first predominating in general statements about the population. 'Patients' never appears. The framing is explicitly respectful and says so: 'this growing detection and awareness of autism requires thoughtful and respectful research to help facilitate communication between people with and without autism' - which frames the goal as bidirectional communication rather than as remediating a deficit. Communication is described as involving 'differences' and 'variability' at least as often as 'difficulties', and the lay summary opens with 'People with autism often struggle with communication differences which traditional clinical measures and language tests cannot fully capture' - locating the inadequacy in the measures rather than in the people. This is among the most careful terminology in the corpus. [RQ1.3] Fully reported with formal testing on every variable. Autistic group: 88 participants, 73 male (83.0%), 11.4 +/- 2.1 years, IQ 99.5 +/- 19.9. Non-autistic group: 70 participants, 40 male (57.1%), 11.5 +/- 1.7 years, IQ 112.1 +/- 12.9. Race and ethnicity are tabulated for both groups (predominantly white, 13 and 8 Hispanic). Age matches (Mann-Whitney p = 0.6044); sex does not (Fisher's exact p = 0.00065); IQ does not (p < 0.001). What distinguishes this study is that both mismatches are tested rather than merely conceded. For sex, the combined model was refitted separately in boys (n = 113, AUC 0.8901, 95% CI 0.8261-0.9541) and girls (n = 45, AUC 0.8067, 95% CI 0.6493-0.9640), neither differing significantly from the full-sample AUC (p = 0.4428 and p = 0.178). For IQ, the misclassification analysis found that IQ was never significantly associated with correct or incorrect classification in any of the three models. The authors nonetheless list loose matching among their limitations - 'Participants were not tightly matched between groups which could result in reduced fit for analysis' - rather than treating the confound tests as closing the question. [RQ1.4] Among the strongest ascertainments in the corpus and comparable to its companion paper. Diagnosis was confirmed by experienced child psychiatrists and clinical psychologists who directly assessed every participant in the autistic and ADHD groups under DSM-IV-TR criteria, followed by a research diagnostic team reviewing 'results of the standardized diagnostic assessments (both videos and scored protocols)' and applying best-estimate procedures. ADOS-2 Module 3 was administered to all participants by research assistants or a senior clinical psychologist trained to research reliability level. Autism was actively ruled out in both comparison subgroups using the ADOS, clinical interview and parent-completed autism questionnaires - so negative cases are excluded on three independent sources rather than assumed. The screening list is extensive and clinically targeted, excluding seizure disorder, cerebral palsy, paediatric stroke, chemotherapy history, sensorimotor handicaps, closed head injury, thyroid disorder, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, current major depressive episode, fetal alcohol syndrome, Tourette's disorder, severe vision impairment, Rett syndrome, current psychoactive medication, non-English speakers and IQ below 70. That 104 of 289 screened participants were excluded 'for not meeting strict diagnostic criteria' indicates the criteria were applied stringently rather than nominally. [RQ1.5] Complete and used analytically throughout. IQ was estimated from a three-subtest WISC-IV short form (Information, Block Design, Vocabulary) with the Sattler and Dumont formula, and the authors note honestly that separate verbal and non-verbal estimates cannot be derived from this short form. The Children's Communication Checklist-2 was completed by parents, with its structure described in detail - ten subscales, the first four averaged into a Structural Language scale and four more into a Pragmatic scale, with the last two measuring behaviours characteristic of autism. ADOS-2 Social Affect and Restricted and Repetitive Behavior scores were computed under the Gotham et al. algorithm. Three objective language-output indices were additionally computed from the task itself: total c-units, total words and activity time. All of these then serve as predictors in the misclassification analysis, which is the paper's most original contribution - they are not merely descriptive but are the variables through which the complementarity of the two modalities is established. [RQ2.1] Three explicit aims, each addressed. First, replicate the voice model of Asgari et al. (2021) and the language model of Salem et al. (2021) and compare their discriminant validity using the same methodology in the same sample - achieved, with language (AUC 0.8748) significantly better than voice (0.7800, DeLong p = 0.036), the difference lying in specificity (0.83 versus 0.69). Second, quantify the gain from combining them - the combined model reached AUC 0.9205, significantly better than voice (p < 0.001) and language (p = 0.033), with accuracy 0.8671, sensitivity 0.8977 and specificity 0.8286; the entire gain is in sensitivity while specificity is unchanged. Third, characterise which participants each model detects - the language model caught children with poorer structural and pragmatic language, less output and one year younger; the voice model caught children with better language profiles and showed no association between language measures and classification success; only nine autistic participants (10.2%) escaped the combined model, and these had the highest IQ and most language output of any subgroup. [RQ2.2] Oregon Health & Science University, with participants recruited through community outreach and referral from OHSU specialty clinics into an fMRI study - so the sample is a research cohort rather than a consecutive clinical series. Recording arrangements are described precisely and with their rationale: 'The microphone was suspended in a cage and placed on a table approximately 3 feet from where the child sat.
