A discrepancy sits unreconciled between the 37 + 41 = 78 preschoolers reported in the results and the 'N = 74 for preschool' stated in the leave-one-out description, and exclusion counts from the two quality-control steps - calibration failure and off-screen fixation - are not reported for either cohort. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'ASD children' and 'toddler ASD' used interchangeably, against 'TD children' and 'typically developing individuals'. The acronym is frequently used adjectivally and occasionally as a bare group label ('toddler ASD, and TD is similar'). The framing is conventional and deficit-oriented - autism 'involves deficits in face processing', gaze is 'aberrant', and the literature on 'gaze abnormalities' is reviewed at length - but the paper is careful about the state of the evidence in a way that softens this: it notes that 'the precise nature of these deficits and the relationships between anomalous face processing and atypical socio-emotional function in ASD remain unclear', and cites a review finding that 'the excessive mouth and diminished eye gaze hypothesis of ASD is not generally supported'. That willingness to report that a widely repeated claim lacks support is uncommon in this corpus. [RQ1.3] Reported per cohort with tests, and both cohorts are matched on both variables. Toddlers: autistic 2.4 +/- 0.5 years and 50 boys to 5 girls, comparison 2.2 +/- 0.6 years and 33 boys to 7 girls, with p = 0.27 for age and p = 0.22 for gender. Preschoolers: autistic 4.6 +/- 0.5 years and 33 boys to 4 girls, comparison 4.8 +/- 0.3 years and 33 boys to 8 girls, with p = 0.11 and p = 0.29. Age and gender were then additionally entered as covariates in every ANCOVA despite already being matched, which is belt-and-braces and appropriate. What is absent is any measure of developmental or cognitive level in either group - no Mullen, Bayley, Griffiths or equivalent - and the authors address this directly rather than omitting it, arguing that 'predominant ASD studies used chronological age instead of developmental age' and that 'in practice, a child transition from Toddler to preschooler is typically based on the chronological age without developmental testing', while conceding that 'future studies may also need to consider adding a developmental test'. The argument is reasonable for defining the cohorts but does not address the confound: two groups matched on chronological age but differing in developmental level would differ in where they look for reasons unrelated to diagnosis, and nothing in the data can separate these. [RQ1.4] DSM-5 diagnosis by experienced physicians with a CARS score above 30 required for children aged 2 and over, described as 'in line with the ADOS standard'. The absence of an observational instrument is stated as the study's first limitation together with its cause - limited access to ADOS and ADI-R in China - which is a candid acknowledgement of a resource constraint rather than a methodological choice. The comparison group is screened more thoroughly than in most studies here: three instruments (the Ages and Stages Questionnaires Chinese Version, the Chinese children warning signs checklist, and the Developmental Screening Parent Questionnaire for Children Aged 0-6) covering communication and language, physical ability, social skills, problem solving and intelligence, administered by a study physician through onsite assessment and parent interview, with exclusion of any psychiatric or neurological history. The authors nonetheless flag the asymmetry: 'we did not assess the CARS in TD Children', so comparison participants were screened on general development but never on autism-specific symptomatology with the same instrument used to establish the cases. [RQ1.5] CARS scores were obtained for the autistic groups only and only for children aged 2 and over, at 32.3 +/- 1.5 in toddlers and 33.0 +/- 2.1 in preschoolers - both close to the cut-off of 30, so the samples sit at the milder end of the CARS range with narrow standard deviations, which limits the severity gradient available for correlation. The severity data are nonetheless used analytically, in a multiple regression of fixation time percentage on CARS with age and gender as covariates across all autistic children, returning no significant association on any area of interest (p values from 0.13 to 0.99). That null is reported without qualification and is important: it means the gaze measures separate the groups on average without tracking how autistic an individual child is, which converges with the same finding in the Keles adult study and bears on whether such measures could serve as severity or outcome measures rather than only as classifiers. No cognitive, language or adaptive measure was collected for either group, and no comorbidity or medication information. [RQ2.1] Goal: determine whether eye-tracking differences between autistic and typically developing children are the same in toddlers and preschoolers, and identify which paradigms discriminate at which age. Main findings: reduced fixation time percentage in nine of ten areas of interest with a main effect of diagnosis, but a main effect of age group on only one area; significant diagnosis-by-age interaction on the eye area, where toddlers did not differ (p = 0.93) but preschoolers did (p = 0.006); single-area classification rankings that largely invert between cohorts, with mouth, upright walking, moving dot and baby face discriminating toddlers and eyes, duck, infant face and fan discriminating preschoolers; full-model accuracy of 80% in toddlers and 71% in preschoolers; only preschool comparison children showing the expected preference for upright biological motion; and no association between any fixation measure and CARS severity. [RQ2.2] A hospital-based child mental health and rehabilitation centre in Shenzhen, with testing conducted in 'a dark and soundproof room' at a fixed 65 cm viewing distance with the child's centre of vision aligned to the monitor centre. This is a tightly controlled laboratory environment rather than a point-of-care setting, which suits the measurement but limits the deployment claim - a dark soundproof room with a calibrated remote tracker is not a paediatric waiting area. The recruitment asymmetry is present but mitigated: autistic children came from the hospital's rehabilitation centre while comparison children came either from a local kindergarten or from routine check-ups at the same hospital's outpatient ward, so a proportion of the comparison group was recruited within the same institution. [RQ2.3] Five short paradigms totalling roughly 40 seconds, each pairing a social element against a non-social competitor within a single display, and each with a stated theoretical rationale drawn from a specific prior literature. The design's strongest feature is its use of position-switched replicates: both the biological motion and the face-versus-dot paradigms were presented twice with left and right positions swapped and the fixation percentages averaged, which controls for any lateral gaze bias - a source of artefact that most paired-display studies in this corpus do not address. The paradigms also span a graded range of social content, from a full face with moving mouth, through point-light biological motion, to a still infant face, against competitors ranging from an abstract moving dot to an electric fan to clipart animals - which is what makes the age-specific ranking analysis informative, since it identifies which level of social content carries signal at which age. The brevity is a practical virtue for 18-month-olds and a limitation for reliability: a 5-second still-image trial yields one fixation percentage per child with no within-child replication from which stability could be estimated. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional with two age cohorts sampled independently rather than followed longitudinally - so the developmental claim rests on a cross-sectional age contrast, which the design cannot distinguish from cohort effects, though this is a standard and reasonable compromise. Ethics reporting is complete: approval by the Ethics Committee of Shenzhen Maternity and Child Healthcare Hospital, written informed consent from legal guardians, and separate written consent obtained specifically for publication of potentially identifiable images or data. Partial overlap with a prior publication by the same group is disclosed rather than concealed: 'A portion of preschool data using paradigm (video clip) data had been used in a previous study... However, this study used more comprehensive paradigms and the findings presented in this study have never been published before.' Raw data are offered on request. [RQ2.5] An SMI RED250 remote tracker at 250 Hz with 0.03 degree spatial resolution, viewing a 22-inch LCD at 1024x768 from 65 cm in a dark, soundproof room, with the child's centre of vision aligned to the screen centre. Calibration used five points with a dynamic pink rabbit as the target, and - importantly - 'those who failed to follow the dynamic pink rabbit fixation did not continue in the experiment', so calibration failure was an exclusion rather than a tolerated source of noise. A second quality step used Gaze Replay path playback before analysis 'to exclude the subjects whose fixation point deviates from the screen to reduce systematic errors'. Both steps are good practice for a toddler paradigm and both are likely to remove children differentially by group, since compliance with a calibration target and sustained on-screen looking are themselves plausibly reduced in autism - yet no exclusion counts are given for either step in either group, which is the most consequential reporting omission in the paper. Fixation detection thresholds are stated (duration above 100 ms, displacement below one degree) and analysis used BeGaze and R-studio 3.5.2. [RQ2.6] Strong on statistics and stimuli, weak on flow and on the classifier. Fully reported: recruitment sources and screening instruments for both groups; the diagnostic basis with its acknowledged limitation; demographics per cohort with tests; every paradigm with duration, content, area-of-interest definition and rationale; the position-switching and averaging procedure; tracker model, sampling rate, spatial resolution, monitor, resolution, viewing distance, room conditions and calibration procedure with its exclusion rule; fixation detection thresholds; the complete statistical model including covariates, variance assumption testing, the weighted least squares substitution, post-hoc correction method and the multivariate-t adjustment for interaction contrasts; means and standard deviations for all ten areas in all four groups; F statistics and p values for all three ANCOVA effects on all ten areas; Cohen's d for every contrast; and the leave-one-out procedure. Not reported: exclusion counts at either quality-control step; the SVM kernel, hyperparameters or implementation; the reconciliation between 78 and 74 preschoolers; and any code. Raw data are offered on request. [RQ2.7] Five limitations are stated and each is substantive, but two passages go considerably beyond the corpus norm. The prevalence discussion is the most valuable: rather than reporting predictive values, the authors explain why they will not, and then calculate the answer - 'using the above toddler values of 80% sensitivity and 82% specificity, and assuming 1% prevalence in the population, the PPV is approximately 4.2%. On the other hand, using these same values, NPV is greater than 99%.' They note that readers can perform the calculation themselves and that omitting predictive values 'is consistent with previous ASD studies on this topic', citing three. The spectrum bias passage is equally direct, naming the phenomenon, identifying its cause in the exclusion of psychiatric and neurological histories from the comparison group, and stating its direction: discriminative ability 'may be overestimated in medical practice'. The other three limitations are the absence of ADOS/ADI-R confirmation with its stated cause, the absence of CARS in comparison children, the small sample without independent validation, and the absence of developmental assessment with a reasoned defence of using chronological age. What is not addressed: that fixation reduction appears across non-social as well as social areas and may therefore index general attention rather than social attention; that the off-area residual is never reported by group; that the two quality-control exclusions may operate differentially by group and their counts are unreported; and the 78-versus-74 discrepancy. [RQ2.9] Five directions, tightly tied to the stated limitations. Validate on independent datasets. Recruit 'a broad spectrum of the ASD and non-ASD participants' to address spectrum bias - the direct remedy for the acknowledged overestimation. Add developmental assessment alongside chronological age. Resolve the biological motion inconsistency, where their toddler comparison group failed to show a preference that prior work reports, with the authors noting that 'the age range for our study is between 1.5 and 3, while the previous study focused only on 2-year-olds, so we cannot exclude the possibility that the discrepancy is due to age range difference'. And exploit the age-specific paradigm rankings: 'elucidating the role of different paradigms in ASD classification across different stages may shed light on developing paradigms for earlier ASD detection, particularly for toddlers between 1.5 and 3 years old or even younger' - which is the concrete translational implication of the study's central finding. [RQ3.1] Visual attention allocation, operationalised as the proportion of stimulus time spent fixating each of ten predefined regions. The construct is deliberately layered across paradigms, moving from face parts (eyes versus mouth), through configural biological motion (upright versus inverted point-light figures), to social-versus-geometric competition (mouthing face versus moving dot), to non-social object tracking (duck, helicopter), to static social-versus-object preference (infant face versus fan). That gradation is what makes the age-comparison informative, since it can localise which level of social content is discriminative at which age. The finding that reduction appears at nearly every level, including for an abstract moving dot and an electric fan, is the study's most consequential result for construct validity and is left uninterpreted: a child who fixates less on the fan as well as less on the baby face is not showing selective social disinterest, and the measure may be indexing how much of the stimulus period was spent fixating anything at all. [RQ3.2] Single modality with no cross-modal fusion, but two forms of within-modality combination are examined and both are informative. The first is combining the ten areas into a single classifier versus using each alone: the full ten-area model reached 80% and 71% while individual areas ranged from significant to indistinguishable from chance under permutation testing, and critically the set of areas exceeding chance differs between cohorts. The second is the within-paradigm pairing, where each social area sits opposite a size-matched non-social competitor in the same display, so the design supports comparing relative preference rather than absolute looking. The biological motion paradigm is analysed this way explicitly, with paired t-tests comparing upright against inverted within each of the four groups - and the result is a clean negative for three of them, with only preschool comparison children showing the expected preference. That the paper runs and reports this within-subject preference analysis, rather than only the between-group percentage comparison, is what allows it to engage substantively with the prior biological motion literature and to identify where it does not replicate. [RQ4.1] A support vector machine on ten interpretable percentages, fitted separately for each age cohort. Modelling is subordinate to the statistical analysis throughout: the paper's primary evidence is a set of ANCOVAs with covariates, variance-assumption testing, post-hoc correction and effect sizes, and classification is used to answer the supplementary question of whether the measures combine usefully and which paradigms contribute at which age. That ordering suits a study whose contribution is a developmental finding rather than a screening product. Fitting the cohorts separately rather than pooling with an age covariate is the decision that makes the age-specific feature rankings possible and is the right one given that the entire hypothesis concerns differential patterns. The classifier itself is under-specified - no kernel, no hyperparameters, no implementation named - which matters less here than it would in a study whose headline was the accuracy, but which prevents replication of the classification component. [RQ4.2] Ten scalar percentages per child, so the unit is unambiguously the participant and leave-one-out cross-validation is genuinely participant-level. Two representational choices deserve note. Averaging the position-switched replicates before analysis removes lateral bias but also discards the only within-child replication in the design, so no reliability estimate is available. And normalising by stimulus duration rather than by on-screen looking time is the choice that produces the study's interpretive ambiguity: because the denominator is total presentation time rather than valid tracked time, a child who looks away, blinks, or loses tracking accrues a lower percentage on every area simultaneously. That is consistent with the observed pattern of reduction across nine of ten areas including non-social ones, and it is precisely the normalisation that Keles and colleagues explicitly avoid by dividing by frames with successful on-screen gaze specifically 'to control for possible individual differences between participants in their total on-screen gaze time'. The contrast between the two studies on this single methodological point is instructive. [RQ4.3] Comprehensive and appropriately chosen. Means and standard deviations for all ten areas across all four groups; F statistics with degrees of freedom and p values for diagnosis, age group and interaction effects on every area; Cohen's d for every group contrast within each cohort; accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for the full model in each cohort; and per-area classification performance plotted against permutation-derived 95% confidence intervals so that non-significant areas are visually identifiable. Reporting effect sizes alongside p values is what makes the developmental comparison legible - the mouth separates toddlers at d = 0.81 and preschoolers at d = 0.44, the eyes separate preschoolers at d = 0.74 and toddlers at d = 0.12 - and these are more informative than the significance pattern alone. Reporting sensitivity and specificity separately exposes the preschool model's weakness, where 81% sensitivity comes with 61% specificity, meaning nearly two in five typically developing preschoolers would be flagged. The deliberate omission of predictive values, with the reasoning and the calculated 4.2% PPV given in the limitations, is a more useful treatment than reporting them uncritically would have been. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is inherent in the design rather than added afterwards, since each feature is a named percentage on a named region and every group difference is reported with its direction and effect size. The per-area classification analysis then functions as a formal importance ranking, tested against permutation rather than asserted, and the finding that the rankings differ substantially between cohorts is the study's central claim. The eye-area result is the clearest example and is properly interpreted: comparison children's eye-looking rises from 17.6% at toddler age to 29.2% at preschool age while autistic children's stays flat at 15.4% and 15.1%, so the group difference emerges developmentally rather than being present from the outset. The authors offer a mechanistic account - that toddlers with typical development use visual mouth information for language acquisition, reducing eye attention, and that as language becomes more auditorily meaningful preschool attention shifts to the eyes - which is testable and which explains both the mouth and eye interactions coherently. Against this, the paper offers no interpretation at all of the finding that fixation is reduced on non-social areas, which is the observation most in tension with the social-attention framing it works within. [RQ4.5] Participant-level leave-one-out cross-validation, described in enough detail to confirm that each held-out child's classifier was 'determined using only the data from the other subjects, omitting the one predicted'. Cohorts were modelled separately, so no information crosses between them. Single-area classifications were tested against non-parametric permutation, which is what establishes that several areas do not exceed chance rather than leaving weak accuracies to be read as weak positives. The statistical analyses are protected by covariate adjustment, variance-assumption testing with an appropriate substitution, Tukey correction and multivariate-t adjustment for the interaction contrasts. Three gaps remain. There is no independent validation cohort, acknowledged. The two quality-control exclusions - calibration failure and off-screen fixation - are described but their counts are not reported, and both plausibly operate differentially by group, so the analysed sample is a compliant subset of unknown size and composition. And the reference standard is DSM-5 plus CARS without observational confirmation, which bounds what any validation can establish. The most valuable validation-adjacent contribution, though, is not internal: by calculating that 80% sensitivity and 82% specificity yields a 4.2% positive predictive value at 1% prevalence, the paper supplies the translation step that converts a cross-validated accuracy into a statement about deployment, and it is the only study in the corpus to do so numerically. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism, eye tracking, percentage of fixation time, machine learning, toddler, preschool, support vector machine. Two of the seven name age bands, which accurately signals that the developmental comparison rather than the classification is the paper's subject. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Psychiatry 13:899521 (2022), in the Child and Adolescent Psychiatry section - a clinical psychiatry venue. Authorship spans the Athinoula A. Martinos Center for Biomedical Imaging and the Departments of Psychiatry and Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School with the Department of Child Psychiatry and Rehabilitation at Shenzhen Maternity and Child Healthcare Hospital, with two co-first authors and two corresponding authors spanning the two sites. The inclusion of a biostatistician from MGH's Department of Medicine is visible in the analysis, which is more statistically careful than any comparable study in the corpus. Funded by Chinese national and provincial sources. The international collaboration also explains the diagnostic constraint being stated so directly: a US-based team publishing on a Chinese cohort has every reason to flag the absence of ADOS and to name its cause. [RQ5.3] 2022. The framing is the standard early-detection argument, but the paper's positioning is developmental rather than translational. Its motivating observation is that 'few studies have investigated the eye tracking differences across different chronological age groups' despite evidence that brain alterations in autism differ across ages, and its specific clinical rationale for the 3-year boundary is that 'a proportion of the children identified with possible autism before age 3 do not meet criteria for autism at later follow-up' while 'many children are not diagnosed with ASD until age 3 or older despite displaying symptoms much earlier'. The literature review is unusually careful about what is and is not established, reporting Frazier's meta-analysis of 122 studies as finding a reliable pattern of gaze abnormality that 'persists across ages and worsens during perception of human interactions' while also noting that 'adding perceptual complexity to stimuli or increasing cognitive load during attention-heavy tasks does not increase gaze abnormalities in autism', and citing a review concluding that 'the excessive mouth and diminished eye gaze hypothesis of ASD is not generally supported'. The comparative claims are likewise measured: rather than asserting superiority, the authors situate their 80% and 71% against a meta-analysis of MRI-based classification reporting sensitivity 0.83 and specificity 0.84 for structural and 0.69 and 0.66 for functional imaging, concluding only that 'our findings based on the eye tracking are comparable with results obtained from sophisticated brain imaging tools' - a comparison whose point is cost and accessibility rather than accuracy.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Double-blinded, multi-site, prospective, active comparator pivotal trial conducted to support FDA market authorisation, registered as NCT04151290 before initiation. Fourteen sites across six US states enrolled 711 children aged 18-72 months with caregiver- or clinician-identified developmental delay concerns between August 2019 and June 2020; 425 completed both Device inputs and specialist evaluation, with COVID-19 accounting for an estimated 100 lost specialist visits and closure of 9 of 14 sites. Completers were 36.2% female, demographically diverse, and clinically representative: specialists diagnosed 122 (28.7%) with autism, 263 (61.9%) with at least one non-autism developmental or behavioural condition, and only 40 (9.4%) as neurotypical. No IQ testing. Code proprietary; de-identified data available on request.
narrative_rows.methods: A gradient boosted decision tree, locked before the trial with abstention thresholds tuned on prior data to hold PPV above 65% and NPV above 85% per FDA agreement, combined three mutually blinded inputs: an 18- or 21-item caregiver questionnaire on a smartphone (median 4:56); two caregiver-recorded home videos of 1.5-5 minutes scored on 28-33 items by analysts holding a master's degree and five years of autism experience, standardised-trained and certified against performance guarantees (median 10:54); and a 13- or 15-item questionnaire completed by a general pediatrics or family medicine physician after a 30-minute in-person or telemedicine visit (~10 min). Output was autism-positive, autism-negative or indeterminate. The reference standard was DSM-5 diagnosis by a specialist with over five years of experience using structured observation, interview, medical review and standardised instruments, independently confirmed by a blinded reviewing specialist with a third adjudicating disagreements by majority.
narrative_rows.outcomes: The Device returned a determinate output for 31.8% (135/425). Within that subset: PPV 80.8% (95% CI 70.3-88.8), NPV 98.3% (90.6-100), sensitivity 98.4% (91.6-100), specificity 78.9% (67.6-87.7), with 63 true positives, 15 false positives, 1 false negative and 56 true negatives. Without the abstention mechanism, sensitivity across all completers would fall to 51.6% (63/122) and specificity to 18.5% (56/303). Of 290 indeterminate cases, 91.0% had at least one neurodevelopmental disorder. All 15 false positives had a non-autism developmental-behavioural condition and none were neurotypical, with one specialist judging a third of them autistic. Severity tracked output: 44 of 65 DSM-5 Level 3 children were classified positive against 1 of 5 Level 1 children. Determinate rate was higher under age 3 (39% versus 26%, p = 0.006), specificity higher at 3 and over (88% versus 67%, p = 0.03). PPV was 60% (12/20) for girls against 88% (51/58) for boys. Mean age at autism-positive output was 2.81 years. The first blinded reviewer agreed with the diagnosing specialist 79% of the time.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Performance applies only to the 31.8% of children the Device classifies; two in three still require specialist evaluation, and without abstention sensitivity and specificity would be 51.6% and 18.5%. The video input is scored by human analysts with a master's degree and five years of autism experience, so the system is a fusion layer over expert judgement rather than automated behaviour analysis, and the authors identify reducing this dependence as a scalability priority. The study was not powered for covariate inference, and the 28-point PPV gap between girls (60%, 12/20) and boys (88%, 51/58) is dismissed on interval overlap. No IQ testing. English only, with non-English families excluded. Higher parental education and lower income than the general population. Smartphone access required. Cost and reimbursement data absent. The reference standard is itself uncertain, with 21% first-reviewer disagreement and diagnosing specialists 'completely certain' only 67% of the time when diagnosing autism. Longitudinal stability of negative and indeterminate outputs is untested. Algorithm and code are proprietary.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This is the study against which the rest of the corpus should be read, and it differs from every other charted paper in kind rather than degree. It is the only one prospectively registered before initiation, the only one to lock its model before evaluation and thereby report an external rather than internal validation, the only one with a blinded multi-specialist consensus reference standard whose own reliability it quantifies, and the only one recruiting consecutively from the population the tool is intended for - so its predictive values are directly deployable rather than requiring the prevalence correction that Kong and colleagues perform hypothetically. Its comparison group is the one nearly every other study here names as necessary future work and does not build: 61.9% of participants had a non-autism developmental condition and only 9.4% were neurotypical, so the tested discrimination is autism versus other developmental concern. Three findings should anchor the synthesis. First, the counterfactual disclosure - sensitivity 51.6% and specificity 18.5% without abstention, against 98.4% and 78.9% within the determinate third - is the clearest available demonstration that reported accuracy is a function of which cases a system is permitted to decline, and it is volunteered rather than extracted. Second, the abstention is principled rather than arbitrary: 91% of declined cases had a neurodevelopmental disorder and severity tracked output cleanly, so the system fails exactly where clinicians also find the presentation ambiguous, and specialist certainty did not differ significantly between classified and declined cases. Third, the errors are clinically adjacent - every false positive had another developmental condition, none was neurotypical, and a third had a specialist who judged them autistic - which reframes what a false positive means in this domain. Against all of this sits the observation that the 'AI' operates on human expert ratings of video rather than on the video itself, which Ko and colleagues criticise by name elsewhere in this corpus; the algorithm and code are proprietary; and seven authors are employed by the manufacturer.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] One consecutively enrolled cohort rather than contrasted groups, with the three-level reference standard producing the comparison structure. Of 711 enrolled, 425 completed both the Device inputs and the specialist evaluation; specialists classified 122 (28.7%) as autism-positive, 263 (61.9%) as autism-negative with at least one other developmental or behavioural condition, and 40 (9.4%) as autism-negative and neurotypical. That composition is the study's decisive structural advantage over every other study in this corpus: the comparison against which the Device is judged is overwhelmingly children with other developmental concerns rather than typically developing children, which is the discrimination a primary care tool actually has to make. Attrition is documented in a flow diagram and its causes disclosed - 126 dropped out before completing Device inputs and a further 160 after completing inputs but before the specialist evaluation, with the COVID-19 national emergency in March 2020 closing 9 of 14 sites, preventing an estimated 100 specialist visits, and the authors estimating the drop-out rate absent COVID at 26.2%. Completers and non-completers are shown to be demographically similar in a side-by-side table. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'patients with ASD', 'a child diagnosed with ASD', 'ASD positive' and 'ASD negative' as output labels. Person-first throughout, with the acronym used as an attribute rather than as a noun for people. The framing is diagnostic and health-systems oriented rather than pathologising: the problems named are wait times, referral bottlenecks, diagnostic disparity and specialist capacity, not deficits in children. The paper is notably careful about the population it serves, repeatedly framing autism as one possibility among many overlapping developmental presentations - 'ASD can co-occur with and/or share many overlapping features of other disorders diagnosed in childhood' - and treating the false positives as children who 'had a non-ASD developmental-behavioral pediatric condition that could potentially benefit from similar early interventions as ASD', which is a clinically constructive reading of an error rather than a defensive one. [RQ1.3] Reported for the whole cohort in unusual demographic depth and used analytically rather than descriptively. Completers were 36.2% female, distributed across five age bands from 18 months to over 5 years, and characterised by race and ethnicity (53.9% non-Hispanic white only, 13.2% Black only, 11.5% Hispanic or Latino only, 13.4% multiple, 4.2% Asian only), parental education across six levels, and parental income across six brackets. Performance is then broken down across every one of these strata with Clopper-Pearson intervals, which no other study in this corpus attempts. The authors are appropriately careful about what this shows: the study 'was not powered for statistical inference on covariates' and differences were assessed 'by examining the overlap of corresponding 95% CIs'. Two age effects did reach significance - a higher determinate rate under 3 (39% versus 26%, p = 0.006) and higher specificity at 3 and over (88% versus 67%, p = 0.03). The sex comparison warrants more caution than the paper gives it: PPV was 60% (12/20) for girls against 88% (51/58) for boys, a 28-point gap resting on 20 determinate positive girls, and reading overlapping intervals as evidence of no difference in an underpowered analysis is the weakest inference in the paper - particularly since diagnostic disparity by sex is one of its stated motivations. The cohort had higher parental education and lower household income than the general US population, both acknowledged, with the income difference attributed plausibly to 'reduced parental participation in the workforce as a result of participants' developmental delays'. [RQ1.4] The strongest reference standard in the corpus, and the one against which others should be judged. Diagnosis was made by board-certified child and adolescent psychiatrists, child neurologists, developmental-behavioural pediatricians or child psychologists with more than five years of autism diagnostic experience, using structured clinical observation (comprising conversation or free play, symbolic interactive play and sensory stimulation), clinician interview and examination, medical and developmental review, and standardised assessment instruments, to reach a DSM-5 determination. That determination was then independently reviewed by a blinded second specialist working from standardised medical history, physical examination findings and video of the initial assessment, with a third specialist adjudicating disagreements and the majority decision defining the standard. The stated purpose is to reduce 'confirmation bias, deindividuation, and homogenized group thinking'. Crucially, the paper also quantifies the reference standard's own reliability rather than treating it as ground truth: the first reviewer agreed with the diagnosing specialist 79% of the time; of the 21% requiring a third opinion, the third sided with the diagnosing specialist 43% of the time and the first reviewer 57%; and diagnosing specialists reported being 'completely certain' only 67% of the time when diagnosing autism, 74% when ruling it out in favour of another condition, and 95% when the child was neurotypical. Reporting the imperfection of one's own gold standard is rare and consequential: it places a ceiling on what any device validated against it can be shown to achieve. [RQ1.5] Extensive on comorbidity and severity, absent on cognition. Specialists recorded all comorbid conditions, tabulated across fifteen diagnostic categories with frequencies, and then cross-tabulated against Device output - showing for instance that children with phonological disorder were classified indeterminate 82.4% of the time while those with intellectual disability received a positive output 66.7% of the time. DSM-5 support-level severity was recorded separately for social communication and restricted repetitive behaviour domains in every autism-positive child, using the maximum where site and reviewing specialists differed, and broken down by output: of 121 with scores, 5 were Level 1, 51 Level 2 and 65 Level 3, with the Device classifying 44 of 65 Level 3 children positive against 1 of 5 Level 1 children. That gradient is the clearest evidence in the paper of what the abstention mechanism is doing - declining on milder and more ambiguous presentations. No IQ or developmental quotient was obtained, and the reason given is sound: 'a large portion of participants were below the age threshold where non-verbal cognitive abilities can be reliably tested with traditional measures of intelligence'. The authors nonetheless flag that 'appropriately powered follow-up studies are needed to confirm Device performance across a range of intellectual levels'. [RQ2.1] Goal: test whether an AI-based diagnostic aid can allow primary care clinicians to diagnose autism directly, reducing referral load and diagnostic delay. Main findings: for the 31.8% of children on which the Device rendered a verdict, PPV was 80.8% and NPV 98.3%, with sensitivity 98.4% and specificity 78.9%; if abstention were removed, sensitivity across all completers would fall to 51.6% and specificity to 18.5%; 91% of the children the Device declined to classify had at least one neurodevelopmental disorder; all 15 false positives had a non-autism developmental condition and none were neurotypical, with one specialist judging a third of them autistic; there was a single false negative; the mean age at which an autism-positive output was rendered was 2.81 years against a national average diagnosis age above 4; and no performance differences were detected across sex, race and ethnicity, income or education, though the study was not powered to test them. [RQ2.2] Fourteen sites across six US states, recruiting children 'representing a population of patients that HCPs would see in their primary care practice' - so the sampling frame is the referral population the tool is intended for, not a research cohort. The participating clinicians are equally representative: 15 physicians trained in general pediatrics or family medicine, spanning 1 to 38 years of post-residency experience, and explicitly 'not recruited on the basis of any special interest or experience of ASD diagnosis, beyond what was delivered as part of their standard training'. That last detail matters more than it might appear: a diagnostic aid evaluated only with enthusiastic autism-interested clinicians would not establish that ordinary primary care physicians can use it. Thirteen point nine percent of clinician assessments were conducted by telemedicine rather than in person, with 'no evidence of performance degradation' when done remotely - an incidental finding produced by the COVID-19 disruption that speaks directly to rural and low-access deployment. [RQ2.3] Three mutually blinded inputs, deliberately mirroring the components of a standard evaluation: 'use of multimodular Device inputs is consistent with current guidelines and recommendations for an evaluation of ASD that include having both caregiver and clinician input, as well as a structured observation of the child'. The video component is the element that distinguishes it from a questionnaire battery, and the rationale given is behavioural rather than technical - clinicians assess 'within a time-constrained clinical encounter where the child may not display behavior characteristic of that seen in the home environment or may become newly behaviorally reactive due to change in environment', so caregiver-recorded home video supplies observation of the child in their ordinary setting. The practical constraints are modest and reported: two videos of 1.5 to 5 minutes, with in-app guidance on framing and lighting; a caregiver questionnaire taking a median 4 minutes 56 seconds; and a clinician questionnaire taking about 10 minutes after a 30-minute visit. Age-banded questionnaire versions differ slightly to reflect developmental trajectories, with the classifier trained to perform equivalently across both. [RQ2.4] Prospective and prospectively registered (NCT04151290) before initiation, conducted August 2019 to June 2020, with each child assessed once by the Device and once by specialists. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: centralised IRB review by IntegReview under protocol number Q170886, approved 19 July 2019, with the subsequent acquisition by Advarra noted, and informed consent from all caregivers. The COVID-19 disruption is disclosed in detail rather than smoothed over - the date of the national emergency, the number of sites closed (9 of 14), the reduced availability of those remaining, the estimate that 100 specialist visits could not be completed, the 97 that were completed afterwards, and the estimated drop-out rate absent the pandemic (26.2%). Data are withheld from public release on patient-sensitivity grounds but offered to qualified researchers under a data-sharing agreement, with the full protocol public on ClinicalTrials.gov. The code is proprietary and not available. [RQ2.5] Consumer smartphones for caregivers plus web portals for clinicians and analysts - no specialised hardware. The substantive resource requirement is human: video analysts must hold at least a master's degree in psychology, occupational therapy, physical therapy, speech-language pathology, special education or a related field with specific autism training, and have at least five years of professional or clinical experience with autistic children. They receive standardised training, must pass certification on previously unseen videos meeting minimum PPV, NPV and abstention-rate guarantees, and undergo ongoing performance review during the study. This is the element that most complicates the scalability claim, and the authors identify it themselves as a research priority: 'improving the scalability of the video component of the Device by decreasing reliance on human video analysts in subsequent generations of the algorithm'. The Device also requires smartphone access, which the authors note 'not all low-income American families may have', and functions only in English, with Mandarin and Spanish versions in development. [RQ2.6] Reporting is at regulatory-trial standard and exceeds every other study in the corpus. Fully specified: trial registration number and protocol availability; IRB name, protocol number and approval date; site count and states; recruitment population; clinician qualifications and experience distribution; participant flow with reasons at each stage and COVID-19 impact quantified; baseline demographics for both completers and all enrolled across age, sex, race and ethnicity, education and income; the complete list of behavioural constructs probed by the questionnaires; item counts per input per age band; video duration requirements and caregiver guidance; video analyst qualification, training and certification requirements; the reference standard procedure including the blinding and adjudication structure; specialist qualifications; the certainty rating scale; median completion times for two of three inputs with the third's estimation method disclosed; the confusion matrix against a three-level standard; performance across every demographic stratum with intervals; severity and comorbidity breakdowns by output; the statistical software, packages and interval method; and the abstention threshold-setting procedure including the FDA-agreed PPV and NPV floors. Not available: the algorithm itself, the feature weights, and the code, all proprietary; and the specific standardised instruments the specialists used are described generically rather than named. [RQ2.7] Substantial and candid, with the central limitation stated as a headline result rather than buried. The abstention rate is not framed as a caveat but as a design feature whose cost is quantified: the Device declined to classify 68.2% of children, and the paper states plainly what would happen otherwise - sensitivity 51.6%, specificity 18.5%. The stated scope follows: 'the goal of the Device is not to enable diagnosis of all presentations of ASD, but to aid primary care HCPs to diagnose the subset of children the Device can confidently determine a recommendation for'. Other limitations acknowledged: not powered for covariate inference; no IQ testing, with the reason and the need for follow-up stated; English only, with non-English families excluded and translations in development; parental education higher and income lower than the general population; smartphone access required; cost and reimbursement data absent, with explicit concern about equitable access for low-income and uninsured families; reliance on human video analysts limiting scalability; and the expectation that abstention rates will vary with the population's composition, being lower in more neurotypical or higher-prevalence populations. What receives insufficient weight: the sex difference in PPV, dismissed on interval overlap in an admittedly underpowered analysis; and the fact that the reference standard's own 21% disagreement rate bounds the achievable ceiling, which is reported but not carried into the interpretation of the results. [RQ2.9] Six directions, all operationally concrete. Reduce dependence on human video analysts in future algorithm generations - the scalability bottleneck. Determine what training primary care clinicians need to use the Device confidently in practice, which is a human-factors question the trial did not address since it used a study protocol rather than routine deployment. Run a registrational study monitoring the stability of Device results against diagnosis over time, 'including establishing a diagnosis later in children who at the time of initial evaluation did not meet diagnostic criteria for ASD' - the follow-up that would establish whether indeterminate and negative outputs remain correct as children develop, and the single most important missing evidence for a tool used at 18-72 months. Power future studies for demographic subgroups. Confirm performance across intellectual levels. And obtain cost and reimbursement data to establish whether deployment would be equitable, with explicit reference to Medicaid sustainability and to families without smartphones or insurance. [RQ3.1] Behaviour is captured through three complementary observational vantage points rather than a single measurement channel, and the design rationale is explicitly clinical rather than technical. Caregiver report captures behaviour across settings and time; home video captures 'rich insight into the child's natural behavior outside of the clinic setting'; and the clinician questionnaire captures structured professional observation within a visit. The constructs probed are enumerated in full and are recognisably the constructs of a clinical autism evaluation - joint attention, integration of communication forms, reciprocal communication, quality of social responses and overtures, directed and responsive smiling, eye contact appropriateness, pretend and creative play alone and with others, imitation, shared interests, offering comfort, repetitive mannerisms, sensory interests, unusual interests - rather than proxy signals such as gaze coordinates or acoustic features. This is the one study in the corpus where the computational input is the same behavioural vocabulary a clinician would use, which is why its outputs can be interpreted directly and why its false positives can be characterised as children with other conditions that would benefit from similar intervention. [RQ3.2] The most consequential fusion result in the corpus, though the fusion itself is inherited from prior work: 'previously published analysis of earlier algorithm iterations demonstrated that combining inputs significantly improved the performance of the algorithm'. What this trial adds is not a demonstration that fusion helps but a demonstration of what fusion plus abstention achieves under prospective conditions on the clinically relevant population. Two properties of the fusion deserve note. The three inputs are mutually blinded, so no channel is contaminated by another - the caregiver does not know what the clinician said, the video analyst does not know either, and none sees the output. And the channels are deliberately heterogeneous in vantage point rather than in modality, combining retrospective caregiver knowledge, naturalistic home observation and structured clinical observation, which is a different fusion logic from the modality-combining designs elsewhere in this review and is justified by reference to diagnostic guidelines rather than to information theory. The trial does not report per-input performance, so the marginal contribution of each channel in this cohort cannot be assessed - a gap relative to the fusion ablations reported by MacFarlane, Han and Liao. [RQ4.1] A gradient boosted decision tree, chosen for a regulated diagnostic aid over deep architectures, and locked before the trial. The model's provenance is described across seven years of prior development: initially trained 'using patient record data from thousands of children with diverse conditions, presentations, and comorbidities' with labels from standardised diagnostic tools, then 'iteratively improved, supplemented with ASD-expert input, and prospectively validated for 7 years prior to this study'. The abstention mechanism is the modelling contribution and is handled with unusual explicitness: thresholds were tuned by cross-validation on training and testing data to hold PPV above 65% and NPV above 85% - floors agreed with the FDA in advance - while minimising the abstention rate. The justification for abstaining rather than always deciding is stated in three parts: it 'provides a safeguard against known machine-learning failure modes, fosters clinician trust through model transparency, and helps flag cases where additional human expertise or data may be needed'. That framing - abstention as a transparency and triage mechanism rather than a performance trick - is the right one, and the paper earns it by quantifying the alternative. [RQ4.2] Three input vectors combined into a single mathematical representation, with 64 questionnaire items per child spread across the channels. The representation is entirely in the vocabulary of clinical behavioural observation rather than in derived signal features, which is what allows the outputs to be audited clinically - the paper can report which comorbidities and which severity levels are associated with each output because the inputs are commensurable with the reference standard's own constructs. The age-banded versions are a considered detail: item content differs slightly between 18-47 and 48-71 months 'in order to best capture the ASD phenotype among children based on developmental trajectories', with the classifier trained to perform equivalently across both, and the trial then reports performance separately by age band and finds a genuine difference in determinate rate and specificity. That is representation design responding to a developmental fact, and it is validated rather than assumed. [RQ4.3] Predictive values were the pre-specified primary endpoints, and the reason given is exactly right for a diagnostic aid: 'the selection of predictive values as primary endpoints reflects the utility of the Device in a broad spectrum of subjects, as these values measure how often in the study population the Device correctly identifies a patient with ASD and how frequently it correctly determines that a patient does not have ASD'. Because the cohort's 28.7% prevalence is that of the referral population the tool would actually serve, these predictive values are directly interpretable in deployment - which is precisely what the accuracy figures reported throughout the rest of this corpus are not. Clopper-Pearson exact intervals accompany every estimate. The confusion matrix is three-by-three against a three-level reference standard rather than two-by-two, so the composition of the errors is visible: all 15 false positives came from the other-condition column and none from the neurotypical column. Performance is stratified across five demographic dimensions with intervals throughout, severity and comorbidity are cross-tabulated against output, and reference-standard reliability and specialist certainty are reported alongside. The one substantive gap is the absence of per-input performance, which would show how much each channel contributes. [RQ4.4] No feature-level interpretability, and the algorithm and code are proprietary - so at the level of mechanism the Device is opaque. What the paper offers instead is case-level interpretability, and it is more clinically useful than a feature ranking would be. The indeterminate group is characterised diagnostically: 91.0% had at least one neurodevelopmental disorder, 71.0% were autism-negative with another condition, 20.0% were autism-positive and 9.0% had no developmental diagnosis - so the abstentions concentrate on the genuinely ambiguous rather than falling randomly. Output is cross-tabulated against DSM-5 severity, showing a clear gradient from 44 of 65 Level 3 children classified positive to 1 of 5 Level 1 children. Output is cross-tabulated against every comorbidity, showing for example that phonological disorder yields abstention 82.4% of the time. And specialist certainty is compared between cases the Device classified and cases it declined - 71% versus 64% completely certain, p = 0.40 - testing whether the Device abstains where clinicians are also uncertain, and finding no significant difference. Taken together these establish what the Device is doing at the level a clinician needs, even though they say nothing about how. [RQ4.5] The validation design is the study's principal contribution to this review and differs in kind from everything else charted here. Rather than resampling within a dataset, the model was locked with thresholds fixed on prior training and testing data, and then evaluated prospectively on consecutively enrolled children whose diagnoses were established afterwards by an independent blinded specialist consensus. All three Device inputs were blinded from one another and from the output; the specialists were blinded to the Device. The trial was registered before initiation, so the endpoints - PPV and NPV with FDA-agreed floors - were pre-specified rather than selected post hoc. Participant flow is fully documented with attrition causes including the COVID-19 disruption quantified. The two features that make this the corpus's benchmark are the population and the disclosure. The population is the referral cohort the tool is meant for, with 28.7% prevalence and only 9.4% neurotypical, so predictive values are directly deployable rather than requiring prevalence correction - the calculation Kong and colleagues perform hypothetically is here unnecessary because the design supplies it directly. The disclosure is the counterfactual: sensitivity 51.6% and specificity 18.5% without abstention, against 98.4% and 78.9% with it. No other paper in this corpus reports what its performance would be under a less favourable operating decision. What remains open is the temporal question the authors themselves identify - whether children given indeterminate or negative outputs at 18-72 months go on to receive autism diagnoses later - which the planned registrational study is designed to address and without which the NPV of 98.3% is a cross-sectional rather than a prognostic figure. [RQ5.1] No keyword list appears in the extracted text. The operative vocabulary is Software as a Medical Device, diagnostic aid, active comparator, predictive value, indeterminate output, abstention, risk control and primary care - a regulatory and health-services register rather than a machine-learning one, which accurately reflects a paper whose contribution is a trial rather than an algorithm. [RQ5.2] npj Digital Medicine 5:57 (2022), a digital health journal published in partnership with Seoul National University Bundang Hospital. Authorship spans 20 affiliations including CHOC Children's, UC Irvine, Stanford, Nationwide Children's, Ohio State, University of Missouri, Arizona State, Children's National, and seven authors affiliated with Cognoa Inc., the device manufacturer, with the corresponding author reachable at a cognoa.com address and also holding a CHOC and UC Irvine appointment. The senior author list includes the Stanford investigator whose group also produced the crowdsourced speech study elsewhere in this corpus and who declares founding Cognoa there. The commercial relationship is transparent from the affiliations and the paper is framed as a regulatory submission, which explains both its methodological rigour - a pivotal trial must satisfy FDA review - and its limits, since the algorithm and code are proprietary and unavailable for independent scrutiny. [RQ5.3] 2022. The framing is a health-systems argument rather than a technical or clinical-deficit one, and it is the most concretely evidenced in the corpus. The problem is specified with figures at each link in the chain: US prevalence 1.9%; mean age of diagnosis over 4 years despite reliable diagnosis being possible at 18 months; an estimated three-year delay between first caregiver concern and diagnosis, longer for children who are non-white, female, of lower socioeconomic status or rural; 27% of autistic children still undiagnosed at age 8; waits of up to 18 months between primary care screening and specialist diagnosis; only about 1% of autistic patients diagnosed by primary care clinicians; roughly 60% of children who fail a screen neither referred nor diagnosed; and 61% of 454 children with an eventual autism diagnosis having screened negative on a common screener in a cohort of over 20,000. The barriers to primary care diagnosis are then named specifically - low confidence with diagnostic tools, lack of specialist training, insufficient time to administer or to review results, and inadequate reimbursement - as is the observation that existing instruments risk overdiagnosis 'in populations with a lower prevalence of ASD, as is the case in primary care' and lose reliability when combination instruments are used stand-alone by time-pressured clinicians. The proposed role follows from this analysis and is correspondingly bounded: not to replace specialist assessment but to let primary care resolve the straightforward cases so that specialist capacity concentrates on the complex ones, with the authors observing that 'reducing tertiary referral loads by even a third could significantly shorten wait times for interventions to begin'.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional acoustic case-control study in Tuscany: 14 autistic children (11 male, 3 female, aged 6-10) recruited through a speech and language therapy service and a disability foundation, diagnosed by a neuropsychiatrist under DSM-5 criteria with no instrument reported, and 14 typically developing children matched on group size, age range and sex ratio with no screening described. No cognitive, language or severity measures in either group. The autistic recordings were reused from a prior thesis project and made in June 2019 by a speech therapist using a tripod-mounted video camera in the children's usual therapy playroom; the comparison recordings were collected later by parents on their own phones at home because COVID-19 prevented in-person collection. Recordings not shared; analysis code publicly released on GitHub.
narrative_rows.methods: Both groups narrated the same six-picture birthday-party story from a commercial storytelling toy. openSMILE 2.1 extracted the 88-parameter eGeMAPS set - chosen over ComParE because 6,376 features would exceed the sample size and over GeMAPS for psychological grounding - spanning frequency, energy and amplitude, and spectral balance families. Mann-Whitney U-tests across all 28 samples selected the 16 significant parameters, which were normalised and used to train decision trees, K-nearest neighbours, random forests and support vector machines under three-fold stratified cross-validation on an 80/20 split giving 22 training and 6 test samples. Ten models were run per method with the best selected and ten-run means also reported.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Sixteen parameters differed significantly: standard deviation of pitch falling slope (p = 0.041), second formant frequency (p = 0.003) and bandwidth (p = 0.033); jitter mean and SD (both p = 0.009), shimmer mean (p = 0.002) and SD (p = 0.001), harmonics-to-noise ratio mean (p = 0.001) and SD (p = 0.002); three loudness functionals; and four spectral measures. Autistic children showed higher mean jitter (0.036 vs 0.024) and shimmer (1.23 vs 1.04) with lower standard deviations, markedly lower harmonics-to-noise ratio (5.04 vs 7.88), higher loudness and higher spectral flux. Best test-set performance was 83% accuracy for decision tree, random forest and SVM, with AUC 88% for decision tree and SVM. Ten-run means were substantially lower: SVM 79.8% (SD 6.75), random forest 70.1%, decision tree 68.2% (SD 16.40), KNN 58.5%.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The two groups were recorded with entirely different equipment in entirely different settings by different people at different times - a tripod-mounted video camera in a therapy playroom versus parents' phones at home - and every reported acoustic family depends directly on microphone type, distance and room acoustics. Harmonics-to-noise ratio is by construction a signal-to-noise measure and differs in exactly the direction the acquisition difference predicts. The authors disclose the divergence and invoke it to discard their loudness results, but retain the voice-quality and spectral results which are equally affected. Feature selection was performed across all 28 samples before splitting, which the authors acknowledge in advance with a supporting citation. The test set contains six children, so 83% accuracy is five of six, and the headline figures are the best of ten runs against means as low as 58.5%. Diagnosis rests on an undescribed neuropsychiatric judgement with no instrument or severity measure, the comparison group was not screened, no cognitive or language measures were obtained, and no ethics approval is reported for either group.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Charted primarily as a cautionary case and secondarily for two contributions that survive its data problems. The cautionary value is specific and complements the leakage examples elsewhere in this corpus: this is the clearest instance of acquisition confounding, where the measurement apparatus rather than the participants differs systematically between groups. It is instructive precisely because the authors understand the mechanism - they discard their own loudness findings on exactly this reasoning and recommend head-mounted microphones for future work - yet do not extend it to jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio and spectral flux, which are no less determined by the recording chain. Any speech study in this review that does not report a single standardised recording arrangement across groups should be read against this example, and harmonics-to-noise ratio in particular should be treated as a candidate proxy for recording quality wherever it appears. The two surviving contributions are the argued case for standardising on a published parameter set, so that acoustic findings become comparable across studies and languages - an argument this review's cross-linguistic study makes independently - and the quality of the feature-family discussion, which reports contradictory prior findings rather than selecting supportive ones, enumerates the loudness literature as containing higher, lower and null results, and states plainly where no comparator literature exists. The paper also declines to claim a classifier, positioning itself as a feature-extraction validity study and disclosing its selection bias in advance, which is a standard of scope discipline that several higher-profile studies in the corpus do not meet.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups of 14, drawn from a homogeneous Tuscan area between Florence, Pistoia and Prato, and matched by construction on group size, age range and sex ratio. The autistic children came from the speech and language therapy service of AUSL Toscana Centro and the Opera Santa Rita foundation, and their recordings were reused from a prior thesis project on discourse and storytelling in autism. The comparison children were recruited separately for this study 'from the same geographical area' with 'the same demographic characteristics'. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The critical structural fact is that the two groups were not merely recruited separately but recorded separately, at different times, by different people, using different equipment, in different environments - a distinction that matters far more for acoustic analysis than for the behavioural comparisons elsewhere in this corpus, and one that the paper discloses fully while underweighting its consequences. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'people with autism', 'autistic people', 'the ASD group', with person-first and identity-first used interchangeably. The register is inconsistent in one respect that stands out: autism is repeatedly referred to as 'the disease' and 'the disorder' - 'to be able to use it during the diagnosis', 'distinguish the speech productions of the disease', 'a turning point in the early diagnosis of the disease' - and participants are twice called 'patients'. Against this, the paper is unusually attentive to correcting a stereotype, arguing from its own pitch data that 'the increasing pitch could suggest chasing away the idea that the speech of people with ASD is robotic, monotonous and without melodic variation, as reported in the past literature', and returning to the point again in the loudness discussion. The historical framing is careful too, quoting Kanner's original observation and noting that 'the researchers ignored this part of Kanner's study in the decades that followed'. [RQ1.3] Matched by design and reported only at that level. Both groups comprise 14 children aged 6 to 10 with 11 males and 3 females. No means, standard deviations or statistical tests are given for age, so the groups are known to share a range rather than shown to be equivalent - and across ages 6 to 10 children's vocal tracts, fundamental frequencies and narrative abilities change substantially, so a within-range imbalance would matter. The sex ratio was chosen deliberately to reflect the DSM-5 epidemiological figure of four males per female, which is a defensible design choice for representativeness though it means only three girls contribute to each group. No IQ, language, adaptive or severity measure was obtained for either group, so cognitive and linguistic level are entirely uncontrolled in a study whose outcome is narrative speech production. The authors identify a related gap themselves, noting that formant and fundamental frequency features are 'sensitive to the speaker's age, gender, and height' and recommending that future work investigate 'the correlation of voice features to the personal characteristics of the speakers'. [RQ1.4] One sentence: 'The diagnosis was made by a neuropsychiatrist according to DSM-5 criteria.' No standardised observational instrument such as ADOS, no interview such as ADI-R, no rating scale, no statement of when the diagnosis was made, whether it was made for this study or taken from clinical records, or what the diagnostic procedure comprised. Recruitment through a speech and language therapy service and a disability foundation indicates that all participants were receiving services, but nothing further is established. The comparison group's status is asserted rather than screened - no instrument, no exclusion criteria, and no statement about family history or developmental concerns. This is among the weakest ascertainments in the corpus and is not acknowledged as a limitation. [RQ1.5] None whatsoever - no cognitive, language, adaptive, severity or comorbidity measure for either group. The absence is particularly consequential here because the outcome is narrative speech elicited from a picture sequence: expressive language level determines how much a child says, how fluently, and with what syntactic complexity, all of which shape the acoustic signal, and it would be expected to differ between a group recruited from speech and language therapy services and a community comparison group. Nothing in the data permits this to be examined, and the paper does not raise it. [RQ2.1] Goal: establish whether acoustic markers of autism reported for English and other languages also appear in Italian, using a standard clinical parameter set, with classification as a check on whether the selected features carry signal. Main findings: 16 of 88 eGeMAPS parameters differed significantly, spanning voice quality (jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio), loudness, pitch dynamics and spectral distribution; best classifiers reached 83% accuracy on a six-sample test set with SVM most consistent across ten runs at a mean of 79.8%; jitter and shimmer were higher on average but less variable in the autistic group, matching a pattern reported in Italian-language-independent adult work; and mean pitch was higher though not significantly, which the authors use to argue against the monotone-speech stereotype. [RQ2.2] Two entirely different settings, and this is the study's defining problem. Autistic children were recorded in June 2019 by a designated speech therapist, in the room where they usually play, during a session that 'started with activities generally done during the treatment session so the child would act in the most spontaneous way', with 'a video camera placed on a tree-legged support'. Comparison children were recorded later by their own parents at home on the parents' phones, because 'due to the COVID-19 pandemic, it was impossible to collect the data in situ'. The clinical setting was designed carefully for the autistic children's comfort, which is good practice for eliciting natural speech and simultaneously guarantees a fixed, distant, uncontrolled microphone position in a room with unknown reverberation. A parent holding a phone produces a close-miked, low-noise, high-signal recording. Since the paper's entire yield is acoustic, the recording chain is not a nuisance variable but a direct competitor for every reported effect. [RQ2.3] Semi-spontaneous narrative from a six-picture sequence depicting a birthday party, from a commercially available storytelling toy, chosen as 'easily interpretable by neurotypical children of different ages'. This is a reasonable elicitation - picture-sequence narration is the standard paradigm in the narrative literature, it produces connected spontaneous speech rather than repetition or reading, and holding the task constant across groups is what the authors correctly identify as the one thing they did preserve when the recording arrangements diverged. Two limitations follow from the design's reuse. The autistic recordings were collected for a different study, on discourse and storytelling, so the elicitation was optimised for qualitative narrative analysis rather than acoustic measurement - which is precisely why the original comparison recordings from that project were unusable. And recording durations, utterance counts and speech quantity are not reported for either group, so it is not known whether the two groups produced comparable amounts of speech, which bears on the stability of every averaged acoustic functional. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, one recording per child, with the two groups recorded at different times separated by the onset of the pandemic. Ethical reporting is incomplete: written consent from caregivers is stated for the autistic group, but no consent statement appears for the comparison group and no ethics committee approval is reported for either. Data are not shared. The analysis code, however, is publicly released on GitHub, which is rare in this corpus and materially improves verifiability of the computational steps even though the recordings themselves are unavailable. [RQ2.5] The acquisition equipment is the study's decisive variable and is reported with enough candour to be evaluated. Autistic group: a video camera on a three-legged support, at an unspecified distance, in a therapy playroom. Comparison group: parents' own phones, model unspecified, at home. No sampling rates, microphone specifications, distances or room characteristics are given for either. The analysis chain is by contrast well specified - openSMILE 2.1 with eGeMAPS, chosen over ComParE because 6,376 features 'vastly outnumbers the sample size', and over GeMAPS for its psychological grounding - with Python, scikit-learn and Jupyter, and public code. The authors' own recommendation for future work is the correct diagnosis of what went wrong: 'it would be necessary that all the participants wear [a microphone] simultaneously from their mouths to ensure that all the variations are due to the actual speech production'. [RQ2.6] Uneven. Fully reported: the elicitation stimulus with its source; both recording arrangements including their divergence and its cause; the feature set with its version, the rationale for choosing it over two alternatives, and a complete table of all extracted feature families with definitions; the selection test; all 16 selected features with group means, standard deviations, outlier counts and exact p-values; the four classifiers; the split proportions and resulting sample sizes; the cross-validation scheme; the number of runs; both best-model and ten-run mean performance; and public code. Not reported: participant age means or tests; any cognitive, language or severity measure; the diagnostic procedure beyond one clause; recording durations, distances, sampling rates or device models; any classifier hyperparameters; comparison-group consent or ethics approval for either group; and any characterisation of speech quantity per child. [RQ2.7] Partially, and in a revealing pattern. The recording divergence is disclosed in full and then defended: 'Even though we are aware that this might eschew our results, we consider that it will not have that significant impact because the storytelling task remained the same, and the quality of the recordings was high (i.e., there was no background noise).' The defence addresses task comparability and the absence of noise in the new recordings, neither of which is the issue - the issue is a systematic difference between two recording chains, which shifts every spectral and voice-quality measure regardless of how clean each chain is individually. The authors nonetheless demonstrate that they grasp the mechanism, because they apply it correctly to their own loudness findings: 'This difference in the results could be caused by the most reported problems: the recording environment and the microphone's position... For these reasons, we decided not to consider the results obtained as relevant for the present.' Having discarded loudness on exactly this reasoning, they retain jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio and the spectral measures, which depend on the same variables. The feature-selection bias is likewise acknowledged in advance with a citation to comparable work in dementia speech, and the scope is explicitly narrowed to feature-extraction validity rather than classification. Not acknowledged: the six-sample test set; that the headline figures are best-of-ten against much lower means; the absence of any diagnostic instrument, severity measure or comparison-group screening; the absence of cognitive and language measures; and the missing ethics approval. [RQ2.9] Five directions, of which two are unusually well targeted. Redesign the recording process so that intensity and pitch can be analysed at all, with the concrete specification that all participants should wear a microphone at a fixed mouth distance - the authors note this must be balanced against 'the necessity of maintaining some environmental comforts for the patients in a clinical condition', which correctly identifies the tension between naturalistic elicitation and acoustic control. Adopt common feature sets across studies so results are comparable across languages, citing De La Fuente and colleagues - a standardisation argument that this review's cross-linguistic study (Lau and colleagues) makes in a different form. The remaining three are larger datasets with feature-subset comparison to build a standard acoustic set for autism; investigation of how voice features relate to speaker age, sex and height; and testing whether the jitter and shimmer pattern seen here in children and reported by Kissine and Geelhand in adults persists across the lifespan, which the authors suggest would be 'a turning point in the early diagnosis'. [RQ3.1] Paralinguistic voice production during narrative, decomposed into four theoretically motivated families rather than treated as an undifferentiated feature vector. Frequency-related parameters index intonation and vocal-tract configuration; voice quality parameters (jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio) index the regularity of vocal fold vibration and are framed as measuring 'the difficulty in controlling the vocal fold vibrations, transforming the production into hoarseness, breathiness, and creaky voice'; loudness indexes intensity and, via its variability, 'the dynamic intonation of autistic speech production'; and spectral parameters index energy distribution.
