Also unaddressed: the absence of any language or cognitive measure in a cohort defined by limited verbal fluency; the use of a single ADOS administration as both the only clinical characterisation and the prediction target; and the absence of an ethics statement. [RQ2.9] No dedicated future-work section, but both stated limitations imply directions and one is developed comparatively. Improving acquisition - the authors' contrast with a four-microphone beamforming setup indicates that better signal-to-noise ratio is the obvious lever, though it would trade against the deployability that a single-microphone setup buys. And relaxing the 20-second, 50-vocalisation minimum, which is framed as a constraint of the deep-learning architecture and which currently excludes the least verbal children. The paper also positions its result against two prior severity-estimation studies - one on Japanese-speaking adolescents using support vector regression and one on English-speaking children achieving a correlation of 0.634 in 33 children - and notes that it achieves 'a similar correlation value (0.606) while using a larger dataset of 132 children', which implicitly frames sample size as the axis along which the field should progress. [RQ3.1] Prosodic and acoustic properties of spontaneous child speech during clinical assessment, grounded in a specific prior literature that the introduction summarises accurately: autistic children have been reported to show 'strange prosody', 'increased pitch variability and pitch range', 'slower speech rate, and prolonged word production', with the observation that 'these studies used manual annotation and inspection of the audio recordings' - which is precisely the dependency the present work is designed to remove. The 48 features are named only in part (pitch, formants, zero-crossing rate, duration), so the operationalisation cannot be fully evaluated from this paper. The construct that the model actually targets, though, is not an acoustic property but a clinical score: the system predicts ADOS raw scores, which aggregate social affect and restricted repetitive behaviour ratings across a 45-minute observation, most of which concerns behaviour the microphone cannot capture. That the model recovers 37% of the variance in such a score from speech acoustics alone is the substantive finding, and it is also the reason the result is hard to interpret mechanistically. [RQ3.2] No cross-modal fusion, but the study performs a well-designed three-way comparison of segmentation inputs feeding an identical downstream model - manual annotation, MFCC-plus-pitch diarization, and x-vector diarization - which isolates the contribution of the segmentation stage cleanly. The result is the paper's most interesting finding and runs against expectation in two ways. Automatic diarization matched or slightly beat manual annotation (R 0.606 and 0.581 against 0.567), which the authors explain rather than merely report: 'the manual segmentation is not perfectly accurate, especially for the child segments. The child speech is often quiet and is sometimes masked by noises, especially when using a distant microphone in a reverberant environment.' And the more sophisticated representation lost: 512-dimensional x-vectors achieved better child-segment accuracy (89.84%) than MFCC plus pitch, yet produced worse downstream severity estimation - so segment-classification accuracy and downstream utility diverge, and optimising the intermediate metric would have selected the worse system. That dissociation between an intermediate objective and the end-to-end outcome is a transferable lesson for any pipeline architecture. [RQ4.1] Two networks in sequence, each matched to its task. Diarization uses a fully connected network with two stacked softmax layers, the second added on cited grounds that it improves final classification, followed by Viterbi decoding to impose temporal coherence on the frame-level outputs - a sensible structure for a sequence-labelling problem. Severity estimation uses a convolutional network with a linear output for regression, trained with RMSprop and hyperparameters selected by random search under five-fold cross-validation, with the selected values reported separately for each segmentation condition. Reporting per-condition hyperparameters is a small but meaningful detail: it shows the comparison between segmentation methods was made with each given its own tuned configuration rather than one set imposed across all three. Neither architecture is described in enough depth to reimplement, with details deferred to a prior publication. [RQ4.2] The representation choice is the study's most considered technical decision. Rather than reducing each recording to a single averaged feature vector - which is what most speech studies in this corpus do - the system builds a 100x48 matrix per child, where each row summarises 48 features over a randomly drawn run of 10 sequential vocalisations. This preserves within-session variability, which matters for a construct like prosodic atypicality that is expressed as inconsistency rather than as a shifted mean, and it supplies a two-dimensional input that a convolutional architecture can exploit. Because the matrix is the input and one prediction is produced per recording, the unit of analysis remains the child despite the internal resampling, so no leakage arises from the 100 correlated rows. The design also implicitly handles variable session length: a child with more vocalisations contributes more distinct draws, but every child yields the same fixed-size matrix. [RQ4.3] Appropriate to a regression problem and reported with variability. Severity estimation uses Pearson correlation and normalised RMSE, each as a mean and standard deviation across 50 repeated splits - so the reader sees not only that R is 0.606 but that its standard deviation is 0.099, which places the manual baseline of 0.567 +/- 0.120 well within the automatic method's variation and correctly supports the paper's cautious claim of 'equivalent or slightly better' rather than a claim of superiority. Diarization is evaluated with the standard diarization error rate, decomposed into substitution, false-accept and missed-detection components with the collar specified, plus recall, precision and accuracy on child segments, and with a stated and reasonable justification for excluding silence errors. The most useful supplementary figure is the total detected vocalisation duration under each condition - 10.85, 11.11 and 10.72 hours - which demonstrates that the three segmentation methods recovered comparable amounts of speech and so that the downstream differences are not simply a matter of one method finding more data. No confidence intervals on the correlations beyond the across-split standard deviations, and no significance test between conditions. [RQ4.4] No feature-level interpretability: the 48 features are not individually reported, no importance analysis is performed, and no acoustic characterisation of severity is offered, so the study contributes a prediction system rather than a finding about how autistic children's speech varies with symptom level. The interpretability that is present operates at the level of the pipeline. The three-way segmentation comparison establishes which stage contributes what, and the finding that automatic diarization outperforms manual annotation is given a mechanistic account grounded in the recording conditions. The dissociation between x-vectors' better segment accuracy and their worse severity estimate is reported without explanation, but it is reported, and it is the kind of intermediate-versus-final metric divergence that a paper optimising only for diarization performance would never have surfaced. [RQ4.5] Among the better-designed validations in the corpus for a regression problem, with one important limitation that is interpretive rather than procedural. The split is by child and repeated 50 times, and - distinctively - each split is constructed so that the ADOS score distribution matches the full sample on four moments: 'we divided the children into training and testing datasets while balancing the distribution of ADOS scores (mean, standard deviation, kurtosis, and skewness) in each dataset'. Matching skewness and kurtosis as well as mean and variance is the right control for a bimodally distributed target, since an unlucky split could otherwise place most of the low-scoring comparison children on one side and inflate or deflate the correlation. Reporting means and standard deviations across the 50 repetitions rather than a single split follows properly. Hyperparameters were tuned by random search under five-fold cross-validation, though whether that tuning sat inside the 50 outer splits or was performed once beforehand is not stated - which leaves some selection optimism unquantified. The substantive limitation is what the correlation measures rather than how it was estimated: computed across a sample where the autistic group averages ADOS 14.6 and the comparison group 3.2, R = 0.606 conflates between-group separation with within-group severity grading, and no within-autism correlation is reported. That is the analysis that would distinguish a severity estimator from a diagnostic classifier expressed on a continuous scale, and it is the same conflation this review has flagged in Kojovic and colleagues. [RQ5.1] No keyword list appears in the extracted text. The operative vocabulary is speaker diarization, severity estimation, diarization error rate, ADOS score and prosodic features - a speech-engineering register applied to a clinical regression target, which accurately describes a paper contributed to a biomedical engineering venue by a signal-processing group working with a clinical centre. [RQ5.2] Proceedings of the 2022 44th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC), DOI 10.1109/EMBC48229.2022.9871523. All authors are at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, spanning biomedical engineering and the Azrieli National Centre for Autism and Neurodevelopment Research, so signal-processing and clinical autism expertise are co-located in a single institution - which shows in the study's access to research-reliable ADOS administration and in the realism of its recording setup. Funded by the Israel Ministry of Science and Technology with a grant number. The work builds explicitly on the same group's prior publications for the vocalisation segmentation method, the 48-feature set and the CNN architecture, so this paper reports an increment - the substitution of automatic diarization for manual labelling - rather than a standalone system. [RQ5.3] 2022. The framing is unusually precise about what the field has and has not done. Prior speech studies 'reported high classification performance' but 'did not estimate the severity of autism symptoms in individual children', and the two exceptions are named and characterised - one on Japanese-speaking adolescents using support vector regression, one on English-speaking children reaching a correlation of 0.634 in 33 participants. The paper also identifies the specific practical dependency it is removing: the earlier acoustic findings on prosody, pitch variability and speech rate all 'used manual annotation and inspection of the audio recordings', which is what makes them non-scalable. Its comparative positioning is likewise concrete rather than promotional: it acknowledges achieving worse diarization error than a four-microphone beamforming study, explains why, notes that a prior 499-hour corpus comprised verbally fluent children whereas this cohort 'mostly do not speak fluently or use little or no phrase speech', and describes its own correlation as 'similar' to the 0.634 of a smaller study rather than as an improvement. Adding a Hebrew-language cohort also extends the linguistic coverage of this corpus, which is otherwise dominated by English with single studies in Italian, Polish, Cantonese and Chinese.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Small controlled observational comparison conducted by a Polish-British collaboration spanning robotics, cognitive and applied psychology, education and rehabilitation medicine. Ten children aged 5.5 to 6.5 years (mean 6.08, SD 0.4) took part, recruited through the kindergartens they attended: five diagnosed with autism and five typically developing, each group comprising four boys and one girl. Diagnoses were recorded in kindergarten files and had been delivered by a multidisciplinary team of a psychiatrist, a psychologist and a pedagogue; the instruments and criteria are not stated. The study was approved by the local research ethics committee at the University of Lower Silesia, guardians were informed of the aims and procedures, and signed consent was obtained both for participation and, separately, for filming. No cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is reported.
narrative_rows.methods: Each child took part in two sessions. A five-minute familiarisation session had NAO introduce itself and perform two short rhythmic dances; after a short break the main experiment followed, comprising the 'Touch me' game with a stationary robot issuing voice commands and then the 'Dance with me' game with a moving robot inviting imitation, each lasting about five minutes. The two scenarios were designed to dissociate routes to the same observable behaviour: a child touching the robot during 'Dance with me' cannot be a response to a voice command and is read instead as imitation, while 'Touch me' precludes spontaneous reactions because the robot does not move. NAO was operated remotely by an experimenter through its standard graphical interface and its onboard sensing was not used for measurement. Sessions were recorded and rated by six competent raters from special education, who counted movement activities and scored interest in the robot and additional movements on 0-5 severity scales at each of a set of defined positions, with the full scale published in an appendix. Analysis used Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis and chi-squared tests; no computational model was fitted and no individual received a predicted class.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Autistic children produced significantly fewer turn-taking behaviours than typically developing children in both game scenarios. Group differences also emerged on interest in the robot and on additional movements, which the authors read as confirming that autistic characteristics were present during the interaction and as supporting the initial diagnoses. Inter-rater reliability across the whole scale was satisfactory at Kendall's W = 0.65 (p < 0.001), and the Additional movements subscale returned Cronbach's alpha of 0.77. No diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, specificity or AUC was computed, and none is claimed.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Five children per group permits detection only of large effects and supports no individual-level inference, and the constraint is not named in the paper. No confidence intervals or effect sizes accompany the group comparisons. Rater blinding to diagnosis is nowhere addressed, which is the principal internal-validity risk in a study where every measurement is a human judgement and the diagnoses were held in the kindergarten records from which participants were recruited. The instruments and criteria behind those diagnoses are not stated. No cognitive or language measure was obtained, so reduced turn-taking in a game the child must first understand cannot be separated from general developmental level. No test-retest data exist for a five-minute protocol proposed as a supplementary assessment tool, although the stability of a six-year-old's engagement with a novel robot across occasions is precisely what such a tool would require. And the robot's own sensors - cameras, microphones, tactile and sonar - are present throughout and used for nothing, which is the study's clearest missed opportunity and the direction its own future work points toward.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Contributes to the review as the clearest example of construct-first paradigm design, and as the upstream complement to the modelling studies charted elsewhere. Where most included studies collect a behavioural stream and ask a model what separates the groups, this one names turn-taking as the target in advance, builds two contrasting robot scenarios specifically to dissociate command-response from imitation, publishes the observational scale that defines the measurement, and quantifies its reliability across six independent raters - the sequence that the automated work generally assumes rather than establishes. Three further properties matter for the synthesis. Both groups were assessed in their own kindergartens under an identical robot-delivered protocol, so the recruitment and setting asymmetry documented across the photograph, audio and thermal branches of this review does not arise, and the elicitation is standardised to a degree no human examiner could match. Its diagnostic ascertainment - a psychiatrist, psychologist and pedagogue working as a team - is genuine clinical judgement, well above the folder-membership, hashtag and questionnaire-threshold labels found elsewhere. And its translational claim is the best-calibrated in the corpus: NAO is 'a supplementary tool, thanks to which specialists can acquire additional diagnostic intuition to be used with standard tools', with the mechanism described as a specialist learning what typical play with the robot looks like and thereby recognising deficits by observation. That is a proposal to calibrate human judgement rather than to replace it, and no other study in this review entertains it. The future-work section also names children themselves among the target users whose cooperation is needed, the only participatory-design commitment in the corpus. What the study cannot supply is any evidence about detection: five children per group, no model, no individual prediction, no accuracy, no rater blinding and no developmental covariate. Its finding that the autistic group differed on additional movements as well as on turn-taking is nonetheless worth carrying forward, since the free-play study charted elsewhere found the restricted-repetitive dimension unreachable in a 90-second sample - suggesting that a robot-mediated task may elicit motor behaviours that unstructured play does not.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Ten children aged 5.5 to 6.5 years (mean 6.08, SD 0.4), recruited through the kindergartens they attended in Poland: five diagnosed with autism and five typically developing, each group comprising four boys and one girl. The sample is the smallest in the review, and its composition is nonetheless carefully constructed - exact sex matching, a 12-month age band, and both groups drawn from the same kindergartens, so the recruitment asymmetry that affects nearly every case-control study charted here does not arise. Diagnoses were taken from kindergarten records and had been delivered by a multidisciplinary team of a psychiatrist, a psychologist and a pedagogue, which is genuine clinical ascertainment even though the instruments and criteria are not stated. No cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is reported. With five children per group, the study can support group-level inference about large effects and cannot support any statement about individual-level discrimination, which is consistent with what it claims. [RQ1.2] Clinical and diagnostic in register, with an unusually clear-eyed account of why existing assessment is difficult. The introduction reviews the screening instruments - M-CHAT, ADEC, CARS-2, ASRS - and observes that because they rest on information from parents and caregivers 'their reliability is limited', with ADOS singled out as the exception 'enriched with interactive protocols'. It then names the differential-diagnosis problem directly: effectiveness 'is compromised by difficulties in differentiating autism from other developmental disorders (for instance, sensory integration disorder, dysphasia, minimal brain dysfunction, e.g., ADHD)', concluding that diagnosis 'often employs a range of clinical tools complemented with long-term observation of the autistic child, often leading to ambiguous diagnostic outcomes'. That is an accurate and specific account of the clinical problem, and the identification of differential diagnosis as the hard case matches the finding of the ADOS-versus-schizophrenia study charted elsewhere in this review. The paper also notes that most robotics work in autism concerns therapy rather than assessment, and positions itself in the smaller assessment literature. 'Autistic children' and 'children with autism' are used interchangeably; no neurodiversity framing appears, but the future-work section names children themselves among the target users whose cooperation is needed to improve the games, which is a participatory commitment absent from the rest of this corpus. [RQ1.3] Age and sex are reported and controlled by design - a 12-month band and exact four-to-one sex matching in each group - which is proportionate handling for a ten-child study and better than several much larger studies in this review manage. What is absent is cognitive and language level, and the omission matters for the construct: turn-taking in a five-minute game depends on understanding the game, and without any developmental measure a general cognitive explanation for reduced turn-taking cannot be separated from an autism-specific one in six-year-olds. No socioeconomic, ancestry or comorbidity information is reported, and the sample is drawn from kindergartens in one Polish city. [RQ1.4] Multidisciplinary clinical diagnosis by a team comprising a psychiatrist, a psychologist and a pedagogue, recorded in kindergarten files. This is real clinical ascertainment and places the study well above the folder-membership, hashtag and questionnaire-threshold labels charted elsewhere in this review - the diagnoses were made by qualified clinicians working together, which is closer to best practice than a single-instrument threshold. Two limitations attach. The instruments, criteria and dates behind those records are not stated, so the standard cannot be characterised further. And the diagnoses were obtained from records rather than confirmed for the study, which means they were known in advance to whoever recruited and, potentially, to the raters - and rater blinding is nowhere addressed, in a study where every measurement is a human judgement. [RQ1.5] No independent severity instrument was administered, but the study's own observational scale carries graded 0-5 severity ratings for interest in the robot and for additional movements at each defined position, so a within-study severity dimension exists. The authors use the group differences on these subscales to argue that the findings 'support the initial ASD diagnoses by showing that autistic symptoms are present in children diagnosed with ASD' - which is a convergent-validity argument for the measurement rather than a severity analysis, and is a reasonable use of the data. No relationship between turn-taking indicators and any severity score is examined. [RQ2.1] The aim is to test whether a dyadic game with a social robot can elicit and reveal turn-taking deficits, as a step toward a robot-enabled diagnostic aid. Five autistic and five typically developing preschoolers each played 'Touch me' and 'Dance with me' with a NAO robot for about five minutes per game, and six raters from special education scored their behaviour from video on a purpose-built scale. Autistic children produced significantly fewer turn-taking behaviours in both scenarios, and group differences also appeared on interest in the robot and on additional movements. Inter-rater reliability was satisfactory (Kendall's W = 0.65, p < 0.001) with subscale alpha 0.77. The study's contribution is the paradigm and its validation rather than a detection result: no model is fitted, no child is assigned a predicted class, and no accuracy is computed or claimed. The authors state the intended use precisely - 'If a specialist has a sense of how a typical child plays with NAO, then they will be able to see possible deficits in the turn-taking of a child with autism by observing him/her' - which is a claim about calibrating human observation, not about automating it. [RQ2.2] The kindergartens the children attended, with a maximum of three children assessed per visit. Both groups were assessed in the same settings under the same protocol, which removes the clinic-versus-school recruitment asymmetry that this review has documented as a confound across the photograph, audio and thermal branches. Bringing a portable robot to a child's own nursery is also the deployment scenario the work envisages, so the data were collected under the conditions in which the method would be used - a property shared with only a few studies in this corpus, notably the population-based one-legged-standing study and the routine-examination work. [RQ2.3] Two purpose-designed five-minute dyadic games preceded by a five-minute familiarisation session, and the paradigm is the study's principal output. Its design merits recording in detail. 'Touch me' uses a stationary robot issuing voice commands; 'Dance with me' uses a moving robot inviting imitation. The two are constructed to dissociate routes to the same observable behaviour, and the authors state the logic explicitly: in 'Dance with me' a child touching the robot 'cannot be classified as a response to the robot's voice command. If at all, this is a phase of some kind of imitation process', while 'the Touch me scenario precludes the emergence of spontaneous child reactions because the NAO robot in this case was not moving'. Designing two conditions so that a single behaviour can be attributed to command-response in one and imitation in the other is a level of construct care that almost nothing else in this review matches - most included studies collect a behavioural stream and ask what separates the groups, whereas this one asks what a given behaviour would mean and builds the paradigm to answer it. Four further properties make the paradigm well suited to the review's concerns: it is short, it requires no verbal response, it is delivered identically to every child by a machine rather than a person - removing examiner variability, which the authors note gives 'predictable and reliable situations' - and it is portable to a kindergarten. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single session per child, with no follow-up or test-retest - the last being a real gap for a five-minute protocol proposed as a diagnostic aid, since the stability of a six-year-old's engagement with a novel robot across occasions is unknown and is exactly what a supplementary assessment tool would need. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: approval from the local research ethics committee at the University of Lower Silesia; legal guardians acquainted with the research aims and procedures; and signed consent forms covering both participation and, separately, the filming of the study. Separate consent for video recording is reported by very few studies in this review. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text. [RQ2.5] A NAO humanoid robot operated remotely by an experimenter through its standard graphical interface, plus video recording. NAO's onboard sensing is not used for measurement at any point, so the robot is a standardised stimulus rather than an instrument - which is the study's defining methodological characteristic and the reason it contains no automated measurement. The equipment cost is nonetheless the highest of the elicitation devices in this review after MRI and thermal imaging: a NAO is a research-grade humanoid platform costing several thousand euros, against the webcam-and-toys protocols charted elsewhere. What it buys is exact reproducibility of the social partner's behaviour, which no human examiner can provide, and the authors identify this as the point. [RQ2.6] Strong for an observational study. Reported: participant numbers, ages with mean and standard deviation, sex composition by group, the diagnostic source and the disciplinary composition of the diagnosing team, the kindergarten setting and the maximum of three children per visit, the two-session structure with familiarisation and both games and their durations, the robot and its remote operation, the number and professional background of the raters, both reliability statistics with their p-value, the statistical tests used, and - most usefully - the complete observational scale with its rating definitions published in an appendix. Publishing the instrument is what makes the paradigm reusable and is the single most valuable disclosure a study of this design can make. Not reported: rater blinding, the diagnostic instruments behind the kindergarten records, funding and competing interests. [RQ2.7] A dedicated limitations section is provided and its principal content is a scoping statement rather than a list of defects: NAO with the proposed software 'can be treated as a supplementary tool, thanks to which specialists can acquire additional diagnostic intuition to be used with standard tools'. The authors add that the games need further development through close cooperation with target users 'including children, psychiatrists/psychologists and therapists', and that the aim is a set of scenarios attractive to children. What is not addressed: the sample of five per group is not named as a constraint, though it permits only large effects to be detected and no individual-level inference at all; rater blinding to diagnosis is nowhere discussed, and is the study's main internal-validity risk since all measurement is human judgement and the diagnoses were on file; the instruments behind those diagnoses are unstated; no cognitive or language measure was obtained, so general developmental level cannot be separated from autism as an explanation for reduced turn-taking; and no test-retest data exist. [RQ2.9] Improve and further develop the game scenarios in close cooperation with target users, explicitly including children alongside psychiatrists, psychologists and therapists; identify scenarios attractive to children; and extend toward a human-robot-interaction-enabled system that supports differentiation of autism symptoms beyond turn-taking. The inclusion of children themselves among the users to be consulted is the only participatory-design commitment in this corpus. The obvious additional steps, not proposed, are blinded rating, a larger sample, a developmental-level covariate, and test-retest assessment. [RQ3.1] Turn-taking, treated as a specific and theoretically motivated construct rather than as a generic behavioural signal - and this is the study's main contribution to the review. Most included studies collect a rich behavioural stream and ask a model what separates the groups; this one names a single element of reciprocal social interaction, designs two contrasting scenarios to elicit it, defines the observable positions that constitute it in a published appendix, and tests whether the groups differ. Two secondary constructs are also measured on 0-5 severity scales: interest in the robot, and additional movements, the latter capturing motor behaviour that the authors treat as stereotypy-adjacent. The finding that autistic children produced significantly fewer turn-taking behaviours in both scenarios is consistent with the free-play study charted elsewhere in this review, which found the social-communication dimension separable in a brief structured sample while the restricted-repetitive dimension was not - here the additional-movements subscale did differ, which is worth noting since it suggests that a robot-mediated task may elicit motor behaviours that a 90-second free-play sample does not. [RQ3.2] None. A single video-recorded interaction stream, coded by human raters. The robot's own sensors - microphones, cameras, sonar, tactile sensors - are all present in the NAO platform and none is used for measurement, which is the study's clearest missed opportunity and the direction its own future-work section points toward. A robot that both elicits and records the interaction would supply exactly the standardised multimodal stream that several other studies in this review construct with far more improvised equipment. [RQ4.1] None. No computational or machine-learning model is fitted at any point, and no automated measurement is performed. The analysis is non-parametric group comparison - Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis and chi-squared - which is the appropriate choice for ordinal ratings from five children per group and is used correctly. For a review of computation-based approaches this study occupies the position immediately upstream of the modelling work: it establishes that a robot-delivered paradigm elicits a measurable group difference on a defined construct, which is the prerequisite for any subsequent automation, and it does not attempt the automation itself. [RQ4.2] Rater-assigned counts of movement activities and 0-5 severity scores per defined position, aggregated into turn-taking indicators for each game. Every value is traceable to a named behaviour with a published definition, so the representation is fully auditable - the opposite end of the interpretability spectrum from the 100,352 DeepFace features or 1,639 landmark values used elsewhere in this review, and a reminder that the constructs those studies attempt to learn were originally defined by exactly this kind of manual specification. [RQ4.3] None of the diagnostic kind, and none claimed. The metrics reported are measurement-quality and inferential statistics: Kendall's W = 0.65 (p < 0.001) for inter-rater reliability across the whole scale, Cronbach's alpha = 0.77 for the Additional movements subscale, and Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis and chi-squared statistics with p-values for the group comparisons. Reporting inter-rater reliability at all is something most observational work in this corpus omits, and it is the appropriate primary metric for a study whose measurements are human judgements. What is absent is any confidence interval or effect size on the group comparisons, which on five per group would have been informative about how large the difference actually is rather than only whether it reached significance. [RQ4.4] Complete, because nothing is opaque. Every measurement is a named behaviour scored against a definition published in an appendix, so any result can be traced to an observable event and independently re-scored - which is precisely what the six-rater reliability analysis does. The conclusion states the intended use in human terms: 'If a specialist has a sense of how a typical child plays with NAO, then they will be able to see possible deficits in the turn-taking of a child with autism by observing him/her.' That formulation is worth recording for the review because it describes an alternative to automation that most of this corpus does not consider - a standardised elicitation device that improves a clinician's calibration, rather than a model that replaces the clinician's judgement. [RQ4.5] Not applicable in the machine-learning sense, since no model is fitted and no individual receives a predicted class - and the corresponding measurement-validation work is done properly. Six independent raters scored the same video material against definitions published in an appendix, inter-rater reliability was assessed with Kendall's W and reported at 0.65 (p < 0.001), and the Additional movements subscale returned an internal-consistency alpha of 0.77. Non-parametric tests appropriate to small ordinal samples were used throughout. The binding limitation is statistical power: with five children per group, only large effects are detectable, no confidence interval or effect size is reported, and nothing in the design supports individual-level inference - which is consistent with the study's own claims, since it asserts a group difference and a paradigm, not a classifier. Two internal-validity issues are unaddressed. Rater blinding to diagnosis is nowhere discussed, and since diagnoses were held in kindergarten records and every measurement is a human judgement, this is the study's main risk of bias. And no cognitive or language measure was obtained, so reduced turn-taking in a game requiring the child to understand the game cannot be separated from general developmental level. Set against the modelling studies in this review, however, the study has one structural advantage that no amount of downstream methodology can substitute for: its measurement instrument is published, its reliability is quantified, and its construct is named in advance. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder; diagnostics; humanoid robot NAO; turn-taking. Compact and accurate, naming the population, the purpose, the apparatus and - unusually - the specific behavioural construct. Very few keyword sets in this corpus identify the construct being measured rather than the method being used. [RQ5.2] Applied Sciences 12(17):8399, MDPI, open access under CC BY; received 10 June 2022, accepted 17 August, published 23 August 2022. An applied-sciences venue with a robotics editorial team. The paper's clinical apparatus - multidisciplinary diagnosis, ethics approval, separate filming consent, inter-rater reliability, a published observational scale - is more complete than that of many papers in clinical venues charted in this review, which suggests the standard came from the authors rather than from the venue: the author list spans robotics, cognitive and applied psychology, psychology, and rehabilitation medicine across four Polish and two British institutions, with all seven authors noted as contributing equally. [RQ5.3] Published August 2022 by a Polish-British collaboration spanning robotics, cognitive psychology, education and rehabilitation medicine. The framing is a well-informed critique of existing assessment: parent- and caregiver-report screening instruments have limited reliability, ADOS is the exception because it is 'enriched with interactive protocols', and diagnostic effectiveness is compromised by the difficulty of differentiating autism from sensory integration disorder, dysphasia and ADHD - so assessment often depends on long-term observation and 'often leading to ambiguous diagnostic outcomes'. For this review the study is valuable in four respects, none of which is a performance figure. It is the corpus's clearest example of construct-first design: rather than collecting a behavioural stream and asking what separates the groups, it names turn-taking as the target, builds two contrasting game scenarios to dissociate command-response from imitation, publishes the observational scale that defines the measurement, and quantifies its reliability across six raters. It brings the assessment to the child - both groups were seen in their own kindergartens under an identical protocol - so the recruitment and setting asymmetry that this synthesis has documented across the photograph, audio and thermal branches does not arise. Its translational claim is the best-calibrated in the corpus: the robot is 'a supplementary tool, thanks to which specialists can acquire additional diagnostic intuition to be used with standard tools', and the mechanism is described as a specialist learning what typical play with NAO looks like and thereby seeing deficits by observation - a proposal to calibrate human judgement rather than to replace it, which no other study here entertains. And its future-work section names children themselves among the target users whose cooperation is required to improve the games, the only participatory-design commitment in this review. What it cannot supply is evidence about detection: five children per group, no model, no individual-level prediction, no accuracy, no rater blinding, and no developmental-level covariate. Its role in the synthesis is therefore as the upstream complement to the modelling studies - a demonstration that a robot-delivered paradigm elicits a measurable group difference on a defined construct, which is the prerequisite that most of the automated work in this corpus assumes rather than establishes.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control classification study in Shenzhen, China, reusing eye-tracking recordings from the authors' earlier experiment (Zhao et al., 2021c). Forty-three children were enrolled and 39 analysed after four tracking failures: 19 with autism, aged 99.6 +/- 25.1 months, 17 male, non-verbal IQ 100.8 +/- 22.7, and 20 typically developing, aged 108.8 +/- 27.0 months, 17 male, IQ 116.1 +/- 22.7 (IQ difference p = .019; age and sex balanced). Autism was established by DSM-IV consensus among two to four psychiatrists rather than by ADOS or ADI-R, to which the authors state they had limited access; no severity measure of any kind was obtained. Each child wore Tobii Pro Glasses 2 (50 Hz, 1920 x 1080 scene camera) during a four-part structured conversation with an interviewer at 80 cm, of which only the longest section - six general 'getting to know you' questions, published in an appendix - was analysed. Participants were not told what the glasses recorded and post-experiment questioning confirmed none had guessed.
narrative_rows.methods: The raw gaze coordinate stream from each child was cut into non-overlapping windows of 1 to 10 s. Six hand-crafted features were computed per window: Shannon entropy of gaze allocation over 10-pixel bins on the x-axis, the y-axis and the 192 x 108 grid of the scene image, plus the maximum spatial range on each axis and in the plane. Windows losing more than 30% of samples were discarded. An SVM with forward feature selection classified each window as ASD-like or TD-like under tenfold cross-validation, with segments - not children - randomly assigned to folds and a single feature subset chosen on all data then reused across folds. A second stage assigned each child a label by comparing the proportion of their windows labelled ASD-like against a threshold, with both the window length and the threshold chosen to maximise accuracy on the same 39 children. A majority-class prediction baseline was computed at each window length as an empirical chance floor for the segment-level results.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Segment classification accuracy rose with window length, stayed above 70% beyond 5 s and peaked at 74.15% for 9 s windows (sensitivity 75.45%, specificity 72.51%) using one feature alone - entropy of gaze allocation in the x-y plane - with additional features slightly degrading performance. It exceeded the majority-class baseline at every length. Child classification peaked at 87.18% (sensitivity 89.47%, specificity 85.00%) at 7 s windows with a 46% threshold, where the underlying segment accuracy was only 72.65%; across the ten window lengths child accuracy ranged 0.77 to 0.87 with optimal thresholds from 0.40 to 0.56. Feature statistics show entropy separating the groups significantly at all ten window lengths while range does so only below 5 s, locating the signal in the irregularity rather than the extent of gaze allocation. Autistic children also took 191 s against 110 s to complete the same six questions (U = 48, p < .01). The authors compare their accuracy to ADOS-2 and ADI-R figures from a meta-analysis while noting their sample is small and homogeneous.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The headline numbers are optimistically biased in three compounding ways that the paper does not discuss. Cross-validation partitioned gaze segments rather than children, so near-duplicate windows from one continuous recording per child appear in both training and test folds and the classifier can key on individual gaze signatures - the leakage Keles et al. measured directly elsewhere in this corpus. The 87.18% is the maximum of a joint search over ten window lengths and an unreported grid of thresholds evaluated on the same 39 children, with the median of the ten reported configurations at 0.78. Forward feature selection ran once on all the data. Beyond validation design, the autistic group's non-verbal IQ was 15 points lower than the controls' and is never adjusted for; the autistic group talked 74% longer, which itself determines the group-linked segment imbalance; the autistic sample excludes children with severe symptoms, IQ below 70, ADHD and medication use; the control group is community-recruited with no autism screening; and no ethics approval or consent statement appears in the report. The authors do state, unusually, that their putatively oculomotor construct is inseparable from visual attention in these data.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Valuable to this review for three reasons beyond its results. First, it is one of the few studies here using a live, unscripted social partner rather than a screen, with head-mounted tracking chosen specifically so head movement is unconstrained, and with participants kept naive to the recording purpose - a control against reactive gaze that almost no other eye-tracking study in the corpus reports. Second, it is a clean instance of the two-stage weak-segment-classifier-plus-aggregation design that recurs across modalities in this corpus, and it shows exactly what that design does and does not buy: aggregating 72.65% segment decisions to an 87.18% child decision looks like a large gain, but because the segments were never participant-disjoint the gain cannot be separated from within-child correlation. Kojovic et al., using the same architecture with a matched participant-wise split, is the controlled comparison. Third, because the authors published a prior study on the identical 39 children using visual fixation features (84.62% alone, 92.31% with conversational length added), this paper offers a rare within-sample comparison of feature families - and reveals that the fused feature carrying much of that earlier gain, conversation length, is close to a direct restatement of the group difference in task duration reported here.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups. Enrolled: 20 ASD and 23 TD. Analysed: 19 ASD and 20 TD, after data from 1 ASD and 3 TD children were dropped for eye-tracking technical failure. Total analysed n = 39. No third or clinical comparison group. The unit of analysis for the model, however, is the gaze behaviour segment, not the child: at 9 s the two groups jointly contribute several thousand segments (exact counts shown only graphically in Fig. 2b), and because ASD sessions were 74% longer on average the ASD group supplies systematically more segments at every window length. [RQ1.2] 'Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)' and 'children with typical development (TD)', used consistently. Person-first throughout ('children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'people with ASD'); the abbreviations ASD and TD are used as group labels in tables and figures. Deficit-oriented vocabulary is used freely in the interpretation - 'social deficits', 'attentional deficit', 'impairments', 'atypical oculomotor performance', 'ASD behaviors' - and the model's output classes are named 'ASD-like' and 'TD-like' behaviours. There is no engagement with neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement statement. [RQ1.3] Age, sex and IQ reported per group with formal group comparisons: age 99.6 +/- 25.1 versus 108.8 +/- 27.0 months (t(37) = 1.09, p = .283); sex 17:2 versus 17:3 male:female (chi-square = .174, p = .676); IQ 100.8 +/- 22.7 versus 116.1 +/- 22.7 (t(37) = 2.45, p = .019). Age range 6-13 years by inclusion. Nothing else: no race or ethnicity, no socioeconomic status, no parental education, no language background, no medication status beyond the exclusion gate, no comorbidity counts. Both groups are drawn from Shenzhen, China, so the sample is culturally homogeneous - relevant because gaze-to-face norms are known to vary cross-culturally and the entire feature set is spatial gaze allocation during a face-to-face conversation. The significant IQ gap deserves emphasis: it is the one variable that separates the groups, and it is neither matched, regressed out, nor discussed as a confound. [RQ1.4] Diagnosis was clinical and consensus-based rather than instrument-based, and the paper is candid about why: 'Due to a limited access to established ASD diagnostic instruments such as ADOS and ADI-R, the accuracy of the ASD diagnosis in the present study was assured through a variety of other rigorous procedures.' Those procedures were DSM-IV criteria applied by a licensed psychiatrist with at least five years' experience, re-evaluation by a senior psychiatrist, and adjudication by at least two further senior psychiatrists if they disagreed. Additional gates: non-verbal IQ >= 70 on Raven's APM, absence of schizophrenia or ADHD, no medication at the time of the experiment, and adequate conversational ability judged by a speech-language psychologist. TD children were community-recruited, Raven-screened to IQ > 70, self/parent-reported free of physical or mental disorder, and with no ASD/ADHD in first-degree relatives. Note the DSM edition: DSM-IV, not DSM-5, in a study published in 2022. Multi-psychiatrist consensus is a defensible reference standard and better than the single-clinician or registry labels used elsewhere in this corpus, but it is unblinded to everything the clinicians already knew about the child, is not quantified for reliability, and yields no severity gradation. [RQ1.5] Cognitive ability: Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices in both groups, non-verbal only, used both as an eligibility gate (IQ >= 70) and as a reported demographic. Language: a qualitative judgement by a speech-language psychologist that the child could sustain average verbal communication - no standardised score. Severity: none. No ADOS calibrated severity score, CARS, SRS, ADI-R algorithm score or any other symptom-quantification instrument was obtained, which is a direct consequence of the stated lack of access to ADOS/ADI-R. The study therefore cannot relate its gaze-entropy features to symptom severity, cannot report where on the spectrum its 19 children sit, and cannot test whether misclassified children were the less severely affected ones. Combined with the exclusion of children with severe symptoms and of those with IQ below 70, the analysed autistic sample is a narrow, cognitively able, verbal slice of the population. [RQ2.1] Two stated goals: first, to test whether gaze behaviour segments produced by autistic and TD children can be classified by machine learning; second, to test whether children themselves can be classified from the proportion of their segments the model labels ASD-like. The framing is explicitly novelty-driven - the authors assert that prior eye-tracking ML studies all extracted features from visual fixation patterns and that 'no study has been found to identify ASD with oculomotor behavior', drawing a conceptual distinction between where attention is directed (fixation) and how the eyes move in the sockets (oculomotor). Findings: segment classification peaked at 74.15% (9 s windows, single feature: entropy of gaze allocation in the x-y plane, sensitivity 75.45%, specificity 72.51%), above the majority-class baseline at every window length; child classification peaked at 87.18% (7 s windows, 46% threshold, sensitivity 89.47%, specificity 85.00%). Feature-level statistics show entropy differences significant at every window length from 1 to 10 s (all p <= .006 for the x-y plane), while range differences are significant only at the shortest windows and fall away beyond 4 s - so the discriminative signal is the irregularity of gaze allocation, not its spatial extent. Secondary observation of substantive interest: ASD children took 191 s to complete the same six-question session against 110 s for TD children (U = 48, p < .01). [RQ2.2] Single site in Shenzhen, China. Autistic children were recruited from a first-class mental health centre (Shenzhen Kangning Hospital / Shenzhen Mental Health Center, the affiliation of the child-psychiatry co-author); TD children came from nearby communities. The recording setting is a controlled but not screen-based one: a face-to-face structured conversation with an interviewer at a fixed 80 cm distance, with the child wearing eye-tracking glasses. This is a clinic-adjacent laboratory setting, not a naturalistic home or classroom setting and not a primary-care setting, so the recruitment path guarantees a spectrum-narrow, already-diagnosed autistic sample facing an unselected community control group - the classic case-control geometry whose accuracy does not transfer to a screening population. [RQ2.3] The paradigm is a structured dyadic conversation, notable in this corpus for being live and social rather than screen-based. Four topic sessions were arranged - Generic question, Hobby sharing, Yes-no question, Question raising - but only the first was analysed, for two stated reasons: gaze behaviour is topic-sensitive so pooling sessions would make segments heterogeneous and harder to classify, and the first session was the longest, yielding the most segments. The six questions of that session are published in an appendix. Two design features deserve credit. Head-mounted rather than remote tracking was chosen deliberately so that head movement is unconstrained and gaze in the scene-camera frame reflects eye-in-socket movement. And the participants were kept naive: they were not told the glasses recorded gaze, were not instructed to keep still, and post-experiment questioning confirmed none had guessed - a control against reactive gaze that most eye-tracking studies in this corpus do not report. The countervailing weakness is that the interviewer is a live human whose own behaviour is not standardised or measured, and who was presumably not blind to group; anything the interviewer did differently with the two groups is baked into the child's gaze. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; no longitudinal component, no follow-up, no repeat testing, no test-retest reliability for the entropy features. Ethics reporting is the weakest element of the paper: the retrieved full text contains no institutional review board statement, no Declaration of Helsinki statement, and no description of parental consent or child assent, despite the study involving minors, a clinical population, and a deliberate withholding of the device's true purpose from participants. The parent study (Zhao et al., 2021c) may carry the approval, but a secondary analysis reusing identifiable behavioural recordings should restate it. What is declared is a conflict-of-interest statement (none) and a detailed funding list of eight grants. [RQ2.5] Tobii Pro Glasses 2 head-mounted eye tracker sampling at 50 Hz, with an integrated 1920 x 1080 scene camera; gaze coordinates exported in pixels by Tobii Pro Lab. Cognitive assessment by Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices. Analysis tooling is not named - no MATLAB, Python, R, scikit-learn or LIBSVM is identified, and the SVM implementation, kernel and hyperparameters are unspecified. Calibration was one-point at the interlocutor's body position within Tobii's recommended 0.5-1.5 m working distance, verified qualitatively by checking that the live-view gaze marker overlapped named targets; no numeric accuracy or precision criterion was applied, and no per-participant tracking-ratio statistic is reported beyond the rule that segments with >30% loss were discarded. [RQ2.6] Split. The experimental side is highly reproducible: the conversation protocol and its six questions are published, the 80 cm distance and 50 Hz sampling are given, the segmentation arithmetic is written out index by index, the binning is exact (10 px bins giving 192 x-bins, 108 y-bins and 20,736 x-y blocks), the Shannon entropy formula is stated, and the 30% data-loss rule is cited to its source. The computational side is not: no code, no data, no preregistration, no SVM kernel or regularisation parameter, no random seed, no scaling procedure, no statement of how many segments existed at each window length in numbers rather than a bar chart, and no specification of the grid of thresholds searched. A reader could re-run the experiment on new children but could not reproduce the reported numbers from the authors' data. [RQ2.7] The authors state three limitations - restricted phenotype (IQ >= 70, verbal, no severe symptoms, 34 of 39 male), restricted and relatively late age band (6-13 years when the clinically decisive window is nearer 3-4), and, in the discussion, the absence of any non-TD clinical comparison. They self-describe the work as 'proof-of-concept'. The unstated limitations are the ones that bear on the headline numbers. (i) Segments, not children, were randomly partitioned into the ten cross-validation folds, so a child's own segments appear in both training and test sets; with only 39 children and thousands of segments, an SVM can learn individual gaze signatures rather than a group property, and the 74.15% is therefore an upper bound of unknown tightness. (ii) The participant-level 87.18% is the maximum over ten window lengths crossed with an unspecified grid of thresholds, all evaluated on the same 39 children - Table 4 shows the neighbouring windows giving 0.77-0.85, so the reported figure sits at the top of its own selection distribution and the honest summary of the method is closer to 'around 0.79 typical, 0.87 at the best of ten'. (iii) Forward feature selection was performed once on all the data and the resulting feature set reused in every fold, so selection is unnested. (iv) The ASD group's IQ was 15 points lower (p = .019) and is never controlled; gaze dispersion during a demanding conversational task is plausibly related to cognitive ability. (v) ASD children spent 74% longer in the session, which both drives the segment-level class imbalance and means the two groups' segments come from conversations of different length and, presumably, different affective character. (vi) No ethics or consent statement. To the authors' credit, the one comparison they do make carefully is the majority-class baseline at the segment level, which is exactly the empirical chance floor the imbalance demands. [RQ2.9] Fuse oculomotor with visual fixation features, since the authors' own earlier work on the same children reached 84.62% from fixation alone and 92.31% with fixation plus conversational length; build a representative ASD oculomotor template on the model of Eraslan et al.'s scan-path trend analysis and classify by similarity to it; pursue the neural basis of gaze irregularity; push the age range down towards the 43-month mean diagnostic age, motivated by evidence of atypical oculomotor behaviour in infants later diagnosed; test against developmental delay and ADHD rather than TD alone; extend to children with more severe presentations and a balanced sex ratio; and separate inherent oculomotor function from visual-attention allocation in unconstrained settings. The last of these is the most interesting, because it is an admission that the paper's central conceptual claim - that it measures oculomotor behaviour rather than attention - is not established by its own data. [RQ3.1] Gaze allocation during live social interaction, reduced to two constructs: regularity, measured as Shannon entropy of the spatial distribution of raw gaze points over 10 px bins (x-axis, y-axis and the 20,736-cell x-y grid), and spatial extent, measured as the maximum distance between the two most remote gaze points on each axis and in the plane. Crucially the representation is deliberately atemporal - gaze allocation 'captured how gaze behavior was mapped spatially without taking into account the temporal information', so no scan path, no fixation/saccade parsing, no dwell time and no areas of interest. The behavioural claim being tested is that autistic children spread gaze more diffusely and less predictably across the visual field during conversation. The results support this for entropy at every window length and for range only at short windows. Two further behaviours are measured but not modelled: conversational duration (191 s versus 110 s, p < .01), which the authors interpret as social-processing difficulty, and, implicitly, the willingness to wear glasses and converse for several minutes, which the sample was selected to guarantee. [RQ3.2] No fusion in this study - a single modality, six features, and the best model uses exactly one of them. The paper is nonetheless one of the more informative in the corpus about fusion, because the authors have a directly comparable prior study on the identical 39 children: Zhao et al. (2021a) reached 84.62% with visual fixation features alone and 92.31% by adding a single non-eye-tracking feature, conversational length. Set beside the present 87.18% from oculomotor features alone, this gives an unusually clean within-sample comparison of three feature families on the same participants - and it also shows how much of the gain in the earlier fusion result came from conversational length, a variable that is essentially a direct measure of the group difference in task duration reported here (191 s versus 110 s). That is worth flagging as a caution about multimodal gains: a fused feature that is itself a near-proxy for group membership will raise accuracy without adding behavioural insight. The authors' recommendation is to fuse oculomotor with fixation features, and, in the longer term, eye tracking with EEG, neuroimaging and kinematics, arguing that segmentation is the enabling technique because it preserves participants who would otherwise be dropped for data loss in any one stream. [RQ4.1] Classical machine learning in two stages. Stage one is a support vector machine classifying individual gaze behaviour segments as ASD-like or TD-like, chosen because 'SVM has been often used in ML studies in the field of ASD' - a popularity rather than a suitability argument, with no comparison against any other classifier. Stage two is a threshold classifier: count the proportion of a child's segments labelled ASD-like and call the child autistic if it exceeds a cut-off tuned to maximise accuracy (46% at the optimal 7 s window). No deep learning, no ensemble, no probabilistic model. The two-stage design - weak per-segment classifier plus aggregation to a strong per-participant decision - is the same multiple-instance shape used by Kojovic et al. in this corpus, and it is a sound idea; the difference is that Kojovic partitioned children before generating segments and this study did not, which is precisely what separates a legitimate aggregation gain from an inflated one. [RQ4.2] Six hand-crafted scalar features per fixed-length window of the raw gaze coordinate stream: entropy_x, entropy_y, entropy_xy, range_x, range_y, range_xy. The window length is itself a modelled hyperparameter, swept from 1 to 10 s. The binning that defines the entropy is spatial and fixed to the scene camera resolution (10 px cells), which means the features are defined in the wearer's own head-centred frame rather than in a world or face-referenced frame - an appropriate choice given head-mounted tracking, but one that makes the features depend on the geometry of where the interviewer sat. No normalisation, standardisation or per-participant centring is described, so between-child differences in absolute gaze spread enter the model directly - the same property that makes segment-level pooling risky. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity at both the segment and participant level, plus an ROC curve for the participant-level threshold sweep (the AUC is not stated numerically). Sensitivity and specificity are defined explicitly and correctly at the segment level. Missing: AUC value, PPV/NPV, F1, confidence intervals of any kind, calibration, and any significance test on the classification results (the t-tests reported are on the features, not the models). The absence of confidence intervals matters at this sample size: with 39 children, the difference between 87.18% (34/39 correct) and the 77% seen at four of the ten window lengths is four children. [RQ4.4] Good by the standards of this corpus, and honest about the limits of its own interpretation. Forward feature selection produces an explicit ranking, and Table 3 shows the striking result that a single feature - entropy of gaze allocation in the x-y plane - achieves the maximum 74.15% and that adding any of the other five slightly reduces accuracy. Table 2 gives group means, SDs and t-tests for all six features at all ten window lengths, letting a reader see that entropy separates the groups at every scale while range does not beyond 4 s. The discussion then supplies a mechanistic account rather than a post-hoc story: higher entropy in the ASD group follows from gaze being distributed more evenly between social and irrelevant regions instead of concentrating on face and body, referencing the authors' own fixation analysis of the same children. And they close by conceding the interpretive cost - 'the atypical oculomotor performance in the children with ASD was inseparable from visual attention in our study' - which is a rare admission that a paper's headline construct is confounded with the one it set out to distinguish itself from. The model is not interrogated at the individual level: no per-child probabilities, no error analysis, no examination of which five children were misclassified. [RQ4.5] This is the paper's weak point and the reason its two headline numbers should be read very differently from each other. Segment level: tenfold cross-validation with random partition of segments. The text is unambiguous that the unit is the segment ('all behavior samples were randomly partitioned into 10 subsamples'), and there is no statement anywhere that a child's segments were kept together. With 19 + 20 children each contributing tens to hundreds of windows from one continuous recording, adjacent segments from one child are near-duplicates in feature space, and the classifier can exploit stable individual gaze idiosyncrasies - the exact leakage that Keles et al. in this corpus quantified directly by identifying individuals from gaze at 35.4% against 6.2% chance. So 74.15% is not an estimate of performance on an unseen child. Participant level: the aggregation is applied to those already-leaky segment labels, and then two further quantities are optimised on the same 39 children - the window length (10 candidates, Table 4 shows accuracies 0.77 to 0.87) and the threshold (a sweep whose grid is not specified, optimal values 0.40 to 0.56). Reporting the maximum of that joint search as the study's accuracy is best-of-many reporting; the median of Table 4 is 0.78. Feature selection is likewise unnested, run once on all data with the chosen subset reused in every fold. What the study does do right is the segment-level chance floor: the majority-class baseline is computed and plotted at every window length precisely because the class imbalance is group-linked, and the SVM beats it throughout. That is more care about chance than most studies here take, which makes the absence of the corresponding participant-level baseline or permutation test more conspicuous. A corrected design would partition the 39 children into folds, generate segments within folds, run forward feature selection inside each training fold, and select the window length and threshold on training children only - and would very likely report a materially lower number, as Cilia et al. found when they moved from image-level to participant-level evaluation of the same data. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: Autism; Behavior segmentation; Entropy; Eye-tracking; Machine learning; Oculomotor. Two are methodological signatures rather than topic labels - 'Behavior segmentation' names the paper's own technique of cutting a continuous gaze recording into short windows, and 'Entropy' names its single discriminative feature - so the keyword set advertises a method rather than a clinical application. 'Oculomotor' is the conceptual claim the paper stakes out against the existing visual-fixation literature. Neither 'diagnosis' nor 'screening' appears, although the abstract closes by proposing to 'promote the automatic screening of ASD'. Terms carried through the body: threshold classifier, gaze allocation, Shannon entropy, support vector machine, forward feature selection, majority class prediction, face-to-face conversation. [RQ5.2] Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders 53:934-946, an Original Paper - a clinically oriented specialist autism journal rather than an engineering or machine-learning venue. The venue choice shows in the reporting profile: participant characterisation, diagnostic procedure, task protocol and feature-level statistics with t-tests at every window length are all reported to clinical standards, while the computational specification (SVM kernel, regularisation, scaling, code) is thin and the cross-validation unit is left ambiguous. The paper was received in an earlier form, accepted 13 July 2022 and published online 1 August 2022 in the 2022 volume year with a 2023 issue assignment. [RQ5.3] Published online 2022, issued 2023, from Shenzhen University's Institute of Human Factors and Ergonomics with the Shenzhen Guangming District Center for Disease Control and Prevention and Shenzhen Kangning Hospital - an engineering-plus-public-health-plus-psychiatry collaboration, funded by eight Chinese grants including the National Natural Science Foundation, the Shenzhen Science and Technology Innovation Committee and a Guangdong Key Realm R&D Program. The framing is incremental and explicitly novelty-staking: the authors argue that all prior eye-tracking classification work has used visual fixation patterns and that 'no study has been found to identify ASD with oculomotor behavior', then draw a conceptual distinction between where attention is directed and how the eyes move in the sockets. The clinical motivation is the standard one for the period - diagnosis depends on clinician experience and caregiver report, is time-consuming and may be biased by subjective factors - and the proposed role is complementary, that eye tracking 'might be incorporated in clinical practice to complement existing diagnostic procedure'. The paper is unusual for 2022 in explicitly flagging that the whole eye-tracking classification literature, its own work included, has only ever tested against typical development.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control classification study at an autism centre in Tehran, Iran, extending the authors' earlier accelerometer-only sensorized toy car. Fifty children aged 3-6 were tested: 28 with autism (mean age 4.63 years), 18 typically developing (mean 4.61), and 4 with other disorders (cerebral palsy, fragile X; mean 5.5), the last group being excluded from all classification results without comment, leaving 46 modelled children at 61% autism prevalence. No diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or process is reported for any group, and no sex, IQ, language, developmental or severity data are given beyond age. Each child played freely with the toy car for 3-5 minutes in a 3 x 4 m room, alone or with a parent or therapist, under the supervision of a centre psychologist. Five autistic children ignored the car entirely; every typically developing child engaged enthusiastically.
narrative_rows.methods: The car concealed an ESP8266 NodeMCU streaming over Wi-Fi by UDP, an ADXL345 triaxial MEMS accelerometer, and two Hall-effect shaft encoders on the front and rear wheels, all battery-powered and hidden inside the body to avoid distracting the child. Play was decomposed into four states identified by the joint sensor signature - not playing (both signals static), playing only with the wheels (encoders active, accelerometer static), playing on the floor (both active) and playing in the air (accelerometer active, encoders static). Forty-four acceleration features from the earlier version (means, variances, five dominant frequencies and their amplitudes per axis, energies, inter-axis correlations, jolt count, duration) were joined by ten new features: seven state-occupancy ratios, the total wheel turn rate, and two tilt counts derived by short-time Fourier transform to recover the car's roll and pitch during wheel play. Two consecutive rounds of backward elimination - first within each modality after examining inter-feature correlation, then across modalities - reduced the set to seven acceleration and three encoder features, which were fused early into one vector per child. A linear-kernel SVM (chosen after testing three kernels), a random forest and an MLP with data augmentation were evaluated under an 80/20 division with 5-fold cross-validation over the 46 children.
narrative_rows.outcomes: The reimplemented accelerometer-only baseline gave 71.11% accuracy (sensitivity 67.14%, specificity 73.00%, precision 80.00%), below the 85% reported for version 1, which the authors attribute to different data, a different collection setup and a from-scratch reimplementation. Adding the encoder features raised accuracy to 78.61%; adding the new roll and pitch features instead gave 75.83%; adding both gave the headline 85.56% (sensitivity 81.67%, specificity 81.00%, precision 87.67%), the claimed improvement of more than ten points. Random forest on all features gave 80.83% accuracy but the best sensitivity and specificity of any configuration (85.48%, 83.67%), and the authors note explicitly that a deployer might prefer it because it would miss fewer autistic children and mislabel fewer typically developing ones. MLP on all features gave 71.11%. The three encoder features surviving selection were the wheels-only play ratio, the not-playing ratio and the total wheel turn rate.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No reference standard is described anywhere: the paper never states how autism was diagnosed in the 28 children, how typical development was established in the 18, or whether the comparison group was screened at all, so the target of the reported accuracy is undefined. The 85.56% is the best cell of a grid spanning three algorithms, three SVM kernels and four feature configurations, evaluated on 46 children with no chance baseline against a 60.9% majority-class floor, no confidence intervals, and roughly nine children per test fold. Two rounds of backward elimination reduced 54 features to 10 on the full sample, with no indication of nesting inside the cross-validation folds. The not-playing ratio - one of three selected encoder features - encodes the fact that five autistic children refused to engage with the toy while every control engaged enthusiastically, so an unknown share of the signal is toy engagement rather than the interest-in-rotating-objects mechanism the hardware was built to capture; the authors' own observation that controls 'played with more energy and moved the car in a wider area' points the same way, and no developmental or motor measure exists to separate autism from general developmental level. The four children with cerebral palsy and fragile X - the only available differential contrast - were collected and dropped. Reported accuracies do not reconcile with the stated sensitivity, specificity and 28:18 class ratio for several rows. Formal ethics review was not obtained, the authors arguing that non-intrusive screening does not require it.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Contributes to this review in four ways. It is the corpus's clearest example of instrumented-object sensing - no camera, microphone, wearable or screen, with the electronics hidden inside an ordinary toy - which sidesteps the acquisition-chain confounds that undermine several video and audio studies here and raises none of the privacy objections that attach to home video capture. Its four-state decomposition is a genuinely good piece of behavioural engineering: two cheap sensors that individually cannot distinguish a spinning wheel from a carried car become, jointly, an interpretable budget of how a child spends a play session, and the ablation across four feature configurations shows the two streams are complementary rather than redundant. It is also one of the few studies whose split unit is the participant by construction, since the whole session collapses to one feature vector, so it is free of the segment-level leakage that inflates much of this literature. Set against that, it is the corpus's outstanding example of an undefined target: a study reporting 85.56% accuracy without stating anywhere how the condition being predicted was ascertained. Finally, its equity framing - low-cost IoT screening for low- and middle-income and rural settings, explicitly tied to the UN Sustainable Development Goals - is a motivation almost absent elsewhere in this corpus and worth carrying into the discussion of what screening tools are actually for, alongside the observation that a device intended for 1-2% population prevalence was validated at 61%.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Three groups recruited, two modelled. Recruited: 28 children with ASD, 18 typically developing children, and 4 children with other disorders (cerebral palsy and fragile X syndrome), total 50, all aged 3-6 years and tested at an autism centre in Tehran. Modelled: 46 subjects, which is exactly 28 + 18, so the four-child other-disorder group is excluded from every classification result without the exclusion being stated. A further subgroup is described but not removed: five of the 28 autistic children 'did not seem interested in playing with the sensorized toy car and neglected it completely', so roughly 18% of the autism group contributed a session of near-zero play. Whether their data were retained is not stated explicitly, but the 46-subject count implies they were, and one of the three selected encoder features is the not-playing ratio. [RQ1.2] 'Children with autism (ASD)', 'children with ASD' and the abbreviation ASD throughout; 'Typically Developed (TD) children' - an idiosyncratic expansion of the usual 'typically developing'. Person-first construction is used consistently ('children with ASD', 'people with ASD'). The clinical framing is medical-model and unhedged: autism is 'a neurodevelopmental disorder that causes problems in social communication and interaction', the targeted behaviours are named as 'symptoms' including 'the obsessive attention to detail' and 'repetitive behaviors', and the conclusion refers to the system as screening 'cognitive deficits'. There is no engagement with neurodiversity perspectives and no autistic-community involvement statement, although the framing of purpose - equitable access to screening in low- and middle-income and rural settings, tied to the UN Sustainable Development Goals - is unusual in this corpus and reflects a genuine health-equity motivation. [RQ1.3] Extremely thin. Table 2 reports only group size, mean age and median age: ASD n = 28, mean 4.63, median 4.0; TD n = 18, mean 4.61, median 4.0; others n = 4, mean and median 5.5. Age is therefore well matched between the two modelled groups, which matters for a motor-play task in 3-6 year olds. Nothing else is reported: no sex distribution for any group, no IQ or developmental quotient, no language level, no socioeconomic status, no race or ethnicity, no comorbidities, no medication.
