It also creates the engineering problem the pipeline is built to solve - the scene contains multiple adults, so person re-identification is needed simply to know which skeleton belongs to the child. The countervailing point is that the sample is a referred clinical series at a tertiary hospital with 29 of 30 children already autistic, which is the opposite of the community screening population the conclusion invokes when it proposes deployment 'in remote areas with underdeveloped medical care'. [RQ2.3] The ADOS-2 response-to-name press, executed as the manual prescribes and left unmodified. The child sits at a table absorbed in toys; the clinician stands behind and to one side and calls the child's name in a natural voice; if the child turns and makes eye contact the item ends, otherwise the call is repeated up to three times at roughly 3 s intervals; then up to two reinforced calls follow, delivered with a changed tone or by a parent. Scoring runs 0 (responds to the first call) through 5 (no response after all five). Two properties make this paradigm unusually well suited to automation. It has a precise onset - the moment the name is spoken - which the ASR component recovers automatically and which the authors correctly identify as removing a source of manual-annotation error; and it has a precise, short response window of 3 s fixed by the protocol itself. Two properties make it hard. The clinically defined response is 'turn and face the implementer with eye contact rather than glance to the side', which is a conjunction of orientation and gaze that no single sensor captures, and which the cascade approximates rather than measures - eye contact per se is never assessed, only head yaw and whether a face was detected by the rear camera. And the caller's position varies between left and right rear, which is why two rear cameras are required and why the head-pose channel depends on the child turning towards whichever camera happens to be behind the caller. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional single session with no follow-up and no test-retest assessment. Since the pipeline is proposed as a clinical scoring aid, the absence of any repeat measurement means nothing is known about whether the same child assessed twice would receive the same automated score. Ethics reporting is minimal but present in both required elements: 'these experiments have passed an ethical review', with no committee, institution or approval number named, and informed consent obtained from the children's parents before each session. A privacy measure is also implemented and disclosed - participants' faces are mosaicked in the published figures, with the authors noting that this may obscure the facial joints they wish to illustrate - and the data are declared confidential rather than released. For video recorded on preschool children with disabilities during clinical assessment, the consent and privacy handling is appropriate; the ethics statement is thinner than the norm and would not satisfy most journals' current reporting requirements. [RQ2.5] Capture: four Hikvision RGB cameras with 2.8 mm lenses mounted at a common height of 1.44 m, recording 1280 x 720 at 25 fps, of which three are used - C1 at the child's left front for body pose and C3/C4 at left and right rear for head pose, the pair being necessary because the clinician may stand on either side. Audio is captured alongside and converted to 16 kHz 16-bit PCM for the speech service. Software stack, all named and all off-the-shelf except for retraining: iFlytek (HKUST Xunfei) real-time speech transcription, a deep fully-convolutional ASR that returns timestamped text and thereby locates each name call; YOLOv3 for person detection, deliberately retrained on more than 1,700 images from the study's own 30 subjects rather than using COCO weights, on accuracy grounds; HRNet for top-down 2-D pose estimation, chosen for its high-resolution feature maintenance and repeated multi-scale fusion; OSNet person re-identification to associate detections across frames and assign a stable ID, without which the child's skeleton could not be distinguished from the clinician's and the parents'; OpenFace for face detection, landmarks and 3-D head Euler angles. Implementation in Python and PyTorch. What is missing is any calibration: the cameras' geometry is fixed and stated but no intrinsic or extrinsic calibration is performed, and the shoulder rotation angle is computed directly in 2-D image coordinates, so a given physical torso rotation maps to different measured angles depending on where the child is seated and how they are oriented with respect to C1. [RQ2.6] Strong on specification, absent on artefacts. Every decision constant is stated numerically - the 3 s response window, the 90 degree and 20 degree shoulder thresholds, the 10-frame (0.4 s) and 8-frame duration thresholds - and the angle computation is written out as three equations from the shoulder vector through the arccosine to the degree conversion. The camera rig, frame rate, resolution, focal length and mounting height are given, as are the roles of each camera, the clinical protocol and its full scoring rule, the exact third-party models used, and the size of the custom detection training set. A competent group could rebuild the system from the paper. What cannot be reproduced is any number in it: the data are declared confidential, the retrained YOLOv3 weights and the 1,700-image annotations are not released, no code is available, and the ASR component is a commercial service whose behaviour may change. There is also no preregistration and no independent evaluation of the perception components (detection, tracking, landmark) in isolation, so their error rates on this population are unknown and are folded silently into the end-to-end figure. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section, though the discussion analyses the two residual errors carefully and the methods contain an important and creditable scope disclaimer - 'although RTN deficiency is closely associated with ASD, our experiment is an assessment of the response to name, not an assessment of autism risk'. The unaddressed limitations are substantial and several are structural. First, there is no validation of any kind: the five decision constants were chosen by hand and reported on the same 30 children, and the one trained component, YOLOv3, was retrained on 1,700 images of those same 30 children, so the detector has seen every participant it is evaluated on. Nothing in the paper estimates performance on an unseen child. Second, no chance baseline is computed, and the sample makes one essential: 17 of 30 children scored 5, so a rule that always predicted non-response would agree with the clinician on a majority of children and on a still larger majority of the 109 calls, since each non-responding child contributes five non-response events. For an ordinal agreement problem of this shape the natural statistic is a weighted kappa, and none is reported. Third, the 109 events are treated as independent for the headline 98.2% although they cluster within 30 children and are strongly serially dependent. Fourth, the reference standard is one unblinded clinician with no second rater and no reliability statistic, on an item that requires a real-time judgement about eye contact from behind the child. Fifth, the shoulder angle is a 2-D image-plane measurement from an uncalibrated fixed camera, so it confounds true rotation with seating position and posture. Sixth, the demographic reporting is too thin to establish for whom the method works. Finally, the framing is inconsistent: the abstract reports agreement with 'clinical diagnosis' and the conclusion invokes early autism screening in underserved regions, while the actual comparator is one clinician's score of one behavioural item in a sample that contains a single non-autistic child. [RQ2.9] No future-work section is provided. The conclusion's forward-looking claims are about deployment rather than research: that the method reduces the professional-knowledge requirement for assessment, provides efficient and objective computer-aided screening, and could support early autism screening in remote areas with underdeveloped medical care. Judged against the evidence, the research steps that would need to come first are clear and unstated: evaluation on children not used to train the detector; a balanced sample containing a meaningful number of non-autistic children so that the item score's discriminative value can be assessed; a second, blinded clinician rater with reported reliability so the reference standard is not one person's judgement; chance-corrected agreement statistics appropriate to an ordinal score; and threshold selection on a development set separate from the evaluation set. The wider point this study raises for the review, and does not itself pursue, is whether automating individual ADOS-2 items one at a time is a viable route to instrument automation - it is the only paper in this corpus attempting it, and the answer depends on error rates the paper cannot currently estimate. [RQ3.1] One behaviour, examined more closely than any other single behaviour in this corpus: response to one's own name. The clinical definition adopted is precise - the child should turn and face the caller with eye contact rather than glance to the side - and the paper's decomposition of it into measurable components is the substantive contribution. Torso orientation is captured as the angle between the left-right shoulder vector at each frame and the same vector at the first frame after the call, so the measurement is relative to the child's own starting posture rather than to an absolute frame. Head orientation is captured as the yaw Euler angle from facial landmarks, with the mere detection of a face by the rear camera also serving as evidence that the child turned towards the caller. Response latency is captured by the ordinal 0-5 score, which encodes how many calls and reinforcements were needed. The authors are explicit about why body pose is needed alongside head pose, and the reasoning is behavioural rather than technical: prior work used head pose and gaze only, but some responsive children turn only the head with little shoulder movement, while some unresponsive children rotate slightly while manipulating toys, so neither channel alone separates response from non-response. What is not measured, despite being in the clinical definition, is eye contact itself - gaze is approximated by head direction on the stated assumption that the two agree, an approximation that is reasonable in general but is exactly the point at which a glance to the side, which the protocol says does not count as a response, becomes indistinguishable from a genuine orienting response. [RQ3.2] Three-stream fusion with a clearly reported ablation, and the fusion architecture is a hand-written cascade rather than a learned combination. Audio and video are fused at the segmentation stage: the ASR stream supplies timestamps for each name call, which cut the video into 3 s response windows, and the authors note that this removes the manual-annotation error that would otherwise attach to onset marking. Body pose and head pose are then fused at the decision stage in a three-branch rule: shoulder rotation above 90 degrees for more than 10 frames gives a positive response outright; shoulder rotation below 20 degrees on every frame gives a negative response outright; and only in the ambiguous 20-90 degree band does head yaw adjudicate, with more than 8 frames of detected yaw giving a positive response. The ablation is reported for the two visual streams and is the paper's central quantitative claim: pose alone gives 83.3% of participants and 95.4% of events, pose plus head pose gives 93.3% and 98.2%. In participant terms that is three additional children correctly scored out of 30, so the confidence interval on the improvement is wide even though the direction is plausible. Two features of this fusion design are worth carrying into the synthesis. It is complementary by explicit behavioural argument rather than by empirical search - each stream is introduced to cover a named failure mode of the other - which is a more defensible basis for multimodality than the accuracy-chasing seen in several other studies here. And the multi-view arrangement is itself a form of fusion driven by the clinical protocol: two rear cameras are required because the caller may stand on either side, so which camera contributes the head-pose evidence depends on the geometry of the assessment rather than on a fixed sensor assignment. [RQ4.1] A hybrid that is unusual in this corpus: four deep neural networks are used as perception front ends, but no model is trained on the behaviour and the decision itself is a hand-written rule. The deep components are YOLOv3 for person detection (retrained on the study's own images rather than using COCO weights, on accuracy grounds), HRNet for top-down 2-D pose estimation (selected for its high-resolution feature maintenance and repeated multi-scale fusion), OSNet re-identification for multi-object tracking (necessary because the scene contains the child, the clinician and a variable number of parents, so the child's skeleton must be identified and followed), OpenFace for facial landmarks and 3-D head Euler angles, and a commercial deep fully-convolutional ASR for name-call timestamps. Above these sits a three-branch threshold cascade with five hand-set constants. The architectural choice is defensible for the task - the clinical scoring rule is itself a deterministic decision tree over observable orienting behaviour, so encoding it directly rather than learning it from 109 examples is the right call at this sample size, and it makes every judgement auditable. The cost is that nothing adapts: the thresholds cannot accommodate a child whose habitual posture or motor control differs, the paper's own two error cases are both threshold-boundary failures, and there is no probability or confidence attached to any judgement, so no case can be flagged as uncertain and referred back to the clinician - which is precisely what an assistive scoring tool ought to do. [RQ4.2] Two scalar angle time series per 3 s response window, each sampled at 25 fps and therefore up to 75 frames long, reduced to threshold-crossing frame counts before the decision. The shoulder rotation series is computed frame by frame as theta_t = arccos(v_0 . v_t / |v_0||v_t|) converted to degrees, where v_t is the vector from the right to the left shoulder joint at frame t and v_0 is the same vector at the first frame after the name call - so the measurement is self-referenced to the child's posture at call onset rather than to any absolute frame, which is a sensible choice that removes dependence on how the child happened to be sitting. The head series is the OpenFace yaw Euler angle, accompanied by an implicit binary of whether a face was detected at all by the relevant rear camera. Both series are then summarised only by counting frames that satisfy a threshold, so the representation discards the shape of the movement entirely: peak angular velocity, smoothness, whether the turn was completed or aborted, and whether the child returned to the toys are all invisible. Nothing is learned from the raw joint coordinates, and no representation of the temporal profile of orienting survives into the decision. [RQ4.3] Accuracy at two aggregation levels (30 participants and 109 test events), sensitivity, specificity, and a 6 x 6 confusion matrix of clinician against predicted 0-5 scores. The positive/negative convention is inverted from ordinary usage and stated explicitly - a true positive is a non-response correctly judged as a non-response - so sensitivity 84.6% refers to detecting failures to respond and specificity 100% to correctly recognising genuine responses. Reporting both aggregation levels and publishing the full score-level confusion matrix is better practice than most of this corpus. But the metric set is wrong for the problem in two ways. First, this is an ordinal agreement task between an automated scorer and a human scorer, for which the appropriate statistic is a weighted kappa or an intraclass correlation, and none is reported - so nothing corrects for the very high chance agreement created by 17 of 30 children scoring 5 and by every one of a non-responding child's five calls being a non-response event. The 98.2% event-level figure in particular is close to uninterpretable without that correction. Second, no confidence intervals are given, and with 30 children a single misclassification moves the participant-level accuracy by 3.3 points, so the reported improvement from 83.3% to 93.3% rests on three children. There is also no AUC, which is defensible since the system emits no score, and no evaluation of the perception components in isolation, so detection, tracking and landmark failures are folded silently into the end-to-end number. [RQ4.4] Fully interpretable by construction, and this is the study's clearest methodological strength. Every judgement reduces to two physically meaningful quantities - degrees of shoulder rotation relative to the child's posture when their name was called, and degrees of head yaw - together with counts of how many of the 75 frames satisfied a stated threshold. Figures 6 and 7 plot both series for worked examples against their thresholds, so a clinician or auditor can replay any decision frame by frame against the video and see exactly why it came out as it did. The design rationale is also explained in behavioural terms rather than defended by performance: shoulder rotation alone fails in two named directions, missing responsive children who turn only the head and falsely flagging unresponsive children who shift slightly while playing with toys, and head pose is introduced specifically to adjudicate that band. Even the duration constant is argued from evidence rather than tuned, being derived from the observation that gaze fixation during concentration lasts at least 0.2 s and then doubled to 0.4 s to allow for timing error in children's rotation. Three interpretability limits remain. Nothing quantifies how close a judgement was to its threshold, so no case can be surfaced as borderline. The perception layer beneath the rule is entirely opaque and unevaluated on this population, so a wrong answer caused by a tracking identity switch would look identical to one caused by a genuine behavioural boundary case. And eye contact, which the clinical definition requires, is never measured - head direction stands in for gaze on an assumption stated but not tested. [RQ4.5] There is no validation strategy, and this is the study's decisive methodological gap. No training/test split, no cross-validation, no development set, no held-out participants: the five decision constants were set by hand and are reported on the same 30 children and 109 calls used to define them, and the single trained component, YOLOv3, was retrained on more than 1,700 images drawn from those same 30 subjects, so the person detector has seen every child it is subsequently evaluated on. Nothing in the paper estimates how the pipeline would behave on a child it has never encountered. Compounding this, no chance-agreement floor is computed although the data make one essential: with 17 of 30 children scoring 5 and each of those children contributing five non-response events, a trivial always-predict-non-response rule would already agree with the clinician on well over half the participants and on a substantially larger share of the 109 calls, so the 98.2% event-level figure is being reported against an unstated and high baseline. For an ordinal agreement problem the correct summary is a weighted kappa or ICC; accuracy without chance correction systematically overstates agreement in exactly this configuration. The 109 events are also treated as independent although they cluster within 30 children and are serially dependent by the protocol's own logic. Finally, the reference standard against which all of this is measured is a single unblinded clinician with no second rater, so even a perfectly validated system could only be shown to reproduce one person's uncorroborated judgements. The corrective study is well within reach of this group and would be worth more than the current numbers: fix the thresholds on a development subset, evaluate on children whose images never entered detector training, add a second blinded rater and report inter-rater reliability, and report weighted kappa alongside accuracy at both aggregation levels. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD); Response to name; Human pose tracking; Head pose estimation; Early screening. Three of the five are computer-vision technique names and one is the specific behaviour targeted, which accurately reflects a paper whose contribution is a perception pipeline for one clinical item. 'Early screening' is the only application term and it overstates the work, since the sample contains a single non-autistic child. Terms carried through the body: multimodal discrimination, shoulder rotation angle, automatic name calling detection, multiple object tracking, person re-identification, Euler angle, yaw, Response to name Dataset, computer-aided diagnosis, ADOS-2 modules. [RQ5.2] Displays 76, article 102360, Elsevier - a display-technology and human-visual-interface journal, recommended for publication by a named handling editor. The venue is an unusual home for a clinical assessment study and explains the emphasis: camera geometry, multi-view capture, pose and landmark estimation and frame-level signal processing are described in detail, while the clinical apparatus around them - demographics, diagnostic scores, rater reliability, chance-corrected agreement - is thin or absent. Received 2 November 2022, revised 25 November 2022, accepted 18 December 2022, available online 5 January 2023. [RQ5.3] Published 2023 by Jilin University's School of Communication Engineering with the Department of Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics of The First Hospital of Jilin University, funded by the Science and Technology Development Plan of Jilin Province and the National Natural Science Foundation of China. The framing is capacity-driven and quantified: the opening cites autism prevalence rising to 1-2%, more than 10 million diagnosed people in China of whom about 3 million are children, and the striking statistic that 'globally, less than 5% of assessments use the ASD gold standard diagnostic tool, which is mainly due to the long test time, complex training of evaluators and high cost'. That last figure is the clearest statement in this corpus of why instrument automation, as opposed to diagnosis replacement, might matter. The paper positions its own contribution against three named prior response-to-name systems (Bidwell, Petric, Liu, Wang), arguing that all previous work relied on face, head pose and gaze while ignoring body pose - so the framing is incremental within a small, well-identified subliterature. Its most creditable move is the methods-section disclaimer that the work assesses response to name and not autism risk, which sits in unresolved tension with the abstract and conclusion.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional case-control classification study in Tehran, Iran. Twenty boys with 'high-performance autism' were recruited from the Daily Rehabilitation Clinic for Children with Special Disorders, affiliated to the Family Institute of Shahid Beheshti University, out of 25 approached - five were excluded for refusing to sit at the computer or for failure to calibrate the eye tracker, and their data were never recorded. Twenty boys from Namjoo public elementary school formed the comparison group, described as 'normal' and 'healthy' with no screening instrument administered and no exclusion criteria stated. Both groups are entirely male, aged roughly 4 to 12 years, and closely matched on age (8.40 +/- 2.45 versus 8.45 +/- 1.90 years). Autism status rests on prior diagnosis by a paediatric psychiatrist and a paediatric clinical psychologist followed by an undescribed comprehensive evaluation; no diagnostic instrument, IQ measure, language measure or severity score was obtained for anyone. Ethics approval was granted by the Research Ethics Committee of Islamic Azad University, Tehran Science and Research Branch (IR.IAU.SRB.REC.1401.152), with parental consent listed as an inclusion criterion for the autistic group.
narrative_rows.methods: A purpose-built two-stage computer game, designed with expert guidance and modelled on picture-exchange practice, used photographs from the Japanese Female Facial Expression database. Stage one required the child to identify which of three candidate faces matched a target; stage two required matching the target expression 'happy' among happy, sad and surprised faces. After familiarisation, 240 game images were presented and gaze was recorded on a stationary eye tracker at Shahid Beheshti University - a device never identified by make, model or sampling rate. Fixations were characterised in MATLAB R2020b by start, duration, end and (X, Y) position. The 1024 x 768 stimulus space was enlarged to accommodate out-of-range samples and partitioned into regions: on each of the three candidate figures, on the reference figure, around each of these, and two outside regions labelled OUT. Fixations were clustered by location and two quantities extracted per region - fixation count and fixation time - giving an 18-feature matrix, evaluated as four nested subsets (around the figures, on the figures, on and around, all features). A multilayer perceptron with hyperbolic tangent hidden activation and sigmoid output was trained by backpropagation with the scaled conjugate gradient algorithm, using 70% of the data for training and 30% for validation and test; the network's layer and node counts are never reported.
narrative_rows.outcomes: The abstract and conclusion report precision 76.6% and accuracy 73.8% for the full feature set, presented as the best of the four subsets. These are the pooled totals across training, validation and test. The corresponding held-out test values in the same table are precision 66.7%, accuracy 58.3%, sensitivity 57.1% and specificity 60.0%, against a 50% chance level. The pattern is uniform across all four subsets: total accuracies of 65.0%, 67.9%, 70.0% and 73.8% conceal test accuracies of 58.3%, 52.8%, 58.3% and 58.3%, with training accuracies of 67.9-78.6% - a train-to-test gap of roughly 20 points in every configuration, never remarked on. Two subsets show unstable held-out behaviour, with test sensitivity of 33.3% for the 'around figures' condition and test specificity of 33.3% for the 'on figures' condition. ROC curves are plotted for all four conditions but no AUC value is given. Arithmetic on the reported percentages establishes that the modelled dataset contains 240 rows split 168/36/36, i.e. six observations per child randomly distributed across partitions.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The study's reported result is a pooled figure that includes training data; its held-out accuracy for the reported best configuration is 58.3% on 36 observations, three observations above chance. The 240 modelled rows come from 40 children at six rows each and are randomly partitioned, so every test row has five siblings from the same child in training - and because the features are per-region fixation counts and durations, which are stable individual looking characteristics, this leaks identity rather than diagnosis. Four feature subsets were compared on the same data and the best reported. Twenty per cent of approached autistic children were excluded for refusing to sit or failing calibration, with no comparable filter on the comparison group and no description of those excluded. The comparison group received no autism screening of any kind. Both groups are entirely male and this is never discussed. No IQ or cognitive measure exists to separate social-attention differences from task-comprehension differences on what is fundamentally a visual matching task. No diagnostic instrument underpins the labels. The eye tracker is never identified, so fixation detection cannot be evaluated. And the stimuli are Japanese faces shown to Iranian children - an other-race face set whose relevance to autistic face processing the paper's own literature review cites without connecting it to its own design.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Three contributions to this review. First, it is the corpus's clearest example of a specific and consequential reporting hazard: a study whose tables are honest and fully disaggregated by partition, but whose abstract, results narrative and conclusion quote the pooled total, so the headline is roughly fifteen points above the study's own held-out result. Anyone reading only the abstract, or citing it in a meta-analysis, would record 73.8% for a method that achieved 58.3% on unseen rows - and this is a failure of presentation rather than of analysis, which makes it both easy to miss and easy to fix. Second, it is a useful negative datapoint on eye-tracking classification: it is one of the few studies here whose held-out figures are visible at all, and they sit close to chance, which is informative context for the much higher figures reported by studies that do not separate their partitions. Third, its stimulus choice is instructive for the corpus's discussion of task design. Iranian children were shown Japanese faces, and the paper's own introduction cites work on differences in same-race versus other-race face processing between autistic and typically developing children, and even quotes that study's 70% accuracy as a comparator - so the confound is one the authors had read about and did not apply to themselves. On the positive side, the game paradigm has properties worth carrying forward: it is engaging rather than passive, every trial has an objectively correct answer so gaze can be interpreted against task demands, and verbal responses were captured alongside gaze - a second modality that was recorded, informally described as consistent with the gaze data, and then left unanalysed.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups of 20, total 40 children, all male, aged roughly 4 to 12 years. The autistic group was drawn from the Daily Rehabilitation Clinic for Children with Special Disorders in Tehran, affiliated to the Family Institute of Shahid Beheshti University; the comparison group came from Namjoo public elementary school. Enrolment and attrition are reported for the autistic group only: 25 children with 'high-performance autism' were selected, of whom 5 (20%) were excluded under the study's stated exclusion criteria - refusing to sit on the chair, or failure to calibrate the eye tracker - and their data were never recorded. No exclusions, and indeed no exclusion criteria at all, are reported for the comparison group, so the two groups passed through different filters. The modelled dataset is not 40 rows but 240: arithmetic on the reported training, validation and test percentages fixes the row count exactly (168 + 36 + 36 = 240, with 132 + 24 + 21 = 177 correct and 177/240 = 73.75% matching the reported 73.8% total), so each child contributes six observations to a randomly partitioned dataset. [RQ1.2] The dominant contrast throughout is 'autistic and normal children', with 'normal' used in the title, abstract, results, discussion and conclusion, supplemented by 'healthy children' and 'typical children'. Framing autistic children against 'normal' peers is the least considered terminology encountered in this corpus and carries an implication - abnormality - that 'typically developing' does not. Autism itself is 'autism disorder' or 'the autism spectrum disorder', characterised by 'communication deficits', 'impairment in social interactions' and the statement that autistic children 'lack the ability to learn the socio-cognitive skills with normal development'. Severity is expressed as 'high-performance autism' and, in one passage discussing robot-assisted education, the text refers to 'students with mental retardation' - outdated in current English usage. Against this, the study's motivation is service-oriented rather than dismissive: it is framed around the shortage of specialists relative to a growing autistic population and the goal of supporting, not replacing, clinical judgement, and the introduction is unusually positive about autistic children's engagement with technology, citing evidence of 'inherent dependence on technology and positive behavior toward computer-based training'. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement statement. [RQ1.3] Table 1 reports sex, group size, and mean and standard deviation of age: autistic 20 male, 8.40 +/- 2.45 years; comparison 20 male, 8.45 +/- 1.90 years, with an overall span of about 4 to 12 years. Age matching is excellent - the means differ by three weeks - though the autistic group is more dispersed. Beyond this, nothing: no IQ or developmental quotient despite the autistic group being labelled high-functioning, no language measure, no adaptive functioning, no comorbidity, no medication, no socioeconomic status, no race or ethnicity, and no autism severity. Two features of the reported demographics deserve emphasis. The sample is 100% male in both groups. This is stated in the table and never mentioned again - not as a design decision, not as a limitation, not in the conclusion - even though the introduction itself notes that autism prevalence is higher in boys, which is a reason to sample boys but not a reason to leave the restriction undiscussed. And the participants are Iranian children in Tehran while the facial stimuli are Japanese women from the JAFFE database, so every trial involves other-race face processing. The paper's own literature review cites work on differences between autistic and typically developing children in processing same-race versus other-race faces, and even reports that study's 70% accuracy as a comparator, yet never connects that literature to its own stimulus choice. [RQ1.4] Weak and under-specified. Autistic status rests on admission to the recruiting clinic, where 'the children were admitted into this clinic based on the diagnosis made by a pediatric psychiatrist and a pediatric clinical psychologist and underwent a comprehensive evaluation', restated in the inclusion criteria simply as 'the diagnosis of autism spectrum disorders made by specialists'. Two clinicians of different disciplines is better than one, and the involvement of a psychiatrist and a clinical psychologist is a reasonable clinical standard, but no diagnostic instrument is named, no DSM or ICD version is cited, the 'comprehensive evaluation' is not described, no diagnosis date or interval to testing is given, and no reliability is quantified. The comparison group is weaker still: children were recruited from a mainstream public elementary school and are called 'normal' and 'healthy', with no screening instrument administered, no exclusion criteria listed and no statement that autism or developmental concerns were ruled out - so undetected autistic traits or other neurodevelopmental conditions in the comparison group cannot be excluded. The autistic group additionally passed two functional gates that shape who was studied: a therapist's judgement that the child had 'relative perception of people's faces', and the ability to sit at a computer and attend to images. Both are defensible for a face-processing task but both further narrow an already high-functioning sample. [RQ1.5] No cognitive, language, adaptive or severity instrument was administered to any participant in either group. The autistic sample is described only as having 'high-performance autism disorder', a label with no accompanying score, cut-off or source, and the conclusion leans on it interpretively - arguing that accuracy above 73% is 'desirable given the status of children with high-performance autism disorder', i.e. that the task is intrinsically harder in a less impaired sample. That is a reasonable argument but it cannot be evaluated, because no measure of functioning or severity exists to place the sample on any scale, nor to check whether the misclassified children were the less affected ones. Two informal proxies appear in the inclusion criteria - a therapist's judgement of the child's face perception, and the capacity to sit and attend at a computer - and both operate as gates rather than as measurements. The absence of IQ is particularly consequential here because the index task is a visual matching task drawn from the same family as nonverbal reasoning tests: any group difference in fixation distribution over candidate figures could as easily reflect differences in matching strategy or task comprehension as differences in social attention, and there is no covariate with which to separate them. [RQ2.1] Goal: to classify autistic from non-autistic children by analysing eye-tracking data captured while they play a purpose-designed computer game, motivated explicitly by the shortage of diagnostic specialists relative to a growing autistic population and the wish for a system 'easily applicable by not-so-expert users'. The game was designed with expert guidance around two objectives drawn from picture-exchange practice: face recognition and facial-expression matching. Findings as reported: precision 76.6% and accuracy 73.8% with all 18 features, which the paper presents as the best of four nested feature subsets and describes as 'a suitable diagnostics system'. Findings as they should be read: those numbers are the TOTAL column of Table 5, pooling training, validation and test rows, and the held-out test values in the same table are precision 66.7%, accuracy 58.3%, sensitivity 57.1% and specificity 60.0% - between 6 and 10 points above a 50% chance level on 36 observations. Across all four feature subsets the pattern is identical and consistent: total accuracies of 65.0-73.8% concealing test accuracies of 52.8-58.3%, with training accuracies of 67.9-78.6%. The gap between training and test performance is present in every configuration and is never remarked on. Two subsets also show unstable held-out behaviour, with test sensitivity of 33.3% for 'around FIGs' and test specificity of 33.3% for 'on FIGs'. [RQ2.2] Single-city, two-source recruitment in Tehran, with testing centralised at one laboratory. Autistic children came from the Daily Rehabilitation Clinic for Children with Special Disorders, a specialist service affiliated to the Family Institute of Shahid Beheshti University; comparison children came from Namjoo public elementary school. All eye tracking took place on one stationary system at the Faculty of Education and Psychology, Shahid Beheshti University, so unlike some studies in this corpus the acquisition chain is identical for both groups and no equipment confound arises. The recruitment geometry is nonetheless the standard clinic-versus-school case-control arrangement at 50% prevalence, and here it is compounded by asymmetric filtering: the autistic group faced five inclusion criteria and two exclusion criteria that removed 20% of those approached, while no criteria at all are stated for the school-recruited comparison group. The children who could not tolerate sitting at the computer or could not be calibrated - plausibly those with greater sensory or attentional difficulty - are precisely those absent from the analysed autistic sample. [RQ2.3] A two-stage computer game built specifically for this study, informed by picture-exchange approaches in which cards depicting facial expressions convey concepts non-verbally. Stage S1 (face recognition): three photographs of Japanese women are displayed in a row beside a target figure, and the child must identify which candidate matches the target. Stage S2 (expression matching): the same women are shown with happy, sad and surprised expressions, with 'happy' as the target. All stimuli come from the JAFFE database. Children were familiarised with example images first, and conditions were checked as suitable before the full run of 240 game images. The design has clear merits - it is engaging rather than passive, it has an objectively correct answer on every trial so gaze can be interpreted against task demands, and it targets a behaviour (facial expression processing) with strong theoretical links to autism. Three features constrain what it can show. The stimuli are other-race for this sample, and the other-race face effect is a documented modulator of both face-processing performance and gaze distribution - the paper cites this literature but not in relation to its own design. Only static images are used, so no dynamic or interactive social content is present. And the analysis discards trial structure entirely: fixations are pooled into region counts and durations, so whether the child looked at the correct candidate, in what order, or how their strategy evolved across 240 trials is not represented, even though the single-child illustration in Fig. 7 shows exactly that kind of trial-level reasoning being informative. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up, no test-retest reliability. Ethics reporting is the strongest element of the paper's governance: approval was obtained from the Research Ethics Committee of Islamic Azad University, Tehran Science and Research Branch, with the approval identifier IR.IAU.SRB.REC.1401.152 stated in a dedicated Ethics subsection and repeated in the declarations - a named committee and a verifiable reference number, which most reports in this corpus do not provide. Consent is handled less completely: parental consent appears as an inclusion criterion for the autistic group only, with no consent statement for the school-recruited comparison children and no mention of child assent. Funding (none received) and competing interests (none) are declared. [RQ2.5] Stimuli: the Japanese Female Facial Expression (JAFFE) database, presented at 1024 x 768. Capture: a stationary eye-tracking system at Shahid Beheshti University, depicted in a photograph but never identified - no manufacturer, model, sampling rate, spatial accuracy or precision figure appears anywhere in the paper, which is a significant omission because every feature is a fixation count or duration and fixation detection depends directly on sampling rate and on the detection algorithm's parameters, neither of which is stated. Analysis: MATLAB R2020b, using fixation detail output (start, duration, end, X, Y) and the Neural Network facilities for the MLP. Calibration was performed and used as a gate, with failure to calibrate an explicit exclusion criterion, but the protocol, point count and accuracy threshold are not described. Out-of-range samples were retained by enlarging the analysis space beyond the stimulus and labelling the surplus 'OUT', which is a pragmatic choice but implies non-trivial tracking error that is never quantified. [RQ2.6] Split between a well-specified experiment and an under-specified model. Reproducible: the game's two stages and objectives, the JAFFE stimulus source, the 240-image protocol, the stimulus resolution and the region segmentation with its named zones, the 18-feature definition as fixation count and fixation time per region, the MATLAB version, the training algorithm (scaled conjugate gradient backpropagation) and the activation functions (tanh hidden, sigmoid output), and the ethics approval identifier. Not reproducible: the eye tracker itself, the fixation-detection parameters, the MLP's hidden-layer count and node counts, the learning rate and iteration count that were 'optimised' by MSE, the random split and seed, and the code. Data are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. The single most consequential reporting gap is not technical but presentational: because the abstract and conclusion quote the pooled total rather than the test column, a reader who does not open the tables will take away a figure roughly 15 points higher than the study's own held-out result. [RQ2.7] The three stated limitations are real but peripheral - no transfer to adults, a desire for richer graph features, and the need for clinically overlapping comparison conditions, the last being a genuinely important acknowledgement that the study can only separate autistic children from unscreened schoolchildren. The unstated limitations dominate. First and most serious, the reported precision and accuracy are pooled across training, validation and test. The tables disaggregate honestly, so the information is present, but the abstract, results narrative and conclusion all quote the total. For the best configuration the held-out accuracy is 58.3% against a 50% chance level - on 36 observations, a difference of three. Second, the modelled rows are not children. Arithmetic on the reported percentages fixes the dataset at 240 rows split 168/36/36 in the MATLAB default proportions, so each of the 40 children contributes six rows that are randomly scattered across the three partitions, and every test row has five siblings from the same child in training. Given that the features are region-level fixation counts and durations, which are strongly stable within an individual, this is a direct route for identity information to leak. Third, four feature subsets were compared on the same data and the best reported as the study's result. Fourth, the stimuli are other-race faces for this sample, an effect the paper's own citations show it is aware of. Fifth, 20% of the approached autistic children were excluded for non-cooperation or calibration failure with no comparable filter on the comparison group and no description of those excluded. Sixth, the sample is entirely male and this is never discussed. Seventh, no IQ or cognitive measure exists to separate social-attention differences from task-comprehension differences on what is essentially a visual matching task. Eighth, ROC curves are displayed without any AUC value, so the one metric that would summarise discriminability across thresholds is shown graphically and not reported numerically. [RQ2.9] Three directions are stated. Enrich the feature set derived from the eye-tracking graph in order to improve precision and accuracy - a reasonable ambition, and one the study has itself left unexploited, since the introduction develops a graph-theoretic framing of fixations as vertices and saccades as edges but no graph metric is ever computed. Extend the classifier to include conditions that overlap with autism so that differential diagnosis becomes possible - the most valuable of the three, and an acknowledgement that separating autistic children from unscreened schoolchildren does not establish clinical utility. And note that a system trained on children will not transfer to adults without retraining. Not mentioned, and more pressing: participant-level validation, reporting held-out rather than pooled performance, an independent cohort, culturally matched stimuli, inclusion of girls, and any cognitive covariate. [RQ3.1] Visual attention during face recognition and facial-expression matching, operationalised entirely spatially. For each defined region of the display - on each of the three candidate figures, on the reference figure, around each of these, and in two regions outside them - two quantities are computed: the number of fixation nodes falling there and the total fixation time spent there. The behavioural hypothesis is the standard one for eye tracking in autism, that autistic and non-autistic children distribute gaze differently when required to compare faces and match expressions, with the paper's own framing that 'the recorded data on eye movements suggest a clear difference between the eye fixation patterns of normal subjects and subjects with autism spectrum disorders'. Two aspects of the operationalisation are worth noting for the synthesis. The regions are defined by task structure (which figure) rather than by facial anatomy - there are no eye, mouth or face-interior areas of interest - so the classic autism finding of reduced eye-region fixation cannot be tested by this feature set at all; what is measured is which stimulus the child compared and how long they dwelt on it, which is closer to a matching-strategy measure than to a social-attention measure. And the distinction between 'on' and 'around' a figure is the study's one attempt to capture a qualitative gaze property, on the implicit reasoning that fixating adjacent to rather than on a face is itself informative; the ablation shows neither subset alone outperforms their union. [RQ3.2] No fusion. A single modality with 18 features from one sensor, and the four reported conditions are nested subsets of that same feature set rather than distinct modalities. One near-miss is worth recording: the discussion states that 'the children's verbal responses to the observed game were also recorded during the test' and that 'the results indicate the significant matching of the provided responses to the recorded eye-tracking patterns'. A second behavioural channel - whether the child correctly identified the target, and what they said - was therefore captured and would have been straightforward to fuse with gaze, all the more so because the task has an objectively correct answer on every one of 240 trials, so accuracy, latency and error patterns were available at no additional cost. None of it is quantified, analysed or entered into the model; the claimed correspondence between speech and gaze is asserted without a single supporting number. This is the same pattern seen in the tablet-based motor study charted elsewhere in this review, where the cognitive-performance channel was deliberately discarded to isolate the motor signal: a second modality present in the raw data and suppressed rather than fused. [RQ4.1] A single shallow multilayer perceptron, trained by error backpropagation using the scaled conjugate gradient algorithm, with hyperbolic tangent activation in the hidden layer and sigmoid activation at the output, implemented in MATLAB R2020b. No alternative classifier was evaluated - no SVM, random forest, logistic regression or even a linear baseline - despite the introduction surveying several such methods, so there is no evidence that the neural network is better suited to 18 features and 240 rows than a simpler model would be. Nor is the network itself specified: the paper devotes a paragraph to explaining that the number of hidden layers and nodes is problem-dependent and then never states what was used, and the iteration count and learning coefficient are described as optimised by MSE without saying on which partition. For a dataset of 240 rows and 18 features, a shallow MLP is a defensible choice and overfitting is the expected risk; the reported train-to-test gaps of roughly 20 points in every configuration are consistent with that risk having materialised. [RQ4.2] An 18-dimensional vector of region-based fixation statistics per observation. The stimulus space, 1024 x 768, was augmented beyond its true extent to accommodate out-of-range gaze samples, then partitioned into named regions: on FIG 1, FIG 2 and FIG 3; on the Reference FIG; around each of these; and two OUT regions below the outer figures. Fixations were clustered by location of node aggregation and two quantities extracted per region - the number of fixation nodes and the fixation time. Four nested subsets of this matrix were evaluated separately: around the figures, on the figures, on and around the figures, and all features. The representation carries no temporal information: no scan-path order, no saccade amplitudes or directions, no transition probabilities between regions, no within-trial dynamics, and no trial-to-trial evolution across the 240 images. This is a notable gap given the introduction's extended development of a graph-theoretic view in which fixations are vertices and saccades are edges - Fig. 6 even displays such a graph for one autistic child - because every quantity that graph representation would naturally yield (degree distribution, edge weights, path structure, transition entropy) is left uncomputed, and the model receives only vertex-region tallies. [RQ4.3] Precision, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, each reported separately for the training, validation and test partitions and for the pooled total, across all four feature subsets - sixty-four numbers in total. The disaggregation is a real reporting virtue and is what makes it possible to see what the study actually achieved: it is only because the tables separate the columns that a reader can recover the held-out test accuracy of 58.3% behind the abstract's 73.8%. Two summary tables then compare precision and accuracy across subsets, again by partition. ROC curves are plotted for all four configurations, but no AUC is reported for any, so the single number that would summarise discriminability independent of threshold is presented only as a picture. Also missing: confidence intervals of any kind, F1, calibration, and any participant-level metric. Given that the test partition contains 36 observations, a confidence interval would have been the most informative addition - at 58.3% on 36 observations the interval comfortably includes chance. [RQ4.4] Limited but honest. The features are individually meaningful - counts and durations of looking at specified places - and the region diagram makes each one concrete. The four-subset comparison functions as a coarse importance analysis, showing that the full set outperforms either the figure regions or their surroundings alone, and the paper's interpretation of this is straightforward and reasonable: more regions provide more detail. A single-child worked example traces the fixation points and times for one trial and shows the child concentrating on the target and the matching candidate before answering correctly, which usefully demonstrates that the raw data are behaviourally interpretable. Against this, no group-level feature analysis is reported at all - no means, no distributions, no effect sizes, no statistical comparison of where the two groups looked - so the paper never states, and cannot state, what visual behaviour distinguishes autistic from comparison children in its own data. It reports only that a network reached a certain accuracy. For a study whose stated purpose is to support specialist decision-making, the absence of any description of the discriminative behaviour is a substantive gap: a clinician can act on 'autistic children fixated less on the reference face' but not on 'an unspecified MLP scored 73.8% pooled across partitions'. [RQ4.5] The weakest element, and it fails on two counts that compound one another. First, the reported performance is not held-out. The abstract, results narrative and conclusion all quote 76.6% precision and 73.8% accuracy, which Table 5 identifies as the TOTAL column - the pooled figure across training, validation and test. The test column of the same table reads 66.7% precision and 58.3% accuracy, with sensitivity 57.1% and specificity 60.0%. The same pattern holds for every feature subset: total accuracies of 65.0-73.8% against test accuracies of 52.8-58.3%, with training accuracies of 67.9-78.6%. A roughly 20-point train-to-test gap in all four configurations is the signature of overfitting on a small dataset, and it is neither reported nor discussed. Second, the split is over observations rather than children. The paper says only that '70 percent of data ... were used for training and the remaining 30 percent for tests and validation', but the reported percentages determine the arithmetic exactly: with 240 rows split 168/36/36 in the MATLAB Neural Network Toolbox default proportions, 78.6% of 168 is 132, 66.7% of 36 is 24, 58.3% of 36 is 21, and (132 + 24 + 21)/240 = 73.75%, reproducing the reported total to the decimal, and the same reconstruction works for the other three subsets. Forty children therefore contribute six rows each, randomly scattered, so every test row has five siblings from the same child in the training set. Because the features are per-region fixation counts and durations - quantities that are highly stable within an individual and reflect that person's habitual looking style as much as their diagnosis - this is a direct channel for identity leakage, and it means even the 58.3% test figure is optimistic relative to a genuinely unseen child. Two further issues: four feature subsets were compared on the same data and the best reported, and no chance baseline, permutation test or confidence interval accompanies any figure, although the balanced design makes chance exactly 50% and the test partition is small enough that three observations separate the reported result from it. The corrective is available and would be worth doing: partition the 40 children, generate observations within partitions, tune the network on training children only, choose the feature subset on a development set, and report test-column figures with confidence intervals as the study's result. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: Artificial neural network; Autism spectrum disorder; Computer games; Eye-tracking. 'Computer games' rather than 'serious games' or 'gamified assessment' reflects the paper's framing of the task as a therapeutic-game artefact repurposed for measurement, and the introduction devotes several paragraphs to games as therapy before turning to classification. No application term - screening, diagnosis, classification - appears in the keywords, although the body text uses 'diagnosis system' freely. Terms carried through the body: therapeutic games, facial emotion recognition, expression matching, fixation duration, fixation count, graph theory, eye-tracking graph, multilayer perceptron, scaled conjugate gradient, confusion matrix. [RQ5.2] Signal, Image and Video Processing 17:4357-4365, Springer - a signal-processing engineering journal, published as an Original Paper. The venue accounts for the reporting balance: the metric tables are exhaustive and correctly disaggregated by training, validation and test partition, and ROC curves are plotted for every configuration, while the clinical apparatus is minimal (no diagnostic instrument, no cognitive measure, no screening of the comparison group) and the eye tracker is never identified. Received 30 March 2023, revised 25 May 2023, accepted 10 June 2023, published online 4 July 2023. [RQ5.3] Published 2023 from the Islamic Azad University Science and Research Branch and Tabriz Branch, with the Institute for Cognitive and Brain Sciences and the Faculty of Education and Psychology of Shahid Beheshti University, Tehran; no funding received. The framing is workforce scarcity: 'since the proper diagnosis of this condition depends on the correct and accurate decision of the specialist, the availability of adequate specialists in this area seems necessary. Unfortunately, the number of these specialists is low with respect to the growing autistic population', leading to the goal of a system 'easily applicable by not-so-expert users'. That is a task-shifting rationale rather than an accuracy-improvement one, and it recurs across the Iranian and Chinese papers in this corpus. The introduction is unusually wide-ranging for a short engineering paper, surveying therapeutic games, socially assistive robots, brain-computer interfaces and fuzzy learning before arriving at its own design, and it conspicuously cites work on same-race versus other-race face processing in autism without applying that literature to its own choice of Japanese stimuli for Iranian children. The conclusion's call to include 'conditions overlapping with autism for differential diagnosis' is a 2023-typical acknowledgement that the case-control geometry is the field's binding constraint.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional diagnostic-classification study with an embedded human benchmark, conducted at the Center for Autism Research, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia. Forty-four adults enrolled and 42 were analysed (15 autistic, 27 neurotypical; two excluded for absent consent to this specific analysis or unprocessable data), all native and fluent English speakers, with the groups matched on chronological age, sex ratio, and WASI-II full-scale and verbal IQ. Diagnostic status was confirmed prospectively for this study by the Clinical Best Estimate process, informed by ADOS-2 Module 4 and adhering to DSM-5 criteria; controls were recruited deliberately as neurotypical rather than merely lacking a diagnosis. In parallel, 19 human raters were recruited - 8 doctoral-level autism experts with extensive training at the centre, and 11 non-experts, mostly BA-level psychology staff with general familiarity but no specialised training - each of whom rated all 42 participants. IRB approval was obtained from CHOP and the work was funded by four NIH grants.
narrative_rows.methods: Participants completed a slightly modified Contextual Assessment of Social Skills: two 3-minute face-to-face conversations with different confederates, one interested and one bored. Only the interested condition was analysed. Confederates were 10 undergraduate or BA-level research staff, blind to diagnostic status and unaware of the dependent variables, trained to speak no more than half the time, to wait 10 s before initiating and 5 s before re-initiating after a pause, and otherwise to converse naturally; the prompt to both parties is quoted verbatim in the paper. Recording used an in-house dual-camera device (two 1080p cameras at 30 fps, back to back on a floor stand between the pair). The computer-vision pipeline fitted a 3D morphable model frame by frame using 3DI, chosen because it learns facial identity across frames - so identity bias is modelled and removed - and accepts camera parameters, which the authors state is critical for separating expression from head pose. The model's default PCA expression basis was replaced by a purpose-built set of 60 localised components so that each dimension maps to a nameable facial region; seven nose and cheek components were discarded, leaving 53 expression dimensions plus yaw, pitch and roll. Windowed cross-correlation was applied to all 56 x 56 ordered pairs of these time series, with 50% window overlap and forward lag only on the second series so that direction is preserved, each pair summarised by the mean and standard deviation of its maximal cross-correlation - 6,272 features per participant. A linear SVM at default C = 1 was evaluated by nested cross-validation with the window length (1, 2, 4 or 6 s; 2 s selected in most folds) as the only tuned hyperparameter, using 10-fold cross-validation repeated 100 times with participant order shuffled. Human raters saw the participant and confederate cropped to head and neck, side by side, with audio removed to match the AI's information, in randomised order, one viewing per video and no revisiting.
narrative_rows.outcomes: The AI pipeline achieved 80.5% average accuracy, against 83.1% for expert clinicians, 78.3% for non-experts and 80.3% for all human raters combined. Model operating characteristics were positive predictive value 0.86, negative predictive value 0.79, sensitivity 0.55 and specificity 0.95 - a conservative classifier that detects just over half the autistic adults while almost never misclassifying a neurotypical one. The study's principal finding concerns errors rather than accuracy: of five participants misclassified by a majority of human raters, four were correctly classified by the model, including the single hardest case, which only 21% of raters got right. Per-participant accuracy of humans and AI correlated at only rho = 0.35, falling to 0.19 once participants correctly classified by at least 95% of raters were removed, and the scatter plot's lower-left quadrant - cases hard for both - is essentially empty. Feature-weight analysis showed head-pose-to-pose correlations carrying the greatest average weight, with pose-eye and mouth-related coordination prominent among the top individual features; against their share of the 6,272-feature pool, pose features are about 2.5 times over-represented in the top 10 and mouth features about 1.6 times.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The comparison group is neurotypical adults recruited as clear cases, so the study establishes separation between well-defined ends of a distribution rather than performance in a population where the alternative to autism is another condition - the authors identify this themselves and call for neurodiverse samples. Sensitivity of 0.55 is reported in a single sentence and never discussed, although a tool that misses 45% of autistic adults cannot serve as the screening technology the conclusion proposes in the direction it proposes; the abstract and conclusion quote only the accuracy. No majority-class baseline is computed, so the 80.5% is not placed against its 64.3% floor, and no confidence intervals, AUC or significance tests accompany any figure - with 42 participants one case is 2.4 accuracy points, and the error-overlap finding rests on five hard cases. The human and AI conditions are not strictly matched, since raters saw the confederate alongside the participant while the model saw only the participant, and raters were told in advance that every case was clear-cut. Only the interested condition of the CASS was analysed, leaving the bored condition - the natural test of whether the coordination signature survives a change in the partner's behaviour - collected but unused. No ADOS-2 severity score is reported despite the instrument having been administered, so it is not possible to check whether the 45% the model missed were the less affected. Participants are cognitively able, verbally fluent adults at a specialist centre.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The most methodologically careful study charted in this review so far, and the only one that asks the question the rest of the corpus takes for granted: not whether a model can classify autism, but whether its classifications tell a clinician anything they did not already know. The premise is stated plainly - an AI tool has negligible utility if its decisions and its errors overlap with the clinician's - and the design follows from it, giving 8 expert clinicians, 11 non-experts and a computer-vision pipeline the identical 3-minute silent videos. The answer is genuinely informative: performance is comparable (80.5% versus 83.1% for experts), but the errors barely overlap, and four of the five participants that a majority of human raters got wrong were classified correctly by the model. That is a different and more useful finding than another accuracy figure, and it reframes the field's evaluation question. Several methodological features also make this the reference point against which other studies here should be read. It is the only study in the corpus that treats facial identity as something to model and subtract rather than as an accidental source of accuracy. Its representation is a coordination analysis rather than a content analysis, and the feature-weight results locate the discriminative signal specifically in cross-channel pairs - head pose with itself, head pose with eye movement - which is a more testable claim than the generic assertion that fusion helps. Its validation is participant-level by construction, nested, repeated 100 times with shuffling, with no feature selection and one tuned hyperparameter. Its interpretability is a design constraint, with the expression basis deliberately rebuilt to be localised at a stated modelling cost. And its reference standard, Clinical Best Estimate with ADOS-2 Module 4, is the strongest here. The counterweight the review should carry forward is the sensitivity of 0.55, which sits alongside Megerian et al.'s FDA pivotal trial and Kong et al.'s prevalence arithmetic as evidence that headline accuracy is the least informative number a study of this kind can report.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Forty-four adults enrolled (17 autistic, 27 neurotypical), of whom two were excluded because they had not consented to this particular set of experiments or their data could not be processed, giving a final sample of 42: 15 autistic and 27 neurotypical, i.e. 35.7% autism prevalence. All were native and fluent English speakers. A second sample is central to the design and is reported with equal care: 19 human raters, comprising 8 expert clinicians (doctoral-level, with extensive autism training at the Center for Autism Research) and 11 non-experts (mostly BA-level psychology staff with some familiarity with autism but no specialised training), all of whom rated all 42 videos. A third group also participates without being analysed: 10 conversation confederates (3 male, 7 female, all native English speakers, undergraduate or BA-level research assistants), semi-randomly assigned by availability and clinical judgement, and blind to participant diagnostic status. The unit of analysis for the model is the participant - one 6,272-dimensional vector each - which is why no within-participant leakage is possible. [RQ1.2] 'Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)' and 'adults with autism' predominate, paired with 'neurotypical (NT) individuals' rather than the more common 'typically developing' or, worse, 'normal'. 'Neurotypical' is a term originating in the autistic community and its use here, in a paper from a major autism research centre, is a meaningful marker: it frames the comparison group as one neurotype among others rather than as a standard of normality. The conclusion goes further, calling for future work 'in predicting ASD diagnosis from neurodiverse samples' - importing 'neurodiverse' as a technical descriptor of a clinically mixed population, which is both an accurate usage and an unusual one in this literature. Clinical description is measured throughout: autism is 'defined by observable behavioral cues - what a person does well or not well, too little or too much', its core traits are 'observable differences in social communication, social reciprocity, nonverbal communication, and relationships', and the word 'differences' rather than 'deficits' is used where most papers in this corpus use the latter. The framing of purpose is also non-replacement: the stated aim is to establish whether AI adds anything beyond clinician judgement, on the explicit premise that 'clinicians would have little interest in or benefit from incorporating AI algorithms if their decisions - and errors - highly overlap with their own'. There is no autistic-community involvement statement. [RQ1.3] The retrieved text states that the groups did not differ significantly on mean chronological age, full-scale IQ, verbal IQ or sex ratio, with the statistics themselves in a table not recoverable from the extracted text. That set of matched variables is nonetheless the most complete in this corpus for a study of this size, and two elements are worth emphasising because their absence undermines so many other studies charted here. IQ was measured with a standardised instrument (WASI-II) in both groups and matched on both full-scale and verbal estimates - so the classification cannot be attributed to a cognitive-ability gap, which is an uncontrolled confound in the majority of studies in this review. And sex ratio was matched rather than left uncontrolled or eliminated by sampling only boys. All participants were native and fluent English speakers by inclusion, which removes language proficiency as a confound in a conversational paradigm but also narrows generalisability. What is not reported in the retrieved text: race or ethnicity, socioeconomic status, comorbidity, medication, and - notably given that ADOS-2 was administered - any severity score. The sample is adults, cognitively able enough to complete an unstructured 3-minute conversation with a stranger, and it is a research-registry population at a specialist centre rather than a community sample. [RQ1.4] The strongest reference standard encountered in this review. Diagnostic status was 'confirmed as part of this study' - established prospectively rather than inherited from records - using the Clinical Best Estimate process, informed by ADOS-2 Module 4 and adhering to DSM-5 criteria. Clinical Best Estimate is the accepted research gold standard precisely because it integrates a standardised observational instrument, developmental history and clinical judgement rather than resting on any single source, and Module 4 is the correct ADOS-2 module for verbally fluent adolescents and adults. Neurotypical status was not merely the absence of a diagnosis: controls were 'recruited specifically as neurotypical controls', and raters were told they were 'clear cases of individuals without autism'. That framing is a genuine strength for a benchmark study - it means the human raters' 80.3% accuracy is not depressed by ambiguous controls - but it is simultaneously the study's central external-validity limit, since the two groups are drawn from the well-separated ends of a distribution that a real screening population fills continuously. The authors say so themselves in the conclusion. Two further points: the ADOS-2 was administered but no calibrated severity score is reported, so the autistic sample's position on the spectrum is unquantified; and the conversation confederates were blind to diagnostic status and unaware of the dependent variables, so the elicitation itself was not differentially shaped by knowledge of group membership - a control that few conversational studies in this corpus implement. [RQ1.5] Cognitive ability was measured properly: WASI-II full-scale and verbal IQ estimates were obtained for the whole sample and compared between groups, with no significant difference. This is the correct handling and it removes the single most pervasive confound in this literature. Language ability is indexed by verbal IQ and by the requirement that all participants be native and fluent English speakers, which matters for a task whose entire stimulus is spontaneous conversation. Autism severity, however, is not reported. ADOS-2 Module 4 was administered as part of the diagnostic process, so calibrated severity scores were almost certainly available, yet none appears - so it is impossible to say where the 15 autistic adults sit on the spectrum, whether the 45% the model failed to detect were the less severely affected, or whether the four participants that humans misjudged but the model caught differed systematically in severity. That last question is the one the paper's own error-overlap analysis makes most interesting, and severity data would have gone a long way towards answering it. No adaptive-functioning, comorbidity or motor measure is reported either. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is not primarily to build a better classifier but to answer a prior question the field has left open: how do AI predictions correspond to human ones? The framing is explicit and is the paper's organising logic - 'the utility of an AI algorithm would be negligible if it provides little information beyond what clinicians can readily infer' - so the study is designed as a benchmark rather than a demonstration. Nineteen raters (8 doctoral-level autism experts, 11 non-experts) and a computer-vision pipeline were given the same 3-minute silent videos of 42 adults in casual conversation. Findings: AI accuracy 80.5%, expert clinicians 83.1%, non-experts 78.3%, all humans 80.3% - so the model performs at approximately expert level on this evidence. The operating characteristics show why accuracy alone is misleading: PPV 0.86, NPV 0.79, specificity 0.95 and sensitivity 0.55, meaning the classifier is highly conservative and detects only just over half the autistic adults. The paper's real result is the error analysis. Of five participants misclassified by a majority of human raters, four were correctly classified by the model, including the hardest case, which only 21% of raters got right. Per-participant accuracy of humans and AI correlated at just rho = 0.35, falling to 0.19 once the participants nearly all raters got right are removed, and the lower-left quadrant of the scatter - hard for both - is essentially empty. Feature weights point to head pose and its coordination with eye movement, and to mouth-related coordination, as the dominant signal, with both categories over-represented in the top-weighted features relative to their share of the feature pool. [RQ2.2] Single site: the Center for Autism Research at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, with the University of Pennsylvania. This is a specialist research centre, and both arms of the study reflect that - the participants are a research-registry sample assessed by Clinical Best Estimate on site, and the 19 raters are the centre's own doctoral clinicians and BA-level staff. The rater sample is therefore an unusually strong human benchmark (these are people who assess autistic adults professionally) and simultaneously a narrow one (they share an institution, a training culture and, plausibly, prior exposure to similar video material). The recording setting is a laboratory room with a floor-standing dual-camera device between the two conversation partners, and the paradigm is a semi-structured assessment rather than a clinical encounter. The recruitment geometry is case-control at 35.7% prevalence with deliberately clear-cut controls, which the authors flag as the key generalisation limit. Against that, the paradigm itself is deliberately designed for scalability outside such settings: the conversation partner is a non-clinician, the interaction lasts three minutes, and the only equipment is a camera - which is the basis for the claim that this could serve as a screening procedure. [RQ2.3] The Contextual Assessment of Social Skills, slightly modified - a semi-structured assessment of conversational ability designed to mimic a real-life first-time encounter. Each participant held two 3-minute face-to-face conversations with two different confederates: an interested condition, in which the confederate engaged verbally and non-verbally, and a bored condition, in which the confederate signalled disengagement through one-word answers, few follow-up questions, neutral affect and reduced eye contact and gesture. Only the interested condition is analysed here. The confederate protocol is specified to an unusual degree: 10 confederates (3 male, 7 female, all native English speakers, undergraduate or BA-level research staff), blind to diagnostic status and unaware of the dependent variables, trained to speak no more than 50% of the time, to wait 10 s before initiating and 5 s before re-initiating after a pause, and otherwise to converse naturally; the prompt given to both parties is quoted verbatim. That combination - a live, unscripted, genuinely social task with a standardised and blinded partner - is close to the ideal for this literature, since it preserves naturalism without letting the partner's behaviour vary with what they believe about the participant. Two design choices constrain the result. Audio was discarded from both the AI and human conditions, so speech content, prosody and turn-taking timing - all diagnostically informative and all captured on the recording - are excluded by design in order to make the human-AI comparison fair.
