The authors state the limitation squarely: participants were recruited without intellectual difficulties but 'we did not obtain any actual IQ values', so the study 'does not adequately take into account the influence of intellectual level', and the sample comprises 'only a small number of mild (high-functioning) cases'. Two consequences follow. Because the FEIT is a cognitive task with a correct answer, intellectual level plausibly affects both recognition accuracy and viewing strategy. And because SRS-2 was used to select which controls were retained, a severity-related variable enters the sampling as well as the description. Notably, no analysis relates any of these severity scores to model output, so the rich phenotyping is used descriptively rather than analytically. [RQ2.1] The stated aim is to test whether modelling the specificity of gaze to particular facial expressions improves classification, on the premise - supported by prior basic research but not previously operationalised - that groups differ in gaze for some emotions and not others. The proposal is to classify each of the 21 or 32 FEIT images separately and then aggregate the per-image decisions with a random forest that learns which images matter, rather than by unweighted voting. Findings, all reported with binomial tests against chance and none oversold. For autistic adults versus controls the weighted CNN reached 0.710 accuracy (sensitivity 0.733, specificity 0.688), significantly above chance and 10 points above the unweighted CNN. For autistic children the weighted models reached 0.667 (weighted CNN sensitivity 0.600, specificity 0.733), significant and 16.7 points above the unweighted CNN, with the weighting raising sensitivity from 0.286 to 0.600. For schizophrenia the best models reached 0.645, only marginally above chance (p = 0.052), and weighting produced no improvement at all. The statistical analysis explains why the method behaves differently across conditions and is the more interesting result: in adults, reduced fixation at the eyes distinguished the schizophrenia group from controls for every one of the seven emotions, but the autistic group from controls for only two (anger and neutral), while scan-path length distinguished autism from controls for six of seven emotions. So the classic reduced-eye-looking signature was present uniformly in schizophrenia and only selectively in autism - which is exactly the condition under which per-image weighting helps for one and not the other. In children, almost no gaze feature reached significance at all, yet the weighted models still exceeded chance. [RQ2.2] Single-country, clinic-linked laboratory testing in Nara and Osaka, Japan, with participants recruited through the psychiatry department of Nara Medical University School of Medicine and Osaka Psychiatric Medical Center and tested on equipment at the Nara Institute of Science and Technology. The setting is a controlled screen-based assessment at a fixed 65 cm viewing distance rather than a naturalistic or point-of-care one, and no deployment scenario is proposed. Recruitment geometry is the standard clinical case-control arrangement, with the important qualification that both clinical groups come from psychiatric services and both are contrasted against the same actively screened control group, which is what makes the parallel comparison meaningful. One setting-related feature is unaddressed: the FEIT is a Western instrument and the participants are Japanese, so every trial involves other-race face processing, in a task whose entire outcome is where on a face the participant looks. Cross-cultural differences in face-scanning are well documented and the paper does not mention them. [RQ2.3] The Facial Emotion Identification Test, a validated instrument that uses morphing to generate expressions at varying intensity, including deliberately weak ones - which is central to the paper's argument, since the finding it converges on concerns subtle rather than prototypical expressions. Each trial: a one-second central fixation cross, then a face for 5 seconds, then a verbal response naming the emotion. Adults saw 21 images (three each of happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust, neutral) and children 32 (eight each of happiness, sadness, anger, surprise), all in random order. Three properties make this among the better paradigms in the corpus. It has an objectively correct answer on every trial, so task performance and gaze behaviour are separately measurable - and the result is striking: FEIT scores were essentially identical across groups (adults 15.5, 14.5 and 14.3 out of 21 for controls, autism and schizophrenia; children 22.1 and 22.2 out of 32), meaning the groups recognised the emotions equally well while looking at the faces differently. Any gaze difference therefore cannot be attributed to differential task success. The stimulus set is systematically structured by emotion, which is what makes per-image weighting meaningful and interpretable rather than an arbitrary ensemble. And the one-second fixation cross standardises the starting gaze position across trials and participants, so scan-path measures begin from a common origin. The paradigm's limitations are the short trial (5 seconds, giving at most 600 gaze samples), the static stimuli, and the copyright restriction that prevents the images being reproduced or shared. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single session per participant, no follow-up and no test-retest reliability for any gaze feature. The two datasets are age-stratified rather than longitudinal - adults and children are separate samples, not the same people at two ages - although the introduction motivates the design partly by an interest in 'the developmental trajectory in processing emotional stimuli in neurodevelopmental conditions', and the parallel analysis does permit a cautious comparison across age groups, which the discussion makes: anger is highly weighted in both the adult and child autism models, suggesting a possible common specificity. Ethics reporting is complete for approval and consent: the data collection was approved by ethics committees at both Nara Medical University and Nara Institute of Science and Technology, the procedure was explained at the start of recording and informed consent obtained, and the formal ethics statement records written informed consent from participants' legal guardian or next of kin. Funding from a single CREST grant is stated, and competing interests are declared as none. [RQ2.5] A Tobii Pro Fusion eye tracker sampling at 120 Hz, with participants seated approximately 65 cm from a 1920 x 1080 display. Fixation and saccade classification used Tobii Pro Lab version 1.145 with its attention filter and the I-VT velocity-threshold algorithm, with the threshold stated explicitly at 100 degrees per second - a level of specificity about event detection that most eye-tracking papers in this corpus omit entirely, and one that matters because fixation counts are meaningless without it. Areas of interest were drawn on the eyes (extending up to the eyebrows), nose and mouth, and were redrawn for each image because mouth size varies with expression, which prevents a systematic bias in mouth-region measurement across emotions. Scan-path length was computed in Python with an algorithm published as pseudocode that segments rather than bridges invalid samples. Modelling used PyTorch with fully tabulated architectures. Clinical instruments: ADOS-2, PANSS, SRS-2, Kikuchi's Scale of Social Skills 18-item, ADHD-RS and CBCL. No calibration procedure is described. [RQ2.6] Among the best-specified studies in the review. Reproducible from the text: the full instrument battery per group, the FEIT protocol with image counts per emotion and exact trial timing, the eye tracker and sampling rate, the viewing distance, the I-VT algorithm with its velocity threshold, the area-of-interest definitions and the per-image redrawing rule, both trial-exclusion rules with the resulting per-emotion trial counts listed exactly, the scan-path computation as pseudocode, both model architectures in a table giving neuron counts and kernel sizes and channel counts, the optimiser, loss function, epoch cap and early-stopping patience, the heat-map construction including the Gaussian sigma and the 34 x 34 centre-cropped downscaling, the three-step strategy adopted specifically because the dataset is small, and the nested leave-one-participant-out scheme with its 8:2 inner split. Statistical procedures are equally explicit, including Welch's t-test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Not available: code, and the FEIT images, which are under copyright and could not even be reproduced as figures. Raw data are offered on request without undue reservation. [RQ2.7] The three stated limitations are well chosen and one is a genuine contribution. Small sample size is acknowledged first. The IQ limitation is stated with unusual candour - participants were recruited without intellectual difficulties but no actual values were obtained, so the study 'does not adequately take into account the influence of intellectual level', and the sample is 'only a small number of mild (high-functioning) cases'. Most valuable is the error analysis, which is the kind of work almost no study in this corpus performs: the authors identified the eight participants misclassified by all four models, inspected their raw data, found that their gaze did not move from the centre at all, checked whether they had simply not engaged with the task, and found that their FEIT recognition scores were normal (18 and 19 of 21 for two autistic adults; 19, 25, 22 and 17 of 32 for four autistic children). The conclusion - that some people complete the task using peripheral vision without moving their eyes - identifies a failure mode intrinsic to gaze-based assessment, quantifies it at 6.5% of adults and 17% of children, and names it as a target for future work. Unstated limitations remain. The statistical analysis treats trials as independent when they cluster within participants at roughly two or three per person per emotion, so Welch's t-tests on 101-172 trials overstate the effective sample size. Control selection by SRS-2 ranking introduces a construct-related variable into the sampling, and the direction of the selection is ambiguous from the text. The adult groups differ by up to six years in mean age and the children's groups by 40 percentage points in sex ratio, neither adjusted. Autistic children scored more than twice as high on the ADHD Rating Scale as controls, an unaddressed comorbidity confound in a gaze task. And Japanese participants viewed Western faces without comment. [RQ2.9] Three directions, each tied to a specific finding. Collect more data to establish validity, the standard response to a small sample. Develop a method that works for participants whose gaze barely moves - which follows directly from the error analysis and is a real methodological problem rather than a generic wish, since a gaze-based classifier that fails on 17% of children because they use peripheral vision has a systematic blind spot that more data alone will not close. And obtain actual IQ values and other individual characteristics so that the relationship between the model and the heterogeneity of the conditions can be examined - an acknowledgement that a high-functioning sample of 15 cannot speak for a spectrum. Not proposed, and worth noting: a direct autism-versus-schizophrenia classifier, which the dataset already supports and which would be the natural differential-diagnosis test; and validation on an independent cohort. [RQ3.1] Visual attention during facial emotion recognition, measured in three ways and analysed separately for each emotion presented. Fixation counts within anatomically defined areas of interest - the eyes region extending up to the eyebrows, the nose and the mouth - index where attention is allocated on the face. Saccade counts index how often gaze shifts. Scan-path length, defined as the mean displacement between consecutive gaze samples, indexes how far and how restlessly the eyes travel. The paper's behavioural hypothesis is the one the field takes for granted, that autistic people look less at the eyes; its finding is that this holds much more clearly for schizophrenia than for autism in these data. In adults, fixation at the eyes separated the schizophrenia group from controls for all seven emotions with p values from .0001 to .01, but separated the autistic group from controls for only two of seven (anger and neutral). What did separate autistic adults from controls, across six of seven emotions, was scan-path length - they moved their gaze further per sample. Fixation at the mouth separated autism from controls for five of seven emotions but never separated schizophrenia from controls. So the two conditions produce distinguishable gaze signatures: schizophrenia is characterised by uniformly reduced eye-region fixation, autism by increased mouth fixation and longer scan paths that vary with the expression shown. In children, almost nothing reached significance - only eye fixation for anger. A secondary behaviour is measured and turns out to be null: emotion recognition accuracy, which was essentially identical across all groups in both datasets, so the gaze differences occur without any difference in task success. [RQ3.2] No cross-sensor fusion, but two forms of within-study integration are central to the design. The first is the CNN's dual input: the gaze heat map is presented alongside the stimulus image, so the network can 'explicitly learn the facial regions and expressions' rather than treating gaze positions as coordinates divorced from what was at those coordinates. Since the same 21 or 32 images are shown to every participant, the image channel functions as a conditioning signal identifying which trial the heat map came from. The second, and the paper's actual contribution, is the aggregation layer: each of the 21 or 32 trials is classified independently and the per-trial decisions are then combined either by unweighted hard voting or by a random forest that learns which stimuli to trust. That is a form of stimulus-level fusion, and unlike most fusion claims in this corpus it is tested against its own ablation across three separate problems with informative results - weighting adds 10 points for autistic adults and 16.7 for autistic children but nothing for schizophrenia. The differential outcome is explained mechanistically rather than left as a number: weighting helps precisely when group differences are selective across stimuli, and is useless when they are uniform. That is a more transferable finding about when multi-stimulus aggregation should be weighted than any of the accuracy comparisons in this review. [RQ4.1] Deliberately small models with a classical aggregation layer, and the modesty is justified rather than incidental. The per-trial classifiers are a three-hidden-layer multilayer perceptron with five neurons per layer, taking three scalar gaze features, and a two-convolutional-layer CNN with 3 x 3 kernels and 8 and 16 channels plus one fully connected layer, taking a 34 x 34 greyscale heat map and the stimulus image. The authors describe a three-step strategy adopted explicitly because the dataset is small: downscale the images to 34 x 34 greyscale after centre-cropping, reduce the CNN to two layers plus one fully connected layer, and use leave-one-participant-out cross-validation to maximise training data. Above the per-trial classifier sits the paper's contribution, an aggregation over the 21 or 32 per-trial decisions by either hard voting or a random forest, the latter learning which stimuli should count. Training used Adam with cross-entropy loss, a 300-epoch cap and early stopping after 15 epochs without validation improvement, with the learning rate optimised inside the nested cross-validation. The authors also justify not using a support vector machine, on the grounds that the per-fold sample size of 630 or 651 trials is adequate relative to a cited prior study - an argument about sample adequacy rather than an unexamined preference for deep learning. [RQ4.2] Two parallel representations, compared directly. The baseline uses three interpretable scalars per trial: number of fixations, number of saccades and scan-path length. The CNN uses a spatial representation: gaze sample positions are set to 1 in an otherwise zero image, blurred with a Gaussian kernel of sigma 10, centre-cropped and downscaled to 34 x 34 greyscale, then paired with the stimulus image so the model sees both where the person looked and what was there. Two observations about this representation. It discards temporal order entirely - a heat map is a spatial density, so the sequence in which regions were visited, which the paper's own scan-path measure partly captures, is unavailable to the CNN. And the aggressive downscaling to 34 x 34 from a 1920 x 1080 display means each pixel spans roughly 56 x 32 display pixels, so the representation can distinguish eyes from mouth but not, say, one eye from the other or the pupil from the eyelid; this is a reasonable trade for a dataset of this size but bounds what the model can learn. One reporting inconsistency: fixation counts of 200-300 in a five-second trial exceed the number of possible fixation events at 120 Hz, so these are gaze samples classified as fixation rather than discrete fixation events, and the label is used loosely throughout. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for four model variants across three classification problems - twelve complete metric triples, reported in a single table with the best in bold. Reporting all three metrics for every ablation condition rather than accuracy alone lets a reader see what the weighting actually does: for children it raises the baseline's sensitivity from 0.333 to 0.667 and the CNN's from 0.286 to 0.600, which is where the accuracy gain comes from, and the paper says so explicitly. The chance-level handling is the most straightforward in the corpus: group sizes were equalised so chance is approximately 50%, and each headline accuracy is tested against it with a binomial test, with all three p-values reported including the one that fails - schizophrenia at p = 0.052, described as marginally significant rather than rounded into significance. Feature importances from the random forest are averaged across cross-validation folds rather than fitted once. Missing: AUC or ROC, confidence intervals, and any precision or predictive-value figure. Given accuracies of 0.645 to 0.710 on samples of 30-31 participants, confidence intervals would be wide and their absence is the main reporting gap - a single participant moves accuracy by about 3 percentage points. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is built into the aggregation design and is then cross-checked against independent evidence, which is the part that distinguishes it. The random forest that weights the 21 or 32 per-image decisions yields an importance per stimulus, averaged over cross-validation folds, and a table maps each face number to its emotion so the importances can be read semantically. The authors then test each importance ranking against the separate statistical analysis. For autistic adults the two highest-weighted images are neutral faces, and the statistics independently show all three gaze features differing significantly on neutral trials - a convergence the authors relate to documented difficulty with subtle expressions, since neutral is the least prototypical stimulus in the set. For autistic children the highest weights fall on surprise and two anger images, and anger is the single emotion showing a significant gaze difference in that dataset. For schizophrenia the top-weighted images are disgust and anger, and here the authors decline to interpret: 'we do not think that feature importance has any particular significance', because the statistics show eye-region fixation differing for every emotion, so no image is distinctive and the ranking is noise. Refusing to build a story around an importance ranking that the underlying statistics do not support is a discipline absent elsewhere in this corpus, and it makes the two interpretations that are offered more credible. The error analysis adds a second layer of interpretability at the individual level, identifying the specific participants the models could not classify and diagnosing why. [RQ4.5] One of the two or three soundest validation designs in this review. The scheme is nested leave-one-participant-out cross-validation: in each outer fold a single participant is held out entirely, with all 21 or 32 of their trials excluded from training, and the inner loop with an 8:2 training/validation split is used to optimise the learning rate. Placing hyperparameter selection inside the outer loop is stated explicitly and is the correct construction; the great majority of studies in this corpus either tune on the test set or do not say. Because the split unit is the participant, the trial-level leakage that inflates results throughout this literature - where a person's own segments appear on both sides of the split - is structurally impossible here, and this matters more than usual because the per-trial classifier operates on individual FEIT images that would otherwise be trivially matched across folds. Class balance was engineered in advance by equalising group sizes, so chance is approximately 50% and is not an artefact of prevalence. And every reported accuracy is tested against that chance level with a binomial test, with the failing result reported as failing. The consequences are visible in the numbers: accuracies of 0.645 to 0.710 rather than the 90-plus figures common in this corpus, which is what a properly participant-disjoint, chance-tested evaluation of gaze features in 30 people looks like. Three residual weaknesses. No confidence intervals accompany any figure, and with 30-31 participants one person is roughly 3 accuracy points, so the 10-point gain from weighting in adults corresponds to about three people. The controls were selected from a larger pool by SRS-2 ranking, so sampling is conditioned on a construct-related variable. And the statistical analysis that motivates the whole approach - and that is used to validate the feature importances - treats trials as independent units when they cluster within participants, without any mixed-effects adjustment, so those p-values are anticonservative even after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia, convolutional neural networks, eye movement, facial emotion recognition. The inclusion of schizophrenia alongside autism is the distinguishing feature and signals the paper's differential-psychiatric framing rather than an autism-screening one; neither 'diagnosis', 'screening' nor 'classification' appears, and the application terms in the body are 'biomarkers' and 'behavioral indicators'. Terms carried through the text: Facial Emotion Identification Test, scan-path length, heat map, hard voting, random forest weighting, nested leave-one-participant-out cross-validation, areas of interest, I-VT, feature importance, peripheral vision. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Digital Health 5:952433, Digital Mental Health section, Original Research, CC BY. Received 25 May 2022, accepted 30 January 2023, published 16 February 2023 - an eight-month review, longer than the Frontiers norm, with two named reviewers and a handling editor from Duke University disclosed as the journal requires. The venue is a digital-health rather than an engineering or clinical-psychiatry journal, and the reporting reflects that mixed audience: clinical instruments and diagnostic procedure are described to psychiatric standards while model architectures, optimiser settings and cross-validation structure are tabulated to engineering standards, and both the statistical analysis and the machine learning are given roughly equal space. Supplementary materials hold the nose-fixation and saccade analyses. [RQ5.3] Published 2023 by the Augmented Human Communication Laboratory at Nara Institute of Science and Technology with the Department of Psychiatry at Nara Medical University School of Medicine and Osaka Psychiatric Medical Center, funded by a single JST CREST grant (JPMJCR19A5). The framing is diagnostic refinement within psychiatry rather than population screening: the opening premise is that experienced psychiatrists identify autism and schizophrenia through interviews, responses and neuropsychological tests, and that 'the discovery of disorder-specific biomarkers and behavioral indicators with sufficient sensitivity is important' to improve that process. Two aspects of the positioning are distinctive for this corpus. The paper's central concern is differentiation between two conditions rather than detection of one - 'since ASD and Sz are often difficult to differentiate, we propose to examine eye movement differences during facial expression recognition for the distinction' - which puts it among the very few studies here that treat the clinically realistic problem. And its contribution is framed as a modelling gap rather than a performance gap: prior basic research had established that gaze differences vary by presented emotion, but 'machine learning models that take this into account have not been examined', so the paper's claim is that a known behavioural fact should be built into the model architecture. The resulting accuracies are modest and are reported without inflation, with binomial tests against chance and a failing result left visible - a tone that stands out against the corpus's prevailing register.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective secondary analysis of usage telemetry from FreeSpeech, an iPad speech-generating augmentative and alternative communication app sold on the Apple iTunes store between January 2012 and May 2014. The app logged every key press, its timing and other on-screen events and transmitted them automatically to a backend server; the authors are explicit that this logging was built for developer debugging rather than research and that the resulting data structure required substantial reprocessing. Across the app's life 6,033 people used it, generating over 2.5 million button presses, with 5,372 retained after 761 were excluded for too few events; usage was international, with 66% of users in the United States. Diagnostic labels come from an optional in-app survey completed voluntarily by 214 users, of whom 180 disclosed a diagnosis: 81 autistic and 99 not, the latter comprising people reporting stroke, ALS, dementia, brain injury, ADHD, unspecified 'other' conditions and no diagnosis. There is no clinical assessment of any kind. Age is reported only as a marginal distribution across six bands with no breakdown by group; no sex, IQ, language, severity or comorbidity data were collected. Participant totals do not reconcile across the text and the two tables. No ethics approval, ethics committee or consent process for research use is reported anywhere.
narrative_rows.methods: All keys and app events were enumerated - 69 unique ones - and partitioned into normal keys, complex keys, normal app events and complex app events, each category assigned a non-overlapping range of integer identifiers so that category membership is recoverable from the value, a scheme the authors call pseudo-semantic. Three modelling views were then constructed. Sequential modelling cuts the identifier stream into non-overlapping windows of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 or 100 consecutive presses, each window becoming a pseudo-sample; temporal modelling substitutes inter-press intervals in milliseconds; spectral modelling counts key or key-category frequencies per session and needs no window. Spatial modelling was considered and rejected because the app is user-customisable, so screen positions are not comparable between people. Classification used radial and polynomial SVMs, a probabilistic neural network, logistic regression, LogitBoost, bagging, stacked autoencoders with one to three encoder layers and deep belief networks with two and three layers, evaluated by ten repetitions of 20-fold cross-validation nested with ten bootstraps for training-sample balancing - with the unit of splitting never stated. Crucially, k-means clustering seeded from the 180 labelled users was used to assign pseudo-labels to the remaining approximately 5,192 users before the headline results were computed.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Simple usage statistics distinguished nothing: session length 2.14 versus 2.10 minutes (p = 0.86), word selects per use 5.6 versus 4.31 (p = 0.166) and word-select frequency 2.99 versus 2.28 per minute (p = 0.147), all non-significant under Holm-Bonferroni correction, and the authors present this null result openly as the motivation for more elaborate modelling. On the 180 human-labelled users, the group's earlier analysis of the same data reached 47-61% across all three modelling views and six window sizes - sequential SVM peaking at 58% at window size 40, temporal at 60%, spectral at 61% with LogitBoost - which is at or barely above a 50% chance level. After k-means pseudo-labelling enlarged the corpus, sequential modelling with an SVM reached 70%, and in the present study stacked autoencoders reached 82% at window size 40, reported as performing consistently across window sizes, with deep belief networks matching only at window size 20. Descriptively the study reports that the app was used across the whole lifespan with heaviest engagement among children under ten, that autistic users had the highest average number of app accesses and produced considerably more unique words than most other diagnostic groups, and that the commonest phrases concerned food, sleep, sport and greetings.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The 82% figure is computed after k-means clustering has assigned labels to roughly 5,192 of about 5,372 users, so approximately 97% of the evaluation data carry machine-generated rather than human-reported labels, and the accuracy is substantially a measure of agreement with a clustering solution. On the 180 users who actually reported a diagnosis, the same data yielded 47-61%, at or near chance. The unit of cross-validation is never stated; each user contributes many windows, no user-level result is reported, and window-level splitting would place every user's own data on both sides of each fold, allowing a classifier to succeed by recognising individuals from their customised key-press habits. Underneath both problems lies a near-structural confound: the comparison group is dominated by stroke, dementia, ALS and brain injury - acquired conditions of adult and later life - while autism is congenital and the app's heaviest users were children under ten, and age is neither reported by group nor adjusted for anywhere, so the classifier may be separating children from older adults. The reference standard is unverified voluntary self- or proxy-report from 3.4% of users with no clinical component and no record of who completed the survey. Accuracy is the only metric; there is no chance baseline, no confidence interval and no class-conditional figure. Participant counts are internally inconsistent across the text and tables. Tuning effort differed between compared classifiers by the authors' own account. And there is no ethics approval, no consent for research use of the telemetry, and no discussion of either, in a dataset drawn largely from disabled children and adults.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Worth charting for what its data source represents rather than for its result. Three features are unique in this corpus. Its participants are AAC users, so its autistic sample is drawn from the minimally verbal end of the spectrum that almost every other study here excludes by requiring children to sit at a screen, follow instructions or hold a conversation - a population whose absence from this literature is a recurring gap that this study incidentally fills. Its comparison group consists of other people who need augmentative communication rather than typically developing controls, so the question posed is the clinically realistic one, stated explicitly as whether autistic users can be distinguished 'from individuals without ASD (but who have need for AAC systems)'. And its behavioural sample consists of real communicative acts serving real purposes in daily life, collected at a scale - 6,033 users, 2.5 million button presses, three continents, two and a half years - that no conventional autism study can reach, which is the authors' central and correct argument. Against this, it is the corpus's clearest illustration of two failure modes. The first is label bootstrapping: a supervised problem on 180 self-reported cases is converted by k-means into a largely self-supervised one on 5,372, after which accuracy rises from near chance to 82% - a progression that reads as methodological improvement and is at least as consistent with the classifier having learned to reproduce a clustering. The second is the unexamined demographic confound, where a comparison group of predominantly older adults with acquired conditions is contrasted against predominantly young children with a congenital one, and age is collected but never used. The paper's own honest reporting of three null t-tests, and its well-reasoned rejection of spatial modelling on customisation grounds, show that the authors were capable of the scrutiny that the classification analysis did not receive. Finally, it is the only included study to build a health classifier from consumer telemetry gathered for debugging, from a population including many disabled children, with no ethics approval, no consent and no discussion of either.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] A very large uncontrolled user population with a very small labelled subset. FreeSpeech attracted 6,033 users between January 2012 and May 2014, of whom 5,372 generated enough events to be usable (761 excluded), collectively producing over 2.5 million button presses. Of these, 214 users voluntarily completed an online survey and 180 disclosed a diagnosis - 81 autistic and 99 non-autistic, which is 3.4% of the usable user base. The non-autistic group is itself clinically diverse: Table III lists 32 users reporting no diagnosis, 49 'other', 12 stroke, 4 ALS, 4 dementia, 4 brain injury and 3 ADHD alongside 88 with autism. Two internal inconsistencies should be recorded: Table III sums to 196 and Table II (age bands) to 235, against stated totals of 180 disclosing a diagnosis and 214 completing the survey, and Table III's 88 autistic users does not match the 81 stated in the text. The modelled unit is neither the user nor the session but the window - a fixed-length run of 10 to 100 consecutive key presses - so a heavy user contributes far more pseudo-samples than a light one, and the effective sample size for the classification experiments is never stated. Critically, the headline result is obtained after k-means clustering has assigned pseudo-labels to the roughly 5,192 users who never disclosed anything, so most of the data underlying the 82% figure carry machine-generated labels. [RQ1.2] 'Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)' and 'individuals with disabilities' predominate, person-first and generally neutral, with the field's own vocabulary of augmentative and alternative communication used precisely throughout. The register is mostly that of assistive-technology research rather than pathology, and the paper is notably interested in what users do with the app rather than in what is wrong with them - the descriptive sections report which phrases people used, how many unique words they produced, and how long they engaged, framed as evidence of the app's usefulness across populations. Against this, deficit language appears in places: AAC systems 'are usually used by individuals with expressive communication disorders who suffer from impairments in speech, language, reading, and/or writing', autism is 'associated with deficits in social interaction', and 'individuals affected with autism' appears once. One passage is garbled in a way that matters: the text states that people with non-autistic communication challenges 'are typically interested in communicating with others, whereas individuals with ASD may be more motivated', which as written contradicts the contrast it is drawing and appears to have lost a negation - a claim about differential communicative motivation in autism that is contentious in the first place and is here left incoherent. There is no neurodiversity framing and no involvement of AAC users or autistic people in the research, which is a notable absence for a study built entirely on the communication attempts of disabled people. [RQ1.3] Almost nothing usable, and the one variable that is reported creates the study's central problem. Age is given only as a distribution over six bands for survey respondents (0-5: 36, 6-10: 39, 11-18: 20, 19-30: 23, 31-50: 45, over 50: 50, unspecified: 22) with no breakdown by diagnosis, and the totals do not reconcile with the stated respondent counts. No sex, race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, IQ, language level or comorbidity data were collected at all. Geographic distribution is reported at country level: 66% of users in the United States, with Europe and Oceania represented. The decisive omission is age by diagnostic group, because the composition of the comparison group makes the confound near-certain rather than speculative. Autism is congenital and the app's heaviest and most frequent users were children aged 10 and under; the non-autistic comparison group is dominated by acquired conditions of adult and later life - stroke, dementia, ALS, brain injury - which the paper's own background section describes as the 'acquired disabilities' category of AAC users, explicitly contrasted with congenital ones. A classifier separating these groups from key-press sequences may therefore be separating a five-year-old learning to request food from a seventy-year-old adapting to post-stroke aphasia, and nothing in the analysis distinguishes that possibility from a genuine autism signature. The paper itself observes in its background that older AAC users approach these systems with greater communicative experience but less technological intuitiveness, producing struggle, frustration and abandonment - which is a description of precisely the age-related usage difference that the classifier could be detecting. [RQ1.4] The weakest reference standard in this review alongside the social-media study. Diagnosis is voluntary self- or proxy-report through an optional online survey embedded in a free commercial app: users 'were asked to disclose their reason for using the application', 214 of 6,033 chose to respond, and 180 named a diagnosis. There is no clinical assessment, no diagnostic instrument, no clinician involvement, no verification, no date of diagnosis, and no record of who completed the survey - the AAC user, a parent, a spouse or a speech-language therapist, each of which would be plausible for a device used by people with communication impairments spanning early childhood to advanced dementia. Because 'refusal to answer the survey did not cause denial of service', respondents are self-selected on unknown characteristics, and they represent 3.4% of usable users. The 'no diagnosis' category (32 users) is particularly ambiguous, since a person using a speech-generating device while reporting no diagnosis may be a therapist, a family member, a curious downloader or someone with an undisclosed condition. The comparison group's composition is simultaneously the study's most interesting feature and a further source of uncertainty: contrasting autism against other communication-impaired populations rather than against typical development is exactly the differential framing this literature usually avoids, but here the comparison group is a convenience aggregate of eight loosely specified categories, one of which is literally labelled 'other' and accounts for half of it. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, language, adaptive-function or autism-severity measure exists for any participant, and none could exist given the data source. This is a substantive gap for a study whose modality is language production: the dataset consists of hundreds of thousands of communicative acts, and the paper reports descriptively that autistic users produced a considerably higher number of unique words than most other diagnostic groups, but no linguistic or communicative competence measure is derived, validated or used. The conclusion identifies the gap without naming it as one, proposing future work on 'how usage patterns can be used to predict quantitative traits of clinical relevance (such as adaptive skills and the severity of the autism presentation)'. Two consequences follow. There is no way to characterise where on the spectrum the 81 autistic users sit, and since they are people who need a speech-generating device they are by construction from the minimally verbal end - a population systematically under-represented in the rest of this corpus, which is a genuine strength of the dataset that the absence of any severity measure prevents the study from exploiting. And the number of unique words used, which the paper reports as evidence of the app's usefulness, is equally readable as a proxy for expressive language level, unmeasured and uncontrolled, and plausibly one of the features the classifier exploits. [RQ2.1] Two goals, and the paper is clearer about the first than the second. The first is to demonstrate that the dense telemetry generated by digital AAC systems is worth analysing at all, which the authors argue has been almost entirely neglected: 'with the exception of one prior report, no efforts have been made to use the dense streams of data collected by digital AACs to derive insights of clinical importance'. The second is the classification question, posed precisely and unusually well: 'can we distinguish individuals with ASD from individuals without ASD (but who have need for AAC systems), based solely on patterns of use?' - the parenthesis matters, because it commits the study to a differential rather than an autism-versus-typical contrast. Findings: conventional usage statistics separate nothing. Session length was 2.14 versus 2.10 minutes (p = 0.86), word selects per use 5.6 versus 4.31 (p = 0.166) and word-select frequency 2.99 versus 2.28 per minute (p = 0.147), none significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction, and the authors present this explicitly as motivation for more advanced modelling. The prior analysis of the same data reached 47-61% across sequential, temporal and spectral views - sequential SVM peaking at 58% at window size 40, temporal at 60%, spectral at 61% with LogitBoost - which is at or barely above chance. Accuracy rose to 70% with sequential modelling only after k-means pseudo-labelling enlarged the training set, and to 82% in the present study with stacked autoencoders at window size 40. Descriptively the study also reports that use spanned the whole lifespan with heaviest engagement among under-10s, that autistic users had the highest average number of app accesses, and that the commonest phrases concerned food, sleep, sport and greetings. [RQ2.2] There is no research setting: the data are telemetry from a free commercial iPad app used by people at home and in daily life across at least three continents over two and a half years, transmitted automatically to a backend server. This is the most naturalistic dataset in the corpus by a wide margin, and the authors are right that it represents a kind of scale that conventional autism research cannot reach - approximately 200 new users per month even at the end of the app's life, and around 1,800 in the busiest month. The corresponding losses are total. Nothing about the context of any interaction is known: whether the user was communicating with a person or exploring the interface, whether a therapist was present, whether the device was being used for its intended purpose, whether the account holder was the person using the screen. The logs were not designed for research and the authors say so plainly - collected 'for developers' debugging purposes and general system usage statistics', with 'little attention... given to the data structure and representation during the app development'. So the study inherits both the reach of consumer telemetry and its complete absence of experimental control, and it is candid about the latter in a way that makes the work easier to appraise. [RQ2.3] None, and its absence defines what the study can and cannot show. There is no task, protocol, prompt, stimulus or elicitation; the behavioural sample is whatever thousands of people chose to do with a communication app over two and a half years. This yields ecological validity that no laboratory paradigm can match - these are real communicative acts serving real needs, not responses to a screen in a clinic - but it also means the behaviour is confounded with everything that varies between users: how the app was configured, who set it up, what vocabulary was loaded, what the user was trying to say, how much support they had, and how long they had owned the device. One design consequence is handled well and is worth recording: the app was fully customisable, so different users operate on different icon arrangements, and the authors correctly reject spatial modelling on this basis - 'between participant or between group analyses are difficult due to the customizability of the app which allows different participants to all potentially create a different base (i.e. set of icons) upon which they operate'. That is a clear-sighted rejection of a representation that would have appeared informative while measuring only how each user had arranged their own screen. The windowing scheme is the substitute for a trial structure, and its trade-off is stated explicitly: longer windows capture more cohesive patterns but produce fewer pseudo-samples and discard short sessions, shorter windows produce more samples but distort the patterns. [RQ2.4] Longitudinal in data span and cross-sectional in analysis: usage covers January 2012 to May 2014 with per-month user and event counts charted, but the classification treats windows as exchangeable and models nothing about change over time. This is a striking missed opportunity, since AAC usage is expected to develop as a user learns the system and, in the acquired-condition groups, may decline with disease progression - and the conclusion identifies 'the stability of predictions over time' as future work. Ethics is the study's most serious deficiency and is entirely absent. There is no institutional review board approval, no ethics committee, no research-ethics statement and no consent process for research use of the telemetry, which was gathered automatically for debugging from a commercial product. The only safeguard reported is that 'all the recorded data were encrypted and de-identified', and the only choice offered to users concerned the optional survey. The population includes 75 users aged 10 or under and a further 20 aged 11-18 among survey respondents alone, plus an unknown number among the roughly 5,192 unlabelled users, and every one of them is a person with a communication impairment whose attempts to speak are the data. Retrospective research use of consumer telemetry from disabled children, without consent or ethical review and without any discussion of either, is a governance gap that a four-page conference format does not excuse. No competing-interests statement appears despite three commercial or industry-lab affiliations among the authors and the app itself having been a commercial product. [RQ2.5] FreeSpeech, an iPad speech-generating AAC application commercially available on the Apple iTunes store from January 2012 to May 2014, with a customisable programmable interface supporting user-modifiable icon arrangement, sentence generation and mapping to synthesised or recorded voices. The app logged all key presses, their timings and other on-screen events and transmitted them automatically to a secure backend on internet connection. No research instrument, sensor or assessment tool was used at any point - the entire measurement apparatus is a consumer application's debug logging. Analysis software, frameworks, library versions and compute are not named anywhere, and neither are the architectures or training settings of the stacked autoencoders and deep belief networks that produce the headline result. The asymmetry is notable: the data-collection platform is described in useful detail while the modelling that generates the paper's claim is described only by algorithm name. [RQ2.6] Partial and uneven. Reproducible in principle: the app's identity and deployment window, the user and event counts, the 12.6% exclusion rule for insufficient events, the survey response numbers, the four-category pseudo-semantic identifier scheme with its non-overlapping ID ranges and the count of 69 unique keys and events, the definitions of sequential, temporal and spectral modelling, the window sizes swept, the classifier inventory, and the repetition and bootstrap counts for both cross-validation schemes. Not reproducible: the unit of cross-validation, which is never stated and determines whether the results mean anything; the k-means configuration, how pseudo-labels were assigned and whether any were checked; the stacked autoencoder and deep belief network architectures and training regimes; the survey instrument; any hyperparameter, seed, code or data. The dataset is telemetry from a discontinued commercial app held by a third-party foundation and is not described as available. Internal consistency is also weak, with three different participant totals recoverable from the text and tables. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section, and the paper's candour is concentrated in the methods rather than in self-appraisal. What is stated plainly and deserves credit: the data were collected for developer debugging with no analytic aim in mind, so the structure required substantial reprocessing; spatial modelling is unusable because the app is customisable; window size trades pattern fidelity against sample count; and the deep belief network was tuned only for one window size, so its poorer results elsewhere may reflect tuning effort rather than capability. What is not addressed is more consequential. The reference standard is unverified voluntary self-report from 3.4% of users with no clinical component. Age is confounded with diagnosis by the structure of the comparison group, which mixes congenital autism against predominantly acquired adult-onset conditions, and no age adjustment or even age-by-group reporting is performed. The headline 82% is computed after k-means assigned pseudo-labels to roughly 5,192 users, so the great majority of the evaluation data carry labels generated by an unsupervised algorithm rather than reported by any person - which makes the accuracy partly a measure of agreement with a clustering solution. The unit of cross-validation is never stated, and with each user contributing many windows, window-level splitting would put a user's own data on both sides of every fold. Accuracy is the only metric. No chance baseline appears. The three participant totals in the text and tables do not reconcile. And there is no ethics approval, no consent for research use, and no discussion of either. [RQ2.9] Three directions, all in the conclusion and all reasonable. Examine the stability of predictions over time - the obvious next step for a dataset spanning two and a half years that is currently analysed cross-sectionally. Predict quantitative traits of clinical relevance such as adaptive skills and the severity of the autism presentation, which acknowledges that the present labels are binary and unverified. And develop 'next generation digital markers and fingerprints for understanding change, variation, and opportunities for growth' - a framing oriented towards monitoring and personalisation rather than diagnosis, which is the more defensible use of this kind of data. Not proposed, and more pressing: obtaining any clinically verified labels, adjusting for or matching on age, reporting user-level rather than window-level performance, evaluating without pseudo-labelling, and addressing the ethical basis for research use of the telemetry. [RQ3.1] Interaction with a speech-generating communication device, treated as a behavioural signal in its own right rather than as a means to an end. Three representations of that behaviour are constructed and compared. Sequential modelling captures which keys are pressed in what order, encoded as a stream of numeric identifiers whose ranges preserve category membership - normal keys, complex keys, normal app events, complex app events - so that the encoding is 'pseudo-semantic' rather than arbitrary. Temporal modelling replaces the identifiers with inter-press intervals in milliseconds, capturing the rhythm of interaction independent of content. Spectral modelling counts how often each key or key category is pressed within a session, discarding order entirely. Spatial modelling is considered and rejected on the well-reasoned grounds that user customisation makes screen positions incomparable across people. What is measured, then, is the pattern of a person's attempts to communicate: how they sequence icons into utterances, how quickly they move between selections, and which parts of their vocabulary they use. Descriptively the paper reports that autistic users accessed the app most frequently and used a considerably higher number of unique words than most other groups, and that the commonest phrases across all users concerned food, sleep, sport and greetings. This is the only study in the corpus whose behavioural sample consists of real communicative acts serving real purposes - and also the only one where the behaviour is fully confounded with how the device happened to be configured, by whom, and for what. [RQ3.2] No fusion. The three usage-pattern representations are alternatives compared against one another rather than channels combined, and the results across them are informative in their own right: sequential modelling peaked at 58% in the prior analysis, temporal at 60% and spectral at 61%, so all three views performed near chance individually, and no attempt is made to combine them. That is a missed opportunity of exactly the kind this review has seen elsewhere, since content (what was said), timing (how fluently) and frequency (which vocabulary) are plausibly complementary rather than redundant descriptions of the same behaviour, and the paper's own results give no reason to prefer any one of them. Two further channels present in the data are also unused. The survey captured age, which is the single most obvious covariate and is reported descriptively but never entered into any model or adjustment. And the app logged what users actually said - the phrase and unique-word analyses in the descriptive section demonstrate that the content is recoverable and interpretable - yet the classification pipeline reduces every key press to a category-preserving integer, discarding lexical content entirely. Given that the paper reports a large descriptive difference in unique-word count between diagnostic groups, the decision not to model content is a substantive choice left unexplained. [RQ4.1] A wide but shallow model comparison. The classical arm comprises radial-basis and polynomial-kernel SVMs, a probabilistic neural network, logistic regression, LogitBoost and bagging; the deep arm comprises stacked autoencoders with one, two and three encoder layers and deep belief networks with two and three layers. The framing is a straightforward representation-learning argument, stated in the discussion: 'feature manipulations and transformations that are being performed in inner layers of deep learning methods such as DBN and SAE are likely to better position such classifiers to stratify usage patterns to expected classes compared to standard classifiers such as SVM and logistic regression'. Two features of the comparison undercut it. Tuning effort was uneven, and the authors say so - the deep belief network was tuned specifically for the 20-key-press window and its weaker results elsewhere are attributed to that, which means the model ranking partly reflects how much attention each classifier received. And the comparison spans two different experiments with different validation schemes and, crucially, different label sets: the 47-61% figures come from the 180 self-reported cases while the 70% and 82% figures come from the pseudo-labelled corpus, so the apparent progression from classical to deep methods is confounded with the change in what was being predicted. The most consequential algorithmic choice is not a classifier at all but the k-means step that generated labels for roughly 5,192 users, which converts a supervised problem on 180 people into a largely self-supervised one on 5,372. [RQ4.2] Fixed-length windows over a pseudo-semantic numeric encoding of the key-press stream. All events and keys across the corpus were enumerated - 69 unique ones despite users being able to add vocabulary - and partitioned into normal keys, complex keys, normal app events and complex app events, with each category assigned a non-overlapping range of integer identifiers so that a value's category is recoverable from its magnitude. That design is a genuine thought: it gives an otherwise arbitrary integer encoding a coarse semantic structure that a model can exploit. The stream is then cut into non-overlapping windows of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 or 100 consecutive presses, each becoming a pseudo-sample; overlapping windows were tested and gave 'no tangible improvement'. Temporal modelling substitutes inter-press intervals for identifiers, and spectral modelling replaces windows with per-session frequency counts. Two properties of this representation matter for interpretation. Users contribute pseudo-samples in proportion to how much they used the app, so heavy users dominate and the effective sample size is never reported. And lexical content is discarded: what a person said is reduced to a category-preserving integer, even though the paper's descriptive analysis shows content to be both recoverable and group-discriminating. [RQ4.3] Average classification accuracy, and nothing else. No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC, ROC curve, confusion matrix or confidence interval appears anywhere for any model - the thinnest metric reporting of any study charted in this review that reports quantitative results. Two consequences follow directly. Because the labelled set is 81 autistic against 99 non-autistic and bootstrapping was used for training-sample balancing, chance is approximately 50%, so the prior analysis's 47-61% range is at or barely above chance while the present 82% is a large gain - but the paper never computes or states the baseline, so a reader must infer it. And because no class-conditional metric is given, it is impossible to tell whether errors fall on autistic or non-autistic users, which matters especially here given that the comparison group is a heterogeneous aggregate of eight categories that the model may separate very unevenly. The one statistical analysis that is reported properly is the negative one: three simple usage measures compared with t-tests under Holm-Bonferroni correction, all non-significant, presented honestly as motivation for the modelling work rather than buried. [RQ4.4] Essentially absent at the model level and moderately good at the data level. No feature importance, saliency, attention, latent-space inspection, error analysis or example-level examination is performed for any classifier, so the paper cannot say what distinguishes autistic from non-autistic usage patterns - only that a stacked autoencoder can tell them apart 82% of the time on a largely pseudo-labelled corpus. This is a particularly costly gap because the alternative explanation is so readily available: with a comparison group dominated by acquired adult-onset conditions and an autism group dominated by young children, the most parsimonious account of the classification is age, and a single look at what the model responds to would have addressed it. What interpretive content exists is descriptive and is genuinely useful for understanding AAC use: usage frequency and duration by age band, average time in app by diagnostic category, the top 14 phrases across the corpus, and unique-word counts by diagnosis showing autistic and stroke users producing considerably more distinct vocabulary than other groups. The pseudo-semantic identifier scheme is designed to make the numeric encoding interpretable, and the rejection of spatial modelling is well argued - but neither is followed through into any analysis of what the models learned. [RQ4.5] The weakest element, with two problems either of which would be decisive on its own. The first is the pseudo-labelling. Only 180 users of approximately 5,372 disclosed a diagnosis; the remainder were assigned labels by k-means clustering seeded from the labelled cases, and the 70% and 82% figures are obtained on this enlarged corpus. So roughly 97% of the evaluation data carry labels generated by an unsupervised algorithm rather than reported by any person, and the reported accuracy is substantially a measure of how well a supervised classifier reproduces a clustering solution - a quantity that can be high regardless of whether the clusters correspond to diagnosis. The contrast with the same data before pseudo-labelling is stark and is visible in the paper's own Table IV: 47-61% across all three modelling views and six window sizes, at or barely above a 50% chance level. The second problem is the unit of cross-validation, which is never stated. The modelling operates on windows, each user generates many windows in proportion to their app use, and neither the earlier leave-one-out-with-100-bootstraps scheme nor the present ten-repetition 20-fold-with-ten-bootstraps scheme is described as partitioning users. If windows were partitioned - the natural reading - then every user's own data appear on both sides of every fold, and since key-press sequences from a customised icon layout are close to an individual signature, the classifier can succeed by recognising users rather than diagnoses. No user-level accuracy is reported anywhere, which is the number the stated research question requires. Compounding both: accuracy is the only metric, no chance baseline is computed, no confidence interval is given, window size was swept with the best reported, and tuning effort differed between the compared classifiers by the authors' own account. The corrective experiment is clear and would be worth more than the present result - partition by user, evaluate only on the 180 verified labels, report sensitivity and specificity at the user level, and adjust for or match on age. [RQ5.1] Title keywords and body terminology rather than a formal keyword list: augmentative and alternative communication, speech-generating devices, usage patterns, stacked autoencoders, autism spectrum disorder, data mining. The framing terms are drawn from data science rather than clinical assessment - 'usage model profiles', 'pseudo-semantic representation', 'pseudo-samples', 'digital markers and fingerprints', 'insight generation from a data science perspective' - and 'screening' does not appear at all, while 'diagnosis classification accuracy' does. The prominence of 'stacked autoencoders' in the title signals that the modelling method is presented as a contribution in its own right. [RQ5.2] 2023 IEEE 13th Annual Computing and Communication Workshop and Conference (CCWC), pages 851-857 - a seven-page general computing conference paper rather than a clinical, assistive-technology or machine-learning venue. The format accounts for some compression, though not for the absence of an ethics statement or of any metric beyond accuracy. The venue choice also explains the paper's structure: roughly half is a literature review of AAC efficacy research, followed by descriptive characterisation of the user base, with the classification experiments occupying comparatively little space and being presented partly as a replication and extension of the same group's earlier report on the same dataset. [RQ5.3] Published 2023 by a distributed group spanning University of Colorado Colorado Springs, Yale, University of Virginia, University of Miami, University of Washington, Seattle Children's Research Institute, Microsoft Research and Van Robotics, funded by NSF and NIH grants, with data provided by the GiveSpeech Foundation. The framing is a data-availability argument rather than a clinical one: the authors contend that AAC research is dominated by single-subject designs and expensive clinical trials requiring 'specialized infrastructure and a great deal of clinical expertise', while the dense telemetry that digital AAC systems generate has been almost entirely ignored - 'with the exception of one prior report, no efforts have been made to use the dense streams of data collected by digital AACs to derive insights of clinical importance'. That is an accurate observation and the study's real contribution is to demonstrate the point. Its positioning within this review is distinctive in three ways. It is the only study whose participants are AAC users, so its autistic sample comes from the minimally verbal end of the spectrum that the rest of the corpus systematically excludes. It is one of very few that pose the differential question explicitly - autism versus others who also need AAC, not autism versus typical development. And it is the only one whose data were generated as a by-product of people using a product for their own purposes, which gives it unmatched ecological validity and simultaneously removes every control that makes a finding interpretable. The paper is also unusual in reporting a null result prominently: three simple usage measures showed no group difference at all, and this is presented as the motivation for the modelling rather than concealed.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Prospective diagnostic study conducted to STARD reporting standards across multiple South Korean sites between 5 August 2021 and 18 July 2022. One hundred and ten children aged 24 to 72 months were screened and 95 (86.4%) completed study measures: 45 autistic (mean age 48.0 +/- 13.4 months, 53.3% boys) recruited from the Seoul National University Hospital Child Psychiatry Outpatient Clinic, a national referral centre, and 50 typically developing (47.9 +/- 12.5 months, 54.0% boys) recruited from day care centres across the country. Enrolment required the ability to sit and no history of visual or auditory deficits. All caregivers completed the Korean CARS-2; children screening positive or prompting caregiver concern were evaluated by a child psychiatrist and received the Korean ADOS-2, with calibrated severity scores reported (total 6.07 +/- 1.6) and modules distributed as 17.8% toddler, 62.2% preverbal or single-word and 20.0% phrase speech. Every child received a standardised cognitive assessment using the Korean Bayley-II or K-WPPSI-IV. Age (p = .99), sex (p > .99) and ethnicity (all Korean) are matched, but best-estimate IQ differs profoundly - 60.1 versus 104 in children under 48 months and 55.1 versus 105 in those older, both p < .001 - and the paper states that conservative criteria were applied deliberately 'to select individuals belonging to clinically distinct groups'. The study was approved by the Yonsei University Health System IRB with written caregiver consent; two authors hold issued patents on the method and a commercial partner assisted with data management, all disclosed.
narrative_rows.methods: A three-task joint attention protocol was designed by adapting the Early Social Communication Scales of Mundy et al., eliciting initiation of joint attention (10-second clips), low-level response to joint attention (5-second clips, object indicated near the child) and high-level response (5-second clips, object indicated across the room). Each child was tested individually in a quiet room, seated on a height-adjustable chair at a table, in a single 10-minute session filmed front-on with a Sony DSC-RX100 IV at 1920 x 1080 and 30 frames per second - no eye tracker, calibration or trained rater. A purpose-built compliance score was computed for every repeated trial and analysed by two-way mixed ANOVA to monitor engagement. Raw frame sequences (224 x 224 x 300 for IJA, 224 x 224 x 150 for RJA) were passed end-to-end to a custom deep learning system combining a CNN, an LSTM and an attention mechanism, with three task-specific models trained for the binary detection problem and three for a three-class severity problem banded from K-CARS-2 scores. Evaluation used 10-fold group-wise cross-validation grouped by individual, with a fixed 0.5 classification threshold and 95% confidence intervals by the Hanley and McNeil method. Grad-CAM at attention peaks, attention-weight plots and agglomerative hierarchical clustering of attention trajectories provided interpretation.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Detection performance was near-ceiling across all three tasks: IJA AUROC 99.6% (95% CI 99.4-99.7) with accuracy 97.6%, precision 95.5% and recall 99.2%; low-level RJA AUROC 99.8% (99.6-99.9) with accuracy 98.8%; high-level RJA AUROC 99.5% (99.2-99.8) with accuracy 98.4%. Severity prediction was substantially lower and clearly task-ordered: IJA AUROC 90.3% (88.8-91.8) with accuracy 84.8% and precision 76.2%, low-level RJA 84.4% with precision 74.7%, high-level RJA 84.2% with precision 68.6%. The IJA advantage for severity was interpreted as reflecting that initiation captures motivational nuance which responsiveness tasks do not, and was independently corroborated by cluster maps in which IJA attention trajectories separated the three severity classes more cleanly. An age-stratified analysis preserved the IJA advantage and showed high-level RJA improving in older children. Interpretability analyses showed the model responding to the intended constructs: triadic gaze shifting between toy and examiner in typically developing children during IJA versus fixation of neither in autistic children; sustained versus fleeting gaze on the indicated toy in low-level RJA; and immediate turning to the distant poster followed by a return to the examiner 'as if seeking approval' versus delayed or absent response in high-level RJA. The compliance analysis found both groups habituating after ten IJA or five RJA repetitions, with autistic children showing comparable initial IJA interest but 'contrasting uninterest in the social cue presented at the beginning of RJA tasks'.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Best-estimate and verbal IQ differ between groups by 44 to 50 points at p < .001 in both age strata - roughly three standard deviations, the largest cognitive separation between compared groups in this review - and no adjustment is attempted, though the authors acknowledge the problem, cite evidence that joint attention differentiates autism after controlling for IQ, and call for external validation in IQ-matched cohorts. Compounding this, the paper states that conservative criteria were applied deliberately to produce 'clinically distinct groups', so the spectrum is truncated at both ends, and there is no developmental-delay or language-disorder comparison group in a sample whose autistic children have mean IQ in the 50s and are 62% preverbal or single-word. Detection AUROCs of 99.5-99.8% are therefore what this design would be expected to produce and are never interrogated. The severity model's three classes include non-autism, so much of its 90.3% AUROC re-solves the detection problem and no within-autism grading result is reported, even though clinician-administered K-ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores were collected and would have supported one; the severity target instead derives from the caregiver-completed K-CARS-2. Specificity is never reported despite STARD adherence, and the class distribution across severity bands is not given, so no chance baseline is computable. The compliance analysis showing autistic children disengaging at the start of RJA tasks is raised as a limitation for severity modelling but not for detection, although an end-to-end model on raw frames could as readily learn disengagement as joint attention. Recruitment channel differs entirely by group, so site co-varies with diagnosis for a model with access to the whole frame. There is no external validation and no test-retest assessment for a system proposed for severity tracking.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: One of the two or three most carefully executed studies in this review, and the clearest illustration of a distinction the corpus badly needs: between a study that is well conducted and a study whose result generalises. Its methodological strengths are substantial and several are unique here. It instruments an already-validated clinical construct rather than searching for a statistical signature, decomposing joint attention into the three forms defined by the Early Social Communication Scales and building a separate model for each - which is what allows its most interesting finding, that all three forms detect autism equally well but only initiation carries severity information. Its cross-validation is group-wise by individual and says so explicitly. Its interpretability work is the most thorough in the corpus and is coupled rather than piecemeal, using attention weights to locate informative time points, Grad-CAM to localise within them, and hierarchical clustering to test whether the pattern holds at dataset level - with the resulting behavioural descriptions matching the constructs the tasks were designed to elicit. Its acquisition is a single consumer camera in a quiet room for ten minutes, with no eye tracker, calibration or trained rater, which makes its scalability claim credible. It reports confidence intervals on all twenty-four estimates, follows STARD, and characterises its participants more completely than anything else here. And its autistic sample is predominantly minimally verbal with mean IQ in the 50s - a population that paradigms requiring screen attention or conversation systematically exclude, so this is one of the few studies in the corpus that speaks to it at all. That last strength is inseparable from the study's central problem: the same fact that makes the sample valuable makes the comparison a 44-50 point IQ gap, and the paper states outright that groups were selected to be clinically distinct. Detection AUROCs of 99.5-99.8% should accordingly be read as evidence that the protocol and pipeline function, not as an accuracy estimate for a referral tool, whose real task is distinguishing autism from developmental delay rather than from a typically developing four-year-old with IQ 105. The severity claim needs a further correction that the paper does not supply: its three classes include non-autism, so it is a graded detection model rather than a within-spectrum severity model, and the K-ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores that would have supported the stronger analysis were collected but not used as a target.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] One hundred and ten children aged 24 to 72 months were screened between 5 August 2021 and 18 July 2022, of whom 95 (86.4%) completed study measures and formed the analytical population: 45 autistic and 50 typically developing. Enrolment criteria were age 24-72 months, ability to sit, and no history of visual or auditory deficits. Recruitment was asymmetric by design - autistic children came from a single national referral centre, the Seoul National University Hospital Child Psychiatry Outpatient Clinic, while comparison children came from day care centres across South Korea, with participants distributed across Seoul (25%), other metropolitan cities (25%) and provinces (50%). The paper states openly that 'conservative inclusion criteria' were applied on both sides 'to select individuals belonging to clinically distinct groups to ensure development of an accurate and precise ASD vs TD classification model' - so the extremity of the contrast is a deliberate design choice, disclosed rather than concealed, and is the single most important fact for interpreting the near-perfect detection results. Each child contributed up to ten IJA clips and five clips per RJA task from a single 10-minute session, and the cross-validation groups by individual so those clips never straddle folds. [RQ1.2] 'Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)' and 'children with typical development (TD)' throughout, person-first and consistent, in the register of a clinical diagnostic journal. Autism is 'a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by abnormal patterns of social interaction and communication', joint attention is 'deficient in children with ASD', and 'infants with this condition, but not those with typical development, appear to lack joint attention' - deficit-framed but factually anchored to the construct being measured rather than generalised. The framing of purpose is assistive: the stated problem is that clinicians 'have had to rely on subjective assessment scores in diagnosing ASD to date' and that validated joint attention manuals such as the Early Social Communication Scales are 'labor-intensive and difficult to implement without trained clinicians and the proper experimental setup', so the target is objectivity and scalability of an existing clinical construct rather than replacement of clinicians. There is no burden or cost rhetoric and no neurodiversity framing. One descriptive passage is worth noting for its observational quality rather than its terminology: in the high-level RJA task, comparison children are described as turning to view the poster 'and then turned back to face the examiner as if seeking approval' - a phenomenological description of shared attention that conveys what the construct actually is. [RQ1.3] The most complete demographic and clinical characterisation in this review, and completeness is what makes the study's central problem visible. Reported per group with formal tests: recruitment source, sex (53.3% versus 54.0% boys, p > .99), age (48.0 +/- 13.4 versus 47.9 +/- 12.5 months, p = .99, with medians and ranges), the proportion under 48 months (46.7% versus 42.0%, p = .80), best-estimate IQ and verbal IQ stratified by age band, K-CARS-2 stratified by age band, and for the autism group K-ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores in total, social affect and restricted-repetitive domains plus module distribution. Ethnicity is reported using NIH categories - all Korean - and geographic distribution is given. Age and sex are matched essentially perfectly, and the 46.7% proportion of girls in the autism group is remarkably high relative to the population sex ratio and to every other autism sample in this corpus, though unexplained. The decisive feature is IQ.
