Best-estimate IQ is 60.1 +/- 15.4 versus 104 +/- 19.1 in children under 48 months and 55.1 +/- 20.8 versus 105 +/- 14.5 in those older, with verbal IQ showing the same 41-45 point gaps, all at p < .001 - a difference roughly three standard deviations wide and the largest cognitive separation between compared groups anywhere in this review. The autism group's mean IQ of 55-60 places it in the range of moderate intellectual disability, and the K-ADOS-2 module distribution (17.8% toddler module, 62.2% preverbal or single-word, 20.0% phrase speech) confirms a predominantly minimally verbal sample. This is a population that most studies in this corpus exclude, which is a genuine strength, but it also means the two groups differ in cognitive and language level as profoundly as they differ in diagnosis. One internal inconsistency: the K-CARS-2 median for the older autism stratum is given as 31.3 with a stated range of 32.0-43.0, which is impossible. [RQ1.4] Strong, staged and transparently described, though with an important detail about which instrument supplies which label. All caregivers completed the Korean Childhood Autism Rating Scale II, a 15-item instrument scored 15 to 60. Children whose scores indicated autism risk, or about whom a caregiver expressed concern, were referred to a child psychiatrist at Seoul National University Hospital for diagnostic evaluation, and the Korean Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule II was administered to those receiving a clinical diagnosis - so the autism label rests on the conjunction of clinician diagnosis and an above-cutoff score on a criterion-standard observational instrument, with calibrated severity scores reported (total CSS 6.07 +/- 1.6, social affect 6.62 +/- 1.8, restricted and repetitive behaviour 6.16 +/- 2.2). Comparison status rests on a below-cutoff K-CARS-2 score together with no parent-reported history of developmental delay or psychiatric condition, so the comparison group is screened rather than merely assumed - though with a caregiver-completed instrument rather than a clinician assessment. Two qualifications matter. The paper states plainly that these conservative criteria were adopted specifically to produce 'clinically distinct groups', so the reference standard is being used to construct maximal separation rather than to sample a clinical spectrum, which the authors disclose but do not connect to their near-ceiling accuracy. And the severity prediction target is derived from K-CARS-2 bands (under 30 non-autism, 30-36 mild or moderate, 37-60 severe) rather than from the K-ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores that were collected and reported - so the clinician-administered severity measure is available in the paper but is not what the severity model predicts. [RQ1.5] Unusually complete on both cognition and severity, and among the best in this review. Cognitive functioning was assessed in every participant using an age-appropriate and ability-appropriate instrument - the Korean Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Second Edition, or the Korean Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, Fourth Edition - and a best-estimate IQ derived, reported separately from verbal IQ and stratified by age band. Severity is measured twice over: K-ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores are reported for total, social affect and restricted-repetitive domains with medians and ranges, and K-CARS-2 total scores are reported by age band for both groups. Module distribution is given, establishing that the autism sample is predominantly preverbal or single-word. What this permits, and what almost no other study in the corpus can do, is a genuine severity-prediction analysis rather than a binary one - and the study takes it up, reporting AUROCs of 84.2-90.3% for a three-class severity task. Two caveats attach. The severity target is the caregiver-completed K-CARS-2 rather than the clinician-administered K-ADOS-2, which is the weaker of the two instruments the study holds. And the three classes include non-autism, so the severity model is not discriminating within the spectrum but performing a graded version of the detection task - which means its 90.3% AUROC is not evidence that the system can grade severity among autistic children, and no within-autism-only result is reported. [RQ2.1] Two objectives, both clinically framed. First, to train deep learning models to distinguish autism from typical development using video of joint attention behaviours; second, to differentiate autism symptom severity from the same data. The motivating argument is precise and is worth recording because it diagnoses the corpus's own problems: prior video-based models are said to be unsuitable for tool development 'due to a lack of automation, the requirements for specialized and expensive equipment, calibration, trained personnel, dependence on human rating of autistic behaviors, and low precision and recall', and the authors attribute that low precision and recall to 'a lack of targeted behavioral biomarkers that can readily discriminate ASD from TD' and to the absence of methods for quantitatively measuring hallmark autism behaviours. Their response is to instrument an existing validated clinical construct rather than to search for a statistical signature. Findings: detection AUROC of 99.6% for IJA, 99.8% for low-level RJA and 99.5% for high-level RJA, with accuracy 97.6-98.8% and confidence intervals throughout. Severity prediction was markedly lower and task-ordered: IJA 90.3% AUROC, low-level RJA 84.4%, high-level RJA 84.2%, with precision falling to 68.6% for high-level RJA. The IJA advantage for severity is interpreted substantively - initiation reflects motivation to share attention and so captures nuance that responsiveness tasks miss - and is corroborated by the cluster maps, where IJA attention-weight trajectories separate the three severity classes more cleanly than the RJA ones. The compliance analysis adds a behavioural finding independent of the models: both groups habituated after ten IJA or five RJA repetitions, but autistic children showed comparable initial interest to comparison children in IJA before declining, while showing 'contrasting uninterest in the social cue presented at the beginning of RJA tasks'. [RQ2.2] Multi-site in the sense that participants were drawn from across South Korea - Seoul, other metropolitan cities and self-governing provinces in equal-ish thirds - but recruitment channels differ completely by group. Autistic children came exclusively from the Child Psychiatry Outpatient Clinic of Seoul National University Hospital, described as receiving referrals of children at high risk of autism from throughout the country; comparison children came from day care centres. This is the standard case-control geometry, and here it is compounded by the deliberate selection of clinically distinct groups. The testing environment itself is standardised and low-tech - a quiet room, a height-adjustable chair, a table, a single consumer camera on a front-facing tripod - and this is presented as a feature, since the protocol is designed to be replicable without specialised equipment, calibration or trained raters. The claim that the setup is 'amenable to computer vision and DL and applicable to a wide range of neuropsychiatric conditions' is credible on the acquisition side; what it does not address is that the model was trained on children drawn from the extreme ends of a clinical distribution. [RQ2.3] The strongest paradigm in this review, judged by the fit between construct, task and measurement. Three tasks were designed by adapting the Early Social Communication Scales manual of Mundy et al. together with validated behaviour-extraction techniques, each targeting one theoretically distinct form of joint attention: initiation, which indexes a child's motivation to share attention and manifests as triadic gaze shifting between object and partner; low-level response, following an indication to a nearby object; and high-level response, following an indication to an object across the room, requiring the child to turn. The decomposition is not arbitrary - it maps onto an established taxonomy with different developmental and clinical significance, and the study's most interesting result is that the three tasks behave differently, with initiation alone carrying severity information. Three further design features deserve credit. The whole protocol takes a single 10-minute session with one consumer camera in a quiet room, so the paradigm is genuinely deployable. Repetition is built in (up to ten IJA trials, five per RJA task), and the authors monitored engagement across repetitions with a purpose-built compliance score analysed by two-way mixed ANOVA, concluding that both groups habituate and recommending that future models be trained on the first five to ten repetitions - a protocol-optimisation finding derived from data rather than assumed. The countervailing concern arises from that same compliance analysis: autistic children showed early disengagement specifically at the start of RJA tasks, so an unknown portion of what the RJA detection models separate is willingness to attend to the examiner at all rather than joint attention per se. The authors raise this as a limitation for severity modelling but not for detection. [RQ2.4] Prospective and cross-sectional: children were enrolled and assessed over an eleven-month window, but each contributed a single 10-minute session with no follow-up, no repeat testing and no test-retest reliability for the model's output - a gap for a system proposed as a severity-assessment tool, since severity assessment implies sensitivity to change. The nearest thing to a temporal analysis is the within-session compliance study across repeated trials, which is genuinely informative about habituation but says nothing about stability across days. Governance is complete and well documented. The study was approved by the Yonsei University Health System Institutional Review Board, caregivers gave written informed consent, and the report follows the STARD reporting guideline for diagnostic accuracy studies - one of very few studies in this corpus to adopt a formal reporting standard, and the reason its participant table, flow accounting and confidence intervals are as complete as they are. Funding is from a Korean government physician-scientist training programme with an explicit no-role statement. The competing-interests disclosure is material and full: two authors hold issued patents on the method and apparatus for diagnosing developmental disability and its severity in toddlers based on joint attention, a third has a patent pending, two report non-financial support from LumanLab Inc, one is affiliated to that company, and the acknowledgements thank LumanLab's administrative, regulatory and data management staff. So the method is patented by its developers and a commercial entity participated in data management - disclosed properly, but without any independent-analysis safeguard of the kind reported by the Duke group elsewhere in this corpus. [RQ2.5] Deliberately minimal. A single Sony DSC-RX100 IV consumer digital camera recording 1920 x 1080 at 30 frames per second from a fixed front-facing viewpoint, a height-adjustable chair and a table in a quiet room. No eye tracker, no depth sensor, no wearable, no markers, no calibration. This is a direct response to the authors' own criticism of prior work for requiring 'specialized and expensive equipment, calibration, trained personnel', and it is what makes the scalability argument credible. Clinical instruments are all named in their Korean validated versions with citations: K-CARS-2, K-ADOS-2, Korean Bayley-II and K-WPPSI-IV. Analysis software is specified to the version number - Python 3.6.8, SciPy 1.4.1, Statsmodels 0.11.1, scikit-learn 0.23.2, Seaborn 0.11.0, Matplotlib 3.3.1 - which is rare in this corpus and is good practice. What the main text does not provide is the network's layer configuration, training hyperparameters or augmentation, though an architecture diagram and training/validation performance appear in supplementary material. [RQ2.6] Among the best in this review on protocol and reporting, incomplete on the model. Fully specified in the main text: recruitment sources and dates, enrolment and exclusion criteria, the staged screening and diagnostic pathway with every instrument named in its validated Korean version, the theoretical source and operational definitions of the three joint attention constructs, the camera model, resolution and frame rate, the exact input tensor dimensions for each task (224 x 224 x 300 for IJA, 224 x 224 x 150 for RJA), the cross-validation scheme with its grouping unit stated explicitly, the classification threshold, the confidence-interval method, and every software package with version. Supplementary materials carry the enrolment flow diagram, the task procedures and acquisition setup, the compliance metric definition, the architecture diagram, training and validation performance, age-stratified results, and all Grad-CAM, attention-plot and cluster-map figures. STARD adherence and a data sharing statement are declared. What is missing is the model itself in reproducible detail - layer sizes, optimiser, learning rate, epochs, augmentation - and any code release. Given that the method is patented, the absence of code is unsurprising but does mean the central artefact cannot be independently checked. [RQ2.7] The two stated limitations are the right two, and one of them is stated more honestly than most papers in this corpus manage: the small sample, and the significant IQ difference between groups. On IQ the authors are candid that 'IQ affects one's ability to perform behavioral tasks', cite external evidence that joint attention differentiates autism after controlling for IQ, and conclude that 'external validation using a larger sample of IQ-matched cohorts with ASD and TD is still warranted'. That is a correct diagnosis of the problem and an appropriate remedy, though no adjustment is attempted in the present analysis and the 44-50 point gap is large enough that it cannot be assumed away by citation. The discussion adds three further self-critical observations about the RJA tasks: that they may lack sensitivity to motivational nuance, that their performance appears developmentally dependent, and that early loss of interest during RJA data collection may have limited the features available for severity modelling. What is not addressed is more consequential than what is. Detection AUROCs of 99.5-99.8% are reported without any interrogation, in a study that states explicitly that groups were selected to be 'clinically distinct' and that documents a three-standard-deviation IQ gap - conditions under which near-perfect separation is close to expected and tells one very little about performance in a clinical population where the question is not autism versus a typically developing four-year-old with IQ 105 but autism versus developmental delay. The severity model's three classes include non-autism, so its 90.3% AUROC largely re-solves the detection problem and provides no evidence of within-autism grading; no autism-only result is reported. Specificity is never reported, in a diagnostic study reported to STARD. The class distribution across the three severity bands is not given. There is no clinical comparison group in a sample whose autistic children have mean IQ 55-60. And the compliance finding that autistic children disengage early from RJA tasks is treated as a limitation for severity but not for detection, although it bears equally on both. [RQ2.9] External validation in larger, IQ-matched cohorts is named as the priority and is the correct one. Beyond that, the authors propose that the standardised video acquisition setup could support large-scale collection of behavioural biomarker datasets 'applicable to a wide range of neuropsychiatric conditions', and offer a concrete protocol recommendation derived from their compliance analysis - that a joint attention-driven model should be trained on the first five to ten repetitions of a task, since both groups habituate beyond that point. Not proposed, and needed: a clinical comparison group so that autism-specificity can be separated from general developmental difference; a within-autism-only severity analysis using the K-ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores the study already holds; reporting of specificity; and test-retest assessment for a system intended to track severity. [RQ3.1] Joint attention, taken as an established clinical construct and instrumented rather than rediscovered - which distinguishes this study from most in the corpus, where the behavioural target is whatever a model finds discriminative. Three forms are elicited and modelled separately. Initiation of joint attention indexes the child's motivation to share attention with another person and is behaviourally realised as a triadic gaze pattern shifting from an object to the partner and back. Low-level response to joint attention is the ability to follow and sustain attention on an object indicated near the child. High-level response requires following an indication to an object across the room, so the child must physically turn. The interpretability analysis then characterises what the model responded to in exactly these terms, and the descriptions are specific enough to be checked against the construct: comparison children showed the triadic shift in IJA while autistic children fixated neither toy nor examiner; comparison children sustained gaze on the indicated toy in low-level RJA while autistic children glanced briefly then looked away; comparison children turned immediately to the distant poster in high-level RJA and then back to the examiner as if seeking approval, while autistic children responded slowly or not at all. Two secondary behaviours are also measured. Task compliance across repeated trials, from which the authors establish that both groups habituate and that autistic children specifically disengage at the start of RJA tasks. And, implicitly, gaze itself - the Grad-CAM heatmaps localise to face and eyes - measured from ordinary video without an eye tracker, which is the study's quiet technical achievement. [RQ3.2] No cross-sensor fusion; a single camera. Two forms of internal integration are central. Architecturally, spatial features from a CNN are combined with temporal modelling by an LSTM and an attention mechanism over frames, so the system represents both what is in each frame and when in the sequence it matters - and the interpretability analysis exploits this composition directly, using attention weights to find the informative time points and Grad-CAM to localise within them, which is a genuinely joint spatial-temporal explanation rather than two separate ones. Conceptually, three separate task-specific models are built rather than one fused model, and the comparison across them is where the study's substantive findings lie: all three tasks detect autism near-perfectly, but only IJA carries severity information, and high-level RJA improves with age. Treating the three joint attention subtypes as separate models and comparing them, rather than pooling all video into one classifier, is what allows the paper to say something about which behaviour matters for which question - a design choice more informative than a fusion gain would have been. The unexploited channel is the compliance score, which is computed for every trial, shown to differ between groups in a diagnostically interesting way, and then used only descriptively rather than as a model input or covariate. [RQ4.1] A single custom architecture combining a convolutional neural network for spatial features, a long short-term memory network for temporal sequence modelling, and an attention mechanism over frames, applied end-to-end to raw video with no hand-crafted features, pose estimation or gaze tracking. The rationale for each component is given: the CNN for frame-level spatial content, the LSTM because it 'was developed to better process sequential data' and the video is time-dependent, and attention to make it possible 'to access and visualize the attention weights across each video sequence according to which frames or video time points contributed most to the model's decision-making' - so the attention mechanism is included at least partly for interpretability rather than purely for performance, which is a defensible and unusual justification. Three separate models are trained, one per joint attention task, with input dimensions matched to task duration (300 frames for the 10-second IJA clips, 150 for the 5-second RJA clips). No alternative architectures or baselines are compared, and no ablation of the CNN, LSTM or attention components is reported, so the contribution of each is unestablished. Grad-CAM, attention plots and agglomerative hierarchical clustering complete the analysis pipeline. [RQ4.2] Raw RGB video frames at 224 x 224, in sequences of 300 (IJA) or 150 (RJA) - a fully end-to-end representation with no intermediate abstraction whatsoever. This is a stronger commitment to learned representation than any other study in this corpus, most of which extract landmarks, poses, gaze coordinates or hand-crafted statistics before modelling. It has two consequences that pull in opposite directions. It removes an entire class of failure - no landmark detector to fail on a child who turns away, no gaze estimator to calibrate, no feature engineering to bias - and it is what allows the same pipeline to work on a task where the child physically turns around, which a face-based method could not handle. But it also means the model has access to everything in the frame: the child's appearance, clothing, posture, the examiner, the room, and anything that co-varies with recruitment site. With autistic children recruited exclusively from one hospital clinic and comparison children from day care centres, and with a 44-50 point IQ difference between groups, an end-to-end model on raw frames has many routes to near-perfect separation that have nothing to do with joint attention. The Grad-CAM analysis is the study's answer to this, and it is a good one as far as it goes - the heatmaps localise to faces and eyes and the described behaviours match the constructs - but it is illustrative rather than systematic, and no quantitative check on background or appearance confounds is reported. [RQ4.3] AUROC, accuracy, precision and recall, each with 95% confidence intervals estimated by the Hanley and McNeil method, reported for all three tasks in both the detection and severity problems - twenty-four interval-bounded estimates, and the most complete uncertainty reporting in this review. That completeness is a direct consequence of adopting the STARD reporting guideline and publishing in a journal that enforces it, and it makes the results checkable in a way that most of this corpus is not. The gaps are nonetheless significant for a diagnostic study. Specificity is never reported, which is an odd omission under STARD and matters because precision and recall alone do not characterise false-positive behaviour at a given prevalence; for the detection models precision is 95.5-98.9% at roughly balanced prevalence, so specificity is evidently high, but it should have been stated. No negative predictive value, no calibration, and no prevalence-adjusted predictive value are given, although the proposed use is referral support in a population where autism prevalence is a few per cent rather than 47%. For the three-class severity problem the class distribution is not reported, so the reader cannot compute a chance baseline, and no baseline is offered. And no permutation test or majority-class comparison accompanies the near-ceiling detection figures. [RQ4.4] The most thorough interpretability work in this review, and unusually it is used to verify the model's reasoning against an independent clinical account rather than to generate a post-hoc narrative. Three techniques operate in sequence. Attention weights across the frame sequence identify which time points drove the decision, plotted per participant. Grad-CAM is then applied specifically at those attention peaks, localising the spatially informative regions within the frames that mattered - so the spatial and temporal explanations are coupled rather than independent. Agglomerative hierarchical clustering of attention-weight trajectories across the test set, displayed as dendrograms with participant identifiers alongside the heatmaps, tests whether the model's temporal decision patterns cluster by class at the dataset level rather than only in selected examples. The results are behaviourally specific and, crucially, match the constructs the tasks were designed to elicit: triadic gaze shifting in IJA, sustained versus fleeting gaze on the indicated object in low-level RJA, and immediate turning with a return to the examiner in high-level RJA. The authors' claim that the system 'made predictions based on salient behavioral differences... in the same way trained specialists diagnose ASD' is therefore supported by evidence rather than asserted. The cluster maps also corroborate the quantitative severity finding independently, showing IJA separating the three severity classes more cleanly than the RJA tasks. Two limits remain. Grad-CAM and attention illustrations are presented for selected participants and time points, so they demonstrate that the model can attend to the right things without establishing that it always does. And no quantitative test rules out appearance, background or site confounds, which an end-to-end model on raw frames from differently recruited groups is exposed to. [RQ4.5] Correctly constructed at the split, and this deserves explicit credit: 'we used 10-fold group-wise (by individual) cross-validation', stated unambiguously, so all clips from a child fall in the same fold and no participant contributes to both training and testing. That is exactly the safeguard most of this corpus omits, and it matters here because each child supplies up to ten IJA and five RJA clips from a single continuous session, which under clip-level splitting would be near-duplicates. Confidence intervals are computed by a named method and reported for every metric, and the classification threshold is fixed at 0.5 rather than tuned. Within its own terms the evaluation is therefore sound, and the near-perfect detection figures cannot be attributed to participant leakage. The problem lies upstream, in what the evaluation is an evaluation of. The paper states that conservative criteria were used deliberately 'to select individuals belonging to clinically distinct groups to ensure development of an accurate and precise ASD vs TD classification model', and the participant table shows a 44-50 point IQ gap at p < .001 with an autism sample that is 62% preverbal or single-word. Separating those two groups is a far easier problem than the clinical question, and AUROCs of 99.5-99.8% are the expected result rather than a surprising one - so the honest reading is that the study demonstrates the protocol and pipeline work, not that the system would perform at this level on the children a referral tool would actually see. The severity analysis inherits the same issue in a specific form: its three classes include non-autism, so a large part of its 90.3% AUROC is the already-solved detection problem, and because no autism-only result is reported there is no evidence that the system grades severity within the spectrum. Further gaps: no external validation, which the authors acknowledge; no clinical comparison group; no specificity; no class distribution for the severity bands and hence no chance baseline; and no adjustment for the IQ difference despite ANCOVA being straightforward and the authors demonstrably comfortable with mixed ANOVA elsewhere in the paper. The corrective study is well specified by the authors themselves - an IQ-matched external cohort - and would be worth considerably more than the present numbers. [RQ5.1] No formal keyword list is carried in the retrieved text; the article is categorised under Psychiatry as an Original Investigation. Governing terms in the title and body: joint attention, deep learning, detection, symptom severity assessment, behavioural biomarker, explainable AI, initiation of joint attention, response to joint attention, Early Social Communication Scales, compliance score, Grad-CAM, attention weights, hierarchical clustering, digitalized measurement. The framing vocabulary is diagnostic-clinical rather than engineering - 'diagnostic study', 'criterion standard diagnostic tool', 'predictive performance' - and 'screening' appears only in reference to the K-CARS-2 stage. [RQ5.2] JAMA Network Open 6(5):e2315174, published 25 May 2023, accepted 10 April 2023, open access under CC-BY, with a correction issued 7 July 2023 for an author contact detail. This is the highest-profile clinical venue of any study in the corpus and the venue standards are visible throughout: adherence to the STARD reporting guideline is declared, the participant table carries formal group comparisons with p values for every characteristic, every performance metric is reported with a 95% confidence interval computed by a named method, funder role and author contributions are itemised, competing interests including issued patents are disclosed in full, and a data sharing statement is provided. Two supplements carry the enrolment flow diagram, task and acquisition procedures, compliance metric, architecture diagram, training and validation performance, age-stratified results and all interpretability figures. The contrast with the conference-proceedings papers elsewhere in this corpus is instructive: the same underlying study reported at a workshop would have shown none of the participant characterisation that makes its IQ confound visible. [RQ5.3] Published 2023 by the Department of Biomedical Systems Informatics at Yonsei University College of Medicine with the Division of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry at Seoul National University College of Medicine and LumanLab Inc, funded by an MD-PhD Physician-Scientist Training Program grant from the Korea Health Industry Development Institute. The framing is a critique of the existing computational literature rather than of clinical practice, and it is one of the sharpest such critiques in the corpus: prior autism-detection models are said to be unsuitable for tool development because of 'a lack of automation, the requirements for specialized and expensive equipment, calibration, trained personnel, dependence on human rating of autistic behaviors, and low precision and recall', with the low performance attributed to the absence of targeted behavioural biomarkers and of methods for quantitatively measuring hallmark autism behaviours. The response - instrument an already-validated clinical construct with a replicable protocol and a consumer camera, rather than search for a statistical signature in whatever data are available - is the study's real contribution and is a template the rest of this literature could usefully follow. Two contextual features should be carried into the synthesis. This is one of very few studies here whose autistic sample is predominantly minimally verbal with mean IQ in the 50s, a population systematically excluded elsewhere by paradigms requiring screen attention or conversation - and simultaneously the study whose groups differ most on IQ, so the two facts are the same fact. And the method is patented by its authors with a commercial entity involved in data management, disclosed fully but without the independent-analysis safeguard reported by the Duke group elsewhere in this corpus.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Secondary computational analysis of a public eye-tracking scanpath image dataset, conducted at Vellore Institute of Technology in India with no new data collection. The dataset comprises 547 visualised scanpath images from 59 children, distributed as two folders - one for typically developing children and one for children diagnosed with autism. Nothing further about the participants is reported: no ages, no sexes, no group sizes, no IQ, no language level, no severity, no comorbidity, and no diagnostic instrument, criteria or clinician. The eliciting task, stimuli, eye tracker and the scheme by which gaze data were rendered into images are likewise not described. The images were split once into 382 training (70%), 108 validation (20%) and 57 test (10%), with the image as the unit of splitting; since 59 children produced 547 images, roughly nine per child, each test image is accompanied by around eight images from the same child in the training and validation sets. The test-set confusion matrix implies 34 typically developing and 23 autism images among the 57 held out. No ethics, funding or competing-interests statement appears.
narrative_rows.methods: Images were converted from RGBA to RGB and then handled along two paths. For a custom convolutional network they were resized to 100x100 and converted to greyscale using the standard luminance weighting, a choice adopted after RGB training proved slow and greyscale was observed to improve accuracy. That network has five levels - 16, 32, 64 and 128 3x3 filters with ReLU and 2x2 max pooling, then flatten to 2048, dense layers of 256 and 128, and a sigmoid output over two classes - and was trained with Adam at learning rate 0.001, binary cross-entropy loss, batch size 64 and 15 epochs. For the proposed pipeline, images were resized to 299x299 with pixel values normalised to [-1, 1] and passed through ImageNet-pretrained InceptionV3, with a 2048-dimensional feature vector taken from the last convolutional layer immediately before global average pooling on the stated rationale that layers near the classifier head carry the most distinctive representations. Those features were fed either to logistic regression or to a two-hidden-layer multilayer perceptron with 200 and 100 neurons. All implementation used TensorFlow on Google Colab. Evaluation was on the single fixed 57-image test set with accuracy, per-class precision, recall and F1, confusion matrices and ROC curves.
narrative_rows.outcomes: The custom CNN reached 71.9% accuracy, InceptionV3 features with logistic regression 78.9%, and InceptionV3 features with an MLP 81.0%. The per-class results are more informative than the headline figures and the authors report them prominently. The custom CNN classified 30 of 34 typically developing images correctly but only 11 of 23 autism images, giving class-wise recall of 0.88 versus 0.48 and F1 of 0.79 versus 0.58 - so a model reported at 71.9% accuracy detected fewer than half the autism cases, below the 59.6% majority-class baseline implied by the same matrix, and the authors state that its 'ability to classify the people affected by ASD was not upto the mark'. Both transfer-learning models were substantially more balanced: logistic regression achieved class-wise precision 0.84/0.72, recall 0.79/0.78 and F1 0.82/0.75, and the MLP 0.83/0.77, 0.85/0.74 and 0.84/0.76. ROC curves are plotted for both but no AUC value is quoted. The conclusion attributes the modest overall accuracy to the dataset containing only 547 images and proposes augmentation and dataset expansion.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The 547 images were split by image rather than by child, so with roughly nine images per child each test image has about eight siblings in training - the same leakage route that recurs across reuses of this dataset. The single fixed split leaves 57 test images with no cross-validation and no confidence intervals, so the 81.0% versus 78.9% comparison the paper draws corresponds to about one image, and no majority-class baseline is computed against an implied 59.6% floor. Greyscale conversion was adopted partly because it improved accuracy on this same data. Nothing at all is reported about the 59 children - no demographics, no clinical characteristics, no group sizes, and no diagnostic procedure - so the quantity being predicted is defined only by folder membership. The task that generated the gaze data is never described, so the paper's own rationale about looking at eyes and mouths cannot be connected to its data. And because the input is a rendered picture rather than a gaze time series, incidental graphical properties such as plotted extent, ink density and line-crossing count are available to the models and indistinguishable from behavioural signal, a question no interpretability analysis addresses. The authors state one limitation - the small dataset - and state it correctly.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The value of this study to the review is comparative rather than evidential. It is the fourth independent reuse of the 547-image scanpath dataset encountered here, and it is the one that reports the lowest accuracy: 81.0% at best, against roughly 97% and 99% reported by other groups on the identical images. Crucially, it shares the same methodological flaw as those higher-scoring reuses - splitting by image rather than by child, so that each of 59 children's roughly nine images straddle the split - yet does not achieve their results. The most plausible reading is that generic ImageNet features passed to a shallow classifier extract less individual-identity information from a rendered trajectory than an end-to-end network trained or fine-tuned on the same images, which means the gap between this paper and the higher-scoring ones is itself evidence about how much of those figures reflects within-child similarity rather than diagnostic signal. Read alongside the source authors' own participant-level correction to around 71% and another group's one-image-per-child leave-one-out figure of 72.88%, this study's 81% sits nearer the defensible end of the range. Two further observations are worth carrying forward. Its per-class reporting demonstrates concretely why aggregate accuracy is inadequate in this literature: a model reported at 71.9% detected 48% of autism cases, a fact visible only because the authors published the confusion matrix and reasoned explicitly that accuracy 'does not give much importance to the class imbalance'. And its recommendation to use generative adversarial networks to expand the dataset should be flagged as a hazard rather than a remedy, since synthesising images from a 547-image corpus and then evaluating on an image-level split would deepen the dependence between training and test data while making it harder to see.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Fifty-nine children contributing 547 scanpath images - the fourth independent reuse of this dataset encountered in this review. The study reports nothing further about who those children were: no counts per group, no ages, no sex, no diagnostic information. The dataset is described purely as two folders, 'TCImages' for typically developing children and 'TSImages' for children diagnosed with autism. The modelled unit is the image, and the split is 382 training, 108 validation and 57 test images with no indication that a child's images were kept together. Because 547 images come from 59 children, each child contributes roughly nine images, so under a random image-level split every test image is accompanied by around eight images from the same child in training or validation. The test-set confusion matrix implies 34 typically developing and 23 autism images among the 57 held out, which is the only class-composition information recoverable anywhere in the paper. [RQ1.2] 'Children with autism spectrum disorder' and 'ASD child' are used alongside 'normal child' and 'TD child', with the autism/normal contrast appearing repeatedly - 'the gaze patterns of a normal child and a child affected with autism', 'differentiate between a TD child and an ASD child'. The framing is medical-model and at times stronger than the evidence warrants: autism is 'a medical condition which is a result of abnormal brain development', characterised by 'abnormal behaviours' and 'fixation abnormality'. Autistic children are described as people who 'refrain from expressing their feeling in the form of facial expressions' and who 'indulge in various repetitive behaviours'. The intent is plainly not hostile - the paper's motivation is that the existing diagnostic process 'consumes a lot of time and energy of both the children and parents' - but the vocabulary of abnormality is used without qualification and the 'normal' contrast term is the one this review has flagged elsewhere as carrying an implication that 'typically developing' does not. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. [RQ1.3] None whatsoever. Not a single demographic or clinical characteristic of the 59 children is reported - no age, no sex, no IQ, no language level, no severity, no comorbidity, no socioeconomic status, no race or ethnicity, and not even the number of children or images in each group. The paper's participant description consists entirely of two folder names. This is the most complete absence of participant information among the included studies, and it follows from the study's nature as a pure dataset-reuse exercise: the authors downloaded images and classified them. The consequence is that nothing can be said about who the model works for, whether the groups were matched on anything, or whether the classification could be driven by an age or sex imbalance between folders - questions that a reader must go to the original dataset publication to answer, and which this paper does not flag as open. [RQ1.4] Absent. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician or process is reported for the 59 children, and the labels are taken directly from the folder structure of the downloaded dataset. The introduction does contain a description of how autism is diagnosed in general practice - initial concern about developmental milestones, paediatrician assessment, referral to a psychologist, child neurologist, speech and language pathologist or developmental paediatrician, then behavioural observation, child and parent interviews, questionnaires and the CARS rating scale - and it correctly observes that 'there are no standard definitive tests like blood test to identify the condition'. But none of this is connected to the actual data. The target being predicted is therefore whichever folder an image sits in, and the study inherits without examination whatever ascertainment the source dataset applied. For a review comparing studies partly on the strength of their reference standards, this is the floor. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, language, adaptive or severity measure appears, and none could, since no participants were assessed by these authors. The absence has a specific analytical cost in this design: the scanpath is a picture of where a child looked during an unreported task, and how much a child looks at all - the number of fixations, the spatial extent covered - varies with attention, developmental level and task compliance. Without any measure of those, a difference in the visual density or spread of the plotted trajectory cannot be separated from a difference in social attention. Since the models are given only the drawing, this is precisely the ambiguity that an interpretability analysis would have addressed, and none is performed. [RQ2.1] The stated aim is to use eye-tracking scanpath images 'as a biological indicator to identify children with autism' and to compare a transfer-learning-plus-classical-classifier pipeline against an end-to-end custom CNN. Findings: the custom CNN reached 71.9% accuracy, InceptionV3 features with logistic regression 78.9%, and InceptionV3 features with an MLP 81.0%. The per-class analysis is the substantive result and the authors present it properly rather than resting on accuracy. The custom CNN's confusion matrix shows 30 of 34 typically developing images correct against only 11 of 23 autism images - class-wise recall of 0.88 versus 0.48, F1 of 0.79 versus 0.58 - so a model reported at 71.9% accuracy is in fact detecting fewer than half the autism cases, and the authors say so: its 'ability to classify the people affected by ASD was not upto the mark'. The transfer-learning models are markedly more balanced, with class-wise F1 of 0.82/0.75 for logistic regression and 0.84/0.76 for the MLP, and the authors conclude on that basis rather than on the accuracy difference alone. The conclusion attributes the modest overall performance to the small dataset and proposes augmentation and dataset expansion. [RQ2.2] There is no study setting: all work was performed on Google Colab using a downloaded public dataset, at Vellore Institute of Technology in India, on images collected elsewhere. No children were recruited, tested, observed or consented for this work. This matters for how the study should be weighted in the review: it contributes no new evidence about autistic children and no new data, and its value lies entirely in being an additional independent modelling attempt on a dataset that several other included studies also use - which makes it a comparison point rather than a primary source. [RQ2.3] Not reported. The paper never states what the children were looking at when the gaze data were recorded, how long the recording lasted, what the display or eye tracker were, or how the scanpaths were rendered into images. It describes only the general definitions of fixation, blink and saccade from the source experiment, and states that the source study 'provides these visualised scanpath images which is used in the work as a biomarker'. So the study models a representation of a behaviour elicited by an unknown task. Two consequences follow for interpretation. Nothing can be said about whether the discriminative signal is social - the whole rationale offered in the introduction concerns looking at eyes and mouths, but if the stimuli were not faces that rationale does not apply. And the rendering choices that turned gaze coordinates into pictures - line width, colour, marker size, axis scaling, whether fixation duration is encoded as circle radius - are properties of the source dataset that determine what a convolutional network can extract, and none is described. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional by inheritance; the study performs no temporal analysis and could not. No ethics statement of any kind appears, which for a secondary analysis of published de-identified images is defensible in substance but is still a reporting omission - the source dataset's approvals are not referenced. No funding statement and no competing-interests declaration appear either. The paper is a four-to-six page conference contribution and these omissions are typical of that format, but they are omissions nonetheless. [RQ2.5] Google Colab and TensorFlow; InceptionV3 pretrained on ImageNet. That is the entirety of the apparatus, because no data were collected. The eye tracker, display, stimuli and recording software that produced the underlying gaze data are not named, so a reader cannot evaluate the measurement chain at all - a striking situation for a study whose stated contribution is to use eye tracking as a biomarker. The description of InceptionV3's architectural innovations (factorised convolutions, asymmetric factorisation, auxiliary classifiers, efficient grid size reduction) is detailed and accurate but is standard exposition rather than anything specific to this application. [RQ2.6] Adequate for the modelling, absent for the data. Reproducible: the source dataset is cited and public; the split counts are given exactly (382/108/57); the preprocessing is fully specified including the RGBA-to-RGB conversion, the 100x100 resize, the greyscale luminance formula, the 299x299 resize for InceptionV3 and the [-1, 1] normalisation; the custom CNN is tabulated layer by layer with kernel counts, sizes and output dimensions at each of five levels; the extraction point in InceptionV3 is named; and the MLP hidden layer sizes, optimiser, learning rate, loss, batch size and epoch count are all given. Not reproducible: the specific train/validation/test split, the random seed, and the mapping from images to children - which is the one piece of information needed to determine whether the evaluation is participant-disjoint. There is also a transcription error in the greyscale formula, where the blue coefficient is given as 0.144 rather than the standard 0.114. [RQ2.7] The single stated limitation is correct and is stated without defensiveness: accuracy is not high, and this is attributed to the dataset containing only 547 images. The authors do not inflate their results - they describe them as promising for future research rather than as a demonstration of feasibility, and they report the custom CNN's poor autism-class performance rather than burying it. What is unaddressed is nonetheless substantial. The split is by image and not by child, so with roughly nine images per child each test image has around eight siblings in training - the mechanism that has produced very high accuracies in other reuses of this same dataset, and one this paper neither invokes nor guards against. A single fixed split of 57 test images cannot support the three-way accuracy comparison the paper draws, since a difference of 81.0% against 78.9% is a single image. No majority-class baseline is computed, though the confusion matrix implies 59.6%, so the custom CNN's 71.9% is roughly twelve points above trivial and its autism-class recall of 0.48 is below it. The greyscale conversion was adopted partly because it improved accuracy, a decision made against the same small dataset. Nothing is reported about the 59 children. And no analysis addresses what visual property of a drawn trajectory the models respond to. [RQ2.9] Two directions, both aimed at the sample-size constraint the authors identify: use data augmentation, specifically generative adversarial networks, to synthesise additional scanpath images, and expand the dataset itself. The first should be flagged as a hazard rather than a solution in this specific setting - generating synthetic scanpath images from a 547-image corpus and then evaluating on an image-level split would compound rather than mitigate the dependence between training and test data, and would do so invisibly. Expanding the dataset is the sound recommendation. Not proposed: splitting by participant, reporting participant-level accuracy, characterising the children, or examining what the models learn. [RQ3.1] Visual scanning behaviour, encoded as a picture. A scanpath is defined correctly in the paper as a spatiotemporal representation of consecutive fixations and saccades that may overlap, and the input to every model is a rendered image of that trajectory. The behavioural claim motivating the work is the standard eye-tracking account of autism - that autistic children look away from eyes and mouths and towards background, with the widely cited 2008 observation about a 15-month-old attending more to the mouth than the eyes given as the example. But the study cannot test that claim, because it never reports what the children were looking at and never inspects what the models attend to. What is actually modelled is the appearance of a line drawing, and the properties of that drawing that a convolutional network could exploit include several that are only indirectly behavioural: the total extent of the plotted region, the density of overplotting, the number of line crossings, the aspect ratio of the traversed area. Some of these are informative about looking behaviour; others would follow from a child simply producing more or fewer gaze samples. The representation makes them indistinguishable, and no analysis in the paper separates them. [RQ3.2] None. A single modality rendered as a single image type, with no fusion, no auxiliary features and no metadata. The three reported models are alternatives compared against each other rather than channels combined. What the comparison does establish, usefully, is a difference in error profile rather than merely in accuracy: the end-to-end CNN is heavily skewed towards the majority class (recall 0.88 versus 0.48) while the ImageNet-pretrained feature extractor plus a simple classifier is balanced (0.85 versus 0.74 for the MLP). That is a real observation about small-sample deep learning - a network trained from scratch on 382 images collapses towards the majority class, while generic pretrained features generalise better - and it is the study's most transferable finding, though the paper frames it in terms of accuracy rather than of what it reveals about training regime. [RQ4.1] Two contrasting approaches. The proposed pipeline uses ImageNet-pretrained InceptionV3 as a fixed feature extractor, taking the 2048-dimensional output of the last convolutional layer before global average pooling on the stated principle that layers close to the classifier head carry the most distinctive representations, and feeds these to either logistic regression or a two-hidden-layer MLP (200 and 100 neurons). The baseline is a custom five-level CNN trained from scratch (16, 32, 64 and 128 3x3 filters, ReLU, 2x2 max pooling at each level, flatten to 2048, dense 256, dense 128, sigmoid output) with Adam at learning rate 0.001, binary cross-entropy, batch size 64 and 15 epochs. The choice is appropriate to the data volume and the result vindicates it: with 382 training images, transfer learning outperforms training from scratch by 9 percentage points and, more importantly, produces a balanced rather than a majority-collapsed classifier. The paper describes InceptionV3 as 'fine-tuned' in one place while describing features as extracted from a fixed layer in another, an ambiguity about whether any weights were updated that is not resolved. [RQ4.2] A rendered scanpath image, resized either to 100x100 greyscale (custom CNN) or 299x299 RGB with pixel values normalised to [-1, 1] (InceptionV3). The greyscale conversion for the CNN is described candidly as an empirical choice: RGB training was slow and 'converting the images to grayscale proved to significantly reduce the training time and an improvement in classification accuracy was also noticed'. That is honest reporting of a decision made partly on observed accuracy, and it is worth noting that if the source rendering used colour to encode anything - fixation order, duration, or which eye - greyscale conversion would discard it, and the paper cannot say whether it did, because the rendering scheme is never described. The deeper representational point is that all temporal information in the original gaze data survives only as visual geometry: sequence order, fixation duration and saccade velocity are recoverable from a drawing only to the extent the renderer encoded them, and the model receives no time series at all. [RQ4.3] Better than the corpus norm for a paper of this scale. Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 are reported per class rather than only in aggregate, confusion matrices are given for the CNN, and ROC curves are plotted for both transfer-learning classifiers. The per-class reporting is what makes the study useful, because it reveals that the custom CNN's 71.9% accuracy conceals autism-class recall of 0.48 - fewer than half the autism images detected, which is below the 59.6% majority-class baseline implied by the confusion matrix. The authors explicitly justify reporting beyond accuracy on the grounds that it 'does not give much importance to the class imbalance in a dataset if at all it exists', which is the right reasoning. Gaps: AUC values are plotted but never quoted numerically; no confidence intervals accompany any figure, although a 57-image test set makes one image worth 1.8 percentage points and therefore makes the 81.0% versus 78.9% comparison uninterpretable; no majority-class baseline is stated; and no participant-level metric is possible given the splitting scheme. [RQ4.4] None. No class activation mapping, saliency analysis, feature visualisation, error analysis or inspection of misclassified images is reported for any of the three models. The methods section instead provides several paragraphs of general exposition on how convolutional layers, pooling variants and InceptionV3's factorisation techniques work - accurate but generic. The absence is more consequential here than in studies that model interpretable features, because the input is a picture of a behaviour rather than the behaviour itself, so there is a genuine open question about whether the models respond to where the gaze went or to incidental graphical properties such as ink density, plotted extent or line crossing count. A single class activation map over a handful of correctly and incorrectly classified scanpaths would have addressed it directly and would have been the most informative addition the paper could have made. [RQ4.5] A single fixed 70/20/10 split of 547 images into 382 training, 108 validation and 57 test, with the image as the unit. Fifty-nine children produced those 547 images, so roughly nine images per child, and nothing in the paper indicates that a child's images were kept together - so on a random split each test image is accompanied by around eight siblings from the same child. This is the same design flaw that recurs across reuses of this dataset, and it is the reason the review treats the family of studies built on it as a triangulation problem rather than as independent evidence. What makes this particular paper informative is that the leakage does not produce a high number: 81.0% at best, against figures near 97-99% reported by other groups on the identical images. The most plausible reading is that generic ImageNet features plus a shallow classifier extract less individual-identity information from a rendered trajectory than an end-to-end network fine-tuned on the same data - so the gap between this study and the higher-scoring reuses is itself evidence about how much of those higher scores is identity rather than diagnosis. Read alongside the source authors' own participant-level correction to around 71% and another group's one-image-per-child leave-one-out result of 72.88%, this study's 81% sits closer to the honest end of the range than to the inflated one, despite sharing the flawed split. Other weaknesses compound the picture: a 57-image test set with no confidence intervals, so the three-way model comparison rests on differences of one or two images; no cross-validation or repeated splits; no chance baseline against an implied 59.6% floor; and one architectural choice (greyscale conversion) made with reference to observed accuracy on the same data. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, scan path, eye tracking, deep learning, transfer learning. Four of five name the method or modality and none names an application - neither screening, diagnosis nor classification appears, although the body text uses 'autism diagnosis technique' and 'second opinion'. Terms carried through the text: visualised scanpath images, biomarker, gaze disparities, fixation abnormality, hybrid classifier model, InceptionV3, feature extraction. [RQ5.2] 2023 2nd International Conference on Vision Towards Emerging Trends in Communication and Networking Technologies (ViTECoN), IEEE - a general communications and networking engineering conference, not a clinical, biomedical or machine-learning venue. That placement explains the paper's balance: substantial textbook exposition of convolutional networks and InceptionV3 architecture aimed at a non-specialist engineering audience, minimal clinical context, and no participant characterisation at all. It also explains the absence of ethics, funding and competing-interests statements, which such venues do not typically require. The paper is short and does not overreach; the reporting gaps are those of the format as much as of the authors. [RQ5.3] Published 2023 by the Department of Computer Science at Vellore Institute of Technology, India, with no reported funding. The framing is the standard workload-and-subjectivity argument: there is no definitive biological test for autism, diagnosis depends on a chain of specialist referrals and subjective instruments, and 'the process of diagnosis itself consumes a lot of time and energy of both the children and parents', so computer-aided methods offering a reliable 'second opinion' are attractive. The paper positions itself within an eye-tracking-for-diagnosis literature that it surveys across several conditions - Parkinson disease, dementia, dyslexia, schizophrenia - before turning to autism, which is a useful reminder that the same modality and often the same architectures are being applied across diagnoses, and that a scanpath classifier reported at 95% for dyslexia and 78.85% for schizophrenia in the cited work is not obviously measuring anything condition-specific. For this review the study's value is not its result but its position: it is the fourth independent reuse of the 547-image dataset encountered here, it applies a different modelling family from the others, and its comparatively modest 81% - obtained under the same image-level splitting that has yielded 97-99% elsewhere - is a useful data point on how much of those higher figures is attributable to method rather than to signal.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Secondary computational analysis of pooled public child-language corpora, conducted at IIIT Delhi with no new data collection. Transcripts of 76 children were drawn from three independently assembled datasets in the CHILDES databank: Eigsti (16 autistic, 16 typically developing, aged 3-6 years, 30-minute free play), Nadig (13 autistic, 25 typically developing, aged 3-7 years, approximately 10 minutes of parent-child free play) and Flusberg (6 autistic, no comparison children, aged 12-26 months, natural mother-child interaction), giving 35 autistic and 41 typically developing children overall. Because Flusberg contributes autistic children exclusively and from an age band no comparison child occupies, corpus membership carries diagnostic information by construction. No individual-level information is reported for any child - no sex, IQ, language level, severity or comorbidity - and no diagnostic instrument, criteria or procedure is described, the labels being inherited as binary clinical status from the three sources. The Eigsti corpus additionally contains a developmental delay group, which is not used. No ethics statement, competing-interests declaration or limitations section appears; funding is acknowledged in full.
narrative_rows.methods: Seventy-seven linguistic features were extracted from the transcripts in three families. Nine semantic-pragmatic measures were specified explicitly against ADOS criteria: mean length of utterance in morphemes, number of distinct word roots, questions initiated by the child, proportion of immediately repeated phrases, child-child discourse coherence and child-partner discourse coherence (both cosine similarities between BERT embeddings of consecutive sentences), echolalia as immediate repetition of the partner's bigrams, proportion of unintelligible units, and unexpected words via TF-IDF. Forty-five part-of-speech tag frequencies formed the lexical family and 23 measures from L2SCA the syntactic complexity family, with CLAN supplying the morphosyntactic baseline. Count-based features were normalised over conversation length, which is necessary given that source sessions range from about 10 to 30 minutes. SHAP analysis on the initial feature set drove elimination to 63 features, apparently before the train-test split. Six classifier families were then compared using an AutoML tool under a stated 90:10 split, with an RBF-kernel SVM retained as best and its C and gamma tuned by grid search with 5-fold cross-validation inside the training data. Accuracy, macro precision, macro recall and macro F1 were reported for every classifier and for seven feature-set configurations, with a majority classifier as the baseline comparator.
narrative_rows.outcomes: The best model, an RBF SVM on all 63 features, reached 94.1% accuracy with macro precision 95%, recall 94% and F1 94%, against a majority-classifier baseline of 56.4% accuracy and 32% macro F1 - a 37.7% relative improvement. Across classifier families, k-nearest neighbours reached 64.7%, logistic regression and gradient boosting 76.5% each, and random forest 88.2%. The feature ablation is the substantive result: morphosyntactic baseline features alone gave 70.59%, syntactic complexity alone 70% (with macro F1 of only 55%, reflecting recall of 58%), part-of-speech frequencies alone 82%, the semantic-pragmatic set alone 82.3%, part-of-speech plus semantic-pragmatic 88.2%, and all three families together 94.1% - so the semantic-pragmatic family matches the lexical family on its own and the three combine additively rather than redundantly, which is precisely the question the study set out to answer. SHAP attribution placed the number of distinct word roots first, with unexpected words and both discourse-coherence measures in the top ten, and the authors related these to prior findings that vocabulary extent differentiates autistic children and that autistic children show reduced global coherence in conversation.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The three pooled corpora differ in age band, session length, conversation partner and transcription convention, and the differences are not label-neutral: Flusberg contributes 6 autistic children and no comparison children, from an age range of 12-26 months that no comparison child occupies, so corpus identity partially predicts diagnosis and corpus-specific artefacts are available to the classifier as diagnostic cues. Since every feature is a language measure in children and the top SHAP contributor is the number of distinct word roots - a canonical developmental index that changes dramatically between 12 months and 8 years - a developmental rather than autism-specific explanation of the result cannot be excluded, and no age, IQ or language-level data exist to adjust for it. The conversation partner varies across corpora and is referred to inconsistently within the paper as therapist, trainer and parent, while child-partner discourse coherence ranks among the top features. SHAP-based feature elimination from 77 to 63 appears to precede the train-test split, and six classifier families were compared with the best reported. All reported accuracies are exact multiples of 1/17, fixing the test set at 17 items rather than the 7 or 8 implied by the stated 90:10 split, so the difference between the headline 94.1% and the next configuration is one child, and no confidence intervals are offered. No reference standard is described for any participant, and the developmental delay group available in the Eigsti corpus - the material for the differential comparison the conclusion says is needed - was not used.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The most substantive feature-engineering contribution in this review's language-based studies, and the one that most directly tests a question the field has left open. Its design principle is worth carrying forward independently of its results: features are specified against ADOS, so every measure has a clinical referent, and the resulting model can be explained in terms a clinician would recognise - echolalia, discourse coherence, initiative in asking questions, vocabulary extent - rather than in embeddings or spectral coefficients. That places it with the joint-attention and facial-complexity studies charted here in the small group that treats interpretability as a design constraint rather than a reporting nicety. Its ablation is the finding to retain: semantic-pragmatic features alone match part-of-speech features (82.3% against 82%), and the three linguistic families combine additively to 94.1%, which establishes that pragmatic measures carry independent signal rather than restating lexical ones. Two of its features are also unusual in this corpus for being genuinely dyadic - echolalia and child-partner coherence are defined by the relation between what the partner said and what the child said next, so they encode interaction rather than individual output, which is what pragmatic assessment actually requires. Its evaluation practice is mixed in an instructive way: it reports a majority-classifier baseline as a named comparator with improvements quantified against it, which most of this corpus omits, while resting its headline on a 17-item test set with unnested feature selection and a six-way classifier search. And its central design decision - pooling three corpora one of which supplies autistic children exclusively, from an age band the comparison group does not reach - is the clearest example in the review of a confound created by dataset assembly rather than by measurement, in a study where the obvious corrective (leave-one-corpus-out validation) was available in the data and not performed.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Seventy-six children assembled from three independent corpora in the CHILDES databank: Eigsti (16 autistic, 16 typically developing, aged 3-6, 30-minute free play), Nadig (13 autistic, 25 typically developing, aged 3-7, approximately 10 minutes of parent-child free play) and Flusberg (6 autistic, no comparison children, aged 12-26 months, natural mother-child interaction), giving 35 autistic and 41 typically developing overall. The composition matters more than the totals. Flusberg contributes autistic children only, so corpus membership is partially informative about diagnosis by construction, and it contributes them from an age band - infancy and early toddlerhood - that no comparison child occupies. The three corpora also differ in session length by a factor of three, in conversation partner, and in transcription era and convention. The paper notes that the Eigsti corpus contains a developmental delay group alongside autism and typical development, but that group is not used. No child-level information beyond corpus, group and corpus-level age range is reported anywhere. [RQ1.2] 'Children with autism (CwA)' is used throughout as the working abbreviation, alongside 'typically developing (TD)' and 'neurotypical', which is a more current pairing than the 'normal' contrast used elsewhere in this corpus. The clinical framing is nonetheless firmly deficit-based and in one respect dated: autism is characterised by 'repetitive and stereotypic behaviours and impaired social and communicative skills collectively called the triads of impairments', a formulation superseded by DSM-5's two-domain structure a decade before this paper. Language differences are described as 'language and communication impairments', 'language atypicalities' and 'aberrant receptive and expressive language development', and the targeted behaviours are 'stereotypic language behaviours'. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. Against this, the paper's motivating concern is a reasonable one about assessment rather than about people - that quantifying behavioural traits 'is cumbersome, and the efficacy of such methods primarily depends on the evaluators' expertise' - and its stated goal is interpretable measurement that a non-expert could follow, which is a service orientation rather than a replacement one. [RQ1.3] Almost nothing at the individual level. Table 1 reports, per corpus, the number of autistic and typically developing participants and an age range: Eigsti 16/16 aged 3-6, Nadig 13/25 aged 3-7, Flusberg 6/0 aged 12-26 months. No sex, IQ, language level, socioeconomic status, race or ethnicity, comorbidity or severity is given for any child, and no group means or matching statistics of any kind are reported. Three consequences follow, all unaddressed. Because the pooled age range spans 12 months to 8 years while the comparison group is confined to 3-7 years, the two groups differ in age distribution by construction - and every feature in the study is a language measure, which in children is dominated by developmental stage. Mean length of utterance and number of distinct word roots, the latter identified by SHAP as the single largest contributor to the model's predictions, are canonical expressive-language milestones that change dramatically between 12 months and 8 years, so an age difference between groups is not a nuisance covariate here but a direct alternative explanation for the headline result. And without IQ or language-level data there is no way to separate an autism-specific pragmatic signature from a general language-delay one, which is precisely what the unused developmental delay group in the Eigsti corpus could have tested. [RQ1.4] Absent as a described procedure. The paper's entire statement on this point is that it 'considered the binary classification problem of classifying a child as having ASD or not, as all three datasets had binary labelling of the clinical status' - so the labels are inherited from three separately assembled research corpora with no account of how autism was diagnosed in any of them, by whom, against which criteria or in which era. Given that the Flusberg corpus records children aged 12-26 months, its labels must derive from a very different ascertainment process from corpora recruiting 3-7 year olds, and pooling them without comment means the target variable is heterogeneous in an unexamined way. ADOS is invoked repeatedly, but as the source of the behavioural constructs the features are designed to mirror - echolalia, back-and-forth interchange, building on statements - rather than as an instrument administered to these children. That is a legitimate and rather elegant use of a diagnostic instrument as a specification for feature engineering, and it should not be confused with having a reference standard. [RQ1.5] No external cognitive, language or severity measure exists, and the absence is more consequential here than in most studies because language is simultaneously the modality, the feature set and the plausible confound. The study computes mean length of utterance in morphemes and number of distinct word roots - both standard expressive-language indices used clinically to characterise developmental level - and uses them as classifier inputs, with the second identified by SHAP as the dominant predictor. In a sample where the autistic group extends down to 12 months and the comparison group does not go below 3 years, that finding is compatible with the model having learned a developmental-language gradient rather than an autism-specific one. Nothing in the analysis distinguishes the two, because no independent measure of language level exists to adjust for. Severity is likewise absent and is named as future work. The gap also blocks the more interesting question the feature set was built to answer: whether pragmatic atypicality - echolalia, poor discourse coherence, failure to initiate questions - is present over and above general language level, which is the clinically meaningful version of the claim. [RQ2.1] The stated objectives are threefold: to automatically extract semantic and pragmatic language features including echolalia, semantic coherence and repetitive language usage; to compare them systematically and identify the most significant; and to build an interpretable assessment system on that basis. The gap the paper identifies in the literature is specific and fair - prior work on semantic-pragmatic features for autism has examined individual measures such as echolalia or pronoun usage in isolation, and 'the cumulative effect of the features and how they complement the lexical, syntactic and other text-based features in the diagnosis of autism has not been analysed'. Findings: the best classifier, an RBF SVM on all 63 retained features, reached 94.1% accuracy with 94% macro F1 against a majority-classifier baseline of 56.4% accuracy and 32% macro F1. The feature-set ablation is the substantive result and is reported in full: morphosyntactic baseline 70.59%, syntactic complexity alone 70%, part-of-speech frequencies alone 82%, semantic-pragmatic features alone 82.3%, part-of-speech plus semantic-pragmatic 88.2%, and all three families 94.1%. So the semantic-pragmatic set matches the lexical set on its own and the three families are complementary rather than redundant, which is exactly the claim the study set out to test. SHAP attribution places the number of distinct word roots first, with unexpected words and both child-child and child-partner discourse coherence in the top ten, and the authors relate each to prior findings on vocabulary extent and on global coherence in autistic conversation. [RQ2.2] No study setting: this is a computational reanalysis conducted at IIIT Delhi on transcripts collected years earlier in North American research laboratories. The three source settings are described only briefly and differ substantially - 30-minute free play sessions in one corpus, roughly 10 minutes of parent-child play in another, and natural mother-child interaction with 12-26 month olds in the third. That heterogeneity is the study's central unexamined problem, because it is not random with respect to the label: one corpus supplies autistic children exclusively. Any systematic difference between the corpora - transcription conventions, how disfluency and unintelligibility were marked, who the partner was, how long the session ran, what era the recording belongs to - is therefore partially aligned with diagnosis. Length-dependent features are normalised over conversation length, which handles the most obvious component, but transcription and partner effects are not addressable by normalisation and are not discussed. [RQ2.3] Three different paradigms pooled as though equivalent. Eigsti recorded 30-minute free play sessions; Nadig recorded approximately 10 minutes of parent-child free play; Flusberg recorded natural mother-child interaction in infants and toddlers. The conversation partner is not held constant and the paper's own terminology drifts - the echolalia feature is defined by repetition of bigrams 'originally spoken by the therapist', the discourse-coherence feature is described as similarity 'between BERT embeddings of consecutive sentences of therapist and child', SHAP results refer to 'trainer-child (t-c) discourse', and the corpus descriptions say the partner was a parent or the mother. Whoever the partner was, they are a live participant whose own language shapes every child-partner feature, and pragmatic behaviour in a child differs systematically with whether the interlocutor is a parent or a clinician. Since child-partner discourse coherence ranks among the top contributing features, this is not a peripheral concern. The countervailing strength is the paradigm's ecological character: these are unstructured natural conversations rather than elicited tasks, so the pragmatic behaviours the features target - taking initiative, building on statements, sustaining a topic - had a genuine opportunity to occur. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional by inheritance, with one session per child and no temporal analysis. The pooling of corpora spanning 12 months to 8 years creates something that looks like developmental range but is not a developmental design, since age is confounded with corpus and with label.
