The discussion's account of why the proposed model outperforms the alternatives is entirely generic and borrowed from the image-processing literature - that convolutional networks are 'successfully used for image denoising' and that convolution 'reduces the high dimensionality of images without losing its information' - with no reference to anything observed in these scan-paths. The absence is compounded by the flattening step, which means the model is not exploiting spatial structure in the way that explanation assumes. For a study whose entire input is a picture of a behaviour, and where incidental graphical properties are as available to the network as behavioural ones, a single class activation map over correctly and incorrectly classified scan-paths would have been the most informative addition possible. [RQ4.5] Two problems compound, and a third makes the result difficult to interpret at all. First, cross-validation partitions the 547 images rather than the 59 children. With roughly nine images per child and no statement that a child's images were kept within a fold, each held-out image is accompanied by around eight siblings from the same child in training - the same route that has produced accuracies from 81% to over 99% across five reuses of this identical dataset, against the source authors' own participant-level figure near 71% and an independent one-image-per-child leave-one-out result of 72.88%. Second, the reported figure is the maximum of an extremely large hyperparameter search: separate sweeps over kernel size, stride, pooling, batch size, optimiser and thirteen architecture configurations, well over a hundred cells in total, every one scored on the same cross-validation with the best bolded and carried forward. No held-out confirmation of the selected configuration is performed, and the 35-point spread between optimisers on identical data shows how much room that search had to exploit. Third, and most consequentially, the headline accuracy cannot be reconciled with the sensitivity and specificity reported for the same model. At 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic images, 77.60% sensitivity and 79.91% specificity give approximately 79.0% accuracy. That implied figure is strikingly consistent with the other honest estimates on this dataset - 81.0% from an independent transfer-learning study, 72.88% from one-image-per-child leave-one-out, and roughly 71% from the source authors' own participant-level correction - which suggests the class-conditional metrics may be the trustworthy ones and the accuracy column an artefact. Either way, the paper reports two irreconcilable characterisations of its own classifier and reconciles neither, so no single number from it can be carried into a synthesis without that caveat. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder (ASD); convolutional neural network (CNN); deep learning; eye-tracking scan path; multi-layer perceptron (MLP); machine learning (ML). Five of six are method labels and none names an application, although the body text speaks of automatic classification, early detection and biomarkers throughout. The coined model name T-CNN-ASD appears in the title and abstract and functions as branding for what is architecturally a small feed-forward network over flattened pixels. [RQ5.2] Information 15(3), article 133, MDPI, open access under CC BY; received 22 January 2024, revised 21 February, accepted 26 February, published 28 February 2024 - a 37-day turnaround from submission to publication. The venue is a general information-science journal rather than a clinical, biomedical or specialist machine-learning one, which is consistent with the paper's shape: twelve tables of hyperparameter sweeps, extensive tutorial exposition of convolutional network components, and no limitations section, ethics statement of its own, funding declaration or competing-interests statement. The compressed review period is worth noting given that the paper's central results table contains an unreconciled arithmetic inconsistency between accuracy and the class-conditional metrics. [RQ5.3] Published 2024 by the Department of Artificial Intelligence at the University of Jordan with Princess Sumaya University for Technology, Amman. The framing is the familiar cost-and-expertise argument, developed at unusual length: diagnosis requires specialised professionals using observation, interviews and questionnaires; current tools are time-consuming because of 'the extensive number of items that need to be checked by the specialist' and rely on 'static human-embedded rules'; and because 'each specialist relies on their own expertise and experience to diagnose autism spectrum disorder', the process suffers 'inconsistencies and a lack of reliability'. The introduction also engages with delayed diagnosis and its causes - limited resources in rural areas and low-income families, shortage of specialist referrals, parental awareness - which locates the work in the access literature. For this review the study's value is as the fifth reuse of the 547-image dataset and as the clearest instance of a specific reporting hazard. It is the only reuse to report sensitivity and specificity alongside accuracy, and those class-conditional metrics imply roughly 79% - close to the independent transfer-learning reuse at 81%, to the one-image-per-child leave-one-out figure of 72.88%, and to the source authors' own participant-level correction near 71%. The 95.59% headline is irreconcilable with them. Whichever number is correct, the paper illustrates why a review of this literature must recompute rather than accept reported accuracies, and why the near-ceiling figures that dominate this dataset's reuse literature should be treated as claims requiring arithmetic verification.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective national cohort study using electronic health records from Tipat Halav, the Israeli Ministry of Health's universal well-baby developmental surveillance programme, delivered by trained nurses and a developmental paediatrician across 503 clinics covering 75% of the population over roughly eleven visits from birth to age six. All 780,610 children born between January 2014 and December 2019 with at least two years of computerised records were included; 1,163 had an autism diagnosis recorded after age two and 774,778 formed the comparison group, giving a population incidence of 0.15%. Cases were ascertained by ICD-9 code (722 children) or by keyword search of provider free-text notes with manual verification that the reference concerned the child rather than a relative (553 children), with acronym collisions such as atrial septal defect screened out. Down syndrome was excluded from the comparison group but Fragile X, tuberous sclerosis and other autism-associated aetiologies were deliberately retained. The autism group was 78.3% male against 51.4% in the comparison group, with higher rates of preterm birth, older mothers, lower gestational age and birth weight, lower nursing rates and far higher parental concern. Mean age at recorded diagnosis was 37.5 months. Approval came from the Ministry of Health Helsinki committee with consent waived on anonymisation grounds; funding was from the Gertner Institute and no conflicts were declared.
narrative_rows.methods: One hundred candidate features were assembled from the records and reduced to 59 on clinical-relevance grounds before modelling, spanning developmental milestone attainment across gross motor, fine motor, language and personal-social domains, birth parameters, post-natal growth percentiles, familial variables and parent-reported concern. The surveillance protocol assesses 60 age-related milestones based partly on the Denver Developmental Screening Test, with 38 checked up to 24 months across nine age bins. Because checkup timing varies and children have multiple entries per milestone, each milestone was reduced to a binary of 'ever passed' versus 'only failed', chosen explicitly to avoid embedding developmental assumptions about never-tested and late-tested records, at the acknowledged cost of not distinguishing children who passed after several attempts. Predictors were capped at 24 months and the outcome restricted to diagnoses recorded after 24 months, a separation adopted deliberately to minimise leakage from diagnosis to predictors. A gradient boosting model was fitted with 3-fold cross-validation over children and compared against logistic regression, random forest and naive Bayes. The high-risk group was defined by the Youden threshold. SHAP quantified feature importance within each fold, with cross-fold stability reported, and the seven leading milestone predictors were tested independently with Fisher's exact tests.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Average test AUC was 0.86 (SD 0.009) with sensitivity 0.75 (SD 0.03) and specificity 0.81 (SD 0.02); training AUC was 0.88, which the authors report as indicating slight overfitting. At the Youden threshold 144,632 children (18.6% of the cohort) were flagged high risk, capturing 874 of the 1,163 cases - an autism incidence of 0.006 in that group against 0.001 in the cohort, a 4.3-fold enrichment, and a positive predictive value of 0.60% that the paper does not compute. The method comparison found almost no advantage for the tree ensemble: logistic regression matched gradient boosting at AUC 0.86 with marginally higher sensitivity (0.77 versus 0.75), random forest reached 0.84 and naive Bayes 0.83. The seven most important milestone predictors, all confirmed at p < 0.001 by independent testing, were vocabulary over ten words, building a tower from cubes, giving a kiss, eating independently with a spoon, knowing at least one body part, composing two-word sentences and saying 2-3 words - four language, two personal-social, one fine motor, all between 12 and 24 months. Male sex, parental developmental concern, non-nursing, older maternal age, lower gestational age and atypical growth percentiles were also key. SHAP rankings were stable across folds, with 15 of 24 unique top-20 features appearing in all three. A boys-only model performed comparably. Children flagged high risk had an odds ratio of 3.29 (95% CI 3.18-3.39) of independent referral for developmental assessment, a variable deliberately excluded from the model.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: Outcome ascertainment is the binding constraint and the authors state it plainly: because diagnoses are captured only when reported during well-baby visits, 'based on the national incidence of ASD, the true positive ASD group is at least 10 times higher in the examined population', so the great majority of autistic children in the cohort sit in the comparison group. That misclassification adds substantial label noise, biases sensitivity and specificity in directions the data cannot resolve, and means the derivable positive predictive value of 0.60% is an underestimate by an unknown factor. Diagnoses also come from two routes with 43.4% ascertained from provider free-text notes, and recording practice varies across 503 clinics with no inter-rater data. Milestone binarisation to ever-passed versus only-failed discards the pattern of delay over repeated attempts, which is arguably the most informative aspect of longitudinal milestone data. The feature set is bounded by what the national protocol records, and plausible early markers outside it - head lag at three months, raising hands to be picked up at six months, nodding at twelve months - are named as missing. Paternal age and family history of autism, both established risk factors, are not routinely collected, and the authors note that the advanced-maternal-age effect may partly proxy paternal age. Positive predictive value is never stated despite the confusion counts making it computable, so the reader must derive that 165 children are flagged per recorded case. And maternal country of birth is reported as associated with diagnosis rate without discussion of whether it entered the model or of the equity implications of a risk score that could encode migration background.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The most important study in this review for translational interpretation, and the only one whose numbers describe deployment rather than a research contrast. Three contributions are decisive. First, it makes the prevalence problem concrete: a well-validated model with AUC 0.86 and 75% sensitivity, applied to a genuine population at 0.15% incidence, produces a high-risk group of 144,632 children containing 874 recorded cases - a positive predictive value of 0.60%, or 165 children flagged for every one with a recorded diagnosis. Every accuracy figure elsewhere in this corpus was obtained at prevalences between 40% and 60%, and this study shows what happens when the same order of discriminative performance meets the real base rate. Second, its method comparison undercuts the algorithmic framing that dominates the rest of the corpus: on real population data with 59 clinically chosen features, logistic regression matched gradient boosting exactly at AUC 0.86 with marginally better sensitivity, and the entire spread across four methods was 0.03 AUC - which suggests that the large algorithm-driven differences reported in small-sample studies elsewhere here are more likely properties of sample size and validation design than of modelling power. Third, its validation design solves problems the rest of the corpus does not have to face and solves them well: a population cohort with no recruitment or spectrum truncation, cross-validation over children, and temporal separation between predictors and outcome imposed explicitly to prevent leakage from diagnosis back to predictors. Two further features deserve emulation. Its limitations section quantifies its own outcome undercount at a factor of ten and states the cost of its representational choices in the same passage as their rationale. And its external validity check - showing that children flagged high risk were 3.29 times more likely to have been independently referred for developmental assessment, using a variable deliberately kept out of the model - is a model of how to interrogate what a high false-positive rate actually consists of. The study also sits at the boundary of the review's modality scope, since its behavioural data are nurse-recorded milestone attainment rather than sensor-derived measurement, and it is worth noting how far that coarse, binary, administratively captured signal goes: whether a two-year-old has ten words, builds a tower, gives a kiss or eats with a spoon.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] A national population cohort rather than a recruited sample - 780,610 Israeli children born between 2014 and 2019 with at least two years of computerised well-baby records, of whom 775,941 entered the analysis: 1,163 with an autism diagnosis recorded after age two and 774,778 without autism or another pervasive developmental or medical condition. This is by four orders of magnitude the largest sample in the review and the only one drawn from an unselected population. Case ascertainment used two routes and both counts are given: 722 children (56.6%) identified by ICD-9 code and 553 (43.4%) by keyword search of provider free-text notes with manual verification that the reference concerned the child rather than a family member. A further 112 children with autism diagnosed before age two were excluded to preserve the temporal separation between predictors and outcome. Conditions sharing the ASD acronym, notably atrial septal defect, were screened out. Down syndrome was excluded from the comparison group but Fragile X, tuberous sclerosis and other autism-associated aetiologies were deliberately retained, on the reasoning that autism has multiple aetiologies and excluding them would narrow the target condition artificially. The resulting incidence of 0.0015 is roughly a tenth of Israel's reported national rate, and the authors state this openly as a limitation. [RQ1.2] 'Children with ASD' and 'typically developing (TD)' children, person-first and consistent. Autism 'manifests through social communication deficits and atypical behaviors' per DSM-5, and the vocabulary of red flags, risk, markers and screening runs throughout - appropriate to a public-health surveillance framing. The register is notably free of the burden and cost rhetoric found elsewhere in this corpus; the motivation offered is access and equity rather than economic saving. Two framing choices are worth recording. The paper repeatedly emphasises heterogeneity as the obstacle to early detection - 'the great heterogeneity in the red flags, onset, and progression of symptoms, and in the divergence of developmental trajectories in ASD' - and treats variation as something a model must accommodate rather than as noise. And it frames the problem partly as one of clinician support rather than clinician replacement, noting that some early signs 'can be easily missed by a healthcare provider during a short checkup visit due to their gradual deviation or subtlety, such as social reciprocity, social smile, and eye contact', and that 'disparities in healthcare screening resources and in provider awareness of individual developmental differences' are themselves barriers. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. [RQ1.3] Extensive and, uniquely in this review, describing a whole population rather than a matched sample. Reported with formal comparisons at a p < 0.001 threshold chosen for the large sample size and multiple comparisons: sex (78.3% male in the autism group against 51.4%), birth year distribution, maternal country of birth (with higher diagnosis rates for mothers born in Russia and Ethiopia), preterm birth rate, maternal age, gestational week, birth weight, nursing status, parental concern rates, and number of well-baby visits (13.7 in the autism group against 11.44, t(775,939) = -23.05, p < 0.001, d = 0.7). Because the design is a population cohort rather than a case-control comparison, these differences are findings about the population rather than confounds introduced by sampling - which is the fundamental difference between this study and every other in the review. Two points nonetheless deserve attention. Sex is both a strong predictor and a strong group difference, and the authors handle it correctly by fitting a boys-only model and reporting that performance remained relatively stable, which is the check that distinguishes a model using sex as one legitimate risk factor from a model that is substantially a sex classifier. Maternal country of birth is reported as associated with diagnosis rate but its role in the model is not made explicit, and a risk score that encoded migration background would raise equity concerns the paper does not address. Absent throughout: IQ, language scores, adaptive functioning and any autism severity measure, none of which exists in the records. [RQ1.4] Routine clinical diagnosis recorded in the health record after age two, ascertained by ICD-9 code for 56.6% of cases and by verified keyword search of provider free-text notes for the remaining 43.4%. There is no research instrument - no ADOS, ADI-R or equivalent - and the well-baby protocol contains no autism-specific screening tool, which the paper states explicitly and which is part of its motivation. Three features of the ascertainment are handled better than the norm in this corpus. The temporal separation is enforced by design: predictors are capped at 24 months and outcomes restricted to diagnoses recorded after 24 months, adopted specifically 'to develop a model that minimizes data leakage from diagnosis to predictors' - a form of leakage control that most studies here do not have to think about and that this one does. Acronym collisions were checked and excluded, and free-text mentions were manually verified to concern the child rather than a relative. And the resulting label noise is quantified rather than glossed: the authors state that 'based on the national incidence of ASD, the true positive ASD group is at least 10 times higher in the examined population', so most autistic children in the cohort sit in the comparison group. That is an unusually candid acknowledgement, and it has an implication the paper does not draw out - that a large share of the flagged false positives may be correctly identified children whose diagnosis was simply never recorded, so both specificity and positive predictive value are understated. The 43.4% of diagnoses ascertained from free text also introduces provider-dependent recording variation, which the authors flag as warranting research into inter-rater differences. [RQ1.5] No autism severity measure exists in the records, and no cognitive, language or adaptive standardised score is available - the well-baby protocol records milestone attainment as pass or fail rather than scaled scores. What the study does have, and uses well, is a proxy for general developmental concern that sits outside the model: referral for extensive developmental assessment due to developmental delay. Because this variable was deliberately excluded from the feature set, it functions as an independent check, and children flagged high risk proved 3.29 times more likely to have been referred (95% CI 3.18-3.39). That is a genuinely informative use of an available clinical variable and it partially answers the question of what the false positives are: many are children whom clinicians independently identified as developmentally concerning. The absence of severity data nonetheless means nothing can be said about which autistic children the model detects - whether the 75% captured differ in presentation from the 25% missed, and whether the model is better at flagging children with co-occurring language or motor delay than those with a more isolated social presentation. Given that four of the seven top milestone predictors are language milestones, the second possibility is live and untested. [RQ2.1] The aim is to build and evaluate a machine learning model predicting later autism diagnosis from routinely collected well-baby records, so that providers can be alerted during ordinary checkups to administer an autism-specific screening tool - the Israeli protocol containing none. Findings: average test AUC 0.86 (SD 0.009) with sensitivity 0.75 and specificity 0.81, against a training AUC of 0.88 that the authors flag as indicating slight overfitting. At the Youden threshold, 18.6% of the cohort (144,632 children) were classified high risk, capturing 874 of 1,163 cases - an autism incidence of 0.006 in that group against 0.001 in the cohort, a 4.3-fold enrichment. The seven most important milestone predictors, all confirmed by independent Fisher's exact tests at p < 0.001, are strikingly ordinary clinical observations: vocabulary over ten words, building a tower from cubes, giving a kiss, eating independently with a spoon, knowing at least one body part, composing two-word sentences and saying 2-3 words. Four are language milestones, two personal-social, one fine motor, and all fall between 12 and 24 months. Other key predictors are male sex, parental developmental concern, non-nursing, older maternal age, lower gestational age and atypical growth percentiles. The most instructive result is the method comparison: logistic regression achieved exactly the same AUC of 0.86 with marginally better sensitivity (0.77 versus 0.75), random forest 0.84 and naive Bayes 0.83 - so gradient boosting gained nothing over a linear model on 59 features, which bears directly on the assumption running through this corpus that model sophistication is where performance comes from. [RQ2.2] The Israeli national well-baby surveillance programme, Tipat Halav, operating across 503 Ministry of Health clinics and covering 75% of the population, with the remaining quarter followed by two health maintenance organisations under identical national guidelines. Services span immunisation, growth monitoring, developmental surveillance and risk detection for mother and child, delivered by nurses with specific maternal and child health training alongside a developmental paediatrician, across approximately eleven visits from birth to age six. This is the only study in the review whose setting is the deployment setting: there is no recruitment, no research protocol, no laboratory and no case-control geometry, and the model is trained on exactly the data that would be available at the moment of use. The equity implication is drawn out explicitly - because the surveillance system is universal and free, a model built on it inherits multi-cultural representativeness that a recruited cohort could not, which the authors contrast with 'disparities in healthcare screening resources and in provider awareness' as barriers to detection. The counterweight is that the model's transferability depends on a health system that most countries do not have, and the authors say so, calling for cross-cultural validation covering 'the expression of signs, parental recognition, interpretation, and reporting levels'. [RQ2.3] There is no experimental paradigm; the behavioural data are generated by routine clinical practice. The surveillance protocol nonetheless functions as a structured behavioural assessment: 60 age-related milestones across gross motor, fine motor, language and personal-social domains, based in part on the Denver Developmental Screening Test, with 38 assessed up to 24 months and between four and nine checked at each of nine age bins from six weeks to six years, results recorded per milestone, plus systematic elicitation of parental concerns about development and hearing at each visit. Two features distinguish this from the elicitation paradigms elsewhere in the review. It is universal and repeated - every child in the population is assessed roughly eleven times by a trained nurse over six years, at zero marginal cost to the research - which is a scale of behavioural observation no research protocol can approach. And it is unoptimised for the task: the milestones were chosen for general developmental surveillance, not for autism detection, so the model works with whatever the protocol happens to record. The authors identify this as a limitation and name specific candidate red flags that fall outside it - head lag at three months, raising hands to be picked up at six months, nodding at twelve months - which is a concrete and testable proposal for improving the instrument rather than the algorithm. [RQ2.4] Genuinely longitudinal in structure and, by the standards of this review, exemplary in its handling of time. Predictors are drawn only from measurements taken up to 24 months and the outcome only from diagnoses recorded after 24 months, an ordering imposed deliberately 'to develop a model that minimizes data leakage from diagnosis to predictors'. Mean age at recorded diagnosis was 37.5 months (SD 13.3), so the model predicts on average more than a year ahead of the clinical event. Follow-up varies by birth cohort, and the authors address this both by noting the smaller autism proportion among 2019 births and by fitting a sensitivity model excluding that year. Within-child longitudinal structure is nonetheless collapsed - milestones are binarised to ever-passed versus only-failed - which the authors name as their first limitation and as a target for future work. Governance is complete: Ministry of Health Helsinki committee approval with number and date, consent waived on anonymisation grounds, extraction and anonymisation performed by dedicated Ministry personnel, access only through a secure platform, funding stated, and no competing interests declared. [RQ2.5] None in the instrumental sense - the study uses no sensor, device or measurement apparatus of its own. Data were extracted and anonymised by the TIMNA project, the Israel Ministry of Health's Big Data Platform, and accessed by researchers through a dedicated secured Ministry platform, with a public URL given for the access route. Analysis used gradient boosting with logistic regression, random forest and naive Bayes comparators and SHAP for attribution; no software package or version is named, which is the one specification gap in an otherwise thoroughly reported methods section. The absence of equipment is the point: the entire input is data that a nurse enters during an ordinary visit, which is why this is the only study in the review whose measurement cost at deployment is zero. [RQ2.6] Among the best-reported studies in the review, constrained only by data-access restrictions. Fully specified: the cohort definition with birth-year window and minimum follow-up requirement; the two-stage case-ascertainment procedure with counts by route and the acronym-collision and family-member checks; the comparison-group definition with its exclusion logic and the explicit reasoning for excluding Down syndrome but retaining other autism-associated aetiologies; the surveillance protocol with milestone counts by domain and age bin and its Denver Developmental Screening Test basis; the milestone binarisation rule with its stated rationale and its stated cost; the reduction from 100 to 59 features on clinical-relevance grounds; the modelling method, cross-validation scheme and Youden-threshold definition; full confusion counts for four comparator methods; and the SHAP fold-stability analysis. Five supplementary tables and figures carry the complete 100-feature list, training performance by fold, performance at multiple thresholds, and boys-only and no-2019 sensitivity models. The data cannot be released publicly for privacy reasons but a formal request route with a URL is provided. Code is not available and no software is named. [RQ2.7] The limitations section is the most substantive in the review and several of its admissions are ones other papers in this corpus would have suppressed. Milestone binarisation cannot distinguish children who passed after repeated attempts from those who passed first time, so a real signal about the pattern of delay is discarded. The feature set is bounded by what the national protocol happens to record, and specific plausible red flags outside it are named. Paternal age and family history of autism, both established risk factors, are not routinely collected, and the authors note that the observed advanced-maternal-age effect may be a proxy for paternal age - an interpretive caution rather than a claim. Most strikingly, they state that 'based on the national incidence of ASD, the true positive ASD group is at least 10 times higher in the examined population', meaning the great majority of autistic children in the cohort are labelled as comparison cases, and they describe this as adding 'a lot of noise to the outcome label' requiring replication with a later stable outcome. And 43.4% of diagnoses came from free-text notes rather than ICD-9 codes, with provider recording practice varying. What is not stated is the positive predictive value, although all the numbers to compute it are given: 874 autism cases among 144,632 flagged children is 0.60%, or 165 children flagged per recorded case. The paper acknowledges 'a cost of high false positive rates' and mounts a partial defence through the developmental-referral analysis, but never puts the figure on the page. It also does not draw out the interaction between its two candid admissions - if the true autism count is ten times higher, then many of those 143,758 apparent false positives are correctly flagged children whose diagnosis was never recorded, so the true PPV is materially better than 0.60% and the true specificity better than 0.81, by an amount the data cannot determine. Finally, maternal country of birth is reported as associated with diagnosis rate without discussion of whether it entered the model or of the equity implications. [RQ2.9] Five directions, all specific and all following from a stated limitation. Model each child's milestone performance pattern over time rather than collapsing to binary attainment, which would restore the delay-trajectory information the current representation discards. Add early signs not currently in the national protocol, with three concrete candidates named. Incorporate paternal age and family history of autism, both known risk factors absent from routine collection. Replicate with a later and more stable outcome label to reduce the label noise the authors quantify. And conduct direct cross-cultural validation before transferring the approach, covering not only sign expression but 'parental recognition, interpretation, and reporting levels' - an acknowledgement that a model built on parent-reported concern and clinician recording is embedded in a particular culture of help-seeking and documentation. The list is notable for containing no proposal to improve the algorithm. [RQ3.1] Developmental milestone attainment across four domains, observed and recorded by trained nurses in routine practice, together with parent-reported concern. This is behavioural data of a different kind from the rest of the review - clinician-mediated, coarse, binary and administratively recorded rather than sensor-derived - and it is worth being explicit that the review includes it at the boundary of its modality scope. What the study demonstrates is how far that coarse behavioural signal goes. The seven most important milestone predictors are all things a nurse can observe in a two-minute interaction: whether a two-year-old has more than ten words, builds a tower from cubes, gives a kiss, eats independently with a spoon, knows a body part, composes two-word sentences, says 2-3 words. Four are language, two personal-social, one fine motor, all falling between 12 and 24 months, and all differ between groups at p < 0.001 on independent testing. The domain distribution is itself informative: language dominates, which is consistent with the wider literature on early markers but also raises the untested possibility that the model preferentially detects autistic children with co-occurring language delay. Parent-reported concern is a further behavioural channel and emerges as a key predictor, which is a finding about the informativeness of parental observation rather than about the child. Notably absent from the recorded protocol, and named by the authors as missed opportunities, are the subtler social behaviours that dominate the rest of this corpus - social reciprocity, social smile, eye contact - which the paper observes 'can be easily missed by a healthcare provider during a short checkup visit due to their gradual deviation or subtlety'. [RQ3.2] Genuine multi-source fusion, and the only study in the review to combine behavioural observation with biological, familial and perinatal data in one model. Five families are integrated: developmental milestone attainment across four domains; birth parameters including gestational age, birth weight and delivery mode; post-natal growth percentiles; familial variables including maternal age, country of birth and nursing status; and parent-reported developmental concern. The rationale for fusion is stated as a scientific argument rather than an accuracy claim: 'prematurity, like other factors, interacts with additional ASD risk factors, such as cesarean delivery, parental age, and birth complications; therefore, there is a need for an integrative/cumulative approach to risk estimation', and these non-linear interactions are what machine learning on large data is expected to capture. The SHAP analysis confirms that the final model draws on all five families, with seven of the top twenty features being milestones and the remainder spanning sex, parent concern, nursing, maternal age, gestational age and growth. The finding that undercuts the fusion rationale is the method comparison: logistic regression, which cannot represent the interactions the argument invokes, achieves an identical AUC of 0.86 with slightly better sensitivity. So the integration of heterogeneous data sources demonstrably helps, while the non-linear modelling that was supposed to exploit their interactions demonstrably does not. [RQ4.1] Gradient boosted decision trees as the primary model, with the mechanism explained in the text - successive trees fitted to the errors of their predecessors, combined stage-wise rather than in parallel - and three comparators: logistic regression, random forest and naive Bayes. Risk stratification used the Youden threshold, defined as the cutoff optimising the balance of sensitivity and specificity. The modelling is deliberately conventional and the paper makes no architectural claim; the contribution is the data and the design. The comparison across methods is the most useful modelling result in the study and cuts against the assumption running through this corpus: logistic regression matched gradient boosting exactly at AUC 0.86 while achieving marginally higher sensitivity (0.77 versus 0.75), with random forest at 0.84 and naive Bayes at 0.83, so the entire spread across four methods is 0.03 AUC. On a genuine population dataset with 59 clinically chosen features, the choice of algorithm is close to irrelevant - which suggests that the very large algorithm-driven performance differences reported elsewhere in this review are more likely properties of small samples and leaky validation than of modelling power. [RQ4.2] A tabular feature vector per child, built from 100 candidate variables reduced to 59 on clinical-relevance grounds before any modelling - a reduction made a priori rather than by data-driven selection, which the paper states explicitly and which removes a source of optimism that data-driven feature selection would introduce. The central representational decision concerns milestones, and it is reasoned carefully. Records vary in the timing of checkups and contain multiple entries per milestone per child, so each milestone was reduced to a binary of 'ever passed' versus 'only failed', chosen specifically 'to avoid attributing a-priori developmental assumptions' to never-tested and late-tested records. The cost is stated in the same paragraph: children who passed after several attempts cannot be distinguished from those who passed immediately, so the pattern of delay - arguably the most diagnostically informative aspect of milestone data - is discarded. Stating a representational trade-off, its motivation and its cost in three sentences is better practice than anything comparable in this corpus. Longitudinal structure within a child is otherwise collapsed, and modelling performance patterns over time is named as the first priority for future work. [RQ4.3] Metric reporting is fitted to the epidemiological setting rather than borrowed from the classification literature, and this is one of the study's clearest strengths. Accuracy is not reported at all - correctly, since at 0.15% incidence a null model achieves 99.85%. What is reported instead: AUC with standard deviation across folds (0.86, SD 0.009), sensitivity (0.75, SD 0.03), specificity (0.81, SD 0.02), training AUC alongside test AUC with an explicit statement that the model is slightly overfit, full true positive, false positive, true negative and false negative counts for all four modelling methods, and the risk stratification expressed as enrichment - 0.006 incidence in the high-risk group against 0.001 in the cohort, a 4.3-fold increase. Supplementary material gives performance at multiple thresholds as multiples of the Youden threshold, with the trade-off against false positives described. The one omission is positive predictive value, which is not stated although the confusion counts make it computable: 874 of 144,632 flagged children, or 0.60%, meaning 165 flagged per recorded case. That figure is the single most important number in the review for understanding what a well-validated model at a realistic base rate delivers, and it is left for the reader to compute. [RQ4.4] SHAP attribution applied within each of the three folds, with fold-to-fold stability quantified explicitly - 15 of 24 unique top-20 features appeared in all three folds, 6 in two and 3 in one. Reporting the stability of an importance ranking across resamples, rather than presenting a single ranking as though it were a property of the data, is a discipline almost absent from this corpus and it materially changes how much weight the ranking can bear. The seven milestone predictors surfaced by SHAP were then tested independently with Fisher's exact tests, all significant at p < 0.001, so the attribution is corroborated by conventional statistics rather than standing alone. The resulting features are directly interpretable and directly actionable by the clinician who would use the model: a nurse can check whether a two-year-old has more than ten words or builds a tower from cubes. Summary and distribution plots for a representative fold appear in the paper with the remaining folds in supplementary material. The one interpretive question left open is whether the model's reliance on language milestones means it preferentially detects autistic children with co-occurring language delay - a question the data could address and the paper does not. [RQ4.5] The strongest validation design in the review, and strong in ways that are structural rather than procedural. Four features stand out. The split unit is the child and the cohort is a whole population, so there is no possibility of within-participant leakage and no case-control sampling to inflate separation. Temporal leakage is controlled by design rather than by hope: predictors are capped at 24 months and outcomes restricted to diagnoses recorded after 24 months, adopted explicitly to prevent information flowing from diagnosis back to predictors - the only study here that faces this problem and the only one that solves it. Feature reduction from 100 to 59 was made a priori on clinical-relevance grounds, so no selection bias enters. And training AUC is reported alongside test AUC with the overfitting acknowledged in the text, rather than concealed. Three-fold cross-validation is modest but adequate at this sample size, and results are stable across folds (SD 0.009). Two internal checks add further confidence: a boys-only model tests whether performance depends on sex, given that sex is both a strong predictor and a strong group difference; and referral for developmental assessment, deliberately excluded from the feature set, serves as an external validity indicator, with high-risk children 3.29 times more likely to have been referred (95% CI 3.18-3.39). The residual limitations are epidemiological rather than methodological: no external cohort or health system has been tested, and the outcome label is substantially incomplete, with the authors estimating the true autism count at ten times the labelled figure - which biases sensitivity and specificity in directions the data cannot resolve. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorders; development; screening; machine learning; electronic health records. The set is balanced between clinical and computational terms, and 'screening' rather than 'diagnosis' correctly names the intended application. Terms running through the text: well-baby checkups, developmental surveillance, milestones, red flags, risk stratification, Youden threshold, SHAP, feature importance, preventative care, developmental trajectories, cumulative risk. [RQ5.2] Children 11(4), article 429, MDPI, open access under CC BY; received 12 March 2024, revised 28 March, accepted 29 March, published 3 April 2024. The venue is a paediatrics journal rather than a computational one, and the reporting reflects that: the cohort definition, case ascertainment, exclusion logic and group comparisons are described to epidemiological standards with effect sizes and a p-value threshold adjusted for sample size, while the modelling is reported adequately but without software versions or hyperparameters. Five supplementary tables and figures carry the full feature list, per-fold training performance, multi-threshold performance and two sensitivity models. The three-week review period is short, though the study's design and reporting do not show the marks of it. [RQ5.3] Published 2024 by the University of Haifa's occupational therapy department with Maccabi Healthcare Services, Tel-Aviv University and the Keshet Autism Center, funded by the Gertner Institute of Health Policy and Epidemiology. The framing is health-services and equity oriented rather than technological: autism diagnosis typically occurs after age three despite behavioural markers being observable in the first two years, the barriers are heterogeneity in presentation, subtlety of early signs during short visits, and 'disparities in healthcare screening resources and in provider awareness', and the proposed remedy is to exploit data a universal surveillance system already collects. The paper is unusual in this corpus for treating the health system as the unit of intervention - its contribution is an alerting layer for a national programme that currently contains no autism-specific screening instrument, not a new measurement device. For the review its importance is threefold. It is the only study reporting performance at a genuine population base rate, and its numbers make the prevalence problem concrete in a way no other study does: an AUC of 0.86 with 75% sensitivity yields a high-risk group of 144,632 children containing 874 recorded cases, a positive predictive value of 0.60%. It shows that on real population data with clinically chosen features, logistic regression matches gradient boosting exactly, which reframes the algorithmic arms race visible across the rest of this corpus. And its limitations section models the standard the field should meet, quantifying its own label noise at a factor of ten and stating the cost of its own representational choices in the same breath as their rationale.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Secondary computational analysis of a public Kaggle image dataset, conducted at the Arab Academy for Science, Technology and Maritime Transport in Alexandria with no data collection of its own. The dataset comprises 2,836 cropped facial photographs, 1,418 labelled autistic and 1,418 not, with the provenance stated explicitly: autistic images 'were sourced from online platforms focusing on autism disorder' and non-autistic images 'randomly gathered from the internet'. Age is claimed as 24-72 months for both classes but is an unverifiable dataset-level assertion about scraped photographs. The number of distinct children is unknown and unrecoverable. No diagnosis, instrument, clinician or verification underlies either label, and no demographic, cognitive, language or severity data exist for any image. A second component uses AffectNet, a general-population facial expression dataset with no autism labels. No ethics approval, consent, funding or competing-interests statement appears.
narrative_rows.methods: Images were preprocessed by the dataset creator (duplicate removal and face cropping), rescaled to [0, 1] and resized - to 96 x 96 in one passage and 224 x 224 x 3 in another, without reconciliation. Augmentation applied rotation, horizontal and vertical flipping, zooming and cropping, brightness and contrast adjustment, noise injection, shearing and scaling; vertical flipping produces upside-down faces and has no rationale for a task premised on facial landmark geometry. The corpus was partitioned once into 2,536 training, 200 validation and 100 test images, with the ordering of augmentation relative to partitioning left ambiguous. Three ImageNet-pretrained networks - MobileNet, Xception and InceptionV3 - were used as feature extractors with two dense layers appended (1,024 neurons, ReLU, L2 at 0.015, dropout 0.4, softmax output), trained with RMSprop at batch size 80 for up to 100 epochs with early stopping on validation loss at patience ten. Separately, five YOLOv8 classification variants and a proposed 11.2-million-parameter model were trained on AffectNet for facial expression recognition. No cross-validation, no repeated splits, and no interpretability analysis of any kind.
narrative_rows.outcomes: MobileNet reached 95% validation accuracy with sensitivity 0.97 and specificity 0.93, alongside 100% training accuracy, with early stopping at 33 epochs; Xception 94% (sensitivity 0.92, specificity 0.95); InceptionV3 89% (sensitivity 0.95, specificity 0.83). The reported confusion matrix gives 131 true positives, 136 true negatives, 9 false positives and 4 false negatives, summing to 280 images - matching neither the stated 200-image validation set nor the 100-image test set. The expression module reports precision 0.988 and mAP50 0.991 for the proposed variant against 0.992 and 0.99 for the smallest YOLOv8 baseline, so the proposed model is marginally outperformed by the lightest comparator on its own task. The two modules are never combined, compared or shown to inform one another, despite the paper's claim to provide 'a more complete picture of a child's condition'.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The two image classes were assembled from different internet sources - autism-focused websites versus random collection - so photographic style, resolution, compression, lighting, background, pose, cropping convention and the demographic composition of the represented populations all differ systematically between classes and are fully available to the classifier. No interpretability analysis is performed that could distinguish a model responding to facial morphology from one responding to image provenance, so the reported accuracy carries no evidential weight about children. Neither label is verified against any diagnosis; an image is autistic because it appeared on an autism website. The number of distinct children is unknown, so split integrity cannot be established even in principle. Augmentation appears to precede partitioning; training accuracy reached 100%; the confusion matrix corresponds to no stated partition; the test set contains 100 images with no confidence intervals, yet model rankings differing by one percentage point are asserted; vertical flipping is applied to faces; and sensitivity and specificity are written as percentages of proportions throughout. There is no limitations section. And no ethics approval, consent or discussion accompanies a study built on photographs of identifiable children that assert a health status about them, while proposing distribution as a consumer mobile application through which families would photograph their own children and receive an autism determination.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Charted as a negative exemplar and as a boundary marker for the review. Three things make it worth recording despite its weakness. First, it identifies where the field stops analysing behaviour: the autism component of this study infers diagnosis from static facial structure, on the explicit premise that autistic children have an 'expanded upper face and a truncated mid-facial region', which is a physiognomic claim adopted from a single citation without engagement with the long and discredited history of inferring conditions from appearance. The attached expression module does concern behaviour but is trained on a general-population emotion dataset with no autism labels and is never linked to the classification result. Second, it is the corpus's most complete instance of class-confounded data collection. The review has already recorded an acoustic study in which autistic children were recorded on a tripod camera and comparison children on parents' phones, contaminating every acoustic feature; here the same failure operates on the entire dataset rather than one feature family, because the two classes were harvested from different parts of the internet. In that earlier case the authors recognised the problem for one feature and discarded it; here it is not recognised at all. Third, and most important for the review's overall argument, the reported 95% accuracy is comparable to or higher than the figures achieved by the most carefully conducted studies charted here - the joint-attention system with ADOS-verified diagnoses and group-wise cross-validation, the facial-complexity study embedded in primary-care surveillance, the human-benchmark comparison against expert clinicians. That a study with no diagnostic verification, no interpretability check, a 100-image test set and a source-confounded dataset produces a comparable number is the clearest available demonstration that reported accuracy in this literature does not order studies by evidential quality. Finally, the ethical position should be recorded plainly: a dataset of identifiable children's photographs scraped without consent, one class collected precisely because those images appeared in autism contexts, used to build a consumer application that would deliver autism determinations to families - proposed without any ethical consideration whatsoever.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] There are no participants in the ordinary sense - the study analyses 2,836 photographs, 1,418 labelled autistic and 1,418 not, obtained from a public Kaggle dataset. The provenance is stated plainly and is the study's decisive feature: 'the images of autistic children's faces were sourced from online platforms focusing on autism disorder, while the images of non-autistic children's faces were randomly gathered from the internet'. So the two classes are not two groups of children assessed under common conditions but two collections of photographs assembled from different corners of the internet for different reasons. The number of distinct children behind the images is unknown and cannot be recovered, so it is impossible to know whether ten photographs represent ten children or one, or whether the same child appears on both sides of the training-test split. Age is stated as 24-72 months for both classes, but this is a claim in the dataset description rather than a verified attribute of scraped photographs. Nothing else about the children is known. [RQ1.2] 'Autistic children' and 'non-autistic children' are the working terms, with 'typically developing (TD)' appearing occasionally. The register is medical-model with some notable slips: autism is 'characterized by early brain abnormalities', and the evaluation section refers to the model having halted 'after evaluating ten patients' when it means an early-stopping patience of ten epochs. The framing that matters, however, is not terminological but conceptual. The paper's premise is physiognomic: it opens by citing research that 'has identified distinct facial features common among autistic children: expanded upper face and a truncated mid-facial region, underscoring the potential of facial analysis in aiding early detection', and the method section asserts that autistic children 'exhibit distinct facial feature variations, showcasing differences in both the arrangement and dimensions of facial landmarks'. Inferring a neurodevelopmental condition from face shape is a claim with a long and discredited history, and the paper adopts it from a single citation with no engagement with that history, no discussion of the evidence base, and no consideration of what a facial autism classifier would mean for the people it classifies. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement - which is a particular absence given that the autistic images were taken from autism-focused websites, that is, from spaces created by and for autistic people and their families, and repurposed as training data without acknowledgement. [RQ1.3] None. No age (beyond an unverifiable dataset-level claim of 24-72 months), sex, race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, cognitive level, language, comorbidity or severity data exist for any image. The omission is more consequential here than in other dataset-reuse studies because the two classes were assembled from different sources: autism-advocacy and awareness websites will over-represent certain countries, ethnicities, family circumstances and photographic conventions relative to a random internet image search, and any such difference is directly available to the classifier as a diagnostic cue. A demographic comparison between the two collections is the minimum check that would begin to address this, and none is attempted. [RQ1.4] There is none, and the substitute is source of retrieval. An image is labelled autistic because it appeared on a website about autism and non-autistic because it did not. No diagnosis, criterion, instrument, clinician or verification underlies either label. Both directions of error are unbounded: an autism-website photograph may depict a sibling, a parent, a stock model or a child whose diagnostic status is unstated, while a randomly gathered photograph may depict an autistic child. Because the label is a property of where a file was found rather than of the person depicted, the quantity the model predicts is image provenance, and the paper's reported 95% accuracy is best read as a measure of how distinguishable the two collections are. That distinguishability has many possible sources - camera type, resolution, JPEG compression, lighting, background, pose, cropping convention, the tendency of advocacy imagery towards particular framings - none of which is examined. [RQ1.5] None, and none is possible. No severity, cognitive, language or adaptive information exists for any image, so nothing can be said about which autistic children the model would detect. The study's proposal - a mobile application for families - would be applied to individual children about whom the model has no information beyond a photograph, and no analysis addresses how the system would behave across the range of presentations, ages, ethnicities or image qualities it would encounter. [RQ2.1] The aim is an AI-powered mobile application that identifies autistic children from facial photographs, combined with a facial expression recognition module, intended for use by families and psychiatrists. Findings: MobileNet reached 95% validation accuracy with sensitivity 0.97 and specificity 0.93, alongside 100% training accuracy; Xception 94% (sensitivity 0.92, specificity 0.95); InceptionV3 89% (sensitivity 0.95, specificity 0.83). The expression module reports precision 0.988 and mAP50 0.991 for the proposed variant - against 0.992 and 0.99 for the smallest YOLOv8 baseline, so the proposed model is marginally worse than the lightest comparator on its own task, a result the paper presents as demonstrating 'a good balance of accuracy and efficiency'. The two modules are never combined, tested against each other, or shown to inform one another, despite the paper's claim to provide 'a more complete picture of a child's condition'. What no result in the paper addresses is what the autism classifier is responding to. Given that the two image classes were assembled from different internet sources, the reported accuracy is consistent with a model that has learned to distinguish autism-website photographs from general internet photographs, and no analysis in the paper can rule that out. [RQ2.2] No study setting exists. Images were downloaded from Kaggle and processed in Google Colab. The absence of a setting is not incidental: because the photographs were captured by unknown people, with unknown devices, in unknown circumstances, for unknown purposes, there is no acquisition chain to standardise and no way to establish that the two classes were photographed comparably. Every other study in this review that uses cameras controls the device, the distance, the lighting or at least the protocol; this one controls nothing, and the two classes are known to come from different sources. [RQ2.3] None. There is no task, protocol or elicitation - the images are photographs. This matters for the review's framing because a facial-photograph classifier is not measuring behaviour at all: it is measuring appearance. The paper's own premise makes this explicit, grounding the approach in claimed morphological differences in the upper face and mid-face rather than in anything the child does. The attached expression recognition module, trained on AffectNet, does concern behaviour, but AffectNet contains adult and general-population faces annotated for emotion and has no autism labels, so that module says nothing about autism and is never linked to the classification result. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional in the trivial sense that photographs have no time dimension. There is no ethics statement, no consent, and no discussion of either. This is the most serious governance failure in the review, and it is worth stating precisely why. The dataset consists of identifiable photographs of children, obtained without their knowledge or their families' consent, in which one class was collected specifically because those images appeared in autism contexts - so the dataset itself asserts a health status about identifiable minors. Training on that dataset propagates the assertion; publishing a mobile application built on it would extend the assertion to new children photographed by whoever downloads it. None of this is acknowledged. No funding statement and no competing-interests declaration appear either. [RQ2.5] Software only: Google Colab with TensorFlow and Keras, three ImageNet-pretrained networks for classification, YOLOv8 variants for expression recognition. No acquisition equipment exists because no data were collected. The imaging characteristics of the source photographs - resolution, sensor, compression, colour profile - are unknown and unexamined, which is precisely the information needed to assess whether the classes are separable on grounds unrelated to the children. [RQ2.6] Reported in outline and internally inconsistent in detail. Available: the dataset composition, the three architectures, the appended layer configuration (1,024 neurons, ReLU, L2 at 0.015, dropout 0.4, softmax output), the RMSprop optimiser, batch size 80, 100-epoch cap with early stopping at patience ten, the augmentation list, and the platform. Unavailable: the Kaggle dataset identifier or version, code, the split assignment or seed, and the image-to-child mapping. Two mutually inconsistent input sizes are given (96 x 96 in the dataset section, 224 x 224 x 3 in the transfer learning section) without reconciliation. The confusion matrix sums to 280 images while the stated validation and test partitions contain 200 and 100. And the order of augmentation relative to partitioning - the single most important procedural fact for interpreting the result - is left ambiguous by the text's ordering of subsections. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section and no constraint is acknowledged anywhere, which for a study with this design is itself the finding. The unaddressed problems begin with the dataset and are not remediable by any modelling choice. Autistic images were scraped from autism-focused websites and non-autistic images gathered randomly from the internet, so the classes differ in provenance and therefore in every photographic property that provenance determines; a model trained to separate them has an easier and entirely non-clinical route to high accuracy, and no analysis in the paper tests which route it took. Neither label is verified against any diagnosis. The number of distinct children is unknown, so split integrity cannot be established even in principle. Augmentation appears to precede partitioning. Training accuracy reached 100%. The confusion matrix does not correspond to any stated partition. Vertical flipping is applied to faces. Sensitivity and specificity are written as percentages of a proportion throughout ('0.97% sensitivity'). The introduction promises a sub-36-month analysis that never appears. The expression module's proposed variant is outperformed by the smallest baseline it is compared against. And no ethics approval, consent or discussion accompanies a system built from photographs of identifiable children and proposed for distribution as a consumer mobile application. [RQ2.9] None is proposed. The introduction states an intention to test the model on images of children below 36 months 'to assess its efficacy in early detection', and no such analysis is reported. The conclusion contains no future-work content beyond restating the results. [RQ3.1] The autism classification component does not target behaviour at all - it targets facial morphology, on the stated premise that autistic children have an 'expanded upper face and a truncated mid-facial region' and 'differences in both the arrangement and dimensions of facial landmarks'. That is a claim about anatomy, not about what a child does, and it places this study outside the behavioural framing that organises the rest of this review. The expression recognition component does target behaviour - emotional facial expression - but it is trained on AffectNet, a general-population emotion dataset with no autism labels, and its output is never connected to the autism classification. So the paper's title claim to identify 'emotional and facial symptoms' rests on two modules that address different constructs on different data and are never integrated. For the review, the study is best understood as marking a boundary: the point at which automated autism detection stops analysing behaviour and begins inferring diagnosis from appearance. [RQ3.2] Claimed but not performed. The paper states that it combines 'facial expression recognition with autism classification, thus providing a more complete picture of a child's condition', but the two components are trained on different datasets for different label spaces, evaluated with different metrics in separate tables, and never joined, compared or shown to inform one another. No fusion architecture, joint training, feature sharing or ablation is described. The claim to combine them is a description of the software containing two modules, not of any analysis relating them. [RQ4.1] Three ImageNet-pretrained networks - MobileNet, Xception and InceptionV3 - used as fixed feature extractors with two dense layers appended (1,024 neurons with ReLU and L2 regularisation at 0.015, dropout 0.4, softmax output), trained with RMSprop under early stopping on validation loss with patience ten. Separately, five YOLOv8 classification variants plus a proposed 11.2-million-parameter model for facial expression recognition. The architectural choices are conventional and appropriate to a small image dataset; the paper notes candidly that batch normalisation and dropout 'didn't notably enhance the models' performance' and that early stopping proved more effective. That candour is worth noting because it is the only self-critical observation in the paper. The reported 100% training accuracy alongside 95% validation accuracy is left without comment. [RQ4.2] Cropped facial photographs, resized (to 96 x 96 in one passage and 224 x 224 x 3 in another) and rescaled to [0, 1], with an extensive augmentation list: rotation, horizontal and vertical flipping, zooming and cropping, brightness and contrast adjustment, noise injection, shearing and scaling. Two elements deserve comment. Vertical flipping produces upside-down faces, which has no rationale for a task premised on facial landmark geometry and would be excluded by anyone reasoning about the construct rather than reaching for a standard augmentation set. And brightness, contrast and noise augmentation are described as helping the model generalise across imaging conditions - which is the right instinct but addresses only the appearance of the problem, since systematic imaging differences between the two source collections would remain available through resolution, compression and framing regardless. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for three models, plus a confusion matrix; precision and mAP50 for the expression module. Reporting sensitivity and specificity rather than accuracy alone is nominally good practice, and the discussion draws the correct general point that the choice between MobileNet and Xception depends on whether missed cases or false positives matter more. But three reporting problems undercut this. The confusion matrix reports 131 + 136 + 9 + 4 = 280 images, which matches neither the stated 200-image validation set nor the 100-image test set, and no explanation is offered. Sensitivity and specificity are written throughout as '0.97%' and '0.93%', conflating proportions with percentages. And no AUC, F1 or confidence interval is given, so a difference of one percentage point between MobileNet and Xception - on a partition of at most a few hundred images - is presented as a meaningful model ranking. [RQ4.4] None, and the absence is the study's central evidential gap rather than a peripheral omission. The paper asserts that its networks work by 'capturing facial features, creating distinctive facial patterns, and evaluating the distances between facial landmarks', and includes a figure of facial landmarks, but no landmark extraction appears in the method and no evidence connects the models' decisions to facial geometry. Given that the two image classes were assembled from different internet sources, the alternative explanation - that the models distinguish autism-website photographs from general internet photographs by their imaging characteristics - is at least as plausible as the stated one, and a single class activation map over correctly and incorrectly classified images would have addressed it directly. No such analysis appears anywhere. [RQ4.5] The design cannot support the claim, and the reasons are structural rather than procedural. A single fixed partition of 2,836 images into 2,536 training, 200 validation and 100 test provides no cross-validation, no repeated splits and no confidence intervals, and the test partition of 100 images makes each image worth a full percentage point. The order of augmentation relative to partitioning is ambiguous, with the text describing the partition and then the augmentation of the full 2,836-image dataset, which if taken at face value places transformed copies of the same photograph on both sides of the split. The number of distinct children behind the images is unknown, so participant-level splitting is not merely absent but impossible, and multiple photographs of the same child may straddle the split undetectably. Training accuracy reached 100%. The confusion matrix corresponds to no stated partition. But none of these is the decisive problem. Because the two classes were assembled from different internet sources, no split of these images - however careful - can distinguish a model that has learned facial morphology from one that has learned image provenance, and no result reported in the paper bears on which it is. The corrective is not a better validation scheme but a different dataset: photographs of diagnostically verified autistic and non-autistic children captured under matched conditions with the same equipment, which is what several other studies in this review provide and what this branch of the literature lacks. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder (ASD), Deep Learning, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Facial Image Analysis, Early Detection, Human-Computer Interaction (HCI), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Transfer Learning, Emotional and Facial Symptom Identification, YOLO Architecture, Augmentation Techniques, Facial Expression Recognition, Assistive Technology. Thirteen keywords for a five-page paper, most of them method labels. 'Emotional and Facial Symptom Identification' is the phrase that carries the paper's conflation of morphology and expression, and 'Assistive Technology' frames a diagnostic classifier as an aid to the people it classifies. [RQ5.2] Proceedings of ICMISI 2024, the International Conference on Machine Intelligence and Smart Innovation, IEEE, pages 87-91 - a five-page general machine-intelligence conference paper with no clinical or biomedical scope. The format accounts for the brevity but not for the absence of an ethics statement, of a limitations section, or of any check on what the classifier responds to. The paper carries internal inconsistencies - two input sizes, a confusion matrix matching no stated partition, sensitivity written as a percentage of a proportion - that a substantive review would be expected to catch. [RQ5.3] Published 2024 by the Department of Computer Engineering at the Arab Academy for Science, Technology and Maritime Transport, Alexandria, with no funding statement. The framing is access and speed - traditional manual assessment is time-consuming, AI 'offers expedited decision-making' - and the deliverable is a consumer mobile application 'designed to be user-friendly for families and psychiatrists alike'. For this review the study functions as a negative exemplar marking the boundary of the field, and it is worth setting out precisely what it exemplifies. First, a label derived from image provenance rather than diagnosis: an image is autistic because it was found on an autism website. Second, class-confounded data collection, in which the two classes come from different sources so that every photographic property distinguishing those sources is available to the classifier - the same failure mode this review has recorded in an acoustic study where autistic and comparison children were recorded on different devices, but here operating on the entire dataset rather than one feature family. Third, a physiognomic premise adopted from a single citation without engagement with the history of inferring conditions from facial structure. Fourth, a proposed consumer deployment - parents photographing their children to receive an autism determination - advanced without diagnostic validation, without any interpretability check on what the model uses, and without ethical consideration of the photographs of identifiable children on which it is built or of the consequences of a false result delivered to a family by an app. The review should record that this branch of the literature exists, that it reports accuracies comparable to or higher than the most carefully conducted studies charted here, and that those accuracies carry no evidential weight.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective algorithm-development study on the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange I, conducted by computer science groups in Pakistan with collaborators in the United States and Saudi Arabia. ABIDE-I supplies 1,112 subjects - 539 autistic and 573 controls - contributed by 17 international sites, each with its own scanner, acquisition protocol and recruitment practice, and each providing T1-weighted structural scans together with a clinical phenotype record. Approximately 65 to 70 phenotype fields were used, and the study's own ranking identifies the ten most influential as ADOS_TOTAL, ADI_R_SOCIAL_TOTAL_A, FIQ, AGE_AT_SCAN, SRS_RAW_TOTAL, ADOS_COMM, ADOS_GOTHAM_SEVERITY, VIQ, PIQ and ADI_R_VERBAL_TOTAL_BV. No age, sex or IQ distributions are reported as sample characteristics, since these variables were entered into the model as features. Diagnosis at the contributing sites rested on clinical judgement supported by ADOS and ADI-R.
narrative_rows.methods: A four-stage architecture. GAMI-Net, a generalised additive model with interactions, processed the phenotype fields through feature-wise subnetworks with pairwise interaction layers and sparse regularisation, producing an interpretable ASD probability embedding. A hybrid CNN-GNN processed the structural scans, with the CNN extracting volumetric features and the GNN modelling relationships between regions of the Harvard-Oxford atlas. An autoencoder compressed both embeddings into a shared 32-dimensional latent space, explicitly to avoid naive concatenation. A hypernetwork then generated subject-specific multilayer perceptron weights for final classification, giving individualised decision boundaries. Evaluation used a single held-out split - described as 70:30 in the methods and as a 20% partition of about 247 subjects in the abstract - together with five-fold stratified cross-validation over the whole dataset. Comparison baselines were TabNet, CNN, LSTM and Bi-LSTM, supported by component ablation studies, SHAP analysis and t-SNE visualisation. SITE_ID was label-encoded during preprocessing; no cross-site harmonisation was applied.
narrative_rows.outcomes: On the held-out split the system achieved 99.40% accuracy, 100% precision, 98.84% recall, 99.42% F1 and 99.99% ROC-AUC. Five-fold stratified cross-validation gave 98.56% accuracy, 98.61% F1, 98.13% precision, 99.12% recall and 99.62% ROC-AUC. The contributions section of the same paper reports a different figure, 'up to 96.4% classification accuracy and an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.92', which is nowhere reconciled with the abstract. The explainability analysis ranked ADOS_TOTAL first among behavioural contributors at 0.278 within GAMI-Net, and ADOS_Gotham_Total first at 0.234 in the final SHAP analysis.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The phenotype stream contains ADOS, ADI-R and SRS totals, which are the scored output of the assessments through which the ABIDE-I sites established the diagnoses used as labels, and the study's own explainability analysis identifies these as the dominant predictors. Because ADOS and ADI-R are administered to diagnose autism and are largely absent for control participants, missingness on these fields is label-informative independently of their values, and no missingness handling is described. A ROC-AUC of 99.99% follows from this arrangement rather than from the architecture, and no partitioning scheme could alter it. Neither evaluation is site-stratified, despite 17 sites with distinct scanners and a substantial literature documenting site as a confound for autism classification on this dataset, and no harmonisation is applied while SITE_ID is label-encoded into the feature space. Age and IQ, which differ between groups in ABIDE-I and predict structural brain measures, are entered as features rather than adjusted for or reported. No confidence intervals accompany any estimate on a 247-subject test set. And the paper reports two mutually inconsistent accuracy figures and two mutually inconsistent split descriptions, with the stated held-out subject count matching neither.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The review's principal representative of the neuroimaging-plus-phenotype branch, and its clearest and most instructive case of target leakage. Its mechanism differs from the questionnaire-dataset studies charted alongside it: there the label was an arithmetic function of the modelled features, whereas here the features are the scored output of the clinical assessment that produced the label - less mechanical, equally circular, and compounded because ADOS and ADI-R are largely absent for controls so that missingness carries the label as well. What makes the study valuable rather than merely flawed is that its own interpretability apparatus exposed the problem. GAMI-Net's additive decomposition isolates each feature's contribution and ranks ADOS_TOTAL first; the SHAP analysis over the fused model ranks ADOS_Gotham_Total first; and the paper reports both transparently, reading them as evidence of clinical alignment. A black-box model on identical inputs would have produced the same 99.99% ROC-AUC with nothing to reveal why, which is the strongest argument this review encounters for interpretable-by-design architectures. Three further points carry into the synthesis.
