[RQ2.3] Two tasks, both taken from ADOS-2 Modules 3 and 4 as administered rather than constructed for the study: interview responses and picture-book story recounting. The choice has one clear advantage and one clear cost. The advantage is standardisation - the same certified administrator elicited both from every participant under a protocol designed to sample social communication, so the elicitation is as comparable across participants as anything in this review. The cost is that the speech analysed was produced during the diagnostic session itself, so the examiner's behaviour toward each participant is part of the context and is unobserved, and the language sample is not independent of the encounter that produced the label. The paper is explicit about what it does with the material: the entire spoken output is evaluated 'without setting specific requirements for text length, speaking duration, or word count', and the analysis addresses 'patterns of lexicogrammar selection from participants' responses' rather than the dynamics of interaction - so turn-taking, latency and interactional contingency are outside scope by design. The contrast between the two tasks is the most valuable feature of the paradigm and is exploited properly: interview is dialogic and socially demanding, picture-book recounting is monologic and scaffolded by the stimulus, and the consistent superiority of interview transcripts across all four models and both annotation methods is a within-study replication of the paper's theoretical claim. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional in analysis, though the corpus was assembled over seven years, with prospective recruitment and retrospective record examination running concurrently. No follow-up, no repeat sampling and no test-retest assessment of the linguistic measures - which matters for an instrument proposed as a diagnostic aid, since stability across occasions is unestablished. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: approval by the Hirosaki University Committee on Medical Ethics under IRB 2013-142, subsequently updated to 2018-168 with the previous number 2015-055 also given; the committee's information security guidelines followed; written consent from participants aged 20 and above and from both participants and guardians for those 19 and under; and anonymisation by alphanumeric identifier with identifiable utterances removed from transcripts. The last of these is a specific privacy measure appropriate to a corpus of personal spoken narratives and is not standard practice in this corpus. Funding from two JSPS KAKENHI grants is itemised and competing interests are declared as none. [RQ2.5] No instrumentation - the data are transcribed ADOS-2 sessions. The apparatus is analytical and is specified adequately: logistic regression on normalised tag frequencies; Bi-LSTM models with 300-dimensional word and hidden vectors trained with Adam at learning rate 0.001, batch size 32, for 50 epochs; and a separate Bi-LSTM sequence labeller for automatic annotation. The most consequential methodological statement concerns what was not done: the hyperparameters 'were adopted from commonly used values and not explored, as preliminary experiments determined that the impact of the search for hyperparameters' was limited. Declining to search hyperparameters on a 135-participant dataset removes a source of optimism that most studies in this corpus exploit heavily, and doing so deliberately and saying so is exceptional. No software package or version is named, which is the one specification gap. [RQ2.6] Strong on conceptual and procedural specification, weaker on artefacts. Reproducible from the text: the participant selection rationale with its critical-period justification, the full diagnostic battery, the ADOS-2 non-spectrum cut-offs applied to the comparison group with observed means, the two elicitation tasks and their ADOS-2 provenance, the Systemic Functional Linguistics annotation scheme with its lexicogrammatical headings, linguistic functions and tag types tabulated at category level, the transfer-comparison method by which the Japanese system network was built, the input construction for each of the four models, all training hyperparameters with the statement that they were not searched, the leave-one-out procedure with the annotation model retrained within each fold, and the evaluation metrics with confidence intervals and McNemar comparisons. Supplementary files carry the tag frequency comparisons. Not available: code, the corpus itself (described in a prior publication rather than deposited), the specific software stack, and any random seed. The annotation scheme's full tag inventory is summarised rather than exhaustively listed in the main text. [RQ2.7] The limitations section is substantive and correctly prioritised. Sample size is named repeatedly as the principal constraint, with the conclusion that the study 'should be viewed as exploratory, aimed at providing initial insights rather than definitive conclusions' - a self-assessment few papers in this corpus offer and fewer still act on. The infeasibility of manual annotation in clinical settings is acknowledged as the reason the automatic annotator exists, and its weakest category (te-clauses, subdivided into eight classifications) is identified with two concrete remedies. Most notably, the McNemar results are interpreted with explicit reference to statistical power: 'the absence of statistically significant differences in our McNemar test results does not definitively indicate the absence of a performance difference between models, particularly in the context of small sample sizes'. Correctly refusing to read non-significance as equivalence is a discipline absent everywhere else in this review. What is not addressed matters nonetheless. IQ was measured in the autistic group at 81-91 and not measured at all in the comparison group, which was selected for average college grade point average - so an unquantified cognitive and educational gap separates the groups in a study of grammatical complexity, and the substitution of grade point average for IQ testing is presented as a selection criterion rather than acknowledged as a limitation. The language samples come from the ADOS-2 sessions that produced the labels, so the elicitation context is the diagnostic encounter itself. The comparison group is three-quarters university students against an autistic group whose educational status is unreported. And the 62.5% female composition of the autistic sample goes unremarked despite the paper's own emphasis on camouflaging. [RQ2.9] Three directions, all concrete. Comprehensive verification with a substantially larger and more diverse participant pool, with the logistical difficulty of achieving this acknowledged rather than waved away. Improvement of the automatic annotation system, particularly for te-clauses, either by sharpening category definitions or by expanding training data - a specific and testable target derived from the study's own error analysis. And extension to other languages through transfer comparison, the same method used to build the Japanese system network, which the authors argue makes the annotation scheme 'applicable to any language'. That last is an unusually ambitious but well-grounded claim, since it rests on a documented linguistic methodology rather than on an assumption that features transfer. Not proposed, and needed: cognitive assessment of the comparison group, and analysis relating model output to the SRS-2, AQ, Vineland-II and ADOS-2 data already collected. [RQ3.1] Lexicogrammatical choice - which options a speaker selects from the grammatical resources their language offers - as an operationalisation of pragmatic impairment. The theoretical grounding is Systemic Functional Linguistics, in which language is a system network of choices and meaning is made by selecting among them, and the clinical construct is defined with care as difficulty in 'adapting language formality based on the situation, interpreting non-literal language (such as idioms, metaphors, irony, and sarcasm), and understanding the nuances of language that affect interpersonal interactions... rather than with the basic structural or grammatical components'. The annotation scheme operationalises this across multiple lexicogrammatical systems, of which the paper details several: modality, where prior work by the first author found autistic individuals less likely to use probability expressions (must, will, may) and evidentiality expressions (seems, looks like, likely, is said, according to) and connected this to inferential reasoning; te-clauses with eight functional subtypes; negotiating particles, comprising twelve Japanese sentence-final and medial particles such as kana, ne, yo and yone that mark attitudinal stance toward a proposition and signal the speaker's claim on the information; and explanative mood. Two features distinguish this target from the rest of the corpus. It is language-specific in a principled way - the particles carrying much of the signal have no English equivalent and were identified through a system network built for Japanese - which is the opposite of the usual practice of applying an English-derived feature set across languages. And the empirical result localises the signal to socially interactive language: interview transcripts discriminated better than narrative recounting in every configuration tested, which is what a pragmatic account predicts and a purely structural account does not. [RQ3.2] Two representations of the same speech are fused and their contributions separately established. The tag stream encodes the linguistic-theoretical description - which lexicogrammatical options were selected - while the text stream encodes the words themselves, and the combined model concatenates tag and word embeddings at each time step so the Bi-LSTM sees both simultaneously. The ablation is reported across four configurations, two tasks and two annotation methods, and its result is instructive precisely because it is modest: on interviews the tag-only linear model reached 0.78, the tag-only Bi-LSTM 0.80, the text-only Bi-LSTM 0.80 and the combined model 0.80-0.82, with McNemar tests finding no significant differences between them. So the theoretically motivated tag representation and the raw word sequence carry largely overlapping information, and combining them adds at most a point or two. The authors report this honestly rather than claiming a fusion benefit, and note that 'the text-DNN and text+tag-DNN models performed almost the same, with the text+tag-DNN model being marginally higher'. That is a more useful contribution to the review's treatment of multimodality than a claimed gain would have been: it shows that an expensive, theory-driven annotation layer can be approximately recovered from surface text by a sequence model, while remaining far more interpretable - which is why the authors retain it. [RQ4.1] Four configurations spanning two model families, with the trade-off between them argued rather than resolved by accuracy. Logistic regression on normalised tag frequencies serves as the interpretable model, retained explicitly because 'in the medical context, interpretability is crucial because we are dealing with human lives' and because it 'allowed us to identify tags that impacted the outputs and quantify these effects'. Bi-LSTM models serve as the performance-oriented alternative, in three variants: tags only, text only, and tags plus text concatenated at each time step. A fifth model, a separate Bi-LSTM sequence labeller, performs automatic annotation and is retrained within each cross-validation fold. Two aspects of the modelling deserve particular credit. Hyperparameters were adopted from standard values and deliberately not searched, on the stated basis that preliminary work showed the search had little impact - which removes a large source of optimism on a 135-participant dataset. And the authors decline to declare a winner: after observing that the linear model was less precise, they write that 'it is not possible to make an unconditional judgment of which model is better', because interpretability and accuracy are not commensurable in a clinical setting. No other study in this corpus refuses to rank its models by accuracy. [RQ4.2] Two representations, both derived from the same transcripts. Tags come from a Systemic Functional Linguistics annotation scheme built for Japanese through transfer comparison, comprising four system networks and eleven or more lexicogrammatical headings each with multiple tag types - modality, te-clauses with eight subtypes, twelve negotiating particles, explanative mood and others. For the linear model the input is a tag-frequency vector normalised by total word count, which discards order. For the Bi-LSTM variants the input is the ordered sequence of tag sets, with each word represented by the sum of the embedding vectors of its tags, giving 300-dimensional tag embeddings; the text model uses 300-dimensional word embeddings; and the combined model concatenates the two at each time step. Annotation was performed both manually and automatically, with both evaluated in parallel throughout, and the automatic annotator achieving a mean F of 0.88 against manual - so the study reports both the ceiling achievable with perfect annotation and the performance obtainable in a setting where manual annotation is impossible. [RQ4.3] The best-calibrated metric reporting in the review after the population EHR study. Accuracy is reported with a 95% confidence interval for every one of sixteen conditions - four models by two tasks by two annotation methods - alongside precision, sensitivity, specificity and AUC. Reporting confidence intervals is what makes the results interpretable at this sample size: the best interview model's interval of [0.75, 0.89] sits clearly above the 52.6% majority-class floor, while the weakest picture-book configuration at 0.60 [0.51, 0.69] does not. Model comparisons are then tested formally with McNemar rather than being asserted from point differences, and the results are tabulated with test statistics and p-values. Most importantly, non-significant comparisons are interpreted correctly: the authors state that non-significance 'does not definitively indicate the absence of a performance difference between models, particularly in the context of small sample sizes', citing the literature on statistical power. Across this corpus, model rankings resting on differences of one or two participants are routinely presented as findings; this is the only study that tests such comparisons and then declines to over-read them. Absent: confusion matrices, and any relation between predictions and the clinical severity variables collected. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is a design constraint, an argument and a reported finding rather than a post-hoc gloss. The features are categories from an explicit linguistic theory, so a model contribution attaches to a nameable grammatical choice - a modality expression, a particular sentence-final particle, a te-clause subtype - rather than to an embedding dimension, and the linear model is retained specifically so those contributions can be identified and quantified. The authors' refusal to declare the deep model superior on accuracy grounds, on the reasoning that interpretability matters differently when 'we are dealing with human lives', is the clearest statement of that principle in the corpus. Group differences in tag frequencies are tabulated in supplementary material. The annotation system's own errors are analysed rather than assumed away, with an overall F of 0.88 and the te-clause identified as the dominant error source together with an explanation of why - it subdivides into eight classifications whose boundaries are hard to define. What is missing is the individual level: no error analysis identifies which participants were misclassified, and no analysis relates model output to the SRS-2, AQ, Vineland-II or ADOS-2 scores the study holds, which would have tested whether the linguistic signal tracks clinical severity. [RQ4.5] Among the two or three soundest validation designs in the review, and sound in ways that require deliberate effort rather than good fortune. The split unit is the participant, with leave-one-out cross-validation formally specified: each of the 135 samples serves once as the test case with the remaining 134 as training data. The step that distinguishes it is the handling of the annotation model. Automatic tag annotation is itself a fitted component, and fitting it once on the whole corpus would leak information from held-out participants into their own annotations; instead the procedure trains the annotator on the training partition of each fold and then uses that fold-specific annotator to label the held-out sample. Very few studies in this corpus recognise that a preprocessing model is a fitted component at all, and none other nests one this carefully. Hyperparameters were adopted from standard values and deliberately not searched, removing the model-selection optimism that inflates most results here. Confidence intervals accompany every accuracy, and model comparisons are tested with McNemar rather than read from point differences, with non-significance correctly not interpreted as equivalence. Two residual concerns are not validation failures but bound what the result means. The comparison group's cognitive and educational level is unmeasured while the autistic group's full-scale IQ is 81-91, so an unquantified ability gap may contribute to the separation. And the transcripts come from the ADOS-2 sessions that produced the labels, so the language sample and the diagnostic judgement arise from the same encounter - which does not leak the label into the features but does mean the model is trained on speech elicited by an examiner who was assessing the participant for autism at that moment. [RQ5.1] No formal keyword list appears in the retrieved text. The organising terms are lexicogrammatical choices, pragmatic impairment, Systemic Functional Linguistics, system network, annotation scheme, corpus of spoken language, Bi-LSTM, leave-one-out cross validation, transfer comparison, differential diagnosis, masking and camouflaging. The vocabulary is drawn from clinical linguistics rather than from machine learning, and the title's framing - 'creating a diagnostic assessment model... by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices' - names a linguistic mechanism rather than an architecture, which is the reverse of the corpus norm. [RQ5.2] PLOS ONE 19(9), article e0311209, published 27 September 2024; received 19 March 2024, accepted 15 September 2024, open access under CC BY, with a named academic editor. Twenty-nine pages, of which a substantial proportion is devoted to the linguistic theory, the annotation scheme and the interpretation of what the tags mean - so the balance is unusual for this corpus, with the machine learning occupying perhaps a quarter of the paper and the linguistic framework the rest. The venue's reporting requirements produce the data availability, funding and competing-interests statements, and the length permits the annotation scheme to be documented at a level that a conference paper could not accommodate. Two supplementary files carry the tag frequency comparisons between groups. [RQ5.3] Published 2024 by the Department of Neuropsychiatry at Hirosaki University with Aomori Chuo Gakuin University and the Natural Language Processing Lab at Tohoku University, funded by two JSPS KAKENHI grants. The framing is diagnostic supplementation grounded in a specific, well-evidenced critique of the gold standard rather than in generic complaints about subjectivity: ADOS-2 does not clearly differentiate autism from ADHD or from the negative symptoms of schizophrenia and other psychiatric comorbidities; masking, compensation and camouflaging can conceal impairment; and adult diagnosis is further hampered because caregiver developmental reports are usually unavailable while self-insight is unreliable. That is a more precise diagnosis of what automated assessment is for than any other paper in this corpus offers, and it leads to a correspondingly bounded claim - language analysis as one input among several, not a replacement. Four features make the study particularly valuable to this review. It is the only one that applies a gold-standard instrument to both groups, so its comparison group is screened rather than assumed. It is the only one that nests a fitted preprocessing component inside its cross-validation. It is the only one that tests model comparisons statistically and then declines to over-read non-significant differences. And it is the only one that refuses to rank its models by accuracy, retaining an interpretable linear model on the explicit ground that interpretability is not commensurable with accuracy in clinical use. Set against these, its unmeasured comparison-group IQ is a real limitation, and its reliance on ADOS-2 transcripts means the speech analysed was produced inside the diagnostic encounter itself - a form of dependence between sample and label that no other language study here faces and that the paper does not discuss.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Secondary computational analysis of a scraped public image dataset, conducted at Andhra University and GITAM Deemed to be University in Visakhapatnam with no data collection. The dataset comprises 2,936 colour facial photographs from Kaggle, evenly divided at 1,468 autistic and 1,468 non-autistic - the same publicly scraped 'Autistic Children Facial Dataset' already charted in this review from a companion study using a 2,836-image version, in which the autistic images were sourced from autism-focused online platforms and the non-autistic images gathered separately from the internet. Labels are the names of two subdirectories, and features were extracted by traversing the directory structure with a label column added to denote 'autistic' or 'non_autistic'. No age, sex, race, cognitive, language, comorbidity or severity information exists for any image, and the number of distinct children is unknown. No diagnostic verification of any kind underlies either class. No ethics approval, consent, funding or competing-interests statement appears.
narrative_rows.methods: Eight feature families were extracted with counts tabulated: 3,000 activations each from ImageNet-pretrained VGG16, ResNet and Inception with fully connected layers excluded; 100 HOG features encoding gradient distributions; 50 LBP features encoding local texture; 50 ORB keypoint and descriptor features; 65 perceptual hash features; and 50 SIFT features. These were combined into three feature vectors of 3,315 dimensions each, pairing the 315 handcrafted features with one backbone's deep features. Five classifiers - random forest, k-nearest neighbours, decision tree, support vector machine and logistic regression - were applied to the handcrafted features alone and to each fused vector. The extraction pipeline is narrated in step-by-step procedural detail down to directory traversal, DataFrame construction and CSV export. No evaluation protocol is described anywhere: the words 'split' and 'validation' do not appear, no cross-validation is reported, and no train-test partition or holdout proportion is stated for any of the twenty tabulated accuracies. No hyperparameters are given for any classifier.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Handcrafted image features alone gave 84.50% accuracy with random forest, 81.20% with logistic regression, 80.00% with decision tree, 78.50% with SVM and 78.00% with k-nearest neighbours. Fusing with ResNet features raised the range to 84.4-90.2%, with SVM and logistic regression best at 90.2% and 90.0%. Fusing with Inception features gave 83.2-94.6%, with SVM best at 94.6%, random forest 91.2% and logistic regression 90.0%. Precision, recall and F1 are reported as identical values to the percentage point in almost every row, without the underlying confusion counts. No AUC, confidence interval or chance baseline is given for any result, and no interpretability analysis of any kind is performed.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: No evaluation protocol is described at all, so none of the twenty reported accuracies can be interpreted as an estimate of performance on unseen data, and the comparison the paper is organised around - handcrafted versus fused features, and among three backbones - cannot be evaluated either, since a resubstitution comparison would favour higher-dimensional representations regardless of generalisation. The dataset's two classes come from different internet sources, so photographic properties are confounded with the label; this matters more here than in the companion study because five of the eight feature families are descriptors that respond directly to gradient structure, texture, keypoint density and global image fingerprint - all functions of resolution, sharpness, compression and lighting - and that feature set alone reaches 84.5%, a result reported without comment. Labels are directory names with no diagnostic verification. The number of distinct children is unknown, so partition integrity could not be established even if a partition had been specified. No demographic information exists. No interpretability analysis is performed that could distinguish a face classifier from a photograph classifier. The title and introduction frame the work as emotion-based while no emotion or expression analysis appears anywhere. And there is no limitations section, no ethics approval, no consent and no discussion of either.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Charted as a second data point on the facial-photograph branch of this literature, and it strengthens three observations already recorded from the companion study on the same scraped dataset. First, the branch is substantial rather than marginal: two independent groups published on this collection in the same year, and this paper's own literature review cites at least half a dozen further facial-image autism classifiers using MobileNetV2, EfficientNet, VGG19 and hybrid vision transformers at accuracies from 88% to 92.5%. Second, its reported accuracies - up to 94.6% - are comparable to or higher than those of the best-conducted studies charted in this review, including the joint-attention system with ADOS-verified diagnoses and the human-benchmark comparison against expert clinicians, which is further evidence that reported accuracy in this literature does not order studies by evidential quality. Third, and specific to this paper, it can report twenty accuracy figures without stating anywhere how training and test data were separated, while narrating the feature-extraction pipeline down to CSV export - an asymmetry that is itself informative about what this branch's peer review is filtering on. One further observation is worth carrying forward as a methodological point rather than a criticism of this study alone. The handcrafted feature set used here consists of HOG, LBP, ORB, PHASH and SIFT: gradient histograms, texture patterns, keypoint descriptors and perceptual hashes. These are the standard toolkit for image retrieval and near-duplicate detection - that is, for telling photographs apart - and they achieve 84.5% on their own. In a dataset whose two classes were harvested from different parts of the internet, that is close to a demonstration of the confound, and it appears in the paper as an intermediate result on the way to a better one.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] There are no participants - 2,936 facial photographs from a Kaggle collection, evenly divided at 1,468 per class, described only as colour images of autistic and non-autistic children. The number of distinct children behind them is unknown and unrecoverable. This is the same publicly scraped 'Autistic Children Facial Dataset' already charted in this review in a companion study which used a 2,836-image version, and the two counts imply different snapshots of a dataset that has been revised. The companion study documents the provenance that this one does not mention: autistic images sourced from online platforms focused on autism, non-autistic images gathered separately from the internet. [RQ1.2] 'Autistic children' and 'non-autistic children', person-first in most constructions but with 'normally developing youngsters' appearing when summarising prior work. The clinical description in the introduction is drawn accurately from DSM criteria and is comparatively careful - reduced sharing of emotions and interests, deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, difficulty adapting behaviour to social contexts, difficulty making friends. The framing of purpose includes an unusual note: technological advancement is described as 'a blessing to the parents who are clueless about managing the condition', which positions the work as parent-facing. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement - a notable absence given that the dataset's autistic images were collected from autism-focused online spaces created by and for that community. The premise that 'autistic children show distinctive patterns' in facial and emotional expression is asserted without citation to any evidence about facial morphology. [RQ1.3] None whatsoever - no age, sex, race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, cognitive level, language, comorbidity or severity data for any image, and no statement that such information is unavailable. The paper does not report even the age range that the dataset's own description carries. As with the companion study, the omission is consequential because the two classes were assembled from different internet sources, and autism-focused online spaces will differ from general internet image collections in the demographics they represent as well as in photographic convention. [RQ1.4] Absent. The labels are the names of two subdirectories in a downloaded folder, and the methods section describes exactly this: features are extracted 'by traversing through the directory structure', with 'a label column added to denote the class label (autistic or non_autistic)'. No diagnosis, instrument, criterion, clinician or verification underlies either class. The quantity the models predict is therefore which folder an image was filed in, and given that the folders were populated from different parts of the internet, the reported accuracies are best read as measures of how distinguishable the two source collections are as image sets. [RQ1.5] None, and none is possible. No severity, cognitive, language or adaptive information exists for any image. [RQ2.1] The stated aim is to improve autism detection accuracy from facial images by combining transfer-learned deep features with handcrafted image descriptors, and to identify the best classifier and feature combination. Findings: handcrafted features alone gave 78.0-84.5% across five classifiers, with random forest best; adding ResNet features raised the range to 84.4-90.2%, with SVM best; and adding Inception features gave 83.2-94.6%, with SVM best at 94.6%. The reported progression - handcrafted alone, then fused with each backbone - is a systematic ablation and is the paper's substantive content. What it cannot establish is what the improvement means, because no evaluation protocol is stated: the words 'split' and 'validation' appear nowhere, no cross-validation is described, and no train-test partition is specified for any of the eighteen reported accuracies. Whether these are held-out figures, training figures, or something else is not determinable from the paper. [RQ2.2] No study setting. Work was performed on a downloaded Kaggle dataset at two universities in Visakhapatnam, India, with no contact with any participant and no acquisition of any kind. [RQ2.3] None. There is no task, protocol or elicitation - the data are photographs. The framing gap is worth stating plainly: the title announces 'Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection' and the introduction argues that 'facial expressions and emotional expressions can help in early detection and diagnosis of ASD', but no expression is labelled, detected, elicited or analysed anywhere in the paper. The features extracted are generic image descriptors, and the classification target is the image's folder. The word 'emotion' does not recur in the method, results or conclusion. So the study measures no behaviour at all while describing itself as behavioural, which places it further outside this review's modality scope than the companion study on the same dataset, that one at least having attached a genuine facial-expression module trained on AffectNet. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional in the trivial sense. No ethics statement, consent, funding declaration or competing-interests statement appears anywhere. As with the companion study, the dataset consists of identifiable photographs of children obtained without their families' knowledge, with one class assembled specifically because those images appeared in autism contexts - so the collection asserts a health status about identifiable minors, and training and publishing on it propagates that assertion. None of this is acknowledged. [RQ2.5] None. Pretrained VGG16, ResNet and Inception networks used as fixed feature extractors with fully connected layers excluded, and five classical classifiers. No hardware, software package, version or hyperparameter is reported. The imaging characteristics of the source photographs - the properties that differ between the two source collections and that HOG, LBP, PHASH and SIFT are designed to capture - are neither reported nor examined. [RQ2.6] Curiously uneven. The feature-extraction pipeline is described at unusual procedural length, narrating library imports, directory traversal, per-image processing, DataFrame construction, label-column addition, merging and CSV export, with exact feature counts tabulated for all eight families. The evaluation is described not at all. A reader is given enough to reconstruct how a 3,315-dimensional feature vector was built and nothing whatever about how the reported accuracies were computed. Also absent: the Kaggle dataset identifier and version, any classifier hyperparameters, any seed, and code. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section and no constraint is acknowledged. The unaddressed problems are the same as for the companion study on this dataset, plus one that is specific to this paper. The dataset's two classes come from different internet sources, so image provenance is confounded with the label - and here the confound is sharper than usual, because five of the eight feature families are handcrafted descriptors that respond directly to gradient structure, texture, keypoint density and perceptual hashing, all of which are functions of resolution, sharpness, compression and lighting rather than of anything about the child. That the handcrafted features alone reach 84.5% is therefore not evidence that facial morphology is informative; it is equally consistent with the two collections being distinguishable as image sets. No diagnostic verification exists for either class. The number of distinct children is unknown. No demographic data are available. Eighteen classifier-feature combinations were evaluated and the maximum reported. And, uniquely among included studies, no evaluation protocol of any kind is described. [RQ2.9] None proposed. The conclusion restates the method and the comparison without identifying any next step. [RQ3.1] None is measured. The paper's framing is behavioural - emotion, facial expression, distinctive patterns shown by autistic children - and its method is not. HOG captures gradient orientation distributions, LBP captures local texture, ORB captures keypoints and their descriptors, PHASH computes a perceptual fingerprint of the whole image, SIFT detects scale-invariant local features, and the three backbones supply generic ImageNet activations. None of these is a measure of expression, movement or any behaviour, and no expression labels exist in the dataset. For the review this study marks the far end of a boundary the companion paper already approached: automated autism detection that has left behaviour behind entirely while retaining behavioural vocabulary. [RQ3.2] Fusion within a single modality and across feature families, systematically ablated. Three feature vectors are constructed, each concatenating the same 315 handcrafted features with one backbone's 3,000 deep features, and results are reported for the handcrafted set alone and for each fused vector across five classifiers. The ablation shows a consistent gain from adding deep features - best accuracy rising from 84.5% with handcrafted features alone to 90.2% with ResNet and 94.6% with Inception - which is a clean comparison and is the paper's only methodological contribution. Its interpretability is destroyed by the absence of an evaluation protocol: without knowing how the accuracies were computed, the gain cannot be attributed to better representation rather than to greater capacity to fit the data. [RQ4.1] Three ImageNet-pretrained backbones used as fixed feature extractors with fully connected layers excluded, and five classical classifiers - random forest, k-nearest neighbours, decision tree, SVM and logistic regression - applied to each of four feature conditions, giving twenty reported model-condition combinations of which eighteen are tabulated. The design is a systematic grid rather than a single proposed model, which is reasonable for a comparison study. No hyperparameters are reported for any classifier, and no rationale is given for the choice of backbones or descriptors beyond their being commonly used. [RQ4.2] A 3,315-dimensional concatenation per image: 3,000 activations from one backbone plus 100 HOG, 50 LBP, 50 ORB, 65 PHASH and 50 SIFT features. The handcrafted component is worth characterising because it determines what a source-provenance confound would look like. HOG encodes gradient distributions, which depend on image sharpness; LBP encodes local texture, which depends on resolution and compression; PHASH is a whole-image fingerprint, which encodes global tone and layout; SIFT and ORB encode keypoint structure, which depends on contrast and focus. Every one of these is a property of the photograph rather than of the face, and all differ systematically between images collected from different sources. That this feature set alone achieves 84.5% is therefore the paper's most diagnostic result, and it is reported without comment. [RQ4.3] Precision, recall, F1 and accuracy, reported as whole percentages for five classifiers across four feature conditions. The set is nominally adequate, but three problems undercut it. Precision, recall and F1 are reported as identical values to the percentage point in almost every row, which for a balanced binary problem is arithmetically possible but is presented without the confusion counts that would let a reader verify it. No AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval appears. And most fundamentally, no evaluation protocol is stated, so it is not determinable what population any of these numbers estimates - they may be held-out, resubstitution, or cross-validated figures, and the paper provides no basis for choosing between those readings. [RQ4.4] None. No feature importance, saliency map, activation visualisation, error analysis or example inspection appears for any of the eighteen combinations. The absence is decisive rather than incidental in this design, because the study's own results contain the material for an interpretability check it does not perform: handcrafted descriptors sensitive to image quality reach 84.5% alone, and a single analysis of which descriptors carry that performance - or a single visualisation of what distinguishes the two classes - would establish whether the model responds to faces or to photographs. [RQ4.5] There is no validation strategy. This is not a case of an inadequate or leaky protocol but of no stated protocol at all: the words 'split' and 'validation' do not occur in the paper, no cross-validation is described, no holdout proportion is given, and no resampling scheme is mentioned, yet twenty accuracy figures are tabulated across four feature conditions and five classifiers. The methods section narrates the feature-extraction pipeline in step-by-step detail down to CSV export and then moves directly to results. Consequently none of the reported numbers can be interpreted as an estimate of performance on unseen data, and the comparison the paper is built around - handcrafted versus fused features, and among the three backbones - cannot be evaluated either, since a resubstitution comparison would favour the higher-dimensional representations regardless of their generalisation. Beneath this sits the same structural problem as in the companion study on this dataset: the two classes were assembled from different internet sources, so no split, however constructed, could separate a model that has learned about faces from one that has learned about photographs; and the number of distinct children is unknown, so images of one child may fall on both sides of any partition undetectably. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder; transfer learning; image features; VGG; ResNet; Inception. Five of six name architectures or feature types; no behavioural, clinical or application term appears. The title's 'Emotion-based' has no counterpart in the keywords, the method or the results, and is the paper's clearest instance of behavioural vocabulary applied to non-behavioural work. [RQ5.2] International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications 15(5), 2024, pages 566 onwards - a general computer-science journal published by The Science and Information Organization, outside the clinical and biomedical literature. The venue accounts for the reporting profile: extensive procedural description of feature extraction, a large comparison grid, and no ethics, funding, competing-interests or limitations statement. It does not account for the absence of an evaluation protocol, which is a scientific rather than a formatting omission. [RQ5.3] Published 2024 by the Department of Computer Science and Systems Engineering at Andhra University with the Department of Applied Psychology at GITAM Deemed to be University, Visakhapatnam. The framing is early detection and parental support, with the observation that diagnosis 'depends predominantly on the aberrations in the functioning of the brain that may not surface in the very early stages' and that technology has been 'a blessing to the parents who are clueless about managing the condition'. The presence of a psychology co-author makes the absence of any diagnostic verification, demographic reporting or ethical consideration more striking rather than less. For this review the study's value is entirely as a second data point on the facial-photograph branch of the literature, and it strengthens three observations already recorded from the companion study on the same dataset. The branch is not small - two independent groups publishing in the same year on the same scraped collection, with a literature review here citing at least half a dozen further examples using facial images, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet and hybrid vision transformers at accuracies from 88% to 92.5%. Its reported accuracies are comparable to or higher than the best-conducted studies in this review, so accuracy in this literature does not order studies by evidential quality. And its methodological reporting can omit the evaluation protocol entirely without that omission preventing publication - which is the strongest available evidence that peer review in this branch is not filtering on the properties that determine whether a number means anything.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective algorithm-development study by a computer science and engineering group at R.M.D. Engineering College, Thiruvallur, India. Two public affective-computing corpora were used: the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces corpus, comprising posed expressions photographed under fixed laboratory conditions with the subject's eyes and lips aligned to standard image coordinates, evaluated across four brightness variants; and the Extended Cohn-Kanade corpus, comprising 327 instructed expression sequences from 118 adult volunteers, of which only the peak frame of each sequence was used. Neither corpus contains autistic participants, autism labels or any clinical ascertainment, and no autism classification, screening or severity-estimation target is modelled anywhere in the paper. A single passing reference in the results to 'the Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression (ASD-FE) dataset and the Extended Cohn-Kanade (CK+) dataset adapted for ASD research' is unsupported by any description, citation, sizing or characterisation in the methods.
narrative_rows.methods: Images were converted to grayscale and resized to 120x110 for a Gabor filter stage and 100x100 for the convolutional network, after intensity normalisation, histogram equalisation, face detection with realignment and background removal, with landmark and local binary pattern descriptors described in the preprocessing account. The proposed architecture couples Weighted Quantum Particle Swarm Optimisation - which encodes the swarm in quaternion rather than Euclidean space, with the quaternion algebra set out through Hamilton's relations - to a Fast Mask Recurrent Convolutional Neural Network. Comparison baselines were a CNN, a linear support vector machine and k-nearest neighbours, with t-values and p-values reported for the differences. No train-test split, cross-validation scheme, held-out set size or partitioning unit is stated anywhere; CK+ is described as testing the model 'on unseen data' after KDEF, implying cross-corpus evaluation, but no cross-corpus result is reported separately.
narrative_rows.outcomes: The hybrid architecture achieved 99.8% accuracy, 99.8% precision, 100% recall and 94% specificity on six-way emotion classification, described as surpassing existing systems, with all baseline comparisons significant at p < 0.01. No confusion matrix, class-wise breakdown, confidence interval or chance baseline accompanies these figures, and the number of emotion classes is stated as six in the abstract, seven in the KDEF description and five in a CK+ figure caption listing 'happy, digest, angry, fear and sad'.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The paper contains no autistic participants, no autism labels and no autism classification target, while its title, keywords, abstract, introduction, problem statement and conclusion are all written in terms of autistic people and the failure of conventional systems to read their faces. The data are posed prototypical expressions from adult volunteers, captured at peak intensity, on a corpus geometrically standardised so that eyes and lips occupy fixed coordinates - the most favourable possible input for facial expression recognition and the furthest from the spontaneous, low-intensity, idiosyncratic expression the paper says it addresses. The introduction itself notes that 'staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones' and that the field lacks spontaneous-stimulus work, without connecting either observation to the study's own design. No validation scheme, split proportion, cross-validation arrangement or partitioning unit is described anywhere, so the reported figures cannot be located relative to any evaluation design. The metric combination of 100% recall with 94% specificity across six classes is unusual and is presented without confusion matrices, class-wise results or a definition of multi-class specificity, and without confidence intervals or a statement of how many runs contributed to the significance tests. The architecture narrative repeatedly describes the optimiser as encoding 'physiological signal characteristics' although no physiological signal is collected or used. And there is no limitations section.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The study contributes to the review not as evidence about autism detection - it contains none - but as its clearest instance of autism framing attached to work with no autism content, and as a marker of what high accuracy on the posed-expression benchmark actually signifies. Every framing element identifies the paper as autism research, and the underlying problem it names is real and under-addressed: autistic people's facial signalling may be atypical in ways that conventional recognition systems misread, with the consequence, as the introduction puts it, that 'these differences can lead to social withdrawal, especially when others react negatively to the atypical responses of individuals with ASD' - a formulation that locates the difficulty partly in others' reactions rather than solely in the autistic person, and which is better than most framing in this corpus. The executed work tests none of it. The evaluation uses instructed prototypical expressions from non-autistic adults, at peak frames, on geometrically standardised images, which is the canonical easy case for this task and one on which very high accuracies have long been achievable. The paper's own introduction supplies the reason this cannot support its stated aim, observing that staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones and that spontaneous-stimulus work is what the field lacks. Read alongside another study charted in this review, which tests the transfer question directly and finds that affect models trained on neurotypical faces estimate arousal and valence poorly in autistic children until fine-tuned on autistic data, the pair makes the synthesis point cleanly: the posed-expression benchmark is close to solved, the autism-relevant expression problem is not, and reported figures move between the two without the distinction being marked. Three procedural defects complete the record - no stated validation scheme of any kind, metrics reported without confusion matrices or class-wise results, and an emotion-class count given as six, seven and five in three different places.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] There are no autistic participants. The Extended Cohn-Kanade corpus supplies 327 sequences from 118 adult volunteers, of which only the peak frame of each sequence is used, giving roughly 2.8 images per person; the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces corpus supplies posed adult expressions photographed under fixed conditions, with its sample size not stated in this paper. Both are general-population affective-computing resources with no autism component, no autism labels and no clinical ascertainment of any kind. The paper's results section mentions once, in passing, 'the Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression (ASD-FE) dataset and the Extended Cohn-Kanade (CK+) dataset adapted for ASD research', but no such dataset is described, cited, sized or characterised anywhere in the methods and no adaptation procedure is specified, while the experiments reported in the results and figures are conducted on brightness variants of KDEF and on CK+ peak frames. The sample is therefore adult, non-autistic, and posed - three respects in which it differs from the population the study's stated purpose concerns, which is autistic children experiencing spontaneous distress. [RQ1.2] The framing is entirely autism-focused and the content is not, which is the record's central observation. The introduction is written with some care about autistic experience: it notes that autistic people 'frequently struggle with self-regulation, emotional interpretation, and understanding and labeling others' emotions', and that 'these differences can lead to social withdrawal, especially when others react negatively to the atypical responses of individuals with ASD' - which locates part of the difficulty in other people's reactions rather than solely in the autistic person, a formulation better than most in this corpus. The conclusion likewise frames the goal as addressing 'the existing challenges faced by conventional facial expression recognition systems when applied to ASD populations, where nuanced facial cues may be misinterpreted or overlooked', which correctly identifies a technology failure rather than a personal deficit. Against this, autism is described as 'a neurological illness', and the phrase 'the minor changes and quirks typical of the facial movements' of autistic people is dismissive. No autistic person is reported as involved, and no autistic person's face appears in the data. [RQ1.3] Not applicable to a study with no clinical groups, and unreported for the corpora used. No age distribution, sex composition or ancestry is given for either KDEF or CK+, although both are documented in their originating publications. The one demographic fact that matters here is implicit and unremarked: both corpora consist of adult volunteers, while the paper's motivating application concerns autistic children, so the modelled population differs from the target population by several decades of facial development as well as by diagnosis. [RQ1.4] None is required by the task as executed, since no autism classification is attempted - the labels are posed emotion categories, which are a strong ground truth for emotion recognition and carry no information about autism. The consequence for this review is that the study cannot contribute evidence on any of the diagnostic questions. Its relevance is instead to the review's treatment of how autism framing attaches to work containing no autism data: a reader relying on the title, abstract, keywords and conclusion would record this as an autism study, and it is not one. [RQ1.5] None. No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists, and none could, since no clinical population was studied. [RQ2.1] The stated aim is to improve recognition of altered facial expressions in autistic people, on the argument that conventional systems misread the nuanced cues that autistic faces produce - a real and under-addressed problem, and the strongest idea in the paper. The executed work is six-way emotion classification on KDEF and CK+, reporting 99.8% accuracy, 99.8% precision, 100% recall and 94% specificity, with significance tests against CNN, linear SVM and k-nearest-neighbour baselines at p < 0.01. The gap between the two is the study's defining feature. The paper's own introduction supplies the reason the executed task cannot address the stated aim, observing that 'research indicates a lack of studies utilizing static or dynamic facial stimuli displaying real, spontaneous emotions' and that 'staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones' - after which the evaluation uses only staged emotions from instructed adult volunteers. A separate study charted in this review tests the transfer question directly and finds that affect models trained on neurotypical faces perform poorly on autistic children and improve substantially only after fine-tuning on autistic data, which is the evidence this study would have needed and did not seek. [RQ2.2] No study setting. Both corpora were collected under laboratory conditions by their original creators, with KDEF in particular geometrically standardised so that eyes and lips fall at fixed image coordinates across all images. That standardisation is the opposite of the conditions the paper's motivating application would face - an autistic child in spontaneous distress, filmed at whatever angle and distance the situation allows - and the mismatch is not discussed. The one robustness check reported, evaluation across four brightness variants of KDEF, addresses illumination but not pose, spontaneity, age or population. [RQ2.3] Instructed posed expression production, as designed into both corpora. This is the canonical easy case for facial expression recognition: prototypical, maximally intense, produced deliberately, and captured at the peak frame - CK+ explicitly uses 'the peak frame of each sequence' because 'it includes the greatest information relating to emotions'. Selecting peak frames maximises separability and is standard practice for benchmarking, but it removes precisely the subtlety the paper claims to address. The paradigm gap is therefore twofold: posed rather than spontaneous, and peak rather than continuous. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element. No ethics statement appears, which is conventional for secondary use of two established consented affective-computing corpora. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text. [RQ2.5] No acquisition equipment. Preprocessing is described in reasonable detail - grayscale conversion, resizing to 120x110 for a Gabor filter stage and 100x100 for the convolutional network, intensity normalisation, histogram equalisation, face detection with realignment, and landmark or local binary pattern feature extraction. The two-resolution arrangement for the two processing stages is a specific and reproducible detail. [RQ2.6] Partial. Reported: both corpora by name, CK+'s 327 sequences from 118 individuals, the peak-frame selection rule, the full preprocessing chain with both working resolutions, the quaternion algebra underpinning the optimiser given as explicit Hamilton relations, the three baseline comparators, and t-values and p-values for the comparisons. Not reported: KDEF's sample size, class distributions for either corpus, any train-test split or cross-validation scheme, the swarm optimiser's own population size and iteration count, the network's hyperparameters, how many runs contributed to the reported means, over what units the t-tests were computed, code, funding and competing interests. The mathematical apparatus is documented and the experimental protocol is not. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section. The most consequential omission is the mismatch between the paper's framing and its content: every framing element - title, abstract, keywords, introduction, problem statement and conclusion - is written in terms of autistic people, while the data are posed expressions from non-autistic adults and no autism label, participant or classification target exists anywhere. The paper also identifies, in its own introduction, the reason its evaluation cannot support its aim - that staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones and that spontaneous stimuli are what the field lacks - without connecting that observation to its own design. Further unstated issues: no validation scheme, split proportion or partitioning unit is given anywhere; the reported metric combination (100% recall with 94% specificity in a six-class problem) is unusual and is presented without confusion matrices, class-wise results or a definition of multi-class specificity; the number of emotion classes is stated as six in the abstract, seven in the KDEF description and five in a CK+ figure caption; and the architecture narrative repeatedly describes the optimiser as encoding 'physiological signal characteristics' although no physiological signal is collected or used. [RQ2.9] None stated. The directions the study most needs are evident from its own framing: evaluate on autistic participants, evaluate on spontaneous rather than posed expression, and test whether a model optimised on posed adult faces transfers to autistic children's faces at all - the last being a question another study in this review answers negatively for a comparable pipeline. [RQ3.1] Prototypical posed emotion in adult volunteers - anger, fear, joy, sadness, surprise and disgust - captured at peak intensity. The construct the paper claims to address is different and considerably harder: the atypical, low-intensity, idiosyncratic facial signalling that autistic people may produce and that conventional recognition systems misread. The paper states that problem clearly and does not test it. For this review the distinction matters because the two constructs have opposite difficulty profiles: posed peak-frame expression is the benchmark case on which affect recognition has long achieved very high accuracy, whereas spontaneous atypical expression in autistic children is where every reported system in this corpus degrades. A 99.8% figure on the first tells a reader nothing about the second. [RQ3.2] None. A single static image modality throughout. The recurring references to encoding 'physiological signal characteristics' and 'physiological signal properties' in quaternion space describe the optimiser's original application domain rather than anything in this study, where no physiological signal is acquired. [RQ4.1] A hybrid of Weighted Quantum Particle Swarm Optimisation with a Fast Mask Recurrent Convolutional Neural Network. The optimiser's distinguishing feature is that it encodes the swarm in quaternion rather than Euclidean space, and the quaternion algebra is set out explicitly through Hamilton's relations, on the stated rationale that this concentrates the search on more productive regions. Comparison against CNN, linear SVM and k-nearest-neighbour baselines with significance tests is more than many papers in this branch offer. What is not reported is the optimiser's own configuration - population size, iteration count, inertia and weighting parameters - or the network's hyperparameters, so the mechanism credited with the improvement cannot be reproduced. [RQ4.2] Grayscale cropped faces at 120x110 for Gabor filtering and 100x100 for convolutional processing, after normalisation, histogram equalisation, face detection and realignment. KDEF images are additionally pre-standardised by the corpus creators so that eyes and lips occupy fixed coordinates, which removes pose and scale variation entirely - a property that raises accuracy and reduces the relevance of the result to any uncontrolled setting. [RQ4.3] Accuracy 99.8%, precision 99.8%, recall 100% and specificity 94%, with t-values and p-values against three baselines at p < 0.01. Three problems. The combination is unusual for a balanced multi-class problem - perfect recall alongside 94% specificity - and no confusion matrix, per-class breakdown or definition of multi-class specificity is supplied to make it interpretable. No confidence intervals accompany any figure, and the number of runs behind the reported means is not stated, so the significance tests cannot be assessed. And no chance baseline is given, though six-way classification would place it near 17% under balance. [RQ4.4] None. No attribution, saliency, feature-importance or error analysis is reported for the classifier. The quaternion formulation is presented in mathematical detail but is a search-space construct, not an explanation of what the network responds to, and the associated claim that it captures physiological signal properties has no referent in the data. [RQ4.5] Not assessable, because no validation scheme is described. The paper states no train-test split proportion, no cross-validation arrangement, no held-out set size and no partitioning unit anywhere. The one hint is that CK+ is used 'to test the WQPSO-FMRCNN model on unseen data' after KDEF, which would be cross-corpus evaluation - the design this review regards most highly, since it tests transfer across acquisition conditions and populations. It is not reported as a separate result, so what would have been the study's strongest methodological feature goes unquantified. Two further points bound the figures. CK+ contributes 327 peak frames from 118 individuals, roughly 2.8 images per person, and whether images of the same individual span any partition is unstated. And KDEF is geometrically standardised with eyes and lips at fixed coordinates, so a classifier operating on it faces none of the pose, scale or framing variation that any real deployment would present. A 99.8% accuracy on peak-frame posed expressions from geometrically aligned adult faces is close to the ceiling that this benchmark has long supported, and is not evidence about the harder problem the paper describes. [RQ5.1] Keywords: hybrid WQPSO, FMRCNN, facial expression recognition, ASD, computational intelligence, healthcare. The inclusion of ASD in the keyword list, alongside an autism-framed title, ensures the paper is indexed and retrieved as autism research - which is how it entered this corpus - although it contains no autism data. That indexing effect is itself a finding for the review: searches for computational autism work will return studies of this kind, and their reported accuracies will enter informal impressions of the field's performance without ever having concerned autistic people. [RQ5.2] Traitement du Signal 41(6), IIETA, open access under CC BY, doi 10.18280/ts.410628; received 12 April 2024, revised 7 August, accepted 20 August, available online 31 December 2024. A signal-processing venue. The review process accepted a paper whose title and abstract promise autism facial expression recognition while its experiments use two general-population posed-expression corpora; whose class count differs across three locations in the text; whose architecture narrative refers repeatedly to physiological signals that are never collected; and which states no validation scheme of any kind. [RQ5.3] Published December 2024 by a computer science and engineering group at R.M.D. Engineering College, Thiruvallur. For this review the study's value lies in what it illustrates rather than in what it measures, and two lessons carry into the synthesis. The first concerns the boundary between autism-framed and autism-evidenced work. Every framing element here - title, keywords, abstract, introduction, problem statement, conclusion - is written in terms of autistic people and the failure of conventional systems to read their faces, which is a real and under-addressed problem stated with some sympathy; and the entire experimental content is six-way emotion classification on posed expressions from non-autistic adult volunteers, evaluated at peak frames on a corpus whose images are geometrically standardised. A reader relying on title and abstract would record 99.8% as an autism result. The second concerns what such figures mean. The paper's own introduction notes that 'staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones' and that the field lacks work on spontaneous stimuli, which is precisely why 99.8% on peak-frame posed adult expressions is near the long-established ceiling for that benchmark and carries no implication for autistic children in spontaneous distress - the application the conclusion invokes. Another study charted in this review tests exactly that transfer and finds that affect models trained on neurotypical faces perform poorly on autistic children and improve materially only after fine-tuning on autistic data. Read together, the two studies make the point cleanly: the emotion-recognition benchmark is solved, the autism-relevant problem is not, and the two are frequently reported as though they were the same. Three further defects should be recorded: no validation scheme, split or partitioning unit is stated anywhere; the reported metrics (100% recall with 94% specificity across six classes) are presented without confusion matrices or class-wise results; and the number of emotion classes is given as six, seven and five in three different places.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional two-group classification study at the Natural and Artificial Cognition Lab, University of Naples Federico II, with the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center. Twenty children aged 3-6 were recruited between 13 February and 21 March 2023: 10 autistic (mean age 4 years, SD 0.94) from the rehabilitation centre where they were receiving psychomotor and speech therapy, and 10 typically developing (mean 3 years 9 months, SD 0.1) from a mainstream pre-primary and primary school in the province of Naples. Autism required a clinical diagnosis confirmed with ADOS-2, administered by healthcare professionals stated explicitly to be independent of the research laboratory and study, together with age 3-6 and absence of comorbid conditions; no ADOS-2 score is reported. Comparison children were selected only on parent and teacher report of no neurodevelopmental disorder and were recruited 'without specific assessment of their pre-existing abilities'. No sex, IQ, developmental, language or severity data exist for either group. The modelled dataset is 738 trajectories, roughly 37 per child, extended to 932 samples for the correlation analysis by adding simulated trajectories. Ethics approval, written parental consent, funder no-role statement and a competing-interests declaration are all reported, and the trajectory data are published openly on GitHub.
narrative_rows.methods: Children played a purpose-built Unity 2D drag-and-drop game on a 12.3-inch Dell Latitude tablet, raised and tilted at about 60 degrees, seated at a table 45-60 cm high with the experimenter 30 cm to their right. The task required dragging an image from the screen centre to a target at one of eight positions spaced 45 degrees apart while avoiding distractors, with identical settings for every participant. No verbal instructions were given: a video tutorial started on pressing play and the image to be moved vibrated as a cue, both introduced explicitly to avoid stressful social situations and improve engagement and autonomy. Finger coordinates were logged at 20 Hz, with recording restricted to completed drags from image to target and only trajectories of 20-69 points retained. Coordinates were then rotation-normalised so that trajectories to different targets became comparable, using the angle between consecutive points computed by atan2 and mapped into 0-360 degrees, with the transformation written out in three numbered equations. Two sequential artificial neural networks were compared, one receiving only the rotated x and y coordinates and one adding velocity and acceleration, evaluated by four-fold cross-validation with a 110-sample validation set described as 15% of the 738 trajectories. A simulation experiment then generated trajectories with average acceleration systematically varied between -5 and +5 cm/s squared, and a robustness analysis simplified trajectories at seven rates from 35% to 90%.
narrative_rows.outcomes: The four-feature model reached 0.90 accuracy against 0.76 for the two-feature model, with a consistently higher distribution across folds and a better ROC curve. The simulation analysis established the role of acceleration directly: across 932 samples, average trajectory acceleration correlated with the model's prediction at r = 0.69 for the two-feature model and r = 0.82 for the four-feature model, both at p < 0.001, with higher acceleration increasing the probability of an autism prediction. The two-feature model's correlation is the more informative of the two, since that model never receives acceleration as an input - so acceleration information is recoverable from the raw coordinate sequence, and the four-feature representation makes it easier to use rather than supplying anything new. The authors conclude accordingly that raw data analysis has potential while the four-feature model excels. No sensitivity, specificity, confusion matrix, AUC value, confidence interval or participant-level result is reported.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The 738 modelled trajectories come from 20 children at roughly 37 each, and four-fold cross-validation partitions trajectories rather than children, with the validation set quoted in samples out of 738 and nothing indicating that folds respected child boundaries. Each validation trajectory therefore has around 36 siblings produced by the same child in the same session with the same hand - and after rotation normalisation those siblings differ only in the noise of execution. Fine motor kinematics at this granularity function close to an individual motor signature, so the reported 0.90 is not an estimate of performance on a child the model has not seen, and no participant-level figure appears anywhere; with 20 children, leave-one-child-out validation would have been trivial to run. Neither group received any developmental or cognitive assessment, and the comparison children were recruited explicitly without assessment of pre-existing abilities, so a general developmental explanation for the motor difference cannot be separated from an autism-specific one in 3-6 year olds. The autistic group's age standard deviation is nearly ten times the comparison group's, so the groups differ in developmental spread even though their means are close. The autistic children were receiving psychomotor therapy at the recruiting centre - direct motor intervention - while the comparison children were not. Comorbidity was excluded, narrowing the sample. No sex data are reported, no model architecture or training hyperparameters are specified, and no class-conditional metric or confidence interval accompanies either accuracy.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Three contributions make this study valuable to the review out of proportion to its sample size. It is the only included study to publish its data openly, at a stated GitHub URL, so its central claim can be independently rechecked - including, by anyone who wishes, under a participant-disjoint split that the paper itself did not perform. Its interpretability method is a template worth propagating: rather than applying post-hoc attribution, it generates synthetic trajectories with acceleration systematically varied across a stated range and measures how the models' predictions move, yielding causal, directional and quantified evidence about the decision function. And its incidental finding is a useful corrective to an assumption running through this literature - the two-feature model, which never receives acceleration as an input, nonetheless correlates with acceleration at r = 0.69, showing that the 14-point accuracy gain from adding derived kinematic features reflects easier access to information already present in the raw sequence rather than new information. Studies throughout this corpus report feature-engineering gains and read them as evidence that the added features capture something; this one shows a case where they do not, and shows it by manipulation. Its task design also deserves noting: the deliberate removal of verbal instruction, replaced by a video tutorial and a vibration cue explicitly to avoid stressful social situations, is the clearest instance in the review of an elicitation designed so that a motor measurement is not contaminated by social demand. Against all this, the study partitions 738 trajectories from 20 children by trajectory, and shares with its companion study from the same group the unaddressed confound that its autistic participants were receiving psychomotor therapy while its comparison participants were not.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Twenty children aged 3-6, recruited between 13 February and 21 March 2023: 10 autistic (mean age 4 years, SD 0.94) from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center where they were receiving psychomotor and speech therapy, and 10 typically developing (mean 3 years 9 months, SD 0.1) from a pre-primary and primary educational institute in the province of Naples. Inclusion for the autistic group required a clinical diagnosis, age 3-6 and absence of comorbid conditions; the only criterion for the comparison group was parent and teacher report of no neurodevelopmental disorder, with the paper stating explicitly that they were recruited 'without specific assessment of their pre-existing abilities'. The modelled unit is not the child but the trajectory: 738 trajectories were retained after filtering, roughly 37 per child, and a further set of computationally generated trajectories brought the correlation analysis to 932 samples. Twenty children is the smallest sample of any included study in this review, and the discrepancy between 20 participants and 738 modelling units is the central interpretive issue. [RQ1.2] 'Children with autism', 'children with a diagnosis of autism' and 'individuals with ASD', person-first and consistent, alongside 'typically developing (TD) children'. Autism is 'a complex and heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder' with the standard two-domain description, and motor differences are called 'motor abnormalities' and 'motor disorders'. The framing is otherwise notably measured and contains one argument worth recording: the paper's opening critique is that autism diagnosis 'is based on subjective observations of behavior' focused on the two core domains, and that 'many other characteristics are overlooked in the diagnostic process, considered non-central to the disorder' - specifically motor characteristics, which 'have always been considered secondary symptoms and not closely related to the syndrome' despite evidence that they precede language and social difficulties. That is an argument for widening what is measured rather than for replacing clinicians, and it is grounded in embodied-cognition theory rather than in an appeal to objectivity alone. The paper also reports the literature on visuospatial ability in autism honestly as conflicting - some studies finding deficits, some no difference, some better performance - rather than selecting the supportive citations. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. [RQ1.3] Thin, and thinner for the comparison group than for the autistic group. Reported: group sizes, age means and standard deviations, recruitment source, and for the autistic group the requirement of an ADOS-2-confirmed diagnosis and absence of comorbidity. Not reported: sex, IQ, developmental level, language ability, socioeconomic status, race or ethnicity, or any severity score. Two features of what is reported deserve attention. The autistic group's age standard deviation is 0.94 years against 0.1 for the comparison group - nearly a tenfold difference in spread - so although the means differ by only three months the autistic group spans a much wider developmental range, which matters for a fine-motor outcome in children aged 3 to 6 where motor control changes rapidly. And no cognitive or developmental assessment was performed on either group; the comparison children were recruited without any assessment of pre-existing abilities, and the autistic group's functioning is inferred rather than measured, from the fact that all 'were able to engage with a tablet, suggesting a moderate level of functioning'. Since the outcome is the smoothness and dynamics of a dragging movement, and both groups were selected without reference to developmental level, a general developmental explanation for the difference cannot be separated from an autism-specific one. A further asymmetry is that the autistic children were undergoing psychomotor therapy at the recruiting centre - direct motor intervention - while the comparison children were not. [RQ1.4] Solid for the autistic group and absent for the comparison group. Autism required a clinical diagnosis confirmed with the ADOS-2, and the paper states something few in this review do: the diagnoses were made 'by healthcare professionals and industry experts who were independent of our research laboratory and study'. Explicit independence between the diagnosing clinicians and the research team removes one route by which knowledge of the study could influence the reference standard, and is worth crediting.
