The discussion also opens a mechanistic direction: since the ADOS-2's apparent autism signal in schizophrenia tracks negative symptoms, and since negative symptoms and autistic social-communication features may both reflect deficits in social cognition supported by overlapping brain regions, the two may be partly the same construct measured under different diagnostic labels. Not proposed, and needed if the model is to progress: blinded administration, item-level inter-rater reliability, a sample that includes the diagnostically ambiguous and comorbid cases the model is intended for, comparable cognitive measurement across groups, and predictive values computed for realistic clinical mixes. [RQ3.1] The full 32-item behavioural repertoire of ADOS-2 Module 4, spanning communication (spoken language level, speech abnormalities, echolalia, stereotyped word use, offering and asking for information, reporting of events, conversation, descriptive gestures, emphatic gestures) and reciprocal social interaction (unusual eye contact, facial expressions directed to the examiner, language production linked with nonverbal communication, shared enjoyment, communication of own affect, comments on others' emotions or empathy, insight into social situations and relationships, responsibility, quality and amount of social overtures, quality of social response), plus imagination and restricted repetitive behaviour items. The item-level table is the study's richest contribution to this review's behavioural synthesis, because it shows that both conditions produce social-communication atypicality but of distinguishable kinds. The autism group scored non-zero more often on asking for information (90.0% against 50.0%), emphatic or emotional gestures (74.0% against 40.0%), unusual eye contact (72.0% against 22.5%), language production linked to nonverbal communication (90.0% against 55.0%) and quality of social overtures (88.0% against 47.5%). The schizophrenia group scored non-zero more often on reporting of events (60.0% against 24.0%), conversation (57.5% against 32.0%), communication of own affect (80.0% against 54.0%) and comments on others' emotions or empathy (75.0% against 34.0%). Roughly speaking, the autistic profile concentrates in the mechanics of nonverbal social exchange - gaze, gesture, the coordination of speech with nonverbal behaviour, the initiation of overtures - while the schizophrenia profile concentrates in the content and organisation of discourse and in affective and empathic commentary. The finding that matters for every behavioural study in this review is that a measure sensitive to social-communication atypicality in general will flag both groups, and that separating them requires attending to which atypicalities are present rather than how many. [RQ3.2] None in the sensor sense - a single observational instrument supplies everything. But the retained six-item model is cross-channel in the same way that the free-play model charted elsewhere is: it combines a discourse-content item (reporting of events), a gesture item (emphatic or emotional gestures), a gaze item (unusual eye contact) and three social-reciprocity items (comments on others' emotions or empathy, responsibility, quality of social overtures). No single channel would have sufficed, and the directions differ by channel - gaze, gesture and overture atypicality point toward autism while discourse and empathic-commentary atypicality point toward schizophrenia. That opposition of signs within one model is what allows a six-item combination to reach an apparent AUC of 0.938 where the algorithm totals, which simply add atypicality across channels, reach 0.56. It is a clean demonstration that summing behavioural abnormality destroys the information needed for differential diagnosis, and it should temper the widespread practice in this corpus of building composite atypicality scores. [RQ4.1] Logistic regression throughout, at three levels: domain scores from each published algorithm as predictors of clinical diagnosis; per-item regressions on dichotomised non-zero indicators to identify predictive items; and a combined six-item model. A further logistic regression within the schizophrenia group predicted ADOS-2 cut-off positivity from the clinical variables that differed between cut-off-positive and cut-off-negative subgroups, returning the PANSS negative scale alone. ROC curves were compared by DeLong's test. With 90 participants and a differential-diagnosis question, regression is the correct tool and no machine learning is attempted or needed - the value of the analysis lies in what the coefficients say, not in maximising a discrimination statistic. The one modelling weakness is the size of the search: six items were chosen from 32 candidates on 90 participants by seeking 'the combination of assessment items with the highest diagnostic predictive accuracy', which is an unregularised selection over a large space, and the holdout result confirms the cost. [RQ4.2] Two representations, compared directly. The instrument's own algorithm domain scores - communication and reciprocal social interaction under the original algorithm, social affect and restricted repetitive behaviour under the revised - which aggregate item ratings into totals against published cut-offs. And a binary per-item vector recording whether each of the 32 items received a non-zero score. The dichotomisation is the more interesting choice and is justified on psychometric rather than convenience grounds: for several items a higher rating denotes a different presentation rather than a more severe one, and the paper works through item B11, quality of social response, where a rating of 1 describes limited, awkward or inconsistent reactions and a rating of 2 describes odd, stereotyped or contextually inappropriate ones - 'there was no clear difference between scores 1 and 2 regarding the severity of ASD symptoms, and the differences were considered to be limited to phenotypic differences in symptoms'. Treating such a scale as ordinal and summing it is exactly what the algorithms do, and the collapse to presence-or-absence of atypicality is part of why the item-level analysis recovers information the totals lose. [RQ4.3] Well chosen for the question and honestly reported. Sensitivity and specificity of both published algorithms against clinical diagnosis, with the false-positive rates given as the headline numbers (45.0% original, 52.5% revised) rather than left to be derived. AUC for both algorithms and for the six-item model, with the interpretive bands stated in advance (excellent 0.90-1, good 0.80-0.90, fair 0.70-0.80, poor 0.60-0.70, bad 0.50-0.60) and DeLong's test for the paired comparison. Odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals for every domain and every retained item. Apparent classification accuracy of 86.6%. And both holdout figures - 85.4% training, 65.3% test. Reporting the drop is the single most valuable reporting decision in this record. Two gaps: the abstract and results present the apparent AUC of 0.938 as the model's discriminative ability without the held-out figure attached, so a reader who does not reach the limitations section will take away the wrong number; and no positive predictive value is computed for any realistic case mix, which for a differential-diagnosis aid would depend on the relative frequency of the two conditions among referred patients. [RQ4.4] Fully interpretable by construction and, unusually, the interpretation is the point rather than a supplement to it. The six predictors are named ADOS-2 items with published behavioural definitions, each reported with an odds ratio, confidence interval and direction, so the model reads as a clinical statement: atypicality in eye contact (OR 34.29), quality of social overtures (OR 10.84) and emphatic or emotional gestures (OR 6.49) points toward autism, while atypicality in reporting of events (OR 0.05), responsibility (OR 0.06) and comments on others' emotions or empathy (OR 0.14) points toward schizophrenia. The complete 32-item table with non-zero proportions and tests lets a reader see the whole profile rather than only the selected six, and the profiles are coherent enough to be taught. The study also performs the construct-validity analysis that this review has repeatedly noted as absent elsewhere: rather than accepting that the ADOS-2 measures autism, it asks what the instrument is measuring in the schizophrenia group and answers with evidence - correlations across all domains with the PANSS negative scale, higher negative-symptom scores in cut-off-positive patients, and cut-off positivity predicted by the negative scale alone. Establishing what a positive score means in a population where it is wrong is a stronger form of interpretability than any saliency map in this corpus. [RQ4.5] The clearest case in the review of a study whose validation honestly undercuts its own headline, and it deserves to be read as a model of reporting rather than as a failure. The six items were selected from 32 candidates using all 90 participants, and the apparent accuracy of 86.6% and AUC of 0.938 come from that same sample - so those figures are development-set performance, not estimates of generalisation. The authors then did what most of this corpus does not: they split the data into training and test samples and reported both results, 85.4% and 65.3%. A twenty-point drop on a single random split of 90 participants is what selection of six binary predictors from 32 candidates should produce, and the authors say so explicitly, naming the number of variables relative to the sample as the cause and concluding that external validation is required. The honest summary of the study's positive finding is therefore that a six-item ADOS-2 combination looks promising and has not yet been shown to generalise. Several further points bear on the validation. The split unit is the participant, so no leakage of the kind that dominates the image and frame-level branches of this review is possible. The comparison baseline is substantive rather than nominal - the instrument's own published algorithms on the same participants - which is more informative than a chance line and makes the negative finding robust to the selection problem entirely, since the algorithms were not fitted here at all. The holdout is a single random split whose proportions and repetition are unstated, and whether item selection was repeated within the training fold is not said; if it was not, the 65.3% is itself optimistic. Administrator blinding to diagnosis is not addressed, and every input is a clinician judgement made after diagnosis was established, so differential expectation is a plausible contributor to the item-level differences. Item-level inter-rater reliability was not computed within the study, although the instrument's published reliability concerns algorithm totals rather than individual items. And the exclusion of comorbid cases from both groups and of severe positive symptoms from the schizophrenia group means that the model was developed on the clean cases and would be deployed on the ambiguous ones. None of this touches the negative result, which is the study's durable contribution: the ADOS-2 algorithms, applied as published by certified administrators to verbally fluent adults with IQ above 85, misclassify 45% to 52% of schizophrenia patients as autistic and achieve AUCs of 0.562 and 0.569 against an independent clinical diagnosis. [RQ5.1] Keywords: schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorder, autism diagnostic observation schedule second edition (printed with a typographical error as 'siagnostic'), differential diagnosis, predictive model. The set is clinically oriented and precise - naming both conditions, the instrument, the diagnostic question and the analytic approach - and would be found by a clinician searching for differential diagnosis rather than by an engineer searching for a method. Terms carried through the body: Module 4, original and revised algorithms, social affect, restricted and repetitive behaviour, PANSS negative scale, cut-off positivity, holdout validation, DeLong's test, non-zero scores. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Psychiatry 15:1493158, Original Research, open access under CC BY; received 13 September 2024, accepted 19 November 2024, published 18 December 2024. Editorial and review handling is disclosed by name as the venue requires. This is a clinical psychiatry journal and the paper reads accordingly: the diagnostic process is described in detail with the explicit exclusion of ADOS-2 and ADI-R from it, the full clinical battery is reported for each group, sample size is justified against a comparable prior study, significance thresholds are stated including a stricter alpha for correlations, AUC interpretive bands are prespecified, effect sizes carry confidence intervals throughout, and the limitations section names overfitting as the explanation for the study's own validation drop. What a computational venue would have added is missing - no code, no data deposit, no statement of the holdout procedure's details - and what a computational venue would have missed is present in full. [RQ5.3] Published December 2024 by psychiatry departments at Showa University and Teikyo University in Tokyo, with no funding of any kind declared and no competing interests, acknowledging a named colleague for teaching the team ADOS-2 administration. The framing is entirely clinical: the two conditions overlap in symptoms, co-occur, cluster in families and share genetic risk, while the features clinicians use to separate them become unavailable in exactly the cases where separation is hardest - when verbal expression is poor, when symptoms are concealed, or when an autistic adult's characteristics did not surface until adolescence. For this review the study is important out of proportion to its size, for four reasons. It is the only included study whose comparison group is another clinical population rather than typical development, and it therefore supplies the evidence that the free-play study charted alongside it identifies as missing when it observes that distinguishing autistic from other non-typically-developing children is the harder and more clinically relevant problem. Its central result is negative and well established: the ADOS-2 - the instrument this literature routinely calls the gold standard and against which computational models are benchmarked - achieved AUCs of 0.562 and 0.569 for autism against schizophrenia in verbally fluent adults, misclassifying 45% to 52% of schizophrenia patients as autistic, with no domain score carrying significant predictive value. That figure should sit beside every high accuracy in this review, because those accuracies were obtained against typically developing comparison groups and none of them has been tested against the discrimination that actually matters in a clinic. Its explanatory finding names the mechanism: what the ADOS-2 detects in schizophrenia is negative-symptom severity, evidenced by correlations across all domains with the PANSS negative scale, by markedly higher negative-symptom scores in cut-off-positive patients, and by a regression in which cut-off positivity is predicted by the negative scale alone - so a measure of social-communication atypicality behaves, in this population, as a measure of negative symptoms. And its own positive contribution is reported with a candour that is rare here: a six-item model reached an apparent AUC of 0.938 and 86.6% accuracy, then fell to 65.3% on a held-out split, and the authors attribute the gap to having six variables in a sample of ninety and conclude that external validation is required. A study that publishes the number that undermines its own headline is a useful counterweight to a corpus in which perfect scores are reported without any held-out check at all.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective algorithm-development study by speech and behaviour-analysis groups at Imperial College London, the University of Augsburg and University Grenoble Alpes, using two existing child speech corpora. The De-Enigma corpus - 55 autistic children aged 4 to 10 from Serbia and the United Kingdom, no control group, 5,368 vocalisation samples over 115 minutes - serves as the pre-training source. The Child Pathological Speech Database - monolingual French-speaking children aged 6 to 18 recruited in Paris, with autism, dysphasia and PDD-NOS groups alongside typically developing controls, 1,722 samples over 62 minutes - serves for fine-tuning and evaluation. CPSD recordings were 'captured in their typical environment, i.e clinic for the LIC subjects and elementary, secondary, and high school for the TD subjects'. Participant counts are internally inconsistent: the control group is described as 64 children (52 male, 12 female) while the corpus as a whole is described as 67 participants (54 male, 13 female), and the number of children in each atypical class is never stated. No age distribution, cognitive measure, language measure or diagnostic procedure is reported for either corpus, and the CPSD diagnostic categories predate DSM-5. Ethics approval is attributed to the dataset administrations rather than a research ethics committee, consent was stated as not required, and the study received no funding.
narrative_rows.methods: Two transfer-learning approaches were compared. Discriminative Fine-Tuning pre-trains on De-Enigma child vocalisations, including both speech and non-speech, then fine-tunes on CPSD. Wav2Vec 2.0 Fine-Tuning uses self-supervised representations pre-trained on 960 hours of unlabelled speech, with quantisation removed so that context representations derive solely from the input waveform, feeding a BLSTM classifier. Two tasks were run on identical folds: binary typicality (typically versus atypically developing) and four-class diagnosis (typically developing, autism, dysphasia, PDD-NOS). Partitioning was 70% training, 15% development, 15% test, with separate female and male test sets carved out for fairness analysis, and splitting was performed by speaker rather than by sample so that all recordings from a child fall in one fold only - stated as a safeguard against the model learning speaker or recording idiosyncrasies and 'deceptively excelling'. Class imbalance was addressed by upsampling the minority class in training while leaving development and test distributions unchanged. Unweighted average recall was the primary metric, supplemented by accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and confusion matrices for each partition. Fairness was assessed by equalised odds, comparing sensitivity and specificity across gender groups. Results were benchmarked against a stated baseline and against published results on the same corpus.
narrative_rows.outcomes: On binary typicality, D-FT reached 94.8% test unweighted average recall and W2V2-FT 91.5%, against a stated baseline of 94.1% and published results of 90.7% and 93.6% on the same corpus. On four-class diagnosis, D-FT reached 60.9% and W2V2-FT 54.3%, against a baseline of 62.4% and published results of 67.1% and 69.4% - so both proposed models fall below the baseline and below prior work on the harder task. The domain-matched pre-training corpus outperformed the far larger unrelated one on both tasks. The fairness results are the study's most consequential finding: for typicality, D-FT sensitivity was 94.8% on the mixed-gender test set but 43.6% on the female set and 61.5% on the male, with accuracy falling from 94.7% to 60.8% and 74.6%; W2V2-FT sensitivity fell from 92.3% to 24.4% and 53.8%. On the diagnosis task, D-FT recall fell from 60.9% to 33.7% for females and 41.3% for males. The gender partitions carry a different class balance from the mixed test set, which accounts for part of the gap, but the magnitude of the collapse indicates that pooled performance substantially overstates what the models have learned. The authors also report a development UAR of 78.0% against the test UAR of 94.8% and flag the discrepancy without explaining its direction.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The recording-setting confound within the evaluation corpus is the decisive unexamined problem: the paper's own dataset description states that atypical children were recorded in clinics and typically developing children in schools, so room acoustics, background noise, microphone and protocol covary perfectly with the binary label, and no acoustic normalisation or channel compensation is reported. Speaker-disjoint splitting, which the authors implement correctly and justify well, offers no protection against a confound that operates at the class level rather than the speaker level. The participant counts cannot both be right - 64 typically developing children within a corpus of 67 participants would leave three for all three atypical classes - and the number of children per diagnostic class is never given, so how many distinct speakers stand behind the 26 test samples per clinical class is unknown, and the value of speaker disjointness cannot be assessed. No age distribution is reported for any group in a corpus spanning 6 to 18 years, across which voice changes fundamentally. No diagnostic procedure is described for either corpus and the categories predate DSM-5. No language measure exists although one of the four classes is a specific language impairment. Nothing is stated about what the children were doing when recorded, which for a prosodic claim removes the ability to separate speaker characteristics from task demands. No uncertainty estimate accompanies any figure, on margins as small as 0.7 points and test sets as small as 26 samples per class. And the development-to-test inversion is noted but unexplained, though a test score sixteen points above development usually indicates that the partitions differ in composition.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Valuable to the review for reasons largely independent of its headline number. It is one of only two included studies whose comparison groups include another clinical population, and the only one to attempt a four-way separation of autism from dysphasia and PDD-NOS - the discrimination that clinical practice requires and that the rest of this corpus does not attempt. Its result on that task is the honest one: 60.9% against a 25% chance level, below the published baseline of 62.4% and below two prior methods on the same data, reported in a comparison table the authors supply themselves. It names the leakage problem precisely and splits by speaker to address it, in language sharper than almost any other paper here. And its equalised-odds fairness testing is the most searching subgroup analysis in the review, with a result that should propagate into the synthesis as a general warning: the same model that reaches 94.8% sensitivity on a pooled test set reaches 43.6% on girls and 61.5% on boys when evaluated on held-out gender partitions, and the second model falls to 24.4% on girls. Almost no other study in this corpus evaluates any subgroup at all, so the extent to which their pooled accuracies conceal comparable deficits is simply unknown - and this paper is the only evidence available on that question. Two cautions travel with it, and they mirror the pattern recorded for the multiscale-attention facial study charted nearby. The binary result rests on a corpus in which the clinical groups were recorded in clinics and the comparison group in schools, so the acoustic environment is a perfect proxy for the label, and none of the study's careful validation machinery addresses a confound at that layer. And the participant accounting is internally contradictory in a way that leaves the study's own leakage safeguard unquantifiable. Read together, the two studies make the review's clearest point about methodological quality: rigour applied downstream of a confounded label produces a well-validated number that cannot be interpreted, and can rank above less careful work whose data are sounder.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two corpora combined, and the participant accounting is the weakest part of the description. De-Enigma contributes 55 autistic children aged 4 to 10, described as 25 from Serbia and 25 from the United Kingdom - a split that does not sum to 55 - with no control group at all, yielding 5,368 vocalisation samples over 115 minutes. The Child Pathological Speech Database contributes monolingual French-speaking children aged 6 to 18, recruited in Paris, carrying diagnoses of autism, dysphasia or PDD-NOS alongside a typically developing group, yielding 1,722 samples over 62 minutes. The CPSD participant counts cannot be reconciled: the control group is said to consist of 64 typically developing children (52 male, 12 female), while the corpus as a whole is said to have 13 female participants contributing 334 samples and 54 males contributing 1,388 - a total of 67, which would leave three children for the autism, dysphasia and PDD-NOS groups combined. The number of children in each atypical class is never stated anywhere in the paper. This is not a bookkeeping quibble. Speaker-disjoint splitting is the study's stated safeguard against leakage, and its protective value depends entirely on how many speakers each class contains: if the 26 autism, 26 dysphasia and 26 PDD-NOS samples in the diagnosis test partition come from one or two children each, then class membership and speaker identity are nearly the same variable, and disjointness across the split cannot separate them. The sex proportions are also stated inconsistently, as 78% and 81% male in the dataset section and as 95% and 90% male in the limitations. Age distributions per group are not reported for either corpus. [RQ1.2] Mixed, with the strongest and weakest language in this corpus sitting a few pages apart. The clinical framing in the introduction is dated and inaccurate: autism is 'a neurological disease correlated by imbalances in the brain', it is 'incurable' though it 'can be managed', and the population is characterised through what it lacks - 'a lack in verbal skills or continuing to be non-verbal'. 'Individuals with ASD' and 'children with ASD' are the standard usages, with 'atypically developing' as the analytic label. Against this, three passages show real care. The fairness section states that bias testing 'is crucial in our experiment, specially that we are adhering to a vulnerable group', and grounds the analysis in the observed male-to-female diagnostic ratio and in the 'female camouflage effect', which suggests females are better at masking autism - one of very few places in this review where under-identification of autistic women is treated as a methodological problem rather than a footnote. The limitations argue that 'non-verbal vocalisations are a form of speech and hold communicative value', which treats the sounds autistic children make as communication rather than as noise to be filtered - a substantive interpretive commitment. And the paper's reflection on research ethics committees as safeguards for child data, and on the difficulty of obtaining such data, shows awareness of the population's vulnerability even though the study's own ethics declaration is thin. No autistic person or community organisation is reported as involved. [RQ1.3] The weakest demographic reporting of any included study, and the gaps are consequential rather than cosmetic. No age distribution is given for any group in either corpus, though the combined range spans 4 to 18 years - the period across which voice undergoes its most profound changes, including the pubertal fall in male fundamental frequency, vocal-tract growth and the maturation of prosody and syntax. If the atypical and typical groups differ in age composition, an age classifier and a diagnosis classifier would be behaviourally identical, and nothing reported allows this to be tested. No IQ, language, adaptive or socioeconomic measure exists, which is particularly striking given that one of the four diagnostic classes is dysphasia - the task asks a model to separate autism from a specific language impairment with no independent measure of language ability in any group. Ancestry is not reported. Sex is reported but inconsistently, at 22% female in De-Enigma and 19% in CPSD in one section and at 5% and 10% in another. The one demographic variable that receives serious analytic attention is sex, through equalised-odds fairness testing - and that analysis returns the study's most important result, showing that performance measured on a mixed-gender partition conceals a substantial deficit for girls. That single finding does more for this review's understanding of demographic confounding than the descriptive tables of most other included studies. [RQ1.4] Absent as an independent element and inherited without description. De-Enigma children are stated to be 'diagnosed with ASD' and CPSD children to carry diagnoses of autism, dysphasia or PDD-NOS, but neither corpus's diagnostic process is described - no instrument, no criteria, no clinician qualification, no date. The typically developing group is characterised only by absence: 'no prior history of difficulties with learning, speech, hearing or general learning', which is a screening statement rather than an assessment. Two features compound this. The CPSD categories are pre-DSM-5, since PDD-NOS was eliminated as a diagnosis in 2013, so the labels encode a superseded nosology whose boundaries with autism were themselves contested - and the four-class task therefore asks a model to reproduce a distinction that the diagnostic system has since abandoned. And the atypical and typical children were recorded in different physical settings, clinic and school respectively, so the label is confounded with the circumstance of recording independently of whatever the diagnoses mean. The paper does not treat the reference standard as a topic at all. [RQ1.5] None. No severity, cognitive, language or adaptive measure is available in either corpus as used here. De-Enigma carries additional annotations for emotion, autistic behaviour and non-verbal vocalisation type, which the authors explicitly set aside as outside their focus - and among these, the autistic-behaviour annotation would have permitted exactly the severity-gradient analysis this review has repeatedly found missing. The four-class diagnosis task partially substitutes for a severity measure by requiring differentiation among clinical categories rather than only from typical development, which is more informative than any single-group severity correlation would have been. [RQ2.1] The aim is to test whether deep transfer learning can compensate for the scarcity of labelled child speech data in autism recognition, by comparing two fine-tuning strategies - discriminative fine-tuning pre-trained on a related child corpus, and Wav2Vec 2.0 fine-tuning pre-trained on 960 hours of unrelated adult speech - across a binary typicality task and a four-class diagnosis task, with fairness testing by gender. The findings are best read against the study's own comparison tables, which the authors supply. On binary typicality, D-FT reached 94.8% unweighted average recall and W2V2-FT 91.5%, against a stated baseline of 94.1% and prior published results of 90.7% and 93.6% on the same corpus - an improvement of 0.7 points over baseline. On four-class diagnosis, D-FT reached 60.9% and W2V2-FT 54.3%, against a baseline of 62.4% and prior results of 67.1% and 69.4% - so both proposed models fall below the baseline and below prior work on the task that actually requires separating autism from other conditions. And the fairness analysis shows that the binary headline does not survive subgroup evaluation: D-FT sensitivity falls from 94.8% on the mixed-gender test set to 43.6% on the female set and 61.5% on the male, with W2V2-FT falling from 92.3% to 24.4% and 53.8%. Publishing a benchmark table showing one's own model below baseline on the harder task, and a fairness table showing a fifty-point sensitivity collapse, is a level of candour this review has encountered in very few papers. [RQ2.2] No primary collection, and the setting structure of the evaluation corpus is the study's central unexamined problem. The CPSD description states that 'recordings of all subjects were captured in their typical environment, i.e clinic for the LIC subjects and elementary, secondary, and high school for the TD subjects'. The atypical classes were therefore recorded in clinical rooms and the typical class in schools, so reverberation, background noise, microphone type and placement, examiner presence and recording protocol all covary perfectly with the binary label - and the entire binary result is trained and tested on this corpus. No acoustic normalisation, channel compensation or noise handling is reported that would mitigate it. The paper does discuss setting as a limitation, but the setting difference it examines is the one between its two corpora (De-Enigma at home, CPSD in laboratory conditions), which affects pre-training rather than the labelled contrast; the within-CPSD clinic-versus-school structure, which is the confound that directly threatens the headline, is never mentioned. This is a clean instance of a pattern the review has documented across modalities - a class label that is inseparable from the circumstances under which the two classes were recorded - arising here in audio rather than in images. [RQ2.3] Not described, for either corpus, and the omission is more damaging here than in most studies because the paper's substantive claim is prosodic. The motivating account is that autistic speech is monotonous, 'lacking the typical variations in pitch, intonation, and expressive elements' - but prosody is determined as much by what a speaker is doing as by who they are. Spontaneous conversation, responding to an adult's questions, reading aloud, repeating modelled utterances and playing all produce systematically different intonation contours. Nothing is stated about what the children in either corpus were doing when recorded, whether an adult or a robot was present, what was said to them, or whether the elicitation differed between the clinic-recorded atypical children and the school-recorded typical ones. De-Enigma was collected within a robot-assisted autism education project, so its vocalisations arise from a specific and unusual interactive context that is not characterised at all. Without a task description, a prosodic difference between groups cannot be attributed to speaker characteristics rather than to what each group was asked to do. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element and no repeat measurement. The ethics reporting is the thinnest of any included study that reports any at all: approval is attributed to 'The Child Pathological Speech Database and De-Engima Project administrations' - the dataset custodians rather than a named research ethics committee - and written informed consent was 'not required from the participants or the participants' legal guardians/next of kin in accordance with the national legislation and institutional requirements'. The contrast with the paper's own introduction is worth noting, since that section reflects specifically on research ethics committees and institutional review boards as safeguards for child data and presents transfer learning as a response to the difficulty of obtaining such data - the topic is raised seriously in the argument and handled formulaically in the declaration. The study received no funding and declares no competing interests, and author contributions are itemised. [RQ2.5] None reported, which is itself a finding. For a speech study, no microphone, sampling rate, channel configuration, recording environment specification or preprocessing chain is given for either corpus. Sample durations are not stated; the reported totals imply mean sample lengths of roughly 1.3 seconds in De-Enigma and 2.2 seconds in CPSD, which are short for prosodic analysis. Computation used two pre-trained model families - a discriminative fine-tuning architecture and Wav2Vec 2.0 with quantisation removed feeding a BLSTM classifier - but no hardware, framework or hyperparameter detail is provided. The absence of acoustic condition reporting is directly connected to the study's principal vulnerability: with the two classes recorded in different physical settings, the properties of the recording chain are exactly what a reader would need to judge whether the signal is speech or room. [RQ2.6] Reported: both corpora with their sources and project pages, sample and duration totals, complete partition tables giving class counts for training, development, test, female and male sets under both tasks, the 70/15/15 split proportions, the speaker-disjoint splitting rule with its stated rationale, the two architectures and their pre-training corpora, the decision to upsample the minority class in training while leaving development and test distributions intact, unweighted average recall as the primary metric, the equalised-odds procedure with its sensitivity and specificity formulae, confusion matrices for every model and partition, and comparison tables against a baseline and against published results on the same dataset. Not reported: code, hyperparameters, sample durations, recording equipment and conditions, the number of children per diagnostic class, age distributions by group, any diagnostic procedure for either corpus, and the number of runs behind each figure. Neither corpus is openly available. The partition tables are the strongest element - they let a reader compute the class balance of every evaluation set, which is what makes the fairness results interpretable and what reveals that the gender test sets differ in composition from the mixed-gender set. [RQ2.7] The limitations section is long, specific and unusually self-critical, covering six issues. The study's original aim - autism recognition in children aged 1 to 3 - was abandoned because data on that population could not be obtained, and the authors say so plainly. The two corpora were collected in different settings, creating domain-shift risk and possible bias toward the more heavily represented one. Class imbalance limited the models, and the authors note that the resampling remedies themselves affect classification performance. Gender imbalance is severe and the fairness testing demonstrates its consequence. The test sets are small and 'not fully representative of the real-world'. And the headline is explicitly qualified: a development UAR of 78.0% against a test UAR of 94.8% is flagged as reflecting corpus-specific characteristics and the additional partitioning, with the conclusion that 'due to the limitations in the dataset, the results reported herein must be carefully interpreted' - reinforced by a citation to a discussion of 'potential over-expectation in speech analysis tasks for real-world application'. What is not addressed is the recording-setting confound within CPSD, where atypical children were recorded in clinics and typical children in schools, which the paper's own dataset description states and which makes acoustic environment a perfect proxy for the binary label. Nor is the participant-count inconsistency resolved, or the number of children per diagnostic class stated - facts that determine how much protection speaker-disjoint splitting actually provides. No age data are available in a corpus spanning 6 to 18 years. No diagnostic procedure is described for either corpus, and the CPSD categories are pre-DSM-5. No language measure exists although one class is a language disorder. Nothing is said about what the children were doing when recorded. And the specific direction of the development-to-test discrepancy - test scoring sixteen points above development - is noted but not explained, though a test score well above a development score usually indicates that the partitions differ in composition rather than that the model improved. [RQ2.9] Four directions are named: stratified sampling to distribute class imbalance evenly across folds; generative adversarial networks for minority-class synthesis, argued to be more representative of real data than SMOTE or ADASYN; extension to children younger than four and to pre-linguistic vocalisations, which the authors argue is supported by their use of non-speech vocalisations from De-Enigma; and continued fairness work given the gender disparities. Not proposed, and needed before the binary result can be interpreted: acoustic normalisation or channel compensation to address the clinic-versus-school recording split, reporting of the number of children per diagnostic class, age distributions by group, and evaluation on a corpus in which both classes were recorded under matched conditions. [RQ3.1] Vocalisation and speech, with the target construct stated as prosodic. The motivating account is specific: autistic speech is monotonous and 'lacks the typical variations in pitch, intonation, and expressive elements that are commonly observed in the speech of typically developing children', a pattern reported to persist into school age. Both speech and non-speech vocalisations are used from De-Enigma, and the authors defend that choice on communicative grounds - 'non-verbal vocalisations are a form of speech and hold communicative value' - and argue it extends the approach toward pre-linguistic assessment in younger children. What the study cannot establish is whether its models respond to that construct. The representation is a learned embedding of the raw waveform, no acoustic analysis or attribution is performed, and prosody is not measured directly at any point, so the models' 94.8% could rest on fundamental-frequency variability, on vocal-tract length, on speaking rate, on the language spoken, on the age of the speaker, or on the reverberation of the room. The four-class task is more informative about the construct than the binary one, because separating autism from dysphasia requires something more specific than general atypicality of speech - and it is precisely there that performance falls to 60.9%, below the baseline of 62.4%. [RQ3.2] None. A single audio modality throughout, with no fusion across sensors, channels or annotation types. The transfer in this study is across datasets and tasks rather than across modalities - discriminative fine-tuning transfers from one child-vocalisation corpus to another, and Wav2Vec 2.0 transfers from 960 hours of unlabelled adult speech to child clinical speech. The comparison between these two transfer sources is the study's clearest methodological result and is worth recording for the review: pre-training on a small, closely related corpus of child autistic vocalisations (D-FT) outperformed pre-training on a vastly larger but unrelated adult speech corpus (W2V2-FT) on both tasks, by 3.3 points on typicality and 6.6 points on diagnosis. Domain proximity beat scale. The caveat is that D-FT's advantage may partly reflect its exposure to De-Enigma's autistic vocalisations, which are class-informative in a way the unlabelled adult corpus is not. [RQ4.1] Two transfer-learning approaches compared head to head. Discriminative fine-tuning pre-trains on De-Enigma child vocalisations and fine-tunes on CPSD - the first application of this technique to autism recognition from speech, according to the authors. Wav2Vec 2.0 fine-tuning uses self-supervised representations pre-trained on 960 hours of unlabelled speech, with the quantisation step removed so that context representations derive solely from the input signal, feeding a BLSTM classifier. Both are appropriate to the data-scarcity problem the study sets out to address, and the comparison is fairly constructed - identical folds for both models and both tasks, a separate development partition, and evaluation on the same test sets. The finding that the smaller, domain-matched pre-training corpus outperforms the much larger unrelated one is the substantive modelling result. Minority-class upsampling was applied in training only, with development and test distributions left intact - a deliberate choice, correctly explained, and one that this review has found in strikingly few papers, since rebalancing the evaluation set is a common and usually silent source of inflation. [RQ4.2] Raw waveform segments per vocalisation, encoded by learned representations - either the discriminatively fine-tuned model's features or Wav2Vec 2.0 context representations. No hand-crafted acoustic descriptors are used in the study's own models, though the ComParE feature set is discussed as background. Sample durations are not stated but can be inferred at roughly 1.3 seconds for De-Enigma and 2.2 seconds for CPSD from the reported totals. Short segments are a real constraint on a prosodic claim: intonation contour, pitch range and expressive variation are properties of utterances and turns rather than of one- to two-second fragments, so the representation may not span the timescale on which the hypothesised difference lives. [RQ4.3] Well chosen and honestly deployed. Unweighted average recall is the primary metric, which is the correct choice for imbalanced classes and sets chance at 50% and 25% for the two tasks. Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 are reported for every model and every partition - mixed-gender, female and male - for both tasks, alongside confusion matrices and sensitivity and specificity by gender for the equalised-odds analysis. Most valuably, two comparison tables place the results in context: one against a baseline and two published studies on the same corpus, the other against published Wav2Vec 2.0 implementations. Those tables show that the study's typicality result exceeds the baseline by 0.7 points, and that its diagnosis result of 60.9% falls below the baseline of 62.4% and below prior results of 67.1% and 69.4%. Reporting a table in which one's own method loses on the harder task is rare in this corpus and should be recorded as such. What is missing is any uncertainty estimate - no confidence intervals, no variance across runs, no significance testing - which matters when the typicality margin over baseline is 0.7 points and when the diagnosis test partition contains 26 samples per clinical class. [RQ4.4] None attempted. No saliency, attribution, acoustic analysis or characterisation of the learned representations is presented, and none is claimed - the models are evaluated purely as classifiers. The only window onto behaviour is the confusion matrices, which the authors do interpret, observing that both models predict typically developing more successfully than atypically developing and attributing this to the class distribution. For a study whose motivating hypothesis is specific and acoustically measurable - reduced variation in pitch, intonation and expressive elements - the absence of any analysis connecting model decisions to prosody is the clearest missed opportunity in the paper, because it is the analysis that would distinguish a model responding to speech from one responding to the acoustics of a clinic room. The fairness analysis partially compensates by revealing something about the models that no saliency map would have: that their apparent competence does not extend to girls. [RQ4.5] Genuinely mixed, with the best-stated splitting principle in this corpus sitting alongside an unexamined confound that undercuts the headline. On the credit side, the splitting is speaker-disjoint and the reasoning is articulated precisely: samples from each child belong to one fold only, 'to prevent the model from over-fitting by learning speaker or recording idiosyncrasies, and therefore deceptively excelling'. That is the leakage problem named accurately, and it is the failure mode this review has documented across the scanpath-image, video-frame and EEG branches where it went unaddressed. A separate development partition is maintained, the same folds serve both tasks for comparability, unweighted average recall is used throughout, minority-class upsampling is confined to training with development and test distributions deliberately left intact, and the results are benchmarked against a baseline and against published work on the same corpus. On the debit side, three problems bound what the 94.8% means. First, speaker disjointness cannot address a confound operating at the class level, and the corpus description states that atypical children were recorded in clinics while typically developing children were recorded in schools - so a model that has learned clinic acoustics transfers perfectly across any speaker boundary, and no acoustic normalisation is reported. Second, the number of children in each atypical class is never stated and the two participant counts given are mutually incompatible; if the diagnostic classes rest on very few speakers, the 26 test samples per class may effectively be one or two voices, and speaker-disjoint splitting offers little protection when class and speaker are nearly the same variable. Third, the development UAR of 78.0% against a test UAR of 94.8% is an inversion that the authors flag but do not explain, and a test score sixteen points above development usually indicates that the partitions differ in composition rather than that the model generalises unusually well - a reading supported by the fairness analysis, in which the same model's sensitivity falls to 43.6% and 61.5% on the female and male partitions. The fairness testing is the most valuable validation act in the paper and deserves emphasis: by evaluating on gender-specific held-out sets rather than only on a pooled test set, it exposes a fifty-point sensitivity gap that pooled reporting concealed entirely. That is a generalisation check almost no other study in this review performs, and its result is a warning about every pooled accuracy in this corpus. Finally, the four-class result is the study's most trustworthy number precisely because it is its worst: 60.9% against a 25% chance level, below the published baseline, on the task that requires distinguishing autism from dysphasia and PDD-NOS rather than from typical development. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, child speech, artificial intelligence, deep learning, transformer, transfer learning, fairness in AI. The inclusion of 'fairness in AI' is the notable element and is earned rather than decorative - the fairness analysis occupies a full section, is grounded in the diagnostic sex ratio and in the female camouflage effect, uses a defined criterion (equalised odds) with stated formulae, and produces the paper's most consequential result. This is the only keyword set in the review to name fairness, and one of very few papers anywhere in the corpus to evaluate subgroup performance at all. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Digital Health 7:1274675, Original Research, open access under CC BY; received 8 August 2023, accepted 28 May 2025, published 18 August 2025, with editor and reviewers disclosed by name. The near two-year interval between submission and acceptance is unusual. The venue is a digital-health rather than a clinical journal, and the paper reads accordingly: the partitioning, metrics, benchmarking and fairness analysis are handled to a good computational standard while the clinical description of the corpora - diagnostic procedures, ages, per-class participant counts, recording conditions - is left almost entirely to the source datasets and is internally inconsistent where it is given. The supplied bibliographic metadata dates the article to 2024 while the article itself is a 2025 publication. [RQ5.3] Published 2025 by speech and behaviour-analysis groups at Imperial College London, the University of Augsburg and University Grenoble Alpes - the GLAM and iBUG laboratories, whose senior authors are central figures in computational paralinguistics and automatic behaviour understanding - with no funding and no declared conflicts. The framing is data-scarcity-driven: obtaining child speech data is hard because ethics committees rightly restrict it, so transfer learning is offered as a way to build usable models from small corpora. For this review the study earns its place on four counts, none of which is its headline. It is one of only two included studies whose comparison groups include another clinical population, and the only one to attempt a four-way separation of autism from dysphasia and PDD-NOS - the discrimination that clinical practice actually requires. It names the leakage problem precisely and splits by speaker to address it, in language sharper than most papers in this corpus manage. It performs equalised-odds fairness testing on held-out gender partitions and publishes a result that undermines its own headline: D-FT sensitivity falls from 94.8% pooled to 43.6% for girls and 61.5% for boys, and W2V2-FT from 92.3% to 24.4% and 53.8% - which should be read as a general warning that pooled accuracies in this literature may conceal large subgroup deficits that nobody has looked for. And it benchmarks itself against a stated baseline and prior work on the same corpus, showing its four-class result at 60.9% against a baseline of 62.4% and prior results of 67.1% and 69.4%, so its own model loses on the harder task. Two cautions travel with it. The binary result rests on a corpus in which the atypical children were recorded in clinics and the typical children in schools - a recording-setting confound perfectly aligned with the class label, stated in the paper's own dataset description and never revisited - so 94.8% may be substantially a measure of room acoustics, and no normalisation is reported that would rule this out. And the participant accounting is internally contradictory, with the number of children in each diagnostic class never stated, which leaves the protective value of the speaker-disjoint splitting unquantifiable. The general lesson matches the one drawn from the multiscale-attention facial study charted nearby: careful validation methodology applied above a confounded data layer produces a well-validated uninterpretable number, and the review should treat the two together.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective digital-phenotyping study by the Department of Information and Computer Sciences at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, using a purpose-built Twitter corpus. English-language tweets carrying #ActuallyAutistic and posted between 1 January 2014 and 31 December 2022 were collected with snscrape; users whose profile descriptions contained 'autism', 'autistic' or 'neurodiverse' were identified, and their full timelines harvested, yielding 3,137,952 tweets from 17,323 users. A control corpus of 3,377,518 tweets from 171,273 users was assembled by excluding the hashtag and sampling 1,000 tweets per day over the same period. No demographic, clinical or diagnostic information exists for any user; the location field was discarded as largely missing or uninformative. The study holds University of Hawaii IRB approval 2023-00248 under expedited review and passed a separate institutional data governance determination of exemption on public-data grounds; user IDs were encrypted and mentions and email addresses anonymised as measures beyond regulatory requirement. Explicit consent was not obtained, which the authors identify as the study's primary limitation, and both the dataset and the trained models were deleted after analysis and never shared outside the author team.
narrative_rows.methods: Text was preprocessed by masking profanity, tokenising, removing non-alphanumeric characters, hyperlinks, user mentions and HTML tags, lowercasing, removing stop words, and applying stemming and lemmatisation, with padding and an unknown token for fixed-length input. Sixteen autism-related hashtags and keywords - including 'actuallyautistic', 'autism', 'autistic', 'neurodiversity', 'neurodivergent', 'adhd', 'diagnosis', 'autismpride' and 'autismspeaks' - were removed on the stated ground that they 'could introduce bias and lead to model overfitting'; since the label is defined by hashtag use, this closes the most direct leakage route. Sentiment was analysed with VADER on both the raw and profanity-censored corpora, and topics were examined for qualitative insight. For tweet-level classification, TF-IDF features were passed through support vector machines, naive Bayes, logistic regression and XGBoost with 5-fold cross-validation on accuracy to select the best algorithm, after which word2vec representations were trained with that algorithm; splitting was at user level, 85:15 for train and test with a further 85:15 division of training into training and validation, explicitly to prevent a user's tweets scattering across the split. For user-profile classification, users with at least five tweets had their preprocessed tweets concatenated into a single document, split 80:20 at user level, and classified by an attention-based bidirectional LSTM over a self-trained embedding layer.
narrative_rows.outcomes: The tweet-level classifier reached 73% accuracy, AUC 0.728 and F1 0.71 using word2vec representations with logistic regression. The user-profile classifier reached AUC 0.78 and F1 0.805 using the attention-based bidirectional LSTM, so aggregating a full timeline improved discrimination over individual posts. Sentiment polarity was almost unchanged between the raw and profanity-censored corpora, indicating that any group difference in polarity is not driven by swearing. Autism-related discussion rose across the nine-year window, which the authors read as increasing engagement of autistic people with the platform. The performance figures are modest by this corpus's standards and are reported identically in the abstract, results and conclusion without amplification.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: There is no clinical validation of any diagnosis: the positive label is use of an advocacy hashtag plus profile keywords, which the authors describe in their own conclusion as 'an imperfect proxy for self-reported autism', and the control group is entirely unscreened. Beyond that, the two classes differ in ways no demographic variable would capture - the positive class is a self-selected community organised around a topic and the negative class is a background platform sample, so they differ in subject matter, audience, posting motivation and network position, and a classifier reaching 73% may be recognising the register of autism self-advocacy rather than any property of autistic language production; removing sixteen keywords attenuates but cannot eliminate this, and no feature analysis is reported that would help decide. The corpora were also assembled by different procedures, full timeline harvesting against daily sampling, so 17,323 users contribute nearly as many tweets as 171,273 and the classes differ in how material was selected as well as in who wrote it. No age, sex, ancestry or socioeconomic information exists for either group, and the #ActuallyAutistic community plausibly differs from a general platform sample on all of them. The authors' bound on control-group contamination assumes population prevalence transfers to Twitter's user base and that non-self-identifying autistic users write like non-autistic ones. No confidence intervals, calibration or predictive value at realistic prevalence are reported. And the English-only restriction over-represents younger and higher-socioeconomic users, which the authors state.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The most distinctive study in the review, and important for reasons that mostly do not concern its accuracy. It is the only included study whose behavioural data are naturally occurring and unelicited, at a scale no laboratory design can approach - 6.5 million posts from 188,596 people across nine years - which makes it the clearest available test of whether ecological validity and volume can substitute for measurement control. The answer is informative: 73% accuracy and AUC 0.728, modest against the 90-plus percent figures reported elsewhere in this corpus from far smaller samples collected under laboratory conditions, and a useful reminder that those higher figures are products of controlled contrasts rather than of stronger signal. It implements two deliberate leakage controls - user-level splitting with the reasoning articulated, and removal of the sixteen autism-related tokens that define its own label, which is the same target-leakage failure this review documents in the questionnaire studies, handled here rather than left in place. It states its label honestly in its own conclusion as hashtag use rather than autism. Its terminology is the most careful in the corpus, and uniquely it explains the community politics behind its inclusion criterion - that #AutismMom and #AutismParent hashtags 'represent the perspectives of neurotypical parents' and that autistic adults' own voices have been 'overshadowed' in research and policy, which is why #ActuallyAutistic exists and why the study samples from it. And it is the only paper anywhere in this review that argues against deploying what it built: having demonstrated feasibility, the authors restrict legitimate use to population-level inference, enumerate the misuse scenarios an individual-level classifier would enable - insurance profiling, university admissions, hiring decisions, government surveillance of citizens - delete both the dataset and the models, and caution researchers against building comparable systems without explicit consent and participatory community-centred design. Set beside the studies charted nearby that scrape identifiable photographs of children from autism support pages with no ethics statement at all, this paper demonstrates that the ethical questions this literature raises are tractable when researchers choose to engage them. The substantive caution is that the study's contrast has several sufficient explanations and it distinguishes none of them - a limitation the authors partly anticipate by declining to present the result as a finding about autistic language at all. The published record shows the article was issued in a corrected version and attracted a formal comment, making it the only included study whose approach generated a documented scholarly exchange.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] The largest sample in this review by an order of magnitude, and the least clinically characterised. The autism corpus comprises 3,137,952 tweets from 17,323 users, identified by their use of #ActuallyAutistic in English-language posts between 1 January 2014 and 31 December 2022 combined with 'autism', 'autistic' or 'neurodiverse' appearing in their profile description, after which all tweets from those users' timelines were collected. The control corpus comprises 3,377,518 tweets from 171,273 users, obtained by a search query excluding the hashtag and sampling 1,000 tweets per day over the same window. No demographic information of any kind exists for either group - no age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic status, cognitive level or comorbidity - and the location field was discarded as largely missing or uninformative, though the authors note that most of the top 20 stated locations were variants of the United Kingdom. Two structural features of the sample deserve emphasis. The tweet counts are near-balanced while the user counts differ tenfold, because the autism group's entire timelines were harvested while control posts were sampled from the platform's daily stream - so the two classes differ in how their material was selected as well as in who produced it, and this is not discussed. And the autism group is not a clinical population but a self-selected online community organised around a hashtag with an explicit advocacy stance, which the paper describes accurately and which bears on everything downstream. [RQ1.2] The most careful terminology in this review, and the only paper here that treats the politics of autism language as part of its subject matter rather than as background. Identity-first language is used throughout - 'millions of individuals are autistic', 'autistic community', 'autistic peers' - alongside 'individuals with autism' in places, and 'neurotypical' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy' for the comparison group. More substantively, the paper explains the origin of its own inclusion criterion in community terms: hashtags such as #AutismMom and #AutismParent 'have represented the perspectives of neurotypical parents, significantly influencing research and policies in this domain', but 'these advocacy groups often overshadow adults with autism, creating a gap in their representation within decision-making processes', and #ActuallyAutistic emerged as 'a paradigm shift ... in the autism rights movement', redirecting attention toward autistic people 'rather than solely focusing on caregivers'. That passage does something no other included study attempts: it recognises that the autism research literature has been shaped disproportionately by parents and professionals rather than by autistic people, and it selects its sample specifically from autistic voices for that reason. The conclusion follows through, calling for 'a more inclusive approach during the model development process that involves the autistic community directly in the ideation and consent processes' and referring to autistic people as a 'marginalized population' whose consent is at issue. The framing is not uniformly neurodiversity-aligned - the introduction still describes autism through misdiagnosis, delayed services and 'negative outcomes later in life' - but the paper is the only one in this corpus to treat the people it studies as a constituency with standing in how they are researched. The published record also shows that the article attracted a formal comment (JMIR Formative Research 2024;8:e59794) and was issued as a corrected version, which indicates that its approach was contested in the literature. [RQ1.3] None available, and the authors are candid about what follows. There is no age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic, cognitive or comorbidity information for any of the 188,596 users, and location was dropped as unusable. The limitations section states the resulting representativeness problem directly: restricting to English 'raises concerns about the lack of diversity in the data, where only English-speaking users from higher socioeconomic groups or younger adults are represented in the data set, as they comprise a larger portion of Twitter users'. Two consequences go further than the paper takes them. The #ActuallyAutistic community is widely observed to include a high proportion of late-diagnosed and self-identifying autistic adults, and a higher proportion of women, than clinically ascertained autism samples - so the demographic distance between the two corpora is likely to be substantial and is entirely unmeasurable, meaning that a sex- or age-linked difference in writing style would be indistinguishable from an autism-linked one. And the two groups differ in a way that no demographic variable captures at all: one is defined by participation in a topic-organised community and the other is a background sample of the platform, so their tweets differ in subject matter, audience, posting motivation and network position before any question of authorship arises. [RQ1.4] None, and the paper's handling of this is the most precise in the review. The positive label is use of #ActuallyAutistic plus autism-related keywords in the profile description - self-identification within an online community. The authors do not claim otherwise at any point: their own conclusion states that the models predict 'use of the #ActuallyAutistic hashtag, an imperfect proxy for self-reported autism', and their first limitation is that 'while we focused on individuals who self-identified as autistic, there is no clinical validation for their diagnosis'. They then reason about contamination in both directions. Users of the hashtag might be parents, caregivers or advocacy organisations rather than autistic people, which they judge rare 'due to the negative social connotations of using #ActuallyAutistic without a diagnosis' - an appeal to community norms rather than evidence, but an informed one, since the hashtag's function within the autism rights movement is precisely to mark first-person testimony. And autistic users who do not self-identify will contaminate the control group, which they bound at roughly the population prevalence, arguing that 'with autism having a prevalence rate of <3%, the model performance should not degrade by more than 3%' - a bound that assumes population prevalence transfers to Twitter's user base and that non-self-identifying autistic users write like non-autistic ones, neither of which is established. What the paper does not consider is that its label might be a design choice rather than a defect: undiagnosed self-identifying autistic adults are precisely the population an access-oriented screening tool would most want to reach, and treating their self-identification as noise assumes that clinical ascertainment is the only valid criterion in a study whose framing elsewhere questions exactly that assumption. [RQ1.5] None. No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists for any user, and none could without linking to clinical records. The corpus retains rich behavioural metadata - account age, friend and follower counts, reply, retweet and like counts, posting source, timestamps - which the authors note could support network or statistical analysis but deliberately do not use. Some of these would function as crude proxies for social engagement and could have supported a gradient analysis of the kind this review has repeatedly found missing; the paper's decision not to pursue them is consistent with its overall restraint about extracting more from the data than it collected consent for. [RQ2.1] The stated objective was 'to study the feasibility of autism screening from Twitter data and discuss the ethical implications of such models' - the ethics being a co-equal aim from the outset rather than an appended caveat, which is unique in this corpus. The technical finding is modest and honestly reported: a tweet-level classifier reached 73% accuracy, AUC 0.728 and F1 0.71 using word2vec representations with logistic regression, and a user-profile classifier reached AUC 0.78 and F1 0.805 using an attention-based bidirectional LSTM. Aggregating a user's full timeline improved discrimination over single tweets, as expected if the signal is a property of a writer rather than of a post. Exploratory analysis found that sentiment polarity was nearly unchanged between the raw and profanity-censored corpora, and that autism-related discussion rose across 2014-2022. The conclusion the authors actually draw is not about accuracy: having demonstrated feasibility, they restrict the legitimate use of such models to 'a broader cross-sectional level' rather than individual prediction, enumerate the misuse scenarios the artefact would enable, delete the data and the models, and caution researchers against building comparable systems without explicit consent and participatory community-centred design. That is the study's contribution and it is a real one. [RQ2.2] No study setting exists in the ordinary sense - the data are public posts scraped from Twitter using snscrape, a library chosen because it avoids the need for platform API keys. The absence of a setting is the point: the data are naturally occurring, produced without observation effects, at a scale no laboratory could approach, at essentially zero collection cost. The corresponding costs are equally structural. Nobody knew they were being studied. The two classes were assembled by different procedures - full timeline harvesting for the autism group, daily sampling for controls - so the corpora differ in composition independently of authorship. The platform's user base is skewed by age, language, geography and socioeconomic status in ways the authors acknowledge. And the positive class is defined by membership in a community organised around a topic, so the contrast is between a self-advocacy discourse and general platform conversation rather than between two comparably situated populations. [RQ2.3] None, and this is the study's chief methodological attraction. There is no elicitation, no examiner, no instruction and no observation effect - people wrote what they wanted to write, at their own pace, over nine years. Against the 90-second free-play sample, the 3-minute video and the 40-minute standardised assessment charted elsewhere in this review, a user's full Twitter timeline is an enormous and ecologically valid behavioural record. What the absence of a paradigm removes is any control over what the two groups were writing about, and here the comparison is unfavourable: because the positive class was selected by participation in a hashtag community, its members were writing about autism, diagnosis, accommodation, sensory experience and ableism far more than a background sample would. Removing the explicit autism keyword list attenuates but cannot eliminate this, since topic pervades vocabulary, syntax and stance well beyond a list of sixteen terms. Naturalistic data therefore buys freedom from task effects at the price of losing any guarantee that the two samples are doing the same thing. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional in analysis but drawing on nine years of longitudinal record, since users' full timelines from 2014 to 2022 were collected - a temporal depth no other included study approaches. That depth is used only descriptively, to show a rising trend in autism-related discussion, and no within-user temporal modelling is attempted. Ethics reporting is by a distance the most thorough in this review. The study holds University of Hawaii Institutional Review Board approval 2023-00248 under expedited review and passed a separate institutional data governance review that deemed it exempt 'due to the inherently public nature of the study data'. The authors then describe measures 'not required by the Institutional Review Board': encrypting user IDs to reduce reidentification risk, and anonymising user mentions and personal information such as email addresses within tweet text. They engage with the consent question substantively rather than resting on the public-data exemption, citing survey evidence that 84% of users were not or only slightly concerned about university research use while observing that 'this leaves a considerable portion of the population who remains concerned', and noting that privacy policies are 'long, with complex legal terms that the users may fail to understand or authorize'. They call for large-scale consent procedures and a regulatory framework for social media data mining. And they act: 'the data set and the model that we built using those data have been deleted. When the data set did exist, it was never shared outside of the original authors.' Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text. [RQ2.5] No instrumentation. snscrape for collection, better-profanity for masking swear words, VADER for lexicon-based sentiment, word2vec and TF-IDF for representation, and an attention-based bidirectional LSTM for user-level classification. The equipment cost of this study is zero and its collection cost is a scraping script - which is precisely why the ethical analysis matters more here than anywhere else in this review. Every other included study is bounded by what a research team can afford to collect from consenting participants; this one is bounded only by what a platform will serve, and the authors' response is to build the model, measure it, describe what it would enable, and destroy it. [RQ2.6] Deliberately partial, with the incompleteness explained rather than concealed. Fully reported: the scraping library, both search queries with their date range, the profile-keyword criterion defining the autism group, the 1,000-per-day sampling rate for controls, the complete preprocessing chain from profanity masking through tokenisation, stop-word removal, stemming and lemmatisation to padding, the full sixteen-item list of removed autism-related keywords, the sentiment tool and the censored-versus-uncensored comparison, the representation methods and model families, the 5-fold cross-validation used for algorithm selection, the 85:15 user-level split for tweet classification with a further 85:15 training-validation division, the 80:20 user split and five-tweet minimum for profile classification, and all corpus counts by group. Not available: the dataset and the trained models, both destroyed, and the code, which is not mentioned. The pipeline is therefore reconstructible and the corpus is not - which is the outcome the authors intend, since re-creating the corpus is the act they argue should not be undertaken without consent. [RQ2.7] Five limitations are stated and the reasoning behind each is unusually developed. There is no clinical validation for any diagnosis, and expert or crowdsourced annotation would help. Hashtag users may be family members, parents, caregivers or advocacy organisations rather than autistic people, though the authors judge this rare given the negative social connotations of using #ActuallyAutistic without a diagnosis. Autistic users who do not self-identify will contaminate the control group, bounded at roughly the population prevalence of under 3%. VADER sentiment may be less accurate than human labelling. And the English-only restriction limits diversity, over-representing younger and higher-socioeconomic users. The authors add a scope restriction that functions as a finding - 'the predictive power of social media is not to be used at an individual level but at a broader cross-sectional level' - and name the consent failure as 'the primary limitation of this study', enumerating misuse scenarios including university admissions, hiring, and government surveillance. What is not addressed is the group-definition confound: the positive class is a community organised around a topic and the negative class is a platform sample, so a classifier could reach 73% by recognising the register of autism self-advocacy rather than any property of autistic language production, and removing sixteen keywords does not close that route. Nor is the structural asymmetry addressed by which the autism group's full timelines were harvested while control posts were sampled daily, so that 17,323 users contribute nearly as many tweets as 171,273 - a difference in how material was selected that is confounded with the label. No demographic data exist for either group in a comparison where the communities plausibly differ in age and sex. No feature analysis is reported for the classifiers, so the interpretive question is left open where it could have been partly answered. And the contamination bound assumes that population prevalence transfers to Twitter's user base and that non-self-identifying autistic users write like non-autistic ones. [RQ2.9] The technical directions named are clinical or crowdsourced annotation to replace hashtag labels, extension beyond English, and use of the retained network metadata. But the direction the paper actually advocates is procedural: 'a more inclusive approach during the model development process that involves the autistic community directly in the ideation and consent processes', supported by research-community work to 'find ways to support large-scale consent procedures' and by 'a regulatory framework for social media data mining'.
