The paper closes by keeping itself 'as a case study of what is currently possible with publicly available' data rather than proposing a successor system. No other study in this review proposes participatory governance as its principal future work, and none argues against the further development of its own method. [RQ3.1] Written language produced in unconstrained public communication - the only such behaviour in the review, and the largest behavioural record it contains. Three analytic layers were applied: sentiment polarity via VADER, computed on both the raw corpus and a profanity-censored version with the two found to be almost identical; topic analysis for qualitative insight; and lexical-distributional modelling through TF-IDF and word2vec for classification. What the study cannot say is which linguistic properties distinguish the groups, because no feature analysis or attribution is reported for the classifiers. The behaviour targeted is therefore best described as 'written register' rather than any specific construct, and the ambiguity between two candidate constructs - autistic language production on the one hand, and participation in an advocacy discourse on the other - is the study's central unresolved question. It is worth noting against this that the authors' preprocessing removes a sixteen-item vocabulary specifically to prevent the second construct from being trivially detectable, which is more than most studies in this corpus do about their own confounds even when they name them. [RQ3.2] None modelled, though the opportunity was substantial and deliberately declined. The curated corpus retains account creation date, friend count, follower count, tweet timestamp, reply count, retweet count, like count, hashtag lists and posting source, and the authors observe that 'other supporting metadata could be used in the future for network analysis or statistical studies'. Fusing behavioural text with network position and engagement metrics would be a natural extension and would plausibly improve discrimination - which is precisely why not doing it, in a paper that concludes such models should not be built without consent, is consistent rather than an oversight. [RQ4.1] A sensible staged progression rather than a single architecture. TF-IDF features were first passed through four classical algorithms - support vector machines, naive Bayes, logistic regression and XGBoost - with 5-fold cross-validation on accuracy used to select the best; word2vec representations were then trained with the selected algorithm and evaluated on a fuller metric set; and an attention-based bidirectional LSTM over a self-trained embedding layer was used for the user-level task, with padding and an unknown token to handle variable tweet lengths. The final tweet-level result comes from word2vec with logistic regression, and the profile-level result from the BiLSTM. The modelling is proportionate: a corpus of 6.5 million tweets can support a deep sequence model, and the authors escalate to one only for the aggregated user-document task where sequence structure and attention have a plausible role. [RQ4.2] TF-IDF vectors and word2vec embeddings at tweet level; a self-trained embedding layer feeding an attention-based BiLSTM over a concatenation of all of a user's preprocessed tweets at profile level, restricted to users with at least five tweets. The representation is the product of aggressive normalisation - profanity masking, removal of non-alphanumerics, links, mentions and HTML, lowercasing, stop-word removal, stemming and lemmatisation - which strips much of the paralinguistic texture of social media writing (capitalisation, punctuation, emoji, elongation) that might itself carry the signal of interest. The most consequential representational decision is the removal of sixteen autism-related tokens including the hashtag that defines the label, on the explicit ground that they 'could introduce bias and lead to model overfitting'. That is a target-leakage control, correctly reasoned, and it is the same failure mode this review documents in the questionnaire-item studies where the label is an arithmetic function of the features - handled here rather than left in place. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, AUC and F1 for both classifiers, with 5-fold cross-validation accuracy for algorithm selection: 73% accuracy, AUC 0.728 and F1 0.71 at tweet level; AUC 0.78 and F1 0.805 at profile level. The figures are modest by this corpus's standards and are presented without inflation - the abstract, results and conclusion all carry the same numbers and none is described as high. What is absent is uncertainty and operating-point reporting: no confidence intervals despite a corpus that would support tight ones, no calibration, and no sensitivity or specificity at any threshold. For a paper that raises screening, the absent quantity is the positive predictive value at population prevalence - at roughly 1-2% base rate, a classifier with AUC 0.78 would place the overwhelming majority of its positive calls on non-autistic people. The authors reach a compatible conclusion by a different route, restricting legitimate use to cross-sectional rather than individual inference, but they do not compute the number that demonstrates why. [RQ4.4] Limited at the model level and thoughtful at the corpus level. Sentiment and topic analyses were run before classification to develop qualitative understanding of the data, and the comparison of sentiment polarity between raw and profanity-censored versions is a genuine methodological check - it establishes that any polarity difference between groups is not simply a difference in swearing. But no attribution, coefficient inspection, attention visualisation or error analysis is reported for either classifier, so what the models responded to is unknown. This is the study's clearest missed opportunity, because inspecting the highest-weighted terms in the word2vec logistic regression would have spoken directly to the interpretive question the paper leaves open - whether 73% reflects something about autistic language or about the vocabulary of a self-advocacy community - and because the prior removal of sixteen autism-related tokens means the answer would have been informative rather than circular. [RQ4.5] Careful on the mechanics and unresolved on the substance, which is the reverse of the pattern in most of this corpus. The mechanics are good. Splitting is at user level with the reasoning stated explicitly - tweets from one user must not scatter across training and test, 'potentially leading to overfitting by the model due to learning user-specific patterns' - and applied to both tasks, 85:15 for tweet classification with a further 85:15 training-validation division, 80:20 for profile classification. Algorithm selection used 5-fold cross-validation with a held-out test partition maintained separately. And the sixteen-token removal list closes the most obvious inflation route, since the label is defined by a hashtag whose presence in the text would otherwise make the task a lookup. Together these are more deliberate leakage controls than most studies in this review implement, and the modest performance obtained is consistent with the controls having worked. What remains unresolved is the construct. The positive class consists of users who chose to participate in a hashtag community organised around autism advocacy; the negative class is a daily sample of general platform conversation. These populations differ in topic, audience, community membership, posting motivation, network position and - plausibly, though unmeasurably - in age, sex and geography. A model reaching 73% accuracy on that contrast may be detecting autistic language production, or the discourse register of self-advocacy, or the difference between a topically coherent community and a background sample, and the study provides no evidence separating them. The corpus construction adds a further asymmetry that is not discussed: the autism group's complete timelines were harvested while control tweets were drawn at 1,000 per day, so 17,323 users supply almost as many tweets as 171,273, and the two classes differ in how their material was sampled as well as in who wrote it. The authors reason carefully about label contamination in both directions and bound the control-group error at the population prevalence, but that bound assumes prevalence transfers to Twitter's user base and that non-self-identifying autistic users write like non-autistic ones. The honest reading is that the study demonstrates a detectable difference between two corpora whose separation has several sufficient explanations, and that its authors' decision to treat the result as a feasibility demonstration rather than a finding about autistic language is the correct one. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism, autism spectrum disorder, machine learning, natural language processing, public health, sentiment analysis, social media analysis, Twitter. The set spans population, method and application domain and includes 'public health', which locates the work in population monitoring rather than individual diagnosis - consistent with the conclusion's restriction of legitimate use to the cross-sectional level. Terms carried through the body: digital phenotyping, #ActuallyAutistic, neurodiversity, weak supervision, VADER, word2vec, attention-based BiLSTM, data governance, participatory research, informed consent. [RQ5.2] JMIR Formative Research 2024;8:e52660, Original Paper, open access. The record carries two notable annotations: the version retrieved is a corrected version, with the correction statement published at JMIR Formative Research 2024;8:e59349, and a formal comment on the article appears at JMIR Formative Research 2024;8:e59794. A published comment on a paper of this kind indicates that its approach was contested in the literature, which is itself part of the paper's significance for this review - it is the only included study whose ethics generated a documented scholarly exchange. JMIR's formative-research track is intended for feasibility and early-stage work, which fits a study whose conclusion is that the thing is possible and should not be done without consent. The venue's structure produced the ethical-considerations section with its IRB number, data-governance determination and description of measures taken beyond regulatory requirement - a section that has no counterpart anywhere else in this corpus. [RQ5.3] Published 2024 by the Department of Information and Computer Sciences at the University of Hawaii at Manoa. The framing is the standard access argument - limited availability of standard tests, misdiagnosis, delayed services, negative outcomes later in life - applied to a data source of unprecedented scale and zero collection cost, with the stated aim of 'enabling support for communities with limited access to diagnostic resources'. For this review the study matters on four counts, only one of which is its performance. It is the only included study whose behavioural data are naturally occurring and unelicited, at a scale - 6.5 million posts from 188,596 people over nine years - that no laboratory design can approach, which makes it the clearest available test of whether ecological validity and scale can substitute for measurement control. The answer it returns is instructive: 73% accuracy and AUC 0.728, modest against the 90-plus percent figures obtained elsewhere in this corpus under laboratory conditions with clinical ascertainment, and obtained despite the vastly larger sample. It implements two deliberate leakage controls - user-level splitting, with the reasoning stated, and removal of the sixteen autism-related tokens that define its own label - which places it among the more careful studies here on mechanics. It is the only paper in this review to discuss its own label honestly enough to state in its conclusion that the model predicts hashtag use rather than autism. And it is the only paper anywhere in the corpus that argues against the deployment of what it built: having demonstrated feasibility, the authors restrict legitimate use to population-level inference, enumerate the misuse scenarios an individual-level classifier would enable - insurance profiling, university admissions, hiring, government surveillance of citizens - delete the dataset and the models, note that the data were never shared outside the author team, and caution researchers against building comparable systems without explicit consent and participatory community-centred design. Set beside the studies charted nearby that scrape identifiable photographs of children from support pages with no ethics statement at all, or that ship an 'AI-driven assistive diagnostic tool' for at-home use on the strength of a model that recomputes a questionnaire's own scoring rule, this paper is the corpus's clearest demonstration that the ethical questions raised by this literature are tractable when researchers choose to engage with them. The substantive caution that travels with it is that its positive class is a self-selected advocacy community and its negative class a background platform sample, so the 73% has several sufficient explanations and the study does not distinguish them - a limitation the authors partially anticipate by declining to treat the result as a finding about autistic language at all.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Prospective case-control classification study nested in the Geneva Autism Cohort at the University of Geneva, with participants recruited between 25 September 2012 and 10 September 2023. One hundred and sixty children aged 1.1 to 5.1 years took part: 80 autistic (48 male, 32 female, mean age 2.68 +/- 0.89 years) meeting DSM-5 criteria with diagnosis supported by gold-standard assessment, and 80 typically developing (48 male, 32 female, mean age 2.46 +/- 0.98 years) screened for absence of known neurological or psychiatric conditions and for no first-degree relative with autism. Both groups underwent the same ADOS assessment in the same setting, so recording context is matched across classes, and sex was matched exactly, giving 40% girls in each group - the highest female representation of any included study. The work was approved by the Faculty of Medicine Ethics Committee at the University of Geneva, with written parental consent for all children and separate specific consent from the child depicted in a figure, their guardian and the examiner for publication of identifying images. Six funding sources are itemised with grant numbers and a no-role statement, and no competing interests are declared.
narrative_rows.methods: ADOS sessions averaging about 46 minutes were recorded and processed through two independent pipelines. For video, OpenPose extracted skeletal keypoints which were plotted over a plain black background at 320x240 resolution - removing face, clothing, body habitus, room and lighting while preserving the interaction between child and examiner - and split into 5-second segments; an ImageNet-pretrained VGG16 with its dense layers removed extracted per-frame features feeding a 512-unit LSTM, 512 fully connected ReLU units and a softmax, with segment predictions retained only above 90% confidence and averaged across the session. For audio, the full undiarised band was normalised to 2-channel 44 kHz 192 kbps to homogenise across the different microphones used over eleven years, split into 10-second segments, and summarised by Librosa into mean MFCCs (150 retained), Mel spectrogram, chromagram, spectral contrast and tonal centroid, fed to a 1D convolutional network with dropout 0.5, trained with Adam at batch size 512 for 30 epochs. The 160 children were split 50-50 into training and test halves of 80, each containing 40 autistic and 40 typically developing children matched for age, sex and ADOS module, with 20% of the training half held out for validation and all hyperparameter selection confined there. Three late-fusion rules were compared: OR, AND, and a decision tree taking the video prediction when its confidence exceeded 60% and otherwise deferring to audio. For interpretation, random regression forests were fitted with all 27 ADOS-2 items as predictors and each network's confidence as outcome, with importance assessed by increase in mean squared error, increase in node purity and p-value, plus a third normalising forest to make the two modalities comparable.
narrative_rows.outcomes: On the held-out 80 children, the video model reached 80.0% accuracy (precision 0.833, recall 0.750, specificity 0.850, NPV 0.773, F1 0.789) and the audio model 78.8% (precision 0.811, recall 0.750, specificity 0.825, NPV 0.767, F1 0.779). The confidence-gated ensemble reached 82.5% (precision 0.861, recall 0.775, specificity 0.875, NPV 0.796, F1 0.816). The OR rule gave sensitivity 0.90 at specificity 0.75 with accuracy 82.5%; the AND rule gave specificity 0.925 at sensitivity 0.60 with accuracy 76.3%. Both networks were simultaneously wrong on only 8.75% of cases, indicating complementary errors despite the small accuracy gain. The interpretability analysis found video confidence most strongly related to initiation of joint attention, quality of social overtures, unusual eye contact and pointing gestures - a coherent nonverbal social-communication cluster - while audio confidence related most strongly to showing behaviour, pointing gesture, unusual sensory exploration and hand mannerisms, none of which is a vocal construct.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The reference standard's independence from the index test is not established: diagnosis was supported by unspecified 'gold standard diagnostic assessments' while the model input is the ADOS recording, so unless the diagnostic session differed from the recorded one the label is partly derived from the material - a milder circularity than in the questionnaire studies, since the model receives raw pose and audio rather than coded items, but one that a single sentence would resolve. No confidence intervals are reported on a test set of 80 children, where one case is worth 1.25 accuracy points and an exact interval around 82.5% spans roughly 72% to 90%; the ensemble's advantage over the video model alone amounts to two children and is not distinguishable from noise. No positive predictive value is computed at any realistic prevalence despite the screening framing, where a specificity of 0.875 would place most positive calls on non-autistic children at a population base rate. The 90% segment-confidence filter on video is an output-selection step whose effect on aggregate accuracy is unquantified. Cognitive and diagnostic-instrument details are deferred to supplementary material. No sex-stratified analysis is reported although the 40% female sample makes one uniquely feasible. The comparison group is typically developing only, so discrimination against other developmental conditions is untested. And the abstract contains two transposition errors - describing high specificity as producing few false negatives and high sensitivity as producing few false positives, and swapping the ensemble's precision and recall - though the results table is internally correct throughout.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: One of the most useful included studies, and the review's clearest example of what an unconfounded design produces. Four features distinguish it. Both groups were recorded under the same ADOS protocol in the same setting, so acquisition context cannot proxy for diagnosis - which removes at a stroke the confound this synthesis has had to record against the scraped-photograph, video-frame and clinic-versus-school audio studies charted nearby. The video input is rendered as skeletal keypoints on a black background, architecturally excluding face, clothing, body habitus, room and lighting, so a video classifier that works must be using movement and interaction dynamics; this is a designed answer to the appearance confound rather than an assertion that none exists, and it is what made a de-identified data release possible when raw recordings could not be shared. Splitting is participant-level and matched on age, sex and ADOS module, with all tuning confined to a validation partition inside the training half. And the interpretability analysis - random regression forests over all 27 ADOS items for both modalities, with a normalisation model making them comparable - produces the review's most valuable methodological finding: the audio model's most predictive items are showing behaviour, pointing, unusual sensory exploration and hand mannerisms, none of them vocal, leading the authors to conclude in their own voice that ambient non-vocal sound from object manipulation contributed to classification, and to note prior evidence that examiners' prosody adapts to child severity such that a full-band model may be reading the adult rather than the child. That result generalises to every study in this corpus using undiarised interaction audio and is examined by none of the others. The performance obtained under these conditions - 80.0% video, 78.8% audio, 82.5% ensemble, on 80 held-out children with sensitivity 0.775 and specificity 0.875 - is the single most useful calibration point this review can offer against the 95-100% accuracies reported elsewhere from confounded or leaked designs: it is roughly what an honest 46-minute multimodal assessment of preschoolers delivers. The study also illustrates a fusion finding worth carrying forward: simple late fusion gained only two children out of eighty over the better single modality and the authors name this as a limitation, yet both networks were simultaneously wrong on only 8.75% of cases, so the complementarity is real and the combination rule rather than the modalities is what fell short.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] One hundred and sixty children aged 1.1 to 5.1 years, enrolled in the Geneva Autism Cohort between 25 September 2012 and 10 September 2023: 80 autistic children (48 male, 32 female, mean age 2.68 +/- 0.89 years) meeting DSM-5 criteria with diagnosis supported by gold-standard assessment, and 80 typically developing children (48 male, 32 female, mean age 2.46 +/- 0.98 years) screened for absence of known neurological or psychiatric conditions and for no history of autism in any first-degree relative. Three features of the sample are worth emphasising. Both groups underwent the same ADOS assessment in the same setting, so the recording context is common to both classes - which removes the setting confound that this review has documented repeatedly across the video, audio and image branches, where clinical groups are recorded in clinics and comparison groups in schools, kindergartens or on the internet. Sex is exactly matched at 48 male and 32 female per group, giving 40% girls, which is by a considerable margin the highest female representation of any included study and the only instance of deliberate exact matching on sex. And the matching extends to the analysis: the 50-50 train-test split was itself constructed so that each half contained 40 autistic and 40 typically developing children matched for age, sex and ADOS module, so the held-out set is not merely disjoint but comparable by construction. The unit of analysis is the child, with segments nested within children and never crossing the split. [RQ1.2] Clinically conventional and, within that idiom, careful and accurate. Autism is 'a group of neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by a wide range of symptoms across two main dimensions: social and nonsocial', and the description that follows is notably precise about heterogeneity - noting that autism 'can be present with or without cognitive and language delay, widening the breadth of clinical presentations', and that 'the heterogeneity of ASD manifestations is a major obstacle to timely diagnosis and personalized medicine'. Person-first phrasing predominates ('children with ASD', 'individuals with autism'), with 'autistic individuals' and 'individuals on the autism spectrum' appearing alongside it. Two aspects of the framing are substantively better than the corpus norm. The description of social symptoms is relational rather than located in the individual: they 'often transcend the isolated instances of behaviors and arise from specific mismatches in the dynamic between agents and their social context' - which is why the study models the child-examiner dyad rather than the child alone, and it is a conceptual position with methodological consequences. And the account of the gold-standard diagnostic procedure treats it as 'the product of convergent clinical and research work over the past four decades', crediting rather than dismissing existing clinical practice, which is a marked contrast to the framing common in the engineering venues where clinical assessment is characterised chiefly as subjective and slow. There is no neurodiversity framing and no reported involvement of autistic people in the design. [RQ1.3] Age and sex are reported per group and exactly matched, and the matching is carried through into the train-test split alongside ADOS module - a three-way matching of the evaluation partition that no other included study performs. Because ADOS module assignment depends on expressive language level, matching on module constrains the groups on a language dimension without measuring it directly, which is a partial substitute for the language measure that is otherwise absent from the main text. Cognitive and developmental assessment details are deferred to supplementary material rather than reported, which is the description's main weakness. Ancestry, socioeconomic status and comorbidity within the autistic group are not reported. The 40% female representation deserves particular note in the context of this review: a speech study charted elsewhere here found that a model reaching 94.8% sensitivity on a pooled test set fell to 43.6% on girls, and that finding is only discoverable in samples where girls are present in reasonable numbers. This study has the sample composition to run that analysis and does not run it - which is a missed opportunity rather than a flaw in the sample. [RQ1.4] Strong in substance and incompletely reported in one respect that matters. Autistic children met DSM-5 clinical criteria with the diagnosis 'further supported by employing gold standard diagnostic assessments', within an established longitudinal cohort staffed by a clinical psychiatry department - so this is genuine clinical ascertainment, not a questionnaire threshold or a dataset label, and it stands among the better reference standards in this review. The comparison group was actively screened rather than merely assumed typical: absence of known neurological or psychiatric conditions, and no first-degree relative with autism, which excludes the elevated-likelihood siblings who would otherwise blur the contrast. The unresolved issue is independence. The model's input is the ADOS recording, and 'gold standard diagnostic assessments' in a paediatric autism cohort ordinarily means ADOS, so the same session that supplied the model's training data may have contributed to the diagnostic label it is trained to predict. That is a circularity of the same family as the questionnaire studies excluded from this review, though far milder in degree - the model sees raw pose and audio rather than the clinician's coded items, so it must rediscover from signal what the clinician judged, rather than reproducing an arithmetic function of its inputs. Still, it means the label is not independent of the material, and the fix would be one sentence: another study in this review states explicitly that neither ADOS nor ADI-R entered its diagnostic process, which is exactly the statement needed here and is absent. The main text also defers the specific instruments to supplementary material, so a reader cannot check. [RQ1.5] ADOS-2 item scores across all 27 items are available and are used analytically rather than descriptively, which is the study's most valuable methodological choice on this axis. Rather than reporting group means and moving on, the authors fit random regression forests with the 27 items as predictors and each network's prediction confidence as the outcome, then calibrate a third model so that the two modalities' importance estimates can be compared on a common scale. This asks - and partly answers - the question this review has repeatedly found unasked: what is the model actually responding to, expressed in clinical terms. The answer for the video model is a coherent nonverbal social-communication cluster (initiation of joint attention, quality of social overtures, unusual eye contact, pointing gestures). The answer for the audio model is not a vocal cluster at all (showing behaviour, pointing gesture, unusual sensory exploration, hand mannerisms), which the authors read as evidence that ambient non-vocal sound contributed to classification. No cognitive or adaptive severity measure is reported in the main text. [RQ2.1] The aim is broad automated screening rather than detection of a single symptom, achieved by combining two neural networks trained on the video and audio channels of the same semi-standardised assessment, and by then asking which clinical features each modality is sensitive to. The performance findings are modest and are not oversold: video alone 80.0% accuracy on the held-out 80 children, audio alone 78.8%, and the best ensemble 82.5% with sensitivity 0.775 and specificity 0.875. Alternative combination rules trade these off - an OR rule reaching sensitivity 0.90 at specificity 0.75, an AND rule reaching specificity 0.925 at sensitivity 0.60 - and the authors present all five variants in one table rather than only the best. The fusion result is honestly negative in the accuracy sense and the authors say so, identifying 'the inability of the simple ensemble model to outperform the individual modalities' as an important limitation; what fusion does provide is complementary errors, with both networks simultaneously wrong on only 8.75% of cases, and operating-point control. The more interesting findings are interpretive. Video confidence tracks initiation of joint attention, quality of social overtures, unusual eye contact and pointing gestures - a coherent nonverbal social-communication cluster. Audio confidence tracks showing behaviour, pointing, unusual sensory exploration and hand mannerisms - which are not vocal constructs, leading the authors to propose that ambient non-vocal sound from object manipulation contributed to the audio classification, and to note prior evidence that examiners' prosody adapts to child severity such that a full-band model may partly be reading the adult. Those two admissions are the study's most valuable output for this review. [RQ2.2] Clinical research assessment sessions in the Geneva Autism Cohort, with both groups undergoing the same ADOS protocol in the same setting. This is the single most important design property of the study for the purposes of this synthesis. Across the video, audio and photograph branches charted here, the recurring failure is that the two classes are recorded under systematically different conditions - clinic against school, autism-advocacy websites against general internet, home videos of stereotypy against kindergarten footage - so that acquisition context is a perfect proxy for the label and no amount of downstream methodological care can separate them. Here the context is common to both classes by construction: same room, same protocol, same examiner role, same equipment. Whatever the models are detecting, it is not the difference between being in a clinic and being at school. The residual acquisition concern is temporal rather than group-related: recordings span eleven years, and audio was explicitly normalised 'to homogenize the audio format from different microphones used for ADOS recordings', so equipment changed over that period - but there is no reason to expect equipment drift to align with diagnosis. [RQ2.3] The ADOS, a semi-structured 40-60 minute assessment comprising free play and activities modelled on everyday play, administered identically to both groups, with average session lengths of about 46 minutes in each partition. The authors set out the paradigm choice as a considered trade-off rather than a default, and their statement of it is the clearest in this review: automating social-symptom measurement has usually required 'over-standardization ... at the expense of less ecological feature presentation', whereas the ADOS activities 'are specifically designed to be representative of naturalistic interactions, with a high amount of prompts aiming at eliciting communication and reciprocal exchanges in a restricted time period'. That formulation identifies exactly what a good behavioural paradigm needs - dense elicitation of the target behaviour within a bounded time, without collapsing into a single narrow construct - and it sits usefully between the two poles this review has charted. At one pole, the 90-second free-play study demonstrated empirically that a brief sample cannot reach restricted and repetitive behaviour at all; at the other, response-to-name and screen-based paradigms deliver a clean readout of one construct. Forty-six minutes of ADOS spans the phenotype, and the interpretability analysis confirms it - the models' confidence relates to joint attention, social overtures, eye contact, pointing, showing, sensory exploration and hand mannerisms, which is most of the diagnostic space. The cost is that the paradigm requires a trained ADOS examiner, so it does not remove the expert bottleneck that motivates the field, and the authors' proposal that this could eventually move to home settings without specialised equipment is aspirational rather than demonstrated. [RQ2.4] The classification analysis is cross-sectional, but the participants are drawn from a longitudinal cohort explicitly established to study early development in autism, and the recruitment window spans eleven years - the longest in this review. No longitudinal modelling or follow-up outcome is reported here. Ethics reporting is complete and in one respect exceeds every other included study: approval by the Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Geneva; written informed consent from a parent or legal guardian for all children; and separately, specific consent obtained from the child depicted in a figure, from their legal guardian and from the examiner for publication of identifying images in an open-access article. That last item is a detail no other paper here reports, and it stands in sharp contrast to the studies charted nearby that train on identifiable photographs of children scraped from support pages without any ethics statement at all. Six funding sources are itemised with grant numbers and a no-role statement, and competing interests are declared as none. [RQ2.5] Standard ADOS session recording equipment, unspecified and heterogeneous across the eleven-year window - which the authors handle by normalising audio to a 2-channel 44 kHz 192 kbps format explicitly 'to homogenize the audio format from different microphones', matched to the parameters of the Urban8K benchmark corpus. Analysis used OpenPose for pose estimation, ImageNet-pretrained VGG16 for video features and Librosa for acoustic features. The equipment story matters for the translational claim: nothing here is specialised. No eye tracker, no motion capture, no wearable, no force plate - a camera and a microphone in a room where an assessment was happening anyway. That places the study alongside the one-legged-standing and free-play studies charted here as instrumentation that a clinic could actually deploy, and unlike them it captures 46 minutes of dense social interaction rather than 90 seconds. The bottleneck it does not remove is the ADOS examiner. [RQ2.6] Among the strongest reproducibility records in the review, and the only one combining published code with a partial data release. Reported in full: the cohort and its eleven-year recruitment window, group sizes with age and sex, the matching variables for the groups and separately for the train-test split, the exact 50-50 participant split with 40-40 composition per half and the 80-20 internal training-validation division, segment lengths for both modalities with the empirical basis for choosing them, the audio normalisation format and its stated rationale, all five acoustic feature families and the 150-MFCC selection, complete architectures for both networks including LSTM units, dense layer sizes, dropout rate, loss function, optimiser, batch size and epoch count with the observation that larger values overfit, the segment aggregation rule and the 90% confidence filter, all three ensemble strategies including the decision tree's 60% threshold, a complete six-metric table for all five models, and the full interpretability procedure with its three importance metrics and cross-modality normalisation model. Training code for both networks is published on GitHub, and a de-identified subsample of pose-estimation videos is deposited on Zenodo with a DOI. What is unavailable is the raw recordings, and the reason given is correct - they 'contain identifiable features such as faces and voices of participants, and as such cannot be shared integrally'. Cognitive and diagnostic-instrument detail is deferred to supplementary material, and no confidence intervals are given. [RQ2.7] One limitation is formally stated - that the simple ensemble could not outperform the individual modalities - and two more consequential ones are volunteered in the discussion without being labelled as such. The authors propose that 'peculiar non-vocal acoustic features (i.e., ambient sound), such as any repetitive sound that would reflect an increased need for sensory stimulation in autistic children (e.g., repeatedly dropping objects or banging them, or perseverating on a musical toy)' contributed to the audio classification, supporting this with their own finding that sensory interests was the ADOS item most correlated with audio-based prediction. And they note prior work showing that examiners attune their prosody to a child's symptom severity, in which 'the psychologist's prosodic cues better predicted the child's autistic symptom severity than the prosody of the child himself' - so a full-band audio model trained on undiarised recordings may be reading the adult's behaviour as much as the child's. Volunteering both is unusual and valuable. What is not addressed: the probable circularity between the ADOS-supported diagnosis and the ADOS-derived model input, which one sentence about whether ADOS entered the diagnostic decision would resolve; the absence of confidence intervals on an 80-child test set, where an exact interval around 82.5% spans roughly 72% to 90% and where the ensemble's 2.5-point advantage over video alone amounts to two children; the absence of any positive predictive value at realistic prevalence in a paper framed around screening, where specificity of 0.875 would place most positive calls on non-autistic children at a population base rate; the unquantified effect of the 90% segment-confidence filter; the eleven-year window across which equipment, personnel and diagnostic practice all changed; the absence of a sex-stratified analysis despite a sample uniquely suited to one; and the restriction of the comparison group to typically developing children, leaving the harder discrimination against other developmental conditions untested. [RQ2.9] More sophisticated fusion architectures that better exploit the complementary strengths of the two modalities - motivated directly by the finding that simple late fusion did not improve accuracy despite the networks failing together on only 8.75% of cases, which is exactly the pattern that a better combination rule should be able to exploit. Beyond that: additional modalities; identification of autism subtypes from behavioural patterns, which the ADOS-item analysis makes plausible; and extension to home settings without specialised equipment. Not proposed, and needed: confidence intervals and a larger test sample; predictive values at realistic prevalence; sex-stratified evaluation; a non-autistic clinical comparison group; and an explicit statement of whether the ADOS recordings used as input contributed to the diagnoses used as labels. [RQ3.1] Two behavioural channels selected to be complementary, and the study's own analysis of what each captures is the most informative such account in the review. The video channel targets whole-body movement and gestural interaction within the child-examiner dyad, and its confidence relates most strongly to initiation of joint attention, quality of social overtures, unusual eye contact and pointing gestures - a coherent nonverbal social-communication cluster, and exactly what one would predict for a model of interactive body motion. The audio channel targets the full acoustic band without diarisation, so it contains child vocalisation, examiner speech and ambient sound from object manipulation - and its confidence relates most strongly to showing behaviour, pointing gesture, unusual sensory exploration and hand mannerisms, which are not vocal constructs at all. The authors draw the correct inference: the audio model is probably keying substantially on non-vocal sound produced by the child's interaction with objects, with sensory interests the single most correlated item, and possibly also on the examiner's prosodic adaptation to the child. This is a rare and important result for the review. It shows that a modality label ('audio') does not determine the construct measured, that a model can succeed by detecting the acoustic signature of behaviour rather than of speech, and that when a recording captures a dyad the model may be measuring the wrong member of it. Any study in this corpus using undiarised interaction audio inherits both possibilities, and none of the others examines them. [RQ3.2] Late fusion of two independently trained networks, with three combination rules compared and all results reported. The honest headline is that fusion did not improve accuracy materially: 82.5% for the confidence-gated ensemble against 80.0% for video alone and 78.8% for audio alone, a gain of two children out of eighty, and the authors name this as an important limitation rather than presenting the ensemble as a success. What fusion does deliver is two things worth recording. First, genuine error complementarity - both networks were simultaneously wrong on only 8.75% of test cases, meaning that roughly 90% of the errors made by one model were correctable in principle by the other, which is precisely the condition under which a better fusion rule should help and is the strongest argument for the authors' own proposed future work. Second, operating-point control: the OR rule yields sensitivity 0.90 at specificity 0.75 and the AND rule yields specificity 0.925 at sensitivity 0.60, so the same two models can be configured for a high-recall screening role or a high-precision confirmatory one. Presenting this as tunability rather than as a single best number is the correct framing for a screening application and is not done elsewhere in this corpus. The interpretability analysis further shows that the two modalities index partly different clinical constructs, which is the substantive justification for combining them at all. [RQ4.1] Two architectures matched to their data. For video, an ImageNet-pretrained VGG16 with its dense layers removed extracts per-frame features from 5-second segments, feeding a 512-unit LSTM, then 512 fully connected ReLU units and a softmax; segment predictions are filtered at 90% confidence and averaged across the session, with the child classified autistic if the mean exceeds 0.5. For audio, five Librosa feature families averaged along the time axis into a one-dimensional vector feed two 1D convolutional layers, max pooling, a third convolutional layer, dropout 0.5, flattening, 512 dense units and a softmax, trained with categorical cross-entropy and Adam at batch size 512 for 30 epochs. Both are conventional and appropriately sized for 160 children; the authors report that larger batch sizes and epoch counts increased validation loss, which indicates that capacity was actively constrained rather than maximised. Fusion is by simple rules rather than a learned combiner - which is both why it underperforms and why the authors identify better fusion as the obvious next step. [RQ4.2] The video representation is the study's most important technical decision and functions as a designed confound control. Rather than modelling raw frames, the authors apply OpenPose and plot the resulting skeletal keypoints over a plain black background at 320x240, 'hence preserving a visual gist of the social interaction between the examiner and the child'. This removes face, expression, clothing, body habitus, skin tone, room, furniture, lighting and every other appearance cue - so a classifier operating on it cannot be exploiting the identity and setting confounds that this review has documented throughout the image-based branch, where models trained on photographs may be recognising where an image came from rather than who is in it. Here the confound is architecturally excluded, not merely unmeasured. It also makes partial data sharing possible, which is why a de-identified pose subsample could be deposited on Zenodo when the raw video could not. The audio representation is the mirror image: the full band with no diarisation, retaining child voice, examiner voice and ambient sound, summarised as time-averaged MFCCs, Mel spectrogram, chromagram, spectral contrast and tonal centroid over 10-second windows. Time-averaging discards temporal structure within each window, so prosodic contour is only weakly represented - consistent with the finding that the audio model's predictive items are gestural and sensory rather than vocal. [RQ4.3] A complete confusion-matrix-derived set - accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, negative predictive value and F1 - reported for all five models in a single table, which is fuller than almost anything else in this corpus and unusual in presenting every ensemble variant rather than the best one. Reporting negative predictive value alongside precision is a further mark of care. Three gaps and two errors. No confidence intervals appear anywhere, on a test set of 80 children where a single case is worth 1.25 accuracy points and an exact binomial interval around 82.5% runs from roughly 72% to 90% - which means the ensemble's advantage over the video model alone, two children, is not distinguishable from noise. No positive predictive value at realistic prevalence is computed, although the paper is framed around screening and the balanced design makes the reported precision of 0.861 an artefact of the 1:1 construction; at a population base rate the same specificity of 0.875 would place the large majority of positive calls on non-autistic children. And the interpretive bands for what counts as good performance are not stated. The two errors are both in the abstract and neither affects the results section: the abstract describes 'higher specificity (92.5%, i.e., few false negatives) or sensitivity (90%, i.e. few false positives)', reversing the meaning of both terms, and gives the ensemble as 'Precision: 0.775, Recall: 0.861' where the table correctly has precision 0.861 and recall 0.775. Table 1 is internally consistent throughout. [RQ4.4] The most substantive interpretability work in the review, and the only instance of a study explaining its models in the vocabulary of the clinical construct rather than in the vocabulary of the input. Random regression forests were fitted with all 27 ADOS-2 items as predictors and each network's prediction confidence as the outcome; importance was assessed through three metrics simultaneously - percentage increase in mean squared error, increase in node purity, and p-value - and a third normalising forest was calibrated on the averaged confidence of both networks so that importances from the two separate models could be placed on a common scale and compared. The design of this analysis is careful in a way that saliency maps elsewhere in this corpus are not, because it produces claims that can be checked against clinical knowledge. The video result is coherent and expected: joint attention initiation, quality of social overtures, unusual eye contact and pointing gestures, a nonverbal social-communication cluster that a model of dyadic body motion should be sensitive to. The audio result is coherent and unexpected: showing behaviour, pointing gesture, unusual sensory exploration and hand mannerisms, none of which is a vocal construct. The authors follow this where it leads rather than around it, proposing that non-vocal ambient sound from object manipulation drove part of the classification and noting that sensory interests was the single most correlated item, and separately raising the possibility that the examiner's prosodic adaptation to the child contributes. An analysis that tells the authors their audio model is probably not listening to speech, reported as such, is worth more to this review than any number of attention heatmaps. [RQ4.5] Among the soundest validation designs in the review, with two residual issues that bound rather than undermine it. The 160 children were split 50-50 into training and test halves of 80, each containing 40 autistic and 40 typically developing children matched for age, sex and ADOS module - so the held-out half is not merely participant-disjoint but constructed to be comparable to the training half on the three variables most likely to drive an artefactual result. That is stronger than a random split and stronger than anything else charted here. Within the training half, 80% trained and 20% validated, and every hyperparameter decision - segment length for both modalities, MFCC count, batch size, epoch count - was made on that validation set with the test children untouched; the authors even report the direction of the failures they observed while tuning, noting that larger batch sizes and epoch counts increased validation loss. Segments are nested strictly within participants, so although tens of thousands of 5- and 10-second clips were generated, none of the within-participant leakage that dominates the image and frame-level branches of this corpus is possible. The reported figures are computed on 80 children. The first residual issue is statistical: 80 test children is small, one case is worth 1.25 accuracy points, no confidence intervals are given, and an exact interval around 82.5% would run from roughly 72% to 90% - so the ensemble's 2.5-point advantage over the video model, two children, cannot be distinguished from noise, and the paper's framing of the ensemble as the best model rests on a difference the data cannot resolve. The second is the reference-standard circularity discussed above: the diagnosis was supported by 'gold standard diagnostic assessments' and the model input is the ADOS session, so unless the diagnostic ADOS was a different session from the recorded one, the label is not independent of the material. The severity of this is limited - the model receives raw pose and undiarised audio rather than coded items, so it must recover from signal what a clinician judged, which is a genuine inference rather than a lookup - but it is not zero, and a single sentence stating whether ADOS entered the diagnostic decision would settle it. Set against these, the design's positive features are substantial: matched recording context across classes, appearance stripped from the video representation by construction, participant-level matched splitting, tuning confined to a validation partition, a complete metric table for every model variant, and an interpretability analysis that identifies a plausible confound in the authors' own audio channel. The reported 78.8% to 82.5% is one of the more trustworthy performance figures in this review. [RQ5.1] Not given as a formal keyword list in the retrieved text. Terms carried through the article: deep learning, multi-modal, ensemble, screening, semi-standardised social interaction, ADOS, pose estimation, OpenPose, digital phenotyping, prosody, diarization, joint attention, social overtures, sensory interests, random regression forest. The vocabulary spans computational and clinical registers evenly, reflecting a psychiatry department doing its own engineering rather than an engineering group applying methods to a clinical dataset. [RQ5.2] PLOS ONE 19(10):e0308388, Research Article, open access under CC BY; received 30 April 2024, accepted 12 July 2024, published 3 October 2024. PLOS ONE's structural requirements produced the data-availability statement, funding itemisation and competing-interests declaration, and the venue's data-sharing policy is visibly what prompted the considered middle position adopted here - raw recordings withheld because they contain faces and voices, a de-identified pose subsample deposited on Zenodo with a DOI, and training code published on GitHub. That is the policy working as intended, and it is worth noting for the review that the same policy which cannot compel raw sharing of identifiable child data did elicit a genuinely useful partial release, made possible by the study's own choice of a skeletal representation. [RQ5.3] Published October 2024 by the Psychiatry Department of the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Geneva with the Geneva School of Economics and Management, funded through a Swiss National Science Foundation Sinergia grant for digital phenotyping of autism, NCCR Synapsy, two further SNSF grants, the Private Foundation of the HUG, a university equipment grant and Fondation Pole Autisme. The framing is clinical and the argument for automation is stated without disparaging existing practice: the gold-standard diagnostic procedure is credited as 'the product of convergent clinical and research work over the past four decades', existing screening questionnaires are described as 'highly valuable' while varying in validity and replicability, and the gap identified is the years-long latency between first observable signs and diagnosis. For this review the study is one of the most useful included, for four reasons that are largely independent of its accuracy. Its recording context is matched across classes - both groups assessed with the same protocol in the same setting - which removes at a stroke the acquisition confound that this synthesis has had to record against the photograph, video-frame and clinic-versus-school audio studies. Its video representation strips appearance by construction, rendering pose as skeleton-on-black, so identity and setting cannot contribute to the classification; that is a designed answer to the confound rather than an assertion that none exists, and it also made partial data sharing possible. Its splitting is participant-level and matched on age, sex and ADOS module, with tuning confined to a validation partition carved from the training half. And its interpretability analysis, which regresses model confidence on all 27 ADOS items across both modalities with a normalisation model to make them comparable, produces the review's clearest demonstration that a modality label does not determine the construct measured: the audio model's most predictive items are showing, pointing, sensory exploration and hand mannerisms rather than anything vocal, and the authors conclude in their own voice that ambient non-vocal sound from object manipulation, and possibly the examiner's prosodic adaptation to the child, contributed to what they had labelled a speech-based classifier. That finding generalises to every study in this corpus using undiarised interaction audio. The performance itself - 80.0% video, 78.8% audio, 82.5% ensemble, on 80 held-out children - is modest, honestly reported, and roughly what one should expect from an unconfounded design, which is itself the most useful calibration this review can offer against the 95-100% figures reported elsewhere. Two cautions travel with it: no confidence intervals on an 80-child test set, where the ensemble's advantage over video alone is two children and cannot be distinguished from noise; and no statement of whether the ADOS sessions used as model input contributed to the diagnoses used as labels, which would take one sentence to resolve.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective algorithm-development study by the LISSI laboratory at Université Paris-Est Créteil with the University of Malaya, funded by a Malaysia-France bilateral grant. The autism data are the Self-Stimulatory Behaviours Dataset - 75 home videos posted to YouTube by parents and caregivers showing children spinning, head banging or arm flapping - of which 73 were retained after two exclusions for video quality, one child per video, split subject-disjointly into 44 children (3,214 seconds) for training, 15 (1,582 seconds) for validation and 14 (1,496 seconds) for test. The autism label rests on the authors' stated position that they are 'confident in the reliability of the parents who uploaded these videos' and therefore consider the children autistic; no clinical assessment exists for anyone. A non-autistic class was assembled from 'facial images of neurotypical youngsters' together with 'facial images of other ASD children', but its size, source and individual count are never reported, and the data-distribution table lists SSBD as the sole database for all three splits. Three further corpora - CK+, IEMOCAP and AffectNet - were used for the affect experiments. No age, sex, ancestry, cognitive or clinical information is reported for any group, and the paper contains no ethics or consent statement.
narrative_rows.methods: A Haar cascade selected frames and cropped faces, with only frames showing an observable face retained. Three architectures were compared across four datasets: a Perceiver transformer (LAMB optimiser, learning rate 0.001 with a three-epoch scheduler, weight decay 0.0001, dropout 0.0001, eight blocks of twelve heads with four cross-attention repetitions, patch size 4, 256x256 latent array), a CNN-WGAN trained with Wasserstein loss, and an ImageNet-pretrained Inception v3 from Keras with top layers removed. The Perceiver was used for autism classification and Inception v3 for affect regression. For autism detection, subjects were kept disjoint across splits and results were computed at 10% and 20% test proportions and under 5-fold cross-validation. The authors additionally created a new annotation layer: five raters, all trained on the software and a written protocol with worked examples, gave continuous arousal and valence ratings from 0 to 5 using mouse, keyboard or joystick while watching each video under supervision, with per-frame values averaged across raters and normalised to the -1 to 1 range, and an inter-annotator correlation matrix reported. Affect models were evaluated in two configurations: trained on AffectNet alone, and trained on AffectNet then fine-tuned on the annotated autism data without freezing layers.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Autism classification from face crops reached 74.5% accuracy with F1 73.7% and recall 73.2% at a 10% test split, 74.8% at 20%, and 75.2% under 5-fold cross-validation - a stable mid-seventies figure across three configurations. Discrete affect recognition reached 93.7-98.4% on laboratory-controlled CK+ and 57.3-62.2% on in-the-wild AffectNet, the controlled-versus-uncontrolled gap being made explicit by the study's own dataset taxonomy. Continuous affect on AffectNet gave concordance correlations of 0.342-0.513 for arousal and 0.373-0.661 for valence against published comparators reaching 0.606 and 0.845. The principal finding concerns transfer: a model trained solely on the neurotypical AffectNet corpus performed poorly on autistic children, while fine-tuning it on the newly annotated autism data produced 'noticeably superior outcomes', leading the authors to conclude that 'it is preferable to have a dataset where the data obtained relates to ASD children and not neurotypical subjects, specifically, when the task is to predict the values for valence and arousal'.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The non-autistic class is never described - not its size, its source, nor the number of individuals in it - so the classification result is a discrimination between two image populations of which only one is characterised, and may reflect a difference between corpora rather than between children; the paper's own data-distribution table, naming SSBD as the sole database across all splits, is inconsistent with a second class existing. Class balance is stated as balanced in the methods and as 'very imbalanced' in the results, leaving no determinable chance baseline for the reported 74.5%. The autism label is an inference from parental upload behaviour with an explicit statement of trust in the uploaders, and sits uneasily beside the authors' own listed limitation that 'existing datasets are not necessarily trustworthy'. Subject-disjointness is guaranteed only for the SSBD half of the data. Cropping to the face discards the stereotypies that define the corpus, which the authors implicitly acknowledge by proposing gesture analysis as future work. No demographic information exists for either class in a study classifying faces, where apparent age and sex-linked morphology are strong drivers. The 5-fold figure is reported as a best-of-folds validation accuracy rather than a mean held-out estimate. No specificity, confusion matrix or confidence interval accompanies the classification. There is no ethics or consent statement for identifiable children's home videos annotated frame by frame for emotional state. And the new annotations, offered as a dataset contribution, cannot be released because the authors 'do not have permission to share data'.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The third study in this review built on the SSBD YouTube corpus, and the one that handles it most carefully on splitting while leaving its result uninterpretable for a different reason. Its splitting practice is a useful counterexample to the frame-level branch: subjects are kept disjoint with the rationale stated, the partition is reported by child and by seconds of video rather than by frame count, and the resulting 74.5% is stable across a 10% split, a 20% split and 5-fold cross-validation. The authors themselves place this beside a cited comparator reporting 94.6% on the Kaggle facial-image corpus, noting only that the comparator used 'the data distribution to obtain better performances' - and this review has charted five Kaggle-corpus studies reporting 81.0% to 99.8% under image-level splitting. The contrast reinforces the synthesis's central observation that figures in the facial-image branch track the splitting and labelling scheme rather than any property of the children. What prevents this study's own figure from being usable is a reporting failure rather than a methodological one: the non-autistic class is never described, so no reader can say what the model discriminates between, and the paper's data table contradicts the existence of that class. The study's durable contribution lies elsewhere, in its affect work. It creates the first continuous arousal and valence annotations for autistic children, describes the protocol fully, reports inter-annotator agreement, and then subjects its own ground truth to sharper criticism than any other paper in this corpus directs at its labels - non-expert raters, reaction-time contamination of averaged continuous ratings, and no mechanism for handling disagreement, all volunteered. And it runs a genuine cross-population transfer test whose result matters well beyond this literature: an affect model trained on a large corpus of neurotypical faces estimates arousal and valence poorly in autistic children, and fine-tuning on autistic data materially improves it. That finding bears directly on the studies in this review that apply generic emotion-recognition models to autistic populations, and on any deployed system that would do the same. Two further items belong in the discussion: the paper's introduction cites Bone and colleagues' failure to reproduce machine-learning autism-diagnosis results on a larger and more balanced dataset, and states that the approach 'will not replace clinicians in terms of their expertise' - restraint that is rare in this branch; and against that, it describes autistic behaviour as 'abhorrent' in a paper whose data are home videos that families made of their own children, with no ethics or consent statement anywhere.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Seventy-three children in the autism class, one per video, from 73 of the 75 videos in the Self-Stimulatory Behaviours Dataset - home recordings posted to YouTube by parents and caregivers showing children spinning, head banging or arm flapping, two videos having been dropped for quality. The split is reported by child and by duration: 44 children and 3,214 seconds in training, 15 children and 1,582 seconds in validation, 14 children and 1,496 seconds in test. That per-child reporting is better than the frame-count reporting typical of this branch. What is entirely absent is the other half of the sample. The methods state only that 'in order to have a complete and balanced database to train this model, we extracted the frames featuring the faces of ASD children and gathered facial images of other ASD children and facial images of neurotypical youngsters' - so a non-autistic class exists, but its size, its source, the number of children in it and their characteristics are nowhere given, and the data-distribution table lists SSBD as the sole database for all three splits, which cannot be true if a second class is present. No age, sex, ancestry, cognitive or language information is available for anyone in either class. For a two-class facial image classifier, the composition of both classes is what determines the meaning of the result, and here only one is described. [RQ1.2] Mixed within a single paper, and the internal tension is worth recording. Some passages are attentive: the term neurotypical is defined explicitly as 'an individual whose neurological development and functioning are considered typical regarding the society's norms and expectations' - a definition that locates typicality in social expectation rather than in biology, which is a neurodiversity-adjacent formulation; the authors relay approvingly that 'ASD is not a disease'; and they observe that differences in emotional perception 'may be the cause for them to experience social and emotional isolation', locating the difficulty in the interaction rather than solely in the person. Against this, the clinical description reproduces the harshest vocabulary in the review: individuals with autism 'typically demonstrate a lack of social interaction and emotional intelligence as well as having repetitive, abhorrent, stigmatized, and fixated behavior'. Calling autistic behaviour abhorrent, in a paper whose data consist of home videos that families posted of their own children, is a serious lapse - and it sits two paragraphs from the statement that autism is not a disease. Elsewhere the register is standard medical ('individuals with ASD', 'ASD children', 'patients'). No autistic person or community is reported as involved in the annotation protocol, in defining what counts as an affective state, or in reviewing the use of family-uploaded videos. [RQ1.3] Absent for both classes, and more consequential than the usual absence because the study classifies faces. No age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic, cognitive or language information is reported for the 73 autistic children or for the undocumented comparison images. Three specific risks follow. Facial classifiers key strongly on apparent age and on sex-linked morphology, and autism is diagnosed roughly four times more often in boys, so an uncontrolled sex imbalance between classes could produce the entire result. The SSBD children were filmed by families who chose to post the footage publicly, which is a self-selected population by geography, language, internet access and disposition. And the comparison images, wherever they came from, will carry their own demographic profile, which cannot be matched because neither profile is known. The paper does note that the borrowed CK+ corpus contains people 'of various genders as well as ethnic backgrounds', so the relevance of demographic composition is recognised for other people's datasets and not applied to its own. [RQ1.4] None, and the paper's account of why is the most candid statement of provenance-based labelling in this review. SSBD videos were 'posted by parents/caregivers on YouTube', collected and annotated for stimming behaviour, and the authors reason: 'Therefore, and in the way the dataset is described, the data only concerns ASD children ... We are also confident in the reliability of the parents who uploaded these videos, and we, therefore, consider that the youngsters presented as the main subject of these videos are all autistic.' The autism label thus rests on two inferences - that a family posting a video of their child stimming implies a diagnosis, and that families are reliable reporters of that diagnosis - and on an explicitly stated act of trust. No clinical assessment, diagnostic instrument, medical record or clinician judgement exists for any child in the corpus. The comparison class is worse still: no basis whatever is offered for the non-autistic label, because the class itself is never described. Two structural consequences follow. Because the positive class comprises children whose families filmed and published their stereotypies, it is drawn from the visibly and severely affected end of the phenotype rather than from any representative spectrum. And because the paper elsewhere lists 'existing datasets are not necessarily trustworthy' as a limitation while simultaneously declaring confidence in these particular uploads, the two statements sit uneasily together. [RQ1.5] No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists. The study's own contribution on this axis is a new continuous affect layer - arousal and valence values for SSBD frames, produced by five trained annotators using continuous rating software with a mouse, keyboard or joystick, on a 0 to 5 scale, normalised to the -1 to 1 range for comparability with published work, with the per-frame values averaged across raters and an inter-annotator correlation matrix reported. This is a genuine measurement contribution and the authors subject it to the sharpest self-criticism in the paper: the annotators 'are not experts in affect and emotion estimation. Therefore, it is impossible to confirm that the information gathered is accurate'; averaging 'is subject to the annotators' reaction times', so that an inattentive rater's lag propagates into the label; and simple averaging 'does not deal with disagreements either'. The stated ambition of automated severity-level assessment, which would 'alert clinicians and parents when aggravation occurs', is not realised - affect level is not severity, and no severity data exist to validate against. The annotations themselves are not released, since the authors do not have permission to share data. [RQ2.1] Two aims are pursued in one pipeline: classify autism from face images, then estimate continuous affect in the identified autistic children, with a view to a longitudinal monitoring platform. The autism classification result is modest and stable - 74.5% accuracy with F1 73.7% and recall 73.2% at a 10% test split, 74.8% at 20%, and 75.2% under 5-fold cross-validation. The affect results are where the substance lies and they are structured as a genuine comparison across conditions: 93.7-98.4% for discrete affect on laboratory-controlled CK+, falling to 57.3-62.2% on in-the-wild AffectNet, with continuous-affect concordance correlations on AffectNet of 0.342-0.513 for arousal and 0.373-0.661 for valence. The finding the paper is built around, and the one worth carrying into the synthesis, is the transfer result: a model trained solely on AffectNet - neurotypical faces - performs poorly on autistic children, while fine-tuning it on the newly annotated autistic data produces 'noticeably superior outcomes', leading the authors to conclude that 'it is preferable to have a dataset where the data obtained relates to ASD children and not neurotypical subjects, specifically, when the task is to predict the values for valence and arousal'. That is an empirical demonstration that affect-recognition tools built on neurotypical populations do not transfer to autistic faces, which has direct implications for every deployed emotion-recognition system and for the several studies in this corpus that apply generic affect models to autistic children. [RQ2.2] No study setting exists. The autism data are home videos filmed by families on unspecified devices in unconstrained conditions and uploaded to YouTube; the comparison images have no stated origin at all. The paper is unusually thoughtful about setting as a variable, opening its dataset section with an explicit taxonomy - a controlled environment is one where 'researchers have a lot of control over factors that can affect the data being collected' and adjust them 'to reduce potential sources of error or bias', while an uncontrolled environment is one where 'data are obtained under natural or actual settings' without manipulation - and it categorises its four corpora accordingly, arguing that spanning both 'helps to understand a model's behavior'. That analysis is carried through rigorously for the affect task, where the drop from 98.4% on CK+ to 62.2% on AffectNet is precisely the controlled-versus-uncontrolled contrast made visible. It is not carried through for the autism task, where the same reasoning would ask whether the positive and negative images were acquired under comparable conditions - and where the paper's silence about the negative class means the question cannot even be posed. [RQ2.3] None for the autism data; the children were filmed by their families for their own purposes. For the affect layer the paper does define a paradigm, and describes it carefully: five annotators, all trained on the software and the protocol beforehand, watched the videos and gave instantaneous ratings of arousal and valence between 0 and 5 using a mouse, keyboard or joystick, with the authors present throughout to ensure the protocol was followed and with worked examples supplied. Ratings were averaged across annotators per frame and normalised to the -1 to 1 range used in the affect literature. The absence of a paradigm on the data side has a specific consequence the study half-recognises: what a child is doing when filmed determines their expression, and in SSBD every autistic child is by construction engaged in a stereotypy while the comparison children are doing something unknown - so the classifier and the affect model are both operating across an uncontrolled difference in activity as well as any difference in the children. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element, despite the stated goal being a longitudinal monitoring platform. There is no ethics statement, no institutional review board reference and no consent statement anywhere in the paper - a full-text search returns no occurrence of the word. The data are identifiable home videos of children, published by their families for reasons of their own, from which faces were cropped and then annotated frame by frame for emotional state by five raters in order to build an autism classifier. Whether families posting a video of their child's stimming for a community of other parents thereby consent to its use as autism training data, and whether a child depicted at two or three years old has any interest in the matter, are questions the paper does not raise. The one place the authors do discuss the trustworthiness of their data concerns label accuracy rather than the ethics of use. Funding under the Malaysia-France Bilateral Research Grant IF040-2021 is declared, competing interests are declared as none, and the data availability statement reads in full: 'The authors do not have permission to share data' - which means the annotations offered as the paper's dataset contribution cannot be obtained. [RQ2.5] No acquisition equipment; the videos were 'shot using various devices in unrestricted natural settings' by families. Analysis used a Haar cascade for frame selection and face cropping, and three architectures whose configurations are reported in useful detail - a Perceiver with the LAMB optimiser at learning rate 0.001 updated every three epochs, weight decay 0.0001, dropout 0.0001, eight transformer blocks of twelve heads with four cross-attention repetitions, patch size 4 and a 256x256 latent array; a CNN-WGAN trained with Wasserstein loss; and an ImageNet-pretrained Inception v3 taken from the Keras applications with top layers excluded. Continuous annotation used dedicated rating software accepting mouse, keyboard or joystick input. The heterogeneity of the source recording devices is acknowledged as a limitation - 'the unconstrained environment and conditions of acquisition and the bad images and videos quality' - but no normalisation, resolution criterion or channel compensation is described that would address it. [RQ2.6] Strong on procedure and empty at the one point that matters most. Well reported: all four datasets with their properties and their categorisation as controlled or uncontrolled, the two SSBD exclusions and the face-observability criterion for frame retention, the annotation protocol with the rater count, training, scale, software modality and supervision, the normalisation equation and the inter-annotator correlation matrix, the split proportions for every dataset, the subject-disjointness rule with per-split child counts and video durations, the complete Perceiver hyperparameter configuration and the evidence that alternatives were tried without gain, the Inception v3 provenance and layer handling, and formal definitions of every metric. Absent: the composition, source and size of the non-autistic image class; the total number of images in any split; code; and the new annotations, which cannot be shared. The first of these is disabling - a reader cannot determine what the classifier's 74.5% is a discrimination between, and the paper's own data-distribution table, which lists SSBD as the sole database across all three splits, is inconsistent with a second class existing at all. [RQ2.7] The stated limitations are unusually honest about measurement and silent about the study's central weakness. Three are listed formally - the scarcity and small size of public autism datasets, that 'existing datasets are not necessarily trustworthy', and the uncontrolled acquisition conditions and poor image quality - and the discussion volunteers three more concerning the annotation layer, each of them a real threat: the five raters 'are not experts in affect and emotion estimation.
