Therefore, it is impossible to confirm that the information gathered is accurate'; averaging their ratings 'is subject to the annotators' reaction times', so inattention produces lag that deviates from the ground truth; and simple averaging 'does not deal with disagreements either'. The introduction also cites Bone and colleagues' finding that on a larger and more balanced dataset they 'were unable to reproduce the results of several works that claim to drastically reduce the time to diagnose autism using machine learning', and the authors state that their own approach 'will not replace clinicians in terms of their expertise'. What is never addressed: the non-autistic class is undescribed, so the classification result is uninterpretable and may reflect a difference between image corpora rather than between children; the class balance is called balanced in the methods and 'very imbalanced' in the results, leaving no determinable chance baseline; the autism label rests on trusting YouTube uploads, which is presented as a warrant rather than examined as a limitation, and sits awkwardly beside the authors' own statement that existing datasets are not necessarily trustworthy; the subject-disjointness guarantee covers only the SSBD half of the data; no demographic information exists for either class in a study classifying faces; and there is no ethics or consent statement for identifiable children's home videos annotated for emotional state. [RQ2.9] Three directions, each tied to an identified weakness. Move from visual-only to audio-visual models. Replace the simple averaging of annotator ratings with a neural multi-label learning approach capable of handling disagreement and reaction-time lag - a direct response to the authors' own critique of their ground truth. And incorporate the subjects' gestures into both tasks, which is the most interesting of the three: the corpus is defined by gestural stereotypy, and cropping to the face discards exactly the behaviour that identifies the children. Not proposed, and prerequisite to interpreting the classification result: documenting the composition and source of the non-autistic class, and evaluating whether the classifier separates children or corpora. [RQ3.1] Two constructs, only one of which the pipeline is well matched to. The classifier targets facial appearance in crops taken from videos whose defining content is self-stimulatory movement - spinning, head banging, arm flapping - so the behaviour that identifies the corpus is cropped away before modelling, leaving whatever differs in the face. The authors recognise this obliquely by proposing gesture analysis as future work. The affect regressor targets emotional expression in the continuous arousal-valence plane, and here the construct choice is well argued: the paper notes that affective computing has concentrated on discrete emotion categories, that 'conventional methods of estimating or quantifying affect in neurotypical individuals are not effective for individuals with mental health disorders', and that no dataset of continuous affect labels for autistic children existed - which the authors then set out to remedy. The resulting demonstration that a neurotypical-trained affect model transfers poorly to autistic faces is a substantive statement about the construct itself: emotional expression in autistic children is not the same measurement problem as in neurotypical adults, and models built on the latter do not simply generalise. [RQ3.2] None implemented. Audio-visual fusion is stated as an aim in the introduction - 'audio-visual cues will also be used to extract emotional features' - and appears in the conclusion as future work, so the paper announces a fusion approach it does not deliver. The related-work section reports a prior audio-visual study reaching about 72%, with the observation that 'the facial expression part shows less accuracy because the features are less discriminative in comparison to the features used for the audio part (screaming and shouting)'. That observation is worth recording alongside the Geneva multimodal study charted elsewhere in this review, which found by a different route that its audio channel's predictive power came largely from non-vocal sound rather than speech: two independent studies pointing to acoustic events accompanying behaviour, rather than facial or vocal expression as such, as the carrier of the signal in in-the-wild recordings. [RQ4.1] Three architectures compared across four datasets and two task types, which is a broader and more systematic comparison than most of this branch attempts. A Perceiver transformer was chosen for autism classification on the grounds of image-classification performance and cross-instance weight sharing; an ImageNet-pretrained Inception v3 emerged as the best affect regressor; a CNN-WGAN was included for its discriminator's sensitivity to image authenticity. The authors report negative tuning results honestly - varying the Perceiver's latent dimension, head count and learning rate produced no improvement over the original paper's configuration - and they explain the Perceiver's poor regression performance mechanistically, attributing it to 'the absence of temporal information'. Comparison against published methods is included for every experiment, and the study's own models lose in several of them, which is reported without softening. [RQ4.2] RGB face crops produced by a Haar cascade, with only frames in which the child's face is observable retained and the number of frames per video varying accordingly. No landmark geometry, no morphometric derivation, no body pose and no temporal sequence for the classifier. Two consequences. Cropping to the face discards the stereotypies that define the corpus, so the classifier cannot use the behaviour that identified these children as autistic in the first place - which the authors implicitly acknowledge by proposing gesture analysis as future work. And retaining only frames with a visible face introduces a selection that could differ systematically between classes, since a child spinning or flapping presents their face to a home camera less consistently than a child photographed for a curated corpus would. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, F1 and recall for classification; mean squared error and concordance correlation coefficient for regression. The regression metric choice is well argued and the argument is worth recording: the authors note that a comparator 'did not report the performances of their approach according to the CCC despite it being the most popular metric for audio and visual affect recognition' and observe that 'it is possible that their approach is very accurate according to MSE but much less accurate according to CCC' - then demonstrate exactly that inversion in their own results, where Inception v3 beats the Perceiver on MSE while losing on CCC. Recognising that two metrics can rank models oppositely, and showing it in one's own data, is a level of measurement care rare in this corpus. The classification reporting is correspondingly weaker: no specificity, no confusion matrix, no confidence intervals, no positive predictive value, and - because the class balance is stated inconsistently - no determinable chance baseline for the reported 74.5%. [RQ4.4] None for the models. No saliency, attribution or feature analysis is reported for the classifier or the regressor, so what distinguishes the two image classes is never examined - which matters especially here, since the undocumented composition of the negative class means an attribution analysis is the only way a reader could tell whether the model responds to children or to corpora. The one transparency contribution is at the measurement layer: an inter-annotator correlation matrix showing each rater's agreement with the mean annotation, accompanied by the authors' own critique of the averaging procedure. That is honest reporting of label quality rather than model interpretability, but in a study whose labels are the weakest link it is arguably the more useful of the two. [RQ4.5] A study with better splitting practice than most of its branch and an unexaminable result, which is an instructive combination. The splitting is genuinely careful for the autism experiment: subjects are disjoint across partitions, the authors state why - 'in order not to distort the results or create overfitting' - and explain how it was achievable, since one child appears in one video. The partition is reported by child and by seconds of video rather than by frame count, which is precisely the disclosure the frame-level studies elsewhere in this review omit. Robustness is probed twice more, by varying the test proportion from 10% to 20% (74.5% to 74.8%) and by 5-fold cross-validation (75.2%), and the authors correctly note that a 5-fold arrangement approximates a 20% test split, so the agreement is expected rather than independent confirmation. All of this is sound. What defeats it is that the classifier's negative class is never described. For a two-class image model, the reported figure is a discrimination between two populations of images, and only one of those populations is characterised; if the non-autistic faces come from a curated corpus such as CK+ or AffectNet - both of which the study uses elsewhere - then the model may be separating home-video frames from studio or scraped photographs, and no splitting scheme could reveal it. The paper's own data-distribution table naming SSBD as the sole database across all three splits is incompatible with a second class existing, so the reporting is not merely incomplete but internally inconsistent. The class balance is likewise contradictory, called balanced in the methods and 'very imbalanced' in the results, which leaves the chance baseline for 74.5% undetermined. Two further points. The subject-disjointness argument rests on a property of SSBD alone, so whatever comprises the negative class has no stated leakage control - and the same corpus, under conventional splitting, was found by another study in this review to contain training-test pairs with cosine similarity up to 0.9714, indicating substantial near-duplication that subject-level splitting is designed to but may not fully address. And the 5-fold figure is reported as 'top-5 validation accuracy', a best-of-folds validation quantity rather than a mean held-out accuracy, so it is weaker evidence than it appears. Set against these, one part of the study's validation design is exemplary and belongs in the synthesis: the affect experiments constitute a true cross-population transfer test - train on neurotypical faces, evaluate on autistic children, then fine-tune - and the result, that the neurotypical-trained model transfers poorly and fine-tuning materially improves it, is both methodologically clean and substantively important. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder, deep learning, discrete affect recognition, continuous affect assessment, SSBD dataset. The set is method- and dataset-facing, with the corpus named explicitly - which is helpful for tracing the SSBD subliterature, of which this review now contains three members. Terms carried through the body: Perceiver, cross-attention, WGAN, Wasserstein loss, Inception v3, arousal, valence, concordance correlation coefficient, self-stimulatory behaviour, in-the-wild, lab-controlled, longitudinal monitoring. [RQ5.2] Biomedical Signal Processing and Control 89:105712, Elsevier; received 24 February 2023, revised 18 October 2023, accepted 5 November 2023, available online 8 November 2023, with a 2024 issue date. A signal-processing venue, and the fingerprints are visible in both directions: the architectural detail, the metric definitions, the four-dataset comparison and the careful argument about MSE versus CCC are all to a good engineering standard, while the absence of any ethics or consent statement for identifiable children's home videos, the undocumented comparison class and the absent demographics passed review without comment. The journal's structure elicited funding, competing-interests, author-contribution and data-availability declarations but has no field that would have prompted a human-subjects statement. [RQ5.3] Published 2023-2024 by the LISSI laboratory at Université Paris-Est Créteil with the Faculty of Computer Science and Information Technology at the University of Malaya, funded by a Malaysia-France bilateral research grant. The framing is affective computing rather than diagnosis: the goal is a platform for longitudinal monitoring that could alert clinicians and parents to deterioration, and the motivating claim is that affect measures developed on neurotypical people do not work for autistic people. For this review the study's value is concentrated in one finding and one contrast. The finding is that a model trained on AffectNet - a large in-the-wild corpus of neurotypical faces - performs poorly at estimating arousal and valence in autistic children, and that fine-tuning it on autistic data produces noticeably better results, from which the authors conclude that data relating to autistic children rather than to neurotypical subjects is what such a task requires. That is a clean empirical demonstration, in a corpus otherwise short of them, that emotion-recognition technology built on general populations does not transfer to autistic faces - which bears on the several studies in this review that apply generic affect models to autistic children, and on any deployed system that would do so. The contrast is between this study's modest, stable, subject-disjoint 74.5% on SSBD face crops and the 94.6% that the authors themselves cite from a study using the Kaggle facial-image corpus, noting only that it was 'on another dataset' whose 'data distribution' the comparator exploited. This review has charted five studies on that Kaggle corpus reporting 81.0% to 99.8% under image-level splitting, against the present study's mid-seventies under subject-level splitting on a different in-the-wild corpus - and the pattern is the one the synthesis has documented throughout: figures in this branch track the splitting and labelling scheme rather than any property of the children. Three cautions travel with the study. The autism label rests on the authors' stated confidence in parents who posted videos of their children stimming, with no clinical ascertainment of any kind. The composition of the non-autistic class is never disclosed, so the classification result cannot be interpreted, and the paper's own data table contradicts its existence. And there is no ethics or consent statement anywhere, in work that crops faces from identifiable children's home videos and has five non-expert raters annotate their emotional states frame by frame - a gap made more conspicuous by the fact that the paper does discuss the trustworthiness of its data, but only as a question about label accuracy.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective algorithm-development study on originally collected thermal imagery, conducted by the Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering at Vignan's Foundation for Science, Technology and Research, Andhra Pradesh, with no funding. Data were collected at Don Guanella Special School, Poonamallee, Chennai: 1,500 thermal images from 30 male autistic children aged 5 to 15, captured with a FLIR USB thermal camera calibrated at emissivity 0.98, distributed across four settings - 500 images from 10 students during outdoor play, 600 from 12 in the classroom, 200 from 4 in the dining area and 200 from 4 on the veranda - plus 20 videos collected for real-time testing that are never analysed. All participants are autistic and male; there is no comparison group, and the classification target is a three-level severity grade whose source is nowhere stated. No age distribution, cognitive level, comorbidity or current medication is recorded. The ethics declaration reads in full: 'Ethical Approval. Not required.', with no institutional review board reference and no consent or assent statement anywhere in the paper.
narrative_rows.methods: A three-stage pipeline. Viola-Jones face detection was followed by denoising with a non-decimated wavelet transform combined with a DnCNN, evaluated against alternative filters on PSNR and SSIM. The Deep Network-based Facial Mood Extraction model - eleven convolutional layers and three dense layers, 5x5 and 3x3 kernels, batch normalisation in blocks conv3 to conv5, 14 million parameters, 160x160 input, trained for 200 epochs with Adam at learning rate 0.0001, batch size 64 and dropout 0.2 - classified five mood categories: neutral, anger, sadness, fear and happiness. Skin temperature was measured directly from the calibrated thermal values. The two feature families were concatenated and passed independently to Random Forest, SVM and K-Nearest Neighbour classifiers predicting severity level 1, 2 or 3. Eighty per cent of the 1,500 images were used for training and 20% for validation, with no participant-level partitioning described and no cross-validation for the severity task. Predicted severity was then mapped to a medication dosage level - lower for level 1, moderate for level 2, higher for level 3 - across a list of agents including metformin, arbaclofen, cannabidiol, oxytocin, bumetanide, lovastatin and trofinetide.
narrative_rows.outcomes: The denoising pipeline outperformed comparison filters on PSNR and SSIM. The DN-FME mood model reached 96.39% accuracy with precision 96.60%, recall 96.53% and F1 96.54%, supported by two ablations: validation accuracy rose monotonically from 0.9521 to 0.9639 as dropout fell from 0.5 to 0.2, and batch normalisation raised it from 0.9378 to 0.9639. For three-class severity classification, Random Forest and SVM both reached 98.33% accuracy (RF precision 0.9848, recall 0.9825, F1 0.9832; SVM 0.9833, 0.9841, 0.9833), with KNN at 90.00%; AUCs were 0.9878, 0.9865 and 0.9268, and Random Forest was fastest at 0.056 seconds. The paper further reports that its classifiers outperform the clinical ABC method across all three severity levels, and that the resulting dosage recommendations 'aligned well with severity levels'.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The paper contains no limitations section. The 80-20 split is over 1,500 images from 30 children - roughly 50 images each - with no participant-level partitioning described and no cross-validation; since severity is a fixed attribute of a child and thermal images of the same child in the same setting are near-duplicates, identifying the individual recovers the label, and a 98.33% three-class accuracy is the expected arithmetic of that arrangement rather than evidence of a thermal severity signature. The severity labels have no stated source anywhere in the paper, so the predicted quantity is undefined, and the claim to outperform the clinical ABC method is logically incoherent if the ABC supplied those labels. Class sizes across the three severity levels are unreported, so no chance or majority-class baseline exists. Skin temperature, the primary feature, was measured across outdoor play, classroom, dining and veranda settings with no ambient compensation or environmental logging, so thermal environment and physical exertion are confounded with any physiological signal, and the four settings drew on overlapping groups of 10, 12, 4 and 4 children whose severity distribution is unstated. Current medication, which itself impairs thermoregulation and correlates with severity by construction, is unrecorded. No feature importance is reported, so whether temperature or mood drives the result is unknown despite Random Forest supplying it without extra work. All 30 participants are male. The 20 videos collected for real-time testing, which would have furnished a genuinely held-out evaluation, are never analysed. And there is no ethics approval, consent or assent for prospectively imaging 30 disabled children at a named residential institution.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This is the only study in the review whose proposed output is a psychiatric medication dosage rather than a diagnosis or a screening flag, and it is charted at length because that destination changes what a leaked accuracy means. Two aspects genuinely merit attention. The modality argument is the best sensor-level answer in this corpus to a problem the synthesis has documented repeatedly: thermal imaging requires no external illumination and, as the authors correctly state, 'is not affected by lighting conditions or skin tone', so it is structurally immune to the demographic and photographic fragility that undermines the visible-spectrum photograph studies charted alongside it. And the clinical motivation is the sharpest statement of the continuous-monitoring case in the review - a 15-minute checklist 'does not capture the full range of daily behavioral variations in children' - acted on by imaging children during play, lessons and meals rather than in a clinic, which is more ecologically valid data collection than almost anything else here. Neither strength survives the execution. The evaluation splits 1,500 images from 30 children at image level with no participant partitioning, so the classifiers can identify individuals and thereby their fixed severity labels; the labels themselves have no stated origin; the comparison against the clinical standard is incoherent if that standard produced the labels; class sizes are unreported so nothing anchors the 98.33%; skin temperature was captured across indoor and outdoor settings with no ambient compensation; current medication, which alters thermoregulation and tracks severity, is unrecorded; and the videos reserved for held-out testing are never analysed. The study also collapses multiple images per child into one fixed label, discarding precisely the within-day variation its own thesis exists to capture. Set beside the review's other high-accuracy results, it makes the strongest available case that leakage is not merely an inferential problem: here it produces a proposal to titrate psychiatric drugs for disabled children, in a paper that itself lists cardiac arrest and kidney failure among the consequences of getting the dose wrong, and that was conducted under the declaration 'Ethical Approval. Not required.' with no consent statement of any kind.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Thirty male autistic children aged 5 to 15, all attending Don Guanella Special School in Poonamallee, Chennai, contributing 1,500 thermal images distributed across four settings within the school: 500 images from 10 students during outdoor play, 600 from 12 students in the classroom, 200 from 4 students in the dining area and 200 from 4 students on the veranda, plus 20 videos collected for real-time testing that are never analysed. Every image is of an autistic child; the study contains no non-autistic participants and no diagnostic task, since the classification target is a three-level severity grade among autistic children only. Four features of the sample bound what can be learned from it. It is entirely male, so nothing reported can be assumed to apply to autistic girls, and the paper does not remark on this. It is small in the way that matters - 30 children, 50 images each - so image counts overstate the effective sample fiftyfold, and the reported 98.33% must be read against that. The children are drawn from a single residential special school, a setting that selects for higher support needs and makes the sample unrepresentative of the autistic population the framework's medication claim addresses. And the four capture settings differ physically in ways that directly affect the primary measurement: outdoor play in Chennai, a classroom, a dining area and an open veranda produce systematically different skin temperatures for reasons unrelated to autism, and the distribution of severity levels across those settings is never reported. [RQ1.2] Medical and deficit-framed throughout, with several formulations that are outdated or inaccurate. Autism is 'a developmental impairment with brain abnormalities', 'a pervasive neurodevelopmental disability', and the introduction speaks of the need for treatments that 'target the underlying abnormalities in the autistic brain'. Prevalence is presented in alarm terms - a rise 'from 1 in 5000 in 1975 to 1 in 45 by 2018' described as 'alarming' and as underscoring urgency - without acknowledging that changing diagnostic criteria and ascertainment account for much of that trend, which makes the framing a claim about incidence that the cited figures do not support. The children themselves appear almost entirely as objects of measurement and dosing: they are 'ASD children' and 'autistic children' whose 'behaviors' are to be monitored continuously so that medication can be adjusted, and no autistic person, family member or advocacy organisation is reported as involved in designing the framework or in judging whether continuous thermal surveillance of children at school is acceptable. One passage is more careful and deserves credit: the discussion of medication notes that 'autistic children may be more sensitive to medication effects and more prone to experiencing adverse drug effects compared to non-ASD children', and the introduction states plainly that the two approved medications 'do not effectively address the core symptoms of ASD and are associated with significant side effects'. That is an accurate and clinically important observation - but it is used to justify more precise dosing rather than to raise any question about the framework's premise that a camera should inform the dose. [RQ1.3] Almost nothing, and the omissions are unusually consequential because the output is a drug recommendation. Reported: age range 5 to 15, sex (all male), and school. Not reported: age distribution, any breakdown by severity level, cognitive or adaptive level, language, comorbidity, current medication, or socioeconomic background. Four specific problems follow. Thermoregulation and facial thermal patterns change substantially between ages 5 and 15, so if severity levels are unevenly distributed by age the classifier may be reading development rather than severity, and nothing reported allows this to be checked. Current medication is itself a determinant of skin temperature - antipsychotics including risperidone impair thermoregulation, which is a documented and clinically monitored effect - so children already on higher doses because they are more severely affected may be thermally distinguishable for pharmacological rather than behavioural reasons, a circularity that would produce exactly the reported result. Comorbid epilepsy, intellectual disability and sensory conditions are common in a special-school population and affect both behaviour and autonomic function. And the all-male sample means the framework has no evidence base for half the population it would be applied to. The one demographic issue the paper does engage is skin tone, and it engages it well: thermal imaging is argued to be preferable to visible-spectrum facial analysis precisely because it 'is not affected by lighting conditions or skin tone', which is a genuine sensor-level answer to a fairness problem that most face-based studies in this review leave unexamined. [RQ1.4] There is none for diagnosis and none stated for severity, and the second gap is the more damaging. All 30 children are described as autistic on the basis of attending a special school; no diagnostic instrument, clinician judgement or record is cited for any of them. The classification target is severity level 1, 2 or 3, and the origin of those labels is nowhere given - not in the dataset description, not in the methodology, not in the results. The Aberrant Behavior Checklist is discussed at length in the introduction as the 58-item instrument clinicians use to grade severity and guide dosage, and it is the obvious candidate, but the paper never states that it was administered to these children, by whom, when, or with what training. Two consequences follow. First, what the classifiers predict is simply unknown, so the 98.33% cannot be interpreted even setting aside the splitting problem. Second, the paper's central comparative claim becomes incoherent: it reports that the machine learning methods 'outperform the clinical ABC method' in classifying severity levels and presents a table comparing their accuracies. If the ABC supplied the labels, a model can at best reproduce it and cannot exceed it, and any apparent excess is measurement of the model's agreement with its own training signal; if some independent criterion existed against which both were scored, the paper does not say what it was. A claim to beat the clinical standard, in a paper proposing to adjust medication, requires the standard to be specified, and it is not. [RQ1.5] The three-level severity grade is the study's only clinical variable, it is the classification target, and its derivation is unstated - so the study has a severity measure in the sense that it predicts one, and none in the sense that it validates against anything documented. No cognitive, adaptive, language or behavioural instrument is reported as administered, and no continuous score is available against which the predicted probability could be correlated. This is the more striking because the study's own rationale is a severity-measurement argument, and a good one: the ABC takes about 15 minutes and 'does not capture the full range of daily behavioral variations in children', so a measure that samples continuously across a school day would in principle capture something a single sitting cannot. That argument is the strongest case for continuous behavioural monitoring anywhere in this review. But the study cannot demonstrate it, because it trains against labels that must themselves have come from a brief assessment of exactly the kind it criticises, and it never examines whether its predictions vary within a child across the day - which is the analysis its own thesis calls for and which its four-setting, multi-image-per-child data would support. [RQ2.1] The aim is a framework for continuous thermal monitoring of autistic children that classifies severity and thereby informs psychiatric medication dosing, motivated by the argument that the ABC's brief administration cannot capture daily behavioural variation and that imprecise dosing risks adverse effects the paper lists as including cardiac arrest, kidney failure, irregular heartbeats and high blood pressure. Three results are reported. The denoising pipeline, combining a non-decimated wavelet transform with a DnCNN, outperformed comparison filters on PSNR and SSIM. The DN-FME facial-mood network reached 96.39% accuracy across five categories - neutral, anger, sadness, fear, happiness - with two properly conducted ablations showing dropout at 0.2 outperforming 0.5 (0.9639 against 0.9521) and batch normalisation adding four points (0.9639 against 0.9378). And the severity classifiers reached 98.33% for Random Forest and SVM with AUCs of 0.9878 and 0.9865, against 90.00% for KNN. The paper then reports that its classifiers outperform the clinical ABC method and presents a severity-to-dosage mapping. The engineering components are competently executed and reported; the clinical components rest on labels of unstated origin, an image-level split that allows the classifiers to identify individual children, and a comparison against a clinical standard that is very likely the source of the labels themselves. [RQ2.2] A residential special school in Chennai, with images captured across four naturalistic contexts during the school day - outdoor play, classroom, dining area and veranda. This is genuinely ecological data collection, and multi-context sampling within an ordinary day is exactly what a continuous-monitoring argument requires; very few studies in this review collect behavioural data in the settings where children actually spend their time. The same feature creates the study's central measurement hazard, and it is specific to this modality. Skin temperature is determined substantially by ambient temperature, solar radiation, airflow and physical exertion, all of which differ sharply between an outdoor playground in Tamil Nadu and an indoor dining hall. No ambient compensation, environmental logging or per-setting normalisation is described, and the image counts by setting (500, 600, 200, 200) come from different and overlapping groups of children (10, 12, 4, 4) whose severity levels are not reported. If severity is unevenly distributed across capture settings - which with 4 children in two of them is likely - then the thermal environment is confounded with the label, and the confound would survive any splitting scheme. A per-setting stratified analysis would have addressed this directly and is not performed. [RQ2.3] None, by design. Images were captured during ordinary school activities with no instruction, elicitation or standardisation, which is the correct choice for a framework whose entire argument is that brief structured assessments miss daily variation. The cost is that nothing is held constant: a child running outdoors, sitting in a classroom and eating a meal differ in exertion, posture, distance from the camera, head angle and thermal environment, and all of these affect both the measured skin temperature and the appearance of the face to a mood classifier. The paper does not report distance to subject, viewing angle, or whether images within a setting were taken in a single session. What is missing is the analysis that this data structure uniquely enables and that the study's own thesis demands: whether a child's predicted state varies across the day and across contexts, which would be evidence of continuous behavioural measurement rather than of static classification. Instead the design collapses multiple images per child into a single per-child severity label, which discards precisely the temporal variation the framework exists to capture. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional despite being framed as continuous monitoring - no child is followed over time, no repeat measurement is analysed, and the 20 videos collected 'for real-time testing to assess the algorithm's performance in dynamic settings' are mentioned once and never reported on. Longitudinal study appears only as future work. The ethics position is the most serious in this review and is stated in five words: 'Ethical Approval. Not required.' There is no institutional review board reference, no ethics committee, no consent statement and no assent statement anywhere in the paper. The participants are 30 disabled children aged 5 to 15, resident at a named special school whose full postal address is printed in the article, thermally photographed during play, lessons and meals, in a study whose declared purpose is to automate adjustment of their psychiatric medication. Who authorised the imaging, whether guardians consented, and whether the children were told what was happening are all unaddressed. This exceeds the ethics gaps recorded elsewhere in this review for the web-scraping studies, because the data here were collected prospectively and in person from a dependent institutionalised population rather than harvested from material families had already made public. The study declares no funding; competing interests are not stated; and the data - identifiable thermal images of these children - are offered to anyone who asks. [RQ2.5] A FLIR USB thermal imaging camera calibrated at an emissivity of 0.98, with analysis in MATLAB 2023a on a Dual-Core E5700. Reporting the emissivity value is good practice and is more acquisition detail than most studies in this review provide. The choice of modality is also well argued on grounds that matter for this corpus: thermal imaging needs no external illumination, is unaffected by lighting conditions, and - the point worth carrying into the synthesis - is 'not affected by ... skin tone', which is a sensor-level answer to the demographic fragility that this review has documented repeatedly in visible-spectrum facial analysis. What is missing is everything needed to interpret an absolute temperature reading: camera model, spatial resolution, noise-equivalent temperature difference, distance to subject, and ambient temperature and humidity at each capture. For a study whose primary feature is skin temperature and whose images span outdoor and indoor settings, the absence of ambient logging is not a minor reporting gap but a limit on what the measurement means. [RQ2.6] Sharply divided between the signal-processing work, which is well documented, and the clinical work, which is not. Reported: the collection site by name and postal address, the camera and its emissivity setting, image counts by capture context with the number of students in each, age range and sex, the denoising pipeline with PSNR and SSIM evaluation against alternatives, the DN-FME architecture with its eleven convolutional and three dense layers, kernel sizes, parameter count and input resolution, the complete hyperparameter table, two ablation tables with numeric results, the three severity classifiers, the AUC values, all metric formulae and the computation-time comparison. Not reported: the origin of the severity labels; the origin of the facial-mood labels, which someone must have assigned to thermal images of these children and which the paper never mentions; the class distribution across severity levels; whether the 80-20 split respected participants; hyperparameters for the three classifiers; ambient conditions; results from the 20 videos; code; and any ethics or consent arrangements. A reader could reimplement the denoising and the mood network and could not reconstruct or evaluate the severity result at all. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section. The future-work paragraph names five extensions - more diverse and representative samples, additional modalities such as speech or genetic information, ensemble models, longitudinal designs, and evaluation in real-world clinical settings - which concede by implication that the present sample is neither diverse nor representative and that nothing has been clinically evaluated, but none of these is allowed to qualify any conclusion. What should have been stated: the 80-20 split is over 1,500 images from 30 children with roughly 50 images each and no participant-level partitioning, so the classifiers can identify the child and thereby the label, and a 98.33% three-class accuracy is the expected arithmetic of that arrangement rather than evidence about thermal signatures of severity. The severity labels have no stated source, so the target is undefined. The comparison against 'the clinical ABC method' is incoherent if the ABC produced those labels. Class sizes are unreported, so no baseline exists. Skin temperature was measured across outdoor and indoor settings without ambient compensation, and if severity is unevenly distributed across settings the environment is confounded with the label. All participants are male. Current medication - itself a determinant of thermoregulation, and correlated with severity by construction - is unrecorded. No feature importance is given, so it is unknown whether temperature or mood drives the result. The 20 held-out videos are never analysed. And there is no ethics approval or consent for prospectively imaging disabled children in an institution. [RQ2.9] Five directions are listed: larger and more diverse samples, additional modalities including speech and genetic information, ensemble models, longitudinal designs to track change over time, and evaluation in real-world clinical settings. The fourth and fifth are the ones the framework actually requires, and their inclusion is a tacit admission that a system proposed for continuous longitudinal monitoring and medication adjustment has been evaluated neither longitudinally nor clinically. Not proposed, and prerequisite to any of the above: participant-disjoint evaluation, disclosure of how severity labels were obtained, per-setting analysis to separate thermal environment from physiological signal, recording of current medication, inclusion of girls, and ethics review. [RQ3.1] Two constructs from one sensor, and the choice is better motivated than most in this review. Facial mood is classified into five categories - neutral, anger, sadness, fear and happiness - and skin temperature is measured directly, on the physiological rationale that pulsating blood flow drives the largest facial temperature variations and that emotional change produces detectable thermal change in facial skin. The target is therefore emotional state and autonomic arousal rather than social communication, gaze or motor stereotypy, which distinguishes this study from nearly all of the corpus and connects it plausibly to the clinical problem it addresses: the medications at issue are prescribed largely for irritability and agitation, so a continuous measure of affective state and arousal is the right construct for titrating them. Three problems attach to the execution. The mood labels for thermal images of these particular children must have been assigned by someone, and the paper never says who or how - so a five-category emotional ground truth exists with no stated provenance, in a population whose facial expression is itself atypical. Skin temperature is confounded with ambient conditions and exertion across four physically different capture settings with no compensation. And no feature importance is reported for the severity classifiers, so whether the discriminative information lies in mood or in temperature - a question with entirely different clinical implications - is unknown. [RQ3.2] Two feature families from a single thermal sensor - learned mood categories and measured temperature - concatenated for severity classification. This is within-modality fusion rather than multi-sensor fusion, and no ablation separates the two contributions, which is the analysis that would give the result whatever interpretive content it might have. The omission is notable because it was free: Random Forest supplies feature importances by default and the paper reports Random Forest results without them. Without that decomposition, an accuracy of 98.33% is consistent with the model reading affective state, with it reading ambient temperature at the moment of capture, and with it reading individual identity across an image-level split - and the study provides no means of distinguishing them. [RQ4.1] A three-stage pipeline, competently constructed at each stage. Viola-Jones face detection, then denoising by a non-decimated wavelet transform combined with a DnCNN, then the DN-FME network - eleven convolutional layers and three dense layers, 5x5 and 3x3 kernels, batch normalisation in blocks conv3 to conv5, 14 million parameters, 160x160 input - and finally Random Forest, SVM and KNN for three-class severity. Model sizing is reasoned rather than assumed: the authors explain that a smaller input resolution and limited data made a dropout of 0.5 counterproductive because it 'resulted in dropping useful information necessary for learning features', and they demonstrate the point with a monotonic table of validation accuracy across seven dropout values. Choosing classical classifiers for the final stage is also appropriate to 30 children. The gap is at that final stage: no hyperparameters are reported for any of the three classifiers, and no tuning procedure is described - so the stage carrying the paper's headline result is the least documented. [RQ4.2] Denoised thermal face images at 160x160 for the mood network, and a concatenation of learned mood output with measured skin temperature for the severity classifiers, whose dimensionality is never stated. Two representational points matter. Absolute skin temperature is only meaningful relative to ambient conditions, and no normalisation or ambient reference is applied, so the same child at the same physiological state would yield different feature values outdoors and indoors. And each image is treated as an independent observation despite 50 coming from each child, so the representation carries no notion of within-child variation - which is exactly what a continuous-monitoring framework should model and what the paper's own critique of the 15-minute ABC assessment implies it should measure. [RQ4.3] A reasonable metric set applied at every stage - PSNR and SSIM for denoising, accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for both classification stages, ROC curves with AUC for severity (RF 0.9878, SVM 0.9865, KNN 0.9268), and computation time - with all formulae defined explicitly. What is missing determines whether any of it can be read. Class sizes across the three severity levels are never given, so neither the chance level nor the majority-class baseline is known and 98.33% has no reference point. There are no confidence intervals, on 1,500 images from 30 children where the effective sample is 30. There are no confusion matrices and no per-class breakdown, so whether the mild and moderate classes are distinguished at all - the clinically important discrimination for dosing - cannot be seen. There is no specificity, and the ROC description conflates specificity with the false positive rate. And the comparison table reporting that the classifiers exceed 'the clinical ABC method' has no stated criterion for either, so the numbers in it cannot be interpreted. [RQ4.4] Present for the mood model at the level of its outputs - five named, clinically legible emotion categories, with two ablations documenting the architectural choices and their numeric effects - and entirely absent for the severity classifiers, which is where a system recommending medication dosages most needs it. No feature importance is reported despite Random Forest providing it without additional work, so it is unknown whether the model responds to skin temperature or to facial mood, to which mood categories, or to which facial regions. Nothing links a severity prediction to any observable property of a child that a clinician could inspect, challenge or corroborate. The paper's own framing makes this gap sharper than usual: it proposes replacing a 58-item instrument, whose items are explicit and auditable, with a classifier whose basis is not reported, and it presents the substitution as an improvement in precision. [RQ4.5] The single sentence describing evaluation is the study's undoing: '80% of the dataset was allocated for training purposes while the remaining 20% was used for performance validation'. The dataset is 1,500 images from 30 children, approximately 50 images each, and no participant-level partitioning is mentioned anywhere - the word 'split' appears nowhere else in the paper, and no cross-validation is performed for the severity task. On the natural reading, about 40 images of every child are in training and 10 in test. Severity is a fixed attribute of a child, so recognising the child suffices to recover the label, and thermal facial images of the same child in the same setting are near-duplicates of one another. A 98.33% three-class accuracy is therefore the expected arithmetic of the arrangement rather than evidence that thermal features encode severity, and the same is true of the AUC of 0.9878. This is the same failure the review has documented in the scanpath-image, video-frame and EEG branches, appearing here in a fourth modality, and it is compounded by four further problems. The severity labels have no stated source, so the quantity being predicted is undefined. The class distribution is unreported, so no baseline exists against which 98.33% could be judged even if the split were sound. The claim that the classifiers 'outperform the clinical ABC method' is incoherent if the ABC supplied the labels, and no alternative criterion is described. And skin temperature, the primary feature, was captured across outdoor play, classroom, dining and veranda settings with no ambient compensation, from overlapping groups of 10, 12, 4 and 4 children whose severity levels are not reported - so if severity is unevenly distributed across settings, thermal environment is confounded with the label in a way that no splitting scheme could remove. The remedy was available and unused: 20 videos were collected 'for real-time testing to assess the algorithm's performance in dynamic settings' and would have provided a genuinely held-out evaluation, but no result from them is reported. What makes this record worth stating at length is the destination of the number. A leaked accuracy in a diagnostic paper produces an overstated claim; here it produces a proposal to set the dose of psychiatric medication for disabled children, in a paper that itself lists cardiac arrest and kidney failure among the consequences of getting the dose wrong. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, facial moods, skin temperature, ASD classification, deep learning, machine learning. The set names the population, both feature families, the task and the methods, and is more balanced than the method-only lists typical of engineering venues in this corpus. Terms carried through the body: thermal imaging, emissivity, Aberrant Behavior Checklist, medication dosage, Non-Decimated Wavelet Transform, DnCNN, PSNR, SSIM, Viola-Jones, DN-FME, continuous monitoring, severity levels. [RQ5.2] Biomedical Signal Processing and Control 100:107009, Elsevier; received 25 November 2023, revised 8 August 2024, accepted 30 September 2024, online 10 October 2024, with a 2025 issue date. The same journal published another study charted in this review, and the pattern is consistent across both: signal-processing components are held to a reasonable standard - denoising evaluated against alternatives on PSNR and SSIM, architectural choices supported by ablation, hyperparameters tabulated - while the clinical apparatus passes without scrutiny. Here that meant an article proposing automated psychiatric medication dosing for children was published with the declaration 'Ethical Approval. Not required.', with no stated source for its outcome labels, with no participant-level validation, and with no limitations section. The journal's declaration structure elicited statements on ethics, funding, data availability and authorship, so the ethics field was completed - with a denial of applicability that went unqueried. [RQ5.3] Published 2024-2025 by the Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering at Vignan's Foundation for Science, Technology and Research in Andhra Pradesh, with data collected at a special school in Chennai and no funding. The framing is pharmacological rather than diagnostic, and this makes the study unique in the review: its output is not a diagnosis or a screening flag but a psychiatric medication dosage level, mapped from a predicted severity grade across a named list of agents including metformin, arbaclofen, cannabidiol, oxytocin, bumetanide, lovastatin and trofinetide. Two things about it deserve to be carried into the synthesis, one positive and one cautionary. The positive: the modality argument is the best-reasoned sensor-level answer in this corpus to a problem the review has documented repeatedly in visible-spectrum facial analysis, since thermal imaging requires no illumination and, as the authors correctly note, 'is not affected by lighting conditions or skin tone' - so a face-based method is proposed that is structurally immune to the demographic fragility that undermines the photograph studies charted here. The clinical motivation is also the sharpest statement of the continuous-monitoring case anywhere in the review: a 15-minute checklist 'does not capture the full range of daily behavioral variations in children', and the children were accordingly imaged during play, lessons and meals rather than in a clinic. The cautionary point is that neither strength is realised. The 80-20 split is over images rather than children, with about 50 images per child, so the classifiers can identify individuals and thereby their fixed severity labels, and 98.33% is what that arrangement produces; the severity labels themselves have no stated source, making the predicted quantity undefined; the claim to outperform the clinical ABC is incoherent if the ABC supplied those labels; class sizes are unreported so no baseline exists; skin temperature was measured across indoor and outdoor settings with no ambient compensation, confounding environment with any physiological signal; no feature importance distinguishes temperature from mood; the 20 videos reserved for real-time testing are never analysed; the sample is entirely male; current medication, which itself alters thermoregulation and correlates with severity by construction, is unrecorded; and there is no limitations section. Above all, the study was conducted on 30 disabled children at a named residential special school under the declaration 'Ethical Approval. Not required.', with no consent or assent statement of any kind, and offers its identifiable thermal images to anyone on request. For a review assessing what this literature does with its findings, this is the clearest case of a leaked accuracy attached to the highest-stakes recommendation in the corpus - a paper that lists cardiac arrest and kidney failure among the consequences of imprecise dosing, and then proposes that an image-level-split classifier of unstated provenance should inform the dose.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective algorithm-development study by groups at the King Salman Center for Disability Research, Riyadh, and three Saudi universities, using the public Kaggle autistic-children facial image corpus: 2,940 RGB images of children stated to be aged 2 to 14, comprising 1,327 in an autistic subfolder and 1,613 in a non-autistic subfolder. The paper describes the construction of the two classes directly - the autistic subfolder holds images of autism, while 'the non-autistic subfolder had images randomly retrieved from web searches'. No child in either class is known to have received a diagnostic assessment, no diagnostic instrument or record is cited, and the number of distinct children behind the images is never stated. No age distribution, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic, cognitive or clinical information is available for either class.
narrative_rows.methods: Images were rescaled to [0, 1] and augmented by 10% shear, 10% zoom and horizontal flipping, described as expanding the training dataset. The corpus was partitioned 80% training, 10% validation and 10% test at image level, with no participant-level partitioning described. Three ImageNet-pretrained architectures - ResNet50, Inception-V3 and VGG-19 - were fine-tuned on 224x224x3 inputs with categorical cross-entropy loss, the SGD optimiser and a maximum of 25 epochs. Evaluation reported per-class precision, recall and F1 with support counts, overall accuracy, weighted averages, confusion matrices, training and validation accuracy and loss curves, an ROC figure for Inception-V3, and a comparison table against ten prior studies using the same corpus.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Inception-V3 reached 98% accuracy (non-autistic precision 98%, recall 97%; autistic precision 97%, recall 98%) with 8 false positives and 5 false negatives on 588 samples; VGG-19 reached 97% with 9 false positives and 7 false negatives; ResNet50 reached 96%. Inception-V3 training accuracy rose to 0.9992 against a validation accuracy of 0.9779, and VGG-19's training accuracy exceeded 0.9854 before a decline the paper notes at epochs 24-25. All three result tables are headed 'Validation results' with support of 294 per class, so the reported figures come from the validation partition; the 10% test partition defined in the methods is never reported on. The paper's own comparison table places ten prior studies on the same corpus between 80.05% and 96%.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The class label records the collection route - an autism-labelled folder against web-search results - which the paper states as a fact of the dataset and never treats as a problem. No diagnostic reference standard exists for any image. No demographic information is available for either class in a study that classifies faces, across an age range of 2 to 14 in which facial appearance changes profoundly, and with a physiognomic premise resting on measurements that vary systematically with age, sex and ancestry. The split is at image level with the number of distinct children unstated, so images of one child can fall on both sides. All reported figures come from the validation partition rather than the defined test partition, so model selection and performance estimation share data. The support counts of 294 per class total 20% of the corpus rather than the stated 10% share and are exactly balanced although the corpus is 1,327 to 1,613, so the evaluation composition cannot be reconstructed and it is unclear whether augmentation reached it. No chance baseline is given against a 54.9% majority class, and no prevalence-adjusted predictive value. The third stated contribution - an analysis of which facial features drive detection - does not appear anywhere in the paper. And the abstract, introduction and results tables disagree about which architectures were compared and which performed best.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The sixth study in this review built on the Kaggle facial-image corpus, and it contributes three things to the synthesis beyond another figure. It states the provenance confound more plainly than any of the others, in its own methods section: the non-autistic images were 'randomly retrieved from web searches' while the autistic images came from an autism collection - which is the whole of the review's case about this corpus, supplied by a paper that draws no conclusion from it. Its Table 1 is the most complete catalogue of the subliterature anywhere in the corpus, listing ten prior studies on these same images at 80.05%, 84.66%, 86%, 87.9%, 89%, 89.87%, 90.5%, 90.67%, 91.3%, 92%, 93.24% and 96%, which documents both the volume of effort invested in a dataset with no diagnostic ascertainment and the fact that the reported accuracies cluster below the 98% claimed here - a figure that is, moreover, a validation rather than a test result. And its introduction contains the only passage in this branch that names the harms of autism identification as such, acknowledging 'the potential for labeling, which may impact the child's self-esteem and social relationships' and 'a risk of overdiagnosis or misdiagnosis, leading to unnecessary interventions and therapies'. That the paper then offers artificial intelligence as the remedy for those risks - without explaining how a classifier trained on web-scraped images with no diagnostic ascertainment would reduce mislabelling - is the clearest instance in the review of the access argument absorbing its own counterargument. The study is otherwise unremarkable: three standard pretrained architectures, standard augmentation, image-level splitting, and a claimed feature-importance analysis that was never performed, in a paper whose own conceded position is that 'the research gap in ASD identification using images persists, despite the proposed system achieving 98% accuracy on a benchmark dataset'.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] There are no participants. The units are 2,940 RGB images from the Kaggle autistic-children facial dataset, split 1,327 autistic and 1,613 non-autistic, described as children aged 2 to 14, organised into two folders. The number of distinct children behind either count is never stated. The decisive fact is the paper's own description of how the two folders were built: 'The autistic subfolder included images of ASD, while the non-autistic subfolder had images randomly retrieved from web searches.' The class label therefore records the collection route rather than any assessment of the child depicted - the same provenance confound this review has recorded for five other studies on this corpus family, stated here more plainly than in any of them. No age distribution, sex, ancestry, cognitive, language or clinical information is available for either class, and no demographic comparison between them is possible. [RQ1.2] Predominantly medical and physiognomic, with one passage of genuine ethical awareness that the paper then argues past. Autism is 'a mental condition characterized by challenges in communication, restricted behaviors, difficulties with speech, non-verbal interaction, and distinctive facial features in children', and is elsewhere called 'this disease'. The physiognomic framing is explicit and forms the study's premise: autistic people 'often present distinct facial morphological characteristics' including 'broader upper faces, wider eyes, shorter nasal bridges, and narrower cheeks', described as 'increasingly recognized as potential biomarkers'. Against this, the introduction contains a paragraph absent from every other paper in this branch, acknowledging the harms of early identification itself: 'A significant concern is the potential for labeling, which may impact the child's self-esteem and social relationships. There is a risk of overdiagnosis or misdiagnosis, leading to unnecessary interventions and therapies.' Naming labelling, self-esteem and overdiagnosis as risks of the enterprise the paper is contributing to is a real acknowledgement. What follows undoes it: the authors propose that these dangers may be mitigated by using artificial intelligence, without explaining how a facial classifier trained on web-scraped images with no diagnostic ascertainment would reduce the risk of mislabelling a child. No autistic person or organisation is reported as involved. [RQ1.3] Absent apart from a stated age range of 2 to 14, and consequential for a facial classifier. No sex distribution, ancestry, socioeconomic, cognitive or clinical information exists for either class, and none could, given how the corpus was assembled. Three risks follow directly. Facial appearance changes profoundly between ages 2 and 14, so an age difference between a class drawn from autism-related material and a class drawn from general web search would be sufficient to produce the reported separation. Autism is diagnosed roughly four times more often in boys and facial classifiers key strongly on sex-linked morphology, so an unmeasured sex imbalance is an untestable alternative explanation. And ancestry composition is likely to differ between an autism-focused collection and a general web search, with no means of checking. The paper's motivating claims are morphometric - upper-face width, eye width, nasal bridge length, cheek narrowness - every one of which varies systematically with age, sex and ancestry, so the demographic gap is not incidental to the hypothesis but fatal to testing it. [RQ1.4] None. The autism label means an image was placed in the autistic subfolder of a Kaggle collection; the non-autistic label means an image was returned by a web search. No child in either class is known to have been assessed, no diagnostic instrument or clinician judgement is cited, and the paper does not identify the absence as a limitation - it reports the folder structure factually and moves on. This is the sixth study in the review resting on this corpus, and the position is unchanged: whatever separation the models achieve, it is a separation between two collections of internet images, and the paper supplies the description that makes this plain. [RQ1.5] None. No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists for any image, and none is possible from a web-assembled corpus. [RQ2.1] The stated aim is to evaluate deep transfer-learning architectures for distinguishing autistic from non-autistic children from facial images, motivated by the cost and delay of conventional assessment and by the premise that autism has a distinct facial phenotype. Results: Inception-V3 98% accuracy, VGG-19 97%, ResNet50 96%, each with per-class precision and recall of 96-98% and confusion matrices on 588 evaluation samples. Two internal inconsistencies bear on how these should be read. The abstract names ResNet50, Inception-V3 and VGG-19 with Inception-V3 best; the introduction names 'ResNet, VGG16, and VGG19' and states that VGG19 achieved the superior 98%, contradicting the paper's own results tables. And all three result tables are headed 'Validation results', with the confusion matrices described as validation-stage - so the headline figures come from the partition used for model selection, while the 10% test partition defined in the methods is never reported on. The paper's own comparison table places this subliterature at 80.05% to 96% across ten prior studies on the same corpus, so a 98% validation figure sits above every published test figure for the same data. [RQ2.2] No study setting exists. The corpus is a third-party Kaggle assembly, and its two classes were built by different procedures - an autism-labelled collection on one side, general web search on the other. As with the other studies on this corpus charted in this review, the collection route is the confound rather than a background detail, because it is the only documented respect in which the two image populations are known to differ. [RQ2.3] None. No task, elicitation or standardisation exists. The children were photographed by whoever took the pictures, for their own purposes, under uncontrolled conditions. This matters for the paper's premise in a specific way: the motivating literature concerns craniofacial morphometry - measurements that require controlled pose, distance and camera geometry to be meaningful - and none of those is available in web-sourced photographs, so even if the morphometric claims were correct the data could not test them. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element. The retrieved text terminates within the discussion section before the declarations, so ethics, funding, data-availability and competing-interest statements could not be assessed from what was available. What can be said is that the paper contains no discussion anywhere in its main text of the ethics of the underlying material - identifiable photographs of children aged 2 to 14, collected from the internet without their families' knowledge or consent, one class specifically from autism-related sources. The introduction does raise the ethical hazards of autism identification in general terms, naming labelling, effects on self-esteem and social relationships, and overdiagnosis, which is more than the rest of this branch offers; it does not extend that concern to the provenance of its own training data. [RQ2.5] No acquisition equipment. Analysis used three ImageNet-pretrained networks on 224x224x3 images with categorical cross-entropy, the SGD optimiser and a 25-epoch cap. Because the images come from unknown cameras under unknown conditions, every acquisition variable is free to vary and, critically, may vary systematically with class given that the two folders were assembled by different routes. [RQ2.6] Adequate on the computational side and empty on the human side. Reported: the corpus with class counts and stated age range, the four augmentation parameters with their values, the 80/10/10 split, the image dimensions, the three architectures, the loss, optimiser and epoch cap, complete per-class precision, recall, F1 and support, confusion matrices, and training and validation curves with specific accuracy and loss trajectories. Not reported: the number of distinct children, any demographic composition, whether the split respected individuals, the composition of the evaluation partition in a form reconcilable with the stated split, hyperparameters beyond the epoch cap, and code. The stated claim of a facial-feature importance analysis has no corresponding section. [RQ2.7] No limitations section appears in the retrieved text, but the introduction contains one honest sentence: 'The research gap in ASD identification using images persists, despite the proposed system achieving 98% accuracy on a benchmark dataset ... Ultimately, clinical validation is necessary to ensure the widespread adoption of this approach in healthcare settings and its practical applicability.' Conceding that a 98% benchmark result leaves the research gap open is unusual in this branch and should be credited. What is not stated: that the non-autistic class was assembled by web search and the autistic class from an autism collection, so the label encodes provenance; that no diagnostic ascertainment exists for any image; that no demographic information is available in a study classifying faces; that the split is at image level with the number of children unknown; that all reported figures come from the validation partition rather than the defined test partition; that the reported support counts are inconsistent with both the stated split proportions and the corpus class ratio; that no chance baseline is given; that the promised feature-importance analysis was not performed; and that the abstract, introduction and results tables disagree about which models were compared and which won. [RQ2.9] Clinical validation is named as necessary for adoption, which is the right requirement. No other direction appears in the retrieved text. Needed and not proposed: reporting of the demographic composition of each class, evaluation on a cohort with documented diagnoses, and any test of whether the classifier's decisions track facial phenotype rather than the collection route of the image. [RQ3.1] Nominally craniofacial morphology; operationally, whatever separates an autism-labelled image folder from a folder of web-search results. The motivating claims are specific and measurable - broader upper faces, wider eyes, shorter nasal bridges, narrower cheeks - but nothing in the pipeline measures any of them: no landmarks are detected, no distances or ratios computed, and the models receive whole RGB images. What the networks can key on is unconstrained and includes apparent age, sex, ancestry, expression, pose, resolution, compression, lighting and background, all of which are free to differ between two folders built by different routes. The paper's third stated contribution was to analyse which facial features drive detection, which would have been the direct test of its own premise; that analysis does not appear. [RQ3.2] None. A single image modality throughout, with no fusion of any kind. [RQ4.1] Three ImageNet-pretrained architectures - ResNet50, Inception-V3 and VGG-19 - fine-tuned with categorical cross-entropy and SGD for up to 25 epochs. Transfer learning from ImageNet is a reasonable default for a 2,940-image corpus, and comparing three families is more informative than reporting one. Two problems attach. The training curves show Inception-V3 reaching 0.9992 training accuracy against 0.9779 validation, and VGG-19 exceeding 0.9854 in training before 'a significant decline in accuracy from epochs 24-25', both of which are signs of fitting to the training set that the paper reports without interpreting. And the introduction's statement that 'VGG16' was among the architectures compared, and that VGG19 achieved the best 98%, contradicts both the abstract and the results tables - an inconsistency about the study's own central claim. [RQ4.2] RGB face images at 224x224x3 with pixel values rescaled to [0, 1], augmented by 10% shear, 10% zoom and horizontal flip. No landmark geometry and no morphometric derivation, so the craniofacial constructs invoked as motivation are not represented at all, and every source-dependent property of the image is retained. [RQ4.3] Per-class precision, recall and F1 with support counts, overall accuracy, weighted averages, confusion matrices for all three models, training and validation curves, an ROC figure for Inception-V3 and a comparison table against ten prior studies on the same corpus. That is a fuller presentation than several papers in this branch. Three defects undercut it. Every table is headed 'Validation results' and the confusion matrices are described as validation-stage, so no held-out test figure is reported despite a test partition being defined. The support counts of 294 per class - 588 in total - are 20% of the corpus rather than the stated 10% validation share, and are exactly balanced although the corpus is 1,327 against 1,613, so the evaluation partition's composition cannot be reconstructed and it is unclear whether augmentation reached it. And no chance baseline, confidence interval or prevalence-adjusted predictive value appears, so a 98% figure has no reference point - at the corpus ratio a trivial majority classifier scores 54.9%, and at a realistic population prevalence the reported precision would not survive. [RQ4.4] Claimed and absent. The third listed contribution is 'Analysis of the specific facial features that contribute most significantly to accurate ASD detection', and the paper contains no such analysis - no saliency map, no attribution, no landmark or region analysis, no feature ranking. This is the one omission that most directly affects the paper's own argument: having asserted specific morphometric differences as the biological basis for the approach, the study had both the motive and the standard tools to test whether its models respond to those regions, and did neither. In their absence, the 98% is compatible with a facial phenotype and equally compatible with the model having learned the photographic character of images that appear in autism-related online collections - and this review has recorded four other studies on this corpus where saliency evidence, where offered, could not distinguish the two either. [RQ4.5] The weakest element, and it fails in three independent ways. First, the split is at image level - 80/10/10 with no mention of participant-level partitioning and no statement of how many distinct children the 2,940 images represent - so in a web-assembled corpus where one child may appear repeatedly, images of the same child can fall on both sides of the boundary. This is the standard failure of this branch and the review has documented it in five prior studies on the same corpus family. Second, and more unusual, every reported figure comes from the validation partition: all three result tables are headed 'Validation results', the confusion matrices are described as validation-stage, and the training curves report validation accuracy as the endpoint, while the 10% test partition defined in the methods section is never reported on anywhere. Model selection and performance estimation therefore share data, and the headline 98% is a selection maximum rather than a held-out estimate. Third, the evaluation partition cannot be reconciled with the described design: 294 samples per class totalling 588 is 20% of 2,940 rather than the stated 10%, and exact class balance is impossible under a random split of a 1,327-to-1,613 corpus - so either the evaluation set was stratified to equal size, or augmentation reached it, or the numbers are misreported, and the paper does not say which. Against all of this sits the confound that no splitting scheme could address: the paper states that the non-autistic images were 'randomly retrieved from web searches' while the autistic images came from an autism collection, so a model that has learned to recognise the photographic character of one source will succeed on perfectly disjoint subjects. The paper's own comparison table, listing ten prior studies on this corpus at 80.05% to 96%, is the most useful thing in it for the review: it shows a subliterature clustered below this study's figure, and the difference between them is a matter of evaluation protocol rather than of signal. [RQ5.1] Keywords: transfer learning, deep learning, diagnosis, disability, mental health. Entirely method- and domain-facing with no term naming autism, the population, the data source or the behaviour - so the paper is hard to locate from a clinically framed search, which is characteristic of this branch. Terms carried through the body: facial phenotype analysis, morphological characteristics, biomarkers, ImageNet, augmentation, confusion matrix, screening. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Medicine 12:1569464, Original Research, open access under CC BY; received 31 January 2025, accepted 16 April 2025, published 21 May 2025, with editor and three reviewers disclosed by name. The venue is a general medical journal rather than an engineering one, which makes the pattern of what passed review notable: a physiognomic premise asserted without measurement, a corpus whose comparison class is described in the paper's own methods as web-search results, no demographic information of any kind, results reported from a validation partition while a defined test partition goes unreported, support counts inconsistent with the stated split, a claimed feature-importance analysis that does not exist, and an introduction that contradicts the abstract and the results tables about which models were compared. The retrieved text ends mid-discussion at Table 8, so the declarations could not be assessed. [RQ5.3] Published May 2025 by groups at the King Salman Center for Disability Research in Riyadh together with King Faisal, Prince Sattam Bin Abdulaziz and Al-Baha Universities. The framing is the standard access argument - conventional diagnosis is time-intensive and costly, creating barriers 'particularly in resource-limited settings' - combined with a physiognomic premise about distinct facial morphology in autism. For this review the paper is the sixth built on the Kaggle facial corpus and adds three things to the record. It states the provenance confound more plainly than any of the others, in its own methods: the autistic folder holds images of autism while 'the non-autistic subfolder had images randomly retrieved from web searches'. It supplies, in its Table 1, the most complete catalogue of the subliterature in the corpus - ten prior studies on the same images reporting 80.05%, 84.66%, 86%, 87.9%, 89%, 89.87%, 90.5%, 90.67%, 91.3%, 92%, 93.24% and 96% - which makes visible both the scale of the effort invested in this dataset and the fact that its reported accuracies cluster below the figure claimed here. And it contains, in its introduction, the only passage in this branch that names the harms of autism identification as such: labelling that 'may impact the child's self-esteem and social relationships', and 'a risk of overdiagnosis or misdiagnosis, leading to unnecessary interventions and therapies'. That the paper then proposes artificial intelligence as the mitigation for those very risks, without explaining how a classifier trained on web-scraped images with no diagnostic ascertainment would reduce mislabelling, is the clearest illustration in the review of how the access argument absorbs its own counterarguments. Three cautions travel with the study: all reported figures are validation-partition results while the defined test partition is never reported on; the evaluation support counts are irreconcilable with both the stated split and the corpus class ratio; and the abstract, introduction and results tables disagree about which architectures were compared and which performed best.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective secondary analysis of archived child speech transcripts, single-authored from The Harker School, San Jose.
