Sixty-four children aged 3 to 6 were assembled from TalkBank: 30 autistic and 34 typically developing, with the autistic children drawn from ASDBank's Eigsti and Nadig corpora and the typically developing children from those two plus CHILDES's Warren and Kuczaj corpora, added deliberately to balance age and sex representation. Developmentally delayed children present in the Eigsti corpus were excluded to keep the task binary. The four source protocols differ: 30-minute play sessions, 10-minute free play with a cleanup period, toy play of unspecified duration, and 30-minute spontaneous speech samples. The paper acknowledges residual imbalance - most participants male, more children aged 3-4 than 5-6 - and explains the sex imbalance by reference to the four-to-one diagnostic ratio, but gives no numerical age or sex composition by diagnostic group and no cognitive, language or clinical measures. Ethics were not sought, on the stated basis that the data are from a public database gathered with informed consent and contain no personal information.
narrative_rows.methods: Stanford's Stanza package parsed sentences and tokens after cleaning that followed TalkBank's transcription guide - symbols removed, bracketed and parenthesised tokens removed as unspoken, 'xxx' and '@<letters>' special-form markers stripped as inconsistently used across datasets, and '&=' tokens removed as non-speech sounds. Six linguistic features were computed - mean length of utterance, mean length of turn, mean word length, number of utterances, total number of words and number of different words - each in a child-alone form and a ratio form expressing the child's value relative to the investigator's, with the three count-based features used only as ratios to normalise for differing transcript lengths. Seven classifiers were compared: logistic regression, Gaussian naive Bayes, random forests, k-nearest neighbours and support vector machines from scikit-learn, a multilayer perceptron with maximum iterations 2000, and a Keras convolutional network with a 1D convolution layer, dense layers, 1D max pooling, ReLU and sigmoid activations and dropout. Cross-validation was rejected because of the small sample; instead each model was trained and evaluated over 50 random 75/25 train-test splits, a number chosen because metric values stabilised and varied by no more than 1% as further splits were added. Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUC were reported, with ROC curves showing individual splits, the mean and a one-standard-deviation band, plus feature-importance plots for logistic regression and random forests and a descriptive analysis of every feature by diagnosis, age band and sex.
narrative_rows.outcomes: The convolutional network reached 84% accuracy and the multilayer perceptron 83%, with recall of 80-81% and precision of 84-86%; logistic regression, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbours and random forests reached 77-80%, and Gaussian naive Bayes about ten points lower - a 5-to-10-point advantage for the neural models. Mean length of utterance was the most important feature for both models supplying importances, confirming a prior finding the paper cites; total number of words was also highly ranked, contradicting a prior study that reported no group difference on it. Typically developing children showed higher values on cMLU, rMLU, rMLT, rUtts and rTNW. The stratified analysis found that mean length of utterance was the only feature consistently increasing with age; that boys aged 3-4 exceeded girls of the same age on the key features while girls aged 5-6 exceeded boys; and that mean length of turn was lower in autistic boys than typically developing boys but higher in autistic girls than typically developing girls. Mean word length carried no interpretable signal, which the author attributes correctly to character counts being a poor proxy for lexical complexity.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The top-ranked predictor, mean length of utterance, is a canonical index of expressive language development, and the paper's own analysis shows it to be the only feature consistently increasing with age; with no independent language or cognitive measure and no age composition reported by diagnostic group, language delay and age cannot be separated from autism as explanations of the result. Part of the typically developing class was drawn from two corpora containing no autistic children and using different recording protocols, so corpus of origin is partly correlated with class; session lengths differ threefold where stated and are unknown for one corpus; and the investigator's role differs across protocols, which matters because half the features are ratios to the investigator's output. Developmentally delayed children available in one source corpus were deliberately excluded, discarding the non-autistic clinical comparison. The headline accuracies were obtained 'after the removal of certain features' selected on the same data, so they are post-selection estimates. Test folds hold sixteen children and no confidence intervals are reported. No model performance is given by age band or sex despite the feature analysis being stratified and finding a diagnosis-by-sex interaction. And the recommendation to use deep learning clinically rests on a 5-to-10-point difference on 64 children, with the margin between the two neural models being one to two points.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: A small conference paper that is more useful to this review than several of the journal articles alongside it, for reasons unrelated to its accuracy figure. Its split unit is the child, its evaluation design is explained and empirically justified - 50 repeated 75/25 splits, the number chosen because metrics stabilised within 1% - and it reports estimate variability through ROC standard-deviation bands rather than a bare point value, which is more honest uncertainty communication than almost anything else in the corpus. Its features are named psycholinguistic constructs with an established literature, so its findings are directly comparable with prior work, and it makes those comparisons explicitly, including where it contradicts them. Its 83-84%, benchmarked against three prior studies at 70-80%, sits in a credible range for a genuinely difficult task and provides a calibration point against the 95-100% figures produced elsewhere in this review by leaked or confounded designs. And its sex-stratified analysis reports a diagnosis-by-sex interaction on mean length of turn - lower in autistic boys than typically developing boys, higher in autistic girls than typically developing girls - which, if real, implies that a classifier trained predominantly on boys would misread girls, the failure another study in this review demonstrated empirically with sensitivity falling from 94.8% pooled to 43.6% for girls. The paper stops at describing the interaction and never evaluates its models by sex, so its own most consequential finding goes untested. Three cautions travel with it: the leading predictor is a developmental language index with no independent language measure available; part of the comparison class comes from corpora containing no autistic children, making corpus of origin partly correlated with class across four protocols that differ in length, structure and investigator role; and the developmentally delayed children present in one source corpus were deliberately excluded, discarding the non-autistic clinical comparison that the review has found almost nowhere else and that this corpus could have supplied at no additional cost.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Sixty-four children aged 3 to 6 - 30 autistic and 34 typically developing - assembled from four archived TalkBank corpora. The autistic children come from ASDBank's Eigsti and Nadig collections; the typically developing children come partly from those same collections and partly from CHILDES's Warren and Kuczaj corpora, added deliberately 'to try to balance demographic (gender and age) representations'. The paper is honest about the residual imbalance, stating that 'most participants are male, and there are more children aged 3-4 than aged 5-6', and it explains the sex imbalance correctly as a consequence of autism being 'almost 4 times as common in boys than in girls'. Numerical age and sex compositions by diagnostic group are not reported, which matters because the paper's own analysis finds that mean length of utterance - the top-ranked predictor - is the only feature that consistently increases with age. Developmentally delayed children present in the Eigsti corpus were deliberately excluded to keep the task binary, which removes the non-autistic clinical comparison group the source data could have supported. The unit of analysis is the child, one transcript and one feature vector each. [RQ1.2] Standard clinical-deficit framing, brief and without the physiognomic or pathologising excesses found elsewhere in this corpus. Autistic children 'commonly have difficulty communicating and interacting with others, show repetitive and restricted behaviors, and have delayed cognitive and movement skills'; the phrase 'there is no permanent cure for ASD' appears, and children are once referred to as 'patients with ASD'. Person-first language predominates. The framing of the access problem is accurate and non-alarmist: diagnosis is difficult because 'there is no medical test', a professional diagnosis from age 2 is considered reliable, and 'some patients with ASD are not diagnosed until after their childhood, and many do not receive a diagnosis at all'. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person is reported as involved. The paper's most careful language is about sex: rather than treating the male preponderance in its sample as a nuisance, it names the four-to-one diagnostic ratio as the cause and then analyses features separately for boys and girls - one of very few studies in this review to treat sex as a substantive variable rather than a sampling artefact. [RQ1.3] Partially reported and, unusually, analytically used. The paper states the age range (3 to 6), acknowledges that boys predominate and that the 3-4 band is larger than the 5-6 band, and explains the sex imbalance by reference to the diagnostic ratio. It does not give numerical age or sex breakdowns by diagnostic group, and no cognitive, language, socioeconomic or ancestry information is available. What distinguishes it from the rest of this corpus is what it does with the demographics it has: rather than reporting them and moving on, it computes every feature separately for autistic and typically developing children, for the two age bands and for boys and girls, and reports the interactions. The results are substantive - mean length of utterance rises with age; boys aged 3-4 exceed girls of the same age on the key features while girls aged 5-6 exceed boys; and mean length of turn is lower in autistic boys than typically developing boys but higher in autistic girls than typically developing girls. That last sex-by-diagnosis interaction, if real, would mean a single classifier trained mostly on boys could systematically misread girls - which is exactly the failure mode a speech study charted elsewhere in this review demonstrated empirically, with sensitivity falling from 94.8% pooled to 43.6% for girls. The gap here is that the paper stops at feature-level description and never evaluates model performance by subgroup, so the implication of its own finding goes untested. [RQ1.4] Inherited from the source corpora and not transmitted. Children are designated autistic or typically developing by the original Eigsti and Nadig investigators, but this paper reports no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician qualification or assessment date. The labels are nonetheless in a different class from those in the web-scraped branches of this review: ASDBank and CHILDES are established research archives whose contributing studies performed documented clinical ascertainment, so the underlying labels are real diagnoses rather than folder membership or hashtag use. The specific weaknesses are that the paper does not tell the reader what those diagnoses rested on, and that the typically developing designation for the Warren and Kuczaj children means only that those corpora were collected from typically developing populations, without any screening described in this paper. [RQ1.5] No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists independently of the modelled features - and this absence is the study's central interpretive problem rather than a routine gap. Mean length of utterance is the single most important predictor in both feature-importance analyses, and MLU is one of the oldest and best-established indices of expressive language development in child language research. Autistic children in this age range frequently have language delay, so a model whose leading feature is MLU may be detecting delayed expressive language rather than autism. Distinguishing the two requires an independent measure of language ability, which the archived transcripts do not supply here and which the paper does not seek. The point is sharpened by the paper's own demographic analysis: it reports that MLU is 'the only feature that consistently significantly increased with age', so the top predictor is simultaneously a developmental index and a diagnostic one, in a sample whose age composition by diagnostic group is not reported. [RQ2.1] The stated aim is to compare classical machine learning against deep learning for autism detection from linguistic features, using more than one data source and paying attention to how features differ across age and sex - three gaps the paper identifies in prior work, the second of which ('all previous studies based their research on a single data source') is a fair criticism of much of this literature. Findings: the convolutional network reached 84% accuracy and the multilayer perceptron 83%, against 77-80% for logistic regression, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbours and random forests, and roughly ten points lower for Gaussian naive Bayes; mean length of utterance was the top-ranked feature for both models that supply importances, confirming one prior study and contradicting another on total number of words; and the demographic analysis found MLU rising with age, a reversal of the sex gap between the 3-4 and 5-6 bands, and a sex-by-diagnosis interaction on mean length of turn. The performance figures are modest, honestly reported, and benchmarked against three prior studies at 70-80%, which places them in a credible range for this task and in sharp contrast to the 95-100% figures elsewhere in this review. What the study cannot establish is what the models detect: its leading feature is a developmental language index, no independent language measure exists, and the age composition of the two groups is unreported. [RQ2.2] No study setting; four archived corpora with different recording protocols. The heterogeneity is presented as a strength - two data banks used 'to better represent the population and make the detection model systems more reliable' - and it is a defensible position against the single-corpus practice the paper criticises. It also creates a partial provenance confound that goes unexamined. The autistic children come only from Eigsti and Nadig; the typically developing children come from those two plus Warren and Kuczaj, which contain no autistic children at all. For that supplemented fraction, corpus of origin is perfectly correlated with class, and the corpora differ in ways that bear directly on the features: session lengths of 30 minutes, 10 minutes, unspecified and 30 minutes respectively; a structured cleanup period in one and not the others; and different investigator roles, which matters because half the features are ratios of the child's output to the investigator's. The paper addresses the transcription-convention side of cross-corpus variation in detail and does not address the protocol side. [RQ2.3] Play-based spontaneous speech, but not one paradigm - four. Eigsti recorded 30-minute play sessions, Nadig 10-minute free play followed by a cleanup period, Warren toy play of unspecified duration and Kuczaj 30-minute spontaneous speech samples. Spontaneous play speech is a good elicitation context for the constructs of interest: it produces enough utterances to estimate MLU stably, it imposes minimal demand, and it captures conversational turn-taking with an adult, which the ratio features exploit. The heterogeneity is handled only partly. The paper normalises the three count-based features as ratios to the investigator specifically 'to normalize for different transcript lengths', which is the right instinct and addresses the most obvious threat. It does not address that a 10-minute free-play session with a cleanup period and a 30-minute spontaneous speech sample differ in more than length - in topic structure, in how much the adult initiates, and in what kinds of utterance are elicited - or that one corpus's session duration is simply unknown. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis of archived transcripts, one session per child, with no follow-up. The ethics position is stated briefly and is defensible: 'The data used in this research is from a publicly available database. The information was gathered with informed consent. This research will not involve any personal information.' Unlike the web-scraping and institutional-imaging studies charted elsewhere in this review, the underlying material was collected for research purposes with consent obtained at source and archived under a governance framework designed for reuse, so a secondary analysis of it raises materially different questions from harvesting children's photographs from support pages or thermally imaging pupils at a special school. Funding and competing interests are not stated. [RQ2.5] No instrumentation. Stanford's Stanza NLP package parsed sentences and tokens; scikit-learn supplied five classical models and the multilayer perceptron; Keras supplied the convolutional network. The computational cost is trivial and the input is text that already exists in a public archive, so this is among the least resource-intensive designs in the review - which is also its limitation, since it inherits whatever the original recordings and transcriptions captured and can add nothing. [RQ2.6] Good for a short conference paper, and notably strong on the preprocessing that determines whether cross-corpus features are comparable. Reported: all four source corpora by name with recording protocols where known, the deliberate exclusion of developmentally delayed children, group sizes, the age range, all six features with both their child-alone and ratio definitions and the reason ratios were used, the NLP package, the token-cleaning rules in detail - symbols removed, bracketed and parenthesised tokens removed as unspoken, 'xxx' and '@<letters>' special-form markers stripped because they are used inconsistently across datasets, '&=' tokens removed as non-speech sounds - the seven models with their library provenance, the convolutional architecture layer by layer, the 75/25 split, the 50 repeated splits with the stability criterion that justified that number, and all five metrics with ROC variability bands. Not reported: age and sex composition by diagnostic group, the source corpora's diagnostic procedures, which features were removed before the headline accuracies, and code. [RQ2.7] Two limitations are stated: limited data, with a call for greater variety of participant backgrounds; and residual noise after feature computation, acknowledged as partly inevitable 'since speech is transcribed in different ways across datasets'. The second identifies cross-corpus heterogeneity at the transcription level, which is the right issue seen from one side. What is not addressed: mean length of utterance, the top predictor, is a developmental language index that the paper's own analysis shows increasing with age, and with no independent language measure and no reported age composition by group, language delay and age cannot be separated from autism; part of the typically developing class comes from corpora containing no autistic children and using different protocols, so corpus of origin is partly correlated with class; session lengths differ threefold where stated and are unknown for one corpus, and the investigator's role differs across protocols although half the features are ratios to the investigator; developmentally delayed children were deliberately excluded, removing the clinical comparison that would have made the result far more informative; the headline accuracies were obtained 'after the removal of certain features' selected on the same data; no confidence intervals accompany estimates from test folds of sixteen children; and no model performance is reported by age band or sex despite the feature analysis being stratified and despite that analysis finding a sex-by-diagnosis interaction. [RQ2.9] Larger and more varied datasets; better preprocessing to reduce transcription noise; and, implied by the mean-word-length finding, lexical complexity measured in phonemes or morphemes rather than characters. Not proposed, and needed: an independent language measure to separate delay from autism; reporting of age and sex composition by diagnostic group; model evaluation stratified by sex, given the interaction the paper itself reports; and reinstatement of the developmentally delayed children as a third class, since the source corpus contains them and the resulting three-way discrimination is what clinical practice requires. [RQ3.1] Structural and quantitative properties of spontaneous speech, operationalised as six standard psycholinguistic descriptors: mean length of utterance, mean length of turn, mean word length, number of utterances, total number of words and number of different words. Two design decisions distinguish this from a generic bag-of-features approach. Each feature was computed both for the child alone and as a ratio to the investigator's value in the same session, and the two versions were compared empirically to see which carried more information - a construct-level question about whether autistic children's speech differs absolutely or relative to their conversational partner's. And the count-based features were used only in ratio form to normalise for transcript length. The results locate the discriminative information in utterance and turn length and in the child's output relative to the adult's, with typically developing children higher on cMLU, rMLU, rMLT, rUtts and rTNW - a coherent picture of shorter utterances, shorter turns and proportionally less talk. Mean word length carried no signal, and the paper draws the right conclusion, that characters are a poor proxy for lexical complexity and that phonemes or morphemes would be the correct unit. The construct that this cannot separate from autism is expressive language level, of which MLU is a canonical index. [RQ3.2] None across modalities - text only, with no acoustic, prosodic or visual information. The ratio features constitute a form of dyadic fusion in that they combine the child's output with the investigator's within a session, which is conceptually similar to the interaction-level modelling in the pose-based studies charted elsewhere in this review and is more than most transcript-based work attempts. Its vulnerability is that the investigator's behaviour is not standardised across the four source corpora, so the denominator of every ratio feature varies by protocol. [RQ4.1] A systematic seven-model comparison spanning logistic regression, Gaussian naive Bayes, random forests, k-nearest neighbours, support vector machines, a multilayer perceptron and a small convolutional network. Comparing classical against neural models on the same features is the paper's stated purpose and is executed evenly - same features, same splits, same metrics. The scale is appropriate for 64 children and twelve features, and the classical models are the ones such data can support. The conclusion drawn from the comparison, however, exceeds it: a 5-to-10-point advantage for neural models on 64 children, with test folds of sixteen and no confidence intervals, is not a stable basis for the recommendation to use deep learning clinically, and the one-to-two-point margin between the multilayer perceptron and the convolutional network is certainly not. [RQ4.2] A vector of at most twelve interpretable linguistic values per child, reduced after a first round comparing the child-alone and ratio forms of each feature. This is the most parsimonious representation in the review and is well matched to the sample: every dimension is a quantity with a published psycholinguistic literature, computed by documented rules from a public archive, so the representation is auditable end to end. Its limitation is that transcript-level aggregation discards everything about how the speech unfolded - no sequence, no timing, no prosody - so constructs such as turn-taking latency or intonation, which the wider literature associates with autistic speech, are outside its reach. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUC for all seven models, with ROC curves that plot the individual splits, the mean curve and a one-standard-deviation band. That variability band is worth singling out: on 64 children with 50 repeated splits it conveys the instability of the estimate more honestly than a point figure, and it is a form of uncertainty reporting that almost no other study in this review provides. Precision and recall are also interpreted correctly in clinical terms, with recall of 80-81% read as a low false-negative rate 'important for ensuring that children with ASD are diagnosed correctly' and precision of 84-86% as protecting children without autism from being misdiagnosed. Missing: confidence intervals, confusion matrices, calibration, and any positive predictive value at a realistic prevalence - the last mattering because the reported precision holds only at the near-balanced sample ratio. [RQ4.4] Among the better-handled in the review, because the features are interpretable by construction and the interpretation is pursued rather than asserted. Feature-importance plots are given for logistic regression and random forests; mean length of utterance emerges as the top predictor in both; and the finding is compared explicitly against prior literature, confirming one study's MLU result and contradicting another's conclusion that total number of words does not differ. The stratified analysis goes beyond importance to describe how each feature behaves across diagnosis, age band and sex, producing the specific and testable claims recorded above. And the negative result on mean word length is interpreted correctly rather than ignored - characters are the wrong unit for lexical complexity, and phonemes or morphemes would be better. What interpretability cannot settle here is the identity of the underlying construct: MLU is a developmental language index and no independent measure of language ability exists in the data, so the models' leading signal is compatible with autism-specific pragmatic difference and with generic expressive language delay, and the paper does not raise the distinction. [RQ4.5] Sound on the mechanics for a study of this size, and unresolved on the confounds. Each child contributes one transcript and one feature vector, so the split unit is the person and no within-participant leakage is possible - which places this study among the minority in the review not exposed to the failure that dominates the image, frame and thermal branches. The evaluation is a 75/25 split repeated over 50 random draws with results averaged, and the choice is both explained and empirically justified: cross-validation was rejected because of small sample size, and 50 repetitions were selected because metrics stabilised, varying by no more than 1% as further splits were added. Stating a stability criterion for the number of repetitions is a level of care that very few papers in this corpus show, and the ROC plots with a one-standard-deviation band around the mean curve carry that honesty into the presentation. Three qualifications bound what this buys. Test folds contain sixteen children, so each averaged estimate rests on very small samples and no confidence interval is given; the headline 83-84% is stated elsewhere in the paper to have been obtained 'after the removal of certain features', a selection made on the same data, so it is a post-selection figure; and repeated random splitting addresses sampling variance and not the three confounds that determine what is being separated. Those are, in order of importance: that the top-ranked feature is a developmental language index with no independent language measure available and no age composition reported by group; that part of the typically developing class comes from corpora containing no autistic children, so corpus of origin is partly correlated with class; and that the four source protocols differ in session length, structure and investigator role, while half the features are ratios to that investigator's output. None of these would be revealed by any splitting scheme, and none is addressed. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder, Natural Language Processing, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Linguistics. Balanced across population, modality and method, and 'Linguistics' in particular signals that the features are psycholinguistic constructs rather than learned embeddings. Terms carried through the body: mean length of utterance, mean length of turn, total number of words, number of different words, TalkBank, CHILDES, ASDBank, Stanza, feature importance, train-test split. [RQ5.2] 2024 IEEE 3rd International Conference on Computing and Machine Intelligence (ICMI), doi 10.1109/ICMI60790.2024.10585946. A short computing-conference paper, single-authored by a student at The Harker School in San Jose - a secondary school - which is worth recording factually because it contextualises both the scale and the character of the work. The paper is careful where a beginner might not be: it splits by participant, justifies its repeated-split design with a stated stability criterion, documents its token-cleaning rules against TalkBank's transcription guide, plots ROC variability bands, compares its feature findings explicitly against three named prior studies including where it contradicts them, and reports modest accuracies without inflation. It is weaker on the clinical reasoning that a conference in computing and machine intelligence would not have prompted: no independent language measure, no age composition by group, a non-autistic clinical comparison deliberately discarded, and a recommendation about clinical model choice resting on a one-to-two-point margin. Set beside several journal papers in this review that report 98-100% from image-level splits on web-scraped corpora, its 84% from a participant-level split on a consented research archive is the more informative result. [RQ5.3] Presented at an IEEE computing conference in 2024 by a single secondary-school author in California. The framing is the standard early-detection argument, stated accurately: 1 in 36 children affected, no medical test, professional diagnosis reliable from age 2, and many children diagnosed late or never. For this review the study is valuable on four counts that have little to do with its accuracy figure. It is one of a small number of included studies whose split unit is the participant and whose evaluation design is both explained and empirically justified - 50 repeated 75/25 splits chosen because metrics stabilised within 1% - and it reports estimate variability through ROC standard-deviation bands rather than a bare point figure. Its features are named psycholinguistic constructs with an established literature, so its results are directly comparable with prior findings, and it makes those comparisons explicitly, confirming one study's mean-length-of-utterance result and contradicting another's on total word count. Its accuracy of 83-84%, benchmarked against three prior studies at 70-80%, sits in a credible range for a genuinely hard task and provides a useful calibration point against the 95-100% figures produced elsewhere in this review by leaked or confounded designs. And its sex-stratified feature analysis reports a diagnosis-by-sex interaction - mean length of turn lower in autistic boys than typically developing boys but higher in autistic girls than typically developing girls - which, if real, means a classifier trained predominantly on boys would misread girls, exactly the failure another study in this review demonstrated empirically with sensitivity falling from 94.8% pooled to 43.6% for girls. Three cautions travel with it. The top-ranked predictor is mean length of utterance, a canonical index of expressive language development that the paper's own analysis shows rising with age, and with no independent language measure and no age composition reported by group, language delay and age cannot be separated from autism as explanations. Part of the typically developing class was drawn from corpora containing no autistic children and using different recording protocols, so corpus of origin is partly correlated with class, and the four protocols differ in session length, structure and investigator role while half the features are ratios to the investigator's output. And the developmentally delayed children present in one source corpus were deliberately excluded to keep the task binary, discarding the non-autistic clinical comparison that would have made the study far more informative and that the review has found almost nowhere else.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective algorithm-development and architecture-comparison study by the School of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Aizu, Japan, funded by the university's Competitive Research Fund. Two public skeleton corpora were used in parallel. The Gait Fullbody Dataset contains 100 children aged 4 to 12 - 50 autistic and 50 typically developing - recorded with a Kinect v2 capturing 25 three-dimensional joint coordinates; each child performed ten walking trials, of which one was retained, 'the most optimal trial ... selected based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation', giving 100 samples. The DREAM dataset contains 61 children aged 3 to 7 recorded with Kinect v1 during robot-assisted therapy, yielding 3,121 samples of which 1,833 were used after the non-spectrum class was excluded; only 10 upper-body joints are recorded. No age distribution by group, sex, cognitive, language or clinical characterisation is available for either corpus, and no diagnostic procedure is described. Both datasets are public and identified, one by Dryad DOI.
narrative_rows.methods: A dual-stream architecture derived from a prior design was optimised. Stream one converts skeleton sequences into Skepxels - spatial image-like encodings - processed by an image classification backbone; stream two embeds relative joint angles into the sequence and applies MSG3D, combining graph convolution over the skeletal topology with temporal convolution. A pairwise Euclidean distance loss aligns the two embeddings during training to promote complementary representations, and the streams are tested separately. Six image backbones were compared - ViT-B as the reference, ConvNeXt-Base, Swin-V2-B, ShuffleNetV2-X2, ResNet-152 and MaxViT-T - and MSG3D was compared against a Stack Transformer in the second stream. Training used SGD at learning rate 0.001 with batch size 12, initially for 30 epochs and extended to 100 after inspecting preliminary learning curves. Evaluation used 10-fold cross-validation: on the Gait dataset, 90 children training against 10 testing per fold, repeated five times for 50 runs; on DREAM, 1,650 samples training against 183 testing per fold, repeated three times, with no participant-level partitioning described. Mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation across runs were reported for every architecture, on an RTX 3090 under a fully versioned Python 3.10 software stack.
narrative_rows.outcomes: On the Gait Fullbody Dataset the six backbones spanned 93.2% to 95.4% average accuracy - ShuffleNetV2-X2 and MaxViT-T at 95.4%, ConvNeXt-Base 95.0%, the ViT-B reference 94.8%, ResNet-152 94.0%, Swin-V2-B 93.2% - with standard deviations of 0.71 to 1.82. On DREAM the same six spanned 68.92% to 70.19%, ConvNeXt-Base highest, with standard deviations of 0.15 to 0.96. Substituting a Stack Transformer for MSG3D in the second stream lowered accuracy, which the authors read as evidence for graph-based models in motion analysis. The most informative pattern in these tables is that architecture choice moves accuracy by 2.2 points on one dataset and 1.3 on the other, against a 25-point gap between the datasets - so performance here is determined by the data rather than the model.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The single modelled walking trial per child was chosen from ten 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation', so the data were selected on the outcome before any model saw them, and no downstream splitting scheme can address this. On DREAM, 1,833 samples from 61 children were split without any participant-level partitioning described, leaving within-participant leakage unaddressed - though notably that leak-prone dataset produced the lower figure, so leakage does not explain the 25-point gap. Neither corpus reports age composition by diagnostic group or any sex information, in a domain where walking kinematics mature substantially between 4 and 12 years and differ by sex from middle childhood. No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC or confusion matrix is reported for any proposed model, so a screening claim rests on accuracy alone. The headline 95.4% is a best-of-six architecture selection on test folds of ten children, where one child is worth ten percentage points and the six backbones span 2.2 points against run-to-run standard deviations reaching 1.82. The DREAM experiment discards the non-spectrum class, making it a discrimination among autism-related labels rather than autism versus non-autism, with the resulting class balance never quantified so no chance baseline exists. No interpretability analysis connects the models to any nameable gait characteristic, despite skeleton data making joint- and phase-level attribution straightforward. And the paper transmits without comment that the Gait dataset's own creators moved from approximately 60% accuracy without augmentation to 92% with seven augmentation techniques applied to 100 samples.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: Contributes four things to the synthesis that are largely independent of its headline figure. Its modality argument fills a coverage gap the review has otherwise left open: diagnosis 'often requires speech-based tests', yet at the early detection stage 'many young children may not yet be able to speak', so a movement-based measure reaches the youngest and least verbal children whom the transcript- and conversation-based studies charted elsewhere here cannot assess at all. Its skeleton representation functions as a designed confound control of the same kind used by the Geneva pose study - face, appearance, clothing, room and lighting are absent by construction - and the paper argues the accompanying privacy advantage explicitly, against anonymity concerns it cites for gaze and video data. Its six-architecture ablation produces a valuable negative result: accuracy spreads of 2.2 and 1.3 percentage points across backbones, against a 25-point gap between the two datasets, showing that in this branch the data and not the model determine performance - a direct corrective to a literature organised around architectural novelty, and reinforced by the paper reporting mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation for every configuration rather than a single best number. And the direction of that 25-point gap is instructive in its own right: the corpus with unaddressed within-participant leakage produced the lower figure, which is a counterexample to the assumption that leakage always explains the highest numbers in a branch, and points instead to sensor coverage - 25 full-body joints against 10 upper-body - as the operative difference. Three cautions travel with it. The Gait dataset's single modelled trial per child was selected on the basis of the diagnosis and a clinician's recommendation, a form of outcome-informed selection that the methods quote and never examine. No sensitivity or specificity is reported for any model, and no demographic data exist for either corpus in a domain where gait varies strongly with age and sex. And the paper supplies, as motivating background, the clearest single piece of evidence in this review for augmentation-driven inflation: a 32-point accuracy gain in the Gait dataset's originating study, from approximately 60% to 92%, produced by applying seven augmentation techniques to a 100-sample corpus.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two public corpora used in parallel. The Gait Fullbody Dataset, created by Al-Jubouri and colleagues, contains 100 children aged 4 to 12 - 50 autistic and 50 typically developing - recorded with a Kinect v2 capturing 25 joint coordinates, with each child performing ten walking trials of which one was retained, giving 100 samples. A separate subset of nine children with severe symptoms is available and is not analysed here. The DREAM dataset contains 61 children aged 3 to 7, recorded with Kinect v1 during robot-assisted therapy, yielding 3,121 samples of which 1,833 were used after the non-spectrum class was excluded; only 10 upper-body joints are recorded, since Kinect v1 detects 20 joints and DREAM omits the lower body. No age distribution, sex, cognitive level, language ability or clinical characterisation is available for either corpus. Two structural facts shape everything downstream. In the Gait dataset each child contributes exactly one sample, so cross-validation necessarily partitions children - a property that arises from the data rather than from a design decision, but that gives this study the participant-level split unit most of the video branch lacks. And that single retained sample was chosen from ten trials 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation', so the modelled data were selected with knowledge of the outcome. [RQ1.2] Predominantly medical, with 'patients with ASD' used repeatedly and autism described as a set of 'complex developmental disabilities' with symptoms such as 'a lack of eye contact and an obsession with certain behaviours'. Two passages show more thought than the register suggests. The introduction gives an accurate and unusually careful account of rising prevalence, noting that the doubling of diagnoses between 2015 and 2024 occurred despite the stricter DSM-5 criteria expected to reduce it, and attributing the net increase to awareness and earlier diagnosis - concluding that 'many patients with ASD have not yet surfaced'. That is the correct reading of the epidemiological trend and stands against the alarm framing used elsewhere in this corpus. And the account of the access barrier is concrete rather than rhetorical: 'the high barrier to visiting a hospital, along with the fact that many children are not yet able to speak. Deciding to visit a hospital often requires recognising signs within the household', with the proposed role for the technology being to give families 'a clearer motivation to visit a hospital' rather than to substitute for assessment. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person is reported as involved. [RQ1.3] Absent for both corpora beyond the stated age ranges of 4 to 12 and 3 to 7 years. No age distribution by diagnostic group, no sex, no cognitive or language measure, no ancestry and no comorbidity. Two of these are specifically damaging for a gait study. Walking kinematics mature substantially across 4 to 12 years - stride length, cadence, arm swing, double-support time and postural stability all change - so if the autistic and typically developing groups differ in age composition, a gait classifier and an age classifier would be behaviourally indistinguishable, and nothing reported allows the check. And gait differs by sex from middle childhood, with no sex information available in either corpus. The DREAM corpus additionally spans 3 to 7 years with ages recorded in months, so finer age information exists in the source data and is not used. The paper does not report demographic composition for either dataset or acknowledge these as confounds. [RQ1.4] Inherited and undescribed for both corpora - no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician qualification or assessment date appears anywhere. The Gait Fullbody Dataset carries binary autistic and typically developing labels from its creators; DREAM carries a three-level label - non-spectrum, ASD and AUT - of which the non-spectrum class was discarded, following the prior study whose architecture this work extends. Discarding the non-spectrum group has a consequence the paper does not draw: the DREAM experiment is then a discrimination between two autism-related categories rather than between autism and non-autism, so its 70.19% is not comparable to the Gait dataset's autism-versus-typical task and the two figures cannot be read as measurements of the same thing. The reference-standard issue that most affects validity, however, is procedural rather than definitional. The methods state that in the Gait dataset each child performed ten walking trials and 'the most optimal trial was selected based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation'. Selecting which of a child's trials enters the dataset on the basis of that child's diagnosis is selection on the outcome: it means the 100 modelled samples are not a random sample of each child's walking but the trial a clinician judged most suitable given what the child was known to have. Whatever separation the models achieve is conditioned on that choice, and no splitting scheme downstream can undo it. [RQ1.5] None used. The Gait Fullbody Dataset includes a subset of nine children with severe symptoms, and the paper's methodology section states that the architecture is proposed 'for ASD detection and severity assessment' - but no severity analysis is performed, no result for the severe subset is reported, and severity appears nowhere in the results. DREAM's three-level labelling likewise encodes a gradient that is collapsed by discarding one class. No cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists for either corpus. [RQ2.1] The aim is to optimise a dual-stream skeleton architecture for autism detection, replacing the vision transformer of a prior design with a convolutional backbone to test whether CNN-based models capture gesture features effectively, and comparing MSG3D against a Stack Transformer in the temporal stream. The headline results are 95.4% on the Gait Fullbody Dataset and 70.19% on DREAM. The more informative findings are in the ablation tables. Across six image backbones the Gait results span 93.2% to 95.4% and the DREAM results 68.92% to 70.19% - so architecture choice moves accuracy by around two points on one dataset and one point on the other, while the gap between the two datasets is 25 points. That is a clean demonstration that in this branch the data determine performance and the model barely matters, which is a useful corrective to a literature organised around architectural novelty. The paper also reports that substituting a Stack Transformer for MSG3D lowered accuracy, and it reports its own reference implementation (ViT-B at 94.8%) alongside the alternatives rather than only the winner. What the study does not establish is what the 25-point gap means: the two corpora differ in sensor generation, joint coverage (25 full-body against 10 upper-body), task (walking against robot-assisted therapy), label structure (autism versus typical against two autism-related classes) and splitting unit (child against sample), and no analysis separates these. [RQ2.2] No study setting. The Gait Fullbody Dataset records walking trials captured by Kinect v2, and DREAM was collected during robot-assisted therapy sessions with Kinect v1. The paper documents the sensor difference carefully - Kinect v2 detects 25 joints, Kinect v1 detects 20, and DREAM omits the lower body leaving 10 - which is exactly the kind of acquisition detail that determines cross-corpus comparability and that most secondary-analysis studies in this review omit. It does not, however, examine the settings themselves: what the children were doing during DREAM sessions, how a robot's presence shapes movement, or whether the walking protocol was standardised in distance, speed or footwear. Within each corpus, both classes were recorded under the same conditions, so the acquisition confound that affects the photograph and clinic-versus-school audio studies charted elsewhere in this review does not arise here - a genuine structural advantage of using purpose-built research corpora. [RQ2.3] Walking trials in one corpus and robot-assisted therapy sessions in the other, neither described in detail. The gait paradigm is well chosen for the review's purposes: walking requires no verbal ability, imposes no social demand, is producible by very young children, and yields a motor signal that can be measured objectively - which the paper argues explicitly, noting that diagnosis 'often requires speech-based tests' but 'at the early detection stage, many young children may not yet be able to speak'. That argument identifies a real gap in the assessment landscape, since the language-based measures charted elsewhere in this review are inapplicable to precisely the youngest and least verbal children for whom early detection matters most. Two things weaken the execution. Only one of ten walking trials per child is retained, and that trial was chosen with knowledge of the diagnosis, so within-child variability - which is itself a candidate marker in motor studies - is discarded by a non-blind procedure. And in DREAM the recorded movements arise from therapy interaction with only upper-body joints available, so the gait construct that motivates the paper is not measurable in the second dataset at all. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element. No ethics statement appears, which is conventional for analysis of two public corpora collected under their originators' governance. The paper does address a related concern substantively, and its argument deserves recording: it notes that prior eye-tracking work 'raised concerns about ensuring anonymity' and identifies 'the issue of privacy protection associated with gaze data', then positions skeleton representation as the answer. Joint coordinates carry no face, appearance, clothing, room or lighting information, so a skeleton corpus is inherently less identifying than the video or photograph corpora that dominate this branch. That is a real privacy property of the modality, argued as a motivation rather than noted as a side effect, and it aligns with the same reasoning that led the Geneva group charted elsewhere in this review to render pose as skeleton-on-black and to release a de-identified pose subsample when raw video could not be shared. Funding from the University of Aizu Competitive Research Fund is declared, competing interests are declared as none, and both datasets are identified with public locations. [RQ2.5] Microsoft Kinect v2 for the Gait Fullbody Dataset, giving 25 three-dimensional joint coordinates, and Kinect v1 for DREAM, giving 20 joints of which 10 upper-body positions are recorded. The paper explains the difference and its consequence for comparability, with a figure contrasting the two joint layouts. Kinect-class depth sensing is consumer hardware, which matters for the deployment argument: skeleton capture requires no markers, no wearables, no calibration by the family and no clinical instrumentation, and produces data that cannot identify the child by appearance. Analysis used Python 3.10 with nine named packages at stated versions on an RTX 3090 with 48 GB RAM, trained with SGD at learning rate 0.001 and batch size 12 - a fuller software and hardware specification than almost any other study in this review provides. [RQ2.6] Among the more reproducible computational records in the corpus. Reported: both datasets with public access locations, one with a Dryad DOI and access date; sensor models, joint counts and the difference between the two Kinect generations with a figure; sample counts for both corpora; the exclusion of the non-spectrum class; the complete software stack with version numbers for nine packages; the hardware; optimiser, learning rate and batch size; the epoch schedule with the reason for its extension; the cross-validation scheme with fold sizes and repetition counts stated separately for each dataset, including why DREAM was run three times rather than five; mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation for every architecture on both datasets; and the specific configuration flag needed to enable Skepxels in the inherited codebase. Not reported: whether DREAM splitting respected participants, any demographic composition, per-class counts for DREAM, sensitivity and specificity, and the authors' own code. [RQ2.7] The conclusion names three limitations: generalisability requires further optimisation, 'particularly for datasets with biased label distributions'; 'the computational complexity of dual-stream models also poses challenges for real-time clinical applications'; and future work should pursue lightweight architectures, improved augmentation and pre-training. Naming one's own computational cost as an obstacle to the clinical use one proposes is candid, and identifying label imbalance as the source of the DREAM shortfall is a reasonable diagnosis even if not the only one. There is no separate limitations section, and several substantial issues go unaddressed. The Gait dataset's single retained trial per child was selected 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation' - the methods quote it and nothing follows. No participant-level partitioning is described for DREAM, where 1,833 samples come from 61 children. No demographic information exists for either corpus, in a domain where gait varies strongly with age and sex. No sensitivity, specificity, AUC or confusion matrix is reported for any proposed model, so a screening claim rests on accuracy alone. The 95.4% is a best-of-six architecture selection on test folds of ten children, where one child is worth ten percentage points and the six backbones span 2.2 points. And the paper reports, without comment, that the Gait dataset's own creators moved from approximately 60% accuracy without augmentation to 92% with seven augmentation techniques - a 32-point gain from augmentation alone, which is as clear a statement of augmentation-driven inflation as this review has found, quoted as background rather than treated as a warning. [RQ2.9] Lightweight architectures to make dual-stream inference tractable in real time; improved augmentation and pre-training; and multimodal extension combining audio and visual data with skeleton. Not proposed, and needed: participant-level partitioning for DREAM; sensitivity and specificity alongside accuracy; demographic reporting and age-stratified analysis; use of all ten walking trials per child rather than one clinician-selected trial, which would both remove the outcome-informed selection and make within-child movement variability available as a feature; and joint-level attribution, which skeleton data make straightforward and which would connect model behaviour to describable gait characteristics. [RQ3.1] Whole-body movement kinematics, and the construct argument is one of the better ones in this review. Gait and gesture are presented as 'prominent behavioural markers' that can be 'efficiently and non-intrusively captured', and the case for preferring them to language-based assessment is made explicitly: diagnosis 'often requires speech-based tests', yet at the early detection stage 'many young children may not yet be able to speak'. That identifies a genuine coverage gap - the transcript-based and conversational measures charted elsewhere in this review are inapplicable to non-speaking and pre-verbal children, who are precisely the population early detection targets. The operationalisation is only partly matched to the argument. In the Gait dataset the construct is walking, measured across 25 full-body joints, which is the right instrument for the claim. In DREAM only 10 upper-body joints are available and the movements arise from therapy interaction, so gait is not measurable and the second experiment addresses a different construct under the same label. And no interpretability analysis connects the models to any nameable movement characteristic, so what aspect of gait the 95.4% reflects - stride variability, arm swing, postural sway, turning - is unknown, despite skeleton data making such an analysis unusually accessible. [RQ3.2] Two representational streams over one sensor, aligned by a pairwise Euclidean distance loss during training and then tested separately. Stream one encodes skeleton sequences as Skepxels for an image backbone; stream two embeds relative joint angles and applies MSG3D, combining graph convolution over the skeletal topology with temporal convolution over time. The design rationale is stated clearly - the loss 'minimises the distance between the Skepxel embedding, which captures spatiotemporal features, and the GCN embedding, which models structural joint relationships', promoting co-learning of complementary representations - and the ablation supports the graph component, with a Stack Transformer substitution lowering accuracy. This is representational rather than sensor fusion, but it is a coherent idea coherently tested. What is missing is a decomposition of how much each stream contributes to the final figure, which would be the natural complement to the architecture ablation that is reported. [RQ4.1] A dual-stream architecture derived from a prior design, with two deliberate substitutions tested: ConvNeXt-Base replacing the original ViT-B in the image stream to assess whether CNN backbones capture gesture features effectively, and a Stack Transformer trialled against MSG3D in the sequence stream. Six image backbones were compared in total - ViT-B, ConvNeXt-Base, Swin-V2-B, ShuffleNetV2-X2, ResNet-152 and MaxViT-T - spanning transformer, convolutional and hybrid families. The comparison is even-handed and the reference implementation is reported alongside the alternatives rather than only the winner. Its most valuable outcome is a negative one: across six architectures the accuracy spread is 2.2 points on one dataset and 1.3 on the other, against a 25-point gap between the datasets, so architectural choice is nearly irrelevant to performance here. For a literature in which most papers are organised around a new architecture, that is a finding worth propagating. [RQ4.2] Three-dimensional joint coordinate sequences, re-expressed two ways - as Skepxel images and as angle-augmented graph sequences. The skeleton representation functions as a designed confound control of the same kind used by the Geneva pose study charted elsewhere in this review: face, expression, clothing, body habitus, room, lighting and background are all absent by construction, so a classifier operating on it cannot exploit the appearance and setting confounds that dominate the photograph branch. It also carries the privacy property the paper argues for, since joint coordinates do not identify a child by appearance. The limitation is coverage: 25 full-body joints in one corpus against 10 upper-body joints in the other, so the two experiments do not measure the same thing, and the paper's own figure contrasting the joint layouts makes this visible without drawing the inference for the 25-point performance gap. [RQ4.3] Accuracy only, but reported with dispersion - average, maximum, minimum and standard deviation across repeated cross-validation cycles for every architecture on both datasets, plus per-epoch accuracy and loss curves. The dispersion reporting is a real strength and is what makes the architecture comparison interpretable: standard deviations of 0.71 to 1.82 on the Gait dataset against a 2.2-point spread between backbones show immediately that the architectural differences are barely larger than run-to-run noise, and the paper is able to note that ShuffleNet was more stable than MaxViT at the same mean accuracy. What is absent is everything a screening claim requires. No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC or confusion matrix is reported for any proposed model, so the balance between missed cases and false alarms is unknown, and no positive predictive value at any realistic prevalence is computed. Accuracy on a 50:50 corpus tells a clinician very little, and on DREAM - where the class distribution is described as biased but never quantified - it tells them nothing at all. [RQ4.4] None attempted, and the omission is more notable here than in most of this review because the modality invites it. Skeleton data are inherently interpretable: joints have names, angles have physical meaning, and time is explicit, so a joint-level or phase-level attribution would map directly onto describable gait characteristics - stride variability, arm swing amplitude and asymmetry, trunk sway, turning smoothness - which are the terms in which the clinical motor literature the paper cites is written. The Geneva pose study charted elsewhere in this review shows what such an analysis yields when its model confidences are regressed on clinical item scores. Here nothing connects the 95.4% to any nameable property of how the children walked, so the study establishes that a classifier can separate the groups and contributes nothing to understanding what it separates them on. Given that no demographic data exist either, the possibility that the models respond to age- or sex-related gait maturation rather than to autism cannot be examined from any direction. [RQ4.5] Two arrangements with materially different properties, reported clearly enough that both can be assessed. On the Gait Fullbody Dataset the split unit is necessarily the child, because each of the 100 children contributes exactly one sample, so 10-fold cross-validation partitions 90 children against 10; each configuration was run through five complete cycles giving 50 training runs, with mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation reported. That is sound practice and the dispersion reporting is better than most of this corpus. On DREAM, 1,833 samples from 61 children were split 1,650 against 183 per fold with no participant-level partitioning described - roughly 30 samples per child distributed across folds - so within-participant leakage is unaddressed. The instructive result is the direction of the difference: the leak-prone dataset produced the lower figure, 70.19% against 95.4%, which means the gap between them cannot be explained by leakage and must lie in sensor coverage, task, label structure or class balance. That inversion is worth carrying into the synthesis, because it is a counterexample to the assumption that leakage always explains the highest numbers in a branch. Three issues nonetheless bound the Gait figure despite its clean split unit. The single sample per child was chosen from ten trials 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation', so the modelled data were selected with knowledge of the outcome - a threat that operates entirely upstream of cross-validation and that no splitting scheme addresses. The 95.4% is the best of six architectures whose spread is 2.2 points against run-to-run standard deviations reaching 1.82, on test folds of ten children where a single child moves accuracy by ten percentage points, so the difference between the reported winner and the reference implementation's 94.8% is not resolvable. And the DREAM experiment discards the non-spectrum class, making it a two-way discrimination among autism-related labels rather than an autism-versus-non-autism task, with the resulting class balance never quantified so that no chance baseline exists for its 70.19%. Finally, the paper transmits without comment the single clearest piece of evidence in this review for augmentation-driven inflation: the Gait dataset's own creators reported approximately 60% accuracy without augmentation and 92% after applying seven augmentation techniques including noise addition, scaling and flipping. A 32-point gain from augmenting a 100-sample dataset is a statement about the augmentation, not about gait, and it is quoted here as motivating background. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism diagnosis; Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs); Convolutional Neural Network (CNN); Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs); effective feature extraction; MSG3D; skeleton points. Almost entirely architectural - six of seven terms name a method or component, with 'autism diagnosis' the only clinical term and no reference to gait, movement, children or screening. Terms carried through the body: Skepxels, dual-stream, pairwise Euclidean distance loss, Kinect, joint angles, gait, gesture, early detection. [RQ5.2] Electronics 14(11):2231, MDPI, open access under CC BY; received 26 April 2025, revised 21 May, accepted 26 May, published 30 May 2025 - a 34-day review cycle. An electronics and computing venue, and the profile matches: the software stack is versioned to nine packages, the hardware is specified, the cross-validation scheme is stated separately for each dataset with fold sizes and repetition counts, and every architecture is reported with mean, max, min and standard deviation. What a clinical venue would have required is absent: no sensitivity or specificity, no demographic composition, no examination of the outcome-informed trial selection quoted in the methods, and no discussion of what the 25-point gap between the two datasets implies about the construct being measured. [RQ5.3] Published May 2025 by the School of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Aizu, Japan, funded by the university's Competitive Research Fund. The framing is screening-oriented and modest in its target: because 'deciding to visit a hospital often requires recognising signs within the household', a video-based assessment could give families 'a clearer motivation to visit a hospital' - an aim scoped as prompting help-seeking rather than replacing assessment, which is among the better-calibrated translational positions in this review. For the synthesis the study contributes four things. Its modality argument fills a real gap: diagnosis 'often requires speech-based tests' yet 'many young children may not yet be able to speak', so a movement-based measure reaches the youngest and least verbal children whom the language-based studies charted elsewhere here cannot assess. Its skeleton representation is a designed confound control, discarding face, appearance, clothing, room and lighting entirely, and the paper argues the accompanying privacy advantage explicitly against the anonymity concerns raised for eye-tracking and video data - the same reasoning that led the Geneva group to render pose as skeleton-on-black. Its architecture comparison produces a valuable negative result: across six image backbones the accuracy spread is 2.2 points on one dataset and 1.3 on the other, against a 25-point gap between the two datasets, so in this branch the data determine performance and the architecture barely matters - a corrective to a literature organised around architectural novelty. And the direction of that 25-point gap is instructive, since the corpus with unaddressed within-participant leakage produced the lower figure, which is a counterexample to the assumption that leakage always explains the highest numbers. Three cautions travel with it. The Gait dataset's single modelled trial per child was chosen from ten 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation' - selection on the outcome, quoted in the methods and never examined. No sensitivity, specificity or confusion matrix is reported for any model, and no demographic data exist for either corpus in a domain where gait varies strongly with age and sex. And the paper transmits, as motivating background, the clearest evidence of augmentation-driven inflation in this review: the Gait dataset's own creators went from approximately 60% accuracy without augmentation to 92% with seven augmentation techniques applied to 100 samples.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Secondary analysis of the publicly available Khozaei et al. cry corpus, collected in Iran under ethics approval from Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences and Health Services in Tehran with comprehensive informed consent from parents or legal guardians. Sixty-two children aged 18 to 54 months contributed: 31 autistic (mean age 35.6 months) and 31 typically developing (mean age 30.8 months), with 24 boys and 7 girls in each group. Autism was established through a four-stage process - the GARS-2 parental questionnaire, a DSM-5-based caregiver interview, direct evaluation and observation by two doctoral-level child clinical psychologists, and separate confirmation by at least one child psychiatrist in a different setting - with the authors noting that ADOS was not administered because no official Farsi version exists. Recordings were made with Sony UX560 and UX512F voice recorders (74.2%) and smartphones running a custom application (25.80%), in WAV at 16-bit and 44.1 kHz, at approximately 25 cm from the child's mouth in quiet environments. Recording settings differed by group: 87.10% of autistic cries came from autism centres and 12.90% from homes, while 54.84% of typically developing cries came from health centres and 45.16% from homes. After excluding pain cries and impure segments, 6.10 +/- 5.05 cry instances were retained per autistic child and 5.39 +/- 3.66 per comparison child. The research was funded by Zoundream AG, a commercial infant-cry-analysis company, with two authors employed by it, one a co-founder holding stock, and a third compensated as a scientific advisory board member.
narrative_rows.methods: Two parallel analyses. Praat computed pitch-based acoustic features per cry pattern, with jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio selected for their established clinical use in voice assessment, and groups compared statistically with means, standard errors and significance coded at three thresholds. Separately, cry audio was converted to 128x128 single-channel spectrogram images and a recurrent convolutional network was trained from scratch, combining three convolutional layers of kernel size 3 with 32 output channels for spatial features and LSTM layers for temporal structure, regularised by dropout of 0.2 in each LSTM layer and by frequency- and time-masking augmentation applied to the training split, optimised with Adam under a cyclic learning rate between 1e-6 and 1e-5 at batch size 16. Training ran for 2,000 epochs, and the model exhibiting the highest validation accuracy was designated the final classifier. No test partition, cross-validation or participant-level splitting is described, and the evaluation unit is the cry instance, as the results table confirms by defining sensitivity and specificity in terms of instance counts.
narrative_rows.outcomes: The statistical comparison found significantly higher jitter and shimmer in autistic children's cries (both p < 0.01) and significantly lower harmonics-to-noise ratio (p < 0.0001), a pattern indicating greater cycle-to-cycle instability in pitch and amplitude together with a noisier, less periodic voice signal, consistent with less stable laryngeal control and replicating the direction reported in prior cry research the authors cite. The recurrent convolutional network reached 90.28% validation accuracy with AUC 90.83%, sensitivity and specificity both 88.64%, precision 95.12% and F-score 91.75%.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The classification result carries no information about performance on a new child. There is no test partition of any kind; the final model was selected as the epoch with the best validation accuracy out of 2,000, so the reported figure is a maximum over 2,000 draws taken on the partition it is reported from; and the evaluation unit is the cry instance with no participant-level splitting described, so with roughly six instances per child from 62 children the network can recognise an individual voice and recover its fixed label. The sensitivity and specificity are likewise instance-level rather than per-child, so they are not the operating characteristics a screening tool would have. The statistical comparison is more defensible but faces three confounds that the paper reports and does not adjust for. The groups differ by 4.8 months in mean age - about 16% of the younger group's mean - during a period of rapid laryngeal and vocal-tract maturation, using measures known to change with that maturation, with no test or adjustment. Recording settings are strongly imbalanced, with 87.10% of autistic cries captured at autism centres against a comparison group split between health centres and homes, and all three measures are sensitive to reverberation, background noise and microphone distance - harmonics-to-noise ratio, the strongest finding at p < 0.0001, being a direct measure of periodic-to-aperiodic energy that ambient noise depresses mechanically. And the eliciting causes of the cries differ between groups. Two device classes were used with no level normalisation reported; GARS-2 scores were collected and are not used for any severity analysis; and the statistical tests appear to be computed over cry instances rather than per-child summaries, leaving their effective sample size unclear.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The only study in the review to analyse pre-linguistic vocalisation, and its construct is its principal contribution. Cry is the earliest behaviour any included study measures: it precedes language, is produced by every child regardless of cognitive or verbal level, requires no cooperation, task compliance or social engagement, and can be captured on a phone at home and repeated indefinitely at no cost. That combination reaches a population nothing else charted here can assess - pre-verbal infants, and children whose developmental level precludes the eye-tracking, conversational and play-based paradigms used elsewhere in this corpus - and the physiological rationale is coherent, since jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio index the stability of laryngeal and respiratory control rather than any social construct. The diagnostic ascertainment behind the corpus is also among the strongest in the review, with four stages culminating in independent confirmation by a child psychiatrist in a separate setting, and the authors explain rather than conceal the absence of ADOS. The competing-interest declaration - itemising employment, co-founder status, stock ownership and advisory compensation by individual, alongside company funding - is the most complete in the corpus and is the standard other commercially sponsored work here should be held to. What the study cannot deliver is evidence about detection. Its classification figure has no held-out test, was taken as the best of 2,000 epochs on the validation set, and is computed over cry instances from children whose other cries were in training - the same failure this review has now documented in scanpath images, video frames, EEG epochs, thermal images and here in cry audio, a fifth modality. And its statistical findings, which are otherwise the more credible half of the paper, are confounded with a 4.8-month age difference and with a recording-setting imbalance in which nearly nine in ten autistic cries came from autism centres, using three measures that all respond to room acoustics. The corrective analyses are available from data the paper already reports - stratify by setting, adjust for age, aggregate per child, and relate the acoustic features to the GARS-2 scores already in hand - which makes this a case where a promising construct is undermined by analyses that were not run rather than by data that were not collected.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Sixty-two children aged 18 to 54 months drawn from the publicly available Khozaei cry corpus collected in Iran: 31 autistic and 31 typically developing, with 24 boys and 7 girls in each group, mean ages 35.6 and 30.8 months. The exact sex matching at 24:7 is a genuine design strength and gives the sample 22.6% girls, higher than most autism research samples in this review. Two features of the sample are less favourable and both are reported without being examined. The mean ages differ by 4.8 months - about 16% of the younger group's mean, in a period of rapid vocal-tract and laryngeal maturation - with no test or adjustment reported, which matters because jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio all vary with vocal development. And the recording settings differ sharply by group: 87.10% of the autistic children's cries were recorded at autism centres and 12.90% at home, while 54.84% of the typically developing children's were recorded at health centres and 45.16% at home. Roughly six cry instances were retained per child (6.10 +/- 5.05 for the autistic group, 5.39 +/- 3.66 for the comparison group), giving an instance-level dataset of around 355 cries from 62 children. No cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is available. [RQ1.2] Clinical and developmental, without pathologising excess. Autism is 'a neurodevelopmental condition', described through 'a wide range of cognitive, social, and communicative challenges' and framed in terms of impact on the child, the family and society across education, healthcare and employment - a systemic rather than individual framing. Person-first phrasing is used consistently ('children with ASD', 'individuals diagnosed with ASD'), and the early-detection argument is made in terms of neuroplasticity and long-term prognosis rather than urgency or alarm. One formulation deserves note for its restraint: the paper states that 'any behavioral cues that raise concerns should be diligently combined with clinical assessments to enable the early identification of atypical development', positioning the technology as an input to clinical judgement rather than a substitute for it. The phrase 'children at risk of ASD' recurs and carries the usual risk framing. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person or family organisation is reported as involved in the work, which is worth noting for a study whose proposed product is an at-home screening tool for caregivers. [RQ1.3] Better than most secondary analyses in this review on sex and worse on age. Sex is matched exactly - 24 boys and 7 girls in both groups - so it is fully controlled, and at 22.6% girls the sample is less male-skewed than most autism research.
