Training and validation curves are reported for all five pairings and read for learning stability, with some pairings noted to show slower learning and greater fluctuation indicating models 'that might struggle with generalization'. A comparison table places the result against two prior studies reporting 0.7500 and 0.8050.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The corpus mixes two sources and the paper reports neither their proportions nor their distribution across classes - the single fact determining whether the mixed design mitigates the branch's provenance confound or introduces a sharper one, since a corpus in which autistic images come predominantly from an Indonesian autism centre and comparison images predominantly from an international web collection would be separable by ancestry, camera and setting alone. The paper's own statement that the network uses 'the texture of the skin' is consistent with that possibility, and a source-held-out evaluation, which the two identifiable sources make directly available, is not performed. No diagnostic ascertainment is described even for the clinic portion, forgoing the study's clearest opportunity to improve on its predecessors. The split is at image level with the number of distinct children unreported; augmentation ordering relative to splitting is unstated, and rotation, flip and contrast variants of one photograph are near-duplicates. No demographic information exists for either class. No specificity, AUC or confusion matrix is reported, so the error profile behind a recall of 0.8182 cannot be inspected, and no chance baseline is stated. There is no ethics or consent statement despite part of the corpus consisting of identifiable photographs of children attending a clinical service, and no limitations section.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: The tenth study in this review on the Kaggle facial-image corpus family, and the only one to supplement it with images from a clinical service - which makes it simultaneously the branch's most interesting variation and its clearest missed opportunity. Adding photographs from an autism centre in Semarang could have anchored part of the corpus in genuine clinical diagnoses, addressing the labelling problem that undermines every other study on these images; instead no ascertainment is described and no source-by-class breakdown is given, so the addition may equally have introduced a sharper confound in which ancestry, camera and setting align with the label. The decisive experiment was in the authors' hands: with two identifiable sources, training on one and testing on the other would have established directly whether the models detect facial phenotype or image provenance, and that single result would have been the most informative in the entire facial-image branch of this review. Three features nonetheless place the study above the branch norm. Its reported 0.8299 is internally consistent and modest, and it benchmarks itself against comparators at 0.7500 and 0.8050 rather than against the high-nineties claims made elsewhere on the same corpus. Its precision-recall discussion is the best in the branch, correctly judging a high-precision low-recall pairing 'less useful for finding all ASD cases' - a screening-oriented reading that almost no other study here articulates. And its account of rising prevalence is accurate where most of this corpus is alarmist, attributing the change from 1 in 150 to 1 in 36 to diagnostic criteria, awareness and detection across a broader age range. Its description of what the network extracts - face shape, expression and skin texture - is also unusually candid about the range of information a whole-image classifier receives, and names precisely the property most likely to track image source rather than the child.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two thousand nine hundred and thirty-six facial images, balanced at 1,468 labelled autistic and 1,468 labelled normal, drawn from two sources - Kaggle and 'data from an autism center in Semarang'. The mixed provenance is what distinguishes this study from the other nine Kaggle-corpus papers charted in this review, and it cuts both ways. Supplementing a web-scraped collection with images from an actual clinical service is in principle an improvement, since clinic-attending children have real diagnoses; but the paper never states how many images came from each source, nor whether the clinic contributed to the autistic class only or to both. If the autistic images are predominantly Indonesian clinic photographs while the comparison images are predominantly international web-scraped ones, the two classes would be separable by ancestry, camera and setting without any facial phenotype being involved - a sharper confound than the pure-Kaggle studies face. The paper's own account of provenance is loose enough to leave this open: the data 'could come from a variety of places, such as clinics, past research, or relevant public statistics'. No age, sex, ancestry, cognitive, language or clinical information is reported for either class, and the number of distinct children behind 2,936 images is never stated. [RQ1.2] Plain and largely accurate, with one notable feature. Autism is 'a developmental disorder that affects how a person talks, interacts with others, and thinks and acts', and the description of the spectrum is correct - conditions 'that used to be called classic autism, Asperger's syndrome, and undefined pervasive developmental disability are now part of ASD. This spectrum shows how different people can have very different symptoms'. 'Normal' is used as the class label for non-autistic children, which is the least careful terminology choice. What sets the framing apart is the treatment of rising prevalence: the paper records the increase from 1 in 150 in the early 2000s to 1 in 36 in 2023 and attributes it correctly to 'changes in how autism is diagnosed, more people and healthcare professionals being aware of it, and better detection of autism across a wider range of ages' - an accurate account that most papers in this corpus replace with an alarm narrative. The Indonesian framing is also specific rather than generic, noting the scarcity of national statistics and the reliance on Ministry of Health reports and local studies. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person is reported as involved. [RQ1.3] Entirely absent, and unusually consequential here. No age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic, cognitive or comorbidity information is reported for either class. The mixed-source corpus makes ancestry a specific rather than generic concern: a Kaggle collection assembled from international web sources and a set of photographs from an autism centre in Semarang would be expected to differ systematically in ancestry, in camera and lighting, and in photographic convention, and the paper's own description of the extracted features - 'the shape of the face, the expression on it, and the texture of the skin' - names skin texture explicitly as something the network uses. Without a source-wise breakdown of the classes, none of this can be examined, and a source-held-out evaluation, which the mixed corpus would have made straightforward, is not performed. [RQ1.4] None described for either source. For the Kaggle portion the labels are folder membership in a collection whose autistic class was harvested from autism-associated online content - the position documented across nine other studies in this review. For the Semarang autism-centre portion, children attending a clinical service would ordinarily carry clinical diagnoses, and this is the one point at which the study could have improved on its predecessors; but no instrument, criteria, clinician, assessment date or procedure is reported, and the paper's provenance sentence explicitly leaves the sources open, saying the data 'could come from a variety of places, such as clinics, past research, or relevant public statistics'. The opportunity to anchor part of the corpus in real diagnoses is therefore present and unrealised. [RQ1.5] None. No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists for any image. [RQ2.1] The aim is to identify a lightweight CNN ensemble that classifies autism from facial photographs accurately enough for deployment on mobile or edge devices. Five pairings were compared - MobileNetV2 with EfficientNetB0, B5 and B7; ResNet50 with EfficientNetB0; VGG16 with EfficientNetB0 - combined by probability averaging or majority voting. The best, MobileNetV2 with EfficientNetB0, reached accuracy 0.8299, precision 0.8514, recall 0.8182 and F1 0.8344, an internally consistent set and among the lower figures in this branch. Two aspects of the reporting are better than the branch norm. The precision-recall trade-off is interpreted in screening terms: ResNet50 with EfficientNetB0 achieved 'higher precision but lower recall, making them less useful for finding all ASD cases', which correctly identifies that a screening instrument's priority is not missing cases. And the learning curves are read substantively for stability and overfitting rather than displayed decoratively, with some pairings noted to show 'slower learning with more fluctuations, indicating less stable models that might struggle with generalization'. The comparison table places the result against two prior studies at 0.7500 and 0.8050 - modest comparators, and the study does not claim to have exceeded the high-nineties figures reported elsewhere in the branch. [RQ2.2] Two settings, imperfectly distinguished. Part of the corpus is the Kaggle collection, which has no setting - the images were harvested from internet sources by a third party. Part comes from an autism centre in Semarang, which is a clinical service setting and the same kind of environment in which the proposed edge-deployed tool would run. The mixture is potentially valuable and is undermined by the absence of any breakdown: without knowing how many images came from each source and how they distribute across the two classes, a reader cannot tell whether the clinic data broadens the corpus or introduces a setting confound aligned with the label. A source-held-out analysis would have answered this directly and is not attempted. [RQ2.3] None. The photographs were taken outside any study, in unknown circumstances, for both portions of the corpus. The paper's description of what the network extracts - face shape, expression and skin texture - underlines the consequence: with no task and no controlled acquisition, expression at the captured instant is free to vary with why the photograph was taken, and skin texture with the camera that took it. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary and clinic-sourced analysis with no longitudinal element. No ethics or consent statement appears anywhere in the paper. This is a more serious omission than for the purely Kaggle-based studies charted elsewhere in this review: part of the corpus consists of facial photographs of children attending an autism centre in Semarang, so identifiable images of clinically attending children were obtained and used with no reported institutional approval and no consent process. Funding and competing interests are not stated. [RQ2.5] No acquisition equipment is described. The architectural argument is explicitly about deployment hardware: MobileNetV2 and EfficientNetB0 were chosen 'because they are fast and have small models', using depthwise separable convolutions and compound scaling so that inference is quick enough for 'devices with limited processing power, like mobile phones or edge devices used in clinical settings'. That is a coherent design rationale for a low-resource context and connects the architecture choice to the stated Indonesian setting, where the paper notes national statistics are scarce. [RQ2.6] Adequate on the pipeline and deficient on the corpus. Reported: total image count and exact class balance, both sources by name, the 80:20 split ratio, the preprocessing and augmentation operations (resizing, normalisation, rotation, flipping, contrast adjustment), all five ensemble pairings with their constituent architectures, both combination rules, the softmax-plus-threshold decision structure, four metrics for each pairing, learning curves for each, and a comparison table against prior work. Not reported: the proportion of images from each source and their distribution across classes, the number of distinct children, whether augmentation preceded splitting, hyperparameters, per-class error breakdowns, ethics arrangements, funding and code. [RQ2.7] No limitations section exists, and the conclusion repeats the results paragraph almost verbatim without critical reflection. What should have been stated: the proportion of Kaggle against Semarang images and their distribution across classes is unreported, which is the single fact determining whether mixing sources mitigates the branch's provenance confound or creates a sharper one aligned with ancestry, camera and setting; no diagnostic ascertainment is described even for the clinic-sourced portion, forgoing the study's clearest opportunity to improve on its predecessors; the split is at image level with the number of distinct children unreported; augmentation ordering relative to splitting is unstated and rotation, flip and contrast variants of one photograph are near-duplicates; no demographic data exist in a study classifying faces; no specificity, AUC or confusion matrix is given, so the error profile behind a recall of 0.8182 is uninspectable; and there is no ethics or consent statement despite part of the corpus coming from a clinical service. [RQ2.9] None separately stated. The step this study most needs is a source-held-out evaluation - training on Kaggle images and testing on Semarang images, or the reverse - which its own mixed corpus makes available and which would establish directly whether the models detect a facial phenotype or the character of an image source. Reporting the source-by-class breakdown would be the prerequisite. [RQ3.1] Facial appearance, described more honestly than in most of this branch. Rather than asserting a specific craniofacial phenotype, the paper says the network finds 'important patterns in the image, such as the shape of the face, the expression on it, and the texture of the skin'. That enumeration is accurate about what a whole-image CNN actually receives, and it names two properties - expression and skin texture - that are not morphological and would vary with photographic circumstance rather than with the child. Naming skin texture as a used feature is particularly pointed in a corpus mixing an internationally scraped collection with photographs from an Indonesian clinic, since skin appearance in an image is jointly determined by ancestry, lighting and camera. No landmark geometry or morphometric quantity is computed anywhere. [RQ3.2] Decision-level ensembling rather than modality fusion. Two CNNs classify independently and their outputs are combined by probability averaging or majority voting, with the stated rationale that this 'makes the system more reliable and accurate by lowering the chance of errors from a single model and making it better at generalizing new data'. Five pairings are compared, which gives real architectural breadth, and the pairings deliberately combine a lightweight backbone with an EfficientNet variant of differing scale. No ablation reports single-model performance against the ensembles, so the claimed ensembling gain is asserted rather than demonstrated. [RQ4.1] Five ensemble pairings of pretrained convolutional networks, combined at the decision level by averaging or voting. The selection criterion is explicitly computational: lightweight architectures using depthwise separable convolutions and compound scaling, chosen for fast inference on constrained hardware. That is an appropriate design goal for a low-resource deployment context and is argued rather than assumed. Comparing five pairings with learning curves for each is more architectural breadth than most single-model papers in this branch offer, and the authors' reading of those curves for stability - identifying which pairings learn smoothly and which fluctuate - is a legitimate diagnostic use rather than a decorative one. [RQ4.2] Resized and normalised face images augmented by rotation, flipping and contrast adjustment. Contrast adjustment is worth noting because it partially normalises a property that would differ systematically between image sources; whether it is sufficient to remove a source signal is untested, and no source-wise analysis is performed. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for each of the five pairings, with training and validation curves. The metric set supports one genuinely useful observation - that a pairing with higher precision but lower recall is 'less useful for finding all ASD cases', which is the correct screening-oriented reading and is articulated in almost no other study in this branch. What is missing is specificity, AUC, confusion matrices and confidence intervals, and no chance baseline is stated despite the exactly balanced construction placing it at 50%. The comparison table cites two prior studies at 0.7500 and 0.8050 rather than the high-nineties figures reported by other Kaggle-corpus work, so the study positions itself against modest comparators. [RQ4.4] None. No attribution, saliency or feature analysis is reported. The omission is pointed here because the paper itself names skin texture among the features the network uses, and because the mixed-source corpus makes it directly testable whether the models respond to image source - a saliency or source-classification analysis would have addressed the study's central ambiguity and neither is attempted. [RQ4.5] An 80:20 image-level split with no cross-validation, no separately described validation partition, and no participant-level partitioning; the number of distinct children behind 2,936 images is never stated. Augmentation by rotation, flipping and contrast adjustment is applied without specifying whether it preceded the split, and such variants of a single photograph are near-duplicates rather than independent observations. These are the standard weaknesses of this branch. What is distinctive here is a confound the mixed corpus introduces and the paper leaves entirely unexamined. The images come from two sources - Kaggle and an autism centre in Semarang - and neither the proportion from each nor their distribution across the two classes is reported. If the clinic supplied predominantly autistic images while the comparison class came predominantly from the international web collection, the classes would be separable by ancestry, camera, lighting and photographic convention without any facial phenotype being involved, and the reported 0.8299 would measure source rather than diagnosis. The paper's own account of what the network extracts - face shape, expression and skin texture - is consistent with that reading. The remedy is available and unused: with two identifiable sources in hand, a source-held-out evaluation, or simply a source-by-class table, would settle the question directly. Two elements of the analysis nonetheless stand above the branch norm: the learning curves are interpreted for stability and overfitting rather than displayed without comment, and the precision-recall trade-off across pairings is read in screening terms, with a high-precision low-recall model correctly judged 'less useful for finding all ASD cases'. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, early detection, ensemble convolutional neural network, facial images, classification, accuracy. Method- and task-facing, with the modality named. The leading keyword field contains the placeholder word 'Component', which suggests a template was not fully edited. [RQ5.2] International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications 16(7):229ff, 2025. An open-access computer science venue, and the profile follows: the ensemble pipeline, augmentation, split ratio and metric tables are documented, while the corpus's dual provenance is left unquantified, no ethics statement appears despite clinic-sourced images, no limitations section is provided, and the conclusion repeats the results paragraph verbatim. An unedited template placeholder survives in the keyword list. [RQ5.3] Published 2025 by an electrical engineering group at Universitas Semarang with collaborators at Institut Kesehatan Indonesia and a Jakarta stem-cell laboratory. For this review the study is the tenth built on the Kaggle facial-image corpus family and the only one to supplement it with images from a clinical service - an autism centre in Semarang - which makes it both the branch's most interesting variation and its clearest missed opportunity. Mixing a web-scraped collection with clinic photographs could have anchored part of the corpus in real diagnoses; instead the paper reports neither the proportion from each source nor how they distribute across the two classes, so a reader cannot tell whether the addition reduces the provenance confound documented across the other nine studies or replaces it with a sharper one, in which Indonesian clinic photographs and international web images are separable by ancestry, camera and setting alone. The paper's own description of what the network extracts - 'the shape of the face, the expression on it, and the texture of the skin' - is unusually candid about the range of information a whole-image CNN receives, and names skin texture, which is exactly the kind of property that tracks image source rather than the child. The remedy was in the study's hands: with two identifiable sources it could have trained on one and tested on the other, and that single experiment would have been the most informative result in the entire facial-image branch of this review. Three further observations. The reported 0.8299 accuracy with precision 0.8514, recall 0.8182 and F1 0.8344 is internally consistent and among the branch's lower figures, and the study benchmarks itself against comparators at 0.7500 and 0.8050 rather than against the high-nineties claims elsewhere. Its precision-recall discussion is the branch's best, correctly judging a high-precision low-recall model 'less useful for finding all ASD cases'. And its account of rising prevalence is accurate where most of this corpus is alarmist, attributing the change from 1 in 150 to 1 in 36 to diagnostic criteria, awareness and broader age-range detection. Against this: no ethics or consent statement anywhere, despite identifiable photographs of children attending a clinical service; no diagnostic ascertainment described even for that portion; no demographic data; image-level splitting with the number of children unreported; no specificity or confusion matrix; and no limitations section.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective secondary analysis of the publicly archived Eye-tracking Dataset to Support the Research on Autism Spectrum Disorder (figshare 20113592, Cilia et al.): 59 children - 29 with ASD, 30 typically developing - viewing static images (faces, objects, scenes) and short videos (cartoon characters, balloons) for about five minutes each at ~60 cm from a 17-inch display, recorded on an SMI RED mobile tracker at 60 Hz. The analysed table holds 1,048,575 gaze-sample rows, one short of Excel's worksheet maximum. Sex composition is 25M/4F in the ASD group against 13M/17F in the TD group; age is given as a single pooled mean of 7.88 years.
narrative_rows.methods: Mean imputation of missing values, label encoding of categorical fields, mutual-information feature selection down to 16 features, min-max normalisation, and reshaping to a single-timestep tensor. Two architectures were fitted: a 64-unit LSTM and a hybrid 1-D CNN plus LSTM, both with dropout, binary cross-entropy, an adaptive optimiser and early stopping. Evaluation used stratified 5-fold cross-validation over the gaze-sample rows.
narrative_rows.outcomes: CNN-LSTM mean accuracy 99.78% (SD 0.11%), per-class precision/recall/F1 of 99.81/99.85/99.83 for non-ASD and 99.72/99.63/99.67 for ASD; the standalone LSTM was lower but still above 99%. A one-sample t-test of the fold accuracies against 95% gave t(4)=14.2, p<0.001. The authors conclude the system successfully diagnosed ASD and shows promise for clinical application.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The paper states none. In fact the result is uninterpretable as diagnostic accuracy for four compounding reasons. (1) The 16-feature input vector includes CARS_Score, the Childhood Autism Rating Scale - a clinician-administered measure of the target condition supplied to the model as a predictor. (2) Cross-validation partitions gaze samples, not children: with roughly 17,800 rows per child, every test fold contains rows recorded milliseconds apart from its own training rows, so the classifier can succeed by identifying individuals. (3) Mutual-information selection and mean imputation were both computed on the full dataset before splitting. (4) The 42.9-point sex gap between groups provides an independent route to high accuracy. No participant-level metric, no specificity, no AUC, no external validation, no ablation without CARS, no ethics statement, and no limitations section appear anywhere in the article.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This study is the review's cleanest single illustration of how several validation failures stack multiplicatively. It sits alongside local_3e88f3ce and local_8253c2ec/local_a0d73248 in the target-leakage group, and alongside the scanpath, video-frame, EEG-epoch, thermal-image, cry-instance and facial-image studies in the within-participant leakage group - but it is the only charted paper that belongs to both simultaneously, at the finest analysis granularity in the corpus. Its 99.78% should be read against local_cd7545e2, where the ADOS-2 itself reaches AUC 0.562 in a clinically relevant discrimination, and against local_7d7f1fcc, where a participant-level matched split over pose data yields 82.5%. It also extends the review's venue finding: an article with no ethics statement and no limitations section, using a diagnostic instrument as a model input, cleared peer review at a clinical journal in 32 days.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups from a single archived dataset: 29 children with ASD and 30 typically developing children, 59 in total. The unit actually analysed is not the child but the gaze sample: 1,048,575 rows. That figure deserves attention - 1,048,576 is the maximum row count of a Microsoft Excel worksheet, so the analysed set is almost certainly a spreadsheet-truncated slice of the source recording rather than the complete data, and the paper never remarks on it. Per-child row counts, per-group row counts and per-fold composition are all unreported. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children diagnosed with ASD, autism group, non-ASD, typically developing (TD) children. Diagnosis-first, deficit-oriented phrasing predominates: children with ASD typically have difficulty focusing, reduced attention to important stimuli, autism and non-autism profiles. There is no mention of autistic community perspectives, no identity-first alternative, and no acknowledgement that the sample carries clinical labels assigned by others. [RQ1.3] Sparse and, where present, alarming. Table 2 reports sex and a single pooled mean age of 7.88 years - no SD, no range, no per-group age. Sex composition is 25 male / 4 female in ASD (86.2% male) versus 13 male / 17 female in TD (43.3% male), a 42.9-point gap. This is the largest sex imbalance in the review's charted corpus, exceeding the 32-point gap in local_4ceee075. Because sex systematically affects gaze behaviour towards faces, a classifier reading gaze coordinates can score highly by learning sex. No race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, language, geography or recruitment source is reported for either group. [RQ1.4] Not confirmed by this study. Labels are inherited wholesale from the figshare dataset. The presence of a CARS_Score field implies that the original collectors administered the Childhood Autism Rating Scale, but this paper reports no cut-off, no administrator qualification, no ADOS or ADI-R, no DSM or ICD criterion, and no statement of who made the diagnoses or when. The TD group's status as non-autistic is likewise asserted rather than evidenced - no screening instrument is named. [RQ1.5] CARS_Score is present in the data but is never reported as a participant characteristic - no mean, no range, no distribution by group. Instead it is consumed as a model input feature. No IQ, developmental quotient, adaptive-behaviour, language or comorbidity measure is reported for any participant. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to implement deep learning on eye-tracking data from social attention tasks to diagnose ASD, and to identify the feature-selection strategy that lets the model reach high accuracy. Note that maximising accuracy is written into the objectives themselves - one of the listed research questions asks for the feature selection strategy that can assist the deep learning model in achieving high accuracy, which is a statement of intent to optimise the reported number rather than to estimate a diagnostic property. The headline finding is CNN-LSTM accuracy 99.78% (SD 0.11%), reported as outperforming previous studies and showing promise for clinical application. [RQ2.2] Data collection setting is described second-hand: a dedicated experimental room, participant seated about 60 cm from a 17-inch display, session length about five minutes, stimulus order varied between participants, infrared reflection tracking. The country, clinic type, recruitment channel and date of the original collection are not stated. The analysis itself was run on a desktop workstation. [RQ2.3] Free viewing of mixed static and dynamic stimuli. Dynamic content comprised short videos with engaging elements such as cartoon characters and balloons designed to attract children's attention; static content comprised images of faces, objects and scenes. No areas of interest are defined, no fixation or saccade extraction is performed, and no social-versus-nonsocial contrast is computed - the abstract's framing as social attention tasks is inherited from the dataset description rather than operationalised in the analysis. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, no follow-up. Ethics reporting is absent entirely - no approval statement, no committee, no consent statement, and the word ethic does not appear in the article. This is a study of clinically labelled disabled children published in a medical journal with a full data-availability statement and no ethics statement of any kind. Only the public status of the source dataset is offered, which addresses data access, not the ethics of the analysis or of the diagnostic claim being made. [RQ2.5] SMI RED mobile eye tracker at 60 Hz with a 17-inch stimulus display, participant at ~60 cm. Compute: 7th-generation Intel Core i7, 8 GB RAM, 16 GB GPU. Software is described only as a suitable computational framework for neural network training - no library, no version, no seed. Calibration procedure, data-quality thresholds and drift handling are not described, which matters because Tracking_Ratio (a data-quality index) is one of the retained features. [RQ2.6] Partial and, on the decisive points, poor. Reproducible: the source dataset is openly archived on figshare with a resolvable URL, and the preprocessing sequence is narrated step by step. Not reproducible: no code, no software or version names, no random seed, no complete hyperparameter specification, no statement of the mutual-information threshold or scores that produced exactly 16 features, no per-fold row counts, and no per-child row counts. A reader cannot verify whether the 16 selected features are the same ones the mutual-information ranking would yield on their machine, nor reconstruct the folds. [RQ2.7] None acknowledged. There is no limitations section, no threats-to-validity paragraph, and no caveat anywhere in the discussion or conclusion. The paper moves directly from 99.78% to promise for clinical application. Every issue this review identifies - row-level splitting, unnested feature selection, CARS as an input, the sex imbalance, imputation before splitting, the Excel-shaped row count - passes unmentioned. [RQ2.9] Two directions: incorporating attention mechanisms into the deep learning models so the model focuses on the most relevant features, and extending to multimodal data combining eye-tracking with other behavioural or physiological signals. Neither addresses the validity problems in the present design; both propose adding capacity to a pipeline whose reported ceiling is already 99.78%. [RQ3.1] Visual attention allocation during free viewing - fixation position (point of regard, left and right eye), gaze direction vectors in three dimensions, and the categorical annotation of what was being looked at (Category_Right, Category_Left) alongside stimulus identity. The behavioural construct is therefore where the child looks, sampled instantaneously, with no aggregation into fixations, saccades, dwell times or AOI proportions. [RQ3.2] No fusion of behavioural modalities - eye tracking only. There is, however, an undeclared fusion of a different kind: the clinical instrument score (CARS) is concatenated with the behavioural features into a single input vector. That is not multimodal behavioural fusion; it is the insertion of the outcome's own measurement instrument into the predictor set. Multimodal work is named as future rather than present. [RQ4.1] Supervised deep learning for binary classification: a standalone LSTM (64 units, dropout, sigmoid) and a hybrid 1-D CNN plus LSTM. The recurrent framing is nominal - the input tensor has exactly one timestep, so the LSTM has no sequence to traverse and reduces to a gated dense transformation of a 16-dimensional vector. The paper says this explicitly (even though the input consisted of only a single timestep) without recognising that it removes the entire justification for the architecture. [RQ4.2] A 16-element tabular vector per gaze sample: trial and stimulus identifiers, Tracking_Ratio, Point_of_Regard right/left X and Y, six gaze-vector components, Category_Right, Category_Left, #Stimulus, and CARS_Score. Min-max scaled to [0,1], reshaped to (1,16). Two of these deserve separate note. CARS_Score is a clinician-administered autism severity instrument: within this dataset it is effectively a monotone function of the label, so its inclusion is direct target leakage and by itself can account for a near-perfect result. Tracking_Ratio is a signal-quality index that plausibly differs systematically between groups for reasons of compliance rather than social attention. Stimulus and trial identifiers encode session structure. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall/sensitivity, F1, per-class values and per-fold confusion matrices; means with standard deviations across the five folds. Missing: specificity as a separate figure, AUC or any threshold-free measure, calibration, positive and negative predictive value at a stated prevalence, and any participant-level metric. Because the analysis unit is the gaze sample, none of the reported numbers is a diagnostic accuracy in the clinical sense - not one figure in the paper describes how often a child would be correctly classified. [RQ4.4] None applied to the model. A Pearson correlation heatmap and the mutual-information ranking characterise the input data before fitting. No post-hoc attribution, no attention weights (attention is proposed as future work), no ablation showing performance with CARS_Score removed - the single experiment that would have settled what the model learned. [RQ4.5] Stratified 5-fold cross-validation on 1,048,575 gaze-sample rows, stratified by class only. This is the review's clearest instance of within-participant leakage at the finest possible granularity: with 59 children and roughly 17,800 rows each, every test fold is virtually guaranteed to contain samples drawn from the same recording session, the same child and the same stimulus presentation as the training rows, differing by fractions of a second. A model can reach 99.78% by recognising individual children rather than autism. Three further defects compound it. First, mutual-information feature selection was run on the whole dataset before cross-validation, so the folds were chosen using their own test labels. Second, mean imputation of missing values was likewise computed over the whole dataset. Third, early stopping restores the weights that minimise loss on the same partition whose accuracy is then reported. The 0.11% standard deviation across folds is presented as evidence of stability; it is better read as confirmation that the five folds are near-identical resamples of one recording set. No participant-level split, no external cohort, and no held-out site is attempted anywhere in the paper. [RQ5.1] autism spectrum disorder; eye-tracking; deep learning; diagnosing; ASD. Purely method-and-condition; nothing on validation, generalisation, participants or clinical deployment. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Medicine 12:1690177 - an open-access general medical journal, not a computing venue. This matters for the review's venue analysis: the paper's audience is clinical, its abstract advises healthcare professionals, and no clinical reviewer flagged the absence of an ethics statement, the absence of a limitations section, or the use of a diagnostic instrument as a model input. [RQ5.3] 2025, published 9 October, 32 days from submission to acceptance. Framing is unqualified diagnostic replacement: the system successfully diagnosed ASD, the approach shows promise for clinical application, assisting healthcare professionals in diagnosing ASD more accurately through advanced artificial intelligence technology. The comparison table positions the contribution purely as a higher accuracy number than nine listed predecessors, with no comparison of study design, split scheme or sample. It belongs to the review's leaderboard genre, in which the reported figure rather than the estimand is the unit of scientific progress.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Primary cross-sectional questionnaire study in Pakistan. A Q-CHAT-10-based instrument was circulated through several rehabilitation centres, collected on paper and via Google Forms, and completed by parents, caregivers, medical staff or clinicians for children aged 2-4 years. The paper states 750 participants, though the reported sex counts (434 male, 308 female) and the split counts (593 train, 149 test) both sum to 742. The test set is 106 autistic-class and 43 non-autistic-class children.
narrative_rows.methods: After removing incomplete rows, binary-encoding categorical fields and deleting the case identifier and the who-completed-the-test field, the authors correlated each Q-CHAT item with the Q-CHAT-10 score and the class label and deleted items A1, A2, A6, A8 and A9 for high correlation. The remaining five items plus age, sex, jaundice and family history were passed to TPOT (10 generations, population 100) over a single random 80/20 split. TPOT returned a BernoulliNB plus RandomForestClassifier ensemble, which the authors then rebuilt manually with the published parameters to verify reproducibility, and compared against six hand-specified baselines.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Autistic class precision 0.83, recall 0.90, F1 0.86; non-autistic class 0.68, 0.53, 0.60; accuracy 0.83 in the results and comparison tables but 78% in the abstract; micro-average ROC 0.87, macro-average ROC 0.81; PR 0.892 and 0.728. Baselines ranged from 0.70 (decision tree) to 0.80 (naive Bayes).
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The label is the Q-CHAT-10 scoring function applied to the same ten items that supply the features, so no clinical diagnosis enters the study and the task is reconstruction of a checklist threshold rather than detection of autism. The correlation-based deletion of five items is arithmetically self-defeating - those items correlate with the score because they are summed into it - and removing them is what pulls the result down from the near-perfect figures other checklist-label studies report to the low 80s. The test set is 71.1% positive, making the majority-class baseline 71.1%; the paper's own SVM row (recall 1.000, precision 0.718, accuracy 0.71) is that trivial classifier, printed without comment. Everything rests on one unseeded 80/20 split with no intervals, the dataset is not shared, respondents were recruited through autism rehabilitation services, comorbid neurological conditions were excluded, and the stated sample size exceeds the accounted-for participants by eight. The authors state only one limitation, the absence of public-dataset evaluation.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This paper is the informative middle term of the review's questionnaire-tabular branch. local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 retain all ten checklist items and report 100% on six metrics; this study deletes five of them and reports 0.83 - the same circular estimand, differing only in how much of the label's own arithmetic was left in the feature set. Read together, the three establish that reported accuracy in this branch is a function of how completely the label's summands survive preprocessing, and nothing else. It is also one of only two included studies (with local_7b468950) whose authors manually re-implemented and verified their own selected model, and its ethics reporting - named committee, protocol number, approval date, consent as an inclusion criterion - stands well above the corpus norm, though the reviewing body is a software engineering department. Its stated novelty, a locally collected Pakistani cohort rather than another reuse of a public high-income-country dataset, is a genuine and rare contribution to the corpus's geographic distribution.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] One group of children aged 2-4 years recruited through Pakistani rehabilitation centres, split by questionnaire outcome rather than by recruitment stream. The paper states 750 participants, but 434 male plus 308 female is 742, and 593 training plus 149 test is also 742; eight children are unaccounted for and the inconsistency is not noted. Class sizes are never stated directly and must be recovered from the test-set support column (106 autistic, 43 non-autistic), implying about 71% positive overall. There is no separate typically developing comparison group in the design sense - both classes come from the same rehabilitation-centre respondent pool, and the questionnaire was described as circulated among trainers and parents of children with autism, which makes the non-autistic class a by-product of scoring rather than a recruited control group. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, ASD traits, autistic class, non-autistic class, children with autism, affected individuals. The introduction is unusually careful in one respect - it states that autism is not a sickness or disease but a lifelong neurological developmental disorder - and unusually careless elsewhere, describing symptoms as tiresome behaviors, deficits in public interactivity, and social disablement. The DSM-5 support levels are laid out at length, then never used. No autistic or community perspective is cited. [RQ1.3] Age band 2-4 years (recorded in months, no mean or SD); 434 male / 308 female overall with no per-class breakdown; jaundice at birth and family history of ASD recorded as binary fields. Nothing on socioeconomic status, urban/rural location, language, education or which rehabilitation centre each child came from - the last being important, since centre could act as a site effect in a dataset pooled across several centres. The paper does report a sex effect in the data (males give more positive Q-CHAT responses) and interprets it as males being more prone to autism, without considering respondent expectation or referral bias. [RQ1.4] Not confirmed for any participant. This is the defining feature of the study: there is no clinical diagnosis anywhere in the pipeline. The label Class/ASD Traits is generated by the Q-CHAT-10 scoring function applied to the same ten items that supply the features. What is modelled is therefore a scoring rule, not a condition. The one screening instrument used is a caregiver checklist completed variously by parents, caregivers, medical staff or clinicians - and the field recording which of those it was was deleted during preprocessing as irrelevant, discarding the only available indicator of measurement heterogeneity. [RQ1.5] None. No IQ, developmental quotient, adaptive behaviour, language level or ASD severity measure. Q-CHAT-10 score is present but is the label's source. Comorbid neurological conditions were an exclusion criterion, so no comorbidity data exist. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to apply automated machine learning (TPOT) to a locally collected Pakistani dataset to determine the likelihood of ASD in children at early stages and to speed up diagnosis, with an explicit framing as one of the first uses of AUTOML for ASD detection on real-world non-high-income-country data. Headline findings: TPOT selected a BernoulliNB plus RandomForest ensemble; autistic-class precision 0.83, recall 0.90, F1 0.86; non-autistic-class precision 0.68, recall 0.53, F1 0.60; accuracy 0.83 in the results tables but reported as 78% in the abstract; micro-ROC 0.87, macro-ROC 0.81. [RQ2.2] Several rehabilitation centres across Pakistan, with responses collected on paper and via Google Forms into a Google Sheet. The authors are candid about the context: there is no proper reporting and tracking of ASD cases in the country, and the data had to be recorded from scratch. Neither the number of centres, their names, their catchment, nor the collection dates are given, so site cannot be treated as a variable and the pooled sample cannot be characterised. [RQ2.3] There is no task or paradigm. The instrument is the ten-item Quantitative Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (Q-CHAT-10) of Allison et al., reproduced in full in Table 2, plus seven auxiliary variables. Behaviour is entirely caregiver-reported and retrospective. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, no follow-up. Ethics reporting is among the better examples in this corpus in form: Declaration of Helsinki compliance, named committee, protocol number BUIC/H11/SE/46113 with an approval date of 3 April 2023, informed parental consent as an inclusion criterion, and exclusion of children with comorbid neurological disorders. The reviewing body is a Software Engineering Department ethical review committee rather than a clinical or psychological board, which is a mismatch given that the study collects health data on disabled children and advertises a diagnostic use. [RQ2.5] No instrumentation - Google Forms for capture, CSV export. Modelling used the TPOT library (10 generations, population 100, remaining parameters default) with scikit-learn estimators. No versions, no hardware, no seed. The full best-pipeline parameter set is given in Table 4, which is more than most papers in this corpus supply. [RQ2.6] Mixed, with one notable strength. The authors manually rebuilt the TPOT-selected pipeline using the exact reported parameters to verify that the automated result was reproducible - a deliberate replication step that almost no other study in this corpus performs, and the paper's best methodological instinct. Against that: the dataset is not deposited, no code is released, no library versions or random seed are given, the single 80/20 split is unseeded, the participant counts do not reconcile, and two different accuracies (78% and 0.83) appear for the same experiment. [RQ2.7] One limitation is stated - no evaluation on public datasets, and the Pakistani rehabilitation-centre sample's demographic and cultural specificity may limit generalisability, with a sensible note that direct comparison against UCI data would itself introduce socio-clinical bias. Unstated: that the label is a deterministic function of the predictors, that five of the ten items were deleted precisely because they predicted the label too well, that the majority-class baseline is 71.1%, that a single unrepeated split underpins every number, that the sample size does not add up, and that respondents were drawn from among parents of children already attending autism rehabilitation services. [RQ2.9] Compare other AUTOML libraries; benchmark the model on public datasets such as the UCI ASD screening data to test robustness across populations. Both are reasonable and directly address the stated limitation, but neither touches the circular label that governs the entire result. [RQ3.1] Early social-communication behaviours as reported by a caregiver: response to name, ease of eye contact, requesting gestures, declarative pointing, pretend play, gaze following, comforting a distressed family member, early speech quality, conventional gestures such as waving goodbye, and prolonged purposeless staring. After correlation-based deletion only five of these (A3 requesting gestures, A4 pointing, A5 pretend play, A7 comforting, A10 staring) remain as predictors. [RQ3.2] No fusion - a single questionnaire modality, augmented by four static fields (age, sex, jaundice, family history). The study belongs to the corpus's questionnaire-tabular branch alongside local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 rather than to any sensor-based branch. [RQ4.1] Automated machine learning by genetic programming: TPOT searched pipelines over classical estimators and returned an ensemble of BernoulliNB and RandomForestClassifier. Six manually specified baselines (SVM, KNN, naive Bayes, logistic regression, decision tree, random forest) were fitted for comparison. No deep learning. [RQ4.2] A nine-field tabular row per child: five binary Q-CHAT items plus age in months, binary sex, binary jaundice and binary family history. The feature-selection step is the analytically decisive move and it runs in an unexpected direction. Items A1, A2, A6, A8 and A9 were removed because they correlated highly with the Q-CHAT-10 score - but the Q-CHAT-10 score is the sum of exactly those items, so high correlation is arithmetic necessity, not redundancy. Deleting them does not remove noise; it removes half of the summands that define the label. The reported 0.83 is thus an estimate of how well five items reconstruct the threshold on all ten, which is why this study lands in the low 80s while local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248, which retained all items, reach 100%. [RQ4.3] Per-class precision, recall and F1 with support, macro and weighted averages, accuracy, a confusion matrix, micro-average ROC 0.87 and macro-average ROC 0.81, and PR values of 0.892 and 0.728. This is a fuller metric set than most of the corpus offers, and unusually the weaker class is reported honestly (non-autistic recall 0.53). Missing: specificity named as such, calibration, predictive values at a stated prevalence, and any confidence interval. The abstract's 78% does not match the 0.83 in the results and comparison tables - the 0.78 in the table is the weighted-average precision/F1 row, so the headline accuracy has been read off the wrong line. [RQ4.4] Pearson item-label correlations guide feature deletion, and the correlation matrix is shown. No post-hoc model explanation - no permutation or Gini importance from the RandomForest component, no partial dependence, no per-case attribution - despite the model family making all of these trivially available. The discussion raises pipeline interpretability as a consideration for AUTOML users but does not act on it. [RQ4.5] A single random 80/20 split: 593 training, 149 test. No cross-validation of the final model, no repeats, no seed, no stratification statement, no interval estimate. TPOT's internal search cross-validates within the training portion, so the pipeline choice is not directly contaminated by the test rows - a cleaner arrangement than most of this corpus - and the manual re-fit with the reported parameters confirms the pipeline is what it claims to be. Two problems dominate nonetheless. First, the validation design cannot address the label's circularity: no split scheme can turn the reconstruction of a checklist threshold into diagnostic accuracy. Second, the test set is 71.1% positive and the paper never states the majority-class baseline, even though it prints it - the SVM comparator's recall of 1.000 at precision 0.718 and accuracy 0.71 is the all-positive classifier, sitting unremarked in the comparison table as though it were a genuine competitor. Read against that baseline, the AUTOML pipeline's contribution is about 12 accuracy points, and the non-autistic recall of 0.53 shows where its errors fall - on precisely the children a screening tool exists to reassure. [RQ5.1] autism spectrum disorder; AUTOML; TPOT. Three terms, one condition and two tooling names - no participants, no validation, no setting, and nothing marking the study's genuine distinguishing feature, which is that the data come from Pakistan. [RQ5.2] Diagnostics 15(15):1859 (MDPI) - an open-access clinical diagnostics journal, with academic editors drawn from the biomedical signal-processing community. The venue's clinical framing did not surface the label circularity or the abstract/table accuracy mismatch in review. [RQ5.3] 2025, published 24 July, 46 days from submission to acceptance including one revision round. Framing is assistive and comparatively restrained: an encouraging approach to improve detection, a first step towards early diagnosis within a few minutes saving time and expense. The novelty claim is placed on the population rather than the accuracy - unlike prior work relying on publicly available datasets from high-income countries, this study uses a locally developed dataset reflecting regional demographics and clinical practices - and that is the paper's real contribution to the corpus. The overreach is concentrated in one sentence claiming the system differentiates intellectual disability disorder from ASD using DSM-5-TR-derived questions, which nothing in the study tests.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective analysis of 2,526 images (1,263 ASD, 1,263 non-ASD) from the Kaggle Autistic Children Facial Image Dataset (imrankhan77), an eleventh reuse in this corpus of the web-scraped autism face collection. An 80-20 stratified image-level split gave 2,020 training and 506 test images, with 5-fold cross-validation inside the training portion; the final evaluation used 200 images selected from the test set. Table 1 additionally reports age bands, sex, six ethnicity categories, urban/rural residence and a four-way facial-morphology partition, all summing exactly to 2,526, none of which exists in the source dataset and none of whose derivation is described.
narrative_rows.methods: Images were resized to 224x224 and augmented by rotation and scaling; landmarks were located with OpenCV and Dlib and refined by a CNN combined with an Active Shape Appearance Model; the landmark configuration was encoded as a Euclidean graph through graph encoder convolutional networks; Randomized Trees ranked geometric features (upper-face breadth, eye spacing, mid-face length) and XGBoost performed the classification. Training used Adam at learning rate 0.001, batch size 32, 500 epochs, on a Windows 10 desktop with 8 GB RAM and an Intel i3 CPU.
narrative_rows.outcomes: At 500 epochs: accuracy 0.985, precision 0.975, recall 0.987, F1 0.925, AUC 0.98, detection accuracy 0.99, miss rate 0.07, fall-out 0.07, and landmark localisation error 0.9 mm. At 100 epochs the same pipeline reports accuracy 0.60 and AUC 0.6. Comparator figures (SVM AUC 0.74, AdaBoost 0.66, MobileNet-V2 0.64) are quoted from one prior paper rather than measured.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The study's premise and its data are different things: every methodological argument concerns depth information available only from 3D scans, while the input is a folder of 2D web photographs processed with a 2D landmark detector, and the reported millimetre localisation error has no metric basis in such images. The labels are Kaggle folder names with no clinical diagnosis behind them. The demographic and facial-morphology table used to argue that the dataset reflects real-world diversity has no source and no described annotation procedure. The headline metrics come from an unexplained 200-image selection from the test set, while the accompanying confusion matrix totals 300 cases and implies accuracy 0.957, precision 0.940 and recall 0.972 - none matching the reported values - and the reported F1 of 0.925 is incompatible with the reported precision and recall. Feature importances, the one output that would show what the model uses, are described but never given. The limitations section is substantive but addresses 3D imaging hardware the study did not use.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This is the eleventh charted reuse of the web-scraped facial-image corpus, and it extends that branch's pattern in a new direction. The other ten vary in model capacity and split protocol while reporting the same kind of number on the same pictures; this one adds an entire imaging modality (3D scanning), a physical measurement (millimetre landmark error) and a demographic annotation layer that the underlying data cannot support. Alongside local_84bcd4ed, which claimed effectiveness for gelotophobia detection without measuring gelotophobia in anyone, it marks the branch's furthest drift between what is claimed and what was measured. Its 0.985 should be read against local_cd7545e2, where the ADOS-2 itself reaches AUC 0.562 in a clinically meaningful discrimination. Its future-work proposal to deploy facial ASD detection in classrooms, in a paper with no ethics statement and no account of where the children's photographs came from, is the corpus's clearest single example of the gap between the ethics gradient's two ends.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] There are no participant groups in any meaningful sense. The unit is the image file: 2,526 images, 1,263 labelled ASD and 1,263 labelled non-ASD, downloaded from a Kaggle re-upload of the web-scraped autism face corpus. The number of distinct children behind those images is never asked, and because the corpus is known to contain multiple images of the same faces, the effective sample is unknown and certainly far below 2,526. An 80-20 split gives 2,020 training and 506 test images, but the headline evaluation is then run on 200 images selected from the test set - and the reported confusion matrix sums to 300 (146 + 141 + 9 + 4), agreeing with neither figure. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autism spectrum disease, autism spectrum condition, ASD patients, affected persons, neurotypical youngsters, non-ASD. The framing is medical-pathological throughout, opening with autism spectrum disease is a neurological disease and treating the face as a biomarker of brain abnormality under the phrase the face predicts the brain. Autistic people are described as patients diagnosed with ASD who often behave in the same way. There is no engagement with autistic perspectives, and no acknowledgement that the study is inferring a neurodevelopmental condition from the appearance of children's faces. [RQ1.3] Table 1 presents an unusually complete-looking demographic breakdown: age bands 2-5 / 6-9 / 10-12 years (850 / 880 / 796), sex 1,340 male and 1,186 female, ethnicity Caucasian 750, Asian 620, African 530, Hispanic 370, Middle Eastern 156 and Indigenous 100, urban 1,480 versus rural 1,046, and a partition by facial structure variation into broad upper face 505, wide-set eyes 725, shorter middle face 625 and narrow jawline 671. Every row sums exactly to 2,526. None of this metadata exists in the cited Kaggle dataset, which distributes only two folders of JPEGs; the paper describes no annotation procedure, no rater, and no automatic estimator for age, ethnicity, urban/rural residence or facial morphology category. The table is presented as evidence that the dataset adequately reflects real-world diversity, minimizing biases in ASD classification. Assigning every one of 2,526 web-scraped photographs - including all 1,263 non-ASD ones - to one of four ASD-associated facial morphology categories is not a description of a dataset; it is an unsourced annotation layer that cannot be verified and that the study's own conclusions then rest on. [RQ1.4] No diagnostic confirmation of any kind. The class labels are Kaggle folder names on images gathered from the open web. No clinical assessment, no instrument, no assessor, no date, and no record of who the children are. The paper does not mention this once, and instead treats the labels as ground truth adequate to support claims about automated ASD screening. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure - none is derivable from a photograph, and none is discussed as missing. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to overcome the failure of 2D face scans and eye tracking to capture subtle facial asymmetries by performing 3D facial landmark localisation with a CNN plus active shape appearance model, encoding inter-landmark geometry as a Euclidean graph, and classifying with Randomized-Trees-guided XGBoost. Headline findings at 500 epochs: accuracy 0.985, precision 0.975, recall 0.987, F1 0.925, AUC 0.98, detection accuracy 0.99, miss rate and fall-out both 0.07, and landmark localisation error 0.9 mm. The central problem is that the premise and the data do not meet: the entire methodological argument is about depth information that 3D scans obtain and 2D images lack, while the actual input is a Kaggle folder of 2D web photographs processed with Dlib's 2D 68-point detector at 224x224. A localisation error quoted in millimetres cannot be established from such images at all, since they carry no scale reference and no metric ground truth. [RQ2.2] No study setting. Images were downloaded; computation ran on a Windows 10 desktop with 8 GB RAM and an Intel i3 CPU. That configuration is worth recording because it is not plausible hardware for training a CNN, a shape model and a graph network for 500 epochs on 2,020 images, and no training time is reported. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. Static photographs, no stimulus, no interaction, no session. The construct measured is facial morphology, though the abstract describes the target as ASD-related behaviours and the keyword list includes eye tracking, which appears nowhere in the method. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. Ethics reporting is absent: the declarations section contains only a conflict-of-interest line. There is no approval, no consent statement, and no consideration of the fact that the corpus consists of photographs of identifiable children scraped from the web and redistributed with an autism label attached. The limitations section does raise a genuine ethical point - that false positives cause unnecessary family stress and false negatives delay intervention - which makes the silence on image provenance more conspicuous rather than less. [RQ2.5] OpenCV and Dlib for landmark detection, Python for the pipeline, XGBoost for classification; Windows 10, 8 GB RAM, Intel i3, no GPU. Training settings: Adam, learning rate 0.001 chosen by grid search over [0.0001, 0.01], batch size 32, 500 epochs, 224x224 input, rotation and scaling augmentation. No versions, no seed, no runtime. [RQ2.6] Low. Positives: the source dataset is publicly linked, the split ratio is stated, and the main optimisation settings are listed. Negatives dominate: no code, no seed, no software versions, no architectural specification sufficient to rebuild CNN-ASAM or the GECN, no landmark count, no XGBoost parameters, no identification of which 200 test images produced the headline numbers, and a Table 1 whose annotations have no reconstructible source. Independent replication is impossible in principle, not merely inconvenient. [RQ2.7] Section 5.1 is a real limitations section and, judged in isolation, a thoughtful one: cost and technical barriers to 3D imaging in clinics, the asymmetric harms of false positives and false negatives, residual demographic bias from underrepresented facial morphologies, lighting effects on scan quality, and computational cost precluding real-time use. Judged against the study, it is misaddressed - four of the five items concern 3D scanning hardware the study never used. Nothing is said about the dataset's web provenance and absent diagnostic labels, about the unexplained demographic annotations, about evaluating on a hand-selected 200-image subset, about the confusion matrix that sums to 300, or about the fact that all comparator figures are quoted from another paper rather than measured. [RQ2.9] Multimodal extension (3D scans plus voice analysis, eye tracking and movement data); explainability to improve clinical trust and transparency; real-world deployment in classrooms and social interactions on mobile or edge devices; robustness to lighting, expression and morphological variation. The classroom-deployment proposal is worth flagging - it would place automated facial ASD screening in schools, applied to children who have not consented and on the basis of a model trained on web-scraped photographs with no diagnostic labels. [RQ3.1] Static facial morphology rather than behaviour: inter-landmark geometry and facial asymmetry, operationalised as upper-face breadth, eye spacing, mid-face length and jawline shape, over landmarks at the eye corners, eyebrows, nose tip, mouth corners and jaw outline. The theoretical warrant offered is that discrepancies in facial landmarks between those with ASD and those without indicate underlying variances in brain development. [RQ3.2] No fusion - a single image modality. The architecture stacks several representations of the same photograph (CNN features, shape-appearance model, landmark graph, boosted trees), which the paper presents as integrating multiple facial features but which is pipeline depth rather than multimodality. Genuine multimodal fusion with voice, gaze and movement is deferred to future work. [RQ4.1] A four-stage hybrid: CNN with Active Shape Appearance Model for landmark localisation; a Euclidean graph over the landmarks encoded by graph encoder convolutional networks; Randomized Trees for feature importance; XGBoost for the final binary decision. Each stage is motivated by a stated deficiency of prior work, in the now-standard architecture-stacking rhetoric of this literature, but no ablation isolates any stage's contribution. [RQ4.2] Nominally a 3D landmark graph; actually a 2D landmark configuration from Dlib applied to 224x224 web photographs, with rotation and scaling augmentation. The depth channel that the entire introduction argues is essential does not exist in the data. This mismatch propagates into the results: the reported landmark localisation error falling from 2.5 mm at 100 epochs to 0.9 mm at 500 epochs is a physical measurement that no part of the input can support, since the images have neither metric calibration nor ground-truth 3D landmark positions. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, loss, AUC, detection accuracy (reported separately from accuracy and never defined), miss rate, fall-out, millimetre localisation error, and a confusion matrix. The abstract claims excellent specificity but no specificity value appears. The internal arithmetic does not hold: the confusion matrix reports 146 true non-ASD, 141 true ASD, 9 false positives and 4 false negatives, summing to 300 cases although the stated final evaluation set is 200 images and the test split is 506. Those cell counts give accuracy 287/300 = 0.957, precision 141/150 = 0.940 and recall 141/145 = 0.972 - none of which match the reported 0.985, 0.975 and 0.987. Separately, F1 is given as 0.925 while precision and recall are 0.975 and 0.987, whose harmonic mean is 0.981; no combination of the reported figures is mutually consistent. [RQ4.4] Claimed but not delivered. Randomized Trees are described at length as revealing which facial features are most relevant for distinguishing between ASD and non-ASD individuals, yet not a single importance value, ranking or plot is reported - the one output that would have shown whether the model attends to facial geometry or to image-provenance artefacts. Explainability is then listed as future work, in a paper whose central claim is that specific facial measurements carry diagnostic information. [RQ4.5] An 80-20 stratified image-level split (2,020 / 506) with 5-fold cross-validation inside the training portion. The cross-validation placement is correct in principle and better than most of this branch. Four problems undo it. First, the split is image-level, not child-level, on a corpus known to contain repeated faces, so the same child can appear on both sides. Second, augmentation by rotation and scaling is described as part of preprocessing rather than as applied within training folds only. Third, and most serious, the headline numbers do not come from the 506-image test set at all: 200 images (100 ASD, 100 non-ASD) were selected from the test set for the final evaluation, with no selection rule stated, which is the definition of a hand-picked evaluation subset - and the accompanying confusion matrix nonetheless totals 300. Fourth, every reported metric is presented as a monotone function of epoch count with the maximum always at the largest value tried (500), and no criterion determined where to stop, so the reported figures are the best point on a curve rather than the output of a prespecified procedure. The cross-validation folds, having been run, are never reported as a mean and standard deviation. [RQ5.1] Facial landmark detection; autism spectrum condition detection; 3D facial landmark; convolutional neural network; eye tracking. The last is a keyword for a modality the study does not use, and 3D facial landmark describes data the study does not have. [RQ5.2] Sadhana 51(1):30 - the Indian Academy of Sciences' general engineering-sciences journal, not a clinical or specialist vision venue. This is relevant to the review's venue analysis: the mismatch between a 2D Kaggle photo set and a paper about 3D scanning, the unsourced demographic table, the absent ethics statement and the internally inconsistent confusion matrix all survived a 324-day review cycle at a general engineering journal. [RQ5.3] Received 4 October 2024, revised 13 March 2025, accepted 24 August 2025 - the longest review cycle among the recently charted studies, and by far the least effective. Framing is diagnostic-replacement with an explicit efficiency argument: enabling more accurate and automated ASD screening, reducing reliance on subjective assessments, and facilitating timely interventions. Positioning is entirely comparative against numbers quoted from a single prior paper, with the contribution expressed as a higher AUC (0.98 against 0.74, 0.66 and 0.64) rather than as an estimate of anything.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Prospective single-site study at Dakshinya Autistic School, Guntur, India. Forty children aged 8-12 with an existing ASD diagnosis (CARS >= 30, DSM-5 criteria applied by experienced physicians in the absence of locally available ADOS/ADI-R) were assigned to four severity classes of ten each. Gaze was recorded with an SMI RED250 at 250 Hz during a ten-second silent movie of a woman articulating English letters, after five-point calibration. Fifty frames per child were segmented and both eyes cropped, producing 4,000 images at 416x416, split 70:15:15. A secondary experiment reused the public Saliency4ASD data (14 ASD, 14 TD).
narrative_rows.methods: After noise removal, calibration drift correction and fixation/saccade segmentation, four scanpath features (x, y, fixation duration, velocity) were extracted and compared across severity levels using dynamic time warping and MultiMatch, with maximal information coefficient scoring. Sequences were padded and masked and passed to a hybrid CNN-RNN (128-unit LSTM layers, softmax output, batch 64, learning rate 0.0001), with GRU, two-layer LSTM, random forest and XGBoost as comparators across four feature combinations. Implementation in MATLAB on a Windows 10 machine with an Intel i5 and 4 GB RAM.
narrative_rows.outcomes: CNN-RNN with (x, d, y) reached accuracy 97.00%, recall 98.24%, F1 97.04%; (x,y,d,v) 95.23%, (y,x) 94.00%, (x,y,v) 90.00%. GRU and 2-LSTM reached 92%, XGBoost 80.25%, RFC 80.80%. The ablation supports the substantive claim that fixation duration and vertical gaze position discriminate severity while velocity does not. On Saliency4ASD the model is reported at 95.93% (full dataset) and 97.95% (eye dataset).
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The 4,000 images derive from 40 children at exactly 100 images each, and the 70:15:15 split is at the image level, so every participant appears in training, validation and test - and the two eyes of a single video frame can fall on opposite sides. Augmentation precedes the split. Cross-validation is claimed four times but never quantified. There is no typically developing group, although the abstract reports gaze differences relative to TD children. The four severity bands in Table 3 are impossible as written: the High class requires CARS above 60 on a scale whose maximum is 60, and the Low and lower-Mild classes lie below the study's own CARS >= 30 eligibility threshold, so the four groups of ten cannot have been produced by the stated rule. Sex is never reported; the Gesell Developmental Scale is collected but never analysed; specificity, FDR and FOR are defined but never given; the stimulus is ten seconds in one section and two minutes in another; a placeholder reading 8-10 children aged x years survives in the introduction; and the literature review carries citations on building energy consumption and distributed generation that belong to a different manuscript.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This study occupies an unusual position in the review. Methodologically it repeats the corpus's dominant failure - a frame-level split that cannot separate participants, here in its most mechanical form, with a constant 100 crops per child - and its 97% belongs with the leakage-inflated figures rather than with local_7d7f1fcc's participant-level 82.5%. But it is also one of the few eye-tracking papers to do genuine behavioural analysis rather than benchmark chasing: the four-way feature ablation and the DTW/MultiMatch contrast produce a falsifiable claim about which aspect of gaze carries severity information (continuous attention, not transitions), and the paper is candid in its abstract that generalisability remains untested. Its ethics reporting - a named committee with a decision reference, parental consent, and a separate publication-specific consent for participants' details and images - places it near the responsible end of the review's ethics gradient with local_7d7f1fcc and local_4b02df7c, and its account of why ADOS and ADI-R were unavailable is the corpus's clearest statement of the infrastructural constraints under which much of this literature is produced. It is the best available illustration that leakage and scientific seriousness are independent axes.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Forty children, all with an existing ASD diagnosis, recruited from Dakshinya Autistic School in Guntur, India, and divided into four severity classes of exactly ten each: low, mild, medium and high. There is no typically developing comparison group, which matters because the abstract nonetheless reports that children with ASD exhibit unique and highly individualized gaze patterns when compared to TD children - a comparison the design cannot support. The only TD data in the paper belong to the separate public Saliency4ASD set (14 ASD, 14 TD) used in a side experiment. Two internal inconsistencies affect the count: the introduction states that in the initial training we enrolled a group of 8-10 children aged x years, with the placeholder x left in the published text, and the analysis unit is not the child but the cropped eye image - 50 frames x 2 eyes x 40 children = 4,000 images, which is what the 70:15:15 split partitions. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, ASD children, autism applicants, participants, TD children, neurotypical. The paper is one of the few in the corpus to define neurotypical explicitly and to note that it refers to individuals whose neurological development conforms to societal norms and expectations - a formulation that recognises the norm as social rather than natural. Elsewhere the register slips (autism applicants as a table heading; the severity ladder low/mild/medium/high applied to children rather than to symptoms). The introduction is unusual in this corpus for framing the research motivation partly around reducing stigma, promoting inclusion, and improving educational and employment outcomes rather than solely around detection. [RQ1.3] Thin. Age is given only as the 8-12 eligibility band, with no mean, SD or per-class distribution. Sex is not reported at all - not even a total male/female count - despite forty children being individually recruited and consented. Nothing on socioeconomic status, language, verbal ability or schooling level, and no per-severity-class characteristics of any kind. The Gesell Developmental Scale is said to have been used to relate eye-tracking data to behavioural and clinical outcomes, but no GDS number appears anywhere in the article. [RQ1.4] Well handled and honestly reported. Diagnoses were made by experienced physicians applying DSM-5 criteria together with CARS scores, and the paper states plainly why gold-standard instruments were not used: ADI-R and ADOS evaluations are not widely available in India. That candour about a real infrastructural constraint compares favourably with the many studies in this corpus that simply assert diagnosis or inherit labels from a download. What undermines it is the severity banding rather than the diagnosis: eligibility required CARS >=30, yet Table 3 assigns ten children to a Low class defined as CARS <=20 and ten more to a Mild class spanning 20 to 40, and a High class defined as CARS >60 when the scale's maximum is 60. The four equal groups cannot have been generated by the stated rule, and the actual CARS distribution is never shown. [RQ1.5] CARS is the only reported measure, and it is the label rather than a covariate. The Gesell Developmental Scale is named but never reported. No IQ, adaptive-behaviour, language or comorbidity data. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to replace largely manual, unscalable eye-tracking analysis with an automated scanpath-based method that classifies autism severity into four levels, and to characterise how gaze features vary across those levels using DTW and MultiMatch similarity. Headline findings: CNN-RNN with features (x, d, y) reaches accuracy 97.00%, recall 98.24%, F1 97.04%, against GRU 92%, 2-LSTM 92%, XGBoost 80.25% and RFC 80.80%. The more interesting finding is the feature ablation: velocity contributes least, and the authors conclude that it is the continuous attention process, as opposed to the transition phases, that reflects atypical visual behaviour - with differences concentrated in attention duration and vertical gaze distribution. [RQ2.2] A single special school (Dakshinya Autistic School, Guntur) supplying participants, with ethics oversight from Government Medical College, Guntur, and analysis at VIT-AP University.
