Phase II predicts a target the authors manufactured with numpy by binning that same Q-CHAT-10 total, from the very features the total is computed on - so 0.9917 measures a classifier reproducing the authors' own arithmetic, and a lookup table would score 1.00. The severity-to-intervention mapping is uncited, has no evidence base, and assigns Intensive Behavioral Intervention to the low-severity band and Pivotal Response Training to the high, inverting the usual intensity gradient. No physical, verbal or behavioural performance measure exists in the data despite Phase II claiming to assess them. The headline 99.99% appears in no results table and exceeds the study's own best figure of 0.99; the printed 10-fold average of 0.986 does not match the mean of the printed folds (0.9876). There is no ethics or consent statement, and no limitations or future-work section. The merged two-region design offered a free external validation - train on one cohort, test on the other - and it is not taken.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This is the fifth charted study built on a Q-CHAT-derived label and the branch's endpoint. local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 reach 100% with all ten items retained; local_ed30e24c reaches a flawless 292 of 292 by adding pre-split SMOTE; local_8ff20c48 falls to 0.83 after deleting five items; and this study reaches 0.99 in Phase I and 0.9917 in Phase II. What distinguishes it is Phase II, which is unique in the corpus: the target variable was written by the authors with numpy as a deterministic function of the predictors, and the resulting accuracy is offered to educators as a basis for real decisions about which intervention an individual autistic child should receive. The rest of the corpus produces uninterpretable diagnostic probabilities; this study produces an uninterpretable placement recommendation, which is a category of harm the review should record separately. The uncited severity-to-intervention mapping - assigning the most intensive intervention to the least affected band - is the clearest instance of clinical content asserted without any clinical input. Its position beside local_7b468950, the Play.Care phase III protocol with a locked algorithm and blinded prospective validation, marks the full range of what this literature currently contains.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] No participants were recruited. Two public toddler screening datasets are merged: the Kaggle ASD Toddler set (1,054 instances, 17 columns) and an online questionnaire dataset covering toddlers aged 12-36 months across regions of Saudi Arabia. The size of the second dataset is never given, the size of the merged set is never given, and the size after SMOTE oversampling is never given - so the number of rows behind every table in the paper is unknown, and it cannot be determined how many are real records and how many synthetic. Class counts are likewise absent. The stated motivation for merging - improving diversity by combining two regions - is the paper's best idea and is never exploited: the two cohorts are pooled rather than used as development and held-out sets. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic children, children with ASD, individuals affected by ASD, high-level and low-level autistic children, autism students. The abstract opens with a genuinely thoughtful observation - that ASD is highly diverse, each affected child is unique, no two autistic children are alike, and what benefits one child may not suit another - and the whole paper is then organised around assigning children to one of six teaching methods on the basis of a checklist total. The severity vocabulary (high-level, moderate-to-high, low-level autistic children) applies the label to the child rather than to support needs, and the framing describes ASD as having a primary origin that is genetic and as significantly affecting cognitive abilities and object recognition. [RQ1.3] None reported. Gender is present as a variable and is named as a factor in the Phase II rationale; ethnicity, region and jaundice exist as columns; no counts, proportions or distributions are printed for any of them. The absence of a regional breakdown is the notable one, since regional diversity is the stated reason for merging the two datasets and the merged column would have made a two-cohort comparison immediate. [RQ1.4] None, and the paper states the label rule plainly enough that this is not in doubt: a 1 is scored for each Q-CHAT-10 item answered Always, Usually or Sometimes, and a total above 3 indicates the presence of potential ASD traits. That threshold is the outcome variable. No clinician, diagnostic instrument, criterion or assessment date exists for any record in either dataset, and the online questionnaire origin of the Saudi data means the respondents were not verified either. [RQ1.5] No validated cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure. The Q-CHAT-10 total is repurposed as a severity index in Phase II, binning children into five severity levels. Q-CHAT-10 is a binary screening instrument with a single cut-off; it was neither designed nor validated to grade severity, and using its total as a severity scale is an unsupported extension that Phase II then rests on entirely. [RQ2.1] Two goals. Phase I: identify ASD from merged toddler screening data using seven classifiers plus a proposed RF-XG voting ensemble, under three feature-selection schemes. Phase II: recommend an appropriate teaching method for each child from their physical, verbal and behavioural performance. Headline findings: RF-XG reaches 0.94 on original features, 0.92 with Bi-Directional Elimination, 0.98 with Boruta and 0.99 with ML-based feature selection; 10-fold cross-validation averages 0.986; and Phase II predicts the teaching-method label at 0.9917. The comparison table separately claims 99.99%, a number that appears in none of the results tables and exceeds every figure the study actually reports. [RQ2.2] No study setting. Two downloaded or pre-existing questionnaire datasets, analysed in Python. No computing environment, runtime or data-handling arrangement is described. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm - an online caregiver questionnaire. Phase II claims to assess children's physical, verbal and behavioural performance, and this claim is unsupported at the most basic level: the dataset contains ten checklist items and a handful of demographic fields, and no physical, verbal or behavioural performance measure of any kind. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. There is no ethics statement, no consent statement and no data-governance statement anywhere in the article. That absence is more consequential here than in most of this corpus, because the output is not a screening probability but a specific educational placement recommendation for individual children, offered to educators as a basis for decisions affecting their learning and development. [RQ2.5] No instrumentation. Python with scikit-learn for modelling; numpy is named specifically as the library used to create the Phase II teaching-method column. No versions, seed, hardware or runtime. [RQ2.6] Low. The one Kaggle dataset is linked and the Q-CHAT-10 label rule is stated explicitly, which is better than most of the branch. Everything else is missing: the second dataset has no accession, the merged dataset that is claimed as a contribution is not deposited, no row counts are reported at any stage (pre-merge, post-merge, post-SMOTE, per class, per split), no hyperparameters are given for any of eight models, no seed or library versions appear, the number and identity of features retained by each of the three selection methods are never stated, and the order of SMOTE relative to the split is unspecified. The manuscript is also visibly an unedited accepted version - the header retains Date of publication xxxx 00, 0000 and the placeholder DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2017.DOI, and the running footer reads VOLUME 4, 2016 throughout. [RQ2.7] None. There is no limitations section and no caveat anywhere. Unmentioned: that the label is a threshold on the summed predictors; that the Phase II target was manufactured by the authors from that same total; that the reported 99.99% appears in no table; that the printed cross-validation average does not equal the mean of the printed folds; that row counts are absent throughout; and that no ethics approval was sought for a study producing educational placement recommendations. [RQ2.9] None stated. There is no future-work section. [RQ3.1] Parent-reported early social-communication behaviours from Q-CHAT-10 - response to name, eye contact, gestures, pointing, pretend play, gaze following, comforting, early speech, staring. No behaviour is observed, and the physical and verbal performance invoked in the Phase II framing does not exist in the data. [RQ3.2] No modality fusion. The only fusion is the merging of two questionnaire datasets from different regions, which is dataset pooling rather than multimodal integration - and, as noted, the regional structure created by that merge is then discarded rather than used for cross-cohort validation. [RQ4.1] Seven classical classifiers - random forest, decision tree, logistic regression, KNN, SVM, gradient boosting, XGBoost - plus an RF-XG voting ensemble presented as the novel contribution. Three feature-selection techniques (Bi-Directional Elimination, Boruta, ML-based selection) are compared. No hyperparameter is reported for any model. [RQ4.2] Tabular rows of ten binary Q-CHAT-10 items plus demographic and history fields, SMOTE-augmented and feature-selected. The ten items are the constituents of the Q-CHAT-10 total whose threshold defines the Phase I label and whose bands define the Phase II label, so in both phases the predictor set arithmetically determines the outcome. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 across four feature conditions, seven classifiers and an ensemble; per-fold cross-validation values; Phase II results; and a state-of-the-art comparison. No AUC, no specificity, no calibration, no confidence interval, and no chance level for either the binary Phase I task or the seven-class Phase II task. Two internal inconsistencies matter. The 10-fold table prints an average accuracy of 0.986 while the ten listed fold accuracies average 0.9876, and it contains a fold reporting recall 0.999 against accuracy 0.988 and another reporting accuracy 0.999 - values out of line with their neighbours. More seriously, the comparison table credits the proposed approach with 99.99% accuracy, positioning it above four quoted literature figures (98.77%, 97.82%, 99.25%, 99.85%), when the study's own best tabulated result is 0.99 and its cross-validated average is 0.986. The headline claim of surpassing the state of the art rests on a number the paper never produced. [RQ4.4] A single feature-ranking figure from the ML-based selection method. No attribution analysis, no examination of which features drive the teaching-method assignment, and no interrogation of why three different feature-selection methods produce accuracies spanning 0.92 to 0.99 on the same data. [RQ4.5] Phase I follows the familiar pattern: an 80:20 split plus 10-fold cross-validation over data whose label is a threshold on the summed predictors, with SMOTE applied at an unstated point relative to the split and feature selection of unstated nesting. Row counts are absent at every stage, so no reported figure can be located to a sample. That much places the study alongside local_ed30e24c, local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 in the circular-label group. Phase II is a different and more serious matter, and it is the reason this record exists. The teaching-method target did not come from any school, therapist, assessment or record: the paper states that a new column named Teaching Method was added to the dataset using the numpy library, containing integers 1 to 6 for six specialised teaching methods plus 0 for no special education needed, and that these were assigned on the basis of severity as analysed from the Q-CHAT-10 score, which is the count of the A1-A10 values. The models are then trained to predict that manufactured column from the other columns - including A1 to A10 themselves. The reported 0.9917 accuracy therefore measures how well a classifier reproduces an arithmetic rule that the authors wrote, applied to the very features they wrote it from. It is not an estimate of anything about children, education or autism; a lookup table would score 1.00. Compounding this, the mapping from severity band to intervention (Pivotal Response Training for high-level, technology-aided instruction for moderate-to-high, PECS for moderate, task analysis for low-to-moderate, Intensive Behavioral Intervention for low) is asserted with no evidence base, no clinical input and no citation, and it inverts the usual intensity gradient by assigning the most intensive intervention to the least affected group. The results are then offered to educators and professionals as a basis for informed decisions about teaching methods that can have a significant impact on the children's learning and development. The merged two-region design offered a genuine external-validation opportunity - train on one cohort, test on the other - and it is not taken. [RQ5.1] Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD); Autism Students Learning; SMOTE; Multi-model Learning; Feature Engineering. Three of five terms name technique; the educational claim that occupies half the paper appears only as Autism Students Learning. [RQ5.2] IEEE Access - a high-volume open-access multidisciplinary engineering journal. The published PDF is the unedited accepted version, retaining template placeholders in the header (Date of publication xxxx 00, 0000; DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2017.DOI) and a VOLUME 4, 2016 footer throughout. No reviewer questioned a fabricated educational-placement target, a 99.99% figure absent from the results, or the absence of any ethics statement in a paper recommending educational interventions for individual children. [RQ5.3] 2025 (accepted version, citation DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2024.3349988). Framing moves beyond diagnosis into intervention allocation: the aim is personalised educational approaches for individuals with ASD, harnessing machine learning to enhance precision in addressing their unique needs, with results said to help educators make informed decisions. The paper opens by insisting that no two autistic children are alike and closes by assigning them to six intervention categories on the basis of a ten-item checklist total that the authors themselves binned. It is the corpus's clearest example of a pipeline whose output is an action taken on a child rather than a probability, built on a target the authors wrote with numpy.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Single-author retrospective analysis of the public toddler Q-CHAT dataset: 1,054 app-submitted records with 19 attributes, 728 labelled autism and 326 control, mean age 25-28 months, 69.7% male within the autism group, spanning eleven ethnic groups. The outcome is the Class/ASD traits field - the Q-CHAT-10 screening result - and the predictor pool contains the ten Q-CHAT items, the Q-CHAT total and demographic fields.
narrative_rows.methods: Preprocessing is published as a numbered algorithm (drop Case_no, handle missing values, one-hot encode ethnicity and respondent, label-encode binary fields, standardise). Three selection methods - chi-squared SelectKBest, RF/Extra Trees importance, and correlation analysis with Pearson, Spearman and VIF - produce four feature subsets, compared against the default set and against Q1-Q10 alone. Four classifiers (LR, KNN, ANN, LR-KNN ensemble) were tuned and evaluated with k-fold cross-validation; no resampling was applied to the 69/31 imbalance. Kruskal-Wallis tests related each item to the class variable, and an iterative analysis tracked sensitivity and specificity as Q1 through Q10 were added one at a time.
narrative_rows.outcomes: With Q1-Q10 alone (41% feature reduction), LR-KNN reached accuracy 0.99, precision 1.00, F1 0.99, MCC 0.98, sensitivity 0.99, specificity 1.00; ANN 0.98/0.98/1.00/0.98/1.00/0.98; LR 0.97 with specificity 0.90; KNN 0.94. Q9, Q6 and Q5 ranked highest across all three selection methods and Q8 and Q10 lowest. In the iterative analysis, age and sex alone gave 99.5% sensitivity.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The label is the Q-CHAT-10 outcome and the predictors are its own items and total, so the reported figures measure recovery of a checklist rule rather than detection of autism. The validation design is under-reported: no split proportions, no value of k, no per-fold results, no statement of whether selection and tuning were nested inside the training partition, and a passage describing tuning followed by training and evaluation on the dataset. The four confusion matrices imply a 317-record test set but disagree on its composition (105/212 for LR, KNN and LR-KNN; 110/207 for the ANN). No chance level is stated, although with 728 of 1,054 positive the majority-class baseline is 69.1% accuracy and 100% sensitivity - which is what the reported 99.5% sensitivity from age and sex alone actually reflects. The ethics statement treats absence of direct human interaction as itself constituting ethical approval. There is no limitations section, and the extracted text ends mid-discussion with no conclusion.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This is the sixth and analytically most useful of the review's Q-CHAT-labelled studies. Where local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 retain all ten items and hit 100%, local_ed30e24c adds pre-split SMOTE and classifies 292 of 292 correctly, local_b9de0d7f manufactures a second target from the same total, and local_8ff20c48 deletes five items and falls to 0.83, this study systematically varies which part of the Q-CHAT arithmetic enters the feature set and reports the result for each configuration. Its subsets separate the total from its summands and combine them, and every configuration containing either performs well - which is the branch's governing mechanism laid out experimentally. The author comes closer than anyone else to naming it, observing that Subset 2 included both the Qchat-10-Score and Q1-Q10 features, which could sometimes mislead the model results, and then treats it as a redundancy problem. Its 99.5% sensitivity from age and sex alone is the corpus's cleanest demonstration that sensitivity without a stated prevalence baseline is uninformative. It is also the branch's most careful study in reporting terms - MCC with an explicit rationale, confusion matrices for all four models, a published preprocessing algorithm, no resampling, an honest title, and a discussion willing to say the results were not entirely satisfactory.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] No participants. 1,054 records from the public toddler Q-CHAT dataset, 728 labelled autism and 326 control - a 69.1% positive rate that the paper reports and, unusually for this branch, leaves in place rather than resampling. The records were submitted through an ASD screening application by parents and other stakeholders, so neither respondent nor child was verified. The confusion matrices imply a test partition of 317 records, though no split proportion is stated; the row totals also differ across models within the same table (105/212 for LR, KNN and LR-KNN but 110/207 for the ANN), which they should not if all four were evaluated on the same partition. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autism traits, ASD traits, toddlers, individuals with ASD, controls, non-ASD individuals. The register is careful and the title is the most honest in this branch of the corpus: predicting autism traits, not diagnosing autism. ASD is described as a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition, controls rather than normals are used for the comparison class, and the stated motivation includes that incorrect diagnoses can have significant implications for families. One slip: the opening sentence calls ASD a complex neuropsychiatric developmental condition. [RQ1.3] Better than most of the branch, though still descriptive only. Age averages 25 to 28 months with a note that labelled cases rise between 25 and 30 months and become more noticeable by 35-36 months. Sex is given only as 69.7% male within the autism group, with no control-group figure. Ethnicity is reported across eleven groups with White Europeans most represented followed by Asians, and the paper states there were no significant ethnic differences in diagnosis rates - the one ethnicity analysis in this branch. Jaundice, family history and respondent type are present. No performance is broken down by any of these, so the demographic detail informs the sample description but not the evaluation. [RQ1.4] None. The outcome is the Class/ASD traits field, the Q-CHAT-10 screening result, applied to app-submitted responses with no clinical assessment, no clinician, no instrument beyond the checklist and no verification of who completed it. The paper's title and abstract are accurate about this - it predicts autism traits, not autism - and that accuracy distinguishes it from several neighbours in the corpus that describe the same label as a diagnosis. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity instrument. The Qchat-10-Score total appears as a predictor in two feature subsets rather than as a participant characteristic. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to identify a minimal feature subset for ASD trait screening in toddlers through systematic feature selection and hyperparameter tuning, and to map Q1-Q10 and the Q-CHAT total onto DSM-5 behavioural domains. Headline findings: using Q1-Q10 alone (a 41% feature reduction) gives the best performance across all classifiers, with the LR-KNN ensemble at accuracy 0.99, precision 1.00, specificity 1.00 and MCC 0.98, followed by ANN 0.98, LR 0.97 and KNN 0.94. Q9, Q6 and Q5 rank consistently highest across chi-squared, tree-importance and correlation methods; Q8 and Q10 lowest. [RQ2.2] No setting. A single-author secondary analysis of a downloaded file; no computing environment or runtime is described. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. The instrument is the ten-item Quantitative Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, administered through a screening app on a five-point frequency scale from never to always, collapsed to binary. Table 1 maps each question to its behavioural construct - response to name, eye contact, finger pointing and so on - which is more transparency about the instrument than most of the branch offers. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. The ethics statement is the notable feature: the dataset was collected via an ASD test screening application, with no direct human interaction, with responses submitted by parents and other stakeholders, ensuring ethical approval for research purposes. Absence of contact between researcher and participant is presented as itself supplying ethical approval. No committee, protocol number, consent statement or data-governance arrangement appears, and no consideration is given to whether app users agreed to research reuse of their children's screening responses. [RQ2.5] No instrumentation. Analytical components: StandardScaler, one-hot and label encoding, SelectKBest with chi-squared, RF and Extra Trees importance, Pearson and Spearman correlation, variance inflation factor, Kruskal-Wallis tests, logistic regression, KNN, a feed-forward ANN and an LR-KNN ensemble. No library names, versions, seed or hardware. [RQ2.6] Moderate, and the strongest in this branch alongside local_ed30e24c. The preprocessing is published as a numbered algorithm specifying every encoding and column operation; the dataset is public; the composition of each of the four feature subsets is listed; the statistical tests and their exact p-values are tabulated; and confusion matrices are printed for all four final models. Missing: split proportions, the value of k in the cross-validation, any per-fold result, final hyperparameter values, the ANN architecture, the ensemble's combination rule, a seed, and code. The extracted PDF also ends mid-discussion after Table 7, so no conclusion or funding statement is available. [RQ2.7] No limitations section, but two candid remarks stand out. The author writes that on reviewing performance across multiple feature subsets, the results obtained were not entirely satisfactory - an unusual admission in a literature where every result is a success. And, discussing Subset 2, that it included both the Qchat-10-Score and Q1-Q10 features, which could sometimes mislead the model results. That second sentence is the closest any of the six Q-CHAT-based studies charted in this review comes to naming the circularity at the centre of the branch: the total and its own summands are both in the feature set, and the label is a threshold on the total. Having noticed it, the paper treats it as a redundancy nuisance and moves on. [RQ2.9] Not available - the extracted text ends mid-discussion and contains no conclusion or future-work section. [RQ3.1] Parent-reported early social-communication behaviours from the Q-CHAT: response to name, ease of eye contact, pointing to express desires, and the remaining seven items, each mapped to a DSM-5 behavioural domain. The item-level analysis produces a consistent ordering - Q9, Q6 and Q5 most informative, Q8 and Q10 least - which is the paper's substantive behavioural claim. [RQ3.2] No fusion - a single questionnaire modality with demographic covariates. The systematic subset comparison is a study of feature configurations within one modality, not multimodal integration. [RQ4.1] Four supervised learners: logistic regression, k-nearest neighbours, a feed-forward artificial neural network, and a soft LR-KNN ensemble presented as the contribution. No tree-based or boosted classifier is used for prediction, though RF and Extra Trees are used for feature ranking. [RQ4.2] Standardised tabular vectors in five configurations: the default 19-attribute set; Subset 1 (chi-squared, ordered by Q1-Q10 with Q9, Q5, Q6 top); Subset 2 (tree importance, retaining both Qchat-10-Score and Q1-Q10); Subset 3 (correlation-based: Qchat-10-Score, sex, jaundice, age, family history, ethnicity, respondent); Subset 4 (minimal: Qchat-10-Score, age, sex, jaundice); and Q1-Q10 alone. The configurations are the study's real object, and their comparison is where its diagnostic value lies - Subsets 3 and 4 keep the Q-CHAT total and drop the items; Q1-Q10 keeps the items and drops the total; Subset 2 keeps both. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, F1, sensitivity, specificity, MCC and a confusion matrix for every model, plus per-subset comparisons and an iterative feature-addition curve. The metric set is the most complete in this branch: MCC is included deliberately because of the class imbalance, and its motivation - that incorrect diagnoses have significant implications for families - is stated. It also does real work, separating LR (accuracy 0.97, MCC 0.92) from ANN (0.98, 0.98). Two problems. No confidence interval accompanies any figure. And the confusion matrices are mutually inconsistent: LR, KNN and LR-KNN each have class totals of 105 and 212, while the ANN's are 110 and 207, so the four models were not all evaluated on the same 317-record partition. [RQ4.4] The most thorough feature analysis in this branch: chi-squared scores, RF and Extra Trees impurity importance, Pearson and Spearman correlations, variance inflation factors, Kruskal-Wallis association tests with exact p-values, a DSM-5 domain mapping for each item, and an iterative curve tracking sensitivity and specificity as Q1 through Q10 are added one at a time. Three items (Q9, Q6, Q5) rank highest under all three methods. The analysis is careful and internally consistent; what limits it is that the label is a threshold on the sum of the very items being ranked, so the Kruskal-Wallis p-values of order 1e-100 and the convergence across three ranking methods are arithmetic consequences rather than empirical discoveries about which behaviours matter. [RQ4.5] The validation design is under-reported - no split proportions, no value of k, no per-fold results, no statement of whether feature selection and tuning were nested inside the training partition, and a passage stating that the manually tuned model is then trained and evaluated on the dataset to ensure generalization, which describes tuning and evaluating on the same data. The confusion matrices imply a 317-record test partition but disagree on its class composition across models (105/212 for three of them, 110/207 for the ANN). Underneath that, the estimand is the branch's usual one: Class/ASD traits is the Q-CHAT-10 outcome and Q1-Q10 are its summands, so predicting the former from the latter is arithmetic recovery. What makes this study analytically valuable to the review is that its own feature-subset experiment maps the circularity almost completely without naming it. Subsets 3 and 4 retain the Qchat-10-Score and discard the items; Q1-Q10 retains the items and discards the total; Subset 2 retains both, and the author observes that this could sometimes mislead the model results. Every configuration containing either the total or its summands performs well, and the reported conclusion - that Q1-Q10 alone gives optimal performance with 41% fewer features - is a statement about which encoding of the label's own arithmetic is most compact. The single most revealing number in the paper is in the iterative analysis: with only the two least significant features, age and sex, sensitivity was 99.5%. With 69.1% of records positive, that is what a near-all-positive classifier produces, and the surrounding text treats it as a baseline from which adding Q1 (sensitivity 97.6%) and Q2-Q4 (92.8%, 91.3%) represents degradation. Read correctly it demonstrates that sensitivity alone is uninformative on this dataset and that the majority-class baseline is 69.1% accuracy - neither point is made, and no chance level appears anywhere in the article. [RQ5.1] machine learning; feature selection; hyperparameter tuning; logistic regression; k-nearest neighbors; artificial neural network. Six terms, all naming technique - autism, ASD, Q-CHAT, toddlers and screening appear in none of them, which is unusual and leaves the keyword list disconnected from the paper's subject. [RQ5.2] Engineering Research Express 7(2):025269 (IOP Publishing) - an open-access general engineering journal. A 132-day review including one revision round did not surface the mutually inconsistent confusion matrices, the missing split proportions and cross-validation k, the unstated chance level, or an ethics statement that treats absence of direct human interaction as constituting ethical approval. [RQ5.3] 2025, published 28 May, 132 days from submission to acceptance. Framing is screening-support rather than diagnostic replacement and is among the most measured in the corpus - the title claims to predict autism traits, the abstract offers a scalable and cost-effective approach for early detection and personalized intervention strategies, and the discussion admits that results across subsets were not entirely satisfactory. The overreach is confined to the closing claim of facilitating the way for integrating ML techniques into clinical settings. Its distinguishing contribution is analytical rather than predictive: by systematically varying which parts of the Q-CHAT arithmetic enter the feature set, it produces the branch's most complete map of why these accuracies are what they are.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional online survey in Spain, nested in a project validating the Spanish CAT-Q. 601 adults participated: 102 with a clinician-made autism diagnosis (72 women, 18 men, 12 non-binary; mean age 36.0, mean age at diagnosis 32.0) and 499 non-autistic adults (399 women, 92 men, 8 non-binary; mean age 33.3). Twelve self-diagnosed respondents and 13 who did not report a gender identity were excluded. Education and self-reported comorbidities are tabulated in full for both groups.
narrative_rows.methods: The 25 CAT-Q-ES Likert items served as predictors for five continuous outcomes: BAPQ Aloofness, Pragmatic Language and Rigid Personality, PHQ-9 total and GAD-7 total. Fifty regression algorithms across Python, R, Matlab and Octave were compared under two-layer 4-fold cross-validation with participant-disjoint, score-range-stratified partitions; hyperparameters were selected by MAE on a validation partition, models refitted on training plus validation, and tested once per trial on an untouched partition. Three further input configurations added gender, autism diagnosis, or both. Code and a sample dataset are on OSF.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Best-regressor correlations between true and predicted scores: Aloofness R=.85 (MAE 5.55, MAPE 9.2%), Pragmatics .82 (5.36, 8.9%), Rigidity .75 (6.94, 11.6%), Depression .58 (4.55, 16.9%), Anxiety .54 (4.00, 19.1%). Winning algorithms were SGD, SVR, Ridge, KNN and boosted trees respectively. Adding gender and/or autism diagnosis changed R by at most .03. A tolerance analysis reports 36.3% of Aloofness predictions within 5% of the true score and just over 60% within 10%.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The authors state four: an 78%-women, highly educated, self-selected online sample, with the recruitment mechanism explained; self-reported diagnoses that could not be verified, mitigated by excluding self-diagnosis and instructing respondents to report only clinician-confirmed conditions; weaker anxiety and depression models, attributed to the criterion-based structure of PHQ-9 and GAD-7 items; and measurement of generalised rather than social anxiety. One limitation is not stated and is the most consequential: predictors and outcomes are self-report questionnaires completed by the same person in the same sitting, so the correlations carry common-method variance, and the CAT-Q-ES items overlap in construct with the BAPQ Aloofness and Pragmatic Language subscales - which is at least as plausible an explanation for the gap between R=.85 for social-trait outcomes and R=.54 for anxiety as the instrument-structure account offered. No external cohort is tested, which the authors themselves require before clinical use.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This is the reference study of the review. Every failure that governs the rest of the corpus is absent here: the analysis unit is the person, the cross-validation partitions are participant-disjoint, hyperparameter selection is nested and never touches the test partition, the outcome is dimensional so no threshold or prevalence artefact arises, the label is not a function of the predictors, the code is deposited, ethics approval and consent are documented, and the limitations are mechanistic rather than formulaic. Its results are correspondingly modest - R=.85 at best, .54 at worst, with only 36% of individual predictions within 5% of the true score - and that contrast is the review's central empirical finding stated in a single study. It should be read alongside local_cd7545e2, where the ADOS-2 itself reaches AUC 0.562 against another clinical group, and local_7d7f1fcc, where a participant-level matched split over pose data yields 82.5%: together these three mark the realistic performance envelope of the field. It is also the only charted study to treat an autistic behaviour as adaptive rather than symptomatic, to analyse non-binary participants as a group rather than excluding them, to compute instrument reliabilities in its own sample, to release working code, and to devote a passage of its discussion to the risk that predictive algorithms in mental health reinforce stigma and pathologise coping strategies.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two groups of adults recruited into one online survey: 102 autistic adults with a clinician-made diagnosis (72 women, 18 men, 12 non-binary) and 499 non-autistic adults (399 women, 92 men, 8 non-binary), 601 in total. The analysis unit is the person throughout, and the four cross-validation partitions are participant-disjoint by construction - each participant appears in exactly one partition. Exclusions are enumerated with reasons: 12 self-diagnosed respondents and 13 who did not report a gender they identified with. This is the only charted study in which the number of people, the number of analysis units and the number of rows in every reported metric are the same figure. [RQ1.2] Autistic adults, autistic individuals, neurodivergent, non-autistic, camouflaging, masking, neurotypical behavior. The framing is identity-first and community-aligned throughout: camouflaging is described as an adaptive social coping strategy rather than a symptom, the paper states explicitly that adapting one's behaviour in social contexts - whether to avoid discrimination or to achieve personal goals - is not inherently pathological and does not necessarily indicate autism, and it warns that mental health professionals should be aware of unintentional reinforcement of stigma and the pathologization of (mal)adaptive social strategies like social camouflaging. Non-binary participants are analysed as a group in their own right rather than dropped, and the paper states its reason for using self-reported gender rather than sex assigned at birth: it better reflects participants' identities. This is the only study in the charted corpus whose language would be recognised as respectful by the population it studies. [RQ1.3] The most complete demographic and clinical reporting in the corpus. Age by group with means, SDs and a tested 2.7-year difference with effect size and confidence interval; mean age at autism diagnosis (32.0 years, SD 12.3); self-reported gender in three categories with between-group tests; full education distribution from no studies to PhD for both groups; and a complete self-reported comorbidity table covering high abilities, ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, specific learning disorder, epilepsy, bipolar disorder, eating disorder, anxiety, depression and sleep disorder, with percentages for both groups. Nationality/residence is stated (Spain). The women-heavy composition (78% overall) is not merely reported but explained and named as the study's most notable limitation, with a mechanism offered - the parent project validates an instrument designed for highly masked autistic adults, especially women, and online studies skew toward respondents with topic interest, higher cognitive ability and moderate-to-high socioeconomic status. [RQ1.4] Self-reported but with real safeguards, and honestly characterised. Participants were asked about a clinically based diagnosis and about which professional made it; the 12 who reported self-diagnosis were excluded; and respondents were instructed to report only clinician-confirmed diagnoses and not diagnoses based on personal feelings of distress. The authors then name the residual uncertainty as a limitation and recommend clinician-based confirmation in future work. No diagnostic instrument was administered by the research team. Importantly, diagnosis is not the prediction target here - it is a covariate tested for incremental value - so the study's central claims do not rest on label accuracy in the way the rest of this corpus does. [RQ1.5] Dimensional and psychometrically characterised. BAPQ Aloofness, Pragmatic Language and Rigid Personality are the autistic-trait outcomes; PHQ-9 and GAD-7 total scores the affective outcomes; CAT-Q-ES compensation, masking and assimilation subscales the predictors. McDonald's omega is computed in this sample for every instrument (CAT-Q-ES .96, GAD-7 .92, PHQ-9 .91, Aloofness .94, Pragmatics .87, Rigidity .92), and the known psychometric weakness of the Spanish BAPQ Pragmatic Language subscale is flagged in advance. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to evaluate whether machine learning on self-reported camouflaging behaviours can predict dimensional autistic traits and anxiety/depression symptoms, and whether knowing a person's gender or autism diagnosis improves that prediction. Headline findings: correlations between true and predicted scores of R=.85 for Aloofness, .82 for Pragmatics and .75 for Rigidity (strong by the pre-specified Colton criterion), against .58 for Depression and .54 for Anxiety (moderate); and adding gender and/or diagnosis changes R by at most .03, from which the authors conclude that this information is already implicit in the camouflaging items. The stated implication is a possible screening aid for people whose autistic traits are masked or subthreshold and whose diagnosis is unclear or not yet established, regardless of gender identity. [RQ2.2] An online REDCap survey hosted at Fundacion Publica Galega de Medicina Xenomica, disseminated through autism associations, institutions, federations, clinical units, research networks and social media, within a broader project validating the CAT-Q for the Spanish population. Recruitment channel is stated and its selection consequences are analysed in the limitations rather than left implicit. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm - a self-report battery completed in one sitting: the 25-item CAT-Q-ES (Likert 1-7) as predictors, and the 36-item BAPQ, the PHQ-9 and the GAD-7 as outcomes. This is the design's central methodological feature and its principal limitation, discussed under RQ4.5. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single administration. Ethics reporting is complete: Declaration of Helsinki, approval by the Ethics Committee of the University of Santiago de Compostela with the code USC 26/2023, informed consent presented in the survey's first section before participation, and participant anonymity preserved throughout collection. Beyond procedural ethics, the discussion contains a substantive ethical analysis absent from every other study charted here - it warns against reinforcing stigma and pathologising adaptive social strategies, insists that algorithmic models should never replace clinical evaluation, and requires that clinicians apply them within a personalised-medicine approach respecting patient autonomy and daily-life context. [RQ2.5] REDCap for capture, with validated data entry, audit trails for tracking data manipulation and export, and automated export procedures. Modelling used fifty regressors implemented in Python, R, Matlab and Octave, with the package and hyperparameter tuning grid for each listed in a supplementary appendix. [RQ2.6] The highest in the charted corpus. Code and a small sample dataset are publicly deposited on OSF - the only working code released by any study in this review. The fifty models, their implementation languages, packages and hyperparameter grids are enumerated in supplementary material. The cross-validation procedure is specified operationally, including partition disjointness, stratification across the score range, the rotation of training/validation/test roles across four trials, and the refit-on-train-plus-validation step. Missing data are quantified (0.30%) and the imputation justified. Exclusions are counted and reasoned. Internal consistencies are computed in-sample for every instrument. The only gap is the full dataset, withheld for confidentiality with a sample released in its place. [RQ2.7] A genuine limitations section, self-critical and mechanistic rather than formulaic. Four limitations are stated with reasoning: the over-representation of women, traced to the parent validation project and to online-recruitment bias toward respondents with topic interest, higher cognitive ability and moderate-to-high socioeconomic status; the inability to verify self-reported diagnoses, with the mitigation described and its residual risk acknowledged; the weaker anxiety and depression models, explained through instrument structure (PHQ-9 and GAD-7 items each map to a distinct diagnostic criterion and so scatter, whereas BAPQ items are interrelated within domain); and the restriction to generalised anxiety, omitting social anxiety, which is the form most closely tied to masking. The one limitation not stated is the shared-method dependence between predictors and outcomes. [RQ2.9] Include clinician-confirmed diagnoses and observational measures of camouflaging alongside self-report; replace criterion-based screeners with dimensional continuous scales for anxiety and depression to reduce scatter; and, before any clinical implementation, cross-validate extensively against health-record data. Each future direction addresses a specific stated limitation, which is rare in this corpus. [RQ3.1] Camouflaging behaviour, decomposed into compensation (copying others' behaviours, preparing scripts for social situations), masking (controlling and adjusting facial and bodily expression to fit in) and assimilation (effortful engagement and pretending to be normal in social situations). The outcomes are dimensional autistic traits - aloof personality, pragmatic language, rigid personality - and depressive and anxious symptoms. The behaviour of interest is therefore an active social strategy rather than a deficit, and the study is the only one in the corpus to treat an autistic behaviour as adaptive rather than symptomatic. [RQ3.2] No modality fusion - a single self-report modality throughout. The nearest analogue is the input-configuration comparison, which tests whether adding gender and/or autism diagnosis to the CAT-Q-ES items improves prediction and finds that it does not. The authors themselves identify observational measurement of camouflaging as the modality this study lacks and recommend adding it. [RQ4.1] Fifty supervised regression algorithms compared under a common protocol - support vector regression, neural networks, linear and regularised linear regressors, decision trees, random forests, boosting ensembles, k-nearest neighbours and Gaussian processes among others. Different algorithms won for different outcomes (SGD for Aloofness, SVR for Pragmatics, Ridge for Rigidity, KNN for Depression, boosted trees for Anxiety), and the winners are simple regularised or instance-based methods rather than deep networks. This is regression to continuous scores rather than the binary classification that dominates the corpus, which removes the threshold and prevalence problems that make most of the charted accuracy figures uninterpretable. [RQ4.2] The 25 raw CAT-Q-ES Likert items, in four configurations: items alone, items plus gender, items plus autism diagnosis, and items plus both. Subscale scores were tested as an alternative input and did not improve accuracy - a negative result the paper reports rather than suppresses. [RQ4.3] Pearson R between true and predicted scores, MAE, MAPE relative to the score range, and RMSE, per outcome and averaged across the four trials, with predicted-versus-true scatter plots against a perfect-agreement diagonal. Correlation magnitudes are interpreted against a pre-specified external criterion (Colton 1974), so strong and moderate are defined before the results rather than after. The tolerance analysis is the most practically informative reporting in the corpus: the best Aloofness model places 36.3% of predictions within 5% of the true score and just over 60% within 10%, which states plainly what the R=.85 does and does not deliver at the individual level. The paper also notes correctly that the lower MAE for Depression and Anxiety reflects their narrower score ranges rather than better prediction, and reads the MAPE accordingly. Two gaps: no confidence intervals or across-trial variance accompany the metrics, and no trivial baseline (for instance, predicting the sample mean) is reported against which the MAE and RMSE could be judged. A minor inconsistency: the abstract gives Rigidity R=.74 and Depression R=.60, while Table 3 gives .75 and .58 for the CAT-Q-ES-only configuration. [RQ4.4] No model-level attribution for the fifty regressors - no coefficients, feature importances or SHAP values are reported, so which camouflaging items carry the signal is not established. The interpretive work is done instead by the input-configuration comparison, which supports a clean negative claim: gender and autism diagnosis add at most .03 to R and 0.10 to MAE, so neither provides information not already implicit in the camouflaging items. That result is the basis for the paper's central applied argument - that the tool could work regardless of gender identity and where a diagnosis is unclear or absent. [RQ4.5] The validation design is the most rigorous in the charted corpus and is reported operationally rather than by name. Two-layer 4-fold cross-validation: 601 participants divided into four partitions that are disjoint at the participant level and stratified so that each spans the full score range; in each of four trials, two partitions train, one validates and one tests, with roles rotating so that every partition serves as test exactly once; for models with tunable hyperparameters, candidates are fitted on the training partitions, selected by MAE on the validation partition, then refitted on training plus validation before a single prediction on the untouched test partition; the four test MAEs are averaged. Hyperparameter selection therefore never sees the test data, the analysis unit is the person, and no participant contributes to both sides of any split - the three failures that account for most of the inflated figures elsewhere in this review are all absent here. Two real limitations remain. The first is the one the paper does not name: predictors and outcomes are self-report questionnaires completed by the same person in the same sitting, so the correlations are inflated by common-method variance, and there is direct construct overlap between camouflaging items (which describe effortful management of social interaction) and the BAPQ Aloofness and Pragmatic Language subscales (which measure social and pragmatic difficulty). The R=.85 for Aloofness should be read as agreement between two overlapping self-descriptions of social experience, not as prediction of an independently ascertained trait - which is precisely why the anxiety and depression models, whose outcomes are less conceptually adjacent to camouflaging, drop to .54 and .58. The authors explain that gap through instrument structure; construct proximity is at least as plausible. The second is that no external cohort is tested, which the paper itself insists on before any clinical use. Set against the corpus, this study is the reference point: a properly nested, participant-level, model-selection-clean design applied to a genuinely dimensional target yields R=.85 at best and .54 at worst, with only 36% of individual predictions landing within 5% of the truth - the realistic ceiling against which the 99% and 100% figures elsewhere in this review should be read. [RQ5.1] ASD; Autism; CAT-Q-ES; Camouflaging; Supervised machine learning; Mental health; Gender. Seven terms covering condition, instrument, construct, method, outcome domain and a demographic dimension analysed substantively - the most informative keyword set in the corpus. [RQ5.2] Research in Autism 128:202712 (Elsevier) - a specialist autism research journal rather than an engineering or general-science venue, and the difference is visible throughout: dimensional outcomes, in-sample psychometrics, effect sizes with confidence intervals for group comparisons, a self-critical limitations section, an ethics analysis of algorithmic screening in mental health, and deposited code. It is the only paper in the corpus published in a venue whose reviewers are subject-matter specialists in autism, and it is also the only one to release code, report internal consistencies, or discuss stigma. [RQ5.3] 2025, accepted 15 September, 133 days with a substantive revision round. Framing is deliberately bounded: the results show the viability of machine learning to predict traits and symptoms and suggest potential for developing a tool that may improve screening in individuals whose diagnosis is unclear or not yet established. The discussion then constrains that further - algorithms should be extensively cross-validated against health records before implementation, should be used as screeners to accelerate referral rather than replace clinical evaluation, and should be applied within a personalised-medicine approach respecting autonomy. Where the rest of this corpus claims diagnosis and delivers checklist arithmetic, this study claims correlation between self-reports and delivers exactly that, with the error bars in view.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective analysis of 2,926 facial images at 224x224 from a public repository - the same Kaggle autism face corpus used by all five studies in the paper's comparison table, and the thirteenth charted reuse of that corpus in this review. The split is 2,526 training, 200 validation and 200 test images; class counts are not reported for any partition, and the number of distinct children is unknown. The paper notes that a cited prior study removed duplicates from this corpus using MD5 hashing, and performs no deduplication itself.
narrative_rows.methods: HyVit-ASD combines a pre-trained torchvision ResNet whose 512-dimensional output is projected to three channels and resized to 224x224, a pre-trained ViT-base with a custom residual ReAttention mechanism, global average pooling and a linear classifier, plus a proposed Attention-Based Augmentation Layer. Training used AdamW at learning rate 1e-5, weight decay 1e-2, cross-entropy loss and CUDA; epoch count, batch size and seed are unreported.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Test set: accuracy 91%, sensitivity 94%, specificity 88%, AUC 95.67%, F-measure 90.99%, G-mean 90.95%, fall-out 0.12, miss rate 0.06. Validation: accuracy 86.5%, AUC 93.65%. Author-fitted baselines reached 71-80% on validation; literature figures on the same corpus range from 64.67% to 92.01%.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The reported 91% rests on a single unrepeated, unseeded image-level split of a web-scraped corpus with no diagnostic labels, no provenance and acknowledged duplicate images that were not removed - so the same child's photographs can appear on both sides. The test set is 200 images, giving a confidence interval of roughly 86-95% that contains almost every entry in the comparison tables the paper ranks itself above, including Xception at 92.01. Validation accuracy is 4.5 points below test accuracy on equal-sized partitions and this inversion is not discussed. The architecture's stated rationale concerns asymmetric facial movements, eye gaze and mouth movements, none of which exists in a still photograph, and the claim that ReAttention focuses on periocular regions is asserted with no attention map or attribution to support it. Neither novel component is parameterised and no ablation isolates either. There is no ethics statement and no account of the images' provenance. The introduction catalogues a specific limitation for roughly twenty prior studies and states none for this one.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This is the thirteenth charted reuse of the web-scraped facial-image corpus, and it is the branch's most explicit statement of its own epistemics: the paper argues that comparison with prior models rests on a solid common foundation precisely because they all use the same dataset. That shared foundation has no diagnostic labels, no provenance and no demographics, so the whole benchmark line is internally comparable and externally uninterpretable. Its 91% falls in the middle of the branch's 81-99.8% range and is consistent with the pattern established across the other twelve - reported accuracy tracks evaluation protocol and model capacity rather than signal. Two features make it worth recording separately. It has the most complete and internally consistent metric reporting in the branch, including specificity and fall-out as numbers. And it contains the corpus's most extensive limitations apparatus, roughly twenty named weaknesses attached to other people's work, with none directed at its own single split, unlabelled data or absent ethics statement - which makes it the clearest example of critical vocabulary functioning as positioning rather than as method.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] No participants. 2,926 images at 224x224, described as curated from public repositories covering diverse demographics and labelled autism or non-autism; the comparison tables identify the source as the same Kaggle facial corpus used by all five of the studies it benchmarks against. The split is 2,526 training, 200 validation and 200 test images. Class counts are never stated for any partition, though the metric arithmetic implies a balanced 200-image test set. The number of distinct children is unknown - and the paper is aware that this matters, because it notes that one cited study cleaned duplicates from the dataset using the MD5 hash algorithm, an acknowledgement that the corpus contains repeated images. No deduplication is performed here. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic and non-autistic children, autistic individuals, ASD children, individuals with ASD and their families. The register is clinical and reasonably neutral - non-autistic rather than normal is used for the comparison class - though the opening sentence describes ASD as a complicated neurological disease and the introduction lists cognitive impairments among its defining characteristics. No autistic or community perspective appears. [RQ1.3] None. The dataset is asserted to cover diverse demographics and the model is claimed to address demographic variability, but no age, sex, ethnicity, geography or recruitment information exists for any image and none is reported. The diversity claim is therefore unverifiable, and the paper's stated advance over prior work on limited generalizability across diverse demographics rests on it. [RQ1.4] None. Labels are the folder assignment of a public image corpus. No clinical diagnosis, instrument, criterion, assessor or date exists for a single image, and unlike several of its neighbours the paper does not even describe the labelling process in passing. The comparison table's premise - that the models being compared share a common foundation because they use the same dataset - makes this the shared and unexamined weakness of the whole benchmark line. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure; none obtainable from photographs. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to overcome the limitations of prior facial-image ASD classifiers - computational cost, pose sensitivity, poor generalisation across demographics - with HyVit-ASD, a hybrid combining a pre-trained ResNet convolutional block, a pre-trained ViT with a custom residual ReAttention mechanism, and an Attention-Based Augmentation Layer. Headline findings: test accuracy 91%, sensitivity 94%, specificity 88%, AUC 95.67%, F-measure 90.99%, G-mean 90.95%, fall-out 0.12, miss rate 0.06, against six models the authors fitted (71-80% validation accuracy) and five literature figures on the same corpus (68-90%). [RQ2.2] No study setting. Images were obtained from a public repository; training used CUDA acceleration with no hardware, runtime or environment described. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. Static photographs. The rationale nonetheless refers repeatedly to movement - the ReAttention mechanism is justified as capturing fine-grained local features critical for ASD biomarkers such as asymmetric facial movements, and as amplifying regions including eye gaze and mouth movements. None of these is present in a still image, so the architecture's stated motivation describes a modality the study does not use. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. Ethics reporting is absent entirely - no approval, no consent, no exemption claim, and no mention of where photographs of identifiable children came from or under what terms they may be reused. The paper does note, in summarising prior work, that web-based screening tools raise privacy concerns, so the category is available to it and simply not applied to its own data. [RQ2.5] No acquisition instrumentation. Modelling used PyTorch with a torchvision pre-trained ResNet and a ViT-base transformer, AdamW at learning rate 1e-5 with weight decay 1e-2, cross-entropy loss and CUDA. No versions, seed, epoch count, batch size or hardware. [RQ2.6] Low. The architecture is described in prose with three equations, and the optimiser, learning rate, weight decay, loss function and split sizes are given - a better start than several neighbours. What is missing prevents replication: no code, no seed, no epoch or batch count, no ResNet depth or ViT variant, no parameterisation for either of the two components claimed as novel (ReAttention and the Attention-Based Augmentation Layer), no list of augmentation transformations, no dataset accession beyond a reference number, no class counts for any partition, and no statement of how the 200-image validation and test sets were drawn from 2,926. [RQ2.7] None of its own. This paper has the corpus's most extensive limitations apparatus pointed entirely outward: the introduction runs through roughly twenty prior approaches and attaches a specific weakness to each - high computational cost and limited generalizability across diverse demographics, sensitivity to non-frontal poses, dependence on iterative expert annotation, computational intensity of heterogeneous data fusion, susceptibility to noise in handcrafted features, laborious EEG preprocessing, expensive eye-tracking hardware, domain shift in EfficientNet on medical images, scarce labelled data, need for high-quality motion sensors, shallow architectures, accuracy sacrificed for deployability, privacy concerns and connectivity dependence in web tools, cultural variability in handwriting, cost and immobilisation requirements of fMRI, and overfitting risk in metaheuristic optimisation. It even observes that cross-validation may not reflect real-world variability, risking overfitting. None of this critical vocabulary is turned on its own single unrepeated image-level split of an unlabelled web corpus. The only self-directed hedge is a clause in the conclusion. [RQ2.9] Hybrid vision transformers and adaptive learning as a direction for future research in ASD classification and medical imaging, and validation on larger, more diverse datasets. The second addresses the study's real gap; the first proposes more of what was just done. [RQ3.1] None. The classification target is static facial appearance. The paper's own account of what the model attends to - periocular regions, eye gaze, mouth movements, asymmetric facial movements - describes dynamic behaviours that a single photograph cannot contain, so the stated biomarker rationale and the actual input are mismatched. [RQ3.2] No fusion of modalities. The hybrid designation refers to combining two vision backbones (ResNet and ViT) over the same image. The introduction reviews multimodal neuroimaging and EEG-plus-eye-tracking work and dismisses both on cost and complexity grounds. [RQ4.1] A three-stage architecture: a ConvBlock in which a pre-trained ResNet produces a 512-dimensional feature vector that is projected by a 1x1 convolution to three channels and interpolated back to 224x224; a TransformerBlock applying a pre-trained ViT-base with a residual ReAttention mechanism; and global average pooling into a linear classifier. The intermediate step is unusual and unexplained - ResNet features are collapsed to a three-channel image-shaped tensor purely so that a pre-trained ViT's input interface can consume them, which discards most of the convolutional representation before the transformer sees it. No ablation tests whether the ConvBlock, the ReAttention module or the ABAL contributes anything. [RQ4.2] 224x224 RGB face crops from the public corpus, with unspecified preprocessing and augmentation plus a proposed Attention-Based Augmentation Layer applying unnamed non-destructive transformations. Neither the augmentation set nor its placement relative to the split is stated. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, AUC, F-measure, G-mean, sensitivity, specificity, fall-out and miss rate, with formulae given, reported for both validation and test, plus a confusion-matrix figure. This is a fuller and better-chosen metric set than most of the facial-image branch offers - specificity and fall-out are reported as numbers rather than merely claimed, and the figures are internally consistent (sensitivity 94% with miss rate 0.06; specificity 88% with fall-out 0.12; their mean 91% matching the reported accuracy on a balanced test set). Two problems. No confidence interval accompanies any figure, and on 200 test images the 95% interval around 91% runs from roughly 86% to 95% - a range that contains almost every entry in the comparison tables, so the claimed ordering among methods is not established. And validation accuracy (86.5%) is lower than test accuracy (91%) by 4.5 points on 200 images each, which is reported without comment. [RQ4.4] Claimed, not shown. The ReAttention mechanism is described as adaptively amplifying diagnostically relevant regions such as eye gaze and mouth movements and as focusing on periocular regions, aligning with clinical studies linking ASD to reduced eye contact. No attention map, saliency overlay, feature attribution or region-level analysis appears anywhere in the paper to support this, and no ablation isolates the module. The claim that the model attends to the periocular region - which would be the study's most interesting finding if demonstrated - is asserted as a design intention and presented as though it were a result. [RQ4.5] A single image-level split of 2,926 images into 2,526 training, 200 validation and 200 test, with no cross-validation, no repetition, no seed and no description of how the split was drawn. Three problems follow. First, the corpus is the widely reused web-scraped autism face collection, which contains duplicate and near-duplicate images of the same individuals; the paper demonstrates awareness of exactly this, noting that a cited study cleaned duplicates from the dataset using the MD5 hash algorithm, and then does not deduplicate, so images of the same child can sit on both sides of the split. Second, the test set is 200 images, giving a 95% confidence interval around 91% of roughly 86-95% - wide enough to contain the great majority of the comparison entries the paper ranks itself above, including MobileNet-V1 at 90.67 and Xception at 92.01, so the reported ordering is not supported. Third, validation accuracy is 4.5 points below test accuracy on partitions of equal size, an inversion that normally indicates split variance rather than generalisation and is reported without remark. Underneath all three sits the problem the whole benchmark line shares and this paper states approvingly: the models being compared have a solid common foundation because they use the same dataset - a dataset with no diagnostic labels, no provenance and no demographic information. A common foundation of that kind makes the numbers comparable to each other and to nothing else. [RQ5.1] Autism spectrum disorder; Vision transformers; Facial image analysis; ReAttention; Early diagnosis; CNN. Four of six terms name architecture; participants, validation and setting are absent. [RQ5.2] International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems 18(3):312-319 - an open-access computing journal. Review appears to have been rapid (received 17 January 2025, revised 4 February 2025) and did not surface the absent ethics statement, the unreported class counts, the 200-image test set behind a four-way ranking claim, or the mismatch between a movement-based biomarker rationale and a still-image input. [RQ5.3] 2025. Framing is diagnostic and confident: the model is a pioneering approach contributing significantly to early diagnosis and intervention strategies, and a powerful tool to enhance ASD diagnosis and improve outcomes for individuals with ASD and their families, hedged only by a clause acknowledging that further validation on larger, diverse datasets is needed. The contribution is expressed as a position in a leaderboard over one public image corpus, and the paper is explicit that this shared corpus is what makes the comparison solid - which is the clearest statement in the review of how this branch understands evidence.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective analysis of the Kaggle ASD Children Facial dataset - 2,940 images, 1,470 autistic and 1,470 non-autistic - the fourteenth charted reuse of this corpus in the review. The methods define an image-level split of 2,540 training images and 400 test images, balanced within each class. No demographic or diagnostic information exists for any image.
narrative_rows.methods: Images were resized (described as adjusting ratio and resolution with the loss of pixels), sharpened by DeepDeblur, a convolution/deconvolution network learning a blurred-to-sharp mapping, then passed to DOCNN, a CNN performing joint denoising and classification with parameters tuned by the Fire Hawk Optimizer. Implementation in MATLAB R2021a. No architecture, learning rate, batch size, epoch count or optimiser budget is reported, and no component is ablated.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Accuracy 96.94%, precision 97.28%, recall 96.62%, F-measure 96.95%. Deblurring: 91.22% blur removed, PSNR 32.75 dB, MSE 0.115, SSIM 0.96, against Deepblur, Wiener filtering and blind deconvolution. Comparison against five literature figures ranging from 92.0% to 96.63%.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The reported accuracy is a resubstitution figure. The results section states that of 2,940 images used for evaluation, 1,430 autism and 1,420 non-autism images were classified correctly - 2,850 correct, 90 wrong - and 2,850/2,940 is exactly 96.94%, so the headline number was computed over the entire dataset including the 2,540 training images, and the 400-image test set defined in the methods produces no reported result. The labels are Kaggle folder names on web-scraped photographs with no clinical diagnosis behind them, and the corpus repeats individuals, so even a correctly executed image-level split would not separate children. Three pipeline components are each claimed as contributions and none is ablated. The deblurring evaluation reports PSNR, MSE and SSIM, which require a sharp ground-truth reference that cannot exist for downloaded images, and no explanation is given. There is no ethics statement, no limitations section and no future work.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This is the fourteenth charted reuse of the web-scraped facial-image corpus and the branch's clearest single instance of a headline figure that is not a held-out estimate at all. Across the branch, reported accuracy has tracked evaluation looseness rather than signal; here the looseness is complete - the test set is defined, described and then not used, and the arithmetic of the confusion matrix makes this checkable from the paper's own numbers. It pairs with local_986436f2, whose headline came from an unexplained 200-image selection out of its test set while its confusion matrix summed to a third figure, as the two cases where the branch's evaluation reporting breaks down entirely rather than merely being optimistic. Its deblurring metrics add a second, less common failure to the review's catalogue: reference-dependent image-quality measures (PSNR, MSE, SSIM) reported for photographs that have no reference, which either means the degradation was synthetic and undisclosed or the metrics were computed against nothing determinable.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] No participants. 2,940 images from the Kaggle ASD Children Facial dataset, balanced at 1,470 autistic and 1,470 non-autistic - the fourteenth charted reuse of this corpus in the review. The number of distinct children is unknown and never raised, and the corpus is known to contain repeated images of the same faces. The paper states a split of 2,540 training images (1,270 per class) and 400 test images (200 per class), but the confusion matrix it then reports covers all 2,940 images, so the population behind the headline figure is the whole dataset rather than the held-out 400. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic and non-autistic faces, autistic patients, children. The register is medical and dated: ASD is introduced as a neurodevelopmental disorder with ineffective brain functions and as a conventional developmental neuro-disorder, and deep learning is credited with developing interactive systems to assist in the reintegration and treatment of autistic patients. No autistic or community perspective appears. [RQ1.3] None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography, socioeconomic status or recruitment source for any image, and no acknowledgement that this information is absent. One of the studies the paper summarises in its own literature review notes that model reliability depends on dataset quality and race factors, so the concern is present in the article's field of view and is not applied to its own data. [RQ1.4] None. Labels are Kaggle folder names on photographs of unknown provenance. No clinical diagnosis, instrument, criterion, assessor or date exists for a single image. The paper opens by observing correctly that there is no medical screening or test like a blood test or scan for ASD and that diagnosis requires developmental history and behavioural assessment - and then treats folder labels on downloaded photographs as sufficient ground truth for a diagnostic classifier. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure; none obtainable from photographs. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to make facial-image ASD screening robust to poor image quality by adding a deblurring stage and a joint denoising-classification network with metaheuristic parameter tuning. Headline findings: accuracy 96.94%, precision 97.28%, recall 96.62%, F-measure 96.95%, against five literature figures between 92.0% and 96.63%; and, for the deblurring stage, 91.22% blur removed with PSNR 32.75 dB and SSIM 0.96 against Deepblur, Wiener filtering and blind deconvolution. [RQ2.2] No study setting. Images downloaded from Kaggle; experiments run in MATLAB R2021a with no hardware, runtime or environment described. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. Static photographs with no stimulus, interaction or session. The construct measured is facial appearance, framed as a diagnostic route parallel to behavioural analysis. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. There is no ethics statement, no consent statement and no exemption claim, and no consideration of where photographs of identifiable children came from or under what terms they may be reused, deblurred, denoised and redistributed in figures - the paper reproduces sample faces at five processing stages in Figure 3. [RQ2.5] No acquisition instrumentation. Implementation in MATLAB R2021a. No toolbox versions, hardware, runtime, seed or code. The proposed pipeline's components - DeepDeblur, DOCNN and the Fire Hawk Optimizer - are described by loss functions and a notation table rather than by any reproducible configuration. [RQ2.6] Very low, with one distinctive problem. The dataset source, class balance, split sizes and MATLAB version are stated, and a 25-symbol notation table with loss definitions (L2, total variation, facial semantic, total) is provided - superficially detailed. But no architecture, learning rate, batch size, epoch count, image resolution, optimiser budget or search space is given; there is no code or seed; the reported result does not correspond to the stated split; and the deblurring evaluation reports PSNR, MSE and SSIM, all of which are computed against a sharp ground-truth reference image. No such reference exists for a photograph downloaded from the web. Either the blur was synthetically added to already-degraded web images so that a reference existed - in which case the deblurring result describes recovery from artificial corruption and says nothing about real image quality - or the metrics were computed against something unstated. The paper does not say which. [RQ2.7] None. There is no limitations section, no threats-to-validity discussion and no caveat. The single occurrence of limitations is a generic sentence in the introduction about facial-feature analysis being affected by image quality and expression variation - which is the problem the paper sets out to solve, not a limitation of its solution. Nothing is said about the dataset's provenance, the absent diagnostic labels, the mismatch between the stated split and the reported evaluation, or the absence of any ablation. [RQ2.9] None. There is no future-work section; the paper ends on the claim of higher accuracy with reduced model complexity. [RQ3.1] None. No behaviour is observed, elicited or measured. The target is static facial appearance recovered from deblurring and denoising. [RQ3.2] No fusion of modalities - a single image source. The pipeline stacks three processing stages (deblurring, denoising, classification) over one photograph, which is depth rather than multimodality. [RQ4.1] A two-stage pipeline: DeepDeblur, a convolution/deconvolution network learning a blurred-to-sharp mapping, followed by DOCNN, a CNN in which one layer set denoises and the next classifies, with a Fire Hawk Optimizer tuning parameters. Three separable components are each claimed as a contribution and none is ablated, so the reader cannot tell whether the deblurring stage, the denoising branch or the metaheuristic contributes anything to the classification result. [RQ4.2] Resized, deblurred and denoised RGB face images at unstated resolution. Resizing is described as adjusting the facial image for ratio and resolution with the loss of pixels - an unusual admission that information is discarded before the pipeline whose purpose is to recover information begins. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure, a confusion matrix and an ROC curve for classification; percentage blur removed, PSNR, MSE and SSIM for deblurring. Specificity is not reported, no AUC value is given numerically, no calibration or predictive values appear, and no confidence interval accompanies any figure. The reported accuracy of 96.94% reconciles exactly with the confusion-matrix counts - 2,850 correct out of 2,940 - which is the problem rather than a reassurance, because 2,940 is the entire dataset and not the 400-image test set the methods section defines. [RQ4.4] None. No saliency, attribution or feature analysis, and no ablation of the three pipeline stages. In a paper whose thesis is that image quality restoration improves ASD detection, no experiment isolates the contribution of restoration to the classification outcome - the deblurring metrics and the classification metrics are reported side by side but never linked. [RQ4.5] This study's decisive problem is that the reported result does not come from its stated evaluation design. The methods define an image-level split of 2,940 images into 2,540 for training and 400 for testing, balanced within each. The results section then states that out of 2,940 images used for evaluation the model correctly classified 1,430 autism images and 1,420 non-autism images, 2,850 correct with 90 misclassified - and 2,850/2,940 is precisely 96.94%, the headline accuracy carried into the abstract and the comparison table. The reported performance is therefore a resubstitution figure computed over the whole dataset, with 86% of the evaluated images having been used to fit the model.
