The 400-image test set is defined and never used to produce a number. Three further issues compound this. The corpus is the web-scraped autism face collection that repeats individuals, so even a correctly executed image-level split would not separate children. The Fire Hawk Optimizer tuned unspecified parameters against an unspecified objective on an unspecified partition. And the comparison table ranks 96.94% against five literature figures spanning 92.0% to 96.63% obtained on different image counts (2,636 to 3,014) under unstated protocols, with the paper asserting that the comparisons are done under the same conditions used in the existing methods to ensure fair comparison - a claim that cannot hold when this study's own figure is a training-set score. [RQ5.1] Autism spectrum disorder; Face recognition; DeepDeblur; Denoising optimized convolutional neural network; Fire hawk optimizer. Four of five terms name pipeline components; face recognition rather than screening or classification is used for the task. [RQ5.2] International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems 18(4) - an open-access computing journal, the same venue as local_6e7174c0. Review did not surface the mismatch between the stated 400-image test set and the 2,940-image evaluation, the absent ethics statement, or the reporting of reference-dependent image-quality metrics for photographs that have no sharp reference. [RQ5.3] 2025 (received 26 October 2024, revised 1 March 2025). Framing is diagnostic and efficiency-oriented: the model is offered for screening and detection of ASD in children, as computer-aided diagnosis, and as achieving higher accuracy with reduced model complexity and less execution time. There is no limitations section and no future work; the contribution is stated entirely as a position above five quoted figures on the same public image corpus, and the paper's own account of why ASD diagnosis is difficult - that there is no blood test or scan and that developmental history and behaviour must be assessed - is not reconciled with what it then does.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective analysis of the public ASD Children Traits dataset from Kaggle (accessed 1 June 2024): 1,985 cases of children aged 1-18 with 28 variables, reduced by expert-guided outlier and inconsistency removal to 634 cases and 19 variables. The retained variables include the ten AQ-10 items, the AQ10 total, the Q-CHAT-10 score, the Social Responsiveness Scale, a CARS severity rating, seven comorbidity flags, demographics and rater type, with the binary ASD_traits field as the target. Class balance is never reported.
narrative_rows.methods: Eight classifiers - random forest, SVM, GBM, XGBoost, C5.0, a neural network, k-NN and logistic regression - were fitted in R with caret 6.0.94 under 10-fold cross-validation with grid-search tuning, and compared by Wilcoxon signed-rank and Friedman tests on fold-wise metrics. Permutation feature importance, LIME and SHAP were applied to the best models. Prompted by the exceptionally high results, the full comparison was repeated at 2-fold, 4-fold and 5-fold.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Under 10-fold cross-validation the neural network achieved accuracy, F1, precision and recall of exactly 1.0000 (prAUC 0.9601); GBM and XGBoost reached 0.9984 with precision 1.0000; logistic regression 0.9858; SVM 0.9874; C5.0 0.9701; random forest 0.9463; k-NN 0.8883 at k=7. The neural network again scored perfectly at 4 and 5 folds but fell to 0.8691 at 2 folds. All three XAI methods identified the A1-A10 behavioural items as dominant and demographic variables as negligible.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The predictor set contains CARS, the Social Responsiveness Scale, the AQ10 total and the Q-CHAT-10 score - four instrument measurements of the target condition - together with the ten AQ-10 items that constitute the AQ10 total, all supplied as predictors of a binary autism-traits label. Perfect classification follows from that arrangement, and the authors' own overfitting investigation, which correctly re-ran the comparison at 2, 4 and 5 folds, cannot detect it because varying the partition does not touch the feature list; the decisive experiment, refitting without the instrument scores, is never run. Preprocessing removed 1,351 of 1,985 records and 9 of 28 variables on unstated criteria before cross-validation, and this step is credited in the abstract with improving generalizability. Class balance is never reported for any partition, so no baseline exists; specificity is never reported for any model; and the claim of applicability across diverse clinical datasets rests on one dataset. The label's own provenance - who assessed these children, with what instrument, against what criterion - is nowhere described.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This study matters to the review as the clearest demonstration that methodological care and a valid estimand are independent. Everything the field's methods literature asks for is present: child-level cross-validation, grid-search tuning, per-fold publication, formal non-parametric model comparison, three explanation methods, a deposited analysis dataset, clinician co-authorship, and an explicit, self-initiated overfitting investigation that no other study in this corpus attempts. The result is accuracy 1.0000. It belongs with local_3e88f3ce, which fed ADOS and ADI-R totals to a model and reached ROC-AUC 99.99%, as the corpus's two instrument-inclusion leakage cases, and with local_ed30e24c, whose careful nested tuning sat downstream of a circular label. Read alongside local_4da2b941, which under a comparably rigorous design and a non-circular target reached R=0.85 at best, it isolates the variable that actually governs reported performance in this literature: not the algorithm, not the resampling scheme, and not the explanation layer, but whether a measurement of the outcome is present among the inputs. Its consent waiver - justified on the ground that prior reuse of the dataset establishes a general consensus regarding its use for research purposes - is also the corpus's most explicit statement of reuse legitimising reuse.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] No participants were recruited. The ASD Children Traits dataset was downloaded from Kaggle: 1,985 cases with 28 variables, covering children aged 1-18. Preprocessing then reduced this to 634 cases and 19 variables - 68% of the records and a third of the variables removed as outliers, inconsistencies or erroneous data identified by clinical experts. Neither the raw nor the preprocessed dataset's class balance is reported anywhere, so the number of ASD and non-ASD cases behind every result in the paper is unknown. This matters more than usual because the introduction states explicitly that ASD assessment datasets tend to over-represent ASD cases and that this can bias models toward the majority class - a problem the authors identify and then never quantify in their own data. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, individuals with ASD, patients, ASD traits, non-ASD. The register is clinical and generally neutral, with person-first phrasing throughout and an explicit concern for quality of life for individuals with ASD. The consistent use of patient for records in a downloaded Kaggle file - patient case identifiers, patient consent, patient information - is worth noting: it treats spreadsheet rows as clinical subjects while the study has no clinical relationship with any of them. [RQ1.3] Variables are present but distributions are not. Age spans 1-18 years with no mean or SD; sex is coded M/F with no counts; ethnicity is coded across 11 categories (Asian, Black, Hispanic, Latino, Middle Eastern, Mixed, Native Indian, Others, Pacifica, South Asian, White European) with no counts; family history and rater type (family member, healthcare professional, other) are recorded. Seven comorbidity flags are retained as model inputs - speech/language delay, learning disorder, genetic disorders, depression, global developmental delay/intellectual disability, social/behavioural issues, anxiety disorder - and not one prevalence figure is given for any of them. The dataset is described as comprehensively capturing socioeconomic status, but no socioeconomic variable appears in either variable table. [RQ1.4] None. The dependent variable is ASD_traits, a binary yes/no field in a Kaggle spreadsheet. No clinical assessment, diagnostic instrument administration, criterion, assessor or date exists for any case, and the originating collection procedure is not described at all. The paper nonetheless frames the task as ASD diagnosis throughout, titles itself Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics, and opens by criticising clinician-administered instruments for introducing variability and potential bias - a criticism made in favour of a label whose provenance is entirely unknown. [RQ1.5] Four instrument scores are present - Social Responsiveness Scale, CARS, AQ10 total and Q-CHAT-10 - and all four are used as model inputs rather than reported as participant characteristics. Not one mean, range or class-wise distribution appears for any of them. This is the study's central analytic problem, examined under RQ4.2 and RQ4.5. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to combine explainable AI with a rigorous, clinically guided preprocessing pipeline to make ML-based ASD diagnosis both accurate and interpretable, and to provide practical R-based guidelines for non-expert clinicians. Headline findings: under 10-fold cross-validation the neural network reached accuracy, precision, recall and F1 of exactly 1.0000, with GBM and XGBoost at 0.9984 and logistic regression at 0.9858; Wilcoxon and Friedman tests confirmed significant differences between models; and PFI, LIME and SHAP all identified the A1-A10 behavioural items as dominant with demographic variables contributing little. [RQ2.2] No study setting. A downloaded Kaggle file analysed in R. The authorship is notable for this corpus - it includes practising paediatric and psychiatric clinicians from a university hospital, and their input is credited with guiding the feature-selection step. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. Tabular records combining AQ-10 item responses, four instrument scores, comorbidity flags and demographics, with a rater field recording whether a family member, healthcare professional or other person completed the assessment. The rater field is retained as a predictor rather than analysed as a source of measurement heterogeneity. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. Ethics is formally addressed and formally waived: ethical review and approval were waived due to the use of publicly available data without any identifiable information, and patient consent was waived because the dataset is widely accepted and publicly available, has been used in numerous research studies establishing a general consensus regarding its use for research purposes, and has been de-identified. The reasoning is at least stated, which distinguishes it from the many charted studies with no ethics statement at all; but the specific argument - that prior reuse establishes a consensus legitimising further reuse - is a citation-count justification for a governance question, and it is offered for a dataset whose own collection consent is never established. [RQ2.5] No instrumentation. R with caret 6.0.94, iml for SHAP and permutation importance, lime for LIME, glmnet and class for two of the models. The paper devotes an entire subsection to arguing that R is accessible to non-expert clinicians and offers practical guidelines for its use - a genuine attempt at translation - and then does not release the script that would make those guidelines operational. [RQ2.6] Split. The artefact-level reporting is among the best in the charted corpus: the source dataset has a URL and access date, the preprocessed 634-case analysis dataset is deposited as a supplementary spreadsheet, fold-by-fold metrics for all eight models appear in an appendix, caret's version is given, each model family is defined by equation, and the k-NN k-sweep is reported in full. The decisive step is nevertheless irreproducible. Preprocessing removed 1,351 of 1,985 records and 9 of 28 variables on the basis of clinical experts identifying inconsistencies and erroneous data, with no criterion stated, no counts per step, no class composition for the removed records and no indication of whether the removal was made blind to the outcome. Since that step is credited in the abstract with improving generalizability and real-world applicability, and since it is the largest single transformation in the pipeline, the study cannot be reproduced in the respect that matters most. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section, but the discussion contains the most genuine act of self-scrutiny in the charted corpus. The authors write that because of the exceptionally high-performance metrics observed in our initial model evaluations, we were concerned about the potential for overfitting, and they respond by re-running the entire comparison at 2-fold, 4-fold and 5-fold. They report that the neural network's perfect scores in certain folds indicate a potential risk of overfitting to specific data characteristics, and that identical metrics for the neural network and k-NN in some tables may indicate redundancy or overfitting in the model implementation or data processing. That instinct is correct and is exercised properly. What it does not reach is the cause: no fold count can diagnose a problem that lies in the feature set rather than the partition, and the one experiment that would have settled it - refitting without the SRS, CARS, AQ10 and Q-CHAT-10 scores - is never run. Unmentioned elsewhere: the unreported class balance, the unspecified 68% record removal, the absence of any external dataset behind a claim of applicability across diverse clinical datasets, and the unknown provenance of the label. [RQ2.9] A single direction: migrate from R to Python for access to more advanced machine-learning libraries and better collaboration with the childcare research community. This is a tooling preference rather than a scientific direction, and it addresses none of the study's own identified concerns - not the overfitting the authors flag, not external validation, and not the missing clinical ground truth. [RQ3.1] Autistic traits as captured by the ten AQ-10 items, characterised in the XAI discussion as communication patterns, repetitive actions and frequency of eye contact. All behaviour is second-hand and questionnaire-mediated, reported by a family member, healthcare professional or unspecified other. [RQ3.2] No modality fusion - a single tabular source. There is, however, a fusion of instrument types within the feature vector that is the study's defining characteristic: AQ-10 item responses, an AQ-10 total, a Q-CHAT-10 total, an SRS score and a CARS severity rating all sit in the same 19-variable input alongside the ASD_traits label they are designed to determine. [RQ4.1] Eight classical classifiers compared under a common protocol - random forest, SVM, gradient boosting machine, XGBoost, C5.0, a neural network, k-nearest neighbours and logistic regression - with grid-search tuning in caret and formal statistical comparison by Wilcoxon signed-rank and Friedman tests. No deep learning on raw signals; the comparison is fair in form and the statistical apparatus is more rigorous than anything else in the charted corpus. [RQ4.2] A 19-field tabular row containing, together: the ten AQ-10 behavioural items, the AQ10 total score, the Q-CHAT-10 score, the Social Responsiveness Scale score, the CARS severity rating, seven comorbidity flags and demographics - with ASD_traits as the target. This is the review's most concentrated instance of target leakage by instrument inclusion. CARS is a clinician-administered autism severity scale; SRS measures social impairment severity; AQ10 and Q-CHAT-10 are autism screening totals whose thresholds define exactly the kind of traits-present label being predicted; and the ten AQ-10 items are the summands of the AQ10 total. Four separate measurements of the target condition, plus the item-level constituents of one of them, are supplied to the model as predictors of that condition. A perfect neural-network score under this arrangement is the expected outcome, not an anomaly - and it explains why even logistic regression, a linear model on 19 variables, reaches 0.9858. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, F1, precision, recall and area under the precision-recall curve, per model and per fold, at four fold counts, with per-fold tables in an appendix. The choice of prAUC is thoughtful and explicitly justified by the expected class imbalance. Two absences matter. Specificity is never reported for any model, so the false-positive behaviour of a system proposed for paediatric screening is invisible; and the class balance is never given, so neither the prAUC baseline nor the majority-class accuracy can be computed. The reported neural-network figures are accuracy 1.0000, F1 1.0000, precision 1.0000 and recall 1.0000 - a model that misclassifies no child in any of ten folds - with prAUC 0.9601, a combination that is itself internally odd, since a classifier with perfect precision and recall should have a precision-recall curve area of 1. [RQ4.4] Three methods, applied properly and to the best models only: permutation feature importance, LIME with reported probability and explanation-fit values, and SHAP, with the authors concluding that SHAP gives the most consistent and reliable explanations for both global and local behaviour. The substantive finding is that the A1-A10 behavioural items dominate while demographic variables such as age and ethnicity contribute little, which the paper reads as evidence that behaviour rather than demography drives ASD prediction and as grounds for clinician trust. The reading is understandable and wrong in an instructive way: the model weights the AQ-10 items heavily because the label is an autism-traits determination made from those items, so the explanation confirms the pipeline's internal arithmetic rather than validating a clinical insight. The XAI apparatus here is the most carefully executed in the charted corpus and is applied to a model whose behaviour it cannot make meaningful. [RQ4.5] On the axes that defeat most of this literature, the design is sound. The analysis unit is the child, the folds partition children, there is no within-participant leakage, hyperparameters are grid-searched, per-fold results are published, model differences are tested with Wilcoxon signed-rank and Friedman statistics rather than eyeballed, and the k-NN sweep is reported. The authors then did what almost no one in this corpus does: they distrusted their own result. Concerned about the potential for overfitting given exceptionally high metrics, they re-ran the full comparison at 2, 4 and 5 folds, observed that the neural network scored perfectly at 4 and 5 folds but fell to 0.8691 at 2, and noted that this indicates a potential risk of overfitting to specific data characteristics. That is the right instinct pointed at the wrong object. Varying the fold count tests partition sensitivity; it cannot detect leakage that lives in the feature set. Here the feature set contains four separate instrument measurements of the target condition - CARS, SRS, AQ10 and Q-CHAT-10 - plus the item-level constituents of the AQ-10 total, all predicting a binary ASD_traits label. Under those conditions accuracy 1.0000 is not overfitting; it is the model reading the answer off the input, and no resampling scheme will change it. Two further issues compound this. The preprocessing removed 68% of the records and a third of the variables through expert identification of inconsistencies and erroneous data, performed on the whole dataset before cross-validation and with no stated criterion, no per-class counts and no indication of outcome blinding - a step credited in the abstract with improving generalizability. And the class balance is never reported, so neither a majority-class baseline nor a prAUC reference exists, and the perfect scores cannot be positioned against anything. The abstract's claim that rigorous preprocessing improved real-world applicability across diverse clinical datasets is made from a single dataset with no external cohort. [RQ5.1] autism spectrum disorder; clinical diagnosis; data preprocessing; healthcare analytics; machine learning; patient outcomes; personalized intervention; explainable artificial intelligence. Eight terms spanning condition, method, application and aspiration; validation and participants are absent, and clinical diagnosis names something the study does not have. [RQ5.2] Diagnostics 14(22):2504 (MDPI) - an open-access clinical diagnostics journal, with paediatric and psychiatric clinicians among the authors. The clinical involvement is real and shaped the feature selection; it did not surface that four instrument measurements of the target condition were sitting in the predictor set, which is precisely the observation clinical expertise is best placed to make. The paper cleared review in 40 days. [RQ5.3] Published 8 November 2024 (indexed here under 2025), 40 days from submission. Framing is translational and confident: the integration of ML and XAI promises to revolutionize intervention strategies, the study successfully developed highly precise and interpretable ML models for ASD diagnosis, and the findings support the adoption of AI-driven diagnostic tools by healthcare professionals and contribute to personalized intervention strategies. The paper positions itself in a comparison table against ten prior studies, with the distinguishing contribution in every row being the absence of XAI in the others - so novelty is claimed on the explanation layer while the estimand goes unexamined. Its most interesting feature is that a team including practising clinicians, applying correct cross-validation, formal statistical testing and three explanation methods, arrived at accuracy 1.0000 and treated it as a result to be defended by resampling rather than as a signal to inspect the feature list.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional primary study in Cordoba, Spain. Ninety-three children aged 32-74 months in three groups - 24 with ASD, 25 with developmental language disorder, 44 typically developing - with both clinical groups recruited from early childhood intervention centres and required to hold a formal DSM-5 diagnosis from a licensed clinical team. Groups were matched on age (F(2,90)=0.041, p=0.959) but differed significantly in sex composition (22/2 and 23/2 male/female in the clinical groups against 22/22 in TD, p<0.01), basic attention and PPVT-III receptive vocabulary.
narrative_rows.methods: Gaze was recorded with a Tobii X2-30 at 30 Hz during an eye-tracking paired preferences task pairing faces (happy, angry, neutral) with objects, after nine-point calibration. Four nested feature sets were derived per child - full (158 variables), secondary (72), prior (60) and basic (24) - and interpretable classifiers were evaluated under stratified 5-fold cross-validation across every group combination, with F1 interpreted against pre-specified bands.
narrative_rows.outcomes: F1 0.912 for DLD versus TD, 0.88 for pooled ASD+DLD versus TD, 0.86 for ASD versus TD, and 0.63 for ASD versus DLD. Naive Bayes and logistic model trees performed best. Broad social versus non-social areas of interest carried the discriminative information; finer variables about specific facial regions and emotions did not improve accuracy. Mean duration of visits to objects emerged as a candidate marker, interpreted as difficulty disengaging attention from objects.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The authors name four: limited experimental scope, sample size, diagnostic instruments that could have been supplemented but were the only ones available, and the provisionality of early-age diagnoses. Three more are visible in the data. The clinical groups are roughly 92% male against 50% in the TD group and differ significantly in receptive vocabulary and basic attention, none of which is adjusted for, so part of the separation from TD may reflect sex and language ability rather than diagnosis. The full feature set carries 158 variables for 93 children, and no confidence interval or across-fold variance is reported for any figure. And the headline results are the best over four feature sets crossed with several algorithms and four group comparisons, without correction or an external cohort. The ASD-versus-DLD result is the least affected by all three, since it shares every methodological feature with the ASD-versus-TD comparison.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This is one of the two studies in the charted corpus not at high overall risk of bias, and it supplies the review's most direct measurement of a quantity the rest of the literature leaves undefined. Almost every included study classifies autism against typical development and reports the resulting figure as diagnostic accuracy. Here the same task, equipment, feature sets, algorithms and cross-validation scheme are applied both ways: F1 0.86 for ASD versus typical development, and F1 0.63 for ASD versus developmental language disorder at nearly balanced class sizes. The 23-point gap is an internally controlled estimate of how much of the corpus's typical ASD-versus-TD performance is autism-specific rather than a general clinical-versus-non-clinical distinction - and the authors draw exactly that conclusion, stating that their approach is more effective as a screening tool than for differential diagnosis. It sits with local_cd7545e2, where the ADOS-2 itself reached AUC 0.562 against schizophrenia with false-positive rates of 45-52%, as the review's two differential-diagnosis calibration points, and with local_4da2b941 and local_7d7f1fcc as evidence of the field's realistic performance envelope. Its negative granularity finding - that broad social/non-social areas of interest outperform fine decompositions by facial region and emotion - is also a useful methodological result for the eye-tracking branch, in which feature elaboration is usually assumed to help.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Ninety-three children aged 32-74 months in three clinically defined groups: 24 with ASD, 25 with developmental language disorder, and 44 typically developing. Both clinical groups were recruited from early childhood intervention centres in Cordoba province and required a formal diagnosis made by a licensed, experienced clinical team. The analysis unit is the child throughout, and each child contributes exactly one row to each of four feature sets. The inclusion of a second clinical group is what distinguishes this study from almost the entire charted corpus: it makes the ASD-versus-DLD comparison possible, and that comparison is where the study's most informative result lies. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, developmental language disorder, neurodevelopmental disorders, typical development, children with ASD, clinical groups. The register is clinical and precise, using DSM-5 language (persistent deficits in social interaction and communication, repetitive and restrictive patterns) without editorialising. Groups are named by diagnosis rather than by normality - the comparison group is typically developing, never normal. There is no autistic-community engagement, but nothing in the language pathologises beyond the diagnostic criteria themselves. [RQ1.3] Among the most complete in the corpus, and reported with statistical tests. Age: TD 53.23 (SD 10.04), ASD 53.50 (10.35), DLD 54.0 (12.14) months, F(2,90)=0.041, p=0.959 - the groups are closely matched on age, which is uncommon here and is demonstrated rather than asserted. Sex: TD 22 boys/22 girls, ASD 22/2, DLD 23/2, chi-squared 20.15, p<0.01 - a large and explicitly tested imbalance which the authors attribute to the higher prevalence of both conditions in males. Basic attention: 87.09 / 73.50 / 73.08, F=13.23, p<0.01. PPVT-III receptive vocabulary standard score: 108.75 / 98.65 / 86.57, F=19.56, p<0.01. Nothing on ethnicity, socioeconomic status or language background. The sex and vocabulary differences matter for the classification results and are not carried into the modelling as covariates. [RQ1.4] Clinically ascertained and honestly qualified. Diagnosis of ASD or DLD was made by a licensed, experienced team of clinicians following DSM-5 and international diagnostic manual guidelines, independently of this study and as a precondition of enrolment at an early intervention centre. Typically developing children are defined by the absence of such enrolment. The authors then add two caveats that few in this corpus offer: that their diagnostic tools could have been supplemented with further assessments but were the only ones available at the time, and that diagnoses at early ages are provisional and may evolve over time, so the findings should be interpreted with caution. [RQ1.5] No autism severity instrument is reported. Instead the study characterises its groups on two dimensions relevant to the task: a basic attention score and PPVT-III receptive vocabulary, both with significant group differences. The absence of a severity measure is a real gap for interpreting the ASD group's heterogeneity, but the inclusion of a standardised language measure is directly to the point, since DLD is the comparison condition. [RQ2.1] The stated aim is to apply explainable machine learning to eye-tracking data from a social attention task in children with ASD, DLD and typical development, to assess classification accuracy across all group combinations and to identify which variables best differentiate the groups. Headline findings: F1 0.912 for DLD versus TD, 0.88 for pooled ASD+DLD versus TD, 0.86 for ASD versus TD, and 0.63 for ASD versus DLD; broad social versus non-social areas of interest carried the signal while finer decompositions by facial region and emotion did not improve accuracy; naive Bayes and logistic model trees performed best; and mean duration of visits to objects emerged as a candidate disorder-specific marker. [RQ2.2] Early childhood intervention centres in the province of Cordoba supplied both clinical groups; testing used a screen-based eye tracker below a 15-inch laptop, with nine-point calibration. The clinical recruitment route is stated, though the room, examiner and whether TD children were tested under identical conditions are not described. [RQ2.3] The eye-tracking paired preferences paradigm: social and non-social images presented side by side, with faces displaying happiness, anger and neutral expressions paired against objects, following established designs (Sasson and Touchstone; Vacas et al.). This is a purpose-built social-attention task drawn from the developmental literature rather than a repurposed video or free-viewing sequence, and the choice is justified by reference to the metrics - fixation duration, fixation count, latency to first fixation - shown to be sensitive to gaze differences across neurodevelopmental conditions. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single session. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: approval by the Research Ethics Committee of Cordoba dated 02/08/2019 with reference number 4393, conducted per the Declaration of Helsinki and local legislation, with families informed of the study's purpose and procedures and written informed consent obtained from legal guardians. The discussion adds an ethically relevant scientific caveat - that early diagnoses are provisional - which bears directly on how the labels should be read. [RQ2.5] Tobii X2-30 remote eye tracker at 30 Hz on a 15-inch laptop screen with Tobii Studio and nine-point calibration using an animated target. The stated spatial accuracy of 36 degrees is a typographic error for 0.36 degrees - as printed the figure would exceed the visual angle of the entire display. The modelling software is not named, and no hyperparameters, tuning procedure or seed is reported for any algorithm, which is the main reporting gap in an otherwise well-specified study. [RQ2.6] Moderate to good on acquisition, thin on modelling. Reproducible: the eye tracker, sampling rate, screen size, calibration procedure, paradigm, stimulus composition and emotion set; the four feature sets by variable count and content; the stratified 5-fold scheme; the F1 interpretive bands, fixed before the results; and an offer of raw data on request. Not reproducible: the modelling workbench, the algorithm settings, whether any tuning occurred and whether it was nested, the seed, per-fold results, and the full variable lists for the 158-, 72-, 60- and 24-variable datasets. [RQ2.7] A short but genuinely self-critical paragraph naming four things: the limited scope of the experiment, the sample size, the diagnostic tools (which could have been supplemented but were the only ones available at the time), and the provisional nature of early-age diagnoses, with an explicit instruction that findings should be interpreted with caution and a call for replication with current behavioural assessments. Not mentioned: that the full variable set has 158 variables for 93 children; that the reported figures are the maximum over four feature sets, several algorithms and four comparisons with no correction; that the sex imbalance between clinical and TD groups (approximately 92% male versus 50%) offers an alternative route to the ASD-vs-TD and DLD-vs-TD separations; and that the significant PPVT-III differences are similarly available. [RQ2.9] Add further explainable algorithms such as gradient boosting trees and explainable boosting machines, and integrate multimodal data combining eye tracking with behavioural, cognitive or neurophysiological measures to improve robustness and clinical applicability. Both are proportionate to the study's own findings. [RQ3.1] Social attention during simultaneous presentation of social and non-social stimuli: preferential looking to faces versus objects, indexed by fixation duration, fixation count, visit duration and latency to first fixation, across areas of interest from whole-stimulus categories down to eyes and mouth and across three emotional expressions. The substantive behavioural finding is about objects rather than faces - mean duration of visits to objects discriminates, which the authors interpret as difficulty disengaging attention from objects rather than as reduced interest in faces. [RQ3.2] No multimodal fusion - eye tracking alone. What the study does instead is a granularity comparison within one modality: four nested feature sets ranging from 24 broad variables to 158 fine-grained ones. The result is a clean negative finding that broad social/non-social area-of-interest variables carry the discriminative information while adding specific facial features and emotion categories does not improve accuracy. Multimodal extension with behavioural, cognitive or neurophysiological measures is named as the next step. [RQ4.1] Interpretable classical classifiers selected for explainability rather than capacity, with naive Bayes and logistic model trees performing best. No deep learning. The algorithm choice follows from the stated aim - to identify which eye-tracking variables discriminate, in a form clinicians can inspect - rather than from a search for maximum accuracy, and this is one of the few studies in the corpus where the modelling choice is subordinated to the scientific question. [RQ4.2] Four nested tabular feature sets per child: full (158 variables), secondary (72), prior (60) and basic (24), differing in how finely stimuli and areas of interest are decomposed. All variables derive from the eye-tracking record; no clinical instrument score, demographic variable or diagnostic measure enters the feature set - a point worth stating explicitly, because it is exactly what separates this study from the corpus's leakage cases. With 93 children and up to 158 variables, three of the four datasets have more variables than participants. [RQ4.3] F1-score only, with precision and recall given by equation. The interpretive bands are stated in advance (0.0-0.5 poor, 0.5-0.7 moderate, 0.8-0.9 good, 0.9-1.0 excellent) and the results are then reported against them, so the descriptions excellent, good and moderate are pre-committed rather than chosen after the fact - a small but genuine discipline. Missing: accuracy, sensitivity and specificity separately, AUC, calibration, confidence intervals, across-fold variance, and any statement of the majority-class baseline. The last matters most for the ASD-versus-DLD comparison, where the classes are nearly balanced (24 versus 25) and F1 0.63 sits only modestly above chance, and for ASD-versus-TD, where the baseline is around 0.65 and the reported 0.86 represents a real but smaller gain than the number suggests in isolation. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is the study's purpose rather than an appendix to it. The four-way feature-set comparison yields a negative result that is reported plainly - fine-grained variables about specific facial areas and emotions do not improve on broad social versus non-social groupings - and the surviving discriminative variable, mean duration of visits to objects, is interpreted theoretically as difficulty disengaging attention from objects, connected to an existing attentional account (Landry and Bryson). This is a claim about behaviour that another laboratory could test, generated by a model whose structure a clinician can inspect, which is the intended use of explainable methods and is rare in this corpus. [RQ4.5] The validation is participant-level and structurally correct: stratified 5-fold cross-validation over 93 children, one row per child, no within-participant duplication, and no clinical instrument score anywhere in the feature set. Three caveats qualify the numbers rather than invalidate them. First, dimensionality - the full dataset carries 158 variables for 93 children, and even the smallest carries 24, so the models operate in a regime where cross-validated estimates over five folds are noisy; no interval or fold variance is reported. Second, selection - the headline figures are the best over four feature sets crossed with several algorithms and four group comparisons, with no correction and no held-out cohort, so they are optimistic by an unquantified margin. Third, confounding - the clinical groups are approximately 92% male against 50% in the TD group (chi-squared 20.15, p<0.01) and differ significantly in receptive vocabulary and basic attention, all of which are plausible correlates of gaze behaviour in a paired-preference task; none is adjusted for, so part of the 0.86 and 0.912 against TD may reflect sex and language ability rather than diagnosis. The result that survives all of this is the one the authors themselves foreground: ASD versus DLD reaches only F1 0.63, at nearly balanced class sizes, and they conclude that the approach is more effective as a screening tool than for differential diagnosis. That conclusion is the correct reading of their own data and is the most valuable single sentence in this part of the corpus, because the two comparisons are internally controlled - same task, same equipment, same pipeline, same analyst - so the gap between 0.86 against typical development and 0.63 against another neurodevelopmental condition isolates how much of the apparent signal is autism-specific rather than clinical-population-general. [RQ5.1] explainable machine learning; autism spectrum disorder; developmental language disorder; eye-tracking; differential diagnosis; computer-aided diagnosis. Six terms naming method, both conditions, modality and - uniquely in this corpus - differential diagnosis, which is what the study actually attempts. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Neuroscience 19:1558621 - an open-access neuroscience journal, with a 127-day review. The venue's disciplinary fit shows in the reporting: matched group characteristics with ANOVA and chi-squared tests, a standardised language measure, a pre-specified interpretive scale for F1, an ethics reference number, and a limitations paragraph that includes the provisionality of early diagnoses. [RQ5.3] 2025, published 24 June, 127 days from submission to acceptance. Framing is deliberately restrained and, unusually, becomes more restrained as the paper proceeds: the abstract reports the ASD-versus-DLD F1 of 0.63 alongside the higher figures rather than burying it, and the conclusion states that the approach is more effective as a screening tool than for differential diagnosis. The clinical claim is limited to a preliminary step toward computer-aided diagnosis. Its contribution to the review is not a performance number but a controlled contrast: by running the same pipeline against a typically developing group and against a second clinical group, it converts the corpus's ubiquitous ASD-versus-TD figure into an interpretable quantity.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective analysis of 547 eye-tracking scanpath images (328 non-ASD, 219 ASD) at 640x480 from a public repository - the Cilia/Carette collection, whose originators appear in the comparison table. The number of distinct children behind the images is never stated; the abstract instead reports the image counts as though they were child counts (328 characteristically emerging children and 219 children with autism), while the methods section gives the correct reading. The viewing task, stimuli and recording equipment of the original collection are not described.
narrative_rows.methods: Images were resized to 640x480, enhanced, converted to arrays and normalised to [0,1], then split into training, validation and test sets, with rotation, shifting and flipping augmentation applied during training via ImageDataGenerator. Four ImageNet-pretrained classifiers were fitted - MobileNet, VGG19, DenseNet169 and a VGG19+MobileNet hybrid - each with a pooling layer, dense layers with ReLU and dropout, a two-unit softmax output, sparse categorical cross-entropy, RMSprop or Adam at learning rate 0.0001, batch sizes 16 and 32, and 100 epochs.
narrative_rows.outcomes: MobileNet reached 100% accuracy with perfect precision, recall and F1 for both classes and ROC 100%; VGG19 92%; DenseNet169 78% (ASD recall 50%). The test partition contains 55 images (33 non-ASD, 22 ASD), a figure recoverable only from the support column. The proposed model is ranked above three prior studies on the same dataset (87%, 90%, 79%), with the advantage attributed to a different preprocessing approach.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The study states none. Its split is at the image level on a scanpath collection in which each child contributes multiple images, so images from the same child's session appear on both sides - the same within-participant leakage documented across the video, EEG-epoch, thermal, cry and facial-image branches, and enough on its own to produce a perfect score. The test set holds 55 images, which the paper never states and which places roughly plus or minus 12 percentage points of sampling noise on every figure: the 78%-to-100% spread across four architectures trained identically is a symptom of that, not a ranking of methods. The viewing task behind the scanpaths is nowhere described, so stimulus identity cannot be excluded as what the classifier reads. Augmentation by rotation and flipping produces gaze traces corresponding to no possible viewing behaviour. There is no dataset accession, no seed, no code, no ethics statement, no limitations section and no future work, and the abstract reports image counts as child counts.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This study extends the review's leakage catalogue to the scanpath-image modality in its purest form, and pairs directly with local_bb4d1f7a, which used the same modality with a fixed 100 crops per child. Its distinctive contribution to the synthesis is the architecture spread: MobileNet 100%, VGG19 92%, DenseNet169 78%, all trained on the same 547 images under the same protocol and evaluated on the same 55 test images. That 22-point range between architectures on identical data is the clearest single demonstration in the corpus that figures from small held-out sets are estimates of noise as much as of method quality - and the paper nevertheless reports the maximum as its headline and ranks it against three prior studies whose reported figures (87%, 90%, 79%) all fall inside its own architectures' range. Its abstract's conversion of 547 images into 547 children is also worth recording alongside local_986436f2's fabricated demographic table as an instance of a dataset being described as something it is not.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] No participants. 547 scanpath images from a public eye-tracking repository, 328 labelled non-ASD and 219 ASD. The abstract converts this image count into a participant count, describing the dataset as scan pathways obtained from 328 characteristically emerging children and 219 children with autism - which would make this one of the larger primary eye-tracking cohorts in the field. The methods section states the correct version, that these are image counts. The source collection is the Cilia/Carette scanpath set, whose originators are cited in the comparison table and in which a few dozen children contributed multiple scanpath images each; the number of distinct children behind the 547 images is never given here. Every reported metric rests on a test partition of 55 images, recoverable only from the support column of the per-class results tables. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, persons diagnosed with ASD, people without ASD, children with autism, characteristically emerging children, ASD children. The phrase characteristically emerging children appears to be a rewording of typically developing and, together with formulations like monotonous and stereotyped behaviors and the commonness of ASD, suggests heavy paraphrasing throughout. The register is otherwise clinical without being pejorative, and there is no autistic-community perspective. [RQ1.3] None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography or recruitment source for any image, and no acknowledgement that this information is absent - despite the introduction discussing sex ratios in ASD prevalence and noting that girls with ASD often have fewer observable symptoms, a point directly relevant to a dataset whose sex composition is unknown. [RQ1.4] None. Labels are inherited from a public image collection with no diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or date reported, and the originating study's diagnostic procedure is not summarised. The paper's opening argument is that conventional ASD assessment relies on subjective criteria and lacks objectivity - a criticism advanced in favour of a label whose ascertainment it never examines. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to automate ASD categorisation from eye-tracking data using deep learning, in response to the cost, delay and subjectivity of conventional assessment. Headline findings: MobileNet reached 100% accuracy with perfect precision, recall and F1 for both classes and ROC 100%; VGG19 92%; DenseNet169 78%; the proposed model is ranked above three prior studies on the same dataset (87%, 90%, 79%). The paper attributes its advantage explicitly to preprocessing - our model achieved high accuracy because we have used a different preprocessing approach from improving dataset. [RQ2.2] No study setting. Images downloaded from an unnamed public repository; the compute environment is tabulated but not quoted in the extracted text. Critically, the acquisition setting of the original data - the viewing task, the stimuli, the eye tracker, the session structure - is nowhere summarised, so a reader cannot say what behaviour the scanpaths record. [RQ2.3] Not reported. The paradigm behind the scanpaths is never described. This matters more than usual for a scanpath dataset, because the geometry of a scanpath image is jointly determined by the child and by the stimulus, and without knowing the stimulus set one cannot tell whether the classifier is reading gaze behaviour or stimulus identity. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. There is no ethics statement, consent statement or exemption claim anywhere in the article, and no consideration of the provenance or consent basis of the underlying eye-tracking recordings of children. [RQ2.5] No acquisition instrumentation described. Modelling used ImageNet-pretrained MobileNet, VGG19 and DenseNet169 backbones with custom heads, Keras ImageDataGenerator for augmentation, RMSprop or Adam at learning rate 0.0001, batch sizes 16 (training) and 32 (validation), and 100 epochs. Parameter tables per model are provided and are more complete than most in this corpus. [RQ2.6] Mixed. Strengths: per-model parameter tables covering base architecture, pooling, dense widths, dropout, output layer, loss, optimiser, learning rate, batch sizes and epochs; and an explicit, correctly ordered preprocessing sequence in which the split precedes augmentation and augmentation is confined to training. Weaknesses: the dataset is described only as a freely accessible public repository with no accession, URL or DOI; the split proportions are never stated and the test size must be inferred from a support column; there is no seed, no code, and no statement of how many children the images come from; and the hybrid model is specified only by a figure. [RQ2.7] None. There is no limitations section and the word limitation does not occur in the article. Nothing is said about the image-level split on a dataset with repeated images per child, about the 55-image test set, about the absence of any description of the underlying task, or about the fact that three architectures trained on the same data under the same protocol span 78% to 100%. [RQ2.9] None. There is no future-work section; the paper closes on the claim that healthcare professionals can use these classifiers to enhance the accuracy rate of ASD diagnosis. [RQ3.1] Visual scanning behaviour, encoded as a rendered scanpath image showing the geometric trace of fixations and saccades. Because the images are treated as pictures rather than as sequences, no fixation duration, saccade amplitude, area-of-interest dwell or temporal ordering is extracted or reported - the behavioural content of the data is entirely implicit in the picture. [RQ3.2] No fusion of modalities - one image source. The hybrid model combines two ImageNet backbones over the same image, which is architectural ensembling rather than multimodality. [RQ4.1] Four transfer-learning classifiers: MobileNet, VGG19, DenseNet169 and a VGG19+MobileNet hybrid, each with ImageNet weights, the top layers removed, a pooling layer, dense layers with ReLU and dropout, and a two-unit softmax output. [RQ4.2] 640x480 scanpath images, enhanced, converted to arrays and normalised to [0,1], with rotation, shifting and flipping augmentation applied during training only. Augmentation of a scanpath image is worth a separate note: flipping and rotating a gaze trace changes its spatial relationship to the stimulus that produced it, so the augmented examples correspond to no possible viewing behaviour - a transformation that is standard for photographs and semantically incoherent for scanpaths. [RQ4.3] Per-class precision, recall, F1 and support, overall accuracy, macro averages, ROC curves and training/validation curves. Specificity is defined by equation and never tabulated. No confidence interval accompanies any figure, and none is possible to infer without the split proportions, which are not stated. The support column is the only place the test-set size appears: 33 non-ASD and 22 ASD, 55 images in total. On 55 images the 95% interval around VGG19's 92% runs from roughly 82% to 98% and around DenseNet169's 78% from roughly 65% to 88%, so the reported ordering of the four architectures - and the ranking against the three prior studies at 87%, 90% and 79% - is not statistically distinguishable. [RQ4.4] None. No saliency, attribution or scanpath-feature analysis, and no ablation of the hybrid. In a study whose premise is that gaze patterns carry diagnostic information, no gaze pattern is identified, and the paper does not report what distinguishes the ASD scanpath images from the others. [RQ4.5] The preprocessing order is handled correctly - the dataset is split before augmentation, and augmentation is applied during training via ImageDataGenerator - which is better than several neighbours in this corpus. Everything else about the evaluation undercuts the result. The split is at the image level on a scanpath collection in which each child contributes multiple images, so images generated from the same child's viewing session sit on both sides of the partition; this is the same within-participant leakage documented across the video, EEG-epoch, thermal, cry and facial-image branches, and it is sufficient to explain a perfect score. The test partition holds 55 images, a figure the paper never states and that must be recovered from a support column, so every reported metric carries roughly plus or minus 11 to 13 percentage points of sampling noise; MobileNet's 100% means 55 of 55 correct. There is no cross-validation, no repetition and no seed, and the spread across four architectures trained identically on the same data - 100%, 92%, 78% and the hybrid - is itself evidence of how unstable a 55-image estimate is, though the paper reads it as a genuine ranking of methods. The comparison against three prior studies on the same dataset (87%, 90%, 79%) is attributed to a different preprocessing approach, when the more parsimonious explanation is that the earlier figures came from evaluations that were less permissive. Finally, the paper never describes the viewing task behind the scanpaths, so it cannot exclude that the classifier is recognising which stimulus produced a trace rather than who produced it. [RQ5.1] autism spectrum disorder; eye tracking; deep learning; VGG19; MobileNet; DenseNet169; hybrid model. Four of seven terms name specific architectures; validation, participants and task are absent. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Medicine 11:1436646 - an open-access clinical journal, accepted in 44 days. A 100% diagnostic accuracy claim, an abstract that reports image counts as child counts, an absent ethics statement, an unstated test-set size and no limitations section all passed clinical review. [RQ5.3] Published 19 July 2024 (indexed here under 2025), 44 days from submission. Framing is unqualified diagnostic assistance: the classifiers are said to demonstrate the potential of eye-tracking data to aid physicians in efficiently and accurately screening for autism, and users and healthcare professionals can utilize these classifiers to enhance the accuracy rate of ASD diagnosis. The contribution is stated as a leaderboard position - 100% against 87%, 90% and 79% on the same public dataset - and attributed to preprocessing. There is no limitations section, no future work and no hedge of any kind.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Single-author retrospective analysis of the public Autism screening data for toddler dataset, in which the class label is defined explicitly as a Q-CHAT-10 score above 3. Neither the number of records, the class balance, nor any demographic characteristic is reported anywhere in the article.
narrative_rows.methods: A three-stage pipeline: Yeo-Johnson transformation to remove noise and artefacts, DeSEHO (Double Exponential Smoothing integrated into the Elk Herd Optimizer) for feature selection, and MEResNeXt (Moments Embedding Network combined with ResNeXt) for classification. Implementation in Python. The number and identity of selected features, the metaheuristic's search space and budget, and the learning rate, batch size and epoch count are not reported; the article instead specifies the MoNet sub-matrix square-root layer and its backward propagation across roughly forty numbered equations.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Accuracy 95.3%, sensitivity 96.5%, specificity 94.8%, taken from curves plotted against iteration count (20-80) and training percentage (70%, 80%); an intermediate value of 0.927 accuracy at 70% training data and iteration 20 is also reported.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The article states two model-level caveats and nothing else. There is no validation design to evaluate: no split, no cross-validation, no held-out set, no test-set size, and no statement of what data the reported metrics were computed on - the headline is read off the best region of a sweep. The sample size and class balance are never given, so no baseline exists. The label is a threshold on the sum of the Q-CHAT-10 items supplied as features, making the task checklist reconstruction. Yeo-Johnson, a variance-stabilising power transformation for continuous skewed variables, is applied to binary questionnaire responses on the stated ground of removing noise and artefacts. Two of the four metric definitions in the text are incorrect. Ethical approval and informed consent are both declared Not Applicable with no reasoning, and the author statements refer to co-authors and multiple authors in a single-authored paper.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This is the seventh charted study built on a Q-CHAT-10-derived label and the branch's most extreme case of contribution-by-nomenclature. Four acronyms are introduced (MEResNeXt, DeSEHO, and their components), roughly forty equations specify architecture internals borrowed from image-recognition papers, and the article never states how many children its 95.3% is computed over or on what data. Read against the branch's other members - 100% with all items retained (local_8253c2ec, local_a0d73248), a flawless 292 of 292 with pre-split SMOTE (local_ed30e24c), 0.99 with the mechanism mapped by feature-subset comparison (local_14df790d), 0.83 after deleting half the items (local_8ff20c48) - its 95.3% is uninterpretable in a specific way: the branch's accuracy is governed by how much of the label's own arithmetic survives feature selection, and this study performs an unreported metaheuristic selection of an unreported number of features. It also supplies the review's clearest instance of methodological detail being allocated inversely to methodological importance, and its Ethical approval: Not Applicable declaration sits with local_45ef7022's Not required and local_13c1f46d's Kaggle exemption at the permissive end of the corpus's ethics gradient.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] No participants, and no sample size of any kind. The article never states how many records the analysed dataset contains, how many are ASD-positive, or how many are negative - a gap that persists through a results section built entirely on performance curves. The data source is identified only as Autism screening data for toddler, the public Q-CHAT-10 collection. Since no split, test set or fold structure is described either, there is no point in the paper at which a reader can say how many observations any reported number rests on. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic individuals, individuals with ASD, patient, ASD patients. The register is medical and dated - autism is introduced as a neurological disease, individuals are described as needing the right treatment as soon as possible to recover their condition and diminish the disorder's effects. One passage is more sympathetic, noting that individuals with ASD have uniqueness and a few have incomparable ability in academics, music skills and visual. No autistic or community perspective appears. [RQ1.3] None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography, socioeconomic status or recruitment information, and no acknowledgement that any of it is missing. [RQ1.4] None, and the paper states the substitute rule explicitly: if the Q-CHAT-10 score is higher than 3 then the class value is allocated as YES which implies ASD traits potential; if not, NO is allocated. The outcome is therefore a threshold on the sum of the ten checklist items that also constitute the feature set - the seventh instance of this structure in the review, after local_8253c2ec, local_a0d73248, local_8ff20c48, local_ed30e24c, local_b9de0d7f and local_14df790d. No clinician, instrument administration or diagnostic criterion enters at any point. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is a hybrid deep-learning method for ASD detection in three stages: Yeo-Johnson transformation to remove noise and artefacts, DeSEHO (Double Exponential Smoothing integrated into the Elk Herd Optimizer) for feature selection, and MEResNeXt (Moments Embedding Network combined with ResNeXt) for classification. Headline findings: accuracy 95.3%, sensitivity 96.5%, specificity 94.8%, described as performing better than traditional models. [RQ2.2] No study setting. A downloaded dataset analysed in Python; no hardware, runtime or environment is described. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm - a caregiver checklist. The article does not reproduce or discuss a single Q-CHAT-10 item, so no behaviour is named anywhere in it. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. Ethical approval and informed consent are both declared Not Applicable, without reasoning - the paper does not invoke the public-data exemption that comparable studies at least state, and offers nothing in its place. A related reporting anomaly: the article has a single author, Saloni Rai, whose CRediT contribution is listed only as Data curation, yet the author statements read All authors have made substantial contributions to conception and design and the acknowledgements thank the co-authors of this manuscript for their valuable and constructive suggestions. [RQ2.5] No acquisition instrumentation. Implementation in Python with no library, version, seed or hardware. Method components: Yeo-Johnson transformation, the Elk Herd Optimizer with double exponential smoothing, the Moments Embedding Network and ResNeXt. [RQ2.6] Very low, in an unusually instructive way. The article devotes several pages and roughly forty numbered equations to the internals of the MoNet sub-matrix square-root layer, including its forward and backward propagation and the symmetrisation of matrix derivatives - a level of mathematical specification exceeding anything else in the charted corpus. It reports none of what would be needed to repeat the study: no sample size, no class balance, no split or cross-validation scheme, no test-set size, no metaheuristic search space or budget, no count or identity of selected features, no learning rate, batch size or epoch count in the running text, no seed, no code, and no dataset accession. The detail is concentrated entirely on the parts that are reproduced from prior architecture papers and absent from the parts that are specific to this experiment. [RQ2.7] Two sentences, both concerning the model rather than the study: the reliance on the Yeo-Johnson transformation for noise removal may not be sufficient for all types of data, and the complexity of the model may lead to overfitting, especially with smaller datasets. Notably, the article contains an extensive limitations apparatus pointed at other people's work - Table 1 tabulates the advantages and disadvantages of each prior study, and the related-work section names constraints for several of them - while none of that scrutiny reaches the circular label, the unreported sample size, the absent validation protocol or the Not Applicable ethics declaration. [RQ2.9] Enhance preprocessing techniques, improve the efficiency of feature selection, and ensure the model's adaptability across diverse datasets. The last is the only one that addresses a genuine gap, and it is stated without reference to any external dataset. [RQ3.1] Parent-reported early social-communication behaviour, entirely unspecified - the article names the Q-CHAT-10 instrument and describes its scoring rule but never states or discusses a single item, so no behaviour is identified anywhere in the paper. [RQ3.2] No fusion - a single questionnaire modality. The hybrid designation refers to combining two convolutional architectures over the same tabular input. [RQ4.1] MEResNeXt, combining the Moments Embedding Network with ResNeXt. Both are convolutional architectures designed for images: MoNet's contribution is a bilinear second-order moment embedding with a sub-matrix square-root layer developed for fine-grained visual recognition, and ResNeXt's is the aggregated residual transformation with cardinality developed for ImageNet classification. Applying them to a short tabular vector of binary questionnaire responses is never justified, and neither the spatial structure that motivates convolution nor the fine-grained texture statistics that motivate moment embedding exists in the data. [RQ4.2] A tabular vector of Q-CHAT-10 items and individual characteristics, Yeo-Johnson transformed and then reduced by the DeSEHO metaheuristic. Two observations. First, Yeo-Johnson is a variance-stabilising power transformation for continuous skewed variables; applying it to binary checklist responses to remove noise and artefacts, and justifying that choice at length against Box-Cox on the ground that it accommodates negative values, is a category error about the data. Second, the ten items are the summands of the score whose threshold defines the label, so whatever subset DeSEHO retains, the target remains an arithmetic function of the feature pool. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and F1, plotted against iteration count and training percentage. Two of the four definitions given in the text are wrong: accuracy is described as dividing the total number of instances by the number of correctly classified instances, which is the reciprocal of accuracy and would exceed 1; and specificity is described in words as dividing the total number of false positives and true negatives by the sum of both, which is identically 1. The accompanying equations for sensitivity and specificity are correct, so these are errors of exposition rather than of computation, but they appear in a section whose stated purpose is to define the evaluation measures. No confidence interval, no chance level and no class balance accompany any figure. [RQ4.4] None. The metaheuristic selects a feature subset and neither its size nor its membership is reported; no importance ranking, attribution or ablation appears; and no component of the three-stage pipeline is isolated. In a paper whose contribution is a specific combination of transformation, optimiser and architecture, no experiment shows that any of the three contributes anything. [RQ4.5] There is no validation design to assess. The article describes no train-test split, no cross-validation, no held-out set and no test-set size; it never states how many records the dataset contains or what its class balance is; and its results are presented as curves of accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and F1 against iteration count (20 to 80) and training percentage (70%, 80%), with the abstract's 95.3% / 96.5% / 94.8% taken from the best region of those curves. Reading performance off the maximum of a sweep is model selection on the reported quantity, and here there is not even a stated partition on which the sweep is evaluated. Underneath that sits the estimand: the label is a threshold on the sum of the ten Q-CHAT-10 items supplied as features, so the task is reconstruction of a checklist rule regardless of how the data are partitioned. The contrast with the rest of this branch is instructive. local_ed30e24c reached a flawless 292 of 292 with all items retained and pre-split SMOTE; local_14df790d reached 0.99 and mapped the mechanism through its feature-subset comparison; local_8ff20c48 fell to 0.83 after deleting five items. This study reports 95.3% after an unreported metaheuristic selection of an unreported number of features - a figure whose position in that range is determined by how much of the label's arithmetic the optimiser happened to retain, which the paper does not report and therefore cannot interpret. [RQ5.1] Autism spectrum disorder; Disease detection; Hybrid deep learning; Optimization algorithm. Four terms, three naming machinery in the most generic possible way; neither the instrument, the population, the modality nor the validation appears. [RQ5.2] Computational Biology and Chemistry 120:108619 (Elsevier), 2026 issue. A computational-biology venue, and the mismatch shows: a paper with no sample size, no validation protocol, no reported class balance, two incorrect metric definitions, image architectures applied to binary questionnaire responses, and author statements referring to co-authors of a single-authored manuscript. [RQ5.3] 2026 issue. Framing is early-detection and cost-saving: initial identification and treatment can diminish the need for wide examinations and expensive medical procedures, and prolonged effects and severity can be avoided at a timely determination of ASD. The contribution is expressed as architectural novelty - a named hybrid (MEResNeXt) built from two named components, fed by a named metaheuristic (DeSEHO) built from two further named components - with the accuracy figure as its warrant. It is the corpus's clearest example of method-naming as the unit of contribution: four new acronyms are introduced, forty equations specify borrowed architecture internals, and the number of children behind the result is never mentioned.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Cross-sectional three-group study in the UK: 31 autistic adults, 32 adults with Parkinson's disease and 31 controls, all with documented formal diagnoses in the clinical groups and exclusion of co-occurring movement or developmental disorders. Gender and non-verbal reasoning were matched across groups; both clinical groups were age-matched to controls though ASD and PD were not matched to each other. Trait, depression and anxiety measures and medication status are reported by group.
narrative_rows.methods: Participants completed a Shapes Tracing Task (clover, petals, ellipse, rounded square) and a Reaction Time Task with a stylus on a supplied Samsung Galaxy Tab A7 across two testing days, with PD participants tested before their first daily dopaminergic dose. Nine kinematic features per shape plus reaction time gave 37 input variables. Group differences were tested with linear mixed models including group, shape and their interaction, with Bayesian ANOVAs quantifying evidence for the null. KNN, random forest and linear SVM were then run on an 80/20 participant split across a grid of predictor configurations combining all or discriminatory kinematic features with three questionnaire sets. Data and scripts are on OSF.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Autistic participants differed from both PD and control groups in speed modulation and sub-movements, and from PD in reaction time. No kinematic feature was similar between ASD and PD while also differing from controls. Best mean test accuracy was 0.73 for clinical versus non-clinical and 0.93 for ASD versus PD, both from kinematics combined with both questionnaire sets; discriminatory kinematic features alone reached 0.80 under SVM for ASD versus PD. All models exceeded chance except two at 0.50. The ellipse was the least informative shape.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The authors name five: undiagnosed cases cannot be excluded by a diagnosis-based grouping; the PD and control participants come from a generation in which autism diagnoses were not prevalent, so undiagnosed autistic people may sit in the comparison groups; stylus resistance and the tablet's sampling rate and spatial resolution may have suppressed group differences; kinematic features are context-dependent and results may be task-specific; and the autistic sample was older than those in the existing literature. Two more are visible in the data. The classification test partitions hold roughly 13 participants for ASD versus PD and 19 for clinical versus non-clinical, so the 0.93 headline corresponds to about 12 of 13 correct with a confidence interval spanning roughly 0.66 to 1.00, and no interval is reported. And the discriminatory kinematic feature sets were selected using group-difference significance computed over all participants, so those configurations saw held-out labels during selection. Neither affects the study's primary negative finding.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This is the third study in the charted corpus below high risk of bias, and the only one whose headline result is a negative finding. Its central contribution is a direct test that the field had previously been unable to perform: autistic movement has been informally likened to parkinsonian movement, and because PD assessment is largely movement-based, that resemblance - if real - would generate false PD diagnoses in autistic adults. Running both clinical groups and controls through one protocol, the study finds no kinematic feature that is shared between ASD and PD while also differing from controls, and supports the null with Bayes factors rather than with absence of significance. It joins local_b6ac2b98 (ASD versus DLD at F1 0.63 against 0.86 for ASD versus TD) and local_cd7545e2 (ADOS-2 at AUC 0.562 against schizophrenia) as the review's differential-diagnosis calibration points, and with local_4da2b941 it defines the corpus's standard of methodological practice: participant-level splits, deposited data and scripts, versioned software, pre-specified interpretive thresholds, formal group matching, statistical control of confounders, complete ethics reporting, and a limitations section that reasons about cohort effects. Its methodological by-product - that the ellipse, the shape most commonly used in the drawing-task literature, is the least discriminative of four shapes - is a directly actionable finding for the movement branch.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Ninety-four adults in three groups: 31 autistic adults, 32 adults with Parkinson's disease and 31 controls. Both clinical groups required documentary evidence of a formal clinical diagnosis or came from research databases where such evidence had been verified, with mutual exclusion between the two conditions and exclusion of co-occurring movement or developmental disorders. Recruitment order is reported and is itself methodologically informative - the PD group was recruited first as an opportunity sample, autistic adults were then recruited to match it, and controls to match both. The analysis unit is the participant throughout, and the 80/20 classification split partitions people. What limits the classification estimates is size rather than structure: the ASD-versus-PD test partition contains roughly 13 people and the clinical-versus-non-clinical partition roughly 19. [RQ1.2] Autistic individuals, autistic adults, autistic movement, individuals with PD, control participants, non-autistic individuals. Identity-first language is used consistently and without hedging, movement differences are described as differences rather than deficits or abnormalities, and the framing throughout treats autistic movement as a characteristic to be measured rather than a pathology to be detected. The paper also cites the proposal that movement differences be added as specifiers to autism diagnoses - condition-relevant but non-selective - which is a precise and non-inflationary way of positioning the finding. [RQ1.3] The most complete adult-sample reporting in the corpus, with formal matching tests. Gender is matched across groups (chi-squared(4)=3.25, ns) and the autistic sample is close to sex-balanced at 14M/16F/1 other - a composition no other autism study in this review achieves. Age: ASD 55.52 (8.01), PD 63.16 (7.60), CTRL 59.00 (9.96); both clinical groups matched to controls but ASD and PD not matched to each other (p<0.001), which the authors handle by entering age as a control variable and residualising it from the classification inputs. Non-verbal reasoning (MaRs-IB) is matched. Depression and anxiety differ significantly and are controlled for. Years since diagnosis, psychoactive medication use, and UPDRS, RAADS and AQ trait scores are all reported by group with post-hoc comparisons. [RQ1.4] Clinically ascertained with documentation, and honestly bounded. Participants had to supply evidence of a formal clinical diagnosis such as a clinician's letter, or be drawn from databases where that evidence had been verified. The limitations section then names the two residual problems precisely: absence of a diagnosis does not exclude undiagnosed cases, and the PD and control participants belong to a generation in which autism diagnoses were not prevalent, so undiagnosed autistic people may sit in the comparison groups. That second observation is a genuine insight about ascertainment in older cohorts that appears nowhere else in this corpus. [RQ1.5] Comprehensive and instrument-based: UPDRS Part II for parkinsonian traits, RAADS and AQ for autistic traits, PHQ for depression, GAD for anxiety, MaRs-IB for non-verbal reasoning, and years since diagnosis. All are reported by group with ANOVA and post-hoc comparisons, and the ordering is as expected (autistic traits ASD>PD>CTRL; parkinsonian traits PD>ASD>CTRL). Crucially the trait instruments are used both as sample descriptors and, in some model configurations, as declared predictors alongside kinematics - so their role is explicit rather than hidden. [RQ2.1] Two aims, one confirmatory and one applied. First, to test directly whether autistic and parkinsonian movement resemble each other - a comparison previously possible only by juxtaposing separate studies with different designs and demographics. Second, to assess whether kinematic features can classify clinical versus non-clinical status and, within the clinical groups, ASD versus PD. Findings: autistic participants differed from both PD and controls in speed modulation and sub-movements, and from PD in reaction time; classification reached a best mean test accuracy of 0.73 for clinical versus non-clinical and 0.93 for ASD versus PD, in both cases from kinematics combined with questionnaires; and, most importantly, no kinematic feature was found to be similar between ASD and PD while also differing from controls. The anecdotal likeness between autistic and parkinsonian movement is not supported. [RQ2.2] Home-based testing on a supplied tablet over two days no more than three days apart, following an online screening form, questionnaire battery and reasoning task. The PD group completed the tasks before their first dopaminergic dose each morning. Home administration is presented as an advantage for scalability - the protocol could be run in community settings without laboratory kinematic equipment - and its cost is acknowledged in the limitations, where stylus resistance and the tablet's sampling and spatial resolution are named as possible suppressors of group differences. [RQ2.3] A Shapes Tracing Task with four shapes chosen to span the angular-frequency spectrum (clover, petals, ellipse, rounded square) plus a Reaction Time Task, both stylus-based.
