The shape design is deliberate and yields a methodological result the review should record: the ellipse was the least useful shape for distinguishing groups, and the authors point out that most drawing tasks in the literature index only elliptical or spiral movements, recommending that future studies span the full angular-frequency range. That is a concrete, actionable finding about task design derived from data. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional with two testing days; no longitudinal follow-up, which the authors identify as limiting their ability to know whether autistic participants later develop PD. Ethics reporting is complete: two Research Ethics Committee approval numbers (ERN_18-1800B and ERN_16-0281AP5), Declaration of Helsinki compliance, fully informed consent, and payment of GBP 10 per hour - remuneration being reported at all is uncommon in this corpus and is relevant to the ethics of research participation. [RQ2.5] Samsung Galaxy Tab A7 with a 10.4-inch 2000x1200 touchscreen and stylus; tasks programmed in PsychoPy and delivered via Pavlovia (PsychoJS 2021.1.4); MaRs-IB on Gorilla. Analysis in R Studio 2022.07.2 (matching), MATLAB 2022a with fitlme (mixed models) and JASP 0.17.2.1 (Bayesian analyses and classification). Every package is named with a version. [RQ2.6] The highest in the charted corpus alongside local_4da2b941. Data and analysis scripts are deposited on OSF; all software is named with versions; the device and its screen specification are given; the outlier rule is stated with the exact percentage removed for each of the nine features; the normalising transformations are listed per variable; the mixed-model formulae are written out including random-effect structure; the feature-selection rule is specified precisely, including how group-by-shape interactions were handled; and the full classification grid is published as a heat map rather than reduced to a headline. The only gaps are the composition of the individual 80/20 draws and whether JASP's parameter optimisation was nested inside the split. [RQ2.7] A genuinely analytical limitations section with five distinct items, each carrying a mechanism: diagnosis-based grouping cannot exclude undiagnosed cases; the PD and control groups come from a generation in which autism diagnoses were not prevalent, so undiagnosed autistic people may be present in them; stylus resistance and tablet sampling and spatial resolution may have suppressed group differences relative to motion tracking; kinematic features are context-dependent and the results may be task-specific; and the autistic sample was older than those in the existing kinematic literature, so apparent contradictions with prior findings may be age effects. Two further issues go unstated: the classification test partitions contain roughly 13 to 19 participants, and the discriminatory feature sets were selected using group-difference tests computed on all participants. [RQ2.9] Employ a range of shapes across the angular-frequency spectrum rather than only ellipses or spirals; investigate kinematic features for early screening in conjunction with clinical assessments; and separate clinically driven movement decline from normal ageing, a need the study itself establishes by demonstrating age effects on several kinematic features. [RQ3.1] Fine motor kinematics during constrained tracing: speed, acceleration, jerk, minimum and maximum speed, number of sub-movements, speed modulation (how sharply speed adapts to trajectory curvature), smoothness via SPARC, and tracing error, plus simple reaction time. The discriminating features are specific and directional - autistic participants showed greater speed modulation and more sub-movements than both other groups, and differed from PD in reaction time - and the paper is careful about mechanism, noting that reported increases in jerk in autism may be epiphenomenal on speed differences because the two quantities are mathematically linked. [RQ3.2] Genuine and declared multimodal fusion, and the study's most useful applied finding. Kinematic features and self-report questionnaire scores are combined in an explicit grid of predictor configurations - kinematics alone, questionnaires alone (ASD, PD, or both) and their combinations - and the combination outperforms either alone for both classification problems (0.73 clinical versus non-clinical; 0.93 ASD versus PD). Because the questionnaire sets are named and separated, the contribution of each modality is visible rather than buried, and the finding that both trait questionnaires together beat either individually is directly interpretable. [RQ4.1] Three standard classifiers - KNN, random forest and linear-kernel SVM - selected on the explicit ground that these three have been used together in comparably sized studies of parkinsonian movement. No deep learning and no novel architecture; results are reported for all three separately and as a mean, so no single algorithm's best run stands in for the finding. [RQ4.2] One row per participant. Thirty-seven kinematic input variables (nine features across four shapes plus one reaction time value), computed as residuals after controlling for age, depression and anxiety and averaged across trials and days; plus three questionnaire sets. A reduced discriminatory kinematic feature set was defined by retaining features, or feature-shape combinations, that showed significant group differences in the mixed models. That selection rule is stated precisely - including that a group-by-shape interaction yielding a difference on only one shape contributes only that shape's value - which is both good reporting and the point at which the design leaks, since the significance tests were computed over all participants including those later held out. [RQ4.3] Test accuracy per algorithm and averaged across the three, with the full grid published as a heat map colour-coded against chance and ordered by mean accuracy - so the reader sees every configuration, including the two that performed at chance, rather than only the maximum. For the group-difference analyses the reporting is fuller still: F statistics, p-values, beta estimates with 95% confidence intervals, and Bayes factors quantifying evidence for the null with interpretive bands stated in advance. What is absent is any interval on the classification accuracies, which matters because the test partitions hold roughly 13 to 19 participants; the 95% interval around the 0.93 headline spans approximately 0.66 to 1.00, and around 0.73 approximately 0.49 to 0.90. [RQ4.4] Substantive and directional. The study identifies which features discriminate (speed modulation, sub-movements, reaction time), in which direction, and between which pairs of groups; which task conditions are informative (the ellipse least so); and where an apparent effect may be an artefact of another (jerk as a possible epiphenomenon of speed). It also uses Bayesian analysis to distinguish absence of evidence from evidence of absence, reporting that low Bayes factors mean there is not strong evidence to conclude that movements were the same between groups where differences were not found - a distinction almost never drawn in this literature. [RQ4.5] The validation design is participant-level and honestly reported, with three qualifications that the review should record rather than treat as disqualifying. The structure is correct: an 80/20 split of participants, with test accuracy computed on held-out people and reported for each of three algorithms and as their mean, and with the entire configuration grid published so that the reported maximum sits visibly among its alternatives, including two models at chance. The qualifications are, first, size - 63 participants in the ASD-versus-PD contrast and 94 in clinical-versus-non-clinical give test partitions of roughly 13 and 19 people, so a 0.93 mean accuracy corresponds to about 12 of 13 correct and carries a confidence interval running from roughly 0.66 to 1.00; no interval is reported. Second, selection - the discriminatory kinematic feature sets were defined by group-difference significance from mixed models fitted on all participants, so configurations using those sets saw the held-out participants' labels during feature selection and are optimistically biased; the all-kinematic-features configurations are unaffected, and the paper's own observation that variability was seen in whether discriminatory or all features yielded stronger accuracy is consistent with the selection buying less than it might. Third, no external cohort, which the authors acknowledge by describing the work as proof-of-concept. Set against the corpus, what makes this study valuable is not its accuracy figure but its structure: the negative result is the primary finding, it is supported by Bayesian evidence for the null rather than by absence of significance, and the classification is offered as a secondary demonstration rather than as a diagnostic claim. [RQ5.1] Autism; Parkinson's disease; Movement; Classification. Four terms, both conditions named, the behavioural domain named, and the analytic task named - with no architecture, no algorithm and no accuracy language. [RQ5.2] Journal of Neurodevelopmental Disorders 18:8, a specialist neurodevelopmental journal, with a 180-day review - the longest among the charted 2026 studies. The disciplinary fit is visible throughout: formal group matching with equivalence tests, mixed models with appropriate random-effect structure, Bayesian evidence for the null, pre-specified interpretive thresholds, deposited data and scripts, complete ethics reporting including participant remuneration, and a limitations section that reasons about cohort effects in ascertainment. [RQ5.3] 2026, accepted 15 December 2025 after 180 days. The framing is unusual for this corpus in that its primary contribution is negative and clinically protective rather than a performance claim. The motivating concern is that PD assessments are primarily movement-based, so autistic people may score highly on PD diagnostic criteria because of autism-related movement differences - a differential-diagnosis risk that matters given rising PD diagnosis rates in autistic populations. The study then finds no kinematic similarity between autism and PD that is also distinct from controls, which addresses that concern directly. The classification work is labelled proof-of-concept, kinematics are proposed for use in conjunction with clinical assessments rather than instead of them, and the applied suggestion - that a tablet-and-stylus protocol could support community-scale assessment without laboratory equipment - is proportionate to what was demonstrated.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective analysis of four public ASD screening datasets from Kaggle and UCI, harmonised into 2,154 records and 15 unified attributes spanning toddlers, children, adolescents and adults, with stratified sampling by age group during merging. Per-cohort and per-class sample counts are not reported. Because no clinician-annotated severity labels exist in the source data - a gap the paper identifies as its motivation - severity labels were constructed as a weighted sum of the A1-A10 items normalised to [0,1] and cut into four ordinal strata (No ASD, Mild, Moderate, Severe) at 0.30, 0.55 and 0.75, with domain weights calibrated to maximise agreement with expert assessments on a sampled subset (Cohen's kappa 0.72, 95% CI 0.69-0.76).
narrative_rows.methods: After mode imputation (validated against median and kNN imputation, under 1.0% deviation), min-max normalisation, label encoding and correlation- plus SHAP-based feature pruning that removed ethnicity, country of residence, respondent type and prior app use, a bidirectional LSTM trained with a chaotic optimiser performed joint binary screening and four-class ordinal severity classification under stratified 10-fold cross-validation with early stopping and class weighting. Author-fitted baselines (SVM, random forest, logistic regression, MLP, unidirectional LSTM) were run under identical preprocessing and validation, and an ablation isolated each architectural component. Severity thresholds were perturbed by 5% and domain weights by 10% across the folds to test labelling stability.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Accuracy 99.10% (toddlers), 97.10% (children), 98.50% (adolescents), 98.10% (adults), with AUROC above 0.99 and a 3-6 point gain over the strongest baselines (SVM 0.911, logistic regression 0.902, random forest 0.928, MLP 0.944, unidirectional LSTM 0.932). Ablation: 0.932 to 0.956 to 0.968 to 0.985 to 0.987. Labelling stability: macro-F1 within 0.6% and kappa within 0.03 under threshold and weight perturbation.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The severity labels are a deterministic function of the model's own inputs, so the reported accuracies measure reconstruction of a scoring rule rather than diagnostic performance - a limitation the paper states itself, five times, and explicitly instructs the reader to apply. Three further issues are not stated. The domain weights defining the label were calibrated on the full dataset before cross-validation, so the target itself was fitted to the data the model is evaluated on. SHAP-based feature pruning requires a fitted model and was likewise performed on the whole dataset. And the expert calibration that provides the study's only external anchor reports kappa 0.72 without stating how many records were expert-labelled, by whom, or against what instrument. Beyond these: no class counts or per-cohort sample sizes are given, so no baseline can be computed; no confidence interval or across-fold variance accompanies any accuracy despite ten folds having been run; ethnicity and country were removed during preprocessing, foreclosing the fairness analysis the future-work section calls for; the optimiser's name is expanded two different ways; and the ablation credits SHAP with a 0.002 accuracy gain that a post-hoc explanation method cannot produce.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This is the eighth charted study built on a checklist-derived label and the only one in the corpus that identifies the circularity itself and bounds its claims accordingly. Its scope paragraph - because the severity labels are deterministically derived from the same behavioural attributes used as model inputs, the subsequent prediction task constitutes a structured function-approximation setting, and high classification performance should be interpreted as evidence of the model's ability to learn stable and interpretable behavioural scoring functions rather than as proof of clinical diagnostic accuracy - states in two sentences what this review had to reconstruct across seven other papers in the same branch. Read alongside them it also supplies a quantitative reading of the branch: a BiLSTM recovers a four-way threshold on a weighted item sum at 97-99%, and SVM, logistic regression and random forest recover it at 90-93%, so the architectural competition running through this literature is a competition to approximate a piecewise-linear function. It is the correct counterexample to local_ed30e24c (292 of 292 read as confirming clinical suitability), local_b9de0d7f (a numpy-generated teaching-method target offered to educators) and local_183eaef4 (accuracy 1.0000 defended by re-running the fold count), because it demonstrates that the problem in this branch has never been the modelling, and that a paper can do the same modelling and report it honestly.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] No participants were recruited. Four public screening datasets from Kaggle and UCI were harmonised into 2,154 records spanning toddlers, children, adolescents and adults, with stratified sampling by age group during merging to preserve cohort proportions. The analysis unit is the record and the cross-validation folds are stratified over records. What is missing is arithmetic: the per-cohort sample sizes, the class counts for the binary screening outcome and the counts for each of the four constructed severity strata are all absent, so the denominator behind every reported accuracy is unknown. The class distribution is characterised only qualitatively, as closely mirroring population-level screening statistics reported in prior paediatric ASD studies. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, participants, developmental cohorts, severity strata. The register is technical and notably free of pathologising language for this corpus; severity is described in terms of DSM-5 functional-support levels rather than as degrees of impairment, and the paper avoids the diagnostic vocabulary its results cannot support. No autistic or community perspective appears. [RQ1.3] Almost none, and by deliberate removal. Age is retained as a continuous normalised feature and cohort membership is preserved through stratified merging, but ethnicity, country of residence, who completed the test and whether the app had been used before were all excluded during feature pruning as low-variance, irrelevant or metadata noise, on the stated ground of eliminating demographic skew. Sex is not reported anywhere. The consequence is that no subgroup analysis by sex, ethnicity or respondent type is possible, and the fairness across populations named in the future-work section cannot be assessed in the present study - the variables required for it were removed. [RQ1.4] None, and the paper is explicit rather than silent about this. The abstract states that reliable severity stratification remains challenging due to the absence of explicit clinician-annotated severity labels; the methods then construct severity labels from the A1-A10 items themselves; and the scope paragraph states that because the severity labels are deterministically derived from the same behavioural attributes used as model inputs, the subsequent prediction task constitutes a structured function-approximation setting. The one external anchor is the weight calibration, in which domain weights were optimised to maximise agreement with independent expert assessments on a randomly sampled subset, achieving Cohen's kappa 0.72 (95% CI 0.69-0.76) - and the paper immediately qualifies this as supporting the internal consistency of the labeling heuristic while not implying external diagnostic validity. Neither the number of expert-labelled records, the identity or qualification of the experts, nor the instrument they used is reported. [RQ1.5] Constructed, not measured. The four ordinal strata are cut points on a weighted sum of A1-A10 normalised to [0,1]: No ASD below 0.30, Mild 0.30-0.55, Moderate 0.55-0.75, Severe at or above 0.75, with the boundaries said to align with DSM-5 functional-support descriptors and percentile interpretations from the Q-CHAT and ADOS-2 literature. No validated severity instrument was administered to anyone. The paper's own framing of this as a controlled behavioural labeling paradigm rather than as severity assessment is accurate and is what distinguishes it from local_b9de0d7f, which generated a six-way teaching-method label from a Q-CHAT total using numpy and then offered the resulting accuracy to educators as a basis for decisions. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is a single-stage framework performing joint screening-level ASD identification and four-level ordinal severity stratification, under an explicitly controlled labelling paradigm, with a bidirectional LSTM as representation learner and a chaotic optimiser for training stability. Headline findings: accuracy 99.10% for toddlers, 97.10% children, 98.50% adolescents and 98.10% adults with AUROC above 0.99, a 3-6 point gain over the authors' own baselines (SVM 0.911, logistic regression 0.902, random forest 0.928, MLP 0.944, unidirectional LSTM 0.932). The framing of these results is the study's distinguishing feature: they are presented as evidence of the model's effectiveness in approximating a deterministic behavioural severity-scoring function rather than independent clinical diagnostic performance. [RQ2.2] No study setting. Public datasets harmonised and analysed computationally; no environment, hardware or runtime is described. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm - screening checklists completed by caregivers or self-report. The paper offers a substantive argument for its architecture choice that deserves recording: although the A1-A10 items are collected in a static format, their ordering is said to be non-arbitrary, with each question progressively evaluating social reciprocity, which is why a bidirectional sequence model is applied. The argument is stated but not tested - no experiment permutes item order to see whether the claimed sequential structure carries any signal. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. Ethical approval and consent to participate are both declared not applicable, with the reasoning stated in full: no direct experimentation with human participants, and all analyses conducted on publicly available, fully anonymised, open-access de-identified datasets from Kaggle and UCI. The declaration is at least reasoned rather than blank. What it does not address is whether the original respondents consented to research reuse - the same gap present across this branch. [RQ2.5] No instrumentation. Analytical components: BiLSTM, a chaotic optimiser (expanded inconsistently as Chaotic Grey Ball Optimizer in the abstract and Chaotic Gradient-Based Optimizer in the methods), SHAP, and standard preprocessing. No software, version, seed or hardware is named in the extracted text. [RQ2.6] Moderate, and unusually strong on the parts that matter most for this branch. The labelling function is specified completely - the weighted index, its normalisation, the four threshold boundaries and the calibration objective - so another group could reconstruct the target variable, which is not true of any comparable study in this review. Three separate sensitivity analyses are reported with quantified deviations: imputation method (mode versus median versus kNN, under 1.0% deviation in macro-F1 and accuracy), severity thresholds perturbed by 5% and domain weights by 10% (macro-F1 within 0.6%, kappa within 0.03). The ablation table isolates each architectural component. Against this: no code, seed, software, versions, layer configuration, learning rate, batch size or epoch count; no per-cohort or per-class sample counts; and the harmonised dataset promised only post-publication. [RQ2.7] This is the study's defining characteristic and the reason it matters to the review. The scope restriction is not confined to a closing limitations paragraph but is stated in the abstract, the contributions list, the labelling section, the training section and the results discussion. Its clearest formulation is in section 3.3: because the severity labels are deterministically derived from the same behavioural attributes used as model inputs, the subsequent prediction task constitutes a structured function-approximation setting; accordingly, high classification performance should be interpreted as evidence of the proposed model's ability to learn stable and interpretable behavioural scoring functions, rather than as proof of clinical diagnostic accuracy. It further states that the labelling kappa supports internal consistency while not implying external diagnostic validity, that SHAP results carry no causal or diagnostic attribution, that performance gains are methodological improvements rather than evidence of clinical diagnostic superiority, and that the datasets are behaviourally constrained. What remains unstated: that the domain weights were calibrated on the full dataset before cross-validation, that SHAP-based feature pruning requires a fitted model and was likewise performed on the full data, that no class counts are reported, and that the ablation credits SHAP with a 0.002 accuracy gain when SHAP is a post-hoc explanation method that cannot alter a model's predictions. [RQ2.9] External validation against independently clinician-annotated severity datasets - named as necessary rather than desirable - plus multimodal fusion (prosody, eye-gaze dynamics), federated learning validation, and prospective clinical trials to enhance sensitivity and ensure fairness across populations. The first directly addresses the study's own stated boundary; the fairness objective is undercut by the removal of ethnicity and country of residence during preprocessing. [RQ3.1] Screening-item behaviours from the A1-A10 instruments, organised into three domains - social communication difficulties, repetitive behaviour and a cognitive assessment component - which supply the weighted terms of the constructed severity index. The correlation analysis relates the composite Q_SCORE to social communication difficulties (r 0.64-0.67) and repetitive behaviour (r 0.45-0.63) and reports moderate inter-item correlations (r 0.10-0.46), read as each item adding unique variance. [RQ3.2] No fusion - a single questionnaire modality. What the study does perform is dataset harmonisation across four age cohorts into a common 15-attribute schema with stratified merging, which is cross-cohort integration rather than multimodal fusion. Multimodal extension with prosody and gaze is named as future work, and the absence of such cues is acknowledged as a constraint of the current data. [RQ4.1] A bidirectional LSTM as a high-capacity representation learner over static questionnaire attributes, trained with a chaotic optimiser that applies controlled chaotic perturbations to diversify gradient updates, described as an alternative to deterministic optimisers such as Adam or RMSProp. Baselines fitted by the authors under identical preprocessing and validation: SVM, random forest, logistic regression, MLP and unidirectional LSTM. The ablation reports a clean monotone progression from 0.932 to 0.987. [RQ4.2] A 15-attribute harmonised row per participant after pruning, with continuous variables min-max normalised and categorical fields label-encoded. The predictor set contains the A1-A10 items and the composite Q_SCORE; the target is a four-level discretisation of a weighted sum of those same A1-A10 items. The label is therefore an arithmetic function of the inputs by construction, and the paper says so. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUROC per cohort and per ablation variant; per-class AUROC curves across the four severity levels and four age groups; Cohen's kappa with a confidence interval for label-expert agreement; and quantified stability under three separate perturbation analyses. The metric set is broad and the sensitivity reporting is a genuine strength. Two gaps. No confidence interval or across-fold variance accompanies any classification accuracy, despite ten folds having been run and despite intervals being reported for the kappa. And no class counts are given for either the binary or the four-level target, so no baseline exists against which a 99.10% can be positioned - which matters particularly for a four-class ordinal problem whose stratum boundaries the authors chose. [RQ4.4] SHAP is applied with its scope explicitly bounded, and the bounding is the point: the contributions list describes it as methodologically bounded explainability, applied to analyse feature utilisation and model consistency without asserting independent clinical causality. That is the correct use of the method under a constructed label, and it is unique in this corpus - the six other Q-CHAT-labelled studies charted here all read their SHAP or feature-importance output as clinical corroboration. Two problems remain. SHAP was also used upstream, as a feature-pruning criterion, which requires a fitted model and was performed on the full dataset before cross-validation. And the ablation table lists BiLSTM + CGBO + SHAP at accuracy 0.987 against BiLSTM + CGBO at 0.985, attributing a 0.002 gain to the addition of SHAP - which is not possible, since a post-hoc explanation method computes attributions for an already-trained model and cannot change its predictions. [RQ4.5] The evaluation is stratified 10-fold cross-validation at the record level with early stopping and class weighting, supported by three quantified sensitivity analyses - imputation method, severity thresholds perturbed by 5%, domain weights perturbed by 10% - showing macro-F1 stable within 0.6% and kappa within 0.03. That is more robustness checking than any other study in this branch performs. But the estimand is settled before any of it, and the paper states the conclusion itself: the severity labels are deterministically derived from the same behavioural attributes used as model inputs, so the task is function approximation and the accuracy figures are not diagnostic accuracy. Read that way, the results are internally coherent and even informative - a BiLSTM recovers a four-way threshold on a weighted sum of ten items with 97-99% accuracy, and simpler models recover it with 90-94%, which quantifies how much architectural capacity the reconstruction of a piecewise-linear scoring rule requires. Three residual issues qualify even that reading. The domain weights were calibrated on the full dataset by optimising kappa against expert labels before cross-validation, so the labelling function itself was fitted to the data the model is then evaluated on. SHAP-based feature pruning was likewise applied to the whole dataset and necessarily requires a fitted model. And the expert calibration - the only external anchor in the study - reports kappa 0.72 without stating how many records were expert-labelled, by whom, or with what instrument, so the one bridge between the constructed label and clinical severity is itself unspecified. Compared against the branch, the difference is not in the estimand but in the interpretation: local_ed30e24c reported 292 of 292 correct as confirming suitability for reliable clinical screening; local_b9de0d7f offered a numpy-generated teaching-method label at 0.9917 to educators; this study reports 99.10% and states in four separate places that it does not mean what it appears to mean. [RQ5.1] Not captured in the extracted text. [RQ5.2] Discover Applied Sciences 8(4):363 (Springer) - an open-access multidisciplinary applied-sciences journal. The venue is not clinical, yet the paper is the most careful in the branch about the boundary between computational and clinical claims, which suggests the discipline of the authors rather than of the reviewers is doing the work here. [RQ5.3] 2026. The framing is the study's principal contribution to this review. Where the rest of the questionnaire branch presents reconstruction of a checklist threshold as diagnostic accuracy, this paper presents the same task as what it is - approximation of a deterministic behavioural scoring function - and repeats that restriction in the abstract, the contributions, the methods, the results and the conclusion. It describes its own labelling as a heuristic with internal consistency but no external diagnostic validity, bounds its SHAP interpretation against causal claims, calls external validation against clinician-annotated data necessary rather than desirable, and requires human oversight for any deployment. The overreach that remains is modest and confined to the discussion, which speaks of diagnostic precision and of stratifying ASD into four functional levels, and to the clinical-integration proposal for electronic health records and e-learning platforms. It is the only study in the branch whose stated conclusions a reader could act on safely.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: A proposed algorithmic framework (MUXAI-ASDBD) evaluated in what the article repeatedly calls simulation across named developmental screening datasets (ASQ, CSBS, PEDS, M-CHAT, STAT) and imaging modalities (MRI, EEG), with code and data cited to a GitHub repository. The sample description is internally contradictory: 10,000 MRI samples in one sentence, 25,000 positive and 1,200 negative cases described as class-balanced in the next, 500 subjects in the CSBS description, and study-population ages given as 0-36 months, 12-36 months and 3-6 years in three separate passages.
narrative_rows.methods: Each modality is split into non-overlapping partitions (six in the methodology, four in the parameter table), each processed by a CNN (ResNet-50 or InceptionV3, 224x224 input, Adam at 0.003, batch 64, 150 epochs, binary cross-entropy), with features aggregated per modality and fused for a softmax classifier. A machine-unlearning mechanism at the summation layer supports subject-level deletion, with an audit protocol requiring the unlearned model to be statistically indistinguishable from one retrained without the deleted subject. The stated evaluation is a 70/15/15 subject-level split with Youden-index thresholding, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, AUC and calibration, paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and an MRI-only ablation.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Maximum diagnostic accuracy of 98%, a 23% reduction in overall error rate, reduced false positives and reduced processing time; unlearning and retraining times of 3.2 s and 5.6 s per partition. None of the named clinical metrics is reported as a number, no confusion matrix appears, and the presented results are bar charts of error rate, false-positive count and precision binned into low, medium and high before and after unlearning.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The two stated limitations concern dataset availability and unlearning overhead. The substantive problems are elsewhere. The sample description contradicts itself - 25,000 positive cases from a 10,000-sample dataset, a 21-to-1 ratio called class balance - and the study population's age is given three incompatible ways in a paper whose entire claim is to address a gap in newborns specifically. No diagnostic label ascertainment is described for any dataset. The evaluation protocol is described in exemplary detail and reports no value from any of its named metrics, while the headline 98% has no denominator and, under the stated class ratio, would sit 2.6 points above a majority-class baseline. Ethics and consent are declared unnecessary because no hospital deployment occurred, and the same passage states the datasets were fully identified. Cybersecurity vocabulary about malicious and fraudulent events survives in the results section, as does a sentence from the response to reviewers.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This study contributes two things to the review, one substantive and one diagnostic. The substantive contribution is its motivating argument, which no other charted study makes: that once a newborn's data enters a training set, most systems have no mechanism to remove its influence if parents withdraw consent, and that this is an obligation under GDPR and HIPAA rather than a courtesy - a point that bears directly on the fourteen studies in this corpus built on web-scraped children's photographs and on the several that waive consent because a dataset is public. The diagnostic contribution is the gap between that framing and the work: the paper obtains no ethical review or consent for its own use of newborn data, reports no value from any of the clinical metrics it names, and contradicts itself about how many children it studied and how old they were. It sits alongside local_e771fb69, which built a federated privacy framework with no ethics statement and evaluated it on nine test cases, as the review's two instances of privacy and governance machinery standing in for research governance.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] No participants and no coherent sample. The methods state within four consecutive sentences that the study utilised MRI datasets of newborns comprising 10,000 samples and that the final dataset included 25,000 positive cases and 1200 negative cases, with class balance maintained. Both claims cannot hold: 25,000 positives cannot come from 10,000 samples, and a ratio of nearly 21 to 1 is not balance. Elsewhere the CSBS description reports 500 subjects, and Table 4, labelled Standard dataset, lists the same identifier range 01-1000 five times over with different family relationships (son, daughter, niece) and a different algorithm name in each row, so it is a results table presented as a data description. No consistent count of children exists anywhere in the article. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, newborns, newborn babies, infants, children, brain disabilities, brain disorder. Autism is grouped throughout with brain disabilities and brain disorders as a single detection target, and the abstract describes ASD as a rising disorder in the brain among newborns. No autistic or community perspective appears. A distinct register intrudes in the results, where false positives are explained as occurring when the system flags safe/normal data as malicious or abnormal, and precision is explained in terms of how likely a nominated event is to be true when the model declares it malicious, fraudulent, or different from the expected behaviour - vocabulary from cybersecurity or fraud detection that has been carried into a paper about newborns. [RQ1.3] None. No sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic or geographic information for any dataset. Age is reported three incompatible ways: newborns aged 0 to 36 months in the title and abstract, children aged 12-36 months in the MRI inclusion criteria, and aged 3-6 years in the CSBS description. Since the paper's central claim is that existing tools are restricted to toddlers above 18 months and that it addresses the gap in newborns, the age of the analysed population is the single most consequential fact in the study and it is stated three different ways. [RQ1.4] None. No diagnostic instrument administration, criterion, assessor or record is described for any dataset. The named sources - ASQ, CSBS, PEDS, M-CHAT and STAT - are developmental screening instruments, not diagnoses, and the paper does not describe how any label was assigned. One results passage categorises outcomes as yes (Y), random (R) - indicating a 50% probability of yes and a 50% probability of no - and not detected (N), which introduces a coin-flip category into what is presented as a diagnostic output. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is a machine-unlearning-integrated explainable AI framework for early ASD and brain-disability detection in newborns, motivated by a genuinely important argument: once a newborn's data is used in training, most models provide no mechanism to remove it if parents withdraw consent, which raises ethical and legal problems under GDPR and HIPAA. Headline findings: a 23% reduction in error rates, reduced false positives, accuracy improved to 98%, and reduced processing time. The results are described as simulation results. [RQ2.2] No study setting. Datasets are said to have been processed in different computing laboratories; a testbed with 32 GB RAM and 2 TB storage is named for timing measurements. The paper states that the work involved no hospital deployments while also claiming, in its contributions list, past experience implementing the system in clinical settings and that the framework can effectively validate itself in real-world clinical implementations. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. Developmental screening instruments and archived imaging. The most concrete behavioural description concerns CSBS items on communication via eye movements (straight, upward, leftward, downward) and repetitive hand and finger movements, recorded as binary responses over 30-second monitoring windows. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. Ethics and consent are declared unnecessary on the stated ground that the work involved no hospital deployments, and the same passage claims that the datasets were fully identified and processed with strict subject-level partitioning, with fully authorised controlled access, audit logging and standard encryption. Fully identified is the opposite of de-identified and appears in a sentence listing privacy safeguards, so it is presumably an error - but it is the operative word in the article's only statement about the identifiability of newborn data. The irony is structural rather than incidental: the paper's entire motivation is that models must be able to forget a newborn's data when parents withdraw consent, and it obtains no consent and no ethical review for its own use of that data. [RQ2.5] No acquisition instrumentation. Model components: ResNet-50 (50 layers) or InceptionV3 (48 layers) at 224x224 input, Adam at learning rate 0.003 (described as increasing), batch size 64, 150 epochs, binary cross-entropy; unlearning and retraining times of 3.2 s and 5.6 s per partition; an inter-modality correlation threshold of 0.65. A testbed with 32 GB RAM and 2 TB storage is named. [RQ2.6] The article makes strong reproducibility claims - a public GitHub repository for both code and data, frozen configuration files, and an explicit statement that the entire pipeline can be replicated end-to-end - and simultaneously makes reproduction impossible by contradicting itself about what was run. The partition count is six in the methodology and four in the parameter table; the sample is 10,000 MRI scans and also 25,000 positives plus 1,200 negatives; the age band is 0-36 months, 12-36 months and 3-6 years in three places; the modality set is MRI, video, audio, text and EEG in one section and MRI, video and text in another. Feature vectors are printed as illustrative example values rather than as results. A sentence from the revision process also survives in the published text, reporting that figures are revised with corrected captions, algorithm numbering is standardized, and placeholder references are replaced with accurate citations. [RQ2.7] Two sentences, both about deployment: the framework depends on the availability and quality of multimodal datasets, which may vary across clinical settings, and repeated unlearning operations can incur overhead at scale. Neither addresses the evidence. Unmentioned: the contradictory sample sizes, the three different age ranges, the absence of any diagnostic label description, the absence of any numeric result table for the headline accuracy, the majority-class baseline implied by the reported class ratio, and the fact that the experiments are described as simulations. [RQ2.9] Not separately developed beyond the deployment limitations. The paper closes on the claim that the framework improved interpretability and diagnostic reliability. [RQ3.1] Developmental screening behaviours as captured by ASQ, CSBS, PEDS, M-CHAT and STAT items - communication through eye movements and repetitive hand and finger movements are the only behaviours described concretely - together with imaging and physiological modalities named but not characterised. [RQ3.2] Multimodal fusion is the framework's structural claim: each modality is partitioned, processed by per-partition CNNs, aggregated into a modality representation, and fused into a single feature vector for a softmax classifier. The claim cannot be evaluated. The modality set differs between sections (MRI, video, audio, text and EEG versus MRI, video and text); no dataset is characterised well enough to know what any modality contains; the fused feature vectors are printed as illustrative example numbers; and no ablation isolates any modality's contribution except a reference to an MRI-only ablation whose results are not shown in the extracted text. [RQ4.1] MUXAI-ASDBD, described as a partitioning-based explainable CNN framework with layer-wise explainability and a machine-unlearning mechanism at the summation layer, using ResNet-50 or InceptionV3 as per-partition feature extractors. Baselines named are CNN, GNN, ACNN, SVM, LSTM and a proposed FCNN-LSTM - a list that does not match the framework the paper is proposing, since the title framework is a partitioned CNN and the proposed baseline is a fully connected LSTM. [RQ4.2] 224x224 images for the CNN backbones; the representation of questionnaire data is never specified, which matters because five of the seven named datasets are questionnaires and a 224x224 convolutional backbone cannot consume a checklist without a stated encoding. Aggregated feature vectors appear in the text as literal illustrative values such as [0.5, 0.6, ..., 0.8] and [0.45, 0.55, ..., 0.75]. [RQ4.3] The named metric set is clinically appropriate and unusually complete for this corpus - sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, ROC AUC and calibration, with thresholds set by the Youden index and significance assessed by paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. None of it is reported. No sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, AUC or calibration value appears in the extracted text, no test statistic or p-value is given, and the phrase all reported with 95 to 98% confidence intervals conflates a confidence level with an interval width. What is actually presented is bar charts of error rate, false-positive count and precision binned into low, medium and high before and after unlearning, plus a headline accuracy of 98% and a 23% error reduction with no denominator. If the stated class ratio of 25,000 positives to 1,200 negatives held, the majority-class baseline would be 95.4% and the headline would be 2.6 points above it. [RQ4.4] Layer-wise explainability is the framework's named contribution and no explainability result is presented. Modality-specific outputs are described in a single sentence as gradient spectrogram features for audio and spatiotemporal attention maps for video, each demonstrating interpretability in a clinically meaningful context, with no figure, attribution or quantitative measure to support the claim in the extracted text. [RQ4.5] The validation section contains, in isolation, the most methodologically literate paragraph of any weak study in this review: a 70/15/15 partition with strict subject-level separation to avoid leakage across folds, stratified sampling to preserve class distribution, Youden-index thresholding on validation data, clinically meaningful metrics including PPV and NPV and calibration, paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, ablation of the MRI-only modality, runtime measurement with means and standard deviations, and a subject-level deletion threat model under which the unlearned model should remain statistically indistinguishable from one retrained without the deleted data, audited by removing specified subjects and validating forgetting against deletion audit sets. Every element of that is the right thing to do. None of it can be assessed, because the article does not report a single number from any of it and because the data description it would apply to is self-contradicting - 10,000 MRI samples yielding 25,000 positive cases, a 25,000-to-1,200 split called class balance, six partitions in one section and four in another, three mutually exclusive age ranges. The experiments are moreover described throughout as simulation results, and the only quantitative outputs shown are before-and-after bar charts binned into low, medium and high. The gap between the methodological vocabulary and the reported evidence is the finding here: this is the corpus's clearest instance of validation language functioning as a genre convention rather than as a description of work performed. [RQ5.1] Autism spectrum disorder; Newborn babies; Machine un-learning; Convolutional neural network; Explainable artificial intelligence. Five terms; the population claim (newborn babies) is the one the article's own data description contradicts three times. [RQ5.2] Alexandria Engineering Journal 145 (2026) 164-181 (Elsevier) - a general engineering journal. Review did not surface a sample description in which 25,000 positive cases are drawn from 10,000 samples and a 21-to-1 ratio is called balanced, three incompatible age ranges for the study population, partition counts differing between sections, a named metric set none of whose values are reported, cybersecurity vocabulary about malicious and fraudulent events in a paper about infants, or a surviving response-to-reviewers sentence in the body text. [RQ5.3] 2026. The framing rests on a genuinely important and under-addressed problem: that once a newborn's data enters a training set there is usually no mechanism to remove it when parents withdraw consent, and that this is a live obligation under GDPR and HIPAA. That argument is correct and is made nowhere else in this corpus. What follows it does not support any of the claims made from it - accuracy improved to 98%, error rates reduced by 23%, false positives reduced, and a framework said to be able to validate itself in real-world clinical implementations and to be implementable in hospital settings. The study reports no confusion matrix, no metric values from its own named metric set, no consistent sample size and no ethics approval, in a paper whose organising principle is the ethical handling of newborns' data.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective analysis of the Self-Stimulatory Behaviour Dataset: 75 YouTube videos of roughly 90 seconds each, uploaded by parents and caretakers of autistic children and annotated by the dataset's originators for the start and finish of each behaviour episode. Frames were extracted with OpenCV, cropped by region-of-interest detection and augmented. The number of distinct children is never reported; the k-fold confusion matrix covers 303 samples. All four target classes - arm flapping, head banging, spinning and normal behaviour - come from videos of autistic children, so there is no non-autistic comparison group.
narrative_rows.methods: A custom CNN-GRU was trained to classify the four behaviour categories, with GRU chosen over LSTM for simpler gating and greater stability under repeated k-fold retraining. VGG16, MobileNet, EfficientNet-B7 and 3D-CNN+LSTM were trained on the same data under identical hyperparameters for comparison. Evaluation used k-fold cross-validation with per-fold means and standard deviations, plus a separate held-out test with its own confusion matrix, and paired t-tests against each baseline at a corrected threshold of 0.0125.
narrative_rows.outcomes: CNN-GRU k-fold accuracy 0.9294 +/- 0.0038 (validation accuracy 0.96, loss 0.16; precision 0.96, recall 0.95-0.96, F1 0.96), against MobileNet 0.9193, 3D-CNN+LSTM 0.8912 and EfficientNet-B7 0.8808, with all four paired comparisons significant. Per class, arm flapping and head banging reached F1 0.98 while spinning and normal behaviour reached 0.94 and 0.93; errors concentrated between spinning and the repetitive classes.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The folds are formed over clips extracted from only 75 videos with no video-level or child-level grouping, so clips sharing a child, room, camera and clothing appear on both sides of every fold - and the per-fold standard deviations below 0.004, presented as evidence of robustness, are better read as evidence that the folds contain much the same material. The number of distinct children is unreported, as are per-class counts and the value of k, so neither the effective sample size nor the chance level can be established. Most fundamentally, the task performed is four-way movement classification within a dataset containing only autistic children, which cannot support the screening and diagnostic claims made in the title and abstract; the paper's own statement that the system is a clinical decision support system and not an independent diagnostic system is the accurate description. There is no ethics or consent statement for the reuse of identifiable children's home videos, whose parent-posted provenance the paper describes explicitly, and a detailed limitations column is applied to eleven prior studies while none is applied to this one.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This study occupies a distinctive position in the review. Its data are the most ecologically valid in the entire corpus - spontaneous self-stimulatory behaviour recorded by families in children's own homes, annotated for when it occurs, with no laboratory, stimulus or instruction - and its comparative design is among the better controlled, with five architectures trained under identical hyperparameters, per-fold standard deviations for every model and paired significance tests at a corrected threshold. It nonetheless repeats the corpus's dominant failure in the video modality, splitting at the clip level over 75 recordings, and it makes the review's clearest category error of a different kind: a within-population behaviour-recognition result presented as ASD screening, when the dataset contains no non-autistic person at all. Read alongside local_b6ac2b98 and local_69b10fe4, which both defined their comparison groups explicitly, it shows that the presence or absence of a meaningful contrast group is a separate axis from validation design, and that a study can be careful about architecture comparison while being silent about what its classes actually contrast. Its ethics silence is also the corpus's sharpest, because the paper itself states that the videos were posted by parents and caretakers on publicly accessible websites and then does not ask whether that constitutes consent to machine learning reuse.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] No participants and no groups. The data are 75 YouTube videos of approximately 90 seconds each from the Self-Stimulatory Behaviour Dataset, uploaded by parents and caretakers, segmented into frame clips by behaviour type using the dataset's original annotations. The number of distinct children is never stated - a consequential omission, since 75 videos may represent fewer than 75 children and the k-fold confusion matrix reports 303 samples, so the analysis unit is the clip. Crucially there is no non-autistic comparison group: all four classes, including normal Behavior, are drawn from videos of autistic children, so the study is a behaviour-recognition problem within one population rather than a diagnostic contrast between populations. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic children, ASD children, ASD youngsters, abnormal Behavioral patterns, stereotypical Behaviors, normal Behavior. The stereotyped/normal opposition is applied to movements rather than to children, which is the more defensible usage, but the framing describes self-stimulatory behaviours as abnormal throughout and the fourth class as normal. No autistic or community perspective appears, and there is no discussion of self-stimulatory behaviour as regulatory rather than pathological. [RQ1.3] None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography or setting information for any child. The videos are consumer home recordings of unknown provenance, and the paper does not report even the age range of the children whose behaviour it classifies. [RQ1.4] None, and not required by the task as executed - but required by the task as described. The videos are annotated for when a behaviour occurs, not for whether the child has a diagnosis; no clinical assessment, instrument or assessor exists for anyone in the dataset. The paper's title nonetheless places the work in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder and its abstract states that the approach facilitates quick, accurate and effective screening of ASD. Those claims do not follow from a four-way discrimination among arm flapping, head banging, spinning and other movement in videos of children who are all autistic. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to classify four behaviour categories - arm flapping, spinning, head banging and normal behaviour - from naturalistic, unstructured video, using a CNN-GRU architecture, in order to help clinicians monitor behavioural trends. Headline findings: CNN-GRU reaches k-fold accuracy 0.9294 +/- 0.0038 and validation accuracy 0.96, outperforming MobileNet (0.9193), 3D-CNN+LSTM (0.8912), EfficientNet-B7 (0.8808) and VGG16, with paired t-tests significant against all four at a corrected threshold of 0.0125. Per class, the two clearly distinct repetitive behaviours (arm flapping, head banging) reach F1 0.98 while spinning and normal behaviour reach 0.94 and 0.93. [RQ2.2] No study setting - the defining property of the data is precisely that there is none. The videos are unstructured home recordings made by families in everyday environments, which is the source of both the design's principal strength (ecological validity, behaviours observed rather than reported) and its principal uncontrolled variance (camera, framing, lighting, distance and activity all vary by video and are perfectly confounded with the child). [RQ2.3] No imposed task. Naturalistic recordings of children engaged in everyday activities, with behaviour episodes delimited by the SSBD annotations of start and finish times. This is the most ecologically valid data source in the charted corpus - no laboratory, no stimulus, no instruction, and behaviours that occurred spontaneously in the child's own environment. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. There is no ethics statement, consent statement or exemption claim anywhere in the article. The omission is more pointed than in the questionnaire studies because the paper itself describes the data's provenance: parents and caretakers posted their videos on websites that are accessible to the public, and the dataset consists of URLs to 75 YouTube videos of identifiable autistic children. Whether a parent posting a home video to YouTube thereby consents to its use as machine learning training data is exactly the question the study needed to address and does not raise. [RQ2.5] No controlled acquisition equipment - the recordings are consumer video of unknown origin. Python OpenCV was used for frame extraction. Region-of-interest detection and cropping were applied to remove background objects, which is the appropriate response to uncontrolled framing. No deep learning framework, version, seed or hardware is named. [RQ2.6] Mixed, with real strengths on the comparative design. Reproducible: the source dataset is public and correctly attributed to its originators, the preprocessing chain is described in order, all five architectures were deliberately trained under identical hyperparameters to make the comparison fair, per-fold standard deviations are reported for every model and metric, and paired t-tests with a corrected significance threshold of 0.0125 are tabulated. Not reproducible: the value of k, the number of frames or clips extracted, the number of distinct children, per-class sample counts, the unit at which folds were formed, the learning rate, batch size and epoch count, any seed, and any code or data-availability statement. [RQ2.7] The paper announces that it will discuss its weaknesses, and the only self-directed remarks concern the data - that SSBD is the sole freely available dataset of its kind, that it is somewhat helpful but does not fully meet the study's conditions, and that no existing dataset does. Against that, a full column of Table 1 assigns a specific limitation to each of eleven prior studies (did not describe the pre-processing and model development steps; need to improve results; implemented a basic CNN model that performs binary classification and was tested on a small dataset). Unmentioned for this study: that folds are formed over clips from 75 videos with no video-level or child-level grouping; that the number of distinct children is unknown; that there is no non-autistic comparison group behind a screening claim; that no ethics statement accompanies the reuse of identifiable children's home videos; and that per-class counts and the chance level are unreported. [RQ2.9] Announced in the paper's structure but not developed in the extracted text. [RQ3.1] Self-stimulatory motor behaviour observed in natural settings: arm flapping, head banging and spinning, against a fourth class of non-stereotyped movement. This is the corpus's clearest instance of behaviour being observed directly rather than inferred from a photograph, a checklist or a questionnaire - the behaviours are the ones clinicians actually watch for, recorded where they actually occur. The confusion-matrix analysis adds a substantive behavioural observation: errors concentrate between spinning and the two repetitive classes, attributed to overlap in motion dynamics, and normal behaviour is moderately confused with the repetitive classes in the held-out test. [RQ3.2] No fusion - video only. The CNN-GRU combination is spatial-plus-temporal modelling within one modality, and the architectural rationale is stated properly: convolutional layers extract spatial features from single frames while autism-related behaviour is a temporal phenomenon requiring sequence modelling across frames. That is a correct justification for a recurrent component, unlike the several studies in this corpus that apply LSTMs to single static inputs. [RQ4.1] A custom CNN-GRU hybrid, with GRU selected over LSTM on the stated grounds of simpler gating, fewer parameters, greater training stability and less overfitting under repeated k-fold retraining. Four comparators - VGG16, MobileNet, EfficientNet-B7 and 3D-CNN+LSTM - were fitted by the authors on the same data under identical hyperparameters, which makes this one of the few architecture comparisons in the corpus that is actually controlled. [RQ4.2] Cropped frame sequences from annotated behaviour segments, after region-of-interest detection to remove irrelevant background and augmentation to reduce overfitting. The ROI step is well motivated for uncontrolled home video, where background and framing differ systematically between recordings. [RQ4.3] Validation accuracy and loss, precision, recall and F1 per architecture; per-fold means with standard deviations for every model and metric; per-class F1; two confusion matrices; learning curves; and paired t-tests with a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of 0.0125. The statistical reporting is among the better examples in this corpus - the standard deviations are given rather than implied, and the multiple-comparison correction is stated explicitly. What is missing bears directly on interpretation: per-class sample counts are not reported, so the 25% chance level for a four-class problem cannot be checked against the actual class balance; the value of k is never given; and the very small per-fold standard deviations (under 0.004 across five architectures) are read as evidence that the model is robust and consistent across the folds when, over clips drawn from only 75 videos, near-identical fold results are equally consistent with folds that are near-identical resamples of the same recordings. [RQ4.4] No model interpretability, but a genuine and clinically sensible error analysis. Spinning is confused with the repetitive classes because of overlapping motion dynamics, and normal behaviour is confused with the repetitive classes in the independent test set - both of which are the errors one would predict from the physics of the behaviours, and both of which point at the harder discrimination (is this movement stereotyped or not?) rather than the easier one (is this flapping or banging?). [RQ4.5] The evaluation is better constructed than most in this corpus and still cannot support the claim the title makes. On the credit side: k-fold cross-validation with per-fold standard deviations reported for all five architectures, an independent test evaluation with its own confusion matrix, identical hyperparameters across models to make the comparison fair, and paired t-tests against every baseline at a corrected threshold. On the debit side, three things. First, the unit: 75 source videos are segmented into clips and the k-fold matrix covers 303 samples, with no video-level or child-level grouping described, so clips from the same recording - same child, same room, same camera, same clothing - fall on both sides of every fold. In naturalistic video this is the strongest available shortcut, because recording identity is far easier to learn than movement type. Second, the reported stability is read backwards: standard deviations below 0.004 across five different architectures are presented as robustness, whereas over clips from 75 videos they indicate that the folds contain much the same material. Third, and separately from any of this, the task is not the task claimed. Four-way discrimination among arm flapping, head banging, spinning and other movement, in videos of children who are all autistic, cannot yield screening for ASD, because no non-autistic person appears anywhere in the data - a screening claim requires a comparison the design does not contain. The paper's own hedge, that the system is intended as a clinical decision support system and not an independent diagnostic system, is the correct reading and sits uneasily beside a title placing the work in diagnoses of ASD and an abstract promising effective screening. [RQ5.1] Autism Spectrum Disorder; Behavior analysis; CNN-GRU; deep learning; naturalistic video. Five terms, and naturalistic video is the one that matters - it names the study's genuine distinguishing property in a corpus dominated by downloaded photographs and checklists. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience 20:1626315, with a 174-day review including a substantial revision. The review did not surface the absent ethics statement for reuse of identifiable children's home videos, the unreported number of distinct children, the absence of a non-autistic comparison behind a screening claim, or the reading of near-zero fold variance as robustness. [RQ5.3] 2026, published 18 March, 174 days from submission with one revision round. The framing is internally split. The objectives section states that the system should be used as a clinical decision support system and not an independent diagnostic system - an accurate and unusually explicit limit. The title, abstract and conclusion pull the other way, placing the work in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder, claiming it facilitates the quick, accurate, and effective screening of ASD, and asserting tremendous potential for real-world clinical implementation. What the study actually demonstrates is that a CNN-GRU distinguishes four movement categories in home video at about 93% under a clip-level split, which is a behaviour-recognition result and a useful one; the screening language is added on top of it.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Secondary analysis of the Spanish BeGaze eye-tracking corpus: 45 children aged roughly 5-8 years, comprising 19 with an ASD diagnosis made externally by neuropaediatricians or clinical psychologists before inclusion and 26 typically developing children. Group characteristics are tabulated - age 75.9 versus 78.1 months, SCQ 12.6 versus 4.7, KBIT-2 108.78 versus 104.3, PPVT-III 50.0 versus 67.3 - and the corpus's ethics approval (Ethics Committee of the Universitat de Valencia, Declaration of Helsinki, guardian informed consent) is reported.
narrative_rows.methods: Children watched a professional storyteller narrating short stories with the face visible, then answered comprehension questions. Six stories were presented, three audio-only and three audio-visual, counterbalanced across participants, with each instance segmented into pre-speech, speech and post-speech phases. Eighteen temporal gaze features were computed over eyes, mouth and nose areas of interest. Six interpretable classifiers were evaluated under five-fold nested cross-validation with participant-independent splits, per-fold class balancing, inner-loop grid search and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, against a per-fold majority-class baseline. Feature importance and SHAP were computed on each fold's test set and averaged.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Best performance 64.1% F1 and 64.5% AUC (logistic regression, audio-visual speech phase), with roughly 55% F1 in the speech phase across both modalities and all models exceeding the majority-class lower bound. Audio-visual stimuli significantly outperformed audio-only in the pre-speech phase but not during or after speech. Per-story means were 57.7 (SD 9.8) audio-only and 64.1 (SD 9.1) audio-visual, with no consistent clustering by narrative content. Feature importance and SHAP converged on mouth fixation time and cross-AOI revisits as the leading discriminators.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The authors state three - a small sample for specific modality/phase pairings limiting generalisation and increasing overfitting risk, the context-specific storytelling task potentially not transferring, and predefined AOIs and fixed intervals limiting granularity - plus separate treatments of the Castilian/Valencian bilingual confound and of clinical viability. The one substantive omission is that the ASD group's receptive vocabulary is markedly lower and is not adjusted for in a task requiring comprehension of narrated stories, so part of the gaze difference may reflect comprehension rather than social attention. No external cohort is tested, and the sample of 45 children means several modality comparisons could not reach significance, which the paper notes each time.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This is the fourth charted study below high risk of bias and the corpus's clearest calibration point for the eye-tracking branch. Its validation design is the most complete in the review - nested five-fold cross-validation with participant-independent splits, inner-loop hyperparameter selection, per-fold class balancing, bootstrap confidence intervals on every estimate, and a per-fold majority-class baseline built in specifically to test whether the gaze features beat class distribution. Under those conditions, with clinician-made diagnoses and a purpose-designed social-attention paradigm, the best result is 64.1% F1 and 64.5% AUC. That figure should be set against the eye-tracking studies charted elsewhere in this review reporting 99.78% (local_7432ffd7, sample-level splits with CARS in the feature set), 100% (local_44d3aef5, 55 scanpath images from a repeated-image collection) and 97% (local_bb4d1f7a, 100 eye crops per child): the difference between them and this study is not the modality, the algorithm or the year, but whether the same child can appear on both sides of the split. It also joins local_b6ac2b98 and local_69b10fe4 in the group of studies that manipulate their stimulus systematically rather than presenting one fixed condition, and its finding that the audio-visual advantage is concentrated before speech onset is a behavioural result rather than a benchmark entry.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Forty-five Spanish children from the BeGaze corpus: 19 with an ASD diagnosis made externally by neuropaediatricians or clinical psychologists before inclusion, and 26 typically developing children, focused on the 5-8 year preschool-to-primary transition. Each child contributed multiple samples - one per story, under two modality conditions and segmented into three temporal phases - and the cross-validation folds are explicitly participant-independent, so the multiplication of samples per child does not leak across the split. This is the correct handling of a repeated-measures design and it is rare in this corpus. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, typically developing children, TYP. The register is measured and clinical without pathologising; gaze differences are framed as attentional and perceptual patterns and as potential biomarkers rather than as deficits, and the comparison group is typically developing throughout. One inherited phrase from the literature review describes eye tracking as quantifying social attention deficits. There is no autistic or community perspective, but nothing in the language overstates. [RQ1.3] Well reported for the variables collected. Group sizes, mean ages with standard deviations, SCQ, KBIT-2 nonverbal intelligence and PPVT-III receptive vocabulary are all tabulated by group, and the pattern is described accurately: nonverbal intelligence comparable across groups (104.3 versus 108.78) while the ASD group shows higher SCQ (12.6 versus 4.7) and markedly lower receptive vocabulary (50.0 versus 67.3). Sex is not reported. Two features deserve note for interpretation. The ASD group's age variability is more than double the comparison group's (SD 19.4 versus 8.8 months), and the receptive-vocabulary gap is large and not adjusted for in the models - in a task whose stimulus is a narrated story, receptive vocabulary is a plausible driver of where a child looks. The paper does address linguistic background separately, devoting a discussion section to the Castilian/Valencian bilingual environment of the recordings. [RQ1.4] Independent and clinician-made: diagnostic classification was conducted externally by qualified specialists (neuropaediatricians or clinical psychologists) prior to inclusion in the corpus, with the SCQ administered separately as a symptomatology measure. The label therefore predates and is unrelated to the gaze data - the property that separates this study from the checklist-threshold and folder-label branches of this review. [RQ1.5] SCQ for autism symptomatology, KBIT-2 for nonverbal intelligence and PPVT-III for receptive vocabulary, all administered by the research team using Spanish-adapted standardised instruments and reported by group with standard deviations. No ADOS or calibrated severity score. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to investigate eye-tracking-based ASD detection during audio-visual storytelling using traditional but explainable machine learning, and to identify which gaze features and which phases of speech carry discriminative information. Headline findings: best performance 64.1% F1 and 64.5% AUC (logistic regression, audio-visual speech phase); around 55% F1 in the speech phase across both modalities; a statistically significant advantage for audio-visual over audio-only stimuli in the pre-speech phase but not during or after speech; and convergent feature-importance and SHAP evidence that mouth fixation time and revisits across facial areas of interest are the most informative features. The abstract states in its second-to-last sentence that performance remains modest. [RQ2.2] The BeGaze corpus was collected in a Spanish research setting with children viewing pre-recorded storytelling clips on screen with AOIs defined over the narrator's face. The bilingual Castilian/Valencian environment of the recorded participants is treated as a methodological factor in its own right rather than left unmentioned. [RQ2.3] A well-designed and unusually informative paradigm. Children watched a professional storyteller narrating short children's stories with the face clearly visible, then answered comprehension questions. Six stories were used, three audio-only and three audio-visual, counterbalanced across participants, and each instance was segmented into pre-speech, speech and post-speech phases. This yields a factorial design in which modality and temporal phase can be varied independently, and it is the only study in the charted corpus that manipulates the stimulus systematically rather than presenting a single fixed stimulus set. The paper also notes what it did not control - that the data were not stratified by story content - and then tests that concern directly in a per-story analysis. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. Ethics reporting is complete for the corpus: approval by the Ethics Committee of the Universitat de Valencia, conduct in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and informed consent from the legal guardians of all participants. Funding is fully itemised across six grants. [RQ2.5] Screen-based eye tracking with predefined AOIs over eyes, nose and mouth; the device model is not named, which is the study's one notable acquisition-reporting gap. Analysis used Scikit-learn, XGBoost and PyTorch on an Intel i7 desktop with 16 GB RAM and no GPU, a configuration the authors highlight deliberately as evidence that the pipeline is deployable without specialised hardware. [RQ2.6] High. The corpus is cited to its source with its ethics approval; participant characteristics are tabulated with standard deviations on four measures; the 18 features are enumerated by area of interest; the factorial design is described in full including story counterbalancing; the grid-search space is published for every algorithm; the nested cross-validation, participant independence, per-fold class balancing and bootstrap interval procedure are all specified; the software stack is named; and per-story and per-condition results are tabulated with variability. Missing: the eye-tracking device, a code or data availability statement, and the number of instances contributing to each modality/phase cell. [RQ2.7] A dedicated limitations section naming three constraints - small sample for specific modality/phase pairings limiting generalisation and increasing overfitting risk; the context-specific storytelling task potentially not transferring to other situations; and predefined AOIs and fixed time intervals limiting analytic granularity - plus a separate section on cultural and linguistic constraints addressing the Castilian/Valencian bilingual environment, and a further section (7.3) that positions the work explicitly against clinical viability benchmarks. The self-assessment is distributed through the discussion rather than confined to a closing paragraph, and it is accurate. The one limitation not raised is the substantial receptive-vocabulary difference between groups, which is measured, reported, and then not adjusted for in a task built on comprehending narrated stories. [RQ2.9] Sequential models that exploit the temporal structure of AOI fixations rather than aggregating them into summary features; larger cross-linguistic cohorts to assess bilingual exposure; and cost-benefit analysis of false positives to define what performance threshold would count as meaningful in low-stakes screening. The last of these is a form of future work no other study in this review proposes - defining the target rather than raising the number. [RQ3.1] Social attention to a speaking face, decomposed by facial region and by time relative to speech onset: fixation count, average fixation duration, dwell-time and fixation-time percentages, normalised dwell coverage and revisits, for the eyes, mouth and nose separately. The substantive behavioural findings are specific and testable - eye revisits and mouth fixation count rank highest in importance, mouth fixation time and cross-AOI revisits emerge as candidate biomarkers under both attribution methods, and the audio-visual advantage is concentrated in the pre-speech phase, which the authors read as anticipatory attention to the mouth before speech begins. [RQ3.2] Modality is manipulated experimentally rather than fused computationally, which is a different and arguably more informative use of the term. By presenting the same storytelling task audio-only and audio-visually and comparing gaze features across the two, the study isolates what the visual speech channel contributes to group discrimination - and finds that it contributes most before speech onset. That is a designed contrast producing an interpretable answer, in contrast to the corpus's several studies that concatenate modalities and report only the combined figure. [RQ4.1] Six classical interpretable classifiers - SVM (linear kernel only, chosen deliberately to preserve interpretability), logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost and a shallow MLP among them - selected explicitly because the study prioritises explainability over capacity.
