SVM was most consistent across conditions; logistic regression gave the single best result. No deep sequence model is used, and the authors give the reason: the corpus is small and the features are lightweight. [RQ4.2] Eighteen AOI-based temporal gaze features per experimental instance, where an instance is one participant viewing one story under one modality in one speech phase. No clinical instrument score, demographic variable or diagnostic measure enters the feature set - the SCQ, KBIT-2 and PPVT-III are reported as sample characteristics and kept out of the model. [RQ4.3] Macro F1 and AUC, chosen explicitly because the data are small and imbalanced, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on every estimate; per-condition, per-phase and per-story breakdowns with standard deviations; paired t-tests between modalities within each phase with full statistics; and - critically - a per-fold majority-class baseline built into the design as a lower bound to test whether the gaze features add anything beyond class distribution. That last element is present in only one other charted study. The reported numbers are correspondingly modest and are described as such: about 55% F1 in the speech phase, 64.1% F1 and 64.5% AUC at best, with the paper noting where differences fail to reach significance and attributing that to the limited number of observations. [RQ4.4] Two attribution methods - model feature importance and SHAP - applied convergently, and computed on each cross-validation fold's test set before averaging, which is the correct placement and is stated explicitly. The result is a ranked feature list dominated by eye revisits, mouth fixation count and mouth fixation-time percentage, interpreted against existing cognitive literature on social attention rather than presented as a novel discovery. The authors also note honestly where interpretation fails: for features beyond the leading ones no clear pattern emerged, which they attribute to the modest performance of the classifiers rather than explaining away. [RQ4.5] This is the most rigorously validated study in the charted corpus, and its result is the corpus's most useful single number. The design is five-fold nested cross-validation with participant-independent splits, class balance preserved within folds, hyperparameter selection confined to the inner loop, retraining on the full training portion before a single outer-fold evaluation, bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on every estimate, and a per-fold majority-class baseline included specifically to test whether the features beat class distribution. Each child contributes multiple samples across stories, modalities and phases, and the participant-independent split is what prevents that from becoming the leakage that inflates most of this literature. The outcome is 64.1% F1 and 64.5% AUC at best and around 55% in most conditions - and the authors state plainly that this positions the work as a research exploration rather than a deployable diagnostic tool, given that benchmarks for clinical viability often exceed 80-90%. Two qualifications remain. The sample is 45 children, and the paper repeatedly notes that the limited number of observations prevents modality differences from reaching significance. And the ASD group's receptive vocabulary is markedly lower (PPVT-III 50.0 versus 67.3), which is measured and reported but not adjusted for in a task requiring comprehension of narrated stories - so part of the gaze difference may be a comprehension difference. Neither qualification changes the study's value to this review, which is calibrative: run with correct participant-level nesting, an explicit trivial baseline, confidence intervals and a purpose-designed social-attention paradigm, eye-tracking classification of autism in children reaches the low sixties. [RQ5.1] Autism spectrum disorder; Early identification in children; Eye-tracking; Audio-visual speech comprehension; Explainable Artificial Intelligence. Five terms covering condition, application, modality, task and method, with the task - audio-visual speech comprehension - named specifically rather than generically. [RQ5.2] Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 10(3), Article ETRA012, the ETRA eye-tracking venue. The disciplinary fit shows in the reporting: participant-independent nested cross-validation, bootstrap intervals, a majority-class lower bound, paired significance testing between conditions, fold-level attribution computation, and an explicit comparison of the achieved performance against published clinical-viability thresholds. [RQ5.3] 2026 (May). The framing is the most disciplined in the review. The abstract concedes in its own body that performance remains modest; the results section opens by observing that the modest overall performances underscore the inherent challenges of detecting ASD from gaze-based features in data-scarce naturalistic settings; and section 7.3 states that roughly 64% F1/AUC positions the work as a research exploration rather than a deployable diagnostic tool, given benchmarks for clinical viability often exceed 80-90%. Value is claimed only for preliminary screening as a complement to human judgement, and the proposed future work includes defining, by cost-benefit analysis, what performance threshold would count as meaningful for low-stakes screening. Set beside the studies in this corpus reporting 99% and 100% from checklist thresholds and web-scraped photographs, its contribution is not a method but a demonstration of what the honest number looks like.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Two datasets analysed under a common ensemble pipeline. Dataset 1 is the public 1,985-record ASD Children Traits collection with 28 attributes - including the Autism Spectrum Quotient, Social Responsiveness Scale, Q-CHAT score and Childhood Autism Rating Scale - and a binary ASD-traits target, with 729 positive (36.72%) and 1,256 negative (63.28%) instances and 283 records carrying missing values. Dataset 2 consists of 100 original clinical samples augmented fourfold to 400, evenly distributed across four severity categories (Mild, Moderate, Severe, Very Severe) with no non-ASD class, and with 4,220 features spanning facial images, voice, motion and physiological signals. No source, citation, country or institution is given for Dataset 2.
narrative_rows.methods: A published algorithm specifies label encoding, z-score normalisation, correlation filtering above 0.90, a stratified 60:20:20 split, conditional SMOTE applied only to the training partition when the class ratio falls below 0.8, and ANOVA F-test feature selection. Five base learners (RF, XGBoost, GB, SVM, LR) plus soft-voting and stacking ensembles and two neural networks were trained, with SHAP and LIME applied to Dataset 1 only. Dataset 2 used a stratified 80/10/10 split and 5-fold stratified cross-validation over the augmented set of 400.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Dataset 1: regularised neural network 97.60% (ROC-AUC 0.998), voting 96.90%, SVM/LR/stacking 96.10%, RF and GB 94.50%, XGBoost 93.70%; logistic regression reports recall 100.00% with ROC-AUC 1.000. Dataset 2: 98.2%. Ablation on Dataset 1 rises from 89.40% (no feature selection, no resampling) to 97.60% through feature selection, SMOTE, ensemble fusion and neural-network regularisation.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The paper states none. Dataset 1's predictor set contains four instruments used to determine autism status - AQ, SRS, Q-CHAT and CARS - alongside the autism-traits label, the same structure that produced accuracy 1.0000 for local_183eaef4 on the identical collection. Its 63.28% majority-class baseline is computable from the paper's own table and never stated. Dataset 2 is unsourced: no citation, country, institution or ethics committee accompanies its 100 clinical samples, and its 80/10/10 split and cross-validation were applied after fourfold augmentation, so transformed copies of the same sample fall on both sides and the 40-sample test partition faces 4,220 features. Dataset 2 also contains no non-ASD class, making its 98.2% a four-class severity result presented in the abstract alongside a binary detection figure. SHAP and LIME are applied only to Dataset 1, omitting the multimodal case where modality attribution would have been informative; precision, recall and F1 are omitted for both neural-network rows; and no confidence interval accompanies any value.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This study is the second charted analysis of the 1,985-record ASD Children Traits dataset, and reading it against local_183eaef4 is instructive: the same collection, the same four embedded instruments, and accuracies of 97.60% here against 1.0000 there, with the difference produced by preprocessing rather than by anything about the data. It also supplies the class balance (63.28% negative) that local_183eaef4 omitted, allowing that study's perfect result to be positioned for the first time. Its own distinctive contributions to the review run in opposite directions. On the positive side it is one of the few studies in this branch to state explicitly that SMOTE was applied only on the training set, preventing data leakage - the exact ordering error that invalidated local_ed30e24c's hold-out - and to publish its whole pipeline as a numbered algorithm. On the negative side, Dataset 2 is the corpus's clearest case of augmentation-crossing-the-split combined with an unsourced dataset: 100 clinical samples of unstated origin inflated to 400, partitioned after augmentation, evaluated on 40 rows against 4,220 features, with an IRB and consent claim that names no committee, institution or country.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two datasets with very different standing. Dataset 1 is 1,985 instances with 28 attributes from public ASD screening databases - the same 1,985-record ASD Children Traits collection analysed by local_183eaef4 - and here, unlike there, its class balance is reported: 729 ASD-positive (36.72%) against 1,256 negative (63.28%), with 283 instances carrying missing values. Dataset 2 consists of 100 original clinical samples augmented fourfold to 400, distributed evenly across four severity categories with no non-ASD class at all, and with no source, citation, country or institution given for the original 100. The number of distinct children behind either dataset is never stated. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, ASD traits. The register is clinical and unremarkable; the framing is service-oriented, opening on the need for clinicians to trust AI tools and closing on healthcare trustworthiness. One sentence in the introduction overreaches in a way worth recording - that machine learning algorithms assess the likelihood of a child being diagnosed with autism from behavioural information, making them a suitable replacement for routine and expensive screening tests. No autistic or community perspective appears. [RQ1.3] Thin for Dataset 1 and absent for Dataset 2. Dataset 1 lists age, sex, ethnicity, jaundice and family history among its features and reports none of their distributions; seven comorbidity indicators are similarly listed as features with no prevalences. Dataset 2 reports no demographic information of any kind for its 100 clinical samples, despite claiming IRB approval and caregiver consent for their collection. [RQ1.4] None for either dataset. Dataset 1's target is a binary ASD-traits field with no diagnostic procedure described, and the dataset's own feature list includes the Autism Spectrum Quotient, Social Responsiveness Scale, Q-CHAT score and Childhood Autism Rating Scale - four instruments used to determine autism status, supplied as predictors of it. This is the same instrument-inclusion leakage documented in local_183eaef4, which used the same 1,985-record dataset and reached accuracy 1.0000. Dataset 2's four severity categories are asserted with no instrument named; clinical experts are said to have verified annotation consistency at Cohen's kappa 0.92, but what they were rating and against what standard is not stated. [RQ1.5] Dataset 1 carries AQ, SRS, Q-CHAT and CARS as features rather than as reported participant characteristics - no mean, range or class-wise distribution appears for any of them. Dataset 2's severity categories are the prediction target with no underlying measure described. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is an ensemble framework that is both accurate and interpretable enough for clinicians to trust, evaluated on a behavioural dataset and a multimodal one. Headline findings: 97.6% accuracy on behavioural data from a regularised neural network (ROC-AUC 0.998) and 98.2% on multimodal data, with all other models above 93%; and an ablation showing accuracy rising from 89.40% (no feature selection, no resampling) through feature selection, SMOTE and ensemble fusion to 97.60% with neural-network regularisation. [RQ2.2] No setting is described for either dataset. Dataset 1 is a public download; Dataset 2's 100 original clinical samples have no stated collection site, country, institution or period, which is difficult to reconcile with the claim that an Institutional Review Board granted approval for their collection. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm for either dataset. Dataset 2's modality descriptions imply that facial images, 10-30 second voice recordings, body-keypoint motion and wearable physiological signals were captured simultaneously with synchronisation errors below 100 ms, which requires a structured session protocol - none is described. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. Ethics is claimed only for Dataset 2, in a short paragraph stating that all participant data were anonymised, written consent was obtained from caregivers, and IRB approval was granted for data collection and analysis, with secure storage, encryption and restricted access. No committee, protocol number, institution or country accompanies any of this, and no ethics statement covers Dataset 1 at all. Given that Dataset 2 is otherwise entirely unsourced, the ethics paragraph is the only evidence offered that its 100 clinical samples exist as described. [RQ2.5] For Dataset 2, vision-based pose estimation and wearable sensors are named without models; ResNet50, VGG16 and MobileNetV2 supply image features at 224x224 with ImageNet normalisation; audio features include MFCC, spectral, temporal, rhythmic and voice-quality measures such as jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio. No software, version, seed or compute environment is given anywhere. [RQ2.6] Sharply divided between the two datasets. Dataset 1's pipeline is one of the better-documented in this branch: the whole sequence is published as a numbered algorithm specifying label encoding, z-score normalisation, the 0.90 correlation-filtering threshold and its retention rule, the 60:20:20 stratified split, the exact SMOTE trigger condition (minority-to-majority ratio below 0.8) with the interpolation formula, the ANOVA F-score expression, and the SHAP and LIME definitions - and the dataset's instance count, feature count, missing-value count and class balance are all tabulated. Dataset 2 is unreproducible in principle: no source, citation, country, institution, ethics committee, participant description or access route exists for the 100 original samples, and its characteristics are conveyed entirely through asserted quality figures (complete data availability, synchronisation below 100 ms, inter-rater kappa 0.92). Neither dataset is accompanied by code, seeds, base-learner hyperparameters or a stated fold count. [RQ2.7] No limitations section appears in the extracted text. A comparison table instead assigns a named limitation to each of roughly fifteen prior studies (few participants, results may not apply widely; tested only in lab settings, not in daily life situations; works best only on similar data, not tested in real-world settings). None of that scrutiny is turned inward. Unmentioned: that four autism instruments sit in Dataset 1's feature set alongside the autism label; that Dataset 2's split partitions augmented copies rather than original samples; that Dataset 2's test partition holds 40 samples against 4,220 features; that Dataset 2 contains no non-ASD class, so its 98.2% is four-class severity rather than detection; that the 63.28% majority-class baseline on Dataset 1 is never stated; and that Dataset 2 has no provenance. [RQ2.9] Not captured in the extracted text. [RQ3.1] Dataset 1: screening-questionnaire responses and comorbidity flags, none of them examined individually. Dataset 2: the most behaviourally specific description in the paper - velocity, acceleration, jerk, movement range, coordination and repetitive behavioural patterns from body keypoints, alongside voice quality and autonomic arousal - describing exactly the kind of multimodal behavioural measurement this literature needs, for a dataset whose existence the paper does not evidence. [RQ3.2] Dataset 2 is presented as genuine four-modality fusion - image, audio, motion and physiological features concatenated into a 4,220-dimensional vector - and the ablation attributes the final gain from 97.80% to 98.2% to multimodal integration. Three things make that uninterpretable. There are 4,220 features for 400 samples, of which only 100 are original. The 400 include augmented copies split across training and test, so the multimodal gain is measured on partly duplicated data. And no modality-level attribution is reported: SHAP and LIME are applied to Dataset 1 only, so the paper cannot say what any modality contributed. A 0.4-point accuracy gain on a 40-sample test set is a single case reclassified. [RQ4.1] Five base learners (random forest, XGBoost, gradient boosting, SVM, logistic regression), soft-voting and stacking ensembles with a logistic-regression meta-learner, and two neural networks - a regularised MLP with L2, batch normalisation and dropout, and a deeper variant with early stopping and adaptive learning-rate scheduling. Predictions are combined by ensemble weighting proportional to validation performance. [RQ4.2] Dataset 1: a reduced tabular vector after correlation filtering above 0.90 and ANOVA F-test selection, drawn from 28 attributes that include the AQ, SRS, Q-CHAT and CARS scores alongside the ASD-traits target. Dataset 2: a 4,220-dimensional concatenation dominated by 4,040 image features, against 400 samples - a ratio of more than ten features per sample, and more than forty per original clinical sample. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC for eight configurations on Dataset 1, plus accuracy and F1 for six ablation configurations on both datasets. Three problems. Precision, recall and F1 are omitted for both neural-network rows, so the two models carrying the headline figures are reported on accuracy and AUC alone. No confidence interval or cross-validation variance accompanies any value. And the reported logistic-regression row - recall 100.00%, precision 87.20%, ROC-AUC 1.000 - is the signature of a model that separates the classes perfectly on the test partition, which on a dataset containing four autism instruments as features is expected rather than notable, and which the paper reads as displaying more false-positive tendencies. The 63.28% majority-class baseline is computable from the paper's own table and is never stated. [RQ4.4] SHAP and LIME are applied, and applied only to Dataset 1 - a choice the abstract states plainly. The consequence is that the paper's interpretability contribution covers the dataset where the answer is predetermined by the presence of AQ, SRS, Q-CHAT and CARS among the features, and omits the dataset where attribution would have been genuinely informative, namely which of four fused modalities carries the signal. No SHAP or LIME output is described in the extracted text. [RQ4.5] The two datasets require separate verdicts. On Dataset 1 the pipeline ordering is right and is unusually well documented: a stratified 60:20:20 split precedes SMOTE, SMOTE is applied only to the training portion and only when the class ratio falls below 0.8, and the paper states this explicitly as preventing data leakage - the ordering that local_ed30e24c got wrong and that most of this branch does not discuss. What the ordering cannot repair is the feature set, which contains the Autism Spectrum Quotient, the Social Responsiveness Scale, the Q-CHAT score and the Childhood Autism Rating Scale as predictors of a binary ASD-traits label. The same dataset produced accuracy 1.0000 for local_183eaef4; here it produces 97.60%, and the difference is attributable to preprocessing choices rather than to anything about autism. Dataset 2 is worse in kind. Its 100 original clinical samples were augmented fourfold to 400, and the stratified 80/10/10 split and 5-fold cross-validation were applied to the augmented set - so rotated, pitch-shifted, coordinate-scaled and noise-added copies of the same clinical sample sit on both sides of the split. The test partition therefore holds 40 samples, of which perhaps ten correspond to distinct originals, evaluated against a 4,220-dimensional feature vector. The reported 98.2% is roughly 39 of 40 correct on data the model has seen transformed versions of. It is also not a detection result: Dataset 2 contains four severity classes and no non-ASD class, so the abstract's presentation of 98.2% accuracy alongside the behavioural detection figure conflates a four-way severity task with binary ASD identification. Neither dataset carries a confidence interval, and the 63.28% majority-class baseline available in the paper's own Table 2 is never used. [RQ5.1] Twelve keywords including ethical AI and healthcare trustworthiness. The list is longer than any other in the corpus and names trust, interpretability, ethics and reliability - all values the paper's Dataset 2 handling does not exemplify. [RQ5.2] Computer Modeling in Engineering & Sciences 146(1):41 (Tech Science Press), 55 days from submission to acceptance. A modelling and engineering venue; review did not surface an entirely unsourced clinical dataset carrying an IRB claim with no committee or institution, a split performed over augmented copies, a four-class severity result reported alongside a binary detection result, or four autism instruments sitting in the predictor set. [RQ5.3] 2026, published 29 January. The framing is trust-centred - the stated goal is a model that is not only good at predicting ASD but also clear in its reasoning, with the title promising to enhance trust, interpretability and reliability in AI-driven healthcare. Against that, the paper reports a 98.2% figure from a dataset it does not source, whose split partitions augmented duplicates, and whose task is not the one the abstract implies; it applies its interpretability methods only to the dataset where they are least informative; and it reproduces the branch's characteristic overreach in describing machine learning as a suitable replacement for routine and expensive screening tests. Its genuine methodological contribution - explicitly confining SMOTE to the training partition and publishing the whole pipeline as an algorithm - is real and is the part of the paper most worth borrowing.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Secondary analysis pooling three prior online experiments with overlapping participants, conducted in the Netherlands. From 959 recruited adults (538 autistic via the Netherlands Autism Register, 421 non-autistic mainly via Prolific Academic), 407 were excluded for missing data from at least one experiment, leaving 286 autistic and 266 non-autistic participants. The autistic group was older (44.2 versus 32.2 years), more often female (71.0% versus 48.9%) and late-diagnosed (mean age at diagnosis 35.6 years); cognitive ability (ICAR-16) was matched. A fully age- and gender-matched subsample of 125 per group was drawn and used as the primary analysis.
narrative_rows.methods: Fifty-four dependent variables from online tasks measuring multisensory perception, emotion recognition and executive function were used to train a random forest, with hyperparameters tuned by GridSearchCV under 3-fold cross-validation and overfitting monitored by the train-test performance gap. No resampling was applied. Three predictor configurations were compared - tasks alone, AQ alone, and both combined - alongside a label-randomisation control. Group differences were tested with Mann-Whitney U and Bonferroni correction. The analysis script is on OSF.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Full sample: accuracy 81.8%, sensitivity 77.1%, specificity 84.1%, F1 77.9%. Age- and gender-matched sample (primary): accuracy 74.0%, sensitivity 69.2%, specificity 79.2%, F1 73.5%. On the matched sample, the AQ alone reached 83% and the combination reached 92%. The label-randomised model performed at chance. Several variables showing no significant group difference under Bonferroni correction carried predictive value in combination; reaction-time variables ranked consistently high.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The authors state the most important one themselves: performance in the unmatched sample is inflated by including age and gender as features given the group disparity, so the matched figure of 74.0% - rather than 81.8% - is the better estimate. They also note that the feature ranking may not generalise across participant ages and that the work is an initial effort. Remaining: diagnosis is self-reported, albeit as a clinician-made diagnosis obtained through a national research register; 407 of 959 recruited participants were excluded for missing data, which may not be at random; the matched subsample is 250 people; and no confidence intervals or cross-validation variance accompany the final estimates.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This study is one of the review's principal calibration points and contributes two things no other charted study does. First, it quantifies demographic confounding directly: the same models reach 81.8% accuracy on the unbalanced sample and 74.0% once age and gender are matched, so roughly eight accuracy points were attributable to demographics alone - a number that bears directly on the many studies in this corpus reporting large unadjusted sex imbalances between groups, including local_7432ffd7 (43-point gap) and local_4ceee075 (32-point gap). Second, it diagnoses the questionnaire branch's two failure modes explicitly and in print: that higher published accuracies were obtained either by predicting whether participants fell above or below an AQ cut-off rather than whether they received an official diagnosis, or by using groups unbalanced on demographic features that were themselves included as predictors, both of which risk sampling biases inflating performance. That is a published statement of exactly what this review reconstructed across seven Q-CHAT-labelled studies. Its own results also set an honest ceiling for adult autism prediction: 74% from a 54-variable performance battery, 83% from the AQ alone, and 92% from both together, in a late-diagnosed, majority-female sample that existing instruments identify least well. It joins local_4da2b941, local_5f57ba19, local_b6ac2b98 and local_69b10fe4 as the studies defining what careful work in this field actually yields, and it is the only one to report the fusion increment in a form that can be checked.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Two recruited groups of adults: 286 autistic and 266 non-autistic in the final dataset, from 959 initially recruited, with 407 excluded for missing data from at least one contributing experiment (per-study exclusion criteria, technical issues, attrition). Autistic participants came from the Netherlands Autism Register and non-autistic participants principally from Prolific Academic. A second, fully age- and gender-matched subsample of 125 per group was drawn by random selection from the unbalanced sample, and it is this matched analysis the paper reports as its primary result. The analysis unit is the person throughout. The attrition is large and is stated plainly with its causes. [RQ1.2] The most carefully handled in the entire corpus, and explicitly so. The paper inserts a parenthetical statement in its opening paragraph that it alternates between person-first and identity-first language to address the varying preferences of the international autism community, citing a published recommendation. Its terminology is consistently difference-based rather than deficit-based - behavioural differences, differences from the norms seen in the non-autistic population - and it justifies its choice of algorithm partly in those terms, noting that random forests capture any patterns that exist in the data and are therefore difference focused rather than deficit focused. It is the only study in the review to make a language decision explicitly, to cite community preference as the reason, and to connect that framing to a methodological choice. [RQ1.3] Complete and analytically load-bearing. Age, gender, ICAR-16 abbreviated IQ, AQ total and age at diagnosis are tabulated for both samples with means, standard deviations and Mann-Whitney tests. The full sample carries large group differences in age (44.2 versus 32.2 years) and gender (71.0% versus 48.9% women), both significant at p<0.001; the matched subsample is exact on both. Cognitive ability is matched in both samples (ICAR 0.54 versus 0.53). The autistic sample is 71% women and late-diagnosed at a mean of 35.6 years - a demographic profile that is the opposite of almost every other autism study in this corpus, and one the paper identifies as particularly difficult to identify. Nothing on ethnicity or socioeconomic status. [RQ1.4] Self-reported formal diagnosis by a registered clinician, with participants drawn from a national research register (NAR) rather than a convenience sample, and non-autistic participants reporting no autism diagnosis. Diagnosis therefore predates and is independent of the task data. The population is explicitly characterised as late-diagnosed, which the paper treats as a strength for the research question - it is precisely the group that existing screening instruments miss - rather than glossing over it. [RQ1.5] AQ-28 total, ICAR-16 abbreviated intelligence, and age at diagnosis, all reported by group with standard deviations and significance tests. The AQ is additionally used as a comparator predictor and a fusion partner, so its role in the modelling is explicit rather than hidden inside a feature vector - the distinction that separates this study from the corpus's instrument-inclusion leakage cases. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to test whether online performance-based measures can predict adult autism diagnosis, whether they add to the most widely used screening questionnaire, and which behavioural variables carry the predictive signal. Headline findings on the age- and gender-matched sample: objective task measures alone reach 74% accuracy (sensitivity 69.2%, specificity 79.2%, F1 73.5%); the AQ alone reaches 83%; the two combined reach 92%. On the unmatched full sample the objective measures reach 81.8%, which the paper states is inflated by including age and gender as features. A label-randomised control performs at chance. Several variables with no significant group difference under Bonferroni correction nevertheless contributed predictive value in combination. [RQ2.2] Entirely online, in Dutch, via the Neurotask platform, on participants' own devices - which the paper presents as the point rather than a compromise, arguing that online performance-based measures offer a marriage of more objective data types with the accessibility of surveys, against neuroimaging approaches that are costly, time-consuming and require laboratory attendance. The battery is described as briefer than a typical movie. [RQ2.3] A battery of online tasks spanning three neuropsychological domains - multisensory perception, emotion recognition and executive function - reused from three prior published experiments with overlapping participants, yielding 54 dependent variables. The design rationale is stated clearly: because autism is heterogeneous, differences in any one neuropsychological domain are inconsistently detected, so the study looks across domains rather than within one. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. Ethics reporting is complete: ethical committee approval from the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam with reference VCWE-2020-041R1, compliance with the Netherlands Code of Conduct for Research Integrity and the revised Declaration of Helsinki, and informed consent from all participants prior to the experiments. Data governance is also handled properly - the register data are restricted for privacy reasons, and the procedure for requesting access through a research proposal and Data Sharing Agreement is documented. [RQ2.5] Participants' own devices, with tasks programmed and delivered online through Neurotask. Analysis in Python with scikit-learn's RandomForest and GridSearchCV, with the script deposited on OSF. [RQ2.6] High, and complete on the axes that matter. The analysis script is publicly deposited; the recruitment sources are named with a justification for the platform chosen; the 407 exclusions are counted with their reasons; the matching procedure is described; demographic, cognitive and AQ characteristics are tabulated with standard deviations and significance tests for both samples; the tuned hyperparameters are enumerated; the tuning procedure and the overfitting criterion are stated; the decision not to resample is stated with its reasoning; and a label-randomisation control is reported. The primary data are restricted by register privacy rules, with the request procedure documented - the correct handling for a national register rather than a gap. [RQ2.7] Distributed through the discussion rather than isolated, and unusually incisive. The paper states that the unmatched sample's higher accuracy is inflated by including age and gender as features and that the matched estimate should be preferred; that the feature ranking may not generalise across participant ages; and that the work represents initial efforts with limits on what can be concluded. Its most valuable limitation, though, is directed outward and applies to a large part of this review's corpus: it notes that studies reporting higher accuracy did so either by using the AQ-10 items to predict whether participants fell above or below an AQ cut-off score rather than whether they received an official diagnosis, or by using groups that were not balanced on demographic features included as predictors - and that this risks sampling biases inflating performance, which the authors accounted for through their matched analysis. That is a precise, published statement of the two mechanisms this review has documented across the questionnaire branch. [RQ2.9] Use feature ranking to remove uninformative measures and shorten the battery; design manipulations that accentuate reaction-time differences in the most sensitive domains, since certain emotional categories and stimulus types are harder to categorise and leave more room for RT differences; and test whether the sensitive measures differ across age groups. [RQ3.1] Neuropsychological performance across three domains rather than a single behavioural marker: multisensory perceptual integration, emotion recognition (with accuracy and reaction time varying by emotional category and stimulus type), and executive function. The substantive behavioural findings are specific - reaction-time variables consistently ranked high in predictive value, and executive function emerged as informative in this adult sample - and the paper is careful that the ranking is sample-dependent. [RQ3.2] Genuine, declared and quantified multimodal fusion, and the study's central result. Objective task measures and the AQ questionnaire are evaluated separately and together on the same matched sample: 74% for tasks alone, 83% for the AQ alone, 92% combined. Because each configuration is reported, the increment attributable to fusion is visible (9 points over the questionnaire alone), and because the feature-importance profile is very similar with and without the AQ, the authors can argue that the two data types contribute information in different ways rather than merely duplicating each other. This is the only study in the charted corpus to report all three configurations and thereby make the fusion claim checkable. [RQ4.1] Random forest, selected with reasons given: capacity to detect sparse signals in high-dimensional data, provision of feature-importance rankings usable for battery optimisation, and the property of being difference-focused rather than deficit-focused. No deep learning and no architecture competition - the modelling is subordinated to the scientific question. [RQ4.2] One row per participant containing 54 task-derived dependent variables, with AQ total and demographic variables added in specified configurations. No dimensionality reduction or feature selection is applied, and no clinical instrument is smuggled in - the AQ's presence is the explicit object of one of the three comparisons. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and F1 for both samples and each configuration, plus a label-randomised control model. The specificity/sensitivity split is reported rather than collapsed into accuracy (matched sample: sensitivity 69.2%, specificity 79.2%), which shows that the model misses roughly a third of autistic adults at the reported operating point - visible precisely because the paper reports it. Missing: confidence intervals, cross-validation variance on the final estimates, and calibration. The chance level is established empirically by the randomisation control rather than asserted. [RQ4.4] Feature importance is used as a scientific instrument rather than as decoration. The headline interpretive result is that several variables showing no significant group difference even under highly conservative Bonferroni correction nonetheless carried predictive value in combination - a finding that only a multivariate model can produce and that the authors read as evidence of complex latent relationships associated with autism rather than as a discovery of new markers. Reaction-time variables ranked consistently high; executive function was informative in this adult sample; and the near-identical importance profile with and without the AQ supports the claim that objective and subjective measures contribute differently. The authors also state the limit: the ranking may not generalise across ages. [RQ4.5] This is one of the two most rigorously evaluated studies in the charted corpus, and its distinctive contribution is the demographic-confounding analysis. The design uses a train/test split with 3-fold cross-validated grid search for hyperparameters and monitors overfitting by the train-test performance gap; adds a label-randomisation control that falls to chance, empirically establishing the baseline rather than assuming it; and declines to resample, stating that neither SMOTE nor undersampling was used. Its decisive move is to run the entire analysis twice - once on the full unbalanced sample and once on a subsample matched 100% on age and gender at 125 per group - and then to report the matched result as primary, stating that performance in the unmatched sample is inflated by the inclusion of age and gender as features given the disparity between groups in those factors. The difference is large: 81.8% unmatched against 74.0% matched, so roughly eight accuracy points in this study were attributable to demographic confounding alone. That number is directly relevant to the rest of this review, in which sex imbalances of 32 points (local_4ceee075) and 43 points (local_7432ffd7) between groups are reported and left unadjusted, and it is the only quantification of that effect anywhere in the corpus. Residual limitations: no confidence intervals or fold variance accompany the final estimates; the matched subsample is 250 people; diagnosis is self-reported rather than verified, albeit through a national register; and 407 of 959 recruited participants were excluded for missing data, which may not be at random. None of these undermines the study's central results, and the authors identify the most important of them themselves. [RQ5.1] Not captured in the extracted text. [RQ5.2] Translational Psychiatry 16:129 (Nature Portfolio) - a clinical and translational psychiatry journal, and the only such venue in the charted corpus. The disciplinary fit is evident throughout: matched-subsample analysis, Bonferroni-corrected group comparisons, a label-randomisation control, sensitivity and specificity reported separately, deposited analysis code, documented data-access procedures, an explicit language statement citing community preference, and a discussion that diagnoses the methodological failures of the prior literature it is compared against. [RQ5.3] 2026. The framing is screening-support and is bounded at every point: the measures may be a promising means of predicting autism, providing complementary information to existing screening questionnaires; the value proposition is triage for expedited assessment given protracted diagnostic wait times, not replacement of clinical assessment; and the reported gain is stated as 9 percentage points over the most popular adult screening questionnaire, with the authors noting that this matters in the context of an estimated 1% population prevalence. The paper is also unusual in reporting a result that undercuts its own headline - that the same models reach 81.8% on the unmatched sample and 74.0% once age and gender are matched - and in choosing the lower figure as its primary estimate.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective analysis of a public eye-tracking scanpath dataset of 28 participants (14 ASD, 14 typically developing), released in anonymised form on Zenodo. No age, sex, cognitive ability, recruitment source, viewing task, eye tracker or diagnostic procedure is reported for the source cohort.
narrative_rows.methods: Each scanpath was truncated or zero-padded to 20 fixations, and nine handcrafted descriptors were computed per trial - fixation count, mean/first/maximum/total fixation duration, total path length, mean saccade amplitude, dispersion and fixation-duration entropy. These were aggregated to one vector per participant via mean and standard deviation, standardised, and classified by a hybrid ensemble combining bagging, boosting and stacking over five base learners. Evaluation used five-fold cross-validation with an explicitly subject-wise protocol adopted to prevent data leakage, a Friedman test on fold-wise F1 scores, and permutation-based feature relevance used solely for interpretation.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Stacking ensemble accuracy 0.9600 (SD 0.0800), precision 0.9750 (0.0500), recall 0.9500 (0.1000), F1 0.9524 (0.0952). Base learners: AdaBoost 0.9267/0.9181, KNN 0.8867/0.8781, random forest 0.8533/0.8374, decision tree 0.8200/0.7657, gradient boosting 0.7800/0.7181.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The authors state the principal one themselves - a single small-scale dataset of 28 participants limits statistical generalisability and the results should be read as a proof-of-concept demonstration. Two further issues are not raised. The within-subject resampling that generates additional subject-level samples is described as occurring during model training without stating whether it precedes or follows the fold split; if it precedes, several vectors derived from the same participant would cross the partition and undermine the subject-wise protocol that is the design's main safeguard. And nothing whatever is reported about the source cohort - no demographics, no viewing task, no equipment, no diagnostic procedure - so what the classifier separates cannot be assessed, and stimulus identity cannot be excluded as a contributor to scanpath geometry. With five folds over 28 people, each test set holds five or six participants, which is what the reported standard deviations of 0.08 on accuracy and 0.095 on F1 record.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This study matters to the review as the eye-tracking branch's counterexample on validation design. Where local_44d3aef5 split 547 scanpath images from a repeated-image collection and reached 100%, local_bb4d1f7a split 100 eye crops per child and reached 97%, and local_7432ffd7 split gaze samples from 59 children and reached 99.78%, this study aggregates to the participant, evaluates subject-wise, and lists leakage prevention among its four stated contributions - and reaches 0.96 with a standard deviation of 0.08 on 28 people, which it labels a proof of concept. It thus demonstrates that participant-level evaluation is straightforward in this modality and that the branch's near-perfect figures are a choice rather than a consequence. Its own weakness is different in kind: an entirely uncharacterised source cohort, with no task, equipment, demographics or diagnostic procedure reported, in a paper co-authored by clinicians. It also reports its fold-wise standard deviations rather than only means, which makes the imprecision of a 28-person estimate visible - and reading those standard deviations against the near-zero fold variance claimed as robustness in local_8d43288c is instructive about what small honest folds actually look like.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Twenty-eight participants, 14 with ASD and 14 typically developing, from a public benchmark eye-tracking dataset released on Zenodo. This is the smallest participant base of any charted study apart from local_e771fb69, and it is the only quantity the paper reports about the people involved - no age, sex, cognitive ability, recruitment source, country or diagnostic procedure appears. Crucially, the analysis unit is the participant: scanpath-level features are aggregated to one vector per person by taking the mean and standard deviation across that person's trials, and the evaluation is described as subject-wise specifically to prevent data leakage. With 28 people and five folds, each test fold holds roughly five or six participants. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, TD, individuals with ASD. The register is clinical and unremarkable; the opening characterisation uses deficits in social communication and the presence of restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, standard DSM phrasing. No autistic or community perspective appears, and no demographic or personal description of the participants is offered at any point. [RQ1.3] None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography, cognitive ability or recruitment information for any of the 28 participants, and no acknowledgement that this information is absent. The paper's own discussion notes that generalisation across demographics and hardware platforms remains a pressing issue in this literature - a concern it identifies and then cannot address, because it reports no demographic variable at all. [RQ1.4] Not described. Labels are inherited from the public dataset with no diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or date reported, and the originating collection's ascertainment procedure is not summarised. This is the study's largest unforced omission, since two of its authors are clinicians - one at a psychiatric hospital and one at a clinical medicine school - and a paragraph characterising the source cohort would have been straightforward. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is a hybrid ensemble integrating bagging, boosting and stacking that operates directly on raw scanpath features rather than on scanpath images, so as to reduce preprocessing overhead and improve interpretability for real-time screening. Headline findings: the stacking ensemble reached accuracy 0.9600 (SD 0.0800), precision 0.9750, recall 0.9500 and F1 0.9524, above every base learner (AdaBoost 0.9267, KNN 0.8867, random forest 0.8533, decision tree 0.8200, gradient boosting 0.7800), and comparable to image-based deep learning models on the same dataset at a fraction of the preprocessing cost. [RQ2.2] No study setting. A public dataset analysed computationally, with no compute environment, runtime or hardware described - which sits awkwardly with a contribution framed around computational efficiency and real-time deployment, since no timing measurement supports it. [RQ2.3] Not reported. The viewing task, stimuli, eye tracker and session structure of the originating collection are nowhere summarised, so a reader cannot say what the participants were looking at when the scanpaths were recorded. For a scanpath analysis this matters, because scanpath geometry is jointly determined by the viewer and the stimulus, and without knowing the stimulus set one cannot exclude stimulus identity as a source of the signal. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. Ethics is declared not required, with reasoning given: the dataset is publicly available, was released in anonymised form by its creators, contains no identifiable personal information, and no new data were collected. The declaration is at least argued rather than blank, and the paper additionally discloses that one author is an editorial board member of the journal and was excluded from the editorial decision - a disclosure no other charted study makes. [RQ2.5] No acquisition instrumentation is described. Modelling components: decision tree, random forest, KNN (k=3), AdaBoost, gradient boosting and a stacking meta-learner. No software, version, seed or hardware. [RQ2.6] Moderate. Reproducible: the source dataset has a DOI; the nine handcrafted scanpath descriptors are enumerated with definitions; the 20-fixation truncation/padding rule, the mean-and-standard-deviation aggregation to participant level, and z-score standardisation are all specified; fold-wise means and standard deviations are tabulated for every model; and the permutation-importance procedure is described with its intended scope. Not reproducible: no code or seed, no software or versions, no hyperparameters beyond k=3, no count of scanpaths per participant, no description of the source task, and no statement of where in the pipeline the within-subject resampling occurs relative to the fold split. [RQ2.7] Stated plainly and correctly, in the discussion rather than in a boilerplate paragraph: although the framework achieved high accuracy, it was evaluated on a single small-scale dataset of 28 participants, which limits the statistical generalizability of the findings, so the reported results should be interpreted as a proof-of-concept demonstration pending validation on larger and more diverse populations. That is the right reading of a 28-person study and it is offered without hedging. What is not raised: that the fold-wise standard deviations (0.08 on accuracy, 0.095 on F1) are large precisely because each fold holds five or six people; that no demographic, task or diagnostic information about the source cohort is reported; and that the within-subject resampling step is not located relative to the split. [RQ2.9] Validation on larger and more diverse datasets, and integration into an end-to-end screening platform. Both follow directly from the stated limitation. [RQ3.1] Visual scanning behaviour reduced to nine interpretable descriptors: number of fixations, mean and maximum and first fixation duration, total fixation duration, total path length, mean saccade amplitude, spatial dispersion of fixations, and fixation-duration entropy as a measure of irregularity in gaze allocation. Operating on these rather than on rendered scanpath images is the paper's central methodological claim, and it is a defensible one - the features are inspectable and the permutation analysis can name which of them matter. [RQ3.2] No modality fusion - eye tracking alone. What is fused is classifiers rather than data: bagging, boosting and stacking are combined within one architecture, with base learners selected by a stated diversity criterion to promote complementary decision boundaries. [RQ4.1] A three-strategy ensemble - bagging, boosting and stacking - over five base learners (decision tree, random forest, KNN k=3, AdaBoost, gradient boosting) with a stacking meta-learner. The base-learner set is chosen by an explicit diversity-aware strategy rather than assembled arbitrarily, and every constituent's performance is reported separately so the ensemble's increment is visible: the best base learner reaches 0.9267 accuracy and the stack 0.9600, a gain of about 3.3 points. [RQ4.2] One vector per participant, formed by aggregating nine scanpath descriptors across that person's trials via mean and standard deviation, after each scanpath was truncated or zero-padded to 20 fixations and before z-score standardisation. The 20-fixation cap is a substantive modelling decision - it discards everything after the twentieth fixation in longer scanpaths and pads shorter ones - and its effect is not tested. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 with fold-wise means and standard deviations for all six models, plus a Friedman test on fold-wise F1 and a permutation-importance ranking. Reporting the standard deviations is a real strength and is also where the study's honest signal lies: an accuracy standard deviation of 0.0800 and an F1 standard deviation of 0.0952 on a five-fold split of 28 people means individual folds ranged widely, which is what five- or six-person test sets produce. On such folds, 0.9600 accuracy corresponds to roughly 27 of 28 participants classified correctly across the full cross-validation, and a single reclassification moves the figure by about 3.6 points. No confidence interval accompanies any estimate and the 50% chance level is never stated. [RQ4.4] Permutation-based feature relevance, with an unusually precise statement of scope: the analysis was performed independently of model selection procedures and served solely as an interpretability tool rather than as a feature selection mechanism. That distinction matters and is drawn correctly - permutation importance computed for interpretation cannot leak into the model, whereas the same computation used to select features would. A full ranking is presented, though the extracted text does not name which descriptors dominated. [RQ4.5] The design gets the structural question right and is limited by size rather than by construction. Subject-wise aggregation and evaluation are adopted explicitly to prevent data leakage and to provide a more realistic estimate of generalisation in clinical settings, and this is listed as one of the paper's four stated contributions - a rare instance in the eye-tracking branch of participant-level splitting being treated as a design requirement rather than overlooked. Set against the branch, that choice is what separates this study's 0.96 on 28 people from local_44d3aef5's 1.00 on 55 scanpath images and local_bb4d1f7a's 0.97 on 100 eye crops per child. Three qualifications remain. First, size: 28 participants across five folds gives test sets of five or six, and the reported standard deviations (0.08 accuracy, 0.095 F1) reflect that directly - the estimate is not wrong, it is imprecise, and the paper says as much in calling the work a proof of concept. Second, the within-subject resampling: additional subject-level samples were generated by resampling scanpaths within each subject and recomputing the aggregated representation, described as occurring during model training; if that augmentation was performed before the fold split rather than inside it, several aggregated vectors derived from the same participant's scanpaths would cross the partition and the subject-wise protocol would be undermined by the very step intended to increase sample diversity. The paper's wording suggests the correct placement but does not state it unambiguously. Third, the source cohort is uncharacterised - no task, no equipment, no diagnostic procedure, no demographics - so what the classifier separates cannot be independently assessed. [RQ5.1] Autism Spectrum Disorder; Bagging; Boosting; Stacking; Ensemble learning; Eye-tracking. Four of six terms name ensemble strategies; participants, task and validation are absent. [RQ5.2] Array 30 (2026) 100753 (Elsevier) - an open-access computer science journal. The author list spans engineering and clinical institutions including a psychiatric hospital, which makes the absence of any description of the source cohort's diagnosis or demographics more notable rather than less. The paper discloses an editorial conflict of interest for one author, which is good practice and uncommon in this corpus. [RQ5.3] 2026. The framing is proportionate and, on the point that matters, correct: the reported results should be interpreted as a proof-of-concept demonstration, pending validation on larger and more diverse populations. The claims that go beyond that are about engineering rather than clinical accuracy - reduced preprocessing overhead by eliminating scanpath-to-image conversion, suitability for real-time screening environments, and a more direct and deployable solution bridging the gap between research prototypes and practical clinical tools - and even those are asserted without any timing measurement. Its contribution to the review is as the eye-tracking branch's demonstration that participant-level evaluation is achievable in this modality and that when it is applied, the resulting figure comes with a standard deviation of eight accuracy points on 28 people.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective analysis of 14,352 annotated facial images of children obtained from the Roboflow platform, labelled autistic or non-autistic with bounding-box annotations. No class counts, split proportions, partition sizes, demographic information or count of distinct children is reported, and the originating collection is not described. Roboflow's export pipeline supplied resizing to 640x640, RGB conversion, normalisation and augmentation for illumination, expression and pose.
narrative_rows.methods: YOLOv8n and YOLOv9c were trained with the Ultralytics framework for 50 epochs at 640x640, with the dataset divided into training, validation and testing groups. Performance was assessed by precision, recall, F1, mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95, with normalised confusion matrices including a Background class, precision-recall and F1-confidence curves, and an informal probe on non-human images.
narrative_rows.outcomes: YOLOv8n: precision 91.95%, recall 92.77%, F1 92.36%, mAP@0.5 94.76%, mAP@0.5:0.95 94.73%. YOLOv9c: 91.29%, 90.29%, 90.79%, 93.32%, 93.21%. In the out-of-distribution probe, YOLOv8n rejected a dog and a leaf while YOLOv9c classified the dog as Autistic and the leaf as Nonautistic.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The study states none. Labels are platform annotations on photographs with no clinical diagnosis behind them. No class counts, split ratios or partition sizes are reported, so no result can be located to a sample, and no chance level can be computed. Augmentation was applied through the Roboflow export pipeline rather than during training, so transformed variants of the same photograph may cross the split - and a 14,352-image set most plausibly derives from a much smaller pool of originals, given that the paper's own literature table cites the roughly 3,000-image public autism face corpus repeatedly. The reported mAP figures are mutually inconsistent: mAP@0.5:0.95 averages precision over IoU thresholds up to 0.95 and cannot sit within 0.11 points of mAP@0.5 for a detector trained on uncalibrated images. An object-detection architecture with a Background class is applied to a single-face whole-image binary question without rationale. And real-time screening is the central claim with no latency or throughput figure anywhere in the paper.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This is the fifteenth charted study in the facial-image branch and it contributes one finding the other fourteen do not. In an informal robustness comparison, one of its two models labelled a photograph of a dog as Autistic and a leaf as Nonautistic. The authors present this as evidence that YOLOv8n filters irrelevant inputs better than YOLOv9c; read as a fact about the task, it demonstrates that a model trained to detect autism from a face will assign an autism label to arbitrary objects unless a background-rejection mechanism intervenes, and that the difference between the two architectures on this dataset is a difference in background handling rather than in anything about autism. No other study in the branch tests a non-face input. Its second distinctive feature is its ethics paragraph, which - alone among the fifteen - states explicitly that given the child's facial data aspect, there is ethical sensitivity, before proceeding on the presumption that a hosting platform's sharing policy implies the original curators obtained consent. Its reported mAP@0.5:0.95 sitting 0.03 points below mAP@0.5 places it with local_986436f2 and local_e04bcd32 among the branch's arithmetically unreconcilable results.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] No participants. 14,352 annotated facial images of children obtained from the Roboflow platform, labelled autistic or non-autistic and carrying bounding-box annotations. No class counts, no split sizes and no count of distinct children appear anywhere. The scale is worth noting against the branch: the paper's own literature table cites the Kaggle autism face corpus repeatedly, and that corpus contains roughly 3,000 images, so a 14,352-image Roboflow set is most plausibly an augmented export of the same underlying photographs - which the paper's description of Roboflow's built-in augmentation at export time supports but never states. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with autism, autistic, non-autistic. The introduction is unusually careful in one respect - it notes that while certain individuals with ASD may also experience cognitive impairment, the majority possess average to above-average intelligence, and that symptoms vary so that some face mild difficulties while others require full-time care. Elsewhere the register is standard for this branch. No autistic or community perspective appears. [RQ1.3] None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography or recruitment information for any image, and no acknowledgement of the absence - although the paper's own literature table repeatedly lists limited dataset diversity and poor generalization as limitations of prior studies using the same kind of data. [RQ1.4] None. Labels are annotations attached to a Roboflow dataset. No clinical diagnosis, instrument, criterion, assessor or date exists for a single image, and the originating collection is not described. The paper's introduction gives an accurate account of how ASD is actually diagnosed - paediatricians or psychologists using developmental history, behavioural observation and instruments including CARS for severity - and then treats platform annotations on downloaded photographs as an adequate substitute. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure; none obtainable from photographs. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is real-time ASD screening from facial images using object detection, with YOLOv8n compared against YOLOv9c to identify the more effective solution. Headline findings: YOLOv8n reached precision 91.95%, recall 92.77%, F1 92.36% and mAP@0.5 94.76%, against YOLOv9c at 91.29%, 90.29%, 90.79% and 93.32%; YOLOv8n showed higher true-positive rates for both classes with fewer misclassifications into the Background class; and, in an out-of-distribution probe, YOLOv8n rejected non-human inputs while YOLOv9c classified a dog as Autistic and a leaf as Nonautistic. [RQ2.2] No setting. Images exported from Roboflow and models trained with the Ultralytics framework; no hardware, runtime or environment is described, which is a notable gap in a paper whose central claim is real-time deployability. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. Static photographs. The construct is facial morphology, with the backbone described as extracting facial symmetry, eye spacing, philtrum width and face shape - a list of dysmorphology features that would require calibrated measurement rather than a detection head trained on uncalibrated web images. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. Ethics is not obtained but is genuinely reasoned about, which distinguishes this study from most of its branch: the authors note that the data comprise only de-identified facial images with no personally identifiable information, state that according to Roboflow dataset sharing policies it is understood that the curators obtained adequate consent and ethical clearance before publication, confirm that no personal or clinical collection took place, and - unusually - write explicitly that given the child's facial data aspect, there is ethical sensitivity. That last sentence is the only acknowledgement anywhere in the fifteen-study facial-image branch that photographing and labelling children's faces raises a question at all. Its weakness is the inference immediately preceding it: consent is presumed from a hosting platform's sharing policy rather than verified. [RQ2.5] No acquisition instrumentation. Roboflow supplied preprocessing (640x640 resize, RGB conversion, normalisation) and augmentation (horizontal flipping and transformations for illumination, expression and pose variation) at export; training used the Ultralytics YOLO framework for 50 epochs. No learning rate, batch size, optimiser, seed or hardware. [RQ2.6] Low. Named: the source platform, the export-time preprocessing and augmentation, the image size, the epoch count and the training framework. Missing: the dataset URL, accession or version; class counts and split proportions; the number of distinct children; optimiser, learning rate, batch size and seed; and any code. The reported metrics also contain an internal inconsistency that cannot be reconciled - mAP@0.5:0.95 sits within 0.11 points of mAP@0.5 for both models, which no genuine detection evaluation produces. [RQ2.7] None for this study. The literature table (Table 2) is unusually thorough in the opposite direction, assigning each of roughly ten prior works a named weakness - limited dataset diversity and challenges generalizing to real-world conditions; overfitting risk with limited data; overfitting in small datasets and poor generalization; low model interpretability and high training time; small and limited dataset, lack of clinical validation, no multimodal analysis. Every one of those applies to the present study and none is claimed by it. Unmentioned: the absent class counts and split ratios, the unstated number of distinct children, the impossible mAP relationship, and the fact that a model trained to detect autism from a face assigned a class label to a dog. [RQ2.9] None stated. [RQ3.1] None. No behaviour is observed or measured; the target is static facial appearance, described in terms of symmetry, eye spacing, philtrum width and face shape. [RQ3.2] No fusion - a single image modality. The paper's own literature table lists no multimodal analysis as a limitation of a cited prior study and does not apply it to itself. [RQ4.1] YOLOv8n and YOLOv9c, single-stage object detectors, applied to a whole-image binary classification problem. The architectural choice is consequential and unexamined: an object detector localises instances within a scene and scores them against a Background class, so the confusion matrices contain Autistic, Non-Autistic and Background categories, and the reported mAP is a localisation-plus-classification measure rather than a diagnostic accuracy. Nothing in the task requires detection - each image contains one face - so the apparatus adds a spatial estimation problem and a third class to a two-class question. [RQ4.2] 640x640 RGB images with bounding boxes, preprocessed and augmented by Roboflow's export pipeline. Because augmentation is applied at export rather than at training time, augmented variants of an image may be distributed across the train, validation and test partitions - the paper gives no information that would exclude this, and gives no split ratio either. [RQ4.3] Precision, recall, F1, mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95 for both models, with normalised confusion matrices, precision-recall curves and F1-confidence curves. The reporting looks complete and contains an impossibility. For YOLOv8n, mAP@0.5 is 94.76% and mAP@0.5:0.95 is 94.73%; for YOLOv9c, 93.32% and 93.21%. mAP@0.5:0.95 averages average precision across ten IoU thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95, so it is bounded above by mAP@0.5 and in practice falls well below it - gaps of twenty to forty points are typical for face-scale objects. A gap of 0.03 points implies that localisation quality is perfect at every threshold up to 0.95, which no detector trained for 50 epochs on uncalibrated web photographs achieves. The two numbers are therefore not both genuine mAP values. No class counts, no split sizes, no chance level and no variance across the repeated runs the paper claims to have performed are reported. [RQ4.4] No formal attribution, but the paper contains an out-of-distribution probe that is the single most informative result in it and is presented only as a robustness comparison between architectures. Given a picture of a dog and a picture of a leaf, YOLOv9c classified the dog as Autistic and the leaf as Nonautistic, while YOLOv8n rejected both. The authors read this as evidence of YOLOv8n's superior filtering. The more important reading is what it reveals about the task: a model trained to detect autism from a photograph will assign an autism label to whatever is placed in front of it unless something else stops it, and the difference between the two architectures here is a difference in background rejection rather than in anything about autism. No other study in this fifteen-strong branch tests its model on a non-face input, and this one does so almost incidentally. [RQ4.5] The evaluation is thinly described and internally inconsistent. The dataset is said to be divided into three groups for testing, validation and training, with the reasoning that such splitting reduces the bias and overfitting possibility - and no ratio, no partition size, no seed and no cross-validation follows. The split is at the image level on a corpus whose per-child composition is unknown, and whose 14,352 images most plausibly derive by augmentation from a much smaller set of underlying photographs, since Roboflow's augmentation was applied at export rather than during training; if so, transformed variants of the same photograph sit on both sides of the partition. Training and evaluation are said to have been carried out multiple times with highly consistent results, and no variance figure supports that claim. Most concretely, the two mAP figures cannot both be genuine: mAP@0.5:0.95 within 0.11 points of mAP@0.5 is arithmetically achievable only under near-perfect localisation at IoU 0.95, which is not attainable here. And the informal robustness probe demonstrates directly that the system's decision surface extends to objects that are not faces, which no reported metric captures. [RQ5.1] Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD); Facial Image Analysis; YOLO; Real-time screening; AI-based Diagnostics. Five terms, two of them deployment claims (real-time screening, AI-based diagnostics) that the paper does not measure - no inference latency or throughput figure appears anywhere despite real-time being the central selling point. [RQ5.2] Journal of Pioneering Medical Sciences 15(1):137-145, a medical sciences journal, 90 days from submission to acceptance. Clinical review did not surface the absent class counts and split ratios, the mAP inconsistency, or the reported finding that one of the two models labels a dog as autistic. [RQ5.3] 2026, published 5 February. Framing is real-time clinical screening: the study is said to facilitate real-time ASD screening, providing healthcare professionals with timely and effective interventions in clinical environments, with mobile and web deployment proposed to reach remote areas. There is no limitations section and no future work, and the contribution is expressed as a position above one quoted prior YOLO result. Its distinguishing features within the branch are two: an ethics paragraph that at least names the sensitivity of children's facial data before proceeding, and an out-of-distribution test that inadvertently shows the model assigning an autism label to a photograph of a dog.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Retrospective analysis of 2,940 facial images balanced at 1,470 per class - the sixteenth charted reuse of the public autism facial-image corpus, identified here only by reference number. No demographic, diagnostic or provenance information accompanies any image, and the number of distinct children is unknown. Results are reported separately for a 70% training phase and a 30% testing phase, with no partition counts or seed.
narrative_rows.methods: Gaussian Gabor filtering enhanced facial features; deep features from VGG16, DenseNet-121 and XceptionNet were concatenated; a wavelet neural network performed classification with parameters tuned by the chimp optimisation algorithm; and Grad-CAM++ produced visual interpretations. Training used ReLU, learning rate 0.01, dropout 0.5, batch size 5 and a stated 50 epochs, on a desktop with an i5-8600K and a GTX 1050 Ti.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Testing phase: average accuracy 98.42%, precision 98.40%, recall 98.42%, F-measure 98.41%, AUC 98.42%. Training phase: 97.75%, 97.80%, 97.75%, 97.76%, 97.75%. Quoted comparators (CONCAT-SDAE, ViT-B, EfficientNet-B4, VGG-19, GBM, RF, KNN) range from 92.10% to 97.76% on precision.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The labels are folder assignments with no diagnostic basis, and the split is a single unseeded image-level partition of a corpus that repeats individuals, so it does not separate children. No component of the four-stage pipeline is ablated, and the chimp optimiser tuned parameters against an unstated objective on an unidentified partition. The testing-phase accuracy exceeds the training-phase accuracy, and the same inversion in the learning curves is read as good generalisation without overfitting rather than as a question about partition independence; the stated 50 epochs also disagree with the 25-epoch curves. Two formal declarations contradict the article: ethics states that it contains no studies with human participants, and data availability states that no datasets were generated or analysed. Privacy preservation is claimed as part of the research gap with no privacy mechanism described. Against all this the paper does state one accurate limitation - that the dataset's lack of demographic information prevents any examination of how facial morphology and expression vary across populations.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This is the sixteenth and final charted reuse of the public autism facial-image corpus, and it closes the branch on two notes worth recording. Its 98.42% sits at the upper end of the branch's 81.0-99.8% range and is produced by the branch's now-standard formula - stack more stages (Gabor filtering, three-backbone fusion, a wavelet classifier, a metaheuristic optimiser, a saliency method), split at the image level, ablate nothing, and report the maximum. Its testing accuracy exceeding its training accuracy, read as good generalisation, is the branch's clearest instance of an anomaly being interpreted as a virtue. But it also contains the branch's most accurate self-diagnosis: a limitation paragraph stating that because the dataset carries no demographic information and because facial morphology and expression vary across demographic groups, the influence of those factors on classification cannot be examined - which is precisely the objection that applies to all sixteen studies, stated plainly by the last of them, in the same article whose formal declarations assert that it involved no human participants and analysed no data.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] No participants. 2,940 images in two balanced classes of 1,470 - the sixteenth charted reuse of the public autism facial-image corpus, identifiable from that exact composition although the paper names only a reference number rather than a repository. The number of distinct children is unknown and never discussed. Results are reported for a 70% training partition and a 30% testing partition with no counts, no seed and no statement of how the split was drawn. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, individuals with ASD, children with ASD. The register is medical and dated - ASD is introduced as a complex psychological disease and later as a critical neurodevelopmental condition with excessive medical expenses - and the symptom list includes repetitive and aggressive behaviours, hyperactivity, and cognitive impairment. Grad-CAM++ is described as providing abnormality detection, which frames the highlighted facial regions as abnormalities rather than as model attention. No autistic or community perspective appears. [RQ1.3] None reported, and the paper is one of the few in this branch to say so and to explain why it matters: expression patterns and facial morphology differ across demographic factors, and because the dataset carries no such information, their influence on ASD classification and on facial-feature learning cannot be clearly examined. That is an accurate statement of the branch's central data problem, made by a study that then proceeds anyway. [RQ1.4] None. Labels are the folder assignments of a public image corpus, with no clinical diagnosis, instrument, criterion, assessor or date for any image, and no description of how the collection was assembled. The introduction gives a conventional account of ASD as requiring thorough clinical testing and then treats folder labels as sufficient ground truth for a system offered as a diagnostic aid in clinical settings. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure; none obtainable from photographs. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is a computationally efficient, privacy-preserving and optimised framework for ASD detection from facial images, combining Gaussian Gabor filtering, fused deep features from VGG16, DenseNet-121 and XceptionNet, a wavelet neural network classifier tuned by the chimp optimisation algorithm, and Grad-CAM++ for visual interpretation. Headline findings: average accuracy 98.42% with precision 98.40%, recall 98.42%, F-measure 98.41% and AUC 98.42% in the 30% testing phase, against quoted comparators from 92.10% to 97.76%. [RQ2.2] No setting. A downloaded dataset analysed in Python 3.6.5 on a desktop with an i5-8600K, 16 GB RAM and a GeForce GTX 1050 Ti - a configuration reported in unusual detail for a study whose stated contribution includes computational efficiency, though no runtime or inference-time measurement accompanies it. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. Static photographs with no stimulus, interaction or session; the construct is facial morphology and expression. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. The ethics declaration is factually wrong rather than merely permissive: this article does not contain any studies with human participants performed by any of the authors, stated for an analysis of 2,940 photographs of children, with consent to participate and consent to publish both marked not applicable.
