It is paired with a data-availability statement asserting that no datasets were generated or analysed during the current study, in an article whose results section reports a full metric grid computed on a 2,940-image dataset. Together the two declarations describe a paper that did not use any data, which is the opposite of what the article reports. The framing also claims the framework is privacy-preserving, with no privacy mechanism of any kind described. [RQ2.5] No acquisition instrumentation. Compute fully specified (Python 3.6.5, i5-8600K, 16 GB RAM, GTX 1050 Ti 4 GB, 250 GB SSD, 1 TB HDD). Training settings: ReLU, learning rate 0.01, dropout 0.5, 50 epochs, batch size 5 - though the accuracy and loss curves are described over 25 epochs, which does not match. [RQ2.6] Low. The compute environment, the four principal training hyperparameters, the class composition and the pipeline order are all given, which is more than several neighbours provide. Against that: the dataset is identified only by a reference number while the formal data statement denies that any dataset was analysed; no split procedure, partition counts or seed appear; the wavelet basis and network topology are unspecified; the chimp optimiser has no stated objective, search space or budget; no code is released; and the epoch count in the text contradicts the epoch axis of the learning curves. [RQ2.7] One stated limitation, and it is the right one: the dataset lacks demographic information, expression patterns and facial morphology vary across demographic factors, and their influence on classification and feature learning therefore cannot be examined - with future work directed at demographically different datasets to assess fairness and generalisability. Within the facial-image branch this is the clearest statement of the problem that undermines all sixteen of its members. What is not stated: that the labels have no diagnostic basis, that the split is at the image level on a corpus that repeats individuals, that the testing-phase accuracy exceeds the training-phase accuracy, that the epoch counts disagree, and that the ethics and data-availability declarations contradict the article's own contents. [RQ2.9] Assessment on demographically different and stable datasets to evaluate fairness and generalisability - proportionate to the stated limitation and the only future direction offered. [RQ3.1] None. No behaviour is observed or measured. The targets are static facial features enhanced by Gabor filtering, with the paper referring to facial cues relevant to ASD and to expression patterns and facial morphology without identifying any specific feature. [RQ3.2] No modality fusion - a single image source. The paper's fusion is across three ImageNet backbones (VGG16, DenseNet-121, XceptionNet) applied to the same photograph, which is representational concatenation rather than multimodality, and no ablation isolates any backbone's contribution. [RQ4.1] A four-stage pipeline: Gaussian Gabor filtering, concatenated features from three pretrained CNNs, a wavelet neural network classifier, and chimp-optimisation parameter tuning, with Grad-CAM++ appended for visualisation. Each stage is named as a contribution and none is ablated, so the reader cannot tell whether the Gabor stage, the three-way fusion, the wavelet classifier or the metaheuristic contributes anything to the reported figure. [RQ4.2] Gabor-filtered facial images encoded as a concatenation of three backbone feature vectors. Neither the input resolution, the fused vector dimensionality, nor the wavelet basis is stated. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure and AUC, per class and averaged, for both phases, with confusion matrices, precision-recall and ROC curves. The reporting is dense and contains one telling relationship: the 30% testing-phase average accuracy (98.42%) is higher than the 70% training-phase average accuracy (97.75%), and the per-class figures move in the same direction. A model that performs better on held-out data than on the data it was fitted to is normally a signal that the partition is not independent - shared or near-duplicate images across the split being the usual cause on this corpus - or that the reported training figure is not a resubstitution score. The paper reads the same inversion in its learning curves as good generalisation without overfitting. No confidence interval, no chance level and no variance across runs accompanies any value. [RQ4.4] Grad-CAM++ is applied and a visual interpretation figure is shown, described as highlighting the most significant facial regions and improving model transparency. The description also calls this abnormality detection, which reframes model attention as pathology. No quantitative attribution is reported, no facial region is named as consistently salient across images, and no test establishes whether the highlighted regions correspond to anything anatomically meaningful rather than to image-provenance artefacts - the question the branch most needs answered and the one a saliency method is least able to settle on unlabelled web photographs. [RQ4.5] The evaluation rests on a single image-level partition of 2,940 photographs into 70% training and 30% testing, with no cross-validation, no repetition, no seed and no statement of how the split was drawn. The corpus repeats individuals, so an image-level split does not separate children, and the number of distinct children is unknown - the same defect documented across the other fifteen members of this branch. Two further features are specific to this paper. First, the accuracy inversion: the testing phase reports 98.42% against the training phase's 97.75%, and the learning curves show validation accuracy exceeding training accuracy, which the authors interpret as evidence of good generalisation. The more usual explanation on this corpus is that the partitions are not independent. Second, the chimp optimisation algorithm tuned the classifier's parameters against an unstated objective on an unstated partition, so the reported test figure may be the outcome of a search evaluated on the data it is then reported against. On top of this, the comparison against seven quoted literature figures (92.10% to 97.76%) is drawn from other papers under unknown protocols, and no component of the four-stage pipeline is ablated. [RQ5.1] Autism Spectrum Disorder; Facial Images; Wavelet Neural Network; Deep Learning; Chimp Optimisation Algorithm. Three of five terms name pipeline machinery; validation, participants and setting are absent. [RQ5.2] Multimedia Tools and Applications 85:300 (Springer), 218 days with a revision round. A multimedia and computing venue. Review did not surface an ethics declaration stating that no human participants were involved in a study of 2,940 children's photographs, a data-availability statement denying that any dataset was analysed, a test accuracy above training accuracy read as good generalisation, or the mismatch between the stated 50 epochs and the 25-epoch learning curves. [RQ5.3] 2026. Framing is diagnostic-aid: the technique is offered as a promising diagnostic aid in clinical settings for the early and non-invasive detection of autism, and the stated research gap is a computationally efficient, privacy-preserving and accurately optimised framework - with no privacy mechanism described and no runtime measured. The contribution is expressed as a position above seven quoted figures. Its one substantive merit within the branch is its limitation paragraph, which states plainly that the dataset's lack of demographic information prevents any assessment of how facial morphology and expression vary across populations, and commits future work to demographically diverse data - the clearest statement of the branch's central problem made by any of its sixteen members, sitting alongside declarations asserting that the study used no data and involved no human participants.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Secondary analysis of the public Kinect V2 dataset Three-dimensional dataset combining gait and full-body movement of children with autism spectrum disorders, available on Zenodo and Dryad: 109 children comprising 50 typically developing, 50 moderate ASD and 9 severe ASD. The typical and moderate groups have real 3D recordings from 25 Kinect joint points with 463 pre-calculated motor features each; the nine severe-ASD children have only 2D phone video, because the original collectors could not deploy Kinect V2 in controlled settings for them. Severe-class feature vectors were therefore synthesised by averaging moderate ASD vectors and adding Gaussian noise.
narrative_rows.methods: A random forest classified three severity levels from 463-dimensional per-child vectors after z-score normalisation, with the repository's seven geometric augmentations deliberately unused. Evaluation combined 5-fold cross-validation with two 20% held-out test sets, one reserved solely for final validation, and the paper states that both are reserved subsets from the same data distribution rather than independent external validation. SHAP produced per-class importance, summary and waterfall analyses.
narrative_rows.outcomes: 84.6 +/- 10.9% accuracy under 5-fold cross-validation and 86.4% on the held-out sets. For the severe class, 100% accuracy on 4 of 4 synthetic cases with a 95% confidence interval of 39.8% to 100.0%. SHAP identified wrist movements, knee trajectories and elbow-to-foot distances as leading biomarkers, with Y-axis features declining and X-axis features increasing across severity levels.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The author states them comprehensively. The severe-ASD class contains no real measurements: its features were generated by averaging moderate ASD vectors and adding Gaussian noise, so the 100% result reflects the ability to distinguish real moderate ASD data from an artificially constructed distribution rather than true clinical severity, its 95% confidence interval runs from 39.8% to 100.0%, and a single misclassification would reduce recall to 75%. The overall sample of 109 is small, and neither held-out set constitutes external validation. Two limitations are not raised: the severity labels' own provenance and instrument are never established, and the three-class majority baseline of approximately 45.9% is never stated against which the 84.6% should be read. The dimensionality - 463 features for roughly 87 training cases - is also unremarked.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This study earns its place in the review not for its accuracy but for its reporting. It is the only charted paper that produces a 100% result and, in the same abstract sentence, explains that the result means nothing clinically and why - because the class in question was synthesised from another class. It computes an exact confidence interval on a 4-of-4 outcome (39.8% to 100.0%), states that one misclassification would move recall to 75%, specifies a minimum sample of 20 to 50 for genuine validation, declines available data augmentation that would have inflated its numbers, and states explicitly that its held-out sets are reserved subsets from the same distribution rather than independent external validation. Read against local_ed30e24c (292 of 292 read as confirming clinical suitability), local_183eaef4 (accuracy 1.0000 defended by re-running fold counts) and local_b9de0d7f (a numpy-generated target offered to educators), it demonstrates that the corpus's characteristic failure is not statistical but rhetorical. Its substantive finding is also worth carrying into the synthesis: Kinect V2 could not be deployed at all for children with severe autism, so the modality that this branch proposes as an objective severity measure is unavailable precisely for the children whose severity most needs measuring.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] One hundred and nine children from a public Kinect V2 dataset: 50 typically developing, 50 moderate ASD and 9 severe ASD. The composition is uneven in a way that determines everything else about the study - the nine severe-ASD children have no Kinect recordings at all, only 2D phone video, because the original collectors could not set up Kinect V2 in controlled laboratory settings for children with severe autism. The severe class in the analysis therefore contains no real motor measurements from any child; its feature vectors were synthesised by averaging moderate ASD vectors and adding Gaussian noise. The analysis unit is the child, one 463-dimensional vector each, and the paper reports this structure openly rather than presenting three comparable groups. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, typical development, moderate ASD, severe ASD. The register is clinical and neutral; motor differences are described as impairments in line with the cited literature, and severity terms are applied to groups rather than to children as labels. One artefact intrudes: the keyword list ends with violence level classification, evidently carried over from an unrelated manuscript. [RQ1.3] Not reported in the extracted text - no age, sex, ethnicity or socioeconomic information for any of the 109 children. The author names this as a gap prospectively rather than leaving it implicit, listing age groups, genders and cultural backgrounds among the dimensions on which generalisation must be tested in future work. [RQ1.4] Inherited from the original collection and not independently established. The three-level grouping (typical, moderate, severe) is used as the classification target and the instrument behind the moderate/severe distinction is not named in the extracted text. What the paper does establish clearly is the provenance chain: ethics approval was obtained by the original collectors from their institutional review board before collection, guardian consent was given, and this study is a secondary analysis of de-identified public data. [RQ1.5] The severity grouping is the outcome rather than a covariate, and no validated severity instrument is named. Given that the study's subject is severity classification, the absence of a stated instrument behind the labels is its largest unaddressed gap - the synthetic-data problem is discussed at length, the label-provenance problem is not. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is objective classification of three ASD severity levels from 3D motor features, identification of the contributing motor biomarkers through SHAP, and evaluation across multiple validation strategies. Headline findings: 84.6 +/- 10.9% accuracy under 5-fold cross-validation and 86.4% on the held-out sets; 100% on the severe class (4 of 4) with a 95% confidence interval of 39.8% to 100.0%; and wrist movements, knee trajectories and elbow-to-foot distances as the leading biomarkers. The abstract itself states that the severe-class result is a methodological proof-of-concept rather than clinical validation because the severe features were synthetically generated. [RQ2.2] The original recordings were made in a controlled laboratory environment for the typical and moderate groups and in clinical settings for the severe group. The reason for that difference is reported and is substantive: Kinect V2 could not be deployed in controlled conditions for children with severe autism, so only phone video was obtained. That is a real, generalisable observation about who this class of technology can and cannot measure, and it is stated plainly rather than worked around silently. [RQ2.3] Gait and full-body movement recorded with 25 Kinect V2 joint points at X, Y and Z coordinates, from which the dataset creators pre-calculated 463 features: inter-joint Euclidean distances, range-of-motion metrics, gait parameters (speed, step length, cycle time) and temporal characteristics. The severe-ASD group was recorded on a Samsung Note 9 in clinical settings, and the paper explains why extracting the same 463 features from that video was technically impossible - missing 3D coordinates, depth information and time-series data. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. Ethics is documented at both levels - institutional review board approval obtained by the original collectors before data collection, guardian written informed consent, and a secondary analysis of publicly available de-identified data in accordance with local legislation and institutional requirements. Both repository locations are given. This is complete provenance reporting for a secondary analysis and is among the best in the corpus. [RQ2.5] Microsoft Kinect V2 capturing 25 joints in three dimensions in real time for the typical and moderate groups; a Samsung Note 9 phone camera for the nine severe-ASD children. The analysis software, versions and seed are not reported. [RQ2.6] High for a secondary analysis. Both repository URLs are given with the note that they contain the same data with full documentation and metadata; the six preprocessing stages are enumerated with exact dataframe dimensions (109 x 466) and class encodings; the decision to use only original rather than the repository's seven geometric augmentations is stated explicitly; the synthetic-generation rule is described precisely enough to reproduce; and both a fold standard deviation and a 95% confidence interval are reported. Missing: model hyperparameters, software and versions, seed and code. [RQ2.7] The most thorough and self-critical limitations discussion in the charted corpus, and the only one in which the paper's own headline result is dismantled by its author. The severe-class analysis is described as the most critical limitation of the study; the reason no real data exist is explained; the synthetic-generation method is named; and the consequence is stated in full - that the reported 100% reflects the model's ability to distinguish between real moderate ASD motor data and an artificially constructed distribution, not between true clinical severity levels. The author further notes that the extremely wide confidence interval indicates high statistical uncertainty and that a single misclassification would reduce recall to 75%, sets a minimum target of 20 to 50 real severe-ASD cases for future work, and states that the two test sets are reserved subsets from the same data distribution rather than independent external validation. The one limitation not raised is the provenance of the severity labels themselves. [RQ2.9] Collect real Kinect-derived severe-ASD data with a stated minimum sample of 20 to 50; test generalisation across age groups, genders and cultural backgrounds on larger datasets from multiple institutions; and run longitudinal studies of how motor biomarkers track severity change, framed as a way to evaluate intervention effectiveness. Each addresses a specific stated limitation. [RQ3.1] Motor function measured directly in three dimensions: inter-joint distances, range of motion, gait speed, step length and cycle time, and temporal characteristics, over 25 skeletal joints. The behavioural claims arising from SHAP are anatomically specific - wrist movements, knee trajectories and elbow-to-foot distances - and are related to motor impairments reported in the prior ASD literature rather than presented as novel discoveries. A structural pattern is also reported: Y-axis features decline (30% to 10% to 0%) and X-axis features increase (70% to 90% to 100%) with increasing severity, though the severe end of that gradient is synthetic. [RQ3.2] No modality fusion - 3D skeletal motion alone. The study's most interesting observation is instead about modality availability: the severe-ASD group could not be captured with the same sensor as the other two, so the modality itself is unavailable for the group whose severity the study most wants to classify. That is a genuine finding about the deployability of depth-sensor assessment and it applies well beyond this paper. [RQ4.1] Random forest, chosen for performance, flexibility and compatibility with SHAP-based interpretation. No architecture competition, no metaheuristic and no deep learning - the modelling is subordinated to the interpretability aim. [RQ4.2] One 463-dimensional feature vector per child, pre-calculated by the dataset creators, z-score normalised, with timestamps omitted. Two aspects deserve note. The dimensionality is high relative to the sample - 463 features for 109 children, of whom roughly 87 are available for training - so the model operates in a regime where a random forest's variable selection is doing most of the work. And the repository's seven geometric augmentations (rotation, mirroring, scaling) were available and deliberately not used, a restraint that several studies in this corpus do not exercise. [RQ4.3] Accuracy with a fold-wise standard deviation (84.6 +/- 10.9%), held-out accuracy (86.4%), per-class results and, for the severe class, an exact binomial confidence interval (39.8%-100.0%) on a 4-of-4 result. Computing and reporting that interval is the single most useful reporting decision in this part of the corpus: it converts an apparently perfect result into a statement that the true accuracy could be anywhere above 40%, and the author draws exactly that inference. The fold standard deviation of 10.9 points is likewise reported rather than smoothed. What is missing: the three-class majority baseline (approximately 45.9%) is never stated, and no per-class sensitivity or specificity is given for the two real classes. [RQ4.4] SHAP applied per class with importance, summary and waterfall plots, yielding anatomically interpretable biomarkers (wrist, knee, elbow-to-foot) that the author relates to established motor findings in autism. The interpretation is properly bounded for the two real classes - the author states that for typical and moderate ASD the approach relies on biomarkers that are anatomically interpretable and reflect systematic motor patterns consistent with the literature - and implicitly withheld for the severe class, whose SHAP profile describes a distribution the author constructed. The reported axis gradient across severity is the clearest illustration: its severe endpoint (X-axis features 100%) is a property of the synthesis procedure rather than of any child. [RQ4.5] The evaluation is competently constructed at the child level - 5-fold cross-validation with a fold standard deviation reported, plus two 20% held-out sets one of which is reserved solely for final validation, and an explicit statement that neither constitutes independent external validation because both are reserved subsets from the same data distribution with the same sensor, protocol and feature pipeline. Against most of this corpus that is exemplary. The decisive issue is the severe class, and the paper states it before any reader could raise it: because no Kinect recordings exist for the nine severe-ASD children, the severe class's feature vectors were created by averaging moderate ASD vectors and adding Gaussian noise. A classifier separating that construction from real moderate data is separating a smoothed, noise-perturbed version of one distribution from the distribution itself, which is a task with a known answer and no clinical content - and the author says so, writing that the 100% result reflects the ability to distinguish real moderate ASD motor data from an artificially constructed distribution, not true clinical severity levels. The 4-of-4 result carries a 95% confidence interval from 39.8% to 100.0%, which the author computes, reports and interprets. Two further qualifications apply to the real two-class portion: 463 features for 109 children is a high-dimensional regime with roughly 87 training cases, and the three-class majority baseline of about 45.9% is never stated against which 84.6% should be read. The study is nonetheless the corpus's clearest demonstration that a near-perfect number can be reported and simultaneously explained away by the person reporting it. [RQ5.1] autism spectrum disorder; motor biomarkers; random forest; SHAP analysis; violence level classification. The last term belongs to a different paper and survives in the published keyword list. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Psychiatry 17:1751654, 107 days with a revision round. A psychiatry venue, and the fit shows in the reporting - confidence intervals on a small-sample result, an explicit statement that held-out sets are not external validation, full provenance for a secondary analysis, and a limitations discussion that identifies the study's own most striking result as uninterpretable. The revision round appears to have strengthened rather than softened these statements, since the synthetic-data caveat appears in the abstract itself. [RQ5.3] 2026, published 23 March. The framing is the most restrained in the charted corpus relative to the numbers reported. The abstract states 100% accuracy for the severe class and, in the same sentence, that this represents a methodological proof-of-concept rather than clinical validation because the features were synthetically generated; the discussion adds that a single misclassification would reduce recall to 75%; the conclusion describes the work as proof-of-concept demonstrating methodological feasibility pending validation on independent datasets; and future work is specified with a minimum sample target. Its contribution to this review is therefore not its accuracy but its demonstration that an author can report a perfect score and simultaneously explain, in the abstract, why it means nothing - the exact move that the corpus's fifteen facial-image studies and seven checklist studies do not make.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Secondary analysis of two public TalkBank child-language corpora: Eigsti et al. (48 children aged 3-6 in three balanced groups of 16 - typically developing, developmental delay, ASD - recorded in 30-minute free-play sessions, with ethnic composition reported) and Nadig and Bang (38 children, 26 typically developing and 12 with ASD, sampled at three time points over a year in parent-child interactions). Participant counts, sex, mean ages, total words and utterance statistics are tabulated by group. In the Nadig corpus the typically developing children average 29-34 months against 53-61 months for the ASD children.
narrative_rows.methods: Transcripts were retrieved via TalkBank APIs and reduced to 52 features covering participant details, utterance statistics, stem words and parts of speech. Logistic regression, a depth-2 random forest and TabNet were tuned by grid search under 5-fold stratified cross-validation and evaluated on Nadig binary, Eigsti binary, the merged data and Eigsti three-class, with six metrics each. SMOTE was applied to the Nadig corpus only and validated by Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests (KS below 0.15, p around 0.99). Overfitting was checked by a train-validation accuracy gap of no more than 4%. Logistic-regression coefficients were averaged across folds for the importance analysis.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Logistic regression reached ROC-AUC 0.93 on Nadig and 0.87 on Eigsti binary; TabNet approximately 0.96 on the merged data; random forest 0.71 on the three-class Eigsti task including developmental delay. Accuracy exceeded 86% on both binary datasets, and a model using only the top four non-part-of-speech features - Mean Length of Utterance, Mean Length of Turn Ratio, age and total words - reproduced nearly the same 86%.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The authors state several: the small size and narrow 3-6 year age range of the corpora, the loss of prosodic information (pitch, rhythm, intonation) that text cannot capture, the overfitting risk from 38-48 participants, and the markedly weaker three-class performance, which they read as showing the need for features specific to developmental delay to reduce misdiagnosis risk. One limitation is documented in their own table and not addressed: in the Nadig corpus the ASD children average roughly two years older than the typically developing children and are more male-weighted, and age is included among the features and named as one of the four carrying the result - so the 0.93 there partly measures developmental stage. The placement of SMOTE relative to the cross-validation folds is unstated, no confidence intervals or fold variance are reported, and the 68.4% majority-class baseline for the imbalanced Nadig corpus is never given.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This study contributes two things to the review. First, it makes privacy the design criterion and states the critique that the rest of the corpus does not: that a major drawback of facial-image approaches is the invasion of privacy, especially for minors, and the need to collect their images over prolonged periods of childhood. That is a direct assessment of the sixteen facial-image studies charted here, several of which reuse web-scraped photographs of identifiable children with no ethics statement, and it is made by a study that then accepts the information cost of its own choice - acknowledging that prosodic markers of atypical speech cannot be represented in text. Its privacy claim is also properly qualified, stating in the abstract that no differential privacy or encryption was implemented. Second, its three-class analysis provides another differential-diagnosis calibration point: the same features and pipeline give ROC-AUC 0.87-0.93 for ASD against typical development and 0.71 once developmental delay is included, joining local_b6ac2b98 (F1 0.86 versus 0.63) and local_69b10fe4 in quantifying how much apparent autism signal is a general clinical-versus-typical distinction. Its own weakness is a clean illustration of the confound local_7b19a959 measured directly: with a two-year age gap between groups and age in the feature set, part of its best result is developmental rather than diagnostic.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Eighty-six children across two independently collected public corpora. Eigsti et al.: 48 children aged 3-6 in three balanced groups of 16 - typically developing, developmental delay and ASD - each recorded in a 30-minute free-play session, with ethnic composition reported (39 White, 3 LatinX, 6 African-American). Nadig and Bang: 38 children, 26 typically developing and 12 with ASD, sampled at three time points over a year in parent-child interactions. The analysis unit is the child throughout, and the two corpora are analysed separately, merged, and - for Eigsti - as a three-class problem. The presence of a developmental-delay group is the design's most valuable feature and is the reason this study can say something the rest of the speech branch cannot. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, typically developing, delayed development. The register is neutral and the paper's framing is unusually ethics-forward: it argues that a major drawback of facial-image approaches is the invasion of privacy, especially for minors, and the need to collect their images over prolonged periods of their childhood, and that MRI-based approaches rely on invasive data collection raising ethical and privacy concerns. One phrase slips - facial features recorded at the onset of the disease - but the overall orientation treats the children's data as something requiring protection rather than as a resource. [RQ1.3] The most complete demographic reporting in the speech branch. Sex, participant counts, mean ages, total words and mean and median utterance lengths are tabulated by group and by sex for both corpora, and Eigsti's ethnic composition is given. That reporting is what makes the study's central confound visible: in the Nadig corpus the typically developing children have mean ages of 29 and 34 months while the ASD children have mean ages of 61 and 53 months, a gap of roughly two years, and the ASD group is 83% male against 58% in the TD group. The authors note the age difference explicitly, attributing it to the significant language delays typically observed in children with ASD - but they then include age in the feature set. [RQ1.4] Inherited from two peer-reviewed developmental-language studies, whose own diagnostic procedures are cited but not summarised. Governance is handled by reference to TalkBank's contribution requirements, which oblige contributing researchers to obtain informed consent from participants or guardians and the necessary ethical approvals before sharing. That is a reasonable basis for secondary analysis of a curated academic repository and is stated rather than assumed - a different situation from the web-scraped and platform-hosted collections elsewhere in this review. [RQ1.5] No severity or cognitive instrument is reported. The Eigsti developmental-delay group provides a partial control for general developmental level in the three-class analysis, which is the closest the study comes to separating autism-specific from delay-general language differences. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to test whether privacy-preserving machine learning on speech transcripts can screen for ASD, on the argument that structured text avoids identifiable biometric data such as raw audio or video. Headline findings: ROC-AUC 0.93 on Nadig and 0.87 on Eigsti binary with logistic regression, approximately 0.96 on the merged data with TabNet, accuracy above 86% on both binary datasets, and a four-feature model reproducing nearly the same 86%. The result the authors themselves flag as important is the three-class Eigsti task, where the best ROC-AUC falls to 0.71. [RQ2.2] No setting of the authors' own. The source recordings were 30-minute free-play sessions (Eigsti) and parent-child interactions at three time points over a year (Nadig), both naturalistic language-sampling protocols from developmental research rather than screening paradigms. [RQ2.3] Naturalistic language sampling rather than a designed classification task, which is a strength - the speech is spontaneous interaction, not an elicited response to a stimulus. The features derived from it are conversational as well as lexical: Mean Length of Turn Ratio measures the child's turn length relative to the adult's, capturing conversational participation rather than isolated production. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional analysis of longitudinally collected data. Ethics rests on TalkBank's stated requirement that contributors obtain informed consent and ethical approval before sharing, which the paper cites explicitly. The privacy argument is the paper's organising claim and it is stated with appropriate qualification: the authors acknowledge that they have not implemented explicit cryptographic privacy measures such as differential privacy or encryption, and claim only that text-based inputs inherently avoid identifiable biometric data. That qualification, placed in the abstract, is more careful than the unqualified privacy-preserving claims made elsewhere in this corpus. [RQ2.5] None for acquisition; transcripts retrieved through TalkBank APIs. Modelling used logistic regression, random forest and TabNet with grid-searched hyperparameters; no software, version or seed is named. [RQ2.6] Moderate to high. Both corpora are public and linked with their source studies cited; participant counts, sex, mean ages, total words and utterance statistics are tabulated by group; the feature count is given; the selected hyperparameters are reported for all three models; the SMOTE validation is quantified with KS statistics and p-values; and the overfitting check is reported as a numerical train-validation gap. Missing: code, seed, software versions, the complete 52-feature list, and the placement of SMOTE relative to the folds. [RQ2.7] Substantive and mostly well aimed. Stated: the small size and limited diversity of the corpora, particularly the narrow 3-6 year age range; the absence of prosodic information - pitch, rhythm, intonation - which text cannot represent and which is indicative of atypical speech in autism, an honest acknowledgement that the privacy advantage carries an information cost; the risk of overfitting given 48 and 38 participants, addressed by a quantified train-validation comparison; and the markedly lower performance on the three-class task, read as showing that features specific to developmental delay are needed to reduce misdiagnosis risk. Not stated: that the ASD and TD groups in the Nadig corpus differ in mean age by roughly two years and that age is one of the four features the paper identifies as carrying the signal. [RQ2.9] Broader age ranges, more diverse environments and dialects, transfer learning from larger speech corpora, features capturing developmental-delay-specific nuances, conversational agents or robotic assistants for scalable screening, and a multimodal extension adding limited prosodic cues while preserving the privacy advantage of text. The last is a considered trade-off rather than a generic call for more modalities. [RQ3.1] Expressive language and conversational participation in spontaneous interaction. The two leading features are behaviourally specific and directionally interpretable: Mean Length of Utterance, where lower values indicate shorter and simpler utterances and are associated with higher ASD likelihood, and Mean Length of Turn Ratio, the child's turn length relative to the adult's, where lower values indicate that the child contributes less to conversational exchange. Both correspond to well-established clinical observations, and the paper relates them accordingly rather than presenting them as discoveries. [RQ3.2] No modality fusion - text alone, deliberately. The paper's argument is that excluding audio and video is the point, since transcripts avoid identifiable biometric data, and it acknowledges the cost: prosodic features indicative of atypical speech cannot be captured in text. Its future-work proposal to add limited prosodic cues while preserving text-level privacy is an explicit privacy-information trade-off, which no other study in this corpus formulates. [RQ4.1] Three classifiers - logistic regression, random forest at maximum depth 2, and TabNet - with logistic regression selected for the interpretability analysis on the basis of its performance. The depth-2 random forest is an appropriate constraint for 38-48 cases and is reported rather than left implicit. [RQ4.2] Fifty-two tabular features per child spanning participant details, utterance statistics, stem words and parts of speech. The inclusion of age among the predictors is the study's principal unaddressed problem: the two groups in the Nadig corpus differ in mean age by roughly two years by the authors' own table, and age is reported as one of the four features that carry the result. [RQ4.3] Six metrics per model per configuration - accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and p-values - with the rationale for each stated. The reporting is complete and the paper draws the right comparison from it: ROC-AUC 0.93 for ASD versus TD in Nadig, 0.87 in Eigsti, roughly 0.96 merged, and 0.71 for the three-class task including developmental delay. Missing: confidence intervals, fold variance, and the majority-class baselines - which matter particularly for Nadig, where 26 TD against 12 ASD gives a 68.4% baseline against a reported accuracy above 86%. [RQ4.4] Well executed. Logistic-regression coefficients were accumulated across all five cross-validation folds and averaged rather than taken from a single fit, and the resulting ranking was then tested by refitting on the top four non-part-of-speech features alone, which reproduced nearly the same 86% accuracy. That reduced-model check is a genuine validation of the importance ranking rather than an assertion, and it supports the paper's privacy argument directly - fewer features means less data collection. The named features are clinically interpretable, and their directions are stated. The one problem is that age is among them, and age is confounded with group. [RQ4.5] The design is sound in structure and limited by two things the paper handles unevenly. Structurally: 5-fold stratified cross-validation at the child level, grid-searched hyperparameters under the same scheme, an explicit overfitting check reporting a train-validation gap of no more than 4% with the small sample sizes named as the reason for checking, SMOTE confined to the one imbalanced corpus and validated by Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests showing near-identical distributions, and six metrics reported for every configuration. That is careful work. Two problems remain. The first is confounding, and it is visible in the paper's own table: in the Nadig corpus the typically developing children average 29 and 34 months while the ASD children average 61 and 53 months - roughly a two-year gap - and the ASD group is 83% male against 58%. Age is then included as a feature and identified as one of the four that carry the signal. A classifier separating a four-year-old from a two-and-a-half-year-old on utterance length and vocabulary is doing developmental rather than diagnostic work, and the Nadig ROC-AUC of 0.93 cannot be separated from that. The Eigsti corpus is better matched (TD 40-45 months, ASD 55-56) and yields a lower 0.87. The second is the placement of SMOTE relative to the folds, which is not stated - though the distributional validation is more than most studies provide. Against these, the study's most valuable number is the one it foregrounds itself: 0.71 for the three-class task including developmental delay, against 0.87-0.93 for ASD versus typical development. The gap is internally controlled - same features, same corpus, same pipeline - and it quantifies how much of the binary performance is autism-specific rather than a general clinical-versus-typical distinction. [RQ5.1] Computational linguistics; Machine learning; Artificial intelligence; Feature importance; Autism spectrum disorder (ASD); Privacy. Privacy as a keyword reflects the paper's organising argument rather than being decorative. [RQ5.2] Scientific Reports 15(1):34134 (Nature Portfolio). A multidisciplinary venue. The reporting reflects it: demographic tables by group and sex, six metrics with stated rationales, a quantified overfitting check, KS validation of the oversampling, and a limitations section that names the information cost of the privacy choice. [RQ5.3] Framing is screening-support and privacy-forward, and both claims are qualified in the abstract itself - the models are described as a foundation for future applications in clinical and educational contexts, and the privacy claim is explicitly limited to the absence of biometric data rather than to any cryptographic guarantee, with the authors stating that they have not implemented differential privacy or encryption. The paper's contribution to this review is twofold. It is the only study in the corpus to make privacy the design criterion and to argue explicitly that facial-image approaches invade the privacy of minors - a critique that applies directly to the sixteen facial-image studies charted here, several of which reuse web-scraped photographs of identifiable children with no ethics statement. And its three-class result (ROC-AUC 0.71 including developmental delay, against 0.87-0.93 against typical development) joins local_b6ac2b98 and local_69b10fe4 as the review's differential-diagnosis calibration points.

narrative_rows.study_design_sample_dataset: Prospective primary study in Brazilian inclusive-education settings. Three trained education professionals supervised 12 children aged 3-6 - six with a clinical ASD diagnosis and six without, matched across age bands - who completed 640 sessions of a purpose-built three-game tablet application over three months. Guardians gave written informed consent for every child and the administering professional signed a consent form after training; children with co-occurring disorders or with disabilities impairing application use were excluded under enumerated criteria.
narrative_rows.methods: Session telemetry (duration, game identity, task-performance fields) was compiled into a tabular dataset partitioned 20% validation with the remaining 80% split 70/30 into training and testing. Seven algorithms - random forest, MLP, deep MLP, KNN, logistic regression, SVM and naive Bayes - were tuned by exhaustive grid search with 5-fold cross-validation, with the complete search space and selected values published, and learning curves plotted for each. Code and dataset are publicly deposited on GitHub.
narrative_rows.outcomes: Random forest 96% accuracy; MLP, deep MLP and SVM 94%; KNN 90%; logistic regression 82%; naive Bayes lower. Learning curves show training accuracy above validation accuracy with no abrupt decline, which the authors read as strong generalisation.
narrative_rows.key_limitations: The authors name six threats - small sample, convenience sampling and selection bias, scope restricted to ASD signs alone, overfitting risk from the reduced sample, absence of longitudinal data, and the ethical implications of school-based screening including stigmatisation and the need for professional training. They do not name the one that determines the result: 640 game sessions come from 12 children, roughly 53 each, and both the initial partition and the 5-fold cross-validation operate on sessions with no participant grouping, so every test fold contains sessions from children whose other sessions trained the model. With six children per class, a session-level split cannot yield a participant-level estimate, and leave-one-child-out validation was available. Compounding this, the paper argues that the high accuracy observed in the models and the robust metrics reinforce the low likelihood of overfitting, and reads high validation accuracy as generalisation - inverting the inference. No feature importance is reported, so nothing establishes which executive-function variables carry the 96%.
narrative_rows.relevance_notes: This study is the review's clearest example of a well-designed study undone by a single validation choice. Almost everything about it is what the field's methods literature asks for: primary collection over three months in the actual deployment setting rather than a laboratory or a download; a purpose-built task grounded in the executive-dysfunction literature rather than a repurposed dataset; age-matched groups with enumerated inclusion and exclusion criteria for both children and staff; dual written consent; the complete hyperparameter search space published for seven algorithms; code and data deposited for replication; claims bounded explicitly to screening rather than diagnosis; and a threats section that raises the risk of stigmatisation from school-based screening and the need for professional training - an ethical concern no other study in this corpus articulates. And the reported 96% is a within-participant figure from 12 children, because the 640 game sessions were split by session. It belongs alongside local_bb4d1f7a (100 eye crops per child), local_8d43288c (frame clips from 75 videos) and local_945300a5 (15 photographs per child) in the corpus's frame-level leakage group, and it is the case where that failure costs the most, since with 12 children leave-one-child-out validation was both obvious and free.
narrative_rows.review_specific_questions: [RQ1.1] Twelve children aged 3-6 years - six with a clinical ASD diagnosis and six without, matched across the same age bands - who together completed 640 game sessions over three months in their own school setting. The recruitment structure is documented in unusual detail: three inclusive-education professionals were recruited with stated inclusion and exclusion criteria, trained on the tool, and supervised the children's use of it, with guardians absent during play. The gap between the number of children and the number of analysis rows is the study's decisive feature: 640 sessions from 12 children is roughly 53 per child, and the dataset is partitioned by session rather than by child. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, typically developing children, atypical and typical children, neurotypicals. The register is educational rather than clinical and the orientation is inclusive - the stated purpose is to let educators tailor teaching to individual needs and promote inclusive education, and the discussion warns against stigmatisation. One phrase dates the framing (ASD as a neuropsychiatric disorder), and the keyword list begins with Phishing, an artefact from an unrelated manuscript. [RQ1.3] Age is reported and controlled by design - children were organised into groups G3, G4 and G5 by age, and the ASD and control groups were matched across those bands specifically to make the samples more homogeneous. Sex is not reported. Nothing on socioeconomic status or ethnicity, though the school-based recruitment in a Brazilian public inclusive-education setting is described. Guardians completed a behavioural anamnesis questionnaire whose contents are not reported. [RQ1.4] Clinical diagnosis is an inclusion criterion - children with a diagnosis form the ASD group and children without form the control group - but the diagnosing procedure, instrument and assessor are not described. The framing is honest about why this matters in context: the study's motivating problem is that a significant number of children with ASD in Brazilian early and primary education remain without an appropriate clinical diagnosis, which leaves educators without information to tailor teaching. The tool is proposed for exactly those undiagnosed children, and is trained on children whose diagnostic status is already known. [RQ1.5] None. Comorbidity and severity are handled by exclusion rather than measurement: three participant profiles are defined - ASD alone, ASD with co-occurring disorders, and children whose disabilities would impair application use - and the scope is restricted to signs of ASD exclusively, with each exclusion criterion enumerated and justified. That is transparent design, and it also means the sample excludes the children for whom screening decisions are hardest. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is a serious-game tablet application combining inclusive-design requirements with machine learning, to give educators a playful, non-invasive ASD screening aid usable inside the school day. Headline findings: random forest reached 96% accuracy, MLP, deep MLP and SVM 94%, KNN 90%, logistic regression 82% and naive Bayes lower, with learning curves showing training accuracy above validation accuracy and no abrupt decline. [RQ2.2] A specialised educational service setting within Brazilian full-day schools, with the games administered by a trained education professional during the child's normal activities and guardians not present. This is the only study in the charted corpus whose data were collected in the setting where the resulting tool would actually be used, and the choice is argued: full-day schools provide a convenient setting, the professional's existing daily relationship with the children was leveraged, and the application was incorporated into planned educational demands. [RQ2.3] Three classical games on a tablet, purpose-designed around executive functions - planning, cognitive flexibility, inhibitory control, working memory and performance monitoring - with the theoretical grounding cited to Pennington and Ozonoff and to Hill. The paradigm is genuinely constructed for the question rather than repurposed, and the games' accessibility and usability requirements were derived from a prior review stage documented in the methodology flowchart. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional analysis of three months of collection. Consent is documented at both levels - guardians signed an Informed Consent Form as the precondition for each child's participation, and the administering professional signed a Free and Informed Consent Form after training - though no ethics committee reference appears in the extracted text. The paper also contains an ethical discussion that no other study in this corpus offers: it states that the ethical implications of early screening in educational settings must be considered, including the risk of stigmatisation and the responsible use of the generated information; that screening should be understood as an initial support for identifying warning signs and guiding the search for specialised clinical evaluation, not as a definitive diagnosis; and that use of the tool should be accompanied by appropriate training for education professionals to reduce misinterpretations and promote an inclusive and respectful approach to differences. For a tool intended to be operated by teachers on undiagnosed children, that is the right set of concerns and it is stated without prompting. [RQ2.5] A tablet running the study's own serious-game application. Modelling used seven standard algorithms with grid-searched hyperparameters; no software, version, seed or compute environment is named. [RQ2.6] High on artefacts. Code and dataset are publicly deposited on GitHub with replication named as the explicit purpose - the second study in the charted corpus to release working code. The full hyperparameter grid and selected values are tabulated for all seven models; the collected data fields are listed with types and example values; inclusion and exclusion criteria are enumerated for both children and professionals; the consent procedure is described at both levels; and the game design and its executive-function rationale are documented through a methodology flowchart. Missing: an ethics committee reference, sex composition, a random seed, software versions, and - most consequentially - any statement of how the 640 sessions were assigned to the training, testing and validation partitions. [RQ2.7] One of the fullest threats-to-validity sections in the corpus, with six distinct items: small sample size as a major constraint on generalisation given the variability among individuals with ASD; convenience sampling as a source of selection bias restricting profile diversity and compromising external validity; the restriction of scope to ASD signs alone, with each exclusion criterion enumerated and justified; overfitting risk from the reduced sample; the absence of longitudinal data, with repeated collections recommended; and the ethical implications of school-based screening including stigmatisation risk. The one thing not identified is the thing that governs the result: that 640 sessions come from 12 children and are partitioned by session. The paper instead argues in the opposite direction, stating that the high accuracy observed in the models and the robust metrics reinforce the low likelihood of overfitting - which reads a symptom as reassurance. [RQ2.9] Longitudinal protocols with additional collections at different time points to assess response stability and tool robustness; larger and more diverse samples to address the convenience-sampling limitation; and training for education professionals as a condition of deployment. Each addresses a stated threat. [RQ3.1] Executive function as elicited by three purpose-built games - planning, cognitive flexibility, inhibitory control, working memory and performance monitoring - captured through session-level telemetry including duration and task-performance fields. This is behaviour observed during a designed task rather than reported on a checklist or inferred from an appearance, and the construct is theoretically motivated rather than chosen for convenience. What the paper does not do is say which behaviours distinguished the groups: no feature importance is reported, so the executive-function framing that justifies the whole design is never connected to a result. [RQ3.2] No modality fusion - game telemetry alone. The behavioural anamnesis questionnaire completed by guardians is collected and not used as a predictor, which keeps the model's inputs clean of parent-report information but also leaves an available modality unexploited. [RQ4.1] Seven algorithms under a single protocol - random forest, MLP, deep MLP, KNN, logistic regression, SVM and naive Bayes - with the full grid search published. The comparison is genuinely controlled and the spread it produces (96% down to 82% and lower) is informative in itself. [RQ4.2] One row per game session, with fields covering session duration in seconds, game identity and task-performance variables, tabulated with data types and examples. The row is a session, not a child, and the paper does not remark on the distinction anywhere. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for all seven models, plus learning curves plotting training and cross-validation accuracy against training-set size. The learning curves are read carefully - training accuracy above validation accuracy is correctly described as expected, and the absence of an abrupt decline is noted - but the reading stops short of asking why validation accuracy is so high at all. No confidence interval, no fold variance and no chance level appears; and the 96% is not related to the effective sample of 12 children. [RQ4.4] None. Random forest was the best model and supplies feature importances at no cost, and none is reported. The study's entire justification is that specific executive functions are impaired in autism and that a game can measure them, so the identification of which game-derived variables carried the signal was both available and central - and it is absent. [RQ4.5] The design is careful everywhere except the one place that determines the answer. Careful: three months of primary collection in the real deployment setting; age-matched groups organised into bands; enumerated inclusion and exclusion criteria for children and professionals; guardian and professional consent; a purpose-built task grounded in the executive-function literature; grid search with 5-fold cross-validation and the full search space published; seven algorithms under one protocol; learning curves inspected per model; code and data deposited; and a six-item threats section including the ethics of school-based screening. Decisive: the analysis unit is the game session. Six hundred and forty sessions from 12 children give roughly 53 sessions per child, and the partition into 20% validation and an 80/70/30 training-testing split - together with 5-fold cross-validation - is performed over sessions with no participant grouping described. Every fold therefore contains sessions from the same children as its training data, played on the same device in the same room with the same supervising professional, so a classifier can reach 96% by recognising individual children rather than autism. With six children per class, no session-level partition can produce a participant-level estimate. Two further points compound this. The learning curves showing high training and validation accuracy are read as suggesting a strong generalization capability, and the paper states elsewhere that the high accuracy observed in the models and the robust metrics reinforce the low likelihood of overfitting - inverting the inference, since under session-level splitting high validation accuracy is what leakage produces. And no feature importance is reported, so there is no evidence about what the 96% is built on. The remedy was available and cheap: with 12 children, leave-one-child-out validation would have given twelve honest folds. [RQ5.1] Phishing; ASD screening; Machine learning; Serious game. The first keyword belongs to an unrelated manuscript and survives in the published article. [RQ5.2] Expert Systems With Applications 295 (2026) 128884 (Elsevier) - an applied AI journal. Review did not surface that 640 analysis rows come from 12 children with no participant-level partitioning, nor the Phishing keyword. [RQ5.3] 2026. The framing is the most appropriately bounded in the primary-data group: the tool is offered as laying the groundwork for future research and practical applications to screen for suspected ASD among children in school settings, and the discussion states explicitly that screening should be understood as an initial support for identifying warning signs and guiding the search for specialised clinical evaluation, not as a definitive diagnosis, with professional training required to reduce misinterpretation and the risk of stigmatisation named. Its contribution to this review is a study that gets almost everything right about design, ethics, transparency and scope - primary collection in the real setting, matched groups, published code and data, a full hyperparameter grid, enumerated criteria, dual consent, and an unprompted discussion of screening ethics - and then reports a 96% that its own validation design cannot support, because 640 game sessions from 12 children were split by session rather than by child.

Genuinely mixed. At the segment level a majority-class baseline is computed and plotted at every window length - an empirically derived chance floor that correctly acknowledges the group-linked class imbalance, and better practice than most studies here. No code, no data, no preregistration, no analysis plan. The dataset is a reuse of the authors' own prior study, which is disclosed clearly, but neither release is available for independent checking.

Three real limitations are stated and the work is self-labelled proof-of-concept; the confound between oculomotor behaviour and visual attention is conceded outright. But nothing is said about segment-level splitting, post hoc threshold selection, unnested feature selection or the IQ difference.

items.notes: None described. No criteria, instrument, clinician, process or date for any diagnosis, and no autism screening of the comparison group. This is the weakest reference-standard reporting encountered so far in this corpus.
Feature subset, algorithm and kernel were all chosen by search on the analysis sample; six configurations are tabulated and the maximum is the abstract's claim. No prespecified operating point.

The apparatus is identical for all children and well specified down to part numbers, with electronics concealed to avoid distraction, which eliminates the acquisition-chain confounds seen elsewhere in this corpus. But the session is unstandardised: 3-5 minutes of free play, with a parent or therapist present or absent unrecorded, no instruction protocol, and no stated sampling rate.
All measurement is sensor-derived and automated; no human rating enters the feature pipeline, so differential observer bias in measurement is not a concern.

The split unit is the child, with one aggregate vector per participant, so no within-child leakage is possible - a real strength relative to most of this corpus. But the cross-validation description is terse and partly self-contradictory ('the training set with 80% of samples and the test set with 20% of the remaining samples'), and the relationship between the single 80/20 split and the 5 folds is not made precise.

Two consecutive rounds of backward elimination reduced 54 features to 10, described in a dedicated section preceding the results with the surviving features named as a fixed outcome and no indication of refitting inside folds. At 46 samples and 54 candidate features this is the regime in which unnested selection produces the largest optimism.

No majority-class baseline (which alone gives 60.9%), no permutation test, no confidence intervals or fold-level spread, no AUC. Test folds contain about nine children, so one child moves fold accuracy by 11 points. Reported accuracies also fail to reconcile with the stated sensitivity, specificity and class ratio in at least three of six rows.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: 46 children for a 54-feature selection problem plus a three-algorithm, three-kernel, four-configuration model search. The authors identify the feature-to-sample ratio as a problem and respond with feature reduction, but the reduction is itself performed on the same small sample.

Hardware reporting is excellent - board, sensor part numbers, encoder type and placement, transport protocol, firmware ecosystem, an ROS interface package - and both feature tables are complete with the final selected subset named. Analysis reporting is absent: no software, no hyperparameters for any of three algorithms, no augmentation scheme, no seeds, no sampling rate, and no diagnostic criteria.

Four metrics across six configurations is a good ablation table, and the SVM/random forest error-profile discussion is a genuine strength. But there is no uncertainty quantification of any kind, no AUC, and the accuracy column does not reconcile with sensitivity, specificity and the 28:18 ratio for several rows. The text also mis-references Table 5 as Table 4.

Data available on request from the corresponding author; hardware and firmware stack described well enough to rebuild; an ROS package developed for integration. No code repository, no preregistration, no analysis plan.

Informed parental consent under the Declaration of Helsinki, anonymised participant IDs, and psychologist supervision are all reported and appropriate. But formal ethics review was not obtained: the IRB statement asserts that non-intrusive screening 'does not require ethics approval as long as the privacy of the participants is considered', substituting an engineering-school proposal acceptance and the autism centre's internal guidelines. For research on 3-6 year old children with developmental disabilities that is not adequate. Funding (none) and conflicts (none) are declared.

No limitations section. The only concessions are that the reimplemented baseline underperformed the original because data and setup differed, and that the system should currently serve as a referral warning rather than a diagnosis. Nothing is said about the missing reference standard, the unnested feature selection, the model search, the engagement confound or the dropped clinical group.

Thirty autistic children from a single rehabilitation centre, comorbidity excluded by design, IQ 59-109, ages 5-10, sex unreported. Excluding comorbidity removes the substantial fraction of autistic children who present with ADHD, anxiety or language disorder, so the modelled population is narrower than the clinical one. No severity data means representativeness cannot be assessed at all.

Typically developing schoolchildren only. No developmental delay, ADHD, motor disorder or language disorder group, so the study cannot address whether the kinematic signature is autism-specific or a general marker of atypical development - a particular concern given that six autistic participants have IQ below the control group's floor.

Age is roughly matched (7 +/- 1.4 versus 6y8m +/- 1) with no test reported. IQ is reported only as ranges, is asymmetric, and is not adjusted for despite the task being a cognitive test and the analysis being restricted to correct trials. Sex is neither matched nor reported. Most specifically, the autistic group was undergoing psychomotor therapy at the recruiting centre while controls were not - a motor-training difference confounded with diagnosis in a study measuring motor kinematics.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: No attrition is reported among the 60 children and all appear in the analysis. But only correctly performed tasks were retained, and neither per-group error rates nor per-child retained-trajectory counts are given, so an unmeasured and plausibly group-dependent amount of data was removed.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: DSM-5 plus ADOS-2 by qualified clinicians for the autism group, with comorbidity excluded; controls excluded for suspected autism signs, developmental abnormality or psychiatric/neurological history, plus exclusion of any child about whom a clinician or teacher was uncertain. Among the strongest in this corpus, weakened only by the non-reporting of ADOS-2 scores and the absence of a screening instrument for controls.

Latent dimensionality chosen by PCA on a latent space fitted to all the data; class-conditional Gaussians used for inference and proposed as clinical thresholds fitted to all 1,500 observations; no prespecified operating point or threshold.

Identical tablet and software for every child, fixed seating geometry (table 65-70 cm, tablet within 20 cm of the edge, examiner opposite), 40 Hz logging, and instructions delivered according to the Leiter-3 manual with gesture guides and no vocal aid. Acquisition does not differ by group, which removes the recording-chain confound that undermines several other studies charted here.

Feature extraction and modelling are fully automated from logged coordinates; no human rating enters the measurement pipeline. The examiner administering the task was presumably not blind to group, but the examiner does not score anything.

The dataset is explicitly 60 children x 25 tasks = 1,500 observations, and 10-fold cross-validation is applied to those observations with no statement that a child's rows were kept together. Each test row therefore has ~22-23 same-child siblings in training. Kinematic profiles are close to individual motor signatures, so the model can separate children rather than groups.

All 12 features are used, so no feature selection occurs, but the two decisions that shape the representation - reducing the latent space from 10 to 2 dimensions via PCA, and fitting the class-conditional bivariate Gaussians - were both made on the complete dataset rather than within training folds.

Accuracy is the only metric: no sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, AUC or confusion matrix, so the error profile is unknown. The +/- 5.6% is a fold standard deviation, not a confidence interval, and carries little meaning under observation-level folds. Chance is unambiguously 50% given the balanced design, but no baseline or permutation test is reported, and no participant-level accuracy is computed despite the participant-level latent plot being presented.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Sixty children for a deep generative model plus predictor. The 1,500-row dataset gives an appearance of adequate sample that the 60 independent units do not support, and the paper itself attributes its need for supervised training to 'the sample size and its characteristics'.

Task, hardware, capture rate, seating, all 12 feature definitions, the extraction package and the full three-term loss with its weighting are specified precisely. The network itself is not: no layer widths, optimiser, learning rate, batch size, epochs, seeds or code, despite two pages of textbook exposition on what neural networks are. The fold-assignment procedure is not described.

One number for the entire classification result, with no class-conditional metrics, no confusion matrix, no AUC and no confidence interval. The participant-level accuracy that the paper's own Figure 3 invites is never computed. Feature effects from the Monte Carlo analysis are presented graphically without effect sizes or uncertainty.
Raw data offered by the authors without undue reservation - a real if informal commitment. No code, no preregistration, no analysis plan, and no deposited dataset.

Approved by the Ethical Committee of Psychological Research of the Department of Humanities, University of Naples Federico II, with written informed consent from legal guardians. The conflict-of-interest statement discloses that two authors were employed by the rehabilitation centre that supplied the autistic participants - material and correctly declared. Funding is not reported.

A single stated limitation, and a conceptual one: that supervision was needed so the model still depends on traditional assessment for ground truth. Nothing about the observation-level cross-validation, the single-metric reporting, the in-sample fitting of the latent structure and class densities, the restriction to correct trials, the IQ asymmetry, the unreported sex distribution, or the psychomotor-therapy confound.

Thirty children from one tertiary hospital, selected only by ADOS-2 module, with a single overall mean age of 3.65 years and no age range, sex, IQ, language or severity data. Twenty-nine of thirty are autistic. Nothing can be established about which children the pipeline works for, and body proportions and postural control vary widely across the 12-month-to-5-year span the included modules cover.

One typically developing child among 30 participants. This is not a comparison group, and no between-group analysis is attempted or possible, yet the paper's framing is early autism screening throughout.

No covariates are measured, so none can be controlled. The specific uncontrolled factor that matters is postural and motor variation with age: the 90 degree shoulder threshold is applied uniformly to children who may differ by several years in development, and it is measured in 2-D image coordinates from a single uncalibrated fixed camera, so seating position and orientation relative to camera C1 confound the angle.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: No attrition is reported and all 30 children appear in the results. Perception failures are acknowledged only anecdotally - one child's mask prevented facial landmark detection - with no systematic accounting of detection, tracking or landmark failure rates across the 109 events.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: A single experienced clinician scores each child, unblinded and while simultaneously conducting the assessment, with no second rater and no inter-rater reliability statistic - on an item requiring a real-time judgement about eye contact made from behind the child. The scoring rule is explicit and well specified, which prevents a worse rating, but the standard is one person's uncorroborated judgement.

Five decision constants set by hand and reported on the same data; the trained detector fitted on images of the same 30 children. No development set, no held-out participants, no prespecified operating point.

The camera rig is fixed and identical across sessions (four cameras, common 1.44 m height, stated focal length, 25 fps, 1280 x 720) and the clinical protocol is followed as written, so acquisition is consistent. But no camera calibration is performed, the caller's side varies between sessions so the contributing rear camera varies, and the number of accompanying parents is deliberately unconstrained - all accepted as realism, at the cost of standardisation.

The automated judgement is fully deterministic and never sees the clinician's score, so the index test is blind to the reference standard by construction. The converse does not hold - but the clinician scored in real time during the session, before any automated output existed.

No split of any kind. Decision thresholds hand-set and evaluated on the same 30 children; YOLOv3 retrained on more than 1,700 images drawn from those same 30 subjects, so the detector has seen every child it is evaluated on. No estimate exists of performance on an unseen participant.

No feature selection occurs - all features are hand-specified and both angle definitions are fixed a priori, which removes selection bias as a mechanism. The threshold constants nonetheless play the same role as fitted parameters and were chosen with the evaluation data in view.

No chance-agreement baseline despite 17 of 30 children scoring 5 and each contributing five non-response events, so the 98.2% event-level figure sits above an unstated and high floor. No weighted kappa or ICC for what is an ordinal agreement problem, no confidence intervals, and the 109 events are treated as independent although they cluster within 30 children and are serially dependent.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Thirty children, of whom one is not autistic. One misclassified child moves participant-level accuracy by 3.3 points, so the headline improvement from 83.3% to 93.3% rests on three children.

Unusually complete for the pipeline: camera count, height, focal length, resolution and frame rate with each camera's role; the clinical protocol and its full 0-5 scoring tree; the angle computation written out as three equations; every threshold constant stated numerically with a rationale for the duration constant; and every third-party model named, including the size of the custom detection training set. A competent group could rebuild the system from the text.

Results are reported at both aggregation levels with the full 6 x 6 score confusion matrix published and the two errors diagnosed concretely - all creditable. But there are no confidence intervals, no chance-corrected agreement statistic, no per-component error rates, and the inverted positive/negative convention, though stated, invites misreading of the sensitivity and specificity figures.

Data declared confidential; no code, no retrained detector weights, no annotations, no preregistration. The reliance on published third-party models partially offsets this at the level of reconstructibility but not of verifiability.

Parental informed consent obtained before each session and faces mosaicked in published figures - appropriate handling for clinical video of preschool children with disabilities. But the ethics statement is a single clause, 'these experiments have passed an ethical review', with no committee, institution or approval number named. Funding and competing interests are declared.

No limitations section. The two error cases are analysed well and the methods contain a correct and creditable scope disclaimer that the study assesses response to name rather than autism risk - but that disclaimer is contradicted by the abstract's 'consistency ... with clinical diagnosis' and by the conclusion's proposal of deployment for early autism screening in remote areas. Nothing is said about the absence of validation, the chance-agreement floor, the single unblinded rater, or the demographic gaps.

Twenty autistic boys with 'high-performance autism' from one Tehran clinic, restricted further to those who could sit at a computer, tolerate calibration and whose face perception a therapist judged adequate; 5 of 25 approached (20%) excluded on those grounds. All male. No severity or cognitive measure, so representativeness is unassessable.

Mainstream schoolchildren described as 'normal' and 'healthy', with no screening instrument, no stated exclusion criteria and no evidence that autism or other conditions were ruled out. No clinical comparison group, which the authors themselves identify as needed for differential diagnosis.

Age is matched to within three weeks and sex is constant by design, which are real strengths. Everything else is uncontrolled: no IQ or cognitive measure on what is fundamentally a visual matching task, no language measure, and no accounting for the fact that the JAFFE stimuli are other-race faces for an Iranian sample - a factor the paper's own literature review shows it is aware of.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Twenty per cent of approached autistic children were excluded before recording, for reasons (refusal to sit, calibration failure) that plausibly correlate with sensory and attentional difficulty, with no characterisation of those children and no comparable filter applied to the comparison group. Out-of-range gaze samples were retained by enlarging the analysis space rather than quantified, and no tracking-ratio or data-loss statistic is reported.
