domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Clinic admission following diagnosis by a paediatric psychiatrist and a paediatric clinical psychologist, with no instrument, criteria version, date or reliability reported, and a comparison group established only by school recruitment and the label 'normal', with no screening.

Four feature subsets compared on the same data with the best reported; network architecture unreported; iteration count and learning coefficient tuned by MSE on an unstated partition; and the quoted operating characteristics taken from the pooled total rather than the test partition.

One eye tracker, one laboratory, one stimulus set and one protocol for both groups, with calibration required before recording - so acquisition does not differ by group. But the eye tracker is never identified by make, model or sampling rate, the fixation-detection parameters are unstated, and no calibration accuracy criterion is given, which matters because every feature is a fixation count or duration.
Feature extraction and classification are automated from logged gaze data; no human rating enters the measurement pipeline.

Arithmetic on the reported percentages fixes the dataset at 240 rows split 168/36/36, i.e. six rows per child randomly scattered across partitions, so every test row has five siblings from the same child in training. Region-level fixation counts and durations are stable individual characteristics, making this a direct leakage channel.

No selection algorithm was used, but four predefined feature subsets were each evaluated on the same data and the best-performing one reported as the study's result, which is selection by another route.

The headline precision and accuracy are pooled across training, validation and test; held-out test accuracies are 52.8-58.3% against a 50% chance floor on 36 observations. No baseline, permutation test or confidence interval is reported, and ROC curves are plotted without AUC values. The consistent ~20-point train-to-test gap across all four configurations is never mentioned.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Forty children, 240 rows, 18 features, and a neural network of unreported size. The 36-observation test partition means a single observation moves test accuracy by 2.8 points, and three observations separate the reported test result from chance.

Task design, stimulus source, region segmentation, feature definitions, MATLAB version, training algorithm and activation functions are all given. Missing: the eye tracker's identity, sampling rate and accuracy; the fixation-detection parameters; the MLP's hidden layers and node counts; the learning rate and iteration count actually used; the split procedure and seed; and the fact, recoverable only by arithmetic, that the modelled units are observations rather than children.

The tables are commendably disaggregated by partition, which is the only reason the held-out figures are recoverable at all. But the abstract, results narrative and conclusion all quote the pooled total, roughly 15 points above the test value, without noting the distinction; no confidence intervals are given anywhere; and ROC curves are shown without AUC.
Data available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. No code, no preregistration, no analysis plan, no deposited dataset.

Ethics approval from a named committee with a verifiable identifier (IR.IAU.SRB.REC.1401.152), stated in its own subsection - better than most reports charted here. But parental consent appears only as an inclusion criterion for the autistic group, with no consent statement for the school-recruited comparison children and no mention of child assent. Funding and competing interests are declared.

Three limitations are stated, of which one - the need for clinically overlapping comparison conditions - is genuinely important. None of the decisive issues is acknowledged: the pooled-versus-held-out reporting, the observation-level split, the train-to-test gap, the subset comparison, the all-male sample, the other-race stimuli, or the differential attrition.

Fifteen autistic adults, verbally fluent native English speakers with IQ comparable to controls, recruited at a specialist research centre and able to hold an unstructured conversation with a stranger. This is the cognitively able end of the adult spectrum, and no severity score is reported to characterise it further.

Neurotypical controls recruited specifically as such and described to raters as clear cases. No clinical comparison group. The authors state the limitation explicitly and call for future work on neurodiverse samples, which is the correct diagnosis of the problem but does not remedy it here.

Groups matched on chronological age, sex ratio, WASI-II full-scale IQ and verbal IQ, with a stated test of each - the most complete matching in this corpus. Native English fluency required of all participants. Confederates blind to diagnostic status and unaware of the dependent variables, so elicitation was not differentially shaped. Facial identity is explicitly modelled and removed at the feature stage.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Two of 44 enrolled participants excluded, with both reasons stated (absent consent for this specific set of experiments; data unavailable for processing), and the resulting 42 fully analysed. The consent-based exclusion indicates granular per-experiment consent.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Clinical Best Estimate informed by ADOS-2 Module 4 and adhering to DSM-5, established prospectively as part of the study rather than inherited from records. Controls deliberately recruited as neurotypical. The only gaps are the absence of a reported ADOS-2 severity score and of a consensus reliability figure.

Linear SVM at default C = 1, no feature selection, one hyperparameter tuned in a nested loop over four values. The representation choices - identity removal, localised basis, exclusion of nose and cheek components and of FACS units - are argued a priori on stated principles rather than selected for performance.

Identical dual-camera device, resolution, frame rate and placement for every participant; a semi-structured paradigm with specified confederate training rules, timing constraints and a verbatim prompt; camera parameters supplied to the 3DMM fitting to decouple expression from pose. No group-dependent acquisition differences.

The pipeline is fully automated and label-free at inference. Confederates were blind to diagnostic status and unaware of the dependent variables. Human raters were necessarily unblinded to the task but were told only that cases were clear-cut, not which was which, and viewed videos in randomised order with a single viewing and no revisiting.

One feature vector per participant makes the split unit the person by construction. Nested cross-validation with 10 folds repeated 100 times with shuffled participant order addresses fold-assignment variance. The 3DMM identity-removal step additionally strips the individual-appearance information that drives leakage elsewhere in this corpus.

No feature selection is performed, so selection bias cannot arise despite 6,272 features. The single tuned hyperparameter is optimised in the inner loop. Regularisation is left at default rather than searched.

Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV are all reported - the most complete metric set here - and per-participant error analyses go beyond summary statistics. But no majority-class baseline (64.3%), permutation test, AUC or confidence interval is given, and the sensitivity of 0.55 is stated once and never discussed while the abstract quotes only accuracy.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Forty-two participants and 6,272 features. The linear model, fixed regularisation and absence of feature selection mitigate the dimensionality, and the nested participant-level scheme means the estimate is honest, but one participant is 2.4 accuracy points and the error-overlap finding rests on five hard cases with no uncertainty quantification.

The paradigm (including confederate training rules and verbatim prompt), hardware, 3DMM method and its rationale, basis construction, exact cross-correlation scheme with lag convention and overlap, feature count derivation, classifier and its fixed C, hyperparameter grid, and validation scheme are all fully specified - as is the entire human-rating protocol. Table 1 demographics were not recoverable from the retrieved text.

Five operating characteristics for the model and three levels of human aggregation, plus two per-participant analyses with a quantified correlation. But no confidence intervals, no AUC, no significance test on the human-versus-AI comparison or the error-overlap claim, and the abstract and conclusion foreground accuracy while omitting the 0.55 sensitivity.

No code, no data, no preregistration, and the modified localised expression basis - the study's most reusable artefact - is not released. The reliance on published components (3DI) partially offsets this for reconstruction but not for verification.

IRB approval from the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia is stated, and the exclusion of two participants for not consenting to this specific set of experiments evidences granular per-experiment consent - a strong governance signal for identifiable facial video. Four NIH grants are itemised. No competing-interests statement appears in the retrieved text.

Six substantive limitations are stated, including several that comparable papers omit entirely: the neurotypical-only comparison group with an explicit call for neurodiverse samples, the adult-only sample, the monadic rather than dyadic analysis, the partial interpretability with a specific statement of where it stops, the sample-size constraint given as the actual reason for the modelling choice, and the need for user research before clinical benefit can be claimed. The unaddressed items are the 0.55 sensitivity, the missing chance baseline, and the unmatched information available to human raters.

One hundred and forty autistic children recruited through hospitals and rehabilitation services with no stated inclusion or exclusion criteria beyond normal or corrected vision, no diagnostic characterisation and no severity or cognitive measure. Representativeness cannot be assessed. The sample is nonetheless large and drawn from multiple sites in two provinces, which is more than most studies here offer.

School-recruited typically developing children with no reported screening for autism or developmental concerns. No clinical comparison group, so the study cannot address whether the viewing signature is autism-specific or a general marker of atypical development or of reduced task engagement.

Age is well matched (4.66 +/- 1.00 versus 4.77 +/- 0.92). Sex is not: 80.0% male in the autistic group against 63.2% in the comparison group, unmatched, unadjusted and unmentioned, in a paper that separately reports higher error rates in boys. No cognitive or developmental measure exists to separate an autism-specific viewing pattern from a general attentional or developmental one, and the authors' own account of grey-mask fixations in 3-4 year olds shows the two are confusable.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Device-level noise handling is specified numerically (merge points below 0.02, delete merged points under 0.1 s) and the minLength filter is analysed rather than assumed, with the authors demonstrating that a stricter setting would preferentially discard autistic children's data - a genuinely careful piece of work. But no attrition, exclusion or data-quality accounting is reported for the 333 children, and no calibration procedure or tracking-ratio statistic is given.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Not described. No instrument, criteria, clinician or process for either group in the main text, and no screening of the comparison group. Table IV lists comparator studies' instruments while leaving the study's own blank.

The Otsu threshold is fitted across training and test subjects together; network size, epochs, batch size, learning rate and minLength were compared on the evaluation data with no development set; and the 60-stimulus shortened protocol is selected in-sample from the same data on which accuracy is reported.

Identical eye tracker, sampling rate, screen, image geometry, viewing distance, display and mask timing and stimulus set for every child, in a consistent therapy-room arrangement with at most two accompanying adults. Acquisition does not differ by group. The absence of a described calibration procedure is the one gap.
The entire pipeline from fixation detection through scoring is automated and label-free at inference; no human rating enters the measurement chain.

Subject-level 50% split repeated over five random permutations with the minimum reported, so all 82 patterns from a child stay together - the correct design for a model that scores individual stimuli. The semantic autoencoder is trained on MS COCO rather than participant data, closing a second potential leakage path.

No feature selection occurs and the full vector enters the model. But the Otsu threshold is fitted transductively across training and test scores, and the stimulus-discriminability ranking that motivates a shortened protocol is computed on the evaluation data.

Accuracy at two aggregation levels, sensitivity, specificity, AUC, ablations, subgroup breakdowns by sex and age, and a five-permutation stability range - a fuller reporting set than almost anything else in this corpus. Missing: confidence intervals, a majority-class baseline (57.6%), and any prevalence-adjusted metric such as PPV, which is the number that matters for the proposed community-screening use.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Three hundred and thirty-three children, 165 in the test set, with 82 stimulus patterns each - by a wide margin the largest sample charted here, and the paper argues explicitly and with supporting visualisation that samples under 100 subjects cannot characterise model performance.

The computational pipeline is specified to reimplementation standard - stimulus protocol, device and its noise rule, superpixel step, autoencoder corpus and loss, full LSTM equations, feature concatenation, weak-supervision labelling, aggregation, thresholding, and a parameter sensitivity table including a reported negative result. The clinical protocol that produced the labels is entirely absent, as are the final architecture dimensions and any calibration procedure.

Two aggregation levels, sensitivity and specificity, AUC, ablations, five-permutation robustness with the minimum reported, and honest subgroup breakdowns that surface unflattering findings. But no confidence intervals, no chance baseline, and no prevalence-adjusted metric for a tool proposed for universal screening.
No code, no data, no stimulus set, no preregistration. Supplementary figures and tables are available through the publisher.

Approval by the Medical Ethics Committee of Northwestern Polytechnical University under protocol 202002032 with Declaration of Helsinki conformity - a named committee with a protocol number, better than most reports here. But no parental consent or child assent statement appears for a study of 333 children aged 3-6, and no competing-interests statement is given. Funding is itemised.

Failure modes are analysed concretely (natural scenes, small objects, edge-placed objects) and the age restriction is stated. The subgroup findings on rehabilitation training and on younger children's inattention are reported honestly and are the paper's most important caveats, though their implications for what the marker measures are not drawn out. Nothing is said about the undescribed reference standard, the sex imbalance, the transductive threshold, or the in-sample parameter and stimulus selection.

Two hundred and twenty-one accounts found by keyword search of public biographies, with no demographic, cognitive or severity information for anyone. Self-disclosure of autism on social media selects a narrow and self-organised slice of the population - verbally fluent, digitally engaged, frequently diagnosed in adulthood - and nothing characterises which slice.

Thirty-one users whose selection is never described, unmatched on any attribute and unscreened for undisclosed autism, supplying the entire 45,000-tweet negative class at roughly 1,450 tweets each. The negative label means 'did not state it publicly', not 'is not autistic'.

No covariate is known so none can be controlled. The specific uncontrolled confound is topic: the positive class was assembled by searching for autism keywords, autism-related vocabulary was not removed from the tweets, and no topic analysis was run, so subject matter is fully confounded with the label. Author identity is a second uncontrolled factor, since the split does not separate writers.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Four cleaning steps are stated clearly and removed 60% of the raw corpus (1,014,723 to 404,627 tweets) - duplicates, retweets, incompletely extracted tweets and cross-platform auto-posts. The reduction is appropriately reported in aggregate but is not broken down by user or group, and how the 90,000-tweet balanced subsample was drawn from the 404,627 is not described.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Unverified self-disclosure in a public biography, with no diagnosis, instrument or verification, and an undescribed, unscreened negative class. The manual exclusion of organisations, advocates and family members is careful and well documented, but it improves the precision of a keyword search rather than establishing a diagnosis.

Best of four models compared on the same split, with grid-searched hyperparameters and no separate validation set. The text representation given to the three classical models is never stated, so the model-family comparison cannot be interpreted.

There is no elicitation protocol at all: the behavioural sample is whatever each user chose to post over five years, unconstrained in topic, audience, length, purpose or timing, spanning both the 140- and 280-character limits. Nothing about the measurement is standardised across users or classes.
Classification is automated and does not consult labels at inference; labels were assigned from profile text before any modelling.

A single random 75/25 split over tweets, not authors. Each of the 31 comparison users has roughly 1,090 of their own tweets in training and 360 in test; the model can succeed by recognising individual writing styles rather than any autism-related property. No performance estimate exists for an unseen writer.

No feature selection is described, but no text representation is described either, and the grid search over classical-model hyperparameters had no validation set separate from the reported test data. No autism-related vocabulary was masked, so the most obvious confound was left in the input.

One random split with no cross-validation, no repetition, no confidence interval and no chance baseline (50% at the tweet level). Full confusion matrices are reported, which is a real strength and exposes the decision tree's near-degenerate behaviour, but sensitivity and specificity are never computed and no user-level metric is given.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Ninety thousand tweets is ample for the models used, but the effective sample is 252 writers and, for the negative class, 31 - which is the number that governs generalisation. The apparent statistical power of a 22,500-tweet test set is illusory given that it contains no new authors.

Data collection is well described - six keywords, three manual exclusion rules with examples, four cleaning steps, date range, counts before and after - and model hyperparameters and the BERT checkpoint are given. But the selection of the 31 comparison users, the text representation for the classical models, BERT's fine-tuning regime and any random seed are all absent.

Full confusion matrices for all four models are published, which is better practice than accuracy alone and is what makes the decision tree's degenerate behaviour visible. But no confidence intervals, no chance baseline, no sensitivity or specificity computed from the counts, no AUC, and no user-level result.

No code, no data, no preregistration. The dataset consists of identifiable individuals' posts and could not be shared straightforwardly, which is a reason to have addressed data governance rather than to omit it.

No ethics approval, no ethics committee, no consent, and no discussion of the ethics of training an autism classifier on identifiable people's public health disclosures harvested without their knowledge. The only privacy measure is redacting username, location and date of birth from two example biographies 'in compliance with Twitter's policies' - a platform-terms consideration, not a research-ethics one. No competing-interests statement. Funding is acknowledged.

Two limitations stated, both about label truthfulness, and both valid. Nothing about the tweet-level split, the 31-user negative class, topic confounding, the absent demographics, the missing user-level metric, or the mismatch between a paper titled 'Early Detection' and a dataset of adult social-media users.

Consecutive well-child attenders at four primary care clinics, with autism ascertained prospectively at 9.2% prevalence - much closer to a deployment population than the case-control norm here. Limits: caregiver education is very high (82.8% college degree), ADOS-T scores are tightly clustered (7.64 +/- 1.69) suggesting a narrow severity band, no cognitive measure exists, and the 40% valid-data threshold silently removes children who could not sustain attention.

Typically developing toddlers from the same clinics, all screened with M-CHAT-R/F - screened rather than assumed, which is better than almost anything else in this corpus. But screen-negative children did not receive ADOS-T, and the developmental-delay comparison that would test differential specificity sits in a supplementary appendix rather than in the main analysis.

Two candidate confounds are handled properly: percentage of missing data and landmark variation are both shown to correlate weakly with the outcome, tested for group difference, and entered as ANCOVA covariates individually and jointly, with the group difference preserved. But three demographic differences - age (3.6 months), sex (29 points) and race/ethnicity (30 points White, 25 points Hispanic/Latino) - are reported and none is adjusted, in a paper that demonstrably knows how to run ANCOVA.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: The most careful treatment in this corpus. Missing points are excluded at the embedding-vector level inside the entropy computation, with a worked example showing why concatenation would bias the estimate; a 40% validity threshold is applied per movie with a cited justification; missing-data percentage is shown not to differ between groups and is used as a covariate. The only gap is that per-movie analysed counts appear graphically rather than in a table.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Universal M-CHAT-R/F within routine care, ADOS-Toddler by a child psychologist for screen-positives and concern-flagged children, ADOS-T totals reported, and the single discordant case disclosed explicitly. Comparison group screened rather than assumed.

Regions chosen a priori with cited rationales; entropy parameters taken from prior literature with a sensitivity appendix; filter cut-off justified physiologically; integration window and validity threshold specified in advance; no feature selection. The only in-sample choice is restricting the secondary classification to social movies.

Identical iPad, camera, frame rate, movie set and 60 cm placement for every child, with a standardised room arrangement (caregiver holds child, others stand behind). Head motion is removed by affine normalisation to a canonical face rather than left as a confound, and camera-relative pose angles are estimated explicitly.

The entire measurement chain from face detection through entropy is automated and label-free. The affect estimator used as comparator was previously validated against human frame-by-frame coding on 136,450 frames with an intraclass correlation of 0.9.

Leave-one-out cross-validation over participants, with one feature vector per child per movie, so within-participant leakage is impossible. The primary claims rest on group comparisons rather than on a fitted predictive model, where cross-validation is not the operative safeguard.
No feature selection occurs - two prespecified features. Preprocessing parameters are fixed a priori from literature and shown insensitive in an appendix, so none is fitted to the outcome.

Effect sizes reported for every statistical comparison and interpreted as a gradient, ANCOVA confound adjustment, DeLong AUC comparisons, and an internal non-social control condition - stronger than anything else here. But the classification arm lacks confidence intervals, quotes no numeric AUC, gives no majority-class baseline (about 91% at 9.2% prevalence), and reports precision and recall arithmetically incompatible with the stated class ratio, implying an undisclosed balancing step.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: 436 participants overall is large for this corpus, but only 40 are autistic, and the analysed number per movie is smaller still after the 40% validity threshold. The authors state directly that the sample 'did not have sufficient power to determine the impact of demographic characteristics on the results', which is the correct acknowledgement given three unadjusted demographic imbalances.

The most complete in this review: recruitment pathway, all exclusion criteria, room and device arrangement, all six movies with durations and content, the full preprocessing chain with justified parameters, the entropy formulation with its missing-data rule and a worked numerical example, the across-subject normalisation, and every statistical test named to the Python function. Five supplementary appendices carry sensitivity and secondary analyses.

Effect sizes accompany every significance test and are interpreted, confound adjustments are reported, and three convergent analyses support the redundancy conclusion. But the classification arm has no confidence intervals, no numeric AUC, no chance baseline, and an unexplained class-handling step.
No code, no data, no stimulus set, no preregistration. The pipeline rests on the group's own previously published components, which aids conceptual reconstruction but not verification.

Duke University Health System IRB approval under two named protocol numbers; written informed consent from caregivers or legal guardians; inability to consent in English or Spanish disclosed as an exclusion criterion. Funding from eight sources itemised with an explicit no-role statement. The competing-interests disclosure is the most detailed in this corpus, covering technology licensed to Apple, patents, company directorships, advisory boards and consulting - and is accompanied by a structural mitigation, with data analysis independently and continuously reviewed by a named conflict-free co-author.

Three limitations stated, all real, including the important one that adult-trained detectors were applied to toddlers and that the sample lacked power to assess demographic effects. Not acknowledged: the unadjusted age, sex and race differences specifically; the in-sample selection of social movies for the classification analysis; the undisclosed class handling; and the fact that ADOS-T scores were obtained but never related to the biomarker.

Fifteen autistic adults and fifteen autistic children recruited through psychiatric services, all without intellectual difficulties but with no IQ measured. The authors state the sample comprises 'only a small number of mild (high-functioning) cases' and that it remains unclear whether findings extend across the spectrum - an accurate self-assessment.

The strongest comparison structure in this review after the human-benchmark study: neurotypical controls actively screened by physicians and psychologists, plus a psychiatric comparison group of 15 adults with schizophrenia assessed with PANSS. The schizophrenia group is not used to build a differential classifier, which is a missed opportunity, but its presence supports the parallel analysis that yields the paper's most valuable finding.

Group sizes were equalised, but by ranking controls on SRS-2 - a variable related to the classified construct. Adult groups differ by up to six years in mean age with very different variances; children's groups are 87% versus 47% male; autistic children score 17.6 against 6.88 on the ADHD Rating Scale, an unaddressed attentional confound in a gaze task. None of these is adjusted. Against this, FEIT recognition scores were equivalent across all groups, so differential task success is excluded as an explanation for the gaze differences.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Two explicit exclusion rules - scan-path length of zero, and a minimum 40% gaze-sample retention - with the resulting per-emotion trial counts listed exactly so attrition is visible. But the eight participants whose gaze never left the centre were retained and misclassified by every model; the error analysis identifies them precisely and diagnoses the cause, which is more than any other study here does, though no handling procedure follows.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: DSM-5 research criteria with ADOS-2 re-evaluation for autism (adult mean total 46.5 +/- 11.9) and PANSS for schizophrenia (67.1 +/- 13.0); controls screened by clinician interview with stated exclusions for psychiatric history, drug abuse, epilepsy, learning delay and communication problems. Every group has an explicit ascertainment procedure.

Three gaze features fixed a priori from cited literature, no feature selection, architectures fixed in advance with a stated small-data rationale, and the learning rate as the only tuned quantity, optimised inside the nested inner loop.

Identical eye tracker, 120 Hz sampling, 65 cm viewing distance, display resolution, stimulus set and trial timing for all participants, with a one-second fixation cross standardising the starting gaze position. The I-VT threshold is stated at 100 degrees per second and areas of interest are redrawn per image so that mouth-region measurement is not biased by expression-dependent mouth size.
The measurement chain from gaze sampling through event classification to modelling is automated and label-free. Verbal emotion responses were scored against an objective key.

Nested leave-one-participant-out cross-validation with all of a held-out person's 21 or 32 trials excluded from training, and the learning rate tuned in the inner loop. Trial-level leakage is structurally impossible, which matters because the per-trial classifier operates on stimulus images shown identically to everyone.
No feature selection occurs. The random-forest weighting layer is trained within folds and its importances averaged across them rather than fitted once on the full sample.

Group sizes equalised so chance is 50%, every accuracy tested against it with a binomial test, and the failing result (schizophrenia, p = 0.052) reported as marginal rather than rounded into significance - the clearest chance handling in this corpus. Missing: confidence intervals, AUC, and any adjustment for the fact that four model variants were compared per problem.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Thirty to thirty-one participants per classification problem, so one person is roughly three accuracy points and the 10-point and 16.7-point weighting gains correspond to about three and five participants. The authors identify small sample size as their first limitation. Per-fold training sets of 630-651 trials give an appearance of adequacy that 30 independent participants do not support.

Instrument battery, FEIT protocol and timing, eye tracker and sampling rate, viewing distance, I-VT threshold, area-of-interest definitions and per-image redrawing, both exclusion rules with resulting trial counts, scan-path pseudocode, both architectures with layer and kernel sizes, optimiser, loss, epoch cap, early-stopping patience, heat-map construction with Gaussian sigma and downscaling, and the nested cross-validation with its inner split - all specified. Statistical procedures named including the Benjamini-Hochberg correction.

Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for all four variants across all three problems, plus binomial tests against chance with the failing p-value shown. Per-emotion means and standard deviations tabulated for every feature. But no confidence intervals anywhere, no AUC, and no correction for comparing four model variants per problem.

Raw data offered by the authors without undue reservation; model architectures fully tabulated and the scan-path algorithm published as pseudocode. No code repository and no preregistration. The FEIT stimuli are under copyright and could not be reproduced even as figures.

Approved by ethics committees at both Nara Medical University and Nara Institute of Science and Technology; the procedure explained and informed consent obtained at the start of recording, with written consent from legal guardians recorded in the formal statement. Funding from a single CREST grant stated; competing interests declared as none.

Three limitations, all substantive: small sample, absence of IQ data with an explicit statement that the sample is mild and high-functioning, and - unusually - a documented failure mode found by inspecting the participants that every model misclassified, showing that some people complete the task using peripheral vision without moving their eyes, quantified at 6.5% of adults and 17% of children. Not acknowledged: the trial-as-unit statistical analysis, the SRS-2-based control selection, and the age and sex imbalances.

Self-selected app downloaders with labels from the 3.4% who chose to complete an optional survey. No criteria, no clinical characterisation, no severity or language measure. The one genuine strength is that AAC users are drawn from the minimally verbal end of the spectrum, a population systematically absent from the rest of this corpus - but nothing in the study characterises them.

Uniquely in this corpus, the comparison group consists of other people who need augmentative communication rather than typically developing controls, which is the clinically realistic contrast. But it is a convenience aggregate of eight categories - 49 'other' and 32 'none' out of 99 - dominated by acquired adult-onset conditions, so it differs from the autism group in age and aetiology as well as diagnosis.

None attempted. Age is collected but reported only as a marginal distribution, never by group, never adjusted - in a design where congenital childhood autism is contrasted against stroke, dementia, ALS and brain injury. The paper's own background section describes older AAC users struggling with non-intuitive interfaces, which is a description of the usage difference the classifier may be detecting. No sex, IQ, language or severity data exist.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: 761 of 6,033 users (12.6%) excluded for too few events, with no characterisation of who they were or how exclusion differed by group. The data were logged for debugging with 'little attention... given to the data structure', so quality is unknown. Participant totals do not reconcile across the text and two tables.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Voluntary self- or proxy-report in an optional in-app survey, no clinical assessment or verification, no record of who answered, and for approximately 97% of the modelled data no human-reported label at all - only a k-means cluster assignment.

Window size swept with the best reported; uneven tuning across compared classifiers acknowledged by the authors; no separate development set; and pseudo-labelling applied before the headline evaluation.

There is no standardisation of any kind: the app is fully user-customisable, so different users operate different icon sets; no context, purpose or communication partner is recorded; and sessions vary without constraint. The authors correctly reject spatial modelling for exactly this reason, which shows they recognised the problem for one representation without extending it to the others.
Logging and modelling are fully automated; labels were self-reported before and independently of any analysis.

The unit of cross-validation is never stated. Users contribute many windows each, no user-level result is reported, and window-level partitioning would place a user's own data on both sides of every fold - with customised icon layouts making key-press sequences close to individual signatures.
No feature selection, but k-means pseudo-labelling of roughly 5,192 users was performed on the whole corpus before classification, so the label set itself is derived from the data being evaluated.

Accuracy is the only metric - no sensitivity, specificity, AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval anywhere. No chance baseline is computed, although bootstrap balancing implies 50%, against which the pre-pseudo-labelling results of 47-61% are at or near chance.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Eighty-one autistic and 99 non-autistic users with human-reported labels, expanded to thousands by pseudo-labelling and to a far larger but unstated number of windows. The apparent scale is a property of the telemetry, not of the labelled evidence.

The data source, encoding scheme, modelling views and window sweep are described clearly, but the elements that determine what the results mean are not: the unit of cross-validation, the k-means configuration and pseudo-label assignment, and the architectures and training regimes of the deep models that produce the headline figure.

Accuracy alone, with no uncertainty quantification of any kind. The one properly reported analysis is the negative t-test result, presented honestly. Three participant totals in the text and tables do not reconcile.
No code, no data, no preregistration. The dataset is telemetry from a discontinued commercial app held by a third-party foundation and is not described as available.

No ethics approval, no ethics committee, no consent for research use of telemetry gathered automatically for debugging, and no discussion of either - in a population including many children under ten and adults with dementia and brain injury. The only safeguard reported is encryption and de-identification. No competing-interests statement despite three commercial or industry-lab affiliations and a commercial data source.

No limitations section. Several real constraints are stated candidly in the methods - the debug-oriented data structure, the unusability of spatial modelling, the window-size trade-off, the uneven classifier tuning - but nothing addresses the reference standard, the age confound, the pseudo-labelling, the splitting unit or the ethics.

Conservative criteria applied deliberately to produce clinically distinct groups, stated by the authors. The autism sample has mean IQ 55-60 and is 62% preverbal or single-word - a population valuably absent from the rest of this corpus, but one selected from the severe end while comparison children are selected from above the screening cutoff, truncating the spectrum at both ends.

Typically developing day care attenders with below-cutoff K-CARS-2 and no parent-reported developmental or psychiatric history. Screened rather than assumed, which is better than most here, but there is no developmental-delay or language-disorder group - a decisive omission when the autism group's mean IQ is in the 50s, since nothing distinguishes an autism signal from a general developmental one.

Age (p = .99), sex (p > .99) and ethnicity are matched or homogeneous, and an age-stratified sensitivity analysis is performed - genuinely careful. But best-estimate and verbal IQ differ by 44-50 points at p < .001 in both age strata, roughly three standard deviations, and no adjustment is attempted despite the authors using mixed ANOVA elsewhere. Recruitment channel also differs completely by group, so site is confounded with diagnosis for an end-to-end model trained on raw frames.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: 110 screened, 95 (86.4%) analysed, with the enrolment flow given in a supplementary figure and the completion rate stated in the abstract. A purpose-built compliance score was computed for every repeated trial and analysed by two-way mixed ANOVA, so engagement is measured rather than assumed - a level of data-quality accounting that few studies here attempt.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Universal K-CARS-2 screening, child psychiatrist diagnosis and K-ADOS-2 with total, social affect and restricted-repetitive calibrated severity scores plus module distribution reported; comparison group screened below cutoff with no parent-reported history. Standardised cognitive assessment of every participant with age-appropriate instruments.

Three task-specific models with input dimensions fixed by task duration, a fixed 0.5 threshold rather than a tuned one, no feature selection and no reported model or hyperparameter search on the evaluation data.

A single consumer camera at fixed resolution and frame rate, front-facing viewpoint, quiet room, height-adjustable chair and table, identical three-task protocol with defined repetition counts, and a single 10-minute session for every child. The protocol was designed for replicability without specialised equipment, calibration or trained raters.
The pipeline is fully end-to-end and automated from raw frames; no human rating enters the index test at any point, which is precisely the dependence the authors set out to eliminate.

Ten-fold group-wise cross-validation with grouping by individual, stated explicitly, so all of a child's up-to-fifteen clips from a single continuous session remain in one fold. This is the correct construction and is unambiguous.
End-to-end learning from raw frames with no feature engineering or selection, so selection bias cannot arise.

AUROC, accuracy, precision and recall each with 95% confidence intervals by a named method for all six models - the most complete uncertainty reporting in this review. But specificity is never reported despite STARD adherence, no chance baseline or permutation test accompanies near-ceiling detection figures, the severity class distribution is unreported so no baseline is computable, and the severity model's inclusion of a non-autism class is not flagged as limiting the within-autism interpretation.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Forty-five autistic and 50 comparison children for an end-to-end CNN-LSTM-attention model on raw video, with the authors naming small sample size as their first limitation. The clip counts give an appearance of data volume that 95 independent children do not support.

Recruitment sources and dates, enrolment and exclusion criteria, every instrument in its validated Korean version, construct definitions with their ESCS source, camera model and settings, exact input tensor dimensions, cross-validation scheme with grouping unit, classification threshold, confidence-interval method and every software package with version number. Supplementary materials carry the flow diagram, task procedures, compliance metric, architecture, training performance and all interpretability figures. Missing: layer configurations, training hyperparameters and code.

Twenty-four interval-bounded estimates across two prediction problems and three tasks, with an age-stratified sensitivity analysis. The omission of specificity and of the severity class distribution are real gaps, but uncertainty reporting is otherwise the most complete in this corpus.

A data sharing statement is provided in a supplement and STARD adherence is declared, but no code is released and the method is covered by issued and pending patents held by the authors, so the central artefact cannot be independently reimplemented or checked.

Yonsei University Health System IRB approval, written caregiver consent, STARD adherence, itemised author contributions, funder no-role statement, and a full competing-interests disclosure covering two issued patents, one pending patent, a company affiliation and non-financial support from LumanLab Inc, whose staff also assisted with data management. Disclosure is complete; unlike the Duke group elsewhere in this corpus, no independent-analysis safeguard accompanies it.

The two stated limitations - small sample and the IQ difference - are the right ones, and the IQ acknowledgement is candid, correctly diagnosed and paired with an appropriate remedy. Three further self-critical observations about the RJA tasks appear in the discussion. But near-ceiling detection performance is never interrogated, the deliberate selection of clinically distinct groups is disclosed in Methods and not revisited in Limitations, and the severity model's inclusion of a non-autism class goes unremarked.

Fifty-nine children inherited from a public dataset, described only as two folders. No age, sex, IQ, language level, severity, comorbidity or group size is reported. Representativeness cannot be assessed even in principle from this paper.
Typically developing children from the source dataset, termed 'normal' throughout. No clinical comparison group, no screening information, and no counts.

No covariates are known and none is controlled. Because the input is a rendered image rather than a gaze time series, incidental graphical properties - plotted extent, ink density, line crossings - are available to the model and are indistinguishable from behavioural signal without an interpretability analysis, which is not performed.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: No attrition, quality or completeness accounting appears. Preprocessing is limited to format and colour conversion and resizing; nothing addresses tracking quality, data loss or how images were rendered, all of which are properties of the source dataset that go unreported.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: None described. Labels are folder names; no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or process is stated for the 59 children, and the source study's procedure is not summarised.
Three models compared on one small test set with the best reported, and greyscale conversion adopted partly because accuracy improved. No prespecified operating point.

Not assessable and not addressed. The eliciting task, stimuli, eye tracker and scanpath rendering scheme are all unreported, so the measurement chain that produced the images cannot be evaluated at all - a striking gap in a study whose stated contribution is to use eye tracking as a biomarker.
Feature extraction and classification are fully automated from image files; no human rating enters the pipeline.

Image-level splitting of 547 images from 59 children with no indication that a child's images were kept together, so each test image has roughly eight siblings in training or validation. No participant-level result is reported.

No feature selection occurs and the InceptionV3 extraction layer is chosen a priori on a stated principle. But the greyscale conversion for the custom CNN was adopted after observing improved accuracy on this dataset, so at least one preprocessing choice saw the evaluation data.

A single fixed split with 57 test images, no cross-validation, no repeated splits and no confidence intervals - so the 81.0% versus 78.9% comparison rests on about one image. No majority-class baseline against an implied 59.6% floor, and AUC values are plotted but never quoted. Per-class metrics and confusion matrices are reported, which is a genuine strength and is what exposes the CNN's 0.48 autism-class recall.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: 382 training images from roughly 59 children for a from-scratch CNN and a transfer-learning pipeline. The authors correctly identify this as the binding constraint on their results.

The modelling side is well specified - split counts, all preprocessing steps with dimensions and formulas, a layer-by-layer CNN table, the InceptionV3 extraction point, MLP hidden sizes, optimiser, learning rate, loss, batch size, epochs, platform and framework. The data side is entirely absent - no participants, no task, no equipment, no rendering scheme - and the image-to-child mapping, the one fact needed to assess the evaluation, is not stated. The greyscale formula contains a transcription error (0.144 for blue rather than 0.114).

Per-class precision, recall and F1 with confusion matrices and ROC curves - better than accuracy alone, and the authors explicitly justify going beyond accuracy because it ignores class imbalance. But no confidence intervals on a 57-image test set, no numeric AUC, and no chance baseline.
The input dataset is public and cited, so the data are available even though this study releases nothing. No code, no split specification, no seed, no preregistration.

No ethics statement, no reference to the source study's approvals, no funding statement and no competing-interests declaration. Defensible in substance for a secondary analysis of published de-identified images, but all four are absent as reporting elements.

One limitation stated, correctly identified as the binding one, with no inflation of the results - the paper calls its own accuracy 'not high' and reports the CNN's poor autism-class performance openly. But nothing is said about the image-level split, the single small test set, the absent participant information or the unexamined question of what the models respond to.

Thirty-five autistic children inherited from three corpora, with no sex, IQ, language level or severity data and no selection criteria applied by these authors. The age span from 12 months to 8 years is not a developmental design but a pooling artefact, since the youngest band contains no comparison children.

Typically developing children from two of the three corpora only, so the comparison group is absent from one entire source and from the youngest age band. The Eigsti corpus contains a developmental delay group - the material for the differential comparison the paper's own conclusion identifies as needed - and it is not used.

None attempted. Age, conversation partner, session length, transcription convention and corpus identity all co-vary with diagnosis to some degree, and every feature is a language measure in children, where developmental stage dominates. Count features are length-normalised, which handles one component; nothing addresses the others.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Speaker information was separated and transcripts cleaned; unintelligible units were retained as a feature rather than discarded, which is behaviourally defensible though it lets transcription-quality differences between corpora enter the model. No attrition or completeness accounting is reported, and no per-corpus data-quality comparison is made.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: None described. Labels are inherited binary clinical status from three independently assembled corpora with no instrument, criteria, clinician or era reported, and no acknowledgement that ascertainment must differ across an age span of 12 months to 8 years.

Feature elimination by SHAP from 77 to 63 appears to precede the split, and six classifier families were compared with the best retained. No prespecified operating point. Hyperparameter search is correctly nested within the training data.

Three different elicitation paradigms pooled - 30-minute free play, 10-minute parent-child play, and natural mother-child interaction with infants - with different partners and transcription conventions. The paper's own terminology for the partner drifts between therapist, trainer and parent, while child-partner discourse coherence is among the top-contributing features.
Feature extraction and classification are fully automated from transcripts; no human rating enters the pipeline, and the transcripts themselves were produced independently of this study.

A single fixed split with no cross-validation of the reported results. The unit is most plausibly the child, which avoids within-child leakage, but the split is random across three heterogeneous pooled corpora one of which contains autistic children only, so corpus identity is available as a shortcut and no leave-one-corpus-out check is performed.

SHAP-driven elimination from 77 to 63 features described on the initially extracted set with no nesting statement - the regime, at 76 samples and 77 candidate features, in which unnested selection produces the largest optimism.

A majority-classifier baseline is computed and reported as the first row of both results tables with improvements quantified against it - better practice than most of this corpus - and four metrics are given for all six classifiers and all seven feature configurations. But no confidence intervals, no AUC, no confusion matrix, and a test set of 17 items in which one child is 5.9 percentage points, so the headline margin over the next configuration is a single child.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Seventy-six children, 77 candidate features, six classifier families compared, and a 17-item test set. The authors do not identify sample size as a limitation, though it constrains every comparison the paper makes.

Every feature is named and defined in a table, including the BERT-cosine coherence construction and the TF-IDF unexpected-word measure; the tools, the feature counts before and after elimination, the classifier family and kernel, and the grid-search-with-5-fold-CV procedure are all stated. Missing: code, the split and seed, the identity of the 63 retained features, the per-corpus composition of the split, and the BERT variant. The stated 90:10 split is inconsistent with the reported accuracies.

Twenty-eight complete metric rows across two tables with a majority baseline - thorough ablation reporting - but no uncertainty quantification of any kind on a 17-item test set, and no confusion matrix or AUC.
The source corpora are public through CHILDES and are cited to their originators, so the inputs are available. No code, no split specification, no preregistration.

No ethics statement, no reference to the source studies' approvals or to CHILDES conditions of use, and no competing-interests declaration. Funding is acknowledged in full. Defensible in substance for secondary analysis of a public corpus, but all are absent as reporting elements.

No limitations section. The only acknowledged constraint is inconsistency in datasets used across the literature, which motivates the majority-classifier comparator. Nothing about the corpus-label confound, the age imbalance, the unnested feature selection, the classifier search, or the 17-item test set.

Fifty-four (or 55) autistic children with no diagnostic characterisation, no IQ, no severity measure and no stated recruitment route. Thirteen of 99 enrolled excluded for invalid data without description. Age spans infancy to adulthood in five bands, so the sample is developmentally heterogeneous in a way no analysis of the diagnosis result accounts for.
Thirty-two typically developing children with no screening information and no clinical comparison group, and with a materially different age and sex profile from the autistic group.

None attempted for the diagnosis analysis, and the study itself supplies the evidence that this matters: scan-path images classify sex within the autistic group at 78.0% and age band at 80.5%, both above the 74.4% achieved for diagnosis, while the groups are 81.5% versus 46.9% male and 31.5% versus 15.6% aged 10 or over. The connection is never drawn.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Thirteen participants excluded for invalid data with no characterisation; no tracking-ratio, data-loss or trial-rejection criteria reported; and no eye-tracker or acquisition parameters given at all, so data quality cannot be assessed. Exposure to individual video clips ranged from 1 to 92 viewings, so the effective stimulus set differs between participants.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Not described. No instrument, criteria, clinician or procedure for either group anywhere in the retrieved text.

Dropout and epoch settings swept with the best reported; augmentation applied at three levels with the highest-augmentation result presented as the finding; multiple representations and stimulus subsets evaluated on the same data with no development set.

The stimulus battery itself is exceptionally well designed and standardised in construct, with explicit controls and foils. But no eye tracker, sampling rate, display, viewing distance or calibration is reported - and gaze velocity, the paper's headline representational addition, is a quantity whose value depends directly on the unreported sampling rate. Participants also viewed different subsets of clips.
Rendering and classification are fully automated from gaze coordinates; no human rating enters the pipeline.

Image-level splitting with roughly sixteen images per child and no subject-disjoint evaluation reported anywhere. Augmented counts quoted for whole datasets rather than training partitions, implying rotated duplicates straddling the split - corroborated by test accuracy rising monotonically with augmentation level to 98.8%.
Augmentation appears to precede splitting. The per-clip ablation that ranks stimulus contributions is computed on the same data used for the headline result.

Training accuracy is reported alongside test accuracy and AUC in every table, which makes the 20-30 point overfitting gap visible and is a real transparency virtue; temporal experiments are repeated three times and averaged. But no sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1 or confusion matrix appears anywhere, no confidence intervals are given, and no chance baseline is computed.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Eighty-six children, and far fewer in the subgroup analyses - the sex-by-age experiment rests on 4 female and 19 male autistic children aged 5-9, expanded to thousands of images by augmentation. Training accuracy of 100% at every setting indicates complete memorisation.

The stimulus constructs, the full 43-clip list with view counts, the rendering and downsampling, the temporal windowing, the velocity formula and colour mapping, the swept hyperparameters, the split ratios and every experimental image count are all specified. Absent: the eye tracker and all acquisition parameters, the diagnostic procedure, the network architectures beyond a figure, the augmentation parameters, and the image-to-participant mapping - the last being the one fact needed to assess every result in the paper.

Fourteen tables with training accuracy, test accuracy and AUC for every configuration, and three-repeat averaging in the temporal experiments - thorough by the standards of this corpus, and the inclusion of training accuracy is genuinely useful. But no class-conditional metric of any kind, no confidence intervals, no chance baseline, and an unresolved 55-versus-54 discrepancy in the sample size.
No code, no data, no preregistration, and no statement on availability of either.

No ethics approval statement, no consent statement and no competing-interests declaration in the retrieved text, for a study involving children including infants. Funding from NIH and the Simons Foundation is stated.

No limitations section. The two constraints acknowledged - too few female autistic participants, and class imbalance depressing AUC - are framed as problems augmentation solves. Nothing about image-level splitting, the augmentation-accuracy relationship, the universal 100% training accuracy, the missing reference standard, or the demographic confound that the paper's own experiments quantify.

Twenty-nine autistic children inherited from a public dataset, with CARS mean 32.97 indicating a mild-to-moderate sample, but no group-level demographics, no inclusion or exclusion criteria and no IQ or language data. Case-control recruitment from specialist clinics against mainstream schools.
Thirty typically developing children from French schools with no reported screening for autism or developmental concerns, and no clinical comparison group.

No covariate is reported by group, so none can be controlled or even checked. The paper's own related-work section notes that removing age as a feature reduced accuracy across all classifiers in a prior study - an observation about gaze-based classifiers drawing on age information that it does not apply to its own work, despite age being available in the dataset.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: No attrition, tracking-quality or trial-rejection information is available, and no rendering specification is given, so what the images represent cannot be assessed. Preprocessing is limited to resizing, colour conversion and flattening.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Specialist clinic evaluation named but not described, CARS used for severity rather than diagnosis, no criteria or clinician detail, and no screening of the comparison group. Inherited rather than authored, but undefined nonetheless.

Over a hundred hyperparameter configurations evaluated on the reporting cross-validation with the maximum taken as the result; no prespecified architecture, optimiser or operating point; no held-out confirmation.

The inherited acquisition is well standardised for its time and better described here than in the other reuses - one eye tracker (SMI Red-m at 250 Hz), a quiet room with white barriers to reduce distraction, a fixed 60 cm viewing distance, and all interaction in the children's first language. But no calibration procedure, tracking criterion or scan-path rendering scheme is reported, and the presence of a live host directing attention in some videos means the elicited behaviour is not uniform across stimuli.
Preprocessing and classification are fully automated from image files; no human rating enters the pipeline.

Ten-round cross-validation over 547 images from 59 children, roughly nine per child, with no indication that a child's images were kept within a fold and no participant-level result reported anywhere.

No feature selection, but hyperparameter selection across more than a hundred configurations was performed on the same cross-validation used to report the result. Notably, augmentation was deliberately avoided on stated and correct grounds, which removes one leakage route that other reuses of this dataset introduce.

The reported accuracy is irreconcilable with the reported sensitivity and specificity at the stated class sizes - 95.59% claimed against approximately 79.0% implied - and the same holds for the multilayer perceptron comparator. The quantity labelled F1 is the harmonic mean of sensitivity and specificity, not F1. No confidence intervals, no AUC, no confusion matrix, and no majority-class baseline against an implied 60.0% floor.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Fifty-nine children and 547 images for a model search spanning well over a hundred configurations. The authors identify no sample-size constraint, and indeed present the absence of augmentation as evidence that the dataset was adequate.

The computational pipeline is documented exhaustively - preprocessing chain with figures, twelve hyperparameter tables with accuracy for every cell, the winning configuration, software versions and hardware. Missing: code, cross-validation implementation and seed, the image-to-child mapping, the scan-path rendering scheme, and any derivation reconciling the reported accuracy with the reported class-conditional metrics.

Sensitivity and specificity are reported alongside accuracy for all five models in two colour conditions, which is better practice than most reuses of this dataset - and is what makes the internal inconsistency detectable. But the three metrics cannot describe the same classifier, F1 is mislabelled, and there are no confidence intervals, no AUC and no confusion matrices.
The source dataset is public and properly cited to its originators, so inputs are available. No code, no seed, no split specification, no preregistration.

The originating study's ethical approvals and Helsinki compliance are cited explicitly, which is appropriate practice for a secondary analysis and more than most dataset-reuse papers in this corpus provide. No funding or competing-interests statement appears in the retrieved text.

No limitations section and no constraint acknowledged anywhere. The self-assessment is uniformly favourable, including the claim that the model 'can accurately classify children with ASD from those with TD without human intervention'.

A whole national birth cohort with no recruitment or selection by the researchers, covering 75% of the population through a universal free surveillance programme. Autism-associated aetiologies such as Fragile X and tuberous sclerosis were deliberately retained rather than excluded, on stated reasoning. The spectrum represented is whatever the population contains.

The comparison group is every other child in the cohort - 774,778 children - with exclusions limited to autism and other pervasive developmental or medical conditions plus Down syndrome. This is a population comparison rather than a recruited control group, the only one in the review.

Because the design is a population cohort, group differences are findings rather than sampling artefacts. Sex is handled correctly through a boys-only sensitivity model, given that it is both a strong predictor and a strong group difference. Maternal country of birth is reported as associated with diagnosis rate without discussion of whether it entered the model or of the equity implications of a risk score encoding migration background.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: The central data problem - variable checkup timing and multiple entries per milestone - is addressed by an explicitly reasoned binarisation rule adopted to avoid embedding developmental assumptions about never-tested and late-tested records, with the cost of that choice stated in the same passage. Variable follow-up by birth year is addressed by a sensitivity model excluding 2019 births.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Routine clinical diagnosis with no research instrument, 43.4% ascertained from provider free-text notes, and an acknowledged tenfold undercount - the authors state that the true autism group is at least ten times larger than the labelled one, so most autistic children are in the comparison group.

Features reduced a priori on clinical grounds, milestone binarisation rule stated with rationale, Youden threshold as an objective cutoff, no hyperparameter search reported, four methods compared rather than the best selected.

The surveillance protocol is nationally standardised with defined milestones at defined age bins, delivered by trained nurses under Ministry guidelines - considerable standardisation for routine data. But measurement is human observation recorded administratively across 503 clinics with no inter-rater reliability data, and the authors note that variation in provider recording practice warrants investigation.
Diagnoses were recorded in routine care years before and independently of the study; model outputs played no part in clinical decisions.

Cross-validation partitions children in a population cohort, so no within-participant leakage is possible; and temporal leakage from diagnosis to predictors is prevented by capping predictors at 24 months and restricting outcomes to diagnoses after 24 months, a control adopted explicitly for that purpose.

The reduction from 100 to 59 features was made before modelling on clinical-relevance grounds and independently of performance, so selection bias does not arise. Milestone binarisation is a fixed rule applied uniformly.

Accuracy is correctly not reported at 0.15% incidence. AUC with fold standard deviation, sensitivity, specificity, full confusion counts for four methods, training alongside test AUC with overfitting acknowledged, enrichment relative to cohort base rate, and multi-threshold performance in supplementary material. The one gap is that positive predictive value is left uncomputed although derivable at 0.60%.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: 775,941 children with 1,163 cases and 59 features. Fold-to-fold variation in AUC is 0.009, and the SHAP top-20 overlaps across folds for 15 of 24 unique features - stability that follows directly from the sample size.

Cohort definition, two-route case ascertainment with counts and verification steps, exclusion logic with reasoning, surveillance protocol with milestone counts by domain and age bin, binarisation rule with rationale and cost, feature reduction basis, modelling method, cross-validation, threshold definition, four-method comparison with confusion counts, and SHAP fold stability. Five supplementary items carry the full feature list, per-fold training performance, multi-threshold results and two sensitivity models. Software and versions are the one omission.

Fold standard deviations on every headline metric, training and test performance side by side with overfitting stated, confusion counts for all comparators, confidence interval on the external validity odds ratio, and a p-value threshold adjusted for sample size with effect sizes throughout the group comparisons. PPV is the sole quantity left uncomputed.

Data cannot be released publicly for privacy and ethical reasons, but a formal request route through the Ministry platform is given with a URL. Extensive supplementary material substitutes in part. No code and no preregistration.

Ministry of Health Helsinki committee approval with number and date, Declaration of Helsinki conformity, consent waived on anonymisation grounds by the committee, extraction and anonymisation by dedicated Ministry personnel, access only through a secure platform, funding stated with grant number, and no competing interests declared.

The most substantive limitations section in the review, quantifying its own outcome undercount at a factor of ten, stating the cost of its representational choices alongside their rationale, naming specific missing predictors and missing milestones, and flagging provider recording variation for further research. The unacknowledged item is the positive predictive value, which the paper's own numbers make computable at 0.60%.

No participants and no selection process; 1,418 photographs scraped from autism-focused websites, with the number of distinct children unknown and no demographic, clinical or severity information available for any image.
Photographs 'randomly gathered from the internet' with no screening and no verification of non-autistic status, drawn from an entirely different source population than the autistic class.

The central confound is the dataset's construction: the two classes differ in source and therefore in imaging characteristics, photographic convention and represented demographics, all of which are available to the classifier and none of which is examined. Augmentation of brightness, contrast and noise addresses only part of the surface of this problem.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: No quality assessment of any kind. Preprocessing was performed by the dataset creator and comprised duplicate removal and face cropping; no resolution, compression, capture-condition or per-class quality comparison is reported.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: The label is where an image was found. No diagnosis, instrument, criterion or verification, and errors are unbounded in both directions.
Three architectures compared with the best reported; augmentation of ambiguous ordering relative to splitting; two inconsistent input sizes; no prespecified operating point.

None is possible. The photographs were captured by unknown people with unknown devices under unknown conditions, and the two classes were assembled from different sources - the opposite of a standardised acquisition chain.
Classification is automated from image files; no human rating enters the pipeline. This is the only domain item in the record not at high concern.
A single fixed partition with augmentation of ambiguous ordering, and an unknown image-to-child mapping that makes participant-level split integrity impossible to establish even in principle.
Augmentation is described after the partition but applied to 'the Kaggle dataset comprising 2,836 facial images', implying transformation of the whole corpus before splitting.

One fixed 100-image test set with no cross-validation, no repeated splits and no confidence intervals; no chance baseline stated despite a balanced design; a confusion matrix summing to 280 that matches no stated partition; 100% training accuracy reported without comment; and a units error in the sensitivity and specificity text throughout.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: 2,536 training images of unknown provenance and unknown child count, with a 100-image test set on which model rankings differing by one percentage point are asserted.

Architectures, appended layers, optimiser, batch size, epochs, early-stopping criterion and augmentation list are given, but the Kaggle dataset identifier, code, split assignment, image-to-child mapping and augmentation ordering are not, and two inconsistent input sizes are stated without reconciliation.
Sensitivity and specificity are reported alongside accuracy, but with a units error throughout, no confidence intervals, no AUC, and a confusion matrix corresponding to no stated partition size.
No code, no dataset identifier or version, no split specification, no preregistration.

No ethics approval, no consent, and no discussion of either, for a study built on photographs of identifiable children obtained without their families' knowledge, in which one class was collected precisely because those images appeared in autism contexts - so the dataset itself asserts a health status about identifiable minors. A consumer mobile application for families is proposed on this basis. No funding or competing-interests statement.
No limitations section and no acknowledged constraint of any kind. The only self-critical observation in the paper is that batch normalisation and dropout did not improve performance.

A large multi-site clinical repository with site-matched case-control recruitment - substantially better provenance than the internet-assembled corpora elsewhere in this review - but no demographic or clinical characterisation is reported and no quality-control exclusions are described.

Controls recruited at the same 17 sites as the autistic participants, which is a real strength. But ABIDE-I controls generally lack ADOS and ADI-R records because those instruments are administered to diagnose autism, so missingness on the model's most important features is itself label-informative.

Age at scan, FIQ, VIQ and PIQ - all of which differ between groups in ABIDE-I and all of which predict structural brain measures - are entered as model features rather than adjusted for or reported. Site is label-encoded rather than harmonised or stratified.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: No missingness handling is described for the phenotype fields, although ADOS, ADI-R and SRS are systematically absent for the control group - which makes the missingness pattern a direct proxy for the label.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Clinical diagnosis supported by ADOS and ADI-R at the contributing sites - the strongest standard in this review.

The index test includes the reference standard's own scored output among its predictors. Architecture components are well specified but hyperparameters are not, and no operating point is prespecified.

Seventeen sites with distinct scanners, field strengths and pulse sequences, with no cross-site harmonisation, intensity normalisation or ComBat-style correction reported, in a dataset where site is a documented confound for this exact task.
Classification is fully automated from stored records and images; no human rater is involved at inference.

Subject-level partitioning prevents within-subject leakage, but target leakage through the ADOS, ADI-R and SRS fields operates on any partition, and no site-stratified or leave-one-site-out evaluation is reported.
GAMI-Net's sparse regularisation prunes features during training; whether pruning was refitted within each cross-validation fold is not stated. Site is label-encoded before splitting.

A ROC-AUC of 99.99% and precision of 100% reported without confidence intervals, without a chance or covariate-only baseline, and with the headline accuracy differing between sections (99.40% against 96.4%) and the split described inconsistently.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
