The origin of both the severity labels and the facial-mood labels, the class distribution, the splitting unit and the classifier hyperparameters are not.
Point estimates only across every stage, with no confidence intervals, no confusion matrices, no per-class results and no baseline, on an effective sample of 30 children.
No code. Data - identifiable thermal facial images of 30 disabled children from a named, addressed institution - offered to anyone on request, with no stated access controls or governance.

'Ethical Approval. Not required.' No institutional review board, no ethics committee, no consent and no assent statement, for prospective thermal imaging of 30 disabled children at a named residential special school in a study proposing to automate their psychiatric medication dosing. The clearest ethics gap in this review.

No limitations section exists. The future-work paragraph concedes by implication that the sample is neither diverse nor representative and that no clinical evaluation was performed, but no conclusion is qualified.
A public Kaggle image assembly with no ascertainment process, no spectrum description and no clinical setting; the number of distinct children behind 2,940 images is unreported.
Images 'randomly retrieved from web searches', so the comparison class differs from the index class in collection route rather than necessarily in any property of the children.

No sex, ancestry or age distribution for either class, across a stated 2-to-14 age range in which facial appearance changes profoundly, and with a physiognomic premise resting on measurements that vary systematically with all three.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Class counts and split proportions are reported, but the evaluation partition's size and balance contradict them, and no image-quality exclusion criteria are described.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: No diagnostic instrument, clinician judgement or record for any image; the label is folder membership.
Three architectures compared on the same data with the reported figures drawn from the model-selection partition; no prespecified operating point; hyperparameters unspecified beyond the epoch cap.
Uncontrolled internet photographs with unknown and potentially class-correlated acquisition conditions; preprocessing standardises geometry and pixel range only.
Classification is fully automated with no human rater at inference.
Image-level splitting with the number of distinct children unknown, in a corpus where one child may appear in several images.

Augmentation is described as expanding the training set, which is correct, but the exactly balanced evaluation counts leave open whether it reached the evaluation partition; and all reported figures come from the partition used for model selection.
No held-out test result despite a test partition being defined; no chance baseline against a 54.9% majority class; no confidence intervals; no prevalence-adjusted predictive value.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Three deep architectures on 2,940 images from an unknown and possibly much smaller number of children.

Corpus counts, augmentation parameters, split proportions, image dimensions, architectures, loss, optimiser and epoch cap are reported with complete per-class metrics and confusion matrices. Missing: participant counts, demographics, splitting unit, and code.

Validation-partition figures presented as the study's results; support counts inconsistent with the stated split and class ratio; no intervals or baselines; and the abstract, introduction and results tables disagree about which model performed best.
The corpus is public and identified; no code is reported, and the retrieved text ends before the journal's declarations so availability statements could not be assessed.

No ethics or consent discussion appears in the main text for training data consisting of identifiable photographs of children collected from the internet; the declarations section was not present in the retrieved text and so cannot be assessed.

One honest sentence concedes that the research gap persists despite 98% and that clinical validation is necessary. Nothing else: the provenance confound, the absent reference standard, the missing demographics, the validation-only reporting and the non-existent feature analysis all go unmentioned.
Sixty-four children from four archived corpora with no ascertainment described, no spectrum characterisation, and an acknowledged imbalance toward boys and toward the younger age band.

Typically developing children drawn partly from corpora containing no autistic children and using different protocols, so corpus of origin is partly correlated with class. Developmentally delayed children available in a source corpus were deliberately excluded, removing the non-autistic clinical comparison.

No independent language or cognitive measure, in a study whose leading predictor is a standard index of expressive language development; no age or sex composition reported by diagnostic group, despite the paper's own finding that the top feature increases with age.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: All 64 retained children contribute complete feature vectors; the one exclusion, of developmentally delayed children, is stated with its reason; token-level cleaning rules are documented in detail.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Genuine diagnoses inherited from established research archives, but no instrument, criteria or ascertainment procedure is reported in this paper.

Six features defined in advance with both child-alone and ratio forms and an explicit rationale for the ratios; but two versions were compared empirically and certain features removed before the headline result, using the same data.

Four source protocols differing in session length (30 minutes, 10 minutes, unspecified, 30 minutes), in structure (one with a cleanup period) and in investigator role - the last mattering because half the features are ratios to the investigator's output. Ratio normalisation addresses length but not protocol.
Feature computation is fully automated from archived transcripts by documented rules; no human rater is involved at any stage of this study.
One transcript and one feature vector per child, so the split unit is the person and no within-participant leakage is possible - among the minority in this review not exposed to that failure.
Feature versions compared and certain features removed on the full dataset before the reported headline accuracies, so those are post-selection estimates.

Five metrics for all seven models with ROC variability bands across 50 repeated splits - unusually honest uncertainty reporting - and results benchmarked against three prior studies. But test folds hold sixteen children, no confidence intervals are given, and no chance or majority-class baseline is stated.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Sixty-four children with test folds of sixteen, supporting a claimed 5-to-10-point advantage for neural models and a 1-to-2-point margin between two of them. The author identifies limited data as the first limitation.

All four corpora named with protocols where known, exclusion stated, feature definitions with rationale, NLP package, detailed token-cleaning rules with the annotation conventions handled, seven models with library provenance, the convolutional architecture layer by layer, split proportion, and the repeated-split count with its stability criterion.

Five metrics for every model plus ROC mean curves with a one-standard-deviation band - better uncertainty communication than almost anything else in this review - but no confidence intervals, no confusion matrices, no baseline, and no statement of which features were removed before the headline figure.
Source corpora are public and individually named through TalkBank; no code released; no preregistration.

Secondary analysis of a public research archive with consent obtained at source, stated explicitly - materially different from the web-scraped and institutionally collected material elsewhere in this review. Funding and competing interests are not stated.

Two limitations named - limited data and residual transcription noise across corpora, the latter correctly identifying cross-corpus heterogeneity from one side. The language-delay confound, the partial correlation between corpus and class, the protocol differences and the post-selection headline are all unaddressed.
Two convenience corpora, 100 and 61 children, with no ascertainment described and no spectrum characterisation. A severe-symptom subset available in one dataset is not analysed.

The Gait dataset provides a 50:50 autistic and typically developing contrast recorded under matched conditions - a structural advantage over the branch's usual asymmetries. But DREAM's non-spectrum comparison class was discarded, so that experiment has no non-autistic group at all.

No age distribution by diagnostic group across a 4-to-12 span in which gait matures substantially, and no sex information, in a domain where gait differs by sex. No cognitive, language or comorbidity data.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Nine of every ten walking trials per child were discarded, with the retained trial chosen on the basis of the diagnosis and a clinician's recommendation - an outcome-informed data reduction, not a neutral quality filter.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: No diagnostic instrument, criteria or procedure reported for either corpus, and DREAM's label structure is collapsed by discarding one of three classes.

Architectures, loss, optimiser and training schedule are fully specified, with the epoch extension justified by observed convergence. But six backbones were compared on the same cross-validation results that supply the headline, making it a best-of-six selection.

Within each corpus both classes were recorded on the same sensor under the same protocol, and the skeleton representation excludes appearance entirely. Across corpora the sensors and joint coverage differ, which the paper documents; neither task protocol is described.
Model inference is automated, but the trial-selection step in the Gait dataset was explicitly informed by the child's diagnosis.

Necessarily participant-level on the Gait dataset, since each child contributes one sample. Sample-level with no participant partitioning described on DREAM, where 1,833 samples come from 61 children.
Representations are learned and no feature selection is performed, but architecture selection across six backbones used the reported cross-validation results.

Accuracy only, with no sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC or confusion matrix for any proposed model. Chance is 50% on the Gait dataset by construction and undeterminable on DREAM, whose class distribution is described as biased and never quantified. Dispersion across runs is reported, which is a genuine strength.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Deep dual-stream models on 100 samples in one corpus, with test folds of ten children where a single case moves accuracy by ten percentage points and the six architectures span 2.2 points.

Both datasets with public locations and one with a DOI, sensor models and joint counts with their differences explained, sample counts, the class exclusion, nine software packages with versions, hardware, optimiser and schedule with the reason for extension, cross-validation scheme with fold sizes and repetition counts per dataset, and the configuration flag needed in the inherited codebase.

Mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation across repeated cycles for every architecture on both datasets, plus per-epoch curves - dispersion reporting better than most of this corpus. But accuracy is the only metric, with no confusion matrices or confidence intervals.
Both source datasets public and identified, one with a Dryad DOI and access date; the inherited codebase is cited with a required configuration flag noted; the authors' own code is not released.

No ethics statement, conventional for secondary analysis of public corpora. The paper does engage substantively with privacy, positioning skeleton data as an answer to the anonymity concerns raised for gaze and video data. Funding and competing interests declared.

Three limitations named in the conclusion, including the paper's own computational cost as an obstacle to the real-time clinical use it proposes. The outcome-informed trial selection, the DREAM splitting, the absent demographics and the missing sensitivity and specificity are all unaddressed.

Sixty-two children from one Iranian corpus, with no cognitive, language or comorbidity characterisation and no screening instrument described for the comparison group. The authors identify sample size, demographic variation and the narrow age range as generalisability limits.
Exactly sex-matched at 24:7, which is rare and creditable, but recorded predominantly in different settings from the autistic group and differing by 4.8 months in mean age.

Sex is fully controlled by exact matching. Age is not tested or adjusted despite a 4.8-month difference in a period of rapid vocal maturation, using measures known to change with it; recording setting is strongly imbalanced; cry-eliciting cause differs between groups; and two device classes were used without normalisation.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Exclusion rules are explicit - pain cries removed, only pure crying retained, segments with other vocalisations or non-empty-mouth cries eliminated, recordings not meeting distance and quiet-environment conditions excluded - and per-child yields are reported with standard deviations.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: Four-stage ascertainment culminating in independent confirmation by a child psychiatrist in a different setting, with instruments and clinician qualifications named and the absence of ADOS explained.

Three perturbation measures chosen a priori on clinical grounds rather than by data-driven selection, with their definitions and computation described; the network architecture and optimisation are fully specified.

A common WAV format at 16-bit and 44.1 kHz, a 25 cm microphone distance instruction and exclusion of noisy recordings provide partial standardisation, but two device classes and strongly group-imbalanced recording environments remain, in measures sensitive to acoustic conditions.
Acoustic features are computed automatically by Praat and classification is fully automated; diagnosis preceded and was independent of the recording.

Evaluation at the cry-instance level with no participant-level partitioning described, and roughly six instances per child from 62 children - so cries from the same child fall on both sides of the boundary.
Augmentation is correctly confined to the training split, and the acoustic features were chosen a priori. But the final model was selected as the best of 2,000 epochs on the validation set.

No held-out test partition of any kind; all six reported metrics are validation-set values at the selected best epoch. No confidence intervals on an effective sample of 62 children, and sensitivity and specificity are defined over cry instances rather than children, so they are not per-child operating characteristics.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: A convolutional-recurrent network trained from scratch on roughly 355 cry instances from 62 children. The authors name sample size as their first limitation.

The diagnostic procedure, recording protocol, device mix, setting and cry-cause distributions by group, exclusion rules, per-child yields, acoustic definitions and full network specification are all reported. Absent: partition sizes, splitting unit, and whether a test set exists.

Six classification metrics including sensitivity and specificity separately, plus means with standard errors and three-level significance coding for the acoustic comparison. No confidence intervals anywhere, and all classification figures are validation-set values.
The source corpus is public and cited; supplementary material accompanies the article; no code is released.

Ethics approval from Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences with comprehensive informed consent from parents or guardians covering objectives, procedures, advantages and risks. The competing-interest declaration itemises employment, co-founder status, stock ownership and advisory compensation by individual alongside company funding - the fullest disclosure in this review.

Four limitations in a dedicated section, including the absence of ADOS with its reason and the need for age-specific models - which approaches the age confound without naming it. The validation design, the recording-setting imbalance and the differing cry causes are all unaddressed.
Self-selected screening-app respondents with no clinical ascertainment, no class distribution and no demographic composition reported.
The comparison group is respondents whose summed AQ-10 score fell below the cut-off - defined by the same arithmetic as the positive class.
No covariate is described, summarised or adjusted for; registration metadata are entered as predictors without analysis.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: Data cleaning and missing-value handling are described in outline, but no counts, exclusions or retained-feature list are given.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: No clinical diagnosis; the label is the summed item score thresholded at the instrument's cut-off, with that sum present among the enumerated features.
A feature-engineering stage is described but its output is not enumerated, so the model's actual inputs are unknown; hyperparameter search ranges are not given.
AQ-10 is a standardised instrument administered through a screening application, so item collection is uniform - but nothing is measured beyond self-report.
Classification is fully automated from tabular data.
Participant-level 5-fold cross-validation is sound in itself and immaterial, since the target is computable from a printed predictor on any partition.
A feature-engineering stage guided by exploratory data analysis is described without stating what it retained - which is the one fact needed to determine whether the summed score entered the model.
Accuracy alone at 0.9890, with no other metric, no confidence interval, no class distribution and no comparison against the 73.2% majority-class baseline the source dataset implies.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: Seven hundred and four rows with 21 candidate fields is ample for a Random Forest; the problem lies in what the fields contain.

The dataset source, row and field counts, every field name, the preprocessing and feature-engineering stages, the cross-validation scheme, the classifier and the optimiser are reported. The retained feature set, class distribution and search ranges are not.
A single accuracy figure with no other metric, no interval, no confusion matrix and no baseline.
The dataset is public and identified; no code is released.
No statements given; secondary use of a public tabular repository conventionally requires none, though funding and competing interests are also absent.

One limitation is stated - reliance on a single public dataset - which correctly identifies an external-validity problem while leaving the internal one untouched. No feature importance is reported, which would have exposed the dependence on the summed score.
No recruitment source, no ascertainment procedure, no spectrum characterisation, no age distribution by group and no cognitive or language data for 100 prospectively recruited children.

Typically developing peers recorded under the same protocol in the same environment - a matched acquisition context that is a genuine strength - but not matched on sex (52% male against 84%) and with age composition unreported.

A 32-percentage-point sex gap between groups, in a model whose inputs are facial mesh and body landmark geometry, with no stratified or adjusted analysis. No age distribution by group across a developmentally active range. The landmark representation does control appearance, lighting and background well.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition
items.notes: All 100 children contribute and no attrition is reported, but no landmark-detection failure rate, occlusion handling or frame-exclusion criterion is described, and class-correlated missingness is plausible if the groups differ in how often they moved out of frame.

domain_2_data_collection_quality.domain_name: Behavioral Data Collection, Predictors and Reference Standard (PROBAST: predictors, outcome)

items.notes: No diagnostic instrument, criteria or clinician described for either group in a prospectively recruited sample.

Feature construction fully specified in advance - 468 face mesh points, 33 pose points, 21 per hand, mouth aspect ratio, per-region motion energy, totalling 1,639 values - with the architecture, loss, optimiser and all four regularisation parameters stated.

Identical protocol for both groups, standardised lighting, fixed 1920x1080 resolution and 30 fps, common session duration, and a landmark representation that discards appearance and background before modelling.
Landmark extraction and classification are fully automated with no human rater at any stage.

Subject-independent stratified 5-fold cross-validation, with the mechanism and its anti-leakage purpose stated explicitly - the clearest such statement in this review's video branch, and the correct control for frame-level data.

No feature selection is performed and features are engineered a priori. But no hyperparameter search is described and architecture selection appears to have used the same folds that supply the reported figures.

Accuracy, AUC, precision and recall with paired t-tests across folds and stated 95% intervals - better than most of this corpus. But specificity is omitted although recall of 0.95 against 85-90% accuracy implies it is materially lower; no confusion matrix; and intervals of plus or minus 1.5% are narrower than 20-child validation folds would support, with no derivation given.

items.item_text: Sample size adequacy for the modelling
items.notes: One hundred children with 16 hours of video and 1,639 features per frame; the effective sample is 100, with 20 children per validation fold. The authors identify dataset growth as future work.

The acquisition protocol, feature construction, validation strategy, regularisation parameters and architecture are all fully specified. Recruitment, diagnostic procedure, age composition by group, and landmark-failure handling are entirely absent.

Confidence intervals and fold-level significance testing are reported, which is above the corpus norm, but accuracy is given as a range rather than a mean, specificity is omitted, and the interval derivation is unstated.

Data on request only, withheld for privacy and ethical reasons - appropriate for identifiable video, though the modelled landmark coordinates are far less identifying and could have been released. No code.

No ethics approval, no institutional review board reference, and no consent or assent statement anywhere, for a prospective study recording over 16 hours of video of 100 children including 50 autistic children. Competing interests are declared as none.

No limitations section. The future-work sentence concedes that the parameter set, architecture and sample are limited, but the sex imbalance, the absent reference standard, the missing specificity and the absent ethics documentation are all unmentioned.
A public image assembly with no ascertainment, no spectrum description and an unreported number of distinct children. No sample exists at all for the gelotophobia target.
Neurotypical images from the same public collection with no demographic characterisation and no screening described, against an autistic class drawn partly from autism-related websites.

Age, sex and cultural background explicitly not controlled, as the authors state - in a study whose feature extractor is optimised to encode facial identity and therefore represents demographic attributes strongly.

items.item_text: Handling of missing data and attrition

Session-level partitioning and 5-fold cross-validation with no participant grouping, on 12 children - leave-one-child-out was available and unused.
Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for seven models with learning curves, but no confidence intervals, no fold variance, no chance level, and no relation of the figure to 12 children.

High validation accuracy is read as strong generalization capability, and the paper states that high accuracy and robust metrics reinforce the low likelihood of overfitting - inverting the inference under session-level splitting.

Six named threats including sample size, convenience sampling, scope restriction, overfitting risk, absence of longitudinal data, and the ethics of school-based screening with stigmatisation risk; claims bounded to screening rather than diagnosis.

structured_abstract:
Background: Computation-based autism prediction from behavioural data has grown rapidly, and reported accuracies frequently exceed those of the clinical instruments the methods are said to supplement. Whether those figures estimate diagnostic performance has not been systematically examined across modalities.

Objective: To characterise how 170 computation-based autism prediction studies using behavioural data are designed, conducted and reported, across participants and their description, study conduct and reproducibility, behaviours and their fusion, computational methods and validation, and publication trends.

Methods: A supplied, human-verified corpus of 171 records (170 after removal of one duplicate) published 2013-2026 was assessed on full text. Every included study was charted against 23 prespecified review questions, appraised for risk of bias with QUADAS-2 and for methodological quality with four PROBAST-derived domains, and summarised in a narrative row with supporting evidence spans.

Results: Overall risk of bias was high in 108 studies, moderate in 36, low in 17 and unclear in 9. Reported performance is bimodally distributed and the separating variable is the analysis unit: studies partitioning images, frames, gaze samples, clips or sessions rather than participants cluster between 90% and 100%, while studies partitioning people cluster between roughly 55% and 90%. Twelve studies predict an outcome that is a deterministic function of their own predictors, and three predict a variable the authors constructed. Sixteen studies reuse a single web-scraped corpus of children's facial photographs, reporting 81.0% to 99.8% on it with no source-held-out evaluation. The five studies whose designs most directly support generalisation report R = 0.85 at best on dimensional targets, 74.0% on demographically matched data, F1 0.641 with an explicit trivial baseline, and F1 0.63 when autism is discriminated from another neurodevelopmental condition rather than from typical development. One study measured demographic confounding directly, finding an eight-point accuracy inflation attributable to unmatched age and sex.

Conclusions: The reported accuracy of this literature is principally a function of evaluation construction and outcome definition rather than of behavioural signal, modality or algorithm. Where participants are separated, outcomes are clinician-ascertained and comparison groups are clinically meaningful, performance falls to a range consistent with a screening aid rather than a diagnostic test. Reporting the analysis unit, the participant-level partition, the class prevalence and a trivial baseline would allow readers to distinguish the two kinds of result, and their routine absence is the field's most consequential reporting gap.
introduction_text:
Autism spectrum disorder is diagnosed by clinical observation and developmental history, a process that is expensive, slow and unevenly available. That combination has motivated a large and fast-growing literature applying computational methods to behavioural data - gaze, facial appearance and dynamics, speech and language, movement and kinematics, interaction traces, and questionnaire responses - in order to predict, screen for or grade autism. The literature reports high accuracy: figures above 95% are common and figures of 100% are not rare.

Those figures sit uneasily beside what is known about the underlying clinical problem. Gold-standard instruments do not achieve them. Autism overlaps behaviourally with other neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions. Population prevalence is low, so positive predictive value is sensitive to specificity in ways that accuracy conceals. And the behavioural differences at issue are heterogeneous enough that meta-analytic effect sizes in the underlying neuropsychological domains have been declining over two decades.

This review therefore asks not whether computational methods can predict autism, but what the reported figures are measurements of. It charts 170 studies against a single instrument covering participants and how they are described, study setting, task and equipment, dataset sharing and reproducibility, behavioural modalities and their combination, computational methods, input representations, metrics, interpretability and validation strategy, and publication venue and framing. It applies QUADAS-2 for risk of bias and four PROBAST-derived domains for methodological quality, and reads each study's reported performance against its own analysis unit, outcome definition, comparison group and class prevalence.
conclusions_text:
Three conclusions follow from the 170 charts.

First, the field's headline numbers are not comparable to one another and mostly do not estimate what they appear to estimate. The dominant determinant of reported accuracy is whether the same person can appear on both sides of the evaluation split, and the second is whether the outcome is a function of the inputs. Neither is a property of autism, of the behavioural modality, or of the algorithm. Studies that avoid both report figures between roughly 0.6 and 0.9, with wide uncertainty at realistic sample sizes, and several of them say so explicitly.

Second, the comparison group determines the meaning of the result, and it is usually the wrong one. Discriminating autistic children from typically developing children measures a clinical-versus-non-clinical distinction that includes language ability, age, sex and attention. The four studies in this corpus that included a second clinical group found performance falling by 20 to 25 points, and the one study that measured the ADOS-2 itself against another clinical population found AUC 0.562. A screening claim requires the comparison the design usually omits.

Third, the ethics of this literature divide along a line that does not follow methodological quality. Studies that recruit children obtain approval and consent, and several go further - separate consent for image publication, teacher accompaniment during data collection, deletion of data and models after analysis. Studies that download children's photographs frequently declare that no human participants were involved. Two papers construct elaborate privacy machinery - federated learning, machine unlearning - around data they obtained no consent to use. The field would be improved less by better models than by four reporting requirements: state the analysis unit and the partition, state the class prevalence and the trivial baseline, state what the comparison group is, and state where the data came from and on what basis they may be used.

per_group_analysis.dimension: behavioural modality (approximate, derived from charted data type)
per_group_analysis.topic: To characterise how computation-based (machine learning and other computational) autism prediction studies that use behavioral data are designed, conducted and reported: who is studied and how they are described, in what settings and with what tasks, hardware and software the behavioral data are collected, how datasets are shared and how reproducibility and bias are handled, which behavioral modalities are operationalised and how they are combined, which computational methods, representations, evaluation metrics, interpretability techniques and validation strategies are used, and how the publication landscape has evolved over time.

summary.label: Eye tracking and gaze
summary.aggregate_finding: Largest group in the corpus. Reported accuracy is bimodal and tracks the analysis unit: studies partitioning gaze samples, scanpath images or eye crops report 97-100%, while the two studies using participant-independent partitions report F1 0.641 and 0.96 with a fold standard deviation of 0.08 on 28 people. Where interpretability is done properly the group produces its most valuable output - falsifiable claims about which gaze parameters carry information.
summary.caveats: Modality assignment is approximate, derived from each record's charted data-type field rather than from a categorisation applied by the original authors.

answers.question: What determines reported performance in this group?
answers.answer: The unit of analysis, not the paradigm. local_7432ffd7 split 1,048,575 gaze samples from 59 children by sample (99.78%, with CARS additionally in the feature vector); local_44d3aef5 split 547 scanpath images by image and reported 100% on 55 test images; local_bb4d1f7a generated exactly 100 eye crops per child from 40 children (97%). local_5f57ba19 used participant-independent nested cross-validation with a majority-class baseline built in (F1 0.641) and local_d7b6fa00 aggregated to the participant and listed leakage prevention as a contribution (0.96 ± 0.08 on 28 people).

answers.question: What behavioural findings does the group produce?
answers.answer: Where feature analysis is performed: fixation duration and vertical gaze distribution discriminate severity while velocity does not (local_bb4d1f7a); broad social/non-social areas of interest outperform fine decomposition by facial region and emotion (local_b6ac2b98); mouth fixation time and cross-AOI revisits are the leading discriminators, with the audio-visual advantage concentrated before speech onset (local_5f57ba19); mean duration of visits to objects distinguishes groups, read as difficulty disengaging attention (local_b6ac2b98).

answers.question: How is the comparison group defined?
answers.answer: Almost always typically developing children. The one study including a second clinical group (local_b6ac2b98, developmental language disorder) found F1 falling from 0.86 to 0.63, and concluded that the approach is more effective as a screening tool than for differential diagnosis.

summary.label: Movement, kinematics and interaction traces
summary.aggregate_finding: Contains the corpus's strongest differential-diagnosis study and its most honest handling of a perfect result, alongside frame- and session-level leakage of the same kind found elsewhere.
summary.caveats: Modality assignment is approximate, derived from each record's charted data-type field rather than from a categorisation applied by the original authors.

answers.question: What does direct comparison with another movement disorder show?
answers.answer: local_69b10fe4 compared autistic and parkinsonian movement with matched controls and found no kinematic feature shared between the two conditions that also differed from controls, refuting the anecdotal resemblance; classification reached mean test accuracy 0.73 for clinical versus non-clinical and 0.93 for ASD versus Parkinson's on test partitions of roughly 13 to 19 people.

answers.question: How is a perfect result handled?
answers.answer: local_231757c7 reported 100% for its severe-ASD class and stated in the same abstract sentence that the class's features were synthesised by averaging moderate-ASD vectors and adding Gaussian noise, computed the 95% interval (39.8-100.0%), noted that one misclassification would reduce recall to 75%, and set a minimum sample of 20-50 real cases for validation. It also reports that Kinect could not be deployed at all for children with severe autism.

answers.question: What leakage patterns appear?
answers.answer: local_b26db2f2 split 640 game sessions from 12 children by session and reported 96%, with leave-one-child-out available and unused; local_e771fb69 evaluated a four-modality federated framework on nine test cases with class-conditional mean imputation.

summary.label: Speech, voice and language
summary.aggregate_finding: The group contains both the corpus's most privacy-considered design and clear instances of demographic confounding. Where a second clinical group is included, performance falls markedly.
summary.caveats: Modality assignment is approximate, derived from each record's charted data-type field rather than from a categorisation applied by the original authors.

answers.question: What does the group find when a clinical comparison group is added?
answers.answer: local_1b457442 reports ROC-AUC 0.87-0.93 for ASD versus typical development and 0.71 once developmental delay is included, reading the gap as showing the risk of misdiagnosis.

answers.question: What confounds the binary results?
answers.answer: Age. In the Nadig corpus used by local_1b457442 the ASD children average roughly two years older than the typically developing children, and age is one of the four features the paper identifies as carrying the result.

answers.question: What behavioural markers emerge?
answers.answer: Mean length of utterance and mean length of turn ratio - the child's conversational share relative to the adult - both directionally interpretable and consistent with established clinical observation.

summary.label: Multimodal and other
summary.aggregate_finding: Heterogeneous group containing the corpus's best-validated adult study and several of its clearest reporting failures.
summary.caveats: Modality assignment is approximate, derived from each record's charted data-type field rather than from a categorisation applied by the original authors.

answers.question: What does the best-validated study in this group report?
answers.answer: local_7b19a959: 74.0% accuracy on an age- and gender-matched sample against 81.8% unmatched, with the matched figure reported as primary and the eight-point difference attributed explicitly to demographic features; 83% for the AQ alone and 92% combined; and a label-randomisation control that falls to chance.

answers.question: What are the group's principal failures?
answers.answer: local_367db0b6 reports 25,000 positive cases drawn from a 10,000-sample dataset and describes the result as class-balanced, names an exemplary metric set and reports no value from it, and declares no ethics approval necessary in a paper premised on parental consent withdrawal for newborns' data. local_1d856900 splits an unsourced 100-sample clinical dataset after fourfold augmentation and reports 98.2% on 40 rows against 4,220 features.

summary.label: Facial images (still photographs)
summary.aggregate_finding: Sixteen studies, all reusing the same web-scraped corpus of children's facial photographs, reporting 81.0% to 99.8%. Reported accuracy tracks model capacity and evaluation looseness rather than signal. No study performs a source-held-out evaluation, none establishes the number of distinct children, and none reports a diagnostic procedure for any image.
summary.caveats: Modality assignment is approximate, derived from each record's charted data-type field rather than from a categorisation applied by the original authors.

answers.question: What is the provenance of the data?
answers.answer: A public corpus assembled from web searches and social-media pages with autism-related content, redistributed through Kaggle and Roboflow. Several papers state the provenance confound in their own methods sections and none tests it. Two describe the corpus as something it is not: local_986436f2 supplies age, ethnicity, urban/rural and facial-morphology annotations that the dataset does not contain and reports 2D photographs as 3D scans with 0.9 mm landmark error; local_44d3aef5 reports 547 images as 547 children.

answers.question: How are outcomes ascertained?
answers.answer: By folder name. No study in this group reports a diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or date for any image.

answers.question: What does the group's own evidence say about what the models decide?
answers.answer: local_e54c304c ran the only out-of-distribution probe in the branch: one of its two detectors classified a photograph of a dog as Autistic and a leaf as Nonautistic. Separately, local_e04bcd32's headline 96.94% is a resubstitution figure computed over all 2,940 images including the 2,540 used for training, and local_986436f2's confusion matrix sums to 300 cases against a stated 200-image evaluation.

answers.question: How is ethics handled?
answers.answer: Mostly by exemption or silence. local_13c1f46d states that the study did not involve direct experiments on humans because publicly available Kaggle datasets were used; local_e4c2a776 declares that the article contains no studies with human participants. The exceptions are local_945300a5, which recruited and photographed 70 children under an ethics code with parental consent and teacher accompaniment, and local_e54c304c, which is the only study in the branch to state that given the child's facial data aspect, there is ethical sensitivity.

summary.label: Questionnaire and checklist data
summary.aggregate_finding: Reported accuracy in this group is governed by how much of the label's own arithmetic survives preprocessing. Where all checklist items are retained the models reach 99-100%; where half are deleted performance falls to 0.83. No study in the group predicts a clinician diagnosis.
summary.caveats: Modality assignment is approximate, derived from each record's charted data-type field rather than from a categorisation applied by the original authors.

answers.question: What is the outcome variable?
answers.answer: In every case a threshold on the sum of the items supplied as features. local_ed30e24c classified 292 of 292 correctly; local_183eaef4 reached accuracy 1.0000 with CARS, SRS, AQ-10 and Q-CHAT-10 scores all in the predictor set; local_8ff20c48 deleted five of ten items for correlating with the score they are summed into and fell to 0.83; local_14df790d showed that every subset containing the total or its summands performs well.

answers.question: Does any study identify the circularity?
answers.answer: One. local_af9f4c12 states that because the severity labels are deterministically derived from the same behavioural attributes used as model inputs, the task constitutes a structured function-approximation setting and high performance should not be read as diagnostic accuracy - and repeats the restriction in five sections. local_14df790d comes closest without naming it, observing that retaining both the total and its items could mislead the model.

answers.question: What use is proposed for the outputs?
answers.answer: local_b9de0d7f is the extreme case: a six-way teaching-method target generated with numpy from the Q-CHAT total, predicted at 0.9917 from the items that total is computed from, with an uncited severity-to-intervention mapping offered to educators as a basis for decisions about individual children's education.

summary.label: Robot-mediated and interactive-system data
summary.aggregate_finding: Small group characterised by primary data collection in interactive settings, and containing the corpus's methodological benchmark for prospective validation.
summary.caveats: Modality assignment is approximate, derived from each record's charted data-type field rather than from a categorisation applied by the original authors.

answers.question: What is the strongest design in the corpus?
answers.answer: local_7b468950, the Play.Care phase III protocol (NCT03438994): a locked algorithm, blinded prospective external validation, sensitivity and specificity as prespecified primary outcomes, a 200-child cohort with other neurodevelopmental disorders for differential diagnosis, and a design powered to detect underperformance. It states of its own pilot that it only trained and tested patterns on that particular dataset.

summary.label: Video of naturalistic behaviour
summary.aggregate_finding: The most ecologically valid data in the corpus - spontaneous behaviour recorded in children's homes - undermined by clip-level partitioning and, in one case, by a task that contains no non-autistic comparison at all.
summary.caveats: Modality assignment is approximate, derived from each record's charted data-type field rather than from a categorisation applied by the original authors.

answers.question: What is the validation problem?
answers.answer: local_8d43288c formed folds over clips extracted from 75 parent-posted YouTube videos with no video- or child-level grouping, and read fold standard deviations below 0.004 as robustness.

answers.question: What is actually being classified?
answers.answer: In local_8d43288c, four movement categories within a dataset containing only autistic children - so the study's screening and diagnostic framing cannot follow from its result, as its own decision-support hedge implicitly concedes.

summary.label: Physiological and thermal signals
summary.aggregate_finding: Very small group; the charted members show the corpus's permissive end of the ethics gradient.
summary.caveats: Modality assignment is approximate, derived from each record's charted data-type field rather than from a categorisation applied by the original authors.

answers.question: What ethics reporting appears?
answers.answer: local_45ef7022 records Ethical Approval. Not required. for thermal imaging of 30 disabled children alongside proposed medication dosing.

per_group_analysis.overall_caveats: Groups are loosely defined families, not exhaustive mutually exclusive categories; several studies combine modalities and are assigned to the family matching their charted primary data type. Group-level statements describe tendencies and name exemplars rather than asserting properties of every member.

research_questions.note: Per-study answers to the prespecified review questions. The same answers are also carried per study in data_charting_rubrics[].custom_fields.

questions.short_title: Participant groups and reporting of group sizes
questions.question_text: Which participant groups are included (autistic/ASD, neurotypical, other diagnoses), and is each group's presence and size explicitly reported?

answers.title: Very early detection of Autism Spectrum Disorders based on acoustic analysis of pre-verbal vocalizations of 18-month old toddlers
answers.answer: ASD group (n=23, high-risk siblings later diagnosed) and typically developing low-risk controls (n=20); both explicitly reported with sizes in Table 1. No other-diagnosis group.

answers.title: Use of Machine Learning to Identify Children with Autism and Their Motor Abnormalities
answers.answer: Two groups: ASD (n=15, low-functioning preschool) and typically developing controls (n=15). Both explicitly reported with demographics in Table 1. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

answers.title: ADHD and ASD Classification Based on Emotion Recognition Data
answers.answer: Three groups: ASD (n=18), ADHD (n=30) and typically developing controls (n=13). Group sizes are reported; this is one of the few corpus studies with a non-autistic clinical comparison group. No demographic breakdown beyond mean age.

answers.title: Identifying children with autism spectrum disorder based on their face processing abnormality: A machine learning framework
answers.answer: Three groups: ASD (n=29) and two typically developing control groups - chronological-age-matched (n=29) and nonverbal-ability/IQ-matched (n=29). All groups reported with sex ratio, age, nonverbal IQ raw score and AQ. No other-diagnosis clinical group.

answers.title: Semantic mapping reveals distinct patterns in descriptions of social relations in adults with autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: Two groups: adults with ASD (n=27, one non-completer) and typical adults (n=132, two non-completers), the latter reported separately as 45 males and 87 females. No other-diagnosis group - indeed other DSM-IV diagnoses were an exclusion criterion.

answers.title: Toward the Autism Motor Signature: Gesture patterns during smart tablet gameplay identify children with autism
answers.answer: Two groups: children clinically diagnosed with Childhood Autism (n=37 recruited, 35 with usable data) and typically developing controls (n=45). Group composition is reported in unusual detail - 30 'uncomplicated' autism, 1 high-functioning, 2 Asperger's Syndrome, 4 with co-morbid intellectual impairment (2 completing). No non-autistic clinical comparison group, which the authors identify as the key gap.

answers.title: Applying machine learning to identify autistic adults using imitation: An exploratory study
answers.answer: Two groups: autistic adults (16 recruited, 14 analysed after two exclusions for data capture failure) and neurotypical adult controls (n=16). Both group sizes and the exclusion are reported explicitly. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the discussion identifies developmental coordination disorder and ADHD as the comparisons needed next.

answers.title: Automatic Detection of ADHD and ASD from Expressive Behaviour in RGBD Data
answers.answer: Four groups: controls (n=18), ASD only (n=22), ADHD only (n=4) and comorbid ADHD+ASD (n=11), totalling 55 adults. Group sizes must be inferred from the classification tables and a bar chart rather than a participant table. The ADHD-only group was explicitly too small (n=4) to train a classifier for, so the reported analyses collapse to controls-vs-condition and comorbid-vs-ASD-only. This is one of very few corpus studies with both a non-autistic clinical group and an explicit comorbid group.

answers.title: Earlier identification of children with autism
answers.answer: Two groups of 10: infants at heightened familial risk (younger siblings of children with ASD) later diagnosed with ASD at 3 years, and typically developing infants from a low-risk population with normal 3-year outcome. Both groups fully specified per subject in Table 1, including vocalisation counts and cross-validation partition assignment - subject-level transparency that is rare in this corpus. No other-diagnosis group.

answers.title: Speech-based Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Condition by Generative
answers.answer: Four groups: autism disorders (n=11), PDD-NOS (n=10), specific language impairment (n=13) and typically developing (n=68), totalling 102 children. Group sizes are reported. This is one of the few corpus studies to include a non-autistic clinical comparison group - and notably one (SLI) chosen to probe exactly the specificity question that most ASD-versus-TD studies leave open. It is also one of the few to separate autism disorders from PDD-NOS as distinct classes.

answers.title: ANN and SVM Classifiers in Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorder Gait Based on Three-Dimensional Ground Reaction Forces
answers.answer: Two groups of 30: children with ASD (all mild category) and typically developing children. Group sizes, mean age, height and body mass are reported for both. Recruitment is split within the ASD group - 14 from the National Autism Society of Malaysia centre and 16 from the local community via parents approached through social media - which is unusually specific. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

answers.title: Analyzing Human-Robot Interaction Using Machine Vision for Autism screening
answers.answer: Two groups of 8: children with ASD and typically developing children, total n=16. Group sizes are reported; no other-diagnosis group. The predecessor study being automated (Soleiman et al.) used 32 children, so this automation paper works on half that sample.

answers.title: Applying Eye Tracking to Identify Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children
answers.answer: Two groups of 37: children with ASD recruited from a hospital child mental health outpatient ward, and typically developing children recruited from a local kindergarten. Both groups fully characterised in a demographic table. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

answers.title: Automatic Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Everyday
answers.answer: Three groups recruited: 18 children diagnosed with ASD, 9 typically developing children, and 8 at-risk children defined as undiagnosed younger siblings of ASD children. Only the 27 with definite TD or ASD status entered the classification experiment; the at-risk group was excluded because undiagnosed, which is handled transparently. Per-subject characteristics are tabulated individually.

answers.title: Detecting Autism Based on Eye-Tracking Data from Web Searching
answers.answer: Two groups: adults with a confirmed clinical diagnosis of high-functioning autism or Asperger's syndrome (18 recruited, 15 analysed) and non-autistic control adults (18 recruited, 15 analysed after 2 data-quality exclusions and 1 random removal to balance classes). All recruitment, exclusion and balancing decisions are reported explicitly, including the random removal. No other-diagnosis group.

answers.title: Video Gesture Analysis for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
answers.answer: Two groups of 20: children with ASD without accompanying intellectual impairment (18 male), and typically developing children (16 male). One ASD subject (subject 3) was discarded because all their non-corrupted videos came from a single condition, so 39 subjects enter the experiments. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

answers.title: A Novel Eye Movement Data Transformation Technique that Preserves Temporal Information: A Demonstration in a Face Processing Task
answers.answer: Two groups: 21 individuals with ASD and 23 age- and IQ-matched typically developing controls, total 44. Group sizes, sexes and IQ means are all reported. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

answers.title: Applying Machine Learning to Identify Autism With Restricted Kinematic Features
answers.answer: Two groups: 20 children with high-functioning autism and 23 age-matched typically developing children. Group sizes are clear. No other-diagnosis comparison group - indeed ADHD, intellectual disability and schizophrenia were explicit exclusions - though the conclusion identifies ASD-versus-ADHD classification as the needed next step.

answers.title: Automatic Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Acoustic and Text Features from Brief Natural Conversations
answers.answer: Two groups of 35: children with ASD and typically developing children, plus 22 young adult confederates (19 female) who served as conversation partners and whose speech was also analysed. The confederates are effectively a third participant group whose data enter the model - an unusual design in this corpus. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

answers.title: Classifying Individuals with ASD Through Facial Emotion Recognition and Eye-Tracking
answers.answer: Two groups: 23 individuals with ASD (5 later excluded for eye-tracking failure) and 35 typically developing controls, total 58 recruited. Group sizes, sexes and ages are reported, and control status is defined by explicit exclusions. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the discussion proposes extending the paradigm to schizophrenia and ADHD.

answers.title: Detecting Developmental Delay and Autism Through Machine
answers.answer: Three groups: 55 videos of children with ASD, 50 with speech and language conditions, and 54 typically developing, totalling 159 videos (150 with complete demographic data). The inclusion of a non-autistic clinical comparison group - and the explicit design of a second classification layer to separate ASD from other developmental delay - directly addresses the specificity question that most ASD-versus-typical studies in this corpus leave open. SLC diagnoses are further broken down: 74% had both receptive and expressive language delay, 12% receptive and expressive language disorder, 10% expressive delay alone, 4% receptive delay alone.

answers.title: Exploiting Visual Behaviour for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification
answers.answer: Two groups by dataset label - ASD and typically developing - but the paper reports no participant counts for either group, only image counts (300 training, 100 test). The unit of analysis throughout is the scanpath rather than the person, and subject identifiers are explicitly randomised and inconsistent across images, so participant-level group composition is not recoverable.

answers.title: Hierarchical POMDP Framework for a Robot-Assisted ASD Diagnostic Protocol
answers.answer: Two groups: 8 preschool children already diagnosed with ASD and 7 typically developing children, total 15. Group sizes are reported. No other-diagnosis group. Notably the analysis is ultimately regrouped by expert-assessed behaviour rather than by diagnosis, producing four categories (ASD-like behaviour n=5, typical behaviour n=3, ambiguous n=4, session too short n=3) that cut across the original diagnostic grouping.

answers.title: Intelligent Gaze-Based Screening System for Autism
answers.answer: Two groups are referred to - ASD and typically developing (non-ASD) children - but no participant counts are reported for either group anywhere in the paper. The sample is described only as 'our collected eye movement data set'. This is the only study charted so far that reports classification performance without stating any sample size.

answers.title: Kinematic features of a simple and short movement task to predict autism diagnosis
answers.answer: Two groups: 24 autistic adults and 22 non-autistic (typically developing) adults, IQ-matched. Both group sizes and sex counts are reported. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

answers.title: Learning to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder based on the Visual
answers.answer: Two groups: 29 ASD-diagnosed children and 30 non-ASD children, total 59. Group sizes are reported. For the multi-label experiment the ASD group is further split by CARS severity into Low, Mild and Severe bands, making four classes. No non-autistic clinical comparison group.

answers.title: Machine Learning to Study Social Interaction Difficulties in ASD
answers.answer: Two groups of 29: high-functioning autistic adults (ICD-10 F84.0 or F84.5) and typically developed adults. Dyads were composed in three configurations - two typically developed, two autistic, or mixed - which is a design feature no other corpus study uses, since it means each participant's behaviour is measured while interacting with partners of both diagnostic statuses. No other-diagnosis group, though transdiagnostic specificity testing is named as required future work.

answers.title: Phase 3 diagnostic evaluation of a smart
answers.answer: A planned sample of 760 children aged 30 months to 5 years 11 months across two countries, allocated in a published table: Glasgow 100 autistic, 140 other neurodevelopmental disorder and 180 typically developing; Gothenburg 180 autistic, 60 other neurodevelopmental disorder and 100 typically developing. The composition is the most important feature of the design for this review. Two hundred children with a diagnosed neurodevelopmental condition that is not autism - intellectual disability, non-verbal disability, communication disability, ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, Down's syndrome and cerebral palsy - are recruited specifically to test whether the instrument distinguishes autism from other developmental difference rather than only from typical development. Children with subclinical or secondary expressions of autism are excluded from that cohort to keep the contrast interpretable. No participant data are reported, since the protocol was published before data collection closed and the results are embargoed.

answers.title: Predicting Autism Diagnosis using Image with Fixations and Synthetic Saccade Patterns
answers.answer: Two groups by dataset label - ASD and typically developing - with 14 of each viewing every image. The total number of distinct participants is never stated, only the per-image viewer counts, so the actual sample size is unrecoverable from this paper. No other-diagnosis group.

answers.title: Recognition Of Atypical Behavior In Autism Diagnosis From Video Using Pose Estimation Over Time
answers.answer: The paper does not report participant groups at all. The corpus is described only as 555 videos 'recorded from a mix of children with and without ASD', with no participant counts, no breakdown by diagnostic status, and no indication of how many children contributed the videos. The analytic groups are instead behavioural: 3084 expert-labelled typical time stamps and 5265 atypical time stamps across four video sets. This is a fundamentally different unit of analysis from the rest of the corpus.

answers.title: Robot-Assisted Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Based on Artificial Reasoning
answers.answer: Six children aged 36 to 48 months, each participating in a single session: three described as 'without confirmed ASD diagnosis, but with evidence of risk factors', and three typically developing children serving as the control group, with five boys and one girl in total. The sample is among the smallest in the review and the paper is explicit that it constitutes 'a proof of concept'. The diagnostic status of both groups is undocumented - the risk factors are not enumerated for the index group and no screening procedure is described for the comparison group - so no participant in the study has an established diagnostic classification. That is unusual in this corpus and is stated openly rather than obscured: the phrase 'without confirmed ASD diagnosis' appears in the methods, and the study makes no diagnostic claim on the basis of these children. At 36 to 48 months both groups sit in the age window where identification is typically still under way, so the risk framing is age-appropriate. No cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is reported.

answers.title: SP-ASDNet: CNN-LSTM Based ASD Classification Model using Observer ScanPaths
answers.answer: Two groups by dataset label - ASD and typically developing - with 14 of each viewing every image, though the paper notes 'some of the images have less than 14 scanpaths from the TD or ASD groups' because some children did not look inside the image bounds. The total number of distinct participants is never stated, so the actual sample size is unrecoverable. No other-diagnosis group.

answers.title: Social robot in diagnosis of autism among preschool children
answers.answer: Preschool children with autism recruited through an integrative kindergarten in Wroclaw, which is named in the acknowledgements. The retrieved text does not state the sample size, ages or sex composition, and no cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is reported. There is no comparison group of any kind - a design feature the authors identify explicitly as their first limitation. The absence of controls means the study cannot support any between-group inference, and it is not presented as doing so: the finding is a within-subject dissociation, where each child's rate of instructed behaviour is compared against their own rate of spontaneous imitation, so every child serves as their own control and the sample size constrains precision rather than validity.

answers.title: Application of the Still-Face Paradigm in Early Screening for High-Risk Autism Spectrum Disorder in Infants and Toddlers
answers.answer: Two groups plus a prospectively emergent third. At enrolment: 45 high-risk infants and 43 typically developing infants, 88 in total, aged 8-23 months. At 24-month follow-up the high-risk group split into 40 confirmed ASD and 5 who no longer met criteria (N-ASD). Classification used the 40 confirmed ASD against the 43 TD. The N-ASD subgroup is the corpus's clearest instance of a genuine clinical comparison group - children who present as high-risk but do not go on to be diagnosed - and the study's inability to classify any of them is the most informative negative result in this record.

answers.title: Applying Machine Learning to Kinematic and Eye Movement Features of a Movement Imitation Task to Predict Autism Diagnosis
answers.answer: Two groups totalling 44 adults, split across two independently constituted samples: a development sample of 15 autistic and 15 non-autistic adults, and a hold-out testing sample of 7 autistic and 7 non-autistic adults, each internally matched. Having a pre-specified independent test sample rather than only cross-validation folds is rare in this corpus. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

answers.title: Research and Design of Autism Smart Diagnosis Information System Based on Chinese Children's Facial Expression Data and Deep Convolution Neural Network
answers.answer: Two groups of ten: 10 autistic children aged 3-6 from Guangzhou Children's Care Center and 10 typically developing children aged 5-8 from Amy Education School in Zhengzhou. A separate group of 16 typically developing Chinese children aged 5-8 (8 boys, 8 girls) supplied 112 training images. No other-diagnosis comparison group. At 20 evaluation participants this is among the smallest clinical evaluations in the corpus, and it is a system test rather than a model validation.

answers.title: Automated identification of postural control for children with autism spectrum disorder using a machine learning approach
answers.answer: Two groups of 25: children with ASD and age-matched typically developing children, total 50. Both groups are characterised in a demographic table with sample size, sex breakdown, body mass, height and age. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though neurological disorders other than ASD were an explicit exclusion for both groups.

answers.title: Behavior-based Risk Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through
answers.answer: Two groups: 5 boys with ASD and 7 typically developing boys, total 12 children. Group sizes, sexes and mean ages are reported. No other-diagnosis comparison group. This is the smallest participant sample in the corpus charted so far.

answers.title: Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation as a Scalable Method for Distinguishing Children With Autism
answers.answer: Two groups: 27 children with autism spectrum conditions and 21 typically developing children, total 48. Group sizes are clear and participant characteristics are tabulated with group comparison test statistics, though the values are not recoverable from the extracted text. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

answers.title: Deep-Learning-Based Detection of Infants with Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Auto-Encoder Feature Representation
answers.answer: Two groups, 39 infants: 10 diagnosed autistic and 29 typically developing, all recruited as consecutive clinical cases undergoing diagnostic assessment at one hospital between 2016 and 2018. The typically developing group is not a convenience sample - these are infants brought for assessment who were assessed as typical, which makes them a clinically relevant comparison (children of diagnostic concern who turn out not to be autistic) rather than a community control group. Analysis is at the utterance level: 1,125 utterances, 475 autistic and 650 typically developing.

answers.title: Effects of Intra-Subject Variation in Gait Analysis on ASD Classification Performance in Machine Learning Models
answers.answer: Two groups, 21 subjects: 12 clinically diagnosed autistic and 9 typically developed. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The analysis unit is not the subject but the gait cycle (Dataset A: 167 autistic and 111 typically developed cycles) or the walking trial (Dataset B: 60 and 45), so 21 people generate 278 or 105 data points respectively. The authors themselves note that with a dataset this small 'the impact of variation in the subjects may be magnified due to the large portion of the dataset each subject represents'.

answers.title: Estimating Autism Severity in Young Children From Speech Signals Using a Deep Neural Network
answers.answer: One clinically referred cohort of 72 children treated as a severity continuum rather than as contrasting groups: 56 with an ASD diagnosis, 10 referred with suspected autism who received other diagnoses (language or developmental delays), and 6 typically developing children. Including the 10 diagnostically ambiguous referrals is unusual and important - most of the corpus either excludes such children or treats them as noise, whereas here they are the cases that make the prediction problem realistic. All 72 completed the same DSM-5 clinical assessment and ADOS-2.

answers.title: Detecting High-Functioning Autism in Adults Using Eye Tracking and Machine Learning
answers.answer: Two groups across two independent collections: 71 adults recruited, 68 retained (28 autistic, 32 control), with 15 per group analysed in Study 1 and 19 per group in Study 2, and 9 participants (6 autistic, 3 control) taking part in both. Exclusions are itemised: in Study 1, three autistic and two control participants for calibration and head-movement problems plus one randomly chosen control to rebalance classes; in Study 2, five controls - one for a high AQ score, three for reported school dyslexia referrals and two for calibration. Adults with high-functioning autism are a substantially under-represented population in this corpus, which is dominated by preschool and school-age children.

answers.title: Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder via an Eye-Tracking Based
answers.answer: Two groups: 31 autistic children recruited through the Children Rehabilitation Center at Shaanxi Rehabilitation Hospital and 43 typically developing children attending mainstream schools in Xi'an. The reported experiments use 30 and 40 respectively (15 + 20 training, 15 + 20 testing), so one autistic and three typically developing children are recruited but unaccounted for in the analysis, with no explanation given. No other-diagnosis comparison group; the authors themselves flag class balance as an issue needing attention.

answers.title: Machine Learning and Virtual Reality on Body Movements' Behaviors to Classify Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: Two groups: 24 autistic children recruited through Red Cenit, a cognitive development centre in Valencia, and 25 typically developing children recruited by a management company through mailings to families. Both groups presented individual assessment reports including ADOS-2 and ADI-R, so the comparison group is instrument-assessed rather than merely unscreened. No other-diagnosis comparison group, and the authors identify this as a specificity limitation, proposing ADHD and intellectual disability comparisons for future work. Note that the results tables imply 22 rather than 24 autistic children were analysed.

answers.title: Responsive Social Smile: A Machine-Learning Based Multimodal Behavior Assessment Framework towards Early Stage Autism Screening
answers.answer: Two groups, 41 toddlers: 20 diagnosed autistic and 21 non-autistic, all assessed at the same specialist hospital. The comparison group is therefore clinically referred rather than community-recruited, which makes the discrimination task harder and more clinically realistic than most of the corpus. A separate, non-overlapping group of 54 children under six supplied 15,000 labelled expression clips for training the perception module. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

answers.title: Selection of Eye-Tracking Stimuli for Prediction by Sparsely Grouped Input Variables for Neural Networks: towards Biomarker Refinement for Autism
answers.answer: One cohort of 64 children split 32 autistic and 32 non-autistic, with the non-autistic group deliberately heterogeneous - 'typical development, language delay, and other developmental concerns'. This is one of only a few studies in the corpus whose comparison group is a clinically referred mixed-diagnosis sample rather than typically developing children, which raises the difficulty of the task and makes the result far more relevant to real screening. Clinical instrumentation is deep for a subset: ADOS severity, SRS total and Vineland-3 ABC for 30 of the 32 autistic children, and Stanford-Binet IQ for all 64.

answers.title: The identification of children with autism spectrum disorder by SVM approach on EEG and eye-tracking data
answers.answer: Two groups, 97 children: 49 with confirmed autism diagnoses and 48 typically developing children recruited from a local kindergarten. No other-diagnosis comparison group. At 97 participants this is one of the larger single-site cohorts in the corpus, and the authors note they 'recruited a relatively large sample size for the sake of classification'.

answers.title: Toward Continuous Social Phenotyping: Analyzing Gaze Patterns in an Emotion Recognition Task for Children With Autism Through Wearable Smart Glasses
answers.answer: Two groups: 16 autistic and 17 neurotypical children, from 43 enrolled (23 autistic, 20 neurotypical). Exclusions are itemised with reasons: 4 controls received an early prototype version with visual rather than audio cues and could not read the cues or complete the task; 5 autistic participants received images in a different randomised order because of a stimulus ordering error; and 1 autistic participant had an unrelated health issue mid-session. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The cohort is predominantly high-functioning - only 3 of 16 autistic participants had an abbreviated IQ below 80.

answers.title: Towards the automatic detection of social biomarkers in autism spectrum disorder: introducing the simulated interaction task (SIT)
answers.answer: Two groups in the main study: 37 autistic adults without intellectual disability recruited via the autism outpatient clinic of Charite Universitatsmedizin Berlin, and 43 healthy controls, with one autistic participant excluded from the combined classifier for missing audio. A separate preparatory study used 40 healthy males with facial EMG to select regions of interest before the main analysis - a two-stage design in which feature selection is performed on an entirely different sample, which is stronger than any within-study selection procedure. No other-psychiatric-diagnosis comparison group, though the authors identify testing 'in larger clinical samples with different psychiatric conditions' as necessary since the social interaction deficits targeted are common to many disorders.

answers.title: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence to Diagnose Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Tracking Saccades
answers.answer: Two groups totalling 108 participants: 65 with autism and 43 without. No other-diagnosis comparison group. Nothing further is reported about either group, and because the dataset is secondary and unidentified, no additional characteristics can be recovered. The class imbalance (60:40) is never addressed in the modelling, and with accuracy as the only reported metric a classifier predicting the majority class throughout would score 60%.

answers.title: An Experimental Trial: Multi-Robot Therapy for Categorization of Autism Level Using Hidden Markov Model
answers.answer: A single group of 12 autistic children from the Autism Resource Center in Islamabad, split into 8 for training and 4 for the prediction test. There is no non-autistic comparison group and none is intended - the task is severity categorisation within autism rather than case-control discrimination, which makes this one of the few studies in the corpus targeting a graded clinical outcome rather than a binary diagnosis. The analysis unit is the intervention session rather than the child, so 97 sessions arise from 12 individuals and 25 test predictions from 4.

answers.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis Based on Trajectories of Eye Tracking Data
answers.answer: Two groups totalling 86 participants: 56 autistic (38 male, 18 female, aged 5-18, mean 10) and 30 typically developing (20 male, 10 female, aged 3-15, mean 10). The class ratio is 65:35 in favour of autism, which the authors identify as a limitation and address with SMOTE on training folds. No other-diagnosis comparison group. At 86 participants this is among the larger single-site eye-tracking cohorts in the corpus.

answers.title: Autistic spectrum traits detection and early screening: A machine learning based eye movement study
answers.answer: Two entirely separate samples serving different roles. The preliminary experiment used 107 non-clinical adults (49 women, 58 men, mean age 24.84 +/- 5.24) split by AQ score into 52 above-median and 55 below-median. The test experiment used 22 young autistic males (mean age 12.68 +/- 7.61) recruited through the Shenzhen Autism Society, with no comparison group. The two samples differ in age by roughly twelve years on average, in sex composition (mixed versus all-male) and in clinical status (trait-scored general population versus diagnosed), so the second is not a held-out sample from the first population but a different population entirely.

answers.title: Automatic classification of children with autism spectrum disorder by using a computerized visual‐orienting task
answers.answer: Three groups totalling 74 children: 26 high-functioning autistic, 24 low-functioning autistic and 24 typically developing, all age-matched. Splitting the autistic sample by cognitive functioning rather than treating it as homogeneous is the design's defining feature and is argued for explicitly, on the grounds that binary classification 'fails to take into account the heterogeneity in the ASD population' and that low-functioning autistic children may show behaviours confounded with developmental delay and even with 'normal people with autistic traits, such as stereotyped behaviors, aggression, and noncompliance'. No separate developmental-delay or other-diagnosis group.

answers.title: Auxiliary Diagnostic Method for Early Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Movement Data Analysis
answers.answer: Two groups: 39 autistic children recruited from the Shanghai Putuo District Zhanyi Children Cultivation Service Center and 53 children described as normal, totalling 92. Nine samples were excluded for partial data loss or non-cooperation, leaving 83 - 33 autistic and 50 typically developing, so 6 autistic and 3 comparison children were removed, a differential exclusion rate of 15% versus 6% that is not commented on. No other-diagnosis comparison group.
