answers.title: Children ASD Evaluation Through Joint Analysis of EEG and Eye-Tracking Recordings With Graph Convolution Network
answers.answer: Two groups of 21 children each, aged 3-6, totalling 42. No other-diagnosis comparison group. Nothing further is reported about either group - no ages beyond the shared range, no sexes, no clinical characterisation - and because no provenance for the dataset is given, nothing can be recovered from a source publication either.

answers.title: Classification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Using Eye Tracking Data Based on Visual Attention Model
answers.answer: A single clinical population of 88 autistic children and adolescents, split by CARS into 39 severe and 49 non-severe, from 91 recruited. There is no typically developing comparison group and none is intended - the research question is whether severity can be graded within autism, which makes this one of very few studies in the corpus addressing gradation rather than detection. Exclusions were calibration problems, eye-tracking record rate below 80% and age over 17, applied to three participants.

answers.title: Classification of Children With Autism and Typical Development Using Eye-Tracking Data From Face-to-Face Conversations: Machine Learning Model Development and Performance Evaluation
answers.answer: Two groups: 20 autistic children recruited from the Child Psychiatry Department of Shenzhen Kangning Hospital and 23 typically developing children from local schools, with four excluded for eye-tracking technical problems leaving 19 and 20. No other-diagnosis comparison group, and the authors identify this as a substantive limitation rather than a scope note: 'it remains unclear whether eye-tracking data could effectively detect ASD from other clinical phenotypes (eg, developmental delay and ADHD)'.

answers.title: Combined Signal Processing Based Techniques and Feed Forward Neural Networks for Pathological Voice Detection and Classification
answers.answer: Three groups, but 19 children in total: 6 autistic (3 boys, 3 girls), 6 with Down syndrome (2 boys, 4 girls) and 7 controls (3 boys, 4 girls), contributing 79, 77 and 99 sustained vowel samples respectively. The inclusion of a Down syndrome group is the design's most valuable feature - it is one of only a handful of studies in the corpus with an other-diagnosis comparison rather than only typical development, enabling the differential question the paper poses. But with six children per clinical group the analysis rests on a very small number of individuals however many samples each provides.

answers.title: Computer-Aided Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Eye-Tracking Study Using Data Visualization and Deep Learning
answers.answer: Two groups of 59 children: 29 autistic and 30 non-autistic, closely matched at 19 males each. The authors explain the age composition candidly rather than presenting it as a design choice - they wanted younger participants for early detection, 'but in our region there were not enough diagnosed children younger than 6 years, and the time it takes to consult a doctor to make a diagnosis can be as long as 2 years'. That is an unusually direct statement of how diagnostic waiting times constrain the very research meant to shorten them. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

answers.title: Computer-aided autism diagnosis based on visual attention models using eye tracking
answers.answer: Two groups totalling 106 children and adolescents: 76 autistic recruited from the Psychiatry Institute of the University of Sao Paulo School of Medicine and 30 typically developing. The class ratio of roughly 2.5:1 favouring autism is not addressed by any balancing procedure and matters for interpreting the reported 90% precision. Notably, participants with psychiatric and neurological comorbidities were deliberately retained rather than excluded, with the authors reasoning from co-occurrence prevalence that excluding them would misrepresent the population. No separate other-diagnosis group, though extending to autism-versus-ADHD discrimination is named as a future direction.

answers.title: Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis
answers.answer: Two groups totalling 55 children aged 4-7: 35 autistic recruited from the Red Cenit Neurocognitive Development Center in Valencia and 20 typically developing recruited by a management company through calls and mailings to families. The 35:20 imbalance is not addressed by any balancing procedure. Both groups are stated to have received the same evaluation scales and procedure before the experiment. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the authors name ADHD inclusion as a priority for future work specifically to 'identify with greater precision the degrees of severity in each disorder'.

answers.title: Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms
answers.answer: Two groups: 20 autistic children recruited from a local psychiatric hospital and 23 typically developing children from nearby communities, with five excluded for camera technical problems leaving 18 and 20. Participants are the same cohort as a companion study by the same group on conversational eye tracking, but the data come from a different conversational session - the yes-no question session rather than the full four-session conversation. No other-diagnosis comparison group. Participants were paid 200 CNY, which is disclosed.

answers.title: Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset
answers.answer: Two groups inherited from the source dataset: 30 autistic and 29 non-autistic children, contributing 219 and 328 scanpath images respectively. The analysis operates on images rather than children throughout, and the 59 participants are never treated as the unit of anything. Following k-means partitioning, the effective analysis units become four image clusters of unstated composition - the paper does not report how many images, or how many children, fall in each cluster, nor the class balance within them, which makes the per-cluster metrics difficult to interpret.

answers.title: Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: Two groups of 13 children each. The autistic group spans three ICD-10 diagnoses - six with F84.9 pervasive developmental disorder unspecified, six with F84.0 autistic disorder and one with F84.5 Asperger syndrome - and includes four children with comorbid mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and one with epilepsy, all reported per participant rather than excluded. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the authors identify developmental coordination disorder and ADHD as necessary additions for establishing whether the motor finding is autism-specific or shared across neurodevelopmental conditions.

answers.title: Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment
answers.answer: Eleven autistic boys recruited from Al Ain Hospital in the United Arab Emirates, all with CARS2 scores between 30 and 36.5 - the mild-to-moderate band - under 16 years of age with a mean of 9.03 years (SD 2.56), and all required to have at least minimal verbal capability, being able to understand verbal communication and answer yes or no. Six of the eleven continued into the long-term study, with no explanation given for the other five. There is no comparison group of any kind, which is consistent with the design: the study measures attention within an intervention rather than discriminating between populations. Two features of the sample are worth recording for the review. Reporting a CARS2 range as an eligibility criterion is more severity characterisation than most included studies provide, and it bounds the population precisely - but because only the range is given rather than per-child scores, within-sample severity variation cannot be related to any outcome. And the eligibility requirements taken together - male, mild to moderate, verbally responsive - define a narrow population, so the system's behaviour with non-speaking or more severely affected children is untested despite the abstract describing the target group as having 'minimal verbal capabilities'.

answers.title: Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning
answers.answer: Two groups of 100 children each: 100 autistic children recruited from the Child Psychiatry Department at Mayo Hospital Lahore and a private autism school, and 100 children described as healthy whose recruitment source is never stated. The comparison group was collected specifically 'to ensure that our model is trained without any class imbalance problem', so its purpose is stated as statistical rather than clinical. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

answers.title: Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism
answers.answer: Two groups from a single neuroimaging cohort: 104 autistic participants recruited of whom 90 were analysed, and 28 typically developing. All 14 exclusions for poor recording quality came from the autistic group, a differential attrition of 13.5% against 0% that is reported but not discussed - and one that plausibly removes the participants whose speech was hardest to capture, potentially the most severely affected. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The 90:28 imbalance is addressed analytically by repeated undersampling rather than left uncorrected.

answers.title: Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images
answers.answer: Two groups from the Saliency4ASD benchmark: 14 autistic children and 14 typically developing children, a balanced 28 in total. Both group sizes are reported, but nothing else about either group is. No other-diagnosis or subthreshold comparison group. The autistic and typically developing children are the same in the training and test partitions - the split is over the 400 images (300 train, 100 test), not over participants.

answers.title: Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data
answers.answer: Two groups from the Saliency4ASD benchmark: 14 autistic and 14 typically developing children, 28 in total. Every one of the 300 training and validation images was viewed by all 28 children, and the 100 test images likewise, so the three partitions are cuts through the same 28 people - 5542 training scanpaths, 1411 validation scanpaths and 2868 test scanpaths all originate from the same fourteen autistic and fourteen typically developing children. This is stated plainly by the authors and is the fact on which their own closing hypothesis turns. No other-diagnosis or subthreshold group.

answers.title: Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children
answers.answer: Three samples, all explicitly sized. Training set: 34 autistic and 34 typically developing children. Testing Set 1: a further 34 and 34, drawn from the same 136-child pool and 'equally distributed' with the training set, matched on diagnosis, age, gender and ADOS module. Testing Set 2: 101 videos from autistic children only, aged 2 to 6.9. The partition is by participant, so the 68 children in Testing Set 1 contributed no data to training - the defining structural strength of the study. Testing Set 2's single-class composition is a real limitation on what it can validate: with no typically developing children, its 80.2% figure is sensitivity alone and cannot detect a model that has drifted toward calling everyone autistic. No other-diagnosis or developmentally-delayed comparison group appears anywhere, so the model is never tested against the discrimination that matters clinically - autism versus other developmental concern - only against typical development.

answers.title: Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities
answers.answer: Two groups of 30, both explicitly sized: 30 children with a DSM-5 and ADOS-2 diagnosis of autism recruited from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center, and 30 typically developing children recruited from a primary school. No other-diagnosis or developmentally-delayed comparison group, which the authors themselves identify as the key gap, noting that the motor signature 'may overlap with other disorders, such as attention deficit disorder, motor coordination disturbance, or general intellectual disabilities'. The two groups come from structurally different settings - a clinic where the autistic children receive ongoing psychomotor and speech therapy, versus a school - so group membership is confounded with familiarity with clinical testing, with the examiner's setting, and potentially with prior therapeutic work on exactly the fine-motor skills being measured. This is not discussed.

answers.title: A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children
answers.answer: Two groups, both explicitly sized: 40 autistic children and 50 typically developing children, 90 in total, aged 3-6. Typically developing children came from a local kindergarten; the autistic children's site is identified only obliquely as 'the school site' where reliable diagnostic information was limited, which suggests a special-education setting but is never stated. No other-diagnosis or developmental-delay comparison group, so the model is tested only against typical development. The class imbalance (40:50) is handled correctly at the validation level by stratified fold construction, and both classes are large enough that the confusion-matrix decomposition is meaningful.

answers.title: AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
answers.answer: Two groups, both explicitly sized and accounted for: 50 typically developing children (27 male) and 44 autistic children (22 male), from an initial 50 ASD-suspected recruits of whom 6 were excluded for ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores below 3. Recruitment sources are named - the Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Division of Seoul National University Hospital for the clinical group and preschools for the comparison group. All 94 children are allocated across the three partitions without overlap: 40 to training and validation, 36 to test set #1, 18 to test set #2. No other-diagnosis comparison group, which matters here because ADHD and developmental coordination disorder were deliberately excluded rather than recruited as contrast groups - so the model is never asked to make the discrimination that would distinguish autism-specific joint-attention impairment from impairment secondary to attention or motor difficulty.

answers.title: Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: Two groups of 40, recruited from special education schools and from regular kindergartens respectively. Both are explicitly sized and their sex composition is identical (33 boys, 7 girls each). No other-diagnosis or developmental-delay comparison group. The recruitment asymmetry is the structural weakness: children attending special education schools and children attending regular kindergartens differ in developmental level, in daily environment, and in familiarity with being assessed, and none of these is measured. With no cognitive or language measure taken, group membership in this study is inseparable from educational placement, and a classifier that separates the two groups at 87.5% cannot be shown to be separating them on autism rather than on the correlates of placement.

answers.title: An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images
answers.answer: Not answerable from this paper. Groups are described only as image classes - 328 non-ASD images and 219 ASD images, 547 in total - and the number of children contributing them is never stated. The paper's entire treatment of participants is one sentence directing the reader elsewhere: 'For more information about participants diagnosed with ASD and non-ASD, see [44]'. This is the only study in the corpus that reports no participant count at all, in either group. Because the source is the same gaze-path collection Cilia and colleagues assembled - 547 images with roughly nine images per child - the underlying sample is a few dozen children, but nothing in this paper permits that inference, and no participant identifier is available to group images by child.

answers.title: Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals
answers.answer: Two groups, with complete flow accounting. 183 individuals were initially recruited (67 autistic, 20 female, 22 at Caltech; 116 typically developing, 33 female, 34 at Caltech). 176 watched Episode A (62 autistic) and 167 watched Episode B (59 autistic); analyses were restricted to the 166 who watched both (58 autistic). Thirteen were then excluded for eye-tracking data quality - specifically, missing or off-screen gaze for more than half of one or both episodes - leaving 48 autistic and 105 typically developing participants. The exclusion was strongly differential: 10 of 58 autistic participants (17.2%) against 3 of 108 controls (2.8%), a figure reported precisely but not discussed. Its direction matters for interpretation: the analysed autistic sample is the subset whose gaze could be tracked reliably throughout 43 minutes of video, which if anything strengthens rather than weakens the paper's conclusion that classification fails, since the participants most likely to produce noisy data were removed. Participants were split across two independent sites, with 17 autistic and 33 control participants at Caltech and the remainder at Indiana University. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

answers.title: Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech
answers.answer: Two groups from a crowdsourced convenience sample: 20 children with a parent-reported autism diagnosis and 38 neurotypical children, 58 in total, contributing 77 videos over four years from 2018 to 2021. Clip counts were deliberately balanced at 425 per class, which means the 20 autistic children contributed roughly 21 clips each against roughly 11 each for the 38 comparison children - so the autistic class is built from fewer children sampled more densely, and each autistic child exerts about twice the influence on the class representation. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The recruitment mechanism is itself distinctive: families downloaded a mobile game, played it at home, and then chose whether to share the recording, so the sample is self-selected among app users willing to disclose a diagnosis and share video of their child.

answers.title: Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection
answers.answer: Two analytic groups from three clinical ones: 88 autistic participants and 70 non-autistic participants, the latter formed by merging children with ADHD and typically developing children. The merge is justified on two stated grounds and both are substantive - preliminary analyses showed no significant difference between the ADHD and typically developing subgroups on any automated language measure, and 'including a non-autistic clinical group alongside TD participants provided an opportunity to more adequately test for the specificity of the results with respect to the presence or absence of autism'. This is the corpus's clearest instance of a study building the specificity test into its comparison group rather than naming it as future work. Flow accounting is complete: 289 screened, 104 excluded for not meeting strict diagnostic criteria, 10 for failing to complete initial assessment, leaving 175 in the parent neuroimaging study (102 ASD, 45 ADHD, 28 TD); 6 autistic participants excluded for untranscribable ADOS sessions due to poor sound quality or non-compliance; and 11 more excluded for analysis - 6 with undefined um proportion because neither um nor uh occurred in the task, 4 without IQ results, and 1 with an acoustically corrupted file. Note that the exclusions fall disproportionately on the autistic group (14 of 17), and that the 6 excluded for producing no filled pauses at all are plausibly among the least verbally fluent.

answers.title: Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers
answers.answer: Three groups identified, two analysed. Of 457 toddlers recruited during well-child checkups at four pediatric primary care clinics, 41 were subsequently diagnosed with autism under DSM-5 and 416 were classified neurotypical. A third group of 12 who screened positive on the M-CHAT-R/F and received a non-autism diagnosis - language delay without autism is the example given - was excluded from analysis because of small sample size. That exclusion is the design's one substantive omission, since those 12 are precisely the children against whom a screening tool must discriminate, and their removal means the reported AUC reflects autism versus typical development rather than autism versus developmental concern. The neurotypical group is nonetheless better ascertained than most comparison groups in this corpus, being formed of two subsets - children with a negative M-CHAT-R/F and no caregiver or physician concern, and children who screened positive or raised concern but were then judged on the ADOS-2 and psychologist clinical judgment to have no developmental or autism-related concerns. The 41:416 ratio is the study's most consequential structural feature: it approximates the base rate a deployed screening tool would encounter, in contrast to the balanced designs that dominate this review.

answers.title: Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study
answers.answer: Four groups across two languages, with recruitment and analysis counts that do not match. Recruited: 55 English-speaking autistic, 39 English-speaking comparison, 28 Cantonese-speaking autistic, 24 Cantonese-speaking comparison. Analysed: 33, 33, 24 and 24 respectively, stated in a parenthesis within the narrative-elicitation section - so 22 of 55 English autistic participants (40%) and 6 of 39 English comparison participants (15%) do not appear in the analysis, with no reason given, no flow diagram, and no comparison between retained and dropped participants. The demographic table reports 28 for the Cantonese autistic group where the analysis text says 24, a further inconsistency. The English participants come from a larger family-genetic study of autism that also enrolled parents and controls; the Cantonese participants were recruited via social media, schools and organisations serving autistic people, and employment programmes for adults previously diagnosed with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism. No other-diagnosis comparison group in either language.

answers.title: Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings
answers.answer: Two groups of 25, recruited through a university clinic, diagnostic or therapeutic centres and schools, and 'matched for age, sex and ethnicity, and nearly matched for intelligence quotients'. The autistic group required a prior clinical diagnosis of idiopathic autism from a multidisciplinary team including a psychiatrist under ICD-10 criteria; the comparison group was excluded for personal or family history of autism, history of developmental disorders, and neurological or psychiatric conditions or suspected genetic syndromes. No other-diagnosis comparison group, which the authors identify as a limitation and propose for future work: 'as we compared individuals with ASD and controls with TD, future studies should include individuals with non-spectrum disorders and other psychiatric conditions'. The design's distinguishing feature is that two further comparators operate on the same 50 participants - two standardised instruments and two human raters - so the study contains four independent classification approaches on one sample rather than one model evaluated in isolation.

answers.title: Development of a visual attention based decision support system for autism spectrum disorder screening
answers.answer: Two groups recruited: 61 toddlers with a clinical DSM-5 autism diagnosis and 72 typically developing toddlers, all aged 26-36 months, from a university-based research centre in Ankara. Recruitment was multi-source for the autistic group - a research centre database, speech and language clinics, and child psychiatrists at accredited hospitals, across both metropolitan and rural areas - and community-based for comparisons. No developmental-delay comparison group, which the authors identify as needed: future work should include 'children with developmental delays'. The critical unresolved issue is that the classification analyses do not appear to use all 133 recruited children. The paper states that 'we used balanced datasets in our study in terms of ASD and TD children distribution... in which all classes had the same number of training samples', and every reported accuracy across all six results tables falls on a 2.5-percentage-point grid while every per-class true positive rate falls on a 0.05 grid - a pattern arithmetically consistent with roughly 20 participants per class and inconsistent with 61 and 72. No exclusion count, flow accounting or subsampling rule is given anywhere, so the number of children behind the headline 87.5% and the basis on which they were selected are both unstated.

answers.title: Different Eye Tracking Patterns in Autism Spectrum Disorder in Toddler and Preschool Children
answers.answer: Two cohorts, each with two groups. Toddler cohort: 55 autistic children (aged 1.5-3, including eight aged 1.6-1.8) and 40 typically developing. Preschool cohort: 37 autistic children (aged 3-5) and 41 typically developing. Autistic participants came from the Child Mental Health and Rehabilitation Center of a maternity and child healthcare hospital; comparison children from a local kindergarten or from routine annual check-ups in the same hospital's outpatient ward. No developmental-delay or other-diagnosis comparison group, and the authors identify the consequence explicitly as spectrum bias. The two-cohort structure is the study's design contribution: rather than treating age as a covariate to be adjusted away, the cohorts are analysed both jointly through a diagnosis-by-age-group interaction and separately through cohort-specific classifiers, which is what permits the finding that different areas of interest discriminate at different ages. A discrepancy sits unreconciled between the 37 + 41 = 78 preschoolers reported in the results and the 'N = 74 for preschool' stated in the leave-one-out description, and exclusion counts from the two quality-control steps - calibration failure and off-screen fixation - are not reported for either cohort.

answers.title: Evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based medical device for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: One consecutively enrolled cohort rather than contrasted groups, with the three-level reference standard producing the comparison structure. Of 711 enrolled, 425 completed both the Device inputs and the specialist evaluation; specialists classified 122 (28.7%) as autism-positive, 263 (61.9%) as autism-negative with at least one other developmental or behavioural condition, and 40 (9.4%) as autism-negative and neurotypical. That composition is the study's decisive structural advantage over every other study in this corpus: the comparison against which the Device is judged is overwhelmingly children with other developmental concerns rather than typically developing children, which is the discrimination a primary care tool actually has to make. Attrition is documented in a flow diagram and its causes disclosed - 126 dropped out before completing Device inputs and a further 160 after completing inputs but before the specialist evaluation, with the COVID-19 national emergency in March 2020 closing 9 of 14 sites, preventing an estimated 100 specialist visits, and the authors estimating the drop-out rate absent COVID at 26.2%. Completers and non-completers are shown to be demographically similar in a side-by-side table.

answers.title: Extraction and Classification of Acoustic Features from Italian Speaking Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.
answers.answer: Two groups of 14, drawn from a homogeneous Tuscan area between Florence, Pistoia and Prato, and matched by construction on group size, age range and sex ratio. The autistic children came from the speech and language therapy service of AUSL Toscana Centro and the Opera Santa Rita foundation, and their recordings were reused from a prior thesis project on discourse and storytelling in autism. The comparison children were recruited separately for this study 'from the same geographical area' with 'the same demographic characteristics'. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The critical structural fact is that the two groups were not merely recruited separately but recorded separately, at different times, by different people, using different equipment, in different environments - a distinction that matters far more for acoustic analysis than for the behavioural comparisons elsewhere in this corpus, and one that the paper discloses fully while underweighting its consequences.

answers.title: Eye Tracking-Based Diagnosis and Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques
answers.answer: Two groups inherited from the Carette et al. dataset: 29 autistic children contributing 219 images and 30 typically developing children contributing 328 images, 547 images from 59 children in total. This paper is more informative than Gaspar and colleagues on the same data, which reported only image counts, since it restates the participant counts and sex composition from the source publication. But the participant structure is then entirely disregarded in the analysis: the 80/20 partition operates on images, so children are not the unit at any stage and images from the same child necessarily span the training and test sets at roughly nine images per participant. No other-diagnosis or developmental-delay comparison group. The class imbalance of 219 to 328 is addressed by differential augmentation of the training and validation partitions - sevenfold for the autistic class, tenfold for the comparison class - rather than by any participant-level consideration.

answers.title: Identification of Social Engagement Indicators Associated With
answers.answer: Two groups from a crowdsourced app population: 68 children with parent-reported autism (53 male, 15 female) contributing 380 videos and 27 neurotypical children (18 male, 9 female) contributing 69 videos, 95 children and 449 videos in total, from approximately 1,000 individuals who downloaded the app. The imbalance is substantial and runs opposite to the direction usual in this corpus - cases outnumber controls by more than two to one at child level and by more than five to one at video level, which the authors identify as the reason for choosing macro- and weighted-average metrics over accuracy. After frame filtering the imbalance is similar (520,536 autistic frames against 99,084), so per-video frame retention was comparable between groups, which is a useful check that the automated quality filters did not operate differentially. No other-diagnosis comparison group.

answers.title: Investigation of Eye-Tracking Scan Path as a Biomarker for Autism Screening Using Machine Learning Algorithms
answers.answer: Two groups inherited from the Carette dataset: 29 autistic children contributing 219 images and 30 typically developing children contributing 328 images, 547 images from 59 children. The participant structure is not merely restated but actually used, which distinguishes this paper from the other two reuses of the same data in this corpus: a 'mini batch dataset that encapsulated only single trials from each of 59 participants' is constructed and evaluated separately. That analysis is the study's most valuable output. The main analyses nonetheless proceed at image level, so in the 70:30 split of 547 images and in the augmented analysis of 2,566 images, images from the same child appear in both training and test at roughly 9.3 images per participant. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The class imbalance of 219 to 328 is not corrected in the original analysis and is partly amplified by uniform augmentation, which preserves the ratio at 1,047 to 1,519.

answers.title: Machine learning models using mobile game play accurately classify children with autism
answers.answer: Two groups from a remotely recruited convenience sample: 28 children with a parent-reported formal autism diagnosis (19 male, 9 female) and 21 neurotypical children (10 male, 7 female, 4 not reporting sex), 49 in total, with data accumulated between April 2017 and February 2021. Recruitment ran through four channels - the app's existing user base, the Hartwell Foundation's KidsFirst autism research database, ResearchMatch.org and Facebook advertisements - which is a more diverse sampling frame than the single-channel recruitment typical here, though all routes select for families with smartphones, internet access and English literacy, and the last two select for research-engaged families. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the diagnostic menu presented to parents included ADHD/ADD, anxiety and speech and language delay, so children with those labels would presumably have been identifiable had they been recruited. The class imbalance is modest (28 to 21) and is handled by SMOTE upsampling applied within each cross-validation split rather than to the whole dataset.

answers.title: Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction
answers.answer: Two groups described only in aggregate: 'more than 80 ASD children and more than 60 normal children', from whom about 4,000 and 3,000 recordings respectively were collected in cooperation with Anhui Medical University, the Anhui Autism Association and special education schools. After quality exclusion 'less than 1/3 of the data was usable', and 511 autistic and 506 comparison recordings were randomly selected for analysis. Participant counts are given imprecisely ('more than'), no exact numbers are stated, and the mapping between children and recordings is never specified - so the analysed sample is roughly six recordings per child but the actual distribution is unknown. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The critical structural fact is that all analysis, splitting and reporting operates on recordings, and children are never used as a unit at any stage.

answers.title: The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation
answers.answer: One cohort of 132 children recorded during routine ADOS-2 assessments, partitioned by diagnosis into 105 autistic and 27 non-autistic. The comparison group is the design feature worth noting: it comprises children 'diagnosed with language or developmental delays or were defined as typically developing', so it is a clinically referred population rather than a screened-typical one. That means the model is fitted across the range of children who actually present for autism assessment, and the regression target spans a continuum from ADOS 0 to 30 rather than two discrete classes. The proportion of the 27 who were developmentally delayed rather than typically developing is not reported, which limits how far the specificity claim can be pushed. No exclusion criteria are stated beyond the downstream requirement of at least 20 seconds and 50 vocalisations of child speech, and how many children that requirement removed is not reported.

answers.title: The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children
answers.answer: Ten children aged 5.5 to 6.5 years (mean 6.08, SD 0.4), recruited through the kindergartens they attended in Poland: five diagnosed with autism and five typically developing, each group comprising four boys and one girl. The sample is the smallest in the review, and its composition is nonetheless carefully constructed - exact sex matching, a 12-month age band, and both groups drawn from the same kindergartens, so the recruitment asymmetry that affects nearly every case-control study charted here does not arise. Diagnoses were taken from kindergarten records and had been delivered by a multidisciplinary team of a psychiatrist, a psychologist and a pedagogue, which is genuine clinical ascertainment even though the instruments and criteria are not stated. No cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is reported. With five children per group, the study can support group-level inference about large effects and cannot support any statement about individual-level discrimination, which is consistent with what it claims.

answers.title: Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach
answers.answer: Two groups. Enrolled: 20 ASD and 23 TD. Analysed: 19 ASD and 20 TD, after data from 1 ASD and 3 TD children were dropped for eye-tracking technical failure. Total analysed n = 39. No third or clinical comparison group. The unit of analysis for the model, however, is the gaze behaviour segment, not the child: at 9 s the two groups jointly contribute several thousand segments (exact counts shown only graphically in Fig. 2b), and because ASD sessions were 74% longer on average the ASD group supplies systematically more segments at every window length.

answers.title: A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features
answers.answer: Three groups recruited, two modelled. Recruited: 28 children with ASD, 18 typically developing children, and 4 children with other disorders (cerebral palsy and fragile X syndrome), total 50, all aged 3-6 years and tested at an autism centre in Tehran. Modelled: 46 subjects, which is exactly 28 + 18, so the four-child other-disorder group is excluded from every classification result without the exclusion being stated. A further subgroup is described but not removed: five of the 28 autistic children 'did not seem interested in playing with the sensorized toy car and neglected it completely', so roughly 18% of the autism group contributed a session of near-zero play. Whether their data were retained is not stated explicitly, but the 46-subject count implies they were, and one of the three selected encoder features is the not-playing ratio.

answers.title: A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities
answers.answer: Two groups of 30, total 60 children aged 5-10 years. ASD group: 30 children, mean age 7 years +/- 1.4, recruited from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center where they were receiving psychomotor and speech therapy, all diagnosed under both DSM-5 criteria and ADOS-2, with no existing comorbidities as an inclusion requirement. TD group: 30 children, mean age 6 years 8 months +/- 1, recruited from a primary school, with no confirmed neurodevelopmental disorder and excluded for suspected autism signs, developmental abnormalities, or any current or past psychiatric or neurological history. All 60 had normal vision and no sensory or motor deficits, and any child about whom a clinician or teacher was uncertain was excluded. No attrition or exclusions after enrolment are reported. The modelled dataset, however, is not 60 rows but 1,500: each child contributed 25 task observations (five tasks at each of five difficulty levels), and it is these observations, not the children, that are the unit of the reported cross-validation.

answers.title: A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation
answers.answer: Thirty children in total: 29 with autism and 1 typically developing, mean age 3.65 years. Selection was by ADOS-2 module - only children assessed with the TM, M1 or M2 modules were included, i.e. children from 12 months upward with little or no fluent oral expression, excluding the M3 and M4 modules used for verbally fluent older children and adults. There is no comparison group in any meaningful sense; the single typically developing participant cannot support a between-group contrast and the paper never attempts one. A second and more relevant unit of analysis exists: 109 individual name-call test events, since each child receives up to five calls (three in natural tone at about 3 s intervals, then up to two reinforced calls by clinician or parent). These 109 events are the denominator for the study's highest reported figure of 98.2%, but they are not independent - they cluster within 30 children and are strongly serially dependent, because a child who ignores the first call usually ignores the remaining four. Table 2 shows the consequence: 17 of the 30 children scored 5, meaning they did not respond to any of the five calls.

answers.title: Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games
answers.answer: Two groups of 20, total 40 children, all male, aged roughly 4 to 12 years. The autistic group was drawn from the Daily Rehabilitation Clinic for Children with Special Disorders in Tehran, affiliated to the Family Institute of Shahid Beheshti University; the comparison group came from Namjoo public elementary school. Enrolment and attrition are reported for the autistic group only: 25 children with 'high-performance autism' were selected, of whom 5 (20%) were excluded under the study's stated exclusion criteria - refusing to sit on the chair, or failure to calibrate the eye tracker - and their data were never recorded. No exclusions, and indeed no exclusion criteria at all, are reported for the comparison group, so the two groups passed through different filters. The modelled dataset is not 40 rows but 240: arithmetic on the reported training, validation and test percentages fixes the row count exactly (168 + 36 + 36 = 240, with 132 + 24 + 21 = 177 correct and 177/240 = 73.75% matching the reported 73.8% total), so each child contributes six observations to a randomly partitioned dataset.

answers.title: Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior
answers.answer: Forty-four adults enrolled (17 autistic, 27 neurotypical), of whom two were excluded because they had not consented to this particular set of experiments or their data could not be processed, giving a final sample of 42: 15 autistic and 27 neurotypical, i.e. 35.7% autism prevalence. All were native and fluent English speakers. A second sample is central to the design and is reported with equal care: 19 human raters, comprising 8 expert clinicians (doctoral-level, with extensive autism training at the Center for Autism Research) and 11 non-experts (mostly BA-level psychology staff with some familiarity with autism but no specialised training), all of whom rated all 42 videos. A third group also participates without being analysed: 10 conversation confederates (3 male, 7 female, all native English speakers, undergraduate or BA-level research assistants), semi-randomly assigned by availability and clinical judgement, and blind to participant diagnostic status. The unit of analysis for the model is the participant - one 6,272-dimensional vector each - which is why no within-participant leakage is possible.

answers.title: Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas
answers.answer: Two groups, with a corpus considerably larger than most in this review. Total recruited: 333 children aged 3-6, comprising 140 with autism (112 boys, 28 girls; mean age 4.66 +/- 1.00 years) and 193 typically developing (122 boys, 71 girls; mean age 4.77 +/- 0.92 years), all with normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Recruitment was multi-centre, from several hospitals and schools across Shaanxi and Fujian provinces. The evaluation set is 165 subjects - 70 autistic and 95 typically developing - formed by a 50% subject-level random split, with robustness checked over five permutations. The paper explicitly frames sample size as a methodological argument rather than a logistical fact: Fig. 14(a) visualises how group separability degrades as more subjects are added, and the discussion states that 'when the number of subjects is less than 100, the test cannot accurately reflect the performance of the model' - a direct criticism of the small-sample studies that dominate this corpus, and one this study is entitled to make. A second unit of analysis exists and is handled correctly: each child contributes 82 stimulus-based viewing patterns, and these are scored individually before being aggregated to a subject-level decision, but the split is by child so the 82 patterns never straddle training and test.

answers.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts
answers.answer: Two groups of Twitter accounts rather than of assessed people: 221 users whose public biography states that they are autistic and 31 users who do not, totalling 252. The imbalance is severe and consequential. Because the modelled dataset was balanced at the tweet level - 45,000 per class from a cleaned pool of 404,627 - each of the 31 comparison users contributes on average about 1,450 tweets while each of the 221 autistic users contributes about 200, a sevenfold difference in per-user concentration. The entire negative class is therefore the writing of 31 individuals. No user was recruited, contacted or aware of the study; the data are historical public posts from 1 January 2017 to 31 January 2022. Cleaning removed 60% of the raw corpus (1,014,723 to 404,627 tweets) by deleting duplicates, retweets, incompletely extracted tweets and cross-platform auto-posts, which is a substantial and appropriately reported reduction, though it is not broken down by user or by group.

answers.title: Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: Four hundred and thirty-six toddlers aged 17-36 months, comprising 40 with autism and 396 typically developing, recruited at four paediatric primary care clinics during routine well-child visits. The recruitment route is the defining feature and separates this study from almost every other in the corpus: children were not enrolled as known cases and known controls, but as consecutive clinic attenders who received the M-CHAT-R/F as part of standard care and were referred for ADOS-Toddler evaluation only if they screened positive or if a caregiver or clinician raised a developmental concern. The resulting 9.2% autism prevalence is far closer to a real screening population than the near-balanced designs elsewhere here. Exclusion criteria are stated in full and are practical rather than diagnostic: known hearing or vision impairment, child too upset, caregiver not interested or without time or needing to care for siblings or unable to consent in English or Spanish, child did not complete the procedures, and missing clinical information. The analysed sample varies by movie because only participants with at least 40% valid landmark data for a given movie were included, and those per-movie counts are shown graphically rather than tabulated - the one place where the participant accounting is less transparent than the rest of the paper.

answers.title: Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders
answers.answer: Two independent datasets and three diagnostic groups. Adults: 15 with autism (9 male, 6 female), 15 with schizophrenia (7 male, 8 female) and 16 controls (8 male, 8 female), the latter selected from 26 available controls in order to equalise group sizes, with the selection made by ranking on SRS-2 score in descending order. Children: 15 with autism (13 male, 2 female) and 15 controls (7 male, 8 female), again reduced from 17 by SRS-2 ranking. The presence of a schizophrenia group is what distinguishes this sample from almost every other in the corpus: it supplies a psychiatric rather than merely a neurotypical contrast, and although no autism-versus-schizophrenia classifier is built, the parallel analyses against a common control group produce the study's most useful finding. Note also that the modelled unit is the trial rather than the participant - each adult contributes 21 trials and each child 32 - but the cross-validation splits by participant, so the two levels are handled correctly in the modelling even though the statistical analysis treats trials as independent.

answers.title: Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders
answers.answer: A very large uncontrolled user population with a very small labelled subset. FreeSpeech attracted 6,033 users between January 2012 and May 2014, of whom 5,372 generated enough events to be usable (761 excluded), collectively producing over 2.5 million button presses. Of these, 214 users voluntarily completed an online survey and 180 disclosed a diagnosis - 81 autistic and 99 non-autistic, which is 3.4% of the usable user base. The non-autistic group is itself clinically diverse: Table III lists 32 users reporting no diagnosis, 49 'other', 12 stroke, 4 ALS, 4 dementia, 4 brain injury and 3 ADHD alongside 88 with autism. Two internal inconsistencies should be recorded: Table III sums to 196 and Table II (age bands) to 235, against stated totals of 180 disclosing a diagnosis and 214 completing the survey, and Table III's 88 autistic users does not match the 81 stated in the text. The modelled unit is neither the user nor the session but the window - a fixed-length run of 10 to 100 consecutive key presses - so a heavy user contributes far more pseudo-samples than a light one, and the effective sample size for the classification experiments is never stated. Critically, the headline result is obtained after k-means clustering has assigned pseudo-labels to the roughly 5,192 users who never disclosed anything, so most of the data underlying the 82% figure carry machine-generated labels.

answers.title: Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: One hundred and ten children aged 24 to 72 months were screened between 5 August 2021 and 18 July 2022, of whom 95 (86.4%) completed study measures and formed the analytical population: 45 autistic and 50 typically developing. Enrolment criteria were age 24-72 months, ability to sit, and no history of visual or auditory deficits. Recruitment was asymmetric by design - autistic children came from a single national referral centre, the Seoul National University Hospital Child Psychiatry Outpatient Clinic, while comparison children came from day care centres across South Korea, with participants distributed across Seoul (25%), other metropolitan cities (25%) and provinces (50%). The paper states openly that 'conservative inclusion criteria' were applied on both sides 'to select individuals belonging to clinically distinct groups to ensure development of an accurate and precise ASD vs TD classification model' - so the extremity of the contrast is a deliberate design choice, disclosed rather than concealed, and is the single most important fact for interpreting the near-perfect detection results. Each child contributed up to ten IJA clips and five clips per RJA task from a single 10-minute session, and the cross-validation groups by individual so those clips never straddle folds.

answers.title: Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking
answers.answer: Fifty-nine children contributing 547 scanpath images - the fourth independent reuse of this dataset encountered in this review. The study reports nothing further about who those children were: no counts per group, no ages, no sex, no diagnostic information. The dataset is described purely as two folders, 'TCImages' for typically developing children and 'TSImages' for children diagnosed with autism. The modelled unit is the image, and the split is 382 training, 108 validation and 57 test images with no indication that a child's images were kept together. Because 547 images come from 59 children, each child contributes roughly nine images, so under a random image-level split every test image is accompanied by around eight images from the same child in training or validation. The test-set confusion matrix implies 34 typically developing and 23 autism images among the 57 held out, which is the only class-composition information recoverable anywhere in the paper.

answers.title: SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism
answers.answer: Seventy-six children assembled from three independent corpora in the CHILDES databank: Eigsti (16 autistic, 16 typically developing, aged 3-6, 30-minute free play), Nadig (13 autistic, 25 typically developing, aged 3-7, approximately 10 minutes of parent-child free play) and Flusberg (6 autistic, no comparison children, aged 12-26 months, natural mother-child interaction), giving 35 autistic and 41 typically developing overall. The composition matters more than the totals. Flusberg contributes autistic children only, so corpus membership is partially informative about diagnosis by construction, and it contributes them from an age band - infancy and early toddlerhood - that no comparison child occupies. The three corpora also differ in session length by a factor of three, in conversation partner, and in transcription era and convention. The paper notes that the Eigsti corpus contains a developmental delay group alongside autism and typical development, but that group is not used. No child-level information beyond corpus, group and corpus-level age range is reported anywhere.

answers.title: Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths
answers.answer: Ninety-nine children were enrolled and 86 had valid eye-gaze data - 54 autistic and 32 typically developing according to Table 1 and the participant text, though the abstract states 55 autistic, an unresolved inconsistency. The 13 excluded participants are not characterised. Participants span the full paediatric age range and are grouped into five bands, with the autistic group distributed 3/11/23/13/4 across 0-1, 2-4, 5-9, 10-17 and 18+ years and the comparison group 5/6/16/5/0. Sex composition differs sharply: 44 male and 10 female among autistic participants (81.5% male) against 15 male and 17 female among comparison participants (46.9% male). The paper states plainly that 'each subject has a different number of recorded ET videos and the data is unbalanced with respect to diagnosis, age, and gender'. The modelled unit is not the child but the scan-path image, one per participant per video clip: 1,012 autistic and 380 typically developing images before augmentation, from 1,414 total clip viewings across 86 children - roughly sixteen images per child, unevenly distributed since Table 6 shows individual clips viewed anywhere from once to 92 times.

answers.title: A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths
answers.answer: Fifty-nine children producing 547 scan-path images - the fifth independent reuse of this dataset encountered in the review. Unlike the other reuses charted here, this paper reports the source participant statistics in a dedicated table: 29 autistic and 30 typically developing children, 38 male (64%) and 21 female (36%), mean age 7.88 years and median 8.1, with CARS mean 32.97 and median 34.50. The image split is 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic, so roughly nine images per child. None of the demographic or clinical variables is broken down by diagnostic group, so it cannot be determined whether the groups were matched on age or sex - the sex ratio of 64% male across the whole sample is compatible with anything from a balanced split to a heavily male autistic group and a balanced comparison group. The 547 images, not the 59 children, are the unit of cross-validation throughout.

answers.title: A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning
answers.answer: A national population cohort rather than a recruited sample - 780,610 Israeli children born between 2014 and 2019 with at least two years of computerised well-baby records, of whom 775,941 entered the analysis: 1,163 with an autism diagnosis recorded after age two and 774,778 without autism or another pervasive developmental or medical condition. This is by four orders of magnitude the largest sample in the review and the only one drawn from an unselected population. Case ascertainment used two routes and both counts are given: 722 children (56.6%) identified by ICD-9 code and 553 (43.4%) by keyword search of provider free-text notes with manual verification that the reference concerned the child rather than a family member. A further 112 children with autism diagnosed before age two were excluded to preserve the temporal separation between predictors and outcome. Conditions sharing the ASD acronym, notably atrial septal defect, were screened out. Down syndrome was excluded from the comparison group but Fragile X, tuberous sclerosis and other autism-associated aetiologies were deliberately retained, on the reasoning that autism has multiple aetiologies and excluding them would narrow the target condition artificially. The resulting incidence of 0.0015 is roughly a tenth of Israel's reported national rate, and the authors state this openly as a limitation.

answers.title: AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: “A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System”
answers.answer: There are no participants in the ordinary sense - the study analyses 2,836 photographs, 1,418 labelled autistic and 1,418 not, obtained from a public Kaggle dataset. The provenance is stated plainly and is the study's decisive feature: 'the images of autistic children's faces were sourced from online platforms focusing on autism disorder, while the images of non-autistic children's faces were randomly gathered from the internet'. So the two classes are not two groups of children assessed under common conditions but two collections of photographs assembled from different corners of the internet for different reasons. The number of distinct children behind the images is unknown and cannot be recovered, so it is impossible to know whether ten photographs represent ten children or one, or whether the same child appears on both sides of the training-test split. Age is stated as 24-72 months for both classes, but this is a claim in the dataset description rather than a verified attribute of scraped photographs. Nothing else about the children is known.

answers.title: An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks
answers.answer: One thousand one hundred and twelve subjects from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange I - 539 autistic and 573 controls - contributed by 17 international sites, each with its own scanner, acquisition protocol and recruitment practice. This is by a wide margin the largest sample in the review apart from the Israeli health-records cohort and the Twitter corpus, and it is the only one that comes with a full clinical phenotype: ADOS totals and subscales, ADOS-Gotham severity, ADI-R social and verbal domain totals, SRS raw totals, and full-scale, verbal and performance IQ. The paper reports none of these as sample characteristics - no age distribution, no sex ratio, no IQ means, no group comparison on anything - because it uses them as model inputs instead. Approximately 65 to 70 phenotype fields enter the classifier. The result is the review's sharpest inversion: the study with the richest clinical characterisation available describes its participants less than almost any other, having redirected that information into the feature vector.

answers.title: Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development
answers.answer: Forty-three children were recruited - 20 autistic and 23 typically developing - and 41 analysed after data from two typically developing children were lost to technical problems, giving 20 autistic and 21 comparison participants aged 6-13 with at least average non-verbal intelligence. This is the same cohort and the same recordings already charted in this review under a different analysis (Zhao et al., oculomotor gaze entropy), where 19 autistic and 20 typically developing children were retained after four were dropped for eye-tracking failure. The two papers therefore analyse overlapping subsets of one conversation dataset with two different sensors on the same videos - eye tracking in one, whole-body movement extracted from the video in the other - which makes them unusually comparable and means they should not be treated as independent evidence in the synthesis. The unit of analysis here is the participant: each child contributes one 23-dimensional coherence vector, computed from their dyad with the interviewer. A further 21 surrogate dyads were constructed for the chance-level control by pairing children and adults from different videos.

answers.title: Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning
answers.answer: One hundred and thirty-five participants aged 14 and above, primarily 14 to 20: 64 diagnosed with autism spectrum and 71 non-autistic. The age floor is a reasoned choice rather than a convenience, selected as post-critical-period for language acquisition with reference to Lenneberg's and Newport's hypotheses, so that the linguistic measures reflect settled grammatical competence rather than ongoing acquisition. The comparison group is deliberately compound: 17 individuals who went through the same comprehensive clinical diagnostic process and were determined to have no psychiatric disorder, and 54 recruited as non-autistic, predominantly college students. Every comparison participant received the ADOS-2 and was confirmed non-spectrum against published cut-offs, with group means reported (Module 3 3.17 and Module 4 4.00 for the clinical subgroup; 2.01 and 4.27 for the recruited subgroup). The autistic cohort deliberately includes co-occurring conditions, displayed in a dedicated figure, on reasoning the authors set out explicitly. Recruitment and retrospective record analysis ran concurrently from September 2013 to October 2020.

answers.title: Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms
answers.answer: There are no participants - 2,936 facial photographs from a Kaggle collection, evenly divided at 1,468 per class, described only as colour images of autistic and non-autistic children. The number of distinct children behind them is unknown and unrecoverable. This is the same publicly scraped 'Autistic Children Facial Dataset' already charted in this review in a companion study which used a 2,836-image version, and the two counts imply different snapshots of a dataset that has been revised. The companion study documents the provenance that this one does not mention: autistic images sourced from online platforms focused on autism, non-autistic images gathered separately from the internet.

answers.title: Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed
answers.answer: There are no autistic participants. The Extended Cohn-Kanade corpus supplies 327 sequences from 118 adult volunteers, of which only the peak frame of each sequence is used, giving roughly 2.8 images per person; the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces corpus supplies posed adult expressions photographed under fixed conditions, with its sample size not stated in this paper. Both are general-population affective-computing resources with no autism component, no autism labels and no clinical ascertainment of any kind. The paper's results section mentions once, in passing, 'the Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression (ASD-FE) dataset and the Extended Cohn-Kanade (CK+) dataset adapted for ASD research', but no such dataset is described, cited, sized or characterised anywhere in the methods and no adaptation procedure is specified, while the experiments reported in the results and figures are conducted on brightness variants of KDEF and on CK+ peak frames. The sample is therefore adult, non-autistic, and posed - three respects in which it differs from the population the study's stated purpose concerns, which is autistic children experiencing spontaneous distress.

answers.title: Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification
answers.answer: Twenty children aged 3-6, recruited between 13 February and 21 March 2023: 10 autistic (mean age 4 years, SD 0.94) from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center where they were receiving psychomotor and speech therapy, and 10 typically developing (mean 3 years 9 months, SD 0.1) from a pre-primary and primary educational institute in the province of Naples. Inclusion for the autistic group required a clinical diagnosis, age 3-6 and absence of comorbid conditions; the only criterion for the comparison group was parent and teacher report of no neurodevelopmental disorder, with the paper stating explicitly that they were recruited 'without specific assessment of their pre-existing abilities'. The modelled unit is not the child but the trajectory: 738 trajectories were retained after filtering, roughly 37 per child, and a further set of computationally generated trajectories brought the correlation analysis to 932 samples. Twenty children is the smallest sample of any included study in this review, and the discrepancy between 20 participants and 738 modelling units is the central interpretive issue.

answers.title: Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain
answers.answer: Not reported. The paper states only that 'different data utilized for the analysis are collected manually, including physical and facial expression data' and that measurements 'are collected from various subjects'. No total sample size, no group sizes, no recruitment route, no eligibility criteria and no setting appear anywhere in the paper. Table 2 displays five individuals as illustrative samples, of whom three are labelled 'Detected' and two 'Not detected', but these are presented as examples of the data format rather than as the study population. A reader cannot determine whether the reported 96.44886% accuracy was computed on tens or thousands of individuals. This is the only included study in the review that reports no sample size at all.

answers.title: Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: Two thousand one hundred and fifty-four respondents across four public screening datasets, modelled separately by age band: toddlers aged 18-36 months (1,054 instances, 728 above and 326 below the screening cut-off), children aged 4-11 (292; 141 and 151), adolescents aged 12-16 (104; 63 and 41), and adults aged 17 and over (704; 189 and 515). The datasets originate from autism screening applications and are aggregated on the UCI Machine Learning Repository and Kaggle. Reporting the class distribution for every band, and discussing whether oversampling was warranted, is better practice than much of this corpus - and the counts also make plain what the 'positive' class is: respondents whose summed responses to ten screening items exceeded the instrument's published cut-off. No participant is known to have received any clinical assessment, no age or sex distribution is reported although both fields are present, and no ethnicity, socioeconomic or comorbidity distribution is given although jaundice at birth and family history of autism are among the tabulated fields.

answers.title: Machine learning’s effectiveness
answers.answer: One hundred and twenty-six five-year-olds - 64 boys and 62 girls - constituting approximately 99% of the five-year-old residents of Sazacho, Nagasaki Prefecture, assessed during their routine preschool medical examinations. This is a whole-population age cohort rather than a recruited sample, and it is the second study in this review with genuinely population-based sampling, alongside the Israeli well-baby records study. Group assignment used the Social Responsiveness Scale, Second Edition completed by mothers, dichotomised at published sex-specific Japanese cut-offs of 53.5 for boys and 52.5 for girls: 19 children (9 boys, 10 girls) fell above and 107 (55 boys, 52 girls) below, giving a 15.1% above-threshold rate. The groups differ sharply on the defining variable (SRS-2 69.79 +/- 23.66 against 31.24 +/- 11.48, t = -6.956, p < 0.001) and not on age (all five) or sex ratio (p = 0.81). The unit of analysis is the child, with one 16-dimensional feature vector each.

answers.title: Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network
answers.answer: There are no participants. The units are images: 2,866 in the Piosenka Kaggle collection, split 1,433 autism-labelled and 1,433 control, described as ages 1-11; and 1,163 face crops extracted with MTCNN from the YTUIA/SSBD video corpus, split after re-clustering into 951 training, 144 validation and 68 test. The number of distinct children behind either figure is unknown and unreported - the paper's own table labels the 2,866 images as 'Total individuals', which is the conflation this review has repeatedly recorded in the image-classification branch. The provenance of each class is stated plainly and is the decisive fact: the autism images were 'taken from websites and Facebook pages that included autism-related content', while the YTUIA positives derive from 100 videos assembled to depict self-stimulatory behaviour, of which 50 came from YouTube and 50 from therapists and professional organisations, with controls being 'YouTube videos featuring kindergarten activities within the relevant age range'. In both corpora, therefore, the class label records where material was found rather than any assessment of the child depicted.

answers.title: Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]
answers.answer: Seventeen boys: 13 autistic aged 10 to 16 and 4 typically developing aged 9 to 16, drawn from the global autism EEG corpus held by the brain-computer interface group at King Abdulaziz University and used with permission. The comparison group of four is the smallest in the review and is too small to characterise typical variation in any EEG measure, let alone to support a claim about detection. The sample is entirely male, which removes sex as a confound and means nothing reported can be assumed to apply to autistic girls. No age distribution by group is given beyond the two ranges, and none of the descriptors this review usually records - cognitive level, language ability, comorbidity, medication, socioeconomic background - is available. The 13:4 ratio also sets the participant-level majority-class baseline at 76.5%, against which the reported 89-94% should be read and never is.

answers.title: Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play
answers.answer: Two hundred and forty-six children aged 1 to 6, recruited in Beijing between January and August 2022 in a matched 1:1 design: 123 autistic (105 male, 18 female, mean age 54.0 months, SD 9.9) and 123 typically developing (103 male, 20 female, mean age 51.1 months, SD 13.5). The autistic children came from a hospital and from autism intervention service centres; the comparison children from a local kindergarten. Groups were matched and formally tested on age (t(224.10) = 1.90, p = 0.0591) and sex (chi-square = 0.031, p = 0.860), and separated on severity as expected (median CARS-2 37.0 against 15.0, Z = -13.90, p < 0.001). Two sample-definition decisions shape what the study can show. Children with current or previous psychiatric diagnoses other than autism, major physical or neurological disease, or any prior psychotropic medication were excluded, which produces an uncomplicated autism group at the cost of representativeness. And 23 children who met clinical criteria but scored below 30 on CARS-2 were removed, so the autistic group is restricted to the more clearly affected end of the spectrum - a restriction the authors identify themselves and connect explicitly to performance inflation. The unit of analysis is the child throughout, with one 81-dimensional indicator vector each.

answers.title: Predictive model using autism
answers.answer: Ninety adults recruited from the outpatient and inpatient services of Showa University Karasuyama Hospital in central Tokyo: 40 with schizophrenia (27 men, 13 women, mean age 33.53 years, SD 10.95) recruited between April 2022 and December 2023, and 50 with autism (35 men, 15 women, mean age 33.80 years, SD 8.39) recruited between October 2018 and December 2020. Both groups required a full-scale IQ above 85 and both were diagnosed under DSM-5 by consensus among several psychiatrists with extensive experience in both conditions. Three features distinguish this sample from almost every other in the review. Both groups are clinical, drawn from the same service, so there is no clinic-versus-community recruitment asymmetry and no typically developing comparison group at all. Both are adults with fluent speech and average or above-average measured ability, which is the population in which differential diagnosis is genuinely difficult and in which most of this corpus's paediatric work has nothing to say. And roughly a third of each group is female (30% and 33%), against the heavy male preponderance typical of autism research samples - a consequence of studying adults presenting to psychiatric services rather than children referred to developmental research. Groups did not differ on age, sex or years of education. The unit of analysis is the participant, with one set of ADOS-2 item codes each.

answers.title: The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech
answers.answer: Two corpora combined, and the participant accounting is the weakest part of the description. De-Enigma contributes 55 autistic children aged 4 to 10, described as 25 from Serbia and 25 from the United Kingdom - a split that does not sum to 55 - with no control group at all, yielding 5,368 vocalisation samples over 115 minutes. The Child Pathological Speech Database contributes monolingual French-speaking children aged 6 to 18, recruited in Paris, carrying diagnoses of autism, dysphasia or PDD-NOS alongside a typically developing group, yielding 1,722 samples over 62 minutes. The CPSD participant counts cannot be reconciled: the control group is said to consist of 64 typically developing children (52 male, 12 female), while the corpus as a whole is said to have 13 female participants contributing 334 samples and 54 males contributing 1,388 - a total of 67, which would leave three children for the autism, dysphasia and PDD-NOS groups combined. The number of children in each atypical class is never stated anywhere in the paper. This is not a bookkeeping quibble. Speaker-disjoint splitting is the study's stated safeguard against leakage, and its protective value depends entirely on how many speakers each class contains: if the 26 autism, 26 dysphasia and 26 PDD-NOS samples in the diagnosis test partition come from one or two children each, then class membership and speaker identity are nearly the same variable, and disjointness across the split cannot separate them. The sex proportions are also stated inconsistently, as 78% and 81% male in the dataset section and as 95% and 90% male in the limitations. Age distributions per group are not reported for either corpus.

answers.title: Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism
answers.answer: The largest sample in this review by an order of magnitude, and the least clinically characterised. The autism corpus comprises 3,137,952 tweets from 17,323 users, identified by their use of #ActuallyAutistic in English-language posts between 1 January 2014 and 31 December 2022 combined with 'autism', 'autistic' or 'neurodiverse' appearing in their profile description, after which all tweets from those users' timelines were collected. The control corpus comprises 3,377,518 tweets from 171,273 users, obtained by a search query excluding the hashtag and sampling 1,000 tweets per day over the same window. No demographic information of any kind exists for either group - no age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic status, cognitive level or comorbidity - and the location field was discarded as largely missing or uninformative, though the authors note that most of the top 20 stated locations were variants of the United Kingdom. Two structural features of the sample deserve emphasis. The tweet counts are near-balanced while the user counts differ tenfold, because the autism group's entire timelines were harvested while control posts were sampled from the platform's daily stream - so the two classes differ in how their material was selected as well as in who produced it, and this is not discussed. And the autism group is not a clinical population but a self-selected online community organised around a hashtag with an explicit advocacy stance, which the paper describes accurately and which bears on everything downstream.

answers.title: Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children
answers.answer: One hundred and sixty children aged 1.1 to 5.1 years, enrolled in the Geneva Autism Cohort between 25 September 2012 and 10 September 2023: 80 autistic children (48 male, 32 female, mean age 2.68 +/- 0.89 years) meeting DSM-5 criteria with diagnosis supported by gold-standard assessment, and 80 typically developing children (48 male, 32 female, mean age 2.46 +/- 0.98 years) screened for absence of known neurological or psychiatric conditions and for no history of autism in any first-degree relative. Three features of the sample are worth emphasising. Both groups underwent the same ADOS assessment in the same setting, so the recording context is common to both classes - which removes the setting confound that this review has documented repeatedly across the video, audio and image branches, where clinical groups are recorded in clinics and comparison groups in schools, kindergartens or on the internet.
