Sex is exactly matched at 48 male and 32 female per group, giving 40% girls, which is by a considerable margin the highest female representation of any included study and the only instance of deliberate exact matching on sex. And the matching extends to the analysis: the 50-50 train-test split was itself constructed so that each half contained 40 autistic and 40 typically developing children matched for age, sex and ADOS module, so the held-out set is not merely disjoint but comparable by construction. The unit of analysis is the child, with segments nested within children and never crossing the split.

answers.title: Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning
answers.answer: Seventy-three children in the autism class, one per video, from 73 of the 75 videos in the Self-Stimulatory Behaviours Dataset - home recordings posted to YouTube by parents and caregivers showing children spinning, head banging or arm flapping, two videos having been dropped for quality. The split is reported by child and by duration: 44 children and 3,214 seconds in training, 15 children and 1,582 seconds in validation, 14 children and 1,496 seconds in test. That per-child reporting is better than the frame-count reporting typical of this branch. What is entirely absent is the other half of the sample. The methods state only that 'in order to have a complete and balanced database to train this model, we extracted the frames featuring the faces of ASD children and gathered facial images of other ASD children and facial images of neurotypical youngsters' - so a non-autistic class exists, but its size, its source, the number of children in it and their characteristics are nowhere given, and the data-distribution table lists SSBD as the sole database for all three splits, which cannot be true if a second class is present. No age, sex, ancestry, cognitive or language information is available for anyone in either class. For a two-class facial image classifier, the composition of both classes is what determines the meaning of the result, and here only one is described.

answers.title: A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features
answers.answer: Thirty male autistic children aged 5 to 15, all attending Don Guanella Special School in Poonamallee, Chennai, contributing 1,500 thermal images distributed across four settings within the school: 500 images from 10 students during outdoor play, 600 from 12 students in the classroom, 200 from 4 students in the dining area and 200 from 4 students on the veranda, plus 20 videos collected for real-time testing that are never analysed. Every image is of an autistic child; the study contains no non-autistic participants and no diagnostic task, since the classification target is a three-level severity grade among autistic children only. Four features of the sample bound what can be learned from it. It is entirely male, so nothing reported can be assumed to apply to autistic girls, and the paper does not remark on this. It is small in the way that matters - 30 children, 50 images each - so image counts overstate the effective sample fiftyfold, and the reported 98.33% must be read against that. The children are drawn from a single residential special school, a setting that selects for higher support needs and makes the sample unrepresentative of the autistic population the framework's medication claim addresses. And the four capture settings differ physically in ways that directly affect the primary measurement: outdoor play in Chennai, a classroom, a dining area and an open veranda produce systematically different skin temperatures for reasons unrelated to autism, and the distribution of severity levels across those settings is never reported.

answers.title: Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: There are no participants. The units are 2,940 RGB images from the Kaggle autistic-children facial dataset, split 1,327 autistic and 1,613 non-autistic, described as children aged 2 to 14, organised into two folders. The number of distinct children behind either count is never stated. The decisive fact is the paper's own description of how the two folders were built: 'The autistic subfolder included images of ASD, while the non-autistic subfolder had images randomly retrieved from web searches.' The class label therefore records the collection route rather than any assessment of the child depicted - the same provenance confound this review has recorded for five other studies on this corpus family, stated here more plainly than in any of them. No age distribution, sex, ancestry, cognitive, language or clinical information is available for either class, and no demographic comparison between them is possible.

answers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features
answers.answer: Sixty-four children aged 3 to 6 - 30 autistic and 34 typically developing - assembled from four archived TalkBank corpora. The autistic children come from ASDBank's Eigsti and Nadig collections; the typically developing children come partly from those same collections and partly from CHILDES's Warren and Kuczaj corpora, added deliberately 'to try to balance demographic (gender and age) representations'. The paper is honest about the residual imbalance, stating that 'most participants are male, and there are more children aged 3-4 than aged 5-6', and it explains the sex imbalance correctly as a consequence of autism being 'almost 4 times as common in boys than in girls'. Numerical age and sex compositions by diagnostic group are not reported, which matters because the paper's own analysis finds that mean length of utterance - the top-ranked predictor - is the only feature that consistently increases with age. Developmentally delayed children present in the Eigsti corpus were deliberately excluded to keep the task binary, which removes the non-autistic clinical comparison group the source data could have supported. The unit of analysis is the child, one transcript and one feature vector each.

answers.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning
answers.answer: Two public corpora used in parallel. The Gait Fullbody Dataset, created by Al-Jubouri and colleagues, contains 100 children aged 4 to 12 - 50 autistic and 50 typically developing - recorded with a Kinect v2 capturing 25 joint coordinates, with each child performing ten walking trials of which one was retained, giving 100 samples. A separate subset of nine children with severe symptoms is available and is not analysed here. The DREAM dataset contains 61 children aged 3 to 7, recorded with Kinect v1 during robot-assisted therapy, yielding 3,121 samples of which 1,833 were used after the non-spectrum class was excluded; only 10 upper-body joints are recorded, since Kinect v1 detects 20 joints and DREAM omits the lower body. No age distribution, sex, cognitive level, language ability or clinical characterisation is available for either corpus. Two structural facts shape everything downstream. In the Gait dataset each child contributes exactly one sample, so cross-validation necessarily partitions children - a property that arises from the data rather than from a design decision, but that gives this study the participant-level split unit most of the video branch lacks. And that single retained sample was chosen from ten trials 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation', so the modelled data were selected with knowledge of the outcome.

answers.title: Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]
answers.answer: Sixty-two children aged 18 to 54 months drawn from the publicly available Khozaei cry corpus collected in Iran: 31 autistic and 31 typically developing, with 24 boys and 7 girls in each group, mean ages 35.6 and 30.8 months. The exact sex matching at 24:7 is a genuine design strength and gives the sample 22.6% girls, higher than most autism research samples in this review. Two features of the sample are less favourable and both are reported without being examined. The mean ages differ by 4.8 months - about 16% of the younger group's mean, in a period of rapid vocal-tract and laryngeal maturation - with no test or adjustment reported, which matters because jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio all vary with vocal development. And the recording settings differ sharply by group: 87.10% of the autistic children's cries were recorded at autism centres and 12.90% at home, while 54.84% of the typically developing children's were recorded at health centres and 45.16% at home. Roughly six cry instances were retained per child (6.10 +/- 5.05 for the autistic group, 5.39 +/- 3.66 for the comparison group), giving an instance-level dataset of around 355 cries from 62 children. No cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is available.

answers.title: Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm
answers.answer: Seven hundred and four respondents to the AQ-10 adult autism screening instrument, drawn from a public Kaggle aggregation of screening-app submissions. The paper reports the row count and the field names and nothing else: no class distribution, no age or sex composition, no ethnicity breakdown, although age, gender and ethnicity are all among the 21 fields it prints. In the source dataset the positive class comprises 189 of 704, giving a majority-class baseline of 73.2% that the paper never states. No respondent is known to have received any clinical assessment. The population is self-selected users of an autism screening application, which is neither a clinical sample nor a population sample.

answers.title: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
answers.answer: One hundred children aged 5 to 9, recruited in Kazakhstan: 50 described as diagnosed with autism and 50 typically developing peers, recorded under a single purpose-designed protocol yielding over 16 hours of video. The sample is balanced 50:50 by group and the acquisition context is common to both, which removes the recruitment and recording asymmetry that affects most of this review's video and image work. Two demographic facts bound what follows. The sex composition differs sharply between groups - the autistic group is approximately 84% male and 16% female, while the comparison group is 52% male and 48% female - a 32-percentage-point gap reported in the results without comment, adjustment or stratified analysis. And no age distribution by group is given, only the shared 5-to-9 range, across which facial proportions, motor coordination and gestural repertoire all change substantially. No cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is available for either group, and no recruitment source is stated.

answers.title: Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of
answers.answer: There are no participants. The units are 2,932 facial images, balanced at 1,466 per class, described in the results as 'collected from platforms such as Kaggle and ASD-related websites'. The number of distinct children behind those images is never stated, and no age, sex, ancestry, cognitive, language or clinical information is available for either class - an absence the authors acknowledge directly, noting that 'demographic variables, such as age, gender, and cultural background, were not explicitly controlled'. This is the seventh study in this review built on the Kaggle facial-image corpus family, and the description of the autistic class as sourced partly from autism-related websites places it squarely in the same category as the others: the label records where an image was found rather than any assessment of the child in it. For the paper's second target, gelotophobia, there are not even images with labels - no person was assessed for gelotophobia by any means, so that half of the study has no sample at all.

answers.title: Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
answers.answer: There are no participants. The units are 2,940 facial images from the Kaggle autistic-children corpus - the eighth study in this review built on this dataset family - with the number of distinct children never stated and no age, sex, ancestry, cognitive, language or clinical information available for either class. The corpus's construction is the determining fact: its autistic images were harvested from autism-related online sources and its comparison images from elsewhere, so the label records where an image was found rather than any assessment of the child in it. This study does not restate that provenance, but it inherits it.

answers.title: Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children
answers.answer: There are no participants. The autism corpus comprises 2,886 images partitioned 2,526 training, 280 testing and 80 validation - the standard split of the Piosenka Kaggle autistic-children collection, which this review has now charted in eight other studies - after poor-quality images were discarded. The emotion corpus supplies 703 training and 130 testing images. The number of distinct children behind either count is never stated, and no age, sex, ancestry, cognitive, language or clinical information is available for any class. The authors name this directly as their first limitation, observing that 'the absence of demographic information such as gender and ethnicity in the utilized Kaggle datasets might hinder the generalization across different populations' - which is a more explicit acknowledgement than most studies on this corpus offer, and which correctly identifies the consequence without identifying the deeper problem, that the corpus's autistic class was harvested from autism-related online sources so that the label records image provenance.

answers.title: Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy
answers.answer: Two thousand nine hundred and thirty-six facial images, balanced at 1,468 labelled autistic and 1,468 labelled normal, drawn from two sources - Kaggle and 'data from an autism center in Semarang'. The mixed provenance is what distinguishes this study from the other nine Kaggle-corpus papers charted in this review, and it cuts both ways. Supplementing a web-scraped collection with images from an actual clinical service is in principle an improvement, since clinic-attending children have real diagnoses; but the paper never states how many images came from each source, nor whether the clinic contributed to the autistic class only or to both. If the autistic images are predominantly Indonesian clinic photographs while the comparison images are predominantly international web-scraped ones, the two classes would be separable by ancestry, camera and setting without any facial phenotype being involved - a sharper confound than the pure-Kaggle studies face. The paper's own account of provenance is loose enough to leave this open: the data 'could come from a variety of places, such as clinics, past research, or relevant public statistics'. No age, sex, ancestry, cognitive, language or clinical information is reported for either class, and the number of distinct children behind 2,936 images is never stated.

answers.title: Diagnosing autism spectrum disorder based on eye tracking technology using deep learning models
answers.answer: Two groups from a single archived dataset: 29 children with ASD and 30 typically developing children, 59 in total. The unit actually analysed is not the child but the gaze sample: 1,048,575 rows. That figure deserves attention - 1,048,576 is the maximum row count of a Microsoft Excel worksheet, so the analysed set is almost certainly a spreadsheet-truncated slice of the source recording rather than the complete data, and the paper never remarks on it. Per-child row counts, per-group row counts and per-fold composition are all unreported.

answers.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Automated Machine Learning
answers.answer: One group of children aged 2-4 years recruited through Pakistani rehabilitation centres, split by questionnaire outcome rather than by recruitment stream. The paper states 750 participants, but 434 male plus 308 female is 742, and 593 training plus 149 test is also 742; eight children are unaccounted for and the inconsistency is not noted. Class sizes are never stated directly and must be recovered from the test-set support column (106 autistic, 43 non-autistic), implying about 71% positive overall. There is no separate typically developing comparison group in the design sense - both classes come from the same rehabilitation-centre respondent pool, and the questionnaire was described as circulated among trainers and parents of children with autism, which makes the non-autistic class a by-product of scoring rather than a recruited control group.

answers.title: Enhanced ASD detection using 3D facial landmark localization with convolutional shape appearance model and graph-randomized XGBoost
answers.answer: There are no participant groups in any meaningful sense. The unit is the image file: 2,526 images, 1,263 labelled ASD and 1,263 labelled non-ASD, downloaded from a Kaggle re-upload of the web-scraped autism face corpus. The number of distinct children behind those images is never asked, and because the corpus is known to contain multiple images of the same faces, the effective sample is unknown and certainly far below 2,526. An 80-20 split gives 2,020 training and 506 test images, but the headline evaluation is then run on 200 images selected from the test set - and the reported confusion matrix sums to 300 (146 + 141 + 9 + 4), agreeing with neither figure.

answers.title: Enhanced multilevel autism classification for children using eye-tracking and hybrid CNN-RNN deep learning models
answers.answer: Forty children, all with an existing ASD diagnosis, recruited from Dakshinya Autistic School in Guntur, India, and divided into four severity classes of exactly ten each: low, mild, medium and high. There is no typically developing comparison group, which matters because the abstract nonetheless reports that children with ASD exhibit unique and highly individualized gaze patterns when compared to TD children - a comparison the design cannot support. The only TD data in the paper belong to the separate public Saliency4ASD set (14 ASD, 14 TD) used in a side experiment. Two internal inconsistencies affect the count: the introduction states that in the initial training we enrolled a group of 8-10 children aged x years, with the placeholder x left in the published text, and the analysis unit is not the child but the cropped eye image - 50 frames x 2 eyes x 40 children = 4,000 images, which is what the 70:15:15 split partitions.

answers.title: Ensemble of Deep Learning with Crested Porcupine Optimizer Based Autism
answers.answer: No participants. The unit is the image: a stated 2,926 facial samples in two classes, Normal and Autism, downloaded from Kaggle. The number of distinct children is unknown and never raised. The stated total does not survive contact with the results: the confusion matrix at 1,000 epochs reports 1,338 correctly recognised normal and 1,362 correctly recognised autism images, which against the per-class accuracies of 95.57% and 97.29% implies about 1,400 images in each class and about 2,800 overall. Those counts also span essentially the whole dataset, which means the reported confusion matrices are not computed on a held-out subset at all.

answers.title: Explainable and secure framework for autism prediction using multimodal eye tracking and kinematic data
answers.answer: Forty-four examples in total - 22 individuals diagnosed with ASD and 22 non-autistic individuals - taken from an open-source movement dataset on Mendeley Data that is neither named nor cited. Nothing else is known about them: not their age band (the introduction discusses both children and adults without saying which these are), not their sex, not their recruitment, not the country, not the year. The 44 examples were divided among three simulated federated clients by an unstated rule, and each client's evaluation rests on nine test cases - a figure that appears nowhere in the text and is recoverable only from the confusion matrices (6 true negatives, 2 true positives, 1 false negative, 0 false positives) and from the fact that every accuracy in Tables 2 through 5 is a multiple of one ninth.

answers.title: Facial Images Dataset for Early Screening of Autism Children Using Convolutional Neural Network
answers.answer: Seventy children in two recruited groups: 35 with autism from a Special Elementary School in Banda Aceh and 35 typically developing children from a State Elementary School in the same city. Each contributed 15 photographs (three expressions x five shots), giving 1,050 images split evenly 525/525. The analysis unit throughout is the image, not the child: the 70/20/10 division yields 369/105/51 images per class, and the reported metrics rest on 102 test images drawn from the same 70 children who supplied the training images. This is genuine primary data collection with a real, separately recruited comparison group - which distinguishes it sharply from the twelve Kaggle-corpus reuses charted in this review - but the group difference is confounded with school of origin, since every autistic child comes from one institution and every comparison child from another.

answers.title: Improving Early Autism Detection with Chi-Square Feature Selection, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI
answers.answer: No groups were recruited. The unit is the questionnaire record: 1,054 cases from the public ASD Toddler dataset (Thabtah, via Kaggle), of which 735 are labelled ASD and 319 non-ASD - a 69.7% positive rate. SVM-SMOTE then expanded the set to 1,456 instances, meaning 402 of the rows subsequently modelled and evaluated are synthetic interpolations rather than children. The 292-case test set (148 ASD, 144 non-ASD) therefore contains an unstated number of synthetic records, and the number of real children behind the reported 100% is never given.

answers.title: Novel Framework for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification and Tailored Education With Effective Data Mining and Ensemble Learning Techniques
answers.answer: No participants were recruited. Two public toddler screening datasets are merged: the Kaggle ASD Toddler set (1,054 instances, 17 columns) and an online questionnaire dataset covering toddlers aged 12-36 months across regions of Saudi Arabia. The size of the second dataset is never given, the size of the merged set is never given, and the size after SMOTE oversampling is never given - so the number of rows behind every table in the paper is unknown, and it cannot be determined how many are real records and how many synthetic. Class counts are likewise absent. The stated motivation for merging - improving diversity by combining two regions - is the paper's best idea and is never exploited: the two cohorts are pooled rather than used as development and held-out sets.

answers.title: Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach
answers.answer: No participants. 1,054 records from the public toddler Q-CHAT dataset, 728 labelled autism and 326 control - a 69.1% positive rate that the paper reports and, unusually for this branch, leaves in place rather than resampling. The records were submitted through an ASD screening application by parents and other stakeholders, so neither respondent nor child was verified. The confusion matrices imply a test partition of 317 records, though no split proportion is stated; the row totals also differ across models within the same table (105/212 for LR, KNN and LR-KNN but 110/207 for the ANN), which they should not if all four were evaluated on the same partition.

answers.title: Predicting autistic traits, anxiety and depression symptoms using camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (CAT-Q-ES): A machine learning study
answers.answer: Two groups of adults recruited into one online survey: 102 autistic adults with a clinician-made diagnosis (72 women, 18 men, 12 non-binary) and 499 non-autistic adults (399 women, 92 men, 8 non-binary), 601 in total. The analysis unit is the person throughout, and the four cross-validation partitions are participant-disjoint by construction - each participant appears in exactly one partition. Exclusions are enumerated with reasons: 12 self-diagnosed respondents and 13 who did not report a gender they identified with. This is the only charted study in which the number of people, the number of analysis units and the number of rows in every reported metric are the same figure.

answers.title: A Computational Method for Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Deep Learning Approach
answers.answer: No participants. 2,926 images at 224x224, described as curated from public repositories covering diverse demographics and labelled autism or non-autism; the comparison tables identify the source as the same Kaggle facial corpus used by all five of the studies it benchmarks against. The split is 2,526 training, 200 validation and 200 test images. Class counts are never stated for any partition, though the metric arithmetic implies a balanced 200-image test set. The number of distinct children is unknown - and the paper is aware that this matters, because it notes that one cited study cleaned duplicates from the dataset using the MD5 hash algorithm, an acknowledgement that the corpus contains repeated images. No deduplication is performed here.

answers.title: Early Detection of ASD from Facial Images Using DeepDeblur and Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network
answers.answer: No participants. 2,940 images from the Kaggle ASD Children Facial dataset, balanced at 1,470 autistic and 1,470 non-autistic - the fourteenth charted reuse of this corpus in the review. The number of distinct children is unknown and never raised, and the corpus is known to contain repeated images of the same faces. The paper states a split of 2,540 training images (1,270 per class) and 400 test images (200 per class), but the confusion matrix it then reports covers all 2,940 images, so the population behind the headline figure is the whole dataset rather than the held-out 400.

answers.title: Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI
answers.answer: No participants were recruited. The ASD Children Traits dataset was downloaded from Kaggle: 1,985 cases with 28 variables, covering children aged 1-18. Preprocessing then reduced this to 634 cases and 19 variables - 68% of the records and a third of the variables removed as outliers, inconsistencies or erroneous data identified by clinical experts. Neither the raw nor the preprocessed dataset's class balance is reported anywhere, so the number of ASD and non-ASD cases behind every result in the paper is unknown. This matters more than usual because the introduction states explicitly that ASD assessment datasets tend to over-represent ASD cases and that this can bias models toward the majority class - a problem the authors identify and then never quantify in their own data.

answers.title: Using explainable machine learning and eye-tracking for diagnosing autism spectrum and developmental language disorders in social attention tasks
answers.answer: Ninety-three children aged 32-74 months in three clinically defined groups: 24 with ASD, 25 with developmental language disorder, and 44 typically developing. Both clinical groups were recruited from early childhood intervention centres in Cordoba province and required a formal diagnosis made by a licensed, experienced clinical team. The analysis unit is the child throughout, and each child contributes exactly one row to each of four feature sets. The inclusion of a second clinical group is what distinguishes this study from almost the entire charted corpus: it makes the ASD-versus-DLD comparison possible, and that comparison is where the study's most informative result lies.

answers.title: Utilizing deep learning models in an intelligent eye-tracking system for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis
answers.answer: No participants. 547 scanpath images from a public eye-tracking repository, 328 labelled non-ASD and 219 ASD. The abstract converts this image count into a participant count, describing the dataset as scan pathways obtained from 328 characteristically emerging children and 219 children with autism - which would make this one of the larger primary eye-tracking cohorts in the field. The methods section states the correct version, that these are image counts. The source collection is the Cilia/Carette scanpath set, whose originators are cited in the comparison table and in which a few dozen children contributed multiple scanpath images each; the number of distinct children behind the 547 images is never given here. Every reported metric rests on a test partition of 55 images, recoverable only from the support column of the per-class results tables.

answers.title: A novel hybrid deep learning model using MEResNext for autism spectrum disorder detection
answers.answer: No participants, and no sample size of any kind. The article never states how many records the analysed dataset contains, how many are ASD-positive, or how many are negative - a gap that persists through a results section built entirely on performance curves. The data source is identified only as Autism screening data for toddler, the public Q-CHAT-10 collection. Since no split, test set or fold structure is described either, there is no point in the paper at which a reader can say how many observations any reported number rests on.

answers.title: An assessment of autistic and parkinsonian movement profiles to inform selective classification algorithms
answers.answer: Ninety-four adults in three groups: 31 autistic adults, 32 adults with Parkinson's disease and 31 controls. Both clinical groups required documentary evidence of a formal clinical diagnosis or came from research databases where such evidence had been verified, with mutual exclusion between the two conditions and exclusion of co-occurring movement or developmental disorders. Recruitment order is reported and is itself methodologically informative - the PD group was recruited first as an opportunity sample, autistic adults were then recruited to match it, and controls to match both. The analysis unit is the participant throughout, and the 80/20 classification split partitions people. What limits the classification estimates is size rather than structure: the ASD-versus-PD test partition contains roughly 13 people and the clinical-versus-non-clinical partition roughly 19.

answers.title: An explainable deep learning framework for screening level autism severity using behavioural data
answers.answer: No participants were recruited. Four public screening datasets from Kaggle and UCI were harmonised into 2,154 records spanning toddlers, children, adolescents and adults, with stratified sampling by age group during merging to preserve cohort proportions. The analysis unit is the record and the cross-validation folds are stratified over records. What is missing is arithmetic: the per-cohort sample sizes, the class counts for the binary screening outcome and the counts for each of the four constructed severity strata are all absent, so the denominator behind every reported accuracy is unknown. The class distribution is characterised only qualitatively, as closely mirroring population-level screening statistics reported in prior paediatric ASD studies.

answers.title: An explainable machine unlearning algorithm framework for early detection of autism spectrum disorder and brain disabilities in newborns
answers.answer: No participants and no coherent sample. The methods state within four consecutive sentences that the study utilised MRI datasets of newborns comprising 10,000 samples and that the final dataset included 25,000 positive cases and 1200 negative cases, with class balance maintained. Both claims cannot hold: 25,000 positives cannot come from 10,000 samples, and a ratio of nearly 21 to 1 is not balance. Elsewhere the CSBS description reports 500 subjects, and Table 4, labelled Standard dataset, lists the same identifier range 01-1000 five times over with different family relationships (son, daughter, niece) and a different algorithm name in each row, so it is a results table presented as a data description. No consistent count of children exists anywhere in the article.

answers.title: Deep learning based approach for Behavior classification in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder using naturalistic videos
answers.answer: No participants and no groups. The data are 75 YouTube videos of approximately 90 seconds each from the Self-Stimulatory Behaviour Dataset, uploaded by parents and caretakers, segmented into frame clips by behaviour type using the dataset's original annotations. The number of distinct children is never stated - a consequential omission, since 75 videos may represent fewer than 75 children and the k-fold confusion matrix reports 303 samples, so the analysis unit is the clip. Crucially there is no non-autistic comparison group: all four classes, including normal Behavior, are drawn from videos of autistic children, so the study is a behaviour-recognition problem within one population rather than a diagnostic contrast between populations.

answers.title: Explainable Children Autism Detection using Gaze Features in Audio-Visual Speech Comprehension
answers.answer: Forty-five Spanish children from the BeGaze corpus: 19 with an ASD diagnosis made externally by neuropaediatricians or clinical psychologists before inclusion, and 26 typically developing children, focused on the 5-8 year preschool-to-primary transition. Each child contributed multiple samples - one per story, under two modality conditions and segmented into three temporal phases - and the cross-validation folds are explicitly participant-independent, so the multiplication of samples per child does not leak across the split. This is the correct handling of a repeated-measures design and it is rare in this corpus.

answers.title: Explainable Ensemble Learning Framework for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Enhancing Trust, Interpretability and Reliability in AI-Driven Healthcare
answers.answer: Two datasets with very different standing. Dataset 1 is 1,985 instances with 28 attributes from public ASD screening databases - the same 1,985-record ASD Children Traits collection analysed by local_183eaef4 - and here, unlike there, its class balance is reported: 729 ASD-positive (36.72%) against 1,256 negative (63.28%), with 283 instances carrying missing values. Dataset 2 consists of 100 original clinical samples augmented fourfold to 400, distributed evenly across four severity categories with no non-ASD class at all, and with no source, citation, country or institution given for the original 100. The number of distinct children behind either dataset is never stated.

answers.title: Finding the forest in the trees: Using machine learning and online cognitive and perceptual measures to predict adult autism diagnosis
answers.answer: Two recruited groups of adults: 286 autistic and 266 non-autistic in the final dataset, from 959 initially recruited, with 407 excluded for missing data from at least one contributing experiment (per-study exclusion criteria, technical issues, attrition). Autistic participants came from the Netherlands Autism Register and non-autistic participants principally from Prolific Academic. A second, fully age- and gender-matched subsample of 125 per group was drawn by random selection from the unbalanced sample, and it is this matched analysis the paper reports as its primary result. The analysis unit is the person throughout. The attrition is large and is stated plainly with its causes.

answers.title: Hybrid ensemble learning for Autism Spectrum Disorder screening using eye-tracking scanpath

answers.title: Screening autism spectrum

The gap between the number of children and the number of analysis rows is the study's decisive feature: 640 sessions from 12 children is roughly 53 per child, and the dataset is partitioned by session rather than by child.

The clinical description is conventional and largely accurate, and one passage is notably careful about heterogeneity: autistic children 'exhibit speech and expressive language abnormalities, which range from a total lack of speech (i.e., non-verbal children) to those who develop normal vocabulary and syntax, but exhibit difficulties with the use of appropriate prosody and pragmatics'. Speech is described as 'abnormal' and 'strange prosody' is quoted from prior work, so the register is deficit-oriented, but the paper is precise about the range rather than treating autistic speech as a single phenotype - and that precision matters here, because the sample is drawn from the less verbal end of that range, which the authors state explicitly when comparing their corpus against prior work on 'verbally fluent children'.

answers.title: The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children
answers.answer: Clinical and diagnostic in register, with an unusually clear-eyed account of why existing assessment is difficult. The introduction reviews the screening instruments - M-CHAT, ADEC, CARS-2, ASRS - and observes that because they rest on information from parents and caregivers 'their reliability is limited', with ADOS singled out as the exception 'enriched with interactive protocols'. It then names the differential-diagnosis problem directly: effectiveness 'is compromised by difficulties in differentiating autism from other developmental disorders (for instance, sensory integration disorder, dysphasia, minimal brain dysfunction, e.g., ADHD)', concluding that diagnosis 'often employs a range of clinical tools complemented with long-term observation of the autistic child, often leading to ambiguous diagnostic outcomes'. That is an accurate and specific account of the clinical problem, and the identification of differential diagnosis as the hard case matches the finding of the ADOS-versus-schizophrenia study charted elsewhere in this review. The paper also notes that most robotics work in autism concerns therapy rather than assessment, and positions itself in the smaller assessment literature. 'Autistic children' and 'children with autism' are used interchangeably; no neurodiversity framing appears, but the future-work section names children themselves among the target users whose cooperation is needed to improve the games, which is a participatory commitment absent from the rest of this corpus.

answers.title: Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach
answers.answer: 'Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)' and 'children with typical development (TD)', used consistently. Person-first throughout ('children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'people with ASD'); the abbreviations ASD and TD are used as group labels in tables and figures. Deficit-oriented vocabulary is used freely in the interpretation - 'social deficits', 'attentional deficit', 'impairments', 'atypical oculomotor performance', 'ASD behaviors' - and the model's output classes are named 'ASD-like' and 'TD-like' behaviours. There is no engagement with neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement statement.

answers.title: A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features
answers.answer: 'Children with autism (ASD)', 'children with ASD' and the abbreviation ASD throughout; 'Typically Developed (TD) children' - an idiosyncratic expansion of the usual 'typically developing'. Person-first construction is used consistently ('children with ASD', 'people with ASD'). The clinical framing is medical-model and unhedged: autism is 'a neurodevelopmental disorder that causes problems in social communication and interaction', the targeted behaviours are named as 'symptoms' including 'the obsessive attention to detail' and 'repetitive behaviors', and the conclusion refers to the system as screening 'cognitive deficits'. There is no engagement with neurodiversity perspectives and no autistic-community involvement statement, although the framing of purpose - equitable access to screening in low- and middle-income and rural settings, tied to the UN Sustainable Development Goals - is unusual in this corpus and reflects a genuine health-equity motivation.

answers.title: A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities
answers.answer: 'Children with autism', 'autism spectrum disorder (ASD)', 'ASD group', 'typically developing (TD) group'. Person-first phrasing predominates but slips into group-as-noun usage in the results and discussion ('classify ASD and TD individuals', 'ASD trajectories', 'the ASD one'). The framing is firmly medical: autism is 'a by-birth neurodevelopmental disorder', characterised by 'communication and social impairment and restricted, repetitive, and stereotyped behaviours', and the target construct is 'motor abnormalities' throughout - abnormality rather than difference. One usage requires comment: the six autistic children with IQ 59-70 are described as having 'mild mental retardation', with the WHO (2016) cited as the source of the classification. That terminology is outdated in English-language practice, where intellectual disability is standard, and its appearance in a 2023 paper is worth noting even allowing for translation from Italian and for the cited WHO/ICD source. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement statement, though the stated purpose - to give clinicians objective quantitative indicators to supplement a process the authors criticise as subjective and examiner-dependent - is a clinician-support rather than a replacement agenda.

answers.title: A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation
answers.answer: 'Autistic children' and 'children with ASD' are both used, with 'autistic children' predominating in the title, abstract and conclusion - identity-first language, which is unusual in this corpus and may reflect translation from Chinese as much as a deliberate stance. Other usages are less careful: 'the number of autistic patients has been rising', 'more than 10 million people have been diagnosed with ASD', and 'children with autism have a low quality of life, require family care, and bring huge economic costs to society'. That last sentence, in the opening paragraph, frames autistic children primarily as a burden and is the starkest instance of deficit-and-cost framing encountered so far in this review. Clinically the vocabulary is standard medical-model: 'neurodevelopmental disorder', 'incidence rate', 'RTN deficiency', 'symptoms', 'no medicine can reliably relieve the symptoms of ASD'. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. Set against this, the study's practical stance towards children is respectful in a way several others here are not: it works within a real clinical assessment rather than imposing an experimental protocol, accepts a flexible number of accompanying parents, and mosaics participants' faces in published figures for privacy even at the cost of obscuring the detected landmarks.

answers.title: Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games
answers.answer: The dominant contrast throughout is 'autistic and normal children', with 'normal' used in the title, abstract, results, discussion and conclusion, supplemented by 'healthy children' and 'typical children'. Framing autistic children against 'normal' peers is the least considered terminology encountered in this corpus and carries an implication - abnormality - that 'typically developing' does not. Autism itself is 'autism disorder' or 'the autism spectrum disorder', characterised by 'communication deficits', 'impairment in social interactions' and the statement that autistic children 'lack the ability to learn the socio-cognitive skills with normal development'. Severity is expressed as 'high-performance autism' and, in one passage discussing robot-assisted education, the text refers to 'students with mental retardation' - outdated in current English usage. Against this, the study's motivation is service-oriented rather than dismissive: it is framed around the shortage of specialists relative to a growing autistic population and the goal of supporting, not replacing, clinical judgement, and the introduction is unusually positive about autistic children's engagement with technology, citing evidence of 'inherent dependence on technology and positive behavior toward computer-based training'. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement statement.

answers.title: Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior
answers.answer: 'Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)' and 'adults with autism' predominate, paired with 'neurotypical (NT) individuals' rather than the more common 'typically developing' or, worse, 'normal'. 'Neurotypical' is a term originating in the autistic community and its use here, in a paper from a major autism research centre, is a meaningful marker: it frames the comparison group as one neurotype among others rather than as a standard of normality. The conclusion goes further, calling for future work 'in predicting ASD diagnosis from neurodiverse samples' - importing 'neurodiverse' as a technical descriptor of a clinically mixed population, which is both an accurate usage and an unusual one in this literature. Clinical description is measured throughout: autism is 'defined by observable behavioral cues - what a person does well or not well, too little or too much', its core traits are 'observable differences in social communication, social reciprocity, nonverbal communication, and relationships', and the word 'differences' rather than 'deficits' is used where most papers in this corpus use the latter. The framing of purpose is also non-replacement: the stated aim is to establish whether AI adds anything beyond clinician judgement, on the explicit premise that 'clinicians would have little interest in or benefit from incorporating AI algorithms if their decisions - and errors - highly overlap with their own'. There is no autistic-community involvement statement.

answers.title: Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas
answers.answer: 'Children with ASD' and 'typically developing (TD) children' are the working terms, used consistently and person-first. But the surrounding framing is the most burden-oriented in this corpus. The introduction states that 'most patients diagnosed with ASD cannot independently live, study and work when they grow up, which places a heavy burden on their families and society', and autistic children are referred to throughout as 'patients' - including in the abstract, where the aim is 'to screen patients with ASD'. Early intervention is motivated by 'reducing the harm caused by the disorder'. Elsewhere the vocabulary is that of deviation from a norm: 'atypical performance', 'abnormalities in ASD', 'abnormal distribution values', and children whose viewing is 'passive in the information exploration process'. Set against this, the study's practical orientation is genuinely equity-driven and its design is respectful of children in a way several others here are not - six minutes of passive viewing, no instructions, no restraint, mother present, stimuli chosen partly to hold attention. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. One passage complicates the picture in an interesting way: the finding that 5-6 year olds who had undergone rehabilitation training scored lower and were more often missed is reported neutrally as a limitation of the model, without remarking that it implies the measured signal is modifiable by intervention - which is a substantive point about what the 'AI-marker' is actually marking.

answers.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts
answers.answer: The terminology is the most internally contradictory in this corpus, and the contradiction is instructive. The search keywords include 'ActuallyAutistic' and 'Aspie' - terms coined and used by autistic people themselves, the first being an identity hashtag that exists precisely to distinguish autistic voices from those speaking about autism, and one that carries an explicit rejection of pathologising language. The paper harvests those self-identifications and then describes the people who wrote them as 'ASD patients', as 'individuals who suffer from ASD', and as 'people that suffer from ASD'; the comparison group is 'people that do not suffer from ASD'. Autism is 'a developmental disability' that 'affects the social and interactive skills of those who have it', which 'appears before the age of three and can last a lifetime'. The framing of value is entirely deficit-and-outcome: 'people who are not diagnosed in childhood have a poorer quality of life'. So the study takes its ground truth from a community that names itself in one register and reports its findings in the opposite one, without noticing. There is no neurodiversity framing, no autistic-community involvement, and no acknowledgement that the data subjects are a self-organised community with stated views about how they are described - or about being classified by algorithms trained on their own posts.

answers.title: Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: 'Toddlers with ASD' and 'typically developing (TD) toddlers', used consistently and person-first throughout, with 'children with autism' also appearing. The register is notably measured for this literature. Autistic children are described as experiencing 'challenges in establishing social communication' and 'differences in use of facial expressions', and the paper speaks of 'atypical' and 'ambiguous' expressions rather than of deficits or abnormality - though 'atypical facial expression' is called an 'early symptom' and the language of biomarkers, symptoms and risk is used throughout. There is no burden framing, no cost-to-society argument, and no claim that autistic people cannot live independently, all of which appear in other papers charted here. Two interpretive passages are worth noting for their care. The explanation offered for the finding is framed as speculation and is symmetrical rather than deficit-laden: typically developing toddlers may respond more predictably because they share an understanding of the movies' social meaning, whereas autistic children's responses 'may be more idiosyncratic' - idiosyncrasy rather than impairment. And the authors note that neutral expressions 'might be interpreted by others as more ambiguous', locating the communicative difficulty in the interpretation as much as in the expression. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement statement.

answers.title: Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders
answers.answer: 'People with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)' and 'people with schizophrenia (Sz)' predominate, person-first, with 'the ASDs' and 'the Szs' appearing as shorthand in the participants section and 'disorder groups' used throughout as the collective term for the clinical samples. The register is clinical-psychiatric and uses 'abnormalities' freely - 'ASD and Sz have abnormalities in cognitive functions, particularly social cognitive functions', 'abnormalities in eye movement during facial expression recognition have also been reported' - and 'atypical gaze patterns' and 'social cognitive deficits' elsewhere. Autism is described as 'a neurodevelopmental disorder, meaning that it does not appear in adulthood but is an innate trait', which is an accurate developmental statement rather than a deficit claim. One passage is notably person-centred in a way the corpus rarely manages: the introduction explains that some people 'have spent their childhood without being diagnosed with ASD' and that in adulthood 'difficulties in real social life may become emerged', sometimes with secondary depressive states leading to a first psychiatric presentation - a description of late diagnosis framed around the person's experience rather than around missed screening opportunities. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement, but there is also no burden or cost rhetoric and no overstated claim.

answers.title: Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders
answers.answer: 'Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)' and 'individuals with disabilities' predominate, person-first and generally neutral, with the field's own vocabulary of augmentative and alternative communication used precisely throughout. The register is mostly that of assistive-technology research rather than pathology, and the paper is notably interested in what users do with the app rather than in what is wrong with them - the descriptive sections report which phrases people used, how many unique words they produced, and how long they engaged, framed as evidence of the app's usefulness across populations. Against this, deficit language appears in places: AAC systems 'are usually used by individuals with expressive communication disorders who suffer from impairments in speech, language, reading, and/or writing', autism is 'associated with deficits in social interaction', and 'individuals affected with autism' appears once. One passage is garbled in a way that matters: the text states that people with non-autistic communication challenges 'are typically interested in communicating with others, whereas individuals with ASD may be more motivated', which as written contradicts the contrast it is drawing and appears to have lost a negation - a claim about differential communicative motivation in autism that is contentious in the first place and is here left incoherent. There is no neurodiversity framing and no involvement of AAC users or autistic people in the research, which is a notable absence for a study built entirely on the communication attempts of disabled people.

answers.title: Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: 'Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)' and 'children with typical development (TD)' throughout, person-first and consistent, in the register of a clinical diagnostic journal. Autism is 'a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by abnormal patterns of social interaction and communication', joint attention is 'deficient in children with ASD', and 'infants with this condition, but not those with typical development, appear to lack joint attention' - deficit-framed but factually anchored to the construct being measured rather than generalised. The framing of purpose is assistive: the stated problem is that clinicians 'have had to rely on subjective assessment scores in diagnosing ASD to date' and that validated joint attention manuals such as the Early Social Communication Scales are 'labor-intensive and difficult to implement without trained clinicians and the proper experimental setup', so the target is objectivity and scalability of an existing clinical construct rather than replacement of clinicians. There is no burden or cost rhetoric and no neurodiversity framing. One descriptive passage is worth noting for its observational quality rather than its terminology: in the high-level RJA task, comparison children are described as turning to view the poster 'and then turned back to face the examiner as if seeking approval' - a phenomenological description of shared attention that conveys what the construct actually is.

answers.title: Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking
answers.answer: 'Children with autism spectrum disorder' and 'ASD child' are used alongside 'normal child' and 'TD child', with the autism/normal contrast appearing repeatedly - 'the gaze patterns of a normal child and a child affected with autism', 'differentiate between a TD child and an ASD child'. The framing is medical-model and at times stronger than the evidence warrants: autism is 'a medical condition which is a result of abnormal brain development', characterised by 'abnormal behaviours' and 'fixation abnormality'. Autistic children are described as people who 'refrain from expressing their feeling in the form of facial expressions' and who 'indulge in various repetitive behaviours'. The intent is plainly not hostile - the paper's motivation is that the existing diagnostic process 'consumes a lot of time and energy of both the children and parents' - but the vocabulary of abnormality is used without qualification and the 'normal' contrast term is the one this review has flagged elsewhere as carrying an implication that 'typically developing' does not. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement.

answers.title: SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism
answers.answer: 'Children with autism (CwA)' is used throughout as the working abbreviation, alongside 'typically developing (TD)' and 'neurotypical', which is a more current pairing than the 'normal' contrast used elsewhere in this corpus. The clinical framing is nonetheless firmly deficit-based and in one respect dated: autism is characterised by 'repetitive and stereotypic behaviours and impaired social and communicative skills collectively called the triads of impairments', a formulation superseded by DSM-5's two-domain structure a decade before this paper. Language differences are described as 'language and communication impairments', 'language atypicalities' and 'aberrant receptive and expressive language development', and the targeted behaviours are 'stereotypic language behaviours'. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. Against this, the paper's motivating concern is a reasonable one about assessment rather than about people - that quantifying behavioural traits 'is cumbersome, and the efficacy of such methods primarily depends on the evaluators' expertise' - and its stated goal is interpretable measurement that a non-expert could follow, which is a service orientation rather than a replacement one.

answers.title: Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths
answers.answer: 'Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)' and 'Typically Developing (TD)' throughout, person-first and consistent, in the register of a computational health-informatics paper. Clinical description is deficit-framed but restrained: autism is 'a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with social communication deficits and repetitive behaviors', with 'deficit in social attention' and 'atypicality in social attention' as the operative constructs. One passage uses 'ASD patients' when summarising prior work. The framing of purpose is unusual for this corpus in being oriented towards heterogeneity rather than detection: the stated motivation is that 'the observed heterogeneity in autism' compounds the subjectivity of clinical assessment, and that 'ASD heterogeneity and proven difficulty to identify generalizable markers of ASD have led to the presumption of the presence of multiple etiologies rather than a single disorder'. That is a defensible scientific position and it drives the study's most interesting experiments. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. One factual error should be noted: the paper states that 'ASD prevalence is found to have a gender bias with one in four individuals with ASD diagnosis being male', which inverts the well-established ratio.

answers.title: A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths
answers.answer: 'Children with ASD' and 'typically developing (TD) children' predominate, person-first, alongside 'individuals with ASD' and 'people with ASD'. Autism is 'a developmental disorder that encompasses difficulties in communication (both verbal and non-verbal), social skills, and repetitive behaviors' and 'a neurodevelopmental disorder that impacts the behavioral and cognitive abilities of children'. The register is medical-model but not pejorative, and the introduction is unusually attentive to autistic people's communicative experience for an engineering paper - it discusses difficulty grasping 'deeper implications in dialogues, resulting in literal understandings and struggles in recognizing indirect messages like sarcasm', and notes that 'clear and specific instructions are necessary for their understanding'. It also engages seriously with heterogeneity, comorbidity (ADHD, anxiety, mood disorders) and the interpersonal-coordination framing of diagnostic conversation. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. One framing choice should be flagged: early detection is motivated partly by 'reduced costs for both individuals and society as a whole', a cost-benefit argument that recurs across this corpus.

answers.title: A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning
answers.answer: 'Children with ASD' and 'typically developing (TD)' children, person-first and consistent. Autism 'manifests through social communication deficits and atypical behaviors' per DSM-5, and the vocabulary of red flags, risk, markers and screening runs throughout - appropriate to a public-health surveillance framing. The register is notably free of the burden and cost rhetoric found elsewhere in this corpus; the motivation offered is access and equity rather than economic saving. Two framing choices are worth recording. The paper repeatedly emphasises heterogeneity as the obstacle to early detection - 'the great heterogeneity in the red flags, onset, and progression of symptoms, and in the divergence of developmental trajectories in ASD' - and treats variation as something a model must accommodate rather than as noise. And it frames the problem partly as one of clinician support rather than clinician replacement, noting that some early signs 'can be easily missed by a healthcare provider during a short checkup visit due to their gradual deviation or subtlety, such as social reciprocity, social smile, and eye contact', and that 'disparities in healthcare screening resources and in provider awareness of individual developmental differences' are themselves barriers. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement.

answers.title: AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: “A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System”
answers.answer: 'Autistic children' and 'non-autistic children' are the working terms, with 'typically developing (TD)' appearing occasionally. The register is medical-model with some notable slips: autism is 'characterized by early brain abnormalities', and the evaluation section refers to the model having halted 'after evaluating ten patients' when it means an early-stopping patience of ten epochs. The framing that matters, however, is not terminological but conceptual. The paper's premise is physiognomic: it opens by citing research that 'has identified distinct facial features common among autistic children: expanded upper face and a truncated mid-facial region, underscoring the potential of facial analysis in aiding early detection', and the method section asserts that autistic children 'exhibit distinct facial feature variations, showcasing differences in both the arrangement and dimensions of facial landmarks'. Inferring a neurodevelopmental condition from face shape is a claim with a long and discredited history, and the paper adopts it from a single citation with no engagement with that history, no discussion of the evidence base, and no consideration of what a facial autism classifier would mean for the people it classifies. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement - which is a particular absence given that the autistic images were taken from autism-focused websites, that is, from spaces created by and for autistic people and their families, and repurposed as training data without acknowledgement.

answers.title: An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks
answers.answer: Conventional clinical framing with a specific rhetorical move worth recording. Autism is 'a complex neurodevelopmental disorder' affecting 'over 1% of the global population', characterised by 'defined problems in social interaction, communication, and flexibility of behavior'. The introduction's argument for automation rests on discrediting the standard instruments: ADOS and ADI-R 'remain subjective, time-consuming, and largely impossible in low-resource environments', and elsewhere they 'relied on subjective behavioral ratings subject to inter-rater bias and with poor scalability, therefore calling for the search for objective biomarkers'. Neuroimaging is contrasted as providing 'objective measures'. That framing is standard in this branch, and here it sits directly against the study's own method, which takes the scored output of those same instruments as its most heavily weighted predictors. A framework motivated by the inadequacy of ADOS and ADI-R cannot be deployed without them. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person is reported as involved.

answers.title: Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development
answers.answer: 'Children with ASD' and 'children with typical development (TD)' throughout, person-first and consistent, with 'autistic children' appearing in the highlights. The clinical framing is standard medical-model - 'persistent social communication impairment is a hallmark symptom', 'atypical behavior in social interaction', 'incapability of social reciprocity', 'failure of normal back-and-forth interaction', 'IMC impairments' - and the introduction's list of autistic social characteristics is unrelievedly deficit-framed. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. Two features of the framing are nonetheless worth noting. The construct is interactional rather than individual: interpersonal motor coordination is a property of a dyad, and the paper is explicit that 'human movement during interpersonal interaction is not a stochastic process' but something two people do together - which locates the measured difference in the interaction rather than solely in the child, even if the interpretation does not follow that through. And the motivation is explicitly about reducing reliance on expert rating: the paper observes that prior work on coordination in autism 'often relied on expert ratings, potentially introducing biases and requiring substantial time', and that studies shortening diagnostic instruments by machine learning leave the objectivity problem untouched because 'the issue of lack of objectivity remains if individuals' behavior is rated by experts'.

answers.title: Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning
answers.answer: 'Autism spectrum (AS)' and 'non-AS' throughout, with 'individuals with AS' as the standard construction - and the choice of 'autism spectrum' rather than 'autism spectrum disorder' is deliberate, appearing even in the running head where the journal's own metadata uses ASD. Clinical description centres on 'pragmatic impairment', defined precisely and non-pejoratively as difficulty with 'the effective use of language in social contexts... rather than with the basic structural or grammatical components' - a distinction most papers in this corpus do not draw. The register is that of clinical linguistics rather than of deficit cataloguing, and the introduction engages seriously with autistic experience in ways rare here: it discusses masking behaviour, compensation strategies and learned camouflaging as phenomena that 'can conceal critical information about impairment, potentially leading to misdiagnosis', and notes that adult diagnosis is hampered because caregiver developmental reports are usually unavailable while 'patient self-insight is unreliable'. That framing treats diagnostic difficulty as a property of the encounter rather than of the person. Deficit vocabulary does appear - 'impairment', 'dysfunction', 'core deficits' - and there is no neurodiversity framing or autistic-community involvement, but the paper's characterisation of what it is measuring is more precise and less totalising than the corpus norm.

answers.title: Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms
answers.answer: 'Autistic children' and 'non-autistic children', person-first in most constructions but with 'normally developing youngsters' appearing when summarising prior work. The clinical description in the introduction is drawn accurately from DSM criteria and is comparatively careful - reduced sharing of emotions and interests, deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, difficulty adapting behaviour to social contexts, difficulty making friends. The framing of purpose includes an unusual note: technological advancement is described as 'a blessing to the parents who are clueless about managing the condition', which positions the work as parent-facing. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement - a notable absence given that the dataset's autistic images were collected from autism-focused online spaces created by and for that community. The premise that 'autistic children show distinctive patterns' in facial and emotional expression is asserted without citation to any evidence about facial morphology.

answers.title: Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed
answers.answer: The framing is entirely autism-focused and the content is not, which is the record's central observation. The introduction is written with some care about autistic experience: it notes that autistic people 'frequently struggle with self-regulation, emotional interpretation, and understanding and labeling others' emotions', and that 'these differences can lead to social withdrawal, especially when others react negatively to the atypical responses of individuals with ASD' - which locates part of the difficulty in other people's reactions rather than solely in the autistic person, a formulation better than most in this corpus. The conclusion likewise frames the goal as addressing 'the existing challenges faced by conventional facial expression recognition systems when applied to ASD populations, where nuanced facial cues may be misinterpreted or overlooked', which correctly identifies a technology failure rather than a personal deficit. Against this, autism is described as 'a neurological illness', and the phrase 'the minor changes and quirks typical of the facial movements' of autistic people is dismissive. No autistic person is reported as involved, and no autistic person's face appears in the data.

answers.title: Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification
answers.answer: 'Children with autism', 'children with a diagnosis of autism' and 'individuals with ASD', person-first and consistent, alongside 'typically developing (TD) children'. Autism is 'a complex and heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder' with the standard two-domain description, and motor differences are called 'motor abnormalities' and 'motor disorders'. The framing is otherwise notably measured and contains one argument worth recording: the paper's opening critique is that autism diagnosis 'is based on subjective observations of behavior' focused on the two core domains, and that 'many other characteristics are overlooked in the diagnostic process, considered non-central to the disorder' - specifically motor characteristics, which 'have always been considered secondary symptoms and not closely related to the syndrome' despite evidence that they precede language and social difficulties. That is an argument for widening what is measured rather than for replacing clinicians, and it is grounded in embodied-cognition theory rather than in an appeal to objectivity alone. The paper also reports the literature on visuospatial ability in autism honestly as conflicting - some studies finding deficits, some no difference, some better performance - rather than selecting the supportive citations. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement.

answers.title: Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain
answers.answer: 'ASD-affected individuals' and 'autism-affected individuals' predominate, with 'ASD-affected children', 'affected children' and 'the individual affected with ASD' appearing throughout - a consistently affliction-framed register. Autism is described as affecting 'the neurological function and also the speech function of children' and as leading to 'uncontrolled aggressive behavior in the affected children', and the case for early detection is made in explicitly economic and burden terms: undetected autism 'may create more economic pressure, affect the family relationship, and also become a burden in social and medical care', and 'the occurrence of ASD has brought a large economic and mental burden to society that leads to severe public health problems'. Elsewhere autism is referred to as a 'defect' and as 'disease growth'. This is the most consistently deficit- and burden-oriented framing in the review, and it is paired with the conflation of autism and sensory processing disorder into a single detection target. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement.

answers.title: Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: Clinical and deficit-oriented, with one formulation that is factually wrong. Autism is described as 'a disorder specified by a genetic neurological condition linked to developmental delays in communication skills, recurring attitudes, difficulties switching between activities, and unexpected responses to senses', and the introduction states that 'if autism is identified early enough it can be treated with better outcomes' - a treatment framing that misdescribes what early intervention does. Against this, the paper's account of the access problem is well sourced and is the most concrete statement of it in the review: it cites over 125,000 individuals waiting for a mental health service examination in England in July 2022 against a recommended three-month wait, with the consequence that 'parents and caregivers [do] not have the necessary support and services early'. That is a real and quantified problem, and it is the reason work of this kind is published, funded and cited. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person or family organisation is reported as involved in designing a tool intended for at-home use by families.

answers.title: Machine learning’s effectiveness
answers.answer: 'Children with autism spectrum disorder' and 'children with high autistic trait' are used precisely and the distinction is maintained throughout - the outcome is consistently named 'High autistic trait group' rather than autism, in the title, abstract, methods, results and conclusion. That precision is unusual in this corpus and matters, because the study measures a screening-questionnaire threshold rather than a diagnosis and says so. Clinical description is standard medical-model - 'deficits in social communication and social interactions and repetitive, restricted behaviors', 'motor impairments', 'balance impairments', 'deficiency in balance ability' - and the introduction opens with a cost framing, citing an estimated lifetime social cost of approximately $3.6 million per individual. Against this, the discussion of why balance matters is developmental and person-centred rather than diagnostic: poor balance 'increases the risk of falls among affected children which diminishes their motivation to participate in physical activities', and balance impairments 'can hinder the development of communication and motor skills, limit the children's integration into mainstream society, and adversely affect their social adaptation abilities'. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement.

answers.title: Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network
answers.answer: Consistently medical and deficit-framed, with the diagnostic label used as an attribute of appearance. Autism is 'a complex neurodevelopmental disorder that affects both cognitive and social development' posing 'a significant concern in modern healthcare'. The facial framing is the distinctive feature: the introduction assembles a physiognomic case - 'craniofacial anomalies make neuro-developmental disorders like ASD more likely to happen', autism severity 'has been associated with a wider intercanthal distance and a lower height of the facial midline', and 'facial asymmetry and facial masculinity are good signs that someone has significant ASD symptoms'. The conclusion instructs clinicians that they 'must recognize these facial traits or regions, as they indicate the condition'. Person-first phrasing appears alongside 'individuals diagnosed with ASD' and 'the non-ASD control group'. There is no neurodiversity framing, no autistic-community involvement, and no acknowledgement that a facial-appearance classifier trained on photographs of children scraped from support and awareness pages carries a different set of ethical questions from a behavioural measurement.

answers.title: Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]
answers.answer: Conventional clinical framing, brief and largely accurate.
