Autism is 'a complex neurodevelopmental condition characterized by a spectrum of challenges, including difficulties in communication, response, attention, social behavior, and repetitive activities', with the addition that autistic people 'exhibit atypical neural activity patterns'. The diagnostic argument is the branch standard: current practice 'predominantly depends on subjective and time-consuming behavioral assessments', so an objective non-intrusive biomarker is needed. Person-first phrasing is used throughout and no pathologising excess appears. No neurodiversity framing is present and no autistic person is reported as involved. The framing is worth recording for the synthesis because it is identical to that of the behavioural studies charted elsewhere in this review - the same dissatisfaction with behavioural assessment motivates both branches, while the electrophysiological branch requires equipment and expertise that the behavioural work is generally chosen to avoid.

answers.title: Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play
answers.answer: Notably careful, and the most consistent use of identity-first language in this corpus. The title and abstract say 'autistic children' and 'neurotypical children'; the body alternates between 'autistic children' and 'children with ASD' without the deficit-laden hedging common elsewhere. Differences are described as differences rather than as deficits - autism is 'a neurodevelopmental condition with distinct patterns in social interaction, communication, and repetitive behavior', autistic children 'often show differences in play development', and the core traits are 'distinct patterns in social interaction and communication, focused interests, and repetitive behaviors'. The opening frames play in terms of what it gives children rather than what it diagnoses: play 'can provide satisfaction and joy, promote quality of life, engender social inclusion, and foster better social outcomes and friendships later in life'. The literature review is also candid about disagreement, noting that 'some studies report no significant differences in symbolic and functional play' and treating the inconsistency as a reason for further work rather than something to be argued past. Two elements pull the other way: the coded behaviour set uses 'unusual' and 'abnormal' as category labels ('unusual sensory seeking behaviors', 'unusual and repetitive hand/body/limb movements', 'abnormal eye contact'), and no autistic person or community organisation is reported as involved in designing the coding scheme, choosing which behaviours count as targets, or interpreting the findings.

answers.title: Predictive model using autism
answers.answer: Consistently medical and diagnostic, which fits the venue and the question. Autism is 'a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and restricted or repetitive behavioral patterns of interest'; participants are 'patients with schizophrenia' and 'participants with ASD'. The framing throughout is nosological rather than functional - the question is which category a person belongs to and how to tell, not what support they need - and the language of the instrument itself supplies terms like 'unusual eye contact' and 'speech abnormalities associated with autism'. What lifts the paper above simple deficit framing is its treatment of overlap. The introduction traces the shared history seriously, from Bleuler's use of 'autistic' as a basic symptom of schizophrenia through modern evidence of co-occurrence, familial clustering and shared genetic risk, and it describes the distinguishing features in clinical detail - the content and duration of delusions, the presence or absence of self-disturbance, the developmental timing of onset - rather than asserting a clean boundary. The discussion then treats the overlap as substantive rather than as measurement error, proposing that negative symptoms in schizophrenia and social-communication features in autism may share underlying deficits in social cognition. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person is reported as involved in the work, but the paper does not pathologise its participants beyond the diagnostic task it sets itself.

answers.title: The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech
answers.answer: Mixed, with the strongest and weakest language in this corpus sitting a few pages apart. The clinical framing in the introduction is dated and inaccurate: autism is 'a neurological disease correlated by imbalances in the brain', it is 'incurable' though it 'can be managed', and the population is characterised through what it lacks - 'a lack in verbal skills or continuing to be non-verbal'. 'Individuals with ASD' and 'children with ASD' are the standard usages, with 'atypically developing' as the analytic label. Against this, three passages show real care. The fairness section states that bias testing 'is crucial in our experiment, specially that we are adhering to a vulnerable group', and grounds the analysis in the observed male-to-female diagnostic ratio and in the 'female camouflage effect', which suggests females are better at masking autism - one of very few places in this review where under-identification of autistic women is treated as a methodological problem rather than a footnote. The limitations argue that 'non-verbal vocalisations are a form of speech and hold communicative value', which treats the sounds autistic children make as communication rather than as noise to be filtered - a substantive interpretive commitment. And the paper's reflection on research ethics committees as safeguards for child data, and on the difficulty of obtaining such data, shows awareness of the population's vulnerability even though the study's own ethics declaration is thin. No autistic person or community organisation is reported as involved.

answers.title: Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism
answers.answer: The most careful terminology in this review, and the only paper here that treats the politics of autism language as part of its subject matter rather than as background. Identity-first language is used throughout - 'millions of individuals are autistic', 'autistic community', 'autistic peers' - alongside 'individuals with autism' in places, and 'neurotypical' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy' for the comparison group. More substantively, the paper explains the origin of its own inclusion criterion in community terms: hashtags such as #AutismMom and #AutismParent 'have represented the perspectives of neurotypical parents, significantly influencing research and policies in this domain', but 'these advocacy groups often overshadow adults with autism, creating a gap in their representation within decision-making processes', and #ActuallyAutistic emerged as 'a paradigm shift ... in the autism rights movement', redirecting attention toward autistic people 'rather than solely focusing on caregivers'. That passage does something no other included study attempts: it recognises that the autism research literature has been shaped disproportionately by parents and professionals rather than by autistic people, and it selects its sample specifically from autistic voices for that reason. The conclusion follows through, calling for 'a more inclusive approach during the model development process that involves the autistic community directly in the ideation and consent processes' and referring to autistic people as a 'marginalized population' whose consent is at issue. The framing is not uniformly neurodiversity-aligned - the introduction still describes autism through misdiagnosis, delayed services and 'negative outcomes later in life' - but the paper is the only one in this corpus to treat the people it studies as a constituency with standing in how they are researched. The published record also shows that the article attracted a formal comment (JMIR Formative Research 2024;8:e59794) and was issued as a corrected version, which indicates that its approach was contested in the literature.

answers.title: Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children
answers.answer: Clinically conventional and, within that idiom, careful and accurate. Autism is 'a group of neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by a wide range of symptoms across two main dimensions: social and nonsocial', and the description that follows is notably precise about heterogeneity - noting that autism 'can be present with or without cognitive and language delay, widening the breadth of clinical presentations', and that 'the heterogeneity of ASD manifestations is a major obstacle to timely diagnosis and personalized medicine'. Person-first phrasing predominates ('children with ASD', 'individuals with autism'), with 'autistic individuals' and 'individuals on the autism spectrum' appearing alongside it. Two aspects of the framing are substantively better than the corpus norm. The description of social symptoms is relational rather than located in the individual: they 'often transcend the isolated instances of behaviors and arise from specific mismatches in the dynamic between agents and their social context' - which is why the study models the child-examiner dyad rather than the child alone, and it is a conceptual position with methodological consequences. And the account of the gold-standard diagnostic procedure treats it as 'the product of convergent clinical and research work over the past four decades', crediting rather than dismissing existing clinical practice, which is a marked contrast to the framing common in the engineering venues where clinical assessment is characterised chiefly as subjective and slow. There is no neurodiversity framing and no reported involvement of autistic people in the design.

answers.title: Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning
answers.answer: Mixed within a single paper, and the internal tension is worth recording. Some passages are attentive: the term neurotypical is defined explicitly as 'an individual whose neurological development and functioning are considered typical regarding the society's norms and expectations' - a definition that locates typicality in social expectation rather than in biology, which is a neurodiversity-adjacent formulation; the authors relay approvingly that 'ASD is not a disease'; and they observe that differences in emotional perception 'may be the cause for them to experience social and emotional isolation', locating the difficulty in the interaction rather than solely in the person. Against this, the clinical description reproduces the harshest vocabulary in the review: individuals with autism 'typically demonstrate a lack of social interaction and emotional intelligence as well as having repetitive, abhorrent, stigmatized, and fixated behavior'. Calling autistic behaviour abhorrent, in a paper whose data consist of home videos that families posted of their own children, is a serious lapse - and it sits two paragraphs from the statement that autism is not a disease. Elsewhere the register is standard medical ('individuals with ASD', 'ASD children', 'patients'). No autistic person or community is reported as involved in the annotation protocol, in defining what counts as an affective state, or in reviewing the use of family-uploaded videos.

answers.title: A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features
answers.answer: Medical and deficit-framed throughout, with several formulations that are outdated or inaccurate. Autism is 'a developmental impairment with brain abnormalities', 'a pervasive neurodevelopmental disability', and the introduction speaks of the need for treatments that 'target the underlying abnormalities in the autistic brain'. Prevalence is presented in alarm terms - a rise 'from 1 in 5000 in 1975 to 1 in 45 by 2018' described as 'alarming' and as underscoring urgency - without acknowledging that changing diagnostic criteria and ascertainment account for much of that trend, which makes the framing a claim about incidence that the cited figures do not support. The children themselves appear almost entirely as objects of measurement and dosing: they are 'ASD children' and 'autistic children' whose 'behaviors' are to be monitored continuously so that medication can be adjusted, and no autistic person, family member or advocacy organisation is reported as involved in designing the framework or in judging whether continuous thermal surveillance of children at school is acceptable. One passage is more careful and deserves credit: the discussion of medication notes that 'autistic children may be more sensitive to medication effects and more prone to experiencing adverse drug effects compared to non-ASD children', and the introduction states plainly that the two approved medications 'do not effectively address the core symptoms of ASD and are associated with significant side effects'. That is an accurate and clinically important observation - but it is used to justify more precise dosing rather than to raise any question about the framework's premise that a camera should inform the dose.

answers.title: Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: Predominantly medical and physiognomic, with one passage of genuine ethical awareness that the paper then argues past. Autism is 'a mental condition characterized by challenges in communication, restricted behaviors, difficulties with speech, non-verbal interaction, and distinctive facial features in children', and is elsewhere called 'this disease'. The physiognomic framing is explicit and forms the study's premise: autistic people 'often present distinct facial morphological characteristics' including 'broader upper faces, wider eyes, shorter nasal bridges, and narrower cheeks', described as 'increasingly recognized as potential biomarkers'. Against this, the introduction contains a paragraph absent from every other paper in this branch, acknowledging the harms of early identification itself: 'A significant concern is the potential for labeling, which may impact the child's self-esteem and social relationships. There is a risk of overdiagnosis or misdiagnosis, leading to unnecessary interventions and therapies.' Naming labelling, self-esteem and overdiagnosis as risks of the enterprise the paper is contributing to is a real acknowledgement. What follows undoes it: the authors propose that these dangers may be mitigated by using artificial intelligence, without explaining how a facial classifier trained on web-scraped images with no diagnostic ascertainment would reduce the risk of mislabelling a child. No autistic person or organisation is reported as involved.

answers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features
answers.answer: Standard clinical-deficit framing, brief and without the physiognomic or pathologising excesses found elsewhere in this corpus. Autistic children 'commonly have difficulty communicating and interacting with others, show repetitive and restricted behaviors, and have delayed cognitive and movement skills'; the phrase 'there is no permanent cure for ASD' appears, and children are once referred to as 'patients with ASD'. Person-first language predominates. The framing of the access problem is accurate and non-alarmist: diagnosis is difficult because 'there is no medical test', a professional diagnosis from age 2 is considered reliable, and 'some patients with ASD are not diagnosed until after their childhood, and many do not receive a diagnosis at all'. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person is reported as involved. The paper's most careful language is about sex: rather than treating the male preponderance in its sample as a nuisance, it names the four-to-one diagnostic ratio as the cause and then analyses features separately for boys and girls - one of very few studies in this review to treat sex as a substantive variable rather than a sampling artefact.

answers.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning
answers.answer: Predominantly medical, with 'patients with ASD' used repeatedly and autism described as a set of 'complex developmental disabilities' with symptoms such as 'a lack of eye contact and an obsession with certain behaviours'. Two passages show more thought than the register suggests. The introduction gives an accurate and unusually careful account of rising prevalence, noting that the doubling of diagnoses between 2015 and 2024 occurred despite the stricter DSM-5 criteria expected to reduce it, and attributing the net increase to awareness and earlier diagnosis - concluding that 'many patients with ASD have not yet surfaced'. That is the correct reading of the epidemiological trend and stands against the alarm framing used elsewhere in this corpus. And the account of the access barrier is concrete rather than rhetorical: 'the high barrier to visiting a hospital, along with the fact that many children are not yet able to speak. Deciding to visit a hospital often requires recognising signs within the household', with the proposed role for the technology being to give families 'a clearer motivation to visit a hospital' rather than to substitute for assessment. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person is reported as involved.

answers.title: Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]
answers.answer: Clinical and developmental, without pathologising excess. Autism is 'a neurodevelopmental condition', described through 'a wide range of cognitive, social, and communicative challenges' and framed in terms of impact on the child, the family and society across education, healthcare and employment - a systemic rather than individual framing. Person-first phrasing is used consistently ('children with ASD', 'individuals diagnosed with ASD'), and the early-detection argument is made in terms of neuroplasticity and long-term prognosis rather than urgency or alarm. One formulation deserves note for its restraint: the paper states that 'any behavioral cues that raise concerns should be diligently combined with clinical assessments to enable the early identification of atypical development', positioning the technology as an input to clinical judgement rather than a substitute for it. The phrase 'children at risk of ASD' recurs and carries the usual risk framing. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person or family organisation is reported as involved in the work, which is worth noting for a study whose proposed product is an at-home screening tool for caregivers.

answers.title: Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm
answers.answer: Brief and conventional. Autism is 'a complex neurological disorder that involves repetitive behaviors, limited interest, and has interpersonal interaction problems', with traditional diagnosis characterised as 'subjective and time-consuming'. Person-first phrasing predominates. The closing statement refers to 'identifying and supporting children with ASD', although the dataset is an adult screening corpus - a slippage between the population studied and the population invoked. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person is reported as involved.

answers.title: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
answers.answer: Conventional medical framing, more dated in places than most of this corpus. Autism is 'a neurodevelopmental disorder' but also 'this disorder' and, in the opening sentence, is placed within 'identification and investigation of diseases'. The characterisation is deficit-based - 'social deficits, difficulties in communication, and atypical patterns of behavior', with key characteristics given as 'avoidance of eye contact, lack of or excessive expression of emotions, and repetitive stereotypical movements'. 'Children with ASD' and 'neurotypical children' are the standard usages, and 'neurotypical' rather than 'normal' is a small point in the paper's favour. The access argument is stated in health-systems terms that are accurate for the setting - 'a shortage of qualified specialists and a high burden on healthcare systems' - and the proposed role is 'earlier identification and timely referral to specialists', which frames the technology as a routing mechanism rather than a replacement for assessment. No neurodiversity framing appears, and no autistic person or family organisation is reported as involved, which is worth noting for a study that recorded 16 hours of video of children without any documented consent process.

answers.title: Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of
answers.answer: Standard clinical framing with an unusually sympathetic account of the second condition. Autism is 'a neurodevelopmental disorder' characterised by 'difficulties in social interactions, communication impairments, repetitive behaviors, and restricted interests', with the spectrum concept explained accurately as reflecting variation in severity and ability. The description of gelotophobia is the paper's best writing and is genuinely person-centred: individuals 'may perceive all laughter as negatively directed at them, interpreting it as a form of mockery or threat, which often leads to social withdrawal and isolation', and the account traces how the belief becomes internalised into 'heightened sensitivity to rejection, feelings of shame, and an increased tendency toward social avoidance'. Framing a condition through the person's experience of it, rather than through observable deficit, is rare in this corpus. The paper also refers to autistic people as 'populations considered socially vulnerable', which is an acknowledgement of social position rather than individual pathology. Against this, the study's method sits awkwardly with its own framing: a condition defined by an internal appraisal of others' intentions is to be detected from a photograph of a face. No autistic person or organisation is reported as involved.

answers.title: Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
answers.answer: Physiognomic and, in one passage, dismissive of families. The premise is stated as fact: 'abnormal facial traits caused by impairment of embryonic development are significantly related to underlying neurological issues', with autistic infants said to show 'wider eyes, a larger mouth, a shorter middle face, a broader top face, and a pronounced philtrum', and the University of Missouri work cited for 'an atypically broad upper face, which includes wide-set eyes' and 'a shorter nose and cheekbones in the middle of their faces'. The abstract states that 'differentiating facial features from normally developing children is a clear way to identify children diagnosed with ASD' - a considerably stronger claim than the cited morphometric literature supports. 'Normal children' is used in the conclusion as the contrast term. The most unfortunate formulation is in the abstract: 'early detection is crucial to help the parents and families in denial and superstition', which attributes diagnostic delay to parental denial and superstition rather than to the access barriers the same paper elsewhere identifies. Against this, the conclusion's framing of the problem is sympathetic and accurate - 'families often encounter difficulties in recognizing and understanding the symptoms of ASD, resulting in delays in seeking diagnosis and treatment' - and the accessibility argument that follows is the paper's best reasoning. No autistic person is reported as involved.

answers.title: Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children
answers.answer: Deficit-framed and, in one passage, seriously mischaracterising. Autism is 'a multifaceted neurological development disability' with 'deficits in social communication and emotion detection', and autistic children are described as 'noted for odd actions or hyper/hypo activity because of aggression, self-aggression, and stereotypical movements'. The most objectionable sentence conflates several distinct things: 'Individuals with a severe form of autism can erupt in dangerous outbursts caused by abnormal facial expressions associated with complex emotional states and mistreatment of autistic children'. Against this, two passages show genuine attention to autistic experience. The introduction observes that 'children with significant autism are non-verbal making it difficult for them to express or understand words' and that 'children who are unable to manage their feelings find it hard to express how they feel' - which frames the emotion-recognition task as serving communication rather than surveillance. And the paper's stated motivation for building a separate emotion model is the best reasoning in it: existing systems are 'primarily trained for healthy ones and consequently missing abnormal facial movements', so a model trained on autistic faces is needed. That is the correct diagnosis of a real problem, and one another study in this review confirms empirically by showing that affect models trained on neurotypical faces transfer poorly to autistic children.

answers.title: Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy
answers.answer: Plain and largely accurate, with one notable feature. Autism is 'a developmental disorder that affects how a person talks, interacts with others, and thinks and acts', and the description of the spectrum is correct - conditions 'that used to be called classic autism, Asperger's syndrome, and undefined pervasive developmental disability are now part of ASD. This spectrum shows how different people can have very different symptoms'. 'Normal' is used as the class label for non-autistic children, which is the least careful terminology choice. What sets the framing apart is the treatment of rising prevalence: the paper records the increase from 1 in 150 in the early 2000s to 1 in 36 in 2023 and attributes it correctly to 'changes in how autism is diagnosed, more people and healthcare professionals being aware of it, and better detection of autism across a wider range of ages' - an accurate account that most papers in this corpus replace with an alarm narrative. The Indonesian framing is also specific rather than generic, noting the scarcity of national statistics and the reliance on Ministry of Health reports and local studies. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person is reported as involved.

answers.title: Diagnosing autism spectrum disorder based on eye tracking technology using deep learning models
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children diagnosed with ASD, autism group, non-ASD, typically developing (TD) children. Diagnosis-first, deficit-oriented phrasing predominates: children with ASD typically have difficulty focusing, reduced attention to important stimuli, autism and non-autism profiles. There is no mention of autistic community perspectives, no identity-first alternative, and no acknowledgement that the sample carries clinical labels assigned by others.

answers.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Automated Machine Learning
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, ASD traits, autistic class, non-autistic class, children with autism, affected individuals. The introduction is unusually careful in one respect - it states that autism is not a sickness or disease but a lifelong neurological developmental disorder - and unusually careless elsewhere, describing symptoms as tiresome behaviors, deficits in public interactivity, and social disablement. The DSM-5 support levels are laid out at length, then never used. No autistic or community perspective is cited.

answers.title: Enhanced ASD detection using 3D facial landmark localization with convolutional shape appearance model and graph-randomized XGBoost
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autism spectrum disease, autism spectrum condition, ASD patients, affected persons, neurotypical youngsters, non-ASD. The framing is medical-pathological throughout, opening with autism spectrum disease is a neurological disease and treating the face as a biomarker of brain abnormality under the phrase the face predicts the brain. Autistic people are described as patients diagnosed with ASD who often behave in the same way. There is no engagement with autistic perspectives, and no acknowledgement that the study is inferring a neurodevelopmental condition from the appearance of children's faces.

answers.title: Enhanced multilevel autism classification for children using eye-tracking and hybrid CNN-RNN deep learning models
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, ASD children, autism applicants, participants, TD children, neurotypical. The paper is one of the few in the corpus to define neurotypical explicitly and to note that it refers to individuals whose neurological development conforms to societal norms and expectations - a formulation that recognises the norm as social rather than natural. Elsewhere the register slips (autism applicants as a table heading; the severity ladder low/mild/medium/high applied to children rather than to symptoms). The introduction is unusual in this corpus for framing the research motivation partly around reducing stigma, promoting inclusion, and improving educational and employment outcomes rather than solely around detection.

answers.title: Ensemble of Deep Learning with Crested Porcupine Optimizer Based Autism
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic children, autistic patients, individuals with ASD, normal controls, Normal class, typically developing children. The pathologising register is unusually strong even for this branch: autism is described as a set of intricate neuro-developmental brain diseases, the comparison class is labelled Normal throughout, and the stated benefit of early recognition is to aid families and parents in superstition and denial. Elsewhere autistic people are said to require treatment and reintegration. There is no autistic or community perspective anywhere in the article.

answers.title: Explainable and secure framework for autism prediction using multimodal eye tracking and kinematic data
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, individuals with ASD, autistic individuals, non-autistic individuals, ASD patients. The register is comparatively neutral for this corpus: the comparison group is called non-autistic rather than normal, autistic individuals is used alongside person-first phrasing, and the introduction notes that the spectrum makes each individual's experience unique. There is no autistic-community engagement and no discussion of how the people in the dataset were labelled or whether they knew their data would be reused.

answers.title: Facial Images Dataset for Early Screening of Autism Children Using Convolutional Neural Network
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with autism, autistic children, autistic condition, typically developing children, normal children, Normal class. The Normal/Autism class labelling runs throughout including in the figures and conclusion. One artefact of manuscript reuse is worth recording: the description of the testing workflow states that the output classifies the child as either a stunted child (label 1) or a normal child (label 0) - terminology from childhood stunting research that has no place in an autism study and that survived into the published text.

answers.title: Improving Early Autism Detection with Chi-Square Feature Selection, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, non-ASD, toddlers, children, ASD presentations. Register is clinical and restrained; the comparison class is called non-ASD rather than normal, and the limitations paragraph shows unusual awareness that ASD presentations vary across populations and cultural contexts. One phrase runs against this: the introduction describes ASD as a complex neuro-developmental abnormality. No autistic or community perspective is cited.

answers.title: Novel Framework for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification and Tailored Education With Effective Data Mining and Ensemble Learning Techniques
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic children, children with ASD, individuals affected by ASD, high-level and low-level autistic children, autism students. The abstract opens with a genuinely thoughtful observation - that ASD is highly diverse, each affected child is unique, no two autistic children are alike, and what benefits one child may not suit another - and the whole paper is then organised around assigning children to one of six teaching methods on the basis of a checklist total. The severity vocabulary (high-level, moderate-to-high, low-level autistic children) applies the label to the child rather than to support needs, and the framing describes ASD as having a primary origin that is genetic and as significantly affecting cognitive abilities and object recognition.

answers.title: Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autism traits, ASD traits, toddlers, individuals with ASD, controls, non-ASD individuals. The register is careful and the title is the most honest in this branch of the corpus: predicting autism traits, not diagnosing autism. ASD is described as a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition, controls rather than normals are used for the comparison class, and the stated motivation includes that incorrect diagnoses can have significant implications for families. One slip: the opening sentence calls ASD a complex neuropsychiatric developmental condition.

answers.title: Predicting autistic traits, anxiety and depression symptoms using camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (CAT-Q-ES): A machine learning study
answers.answer: Autistic adults, autistic individuals, neurodivergent, non-autistic, camouflaging, masking, neurotypical behavior. The framing is identity-first and community-aligned throughout: camouflaging is described as an adaptive social coping strategy rather than a symptom, the paper states explicitly that adapting one's behaviour in social contexts - whether to avoid discrimination or to achieve personal goals - is not inherently pathological and does not necessarily indicate autism, and it warns that mental health professionals should be aware of unintentional reinforcement of stigma and the pathologization of (mal)adaptive social strategies like social camouflaging. Non-binary participants are analysed as a group in their own right rather than dropped, and the paper states its reason for using self-reported gender rather than sex assigned at birth: it better reflects participants' identities. This is the only study in the charted corpus whose language would be recognised as respectful by the population it studies.

answers.title: A Computational Method for Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Deep Learning Approach
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic and non-autistic children, autistic individuals, ASD children, individuals with ASD and their families. The register is clinical and reasonably neutral - non-autistic rather than normal is used for the comparison class - though the opening sentence describes ASD as a complicated neurological disease and the introduction lists cognitive impairments among its defining characteristics. No autistic or community perspective appears.

answers.title: Early Detection of ASD from Facial Images Using DeepDeblur and Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic and non-autistic faces, autistic patients, children. The register is medical and dated: ASD is introduced as a neurodevelopmental disorder with ineffective brain functions and as a conventional developmental neuro-disorder, and deep learning is credited with developing interactive systems to assist in the reintegration and treatment of autistic patients. No autistic or community perspective appears.

answers.title: Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, individuals with ASD, patients, ASD traits, non-ASD. The register is clinical and generally neutral, with person-first phrasing throughout and an explicit concern for quality of life for individuals with ASD. The consistent use of patient for records in a downloaded Kaggle file - patient case identifiers, patient consent, patient information - is worth noting: it treats spreadsheet rows as clinical subjects while the study has no clinical relationship with any of them.

answers.title: Using explainable machine learning and eye-tracking for diagnosing autism spectrum and developmental language disorders in social attention tasks
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, developmental language disorder, neurodevelopmental disorders, typical development, children with ASD, clinical groups. The register is clinical and precise, using DSM-5 language (persistent deficits in social interaction and communication, repetitive and restrictive patterns) without editorialising. Groups are named by diagnosis rather than by normality - the comparison group is typically developing, never normal. There is no autistic-community engagement, but nothing in the language pathologises beyond the diagnostic criteria themselves.

answers.title: Utilizing deep learning models in an intelligent eye-tracking system for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, persons diagnosed with ASD, people without ASD, children with autism, characteristically emerging children, ASD children. The phrase characteristically emerging children appears to be a rewording of typically developing and, together with formulations like monotonous and stereotyped behaviors and the commonness of ASD, suggests heavy paraphrasing throughout. The register is otherwise clinical without being pejorative, and there is no autistic-community perspective.

answers.title: A novel hybrid deep learning model using MEResNext for autism spectrum disorder detection
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic individuals, individuals with ASD, patient, ASD patients. The register is medical and dated - autism is introduced as a neurological disease, individuals are described as needing the right treatment as soon as possible to recover their condition and diminish the disorder's effects. One passage is more sympathetic, noting that individuals with ASD have uniqueness and a few have incomparable ability in academics, music skills and visual. No autistic or community perspective appears.

answers.title: An assessment of autistic and parkinsonian movement profiles to inform selective classification algorithms
answers.answer: Autistic individuals, autistic adults, autistic movement, individuals with PD, control participants, non-autistic individuals. Identity-first language is used consistently and without hedging, movement differences are described as differences rather than deficits or abnormalities, and the framing throughout treats autistic movement as a characteristic to be measured rather than a pathology to be detected. The paper also cites the proposal that movement differences be added as specifiers to autism diagnoses - condition-relevant but non-selective - which is a precise and non-inflationary way of positioning the finding.

answers.title: An explainable deep learning framework for screening level autism severity using behavioural data
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, participants, developmental cohorts, severity strata. The register is technical and notably free of pathologising language for this corpus; severity is described in terms of DSM-5 functional-support levels rather than as degrees of impairment, and the paper avoids the diagnostic vocabulary its results cannot support. No autistic or community perspective appears.

answers.title: An explainable machine unlearning algorithm framework for early detection of autism spectrum disorder and brain disabilities in newborns
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, newborns, newborn babies, infants, children, brain disabilities, brain disorder. Autism is grouped throughout with brain disabilities and brain disorders as a single detection target, and the abstract describes ASD as a rising disorder in the brain among newborns. No autistic or community perspective appears. A distinct register intrudes in the results, where false positives are explained as occurring when the system flags safe/normal data as malicious or abnormal, and precision is explained in terms of how likely a nominated event is to be true when the model declares it malicious, fraudulent, or different from the expected behaviour - vocabulary from cybersecurity or fraud detection that has been carried into a paper about newborns.

answers.title: Deep learning based approach for Behavior classification in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder using naturalistic videos
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic children, ASD children, ASD youngsters, abnormal Behavioral patterns, stereotypical Behaviors, normal Behavior. The stereotyped/normal opposition is applied to movements rather than to children, which is the more defensible usage, but the framing describes self-stimulatory behaviours as abnormal throughout and the fourth class as normal. No autistic or community perspective appears, and there is no discussion of self-stimulatory behaviour as regulatory rather than pathological.

answers.title: Explainable Children Autism Detection using Gaze Features in Audio-Visual Speech Comprehension
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, typically developing children, TYP. The register is measured and clinical without pathologising; gaze differences are framed as attentional and perceptual patterns and as potential biomarkers rather than as deficits, and the comparison group is typically developing throughout. One inherited phrase from the literature review describes eye tracking as quantifying social attention deficits. There is no autistic or community perspective, but nothing in the language overstates.

answers.title: Explainable Ensemble Learning Framework for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Enhancing Trust, Interpretability and Reliability in AI-Driven Healthcare
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, ASD traits. The register is clinical and unremarkable; the framing is service-oriented, opening on the need for clinicians to trust AI tools and closing on healthcare trustworthiness. One sentence in the introduction overreaches in a way worth recording - that machine learning algorithms assess the likelihood of a child being diagnosed with autism from behavioural information, making them a suitable replacement for routine and expensive screening tests. No autistic or community perspective appears.

answers.title: Finding the forest in the trees: Using machine learning and online cognitive and perceptual measures to predict adult autism diagnosis
answers.answer: The most carefully handled in the entire corpus, and explicitly so. The paper inserts a parenthetical statement in its opening paragraph that it alternates between person-first and identity-first language to address the varying preferences of the international autism community, citing a published recommendation. Its terminology is consistently difference-based rather than deficit-based - behavioural differences, differences from the norms seen in the non-autistic population - and it justifies its choice of algorithm partly in those terms, noting that random forests capture any patterns that exist in the data and are therefore difference focused rather than deficit focused. It is the only study in the review to make a language decision explicitly, to cite community preference as the reason, and to connect that framing to a methodological choice.

answers.title: Hybrid ensemble learning for Autism Spectrum Disorder screening using eye-tracking scanpath
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, TD, individuals with ASD. The register is clinical and unremarkable; the opening characterisation uses deficits in social communication and the presence of restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, standard DSM phrasing. No autistic or community perspective appears, and no demographic or personal description of the participants is offered at any point.

answers.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Facial Images and AI-Based Deep Learning Models
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with autism, autistic, non-autistic. The introduction is unusually careful in one respect - it notes that while certain individuals with ASD may also experience cognitive impairment, the majority possess average to above-average intelligence, and that symptoms vary so that some face mild difficulties while others require full-time care. Elsewhere the register is standard for this branch. No autistic or community perspective appears.

answers.title: Multimodal fusion of deep transfer learning with wavelet neural network for autism spectrum disorder detection using facial images
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, individuals with ASD, children with ASD. The register is medical and dated - ASD is introduced as a complex psychological disease and later as a critical neurodevelopmental condition with excessive medical expenses - and the symptom list includes repetitive and aggressive behaviours, hyperactivity, and cognitive impairment. Grad-CAM++ is described as providing abnormality detection, which frames the highlighted facial regions as abnormalities rather than as model attention. No autistic or community perspective appears.

answers.title: SHAP-based explainable AI framework for autism severity classification using 3D motor biomarkers
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, typical development, moderate ASD, severe ASD. The register is clinical and neutral; motor differences are described as impairments in line with the cited literature, and severity terms are applied to groups rather than to children as labels. One artefact intrudes: the keyword list ends with violence level classification, evidently carried over from an unrelated manuscript.

answers.title: Screening autism spectrum
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, typically developing, delayed development. The register is neutral and the paper's framing is unusually ethics-forward: it argues that a major drawback of facial-image approaches is the invasion of privacy, especially for minors, and the need to collect their images over prolonged periods of their childhood, and that MRI-based approaches rely on invasive data collection raising ethical and privacy concerns. One phrase slips - facial features recorded at the onset of the disease - but the overall orientation treats the children's data as something requiring protection rather than as a resource.

answers.title: Towards screening of children students with autism spectrum disorder based on executive functions with serious game and machine learning approaches
answers.answer: ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, typically developing children, atypical and typical children, neurotypicals. The register is educational rather than clinical and the orientation is inclusive - the stated purpose is to let educators tailor teaching to individual needs and promote inclusive education, and the discussion warns against stigmatisation. One phrase dates the framing (ASD as a neuropsychiatric disorder), and the keyword list begins with Phishing, an artefact from an unrelated manuscript.

questions.short_title: Sample size, age, gender and matching
questions.question_text: What are the sample size, age range and mean/SD, and gender distribution per group, and are comparison groups matched on age and/or gender?

answers.title: Very early detection of Autism Spectrum Disorders based on acoustic analysis of pre-verbal vocalizations of 18-month old toddlers
answers.answer: ASD n=23, 15M/8F, age 18 +/- 0.42 months; controls n=20, 13M/7F, age 18 +/- 0.23 months. Controls explicitly described as age-matched; gender matching not claimed.

answers.title: Use of Machine Learning to Identify Children with Autism and Their Motor Abnormalities
answers.answer: ASD n=15, 3F/12M, chronological age 3;5 +/- 7.7 (2.8-4.6 yrs), IQ 75 +/- 13.4; TD n=15, 2F/13M, chronological age 2;6 +/- 5.2 (1.7-2.9 yrs), IQ 105 +/- 12.7. Matched on mental age (2;6 vs 2;7, n.s.) and gender-balanced, but NOT chronological-age matched (p<0.001) and IQ differed (p<0.001).

answers.title: ADHD and ASD Classification Based on Emotion Recognition Data
answers.answer: ASD n=18 (mean age 10.5), ADHD n=30 (mean 9.46), control n=13 (mean 9.22). No standard deviations, no age ranges, and no gender distribution for any group. No matching procedure and no statistical test of group comparability is reported. Class imbalance was handled after the fact by random oversampling to 30 per group.

answers.title: Identifying children with autism spectrum disorder based on their face processing abnormality: A machine learning framework
answers.answer: ASD n=29, 25M/4F, age 7.90 (1.45), NVIQ raw 22.29 (10.80), AQ 85.48 (14.90). TD-Age n=29, 25M/4F, age 7.86 (1.38), NVIQ 29.90 (9.96), AQ 62.74 (12.57). TD-Ability n=29, 25M/4F, age 5.74 (1.01), NVIQ 22.28 (7.90), AQ 64.03 (12.21). Age matching holds for TD-Age (t=0.09, n.s.) and ability matching holds for TD-Ability (t=0.00); sex ratio identical across all three groups. This double-matching design is stronger than most of the corpus.

answers.title: Semantic mapping reveals distinct patterns in descriptions of social relations in adults with autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: ASD n=27, 4 female / 23 male, age 34.80 (15.90), full-scale IQ 106.30 (16.30), verbal IQ 107.00 (17.00). Typical males n=45, age 27.70 (10.00), verbal IQ 117.00 (12.00); typical females n=87, age 22.80 (6.90), verbal IQ 116.00 (23.00). Matching is claimed on age and verbal IQ and no significant baseline difference was found by one-way ANOVA (except AQ), but the means differ substantially and the group sizes are very unequal (27 vs 132). Gender is markedly mismatched and in opposite directions - the authors acknowledge the ASD group's male preponderance and name the shortage of female ASD participants as a limitation. Adults only; no early-diagnosis relevance.

answers.title: Toward the Autism Motor Signature: Gesture patterns during smart tablet gameplay identify children with autism
answers.answer: Autism n=37 (12 female / 25 male), mean age 4 years 5 months (SD 11 months), range 3-6 years. Control n=45 (13 female / 32 male), mean age 4 years 7 months (SD 11 months). Explicitly both age-matched and gender-matched - one of relatively few corpus studies to match on both. Female representation (32%) is unusually high for this literature. Very young sample, directly relevant to early identification, though all children were already diagnosed.

answers.title: Applying machine learning to identify autistic adults using imitation: An exploratory study
answers.answer: ASC n=14 analysed (16 recruited), mean age 32 +/- 7.69 years, mean WASI IQ 118.5 +/- 12.02. Controls n=16, mean age 29.31 +/- 8.38, mean IQ 119.8 +/- 11. Age and IQ did not differ significantly (age t(28) = 0.7, p = 0.49; IQ t(28) = -0.31, p = 0.76) - so unusually for this corpus the groups are matched on IQ as well as age, and the matching is statistically verified rather than merely asserted. Sex matching is claimed but no male/female counts are given for either group. Adults only, so no early-diagnosis relevance. Both groups are high-IQ (mean ~119), which bounds generalisability considerably.

answers.title: Automatic Detection of ADHD and ASD from Expressive Behaviour in RGBD Data
answers.answer: Poorly reported. Total n=55 adults over 18. Group sizes are recoverable (18 control, 22 ASD only, 4 ADHD only, 11 comorbid) but only from the results tables. Median age per group and gender distribution per group are presented solely as bar charts (Figs. 2 and 3) with no numeric values, no standard deviations and no age range. No matching procedure, and no statistical test of age or gender comparability between groups, is reported. Adults only, so no early-diagnosis relevance.

answers.title: Earlier identification of children with autism
answers.answer: ASD n=10 (5 male, 5 female); TD n=10 (5 male, 5 female). All infants exactly 10 months old at recording, so age is matched by design with no variance. Gender is exactly balanced within and across groups, and the authors additionally describe the sample as family-language-balanced. This is one of the very few corpus studies with perfect sex balance - though at n=20 total it is also among the smallest. Highly relevant to early diagnosis: 10 months is the youngest recording age in the corpus, with outcome ascertained 26 months later.

answers.title: Speech-based Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Condition by Generative
answers.answer: Sample sizes are given (11 AD, 10 PDD-NOS, 13 SLI, 68 TD) but no age, no age range, no standard deviation and no gender distribution is reported anywhere in the paper. Matching is asserted - patients matched among themselves for age, sex, academic grades and lexical abilities, and TD children matched to patients for age and sex at a 2:1 ratio - but with no numbers and no statistical verification. Absence of any age data makes the study impossible to place in the early-diagnosis timeline.

answers.title: ANN and SVM Classifiers in Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorder Gait Based on Three-Dimensional Ground Reaction Forces
answers.answer: ASD n=30, mean age 8.63 +/- 2.16 years, height 1.29 +/- 0.14 m, mass 31.21 +/- 14.20 kg. TD n=30, mean age 9.52 +/- 1.96 years, height 1.27 +/- 0.13 m, mass 28.03 +/- 10.57 kg. No gender distribution is reported for either group, and no age matching is claimed or statistically tested despite a ~0.9-year mean difference - material for a gait study in children, where maturation changes force profiles. Height and body mass are reported, which is appropriate since GRF amplitudes are normalised to body weight, but the large mass SD in the ASD group (14.20 kg) is not discussed.

answers.title: Analyzing Human-Robot Interaction Using Machine Vision for Autism screening
answers.answer: ASD n=8, age range 2.1-4.1 years. TD n=8, age range 2.11-7.6 years. No means, no standard deviations, and no gender distribution for either group. The groups are not age-matched and the mismatch is substantial - the control range extends to 7.6 years while no autistic child was older than 4.1 - which is a serious confound for a measure based on where a child physically positions themselves relative to a robot, since approach behaviour, mobility and social confidence all change markedly between age 2 and age 7. Very young sample, so relevant in principle to early screening.

answers.title: Applying Eye Tracking to Identify Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children
answers.answer: ASD n=37, 33 boys / 4 girls, age 4.6 +/- 0.7 years, CARS 34.4 +/- 7.8. TD n=37, 27 boys / 10 girls, age 4.8 +/- 0.4 years. Age matched by design with no significant difference (p = 0.17), and gender difference non-significant by chi-square (p = 0.14) - though the actual distributions are 89% versus 73% male, so the matching is statistically defensible rather than close. Narrow 4-6 year age band by inclusion criterion, directly relevant to early screening but, as the authors note, leaving open whether the finding generalises to younger children.

answers.title: Automatic Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Everyday
answers.answer: This is the study's weakest reporting. Sample sizes are clear (18 ASD, 9 TD, 8 at-risk) and every subject's individual age, gender and diagnosis is listed in Table 1, but no group-level age mean, SD or gender distribution is computed anywhere, and no matching or comparability test is performed. Ages span 3 months to 17 years at recruitment. Inspecting Table 1, the ASD group includes children aged 2, 3 and 4 years while the TD group includes 16-year-olds, so the groups are grossly unmatched on age - a decisive confound for acoustic voice features, which change dramatically across childhood and adolescence.

answers.title: Detecting Autism Based on Eye-Tracking Data from Web Searching
answers.answer: ASD n=15 analysed (9 male, 6 female), mean age 37 +/- 9.14 years, mean 16 +/- 3.33 years of formal education. Control n=15 analysed (8 male, 7 female), mean age 33.66 +/- 8.6 years, mean 18.35 +/- 2.47 years of formal education. No formal matching procedure or comparability test is reported, though age and gender are close in practice. At 40% and 47% female, this is by a wide margin the most gender-balanced sample in the corpus - most comparable studies are 80-90% male. Adults only, and the authors explicitly acknowledge that web tasks are unsuitable for the young children where early detection would matter most. Education differs by about 2.3 years in the controls' favour, which is not discussed.

answers.title: Video Gesture Analysis for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
answers.answer: ASD n=20 (18 male, 2 female), age 9.8 +/- 1.5 years, WISC-IV Full Scale IQ 98.5 +/- 11.1. TD n=20 (16 male, 4 female), age 9.5 +/- 1.5 years, Full Scale IQ 102.8 +/- 9.4. Matching is verified statistically on both age (t38 = -0.665, p = 0.510) and IQ (t38 = 1.325, p = 0.193), and gender is matched by design. This is among the best-matched samples in the corpus - age, gender and IQ all matched with tests reported - though both groups are male-dominated (90% and 80%) and the ASD group is restricted to children without intellectual impairment.

answers.title: A Novel Eye Movement Data Transformation Technique that Preserves Temporal Information: A Demonstration in a Face Processing Task
answers.answer: ASD n=21 (2 female, 10%), mean age 16.27, range 11-29, mean full-scale IQ 109.4. TD n=23 (5 female, 22%), mean age 16.31, range 10-21, mean full-scale IQ 112.3. Groups are described as age- and IQ-matched and the means are indeed near-identical, though the ASD age range extends to 29 while no control exceeded 21, and no standard deviations or formal comparison tests are reported. All participants had full-scale IQ above 85, so the sample is restricted to average-or-above intellectual ability. Both groups are heavily male. Adolescents and adults, so no early-diagnosis relevance.

answers.title: Applying Machine Learning to Identify Autism With Restricted Kinematic Features
answers.answer: ASD n=20, TD n=23, described as age-matched with an inclusion range of 6-13 years. Demographic details including ages and sexes are presented in Table 1, which is not recoverable from the extracted text, so exact means, standard deviations and sex ratios cannot be charted here. Non-verbal IQ was assessed with Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices as an inclusion criterion (average ability required) but the values are likewise in the unrecoverable table. Age matching is claimed and a demographic comparison is tabulated, which is better practice than most of the corpus.

answers.title: Automatic Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Acoustic and Text Features from Brief Natural Conversations
answers.answer: ASD n=35, mean age 11.42 +/- 2.51, full-scale IQ 105.51, verbal IQ 104.97, non-verbal IQ 104.63. TD n=35, mean age 10.57 +/- 2.82, full-scale IQ 107.14, verbal IQ 105.83, non-verbal IQ 105.97. Age difference non-significant (t=1.33, p=0.19); IQ differences non-significant on all three measures (p=0.6, 0.78, 0.68); sex ratio matched by design and non-significant (chi-square=0.06, p=0.8). This is among the best-matched samples in the corpus - matched and tested on full-scale, verbal and non-verbal IQ as well as sex. The one defect is that the printed sex counts ('13 f., 12 m.' and '11 f., 14 m.') sum to 25 rather than the stated 35 per group.

answers.title: Classifying Individuals with ASD Through Facial Emotion Recognition and Eye-Tracking
answers.answer: ASD n=23 (20 male, 87%), age 12.74 +/- 2.45 years, range 8-17, IQ range 58-137. TD n=35 (25 male, 71%), age 14.11 +/- 5.09 years, range 8-34. Neither age nor sex was matched by design, but both differences were tested and found non-significant (p=0.241 and p=0.171). The control age range nonetheless extends to 34 while no autistic participant exceeded 17, so the groups differ substantially in composition even though means do not differ significantly - the control SD is more than double the ASD SD. IQ is given only as a range for the ASD group with no control values and no use as a covariate.

answers.title: Detecting Developmental Delay and Autism Through Machine
answers.answer: ASD n=50 (36 male, 72%), mean age 2.51 (0.70) years. SLC n=50 (31 male, 46%), mean age 2.73 (0.51). TD n=50 (23 male, printed as 62% though the count implies 46%), mean age 2.40 (0.59). Ages are close across groups but no matching or comparability testing is reported. Sex is substantially imbalanced between the two clinical groups (72% versus 46% male), which is a material confound for the ASD-versus-SLC layer. The demographic table also shows a marked socioeconomic gradient: 96% of ASD families earned over 30,000 taka versus 80% of SLC and only 26% of TD families, and 100% of ASD and TD families were urban versus 78% of SLC. Very young sample (18 months to 4 years), directly relevant to early detection.

answers.title: Exploiting Visual Behaviour for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification
answers.answer: Not reported at any level. No sample sizes, no ages, no age ranges, no standard deviations, no gender distribution, and no matching information for either group. The authors state explicitly that age 'is not available in the given dataset' and treat this as a substantive limitation on their model, since they cite evidence that ASD fixation behaviour differs markedly between toddlers, young children and grown-up children. This is the least participant-characterised study in the corpus so far.

answers.title: Hierarchical POMDP Framework for a Robot-Assisted ASD Diagnostic Protocol
answers.answer: Only group sizes are reported: 8 ASD and 7 typically developing preschool children, matched by mental age. No chronological ages, no age ranges, no standard deviations, and gender is explicitly disregarded - 'Gender was not considered'. Mental-age matching is claimed but no values or comparison are given. The research targets ages 2-6, so the sample is directly relevant to early diagnosis, but nothing about its composition can be verified.

answers.title: Intelligent Gaze-Based Screening System for Autism
answers.answer: Nothing is reported. No sample sizes, no ages, no age range, no standard deviations, no gender distribution and no matching information for either group. The paper's motivation depends on early screening before age 2, but the age of the children actually tested is never stated, so it cannot be established whether the system was evaluated in the population it targets.

answers.title: Kinematic features of a simple and short movement task to predict autism diagnosis
answers.answer: ASC n=24 (9 female, 37.5%), mean age 31.5 years. TD n=22 (7 female, 31.8%), mean age 30.8 years. Groups are stated to be IQ matched, but no IQ values, no age standard deviations, no age ranges and no statistical comparisons are reported. Female representation is comparatively high for this literature. Adults only, so no early-diagnosis relevance.

answers.title: Learning to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder based on the Visual
answers.answer: Reported only at whole-sample level: 59 children, 38 male (64%) and 21 female (36%), mean age 7.88 years and median 8.1 years, with age and CARS distributions shown as box plots. No per-group age means, standard deviations, ranges or sex breakdowns are given, and no matching procedure or comparability test is reported. This makes it impossible to assess whether the ASD and non-ASD groups differ in age or sex - a material gap since gaze behaviour changes markedly across childhood. The sample is school-aged (around 8 years), so despite the paper's early-detection framing it does not test the youngest ages.

answers.title: Machine Learning to Study Social Interaction Difficulties in ASD
answers.answer: Only the group sizes are reported in this paper: 29 autistic and 29 typically developed adults. No ages, no age ranges, no standard deviations, no sex distribution, and no matching information or comparability testing - all deferred to a companion manuscript described as under revision. For a Perspective article this is understandable, but it means the classification result cannot be assessed for demographic confounding from this paper alone. Adults only, so no early-diagnosis relevance.

answers.title: Phase 3 diagnostic evaluation of a smart
answers.answer: Not reportable, since no participants had been analysed. The design nonetheless specifies more clinical characterisation than almost any completed study in this corpus: parents of children in both clinical cohorts complete the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, the ESSENCE Questionnaire, and either the Adaptive Behavior Assessment System-3 or the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales-II, so behavioural difficulties, neurodevelopmental symptom breadth and adaptive functioning will all be available alongside the diagnostic label. The pilot study on which the trial builds used age- and gender-matched controls, and the age window is tightly bounded at 30 months to 5 years 11 months.

answers.title: Predicting Autism Diagnosis using Image with Fixations and Synthetic Saccade Patterns
answers.answer: Sparse. 14 ASD and 14 TD children viewed each of 300 images, but the number of distinct children is not reported. Age is given only for the ASD group: 5 to 12 years, mean 8. No control age data, no gender data for either group, no matching procedure and no comparability testing. Given that gaze behaviour changes substantially between ages 5 and 12, and that no control ages are reported at all, demographic confounding cannot be assessed.

answers.title: Recognition Of Atypical Behavior In Autism Diagnosis From Video Using Pose Estimation Over Time
answers.answer: Nothing reported. No participant counts, no ages, no age ranges, no gender distribution, no matching information, and no diagnostic breakdown. The only quantitative description of the corpus is at video and time-stamp level: four sets comprising 235, 101, 177 and 42 video clips (555 total) yielding 4465, 2048, 1545 and 291 time stamps (8349 total), split 3084 typical and 5265 atypical. Since the number of contributing children is never stated, even the ratio of episodes to participants is unknown.

answers.title: Robot-Assisted Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Based on Artificial Reasoning
answers.answer: Age and sex are reported at the level the sample allows - a 36-to-48-month band and a five-boys-one-girl composition - and nothing else. No cognitive, language, adaptive, socioeconomic or comorbidity measure was obtained, which in three-year-olds means that any behavioural difference between the groups could reflect general developmental level rather than autism risk. The absence matters particularly for the reported finding, since initiation of joint attention develops rapidly across this age range and neither group's developmental level is characterised. The risk factors that define the index group are also not enumerated, so what distinguishes the two groups is not stated in any measurable form.

answers.title: SP-ASDNet: CNN-LSTM Based ASD Classification Model using Observer ScanPaths
answers.answer: Nothing reported. No participant counts beyond 14 viewers per image per group, no ages, no age ranges, no standard deviations, no gender distribution, and no matching or comparability information for either group. The paper notes that scanpath counts per image vary because some children looked outside the image, but gives no participant-level accounting.

answers.title: Social robot in diagnosis of autism among preschool children
answers.answer: Not reported. The retrieved text gives no sample size, age, sex, cognitive level, language ability, socioeconomic background or comorbidity information for the participating children. For a paired within-subject design the omissions are less damaging than they would be in a group comparison - the contrast being tested is internal to each child, so demographic differences cannot confound it - but they prevent any statement about which children the finding applies to, and they leave developmental level unmeasured in a study whose construct is spontaneous imitation of a robot.

answers.title: Application of the Still-Face Paradigm in Early Screening for High-Risk Autism Spectrum Disorder in Infants and Toddlers
answers.answer: High-risk: n = 45, 40 male / 5 female (11% female), mean age 19.71 +/- 3.43 months. Typically developing: n = 43, 32 male / 11 female (26% female), mean age 16.40 +/- 4.70 months. The age difference is significant (t = 3.80, p < 0.01) and is the authors' first stated limitation, with the explicit rationale that matching on age would unmatch developmental level. Gesell developmental quotients differ significantly on adaptive (80.29 vs 92.98), fine motor (86.64 vs 93.70), language (60.84 vs 86.51) and personal-social (78.80 vs 92.28) domains; only gross motor is comparable (92.02 vs 92.77). Sex distributions were nominally matched by design with a non-significant chi-square (p = 0.08) but differ visibly. All participants are from the Nanjing area of China, with no ethnicity or socioeconomic reporting.

answers.title: Applying Machine Learning to Kinematic and Eye Movement Features of a Movement Imitation Task to Predict Autism Diagnosis
answers.answer: Development sample: 15 autistic (3 female, 12 male), mean age 33.1, mean IQ 122.0; 15 non-autistic (3 female, 12 male), mean age 32.2, mean IQ 124.8. Age p = 0.73, IQ p = 0.51. Independent test sample: 7 autistic (4 female, 3 male), mean age 28.16, mean IQ 122.14; 7 non-autistic (4 female, 3 male), mean age 27.90, mean IQ 126.29. Age p = 0.95, IQ p = 0.46. Groups are matched for age, gender, handedness and IQ within each sample, with all comparisons tested and reported - unusually thorough. The two samples differ in sex composition (20% female in development versus 57% in testing) and marginally in age (p = 0.06), which the authors flag explicitly and turn into a strength: generalisation held despite the demographic shift. Both samples are high-IQ (means 122-126) adults, which bounds the population addressed.

answers.title: Research and Design of Autism Smart Diagnosis Information System Based on Chinese Children's Facial Expression Data and Deep Convolution Neural Network
answers.answer: Autistic group: 10 children, 5 boys and 5 girls, aged 3-6, recruited through Guangzhou Children's Care Center. Control group: 10 children, 5 boys and 5 girls, aged 5-8, recruited through Amy Education School in Zhengzhou. Sex is balanced within and across groups, which is unusual for this corpus. Age is not: the ranges barely overlap and the autistic children are systematically younger, which matters because facial expression production, imitation compliance and attention to a screen prompt all change substantially between 3 and 8 years. Recruitment site is fully confounded with group. No means, standard deviations, IQ, developmental level, ethnicity or socioeconomic information is reported for either group.

answers.title: Automated identification of postural control for children with autism spectrum disorder using a machine learning approach
answers.answer: ASD n=25 (14 female, 11 male), age 6.9 (1.8) years, body mass 32.7 (11.5) kg, height 126 (13) cm. TD n=25 (10 female, 15 male), age 7.2 (2.0) years, body mass 30.3 (12.4) kg, height 128 (12) cm. Recruitment range 5-12 years. Groups are explicitly age-matched with near-identical means and overlapping standard deviations, and anthropometrics are reported and closely comparable - which matters for postural measures since body mass and height affect sway. Sex is not matched, with the ASD group 56% female against 40% in controls, but both proportions are far higher than the corpus norm, making this one of very few studies here where autistic girls are well represented. Sample size is justified by an a priori power analysis (power 0.80) against previously published postural sway data, indicating 10-13 per group would suffice for the group comparison, with the larger n=25 chosen because 'a larger sample size will improve the accuracy and success of machine learning classifiers'.

answers.title: Behavior-based Risk Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through
answers.answer: ASD n=5 (all male), mean age 8.2 +/- 1.10 years. TD n=7 (all male), mean age 7.43 +/- 2.30 years. Overall age range 5-10 years. No matching procedure or comparability test is reported; the group means differ by about 0.8 years and the control group's standard deviation is more than double the ASD group's. Both groups are exclusively male, which the authors explicitly list as a limitation - 'the inclusion of a single gender' - making this one of the few corpus studies to name sex homogeneity as a limitation rather than leave it unremarked. Total interaction time is reported per group (3931 s TD, 3442 s ASD), described as making the datasets comparable in size.

answers.title: Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation as a Scalable Method for Distinguishing Children With Autism
answers.answer: 27 ASC and 21 TD children aged 8-12 years. Participant characteristics including means, standard deviations, ranges and group comparison test statistics are presented in Table 1, but the values are not recoverable from the extracted text, so age and sex matching cannot be independently verified in this charting. IQ is controlled by inclusion criterion - full-scale IQ of at least 80 or at least one WISC-V index score of at least 80 - which restricts the sample to children of broadly average or above cognitive ability. General motor ability was additionally measured with the Movement Assessment Battery for Children-2 specifically 'to account for autism-associated differences in general motor abilities', which is an unusually thoughtful covariate choice for an imitation study since it separates imitation-specific from general motor difficulty.

answers.title: Deep-Learning-Based Detection of Infants with Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Auto-Encoder Feature Representation
answers.answer: Autistic group: n = 10, 4 male / 6 female, mean age 19.20 +/- 2.52 months, all aged 12-24 months. Typically developing group: n = 29, 19 male / 10 female, mean age 14.72 +/- 2.45 months, all aged 6-18 months. Age separation is near-total: every infant in the 6-12 month band is TD and every infant in the 18-24 month band is ASD, with overlap confined to the 12-18 month band. The sex ratio is inverted relative to autism's usual epidemiology (40% male in the autistic group versus 66% in the TD group) and is not addressed. Country and site are single (South Korea, SNUBH); no socioeconomic or ethnicity data. Per-infant age, sex, initial diagnosis date and definite final diagnosis date are tabulated for all 39 participants, which is unusually transparent. Note that the running text states the ASD mean age as 14.72 months, contradicting the table - an apparent transposition with the TD figure.

answers.title: Effects of Intra-Subject Variation in Gait Analysis on ASD Classification Performance in Machine Learning Models
answers.answer: None reported. The paper gives group sizes (12 autistic, 9 typically developed) and nothing else: no ages, no age ranges, no sex distribution, no ethnicity, no socioeconomic information, no country of collection, and no statement about matching on any variable. This is the least participant characterisation of any included study in the corpus, and it means the reported group difference cannot be attributed to autism rather than to age, sex, height, leg length or any other determinant of gait timing - all of which the eight features measure directly.

answers.title: Estimating Autism Severity in Young Children From Speech Signals Using a Deep Neural Network
answers.answer: Group sizes and diagnostic composition are given (56 ASD, 10 other diagnoses, 6 TD) and ADOS module distribution is reported (toddler module 10, module 1 19, module 2 31, module 3 12), indicating a young cohort spanning a wide language-ability range. Ages and sexes were tabulated in Tables 1 and 4 but those tables did not survive text extraction, so the numbers cannot be reported here. What can be established is that age was handled analytically rather than by matching: age was correlated against all 60 features and found to relate mainly to vocalisation rate, duration and count, with little overlap with the features predicting severity, and train and test sets were matched on age and behavioural characteristics. All participants are Hebrew-speaking children assessed at a single Israeli centre; no ethnicity or socioeconomic reporting.

answers.title: Detecting High-Functioning Autism in Adults Using Eye Tracking and Machine Learning
answers.answer: Group sizes and exclusions are fully itemised, and functional and educational characteristics are reported in unusual detail: all participants were highly independent adults with no caregiver; 20 autistic participants were employed or in higher education and 8 lived independently on disability benefits; among the autistic group 8 had completed high school, 8 held bachelor's and 3 master's degrees, against 3, 10 and 5 plus one PhD in the control group. All but one participant used the web daily. Ages and sex distributions were tabulated in Table I but that table did not survive extraction. The visible education imbalance favouring controls is not adjusted for, and matters for tasks that are fundamentally reading and information-search tasks. Ethnicity and socioeconomic status are not reported; recruitment was from Wolverhampton and Birmingham.

answers.title: Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder via an Eye-Tracking Based
answers.answer: Autistic group: n = 31, aged 1.8-8 years, mean 4.67 +/- 1.59. Typically developing group: n = 43, aged 2.5-7 years, mean 4.15 +/- 0.98. Age is reported but not tested: the means differ by about half a year, the spreads differ substantially (SD 1.59 versus 0.98), and the ranges are asymmetric, with only the autistic group including children under 2.5 or over 7. Free-viewing behaviour changes rapidly across 2-8 years, and age is not entered into or controlled by the model.
