Sex is not reported at all for either group, nor is IQ, developmental level, socioeconomic status or ethnicity. All participants are from Xi'an.

answers.title: Machine Learning and Virtual Reality on Body Movements' Behaviors to Classify Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: Autistic group: n = 24, 21 male and 3 female (87.5% male), mean age 5.13 +/- 1.35 years. Typically developing group: n = 25, 16 male and 9 female (64% male), mean age 4.86 +/- 0.91 years. Overall range 4-7 years. The age difference is small but untested and the spreads differ. The sex imbalance is substantial and unaddressed, which matters because the dependent variable is body movement magnitude. Critically, the authors state plainly that 'the experimental groups were not matched on measures related to the intelligence quotient performance, cognitive abilities, and motor comorbidities (e.g., dyspraxia)' and that this limits confidence that the observed differences are attributable to autism. No ethnicity or socioeconomic reporting; single site in Valencia.

answers.title: Responsive Social Smile: A Machine-Learning Based Multimodal Behavior Assessment Framework towards Early Stage Autism Screening
answers.answer: Reported only for the pooled cohort: 41 children aged 12-32 months, mean 23.34 months, 33 boys and 8 girls. No group-wise ages, standard deviations, sex splits or matching tests are given, and an age-by-diagnosis figure is shown but its values are not tabulated. This is a material gap: with a 12-32 month range, responsive social smiling to scripted verbal prompts changes substantially with age, so an age difference between groups would directly produce the observed effect. The authors note the 4:1 male:female ratio matches autism epidemiology, which speaks to representativeness but not to between-group balance. No IQ, developmental, socioeconomic or ethnicity data; single site in Guangzhou.

answers.title: Selection of Eye-Tracking Stimuli for Prediction by Sparsely Grouped Input Variables for Neural Networks: towards Biomarker Refinement for Autism
answers.answer: Reported for the whole cohort only: 64 children, mean age 76.32 +/- 16.3 months (about 6.4 years), 43 male and 21 female. Group-wise ages and sexes are not tabulated; the paper states there is 'no significant difference for age and sex between the ASD and non-ASD population' without giving means or test statistics. Stanford-Binet IQ was obtained for all participants, which is unusual and important, though group-wise IQ is likewise not reported - a notable gap given that IQ turned out to be the one clinical variable the eye-tracking features could predict. No ethnicity or socioeconomic reporting. The authors flag that findings 'may reflect developmental properties of ASD specific to the school-age period'.

answers.title: The identification of children with autism spectrum disorder by SVM approach on EEG and eye-tracking data
answers.answer: Autistic group: n = 49, 39 male and 10 female, mean age 4.29 +/- 1.07 years. Typically developing: n = 48, 36 male and 12 female, mean age 4.26 +/- 1.00 years. The authors state there were no statistical differences in age or gender between groups, and the reported means and SDs bear that out - this is among the best-matched pairs in the corpus, on the two variables most likely to confound gaze during face viewing at this age. Both groups span 3-6 years. No IQ, developmental level, socioeconomic or ethnicity data; recruitment routes differ between groups (clinical for autism, a local kindergarten for controls), which is not addressed.

answers.title: Toward Continuous Social Phenotyping: Analyzing Gaze Patterns in an Emotion Recognition Task for Children With Autism Through Wearable Smart Glasses
answers.answer: Autistic group: n = 16, 13 male (81%) and 3 female, mean age 12.13 +/- 3.31 years, range 6-17; SCQ 18.86 +/- 6.43; ABIQ 102.75 +/- 19.54 (range 55-133); SRS-2 total 78.85 +/- 11.13. Neurotypical group: n = 17, 9 male (53%) and 8 female, mean age 11.53 +/- 2.48, range 8-17; SCQ 1.82 +/- 1.07; ABIQ 108.94 +/- 9.58 (91-129); SRS-2 total 44.41 +/- 8.11. Comorbidities and current medications are itemised for the 11 autistic participants who completed the survey - methylphenidate in 3, sertraline in 2, and single instances of arginine vasopressin, guanfacine, carbamazepine, aripiprazole and dexmethylphenidate, with only 4 of 11 unmedicated against 15 of 17 controls. This is the most complete participant characterisation in the corpus. The sex imbalance (81% versus 53% male) is named by the authors as a limitation, and the ABIQ distribution shows the autistic cohort is predominantly high-functioning with wider spread than controls.

answers.title: Towards the automatic detection of social biomarkers in autism spectrum disorder: introducing the simulated interaction task (SIT)
answers.answer: Autistic group: n = 37, 18 female (49%), mean age 36.89 years, range 22-62. Control group: n = 43, 22 female (51%), mean age 33.14 years, range 18-49. The sex balance is the most striking feature - essentially even in both groups, against the 4:1 male predominance typical of autism cohorts including most in this corpus - and it enables the paper's per-gender analysis showing better detection of women (33 of 39 versus 25 of 40, p = 0.048), which the authors interpret through the finding that women require more severe symptoms to receive a diagnosis. Age is not matched, with the autistic group 3.75 years older and extending 13 years further, and the classifier demonstrably picks this up (class probability correlated with age at rs = 0.35, p = 0.001). Verbal intelligence was confirmed sufficient by the Wortschatztest but no IQ values are reported. No ethnicity or socioeconomic data; single clinic recruitment.

answers.title: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence to Diagnose Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Tracking Saccades
answers.answer: None reported. The entire participant description is 'a total of 65 participants with ASD and 43 with no autism present; these were closely related in terms of patients of similar ages and genders'. No ages, no age ranges, no sex counts, no ethnicity, no socioeconomic information, no country, no recruitment route and no statistical test of the asserted matching. This is the least participant characterisation of any included study in the corpus. It matters directly here because saccade latency, peak velocity and accuracy all change substantially across childhood and adolescence, so an unreported age difference would reproduce every group difference the paper describes.

answers.title: An Experimental Trial: Multi-Robot Therapy for Categorization of Autism Level Using Hidden Markov Model
answers.answer: Twelve children, 11 male and 1 female, aged 4.2 to 7.5 years with a mean of 6.5 and standard deviation 0.98, described as of Asian background. Per-child age, sex, autism type and mean joint attention and imitation performance are tabulated individually, which is good practice and is what makes the internal inconsistency between the tables detectable. No IQ, language, adaptive functioning, comorbidity or socioeconomic information. The sex ratio of 11:1 is more extreme than population estimates and the single girl is in the test set. Age is not related to performance anywhere in the analysis despite a 3.3-year span across which joint attention and imitation both develop substantially.

answers.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis Based on Trajectories of Eye Tracking Data
answers.answer: Autistic group: 56 participants, 38 male and 18 female, aged 5-18 with mean 10. Typically developing: 30 participants, 20 male and 10 female, aged 3-15 with mean 10. Means match exactly and sex proportions are close (68% versus 67% male), but the age ranges differ at both ends, no standard deviations are given, and no statistical test of matching is reported. The age span is wide - 3 to 18 years - across which gaze-following and anticipation in joint attention change substantially, and age is neither modelled nor controlled. CARS scores are reported for both groups (33-45, mean 34.5 for autism; below 30 for typical development), which is more clinical detail than most of the corpus provides. No IQ, language, comorbidity, ethnicity or socioeconomic data.

answers.title: Autistic spectrum traits detection and early screening: A machine learning based eye movement study
answers.answer: Preliminary experiment: 107 adults, 49 women and 58 men, mean age 24.84 +/- 5.24 years, mean AQ 21.0 +/- 5.2. The two label groups are closely matched - 25 women and 30 men at 24.7 +/- 5.2 years versus 24 women and 28 men at 25.0 +/- 5.3 - which is good practice, although the reported group AQ means of 16.6 for the high-trait group and 25.7 for the low-trait group are transposed relative to their labels. Test experiment: 22 participants, all male, mean age 12.68 +/- 7.61 years, with no age range, AQ, IQ, severity, comorbidity or socioeconomic data. The demographic gulf between the two samples is the study's central design flaw and is never addressed.

answers.title: Automatic classification of children with autism spectrum disorder by using a computerized visual‐orienting task
answers.answer: Typically developing: 24 children, 18 male and 6 female, 5.24 +/- 0.81 years, Raven raw 22.17 +/- 9.03, PPVT raw 80.38 +/- 30.16, SCQ 8.50 +/- 5.13. High-functioning autistic: 26 children, 23 male and 3 female, 5.08 +/- 0.83 years, Raven 20.77 +/- 10.83, PPVT 77.44 +/- 22.39, SCQ 12.23 +/- 6.92. Low-functioning autistic: 24 children, 19 male and 5 female, 4.98 +/- 1.09 years, Raven 11.00 +/- 2.00, PPVT 22.88 +/- 12.30, SCQ 17.32 +/- 5.23. All three groups are age-matched with no significant pairwise differences, and the high-functioning and typically developing groups are additionally matched on both nonverbal intelligence (t(48) = -.49, p = .624) and verbal intelligence (t(46) = -.95, p = .356) - so the critical contrast is IQ-controlled, which almost no other study in this corpus achieves. Sex proportions differ (75%, 88%, 79% male) and are not tested; the authors name this as a limitation. No ethnicity or socioeconomic data; recruitment from a Beijing specialised preschool for the clinical groups.

answers.title: Auxiliary Diagnostic Method for Early Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Movement Data Analysis
answers.answer: Autistic group: 39 children, 29 boys and 10 girls, aged 4-10. Comparison group: 53 children, 27 boys and 26 girls, aged 2-15. No means, standard deviations, matching statement or statistical test is reported for either variable. Both differences are substantial: the comparison group is 51% male against 74%, and its age range brackets the clinical group at both ends, including children five years younger and five years older than any autistic participant. For a six-minute passive-viewing task with an abstract point-light stimulus, where the strongest feature is failure to maintain trackable gaze, an age spread from 2 to 15 years in one group only is a first-order confound. No IQ, language, severity, comorbidity or socioeconomic data.

answers.title: Children ASD Evaluation Through Joint Analysis of EEG and Eye-Tracking Recordings With Graph Convolution Network
answers.answer: Almost nothing. Two groups of 21 children aged between 3 and 6, with the single sentence 'No statistical differences in age and gender are observed between ASD and TD groups' offered in place of any figures - no means, standard deviations, sex counts or test statistics for either variable. For a study whose gaze features are cumulative fixation durations during face and social viewing, and whose EEG features include entropy measures that change substantially across early childhood, a three-year age band with no distributional information is a material gap. No IQ, language, severity, comorbidity, ethnicity or socioeconomic data.

answers.title: Classification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Using Eye Tracking Data Based on Visual Attention Model
answers.answer: Non-severe group: 49 participants, 27 male and 22 female, aged 3-16 with mean 8.8 +/- 3.2, CARS 30-36 with mean 33.1 +/- 2.0. Severe group: 39 participants, 12 male and 27 female, aged 3-16 with mean 8.7 +/- 3.9, CARS 36.5-46.5 with mean 39.4 +/- 2.6. Age is well matched (p = 0.900) with identical ranges. Sex is not: 55% male against 31%, p = 0.02, so the severe group is majority female against a population sex ratio of roughly 3:1 male. The authors engage with this substantively, citing literature both supporting and contesting greater severity in autistic females and noting that the ratio falls to 2:1 when restricted to low-functioning or intellectually disabled subgroups - but they do not adjust for sex in the model. Vineland scores were significantly lower in the severe group (p = 0.0006) while Repetitive Behavior Scale scores did not differ (p = 0.104). No IQ data, which the authors identify as a limitation.

answers.title: Classification of Children With Autism and Typical Development Using Eye-Tracking Data From Face-to-Face Conversations: Machine Learning Model Development and Performance Evaluation
answers.answer: Autistic group: 19 analysed, 17 male and 2 female, mean age 99.6 +/- 25.1 months, mean IQ 100.8 +/- 22.7. Typically developing group: 20 analysed, 17 male and 3 female, mean age 108.8 +/- 27.0 months, mean IQ 116.1 +/- 22.7. Age (p = .28) and sex ratio (p = .68) are well matched and formally tested. IQ is not - the groups differ by 15.3 points (p = .02) - and this is reported in the demographic table but not adjusted for anywhere in the modelling, which matters given that the single most informative feature is how long a child took to complete a conversation. Only four girls participated in total, which the authors name as a limitation with the specific rationale that autistic males and females differ in behavioural presentation, cognitive domains and emotions. No ethnicity or socioeconomic data.

answers.title: Combined Signal Processing Based Techniques and Feed Forward Neural Networks for Pathological Voice Detection and Classification
answers.answer: Almost none. Nineteen children aged 5-14, with sex counts by group but no ages, means, standard deviations or matching test for any group. The 5-14 range is the critical gap: fundamental frequency, jitter, shimmer and formant structure all change substantially across childhood and pubertal onset falls inside this window, so any group age difference would directly produce the acoustic differences the classifier exploits. Sex is likewise a primary determinant of these features and is balanced only by count across very small groups. No IQ, severity, comorbidity, language ability, socioeconomic or recruitment information.

answers.title: Computer-Aided Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Eye-Tracking Study Using Data Visualization and Deep Learning
answers.answer: Autistic group: 29 children, 19 male, chronological age 7 years 7 months (SD 2 years 6 months), CARS 32.9 +/- 6.4, ECSP total 141.1 +/- 50.3. Non-autistic group: 30 children, 19 male, chronological age 8 years 0 months (SD 2 years 8 months), CARS exactly 15 with zero variance, ECSP total 139.18 +/- 49.5. Ages and sex ratios are closely comparable though no test is reported. Two features of the clinical data deserve note: the non-autistic group's CARS of 15 with zero standard deviation is the instrument's floor, so the measure carries no within-group variance; and ECSP developmental ages of approximately 23-24 months in both groups reflect a ceiling effect of an instrument designed for much younger children, not a meaningful developmental estimate for eight-year-olds. No IQ, ethnicity or socioeconomic data.

answers.title: Computer-aided autism diagnosis based on visual attention models using eye tracking
answers.answer: Group sizes and sex splits are given - 76 autistic (49 male, 27 female) and 30 typically developing (20 male, 10 female) - with a single 3-18 year age range for the whole sample. No group-wise ages, means, standard deviations, matching statement or statistical test appears anywhere. The authors treat the breadth as a virtue, describing the dataset as 'heterogeneous in terms of age, gender and CARS' and citing this as a strength relative to comparison studies, which is a legitimate external-validity argument. But a fifteen-year age span with no group comparison is a gap on a paradigm where preference for biological over geometric motion is developmentally graded. Per-participant clinical data including WISC, Repetitive Behavior Scale and Vineland where obtainable are deposited in supplementary material, which is better practice than most of the corpus.

answers.title: Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis
answers.answer: Autistic group: 35 children, mean age 5.26 +/- 0.51 years. Typically developing group: 20 children, mean age 4.75 +/- 0.77 years. Sex is not reported for either group anywhere in the paper - a striking omission in autism research. The six-month age difference is untested. Most importantly, the authors state directly that 'experimental groups were not matched on sociodemographics, IQ, or cognitive ability, limiting the generalization of the model', and recommend treating these as moderators in future work. The only stated exclusion criteria were wearing glasses or having an ocular alteration or pathology. ADOS-2 module 1 administration indicates the autistic sample is minimally verbal, which is important context for the study's central finding.

answers.title: Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms
answers.answer: Eligibility required ages 6-13 in both groups, at least average nonverbal intelligence (IQ 70 or above by Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices) in the autistic group, and absence of physical or mental disorder plus no autism or ADHD in first-degree relatives for the comparison group. Group-wise ages, sexes and IQ appear in Table 1, which did not survive text extraction; the companion study on the same cohort reports mean ages of 99.6 and 108.8 months, sex ratios of 17:2 and 17:3, and a significant 15-point IQ difference favouring the comparison group. That IQ gap matters here too, and the study handles it better than most: age and IQ are both entered as random factors in the mixed-effects models used to establish which features discriminate, so the reported kinematic differences are adjusted for both. No ethnicity or socioeconomic data.

answers.title: Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset
answers.answer: Reported entirely at second hand and only for the whole sample: 59 participants, 38 male (64%) and 21 female (36%), aged approximately 3 to 13 years, recruited from schools in the Hauts-de-France region. No group-wise ages, sexes, means or standard deviations appear, and no matching is discussed. The source study reports mean ages of 7 years 7 months and 8 years 0 months by group, so the information exists but is not carried over.

answers.title: Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: Autistic group: 13 children, 8 male and 5 female, aged 44-82 months, mean 66.23 +/- 11.56. Typically developing group: 13 children, 4 male and 9 female, aged 43-71 months, mean 60.08 +/- 9.54. Age matching is formally tested and confirmed (t(24) = 1.480, p = 0.152). Sex is not: 38% female against 69% female, an inversion of the usual direction, reported per participant but never tested or mentioned. Handedness was assessed behaviourally by asking children to draw and confirmed by caregivers or clinicians, with two left-handed children and two of unclear handedness, and left-hand trials from three autistic children were discarded because markers could not be placed on their left arms due to compliance problems. Per-participant ADOS totals, modules, ages, sexes, ICD-10 codes, comorbidities and handedness are all tabulated - the most complete individual-level characterisation in the corpus. No IQ or cognitive measures, which the authors name as a limitation.

answers.title: Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment
answers.answer: Age is reported as a mean with standard deviation and severity as a CARS2 eligibility range, both of which exceed the corpus norm. Sex is not a variable, since all eleven participants are male. What is absent is cognitive and language measurement: the verbal-response criterion is a functional floor rather than an assessed level, so the children's language ability is bounded below and not otherwise characterised, and no IQ, adaptive or developmental measure was obtained. Since the outcome is attention during a verbally mediated robot interaction, and the sound-response component of the score is a speech-latency measure, language ability is directly implicated in the measurement and is unmeasured. No socioeconomic, ancestry or comorbidity information is reported.

answers.title: Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning
answers.answer: Essentially none. No ages, means, standard deviations, sex counts or matching statistics are reported for either group. The age eligibility is stated inconsistently - under 12 in the abstract and under 10 in the methods. Sex, age and birth order are model features while remaining undescribed at group level, so the classifier's reliance on demographic separation cannot be assessed. Histograms of the distributions are presented as figures but no counts are given in text or table. No socioeconomic data beyond parental education, which is itself a model feature.

answers.title: Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism
answers.answer: Autistic group: 90 participants, 75 male (80.6%), mean age 10.84 +/- 2.20 (7.8-15.3), WISC-IV full-scale IQ 99.0 +/- 20.0. Comparison group: 28 participants, 12 male (40.0%), mean age 10.96 +/- 1.54 (7.0-15.0), IQ 113.4 +/- 12.3. Age, race and ethnicity show no significant difference. Two variables do: sex (p < 0.001) and IQ (p = 0.005). The IQ difference is addressed by a matched-pair replication; the sex difference is acknowledged but not tested. Given that pitch is sex-dependent and is one of the two features retained, and that the comparison group is 60% female against the autistic group's 19%, the sex imbalance is the more consequential of the two. Race is 86% white in both groups, and Hispanic ethnicity 14-18%, so the sample is demographically narrow but balanced.

answers.title: Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images
answers.answer: Only group sizes are given: 14 and 14. Age, sex, IQ, language level and severity are all absent for both groups, and no matching of any kind is described or possible to verify. This is the least-characterised sample in the corpus. The gap matters more here than it would elsewhere because the paper's own Discussion devotes four bullet points to how fixation behaviour changes with age - contrasting toddlers around 21 months, children under ten and those over twenty - and concludes that 'selection of necessary features for modelling fixation behaviour of subjects should be varied based on the corresponding age', immediately followed by the admission that 'the presented model does not consider the age information'. The authors thus diagnose the omission precisely without being able to remedy it, because the benchmark they inherited does not carry the variable.

answers.title: Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data
answers.answer: Sample sizes are given (14 and 14) and, unlike the companion paper on the same dataset, ages are partially reported: 'the age of children with ASD lied in the range from 5 to 12 years old (8 years old on average)'. No standard deviation. Critically, no age information at all is given for the typically developing group, so age matching cannot be assessed even coarsely. Sex distribution, IQ, language level and severity are absent for both groups. The demographic reporting therefore covers one variable in one of two groups - better than nothing, but insufficient to know whether the two groups are comparable on the variable the authors' own literature review identifies as decisive for gaze behaviour.

answers.title: Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children
answers.answer: Autistic group in the main pool: 68 children, 2.80 +/- 0.92 years, range 1.2-5.1. Typically developing group: 68 children, 2.55 +/- 0.97 years, same range. Testing Set 2: 101 autistic children, 3.46 +/- 1.16 years, range 2-6.9. Groups are stated to be matched for diagnosis, age, gender and ADOS module, with the sex distribution given in supplementary Table S1 rather than the main text - the only demographic detail displaced to supplementary material. Matching on ADOS module is a subtler control than most studies apply: module assignment depends on expressive language level, so matching on it partially equates the groups on language, which for a non-verbal-behaviour classifier removes an obvious alternative explanation. The comparison group is nonetheless typically developing rather than developmentally delayed, so age and module matching cannot equate general developmental level - and best-estimate IQ, which is measured, is not reported as matched and correlates with the model output.

answers.title: Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities
answers.answer: Autistic group: 30 children, mean age 7 years (SD 1.4), IQ range 59-109 on the Leiter-3, with six children between 59 and 70. Comparison group: 30 children, mean age 6 years 8 months (SD 1), IQ range 74-110. Age is close but no test of the difference is reported and matching is not claimed as a procedure. Two reporting gaps are consequential. Sex is not reported for either group anywhere in the paper - no counts, no proportions, no statement that groups were balanced - which is a complete omission of a variable that affects both autism prevalence and fine motor development at these ages. And IQ is given only as a range, with no mean or standard deviation, so the extent of the cognitive difference between groups cannot be quantified even though the authors concede it is a confound: the autistic range extends 15 points lower at the bottom and the distributions within those ranges are unknown. The comparison group's lower bound of 74 is itself notable, sitting in the borderline range.

answers.title: A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children
answers.answer: Group sizes (40 and 50) and the 3-6 age range appear in the running text; ages, sex distribution and the four questionnaire scores are tabulated in Table I with p values from two-independent-sample t-tests, but the table did not render in the extracted text so the values cannot be recovered. That the comparison was made formally and reported with p values is to the study's credit and distinguishes it from the several studies here that report no demographic testing at all. What is not addressed is whether any demographic difference that did emerge was subsequently controlled for - no covariate adjustment or matched-subsample analysis appears anywhere. No IQ, developmental quotient, language level or adaptive functioning measure was collected for either group, which for a 3-6-year-old sample leaves the most obvious alternative explanation - general developmental level - entirely unaddressed.

answers.title: AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
answers.answer: Fully reported and formally tested, which is uncommon in this corpus. Autistic group: 44 children, 22 male (50.0%), 46.9 +/- 13.0 months, median 49.0, range 24-68. Comparison group: 50 children, 27 male (54.0%), 47.9 +/- 12.5 months, median 48.5, range 25-72. Age p = 0.697 by t-test; sex p = 0.857 by chi-squared; both groups therefore genuinely matched on the two standard demographic variables and shown to be so. The decisive difference is cognitive: best-estimate IQ 104 +/- 17.4 in the comparison group against 58.8 +/- 18.6 in the autistic group, p < 0.001 - a 45-point gap placing the autistic group's mean firmly within the intellectual disability range. IQ was measured with the Korean WPPSI-IV or the Korean Bayley Scales depending on the child. The gap is acknowledged as the study's chief limitation but is not addressed analytically: no covariate adjustment, no IQ-matched subsample, no stratified analysis. Since joint attention emerges developmentally and is sensitive to cognitive level, and since the autistic group averages roughly a 45-point deficit, a substantial part of the classification could reflect developmental level rather than autism specifically.

answers.title: Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: Autistic group: 40 children, 33 boys and 7 girls, aged 3-6, mean 4.6 years with a standard deviation of 9 months. Comparison group: 40 children, 33 boys and 7 girls, aged 3-6, mean 4.8 years, SD 7 months. The paper states 'no significant difference in age or sex existed between the two groups' but reports no test statistic or p value for either. Sex is matched exactly, which is a stronger match than most studies here achieve. What is entirely absent is any measure of cognitive, language or adaptive functioning - a serious gap in a 3-to-6-year-old sample where developmental level varies widely, where EEG spectral power changes rapidly with age and maturation, and where the two groups were drawn from educational settings that themselves sort on developmental level. No IQ, no developmental quotient, no language measure, no severity score.

answers.title: An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images
answers.answer: Nothing. No ages, no sexes, no group sizes in people, no cognitive or language measures, no matching, and no statement that any of these are unavailable. The only quantities reported about the sample are image counts per class. This is the least characterised sample in the corpus, exceeding even Mazumdar, which at least reported that 14 autistic and 14 typically developing children contributed the data.

answers.title: Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals
answers.answer: Fully reported with formal testing on every variable, in a table with test statistics and p values. Autistic group: 48 adults, 79.2% male, 27.69 +/- 5.37 years (18-41), full-scale IQ 111.38 +/- 14.98 (84-150), ADOS CSS-Overall 7.04 +/- 1.98 (3-10), AQ 28.06 +/- 7.67. Comparison group: 105 adults, 70.5% male, 27.09 +/- 7.29 years (19-55), full-scale IQ 110.01 +/- 10.20 (85-136), AQ 15.70 +/- 6.41. None of age (t(151) = -0.501, p = 0.617), sex (chi-squared = 0.864, p = 0.353) or IQ (t(140) = -0.637, p = 0.525) differed; only AQ did (t(151) = -10.314, p < 0.001), as it should. Eleven participants with missing IQ scores were explicitly excluded from that comparison and the exclusion is footnoted. This is the only study in the corpus to equate IQ between groups in a well-powered sample rather than acknowledging an IQ gap as a limitation, and the equating was achieved by restricting recruitment to adults with IQ in the normal range - a design choice the authors justify on the grounds of reducing 'variation related to general inattention, difficulty following instructions, or difficulty understanding the video stimuli', while acknowledging that it limits generalisation.

answers.title: Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech
answers.answer: Reported, and the reporting reveals the study's central problem. Autistic group: 20 children, 19 male (95%) and 1 female, median age 5 years. Comparison group: 38 children, 15 male (39%), 22 female (58%) and 1 unspecified, median age 9.5 years. Overall age range 3-12. Two large imbalances follow. The 4.5-year median age gap is the more serious and is never mentioned anywhere in the paper - not in the limitations, not in the discussion - despite being the single variable that most determines the acoustics of a child's voice across this range: fundamental frequency falls, formants shift with vocal-tract growth, articulation stabilises, disfluency declines and utterance length increases substantially between 5 and 9.5 years. The sex imbalance is the reverse - 95% versus 39% male - and this one is acknowledged, quantified and benchmarked, with the authors noting that even the naturally skewed 4:1 to 3:1 population ratio would predict only 75-80% male, so their split exceeds expectation, and concluding that the dataset 'may still not be completely representative of real-world conditions'. Combining the two, the autistic group is younger and almost entirely male while the comparison group is older and majority female, so the groups differ systematically on both determinants of child vocal acoustics before diagnosis is considered. No IQ, language level, developmental measure or matching procedure is reported.

answers.title: Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection
answers.answer: Fully reported with formal testing on every variable. Autistic group: 88 participants, 73 male (83.0%), 11.4 +/- 2.1 years, IQ 99.5 +/- 19.9. Non-autistic group: 70 participants, 40 male (57.1%), 11.5 +/- 1.7 years, IQ 112.1 +/- 12.9. Race and ethnicity are tabulated for both groups (predominantly white, 13 and 8 Hispanic). Age matches (Mann-Whitney p = 0.6044); sex does not (Fisher's exact p = 0.00065); IQ does not (p < 0.001). What distinguishes this study is that both mismatches are tested rather than merely conceded. For sex, the combined model was refitted separately in boys (n = 113, AUC 0.8901, 95% CI 0.8261-0.9541) and girls (n = 45, AUC 0.8067, 95% CI 0.6493-0.9640), neither differing significantly from the full-sample AUC (p = 0.4428 and p = 0.178). For IQ, the misclassification analysis found that IQ was never significantly associated with correct or incorrect classification in any of the three models. The authors nonetheless list loose matching among their limitations - 'Participants were not tightly matched between groups which could result in reduced fit for analysis' - rather than treating the confound tests as closing the question.

answers.title: Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers
answers.answer: Reported in full and tested, and the picture is one of multiple significant imbalances. Autistic group: 41 toddlers, 70.7% male, 24.38 +/- 4.73 months. Neurotypical group: 416 toddlers, 50.2% male, 20.59 +/- 3.18 months. Age differs significantly by ANOVA, sex by chi-squared. Two further significant differences appear in the demographic table and are less commonly reported elsewhere in this corpus: Hispanic ethnicity (29.3% versus 7.5%) and caregiver education, where 85.6% of neurotypical caregivers held a four-year college degree or more against 53.7% of autistic caregivers. Age and the proportion of missing data were entered as ANCOVA covariates and did not affect the between-group results; sex was not covaried, with the authors stating that the sample 'did not offer sufficient power to determine the influence of biological and demographic characteristics, such as sex'; ethnicity and caregiver education are reported but never revisited. The last is worth attention in this particular paradigm, since the measurement is of a toddler sitting on a caregiver's lap with 'no special instructions given regarding how to hold the child', so any systematic difference in how caregivers positioned or settled their children would enter the signal directly. Cognitive ability differs markedly - the autistic group's Mullen Early Learning Composite averages 63.64 - and no Mullen data were collected for the neurotypical group, so the difference cannot be quantified or adjusted.

answers.title: Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study
answers.answer: Tabulated with within-language significance testing, and the picture differs sharply between the two language groups. Cantonese: autistic 19 male : 9 female, 17.83 +/- 9.24 years, IQ 108.54 +/- 10.92; comparison 17 male : 7 female, 18.88 +/- 8.70 years, IQ 115.08 +/- 10.13 - well matched on sex and age, with an IQ gap. English: autistic 29 male : 4 female, 15.96 +/- 7.38 years, IQ 104.13 +/- 14.34; comparison 15 male : 18 female, 19.31 +/- 5.35 years, IQ 111.03 +/- 13.79 - a 42-percentage-point sex imbalance in opposite directions, a three-year age gap, and an IQ gap. The authors identify this asymmetry themselves, referring to 'differences in gender and age observed between the English (but not Cantonese) groups', and run a post-hoc analysis in supplementary material to rule them out as confounds in the English f0 classification. That the confounds are concentrated in the English sample matters because the English intonation model is the only intonation classification that reached significance, and f0 is strongly sex-dependent: an autistic group that is 88% male compared against a group that is 55% female differs in mean pitch for reasons unrelated to diagnosis. Age ranges are wide in every group (6-35 years overall), spanning pre- and post-pubertal voice change. IQ was assessed with Wechsler scales in English and the TONI-4 in Cantonese, so cognitive level is not comparable across languages even though both language groups show a difference favouring comparison participants.

answers.title: Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings
answers.answer: Reported with tests for every variable. Autistic group: 25 participants, 14.55 +/- 5.46 years (7.1-24.6), non-verbal IQ 109.08 +/- 13.04 (80-140), verbal IQ 106.62 +/- 19.70 (72-131). Comparison group: 25 participants, 14.38 +/- 5.83 years (7.3-25.3), non-verbal IQ 114.64 +/- 12.50 (80-134), verbal IQ 113.12 +/- 14.33 (85-141). Age matches closely (p = 0.92) and both IQ measures are non-significant (p = 0.13 and p = 0.20), though the authors describe the match as 'nearly matched' and list imperfect IQ matching among their limitations - an appropriately cautious reading, since a five-to-six point gap in both verbal and non-verbal IQ at n = 25 per group is underpowered to detect. Verbal IQ matters particularly here because the outcome is narrative language. The one reporting gap is sex: the groups are stated to be matched on sex and ethnicity, but no counts, proportions or test are given for either, so the claim cannot be verified. The age range is wide (7 to 25 years), spanning most of narrative development, and the authors note they could not stratify by age, sex or IQ at this sample size.

answers.title: Development of a visual attention based decision support system for autism spectrum disorder screening
answers.answer: Reported with tests, and the picture is one of a single successful match against two large failures. Age: 34.85 months for the autistic group against 32.90 for comparisons, p = 0.07 - matched, though marginally, and matching on age was the stated design intention. Sex: 37:24 against 38:34, reported as p = 0.00, acknowledged in the limitations. Development: Bayley-III cognitive scores of 77.79 against 98.0 and language scores of 67.70 against 101.27, both p < 0.001. The language gap of 33.6 standard score points is the largest developmental difference reported in any study in this corpus, and the cognitive gap of 20 points places the autistic group's mean more than one standard deviation below the comparison group's. Neither is adjusted for, stratified on, or listed as a limitation. The authors' stated reason for matching only on age is that 'the study involved a passive viewing paradigm and did not require cognitive or language processing skills', which conflates task demands with developmental sensitivity: no response was required, but where a 30-month-old looks when a conversing adult and child compete against a spinning animation is itself a developmental milestone, and a group averaging a 34-point language deficit would be expected to attend differently to a social interaction scene for reasons that are not specific to autism. Standard deviations are not reported for age or for either Bayley score.

answers.title: Different Eye Tracking Patterns in Autism Spectrum Disorder in Toddler and Preschool Children
answers.answer: Reported per cohort with tests, and both cohorts are matched on both variables. Toddlers: autistic 2.4 +/- 0.5 years and 50 boys to 5 girls, comparison 2.2 +/- 0.6 years and 33 boys to 7 girls, with p = 0.27 for age and p = 0.22 for gender. Preschoolers: autistic 4.6 +/- 0.5 years and 33 boys to 4 girls, comparison 4.8 +/- 0.3 years and 33 boys to 8 girls, with p = 0.11 and p = 0.29. Age and gender were then additionally entered as covariates in every ANCOVA despite already being matched, which is belt-and-braces and appropriate. What is absent is any measure of developmental or cognitive level in either group - no Mullen, Bayley, Griffiths or equivalent - and the authors address this directly rather than omitting it, arguing that 'predominant ASD studies used chronological age instead of developmental age' and that 'in practice, a child transition from Toddler to preschooler is typically based on the chronological age without developmental testing', while conceding that 'future studies may also need to consider adding a developmental test'. The argument is reasonable for defining the cohorts but does not address the confound: two groups matched on chronological age but differing in developmental level would differ in where they look for reasons unrelated to diagnosis, and nothing in the data can separate these.

answers.title: Evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based medical device for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: Reported for the whole cohort in unusual demographic depth and used analytically rather than descriptively. Completers were 36.2% female, distributed across five age bands from 18 months to over 5 years, and characterised by race and ethnicity (53.9% non-Hispanic white only, 13.2% Black only, 11.5% Hispanic or Latino only, 13.4% multiple, 4.2% Asian only), parental education across six levels, and parental income across six brackets. Performance is then broken down across every one of these strata with Clopper-Pearson intervals, which no other study in this corpus attempts. The authors are appropriately careful about what this shows: the study 'was not powered for statistical inference on covariates' and differences were assessed 'by examining the overlap of corresponding 95% CIs'. Two age effects did reach significance - a higher determinate rate under 3 (39% versus 26%, p = 0.006) and higher specificity at 3 and over (88% versus 67%, p = 0.03). The sex comparison warrants more caution than the paper gives it: PPV was 60% (12/20) for girls against 88% (51/58) for boys, a 28-point gap resting on 20 determinate positive girls, and reading overlapping intervals as evidence of no difference in an underpowered analysis is the weakest inference in the paper - particularly since diagnostic disparity by sex is one of its stated motivations. The cohort had higher parental education and lower household income than the general US population, both acknowledged, with the income difference attributed plausibly to 'reduced parental participation in the workforce as a result of participants' developmental delays'.

answers.title: Extraction and Classification of Acoustic Features from Italian Speaking Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.
answers.answer: Matched by design and reported only at that level. Both groups comprise 14 children aged 6 to 10 with 11 males and 3 females. No means, standard deviations or statistical tests are given for age, so the groups are known to share a range rather than shown to be equivalent - and across ages 6 to 10 children's vocal tracts, fundamental frequencies and narrative abilities change substantially, so a within-range imbalance would matter. The sex ratio was chosen deliberately to reflect the DSM-5 epidemiological figure of four males per female, which is a defensible design choice for representativeness though it means only three girls contribute to each group. No IQ, language, adaptive or severity measure was obtained for either group, so cognitive and linguistic level are entirely uncontrolled in a study whose outcome is narrative speech production. The authors identify a related gap themselves, noting that formant and fundamental frequency features are 'sensitive to the speaker's age, gender, and height' and recommending that future work investigate 'the correlation of voice features to the personal characteristics of the speakers'.

answers.title: Eye Tracking-Based Diagnosis and Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques
answers.answer: Sex composition is restated from the source publication and is the only demographic information given: the autistic group comprises 25 males and 4 females (86.2% male) and the comparison group 13 males and 17 females (43.3% male). That 43-percentage-point difference, running in opposite directions between groups, is reported in a single sentence and never mentioned again - not analysed, not covaried, not listed as a limitation, and not discussed anywhere in a 27-page paper. It matters because the classifier operates on rendered scanpath images, and any systematic difference in viewing behaviour, screen coverage or trace density associated with sex would be absorbed directly into the texture features. No ages, no age range, no IQ, no language level, no severity and no matching of any kind. Given that the same dataset elsewhere in this corpus is analysed by Gaspar and colleagues with no participant information at all, the restatement here is an improvement in reporting that is not accompanied by any improvement in analysis.

answers.title: Identification of Social Engagement Indicators Associated With
answers.answer: Reported only in aggregate and incompletely. Sex is given as 53 male and 15 female in the autistic group against 18 male and 9 female in the comparison group - 77.9% versus 66.7% male - with no test and no discussion. Age is reported only as an overall range of 2 to 15 years, with the distribution shown in a figure and no group means, medians, standard deviations or tests in the text, and one comparison-group child not providing an age at all. That is the study's most consequential reporting gap: gaze allocation, sustained attention, and willingness to engage in a charades game with a parent all change enormously between a 2-year-old and a 15-year-old, and the analysis pools the entire range without stratifying, covarying or reporting whether the groups are comparable. No IQ, language, adaptive or severity measure for either group, and no exclusion criteria described.

answers.title: Investigation of Eye-Tracking Scan Path as a Biomarker for Autism Screening Using Machine Learning Algorithms
answers.answer: Nothing. No ages, no sexes, no group sizes beyond the participant and image counts, no IQ, no language level and no matching of any kind for either group. The literature review mentions in passing that a different Carette study involved children aged 8 to 10, but no demographic information is given for the participants whose images are analysed here. This is a lesser omission than in the two companion reuses of the same data only in that participant counts are stated and, uniquely, used; on every other demographic variable the study is silent.

answers.title: Machine learning models using mobile game play accurately classify children with autism
answers.answer: The weakest demographic reporting relative to the paper's methodological care elsewhere. Sex is given as 19 male and 9 female among autistic children and 10 male, 7 female and 4 unspecified among comparison children - so 67.9% versus 47.6% male among those reporting - with no comparison or discussion. Age is reported only as a whole-sample figure of 7.10 +/- 5.82 years, with no group-specific means, and that figure is arithmetically implausible: with inclusion restricted to ages 3 to 12, a standard deviation of 5.82 cannot arise, since the entire range spans nine years. Whether this is a transcription error or a computation over a different variable cannot be determined. No IQ, language, adaptive or severity measure for either group. The authors identify the consequence in their limitations - 'the sample size was too small to evaluate the predictive power of our models across various demographic dimensions, including gender, ethnicity, nationality, age and other diagnosis' - and commit to demographic fairness validation as recruitment expands, which is the right commitment but does not substitute for reporting what was collected.

answers.title: Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction
answers.answer: Nothing whatsoever. No ages, no age ranges, no sexes, no IQ, no language level, no matching and no statistical comparison of any kind for either group. Even the participant counts are approximate. This is the least characterised sample in the corpus among studies that collected their own data rather than reusing a public benchmark - the benchmark-reuse papers at least have the excuse of inheriting an undocumented dataset, whereas this group recruited the children themselves over roughly two years and reports none of what they must have known. For a speech study the omission of age is especially consequential, since fundamental frequency, formant structure and articulatory precision change substantially across childhood and would separate any two groups differing in age composition.

answers.title: The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation
answers.answer: Reported compactly and adequately for both groups: 105 autistic children aged 3.7 +/- 1.3 years, 80.0% male, ADOS 14.6 +/- 6.5; and 27 non-autistic children aged 3.1 +/- 1.5 years, 77.8% male, ADOS 3.2 +/- 3.7. The groups are close on sex (a 2.2-point difference) and reasonably close on age (0.6 years), though neither is formally tested and matching is not claimed. The overall age range of 1 to 7 years is given in the discussion. What is absent is any cognitive, language or adaptive measure, which is a real gap for a study whose predictor is speech and whose sample is described as 'mostly do not speak fluently or use little or no phrase speech' - expressive language level would be the obvious covariate, and it plausibly mediates both the acoustic features and the ADOS score. Ethnicity and socioeconomic information are not reported.

answers.title: The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children
answers.answer: Age and sex are reported and controlled by design - a 12-month band and exact four-to-one sex matching in each group - which is proportionate handling for a ten-child study and better than several much larger studies in this review manage. What is absent is cognitive and language level, and the omission matters for the construct: turn-taking in a five-minute game depends on understanding the game, and without any developmental measure a general cognitive explanation for reduced turn-taking cannot be separated from an autism-specific one in six-year-olds. No socioeconomic, ancestry or comorbidity information is reported, and the sample is drawn from kindergartens in one Polish city.

answers.title: Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach
answers.answer: Age, sex and IQ reported per group with formal group comparisons: age 99.6 +/- 25.1 versus 108.8 +/- 27.0 months (t(37) = 1.09, p = .283); sex 17:2 versus 17:3 male:female (chi-square = .174, p = .676); IQ 100.8 +/- 22.7 versus 116.1 +/- 22.7 (t(37) = 2.45, p = .019). Age range 6-13 years by inclusion. Nothing else: no race or ethnicity, no socioeconomic status, no parental education, no language background, no medication status beyond the exclusion gate, no comorbidity counts. Both groups are drawn from Shenzhen, China, so the sample is culturally homogeneous - relevant because gaze-to-face norms are known to vary cross-culturally and the entire feature set is spatial gaze allocation during a face-to-face conversation. The significant IQ gap deserves emphasis: it is the one variable that separates the groups, and it is neither matched, regressed out, nor discussed as a confound.

answers.title: A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features
answers.answer: Extremely thin. Table 2 reports only group size, mean age and median age: ASD n = 28, mean 4.63, median 4.0; TD n = 18, mean 4.61, median 4.0; others n = 4, mean and median 5.5. Age is therefore well matched between the two modelled groups, which matters for a motor-play task in 3-6 year olds. Nothing else is reported: no sex distribution for any group, no IQ or developmental quotient, no language level, no socioeconomic status, no race or ethnicity, no comorbidities, no medication. The absence of sex counts is a deliberate, argued choice rather than an oversight - the authors state they did not balance sex because play complexity and toy engagement with car-like toys have been shown to be similar across sexes in autistic children - but declining to balance a variable is not a reason to decline to report it, and without the counts a reader cannot check whether the two groups happened to differ. Given that all children were recruited at a single autism centre in Tehran, the sample is also culturally and geographically homogeneous, which is worth noting for a device whose selling point is deployment in homes worldwide.

answers.title: A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities
answers.answer: Partial. Reported: group sizes (30/30), mean and SD of age per group (7 +/- 1.4 versus 6 years 8 months +/- 1), age range 5-10, and IQ ranges per group from the Leiter-3 (ASD 59-109, TD 74-110), with the note that six autistic children scored between 59 and 70 and that no severe or profound impairment was present. Recruitment source is given for both groups. Not reported: sex distribution for either group - a striking omission in a 60-child study where sex ratio is both clinically salient and trivially available; race or ethnicity; socioeconomic status; parental education; language level; medication; and any positive comorbidity data, since comorbidity was an exclusion criterion. Two features of what is reported deserve emphasis. First, IQ is given only as a range, with no mean or SD, so the distributions cannot be compared - yet the ranges are visibly asymmetric and six autistic children sit below the TD group's floor of 74, which matters because the index task is a reimplementation of a cognitive test and the analysis is restricted to correctly performed trials. Second, the two groups differ systematically in more than diagnosis: the autistic children were recruited from a rehabilitation centre and were actively receiving psychomotor therapy, i.e. motor intervention, while the controls came from a mainstream school, so exposure to motor training is confounded with group membership in a study whose outcome is motor kinematics.

answers.title: A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation
answers.answer: The thinnest demographic reporting of any included study charted so far. What is given: n = 30, of whom 29 autistic and 1 typically developing; a single overall mean age of 3.65 years; and the ADOS-2 modules from which participants were drawn (TM, M1, M2), which implies limited or absent fluent language across the sample. What is absent: sex distribution, age range or standard deviation, per-group age, IQ or developmental quotient, language level beyond the module implication, socioeconomic status, race or ethnicity, comorbidity, medication, and any ADOS-2 total, algorithm or comparison score. Because the sample is 29 autistic children and 1 control, the usual concern about group matching does not arise, but a different problem does: without age spread, sex, or developmental level it is impossible to judge for whom the vision pipeline works. Body proportions, head size, motor control and sitting posture all vary sharply across the 12-month to roughly 5-year span that modules TM through M2 encompass, and a shoulder-rotation threshold of 90 degrees measured in 2-D image coordinates is not obviously age-invariant. All data come from one hospital in Changchun, so the sample is also geographically and culturally homogeneous.

answers.title: Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games
answers.answer: Table 1 reports sex, group size, and mean and standard deviation of age: autistic 20 male, 8.40 +/- 2.45 years; comparison 20 male, 8.45 +/- 1.90 years, with an overall span of about 4 to 12 years. Age matching is excellent - the means differ by three weeks - though the autistic group is more dispersed. Beyond this, nothing: no IQ or developmental quotient despite the autistic group being labelled high-functioning, no language measure, no adaptive functioning, no comorbidity, no medication, no socioeconomic status, no race or ethnicity, and no autism severity. Two features of the reported demographics deserve emphasis. The sample is 100% male in both groups. This is stated in the table and never mentioned again - not as a design decision, not as a limitation, not in the conclusion - even though the introduction itself notes that autism prevalence is higher in boys, which is a reason to sample boys but not a reason to leave the restriction undiscussed. And the participants are Iranian children in Tehran while the facial stimuli are Japanese women from the JAFFE database, so every trial involves other-race face processing. The paper's own literature review cites work on differences between autistic and typically developing children in processing same-race versus other-race faces, and even reports that study's 70% accuracy as a comparator, yet never connects that literature to its own stimulus choice.

answers.title: Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior
answers.answer: The retrieved text states that the groups did not differ significantly on mean chronological age, full-scale IQ, verbal IQ or sex ratio, with the statistics themselves in a table not recoverable from the extracted text. That set of matched variables is nonetheless the most complete in this corpus for a study of this size, and two elements are worth emphasising because their absence undermines so many other studies charted here. IQ was measured with a standardised instrument (WASI-II) in both groups and matched on both full-scale and verbal estimates - so the classification cannot be attributed to a cognitive-ability gap, which is an uncontrolled confound in the majority of studies in this review. And sex ratio was matched rather than left uncontrolled or eliminated by sampling only boys. All participants were native and fluent English speakers by inclusion, which removes language proficiency as a confound in a conversational paradigm but also narrows generalisability. What is not reported in the retrieved text: race or ethnicity, socioeconomic status, comorbidity, medication, and - notably given that ADOS-2 was administered - any severity score. The sample is adults, cognitively able enough to complete an unstructured 3-minute conversation with a stranger, and it is a research-registry population at a specialist centre rather than a community sample.

answers.title: Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas
answers.answer: Reported: group sizes, sex counts and mean and standard deviation of age for both groups, plus normal or corrected vision as the only participant criterion. Age is well matched (4.66 +/- 1.00 versus 4.77 +/- 0.92). Sex is not: the autistic group is 80.0% male (112 of 140) and the comparison group 63.2% male (122 of 193), a difference of nearly 17 percentage points that is neither tested, matched, adjusted nor mentioned. This omission is more consequential here than in most studies because the paper's own subgroup analysis reports that 'the groups of boys presented higher error rates than the groups of girls' - so sex is demonstrably related to model performance and is also unequally distributed between the classes. Not reported at all: IQ or developmental level, language ability, socioeconomic status, comorbidity, medication, and any autism severity measure. Recruitment sites are described qualitatively as areas 'where medical conditions are relatively poor', which is the closest the paper comes to a socioeconomic characterisation and is offered as a strength of external validity rather than as a demographic variable. The absence of any cognitive measure is a real limitation for a passive-viewing task in 3-6 year olds, since the capacity to sit still and attend to a screen for six minutes varies sharply with developmental level - and the paper's own analysis of why specificity is lowest in the youngest children turns on exactly that capacity.

answers.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts
answers.answer: None whatsoever. No age, sex, race or ethnicity, socioeconomic status, education, nationality, language background, comorbidity or medication is available for any of the 252 users in either group, and none is estimated or discussed. Three consequences follow. First, the sample is necessarily adolescents and adults, since Twitter requires account holders to be at least 13 - which sits at odds with a paper titled 'Early Detection' and motivated in its opening pages entirely by the value of diagnosing children before the age of three, a mismatch the text never addresses. Second, no matching of any kind was possible between the 221 autistic and 31 comparison users, and none was attempted, so any demographic difference between the groups - in age, sex, nationality, education, topic interests, or how much they tweet - is fully confounded with the label. Third, the only English-language requirement is stated for the tweets, but the chosen model is BERT-base-multilingual-cased, a multilingual checkpoint, which suggests the corpus may not be uniformly English. The one participant characteristic that is described in detail is not demographic but procedural: the manual exclusion of organisational accounts, self-described advocates and family members from the autistic group, which is careful work and is the paper's strongest methodological passage.

answers.title: Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: The most complete demographic reporting in this corpus, and the completeness is what makes the imbalances visible. Table 1 gives, per group: sex (autistic 77.5% male versus typically developing 48.9%), race (White/Caucasian 47.5% versus 77.7%; African American 15.0% versus 8.6%; other 37.5% versus 13.6%), Hispanic/Latino ethnicity (32.5% versus 7.3%), M-CHAT-R/F positivity (87.5% versus 0.25%), ADOS-T total (7.64 +/- 1.69 in the autistic group), and age in months (24.21 +/- 4.72 versus 20.62 +/- 3.21). Caregiver education is reported for the whole sample: 82.8% college degree, 15.5% more than high school, 1.8% no high school. Three of these differences matter and none is adjusted for. The age gap of 3.6 months is large at 17-36 months, a period of rapid change in facial expressivity, affect regulation and attention, and it runs in the direction that would be expected to produce more, not less, behavioural regulation in the older autistic group - so it does not obviously explain the finding, but it is a live confound in a study that goes to the trouble of ANCOVA-adjusting two other covariates. The sex difference reflects autism's true sex ratio rather than a sampling error, but sex differences in facial expressivity in toddlerhood are documented. The racial and ethnic difference is the one with a technical as well as a demographic dimension: the autistic group is 30 percentage points less White and over four times as likely to be Hispanic/Latino, and the paper's own stated limitation is that landmark and affect detectors were trained primarily on adults - detector accuracy is also known to vary by skin tone and facial morphology, so differential measurement error across groups cannot be excluded. The authors acknowledge the general problem, stating that the sample 'did not have sufficient power to determine the impact of demographic characteristics on the results'.

answers.title: Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders
answers.answer: Reported per group in two tables and more completely than most in this corpus, though with gaps. Adults: n and sex ratio, age, Kikuchi's Scale of Social Skills 18-item, SRS-2, FEIT score, ADOS-2 and PANSS as applicable. Children: n and sex ratio, age, SRS-2, FEIT score, ADHD-RS and CBCL. Three imbalances are visible and none is adjusted. The adult groups span six years of mean age (Sz 26.0 +/- 5.85, control 29.3 +/- 3.72, ASD 32.1 +/- 9.13) with very different variances, and age affects both gaze behaviour and face processing. The children's groups differ sharply in sex - 13:2 male:female in the autistic group against 7:8 in controls, so 87% versus 47% male - which is the largest sex imbalance in a matched-design study charted here. And autistic children scored more than twice as high on the ADHD Rating Scale as controls (17.6 +/- 10.2 versus 6.88 +/- 9.40), so attentional difficulty is confounded with diagnosis in a task whose outcome is where the eyes go. Not measured at all: IQ, which the authors identify as a limitation and which matters because they characterise the sample as high-functioning without being able to quantify it; and race or ethnicity, relevant here because Japanese participants viewed the FEIT's Western facial stimuli, an other-race configuration that goes unremarked. What is unusually well reported is the phenotypic battery: SRS-2 in both datasets, ADOS-2 totals for autistic adults, PANSS for schizophrenia, plus social-skills and behaviour-checklist measures, with a clear explanation of why SRS-2 was not administered to the schizophrenia group.

answers.title: Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders
answers.answer: Almost nothing usable, and the one variable that is reported creates the study's central problem. Age is given only as a distribution over six bands for survey respondents (0-5: 36, 6-10: 39, 11-18: 20, 19-30: 23, 31-50: 45, over 50: 50, unspecified: 22) with no breakdown by diagnosis, and the totals do not reconcile with the stated respondent counts. No sex, race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, IQ, language level or comorbidity data were collected at all. Geographic distribution is reported at country level: 66% of users in the United States, with Europe and Oceania represented. The decisive omission is age by diagnostic group, because the composition of the comparison group makes the confound near-certain rather than speculative. Autism is congenital and the app's heaviest and most frequent users were children aged 10 and under; the non-autistic comparison group is dominated by acquired conditions of adult and later life - stroke, dementia, ALS, brain injury - which the paper's own background section describes as the 'acquired disabilities' category of AAC users, explicitly contrasted with congenital ones. A classifier separating these groups from key-press sequences may therefore be separating a five-year-old learning to request food from a seventy-year-old adapting to post-stroke aphasia, and nothing in the analysis distinguishes that possibility from a genuine autism signature. The paper itself observes in its background that older AAC users approach these systems with greater communicative experience but less technological intuitiveness, producing struggle, frustration and abandonment - which is a description of precisely the age-related usage difference that the classifier could be detecting.

answers.title: Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: The most complete demographic and clinical characterisation in this review, and completeness is what makes the study's central problem visible. Reported per group with formal tests: recruitment source, sex (53.3% versus 54.0% boys, p > .99), age (48.0 +/- 13.4 versus 47.9 +/- 12.5 months, p = .99, with medians and ranges), the proportion under 48 months (46.7% versus 42.0%, p = .80), best-estimate IQ and verbal IQ stratified by age band, K-CARS-2 stratified by age band, and for the autism group K-ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores in total, social affect and restricted-repetitive domains plus module distribution. Ethnicity is reported using NIH categories - all Korean - and geographic distribution is given. Age and sex are matched essentially perfectly, and the 46.7% proportion of girls in the autism group is remarkably high relative to the population sex ratio and to every other autism sample in this corpus, though unexplained. The decisive feature is IQ. Best-estimate IQ is 60.1 +/- 15.4 versus 104 +/- 19.1 in children under 48 months and 55.1 +/- 20.8 versus 105 +/- 14.5 in those older, with verbal IQ showing the same 41-45 point gaps, all at p < .001 - a difference roughly three standard deviations wide and the largest cognitive separation between compared groups anywhere in this review. The autism group's mean IQ of 55-60 places it in the range of moderate intellectual disability, and the K-ADOS-2 module distribution (17.8% toddler module, 62.2% preverbal or single-word, 20.0% phrase speech) confirms a predominantly minimally verbal sample. This is a population that most studies in this corpus exclude, which is a genuine strength, but it also means the two groups differ in cognitive and language level as profoundly as they differ in diagnosis. One internal inconsistency: the K-CARS-2 median for the older autism stratum is given as 31.3 with a stated range of 32.0-43.0, which is impossible.

answers.title: Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking
answers.answer: None whatsoever. Not a single demographic or clinical characteristic of the 59 children is reported - no age, no sex, no IQ, no language level, no severity, no comorbidity, no socioeconomic status, no race or ethnicity, and not even the number of children or images in each group. The paper's participant description consists entirely of two folder names. This is the most complete absence of participant information among the included studies, and it follows from the study's nature as a pure dataset-reuse exercise: the authors downloaded images and classified them. The consequence is that nothing can be said about who the model works for, whether the groups were matched on anything, or whether the classification could be driven by an age or sex imbalance between folders - questions that a reader must go to the original dataset publication to answer, and which this paper does not flag as open.

answers.title: SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism
answers.answer: Almost nothing at the individual level. Table 1 reports, per corpus, the number of autistic and typically developing participants and an age range: Eigsti 16/16 aged 3-6, Nadig 13/25 aged 3-7, Flusberg 6/0 aged 12-26 months. No sex, IQ, language level, socioeconomic status, race or ethnicity, comorbidity or severity is given for any child, and no group means or matching statistics of any kind are reported. Three consequences follow, all unaddressed. Because the pooled age range spans 12 months to 8 years while the comparison group is confined to 3-7 years, the two groups differ in age distribution by construction - and every feature in the study is a language measure, which in children is dominated by developmental stage. Mean length of utterance and number of distinct word roots, the latter identified by SHAP as the single largest contributor to the model's predictions, are canonical expressive-language milestones that change dramatically between 12 months and 8 years, so an age difference between groups is not a nuisance covariate here but a direct alternative explanation for the headline result. And without IQ or language-level data there is no way to separate an autism-specific pragmatic signature from a general language-delay one, which is precisely what the unused developmental delay group in the Eigsti corpus could have tested.

answers.title: Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths
answers.answer: Age band and sex are reported per group in two tables and nothing else is. No IQ, language level, severity, comorbidity, medication, socioeconomic status, race or ethnicity appears anywhere, and no exact ages, means or statistical comparisons are given. The two variables that are reported are the two that matter most here, and both are badly imbalanced. Sex: 81.5% male in the autistic group against 46.9% in the comparison group, a difference of nearly 35 percentage points. Age: 31.5% of autistic participants are aged 10 or over against 15.6% of comparison participants, and all four participants aged 18 or over are autistic while all remaining comparison participants are under 18. Ordinarily these would be recorded as uncontrolled confounds of unknown magnitude. What makes this study distinctive is that it measures their magnitude itself: its own experiments show that scan-path images predict sex within the autistic group at 78.0% accuracy with AUC 0.850, and age band within the autistic group at 80.5% with AUC 0.868. Both figures exceed the 74.4% achieved for diagnosis. So the study demonstrates that its input representation carries demographic information at least as strongly as diagnostic information, in a sample where the demographics differ substantially between diagnostic groups - and the two results are presented in consecutive sections without the connection being drawn.

answers.title: A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths
answers.answer: Better than the other reuses of this dataset, which typically report nothing, but still incomplete and entirely inherited. Table 1 gives, for the sample as a whole: 59 participants, 38 male and 21 female (64%/36%), 29 autistic and 30 typically developing, mean age 7.88 years and median 8.1, and CARS mean 32.97 and median 34.50. No variable is reported by group, so age matching, sex balance between groups and the severity distribution within the autistic group are all unavailable. The CARS figures nonetheless carry information the paper does not use: a mean of 32.97 with median 34.50 places the autistic sample in the mild-to-moderate band on that instrument, which characterises the spectrum position of the group better than most studies in this corpus manage - and the paper's own introduction notes that eye-tracking markers have been linked to a more severely affected subtype, so relating CARS to model output was both possible and thematically invited. Nothing else is available: no IQ, language level, comorbidity, medication or socioeconomic data, and no race or ethnicity beyond the participants being French-speaking children from the Hauts-de-France region.

answers.title: A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning
answers.answer: Extensive and, uniquely in this review, describing a whole population rather than a matched sample. Reported with formal comparisons at a p < 0.001 threshold chosen for the large sample size and multiple comparisons: sex (78.3% male in the autism group against 51.4%), birth year distribution, maternal country of birth (with higher diagnosis rates for mothers born in Russia and Ethiopia), preterm birth rate, maternal age, gestational week, birth weight, nursing status, parental concern rates, and number of well-baby visits (13.7 in the autism group against 11.44, t(775,939) = -23.05, p < 0.001, d = 0.7). Because the design is a population cohort rather than a case-control comparison, these differences are findings about the population rather than confounds introduced by sampling - which is the fundamental difference between this study and every other in the review. Two points nonetheless deserve attention. Sex is both a strong predictor and a strong group difference, and the authors handle it correctly by fitting a boys-only model and reporting that performance remained relatively stable, which is the check that distinguishes a model using sex as one legitimate risk factor from a model that is substantially a sex classifier. Maternal country of birth is reported as associated with diagnosis rate but its role in the model is not made explicit, and a risk score that encoded migration background would raise equity concerns the paper does not address. Absent throughout: IQ, language scores, adaptive functioning and any autism severity measure, none of which exists in the records.

answers.title: AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: “A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System”
answers.answer: None. No age (beyond an unverifiable dataset-level claim of 24-72 months), sex, race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, cognitive level, language, comorbidity or severity data exist for any image. The omission is more consequential here than in other dataset-reuse studies because the two classes were assembled from different sources: autism-advocacy and awareness websites will over-represent certain countries, ethnicities, family circumstances and photographic conventions relative to a random internet image search, and any such difference is directly available to the classifier as a diagnostic cue. A demographic comparison between the two collections is the minimum check that would begin to address this, and none is attempted.

answers.title: An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks
answers.answer: Available in unusual depth and reported not at all. ABIDE-I supplies age at scan, sex, handedness, full-scale, verbal and performance IQ, medication status at several sites and site identity for every subject, and the paper enters age, FIQ, VIQ and PIQ into the model - AGE_AT_SCAN ranks fourth and FIQ third among behavioural contributors - while reporting no group means, no distributions and no comparisons for any of them. Three consequences follow.
