ABIDE-I's autistic and control groups differ in age composition at several contributing sites, and age is a strong predictor of structural brain measures across the childhood-to-adult range the dataset spans, so an unexamined age difference is a live alternative explanation for part of the imaging stream's contribution. IQ differs systematically between groups in ABIDE-I and is entered as a predictor, so part of what the model separates is cognitive ability rather than autism. And sex is not reported at all, in a repository that is heavily male-weighted. Treating covariates as features rather than as things to be described or adjusted for is a defensible modelling choice for maximising accuracy and an indefensible one for supporting a diagnostic claim, and the paper does not distinguish the two purposes.

answers.title: Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development
answers.answer: Reported per group with formal tests for the three variables collected: sex 18:2 versus 17:4 male:female (chi-square = 0.671, p = .413), age 99 +/- 24.6 versus 114 +/- 24.8 months (t(39) = 1.89, p = .066), and non-verbal IQ 102 +/- 22.7 versus 118 +/- 16.2 (t(39) = 2.54, p = .015). Nothing else: no race or ethnicity, socioeconomic status, parental education, language measure, medication or severity. Two of the three reported variables are problematic and neither is handled. The IQ difference of 16 points is significant and unadjusted, and it matters here because interpersonal coordination has been reported to correlate with social cognition, so the group difference in coordination could reflect the group difference in cognitive ability. The age difference of 15 months falls just short of significance but is substantial in a 6-13 year range where motor control and conversational competence change considerably, and the direction - the autistic group younger - is the direction that would independently predict less mature coordination. The sample is also 85% male and drawn entirely from Shenzhen, and the eligibility requirement of at least average non-verbal intelligence excludes the substantial proportion of autistic children with intellectual disability. The authors identify sex ratio and severity range among their stated limitations but not IQ or age.

answers.title: Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning
answers.answer: Reported asymmetrically, and the asymmetry is the study's principal weakness. For the autistic group: age 18 +/- 3.48, sex 24 male to 40 female, ADOS-2 Module 3 and 4 totals, SRS-2 total 85.53 +/- 9.00, WISC-IV full-scale IQ 81.22 +/- 14.42 and WAIS-III full-scale IQ 91.33 +/- 20.12, Vineland-II adaptive composite 64.83 +/- 22.53, AQ 36.64 +/- 8.04, and PARS-TR scores for preschool and for adolescent/adult items. This is the most complete clinical characterisation of an autistic sample anywhere in the review. For the comparison group: age 19 +/- 2.77, sex 39 male to 32 female, ADOS-2 totals - and then nothing except a college grade point average range of 2.4 to 2.8, with the authors stating plainly that 'IQ testing was not part of our methodology'. The consequence is a confound that cannot be assessed: the autistic group has measured full-scale IQ between 81 and 91, while the comparison group is three-quarters university students selected for average academic standing, so the groups almost certainly differ substantially in cognitive and educational level, in a study whose entire outcome is the range and complexity of grammatical choices a speaker makes. Two further features deserve note. Age differs significantly (p = 0.00) but by only about a year, so the significance reflects sample size rather than a meaningful gap. And the autistic sample is 62.5% female - the only female-majority autistic cohort in this review, and by a very wide margin - which is unremarked despite the paper's own extended discussion of camouflaging, a phenomenon reported disproportionately in autistic women and directly relevant to whether linguistic markers would be detectable in this sample.

answers.title: Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms
answers.answer: None whatsoever - no age, sex, race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, cognitive level, language, comorbidity or severity data for any image, and no statement that such information is unavailable. The paper does not report even the age range that the dataset's own description carries. As with the companion study, the omission is consequential because the two classes were assembled from different internet sources, and autism-focused online spaces will differ from general internet image collections in the demographics they represent as well as in photographic convention.

answers.title: Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed
answers.answer: Not applicable to a study with no clinical groups, and unreported for the corpora used. No age distribution, sex composition or ancestry is given for either KDEF or CK+, although both are documented in their originating publications. The one demographic fact that matters here is implicit and unremarked: both corpora consist of adult volunteers, while the paper's motivating application concerns autistic children, so the modelled population differs from the target population by several decades of facial development as well as by diagnosis.

answers.title: Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification
answers.answer: Thin, and thinner for the comparison group than for the autistic group. Reported: group sizes, age means and standard deviations, recruitment source, and for the autistic group the requirement of an ADOS-2-confirmed diagnosis and absence of comorbidity. Not reported: sex, IQ, developmental level, language ability, socioeconomic status, race or ethnicity, or any severity score. Two features of what is reported deserve attention. The autistic group's age standard deviation is 0.94 years against 0.1 for the comparison group - nearly a tenfold difference in spread - so although the means differ by only three months the autistic group spans a much wider developmental range, which matters for a fine-motor outcome in children aged 3 to 6 where motor control changes rapidly. And no cognitive or developmental assessment was performed on either group; the comparison children were recruited without any assessment of pre-existing abilities, and the autistic group's functioning is inferred rather than measured, from the fact that all 'were able to engage with a tablet, suggesting a moderate level of functioning'. Since the outcome is the smoothness and dynamics of a dragging movement, and both groups were selected without reference to developmental level, a general developmental explanation for the difference cannot be separated from an autism-specific one. A further asymmetry is that the autistic children were undergoing psychomotor therapy at the recruiting centre - direct motor intervention - while the comparison children were not.

answers.title: Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain
answers.answer: None. No age, sex, race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, cognitive level, language ability, severity or comorbidity information appears for any individual, and no statement acknowledges the absence. The only individual-level variables reported anywhere are the eleven columns of Table 2 - seven emotion probabilities, two emotion aggregates, body temperature and heart rate - shown for five people.

answers.title: Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: Present as data fields and absent as reported characteristics. Age, gender, ethnicity, jaundice at birth, family history of autism, country of residence, prior app use and who completed the test are all columns in the datasets, and all but two of the twenty-one fields were retained for modelling - but no distribution, group comparison or descriptive statistic is reported for any of them. Age is handled structurally rather than statistically, by fitting a separate model per band, which is defensible since Q-CHAT-10 and AQ-10 are age-calibrated instruments. The one field whose treatment deserves comment is 'Who_completed_the_test', which the paper discusses: for the toddler and child datasets the items are answered by a parent, relative or health professional rather than by the person being screened, so the modelled data are one person's report about another, and the identity of that reporter is itself a predictor. That the respondent's relationship to the person is available as a feature underlines what the dataset contains - a record of someone's judgements, not of anyone's behaviour.

answers.title: Machine learning’s effectiveness
answers.answer: Sparse but well controlled by design rather than by adjustment. Reported: group sizes, sex ratio with a chi-square test (p = 0.81), age with a t-test (non-significant, and in any case every participant was five years old by inclusion criterion), and SRS-2 total scores per group with a t-test. Not measured: IQ, developmental level, language, adaptive functioning, socioeconomic status, comorbidity or medication. Two features of the design substitute effectively for adjustment on the variables that matter most in a postural study. Restricting the sample to a single age year removes the age confound that troubles most motor studies in this review - postural control changes rapidly between three and six, and every other motor study charted here spans several years. And the sex-specific SRS-2 cut-off means that sex is handled within the outcome definition rather than left as a group difference, which combined with the balanced observed ratio makes sex an unlikely driver. What remains unaddressed is developmental level: no cognitive or motor-development measure was obtained, so at an age when balance is still maturing a general developmental explanation cannot be distinguished from an autistic-trait-specific one. The sample is also drawn entirely from one small Japanese municipality, so the SRS-2 cut-offs, though taken from published Japanese population distributions, are applied to a single local cohort.

answers.title: Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network
answers.answer: Almost entirely absent, and the paper marks the absence in its own table. Age is given as a range of 1-11 for dataset 1 and not at all for dataset 2; the sex distribution is recorded as 'Females/Males: -' with the note 'Gender distribution unspecified'; and no information exists on ancestry, socioeconomic status, cognitive level, language, comorbidity or medication for either class. No between-class comparison of any characteristic is possible, and none is attempted. Two consequences follow directly. Because autism is diagnosed roughly four times more often in boys, and because facial classifiers are known to key strongly on sex-linked morphology, an unmeasured sex imbalance between classes is a live and untestable alternative explanation for the entire result. And because the two classes were harvested from different regions of the internet - autism advocacy and support content on one side, general and kindergarten content on the other - they are likely to differ in the geography, ancestry and photographic circumstances of the children depicted, none of which can be checked. The reported cross-dataset transfer does not resolve this, since both corpora were constructed on the same principle.

answers.title: Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]
answers.answer: Almost entirely absent. Sex is fully controlled by the sample being all-male; age is given only as two overlapping ranges (10-16 and 9-16) with no distribution or group comparison; and no cognitive, language, comorbidity, medication or socioeconomic information exists. Two specific risks follow. EEG spectral characteristics change substantially across the 9-to-16 window - the alpha peak rises in frequency, slow-wave power declines, and the maturational trajectory is well documented - so an age difference between a 13-child and a 4-child group would be sufficient to separate them on spectral features, and nothing reported allows the check. And medication is unrecorded, although antiepileptics and antipsychotics both alter EEG spectra and are more common in an autistic than in a comparison sample.

answers.title: Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play
answers.answer: Age and sex are reported per group with formal matching tests, severity is reported with a group comparison, and comorbidity and medication are controlled by explicit exclusion criteria - a considerably fuller demographic account than most of this corpus. What is absent is cognitive and language level, and that absence is consequential rather than incidental. The strongest single predictor in the final model is the duration of socially oriented vocalisations and verbalisations, and the candidate pool contained counts and proportions of vocalisations using words; without an expressive language measure, a group difference in language level cannot be separated from a group difference in the social orientation of speech. The age matching also deserves a closer reading than the p-value alone gives it. The means differ by 2.9 months at p = 0.0591, but the standard deviations differ substantially (9.9 against 13.5), so the distributions are not the same shape - and in a sample spanning 1 to 6 years, functional and imaginative play increase steeply with age. Four of the five retained predictors are quantities of object play, and the model does not adjust for age, so part of what the nomogram encodes may be developmental level rather than autism. Socioeconomic status, ancestry and parental education are not reported, and the sample is drawn entirely from Beijing.

answers.title: Predictive model using autism
answers.answer: Better characterised on the clinical side than any other included study and weaker on one specific comparison. Reported and compared: age, sex, years of education, and Autism Spectrum Quotient totals for both groups. The schizophrenia group additionally has PANSS positive, negative, general psychopathology and total scores, DIEPSS drug-induced extrapyramidal symptom severity, chlorpromazine-equivalent antipsychotic dosage, age at onset and duration of illness - and all of these are used analytically, in correlations with ADOS-2 scores and in comparisons between cut-off-positive and cut-off-negative subgroups. That depth is what allows the study's most important finding, that ADOS-2 positivity in schizophrenia tracks negative-symptom severity. The gap is intelligence. Both groups were screened at a full-scale IQ above 85, but with different instruments - WAIS-III administered directly to the autism group, the Japanese Adult Reading Test estimating premorbid ability in the schizophrenia group - and the authors state that they were therefore 'unable to accurately compare intelligence between patients with schizophrenia and ASD'. This is not a minor asymmetry: JART is a reading-based estimate of premorbid rather than current function, and schizophrenia commonly involves cognitive decline from premorbid levels, so the two groups may be matched on a threshold while differing substantially in current cognitive ability. Since ADOS-2 Module 4 requires fluent speech and several discriminating items concern the structure and content of conversation, an uncontrolled difference in current verbal ability is a live alternative explanation for part of the item-level pattern. Ancestry and socioeconomic status beyond education are not reported.

answers.title: The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech
answers.answer: The weakest demographic reporting of any included study, and the gaps are consequential rather than cosmetic. No age distribution is given for any group in either corpus, though the combined range spans 4 to 18 years - the period across which voice undergoes its most profound changes, including the pubertal fall in male fundamental frequency, vocal-tract growth and the maturation of prosody and syntax. If the atypical and typical groups differ in age composition, an age classifier and a diagnosis classifier would be behaviourally identical, and nothing reported allows this to be tested. No IQ, language, adaptive or socioeconomic measure exists, which is particularly striking given that one of the four diagnostic classes is dysphasia - the task asks a model to separate autism from a specific language impairment with no independent measure of language ability in any group. Ancestry is not reported. Sex is reported but inconsistently, at 22% female in De-Enigma and 19% in CPSD in one section and at 5% and 10% in another. The one demographic variable that receives serious analytic attention is sex, through equalised-odds fairness testing - and that analysis returns the study's most important result, showing that performance measured on a mixed-gender partition conceals a substantial deficit for girls. That single finding does more for this review's understanding of demographic confounding than the descriptive tables of most other included studies.

answers.title: Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism
answers.answer: None available, and the authors are candid about what follows. There is no age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic, cognitive or comorbidity information for any of the 188,596 users, and location was dropped as unusable. The limitations section states the resulting representativeness problem directly: restricting to English 'raises concerns about the lack of diversity in the data, where only English-speaking users from higher socioeconomic groups or younger adults are represented in the data set, as they comprise a larger portion of Twitter users'. Two consequences go further than the paper takes them. The #ActuallyAutistic community is widely observed to include a high proportion of late-diagnosed and self-identifying autistic adults, and a higher proportion of women, than clinically ascertained autism samples - so the demographic distance between the two corpora is likely to be substantial and is entirely unmeasurable, meaning that a sex- or age-linked difference in writing style would be indistinguishable from an autism-linked one. And the two groups differ in a way that no demographic variable captures at all: one is defined by participation in a topic-organised community and the other is a background sample of the platform, so their tweets differ in subject matter, audience, posting motivation and network position before any question of authorship arises.

answers.title: Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children
answers.answer: Age and sex are reported per group and exactly matched, and the matching is carried through into the train-test split alongside ADOS module - a three-way matching of the evaluation partition that no other included study performs. Because ADOS module assignment depends on expressive language level, matching on module constrains the groups on a language dimension without measuring it directly, which is a partial substitute for the language measure that is otherwise absent from the main text. Cognitive and developmental assessment details are deferred to supplementary material rather than reported, which is the description's main weakness. Ancestry, socioeconomic status and comorbidity within the autistic group are not reported. The 40% female representation deserves particular note in the context of this review: a speech study charted elsewhere here found that a model reaching 94.8% sensitivity on a pooled test set fell to 43.6% on girls, and that finding is only discoverable in samples where girls are present in reasonable numbers. This study has the sample composition to run that analysis and does not run it - which is a missed opportunity rather than a flaw in the sample.

answers.title: Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning
answers.answer: Absent for both classes, and more consequential than the usual absence because the study classifies faces. No age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic, cognitive or language information is reported for the 73 autistic children or for the undocumented comparison images. Three specific risks follow. Facial classifiers key strongly on apparent age and on sex-linked morphology, and autism is diagnosed roughly four times more often in boys, so an uncontrolled sex imbalance between classes could produce the entire result. The SSBD children were filmed by families who chose to post the footage publicly, which is a self-selected population by geography, language, internet access and disposition. And the comparison images, wherever they came from, will carry their own demographic profile, which cannot be matched because neither profile is known. The paper does note that the borrowed CK+ corpus contains people 'of various genders as well as ethnic backgrounds', so the relevance of demographic composition is recognised for other people's datasets and not applied to its own.

answers.title: A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features
answers.answer: Almost nothing, and the omissions are unusually consequential because the output is a drug recommendation. Reported: age range 5 to 15, sex (all male), and school. Not reported: age distribution, any breakdown by severity level, cognitive or adaptive level, language, comorbidity, current medication, or socioeconomic background. Four specific problems follow. Thermoregulation and facial thermal patterns change substantially between ages 5 and 15, so if severity levels are unevenly distributed by age the classifier may be reading development rather than severity, and nothing reported allows this to be checked. Current medication is itself a determinant of skin temperature - antipsychotics including risperidone impair thermoregulation, which is a documented and clinically monitored effect - so children already on higher doses because they are more severely affected may be thermally distinguishable for pharmacological rather than behavioural reasons, a circularity that would produce exactly the reported result. Comorbid epilepsy, intellectual disability and sensory conditions are common in a special-school population and affect both behaviour and autonomic function. And the all-male sample means the framework has no evidence base for half the population it would be applied to. The one demographic issue the paper does engage is skin tone, and it engages it well: thermal imaging is argued to be preferable to visible-spectrum facial analysis precisely because it 'is not affected by lighting conditions or skin tone', which is a genuine sensor-level answer to a fairness problem that most face-based studies in this review leave unexamined.

answers.title: Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: Absent apart from a stated age range of 2 to 14, and consequential for a facial classifier. No sex distribution, ancestry, socioeconomic, cognitive or clinical information exists for either class, and none could, given how the corpus was assembled. Three risks follow directly. Facial appearance changes profoundly between ages 2 and 14, so an age difference between a class drawn from autism-related material and a class drawn from general web search would be sufficient to produce the reported separation. Autism is diagnosed roughly four times more often in boys and facial classifiers key strongly on sex-linked morphology, so an unmeasured sex imbalance is an untestable alternative explanation. And ancestry composition is likely to differ between an autism-focused collection and a general web search, with no means of checking. The paper's motivating claims are morphometric - upper-face width, eye width, nasal bridge length, cheek narrowness - every one of which varies systematically with age, sex and ancestry, so the demographic gap is not incidental to the hypothesis but fatal to testing it.

answers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features
answers.answer: Partially reported and, unusually, analytically used. The paper states the age range (3 to 6), acknowledges that boys predominate and that the 3-4 band is larger than the 5-6 band, and explains the sex imbalance by reference to the diagnostic ratio. It does not give numerical age or sex breakdowns by diagnostic group, and no cognitive, language, socioeconomic or ancestry information is available. What distinguishes it from the rest of this corpus is what it does with the demographics it has: rather than reporting them and moving on, it computes every feature separately for autistic and typically developing children, for the two age bands and for boys and girls, and reports the interactions. The results are substantive - mean length of utterance rises with age; boys aged 3-4 exceed girls of the same age on the key features while girls aged 5-6 exceed boys; and mean length of turn is lower in autistic boys than typically developing boys but higher in autistic girls than typically developing girls. That last sex-by-diagnosis interaction, if real, would mean a single classifier trained mostly on boys could systematically misread girls - which is exactly the failure mode a speech study charted elsewhere in this review demonstrated empirically, with sensitivity falling from 94.8% pooled to 43.6% for girls. The gap here is that the paper stops at feature-level description and never evaluates model performance by subgroup, so the implication of its own finding goes untested.

answers.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning
answers.answer: Absent for both corpora beyond the stated age ranges of 4 to 12 and 3 to 7 years. No age distribution by diagnostic group, no sex, no cognitive or language measure, no ancestry and no comorbidity. Two of these are specifically damaging for a gait study. Walking kinematics mature substantially across 4 to 12 years - stride length, cadence, arm swing, double-support time and postural stability all change - so if the autistic and typically developing groups differ in age composition, a gait classifier and an age classifier would be behaviourally indistinguishable, and nothing reported allows the check. And gait differs by sex from middle childhood, with no sex information available in either corpus. The DREAM corpus additionally spans 3 to 7 years with ages recorded in months, so finer age information exists in the source data and is not used. The paper does not report demographic composition for either dataset or acknowledge these as confounds.

answers.title: Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]
answers.answer: Better than most secondary analyses in this review on sex and worse on age. Sex is matched exactly - 24 boys and 7 girls in both groups - so it is fully controlled, and at 22.6% girls the sample is less male-skewed than most autism research. Mean ages are reported per group at 35.6 and 30.8 months, but no statistical comparison is made and no adjustment is applied, despite a 4.8-month difference spanning a developmental window in which laryngeal control, vocal-tract length and respiratory coordination all change substantially. The three features that reached significance - jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio - are exactly the measures known to vary with vocal maturation, so an age difference of this magnitude is a competing explanation for the group findings and no analysis distinguishes them. The authors come close to the point in their limitations, noting that 'cry characteristics may evolve as children grow, potentially influencing model accuracy, making it essential to explore age-specific models', but treat it as a generalisability issue rather than as a confound within their own comparison. No cognitive, language, adaptive, socioeconomic or comorbidity data are available, and the sample is entirely Iranian and Farsi-speaking, which the authors identify as limiting cultural generalisability.

answers.title: Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm
answers.answer: Present as fields and absent as reported characteristics. Age, gender, ethnicity, jaundice at birth, family history of autism, country of residence, prior app use and who completed the test are all among the 21 columns the paper enumerates, and all are candidates for the model; none is described, summarised or analysed. The consequence is that nothing can be said about who the 704 respondents were, and no confounding can be assessed - though the question is largely moot given that the outcome is computable from the inputs.

answers.title: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
answers.answer: Sex is reported per group and is badly imbalanced; everything else is absent. The autistic group is approximately 84% male and the comparison group 52% male, so the two classes differ by around 32 percentage points on a variable that directly shapes every input the model receives. The feature vector comprises 468 facial mesh points, 33 pose points and 42 hand landmark points, together with a mouth aspect ratio derived from lip geometry - facial morphology, body proportion and posture are all sex-linked from middle childhood, and a network given these coordinates could achieve substantial separation by distinguishing boys from girls without representing anything about autism. This is the same failure mode that a speech study charted elsewhere in this review exposed empirically, where sensitivity collapsed from 94.8% pooled to 43.6% for girls; here the imbalance is in the sample rather than in the evaluation, so it inflates rather than conceals. No sex-stratified analysis, adjustment or discussion appears. No age distribution by group is reported despite a 5-to-9 range in which facial and motor development changes markedly; no cognitive, language, socioeconomic or ancestry information exists; and comorbidity is not recorded. The landmark representation does control for one class of confound well - appearance, clothing, skin tone, lighting and room are all discarded before modelling - which makes the uncontrolled demographic variables the more conspicuous.

answers.title: Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of
answers.answer: Entirely absent, and acknowledged as such. No age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic, cognitive or comorbidity information exists for either image class, and the authors state plainly that age, gender and cultural background 'were not explicitly controlled'. Two consequences follow that the acknowledgement does not address. Facial classifiers key strongly on apparent age and on sex-linked morphology, and autism is diagnosed roughly four times more often in boys, so an unmeasured sex imbalance between a class harvested from autism-related sources and a class harvested elsewhere is a live and untestable alternative explanation for the reported 92%. And DeepFace, the feature extractor, is a face-recognition library whose embeddings are optimised to encode individual identity - which makes demographic attributes among the properties most strongly represented in the 100,352 features fed to the classifier. Comorbidity is a further specific gap here, since the paper's own second target is a comorbid condition whose prevalence in autism it puts at up to 45%, yet no comorbidity is recorded for any image.

answers.title: Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
answers.answer: Entirely absent. No age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic, cognitive or comorbidity information exists for either image class, and none could, given how the corpus was assembled. The omission is consequential because the study's own motivating claims are morphometric - upper-face breadth, eye spacing, nose length, mid-face proportions, philtrum prominence - and every one of these varies systematically with age, sex and ancestry. A model reading whole face crops from two internet-sourced folders has access to all three, and nothing reported allows any of them to be excluded as the operative signal.

answers.title: Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children
answers.answer: Absent, and identified as absent by the authors. No age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic, cognitive or comorbidity information exists for either corpus, and the limitations section names gender and ethnicity specifically as missing in a way that constrains generalisation. Two consequences go beyond what is acknowledged. Facial classifiers key strongly on apparent age and sex-linked morphology, and autism is diagnosed roughly four times more often in boys, so an unmeasured sex imbalance between a class harvested from autism-related sources and a class harvested elsewhere could produce the entire separation. And the paper's own motivating claim is morphological - that autistic children 'show morphological differences within their face' - which is precisely the kind of quantity that varies with age, sex and ancestry, none of which is recorded.

answers.title: Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy
answers.answer: Entirely absent, and unusually consequential here. No age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic, cognitive or comorbidity information is reported for either class. The mixed-source corpus makes ancestry a specific rather than generic concern: a Kaggle collection assembled from international web sources and a set of photographs from an autism centre in Semarang would be expected to differ systematically in ancestry, in camera and lighting, and in photographic convention, and the paper's own description of the extracted features - 'the shape of the face, the expression on it, and the texture of the skin' - names skin texture explicitly as something the network uses. Without a source-wise breakdown of the classes, none of this can be examined, and a source-held-out evaluation, which the mixed corpus would have made straightforward, is not performed.

answers.title: Diagnosing autism spectrum disorder based on eye tracking technology using deep learning models
answers.answer: Sparse and, where present, alarming. Table 2 reports sex and a single pooled mean age of 7.88 years - no SD, no range, no per-group age. Sex composition is 25 male / 4 female in ASD (86.2% male) versus 13 male / 17 female in TD (43.3% male), a 42.9-point gap. This is the largest sex imbalance in the review's charted corpus, exceeding the 32-point gap in local_4ceee075. Because sex systematically affects gaze behaviour towards faces, a classifier reading gaze coordinates can score highly by learning sex. No race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, language, geography or recruitment source is reported for either group.

answers.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Automated Machine Learning
answers.answer: Age band 2-4 years (recorded in months, no mean or SD); 434 male / 308 female overall with no per-class breakdown; jaundice at birth and family history of ASD recorded as binary fields. Nothing on socioeconomic status, urban/rural location, language, education or which rehabilitation centre each child came from - the last being important, since centre could act as a site effect in a dataset pooled across several centres. The paper does report a sex effect in the data (males give more positive Q-CHAT responses) and interprets it as males being more prone to autism, without considering respondent expectation or referral bias.

answers.title: Enhanced ASD detection using 3D facial landmark localization with convolutional shape appearance model and graph-randomized XGBoost
answers.answer: Table 1 presents an unusually complete-looking demographic breakdown: age bands 2-5 / 6-9 / 10-12 years (850 / 880 / 796), sex 1,340 male and 1,186 female, ethnicity Caucasian 750, Asian 620, African 530, Hispanic 370, Middle Eastern 156 and Indigenous 100, urban 1,480 versus rural 1,046, and a partition by facial structure variation into broad upper face 505, wide-set eyes 725, shorter middle face 625 and narrow jawline 671. Every row sums exactly to 2,526. None of this metadata exists in the cited Kaggle dataset, which distributes only two folders of JPEGs; the paper describes no annotation procedure, no rater, and no automatic estimator for age, ethnicity, urban/rural residence or facial morphology category. The table is presented as evidence that the dataset adequately reflects real-world diversity, minimizing biases in ASD classification. Assigning every one of 2,526 web-scraped photographs - including all 1,263 non-ASD ones - to one of four ASD-associated facial morphology categories is not a description of a dataset; it is an unsourced annotation layer that cannot be verified and that the study's own conclusions then rest on.

answers.title: Enhanced multilevel autism classification for children using eye-tracking and hybrid CNN-RNN deep learning models
answers.answer: Thin. Age is given only as the 8-12 eligibility band, with no mean, SD or per-class distribution. Sex is not reported at all - not even a total male/female count - despite forty children being individually recruited and consented. Nothing on socioeconomic status, language, verbal ability or schooling level, and no per-severity-class characteristics of any kind. The Gesell Developmental Scale is said to have been used to relate eye-tracking data to behavioural and clinical outcomes, but no GDS number appears anywhere in the article.

answers.title: Ensemble of Deep Learning with Crested Porcupine Optimizer Based Autism
answers.answer: None whatsoever. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography, socioeconomic status or recruitment source - the dataset carries none and the paper requests none. This is notable in comparison with local_986436f2, which reused a sibling of the same corpus and supplied an elaborate demographic table that the data cannot support; here the same absence is simply left unremarked. The abstract's claim about the facial evolution of newborns with ASD is particularly untethered, since nothing in the data identifies any subject's age, let alone a neonate.

answers.title: Explainable and secure framework for autism prediction using multimodal eye tracking and kinematic data
answers.answer: None. Not a single demographic characteristic is reported for the 44 people - no age, sex, ethnicity, geography, language or clinical background. This is a striking omission in a paper whose entire argument concerns the responsible, privacy-preserving handling of sensitive personal health data: the study invokes GDPR and HIPAA in its abbreviation table while reporting nothing at all about the individuals whose data it processes, and without asking whether they consented to this reuse.

answers.title: Facial Images Dataset for Early Screening of Autism Children Using Convolutional Neural Network
answers.answer: Thin, and internally inconsistent where present. Age is given as 3 to 14 years in the acquisition narrative and 5 to 15 years in Table I and again in the results; no mean, SD or per-group distribution is provided. Sex is not reported at all. No socioeconomic, ethnic, linguistic or verbal-ability information. The exclusion criteria are unusually explicit for this corpus - children with colds, diarrhoea, lung infections, epilepsy or flu were excluded from both groups, and autistic participants with intellectual disability, cerebral palsy or Down syndrome were excluded - which controls the sample tightly but also removes the co-occurring conditions most likely to be present in a real screening population and narrows the autistic group to those without intellectual disability.

answers.title: Improving Early Autism Detection with Chi-Square Feature Selection, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI
answers.answer: Almost none reported, though several demographic variables are present in the data and used as predictors. Age is given only as the dataset's 12-36 month scope. Sex, ethnicity and region exist as columns - sex and jaundice are named in the SHAP analysis as low-importance features - but no counts, proportions or distributions are printed for any of them, and no subgroup breakdown is performed. Ethnicity and region are label-encoded into ordinal integers, a transformation that imposes an arbitrary ordering on nominal categories and is not discussed.

answers.title: Novel Framework for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification and Tailored Education With Effective Data Mining and Ensemble Learning Techniques
answers.answer: None reported. Gender is present as a variable and is named as a factor in the Phase II rationale; ethnicity, region and jaundice exist as columns; no counts, proportions or distributions are printed for any of them. The absence of a regional breakdown is the notable one, since regional diversity is the stated reason for merging the two datasets and the merged column would have made a two-cohort comparison immediate.

answers.title: Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach
answers.answer: Better than most of the branch, though still descriptive only. Age averages 25 to 28 months with a note that labelled cases rise between 25 and 30 months and become more noticeable by 35-36 months. Sex is given only as 69.7% male within the autism group, with no control-group figure. Ethnicity is reported across eleven groups with White Europeans most represented followed by Asians, and the paper states there were no significant ethnic differences in diagnosis rates - the one ethnicity analysis in this branch. Jaundice, family history and respondent type are present. No performance is broken down by any of these, so the demographic detail informs the sample description but not the evaluation.

answers.title: Predicting autistic traits, anxiety and depression symptoms using camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (CAT-Q-ES): A machine learning study
answers.answer: The most complete demographic and clinical reporting in the corpus. Age by group with means, SDs and a tested 2.7-year difference with effect size and confidence interval; mean age at autism diagnosis (32.0 years, SD 12.3); self-reported gender in three categories with between-group tests; full education distribution from no studies to PhD for both groups; and a complete self-reported comorbidity table covering high abilities, ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, specific learning disorder, epilepsy, bipolar disorder, eating disorder, anxiety, depression and sleep disorder, with percentages for both groups. Nationality/residence is stated (Spain). The women-heavy composition (78% overall) is not merely reported but explained and named as the study's most notable limitation, with a mechanism offered - the parent project validates an instrument designed for highly masked autistic adults, especially women, and online studies skew toward respondents with topic interest, higher cognitive ability and moderate-to-high socioeconomic status.

answers.title: A Computational Method for Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Deep Learning Approach
answers.answer: None. The dataset is asserted to cover diverse demographics and the model is claimed to address demographic variability, but no age, sex, ethnicity, geography or recruitment information exists for any image and none is reported. The diversity claim is therefore unverifiable, and the paper's stated advance over prior work on limited generalizability across diverse demographics rests on it.

answers.title: Early Detection of ASD from Facial Images Using DeepDeblur and Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network
answers.answer: None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography, socioeconomic status or recruitment source for any image, and no acknowledgement that this information is absent. One of the studies the paper summarises in its own literature review notes that model reliability depends on dataset quality and race factors, so the concern is present in the article's field of view and is not applied to its own data.

answers.title: Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI
answers.answer: Variables are present but distributions are not. Age spans 1-18 years with no mean or SD; sex is coded M/F with no counts; ethnicity is coded across 11 categories (Asian, Black, Hispanic, Latino, Middle Eastern, Mixed, Native Indian, Others, Pacifica, South Asian, White European) with no counts; family history and rater type (family member, healthcare professional, other) are recorded. Seven comorbidity flags are retained as model inputs - speech/language delay, learning disorder, genetic disorders, depression, global developmental delay/intellectual disability, social/behavioural issues, anxiety disorder - and not one prevalence figure is given for any of them. The dataset is described as comprehensively capturing socioeconomic status, but no socioeconomic variable appears in either variable table.

answers.title: Using explainable machine learning and eye-tracking for diagnosing autism spectrum and developmental language disorders in social attention tasks
answers.answer: Among the most complete in the corpus, and reported with statistical tests. Age: TD 53.23 (SD 10.04), ASD 53.50 (10.35), DLD 54.0 (12.14) months, F(2,90)=0.041, p=0.959 - the groups are closely matched on age, which is uncommon here and is demonstrated rather than asserted. Sex: TD 22 boys/22 girls, ASD 22/2, DLD 23/2, chi-squared 20.15, p<0.01 - a large and explicitly tested imbalance which the authors attribute to the higher prevalence of both conditions in males. Basic attention: 87.09 / 73.50 / 73.08, F=13.23, p<0.01. PPVT-III receptive vocabulary standard score: 108.75 / 98.65 / 86.57, F=19.56, p<0.01. Nothing on ethnicity, socioeconomic status or language background. The sex and vocabulary differences matter for the classification results and are not carried into the modelling as covariates.

answers.title: Utilizing deep learning models in an intelligent eye-tracking system for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis
answers.answer: None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography or recruitment source for any image, and no acknowledgement that this information is absent - despite the introduction discussing sex ratios in ASD prevalence and noting that girls with ASD often have fewer observable symptoms, a point directly relevant to a dataset whose sex composition is unknown.

answers.title: A novel hybrid deep learning model using MEResNext for autism spectrum disorder detection
answers.answer: None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography, socioeconomic status or recruitment information, and no acknowledgement that any of it is missing.

answers.title: An assessment of autistic and parkinsonian movement profiles to inform selective classification algorithms
answers.answer: The most complete adult-sample reporting in the corpus, with formal matching tests. Gender is matched across groups (chi-squared(4)=3.25, ns) and the autistic sample is close to sex-balanced at 14M/16F/1 other - a composition no other autism study in this review achieves. Age: ASD 55.52 (8.01), PD 63.16 (7.60), CTRL 59.00 (9.96); both clinical groups matched to controls but ASD and PD not matched to each other (p<0.001), which the authors handle by entering age as a control variable and residualising it from the classification inputs. Non-verbal reasoning (MaRs-IB) is matched. Depression and anxiety differ significantly and are controlled for. Years since diagnosis, psychoactive medication use, and UPDRS, RAADS and AQ trait scores are all reported by group with post-hoc comparisons.

answers.title: An explainable deep learning framework for screening level autism severity using behavioural data
answers.answer: Almost none, and by deliberate removal. Age is retained as a continuous normalised feature and cohort membership is preserved through stratified merging, but ethnicity, country of residence, who completed the test and whether the app had been used before were all excluded during feature pruning as low-variance, irrelevant or metadata noise, on the stated ground of eliminating demographic skew. Sex is not reported anywhere. The consequence is that no subgroup analysis by sex, ethnicity or respondent type is possible, and the fairness across populations named in the future-work section cannot be assessed in the present study - the variables required for it were removed.

answers.title: An explainable machine unlearning algorithm framework for early detection of autism spectrum disorder and brain disabilities in newborns
answers.answer: None. No sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic or geographic information for any dataset. Age is reported three incompatible ways: newborns aged 0 to 36 months in the title and abstract, children aged 12-36 months in the MRI inclusion criteria, and aged 3-6 years in the CSBS description. Since the paper's central claim is that existing tools are restricted to toddlers above 18 months and that it addresses the gap in newborns, the age of the analysed population is the single most consequential fact in the study and it is stated three different ways.

answers.title: Deep learning based approach for Behavior classification in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder using naturalistic videos
answers.answer: None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography or setting information for any child. The videos are consumer home recordings of unknown provenance, and the paper does not report even the age range of the children whose behaviour it classifies.

answers.title: Explainable Children Autism Detection using Gaze Features in Audio-Visual Speech Comprehension
answers.answer: Well reported for the variables collected. Group sizes, mean ages with standard deviations, SCQ, KBIT-2 nonverbal intelligence and PPVT-III receptive vocabulary are all tabulated by group, and the pattern is described accurately: nonverbal intelligence comparable across groups (104.3 versus 108.78) while the ASD group shows higher SCQ (12.6 versus 4.7) and markedly lower receptive vocabulary (50.0 versus 67.3). Sex is not reported. Two features deserve note for interpretation. The ASD group's age variability is more than double the comparison group's (SD 19.4 versus 8.8 months), and the receptive-vocabulary gap is large and not adjusted for in the models - in a task whose stimulus is a narrated story, receptive vocabulary is a plausible driver of where a child looks. The paper does address linguistic background separately, devoting a discussion section to the Castilian/Valencian bilingual environment of the recordings.

answers.title: Explainable Ensemble Learning Framework for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Enhancing Trust, Interpretability and Reliability in AI-Driven Healthcare
answers.answer: Thin for Dataset 1 and absent for Dataset 2. Dataset 1 lists age, sex, ethnicity, jaundice and family history among its features and reports none of their distributions; seven comorbidity indicators are similarly listed as features with no prevalences. Dataset 2 reports no demographic information of any kind for its 100 clinical samples, despite claiming IRB approval and caregiver consent for their collection.

answers.title: Finding the forest in the trees: Using machine learning and online cognitive and perceptual measures to predict adult autism diagnosis
answers.answer: Complete and analytically load-bearing. Age, gender, ICAR-16 abbreviated IQ, AQ total and age at diagnosis are tabulated for both samples with means, standard deviations and Mann-Whitney tests. The full sample carries large group differences in age (44.2 versus 32.2 years) and gender (71.0% versus 48.9% women), both significant at p<0.001; the matched subsample is exact on both. Cognitive ability is matched in both samples (ICAR 0.54 versus 0.53). The autistic sample is 71% women and late-diagnosed at a mean of 35.6 years - a demographic profile that is the opposite of almost every other autism study in this corpus, and one the paper identifies as particularly difficult to identify. Nothing on ethnicity or socioeconomic status.

answers.title: Hybrid ensemble learning for Autism Spectrum Disorder screening using eye-tracking scanpath
answers.answer: None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography, cognitive ability or recruitment information for any of the 28 participants, and no acknowledgement that this information is absent. The paper's own discussion notes that generalisation across demographics and hardware platforms remains a pressing issue in this literature - a concern it identifies and then cannot address, because it reports no demographic variable at all.

answers.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Facial Images and AI-Based Deep Learning Models
answers.answer: None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography or recruitment information for any image, and no acknowledgement of the absence - although the paper's own literature table repeatedly lists limited dataset diversity and poor generalization as limitations of prior studies using the same kind of data.

answers.title: Multimodal fusion of deep transfer learning with wavelet neural network for autism spectrum disorder detection using facial images
answers.answer: None reported, and the paper is one of the few in this branch to say so and to explain why it matters: expression patterns and facial morphology differ across demographic factors, and because the dataset carries no such information, their influence on ASD classification and on facial-feature learning cannot be clearly examined. That is an accurate statement of the branch's central data problem, made by a study that then proceeds anyway.

answers.title: SHAP-based explainable AI framework for autism severity classification using 3D motor biomarkers
answers.answer: Not reported in the extracted text - no age, sex, ethnicity or socioeconomic information for any of the 109 children. The author names this as a gap prospectively rather than leaving it implicit, listing age groups, genders and cultural backgrounds among the dimensions on which generalisation must be tested in future work.

answers.title: Screening autism spectrum
answers.answer: The most complete demographic reporting in the speech branch. Sex, participant counts, mean ages, total words and mean and median utterance lengths are tabulated by group and by sex for both corpora, and Eigsti's ethnic composition is given. That reporting is what makes the study's central confound visible: in the Nadig corpus the typically developing children have mean ages of 29 and 34 months while the ASD children have mean ages of 61 and 53 months, a gap of roughly two years, and the ASD group is 83% male against 58% in the TD group. The authors note the age difference explicitly, attributing it to the significant language delays typically observed in children with ASD - but they then include age in the feature set.

answers.title: Towards screening of children students with autism spectrum disorder based on executive functions with serious game and machine learning approaches
answers.answer: Age is reported and controlled by design - children were organised into groups G3, G4 and G5 by age, and the ASD and control groups were matched across those bands specifically to make the samples more homogeneous. Sex is not reported. Nothing on socioeconomic status or ethnicity, though the school-based recruitment in a Brazilian public inclusive-education setting is described. Guardians completed a behavioural anamnesis questionnaire whose contents are not reported.

questions.question_text: How is autism diagnosed or confirmed (which standardized instruments, criteria, assessors)?

answers.title: Very early detection of Autism Spectrum Disorders based on acoustic analysis of pre-verbal vocalizations of 18-month old toddlers
answers.answer: Blinded experienced clinician at age three using medical history, ADOS and ADI-R; ADOS Module 1 sessions also provided the recordings.

answers.title: Use of Machine Learning to Identify Children with Autism and Their Motor Abnormalities
answers.answer: DSM-IV-TR diagnosis by a child neuropsychiatrist specialised in autism, independently confirmed by a child psychologist via direct observation and parent discussion. ADOS was administered to only 7 of the 15 ASD children, so the gold-standard instrument does not cover the whole clinical sample.

answers.title: ADHD and ASD Classification Based on Emotion Recognition Data
answers.answer: ASD: DSM-IV-R diagnostic criteria. ADHD: Turkish version of K-SADS-PL. Both applied at the Marmara University Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Outpatient Department under the supervision of the department head. No ADOS or ADI-R.

answers.title: Identifying children with autism spectrum disorder based on their face processing abnormality: A machine learning framework
answers.answer: Diagnosis by experienced clinicians against DSM-IV criteria, confirmed with the Chinese AQ-Child. The authors explicitly state that ADI-R and ADOS were unavailable to them - so no gold-standard observational instrument was used.

answers.title: Semantic mapping reveals distinct patterns in descriptions of social relations in adults with autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: DSM-IV criteria for Asperger's Disorder, high-functioning autism or PDD-NOS with IQ >= 70, assessed at an academic developmental neuropsychiatry clinic. ADOS was administered (group mean 12.40, SD 3.89) and the SCL-90 was used to exclude other DSM-IV diagnoses. This is one of the better-specified diagnostic pipelines in the corpus.

answers.title: Toward the Autism Motor Signature: Gesture patterns during smart tablet gameplay identify children with autism
answers.answer: Clinical diagnosis of Childhood Autism per ICD-10 (2010 Edition) by medical practitioners in specialist clinics, with a clinician questionnaire on symptom severity and intellectual/social functioning; children with uncertain diagnosis were excluded. No ADOS, ADI-R or other standardised observational instrument was used - a notable weakness given the strength of the rest of the design.

answers.title: Applying machine learning to identify autistic adults using imitation: An exploratory study
answers.answer: Not reported in this paper. The ASC participants come from a previously published experiment and no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or confirmation procedure is described - the reader is referred to the source publication. Given that diagnostic status is the classification target, this is the study's most significant reporting gap.

answers.title: Automatic Detection of ADHD and ASD from Expressive Behaviour in RGBD Data
answers.answer: Clinical groups: prior clinical diagnosis of ADHD and/or ASD, recruited through the Nottingham City Asperger Service and ADHD Clinic; the diagnostic instruments and criteria behind those prior diagnoses are not described. Controls: actively screened out using two validated instruments with stated thresholds - Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale Part A (threshold 4) and AQ-10 (threshold 6). The control screening is more rigorously specified than the case ascertainment, which is the reverse of the usual pattern in this corpus.

answers.title: Earlier identification of children with autism
answers.answer: ASD diagnosis at 3 years of age using DSM-5 criteria within the EASE longitudinal cohort; TD status confirmed by normal outcome at the same 3-year assessment. The specific instruments used at the 3-year assessment are not named in this paper. Group membership was withheld from the annotator during segmentation.

answers.title: Speech-based Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Condition by Generative
answers.answer: Clinical diagnosis under DSM-IV criteria in two university departments of child and adolescent psychiatry in Paris. Control status established by teacher questionnaire excluding learning disorders. No standardised autism instrument (no ADOS, ADI-R or questionnaire measure) is reported, and no inter-rater reliability is given for the clinical diagnoses that serve as ground truth for a four-way task.

answers.title: ANN and SVM Classifiers in Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorder Gait Based on Three-Dimensional Ground Reaction Forces
answers.answer: Not reported. Participants are described only as 'previously diagnosed with a mild category of ASD' with no instrument, diagnostic criteria, diagnosing clinician or confirmation procedure named. Control status is asserted rather than screened. Since diagnostic label is the classification target, this is the study's most serious reporting gap.

answers.title: Analyzing Human-Robot Interaction Using Machine Vision for Autism screening
answers.answer: Diagnosis by a clinical team - a developmental-behavioural pediatrician and a child psychologist - with a child psychiatrist validating the psychologist's initial evaluation. This multi-clinician process is described in more detail than most corpus studies, but no standardised instrument is named (no ADOS, ADI-R, GARS or SCQ), despite the introduction reviewing exactly such instruments. Control status was established by attendance at mainstream daycare and absence of observed cognitive deficit, with no screening instrument.

answers.title: Applying Eye Tracking to Identify Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children
answers.answer: DSM-5 diagnosis by experienced physicians plus a CARS score above 30 as an explicit inclusion criterion. The authors state directly that ADI-R and ADOS were unavailable in China and list the absence of confirmation with validated diagnostic instruments as their first limitation - an unusually forthright acknowledgement. Controls were screened by a licensed physician to exclude any psychiatric or neurological history including ASD, which is a stronger control-status procedure than most corpus studies.

answers.title: Automatic Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Everyday
answers.answer: Not reported at all. Children are described as 'diagnosed with ASD' with no instrument, no criteria, no diagnosing professional and no date. TD status is asserted without any screening. At-risk status is defined purely by sibling relationship. Given that diagnostic label is the classification target and the paper proposes a screening tool, the complete absence of reference-standard information is the study's most serious gap.

answers.title: Detecting Autism Based on Eye-Tracking Data from Web Searching
answers.answer: A confirmed clinical diagnosis of autism 'as verified by the charity organisation' through which participants were recruited - no instrument, criteria or clinician is named, and verification is delegated to a third-party organisation. By contrast, control status is established rigorously with the Autism Quotient, with an explicit threshold (none above 32) and a rationale (the AQ is used by UK general practitioners as pre-referral screening). As in several other corpus studies, the control ascertainment is better specified than the case ascertainment.

answers.title: Video Gesture Analysis for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
answers.answer: DSM-5 criteria, with both ADOS-2 and ADI-R administered by two experienced professionals. This is the most complete diagnostic ascertainment encountered in the corpus to date - the two instruments that the literature identifies as having the highest sensitivity and specificity, both applied, by two independent experienced assessors.

answers.title: A Novel Eye Movement Data Transformation Technique that Preserves Temporal Information: A Demonstration in a Face Processing Task
answers.answer: Among the strongest in the corpus: all ASD participants had prior clinical diagnoses under WHO ICD-10 criteria, and all diagnoses were additionally confirmed by the research team using ADOS-2, described accurately as 'a standardized, validated instrument for the assessment of autism spectrum conditions'. Control status was established by absence of any history of autism spectrum or other neurodevelopmental disorders. Independent re-confirmation with a gold-standard instrument, rather than reliance on prior diagnosis alone, is uncommon here.

answers.title: Applying Machine Learning to Identify Autism With Restricted Kinematic Features
answers.answer: Confirmed diagnosis of high-functioning autism by a licensed psychiatrist using DSM-IV criteria, with Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices confirming average non-verbal intellectual ability and explicit exclusion of ADHD, intellectual disability and schizophrenia. No ADOS or ADI-R. The exclusion of common comorbidities is unusually explicit and is a design strength for internal validity, though it narrows the population.

answers.title: Automatic Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Acoustic and Text Features from Brief Natural Conversations
answers.answer: The strongest reference standard in the corpus: diagnoses were confirmed for the ASD group and ruled out for the TD group using the Clinical Best Estimate process informed by ADOS-2 and adhering to DSM-5 criteria. Crucially the same rigorous process was applied to controls, not just cases - the inverse of the common corpus pattern where control screening is better specified than case ascertainment. Symptom severity was additionally characterised with ADOS-2 Calibrated Severity Scores and the Social Communication Questionnaire for both groups.

answers.title: Classifying Individuals with ASD Through Facial Emotion Recognition and Eye-Tracking
answers.answer: Diagnosis based on testing with standardized instruments, review of diagnostic history and prior evaluations, and DSM criteria confirmed by clinical research staff - a multi-source ascertainment described in more procedural detail than most corpus studies, though the specific instruments are not named. Control status established by requiring no psychiatric history, no developmental delay and no previous special education.

answers.title: Detecting Developmental Delay and Autism Through Machine
answers.answer: MCHAT (Bangla version) administered to all children, followed by clinical evaluation by a developmental psychologist and a child health physician to assign ASD, SLC or TD. ADOS was administered to only 28 of 50 ASD children, with the reason given explicitly - families could not commit the time required, 'a common problem for families in low-resource areas'. This partial gold-standard coverage is disclosed transparently and is itself an informative observation about diagnostic feasibility in the target setting. MCHAT scores are reported per group (13.5 ASD, 2 TD, 0.08 SLC), giving some quantitative separation.

answers.title: Exploiting Visual Behaviour for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification
answers.answer: Not reported. Class labels are inherited from the Saliency4ASD challenge dataset with no description of how the original diagnoses were established, what instruments were used, or how typically developing status was confirmed.

answers.title: Hierarchical POMDP Framework for a Robot-Assisted ASD Diagnostic Protocol
answers.answer: Not reported. Children are described as 'already diagnosed with ASD' with no instrument, criteria, clinician or date, and typically developing status is asserted without screening. The protocol tasks are modelled on ADOS, but ADOS itself was not administered as a reference standard. Instead, the validation comparator is a post-hoc expert judgement of behaviour from de-identified transcripts - which is a reasonable choice given the authors' observation that behaviour and diagnosis diverged, but it means no gold-standard diagnostic anchor exists in the study.

answers.title: Intelligent Gaze-Based Screening System for Autism
answers.answer: Not reported. No diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or confirmation procedure is described for the ASD group, and typically developing status is asserted without any screening. Since diagnostic label is the classification target and the paper proposes a clinical screening tool, the complete absence of reference-standard information is disqualifying for any diagnostic-accuracy claim.

answers.title: Kinematic features of a simple and short movement task to predict autism diagnosis
answers.answer: Not reported. Participants are described simply as autistic adults with no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or verification procedure named, and control status is asserted without screening. Given that diagnosis is the prediction target, this is the study's principal reporting gap - though the same research group's companion 2020 paper documents its ascertainment more fully.

answers.title: Learning to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder based on the Visual
answers.answer: ASD-diagnosed children were examined in multidisciplinary ASD specialty clinics, with autism intensity rated by psychologists using CARS. Typically developing status rests on recruitment from mainstream schools plus careful consideration of parental reports of any possible concerns. No ADOS, ADI-R or structured screening instrument is used, and CARS serves both as the severity measure and, implicitly, as part of the diagnostic characterisation - which matters because CARS bands are later used as the multi-label prediction target.

answers.title: Machine Learning to Study Social Interaction Difficulties in ASD
answers.answer: Diagnosis confirmed independently by two medical specialists in clinical interviews according to ICD-10 criteria, supplemented by extensive neuropsychological examination, with the sample restricted to F84.0 high-functioning autism and F84.5 Asperger syndrome. Independent double confirmation by two specialists is stronger than most corpus studies, though no standardised observational instrument is named. Control status is asserted with no screening instrument reported.

answers.title: Phase 3 diagnostic evaluation of a smart
answers.answer: Clinical diagnosis of autism made independently of the study on DSM-5 criteria or the equivalent ICD-10 framework, against which the algorithm's blinded classification will be compared once data collection closes. Two features distinguish this from every other reference standard in the review. The comparison is prospective and blinded - the classifier is locked and applied to data 'obtained independently of the Play.Care software engineers and commercial concerns', with results embargoed until collection is complete - so the index test cannot be tuned to the labels. And the standard is supplemented rather than replaced by questionnaire data: SDQ, ESSENCE and an adaptive behaviour scale are collected for both clinical cohorts, so a positive or negative classification can be examined against symptom breadth and adaptive functioning rather than only against a binary label.

answers.title: Predicting Autism Diagnosis using Image with Fixations and Synthetic Saccade Patterns
answers.answer: Not reported. Class labels are inherited from the Saliency4ASD challenge dataset with no description of diagnostic instrument, criteria or procedure for either group.

answers.title: Recognition Of Atypical Behavior In Autism Diagnosis From Video Using Pose Estimation Over Time
answers.answer: Not reported at participant level. Expert physicians reviewed videos through the NODA platform and tagged time stamps as typical or atypical behaviour, and each video is stated to have been 'annotated by several expert physicians' - but no diagnostic instrument, criteria, or per-child diagnostic outcome is described, and no inter-rater agreement statistic is given despite multiple annotators. The ground truth for classification is therefore expert behavioural judgement rather than diagnosis.

answers.title: Robot-Assisted Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Based on Artificial Reasoning
answers.answer: None, and the paper says so rather than implying otherwise. The index group comprises 'three children without confirmed ASD diagnosis, but with evidence of risk factors', with the risk factors unspecified and no instrument, screening tool or clinician assessment reported; the comparison group is described as typically developing with no screening procedure. This is a genuinely undetermined diagnostic status on both sides, which the study handles by making no diagnostic claim - it reports a behavioural pattern difference and suggests it 'can be used as evidence to improve the ASD diagnosis' rather than asserting that the groups were correctly separated. For the review the relevant observation is that the transparency is a virtue while the underlying limitation is severe: a behavioural difference between three children with unspecified risk factors and three children of unverified typical development cannot support an inference about autism, and the paper's proof-of-concept framing is the correct standing for it.

answers.title: SP-ASDNet: CNN-LSTM Based ASD Classification Model using Observer ScanPaths
answers.answer: Not reported. Class labels are inherited from the Saliency4ASD challenge dataset with no description of how diagnoses were established or how typically developing status was confirmed.

answers.title: Social robot in diagnosis of autism among preschool children
answers.answer: Not described in the retrieved text. Children were recruited through an integrative kindergarten and are stated to have autism, with no instrument, criteria, clinician or date given. The group's 2022 study on a related sample reports that diagnoses were delivered by a multidisciplinary team of a psychiatrist, a psychologist and a pedagogue and recorded in kindergarten files, which is likely the same route; if so the underlying ascertainment is genuine clinical judgement, well above the folder-membership and questionnaire-threshold labels charted elsewhere in this review. As reported here, however, the standard is undocumented. The absence matters less than usual because the study makes no diagnostic claim - it does not attempt to distinguish autistic from non-autistic children, and its within-subject finding does not depend on the label being correct for any classification purpose.

answers.title: Application of the Still-Face Paradigm in Early Screening for High-Risk Autism Spectrum Disorder in Infants and Toddlers
answers.answer: The strongest ascertainment in the corpus's infant-screening strand, because it is prospective rather than concurrent. Entry to the high-risk group required a positive M-CHAT plus a pediatric psychiatrist's judgement that the child met DSM-5 core criteria while under 24 months. At 2 years every high-risk child was re-evaluated with both the ADI-R and the ADOS, and clinically diagnosed by two pediatric psychiatrists against DSM-5; all confirmed cases reached cut-off on both instruments. Exclusions removed Rett syndrome, fragile X, isolated language disorder, intellectual disability, craniocerebral trauma and neurological illness. Typically developing status rests on exclusion criteria plus Gesell assessment rather than a positive screen.

answers.title: Applying Machine Learning to Kinematic and Eye Movement Features of a Movement Imitation Task to Predict Autism Diagnosis
answers.answer: Not described in this paper. The experimental protocol, stimuli and by implication the diagnostic ascertainment are referred to a prior publication by Gowen et al. This is the study's principal reporting gap - as with the same group's 2019 paper, the diagnostic basis for the class labels is not stated in the analysis paper itself.

answers.title: Research and Design of Autism Smart Diagnosis Information System Based on Chinese Children's Facial Expression Data and Deep Convolution Neural Network
answers.answer: One sentence: 'The selected children with autism were diagnosed by a professional physician.' No instrument, criteria, date or diagnostician detail. The paper describes ICD-10, DSM-IV, ABC, CARS and CABS as the instruments the collaborating hospitals use, and analyses their facial-expression-related items in detail to motivate the design, but does not state which if any were applied to these ten children. Typically developing status rests entirely on parents answering that their child had no history of autism.

answers.title: Automated identification of postural control for children with autism spectrum disorder using a machine learning approach
answers.answer: A prior diagnosis of ASD by a physician or a licensed psychologist was an inclusion criterion, but no diagnostic instrument, criteria or confirmation procedure is described, and no autism-trait screening was applied to controls. Two further inclusion requirements - the ability to understand and communicate with examiners and the ability to perform the required tasks - restrict the ASD sample to children who could follow standing instructions, which bounds generalisability toward more able children.

answers.title: Behavior-based Risk Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through
answers.answer: Not reported. No diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or confirmation procedure is described for the ASD group, and typically developing status is asserted without screening. Given that diagnostic label is the classification target, this is the study's most fundamental reporting gap, though it is partly a consequence of the two-page format.

answers.title: Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation as a Scalable Method for Distinguishing Children With Autism
answers.answer: The most complete diagnostic ascertainment in the corpus alongside Cho et al. (2019): DSM-5 criteria confirmed on site by research-reliable assessors using ADOS-2 (module 3 for all participants, ensuring comparability), the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised, and the parent-report SRS-2. Using all three of the field's principal instruments, applied by research-reliable assessors, and standardising the ADOS module across participants, is a materially stronger reference standard than the 'prior clinical diagnosis' that most of this corpus relies on.

answers.title: Deep-Learning-Based Detection of Infants with Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Auto-Encoder Feature Representation
answers.answer: The most thorough in the corpus. Every participant was assessed with seven instruments: ADOS-2, ADI-R, BeDevel-Interview, BeDevel-Play, K-CARS (refined from CARS-2), the Social Communication Questionnaire and the Social Responsiveness Scale. The final diagnosis was the best clinical estimate by a licensed child psychiatrist against DSM-5 criteria using all available information.
