Main findings: conventional classifiers performed at or near chance on the original images (deep SVM AUC 51.50%, decision jungle 60.40%, boosted decision tree 67.60%); the convolutional network reached AUC 78.00% on the same images; rotation augmentation raised the network to AUC 97.00%, which the authors attribute to data contamination; and the participant-level subset of 59 images evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation yielded 72.88% accuracy with sensitivity 58.62% and specificity 86.67%.

answers.title: Machine learning models using mobile game play accurately classify children with autism
answers.answer: Goal: determine whether the GuessWhat game generates a signal separating autistic from neurotypical children using only objective gameplay metadata, as a step toward an easily deployed remote screening tool. Main findings: AU-ROC 0.745 with recall 0.769 for the best model (random forest on duration features); duration features significantly more important than accuracy features (t = 5.15, p = 1e-5); accuracy features uninformative because they cluster at ceiling in both groups; three of four classifiers improved or held when accuracy features were removed; and disgust, surprise and sadness prompts carried the most importance among duration features.

answers.title: Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction
answers.answer: Goal: compare three acoustic feature constructions derived from time-frequency ICA for distinguishing autistic from comparison children's speech. Main findings: unmixing-matrix features reached 98.51% accuracy with SVM and 95.59% with CNN; separated frequency-point sequences reached only 59.71% and 55.19%, this being the best of 256 sequences; cepstral features on separated signals reached 91.00-92.89% with SVM, with PLP best and MFCC worst; and SVM outperformed CNN under every condition, which the authors attribute to the small dataset.

answers.title: The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation
answers.answer: Goal: build an end-to-end system that locates child speech within a full ADOS recording and estimates autism severity from it, and determine whether automatic diarization can replace manual annotation. Main findings: MFCC-plus-pitch diarization achieved a 26.91% diarization error rate against x-vectors' 89.84% child-segment accuracy; severity estimation reached Pearson R 0.606 +/- 0.099 with NRMSE 0.248 with automatic diarization, against 0.567 +/- 0.120 and 0.261 with manual segmentation; and automatic diarization therefore matched or slightly exceeded manual annotation, which the authors attribute to imperfect manual labelling of quiet child speech in a reverberant room.

answers.title: The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children
answers.answer: The aim is to test whether a dyadic game with a social robot can elicit and reveal turn-taking deficits, as a step toward a robot-enabled diagnostic aid. Five autistic and five typically developing preschoolers each played 'Touch me' and 'Dance with me' with a NAO robot for about five minutes per game, and six raters from special education scored their behaviour from video on a purpose-built scale. Autistic children produced significantly fewer turn-taking behaviours in both scenarios, and group differences also appeared on interest in the robot and on additional movements. Inter-rater reliability was satisfactory (Kendall's W = 0.65, p < 0.001) with subscale alpha 0.77. The study's contribution is the paradigm and its validation rather than a detection result: no model is fitted, no child is assigned a predicted class, and no accuracy is computed or claimed. The authors state the intended use precisely - 'If a specialist has a sense of how a typical child plays with NAO, then they will be able to see possible deficits in the turn-taking of a child with autism by observing him/her' - which is a claim about calibrating human observation, not about automating it.

answers.title: Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach
answers.answer: Two stated goals: first, to test whether gaze behaviour segments produced by autistic and TD children can be classified by machine learning; second, to test whether children themselves can be classified from the proportion of their segments the model labels ASD-like. The framing is explicitly novelty-driven - the authors assert that prior eye-tracking ML studies all extracted features from visual fixation patterns and that 'no study has been found to identify ASD with oculomotor behavior', drawing a conceptual distinction between where attention is directed (fixation) and how the eyes move in the sockets (oculomotor). Findings: segment classification peaked at 74.15% (9 s windows, single feature: entropy of gaze allocation in the x-y plane, sensitivity 75.45%, specificity 72.51%), above the majority-class baseline at every window length; child classification peaked at 87.18% (7 s windows, 46% threshold, sensitivity 89.47%, specificity 85.00%). Feature-level statistics show entropy differences significant at every window length from 1 to 10 s (all p <= .006 for the x-y plane), while range differences are significant only at the shortest windows and fall away beyond 4 s - so the discriminative signal is the irregularity of gaze allocation, not its spatial extent. Secondary observation of substantive interest: ASD children took 191 s to complete the same six-question session against 110 s for TD children (U = 48, p < .01).

answers.title: A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features
answers.answer: Goal: to extend the group's existing accelerometer-only sensorized toy car by adding wheel shaft encoders, testing whether autistic children's documented interest in rotating objects can be captured as a second sensing modality and whether fusing it with movement features improves screening accuracy. The comparison is deliberately internal - the authors state they do not wish to compare their accuracy against other modalities in the literature, only against their own version 1. Findings: the reimplemented accelerometer-only baseline achieved 71.11% accuracy on the new data (lower than the 85% reported for version 1, attributed to different data, different collection setup and a from-scratch reimplementation); adding encoder features gave 78.61%; adding new roll/pitch acceleration features instead gave 75.83%; adding both gave 85.56% with sensitivity 81.67%, specificity 81.00% and precision 87.67% - the claimed improvement of more than 10 percentage points over baseline. Of the ten features surviving two rounds of backward elimination, three came from the encoders: the ratio of wheels-only play to total playtime, the not-playing ratio, and the total wheel turn rate. A secondary and arguably more informative finding is that random forest on the full feature set gave lower accuracy (80.83%) but the best sensitivity and specificity of any configuration (85.48%, 83.67%), which the authors flag as a reason a deployer might prefer it - a rare instance in this corpus of explicitly preferring a model on error-profile grounds rather than on headline accuracy.

answers.title: A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities
answers.answer: Goal: to move beyond descriptive comparison of touchscreen motion features - which the group's own earlier work (Simeoli et al., 2020) had found insufficient to distinguish the groups significantly - by using a variational autoencoder to learn a low-dimensional latent distribution of movement, and then to interrogate that latent space to identify which kinematic features drive classification and at what values. The framing is explicitly dual: not merely a diagnostic classifier but 'a new quantitative method to assess ASD', with the theoretical grounding in embodied cognition and predictive coding and the claim that motor abnormality is an underrated defining feature of autism. Findings: task-level cross-validated accuracy 91.2% +/- 5.6%; a latent space in which the two groups occupy distinct, approximately Gaussian regions, with cleaner separation when participants are plotted as the mean of their 25 tasks than task by task; latent structure stable across initialisations up to rotation; and, from Monte Carlo perturbation of one feature at a time, the finding that sdSpeed, MaxAcceleration, MinAcceleration and sdAcceleration have the largest capacity to move a participant across the latent space and reverse their classification, while sdDC, MeanSpeed, MaxSpeed and MeanLength map preferentially into the TD region and are judged marginal. The fitted class densities give signed rules - higher MaxAcceleration and sdAcceleration, and lower MaxSpeed and MinAcceleration, increase the probability of ASD assignment - which the authors offer to clinicians as candidate threshold values.

answers.title: A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation
answers.answer: Goal: to automate the judgement of response to name during real clinical ADOS-2 assessments, by combining automatic speech recognition (to timestamp the name calls) with human pose tracking (to measure shoulder rotation) and head pose estimation (to measure head yaw), and to show that adding body pose to the head-pose-only approach used in prior work improves agreement with clinicians. Three contributions are claimed: a four-camera multi-view capture rig; a 'Response to name Dataset' drawn from live ADOS-2 screening rather than a controlled laboratory protocol, with more natural child behaviour and an unrestricted number of accompanying parents; and the finding that combining shoulder rotation angle, head pose and response duration improves accuracy over pose alone. Findings: shoulder pose alone agreed with the clinician for 25 of 30 children (83.3%) and 104 of 109 calls (95.4%); adding head pose raised this to 28 of 30 (93.3%) and 107 of 109 (98.2%), with sensitivity 84.6% and specificity 100% under an inverted convention in which the 'positive' class is non-response. The two residual participant-level errors are diagnosed concretely: one child responded too slowly to accumulate the required 10 frames above the shoulder threshold and was also wearing a mask, which blocked the facial-landmark fallback; the other turned their head too fast for 8 frames of yaw to be detected. The score-level confusion matrix shows the modal outcome to be clinician 5 / predicted 5 in 17 children.

answers.title: Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games
answers.answer: Goal: to classify autistic from non-autistic children by analysing eye-tracking data captured while they play a purpose-designed computer game, motivated explicitly by the shortage of diagnostic specialists relative to a growing autistic population and the wish for a system 'easily applicable by not-so-expert users'. The game was designed with expert guidance around two objectives drawn from picture-exchange practice: face recognition and facial-expression matching. Findings as reported: precision 76.6% and accuracy 73.8% with all 18 features, which the paper presents as the best of four nested feature subsets and describes as 'a suitable diagnostics system'. Findings as they should be read: those numbers are the TOTAL column of Table 5, pooling training, validation and test rows, and the held-out test values in the same table are precision 66.7%, accuracy 58.3%, sensitivity 57.1% and specificity 60.0% - between 6 and 10 points above a 50% chance level on 36 observations. Across all four feature subsets the pattern is identical and consistent: total accuracies of 65.0-73.8% concealing test accuracies of 52.8-58.3%, with training accuracies of 67.9-78.6%. The gap between training and test performance is present in every configuration and is never remarked on. Two subsets also show unstable held-out behaviour, with test sensitivity of 33.3% for 'around FIGs' and test specificity of 33.3% for 'on FIGs'.

answers.title: Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior
answers.answer: The stated goal is not primarily to build a better classifier but to answer a prior question the field has left open: how do AI predictions correspond to human ones? The framing is explicit and is the paper's organising logic - 'the utility of an AI algorithm would be negligible if it provides little information beyond what clinicians can readily infer' - so the study is designed as a benchmark rather than a demonstration. Nineteen raters (8 doctoral-level autism experts, 11 non-experts) and a computer-vision pipeline were given the same 3-minute silent videos of 42 adults in casual conversation. Findings: AI accuracy 80.5%, expert clinicians 83.1%, non-experts 78.3%, all humans 80.3% - so the model performs at approximately expert level on this evidence. The operating characteristics show why accuracy alone is misleading: PPV 0.86, NPV 0.79, specificity 0.95 and sensitivity 0.55, meaning the classifier is highly conservative and detects only just over half the autistic adults. The paper's real result is the error analysis. Of five participants misclassified by a majority of human raters, four were correctly classified by the model, including the hardest case, which only 21% of raters got right. Per-participant accuracy of humans and AI correlated at just rho = 0.35, falling to 0.19 once the participants nearly all raters got right are removed, and the lower-left quadrant of the scatter - hard for both - is essentially empty. Feature weights point to head pose and its coordination with eye movement, and to mouth-related coordination, as the dominant signal, with both categories over-represented in the top-weighted features relative to their share of the feature pool.

answers.title: Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas
answers.answer: The goal is explicitly infrastructural rather than merely methodological: to build a screening method that works where the constraints are affordability, child-friendliness and the absence of professionals, which the authors identify as the three barriers to autism screening in remote areas. The technical contribution is the dynamic viewing pattern - gaze treated as an ordered trajectory over both viewing time and the stimulus set, rather than as a static distribution of fixations - together with a pipeline that encodes each fixation semantically via an autoencoder, scores each stimulus sequence with an LSTM, and aggregates 82 stimulus scores into a subject decision. Findings: subject-level accuracy 96.73% with sensitivity 96.85% and specificity 96.63% on 165 test children, stable above 95.76% across five random subject-level splits. The supporting analyses are more informative than the headline. Conventional hand-crafted features reproduce the expected group differences - autistic children make fewer fixations with longer saccades, look less at faces and other salient objects, take longer to notice them, and dwell more on background and on the grey mask - but the authors state plainly that these differences are 'not sufficiently significant to directly use these hand-crafted features for classification'. A time-delay embedding analysis then shows that between-group distance grows with the length of the pattern section used and with the number of stimuli included, and that for sections shorter than five fixations the within-autism variability exceeds the between-group difference - a quantitative argument that separability is manufactured by using more temporal and more stimulus context, not merely asserted. Ablation confirms both feature families contribute (semantic 94.85%, low-level 93.33%, combined 96.73%) and that sequence modelling beats fixation-histogram and stacked-fixation baselines.

answers.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts
answers.answer: The stated objective is to build models 'capable of diagnosing ASD through the analysis of texts posted by users who disclose their condition in their biographies', motivated by the scarcity of specialists and the value of early diagnosis. Three contributions are claimed: a new Twitter dataset of 404,627 tweets from 252 users of whom 221 disclose autism; application of several machine-learning techniques to build predictive models; and comparison of classical machine learning against deep learning. Findings: BERT-base-multilingual-cased, used untuned, reached 84.3% accuracy and F1 0.84, outperforming XGBoost at 71.6% (F1 0.74), decision trees at 61.2% (F1 0.72) and k-nearest neighbours at 60.8% (F1 0.67), all three of which were hyperparameter-tuned by grid search. The authors present this as the paper's headline - that a default deep model beats optimised classical ones - and describe the result as 'quite astonishing'. The confusion matrices they report, to their credit, reveal more than the accuracies do: the decision tree produced 11,229 true positives against just 41 false negatives, meaning it labelled nearly every tweet autistic and achieved 99.6% sensitivity at 22.6% specificity - close to a degenerate classifier, which its 61.2% accuracy and 0.72 F1 conceal. BERT's counts correspond to sensitivity 82.1% and specificity 86.5%. No user-level result is reported for any model.

answers.title: Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: Three questions, stated as hypotheses in advance. Whether the complexity of facial landmark dynamics differentiates autistic from typically developing toddlers; whether that complexity is higher specifically in the eyebrow region, on the basis of prior work on eyebrow raising in this cohort, and the mouth region, on the basis of atypical vocalisation literature; and whether the complexity measure adds information beyond the group's own previously published affect-based analysis or merely duplicates it. Findings: autistic toddlers showed significantly higher multiscale entropy in both regions, with a clear social/non-social gradient - during social movies p < .0001 with large to very large effect sizes (r = .51-.82), during non-social movies still significant but only medium (r = .32-.40). Integrated entropy over the first 20 scales gave p < .00001 with large or very large effects for all social movies. Eyebrows and mouth did not differ from each other (p > .05, r < 0.1), so the hypothesis of regional specificity was not supported in the sense of one region dominating. The autistic group also showed a significantly wider range of integrated entropy across the six movies (eyebrows p = .001, r = .33; mouth p = .0002, r = .39), meaning their facial responsiveness varied more between contents. On the third question, correlations between integrated entropy and positive-affect energy were moderate for two movies and negligible for four, and adding affect to the classifier did not improve on entropy alone - while affect alone performed worse - so the measures are largely independent and the complexity measure is the more informative of the two. Classification with a decision tree on social movies gave 76.6-78.3% accuracy with entropy alone; logistic regression gave odds ratios up to 1.8 for entropy against 0.8 for affect.

answers.title: Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders
answers.answer: The stated aim is to test whether modelling the specificity of gaze to particular facial expressions improves classification, on the premise - supported by prior basic research but not previously operationalised - that groups differ in gaze for some emotions and not others. The proposal is to classify each of the 21 or 32 FEIT images separately and then aggregate the per-image decisions with a random forest that learns which images matter, rather than by unweighted voting. Findings, all reported with binomial tests against chance and none oversold. For autistic adults versus controls the weighted CNN reached 0.710 accuracy (sensitivity 0.733, specificity 0.688), significantly above chance and 10 points above the unweighted CNN. For autistic children the weighted models reached 0.667 (weighted CNN sensitivity 0.600, specificity 0.733), significant and 16.7 points above the unweighted CNN, with the weighting raising sensitivity from 0.286 to 0.600. For schizophrenia the best models reached 0.645, only marginally above chance (p = 0.052), and weighting produced no improvement at all. The statistical analysis explains why the method behaves differently across conditions and is the more interesting result: in adults, reduced fixation at the eyes distinguished the schizophrenia group from controls for every one of the seven emotions, but the autistic group from controls for only two (anger and neutral), while scan-path length distinguished autism from controls for six of seven emotions. So the classic reduced-eye-looking signature was present uniformly in schizophrenia and only selectively in autism - which is exactly the condition under which per-image weighting helps for one and not the other. In children, almost no gaze feature reached significance at all, yet the weighted models still exceeded chance.

answers.title: Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders
answers.answer: Two goals, and the paper is clearer about the first than the second. The first is to demonstrate that the dense telemetry generated by digital AAC systems is worth analysing at all, which the authors argue has been almost entirely neglected: 'with the exception of one prior report, no efforts have been made to use the dense streams of data collected by digital AACs to derive insights of clinical importance'. The second is the classification question, posed precisely and unusually well: 'can we distinguish individuals with ASD from individuals without ASD (but who have need for AAC systems), based solely on patterns of use?' - the parenthesis matters, because it commits the study to a differential rather than an autism-versus-typical contrast. Findings: conventional usage statistics separate nothing. Session length was 2.14 versus 2.10 minutes (p = 0.86), word selects per use 5.6 versus 4.31 (p = 0.166) and word-select frequency 2.99 versus 2.28 per minute (p = 0.147), none significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction, and the authors present this explicitly as motivation for more advanced modelling. The prior analysis of the same data reached 47-61% across sequential, temporal and spectral views - sequential SVM peaking at 58% at window size 40, temporal at 60%, spectral at 61% with LogitBoost - which is at or barely above chance. Accuracy rose to 70% with sequential modelling only after k-means pseudo-labelling enlarged the training set, and to 82% in the present study with stacked autoencoders at window size 40. Descriptively the study also reports that use spanned the whole lifespan with heaviest engagement among under-10s, that autistic users had the highest average number of app accesses, and that the commonest phrases concerned food, sleep, sport and greetings.

answers.title: Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: Two objectives, both clinically framed. First, to train deep learning models to distinguish autism from typical development using video of joint attention behaviours; second, to differentiate autism symptom severity from the same data. The motivating argument is precise and is worth recording because it diagnoses the corpus's own problems: prior video-based models are said to be unsuitable for tool development 'due to a lack of automation, the requirements for specialized and expensive equipment, calibration, trained personnel, dependence on human rating of autistic behaviors, and low precision and recall', and the authors attribute that low precision and recall to 'a lack of targeted behavioral biomarkers that can readily discriminate ASD from TD' and to the absence of methods for quantitatively measuring hallmark autism behaviours. Their response is to instrument an existing validated clinical construct rather than to search for a statistical signature. Findings: detection AUROC of 99.6% for IJA, 99.8% for low-level RJA and 99.5% for high-level RJA, with accuracy 97.6-98.8% and confidence intervals throughout. Severity prediction was markedly lower and task-ordered: IJA 90.3% AUROC, low-level RJA 84.4%, high-level RJA 84.2%, with precision falling to 68.6% for high-level RJA. The IJA advantage for severity is interpreted substantively - initiation reflects motivation to share attention and so captures nuance that responsiveness tasks miss - and is corroborated by the cluster maps, where IJA attention-weight trajectories separate the three severity classes more cleanly than the RJA ones. The compliance analysis adds a behavioural finding independent of the models: both groups habituated after ten IJA or five RJA repetitions, but autistic children showed comparable initial interest to comparison children in IJA before declining, while showing 'contrasting uninterest in the social cue presented at the beginning of RJA tasks'.

answers.title: Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking
answers.answer: The stated aim is to use eye-tracking scanpath images 'as a biological indicator to identify children with autism' and to compare a transfer-learning-plus-classical-classifier pipeline against an end-to-end custom CNN. Findings: the custom CNN reached 71.9% accuracy, InceptionV3 features with logistic regression 78.9%, and InceptionV3 features with an MLP 81.0%. The per-class analysis is the substantive result and the authors present it properly rather than resting on accuracy. The custom CNN's confusion matrix shows 30 of 34 typically developing images correct against only 11 of 23 autism images - class-wise recall of 0.88 versus 0.48, F1 of 0.79 versus 0.58 - so a model reported at 71.9% accuracy is in fact detecting fewer than half the autism cases, and the authors say so: its 'ability to classify the people affected by ASD was not upto the mark'. The transfer-learning models are markedly more balanced, with class-wise F1 of 0.82/0.75 for logistic regression and 0.84/0.76 for the MLP, and the authors conclude on that basis rather than on the accuracy difference alone. The conclusion attributes the modest overall performance to the small dataset and proposes augmentation and dataset expansion.

answers.title: SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism
answers.answer: The stated objectives are threefold: to automatically extract semantic and pragmatic language features including echolalia, semantic coherence and repetitive language usage; to compare them systematically and identify the most significant; and to build an interpretable assessment system on that basis. The gap the paper identifies in the literature is specific and fair - prior work on semantic-pragmatic features for autism has examined individual measures such as echolalia or pronoun usage in isolation, and 'the cumulative effect of the features and how they complement the lexical, syntactic and other text-based features in the diagnosis of autism has not been analysed'. Findings: the best classifier, an RBF SVM on all 63 retained features, reached 94.1% accuracy with 94% macro F1 against a majority-classifier baseline of 56.4% accuracy and 32% macro F1. The feature-set ablation is the substantive result and is reported in full: morphosyntactic baseline 70.59%, syntactic complexity alone 70%, part-of-speech frequencies alone 82%, semantic-pragmatic features alone 82.3%, part-of-speech plus semantic-pragmatic 88.2%, and all three families 94.1%. So the semantic-pragmatic set matches the lexical set on its own and the three families are complementary rather than redundant, which is exactly the claim the study set out to test. SHAP attribution places the number of distinct word roots first, with unexpected words and both child-child and child-partner discourse coherence in the top ten, and the authors relate each to prior findings on vocabulary extent and on global coherence in autistic conversation.

answers.title: Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths
answers.answer: The stated objective is to test whether scan-path images - spatial representations of gaze - can stratify autism from typical development, and then whether they also capture the age and sex variation that makes autism biomarkers hard to generalise. The two contributions claimed are incorporating temporal information into scan-path images and infusing gaze velocity into them. Findings, in the paper's own summary order: spatial scan-paths separate autism from typical development at 74.4% test accuracy (AUC 0.68-0.72); scan-paths separate 2-4 year old from 10-17 year old autistic children at 80.5% (AUC 0.868); scan-paths separate male from female autistic children at 78.0% (AUC 0.850); and within the 5-9 year autistic subgroup they separate male from female at 98.8%. Temporal windowing shows the first three seconds of viewing discriminate best (76.3%) with a monotone decline to 70.2% by 12-15 seconds. Velocity-based colour coding raises the 3-6 second window from 71.74% to 80.25% (AUC 0.839), the paper's headline representational result. Per-clip ablation ranks the contribution of individual videos, with Theory of Mind and Dyadic Bid clips mattering most. The authors read the age and sex results as evidence that scan-paths capture heterogeneity; they can equally be read as evidence that the diagnostic result is confounded, since the two groups differ substantially on both variables.

answers.title: A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths
answers.answer: The stated aim is to build an enhanced convolutional deep network for autism identification from eye-tracking scan-path images, with an explicit methodological claim distinguishing it from prior work: 'we addressed the issue of working with a dataset containing a small number of images without utilizing augmentation. Whereas many earlier studies depended on augmenting image data to improve outcomes, we maintained the original image count and achieved superior performance.' That is a defensible and welcome position, since augmentation on a 547-image corpus split at image level compounds dependence between training and test data, as another study in this corpus demonstrates directly. Findings: 95.59% accuracy for greyscale images with two hidden layers of 300 and 150 neurons, kernel size 3, stride 1, Adam optimiser and 20% dropout; 94.69% with colour. Comparators on the same data reach 61.3% for k-nearest neighbours, 67.7% for decision tree, 69.60% for random forest and 94.69% for a multilayer perceptron. Optimiser choice dominates everything else: Adam and Nadam give 81-95%, RMSprop and AdaMax 85-94%, while SGD and Adadelta collapse to 56-62% - a 35-point spread that indicates the result is highly sensitive to optimisation rather than robustly present in the data. The decisive problem is that the same results table reports sensitivity 77.60% and specificity 79.91% alongside the 95.59% accuracy, and those three figures cannot describe the same classifier: with 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic images they imply an accuracy near 79%.

answers.title: A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning
answers.answer: The aim is to build and evaluate a machine learning model predicting later autism diagnosis from routinely collected well-baby records, so that providers can be alerted during ordinary checkups to administer an autism-specific screening tool - the Israeli protocol containing none. Findings: average test AUC 0.86 (SD 0.009) with sensitivity 0.75 and specificity 0.81, against a training AUC of 0.88 that the authors flag as indicating slight overfitting. At the Youden threshold, 18.6% of the cohort (144,632 children) were classified high risk, capturing 874 of 1,163 cases - an autism incidence of 0.006 in that group against 0.001 in the cohort, a 4.3-fold enrichment. The seven most important milestone predictors, all confirmed by independent Fisher's exact tests at p < 0.001, are strikingly ordinary clinical observations: vocabulary over ten words, building a tower from cubes, giving a kiss, eating independently with a spoon, knowing at least one body part, composing two-word sentences and saying 2-3 words. Four are language milestones, two personal-social, one fine motor, and all fall between 12 and 24 months. Other key predictors are male sex, parental developmental concern, non-nursing, older maternal age, lower gestational age and atypical growth percentiles. The most instructive result is the method comparison: logistic regression achieved exactly the same AUC of 0.86 with marginally better sensitivity (0.77 versus 0.75), random forest 0.84 and naive Bayes 0.83 - so gradient boosting gained nothing over a linear model on 59 features, which bears directly on the assumption running through this corpus that model sophistication is where performance comes from.

answers.title: AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: “A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System”
answers.answer: The aim is an AI-powered mobile application that identifies autistic children from facial photographs, combined with a facial expression recognition module, intended for use by families and psychiatrists. Findings: MobileNet reached 95% validation accuracy with sensitivity 0.97 and specificity 0.93, alongside 100% training accuracy; Xception 94% (sensitivity 0.92, specificity 0.95); InceptionV3 89% (sensitivity 0.95, specificity 0.83). The expression module reports precision 0.988 and mAP50 0.991 for the proposed variant - against 0.992 and 0.99 for the smallest YOLOv8 baseline, so the proposed model is marginally worse than the lightest comparator on its own task, a result the paper presents as demonstrating 'a good balance of accuracy and efficiency'. The two modules are never combined, tested against each other, or shown to inform one another, despite the paper's claim to provide 'a more complete picture of a child's condition'. What no result in the paper addresses is what the autism classifier is responding to. Given that the two image classes were assembled from different internet sources, the reported accuracy is consistent with a model that has learned to distinguish autism-website photographs from general internet photographs, and no analysis in the paper can rule that out.

answers.title: An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks
answers.answer: The stated aim is an interpretable, personalised multimodal framework that combines structured behavioural phenotypes with structural MRI, addressing what the authors identify as two gaps in prior work: the absence of principled fusion strategies and insufficient attention to explainability and personalisation. The architecture is genuinely thoughtful - GAMI-Net for transparent additive modelling of tabular clinical data, a CNN-GNN pair to capture both voxel-level structure and inter-region relationships over the Harvard-Oxford atlas, an autoencoder to fuse into a shared 32-dimensional space rather than concatenating naively, and a hypernetwork generating subject-specific classifier weights so that decision boundaries adapt per individual. Reported results are 99.40% accuracy, 100% precision, 98.84% recall and 99.99% ROC-AUC on a held-out split, and 98.56% accuracy with 99.62% ROC-AUC under five-fold stratified cross-validation. The explainability analysis identifies ADOS_TOTAL and ADOS_Gotham_Total as the dominant predictors. Read together, these findings say that a model given the diagnostic instrument scores reproduces the diagnosis nearly perfectly, which is what one would expect and which the architecture's sophistication does not alter. The paper's own contributions section states a different and lower figure - 96.4% accuracy and AUC 0.92 - that is not reconciled with the abstract anywhere.

answers.title: Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development
answers.answer: Two objectives: to quantify interpersonal motor coordination, described as 'an omnipresent yet least studied behavioral characteristic in ASD', and to test whether coordination features can classify autistic from typically developing children. The methodological rationale for cross wavelet analysis is stated explicitly and is the paper's reason for existing: the group's earlier analysis of these same recordings used complexity matching to quantify overall coordination across the conversation and 'failed to find significant differences in IMC between the ASD and TD children', whereas cross wavelet analysis resolves coordination at separate movement frequencies and so 'could provide a more detailed picture', while also generating many candidate features for classification. Findings: coherence was significantly lower in the autistic group at six of 23 time scales, all at the faster end (0.1-0.9 s), with both groups exceeding the pseudo-pair chance level, so real coordination was occurring in both and differed in degree. Classification on original coherence features reached 85.37% (specificity 95.24%, sensitivity 75.00%) with five features, of which four were among the significantly different ones. Constructing 57 derived features by summing subsets of the six significant coherences raised the best result to 92.68% (specificity 95.24%, sensitivity 90.00%) with a decision tree using three of them. The specificity is identical across both conditions, so the whole improvement is a rise in sensitivity from 75% to 90% - three additional autistic children out of twenty.

answers.title: Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning
answers.answer: The study begins from a specific and well-evidenced clinical problem rather than from a technical opportunity: ADOS-2, the gold standard, has documented limitations for adolescents and adults, because it does not clearly separate autism from ADHD or from the negative symptoms of schizophrenia and other psychiatric comorbidities, and because masking, compensation and camouflaging can conceal impairment. The proposed remedy is a comprehensive mapping of pragmatic impairment through lexicogrammatical analysis, which the authors note has not previously been attempted - prior linguistic work examined single grammatical areas such as modality, relative clauses or syntax, leaving 'the overall picture of the impairment... uncharted'. Findings: on interview transcripts the combined text-plus-tag Bi-LSTM reached 0.82 accuracy (95% CI 0.75-0.89) with AUC 0.90 under automatic annotation, and 0.80 (0.73-0.87) with sensitivity 0.73 and specificity 0.87 under manual annotation. The tag-only linear model reached 0.78 and the text-only model 0.80, and McNemar tests found no significant differences between them on the interview task. The substantive result is the task contrast: every model performed better on interviews than on picture-book recounting, where the linear model fell to 0.60-0.64 and the best model reached 0.78. The authors interpret this as evidence that the discriminative signal lies in socially interactive language use rather than in narrative production generally, which is exactly what a pragmatic-impairment account predicts and is a stronger form of evidence than a single accuracy figure.

answers.title: Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms
answers.answer: The stated aim is to improve autism detection accuracy from facial images by combining transfer-learned deep features with handcrafted image descriptors, and to identify the best classifier and feature combination. Findings: handcrafted features alone gave 78.0-84.5% across five classifiers, with random forest best; adding ResNet features raised the range to 84.4-90.2%, with SVM best; and adding Inception features gave 83.2-94.6%, with SVM best at 94.6%. The reported progression - handcrafted alone, then fused with each backbone - is a systematic ablation and is the paper's substantive content. What it cannot establish is what the improvement means, because no evaluation protocol is stated: the words 'split' and 'validation' appear nowhere, no cross-validation is described, and no train-test partition is specified for any of the eighteen reported accuracies. Whether these are held-out figures, training figures, or something else is not determinable from the paper.

answers.title: Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed
answers.answer: The stated aim is to improve recognition of altered facial expressions in autistic people, on the argument that conventional systems misread the nuanced cues that autistic faces produce - a real and under-addressed problem, and the strongest idea in the paper. The executed work is six-way emotion classification on KDEF and CK+, reporting 99.8% accuracy, 99.8% precision, 100% recall and 94% specificity, with significance tests against CNN, linear SVM and k-nearest-neighbour baselines at p < 0.01. The gap between the two is the study's defining feature. The paper's own introduction supplies the reason the executed task cannot address the stated aim, observing that 'research indicates a lack of studies utilizing static or dynamic facial stimuli displaying real, spontaneous emotions' and that 'staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones' - after which the evaluation uses only staged emotions from instructed adult volunteers. A separate study charted in this review tests the transfer question directly and finds that affect models trained on neurotypical faces perform poorly on autistic children and improve substantially only after fine-tuning on autistic data, which is the evidence this study would have needed and did not seek.

answers.title: Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification
answers.answer: Two objectives, both methodological rather than clinical. First, to test whether raw motion trajectories alone - unprocessed x and y coordinates - carry enough information to classify autistic from typically developing children, or whether derived kinematic features are needed; the comparison is motivated by the group's own prior work, which had found that maximum and minimum acceleration and standard deviations of speed and acceleration were the leading contributors in a feature-based model. Second, to test the specific role of acceleration by generating synthetic trajectories with systematically varied acceleration and observing how the models respond. Findings: the four-feature model reached 0.90 accuracy against 0.76 for the two-feature model, with a consistently higher fold-wise distribution and a better ROC curve, so derived features help substantially. But the simulation analysis complicates the simple reading: acceleration correlated with the two-feature model's predictions at r = 0.69 despite that model never receiving acceleration as an input, and with the four-feature model's at r = 0.82, both at p < 0.001 over 932 samples, with higher acceleration increasing the probability of an autism prediction in both. So the information is present in the raw coordinate sequence and the four-feature representation makes it easier to use rather than supplying something new - a conclusion the authors reach and state, writing that their findings 'support the potential of raw data analysis in objectively assessing motor behaviors related to autism' while the four-feature model 'excels'.

answers.title: Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain
answers.answer: The stated aim is a detection model for autism and visual sensory processing disorder that combines facial expression data with heart rate and body temperature, using a purpose-designed hybrid optimisation algorithm to select features and tune network parameters. Findings: the proposed method reached 96.44886% accuracy, 96.2963% sensitivity, 96.50485% specificity and 91% precision. Four metaheuristic comparators using the identical network architecture clustered within one percentage point (95.45-95.74%), and four conventional classifiers were substantially lower (81.5-86.6%). The tight clustering of the metaheuristic variants is the most interpretable result in the paper: it indicates that the choice among optimisation algorithms contributes about one accuracy point while the network architecture contributes about ten, which somewhat undercuts the paper's central claim that the novel optimiser is the contribution. Against this, the results cannot be evaluated because the dataset on which they were computed is never described, and the two accounts of the validation scheme - a variable learning-percentage split illustrated at 65/35, and 5-fold cross-validation defined among the evaluation measures - are not reconciled or tied to the reported figures.

answers.title: Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: The stated aim is to improve the precision and speed of early autism diagnosis by optimising one-dimensional convolutional networks with the Tree-structured Parzen Estimator across four age-specific datasets, and to deploy the result as an interactive diagnostic tool. The methodological argument is coherent and specific: prior work on these datasets relied on predefined hyperparameters or on exhaustive grid search, which the authors correctly characterise as 'computation-intensive and inefficient', and an adaptive Bayesian alternative is a sensible remedy. The result reported is 100% on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation coefficient and AUC-ROC in every age band, attributed to the optimisation. The alternative explanation is complete and requires nothing of the model: the class label in these datasets is the summed item score thresholded at the instrument's cut-off, the items are among the inputs, and the sum itself is among the tabulated fields, so the model is being asked to reproduce a deterministic function of its own predictors. On that reading the baseline models' shortfall reflects optimisation difficulty rather than any information limit, and the optimised models' perfection reflects the arithmetic. The paper's own literature review is consistent with this: it tabulates the subliterature at 97.15% to 100% on these datasets, and notes one comparator - using physical fitness tests, brain scans and severity assessments on recruited participants - reaching 77.99%, roughly twenty-two points lower.

answers.title: Machine learning’s effectiveness
answers.answer: The aim is to test whether machine-learning analysis of movement during the one-legged standing test can identify five-year-olds with high autistic traits, motivated by a specific timing gap: autism can be detected at 14 months and diagnosed reliably by two years, yet over 70% of affected children are not diagnosed until after 51 months, so screening before elementary school entry is needed. Balance is chosen because prior behavioural work reports that autistic children show smaller centre-of-pressure shift, more repetitive centre-of-pressure patterns and less complex postural control in both static and dynamic states, and because the one-legged standing test is already a standard clinical assessment - so the measurement can be added to a routine examination at essentially no cost. Findings: accuracy, sensitivity and specificity all reached 1.000 for the study's proposed variable set (correlations between centre-of-pressure and shoulder, right trunk and right knee angles) and for the combined set, while the conventional variable set based on prior literature performed less well on accuracy and sensitivity though it also achieved specificity of 1.000. SHAP attribution identified shoulder, hip and trunk as the dominant contributors. And SRS-2 total correlated positively with predicted probability across all three variable sets. The substantive claim is therefore not that balance differs in magnitude but that the coordination between upper body and the shifting base of support differs - the conventional sway measures are the weaker predictors and the novel correlation measures are what produce the separation.

answers.title: Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network
answers.answer: The stated aim is to improve facial-image-based autism detection by combining squeeze-and-excitation channel attention, multiscale feature fusion and convolutional networks with automated hyperparameter search using the white shark optimisation algorithm, motivated by four claimed gaps in prior work: limited modelling of long-range dependencies by CNNs, insufficient local inductive bias when images are treated as token sequences, weak interpretability, and inadequate splitting strategies. The headline finding is 95.36% accuracy, 92.62% precision and 95.5% F1 - a triple that is arithmetically consistent with a recall of 98.6% and a specificity of 92.2% at the reported 1:1 ratio, which is worth noting because internal inconsistency is common in this branch. Three secondary findings carry more weight than the headline. The ablation shows that the paper's own multiscale fusion contribution reduces accuracy relative to squeeze-and-excitation alone when the hyperparameter search is removed (0.85 against 0.89), and the authors state this plainly rather than burying it. The leakage investigation on the video-derived corpus found a maximum training-test cosine similarity of 0.9714 before intervention, which is direct evidence that naive frame-level splitting of that dataset - the standard practice in the papers it is drawn from - leaks. And bidirectional cross-dataset evaluation reached 89-90%, which the paper presents as robustness and which is better read as evidence that whatever the model has learned is common to two corpora built by the same web-scraping principle.

answers.title: Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]
answers.answer: The aim is to compare a broader range of neural architectures on EEG-derived features than prior work has done, on the argument that existing studies have explored a limited set of models and feature combinations. Four architectures were fitted to eleven linear and non-linear time- and frequency-domain features: a custom neural network reached 94.02% accuracy, an LSTM 93.83%, a deep neural network 91.98% and a convolutional network 89.02%, with precision, recall, specificity and F1 reported for each. The comparison is even-handed and includes the lowest performer rather than only the winner. What the study cannot establish is what those figures mean. With 17 participants the accuracies must have been computed over EEG epochs rather than people, no validation scheme of any kind is described, and with four control children a participant-disjoint evaluation would leave at most one control in any held-out set. The paper's own comparison table is the most useful thing in it for this review, and its pattern is discussed below.

answers.title: Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play
answers.answer: The aim was to measure functional and imaginative play together with other core autistic traits during a brief free play task, characterise the group differences, and build from them a clinical prediction model capable of screening children aged 1 to 6 - explicitly extending prior work that had examined play behaviours alone. Directional hypotheses were stated in advance, including the prediction that repetitive behaviour frequency would not differ between groups because the session would be too short for it to emerge. The findings: autistic children showed less functional and less imaginative play, and reduced eye contact, facial expression and vocalisation. Restricted and repetitive behaviours did not separate the groups, exactly as predicted - the reported odds ratios for stereotyped language use, repetitive hand and body movements and unusual sensory seeking are numerically enormous with confidence intervals spanning zero to infinity and p-values near 1, the signature of behaviours almost never observed in a 90-second window. Stepwise regression retained five predictors, all in the protective direction: duration of socially oriented vocalisations (OR 0.940), total counts of functional play (OR 0.639), and play time with miniature or representational toys (OR 0.985), cause-and-effect toys (OR 0.973) and construction toys (OR 0.958). The nomogram reached AUC 0.826 (95% CI 0.776-0.877) with sensitivity 85.4% and specificity 68.3% at a cut-off of 0.399. The confirmed negative prediction about repetitive behaviour is worth as much as the positive findings: it demonstrates that the task samples the social-communication and play dimensions of the phenotype and not the restricted-repetitive dimension, which bounds what any model built on it can claim to detect.

answers.title: Predictive model using autism
answers.answer: The aim was to identify similarities and differences in the symptoms of schizophrenia and autism, establish a more objective method of differential diagnosis, and characterise autistic features in schizophrenia - motivated by a clinical problem the introduction sets out at length: the two conditions co-occur, cluster in families, share genetic risk and produce overlapping presentations, while the features that distinguish them (the content and duration of delusions, self-disturbance, developmental timing) are precisely the ones that become unavailable when verbal expression is poor, when symptoms are concealed, or when a high-functioning autistic adult's characteristics did not surface until adolescence. The findings answer that question in three parts. The ADOS-2's own algorithms failed: 45.0% and 52.5% of the schizophrenia group screened positive on the original and revised algorithms, AUCs were 0.562 and 0.569, and no domain score of either algorithm carried significant predictive value. An item-level model built on six items - A7 reporting of events, A10 emphatic or emotional gestures, B1 unusual eye contact, B6 comments on others' emotions or empathy, B8 responsibility, B9 quality of social overtures - reached apparent accuracy 86.6% and AUC 0.938, significantly outperforming both algorithms by DeLong's test, but dropped to 65.3% under holdout validation. And the autistic-looking features in schizophrenia proved to be negative symptoms: ADOS-2 scores correlated with the PANSS negative scale, cut-off-positive patients had higher negative-symptom scores than cut-off-negative patients, and cut-off positivity was predicted by the negative scale alone. The negative finding is the durable one. The positive finding is a promising direction whose own validation shows it is not yet ready.

answers.title: The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech
answers.answer: The aim is to test whether deep transfer learning can compensate for the scarcity of labelled child speech data in autism recognition, by comparing two fine-tuning strategies - discriminative fine-tuning pre-trained on a related child corpus, and Wav2Vec 2.0 fine-tuning pre-trained on 960 hours of unrelated adult speech - across a binary typicality task and a four-class diagnosis task, with fairness testing by gender. The findings are best read against the study's own comparison tables, which the authors supply. On binary typicality, D-FT reached 94.8% unweighted average recall and W2V2-FT 91.5%, against a stated baseline of 94.1% and prior published results of 90.7% and 93.6% on the same corpus - an improvement of 0.7 points over baseline. On four-class diagnosis, D-FT reached 60.9% and W2V2-FT 54.3%, against a baseline of 62.4% and prior results of 67.1% and 69.4% - so both proposed models fall below the baseline and below prior work on the task that actually requires separating autism from other conditions. And the fairness analysis shows that the binary headline does not survive subgroup evaluation: D-FT sensitivity falls from 94.8% on the mixed-gender test set to 43.6% on the female set and 61.5% on the male, with W2V2-FT falling from 92.3% to 24.4% and 53.8%. Publishing a benchmark table showing one's own model below baseline on the harder task, and a fairness table showing a fifty-point sensitivity collapse, is a level of candour this review has encountered in very few papers.

answers.title: Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism
answers.answer: The stated objective was 'to study the feasibility of autism screening from Twitter data and discuss the ethical implications of such models' - the ethics being a co-equal aim from the outset rather than an appended caveat, which is unique in this corpus. The technical finding is modest and honestly reported: a tweet-level classifier reached 73% accuracy, AUC 0.728 and F1 0.71 using word2vec representations with logistic regression, and a user-profile classifier reached AUC 0.78 and F1 0.805 using an attention-based bidirectional LSTM. Aggregating a user's full timeline improved discrimination over single tweets, as expected if the signal is a property of a writer rather than of a post. Exploratory analysis found that sentiment polarity was nearly unchanged between the raw and profanity-censored corpora, and that autism-related discussion rose across 2014-2022. The conclusion the authors actually draw is not about accuracy: having demonstrated feasibility, they restrict the legitimate use of such models to 'a broader cross-sectional level' rather than individual prediction, enumerate the misuse scenarios the artefact would enable, delete the data and the models, and caution researchers against building comparable systems without explicit consent and participatory community-centred design. That is the study's contribution and it is a real one.

answers.title: Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children
answers.answer: The aim is broad automated screening rather than detection of a single symptom, achieved by combining two neural networks trained on the video and audio channels of the same semi-standardised assessment, and by then asking which clinical features each modality is sensitive to. The performance findings are modest and are not oversold: video alone 80.0% accuracy on the held-out 80 children, audio alone 78.8%, and the best ensemble 82.5% with sensitivity 0.775 and specificity 0.875. Alternative combination rules trade these off - an OR rule reaching sensitivity 0.90 at specificity 0.75, an AND rule reaching specificity 0.925 at sensitivity 0.60 - and the authors present all five variants in one table rather than only the best. The fusion result is honestly negative in the accuracy sense and the authors say so, identifying 'the inability of the simple ensemble model to outperform the individual modalities' as an important limitation; what fusion does provide is complementary errors, with both networks simultaneously wrong on only 8.75% of cases, and operating-point control. The more interesting findings are interpretive. Video confidence tracks initiation of joint attention, quality of social overtures, unusual eye contact and pointing gestures - a coherent nonverbal social-communication cluster. Audio confidence tracks showing behaviour, pointing, unusual sensory exploration and hand mannerisms - which are not vocal constructs, leading the authors to propose that ambient non-vocal sound from object manipulation contributed to the audio classification, and to note prior evidence that examiners' prosody adapts to child severity such that a full-band model may partly be reading the adult. Those two admissions are the study's most valuable output for this review.

answers.title: Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning
answers.answer: Two aims are pursued in one pipeline: classify autism from face images, then estimate continuous affect in the identified autistic children, with a view to a longitudinal monitoring platform. The autism classification result is modest and stable - 74.5% accuracy with F1 73.7% and recall 73.2% at a 10% test split, 74.8% at 20%, and 75.2% under 5-fold cross-validation. The affect results are where the substance lies and they are structured as a genuine comparison across conditions: 93.7-98.4% for discrete affect on laboratory-controlled CK+, falling to 57.3-62.2% on in-the-wild AffectNet, with continuous-affect concordance correlations on AffectNet of 0.342-0.513 for arousal and 0.373-0.661 for valence. The finding the paper is built around, and the one worth carrying into the synthesis, is the transfer result: a model trained solely on AffectNet - neurotypical faces - performs poorly on autistic children, while fine-tuning it on the newly annotated autistic data produces 'noticeably superior outcomes', leading the authors to conclude that 'it is preferable to have a dataset where the data obtained relates to ASD children and not neurotypical subjects, specifically, when the task is to predict the values for valence and arousal'. That is an empirical demonstration that affect-recognition tools built on neurotypical populations do not transfer to autistic faces, which has direct implications for every deployed emotion-recognition system and for the several studies in this corpus that apply generic affect models to autistic children.

answers.title: A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features
answers.answer: The aim is a framework for continuous thermal monitoring of autistic children that classifies severity and thereby informs psychiatric medication dosing, motivated by the argument that the ABC's brief administration cannot capture daily behavioural variation and that imprecise dosing risks adverse effects the paper lists as including cardiac arrest, kidney failure, irregular heartbeats and high blood pressure. Three results are reported. The denoising pipeline, combining a non-decimated wavelet transform with a DnCNN, outperformed comparison filters on PSNR and SSIM. The DN-FME facial-mood network reached 96.39% accuracy across five categories - neutral, anger, sadness, fear, happiness - with two properly conducted ablations showing dropout at 0.2 outperforming 0.5 (0.9639 against 0.9521) and batch normalisation adding four points (0.9639 against 0.9378). And the severity classifiers reached 98.33% for Random Forest and SVM with AUCs of 0.9878 and 0.9865, against 90.00% for KNN. The paper then reports that its classifiers outperform the clinical ABC method and presents a severity-to-dosage mapping. The engineering components are competently executed and reported; the clinical components rest on labels of unstated origin, an image-level split that allows the classifiers to identify individual children, and a comparison against a clinical standard that is very likely the source of the labels themselves.

answers.title: Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: The stated aim is to evaluate deep transfer-learning architectures for distinguishing autistic from non-autistic children from facial images, motivated by the cost and delay of conventional assessment and by the premise that autism has a distinct facial phenotype. Results: Inception-V3 98% accuracy, VGG-19 97%, ResNet50 96%, each with per-class precision and recall of 96-98% and confusion matrices on 588 evaluation samples. Two internal inconsistencies bear on how these should be read. The abstract names ResNet50, Inception-V3 and VGG-19 with Inception-V3 best; the introduction names 'ResNet, VGG16, and VGG19' and states that VGG19 achieved the superior 98%, contradicting the paper's own results tables. And all three result tables are headed 'Validation results', with the confusion matrices described as validation-stage - so the headline figures come from the partition used for model selection, while the 10% test partition defined in the methods is never reported on. The paper's own comparison table places this subliterature at 80.05% to 96% across ten prior studies on the same corpus, so a 98% validation figure sits above every published test figure for the same data.

answers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features
answers.answer: The stated aim is to compare classical machine learning against deep learning for autism detection from linguistic features, using more than one data source and paying attention to how features differ across age and sex - three gaps the paper identifies in prior work, the second of which ('all previous studies based their research on a single data source') is a fair criticism of much of this literature. Findings: the convolutional network reached 84% accuracy and the multilayer perceptron 83%, against 77-80% for logistic regression, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbours and random forests, and roughly ten points lower for Gaussian naive Bayes; mean length of utterance was the top-ranked feature for both models that supply importances, confirming one prior study and contradicting another on total number of words; and the demographic analysis found MLU rising with age, a reversal of the sex gap between the 3-4 and 5-6 bands, and a sex-by-diagnosis interaction on mean length of turn. The performance figures are modest, honestly reported, and benchmarked against three prior studies at 70-80%, which places them in a credible range for this task and in sharp contrast to the 95-100% figures elsewhere in this review. What the study cannot establish is what the models detect: its leading feature is a developmental language index, no independent language measure exists, and the age composition of the two groups is unreported.

answers.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning
answers.answer: The aim is to optimise a dual-stream skeleton architecture for autism detection, replacing the vision transformer of a prior design with a convolutional backbone to test whether CNN-based models capture gesture features effectively, and comparing MSG3D against a Stack Transformer in the temporal stream. The headline results are 95.4% on the Gait Fullbody Dataset and 70.19% on DREAM. The more informative findings are in the ablation tables. Across six image backbones the Gait results span 93.2% to 95.4% and the DREAM results 68.92% to 70.19% - so architecture choice moves accuracy by around two points on one dataset and one point on the other, while the gap between the two datasets is 25 points. That is a clean demonstration that in this branch the data determine performance and the model barely matters, which is a useful corrective to a literature organised around architectural novelty. The paper also reports that substituting a Stack Transformer for MSG3D lowered accuracy, and it reports its own reference implementation (ViT-B at 94.8%) alongside the alternatives rather than only the winner. What the study does not establish is what the 25-point gap means: the two corpora differ in sensor generation, joint coverage (25 full-body against 10 upper-body), task (walking against robot-assisted therapy), label structure (autism versus typical against two autism-related classes) and splitting unit (child against sample), and no analysis separates these.

answers.title: Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]
answers.answer: Two aims: to identify acoustic differences between autistic and typically developing children's cries, and to test whether deep learning can classify them. The statistical result is coherent and physiologically interpretable - significantly higher jitter (p < 0.01) and shimmer (p < 0.01) and significantly lower harmonics-to-noise ratio (p < 0.0001) in the autistic group, which together describe greater cycle-to-cycle instability in both pitch and amplitude and a noisier, less periodic voice signal, consistent with less stable laryngeal and respiratory control. The direction replicates prior cry work the authors cite. The classification result was 90.28% accuracy with AUC 90.83%, sensitivity and specificity both 88.64%, precision 95.12% and F-score 91.75%. The two halves of the study are of very different evidential weight. The acoustic comparison is a straightforward group contrast on prespecified clinical measures and stands or falls on the confounds - age, recording setting, cry cause - none of which is adjusted. The classification figure additionally rests on a validation-set maximum selected across 2,000 epochs with no held-out test partition and no participant-level splitting, so it carries essentially no information about performance on a new child, and the paper does not connect the network's behaviour to the interpretable acoustic features it identified.

answers.title: Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm
answers.answer: The stated aim is to improve autism prediction with a Bayesian-optimised Random Forest, motivated by the subjectivity and slowness of conventional assessment. The reported result is 0.9890 accuracy, described as highly promising and as providing 'recommendations for a verified diagnostic technique when implemented'. The alternative explanation is complete: the class variable is the summed AQ-10 item score thresholded at the instrument's cut-off, the ten items are inputs, and the sum itself is printed among the study's own feature list with no removal step described - so the model is recovering a threshold rule from its own predictor, a task a single decision stump would solve. The paper attributes the accuracy to Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation of the ensemble.

answers.title: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
answers.answer: The aim is an automated method for detecting autism from facial and motor features extracted from video, motivated by the subjectivity of expert observation, the weakness of early behavioural signs, and a shortage of specialists. The pipeline extracts 1,639 numerical parameters per frame using MediaPipe face mesh, pose and hands, adds a mouth aspect ratio and per-region motion energy, and models the sequence with a hybrid CNN+LSTM. Reported results: 90% accuracy on training data, 85-90% on validation, recall 0.95 and AUC above 0.9042, with the hybrid significantly outperforming single-architecture baselines at p < 0.05 by paired t-tests across folds. Heat map and movement-energy analyses showed group differences in motor activity and facial expression. The performance is modest and in a credible range for this task, and it is benchmarked against external comparators rather than presented in isolation. What the study cannot establish is what the separation reflects: the autistic group is 84% male against 52% in the comparison group, and the inputs are facial and body geometry, so sex is a live alternative explanation that no reported analysis excludes.

answers.title: Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of
answers.answer: The stated aim is a dual diagnostic framework detecting both autism and gelotophobia, motivated by evidence that gelotophobia affects around 6% of neurotypical people but up to 45% of autistic people, with prevalence reaching 41.98% in adolescents with high-functioning autism - a genuine and under-studied comorbidity, and the identification of it as a target is the paper's most interesting idea. The reported findings are 92% overall accuracy for autism identification using DeepFace features and a multilayer perceptron, with 10-fold cross-validation on the training portion, and qualitative statements for gelotophobia: the system classified it successfully where facial expressions were clear, DeepFace alone was insufficient where cues were ambiguous, and adding the questionnaire improved reliability. The evidential standing of the two halves is entirely different. The 92% is a real number from a real classification experiment, subject to the provenance and splitting problems that this review has recorded for six other studies on the same corpus. The gelotophobia statements are descriptions of an intended workflow, since no gelotophobia assessment was performed on any person and no metric of any kind is reported for that task.

answers.title: Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
answers.answer: The aim is autism detection from facial images alone, using pretrained convolutional networks as feature extractors with a simple downstream classifier. Five extractors - MobileNet, Xception, VGG16, VGG19 and EfficientNet - were compared across three preprocessing configurations, with augmentation applied, and the best combination reached 88.33% accuracy on test data, supported by a confusion matrix. The figure is the second-lowest among the eight Kaggle-corpus studies charted in this review, which range from 81.0% to 99.8%, and the architecture is the one least able to memorise: frozen pretrained extractors with a logistic-regression head have far fewer fitted parameters than the end-to-end fine-tuned networks used elsewhere on the same images. Whether the lower figure reflects that restraint or simply a different split cannot be determined, because no validation scheme is described.

answers.title: Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children
answers.answer: Two aims are pursued. The first is autism prediction from facial images using a hybrid architecture, justified by the argument that 'a single CNN is utilized within most studies which limits generalization. Therefore hierarchical features with fine grains are not obtained' - so combining ResNet50V2 and InceptionV3 should capture features at multiple granularities. The second, and the paper's better idea, is emotion recognition trained specifically on autistic children's faces, on the reasoning that existing systems are 'primarily trained for healthy ones and consequently missing abnormal facial movements'. The reported results diverge sharply in credibility. The emotion model reached 73.33% on six classes against a VGG16-plus-Random-Forest baseline at 57.33%, with precision 72.26, recall 73.33, specificity 83.90 and F1 70.38 - a modest, internally coherent figure on a genuinely hard task, and one consistent with the difficulty another study in this review documents for affect recognition in autistic children. The autism model's reported set is not coherent: 'accuracy = 95, precision = 0.96, sensitivity/recall = 0.94, Specificity = 42.5, F1 = 0.95 and AUC = 78'. On a balanced 280-image test set, recall 0.94 with specificity 0.425 yields roughly 68% accuracy, not 95%; precision 0.96 is impossible alongside specificity 0.425 at a 1:1 ratio, where the implied 80 false positives against 132 true positives would give precision near 0.62; and an AUC of 0.78 is incompatible with an accuracy of 0.95. The figures cannot all be right and no reconciliation is offered.

answers.title: Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy
answers.answer: The aim is to identify a lightweight CNN ensemble that classifies autism from facial photographs accurately enough for deployment on mobile or edge devices. Five pairings were compared - MobileNetV2 with EfficientNetB0, B5 and B7; ResNet50 with EfficientNetB0; VGG16 with EfficientNetB0 - combined by probability averaging or majority voting. The best, MobileNetV2 with EfficientNetB0, reached accuracy 0.8299, precision 0.8514, recall 0.8182 and F1 0.8344, an internally consistent set and among the lower figures in this branch. Two aspects of the reporting are better than the branch norm. The precision-recall trade-off is interpreted in screening terms: ResNet50 with EfficientNetB0 achieved 'higher precision but lower recall, making them less useful for finding all ASD cases', which correctly identifies that a screening instrument's priority is not missing cases. And the learning curves are read substantively for stability and overfitting rather than displayed decoratively, with some pairings noted to show 'slower learning with more fluctuations, indicating less stable models that might struggle with generalization'. The comparison table places the result against two prior studies at 0.7500 and 0.8050 - modest comparators, and the study does not claim to have exceeded the high-nineties figures reported elsewhere in the branch.

answers.title: Diagnosing autism spectrum disorder based on eye tracking technology using deep learning models
answers.answer: The stated goal is to implement deep learning on eye-tracking data from social attention tasks to diagnose ASD, and to identify the feature-selection strategy that lets the model reach high accuracy. Note that maximising accuracy is written into the objectives themselves - one of the listed research questions asks for the feature selection strategy that can assist the deep learning model in achieving high accuracy, which is a statement of intent to optimise the reported number rather than to estimate a diagnostic property. The headline finding is CNN-LSTM accuracy 99.78% (SD 0.11%), reported as outperforming previous studies and showing promise for clinical application.

answers.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Automated Machine Learning
answers.answer: The stated goal is to apply automated machine learning (TPOT) to a locally collected Pakistani dataset to determine the likelihood of ASD in children at early stages and to speed up diagnosis, with an explicit framing as one of the first uses of AUTOML for ASD detection on real-world non-high-income-country data. Headline findings: TPOT selected a BernoulliNB plus RandomForest ensemble; autistic-class precision 0.83, recall 0.90, F1 0.86; non-autistic-class precision 0.68, recall 0.53, F1 0.60; accuracy 0.83 in the results tables but reported as 78% in the abstract; micro-ROC 0.87, macro-ROC 0.81.
