The paper's headline claim concerns the effect of feature selection, and the reader cannot determine how many or which features that selection produced.

answers.title: Novel Framework for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification and Tailored Education With Effective Data Mining and Ensemble Learning Techniques
answers.answer: Low. The one Kaggle dataset is linked and the Q-CHAT-10 label rule is stated explicitly, which is better than most of the branch. Everything else is missing: the second dataset has no accession, the merged dataset that is claimed as a contribution is not deposited, no row counts are reported at any stage (pre-merge, post-merge, post-SMOTE, per class, per split), no hyperparameters are given for any of eight models, no seed or library versions appear, the number and identity of features retained by each of the three selection methods are never stated, and the order of SMOTE relative to the split is unspecified. The manuscript is also visibly an unedited accepted version - the header retains Date of publication xxxx 00, 0000 and the placeholder DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2017.DOI, and the running footer reads VOLUME 4, 2016 throughout.

answers.title: Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach
answers.answer: Moderate, and the strongest in this branch alongside local_ed30e24c. The preprocessing is published as a numbered algorithm specifying every encoding and column operation; the dataset is public; the composition of each of the four feature subsets is listed; the statistical tests and their exact p-values are tabulated; and confusion matrices are printed for all four final models. Missing: split proportions, the value of k in the cross-validation, any per-fold result, final hyperparameter values, the ANN architecture, the ensemble's combination rule, a seed, and code. The extracted PDF also ends mid-discussion after Table 7, so no conclusion or funding statement is available.

answers.title: Predicting autistic traits, anxiety and depression symptoms using camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (CAT-Q-ES): A machine learning study
answers.answer: The highest in the charted corpus. Code and a small sample dataset are publicly deposited on OSF - the only working code released by any study in this review. The fifty models, their implementation languages, packages and hyperparameter grids are enumerated in supplementary material. The cross-validation procedure is specified operationally, including partition disjointness, stratification across the score range, the rotation of training/validation/test roles across four trials, and the refit-on-train-plus-validation step. Missing data are quantified (0.30%) and the imputation justified. Exclusions are counted and reasoned. Internal consistencies are computed in-sample for every instrument. The only gap is the full dataset, withheld for confidentiality with a sample released in its place.

answers.title: A Computational Method for Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Deep Learning Approach
answers.answer: Low. The architecture is described in prose with three equations, and the optimiser, learning rate, weight decay, loss function and split sizes are given - a better start than several neighbours. What is missing prevents replication: no code, no seed, no epoch or batch count, no ResNet depth or ViT variant, no parameterisation for either of the two components claimed as novel (ReAttention and the Attention-Based Augmentation Layer), no list of augmentation transformations, no dataset accession beyond a reference number, no class counts for any partition, and no statement of how the 200-image validation and test sets were drawn from 2,926.

answers.title: Early Detection of ASD from Facial Images Using DeepDeblur and Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network
answers.answer: Very low, with one distinctive problem. The dataset source, class balance, split sizes and MATLAB version are stated, and a 25-symbol notation table with loss definitions (L2, total variation, facial semantic, total) is provided - superficially detailed. But no architecture, learning rate, batch size, epoch count, image resolution, optimiser budget or search space is given; there is no code or seed; the reported result does not correspond to the stated split; and the deblurring evaluation reports PSNR, MSE and SSIM, all of which are computed against a sharp ground-truth reference image. No such reference exists for a photograph downloaded from the web. Either the blur was synthetically added to already-degraded web images so that a reference existed - in which case the deblurring result describes recovery from artificial corruption and says nothing about real image quality - or the metrics were computed against something unstated. The paper does not say which.

answers.title: Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI
answers.answer: Split. The artefact-level reporting is among the best in the charted corpus: the source dataset has a URL and access date, the preprocessed 634-case analysis dataset is deposited as a supplementary spreadsheet, fold-by-fold metrics for all eight models appear in an appendix, caret's version is given, each model family is defined by equation, and the k-NN k-sweep is reported in full. The decisive step is nevertheless irreproducible. Preprocessing removed 1,351 of 1,985 records and 9 of 28 variables on the basis of clinical experts identifying inconsistencies and erroneous data, with no criterion stated, no counts per step, no class composition for the removed records and no indication of whether the removal was made blind to the outcome. Since that step is credited in the abstract with improving generalizability and real-world applicability, and since it is the largest single transformation in the pipeline, the study cannot be reproduced in the respect that matters most.

answers.title: Using explainable machine learning and eye-tracking for diagnosing autism spectrum and developmental language disorders in social attention tasks
answers.answer: Moderate to good on acquisition, thin on modelling. Reproducible: the eye tracker, sampling rate, screen size, calibration procedure, paradigm, stimulus composition and emotion set; the four feature sets by variable count and content; the stratified 5-fold scheme; the F1 interpretive bands, fixed before the results; and an offer of raw data on request. Not reproducible: the modelling workbench, the algorithm settings, whether any tuning occurred and whether it was nested, the seed, per-fold results, and the full variable lists for the 158-, 72-, 60- and 24-variable datasets.

answers.title: Utilizing deep learning models in an intelligent eye-tracking system for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis
answers.answer: Mixed. Strengths: per-model parameter tables covering base architecture, pooling, dense widths, dropout, output layer, loss, optimiser, learning rate, batch sizes and epochs; and an explicit, correctly ordered preprocessing sequence in which the split precedes augmentation and augmentation is confined to training. Weaknesses: the dataset is described only as a freely accessible public repository with no accession, URL or DOI; the split proportions are never stated and the test size must be inferred from a support column; there is no seed, no code, and no statement of how many children the images come from; and the hybrid model is specified only by a figure.

answers.title: A novel hybrid deep learning model using MEResNext for autism spectrum disorder detection
answers.answer: Very low, in an unusually instructive way. The article devotes several pages and roughly forty numbered equations to the internals of the MoNet sub-matrix square-root layer, including its forward and backward propagation and the symmetrisation of matrix derivatives - a level of mathematical specification exceeding anything else in the charted corpus. It reports none of what would be needed to repeat the study: no sample size, no class balance, no split or cross-validation scheme, no test-set size, no metaheuristic search space or budget, no count or identity of selected features, no learning rate, batch size or epoch count in the running text, no seed, no code, and no dataset accession. The detail is concentrated entirely on the parts that are reproduced from prior architecture papers and absent from the parts that are specific to this experiment.

answers.title: An assessment of autistic and parkinsonian movement profiles to inform selective classification algorithms
answers.answer: The highest in the charted corpus alongside local_4da2b941. Data and analysis scripts are deposited on OSF; all software is named with versions; the device and its screen specification are given; the outlier rule is stated with the exact percentage removed for each of the nine features; the normalising transformations are listed per variable; the mixed-model formulae are written out including random-effect structure; the feature-selection rule is specified precisely, including how group-by-shape interactions were handled; and the full classification grid is published as a heat map rather than reduced to a headline. The only gaps are the composition of the individual 80/20 draws and whether JASP's parameter optimisation was nested inside the split.

answers.title: An explainable deep learning framework for screening level autism severity using behavioural data
answers.answer: Moderate, and unusually strong on the parts that matter most for this branch. The labelling function is specified completely - the weighted index, its normalisation, the four threshold boundaries and the calibration objective - so another group could reconstruct the target variable, which is not true of any comparable study in this review. Three separate sensitivity analyses are reported with quantified deviations: imputation method (mode versus median versus kNN, under 1.0% deviation in macro-F1 and accuracy), severity thresholds perturbed by 5% and domain weights by 10% (macro-F1 within 0.6%, kappa within 0.03). The ablation table isolates each architectural component. Against this: no code, seed, software, versions, layer configuration, learning rate, batch size or epoch count; no per-cohort or per-class sample counts; and the harmonised dataset promised only post-publication.

answers.title: An explainable machine unlearning algorithm framework for early detection of autism spectrum disorder and brain disabilities in newborns
answers.answer: The article makes strong reproducibility claims - a public GitHub repository for both code and data, frozen configuration files, and an explicit statement that the entire pipeline can be replicated end-to-end - and simultaneously makes reproduction impossible by contradicting itself about what was run. The partition count is six in the methodology and four in the parameter table; the sample is 10,000 MRI scans and also 25,000 positives plus 1,200 negatives; the age band is 0-36 months, 12-36 months and 3-6 years in three places; the modality set is MRI, video, audio, text and EEG in one section and MRI, video and text in another. Feature vectors are printed as illustrative example values rather than as results. A sentence from the revision process also survives in the published text, reporting that figures are revised with corrected captions, algorithm numbering is standardized, and placeholder references are replaced with accurate citations.

answers.title: Deep learning based approach for Behavior classification in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder using naturalistic videos
answers.answer: Mixed, with real strengths on the comparative design. Reproducible: the source dataset is public and correctly attributed to its originators, the preprocessing chain is described in order, all five architectures were deliberately trained under identical hyperparameters to make the comparison fair, per-fold standard deviations are reported for every model and metric, and paired t-tests with a corrected significance threshold of 0.0125 are tabulated. Not reproducible: the value of k, the number of frames or clips extracted, the number of distinct children, per-class sample counts, the unit at which folds were formed, the learning rate, batch size and epoch count, any seed, and any code or data-availability statement.

answers.title: Explainable Children Autism Detection using Gaze Features in Audio-Visual Speech Comprehension
answers.answer: High. The corpus is cited to its source with its ethics approval; participant characteristics are tabulated with standard deviations on four measures; the 18 features are enumerated by area of interest; the factorial design is described in full including story counterbalancing; the grid-search space is published for every algorithm; the nested cross-validation, participant independence, per-fold class balancing and bootstrap interval procedure are all specified; the software stack is named; and per-story and per-condition results are tabulated with variability. Missing: the eye-tracking device, a code or data availability statement, and the number of instances contributing to each modality/phase cell.

answers.title: Explainable Ensemble Learning Framework for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Enhancing Trust, Interpretability and Reliability in AI-Driven Healthcare
answers.answer: Sharply divided between the two datasets. Dataset 1's pipeline is one of the better-documented in this branch: the whole sequence is published as a numbered algorithm specifying label encoding, z-score normalisation, the 0.90 correlation-filtering threshold and its retention rule, the 60:20:20 stratified split, the exact SMOTE trigger condition (minority-to-majority ratio below 0.8) with the interpolation formula, the ANOVA F-score expression, and the SHAP and LIME definitions - and the dataset's instance count, feature count, missing-value count and class balance are all tabulated. Dataset 2 is unreproducible in principle: no source, citation, country, institution, ethics committee, participant description or access route exists for the 100 original samples, and its characteristics are conveyed entirely through asserted quality figures (complete data availability, synchronisation below 100 ms, inter-rater kappa 0.92). Neither dataset is accompanied by code, seeds, base-learner hyperparameters or a stated fold count.

answers.title: Finding the forest in the trees: Using machine learning and online cognitive and perceptual measures to predict adult autism diagnosis
answers.answer: High, and complete on the axes that matter. The analysis script is publicly deposited; the recruitment sources are named with a justification for the platform chosen; the 407 exclusions are counted with their reasons; the matching procedure is described; demographic, cognitive and AQ characteristics are tabulated with standard deviations and significance tests for both samples; the tuned hyperparameters are enumerated; the tuning procedure and the overfitting criterion are stated; the decision not to resample is stated with its reasoning; and a label-randomisation control is reported. The primary data are restricted by register privacy rules, with the request procedure documented - the correct handling for a national register rather than a gap.

answers.title: Hybrid ensemble learning for Autism Spectrum Disorder screening using eye-tracking scanpath
answers.answer: Moderate. Reproducible: the source dataset has a DOI; the nine handcrafted scanpath descriptors are enumerated with definitions; the 20-fixation truncation/padding rule, the mean-and-standard-deviation aggregation to participant level, and z-score standardisation are all specified; fold-wise means and standard deviations are tabulated for every model; and the permutation-importance procedure is described with its intended scope. Not reproducible: no code or seed, no software or versions, no hyperparameters beyond k=3, no count of scanpaths per participant, no description of the source task, and no statement of where in the pipeline the within-subject resampling occurs relative to the fold split.

answers.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Facial Images and AI-Based Deep Learning Models
answers.answer: Low. Named: the source platform, the export-time preprocessing and augmentation, the image size, the epoch count and the training framework. Missing: the dataset URL, accession or version; class counts and split proportions; the number of distinct children; optimiser, learning rate, batch size and seed; and any code. The reported metrics also contain an internal inconsistency that cannot be reconciled - mAP@0.5:0.95 sits within 0.11 points of mAP@0.5 for both models, which no genuine detection evaluation produces.

answers.title: Multimodal fusion of deep transfer learning with wavelet neural network for autism spectrum disorder detection using facial images
answers.answer: Low. The compute environment, the four principal training hyperparameters, the class composition and the pipeline order are all given, which is more than several neighbours provide. Against that: the dataset is identified only by a reference number while the formal data statement denies that any dataset was analysed; no split procedure, partition counts or seed appear; the wavelet basis and network topology are unspecified; the chimp optimiser has no stated objective, search space or budget; no code is released; and the epoch count in the text contradicts the epoch axis of the learning curves.

answers.title: SHAP-based explainable AI framework for autism severity classification using 3D motor biomarkers
answers.answer: High for a secondary analysis. Both repository URLs are given with the note that they contain the same data with full documentation and metadata; the six preprocessing stages are enumerated with exact dataframe dimensions (109 x 466) and class encodings; the decision to use only original rather than the repository's seven geometric augmentations is stated explicitly; the synthetic-generation rule is described precisely enough to reproduce; and both a fold standard deviation and a 95% confidence interval are reported. Missing: model hyperparameters, software and versions, seed and code.

answers.title: Screening autism spectrum
answers.answer: Moderate to high. Both corpora are public and linked with their source studies cited; participant counts, sex, mean ages, total words and utterance statistics are tabulated by group; the feature count is given; the selected hyperparameters are reported for all three models; the SMOTE validation is quantified with KS statistics and p-values; and the overfitting check is reported as a numerical train-validation gap. Missing: code, seed, software versions, the complete 52-feature list, and the placement of SMOTE relative to the folds.

answers.title: Towards screening of children students with autism spectrum disorder based on executive functions with serious game and machine learning approaches
answers.answer: High on artefacts. Code and dataset are publicly deposited on GitHub with replication named as the explicit purpose - the second study in the charted corpus to release working code. The full hyperparameter grid and selected values are tabulated for all seven models; the collected data fields are listed with types and example values; inclusion and exclusion criteria are enumerated for both children and professionals; the consent procedure is described at both levels; and the game design and its executive-function rationale are documented through a methodology flowchart. Missing: an ethics committee reference, sex composition, a random seed, software versions, and - most consequentially - any statement of how the 640 sessions were assigned to the training, testing and validation partitions.

questions.question_text: Which limitations do the authors acknowledge?

answers.title: Very early detection of Autism Spectrum Disorders based on acoustic analysis of pre-verbal vocalizations of 18-month old toddlers
answers.answer: Reported/identifiable bias: very small sample (n=43); single national cohort; high-risk-sibling recruitment means the ASD group is not a general-population sample; male-skewed (28/43 male); English-speaking homes only; instance-level analysis with unequal vocalisation counts per group (2592 control vs 1930 ASD instances). Authors acknowledge only that non-ASD language-disorder toddlers were not included. Reviewer-identified: probable subject leakage in cross-validation and absence of any external validation.

answers.title: Use of Machine Learning to Identify Children with Autism and Their Motor Abnormalities
answers.answer: Reported by the authors: very small sample; classifier highly specific to the training sample (preschool, low-functioning); need for females, high-functioning children and adults; no ADOS on the full sample; no other neurodevelopmental comparison groups; predictive value constrained by population base rate. Identifiable in review: strong male skew (25/30 male); chronological-age and IQ imbalance between groups confounded with diagnosis; single-site recruitment; maximum-over-feature-subsets accuracy reporting; feature selection not demonstrably nested within the LOO loop.

answers.title: ADHD and ASD Classification Based on Emotion Recognition Data
answers.answer: Reported by the authors: class imbalance across groups, attributed to 'technical problems' and corrected by random oversampling to 30 per group. Identifiable in review: very small control group (n=13); no gender data at all, so sex bias cannot be assessed in a literature where ASD samples are typically male-skewed; no age matching; single-site outpatient recruitment; no reported handling of ASD-ADHD comorbidity despite a three-way design; post-hoc selection of the best-performing class grouping and classifier; oversampling apparently applied before rather than within validation; and no validation scheme reported, so all accuracies are of unknown optimism.

answers.title: Identifying children with autism spectrum disorder based on their face processing abnormality: A machine learning framework
answers.answer: Reported by the authors: sample prevalence (33% ASD) far exceeds population prevalence (~1%), so positive predictive value in practice would be much lower; face-scanning is age- and culture-adapted so the model may not transfer across ages or cultures; ASD sample characteristics such as symptom severity and cognitive function may drive scanning patterns; sample size is small for pattern classification. Identifiable in review: strong male skew (25/29, ~86% male, replicated across all groups); single-country Chinese sample with race-specific face stimuli; diagnosis confirmed by questionnaire (AQ-Child) rather than ADOS/ADI-R; cluster number K and decision threshold tuned for maximum accuracy on the same data; K-means quantisation fitted on all participants including the held-out test participant, a subtle transductive leak; and the direction of the discriminative-region effects is stated inconsistently between Results and Discussion.

answers.title: Semantic mapping reveals distinct patterns in descriptions of social relations in adults with autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: Reported by the authors: small patient sample, especially few female participants with ASD, with an explicit note that male and female ASD participants may differ in language patterns; the model omits word ordering and phrase-level effects; the prompted format may not capture core language-generation deficits; mechanisms are not disambiguated. Identifiable in review: group sizes are very unequal (27 vs 132) and gender is imbalanced in opposite directions between groups (85% male ASD vs 66% female typical) while gender is not matched - a serious confound for a language-production measure; the ASD group is also on average 7-12 years older; the sample is high-functioning adults (IQ >= 70, mean verbal IQ ~107) so results cannot extend to the wider spectrum; no statement that LSI was refitted within cross-validation folds; and 59% White in the ASD group with no other ethnicity analysis.

answers.title: Toward the Autism Motor Signature: Gesture patterns during smart tablet gameplay identify children with autism
answers.answer: Reported by the authors, unusually thoroughly: IQ was not controlled and could confound; recruitment from particular specialist institutions gives only a subgroup of the spectrum and this 'inherent selection bias in our autism group may have facilitated machine learning differential power'; machine learning is sensitive to sample size so wider recruitment and larger numbers are needed; and the comparison is against children with no concern for ASD rather than against the clinically relevant ASD-versus-ASD-like contrast. Identifiable in review: 247 features against 82 children; feature importance assessed univariately by KS distance rather than from the models; the reported AUC is the best of four algorithm variants across two games plus their average; and two authors are affiliated with the commercial developer with explicit commercialisation ambitions, disclosed by affiliation but not as a competing-interests statement.

answers.title: Applying machine learning to identify autistic adults using imitation: An exploratory study
answers.answer: Reported by the authors: small sample size is named as the study's limitation; ASC heterogeneity means generalisation to a wider population 'remains to be tested'; and comparison against other motor-deficit groups (developmental coordination disorder, ADHD) is needed to know whether the profile is autism-specific. Identifiable in review: no diagnostic instrument is reported for the ASC group at all; both groups have mean IQ near 119, so the sample represents only high-IQ verbally able adults; sex counts are never given despite sex-matching being claimed; 6% of ASC trials and 2% of control trials were excluded for recording or imitation errors, an asymmetry that is disclosed but not analysed; and the reported 86.7% is the best cell of a grid spanning three feature-selection methods, four-plus classifiers and eight conditions, so some selection optimism survives even the nested validation.

answers.title: Automatic Detection of ADHD and ASD from Expressive Behaviour in RGBD Data
answers.answer: No limitations section exists, so nothing is acknowledged by the authors beyond the ADHD-only group being too small to model. Identifiable in review: severe class imbalance (18 controls vs 37 condition) reported only as accuracy, where always predicting 'condition' would already score 67%; group sizes of 4 and 11 in two of the four cells; ages and genders never reported numerically and never matched or tested, so demographic confounding cannot be assessed at all; a very high-dimensional feature vector (six feature families x 12 segments) against 55 subjects with greedy forward selection not stated to be nested inside the leave-one-subject-out loop - the single most likely explanation for 37/37 and 22/22 perfect recall on the majority classes; single-site recruitment; and no ethnicity data.

answers.title: Earlier identification of children with autism
answers.answer: Reported by the authors: the small number of subjects limits the impact of the results, and a genuine performance difference between SVM and deep learning 'might only become evident on a dataset with a considerably higher number of vocalisations'. They also note that a proportion of ASD infants' vocalisations carry no acoustic atypicality, and disclose pacifier use as a possible source of error for one misclassified control. Identifiable in review: n=20 makes the 75% subject-level figure equivalent to 15/20 correct with a very wide confidence interval; the headline 75% uses per-fold optimised thresholds rather than the fixed 0.5 threshold (70%); vocalisation counts are unbalanced between groups (259 ASD vs 425 TD) and per subject (9 to 98), so subject-level ratios rest on very different amounts of evidence; 54 of 88 features are declared significant with no multiple-comparison correction, so a substantial share are likely false positives; and the high-familial-risk sibling design means the ASD group is not representative of general-population screening.

answers.title: Speech-based Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Condition by Generative
answers.answer: Reported by the authors: small corpus size in ASC research generally is the paper's motivating problem, and they cite prior work warning that high accuracies on small datasets 'may lead to potential confounds'. Identifiable in review: severe class imbalance (68 TD versus 11 AD children, 4547 versus 149 test-set utterances by the confusion matrices) with the reported UAR concealing near-floor autism recognition; no age or sex data reported at all, so demographic bias cannot be assessed; matching is asserted without numbers; single-country, monolingual, verbally able children only, which excludes minimally verbal autistic children entirely; evaluation is at utterance rather than child level; and the best-layer selection differs between feature sets in a way that suggests the layer choice is being read off test performance rather than validation - the eGeMAPS validation UARs are essentially flat across layers (39.33-40.92%) while the test UARs vary by more than a point.

answers.title: ANN and SVM Classifiers in Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorder Gait Based on Three-Dimensional Ground Reaction Forces
answers.answer: Reported by the authors: only that evaluation on a larger dataset is needed to confirm the observations - there is no limitations section as such. Identifiable in review: feature selection by SWDA used group labels on the full dataset before cross-validation, and the exhaustive hyperparameter grid search (three SVM kernels, six C values, three polynomial degrees, 21 gamma values, 50 ANN hidden-layer sizes) was likewise performed outside the folds, so 93.3% is not an unbiased generalisation estimate; the reported figure is also the best of four classifier configurations; no gender data at all, so sex bias cannot be assessed in a literature with strong male skew; groups differ by ~0.9 years in mean age with no matching test, and gait matures with age; body mass SD is large and unequal; ASD recruitment is split across a specialist centre and social-media outreach with no comparison between subgroups; only one stance phase of one limb from one trial represents each child, so within-subject gait variability - itself a reported feature of autistic movement - is entirely discarded.

answers.title: Analyzing Human-Robot Interaction Using Machine Vision for Autism screening
answers.answer: Reported by the authors: the limited number of cases is explicitly named as a limitation, with a stated plan to run on more children; and the method is acknowledged to fail on shy typically developing children, which the authors address by arguing it should be combined with other screening methods rather than used alone. Identifiable in review: control age range (2.11-7.6 years) roughly doubles the ASD range (2.1-4.1) with no matching, confounding age with group in a spatial-approach measure; no gender data despite a strongly sex-skewed condition; no diagnostic instrument; the best of five classifiers across three feature configurations is reported with no nesting of that selection inside the 8-fold cross-validation; the stacking layer degrades four of five classifiers, so the 81.3% may reflect a fortunate combination rather than a real gain; and post-hoc explanations of the four first-layer errors (shyness, high functioning) are unmeasured narrative rather than data.

answers.title: Applying Eye Tracking to Identify Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children
answers.answer: Reported by the authors in an explicit five-point limitations list: ADOS/ADI-R unavailable so diagnoses rest on DSM-5 and CARS alone; no IQ or adaptive-behaviour measure of functional level; relatively small sample requiring larger-sample validation; unknown whether findings are specific to the 4-6 age group; and no direct comparison against or combination with other eye-tracking paradigms. Identifiable in review: gender is imbalanced in practice (89% vs 73% male) despite a non-significant chi-square on n=74; the control group has no GDS or functional data so the correlational analysis cannot be contrasted across groups; single-site recruitment with an ethnically homogeneous sample viewing an Asian female face, leaving cross-cultural transfer untested; whether AOI selection was nested inside the five-fold cross-validation is unstated; and the paper reports two mutually inconsistent sets of accuracy figures for the same analysis.

answers.title: Automatic Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Everyday
answers.answer: Reported by the authors, unusually thoroughly for a conference paper: large variance in data volume per subject (4 to 1968 recordings) driven by device-usage preference rather than condition; real-life data errors including interrupted tests and parents completing tests on the child's behalf, which would overestimate development level; varying background noise across subjects; absence of speaker diarization so child and parent speech cannot be separated; ASR error rates that increase precisely when child speech is atypical, undermining the linguistic features; and misclassification associated with low data volume for two of the three errors. They also deliberately excluded age and gender as features because 'in the subject recruitment process, it is possible that age and gender information have some implicit connection with the label'. Identifiable in review: that same recruitment confound is not addressed at the sample level - ages span 3 months to 17 years with toddlers over-represented in the ASD group and teenagers among the TD group, entirely unmatched, so acoustic maturation is confounded with diagnosis; 18 ASD versus 9 TD with only 27 analysed; no diagnostic instrument whatsoever; no ethics or consent statement; and the 17-month longitudinal structure is collapsed to a single averaged vector, discarding the developmental information the design was uniquely placed to capture.

answers.title: Detecting Autism Based on Eye-Tracking Data from Web Searching
answers.answer: Reported by the authors in a dedicated Limitations subsection: the 0.75 accuracy compares unfavourably with the 71-86.7% range reported for fMRI classifiers, which they attribute partly to the data not having been collected for classification; web-searching tasks are unsuitable for the very young children in whom early detection would be most valuable, so a different task would be needed to reach them; and the sample is not large, though they note it exceeds the 12-per-group benchmark study they compare against. Identifiable in review: no diagnostic instrument is named, with verification delegated to the recruiting charity; formally diagnosed intellectual disability is an exclusion criterion so results apply only to high-functioning adults; control education exceeds autistic education by 2.3 years, undiscussed; the headline is selected across two tasks, two AOI schemes, four feature sets and multiple page subsets - though every alternative is reported with confidence intervals, making the selection auditable; and the participant-level aggregation rule (majority vote over behaviours) is a design choice whose sensitivity is not explored.

answers.title: Video Gesture Analysis for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
answers.answer: There is no limitations section, so nothing is formally acknowledged, though the authors do report the difficulty candidly in the results - the large per-subject standard deviation is presented as evidence that 'finding a very general pattern in the video, that could be unique in distinguishing autistic subjects, is a challenging task', and TD subjects being classified better than ASD ones is read as 'evidence of the fact that autistic spectrum disorders comprise indeed a very wide spectrum of variability'. Identifiable in review: n=39 makes 0.82 equal to 32 of 39 children; the ASD group excludes intellectual impairment and is IQ-matched to controls, so results cannot extend to the broader spectrum; both groups are 80-90% male; the per-subject table shows several ASD children classified confidently wrong (subjects 7, 17 and 20 at 0.15, 0.16 and 0.31), which a single aggregate figure would conceal; the 0.5 threshold on averaged frame probabilities is a lenient decision rule and performance collapses below chance above a 0.9 threshold; and single-site recruitment with one fixed camera viewpoint leaves transfer entirely untested.

answers.title: A Novel Eye Movement Data Transformation Technique that Preserves Temporal Information: A Demonstration in a Face Processing Task
answers.answer: The paper has no dedicated limitations section, since it is framed as a methods demonstration. It does report transparently that Experiment 1 data were reused from a companion paper and why. Identifiable in review: the absolute accuracies of 53.9% and 55.5% are barely above chance and correspond to a 1.6 percentage point improvement, so while the temporal claim is statistically supported the practical discriminability is negligible - a fact the paper does not emphasise; the unit of analysis is a single two-second trial rather than a person, so no participant-level diagnostic estimate exists; the ASD age range extends to 29 against a control maximum of 21 despite matched means; both groups are heavily male on very small female counts; all participants have IQ above 85, so the sample excludes much of the spectrum; and trials with no AOI transitions in either eye were excluded, which may remove disproportionately many ASD trials given the noted tendency toward stray fixations.

answers.title: Applying Machine Learning to Identify Autism With Restricted Kinematic Features
answers.answer: Reported by the authors in a dedicated Limitations section that is notably candid: only high-functioning children were recruited to ensure task compliance, and whether low-functioning patients could perform the task 'remains an open question'; and 'obviously, this motor task would not work for children less than 2 years old, which suggests that this motor task would not function for the early screening of ASD' - an explicit concession that the method cannot serve early screening, which almost no other corpus study makes. They further note that motion-capture approaches can quantify low-level stereotyped movement but not higher-level RRB such as circumscribed interest. Identifiable in review: the t-test screen from 18 to 9 features used the full labelled dataset before cross-validation, and forward feature selection then selected the combination maximising classification accuracy, so 88.37% is a maximum over a search using the evaluation criterion; the best of five classifiers and four k values is reported; sensitivity and specificity are reversed between abstract and discussion; the direction of the velocity features carrying most of the signal is not reported; exclusion of ADHD, intellectual disability and schizophrenia makes the discrimination easier than the clinical task; and demographic detail resides in a table that is not reproduced in the running text.

answers.title: Automatic Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Acoustic and Text Features from Brief Natural Conversations
answers.answer: Reported by the authors: performance is limited by 5-minute samples and generic topics compared with ADOS evaluations designed to elicit ASD-like features; human raters outperformed the model, which the authors read as evidence that the feature set fails to capture topicality, relevance, appropriateness and conversational flow at a turn-by-turn level; ASD is harder to predict than TD because of phenotypic heterogeneity; and the approach 'is not yet valuable as a method for diagnosing ASD, which still needs to be diagnosed by expert clinicians'. Identifiable in review: the demographic table's sex counts sum to 25 rather than 35 in both groups; the confederate features that are among the most consistently selected mean part of the signal is an interlocutor's response to the child rather than the child's own behaviour, which limits transfer to any self-administered or partner-free screening context; all participants were native English speakers at a single site, with no ethnicity or socioeconomic data; confederates were 19 of 22 female, so partner-sex variation is minimal; and n=70 makes 75.71% equal to 53 of 70 children.

answers.title: Classifying Individuals with ASD Through Facial Emotion Recognition and Eye-Tracking
answers.answer: No dedicated limitations section. The introduction acknowledges at field level that eye-tracking results 'can be impacted by sample size, age, developmental level and IQ, variation in stimuli, and task effort and objective', but the study does not then control for these. Identifiable in review: the two eye trackers are confounded with group - all ASD subjects used the 300 Hz TX300 while 29 of 35 controls used the 60 Hz X2-60 - and the most important model features (fixation frequency, fixation duration, fixation time, saccade amplitude) are exactly the measures a fivefold sampling-rate difference would bias, yet the authors dismiss this in one sentence; five ASD subjects were excluded for eye-tracking capture failure with no controls excluded, a group-dependent attrition that could itself reflect the behaviour being measured; control ages extend to 34 versus an ASD maximum of 17, with a control SD more than double the ASD SD; IQ is reported only as an ASD range and never controlled; two display sizes were used; and the reported equations define sensitivity in terms of TN and specificity in terms of TP, inverting the standard definitions.

answers.title: Detecting Developmental Delay and Autism Through Machine
answers.answer: Reported by the authors in a dedicated limitations section that diagnoses the transfer gap in three specific ways: the source classifiers were trained on clinical scoresheets rather than features obtained from live video; those scoresheets came from formal clinical assessments of US children and 'do not capture a culturally diverse set of behavioral nuances'; and the classifiers were built to separate typical development from autism whereas this dataset contains other delays including SLCs. They also hypothesise that raters sharing the children's linguistic and sociocultural background would improve performance. Identifiable in review: sex is markedly imbalanced between the ASD and SLC cohorts (72% versus 46% male), directly confounding the second classification layer; family income differs sharply across groups (96% of ASD families above 30,000 taka versus 26% of TD families), as does residence; stunting data are missing entirely for the TD cohort; ADOS covered only 28 of 50 ASD children; the demographic table's gender percentages are inconsistent with their counts; and the senior author founded a company developing paediatric digital health solutions, disclosed as a conflict of interest.

answers.title: Exploiting Visual Behaviour for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification
answers.answer: Reported by the authors, and unusually thoughtfully for a four-page workshop paper: ASD fixation behaviour changes with age, with toddlers, young children and grown-up children differing markedly and adults with ASD showing no visible difference in fixation duration between objects and non-objects, so 'the ASD subject age is very important for detecting the condition' - yet age was unavailable in the dataset; and fixation behaviour also depends on image content, since young ASD children do not differ from TD children on scenes containing both faces and objects of circumscribed interest, so 'ASD condition cannot be generalized over age, fixation behaviour, and image content' whereas the model generalises all features over all subjects. Identifiable in review: specificity of 50.56% is chance level and the model is therefore near-useless for ruling out ASD, which the summary framing of '60% accuracy' obscures; no participant counts, ages or genders exist at all; subject identity is not consistent across images so subject-independent evaluation is impossible and the same person's scanpaths can appear in both training and test sets; the unit of analysis is a scanpath not a person, so this is not a person-level diagnostic result; and no feature importance is reported despite the model providing it natively.

answers.title: Hierarchical POMDP Framework for a Robot-Assisted ASD Diagnostic Protocol
answers.answer: Reported by the authors, with notable candour: the sample size 'is not large'; because each task runs once the robot makes only three decisions, which 'does not necessarily warrant a use of POMDP'; social cue detection algorithms are 'not accurate enough for fully autonomous execution' so the robot is only semi-autonomous with an operator supplying critical observations; not all children completed all tasks, some because of robot failures and some through fear or refusal; in four cases robot failure ended the session because children would not continue; and crucially, typically developing children 'sometimes exhibit autistic behavior, and vice versa', which the authors attribute to the ASD group being in daily intervention and unafraid of the robot while typically developing children were shy and wary. Identifiable in review: no ages, genders or diagnostic instrument; no ethics or consent statement despite two-way-mirror video of preschoolers; observation probabilities elicited by clinician survey rather than estimated from data; no quantitative performance metric whatsoever; and the confidence-scaling parameter was tuned until 'more appropriate' belief values emerged, which is a judgement call rather than a fitted value.

answers.title: Intelligent Gaze-Based Screening System for Autism
answers.answer: Reported by the authors: only that the model should be replicated with larger datasets to validate performance, and that other classification techniques should be compared. No limitations section exists. Identifiable in review: no sample size is reported, so the precision of the four performance figures is unknowable; no ages, genders or diagnostic procedure, so demographic and ascertainment bias cannot be assessed; no stimulus, ROI or feature specification, so the measurement cannot be evaluated; methods sections are written partly in the future tense, suggesting the system was planned rather than fully executed at time of writing; the claim that a high AUC means the model 'works well regardless of the class distribution (i.e. when data are new/unknown)' conflates class-distribution invariance with generalisation to new data; and the study is framed around screening before age 2 while never reporting the age of any participant.

answers.title: Kinematic features of a simple and short movement task to predict autism diagnosis
answers.answer: No dedicated limitations section, but the paper's entire framing is a limitation critique aimed at its own field: prior kinematic studies achieving 86.7-96.7% 'used K-fold Cross-Validation, which was demonstrated to produce overoptimistic performance estimates, especially when a sample size is small' and did not assess whether performance differed significantly from random guessing. The conclusion adds that large parametric effect sizes 'do not necessarily translate to high ML classification performance'. Identifiable in review: no diagnostic instrument named; IQ matching claimed without values; no age standard deviations or ranges; adults only; n=46 so 71% is roughly 33 of 46 correct, with no confidence interval reported though accuracy distributions are plotted; the best of four pipelines is highlighted, though all four including the two non-significant ones are reported in full; and outlier replacement with group means (1.4% of data points) uses group information, a minor leakage route not discussed.

answers.title: Learning to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder based on the Visual
answers.answer: Reported by the authors in a brief limitations section: the relatively small number of participants, and the fairly short duration of the video scenarios, with longer scenarios possibly allowing a richer visual representation. Identifiable in review and more consequential: the unit of analysis is the image not the child, with 547 images from 59 children plus 2,735 augmented synthetic derivatives, and no statement that cross-validation was participant-independent - so images and their own augmented near-duplicates can span the training and test folds, which would inflate the reported AUC substantially; no per-group age or sex data at all; the qualitative observation that the ASD exemplar looked toward the bottom of the screen where the eye tracker was physically located raises the possibility of apparatus-driven signal; the multi-label experiment predicts CARS bands from data collected on children whose diagnosis was itself characterised by CARS, which is partly circular; and the work was funded by a commercial healthcare IT company, acknowledged but not declared as a competing interest.

answers.title: Machine Learning to Study Social Interaction Difficulties in ASD
answers.answer: Reported by the authors: the sample size is 'rather limited', so the next step must be applying the algorithm to a completely new and larger dataset; transdiagnostic specificity across psychiatric conditions is untested; and Motion Energy Analysis retains 'a subjective component' because regions of interest are drawn manually, even though pixel-change detection is automatic. The paper also criticises the wider literature for circularity where classifiers are trained on clinician-derived features. Identifiable in review: no participant ages, sexes or matching information are reported in this paper at all; specificity of 55.2% means the model misclassifies nearly half of controls, so the headline accuracy rests on an unbalanced error profile; the dyadic design means each participant's synchrony was measured while interacting with partners of differing diagnostic status, a potential source of variance that is not analysed; one entire task was dropped because a single dyad misunderstood instructions; and the sample is high-functioning adults only.

answers.title: Phase 3 diagnostic evaluation of a smart
answers.answer: The protocol's account of its predecessor's limitations is the most methodologically literate passage in this corpus, and it names both failure modes that this review has documented repeatedly. On selection: the pilot's 82 children came from 'a small number of specialist day-care centres in Poland. Such limited subject recruitment is prone to selection bias and site-specific effects and precludes assessment of predictive value in population-based settings.' On evaluation: 'the pilot study employed the same dataset to train and test the machine learning algorithm. It did so with 10 repetitions of a 10-fold cross-validation procedure that is not prone to overfitting. Nevertheless, it only trained and tested patterns on that particular dataset.' That second sentence is important - it concedes that repeated cross-validation, which most studies in this review treat as sufficient, does not establish generalisation beyond the dataset it is computed on. Both concerns are then addressed structurally rather than rhetorically. Two design points remain unstated: recruitment through specialist services means population-prevalence predictive value will still not be directly estimable, and the algorithm remains a commercial black box, so a positive result would show that the instrument works without showing what it measures.

answers.title: Predicting Autism Diagnosis using Image with Fixations and Synthetic Saccade Patterns
answers.answer: Reported by the authors only briefly: 'The performance gap may be caused by the imbalanced distribution of training and test dataset and lacking of training images'. They also note, when citing the prior 92% adult result, that it 'may not be directly applicable to gaze patterns from children' - a caution about transfer that few corpus papers offer about their own antecedents. Identifiable in review: the internal split is partitioned by image, not by participant, so the same child's scanpaths appear in both internal training and validation, which is the most likely reason internal accuracy exceeds blind test accuracy by 6-11 points; the number of distinct participants is never stated; no control ages, no genders, no diagnostic information; specificity on the blind test collapses to 0.282-0.471, meaning the models achieve their apparent sensitivity largely by over-calling ASD; and the unit of analysis is the scanpath rather than the person, so no person-level estimate exists.

answers.title: Recognition Of Atypical Behavior In Autism Diagnosis From Video Using Pose Estimation Over Time
answers.answer: No dedicated limitations section. The authors note only that the approach could be improved by combining RGB and audio modalities and by moving to 3D trajectories. Identifiable in review and more consequential: the classification target is episode-level expert-labelled behaviour rather than participant diagnosis, so the reported figures are not diagnostic accuracy despite the paper's 'ASD prediction' framing; no participant counts, ages, genders or diagnostic status are reported, so the corpus composition and any demographic confounding are unknowable; the train/test partitioning basis is unstated with 8349 episodes from 555 videos, making episode-level leakage across the split highly likely; class imbalance (5265 atypical to 3084 typical) is unaddressed and is consistent with the 0.92 recall against 0.66 AUC, indicating a majority-class-biased classifier; the imputation ablation shows three conditions performing identically on accuracy, precision and recall yet the text claims 'the classifier benefits a lot from interpolation'; multiple expert annotators are mentioned with no inter-rater agreement reported; and there is no ethics or consent statement for home video of children.

answers.title: Robot-Assisted Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Based on Artificial Reasoning
answers.answer: There is no dedicated limitations section, but the paper's self-description is honest at the points that matter: the evaluation is labelled 'a proof of concept', the index group is described as 'without confirmed ASD diagnosis', and the vision pipeline's occlusion failures are reported rather than omitted. The introduction also identifies the gap in prior work accurately - early robot-assisted diagnostic systems 'have primarily been open loop and remotely operated systems. However, these approaches are unable to perform autonomous feedback to enhance the interaction' - which is the specific deficiency the closed-loop architecture addresses. What is not addressed: six children in single sessions cannot support a behavioural claim, and no statistical test, effect size or uncertainty estimate accompanies the reported difference; neither group has documented diagnostic status; the mediator order is not counterbalanced, confounding the key finding with order, fatigue and novelty; no ethics approval is reported; no developmental measure was obtained in three-year-olds, so general developmental level cannot be separated from autism risk; and the behavioural finding rests on automated visual-focus-of-attention estimates with no reliability check against human coding, in a pipeline whose occlusion problems the paper itself reports.

answers.title: SP-ASDNet: CNN-LSTM Based ASD Classification Model using Observer ScanPaths
answers.answer: Reported by the authors: the blind-test performance 'is much lower than that of the validation dataset, which could indicate the submitted models being overfitted', with a call to further investigate the structure of visual attention to mitigate this. They also note candidly that SalGAN was trained on SALICON, 'collected from subjects over a large age range and thus not perfectly reflected the saliency distribution of the children', and that no public large-scale child saliency dataset exists to retrain it. They further acknowledge that the influence of saliency prediction quality on final classification has not been exhaustively tested. Identifiable in review: the internal split is partitioned by image, not participant, so the same children appear in both training and validation; model selection across two CNN variants, three feature dimensionalities and two normalisation settings was performed on that same validation set, compounding optimism; no participant counts, ages, genders or diagnostic information exist; the unit of analysis is the scanpath rather than the person; and blind-test precision of 0.5319-0.5684 with recall up to 0.8771 for model A indicates the best-recall model achieves it by over-calling ASD.

answers.title: Social robot in diagnosis of autism among preschool children
answers.answer: Two limitations are stated and both are correctly identified. The first is the absence of a comparison group - 'we observed only autistic children interacting with the robot' - with the remedy given as comparison against typically developing children, which the group subsequently carried out. The second is more valuable and is rare in this corpus: 'the especially challenging task is to differ autism from other similar disorders. Thus, the other direction of our future studies is to observe the interactions performed by the robot and the children with other disorders.' Committing to a non-autistic clinical comparison is a commitment almost no study in this review makes, and the one included study that does test autism against another clinical population found the field's gold-standard observational instrument achieving an AUC of 0.562 - which is the evidence that this stated priority is the right one. What is not addressed: sample size and participant characteristics are unreported; no diagnostic ascertainment is described; inter-rater reliability is not quantified for this study; rater blinding to the hypothesis is not discussed; and no developmental measure separates general cognitive level from autism as an explanation for reduced spontaneous imitation.

answers.title: Application of the Still-Face Paradigm in Early Screening for High-Risk Autism Spectrum Disorder in Infants and Toddlers
answers.answer: Two limitations are stated: the groups could not be age-matched because autistic children generally have delayed development, so matching on age would unmatch developmental level; and the sample was small. The N-ASD failure is discussed candidly - 'the 5 N-ASD was not classified correctly', attributed to class imbalance and to only ten indicators per sample, with identifying N-ASD from ASD named as a goal for future work. The contrary finding on negative emotion is also flagged as needing further validation. Identifiable in review but not acknowledged: the verification step is largely circular, since 40 of the 45 high-risk children used to verify the SVM were in its training set; the age gap coincides with significant differences in four of five developmental quotients, so group separation may partly reflect developmental level rather than autism; features were selected by group-difference t-tests computed on the full dataset before cross-validation, which leaks label information into the feature set; and the reported accuracies do not exactly match the tabulated confusion matrices.

answers.title: Applying Machine Learning to Kinematic and Eye Movement Features of a Movement Imitation Task to Predict Autism Diagnosis
answers.answer: The paper's framing is itself a critique of prior work's limitations rather than only its own. On the field: prior kinematic ML studies 'had small sample sizes and achieved high classification accuracy', but 'models developed with small sample/high dimensional data are prone to fit noise and not necessarily an underlying pattern separating classes', and those studies 'did not avoid pooling training and validation data while developing their ML models and did not take other steps to control for the fitting of random noise', were 'not tested with independent data', and did not assess statistical significance. On their own work they acknowledge the difficulty of small-sample high-dimensional pattern recognition requiring careful handling of both validation and feature selection. Identifiable in review: 44 adults total with a 14-participant test set means 78% is roughly 11 of 14 correct; the diagnostic ascertainment is entirely absent from this paper; both samples are high-IQ adults; the reported headline is the best across several feature-selection variants; and the marked sex-composition difference between samples, while turned into a generalisation argument, also means the independent test provides limited evidence about performance in a comparably composed sample.

answers.title: Research and Design of Autism Smart Diagnosis Information System Based on Chinese Children's Facial Expression Data and Deep Convolution Neural Network
answers.answer: The authors acknowledge that the algorithm 'is affected by the environment and light' and that accuracy suffers accordingly, noting that two typically developing children scored 57.1%; that errors concentrate on disgust and surprise because those expressions involve only minor local facial change and some participants produced them weakly; and that more real samples are needed. They do not acknowledge the design's central problems. No model is trained on autism labels, so a proxy task's failure rate is being treated as a diagnostic signal, and the design cannot separate non-imitation, atypical imitation, developmental immaturity and out-of-distribution faces from autism. The groups differ in age (3-6 versus 5-8) and are fully confounded with recruitment site. The supplementary training images came from typically developing 5-8 year olds, the control group's own population, which biases the classifier toward recognising control-group faces. The 60% threshold is fitted to the same 20 children it is evaluated on. And the abstract's 81.4% is the expression recognition rate in typically developing children, not a diagnostic accuracy, yet is presented as 'the accuracy of facial expression recognition of this system'.

answers.title: Automated identification of postural control for children with autism spectrum disorder using a machine learning approach
answers.answer: Reported by the authors only briefly, in the abstract and conclusions: 'By increasing the sample size and analyzing more data/features of postural control, a better classification performance would be expected'. There is no dedicated limitations section. Identifiable in review: n=50 with five-fold cross-validation means roughly 10 children per test fold, so 0.900 accuracy is about 45 of 50 correct and the exact 1.000 specificity and precision reflect zero false positives among 25 controls - values that will not be stable at this scale; the headline is the best of six algorithms evaluated on the same cross-validation with no nested selection or external validation; no diagnostic instrument is named; inclusion criteria requiring comprehension of instructions and task performance restrict the ASD sample to more able children; sex is not matched (56% versus 40% female); and the negative sample entropy result contradicts two prior studies cited in the introduction without the discrepancy being discussed in the extracted text.

answers.title: Behavior-based Risk Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through
answers.answer: Reported by the authors, and unusually directly for the format: the work 'is limited by the number of participants, the inclusion of a single gender and the exclusive use of behaviors available from video data', and given the 0.1787 false negative rate 'this method cannot be claimed to be ready to be used singularly as a diagnostic tool for ASD'. Identifiable in review and more consequential: the evaluation unit is the 1-second data window rather than the child, with approximately 18,597 data points per subject and a single 80/20 split whose partitioning level is unstated - so windows from the same child are almost certainly split across training and validation, making the reported accuracy a within-child figure rather than a person-level detection estimate; 12 children cannot support a person-level estimate regardless; no diagnostic instrument is reported; ages are unmatched with markedly unequal variances; validation and test sets are not distinguished; and no feature-level interpretation is offered so nothing is learned about what distinguishes the groups behaviourally.

answers.title: Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation as a Scalable Method for Distinguishing Children With Autism
answers.answer: Reported by the authors, and addressed unusually rigorously rather than merely acknowledged. On sample size, they concede that 27 ASC and 21 TD 'can be considered relatively small' given phenotypic heterogeneity, then argue quantitatively that the method does not suffer from a sample size problem: invoking the 1-in-10 rule for the three-variable metric learning (30 samples needed, approximately 90 used), and applying Raudys's formula for SVM expected error with p=3, delta=3.83 and n=13 per class to derive a 5.9% expected error against a 2.8% infinite-sample floor. They also note their parameter-to-sample ratio is more favourable than two named prior autism motor studies (40 parameters from 30 subjects, and 7 parameters from 30 subjects). On scalability they concede that Kinect imperfections 'require some manual processing that can be time-consuming'. Identifiable in review: 48 children means 87.2% is roughly 42 correct; the headline is the better of two scoring methods evaluated on the same folds; IQ at or above 80 and ages 8-12 bound generalisability; and the demographic table is not recoverable from the extracted text so matching cannot be verified.

answers.title: Deep-Learning-Based Detection of Infants with Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Auto-Encoder Feature Representation
answers.answer: Explicitly acknowledged: the data set is insufficient, dispersed and unbalanced; performance is 'relatively poor in comparison to the general classification tasks based on deep learning'; the improvement from joint optimisation is 'only marginal'; the BLSTM was deliberately kept small (eight cells) to match prior work rather than to maximise performance; and comparison with the prior study is only indirect because feature selection did not reproduce. Not acknowledged: the near-disjoint age distributions between groups, on the variable that most strongly governs infant vocalisation; the inverted sex ratio; the utterance-level rather than infant-level splitting, which allows the same child's voice into both training and evaluation folds; and the transposed precision and recall labels in the results table. Reading the confusion matrices directly also shows that autistic-class sensitivity is only 45.3% even for the best model, a figure the accuracy and UAR headline numbers obscure.

answers.title: Effects of Intra-Subject Variation in Gait Analysis on ASD Classification Performance in Machine Learning Models
answers.answer: Acknowledged with unusual directness in one respect and not at all in others. The authors state that training and testing folds 'can both contain data points from the same subject and even from the same trial', judge the impact 'potentially limited', and choose 10-fold over leave-one-out on that basis - naming the leakage and then reasoning past it rather than eliminating it by splitting on participants. They also acknowledge the small dataset, the class imbalance, that averaging reduces the data available for training, and that the SVM's apparent 100% recall was a degenerate single-class predictor with 'no use in real world applications'. Not acknowledged: that grid search selected hyperparameters on the same cross-validation whose scores are reported, so every figure is optimistically biased; that no participant characteristic is reported, so nothing rules out age, sex or stature as the discriminated variable in features that are all durations; that no diagnostic instrument is named; and that no ethics approval is stated. The paper describes itself as a 'preliminary investigation', which is a fair self-assessment.

answers.title: Estimating Autism Severity in Young Children From Speech Signals Using a Deep Neural Network
answers.answer: Acknowledged: that speaker labelling was manual and that automatic diarization is needed for a fully automated system; that recordings are short clinic sessions rather than naturalistic home recordings; that the shorter-response-latency finding contradicts prior English-language work and needs replication; that feature utility may change with age and requires longitudinal testing; and, implicitly but importantly, that single-split results overstate robustness. Identifiable in review but not stated: RMSE 4.65 on a 0-30 scale is a large absolute error against which the phrase 'remarkably accurate prediction' sits uneasily; architecture and hyperparameters were selected by trying combinations, apparently outside the 50-split evaluation, so the reported means carry model-selection optimism; only 6 typically developing children means the low end of the severity range is thinly sampled, which inflates correlation through range restriction at one end and thin support at the other; and no ethics approval is reported for full clinical session audio.

answers.title: Detecting High-Functioning Autism in Adults Using Eye Tracking and Machine Learning
answers.answer: Acknowledged: that web-searching tasks are unsuitable for very young children; that the sample is small, 'comparable with those of state-of-the-art fMRI studies for autism detection but smaller than the number needed for large validation studies'; that the design cannot explain why some pages discriminate better than others, nor why the harder Synthesis task did not outperform Search; that testing on independently collected data is not currently feasible because the data are task-specific and no comparable independent dataset exists; and, in a footnote, that the better accuracy under the longer browse limit might reflect the different pages and participants rather than the time limit itself. Identifiable in review but not acknowledged: the headline accuracies are maxima over a large configuration space - task, AOI definition, feature set, split ratio and every page subset - selected on the same 100 splits that produce the reported means, so the confidence intervals describe split variability but not selection uncertainty; and the control group's visibly higher educational attainment is left unadjusted in tasks that are fundamentally reading and search tasks.

answers.title: Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder via an Eye-Tracking Based
answers.answer: Acknowledged and unusually specific: the sample of 31 and 43 children is small and needs large-scale replication; class balance 'is also a problem that needs attention in the validation of our machine learning based model'; severity subdivision is not addressed; and data validity is limited because distracted typically developing children 'may generate meaningless eye movement', which the error analysis identifies as the reason specificity trails sensitivity. Not acknowledged: the Otsu threshold is computed on the score distribution being classified, including at test time, so the decision boundary uses test data and would not be available when assessing a single child; the abstract's 94.28% is the best of five permutations rather than the average; comparisons against Liu and Jiang and Zhao are across different datasets and cannot establish superiority; age differs between groups in mean, spread and range without any test or adjustment; sex is unreported; the control group is unscreened; and no ethics approval is stated.

answers.title: Machine Learning and Virtual Reality on Body Movements' Behaviors to Classify Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: Acknowledged with unusual candour: the sample is small and precludes a genuine test set; autism's heterogeneity means larger training groups would be needed for generalisation; other neurodevelopmental comparison groups are absent, so the classifier may separate neurodevelopmental difference generally rather than autism specifically; the groups were not matched on IQ, cognitive ability or motor comorbidities, which the authors say directly limits attributing the differences to autism; and the stimulus order was not counterbalanced. Not acknowledged: the Wilcoxon signed-rank test is a paired test applied here to independent groups, where Mann-Whitney U is required, so the reported per-joint significances are unverified; 24 models were built and hyperparameters tuned to maximise kappa on the same leave-one-out estimate reported as the result, making 89.36% a best-of-many figure on 47 children where one child is worth 2.13 points; the sex distributions differ substantially on a motor outcome; the analysed sample appears to be 47 not 49; and the quantity called 'frequency' throughout is mean displacement, a magnitude.

answers.title: Responsive Social Smile: A Machine-Learning Based Multimodal Behavior Assessment Framework towards Early Stage Autism Screening
answers.answer: Acknowledged: that a single protocol is insufficient - 'using the responsive social smile score alone cannot give a very comprehensive ASD classification' - and that fusing multiple protocols is needed; that autistic children are heterogeneous, making single-aspect screening hard; and, through the failure case study, that most residual errors are smiles that occurred but were not responses to the designed stimulus. Not acknowledged: that group-wise ages and sexes are never reported, so age and sex confounding cannot be excluded in a 12-32 month cohort; that the diagnostic reference standard is a bare DSM-IV clinical judgement with no instrument; that 80.49% is the best of four classifiers on 41 children where one child is worth 2.4 points - the same size as the gap the human-score ablation reveals; that stimulus scoring is evaluated at the trial level so the same child appears across folds; and that no ethics approval is reported.

answers.title: Selection of Eye-Tracking Stimuli for Prediction by Sparsely Grouped Input Variables for Neural Networks: towards Biomarker Refinement for Autism
answers.answer: Acknowledged with unusual directness: 'We acknowledge that the validation performance might be over-optimistic and does not represent real-world performance for ASD/non-ASD classification'; only 64 participants with just 30 having full ADOS, Vineland and SRS measurement; limited power to characterise autism heterogeneity; results possibly specific to the school-age period; selected paradigms not guaranteed stable across runs because the p > n problem may have no unique optimum; and that much remains before eye tracking can be used practically for treatment optimisation or long-term outcome prediction. Identifiable in review but not stated: group-wise ages, sexes and IQs are asserted as balanced but never tabulated, which matters greatly given that IQ is the one variable the features do predict; the sparsity operating point, the hyperparameters and the identification of SGIN as best were all determined against the same 10-fold estimate; and the non-autistic group's heterogeneity, while a design strength, means the classifier's target is 'autism versus other developmental presentations', which is not the same construct as 'autism versus typical development' and complicates comparison with the rest of this corpus.

answers.title: The identification of children with autism spectrum disorder by SVM approach on EEG and eye-tracking data
answers.answer: Acknowledged: that the cohort begins at age 3 and that 'diagnosis of autism at earlier ages is a pressing clinical need', with a stated plan to recruit children aged 2 or younger; and that more features should be extracted from both modalities. The paper also usefully concedes a limitation of its own EEG modality, noting that 'no differences in EEG were found in some previous studies, especially for high functioning autism' and concluding that 'using only EEG evaluation may be insufficient to identify children with this complex disease'. Not acknowledged, and decisive: no validation scheme of any kind is described, so the reported accuracies have no established out-of-sample interpretation; mRMR uses class labels with no indication of nesting within any resampling; the headline 85.44% is the maximum of a curve swept over one to forty-five features, so the operating point was selected on the reported data; the identity of the selected features is never given; recruitment routes differ systematically between groups; and no severity or functioning measure is reported despite heterogeneity being central to the paper's own argument.

answers.title: Toward Continuous Social Phenotyping: Analyzing Gaze Patterns in an Emotion Recognition Task for Children With Autism Through Wearable Smart Glasses
answers.answer: The most complete limitations section in the corpus, with five named items. Age range 6-17 'is not representative of children who are in critical periods of development for cognition and speech'. Gender imbalance of 13:3 in the autistic cohort against 9:8 in controls, with the authors noting that gender differences exist on emotion recognition and gaze tasks and 'may have been exacerbated by our imbalanced cohorts'. Limited spectrum coverage, since only 3 of 16 autistic participants had ABIQ below 80 so 13 are high-functioning. A chinrest added after the first four participants because of head movement, with the explicit admission that 'more ASD subjects took part in the study later on. This confound may be exploited by the classifiers'. And nonstandard eye tracking - the custom system was never evaluated against a standard tracker, the mount shifted requiring recalibration and extensive manual annotation, and it 'occluded roughly 15% of the field of view in the lower region for most participants, which may have had a greater distracting effect on participants in the ASD group with tactile sensitivities'. The discussion adds an ethological caution: static 6-second photographs are 'quite divergent from real-life social interactions with moving children and fleeting displays of facial emotion', and the field 'does not have enough information to know how divergent our experimental data might be from the ecologically valid situations'.

answers.title: Towards the automatic detection of social biomarkers in autism spectrum disorder: introducing the simulated interaction task (SIT)
answers.answer: Acknowledged with unusual thoroughness. On the age bias: 'older participants in both groups were more often labeled as autistic than young participants by the machine-learning classifiers, as the classifier was probably picking up a tendency of higher age in the ASD group. This age bias points to the strong need of careful testing for confounders and biases in training data for all kind of machine-learning diagnostic methods.'
