On gaze: the null result is attributed to appearance-based estimation being 'not sensitive enough to detect the subtle gaze dysfunctions present in ASD', with a caution that the null 'has to be interpreted with caution'. On the paradigm: the prerecorded actress cannot adapt to answer length, and future versions should provide tailored responses and partners matched on gender, age or ethnicity since similarity enhances mimicry. On the HNR finding: interpretation 'is not straightforward, given the lack of reference studies', with conflicting prior findings acknowledged and the possibility raised that groups differ in speaking-to-pause ratios. On multiplicity: the authors note that automated analysis 'allows the comparison of many different aspects of behavior' so 'the problem of multiple testing remains', which is why they favour the multivariate machine learning approach. Not acknowledged: the reported direction of the HNR effect contradicts the tabulated medians, which are lower rather than higher in autism; and the age confound, though identified, is not adjusted for in the headline accuracy.

answers.title: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence to Diagnose Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Tracking Saccades
answers.answer: Acknowledged: that only 108 individuals were used and more would produce a more diverse and robust classifier with better performance on edge cases; that restricting to six features may have cost accuracy; and that Azure ML Studio prevented direct hyperparameter tuning. Not acknowledged, and decisive: mutual-information feature selection was applied to the full dataset before splitting, so supervised selection sits outside the cross-validation loop; no participant characteristics are reported so no confound can be excluded; the dataset's provenance, diagnostic basis and collection ethics are entirely unstated; only accuracy is reported for a proposed diagnostic test, with no sensitivity or specificity and an unlabelled ROC curve; the 60:40 class imbalance means a majority-class predictor scores 60%; the abstract's 88-91% range is unexplained against the text's single figure of 88%; the comparator set includes regression methods that are not binary classifiers; and every descriptive group difference is asserted without a statistic.

answers.title: An Experimental Trial: Multi-Robot Therapy for Categorization of Autism Level Using Hidden Markov Model
answers.answer: Essentially none. The paper has no limitations section, and the only self-critical remark is a defence of the sample size on the ground that 'the presented work is based on previous research that also uses a similar number of subjects'. Identifiable in review and unaddressed: Table 2 assigns each test child a single autism type (one mild, three minimal) while Table 4 records 12 mild and 13 minimal actual categories across 25 test sessions, which cannot be reconciled without an unexplained within-child change in CARS category, and until resolved makes the reported accuracy and kappa uninterpretable; the kappa treats 25 sessions from 4 children as independent, inflating the effective sample about sixfold; the two observables are binned to three levels each using thresholds set with the therapist who also supplied the labels; the conditional independence assumption is contradicted by the design, since the imitation module is activated by joint attention; the severity labels 'minimal' and 'mild' are never mapped to the DSM levels the introduction describes; and the claim that no therapist is needed is undercut by the fact that every training label comes from a therapist's CARS assessment.

answers.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis Based on Trajectories of Eye Tracking Data
answers.answer: Acknowledged: the dataset is imbalanced and synthetic sampling is a stopgap pending more real data; region demarcation still requires a therapist and automatic identification would make the method faster; and accuracy could be improved with other methods such as genetic algorithms for meta-classifier construction. The low specificity is noted and defended rather than treated as a limitation - the authors argue that 'our major goal is to capture all possible individuals with the disorder' and that highly sensitive tests suit early rule-out. Not acknowledged: the reported 75% is the maximum over 511 classifier subsets, three ensemble strategies, swept thresholds, five balancing methods and per-segment hyperparameter grids, all selected on the same 10-fold estimate with no outer validation loop, so the figure is optimistically biased and the segment-1-3-8 finding is a selection outcome rather than an independent result; the practical consequence of 53% specificity - referring roughly half of typically developing children onward - is not discussed; ages span 3-18 with different ranges per group and no adjustment; CARS scores are collected but never related to model output; and no ethics approval is reported.

answers.title: Autistic spectrum traits detection and early screening: A machine learning based eye movement study
answers.answer: Acknowledged: aGlass stability and accuracy are insufficient; VR was rejected by some autistic participants; small samples in both experiments make bias inevitable; not all scenes containing social stimuli discriminate, so scene design should involve a specialist psychologist and several scenes should be compared. Most valuably, the authors report and interpret the recall instability across experiments, concluding that 'the data patterns of the adults we recruited in the preliminary experiment are somehow different from those autistic adults'. Not acknowledged: that the preliminary positive class is a median split of a general-population trait distribution well below the AQ clinical cut-off, so the models were never trained on autism; that Table 2's group AQ means are transposed; that age and sex are model features while the test sample differs sharply from the training population on both; that the test experiment has no negative cases so specificity is unmeasured and recall alone cannot distinguish a good model from one biased toward positive prediction; that the ensemble's AUC of 0.90 is inconsistent with constituent AUCs of 0.57-0.68; and that outlier replacement by the mean is unspecified in both criterion and timing.

answers.title: Automatic classification of children with autism spectrum disorder by using a computerized visual‐orienting task
answers.answer: Acknowledged with four specific limitations: still rather than dynamic directional cues, whereas dynamic cues predominate in daily life; the attention-sustaining phase distinguishes this paradigm from conventional visual-orienting tasks and may itself drive the group differences, so future work should test whether the algorithms can separate autism from attention deficits; too few girls to test sex-specific performance, with the specific rationale that 'autistic girls exhibit more typical social attention than do autistic boys'; and that 'the predictive power of automatic classification techniques is constrained by the base rate of ASD in the population', so direct comparison against current diagnostic methods requires caution. The absence of ADOS and ADI-R is disclosed with its reason. Identifiable in review but not stated: the low-functioning group's 5.7% success rate means these children largely failed the task, so their classification may reflect general non-engagement rather than a visual-orienting deficit specifically; and the criterion for assigning children to that group included failure to complete the Raven's test, which partly conflates cognitive level with capacity to complete a structured assessment of the same general kind as the outcome task.

answers.title: Auxiliary Diagnostic Method for Early Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Movement Data Analysis
answers.answer: Acknowledged: the dataset is limited so 'comparisons cannot be simply drawn with other existing diagnostic methods, and more samples are needed for further analysis'; the clap-prediction feature 'needs to be further justified' given its weak correlation; and the hyperparameters were empirically set with the explicit note that 'different values could be set to gain a better performance'. The refutation of hypothesis 2 is reported clearly and the interpretation revised. Not acknowledged: no diagnostic instrument or criteria are reported for either group; no ethics approval; groups differ substantially in age (4-10 versus 2-15) and sex (74% versus 51% male) with no test or adjustment; validation is a single random split with no cross-validation or repetition, so the 40-child result carries wide sampling uncertainty; the correlation analysis validating the feature hypotheses used the full dataset including the test half; exclusion rates differ between groups (15% versus 6%); and the most predictive feature family, area0, is defined by the tracker's failure to resolve gaze, conflating attentional signal with equipment dropout.

answers.title: Children ASD Evaluation Through Joint Analysis of EEG and Eye-Tracking Recordings With Graph Convolution Network
answers.answer: Essentially none. The paper has no limitations section and offers no caveats on sample size, generalisability or validation design. Identifiable in review: the reported accuracies are arithmetically incompatible with a participant-level 80/20 split of 42 children and correspond instead to 19 of 20, 14 of 19 and 15 of 19 samples, which combined with 4-second EEG epoching implies segment-level splitting and hence leakage across the train/test boundary; no diagnostic instrument or criteria are reported for either group; age and sex matching is asserted with no figures; the t-tests and covariance thresholds defining the graph structure were computed on the full dataset including test samples; validation is a single unrepeated split with no confidence intervals; and the reduction from 128 to 8 electrodes is justified only computationally.

answers.title: Classification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Using Eye Tracking Data Based on Visual Attention Model
answers.answer: Acknowledged: that the saliency-map approach needs testing with different visual inputs 'in order to validate the relevant features'; that the age range is restricted to 3-16 while autism is lifelong; that the sample is small; and that the sex imbalance between groups is a limitation. Analysing IQ as an additional feature is proposed. Not acknowledged: the reported accuracy of 88% is inconsistent with the reported error rate of 25% and with the reported sensitivity and specificity, and coincides exactly with the separately reported maximum ROC AUC; ReliefF feature selection is not stated to be nested within cross-validation folds, so the group-specific feature sets that constitute the paper's main finding may have been chosen using all the data; and the 20-frame decision threshold was fitted by Youden index on the same ROC used for evaluation.

answers.title: Classification of Children With Autism and Typical Development Using Eye-Tracking Data From Face-to-Face Conversations: Machine Learning Model Development and Performance Evaluation
answers.answer: Acknowledged extensively and specifically: the sample excludes severe presentations and children below 6 or above 13, so the work is 'proof-of-concept research'; only four girls participated, and autistic males and females differ across behavioural, cognitive and emotional domains; severity was not measured; head-mounted eye tracking may itself affect autistic children's behaviour and contactless methods are needed; only fixation percentage was computed while counts, entropy, revisits and oculomotor measures were available; only autism versus typical development was tested, leaving discrimination from other clinical phenotypes unknown; and live interaction introduces uncontrollable subjective factors, with the honest observation that 'no human being can be expected to behave exactly the same way when interacting with different people'. Not acknowledged: forward feature selection maximises the same leave-one-out accuracy that is reported, so the headline is not an unbiased estimate, and the maximum is quoted across 21 feature counts, four classifiers and three feature sets; and IQ differs significantly between groups with no adjustment, despite the leading feature being conversation duration.

answers.title: Combined Signal Processing Based Techniques and Feed Forward Neural Networks for Pathological Voice Detection and Classification
answers.answer: None. There is no limitations section and no caveat anywhere on sample size, validation design, generalisability or the absence of clinical characterisation. The nearest approach is the acknowledgement that hidden neuron counts have no exact formula and were fixed by trial. Identifiable in review: 255 samples derive from only 19 children with roughly 13 samples each, and the 70/15/15 partition operates over samples with no statement that speakers were kept together, which alone would explain the perfect accuracies; hidden neuron counts were tuned to maximise the reported accuracy for each feature set and task; no diagnostic instrument is reported for either clinical group; ages are given only as a collective 5-14 range in a domain where voice changes with maturation; no ethics or consent statement exists; and the sustained vowel task cannot express the prosodic properties the paper itself identifies as characterising autistic speech.

answers.title: Computer-Aided Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Eye-Tracking Study Using Data Visualization and Deep Learning
answers.answer: Acknowledged: the small participant count as the primary limitation; the inability to access ADI-R and ADOS-G scores, which 'limits the interpretation of our results'; the short duration of video scenarios, since 'perhaps longer scenarios might have allowed for a richer representation of the gaze behavior'; the restricted age group; the absence of a benchmark dataset in the autism literature making cross-study comparison difficult; and hardware and software costs as barriers to clinical adoption. The performance decline under participant-level splitting is reported as expected rather than hidden. Not acknowledged: the MIC of 0.79 is computed per image rather than per child, so 547 observations derive from 59 individuals; and because every non-autistic child scores the CARS floor of 15 with zero variance, that correlation largely reflects the between-group difference rather than a severity gradient within autism. Also unremarked: augmented copies of an image share its participant, which would compound leakage in the image-level condition, and three training epochs is very few.

answers.title: Computer-aided autism diagnosis based on visual attention models using eye tracking
answers.answer: Acknowledged with unusual directness on one point. The authors anticipate the objection that using the same video for training and diagnosis constitutes contamination, state it themselves - 'although it could be interpreted as contamination and biasing of learning' - and describe their mitigation: only 700 sampled pixels per map enter learning, 50 frames are withheld entirely for diagnosis, and negatives are randomly drawn, which they argue 'approximates a scenario of usage of different videos'. They also note the optical-flow threshold is stimulus-specific, identify dataset construction as the field's binding constraint, and flag intent to release data. Not acknowledged: sensitivity of 69% is not discussed at all despite being the weakest metric and the one that matters for screening; the 2.5:1 class ratio inflates precision and is unaddressed; genetic algorithm selection is not stated to be nested within folds although the selected feature sets are the paper's main interpretive claim; the 28-vote threshold was fitted by Youden on the reported ROC; and no group-wise ages are given across a 3-18 year span.

answers.title: Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis
answers.answer: Acknowledged with unusual completeness. The sample is small, the feature count high, and 'the models were not applied to an independent sample'; the authors state directly that 'data from all participants were used to validate the model; therefore, the reported results correspond to the cross-validation process', offering the 20 iterations and low standard deviations as partial mitigation. Groups were not matched on sociodemographics, IQ or cognitive ability. The macro-level area-of-interest approach 'presented some limitations in terms of recognition of specific eye gaze patterns related to specific areas, such as face areas (i.e., eyes and mouth)'. Eye-tracking glasses may not be accepted by young children and both they and the CAVE are expensive, limiting clinical deployment. Training took about 20 hours even parallelised. Not acknowledged: the feature subset and model were both chosen on the same repeated cross-validation that produces the reported metrics, across five algorithms and ten datasets, so the headline is a maximum over roughly fifty fits; participant sex is never reported; and the minimally verbal composition implied by ADOS-2 module 1 may bound the generality of the reversed social-attention finding.

answers.title: Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms
answers.answer: Acknowledged: the small sample, attributed to 'the great difficulty of recruiting a large sample of ASD participants and having them complete the motor tasks', with leave-one-out cross-validation and the small number of retained features offered as mitigation against overfitting; autism's heterogeneity requiring larger and more varied samples; and the age range of 6-13 being 'much older than the mean age at diagnosis', so the study 'could only be viewed as an initial examination of social head behaviors in an older sample to establish proof of concept'. The instructed-gesture confound is also raised directly as an explanation for the frequency null. Not acknowledged: the exhaustive search evaluated 63 feature subsets across five classifiers on the same leave-one-out estimate that is reported, so the headline is a maximum over 315 fits; the abstract and results disagree on which two features produced it; and OpenFace tracking failure was fifteen times higher in the autistic group (3.46% versus 0.23%), which is reported but never examined as a possible source of the group difference.

answers.title: Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset
answers.answer: None. There is no limitations section and no caveat on sample size, validation design, cluster interpretation or generalisability. Identifiable in review: ten-fold cross-validation operates over 547 images from 59 children with no statement that a child's images were confined to one fold, and the source study demonstrated on these same images that participant-level splitting reduces accuracy from approximately 90% to approximately 71%; k-means clustering was performed on the full image set before classification, so cluster membership was determined using test images; the headline is the best of 45 cluster-by-classifier cells with no multiplicity correction or confidence intervals; the abstract quotes 87% against the table's 88.89%; several reported cells are near-degenerate single-class predictors that are not flagged; and no clinical or behavioural interpretation of any result is offered.

answers.title: Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: Acknowledged: the sample was 'relatively small and likely not able to capture the full heterogeneity of ASD'; intellectual disability was not measured despite being a known source of variability affecting motor planning and coordination; and only autism and typical development were contrasted, whereas motor difficulties occur across neurodevelopmental disorders so additional diagnostic classes would 'facilitate a dimensional acknowledgment of atypical development'. Practical constraints are also disclosed, including that left-arm markers could not be placed on three autistic children due to compliance problems. Not acknowledged: the abstract reports 0.947 as classification accuracy when it is the subject-level AUC, with trial-level accuracy being 0.739; the sensitivity and specificity are taken at an operating point optimised on the same ROC used to characterise performance; the sex imbalance of 38% versus 69% female is tabulated but never tested or discussed; and the severity correlation rests on 13 observations with a visibly influential high-ADOS point.

answers.title: Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment
answers.answer: The introduction contains an unusually clear analysis of the field's constraints, which functions as a limitations discussion of the wider literature: most preprogrammed robot systems 'have fixed behavior (i.e., they are unable to autonomously perform adaptable closed-loop interactions), are not tailored to the individual needs of patients, and cannot keep track of their recovery progress', while adaptive systems 'need high-performance hardware, such as GPUs chips, to process real-time data' and 'are not yet reliable outside controlled research' settings. The discussion reports a practical failure - children handling the chest display in early sessions, depressing scores, addressed by fixing the display - and the causal claim about attention improvement is labelled a hypothesis. What is not addressed: there is no control condition, so the seven-week rise in attention scores cannot be separated from familiarisation with the robot, task practice, maturation or study attention, and the score's own components would be expected to rise as a child grows comfortable with the apparatus. Attrition of 5 of 11 children is unexplained, and if disengagement drove it then the trend is computed on the children who were already engaging. The 82.4% agreement is computed over sessions clustered within children with no adjustment, no chance-corrected statistic and no confidence interval, and no reliability estimate exists for the therapist ratings serving as the standard. Scoring constants are operator-set per child, so scores are not comparable across children. And equating a detected face with attending is a strong assumption for children who may attend without orienting.

answers.title: Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning
answers.answer: Acknowledged: the dataset should be enlarged for reliability; the model 'should be used with care and under supervision of some professional'; and 'this is a local dataset which should not be applied elsewhere in the world without consultation'. The last two are genuine scoping cautions that most of the corpus omits. Not acknowledged: no diagnostic instrument for either group; a single 80/20 split with a 40-child test set and no cross-validation; SelectKBest's k tuned to give the best results; the maximum reported across 27 cells; no group demographics despite sex, age and birth order being model features; no ethics approval; recall bias in retrospective caregiver report, which differs systematically between parents of diagnosed and undiagnosed children; and, most consequentially, the presentation of single-group frequencies about maternal vaccination and parental smoking as observations about autism without any control comparison or base rate.

answers.title: Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism
answers.answer: Acknowledged directly: 'These results were not adjusted for multiple comparisons and should be viewed as preliminary. They require replication in larger samples, more balanced with respect to IQ and gender composition'. The study is described as a proof of concept and a pilot analysis. The IQ imbalance is not only acknowledged but addressed by a matched-pair replication. Not acknowledged: the sex imbalance receives no matched-subsample check despite being larger and more directly relevant, since pitch is sex-dependent and is one of the two retained features; the finding of lower pitch in autism runs contrary to a substantial part of the prosody literature and this discrepancy is never noted; all 14 exclusions for recording quality came from the autistic group; and RFECV and the choice of best conversational activity were both performed across the reported cross-validation without an outer loop.

answers.title: Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images
answers.answer: Unusually forthright, and volunteered rather than buried. The Discussion opens by conceding the model 'can reach at most 60% accuracy in detecting ASDs' and then sets out four substantive reasons the task is hard - that fixation behaviour changes with age across toddlers, young children and adults; that at-risk toddlers can match typically developing toddlers on face fixation duration so the signal is age-dependent in kind rather than degree; that in scenes containing both faces and objects of circumscribed interest young autistic children do not differ from typically developing ones while older children show a non-object bias; and that consequently features should be selected per age band, which this model does not do. The Conclusion repeats that 'there is room for improvement'. What is not acknowledged: that classification is per scanpath rather than per child; that 23 classifiers were compared before one was selected; that specificity of exactly 0.50 means chance performance on the typically developing group; and the complete absence of participant characterisation and diagnostic provenance.

answers.title: Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data
answers.answer: Substantially acknowledged, and in the most important place. The authors state that scanpath-only performance rivalling scanpath-plus-image is 'a surprising result as the scan-path itself contains no direct information about the visual stimuli', note that it contradicts the premise of their own design and of every study in their related-work section, and offer the explanation that 'the dataset is too small in terms of the number of subjects - only 14 ASD and 14 TD children were included. As such, there might be a systematic bias in terms of the gaze patterns between these two groups'. They also concede they have not mapped learned features back to explainable entities. What is not acknowledged: that the same-28-children-in-every-split design makes this bias exploitable rather than merely present, so it bounds the validity of the 62.13% rather than only explaining an anomaly; that the validation-to-test ranking reversals (LSTM best on validation, worst of three on test) indicate the validation set is too similar to training to guide model selection, which they note descriptively without drawing the inference; that specificity is weak throughout, 0.537 for the best model and 0.44-0.57 across variants, so performance rests disproportionately on the autistic class; and that the supporting KS test treats thousands of scanpaths from 28 children as independent observations.

answers.title: Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children
answers.answer: The study's weakest aspect: there is no limitations section, and the Discussion is uniformly positive. Only one caveat is stated anywhere - that 'the current level of analysis prevents us from drawing solid conclusions on what is represented in the NN' - and it is offered in support of the future-work agenda rather than as a constraint on the claims. Four issues go unaddressed. OpenPose extracts keypoints for all persons present and the videos contain examiner and often caregiver alongside the child, so the model may be reading clinician behaviour, which is systematically different when a clinician is eliciting from a child who does not respond; nothing in the paper isolates the child. The clinical-validity correlations are computed across a mixed two-group sample where severity is near-floor in one group, so they largely re-express the group difference rather than demonstrating within-group grading. ASD probability correlates inversely with IQ and adaptive functioning, raising a developmental-level confound that is reported without comment. And the single null in the entire correlation table is the VABS-II motor subdomain (-0.186, p = 0.066) - the domain a pose-based classifier would most be expected to track - which passes without remark. Testing Set 2 is also presented as endorsing 'the model's stability' without noting that a single-class sample cannot detect loss of specificity.

answers.title: Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities
answers.answer: Substantially candid on the scientific limitations and silent on the methodological one. Acknowledged, in a dedicated passage: the small sample, with replication needed 'to validate this method on a new not trained dataset' and an explicit question of whether the algorithm 'could remain predictive also for a greater sample or if it requires to be retrained'; the IQ confound, stated directly as 'we were not able to exclude intelligence as confounders', with the mitigation that most participants were high functioning and that analysing only universally-passed items limits cognitive interference; and - the most valuable admission in the paper - that the motor signature 'may overlap with other disorders, such as attention deficit disorder, motor coordination disturbance, or general intellectual disabilities', reinforced by the observation that sensory integration dysfunction, their explanatory mechanism, is also found in ADHD, so 'future extensions of this work should include other neurodevelopmental disabilities in order to verify the specificity of these motor signatures for ASD'. Not acknowledged: that the cross-validation folds split task-level samples rather than children, so the same child's data appears on both sides; that the headline 93% is the best of ten fold models while the cross-validated estimate is 88 +/- 3%; that hidden-layer width, feature ranking and the reported operating point were all selected on the same cross-validation used for reporting; and that cases and comparisons were recruited from systematically different settings.

answers.title: A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children
answers.answer: Only two limitations are stated, and both are engineering constraints rather than threats to validity: that deployment requires EEG and eye-tracking data to be available simultaneously, and that training three SDAE models costs more computation than one. Unaddressed: the diagnostic reference standard rests on parent-report questionnaires, which the authors themselves flag as a data-access compromise in the Methods but never carry into the interpretation of their results; the two groups were recruited from different institutional settings; no cognitive or developmental measure was collected in a 3-6-year-old sample, leaving developmental level uncontrolled; the >70% screen-looking-time gate may exclude children differentially by group with no count reported; the EEG segment yield differs markedly between groups (20.4 versus 27.2 clean segments), which the paper states in passing and never discusses despite its implication that artifact burden - and hence measurement noise - is itself group-dependent; hyperparameter selection is undescribed; there is no external validation cohort; and 90 children is a small sample for a model with three stacked networks. The Conclusion's claim that the framework 'can automatically learn and fuse useful information... without the need of much more diagnostic expert experience' is also stronger than a study whose labels came from parent questionnaires can support.

answers.title: AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
answers.answer: One limitation is stated and it is the right one: 'there is a statistically significant difference in IQ between the ASD and TD children. IQ is known to affect one's ability to perform behavioral tasks and joint attention', followed by the conclusion that 'a replication study using a sample of IQ-matched ASD and TD cohorts is therefore required'. The framing is honest, though the accompanying defence - that 'even when IQ is considered, joint attention still proved to be an important trait to differentiate ASD from TD children' - rests on a citation to prior literature rather than on any analysis of the present data, and no covariate adjustment or matched subsample is attempted despite IQ being measured for every child. Unaddressed: that test metrics are computed over clips rather than children, so effective sample sizes are 36 and 18 rather than 416 and 184; that the training set comprises only 32 children; that the target behaviour is separately scored by a human rater in this very study with near-complete group separation, so the model automates an existing measurement rather than revealing a new one; that ADHD and developmental coordination disorder were excluded rather than used as contrast groups, leaving specificity untested; that the examiner responds contingently to the child; and that the closing comparison against prior models reporting 0.70-0.80 accuracy is made without any statistical test and across incomparable populations.

answers.title: Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: Two limitations are stated. The sample is 'relatively small' and should be extended. And the data 'have nonstationary characteristics, and the recording environments are changing', so that 'across-day variability exists in recording conditions', motivating future work on models that adapt over time - a limitation rarely raised in this corpus and a real one for consumer EEG. Not acknowledged: that the 12 EEG features were selected by t-tests computed across all 80 children before leave-one-out cross-validation, so the held-out child's label informed feature selection; that the gaze cluster count K was chosen from the experimental results; that the headline 87.50% is the best across three classifiers; that autism was established by DSM-5 criteria alone with no instrument, assessor or setting described; that no cognitive, language or severity measure was taken in a preschool sample; and that the two groups were recruited from special education schools and regular kindergartens respectively, so educational placement is confounded with diagnosis.

answers.title: An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images
answers.answer: Three limitations are stated and none concerns validity. The dataset has a 'low number of participants'; the video scenarios were short, so images carry limited information and 'more extended scenarios should be allowed'; and 'the current version of this work is limited by the reduced number of samples of the eye-tracking dataset. We included a data augmentation step to generate synthetic samples to enlarge the training and testing data to overcome this issue'. That last sentence is the paper's most significant disclosure and is offered as a solution rather than as a problem: augmenting the testing data means near-duplicate transformations of the same source images populate both sides of the evaluation, which is exactly what a test set must exclude. Unaddressed: that no split or cross-validation protocol is described at all; that images from the same child cannot be separated because no participant identifiers exist; that the metaheuristic optimises hyperparameters against what appears to be the reported data; that grayscale conversion discards the velocity, acceleration and jerk information encoded in colour; that no participant characteristics or diagnostic procedures are known; and that the 17-to-26-point gap over conventional classifiers on identical data warrants explanation.

answers.title: Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals
answers.answer: Three limitations are stated, each substantive and each with a proposed remedy - the most serious limitations section in the corpus. First, the sample is relatively small and 'not representative of ASD in general', and consists of adults with IQ in the normal range, so 'it remains unclear if our findings would generalize to children and individuals with lower IQ'; the inclusion of comorbid depression, anxiety and ADHD is folded into this as a further open question. Second, only two temporal blocks were collected, both on the same day, so within-individual precision is limited both by measurement error and potentially by state-dependent change, and longer-term longitudinal data across more diverse stimuli would be needed. Third, and most carefully argued, the interpretation rests on having measured only eye movements: 'It remains possible that other dependent measures - performance tasks or questionnaires based on interpreting the videos, or neuroimaging - would have revealed higher variability in ASD', including the specific alternative that autistic people might have unreliable cognition that they compensate for. The authors then argue against their own alternative rather than merely listing it, noting that 'eye movements are not under strong volitional control' and the stimuli are highly engaging, so 'a top-down compensatory mechanism thus seems implausible'. Two issues go unremarked: the differential exclusion rate for gaze data quality (17% of autistic participants versus 3% of controls), and the fact that the two sites used different diagnostic confirmation procedures.

answers.title: Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech
answers.answer: Three limitations are stated, one of them thoroughly. The sex imbalance is quantified precisely (95% versus 39% male), benchmarked against the expected 4:1 to 3:1 population ratio, and the conclusion drawn that the dataset 'may still not be completely representative of real-world conditions' - among the more careful demographic self-assessments in the corpus. The unverified nature of parent-reported diagnoses is conceded directly. The small dataset and the non-scalability of manual splicing are both raised, with automatic blind source separation named as the necessary but difficult alternative. What is absent is the study's largest problem: the 4.5-year median age gap between groups appears once, in a single sentence of the demographics paragraph, and is never mentioned again - not in the limitations, not in the discussion, not as a caveat on the accuracy figures. No age-matched analysis, age covariate or age-only baseline is attempted. Also unaddressed: that the autistic class is built from 20 children sampled at roughly 21 clips each while the comparison class draws on 38 children at roughly 11 each; that metrics are clip-level rather than child-level despite the folds being child-disjoint; that no acoustic characterisation of any kind is reported; and that the prosodic rationale in the introduction is not reflected in any feature actually used.

answers.title: Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection
answers.answer: The most complete limitations section in the corpus, running to ten distinct items, several of which the authors were under no obligation to raise. Sample scope: ages 7-17 only; all participants had IQ in the normal range; all were fluent English speakers assessable with Module 3, so 'it is important for future studies to include individuals with lower IQ and less verbal participants'. Design: 'Participants were not tightly matched between groups which could result in reduced fit for analysis', notwithstanding the confound tests. Features: the set was deliberately limited to previously validated measures and should be expanded and tested component by component. Preprocessing: 'We do not know the full impact of denoising on voice features and results', with a recommendation to control microphone quality and placement to reduce the need for it. Setting: the samples come from ADOS administrations in a clinical research setting and cannot be generalised to other contexts, and because 'ADOS administration focuses on eliciting autistic features... it is possible that our results are overestimated compared to what would be obtained with more naturalistic conversational samples'. Reliability: test-retest and short-term stability are unknown. Transcription: manual transcription is costly and labour-intensive, and 'though the transcribers went through extensive training and regular consistency reviews, we do not have transcription reliability results'. In the discussion the authors additionally raise, unprompted, that examiners may have facilitated and maximised the language output of the more able participants, citing Bone et al., and that parents' CCC-2 scores 'could have been negatively biased in this subset due to their child's ASD diagnosis'.

answers.title: Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers
answers.answer: Three limitations are stated and each is substantive. The sample, though large overall, contained only 41 autistic children and therefore 'did not offer sufficient power to determine the influence of biological and demographic characteristics, such as sex'. Data from all participants were not used in every analysis because of the 40% attendance threshold. And 'the autistic and neurotypical group differed in cognitive ability and, thus, it is not clear the degree to which differences in cognition contributed to our findings' - a direct acknowledgement that the study's most likely alternative explanation is unresolved. A fourth limitation appears not in the limitations section but in the discussion, and is arguably the most important: inspection of videos from high-movement toddlers 'revealed that the movement involves not just the head but also the upper body including trunk and shoulders, which were not captured by our computer vision algorithm, as we focused solely on the face in this study'. That reframes the construct from head movement to whole-body postural instability, and the authors follow it with a serious engagement with the postural-sway literature. What goes unaddressed: the significant ethnicity and caregiver-education differences, never revisited after the demographic table; the exclusion of the 12 children with non-autism diagnoses, which removes the clinically decisive contrast; the wide confidence intervals on the per-movie AUCs; and the internal contradiction between the Results' positive Mullen correlations and the Discussion's statement that lower-ability children moved more.

answers.title: Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study
answers.answer: Three limitations are stated, each substantive. The wide age range across groups and the small number of females are raised together, with the authors arguing that robust classification despite these may indicate 'aspects of prosodic profiles of ASD which are relatively age and gender invariant', supported by the post-hoc analysis, while conceding that 'future studies with larger samples are needed to confirm whether findings reported here extend to both males and females and different age ranges where prosodic abilities may vary'. The absence of language ability measures for group matching is identified with a precise mechanism - baseline language ability covaries with age and autism severity and influences pitch in particular. And the restriction to two languages is named, with specific proposals for extension. What goes unaddressed: the unexplained loss of 40% of the English autistic sample between recruitment and analysis; the discrepancy between the demographic table and the analysis counts for the Cantonese autistic group; the absence of any recording specification; the use of different IQ instruments across language groups, which makes the two samples non-comparable on cognitive level; and the fact that the sex imbalance falls precisely on the English intonation model, the one f0 classification that reached significance.

answers.title: Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings
answers.answer: Six limitations are stated, all substantive. The sample is small with a wide age range and imperfect IQ matching, so 'we were not able to divide our sample into subgroups based on age, sex or IQ level'. The sample includes only fluently speaking participants without intellectual disability, so results 'might not apply to everyone on the autism spectrum' - followed by an unusually thoughtful observation that this may mean the figures 'show the upper limit of diagnostic possibilities from the closed text data only'. Only one narrative context was tested, with the authors noting prior evidence that less structured tasks are harder for autistic participants. No non-spectrum clinical comparison group was included. The approach requires high-quality transcription, which remains difficult to automate for spontaneous speech. And the models offer no interpretability. The authors additionally volunteer, when discussing why their instruments outperformed published validation figures, that 'participants in our sample were carefully selected with clear signs of ASD among individuals in the ASD group and lack of developmental problems among individuals in the TD group' - a candid acknowledgement that the sample is easier than a clinical population, which qualifies their own headline comparison. Not addressed: that only the best classifier per input combination is reported, over three families and a 27-point grid; the absence of any confidence interval on figures derived from 25 cases per class; and the unreported sex composition.

answers.title: Development of a visual attention based decision support system for autism spectrum disorder screening
answers.answer: Four limitations are stated. Class balance is treated most carefully and is the best-argued passage in the paper: the authors note that 'we need the true ratio of children with ASD to TD children, 1 in every 54 children, to test the usefulness of the DSS for predicting how DSS would perform on a sample representative of the population' - correctly identifying that a balanced design overstates deployment performance, which very few studies in this corpus acknowledge. They then undercut it with a non-sequitur: 'Despite missing this class imbalance, our results show over 80% accuracy and AUC ROC values (for SVM and RF) which indicates that the proposed DSS can also handle class imbalance.' Performance on balanced data carries no information about performance under 1-in-54 prevalence, where positive predictive value would collapse. The sex imbalance is acknowledged. The 12.5% false-negative rate is acknowledged and attributed to clinical heterogeneity, with a call to characterise those children's symptom profiles. Sample size is acknowledged. Not acknowledged: the 20-point cognitive and 34-point language gaps between groups; the discrepancy between recruited and analysed sample sizes; that 87.5% is the maximum across 24 configurations; the absence of an observational diagnostic instrument; the laboratory setting relative to the paper's own call for less intrusive screening; and the absence of any ethics statement.

answers.title: Different Eye Tracking Patterns in Autism Spectrum Disorder in Toddler and Preschool Children
answers.answer: Five limitations are stated and each is substantive, but two passages go considerably beyond the corpus norm. The prevalence discussion is the most valuable: rather than reporting predictive values, the authors explain why they will not, and then calculate the answer - 'using the above toddler values of 80% sensitivity and 82% specificity, and assuming 1% prevalence in the population, the PPV is approximately 4.2%. On the other hand, using these same values, NPV is greater than 99%.' They note that readers can perform the calculation themselves and that omitting predictive values 'is consistent with previous ASD studies on this topic', citing three. The spectrum bias passage is equally direct, naming the phenomenon, identifying its cause in the exclusion of psychiatric and neurological histories from the comparison group, and stating its direction: discriminative ability 'may be overestimated in medical practice'. The other three limitations are the absence of ADOS/ADI-R confirmation with its stated cause, the absence of CARS in comparison children, the small sample without independent validation, and the absence of developmental assessment with a reasoned defence of using chronological age. What is not addressed: that fixation reduction appears across non-social as well as social areas and may therefore index general attention rather than social attention; that the off-area residual is never reported by group; that the two quality-control exclusions may operate differentially by group and their counts are unreported; and the 78-versus-74 discrepancy.

answers.title: Evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based medical device for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: Substantial and candid, with the central limitation stated as a headline result rather than buried. The abstention rate is not framed as a caveat but as a design feature whose cost is quantified: the Device declined to classify 68.2% of children, and the paper states plainly what would happen otherwise - sensitivity 51.6%, specificity 18.5%. The stated scope follows: 'the goal of the Device is not to enable diagnosis of all presentations of ASD, but to aid primary care HCPs to diagnose the subset of children the Device can confidently determine a recommendation for'. Other limitations acknowledged: not powered for covariate inference; no IQ testing, with the reason and the need for follow-up stated; English only, with non-English families excluded and translations in development; parental education higher and income lower than the general population; smartphone access required; cost and reimbursement data absent, with explicit concern about equitable access for low-income and uninsured families; reliance on human video analysts limiting scalability; and the expectation that abstention rates will vary with the population's composition, being lower in more neurotypical or higher-prevalence populations. What receives insufficient weight: the sex difference in PPV, dismissed on interval overlap in an admittedly underpowered analysis; and the fact that the reference standard's own 21% disagreement rate bounds the achievable ceiling, which is reported but not carried into the interpretation of the results.

answers.title: Extraction and Classification of Acoustic Features from Italian Speaking Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.
answers.answer: Partially, and in a revealing pattern. The recording divergence is disclosed in full and then defended: 'Even though we are aware that this might eschew our results, we consider that it will not have that significant impact because the storytelling task remained the same, and the quality of the recordings was high (i.e., there was no background noise).' The defence addresses task comparability and the absence of noise in the new recordings, neither of which is the issue - the issue is a systematic difference between two recording chains, which shifts every spectral and voice-quality measure regardless of how clean each chain is individually. The authors nonetheless demonstrate that they grasp the mechanism, because they apply it correctly to their own loudness findings: 'This difference in the results could be caused by the most reported problems: the recording environment and the microphone's position... For these reasons, we decided not to consider the results obtained as relevant for the present.' Having discarded loudness on exactly this reasoning, they retain jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio and the spectral measures, which depend on the same variables. The feature-selection bias is likewise acknowledged in advance with a citation to comparable work in dementia speech, and the scope is explicitly narrowed to feature-extraction validity rather than classification. Not acknowledged: the six-sample test set; that the headline figures are best-of-ten against much lower means; the absence of any diagnostic instrument, severity measure or comparison-group screening; the absence of cognitive and language measures; and the missing ethics approval.

answers.title: Eye Tracking-Based Diagnosis and Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques
answers.answer: There is no limitations section, and no limitation is stated anywhere in the paper. Nothing is acknowledged about the image-wise split, the pooled headline accuracy, the absence of participant information, the sex imbalance restated in the methods, the lack of diagnostic provenance, the absence of any behavioural interpretation, or the single fixed split without repetition or confidence intervals. The conclusion instead asserts that all three systems 'achieved superior results' and 'promising results', and the future work proposes only to concatenate the feature families - an architectural extension that would address none of the above. This is the least self-critical paper in the corpus.

answers.title: Identification of Social Engagement Indicators Associated With
answers.answer: Two limitations are stated and both are real. Class imbalance is identified as the reason macro-averaged and weighted-average statistics diverge, with dataset augmentation proposed as the remedy. More importantly, the interpretability of the areas of interest is conceded directly: 'due to camera motion and variation in the location of the smartphone relative to the parent's face, the gaze fixation maps are difficult to interpret qualitatively, and AOIs cannot be definitely matched to a parent's specific facial regions'. That is the central caveat on the whole study and the authors state it plainly rather than gesturing at eye contact or mouth-looking. What is not acknowledged: that diagnostic labels are unverified parent report, conceded by the same group in their companion speech paper but absent here; that the sample spans thirteen years of childhood with no age reporting, matching or covariate adjustment; that weighted-average recall of 0.656 falls below the roughly 0.80 a majority-class predictor would achieve on a test set of 43 autistic and 11 comparison videos; and that no confidence intervals, permutation tests or baselines accompany the classification results, in contrast to the rigour applied to the group comparisons.

answers.title: Investigation of Eye-Tracking Scan Path as a Biomarker for Autism Screening Using Machine Learning Algorithms
answers.answer: Two limitations are stated and the first is the most substantive limitation statement in this part of the corpus. It identifies the structural problem with the available data infrastructure: 'A few open-access ET datasets are available; however, they combine multiple ETSP images from a small set of participants rather than a single trial from a large group, making them unsuitable for reliable ASD screening.' That is a correct and generalisable diagnosis, and it is reinforced in the discussion where the authors attribute their own augmented result to 'possible data contamination as similar replicates are entered into the training set, as seen in the testing dataset'. The second limitation concerns collection quality, recommending that clinicians ensure the child attends to the tracker in a distraction-free environment. What is not acknowledged: that the abstract, keywords and conclusion all lead with the 97.00% figure the discussion attributes to contamination; that images from the same child span the training and test partitions even without augmentation; that principal component analysis was fitted on the full dataset before splitting; that rotation by 45 and 60 degrees produces physically impossible gaze traces; that the participant-level result rests on 59 samples with no confidence interval; and that greyscale conversion discards the colour-encoded derivative information the source images carry.

answers.title: Machine learning models using mobile game play accurately classify children with autism
answers.answer: Two limitations are stated and both are substantive, and one further caveat appears in the discussion that is arguably more important than either. The stated limitations are that the sample is too small to evaluate performance across demographic dimensions - gender, ethnicity, nationality, age and co-occurring diagnoses - with a commitment to demographic fairness validation as recruitment expands; and that the study should be reproduced 'in a clinical setting in which the person displaying the prompts to the child is neither a parent nor informed of the child's diagnosis', which would remove both parental leniency in labelling and the unblinding of the person generating the labels. The discussion caveat is the one that bears on the headline: 'the duration-based measures in this study could capture the speed with which a parent marks a prompt as correct as opposed to the speed with which it takes the child to answer the prompt' - so the feature family carrying nearly all the signal may be measuring the parent. The authors also diagnose why the accuracy features failed, attributing the ceiling effect to 'parents incorrectly labeling or a game design that was too easy for the majority of children regardless of diagnosis'. Not acknowledged: the implausible age standard deviation; the absence of any group-specific demographics; and the unit-of-analysis ambiguity.

answers.title: Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction
answers.answer: There is no limitations section and only one limitation is acknowledged anywhere - that the dataset is small, offered as the explanation for the CNN underperforming the SVM and as the motivation for the sole future direction. Not acknowledged: that recordings from the same child are distributed across training and test; that the sample is entirely uncharacterised demographically and clinically; that no diagnostic procedure is reported; that the 59.71% figure for Method 2 is the maximum over 256 frequency sequences; that Method 2's near-chance result is difficult to reconcile with Method 1's near-perfect one; that the two-channel configuration underpinning the whole method is never described; that less than a third of collected recordings were usable and the loss was driven by the autistic children's pronunciation difficulty, so the analysed autistic sample is the more verbally able subset; and that no ethics approval is reported.

answers.title: The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation
answers.answer: Two limitations are stated, both technical and both substantive. The audio quality achieved with a single distant microphone in a reverberant room, quantified as 12 +/- 5 dB signal-to-noise ratio for child speech, is named and contextualised against prior work using four microphones with beamforming. And the requirement for a minimum of 20 seconds of child speech comprising at least 50 vocalisations is acknowledged as a constraint of the deep-learning approach. What is not acknowledged is the more consequential interpretive issue: the correlation of 0.606 is computed across a sample containing two well-separated clusters, with the autistic group averaging ADOS 14.6 and the comparison group 3.2, so a large part of the association reflects group membership rather than graded severity within either group. No within-autism correlation is reported, and without it the claim to estimate severity rather than to detect diagnosis is not established. Also unaddressed: the absence of any language or cognitive measure in a cohort defined by limited verbal fluency; the use of a single ADOS administration as both the only clinical characterisation and the prediction target; and the absence of an ethics statement.

answers.title: The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children
answers.answer: A dedicated limitations section is provided and its principal content is a scoping statement rather than a list of defects: NAO with the proposed software 'can be treated as a supplementary tool, thanks to which specialists can acquire additional diagnostic intuition to be used with standard tools'. The authors add that the games need further development through close cooperation with target users 'including children, psychiatrists/psychologists and therapists', and that the aim is a set of scenarios attractive to children. What is not addressed: the sample of five per group is not named as a constraint, though it permits only large effects to be detected and no individual-level inference at all; rater blinding to diagnosis is nowhere discussed, and is the study's main internal-validity risk since all measurement is human judgement and the diagnoses were on file; the instruments behind those diagnoses are unstated; no cognitive or language measure was obtained, so general developmental level cannot be separated from autism as an explanation for reduced turn-taking; and no test-retest data exist.

answers.title: Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach
answers.answer: The authors state three limitations - restricted phenotype (IQ >= 70, verbal, no severe symptoms, 34 of 39 male), restricted and relatively late age band (6-13 years when the clinically decisive window is nearer 3-4), and, in the discussion, the absence of any non-TD clinical comparison. They self-describe the work as 'proof-of-concept'. The unstated limitations are the ones that bear on the headline numbers. (i) Segments, not children, were randomly partitioned into the ten cross-validation folds, so a child's own segments appear in both training and test sets; with only 39 children and thousands of segments, an SVM can learn individual gaze signatures rather than a group property, and the 74.15% is therefore an upper bound of unknown tightness. (ii) The participant-level 87.18% is the maximum over ten window lengths crossed with an unspecified grid of thresholds, all evaluated on the same 39 children - Table 4 shows the neighbouring windows giving 0.77-0.85, so the reported figure sits at the top of its own selection distribution and the honest summary of the method is closer to 'around 0.79 typical, 0.87 at the best of ten'. (iii) Forward feature selection was performed once on all the data and the resulting feature set reused in every fold, so selection is unnested. (iv) The ASD group's IQ was 15 points lower (p = .019) and is never controlled; gaze dispersion during a demanding conversational task is plausibly related to cognitive ability. (v) ASD children spent 74% longer in the session, which both drives the segment-level class imbalance and means the two groups' segments come from conversations of different length and, presumably, different affective character. (vi) No ethics or consent statement. To the authors' credit, the one comparison they do make carefully is the majority-class baseline at the segment level, which is exactly the empirical chance floor the imbalance demands.

answers.title: A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features
answers.answer: The paper has no limitations section, and the omission is felt. What it does concede is narrow but honest: that the reimplemented baseline underperforms the original because the data and collection setup differed and the optimisation may not have matched; and, in the future-work paragraph, that at this stage the system should serve as a warning to prompt expert referral rather than as a diagnostic tool. The unacknowledged limitations are substantial. (i) No reference standard is described for any group, so the classification target is undefined. (ii) Six model/feature configurations are reported in Table 5 and the maximum is presented as the result, with no penalty for selection; the honest reading of an SVM chosen among three kernels, three algorithms and four feature sets on 46 children is that 85.56% is the top of a search distribution whose other members run 71-81%. (iii) Feature selection by two rounds of backward elimination over all 46 children's data, described before and separately from the evaluation, appears unnested, which on a 54-feature vector and 46 samples is exactly the regime where selection bias is largest. (iv) The engagement confound is stated in the text and then never revisited: five autistic children ignored the car entirely, all TD children were 'very interested', and the not-playing ratio is one of the three encoder features selected into the final model - so part of the classifier's discriminative power is a measure of whether the child engaged with the toy at all, which is a real behavioural difference but not the attention-to-rotating-objects mechanism the paper claims to have captured. (v) No developmental or motor measure exists to rule out general developmental level as the driver, despite the authors' own observation that TD children 'played with more energy and moved the car in a wider area'. (vi) The four CP/fragile X children were recruited and dropped. (vii) The reported metrics do not fully reconcile: at 28 ASD and 18 TD, row 6's sensitivity of 81.67% and specificity of 81.00% imply an accuracy near 81.4%, not 85.56%, and rows 1 and 4 show similar discrepancies, so either the class balance within folds differs from the overall sample or the columns are not all computed on the same basis.

answers.title: A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities
answers.answer: The stated limitation is real but tangential: that supervision was required at the outset, so the ground truth still comes from traditional assessment, whereas an ideal VAE application would organise the latent space unsupervised. The unstated limitations are more consequential. The decisive one is the validation unit. The dataset is described unambiguously as 1,500 x 12 observations built from 60 children x 25 tasks, and 10-fold cross-validation is applied to those observations. Nothing indicates that a child's 25 rows were kept together, so in a standard k-fold split roughly 22-23 of each test observation's sibling rows - same child, same hand, same session, adjacent difficulty levels - are in the training set. A model with a 12-dimensional input and a 2-dimensional latent bottleneck can readily encode a child's individual motor signature, and the reported 91.2% is therefore substantially a measure of within-child consistency rather than of between-child generalisation. The tell is in the paper's own figures: Figure 3, which averages a participant's 25 tasks to a single point, shows cleaner separation than the task-level Figure 2, yet no accuracy is computed at that level, which is exactly the number a participant-disjoint evaluation would produce. Beyond validation: accuracy is the only metric reported, with no sensitivity, specificity, AUC or confusion matrix; the reduction from 10 to 2 latent dimensions was chosen by PCA on a latent space fitted to all the data; the analysis is restricted to correctly performed tasks, conditioning on cognitive success in a way that plausibly differs by group and is never quantified; IQ ranges are asymmetric with six autistic children below the TD floor and no means, SDs or test reported; sex is not reported at all; and the autistic group was in active psychomotor therapy while controls were not, confounding motor training with diagnosis in a study of motor kinematics.

answers.title: A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation
answers.answer: There is no limitations section, though the discussion analyses the two residual errors carefully and the methods contain an important and creditable scope disclaimer - 'although RTN deficiency is closely associated with ASD, our experiment is an assessment of the response to name, not an assessment of autism risk'. The unaddressed limitations are substantial and several are structural. First, there is no validation of any kind: the five decision constants were chosen by hand and reported on the same 30 children, and the one trained component, YOLOv3, was retrained on 1,700 images of those same 30 children, so the detector has seen every participant it is evaluated on. Nothing in the paper estimates performance on an unseen child. Second, no chance baseline is computed, and the sample makes one essential: 17 of 30 children scored 5, so a rule that always predicted non-response would agree with the clinician on a majority of children and on a still larger majority of the 109 calls, since each non-responding child contributes five non-response events. For an ordinal agreement problem of this shape the natural statistic is a weighted kappa, and none is reported. Third, the 109 events are treated as independent for the headline 98.2% although they cluster within 30 children and are strongly serially dependent. Fourth, the reference standard is one unblinded clinician with no second rater and no reliability statistic, on an item that requires a real-time judgement about eye contact from behind the child. Fifth, the shoulder angle is a 2-D image-plane measurement from an uncalibrated fixed camera, so it confounds true rotation with seating position and posture. Sixth, the demographic reporting is too thin to establish for whom the method works. Finally, the framing is inconsistent: the abstract reports agreement with 'clinical diagnosis' and the conclusion invokes early autism screening in underserved regions, while the actual comparator is one clinician's score of one behavioural item in a sample that contains a single non-autistic child.

answers.title: Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games
answers.answer: The three stated limitations are real but peripheral - no transfer to adults, a desire for richer graph features, and the need for clinically overlapping comparison conditions, the last being a genuinely important acknowledgement that the study can only separate autistic children from unscreened schoolchildren. The unstated limitations dominate. First and most serious, the reported precision and accuracy are pooled across training, validation and test. The tables disaggregate honestly, so the information is present, but the abstract, results narrative and conclusion all quote the total. For the best configuration the held-out accuracy is 58.3% against a 50% chance level - on 36 observations, a difference of three. Second, the modelled rows are not children. Arithmetic on the reported percentages fixes the dataset at 240 rows split 168/36/36 in the MATLAB default proportions, so each of the 40 children contributes six rows that are randomly scattered across the three partitions, and every test row has five siblings from the same child in training. Given that the features are region-level fixation counts and durations, which are strongly stable within an individual, this is a direct route for identity information to leak. Third, four feature subsets were compared on the same data and the best reported as the study's result. Fourth, the stimuli are other-race faces for this sample, an effect the paper's own citations show it is aware of. Fifth, 20% of the approached autistic children were excluded for non-cooperation or calibration failure with no comparable filter on the comparison group and no description of those excluded. Sixth, the sample is entirely male and this is never discussed. Seventh, no IQ or cognitive measure exists to separate social-attention differences from task-comprehension differences on what is essentially a visual matching task. Eighth, ROC curves are displayed without any AUC value, so the one metric that would summarise discriminability across thresholds is shown graphically and not reported numerically.

answers.title: Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior
answers.answer: The stated limitations are unusually well chosen and include several that comparable papers omit: the sample is too small for deep learning, and this is given as the actual reason for the modelling choice rather than left implicit; the interpretability achieved is partial, and the authors specify exactly where it stops (they cannot resolve upper lip from mouth corner); the comparison group is neurotypical, and the conclusion states that a real patient 'may not be NT but may not have ASD either', calling for neurodiverse samples; the participants are adults when early diagnosis is where the clinical value lies; the analysis is monadic and discards the confederate; and whether clinicians actually benefit requires user research not yet performed. What is not addressed matters too. The sensitivity of 0.55 appears in a single sentence alongside three other operating characteristics and is never revisited, yet it is arguably the study's most consequential number: a tool that misses 45% of autistic adults cannot function as the screening technology the conclusion proposes, at least not in the direction the conclusion proposes it - though it could function well in the opposite direction, since NPV 0.79 and specificity 0.95 make a positive prediction informative. The abstract and conclusion report only accuracy. No majority-class baseline is computed, though at 15 versus 27 the floor is 64.3%, so the model's 80.5% represents a 16-point gain rather than the 30-point gain a reader assuming balance would infer. The human and AI conditions are not strictly matched - raters saw participant and confederate side by side while the model saw only the participant, so if anything the humans had more information, which strengthens rather than weakens the paper's conclusion but should be stated. Raters were also told that every case was clear-cut. No confidence intervals accompany any figure, and with 42 participants one case is 2.4 percentage points. And the bored condition was collected and never used.

answers.title: Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas
answers.answer: The stated limitations are concrete and unusually specific about failure modes: the model is trained only on 3-6 year olds and applies only there; natural scenes with small between-group differences and few training examples are hard; small objects defeat the semantic encoder; and images with objects near the edge cause false positives because typically developing children's exploratory fixations also land on the grey mask. Two further constraints appear as subgroup findings rather than caveats and are more interesting than either: sensitivity is lowest in 5-6 year olds because some had undergone rehabilitation training teaching them to attend to social information, prompting the statement that 'the model is more suitable for the initial screening of children who have not undergone rehabilitation training'; and specificity is lowest in 3-4 year olds because they cannot sustain attention to the screen. Taken together these say that the measured signal is erased by intervention at one end of the age range and mimicked by ordinary inattention at the other, which bears directly on what the proposed 'AI-marker' represents - a point the paper reports but does not draw out. The unstated limitations are led by the absence of any described diagnostic reference standard, without which the target of a 96.73% accuracy is undefined. Others: sex is imbalanced between groups by 17 percentage points and never mentioned, despite the paper's own finding that error rates differ by sex; the Otsu decision threshold is fitted on training and test scores together, so the operating point is chosen with sight of the test distribution; architecture, learning parameters and the minLength value were compared on the evaluation data with no separate development set; the stimulus-discriminability ranking used to justify a shortened protocol is derived from the same data on which accuracy is reported; there is no majority-class baseline (57.6%) or confidence interval; and no prevalence-adjusted metric is offered despite the paper proposing population-scale screening.

answers.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts
answers.answer: The two stated limitations are correctly identified and concern label validity: users may give false information in their biographies, and tweets may be written by someone other than the account owner. Everything else is unaddressed, and several of the omissions are decisive. The split is random over 90,000 tweets, not over the 252 users, so every author in the test set has the great majority of their own tweets in training; for the comparison class this is extreme, since 31 people supply all 45,000 negative tweets, meaning roughly 1,090 of each comparison user's tweets are available to help classify their remaining 360. A model that learned to recognise 31 individual writing styles would score very well and would have learned nothing about autism. There is no control for topic, in a design where the positive class was assembled by searching for autism keywords and no autism vocabulary was removed from the text. The 31 comparison users are undescribed, unmatched and unscreened, so undisclosed autistic people may sit in the negative class and any group difference in age, nationality, profession or interests is confounded with the label. No demographic data exist. Hyperparameters were grid-searched with no separate validation set. No user-level metric is reported although per-user aggregation is the only form in which such a system could be used. And the framing gap is never acknowledged: a paper titled 'Early Detection', motivated by diagnosing children before age three, is trained entirely on adult social-media users.

answers.title: Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: The three stated limitations are accurate and appropriately weighted: adult-trained landmark and affect detectors applied to toddlers, the possibility that other complexity measures would discriminate better, and insufficient power to determine how demographic characteristics affect the results. The last is an honest acknowledgement of a real problem, since the groups differ substantially on three demographic axes. The unstated limitations are fewer than in any other study charted here but include some that matter. The 3.6-month age gap between groups is never adjusted for, which is conspicuous in a paper that constructs ANCOVA models for two other covariates - the direction of the gap makes it an unlikely explanation of the finding, but it should have been modelled.
