The racial and ethnic composition differs sharply (47.5% versus 77.7% White; 32.5% versus 7.3% Hispanic/Latino), and this interacts with the acknowledged limitation about the detectors: landmark localisation accuracy varies with facial morphology and skin tone, so differential measurement error is a specific possibility, not a generic caveat. The decision to run the classification only on social movies was taken after seeing which movies produced larger effect sizes in the same data. No class handling is described for the decision tree, and the reported precision of about 70% with recall near 89% cannot arise from a 40:396 ratio without some balancing, so an undisclosed step exists in the classification pipeline. Per-movie analysed sample sizes appear only in figures. And ADOS-T totals were collected but never correlated with the entropy measure, leaving the biomarker's relationship to severity untested.

answers.title: Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders
answers.answer: The three stated limitations are well chosen and one is a genuine contribution. Small sample size is acknowledged first. The IQ limitation is stated with unusual candour - participants were recruited without intellectual difficulties but no actual values were obtained, so the study 'does not adequately take into account the influence of intellectual level', and the sample is 'only a small number of mild (high-functioning) cases'. Most valuable is the error analysis, which is the kind of work almost no study in this corpus performs: the authors identified the eight participants misclassified by all four models, inspected their raw data, found that their gaze did not move from the centre at all, checked whether they had simply not engaged with the task, and found that their FEIT recognition scores were normal (18 and 19 of 21 for two autistic adults; 19, 25, 22 and 17 of 32 for four autistic children). The conclusion - that some people complete the task using peripheral vision without moving their eyes - identifies a failure mode intrinsic to gaze-based assessment, quantifies it at 6.5% of adults and 17% of children, and names it as a target for future work. Unstated limitations remain. The statistical analysis treats trials as independent when they cluster within participants at roughly two or three per person per emotion, so Welch's t-tests on 101-172 trials overstate the effective sample size. Control selection by SRS-2 ranking introduces a construct-related variable into the sampling, and the direction of the selection is ambiguous from the text. The adult groups differ by up to six years in mean age and the children's groups by 40 percentage points in sex ratio, neither adjusted. Autistic children scored more than twice as high on the ADHD Rating Scale as controls, an unaddressed comorbidity confound in a gaze task. And Japanese participants viewed Western faces without comment.

answers.title: Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders
answers.answer: There is no limitations section, and the paper's candour is concentrated in the methods rather than in self-appraisal. What is stated plainly and deserves credit: the data were collected for developer debugging with no analytic aim in mind, so the structure required substantial reprocessing; spatial modelling is unusable because the app is customisable; window size trades pattern fidelity against sample count; and the deep belief network was tuned only for one window size, so its poorer results elsewhere may reflect tuning effort rather than capability. What is not addressed is more consequential. The reference standard is unverified voluntary self-report from 3.4% of users with no clinical component. Age is confounded with diagnosis by the structure of the comparison group, which mixes congenital autism against predominantly acquired adult-onset conditions, and no age adjustment or even age-by-group reporting is performed. The headline 82% is computed after k-means assigned pseudo-labels to roughly 5,192 users, so the great majority of the evaluation data carry labels generated by an unsupervised algorithm rather than reported by any person - which makes the accuracy partly a measure of agreement with a clustering solution. The unit of cross-validation is never stated, and with each user contributing many windows, window-level splitting would put a user's own data on both sides of every fold. Accuracy is the only metric. No chance baseline appears. The three participant totals in the text and tables do not reconcile. And there is no ethics approval, no consent for research use, and no discussion of either.

answers.title: Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: The two stated limitations are the right two, and one of them is stated more honestly than most papers in this corpus manage: the small sample, and the significant IQ difference between groups. On IQ the authors are candid that 'IQ affects one's ability to perform behavioral tasks', cite external evidence that joint attention differentiates autism after controlling for IQ, and conclude that 'external validation using a larger sample of IQ-matched cohorts with ASD and TD is still warranted'. That is a correct diagnosis of the problem and an appropriate remedy, though no adjustment is attempted in the present analysis and the 44-50 point gap is large enough that it cannot be assumed away by citation. The discussion adds three further self-critical observations about the RJA tasks: that they may lack sensitivity to motivational nuance, that their performance appears developmentally dependent, and that early loss of interest during RJA data collection may have limited the features available for severity modelling. What is not addressed is more consequential than what is. Detection AUROCs of 99.5-99.8% are reported without any interrogation, in a study that states explicitly that groups were selected to be 'clinically distinct' and that documents a three-standard-deviation IQ gap - conditions under which near-perfect separation is close to expected and tells one very little about performance in a clinical population where the question is not autism versus a typically developing four-year-old with IQ 105 but autism versus developmental delay. The severity model's three classes include non-autism, so its 90.3% AUROC largely re-solves the detection problem and provides no evidence of within-autism grading; no autism-only result is reported. Specificity is never reported, in a diagnostic study reported to STARD. The class distribution across the three severity bands is not given. There is no clinical comparison group in a sample whose autistic children have mean IQ 55-60. And the compliance finding that autistic children disengage early from RJA tasks is treated as a limitation for severity but not for detection, although it bears equally on both.

answers.title: Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking
answers.answer: The single stated limitation is correct and is stated without defensiveness: accuracy is not high, and this is attributed to the dataset containing only 547 images. The authors do not inflate their results - they describe them as promising for future research rather than as a demonstration of feasibility, and they report the custom CNN's poor autism-class performance rather than burying it. What is unaddressed is nonetheless substantial. The split is by image and not by child, so with roughly nine images per child each test image has around eight siblings in training - the mechanism that has produced very high accuracies in other reuses of this same dataset, and one this paper neither invokes nor guards against. A single fixed split of 57 test images cannot support the three-way accuracy comparison the paper draws, since a difference of 81.0% against 78.9% is a single image. No majority-class baseline is computed, though the confusion matrix implies 59.6%, so the custom CNN's 71.9% is roughly twelve points above trivial and its autism-class recall of 0.48 is below it. The greyscale conversion was adopted partly because it improved accuracy, a decision made against the same small dataset. Nothing is reported about the 59 children. And no analysis addresses what visual property of a drawn trajectory the models respond to.

answers.title: SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism
answers.answer: There is no limitations section, and the omissions matter more than in most studies of this type because several are specific to the pooling strategy. The three corpora differ in age band, session length, conversation partner and transcription convention, and - decisively - the Flusberg corpus contributes 6 autistic children and no comparison children, so corpus membership is partially predictive of diagnosis and corpus-specific artefacts are available to the classifier as diagnostic cues. The autistic group therefore extends to 12 months while the comparison group starts at 3 years, in a study whose features are language measures and whose top SHAP contributor is the number of distinct word roots - a canonical developmental index. Feature elimination by SHAP from 77 to 63 features is described before the train-test split with no statement of nesting, so the retained set saw the evaluation data. Six classifiers were compared and the best reported. All accuracies are multiples of 1/17, implying a 17-item test set rather than the 7 or 8 that a 90:10 split of 76 children would give, and no confidence interval accompanies a comparison in which one child moves accuracy by 5.9 points - so the 94.1% versus 88.2% difference between the best model and the next is one child. No demographic or cognitive data exist for any participant. And the Eigsti corpus's developmental delay group, which would have supported the differential comparison the conclusion identifies as needed, was present in the source material and not used. What the paper does do well on the evaluation side is report a majority-classifier baseline as a named comparator in both results tables, which is better practice than most of this corpus.

answers.title: Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths
answers.answer: There is no limitations section, and the two constraints acknowledged in passing - too few female autistic participants for sex analysis outside the 5-9 band, and class imbalance depressing AUC - are both treated as problems that augmentation solves rather than as bounds on inference. The unaddressed issues are severe and partly self-documented. The splitting unit is the scan-path image, and with roughly sixteen images per child each test image has about eleven siblings from the same participant in training; no subject-disjoint result appears anywhere in the paper. Augmentation compounds this: image counts after augmentation are quoted for the whole dataset rather than for the training partition, and the sex-by-age experiment shows test accuracy rising monotonically with augmentation level - 85.07% at 961/957 images, 85.81% at 1,276/1,259, and 98.84% at 3,121/2,905 - which is the characteristic signature of rotated duplicates falling on both sides of the split, since a genuine signal does not strengthen with synthetic replication. The 98.8% is nonetheless presented as evidence of 'substantial difference' between male and female autistic children. Training accuracy is 100% or within a fraction of it in essentially every table while test accuracy ranges from 67% to 81%, a twenty-to-thirty point gap noted once as 'a gap in performance' and never analysed. And the study's own results contain the material for its strongest self-critique: it shows that scan-path images encode age at 80.5% and sex at 78.0% within the autistic group, both higher than the 74.4% achieved for diagnosis, in a sample where the autistic group is 81.5% male against 46.9% and twice as likely to be aged 10 or over. Those two facts are reported four pages apart and never brought together. Beyond this: no reference standard, no IQ or severity measure despite an abstract that invokes intellectual impairment, no ethics or consent statement, no eye-tracker description, no sensitivity or specificity, no confidence intervals, and an unresolved discrepancy between 55 and 54 autistic participants.

answers.title: A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths
answers.answer: There is no limitations section and no constraint of any kind is acknowledged; the paper's self-assessment is uniformly favourable. The problems are correspondingly unaddressed and one is arithmetic rather than methodological. First, the reported metrics are mutually incompatible: Table 9 gives the proposed model 95.59% accuracy, 77.60% sensitivity and 79.91% specificity, but with 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic images those sensitivity and specificity values imply an accuracy of approximately 79.0%. The same holds for the multilayer perceptron comparator (94.69% reported against an implied 73.6%). Either the accuracy figures come from a different computation than the class-conditional ones, or one set is in error; the paper does not reconcile them, and a reader cannot determine which number describes the model. Second, the quantity labelled F1 is defined in Equation (4) as the harmonic mean of sensitivity and specificity, which is not F1. Third, cross-validation partitions the 547 images rather than the 59 children, so each held-out image has roughly eight siblings from the same child in training - the recurring leakage route in this dataset's reuse literature. Fourth, more than a hundred hyperparameter configurations were evaluated on that same cross-validation and the maximum reported as the result, with no independent confirmation; the 35-point spread between optimisers shows how much of the outcome depends on that search. Fifth, images are flattened to one dimension before entering a model described throughout as convolutional. Sixth, no majority-class baseline is computed against an implied 60.0% floor. And the CARS severity data the dataset carries, and which the introduction's discussion of severity-linked subtypes invites using, are reported and then ignored.

answers.title: A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning
answers.answer: The limitations section is the most substantive in the review and several of its admissions are ones other papers in this corpus would have suppressed. Milestone binarisation cannot distinguish children who passed after repeated attempts from those who passed first time, so a real signal about the pattern of delay is discarded. The feature set is bounded by what the national protocol happens to record, and specific plausible red flags outside it are named. Paternal age and family history of autism, both established risk factors, are not routinely collected, and the authors note that the observed advanced-maternal-age effect may be a proxy for paternal age - an interpretive caution rather than a claim. Most strikingly, they state that 'based on the national incidence of ASD, the true positive ASD group is at least 10 times higher in the examined population', meaning the great majority of autistic children in the cohort are labelled as comparison cases, and they describe this as adding 'a lot of noise to the outcome label' requiring replication with a later stable outcome. And 43.4% of diagnoses came from free-text notes rather than ICD-9 codes, with provider recording practice varying. What is not stated is the positive predictive value, although all the numbers to compute it are given: 874 autism cases among 144,632 flagged children is 0.60%, or 165 children flagged per recorded case. The paper acknowledges 'a cost of high false positive rates' and mounts a partial defence through the developmental-referral analysis, but never puts the figure on the page. It also does not draw out the interaction between its two candid admissions - if the true autism count is ten times higher, then many of those 143,758 apparent false positives are correctly flagged children whose diagnosis was never recorded, so the true PPV is materially better than 0.60% and the true specificity better than 0.81, by an amount the data cannot determine. Finally, maternal country of birth is reported as associated with diagnosis rate without discussion of whether it entered the model or of the equity implications.

answers.title: AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: “A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System”
answers.answer: There is no limitations section and no constraint is acknowledged anywhere, which for a study with this design is itself the finding. The unaddressed problems begin with the dataset and are not remediable by any modelling choice. Autistic images were scraped from autism-focused websites and non-autistic images gathered randomly from the internet, so the classes differ in provenance and therefore in every photographic property that provenance determines; a model trained to separate them has an easier and entirely non-clinical route to high accuracy, and no analysis in the paper tests which route it took. Neither label is verified against any diagnosis. The number of distinct children is unknown, so split integrity cannot be established even in principle. Augmentation appears to precede partitioning. Training accuracy reached 100%. The confusion matrix does not correspond to any stated partition. Vertical flipping is applied to faces. Sensitivity and specificity are written as percentages of a proportion throughout ('0.97% sensitivity'). The introduction promises a sub-36-month analysis that never appears. The expression module's proposed variant is outperformed by the smallest baseline it is compared against. And no ethics approval, consent or discussion accompanies a system built from photographs of identifiable children and proposed for distribution as a consumer mobile application.

answers.title: An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks
answers.answer: One limitation is conceded, in the abstract: because evaluation used stratified cross-validation and a single held-out split, 'future research should seek to validate the framework on larger, multi-site datasets and different partitioning schemes to guarantee robustness over heterogeneous populations'. That identifies partitioning as the issue, which is correct in kind, though ABIDE-I is already multi-site and the specific partitioning needed - leave-one-site-out - is available within it. What is not addressed: the phenotype stream contains the ADOS, ADI-R and SRS totals from which the diagnosis was derived, and the study's own explainability analysis ranks them first, so the reported accuracy substantially measures the model's ability to reproduce a clinical judgement from that judgement's own scored output. Missingness on those fields is additionally label-informative, since controls in ABIDE-I generally do not receive ADOS or ADI-R. No cross-site harmonisation is applied and site is label-encoded into the feature space. Age and IQ, which differ between groups in this dataset, are entered as predictors rather than adjusted for. The accuracy figures are internally inconsistent between sections, as are the split descriptions. And no confidence intervals accompany estimates on a 247-subject test set.

answers.title: Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development
answers.answer: The stated limitations are three and are given in a single abstract sentence: sample size, sex ratio, and the absence of severity variation. All are real. What is not addressed is more consequential. The headline 92.68% depends on features constructed from the six coherence values found statistically significant in a group comparison using all 41 participants, and those derived features were then evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation on the same 41 - so although no participant's data trained the model that classified them, every participant's diagnosis informed which features existed. The paper presents this as a methodological contribution: 'our analysis demonstrated that combining original features improved classification performance... by creating novel features through the summation of statistically significant features', and offers larger Cohen's d values as the explanation. The larger effect sizes are precisely what selection on significance produces, so the explanation and the artefact are the same thing. Second, four classifiers were compared across two feature conditions over 63 candidate features with the maximum reported, and no confidence interval accompanies a figure where one participant is 2.4 percentage points. Third, the autistic group's non-verbal IQ is 16 points lower at p = .015 and its mean age 15 months younger at p = .066, neither adjusted, in a study of motor coordination. Fourth and most substantively, the paper's own prior analysis of these identical recordings using complexity matching found no significant group difference in coordination, while the present analysis using cross wavelet analysis finds one - the discrepancy is acknowledged in the literature review as a general feature of a divergent field but is never confronted as a fact about this dataset, and it is the single most informative observation available about how much analytic choice determines the result.

answers.title: Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning
answers.answer: The limitations section is substantive and correctly prioritised. Sample size is named repeatedly as the principal constraint, with the conclusion that the study 'should be viewed as exploratory, aimed at providing initial insights rather than definitive conclusions' - a self-assessment few papers in this corpus offer and fewer still act on. The infeasibility of manual annotation in clinical settings is acknowledged as the reason the automatic annotator exists, and its weakest category (te-clauses, subdivided into eight classifications) is identified with two concrete remedies. Most notably, the McNemar results are interpreted with explicit reference to statistical power: 'the absence of statistically significant differences in our McNemar test results does not definitively indicate the absence of a performance difference between models, particularly in the context of small sample sizes'. Correctly refusing to read non-significance as equivalence is a discipline absent everywhere else in this review. What is not addressed matters nonetheless. IQ was measured in the autistic group at 81-91 and not measured at all in the comparison group, which was selected for average college grade point average - so an unquantified cognitive and educational gap separates the groups in a study of grammatical complexity, and the substitution of grade point average for IQ testing is presented as a selection criterion rather than acknowledged as a limitation. The language samples come from the ADOS-2 sessions that produced the labels, so the elicitation context is the diagnostic encounter itself. The comparison group is three-quarters university students against an autistic group whose educational status is unreported. And the 62.5% female composition of the autistic sample goes unremarked despite the paper's own emphasis on camouflaging.

answers.title: Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms
answers.answer: There is no limitations section and no constraint is acknowledged. The unaddressed problems are the same as for the companion study on this dataset, plus one that is specific to this paper. The dataset's two classes come from different internet sources, so image provenance is confounded with the label - and here the confound is sharper than usual, because five of the eight feature families are handcrafted descriptors that respond directly to gradient structure, texture, keypoint density and perceptual hashing, all of which are functions of resolution, sharpness, compression and lighting rather than of anything about the child. That the handcrafted features alone reach 84.5% is therefore not evidence that facial morphology is informative; it is equally consistent with the two collections being distinguishable as image sets. No diagnostic verification exists for either class. The number of distinct children is unknown. No demographic data are available. Eighteen classifier-feature combinations were evaluated and the maximum reported. And, uniquely among included studies, no evaluation protocol of any kind is described.

answers.title: Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed
answers.answer: There is no limitations section. The most consequential omission is the mismatch between the paper's framing and its content: every framing element - title, abstract, keywords, introduction, problem statement and conclusion - is written in terms of autistic people, while the data are posed expressions from non-autistic adults and no autism label, participant or classification target exists anywhere. The paper also identifies, in its own introduction, the reason its evaluation cannot support its aim - that staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones and that spontaneous stimuli are what the field lacks - without connecting that observation to its own design. Further unstated issues: no validation scheme, split proportion or partitioning unit is given anywhere; the reported metric combination (100% recall with 94% specificity in a six-class problem) is unusual and is presented without confusion matrices, class-wise results or a definition of multi-class specificity; the number of emotion classes is stated as six in the abstract, seven in the KDEF description and five in a CK+ figure caption; and the architecture narrative repeatedly describes the optimiser as encoding 'physiological signal characteristics' although no physiological signal is collected or used.

answers.title: Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification
answers.answer: The stated limitations are four and are well chosen: small sample size, exclusive reliance on a tablet as the tracking device, the absence of longitudinal observation, and the absence of complementary measures - with the specific and useful suggestion that manual and ocular movement data be coordinated to characterise hand-eye patterns. The authors also call for cross-validation against other diagnostic tools. What is not addressed is the relationship between 20 children and 738 modelling units. Cross-validation partitions trajectories, and with roughly 37 trajectories per child each validation trajectory has around 36 siblings from the same child in training; movement kinematics are close to an individual motor signature at this granularity, so a model can separate children rather than groups and report high accuracy. No participant-level result appears anywhere, and the paper does not state whether folds respected child boundaries. Three further omissions matter. Neither group received any developmental or cognitive assessment, and the comparison children were recruited explicitly without assessment of pre-existing abilities, so a general developmental explanation cannot be excluded in a fine-motor task with 3-6 year olds. The autistic group's age standard deviation is nearly ten times the comparison group's, so the groups differ in developmental spread. And the autistic children were receiving psychomotor therapy at the recruiting centre while the comparison children were not, confounding motor training with diagnosis in a study of motor kinematics - the same confound this review recorded in the group's companion study on a different sample, and unaddressed in both.

answers.title: Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain
answers.answer: There is no limitations section and no constraint is acknowledged. The unaddressed problems begin with the impossibility of assessment: without a sample size, participant description, recruitment procedure, task, equipment or diagnostic standard, the study cannot be evaluated, replicated or interpreted, and its reported metrics - given to five decimal places - have no stated denominator. The target conflates autism with visual sensory processing disorder into one binary label. The validation scheme is described twice in mutually inconsistent terms and neither description is connected to the reported results. Feature selection optimises a fitness function involving inter- and intra-class similarity, which requires class labels, with no statement that this was confined to training data. No ethics approval or consent is reported for manual collection of physiological and facial data from human participants. And the paper's own worked example is the clearest evidence about what its labels track: of the five individuals in Table 2, the three labelled 'Detected' have body temperatures of 100.4, 95.5 and 103 with heart rates of 102, 62 and 133, while the two labelled 'Not detected' have 98.5 and 99.5 with heart rates of 85 and 89. Two of the three positives are febrile or hypothermic and two are tachycardic; both negatives are within normal range on both measures. In the only data the paper displays, the label separates people with abnormal vital signs from people without.

answers.title: Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: No limitations section exists, and the paper's critical attention is directed entirely at prior work: small sample sizes, narrow diagnostic focus, dependence on predefined hyperparameters, and the inefficiency of grid search. What should have been stated: the class variable is computed from the modelled features by summation and thresholding, so the task contains no uncertainty and the perfect scores are arithmetic rather than empirical; no respondent in any dataset is known to have received a diagnostic assessment; no positive predictive value is computed at any realistic prevalence for a tool proposed for at-home use, where the base rate would be far below the 61-69% positive rates in the training data; no feature ablation isolates what the registration metadata contribute independently of the items, which would have been the single most informative experiment available; and the deployed tool presents the output of the Q-CHAT-10 and AQ-10 scoring rules to parents as an artificial-intelligence diagnosis without indicating that this is what it is.

answers.title: Machine learning’s effectiveness
answers.answer: The limitations passage is among the most self-critical in this review and names four constraints, one of them unprompted by convention. The target is a screening cut-off rather than a diagnosis, and the authors recommend that clinical assessment be integrated alongside the SRS-2. The above-threshold sample is small at around 20, and the class imbalance is acknowledged as the reason for choosing leave-one-out cross-validation 'to avoid polarization of prediction toward the Low autistic trait group'. Only an SVM was tried. And external validation on other regions and institutions is needed. Most notably, the authors state the specific hazard their own validation choice creates: 'LOOCV can also produce optimistic performance estimates due to the small test set in each iteration. In addition, it can be unstable when the dataset contains noise or outliers, as individual data points can disproportionately influence the results. These limitations emphasize the need for cautious interpretation of our results.' Naming the optimism of one's own evaluation scheme is rare here. What is not addressed is the more consequential question. The paper states that the procedure 'simultaneously selected the 16 explanatory variables and optimized the hyperparameter', with three to five variables plus a cost parameter chosen per model from sixteen candidates on 126 participants of whom 19 are positive - and it does not say whether that selection occurred inside each leave-one-out fold. If it did not, unnested selection on this configuration would by itself be sufficient to produce accuracy, sensitivity and specificity of exactly 1.000, and the perfect scores would carry no information. Also unaddressed: no majority-class baseline against an 84.9% floor, no positive predictive value despite a genuinely population-based design that could support one, no developmental measure to separate autistic-trait effects from general motor maturation in five-year-olds, and single-informant SRS-2 with no reliability estimate.

answers.title: Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network
answers.answer: Two limitations are stated and both are real. The computational cost of a deep multiscale attention architecture combined with metaheuristic search is acknowledged as a barrier to real-time deployment. And the interpretability claim is qualified honestly: 'clinical users or experts did not validate our heatmaps, limiting our ability to assess their potential clinical utility', with a concrete remedy proposed. The ablation discussion adds a third, unprompted admission - that multiscale fusion alone did not improve on squeeze-and-excitation alone. What is not stated is more consequential. The provenance confound is never raised, although the paper supplies the evidence for it in its own description of where the images came from. No diagnostic reference standard exists for either corpus and this is not identified as a limitation. Demographics are absent and marked as absent, yet the possibility that age, sex or ancestry imbalance drives the result is not discussed. The 1:1 class ratio bears no relation to prevalence and no positive predictive value is computed. The confidence intervals - uniformly the mean plus or minus 0.4 points, on a test set of 68 images where one image is worth 1.47 points - cannot be describing the uncertainty in the accuracy estimate; an exact binomial interval around 95% on 68 images runs from roughly 87% to 99%. The cross-dataset result is offered as robustness without noting that both corpora were built the same way. And the ethics of the underlying images is untouched.

answers.title: Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]
answers.answer: There is no limitations section. What should have been stated, in order of consequence: no validation scheme of any kind is described, so the reported 89-94% cannot be placed relative to any evaluation design, and with 17 participants those figures must derive from epoch-level evaluation where a participant-disjoint arrangement is barely constructible from four controls. The participant-level majority-class baseline is 76.5% and is never stated. The comparison group of four children is too small to characterise typical EEG variation. No age distribution by group is given across a 9-to-16 window in which EEG spectra change substantially, and medication - which alters EEG directly and differs between such groups - is unrecorded. No diagnostic ascertainment is described. No feature-importance analysis identifies which of the eleven descriptors separates the groups, which would have been the study's most transferable finding. And the paper's own comparison table displays a pattern it does not comment on, discussed below.

answers.title: Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play
answers.answer: Five limitations are enumerated and they are well chosen - three of them identify problems that most papers in this corpus leave to the reader. The 90-second task does not fully capture social interaction, communication or repetitive behaviours, and should be lengthened with opportunities for child-initiated interaction. The sample is predominantly male, limiting generalisability across gender-specific presentations. Children scoring below 30 on CARS-2 were excluded, 'which may have resulted in selection bias by including only those with more pronounced characteristics of autism. Consequently, the performance of the clinical prediction model may be overestimated' - a statement of spectrum truncation and its effect on performance that is more direct than anything else in this review. The sample is small for prediction-model development and both the coding scheme and the model need further reliability and validity evaluation across age groups, language levels and presentations. And only autistic and typically developing groups were compared, whereas 'in the real clinical setting, it is more challenging to distinguish ASD children from non-ASD children, such as those with IDD, than distinguish ASD children from TD children'. What is missing is the optimism arising from the analysis itself: five predictors were selected from 81 candidates using the same 246 children whose data yield the reported AUC, sensitivity and specificity, and the operating cut-off was chosen from the same ROC curve, so the headline figures are apparent performance and no optimism-corrected estimate is reported although a bootstrap was run. Also unaddressed: predictive values are quoted at the matched 50% prevalence with no recalculation for a screening base rate; no language or cognitive measure exists although the strongest predictor is socially directed speech; age is matched at the mean but not adjusted for, in a 1-to-6-year sample where four of five predictors are play-quantity measures; the recruitment asymmetry between clinical services and a kindergarten is not discussed; and coder blinding to group is not stated.

answers.title: Predictive model using autism
answers.answer: Four limitations are stated and the fourth is the most consequential and the most creditable. The sample is small and the findings require careful interpretation. No upper age limit was applied, which may have caused an age imbalance, though the authors judge the impact limited given the similar ranges, means and standard deviations. Intelligence could not be compared because JART was used in one group and WAIS-III in the other. And: 'the holdout validation result of the Predictive Model showed a decrease in diagnostic accuracy. The model had six variables, which was a large number compared to the number of samples; hence, the AUC may have increased due to overfitting. Therefore, additional validation of the model using external data is required.' Reporting a held-out accuracy of 65.3% against a training accuracy of 85.4%, and naming overfitting as the explanation, places this paper in a very small minority within this corpus - most studies that perform such a check report only the favourable figure, and several report perfect scores without any check at all. What is not stated: whether ADOS-2 administrators were blind to diagnosis, which matters because every input is a clinician judgement; that item-level inter-rater reliability was never established within this study although the analysis operates at that granularity while the instrument's published reliability is at algorithm level; that the two groups were recruited two years apart in non-overlapping windows; that the abstract and results still present AUC 0.938 as the model's discriminative ability with the 65.3% figure confined to the body; that excluding comorbidity from both groups and severe positive symptoms from the schizophrenia group removes precisely the ambiguous cases the model is for; and that no positive predictive value is computed for any realistic clinical case mix.

answers.title: The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech
answers.answer: The limitations section is long, specific and unusually self-critical, covering six issues. The study's original aim - autism recognition in children aged 1 to 3 - was abandoned because data on that population could not be obtained, and the authors say so plainly. The two corpora were collected in different settings, creating domain-shift risk and possible bias toward the more heavily represented one. Class imbalance limited the models, and the authors note that the resampling remedies themselves affect classification performance. Gender imbalance is severe and the fairness testing demonstrates its consequence. The test sets are small and 'not fully representative of the real-world'. And the headline is explicitly qualified: a development UAR of 78.0% against a test UAR of 94.8% is flagged as reflecting corpus-specific characteristics and the additional partitioning, with the conclusion that 'due to the limitations in the dataset, the results reported herein must be carefully interpreted' - reinforced by a citation to a discussion of 'potential over-expectation in speech analysis tasks for real-world application'. What is not addressed is the recording-setting confound within CPSD, where atypical children were recorded in clinics and typical children in schools, which the paper's own dataset description states and which makes acoustic environment a perfect proxy for the binary label. Nor is the participant-count inconsistency resolved, or the number of children per diagnostic class stated - facts that determine how much protection speaker-disjoint splitting actually provides. No age data are available in a corpus spanning 6 to 18 years. No diagnostic procedure is described for either corpus, and the CPSD categories are pre-DSM-5. No language measure exists although one class is a language disorder. Nothing is said about what the children were doing when recorded. And the specific direction of the development-to-test discrepancy - test scoring sixteen points above development - is noted but not explained, though a test score well above a development score usually indicates that the partitions differ in composition rather than that the model improved.

answers.title: Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism
answers.answer: Five limitations are stated and the reasoning behind each is unusually developed. There is no clinical validation for any diagnosis, and expert or crowdsourced annotation would help. Hashtag users may be family members, parents, caregivers or advocacy organisations rather than autistic people, though the authors judge this rare given the negative social connotations of using #ActuallyAutistic without a diagnosis. Autistic users who do not self-identify will contaminate the control group, bounded at roughly the population prevalence of under 3%. VADER sentiment may be less accurate than human labelling. And the English-only restriction limits diversity, over-representing younger and higher-socioeconomic users. The authors add a scope restriction that functions as a finding - 'the predictive power of social media is not to be used at an individual level but at a broader cross-sectional level' - and name the consent failure as 'the primary limitation of this study', enumerating misuse scenarios including university admissions, hiring, and government surveillance. What is not addressed is the group-definition confound: the positive class is a community organised around a topic and the negative class is a platform sample, so a classifier could reach 73% by recognising the register of autism self-advocacy rather than any property of autistic language production, and removing sixteen keywords does not close that route. Nor is the structural asymmetry addressed by which the autism group's full timelines were harvested while control posts were sampled daily, so that 17,323 users contribute nearly as many tweets as 171,273 - a difference in how material was selected that is confounded with the label. No demographic data exist for either group in a comparison where the communities plausibly differ in age and sex. No feature analysis is reported for the classifiers, so the interpretive question is left open where it could have been partly answered. And the contamination bound assumes that population prevalence transfers to Twitter's user base and that non-self-identifying autistic users write like non-autistic ones.

answers.title: Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children
answers.answer: One limitation is formally stated - that the simple ensemble could not outperform the individual modalities - and two more consequential ones are volunteered in the discussion without being labelled as such. The authors propose that 'peculiar non-vocal acoustic features (i.e., ambient sound), such as any repetitive sound that would reflect an increased need for sensory stimulation in autistic children (e.g., repeatedly dropping objects or banging them, or perseverating on a musical toy)' contributed to the audio classification, supporting this with their own finding that sensory interests was the ADOS item most correlated with audio-based prediction. And they note prior work showing that examiners attune their prosody to a child's symptom severity, in which 'the psychologist's prosodic cues better predicted the child's autistic symptom severity than the prosody of the child himself' - so a full-band audio model trained on undiarised recordings may be reading the adult's behaviour as much as the child's. Volunteering both is unusual and valuable. What is not addressed: the probable circularity between the ADOS-supported diagnosis and the ADOS-derived model input, which one sentence about whether ADOS entered the diagnostic decision would resolve; the absence of confidence intervals on an 80-child test set, where an exact interval around 82.5% spans roughly 72% to 90% and where the ensemble's 2.5-point advantage over video alone amounts to two children; the absence of any positive predictive value at realistic prevalence in a paper framed around screening, where specificity of 0.875 would place most positive calls on non-autistic children at a population base rate; the unquantified effect of the 90% segment-confidence filter; the eleven-year window across which equipment, personnel and diagnostic practice all changed; the absence of a sex-stratified analysis despite a sample uniquely suited to one; and the restriction of the comparison group to typically developing children, leaving the harder discrimination against other developmental conditions untested.

answers.title: Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning
answers.answer: The stated limitations are unusually honest about measurement and silent about the study's central weakness. Three are listed formally - the scarcity and small size of public autism datasets, that 'existing datasets are not necessarily trustworthy', and the uncontrolled acquisition conditions and poor image quality - and the discussion volunteers three more concerning the annotation layer, each of them a real threat: the five raters 'are not experts in affect and emotion estimation. Therefore, it is impossible to confirm that the information gathered is accurate'; averaging their ratings 'is subject to the annotators' reaction times', so inattention produces lag that deviates from the ground truth; and simple averaging 'does not deal with disagreements either'. The introduction also cites Bone and colleagues' finding that on a larger and more balanced dataset they 'were unable to reproduce the results of several works that claim to drastically reduce the time to diagnose autism using machine learning', and the authors state that their own approach 'will not replace clinicians in terms of their expertise'. What is never addressed: the non-autistic class is undescribed, so the classification result is uninterpretable and may reflect a difference between image corpora rather than between children; the class balance is called balanced in the methods and 'very imbalanced' in the results, leaving no determinable chance baseline; the autism label rests on trusting YouTube uploads, which is presented as a warrant rather than examined as a limitation, and sits awkwardly beside the authors' own statement that existing datasets are not necessarily trustworthy; the subject-disjointness guarantee covers only the SSBD half of the data; no demographic information exists for either class in a study classifying faces; and there is no ethics or consent statement for identifiable children's home videos annotated for emotional state.

answers.title: A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features
answers.answer: There is no limitations section. The future-work paragraph names five extensions - more diverse and representative samples, additional modalities such as speech or genetic information, ensemble models, longitudinal designs, and evaluation in real-world clinical settings - which concede by implication that the present sample is neither diverse nor representative and that nothing has been clinically evaluated, but none of these is allowed to qualify any conclusion. What should have been stated: the 80-20 split is over 1,500 images from 30 children with roughly 50 images each and no participant-level partitioning, so the classifiers can identify the child and thereby the label, and a 98.33% three-class accuracy is the expected arithmetic of that arrangement rather than evidence about thermal signatures of severity. The severity labels have no stated source, so the target is undefined. The comparison against 'the clinical ABC method' is incoherent if the ABC produced those labels. Class sizes are unreported, so no baseline exists. Skin temperature was measured across outdoor and indoor settings without ambient compensation, and if severity is unevenly distributed across settings the environment is confounded with the label. All participants are male. Current medication - itself a determinant of thermoregulation, and correlated with severity by construction - is unrecorded. No feature importance is given, so it is unknown whether temperature or mood drives the result. The 20 held-out videos are never analysed. And there is no ethics approval or consent for prospectively imaging disabled children in an institution.

answers.title: Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: No limitations section appears in the retrieved text, but the introduction contains one honest sentence: 'The research gap in ASD identification using images persists, despite the proposed system achieving 98% accuracy on a benchmark dataset ... Ultimately, clinical validation is necessary to ensure the widespread adoption of this approach in healthcare settings and its practical applicability.' Conceding that a 98% benchmark result leaves the research gap open is unusual in this branch and should be credited. What is not stated: that the non-autistic class was assembled by web search and the autistic class from an autism collection, so the label encodes provenance; that no diagnostic ascertainment exists for any image; that no demographic information is available in a study classifying faces; that the split is at image level with the number of children unknown; that all reported figures come from the validation partition rather than the defined test partition; that the reported support counts are inconsistent with both the stated split proportions and the corpus class ratio; that no chance baseline is given; that the promised feature-importance analysis was not performed; and that the abstract, introduction and results tables disagree about which models were compared and which won.

answers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features
answers.answer: Two limitations are stated: limited data, with a call for greater variety of participant backgrounds; and residual noise after feature computation, acknowledged as partly inevitable 'since speech is transcribed in different ways across datasets'. The second identifies cross-corpus heterogeneity at the transcription level, which is the right issue seen from one side. What is not addressed: mean length of utterance, the top predictor, is a developmental language index that the paper's own analysis shows increasing with age, and with no independent language measure and no reported age composition by group, language delay and age cannot be separated from autism; part of the typically developing class comes from corpora containing no autistic children and using different protocols, so corpus of origin is partly correlated with class; session lengths differ threefold where stated and are unknown for one corpus, and the investigator's role differs across protocols although half the features are ratios to the investigator; developmentally delayed children were deliberately excluded, removing the clinical comparison that would have made the result far more informative; the headline accuracies were obtained 'after the removal of certain features' selected on the same data; no confidence intervals accompany estimates from test folds of sixteen children; and no model performance is reported by age band or sex despite the feature analysis being stratified and despite that analysis finding a sex-by-diagnosis interaction.

answers.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning
answers.answer: The conclusion names three limitations: generalisability requires further optimisation, 'particularly for datasets with biased label distributions'; 'the computational complexity of dual-stream models also poses challenges for real-time clinical applications'; and future work should pursue lightweight architectures, improved augmentation and pre-training. Naming one's own computational cost as an obstacle to the clinical use one proposes is candid, and identifying label imbalance as the source of the DREAM shortfall is a reasonable diagnosis even if not the only one. There is no separate limitations section, and several substantial issues go unaddressed. The Gait dataset's single retained trial per child was selected 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation' - the methods quote it and nothing follows. No participant-level partitioning is described for DREAM, where 1,833 samples come from 61 children. No demographic information exists for either corpus, in a domain where gait varies strongly with age and sex. No sensitivity, specificity, AUC or confusion matrix is reported for any proposed model, so a screening claim rests on accuracy alone. The 95.4% is a best-of-six architecture selection on test folds of ten children, where one child is worth ten percentage points and the six backbones span 2.2 points. And the paper reports, without comment, that the Gait dataset's own creators moved from approximately 60% accuracy without augmentation to 92% with seven augmentation techniques - a 32-point gain from augmentation alone, which is as clear a statement of augmentation-driven inflation as this review has found, quoted as background rather than treated as a warning.

answers.title: Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]
answers.answer: Four limitations are stated in a dedicated section and they are reasonable as far as they go: generalisability limited by sample size, demographic variation and the 18-to-54-month age range; cry characteristics changing with growth, making age-specific models necessary; the absence of ADOS because no official Farsi version exists; and the need for larger datasets and refined diagnostic methods. The second of these comes close to identifying the age confound but treats it as a generalisability question rather than as a threat to the group comparison in hand. What is not addressed is more consequential. The classification result has no held-out test partition, the final model was selected as the best of 2,000 epochs on the validation set, and the evaluation unit is the cry instance with no participant-level splitting described - so with roughly six instances per child, the network can identify a voice and recover its fixed label, and 90.28% is a selection maximum on data it has partly seen. The recording-setting imbalance is reported in the methods and presented as a strength when 87.10% of autistic recordings came from autism centres against a comparison group split between health centres and homes, and the three significant acoustic measures are all sensitive to room acoustics and background noise. The 4.8-month age difference is not tested or adjusted. Cry causes differ between groups and are not adjusted. Two device classes are used with no normalisation reported. GARS-2 scores exist and are not used for any severity analysis. And the statistical tests appear to be computed over cry instances rather than per-child summaries, so their effective sample size is unclear.

answers.title: Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm
answers.answer: One limitation is stated and is correct as far as it goes: 'A limitation of this work is its heavy reliance on a single public Kaggle dataset, which may limit the model's generalizability. Future studies should address this by incorporating diverse datasets to enhance the model's applicability across different populations.' That identifies an external-validity problem while leaving the internal one untouched - the issue is not that one dataset was used but that within it the label is computable from the features. Also unstated: no class distribution or majority-class baseline despite the source dataset's 73.2% negative rate; only accuracy reported, with no precision, recall, specificity, AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval; no feature importance despite Random Forest supplying it without cost, which would have exposed the dependence on 'result' immediately; and no clinical ascertainment for any respondent.

answers.title: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
answers.answer: There is no limitations section. The introduction's future-work sentence - calling for 'extension of the parameter set, utilization of deeper architectures, growth of dataset size, and optimization towards real-time high-accuracy performance' - concedes by implication that the parameter set, architecture and sample are limited, but nothing qualifies a conclusion. What should have been stated, in order of importance: the autistic group is 84% male against 52% in the comparison group, and the model's inputs are facial mesh and body landmark geometry, so a substantial part of the separation could be sex discrimination, and no stratified or adjusted analysis is reported. No diagnostic reference standard is described for a prospectively recruited sample, so the predicted label is undefined. There is no ethics approval or consent statement for a study recording 16 hours of video of 100 children. No age distribution by group is given across a 5-to-9 range in which facial and motor development changes substantially. All reported figures are cross-validation results with no independent held-out test, so architecture selection and performance estimation share data. No specificity or confusion matrix is reported, and with recall at 0.95 and accuracy at 85-90%, specificity must be materially lower than recall - a fact the reported metrics conceal. The stated 95% confidence intervals of plus or minus 1.5% are narrower than 100 children in 5-fold cross-validation would ordinarily support and their derivation is not given. And no ablation separates the face, pose and hand streams, so the study cannot say which behaviour carries the signal.

answers.title: Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of
answers.answer: The limitations section is one of the better ones in this branch and names five issues: the corpus of public 2D images may not represent the diversity of facial expressions in the target groups because age, gender and cultural background were not controlled; ten-fold cross-validation mitigates overfitting but there is no external validation cohort; subtle emotional states such as fear and disgust are hard to distinguish because they involve minimal muscle movement; the approach uses only static images while real interactions are dynamic and multimodal; and the advanced architectures and multimodal inputs proposed as future work were not implemented. Naming uncontrolled demographics and the absence of external validation directly is creditable. What is not addressed: the autistic images come from autism-related websites, so the label records provenance rather than diagnosis, and no diagnostic reference standard exists for autism at all; the split is at image level with the number of distinct children unreported, opening the leakage route that this review has documented for six other studies on this corpus family, and DeepFace's identity-optimised embeddings make that exposure greater than for a generic feature extractor; the 92% is reported as spanning training and testing together with no separate held-out figure; no sensitivity, specificity, confusion matrix or interval is given for autism and no metric at all for gelotophobia; the feature-to-image ratio is about 34 to 1; and above all, the GELOPH<15> was never administered to anyone, so the gelotophobia component - the paper's headline contribution - has no ground truth, no evaluation and no measured result, while the conclusion claims its effectiveness has been demonstrated.

answers.title: Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
answers.answer: No limitations section exists. What should have been stated: the corpus's autistic class is harvested from autism-related online sources, so the label encodes provenance and no diagnostic ascertainment exists for any image; no validation scheme, split proportion or partitioning unit is described anywhere and the number of distinct children is unreported, leaving the standard leakage route for this corpus open and unexaminable; augmentation by zoom and brightness is applied without stating whether it was confined to training, and brightness or zoom variants of a single photograph appearing on both sides of a split are near-duplicates rather than independent observations; no demographic information exists for either class in a study classifying faces, while the study's own motivating morphometric quantities all vary with age, sex and ancestry; only accuracy is reported, with no sensitivity, specificity, interval or chance baseline; and the physiognomic premise is neither measured nor tested against model behaviour.

answers.title: Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children
answers.answer: A dedicated limitations section names six issues and is among the more candid in this branch: missing demographic information on gender and ethnicity limiting generalisation across populations; a small image count possibly yielding a less robust model; analysis restricted to static images so that 'facial cues that were dynamic like gaze direction and micro-expressions were not captured'; no validation on independent clinical datasets; no explainable-AI visualisation, limiting clinical interpretability; and CPU-based training restricting tuning. The methods add that only a single split was performed, with the computational reason given. What is not addressed is more consequential. The autism model's reported metrics are mutually inconsistent - accuracy 95% cannot hold alongside specificity 42.5% and recall 94% on a balanced test set, and precision 0.96 cannot hold alongside specificity 0.425 at a 1:1 ratio - and no reconciliation appears anywhere, so the headline figure is uninterpretable. If the specificity is the accurate value then the model misclassifies more than half of non-autistic children, which is below chance and would be the paper's most important result. The corpus's provenance confound is unmentioned, no diagnostic ascertainment exists, the image-level split leaves subject overlap unexaminable since the number of distinct children is unreported, the quality filter introduces an unreported selection, and no chance baseline is given.

answers.title: Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy
answers.answer: No limitations section exists, and the conclusion repeats the results paragraph almost verbatim without critical reflection. What should have been stated: the proportion of Kaggle against Semarang images and their distribution across classes is unreported, which is the single fact determining whether mixing sources mitigates the branch's provenance confound or creates a sharper one aligned with ancestry, camera and setting; no diagnostic ascertainment is described even for the clinic-sourced portion, forgoing the study's clearest opportunity to improve on its predecessors; the split is at image level with the number of distinct children unreported; augmentation ordering relative to splitting is unstated and rotation, flip and contrast variants of one photograph are near-duplicates; no demographic data exist in a study classifying faces; no specificity, AUC or confusion matrix is given, so the error profile behind a recall of 0.8182 is uninspectable; and there is no ethics or consent statement despite part of the corpus coming from a clinical service.

answers.title: Diagnosing autism spectrum disorder based on eye tracking technology using deep learning models
answers.answer: None acknowledged. There is no limitations section, no threats-to-validity paragraph, and no caveat anywhere in the discussion or conclusion. The paper moves directly from 99.78% to promise for clinical application. Every issue this review identifies - row-level splitting, unnested feature selection, CARS as an input, the sex imbalance, imputation before splitting, the Excel-shaped row count - passes unmentioned.

answers.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Automated Machine Learning
answers.answer: One limitation is stated - no evaluation on public datasets, and the Pakistani rehabilitation-centre sample's demographic and cultural specificity may limit generalisability, with a sensible note that direct comparison against UCI data would itself introduce socio-clinical bias. Unstated: that the label is a deterministic function of the predictors, that five of the ten items were deleted precisely because they predicted the label too well, that the majority-class baseline is 71.1%, that a single unrepeated split underpins every number, that the sample size does not add up, and that respondents were drawn from among parents of children already attending autism rehabilitation services.

answers.title: Enhanced ASD detection using 3D facial landmark localization with convolutional shape appearance model and graph-randomized XGBoost
answers.answer: Section 5.1 is a real limitations section and, judged in isolation, a thoughtful one: cost and technical barriers to 3D imaging in clinics, the asymmetric harms of false positives and false negatives, residual demographic bias from underrepresented facial morphologies, lighting effects on scan quality, and computational cost precluding real-time use. Judged against the study, it is misaddressed - four of the five items concern 3D scanning hardware the study never used. Nothing is said about the dataset's web provenance and absent diagnostic labels, about the unexplained demographic annotations, about evaluating on a hand-selected 200-image subset, about the confusion matrix that sums to 300, or about the fact that all comparator figures are quoted from another paper rather than measured.

answers.title: Enhanced multilevel autism classification for children using eye-tracking and hybrid CNN-RNN deep learning models
answers.answer: Three limitations are stated: small-scale datasets typical of ASD research; the practice of retaining valid scanpaths across paradigms, which produces inconsistent sample sizes across subjects; and eye-tracking reliability problems from calibration precision, subject cooperation and equipment limits. All three are real and specific. Unmentioned: that the 70:15:15 split is at the eye-image level so every participant appears in all three subsets; that there is no TD group despite the abstract's TD comparison; that the CARS bands defining the four classes are arithmetically impossible and inconsistent with the eligibility threshold; that the external comparison is against a different task on a different dataset; that specificity, FDR and FOR are defined but never reported; and that the asserted cross-validation is never quantified.

answers.title: Ensemble of Deep Learning with Crested Porcupine Optimizer Based Autism
answers.answer: None. The article contains no limitations section, no threats-to-validity discussion, and no caveat of any kind. Nothing is said about the dataset's web provenance, the absence of diagnostic labels, the evaluation counts that span the whole dataset, the epoch-wise selection of the reported figure, or the fact that all comparator numbers are quoted rather than measured.

answers.title: Explainable and secure framework for autism prediction using multimodal eye tracking and kinematic data
answers.answer: None. There is no limitations section. Nothing is said about 44 examples being the entire dataset, about nine-case test sets, about accuracies quantised to multiples of one ninth, about class-mean imputation using the outcome label, about the contradictory normalisation account, about the absent ethics statement, or about the three federated clients being partitions of a single small file rather than independent institutions.

answers.title: Facial Images Dataset for Early Screening of Autism Children Using Convolutional Neural Network
answers.answer: None stated. There is no limitations section. The image-level split across 15 photographs per child, the school-based group assignment standing in for diagnosis, the confounding of group with institution, the absence of any per-expression analysis, and the 102-image test set all pass without comment. The one candid admission is incidental: the study does not record the total number of augmentations applied in the code.

answers.title: Improving Early Autism Detection with Chi-Square Feature Selection, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI
answers.answer: A real limitations paragraph, and better than most: the results rest on a single public dataset which may not capture the full diversity of ASD presentations across populations and cultural contexts, real-world deployment would require external validation on larger and more heterogeneous cohorts, and additional modalities such as genetic or neuroimaging data could be integrated. What it does not question is the result itself. A model that classifies 292 consecutive cases without a single error is treated as an achievement to be explained by good feature selection rather than as a signal that the target is recoverable from the inputs by construction. Also unmentioned: that SMOTE preceded the split, that the label is the Q-CHAT-10 outcome rather than a diagnosis, and that a fifth of the evaluated instances are synthetic.

answers.title: Novel Framework for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification and Tailored Education With Effective Data Mining and Ensemble Learning Techniques
answers.answer: None. There is no limitations section and no caveat anywhere. Unmentioned: that the label is a threshold on the summed predictors; that the Phase II target was manufactured by the authors from that same total; that the reported 99.99% appears in no table; that the printed cross-validation average does not equal the mean of the printed folds; that row counts are absent throughout; and that no ethics approval was sought for a study producing educational placement recommendations.

answers.title: Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach
answers.answer: No limitations section, but two candid remarks stand out. The author writes that on reviewing performance across multiple feature subsets, the results obtained were not entirely satisfactory - an unusual admission in a literature where every result is a success. And, discussing Subset 2, that it included both the Qchat-10-Score and Q1-Q10 features, which could sometimes mislead the model results. That second sentence is the closest any of the six Q-CHAT-based studies charted in this review comes to naming the circularity at the centre of the branch: the total and its own summands are both in the feature set, and the label is a threshold on the total. Having noticed it, the paper treats it as a redundancy nuisance and moves on.

answers.title: Predicting autistic traits, anxiety and depression symptoms using camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (CAT-Q-ES): A machine learning study
answers.answer: A genuine limitations section, self-critical and mechanistic rather than formulaic. Four limitations are stated with reasoning: the over-representation of women, traced to the parent validation project and to online-recruitment bias toward respondents with topic interest, higher cognitive ability and moderate-to-high socioeconomic status; the inability to verify self-reported diagnoses, with the mitigation described and its residual risk acknowledged; the weaker anxiety and depression models, explained through instrument structure (PHQ-9 and GAD-7 items each map to a distinct diagnostic criterion and so scatter, whereas BAPQ items are interrelated within domain); and the restriction to generalised anxiety, omitting social anxiety, which is the form most closely tied to masking. The one limitation not stated is the shared-method dependence between predictors and outcomes.

answers.title: A Computational Method for Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Deep Learning Approach
answers.answer: None of its own. This paper has the corpus's most extensive limitations apparatus pointed entirely outward: the introduction runs through roughly twenty prior approaches and attaches a specific weakness to each - high computational cost and limited generalizability across diverse demographics, sensitivity to non-frontal poses, dependence on iterative expert annotation, computational intensity of heterogeneous data fusion, susceptibility to noise in handcrafted features, laborious EEG preprocessing, expensive eye-tracking hardware, domain shift in EfficientNet on medical images, scarce labelled data, need for high-quality motion sensors, shallow architectures, accuracy sacrificed for deployability, privacy concerns and connectivity dependence in web tools, cultural variability in handwriting, cost and immobilisation requirements of fMRI, and overfitting risk in metaheuristic optimisation. It even observes that cross-validation may not reflect real-world variability, risking overfitting. None of this critical vocabulary is turned on its own single unrepeated image-level split of an unlabelled web corpus. The only self-directed hedge is a clause in the conclusion.

answers.title: Early Detection of ASD from Facial Images Using DeepDeblur and Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network
answers.answer: None. There is no limitations section, no threats-to-validity discussion and no caveat. The single occurrence of limitations is a generic sentence in the introduction about facial-feature analysis being affected by image quality and expression variation - which is the problem the paper sets out to solve, not a limitation of its solution. Nothing is said about the dataset's provenance, the absent diagnostic labels, the mismatch between the stated split and the reported evaluation, or the absence of any ablation.

answers.title: Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI
answers.answer: There is no limitations section, but the discussion contains the most genuine act of self-scrutiny in the charted corpus. The authors write that because of the exceptionally high-performance metrics observed in our initial model evaluations, we were concerned about the potential for overfitting, and they respond by re-running the entire comparison at 2-fold, 4-fold and 5-fold. They report that the neural network's perfect scores in certain folds indicate a potential risk of overfitting to specific data characteristics, and that identical metrics for the neural network and k-NN in some tables may indicate redundancy or overfitting in the model implementation or data processing. That instinct is correct and is exercised properly. What it does not reach is the cause: no fold count can diagnose a problem that lies in the feature set rather than the partition, and the one experiment that would have settled it - refitting without the SRS, CARS, AQ10 and Q-CHAT-10 scores - is never run. Unmentioned elsewhere: the unreported class balance, the unspecified 68% record removal, the absence of any external dataset behind a claim of applicability across diverse clinical datasets, and the unknown provenance of the label.

answers.title: Using explainable machine learning and eye-tracking for diagnosing autism spectrum and developmental language disorders in social attention tasks
answers.answer: A short but genuinely self-critical paragraph naming four things: the limited scope of the experiment, the sample size, the diagnostic tools (which could have been supplemented but were the only ones available at the time), and the provisional nature of early-age diagnoses, with an explicit instruction that findings should be interpreted with caution and a call for replication with current behavioural assessments. Not mentioned: that the full variable set has 158 variables for 93 children; that the reported figures are the maximum over four feature sets, several algorithms and four comparisons with no correction; that the sex imbalance between clinical and TD groups (approximately 92% male versus 50%) offers an alternative route to the ASD-vs-TD and DLD-vs-TD separations; and that the significant PPVT-III differences are similarly available.

answers.title: Utilizing deep learning models in an intelligent eye-tracking system for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis
answers.answer: None. There is no limitations section and the word limitation does not occur in the article.
