answers.title: Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach
answers.answer: Standardised tabular vectors in five configurations: the default 19-attribute set; Subset 1 (chi-squared, ordered by Q1-Q10 with Q9, Q5, Q6 top); Subset 2 (tree importance, retaining both Qchat-10-Score and Q1-Q10); Subset 3 (correlation-based: Qchat-10-Score, sex, jaundice, age, family history, ethnicity, respondent); Subset 4 (minimal: Qchat-10-Score, age, sex, jaundice); and Q1-Q10 alone. The configurations are the study's real object, and their comparison is where its diagnostic value lies - Subsets 3 and 4 keep the Q-CHAT total and drop the items; Q1-Q10 keeps the items and drops the total; Subset 2 keeps both.

answers.title: Predicting autistic traits, anxiety and depression symptoms using camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (CAT-Q-ES): A machine learning study
answers.answer: The 25 raw CAT-Q-ES Likert items, in four configurations: items alone, items plus gender, items plus autism diagnosis, and items plus both. Subscale scores were tested as an alternative input and did not improve accuracy - a negative result the paper reports rather than suppresses.

answers.title: A Computational Method for Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Deep Learning Approach
answers.answer: 224x224 RGB face crops from the public corpus, with unspecified preprocessing and augmentation plus a proposed Attention-Based Augmentation Layer applying unnamed non-destructive transformations. Neither the augmentation set nor its placement relative to the split is stated.

answers.title: Early Detection of ASD from Facial Images Using DeepDeblur and Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network
answers.answer: Resized, deblurred and denoised RGB face images at unstated resolution. Resizing is described as adjusting the facial image for ratio and resolution with the loss of pixels - an unusual admission that information is discarded before the pipeline whose purpose is to recover information begins.

answers.title: Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI
answers.answer: A 19-field tabular row containing, together: the ten AQ-10 behavioural items, the AQ10 total score, the Q-CHAT-10 score, the Social Responsiveness Scale score, the CARS severity rating, seven comorbidity flags and demographics - with ASD_traits as the target. This is the review's most concentrated instance of target leakage by instrument inclusion. CARS is a clinician-administered autism severity scale; SRS measures social impairment severity; AQ10 and Q-CHAT-10 are autism screening totals whose thresholds define exactly the kind of traits-present label being predicted; and the ten AQ-10 items are the summands of the AQ10 total. Four separate measurements of the target condition, plus the item-level constituents of one of them, are supplied to the model as predictors of that condition. A perfect neural-network score under this arrangement is the expected outcome, not an anomaly - and it explains why even logistic regression, a linear model on 19 variables, reaches 0.9858.

answers.title: Using explainable machine learning and eye-tracking for diagnosing autism spectrum and developmental language disorders in social attention tasks
answers.answer: Four nested tabular feature sets per child: full (158 variables), secondary (72), prior (60) and basic (24), differing in how finely stimuli and areas of interest are decomposed. All variables derive from the eye-tracking record; no clinical instrument score, demographic variable or diagnostic measure enters the feature set - a point worth stating explicitly, because it is exactly what separates this study from the corpus's leakage cases. With 93 children and up to 158 variables, three of the four datasets have more variables than participants.

answers.title: Utilizing deep learning models in an intelligent eye-tracking system for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis
answers.answer: 640x480 scanpath images, enhanced, converted to arrays and normalised to [0,1], with rotation, shifting and flipping augmentation applied during training only. Augmentation of a scanpath image is worth a separate note: flipping and rotating a gaze trace changes its spatial relationship to the stimulus that produced it, so the augmented examples correspond to no possible viewing behaviour - a transformation that is standard for photographs and semantically incoherent for scanpaths.

answers.title: A novel hybrid deep learning model using MEResNext for autism spectrum disorder detection
answers.answer: A tabular vector of Q-CHAT-10 items and individual characteristics, Yeo-Johnson transformed and then reduced by the DeSEHO metaheuristic. Two observations. First, Yeo-Johnson is a variance-stabilising power transformation for continuous skewed variables; applying it to binary checklist responses to remove noise and artefacts, and justifying that choice at length against Box-Cox on the ground that it accommodates negative values, is a category error about the data. Second, the ten items are the summands of the score whose threshold defines the label, so whatever subset DeSEHO retains, the target remains an arithmetic function of the feature pool.

answers.title: An assessment of autistic and parkinsonian movement profiles to inform selective classification algorithms
answers.answer: One row per participant. Thirty-seven kinematic input variables (nine features across four shapes plus one reaction time value), computed as residuals after controlling for age, depression and anxiety and averaged across trials and days; plus three questionnaire sets. A reduced discriminatory kinematic feature set was defined by retaining features, or feature-shape combinations, that showed significant group differences in the mixed models. That selection rule is stated precisely - including that a group-by-shape interaction yielding a difference on only one shape contributes only that shape's value - which is both good reporting and the point at which the design leaks, since the significance tests were computed over all participants including those later held out.

answers.title: An explainable deep learning framework for screening level autism severity using behavioural data
answers.answer: A 15-attribute harmonised row per participant after pruning, with continuous variables min-max normalised and categorical fields label-encoded. The predictor set contains the A1-A10 items and the composite Q_SCORE; the target is a four-level discretisation of a weighted sum of those same A1-A10 items. The label is therefore an arithmetic function of the inputs by construction, and the paper says so.

answers.title: An explainable machine unlearning algorithm framework for early detection of autism spectrum disorder and brain disabilities in newborns
answers.answer: 224x224 images for the CNN backbones; the representation of questionnaire data is never specified, which matters because five of the seven named datasets are questionnaires and a 224x224 convolutional backbone cannot consume a checklist without a stated encoding. Aggregated feature vectors appear in the text as literal illustrative values such as [0.5, 0.6, ..., 0.8] and [0.45, 0.55, ..., 0.75].

answers.title: Deep learning based approach for Behavior classification in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder using naturalistic videos
answers.answer: Cropped frame sequences from annotated behaviour segments, after region-of-interest detection to remove irrelevant background and augmentation to reduce overfitting. The ROI step is well motivated for uncontrolled home video, where background and framing differ systematically between recordings.

answers.title: Explainable Children Autism Detection using Gaze Features in Audio-Visual Speech Comprehension
answers.answer: Eighteen AOI-based temporal gaze features per experimental instance, where an instance is one participant viewing one story under one modality in one speech phase. No clinical instrument score, demographic variable or diagnostic measure enters the feature set - the SCQ, KBIT-2 and PPVT-III are reported as sample characteristics and kept out of the model.

answers.title: Explainable Ensemble Learning Framework for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Enhancing Trust, Interpretability and Reliability in AI-Driven Healthcare
answers.answer: Dataset 1: a reduced tabular vector after correlation filtering above 0.90 and ANOVA F-test selection, drawn from 28 attributes that include the AQ, SRS, Q-CHAT and CARS scores alongside the ASD-traits target. Dataset 2: a 4,220-dimensional concatenation dominated by 4,040 image features, against 400 samples - a ratio of more than ten features per sample, and more than forty per original clinical sample.

answers.title: Finding the forest in the trees: Using machine learning and online cognitive and perceptual measures to predict adult autism diagnosis
answers.answer: One row per participant containing 54 task-derived dependent variables, with AQ total and demographic variables added in specified configurations. No dimensionality reduction or feature selection is applied, and no clinical instrument is smuggled in - the AQ's presence is the explicit object of one of the three comparisons.

answers.title: Hybrid ensemble learning for Autism Spectrum Disorder screening using eye-tracking scanpath
answers.answer: One vector per participant, formed by aggregating nine scanpath descriptors across that person's trials via mean and standard deviation, after each scanpath was truncated or zero-padded to 20 fixations and before z-score standardisation. The 20-fixation cap is a substantive modelling decision - it discards everything after the twentieth fixation in longer scanpaths and pads shorter ones - and its effect is not tested.

answers.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Facial Images and AI-Based Deep Learning Models
answers.answer: 640x640 RGB images with bounding boxes, preprocessed and augmented by Roboflow's export pipeline. Because augmentation is applied at export rather than at training time, augmented variants of an image may be distributed across the train, validation and test partitions - the paper gives no information that would exclude this, and gives no split ratio either.

answers.title: Multimodal fusion of deep transfer learning with wavelet neural network for autism spectrum disorder detection using facial images
answers.answer: Gabor-filtered facial images encoded as a concatenation of three backbone feature vectors. Neither the input resolution, the fused vector dimensionality, nor the wavelet basis is stated.

answers.title: SHAP-based explainable AI framework for autism severity classification using 3D motor biomarkers
answers.answer: One 463-dimensional feature vector per child, pre-calculated by the dataset creators, z-score normalised, with timestamps omitted. Two aspects deserve note. The dimensionality is high relative to the sample - 463 features for 109 children, of whom roughly 87 are available for training - so the model operates in a regime where a random forest's variable selection is doing most of the work. And the repository's seven geometric augmentations (rotation, mirroring, scaling) were available and deliberately not used, a restraint that several studies in this corpus do not exercise.

answers.title: Screening autism spectrum
answers.answer: Fifty-two tabular features per child spanning participant details, utterance statistics, stem words and parts of speech. The inclusion of age among the predictors is the study's principal unaddressed problem: the two groups in the Nadig corpus differ in mean age by roughly two years by the authors' own table, and age is reported as one of the four features that carry the result.

answers.title: Towards screening of children students with autism spectrum disorder based on executive functions with serious game and machine learning approaches
answers.answer: One row per game session, with fields covering session duration in seconds, game identity and task-performance variables, tabulated with data types and examples. The row is a session, not a child, and the paper does not remark on the distinction anywhere.

questions.question_text: Which evaluation metrics are reported?

answers.title: Very early detection of Autism Spectrum Disorders based on acoustic analysis of pre-verbal vocalizations of 18-month old toddlers
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, AUC. Headline: 97.7% / 95.6% / 100.0% / 0.97 (PNN, FC3).

answers.title: Use of Machine Learning to Identify Children with Autism and Their Motor Abnormalities
answers.answer: Accuracy, specificity, sensitivity. Headline: 96.7% / 93.8% / 100% at seven features; mean across feature-subset sizes 84.9% / 89.1% / 82.2%. No AUC, F1 or confidence intervals.

answers.title: ADHD and ASD Classification Based on Emotion Recognition Data
answers.answer: Accuracy only - reported as best and mean across the three data types. No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC or confidence intervals, which is a serious gap for imbalanced clinical classes.

answers.title: Identifying children with autism spectrum disorder based on their face processing abnormality: A machine learning framework
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, ROC curves and AUC - a fuller metric set than most corpus studies of this period. Headline: 88.51% accuracy / 93.10% sensitivity / 86.21% specificity / AUC 89.63%. No confidence intervals; a significance marker (p<0.001) is attached to the overall accuracy.

answers.title: Semantic mapping reveals distinct patterns in descriptions of social relations in adults with autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: AUC (the primary metric), classification correct rate, sensitivity, specificity, ROC curves, and - unusually - the variance of performance across folds. Headline: AUC 0.82 for SVM (variance 0.12), 0.71 quadratic, 0.67 linear; sensitivity 0.50-0.52 and specificity 0.68-0.74 at the optimal threshold. Chance comparison by two-tailed t-test with Bonferroni correction.

answers.title: Toward the Autism Motor Signature: Gesture patterns during smart tablet gameplay identify children with autism
answers.answer: AUC as the primary metric, reported with standard deviation across repetitions - a rarity in this corpus - plus sensitivity and specificity quoted at two explicitly stated thresholds (0.50 and 0.55) and full ROC curves. Headline: AUC 0.932 average, 0.926 Creativity, 0.848 Sharing; 83% sensitivity / 85% specificity at threshold 0.50 on Creativity. No accuracy figure is emphasised, though the abstract translates the result as 'up to 93% accuracy', conflating AUC with accuracy.

answers.title: Applying machine learning to identify autistic adults using imitation: An exploratory study
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, reported per classifier with averages and standard deviations across methods; the true positive and true negative definitions and class sizes (P=14, N=16) are stated explicitly. Headline: 86.7% accuracy, 85.7% sensitivity, 87.5% specificity (linear SVM, nine features). No AUC, F1 or confidence intervals.

answers.title: Automatic Detection of ADHD and ASD from Expressive Behaviour in RGBD Data
answers.answer: Classification accuracy only, supported by raw per-class correct/incorrect counts (which is at least transparent enough to recover the confusion matrix). No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC or confidence intervals - a significant gap given the 18-vs-37 and 11-vs-22 class imbalances, where the reported accuracies of 96.4% and 93.9% cannot be compared against the relevant majority-class baselines of 67% and 67% without recomputation.

answers.title: Earlier identification of children with autism
answers.answer: Unweighted average recall as the primary metric with weighted average recall alongside, both reported with standard deviations across folds; full vocalisation-level confusion matrices for both classifiers; and subject-level accuracy at two explicitly stated thresholds. Using UAR rather than accuracy is the methodologically correct choice for the unbalanced 259-vs-425 vocalisation split, and this is one of the few corpus studies to make it.

answers.title: Speech-based Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Condition by Generative
answers.answer: Unweighted average recall only, chosen explicitly because the four-class task is imbalanced - the methodologically correct choice, and reported on both validation and test partitions. Full four-by-four confusion matrices are published for the best system under each feature set, which is unusually transparent and is what makes the near-floor autism-class performance visible. One-sided z-tests compare systems. No accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1 or AUC, and no per-child metric.

answers.title: ANN and SVM Classifiers in Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorder Gait Based on Three-Dimensional Ground Reaction Forces
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, reported for all four classifier configurations. Headline: 93.3% accuracy, 96.7% sensitivity, 90.0% specificity for the ANN. No AUC, F1, precision, confidence intervals or fold-level variance, despite averaging over ten folds and ten iterations where a standard deviation would have been readily available.

answers.title: Analyzing Human-Robot Interaction Using Machine Vision for Autism screening
answers.answer: Accuracy only, reported for five classifiers across three feature configurations, supplemented by narrative false-positive and false-negative counts (2 and 1 for the final model). No sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, AUC or confidence intervals, though the raw counts allow them to be derived: with 8 per group, 2 FP and 1 FN gives sensitivity 87.5% and specificity 75%.

answers.title: Applying Eye Tracking to Identify Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, with a permutation-derived p-value establishing that accuracy exceeds chance. Headline: 85.1% / 86.5% / 83.8% (p<0.001). No AUC, F1 or confidence intervals. A contradictory second set of figures (82.8% / 79.3% / 86.2%) appears in the Discussion for what is described as the same analysis, and is never reconciled.

answers.title: Automatic Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Everyday
answers.answer: Unweighted average F1-score as the primary metric, selected explicitly because the classes are unbalanced (18 ASD vs 9 TD) - the methodologically correct choice and one only a minority of corpus studies make. Accuracy (88.9%) and a confusion matrix are also reported, along with per-single-source F1 scores enabling the fusion ablation. No sensitivity, specificity, AUC or confidence intervals.

answers.title: Detecting Autism Based on Eye-Tracking Data from Web Searching
answers.answer: Classification accuracy, reported with 95% confidence intervals for every single configuration in every table - the only study in the corpus to do this systematically - plus confusion matrices for the two best results showing balanced per-class performance (0.722 control, 0.706 ASD for the best browse model). No sensitivity, specificity, F1 or AUC as such, though the confusion matrices permit their derivation.

answers.title: Video Gesture Analysis for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
answers.answer: Per-subject averaged accuracy with standard deviation, detection accuracy at a stated threshold, a full confusion matrix with per-class precision and recall (ASD 83.33% precision / 78.95% recall; TD 80.95% precision / 85.00% recall), and a threshold sensitivity curve from 0.5 to 0.95. No AUC or confidence intervals, but the reporting is more complete than accuracy-only studies and the full per-subject accuracy table is published, which allows a reader to see the distribution rather than only its mean.

answers.title: A Novel Eye Movement Data Transformation Technique that Preserves Temporal Information: A Demonstration in a Face Processing Task
answers.answer: Classification accuracy averaged over folds and iterations, with a paired t-test between the two models, confusion matrices for both, and permutation-based verification against chance. Group-level distributional differences are tested separately with the non-parametric Cramer test with reported statistics, critical values and p-values for each eye. The reporting is statistically thorough, though absolute accuracy is the only classification metric and no sensitivity, specificity or AUC is given.

answers.title: Applying Machine Learning to Identify Autism With Restricted Kinematic Features
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for the best model of each of the five classifiers, plus a confusion matrix for the winning model and a plot of accuracy against number of features for all classifiers - which usefully exposes how performance varies with model size. Headline: 88.37% accuracy, AUC 0.8815. Sensitivity and specificity values (91.3% and 85%) are reported but with their labels swapped between the abstract and the discussion, leaving the assignment formally ambiguous. No confidence intervals or significance testing against chance.

answers.title: Automatic Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Acoustic and Text Features from Brief Natural Conversations
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 per class and averaged, plus a ROC curve with AUC - and, unusually, the identical metric set computed for human raters so the two can be read side by side. Headline: 75.71% accuracy, AUC 75.43%, with the per-class asymmetry (TD 85.71%, ASD 65.71%) reported prominently rather than buried in an average. No confidence intervals.

answers.title: Classifying Individuals with ASD Through Facial Emotion Recognition and Eye-Tracking
answers.answer: AUC, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, reported for every feature family at every unit of analysis - a 3x4 results table that is among the most complete in the corpus and permits direct assessment of what each component contributes. Headline subject-level combined: AUC 0.935, accuracy 86.2%, sensitivity 91.3%, specificity 82.9%. No confidence intervals or confusion matrices. The printed formulas define sensitivity as TN/(TN+FP) and specificity as TP/(TP+FN), which reverses the conventional definitions and is presumably a transcription error, though it leaves the labelling of the reported values formally ambiguous.

answers.title: Detecting Developmental Delay and Autism Through Machine
answers.answer: AUC and sensitivity with standard deviations for both layers, and AUC with standard deviation for the source-classifier transfer test, plus ROC curves. Reporting sensitivity alongside AUC is appropriate for a screening framing, and reporting standard deviations across folds is better than corpus norm. However specificity is not reported for either layer, which matters given that layer one is explicitly optimised for sensitivity - so the false-positive burden of the first-stage triage is not quantifiable from the paper.

answers.title: Exploiting Visual Behaviour for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification
answers.answer: The fullest metric set in the corpus so far: accuracy (59.30%), recall/sensitivity (68.43%), specificity (50.56%), F1 (61.64%), precision (56.96%) and AUC-ROC (59.50%), all reported together for the held-out test set. Reporting specificity alongside recall is what makes the result interpretable - it shows recall is achieved largely by over-calling ASD, with specificity at chance. No confidence intervals or per-class confusion matrix.

answers.title: Hierarchical POMDP Framework for a Robot-Assisted ASD Diagnostic Protocol
answers.answer: None. No accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1 or AUC is reported, and no confusion matrix. The outputs are belief distributions over three latent states, plotted as frequency histograms per expert-assigned behavioural category. This means the study contributes no diagnostic accuracy estimate, and it should be excluded from any quantitative synthesis of performance - a point worth recording explicitly since its framing as a diagnostic protocol might otherwise invite inclusion.

answers.title: Intelligent Gaze-Based Screening System for Autism
answers.answer: Accuracy (88.6%), specificity (92.31%), sensitivity (86.63%) and AUC (0.96) - a reasonably complete metric set on its face, and the authors explicitly motivate reporting all four. But with no sample size reported, none of the figures carries an interpretable precision, and the two-decimal specificity (92.31%, consistent with 12 of 13) hints at a very small test set. No confusion matrix, confidence intervals or significance testing.

answers.title: Kinematic features of a simple and short movement task to predict autism diagnosis
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and a permutation p-value for each of the four pipelines, plus accuracy distributions across the 100 nested cross-validation repetitions and confusion matrices for all four models. Reporting non-significant results with their p-values (0.113 and 0.148) alongside significant ones is rare in this corpus. No AUC or confidence intervals, though the plotted distributions convey spread.

answers.title: Learning to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder based on the Visual
answers.answer: AUC with standard deviation across cross-validation folds, plotted as ROC curves for all four neural architectures, plus a normalised confusion matrix for the multi-label severity model. AUC is a reasonable primary metric, and reporting fold standard deviations is better than corpus norm. However no accuracy, sensitivity, specificity or precision is given for the binary task, and no confidence intervals, so the per-class error profile of the main result cannot be assessed.

answers.title: Machine Learning to Study Social Interaction Difficulties in ASD
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, AUC and raw true/false positive and negative counts, plus a decision-score plot showing each participant's position relative to the decision boundary. Reporting the raw counts (28/16/13/1) is what makes the error profile legible - the model's 75.9% accuracy comes with 96.6% sensitivity but only 55.2% specificity, meaning 13 of 29 controls were called autistic. No confidence intervals.

answers.title: Phase 3 diagnostic evaluation of a smart
answers.answer: Sensitivity and specificity as prespecified primary outcomes for the autism-versus-typical comparison, and accuracy for the autism-versus-other-neurodevelopmental-disorder comparison as a secondary outcome. Choosing sensitivity and specificity rather than accuracy as the primary measures is correct for a diagnostic instrument and is done by almost no other study in this corpus, most of which report accuracy alone on balanced designs. The sample size justification is expressed in the same terms and is worth quoting for the synthesis: if sensitivity or specificity is as high as 90%, the study has 80% power to show it exceeds 83.0% and 90% power to show it exceeds 81.9%; and 'if the sensitivity (or specificity) is only 70%, there will be 91% power to show that it is below 80%. That is, if the Play.Care assessment is underperforming, which is the major concern of healthcare services, this study has a high probability of detecting it.' Powering a study to detect its own instrument's failure, and stating that this is the point, is unique in this review.

answers.title: Predicting Autism Diagnosis using Image with Fixations and Synthetic Saccade Patterns
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for all three models on both the internal validation split and the organiser's blind test set. Reporting the full metric set twice, on two evaluation regimes, is what makes this paper informative: the sensitivity-specificity asymmetry on the blind test (0.807 sensitivity against 0.282 specificity for the full synthetic saccade model) shows the models are largely defaulting to the ASD label, which a single accuracy figure would conceal.

answers.title: Recognition Of Atypical Behavior In Autism Diagnosis From Video Using Pose Estimation Over Time
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall and AUC, reported consistently across three imputation conditions and against the RGB baseline, plus frame-annotation rates before and after pose-estimator retraining. Reporting AUC alongside accuracy is what makes the result interpretable: 0.72 accuracy with 0.92 recall but only 0.66 AUC indicates a classifier operating close to the majority class rather than discriminating well, which the accuracy figure alone would conceal.

answers.title: Robot-Assisted Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Based on Artificial Reasoning
answers.answer: No diagnostic metric of any kind, and none claimed. What is reported is vision-pipeline performance for the case study, presented in a figure and accompanied by an account of the occlusion problems encountered, plus qualitative descriptions of joint-attention events by group and mediator. The absence of any statistical test on the behavioural comparison is the study's main analytic gap, though with three children per group no test would carry weight; the more consequential omission is the lack of any reliability check of the automated attention estimates against human coding, which is the validation the measurement infrastructure needs and which the study's own tagged behaviour categories would have supported.

answers.title: SP-ASDNet: CNN-LSTM Based ASD Classification Model using Observer ScanPaths
answers.answer: Validation accuracy across six model configurations; accuracy, recall, precision and F1 on the organiser's blind test set for three submitted models; and a frequency distribution of per-image accuracy across the validation set. Reporting precision and recall separately on the blind test is what makes the error profile visible - model A achieves 0.8771 recall against 0.5319 precision, revealing it is largely defaulting to the ASD label. No AUC, specificity or confidence intervals.

answers.title: Social robot in diagnosis of autism among preschool children
answers.answer: One inferential statistic - Wilcoxon signed-rank W = 21, p = 0.028 - and no diagnostic accuracy metric of any kind, which is appropriate given that no classification is attempted. What is missing is an effect size and a confidence interval, which on a small paired sample would have conveyed the magnitude of the dissociation rather than only its statistical detectability, and inter-rater reliability for the coding on which the statistic rests.

answers.title: Application of the Still-Face Paradigm in Early Screening for High-Risk Autism Spectrum Disorder in Infants and Toddlers
answers.answer: Overall accuracy per algorithm per episode, plus an SVM confusion matrix. Deriving from the matrix: SF episode sensitivity 85.0% and specificity 83.7%; FF episode sensitivity 87.5% and specificity 76.7%, so the still-face episode's advantage lies in specificity. No AUC, precision, recall or F1 is reported directly, although the paper does discuss 'low recall rate of N-ASD samples'. Accuracy is additionally stratified across four age bands to test whether misclassification clusters by age; no regularity was found.

answers.title: Applying Machine Learning to Kinematic and Eye Movement Features of a Movement Imitation Task to Predict Autism Diagnosis
answers.answer: Classification accuracy at both development and independent-testing stages, reported side by side per algorithm and per instruction block - the side-by-side presentation is what makes the generalisation claim checkable. Kuncheva's index quantifies feature selection stability as a second reported outcome, treated as co-equal with accuracy. Statistical significance p-values accompany the accuracies, and accuracy distributions are shown as box plots. No sensitivity, specificity or AUC.

answers.title: Research and Design of Autism Smart Diagnosis Information System Based on Chinese Children's Facial Expression Data and Deep Convolution Neural Network
answers.answer: Only recognition rate: the proportion of seven prompted expressions the classifier assigned to the prompted category, reported per expression, per child and per group. No sensitivity, specificity, AUC, precision, recall, F1, confusion matrix or statistical test. Because the threshold rule reduces to a binary decision on 20 children, sensitivity of 10/10 and specificity of 8/10 could be derived, but the paper does not do so and the threshold was chosen on these same data.

answers.title: Automated identification of postural control for children with autism spectrum disorder using a machine learning approach
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision and F1, with all five formulas printed explicitly and 'positive' defined as ASD - a level of metric transparency few corpus studies match - plus confusion matrices for every classifier in an appendix. Headline: 0.900 accuracy, 1.000 specificity, 1.000 precision, 0.898 F1, 0.826 sensitivity for naive Bayes. No AUC and no confidence intervals, which matters given that specificity and precision of exactly 1.000 on 25 controls carry wide uncertainty.

answers.title: Behavior-based Risk Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision and recall for all three classifiers, plus a confusion matrix for the CNN from which the 0.1787 false negative rate is derived and discussed. Reporting the false negative rate explicitly, and using it to disclaim diagnostic readiness, is better practice than the corpus norm of quoting accuracy alone. Training accuracy and loss are also given. No AUC, F1, confidence intervals or per-class breakdown beyond the confusion matrix, and no significance testing.

answers.title: Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation as a Scalable Method for Distinguishing Children With Autism
answers.answer: Classification accuracy for the diagnostic comparison, but the evaluation is much broader than classification: Spearman correlations for construct validity against the expert standard, correlations across repeated trials for test-retest reliability, correlations with two independent symptom instruments for clinical validity, and group comparison significance testing. Reporting reliability alongside validity and accuracy is close to unique in this corpus and reflects a psychometric rather than purely machine-learning framing. No sensitivity, specificity or AUC is reported, which is the main metric gap.

answers.title: Deep-Learning-Based Detection of Infants with Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Auto-Encoder Feature Representation
answers.answer: Full confusion matrices for all four models, plus accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and unweighted average recall - UAR explicitly adopted from the INTERSPEECH 2009 Emotion Challenge because the classes are imbalanced. Reporting UAR alongside accuracy is good practice and rare in this corpus. Two caveats: precision and recall are transposed in the table (the printed 0.4526 for the AE model is autistic-class recall, as the reported UAR confirms), and all metrics are utterance-level, so no per-infant performance can be derived. Derived from the matrices, autistic-class sensitivity is 45.3% (AE), 41.3% (eGeMAPS-88), 35.8% (eGeMAPS-54) and 13.1% (SVM), against specificities of 84.9%, 84.8%, 84.2% and 97.2%.

answers.title: Effects of Intra-Subject Variation in Gait Analysis on ASD Classification Performance in Machine Learning Models
answers.answer: Accuracy, recall, precision and F1, with accuracy and F1 designated primary and the other two used for extended analysis. Reporting all four is what makes the SVM's degeneration detectable - accuracy 50% with recall 100% and precision 50% is diagnostic of a single-class predictor, and the authors correctly identify it as such. Precision was also the grid-search selection metric, chosen on the stated grounds that the application is identifying autistic from non-autistic people. Missing: AUC, confusion matrices, per-fold variance, confidence intervals, and any statistical test of the difference between Dataset A and Dataset B results - so the headline improvement from 68.75% to 76.67% on 105 data points is reported without any indication of whether it exceeds noise.

answers.title: Estimating Autism Severity in Young Children From Speech Signals Using a Deep Neural Network
answers.answer: RMSE and Pearson correlation against clinician-assigned ADOS total, reported as mean +/- standard deviation over 50 splits and shown as histograms, plus scatter plots for one representative split. Reporting the across-split standard deviation and interpreting it is the distinguishing feature: it reveals that models with respectable means (SVR at R = 0.51, FC-DNN 2 at 0.31) were also wildly unstable (SD 0.17 and 0.25), while the two matrix-input models were stable at SD 0.09. Because the task is regression, no sensitivity, specificity or AUC applies; but no calibration analysis or error-versus-severity breakdown is given, so whether error concentrates at particular ADOS ranges is unknown, and with only 6 typically developing children the low end is thinly supported.

answers.title: Detecting High-Functioning Autism in Adults Using Eye Tracking and Machine Learning
answers.answer: Mean accuracy over 100 random participant-level splits with 95% confidence intervals, reported for every one of the 12 task-by-AOI configurations and for individual pages and page combinations. Confidence intervals are used substantively - the authors read them as showing 'the models are robust in their predictions'. Confusion matrices exist but are deposited rather than printed, and no sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1 or AUC appears in the paper. For a screening application where the cost of false negatives and false positives differ, this omission matters more than for a purely comparative study.

answers.title: Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder via an Eye-Tracking Based
answers.answer: Accuracy at three aggregation levels (piece, scanpath, subject) plus sensitivity and specificity, tabulated per permutation and per ablation condition. Reporting accuracy at all three granularities is a real methodological contribution: it makes the value of hierarchical evidence integration measurable (87.16 to 88.03 to 93.15 percent) rather than assumed, and it is the kind of reporting that would expose segment-level inflation in studies that report only the finest granularity. Missing: AUC, confusion matrices, confidence intervals, and any statistical comparison between conditions - on a 35-child test set, where one subject is worth 2.86 points, the differences between permutations and between some ablation conditions amount to one or two children.

answers.title: Machine Learning and Virtual Reality on Body Movements' Behaviors to Classify Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: Accuracy, true positive rate, true negative rate, Cohen's kappa and retained feature count, tabulated for all 24 models. Reporting the full factorial rather than a selected best is good practice and is what allows an external reader to see both the multiplicity problem and the confusion-matrix imbalances - the pooled head model achieves 82.98% with 100% sensitivity but 68% specificity, while the pooled trunk model achieves identical accuracy with 63.64% sensitivity and 100% specificity, which the paper notes explicitly. Including Cohen's kappa is unusual in this corpus and appropriate given the near-balanced classes. Missing: confidence intervals, AUC, and any statistical comparison between models, which matters when adjacent accuracies differ by one or two children.

answers.title: Responsive Social Smile: A Machine-Learning Based Multimodal Behavior Assessment Framework towards Early Stage Autism Screening
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity with full confusion matrices at both stages, and - most valuably - a four-classifier comparison run twice, once on predicted stimulus scores and once on clinicians' scores. That paired table is the paper's best methodological contribution: it decomposes total error into the perception stage and the protocol stage, showing the perception stage contributes about 2.4 accuracy points. No AUC, no confidence intervals, no statistical test, and no per-stimulus analysis. The cross-study comparison table against eye-movement, hand-imitation, prosody and neuroimaging methods is drawn from different populations and age ranges and cannot support relative claims, though the paper presents it as context rather than as competition, noting its own cohort is the youngest at 1-3 years.

answers.title: Selection of Eye-Tracking Stimuli for Prediction by Sparsely Grouped Input Variables for Neural Networks: towards Biomarker Refinement for Autism
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and AUC, all plotted as functions of the number of sparsified groups rather than reported as single points - so the deliverable is a trade-off curve between battery length and discriminative power, which is exactly the quantity a biomarker designer needs. Pearson correlation for the four regression targets, likewise plotted against sparsity, with random guessing anchored at r = 0. Selection stability is quantified as discard probability per paradigm over 100 bootstrap runs. No confidence intervals on the accuracy curves and no statistical test between methods.

answers.title: The identification of children with autism spectrum disorder by SVM approach on EEG and eye-tracking data
answers.answer: Accuracy and AUC only, but reported for every modality and stimulus condition separately, which is what makes the fusion ladder legible. Missing: sensitivity, specificity, confusion matrices, confidence intervals, and any statistical test of the differences between modality conditions - so whether 85.44% is significantly better than 75.89% on 97 children is not established. The accuracy-versus-feature-count curve is plotted, which is transparent about the sweep but also makes explicit that the headline is a maximum rather than a pre-specified operating point.

answers.title: Toward Continuous Social Phenotyping: Analyzing Gaze Patterns in an Emotion Recognition Task for Children With Autism Through Wearable Smart Glasses
answers.answer: Leave-one-participant-out accuracy paired with a Monte Carlo shuffling P value for every one of 60 grid cells (15 feature combinations by four trial conditions), plus cross-validation confusion matrices for the full model. Shuffling tests ran 2,500 iterations and were checked for convergence. Bonferroni correction is applied when interpreting significance across the grid, and the authors note which results survive it and which do not. Reporting a permutation-based significance test for every reported accuracy is unique in this corpus and is precisely what distinguishes an accuracy from a finding at this sample size. No sensitivity, specificity or AUC.

answers.title: Towards the automatic detection of social biomarkers in autism spectrum disorder: introducing the simulated interaction task (SIT)
answers.answer: AUC per modality and combined, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity at a stated threshold, McNemar tests against a majority-vote baseline and against expert raters, correlations of predicted class probability with ADOS severity and with age, per-gender classification breakdowns, and supplementary confusion matrices and ROC curves for every classifier. Two of these are almost unique in the corpus. Comparing against a majority-vote baseline establishes that the accuracy exceeds trivial prediction. Correlating predicted probability with ADOS establishes that the model's continuous output has clinical meaning beyond the binary decision - and correlating it with age reveals the confound.

answers.title: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence to Diagnose Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Tracking Saccades
answers.answer: Accuracy alone, at 88% in the text and 88-91% in the abstract, with a plotted ROC curve whose AUC is never stated. For a paper proposing to replace multidisciplinary diagnostic assessment with a single test, the absence of sensitivity and specificity is the critical omission - these are the quantities that determine whether such a test would be usable, and with 60% of the sample autistic, accuracy alone cannot distinguish a useful classifier from one biased toward the majority class. No confusion matrix, no confidence interval, no per-fold variability and no statistical comparison against any baseline.

answers.title: An Experimental Trial: Multi-Robot Therapy for Categorization of Autism Level Using Hidden Markov Model
answers.answer: Accuracy (19 of 25, 76%) and Cohen's kappa (0.52, p = 0.009) against clinician CARS categorisation. Reporting kappa rather than accuracy alone is appropriate for an agreement study and is better practice than most of the corpus. But the kappa's n = 25 counts sessions rather than children, so its significance is overstated; no confidence interval accompanies it; and no sensitivity, specificity or per-class breakdown is given, though the individually tabulated 25 test rows allow these to be derived - three false-mild and three false-minimal errors, symmetric across classes.

answers.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis Based on Trajectories of Eye Tracking Data
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity, precision, specificity and F1 for the best configuration of each ensemble strategy. Reporting all five is what makes the result honestly interpretable and exposes the sensitivity-specificity imbalance that accuracy alone would conceal - the equal-weight ensemble achieves an F1 of 0.81 while correctly classifying only 30% of typically developing participants. No AUC, no confidence intervals, no per-fold variability and no statistical comparison between strategies, so whether 0.75 differs meaningfully from 0.71 on 86 participants is not established.

answers.title: Autistic spectrum traits detection and early screening: A machine learning based eye movement study
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUC for all eight models in the preliminary experiment - a complete and transparent table - but recall alone in the test experiment, because the test sample contains no negative cases. That asymmetry matters: recall of 0.77 on an all-positive sample is uninformative about discrimination, since any model with a positive prediction bias scores well. The reported ensemble AUC of 0.90 against constituent AUCs of 0.57-0.68 is also internally implausible, since averaging or voting over models with AUC at most 0.68 cannot ordinarily yield 0.90.

answers.title: Automatic classification of children with autism spectrum disorder by using a computerized visual‐orienting task
answers.answer: Complete: overall accuracy, per-class sensitivity and specificity, full confusion matrices and per-class ROC AUC for the three-class problem, the same for the collapsed binary problem, and accuracy for both cross-group generalisation tests. The confusion matrix is interpreted substantively rather than merely reported - errors concentrate on mislabelling the other groups as high-functioning, which the authors relate to that group's intermediate behavioural position and which explains its lowest specificity. Reporting the binary result alongside the three-class result quantifies exactly what collapsing heterogeneity buys: 93.24% versus 81.08%.

answers.title: Auxiliary Diagnostic Method for Early Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Movement Data Analysis
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity with confusion matrices for all three classifiers - adequate for a diagnostic framing and better than accuracy alone. The reported figures make the asymmetry visible: the best model detects 12 of 15 autistic children while correctly classifying 25 of 25 typically developing children, so it misses one autistic child in five. No AUC, precision, F1, confidence interval, per-split variability or statistical comparison between models, and with only 40 test children a single participant is worth 2.5 accuracy points, so the 0.93 versus 0.90 difference between the top two models is one child.

answers.title: Children ASD Evaluation Through Joint Analysis of EEG and Eye-Tracking Recordings With Graph Convolution Network
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for the proposed model and all three comparators, plus t-statistics and p-values for every feature. Reporting all four metrics across a full ablation is good practice, and the single-modality baselines make the fusion gain directly readable. Missing: AUC, confusion matrices, confidence intervals and any statistical test between models - and with a test set of roughly 20 samples, the difference between 0.95 and 0.81 is about three samples. That all four metrics for the proposed method are exactly 0.9500 indicates a balanced test set of 20 with a single error.

answers.title: Classification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Using Eye Tracking Data Based on Visual Attention Model
answers.answer: Precision, sensitivity, specificity, error and accuracy plus a ROC curve with mean and maximum AUC - a full set on paper, but the values do not reconcile. Error of 25% implies accuracy of 75%; sensitivity of 87% with specificity of 60% on a 39-severe, 49-non-severe split implies roughly 72%; and the headline 88% matches the separately reported maximum AUC of 0.88 exactly. The internally consistent reading is that the classifier achieves roughly 75% accuracy with 87% sensitivity and 60% specificity, and that mean AUC is 0.85. That specificity of 60% is the more informative figure for a severity-grading tool: two in five non-severe participants would be labelled severe.

answers.title: Classification of Children With Autism and Typical Development Using Eye-Tracking Data From Face-to-Face Conversations: Machine Learning Model Development and Performance Evaluation
answers.answer: Comprehensive. Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for every classifier under every feature set; a confusion matrix for the best model; an accuracy-versus-feature-count curve for all four classifiers; a table showing the incremental contribution of each successively added feature; and full Mann-Whitney comparisons for all 16 fixation features and all session lengths. Crucially, a majority-class baseline of 51.3% is computed and explicitly compared, which is the check almost every other study in the corpus omits. The one gap is that no confidence intervals accompany any figure, and with 39 participants a single misclassification is worth 2.6 accuracy points.

answers.title: Combined Signal Processing Based Techniques and Feed Forward Neural Networks for Pathological Voice Detection and Classification
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for all seven individual and four combined feature sets across all three tasks - 33 conditions in total - plus processing time comparisons and hidden-neuron sensitivity curves. The coverage is unusually complete, and the processing time analysis is a practical dimension few studies report, showing MFCC and RASTA-PLP to be cheapest because jitter and shimmer require fundamental frequency estimation and GNE requires Hilbert envelope extraction and cross-correlation per glottal cycle. Missing: confidence intervals, confusion matrices, and any statistical test - and with perfect scores reported in six of 33 conditions, the metrics carry no information about where the model fails.

answers.title: Computer-Aided Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Eye-Tracking Study Using Data Visualization and Deep Learning
answers.answer: ROC curves with AUC and cross-fold standard deviation, plus accuracy, recall and precision, reported twice - once for each splitting regime - together with training and validation loss curves. Reporting the same metrics under both regimes is what makes the comparison legible and is the paper's key methodological contribution. Missing: confusion matrices, confidence intervals on the accuracy figures, and per-class breakdown for the participant-level condition, where only accuracy is quoted.

answers.title: Computer-aided autism diagnosis based on visual attention models using eye tracking
answers.answer: Precision, sensitivity, specificity and AUC with fold-wise standard deviation, ROC curves for all five folds, a six-row comparison of classifier and selection combinations, and a table of published AUCs from three comparable studies for external context. Reporting standard deviation across folds is what reveals the stability benefit of feature selection. The gap is that sensitivity of 69% is reported but never discussed, and no confusion matrix or confidence interval accompanies it - on a sample where 76 of 106 participants are autistic, missing 31% of them is the most consequential number in the paper.

answers.title: Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis
answers.answer: Six metrics - accuracy, kappa, AUC, F1, sensitivity and specificity - each with a standard deviation across 20 cross-validation iterations, reported for the best model on every one of ten datasets. Including kappa alongside accuracy is appropriate given the 35:20 imbalance and is done consistently. The standard deviations are used substantively: the model on the 13 significant features is noted to have 'the lowest standard deviations, showing the highest consistency', which is a real finding distinct from mean accuracy. Missing: confusion matrices, confidence intervals, and any statistical comparison between the ten datasets, so whether 0.86 differs meaningfully from 0.84 on 55 children is not established - and the standard deviation of 0.10 on the best model spans that gap.

answers.title: Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for each classifier's best model, ROC curves for all five, and an accuracy-versus-feature-count plot. Reporting all five classifiers rather than only the winner allows the reader to see that the result is robust across model families. Missing: confusion matrices, confidence intervals and any statistical comparison between classifiers - on 38 participants one case is worth 2.6 accuracy points, so the spread from 81% to 92.11% is about four cases.

answers.title: Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset
answers.answer: Eight metrics for all nine classifiers on all five datasets, which is comprehensive in coverage and is the paper's strongest feature. Reporting specificity and fall-out alongside sensitivity is what makes the degenerate cells visible: in cluster 1, naive Bayes and SVM both show 73.3% accuracy with 26.7% specificity and exactly 0.500 AUC, and the best model itself pairs 88.9% sensitivity with only 69.4% specificity. Missing: confidence intervals, confusion matrices, cluster composition, and any statistical comparison - so whether 88.89% differs meaningfully from 77.8% is not established.

answers.title: Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: Trial-level accuracy reported as a mean and in bands across participants, plus a subject-level ROC with AUC and the sensitivity and specificity at its optimal operating point. Reporting the distribution of per-child accuracy rather than only the mean is valuable - it shows five of 26 children classified below 0.6, which a summary figure would hide. The weakness is presentational: the abstract's 'classification accuracy reached up to 0.947' conflates AUC with accuracy, no subject-level accuracy is given directly, and the operating point yielding 0.846 sensitivity and 0.923 specificity is selected on the same curve. Comparison against ADOS's own published sensitivity and specificity is a useful external anchor that few studies provide.

answers.title: Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment
answers.answer: One agreement figure - 82.4%, from 6 mismatches in 34 sessions against the therapist's 0-100 attention ratings - plus session-by-session attention scores for the longitudinal arm. The metric is the right kind for the claim, since concurrent agreement with a clinician's judgement of the same construct is what a therapy-support measure needs to demonstrate, and the paper describes it correctly as matching therapist assessments rather than as diagnostic accuracy. Three gaps: no chance-corrected statistic such as Cohen's kappa, so the proportion of agreement attributable to the marginal distribution of therapist ratings is unknown; no adjustment for the clustering of 34 sessions within 6 children; and no reliability estimate for the therapist ratings themselves, so the achievable ceiling is unknown.

answers.title: Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning
answers.answer: Accuracy for all 27 combinations, confusion matrices for nine algorithms under one scheme, and ROC curves. Providing the confusion matrices is what allows sensitivity and specificity to be derived - random forest and SVM both achieve 18 of 20 autistic children detected with all 20 comparison children correctly classified - even though the paper states these were calculated but does not tabulate them. Missing: confidence intervals, any statistical comparison, and any acknowledgement that a 40-child test set makes each case worth 2.5 accuracy points.

answers.title: Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism
answers.answer: AUC with 95% confidence intervals, sensitivity, specificity and accuracy, reported for three feature configurations and seven activity configurations, every one alongside the chance baseline. Reporting confidence intervals on AUC allows the differences between conditions to be assessed - the prosody interval (81.11-83.35) does not overlap the articulation interval (66.62-69.35), so that comparison is supported, while the intervals for the four individual activities largely overlap, so the ranking among them is weaker than the point estimates suggest. Missing: confusion matrices and per-fold variability.

answers.title: Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images
answers.answer: Seven metrics - accuracy, recall, precision, F1, specificity, false positive rate and false negative rate - reported for the proposed model and all seven competing entries in a single table, which is the most complete comparative reporting in the corpus and allows failure modes to be read directly. It shows, for instance, that SP-ASDNET_1's apparently strong 0.87 recall comes with 0.25 specificity and a 0.75 false positive rate, meaning it classifies almost everything as autistic - a pathology that accuracy alone would have hidden. Applied to RM3ASD itself, the same table shows specificity of exactly 0.50 against recall of 0.68, so the model performs at chance on typically developing children and its accuracy advantage rests entirely on the autistic class. No confidence intervals, no significance testing, and no confusion matrices.

answers.title: Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for every one of roughly twenty configurations, on both validation and blind test, with standard deviations across two or three runs on validation - the most complete metric reporting in the corpus, and complete enough to read failure modes directly. Doing so is instructive: specificity is the consistent weakness, at 0.537 for the best test model and dropping as low as 0.35 for BrMLP-F and 0.44-0.48 for several others, against sensitivities of 0.71-0.78 - so most configurations lean toward calling children autistic, and accuracy alone would conceal this. The final comparison table adds F1 and flags, with an asterisk and a footnote, that two competitor AUCs were computed over binary labels as the mean of sensitivity and specificity because probability scores were unavailable - a precision about the comparability of borrowed numbers that is rare anywhere in this literature. No confidence intervals and no significance testing between methods, so the 62.13% versus 59.84% margin over the nearest competitor is a comparison of point estimates.

answers.title: Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1 on the balanced held-out set - a complete set for a binary task, and one that shows the model is not trading sensitivity for specificity (0.854 against 0.765, the most balanced profile among the higher-accuracy studies in this corpus). Two additional evaluations go beyond the standard panel and are more informative than any of them. Accuracy as a function of input video length quantifies the deployment tradeoff directly, showing ~70% at 10 minutes rising to 81% at full length - a dose-response curve for evidence, which no other study here provides. And prediction consistency within an individual, reported as the cumulative incidence of the segment length needed for 100% stable class attribution across randomly drawn windows, measures whether a single child would receive the same answer twice - a reliability question distinct from accuracy and one that matters more for a screening tool than the point estimate does. Missing: no confidence intervals on any figure, no confusion matrix, and no significance test against a trivial baseline such as age.

answers.title: Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and an ROC curve - an adequate panel, and the specificity/sensitivity asymmetry (0.98 versus 0.87) is reported rather than collapsed into accuracy. Two supplementary reporting choices are better than the corpus norm. Training-accuracy curves are shown with mean and 90% bootstrapped confidence intervals across all replications, so training stability is visible rather than asserted, and the authors state they 'checked that no overfitting is present in every fold'. And the feature-ablation curve reports accuracy, sensitivity and specificity jointly as a function of how many features are retained, which shows the graceful-then-sharp degradation pattern (78% at five features, 52% at one) and demonstrates that the result does not hinge on a single variable. What is missing bears directly on the headline: no confidence interval on the reported 93%, no confusion matrix, no per-fold table that would let a reader see the spread from which the best fold was drawn, and no comparison against a trivial baseline such as age or IQ - the latter especially relevant given that the authors concede IQ is an uncontrolled confound.

answers.title: A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity with fold-wise standard deviations, ROC curves with AUC for all four models, and complete confusion matrices for all four - a full panel, and reported comparatively rather than only for the winning model. Reporting standard deviations across folds supports one of the paper's substantive claims, that MMSDAE 'presents the best stability and robustness with the smallest standard deviation among all compared methods', which is a claim about variance that accuracy alone cannot carry. The confusion matrices are the most useful element, since they convert an accuracy comparison into a diagnosis of where each model fails and thereby ground the complementarity argument. Missing: no confidence intervals on the reported means, no statistical test of the difference between models despite the word 'significantly' being used repeatedly of differences that are never tested, no per-fold table, and no comparison against a trivial baseline such as age - which for 3-to-6-year-olds is a real omission given that both resting EEG spectra and gaze behaviour change rapidly across that band.

answers.title: AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and full confusion matrices for both testing sets, plus training and validation accuracy - a complete panel for a conference paper, and reported for both test sets rather than only the better one. The confusion matrices make the error structure legible: on test set #1, 23 of 198 typically developing clips were called autistic against 12 of 218 autistic clips called typical, so the model errs toward false positives, and precision (0.900) sits below recall (0.945) accordingly. Two things are missing and one is consequential. There are no confidence intervals and no per-child accuracy, and since the metrics are computed over 416 and 184 clips originating from only 36 and 18 children, clips from the same child are not independent and the apparent precision of the estimates is overstated - the paper itself describes averaging probabilities per subject for training and validation but does not do so for testing. And there is no comparison against a trivial baseline; given a 45-point IQ gap, a baseline using developmental level alone would be the informative comparator.

answers.title: Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: Accuracy only, plus confusion matrices - no sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, ROC or AUC is reported by name, though the confusion matrices supply per-class rates from which sensitivity and specificity can be read (85.0% and 90.0% for the fused model). No confidence intervals, no variance across leave-one-out iterations, and no statistical test of any comparison, despite the text repeatedly describing differences as significant ('significantly greater than that obtained using a single modality', 'can significantly improve the classification accuracy') where no test was performed. The reporting of both best and average accuracy per modality is a genuine strength that partly offsets this, since it makes classifier-dependence visible. The absence of any trivial baseline is a real gap given that the two groups differ in educational placement and no developmental measure was taken.

answers.title: An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images
answers.answer: The most complete metric panel in the corpus in form - accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, Matthews correlation coefficient and F1, each with average, median and standard deviation over 30 runs, plus a confusion matrix, ROC curves with AUC for four classifiers, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for every optimiser comparison. Including MCC is good practice for imbalanced classes and is rare here. The apparatus is nonetheless measuring the wrong thing. The 30 runs vary only the metaheuristic's random seed, not the data partition, so the sub-0.0015 standard deviations quantify optimiser stability rather than generalisation variance, and they should not be read as precision of the accuracy estimate. The Wilcoxon p-values of 5e-12 test whether one optimiser reliably beats another across seeds - a valid question about algorithms and an irrelevant one about autism. And the confusion matrix's 1,423 instances cannot be located in any described partition, since no split is specified; it corresponds to about 20% of the 7,111 augmented images, which is the only reading consistent with the paper's own statement that augmentation enlarged the testing data.

answers.title: Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals
answers.answer: The most statistically careful reporting in the corpus, and the one that determines the paper's central conclusion. Group differences are reported as Cohen's d with bootstrap confidence intervals from 10,000 resamples rather than as p values alone, with the authors stating they 'preferred Cohen's d to provide a practical estimate for the magnitude of an effect of interest... rather than just reporting the results of statistical tests'. Reliability is reported as Spearman's rho with a bootstrap test of the between-group difference in reliability - testing not whether each group is reliable but whether they differ in reliability, which is the actual hypothesis. Fingerprinting accuracy is tested against a permutation null with 10,000 label shuffles. Most importantly, classification accuracy is compared to an empirically derived chance level of 0.607 rather than to an assumed 0.500 - a distinction that entirely changes the reading of the 0.618 result, since against a nominal 50% baseline it would have appeared as a modest success. FDR correction is applied throughout. And per-participant classification frequencies across 10,000 iterations are reported, revealing that the aggregate accuracy conceals a bimodal structure: 95 participants classified correctly more than 75% of the time and 32 misclassified more than 75% of the time, 22 of those autistic. Reporting who is misclassified, rather than only how often, is what converts a null accuracy into a substantive finding about heterogeneity.

answers.title: Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech
answers.answer: Five metrics per model, each as mean and standard deviation across five folds, plus per-fold and mean ROC curves and confusion matrices for all three - complete and comparative reporting. The standard deviations do real work here and are worth reading closely: the random forest's recall SD is 0.247, larger than the entire performance gap between models, indicating that its per-fold recall swings wildly, while its accuracy SD is only 0.013 - a pattern signalling that it trades sensitivity against specificity differently in each fold. Wav2vec's AUROC SD of 0.077 against the CNN's 0.010 similarly shows the CNN is the more stable model despite the authors' expectation that the 95-million-parameter transformer would be 'more robust'. The confusion matrices add a real finding: both deep models produce few false positives while the random forest produces many, with all three having similar false negative rates. What is missing is any comparison against a trivial baseline - given a 4.5-year median age difference between groups, an age-only classifier is the obvious comparator and would establish how much of the 79.3% is diagnostic at all.

answers.title: Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC with 95% confidence intervals for all three models, with DeLong tests for every pairwise AUC comparison - the appropriate test for correlated ROC curves derived from the same participants, and one that almost no other study in this corpus uses. The confidence intervals do real work: the voice model's interval (0.7076-0.8525) and the combined model's (0.8768-0.9641) do not overlap, so that comparison is visibly supported, whereas the language and combined intervals do overlap and the DeLong test is correspondingly marginal at p = 0.033. Reporting sensitivity and specificity separately is what makes the complementarity finding legible - the voice model's specificity of 0.6857 is the weakness that the language model repairs, and the combined model's unchanged specificity alongside raised sensitivity is the signature of the two modalities catching different people. The misclassification analysis adds a class of evidence absent elsewhere: Mann-Whitney comparisons of age, IQ, two CCC-2 scales, two ADOS domains and three task indices between detected and missed participants, for each of the three models separately, with the counterpart analysis for non-autistic participants in supplementary material. No chance or trivial baseline is reported, which is the one gap.

answers.title: Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers
answers.answer: The most complete statistical reporting in the corpus for a study of this kind. Every group comparison carries an effect size r alongside its p value; the mixed ANOVAs report F with degrees of freedom for group, movie type and their interaction; entropy comparisons are reported per scale across all 30 multiscale resolutions rather than only for the integrated summary; every AUC carries a Hanley-McNeil 95% confidence interval; and classifier configurations are compared by a stated variance-based criterion with the explicit rule that models are 'considered not significantly different' if the interval spans zero. The confidence intervals are essential to reading the result honestly and the paper does not hide what they show: for Blowing-Bubbles the entropy AUC interval runs 0.53 to 0.75, so that single-movie result barely excludes chance, and the intervals on the individual-movie AUCs are uniformly wide because only about 30 autistic children contribute to each. The headline 0.85 is correspondingly better supported than the per-movie figures. Also reported are the attention rates for both groups and the per-movie participant counts after the data-quality gate, both of which bear on whether the measurement was equally successful in the two groups.

answers.title: Cross-linguistic patterns of speech prosodic differences in autism: A machine learning study
answers.answer: Median AUC across 5,001 iterations with permutation-derived p values, reported alongside accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for every one of the six configurations, with the full AUC distributions displayed as boxplots and aggregated confusion matrices provided. Reporting the median across iterations with its distribution rather than a single point estimate is the correct summary for a repeated cross-validation, and it makes the stability of each result visible. The permutation testing is what carries the paper's central negative claims - without it, a Cantonese intonation AUC of 0.620 and a combined intonation AUC of 0.559 might have been reported as weak but positive results, whereas the permutation p values of 0.507 and 0.509 establish them as indistinguishable from chance. The sensitivity and specificity breakdown adds a further observation the authors draw out: the significant English intonation model has good sensitivity (0.758) but poor specificity (0.606), so it tends to call typically developing participants autistic, while the rhythm models are balanced across classes. No confidence intervals accompany the AUCs, and no formal test compares one model against another - the rhythm-versus-intonation contrast rests on one being significant and the other not, rather than on a test of their difference.

answers.title: Detecting autism from picture book narratives using deep neural utterance embeddings
answers.answer: Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value - clinically appropriate metrics reported identically for all ten rows of the comparison table. Reporting PPV and NPV alongside sensitivity and specificity is uncommon here and is meaningful in this design because the class balance is 25:25, so the predictive values are directly interpretable as performance at 50% prevalence. The table's real contribution is its scope: six model configurations, two human raters and two standardised instruments, all evaluated on the same 50 participants with the same four metrics, which allows the reader to locate the models between a human floor and an instrument ceiling rather than against an absent baseline. What is missing matters at this sample size. There is no AUC, no confidence interval and no significance test anywhere, so a sensitivity of 0.72 represents 18 of 25 correct and carries a binomial confidence interval running from roughly 0.51 to 0.88 - wide enough that the differences among the six configurations, and between the models and the raters, are not established. Nor is any chance or trivial baseline reported, though the balanced design makes 0.50 the natural reference and the human raters serve a similar function empirically.

answers.title: Development of a visual attention based decision support system for autism spectrum disorder screening
answers.answer: Seven metrics per class per configuration - true positive rate, false positive rate, precision, recall, F-measure, ROC area and accuracy - across six full tables, plus two summary tables and two figures. This is among the most complete metric reporting in the corpus, and reporting per class rather than only overall is what makes the study's central asymmetry visible: across every configuration the true positive rate for the autistic class is lower than for comparisons, and in the best model it is 0.800 against 0.950, so the system misses one autistic toddler in five while correctly clearing nineteen comparisons in twenty. For a screening instrument that asymmetry is the wrong way round, and the authors flag the 12.5% false-negative rate explicitly. What is missing: no confidence intervals on any of the 24 accuracy figures, no significance test between configurations, and no chance or demographic baseline - the last being consequential given the 34-point language gap, since a classifier using Bayley language score alone would likely perform comparably and would establish how much of the 87.5% is attributable to gaze rather than to development.

answers.title: Different Eye Tracking Patterns in Autism Spectrum Disorder in Toddler and Preschool Children
answers.answer: Comprehensive and appropriately chosen. Means and standard deviations for all ten areas across all four groups; F statistics with degrees of freedom and p values for diagnosis, age group and interaction effects on every area; Cohen's d for every group contrast within each cohort; accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for the full model in each cohort; and per-area classification performance plotted against permutation-derived 95% confidence intervals so that non-significant areas are visually identifiable. Reporting effect sizes alongside p values is what makes the developmental comparison legible - the mouth separates toddlers at d = 0.81 and preschoolers at d = 0.44, the eyes separate preschoolers at d = 0.74 and toddlers at d = 0.12 - and these are more informative than the significance pattern alone. Reporting sensitivity and specificity separately exposes the preschool model's weakness, where 81% sensitivity comes with 61% specificity, meaning nearly two in five typically developing preschoolers would be flagged. The deliberate omission of predictive values, with the reasoning and the calculated 4.2% PPV given in the limitations, is a more useful treatment than reporting them uncritically would have been.

answers.title: Evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based medical device for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: Predictive values were the pre-specified primary endpoints, and the reason given is exactly right for a diagnostic aid: 'the selection of predictive values as primary endpoints reflects the utility of the Device in a broad spectrum of subjects, as these values measure how often in the study population the Device correctly identifies a patient with ASD and how frequently it correctly determines that a patient does not have ASD'.
