Because the cohort's 28.7% prevalence is that of the referral population the tool would actually serve, these predictive values are directly interpretable in deployment - which is precisely what the accuracy figures reported throughout the rest of this corpus are not. Clopper-Pearson exact intervals accompany every estimate. The confusion matrix is three-by-three against a three-level reference standard rather than two-by-two, so the composition of the errors is visible: all 15 false positives came from the other-condition column and none from the neurotypical column. Performance is stratified across five demographic dimensions with intervals throughout, severity and comorbidity are cross-tabulated against output, and reference-standard reliability and specialist certainty are reported alongside. The one substantive gap is the absence of per-input performance, which would show how much each channel contributes.

answers.title: Extraction and Classification of Acoustic Features from Italian Speaking Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.
answers.answer: Accuracy, recall, precision, F1 and AUC, reported on both training and test sets for the best model of each method, plus means and standard deviations across ten runs. Reporting training alongside test performance is what allows overfitting to be diagnosed and the authors use it that way. Reporting the ten-run distribution rather than only the maximum is better practice still, and it substantially deflates the headline: SVM's mean accuracy is 79.8% against a best of 83%, the decision tree's mean is 68.2% against a best of 83%, and KNN's mean is 58.5%. What no metric can repair is the denominator. The test set contains six children, so 83% accuracy is five of six and 100% recall is three of three; a single reclassified child moves accuracy by 17 percentage points, and no confidence interval accompanies any figure. With 22 training and 6 test samples, and a further split into three cross-validation folds within the training set, the effective sample at every stage is too small for the metrics to discriminate between methods.

answers.title: Eye Tracking-Based Diagnosis and Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for all six configurations, with confusion matrices and, for the neural network pipeline, separate training, validation and test figures. Reporting the three phases separately is genuinely useful and is what allows the headline to be diagnosed: the ANN achieved 100% on training and validation and 98.7% at test, and the abstract's 99.8% is described as 'the overall accuracy' - so it pools performance on data the model was fitted to with performance on held-out data. The correct held-out figure is 98.7%, on 109 images. Two internal inconsistencies also appear: GoogleNet is reported with 93.6% accuracy but 99.48% AUC while ResNet-18 has higher accuracy (97.6%) and lower AUC (97.56%), a pattern that would require explanation and receives none; and GoogleNet's per-class accuracies of 97.7% and 90.9% are difficult to reconcile with its stated 94.5% sensitivity and 94.5% specificity. No confidence intervals, no repeated splits, no significance tests and no baseline of any kind accompany any figure.

answers.title: Identification of Social Engagement Indicators Associated With
answers.answer: Two very different standards are applied to the two halves of the paper, and the contrast is instructive. The group comparisons are analysed with exemplary conservatism: two-sided permutation tests with 100,000 rearrangements at every location, Bonferroni correction applied to both families, and the correction's stringency explicitly noted as reducing Type 1 error at the cost of power. Reporting one significant region from 16 and one transition from 61 under that regime is a credible finding precisely because 15 and 60 negatives are reported alongside. The classification results receive no equivalent treatment - four metrics for three configurations with no confidence intervals, no permutation null and no baseline. The metric choice is nonetheless well reasoned, with macro- and weighted-average precision and recall selected over accuracy because of the imbalance and the divergence between them correctly interpreted as class-dependent performance. What is missing is the comparison that would locate the result: with 43 autistic and 11 comparison videos in the test set, always predicting autism yields weighted-average recall around 0.80, above the reported 0.656.

answers.title: Investigation of Eye-Tracking Scan Path as a Biomarker for Autism Screening Using Machine Learning Algorithms
answers.answer: The metric panel is a deliberate improvement on the field's convention and is argued as such: 'In contrast to the previously reported studies, we evaluate the model performance using the area under the ROC curve (AUC), specificity, sensitivity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative prediction value (NPV).' Reporting PPV and NPV alongside sensitivity and specificity is uncommon here and is what makes the participant-level result legible - sensitivity 58.62% against specificity 86.67% shows immediately that the model detects comparison children far better than autistic ones, which a single accuracy figure would conceal. All four models are reported in every data condition with all five metrics, so the deterioration of the conventional models and the improvement of the network under augmentation are both fully visible. Two gaps: no confidence intervals accompany any figure, which matters most for the 59-sample participant-level result; and Table 6 labels 72.88 as AUC while the discussion describes it as 'an overall accuracy of 72.88%', with the arithmetic (17 + 26 correct of 59) confirming it is accuracy, so the participant-level table header is mislabelled.

answers.title: Machine learning models using mobile game play accurately classify children with autism
answers.answer: Mean AU-ROC, recall, accuracy and precision reported for all four classifiers under both feature conditions - sixteen complete result rows - with the values being means across 28 nested cross-validation iterations rather than single-split point estimates, and with distributions bootstrapped from those 28 sets. Reporting the full grid rather than only the winner exposes the tradeoff structure: linear SVM has the best precision on the full feature set while tree methods have the best recall, and XGBoost is the only model that degrades on the reduced set. The metric-selection reasoning is also made explicit, with the authors arguing for choosing 'the model that results in the highest average of AU-ROC and Recall' and undertaking to discuss the practical considerations of each metric. What is missing: no confidence intervals are printed despite distributions having been bootstrapped, and no chance or trivial baseline is reported - which matters at n = 49, where an AU-ROC of 0.745 estimated over 28 folds of roughly 12 held-out children each carries substantial uncertainty.

answers.title: Speech Signal Analysis of Autistic Children Based on Time-Frequency Domain Distinguishing Feature Extraction
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 reported for both classifiers under all six feature conditions - a complete and consistently applied panel, and the metric definitions are given. Reporting all three methods including the near-chance one is to the paper's credit, since Method 2's 59.71% could easily have been omitted. What is missing bears directly on how the numbers should be read. There is no confidence interval anywhere, on a test set of 181 recordings where a single reclassification moves accuracy by half a percentage point. There is no chance or trivial baseline, so Method 2's result is uninterpretable as stated - especially given that it is the maximum over 256 candidate frequency sequences, a selection that would elevate the apparent performance of pure noise. And there is no per-child aggregation, so the reported figures describe how well one-second recordings are classified rather than how well children are.

answers.title: The Impact of Speaker Diarization on DNN-based Autism Severity Estimation
answers.answer: Appropriate to a regression problem and reported with variability. Severity estimation uses Pearson correlation and normalised RMSE, each as a mean and standard deviation across 50 repeated splits - so the reader sees not only that R is 0.606 but that its standard deviation is 0.099, which places the manual baseline of 0.567 +/- 0.120 well within the automatic method's variation and correctly supports the paper's cautious claim of 'equivalent or slightly better' rather than a claim of superiority. Diarization is evaluated with the standard diarization error rate, decomposed into substitution, false-accept and missed-detection components with the collar specified, plus recall, precision and accuracy on child segments, and with a stated and reasonable justification for excluding silence errors. The most useful supplementary figure is the total detected vocalisation duration under each condition - 10.85, 11.11 and 10.72 hours - which demonstrates that the three segmentation methods recovered comparable amounts of speech and so that the downstream differences are not simply a matter of one method finding more data. No confidence intervals on the correlations beyond the across-split standard deviations, and no significance test between conditions.

answers.title: The Use of Social Robots in the Diagnosis of Autism in Preschool Children
answers.answer: None of the diagnostic kind, and none claimed. The metrics reported are measurement-quality and inferential statistics: Kendall's W = 0.65 (p < 0.001) for inter-rater reliability across the whole scale, Cronbach's alpha = 0.77 for the Additional movements subscale, and Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis and chi-squared statistics with p-values for the group comparisons. Reporting inter-rater reliability at all is something most observational work in this corpus omits, and it is the appropriate primary metric for a study whose measurements are human judgements. What is absent is any confidence interval or effect size on the group comparisons, which on five per group would have been informative about how large the difference actually is rather than only whether it reached significance.

answers.title: Use of Oculomotor Behavior to Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development: A Novel Implementation of the Machine Learning Approach
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity at both the segment and participant level, plus an ROC curve for the participant-level threshold sweep (the AUC is not stated numerically). Sensitivity and specificity are defined explicitly and correctly at the segment level. Missing: AUC value, PPV/NPV, F1, confidence intervals of any kind, calibration, and any significance test on the classification results (the t-tests reported are on the features, not the models). The absence of confidence intervals matters at this sample size: with 39 children, the difference between 87.18% (34/39 correct) and the 77% seen at four of the ten window lengths is four children.

answers.title: A Sensorized Toy Car for Autism Screening Using Multi-Modal Features
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and precision, reported for all six classifier/feature configurations in a single table, plus a confusion matrix for the best model. Reporting four metrics across a full ablation grid rather than one number for one model is better practice than much of this corpus. What is missing: AUC or ROC, F1, any confidence interval or standard deviation across the five folds, calibration, and any translation of the operating point to a screening context - no PPV or NPV at a plausible population prevalence, despite the paper's entire argument being about population-level screening access. At the study's own 60.9% prevalence a precision of 87.67% is unremarkable; at a 1-2% community prevalence, sensitivity 81.7% with specificity 81.0% would give a positive predictive value in the low single digits, which is the number that matters for a device proposed for home and daycare use. There is also an internal consistency problem: for several rows the reported accuracy cannot be recovered from the reported sensitivity and specificity given the 28:18 class ratio - row 6 implies about 81.4% rather than 85.56%, row 4 about 72.3% rather than 78.61%, and row 1 about 77.3% rather than 71.11% - so the columns appear not to be computed on a common basis.

answers.title: A deep learning latent variable model to identify children with autism through motor abnormalities
answers.answer: Accuracy alone: 91.2% +/- 5.6% across 10 folds. This is the thinnest metric reporting of any study charted in this review that reports a headline number at all. There is no sensitivity, no specificity, no precision or recall, no F1, no AUC or ROC curve, no confusion matrix, and no per-class breakdown, so it is impossible to tell whether errors fall preferentially on autistic or typically developing observations - which is precisely the information a clinician evaluating a screening aid needs. The +/- 5.6% is a fold standard deviation, not a confidence interval, and with observation-level folds it does not carry the meaning it would under participant-level splitting. There is also no participant-level accuracy at all, despite Figure 3 plotting exactly the per-participant aggregation that would yield one, and despite the paper's own observation that the separation is clearer at that level. The balanced design (750 versus 750) at least makes 50% the unambiguous chance floor, so no prevalence adjustment is needed to read the number - but nor is any positive or negative predictive value offered for the screening use the discussion proposes.

answers.title: A multimodal discrimination method for the response to name behavior of autistic children based on human pose tracking and head pose estimation
answers.answer: Accuracy at two aggregation levels (30 participants and 109 test events), sensitivity, specificity, and a 6 x 6 confusion matrix of clinician against predicted 0-5 scores. The positive/negative convention is inverted from ordinary usage and stated explicitly - a true positive is a non-response correctly judged as a non-response - so sensitivity 84.6% refers to detecting failures to respond and specificity 100% to correctly recognising genuine responses. Reporting both aggregation levels and publishing the full score-level confusion matrix is better practice than most of this corpus. But the metric set is wrong for the problem in two ways. First, this is an ordinal agreement task between an automated scorer and a human scorer, for which the appropriate statistic is a weighted kappa or an intraclass correlation, and none is reported - so nothing corrects for the very high chance agreement created by 17 of 30 children scoring 5 and by every one of a non-responding child's five calls being a non-response event. The 98.2% event-level figure in particular is close to uninterpretable without that correction. Second, no confidence intervals are given, and with 30 children a single misclassification moves the participant-level accuracy by 3.3 points, so the reported improvement from 83.3% to 93.3% rests on three children. There is also no AUC, which is defensible since the system emits no score, and no evaluation of the perception components in isolation, so detection, tracking and landmark failures are folded silently into the end-to-end number.

answers.title: Classification of autistic and normal children using analysis of eye-tracking data from computer games
answers.answer: Precision, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, each reported separately for the training, validation and test partitions and for the pooled total, across all four feature subsets - sixty-four numbers in total. The disaggregation is a real reporting virtue and is what makes it possible to see what the study actually achieved: it is only because the tables separate the columns that a reader can recover the held-out test accuracy of 58.3% behind the abstract's 73.8%. Two summary tables then compare precision and accuracy across subsets, again by partition. ROC curves are plotted for all four configurations, but no AUC is reported for any, so the single number that would summarise discriminability independent of threshold is presented only as a picture. Also missing: confidence intervals of any kind, F1, calibration, and any participant-level metric. Given that the test partition contains 36 observations, a confidence interval would have been the most informative addition - at 58.3% on 36 observations the interval comfortably includes chance.

answers.title: Comparison of Human Experts and AI in Predicting Autism from Facial Behavior
answers.answer: The most complete metric set in this corpus for a study of this type. The AI model is characterised by accuracy (80.5%), sensitivity (0.55), specificity (0.95), positive predictive value (0.86) and negative predictive value (0.79) - reporting PPV and NPV alongside sensitivity and specificity is rare here and is the reporting that lets a reader see the model's actual clinical shape, namely a conservative rule whose positive calls are trustworthy and whose negative calls are not. Human performance is reported at three levels of aggregation: all raters (80.3%), experts (83.1%) and non-experts (78.3%). Beyond summary metrics, the study reports two per-participant analyses that carry more information than any accuracy figure: a table listing the five participants misclassified by a majority of human raters together with the AI's prediction for each, and a scatter plot of per-participant human accuracy against per-participant AI accuracy with the correlation quantified (rho = 0.35, and rho = 0.19 after excluding participants that 95%+ of raters classified correctly). Missing: AUC, confidence intervals, and any statistical test of the human-versus-AI difference or of the error-overlap claim - the rho values and the empty lower-left quadrant are reported descriptively, with no significance test or bootstrap, and with 42 participants and five hard cases the error-overlap finding rests on a small number of observations.

answers.title: Dynamic Viewing Pattern Analysis: Towards Large-Scale Screening of Children With ASD in Remote Areas
answers.answer: Accuracy at two levels of aggregation (A1 for stimulus-based patterns, A2 for subjects), sensitivity, specificity, ROC analysis and AUC, with results additionally broken down by sex and by age band and by ablation condition. Reporting sensitivity and specificity alongside accuracy is the minimum this literature should meet and is met here; adding subgroup breakdowns, and reporting them honestly when they are unflattering, goes beyond it. Robustness is addressed by repeating the subject-level split five times and reporting the minimum (95.76%) rather than only the mean. What is missing: confidence intervals; a majority-class baseline, which at 42.4% autism in the test set would be 57.6%; and any prevalence-adjusted metric such as positive predictive value, which is the number that matters for the community-screening application the paper proposes. At a population prevalence near 1-2%, sensitivity 96.85% with specificity 96.63% would yield a positive predictive value in the range of roughly 22-37% - far better than most operating points in this corpus, and a calculation the paper would have benefited from making explicit given how strongly it frames itself as a universal screening tool. The 82 stimulus-level scores are also not independent within a child, which affects the interpretation of A1 though not of A2.

answers.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder through AI-Powered Analysis of Social Media Texts
answers.answer: Accuracy and F1 for each model, together with full confusion matrices giving true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives - and the confusion matrices are the most valuable thing in the results, because they expose behaviour the summary metrics hide. The decision tree's counts (tp 11,229, fn 41, tn 2,540, fp 8,690) show a model that assigned almost every tweet to the autistic class: 99.6% sensitivity against 22.6% specificity, reported as 61.2% accuracy and F1 0.72, both of which make it look like a mediocre classifier rather than a near-degenerate one. BERT's counts give sensitivity 82.1% and specificity 86.5%, reasonably balanced. Publishing the raw counts for all four models is good practice and lets a reader recover what the headline numbers conceal. What is missing: sensitivity, specificity, precision and recall are never named or computed even though the counts are present; there is no AUC; there are no confidence intervals; there is no majority-class baseline, though the balanced tweet-level design makes it 50%; and there is no user-level metric, which is the only level at which the proposed application would operate. F1 is also computed with the autistic class as positive, which given the balanced tweet-level design is defensible but is never stated.

answers.title: Exploring Complexity of Facial Dynamics in Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: Two metric sets for two purposes, both appropriate. For the primary group comparisons: exact p-values with effect size r reported for every test at every scale and every movie, ANCOVA-adjusted significance after controlling for missing-data percentage and landmark variation individually and jointly, Spearman correlations for the redundancy analysis, and within-group Wilcoxon tests for the eyebrow-versus-mouth comparison. Reporting effect sizes systematically alongside p-values, and interpreting them (medium for non-social, large to very large for social), is better statistical practice than anything else in this corpus and is what allows the social/non-social gradient to be read as a graded finding rather than a binary significant/not-significant one. For the secondary classification: accuracy, precision and recall for three feature sets across four movies under leave-one-out cross-validation, ROC curves with AUCs compared by DeLong's method, and logistic-regression odds ratios. Gaps: no confidence intervals on any classification metric; AUC values are shown graphically but not quoted numerically in the retrieved text; no majority-class baseline, which at 9.2% prevalence would be about 91% and therefore above the reported accuracies; and no positive or negative predictive value at the study's own prevalence, which for a primary-care screening tool is the number that would matter most. The precision-recall combination reported (about 70% and about 89%) is also arithmetically incompatible with a 40:396 class ratio, implying an undisclosed balancing step.

answers.title: Eye-movement analysis on facial expression for identifying children and adults with neurodevelopmental disorders
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for four model variants across three classification problems - twelve complete metric triples, reported in a single table with the best in bold. Reporting all three metrics for every ablation condition rather than accuracy alone lets a reader see what the weighting actually does: for children it raises the baseline's sensitivity from 0.333 to 0.667 and the CNN's from 0.286 to 0.600, which is where the accuracy gain comes from, and the paper says so explicitly. The chance-level handling is the most straightforward in the corpus: group sizes were equalised so chance is approximately 50%, and each headline accuracy is tested against it with a binomial test, with all three p-values reported including the one that fails - schizophrenia at p = 0.052, described as marginally significant rather than rounded into significance. Feature importances from the random forest are averaged across cross-validation folds rather than fitted once. Missing: AUC or ROC, confidence intervals, and any precision or predictive-value figure. Given accuracies of 0.645 to 0.710 on samples of 30-31 participants, confidence intervals would be wide and their absence is the main reporting gap - a single participant moves accuracy by about 3 percentage points.

answers.title: Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders
answers.answer: Average classification accuracy, and nothing else. No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC, ROC curve, confusion matrix or confidence interval appears anywhere for any model - the thinnest metric reporting of any study charted in this review that reports quantitative results. Two consequences follow directly. Because the labelled set is 81 autistic against 99 non-autistic and bootstrapping was used for training-sample balancing, chance is approximately 50%, so the prior analysis's 47-61% range is at or barely above chance while the present 82% is a large gain - but the paper never computes or states the baseline, so a reader must infer it. And because no class-conditional metric is given, it is impossible to tell whether errors fall on autistic or non-autistic users, which matters especially here given that the comparison group is a heterogeneous aggregate of eight categories that the model may separate very unevenly. The one statistical analysis that is reported properly is the negative one: three simple usage measures compared with t-tests under Holm-Bonferroni correction, all non-significant, presented honestly as motivation for the modelling work rather than buried.

answers.title: Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: AUROC, accuracy, precision and recall, each with 95% confidence intervals estimated by the Hanley and McNeil method, reported for all three tasks in both the detection and severity problems - twenty-four interval-bounded estimates, and the most complete uncertainty reporting in this review. That completeness is a direct consequence of adopting the STARD reporting guideline and publishing in a journal that enforces it, and it makes the results checkable in a way that most of this corpus is not. The gaps are nonetheless significant for a diagnostic study. Specificity is never reported, which is an odd omission under STARD and matters because precision and recall alone do not characterise false-positive behaviour at a given prevalence; for the detection models precision is 95.5-98.9% at roughly balanced prevalence, so specificity is evidently high, but it should have been stated. No negative predictive value, no calibration, and no prevalence-adjusted predictive value are given, although the proposed use is referral support in a population where autism prevalence is a few per cent rather than 47%. For the three-class severity problem the class distribution is not reported, so the reader cannot compute a chance baseline, and no baseline is offered. And no permutation test or majority-class comparison accompanies the near-ceiling detection figures.

answers.title: Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking
answers.answer: Better than the corpus norm for a paper of this scale. Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 are reported per class rather than only in aggregate, confusion matrices are given for the CNN, and ROC curves are plotted for both transfer-learning classifiers. The per-class reporting is what makes the study useful, because it reveals that the custom CNN's 71.9% accuracy conceals autism-class recall of 0.48 - fewer than half the autism images detected, which is below the 59.6% majority-class baseline implied by the confusion matrix. The authors explicitly justify reporting beyond accuracy on the grounds that it 'does not give much importance to the class imbalance in a dataset if at all it exists', which is the right reasoning. Gaps: AUC values are plotted but never quoted numerically; no confidence intervals accompany any figure, although a 57-image test set makes one image worth 1.8 percentage points and therefore makes the 81.0% versus 78.9% comparison uninterpretable; no majority-class baseline is stated; and no participant-level metric is possible given the splitting scheme.

answers.title: SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism
answers.answer: Accuracy, macro precision, macro recall and macro F1, reported for every one of six classifiers and every one of seven feature-set configurations, with a majority classifier as the first row of both tables. Macro averaging suits the near-balanced 35:41 split, and including the majority baseline as a named comparator - with improvements quantified against it - is better practice than most studies charted here, particularly given the authors' explicit rationale that inconsistency in the datasets used across the literature makes cross-study comparison unreliable. The gaps are nonetheless serious at this sample size. No confidence interval is reported anywhere, and since every accuracy is an exact multiple of 1/17 the test set contains 17 items, so one child is 5.9 percentage points and the difference between the headline 94.1% and the next-best 88.2% is a single child. No confusion matrix, no AUC, and no sensitivity or specificity named as such. The majority-classifier figure of 56.4% also does not correspond to the 53.9% implied by the overall class ratio, so it appears to be computed on a particular split, which is not stated.

answers.title: Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths
answers.answer: Training accuracy, test accuracy and AUC for every configuration across fourteen tables - and the decision to report training accuracy is worth crediting, because it makes visible what most papers in this corpus conceal: the models reach 100% training accuracy in essentially every experiment while testing between 67% and 81%. A reader can therefore see the overfitting directly rather than having to infer it. AUC is also reported throughout, which is better than accuracy alone, and the paper reasons about the gap between accuracy and AUC, correctly attributing the low AUC to class imbalance in the training data. Against this, no sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1 or confusion matrix appears anywhere, so nothing is known about the error profile or about which class the models fail on. No confidence intervals are given; the temporal experiments are repeated three times and averaged, which gives some sense of stability, but the diagnosis and stratification headlines rest on single splits. And no chance baseline is stated, although after augmentation the classes are near-balanced.

answers.title: A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and a mislabelled F1, reported for the proposed model and all four comparators in both greyscale and colour conditions - and this fuller metric set is what exposes the paper's central problem. Reporting sensitivity and specificity alongside accuracy is good practice, but here the three quantities cannot describe the same classifier: at 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic images, the reported 77.60% sensitivity and 79.91% specificity imply an accuracy of about 79.0%, not the 95.59% claimed, and the multilayer perceptron shows the same pattern (94.69% claimed against about 73.6% implied). The discrepancy is not small and is not reconciled anywhere. Separately, Equation (4) defines F1 as 2 x (Sensitivity x Specificity) / (Sensitivity + Specificity), which is the harmonic mean of sensitivity and specificity - a balanced-accuracy variant - rather than the F1 score, so the column labelled F1 does not mean what its name implies. Also missing: AUC, confusion matrices, confidence intervals, and any majority-class baseline against an implied 60.0% floor.

answers.title: A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning
answers.answer: Metric reporting is fitted to the epidemiological setting rather than borrowed from the classification literature, and this is one of the study's clearest strengths. Accuracy is not reported at all - correctly, since at 0.15% incidence a null model achieves 99.85%. What is reported instead: AUC with standard deviation across folds (0.86, SD 0.009), sensitivity (0.75, SD 0.03), specificity (0.81, SD 0.02), training AUC alongside test AUC with an explicit statement that the model is slightly overfit, full true positive, false positive, true negative and false negative counts for all four modelling methods, and the risk stratification expressed as enrichment - 0.006 incidence in the high-risk group against 0.001 in the cohort, a 4.3-fold increase. Supplementary material gives performance at multiple thresholds as multiples of the Youden threshold, with the trade-off against false positives described. The one omission is positive predictive value, which is not stated although the confusion counts make it computable: 874 of 144,632 flagged children, or 0.60%, meaning 165 flagged per recorded case. That figure is the single most important number in the review for understanding what a well-validated model at a realistic base rate delivers, and it is left for the reader to compute.

answers.title: AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: “A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System”
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for three models, plus a confusion matrix; precision and mAP50 for the expression module. Reporting sensitivity and specificity rather than accuracy alone is nominally good practice, and the discussion draws the correct general point that the choice between MobileNet and Xception depends on whether missed cases or false positives matter more. But three reporting problems undercut this. The confusion matrix reports 131 + 136 + 9 + 4 = 280 images, which matches neither the stated 200-image validation set nor the 100-image test set, and no explanation is offered. Sensitivity and specificity are written throughout as '0.97%' and '0.93%', conflating proportions with percentages. And no AUC, F1 or confidence interval is given, so a difference of one percentage point between MobileNet and Xception - on a partition of at most a few hundred images - is presented as a meaningful model ranking.

answers.title: An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC under two evaluation schemes, with ablation tables, ranked SHAP contributions and t-SNE visualisation. The metric set is adequate and the dual evaluation scheme is more than most of this branch reports. Three problems. The figures are internally inconsistent: the abstract and results report 99.40% accuracy with 99.99% ROC-AUC, while the contributions section reports 'up to 96.4% classification accuracy and an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.92', and no reconciliation is offered. The split description is likewise inconsistent, given as 70:30 in the methods and as a 20% held-out set of about 247 subjects in the abstract, where 20% of 1,112 is 222. And no confidence intervals accompany any estimate, on a test set of roughly 247 subjects where a 95% interval around 99.4% would still span about a point and a half. A ROC-AUC of 99.99% on a diagnostic task is in any case a figure that should prompt a search for leakage rather than a claim of state-of-the-art performance.

answers.title: Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for the best model in each of the two feature conditions, plus ROC curves for all four classifiers and Cohen's d for the derived features. Reporting sensitivity and specificity separately is what makes the study's key numerical detail visible: specificity is 95.24% in both conditions, identical to the decimal, so the entire improvement from 85.37% to 92.68% consists of sensitivity rising from 75.00% to 90.00% - that is, three more of twenty autistic children correctly classified, with no change at all in performance on the comparison group. On a sample of 41 where one participant is 2.4 percentage points, a three-participant difference obtained after selecting features on the outcome is not a stable result, and no confidence interval, permutation test or majority-class baseline is offered against which to judge it. AUC values are not quoted numerically despite ROC curves being plotted. The statistical analysis by contrast is properly equipped, with ANOVA across three groups including the surrogate control, Fisher's LSD post-hoc tests, and effect sizes.

answers.title: Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning
answers.answer: The best-calibrated metric reporting in the review after the population EHR study. Accuracy is reported with a 95% confidence interval for every one of sixteen conditions - four models by two tasks by two annotation methods - alongside precision, sensitivity, specificity and AUC. Reporting confidence intervals is what makes the results interpretable at this sample size: the best interview model's interval of [0.75, 0.89] sits clearly above the 52.6% majority-class floor, while the weakest picture-book configuration at 0.60 [0.51, 0.69] does not. Model comparisons are then tested formally with McNemar rather than being asserted from point differences, and the results are tabulated with test statistics and p-values. Most importantly, non-significant comparisons are interpreted correctly: the authors state that non-significance 'does not definitively indicate the absence of a performance difference between models, particularly in the context of small sample sizes', citing the literature on statistical power. Across this corpus, model rankings resting on differences of one or two participants are routinely presented as findings; this is the only study that tests such comparisons and then declines to over-read them. Absent: confusion matrices, and any relation between predictions and the clinical severity variables collected.

answers.title: Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms
answers.answer: Precision, recall, F1 and accuracy, reported as whole percentages for five classifiers across four feature conditions. The set is nominally adequate, but three problems undercut it. Precision, recall and F1 are reported as identical values to the percentage point in almost every row, which for a balanced binary problem is arithmetically possible but is presented without the confusion counts that would let a reader verify it. No AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval appears. And most fundamentally, no evaluation protocol is stated, so it is not determinable what population any of these numbers estimates - they may be held-out, resubstitution, or cross-validated figures, and the paper provides no basis for choosing between those readings.

answers.title: Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed
answers.answer: Accuracy 99.8%, precision 99.8%, recall 100% and specificity 94%, with t-values and p-values against three baselines at p < 0.01. Three problems. The combination is unusual for a balanced multi-class problem - perfect recall alongside 94% specificity - and no confusion matrix, per-class breakdown or definition of multi-class specificity is supplied to make it interpretable. No confidence intervals accompany any figure, and the number of runs behind the reported means is not stated, so the significance tests cannot be assessed. And no chance baseline is given, though six-way classification would place it near 17% under balance.

answers.title: Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification
answers.answer: Binary accuracy, reported as a distribution across cross-validation folds rather than as a single point, which conveys stability better than a bare figure; ROC curves for both models; and Pearson correlations with p-values for the acceleration analysis. Reporting the fold-wise distribution is good practice and is rare in this corpus. But the metric set is otherwise thin for a diagnostic claim: no sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1 or confusion matrix is given, so the error profile is unknown and it cannot be determined whether the models fail preferentially on autistic or comparison trajectories; no AUC value is quoted despite ROC curves being plotted; and no confidence interval accompanies either headline accuracy. No majority-class baseline is stated. Since the modelled unit is the trajectory rather than the child, no participant-level metric of any kind is available - which is the figure a clinical claim would require.

answers.title: Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain
answers.answer: Ten metrics defined by numbered equation - accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, false positive rate, false negative rate, negative predictive value, false discovery rate, F1-score and Matthews correlation coefficient - reported across two comparison tables to five decimal places. The precision of the reporting is inversely related to its informativeness: five decimal places imply a sample size in the hundreds of thousands, while the sample size is never stated. The metrics are also internally revealing in one respect: precision of 91% alongside sensitivity of 96.3% and specificity of 96.5% implies a positive class comprising roughly a quarter of the sample, information the paper does not supply directly. Three different headline figures appear - 96% accuracy with 93% F1 in the abstract, 96.44% accuracy with 91% precision in the conclusion, and 96.44886% with 91% in Table 3 - and the abstract's F1 value is not reproduced anywhere else. No confusion matrix, confidence interval or AUC appears.

answers.title: Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: Six metrics reported for baseline and optimised models across all four datasets - accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation coefficient and AUC-ROC. Including the Matthews correlation coefficient is good practice for imbalanced tabular data and is rare in this corpus, and class distributions are reported for every band so that majority-class baselines are computable at 69%, 52%, 61% and 73%. None of those baselines is stated or compared against, and no confidence intervals are given. The decisive reporting failure is not in the metric set but in its interpretation: six independent-looking metrics all reaching exactly 100% simultaneously, in four separate datasets, is a signature of a degenerate task rather than a converging body of evidence, and the paper reads it as the latter.

answers.title: Machine learning’s effectiveness
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for each of three variable sets, reported alongside the named variables and cost parameter of each best model; SHAP values displayed for all participants; and correlations between SRS-2 total and predicted probability. Reporting sensitivity and specificity separately is essential at 15.1% prevalence and is done. But three gaps matter. No majority-class baseline is stated, so the reported 1.000 is not placed against the 84.9% floor that a trivial all-negative classifier would achieve - although sensitivity of 1.000 does establish that all 19 positives were caught, which a trivial classifier could not do. No AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval appears; on 19 positives, an exact binomial interval around a sensitivity of 1.000 would extend below 0.82, which is the figure a reader needs. And no positive predictive value is computed, despite the population-based design making it directly meaningful - at the observed 15.1% prevalence and perfect specificity it would be 1.000, but any realistic degradation in specificity would move it sharply, and that sensitivity analysis is exactly what a screening proposal requires.

answers.title: Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network
answers.answer: The broadest metric set in this branch: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Cohen's kappa, specificity, AUC and AUC-PR, with confusion matrices, ROC and precision-recall curves, means and standard deviations across runs, 95% intervals, McNemar's test and paired t-tests. The apparatus is well beyond what most facial-image papers in this review report, and the headline triple is internally coherent - 95.36% accuracy with 92.62% precision and 95.5% F1 implies recall 98.6% and specificity 92.2% at a 1:1 ratio, which reproduces the stated accuracy exactly. Two failures nonetheless undercut the reporting. The intervals are not compatible with the data: every one is the mean plus or minus 0.4 percentage points, accompanied by a standard deviation of 0.03, on test sets as small as 68 images where a single misclassification moves accuracy by 1.47 points; an exact binomial interval around 95% on 68 images spans roughly 87% to 99%. And no positive predictive value is computed for any realistic prevalence, despite a 1:1 class ratio that exists only because the datasets were assembled that way - at a population rate near 1-2%, a specificity of 92% would place the great majority of positive calls on non-autistic children.

answers.title: Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1 for all four architectures. Reporting specificity is appropriate at a 13:4 class ratio and more than several studies in this review provide. Three gaps: no confidence intervals on figures derived from 17 participants; no confusion matrices or class-wise breakdowns; and no chance or majority-class baseline, although the participant-level ratio places a trivial all-autistic classifier at 76.5%, so the reported 89-94% represents a much smaller increment over the trivial solution than the raw numbers suggest.

answers.title: Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play
answers.answer: The fullest metric reporting in the review's behavioural branch. AUC 0.826 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.776-0.877; sensitivity 85.4%; specificity 68.3%; positive predictive value 72.9%; negative predictive value 82.4%, all at a stated cut-off of 0.399; Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness of fit; a calibration curve relating predicted to observed probabilities; density plots for the retained indicators; and odds ratios with confidence intervals and p-values at both the univariate and multivariate stages for every indicator. Reporting discrimination, calibration, predictive values and per-predictor uncertainty together is what a prediction-model study should do and what almost no other paper in this corpus does. Three qualifications. The predictive values are computed at the 1:1 prevalence the matched design created; at a realistic screening base rate, a specificity of 68.3% would place the great majority of positive calls on non-autistic children, and this recalculation is exactly what the paper's screening proposal requires and does not perform. The reported AUC is apparent rather than optimism-corrected, despite a bootstrap having been run for that purpose. And the operating cut-off of 0.399 was chosen from the same ROC curve on which the sensitivity and specificity are then quoted, so that pair is a best-of-curve selection rather than a prespecified operating point.

answers.title: Predictive model using autism
answers.answer: Well chosen for the question and honestly reported. Sensitivity and specificity of both published algorithms against clinical diagnosis, with the false-positive rates given as the headline numbers (45.0% original, 52.5% revised) rather than left to be derived. AUC for both algorithms and for the six-item model, with the interpretive bands stated in advance (excellent 0.90-1, good 0.80-0.90, fair 0.70-0.80, poor 0.60-0.70, bad 0.50-0.60) and DeLong's test for the paired comparison. Odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals for every domain and every retained item. Apparent classification accuracy of 86.6%. And both holdout figures - 85.4% training, 65.3% test. Reporting the drop is the single most valuable reporting decision in this record. Two gaps: the abstract and results present the apparent AUC of 0.938 as the model's discriminative ability without the held-out figure attached, so a reader who does not reach the limitations section will take away the wrong number; and no positive predictive value is computed for any realistic case mix, which for a differential-diagnosis aid would depend on the relative frequency of the two conditions among referred patients.

answers.title: The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech
answers.answer: Well chosen and honestly deployed. Unweighted average recall is the primary metric, which is the correct choice for imbalanced classes and sets chance at 50% and 25% for the two tasks. Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 are reported for every model and every partition - mixed-gender, female and male - for both tasks, alongside confusion matrices and sensitivity and specificity by gender for the equalised-odds analysis. Most valuably, two comparison tables place the results in context: one against a baseline and two published studies on the same corpus, the other against published Wav2Vec 2.0 implementations. Those tables show that the study's typicality result exceeds the baseline by 0.7 points, and that its diagnosis result of 60.9% falls below the baseline of 62.4% and below prior results of 67.1% and 69.4%. Reporting a table in which one's own method loses on the harder task is rare in this corpus and should be recorded as such. What is missing is any uncertainty estimate - no confidence intervals, no variance across runs, no significance testing - which matters when the typicality margin over baseline is 0.7 points and when the diagnosis test partition contains 26 samples per clinical class.

answers.title: Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism
answers.answer: Accuracy, AUC and F1 for both classifiers, with 5-fold cross-validation accuracy for algorithm selection: 73% accuracy, AUC 0.728 and F1 0.71 at tweet level; AUC 0.78 and F1 0.805 at profile level. The figures are modest by this corpus's standards and are presented without inflation - the abstract, results and conclusion all carry the same numbers and none is described as high. What is absent is uncertainty and operating-point reporting: no confidence intervals despite a corpus that would support tight ones, no calibration, and no sensitivity or specificity at any threshold. For a paper that raises screening, the absent quantity is the positive predictive value at population prevalence - at roughly 1-2% base rate, a classifier with AUC 0.78 would place the overwhelming majority of its positive calls on non-autistic people. The authors reach a compatible conclusion by a different route, restricting legitimate use to cross-sectional rather than individual inference, but they do not compute the number that demonstrates why.

answers.title: Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children
answers.answer: A complete confusion-matrix-derived set - accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, negative predictive value and F1 - reported for all five models in a single table, which is fuller than almost anything else in this corpus and unusual in presenting every ensemble variant rather than the best one. Reporting negative predictive value alongside precision is a further mark of care. Three gaps and two errors. No confidence intervals appear anywhere, on a test set of 80 children where a single case is worth 1.25 accuracy points and an exact binomial interval around 82.5% runs from roughly 72% to 90% - which means the ensemble's advantage over the video model alone, two children, is not distinguishable from noise. No positive predictive value at realistic prevalence is computed, although the paper is framed around screening and the balanced design makes the reported precision of 0.861 an artefact of the 1:1 construction; at a population base rate the same specificity of 0.875 would place the large majority of positive calls on non-autistic children. And the interpretive bands for what counts as good performance are not stated. The two errors are both in the abstract and neither affects the results section: the abstract describes 'higher specificity (92.5%, i.e., few false negatives) or sensitivity (90%, i.e. few false positives)', reversing the meaning of both terms, and gives the ensemble as 'Precision: 0.775, Recall: 0.861' where the table correctly has precision 0.861 and recall 0.775. Table 1 is internally consistent throughout.

answers.title: Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning
answers.answer: Accuracy, F1 and recall for classification; mean squared error and concordance correlation coefficient for regression. The regression metric choice is well argued and the argument is worth recording: the authors note that a comparator 'did not report the performances of their approach according to the CCC despite it being the most popular metric for audio and visual affect recognition' and observe that 'it is possible that their approach is very accurate according to MSE but much less accurate according to CCC' - then demonstrate exactly that inversion in their own results, where Inception v3 beats the Perceiver on MSE while losing on CCC. Recognising that two metrics can rank models oppositely, and showing it in one's own data, is a level of measurement care rare in this corpus. The classification reporting is correspondingly weaker: no specificity, no confusion matrix, no confidence intervals, no positive predictive value, and - because the class balance is stated inconsistently - no determinable chance baseline for the reported 74.5%.

answers.title: A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features
answers.answer: A reasonable metric set applied at every stage - PSNR and SSIM for denoising, accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for both classification stages, ROC curves with AUC for severity (RF 0.9878, SVM 0.9865, KNN 0.9268), and computation time - with all formulae defined explicitly. What is missing determines whether any of it can be read. Class sizes across the three severity levels are never given, so neither the chance level nor the majority-class baseline is known and 98.33% has no reference point. There are no confidence intervals, on 1,500 images from 30 children where the effective sample is 30. There are no confusion matrices and no per-class breakdown, so whether the mild and moderate classes are distinguished at all - the clinically important discrimination for dosing - cannot be seen. There is no specificity, and the ROC description conflates specificity with the false positive rate. And the comparison table reporting that the classifiers exceed 'the clinical ABC method' has no stated criterion for either, so the numbers in it cannot be interpreted.

answers.title: Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: Per-class precision, recall and F1 with support counts, overall accuracy, weighted averages, confusion matrices for all three models, training and validation curves, an ROC figure for Inception-V3 and a comparison table against ten prior studies on the same corpus. That is a fuller presentation than several papers in this branch. Three defects undercut it. Every table is headed 'Validation results' and the confusion matrices are described as validation-stage, so no held-out test figure is reported despite a test partition being defined. The support counts of 294 per class - 588 in total - are 20% of the corpus rather than the stated 10% validation share, and are exactly balanced although the corpus is 1,327 against 1,613, so the evaluation partition's composition cannot be reconstructed and it is unclear whether augmentation reached it. And no chance baseline, confidence interval or prevalence-adjusted predictive value appears, so a 98% figure has no reference point - at the corpus ratio a trivial majority classifier scores 54.9%, and at a realistic population prevalence the reported precision would not survive.

answers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUC for all seven models, with ROC curves that plot the individual splits, the mean curve and a one-standard-deviation band. That variability band is worth singling out: on 64 children with 50 repeated splits it conveys the instability of the estimate more honestly than a point figure, and it is a form of uncertainty reporting that almost no other study in this review provides. Precision and recall are also interpreted correctly in clinical terms, with recall of 80-81% read as a low false-negative rate 'important for ensuring that children with ASD are diagnosed correctly' and precision of 84-86% as protecting children without autism from being misdiagnosed. Missing: confidence intervals, confusion matrices, calibration, and any positive predictive value at a realistic prevalence - the last mattering because the reported precision holds only at the near-balanced sample ratio.

answers.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning
answers.answer: Accuracy only, but reported with dispersion - average, maximum, minimum and standard deviation across repeated cross-validation cycles for every architecture on both datasets, plus per-epoch accuracy and loss curves. The dispersion reporting is a real strength and is what makes the architecture comparison interpretable: standard deviations of 0.71 to 1.82 on the Gait dataset against a 2.2-point spread between backbones show immediately that the architectural differences are barely larger than run-to-run noise, and the paper is able to note that ShuffleNet was more stable than MaxViT at the same mean accuracy. What is absent is everything a screening claim requires. No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC or confusion matrix is reported for any proposed model, so the balance between missed cases and false alarms is unknown, and no positive predictive value at any realistic prevalence is computed. Accuracy on a 50:50 corpus tells a clinician very little, and on DREAM - where the class distribution is described as biased but never quantified - it tells them nothing at all.

answers.title: Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]
answers.answer: A fuller metric set than most of this branch: accuracy 90.28%, AUC 90.83%, sensitivity 88.64%, specificity 88.64%, precision 95.12% and F-score 91.75%, with sensitivity and specificity reported separately and defined explicitly in the table as counts of autistic and typically developing instances. The statistical analysis reports means with standard errors and codes significance at three thresholds. Two problems limit what any of it means. Every classification figure is a validation-set value with no held-out test, taken at the best of 2,000 epochs, so all six metrics inherit the same selection optimism. And the instance-level definition of sensitivity and specificity means these are not per-child operating characteristics: a screening tool's sensitivity is the proportion of autistic children it flags, not the proportion of their individual cries, and with six cries per child the two quantities can differ substantially. No confidence intervals accompany any figure, on an effective sample of 62 children.

answers.title: Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm
answers.answer: Accuracy alone, at 0.9890. No precision, recall, specificity, F1, AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval is reported, and no class distribution is given, so the figure cannot be compared against the 73.2% majority-class baseline that the source dataset implies. For a screening application, sensitivity and specificity are the quantities that matter and neither is provided.

answers.title: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
answers.answer: Accuracy, AUC, precision and recall, with paired t-tests across the 5-fold results at p < 0.05 and 95% confidence intervals for accuracy, precision, recall and F1 stated to lie within plus or minus 1.5%. Reporting intervals and fold-level significance testing at all places the study above most of this corpus. Three problems limit the reporting. Specificity is not given, and with recall at 0.95 and accuracy at 85-90% on a balanced sample, specificity must be substantially below recall - roughly 75-85% by arithmetic - so the metric that a screening application most needs is the one omitted, and the model's error profile is asymmetric in a direction the reported figures obscure. No confusion matrix appears. And the stated interval of plus or minus 1.5% is narrower than 100 children in 5-fold cross-validation would normally support, with 20 children per validation fold meaning a single child moves fold accuracy by 5 percentage points; the derivation of the interval is not stated, so whether it describes across-fold variation or something else cannot be determined.

answers.title: Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of
answers.answer: Thin, and thinner still for the second target. For autism, accuracy alone is reported at 92%, described as holding 'across both training and testing datasets' - a formulation that conflates the two and gives no separate held-out figure, on a test partition of 279 images where a 95% interval would span roughly plus or minus 3 points before any leakage consideration. No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval appears. For gelotophobia, no quantitative metric of any kind is reported: the results state that the system 'successfully classified gelotophobia in cases where facial expressions were clear' and that DeepFace alone was insufficient otherwise, neither of which has a denominator, a comparison or a ground truth. A paper whose stated objective is 'to develop a deep learning-based diagnostic system ... to detect gelotophobia' reports no number for that detection.

answers.title: Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
answers.answer: Accuracy of 88.33% with a confusion matrix presented as a figure. No precision, recall, specificity, F1, AUC or confidence interval is reported in the retrieved text, and no chance baseline is stated - although a confusion matrix at least permits per-class errors to be read off, which several studies on this corpus do not provide. Notably, no accuracy figures are broken out for the five extractors or the three preprocessing configurations individually, so the comparisons the study set up are not reported in a form that supports conclusions about them.

answers.title: Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children
answers.answer: The fullest metric reporting of any Kaggle-corpus study in this review - accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, F1 and AUC for the autism model, six measures plus confusion matrices for emotion - and that completeness is what makes the problem visible. The autism figures are 'accuracy = 95, precision = 0.96, sensitivity/recall = 0.94, Specificity = 42.5, F1 = 0.95 and AUC = 78'. These cannot all be correct. On the stated balanced 280-image test set, a recall of 0.94 recovers about 132 of 140 positives while a specificity of 0.425 recovers about 60 of 140 negatives, giving 192 correct and an accuracy near 68%. The same figures imply about 80 false positives, so precision would be near 0.62 rather than 0.96. And an AUC of 0.78 is not compatible with 95% accuracy on balanced classes. Reporting specificity at all is what exposes this - the seven other Kaggle-corpus studies charted here that report accuracy alone would have concealed an identical failure. If the specificity of 42.5% is the accurate figure, the model correctly identifies fewer than half of non-autistic children, which is worse than chance and is the study's most important result. The emotion metrics, by contrast, are internally consistent and modest.

answers.title: Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Using Lightweight Ensemble CNN Based on Facial Images for Improved Diagnostic Accuracy
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for each of the five pairings, with training and validation curves. The metric set supports one genuinely useful observation - that a pairing with higher precision but lower recall is 'less useful for finding all ASD cases', which is the correct screening-oriented reading and is articulated in almost no other study in this branch. What is missing is specificity, AUC, confusion matrices and confidence intervals, and no chance baseline is stated despite the exactly balanced construction placing it at 50%. The comparison table cites two prior studies at 0.7500 and 0.8050 rather than the high-nineties figures reported by other Kaggle-corpus work, so the study positions itself against modest comparators.

answers.title: Diagnosing autism spectrum disorder based on eye tracking technology using deep learning models
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall/sensitivity, F1, per-class values and per-fold confusion matrices; means with standard deviations across the five folds. Missing: specificity as a separate figure, AUC or any threshold-free measure, calibration, positive and negative predictive value at a stated prevalence, and any participant-level metric. Because the analysis unit is the gaze sample, none of the reported numbers is a diagnostic accuracy in the clinical sense - not one figure in the paper describes how often a child would be correctly classified.

answers.title: Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Automated Machine Learning
answers.answer: Per-class precision, recall and F1 with support, macro and weighted averages, accuracy, a confusion matrix, micro-average ROC 0.87 and macro-average ROC 0.81, and PR values of 0.892 and 0.728. This is a fuller metric set than most of the corpus offers, and unusually the weaker class is reported honestly (non-autistic recall 0.53). Missing: specificity named as such, calibration, predictive values at a stated prevalence, and any confidence interval. The abstract's 78% does not match the 0.83 in the results and comparison tables - the 0.78 in the table is the weighted-average precision/F1 row, so the headline accuracy has been read off the wrong line.

answers.title: Enhanced ASD detection using 3D facial landmark localization with convolutional shape appearance model and graph-randomized XGBoost
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, loss, AUC, detection accuracy (reported separately from accuracy and never defined), miss rate, fall-out, millimetre localisation error, and a confusion matrix. The abstract claims excellent specificity but no specificity value appears. The internal arithmetic does not hold: the confusion matrix reports 146 true non-ASD, 141 true ASD, 9 false positives and 4 false negatives, summing to 300 cases although the stated final evaluation set is 200 images and the test split is 506. Those cell counts give accuracy 287/300 = 0.957, precision 141/150 = 0.940 and recall 141/145 = 0.972 - none of which match the reported 0.985, 0.975 and 0.987. Separately, F1 is given as 0.925 while precision and recall are 0.975 and 0.987, whose harmonic mean is 0.981; no combination of the reported figures is mutually consistent.

answers.title: Enhanced multilevel autism classification for children using eye-tracking and hybrid CNN-RNN deep learning models
answers.answer: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, false discovery rate, false omission rate and AUC are all defined by equation, which reads as thorough; only accuracy, recall and F1 are then reported for the within-study experiments, and specificity, FDR and FOR appear as numbers nowhere. A four-class confusion matrix is shown and discussed sensibly - low and medium separate better than mild and high. The Saliency4ASD table reports accuracy and AUC together (95.93/95.82 and 97.95/97.84). The 25% four-class chance level is never stated, and no metric carries an interval.

answers.title: Ensemble of Deep Learning with Crested Porcupine Optimizer Based Autism
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall, F-score and G-measure, per class and averaged, at 500 through 2,500 epochs; ROC curves described qualitatively; a Gabor ablation with training time and a computational-cost index whose units are not given. No specificity, no numeric AUC, no calibration, no predictive values at a stated prevalence, and no confidence interval anywhere. The reported average of 96.43% is not one measurement but the best of five epoch settings, carried into both the abstract and the comparison table against baselines evaluated under unknown conditions in other papers.

answers.title: Explainable and secure framework for autism prediction using multimodal eye tracking and kinematic data
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1, reported per client, per feature subset, per local model and for the global model in both scenarios. No specificity, no AUC, no calibration, no predictive values and no confidence interval anywhere. The metric grid is dense and the reported values are internally revealing: they take only the values 0.11, 0.22, 0.33, 0.44, 0.55, 0.66, 0.77, 0.88 and 1.00, which are the achievable accuracies on nine test cases. The headline of 99.99% is that same 9/9 restated, and the paper describes it as flawless classification performance. One tabulated value, Client 3 on L_Attention at 0.01, is not a multiple of one ninth and is presumably a typographic corruption of 0.11.

answers.title: Facial Images Dataset for Early Screening of Autism Children Using Convolutional Neural Network
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and a confusion matrix, with sensitivity and specificity defined by formula but specificity never reported numerically. The reported figures reconcile exactly with the confusion-matrix cells - 92 of 102 correct gives 0.902; 47 of 51 predicted-positive gives 0.922; 47 of 53 actual-positive gives 0.887 - which is a level of internal consistency several other studies in this corpus fail to achieve. What is absent is any interval: with 102 test images the 95% confidence interval around 0.90 runs from roughly 0.83 to 0.95, so the comparison against the quoted literature figures of 87%, 88%, 89.2%, 90% and 92% is not discriminating. The abstract also describes the evaluation as using a nuisance matrix.

answers.title: Improving Early Autism Detection with Chi-Square Feature Selection, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and log loss for all twelve configurations, plus a confusion matrix and SHAP plots for the best model. The log loss column deserves credit: it is the only calibration-sensitive measure reported by any study charted in this review, and it does real work here - Decision Tree posts 0.938 accuracy with a log loss of 2.223, exposing badly miscalibrated probabilities that accuracy alone would hide. Against that, no confidence interval accompanies any figure, and neither baseline is stated (50.7% on the balanced test set, 69.7% majority-class on the original data). The F1 score is also described as the geometric mean of precision and recall, when it is the harmonic mean.

answers.title: Novel Framework for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification and Tailored Education With Effective Data Mining and Ensemble Learning Techniques
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 across four feature conditions, seven classifiers and an ensemble; per-fold cross-validation values; Phase II results; and a state-of-the-art comparison. No AUC, no specificity, no calibration, no confidence interval, and no chance level for either the binary Phase I task or the seven-class Phase II task. Two internal inconsistencies matter. The 10-fold table prints an average accuracy of 0.986 while the ten listed fold accuracies average 0.9876, and it contains a fold reporting recall 0.999 against accuracy 0.988 and another reporting accuracy 0.999 - values out of line with their neighbours. More seriously, the comparison table credits the proposed approach with 99.99% accuracy, positioning it above four quoted literature figures (98.77%, 97.82%, 99.25%, 99.85%), when the study's own best tabulated result is 0.99 and its cross-validated average is 0.986. The headline claim of surpassing the state of the art rests on a number the paper never produced.

answers.title: Predicting autism traits using Q-CHAT behavioral features: a machine learning approach
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, F1, sensitivity, specificity, MCC and a confusion matrix for every model, plus per-subset comparisons and an iterative feature-addition curve. The metric set is the most complete in this branch: MCC is included deliberately because of the class imbalance, and its motivation - that incorrect diagnoses have significant implications for families - is stated. It also does real work, separating LR (accuracy 0.97, MCC 0.92) from ANN (0.98, 0.98). Two problems. No confidence interval accompanies any figure. And the confusion matrices are mutually inconsistent: LR, KNN and LR-KNN each have class totals of 105 and 212, while the ANN's are 110 and 207, so the four models were not all evaluated on the same 317-record partition.

answers.title: Predicting autistic traits, anxiety and depression symptoms using camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (CAT-Q-ES): A machine learning study
answers.answer: Pearson R between true and predicted scores, MAE, MAPE relative to the score range, and RMSE, per outcome and averaged across the four trials, with predicted-versus-true scatter plots against a perfect-agreement diagonal. Correlation magnitudes are interpreted against a pre-specified external criterion (Colton 1974), so strong and moderate are defined before the results rather than after. The tolerance analysis is the most practically informative reporting in the corpus: the best Aloofness model places 36.3% of predictions within 5% of the true score and just over 60% within 10%, which states plainly what the R=.85 does and does not deliver at the individual level. The paper also notes correctly that the lower MAE for Depression and Anxiety reflects their narrower score ranges rather than better prediction, and reads the MAPE accordingly. Two gaps: no confidence intervals or across-trial variance accompany the metrics, and no trivial baseline (for instance, predicting the sample mean) is reported against which the MAE and RMSE could be judged. A minor inconsistency: the abstract gives Rigidity R=.74 and Depression R=.60, while Table 3 gives .75 and .58 for the CAT-Q-ES-only configuration.

answers.title: A Computational Method for Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children Using Deep Learning Approach
answers.answer: Accuracy, AUC, F-measure, G-mean, sensitivity, specificity, fall-out and miss rate, with formulae given, reported for both validation and test, plus a confusion-matrix figure. This is a fuller and better-chosen metric set than most of the facial-image branch offers - specificity and fall-out are reported as numbers rather than merely claimed, and the figures are internally consistent (sensitivity 94% with miss rate 0.06; specificity 88% with fall-out 0.12; their mean 91% matching the reported accuracy on a balanced test set). Two problems. No confidence interval accompanies any figure, and on 200 test images the 95% interval around 91% runs from roughly 86% to 95% - a range that contains almost every entry in the comparison tables, so the claimed ordering among methods is not established. And validation accuracy (86.5%) is lower than test accuracy (91%) by 4.5 points on 200 images each, which is reported without comment.

answers.title: Early Detection of ASD from Facial Images Using DeepDeblur and Denoising Optimized Convolutional Neural Network
answers.answer: Accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure, a confusion matrix and an ROC curve for classification; percentage blur removed, PSNR, MSE and SSIM for deblurring. Specificity is not reported, no AUC value is given numerically, no calibration or predictive values appear, and no confidence interval accompanies any figure. The reported accuracy of 96.94% reconciles exactly with the confusion-matrix counts - 2,850 correct out of 2,940 - which is the problem rather than a reassurance, because 2,940 is the entire dataset and not the 400-image test set the methods section defines.

answers.title: Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI
answers.answer: Accuracy, F1, precision, recall and area under the precision-recall curve, per model and per fold, at four fold counts, with per-fold tables in an appendix. The choice of prAUC is thoughtful and explicitly justified by the expected class imbalance. Two absences matter. Specificity is never reported for any model, so the false-positive behaviour of a system proposed for paediatric screening is invisible; and the class balance is never given, so neither the prAUC baseline nor the majority-class accuracy can be computed. The reported neural-network figures are accuracy 1.0000, F1 1.0000, precision 1.0000 and recall 1.0000 - a model that misclassifies no child in any of ten folds - with prAUC 0.9601, a combination that is itself internally odd, since a classifier with perfect precision and recall should have a precision-recall curve area of 1.

answers.title: Using explainable machine learning and eye-tracking for diagnosing autism spectrum and developmental language disorders in social attention tasks
answers.answer: F1-score only, with precision and recall given by equation.
