The scheme is nested leave-one-participant-out cross-validation: in each outer fold a single participant is held out entirely, with all 21 or 32 of their trials excluded from training, and the inner loop with an 8:2 training/validation split is used to optimise the learning rate. Placing hyperparameter selection inside the outer loop is stated explicitly and is the correct construction; the great majority of studies in this corpus either tune on the test set or do not say. Because the split unit is the participant, the trial-level leakage that inflates results throughout this literature - where a person's own segments appear on both sides of the split - is structurally impossible here, and this matters more than usual because the per-trial classifier operates on individual FEIT images that would otherwise be trivially matched across folds. Class balance was engineered in advance by equalising group sizes, so chance is approximately 50% and is not an artefact of prevalence. And every reported accuracy is tested against that chance level with a binomial test, with the failing result reported as failing. The consequences are visible in the numbers: accuracies of 0.645 to 0.710 rather than the 90-plus figures common in this corpus, which is what a properly participant-disjoint, chance-tested evaluation of gaze features in 30 people looks like. Three residual weaknesses. No confidence intervals accompany any figure, and with 30-31 participants one person is roughly 3 accuracy points, so the 10-point gain from weighting in adults corresponds to about three people. The controls were selected from a larger pool by SRS-2 ranking, so sampling is conditioned on a construct-related variable. And the statistical analysis that motivates the whole approach - and that is used to validate the feature importances - treats trials as independent units when they cluster within participants, without any mixed-effects adjustment, so those p-values are anticonservative even after Benjamini-Hochberg correction.

answers.title: Large-scale Investigations of AAC Usage Patterns: Trends, Autism, and Stacked Autoencoders
answers.answer: The weakest element, with two problems either of which would be decisive on its own. The first is the pseudo-labelling. Only 180 users of approximately 5,372 disclosed a diagnosis; the remainder were assigned labels by k-means clustering seeded from the labelled cases, and the 70% and 82% figures are obtained on this enlarged corpus. So roughly 97% of the evaluation data carry labels generated by an unsupervised algorithm rather than reported by any person, and the reported accuracy is substantially a measure of how well a supervised classifier reproduces a clustering solution - a quantity that can be high regardless of whether the clusters correspond to diagnosis. The contrast with the same data before pseudo-labelling is stark and is visible in the paper's own Table IV: 47-61% across all three modelling views and six window sizes, at or barely above a 50% chance level. The second problem is the unit of cross-validation, which is never stated. The modelling operates on windows, each user generates many windows in proportion to their app use, and neither the earlier leave-one-out-with-100-bootstraps scheme nor the present ten-repetition 20-fold-with-ten-bootstraps scheme is described as partitioning users. If windows were partitioned - the natural reading - then every user's own data appear on both sides of every fold, and since key-press sequences from a customised icon layout are close to an individual signature, the classifier can succeed by recognising users rather than diagnoses. No user-level accuracy is reported anywhere, which is the number the stated research question requires. Compounding both: accuracy is the only metric, no chance baseline is computed, no confidence interval is given, window size was swept with the best reported, and tuning effort differed between the compared classifiers by the authors' own account. The corrective experiment is clear and would be worth more than the present result - partition by user, evaluate only on the 180 verified labels, report sensitivity and specificity at the user level, and adjust for or match on age.

answers.title: Development and Validation of a Joint Attention-Based Deep Learning System for Detection and Symptom Severity Assessment of Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: Correctly constructed at the split, and this deserves explicit credit: 'we used 10-fold group-wise (by individual) cross-validation', stated unambiguously, so all clips from a child fall in the same fold and no participant contributes to both training and testing. That is exactly the safeguard most of this corpus omits, and it matters here because each child supplies up to ten IJA and five RJA clips from a single continuous session, which under clip-level splitting would be near-duplicates. Confidence intervals are computed by a named method and reported for every metric, and the classification threshold is fixed at 0.5 rather than tuned. Within its own terms the evaluation is therefore sound, and the near-perfect detection figures cannot be attributed to participant leakage. The problem lies upstream, in what the evaluation is an evaluation of. The paper states that conservative criteria were used deliberately 'to select individuals belonging to clinically distinct groups to ensure development of an accurate and precise ASD vs TD classification model', and the participant table shows a 44-50 point IQ gap at p < .001 with an autism sample that is 62% preverbal or single-word. Separating those two groups is a far easier problem than the clinical question, and AUROCs of 99.5-99.8% are the expected result rather than a surprising one - so the honest reading is that the study demonstrates the protocol and pipeline work, not that the system would perform at this level on the children a referral tool would actually see. The severity analysis inherits the same issue in a specific form: its three classes include non-autism, so a large part of its 90.3% AUROC is the already-solved detection problem, and because no autism-only result is reported there is no evidence that the system grades severity within the spectrum. Further gaps: no external validation, which the authors acknowledge; no clinical comparison group; no specificity; no class distribution for the severity bands and hence no chance baseline; and no adjustment for the IQ difference despite ANCOVA being straightforward and the authors demonstrably comfortable with mixed ANOVA elsewhere in the paper. The corrective study is well specified by the authors themselves - an IQ-matched external cohort - and would be worth considerably more than the present numbers.

answers.title: Predicting autism in children at an early stage using eye tracking
answers.answer: A single fixed 70/20/10 split of 547 images into 382 training, 108 validation and 57 test, with the image as the unit. Fifty-nine children produced those 547 images, so roughly nine images per child, and nothing in the paper indicates that a child's images were kept together - so on a random split each test image is accompanied by around eight siblings from the same child. This is the same design flaw that recurs across reuses of this dataset, and it is the reason the review treats the family of studies built on it as a triangulation problem rather than as independent evidence. What makes this particular paper informative is that the leakage does not produce a high number: 81.0% at best, against figures near 97-99% reported by other groups on the identical images. The most plausible reading is that generic ImageNet features plus a shallow classifier extract less individual-identity information from a rendered trajectory than an end-to-end network fine-tuned on the same data - so the gap between this study and the higher-scoring reuses is itself evidence about how much of those higher scores is identity rather than diagnosis. Read alongside the source authors' own participant-level correction to around 71% and another group's one-image-per-child leave-one-out result of 72.88%, this study's 81% sits closer to the honest end of the range than to the inflated one, despite sharing the flawed split. Other weaknesses compound the picture: a 57-image test set with no confidence intervals, so the three-way model comparison rests on differences of one or two images; no cross-validation or repeated splits; no chance baseline against an implied 59.6% floor; and one architectural choice (greyscale conversion) made with reference to observed accuracy on the same data.

answers.title: SPASHT: Semantic and Pragmatic Speech Features for Automatic Assessment of Autism
answers.answer: The weakest dimension, and the problems compound. The reported scheme is a single 90:10 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation used inside the training data only for SVM hyperparameter selection - which is the correct placement for hyperparameter tuning and is stated clearly. But three issues sit above it. First, the arithmetic does not match the description: every reported accuracy is an exact multiple of 1/17 (64.7, 70.59, 76.5, 82.3, 88.2, 94.1 per cent), which fixes the test set at 17 items, roughly 22% of 76 rather than the stated 10%, and the discrepancy is unexplained. Whatever the intended design, a 17-item test set means one child is worth 5.9 percentage points, so the headline 94.1% is 16 of 17 correct and its margin over the next-best configuration is one child - a difference no confidence interval is offered for and none would support. Second, SHAP-based elimination from 77 to 63 features is described as performed on the initially extracted set with no indication of nesting inside the split, so the retained feature set was chosen with sight of the evaluation data; on 76 samples and 77 candidate features this is exactly the regime in which unnested selection produces substantial optimism. Third, six classifier families were compared and the best retained, with a 30-point spread between the worst and best, so the reported figure is the maximum of a search. Beneath all of this lies the pooling problem, which no amount of correct splitting would fix: because the Flusberg corpus contributes autistic children only and from a much younger age band, corpus identity partially predicts diagnosis, and a random split across pooled corpora cannot separate a linguistic signature from a corpus signature. The corrective design is available in the data and would be far more informative - leave-one-corpus-out validation, which would show directly whether features learned on Eigsti and Flusberg transfer to Nadig and vice versa, together with nesting the SHAP elimination and reporting the ablation ordering rather than point accuracies.

answers.title: Stratification of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder Through Fusion of Temporal Information in Eye-gaze Scan-Paths
answers.answer: The weakest element, and the paper contains the evidence for its own strongest critique. The splitting unit is the scan-path image at 7:3 or 75:25, and no participant-level or subject-disjoint evaluation is reported anywhere in twenty pages. With 86 participants generating 1,414 clip viewings, each child contributes roughly sixteen images, so a random image-level split places about eleven of a test child's own scan-paths in training - and scan-paths from one child viewing different clips share that child's habitual gaze extent, saccade amplitude and scanning style. Rotation-based augmentation makes this worse rather than better, because augmented counts are quoted for the whole dataset rather than for training partitions, implying that rotated copies of a single scan-path can appear on both sides of the split. The sex-by-age experiment then supplies near-direct evidence of this: test accuracy rises monotonically with augmentation level, from 85.07% at 961/957 images through 85.81% at 1,276/1,259 to 98.84% at 3,121/2,905. A real signal does not strengthen when synthetic copies are added; a duplicate-leakage artefact does exactly this. The 98.8% is nevertheless reported as the paper's most striking stratification result. Training accuracy of 100% in almost every table confirms complete memorisation at every setting. Layered on top of the leakage is a confound the paper documents without recognising: it establishes that scan-path images predict age band at 80.5% and sex at 78.0% within the autistic group - both above the 74.4% achieved for diagnosis - while its diagnostic groups differ by 35 percentage points in sex composition and by a factor of two in the proportion aged 10 or over. Taken together these mean the headline diagnosis figure cannot be attributed to autism-related looking patterns rather than to age and sex. The corrective design is straightforward and would be genuinely valuable given the quality of the stimulus battery: split by participant, augment only within training folds, and evaluate diagnosis within age-and-sex-matched strata using the paper's own demographic classifiers as a check.

answers.title: A Convolutional Deep Neural Network Approach to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye-Tracking Scan Paths
answers.answer: Two problems compound, and a third makes the result difficult to interpret at all. First, cross-validation partitions the 547 images rather than the 59 children. With roughly nine images per child and no statement that a child's images were kept within a fold, each held-out image is accompanied by around eight siblings from the same child in training - the same route that has produced accuracies from 81% to over 99% across five reuses of this identical dataset, against the source authors' own participant-level figure near 71% and an independent one-image-per-child leave-one-out result of 72.88%. Second, the reported figure is the maximum of an extremely large hyperparameter search: separate sweeps over kernel size, stride, pooling, batch size, optimiser and thirteen architecture configurations, well over a hundred cells in total, every one scored on the same cross-validation with the best bolded and carried forward. No held-out confirmation of the selected configuration is performed, and the 35-point spread between optimisers on identical data shows how much room that search had to exploit. Third, and most consequentially, the headline accuracy cannot be reconciled with the sensitivity and specificity reported for the same model. At 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic images, 77.60% sensitivity and 79.91% specificity give approximately 79.0% accuracy. That implied figure is strikingly consistent with the other honest estimates on this dataset - 81.0% from an independent transfer-learning study, 72.88% from one-image-per-child leave-one-out, and roughly 71% from the source authors' own participant-level correction - which suggests the class-conditional metrics may be the trustworthy ones and the accuracy column an artefact. Either way, the paper reports two irreconcilable characterisations of its own classifier and reconciles neither, so no single number from it can be carried into a synthesis without that caveat.

answers.title: A Prediction Model of Autism Spectrum Diagnosis from Well-Baby Electronic Data Using Machine Learning
answers.answer: The strongest validation design in the review, and strong in ways that are structural rather than procedural. Four features stand out. The split unit is the child and the cohort is a whole population, so there is no possibility of within-participant leakage and no case-control sampling to inflate separation. Temporal leakage is controlled by design rather than by hope: predictors are capped at 24 months and outcomes restricted to diagnoses recorded after 24 months, adopted explicitly to prevent information flowing from diagnosis back to predictors - the only study here that faces this problem and the only one that solves it. Feature reduction from 100 to 59 was made a priori on clinical-relevance grounds, so no selection bias enters. And training AUC is reported alongside test AUC with the overfitting acknowledged in the text, rather than concealed. Three-fold cross-validation is modest but adequate at this sample size, and results are stable across folds (SD 0.009). Two internal checks add further confidence: a boys-only model tests whether performance depends on sex, given that sex is both a strong predictor and a strong group difference; and referral for developmental assessment, deliberately excluded from the feature set, serves as an external validity indicator, with high-risk children 3.29 times more likely to have been referred (95% CI 3.18-3.39). The residual limitations are epidemiological rather than methodological: no external cohort or health system has been tested, and the outcome label is substantially incomplete, with the authors estimating the true autism count at ten times the labelled figure - which biases sensitivity and specificity in directions the data cannot resolve.

answers.title: AI-Powered Human-Computer Interaction Assisting Early Identification of Emotional and Facial Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: “A Deep Learning-Based Enhanced Facial Feature Recognition System”
answers.answer: The design cannot support the claim, and the reasons are structural rather than procedural. A single fixed partition of 2,836 images into 2,536 training, 200 validation and 100 test provides no cross-validation, no repeated splits and no confidence intervals, and the test partition of 100 images makes each image worth a full percentage point. The order of augmentation relative to partitioning is ambiguous, with the text describing the partition and then the augmentation of the full 2,836-image dataset, which if taken at face value places transformed copies of the same photograph on both sides of the split. The number of distinct children behind the images is unknown, so participant-level splitting is not merely absent but impossible, and multiple photographs of the same child may straddle the split undetectably. Training accuracy reached 100%. The confusion matrix corresponds to no stated partition. But none of these is the decisive problem. Because the two classes were assembled from different internet sources, no split of these images - however careful - can distinguish a model that has learned facial morphology from one that has learned image provenance, and no result reported in the paper bears on which it is. The corrective is not a better validation scheme but a different dataset: photographs of diagnostically verified autistic and non-autistic children captured under matched conditions with the same equipment, which is what several other studies in this review provide and what this branch of the literature lacks.

answers.title: An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Multimodal Autism Diagnosis Using XAI GAMI-Net and Hypernetworks
answers.answer: The subject is the analytic unit under both evaluation schemes, so the within-subject leakage that dominates the image, frame, EEG, thermal and cry branches of this review does not arise. What arises instead is target leakage of the most direct kind, and it operates through two channels simultaneously. First, the recorded values: ADOS_TOTAL, ADOS_COMM, ADOS_GOTHAM_SEVERITY, ADI_R_SOCIAL_TOTAL_A, ADI_R_VERBAL_TOTAL_BV and SRS_RAW_TOTAL are the scored output of the assessments through which the ABIDE-I sites established the diagnoses that constitute the label, and the study's own explainability analysis ranks them first and second among all contributors. Second, missingness: ADOS and ADI-R are administered to establish an autism diagnosis and are largely absent for control participants in ABIDE-I, so the presence or absence of a value on these fields carries the label independently of its magnitude, and no imputation or missingness-handling procedure is described that would neutralise it. A ROC-AUC of 99.99% is the expected consequence, and no partitioning scheme - subject-level, site-level or otherwise - could alter it. Three further issues are secondary but real. Neither evaluation is site-stratified, despite 17 sites with distinct scanners and protocols and a substantial literature documenting site as a confound for autism classification on this dataset; SITE_ID is label-encoded into the preprocessing, and no leave-one-site-out result is reported. Age and IQ, which differ between groups in ABIDE-I, are entered as predictors rather than adjusted for, so part of the residual signal is cognitive ability and developmental stage. And the reported accuracy and split descriptions are mutually inconsistent between sections. The remedy is straightforward and would make the study genuinely informative: refit with the six instrument-derived fields removed, run leave-one-site-out, and report an age-and-IQ-only baseline. The architecture is well enough constructed that the resulting numbers would be worth having.

answers.title: Interpersonal Motor Coordination in Children with Autism and the Establishment of Machine Learning Models to Objectively Classify Children with Autism and Typical Development
answers.answer: Structurally sound at the level of splitting and compromised at the level of feature construction, and the two need to be separated. The splitting is correct and clearly described: leave-one-out cross-validation with each of 41 iterations training on 40 participants and testing on the remaining one, with each participant contributing a single feature vector, so within-participant leakage is impossible - the same standard achieved by the best studies in this review and not by most. The chance-level handling in the statistical analysis is better still: the pseudo-pair surrogate group, constructed by pairing a child's movement with an adult's from a different video, is an empirically derived null for a synchrony measure, which is the appropriate control because coherence between any two quasi-periodic signals is non-zero by default. Very few studies in this corpus construct a surrogate null of this kind. The compromise lies elsewhere. The 92.68% headline is achieved with features built by summing the six coherence values that a group comparison on all 41 participants had identified as significantly different. Leave-one-out cross-validation then evaluates those features on the same 41 participants. No participant's data trains the model that classifies them, but every participant's diagnosis determined which features the model could choose from, so the evaluation is not label-blind and the derived-feature result is optimistically biased by an amount the design cannot quantify. The paper's own explanation confirms the mechanism without naming it: the improvement is attributed to 'higher Cohen's d values' for the derived features, and higher effect sizes are exactly what selecting and summing on significance produces. The original-feature result of 85.37% is the more trustworthy figure, though even there four of the five selected features were among the significant ones and it is not stated whether forward feature selection was nested inside the loop. Two further points: four classifiers across two feature conditions and 63 candidate features were compared with the maximum reported; and no confidence interval accompanies a comparison in which the entire improvement is three children.

answers.title: Creating a diagnostic assessment model for autism spectrum disorder by differentiating lexicogrammatical choices through machine learning
answers.answer: Among the two or three soundest validation designs in the review, and sound in ways that require deliberate effort rather than good fortune. The split unit is the participant, with leave-one-out cross-validation formally specified: each of the 135 samples serves once as the test case with the remaining 134 as training data. The step that distinguishes it is the handling of the annotation model. Automatic tag annotation is itself a fitted component, and fitting it once on the whole corpus would leak information from held-out participants into their own annotations; instead the procedure trains the annotator on the training partition of each fold and then uses that fold-specific annotator to label the held-out sample. Very few studies in this corpus recognise that a preprocessing model is a fitted component at all, and none other nests one this carefully. Hyperparameters were adopted from standard values and deliberately not searched, removing the model-selection optimism that inflates most results here. Confidence intervals accompany every accuracy, and model comparisons are tested with McNemar rather than read from point differences, with non-significance correctly not interpreted as equivalence. Two residual concerns are not validation failures but bound what the result means. The comparison group's cognitive and educational level is unmeasured while the autistic group's full-scale IQ is 81-91, so an unquantified ability gap may contribute to the separation. And the transcripts come from the ADOS-2 sessions that produced the labels, so the language sample and the diagnostic judgement arise from the same encounter - which does not leak the label into the features but does mean the model is trained on speech elicited by an examiner who was assessing the participant for autism at that moment.

answers.title: Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection by Leveraging Transfer Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms
answers.answer: There is no validation strategy. This is not a case of an inadequate or leaky protocol but of no stated protocol at all: the words 'split' and 'validation' do not occur in the paper, no cross-validation is described, no holdout proportion is given, and no resampling scheme is mentioned, yet twenty accuracy figures are tabulated across four feature conditions and five classifiers. The methods section narrates the feature-extraction pipeline in step-by-step detail down to CSV export and then moves directly to results. Consequently none of the reported numbers can be interpreted as an estimate of performance on unseen data, and the comparison the paper is built around - handcrafted versus fused features, and among the three backbones - cannot be evaluated either, since a resubstitution comparison would favour the higher-dimensional representations regardless of their generalisation. Beneath this sits the same structural problem as in the companion study on this dataset: the two classes were assembled from different internet sources, so no split, however constructed, could separate a model that has learned about faces from one that has learned about photographs; and the number of distinct children is unknown, so images of one child may fall on both sides of any partition undetectably.

answers.title: Enhanced Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression Recognition Using Hybrid Weighed
answers.answer: Not assessable, because no validation scheme is described. The paper states no train-test split proportion, no cross-validation arrangement, no held-out set size and no partitioning unit anywhere. The one hint is that CK+ is used 'to test the WQPSO-FMRCNN model on unseen data' after KDEF, which would be cross-corpus evaluation - the design this review regards most highly, since it tests transfer across acquisition conditions and populations. It is not reported as a separate result, so what would have been the study's strongest methodological feature goes unquantified. Two further points bound the figures. CK+ contributes 327 peak frames from 118 individuals, roughly 2.8 images per person, and whether images of the same individual span any partition is unstated. And KDEF is geometrically standardised with eyes and lips at fixed coordinates, so a classifier operating on it faces none of the pose, scale or framing variation that any real deployment would present. A 99.8% accuracy on peak-frame posed expressions from geometrically aligned adult faces is close to the ceiling that this benchmark has long supported, and is not evidence about the harder problem the paper describes.

answers.title: Enhancing early autism diagnosis through machine learning: Exploring raw motion data for classification
answers.answer: The decisive weakness, and it is structural rather than procedural. The dataset is 738 trajectories from 20 children, roughly 37 each, and evaluation uses four-fold cross-validation with a 110-sample validation set described as 15% of the trajectory dataset. The unit is explicitly the trajectory: the validation size is quoted in samples out of 738, and nothing in the paper indicates that a child's trajectories were kept within a fold. Under a random trajectory-level split, each validation trajectory is accompanied by approximately 36 siblings produced by the same child in the same session with the same hand, differing only in which of eight targets was approached - and after rotation normalisation even that difference is removed. Fine motor kinematics at this granularity function close to an individual motor signature, so a model can separate children rather than groups and report high accuracy; the reported 0.90 is therefore not an estimate of performance on a child the model has not seen, and no participant-level figure appears anywhere. With only 20 children, a participant-disjoint scheme would have been straightforward - leave-one-child-out would give exactly 20 folds - and would have produced the number a clinical claim requires. Three secondary points compound this. No chance baseline, confidence interval or class-conditional metric accompanies either accuracy. The simulation and simplification analyses, which are the study's strongest contribution, are conducted on the same trained models and the same underlying trajectories. And the two feature sets were compared without model architecture being specified, so the 14-point difference cannot be checked against differences in capacity. The corrective is simple and the open data release makes it possible for others to perform: partition the 20 children, retrain, and report participant-level accuracy alongside sensitivity and specificity.

answers.title: Hybrid weight optimized deep learning for autism and visual sensory processing disorder detection: A heuristic strategy on medical domain
answers.answer: Not assessable, and not assessable in a stronger sense than any other study in this review. The paper gives two accounts of its evaluation that are not reconciled: one describing a variable 'learning percentage' divided into five values with the complement used for testing, illustrated at 65% training and 35% testing; and another defining 5-fold cross-validation within the list of evaluation measures. Neither is linked to the reported figures, and neither states a unit of splitting - which is unrecoverable in any case, since the number of individuals contributing the data is never given, so it cannot be determined whether the rows being split are people or repeated measurements from people. Feature selection optimises a fitness function that uses inter- and intra-class similarity, and therefore class labels, with no statement that it was confined to training partitions. No chance baseline, class distribution, confusion matrix or confidence interval is reported. Underneath all of this lies the fact that the reported 96.44886% accuracy has no stated denominator: a reader cannot say whether it was computed on ten individuals or ten thousand, nor what proportion of them carried each label, nor what condition they were in when measured. The figure is not an estimate of anything that can be identified.

answers.title: Bayesian optimization of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNN) for early diagnosis of Autistic Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: The mechanics are sound and irrelevant. Each respondent contributes one row, so the split unit is the person and within-participant leakage cannot occur; the 80/20 partition sizes are tabulated for all four datasets; class distributions are reported and the decision not to oversample is explained rather than assumed, which avoids the synthetic-minority inflation affecting several comparators in the paper's own literature review. All of this is better practice than much of this corpus. It has no bearing on the reported result, because the target in these datasets is computed from the predictors: the class is the summed A1-A10 score thresholded at the instrument's published cut-off, the ten items are model inputs, and the sum itself appears among the tabulated fields. A model with access to either can recover the label exactly, on any partition, under any validation scheme, with any architecture. Scores of 100% on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation coefficient and AUC-ROC across four independent datasets simultaneously are the arithmetic consequence of that arrangement, and the paper's attribution of them to Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation misidentifies the cause. This is target leakage in its most complete form - more complete than the neuroimaging study charted alongside it, where the features summarised a clinical judgement, since here the label is a closed-form function of the inputs. The paper's own comparison table is the strongest available evidence that this is systematic rather than idiosyncratic: it places the subliterature on these datasets at 97.15% to 100%, and records one comparator using genuinely independent measurements - physical fitness tests, brain scans and severity assessments on recruited participants - at 77.99%.

answers.title: Machine learning’s effectiveness
answers.answer: Correct on the split unit and ambiguous on the step that matters. The evaluation is leave-one-out cross-validation over 126 participants, each contributing one 16-dimensional vector, so the unit is the person and within-participant leakage is impossible. The class imbalance is acknowledged and drives the choice of scheme, with the authors stating that with around 20 above-threshold samples they 'were forced to use LOOCV to avoid polarization of prediction toward the Low autistic trait group'. They then state the risk this creates in their own words - that leave-one-out 'can also produce optimistic performance estimates due to the small test set in each iteration' and 'can be unstable when the dataset contains noise or outliers' - and conclude that their results need cautious interpretation. That is the right instinct, but it does not reach the decisive issue. The methods state that the procedure 'simultaneously selected the 16 explanatory variables and optimized the hyperparameter', and three to five variables plus a cost parameter were retained per model from sixteen candidates on 126 participants of whom 19 are positive. Whether that joint selection was repeated inside each of the 126 folds is not stated anywhere in the main text. If it was not - and the sentence's placement before the description of cross-validation suggests it may not have been - then the selection saw every participant's label, and on this configuration that alone is sufficient to produce accuracy, sensitivity and specificity of exactly 1.000. Perfect scores on all three metrics for a behavioural measurement in five-year-olds are not a plausible property of the phenomenon, and unnested selection is the most parsimonious explanation. Three further points: no majority-class baseline is given against an 84.9% floor; no confidence interval accompanies a sensitivity estimated on 19 positives; and the three variable sets were compared on the same 126 participants. The corrective is straightforward and would leave the study's substantive contribution intact - nest the selection, report the resulting accuracy with an interval, and add the positive predictive value that the population-based design uniquely permits.

answers.title: Multiscale attention-based network to enhance detection and classification of autism spectrum disorders using convolutional neural network
answers.answer: The most developed validation section in the facial-image branch of this review, and worth recording carefully because it is the one place where a paper in that branch takes leakage seriously. The authors recognised that the video-derived corpus risks subject-level and temporal leakage under frame-level splitting, and rather than asserting the problem away they measured it: ResNet-50 features for all 1,163 images, maximum training-test cosine similarity of 0.9714, correctly interpreted as 'a substantial likelihood of leakage'. They then applied K-Means over the deep features, swept cluster counts from 30 to 150, split clusters rather than images 80/10/10, and reassigned test images exceeding 0.90 similarity to a training image back into the training set, adopting the 100-cluster configuration for its balance of test-set size (68 images), final similarity (0.8989) and reassignment count (28). The same check on the Piosenka corpus returned 0.90, and the original split was kept. Compared with the four other Piosenka-based papers charted here, all of which split images without comment, this is a substantial advance. Three qualifications bound it. Perceptual similarity is a proxy for identity and not a measurement of it - two images of one child under different lighting can fall below any threshold while two different children in matched conditions can exceed it - so the paper's claim to have confirmed 'the absence of subject- or frame-level leakage' asserts more than a cosine threshold can support. The reassignment step edits the test set using the model's own feature space, moving out precisely the images most similar to training data, which makes the reported performance conditional on a data-dependent curation rule. And the leakage machinery addresses only within-corpus duplication; it does nothing about the confound that determines what the labels mean, since a model that has learned to recognise images sourced from autism-related web content will do so equally well on perfectly disjoint subjects. The cross-dataset evaluation deserves the same reading. Training on one corpus and testing on the other reached 89-90% in both directions, which the paper offers as robustness. But both corpora were built by the same principle - autism-labelled material harvested from autism-associated online sources, controls from general online sources - so a confound common to both transfers exactly as a genuine phenotype would. Transfer between two datasets that share a construction bias is not independent confirmation; transfer to a clinically ascertained cohort would be, and is not attempted. The remaining gaps are the unstated evaluation partition for the hyperparameter fitness, the absence of any chance or prevalence baseline, and confidence intervals incompatible with the test set sizes.

answers.title: Performance Evaluation of Neural Network Models for Autism Detection Using EEG Data [REC04023]
answers.answer: The study reports no validation scheme at all, and the sample structure makes the omission decisive. With 13 autistic and 4 typically developing participants, accuracies of 89.02% to 94.02% cannot have been computed over people - 17 cases cannot produce those percentages - so they must be computed over EEG epochs or windows, and the paper never states how many segments were extracted, how long they were, how they distribute across participants, or how they were partitioned. With four control children, any participant-disjoint evaluation would place at most one control in a held-out set, which would make the reported specificity uninterpretable; the natural reading is therefore that segments from the same children appear on both sides of the boundary, and that the networks are separating individuals rather than groups. This is the same failure the review has documented for scanpath images, video frames, thermal images and cry instances, arising here in a fifth modality, and it is compounded by the absence of a stated majority-class baseline: at 13 against 4, a classifier that predicts autism for everything scores 76.5% at participant level, so the headline numbers represent a far smaller gain than they appear to. The paper's own comparison table is the most useful evidence in the study and it points the same way. It lists participant counts of 16/46, 10/5, 34/11, 10/10, 15/0 and 13/4 alongside accuracies of 92.9%, 93%, 72.77%-90.57%, 81%, 91.12% and 89.02%-94.02% - and one outlier at 212/199 participants reporting 56% to 64%. The single study in the table with a sample an order of magnitude larger than the rest reports by far the lowest accuracy, and the authors reproduce this pattern without comment. That inverse relationship between sample size and reported performance is the same one this review has traced through the behavioural branches, and its appearance in a table assembled by the authors themselves makes it the study's most transferable contribution.

answers.title: Prediction for children with autism spectrum disorder based on digital behavioral features during free play
answers.answer: The weakest link in an otherwise carefully executed study, and instructive precisely because everything upstream is done well. Eighty-one indicators were reduced by group-difference testing and clinical judgement, then by univariate logistic regression, then by stepwise logistic regression, and the resulting five-predictor model's AUC, sensitivity, specificity and predictive values were computed on the same 246 children that drove every one of those selection steps. The operating threshold of 0.399 was likewise read off that same ROC curve. Selecting five predictors from 81 candidates on 123 events produces substantial optimism, and the standard remedy - bootstrap resampling that repeats the entire selection procedure within each resample to yield an optimism-corrected estimate - was partially performed but not reported that way: the bootstrap is described as validating the model, and the calibration curve and Hosmer-Lemeshow test address probability calibration and fit rather than out-of-sample discrimination, so no corrected AUC appears anywhere. There is no held-out set, no cross-validation and no external cohort. What makes this worth stating carefully is that the study's other validity properties are unusually sound - the split unit is the child throughout with no possibility of within-participant leakage, the diagnosis is a real clinical best-estimate judgement rather than a questionnaire threshold, the groups are matched and tested on age and sex, the comparison prediction about repetitive behaviour was made in advance and confirmed, and the authors themselves identify spectrum truncation as a source of performance inflation. The likely direction of error is therefore known and the likely magnitude is modest by this corpus's standards: an AUC of 0.826 with sensitivity 85.4% and specificity 68.3% is a plausible figure for this task, and the paper's own honesty about the CARS-2 floor points the same way. Two further items belong here. Coder blinding to group is not stated, and with autistic children recruited from hospitals and intervention centres and controls from a kindergarten, the recordings themselves may reveal group membership - which matters more in a human-coded study than in an automated one, because every one of the 81 indicators passes through a coder's judgement. And the predictive values that a screening claim depends on are quoted at the 50% prevalence of a matched design, with no recomputation for the base rate of any population in which the tool would be used.

answers.title: Predictive model using autism
answers.answer: The clearest case in the review of a study whose validation honestly undercuts its own headline, and it deserves to be read as a model of reporting rather than as a failure. The six items were selected from 32 candidates using all 90 participants, and the apparent accuracy of 86.6% and AUC of 0.938 come from that same sample - so those figures are development-set performance, not estimates of generalisation. The authors then did what most of this corpus does not: they split the data into training and test samples and reported both results, 85.4% and 65.3%. A twenty-point drop on a single random split of 90 participants is what selection of six binary predictors from 32 candidates should produce, and the authors say so explicitly, naming the number of variables relative to the sample as the cause and concluding that external validation is required. The honest summary of the study's positive finding is therefore that a six-item ADOS-2 combination looks promising and has not yet been shown to generalise. Several further points bear on the validation. The split unit is the participant, so no leakage of the kind that dominates the image and frame-level branches of this review is possible. The comparison baseline is substantive rather than nominal - the instrument's own published algorithms on the same participants - which is more informative than a chance line and makes the negative finding robust to the selection problem entirely, since the algorithms were not fitted here at all. The holdout is a single random split whose proportions and repetition are unstated, and whether item selection was repeated within the training fold is not said; if it was not, the 65.3% is itself optimistic. Administrator blinding to diagnosis is not addressed, and every input is a clinician judgement made after diagnosis was established, so differential expectation is a plausible contributor to the item-level differences. Item-level inter-rater reliability was not computed within the study, although the instrument's published reliability concerns algorithm totals rather than individual items. And the exclusion of comorbid cases from both groups and of severe positive symptoms from the schizophrenia group means that the model was developed on the clean cases and would be deployed on the ambiguous ones. None of this touches the negative result, which is the study's durable contribution: the ADOS-2 algorithms, applied as published by certified administrators to verbally fluent adults with IQ above 85, misclassify 45% to 52% of schizophrenia patients as autistic and achieve AUCs of 0.562 and 0.569 against an independent clinical diagnosis.

answers.title: The Noor Project: fair transformer transfer learning for autism spectrum disorder recognition from speech
answers.answer: Genuinely mixed, with the best-stated splitting principle in this corpus sitting alongside an unexamined confound that undercuts the headline. On the credit side, the splitting is speaker-disjoint and the reasoning is articulated precisely: samples from each child belong to one fold only, 'to prevent the model from over-fitting by learning speaker or recording idiosyncrasies, and therefore deceptively excelling'. That is the leakage problem named accurately, and it is the failure mode this review has documented across the scanpath-image, video-frame and EEG branches where it went unaddressed. A separate development partition is maintained, the same folds serve both tasks for comparability, unweighted average recall is used throughout, minority-class upsampling is confined to training with development and test distributions deliberately left intact, and the results are benchmarked against a baseline and against published work on the same corpus. On the debit side, three problems bound what the 94.8% means. First, speaker disjointness cannot address a confound operating at the class level, and the corpus description states that atypical children were recorded in clinics while typically developing children were recorded in schools - so a model that has learned clinic acoustics transfers perfectly across any speaker boundary, and no acoustic normalisation is reported. Second, the number of children in each atypical class is never stated and the two participant counts given are mutually incompatible; if the diagnostic classes rest on very few speakers, the 26 test samples per class may effectively be one or two voices, and speaker-disjoint splitting offers little protection when class and speaker are nearly the same variable. Third, the development UAR of 78.0% against a test UAR of 94.8% is an inversion that the authors flag but do not explain, and a test score sixteen points above development usually indicates that the partitions differ in composition rather than that the model generalises unusually well - a reading supported by the fairness analysis, in which the same model's sensitivity falls to 43.6% and 61.5% on the female and male partitions. The fairness testing is the most valuable validation act in the paper and deserves emphasis: by evaluating on gender-specific held-out sets rather than only on a pooled test set, it exposes a fifty-point sensitivity gap that pooled reporting concealed entirely. That is a generalisation check almost no other study in this review performs, and its result is a warning about every pooled accuracy in this corpus. Finally, the four-class result is the study's most trustworthy number precisely because it is its worst: 60.9% against a 25% chance level, below the published baseline, on the task that requires distinguishing autism from dysphasia and PDD-NOS rather than from typical development.

answers.title: Using #ActuallyAutistic on Twitter for Precision Diagnosis of Autism
answers.answer: Careful on the mechanics and unresolved on the substance, which is the reverse of the pattern in most of this corpus. The mechanics are good. Splitting is at user level with the reasoning stated explicitly - tweets from one user must not scatter across training and test, 'potentially leading to overfitting by the model due to learning user-specific patterns' - and applied to both tasks, 85:15 for tweet classification with a further 85:15 training-validation division, 80:20 for profile classification. Algorithm selection used 5-fold cross-validation with a held-out test partition maintained separately. And the sixteen-token removal list closes the most obvious inflation route, since the label is defined by a hashtag whose presence in the text would otherwise make the task a lookup. Together these are more deliberate leakage controls than most studies in this review implement, and the modest performance obtained is consistent with the controls having worked. What remains unresolved is the construct. The positive class consists of users who chose to participate in a hashtag community organised around autism advocacy; the negative class is a daily sample of general platform conversation. These populations differ in topic, audience, community membership, posting motivation, network position and - plausibly, though unmeasurably - in age, sex and geography. A model reaching 73% accuracy on that contrast may be detecting autistic language production, or the discourse register of self-advocacy, or the difference between a topically coherent community and a background sample, and the study provides no evidence separating them. The corpus construction adds a further asymmetry that is not discussed: the autism group's complete timelines were harvested while control tweets were drawn at 1,000 per day, so 17,323 users supply almost as many tweets as 171,273, and the two classes differ in how their material was sampled as well as in who wrote it. The authors reason carefully about label contamination in both directions and bound the control-group error at the population prevalence, but that bound assumes prevalence transfers to Twitter's user base and that non-self-identifying autistic users write like non-autistic ones. The honest reading is that the study demonstrates a detectable difference between two corpora whose separation has several sufficient explanations, and that its authors' decision to treat the result as a feasibility demonstration rather than a finding about autistic language is the correct one.

answers.title: Video-audio neural network ensemble for comprehensive screening of autism spectrum disorder in young children
answers.answer: Among the soundest validation designs in the review, with two residual issues that bound rather than undermine it. The 160 children were split 50-50 into training and test halves of 80, each containing 40 autistic and 40 typically developing children matched for age, sex and ADOS module - so the held-out half is not merely participant-disjoint but constructed to be comparable to the training half on the three variables most likely to drive an artefactual result. That is stronger than a random split and stronger than anything else charted here. Within the training half, 80% trained and 20% validated, and every hyperparameter decision - segment length for both modalities, MFCC count, batch size, epoch count - was made on that validation set with the test children untouched; the authors even report the direction of the failures they observed while tuning, noting that larger batch sizes and epoch counts increased validation loss. Segments are nested strictly within participants, so although tens of thousands of 5- and 10-second clips were generated, none of the within-participant leakage that dominates the image and frame-level branches of this corpus is possible. The reported figures are computed on 80 children. The first residual issue is statistical: 80 test children is small, one case is worth 1.25 accuracy points, no confidence intervals are given, and an exact interval around 82.5% would run from roughly 72% to 90% - so the ensemble's 2.5-point advantage over the video model, two children, cannot be distinguished from noise, and the paper's framing of the ensemble as the best model rests on a difference the data cannot resolve. The second is the reference-standard circularity discussed above: the diagnosis was supported by 'gold standard diagnostic assessments' and the model input is the ADOS session, so unless the diagnostic ADOS was a different session from the recorded one, the label is not independent of the material. The severity of this is limited - the model receives raw pose and undiarised audio rather than coded items, so it must recover from signal what a clinician judged, which is a genuine inference rather than a lookup - but it is not zero, and a single sentence stating whether ADOS entered the diagnostic decision would settle it. Set against these, the design's positive features are substantial: matched recording context across classes, appearance stripped from the video representation by construction, participant-level matched splitting, tuning confined to a validation partition, a complete metric table for every model variant, and an interpretability analysis that identifies a plausible confound in the authors' own audio channel. The reported 78.8% to 82.5% is one of the more trustworthy performance figures in this review.

answers.title: Video-based continuous affect recognition of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using deep learning
answers.answer: A study with better splitting practice than most of its branch and an unexaminable result, which is an instructive combination. The splitting is genuinely careful for the autism experiment: subjects are disjoint across partitions, the authors state why - 'in order not to distort the results or create overfitting' - and explain how it was achievable, since one child appears in one video. The partition is reported by child and by seconds of video rather than by frame count, which is precisely the disclosure the frame-level studies elsewhere in this review omit. Robustness is probed twice more, by varying the test proportion from 10% to 20% (74.5% to 74.8%) and by 5-fold cross-validation (75.2%), and the authors correctly note that a 5-fold arrangement approximates a 20% test split, so the agreement is expected rather than independent confirmation. All of this is sound. What defeats it is that the classifier's negative class is never described. For a two-class image model, the reported figure is a discrimination between two populations of images, and only one of those populations is characterised; if the non-autistic faces come from a curated corpus such as CK+ or AffectNet - both of which the study uses elsewhere - then the model may be separating home-video frames from studio or scraped photographs, and no splitting scheme could reveal it. The paper's own data-distribution table naming SSBD as the sole database across all three splits is incompatible with a second class existing, so the reporting is not merely incomplete but internally inconsistent. The class balance is likewise contradictory, called balanced in the methods and 'very imbalanced' in the results, which leaves the chance baseline for 74.5% undetermined. Two further points. The subject-disjointness argument rests on a property of SSBD alone, so whatever comprises the negative class has no stated leakage control - and the same corpus, under conventional splitting, was found by another study in this review to contain training-test pairs with cosine similarity up to 0.9714, indicating substantial near-duplication that subject-level splitting is designed to but may not fully address. And the 5-fold figure is reported as 'top-5 validation accuracy', a best-of-folds validation quantity rather than a mean held-out accuracy, so it is weaker evidence than it appears. Set against these, one part of the study's validation design is exemplary and belongs in the synthesis: the affect experiments constitute a true cross-population transfer test - train on neurotypical faces, evaluate on autistic children, then fine-tune - and the result, that the neurotypical-trained model transfers poorly and fine-tuning materially improves it, is both methodologically clean and substantively important.

answers.title: A novel thermal imaging-based framework for continuous ASD classification and behavior analysis using facial mood and skin temperature features
answers.answer: The single sentence describing evaluation is the study's undoing: '80% of the dataset was allocated for training purposes while the remaining 20% was used for performance validation'. The dataset is 1,500 images from 30 children, approximately 50 images each, and no participant-level partitioning is mentioned anywhere - the word 'split' appears nowhere else in the paper, and no cross-validation is performed for the severity task. On the natural reading, about 40 images of every child are in training and 10 in test. Severity is a fixed attribute of a child, so recognising the child suffices to recover the label, and thermal facial images of the same child in the same setting are near-duplicates of one another. A 98.33% three-class accuracy is therefore the expected arithmetic of the arrangement rather than evidence that thermal features encode severity, and the same is true of the AUC of 0.9878. This is the same failure the review has documented in the scanpath-image, video-frame and EEG branches, appearing here in a fourth modality, and it is compounded by four further problems. The severity labels have no stated source, so the quantity being predicted is undefined. The class distribution is unreported, so no baseline exists against which 98.33% could be judged even if the split were sound. The claim that the classifiers 'outperform the clinical ABC method' is incoherent if the ABC supplied the labels, and no alternative criterion is described. And skin temperature, the primary feature, was captured across outdoor play, classroom, dining and veranda settings with no ambient compensation, from overlapping groups of 10, 12, 4 and 4 children whose severity levels are not reported - so if severity is unevenly distributed across settings, thermal environment is confounded with the label in a way that no splitting scheme could remove. The remedy was available and unused: 20 videos were collected 'for real-time testing to assess the algorithm's performance in dynamic settings' and would have provided a genuinely held-out evaluation, but no result from them is reported. What makes this record worth stating at length is the destination of the number. A leaked accuracy in a diagnostic paper produces an overstated claim; here it produces a proposal to set the dose of psychiatric medication for disabled children, in a paper that itself lists cardiac arrest and kidney failure among the consequences of getting the dose wrong.

answers.title: Application of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare for diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: The weakest element, and it fails in three independent ways. First, the split is at image level - 80/10/10 with no mention of participant-level partitioning and no statement of how many distinct children the 2,940 images represent - so in a web-assembled corpus where one child may appear repeatedly, images of the same child can fall on both sides of the boundary. This is the standard failure of this branch and the review has documented it in five prior studies on the same corpus family. Second, and more unusual, every reported figure comes from the validation partition: all three result tables are headed 'Validation results', the confusion matrices are described as validation-stage, and the training curves report validation accuracy as the endpoint, while the 10% test partition defined in the methods section is never reported on anywhere. Model selection and performance estimation therefore share data, and the headline 98% is a selection maximum rather than a held-out estimate. Third, the evaluation partition cannot be reconciled with the described design: 294 samples per class totalling 588 is 20% of 2,940 rather than the stated 10%, and exact class balance is impossible under a random split of a 1,327-to-1,613 corpus - so either the evaluation set was stratified to equal size, or augmentation reached it, or the numbers are misreported, and the paper does not say which. Against all of this sits the confound that no splitting scheme could address: the paper states that the non-autistic images were 'randomly retrieved from web searches' while the autistic images came from an autism collection, so a model that has learned to recognise the photographic character of one source will succeed on perfectly disjoint subjects. The paper's own comparison table, listing ten prior studies on this corpus at 80.05% to 96%, is the most useful thing in it for the review: it shows a subliterature clustered below this study's figure, and the difference between them is a matter of evaluation protocol rather than of signal.

answers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Linguistic Features
answers.answer: Sound on the mechanics for a study of this size, and unresolved on the confounds. Each child contributes one transcript and one feature vector, so the split unit is the person and no within-participant leakage is possible - which places this study among the minority in the review not exposed to the failure that dominates the image, frame and thermal branches. The evaluation is a 75/25 split repeated over 50 random draws with results averaged, and the choice is both explained and empirically justified: cross-validation was rejected because of small sample size, and 50 repetitions were selected because metrics stabilised, varying by no more than 1% as further splits were added. Stating a stability criterion for the number of repetitions is a level of care that very few papers in this corpus show, and the ROC plots with a one-standard-deviation band around the mean curve carry that honesty into the presentation. Three qualifications bound what this buys. Test folds contain sixteen children, so each averaged estimate rests on very small samples and no confidence interval is given; the headline 83-84% is stated elsewhere in the paper to have been obtained 'after the removal of certain features', a selection made on the same data, so it is a post-selection figure; and repeated random splitting addresses sampling variance and not the three confounds that determine what is being separated. Those are, in order of importance: that the top-ranked feature is a developmental language index with no independent language measure available and no age composition reported by group; that part of the typically developing class comes from corpora containing no autistic children, so corpus of origin is partly correlated with class; and that the four source protocols differ in session length, structure and investigator role, while half the features are ratios to that investigator's output. None of these would be revealed by any splitting scheme, and none is addressed.

answers.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Using Skeleton-Based Body Movement Analysis via Dual-Stream Deep Learning
answers.answer: Two arrangements with materially different properties, reported clearly enough that both can be assessed. On the Gait Fullbody Dataset the split unit is necessarily the child, because each of the 100 children contributes exactly one sample, so 10-fold cross-validation partitions 90 children against 10; each configuration was run through five complete cycles giving 50 training runs, with mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation reported. That is sound practice and the dispersion reporting is better than most of this corpus. On DREAM, 1,833 samples from 61 children were split 1,650 against 183 per fold with no participant-level partitioning described - roughly 30 samples per child distributed across folds - so within-participant leakage is unaddressed. The instructive result is the direction of the difference: the leak-prone dataset produced the lower figure, 70.19% against 95.4%, which means the gap between them cannot be explained by leakage and must lie in sensor coverage, task, label structure or class balance. That inversion is worth carrying into the synthesis, because it is a counterexample to the assumption that leakage always explains the highest numbers in a branch. Three issues nonetheless bound the Gait figure despite its clean split unit. The single sample per child was chosen from ten trials 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation', so the modelled data were selected with knowledge of the outcome - a threat that operates entirely upstream of cross-validation and that no splitting scheme addresses. The 95.4% is the best of six architectures whose spread is 2.2 points against run-to-run standard deviations reaching 1.82, on test folds of ten children where a single child moves accuracy by ten percentage points, so the difference between the reported winner and the reference implementation's 94.8% is not resolvable. And the DREAM experiment discards the non-spectrum class, making it a two-way discrimination among autism-related labels rather than an autism-versus-non-autism task, with the resulting class balance never quantified so that no chance baseline exists for its 70.19%. Finally, the paper transmits without comment the single clearest piece of evidence in this review for augmentation-driven inflation: the Gait dataset's own creators reported approximately 60% accuracy without augmentation and 92% after applying seven augmentation techniques including noise addition, scaling and flipping. A 32-point gain from augmenting a 100-sample dataset is a statement about the augmentation, not about gait, and it is quoted here as motivating background.

answers.title: Automatic Cry Analysis Deep Learning for Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder in Early Childhood [REC01905]
answers.answer: Three compounding failures make the reported 90.28% uninterpretable, and none is discussed. First, there is no test partition: accuracy, AUC, sensitivity, specificity, precision and F-score are all validation-set figures, and no held-out evaluation of any kind appears in the paper. Second, the final model was chosen as the epoch with the best validation accuracy out of 2,000 - so the reported number is a maximum over 2,000 draws taken on the very partition it is reported from, an optimistic selection whose inflation on a small validation set is substantial. Third, the evaluation unit is the cry instance rather than the child, as Table 1's own definitions confirm, and no participant-level partitioning is described anywhere; with roughly six instances per child from 62 children, cries from the same child will fall on both sides of the boundary, so the network can recognise an individual voice and recover that child's fixed label. This is the same failure documented in this review for scanpath images, video frames, EEG epochs and thermal images, appearing here in a fifth modality. Set against this, the statistical analysis is a separate and more defensible piece of work - a prespecified comparison of three clinically established measures, replicating a direction reported in prior cry research, with significance at p < 0.01 and p < 0.0001. But it faces its own confounds, all reported in the paper and none adjusted: the groups differ by 4.8 months in mean age during a period of rapid vocal maturation, using measures that change with that maturation; 87.10% of autistic recordings came from autism centres against a comparison group split between health centres and homes, and all three measures are sensitive to room acoustics and background noise, with harmonics-to-noise ratio - the strongest finding - being a direct measure of periodic-to-aperiodic energy that ambient noise depresses mechanically; the eliciting causes of the cries differ between groups; two device classes were used; and the tests appear to be computed over cry instances rather than per-child means, leaving their effective sample size unclear. The corrective analyses are all available from data the paper already reports - stratify by recording setting, adjust for age, aggregate per child, and correlate the acoustic features with the GARS-2 scores already collected.

answers.title: Enhancing Early Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Bayesian-Optimized Random Forest Algorithm
answers.answer: Sound mechanics on a task with no uncertainty in it. Each respondent contributes one row so the split unit is the person, and 5-fold cross-validation is appropriate for 704 rows - both better than several comparators in this branch. Neither bears on the result. The outcome variable 'Class/ASD' is the summed A1-A10 score thresholded at the AQ-10 cut-off; the ten items are inputs; and 'result', the sum itself, is printed among the paper's own enumerated feature list with no feature-selection step removing it described. A model with access to either the items or the sum recovers the label exactly, on any partition, under any resampling scheme, with any classifier - and 0.9890 accuracy is a figure a single decision stump on the 'result' column would reach or exceed. This is the third study in the review resting on the UCI-derived autism screening tables, and the pattern is identical across all three: careful analytic practice above a label that is a closed-form function of the features. The paper's own stated limitation, that reliance on a single dataset may limit generalisability, correctly names an external-validity concern while leaving the internal one entirely unaddressed - which is the characteristic failure of this subliterature, since diversifying the datasets would change nothing if each new dataset carries the same arithmetic relationship between its items and its label.

answers.title: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
answers.answer: Strong where this review's video branch is usually weakest, and unexamined where this particular sample is weakest. The splitting is subject-independent stratified 5-fold cross-validation, and the paper states both the mechanism and the purpose: 'To provide strong model validation and prevent data leakage ... The dataset was divided on a subject-independent basis such that data from the same participant was not included in both training and validation datasets.' In a corpus of frame-level data from 100 children, where naive splitting would place frames of the same child on both sides and produce a near-perfect figure, this is exactly the right control, and it is named as such - the clearest anti-leakage statement in this review's video branch. Stratification preserves class ratio across folds; four overfitting controls are specified with their parameters; and the resulting figure of 85-90% is modest and plausible, benchmarked against external comparators rather than presented in isolation. The remaining issues are of two kinds. Procedurally, all reported figures are cross-validation results with no independent held-out test, so architecture selection and performance estimation share the same folds; the reported accuracy is a range rather than a mean with fold-level detail; specificity is not reported although recall of 0.95 against 85-90% accuracy implies it is materially lower; and the stated plus-or-minus 1.5% intervals are narrower than 20-child validation folds would ordinarily support, with no derivation given. Substantively, and more importantly, subject-independence protects against recognising an individual across the split but offers no protection against a group-level confound, and this sample has a severe one: the autistic group is approximately 84% male and the comparison group 52%, while the model's inputs are 468 facial mesh points and 75 body and hand landmarks, all encoding sex-linked morphology and posture. A classifier that separates boys from girls would perform equally well on unseen children and would be entirely consistent with the reported figures. The study is therefore a clear illustration of a distinction the synthesis should draw: leakage control and confound control are different problems, and closing the first - which this paper does deliberately and well - leaves the second untouched.

answers.title: Data Mining–Based Model for Computer-Aided Diagnosis of
answers.answer: Two separate problems, of different kinds. For the autism task, the evaluation is a 90.48/9.51 image-level split into 2,653 training and 279 testing images, with 10-fold cross-validation on the training portion. The number of distinct children behind 2,932 images is never stated and no participant-level partitioning is described, so in a web-assembled corpus where a single child may contribute several images, images of the same child can fall on both sides of the boundary - the failure this review has now recorded for six other studies on this corpus family. The exposure is greater here than usual because DeepFace's features are optimised for face identity, so the representation is specifically good at the thing an image-level split leaves exploitable. Compounding this, the reported 92% is described as spanning 'both training and testing datasets', so no held-out figure is given separately, and no per-class metric or interval accompanies it. The authors do identify the absence of an external validation cohort, correctly noting that 10-fold cross-validation addresses overfitting but not generalisability. None of this touches the more basic issue that the autistic images were harvested from autism-related websites, so the label encodes provenance and no splitting scheme could separate that from a facial phenotype. For the gelotophobia task, the problem is not validation but the absence of anything to validate. The ethics section states that the GELOPH<15> 'was not directly administered to participants in this study' and that 'no direct contact with human participants occurred', which contradicts the abstract's assertion that it 'was administered to confirm the diagnosis' and means that no image in the corpus carries a gelotophobia label of any kind. There is therefore no ground truth, no held-out set, no metric and no result - and the conclusion nonetheless states that the study 'demonstrates the effectiveness of combining deep learning techniques with validated diagnostic tools for detecting gelotophobia'. Across this whole review, this is the only instance of a primary claim for which no measurement of any kind was performed, and it is worth distinguishing in the synthesis from the many studies whose measurements are confounded or inflated.

answers.title: Deep Learning-Based Feature Extraction from Children's Facial Images for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
answers.answer: No validation scheme is described anywhere. The retrieved text states no train-test split proportion, no cross-validation arrangement, no held-out set size and no partitioning unit, while reporting accuracy 'on test data' and presenting a confusion matrix - so a test partition existed and its construction is unstated. The number of distinct children behind 2,940 images is likewise unreported, so whether images of the same child appear on both sides of the boundary cannot be determined; this is the standard failure of the corpus family and is documented in this review for seven other studies on the same images. Augmentation compounds the concern: zoom and brightness variants of a single photograph are near-duplicates rather than independent observations, and the paper does not state whether augmentation preceded or followed splitting - a distinction that another study in this review makes decisive, reporting that its dataset's originators moved from roughly 60% to 92% accuracy by applying seven augmentation techniques to a 100-sample corpus. Two features nonetheless make this study's figure among the more plausible in its branch. Its 88.33% is the second-lowest of the eight Kaggle-corpus studies charted here, which span 81.0% to 99.8%. And its architecture is the one least able to memorise, since frozen pretrained extractors with a logistic-regression head fit only a linear function of fixed embeddings, whereas the higher-scoring studies on the same images fine-tune millions of parameters end to end. Neither observation can be confirmed without the split description, and none of it touches the provenance confound: a model that has learned to recognise images sourced from autism-related web content will perform identically on perfectly subject-disjoint partitions.

answers.title: Deep learning-based detection of autism spectrum disorder and emotion recognition in children
answers.answer: Two failures of different kinds, and the reporting quality that exposes the second is worth crediting. The first is standard for this corpus family: the split is at image level, 2,526 training against 280 testing and 80 validation, with the number of distinct children behind 2,886 images unreported, so in a web-assembled collection where a child may appear in several photographs, images of one child can fall on both sides of the boundary. Stratified random sampling was used and is correctly described as preserving class proportions across partitions - but stratification balances classes, not subjects, and the paper does not consider subject overlap. The authors do state candidly that 'the dataset was split only once, and the procedure was not repeated due to the high computational expense of training deep learning models', which names a real limitation with its reason and is more forthcoming than most of this branch. The second failure is arithmetic and more serious. The autism model's reported metrics - accuracy 95, precision 0.96, recall 0.94, specificity 42.5, F1 0.95, AUC 78 - are mutually incompatible on the stated balanced test set: recall 0.94 with specificity 0.425 gives roughly 68% accuracy, precision would be near 0.62 rather than 0.96, and an AUC of 0.78 cannot accompany 95% accuracy. No reconciliation is offered anywhere.
