It situates itself in a programme of prior work on rapid mobile ASD detection from short home videos, and its central empirical contribution - measuring how far those US-validated classifiers transfer - is the kind of external validation this corpus otherwise almost entirely lacks.

answers.title: Exploiting Visual Behaviour for Autism Spectrum Disorder Identification
answers.answer: 2019. The related-work section surveys the eye-tracking-plus-machine-learning turn in some breadth, citing web-browsing gaze classification, saccade-based classification on six subjects, and a 700-image saliency study finding stronger centre bias and reduced saliency for faces in ASD. It also cites contrary evidence - that social orienting is 'not qualitatively impaired' in ASD and that the excess-mouth, diminished-eye gaze hypothesis has poor support - making it one of the few corpus papers to acknowledge that the underlying behavioural claims are contested. The existence of a dedicated Grand Challenge with a shared dataset is itself evidence of the field's move toward benchmark-based evaluation around 2019.

answers.title: Hierarchical POMDP Framework for a Robot-Assisted ASD Diagnostic Protocol
answers.answer: 2019. The paper positions itself as 'one of the first applications of humanoid robots in the diagnostics procedure', distinguishing diagnostic from the much commoner therapeutic robot applications and noting that diagnostic use 'brings forth some additional requirements and challenges, especially in terms of data acquisition and reasoning'. It observes that the complexity of the diagnostic process 'imposes constraints on the robotic applications in form of the need for efficient processing and reasoning algorithms', which results in a 'low number of robotic applications in ASD diagnosis'. It also documents that most robot-autism research still uses 'some form of Wizard-of-Oz approach with various degrees of autonomy', and that observations are typically 'collected through analysis of video recordings, which is a common technique in this field' - an accurate characterisation of the robot strand of this corpus.

answers.title: Intelligent Gaze-Based Screening System for Autism
answers.answer: 2019. The literature review is the paper's strongest section and characterises the field carefully: screening has 'evolved recently from subjective clinical assessments to objective metrics acquired from sensing devices such as gaze-tracking, motion sensors, and speech analytics'; machine learning in autism has 'largely focused on how to select the most effective features from a large feature set on the clinical diagnostic tools to shorten the diagnosis time'; and, most pointedly, 'all presented studies adopted machine learning differently yet there is no automatic prediction model integrated within a screening tool to be used in clinics'. It also documents a geographic gap - a shortage of Arabic-language autism research and uncertain prevalence estimates of 1.4, 29 and 59 per 10,000 children in Oman, the UAE and Saudi Arabia - which is a dimension of coverage bias not raised elsewhere in this corpus.

answers.title: Kinematic features of a simple and short movement task to predict autism diagnosis
answers.answer: 2019. The paper explicitly characterises the state of kinematic autism classification: three prior studies using tablet gameplay sensors, reach-and-throw tracking and movement imitation achieved 'high classification accuracy rates of 86.7% to 96.7%', but 'these studies used K-fold Cross-Validation, which was demonstrated to produce overoptimistic performance estimates, especially when a sample size is small' and did not test significance against chance. This is the corpus's most direct statement that its own literature's headline accuracies are methodologically inflated, and the paper's 71% is offered as the corrected estimate for a comparable task.

answers.title: Learning to Predict Autism Spectrum Disorder based on the Visual
answers.answer: 2019. The related-work section surveys the eye-tracking evidence base - shorter and less frequent saccades in high autistic traits, longer fixation on dynamic geometric images in ASD toddlers, declining eye fixation in infants aged 2 to 6 months who later developed ASD, and cohort evidence for eye tracking as an objective measure of autism risk and severity - and then the machine-learning turn, citing RNN classification of Fragile X from gaze during conversation (86-91%) and the authors' own earlier saccade-feature model on 17 children. It positions the visual-representation approach as novel: 'It is claimed that such approach has not been applied before in the context of ASD, to the best of our knowledge'. The accompanying dataset release and deployed web service also document the field's move toward shared benchmarks and demonstrable tooling around 2018-2019.

answers.title: Machine Learning to Study Social Interaction Difficulties in ASD
answers.answer: 2019. The paper provides one of the corpus's most explicit critical surveys of its own field. It notes that early machine-learning work in autism aimed at shortening ADOS and ADI-R administration by item reduction, 'yielding a classification accuracy of autism vs. typically-developing individuals of up to 99.9%', but warns that in such studies 'the features utilized for classification are still highly subjective and not independent of the respective clinician who bases the diagnostic decision on just those features (circularity)'. It catalogues the kinematic strand (96.7%, 92.5%, 93% from staged movement tasks) and observes that 'the movements under investigation were staged, thus, highly unnatural', arguing for a move to naturalistic interaction. And it identifies simple cross-validation and leave-one-out as sources of unstable and optimistic estimates. Together these amount to a diagnosis of three distinct methodological problems in the 2015-2019 literature that this corpus documents.

answers.title: Phase 3 diagnostic evaluation of a smart
answers.answer: Published July 2019 by a collaboration between the University of Strathclyde, the University of Glasgow, the University of Aberdeen, the Gillberg Neuropsychiatry Centre at Gothenburg, and Harimata sp. z o.o., funded through a Horizon 2020 SME Instrument subcontract. For this review the article is the methodological benchmark against which the rest of the corpus can be read, and it earns that position on six counts. The algorithm is locked before the evaluation data exist and applied by investigators separate from its developers, with results embargoed until collection closes - so none of the tuning, selection or leakage mechanisms documented across the other 130-odd included studies can operate. Sensitivity and specificity are prespecified as primary outcomes rather than accuracy. A 200-child cohort with other neurodevelopmental disorders is recruited to test differential diagnosis as a prespecified secondary outcome, making this the only powered study in the corpus to address the question the free-play and robot studies name as the hardest and that the ADOS-versus-schizophrenia study shows the field's gold-standard instrument failing. The sample size is justified with power calculations framed around detecting underperformance, with the protocol stating that 'if the Play.Care assessment is underperforming, which is the major concern of healthcare services, this study has a high probability of detecting it'. The commercial interest is managed structurally, with academic investigators holding no equity, company board members with vesting options identified individually, and the analysis blinded to the developers. And the protocol is registered and published before any result exists. Beyond the design, one passage deserves to be carried into the synthesis verbatim, because it states the inferential problem that most of this corpus leaves unexamined: the pilot 'employed the same dataset to train and test the machine learning algorithm. It did so with 10 repetitions of a 10-fold cross-validation procedure that is not prone to overfitting. Nevertheless, it only trained and tested patterns on that particular dataset.' Repeated cross-validation establishes consistency within a dataset and not generalisation beyond it - and the entire trial exists because its authors took that distinction seriously about a 93% figure of their own. What the article cannot supply is a result: it is registered as NCT03438994 with status 'Pre-results', and no participant data are reported.

answers.title: Predicting Autism Diagnosis using Image with Fixations and Synthetic Saccade Patterns
answers.answer: 2019. The paper documents the state of gaze-based autism classification concisely: atypical visual attention 'sometimes emerged even before the onset of the disorder', with delayed attentional disengagement in infants correlating with later toddlerhood diagnosis, but 'a holistic automated diagnosis tool remain elusive'. It cites the 92% accuracy reported for deep-network gaze classification in 20 high-functioning ASD and 19 typically developed adults and immediately qualifies that this 'may not be directly applicable to gaze patterns from children' - one of the few instances in the corpus of a paper explicitly discounting a headline result it builds upon. The existence of the Saliency4ASD challenge itself evidences the field's move toward shared benchmarks with blind evaluation around 2019.

answers.title: Recognition Of Atypical Behavior In Autism Diagnosis From Video Using Pose Estimation Over Time
answers.answer: 2019. The related-work survey characterises the field as having grown 'in the last couple of decades' around home-video behaviour analysis, infant observation scales, facial expression quantification with IQ-matched controls, caregiver-child interaction analysis, and multimodal eye-movement classification - and then identifies a specific gap: 'none of them focused on studying full body pose movement over time as an indicator of atypical behaviors', with most work 'focusing on specific body parts of children (e.g. face)'. This is an accurate characterisation of the corpus, where face and gaze dominate and full-body pose is rare. The commercial NODA platform also documents the emergence of remote video-based autism assessment as a deployed service by 2019.

answers.title: Robot-Assisted Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Based on Artificial Reasoning
answers.answer: Published 2019 by a group at the Universidade Federal do Espirito Santo in Brazil. The framing identifies the problem precisely: autism signs may be observable before ten months while reliable diagnosis is only possible at 18 to 24 months, diagnosis 'is usually performed through several sessions of behavioral observation, exhaustive screening, and manual coding behavior', and automated video coding could 'help the clinicians to reduce the delay'. For this review the study contributes three things, none of them a detection result. It builds the most developed measurement infrastructure in the corpus - an unstructured, scalable multi-camera RGBD network on ROS in which each node performs local face analysis and a fusion node computes visual focus of attention through a Hidden Markov Model - and it does so from cited open-source components, addressing directly the occlusion problem that limits single-camera gaze measurement with a moving child in a room containing two adults and a robot. It specifies its construct more precisely than anything else here, decomposing joint attention into initiation, response and request-initiation subtypes and reporting its finding at that level rather than in aggregate. And it closes the loop between measurement and robot behaviour, with the reasoning module modifying the robot's gaze, expression and rewards according to the child's performance - a design the introduction motivates by observing that earlier robot-assisted diagnostic systems 'have primarily been open loop and remotely operated' and 'are unable to perform autonomous feedback to enhance the interaction'. Its behavioural claim, however, cannot be relied on: six children in single sessions, no documented diagnostic status in either group, no ethics approval reported, an uncounterbalanced mediator order that confounds the key finding with order and novelty, no developmental measure in three-year-olds, and no reliability check of the automated attention estimates against human coding. The paper's own framing is appropriately modest - 'a proof of concept', a group 'without confirmed ASD diagnosis', and a conclusion that the observed pattern 'can be used as evidence to improve the ASD diagnosis' rather than that it discriminates.

answers.title: SP-ASDNet: CNN-LSTM Based ASD Classification Model using Observer ScanPaths
answers.answer: 2019. The paper documents the intersection of two technical trends: deep saliency prediction models (EML-Net, SalGAN, SAM with attention mechanisms) that have displaced conventional saliency models since 2014, and the application of those models to autism classification. It notes that a saliency prediction dataset for children with ASD exists but comprises only 13 children over 500 images, and cites a prior deep architecture performing ASD classification from sets of images along with an algorithm for selecting the most discriminative image contents. The existence of the Saliency4ASD challenge with a blind test track is itself evidence of the field's move toward benchmark evaluation, and the fact that two entries in this corpus independently report the same validation-to-test collapse makes that benchmark unusually informative.

answers.title: Social robot in diagnosis of autism among preschool children
answers.answer: Presented in 2019 at an automation and robotics conference by a Polish collaboration between the Department of Cybernetics and Robotics at Wroclaw University of Science and Technology and the Research Unit for Cognitive and Applied Psychology at the University of Lower Silesia - the same group whose 2022 follow-up is charted separately in this review. The framing is distinctive: rather than presenting a method, the paper presents a stage in an interdisciplinary development process, arguing that diagnostic human-robot interaction 'implies the need of close cooperation between psychologists and engineers' and delivering both a psychological result and a set of engineering requirements as co-equal outputs. For the synthesis the study contributes three things. Its finding is a within-construct dissociation rather than a group difference: autistic children performed significantly more behaviours when instructed than spontaneously in imitation (W = 21, p = 0.028), which the authors read as a deficit in automatic rather than intentional turn-taking. That is a claim about the structure of the difficulty, and the measurement principle behind it - separating prompted from unprompted performance to distinguish capacity from spontaneous deployment - has wide application in a corpus where most behavioural measures collapse the two. Its design demonstrates that a paired within-subject contrast can extract an interpretable result from a sample far too small for any classifier, which several similarly sized between-group studies charted here might usefully have adopted. And its stated future direction identifies the field's hardest problem correctly: 'the especially challenging task is to differ autism from other similar disorders', with a commitment to observe robot interactions with children who have other developmental conditions. Almost no study in this review makes that commitment, and the one included study that does test autism against another clinical group found the field's gold-standard observational instrument achieving an AUC of 0.562 - which is the evidence that this priority is the right one. What the study cannot supply is any detection result: no comparison group, no model, no classification, no accuracy, an unreported sample size and no diagnostic ascertainment described.

answers.title: Application of the Still-Face Paradigm in Early Screening for High-Risk Autism Spectrum Disorder in Infants and Toddlers
answers.answer: 2020. The framing is the diagnostic delay gap: autism can currently be diagnosed at 2 years but 'age at ASD diagnosis is still 40 months or even later', and Chinese prevalence estimates rose from 0.07% to 1.8%. The authors position video-based behavioural coding as the objective alternative to the retrospective parent interviews and rating scales that dominated earlier work, which they characterise as 'highly subjective and unfavorable for widespread promotion'. They also note that machine-learning screening had by then reached over 80% accuracy using EEG and brain imaging, and argue that combining social behavioural indicators with biological indicators is the necessary next step - positioning this paper as supplying the behavioural half of that combination.

answers.title: Applying Machine Learning to Kinematic and Eye Movement Features of a Movement Imitation Task to Predict Autism Diagnosis
answers.answer: 2020. The paper gives one of the corpus's sharpest field characterisations. On the clinical problem: UK average waiting time between initial concerns and clinical diagnosis exceeds three years, adult diagnostic instruments 'have only been validated for use with children', and adult diagnosis is 'less accurate, more subjective and lengthier'. On the methodological problem: 'only a handful of ML studies used kinematic data for autism prediction. All studies had small sample sizes and achieved high classification accuracy', but such models 'are prone to fit noise', and to the authors' knowledge those studies 'did not avoid pooling training and validation data', were not tested with independent data, and did not assess statistical significance. This paper is the corrective demonstration that follows from that diagnosis.

answers.title: Research and Design of Autism Smart Diagnosis Information System Based on Chinese Children's Facial Expression Data and Deep Convolution Neural Network
answers.answer: 2020. The framing is epidemiological and economic rather than methodological: prevalence rising from 3-5 per 10,000 in the 1980s to 2.76% among US children aged 3-14 by 2016; an estimated 10 million people with autism in China including 2 million children, growing by nearly 200,000 annually, with no national statistical survey; 33% of parents reporting that caregiving seriously affected their careers with an average annual income loss of 30,957 yuan. Against that, the paper identifies the bottleneck as clinical throughput and subjectivity - one to two hours per diagnosis, results 'easily disturbed by external factors such as hospital level, physician's subjective level, patient's education level, age' - and positions an app-deliverable CNN system as the answer, with explicit emphasis on remote and underdeveloped areas. The paper is a clear marker of the corpus's deployment-first strand, in which access and cost arguments substitute for validation.

answers.title: Automated identification of postural control for children with autism spectrum disorder using a machine learning approach
answers.answer: 2020. The paper situates itself carefully in two literatures. On postural control it notes that reduced postural stability in ASD is 'well-established', with prior force-plate studies reporting greater sway displacement, areas, standard deviations, velocities and root mean square, and two studies reporting decreased COP complexity. On machine learning it observes that classifiers have already distinguished impaired postural stability in multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease and vestibular dysfunction, and have been applied in autism to eye gaze, cognitive function, pregnancy risk factors and hand movements - but concludes that 'to our knowledge, there has been no study that utilized machine learning approaches to study postural control features in children with ASD'. It thus documents the transfer of an established clinical-biomechanics method into the autism domain.

answers.title: Behavior-based Risk Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder Through
answers.answer: 2020. The brief related-work statement characterises prior machine-learning approaches to ASD diagnosis as based on standardised assessment data, brain imaging datasets, and kinematic analysis of upper-body movement during specialised tasks. The paper positions its own contribution against these as using 'only behavioral data captured through video recordings of a naturalistic interaction with social robots' with unrestricted movement and no obtrusive sensors - articulating the corpus-wide trend away from constrained laboratory tasks and toward naturalistic, sensor-free observation.

answers.title: Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation as a Scalable Method for Distinguishing Children With Autism
answers.answer: 2020. The paper characterises the field precisely along two axes. On imitation assessment, it notes that human observation coding remains the standard but is 'subjective and time-consuming and requires intensive coder training', rendering it 'impractical for use in clinics and home settings', and that prior automated approaches are either rule-based with 'very limited generalizability' or DTW-based but reduced to dichotomous or categorical outputs that waste the continuous distance metric. On machine learning it makes a specificity critique that bears directly on this corpus: prior studies classifying autism from motor patterns 'did not directly assess imitation ability even when some tasks involved imitation', so 'it is unclear if the observed differences represent general motor abnormalities or specific imitation impairments' - a limitation that 'restricts the use of these methods for intervention purposes'.

answers.title: Deep-Learning-Based Detection of Infants with Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Auto-Encoder Feature Representation
answers.answer: 2020. The framing cites prevalence rising from 1 in 150 children in 2000 to 1 in 54 in 2016, and identifies the bottleneck as the gold-standard behavioural assessments themselves - time-consuming, requiring multidisciplinary teams, and unstable because of accessibility, subjectivity and 'interpretive bias between professions'. Its most distinctive contribution to the corpus's framing is a data-availability argument: it names infant anonymity requirements and parental non-recognition at early developmental stages as the structural reasons the field's data is small, dispersed by sex, age and vocalisation count, and unrefined, and it observes that 'these problems were typically overlooked by previous research with controlled and small amounts of data'. The method is then designed for those conditions rather than assuming they will be solved.

answers.title: Effects of Intra-Subject Variation in Gait Analysis on ASD Classification Performance in Machine Learning Models
answers.answer: 2020. The framing is a shift in the field's evidential basis: research on autism detection 'traditionally focused on behavioural aspects' but has moved toward 'more objective alternatives' such as gait analysis, on the argument that instrumented measurement 'can identify ASD with more confidence when compared to behavioural assessments recorded by human beings'. The paper situates itself against a set of prior results it reports at face value - 95%, 89% and 100% for random forest, KNN and SVM on adolescent scan data, 96.2% for a PART classifier on gaze and demographic data - and against gait datasets of 60 subjects (30/30) and 44 subjects (12/32). Its own contribution is to notice that these studies differ in how each subject is represented and that this choice has not been examined, which makes it one of the few papers in the corpus whose motivation is a defect in the literature's methodology rather than a clinical need.

answers.title: Estimating Autism Severity in Young Children From Speech Signals Using a Deep Neural Network
answers.answer: 2020. The framing is unusual in this corpus for arguing about tooling as much as about clinical need. It identifies LENA as the dominant platform for automated speech analysis in autism and objects on methodological grounds - LENA 'is not an open-source software and it is, therefore, not possible to further develop the LENA algorithms nor assess their utility in estimating ASD severity' - making open, inspectable pipelines part of the paper's motivation. It also notes that only a few studies had attempted severity estimation rather than binary classification, citing one that explained about 40% of the variance in Social Affect scores from 33 English-speaking children, and positions itself as the first application of these features and deep learning to Hebrew, arguing that the results 'highlight the utility of speech analyses for estimating ASD severity at very young ages, regardless of the child's spoken language or their cultural environment'.

answers.title: Detecting High-Functioning Autism in Adults Using Eye Tracking and Machine Learning
answers.answer: 2020. The framing is unusual in taking the measure of its own field before contributing to it. It positions resting-state fMRI as the state of the art for adult autism detection from behavioural data, quoting 79-86% under leave-one-out and 71-83% on unseen data, and notes the practical objection that fMRI is expensive, obtrusive and unsuitable for pregnant women or people with sensory issues, metal implants, claustrophobia or head trauma. It then singles out the EEG (94%) and speech (93%) results as 'potentially overoptimistic' for segment-level splitting, and observes of a comparable child eye-tracking study reporting 85.1% that there was 'no note on how the data was split'. Against that background it positions its own 74-75% as comparable to fMRI at far lower cost, and frames the adult high-functioning population as the underserved case: symptoms are less obvious, lifelong coping strategies mask presentation, and 'unlike for children, critical incidents with adults are not monitored by school staff or parents'.

answers.title: Identification of Autism Spectrum Disorder via an Eye-Tracking Based
answers.answer: 2020. The framing combines an access argument with a methodological one. On access: autism diagnosis 'usually relies on a multidisciplinary team of experts, which is relatively difficult to achieve, especially for economically underdeveloped areas', and eye trackers are 'affordable, portable, and easy to operate' so 'they can also be used in poor and remote areas'. On method: the paper's specific criticism of the existing eye-tracking literature is that models 'have usually utilized statistical analysis to discover the differences between the two classes' and so 'have high requirements for selecting the stimuli and indicators of eye movement for analysis', and that they analyse static fixations while 'the actual eye movement is a dynamic process'. Protocol duration is treated as a competitive dimension in its own right - the paper contrasts its short recording against comparators needing 10 or 10-45 minutes - reflecting a field increasingly aware that attention span, not accuracy alone, bounds what is deployable with young children.

answers.title: Machine Learning and Virtual Reality on Body Movements' Behaviors to Classify Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: 2020. The framing is a critique of the gold standard on two grounds simultaneously - objectivity and ecological validity. On objectivity: 'since in ADOS examiner has to judge a child's performance giving scoring and rating, evaluation relies on the examiner's expertise and subjectivity; likewise, in ADI-R ASD diagnosis is based on caregivers' reports rather than on objective evaluation'. On ecology: the limitation is 'the absence of both objective assessment methods and the ecological validity of the setting'. Virtual reality is offered as addressing both at once - a controlled, repeatable environment that is nonetheless a simulated real-life scene, with sensory content that can be manipulated in ways a clinic room cannot. The paper positions itself as 'the first attempt to discriminate ASD children from children with typical neurodevelopment using body movements parameters of an imitation VR task and machine learning', and situates repetitive behaviour as an under-studied criterion domain relative to social communication.

answers.title: Responsive Social Smile: A Machine-Learning Based Multimodal Behavior Assessment Framework towards Early Stage Autism Screening
answers.answer: 2020. The framing is about clinician workload and the limits of subjective scoring in a specific, unusually difficult case. The paper argues that the responsive social smile differs from other screening indicators because it lacks clear benchmarks and is 'evaluated by emotion description', that assessing 'children's emotions on small faces' while simultaneously running the experiment is error-prone, and that 'remembering every score for different social stimuli during the screening or perform the behavior scoring after the test is very subjective and labor-intensive'. Its comparison table is a useful snapshot of the 2020 field - eye movement at 88.51%, hand imitation at 86.70%, prosody at 76.00%, neuroimaging at 70.00% - and its accompanying observation is that 'cost and age requirements prevent some accurate ASD screening methods among children', with neuroimaging singled out as both expensive and impractical for young children who cannot stay still. Its own cohort at 12-32 months is the youngest in that table.

answers.title: Selection of Eye-Tracking Stimuli for Prediction by Sparsely Grouped Input Variables for Neural Networks: towards Biomarker Refinement for Autism
answers.answer: 2020. The framing is explicitly regulatory and infrastructural rather than clinical-need-driven: it situates itself among 'large-scale ongoing efforts in progress to develop next generation biomarker applications', cites the FDA-NIH Biomarker Working Group, and identifies validation studies aimed at markers of treatment response, predictors of later outcomes and subgrouping for intervention response. Its diagnosis of the field's practical bottleneck is precise and rarely stated elsewhere in this corpus: 'the longer the session associated with a biomarker, the more burdensome that biomarker becomes, and the less likely it will be to see practical implementation', with long batteries 'often stressful for young children and infants' and shorter sessions reducing burden, improving data quality and requiring less staff time. It also criticises current selection practice - 'straightforward winnowing of experimental batteries based on independent trial discriminability' - for ignoring interrelationships between trials that machine learning can capture, while warning that overfitting risk in the large-p small-n regime demands specialised techniques.

answers.title: The identification of children with autism spectrum disorder by SVM approach on EEG and eye-tracking data
answers.answer: 2020. The framing is the standard objectivity argument - 'clinical diagnosis is mainly based on behavioral scale tests including the autism behavior checklist and Childhood Autism Rating Scale' and 'due to subjectivity, evaluation results may not be very accurate' - but with a more specific biomarker orientation than most: biomarkers are defined as objective indicators of biological processes used 'for diagnosis, outcome predictions, and treatment prediction', with high accuracy, reliability and validity named as prerequisites for clinical use. The paper's distinctive contribution to the corpus's framing is its argument for why single-modality approaches fail: it cites a review finding a U-shaped profile of EEG power alterations in autism (excess low- and high-frequency power, deficient alpha), then notes that other studies found no EEG differences at all, particularly in high-functioning autism, and concludes that heterogeneity makes EEG alone insufficient. Eye tracking is added specifically because 'atypical face processing' has been found across all presentations. That is a heterogeneity-driven rationale for fusion rather than a generic more-data-is-better argument, and it is unusual in this literature.

answers.title: Toward Continuous Social Phenotyping: Analyzing Gaze Patterns in an Emotion Recognition Task for Children With Autism Through Wearable Smart Glasses
answers.answer: 2020. The framing is the gap between where social skills are practised and where they are measured: emotion recognition and eye contact skills 'are important to improve social functioning, but the methods currently used to measure and track such skills are delivered in clinical settings or via trained administrators outside the social context where these skills are practiced'. The proposed remedy is mobile and wearable machine learning platforms enabling continuous phenotyping during natural social interactions. The paper's most valuable contribution to the field's self-understanding is its retraction of a prior assumption, stated explicitly: 'The prevailing belief in the literature was that facial attention differences are very clear in ASD, so we hypothesized that distraction ratios across an emotion recognition task alone were enough to distinguish ASD vs NC reliably. We now believe that integrating further subtlety through robust gaze-tracking hardware will be required to design a phenotyping marker from this effect.' It also reports that later generations of the same research group's system abandoned the eye tracker entirely because of bulkiness and calibration problems - a rare disclosure of a technology's practical failure trajectory.

answers.title: Towards the automatic detection of social biomarkers in autism spectrum disorder: introducing the simulated interaction task (SIT)
answers.answer: 2020. The framing is distinctive in locating the problem in the measurement instrument rather than in access or cost alone. For general cognition, standardised tests exist - the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, the Mini Mental State Examination - but 'quantifying social interaction deficits is still in its infancy', so clinicians rely on the clinical gaze, which 'practitioners need many years of training to acquire' and which is 'difficult to verbalize, teach, quantify, standardize, and validate'. The paper's own expert-rating data then substantiate this claim empirically: eight experienced clinicians rating the same videos ranged from 0.56 to 1.00 accuracy, with performance correlating with months of experience. The population argument is equally specific - adults with average or above-average intelligence are diagnosed late because they develop camouflaging strategies, and 'to the best of our knowledge, no existing approach focuses on adults with ASD and normal intelligence levels despite the high need for access to diagnosis'. The paper is also careful about its own claim, stating that the SIT 'is not meant to substitute traditional clinical assessment but rather to allow additional information about the client's social communication abilities at an early stage of the diagnostic process'.

answers.title: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence to Diagnose Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Tracking Saccades
answers.answer: 2020. The framing is access and throughput: CDC prevalence of 1 in 54, an estimate of 'two undiagnosed cases for every three accurately diagnosed', and a description of comprehensive developmental evaluation as requiring 'a multidisciplinary team consisting of a psychologist, neurologist, psychiatrist, speech therapist, and may include others' conducting in-depth neurological, cognitive and language testing, with no single medical test available. Two framing points are distinctive within this corpus. First, the sex argument - girls with subtler presentations who are 'better at copying stereotypical social patterns' go undiagnosed into adulthood - correctly identifies camouflaging as a diagnostic failure mode, although the study then reports no sex data. Second, the rationale for choosing saccades over social gaze is temporal rather than practical: sensorimotor abnormalities are said to be present 'prior to the identification of social and cognitive deficits', which would make an oculomotor marker earlier-detectable in principle than the social behaviours clinical diagnosis relies on. The paper also states that saccades in autism are an under-researched area, which is broadly consistent with this corpus, where gaze studies overwhelmingly examine where people look rather than how their eyes move.

answers.title: An Experimental Trial: Multi-Robot Therapy for Categorization of Autism Level Using Hidden Markov Model
answers.answer: 2021. The framing combines prevalence growth (CDC estimates moving from 1 in 59 to 1 in 54) with a claim that autism is 'the fastest-growing developmental disorder in the USA with a 6% to 15% increase in rate per year'. Distinctively for this corpus, it invokes COVID-19 as a driver: 'especially under the current COVID-19 situation, the current research trends are focusing online for technology-based therapies', which situates robot-mediated intervention within a pandemic-era shift toward remote and technology-delivered care. The rationale for robots is given as controllability, accuracy, low cost and adaptability, plus the claim that autistic children are drawn to robots because of their predictable behaviour. The specific gap claimed is that existing robot therapies improve skills but cannot label severity, and the authors note a prior HMM attempt that 'failed to produce hidden Markov models that are indicative of a person's level of autism'.

answers.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis Based on Trajectories of Eye Tracking Data
answers.answer: 2021. The framing identifies a specific methodological gap rather than a general access problem: joint attention is 'an important marker to differentiate children with ASD from 12 months onwards', its verification 'requires the therapist's experience, attention and time spent, considering that the specialist's observation not using any tools is the most common practice', and the obstacle to automating it is technical - 'the studies cited in the literature that use ET signals combined with computational methods do not process trajectory data or ignore that the paradigm involves the displacement of regions of interest'. The developmental grounding is unusually explicit for this corpus, linking gaze-following to inferences about intentions and motivations and framing anticipation as 'the action of providing a view of the immediate future based on the immediate past', which 'appears to be difficult in ASD'. That framing directly motivates the anticipation feature, giving the paper a rare coherence between construct, feature design and analysis.

answers.title: Autistic spectrum traits detection and early screening: A machine learning based eye movement study
answers.answer: 2021. The framing is unusually specific about health-system context in China. It describes the two-stage screening structure recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics, notes that 'approximately 50% of the time is carried out with staff assistance' even for parent-completed tools, and that assessment can 'continue for months if the symptoms are not sufficiently obvious'. On China specifically it observes that 'the study of mental diseases used to be marginalized due to the conservative culture and weak science consciousness', that 'a majority of child health care institutions in China have not incorporated early ASD screening into their daily work', and that parents and primary health care staff lack awareness of early behavioural characteristics. It also positions itself against two named Chinese eye-tracking studies reporting 88.51% and 85.1%, criticising both for using only a face on a computer screen, and grounds that criticism in a substantive claim from the literature - that social attention in autism appears normal when social information is presented statically or in isolation, which is the argument for immersive scenes.

answers.title: Automatic classification of children with autism spectrum disorder by using a computerized visual‐orienting task
answers.answer: 2021. The framing is a systematic critique of three methodological patterns in the existing literature, each with a named remedy. First, that behavioural features in prior work 'often relied on manually labeled features such as the retrospective coding of children's behaviors in videotapes' which 'were essentially based on subjective ratings, which reduced the appeal of using machine learning algorithms' - remedied by using raw gaze samples. Second, that most studies performed binary classification, which 'fails to take into account the heterogeneity in the ASD population' - remedied by three-class classification including functioning level. Third, that brain-imaging classification 'is generally limited to adults or older children (over 7 years)' so that 'the application of machine learning to young children or infants, who are arguably in more need of automatic classification, is challenging' - remedied by a 15-minute child-friendly eye-tracking task. To these it adds the selection-inflation critique, singling out a named study reporting 96.7% after selecting an optimal feature set from 15 participants per group and noting that such practice 'is currently prevalent among medical studies with the machine learning techniques, and its overestimation of prediction accuracy should be cautioned'. That is the most precise methodological self-awareness in the corpus.

answers.title: Auxiliary Diagnostic Method for Early Autism Spectrum Disorder Based on Eye Movement Data Analysis
answers.answer: 2021. The framing is the standard subjectivity argument - diagnosis 'mainly relies on experts' comprehensive clinical analysis of children, which is usually subjective and highly dependent on doctors' individual professional skills' - with an added emphasis on pre-verbal assessment, aiming to 'diagnose children without linguistic ability in an early stage'. Its distinctive contribution to the corpus's framing is a preference for structured over unstructured data: it observes that 'most of the studies focus on unstructured data, which has complicated correlations among numerous parameters' and argues that 'it is highly desired to develop an effective auxiliary diagnostic method for ASD with the utilization of structured data'. That is an argument for interpretability over raw predictive power, and it is one of the few places in this corpus where the trade-off is stated as a design principle rather than discovered after the fact. The biological motion rationale is also well grounded, citing the classic finding of strong visual sensitivity to biological movement in typical viewers against reports of abnormal gaze to point-light displays in autism.

answers.title: Children ASD Evaluation Through Joint Analysis of EEG and Eye-Tracking Recordings With Graph Convolution Network
answers.answer: 2021. The framing is a two-stage critique. First, that single-modality analysis is inherently limited because 'the bio-marker information carried by the bio-signal of a single-modality is likely insufficient or distorted' - an argument for fusion on information-theoretic rather than merely empirical grounds. Second, and more specific, that existing fusion work 'mainly rely on feature-level fusion or decision-level fusion' and that 'these simple kinds of fusion strategies may not make full use of modality-cross information, thus the performances are largely limited'. The paper then demonstrates this empirically by implementing both a feature-concatenation baseline and a deep network over concatenated features, and showing the latter performs worst. It also grounds the cross-modal premise in developmental neuroscience, citing work linking frontolimbic connectivity at 6 months to responding-to-joint-attention at 9 months, and studies finding eye-tracking and EEG measures correlated during social stimulation - so the fusion argument rests on a claimed functional relationship rather than on an assumption that more data helps.

answers.title: Classification of Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Using Eye Tracking Data Based on Visual Attention Model
answers.answer: 2021. The framing is that severity classification is under-explored relative to diagnosis - 'although we know little about its potential use in severity classification, in literature there are some important clues about the use of eye tracking in symptom severity' - and it assembles those clues carefully: a reported correlation of r = -0.52 between fixation on social stimuli and ADOS social scores; evidence that geometric preference predicts later symptom severity and joint-attention gaze shifting; and a finding that autistic children preferring the geometric side scored worse on ADOS, Mullen and Vineland alike. Its methodological argument is that region-of-interest analysis, which dominates the field, discards information: 'although using all the image information and visual attention models... could be more informative'. It builds directly on a 2015 three-level saliency study that found semantic features important in characterising autistic viewing and 'suggesting top-down impairments', and extends that from diagnosis to severity - which is a genuinely incremental and well-posed research question rather than a reapplication of an existing method to a new dataset.

answers.title: Classification of Children With Autism and Typical Development Using Eye-Tracking Data From Face-to-Face Conversations: Machine Learning Model Development and Performance Evaluation
answers.answer: 2021. The framing is a specific critique of ecological validity in the existing eye-tracking literature. The paper observes that prior data 'were primarily obtained by having participants watch images (ie, videos, pictures, web pages)' but that 'human gaze behavior is highly context-sensitive', that experimental setting and cognitive load influence visual attention, that face-to-face interaction is 'much more perceptually and cognitively difficult' than image watching, and that 'the presence of the social partner elicits a different pattern of both neural response and gaze behavior' - concluding that image-viewing findings 'could not be directly generalized to the scenario of natural social interaction'. It also situates itself on age, noting a meta-analytic mean diagnosis age of 60.48 months and arguing that future work should examine younger children than its own 6-13 range. And it is unusually explicit that the field has not yet addressed differential diagnosis: 'our study and most others only classified individuals with ASD and TD... More scientific endeavor is certainly required before a practical ML model that could detect ASD from different conditions is established.'

answers.title: Combined Signal Processing Based Techniques and Feed Forward Neural Networks for Pathological Voice Detection and Classification
answers.answer: 2021. The framing is unusual and revealing: autism is introduced not as a neurodevelopmental condition but as one of two 'voice disabilities' within a paper about pathological voice detection, alongside Down syndrome, in a context where '1.2% of the world's total population is facing some type of voice disability'. Prevalence figures are given for both conditions in the United States and India (1 in 59 and 23 per 10,000 for autism; 1 in 700 and 1 in 1250 for Down syndrome). The critique of existing diagnosis is brief - ADOS-R and ADI-R 'require standardized structures for capturing the behaviors and found to be very difficult' - and the paper's real intellectual investment is in the acoustic literature, which it reviews carefully across five prior Down syndrome voice studies with their specific findings on fundamental frequency, jitter and shimmer. Its stated novelty is the differential task: prior work 'analyzed the variability of acoustic features in the voice produced by children with ADS, DS and normal children' but 'there has been no attempt to classify both'.

answers.title: Computer-Aided Screening of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Eye-Tracking Study Using Data Visualization and Deep Learning
answers.answer: 2021. The framing is conventional on diagnosis - hours of clinical examination, symptom variation, susceptibility to human bias - but two observations are distinctive. First, an unusually frank statement of how service capacity shapes research: the sample is school-aged rather than preschool because 'in our region there were not enough diagnosed children younger than 6 years, and the time it takes to consult a doctor to make a diagnosis can be as long as 2 years', so the very diagnostic delay the tool is meant to address prevented studying the age group where it would matter most. Second, an argument about acceptance rather than accuracy: 'parents seem to have high acceptance of eye tracking as part of the clinical evaluation because the visual results are easier to understand than is the ADI cutoff', and 'for some parents, a lack of an objective measure can lead to delayed or diminished acceptance of the clinical diagnosis'. That reframes the value of objective measurement as communicative as well as diagnostic, a consideration essentially absent elsewhere in this corpus. The paper also identifies the absence of a benchmark dataset as an obstacle to comparing methods, and responds by releasing its own.

answers.title: Computer-aided autism diagnosis based on visual attention models using eye tracking
answers.answer: 2021. The framing is a precise methodological critique rather than a general appeal to objectivity. Region-of-interest methods carry two costs: annotation burden, since every ROI must be marked on every frame of every video, and information loss, since aggregating within a region discards 'which visual features of sub parts of an image had a more fixed gaze'. The paper grounds its alternative in attention theory, distinguishing bottom-up circuits driven by image properties from top-down circuits using prior knowledge and social rules, and traces the computational lineage from the Koch model through Itti's implementation to the supervised saliency models of Borji and Judd. It positions its own advance as extending these from static images to video, citing the argument that video 'can contribute with more discoveries because the videos have temporal information'. It also situates itself quantitatively against prior work, tabulating AUCs of 0.71, 0.71 and 0.86 from three published studies against its own 0.82, and noting that its sample is larger and more heterogeneous in age, sex and severity than the comparators.

answers.title: Eye gaze as a biomarker in the recognition of autism spectrum disorder using virtual reality and machine learning: A proof of concept for diagnosis
answers.answer: 2021. The framing combines three arguments. On objectivity, that assessment 'relies on children's observable behaviors and parents' interview responses, which clinicians rate according to their expertise and subjectivity', with the specific addition that 'social desirability bias has been found to affect the veracity of parents' responses'. On ecological validity, that assessment 'occurs in laboratories or clinical settings lacking ecological validity that could offer a deeper understanding of real-life abilities'. And on timing, that 'many ASD dimensions are internal and do not manifest until 2-3 years of age', lengthening diagnosis. Its most valuable contribution to the corpus's framing is a careful review of the inconsistency in the social-attention literature: it catalogues studies finding reduced social attention, four finding increased social preference, and eight finding no difference, and identifies the moderators as static versus dynamic stimuli and level of social content - citing meta-analytic evidence that autistic children attended less to social stimuli specifically 'when the social content was higher (i.e., the number of people exceeded one)'. Its own contrary result is then argued within that framework rather than against it.

answers.title: Identifying Autism with Head Movement Features by Implementing Machine Learning Algorithms
answers.answer: 2021. The framing combines diagnostic delay with a specific argument for motor markers. On delay, it cites more than a year on average between initial screening and confirmed diagnosis in the United States, and a 35-country meta-analysis giving a mean diagnosis age of 60.48 months, falling to 43.18 months among children aged ten or under. On motor markers, it assembles evidence of atypical motor function in postural control, gait stability, arm movements and gross and fine motor control, and of delayed motor development in infancy that 'could subsequently contribute to the social impairments' - so motor features are argued to be developmentally upstream of the social criteria, not merely correlated with them. It then identifies head movement specifically as documented but unexploited, citing stereotyped head rolling, shaking and banging, greater head turning displacement and velocity when viewing social stimuli, and slower and less frequent head turning in response to name. Its closing claim is notably strong: 'the current diagnostic system of ASD, which are established on behavioral evaluation of social communication and restricted and repetitive behavior, would be greatly challenged' by combining features across neuroimaging, eye tracking, EEG and motion capture.

answers.title: Machine Learning Model To Predict Autism Investigating Eye-Tracking Dataset
answers.answer: 2021. The framing is brief and largely a literature enumeration, cataloguing prior eye-tracking autism work including the source dataset's own publications, web-page gaze studies, video-based screening paradigms, geometric-preference subtyping and autism risk indices. Its stated motivation is that 'there are needed a elaborated work that can explore significant factors of eye-signs for detecting autism', though the analysis performed does not in fact explore any factors. Its most interesting incidental observation is the honest one that motivates the clustering: 'these scanpath images were almost similar for normal and autistic children', which is a candid statement that the raw visual difference between groups is small - consistent with the source study's finding that participant-level accuracy sits near 71%.

answers.title: Motor synergies: Evidence for a novel motor signature in autism spectrum disorder
answers.answer: 2021. The framing is developmental and causal rather than diagnostic-efficiency driven. It argues that 'low-order impairments of sensory processing and motor coding during the early stages of life may impact the acquisition of more complex abilities, including socio-communicative skills and cognitive functions', and assembles evidence of pervasive sensorimotor impairment across posture, balance, gait, aiming movements, eye-hand coordination, force control and handwriting - proposing that these 'scattered disturbances presumably arise from a limited number of common dysfunctional mechanisms'. Its most distinctive contribution to the corpus's framing is a methodological criticism aimed at its own field: that standardised symptom assessments 'are often only used to assign group labels (i.e. ASD vs. neurotypical)', and that 'this approach has prevented understanding the impact of motor differences in the heterogeneous expression of ASD symptoms'. The paper then acts on that criticism by correlating every kinematic measure against ADOS totals within the autistic group, which is what yields its central dissociation.

answers.title: Personalized Robot Interventions for Autistic Children: An Automated Methodology for Attention Assessment
answers.answer: Published 2021 by a group at United Arab Emirates University with Al Ain Hospital, and collaborators at RIKEN, the University of New South Wales, Western Sydney University and the University of Malaya. The framing separates it from most of this corpus: the problem identified is not detection but the cost of repeated assessment during therapy - assessment 'is typically performed at the time of enrollment and repeated during long-term therapy to measure progress', and if it 'could be repeated more frequently to trace the severity and development of symptoms, then therapists could implement more efficacious diagnostic and therapeutic options, and patients and their parents would be better motivated to withstand long, repetitive therapy sessions'. For this review the study contributes three things that the detection-oriented literature does not. It closes the loop: the automated attention measure feeds back into the interaction scenario, which adapts to each child's score history across sessions, so measurement serves intervention rather than terminating in a classification - no other study in the corpus implements this. It demonstrates what is achievable without any learned model: three transparent rules with operator-adjustable constants, running at 1 Hz on a phone camera mounted to the robot the child is attending to, agreeing with the treating therapist's judgement on 28 of 34 sessions. And it is longitudinal, tracking six children across a seven-week course, in a corpus that is otherwise almost entirely cross-sectional. Its evidential weight is nonetheless limited in ways that should be stated: there is no comparison group and no control condition, so the observed rise in attention cannot be separated from familiarisation, practice or maturation; 5 of 11 children did not complete and no reason is given; the 82.4% is an uncorrected agreement rate over sessions clustered within six children, against a therapist standard of unknown reliability; and the population is narrow - male, mild to moderate, verbally capable - despite the abstract describing the target as children with minimal verbal capabilities. The authors' own restraint is worth noting: the causal claim is presented as a hypothesis, and the system is positioned as a tool for therapists rather than as a diagnostic instrument.

answers.title: Predictive Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) using Machine Learning
answers.answer: 2021. The framing is about data absence rather than methodological gap, and on that point it is informative and specific. The authors note that 'no reliable epidemiological data on the prevalence of autism exists' for South Asia, that Pakistan does not track or report autism cases, that the country's only government-run child psychiatry department averages two patients a day, and that 'even in that department, no such reasonable measures have been taken to store data in any format', so data 'had to be collected from scratch'. That account of health-system data infrastructure is a genuine contribution to the corpus's picture of where this research happens and under what constraints, and it distinguishes the paper's problem from the throughput and objectivity arguments that dominate elsewhere. The scientific execution does not match the framing: the stated aim of identifying causes for lifestyle modification is beyond what a 200-child cross-sectional questionnaire without diagnostic ascertainment can address, and the conclusions drawn from it are single-group frequencies presented without comparison.

answers.title: Quantifying Voice Characteristics for Detecting Autism
answers.answer: 2021. The framing is the most precisely targeted in the corpus. Rather than arguing that clinical assessment is subjective in general, it identifies exactly where prosody falls through the diagnostic net: ADOS-2 Module 3 contains one item rating 'Speech abnormalities associated with autism (Intonation/Volume/Rhythm/Rate)' on a 0-2 scale where an abnormal score 'represents a composite of abnormal features crudely lumped together'; the SRS contains one item on unusual tone of voice; and 'there is no reference to speech or voice quality in any of the 7 diagnostic criteria laid out in' DSM-5. It also identifies a technical rather than clinical obstacle - that existing pitch detection algorithms produce octave errors on quasi-periodic disordered speech and lack the resolution to capture fine perturbation - and addresses it with a model previously validated on other clinical populations. Its account of why prior pitch findings conflict is likewise specific, attributing heterogeneity to variation in voice sampling context, from home recordings to structured caregiver interactions to professional evaluations 'with varying social and cognitive demands', and then testing that account directly by comparing four conversational contexts within one dataset.

answers.title: Early detection of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder based on visual exploration of images
answers.answer: 2021 (submitted 2020, revised December 2020). Framed as early detection enabling early intervention, with the standard supporting claim that symptoms appear in the first two years and that early programmes let children enter kindergarten alongside typically developing peers - though the model is applied to school-age children of unstated age and could not address toddlers, whose viewing behaviour the paper's own Discussion says differs qualitatively. The more distinctive feature of the framing is what surrounds it: this is a challenge paper, so its comparative claim is against seven named competitor methods on a shared test set rather than against the literature at large, and its headline number is a modest 0.59 stated without inflation. The corpus contains few papers that report a result this weak, and its presence is a useful corrective - the same modality that yields 90%-plus in single-laboratory studies yields 0.53-0.59 across all eight entries when the data are fixed and shared.

answers.title: Predicting ASD Diagnosis in Children with Synthetic and Image-based Eye Gaze Data
answers.answer: 2021 (submitted May 2020, revised January 2021), extending a 2019 ICME Grand Challenge submission. The framing is the standard early-detection argument, sharpened by specific epidemiological figures on the diagnostic delay and by the claim that scanpath-only classifiers would be computationally light enough for mobile deployment. What distinguishes this paper's position in the literature is not its framing but its evaluative stance: it is one of the few here written in explicit competition with named alternatives on a shared blind test set, reporting its own prior submission's weaker numbers alongside the improved ones, and it treats the failure of its own central idea as a finding rather than an embarrassment. Its related-work section is also unusually careful about generalisation, noting that a 92%-accuracy adult study 'may not directly translate to ASD diagnosis among children' because children's and adults' gaze patterns differ - a caution that other papers in this corpus citing the same adult results do not observe.

answers.title: Using 2D video-based pose estimation for automated prediction of autism spectrum disorders in young children
answers.answer: 2021 (received March, accepted July). The framing is the standard early-detection argument but stated with unusual precision and with quantities attached: autism is detectable at 14 months and with high certainty before two years, yet over 70% of affected children are not diagnosed before 51 months; children diagnosed before age two can gain up to 20 IQ points over the following year, while those diagnosed after four 'will not show any substantial cognitive gain even with adequate intervention'. That last figure converts the diagnostic delay from an inconvenience into a quantified loss and is the strongest version of the early-detection premise in this corpus. The critique of existing tools is equally specific - most screening tests are questionnaire-based, perform with low to moderate accuracy, and are 'prone to recall and subjectivity bias'. What most distinguishes the paper's positioning, though, is its critique of the prior computational literature rather than of clinical practice: it names the field's dominant paradigm - single-feature extraction from controlled prompts - as the limitation to be overcome, and argues that a construct defined by the decoupling of behaviours from one another cannot be measured by indexing those behaviours one at a time. The Discussion is also careful about scope in a way few papers here are, stating that diagnosis 'is unlikely to be set on the track of automated performance before long' and positioning the contribution as screening that catalyses referral.

answers.title: Using Technology to Identify Children With Autism Through Motor Abnormalities
answers.answer: 2021 (received November 2020, published May 2021). The framing is the standard critique of observational diagnosis - it 'requires a lot of time', relies on 'the interpretative skills of clinicians', and 'take a long time without being able to deliver an objective and shareable result' - but the paper adds a more specific diagnosis of the field's problem: 'one of the main gaps in the diagnosis of autism is related to the lack of a quantitative evaluation of the disorder; in fact, although the variability within the disorder is known, there is still no valid method to recognize and categorize these differences'. The target is therefore the absence of graded measurement rather than subjectivity as such. A second framing move is methodological and unusual for this corpus: the authors argue explicitly that classical group-difference statistics are the wrong instrument here, 'since several interactions of motion variables could, actually, affect the presumed typical autistic motor pattern, we cannot assume that there must necessarily be movement variables typical of autism', and cite Yarkoni and Westfall to justify a predictive rather than exploratory approach. That is a considered epistemic position rather than a default. The paper also positions itself in a specific lineage - Anzulewicz's iPad gameplay study with 262 features reaching 'up to 93% accuracy', Crippa's upper-limb kinematics at 96.7% - and its own 93% lands squarely on the number it cites, which the Discussion treats as convergent confirmation rather than as an occasion to ask whether the two studies share a validation design.

answers.title: A Multimodal Approach for Identifying Autism Spectrum Disorders in Children
answers.answer: 2022 (submitted September 2021, published July 2022). The framing combines the standard prevalence appeal (1 in 54 per US CDC) with two more specific claims: that 'there is limited understanding of the neural patterns behind ASD and the severity of the disease', and that 'there is a lack of experienced experts for ASD diagnosis' - the second being a workforce argument that is more concretely relevant in the Chinese context the study is situated in than the objectivity arguments that dominate elsewhere in this corpus. The paper's distinctive positional claim is methodological: that 'most existing methods mainly rely on a single modality with limited information and often cannot achieve satisfactory performance', and that since autism has 'abnormal manifestations from the cellular level to the behavioral level' no single level of measurement can suffice. Its related-work section is unusual in citing single-modality accuracy figures from both literatures side by side - 92.34% and 96.44% for EEG, 88.51% and 85.1% for eye tracking - which sets up the fusion argument but also, unintentionally, shows that the highest reported unimodal figures already exceed this study's own unimodal results (81.11% and 86.67%), a discrepancy that goes unremarked and that most likely reflects differences in validation design rather than in signal quality.

answers.title: AI-assisted Initiation to Joint Attention Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
answers.answer: 2022. The framing combines the usual prevalence and early-intervention arguments (1 in 59, billions in socio-economic burden, improved outcomes from early detection) with a workforce argument that is more specific and more relevant to the deployment claim: early detection 'does not appear to be feasible, especially in regions where there is a scarcity of mental health specialists'. What distinguishes this paper's positioning is its critique of the immediately preceding work rather than of clinical practice in general. It observes that the Cognoa system, which obtained FDA marketing authorisation, 'may be considered not fully automated as it uses as input for the machine learning model not the actual videos, but human ratings corresponding to the quality of behavior conveyed in each video' - a precise and correct distinction between automating inference and automating measurement that no other paper in this corpus draws. And it criticises Zunino's grasping-kinematics classifier on the ground that 'the targeted gesture is not generally considered an indication of ASD behavior by most mental health specialists', which is a criterion of clinical construct validity rather than of accuracy. Those two criticisms jointly define the paper's design: raw video in, and a behaviour clinicians already accept as diagnostic as the target. The conclusion's comparative claim - higher accuracy and F1 than prior models reporting 0.70-0.80 - is asserted without statistical test and across studies with different populations and IQ distributions, which sits oddly against the care of the critique that opens the paper.

answers.title: Application of Machine Learning Techniques to Detect the Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
answers.answer: 2022. The framing is standard in its premises - 1 in 54 prevalence, 'a tremendous economic and mental burden to society', existing methods 'depend on the assessment of experts, which are subjective and costly' - but two elements are distinctive. The critique of current tools is concrete rather than generic, citing the M-CHAT as a case where a parent questionnaire 'is administered by specialists in rigorously controlled clinical settings, usually taking hours to complete', so the objection is to throughput rather than to validity. And the aetiological framing is unusually non-deterministic for this literature: the paper cites 'an emerging view is that the atypical behavior of ASD children may be caused by early brain adaptation to an adverse environment, rather than a result of ongoing neural pathology', which recasts early intervention as preventing maladaptive adaptation during a period of plasticity rather than as treating a fixed pathology. That framing then does argumentative work, supplying the paper's justification for including EEG at all - that 'atypical brain development in children with ASD appears earlier than atypical behavior, and the critical period of early intervention will be missed if the detection is based on behavioral data'. The claimed contributions are explicitly comparative: that prior work has applied each modality separately, that 'studies on data fusion are few', and that 'the discriminative powers of different data modalities are unclear' - a gap the study does address, and the modality-ranking result is its most transferable finding whatever the absolute accuracies are worth.

answers.title: An optimized Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for the classification of the autism spectrum disorder by using gaze tracking images
answers.answer: 2022 (received October 2021, revised February 2022). The framing is the standard objectivity argument in a strong form: 'the accurate diagnosis of ASD is usually affected since it is linked to the judgment of an expert, which produces biases related to the lack of objectivity', with the gold standard characterised as requiring 'multiple sessions and a qualified professional', hence 'time and... high cost'. The proposed role is appropriately modest - 'automatic screening tools can accelerate the diagnosis by identifying which individual require a complete autism assessment' - and the discussion repeats that the method 'permits the experts to provide a preliminary overview that guides diagnosis to more complex stages and tests'. Two features of the background are worth noting against the corpus. The clinical description is the least accurate here, framing autism as a condition from which children 'deteriorate' without early medical prescription and cataloguing 'red flags' at 12, 14 and 18 months. And the paper's positioning of its own novelty - 'to the best of our knowledge, this is the first time KELM is used for ASD classification by using gaze tracking images' - is a claim about the pairing of an algorithm with a dataset rather than about any question concerning autism, which is a fair statement of what the study contributes.

answers.title: Atypical gaze patterns in autistic adults are heterogeneous across but reliable within individuals
answers.answer: 2022. The framing is a deliberate inversion of the rest of this literature. Rather than arguing that clinical diagnosis is subjective and that automated classification would be objective, the paper starts from the premise that autism 'has so far defied any simple diagnostic markers or cognitive mechanisms' and asks what property of the data would have to hold for classification to be possible at all. It then names the field's characteristic omission precisely: 'Across ASD eye tracking studies, this is a major unanswered question: what portion of the variance in findings can be assigned to between-individual variability, and what portion can be assigned to within-individual variability?' - and observes that 'individual-level reliability is a prerequisite for successful classification and prediction'. That reframing converts a methodological question into a substantive one and produces a result the accuracy-maximising literature could not have produced: a demonstration that the measurement is reliable, the group difference is real and replicable, and the classifier nonetheless fails, because reliability and classifiability are different properties. The paper's positioning of eye tracking is correspondingly measured - it emphasises the modality's practical advantages, its applicability from infancy to adulthood, its resistance to volitional control and its emerging feasibility on phones and over the internet - while directing those advantages toward subtype discovery, longitudinal monitoring and intervention assessment rather than toward diagnosis.

answers.title: Classifying Autism From Crowdsourced Semistructured Speech
answers.answer: 2022. The framing combines the usual epidemiological appeal with two access statistics that are more concrete than the corpus norm: 83.86% of American counties have no autism diagnostic resources at all, and the delay from first consultation to diagnosis averages over two years, pushing typical diagnosis past age four with documented downstream consequences including higher psychotropic medication use, lower IQ and reduced language aptitude. The distinctive positioning, though, is a critique of the immediately preceding speech literature on deployability rather than on accuracy. The authors name two studies achieving comparable or better results - one using 'a specialized biosensor device with 4 directional microphones', another 'multiple wireless microphones, providing high purity recordings at a central recording location (a hospital)' - and argue that such work 'does not accelerate the process of autism detection' precisely because the conditions that produce clean data are the conditions that prevent scaling. They then add a validity argument alongside the logistical one: recording in unfamiliar settings with unfamiliar adults may itself alter the behaviour being measured. That pairing - that laboratory control buys signal quality at the cost of both reach and ecological validity - is the sharpest statement of the deployment-versus-fidelity tradeoff in this review, and it is the axis along which this study should be compared with Asgari and colleagues, who took the opposite position and gained interpretability, clinical characterisation and confound control in exchange for requiring a clinical ADOS session.

answers.title: Combining voice and language features improves automated autism detection
answers.answer: 2022. The framing is unusual for this corpus in three respects. First, it declines the diagnostic frame outright: 'This work (past and current) is not currently intended to be employed for diagnostic or screening purposes. Rather, our methodology uses already-established diagnosis as an external criterion against which we can validate (in the sense of discriminant validity) these voice and language measures.' The target is outcome measures for trials and longitudinal studies, and the paper closes on that application. Second, the critique of existing instruments is specific rather than generic - conventional tests like the CELF-4 and PPVT 'evaluate structural aspects of language' and must be augmented by natural language sampling; parent-report instruments such as the CCC-2 have validity limits 'as illustrated in treatment studies that have shown caregiver reports to be susceptible to the placebo effect'; and, echoing the group's companion paper, the ADOS and SRS 'include only one item each on voice quality' despite prosodic difference being a cited characteristic of autism. Third, the epidemiological framing is calibrated rather than alarmist, citing a worldwide prevalence range of 0.043% to 2.68% and noting that 'reasons for the increasing prevalence rate are uncertain' - written by an author who has published extensively on exactly that question. The comparison against prior work is likewise careful, noting that Tanaka et al.'s sample of four autistic and two typically developing participants made its findings 'unreliable', and that the sampling contexts of the compared studies differed from this one so that 'examination of contextual effects should be vigorously pursued'.

answers.title: Complexity analysis of head movements in autistic toddlers
answers.answer: 2022-2023. The framing is developmental and mechanistic rather than diagnostic, positioning head movement as 'one of the early sensorimotor signs associated with autism' and situating it within an established literature on motor differences - stereotypies, fine and gross motor impairment, motor planning and coordination, asymmetry in home videos of infants later diagnosed, and documented difficulties in gait, balance, postural control, movement accuracy, manual dexterity and praxis. What distinguishes the positioning is that the paper engages directly with a competing published interpretation and produces evidence against it: Martin and colleagues found head movement differences only during social stimuli and proposed that autistic children use head movements to modulate their perception of social scenes, whereas this study finds differences during both content types and states plainly that 'our data do not support the hypothesis that the head movements of the autistic toddlers were used to modulate the perception of social stimuli, per se'. It then offers alternatives without overclaiming, noting that 'the nature of these differences in head movement dynamics is not fully understood'.
